en.meaning: to have many connections; to be well connected
examples[].german: He knows a lot of people, so you can ask him for anything.
Thanks to my well-connected senior, I found a good part-time job.
My father is widely known in town and gets greeted wherever he goes.
en.notes: 顔が広い literally means "the face is wide" and means that someone knows many people and is known everywhere. Before a noun, が usually becomes の: 顔の広い人. Related but different: 顔が利く "to have influence, to be able to pull strings" and 顔を出す "to drop by, to show up". A neutral, everyday expression with a positive tone.

en.meaning: to drop by briefly; to make an appearance
examples[].german: I dropped by the party for a bit.
If you have time, go visit your parents' home once in a while.
The sun came out from between the clouds.
en.notes: 顔を出す literally means "to stick out one's face" and usually means "to drop by briefly, to make an appearance". The place takes に: パーティーに顔を出す, 会社に顔を出す, 実家に顔を出す; often with ちょっと or たまには. It sounds more casual than 出席する "to attend" and stresses that you are only there briefly. It can also mean that something hidden "comes into view": 太陽が顔を出す. Similar is 顔を見せる "to show oneself".

en.meaning: to lend a hand; to help
examples[].german: Could you help me with my move?
I helped an old woman who was carrying heavy luggage.
I have no intention of helping with anything wrong.
en.notes: 手を貸す literally means "to lend a hand" and corresponds to "to give someone a hand, to help". The thing one helps with, or the person, takes に: 引っ越しに手を貸す, お年寄りに手を貸す; as a request 手を貸してくれませんか. The counterpart from the point of view of the person seeking help is 手を借りる (猫の手も借りたい). Compared with 手伝う it sounds somewhat more figurative and can also be used negatively: 悪いことに手を貸す "to be party to something wrong".

en.meaning: mind your own business; unsolicited advice
examples[].german: Don't interfere in my life. Mind your own business.
My relatives told me to get married soon, but I just thought: mind your own business.
"You should get a haircut." "Mind your own business!"
en.notes: お世話 means "care, help"; 大きな "big" turns it ironically into "too much unrequested care". It is used to bluntly reject interference or unasked advice: 大きなお世話だ "It's none of your business!". 余計なお世話 means the same. Because it is impolite, it is only said to close acquaintances or in anger, never to superiors. The opposite in tone is the thank-you formula お世話になります.

en.meaning: feelings get across; to understand each other
examples[].german: Even if the languages differ, feelings do get across.
After talking many times, my feelings finally got through to my mother.
en.notes: 気持ちが通じる means that feelings or one's intentions reach the other person and are understood. 気持ち stands as the subject before が; に can name the person who understands. 通じる is used here without を, for "to be understood". One can also say that feelings become understandable despite different languages.

en.meaning: to be unable to stand up to someone; to be indebted to someone
examples[].german: She always helps me, so I can never stand up to her.
My father can't stand up to my mother.
Apparently even the company president can't hold his head up before the chairman who founded the company.
en.notes: 頭が上がらない literally means "unable to raise one's head": you cannot face someone as an equal because you are indebted to them or inferior to them. The person takes に, often with は: 〜には頭が上がらない. Reasons are gratitude (having received a lot of help), debts or authority; humorously also about spouses: 父は母に頭が上がらない. The form is fixed in the negative and behaves like an い-adjective (頭が上がらなかった).

en.meaning: one who ventures out may meet with good or bad luck
examples[].german: Running into an old friend on a walk - a dog that walks will bump into a stick.
Let's go out rather than stay home. They say a dog that walks bumps into a stick.
If you meddle in things that don't concern you, you'll get a bitter lesson.
en.notes: 犬も歩けば棒に当たる literally means "even a dog that walks around bumps into a stick". Originally (Iroha karuta of the Edo period) it was a warning: if you meddle unnecessarily, you get beaten. Today it is mostly understood positively: if you become active, you unexpectedly run into luck. It is quoted after a surprising event or as encouragement, e.g. with って言うし or だね. Which reading is meant depends on the context.

en.meaning: fortune comes to the house where there is laughter
examples[].german: Especially in hard times, let's laugh. Fortune comes to the house where there is laughter.
A paper with the words "Fortune comes to those who laugh" is stuck on the wall of the shop.
Seeing the always smiling family, I think: fortune comes to the house where there is laughter.
en.notes: 笑う門には福来たる literally means "fortune comes to the gate where there is laughter"; 門 is read かど here and stands for house and family, and 来たる is a classical form of 来る. It means: whoever stays cheerful attracts good fortune. It is said encouragingly in hard times or as a life motto; it also appears on New Year cards and good-luck charms. The spelling 笑う門には福来る is also common. It is quoted unchanged, often with だよ or って言うでしょ.

en.meaning: penny wise, pound foolish (lit. buying cheap goods, losing money)
examples[].german: It broke again right away. Buy cheap, lose money.
So that we don't end up penny wise and pound foolish, let's choose something good even if it costs a little more.
"Buying cheap means losing money" is my mother's catchphrase, and she always checks the quality before buying.
en.notes: 安物買いの銭失い literally means "buying cheap goods, losing money"; 銭 is an old word for money. It means: if you skimp on quality, you soon have to buy again and end up paying more - "buy cheap, buy twice". It is said about oneself after a bad purchase or as advice before shopping: 安物買いの銭失いにならないように. It is quoted unchanged and used like a noun with だ.

en.meaning: money goes from hand to hand; money comes and goes
examples[].german: It's fine even if you have no money. Money comes and goes.
Using the saying "money circulates in the world", my father always spends his money right away.
If tourists spend money, it reaches the local people too. Money really does circulate.
en.notes: 金は天下の回り物 literally means "money is something that goes around the world". It means: money does not stay with one person but constantly changes hands - if you have none now, you will get some again sometime. It is said consolingly to someone short of money or half jokingly as a justification for spending. The reading is かね, not きん; 回り物 means "something that circulates". Quoted unchanged, mostly with だ/だよ/だから.

en.meaning: birds of a feather flock together
examples[].german: You both like books, don't you. Birds of a feather flock together.
All of his friends are always late. That's birds of a feather for you.
When I joined the hobby club, everyone had a similar personality, and I realized that birds of a feather flock together.
en.notes: 類は友を呼ぶ literally means "like calls friends" and corresponds to "birds of a feather flock together". It is said when people with similar interests or traits come together - neutral or slightly ironic, especially with bad habits. Common patterns: 類は友を呼ぶだね, 類は友を呼ぶというやつだ, 類は友を呼ぶと実感する. Colloquially there is the short form 類友.

en.meaning: the riper the rice, the lower it bows - true greatness shows in humility
examples[].german: That professor is very humble. "The riper the ear of rice, the lower it bows," as they say.
Seeing him treat everyone politely even after becoming company president, I remember the saying "the riper the ear of rice, the lower it bows."
My grandfather's favorite saying was "The riper the ear of rice, the lower it bows."
en.notes: Literally: "The more it bears, the lower the ear of rice bows its head." 実る means "to ripen, to bear fruit", 頭を垂れる "to lower one's head", and かな is a classical exclamatory particle as in haiku. It means: those who are truly educated or important remain humble. The saying is quoted in praise of a humble person or as a reminder to the successful; the variant 実るほど頭の下がる稲穂かな is also common.

en.meaning: to hold someone back; to get in someone's way
examples[].german: I don't want to hold the team back.
Rather than dragging others down, you should make an effort yourself.
My math score dragged me down, and I couldn't get into the school I wanted.
en.notes: 足を引っ張る literally means "to pull by the leg". It means, on the one hand, to unintentionally set a group back (チームの足を引っ張る "to hold the team back"), and on the other, to deliberately harm someone out of envy (人の足を引っ張る). Things can also be the subject: 数学の点数が足を引っ張った "the math score dragged everything down". Neutral and very common.

en.meaning: the mouth is the source of misfortune - careless words bring trouble
examples[].german: I said something unnecessary and made him angry. The mouth is the source of misfortune.
Think carefully before posting on social media. The mouth is the source of misfortune.
Since they say the mouth is the source of misfortune, I make a point of not badmouthing my boss.
en.notes: 口は災いの元 literally means "the mouth is the origin of misfortune": careless words get you into trouble. It is said after a verbal slip (about oneself or others) or as a warning to be careful; typical: 〜。口は災いの元だ, 口は災いの元というから〜. An older variant is 口は禍の門. In content it corresponds to "silence is golden", but stresses the harm more.

en.meaning: after the rain the ground hardens - a quarrel strengthens a relationship
examples[].german: After the big fight, their relationship became even stronger. After the rain, the ground hardens.
We lost the game and argued, but since then the team has come together. After the rain, the ground hardens.
Since my parent and I have said what we really think to each other, we can talk better than before. That is exactly what this saying means.
en.notes: 雨降って地固まる literally means "it rains, and the ground hardens" (地 is read じ here). It means: after a quarrel or crisis, a relationship or group becomes stronger than before. It is said in retrospect after a reconciliation, often with だ/だね or 〜とはこのことだ. It is a popular saying in wedding speeches and in team conflicts. The verbs stand in a classically terse form and are not changed.

examples[].german: Don't waste time. Time is money.
Time is money, so I study English during my commute.
The company president says "time is money" and always ends meetings within thirty minutes.
en.notes: 時は金なり is the Japanese translation of "Time is money" (Benjamin Franklin); なり is the classical copula instead of だ. It means: time is precious and should not be wasted. It is quoted as an admonition or to justify efficient behavior, often with だから or と言って. In everyday life it is used unchanged, e.g. 時は金なりだよ; the reading of 金 is かね.

en.meaning: to bring shame on someone; to tarnish someone's reputation
examples[].german: With a failure like that, he brought shame on the company.
Don't do anything that would bring shame on your parents.
I am sorry for having brought shame on the teacher who recommended me.
en.notes: 顔に泥を塗る literally means "to smear mud on someone's face" and means to embarrass someone through one's own misconduct or to damage their reputation, typically parents, teachers, superiors or one's own company: Xの顔に泥を塗る. The expression is serious and is often used in admonitions or apologies. Related: 顔をつぶす "to make someone lose face". Neutral to elevated.

examples[].german: They noticed I was in a hurry, took advantage of it, and charged me a high price.
The other side knew we could not refuse and demanded unreasonable terms.
A business that exploits its customers' predicament does not last long.
en.notes: 足元を見る literally means "to look at the feet": in the past, palanquin bearers judged by a traveler's feet how tired he was and then demanded more money. Figuratively it means to exploit another person's predicament or weakness, especially over the price. Often in the passive: 足元を見られる "to be taken advantage of". The literal meaning (足元に気を付ける "watch your step") is to be distinguished from this. Neutral.

en.meaning: to stir up a hornet's nest; to bring trouble on oneself
examples[].german: If you ask unnecessary questions, you'll stir up trouble.
I asked for a discount and was charged a fee instead: a case of asking for trouble.
Clumsy excuses will only backfire, so you'd better apologize honestly.
en.notes: 薮蛇 is the short form of 薮をつついて蛇を出す "to poke around in the bushes and flush out a snake". It refers to trouble that one brings on oneself through unnecessary action, just like "to let sleeping dogs lie" gone wrong. Typical are 薮蛇になる and 薮蛇だ. It is often written in hiragana (やぶへび); the standard spelling is 藪蛇, and 薮 is a simplified variant. Colloquial.

en.meaning: to wait eagerly; to crane one's neck
examples[].german: I am waiting eagerly for her return.
The children are eagerly waiting for Christmas.
We are looking forward very much to your reply.
en.notes: 首を長くする literally means "to make one's neck long", like someone craning to see whether the person they are expecting is coming yet. It practically always appears in the form 首を長くして待つ "to wait eagerly"; what one is waiting for is marked by を. In letters and emails, お返事を首を長くしてお待ちしております is a friendly formula. Neutral, warm in tone.

en.meaning: sometimes you have to lose in order to gain
examples[].german: Even if we run a deficit at first, let's invest in the future. You have to lose to gain.
In the spirit of "lose a little, gain a lot", we gave out free coffee on the opening day.
Even among friends, it pays to give way a little, as you gain in the end.
en.notes: 損して得取れ literally means "take a loss and take a gain": whoever accepts a small loss at first obtains a bigger advantage later. It is a classic merchants' saying, for example for introductory discounts or free samples, but it is also applied to personal relationships. Typical frames: 損して得取れだ / 損して得取れで. Neutral.

examples[].german: Even that chef sometimes burns the food. Even the best make mistakes.
For such an experienced teacher to get a calculation wrong, even masters slip up, don't they?
There was a typo in the famous author's new book, but even the best slip up now and then, I suppose.
en.notes: Literally "even 弘法 (弘法大師, the monk 空海) makes a slip of the brush": even Japan's most famous calligrapher made mistakes. It means that even a master of a field can get something wrong. It is used leniently about experts whose blunder is surprising, never about oneself, since that would declare oneself a master. Often also without に as 弘法も筆の誤り. Similar is 猿も木から落ちる ("even monkeys fall from trees"), which sounds a little more casual.

en.meaning: there are kind people everywhere; the world is not full of only bad people
examples[].german: When I was in trouble, a stranger helped me. There are kind people everywhere.
I lost my wallet, but someone had turned it in to the police box. There really are good people everywhere.
As the proverb says, there are kind people everywhere: many people were very kind to me on my trip.
en.notes: 渡る世間に鬼はなし literally means "in the world one passes through, there are no demons": even among strangers one finds helpful, kind people everywhere. One usually says it after unexpectedly receiving help. なし is the classical form of ない; JMdict lists the saying under 渡る世間に鬼はない. Also well known is the TV series 渡る世間は鬼ばかり, which ironically reverses the proverb. Neutral.

en.meaning: good things come to those who wait; patience pays off
examples[].german: Don't be impatient about the result. Good things come to those who wait.
The interview is over now. Let's just wait and see: let's get some rest today.
There's no point checking every day whether the stock price is rising. Good things come to those who wait.
en.notes: Literally "wait for good fortune while sleeping": 果報 is "good fortune, a good fate", and 寝て待て is the imperative "sleep and wait". It means that someone who has done what they could should calmly await the result instead of driving themselves crazy; it is not a call to laziness. Typical as encouragement after exams, job applications or negotiations: 果報は寝て待てだよ／果報は寝て待てと言うし. Colloquial-neutral; ironically also said about someone who does nothing at all and still hopes for luck.

en.meaning: kindness comes back to you; those who do good will be treated well
examples[].german: If you are kind to others, it comes back to you someday. Kindness pays off.
I helped my neighbor when he was in need, and now he has helped me. How true: one good turn deserves another.
As the saying goes, kindness comes back: my volunteer experience even helped me in my job hunt.
en.notes: Literally "compassion is not (only) for the sake of others": ならず is the classical negation of なり (= だ). It means that kindness returns to oneself by a roundabout route. The proverb is very often misunderstood as "helping does the other person no good, it spoils them"; this reading is considered a mistake, even though JMdict lists it as a second meaning. Typical embedding: 情けは人のためならずと言うように／〜とはよく言ったものだ. Slightly elevated, but universally known.

en.meaning: learn from the mistakes of others
examples[].german: Seeing my colleague's habit of being late made me reflect. One should learn from other people's behavior.
Seeing someone talk loudly on the phone on the train, I thought I should correct my own behavior by watching others.
I pointed out a mistake in my subordinate's report, and then found the same mistake in my own documents. Watch others and fix yourself.
en.notes: Literally "look at other people's behavior and correct your own": 振り is "manners, conduct", and 我が is archaic for "my, own". One uses it when, from other people's bad behavior, one realizes that one makes similar mistakes oneself, that is, self-criticism rather than mocking others. Typical: 〜を見て、人の振り見て我が振り直せだと思った. A well-known maxim from school and upbringing; the imperative 直せ is fixed.

en.meaning: even in poor condition, something valuable remains valuable
examples[].german: Even though it is old, this watch is a brand-name item. Quality stays quality.
The veteran, close to retirement, scored the winning goal. Class is class.
Even though business results have dropped, that company's technical strength is still first-rate.
en.notes: Literally "even rotten, still a sea bream": the 鯛 is regarded in Japan as the noblest fish for celebrations. It means that something or someone of high rank keeps its value even after decline, age or a slump. Typical for former stars, long-established companies or brands: さすが、腐っても鯛だ. Slightly jocular; said directly about a person who is present it can come across as rude, because 腐っても "even if run down" resonates in it.

en.meaning: walls have ears; be careful, someone may be listening
examples[].german: Let's not talk about secrets here. Walls have ears.
You'd better not badmouth your boss at the company. Walls have ears.
You never know who is listening, so don't say your password out loud on the train.
en.notes: Literally "the wall has ears, the paper sliding door has eyes": あり is the classical form of ある, and 障子 is the paper-covered sliding door. A warning that conversations are easily overheard or watched, equivalent to "walls have ears". Often only the first half is used: 壁に耳ありだから小声で. Typical as a reminder against gossip in the office or confidential topics in public; neutral to jocular.

en.meaning: neither one thing nor the other; not suited to either purpose
examples[].german: This room is too small for an office and too big for a storeroom. Neither one thing nor the other.
This bag is too small for travel and too big for everyday use. It doesn't fit anywhere properly.
There are a few applicants, but none is quite right, so we just can't decide.
en.notes: Literally "too short for an obi (kimono sash), too long for a tasuki": a 襷 is the cord used to tie up kimono sleeves, and 短し／長し are classical adjective forms. It means something halfway that is really suitable for neither of the two possible purposes. Typical with sizes, quantities, time spans or candidates, often in the pattern 〜には〜し、〜には〜。帯に短し襷に長しだ. Neutral, usually said with a sigh.

en.meaning: to get angry; to be irritated
examples[].german: His attitude made me angry.
No matter how many times I tell him, he doesn't understand, which really irritates me.
I was so angry at my own mistake that I couldn't sleep.
en.notes: 腹が立つ literally means "the belly stands up" - in Japanese the belly is regarded as the seat of feelings. It means "to get angry, to be irritated" and mostly describes one's own anger; the trigger takes に: 彼の態度に腹が立つ, 腹が立って仕方がない. For other people one rather uses the transitive form 腹を立てる (彼は腹を立てた). Compared with 怒る, which can also mean visibly scolding, 腹が立つ stresses the inner feeling; more colloquial are 頭にくる and むかつく.

examples[].german: Without taking risks there is no success. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.
True to the saying "nothing ventured, nothing gained," he boldly founded a company abroad.
Resolved to take the risk, the reporter set out to cover the dangerous region.
en.notes: Literally: "he who does not enter the tiger's den (虎穴) does not get the tiger cub (虎子)"; 入らずんば is a classical conditional form "if one does not enter", 得ず a classical negation. The proverb comes from a Chinese chronicle and means that great gain is only available through risk. It sounds elevated and resolute and often appears with と言うように or の覚悟で. The counterpart is 君子危うきに近寄らず (the wise man avoids danger).

en.meaning: what's done cannot be undone; spilled water cannot be returned to the tray
examples[].german: What has been said cannot be taken back. What's done is done.
My ex said she wanted to get back together, but what's done is done.
Even if I regret quitting the company, what's done is done and I can't go back.
en.notes: Literally: "spilled water (覆水) does not return to the tray (盆)"; 盆 is a tray or shallow dish here, not the Obon festival. The saying goes back to a Chinese anecdote about 太公望: when his wife, who had left him, wanted to return, he poured water on the ground and demanded that she gather it up again. It therefore suits broken relationships and irrevocable words or deeds in particular. Typical at the end of a sentence: …覆水盆に返らずだ; close in content is 後悔先に立たず ("regret always comes too late").

en.meaning: a drop in the bucket; futile effort
examples[].german: The debt is so large that paying back a little is a drop in the bucket.
In the scorching heat, sprinkling water in front of the house was futile.
Considering the scale of the damage, the government's relief funds are a drop in the bucket.
en.notes: 焼け石に水 literally means "water on a red-hot stone": the water evaporates immediately without cooling the stone. It means help or a measure that remains ineffective given the size of the problem, just like "a drop in the bucket". Typical are 〜ても焼け石に水だ and 焼け石に水の対策. 雀の涙, by contrast, only stresses that an amount is tiny, not the ineffectiveness.

examples[].german: In a suit, he looks amazingly impressive. Fine feathers make fine birds.
Seeing his daughter in a furisode at her coming-of-age ceremony, her father laughed, "Fine clothes make the person."
I was told "clothes make the man," but I wonder if that was a compliment.
en.notes: 馬子 was formerly a simple packhorse driver; 馬子にも衣装 therefore means "even a horse driver looks good in fine clothes". It corresponds to "clothes make the man", but is a teasing, backhanded compliment: one says it jokingly about family members, close friends or oneself; toward strangers or superiors it would be rude. 馬子 has nothing to do with 孫 "grandchild", even though both are read まご.

en.meaning: good medicine tastes bitter; honest advice is hard to hear
examples[].german: I was told harsh things, but good medicine tastes bitter.
They say good medicine tastes bitter, so I'll accept the teacher's strict remarks with an open mind.
It is precisely the subordinates' uncomfortable opinions that are bitter medicine and good for the company.
en.notes: Literally: "good medicine is bitter in the mouth"; 苦し is the classical form of 苦い. The proverb of Chinese origin says that honest, helpful advice is often unpleasant to hear, and it is frequently paired with 忠言耳に逆らう ("loyal advice grates on the ear"). It is used to accept harsh criticism as useful: 良薬は口に苦しと言うから…, …良薬は口に苦しだ. Related is the expression 耳が痛い for unpleasant truths.

en.meaning: ignorance is bliss; what you don't know can't hurt you
examples[].german: He doesn't know that people are badmouthing him. Ignorance is bliss.
My father is blithely traveling, unaware that the stocks he owns are crashing. This is what they mean by ignorance is bliss.
When it comes to what's in this soup, sometimes ignorance is bliss.
en.notes: Literally: "not knowing is Buddha": whoever knows nothing about something unpleasant remains as serene as a Buddha. 知らぬ is the classical negation of 知る. Often said ironically of someone who is the only one who suspects nothing: 知らぬが仏とはこのことだ, or as advice that one had better not find something out. Do not confuse it with 言わぬが花 ("some things are better left unsaid"), a proverb of its own.

en.meaning: to reap what one has sown; to bear the consequences of one's own actions
examples[].german: His lies were exposed and he lost people's trust. He brought it on himself.
You skipped studying for the exam, so failing is your own fault.
Even if he brought it on himself, I feel sorry that he lost everything.
en.notes: 身から出た錆 literally means "rust that comes from the blade itself"; 身 is the blade of a sword here, which rusts through its owner's negligence. It means misfortune one has brought upon oneself through one's own misconduct. Typical are 身から出た錆だ and 身から出た錆とはいえ; often also in kana, 身から出たさび. Equivalent in meaning, but more sober and more literary, is 自業自得.

en.meaning: one easily overlooks what is close at hand (lit.: it is dark under the lamp stand)
examples[].german: The key I had been looking for all along was in my pocket. What's right under your nose is easy to miss.
The culprit was right next to the victim the whole time. It really is darkest under the lamp.
I went far to find a good restaurant, but there was a well-known one right in my neighborhood.
en.notes: 灯台 here does not mean a lighthouse but the old lamp stand or oil-lamp holder: directly under the lamp there is shadow. The proverb says that one most easily overlooks what is closest at hand: the object one is looking for in one's own pocket, the culprit in one's immediate circle, the good restaurant in the neighborhood. It is usually placed at the end as a comment (灯台下暗しだ) or connected with で. 下 is read もと here.

en.meaning: when the money runs out, the relationship ends
examples[].german: Since he went bankrupt, he has no friends left. When the money runs out, so does the friendship.
When the sponsor disappeared, the team's other associates also left one after another. When the money ran out, the ties ended.
Friends you only keep through money are gone as soon as the money is gone.
en.notes: Literally "the break in the money is the break in the bond": 切れ目 is "end, break", and 縁 is "relationship, connection". The proverb says cynically that relationships based on money end as soon as the money is gone, whether friendships, love affairs or business partners. Often bitter in hindsight or as a warning: 結局、金の切れ目が縁の切れ目だった. Neutral, widely used.

en.meaning: to take someone's side; to stand up for someone
examples[].german: I wish you would stop always taking my little brother's side.
That teacher only ever takes the side of students with good grades.
I don't intend to take either side, but I understand what he is saying, too.
en.notes: 肩を持つ literally means "to hold someone's shoulder" and means to take someone's side in a dispute: 〜の肩を持つ. It often carries an accusation of partiality (いつもあの人の肩を持つ). More neutral alternatives are 味方する "to be on someone's side" or 応援する "to support". Colloquial and neutral.

en.meaning: one is influenced by one's surroundings; a man is known by the company he keeps
examples[].german: If you hang out with bad company, you turn bad yourself. You become like those you associate with.
They say you become like the company you keep, so choose your friends carefully.
Surrounded by studious peers, I caught the bug, and now I study every day too.
en.notes: Literally: "whoever mixes with vermilion (朱) turns red"; 交われば is the conditional form of 交わる "to associate, to mingle". The proverb says that one is shaped by one's company, usually as a warning against bad company, but it can also stand positively for an inspiring environment. It is quoted with と言うから or followed by だ／で. Similar, but somewhat differently oriented, is 類は友を呼ぶ (birds of a feather flock together).

examples[].german: I didn't eat breakfast, so I'm hungry.
After club activities, I'm always really hungry.
Man, I'm hungry. Let's go eat some ramen.
en.notes: Literally "the belly (腹) shrinks (減る)" - "to get hungry". Mostly in the past tense: 腹が減った "I'm hungry"; in casual conversation が is often dropped: 腹減った. The expression is rough colloquial speech and rather masculine; neutrally and politely one says お腹が空いた. It lives on in the proverb 腹が減っては戦ができぬ "you can't fight on an empty stomach".

en.meaning: to take a lot of effort; to be time-consuming
examples[].german: Homemade cooking takes a lot of effort, but it is delicious.
Processing this document takes a lot of trouble, so please submit it early.
My youngest is still small and takes a lot of care in all sorts of ways.
en.notes: 手間 means "labor, time and effort"; 手間がかかる means "to require a lot of effort, to be troublesome". The thing takes が or は as topic: この料理は手間がかかる. It is intensified with とても or すごく; about people one says 手間がかかる子 "a child who needs a lot of care". The transitive counterpart is 手間をかける "to put effort in", politely お手間を取らせてすみません "sorry for the trouble". Similar is 面倒だ, but it stresses the annoyance more.

en.meaning: change of pace, change of scenery, diversion
examples[].german: I went for a walk for a change of pace.
Rearranging the furniture was a nice change of scenery.
When you're tired of studying, you should take a little break.
en.notes: 気分転換 is composed of 気分 "mood, humor" and 転換 "switch, change" and means "change of pace, change of scenery, diversion": a small interruption to clear one's head. Typical frames are 気分転換に〜する "to ... for a change of pace", 気分転換をする and 〜はいい気分転換になる. It is a noun (also possible as a する-verb), not a verb phrase. Similar is 息抜き "breather", which stresses relaxation from work more strongly.

examples[].german: Let's go home before it gets dark.
As a child, I used to play in the park until dusk.
It gets dark early in winter, doesn't it?
en.notes: Literally "the day / sun (日) comes to an end (暮れる)" - "dusk falls, evening comes". Typical frames: 日が暮れる前に "before it gets dark", 日が暮れるまで "until dusk", 日が暮れるのが早い. The counterpart is 夜が明ける "dawn breaks"; 日が沈む, on the other hand, only describes the sinking of the sun. The related noun is 日暮れ "dusk".

examples[].german: Don't hold back. Don't be so formal with me.
You could have told me if you were moving. Why are you being so distant?
We're best friends, so paying me as thanks is way too formal.
en.notes: 水臭い literally means "watery, diluted" (for example of thin sake). Figuratively it means "distant, too formal" toward people who are close to you. It is almost always used as a friendly reproach when a friend does not accept help, keeps something secret or is excessively polite: 水臭いなあ, 水臭いこと言うなよ, 水臭いじゃないか. It does not suit strangers or superiors. It is an ordinary い-adjective.

examples[].german: Time really flies.
As time went on, I got used to my new job as well.
This bread gets hard as time passes, so please eat it soon.
en.notes: 経つ "to pass (of time)" with 日 "day": "the days pass". Common frames: 日が経つのが早い "time passes quickly", 日が経つにつれて "as time goes by". For concrete periods one says 三日経つ or 一年が経つ. Do not confuse it with the identically read 立つ "to stand"; it is also written 日がたつ in kana. Neutral.

en.meaning: it is convenient; it suits one's schedule
examples[].german: Is tomorrow afternoon convenient for you?
Let's hold the meeting on a day that suits everyone.
He only ever says things that are convenient for himself.
en.notes: 都合 means "circumstances, schedule"; 都合がいい means "it suits, it is convenient". Typical when arranging appointments: 明日は都合がいいですか, more politely ご都合はいかがですか; the opposite is 都合が悪い. Before nouns usually 都合のいい日. With 自分に it can have a negative meaning of "self-serving, whatever suits oneself": 自分に都合のいい話. In formal writing also 都合がよい.

en.meaning: to be too heavy a burden; to be beyond one's capacity
examples[].german: This job is too much of a burden for a newcomer.
The role of leader is too heavy a burden for me.
Giving a speech in place of the company president is a bit much for me.
en.notes: 荷が重い literally means "the load is heavy" and means that a task or responsibility is too big for someone. The person concerned takes には: 新人には荷が重い, 私には荷が重すぎます; the latter is a modest way of declining a task. Related are 重荷 "burden" and 肩の荷が下りる "a load is lifted from one's shoulders". It behaves like an い-adjective (荷が重すぎる, 荷が重かった).

examples[].german: I killed time on my smartphone while waiting for the train.
I had time before the meeting, so I killed time in a bookstore.
In the hospital, all I could do to pass the time was watch TV.
en.notes: 暇を潰す literally means "to crush free time" and means "to kill time", mostly while waiting or out of boredom. The means takes で: スマホで暇を潰す, 本屋で暇を潰す. Equivalent is 時間を潰す; the related noun is 暇つぶし (暇つぶしに〜する "to do as a pastime"). The expression is neutral to colloquial and does not have the negative undertone of "wasting time" (時間を無駄にする).

en.meaning: to be stubborn; to think inflexibly
examples[].german: The department head is inflexible and doesn't accept new proposals.
They say people become set in their ways as they age, but my grandmother loves new things.
So that no one calls me inflexible, I try to listen to various opinions.
en.notes: 頭が固い literally means "the head is hard" and describes someone who stubbornly clings to their own ideas and does not accept anything new. The opposite is 頭が柔らかい "to think flexibly"; with なる one says 頭が固くなる "to become set in one's ways". A similar insult is 石頭. Besides 固い, the spelling 堅い is also seen, but not 硬い. Neutral to colloquial, judgmental.

en.meaning: to fuel up beforehand; to eat something before setting out
examples[].german: Let's get something to eat before we set out.
Before the match, I ate a bit of rice balls to fuel up.
Food first. We can talk afterwards.
en.notes: 腹ごしらえ is composed of 腹 "belly" and こしらえ (from 拵える "to prepare"): "preparing the stomach", that is, fortifying oneself with a meal before an exertion. Typical are 腹ごしらえをする, 〜の前に腹ごしらえ, まずは腹ごしらえだ. It is a noun or する-verb and, because of 腹, sounds casual, somewhat masculine and colloquial; more neutral would be 先に何か食べておく.

en.meaning: the conversation gets lively; to chat animatedly
examples[].german: We met after a long time and had a lively conversation.
When we found out we had a hobby in common, we got talking even though it was our first meeting.
The conversation didn't flow on the date, which was awkward.
en.notes: 話が弾む literally means "the conversation bounces (like a ball)" and means "to chat animatedly, for the conversation to pick up". The topic takes で: 昔の話で話が弾む, 共通の趣味で話が弾む. The negative 話が弾まない "the conversation doesn't get going" is also common. It is intransitive; the participants are not the subject, 話 is the subject. The expression is neutral and very everyday.

en.meaning: to spend money like water; to be extravagant
examples[].german: He spends money like water.
The public is angry at politicians who throw tax money around.
The man who won the lottery spent his prize money like water and lost all of it within a year.
en.notes: Literally "to use like hot and cold water": 湯水 stands for something that seems available without limit. It means extravagant spending, almost always with お金, 税金 or 予算 as the object: 〜を湯水のように使う. Reproachful and critical, common in the media about tax money; the verb conjugates normally (使って, 使った). More neutral and general is 無駄遣いする "to waste".

en.meaning: a bolt from the blue; completely unexpected
examples[].german: The sudden dismissal came as a bolt from the blue.
The sale of the parent company was a bolt from the blue for the employees.
My brother is getting married next month? That's news to me!
en.notes: 寝耳に水 literally means "water in the ear while one is asleep": news hits one completely unprepared and shocks. It is mostly about unpleasant news such as layoffs, closures or scandals. Typical are 〜は寝耳に水だった and 寝耳に水の話／出来事. Synonymous but more elevated is 青天の霹靂.

en.meaning: to be swamped with work; to be under work pressure
examples[].german: I'm swamped with work every day and have no time to rest.
At the end of the fiscal year I'm swamped with work and have no time to talk with my family.
I gave up my life of being chased by work and moved to the countryside.
en.notes: 仕事に追われる is the passive of 追う "to chase": literally "to be chased by work", that is, "to be swamped with work, to work constantly under time pressure". The cause takes に; the pattern also works for other things: 家事に追われる, 締め切りに追われる, 時間に追われる. Common in the progressive form 追われている or as a て-form with a consequence: 仕事に追われて休む暇もない. Neutral, very common in everyday life and the media.

en.meaning: to show one's skill; to make full use of one's abilities
examples[].german: We enjoyed the dish that the chef put all his skill into.
On the weekend, my father showed what he can do in the kitchen and made curry for the family.
The new department head is to put his full ability into rebuilding the company.
en.notes: Literally "to swing the arm": 腕 stands here for "skill, dexterity". It means to bring one's skill fully to bear, especially in cooking or in manual and professional work: 料理の腕を振るう, 〜に腕を振るう. Positive, neutral to slightly elevated (restaurant advertising, reports). Do not confuse with 腕を磨く "to hone one's skills" and 腕が上がる "to get better". Rarely also written 腕を揮う.

en.meaning: to come of age; to become a full-fledged member
examples[].german: I want to become a full-fledged craftsman soon.
Let's keep working a bit longer until my son is independent.
It is said that it takes ten years to become a full-fledged chef.
en.notes: 一人前 literally means "a portion for one person" (as with food: 寿司一人前) and refers to someone who counts as a full person. 一人前になる therefore means "to become an adult and independent" or, in a profession, "to have completed one's training, to master one's craft". Typical are 一人前の職人／社会人になる and the transitive 一人前に育てる ("to raise into a full-fledged ..."). Neutral; there is also the disparaging 一人前の口をきく ("to talk as if one were already somebody").

en.meaning: to feel ashamed; to feel small in front of others; to be in an awkward position
examples[].german: I make a lot of mistakes, so I feel small at work.
These days smoking is banned almost everywhere, so smokers are made to feel small.
I was the only one among my siblings to fail the university exam, and I felt awkward at the family gathering.
en.notes: Literally "the width of the shoulders is narrow": 肩身 stands for one's standing in front of others. It means the oppressive feeling of having to be ashamed or make oneself small before others, because one has failed, belongs to a minority or is a burden on others. Typical: 〜で肩身が狭い, 肩身の狭い思いをする. Unlike 恥ずかしい, it stresses one's social position, that is, the feeling of having hardly any room or standing.

en.meaning: to be riveted; to be glued (to a spot)
examples[].german: With the deadline coming up, I'm nailed to my desk.
During the World Cup final, the whole country was glued to the TV.
The child's eyes were riveted on the cakes in the shop window.
en.notes: Literally "to be nailed down": 釘付け is actually the nailing down. It means that one cannot tear oneself away from a place or sight, out of fascination, fright or duty. Typical frames: テレビに釘付けになる, 目が〜に釘付けになる, その場に釘付けになる. The transitive side is 釘付けにする "to rivet, to hold someone fast" (観客を釘付けにする). Neutral, common in the media and daily life.

en.meaning: to dodge the issue; to fob someone off; to do something only superficially
examples[].german: He did not answer the question and dodged the issue.
Instead of real measures, they just put up posters and left it at that.
I was asked to give a speech but wasn't prepared, so I got by with a short greeting.
en.notes: Literally "to muddy the tea": someone who cannot do the tea ceremony just stirs the tea somehow until it is cloudy and pretends. It means to evade a matter with a half-hearted, superficial answer or makeshift solution: 適当な返事でお茶を濁す, 〜だけでお茶を濁す. Similar are 言葉を濁す (to be vague, only in speech) and ごまかす (to cover up); お茶を濁す stresses the half-hearted, provisional. Neutral, mostly critical.

examples[].german: I held my breath at the beauty of the scenery.
At the moment of the accident, the spectators all gasped at once.
The game stayed breathtaking until the very end.
en.notes: 息を呑む literally means "to swallow one's breath": from astonishment, fright or suspense, one's breath catches. Typical frames are 〜に息を呑む (美しさに息を呑む), 息を呑むほど美しい and 息を呑む展開／光景. The kanji 呑 is not on the Jōyō list, so newspapers usually write 息をのむ; 息を飲む is also widespread. To be distinguished are 息を止める (deliberately holding one's breath, e.g. underwater) and 息を殺す (breathing quietly so as not to be noticed).

en.meaning: to save face; to keep one's reputation intact
examples[].german: With this proposal, the boss will probably be able to save face.
Thanks to everyone's cooperation, I saved face as the organizer.
If we can't deliver the goods by the agreed date, the senior colleague who introduced us will lose face.
en.notes: Literally "the face stands": 顔 stands for standing and honor. It means that someone's reputation is preserved, usually thanks to the behavior of others: 〜の顔が立つ, negative 顔が立たない. The transitive counterpart 顔を立てる means "to save someone's face, to show someone honor" (部長の顔を立てる); the opposite is 顔が潰れる／顔を潰す "to lose face / to embarrass someone". Typical at work and in the family, where consideration for hierarchy counts.

en.meaning: not to be worth it; to be out of proportion
examples[].german: This job is hard but the pay is low, so it isn't worth it.
Spending three hours round trip for a 1,000-yen purchase isn't worth it.
If the job is that dangerous, this amount isn't worth it.
en.notes: 割 here is the ratio and 合う means "to fit": literally "doesn't fit the ratio" - the effort, risk or cost is out of proportion to the return. Usually a contrast with のに or わりに precedes it: 大変なのに安くて割に合わない. The positive form 割に合う ("it pays off") is rarer, often negated as 割に合う仕事じゃない; variant 割が合わない. Not to be confused with the adverb 割に／割と ("fairly, relatively"). Neutral to colloquial.

en.meaning: to take command; to take charge
examples[].german: She is in charge of the project.
At the school festival, the student council president was in charge of the whole thing.
Because the company president is in the hospital, the vice president will take charge of the company.
en.notes: Literally "to wave the commander's baton": 采配 is the tasseled baton with which generals used to direct their troops. Today it means to take over leadership and command, for example for projects, events or in a company: 〜の采配を振る. Also used as 采配を振るう. Neutral to slightly elevated; 采配 alone often refers to a coach's tactical decisions: 監督の采配が当たった.

en.meaning: to act on principle; to follow the proper channels
examples[].german: In everything, it is important to follow the proper procedure.
If you want to change jobs, you should first inform your current boss properly before going further.
He is a man who sticks to his principles even when it costs him, so he can be trusted.
en.notes: Literally "to pass a thread through": 筋 means "logic, correct procedure, principle" here. It means to act consistently by principle and decency and to follow the proper channels, for example informing one's superior first before doing something: 〜に筋を通す. The opposite is 筋が通らない "illogical, not proper". Positive in tone, typical in business and politics.

en.meaning: to catch fire; to get fired up (motivation)
examples[].german: Seeing my rival's success fired up my motivation.
Since it was featured on social media, this shop's popularity has taken off.
The wind is so strong that the candle won't light.
en.notes: Literally "fire attaches": something catches fire or can be lit (ろうそくに火がつく). Figuratively, feelings, arguments or a trend suddenly flare up: やる気に火がつく ("motivation is fired up"), 人気に火がつく ("suddenly becomes popular"), 議論に火がつく. What starts to burn takes に. It is the intransitive partner of 火をつける ("to light, to kindle"): 彼の言葉が私のやる気に火をつけた. The kanji can also be written 火が付く／点く; neutral.

en.meaning: to have a prospect in sight; to see a way forward
examples[].german: At last there is a prospect of finishing the project.
Because of the heavy rain, there is no prospect yet of when trains will resume.
I was relieved that I could finally see a way to pay back my debt.
en.notes: めど means "goal, prospect"; 目処 is an ateji spelling, and it is often written in hiragana (also 目途). 目処が立つ means that an end or a solution becomes foreseeable: 完成の目処が立つ, 復旧の目処が立たない (very common in the news). The transitive counterpart is 目処をつける "to create a prospect, to roughly get something under way". Neutral, very common in business and the media.

en.meaning: to hold two jobs at once; to play a double role
examples[].german: He works as both a company employee and a writer.
A professional baseball player who plays both pitcher and batter is the talk of the town.
I got tired of juggling two jobs, so I quit my company to concentrate on composing.
en.notes: 二足のわらじを履く literally means "to wear two pairs of straw sandals (わらじ)". Originally, in the Edo period, it referred to people with incompatible roles, such as gamblers who also worked as police informants; today it means, neutrally to appreciatively, to hold two jobs or roles at once. Typical frame: AとBの二足のわらじを履く. わらじ is usually written in kana, less often 草鞋.

en.meaning: to sprout; to begin to show success
examples[].german: Years of research have finally begun to bear fruit.
When spring came, the seeds I sowed sprouted.
The manga artist who hadn't sold for years has finally made it.
en.notes: 芽 is "sprout, bud"; 芽を出す literally means "to put out a sprout" (seeds, plants). Figuratively, efforts, talents or projects show first successes, or a previously unknown person makes a breakthrough. The intransitive variant 芽が出る is at least as common, especially in the negative: なかなか芽が出ない ("just can't get a breakthrough"). The opposite image is 芽を摘む ("to nip in the bud"). Neutral, figurative.

en.meaning: to be thrifty; to keep a tight hold on the purse
examples[].german: My mother is thrifty and doesn't allow waste.
Because of the bad economy, consumers are keeping a tight hold on their money.
My husband is so tight-fisted that he hardly ever agrees when I bring up travel plans.
en.notes: Literally "the string of the purse is tight"; in the past, purses were tied shut with a cord. It means that someone is reluctant to spend money: thrifty to stingy. Related: 財布の紐を締める "to tighten one's belt", 財布の紐を緩める "to spend money more freely", 財布の紐を握る "to control the household money". Neutral; in business news also about consumers: 消費者の財布の紐が固い. Also written 財布のひもが堅い.

en.meaning: to be short of money; to have no money
examples[].german: It's before the bonus, so I'm short of cash.
I'm broke this month because of the move, so I'll pass on the drinking party.
For students short on money, the cheap prices at this set-meal restaurant are a blessing.
en.notes: Literally "the breast pocket is cold": 懐 is the fold of the kimono in front of the chest in which money used to be carried. It means that one has little money at the moment; similar is 懐が寂しい, the opposite is 懐が温かい. Typical: 給料日前で懐が寒い. Colloquial and slightly jocular; it describes a temporary situation, not real poverty (for that, 貧乏).

en.meaning: to puff out one's chest; to be proud
examples[].german: Walk with your chest out, confidently.
We lost the game, but let's go home with our heads held high.
I want to become able to be proud of my work.
en.notes: 胸を張る literally means "to stretch the chest", i.e. to stand upright with the chest thrust out. Figuratively it means being confident and proud without having to feel ashamed: 胸を張って歩く, 胸を張れる仕事. Unlike 威張る "to show off, to act important", it is usually meant positively. Neutral, often used in encouragement.

en.meaning: to spare no expense; to not let money matter
examples[].german: I spare no expense on my children's education.
The collector bought up old stamps regardless of cost.
It's a once-in-a-lifetime trip, so this time I decided not to worry about money.
en.notes: 糸目 are the guide strings of a kite: without them it flies off uncontrolled. 金に糸目をつけない therefore means to spend money without any limit, to spare no expense. Typical are 〜には金に糸目をつけない and adverbial 金に糸目をつけずに買う／集める. The expression is used almost only in the negative; an affirmative form is not usual.

en.meaning: to be in financial straits; to be deep in debt
examples[].german: I have so many debts that I'm in financial straits.
Sales dropped, and the shop manager ended up unable to move because of debt.
If you shop too much on your card, you'll soon be up to your neck in debt.
en.notes: Literally "the neck cannot turn": one is so deep in debt that one can no longer move. Almost always linked with 借金: 借金で首が回らない, 首が回らなくなる. Only the negative form is idiomatic; there is also the literal meaning "cannot turn one's head", for example with a stiff neck. Colloquial-neutral; similar is 火の車 "in utmost financial distress".

en.meaning: to exceed the budget; to run a deficit
examples[].german: I went over budget on the trip.
The party cost 10,000 yen more than planned, so the organizer paid the difference.
I thought it was cheap when I bought it, but the shipping costs put me over budget.
en.notes: Literally "the feet stick out", as from under a blanket that is too short. It means that expenses exceed the budget: 予算から足が出る, 一万円足が出た. More rarely it means that a secret comes out; for that, however, 足がつく "to leave a trail" is much more common. Neutral and everyday; similar is 赤字になる "to go into the red".

en.meaning: to recoup one's costs; to get one's money's worth
examples[].german: I ate a lot at the all-you-can-eat and got my money's worth.
The annual fee is high, so unless I use it a lot I won't get my money's worth.
Opening the shop cost a lot of money, but I recouped it in three years.
en.notes: 元 here is the invested money, the cost; 取る means "to take back". Literally "to take back what was put in": to use something so much or earn so much from it that the expense was worth it. Typical with flat prices and investments: 食べ放題で元を取る, 定期券の元を取る. Very common in the potential form 元が取れる／元が取れない. Colloquial to neutral; not to be confused with 元 "former, original".

en.meaning: to be flush with cash; to have a lot of money
examples[].german: I got my bonus, so I'm flush with cash.
I'm flush today, so dinner is on me.
While I was still flush after winning at the horse races, I bought the camera I had wanted.
en.notes: Literally "the breast pocket is warm": 懐 is the kimono fold in which money used to be carried. It means that one is well off at the moment, often temporarily after payday, a bonus or winnings. Opposite: 懐が寒い／懐が寂しい. Also written 懐が暖かい. Colloquial, often used jokingly as a reason to treat others.

en.meaning: to use someone as a source of money
examples[].german: She is only using him as a source of money.
The fraud ring had been using elderly people as a source of money.
Stop living like that, treating your parents like a cash cow.
en.notes: 金づる (also 金蔓) is literally a "money vine", a vine from which one can pull money, that is, a source of money or a wealthy patron. 〜を金づるにする means to exploit someone as a source of money; passive 金づるにされる. Clearly derogatory and colloquial; neutral words would be スポンサー or 資金源. Mostly written in hiragana.

en.meaning: to have not a single sen left; to be completely broke
examples[].german: It's right before payday, and there isn't a single sen left in my wallet.
After paying rent and electricity, nothing is left.
I spent too much on the trip, and not a single sen of my bonus was left.
en.notes: 銭 is an old coin unit (one hundredth of a yen) that now survives only in set phrases. 一銭も + negative means "not a single penny": 一銭も残らない "not a penny is left", typical after expenses: 〜を払ったら一銭も残らない. For the current state one says 一銭も残っていない. Same pattern: 一銭も払わない, 一銭にもならない ("brings in not a penny"); in everyday speech 一円も is just as common. Colloquial and emphatic.

en.meaning: to be generous with money; to be free-handed
examples[].german: He is generous with money, so he often treats us.
That president is free-handed and even paid for the entire company trip.
Being generous is fine, but you should save a bit as well.
en.notes: 金離れ is literally "parting from money", that is, the way someone spends money. 金離れがいい means to pay generously and without hesitation, for example for invitations, gifts or tips. Opposite: 金離れが悪い or 財布の紐が固い. Neutral to appreciative and not necessarily wasteful; for that one says 湯水のように使う. Instead of いい, よい is also used; it conjugates via よ-: よくて, よかった.

en.meaning: to let someone take the credit; to let someone shine
examples[].german: I let the junior take the credit.
The department head deliberately stayed quiet in the meeting so the newcomer could shine.
I played shogi with my grandson and let him win in the end.
en.notes: Literally "to let someone hold the flowers": one leaves the glory or the victory to someone else although one could have shone oneself, usually out of consideration, for example toward juniors, guests or superiors. Structure: 〜に花を持たせる (causative of 持つ). Neutral and positive-modest; typical at work, in sports and in games. Do not confuse with 花を添える "to add some further beauty to something".

en.meaning: the situation changes; the wind shifts
examples[].german: The direction of public opinion has changed.
The wind changed in the afternoon, and it suddenly got cold.
A goal in the second half changed the course of the game.
en.notes: 風向き "wind direction" + 変わる "to change": literally the wind shifts; figuratively the situation, mood or public opinion turns, often unexpectedly. Usually preceded by 〜の: 世論の風向きが変わる, 試合の風向きが変わる. The transitive form is 風向きを変える ("to turn the tide"). Neutral, common in news and sports reports. Reading かざむき (less often かぜむき).

en.meaning: to hone one's skills; to perfect one's skill
examples[].german: I want to improve my cooking skills.
He honed his bread-making skills in France for three years.
I'm honing my tennis skills every day in preparation for the tournament.
en.notes: 腕を磨く literally means "to polish the arm"; 腕 stands for skill and ability here. Typical is 〜の腕を磨く with a field: 料理の腕, テニスの腕. Related expressions are 腕を上げる / 腕が上がる "to get better" and 腕がいい "to be skilled". Neutral, often used for crafts, sports and cooking.

en.meaning: to hear through the grapevine; to learn indirectly
examples[].german: I heard through the grapevine that he got married.
I heard through the grapevine that a former colleague opened a cafe in the countryside.
I was relieved to hear through the grapevine that my teacher is doing well.
en.notes: Literally "to hear by the letter of the wind": 風の便り is news whose source is unclear and which has somehow been carried to you. Typical for news about acquaintances with whom one no longer has direct contact: 〜と風の便りに聞いた, often with らしい or そうだ. Slightly poetic, but also used in conversation; unlike 噂, it does not sound like gossip but rather nostalgic.

en.meaning: it looks like trouble; the situation is getting worrying
examples[].german: The meeting is starting to look troublesome.
The sky looks threatening, so let's take an umbrella.
The relationship between the two seems to be getting shaky.
en.notes: 雲行き is "the movement of the clouds" and 怪しい is "suspicious, worrying". Literally the sky looks like rain; figuratively a situation threatens to go wrong - negotiations, meetings, relationships, the economy. Very common as a development: 雲行きが怪しくなる／怪しくなってきた ("something is brewing"). Whose situation is meant takes の: 会議の雲行き. Neutral.

en.meaning: to be deeply rooted; to be a fundamental problem
examples[].german: This problem is deeply rooted and cannot be solved easily.
The conflict between the two countries has deep historical roots.
The bad blood between those two runs deep and won't be fixed by a short talk.
en.notes: Literally "the root is deep": it refers to problems, conflicts or feelings whose causes reach far back and which are therefore hard to resolve: 根が深い問題, 〜の対立は根が深い. Neutral, also used in the news; equivalent but more written is the single word 根深い. Do not confuse with 根はいい／根は優しい, where 根 means "basic character".

en.meaning: leave no mess behind when you go; to make a clean exit
examples[].german: When I left the company, I did the handover cleanly.
Before moving, I cleaned the room thoroughly, as one should leave properly.
When we leave the campsite, let's take all the trash back with us and leave no trace.
en.notes: Literally "the bird that takes off does not muddy (the water) behind it": water birds leave clear water when they fly off. It means to leave a place, a post or a task properly: tidying up, handing over cleanly, leaving no trouble behind. Typical for resignation, moving or departure: 立つ鳥跡を濁さずと言うから／立つ鳥跡を濁さずの気持ちで. Neutral, positive and admonishing; the opposite is 後は野となれ山となれ "after me, the deluge".

en.meaning: to take criticism calmly, like a willow in the wind
examples[].german: She brushes off criticism like a willow in the wind.
No matter what the boss says, he shrugs it off and doesn't mind.
The best way to deal with online insults is to let them roll off you.
en.notes: 柳に風 literally means "wind against the willow": the pliant willow yields to the wind and does not break. It means calmly letting criticism, mockery or attacks bounce off without fighting back. Typical is 柳に風と受け流す, also 柳に風で気にしない. Depending on the context it sounds appreciative (composed) or slightly critical (won't be told anything).

en.meaning: to listen attentively; to lend an ear
examples[].german: You should listen attentively to your subordinates' opinions.
At the press conference, the prime minister said, "We will listen to the voice of the people."
I closed my eyes and listened to the sound of the waves.
en.notes: Literally "to tilt the ear": to listen attentively and seriously, especially to opinions, requests or criticism: 〜に耳を傾ける. Somewhat more elevated than 聞く and stresses the willingness to engage with the other person; typical in speeches, politics and leadership contexts (国民の声に耳を傾ける). The opposite is 耳を貸さない "to turn a deaf ear". Also for music or sounds: 波の音に耳を傾ける.

examples[].german: Please don't butt into other people's conversations.
This is a family matter, so it's not for outsiders to interfere.
Excuse me, may I cut in for a moment?
en.notes: Literally "to wedge in one's mouth": to interfere uninvited in a conversation or in other people's affairs: 人の話に口を挟む. Mostly reproachful and often negated or used as a request: 口を挟まないで. Similar is 口出しする (to interfere, more general). As a polite opening to briefly interject: ちょっと口を挟んでもいいですか.

en.meaning: to be impatient; to be short-tempered
examples[].german: My father is short-tempered, so he gets angry quickly.
I am impatient, so I hate standing in long lines.
The impatient customer left after waiting only five minutes.
en.notes: 気が短い literally means "the temper is short" and describes someone who is impatient and quickly irritated. The opposite is 気が長い "patient". Similar is せっかち "hasty, impatient", which, however, stresses haste rather than irritability; 短気 is the corresponding noun or な-adjective. Neutral, often used to describe oneself.

en.meaning: to be eloquent; to be able to speak fluently
examples[].german: She is a very fluent talker.
I've had too much to drink, and my tongue is getting heavy.
With tongue twisters my tongue just won't cooperate, and I can hardly say them well.
en.notes: Literally "the tongue turns": to speak fluently and skillfully. Positive or ironic ("he talks like a waterfall"), often with よく: よく舌が回る. The negative 舌が回らない is very common: one cannot speak clearly, for example from tiredness, when drunk or with tongue twisters (similar to ろれつが回らない). Colloquial-neutral.

en.meaning: to be vague; to beat around the bush
examples[].german: He never says what he really thinks and always beats around the bush.
Asked about his possible resignation, the minister gave a vague reply.
When I asked my son about his test result, he said evasively, "Oh, so-so."
en.notes: Literally "to muddy the words": to answer deliberately vaguely to avoid a clear statement, out of politeness, uncertainty or because one wants to hide something. Typical: 〜について言葉を濁す, 〜と聞かれて言葉を濁した. Unlike お茶を濁す (to deal with a matter half-heartedly), it refers only to speaking. Neutral; frequent in news about politicians.

en.meaning: to search one's conscience; to reflect
examples[].german: Put your hand on your heart and think about it.
I searched my conscience as to why my friends had drifted away.
If you search your conscience, you should know who is to blame.
en.notes: Literally "to put one's hand on one's chest": to reflect and honestly examine one's own conscience. Almost always in the form 胸に手を当てて考える／考えてみる, often as a reproachful demand to someone who does not see their own guilt: 胸に手を当ててよく考えなさい. It can also be meant literally, for example when swearing an oath. Neutral to sternly admonishing.

en.meaning: for the conversation to blossom; to get chatting
examples[].german: Meeting my old friend again, we got into a lively conversation.
At the class reunion, we chatted enthusiastically about memories of our school days.
Some anime fans got together, and the talk about their favorite series blossomed.
en.notes: Literally "flowers bloom in the conversation": a conversation becomes lively and animated, usually among friends about shared memories or interests: 思い出話に花が咲く, 〜の話に花が咲く. Almost always told in the past tense (咲いた). Positive and neutral; similar is 話が弾む "the conversation gets going".

en.meaning: to speak casually, without polite forms; to talk (disrespectfully) as an equal
examples[].german: It's rude to speak casually to a senior.
The newcomer spoke casually to the company president, and everyone was shocked.
We're the same age, so let's talk casually.
en.notes: ため口 (often written タメ口) is the casual way of speaking among equals, without です／ます and without keigo; 口を利く means "to speak, to address someone". Among friends this is normal, but toward elders, superiors or 先輩 it counts as disrespectful, so 〜にため口を利く usually sounds reproachful. More neutral are ため口で話す and the offer ため口でいいよ ("you can speak casually with me"). Colloquial; 利く is often written in kana.

en.meaning: to fall for someone's smooth talk; to be talked into something
examples[].german: I fell for the salesman's patter and bought something expensive.
An acquaintance talked me into a dubious investment, and I lost a lot of money.
Don't fall for his smooth talk. He always just says what sounds good.
en.notes: 口車 is skillful, glib talk with which one wins someone over; 口車に乗る means to fall for it and be talked into something. Typical are 〜の口車に乗る and the passive 口車に乗せられる; the transitive counterpart is 〜を口車に乗せる. It is about persuasion or deception, not just praise; for flattery people rather say おだてに乗る.

en.meaning: to hit the nail on the head; to hit the mark
examples[].german: She hit the nail on the head, and I couldn't say anything.
"You don't really want to go, do you?" Caught out, I smiled wryly.
My mother sees through my lies immediately and always hits the mark.
en.notes: 図星 is literally the center of a target, and 指す is "to point at". 図星を指す means to hit exactly on someone's hidden thoughts or sore spots. Especially common in the passive from the viewpoint of the person found out: 図星を指される; in conversation, short 図星だ！ "Bull's-eye!". Colloquial-neutral; similar to 言い当てる, but 図星 stresses that it is uncomfortable for the person concerned.

en.meaning: to read the room; to gauge the atmosphere correctly
examples[].german: He is good at reading the room.
Everyone was tired, so I read the room and cut my talk short.
I don't want to be seen as someone who can't read the room.
en.notes: Literally "to read the air": to grasp the unspoken mood and expectations of a group and adjust one's behavior accordingly, for example by staying quiet, giving in, or ending a conversation. Typical patterns are 空気を読んで〜する and 空気を読むのが上手／苦手. The potential form 空気が読めない criticizes a lack of tact and can be hurtful; the related 場の空気 means "the atmosphere in the room". Colloquial to neutral; it refers to a social judgment, not literal reading.

en.meaning: the future is uncertain (lit. one sun ahead is darkness)
examples[].german: You never know what will happen in life. The future is uncertain.
For the industry leader to go bankrupt, you really never know what's coming.
In politics, they say you never know what's around the corner, but nobody expected this election result.
en.notes: Literally "one sun ahead is darkness": 一寸 is an old unit of length of about three centimeters. It means that nobody knows what will happen even in the near future, often with a view to sudden misfortune, but also soberly about politics and business (政界は一寸先は闇). Neutral; mostly stands with だ or と言われる. Related but more optimistic: 明日は明日の風が吹く.

en.meaning: there is luck in what is left over
examples[].german: The last remaining cake was the most delicious. There's luck in leftovers.
I drew a lot last and won first prize. There's luck in what's left.
Sorry you're last. But they say there's luck in what's left over.
en.notes: 残り物 means "leftovers, remains" and 福 means "luck, blessing": literally "there is luck in the leftovers". It is said when someone chooses last, draws a lot or has their turn last - as consolation or encouragement in the sense of "the best comes last". Typical when drawing lots or distributing gifts or food, often quoted with って言う. Neutral, friendly and jokingly; variant 余り物には福がある.

en.meaning: to open one's eyes wide; to be astonished
examples[].german: I opened my eyes wide at her transformation.
When she heard the price, my mother opened her eyes wide.
The children stared wide-eyed at the size of the elephant they were seeing for the first time.
en.notes: 目を丸くする literally means "to make one's eyes round" and describes visible astonishment or amazement, mostly reported in the past tense: 〜に目を丸くした or 目を丸くして驚く. The cause of the astonishment is marked with に. Similar is the more elevated 目を見張る "to open one's eyes wide, to marvel (often in admiration)"; the colloquial 目が点になる, by contrast, expresses speechless bewilderment. Neutral, common in narratives and reports.

en.meaning: to be attentive; to be thoughtful
examples[].german: She is thoughtful, so everyone likes her.
This hotel is attentive down to the smallest details.
I wish I could have said something clever in my speech.
en.notes: 気が利く means being attentive and noticing on one's own what others need - high praise in Japanese everyday life. The negative 気が利かない is a common reproach. Before nouns, 気の利いた "clever, fitting, well done" is often used: 気の利いたプレゼント, 気の利いた一言. Do not confuse it with 気をつける "to watch out" or 気を使う "to be considerate, to worry about others". Neutral.

en.meaning: better safe than sorry (lit. a cane before you fall)
examples[].german: Taking out insurance is a precaution: better safe than sorry.
As a precaution, I back up my data every week.
When I go to the mountains, I always take rain gear and a map just in case.
en.notes: Literally "the cane before one falls": 転ばぬ is the classical negation of 転ぶ. It means taking precautionary measures before something happens, such as insurance, data backups or an umbrella. Mostly stands with だ or as 転ばぬ先の杖として. Neutral, slightly didactic; similar is 備えあれば憂いなし "if you are prepared, you have nothing to worry about".

en.meaning: do good things quickly; never put off a good deed
examples[].german: When you get an idea, act on it right away.
Do good things without delay - let's apply today.
If you've found a good room, don't hesitate. Let's contact them right away.
en.notes: 善 means "the good" and 急げ is the imperative of 急ぐ: literally "With the good - hurry!". It means: if you plan something good or worthwhile, do it immediately before the opportunity passes. Often used as a prompt to act: 善は急げだ、すぐ〜しよう or 善は急げで早速〜. Similar is 思い立ったが吉日. Neutral, in everyday life often half jokingly.

en.meaning: the child is father of the man; the character formed in childhood lasts a lifetime (lit. the soul of a three-year-old until a hundred)
examples[].german: A childhood personality doesn't change. The child is father of the man.
My grandfather is said to have been a poor loser since he was little, and even now he takes games seriously. The child is father of the man, isn't it.
They say that what is learned young lasts, so I want her to get into the habit of greeting people while she is small.
en.notes: Literally "the soul of a three-year-old until a hundred": 三つ子 means "three-year-old child" here, not "triplets". It means that character and habits from early childhood last a lifetime, for better or worse. It is not about learning but about the unchangeable core of a person. Neutral, often said with a smile about adults, or as an argument for early upbringing: 三つ子の魂百までと言うから.

en.meaning: to love doing something without being good at it; an enthusiastic amateur
examples[].german: I'm not good at golf, but I love it and go every week.
"You play the piano well!" "Not at all, I just enjoy it more than I'm good at it."
My father loves writing haiku and has kept at it for thirty years, though he has no great talent for it.
en.notes: Literally "the side-fondness of the unskilled": 下手 means "unskilled", and 横好き is a fondness for something that actually does not suit one. It refers to someone who pursues a hobby with great enthusiasm although they are bad at it. Mostly said modestly about oneself: 下手の横好きで〜を続けています; said about others it sounds mocking. Neutral to modest-polite; the phrase is a noun and stands with だ／です or で.

en.meaning: speak of the devil (lit. talk of rumors and the shadow appears)
examples[].german: We were talking about him, and he showed up. Speak of the devil.
"I haven't seen Mr. Tanaka lately." "Speak of the devil, look, here he comes."
They say "speak of the devil", but I was amazed when the department head actually walked into the room.
en.notes: Literally "if you talk about someone, his shadow falls in": just when you are talking about a person, he turns up. Usually shortened to 噂をすれば影 or just 噂をすれば… as soon as the person walks in. Colloquial and jocular, equivalent to "speak of the devil". 差す is also written 射す or さす.

en.meaning: the eyes say as much as the mouth; eyes speak louder than words
examples[].german: You can tell her feelings from her eyes. The eyes say as much as words.
The child said nothing but stared at the present. This is just what they mean by the eyes saying as much as the mouth.
They say the eyes speak, so look the other person in the eye when you talk in an interview.
en.notes: Literally "the eyes say as much as the mouth": ほど expresses equivalence here ("to the same degree as"). It means that looks reveal feelings and intentions just as clearly as words, for example when someone is silent but you can see from the eyes what they think. Neutral, rather cultured and literary; mostly stands as a sentence of its own, with と言う or in 〜とはこのことだ.

en.meaning: yield to those in power; don't challenge the stronger
examples[].german: Don't go against your boss. If you can't beat them, join them.
I wasn't convinced, but I followed the company line on the principle of going along with those in power.
The way of living by always yielding to the powerful doesn't suit me.
en.notes: Literally: "let yourself be wrapped by long things"; 巻かれろ is the imperative of the passive of 巻く. It means: one cannot prevail against the powerful or one's superiors, so it is better to submit. The expression sounds resigned or cynical and is often rejected (長い物には巻かれろという生き方は嫌だ). Related is 寄らば大樹の陰 (seeking shelter with the powerful).

en.meaning: to forgive and forget; to let bygones be bygones
examples[].german: Let's let bygones be bygones.
Since he apologized properly, I decided to let this matter go.
After being told such terrible things, I can't simply forgive and forget.
en.notes: 水に流す literally means "to let flow away in the water" and means to forgive past quarrels or offenses and not speak about them any more. Typical: 過去のことは水に流す, 今回のことは水に流す. In the negative potential form it expresses that one cannot forgive something: 水に流せない. Neutral, common in reconciliation situations.

en.meaning: windfall; unexpected good luck (short for 棚からぼたもち)
examples[].german: Getting a present unexpectedly is a real windfall.
The other team didn't show up to the match, so we advanced to the final by a stroke of luck.
Thanks to my senior colleague quitting, I became section chief by sheer luck.
en.notes: 棚ぼた is the colloquial short form of 棚からぼたもち: literally, a sweet rice cake (ぼたもち) falls from the shelf (棚) into one's mouth, a piece of luck for which one has done nothing. Typical are まさに棚ぼただ, 棚ぼたで〜 and 棚ぼた式に; one says it half jokingly, sometimes slightly disparagingly, about an undeserved gain. The full form is also common, but in conversation one mostly hears the short form.

en.meaning: everyone is different; ten people, ten colors
examples[].german: When it comes to food, everyone has their own taste.
Everyone studies in their own way, so please find the method that suits you.
Even though everyone watched the same film, the impressions were all different.
en.notes: 十人十色 literally means "ten people, ten colors": every person has their own preferences, views and peculiarities. It is used to calmly state differences, mostly in the pattern 〜は十人十色だ (好み・考え方・生き方は十人十色). Note the reading: 十色 is read といろ here, not じゅういろ. In casual conversation the same thing is often simply said with 人それぞれ "everyone is different".

en.meaning: persistence is strength; constant dripping wears away the stone
examples[].german: If you practice a little every day, you'll get good. Persistence is strength.
Because I kept jogging every morning, I was able to run the whole marathon. Persistence is strength.
"Persistence is strength" is written on the classroom wall.
en.notes: 継続 means "continuation, sticking with it", 力 means "strength", and なり is the classical copula (equivalent to である). Literally "sticking with it is strength": whoever keeps going steadily becomes strong, even if each step is small. A popular motto in school, sports and work, often on posters or as a watchword; in a sentence it usually ends with だ or ですね. Slightly elevated because of なり, but ubiquitous.

en.meaning: God helps those who help themselves
examples[].german: First, do your best on your own. God helps those who help themselves.
As they say, God helps those who help themselves; he kept at it, and eventually his chance came.
My grandfather's favorite saying was "God helps those who help themselves."
en.notes: The proverb is the Meiji-era translation of "Heaven helps those who help themselves" from Samuel Smiles's "Self-Help". 助くる and 助く are classical forms of 助ける: "Heaven helps those who help themselves". It encourages making an effort rather than waiting for outside help. The tone is elevated; it is quoted with と言うように or as a life motto.

en.meaning: fall seven times, get up eight; never give up
examples[].german: No matter how many times you fail, the spirit of getting back up is important.
My grandfather's life was truly one of falling down and getting back up.
Taking "fall seven times, get up eight" as his motto, he rebuilt the company.
en.notes: Literally "seven (七) falls (転), eight (八) risings (起)": one falls seven times and gets up eight times. It is the Sino-Japanese reading of the proverb 七転び八起き, which is much more common in daily life; 七転八起 sounds written-language and often appears as a motto. Typical are 七転八起の精神 or 七転八起の人生. Do not confuse with 七転八倒（しちてんばっとう）, which means "to writhe in pain".

en.meaning: to give the strong even more strength; twice as strong
examples[].german: If he joins the team, it will be unbeatable.
My mother is a good cook, and with a new oven she'd be unstoppable.
If you can speak both English and Chinese, you'll have a great advantage in job hunting.
en.notes: 鬼 is the Japanese ogre and 金棒 an iron-studded club. An already strong ogre gets an iron club on top: someone who is already strong or capable becomes unbeatable through an extra advantage. Mostly predicative in conditional sentences: AがあればBは鬼に金棒だ, AとBが組めば鬼に金棒. Always meant positively; neutral, popular in sports, work and everyday life.

en.meaning: let sleeping dogs lie; leave well alone (lit. a god you do not touch brings no curse)
examples[].german: You'd better stay out of that matter. Let sleeping dogs lie.
On days when the department head is in a bad mood, I try not to talk to him at all.
I've decided not to meddle in my sister and her husband's quarrels. Let sleeping dogs lie, as they say.
en.notes: Literally "a god one does not touch brings no curse": 触らぬ is the classical negation of 触る, and 祟り is the curse of a deity. It means keeping away from delicate matters or moody people so as not to bring trouble on oneself. Mostly added afterwards as a justification: 〜。触らぬ神に祟りなしだ or 触らぬ神に祟りなしと思って. Colloquial-neutral; equivalent to "let sleeping dogs lie".

en.meaning: spare the rod and spoil the child (lit.: let a beloved child travel); let those you love gain experience
examples[].german: I'm worried, but you have to let a beloved child go out into the world, so I let him go alone.
They say you should let a beloved child travel, so I'm thinking of letting my daughter study abroad.
Since children grow through challenges, we sent our son to a dormitory famous for its strictness.
en.notes: Literally: "let your beloved child travel"; させよ is the classical imperative of させる. In the past, travel was arduous and dangerous, so whoever loves their child should let them experience hardship rather than pamper them. It is used when parents let their children go, for example for time abroad, boarding school or training away from home. The kanji 可愛い is often also written in kana: かわいい子には旅をさせよ.

en.meaning: in for a penny, in for a pound (lit.: if you eat poison, eat the plate too)
examples[].german: Now that we've come this far, in for a penny, in for a pound. Let's see it through.
My diet is shot anyway. Might as well go all the way and order dessert too.
Having once gotten involved in fraud, he went on to commit even more crimes, figuring he might as well.
en.notes: Literally: "if you are going to eat poison, then also the plate"; 食らわば is a classical conditional form of 食らう. Originally it means: whoever has once committed a wrong may as well carry it through completely. Today it is often used jokingly, for example when abandoning good resolutions, or in the sense of "in for a penny, in for a pound". The tone is colloquial and slightly defiant.

examples[].german: This is no time to be wasting time in a place like this.
