Where have you been dawdling? You're already an hour late.
If you loiter during work, the section chief will scold you.
en.notes: 油を売る literally means "to sell oil": in the Edo period, hair-oil sellers chatted with their customers for a long time while the viscous oil slowly dripped. So it means to dawdle during work or on the way and waste time chatting. Almost always in the progressive form: どこで油を売っていたの？ Colloquial, mostly reproachful.

en.meaning: a fox borrowing the tiger's might; relying on another's power to intimidate others
examples[].german: Throwing around the department head's name to act important: that's a fox in a tiger's clothing.
He swaggers just because he is the president's son, and people badmouth him as a fox borrowing the tiger's might.
That country, which acts boldly with the backing of a great power, is like a fox borrowing the tiger's might.
en.notes: Literally: "the fox who borrows the authority (威) of the tiger", after an old Chinese fable in which the fox walks ahead of the tiger and the other animals flee out of fear of the tiger. It means a small person who relies on the power of someone more powerful in order to put on airs and intimidate others, for example with the name of the boss or one's parents. Typical: 〜は虎の威を借る狐だ, 虎の威を借る狐のように. Not the same as "to strut in borrowed feathers" (passing off others' achievements as one's own).

en.meaning: tomorrow a different wind will blow; tomorrow is another day
examples[].german: Let's forget about today. Tomorrow a different wind will blow.
I failed the exam, but tomorrow is another day. Let's try again.
He always says "tomorrow is another day" and doesn't save money.
en.notes: Literally "tomorrow the wind of tomorrow will blow": tomorrow the circumstances will be different, so there is no need to worry unnecessarily today. It is said to console or to switch off after a bad day; depending on tone calm or carefree, similar to "tomorrow is another day". Often with よ or さ at the end of the sentence or quoted with と言って. 明日 is read あした here. Colloquial to neutral.

en.meaning: to repay kindness with ingratitude; to be ungrateful
examples[].german: After helping him so much, he betrays me. This is what repaying kindness with spite means.
Handing over information about the company that trained you to a rival firm is an act of repaying kindness with spite.
I don't want to do anything that repays my kind teacher with ingratitude.
en.notes: Literally "to repay a favor with enmity": 恩 is a favor received, and 仇（あだ） is enmity or harm. It means serious ingratitude, harming or betraying someone who has helped you. Typical: 恩を仇で返すようなことをする, 恩を仇で返すとはこのことだ. Strongly censuring; the opposite is 恩返しをする or 恩に報いる "to show gratitude".

en.meaning: there is no smoke without fire
examples[].german: That rumor may be true. They say there is no smoke without fire.
The politician denies it, but they also say there's no smoke without fire.
That shop has many bad reviews. There's no smoke without fire, so let's not go.
en.notes: Literally "where there is no fire, no smoke rises": 立たぬ is the classical negation of 立つ; the modern 火のない所に煙は立たない is also used. It means that there is usually something true in a rumor. Typical with と言う／と言うから／とも言う and in connection with 噂 or scandals. Neutral; corresponds exactly to "no smoke without fire".

en.meaning: life is the most important thing; without life, nothing is possible
examples[].german: Don't overwork yourself. Life comes first.
Our house was washed away, but the whole family is safe. As long as we're alive, that's what matters.
If the weather is bad, the courage to turn back is also important. After all, without your life, nothing else matters.
en.notes: 物種 means "seed, origin of all things"; 命あっての物種 therefore means: only someone who is alive can achieve anything at all. It is used to warn against dangerous recklessness or overwork, or to console after a loss in which life was spared (家は失ったが命あっての物種だ). Colloquial, often with だよ／だからね. 物種 is read ものだね.

en.meaning: wherever you live becomes home; you get used to anything
examples[].german: I didn't like it at first, but you get used to anywhere, and now I love this town.
It's a small apartment, but home is where you make it.
You're probably anxious about being transferred to the countryside, but they say you get used to anywhere.
en.notes: 住めば is the ば-form of 住む ("if you live there") and 都 means "capital", here the best place of all. Literally "if you live there, it is the capital": you get used to any place of residence, and over time you come to like it. Typical with moves, small apartments or transfers, often as 住めば都で… or 住めば都って言うよ. Neutral, comforting.

en.meaning: even the longest journey begins with a single step
examples[].german: A journey of a thousand ri begins with a single step, so let's get started.
Memorizing two thousand kanji is tough, but a journey of a thousand ri begins with a single step. Today I'll learn five.
The company president said "a journey of a thousand ri begins with a single step" and started with a small shop.
en.notes: 千里 means "a thousand ri" (an old unit of length, one ri is about 3.9 km), 一歩 means "one step", and も means "even": literally "even a road of a thousand ri begins with one step", originally from the Daodejing. It means that big goals are only reached by starting small and proceeding step by step. Typical as encouragement before a big undertaking: 千里の道も一歩からだから、まず〜. Neutral, slightly elevated.

en.meaning: to give a firm warning; to caution in advance
examples[].german: I cautioned him in advance not to be late.
I was warned, "Don't tell anyone about this."
The government warned companies firmly to refrain from raising prices.
en.notes: 釘を刺す literally means "to drive in a nail" (to secure something). Figuratively: to firmly warn someone in advance so that they do not make a mistake or break a promise later. Typical frames are 〜ように釘を刺す, 「…」と釘を刺す and 〜に釘を刺す, often with 〜ておく; passive 釘を刺される. Unlike the neutral 念を押す ("to confirm once more"), 釘を刺す sounds sterner and more warning.

en.meaning: to be extremely cautious (lit. to tap even a stone bridge before crossing it)
examples[].german: He is the type to tap a stone bridge before crossing it, so decisions take him a long time.
When making a big purchase, it's just right to be extremely careful.
That bank is run with extreme caution, so it is stable even in a recession.
en.notes: Literally "to tap a stone bridge before crossing it": one double-checks even what is safe. Depending on context, it is either praise (thorough, prudent) or mildly critical (overcautious, hesitant). Typical: 石橋を叩いて渡る性格／タイプ, 石橋を叩いて渡るような〜. A humorous intensification: 石橋を叩いても渡らない "so cautious that one never acts at all". Neutral; the verb is conjugated normally (渡って, 渡った).

en.meaning: practice makes perfect (lit. get used to it rather than learn it)
examples[].german: Don't just read textbooks; practice beats study.
Driving is something you learn by doing, so it's good to drive a little every day.
Japanese conversation is learn-by-doing. Please try speaking as much as you can.
en.notes: 習う means "to be taught, to learn", より means "rather than", and 慣れろ is the imperative of 慣れる "to get used to". Literally "get used to it rather than being taught": skills are acquired through practice, not theory. Often said by teachers, coaches or experienced people, for example about languages, sports or driving. The imperative is part of the fixed saying here and is not impolite; it usually ends with だ／だよ／です.

en.meaning: an old person doing things unsuited to their age; recklessness in old age
examples[].german: Skydiving at sixty is a bit much for your age.
People might laugh and say I'm too old for this, but at seventy I'm taking on a full marathon.
Grandpa, climbing onto the roof is far too reckless at your age.
en.notes: Literally: "the cold water of the old"; an old person who bathes in cold water or drinks cold water harms himself. It means reckless behavior that is no longer appropriate for one's age. Said directly to older people it sounds mocking; the self-ironic use is very common: 年寄りの冷や水と言われるかもしれないが…. Typical are 〜とは年寄りの冷や水だ and 〜なんて年寄りの冷や水だよ.

en.meaning: you learn from mistakes; failure is the path to success
examples[].german: Don't be discouraged. Failure is the mother of success.
The experiment failed again, but let's treat failure as the foundation of success and try once more.
The company president always says "failure is the foundation of success" and lets us take on new challenges.
en.notes: Literally: "failure is the origin (もと) of success" - you learn from mistakes, and they ultimately lead to success. The saying is used mainly to console and encourage, for example after a botched exam or a failed attempt, often with だよ or 「…」って言うでしょ. もと is also written 元 or 基; the variant 失敗は成功の母 sounds somewhat more elevated. Someone who merely uses it to excuse themselves without learning anything, however, seems unconvincing.

en.meaning: to turn misfortune into good fortune
examples[].german: Thanks to the injury I found a new job. Misfortune turned into good fortune.
I was hospitalized after an accident, but it turned out for the best: I met my current wife at the hospital.
After the fire at the factory, we renewed all the equipment and managed to turn disaster into gain.
en.notes: Literally: "to turn (転じて) misfortune (禍) and make (為す) it good fortune (福)": to draw an advantage from a misfortune through one's own action. The more common form in everyday life is 災い転じて福となす (without を, with 災い and なす in kana). It is used in retrospect (…で、禍を転じて福と為すことができた) or as a resolution. The tone is rather elevated; similar is 怪我の功名, which, however, means a more accidental stroke of luck.

en.meaning: too blunt; without any sugarcoating; sobering directness
examples[].german: If you put it that way, it's rather too blunt.
"In the end, good-looking people are popular" is a pretty blunt way of putting it.
The students were disappointed by the blunt conclusion that effort cannot beat talent.
en.notes: Literally "neither body (of the vessel) nor lid": everything lies open, nothing remains covered. It refers to a statement so direct and sober that it destroys any subtlety, hope or charm. Typical as a reaction: それを言ったら身も蓋もない, 身も蓋もない言い方. Colloquial and slightly reproachful: possibly accurate in substance, but tactless. Also written 身もふたもない.

examples[].german: I try to do one good deed every day.
As my good deed for the day, I picked up trash on the road.
en.notes: 一日一善 is the motto of doing one good deed every day. As a noun it stands, for example, with を in 一日一善を心がける, to set oneself this daily goal. The reading is いちにちいちぜん; 一善 here means a good deed. The compound formulates a resolution, not a statement that everyone fulfills it.

en.meaning: to ignore one's own faults while criticizing others
examples[].german: Don't criticize others while ignoring your own faults.
He overlooks his own lateness but keeps blaming his subordinates for theirs.
I'm no better myself, but you should go to bed earlier.
en.notes: 棚に上げる literally means "to put on the shelf", that is, to remove from view. It almost always appears in the frame 自分のこと(は)棚に上げて…: one passes over one's own weaknesses while criticizing others. Self-ironically one says 自分のことは棚に上げて言うけど "I'm no better myself, but...". The noun 棚上げ(する), on the other hand, usually means "to shelve a problem or plan".

examples[].german: I haven't heard from my son, but no news is good news, I suppose.
The hospital hasn't contacted me about the test results. I hope no news is good news.
You're worrying too much. They say no news is good news, don't they.
en.notes: 便り means "news, letter": literally "that no news comes is good news" - it corresponds to "no news is good news". It is said for reassurance when children, friends or an office haven't been in touch for a long time: if something had happened, you would have heard. The の in 便りのない replaces が in the relative clause; also 便りがないのは良い便り, with よい often in kana. Often quoted with って言う or as だろう／と思う. Neutral.

en.meaning: to lay a hand on; to meddle; to hit
examples[].german: You shouldn't meddle in things you know nothing about.
Please don't stick your hand out of the window.
Even if a fight breaks out, you must not lay a hand on the other person.
en.notes: 手を出す has different meanings depending on the context. With an activity, it means to get involved in it or try it. Toward a person, it can mean to become physically violent. With a location such as 窓から, the hand is meant literally. The phrase before the expression, such as 相手に or 窓から, helps distinguish the meanings.

en.meaning: to wake up; to come to one's senses
examples[].german: I woke up at six in the morning.
He realized the lie and finally came to his senses.
en.notes: 目を覚ます first means to wake up. The eyes stand as the object before を, even though the person himself or herself wakes from sleep. Figuratively, the expression can also mean to come to one's senses or to see through a false idea. The context decides whether sleep or a realization is meant; 覚ます becomes 覚ました.

en.meaning: to get angry; to be furious
examples[].german: His attitude makes me angry.
Even when I get angry, I try not to speak loudly.
en.notes: 頭に来る is a colloquial expression for getting angry. The head is not an actual place of movement here. The cause can be given with に, as in あの人の態度には. In the past tense it is 頭に来た（あたまにきた）. The expression clearly conveys personal annoyance and is less suited to a factual report.

en.meaning: to catch the eye; to attract attention
examples[].german: The red dress caught the eye.
The store put up a large sign to attract customers' attention.
en.notes: 目を引く means to attract attention. The eye-catching object stands as the subject before が, as in 赤いドレスが目を引いた. Whose attention is meant can be given with 客の目. Unlike looking at something, the expression describes an object that stands out or is designed so that others notice it.

examples[].german: I noticed the mistake.
After I arrived at the station, I realized that I didn't have my wallet.
en.notes: 気が付く means to notice something or become aware of it. The 気が is a fixed part of the phrase. With に you name what is noticed; a whole situation can be attached with ことに. The final part is a godan verb: 気が付きます, 気が付いて, 気が付いた.

en.meaning: to be on one's mind; to worry; to be curious
examples[].german: I'm curious about the exam results.
It worries me that the child comes home late.
en.notes: 気になる means that something occupies one's attention. With an exam result it can mean curiosity or anxious anticipation; with a child coming home late, rather worry. The object stands before が. This is not the same as 気に入る, which expresses liking: even something unpleasant can be 気になる.

en.meaning: to be in the way; to be a hindrance
examples[].german: This luggage is in the way.
Voices are disturbing my studying, so please be quiet.
en.notes: 邪魔になる means that something stands in the way or hinders an activity. A piece of luggage can block the path physically; 話し声 can disturb studying. 邪魔になっている means the obstruction is happening right now. The person or activity that is disturbed can be named with の or に. Unlike 邪魔する, the expression describes the obstacle itself.

en.meaning: to get help; to ask for someone's help
examples[].german: I got a friend's help with moving.
I can't do it alone, so may I ask for a little help?
en.notes: 手を借りる uses "hand" figuratively for a person's help. With 友達の手, you name whose support you are using. The te-form 手を借りて can connect to the action in which help is given. The polite question 手を借りてもいいですか asks for assistance and does not mean that one borrows a hand as an object.

en.meaning: to go to great lengths; to take pains
examples[].german: He went to great lengths for me.
It took a great deal of effort to find a new business partner.
Thank you very much for all the trouble you have taken on this occasion.
en.notes: 骨を折る literally means "to break a bone" (but for that one usually says 骨折する), and figuratively "to take great pains for something or someone". Often with てくれる for others' efforts: 私のために骨を折ってくれた. The noun 骨折り appears in the polite thank-you formula お骨折りいただき. Neutral to polite.

en.meaning: to reach one's ears; to get into one's ear
examples[].german: A strange rumor reached my ears.
While swimming in the pool, water got into my ear.
en.notes: 耳に入る can mean figuratively that news or a rumor reaches you. It does not say that you deliberately asked for it. With water, the literal use is possible: it gets into the ear. What reaches you or gets into the ear stands before が; 入る becomes 入った in the past tense.

en.meaning: to catch one's eye; to come into view
examples[].german: A beautiful flower caught my eye.
While looking for my wallet, I noticed the key under the desk.
en.notes: 目に入る means that you notice something or it comes into view, often without explicitly looking for it. The perceived object stands before が. It can be a lovely sight while walking by or something else that stands out during a search. The somewhat similar expression 目を引く, by contrast, emphasizes that something attracts attention.

en.meaning: to raise a hand; to give up; to hit
examples[].german: Those who have a question, please raise your hand.
The other side was stronger, and I finally gave up.
You must not hit a child.
en.notes: 手を上げる can literally mean to raise a hand, for example to ask a question. In a conflict, it can also mean to give up or surrender. With a person before に, it often means that someone is about to strike or becomes physically violent toward them. The context is therefore decisive; 上げる is an ichidan verb and becomes 上げて.

en.meaning: to be a fast runner; to spoil quickly (food)
examples[].german: This fish spoils quickly, so eat it soon.
I ran with a friend who is a fast runner.
en.notes: For people, 足が速い means to be able to run or walk fast. For food, the identically read expression can mean that it spoils quickly; for this, the spelling 足が早い is especially common. The sentence about the fish therefore describes its short shelf life, not its swimming speed. In the first sentence, the additional 早く食べて means "eat it soon"; this 早く refers to the timing of eating.

en.meaning: to be considerate; to pay attention to others
examples[].german: I got tired from being so attentive to the guests.
Please don't go to so much trouble.
en.notes: 気を使う describes attentive consideration for others, often with the effort of not causing anyone trouble. に names the person you are looking after. 気を使わないでください can mean in a friendly way: please don't go to any trouble. The godan verb 使う becomes 使って and 使わない; the expression keeps を.

examples[].german: Every morning I wash my face before eating breakfast.
I had mud on my face, so I washed it.
en.notes: 顔を洗う is an everyday action: to wash one's face. 顔 stands before を as the body part being washed; that it is one's own is normally clear from the context. 洗う is a godan verb: 洗います, 洗って and 洗いました. With 洗ってから you can present the washing as a step before another action.

en.meaning: to mention someone's name; to bring up a name
examples[].german: Please don't mention his name in the meeting.
The teacher mentioned my name in front of everyone and praised me.
en.notes: 名前を出す means to mention a name in conversation or bring it up. The person can stand before 名前 with の, as in 彼の名前. 会議で names the occasion at which the name is to come up. 出さないでください asks that it be left unmentioned; 出す is a godan verb here, becoming 出さない or 出して.

en.meaning: to be of help; to be a support
examples[].german: He helped me when I was in trouble.
If you have any problems, I'll help you.
en.notes: 力になる means to stand by someone and be helpful. 誰かの力になる names the person supported; 力 here means the help they can rely on. なってくれた expresses that someone gave this help for the speaker's benefit. 力になります is suitable as an offer of support.

en.meaning: to take time; to take long
examples[].german: This work takes time.
If you use the new machine, it doesn't take very long.
en.notes: 時間がかかる states the time a task requires. Without further qualification, the phrase can mean that something takes a long time; 少し or あまり changes this assessment. あまり時間がかかりません means it doesn't take very long. かかる is a godan verb with かかります and かかった; in the basic construction 時間 stands before が.

en.meaning: to cost money; to be expensive
examples[].german: Educating children costs a lot of money.
It doesn't cost anything to enter this park.
en.notes: お金がかかる describes that money is needed for something. The activity or thing can be named with に or には, as in 子供の教育には. In a negative statement, お金はかかりません can explicitly say that no costs arise. かかる becomes かかります and かかりません; お金 is the money required.

en.meaning: to dawdle on the way; to take detours
examples[].german: Don't dawdle; go straight home.
I dawdled on the way home from school and got scolded by my mother.
I took many detours after finishing university, but I finally became a teacher.
en.notes: 道草を食う literally means "to eat grass at the roadside", like a horse that stops on the way and grazes. It means to dawdle or linger along the way, classically on the way home from school; more briefly people also say 道草する. Figuratively it denotes detours in life or career. 食う is used here quite neutrally despite its rough sound; 道草を食べる is not used.

en.meaning: to reply; to give an answer
examples[].german: Answer the teacher.
I'll reply by email tomorrow.
en.notes: 返事をする means to give a reply, orally or in writing. に names the recipient, while メールで gives the medium. 先生に返事をしなさい is a direct command from a person in authority; for a polite request, 返事をしてください is suitable. The verb する becomes します, して and しなさい.

en.meaning: to step away from one's seat; to be away briefly
examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka is away from his desk.
I need to make a phone call, so may I step away for a moment?
en.notes: 席を外す means to temporarily leave one's own seat, for example during a meeting or at one's workplace. 席を外しています often describes that someone is currently away from their desk and not reachable. With 外してもいいですか you ask permission to step away briefly. 外す is a godan verb, becoming 外して and 外しました.

examples[].german: I asked for directions to the station.
When asking for directions, it's handy to show a map.
en.notes: 道を聞く means to ask for directions. The destination can stand before への道, as in 駅への道; with 人に you name the person being asked. 聞く means "to ask" in this combination. It is a godan verb: 聞きます, 聞いて and 聞いた. A map can help show which way you are asking about.

en.meaning: to make a phone call; to call
examples[].german: I called my mother.
Please don't make phone calls here.
en.notes: 電話をかける means making a call. に names the person or place called, for example 母に. 電話 stands before を; かける is an ichidan verb and becomes かけます, かけて or かけない. Here では can emphasize the place where calls should not be made.

en.meaning: to make tea; to brew tea
examples[].german: I made tea for the guests.
Please wait here while I make the tea.
en.notes: お茶を入れる means to prepare tea. お客さんに names the people the tea is made for; お茶 remains the object before を. 入れる is an ichidan verb here, with 入れます and 入れて. お茶を入れる間 names the span of time during which one is preparing the tea.

examples[].german: It is important to keep promises.
It was raining, but I kept my promise and went to meet my friend.
en.notes: 約束を守る means to stick to a promise. 約束 is the object before を; with 約束を守ること the action becomes the topic as the keeping of promises. 守る is a godan verb: 守ります and 守って. The expression can describe a general rule or a personal promise that was actually kept.

examples[].german: Let's take a photo together.
May I take photos in this art museum?
en.notes: 写真を撮る is the usual combination for taking a photo. 写真 stands before を; 撮る is a godan verb, becoming 撮ります and 撮って. 撮りましょう invites someone to take a photo, while 撮ってもいいですか asks for permission. With 一緒に it can mean that you want to be in the picture together.

examples[].german: Every morning I take a walk in the park.
Let's take a short walk once the rain stops.
en.notes: 散歩をする describes taking a walk. The place usually stands before で, for example 公園で; a time expression can come first. 散歩 is a noun that expresses an activity here with を and する. 散歩をしましょう is an invitation to go for a walk. The shorter 散歩する is also common.

en.meaning: to go shopping; to do the shopping
examples[].german: On weekends I go shopping at the supermarket.
The shops are closed at night, so I shopped on the internet.
en.notes: 買い物をする means to shop or to run errands. The place or medium stands before で: スーパーで names the supermarket, インターネットで shopping on the internet. 買い物 is the noun and する the verb; here they are linked by を. Besides regular shopping, the expression can also refer to a single purchase made.

examples[].german: It's cold, so be careful not to catch a cold.
I caught a cold, so I took yesterday off from work.
en.notes: 風邪を引く means to catch a cold. 風邪 stands before を as the illness; 引く is a godan verb and becomes 引いた, 引きます or 引かない. 風邪を引かないようにね is a caring request between close people. With 風邪を引いたので you can explain why you skipped an activity.

en.meaning: to get carried away; to get cocky
examples[].german: Don't get carried away just because you were praised.
The moment I let him off once, he got completely cocky.
If you get cocky just because you've sold a little, you'll fail soon.
en.notes: 図に乗る means to become overconfident and brazen through success, praise or other people's indulgence. According to the common explanation, 図 originally referred to a tonal change point in Buddhist chanting; whoever hits it well becomes bold. The expression is clearly reproachful and often appears in the prohibition 図に乗るな or as 図に乗って…. The similar 調子に乗る is broader and can also mean "to get into the swing of things" neutrally; 図に乗る is always negative.

en.meaning: to put one's heart into something; to do with heart and soul
examples[].german: I wrote the letter with all my heart.
I cooked for my mother with a lot of love.
If you sing with all your heart, your feelings will surely come across.
en.notes: Literally "to put the heart (心) into it (込める)": to do something with devotion and genuine feelings. Mostly adverbial in the て-form: 心を込めて書く／作る／歌う, or before a noun: 心を込めた料理. The intransitive counterpart shows in 心のこもったプレゼント "a gift that comes from the heart". Similar is 気持ちを込める. Also in kana: 心をこめて.

en.meaning: to put effort into; to focus on; to apply force
examples[].german: The company is focusing on developing new products.
This jar's lid won't open, even if I put force into it.
This year I want to put more effort into studying Japanese.
en.notes: Literally "to put strength (力) into it (入れる)". Physically it means "to apply force, to tense": 手に力を入れる. Figuratively, the target is marked with に: 〜に力を入れる "to place special emphasis on, to put particular effort into" - typical for companies, schools or personal resolutions. The opposite is 力を抜く "to ease off". Intransitively it is 力が入る: 肩に力が入る "to be tense".

en.meaning: to open a way; to pave the way
examples[].german: The effort opened up a new path.
This discovery paved the way for the development of new drugs.
The villagers cleared the snow and opened the road for us.
en.notes: Literally "to open a path": concretely to clear a path, figuratively "to pave the way, to open up new possibilities". Often 〜への道を開く or 〜に道を開く; the subject is often an achievement or discovery. 開く is read ひらく here, not あく; sometimes also written 拓く. Intransitively it is 道が開ける "a path opens up". Rather elevated, written style (news, speeches).

en.meaning: things move quickly; that makes it easy; to catch on quickly
examples[].german: He is quick on the uptake, which is a big help.
Oh, you know Mr. Tanaka? Then this is easy.
It's quicker if you ask the department head directly.
en.notes: Literally "the talk is quick": a matter can be settled without long explanations, because the other person understands right away or the situation is favorable. Very common: それなら話が早い "Then it's easy" and 話が早くて助かる as praise for someone who catches on quickly. Do not confuse it with "speaking fast" (早口) or 話が長い "to be long-winded". Colloquial to business-neutral.

en.meaning: to bow one's head; to humble oneself; to apologize
examples[].german: After making a mistake, I apologized to my boss.
To borrow money, I humbly asked my older brother.
The students bowed to the teacher and said, "Thank you very much."
en.notes: Literally "to lower the head": to bow, and figuratively to apologize or to humbly ask for something (頭を下げて頼む). The person is marked with に: 上司に頭を下げる. While お辞儀をする is the neutral polite bow, 頭を下げる emphasizes apology, a request or subordination. Note: the intransitive 頭が下がる means "to feel respect" (彼の努力には頭が下がる).

en.meaning: to look over; to skim through
examples[].german: Please look over the documents.
Every morning I skim the newspaper before I leave the house.
Before the exam, I looked over my notes once more.
en.notes: Literally "to pass the eyes through": to look through or skim something without studying it thoroughly. The particle に is important: 書類に目を通す, not を. Very common at work: 目を通しておいてください; very polite お目通しください. In contrast to 読む, 目を通す emphasizes quickly checking the content, not reading thoroughly.

en.meaning: to take measures; to settle; to come to an agreement
examples[].german: Let's take action before the problem gets bigger.
All right, let's settle on 5,000 yen.
A good idea occurred to me, and I clapped my hands without thinking.
en.notes: 手 here means "means, move": 手を打つ mainly means "to take measures", often preventively: 早めに手を打つ, 何か手を打たないと. In negotiation it means "to settle, to come to an agreement", with で for the price: 五千円で手を打とう. Literally it is also "to clap one's hands", for example when an idea occurs to you. Neutral; more formal would be 対策を取る.

en.meaning: to open one's mouth; to begin to speak
examples[].german: He wouldn't open his mouth for a long time.
Every time he opens his mouth, he complains.
For a while nobody spoke, but then the company president began to speak.
en.notes: 口を開く (ひらく) means "to open one's mouth" in the sense of "to begin to speak, to express oneself" - often after a silence: やっと口を開いた. With ば: 口を開けば〜ばかり "every time he opens his mouth...". The purely physical opening, for instance at the dentist, is 口を開ける (あける). The opposite is 口を閉ざす "to fall silent". Slightly elevated, frequent in narratives.

en.meaning: to settle down; to apply oneself seriously to something
examples[].german: Let's settle down and study seriously.
I was transferred constantly, but I'd like to finally settle down in this town.
We need to take our time and discuss this problem thoroughly.
en.notes: Literally "to set the hips down firmly": one sits down and stays. Figuratively it means (1) "to apply oneself calmly and seriously to something", mostly adverbial 腰を据えて取り組む/考える/勉強する, and (2) "to settle down in a place": 〜に腰を据える. The opposite is a half-hearted, unsteady attitude; the intransitive phrase 腰が据わらない ("not to stay on task") fits here. Neutral to slightly elevated.

en.meaning: to stretch one's legs; to go a bit farther; to make a side trip
examples[].german: I made a side trip as far as Kyoto.
When I stretch my legs in a big bath, my tiredness goes away.
Since we're here anyway, shall we go a little farther and see the sea?
en.notes: Literally "to stretch out the legs", for example in a bathtub. Figuratively it means "to make a side trip, to go a bit farther", with まで for the destination: 京都まで足を伸ばす. In this travel meaning 足を延ばす (延ばす "to extend") is also written. Unlike 寄る "to drop by on the way", it is about extending the route beyond the actual destination. Neutral.

examples[].german: That is a selfish proposition.
Wanting a raise without doing anything is way too much to ask.
He only contacts me when he is in trouble; he really is self-serving.
en.notes: 虫がいい describes expectations or demands that brazenly consider only one's own advantage. 虫 stands here for one's inner mood, as in 虫が好かない or 虫の居所が悪い. Typical are 虫のいい話, 虫のいい考え and above all 虫がよすぎる "that is too brazen". Unlike わがまま or 自分勝手, which mean generally selfish behavior, 虫がいい specifically criticizes a one-sidedly convenient calculation.

en.meaning: to droop one's shoulders; to be disappointed
examples[].german: I failed the exam and was crestfallen.
The players who lost the match went home with drooping shoulders.
Don't be so downcast. You can just try hard again.
en.notes: Literally "to drop the shoulders": to be visibly disappointed or dejected. The expression mainly describes outward posture, often in narratives about others: 肩を落として帰る. The mere feeling is がっかりする; 気を落とす rather emphasizes the inner loss of courage and often appears in consolation. With ないで also as encouragement: そんなに肩を落とさないで.

en.meaning: to tilt one's head; to doubt; to be puzzled
examples[].german: I was skeptical about his explanation.
When you call our dog by name, it tilts its head.
Even the store manager is puzzled about why it suddenly stopped selling.
en.notes: 傾げる means "to tilt": to tilt the head as a gesture of doubt or wonder. The cause is marked with に: 説明に首を傾げる "to be puzzled by the explanation". Common in reports: 専門家も首を傾げている "even experts are baffled". Literal also for animals. Do not confuse it with 首を振る "to shake one's head". Often in kana: 首をかしげる.

en.meaning: one's heart leaps; to feel cheerful and excited
examples[].german: My heart leaps with joy when I make travel plans.
Because I'm finally meeting my friends again, my heart has been leaping since morning.
When the flowers bloom in spring, one's heart naturally lifts.
en.notes: 弾む means "to bounce, to hop (like a ball)": the heart bounces with anticipation or happiness - "to be in high spirits, to feel cheerful". Often with the cause + と or ので: 旅行のことを考えると心が弾む. Before nouns also 心弾む春. Related are 声が弾む "to sound cheerful" and 話が弾む "the conversation gets lively". Somewhat more elevated than the everyday わくわくする.

en.meaning: to touch the heart; to move someone deeply
examples[].german: Her speech touched everyone's heart.
I was deeply moved by the child's kind words.
If you want to see a film that really touches you, I recommend this one.
en.notes: Literally "to strike the heart": words, a speech or an act deeply move someone. The subject is the thing that moves; the person is marked with の: 人々の心を打つ. The person who is moved usually uses the passive: 〜に心を打たれる. Before nouns: 心を打つ話. 胸を打つ means the same; 感動する is more everyday. Rather elevated.

en.meaning: to lose heart; to be discouraged
examples[].german: Don't lose heart, there's always next time.
Because he can't find a job, my older brother is completely discouraged.
What happened with your father must have been hard. Please don't lose heart.
en.notes: Literally "to drop the spirit (気)": to lose heart after a failure or loss. Very common as consolation: 気を落とさないで(ください); in condolences also the very polite お気を落とさずに. For description, the ている-form is usually used: すっかり気を落としている. がっかりする is rather brief disappointment, 落ち込む colloquially "to be depressed", 肩を落とす the visible posture.

en.meaning: to not feel like it; to be reluctant
examples[].german: I don't feel like going out today.
Thank you for inviting me, but I'm not really up for it this time.
Even work you don't feel like doing has to be finished.
en.notes: Literally "the spirit (気) doesn't move forward": an inner reluctance toward something you should do or are invited to. Typical: 〜のは気が進まない, あまり／どうも気が進まない, before a noun 気が進まない仕事. Popular as a soft, polite refusal: ちょっと気が進まないんです. Compared with the direct 〜たくない, it sounds more reserved; やる気がない means a general lack of motivation.

en.meaning: to pull oneself together; to take heart again
examples[].german: It didn't work out, but let's pick ourselves up and try once more.
The match was canceled because of rain, but I pulled myself together and went to practice anyway.
After crying a little, she composed herself and continued speaking.
en.notes: Literally "to take the spirit anew" (取り直す "to take again"): to recover after a setback or disappointment. Almost always in the て-form, followed by the next action: 気を取り直して、もう一度. Unlike 立ち直る, which describes a longer recovery, this is a brief inner restart. Similar is 元気を出す "to cheer up". Neutral.

en.meaning: to be well known; to be a familiar face
examples[].german: He is a familiar face in this town.
Since she started appearing on TV, she has gradually become better known.
That actor is so well known that he reportedly goes out in a hat and mask.
en.notes: Literally "the face (顔) sells (売れる)": someone is known to the public or within a certain circle. Mostly in the ている-form: この町で顔が売れている; the development is shown by 顔が売れてきた "is becoming better and better known". Similar is 名が売れる. Do not confuse it with 顔が広い "to know many people, to be well connected". Neutral to colloquial.

en.meaning: to make arrangements; to pull strings behind the scenes
examples[].german: He had arranged everything beforehand behind the scenes.
Apparently my father pulled strings in the background and got me into that company.
He gently put his arm around her shoulders.
en.notes: Literally "to move the hand around": to make arrangements in the background, to use connections, to pull the strings. Common are 裏で手を回す or 〜に手を回す (whom one turns to) and 手を回しておく "to arrange in advance". Often with a slightly negative flavor of exerting influence. Literally it also means "to put an arm around someone": 肩に手を回す. Distinguish from 手を打つ "to take measures".

en.meaning: to take a lot of effort; to be demanding
examples[].german: Small children take a lot of work.
This dish is delicious, but it takes a lot of effort to make.
Our oldest child didn't need much care, so it was easy.
en.notes: 手 here stands for "work, care": 手がかかる means "to take a lot of effort, to need a lot of looking after, to be laborious" - with children, pets, the sick, or with tasks such as cooking. Before nouns usually 手のかかる子／料理. Negated it is praise: 手のかからない子 "an easy, independent child". Similar is 手間がかかる, which rather emphasizes the time and labor involved. かかる is mostly in kana.

examples[].german: Please don't believe completely groundless rumors.
The weekly magazine's article was a fabricated story.
Being accused of totally baseless things really made me angry.
en.notes: 根も葉もない literally means "to have neither roots nor leaves": a claim has no basis whatsoever. It almost always appears attributively before 噂, 嘘, 話, 中傷 or こと. It is inflected like an い-adjective (根も葉もなかった). The written equivalent in official denials is 事実無根.

en.meaning: to be beyond one's ability; to be unmanageable
examples[].german: This problem is beyond my ability.
That child does nothing but mischief, and the parents can no longer handle him.
The fire grew so big that it was no longer under control.
en.notes: 負う means "to carry, to take on": 手に負えない means "one cannot handle it with one's own hands" - too difficult, out of control, no longer tameable. The person who is overwhelmed is marked with の: 私の手に負えない, 親の手に負えない. Also used of people and things: 手に負えない子供, 火が手に負えなくなる. Polite: 手に負えません. Neutral, more expressive than a bare 無理.

en.meaning: to come face to face; to meet
examples[].german: I run into the same person on the train every day.
We just had an argument, so it's awkward to face him.
This is the first time these two teams have met in the final.
en.notes: Literally "to bring the faces together": to meet each other in person, to face one another. The other person is marked with と: 〜と顔を合わせる. Often used for regular or unavoidable meetings and for discomfort: 顔を合わせるのが気まずい. In sports and performances it means "to face each other, to appear together". Unlike the neutral 会う, it emphasizes direct confrontation; the noun 顔合わせ is a first get-to-know-you meeting.

en.meaning: to take a break; to catch one's breath
examples[].german: It's important to take a break once in a while, too.
Studying only for exams is tiring, so take a break every now and then.
I'm so busy that I don't even have time to catch my breath.
en.notes: Literally "to let the breath (息) out (抜く)": to release tension, to take a short breather. Much more common is the noun 息抜き "breather": 息抜きに散歩する. Typical frames: たまには息を抜く, 息を抜く時間もない. Do not confuse it with 手を抜く "to slack off, to not put in effort", which is negative. Neutral, used in everyday life and at work or study.

en.meaning: to make up one's mind; to resolve
examples[].german: I made up my mind and changed jobs.
Stop agonizing forever - why don't you make up your mind already?
The company president seems to have resolved to sell the company.
en.notes: In Japanese, 腹 "belly" is regarded as the seat of inner resolve; 腹を決める therefore means "to make a firm decision", usually for a hard or risky decision. The content is often marked with と: 会社を辞めると腹を決める. 腹をくくる and 覚悟を決める mean the same; 決心する is more neutral. Colloquial, sounds determined and somewhat gutsy.

examples[].german: I got goose bumps when I heard the scary story.
When I went out lightly dressed, I got goose bumps from the cold.
Her singing voice was so beautiful that I got goose bumps.
en.notes: Literally "the bird skin (鳥肌) stands up": the skin looks like that of a plucked chicken. Originally it describes goose bumps from cold, fear or disgust. Today it is also very often used positively for deep emotion, for example at music or sports, although some feel this is not standard usage. The verb 立つ is intransitive and conjugates normally (鳥肌が立った). Colloquially one also says 鳥肌もの ("something that gives you goose bumps") or simply 鳥肌！.

examples[].german: When I heard the news, I couldn't believe my ears.
When I heard I'd won the lottery, I could hardly believe my ears.
Words came out of the teacher's mouth that were hard to believe.
en.notes: Literally "to doubt the ears": to hear something so surprising that one can hardly believe it. Almost always in the past tense: 〜を聞いて耳を疑った. Before nouns: 耳を疑うような話／ニュース "an unbelievable story/piece of news". The counterpart for things seen is 目を疑う. Neutral, common in narratives and reports; often intensified with 思わず.

en.meaning: to close one's eyes; (euphemistically) to die
examples[].german: Please close your eyes and breathe deeply and slowly.
When I close my eyes, the scenery of my hometown comes to mind.
My grandmother, surrounded by her family, quietly closed her eyes for good.
en.notes: 閉じる "to close": 目を閉じる means "to close one's eyes", for example to relax, think or remember. More colloquial is 目をつぶる, which also means "to turn a blind eye, to overlook something" - 目を閉じる does not normally have this meaning. In elevated style, 静かに目を閉じる serves as a euphemism for "to die". Opposite: 目を開ける. Intransitive: 目が閉じる.

examples[].german: I shed tears watching the movie.
The players who won were all shedding tears of joy.
She said nothing and quietly shed tears.
en.notes: 涙を流す means "to shed tears" and is more descriptive than 泣く: it emphasizes the visible tears, often silent and also from joy or emotion, e.g. うれし涙を流す, 感動して涙を流す. Common in narratives and reports. Intransitively one says 涙が流れる or 涙が出る "tears come to my eyes". Neutral to slightly elevated.

en.meaning: to be overwhelmed with emotion; one's heart is full
examples[].german: I was overcome with emotion at the graduation ceremony.
Everyone's warm words filled my heart.
At my daughter's wedding I was so choked up that I couldn't eat anything.
en.notes: Literally "the chest (胸) becomes full": to be overwhelmed by feelings such as joy, gratitude, emotion or sadness, so that one can hardly speak or eat. The trigger is marked with に or で: 感謝の気持ちで胸がいっぱいになる. いっぱい is mostly written in kana. Do not confuse it with お腹がいっぱい "to be full (of food)". Neutral, often at celebrations and farewells.

en.meaning: to turn a blind eye; to overlook something
examples[].german: Please turn a blind eye just this once.
I decided to overlook the newcomer's small mistakes.
Close your eyes and take a slow, deep breath.
en.notes: 目をつぶる literally means "to close one's eyes" (the more neutral word is 目を閉じる). Figuratively, 〜に目をつぶる means "to turn a blind eye to something, to deliberately overlook something", typically for small mistakes or rule violations: ミスに目をつぶる. Similar is 大目に見る "to be lenient". つぶる is almost always written in hiragana (rarely 瞑る); it is a godan verb ending in -ru.

en.meaning: to succeed; to start to bear fruit (talent or effort)
examples[].german: After keeping at it for ten years, it has finally paid off.
As a comedian, he did not make his breakthrough for many years.
In spring, sprouts came up from the seeds I had sown in the garden.
en.notes: 芽が出る literally means "a sprout comes out", that is, "to sprout"; it is also used quite normally this way for plants. Figuratively it means that success finally comes after a long time, or that someone makes a breakthrough as an artist, athlete and so on. The negative is particularly common: なかなか芽が出ない "just not making a breakthrough". The transitive counterpart of 出る is 出す: 芽を出す.

en.meaning: to fall seven times, get up eight; never give up
examples[].german: Let's do our best in the spirit of "fall seven times, get up eight".
Life is full of ups and downs, so don't get discouraged by one failure.
My grandfather's life was truly one of falling seven times and getting up eight.
en.notes: 七転び八起き literally means "fall down seven times, get up eight times": one does not let setbacks get one down and keeps getting back up. It also denotes the ups and downs of life: 七転び八起きの人生. Typical are 七転び八起きの精神 and 人生は七転び八起きだ. The proverb is associated with the Daruma figure, which rights itself again and again. Neutral, encouraging.

en.meaning: perseverance pays off (lit. even on a stone, three years)
examples[].german: They say perseverance pays off, so let's hang in there a little longer.
To the new employee who wanted to quit right away, the department head said, "Patience pays off, you know."
Perseverance pays off: practicing the piano has finally started to be fun.
en.notes: 石の上にも三年 literally means "even on a (cold) stone, three years": if you just sit on it long enough, even a stone becomes warm. It means that patience and perseverance pay off in the end. It is often said to new employees who want to quit quickly; typical frames are 〜と言うから / 〜で. Neutral, somewhat preachy.

en.meaning: to prefer the practical to the beautiful (lit. dumplings over flowers)
examples[].german: I went to see the cherry blossoms, but ended up just eating, preferring dumplings to flowers.
My child prefers dumplings to flowers: even when traveling, he's more into the food than the scenery.
"I'm happier with tasty sweets than with a bouquet." "Dumplings over flowers, huh?"
en.notes: 花より団子 literally means "dumplings rather than blossoms": at cherry blossom viewing (花見) many people are more interested in eating and drinking than in the blossoms. The proverb describes someone who prefers practical or material benefit (above all food) to beauty. It is mostly said jokingly about oneself or friends: 花より団子で〜, まさに花より団子だ, 私は花より団子タイプ. It stands as a noun with だ or で and is not meant as an insult.

en.meaning: seeing is believing; a picture is worth a thousand words (lit. hearing a hundred times is not like seeing once)
examples[].german: Seeing is believing, so let's go and see it for real.
It's completely different from seeing it in photos. Seeing is believing, isn't it.
As the saying goes, seeing is believing: touring the factory, I understood the process well.
en.notes: 百聞は一見に如かず literally means "hearing a hundred times does not equal seeing once"; 如かず is the classical negation of 如く "to equal". One says it to encourage someone to see something for themselves, or after having understood something on the spot. Typical frames: 百聞は一見に如かずだ / 〜というように. Slightly elevated but universally known; 如かず is often written in hiragana as well.

en.meaning: more haste, less speed (lit. if you are in a hurry, take the detour)
examples[].german: More haste, less speed: let's study carefully from the basics.
They say more haste, less speed, so let's take the usual road rather than an unfamiliar shortcut.
More haste, less speed. If you write in a rush, you'll only make more mistakes.
en.notes: 急がば回れ literally means "if you are in a hurry, take the detour": 急がば is a classical conditional form of 急ぐ, and 回れ is the imperative of 回る. It means that the safe, thorough way gets you to the goal faster in the end than a risky shortcut. Typical frames: 急がば回れで… or 急がば回れと言うから…. Neutral and very common.

en.meaning: when in Rome, do as the Romans do (lit. when you enter a village, follow its rules)
examples[].german: If you are in Japan, then when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
When in Rome: I want to get used to the way things are done at the new company.
They say you should do as the locals do, so let's take our shoes off here.
en.notes: 郷に入っては郷に従え literally means "when you enter a village, follow the village": you should adapt to the customs of the place or group you come into. Watch the readings: 郷 is read ごう here (not きょう), and 入って is いって (classical, not はいって). It applies not only to countries but also to new companies, schools or families. Neutral, very well known.

en.meaning: he who chases two hares catches none
examples[].german: He who chases two hares catches none, so let's focus on one.
I tried to give my all to both work and studying for a qualification, but he who chases two hares catches none, and I ended up doing both halfway.
They say he who chases two hares catches none; why don't you narrow your club activities down to one?
en.notes: The proverb literally reads "he who chases two hares (兎) does not obtain even one"; 一兎をも得ず is a classical negation. It warns against pursuing several goals at once and ending up reaching none. It is quoted with と言う／と言うから or followed by だ／で; abbreviated, people also say 二兎を追う. The counterpart is 一石二鳥 (killing two birds with one stone).

en.meaning: it is easier than expected (lit.: giving birth is easier than worrying about it)
examples[].german: It's easier done than worried about, so let's try it first.
I was nervous about my first speech, but it was easier than I feared, and it went well.
I was anxious about living alone, but it turned out to be much easier than expected.
en.notes: Literally: "giving birth (産む) is easier (易し, classical form of 易しい) than worrying (案ずる) about it". The proverb says that something one is afraid of is usually easier in the doing than feared. It is used as encouragement beforehand (案ずるより産むが易しだから、やってみよう) or in retrospect (やってみたら案ずるより産むが易しだった). The related 習うより慣れよ, by contrast, stresses learning by practice.

en.meaning: two heads are better than one (lit.: three people together have the wisdom of Monju)
examples[].german: Two heads are better than one, so let's think together.
Don't agonize alone; talk to us. They say two heads are better than one, right?
Working together as three, we finally solved the difficult puzzle.
en.notes: Literally: "when three people gather (寄れば), the wisdom of Monju (文殊) arises"; 文殊 is the bodhisattva of wisdom (Manjushri). It means that even ordinary people can come up with good ideas together. It is used to invite joint thinking or to comment on a team result, often with って言うでしょう. The counterpart is 船頭多くして船山に上る (too many cooks spoil the broth).

en.meaning: to happen to hear; to come to one's ears
examples[].german: I have heard that rumor before.
That's a word you hear a lot lately, isn't it.
At the station I happened to overhear that the two are getting married.
en.notes: 耳にする literally means "to make something one's ear" and means "to (happen to) hear, to get wind of". Unlike 聞く, which can also mean listening actively or asking, 耳にする describes casually catching rumors, news or words: 噂を耳にする, よく耳にする言葉, 〜という話を耳にした. It is transitive with を; the intransitive variant is 耳に入る "to reach one's ears". The expression sounds somewhat more refined than 聞く; parallel to it there is 目にする "to catch sight of".

en.meaning: many a little makes a mickle (lit. even dust becomes a mountain when piled up)
examples[].german: Even 100 yen a day comes to more than 30,000 yen in a year: many a little makes a mickle.
Even if it is only five minutes of study at a time, little by little adds up, so let's keep going.
Even leaving the lights on adds up, and the electricity bill goes up.
en.notes: 塵も積もれば山となる literally means "even dust becomes a mountain when it piles up": small amounts or efforts add up to something big. It is used positively for saving money or studying, but also as a warning about small wastes. Typical frames: 塵も積もれば山となるで… or 〜と言うから. In daily life often only the first half is quoted, or ちりも is written in hiragana. Neutral.

en.meaning: even a master makes mistakes (lit. even monkeys fall from trees)
examples[].german: They say even monkeys fall from trees, so don't let your guard down.
Even professional chefs sometimes fail. Even monkeys fall from trees.
My brother, who is good at math, made a calculation error - that's exactly what "even monkeys fall from trees" means.
en.notes: 猿も木から落ちる literally means "even monkeys fall from trees": even someone who is excellent at something makes a mistake once. It is said when an expert has a mishap, as consolation or as a warning to be careful; typical are 猿も木から落ちるというから〜 and 猿も木から落ちるとはこのことだ. Similar proverbs are 弘法にも筆の誤り and 河童の川流れ. Use it carefully with superiors, since you are indirectly comparing them to a monkey.

en.meaning: like father, like son (lit. a frog's child is a frog)
examples[].german: Your father was a doctor too. Like father, like son.
Her mother was also good at singing, so like mother, like daughter.
Like father, like son: in the end I too became an ordinary office worker like my father.
en.notes: 蛙の子は蛙 literally means "a frog's child is a frog". Today it mostly means that children inherit their parents' talent or profession: 蛙の子は蛙だね. Originally it was meant more modestly: the children of ordinary parents remain ordinary; it is also used this way in self-deprecation. The counterpart is 鳶が鷹を生む "a hawk is born of a kite" (an exceptional child of ordinary parents). Neutral.

en.meaning: the frog in the well does not know the ocean (narrow-minded)
examples[].german: See more of the world. You're a frog in a well.
I was the best in my hometown, but at the national tournament I was made to realize that I had been a frog in a well.
Since I started working abroad, I truly understand what the saying about the frog in the well means.
en.notes: Literally: "the frog in the well does not know the great ocean"; 蛙 is read classically as かわず here, and 知らず is a classical negation. The proverb of Chinese origin criticizes someone who knows only his own small world and therefore overestimates himself. It is often shortened to 井の中の蛙, also self-critically (自分は井の中の蛙だった). In Japan there is a later positive continuation: されど空の深さを知る.

en.meaning: the grass is always greener on the other side
examples[].german: They say the grass is always greener on the other side, but my life isn't bad either.
Your friend's company looks better to you simply because the grass is always greener elsewhere.
Other families look happy, but things always look nicer at other people's places.
en.notes: 隣の芝生は青い literally means "the neighbor's lawn is green" (青い here stands for lush green). It means that what others have always seems better than what one has oneself. The variant 隣の芝生は青く見える is also common; typical frames are 〜というけど and 〜ってことだよ. The proverb is a borrowing from English and sounds modern and neutral.

en.meaning: pearls before swine (lit. gold coins for a cat)
examples[].german: Giving an expensive watch to a child is like giving a gold coin to a cat.
If you bought an expensive computer but only use it for email, it's wasted on you.
That specialist book was far too difficult for me; it was truly wasted on me.
en.notes: 猫に小判 literally means "(giving) a gold coin to a cat"; 小判 was an oval gold coin of the Edo period. It means that something valuable is completely wasted on someone who cannot appreciate it - like "pearls before swine". Typical is the pattern 〜に〜をあげても猫に小判だ. Said about others it can sound derogatory; said self-deprecatingly about oneself it is harmless. A proverb with the same meaning is 豚に真珠.

en.meaning: to preach to deaf ears (lit. a prayer in a horse's ear)
examples[].german: No matter how many times I warn him, it's like talking to a brick wall.
However often I tell my son to study, it goes in one ear and out the other, and he just plays video games.
I advised the department head to quit smoking for his health, but it fell on deaf ears.
en.notes: Literally "to recite a prayer (念仏, the Buddhist invocation of Amida) into a horse's ear": the horse does not understand the pious text, no matter how often it is repeated. It means that advice or admonitions have no effect at all on someone, that is, "preaching to deaf ears". Typical frames are 何度言っても馬の耳に念仏だ or 彼に注意しても馬の耳に念仏. The expression is colloquial and critical and is said about third parties; said directly to a superior it would be rude. Synonymous are the rarer variant 馬の耳に風 and the four-character expression 馬耳東風.

en.meaning: the nail that sticks out gets hammered down; those who stand out are cut down to size
examples[].german: In Japan, it is said that the nail that sticks out gets hammered down.
Afraid of standing out and being attacked, I couldn't voice my opinion in the meeting.
If you stand out too much as a newcomer, you'll be cut down to size.
en.notes: 出る杭は打たれる literally means "the stake that sticks out gets hammered in". It means that anyone who stands out, is too talented or pushes themselves forward too much will be attacked or cut down to size. It is often cited to explain the pressure to conform in groups; there is also the counter-saying 出過ぎた杭は打たれない "a stake that sticks out far enough is no longer hammered down". Neutral, often critical and reflective.

en.meaning: the early bird catches the worm (lit. rising early brings three mon of profit)
examples[].german: The early bird catches the worm, so let's get up early from tomorrow.
Because I got up early, I was able to see a beautiful sunrise. Getting up early really pays off.
My grandfather always used to say, "The early bird catches the worm."
en.notes: 早起きは三文の徳 literally means "rising early brings three mon of profit"; 三文 was a very small sum of money. Originally, then: getting up early brings a small advantage - today generally "the early bird catches the worm". It is said as an admonition or when getting up early has paid off: 早起きは三文の徳だね. It is also written 三文の得. It is mostly quoted unchanged, often with だから or って言うし.

en.meaning: it hurts to hear (because it is true)
examples[].german: The teacher's words hurt because they are true.
When I'm told to go to bed earlier, it stings because it's true.
It's hard to hear, but you are absolutely right.
en.notes: 耳が痛い literally means "the ears hurt" and figuratively means that criticism or a reprimand is uncomfortable because it hits the mark exactly. Typical are 耳が痛い話 and 〜と言われると耳が痛い; with it, one often admits that the reproach is justified. Literally it can also simply mean "to have an earache". Neutral, common in conversation and columns.

en.meaning: windfall; unexpected good luck (lit. a rice cake falls from the shelf)
examples[].german: Winning the lottery is a real windfall.
My senior colleague suddenly quit, so I became the leader quite unexpectedly.
The opposing team withdrew, so we got into the final as a pure windfall.
en.notes: Literally "a ぼたもち falls from the shelf (棚)", that is, a rice cake covered in sweet bean paste falls straight into one's open mouth. It means unexpected good luck for which one did nothing. In colloquial speech the short form 棚ぼた is very common, often used adjectivally: 棚ぼたの勝利, 棚ぼた式に. The expression is casual and slightly jocular; it does not fit hard-earned success, as it stresses precisely the element of chance. A rarer spelling is 棚から牡丹餅.

en.meaning: to be careful; to watch out
examples[].german: Please watch out for cars.
Please take good care of your health.
en.notes: 気をつける means to watch out or to be mindful. With に you name what the attention is directed at. 車に気をつけて is a warning about vehicles; 体に気をつけて can serve as a friendly wish for good health. The expression contains を and the ichidan verb つける, whose request form is 気をつけてください. 気を付ける is the same expression in a different spelling.

en.meaning: to cheer up; to take heart
examples[].german: Cheer up! Tomorrow will surely be a good day.
I told a friend who had failed the exam to cheer up.
en.notes: 元気を出す encourages someone to regain confidence after a disappointment. The request 元気を出して often corresponds to "Cheer up". 元気 stands before を as what one should muster again; 出す becomes 出して or 出しました. The expression thus describes a change, not just the state of being healthy.

en.meaning: to feel unwell; to feel sick; to be creepy
examples[].german: I ate too much and felt sick.
This dark room is creepy because of the strange noises.
en.notes: 気持ちが悪い can express physical discomfort or an unpleasant, creepy impression. After eating too much, it usually means feeling nauseous. For a sound or a sight, on the other hand, the expression can mean that one finds it repulsive or creepy. The i-adjective 悪い becomes 悪くなる with なる.

en.meaning: to disturb; to get in the way
examples[].german: Please don't disturb me while I'm studying.
I'm sorry for disturbing you at work.
Whenever I'm reading a book, our cat always comes to disturb me.
en.notes: 邪魔 originally consisted of 邪 "evil" and 魔 "demon" - in Buddhism, a demon that disturbs practice. 邪魔をする means "to disturb, to hinder someone"; the person or activity is marked with の: 勉強の邪魔をする, 人の邪魔をする. Often を is dropped (邪魔する), and お邪魔します is the set polite formula when entering someone else's home. Merely "being in the way" without intent is expressed with 邪魔になる or 邪魔だ.

en.meaning: to receive help; to be looked after; to be indebted to someone
examples[].german: Many people helped me in Japan.
Thank you for your continued support.
Thank you so much for everything over these three years.
en.notes: Literally: 世話 "care, looking after" and になる "to come to one" - you receive the care or help of others and are therefore in their debt. The benefactor is marked with に: 先生にお世話になる; almost always with the polite お. Set formulas are いつもお世話になっております as an opening for business emails and phone calls, and お世話になりました when parting. Actively, "to take care of someone" is 世話をする.

en.meaning: to overdo it; to push oneself too hard
examples[].german: Don't overdo it, and get plenty of rest.
Even though I had a fever, I forced myself to go to the office.
I didn't have much money, but I stretched myself and bought an expensive bag.
en.notes: Literally: 無 "without" and 理 "reason" - 無理 is the unreasonable, the impossible; 無理をする means "to overreach, to take on too much". 無理をしないでね or 無理しないで is a caring phrase toward people who are ill or stressed. With the て-form, 無理をして〜する describes forcing something despite poor conditions. Do not confuse it with 無理だ "that's impossible".

en.meaning: to be absorbed in something; to be fascinated by something
examples[].german: The children are absorbed in their game.
I was so absorbed in my book that I forgot to get off at the station.
He is crazy about his new girlfriend.
en.notes: Literally: 夢 "dream" and 中 "in the middle of" - as in a dream, forgetting everything else. 夢中になる means "to become absorbed in something, to be captivated or crazy about it"; the object is marked with に: ゲームに夢中になる, 彼女に夢中だ. With the て-form, 夢中になって〜する describes forgetting other things because of it. The state is expressed with 夢中になっている or 夢中だ; the register is neutral.

en.meaning: to read someone's mood from their face; to watch someone's reactions
examples[].german: She is always watching her boss's expression.
The child cautiously watched his parents' faces and said, "I want a video game."
Stop always reading other people's faces and say your own opinion.
en.notes: 顔色を窺う literally means "to observe the color of the face": you anxiously watch another person's expression to gauge their mood and not to upset them. Typical are 上司/親の顔色を窺う and 人の顔色ばかり窺う, which criticizes a dependent, conformist attitude. The kanji 窺う is rare; it is mostly written 顔色をうかがう. Not to be confused with 伺う "to visit, to ask (humble)". Related is 空気を読む "to read the room", which is more neutral.

en.meaning: to feel dizzy; to be extremely busy
examples[].german: At the end of the year I'm so busy my head spins.
I rode the teacup ride so many times that I got dizzy.
Moving and a new job coincided, so my days are a whirl.
en.notes: 目が回る literally means "the eyes spin". First, physically, it means "to feel dizzy", for example after a merry-go-round; medically more neutral is めまいがする. Second, and very commonly, it describes extreme busyness in an exaggerated way: 目が回るほど忙しい, 目が回る忙しさ, 目が回る毎日. In this meaning it is almost always used attributively or with ほど before 忙しい. It is intransitive and colloquial.

en.meaning: to have a loose tongue; to be unable to keep a secret
examples[].german: She has a loose tongue, so don't tell her any secrets.
When he drinks, the department head suddenly becomes talkative.
Because I couldn't keep my mouth shut, the surprise for my friend was spoiled.
en.notes: 口が軽い literally means "the mouth is light" and describes someone who blabs secrets and cannot keep anything to himself. The opposite is 口が堅い "discreet". With なる it describes a state: お酒を飲むと口が軽くなる "when drinking, one becomes talkative". Not to be confused with 口が悪い "to have a sharp, hurtful tongue". Neutral, clearly negative in evaluation.

en.meaning: to be proud (of someone/something); to have a prominent nose
examples[].german: I'm proud that my son passed the university entrance exam.
The students won the national championship, and their teacher is very proud too.
He has a prominent nose and big eyes.
en.notes: 鼻が高い literally means "the nose is high" and means "to be proud", especially of the achievements of family, students or one's own group: 息子が合格して鼻が高い. It is meant positively and is not the same as showing off: "to boast" is 鼻にかける, "to get conceited" is 天狗になる. Literally, 鼻が高い can also mean "to have a prominent, high nose". It behaves like an い-adjective (鼻が高かった, 鼻が高くて).

en.meaning: to be slow to act; to be reluctant to get moving
examples[].german: He is slow to act and hardly ever takes action.
I know I should clean, but on days off I just can't get myself going.
I persuaded my reluctant husband and finally took him to the hospital.
en.notes: 腰が重い literally means "the hips are heavy" and means "to find it hard to get going, to get started only reluctantly". It is not about back pain (that would be 腰が痛い) but about a lack of willingness to tackle something: 腰が重くてなかなか〜しない. The opposite is 腰が軽い "quick to act, helpful". Similar is なかなか腰が上がらない. The expression is neutral and behaves like an い-adjective.

en.meaning: to be at a loss; to rack one's brains
examples[].german: I'm at my wits' end over my debt problem.
Sales have dropped, and the company president is at a loss.
The exam questions were so difficult that I involuntarily held my head in my hands.
en.notes: 頭を抱える literally means "to hold one's head (in one's hands)" - the gesture of despair. It means "to be at a loss, to rack one's brains over a problem". The cause takes に or で: 借金の問題で頭を抱える, 難問に頭を抱える; often in the progressive form 頭を抱えている. Similar are 頭が痛い "something is a headache" and 悩む "to worry, to brood"; 頭を抱える stresses the hopelessness more.

en.meaning: to feel heartache; to feel pained
examples[].german: It pains me to see the news from the disaster area.
When I think about how I couldn't keep my promise, it still hurts to this day.
I suddenly had chest pain after running, so I went to the hospital.
en.notes: 胸が痛む literally means "the chest aches". Physically it can mean real chest pain, but mostly it means "it hurts in the heart": pity, guilt or sorrow. Typical patterns are 〜を見て/聞いて胸が痛む and 〜と思うと胸が痛む. The transitive counterpart is 胸を痛める "to worry (about someone), to be distressed". The expression is neutral to slightly elevated and also suits news and letters.

en.meaning: to feel heavy-hearted; to dread the thought
examples[].german: I feel heavy-hearted when I think about tomorrow's meeting.
I have to give him bad news, so I'm dreading it.
The Monday after a long holiday weekend somehow feels heavy.
en.notes: 気が重い literally means "the mind is heavy" and describes a depressed feeling about something unpleasant that lies ahead. Typical are 〜と思うと/考えると気が重い or 〜ので気が重い; the occasion is often a meeting, bad news or the start of the week. Similar is 気が進まない "not to feel like it", which expresses more reluctance, while 憂鬱 means a more general gloom. It behaves like an い-adjective.

en.meaning: a weight is lifted off one's shoulders; to be relieved of a burden
examples[].german: When the project was over, a weight was lifted off my shoulders.
Now that all the children have become independent, I'm finally free of that responsibility.
The important presentation went off without a hitch, and I feel truly relieved.
en.notes: 肩の荷が下りる literally means "the load on the shoulders is unloaded" and corresponds to "a weight is lifted off one's shoulders". One says it when a responsibility or worry ends: 〜が終わって肩の荷が下りた, やっと肩の荷が下りた, often together with ほっとする. The transitive counterpart is 肩の荷を下ろす "to free oneself of a burden". Compare 荷が重い "to be too heavy a burden". The expression is neutral and mostly used in the past tense.

en.meaning: to go somewhere in person; to visit a place
examples[].german: Thank you very much for making the trip all the way here.
The reporter went to the scene many times to listen to people.
Please also stop by the local art museum once.
en.notes: 足を運ぶ literally means "to carry one's feet" and means "to (specially) go somewhere, to visit a place". Unlike 行く or 来る, it stresses the effort and trouble of the visit, which is why it is typical in thank-you phrases: わざわざ足を運んでいただき, ありがとうございます. The destination takes に or へ: 現場に何度も足を運ぶ, 美術館に足を運ぶ. The expression is polite to elevated and common in business language, advertising and reportage.

en.meaning: to lose patience; to be fed up with someone
examples[].german: I'm fed up with his lies.
I've completely lost patience with my subordinate who is late no matter how many times I warn him.
The public, too, is fed up with politicians who are all talk.
en.notes: 愛想が尽きる literally means "the amiability is used up": you have finally had enough of someone and want nothing more to do with them. The person or their behavior takes に: 彼の嘘に愛想が尽きた, もう愛想が尽きた. The transitive counterpart is 愛想を尽かす (〜に愛想を尽かす, passive 愛想を尽かされる "someone has had enough of you"). 愛想 is usually read あいそ here, less often あいそう. The expression is clearly stronger than 嫌になる.

en.meaning: to be good at getting things done; to be efficient
examples[].german: She knows how to get things done, so she works fast.
He is shrewd: he always skillfully hands off the troublesome work to others.
I'm not efficient, so I always end up working overtime.
en.notes: 要領がいい literally means "to grasp the main point (要領) well" and describes someone who gets things done skillfully and efficiently. Depending on context, criticism can also resonate: "clever, cunning" - someone who skillfully avoids unpleasant work or sells themselves well. The opposite is 要領が悪い "clumsy, inefficient"; not to be confused with 要領を得ない "unclear, not to the point". It behaves like いい: 要領がよくて, 要領がよかった.

en.meaning: to devote oneself intensely to work; to work without a break
examples[].german: I studied so intensely that my health suffered.
Don't overdo it; take a little rest.
I worked without a break and finished the model in one day.
en.notes: 根を詰める: 根 is read こん here and means "perseverance, energy" (as in 根気), not ね "root". The expression means "to bury oneself in a task without a break, to wear oneself out". Typical are 根を詰めて働く/勉強する/作業する and the caring admonition あまり根を詰めないでね "don't overdo it". It describes intense, often too intense concentration on a task; neutral to slightly elevated.

examples[].german: I don't want people meddling in my problems.
My mother even interferes in the choice of my marriage partner.
The department head interferes even in minor details, which bothers everyone.
en.notes: 口を出す literally means "to stick out one's mouth" and means "to (uninvited) butt in, to interfere". The matter takes に: 人のことに口を出す, 〜にまで口を出す "to interfere even in ...". The expression is clearly negative; as a noun there is 口出し (口出しする, 口出しするな). Related is 口を挟む, which rather means "to cut in on someone" in an ongoing conversation, whereas 口を出す refers to other people's decisions and affairs.

en.meaning: to be caught in the middle; to be in a dilemma
examples[].german: I'm caught in the middle between my boss and my subordinates.
My husband was caught between his mother and me and couldn't say anything.
A store manager is often caught between customers and headquarters.
en.notes: 板挟み originally refers to being squeezed between two boards (板 "board", 挟む "to pinch"). 板挟みになる therefore means "to be caught between two fronts", when you have to satisfy two sides with conflicting expectations. Typical is A と B の板挟みになる, for example between boss and team or spouse and parents; also 板挟みに苦しむ. Similar is ジレンマ, but that rather means a choice between two options, not between people.

en.meaning: to be itching to show one's skills
examples[].german: I'm itching to show what I can do, having entered the cooking contest.
I've been given a big job for the first time in a long while, and I can't wait to get started.
Hearing that they would be fighting a strong opponent, the players seem to be itching to go.
en.notes: 腕が鳴る literally means "the arm rings/cracks" and describes the eager anticipation of finally being allowed to show one's skill: one is burning to get started. Usually one speaks this way about oneself before a challenge: 腕が鳴るよ. Unlike 腕を磨く (to improve one's skill), this is about eagerness to act. Neutral to colloquial.

en.meaning: to be speechless with admiration; to be deeply impressed
examples[].german: I was speechless with admiration at his piano skills.
Even the expert marveled at the child's sharp question.
Everyone marvels at how good her Japanese is.
en.notes: 舌を巻く literally means "to roll up one's tongue" and means to be so amazed at someone's skill or achievement that words fail. The cause is marked with に: 〜の腕前に舌を巻く. Unlike 目を丸くする (general astonishment), it always expresses admiration for an ability. Slightly elevated, common in reports.

en.meaning: to have a trained eye; to be a connoisseur
examples[].german: Having been exposed to art for many years, I have a trained eye.
Many customers at this shop have a discerning eye, so we pay attention to quality.
If you only look at luxury goods, your eye becomes refined and you can no longer be satisfied with cheap things.
en.notes: 目が肥える literally means "the eyes grow fat" and means to gain a trained, demanding eye through much experience with good things, for example for art, fashion or antiques. Mostly used as a state, 目が肥えている, or attributively, 目の肥えた客. For food one says 舌が肥える instead, for music 耳が肥える. Neutral.

en.meaning: necessity knows no law; one must set priorities
examples[].german: It's expensive, but needs must, so I have no choice but to buy it.
Out of necessity, I sold my beloved guitar.
We were short of staff, so I thought I had no choice and went to work on my day off, too.
en.notes: 背に腹は代えられない literally means "you cannot trade your belly for your back": to protect the more important thing (the belly with the organs), you must sacrifice the less important. One says it when doing something unpleasant out of necessity because there is no other choice. In written language 背に腹は代えられず also occurs; the spelling 換えられない is also found. Neutral.

en.meaning: to forget the danger once it is over; to be ungrateful
examples[].german: Have you already forgotten last year's mistake? Once it's over, you forget how bad it was.
After the earthquake everyone bought disaster-preparedness supplies, but once the danger had passed, nobody cares about it now.
As soon as he recovered from his illness, he started staying up late again. This is exactly what it means to forget the pain once it's over.
en.notes: 喉元過ぎれば熱さを忘れる literally means "once it has passed the throat, you forget the heat". It means that one quickly forgets hardship, danger or suffering as soon as it is over, and likewise the help one received back then. It is used critically about people who learn nothing from experience; typical frames are 〜で, 〜とはこのことだ. Neutral.

en.meaning: relaxed and familiar; at ease (with someone)
examples[].german: She is a friend I can be completely at ease with.
A drink with close friends you can be yourself with is the best.
I'm so close to my older brother that I can talk to him about anything.
en.notes: 気が置けない means "so familiar that one does not have to hold back or put on a front" (from 気を置く "to be on one's guard, to keep one's distance"). It is praise for close friends: 気が置けない友人, 気が置けない仲. Note: many Japanese today wrongly understand it as "he cannot be trusted", but the correct meaning is positive. Neutral, rather elevated.

en.meaning: to speak frankly and honestly; to open one's heart
examples[].german: Let's have a frank talk for once.
I need to have a frank talk with the president once.
After a frank discussion, the two of them made up.
en.notes: 腹を割って話す literally means "to cut open the belly and talk"; in Japanese the belly is regarded as the seat of one's true intentions. It means an open, honest conversation without ulterior motives, often to clear up misunderstandings. Also common as 腹を割って話し合う "to talk things out openly". Neutral, used rather in personal or professional conflict situations.

en.meaning: to be discreet; to keep a secret
examples[].german: She can keep a secret, so it's fine to tell her secrets.
This job involves many secrets, so we are looking for a discreet person.
I consulted him believing he could keep a secret, but he told everyone.
en.notes: 口が堅い literally means "the mouth is firm" and describes someone who is discreet and keeps secrets to themselves - clear praise. The opposite is 口が軽い. Attributively one says 口の堅い人. The spelling with 堅い (firm, reliable) is usual; 固い also occurs. Neutral.

en.meaning: to cut corners; to slack off
examples[].german: You must not cut corners at work.
Even when playing tennis with us kids, my father never goes easy.
On busy days, I think it's fine to cut corners a bit when cooking.
en.notes: 手を抜く literally means "to pull out the hand" and means "to work carelessly, take shortcuts, spare oneself". The area is marked with の or で: 掃除の手を抜く, 仕事で手を抜く. In competition it means "not playing at full strength": 子供相手でも手を抜かない. The related noun is 手抜き (手抜き工事 "shoddy construction work", 手抜き料理 "a quick meal without effort"). Depending on context it is critical or, with 少し手を抜く, quite relaxed.

en.meaning: to order people around; to boss someone around arrogantly
examples[].german: That company president is famous for ordering his employees around.
Just because you're a senior, it's not good to boss juniors around.
My younger brother orders our parents around and does nothing himself.
en.notes: 顎で使う literally means "to use with the chin" - one gives orders merely with a nod of the head, without lifting a finger oneself. It means to order others around arrogantly: Xを顎で使う.
