The expression is clearly derogatory and is used for superiors, older colleagues or family members. 顎 is often written in hiragana (あごで使う). Colloquial.

en.meaning: to be completely helpless; to be unable to do anything
examples[].german: That problem was so difficult that I was completely helpless.
The opposing team was so strong that we couldn't do anything.
Without funds, our hands are tied.
en.notes: 手も足も出ない literally means "neither hands nor feet come out" and means to be completely powerless against an opponent or a problem. Typical with tasks that are too hard, superior opponents or lack of money. Do not confuse it with 手が出ない "cannot afford something, cannot get at it". Almost always in the past: 手も足も出なかった. Neutral.

en.meaning: to be in a tight spot; to be pressed for time
examples[].german: The deadline is near, and now I'm under pressure.
It was only a week before the exam that I finally got a fire under me.
If I'm not under pressure, I can't get serious.
en.notes: 尻に火がつく literally means "the backside catches fire" and describes a matter becoming so urgent that one finally has to act - typically shortly before a deadline. Often やっと尻に火がついた "now it's finally burning". More polite is お尻に火がつく. Also spelled 尻に火が付く. Colloquial, slightly crude.

en.meaning: to devote oneself; to work oneself to the bone
examples[].german: He works himself to the bone for his family.
My mother devoted herself to raising the three of us.
Even if employees work themselves to the bone, their salaries hardly rise.
en.notes: 身を粉にする literally means "to turn one's own body into powder"; 粉 is read こ here, not こな. It means to sacrifice oneself to the point of exhaustion for someone or something. Almost always in the form 身を粉にして働く, often for parents who slave away for their family. Neutral to slightly elevated.

en.meaning: to get along well; to click with someone
examples[].german: I think I'll get along with the new coworker.
The two have opposite personalities, yet strangely they get along.
He's not a bad person, but somehow I don't click with him.
en.notes: 馬が合う literally means "the horse fits" - originally, rider and horse were in harmony. Today it means that two people get along well right away, often for no explainable reason. The partner takes と: Xとは馬が合う. Very similar is 気が合う; the negative 馬が合わない is also common. Neutral, colloquial.

en.meaning: to have free time; to have nothing to do at the moment
examples[].german: Could you help me when you have a moment?
Is anyone free right now?
I'll be free in the afternoon, so I will look at the materials then.
en.notes: 手が空く literally means "the hands become free" and means to have no work at the moment and so have time for something else. Typical are 手が空いたら… "when you have a moment" and 手が空いている人. The opposite is 手が離せない "cannot get away right now"; similar is 暇がある, which, however, means more generally "to have free time". 空く is read あく here. Neutral, very common in the workplace.

en.meaning: to speak frankly; to not mince words
examples[].german: She is known for her blunt way of speaking.
To put it bluntly, this project is not interesting.
My grandmother speaks her mind, and she plainly complains even about my clothes.
en.notes: 歯に衣着せぬ literally means "to put no clothes on one's teeth" (衣 is read きぬ here, not ころも); 着せぬ is a classical negation. It means to give one's opinion openly without sugarcoating. It mostly stands attributively: 歯に衣着せぬ発言／物言い／批評／人; adverbially it is 歯に衣着せずに言う. Depending on context it sounds appreciative (honest) or slightly critical (tactless).

en.meaning: to take someone as an example (lit.: to brew and drink the dirt under someone's nails)
examples[].german: He is so hardworking that one should take him as an example.
Take an example from your big brother for once!
I'd love to hold him up to my staff as a shining example.
en.notes: Literally: "to boil the dirt under (someone's) fingernails and drink it", in the hope of picking up some of that person's virtues. The expression is half joking, half reproachful and almost always appears in the frame 〜の爪の垢を煎じて飲ませたい／飲みなさい: one holds up a role model to someone. For the neutral statement "to take an example from" people say 見習う or 手本にする.

en.meaning: to have something up one's sleeve; to have ulterior motives
examples[].german: There seem to be ulterior motives behind that smile.
He was silent, looking like he had something up his sleeve.
He's suddenly being nice; he must have something in mind.
en.notes: 腹に一物 literally means "one thing in the belly"; in Japanese the belly is considered the seat of hidden intentions (cf. 腹黒い, 腹を探る). It means secretly having ulterior motives or a plan. It is mostly followed by ある: 腹に一物ある, 腹に一物ありそうだ, 腹に一物ある人; 胸に一物 means the same. 一物 is read いちもつ here.

en.meaning: to get one's hands on; to obtain
examples[].german: I finally got my hands on the limited-edition item.
After a lot of hard work, I got my dream home.
Where did you get that information?
en.notes: 手に入れる literally means "to put into the hand" and means "to get, obtain, procure". It often stresses that something was hard to get: 限定品, チケット, 情報, 夢のマイホームを手に入れる. Unlike 買う, the way does not matter (purchase, gift, prize), and it sounds more everyday than 得る. Transitive with を; the intransitive counterpart is 手に入る "to fall into one's hands, to be available" (このチケットはなかなか手に入らない).

en.meaning: to take to heart; to engrave on one's mind
examples[].german: I will take my senior's advice to heart and do my best.
We will take this failure to heart and work to prevent a recurrence.
I still keep my father's words, "Don't cause trouble for others," engraved on my heart.
en.notes: 肝に銘じる literally means "to engrave into the liver"; the liver (肝) was regarded as the seat of the spirit. One firmly imprints a lesson, a piece of advice or a mistake in order to act accordingly in the future: 〜を肝に銘じる. It is very typical in formal apologies and resolutions (肝に銘じます); there is also the older form 肝に銘ずる. Less solemn are 心に刻む or simply 覚えておく.

en.meaning: to be singled out; to be chosen for something
examples[].german: He was singled out as the leader of the new project.
The company chose the young Mr. Tanaka to head the restructuring.
I still don't know why I was the one chosen.
en.notes: 白羽の矢が立つ goes back to a legend: a god demanding a maiden sacrifice shot a white-feathered arrow onto the roof of the chosen house. Originally negative, it now mostly means, positively, "to be singled out from many": 〜に白羽の矢が立つ, transitive 〜に白羽の矢を立てる. The form 白羽の矢が当たる is a common mistake. Typical in personnel and sports reports.

en.meaning: as alike as two peas in a pod; strikingly similar
examples[].german: Those twins are identical and cannot be told apart.
She is the spitting image of her mother when she was young.
In town I saw someone who looked just like a celebrity.
en.notes: 瓜二つ literally means "a melon in two halves": the two cut surfaces look exactly the same. It almost always refers to the outward resemblance of people, especially faces: AとBは瓜二つだ, AはBに瓜二つだ, 瓜二つの顔／人. It is stronger than the more general そっくり, which also fits things, voices or behavior.

en.meaning: utterly dejected, like a wilted plant
examples[].german: He failed the exam and is down in the dumps.
The players who were scolded by the coach hung their heads dejectedly.
The child who was full of energy a moment ago is crestfallen now that his toy was taken away.
en.notes: 青菜に塩 literally means "salt on green vegetables": salted leafy greens wilt immediately. It describes someone who is suddenly completely dejected and hangs his head. Typical frames are 青菜に塩のようにしょげる／しょんぼりする or 青菜に塩でうなだれる; also predicatively 青菜に塩だ. The expression is vivid and colloquial.

en.meaning: just what was needed; a lucky coincidence
examples[].german: I was thinking about moving, and a friend just happened to introduce me to a good place; it was perfect timing.
He offered to help, so I took him up on it as a godsend.
For the cash-strapped company, the partnership offer was a godsend.
en.notes: 渡りに船 literally means "a boat just when you want to cross": exactly at the right moment, the help or opportunity one needed presents itself. Typical are 渡りに船だ, 渡りに船の話／申し出 and 渡りに船とばかりに "seizing the opportunity right away". Unlike 棚からぼた餅 (unearned luck without any effort of one's own), 渡りに船 stresses that something comes along perfectly timed for an existing need.

en.meaning: to get along well; to be on the same wavelength
examples[].german: I clicked with him from the first time we met.
I don't really get along with my new roommate.
Traveling with friends you click with is really fun.
en.notes: Literally "the spirit (気) fits together (合う)": two people have a similar nature and understand each other right away. The person is marked with と: 彼とは気が合う; before a noun, が usually becomes の: 気の合う友達. Unlike 仲がいい, which describes an existing good relationship, 気が合う emphasizes the natural match of characters. Negated: 気が合わない "cannot get along". Neutral, common in everyday life and at work.

en.meaning: to have a good eye; to have good taste
examples[].german: Choosing this painting shows you have a good eye.
This is the most popular wine this year. You have a good eye, sir.
Tanaka has a good eye, so I asked him to help me pick a present.
en.notes: Literally "the eye (目) is high (高い)": someone has fine judgment and recognizes quality. It is almost always praise for others, especially as a polite phrase from sales staff: お客様、お目が高いですね. One does not say it about oneself. Do not confuse it with 鼻が高い "to be proud"; similar is 目が肥えている "to have a refined taste through a lot of experience".

en.meaning: to get along well; to be on good terms
examples[].german: Those two get along very well.
In my new class, I became friends with everyone.
en.notes: 仲がいい describes a good personal relationship. The people involved can stand together as the topic: あの二人は仲がいい. With と you name the person you get along well with. Before なる, いい becomes よく: 仲がよくなる means that the relationship improves or that people grow closer.

en.meaning: to call out to someone; to speak to someone
examples[].german: I spoke to a person who was in trouble.
The next time everyone goes out for a drink, let me know too!
During the match, we all called out to the players to cheer them on.
en.notes: Literally "to hang a voice (声) on someone"; the person is marked with に: 〜に声をかける. It means to speak to or greet someone, but also "to let someone know, to invite" (今度声をかけてね) and "to cheer on". Passive 声をかけられる "to be spoken to", for example by strangers. Unlike 話しかける "to start a conversation", 声をかける is broader. かける is usually written in kana, less often 掛ける.

examples[].german: The new president's policy platform was announced.
The prime minister delivered a policy speech in the Diet.
Administrative rights over Okinawa were returned to Japan in 1972.
en.notes: 施政 is the exercise of governmental power, i.e. the practical running of a state, and occurs almost only in fixed combinations in official and press language. Important are 施政方針 ("government program") and 施政方針演説, the prime minister's policy address at the start of the ordinary Diet session, as well as 施政権 ("administrative authority"), for example regarding the return of Okinawa. Do not confuse it with the identically read 市政 ("city administration") and 姿勢 ("attitude, posture").

examples[].german: Governance of the colony continued for many years.
At that time, this island was under British rule.
With scandals continuing, strengthening corporate governance is being called for.
en.notes: 統治 is the governing and ruling of a country or territory by an authority; as a する-verb it is transitive: 国を統治する. Typical: 植民地統治, 〜の統治下にある ("to be under the rule of ..."), 統治者, 統治機構. In business, 企業統治 stands for "corporate governance". 支配 is broader and sounds more like oppression, whereas 統治 suggests the orderly exercise of rule.

examples[].german: The separation of powers is a basic principle of the modern state.
The separation of powers means dividing the three powers of legislature, executive and judiciary.
Government pressure on the courts was criticized as undermining the separation of powers.
en.notes: 三権分立 is composed of 三権 ("the three powers": 立法, 行政, 司法) and 分立 ("to exist separately side by side") and denotes the separation of powers as described by Montesquieu. In Japan the powers rest with the 国会, 内閣 and 裁判所. The word appears in textbooks, constitutional debates and commentaries, often in phrases like 三権分立を守る or 三権分立を揺るがす.

examples[].german: Pacifism has been regarded as the fundamental national principle of postwar Japan.
That country has made perpetual neutrality its national principle.
The three non-nuclear principles are said to be a national principle of Japan.
en.notes: 国是 is the fundamental, long-term guiding principle of a state's policy. Typical are 〜を国是とする "to make ... one's national principle" and 〜は〜の国是だ. Unlike 国策 "concrete national policy", 国是 means an immovable principle. Analogous terms are 社是 "company motto" and 党是 "party principle". Very formal, typical of editorials and speeches.

examples[].german: Artificial dialysis is a treatment that replaces kidney function.
My father goes to the hospital for dialysis three times a week.
Dialysis takes about four hours each time, so balancing it with work is hard.
en.notes: 透析 is "dialysis"; in medical practice mostly 人工透析 or 血液透析 ("hemodialysis") and 腹膜透析 ("peritoneal dialysis"). Patients say 透析を受ける or 透析に通う; a dialysis patient is a 透析患者. In chemistry, 透析 also denotes the separation process through a membrane (transitive: 溶液を透析する).

examples[].german: Chronic alcohol consumption can cause liver cirrhosis.
If hepatitis is left untreated, it can progress to cirrhosis.
My uncle was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis and quit drinking completely.
en.notes: 肝硬変 is "liver cirrhosis": 肝 ("liver") and 硬変 ("hardening"). Common causes are chronic hepatitis (B型肝炎, C型肝炎) and alcohol; a consequent risk is 肝がん. Typical are 肝硬変になる, 肝硬変と診断される and 肝炎から肝硬変に進む. A precursor is often 脂肪肝 ("fatty liver").

en.meaning: collagen disease; autoimmune connective tissue disease
examples[].german: Collagen diseases are a group of disorders in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue.
Joint pain and a low-grade fever continued, and tests showed it was a collagen disease.
Collagen diseases are known to be common in young women.
en.notes: 膠原病 is a collective term for systemic autoimmune diseases of the connective tissue ("collagen diseases"), such as 全身性エリテマトーデス, 強皮症 or, in a broader sense, 関節リウマチ. 膠原 means "collagen" (膠 = "glue"). Caution: it sounds exactly like 抗原 ("antigen") but has nothing to do with it. It is treated in the department of 膠原病内科 or リウマチ科.

examples[].german: In autoimmune diseases, the immune system mistakenly attacks normal cells.
This disease is thought to be caused by an autoimmune mechanism.
My sister has an autoimmune thyroid disease and keeps taking medication.
en.notes: 自己免疫 is "autoimmunity", i.e. an immune reaction against the body itself. The word appears almost always in compounds: 自己免疫疾患 ("autoimmune disease"), 自己免疫性肝炎, 自己免疫性甲状腺疾患, plus 自己抗体 ("autoantibody"). 自己 is the formal "self", 免疫 "immunity".

examples[].german: Overuse of antibiotics promotes the emergence of resistant bacteria.
Colds are caused by viruses, so antibiotics don't work.
Please finish the antibiotics to the end, even if your symptoms subside.
en.notes: 抗生物質 is the "antibiotic": 抗生物質を飲む, 抗生物質を出す／処方する, 抗生物質が効く. In clinics the short form 抗生剤 is often heard; in technical language today mostly 抗菌薬. They do not work against viruses, including ordinary colds; wrong use promotes 耐性菌.

examples[].german: The emergence of drug-resistant bacteria is a worldwide public health threat.
If antibiotics are used carelessly, resistant bacteria arise more easily.
An infection with resistant bacteria spread in the hospital, and the ward was temporarily closed.
en.notes: 耐性菌 are "resistant bacteria", bacteria against which antibiotics no longer work: 耐性 ("resistance, tolerance") + 菌 ("bacterium"). Technically it is also 薬剤耐性菌 or 多剤耐性菌 ("multidrug-resistant bacteria"), a well-known example being MRSA. Typical verbs are 耐性菌が生まれる／出現する／広がる; particularly feared is 院内感染 ("hospital-acquired infection") by 耐性菌.

examples[].german: Chemotherapy is one of the main pillars of cancer treatment.
After the surgery, I received chemotherapy to prevent a recurrence.
My hair fell out because of the side effects of chemotherapy.
en.notes: 化学療法 is "chemotherapy"; in conversation with patients one often says 抗がん剤治療, among doctors also shortened to 化療. Typical are 化学療法を受ける／行う, 化学療法の副作用 (hair loss, nausea). Together with 手術 and 放射線療法 it forms the three classic pillars of cancer treatment.

examples[].german: Radiation therapy is a treatment that targets and destroys tumor cells.
Radiation therapy is delivered in small daily doses over several weeks.
Because the tumor is in a place where surgery is difficult, we chose radiation therapy.
en.notes: 放射線療法 is "radiation therapy"; in daily life and on clinic signs, 放射線治療 means the same and is more common. Irradiation is described with 放射線を当てる or, technically, 照射する. It is often chosen when surgery is difficult, and combined with 化学療法.

examples[].german: Immunotherapy is a new treatment that uses the body's immune power to fight cancer.
I started sublingual immunotherapy to treat my cedar pollen allergy.
The effectiveness of some immunotherapies has not yet been sufficiently proven.
en.notes: 免疫療法 denotes treatments that use or modulate the immune system. In cancer medicine one speaks of がん免疫療法 (e.g. with 免疫チェックポイント阻害薬), for allergies of アレルゲン免疫療法 or 舌下免疫療法 ("sublingual immunotherapy"). Since private clinics also offer unproven 免疫療法, the word often appears in the media with critical remarks.

en.meaning: national sovereignty; sovereign power of the state
examples[].german: The highest organ of state power is the Diet.
Article 9 of the Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right of the nation.
In the Meiji era, there were people who advocated expanding national power.
en.notes: 国権 is the power of the state, i.e. the sovereign rights of a state. It is known above all from the Constitution: 国会は国権の最高機関である (Art. 41) and 国権の発動たる戦争 "war as a sovereign right of the nation" (Art. 9). Historically, in the Meiji era it stands opposed to 民権 "people's rights" (国権論 vs. 民権論). A very formal, legal-political word; in everyday speech one rather says 国の権力 or 主権.

examples[].german: Palliative care reduces the patient's suffering and improves quality of life.
Palliative care is not only for terminal patients.
My mother spent her last few months peacefully in a palliative care ward.
en.notes: 緩和ケア is "palliative care": 緩和 ("relief") + ケア. It relieves pain and emotional burden and today often begins already at diagnosis, not only at the end of life. Typical are 緩和ケアを受ける, 緩和ケア病棟 ("palliative care ward") and ホスピス. 緩和 alone is also known from 規制緩和 ("deregulation").

examples[].german: The safety of new drugs is confirmed through clinical trials.
We are recruiting patients to participate in a clinical trial of a new drug.
This vaccine has entered the final stage of clinical trials.
en.notes: 臨床試験 is a "clinical trial" on humans: 臨床試験を行う, 臨床試験に参加する, 臨床試験の段階. 臨床 means "at the bedside, clinical". Trials for drug approval are specifically called 治験; this word is seen more often in everyday life, e.g. in ads for 治験ボランティア.

examples[].german: An epidemiological survey revealed the pattern of spread of the infectious disease.
According to epidemiological research, smokers have a higher risk of lung cancer.
I studied public health at university and specialize in epidemiology.
en.notes: 疫学 is "epidemiology"; 疫 means "epidemic" as in 疫病 and 免疫. Typical are 疫学調査 (e.g. the contact tracing by public health centers), 疫学的, 疫学者 and 疫学の研究. Today epidemiology studies not only infections but also associations such as smoking and cancer.

examples[].german: The morbidity rate among the elderly is higher than among young people.
My father contracted diabetes in his fifties.
Staff who have contracted an infectious disease cannot come to work until they recover.
en.notes: 罹患 is the medical-statistical technical term for "to fall ill with something"; as a する-verb the disease takes に: がんに罹患する. In everyday speech one says 病気にかかる instead. It is common in compounds such as 罹患率 ("morbidity rate, incidence") or 罹患者 ("affected persons"). Since 罹 is not a Jōyō kanji, authorities often write り患.

examples[].german: The prevalence of diabetes is trending upward worldwide.
In this region, the prevalence of hypertension is higher than the national average.
The survey found that the prevalence of hay fever had roughly doubled compared with ten years ago.
en.notes: 有病率 is an epidemiological technical term: the share of the population suffering from a disease at a given point in time. To be distinguished from 罹患率, which measures new cases in a period. Typical are 〜の有病率, 有病率が高い／低い and 有病率が増加する. The word is encountered almost only in statistics, reports and news.

examples[].german: The case fatality rate of this infectious disease is reported to be about two percent.
Ebola hemorrhagic fever is known for its extremely high case fatality rate.
If treatment is started early, the fatality rate can be reduced significantly.
en.notes: 致死率 denotes the share of those who fall ill with a disease and die of it (case fatality). Do not confuse it with 死亡率, which gives mortality relative to the whole population. Common are 致死率が高い／低い, 致死率を下げる and statements such as 致死率〇パーセント. Related is 致死量 ("lethal dose").

examples[].german: The incubation period of this disease is usually two to four weeks.
Even during the incubation period, it is possible to pass it on to other people.
If no symptoms appear even after the incubation period has passed, the person is considered not to be infected.
en.notes: 潜伏期間 is the time between infection and the appearance of symptoms; the shorter form 潜伏期 is also used. 潜伏 on its own means "to lie hidden" and is also used for culprits who have gone into hiding. Typical expressions: 潜伏期間は〇日, 潜伏期間中, 潜伏期間を過ぎる. Common in health information and the news.

examples[].german: Identifying the pathogen is essential for developing an effective treatment.
Viruses, bacteria and anything else that causes disease are collectively called pathogens.
In operating rooms, strict controls are in place so that no pathogens are brought in.
en.notes: 病原体 is the umbrella term for anything that causes disease: viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites. 病原菌, by contrast, refers only to bacteria or germs. Common combinations: 病原体を特定する, 病原体に感染する, 病原体が侵入する. The word belongs to technical language; in everyday speech people tend to say ウイルス or 菌.

examples[].german: Influenza spreads mainly through droplet infection.
To prevent droplet infection, please wear a mask when you have a cough.
Partitions were installed on the tables to reduce droplet infection during conversation.
en.notes: 飛沫感染 is infection via droplets released when coughing, sneezing or speaking; 飛沫 on its own means "spray, droplets". Its sister terms are 接触感染 ("contact infection") and 空気感染 ("airborne transmission"). Typical: 飛沫感染で広がる, 飛沫感染を防ぐ. Since the Covid period the word has also become very familiar in everyday announcements.

examples[].german: Hand washing is the most basic way to prevent contact infection.
Caution is also needed against contact infection via doorknobs and train straps.
This bacterium is spread mainly by contact infection, so please avoid sharing towels.
en.notes: 接触感染 is transmission through direct touch or via objects such as doorknobs and towels. It usually appears alongside 飛沫感染 and 空気感染 when routes of transmission are explained. Typical frames: 接触感染でうつる, 接触感染を防ぐ／予防する. Register: technical language, but also common in hygiene advice.

examples[].german: Martial law was declared after the coup.
The government imposed martial law on the capital.
Martial law was finally lifted after three months.
en.notes: 戒厳令 is the decree by which the military takes over state authority in an area, i.e. the imposition of martial law. Typical verbs: 戒厳令を敷く (also 布く) "to impose", 戒厳令が発令される, 戒厳令を解除する "to lift", 戒厳令下で "under martial law". Not to be confused with 緊急事態宣言, a civil state of emergency without military rule (as during the coronavirus pandemic). A word from news and history.

examples[].german: Surgical instruments are thoroughly sterilized before use.
This gauze is already sterilized, so you can take it out of the bag and use it as it is.
In the laboratory, used culture medium is sterilized at high temperature and pressure before being discarded.
en.notes: 滅菌 means to kill all microorganisms completely, which makes it stricter than 殺菌 ("killing germs"), 消毒 ("disinfecting") or the advertising word 除菌 ("reducing germs"). As a する-verb it is transitive: 器具を滅菌する, often in the passive 滅菌される. Very common is 滅菌済み ("sterile-packed").

examples[].german: Congenital heart disease is a heart abnormality that is present from birth.
My son has a congenital heart disease and had surgery right after he was born.
This disease is not congenital; its cause is lifestyle.
en.notes: 先天性 is a noun that stands attributively with の or directly before a disease name: 先天性の病気, 先天性心疾患. It is mainly medical; for general talents people say 先天的な才能 or 生まれつき. The opposite is 後天性 ("acquired").

examples[].german: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome is a disease that destroys the immune system.
His hearing loss is not congenital but acquired, caused by an accident.
Many acquired diseases can be prevented by reviewing one's lifestyle.
en.notes: 後天性 means "acquired only after birth" and is the opposite of 先天性. It appears with の or as the first element of disease names: 後天性の難聴, 後天性免疫不全症候群 (AIDS). Outside medicine, the な-adjective 後天的 (後天的な能力) is used more often.

examples[].german: Hereditary diseases are caused by genetic abnormalities passed from parents to children.
This disease is said to be hereditary.
The doctor explained that my mother's illness is not hereditary.
en.notes: 遺伝性 denotes the property of being "hereditary". It mostly stands before nouns, directly or with の: 遺伝性疾患 ("hereditary disease"), 遺伝性の病気; also 遺伝性がある/ない. The form 遺伝性な is rare. Distinguish it from 遺伝的 ("genetic, by inheritance", e.g. 遺伝的な要因) and 先天性 ("congenital"), which does not necessarily mean inherited. Medical terminology, also used in health articles.

examples[].german: The basal metabolic rate tends to decline with age.
If you exercise and build muscle, your metabolism goes up and you gain weight less easily.
Babies have an active metabolism, so they sweat a lot.
en.notes: 代謝 is metabolism; in everyday speech you hear especially 代謝がいい／悪い, 代謝を上げる and 基礎代謝 ("basal metabolic rate"). Even more common is 新陳代謝, which is also used figuratively for the renewal of an organization. In this second sense of "renewal", 代謝 can occur as an intransitive する-verb, but this is rare.

examples[].german: Thyroid hormones play an important role in regulating metabolism.
During puberty, the hormone balance changes greatly.
Let's grill and eat offal at the place near the station tonight.
en.notes: ホルモン is the hormone; typical are ホルモンバランス, ホルモンが分泌される and 女性ホルモン／成長ホルモン. Caution: in a food context ホルモン means grilled offal (ホルモン焼き), which is a popular dish in Japan. The word is always written in katakana.

examples[].german: The endocrine system regulates bodily functions through hormones.
Thyroid diseases can be treated at an endocrinology department.
Some chemical substances may disrupt the workings of the endocrine system.
en.notes: 内分泌 is internal secretion, that is, the release of hormones directly into the blood; the opposite is 外分泌 (e.g. sweat, saliva). It mostly appears in compounds: 内分泌系 ("hormone system"), 内分泌内科 ("endocrinology"), 内分泌かく乱物質 ("hormonally active pollutants"). In technical language the reading ないぶんぴ is also heard.

examples[].german: Stress can cause the balance of the autonomic nervous system to break down.
I keep staying up late, so my autonomic nervous system seems to be out of balance.
My older sister was diagnosed with autonomic dysfunction and has been off work for a while.
en.notes: 自律神経 is the vegetative (autonomic) nervous system, which consists of the 交感神経 and the 副交感神経. In everyday speech 自律神経が乱れる ("to get out of balance") is very common, for example with stress or lack of sleep, as is 自律神経を整える. The condition 自律神経失調症 ("autonomic dysfunction") is a common diagnosis in Japan.

examples[].german: When the sympathetic nervous system is excited, the heart rate increases.
When I get nervous, my sympathetic nerves kick in and my hands sweat.
Looking at your phone before bed stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and makes it hard to fall asleep.
en.notes: 交感神経 is the sympathetic nervous system, the part of the 自律神経 that works during tension, stress and activity. Typical expressions: 交感神経が働く, 交感神経が優位になる, 交感神経が刺激される. Its counterpart is 副交感神経. The word often appears in health guides and TV programs.

examples[].german: When the parasympathetic nervous system becomes dominant, you enter a relaxed state.
Soaking slowly in a lukewarm bath makes it easier for the parasympathetic nervous system to work.
Deep breathing is said to have the effect of boosting the parasympathetic nervous system.
en.notes: 副交感神経 is the parasympathetic nervous system, the "rest nerve" of the 自律神経, active during relaxation, sleep and digestion. Typical are 副交感神経が優位になる, 副交感神経が働く and 副交感神経を高める. It is almost always mentioned in contrast to 交感神経, for example in relaxation tips.

en.meaning: political upheaval; change of power; political crisis
examples[].german: A sudden political upheaval threw the political situation into confusion.
A military-led change of power occurred in that country.
The prime minister resigned amid the political crisis, and a new government was launched.
en.notes: 政変 is a sudden change in power: from the fall of a cabinet, through a power struggle at court, to a coup. Typical: 政変が起きる/起こる, 政変で失脚する, 宮廷政変 "palace revolt". To be distinguished from this are 政局 "political situation, power games" and クーデター "violent coup d'etat", which is a form of 政変; 革命 means a fundamental overthrow of the system.

examples[].german: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter involved in regulating mood.
Neurotransmitters such as dopamine are related to motivation and pleasure.
This medicine improves depressive symptoms by adjusting the amount of neurotransmitters in the brain.
en.notes: 神経伝達物質 is the technical term for messenger substances such as ドーパミン, セロトニン or アドレナリン that transmit signals between nerve cells. Typical verbs: 神経伝達物質が放出される, 〜を分泌する, 〜の量を調整する. This long compound belongs in technical texts and popular-science articles; in conversation people often simply say 脳内物質.

examples[].german: Drugs exert their effect by binding to specific receptors.
Many receptors that sense taste are lined up on the surface of the tongue.
Viruses use receptors on the cell surface as a foothold to invade.
en.notes: 受容体 is the receptor to which a substance such as a hormone, drug or virus binds; レセプター is also used with the same meaning. Typical expressions: 受容体に結合する, 〜の受容体, 受容体を介して. It also refers to sensory receptors, for example for taste or light. Purely technical language.

examples[].german: Anti-inflammatory drugs have the effect of reducing pain and swelling.
Ginger is said to have an anti-inflammatory effect.
To reduce the swelling, the doctor prescribed an anti-inflammatory ointment.
en.notes: 抗炎症 is made up of the prefix 抗 ("anti-, against") and 炎症 ("inflammation") and almost never stands alone but as a first element: 抗炎症作用 ("anti-inflammatory effect"), 抗炎症薬／抗炎症剤 ("anti-inflammatory agent"). The same pattern forms 抗菌, 抗ウイルス or 抗酸化. Typical of package inserts, health articles and technical texts.

examples[].german: Painkillers relieve suffering by blocking pain signals.
After having a tooth pulled at the dentist, I was given two days' worth of painkillers.
This poultice contains an ingredient with a pain-relieving effect.
en.notes: 鎮痛 means "pain relief" and appears almost always in compounds: 鎮痛剤／鎮痛薬 ("painkiller"), 鎮痛作用, 鎮痛効果, 解熱鎮痛剤. In conversation people usually say 痛み止め instead of 鎮痛剤. As a する-verb, 鎮痛する hardly occurs; people rather say 痛みを抑える／和らげる.

examples[].german: We gave a fever reducer to bring down the high fever.
After I took a fever reducer, my temperature went down in about an hour.
Please keep your child away from nursery until two days after the fever has gone down.
en.notes: 解熱 means "fever reduction" and mostly appears in 解熱剤 ("fever-reducing medicine") or 解熱鎮痛剤. As an intransitive する-verb, 解熱する means "the fever goes down", typical in doctors' instructions and school rules (解熱後二日). In everyday speech people say 熱が下がる, and 熱冷まし for the medicine. Watch the reading: げねつ, not かいねつ.

examples[].german: Diuretics make the body excrete excess water.
Coffee has a diuretic effect, so if you drink too much you need the toilet more often.
The doctor prescribed a diuretic to get rid of the swelling in my legs.
en.notes: 利尿 is the excretion of urine or its promotion and occurs practically only in compounds: 利尿作用 ("diuretic effect"), 利尿剤／利尿薬 ("diuretic"). In everyday life you mostly hear コーヒーには利尿作用がある. Do not confuse it with 排尿 ("urination"), which denotes the act itself.

examples[].german: Diabetic patients need to manage their blood sugar level strictly.
To prevent my blood sugar level from rising sharply after meals, I eat vegetables first.
At my health checkup I was told that my blood sugar level is somewhat high.
en.notes: 血糖値 is the blood sugar value; typical are 血糖値が上がる／下がる, 血糖値が高い, 血糖値を測る and 血糖値の急上昇 after eating. The word is not only medical but constantly appears in health checkups, advertising and diet guides. 血糖 alone ("blood sugar") is rarer than 血糖値.

examples[].german: High cholesterol is a risk factor for arteriosclerosis.
At my health checkup I was told that my cholesterol level is high.
I am careful about my diet in order to reduce bad cholesterol.
en.notes: コレステロール is "cholesterol"; in everyday speech it is usually about blood values: コレステロール値が高い, コレステロールを下げる. Colloquially a distinction is made between 善玉コレステロール (HDL, "good") and 悪玉コレステロール (LDL, "bad"). 高コレステロール (血症) is an elevated cholesterol level. The word is ubiquitous in health topics and is always written in katakana.

examples[].german: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord.
Alcohol has the effect of suppressing the activity of the central nervous system.
If the central nervous system is damaged, recovery takes a long time.
en.notes: 中枢神経 refers to the brain and spinal cord; more precisely the system is called 中枢神経系. 中枢 on its own means "center, control point" and is also used figuratively (政治の中枢). Typical expressions: 中枢神経に作用する, 中枢神経を抑制する／刺激する. The opposite is 末梢神経.

examples[].german: Diabetes can cause peripheral neuropathy.
Numbness in the hands and feet can be caused by an abnormality of the peripheral nerves.
The peripheral nerves spread from the brain and spinal cord throughout the body like a net.
en.notes: 末梢神経 are the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, which branch out to the hands and feet; the opposite is 中枢神経. Common is 末梢神経障害 ("neuropathy"), often linked with しびれ ("numbness, tingling"). 末梢 alone means "tip, periphery"; 末梢的 means "peripheral, of minor importance" in the figurative sense. Since 梢 is not a Jōyō kanji, 末しょう is occasionally written.

examples[].german: The dictator carried out a purge of the opposition.
Many people were executed in Stalin's Great Purge.
The new leader purged his former close aides one after another.
en.notes: 粛清 is the (often bloody) purge in which a regime or party eliminates opponents and unwelcome members: 〜を粛清する, 〜が粛清される, 大粛清 "the Great Purge" under Stalin. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 粛正 "strict crackdown, enforcing discipline", as in 綱紀粛正 "restoring official discipline". A word from history and political reporting.

examples[].german: In the treatment of stroke, prompt action after onset is the key.
My grandfather collapsed from a stroke and was taken away by ambulance.
As an after-effect of the stroke, I can't move my right hand well.
en.notes: 脳卒中 is the umbrella term for strokes and includes 脳梗塞 ("cerebral infarction"), 脳出血 ("cerebral hemorrhage") and くも膜下出血. Typical expressions: 脳卒中で倒れる ("to suffer a stroke"), 脳卒中を起こす, 脳卒中の後遺症 ("after-effects"). The word is medical, but also common in everyday life and in the news.

examples[].german: A memory test is effective for the early detection of dementia.
Since my mother developed dementia, the family has been taking turns caring for her.
I worry whether it is just forgetfulness or the beginning of dementia.
en.notes: 認知症 has been the official term for dementia since 2004 and replaced 痴呆, which was felt to be derogatory. Typical are 認知症になる, 認知症が進む ("to progress"), 認知症の母 and 認知症の介護. In everyday speech it is often deliberately distinguished from harmless forgetfulness (物忘れ).

examples[].german: Epilepsy is a disease in which seizures occur due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
He has chronic epilepsy, so he takes his medicine every day without fail.
A man had an epileptic seizure on the train, and passengers called a station attendant.
en.notes: てんかん ("epilepsy") is almost always written in hiragana, because the kanji 癲癇 are very difficult and not Jōyō. Typical expressions: てんかんの発作, てんかん発作を起こす, てんかんの持病がある. Beware of homophones such as 転換 ("change over") or 展観; context decides.

examples[].german: Bacterial pneumonia can be treated with antibiotics.
I let my cold drag on, developed pneumonia, and was hospitalized for a week.
Elderly people need to be careful about aspiration pneumonia, which occurs when food enters the windpipe.
en.notes: 肺炎 is pneumonia; typical are 肺炎になる, 肺炎を起こす and 風邪をこじらせて肺炎になる ("a neglected cold turns into pneumonia"). In older people, 誤嚥性肺炎 ("aspiration pneumonia") is a frequent topic. The word is an everyday one, not a purely technical term.

examples[].german: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease spread by airborne transmission of the tubercle bacillus.
In the past, tuberculosis was feared as an incurable disease.
I was worried about a persistent cough and got tested, and it turned out to be tuberculosis.
en.notes: 結核 is tuberculosis; the pathogen is called 結核菌. Typical are 結核にかかる, 結核で亡くなる and 結核の検査. It was once regarded as a national disease that cost many writers their lives; today it is rare, but has not disappeared. The second sense "concretion" is purely technical and rare.

examples[].german: Sepsis is a serious, life-threatening condition in which an infection has spread throughout the body.
Bacteria entered through the wound, and he developed sepsis and was taken to the intensive care unit.
If treatment for sepsis is not started early, it can even cost a person's life.
en.notes: 敗血症 is sepsis, colloquially "blood poisoning": an infection spreads through the blood to the whole body. Typical are 敗血症を起こす, 敗血症になる, 敗血症で亡くなる and 敗血症性ショック. The word is medical, but appears in news reports about causes of death.

examples[].german: Iron-deficiency anemia is caused by a lack of iron.
I fainted from anemia in the middle of the morning assembly.
The reason I tire easily lately might be that I am a bit anemic.
en.notes: 貧血 is medically anemia ("lack of blood"), e.g. 鉄欠乏性貧血. Colloquially, however, 貧血 (貧血を起こす, 貧血で倒れる) also stands for sudden dizziness and fainting, even when medically what is meant is rather 立ちくらみ or circulation problems. Common is 貧血気味 ("slightly anemic").

examples[].german: Leukemia is caused by abnormal proliferation of white blood cells in the bone marrow.
She was diagnosed with leukemia in her teens, but after treatment she is now working in good health.
Calls are being made to register as donors with the bone marrow bank in order to save leukemia patients.
en.notes: 白血病 is leukemia, literally "white-blood disease"; a distinction is made between 急性 ("acute") and 慢性 ("chronic") forms. Typical are 白血病と診断される, 白血病を発症する and 白血病の治療. The word often comes up in connection with 骨髄移植 and donor registration (骨髄バンク).

examples[].german: Stem cell research is contributing greatly to the development of regenerative medicine.
iPS cells are a kind of stem cell that can become various kinds of cells.
Hematopoietic stem cells produce blood cells inside the bone marrow.
en.notes: 幹細胞 is the stem cell; 幹 means "trunk (of a tree)", i.e. the cell from which other cells "branch off". Well-known types are iPS細胞, ES細胞 and 造血幹細胞 ("blood-forming stem cells"). Typical frames: 幹細胞研究, 幹細胞を培養する／移植する. Technical language, but frequent in science news.

examples[].german: The puppet regime merely followed the will of the great power.
Manchukuo was a puppet state of Japan.
The new president is said to be nothing but a puppet of the former chairman.
en.notes: 傀儡 originally means "puppet", but is today used almost only figuratively: a person or government controlled by others. Typical are 傀儡政権 "puppet government", 傀儡国家 "puppet state" and 〜の傀儡にすぎない "is merely a puppet of ...". For the actual theater puppet one says あやつり人形 or マリオネット today. Derogatory and rather written.

examples[].german: Regenerative medicine is an innovative field that repairs damaged tissues and organs.
If regenerative medicine becomes practical, fewer people may have to wait for organ transplants.
At this hospital, clinical research on regenerative medicine using iPS cells is being carried out.
en.notes: 再生医療 is regenerative medicine, which restores damaged tissue or organs using cells. 再生 means "restoration, regeneration" (also "playback" for videos), 医療 "medical care". In Japan the word is closely tied to iPS cell research; typical are 再生医療の実用化 and 再生医療の研究.

examples[].german: Gene therapy aims at a fundamental cure of hereditary diseases.
Thanks to gene therapy, the boy became able to walk on his own legs.
Some voices point out ethical problems with gene therapy.
en.notes: 遺伝子治療 is gene therapy, i.e. treatment by introducing or altering genes (遺伝子). Typical are 遺伝子治療を受ける, 遺伝子治療薬 and 遺伝子治療の臨床試験. Do not confuse it with 遺伝性 ("hereditary"), which describes the disease. In debates, ethical questions are often pointed out.

examples[].german: Internal medicine is a medical specialty centered on drug therapy.
Since my fever and cough continued, I went to a nearby internal medicine clinic.
I asked at the reception whether I should go to internal medicine or surgery.
en.notes: 内科 is internal medicine, or the internal medicine department or practice. In Japan, with a cold, fever or stomach problems one typically goes to a 内科, rather than to a "family doctor"; one says 内科を受診する or 内科にかかる. The counterpart is 外科; the doctor is called 内科医.

examples[].german: When a surgical intervention is necessary, a quick decision is required.
My older brother works as a surgeon at a university hospital.
I had cut my finger deeply, so I had it stitched up in surgery.
en.notes: 外科 is surgery as a field and as a department; one goes there with injuries or when an operation is needed. Derivatives: 外科医 ("surgeon"), 外科手術, 外科的 ("surgical"). Note the reading: げか, not がいか. The counterpart is 内科; specialties are, for example, 整形外科 or 脳外科.

examples[].german: Orthopedics specializes in treating fractures and joint diseases.
I hurt my wrist in a fall, so I had an X-ray taken at the orthopedic clinic.
My lower back pain is severe, so I go to the orthopedic clinic once a week.
en.notes: 整形外科 is orthopedics: bone fractures, joints, back and knee pain. A trap for learners: cosmetic surgery is called 美容整形, and the short 整形 alone colloquially usually means cosmetic surgery; plastic and reconstructive surgery is 形成外科. Typical: 整形外科に通う, 整形外科でレントゲンを撮る.

examples[].german: Glaucoma is a disease that should be checked regularly at an ophthalmologist.
My eyes were itchy and bloodshot, so I went to the eye doctor.
Before getting contact lenses, you need to have an examination at an eye clinic.
en.notes: 眼科 is ophthalmology or the eye doctor's practice; the doctor is called 眼科医, colloquially also 目医者. People say 眼科に行く, 眼科で診てもらう or 眼科を受診する. 眼 is read がん here, as in 眼球 or 近眼.

examples[].german: Obstetricians protect the safety of mother and fetus during childbirth.
In rural areas there is a shortage of obstetricians, and the number of hospitals where one can give birth is decreasing.
My wife's due date is near, so I checked out the obstetrics ward beforehand.
en.notes: 産科 is obstetrics or the maternity department; it is mostly combined with gynecology as 産婦人科, and this name is more common in everyday speech. The doctor is called 産科医; the shortage of 産科医 in rural areas is a well-known social issue. Typical: 産科の病棟, 産科を受診する.

examples[].german: Pediatrics is the medical department that specializes in children's development and diseases.
My child ran a high fever in the middle of the night, so I took him to the pediatrician first thing in the morning.
The waiting room of the pediatrics clinic has picture books and toys.
en.notes: 小児科 is pediatrics or the pediatrician's practice; 小児 ("small child, child") is a formal word for 子ども. People say 小児科に連れて行く, 小児科にかかる; the doctor is called 小児科医. In Japan it mostly treats children up to about the end of junior high school.

examples[].german: Dermatology treats atopic dermatitis and acne.
The spot where an insect bit me started to swell, so I got medicine at the dermatologist.
The dermatologist recommended that I apply sunscreen every day.
en.notes: 皮膚科 is dermatology or the skin doctor's practice; you go there with rash, acne, itching or insect bites. Typical: 皮膚科に行く, 皮膚科で薬をもらう, 皮膚科の先生. For purely cosmetic treatments there is a separate 美容皮膚科.

examples[].german: Urology specializes in diseases of the kidneys, bladder and so on.
There was blood in my urine, so I went to see a urologist.
My prostate value was high at the health checkup, and I was advised to be retested at urology.
en.notes: 泌尿器科 is urology: kidneys, urinary tract, bladder and prostate. 泌尿器 means "urinary organs"; 泌 is read ひ here, whereas in 分泌 (ぶんぴつ) it is read ぴつ. Typical: 泌尿器科を受診する, 泌尿器科で検査を受ける. The subject is regarded as somewhat embarrassing, so the visit is often put off for a long time.

examples[].german: A plot to bring down a political rival was exposed.
We fell completely into the enemy's trap.
There is a theory that the incident was a plot by the intelligence agency.
en.notes: 謀略 is a secretly devised plan to harm an opponent, especially in politics, war and intelligence work. Typical: 謀略をめぐらす "to scheme", 謀略にかかる/はまる "to fall victim to a plot", 謀略戦, 謀略説 "conspiracy theory (about an event)". Similar are 陰謀 "conspiracy" (more focused on secrecy) and 策略 "ruse, trick", which sounds more neutral.

examples[].german: Otolaryngology treats hearing loss and sinusitis.
My child complained of ear pain, so I took him to the ENT clinic.
During hay fever season, the ENT clinic is always crowded.
en.notes: 耳鼻咽喉科 is otolaryngology (ear, nose and throat medicine); 耳 "ear", 鼻 "nose", 咽喉 "pharynx and throat". In everyday speech people almost always say the short 耳鼻科; the full form appears on signs and in official texts. Typical: 耳鼻咽喉科を受診する, 耳鼻咽喉科に連れて行く. It is especially crowded there during the hay fever season.

examples[].german: Rehabilitation after a stroke is essential for functional recovery.
After my knee surgery, I continued rehabilitation for three months.
Even after leaving the hospital, I go to rehabilitation twice a week.
en.notes: リハビリテーション is rehabilitation after illness or injury; in everyday speech people almost always say the short リハビリ (リハビリをする／受ける, リハビリに通う). The long form appears in technical texts and in names of clinics and departments. Figuratively, リハビリ is also used for athletes after an injury or a long break.

examples[].german: Physical therapy is a treatment that promotes recovery of motor function.
Under the guidance of a physical therapist, I do walking training every day.
My shoulder pain continues, so I am going to receive physical therapy.
en.notes: 理学療法 is physiotherapy: exercises, massage, heat or electrical treatment to restore mobility. The specialist is called 理学療法士 (PT). Distinguish it from 作業療法 ("occupational therapy"), which trains everyday activities. In everyday speech people usually just say リハビリ.

examples[].german: Occupational therapy supports independence in activities of daily living.
In occupational therapy, you practice everyday movements such as cooking and changing clothes.
My mother works at a psychiatric hospital as an occupational therapist.
en.notes: 作業療法 is occupational therapy; 作業 means "activity" here, that is, cooking, dressing, handicrafts or writing as practice for everyday life. The specialist is called 作業療法士 (OT). Unlike 理学療法, which trains basic movements such as walking, 作業療法 aims at independence in daily life and is also used in psychiatry.

examples[].german: Plasma contains various proteins and electrolytes.
About 55% of blood is made up of plasma.
Today I gave a plasma donation at the blood donation room.
en.notes: 血漿 is "blood plasma", the liquid part of the blood without the blood cells (血球). Do not confuse it with 血清 ("serum"), which is plasma without clotting factors. Typical combinations: 血漿成分献血 ("plasma donation"), 血漿製剤 ("plasma preparation"), 血漿タンパク. The character 漿 is rare; texts sometimes write 血しょう. Technical word of medicine and biology.

examples[].german: Platelets play an important role in promoting blood clotting when bleeding occurs.
Because of the effects of anticancer drugs, my platelets decreased and I started bruising easily.
Today I donated platelets at the blood donation room.
en.notes: 血小板 are the platelets (thrombocytes), which initiate blood clotting after injuries. Typical are 血小板が減る／少ない, 血小板の数 and 血小板減少症. When donating blood, one can specifically donate platelets (血小板の成分献血). Literally: "small plates in the blood".

examples[].german: Red blood cells carry oxygen to the tissues throughout the body.
In my blood test I was told that my red blood cell count is low.
Under a microscope, red blood cells have the shape of a disc that is dented in the middle.
en.notes: 赤血球 is the medical term for "red blood cells"; the building blocks are 赤 "red", 血 "blood" and 球 "sphere". Typical combinations are 赤血球数 "red blood cell count", 赤血球が減る/少ない (e.g. in anemia, 貧血) and 赤血球が酸素を運ぶ. Its counterparts are 白血球 "white blood cells" and 血小板 "platelets". The word is neutral and appears equally in biology class, in doctor's letters and in health articles.

examples[].german: White blood cells attack pathogens that have invaded the body.
Your white blood cell count is high, so there may be inflammation somewhere.
My white blood cells decreased due to the side effects of anticancer drugs.
en.notes: 白血球 are the "white blood cells" (白 "white", 血 "blood", 球 "sphere"), the body's defense cells. In everyday speech you hear the word mainly with blood values: 白血球が多い/増えている points to inflammation or infection, 白血球が少ない/減少する occurs for example after chemotherapy. Do not confuse it with 白血病 "leukemia", which differs by only one character. The counterpart is 赤血球.

examples[].german: Lymph nodes are an important component of the immune system.
I caught a cold and the lymph nodes in my neck are swollen.
For swollen legs, massage that improves the flow of lymph is effective.
en.notes: リンパ is "lymph" or the lymphatic system; the word comes from Dutch/Latin and is today written almost only in katakana (the old kanji spelling 淋巴 is rare). It mostly appears in compounds: リンパ節 "lymph node", リンパ液 "lymph fluid", リンパ球 "lymphocyte", リンパ腫 "lymphoma". Colloquially people say リンパが腫れる and mean swollen lymph nodes; in cosmetics and wellness, リンパマッサージ "lymphatic drainage" is a common word.

examples[].german: The colloid osmotic pressure of plasma regulates the movement of water between tissues.
When albumin decreases, the colloid osmotic pressure drops and swelling occurs more easily.
A question about colloid osmotic pressure came up in the nursing school exam.
en.notes: 膠質浸透圧 is a physiological technical term: 膠質 "colloid" (literally "glue-like substance") + 浸透圧 "osmotic pressure". It refers to the pressure generated mainly by plasma proteins such as albumin (アルブミン) in the blood vessels, which keeps water inside the vessel. Synonymous but somewhat more modern is コロイド浸透圧. Typical: 膠質浸透圧が低下する → 浮腫 "edema" develops. The word occurs practically only in textbooks and clinical texts.

examples[].german: They won over the opposition and got the bill passed.
The government tried to win over local residents by promising subsidies.
The boss is trying to win over his staff with sweets.
en.notes: 懐柔 means to bring someone over to one's side by concessions, favors or friendly accommodation, often with calculating intent: 〜を懐柔する, 懐柔策 "conciliatory policy", 懐柔を図る, 懐柔工作. In contrast to 説得 "convincing with arguments", it is about benefits rather than reasons; なだめる means only "to calm, soothe". Rather written, but it can also appear jokingly in everyday speech.

examples[].german: A deficiency of clotting factors causes hemophilia.
When liver function declines, clotting factors are no longer produced in sufficient amounts.
A clotting factor preparation was administered before the surgery.
en.notes: 凝固因子 are the "clotting factors" in the blood: 凝固 "coagulation, solidification" + 因子 "factor". In medicine they are usually named with Roman numerals (第VIII因子 "factor VIII"). Typical combinations: 凝固因子が欠乏する/不足する, 凝固因子製剤 "clotting factor preparation". The related verb is 血液が凝固する "the blood clots"; colloquially people rather say 血が固まる. Purely technical vocabulary.

examples[].german: Peritoneal dissemination refers to a state in which cancer has spread within the abdominal cavity.
When spring comes, the sowing of soybeans begins in the fields.
The test results showed that the cancer had disseminated to the pleura.
en.notes: 播種 literally means "to sow seeds" (播 = sow, 種 = seed) and is used technically in agriculture and horticulture: 播種機 ("seeder"), 播種期; in everyday speech people say 種まき. In medicine it denotes the "spreading" of cancer cells into a body cavity, for example 腹膜播種 or がんが胸膜に播種する; also 播種性 ("disseminated"). As a する-verb it is transitive (種を播種する) or, in medicine, intransitive.

examples[].german: Laparoscopic surgery allows faster recovery than conventional open abdominal surgery.
Gallbladder surgery is often performed using a laparoscope.
Since it is laparoscopic surgery, the wounds will be small.
en.notes: 腹腔鏡 is the "laparoscope", an endoscope for the abdominal cavity. In medicine 腹腔 is mostly read ふくくう (otherwise also ふっこう). Very common is 腹腔鏡手術 or 腹腔鏡下手術 ("laparoscopic surgery, keyhole surgery"), as opposed to 開腹手術 ("open abdominal surgery"). The umbrella term is 内視鏡 ("endoscope"). Typical: 腹腔鏡で手術する, 腹腔鏡を挿入する.

examples[].german: A cardiac catheterization confirms the narrowing of the coronary arteries.
After the surgery, a catheter remained in my urethra for a while.
The nurse slowly removed the catheter for me.
en.notes: カテーテル is the "catheter", a thin tube that is inserted into vessels, urinary tract and so on. People say カテーテルを入れる/挿入する and カテーテルを抜く. Common compounds: 心臓カテーテル検査 "cardiac catheterization" (in hospital jargon shortened to カテ), 尿道カテーテル "urinary catheter", カテーテル治療. The word is completely commonplace in the hospital; patients use it too.

examples[].german: A stent is placed in the coronary artery to restore blood flow.
My father collapsed from a heart attack and had two stents put in.
I hear that with stent treatment you don't need to have your chest opened.
en.notes: ステント is a "stent", a small mesh tube that keeps narrowed vessels or ducts open. The typical technical verb is ステントを留置する "to place a stent (and leave it there)"; in conversation people simply say ステントを入れる. Common in ステント治療 and 冠動脈ステント. Mostly in connection with cardiac catheter procedures (カテーテル治療) for angina pectoris or heart attack.

examples[].german: A ventilator is attached to severely ill patients to assist their breathing.
My grandfather was connected to a ventilator for a week.
Because of the epidemic of an infectious disease, the hospital ran out of ventilators.
en.notes: 人工呼吸器 is the "ventilator": 人工呼吸 "artificial respiration" + 器 "device". People say 人工呼吸器を装着する/つける and 人工呼吸器を外す; 人工呼吸器につながれる means "to be hooked up to a ventilator". Do not confuse it with 人工呼吸 alone, which also means mouth-to-mouth resuscitation in first aid. In hospital routine the loanword ベンチレーター is also heard.

examples[].german: Defibrillation must be performed immediately for ventricular fibrillation.
Before the ambulance crew arrived, a station attendant applied defibrillation with an AED.
In the life-saving course, we also practiced how to use a defibrillator.
en.notes: 除細動 is "defibrillation": literally the removal (除) of fibrillation (細動, ventricular or atrial fibrillation). People say 除細動を行う/かける. The device is called 除細動器; the publicly installed lay defibrillator is the AED (自動体外式除細動器), which in everyday speech is almost always just called "AED". The word itself is technical language from emergency medicine and first-aid courses.

examples[].german: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is a basic skill in emergency medicine.
The man whose heart had stopped was miraculously revived by the treatment of the ambulance crew.
Under the new mayor, the run-down shopping street is being revived.
en.notes: 蘇生 means "resuscitation" and can be used as an intransitive する-verb: 患者が蘇生した "the patient was resuscitated / came round". Common in technical use are 心肺蘇生(法) "cardiopulmonary resuscitation" and 蘇生措置 "resuscitation measures"; 蘇生させる means "to resuscitate someone". Figuratively it can also mean the revival of a town or company, but this is elevated. The everyday word is 生き返る; 復活 rather means a comeback.

examples[].german: Critically ill patients receive 24-hour monitoring in the intensive care unit.
The accident victim was taken to the intensive care unit unconscious.
My mother was able to move from the intensive care unit to a general ward.
en.notes: 集中治療室 is the "intensive care unit" (literally "room for concentrated treatment"). In everyday speech and in the news people usually say the short ICU (アイシーユー); there are also specialized units such as CCU (cardiac) or NICU (newborns). Typical: 集中治療室に運ばれる/入る "to be taken to / enter the intensive care unit", 集中治療室で治療を受ける, 集中治療室から一般病棟に移る "to be moved from intensive care to a normal ward".

examples[].german: Continuous monitoring of vital signs allows changes in the patient's condition to be detected early.
The patient's vital signs after the surgery are stable.
The paramedic first checked the vital signs.
en.notes: バイタルサイン are the "vital signs": pulse, blood pressure, respiration, body temperature (often also level of consciousness). In nursing jargon this is shortened to バイタル: バイタルを測る/チェックする. Typical combinations: バイタルサインが安定している "the vital signs are stable", バイタルサインを確認する. The word belongs to the technical language of nursing, emergency services and clinics.

examples[].german: The ties between politicians and vested interests are seen as a problem.
The great powers competed over railway and mining concessions in China.
Large development projects easily become entangled with vested interests.
en.notes: 利権 are rights or concessions that bring profit, such as 石油利権 "oil concessions". In domestic politics the word usually has a negative connotation: lucrative vested interests that politicians, officials and companies flock to. Typical: 利権を握る, 利権に群がる, 利権が絡む "vested interests are involved", 利権争い, 利権政治. Not to be confused with 権利 "right" - the same characters in reverse order.

examples[].german: Preventive medicine is a field aimed at preventing disease and promoting health.
From the standpoint of preventive medicine, we recommend an annual health checkup.
To hold down medical costs, the government has begun putting effort into preventive medicine.
en.notes: 予防医学 is "preventive medicine": 予防 "prevention" + 医学 "medicine (as a science)". It denotes a field of study, not an individual measure; for concrete preventive care people say 予防 or 健康診断 "health checkup". Typical: 予防医学の観点から "from the viewpoint of preventive medicine", 予防医学に力を入れる. Related is 治療医学 "curative medicine" as its opposite. Rather formal, in technical texts, politics and health journalism.

examples[].german: Improving public health raises the health level of society as a whole.
The development of water and sewage systems was a major turning point in the history of public health.
Leaving garbage lying around becomes a public health problem.
en.notes: 公衆衛生 means "public health" in the sense of hygiene and health protection of the population: 公衆 "the public" + 衛生 "hygiene". It covers infection control, water supply, food hygiene and so on. Typical: 公衆衛生の向上, 公衆衛生上の問題 "a public health problem", 公衆衛生学 as a subject. Rather formal; in everyday speech people simply say 衛生 or 衛生面.

examples[].german: Obtaining informed consent before surgery is an ethical obligation.
Before taking part in the clinical trial, I received an explanation of informed consent from the doctor.
The patient's side sued the hospital, claiming that informed consent had been insufficient.
en.notes: インフォームドコンセント is the patient's "informed consent" after the doctor's explanation, taken over from English. Typical: インフォームドコンセントを得る/取る, インフォームドコンセントが不十分だ. Because the word is long and incomprehensible to many patients, authorities recommend the Japanese paraphrase 説明と同意; in conversation people often simply say 十分な説明を受ける. It belongs to medical ethics, clinics and law.

examples[].german: The results of clinical research led to the development of a new treatment.
This new drug is still at the clinical trial stage.
Not only in research, I have also worked ten years in clinical practice.
en.notes: 臨床 literally means "at the sickbed" (臨 "to face something" + 床 "bed") and denotes practical work with patients as opposed to basic research (基礎). It almost always stands attributively: 臨床研究, 臨床試験 "clinical trial", 臨床医 "clinician", 臨床の現場 "clinical practice". As a noun there is also 臨床に携わる "to be engaged in patient care". Also well known is 臨床心理士 "clinical psychologist".

examples[].german: Drug discovery using AI is shortening the time needed for new drug development.
After studying at university, she works on drug discovery research at a pharmaceutical company.
Drug discovery takes more than ten years and an enormous amount of money.
en.notes: 創薬 means "drug development, drug discovery research" (創 "create" + 薬 "medicine") and denotes the whole process from the search for drug candidates to the new medicine. It is a relatively young technical word from the pharmaceutical industry and science policy: 創薬研究, 創薬ベンチャー, AI創薬. In everyday speech people rather say 新薬の開発 or 薬を開発する; 創薬 itself is not used as a する-verb.

examples[].german: Molecularly targeted drugs selectively attack cancer cells.
There is still no effective treatment drug for this disease.
The earlier you take a flu medicine after onset, the more effective it is.
en.notes: 治療薬 is a "drug for treating" a particular disease, often with the disease name before it: 糖尿病の治療薬, インフルエンザ治療薬, 分子標的治療薬. It is distinct from 予防薬 "preventive drug" and ワクチン "vaccine". 特効薬, by contrast, is a "miracle cure" that works instantly. The general everyday word is simply 薬; 治療薬 sounds more technical and occurs in the news and in conversations with doctors.

examples[].german: When there is no fundamental cure, symptoms are managed with symptomatic treatment.
Cold medicine is symptomatic treatment, so it only eases the fever and cough.
Merely handing out subsidies is only a stopgap measure, and the declining birthrate will not stop.
en.notes: 対症療法 is "symptomatic treatment", which treats only the symptoms (症), not the cause (対 = directed at); the opposite is 原因療法 or 根治療法. Figuratively it also means "stopgap, patchwork", for example with political measures: 対症療法にすぎない "is merely fighting symptoms". Note: the spelling 対処療法 is a very widespread mistake; the correct one is 対症 "against the symptom".

examples[].german: We aim at a radical cure of the cancer through surgery.
This disease is hard to cure completely with medicine alone.
If it can be found early, a radical operation is possible.
en.notes: 根治 means "complete cure, healing at the root" (根 "root" + 治 "heal"); the reading こんじ is also widespread. As a する-verb: 病気を根治する "to cure a disease completely" or intransitive 病気が根治する. Typical are 根治を目指す, 根治手術, 根治療法 (the opposite of 対症療法). 完治 also means "completely cured", but emphasizes the result, whereas 根治 rather emphasizes the removal of the cause. Also figuratively: 不正を根治する "to eliminate abuses from the ground up".

examples[].german: The balance of the gut microbiota affects the health of the whole body.
Yogurt and natto are said to increase intestinal bacteria.
Taking antibiotics can sometimes reduce even the intestinal bacteria.
en.notes: 腸内細菌 are the "intestinal bacteria" (腸 "intestine" + 内 "inside" + 細菌 "bacteria"). The totality is called 腸内細菌叢 technically, and 腸内フローラ "gut flora" in popular usage. Common expressions: 腸内細菌のバランス, 善玉菌 "good bacteria" and 悪玉菌 "bad bacteria", 腸内環境を整える "to bring the intestinal environment into balance". The word is very widespread in advertising for yogurt and dietary supplements.

examples[].german: The mucous membrane of the stomach can be damaged by infection with Helicobacter pylori.
In winter the air is dry, and the mucous membranes of the nose and throat easily weaken.
I ate something hot in a hurry and burned the mucous membrane in my mouth.
en.notes: 粘膜 is the "mucous membrane" (粘 "sticky" + 膜 "membrane"). Mostly with a body part before it: 胃の粘膜 "gastric mucosa", 鼻の粘膜, 口の中の粘膜. Typical: 粘膜が荒れる "the mucous membrane is irritated", 粘膜が乾燥する, 粘膜を保護する. Do not confuse it with 鼓膜 "eardrum" or 角膜 "cornea". The word is medical, but also familiar from advertising for lozenges and nasal sprays.

examples[].german: Construction-tribe lawmakers argued for expanding the budget for public works.
The reform was watered down by the resistance of the agriculture-tribe lawmakers.
The collusion between policy-tribe lawmakers and bureaucrats was criticized.
en.notes: 族議員 are lawmakers who are closely tied to a particular ministry and its industry and represent its interests in parliament. They are formed with 〜族: 建設族, 道路族, 農林族, 厚労族 etc. The word sounds critical because it hints at clientelism and 癒着 "collusion" with the bureaucracy and business. Typical for political commentary in newspapers.

examples[].german: When the cartilage in a joint wears down, osteoarthritis develops.
As I got older, the cartilage in my knees wore away, and stairs became hard.
At the izakaya I ordered fried cartilage.
en.notes: 軟骨 is "cartilage" (軟 "soft" + 骨 "bone"), e.g. 関節の軟骨, 耳の軟骨, 鼻の軟骨. Typical: 軟骨がすり減る "the cartilage wears away". In addition, 軟骨 (often in kana なんこつ) is also a dish: fried or grilled chicken cartilage, popular in izakaya and as yakitori (軟骨の唐揚げ). The counterpart in the body is 硬骨 "bone (in the narrow sense)", in everyday speech simply 骨.

examples[].german: Anterior cruciate ligament injury is a common injury among athletes.
I twisted my ankle and hurt a ligament.
The ace tore a ligament in his knee, and his season is hopeless.
en.notes: 靭帯 is the "ligament" that connects bones at joints. The official spelling is 靱帯; 靭帯 is the variant common in the media, and both are read じんたい. Typical combinations: 靭帯を痛める/損傷する, 靭帯が切れる/断裂する "a ligament tears", 前十字靭帯 "anterior cruciate ligament". Distinguish it from 腱 "tendon", which connects muscle and bone. Frequent in sports news.

examples[].german: Rupture of the Achilles tendon can occur from sudden exercise.
I used my smartphone too much every day and hurt a tendon in my wrist.
Weak defense is this team's Achilles heel.
en.notes: 腱 is the "tendon" that connects a muscle to bone; by contrast, 靭帯 connects bone to bone. 腱 rarely stands alone, mostly in compounds: アキレス腱 "Achilles tendon" (also figuratively "Achilles heel, weak point"), 腱鞘炎 "tendon sheath inflammation", 腱を切る "to tear a tendon". Because the kanji is difficult, the media sometimes also write けん in kana.

examples[].german: A herniated disc is one of the main causes of lower back pain.
When I lifted a heavy load, I hurt a disc in my lower back.
On the MRI you can see that the disc is slightly compressed.
en.notes: 椎間板 is the "intervertebral disc" between two vertebrae (椎 "vertebra" + 間 "between" + 板 "plate"). By far the most common context is 椎間板ヘルニア "slipped disc", in everyday speech often just called ヘルニア. Further combinations: 腰椎の椎間板 "disc of the lumbar spine", 椎間板がすり減る/つぶれる. The word is medical, but patients with back problems know it well.

examples[].german: Osteoporosis is a disease in which a decrease in bone density raises the risk of fracture.
My grandmother has osteoporosis, and she broke a leg bone just from falling.
To prevent osteoporosis, calcium and moderate exercise are important.
en.notes: 骨粗鬆症 is "osteoporosis", literally "disease of bones that become coarse (粗) and loose (鬆)". Because 鬆 is not an everyday kanji, media and brochures mostly write 骨粗しょう症. Typical combinations: 骨粗鬆症になる, 骨粗鬆症を予防する, 骨粗鬆症による骨折. Closely linked to 骨密度 "bone density"; women after menopause (閉経後) in particular are affected.

examples[].german: Hyperlipidemia increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.
At my health checkup I was told I have hyperlipidemia, so I decided to review my diet.
High blood pressure and hyperlipidemia often progress without any subjective symptoms.
en.notes: 高脂血症 is "hyperlipidemia", i.e. too-high blood fat values (高 "high" + 脂 "fat" + 血 "blood" + 症 "disease"). In the Japanese guidelines the term was largely replaced in 2007 by 脂質異常症 "dyslipidemia", but 高脂血症 is still widespread in everyday speech and among patients. Typically in a series with 高血圧 and 糖尿病 as 生活習慣病 "lifestyle diseases". Colloquially people often simply say コレステロールが高い.

examples[].german: Gout develops when a high uric acid level continues.
The big toe suddenly swelled in the middle of the night, and I realized it was a gout attack.
The department head, who likes beer, has been cutting back on alcohol since he got gout.
en.notes: 痛風 is "gout", literally "pain-wind"; the popular explanation of the name is that it hurts even when just a breath of wind touches the spot. The cause is a too-high 尿酸値 "uric acid level"; typical is the sudden 痛風発作 "gout attack", often in the big toe. People say 痛風になる/を発症する. Triggers are said to be プリン体 "purines" in beer and organ meats, which is why the word often comes up in conversations about drinking habits.

examples[].german: Hyperthyroidism is a disease in which metabolism becomes abnormally active.
I tire easily, so I had a test, and my thyroid function was weak.
The front of your neck is swollen, so please have your thyroid examined.
en.notes: 甲状腺 is the "thyroid gland" (甲状 "shield-shaped" + 腺 "gland"). Common compounds: 甲状腺ホルモン, 甲状腺機能亢進症 "overactive thyroid" (well known is バセドウ病 "Graves' disease"), 甲状腺機能低下症 "underactive thyroid", 甲状腺がん. People say 甲状腺が腫れる "the thyroid is enlarged". The word is medical, but generally known.

examples[].german: The pancreas is an organ with the endocrine function of secreting insulin.
Pancreatic cancer is said to be difficult to detect early.
Some people damage their pancreas by drinking too much alcohol.
en.notes: 膵臓 is the "pancreas"; it produces digestive juices (膵液) and insulin. Important combinations: 膵臓がん "pancreatic cancer" (considered hard to detect early), 膵炎 "pancreatitis", 膵臓の機能. Because of the difficult kanji, the media sometimes write すい臓. The word is widespread in health topics and the news.

examples[].german: The adrenal glands secrete cortisol, a stress hormone.
The adrenal glands are small organs located above the left and right kidneys.
I was prescribed an adrenal corticosteroid ointment for my eczema.
en.notes: 副腎 is the "adrenal gland" (副 "secondary" + 腎 "kidney"), which sits on top of the kidneys and produces hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline. Common compounds: 副腎皮質 "adrenal cortex", 副腎皮質ホルモン "corticosteroids" (also for steroid ointments, ステロイド), 副腎髄質. The word is purely medical; do not confuse it with 腎臓 "kidney".

examples[].german: The prime minister's resignation threw the political situation into turmoil.
The Diet is preoccupied with political maneuvering rather than policy debate.
The submission of a no-confidence motion against the cabinet suddenly heightened political tension.
en.notes: 政局 is the political situation, especially with regard to power struggles, government stability and party tactics. In Japanese political language it is often contrasted with 政策 ("substantive policy"): 政局より政策を. Typical: 政局が混乱する, 政局が緊迫する, 政局が流動化する, 政局になる ("to turn into a power struggle"). For the general (also international) situation, one rather uses 情勢.

en.meaning: administrative vice-minister; top career official of a ministry
examples[].german: The administrative vice-minister oversees the administrative affairs within the ministry.
He rose all the way to administrative vice-minister of finance.
The administrative vice-minister resigned, taking responsibility for the scandal.
en.notes: 事務次官 is the highest career civil servant of a ministry and heads the administration under the minister - comparable to a permanent secretary. Unlike the 副大臣 and 政務官, who are appointed as politicians, the 事務次官 is at the top of the civil service career: 〜事務次官まで上り詰める. Often with the ministry's name: 財務事務次官, 外務事務次官. It is also shortened to 次官.

examples[].german: Cholecystitis is often caused by gallstones.
I have gallstones, so I had surgery to remove my gallbladder.
The gallbladder is an organ that stores bile produced in the liver.
en.notes: 胆嚢 is the "gallbladder", which stores the bile (胆汁) produced in the liver. Because of the difficult character 嚢, it is often written 胆のう. Typical words: 胆嚢炎 ("gallbladder inflammation"), 胆石 ("gallstone"), 胆嚢摘出 ("removal of the gallbladder"). 胆 alone also stands for "courage" (大胆, 胆力). Medical terminology, but familiar in conversations with doctors.

examples[].german: The spleen is involved in destroying aged red blood cells and in immune function.
My spleen ruptured in a traffic accident, and I had emergency surgery.
The spleen is located behind and to the left of the stomach.
en.notes: 脾臓 is the "spleen" (脾 "spleen" + 臓 "organ"). Typical contexts are 脾臓が腫れる "the spleen is enlarged" (脾腫) and, after accidents, 脾臓破裂 "ruptured spleen" or 脾臓を摘出する "to remove the spleen". In everyday life the word hardly plays a role; you encounter it in anatomy, in conversations with doctors and in accident reports. Because of the rare kanji, ひ臓 is also found.

examples[].german: Air is drawn into the lungs through contraction of the diaphragm.
Hiccups are caused by spasms of the diaphragm.
When you sing, be aware of your diaphragm and project your voice from your belly.
en.notes: 横隔膜 is the "diaphragm", the membrane (膜) that separates (隔) crosswise (横) the chest cavity from the abdominal cavity. Typical: 横隔膜が収縮する, 横隔膜を使って呼吸する (abdominal breathing, 腹式呼吸). Hiccups (しゃっくり) are explained as 横隔膜のけいれん. In 焼肉, the beef diaphragm is known as ハラミ or サガリ.

examples[].german: Retinal detachment carries the risk of blindness if not treated promptly.
Light entering the eye passes through the lens and forms an image on the retina.
People with diabetes should have their retinas examined regularly.
en.notes: 網膜 is the "retina" of the eye (網 "net" + 膜 "membrane"). Common combinations: 網膜剥離 "retinal detachment", 網膜に映る "to be projected on the retina", 糖尿病網膜症 "diabetic retinopathy". Distinguish it from 角膜 "cornea" (at the front) and 水晶体 "lens". Figuratively, 網膜に焼きつく is used for an image that has burned itself into the memory.

examples[].german: Vision can be restored through a corneal transplant.
I slept with my contact lenses in and scratched my cornea.
LASIK is a surgery that corrects vision by reshaping the cornea with a laser.
en.notes: 角膜 is the "cornea" of the eye (角 "horn" + 膜 "membrane"); for the callus on the feet, by contrast, people say 角質 or たこ. Typical combinations: 角膜移植 "corneal transplant", 角膜に傷がつく "the cornea gets injured", 角膜炎. Frequent in connection with contact lenses and laser surgery such as レーシック. Do not confuse it with 網膜 "retina".

examples[].german: A cataract is an eye disease in which the lens becomes cloudy and white.
The eye focuses by changing the thickness of the lens.
In the surgery, the clouded lens was replaced with an artificial lens.
en.notes: 水晶体 is the "lens of the eye"; literally "crystal body". For cameras and glasses, by contrast, people say レンズ. The eye focuses as the ciliary muscle changes the thickness of the 水晶体. In a cataract (白内障) the lens becomes cloudy: 水晶体が濁る. Other parts of the eye are 角膜 ("cornea") and 網膜 ("retina"). A technical word, but one that often comes up in conversations with doctors about the eyes.

examples[].german: As otitis media progresses, the eardrum may perforate.
I cleaned too deep with an ear pick and damaged my eardrum.
When I stood in front of the speakers at the concert, it was so loud that my eardrums felt like they would burst.
en.notes: 鼓膜 is the "eardrum" (鼓 "drum" + 膜 "membrane"). People say 鼓膜が破れる "the eardrum bursts" (technically 鼓膜が穿孔する) and 鼓膜を傷つける. Colloquially and exaggerating: 鼓膜が破れそうな音/声 "ear-splittingly loud". Related are 中耳 "middle ear" and 中耳炎 "otitis media".

examples[].german: The cochlea is the organ that converts sound vibrations into nerve signals.
If you keep listening to loud sounds, the cells of the cochlea can be damaged, leading to hearing loss.
The name 蝸牛 comes from the fact that its spiral shape resembles a snail.
en.notes: 蝸牛 literally means "snail"; in the reading かぎゅう it is the anatomical technical term for the "cochlea" in the inner ear. The animal itself is called かたつむり (same kanji, different reading) or でんでんむし in everyday speech. Common in technical use: 蝸牛管 "cochlear duct", 蝸牛の有毛細胞 "hair cells of the cochlea"; the cochlear implant, by contrast, is called 人工内耳. The reading かぎゅう occurs practically only in medical and literary texts.

examples[].german: The cerebral cortex is the brain region that governs cognition and sensory processing.
Compared with other animals, humans have a highly developed cerebral cortex.
A stroke damaged part of my cerebral cortex, and words became hard to produce.
en.notes: 大脳皮質 is the "cerebral cortex": 大脳 "cerebrum" + 皮質 "cortex". It is divided into lobes, e.g. 前頭葉 "frontal lobe" and 側頭葉 "temporal lobe". Typical combinations: 大脳皮質が〜を司る "is responsible for ...", 大脳皮質の働き, 大脳皮質が発達する. A technical term from neurology, psychology and popular-science books about the brain.

examples[].german: The cerebellum is involved in motor coordination and maintaining balance.
It is thanks to the cerebellum that the body remembers how to ride a bicycle.
I had an infarction in my cerebellum and became unable to walk straight.
en.notes: 小脳 is the "cerebellum" (小 "small" + 脳 "brain"), the counterpart of 大脳 "cerebrum"; in addition there is 脳幹 "brain stem". It controls balance and coordination of movement; failures lead, for example, to ふらつき "staggering". Typical: 小脳の働き, 小脳梗塞 "cerebellar infarction". Well known is the disease 脊髄小脳変性症. A technical word, but generally known from biology class.

examples[].german: The parliamentary secretary attended the press conference on behalf of the minister.
He was appointed parliamentary secretary of foreign affairs after being elected just twice.
The vice-minister and the parliamentary secretary inspected the disaster area.
en.notes: 政務官 is the short form of 大臣政務官, a political post existing since 2001: lawmakers who support the minister in particular areas of responsibility. In the hierarchy: 大臣 > 副大臣 > 政務官.
