examples[].german: It is important not to neglect daily study.
After many years of diligent training, he finally became a full-fledged craftsman.
Young researchers are devoting themselves to study abroad.
en.notes: 研鑽 means to deepen and hone knowledge or skill through persistent study (研 "to polish", 鑽 "to drill"). It is an elevated, literary word, typical in fixed combinations: 研鑽を積む, 研鑽に励む, 日々の研鑽, 自己研鑽 "self-improvement". Because 鑽 is not a jōyō kanji, newspapers often write 研さん. More everyday are 勉強 or 努力; 修業, by contrast, emphasizes practical training under a master.

examples[].german: Judicial review of the administrative action was demanded.
Highly political questions are sometimes excluded from judicial review.
In the United States, the system of judicial review was established by case law.
en.notes: 司法審査 is the review of laws or administrative action by the courts. In Japan, one usually speaks more concretely of 違憲審査 or 違憲立法審査権 "power of judicial review". Typical: 司法審査の対象となる/外とされる, 司法審査を求める. According to the doctrine of 統治行為 "acts of state", highly political questions can be exempted from 司法審査. Legal technical term.

examples[].german: A support system for students who refuse to attend school was set up.
Our son has not been going to school since the autumn of his second year of middle school.
The number of free schools that children who don't attend regular school can go to is increasing.
en.notes: 不登校 designates longer absence from school for psychological or social reasons, not because of illness or poverty; the Ministry of Education counts pupils with at least 30 days of absence per year. Typical: 不登校になる, 不登校の児童・生徒, 不登校気味. The older expression 登校拒否 "school refusal" is avoided today because it implies a conscious refusal. Occasional skipping school, by contrast, is called サボる or ずる休み.

examples[].german: Efforts to eradicate bullying are being strengthened.
He was badly bullied when he was in elementary school.
I quit my job because I was suffering from bullying at work.
en.notes: いじめ is the noun for the transitive verb いじめる "to torment, to bully" (〜をいじめる) and is almost always written in kana. Someone who is bullied いじめに遭う or いじめを受ける; the perpetrator is the いじめっ子, the victim the いじめられっ子. The word applies to school as well as the workplace (職場のいじめ), where パワハラ is often said. Harmless teasing, by contrast, is called からかう.

examples[].german: Classroom breakdown is a serious problem for teachers.
After the homeroom teacher changed, that class fell into a state of classroom breakdown.
To prevent classroom breakdown, some schools have two teachers teach each lesson.
en.notes: 学級崩壊 is a term in use since the late 1990s for a class in which teaching is no longer possible: pupils walk around, don't listen, ignore the teacher. It concerns mainly elementary schools. 学級 is the official word for "school class" (in everyday speech クラス), 崩壊 means "collapse". Typical: 学級崩壊が起きる, 学級崩壊の状態に陥る, 学級崩壊を防ぐ. Distinguish from 校内暴力 "violence in schools".

examples[].german: He used the early-admission system and entered university at sixteen.
She moved to graduate school early, after only the third year of her undergraduate studies.
In Japan there are still few cases of early admission.
en.notes: 飛び入学 designates early transfer to the next educational level without completing the current one: from high school to university or from undergraduate study to graduate school. In Japan this has been possible at some universities since 1998, but is rare. Do not confuse it with 飛び級 "skipping a grade" within the same school, which is not provided for in Japanese compulsory schooling. Typical: 飛び入学で入る, 飛び入学制度.

examples[].german: Criticism of cram-style education is growing.
Knowledge learned by cramming is forgotten as soon as the exam is over.
I got sick from packing in too many appointments.
en.notes: 詰め込み is the noun for the transitive verb 詰め込む "to stuff in, to pack full". In an educational context it stands for cramming knowledge: 詰め込み教育, 詰め込み式 / 詰め込み型の勉強, with ゆとり教育 as the opposite. Beyond that it applies to anything overloaded: 詰め込みすぎ "too much at once" with suitcases, appointments or texts. Studying through the night shortly before an exam is called 一夜漬け.

examples[].german: The merits and demerits of yutori education are being debated.
With yutori education, class hours and the content of learning were drastically reduced.
He belongs to the generation that went through yutori education, but he dislikes being called part of the "yutori generation".
en.notes: ゆとり教育 designates the Japanese education policy of roughly 2002 to 2010, which, as a response to 詰め込み教育, cut learning content and class hours, introduced the five-day week and promoted cross-curricular learning. ゆとり means "leeway, composure". After weaker PISA results it was rolled back (脱ゆとり). The generation affected is called ゆとり世代, often used pejoratively.

examples[].german: The importance of lifelong learning has come to be widely recognized.
My mother is learning calligraphy at the city's lifelong learning center.
After retirement, I plan to attend the university's open lectures as lifelong learning.
en.notes: 生涯学習 ("learning throughout life", 生涯 "lifetime") is an education-policy term for all learning activities after school: community courses, hobbies, continuing education in old age. Typical are 生涯学習センター, 生涯学習講座 and 生涯学習として〜を学ぶ. For job-related continuing education, one rather says リカレント教育 or リスキリング; 社会教育 is the administrative term for adult education.

examples[].german: Japan's literacy rate is among the highest in the world.
Improving the literacy rate leads to a reduction in poverty.
Japan in the Edo period is said to have had a high literacy rate.
en.notes: 識字率 is made up of 識字 "being able to read and write" and 率 "rate" and is a technical term from statistics, development policy and history. Typical: 識字率が高い / 低い, 識字率が向上する, 識字率を上げる. Related is 識字教育 "literacy education". The older word 文盲 for illiteracy is considered discriminatory today; one says 非識字.

examples[].german: Customary law is also an important source of law.
In Japan, there is debate over whether court precedents count as a source of law.
In Islamic law, the Koran is regarded as the primary source of law.
en.notes: 法源 is a term of legal science: the sources from which law arises, such as 成文法 "written law", 慣習法 "customary law", 判例 "case law" and 条理 "general legal principles". Typical: 〜は法源の一つである, 〜が法源にあたるか. Note: it is read the same as 方言 "dialect". Almost only in textbooks and technical texts.

examples[].german: In the general education course, you study a wide range of fields.
After finishing the general education course, you move on to the specialized course from the third year.
At the University of Tokyo, everyone studies in the general education course for the first two years.
en.notes: 教養課程 is the general-education stage of the first one or two years at Japanese universities, in which courses from many areas are taken before moving on to specialized study (専門課程). 教養 here means "general education", 課程 "stage of study". The corresponding courses are called 教養科目 or 一般教養, in student slang abbreviated 般教. Typical: 教養課程で学ぶ, 教養課程を終える.

examples[].german: Three professors are in charge of reviewing the dissertation.
I have to submit my thesis by the end of January.
His dissertation was later published as a book.
en.notes: 学位論文 is the umbrella term for any paper with which an academic degree is earned: 卒業論文 (卒論, bachelor's thesis), 修士論文 (修論, master's thesis) and 博士論文 (博論, doctoral dissertation). The word is formal and appears in examination regulations and library catalogs; in conversation people usually name the specific kind. Typical: 学位論文を提出する / 審査する / 執筆する.

examples[].german: In the oral examination, we had a question-and-answer session about the research content.
In this school's entrance exam, there is an oral examination after the written exam.
I was relieved when I got through the oral defense of my dissertation.
en.notes: 口頭試問 ("oral examination questions") is a formal term for an oral exam, especially the defense of a thesis or dissertation and the oral parts of entrance exams. Typical: 口頭試問を受ける / 行う, 口頭試問に合格する. More general is 口頭試験; 面接 is an interview or selection interview, 筆記試験 the written exam.

examples[].german: I forgot to write my name on the answer sheet.
I couldn't finish writing my answers within the time limit.
The graded exams will be returned in class next week.
en.notes: 答案 is what one hands in in writing during an exam: the completed exam paper or the answers on it. The blank sheet is called 答案用紙. Typical: 答案を書く / 提出する / 採点する / 返却する, 模範答案 "model answer". To be distinguished from 解答 (the solution to a problem, also in an answer booklet) and 回答 (a reply to a survey or inquiry).

examples[].german: It is tough to grade over a hundred exam papers.
That teacher is famous for being a strict grader.
The scoring method in figure skating is very complicated.
en.notes: 採点 is the awarding of points, that is, correcting and grading exams, but also the scoring by judges in sports or competitions. As a transitive する-verb: 答案を採点する. Typical: 採点が甘い / 厳しい "to grade leniently / strictly", 採点基準, 自動採点; karaoke machines have a 採点機能. 評価 is broader (overall assessment), 成績 the result.

examples[].german: When the parents saw the report card, they were surprised.
University grade reports can be checked online.
The results sheet for the mock exam was sent from the cram school.
en.notes: 成績表 is an overview of grades or results achieved. In elementary and middle schools the report card is usually called 通知表 (older 通信簿); 成績表 is used more generally and at universities. An officially certified transcript for applications, on the other hand, is a 成績証明書. Typical: 成績表をもらう / 見る / 確認する.

examples[].german: I failed the main exam but passed the makeup exam.
Students who missed the final exam because of illness can take a makeup exam.
The experimental result was not confirmed in replication studies by other researchers.
en.notes: 追試 is the short form of 追試験 and in school designates a makeup exam for those who were absent; colloquially it is often also used for the retake exam after failing (more precisely 再試 / 再試験). Typical: 追試を受ける, 追試になる. In science, 追試 means the replication of an experiment by others (実験を追試する, 追試で確認される).

examples[].german: You must retake subjects that you failed.
In the retake class I sit with first-years, which is a bit awkward.
Students retaking a course can register for it with priority.
en.notes: 再履修 is a university term: 再 "again" + 履修 "to take a course", that is, to take a failed course once more. As a する-verb: 科目を再履修する; students say 再履 (さいり) for short. Distinguish from 留年 "repeating a whole year" and 追試 / 再試 (only the exam is repeated).

examples[].german: The Imperial Rescript on Education set out the basic philosophy of prewar education.
The Imperial Rescript on Education was promulgated in 1890.
After the war, the Imperial Rescript on Education lost its force by a resolution of the Diet.
en.notes: 教育勅語 is the education edict issued in 1890 in the name of the Meiji Emperor (勅語 "words of the Emperor"). It stressed loyalty to the Emperor, filial piety and obedience and was solemnly read aloud in schools until 1945. In 1948 it was declared invalid by parliamentary resolutions. Today the word appears in historical texts and in political debates about moral education; it is a historical technical term.

examples[].german: The decision was made on the basis of the principle of good faith.
Under the doctrine of abuse of the right to dismiss, a dismissal without reasonable grounds is invalid.
This ruling is correct in terms of legal principle, but out of step with the public's sense.
en.notes: 法理 refers to a legal principle derived from the legal system as a whole or from case law, and often not stated explicitly in the statute. Typical are fixed combinations like 信義則の法理 or 解雇権濫用法理, usually with に基づく or に照らして. Compared with 法律 "the individual law" and 原則 "principle" in general, 法理 is a technical word from legal science and case law; it hardly appears in everyday life.

examples[].german: There are opinions that the duration of compulsory education should be extended.
Compulsory education in Japan is nine years, covering elementary and middle school.
In compulsory education, textbooks are handed out free of charge.
en.notes: 義務教育 is compulsory schooling; in Japan it covers nine years (6 years 小学校, 3 years 中学校). Legally, the obligation lies with the parents to send their children to school. Typical: 義務教育を受ける / 終える, 義務教育課程, 義務教育の無償. High school (高校) is not part of it, although almost everyone attends.

examples[].german: Making higher education free of charge is being considered as a policy.
The proportion of people with higher education is increasing year by year.
Institutions of higher education include, besides universities, junior colleges and vocational schools.
en.notes: 高等教育 is tertiary education: universities, junior colleges (短大), colleges of technology (高専, from the 4th year) and vocational schools. Caution: despite its name, 高等学校 (高校) is the high school and belongs to 中等教育. The three levels are called 初等教育, 中等教育 and 高等教育. Typical: 高等教育を受ける, 高等教育機関, 高等教育の無償化.

examples[].german: This author's prose is concise and beautiful.
He started out as a poet but later turned to prose.
What he says is always prosaic and without any dreams.
en.notes: 散文 is prose, that is, text without meter or syllable pattern, in contrast to 韻文. It often appears in literary criticism: 散文詩 "prose poem", 散文作品, 散文家. Derived from it is 散文的 "prosaic", figuratively also "sober, unimaginative". For a single novel or story, one says concretely 小説 or 随筆.

examples[].german: It is important to understand the difference between verse and prose.
In the past, even history and laws were sometimes written in verse so that they would be easy to remember.
This work is a tragedy written in verse.
en.notes: 韻文 is metrical language, that is, text with a fixed rhythm, syllable pattern or rhyme (韻 "rhyme, sound"). In Japanese poetry it relies less on rhyme than on syllable count, for example the 五七調 in 和歌 and 俳句. The opposite is 散文. The term is literary-scholarly and formal; in everyday speech one simply says 詩. "To rhyme" is 韻を踏む.

examples[].german: In Japanese poetry, the changing of the four seasons is sung.
She grew up familiar with poetry from early childhood.
On the poetry shelf of the library, I found an old poetry collection.
en.notes: 詩歌 (しいか, less often しか) is an elevated collective term for poetry: originally Chinese poems (漢詩) and Japanese song poetry (和歌), today lyric poetry in general including 短歌 and 俳句. It designates the genre, not a single poem; for that one says 詩 or 歌. Typical: 詩歌に親しむ, 詩歌を詠む, 詩歌集.

examples[].german: The Man'yōshū contains over four thousand waka poems.
A waka consists of 31 syllables in the pattern 5-7-5-7-7.
The aristocrats of the Heian period composed waka to convey their feelings to one another.
en.notes: 和歌 ("Japanese song") is the classical Japanese poetic form in contrast to the Chinese 漢詩; usually the 短歌 with 31 morae in the pattern 5-7-5-7-7 is meant. Poems are 詠む (よむ), not 書く, and counted with 首: 一首, 百人一首. Famous collections are the 万葉集 and the 古今和歌集. The modern form is called 短歌.

examples[].german: His lyric poetry expresses delicate emotions.
While the epic narrates events, lyric poetry sings of the poet's heart.
When I was young, I often wrote love poems.
en.notes: 抒情詩 is lyric poetry in the narrower sense: poems that express the feelings and moods of the poet (抒情 "expression of feeling"). Because 抒 is not a jōyō kanji, today it is often written 叙情詩. Opposites are 叙事詩 "epic" (narrates events) and 劇詩 "dramatic poetry". Related is the adjective 抒情的 / 叙情的 "lyrical, emotional".

examples[].german: Bashō's travel writings have high literary value.
On weekends I often watch travel programs on TV.
She traveled around Asia and compiled her experiences into a travelogue.
en.notes: 紀行 ("record of a journey") is a literary term for travel accounts. It rarely stands alone; typical are 紀行文 "travel prose", 紀行番組 "travel documentary on TV" and titles like 〜紀行. The best-known example is Bashō's おくのほそ道. In everyday speech, one rather says 旅行記 or simply 旅の記録.

examples[].german: Shakespeare's plays are still performed today.
She writes not only novels but also plays.
The novel was rewritten as a play and performed on stage.
en.notes: 戯曲 is a stage play as a literary text, that is, the written drama. The performance itself is called 劇 or 芝居; 脚本 is the script (also for film), 台本 the actors' working script. The author is a 劇作家. Typical: 戯曲を書く, 戯曲化する "to dramatize", 戯曲集.

examples[].german: He completed a full-length novel over five years.
The director's first feature-length animated film has been released.
I like short stories better than novels because they are easy to read.
en.notes: 長編 (also 長篇) designates a voluminous work and usually comes before the genre: 長編小説 "novel", 長編映画 "feature film", 長編アニメ. Used alone it usually means a novel: 初の長編. The gradation is 長編 – 中編 – 短編 – 掌編.

en.meaning: laws and ordinances; statutes and regulations
examples[].german: There is an obligation to comply with the relevant laws and regulations.
That act may violate laws and regulations.
We revised our internal company rules in line with the amendments to the laws and regulations.
en.notes: 法令 is the collective term for laws (法律) and the administrative ordinances based on them (政令, 省令 etc.), i.e. all rules of law in force. Common: 法令を守る/遵守する, 法令に違反する, 法令に基づく; "compliance" in companies is often 法令遵守. In contrast to 法律 ("a law passed by parliament"), 法令 also includes regulations of the executive; the tone is official and written.

examples[].german: A short story collection was nominated for a literary prize.
On the commuter train I read a short story.
His short film won an award at an international film festival.
en.notes: 短編 (also 短篇) denotes a short work and mostly stands before the genre: 短編小説 "short story", 短編映画 "short film", 短編集 "story collection". Used alone, it mostly means a short story. Opposites are 中編 and 長編; even shorter is 掌編.

examples[].german: I entered a contest for flash fiction under a thousand characters.
Kawabata Yasunari's "Palm-of-the-Hand Stories" is a representative work of flash fiction.
It is my daily routine to read one flash fiction piece before bed.
en.notes: 掌編 ("work the size of a palm", 掌 "palm of the hand") is a very short story, often only one to a few pages; mostly as 掌編小説. A well-known example is Kawabata's collection 掌の小説. A similar, more entertaining term is ショートショート, coined by 星新一. The word is literary and rare; the gradation is 長編 – 中編 – 短編 – 掌編.

examples[].german: Miyazawa Kenji's children's stories are popular with adults too.
I read my child a children's story before bedtime.
"The Little Mermaid" is one of Andersen's fairy tales.
en.notes: 童話 are stories for children, usually written by a single author: アンデルセン童話, グリム童話, the tales of 宮沢賢治. Traditional folktales such as 桃太郎 are more often called 昔話 or 民話. おとぎ話 also means "fairy tale" and is used figuratively for unrealistic ideas. Typical: 童話を読み聞かせる, 童話作家, 創作童話.

examples[].german: There is a danger that oral traditions will disappear before they are written down.
A legend about a dragon still survives in this village.
Passing on the craftsmen's skills to the younger generation is not easy.
en.notes: 伝承 designates both the process of handing down from generation to generation (伝承する, transitive: 技を次の世代に伝承する) and the handed-down material itself, that is, legends and folk traditions (村に残る伝承). Typical combinations are 口頭伝承 "oral tradition", 民間伝承 "folk tradition" and 〜にまつわる伝承. Distinguish 伝説 "legend" (a concrete tale) and 伝統 "tradition" as a custom or practice; 伝承 emphasizes the passing on.

examples[].german: There are activities to keep telling the folktales of the Tōhoku region.
My grandmother often told me folktales before bed.
This picture book is based on folktales from all over Japan.
en.notes: 民話 is the collective term for folk narratives passed on orally among the people: fairy tales, legends, comic tales. In everyday speech one rather says 昔話 "old story, fairy tale" (those that begin with むかしむかし); 民話 sounds somewhat more factual and is used in folklore studies, libraries and educational projects. 童話, on the other hand, are children's stories, including ones written by authors such as Andersen's. Typical: 民話を語り継ぐ, 〜地方の民話, 民話集.

examples[].german: I read a book collecting anecdotes about historical figures.
Numerous anecdotes that speak of his kindness survive.
In his speech, the company president shared an anecdote from the founding days.
en.notes: 逸話 is a little-known, often revealing anecdote about a person that is missing from official accounts (逸 "escaped, hidden"). Typical are 〜にまつわる逸話, 逸話が残る, 逸話を残す and 〜を物語る逸話 "an anecdote that shows ...". In conversation one mostly says エピソード, which also fits one's own experiences; 逸話 sounds more written and almost always refers to famous people or events. Do not confuse it with 挿話 "inserted episode" within a narrative.

examples[].german: Episodes unrelated to the main plot give the story depth.
A story inserted in the middle of the lecture made the audience laugh.
This novel contains several inserted episodes depicting the hero's boyhood.
en.notes: 挿話 (挿 "to insert") is a side story inserted into a larger narrative, speech or work that does not belong to the main thread (本筋). The word is literary and appears mainly in literary criticism and descriptions of works; in everyday speech one says エピソード. In contrast to 逸話, which means an anecdote about a person, 挿話 emphasizes the position within a larger whole. Typical: 挿話を挟む, 挿話が含まれる.

examples[].german: A famous critic contributed the preface.
The preface describes how the author came to write this book.
Even busy people can grasp the overall picture of the book just by reading the preface.
en.notes: 序文 is the preface at the beginning of a book. The common, less formal word is まえがき (also はしがき); 序文 sounds more elevated and is often used when someone other than the author writes the preface: 序文を寄せる "to contribute a preface". The counterpart is 跋文 or あとがき. In scholarly works the introductory chapter is rather called 序論 or 序章, not 序文.

examples[].german: The afterword recorded the author's motivation for writing.
My former teacher contributed an afterword to this haiku collection.
The afterword is placed at the end of the book and is the counterpart to the preface.
en.notes: 跋文 is the afterword at the end of a book and the counterpart to 序文. The word is very literary; the character 跋 is known almost only from this word. It appears mainly in traditional works and in poetry and haiku collections (歌集, 句集), often written by a teacher or friend: 跋文を寄せる. In an ordinary book the afterword is called あとがき. It is not to be equated with "epilogue" as the closing part of a story (エピローグ).

examples[].german: An explanatory note is attached at the end of the paperback edition.
An expert explained the background of the news in an easy-to-understand way.
In baseball broadcasts, a former player handles the commentary.
en.notes: 解説 is a knowledgeable explanation for an audience: commentary on news or sports broadcasts, explanatory texts in a museum, or the afterword essay in a paperback (巻末解説). As a transitive する-verb: 〜を解説する. 説明 is the general everyday word for "to explain" (also for directions or excuses); 解説 presupposes specialist knowledge. Derivatives: 解説者 "commentator", 解説書 "handbook, companion book".

examples[].german: The judge handed down the verdict against the defendant.
After serving as an assistant judge, she became a judge at forty.
A US federal judge temporarily blocked the enforcement of the law.
en.notes: In Japan, 判事 is actually an official rank designation for professional judges (below it stands the 判事補 "assistant judge"); the general word for "judge" is 裁判官. In news, 判事 is read mainly in 最高裁判事 and for foreign courts, e.g. 米連邦判事. In everyday speech and conversation, 裁判官 is mostly used; the presiding judge of a panel is called 裁判長.

examples[].german: Detailed annotations are indispensable for classical works.
This book is easy to read because difficult words come with notes.
Many scholars have added commentary to the Tale of Genji.
en.notes: 註釈 is the older spelling of 注釈; today one mostly writes 注釈, while 註 is still found in classical and scholarly texts. It means explanatory notes on a text, from individual word explanations to detailed commentary: 註釈を付ける, 註釈を加える, 註釈書. A footnote in the narrower sense is 脚注, a single note simply 注. Figuratively, 注釈 also means an explanatory remark: 注釈なしで "without further explanation".

examples[].german: In the critical edition, errors in the original text have been corrected.
He compares Edo-period manuscripts and establishes a critical text.
This complete works edition was published after rigorous critical editing by specialists.
en.notes: 校訂 is the philological work of producing the most correct text possible by comparing different manuscripts and editions; the result is called 校訂本 or 校訂版. Not to be confused with 校正 "proofreading" (finding printing errors), 校閲 "review of content", and the homophone 改訂 "revision by the author" (改訂版 "revised edition"). As a transitive する-verb: 本文を校訂する.

examples[].german: Consulting the original source rather than the translation is the foundation of research.
Someday I'd like to read Shakespeare in the original.
When quoting, please always state the original source.
en.notes: 原典 is the original text or the primary source on which translations, quotations or adaptations are based. Set phrases: 原典に当たる "to consult the original source", 原典で読む "to read in the original", 原典を明記する. Distinguish: 原作 is the source of a film adaptation or manga, 原文 the exact wording of a sentence in the original, 出典 the source citation of a quotation.

examples[].german: This complete works edition uses the first edition as its base text.
Depending on which manuscript is chosen as the base text, the text changes slightly.
I added notes to passages that seem to be errors in the base text.
en.notes: 底本 is a technical term of textual scholarship: the edition or manuscript that serves as the textual basis for an edition, translation or copy. Typical is 〜を底本とする / 〜を底本にする. Beware the homophone 定本 (ていほん) "authoritative, definitive edition"; to avoid confusion, 底本 is sometimes read そこほん in specialist jargon. The rare meaning "draft" plays hardly any role in current usage.

examples[].german: Valuable manuscripts are held in the library.
Before printing technology spread, books were transmitted by handwritten copies.
The monks spent years making copies of the Bible.
en.notes: 写本 is a hand-copied book, that is, a manuscript in the sense of a codex, in contrast to the printed book (刊本, 版本) and the original (原本). Before the spread of printing, texts were transmitted through 写本, which is why there are often several divergent 写本 of one work. An ordinary copy is called 写し or コピー; the manuscript of a present-day author is 原稿.

examples[].german: The writer's manuscript shows many traces of revision.
The author's autograph manuscript was found in a used bookstore.
This manuscript was never published and remained in the possession of the bereaved family.
en.notes: 稿本 is an elevated, technical word for the handwritten manuscript or draft of a work, especially when it has survived as a document. In everyday speech and in publishing, one says 原稿; a provisional draft is 草稿. Common in literary and archival contexts: 自筆稿本 "autograph manuscript". Do not confuse it with the homophone 校本 "collated edition".

examples[].german: He refined the text through repeated revisions.
Polish your report once more before submitting it.
During revision, I cut nearly half of the sentences.
en.notes: 推敲 is the repeated polishing of the wording of one's own text. The word goes back to the Chinese poet Jia Dao, who wavered for a long time over whether to write "push the gate" (推) or "knock at the gate" (敲) in his verse. Typical: 推敲を重ねる, 文章を推敲する (transitive). Distinguish 校正 "proofreading for errors" and 添削 "correcting someone else's text", for example by a teacher.

examples[].german: The magnum opus, three years in the making, is finally finished.
The writer finally finished her novel the day before the deadline.
Once the manuscript is finished, I plan to go on a trip for a while.
en.notes: 脱稿 (脱 "to come out", 稿 "manuscript") means to finish writing a manuscript, a word from the world of authors, journalists and scholars. It is used both transitively (長編を脱稿する) and intransitively (原稿が脱稿する). Related terms: 起稿 "to begin writing" and 入稿 "to hand the manuscript to the publisher or printer". In everyday speech one simply says 書き上げる.

examples[].german: I published my research results as a book.
I am pleased to announce that my first novel has been published.
To commemorate his eightieth birthday, the professor published his autobiography.
en.notes: 上梓 literally means "to put on catalpa wood (梓)", because printing blocks used to be cut from this wood; today it means, in an elevated way, "to publish a book". It is used for books, mostly in polite announcements about one's own works or those of respected persons: 〜を上梓する, 上梓いたしました. Neutral are 出版 and 刊行; 上梓 does not fit magazines or newspapers.

examples[].german: That book is out of print and hard to obtain.
Sales dropped, and that dictionary went out of print last year.
I finally found the out-of-print book in a secondhand bookstore.
en.notes: 絶版 is the state in which a book is no longer printed and the publisher has permanently taken it out of its list: 絶版になる, 絶版にする, 絶版の本. To be distinguished from it is 品切れ "temporarily unavailable" (often 品切れ重版未定). The term for revival is 復刊. For CDs and other products, one says 廃盤.

examples[].german: The prosecutor gave the opening statement.
The prosecutor in charge questioned me once more.
He passed the bar exam and chose a career as a prosecutor.
en.notes: 検事 is the public prosecutor, strictly speaking a rank within the prosecution service; the general term for all prosecutors is 検察官, and the authority is called 検察 or 検察庁. In news and crime dramas, 検事 is the usual term for the person: 担当検事, 検事総長 "Prosecutor General". The opponent in court is the defense counsel (弁護人, generally 弁護士).

examples[].german: In response to readers' requests, the classic was reissued.
The magazine that had been suspended resumed publication after ten years.
Many voices call for a reissue of the out-of-print manga.
en.notes: 復刊 means to bring out an out-of-print (絶版) book again, but also that a discontinued magazine or newspaper appears again. Transitive: 名著を復刊する; for periodicals also intransitive: 雑誌が復刊する. Distinguish 重版 or 再版 "reprint of a title that is still available" and 復刻 "faithful new edition, facsimile". Counterpart for periodicals: 休刊 "temporary suspension".

examples[].german: He is acclaimed as a writer who established a style of his own.
A thesis and a letter call for different styles.
This author's style has rhythm and is easy to read.
en.notes: 文体 has two meanings: an author's personal writing style (独自の文体, 簡潔な文体) and the linguistic form of a text, such as 口語体/文語体 or です・ます体 and だ・である体. In the second meaning, one speaks of keeping the 文体 of a text consistent (文体を統一する). 作風 is the artistic style of a work as a whole (themes, atmosphere), not just the language; スタイル is more general and more colloquial.

examples[].german: It is a fine piece of writing that makes skillful use of rhetorical devices.
His speech is so overloaded with rhetoric that the content doesn't come across.
Rhetoric as a discipline developed in ancient Greece.
en.notes: 修辞 is the artful shaping of language, that is, stylistic devices and rhetorical turns; the discipline is called 修辞学, an individual device 修辞法. Typical: 修辞を駆使する, 修辞に凝る. In present-day usage レトリック is more common and can also mean pejoratively "mere rhetoric, wordplay". Technical term: 修辞疑問 "rhetorical question".

examples[].german: In fairy tales, personification is often applied to animals.
"The wind whispers" is an expression that uses personification.
If you use personification in an essay, the writing becomes more lively.
en.notes: 擬人法 is personification as a stylistic device: human actions or feelings are attributed to things, animals or natural phenomena, for example 風がささやく or 花が笑う. One says 擬人法を使う／用いる. To be distinguished from it is 擬人化（する）, which means humanizing in general, for example with mascots or anime characters. 擬人法 belongs to the technical language of rhetoric and composition teaching.

examples[].german: The meter of waka is based on the 5-7-5-7-7 syllable pattern.
In translation, it is difficult to reproduce the meter of the original poem.
In phonetics, intonation and accent are called prosody.
en.notes: 韻律 is, in poetry, the meter or rhythm of a poem, that is, the rules for syllable count, stress or rhyme. Japanese poetry such as waka and haiku is based on the number of morae (音数律), not on stress. In linguistics, 韻律 also means "prosody", that is, intonation, accent and rhythm of spoken language. Related: 押韻 "rhyme", 韻を踏む "to rhyme".

examples[].german: In Chinese poetry, the rules of rhyme are strictly observed.
In rap, skill at rhyming is appreciated.
This poem rhymes at the end of each line.
en.notes: 押韻 is the technical term for "rhyme, rhyming"; in everyday speech one says 韻を踏む "to rhyme". It occurs mainly in literary studies, in Chinese poetry (漢詩) and today in rap. Subtypes: 脚韻 "end rhyme" and 頭韻 "alliteration". As a する-verb it is mostly used intransitively (各行が押韻している). Classical Japanese poetry has hardly any rhymes; it relies on syllable count (韻律).

examples[].german: The way you punctuate changes the impression a text gives.
Elementary school pupils' compositions have little punctuation and are hard to read.
Recently, more and more young people send messages without any punctuation.
en.notes: 句読点 is the umbrella term for Japanese punctuation marks: 句点 "。" (end of sentence) and 読点 "、" (comma); they are put in place with 打つ or 付ける: 句読点を打つ. Note the reading: 読 is read とう here. In a broader sense the word can also include other punctuation marks. In some technical and official documents, the marks "．，" are used instead of "。、".

examples[].german: I published a research book with detailed bibliographic information attached.
I checked the book's bibliographic information in the library search system.
He compiled a bibliography of Sōseki studies.
en.notes: 書誌 designates a bibliography in the sense of a list of books on an author or topic, but also the description of books themselves; the discipline is called 書誌学. It most often appears in compounds such as 書誌情報 or 書誌データ "bibliographic data" (author, title, publisher, year), for example in library catalogs. The list of references at the end of a paper, by contrast, is called 参考文献.

examples[].german: His book collection exceeds ten thousand volumes.
This library boasts a collection of about 500,000 volumes.
Every time I move, I'm troubled by how many books I own.
en.notes: 蔵書 are the books owned by a person or an institution, both a private book collection and the holdings of a library. Typical: 蔵書が〜冊ある, 〜冊の蔵書を誇る, 蔵書を整理する. Derivatives: 蔵書家 "book collector", 蔵書印 "ownership stamp", 蔵書検索 "catalog search". The word is neutral to elevated; in everyday speech one also simply says 持っている本.

examples[].german: New economic measures were decided at the cabinet meeting.
The government approved a new policy by cabinet decision.
After the cabinet meeting, the Chief Cabinet Secretary held a press conference.
en.notes: 閣議 is the meeting of the Japanese cabinet (内閣) chaired by the prime minister; regular meetings (定例閣議) take place on Tuesday and Friday mornings. Very common is 閣議決定 ("cabinet decision"), also as a する-verb: 〜を閣議決定する. The ministers are called 閣僚. Typical news language: 閣議で決定する, 閣議後の記者会見.

examples[].german: The suspect was taken into custody.
The police are continuing to interrogate the suspect.
A suspect has the right to appoint defense counsel.
en.notes: 被疑者 is the technical term for a person suspected of a crime before charges are filed; after indictment, the person becomes a 被告人. Newspapers and TV almost always say 容疑者 instead of 被疑者, whereas 被疑者 is the language of the police, the judiciary and statutes. Typical: 被疑者を逮捕する, 被疑者の取り調べ, 被疑者の身柄を拘束する.

examples[].german: The secondhand book bore the ownership stamp of its former owner.
All the books in the library carry a library stamp.
My grandfather loved to use an ownership stamp he had carved himself.
en.notes: 蔵書印 is a stamp with which an owner or a library marks books as its property; it is pressed with 押す: 蔵書印を押す. A pasted-in bookplate sheet, by contrast, is called 蔵書票. In book research, 蔵書印 are important because they show whose hands an old book has passed through. The word belongs to the technical language of libraries and antiquarian bookshops.

examples[].german: With pocket paperbacks, you can read masterpieces at affordable prices.
There is a small class library at the back of the classroom.
That novel is said to come out as a paperback next month.
en.notes: 文庫 has two main meanings: a book collection or library (学級文庫 "class library", also in names like 東洋文庫) and, as the short form of 文庫本, the small Japanese paperback in A6 format. Publishers' series are also called this, for example 岩波文庫. 文庫化 means that a book first published in hardcover (単行本) comes out as a paperback. 新書 is another, somewhat taller format, mostly for nonfiction.

examples[].german: A new-format edition of Natsume Sōseki's complete works has been released.
I borrowed the complete works of Miyazawa Kenji from the university library.
This CD is the complete set of Beethoven's symphonies.
en.notes: 全集 is the complete edition of all of an author's works (漱石全集) or a comprehensive series on a subject (世界文学全集, 美術全集); it often stands as a suffix directly after the name. By contrast, 選集 contains only a selection, and 著作集 contains collected writings without claiming to be complete. In music, too, one speaks of e.g. 交響曲全集 "the complete symphonies".

examples[].german: Her work was also included in the anthology of modern poetry.
The complete works were too expensive, so I started with a selected edition first.
To mark the fiftieth anniversary of his death, a selection of the poet's works was compiled.
en.notes: 選集 is a selected edition: chosen works of one author (〜選集) or an anthology on a theme. The counterpart is 全集 "complete works"; collections by several authors are now often also called アンソロジー. Typical: 選集を編む "to compile a selection", 選集に収録される. Caution: 選集 sounds exactly like 先週 "last week"; in classical texts the spelling 撰集 is also found.

examples[].german: Her first poetry collection received high praise.
The Man'yōshū is Japan's oldest waka collection.
In music class, we sang in chorus while looking at the songbook.
en.notes: 歌集 is above all a collection of 和歌 or 短歌 (poems in the 5-7-5-7-7 pattern), whether a classical anthology such as the 万葉集 or the volume of a modern tanka poet. To be distinguished: 句集 "haiku collection" and 詩集 "poetry volume" with free, modern verse. In addition, 歌集 can designate a songbook with lyrics and music, for example at school. 処女歌集 means "one's first own tanka volume".

examples[].german: Publishing a haiku collection is the dream of every haiku poet.
I read Bashō's haiku collection and looked up the seasonal words.
My grandmother self-published her first haiku collection at eighty.
en.notes: 句集 is a collection of haiku (俳句), each counted as one 句; senryū collections can also be called this. Haiku poets (俳人) typically publish their works as a 句集; one says 句集を出す, 句集を編む. Counterparts are 歌集 for tanka and 詩集 for modern poetry. Many amateur poets bring out their 句集 through self-publishing (自費出版).

examples[].german: The author's collected letters offer a glimpse of the creative process.
The prime minister sent a letter to the president.
This is a letter that Sōseki addressed to one of his disciples.
en.notes: 書簡 is the formal, literary word for "letter"; in everyday speech one says 手紙. It appears in diplomacy (首相に書簡を送る, 公開書簡 "open letter"), in literary studies (書簡集 "collection of letters", 書簡体小説 "epistolary novel") and in official contexts. A personal letter from a head of state is called 親書. One says 書簡を送る, 書簡を宛てる, 書簡を交わす.

examples[].german: The Tosa Diary is regarded as the pioneer of diary literature.
In the Heian period, many works of diary literature were written by women.
The appeal of diary literature lies in the fact that the movements of the author's heart are depicted in detail.
en.notes: 日記文学 is a genre term in Japanese literary history for literarily shaped diaries, above all from the Heian period: 土佐日記, 蜻蛉日記, 紫式部日記, 更級日記. They were mostly written in kana, often by court ladies, and contain recollections, poems and partly invented elements; they are thus not mere records like a private 日記. The term appears mainly in school and literary studies.

examples[].german: The defendant pleaded not guilty.
At the trial, the defendant was questioned.
The presiding judge asked the defendant whether he had anything to say at the end.
en.notes: 被告人 is the defendant in a criminal trial, i.e. the person against whom charges (起訴) have been filed; before that, the person is called 被疑者 or, in the media, 容疑者. Not to be confused with 被告 ("defendant" in a civil suit, the opposing party of the 原告); however, the media also often shorten it to 被告 in criminal trials and attach it to the name (山田被告). Typical: 被告人質問, 被告人に判決を言い渡す.

examples[].german: The boundary between pure literature and popular literature is becoming blurred.
The Naoki Prize is the best-known award for popular literature.
Historical novels and detective novels are classified as popular literature.
en.notes: 大衆文学 is literature for a broad audience with a focus on entertainment: historical novels, crime fiction, romance. The opposite is 純文学 "pure, artistic literature"; the most important prize for 大衆文学 is the 直木賞, for 純文学 the 芥川賞. Today in everyday speech one often says エンタメ小説; the older 通俗小説 sounds pejorative.

examples[].german: The Akutagawa Prize is an award given to new writers of pure literature.
Serious literature seems difficult, and I can hardly bring myself to try it.
She is a writer who writes both serious literature and popular novels.
en.notes: 純文学 designates artistically ambitious literature in which language and inner life matter more than plot and entertainment. The opposite is 大衆文学 or 大衆小説, or today エンタメ小説. The distinction is reflected in the prizes: the 芥川賞 is for 純文学, the 直木賞 for popular literature. Typical are 純文学作家 and 純文学を読む; the word sounds somewhat elevated and is often also used slightly ironically for "heavy fare".

examples[].german: Her debut work sent shock waves through the literary world.
He made his debut in the literary world at twenty.
The writer disliked socializing in literary circles and lived in the countryside.
en.notes: 文壇 designates the literary world as a social community of writers, critics and publishers, the literary scene. Typical: 文壇にデビューする, 文壇に登場する, 文壇の大御所 "grand old figure of the literary scene". Following the same pattern there are 画壇 (painting), 歌壇 (tanka) and 論壇 (journalism and commentary). The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned but is common in arts pages and literary history.

examples[].german: The literary giants of the Meiji era contributed to the formation of modern Japanese.
Many literary giants once stayed at this inn.
The great Russian writer Tolstoy wrote "War and Peace".
en.notes: 文豪 is an honorific expression for a great, universally recognized writer, usually a classic such as 夏目漱石 or トルストイ. It is hardly used for living authors or newcomers; neutral are 作家 or 小説家. Typical combinations: 明治の文豪, ロシアの文豪, 文豪ゆかりの宿 "an inn associated with a great writer".

examples[].german: He continued his writing activities throughout his life.
Since retiring, he has devoted himself to writing.
I wrote "writer" in the occupation field of the form.
en.notes: 著述 is the writing of books, especially nonfiction and scholarly books, as well as the resulting work. Typical: 著述活動 "writing activity", 著述に専念する, 著述業 as an occupational title "freelance author". 執筆 refers rather to the writing of a specific text, 著書 to an author's finished book. As a transitive する-verb (〜を著述する) it is rare; usually the noun is used.

examples[].german: I am currently starting work on a new book.
The author of this article is a former newspaper reporter.
She writes an essay for a magazine every month.
en.notes: 執筆 is writing a text for publication - a novel, article, column - and sounds more formal than 書く. Typical: 〜の執筆に取りかかる, 執筆中, 原稿を執筆する, 雑誌に執筆する "to write for a magazine". Derivatives: 執筆者 "author, writer", 執筆活動. For private letters or notes, one does not say 執筆 but simply 書く.

examples[].german: He depicts everyday life in a detached style.
The author recounts his failures in a style full of humor.
Calligraphy works written with powerful brushstrokes are on display.
en.notes: 筆致 is the "touch" of a work: originally the brushwork in calligraphy and painting, figuratively the tone and the way a text is written. A descriptive adjective almost always comes before it: 軽妙な筆致 "light-footed style", 淡々とした筆致, 力強い筆致, and usually で描く / でつづる follows. In contrast to 文体, which describes the linguistic form, 筆致 emphasizes the impression and attitude; the word is typical of reviews.

en.meaning: laying down one's pen; finishing writing
examples[].german: Illness forced him to lay down his pen.
With this, I lay down my pen.
It was only near dawn that he finally put down his pen.
en.notes: 擱筆 (擱 "to put down", 筆 "brush") means to lay down the pen, that is, to stop writing, mostly at the end of a letter, preface or essay: 以上をもって擱筆する "with this I end my remarks". More rarely it means to give up writing altogether. The word is very literary and intransitive; the opposite is 起筆. Distinguish: 脱稿 "to finish a manuscript" and 絶筆 "last work before death".

en.meaning: last work; final piece of writing
examples[].german: The unfinished final work was published posthumously.
This painting became the painter's last work.
This letter, written on his sickbed, became his last piece of writing.
en.notes: 絶筆 is the last work that a writer, painter or calligrapher created before his death; the typical phrase is 〜が絶筆となる "became his last work". More rarely it means to give up writing altogether. Related are 遺稿 "posthumous manuscripts" and 遺作 "last, often posthumously published work"; 絶筆 emphasizes that nothing was produced afterwards.

examples[].german: The bereaved family organized the posthumous manuscripts and published them.
An unpublished manuscript was found in the study.
After his death, a collection of his posthumous writings was published.
en.notes: 遺稿 are manuscripts left behind by a deceased person that remained unpublished during his lifetime; collected, they appear as 遺稿集. Typical: 遺稿を整理する, 遺稿が見つかる, 遺稿を出版する. Distinguish: 遺作 "last work" (also paintings, films), 絶筆 "the last thing written". Beware, many homophones: 以降, 意向, 移行.

examples[].german: A confession obtained by coercion has no evidentiary value.
The suspect confessed to the crime during interrogation.
At trial, the defendant retracted his confession and claimed innocence.
en.notes: 自白 is a confession, above all in criminal proceedings; as a する-verb it is transitive: 犯行を自白する. Typical combinations: 自白を強要する ("to force"), 自白を引き出す, 自白を翻す ("to retract a confession"). Close in meaning is 白状する, which is more colloquial and also covers everyday matters ("to confess, admit"); 告白, by contrast, is a confession of feelings or secrets, such as a declaration of love.

examples[].german: I had someone ghostwrite the speech manuscript for me.
I wrote a letter on behalf of my visually impaired grandmother.
Many celebrity autobiographies are said to be ghostwritten.
en.notes: 代筆 means to write something in place of another: a letter for someone who cannot write, a form, or a speech or a book as a ghostwriter. Transitive: 手紙を代筆する; one asks for it with 代筆を頼む or 代筆してもらう. For professional ghostwriting one also says ゴーストライター. With signatures and official documents, 代筆 can be legally delicate.

examples[].german: Rhyming at the end of a poem creates a musical effect.
This song's lyrics rhyme, so they are easy to remember.
In Chinese poems, characters of the same rhyme class are placed at the end of lines.
en.notes: 韻 is rhyme and occurs almost always in the set phrase 韻を踏む "to rhyme"; the technical term for it is 押韻. In Chinese phonology, 韻 also designates the rhyming final of a character, according to which characters are divided into rhyme classes, which is important for 漢詩. In compounds, 韻 also stands for aftersound or mood: 余韻 "lingering resonance", 韻律 "meter".

examples[].german: I'm taking a lecture on the history of Japanese literature.
This work is a masterpiece that will go down in literary history.
I learned authors and work titles from the literary history textbook.
en.notes: 文学史 is the history of literature as a subject and as an account: 日本文学史, 文学史の講義, 文学史の教科書. A common phrase is 文学史に残る "to go down in literary history" or 文学史に名を残す. The word is neutral and familiar from school; in Japanese language class in Japan, one learns authors, works and periods in the subject 文学史.

examples[].german: Learning the methods of literary criticism deepens one's understanding of works.
He is a novelist and at the same time known for his sharp literary criticism.
That critique discusses the work in connection with social problems.
en.notes: 文芸批評 is literary criticism as a discipline and as a text form that interprets and evaluates works. Synonymous and today somewhat more common is 文芸評論; the person who writes it is a 批評家 or 評論家. The review of a single new publication, on the other hand, is called 書評 "book review". Typical: 文芸批評の手法, 文芸批評を書く, 〜の文芸批評で知られる.

examples[].german: I infer the meaning of a word from its context.
That remark was taken out of context.
I think about Japanese diplomacy within its historical context.
en.notes: 文脈 is first of all the linguistic context of a text: 文脈から意味を推測する, 文脈に合わない. In a broader sense it means the background or circumstances of a matter: 歴史的な文脈, 〜という文脈で語られる. A common criticism is 文脈を無視して切り取る "to take out of context". Close in meaning are コンテキスト, 前後関係 and 脈絡 (more "logical coherence": 脈絡のない話).

examples[].german: I was moved by the meaningful words.
Grandfather's words are short but rich in meaning.
This poem seems simple at first glance, but it has great depth.
en.notes: 含蓄 is the deeper, unspoken content of words or texts, what resonates between the lines. It is positive and appears almost always in fixed combinations: 含蓄のある言葉 "suggestive, meaningful words", 含蓄に富む, 含蓄が深い. To be distinguished is 含み (含みのある言い方), which rather means a hidden intention or hint. The word is literary and elevated.

examples[].german: A political allegory is hidden in this story.
Each of Aesop's fables carries an instructive moral.
The hourglass painted in the picture is said to be an allegory of the brevity of life.
en.notes: 寓意 is the real message hidden in a story, picture or symbol: "allegory", "moral", "allegorical meaning". Typical are 寓意が込められている／隠されている, 寓意を読み取る and 寓意的な作品. Related is 寓話 "fable, parable" as a text genre; 比喩 is any figurative expression (metaphor, simile), without a lesson necessarily lying behind it. Literary, especially in literary and art criticism.

examples[].german: Writing full of wit entertains readers.
In Sōseki's novels, even sharp social criticism is studded with humor.
He lightened the mood in the hall with a speech laced with wit.
en.notes: 諧謔 is an elevated, literary expression for witty jokes, banter and humorous irony. Typical are 諧謔に富む, 諧謔を交える, 諧謔精神 and 諧謔的な文体. In everyday speech one says ユーモア or 冗談 instead; 諧謔 appears mainly in literary criticism and demanding texts and sounds more intellectual, often with a touch of self-irony or satire. It is practically always written in kanji.

examples[].german: A melancholy melody creates the atmosphere of the work.
A certain wistfulness hangs over the harbor town at dusk.
His back conveyed the pathos of a man who had just reached retirement.
en.notes: 哀愁 is a quiet, wistful sadness that is perceived more as a mood or aura than as acute pain. Typical combinations are 哀愁が漂う, 哀愁を帯びる, 哀愁を感じる and 哀愁のある声. Unlike 悲しみ (concrete grief), 哀愁 often has an aesthetic, almost beautiful overtone; 郷愁 is specifically longing for home or the past. Somewhat elevated, used in descriptions of music, film and moods; jokingly also 背中に哀愁が漂う about tired men.

examples[].german: Poems rich in lyrical feeling resonate in readers' hearts.
Her songs captivate many fans with their lyrical melodies.
In class, we learned about the difference between epic and lyric poetry.
en.notes: 叙情 designates the expression of personal feelings and moods in poetry, music or painting, the "lyrical" in the sense of the emotional. It mostly appears in compounds: 叙情詩 "lyric poem", 叙情的 "lyrical, emotional", 叙情豊か. The opposite is 叙事 "factual narration of events" (叙事詩 "epic"). The original spelling is 抒情; 叙情 is the replacement spelling in use today; both are correct. Literary, from literary and art criticism.

examples[].german: The suspect exercised the right to remain silent.
Before the interrogation, the police officer informed him that he had the right to remain silent.
When my mother was asked her age, she said with a laugh, "I'll exercise my right to remain silent."
en.notes: 黙秘権 is the right of the suspect or defendant to refuse to testify; fixed combinations are 黙秘権を行使する and 黙秘権を告知する (advisement by the police or court). The silence itself is called 黙秘 (黙秘する, 完全黙秘). In everyday speech one jokingly says 黙秘権を行使します or simply 黙秘します when one does not want to answer an uncomfortable question.

examples[].german: The ability to accurately analyze complex sentence structures is required.
In exam English, you often memorize important constructions together with example sentences.
The program doesn't run because it contains a syntax error.
en.notes: 構文 is the structure of a sentence or a fixed grammatical construction. In school teaching, 構文 often means sentence patterns such as "so ... that" in English (英語の構文を覚える). In linguistics and computer science it stands for "syntax": 構文解析 "parsing", 構文エラー "syntax error". Distinction: 文法 is grammar as a whole, 文型 a sentence pattern or sentence type, 文体 style. Neutral to technical.

examples[].german: If you trace the etymology of this word, you end up at Latin.
The origin of "arigatō" is said to be the old "arigatashi" (hard to come by).
Knowing the origin of a word makes it easier to remember.
en.notes: 語源 is the origin of an individual word or expression. Typical are 語源をたどる／調べる, 〜の語源は…だ, …に語源がある, as well as 語源説 "theory about a word's origin" and 語源学 "etymology (as a field)". 由来 and 起源 are more general and also apply to customs, names or the origin of life; 語源 refers only to words. Neutral and also common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: Conjugated forms are made by attaching affixes to the verb stem.
In "takai", "taka" is the stem and "i" is the inflectional ending.
A na-adjective modifies a noun by attaching "na" to its stem.
en.notes: 語幹 is the unchanging part of an inflectable word; the changing part is called 活用語尾 "inflectional ending" (語尾 for short). In Japanese school grammar, for example, the stem of 高い is 高, of 静かだ it is 静か. Not to be confused with 語根 "root" (etymological core) and 語源 "word origin". A technical grammar term, neutral.

examples[].german: "O" and "go" are typical Japanese prefixes.
"Fu", "mu" and "hi" are prefixes that express negation.
The English "un-" is a prefix that reverses the meaning of a word.
en.notes: 接頭辞 is the linguistic word for "prefix", that is, an element that comes before a word, like お／ご or the negations 不・無・非・未. In school grammar 接頭語 is also common; both mean practically the same. The counterpart is 接尾辞 "suffix". Typical phrases: 接頭辞が付く／接頭辞を付ける.

examples[].german: "Teki" is a suffix attached to nouns.
"Tachi" and "san", which refer to people, are also a kind of suffix.
In English, adding the suffix "-ness" turns a word into a noun.
en.notes: 接尾辞 is the technical word for "suffix", an element that attaches to the end of a word: 的, 化, 性 make new words from nouns, さん・様・たち attach to names or persons. In school grammar there is also 接尾語 with the same meaning. The counterpart is 接頭辞 "prefix". One says 接尾辞が付く or 名詞に接尾辞を付ける.

examples[].german: Colloquial and literary language differ in grammar.
In classical Japanese textbooks, a translation into modern Japanese is given next to the original text.
"Jan" is colloquial, so you should not use it in reports.
en.notes: 口語 has two meanings: "spoken colloquial language" and, in the history of language, "modern Japanese" in contrast to the classical 文語. Typical are 口語的な表現, 口語体 and 口語訳 "rendering of a classical text into modern Japanese". In everyday speech, one rather says 話し言葉 for spoken language; 口語 is the more technical term. Neutral to technical.

examples[].german: We decipher classics written in classical literary language.
The Meiji Constitution is written in classical literary language and is therefore hard for people today to read.
In high school classics class, I learned classical grammar from scratch.
en.notes: 文語 means above all the classical written language based on Heian-period Japanese, which was used for laws, newspapers and literature until the Meiji period (文語体, 文語文法). The opposite is 口語 "modern (spoken) Japanese". For "written language" in the modern sense, that is, the written style of present-day texts, one rather says 書き言葉. A technical term, literary.

examples[].german: Many people are bilingual in the standard language and a dialect.
Since moving to Tokyo, I've been trying to speak standard Japanese.
News announcers are trained to read with standard-language accent.
en.notes: 標準語 is the standardized language; in Japanese it is the standard variety based on the speech of Tokyo. The opposite is 方言 "dialect"; typical are 標準語で話す and 標準語に直す. Specialists and NHK prefer to speak of 共通語 today, because 標準語 sounds like a prescribed "correct" language; in everyday speech, however, 標準語 is the more common word. Neutral.

en.meaning: common language, lingua franca, standard language
examples[].german: English functions as an international common language.
Even students from the provinces speak standard Japanese in class.
In multi-ethnic states, a common language that connects different ethnic groups is needed.
en.notes: 共通語 has two meanings: a lingua franca between speakers of different languages (e.g. 国際共通語としての英語) and the standard variety of Japanese understood nationwide. In the second meaning, it is the more neutral technical term for what is called 標準語 in everyday speech: it describes the language actually used in common, without a claim to a norm. The opposite is 方言. Neutral, common in the media and linguistics.

examples[].german: Because of the influence of one's native language, the pronunciation of a foreign language can be difficult.
His native language is Spanish, but he also speaks Japanese almost perfectly.
All the instructors of this course are native speakers of English.
en.notes: 母語 is the language one first acquired as a child. It is deliberately distinguished from 母国語 "language of one's home country", because 母国語 equates country and language, which often does not fit multilingual people or children of immigrants. Linguistics and education therefore prefer 母語; in everyday speech both are heard. Common: 母語話者 "native speaker" (colloquially ネイティブ). Neutral to technical.

examples[].german: The court issued an arrest warrant.
The police obtained a warrant and searched the man's home.
It is not permitted to search the contents of a smartphone without a warrant.
en.notes: 令状 is a written order, today above all the court order in criminal proceedings: 逮捕令状 (usually shortened to 逮捕状 "arrest warrant"), 捜索令状 ("search warrant"). Typical verbs: 令状を請求する ("to apply for", by the police or prosecution), 令状を出す/発付する (by the court), 令状を示す. 令状なしで means "without a warrant". Historically, 召集令状 was the draft notice (colloquially 赤紙).

examples[].german: Wago are words native to the Japanese language.
"Hajimeru" is a native Japanese word, and "kaishi suru" is the Sino-Japanese word with the same meaning.
Using many native Japanese words gives a text a softer impression.
en.notes: 和語 (also やまとことば) are the originally Japanese words that were not borrowed from Chinese or other languages; in kanji they are mostly written with the kun reading (山, 話す, 美しい) or in hiragana. Together with 漢語 and 外来語 they form the three layers of the vocabulary. 和語 sound softer and more everyday, 漢語 more concise and formal; there are often pairs like 決める／決定する. A technical term from linguistics and language teaching.

examples[].german: Sino-Japanese words are often used in technical terminology.
Sino-Japanese words are read with the on reading and give a stiffer impression than native words.
In texts for children, difficult Sino-Japanese words are avoided as much as possible.
en.notes: 漢語 are words of Chinese origin or kanji compounds formed on the Chinese pattern with the on reading (勉強, 経済, 開始). Words coined in Japan, such as 哲学, also count; they are called 和製漢語. 漢語 sound more formal and concise than 和語 and dominate technical, official and newspaper language. Rarely, 漢語 also means "the Chinese language"; today one says 中国語 for that. A technical term, neutral.

examples[].german: "Keshigomu" is a hybrid word mixing a native Japanese word and a loanword.
The Japanese vocabulary can be divided by origin into four groups: native, Sino-Japanese, loanwords and hybrid words.
Hybrid words such as "haburashi" (toothbrush) and "shōene" (energy saving) also come up often in everyday conversation.
en.notes: 混種語 is a term in the Japanese classification of words by origin (語種): the vocabulary is divided into 和語 (native), 漢語 (Sino-Japanese), 外来語 (Western loanwords) and 混種語. A 混種語 is composed of parts of different origins, for example 消し＋ゴム or 歯＋ブラシ. The word appears almost only in textbooks, grammar explanations and linguistics.

examples[].german: "Mujun" (contradiction) is an idiom derived from an old Chinese anecdote.
In Japanese class, we researched and presented the origins of idioms from classical stories.
"Dasoku" (a superfluous addition) and "gojippo hyappo" (six of one, half a dozen of the other) are also commonly used idioms from old stories.
en.notes: 故事成語 are fixed expressions that go back to an incident or story from ancient China (故事 "handed-down story" + 成語 "set phrase"), such as 矛盾, 蛇足, 五十歩百歩 or 四面楚歌. They partly overlap with 四字熟語 but differ from ことわざ (folk proverbs) and 慣用句 (idioms without a clear source). Typical is 故事成語の由来を調べる; the word belongs to school teaching and educated language.

en.meaning: homophone; word with the same sound
examples[].german: Japanese has a great many homophones.
"Kōen" (park) and "kōen" (lecture) are homophones, so when speaking you tell them apart from context.
Because there are so many homophones, it is easy to make conversion errors on a computer.
en.notes: 同音異義語 are words with the same pronunciation (the same kana spelling) but different meanings and usually different kanji, e.g. 公園／講演／後援. Because of the many Sino-Japanese words, Japanese is especially rich in them, which makes puns (だじゃれ) possible and easily leads to errors in kana-to-kanji conversion. Related terms: 同訓異字 "same kun reading, different kanji" (会う／合う) and 多義語 "a word with several meanings". Technical term, neutral.

en.meaning: synonym; word with a similar meaning
examples[].german: I understand the subtle differences in nuance between synonyms.
"Utsukushii" and "kirei" are synonyms, but they are used a little differently.
When the same word keeps recurring in a report, I look for alternatives in a thesaurus.
en.notes: 類義語 are words with a similar but not completely identical meaning, such as 上がる／登る. 同義語, by contrast, means words that are strictly identical in meaning; in language teaching 類義語 is usually used, because true synonyms are rare. The opposite term is 対義語 or 反対語 "antonym". A thesaurus is called 類語辞典 or 類義語辞典. Neutral, from linguistics and teaching.

examples[].german: The antonym of "good" is "evil".
What is the opposite of "agaru" (to rise)?
This dictionary lists not only synonyms but also antonyms.
en.notes: 対義語 is the word for "antonym"; equivalent are 反対語 (more everyday) and 反意語／反義語 (technical). The opposite term is 類義語 or 同義語 "synonym". A typical question: 〜の対義語は何ですか. The word often appears in dictionaries and exam questions; in conversation people usually just say 反対の言葉.

examples[].german: The phonological system of Japanese is relatively simple.
Ancient Japanese had phonological distinctions that no longer exist today.
He is studying Japanese phonology in graduate school.
en.notes: 音韻 refers to the sounds of a language as a system of meaning-distinguishing units, i.e. the phonological level. It mostly appears in compounds: 音韻論 "phonology", 音韻体系 "sound system", 音韻変化 "sound change". Distinctions: 音声 concerns the sounds as actually articulated, the physical sounds (音声学 "phonetics"), while 音素 is the single smallest unit of this system. Technical term; hardly used in everyday life.

examples[].german: Japanese is classified as an open-syllable language.
"Nippon" has two syllables, but counted in morae it has four.
When you learn English words, try pronouncing them syllable by syllable.
en.notes: 音節 is the syllable as a phonetic unit made up of a vowel as the nucleus and possibly surrounding consonants. For Japanese, the distinction from 拍 (mora) is important: long vowels, ん and the small っ each form a mora of their own, but not a syllable of their own – とうきょう has two syllables but four morae. Typical terms are 開音節 "open syllable" (ends in a vowel), 閉音節 "closed syllable" and 一音節ずつ. Technical term, also used neutrally in language teaching.

examples[].german: The police are pushing ahead with the investigation of the case.
The police launched an investigation on suspicion of fraud.
With few clues to the culprit, the investigation is struggling.
en.notes: 捜査 is a criminal investigation by the police or prosecution; as a する-verb it is transitive: 事件を捜査する. Common combinations: 捜査を進める, 捜査に乗り出す ("to launch an investigation"), 捜査が難航する ("to stall"), 捜査線上に浮かぶ ("to come under the investigators' scrutiny"). Not to be confused with 捜索 ("search" for persons or things) and 調査 ("investigation, survey" without criminal connection); 操作 ("operation, handling") sounds the same.

examples[].german: The distinction between phonemes varies from language to language.
In English r and l are different phonemes, but in Japanese they are not distinguished.
"Kasa" and "kata" differ in only a single phoneme.
en.notes: 音素 is the smallest meaning-distinguishing sound unit of a language, e.g. /k/ or /a/. Whether two sounds are different 音素 is shown by minimal pairs such as かさ／かた. Distinctions: 音節 is the syllable, 拍 the mora, 音韻 the sound system as a whole; 形態素, by contrast, is the smallest meaning-bearing unit. Purely a technical term of linguistics.

examples[].german: The rhythm of Japanese is based on morae.
In a waltz, one measure consists of three beats.
After pausing for a beat, he answered slowly.
en.notes: 拍 is the "beat" in a musical measure and also the linguistic term for the mora, the basic rhythmic unit of Japanese; it also serves as a counter (三拍, 四拍). In Japanese every kana, including ん, っ and a long vowel, counts as one 拍: きって has three 拍. In linguistics one also says モーラ. Well-known derivations are 拍手 "applause" and 拍子 "beat, rhythm"; the phrase 一拍置く means "to pause briefly".

examples[].german: Chinese is a tonal language with four tones.
If you get the tone wrong, the word takes on a completely different meaning.
Vietnamese has six tones, more than Chinese.
en.notes: 声調 refers in linguistics to the meaning-distinguishing pitch contour of a syllable in tonal languages such as Chinese, Thai or Vietnamese (声調言語 "tonal language"). Japanese, by contrast, has no 声調 but a pitch accent at word level (アクセント). The older meaning "tone of voice" is rare and literary. For sentence melody one says イントネーション or 抑揚. Technical term, written language.

examples[].german: The accent patterns differ between the Tokyo and Kansai dialects.
His Japanese has a slight French accent.
I added an accent to the white shirt with a red scarf.
en.notes: In Japanese, アクセント mainly means the pitch accent of a word (高低アクセント): 箸 and 橋 differ only in their アクセント. In English, by contrast, it means stress accent (強弱アクセント). A foreign-language accent is also called アクセント; for the regional coloring of a dialect, one more often says 訛り. In fashion and design it means "accent, eye-catcher": アクセントをつける. Neutral.

examples[].german: In questions the intonation rises.
He is from Kansai, and you can tell from his intonation even when he speaks standard Japanese.
Depending on the intonation, "sō desu ka" can sound surprised or sarcastic.
en.notes: イントネーション is the pitch movement over a whole sentence or utterance, such as the rise at the end of a question. It differs from the アクセント, which fixes the pitch within a single word. In everyday use, however, イントネーション is also used loosely for the typical speech melody of a dialect (関西のイントネーション). A Japanese synonym is 抑揚 "intonation, modulation". Neutral.

examples[].german: Morphological analysis is the foundation of natural language processing.
"Tabesaserareta" can be divided into several morphemes.
"Hondana" (bookshelf) is made up of the two morphemes "hon" and "tana".
en.notes: 形態素 is the smallest meaning-bearing unit of a language: 食べさせられた, for example, consists of 食べ, させ, られ and た. To be distinguished are 音素, the smallest meaning-distinguishing sound unit without a meaning of its own, and 単語, which can consist of several 形態素. Particularly well known is 形態素解析 "morphological analysis": since Japanese is written without spaces, programs use it to split texts into words. Technical term from linguistics and computer science.

examples[].german: Japanese is classified as an agglutinative language.
In agglutinative languages, units of meaning are strung together one after another, as in tabe-sase-rare-ta.
Turkish and Korean are also agglutinative languages, like Japanese.
en.notes: 膠着語 literally means "glued language" (膠 "glue", 着 "stick"): grammatical elements such as particles and auxiliary suffixes are attached one after another to an unchanging stem, and each usually carries only one function. These include Japanese, Korean, Turkish, Finnish and Hungarian. The opposite terms are 屈折語 "inflecting language" and 孤立語 "isolating language". Purely a technical term of linguistic typology.

examples[].german: Chinese is a representative example of an isolating language.
In isolating languages words do not change form, so grammatical relations are expressed by word order.
Vietnamese is also isolating; tense is indicated by a word placed before the verb.
en.notes: 孤立語 is a language whose words do not change form; grammatical relations are expressed by word order and separate function words. Classic examples are Chinese and Vietnamese. Not to be confused with a genetically isolated language with no known relatives, such as Basque – for that one says 孤立した言語. Together with 膠着語 and 屈折語 it forms the classic typology. Purely a technical term.

examples[].german: The suspect's case was referred to prosecutors on paper, without an arrest.
The arrested man was referred to prosecutors the next day.
The police referred the driver who caused the accident to the prosecutors.
en.notes: 送検 means that the police hand a case over to the public prosecutor's office, which then decides on indictment; in the news mostly in the passive: 容疑者が送検された. With 身柄送検, the arrested suspect is sent along; with 書類送検, only the files go to the prosecutor's office and the suspect remains at large. The word is the language of the police and media; in the law, the procedure is called 送致.

examples[].german: The basic word order in Japanese is SOV.
Word order in Japanese is relatively free: you can say 「昨日私は」 as well as 「私は昨日」.
When writing in English, a sentence becomes unintelligible if the word order is wrong.
en.notes: 語順 is the order of words or sentence elements. Typical are 語順が自由だ, 語順を入れ替える, 基本語順 and type labels such as SOV型／SVO型. In Japanese, particles mark the roles, so the order before the predicate is quite free; what is fixed, however, is that the predicate comes last and modifiers come first. Neutral, common in language teaching.

examples[].german: In Japanese, the predicate comes at the end of the sentence.
In the sentence "Zō wa hana ga nagai", "nagai" is the predicate.
In Japanese, not only verbs but also adjectives can form a predicate on their own.
en.notes: 述語 is the predicate, that is, the part of the sentence that says what the subject does, what it is like, or what it is: a verb, an adjective, or noun + だ. It forms a pair with 主語 (主語と述語, 主述関係); a common writing mistake is that 主語と述語がねじれている, that is, they do not match. In logic, 述語 stands for "predicate" as in 述語論理. A technical term from grammar and teaching.

examples[].german: In Japanese, the subject is often omitted.
This sentence has no subject, but from the context you can tell it is "I".
When you write long sentences, check whether the subject and predicate correspond.
en.notes: 主語 is the subject of a sentence; in Japanese it is usually marked with が and very often omitted when it is clear from the context. Important: は marks the topic (主題), not necessarily the subject - in 象は鼻が長い, 象 is the topic and 鼻 is the subject. Typical: 主語を省略する, 主語と述語. In internet slang, 主語が大きい means "to generalize too broadly" (e.g. "the Japanese" instead of "I"). Neutral, a grammar term.

examples[].german: A transitive verb is a verb that takes an object.
In 「パンを食べる」 the object is 「パン」.
In English the object is placed right after the verb.
en.notes: 目的語 is the object of a sentence; the direct object is marked in Japanese with を, the indirect object (間接目的語) usually with に. With some predicates the object takes が: 日本語がわかる, 水が飲みたい. Motion verbs with を such as 道を歩く or 空を飛ぶ, on the other hand, have no 目的語 in the strict sense; they remain intransitive. Grammatical term, neutral.

examples[].german: The modifier is placed before the word it modifies.
In 「赤い花」, 「赤い」 is the modifier that modifies 「花」.
If the modifiers are too long, the sentence becomes hard to understand.
en.notes: 修飾語 is a word or expression that describes another word (被修飾語) more closely. One distinguishes 連体修飾語, which modifies a noun (attribute: 赤い花), and 連用修飾語, which modifies a verb or adjective (adverbial: ゆっくり歩く). In Japanese the 修飾語 always comes before the word it modifies, even when it is a whole relative clause. Grammatical term, neutral.

examples[].german: 「開く（ひらく）」 can be used both as an intransitive and as a transitive verb.
「閉まる」 in 「窓が閉まる」 is an intransitive verb.
Pairs of intransitive and transitive verbs are a place where learners of Japanese often make mistakes.
en.notes: 自動詞 is the "intransitive verb", the counterpart of 他動詞. Japanese has many pairs: ドアが開く（あく）／ドアを開ける, 窓が閉まる／窓を閉める; the 自動詞 takes が and describes a process without an acting person. Caution: motion verbs such as 歩く or 渡る take を for the path (公園を歩く) and are still 自動詞. Some verbs such as 開く（ひらく） are both.

examples[].german: It is important to learn the correspondences between intransitive and transitive verbs.
「開ける」 in 「ドアを開ける」 is transitive, while 「開く」 in 「ドアが開く」 is intransitive.
In dictionaries, transitive verbs are often marked with the symbol 「他」.
en.notes: 他動詞 is a transitive verb that takes a direct object with を; its counterpart is 自動詞. Many verbs form pairs: 開ける／開く, 壊す／壊れる, 出す／出る – the 他動詞 emphasizes the agent, the 自動詞 the process. Note: verbs of moving through a space such as 道を歩く or 空を飛ぶ do take を but are 自動詞. In dictionaries 他動詞 is often marked with 他. Grammatical term.

examples[].german: Causative expressions mean making or letting someone do something.
The causative passive 「飲まされた」 expresses resentment at having been forced to drink.
In the past, cattle and horses were put to work in farming.
en.notes: 使役 is the causative in grammar, i.e. "to make or let someone do something": 使役形 (書かせる, 食べさせる), 使役文, 使役受身 (書かされる, 食べさせられる) for "to be forced to". The person who is to act is marked with に or を. The original meaning "to put someone to work" lives on in 使役する and 使役動物 "working animal", but it is literary and rare. Technical term.

examples[].german: The Japanese passive also has a usage called the adversative passive.
In negotiations you should not stay on the defensive but make proposals yourself.
In judo you begin with practicing how to fall.
en.notes: 受身 (also 受け身) is the passive in grammar: 受身形 (書かれる, 食べられる), 受身文. A Japanese particularity is 迷惑の受身, the indirect passive for inconveniences (雨に降られた, 隣の人にたばこを吸われた). Outside grammar, 受身 means "passive, defensive attitude" (受身になる, 受身の姿勢) and, in judo, "breakfall" (受身を取る). Neutral.

examples[].german: The first trial hearing is scheduled to be held next month.
The defendant admitted the charges at the first hearing.
Anyone can attend a public trial as a spectator.
en.notes: 公判 is the public main hearing in a criminal trial, after the indictment (起訴) and before the verdict. Very common in the news: 初公判 ("first hearing"), 公判が開かれる, 公判で起訴内容を認める/否認する. More general is 裁判 ("court proceedings", also civil); 公判 is a technical term of criminal procedure.

examples[].german: How the potential form is made differs depending on the verb group.
The potential form of 「話す」 is 「話せる」, and that of 「食べる」 is 「食べられる」.
Recently you often hear "ra-dropped" potential forms such as 「見れる」 too.
en.notes: 可能形 is the potential form of the verb: 書く→書ける, 食べる→食べられる, 来る→来られる, する→できる. The object often switches from を to が: 日本語が話せる. Colloquially widespread are ら抜き言葉 such as 見れる instead of 見られる, which are considered incorrect in formal texts. The term comes from Japanese-as-a-foreign-language teaching; school grammar speaks of 可能動詞 or the auxiliary verb られる.

examples[].german: The volitional form expresses the speaker's intention.
The volitional form of 「行く」 is 「行こう」, and that of 「食べる」 is 「食べよう」.
If you attach 「と思う」 to the volitional form, you can express plans, as in 「旅行しようと思う」.
en.notes: 意志形 (also 意向形) is the volitional form: 行く→行こう, 食べる→食べよう, する→しよう, 来る→来よう. On its own it means "let's ..." or "I will ..." (一緒に行こう); with と思う it expresses an intention (旅行しようと思う); with とする it means "to try" or "to be about to" (出かけようとしたとき). The term comes from Japanese-as-a-foreign-language teaching; school grammar speaks of 未然形＋う／よう.

examples[].german: The imperative is rarely used in everyday conversation.
「急げ」 and 「やめろ」 are imperatives and sound quite rough.
The traffic sign 「止まれ」 is a typical example of the use of the imperative.
en.notes: 命令形 is the imperative form: 書く→書け, 食べる→食べろ, する→しろ, 来る→来い. It sounds very direct and rough and in everyday life is used almost only among close friends, in sports, in emergencies, on signs (止まれ) or in quoted commands. Polite requests are formed with 〜てください or 〜なさい. In exams and instructions, the written variant ending in よ appears: 次の問いに答えよ. Grammatical term, also one of the six conjugation forms of school grammar.

examples[].german: The conditional form is used in sentence patterns that express conditions.
The conditional form of 「行く」 is 「行け」, and adding 「ば」 gives 「行けば」.
In classical grammar one learns the realis form (已然形) instead of the conditional form.
