The opposite term is 直音 (syllables with a normal-size kana). There is a risk of confusion when reading with syllable sequences like びよういん "beauty salon" versus びょういん "hospital".

en.meaning: seion; kana without dakuten (e.g. か, さ, た)
examples[].german: Distinguishing seion and dakuon is a basic point of Japanese.
If you add a dakuten to 「か」, the seion becomes the dakuon 「が」.
In rendaku, the first seion of the second word changes into a dakuon.
en.notes: 清音 are, in Japanese kana teaching, all syllables without dakuten (゛) or handakuten (゜), e.g. か, さ, た, は, but also あ, な, ま etc. It is therefore a writing term and not exactly the same as phonetic "voiceless": な and ま are voiced and are nevertheless 清音. The opposite terms are 濁音 (が, ざ, だ, ば) and 半濁音 (ぱ). In 連濁 the first 清音 of the second word becomes a 濁音 (ほん + たな → ほんだな).

examples[].german: Dakuon are written by adding a dakuten.
Many monster names, like Godzilla, begin with a dakuon.
In native Japanese words, a dakuon rarely comes at the beginning of a word.
en.notes: 濁音 are the syllables with dakuten (゛, colloquially てんてん): が, ざ, だ, ば and their series; phonetically they have a voiced consonant. The opposite terms are 清音 (か, さ, た, は) and 半濁音 (ぱ). The character is called 濁点, the sound 濁音. Genuine Japanese words (和語) rarely begin with a 濁音; many Japanese perceive 濁音 as "heavy, rough", which is why e.g. monster names often start with them.

examples[].german: Handakuon refers to the sounds of the 「ぱ」 row.
If you add a circle to 「は」, it becomes the handakuon 「ぱ」.
Excluding loanwords, many words beginning with a handakuon are onomatopoeia.
en.notes: 半濁音 are only the syllables of the ぱ-row (ぱ, ぴ, ぷ, ぺ, ぽ), written with the small circle 半濁点 (゜, colloquially まる). The name "half-voiced" is traditional; phonetically, p is actually voiceless. Originally Japanese words with a 半濁音 at the beginning are almost only onomatopoeia such as ぱらぱら or ぴかぴか; otherwise they occur mainly in loanwords and after っ or ん (いっぱい, さんぽ).

examples[].german: Assimilation can occur under the influence of adjacent sounds.
The 「ん」 assimilates to the following sound and is pronounced [m] in 「さんま」.
It takes time for immigrants to assimilate into local society.
en.notes: 同化 generally means "adjustment, assimilation" and, as a する-verb, is mostly intransitive: 社会に同化する "to assimilate into society", plus 同化政策 "assimilation policy". In phonetics it denotes the adjustment of a sound to its neighboring sounds, for instance when ん before m/b/p is pronounced as [m]. In biology 同化 stands for anabolism; the opposite term is in each case 異化.

examples[].german: Dissimilation is a phenomenon in which the succession of the same sound is avoided.
Inside the body, assimilation and catabolism are constantly taking place.
In Brecht's theater, the alienation effect is emphasized.
en.notes: 異化 is the opposite term to 同化. In phonetics it denotes dissimilation, i.e. the becoming unlike of identical or similar sounds. In biology 異化 means catabolism (breakdown); 同化 and 異化 together make up metabolism. In art and literary theory 異化 stands for "defamiliarization", known from 異化効果 (Brecht's alienation effect). The word is technical throughout.

examples[].german: In civil proceedings, the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff.
In criminal trials, the prosecution bears the burden of proof.
Some argue that in pollution lawsuits, companies should bear the burden of proof.
en.notes: 挙証責任 is the burden of proof: a party must prove a fact, otherwise it bears the disadvantage. Synonymous and somewhat more common is 立証責任; both are technical language. Typical: 挙証責任を負う, 挙証責任がある, 挙証責任の転換 ("reversal of the burden of proof"). In criminal proceedings, it lies in principle with the prosecution (検察側).

examples[].german: Historical novels require meticulous historical research.
The period research for this drama is handled by a university professor.
Based on an old picture scroll, I researched the clothing of the time.
en.notes: 考証 is the investigation of historical matters on the basis of evidence such as old documents, pictures or objects; as a する-verb, transitive: 衣装を考証する. Very common is 時代考証, the historical consultation for films, series and historical novels. In contrast to 検証 ("verification" in general), 考証 almost always relates to history and sources. Register: written, technical.

en.meaning: various versions of a text; all extant texts
examples[].german: Compare the various texts to establish the most accurate text.
Many different texts of the Heike Monogatari have been handed down.
It took ten years to sort out the lineage of the text versions.
en.notes: 諸本 is a word of textual philology: all the transmitted manuscripts, prints and editions of a particular work taken together, e.g. 平家物語の諸本. 諸 means "various, all", 本 here "copy, version". Typical combinations are 諸本を比較する, 諸本を校合する and 諸本の系統 (lines of transmission). A single deviating version is called 異本, a manuscript 写本.

examples[].german: I collated different manuscripts and examined the differences.
Collating it with the original turned up three errors.
Before transcribing a text, I make it a rule to collate it with several copies.
en.notes: 校合 (きょうごう, more rarely こうごう) is the comparison of a text with another version or the original in order to determine differences (異同) and errors; as a する-verb, transitive: 写本を校合する. It is a word of philology and publishing. Related are 校正 ("proofreading" of printer's proofs) and 校訂 (producing a critically cleaned text on the basis of the comparison).

examples[].german: The publisher and the publication date are noted in the colophon.
When citing, please check the year of publication on the colophon.
Looking at the colophon, this book was already in its tenth printing.
en.notes: 奥付 is the page at the end of a Japanese book with the bibliographic details: title, author, publisher, publication date, and edition and printing (e.g. 初版第三刷). It roughly corresponds to the imprint page, but it comes at the back (奥 means "far back, inside"). For references, you look up the publication year in the 奥付. Typical phrases: 奥付を見る, 奥付に記載されている.

examples[].german: A beautifully designed book is a joy to hold.
The design of this book was done by a famous designer.
The book got a new design when it was reissued as a paperback.
en.notes: 装丁 is the outer design of a book: binding, cover, dust jacket, typography and materials. It is also written 装幀 and 装釘; the designer is called 装丁家. As a transitive する-verb: 本を装丁する. It concerns the book as an object, not its content; for pictures within the text one says 挿絵, and for cover pictures 表紙絵 or カバーイラスト.

examples[].german: The illustrations enrich the world of the story.
As a child, I only read books with lots of illustrations.
He draws the illustrations for a serialized novel in the newspaper.
en.notes: 挿絵 are pictures inserted into a text, in books, newspaper serials or textbooks; 挿 means "to insert". Typical phrases: 挿絵を描く, 挿絵入りの本, 挿絵画家. The more everyday イラスト today is broader and means any illustration; 挿絵 sounds somewhat more traditional and stresses the connection to the text. A picture at the front of a book, on the other hand, is called 口絵.

examples[].german: A portrait of the author was printed in the frontispiece.
The first edition came with a brightly colored frontispiece.
This light novel introduces its characters on color pages at the start of the book.
en.notes: 口絵 is the picture or the picture pages at the very front of a book or magazine, often printed in color on better paper; the frontispiece. 口 here stands for "beginning, entrance". By contrast, 挿絵 are the illustrations within the text. Typical are カラー口絵 and 口絵に載る; in light novels, color 口絵 showing the characters are common.

examples[].german: The old character forms are also called 正字.
In the test, write the correct characters, not abbreviated forms.
This dictionary also gives the traditional form for the kanji in its headwords.
en.notes: 正字 is the "correct, standard character", in contrast to 誤字 (wrong character), 俗字 (popular form) and 略字 (abbreviated form). In Japanese usage, 正字 often means the traditional, unsimplified forms based on the Kangxi dictionary, i.e. in practice the 旧字体 such as 國 or 學. It follows that 正字 specifically does not refer to the standard form in common use today (新字体).

examples[].german: Abbreviated characters are handy when writing by hand.
Please do not use abbreviated forms in official documents.
Grandfather's notes are full of abbreviated characters and very hard to read.
en.notes: 略字 is a simplified, abbreviated form of a kanji, as it appears mainly in handwriting (e.g. the handwritten 门 for 門). Many of today's standard forms (新字体) developed from such 略字. In official documents and exams, non-standard 略字 are not considered correct; the opposite term is 正字. Rarely, 略字 also means "abbreviation, acronym".

examples[].german: Prewar books are printed in the old character forms.
The old form of 「国」 is 「國」.
Some people named Saitō use the old form 「齋」 in their family name.
en.notes: 旧字体 are the kanji forms that were standard in Japan until the script reform after World War II, e.g. 國 (now 国), 學 (学) or 體 (体). The opposite term is 新字体. You encounter them in prewar prints, on old signs and in family names (齋藤, 髙橋) that many people deliberately keep. They are not the same as traditional Chinese characters, but overlap with them a great deal.

examples[].german: Fines are paid into the national treasury.
The national treasury bears half of the cost of this project.
Property without heirs ultimately reverts to the national treasury.
en.notes: 国庫 is the state treasury, i.e. the state as the holder of public funds. Typical combinations: 国庫に納める/入る ("to flow into the treasury"), 国庫に返納する, 国庫に帰属する ("to revert to the state"), 国庫負担, 国庫補助金 ("state subsidy"). The word is official and written; in everyday speech one rather says 国のお金 or 税金. Not to be confused with 金庫 ("safe").

examples[].german: The new character forms were introduced by the postwar language reform.
The character 「學」 is written 「学」 in the new form.
Chinese simplified characters and Japanese shinjitai often look different.
en.notes: 新字体 are the simplified kanji forms introduced after the war with the 当用漢字 list and its table of character shapes (1949), and standard in Japan today, e.g. 学 instead of 學. The opposite term is 旧字体. Do not confuse them with Chinese simplified characters (簡体字): the two reforms often simplified differently, e.g. Japanese 広 versus Chinese 广.

examples[].german: I majored in Japanese literature and studied Heian literature.
My grandfather taught Japanese literature at university.
Recently, the name 日本文学 is often used instead of 国文学.
en.notes: 国文学 means both "Japanese literature" as a subject matter and the field of study "Japanese literary studies" (国文学科, 国文学を専攻する). As in 国語, 国 means "one's own country" from the Japanese point of view. Counterparts are 外国文学 and, for the language, 国語学. As with 日本語学, some universities now replace the name with 日本文学.

examples[].german: I learned the basics in the introduction to linguistics course.
As an overview of psychology, this book is very easy to understand.
I will first give an overview of the problem and then give specific examples.
en.notes: 概論 is an introductory overall survey of a subject and very often appears as a suffix in course and book titles: 言語学概論, 経済学概論. Unlike 入門 ("a start for beginners"), 概論 stresses the systematic overview; a 序論, by contrast, is the introduction to a single text. In curricula, the 概論 is often followed by the 各論. Use as a する-verb is rare.

examples[].german: After finishing the overview, we move on to the specific topics.
Many people are in favor of reforms in general but against each concrete measure.
Medical textbooks are divided into a general part and a specific part.
en.notes: 各論 is the individual treatment or the "special part" of a topic, point by point; the opposite term is 総論 ("general part"). Textbooks (e.g. law, medicine) are often divided into 総論 and 各論. A very well-known phrase is 総論賛成、各論反対: to be in favor in principle but against every concrete implementation. Typical are 各論に入る and 各論で議論する.

examples[].german: The general part presents the overall picture of the research.
I agree in general, but there are problems in the details.
This report stays at the general level and contains no concrete proposals.
en.notes: 総論 is the "general part" or overall treatment of a topic, as opposed to 各論, the individual questions. In specialist books the opening chapter is often called 総論 (民法総論, 総論部分). In discussions, 総論 is also used somewhat critically for statements that stay general, especially in 総論賛成、各論反対. Register: formal, administration, scholarship.

examples[].german: The aim and method of the research are stated in the introduction.
A thesis is structured in three parts: introduction, main body and conclusion.
The introduction is so long that it hardly gets to the point.
en.notes: 序論 is the introduction of a scholarly work or treatise, in which the research question, aim and method are set out; the classic structure is 序論・本論・結論. An author's foreword is more often called 序文 or まえがき, and in term papers はじめに is also common. 概論, on the other hand, is an overview of a whole field. Register: academic, written.

examples[].german: The abstract of the paper is to be summarized in no more than 300 characters.
The conference's book of abstracts contains the summaries of the presentations.
Parts of the writer's diary were excerpted and published in a magazine.
en.notes: 抄録 has two uses: the short version of an essay or talk (abstract), e.g. 論文の抄録 or 学会の抄録集, and copying or reproducing a text in excerpts, as a transitive する-verb: 日記を抄録する. In everyday speech one more often says 要約 or 要旨, and in the natural and medical sciences also アブストラクト. Register: technical, written.

examples[].german: A list of references is placed at the end of the paper.
Be sure to state your references in the report.
How to format references differs slightly depending on the field.
en.notes: 参考文献 are the sources one has consulted for a piece of work, and also the list of them at the end (bibliography). Typical: 参考文献を挙げる, 参考文献一覧, 参考文献リスト. In the narrower sense, 引用文献 are only the works quoted directly, while 参考文献 also includes literature that was merely consulted. Register: academic, but also common in school presentations.

examples[].german: Fixed asset tax is assessed by the municipality.
The electricity bill includes a renewable energy surcharge.
Japan's public pension is run on a pay-as-you-go basis.
en.notes: 賦課 is the official imposition of taxes, levies or fees; as a する-verb it is transitive: 税を賦課する. The authority is the subject, the levy the object. Well known are 賦課金 (e.g. 再エネ賦課金 on the electricity bill) and 賦課方式 (the pay-as-you-go system of pensions). Equivalent in meaning but more everyday are 課す and 課税する; 賦課 is purely administrative language.

examples[].german: Interdisciplinary research can sometimes produce new insights.
Environmental problems need to be tackled in an interdisciplinary way.
Next year, the university will get a new interdisciplinary faculty.
en.notes: 学際的 is a な-adjective: 学際的な研究, adverbially 学際的に取り組む. 学際 literally means "between the sciences" (際 = border, as in 国際). Similar in meaning but more colloquial are 分野横断的 or 分野を越えた; 総合的, by contrast, means more "comprehensive". Typical of university and research policy, e.g. 学際的なプロジェクト.

examples[].german: With his encyclopedic knowledge, he can answer any question.
In the lectures of the professor, who is known for his vast learning, the topics keep branching out one after another.
My grandfather was extremely well read and remembered every date in history.
en.notes: 博覧強記 is made up of 博覧 "having read a lot, widely read" and 強記 "a strong memory"; it means someone who has read a great deal and remembers everything, that is, enormous, encyclopedic knowledge. It is a laudatory, rather literary yojijukugo, typically used as 博覧強記の人, 博覧強記で知られる or 博覧強記を誇る, mostly about scholars and writers.

examples[].german: I was moved to see how splendidly my former student had grown up.
For the teacher's retirement celebration, his former students gathered from all over the country.
He was a student of mine in my university days.
en.notes: 教え子 is a pupil or student seen from the teacher's point of view, especially a former one: 私の教え子, 昔の教え子. Unlike 生徒 or 学生, it expresses the personal relationship with one's own teacher; 弟子, by contrast, stresses training under a master (art, craft, martial arts). The word always refers to a particular teacher: a teacher says 私の教え子, and about oneself one says 田中先生の教え子です.

en.meaning: debt of gratitude to one's teacher; scholarly patronage received
examples[].german: I continue my research to repay the debt I owe my mentor.
What I owe to my supervisor from my graduate school days is immeasurable.
This book is dedicated to the late Professor Tanaka, to whom I owe an immense scholarly debt.
en.notes: 学恩 is the debt of gratitude owed to a teacher or scholar for the instruction and scholarly support received, that is, the kindness shown, not the feeling of gratitude itself. It is an elevated word from the academic world, typical in forewords and obituaries: 学恩を受ける, 学恩に報いる, 学恩に感謝する. Related are 恩師 (a revered teacher) and 師恩.

examples[].german: The book was finally published after going through editorial review.
She works in the checking department of a newspaper, verifying the facts in articles.
I had a specialist review the translation and corrected the terminology.
en.notes: 校閲 is the review of a manuscript's content before publication: facts, names, figures, contradictions and wording. It is distinguished from 校正, proofreading of the printer's proofs for typos and typesetting errors. Newspapers and publishers have their own 校閲部; as a transitive する-verb: 原稿を校閲する. If a professional authority stands behind a work and is responsible for its content, one more often speaks of 監修.

examples[].german: The first edition of this book is already out of print.
I found a first edition of Sōseki at a secondhand bookshop.
The errors of the first edition were corrected in the second edition.
en.notes: 初版 is the first edition of a book. In Japan one distinguishes 版 (edition; with changes to the content: 第二版, 改訂版) and 刷 (printing without changes): 初版第一刷 is the very first printing. 初版本 is a copy of the first edition, often a collector's item. Counterparts are 重版 or 増刷 (reprint) and 再版 (new edition).

examples[].german: A reprint was decided right after it went on sale.
After it was featured on TV, it went back to press many times.
Several misprints were corrected at the time of the reprint.
en.notes: 重版 is a further printing of a book with (almost) unchanged content, that is, a reprint; a synonym is 増刷. A 重版 is a sign of good sales, typically: 重版が決まる, 重版がかかる, 重版出来 (じゅうはんしゅったい, "reprint has come out"). As a transitive する-verb: 本を重版する. If the content is revised, one speaks of 改訂版, not 重版.

examples[].german: A supplemented and revised edition has been newly published.
New material was added to expand the ten-year-old book.
Two chapters have been added to the enlarged edition.
en.notes: 増補 means adding content to an existing work, supplementing and expanding it; as a transitive する-verb: 旧著を増補する. It is most often found in book titles such as 増補版 and 増補改訂版 ("enlarged and revised edition"). 改訂 means revising what exists, 増補 means adding to it; a mere reprint is 重版.

examples[].german: Work on revising the textbook is under way.
A revised edition of that dictionary has come out for the first time in ten years.
We revised the outdated data and renewed the manual.
en.notes: 改訂 is the revision of a text, such as a book, textbook or dictionary: 改訂版, 改訂する (transitive), 教科書の改訂. Careful, homophone: 改定 (same reading) means changing rules, prices or contracts (料金の改定, 規則の改定). Rule of thumb: texts are 改訂, stipulations are 改定. 増補 refers specifically to adding content.

en.meaning: auction by court order; foreclosure sale
examples[].german: The mortgaged property was put up for foreclosure auction.
He could no longer pay the loan, and his home was put up for foreclosure auction.
He buys foreclosure properties cheaply, renovates them and rents them out.
en.notes: 競売 is read けいばい in legal language and mainly means the judicial compulsory auction, for example of real estate whose loan was not repaid; typical: 競売にかける/かけられる, 競売物件, 競売で落札する. General auctions are rather called きょうばい or simply オークション. As a する-verb it is rare; it usually appears as a noun with にかける.

en.meaning: word definition; explanation of a word
examples[].german: I looked up the exact meaning by consulting the definition in the dictionary.
This Japanese dictionary has a reputation for easy-to-understand definitions.
In classical Japanese class, we first go over the explanations of the difficult words.
en.notes: 語釈 is the explanation of a word's meaning, above all the definition text in a dictionary or the word explanation in an annotated edition of classical texts. Typical: 辞書の語釈, 語釈が分かりやすい, 語釈を付ける. 語義 is the word's meaning itself, 語釈 is its explanation; 注釈 is more general, any note on a text.

examples[].german: The meaning of a word can change over time.
In this dictionary, example sentences are given for each sense.
「確信犯」 is often used in a sense different from its original meaning.
en.notes: 語義 is the meaning of a word as an object of language study, for instance in dictionaries or semantics: 語義の変化, 語義ごとに, 本来の語義. In everyday speech one simply says 意味; 語義 sounds technical. 語釈 is the explanatory definition, 語義 the meaning itself. A word with many 語義 is called 多義語.

examples[].german: The meaning of a polysemous word is determined by the context.
「かける」 is one of the most typical polysemous words in Japanese.
Can you explain the difference between a polysemous word and a homonym?
en.notes: 多義語 is a word with several related meanings (polysemy), e.g. かける or とる. To be distinguished from it is 同音異義語: different words with the same reading but unrelated meanings (橋 and 箸). With a 多義語, the context (文脈) decides the meaning; in dictionaries the 語義 are numbered.

en.meaning: feel for words; nuance (of a word)
examples[].german: I want to become able to pick up the subtle differences in nuance between words.
He has a keen feel for language and is very good at choosing his words.
「亡くなる」 has a softer nuance than 「死ぬ」.
en.notes: 語感 has two meanings: a person's feel for language (語感が鋭い "to have a fine sense of language") and the nuance or connotation a word has (柔らかい語感, 語感が悪い). It does not mean the objective meaning (語義) but the impression a word makes when heard or read. Both uses are neutral to slightly elevated.

en.meaning: usage; how a word is used
examples[].german: This usage is peculiar to written language.
I was told that this way of putting it is incorrect as usage.
I bought a study book that explains English usage in detail.
en.notes: 語法 refers to the rules for how words are actually used and combined, that is, word usage and grammar in detail. Typical are 語法の誤り, 語法上正しい and 英語の語法 (a popular topic of study books). 文法 is the whole grammatical system, 用法 the way a particular word is used; 語法 lies in between and stresses concrete usage.

en.meaning: word history; history of a word
examples[].german: If you trace the history of a word, you can see how its meaning changed.
Some Japanese dictionaries have a special section on word history.
If you look into the history of 「やばい」, it goes back to the Edo period.
en.notes: 語誌 is the history of an individual word: its first attestations, its changes in form and meaning, and its spread. Large dictionaries such as the 日本国語大辞典 have their own 語誌 sections. Unlike 語源 ("etymology, origin"), 語誌 follows the whole further development. The rare meaning "glossary" plays hardly any role in present-day usage.

examples[].german: The classification of parts of speech differs from language to language.
In a dictionary, the part of speech is written after the headword.
Japanese school grammar divides words into ten parts of speech.
en.notes: 品詞 is the part of speech. Japanese school grammar (学校文法) distinguishes ten 品詞: 名詞, 動詞, 形容詞, 形容動詞, 副詞, 連体詞, 接続詞, 感動詞, 助動詞 and 助詞. Typical phrases are 品詞を判別する, 品詞分解 (breaking a sentence down into its parts of speech, especially in 古文 classes) and 品詞の分類. Register: technical, but generally known from school.

examples[].german: Yōgen refers to independent words that inflect.
Adjectives of both kinds are also included among yōgen.
The distinction between taigen and yōgen is basic to Japanese grammar.
en.notes: 用言 is a term of Japanese grammar for independent words that inflect and can form a predicate on their own: 動詞, 形容詞 (い-adjectives) and 形容動詞 (な-adjectives). The opposite term is 体言, the non-inflecting words such as nouns and pronouns. The pairing 体言・用言 matters for rules such as 用言の連用形 or 体言止め.

examples[].german: Taigen are independent words that do not inflect.
In Japanese grammar, nouns and pronouns are grouped together as taigen.
This verse ends with a noun, that is, with the stylistic device taigen-dome.
en.notes: 体言 is a technical term of Japanese school grammar (国文法) for independent, non-inflecting words that can be a subject, in practice nouns including pronouns and numerals. The counterpart is 用言 (verbs and adjectives, which inflect). The term is well known from 連体形 ("the form before a 体言") and 体言止め, the stylistic device of ending a sentence or verse with a noun. The word hardly appears in everyday life.

examples[].german: Particles and auxiliary verbs are classified as dependent words.
Dependent words cannot form a phrase on their own.
Of the dependent words, only auxiliary verbs inflect.
en.notes: 付属語 are, in Japanese school grammar, the words that cannot form a 文節 (phrase) alone and are always attached to a 自立語: 助詞 (particles) and 助動詞 (auxiliary verbs). The opposite term is 自立語. Of the 付属語, only the 助動詞 inflect. Do not confuse with suffixes such as 〜さ or 〜的, which count as 接尾語 in word formation. Older spelling: 附属語.

en.meaning: deposit (with a public office); security deposit
examples[].german: The debtor deposited the payment with the Legal Affairs Bureau.
Because the landlord would not accept the rent, I deposited it with the deposit office.
Because he received too few votes, his election deposit was forfeited.
en.notes: 供託 is the deposit of money or securities with a state deposit office (供託所, in Japan the 法務局), for example when a creditor refuses payment: 家賃を供託する. Best known is 供託金, the deposit that election candidates must lodge and lose if they get too few votes (供託金が没収される). As a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を法務局に供託する.

examples[].german: Nouns and verbs are examples of independent words.
Every phrase contains exactly one independent word.
Of the independent words, those that inflect are called yōgen.
en.notes: 自立語 are, in Japanese school grammar, the words with a meaning of their own that can form a 文節 (phrase) alone: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, 連体詞, conjunctions and interjections. Every 文節 begins with exactly one 自立語, optionally followed by 付属語 (particles, auxiliary verbs). Inflecting 自立語 are called 用言, and non-inflecting ones that can be a subject 体言. A purely technical term from grammar class and linguistics.

examples[].german: Oral literature is important in cultures without writing.
The Yukar is the epic poem that represents Ainu oral literature.
Folktales and folk songs are also studied as a form of oral literature.
en.notes: 口承文学 is literature that is passed on orally (口承 "handed down from mouth to mouth") rather than in writing: myths, epics, tales, legends, folk songs. The opposite term is literature fixed in writing (記載文学). Synonymous are 口承文芸 and, more generally, 口頭伝承. A scholarly term from folklore studies, ethnology and literary studies; 口承 alone appears in, for example, 口承で伝わる "to be handed down orally".

examples[].german: Studying literary theory opens up new ways of reading works.
I am specializing in literary theory in graduate school.
The essay is written drawing on feminist literary theory.
en.notes: 文学理論 is literary theory as an academic field: structuralism, reception aesthetics, deconstruction, feminist theory, etc. Typical are 文学理論を学ぶ/専攻する and 〜の文学理論を踏まえる. Closely related is 批評理論 ("critical theory, theory of literary criticism"); 文学論, by contrast, refers more to an individual treatise on literature, such as 夏目漱石の『文学論』. Elevated, academic vocabulary.

examples[].german: A short story was published in the literary magazine.
In high school I joined the literature club and wrote novels.
This publisher is stronger in practical books than in literary works.
en.notes: Like 文学, 文芸 means "literature", but it stresses the literary as an art and as creative work, and it appears mainly in fixed compounds: 文芸誌 (literary magazine), 文芸部 (literature club at schools), 文芸書 ("belles-lettres"), 文芸作品, 文芸評論. 文学, by contrast, is the more general word, also used for the field of study (文学部, 日本文学). In the older, broader sense, 文芸 covers literature and the arts in general.

examples[].german: The language of the time can be inferred from ancient inscriptions.
The inscription on the stone monument in the park had become hard to read after years of wind and rain.
The inscription on the memorial has the names of the people who died in the earthquake carved into it.
en.notes: 碑文 is the text on a 碑, that is, a memorial stone, monument or gravestone. Typical combinations: 碑文を刻む "to carve an inscription", 碑文を読む/解読する, 碑文に記される. For inscriptions on metal (bells, swords, mirrors) one more often says 銘文; the epitaph in the narrower sense is called 墓碑銘. Written language, frequent in archaeology, history and museum texts.

examples[].german: I deciphered the inscription engraved on the sword.
The inscription on this bell records the year in which it was cast.
The inscription on an iron sword unearthed from an ancient burial mound gave an important clue to the study of ancient history.
en.notes: 銘文 is an engraved or cast inscription, above all on metal objects such as bells, swords, bronze mirrors or vessels; 碑文, by contrast, is for inscriptions on stone monuments. The single word 銘 also appears as a swordsmith's signature (刀の銘) and in 座右の銘 "personal motto". Typical: 銘文を刻む, 銘文を解読する. Technical vocabulary from archaeology and art history.

examples[].german: It was a work that left a refreshing impression after reading.
The ending of this novel is so heavy that it doesn't leave a very good feeling afterwards.
In the book review, I wrote not only about the story but also about the impression the book leaves.
en.notes: 読後感 is the feeling that remains after reading a book, so more a mood than a fully formed opinion (for that one says 感想). Typical combinations: 読後感がいい／悪い, 爽やかな読後感, 読後感を残す. The word comes from book criticism and reviews, but is also used in everyday talk about novels and manga.

examples[].german: I was chosen for an honorable mention in the contest.
It isn't flashy, but it is a quite good piece of work.
This short story collection is full of fine pieces.
en.notes: 佳作 has two uses: in general it is a successful, good work, a compliment but one step below 傑作 or 名作, typically in なかなかの佳作 or 佳作ぞろい. In competitions, 佳作 denotes the award below the actual prizes, roughly "honorable mention": 佳作に選ばれる, 佳作に入る, 選外佳作. Rather written language, but commonplace in competition results and reviews.

en.meaning: failure; poor work; piece of junk
examples[].german: It was savaged by critics as a poor piece of work.
Honestly, the final installment of the series was a dud.
Don't be afraid of writing duds; just write as much as you can.
en.notes: 駄作 is a failed, worthless work; 駄 means "inferior" as in 駄菓子 or 駄洒落. The word is clearly derogatory, but quite common when talking about films, books or games: 駄作だった, 駄作と酷評される. The opposites are 名作, 傑作 and 佳作; more neutral for "mediocre" is 凡作. One also uses it self-deprecatingly about one's own work.

examples[].german: There are masterpieces that continue to be read across the ages.
During summer vacation I read several masterpieces of world literature.
This film is a masterpiece that makes me cry every time I watch it.
en.notes: 名作 is a famous, widely recognized work - a classic in literature, film, music or games: 不朽の名作, 世界の名作, 名作映画. 傑作, by contrast, stresses outstanding quality, often in relation to an artist's overall output (最高傑作). For books, including nonfiction, there is 名著; for pieces of music 名曲; for paintings 名画. Neutral and very common.

examples[].german: A mortgage was registered on the property.
He put his house up as collateral and borrowed money from the bank.
Since the loan was paid off, I went through the procedure to cancel the mortgage.
en.notes: 抵当 is security for a loan, above all real estate; the right to it is called 抵当権 ("mortgage, lien on land"). Typical: 家を抵当に入れる ("to mortgage a house"), 抵当権を設定する/抹消する, 抵当に取る. More general is 担保 ("security" of any kind); 質 (しち) is the pledge of movable items at the pawnbroker.

en.meaning: posthumous work; last work (of a deceased person)
examples[].german: The unfinished posthumous work was published after his death.
This painting became the painter's last work.
The late director's last film will be released next month.
en.notes: 遺作 is the work a deceased person left behind, usually their last, often unfinished or published only after death. Typical frame: 〜が遺作となる "became his/her last work", 遺作展 "exhibition of late works". Related are 遺稿 (a manuscript left behind) and 絶筆 (the last thing written or painted). Neutral to written register, frequent in obituaries and cultural news.

examples[].german: Her first work became a bestseller.
It is said that everything that makes an author is already in their first work.
His first work was a poetry collection he self-published as a student.
en.notes: 処女作 is the first published work of an author or artist; 処女 here means "first-time, untouched" as in 処女航海 (maiden voyage). Because of the secondary meaning "virgin", some people avoid it in favor of デビュー作 (more casual, also used for film and music) or 第一作. Typical: 〜の処女作, 処女作で賞を取る. Neutral, common in literary criticism and biographies.

examples[].german: 「坊っちゃん」 is one of Natsume Sōseki's best-known works.
This film is said to be the director's signature work.
In the job interview, I was told to show three of my representative works.
en.notes: 代表作 is the work that is most typical of an author, artist, director or musician and for which they are known: 〜の代表作, 代表作に挙げる, 代表作となる. It stresses fame and representativeness, not necessarily the highest quality; for that one says 傑作 or 名作. It applies to novels, films, paintings, songs and even a company's products.

examples[].german: The original was reworked into a stage version.
In his later years, the author revised his youthful works again and again.
Reworking a work without the permission of its original author can be a copyright infringement.
en.notes: 改作 means reworking an existing work, one's own or someone else's; as a transitive する-verb: 作品を改作する. Distinctions: 翻案 transfers material to another era, culture or genre, 脚色 adapts it for stage or film, and 改訂 corrects and updates a text (e.g. a textbook). Written language, mainly in literary and theater contexts.

examples[].german: It is a Japanese-language play freely adapted from Shakespeare's drama.
A foreign mystery novel was adapted, with the setting moved to Japan.
The rakugo story 「死神」 is said to be an adaptation of a Grimm fairy tale.
en.notes: 翻案 means taking over the plot and material of a (often foreign) work and adapting it to another time, country or genre; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を翻案する. Unlike 翻訳 (translation), the content is freely reshaped; 改作 is the more general "rework". 翻案小説 were widespread in the Meiji period; in copyright law there is the term 翻案権. Written language.

examples[].german: It is important to put the theory of pedagogy into practice.
I studied education at university and became an elementary school teacher.
From a pedagogical point of view, this way of assigning homework is problematic.
en.notes: 教育学 is the science of education and upbringing, that is, pedagogy or education studies as a field of study: 教育学を学ぶ/専攻する, 教育学の観点から. Subfields include 教育心理学 and 教育社会学. Careful: 教育学部 "Faculty of Education" is 教育＋学部, not 教育学＋部. The word is academic; for education itself one simply says 教育.

examples[].german: I decided to enroll because I sympathized with the school's educational philosophy.
The founder's educational ideals live on to this day in the school motto.
In the interview, I was asked how I understand the school's educational philosophy.
en.notes: 教育理念 is the fundamental educational ideal or guiding principle of a school, university or company (理念 "guiding idea, basic principle"). It typically appears on websites and in brochures: 本校の教育理念, 教育理念に共感する, 教育理念を掲げる. More concrete are 教育方針 ("educational policy") and 校訓 (school motto); private schools also speak of 建学の精神. Formal and written language.

examples[].german: The degree conferral ceremony takes place in March.
The dissertation passed review, and the conferral of the degree has been decided.
This university has published its own policy on awarding degrees.
en.notes: 学位授与 is the formal conferral of an academic degree (授与 "to confer ceremonially", also used for prizes and decorations). Verbally: 学位を授与する or, passive, 学位が授与される; from the students' point of view one says 学位を取得する "to obtain a degree". Fixed combinations: 学位授与式 (graduation ceremony, in everyday speech often simply 卒業式) and 学位授与の方針 (a university's "diploma policy"). Official, formal style.

examples[].german: You need a license to take up a teaching position.
My father worked as a teacher for nearly forty years until retirement.
I am taking teacher-training courses at university.
en.notes: 教職 is the teaching profession as an occupation or office and sounds more formal than 教師 or 先生. Typical combinations: 教職に就く "to become a teacher", 教職を務める, 教職を離れる/去る. 教職課程 are the teacher-training modules taken at Japanese universities alongside the main course of study; 教職員 means teachers and other school staff together. The meaning "instruction of laypeople" (religious) is rare.

examples[].german: I revised the paper following my supervisor's advice.
When you are in trouble, it is good to ask an expert for advice.
A senior colleague gave me advice about changing jobs.
en.notes: 助言 is factual, rather formal advice; in conversation アドバイス is more common. Typical combinations: 助言を求める/受ける/与える, 〜の助言に従う, and as a する-verb 人に助言する. Distinctions: 忠告 is warning, admonishing advice, and 勧告 is an official recommendation, for example from an authority. The word fits well in work, study and counseling situations.

examples[].german: The contract was terminated due to non-performance of the obligation.
The company went bankrupt carrying large debts.
The national debt keeps growing year after year.
en.notes: 債務 is the legal obligation to perform something, usually a monetary debt; the counterpart is 債権 ("claim"), and the parties are called 債務者 and 債権者. Typical: 債務を負う, 債務を返済する, 債務不履行 ("non-performance"), 債務超過 ("insolvency, liabilities exceeding assets"). In everyday life, for debts one rather says 借金; 債務 is matter-of-fact and formal, and common in business and law.

en.meaning: narrative trick; deceiving the reader through the way the story is told (mystery)
examples[].german: Mystery novels that use narrative tricks are popular.
I realized the narrative trick in the very last line and reread everything from the beginning.
Because it uses a narrative trick, this novel is difficult to adapt for film.
en.notes: 叙述トリック is a term from the Japanese mystery scene: it is not the characters but the reader who is deceived, through the way the story is told, for example a concealed gender, a hidden time level or the narrator's true identity. The counterpart is the 物理トリック at the crime scene. Typical: 叙述トリックを使う, 叙述トリックに騙される. Common fan jargon in reviews.

examples[].german: The technique of the unreliable narrator is attracting attention.
The narrator of this novel is a cat.
My grandmother was known in the village as a teller of old tales.
en.notes: 語り手 (from 語る "to narrate" + 手 "person") is, on the one hand, the narrating voice of a literary text, which is not identical with the author (作者): 一人称の語り手, 信頼できない語り手. On the other hand, it denotes a person who recites stories orally. Distinctions: 話し手 is the speaker in a conversation (counterpart 聞き手), and ナレーター is the voice-over speaker in film or television.

examples[].german: Changing the viewpoint character gives the story many layers.
In this chapter, the viewpoint switches to the culprit.
What the viewpoint character doesn't know is not revealed to the reader either.
en.notes: 視点人物 is the character from whose perspective a scene is narrated, especially in third-person limited narration. It is not necessarily the 語り手 (narrator) or the 主人公 (protagonist). Typical: 視点人物が変わる/切り替わる, 視点人物を固定する. A technical term from literary studies and writing guides; in fan circles also 視点キャラ.

en.meaning: ensemble drama; story with multiple protagonists
examples[].german: It is an ensemble drama woven together by a diverse cast of characters.
This film is an ensemble piece depicting people who happened to be at the airport on the same day.
With ensemble stories that have no protagonist, it is hard to remember all the characters.
en.notes: 群像劇 is a film, play or novel in which many characters are equally at the center and several storylines run in parallel, without a single protagonist; an "ensemble piece". 群像 alone means a group of figures, for example in sculpture or in 青春群像. Typical: 〜を描いた群像劇, 群像劇として描く. Neutral, frequent in film and book reviews.

examples[].german: Western poetry's metrical feet include the iamb, among others.
In iambic pentameter, a line consists of five metrical feet.
In this Chinese poem, the final characters of the second and fourth lines serve as the rhyme.
en.notes: 韻脚 has two meanings: in Western metrics it is the metrical foot, a fixed sequence of stressed and unstressed syllables such as 弱強格 (iamb) or 強弱格 (trochee); 詩脚 is synonymous. In Chinese poetry (漢詩), it denotes the rhyming character at the end of a line. A purely technical term of prosody; "to rhyme" is generally 韻を踏む.

examples[].german: The textual variants between the manuscripts were recorded in detail.
Different versions of this waka have been handed down depending on the manuscript.
In the critical edition, the main variants are noted below the main text.
en.notes: 異文 is a term of textual criticism: a passage whose wording in one manuscript or edition differs from other transmissions. Typical: 異文がある/伝わる, 異文を記録する/注記する, 〜による異文. To be distinguished from it is 異本 (a divergent manuscript or edition as a whole). Do not confuse with 異文化 "foreign culture", which consists of 異＋文化. Technical language of philology.

en.meaning: letter (of an alphabet); source kanji of a kana
examples[].german: The source characters of hiragana derive from the cursive forms of kanji.
The source character of 「あ」 is the kanji 「安」.
The Russian alphabet has 33 letters.
en.notes: 字母 has two main uses in Japanese: in the history of writing it is the kanji from which a kana originated (「あ」の字母は「安」). In general it denotes the letters of an alphabet, e.g. ロシア語の字母. In printing, it also meant the casting matrix for type. A technical word from the history of writing and linguistics; for "letter" in everyday speech one says 文字 or アルファベット.

en.meaning: spirit of language; magical power of words
examples[].german: The idea of kotodama has existed in Japan since ancient times.
The Man'yōshū has a poem that sings of Japan as a 「言霊の幸わう国」 (land where the power of words brings blessing).
People avoid saying 「落ちる」 in front of exam candidates because they care about kotodama.
en.notes: 言霊 is the old Japanese belief that words have a power of their own to take effect: what one utters can become reality. The word often appears in 言霊信仰 or 言霊の思想. To this day the idea lives on in 忌み言葉, words one avoids at weddings (切れる, 別れる) or before exams (落ちる, 滑る). A cultural-religious term, neutral to elevated.

en.meaning: binding commitment; word one can be held to
examples[].german: I moved the negotiation forward after getting the other party's commitment.
At the press conference, the minister answered carefully so as not to commit himself.
I carelessly said 「やります」, and now my boss has pinned me down on it.
en.notes: 言質 is a statement one can later hold someone to, a binding commitment. It almost always appears in fixed combinations: 言質を取る "to take someone at their word, to extract a commitment", 言質を与える "to commit oneself", 言質を取られる "to be pinned down on something". The correct reading is げんち; げんしつ is often heard, but is traditionally regarded as a misreading. Typical of politics, negotiations and business.

examples[].german: The report does not mention that problem.
The prime minister avoided referring to the tax increase.
In your paper, you should also refer to previous research.
en.notes: 言及 means to come to speak of something or to refer to it. As an intransitive する-verb it takes に or について: 〜に言及する, 〜について言及する; also common is 言及を避ける/控える "to not bring something up". It is formal and typical of reports, news and academic texts; in conversation one more often says 触れる (話に触れる). Compared with 指摘 ("to point out a matter"), 言及 is more neutral.

examples[].german: The seller was held responsible for the defects of the building.
The disposition was revoked on the grounds that there was a flaw in the procedure.
A roof leak was found after handover, and we demanded repair as a defect.
en.notes: 瑕疵 means "blemish, defect", above all in law: a defect in a thing (建物の瑕疵) or a legal flaw in a procedure or declaration of intent (手続きに瑕疵がある). The former 瑕疵担保責任 ("warranty for defects") has been called 契約不適合責任 in the Civil Code since 2020, but 瑕疵 remains common in construction law and contracts. The characters are difficult; one often sees かし or furigana. In everyday life, one says 欠陥 or 不具合.

examples[].german: It is important to understand the intention behind an utterance accurately.
A child's first utterances most often appear around the age of one.
The speech recognition system converts the user's speech into text.
en.notes: 発話 is a technical term of linguistics for a concrete linguistic utterance or for speaking itself: 発話の意図, 子どもの発話, 発話する. The speech act in the sense of pragmatics is more precisely called 発話行為. In everyday speech one doesn't say 発話 but 話す or 言う; 発言 is a contribution to a discussion, for example in a meeting. Also common in speech recognition and speech therapy.

examples[].german: Discourse analysis is an important research area of linguistics.
On the 50th anniversary of the end of the war, a statement by the prime minister was released.
In the hospital lounge, the patients were chatting happily.
en.notes: 談話 has three uses: a formal word for "conversation, talk" (談話する, 談話室 "lounge"), an official statement that has not been formally resolved (首相談話, 官房長官談話, such as the well-known 村山談話), and in linguistics "discourse" (談話分析). For an ordinary conversation, one says 会話 or 話 in everyday speech; 談話 sounds elevated or official.

examples[].german: Graphemics studies the structure and function of writing systems.
In studies of Japanese writing, the choice between kanji and kana is often discussed.
In the lecture on writing theory, we learned the difference between phonographic and logographic scripts.
en.notes: 文字論 is the subfield of linguistics that studies writing and writing systems, that is, graphemics or theory of writing. In Japanese this often concerns the interplay of kanji, hiragana and katakana, and 表語文字 (logographic script) and 表音文字 (phonographic script). Related is 文字学, which more traditionally studies the origin and forms of individual characters, especially kanji. A purely academic term.

examples[].german: Contrastive linguistics compares and contrasts two languages.
Unlike comparative linguistics, contrastive linguistics does not ask about the genealogy of languages.
Findings of contrastive linguistics are also useful for foreign language teaching.
en.notes: 対照言語学 compares two or more languages synchronically, that is, in their present state, to work out similarities and differences, often with foreign language teaching in mind. To be distinguished from it is 比較言語学, historical-comparative linguistics, which asks about language relationships and common proto-languages. Adjectivally: 対照言語学的な研究. An academic technical term.

examples[].german: In business emails, you need to use appropriate respectful expressions.
Introductory phrases such as 「恐れ入りますが」 are also a kind of respectful expression.
Even without using keigo, you can express respect through your choice of words.
en.notes: 敬意表現 is any linguistic form with which one expresses respect and consideration toward the other person. The term is broader than 敬語 (the grammatical honorific forms 尊敬語, 謙譲語, 丁寧語): it also includes introductory phrases such as 恐れ入りますが, indirect requests and considerate word choice. Still more general is 待遇表現, which also includes derogatory expressions. A technical term from language policy and Japanese language teaching.

examples[].german: The 「い」 in 「書いて」 is a change due to onbin.
「読んで」 is an example of the nasal onbin, and 「待って」 of the geminate onbin.
「ありがとう」 is also a form that changed from 「ありがたく」 through the u-onbin.
en.notes: 音便 is a historical sound change for easier pronunciation, especially in the て／た-form of verbs: イ音便 (書いて), 促音便 (待って), 撥音便 (読んで) and ウ音便 (ありがたく → ありがとう, おはやく → おはよう). It explains why the て-form of godan verbs looks so irregular. The word is a grammatical technical term; one says 音便が起こる or 〜は音便による変化だ.

en.meaning: phonetic shift; sound change away from spelling
examples[].german: The difference between historical and modern kana orthography is related to tenko.
Reading 「かは」 as "kawa" is a result of the ha-row sound change.
Pronouncing the particle 「は」 as "wa" is also a remnant of tenko.
en.notes: 転呼 (short for 転呼音) is a sound change by which pronunciation moves away from the traditional kana spelling. The most important example is the ハ行転呼: inside a word, は・ひ・ふ・へ・ほ became わ・い・う・え・お, hence かは → かわ, おもふ → おもう. The pronunciation of the particles は and へ as "wa" and "e" also goes back to it. A technical term of historical linguistics.

examples[].german: Traces of vowel harmony can be seen in Old Japanese.
Turkish and Finnish have vowel harmony.
In languages with vowel harmony, the vowel of a suffix changes to match the vowels of the stem.
en.notes: 母音調和 is vowel harmony: in a word only vowels from the same group (for example front or back vowels) may occur, and suffixes adapt their vowel to the stem. Well-known examples are Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian and Mongolian. For Old Japanese (上代日本語), a remnant of vowel harmony is discussed. A purely linguistic technical term.

examples[].german: Reading 「因縁」 as 「いんねん」 is an example of renjō.
Reading 「天皇」 as 「てんのう」 is also due to renjō.
In a class on the history of the Japanese language, I learned about the phenomenon called renjō for the first time.
en.notes: 連声 is generally "sandhi"; in Japanese it specifically means a historical sound change in kanji compounds: if the first element ends in n (or formerly m, t) and the second begins with a vowel, y or w, this becomes na-, ni-, no- etc.: 因縁 いん＋えん → いんねん, 観音 かん＋おん → かんのん, 天皇 てん＋おう → てんのう. Today no new cases arise. The word is purely technical (phonology, language history).

examples[].german: Measures were taken to improve the quality of teaching and study.
In running a university, you have to consider both management and academic affairs.
The vice president in charge of academic affairs is pushing ahead with curriculum reform.
en.notes: 教学 means "teaching and study" and today appears mainly in university administration: 教学部門 or 教学担当 stand for the academic side, as opposed to 経営 (finance, administration); 教学改革 is a study reform. In Buddhist contexts, 教学 denotes the doctrine or dogmatics of a school (天台教学). A formal, official word; in everyday speech one says 教育.

examples[].german: A bona fide third party is protected.
What I said with good intentions ended up hurting the other person instead.
Fraud that takes advantage of people's goodwill is on the rise.
en.notes: 善意 means in everyday life "good intention, goodwill": 善意で, 善意の寄付, 人の善意を利用する. In law it has a quite different, technical meaning: 善意 there means not knowing a certain fact ("good faith"), without any moral evaluation, e.g. 善意の第三者. The counterpart is 悪意 ("knowing the fact"). For everyday "goodwill", 好意 is also common, which expresses more personal affection.

examples[].german: She enjoys an international reputation.
With that novel, he suddenly gained fame as a writer.
A single scandal destroyed the reputation he had built up over many years.
en.notes: 名声 is the good reputation, fame and standing that someone enjoys in public, always positive. Typical combinations: 名声を博する/得る/高める, 名声が高まる, 名声が地に落ちる "the reputation is ruined". 評判 is more everyday and can also be bad (評判が悪い); 名誉 is "honor", 有名 simply "well-known". Elevated style.

examples[].german: That decision is a matter that affects the government's prestige.
The two countries staged a space race with their prestige at stake.
A string of scandals has badly shaken the police's standing.
en.notes: 威信 is the prestige and dignity that an institution, a state or a leader projects outward: 国家の威信, 政府の威信. Typical: 威信をかける "to stake one's whole prestige", 威信が揺らぐ/失墜する, 威信を保つ/回復する. Unlike 名声 (personal fame), it concerns authority and respect; 権威 stresses authority based on power or expertise. Formal, frequent in the news.

examples[].german: The aristocratic class enjoyed many privileges.
Being allowed to fail is the privilege of the young.
The diplomat escaped arrest thanks to diplomatic immunity.
en.notes: 特権 is a prerogative that belongs only to certain persons or groups: 特権を持つ/与える/享受する/乱用する, 特権階級, 外交特権 "diplomatic immunity". Casually it can also mean "privilege" in a figurative sense: 若者の特権. 権利 is a general right that can belong to everyone; 特典 is a perk, for example for customers or members.

examples[].german: I am prepared to fully carry out my duty as a leader.
Parents have a duty to educate their children.
Companies must fulfill their social responsibility for environmental protection.
en.notes: 責務 is the duty and responsibility that falls to one because of a role or position. Typical: 責務を果たす/全うする/負う, 〜としての責務, 社会的責務. 責任 is more general and also includes liability and blame (責任を取る); 義務 is more the (legal) obligation, and 任務 a concrete assignment. 責務 sounds formal and solemn, as in speeches and official texts.

examples[].german: Modesty is regarded as a virtue in Japanese culture.
The attitude of regarding endurance as a virtue is one cause of overwork.
Punctuality is probably regarded as a virtue in every country.
en.notes: 美徳 is a virtue or a trait regarded as good: 〜を美徳とする, 〜は美徳とされる, 日本人の美徳. The opposite is 悪徳. The term is also often used critically, for example when endurance or restraint is exalted as a virtue (我慢を美徳とする風潮). 徳 alone means more moral integrity (徳が高い), and 長所 simply a strength. Neutral to elevated.

examples[].german: There is no end to consumers falling for fraudulent sales practices.
An unscrupulous company charged me an exorbitant repair bill.
Sloth has been counted among the vices since ancient times.
en.notes: 悪徳 as a noun means "vice, immorality" and is the opposite of 美徳; used this way it sounds rather literary. Today it is much more often found as a modifier before a noun in the sense of "unscrupulous, fraudulent": 悪徳商法 (fraudulent sales methods), 悪徳業者, 悪徳弁護士. For individual bad habits one more often says 悪癖 or 悪い癖.

examples[].german: We should not be bound by outdated customs but take in new ideas.
The young people who tried to break the old customs were isolated in the village.
The novel is set in a remote mountain village bound by old customs.
en.notes: 因習 is a time-honored custom that is felt to be outdated and constraining; the word is clearly negative. Typical: 因習にとらわれる/縛られる, 因習を打破する, 古い因習, 因習的な村. An older spelling is 因襲. Neutral, by contrast, are 習慣 (habit) and 慣習 (custom, also in law), and positive is 伝統 (tradition). Written language.

examples[].german: The exclusion of foreigners leads to the division of society.
An organization that shuts out people with different opinions will not last long.
In the early 20th century, a movement to exclude Japanese immigrants arose in the United States.
en.notes: 排斥 means actively excluding, pushing out or boycotting people, groups or goods; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を排斥する, passive 排斥される. Fixed combination: 排斥運動 "boycott or exclusion movement". 排除 is more general "to eliminate, remove" (also obstacles), 差別 is discrimination, and 疎外 is more the state of being left out or alienated. Formal, frequent in history and politics.

examples[].german: Advancing urbanization produces a sense of alienation from the local community.
Right after changing schools, I felt left out in the class.
Marx argued that workers are alienated from their own labor.
en.notes: 疎外 means to exclude someone or to become alien to something; a transitive する-verb, but mostly used in the passive: 疎外される "to be excluded". Most common is 疎外感 "the feeling of being left out" (疎外感を覚える/味わう). In philosophy and sociology it is "alienation" (人間疎外, 労働の疎外). Colloquially, for being excluded from a group one says 仲間外れ; actively driving someone out is more 排斥.

examples[].german: Policies to promote harmony between ethnic groups were implemented.
After the election, the new president appealed for national reconciliation.
A joint training session was held to bring together the employees of the two merged companies.
en.notes: 融和 is the growing together and reconciliation of groups that were previously separate or hostile: 融和を図る/促進する/訴える, 民族の融和, 融和ムード. As a する-verb it is intransitive (両国が融和する). 和解 stresses the settlement of a concrete dispute, 調和 the harmony of elements (色の調和). Careful: the identically read 宥和 means "appeasement" (宥和政策 = appeasement policy). Formal, typical of politics and news.

en.meaning: House of Councillors (upper house of the Japanese parliament)
examples[].german: The House of Councillors election will be held next month.
The House of Councillors cannot be dissolved, and half of its members are re-elected every three years.
The bill passed the House of Representatives and was sent to the House of Councillors.
en.notes: 参議院 is the upper house of the Japanese parliament (国会), abbreviated 参院. Its members (参議院議員) serve six-year terms; every three years half of the seats are up for election, and unlike the 衆議院 it cannot be dissolved. Typical: 参議院選挙 (short 参院選), 参議院で可決する, 参議院に送られる.

examples[].german: A possessor in bad faith has a duty to return the item.
A malicious post spread across the internet.
His words were harsh, but I think he meant no harm.
en.notes: 悪意 means in everyday life "ill will, malice": 悪意がある/ない, 悪意のある書き込み, 悪意に満ちた. In law, by contrast, it is a technical term: 悪意 means knowing a certain fact ("bad faith"), entirely without any intention of harming anyone; the counterpart is 善意. To be distinguished is 故意 ("intent"), which refers to intention in committing an act.

examples[].german: The split within the party is hampering the running of the government.
Cells multiply through repeated division.
Because of differences of opinion, the band split into two.
en.notes: 分裂 means that a whole breaks up into parts from within; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 党が分裂する, 〜に分裂する. It is used for organizations (党内分裂) but also in natural science: 細胞分裂, 核分裂. 分割, by contrast, is deliberate, transitive dividing (〜を分割する), and 分断 is cutting apart or separating, often from outside (社会の分断). Neutral to formal.

examples[].german: Protest movements against the exploitation of workers spread.
Making people work long hours for low pay is clearly exploitation.
Making people work unpaid on the grounds that "you love your job" is called passion exploitation.
en.notes: 搾取 is the exploitation of people, especially of their labor; as a transitive する-verb: 労働者を搾取する, passive 搾取される. Fixed expressions: 中間搾取 (exploitation by middlemen), 搾取工場 ("sweatshop") and, newer and colloquial, やりがい搾取, exploitation by appealing to one's passion for the work. The literal meaning "to squeeze out, to milk" is rare. 酷使 means "to overwork".

examples[].german: The suppression of freedom of speech shakes the foundations of democracy.
Ethnic minorities have been oppressed by the government for years.
If you keep suppressing your anger, it harms your mental health.
en.notes: 抑圧 refers to the forcible or systematic holding down of people, freedoms or feelings; as a transitive する-verb: 自由を抑圧する, passive 抑圧される. Typical are 抑圧された人々 and 〜に対する抑圧. Unlike 弾圧 ("violent suppression" by the state or police, very concrete), 抑圧 is more general and also used psychologically (感情を抑圧する "to repress feelings"). 抑制, by contrast, just means "to curb, restrain" neutrally (costs, inflation). Written language.

examples[].german: The government's repression of dissidents was condemned internationally.
In the Edo period, Christianity suffered harsh persecution.
The military put down the peaceful demonstration by force.
en.notes: 弾圧 is the violent suppression of opponents, religious groups or free speech by a power, usually the state: 〜を弾圧する, 弾圧を受ける, 弾圧を加える, 言論弾圧, 宗教弾圧. 抑圧 is more general (also feelings or social constraints), and 鎮圧 means putting down a concrete uprising. Typical of news, history and politics.

examples[].german: Many people went into exile to escape religious persecution.
He was persecuted because of his political opinions.
At this museum, you can learn about the history of the persecution of the Jews by the Nazis.
en.notes: 迫害 is the targeted persecution and harassment of people because of religion, origin or conviction. Mostly passive: 迫害を受ける or 迫害される "to be persecuted"; active 〜を迫害する. Typical combinations: 宗教的迫害, 迫害から逃れる, ユダヤ人迫害. Unlike 抑圧 ("suppression" of freedoms), 迫害 stresses the oppression and suffering of concrete groups; in asylum law 迫害 is the technical term for "persecution". Written language.

examples[].german: Granting protection to political refugees is an obligation under international law.
She grew up under her parents' protection without wanting for anything.
The painter was able to continue his work with the patronage of an influential merchant.
en.notes: 庇護 is the protection that a stronger party grants a weaker one, often with the image of a "protecting wing". Typical: 〜の庇護のもとで（育つ）, 庇護を受ける, 庇護を与える, 庇護する. In asylum law it stands for "protection/asylum" (庇護申請 "asylum application"). In everyday speech one more often says 保護 or 守る; 庇護 sounds elevated and stresses dependence on the protector (parents, patron, state). Since 庇 is not a jōyō kanji, newspapers often add a reading aid.

examples[].german: Both sides agreed to follow the ruling of the arbitration committee.
The labor commission issued a ruling rejecting the company's position.
The association ruled the result of that match invalid.
en.notes: 裁定 is the binding decision of a competent body in a dispute: an arbitration panel, an authority, a judging panel. Typical: 裁定を下す "to issue a ruling", 裁定に従う, 〜と裁定する. Unlike 判決 (the judgment of an ordinary court) and 判定 (an assessment, e.g. by score judges, ビデオ判定), 裁定 refers more to arbitration and official decisions, for example in labor law or a sports federation. Written language.

examples[].german: Strengthening local self-government is essential for the development of democracy.
At our apartment building's residents' association, we discussed the rules for taking out the garbage.
The residents of that region are demanding broader autonomy.
en.notes: 自治 means "self-government, autonomy": a group manages its own affairs. Very common in compounds: 地方自治 "local self-government", 自治体 "municipality, local public body", 自治会 "neighborhood or residents' association", 学生自治 / 自治区 "autonomous region". On its own it mostly appears with を認める / を求める. Unlike 独立 ("independence"), with 自治 one remains part of a larger whole. Neutral to official.

examples[].german: We are putting great effort into awareness-raising activities on human rights.
He always reads self-improvement books on the commuter train.
I was greatly inspired by my senior colleague's way of working.
en.notes: 啓発 means to awaken someone's awareness or knowledge: "enlightenment, raising awareness, inspiration". Very common: 啓発活動 "awareness-raising work", 意識を啓発する, 啓発ポスター, and 自己啓発 "self-improvement, personal development" (自己啓発本 = self-help literature). The passive 啓発される means "to be stimulated, inspired". The historical "Enlightenment" of philosophy, by contrast, is 啓蒙. Neutral to official.

examples[].german: Sensationalist reporting may foster social unrest.
The weekly magazine covered the case with lurid headlines.
The advertisement was criticized as too provocative.
en.notes: 煽情 is the deliberate stirring up of emotions, especially in the media. Almost only as 煽情的（な）: 煽情的な報道 "sensationalist reporting", 煽情的な見出し. It can also mean sexually provocative (煽情的な服装, 煽情的なポーズ). Today it is mostly written 扇情 or 扇情的, since 煽 is not a jōyō kanji. Related is 煽る "to stir up, incite". Written language, critical and judgmental.

examples[].german: I entrusted the lawsuit to a lawyer.
If a representative handles the procedure, a power of attorney is required.
The company president delegated the authority to approve to the department head.
en.notes: 委任 means to transfer a task or authority to someone to carry out at their own discretion; as a する-verb it is transitive: AにBを委任する. Typical: 権限を委任する, 委任状 ("power of attorney"), 委任契約. Close in meaning are 委託 ("commission, outsourcing", rather business) and 一任 ("to leave entirely to someone"); 任せる is the everyday word.

examples[].german: Deceit toward the public must never be tolerated.
The "eco-friendly" advertising is full of deception.
Convincing yourself that "it's not my fault" is self-deception.
en.notes: 欺瞞 is deliberate deception, the pretense of false facts, often in a moral or political context. Typical: 欺瞞に満ちた, 欺瞞的な, 欺瞞行為, 自己欺瞞 "self-deception". Unlike 詐欺 (fraud as a crime to obtain money) and だます (colloquial "to trick"), 欺瞞 sounds elevated and criticizes hypocrisy: 〜は欺瞞だ "... is eyewash". As a verb, 欺瞞する is hardly used.

examples[].german: He tried to bring down his political rival by despicable means.
Deceiving elderly people and taking their money is a despicable crime.
Attacking people anonymously is cowardly and low.
en.notes: 卑劣 describes morally contemptible, cowardly behavior, especially underhanded action against the defenseless. As a な-adjective: 卑劣な手段, 卑劣な犯行, 卑劣な男; predicative 卑劣だ. Frequent in news about fraud or attacks (卑劣な犯罪). Stronger and more moral than ずるい ("unfair, mean" in everyday speech) and more formal than 汚い ("dirty, unfair"). The card type "adjective" here means a な-adjective.

examples[].german: He embezzled a huge sum of money by cunning methods.
In folktales, the fox is often portrayed as a sly animal.
He maneuvered craftily and shifted the responsibility onto his subordinates.
en.notes: 狡猾 means "sly, crafty": clever, but in an underhanded, self-serving way. Always negative, unlike 賢い ("clever") or 抜け目ない ("shrewd, savvy", rather neutral). Typical: 狡猾な手口, 狡猾な男, 狡猾に立ち回る. In everyday speech one more often says ずる賢い. Written language; neither kanji is a jōyō kanji, so a reading aid is often added.

examples[].german: Power tends to corrupt people.
Since entering university, he has been leading a dissolute life, doing nothing but playing around.
The successive corruption cases show the moral decay of politics.
en.notes: 堕落 is the moral descent of a person or institution: "depravity, corruption". As an intransitive する-verb: 人が堕落する, 堕落した生活; causative 〜を堕落させる "to corrupt". Also common: 政治の堕落, 堕落した政治家. In the religious sense it is the "Fall" or falling away from the faith. In contrast to 衰退 ("decline" of power or economy), 堕落 is always about morals and way of life.

examples[].german: Voices lamenting the decay of society are growing louder.
This film captures well the decadent atmosphere of the fin de siècle.
In the chaos of the postwar period, public morals in the cities declined greatly.
en.notes: 退廃 is the moral or cultural decay of a society, era or artistic movement; the older spelling is 頽廃. Very common is the adjective 退廃的 "decadent" (退廃的な雰囲気, 退廃的な美). As an intransitive する-verb: 風紀が退廃する. For purely material decay of buildings, one more often says 荒廃 or 老朽化. The word is written language.

examples[].german: Civil servants are expected to have an upright attitude.
The governor was a man of integrity and never accepted bribes.
Above all, integrity is needed at the top of an organization.
en.notes: 廉潔 means "honest and incorruptible", especially in dealing with money and power. It is used as a な-adjective (廉潔な人物, 廉潔な姿勢) or as a noun (廉潔さ, 廉潔を旨とする). The word is rare and very elevated; more common are 清廉 and the four-character phrase 清廉潔白. Typical context: the ethics of civil servants and politicians.

examples[].german: Only a person of unblemished integrity is fit to be a leader.
The minister, who had come under suspicion, insisted on his innocence at a press conference.
My grandfather was a man of integrity and was trusted by the people of the town.
en.notes: 清廉 means "pure, honest", especially free from greed and corruptibility. Mostly in the phrase 清廉潔白 "spotless, with a clean slate" (清廉潔白な人, 清廉潔白を主張する "to protest one's innocence"). Alone as a な-adjective: 清廉な人柄, 清廉な政治家. Equal in meaning but rarer is 廉潔. Elevated; in everyday speech one more often says 正直 or まじめ.

examples[].german: His devoted work for social welfare was recognized.
My mother nursed my sick grandmother devotedly.
She devoted her whole life to supporting refugees.
en.notes: 献身 is selfless devotion to a person or cause. Very common adverbially or adjectivally: 献身的に看病する, 献身的な努力 / 支え. As an intransitive する-verb with に: 〜に献身する "to devote oneself to ...". Unlike 犠牲 ("sacrifice"), 献身 stresses active, voluntary devotion; 貢献, by contrast, only means "to make a contribution". Neutral to elevated, strongly positive.

examples[].german: International aid based on a spirit of philanthropy is called for.
The motto of France is 「自由・平等・博愛」 ("liberty, equality, fraternity").
The Red Cross was founded on the principle of love for humanity.
en.notes: 博愛 is love for all people without distinction: "love of humanity, brotherhood". Typical: 博愛主義 "philanthropy", 博愛精神, 博愛の心. Known from the motto of the French Revolution 自由・平等・博愛 "liberty, equality, fraternity". Unlike 慈善 ("charity" as concrete help), 博愛 denotes the attitude. Elevated, hardly used in everyday conversation.

examples[].german: Building economically reciprocal relations benefits both countries.
The two leaders agreed to promote a mutually beneficial strategic relationship.
This exchange between universities is based on the principle of reciprocity.
en.notes: 互恵 means "reciprocity, mutual benefit", especially in diplomacy and trade. It appears almost only in compounds or with 的: 互恵関係, 互恵的な協力, 互恵主義, 互恵の精神. Well known is 戦略的互恵関係 "strategic relationship of mutual benefit" (Japan-China relations). In everyday speech one says お互いのためになる or ウィンウィン. Very formal.

en.meaning: disposal of government property; sale of state assets
examples[].german: The sale of state-owned land became an issue.
The city sold land it no longer used to a private company.
This shop deals in surplus equipment from the Self-Defense Forces.
en.notes: 払い下げ is the sale of state or agency property that is no longer needed to private parties; the verb is 払い下げる (transitive: 土地を企業に払い下げる). Common in 国有地の払い下げ, often in connection with scandals over sales at too low a price. 払い下げ品 are decommissioned goods, such as equipment of the Self-Defense Forces. The opposite direction (purchase by the state) is 買い上げ.

examples[].german: Fewer and fewer people belong to the generation that experienced the destitution of the postwar years.
Due to repeated wars, the domain's finances fell into dire straits.
Unemployment dragged on, and the family lived enduring great hardship.
en.notes: 窮乏 denotes a state of bitter poverty and deprivation in which even the necessities are lacking. Typical: 窮乏生活, 財政の窮乏 "financial distress (of public budgets)", 窮乏に耐える; as an intransitive する-verb 生活が窮乏する. Stronger and more literary than 貧乏 ("poor, poverty" in everyday speech) and more formal than 困窮 (similar, "hardship", frequent in official language: 生活困窮者). Mainly in historical or economic texts.

examples[].german: History has seen the rise and fall of empires again and again.
This novel depicts the rise and fall of the warlords of the Sengoku period.
In the IT industry, companies rise and fall at a furious pace.
en.notes: 興亡 is the "rise and fall" of states, dynasties, companies or cultures; 興 "to flourish", 亡 "to perish". Typical: 国家の興亡, 興亡の歴史, 〜の興亡を描く, and the four-character phrases 興亡盛衰 and 栄枯盛衰 ("prosperity and decline"). Unlike 盛衰 ("ups and downs", also for customs or fashions), 興亡 stresses the emergence and disappearance of whole powers. Written language, especially in history texts.

examples[].german: We are currently in a transitional period from the old system to the new one.
Adolescence is said to be the transitional period from child to adult.
This is merely a transitional measure and will be reviewed next year.
en.notes: 過渡 means "transition from the old to the new" and occurs practically only in compounds: 過渡期 "transitional period", 過渡的（な） "provisional, transitional", 過渡的措置 "transitional measure", and in engineering 過渡現象 "transient phenomenon". 過渡 hardly stands alone. The old meaning "ferry, crossing" is obsolete. In everyday speech, for individual processes, one says 移行 or 切り替え. Neutral to written.

examples[].german: New talent was brought in to pursue the renewal of the organization.
Following the scandal, the company replaced its entire management.
The design of the app was completely overhauled.
en.notes: 刷新 is a fundamental renewal in which the old and its abuses are eliminated. As a transitive する-verb: 組織を刷新する, 人事を刷新する, デザインを刷新する; passive 刷新される. Typical after scandals: 人心の刷新 "a fresh start to regain trust". Stronger than 改善 ("improvement") and more concrete than 改革 ("reform" of systems); 更新, by contrast, only means "to update, renew (a contract)". Neutral to formal, often in business and politics.

examples[].german: The rise of emerging nations is changing the international order.
Far-right parties are on the rise in many countries.
This season, the emergence of young players stood out.
en.notes: 台頭 is the emergence and strengthening of a new force that was previously in the background: "rise, gaining strength". As an intransitive する-verb: 新興国が台頭する, 〜の台頭. Frequent for states, movements, ideologies and young talents (若手の台頭). Unlike 上昇 ("rise" of values) and 出世 ("career" of a person), 台頭 describes emerging in the balance of power, often with a slightly threatening undertone (ナショナリズムの台頭). Also written 擡頭 (outdated).

examples[].german: Internal conflicts intensified and the organization fell apart.
With the collapse of the Edo shogunate, the age of the samurai ended.
When the key members left, the plan collapsed all at once.
en.notes: 瓦解 literally means "to fall apart like roof tiles": the sudden, complete collapse of an organization, regime or plan as soon as one part gives way. As an intransitive する-verb: 組織が瓦解する, 政権の瓦解. Unlike 崩壊 (generally "collapse, caving in", also of buildings), 瓦解 is used only figuratively. Written language, typical in history and political reports.

en.meaning: to be on the verge of; to be close to
examples[].german: That company is on the verge of bankruptcy.
This bird is in danger of extinction.
The town, facing a financial collapse, embarked on bold reforms.
en.notes: 瀕する means "to stand directly before something bad" and always takes に: 危機に瀕する, 絶滅の危機に瀕した動物, 倒産に瀕する, 死に瀕する. Almost always in the form 瀕している or attributively 〜に瀕した. It is more elevated than 〜しそうだ or 寸前だ and occurs mainly in news and factual texts. The noun 瀕死 "near death" (瀕死の重傷) belongs with it.

examples[].german: A statement denouncing the government's negligence was released.
The reporter sharply denounced the company's wrongdoing in his article.
The legislator who made discriminatory remarks was denounced from all quarters.
en.notes: 糾弾 is the public, sharp denunciation of misconduct or responsibility: "to denounce, to pillory". As a transitive する-verb: 不正を糾弾する, 責任を糾弾する; passive 糾弾される, or 糾弾を浴びる / 受ける. Stronger than 批判 ("criticism") and 非難 ("reproach, blame"); 糾弾 presupposes that someone is to be held accountable. Written language, frequent in politics and the media.

examples[].german: An international framework for the protection of human rights is gradually being put in place.
As criticism mounted, he alone stood up for his colleague.
The organization is calling for the defense of freedom of expression.
en.notes: 擁護 means to protect something valuable against attack or to stand up for someone: "to defend, protect, advocate". Typical: 人権擁護, 憲法擁護, 〜を擁護する発言. Unlike 防衛 (military defense) and 保護 ("protection" of the weak, of nature), 擁護 is often about principles or defending a person against criticism. Neutral to formal.

en.meaning: to advocate; to proclaim; to recite
examples[].german: He is loudly advocating the need for social reform.
The monk was quietly reciting a sutra.
In the meeting, only one person raised an objection to the plan.
en.notes: 唱える is transitive (〜を唱える) and has three uses: reciting formulas aloud (お経を唱える "to recite sutras", 呪文を唱える "to speak a spell"), calling something out loud (万歳を唱える "to cheer banzai") and publicly advocating an opinion (新説を唱える, 異議を唱える "to raise an objection"). In the last sense it is more elevated than 主張する and stresses putting forward a new or dissenting position. Do not confuse with 歌う ("to sing") or 述べる ("to state").

examples[].german: Heated debate took place in the Budget Committee.
My daughter joined the executive committee for the school festival.
The election administration commission announced the final voter turnout.
en.notes: 委員会 is a committee or commission: in parliament (予算委員会), in government bodies (選挙管理委員会, 教育委員会) and quite commonly in schools and clubs (文化祭の実行委員会). Members are called 委員, the chair 委員長. Typical: 委員会を設置する, 委員会で審議する, 委員会に入る. In contrast to 会議 ("meeting"), 委員会 refers to the body itself, but can also mean its meeting.

examples[].german: Measures to stop the spread of drug abuse are urgently needed.
In winter, influenza spreads easily in schools.
A resigned attitude of "nothing will change anyway" had spread throughout the company.
en.notes: 蔓延 describes the uncontrolled spread of something undesirable, like vines overgrowing everything: diseases, drugs, corruption, moods. As an intransitive する-verb: 感染症が蔓延する, 〜の蔓延を防ぐ. Since 蔓 is not a jōyō kanji, government agencies write まん延 (e.g. まん延防止等重点措置 during the Covid period). Unlike neutral 普及 ("spread" of technology) and 広がる, 蔓延 is always negative. Written language.

examples[].german: The eradication of poverty is a common goal of the international community.
Smallpox was eradicated through vaccines.
The school created new rules to eradicate bullying completely.
en.notes: 根絶 literally means "to cut at the root": to eliminate something evil completely and finally. As a transitive する-verb: 暴力を根絶する, passive 根絶される; common: 〜の根絶を目指す. Similar is 撲滅, which stresses the active fight (campaigns, slogans), while 根絶 stresses the complete result (天然痘は根絶された). 絶滅, on the other hand, is the extinction of species. Written language.
