examples[].german: A nationwide campaign to stamp out crime was launched.
A poster saying 「飲酒運転撲滅」 is put up in front of the station.
The farmers are working together to exterminate the pests.
en.notes: 撲滅 means "to wipe out by determined fighting" and stands above all for campaigns against crime, diseases or pests. Very common as a compound with the target in front: 犯罪撲滅, 飲酒運転撲滅, がん撲滅, 害虫撲滅; as a verb 〜を撲滅する. Compared with 根絶 ("to pull out by the root", result), 撲滅 stresses the fight itself and has a poster-like feel, typical for slogans and posters. Written language.

examples[].german: Protecting human dignity is the fundamental principle of law.
In nursing care, it is important to use language that does not hurt the dignity of the elderly.
The debate over death with dignity continues to this day.
en.notes: 尊厳 is the inviolable dignity of a human being or of something sublime. Typical: 人間の尊厳, 個人の尊厳 (a constitutional term), 尊厳を守る / 傷つける / 保つ, 尊厳死 "dying with dignity (passive euthanasia)". Unlike 威厳 ("dignified bearing, authority" of a person) and プライド / 誇り ("pride"), 尊厳 denotes a value that belongs to everyone. Elevated, frequent in law, medicine and ethics.

examples[].german: Raising citizens with respect for the law supports the foundation of society.
After a series of scandals, employees' awareness of the law is being questioned.
The union began a work-to-rule action to demand wage increases.
en.notes: 遵法 means "to obey the laws, law-abidingness". It appears almost only in compounds: 遵法精神, 遵法意識, 遵法闘争 "work-to-rule" (a form of labor action in which regulations are followed overly strictly). Also written 順法. For "compliance" in companies, one says 法令遵守 or コンプライアンス; the verb "to keep rules" is 守る or 遵守する. Formal, official.

examples[].german: The constitution should be amended on the basis of the general will of the people.
This was decided as the collective will of all the club members.
It was not easy to bring together a common will among the residents.
en.notes: 総意 is the common will or consensus of all members of a group. Typical: 国民の総意, 全員の総意, 〜の総意として, 総意に基づく. Known from Article 1 of the Japanese Constitution (天皇の地位は…日本国民の総意に基く). Unlike 合意 ("agreement" between parties after negotiation) and 多数意見 ("majority opinion"), 総意 denotes the will of the whole. Formal.

examples[].german: The weakening of the sense of belonging is leading to the decline of local communities.
The two countries have been in conflict for years over who the island belongs to.
The copyright of this work belongs to the company.
en.notes: 帰属 means that something belongs to, or is attributed to, a group, a state or a person: 〜に帰属する. Common are 帰属意識 "sense of belonging", 領土の帰属 "sovereignty over a territory" and, legally, 権利は〜に帰属する. For everyday membership in a company, club or department, one says 所属. The word is formal and appears in law, politics and sociology.

examples[].german: Policies promoting social inclusion are attracting attention.
Organizations that can embrace diverse values are the strong ones.
In logic, the concept "dog" is subsumed under the concept "animal".
en.notes: 包摂 means "to include, to encompass". In social policy, 社会的包摂 is the technical term for "social inclusion" (opposite 社会的排除), and also 包摂的な社会. In logic and philosophy, 包摂 means "subsumption": a concept is placed under a more general one (AはBに包摂される). As a verb it is transitive: 〜を包摂する. In everyday speech one more often says 含む or 受け入れる; for inclusion in schools also インクルージョン. Technical and written language.

examples[].german: Economic imbalance between regions is causing social problems.
A trade imbalance has persisted between the two countries for years.
The gender ratio in this faculty is unbalanced.
en.notes: 不均衡 is an imbalance between quantities that should actually be in balance: trade, income, regions, nutrition. Used as a noun (貿易不均衡, 需給の不均衡) and as a な-adjective (不均衡な配分). Opposite: 均衡 "balance". More neutral and technical than 格差 ("gap, inequality" between groups) and more formal than アンバランス or バランスが悪い in everyday speech. Frequent in economics and statistics.

examples[].german: Small parliamentary groups joined forces and voted in favor of the bill.
The two parties formed a joint parliamentary group in the House of Representatives.
An independent lawmaker joined that parliamentary group.
en.notes: 会派 is, in the Japanese parliament, a group of lawmakers registered with the respective house, similar to a parliamentary caucus. A 会派 can correspond to one party, but can also include several parties or independents (統一会派を組む/結成する). Speaking time and committee seats depend on the number of members. More generally, 会派 also means "school, faction" in religion or art; in politics it is technical.

examples[].german: The conflict between environmental protection and economic development is an important issue of modern society.
The novel portrays a protagonist suffering from the conflict between duty and affection.
The antagonism between father and son is at the center of this family saga spanning three generations.
en.notes: 相克 is the conflict of two forces that exclude each other and cannot be reconciled: 理性と感情の相克, 〜と〜の相克. Also written 相剋. It originally comes from the theory of the five elements (相克 "mutual overcoming", opposite 相生). Compared with 対立 ("opposition, confrontation") and 葛藤 ("inner conflict"), 相克 sounds literary and stresses a fateful incompatibility. Written language, often in essays and literary criticism.

examples[].german: Selfish behavior is weakening the cohesion of the community.
His decision did not come from egoism.
Thinking only of your own interests is too selfish.
en.notes: 利己 means "self-interest" and appears almost only in 利己的（な） "selfish" and 利己主義 "egoism (as an attitude)". 利己的な遺伝子 is the Japanese title of Dawkins' "The Selfish Gene". Opposite: 利他. In everyday speech one more often says 自分勝手, わがまま or 自己中（心的）; 利己的 sounds more objective and analytical. Formal.

examples[].german: The altruistic spirit forms the foundation of social welfare.
Altruistic behavior is also observed in some animals.
That business owner has made the "spirit of altruism" a pillar of his management.
en.notes: 利他 means "unselfishness, acting for the benefit of others" and mostly appears in 利他的（な） "altruistic" and 利他主義 "altruism". Opposite: 利己. In Buddhism, 利他 is a central value (自利利他 "benefiting oneself and others"). In everyday speech one more often says 人のために or 思いやりがある; 利他的 sounds objective, e.g. in psychology, biology or corporate philosophy.

examples[].german: Passing on the techniques of traditional crafts to the next generation is an urgent task.
As a souvenir from Kanazawa, I bought a lacquerware craft piece.
She is studying textile arts (dyeing and weaving) at university.
en.notes: 工芸 is craft art: objects that are both practical and beautiful (ceramics, lacquerware, textiles, woodwork). Typical: 伝統工芸, 工芸品, 工芸家, 美術工芸, 民芸 (folk craft). Unlike 美術 ("fine art"), 工芸 stresses use and craft technique; 手芸, by contrast, is handicraft such as knitting or embroidery as a hobby. Neutral.

examples[].german: Noh theater is registered as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of UNESCO.
At the weekend, I saw a performance at a Noh theater for the first time.
His family is a Noh family going back generations.
en.notes: 能楽 is the umbrella term for the classical stage art made up of 能 (serious masked drama with song and dance) and 狂言 (comic interludes). Typical: 能楽堂 "Noh theater", 能楽師 "Noh performer". In conversation one usually just says 能 (能を見に行く); 能楽 sounds more formal and appears in programs, specialist texts and names of institutions.

examples[].german: Performances of traditional Japanese music have a unique way of handling pauses.
I like Japanese music better than Western music because I can understand the lyrics.
My daughter plays the koto in her high school's traditional Japanese music club.
en.notes: 邦楽 has two meanings: in a cultural context, traditional Japanese music (koto, shamisen, shakuhachi, 邦楽器 "Japanese instruments"); in everyday speech and in record shops, however, simply "Japanese music" as opposed to 洋楽, including J-pop and Japanese rock (邦楽コーナー, 邦楽ロック). Which meaning is intended depends on the context. For traditional music in the narrower sense, one also says 和楽 or 伝統音楽.

examples[].german: Western music was introduced to Japan in earnest after the Meiji period.
Since junior high school I've listened to almost nothing but Western music.
I study English by translating the lyrics of Western songs.
en.notes: 洋楽 is "Western music". Historically it means the European art music introduced since the Meiji period; today in everyday speech it mainly means Western, mostly English-language, pop music (洋楽を聴く, 洋楽ファン, 洋楽ロック). The opposite term is 邦楽. For classical music, one nowadays more often says クラシック（音楽）. Neutral.

examples[].german: The folk songs of each region reflect the climate and way of life of that place.
At the Bon dance, everyone dances to the local folk songs.
My grandmother reportedly won a folk song contest when she was young.
en.notes: 民謡 are traditional folk songs of a region; in Japan they are often work songs or festival songs with a characteristic singing technique and shamisen accompaniment (津軽民謡, 民謡歌手). They are sung and danced to at 盆踊り. Unlike 童謡 ("children's song") and 演歌 (sentimental ballad), 民謡 are handed down anonymously. Western folk songs are also called 民謡 (ドイツ民謡). Neutral.

examples[].german: Japanese dance is a performing art that has perfected the beauty of movement.
My older sister has been learning classical Japanese dance since she was a child.
Folk dances from various countries were performed at the school festival.
en.notes: 舞踊 is dance as a performing art. Most often in 日本舞踊 "classical Japanese dance", and also 民族舞踊 "folk dance", 舞踊家, 舞踊団. In everyday speech, for dancing in general one says ダンス or 踊り / 踊る; 舞踊 sounds art-related and formal. 舞 stresses calm, circling movements, 踊 rhythmic jumping. Do not confuse with 舞踏 (Western ballroom dancing, Butō).

examples[].german: Ankoku butoh is an avant-garde form of physical expression that originated in Japan.
Cinderella went to the prince's ball.
In the Meiji era, Western-style balls were held at the Rokumeikan.
en.notes: 舞踏 first denotes dance, especially Western ballroom dancing: 舞踏会 "ball" (シンデレラの舞踏会), 舞踏曲 "dance music". It is also the name of the Japanese avant-garde dance form Butō that emerged in the 1950s (暗黒舞踏, often also in katakana ブトー). Unlike 舞踊 (dance as a stage art, especially 日本舞踊), 舞踏 now sounds slightly old-fashioned or technical. Formal.

examples[].german: A party disciplinary measure was imposed on the rebel lawmaker.
He was expelled for violating party discipline.
The party's disciplinary committee will decide the punishment next week.
en.notes: 党紀 is the discipline and order within a party. Typical: 党紀に違反する, 党紀を乱す, 党紀処分 ("party punishment", from a warning to 除名 "expulsion"), 党紀委員会. Pronounced the same is 党規 ("party statutes, party rules"); 党紀 stresses discipline. Violations often arise when lawmakers vote against the 党議拘束 ("party whip").

examples[].german: The spirit of elegance that sings of nature dwells in haiku.
There is a bamboo water pipe in the moss-covered garden, a truly refined atmosphere.
My grandfather was a cultured man who practiced tea ceremony and calligraphy.
en.notes: 風雅 is refined, cultivated elegance in the sense of traditional aesthetics, and also the pursuit of poetry, tea ceremony and calligraphy itself (風雅の道). As a な-adjective: 風雅な庭, 風雅な暮らし; also 風雅を解する "to have a sense for the refined". Compared with 優雅 ("graceful, elegant", also in a modern lifestyle), 風雅 is strongly literary and tied to nature and poetry; 風流 is similar but more common. Elevated.

examples[].german: The autumn foliage has an exceptional charm.
We walked through an atmospheric hot spring town with cobbled alleys.
A cityscape of nothing but new buildings is convenient but lacks charm.
en.notes: 情趣 is the atmospheric, emotionally charged air that something radiates and that touches the heart: 情趣がある, 情趣あふれる町並み, 情趣に欠ける. Close in meaning are 情緒 (more common, also 下町情緒) and 趣 ("charm, flair"), which is the most common in everyday speech. 情趣 is written language and is used mainly for landscapes, seasons and classical literature.

examples[].german: The beauty of yūgen pervades the world of Noh.
The mountain temple, wrapped in mist, was filled with a mysterious atmosphere.
The audience listened quietly to the profound tone of the shakuhachi.
en.notes: 幽玄 is a fundamental concept of Japanese aesthetics: a deep, mysterious beauty that suggests more than it shows. It particularly shapes 能 and classical poetry (幽玄の美, 幽玄の世界). As a な-adjective it now also describes mist-shrouded landscapes, dimly lit temples or music: 幽玄な雰囲気. Related are わび・さび (simple, transient beauty); 幽玄, by contrast, stresses the unfathomable. Elevated.

examples[].german: Developing a uniquely Japanese aesthetic eye requires years of training.
I go to a cosmetic dentist to have my teeth straightened.
This building is highly regarded not only for its functionality but also aesthetically.
en.notes: 審美 is the judging of beauty and appears almost only in compounds: 審美眼 "an eye for beauty, connoisseur's eye" (審美眼がある / を養う), 審美的（な） "aesthetic", 審美歯科 "cosmetic dentistry". The philosophy of aesthetics is called 美学 (formerly also 審美学). 審美 hardly stands alone; in everyday speech one says センス or 美的感覚. Written or technical language.

examples[].german: This sculptor's sense of form is unique and innovative.
In this film, the design of the monsters is very realistic.
Ancient pottery has a simple formal beauty.
en.notes: 造形 is the shaping of forms, especially in the visual arts: sculpture, plastic art, design, figures. Typical: 造形美術 "visual arts", 造形美 "formal beauty", 造形作家, キャラクターの造形 "character design". As a する-verb it is hardly used; one more often says 形を作る or 造形を手がける. Also written 造型. Unlike デザイン (design in general), 造形 stresses three-dimensional, physical form. Neutral to technical.

examples[].german: The changes in architectural styles reflect the aesthetic sense of each era.
Please submit the application on the prescribed form.
Because of the epidemic, people's way of life has changed greatly.
en.notes: 様式 denotes a fixed form or style, especially in compounds: 建築様式 "architectural style", 生活様式 "way of life", 行動様式 "behavior pattern". In government offices and companies, 様式 also means the prescribed form template, such as 所定の様式 "the prescribed form". Compared with スタイル, 様式 is more objective and more written; for an artist's personal style one more often says 作風 or スタイル.

examples[].german: Simple beauty free of excessive ornament is a characteristic of Japanese culture.
The wedding venue was decorated with white flowers.
Since this watch has little decoration, the dial is easy to read.
en.notes: 装飾 is the decorative design of rooms, buildings or objects; as a transitive する-verb: 会場を花で装飾する, passive 装飾される. Common compounds are 室内装飾 "interior decoration" and 装飾品 "ornament, accessory"; 装飾的 means "decorative", and for texts also pejoratively "overloaded". In everyday speech one mostly says 飾り or 飾る or デコレーション; 装飾 sounds more objective and relates to art, architecture or design.

examples[].german: The technique of metal inlay has been handed down since ancient times.
The sword guard of this sword is decorated with gold inlay.
The craftsman inlaid thin silver lines into the ebony box.
en.notes: 象嵌 is a craft technique in which gold, silver, mother-of-pearl or the like is set into a cut surface of metal, wood or ceramic. Typical phrases are 象嵌を施す "to apply inlay work", 金象嵌 "gold inlay" and 象嵌細工 "inlay work"; as a transitive する-verb: 銀を象嵌する. For mother-of-pearl inlay in lacquer there is the separate term 螺鈿. The word is a technical term from art and craft and is also written 象眼.

examples[].german: Arita ware is one of Japan's representative ceramics.
Ceramics break easily, so please pack them carefully.
At the museum, I saw an exhibition of old Chinese ceramics.
en.notes: 陶磁器 is the collective term for 陶器 "earthenware, pottery" (made of clay, rather thick and porous) and 磁器 "porcelain" (thin, hard and light). One speaks of 陶磁器の産地 "ceramics region" or 陶磁器を焼く "to fire ceramics"; regional wares carry the ending 〜焼, as in 有田焼 or 備前焼. In everyday speech, for tableware one mostly says 焼き物 or 器; 陶磁器 sounds objective, as in museums, trade or shipping notices.

examples[].german: This pottery is a renowned kiln with a history of over three hundred years.
On a trip, I visited a pottery and tried the potter's wheel.
Buying directly from the pottery is often cheaper than from a shop.
en.notes: 窯元 is the pottery or ceramics workshop that operates its own kiln, and also its owner or master potter. The kiln itself is only called 窯; 窯元 always means the business or the person behind it. Typical are 窯元を訪ねる, 窯元めぐり "tour of potteries" and 窯元直売 "direct sales from the pottery". 蔵元, for sake and soy sauce breweries, is formed similarly.

examples[].german: A new platform was adopted at the party convention.
The party's platform upholds pacifism.
The newspaper company has set a code of ethics that its reporters must follow.
en.notes: 綱領 are the principles or program of an organization, above all the basic platform of a party: 党の綱領, 綱領を採択する/改定する, 綱領に掲げる. Outside politics it appears in 倫理綱領 ("code of ethics") of professional associations or newspapers. Compared with 公約 ("campaign pledge") and マニフェスト, 綱領 is long-term and fundamental; the word is formal and written.

examples[].german: The skill of master craftsmen is attracting attention from around the world.
Master temple carpenters were gathered for the restoration of the temple.
These kitchen knives are handmade one by one by a master with fifty years in the trade.
en.notes: 匠 is a masterly craftsman whose skill has matured over many years; the word sounds appreciative and somewhat elevated. Fixed is 匠の技 "masterly craftsmanship", especially in advertising and media about traditional crafts. Neutrally one says 職人 "craftsman"; 名匠 and 巨匠 stress fame even more, 巨匠 above all for artists. As a component, 匠 is also in 意匠 "design, ornamental design".

examples[].german: Tea bowls made by great masters have high value as works of art as well.
This Buddha statue is said to be the work of a famous master of the Kamakura period.
A sword by a swordsmith known as a master was sold at auction for a high price.
en.notes: 名匠 is a famous, outstanding master, especially in the crafts (swordsmiths, potters, sculptors), occasionally also for directors or chefs. Typical are 名匠の作 "work of a famous master" and 名匠の手による "made by a master's hand". Compared with 匠, 名匠 highlights fame; 巨匠 is more used for great artists in painting, music and film. Do not confuse with the similar-sounding 名称 "name, designation".

examples[].german: The new film by a master of the film world was screened at an international film festival.
Famous paintings by the great masters of the Renaissance are gathered in this exhibition.
He too, unknown in his youth, is now called a great master.
en.notes: 巨匠 is a "grand master" with an outstanding reputation in art, music, literature or film, e.g. 映画界の巨匠, ルネサンスの巨匠 or 巨匠と呼ばれる指揮者. It is a respectful, often journalistic term for recognized, usually older figures. For craftsmen, 名匠 or 匠 fit better, and for masters in games such as shōgi or Go, 名人.

examples[].german: The achievements of the master who trained many disciples are immeasurable.
He became a disciple of a great master at fifteen.
Confucius is said to have had three thousand disciples.
en.notes: 門弟 is a pupil who has been accepted into a master's school, for example in martial arts, tea ceremony, painting or classical scholarship. Typical are 門弟となる "to become a disciple", 門弟を育てる and the classic image of Confucius's three thousand disciples. The word is elevated and somewhat old-fashioned; 門人 is synonymous, and the normal everyday term is 弟子. For pupils of an ordinary school one says 生徒 or 学生, never 門弟.

en.meaning: secret of an art; deepest teaching
examples[].german: Mastering the deepest secrets of the martial arts requires lifelong training.
Before his death, the master passed on the secret teachings to his only disciple.
The game's protagonist unleashed his ultimate technique in the final boss fight.
en.notes: 奥義 are the deepest, often secretly transmitted teachings or techniques of an art, which a master passes on only to advanced pupils. Typical verbs are 奥義を極める "to master completely", 奥義を伝授する or 奥義を授ける "to pass on" and 奥義を会得する "to acquire". Besides おうぎ, the reading おくぎ is also possible; related are 秘伝 "secret teaching" and 極意 "core, innermost secret". In manga and video games, 奥義 also denotes a character's strongest special technique.

examples[].german: The quintessence of Japanese culture is concentrated in this work.
It is said that the essence of the tea ceremony lies in the spirit of welcoming guests.
This book sums up the essence of the author's forty years of research.
en.notes: 精髄 is the most essential thing, the innermost core of a culture, teaching or art. It almost always appears with の: 日本文化の精髄, 思想の精髄; typical verbs are 精髄に触れる, 精髄を伝える and 精髄が凝縮される. More common and synonymous is 真髄 (also written 神髄); エッセンス sounds more colloquial. The word is written language and elevated.

examples[].german: The secret of cooking is to bring out the flavor of the ingredients to the fullest.
After long training, the disciple was entrusted with the innermost secret of swordsmanship by his master.
After ten years of work, I have finally grasped the essence of customer service.
en.notes: 極意 is the innermost secret or real essence of an art or skill, originally from martial arts and traditional arts: 剣の極意, 極意を授ける／伝授する, 極意をつかむ. Today it also appears casually in book titles such as 仕事の極意 or 会話の極意. コツ is an everyday "knack", 秘訣 a "secret recipe"; 極意 sounds the deepest and most elevated.

examples[].german: The movements of Noh have a refined beauty with no waste.
Her bearing is very graceful, and you can sense her good upbringing.
I learned from my grandmother how to move when wearing a kimono.
en.notes: 所作 denotes the way one moves and behaves, especially the formalized, beautiful movements in tea ceremony, Noh, Kabuki or martial arts. One says 所作が美しい, 所作を身につける or 美しい所作. Unlike neutral 動作 "movement, action", 所作 stresses posture and grace; 仕草 are rather small, involuntary gestures, and 立ち居振る舞い is behavior as a whole. In Kabuki, 所作事 is a dance piece.

examples[].german: In traditional Japanese arts, mastering the forms is considered fundamental.
At the karate tournament, she won the kata division.
With formulaic thinking, no new ideas are born.
en.notes: 型 refers to a fixed form or pattern: in martial arts and traditional arts the set sequence of movements (kata), but also a mold, a model or a convention. Important phrases are 型を覚える, 型にはまる "to be formulaic" as well as 型にはまらない and 型破り "unconventional". As a suffix it is read がた: 血液型, 新型, 大型. Distinction: 形 is the outer shape, 型 the prescribed pattern according to which something is made.

examples[].german: Various schools exist in the art of flower arrangement.
Even in karate, the kata and stances differ depending on the style.
He has been in contact with many calligraphers across school lines.
en.notes: 流派 is a school or style in an art or martial art that hands down its own teaching and technique, for example in ikebana, tea ceremony or karate. One says 流派に属する, 流派を開く "to found a school" and 流派を超えて "across schools". The names of such schools often end in 〜流, and at their head there is often an 家元. For scholarly or philosophical currents one more often says 学派.

examples[].german: The founding convention of the new party was held on a grand scale.
The party took power only ten years after its founding.
They founded a party under the banner of abolishing the consumption tax.
en.notes: 結党 is the founding of a political party; as a する-verb it is mostly intransitive (新党が結党する), but also transitive (新党を結党する). Typical: 結党大会, 結党以来, 結党〇周年. The opposite is 解党 ("dissolution of a party"). For groups in general, one says 結成する; 結党 is limited to parties and belongs to the language of the news.

en.meaning: head of a school of art; iemoto
examples[].german: The iemoto system plays an important role in passing on traditional Japanese culture.
In his twenties, he succeeded as head of an ikebana school.
Only a limited number of disciples can receive instruction directly from the head of the school.
en.notes: 家元 is the usually hereditary head of a school in traditional arts such as tea ceremony, ikebana, Noh, dance or music, and often also the family that runs the school. The 家元制度 regulates teaching authority and artist names; the title is usually passed on within the family: 家元を継ぐ. Respectfully one also says お家元; the designated successor is generally called 次期家元.

examples[].german: The shortage of successors for intangible cultural properties is a serious problem.
It is important to pass local festivals on to the next generation.
After the king's death, his eldest son succeeded to the throne.
en.notes: 継承 is taking over and carrying on something handed down: rights, offices, traditions or techniques; as a transitive する-verb: 伝統を継承する, 王位を継承する. Common are 継承者 "successor, heir", 王位継承 "succession to the throne" and, in computing, "inheritance" (クラスの継承). For inheriting property, one says 相続 instead; in everyday speech 継承する is often replaced by 受け継ぐ or 引き継ぐ.

examples[].german: Learning art begins with imitation and leads to originality.
Imitations of famous brands are sold online.
Small children learn by imitating the speech and behavior of the adults around them.
en.notes: 模倣 is imitating or copying a model; as a transitive する-verb: 手本を模倣する. It is objective to written language and is often the opposite of 独創 or 創造; in everyday speech one says 真似 or 真似する. Common compounds are 模倣品 "imitation product, counterfeit" and 模倣犯 "copycat criminal". Depending on the context it sounds neutral (learning by imitation) or derogatory (plagiarism).

examples[].german: Original ideas make this artist's works stand out.
The originality of this paper was highly rated.
His cooking builds on tradition yet is full of originality.
en.notes: 独創 is producing something entirely one's own, not imitated. It seldom stands alone; it mostly appears as 独創的 "original", 独創性 "originality" or in phrases such as 独創に富む "rich in originality". The opposite term is 模倣 "imitation"; similar are 独自 "one's own, independent" and 創造 "creation", while オリジナリティ sounds more colloquial.

examples[].german: The Tale of the Heike is a masterpiece of Japan's epic literature.
The Iliad is an ancient Greek epic poem about the Trojan War.
His novels are written in a narrative style that holds back emotion.
en.notes: 叙事 is the factual presentation of events and facts, without putting one's own feelings in the foreground. It hardly occurs on its own; the usual forms are 叙事詩 "epic, epic poetry", 叙事文学 and 叙事的 "epic, narrative". The opposite is 叙情 (also 抒情) "lyric poetry, expression of feeling", e.g. 叙情詩 "lyric poem". The word belongs to the technical language of literary studies.

en.meaning: to compose (a poem); to write a poem
examples[].german: Composing poems about the beauties of nature (flowers, birds, wind and moon) is the foundation of waka.
Seeing the beautiful scenery on my trip, I tried composing a haiku.
Mt. Fuji has been celebrated in many waka poems since ancient times.
en.notes: 詠む means "to compose a poem (waka, tanka, haiku)" and is used only for poetry: 歌を詠む, 一句詠む for a haiku, 一首詠む for a tanka. In the form 〜に詠まれる it means "to be celebrated in poems", e.g. 富士山は多くの歌に詠まれてきた. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 読む "to read"; for prose one says 書く, and for reciting rather 吟じる or 朗読する.

examples[].german: The sight of him reciting Chinese poems in a resonant voice was impressive.
Whenever my grandfather had had some drink, he would invariably recite old poems.
At the shigin recital, the students each recited a Chinese poem in turn.
en.notes: 吟じる means to recite a poem in a solemn, melodic voice, above all Chinese poems (漢詩) or waka in the style of 詩吟. 吟ずる is synonymous and somewhat more classical; less often it also means "to compose a poem". Compared with the neutral 朗読する "to read aloud", 吟じる stresses the sung, drawn-out delivery; typical is 朗々と吟じる "to recite in a resonant voice". The word is elevated and literary.

en.meaning: to brew; to create; to bring about
examples[].german: This work creates a unique atmosphere.
The prime minister's careless remark is stirring up controversy.
This brewery makes sake using traditional methods.
en.notes: 醸す originally means "to brew sake or soy sauce by fermentation"; today it is used mainly in a figurative sense. Very common are 物議を醸す "to stir up controversy" and the compound 醸し出す "to give off, create an atmosphere", e.g. 雰囲気を醸し出す. The word is literary; in everyday speech one says 造る (酒を造る) for brewing and rather 雰囲気がある for the mood.

en.meaning: to cultivate (an art); to indulge in moderation
examples[].german: The number of people who practice the tea ceremony is growing even among the younger generation.
I only drink alcohol occasionally and in moderation, never much.
My grandfather has been writing haiku since his youth.
en.notes: 嗜む means to pursue an art, a sport or a luxury item with interest and in moderation: 茶道を嗜む, 俳句を嗜む, お酒を少々嗜む. It sounds cultured and modest and therefore suits self-introductions well; the more neutral alternative is 趣味にしている. It is mostly written in kana (たしなむ). The noun 嗜み means "knowledge, skill" and also "decorum, good manners" (大人の嗜み).

en.meaning: to spin; to weave together (words, stories); to tell
examples[].german: I take my hat off to the imagination of the author who spins stories.
My grandmother turned the spinning wheel and spun thread from sheep's wool.
Fighting back tears, she put her words together one by one.
en.notes: 紡ぐ literally means "to spin fibers such as cotton, wool or silk into thread": 糸を紡ぐ, 綿を紡ぐ. Figuratively and in literary use it means to piece together words, stories or memories with care: 言葉を紡ぐ, 物語を紡ぐ, 歴史を紡ぐ. This figurative use is now more common and sounds poetic. "To weave" in the literal sense is 織る instead.

examples[].german: Three members announced their departure from the party because of differences in policy.
He submitted his resignation from the party to the party headquarters.
The lawmaker who left the party ran as an independent in the next election.
en.notes: 離党 is voluntarily leaving a party; as a する-verb it is intransitive, yet the party still takes を: 自民党を離党する. Typical: 離党届を出す, 離党を表明する, 離党に追い込まれる. Equivalent in meaning, but sounding somewhat harsher, is 脱党; expulsion by the party is called 除名. The opposite is 入党.

examples[].german: Appreciating art enriches the heart.
My hobby is watching movies.
Please view the works quietly in the museum.
en.notes: 鑑賞 is the enjoying, understanding viewing or listening to art: 美術鑑賞, 音楽鑑賞, 映画鑑賞; as a transitive する-verb: 絵画を鑑賞する. 映画鑑賞 and 音楽鑑賞 are standard answers to the question about one's hobby. Not to be confused with the similar-sounding words 観賞 "viewing nature, flowers or ornamental fish" (観賞魚), 感傷 "sentimentality" and 干渉 "interference".

examples[].german: He was inducted into the music hall of fame.
Universities are often called temples of learning.
This theater has long been loved as a temple of classical music.
en.notes: 殿堂 is originally a magnificent hall or temple building; today it is mostly used figuratively for an institution regarded as the supreme place of a field: 学問の殿堂 "temple of learning", 芸術の殿堂. Very common is 殿堂入り "induction into the hall of fame", also in sports (野球殿堂) and in rankings. The word is elevated; do not confuse it with the homophones 伝道 "missionary work" and 電動 "electric".

examples[].german: Stone monuments inscribed with verses by Matsuo Basho stand all over the country.
A monument mourning the victims of the war stands in the park.
The characters carved into the monument have weathered and are almost unreadable.
en.notes: 碑 is an inscribed stone commemorating a person, an event or a poem; read on its own it is ひ, poetically also いしぶみ. It mostly appears in compounds: 記念碑 "monument", 慰霊碑 "memorial for the dead", 石碑, 句碑 and 歌碑 for engraved haiku and waka respectively. Typical verbs are 碑を建てる and 碑に刻む. A gravestone, by contrast, is 墓石, and a statue 銅像.

examples[].german: Horyu-ji has the oldest buildings in Japan designated as national treasures.
The main keep of Himeji Castle is designated a national treasure.
My grandfather is a ceramic artist who was certified as a Living National Treasure.
en.notes: 国宝 is a cultural property officially designated a national treasure, the highest rank above 重要文化財; one says 国宝に指定する or 国宝に指定されている. 人間国宝 is the popular term for holders of outstanding traditional skills ("Living National Treasure"). In colloquial speech 国宝級 praises something as extraordinary, e.g. 国宝級の美しさ.

examples[].german: This Buddha statue is designated an important cultural property.
Photography is prohibited inside the building, which is an important cultural property.
The main hall, an important cultural property, burned down in the fire.
en.notes: 重要文化財 is a statutory protection category for buildings, works of art and documents of special value; the most outstanding of them are additionally declared 国宝. One says 重要文化財に指定する or 指定されている; in the media and guidebooks the abbreviation 重文 is common. The word is official and matter-of-fact and is found mainly on information signs, in travel guides and in the news.

examples[].german: He has the strong will to stand by his convictions.
"Always keep your promises" is my principle.
The constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of creed.
en.notes: 信条 is a firm principle by which one lives or acts, and in the religious sense a creed. Typical are 〜を信条とする "to make something one's principle", 信条を貫く and 私の信条は〜だ. In legal texts 信条 stands for ideological conviction, for example in the constitution's ban on discrimination. Compared with 信念 "firm conviction", 信条 stresses more a rule of life that can be put into words.

examples[].german: Understanding the differences between the doctrines of the various denominations is the foundation of religious studies.
According to Catholic doctrine, divorce is not permitted.
That religious group attracted followers by putting forward its own doctrine.
en.notes: 教義 is the binding teaching of a religion or faith community, its articles of faith. Typical phrases are 教義に従う, 教義に反する, 教義を説く and 教義を掲げる. Figuratively it can also mean the rigid doctrine of an ideology; "dogmatic", however, is 教条的. Distinctions: 教え is the general, softer word for "teaching", 経典 the scripture in which the teaching is written.

examples[].german: Monks keep strict precepts and devote themselves to training.
Under Islamic religious law, eating pork is forbidden.
The monk who broke the precepts was driven out of the temple.
en.notes: 戒律 are the religious commandments and rules of conduct that believers, monks or nuns must observe, e.g. dietary and abstinence rules. Typical verbs are 戒律を守る, 戒律を破る and 戒律に従う; 厳しい戒律 is a common combination. Figuratively, the strict rules of a group can also be called this. Distinctions: 規則 are secular regulations, 教義 the content of the faith, 戒律 the rules for living.

examples[].german: Some practitioners aim at purifying the mind through asceticism.
After six years of asceticism, Buddha realized that it was not the path to enlightenment.
Commuting an hour on a packed train is truly an ordeal.
en.notes: 苦行 is religious asceticism in which one seeks to purify mind and body through fasting, cold or pain; as an intransitive する-verb it is rare (苦行する), the usual forms being 苦行を積む and 苦行に耐える. Colloquially, and often with exaggeration, it denotes any agonizingly tedious activity: 〜はまさに苦行だ. Distinction: 修行 is religious or artistic training in general, while 苦行 stresses deliberate suffering.

examples[].german: In Zen practice, enlightenment is regarded as the ultimate goal.
Tradition has it that Buddha attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.
He is quick on the uptake, so explaining it once is enough.
en.notes: 悟り is, in Buddhism, enlightenment, the awakening to the truth; fixed is 悟りを開く "to attain enlightenment". It also means in general "understanding, grasp", for example 悟りが早い "quick to understand". It is the noun of the verb 悟る "to realize, comprehend". Colloquially, さとり世代 denotes a sober young generation without strong desires.

examples[].german: The number of young people joining parties is on an upward trend.
He joined the Communist Party when he was a university student.
To join the party, you have to pay dues every year.
en.notes: 入党 is joining a political party; as a する-verb it is intransitive with に: 共産党に入党する. Typical: 入党を申し込む, 入党手続き, 入党を勧める. The opposite is 離党; for associations and clubs one says 入会 in general. The word belongs to the language of politics and the news.

en.meaning: liberation; release from the cycle of rebirth
examples[].german: In Buddhism, liberation means release from worldly desires.
In Buddhism, release from the cycle of rebirth is considered the final goal.
The entrance exams are over, and I finally feel freed from the days of nonstop studying.
en.notes: 解脱 is, in Buddhism, liberation from desires and from the cycle of rebirth; as an intransitive する-verb: 輪廻から解脱する, 煩悩から解脱する. It is a religious technical term; closely related are 悟り "enlightenment" and 涅槃 "nirvana". It is also said jokingly when one feels freed from a burdensome duty. For worldly liberation one normally uses 解放.

examples[].german: The idea of samsara and reincarnation originates in Indian philosophy.
Buddhism teaches that living beings go through the cycle of rebirth again and again even after death.
For people who believe in reincarnation, death is not the end.
en.notes: 輪廻 is the Buddhist-Hindu cycle of death and rebirth; mostly in the fixed combination 輪廻転生. Typical are 輪廻を繰り返す, 輪廻から抜け出す and 輪廻を信じる; more rarely as an intransitive する-verb "to be reborn". Liberation from it is called 解脱. The word is religious-philosophical; in everyday speech one says rather 生まれ変わり "rebirth".

examples[].german: It is said that the karma of past lives determines one's fate in this life.
Not being able to cast off desire is probably what is called human karma.
The department head, losing patience at the lack of a reply, phoned the client himself.
en.notes: 業 (ごう) is the Buddhist term "karma": deeds and their consequences, which work beyond lifetimes, also in the sense of fate. Fixed phrases are 業が深い "sinful, heavily burdened", 人間の業 "the inescapable nature of humans" and 業を煮やす "to boil with impatience". Do not confuse it with the reading ぎょう (職業, 卒業) or わざ "technique". Related: 自業自得.

examples[].german: The New Year's Eve bell is rung to drive away the 108 worldly desires.
Even when I sit in zazen, my worldly desires don't easily go away.
I'm on a diet, but when I see cake, temptation stirs.
en.notes: 煩悩 are, in Buddhism, the mental defilements such as greed, hatred and delusion that cause suffering; traditionally one speaks of 百八つの煩悩. Typical phrases are 煩悩を払う, 煩悩を断ち切る and 煩悩にとらわれる. In everyday speech it is often used jokingly for small cravings, such as a longing for sweets or laziness. 子煩悩, on the other hand, is praise: "doting on one's own children".

examples[].german: Buddha's compassion is poured out equally on all sentient beings.
The king showed mercy even to the defeated enemy.
"Please, have mercy," the man begged the judge.
en.notes: 慈悲 is originally the Buddhist virtue of kindness and compassion for all beings; in general "mercy, grace". Typical phrases are 慈悲深い "merciful", 慈悲をかける "to show mercy" and the pleading request どうかお慈悲を. The opposite is 無慈悲 "merciless". Compared with 同情 "sympathy" and 思いやり "consideration", 慈悲 sounds exalted and religiously colored.

examples[].german: The bodhisattva Kannon is worshipped as a being who saves sentient beings from suffering.
The Jizo statues by the roadside are the bodhisattva Jizo.
My grandmother was as kind as a bodhisattva.
en.notes: 菩薩 is, in Mahayana Buddhism, a being who strives for enlightenment but vows to save all other beings first. It often appears as a title after the name: 観音菩薩, 地蔵菩薩, 弥勒菩薩. In rank, 菩薩 stands below 如来, the perfected Buddha. Figuratively, 菩薩のような人 denotes an exceptionally kind person.

examples[].german: Amida Nyorai is revered as the principal object of worship of the Jodo school.
Yakushi Nyorai has long been worshipped as the Buddha who heals illness.
When we entered the main hall, a golden statue of a Buddha sat quietly there.
en.notes: 如来 is an honorific title for a perfected Buddha who has attained enlightenment; it follows the name: 阿弥陀如来, 薬師如来, 大日如来. In the ranking of Buddhist figures, 如来 stands above 菩薩, 明王 and 天. On temple visits the word appears mainly in names of statues (如来像) and main halls.

examples[].german: After attaining enlightenment, the Buddha taught his disciples.
The Buddha's teachings eventually spread throughout Asia.
The place where the Buddha was born is in present-day Nepal.
en.notes: 仏陀 is the kanji spelling of "Buddha", today mostly written in katakana as ブッダ. It refers above all to the historical Buddha, who in everyday speech is rather called お釈迦様 or 釈迦. ほとけ／仏, by contrast, denotes buddhas in general and also the deceased. Typical: 仏陀の教え, 仏陀が悟りを開く.

examples[].german: The Heart Sutra is one of the most widely read Buddhist sutras.
Many sutras reached China from India via the Silk Road.
He is translating old sutras into modern language.
en.notes: 経典 (きょうてん) are above all the Buddhist sutras, and in general also the holy scriptures of other religions such as the Bible or the Koran. Typical verbs are 経典を読む, 経典を唱える and 経典を翻訳する. Read けいてん, the same spelling denotes the Confucian classics. Distinctions: お経 is the everyday word for the sutras that are recited, 聖典 stresses the sacred character of a text, 教典 the doctrinal text.

examples[].german: Every religion has its own sacred scriptures.
The Koran is the holy book of Islam.
This book is regarded as the bible among mountaineering enthusiasts.
en.notes: 聖典 is the holy scripture of a religion, such as the Bible, the Koran or the Vedas; the word stresses the sacred, authoritative character. Figuratively, a standard work that is revered almost cultishly in a group is called 〜の聖典 ("the bible of ..."). Distinctions: 経典 refers mainly to Buddhist sutras, 聖書 specifically to the Christian Bible.

en.meaning: House of Representatives (lower house of the Japanese parliament)
examples[].german: The House of Representatives will be dissolved and a general election held.
The term of a House of Representatives member is four years.
On the budget, the House of Representatives' resolution takes precedence.
en.notes: 衆議院 is the lower house of the Japanese parliament, abbreviated 衆院. The term is four years, but the house can be dissolved early (解散), after which a general election (総選挙) follows. On the budget, treaties and the election of the prime minister, it takes precedence over the 参議院 (衆議院の優越). Typical: 衆議院議員, 衆議院を解散する, 衆議院を通過する.

examples[].german: Two political parties formed a coalition government.
The ruling party formed a coalition with part of the opposition.
We solved simultaneous equations in math class.
en.notes: 連立 in politics means "coalition": 連立政権, 連立を組む, 連立与党, 連立を離脱する ("to leave the coalition"). The basic meaning is "to exist side by side", hence also the mathematical term 連立方程式 ("system of equations"). As a する-verb it is intransitive and rare; it mostly appears as a noun or in compounds. A looser alliance is called 連携 or 協力.

examples[].german: A dispute arose between the schools over the interpretation of the doctrinal texts.
That religious group takes a book compiling its founder's words as its doctrinal text.
Every morning the believers read a passage from the doctrinal text aloud.
en.notes: 教典 is a text in which the teaching of a religion is set down, especially in newer faith communities and schools; also an authoritative textbook. It is read the same as 経典, which mainly means Buddhist sutras; in conversation, context or the paraphrase 教えの本 therefore often helps. Typical are 教典を読む, 教典の解釈 and 〜を教典とする.

examples[].german: In the Edo period, the religion of the population was controlled through official religious inspections.
The monk who had gone against the teachings of his sect was severely punished.
en.notes: 宗門 is an older, formal word for a religious denomination or community, today mainly in history and in the usage of the temple organizations themselves. Well known is 宗門改め, the religious inspection of the Edo period, with which the shogunate tracked down Christians and assigned every household to a temple. In everyday speech today one says 宗派 instead.

en.meaning: missionary work; propagation of a faith
examples[].german: Buddhism spread across the world through missionary activity abroad.
In the 16th century, missionaries began propagating Christianity in Japan.
I got my friend into my favorite anime, and now he is completely hooked.
en.notes: 布教 is spreading a religion and recruiting new believers, regardless of the religion; as a transitive する-verb: 教えを布教する, but more often 布教活動 "missionary activity". For Christian missions 伝道 and 宣教 are also usual. Colloquially and jokingly, one speaks of 布教 when someone wants to get friends excited about their favorite hobby, series or band.

examples[].german: Francis Xavier was a pioneer of missionary work in Japan.
He went to Africa as a missionary.
On Sundays, believers preach in front of the station.
en.notes: 伝道 is the proclamation of a religion, above all Christian mission and evangelism; as a する-verb: 伝道する. Common are 伝道活動, 伝道師 "preacher, missionary" and 伝道の旅. Close in meaning are 布教 (religion-neutral) and 宣教. Do not confuse it with the homophones 伝導 "conduction (of heat, electricity)", 殿堂 "hall" and 電動 "electrically powered".

examples[].german: Forced conversion is an act that violates freedom of religion.
He converted to Islam when he got married.
In the Sengoku period, some daimyo converted to Christianity.
en.notes: 改宗 is conversion to another religion or denomination; as an intransitive する-verb with に: キリスト教に改宗する, also 〜から〜に改宗する. Forced conversion is called 強制改宗. Jokingly it is also used for a change of preference, for example when switching to a different smartphone. Distinction: 帰依 stresses inner devotion, 改宗 the change itself.

en.meaning: devotion to a faith; taking refuge
examples[].german: Taking refuge in the Three Jewels is the starting point of a Buddhist.
In his later years, he devoted himself deeply to Buddhism.
In the Kamakura period, many samurai embraced Zen.
en.notes: 帰依 means to entrust oneself entirely to a faith, a Buddha or a revered teacher and to take refuge in it; as an intransitive する-verb with に: 仏教に帰依する, 三宝に帰依する. It stresses inner devotion, whereas 改宗 only denotes the change of religion. The word is religious and literary and often occurs in biographies and historical accounts; 深く帰依する is a common combination.

examples[].german: A prayer for a bountiful harvest was held at the shrine.
Since it is my unlucky year, I had a prayer for warding off misfortune performed at the shrine.
We had prayers said at the temple for my mother's recovery.
en.notes: 祈祷 is a formal, ritual prayer, usually performed by priests or monks on someone's behalf, for example for health, harvest or protection from misfortune; as a する-verb: 祈祷する, often 祈祷を受ける, 祈祷してもらう. Related are 祈祷師 "prayer healer" and 厄除け祈祷 "prayer to ward off misfortune". The general word for "prayer" is 祈り or お祈り; 祈願 stresses the concrete wish. Traditionally it is also written 祈禱.

examples[].german: Many exam candidates visit shrines to pray for passing their exams.
At New Year we went to the shrine as a family and prayed for good health for the year.
Before the season opened, the team prayed for victory.
en.notes: 祈願 is the formal request for divine help for a specific goal, usually at a shrine or temple. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を祈願する (安全を祈願する). Very common in compounds such as 合格祈願, 必勝祈願 or 家内安全, which one reads on amulets and votive plaques. More general is 祈り "prayer"; 祈祷 stresses the ritual performed by a priest.

examples[].german: Meditation experiences at Zen temples are popular among tourists.
I make a point of meditating with my eyes closed for ten minutes every morning.
He sat by the window, quietly lost in meditation.
en.notes: 瞑想 is "meditation" in the general sense, both religious and secular for relaxation. Intransitive する-verb: 目を閉じて瞑想する; to become completely absorbed in thought is 瞑想にふける. The spelling 冥想 also occurs. 座禅, by contrast, is specifically the seated meditation of Zen; modern mindfulness practice is often called マインドフルネス.

examples[].german: Citizens staged a protest against the government's decision.
The manager protested vehemently against the umpire's call.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs lodged a strong protest with the other country.
en.notes: 抗議 is a protest or objection against a decision or action; as a する-verb it mostly takes に: 審判に抗議する, 決定に抗議する. Typical: 抗議デモ, 抗議文, 厳重に抗議する (diplomatic), 抗議が殺到する. To be distinguished are 反対 ("being against", without an active complaint), 異議 ("formal objection", 異議あり) and the colloquial 文句を言う ("to complain, grumble").

examples[].german: By practicing zazen one can attain inner stillness.
On the weekend I tried a zazen session at a temple.
My legs went numb during zazen, and I couldn't stand up.
en.notes: 座禅 is the seated meditation of Zen Buddhism, usually in the lotus or half-lotus position. The fixed combination is 座禅を組む "to sit down for zazen, to practice zazen"; also 座禅をする. The original spelling 坐禅 is used mainly by Zen temples. Anyone who nods off gets a blow on the shoulder with the wooden stick 警策.

examples[].german: The voice of the monk reciting sutras echoed through the hall.
At the funeral, the mourners offer incense while the monk recites the sutras.
On my grandfather's death anniversary, a monk came to our house and recited sutras.
en.notes: 読経 is the loud, rhythmic recitation of Buddhist sutras by monks, for example at funerals and memorial services. Besides どきょう, the reading どっきょう is also in use. As an intransitive する-verb: 僧侶が読経する; common is 読経の声. In everyday speech one usually says more simply お経を読む or お経をあげる.

examples[].german: A memorial service for the first anniversary of the deceased's death was held.
After the 49th-day memorial service, the interment of the ashes was completed.
A memorial service to mourn the victims of the earthquake was held at the temple.
en.notes: 法要 is a Buddhist ceremony, above all the memorial service for the deceased on fixed dates (四十九日, 一周忌, 三回忌). One says formally 法要を営む or neutrally 法要を行う. The everyday counterpart is 法事; 法要 sounds more formal and often appears in invitations and newspaper reports.

en.meaning: memorial service; offering for the dead
examples[].german: Ancestor memorial rites are an important aspect of Japan's Buddhist culture.
At Obon I go back to my parents' home to honor the ancestors.
I didn't throw away the old dolls but had them ritually laid to rest at a temple.
en.notes: 供養 means to offer the deceased or Buddhas offerings, prayers and sutra recitations in order to comfort the souls. As a transitive する-verb: 先祖を供養する, 霊を供養する. In Japan one also bids things farewell ritually: at a 人形供養 or 針供養, worn-out dolls or sewing needles are gratefully "buried". 法要 is the individual ceremony, 供養 rather the act and intention of remembrance.

en.meaning: transfer of merit; prayer for the dead
examples[].german: A service was held to dedicate merit to the deceased.
The head priest prayed for the souls of the war dead.
At the end of the sutra recitation, a dedication text is chanted.
en.notes: 回向 is a Buddhist technical term: the "turning toward" others, especially the deceased, of the merit (功徳) earned through sutra recitation or good deeds, in order to further their spiritual welfare. From this comes the meaning "prayer for the repose of the soul". Patterns: 功徳を故人に回向する, 霊に回向する. The word is highly technical; in everyday speech one says 供養.

examples[].german: The initiation ritual in esoteric Buddhism is carried out in secret.
Kukai conferred the kanjo initiation on Saicho at Takaosanji temple.
On Mt. Koya, ordinary people too can receive a kechien kanjo initiation.
en.notes: 灌頂 is, in esoteric Buddhism (密教, esp. Shingon and Tendai), the initiation in which water is poured over the disciple's head in order to transmit teachings or the rank of master to him. Typical are 灌頂を受ける / 灌頂を授ける as well as 結縁灌頂 (initiation for laypeople) and 伝法灌頂 (master's initiation). The reading かんちょう also occurs. Not an everyday word; it has only a distant connection with anointing in the Christian sense.

examples[].german: After the ordination ceremony, he formally became a monk.
She was ordained at fifty and began a new life as a nun.
As heir to the temple, he was ordained at the age of ten.
en.notes: 得度 is ordination: one takes the vows, receives a Buddhist name and enters the state of monk or nun, usually with a shaved head. Intransitive する-verb: 得度する; the ceremony is called 得度式. Similar in meaning is 出家 "to leave home, become a monk", which sounds more general; 得度 denotes the formal rite.

examples[].german: Nirvana is the ultimate state of liberation from all suffering.
Tradition has it that the Buddha entered nirvana at the age of eighty.
I saw a huge reclining Buddha statue at a temple in Thailand.
en.notes: 涅槃 is the state of complete liberation from desire and suffering, the final goal of Buddhist practice. At the same time it denotes the death of the Buddha: 涅槃に入る "to enter nirvana". Well-known compounds are 涅槃像 "reclining Buddha" and 涅槃会, the memorial service for the Buddha's death on February 15. The katakana form ニルヴァーナ is rare.

examples[].german: The goal of Buddhist practice is to cross from this shore to the other shore.
The Sanzu River is said to be the boundary between this shore and the other shore.
The novel depicts the grief of those left behind on this shore.
en.notes: 此岸 is "this shore": the world of the living, full of suffering and desire, as opposed to 彼岸 "that shore", the beyond or enlightenment. The word almost always appears paired with 彼岸 (此岸と彼岸, 此岸から彼岸へ) and is Buddhist-literary. 此 is an old spelling for この. While お彼岸, the memorial week around the equinox, is known to everyone, 此岸 hardly occurs in everyday speech.

examples[].german: The Pure Land teachings were widely accepted by the common people in the late Heian period.
The Phoenix Hall of Byodo-in was built to recreate the Pure Land paradise on earth.
Our family's denomination is Jodo Shinshu.
en.notes: 浄土 is the "Pure Land", a world without suffering created by a Buddha; usually Amida's western paradise is meant (極楽浄土, 西方浄土). From it derive the schools 浄土宗 and 浄土真宗, whose believers hope to be reborn in the Pure Land by reciting the 念仏 (浄土に往生する). Figuratively it can denote a paradisiacally peaceful place; in everyday speech one rather says 楽園 for this.

examples[].german: A large demonstration took place in front of the Diet building.
The shop assistant gave me a demo of the new camera.
en.notes: デモ can refer to a protest rally or to a demonstration. In front of a parliament building with many participants, the protest is usually meant. With an app or a device, on the other hand, デモ can show how something works. The katakana form belongs to these nouns; the similar-sounding でも is used differently as a grammatical connective.

examples[].german: It is taught that by reciting the nenbutsu one can be reborn in paradise.
Soaking in the open-air bath, I murmured, "Ahh, this is heaven."
The job ad made it look easy, but it was heaven to hear about and hell to see.
en.notes: 極楽 is originally Amida's paradise (short for 極楽浄土) and the opposite of 地獄 "hell". In everyday speech it is often used jokingly for supreme comfort, for example in a hot bath: 「ああ、極楽極楽」. Fixed phrases are 極楽往生 "to die peacefully and enter paradise" and 聞いて極楽見て地獄 "sounds heavenly, is in reality hell". 天国 is the word for "heaven" with a Christian coloring.

examples[].german: The concept of reincarnation forms the core of Eastern thought.
Do you believe in reincarnation?
In Buddhism, it is said that through enlightenment one can be freed from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth.
en.notes: 輪廻転生 is a yojijukugo made of 輪廻 "cycle of birth and death" and 転生 "rebirth in another form": the doctrine that all beings are reborn again and again after death. Besides りんねてんしょう, りんねてんせい is also common. Typical: 輪廻転生を信じる, 輪廻転生から解脱する; often one says just 輪廻. In pop culture, 転生 on its own is very popular, for example in novels about rebirth in another world.

en.meaning: passing into paradise; peaceful death; being at a loss
examples[].german: At the moment of death, he passed away peacefully.
On the way home I got caught in a sudden downpour, and I was totally stuck.
Because of heavy snow, the car got stuck, and we spent the night in the vehicle.
en.notes: 往生 means in Buddhism "to go over to the Pure Land and be reborn there" and is therefore a euphemism for a peaceful death: 往生を遂げる, especially 大往生 "death in old age after a fulfilled life". Colloquially and somewhat old-fashioned, 往生する also means "to not know what to do, to be in a fix". Derived from it is 立ち往生 "to get stuck, be stranded" (train, car, speaker). Intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: Mahayana Buddhism teaches that all sentient beings can attain buddhahood.
It is said that if you still cling to this world, you cannot rest in peace.
At my grandmother's grave, I put my hands together: "Please rest in peace."
en.notes: 成仏 literally means "to become a Buddha", that is, to attain enlightenment. In everyday speech it mainly means that a deceased person finds peace and does not wander as a ghost: 安らかに成仏してください, and in the negative 成仏できない for a restless soul. In contrast to 往生 (rebirth in the Pure Land), 成仏 stresses buddhahood or the repose of the soul. Intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: It is believed that one can gain merit by accumulating good deeds.
Many people want to accumulate merit by doing the Shikoku pilgrimage.
Copying sutras is said to bring great merit.
en.notes: 功徳 is the religious merit one earns through good deeds, donations or sutra recitation, and at the same time the blessing that arises from it. The fixed combination is 功徳を積む "to accumulate merit"; also 功徳がある "to be beneficial". Note: the reading is くどく, not こうとく. Close in meaning is ご利益 "blessing, benefit (from gods or Buddhas)", which stresses rather the concrete advantage for the believer.

examples[].german: He repented of his sins and began a new life.
Everyone lives carrying some kind of guilt.
The protagonist kept suffering over the depth of his sins.
en.notes: 罪業 is a Buddhist-flavored term for sin in the sense of bad karma: misdeeds whose consequences one must bear in this or a later life. Typical are 罪業を背負う, 罪業が深い and 罪業を懺悔する. More general and everyday is 罪 "guilt, sin, offense"; 罪業 sounds heavy, literary and religious.

examples[].german: Pressing his hands together before the Buddha, he repented of his past errors.
The trainee monks repent of their conduct every morning.
In his later years, he wrote his autobiography in the spirit of a confession of the mistakes of his youth.
en.notes: 懺悔 is the remorseful confession of one's own transgressions. Today it is generally read ざんげ, also in the Christian context (懺悔室 "confessional"); in Buddhism the reading さんげ is also traditionally used. As a transitive する-verb: 罪を懺悔する. In everyday speech it is often used half-jokingly for a confession; 後悔 by contrast is mere regret without confession.

examples[].german: A sense of atonement changed his life greatly.
In Christianity, Jesus' death on the cross is regarded as atonement for humankind.
The defendant made an atonement donation before the verdict.
en.notes: 贖罪 is "atonement": to answer for guilt one has incurred through deeds or sacrifice. In Christian theology it denotes the redemption of humankind through the death of Jesus. In a secular sense it appears in 贖罪の意識 "the need to atone for guilt" and in criminal law as 贖罪寄付, a donation by the offender as a sign of remorse. The more everyday word for making amends is 償い (償う).

examples[].german: An ascetic life is led in the monastery.
For the month before the tournament, I gave up sweets and alcohol and lived like an ascetic.
If you deny yourself too much, you actually build up stress.
en.notes: 禁欲 is the deliberate renunciation of desires and pleasures such as sex, alcohol or luxury, whether religiously motivated as in monasticism or for personal reasons. Common in 禁欲的な生活 "ascetic life", 禁欲生活を送る and, as an intransitive する-verb, 禁欲する. Milder terms are 節制 "moderation" and 我慢 "holding oneself back"; 禁欲 means strict renunciation.

examples[].german: Keeping a pure heart is the basis of religious practice.
Climbers in white garb ascend the mountain chanting "rokkon shojo".
Buddhism aims at a pure state free of worldly desires.
en.notes: 清浄 means "pure, free of dirt and defilement". In religious contexts (Buddhism, Shinto) it is read しょうじょう, for example in 六根清浄, the chant of mountain pilgrims, or in 清浄な心. In the technical and everyday sense, by contrast, it is read せいじょう: 清浄な空気, 空気清浄機 "air purifier". Grammatically it is a noun and な-adjective (清浄な, 清浄に保つ).

examples[].german: A constitutional amendment requires a majority in favor in a national referendum.
The United Kingdom decided to leave the EU by referendum.
A national referendum has never yet been held in Japan.
en.notes: 国民投票 is a nationwide referendum. In Japan it is provided for only for constitutional amendments (憲法改正の国民投票) and has never been carried out so far; votes at the municipal or prefectural level are called 住民投票. Typical: 国民投票を行う/実施する, 国民投票にかける, 国民投票で可決/否決される. 国民投票 is also used for referendums in other countries.

examples[].german: In Shinto, rituals for purging impurity are emphasized.
It is said that salt is scattered after a funeral to purify the impurity of death.
The child's unblemished smile refreshed my heart.
en.notes: 穢れ is a key concept of Shinto: ritual impurity that arises mainly through contact with death, blood or illness and is removed by 祓い or 禊 (穢れを祓う, 穢れを清める). Figuratively it also stands for a moral stain: 穢れのない心. The verb is intransitive 穢れる, transitive 穢す. It is often also written 汚れ; do not confuse it with よごれ "physical dirt" without ritual meaning.

examples[].german: At the great purification at the end of the year, the impurities of the year are cleansed.
Since I bought a new car, I had a traffic-safety purification rite done at a shrine.
Since this is my unlucky year, I had a purification rite performed at the shrine.
en.notes: 祓い is the Shinto purification ceremony in which a priest drives away impurity (穢れ) and misfortune. In everyday speech one almost always says お祓い: お祓いを受ける, お祓いしてもらう, for example for a new car, in an unlucky year (厄祓い) or before building a house. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 払い "payment". The great purification ritual on June 30 and December 31 is called 大祓 (おおはらえ).

examples[].german: The ascetic practice of misogi under a waterfall is still carried out in some places today.
In the Kojiki, Izanagi performs misogi in a river and washes away his impurity.
The lawmaker who had caused a scandal won the election and said, "The misogi is done."
en.notes: 禊 is the ritual purification of the body with water, in a river, in the sea or under a waterfall, to wash off impurity (穢れ); myth traces it back to the god イザナギ. One says 禊をする or 禊を行う; the spelling 禊ぎ also occurs. In politics and the media it is used figuratively: a politician who is reelected after a scandal declares 禊は済んだ "the matter has been atoned for".

examples[].german: The sacred object of this shrine is the mountain itself.
The Nachi Falls are enshrined as the goshintai of Hiryu Shrine.
The goshintai is kept deep inside the main hall and cannot be seen by the general public.
en.notes: 御神体 is the object in which, according to Shinto belief, the deity of a shrine dwells, for example a mirror, a sword, a rock, a waterfall or a whole mountain. It is usually kept hidden in the main sanctuary (本殿) and not shown publicly. Today it is often written ご神体; the prefix 御 expresses reverence, and the neutral form 神体 is rarer. Do not confuse it with 御本尊, the main object of worship of a Buddhist temple.

en.meaning: Shinto; the way of the gods
examples[].german: Shinto is a polytheistic belief system native to Japan.
In Japan, many people hold weddings in the Shinto style and funerals in the Buddhist style.
Before the war, State Shinto was built into the education of the people.
en.notes: 神道 is Japan's native religion, with the worship of countless deities (八百万の神) in nature, ancestors and places. Note the reading: しんとう, not しんどう. Typical contrast: 神道 and 仏教, shrine 神社 and temple 寺. Compounds: 国家神道 "State Shinto" (until 1945), 神道式 "in the Shinto style" (for a wedding also 神前式).

examples[].german: On the shrine grounds towers a sacred tree more than a thousand years old.
On the day of the summer festival, many food stalls line up on the shrine grounds.
Please refrain from smoking on the temple grounds.
en.notes: 境内 is the enclosed precinct of a shrine or temple, usually counted from the torii or the temple gate. Typical: 境内に入る, 境内を散歩する, 境内で (as the site of festivals and markets), 境内の桜. On signs one often reads 境内での〜はご遠慮ください. For secular properties of schools, companies or houses, one says 敷地 instead.

examples[].german: The monk walked through the town collecting alms and chanting sutras.
At my grandfather's funeral, we had a priest recite the sutras.
After finishing university, he chose the path of becoming a monk.
en.notes: 僧侶 is the neutral, somewhat formal word for Buddhist monks and priests. In everyday speech one says お坊さん, and for the head of a temple 住職 or 和尚. For Christian clergy one uses 牧師 or 神父, for Shinto priests 神主 or 神職. Typical: 僧侶になる, 僧侶にお経をあげてもらう.

en.meaning: head priest of a temple; abbot
examples[].german: The abbot of this temple is also keen on the region's cultural activities.
I consulted the head priest about the date of the memorial service.
My father retired, and my older brother succeeded him as head priest of the temple.
en.notes: 住職 is the head of a Buddhist temple, who lives there and manages it; the post is often passed from father to son (住職を継ぐ). Respectful address: ご住職 or, depending on the school, 和尚さん. More general are 僧侶 and colloquially お坊さん "monk". The Shinto counterpart at a shrine is 宮司.

en.meaning: chief priest of a Shinto shrine
examples[].german: The festival began when the chief priest recited the ritual prayer.
The post of chief priest of this shrine has been held by the same family for generations.
At the groundbreaking ceremony, the chief priest purified the land and prayed for safety in the construction.
en.notes: 宮司 is the highest priest of a Shinto shrine. Below him are ranks such as 禰宜 and 権禰宜; Shinto priests in general are called 神職 or, colloquially, 神主さん. Note the reading: ぐうじ, not きゅうじ. The Buddhist counterpart at a temple is 住職.

examples[].german: Switzerland is a typical country that employs direct democracy.
Direct democracy was practiced in ancient Athens.
The residents' referendum is a system that incorporates the idea of direct democracy.
en.notes: 直接民主制 is "direct democracy" as a system of state or government in which citizens themselves decide on substantive questions; the counterpart is 間接民主制. 直接民主主義 refers more to the idea or principle, while 制 stresses the institution. Typical combinations are 直接民主制を採用する/取り入れる; in Japan, 住民投票 ("residents' referendum") and リコール ("recall") are regarded as elements of it. A technical word from politics and civics.

examples[].german: The sight of a shrine maiden performing kagura has a mystical beauty.
For just the first three days of the New Year, I worked a part-time job as a shrine maiden at a shrine.
The shamanesses of ancient times are said to have conveyed the words of the gods in a trance.
en.notes: 巫女 are young women in a white top and red hakama who help with rituals at the shrine, perform the sacred dance 神楽 and hand out amulets; at New Year many female students are hired as temporary help (巫女のアルバイト). Historically 巫女 also denotes a shamaness who proclaims the words of the gods in a trance. The actual priests are 神職 or 神主; 巫女 is not a consecrated priestly office.

examples[].german: A norito is a prayer to the gods set down in ancient language.
While the priest was reciting the norito, the attendees kept their heads bowed.
At the wedding, the chief priest recited a norito celebrating the couple's new start.
en.notes: 祝詞 is the prayer composed in Old Japanese that a Shinto priest recites before the gods at ceremonies. Fixed combinations: formally 祝詞を奏上する, otherwise 祝詞をあげる. The reading のりと is irregular; read しゅくし, the same characters mean "words of congratulation" (usually written 祝辞). What is meant is always the text or its recitation, not the whole ceremony.

examples[].german: At New Year, one receives an ofuda at the shrine and enshrines it on the household altar.
A fire-prevention ofuda is stuck on the pillar in the kitchen.
Old ofuda are returned to the shrine at the end of the year.
en.notes: 御札 (usually written お札) is an amulet of paper or wood bearing the name of the deity and the seal of the shrine or temple, which one sets up at home on the 神棚 or attaches to a wall or door. One says 御札を受ける or いただく, not "to buy". Smaller and portable is お守り. Note: お札 read おさつ is a "banknote"; only おふだ is the amulet.

examples[].german: Offerings were presented before the shrine with prayers for a bountiful harvest.
At the autumn festival, local children dedicate kagura dances to the gods.
A sake brewing company donated sake barrels to the shrine.
en.notes: 奉納 is the solemn offering of gifts or performances to gods and Buddhas: sake barrels, votive plaques, lanterns, but also dances, sumo or music. Transitive する-verb: 〜を神社に奉納する; as a modifier in 奉納相撲, 奉納演奏, 奉納品. In contrast to 供える "to set out, offer (food etc.)", 奉納 stresses the formal act of dedication; the donors are often named on plaques or stone lanterns.

examples[].german: You write a wish on an ema and dedicate it at the shrine.
At the Tenmangu shrine, the ema of exam candidates praying to pass hung in rows.
Ema often depict the zodiac animal of that year.
en.notes: 絵馬 is a small wooden plaque on which one writes a wish and one's name and hangs it at a shrine or temple (絵馬を掛ける, 絵馬を奉納する). The name recalls that in the past living horses were donated and later replaced by pictures of horses; today many 絵馬 show the zodiac animal of the year. Especially well known are exam wishes at shrines of the god of scholars, Tenjin.

examples[].german: In an unlucky year, many people have a ritual to ward off misfortune performed.
In my unlucky year at forty-two, I went to the shrine with my family to have misfortune warded off.
It was a terrible year, so let's go out for a good drink to shake off the bad luck.
en.notes: 厄払い is a ritual for warding off misfortune, especially in the 厄年, the years of life considered dangerous (around 42 for men, 33 for women). It is usually performed at a shrine: 厄払いをしてもらう, 厄払いに行く. Variants are the spelling 厄祓い and 厄除け, which is more usual at temples and for amulets. Colloquially it is also used figuratively: after a run of bad luck, 厄払いに飲みに行く.

examples[].german: The syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism is a unique phenomenon in Japanese religious history.
The fact that there is a shrine on temple grounds is a remnant of the fusion of Shinto and Buddhism.
The Meiji government issued an edict of separation and rejected the blending of Shinto and Buddhism.
en.notes: 神仏習合 is a yojijukugo made of 神 "Shinto gods", 仏 "Buddhas" and 習合 "fusion": the blending of Shinto and Buddhism that grew over more than a thousand years, in which Shinto gods were interpreted, for example, as manifestations of Buddhas (本地垂迹). The Meiji government officially ended it in 1868 with the 神仏分離令; the opposite term is therefore 神仏分離. A technical term of religious history, but common in travel guides.

en.meaning: anti-Buddhist movement of the Meiji period
examples[].german: Many temples were destroyed in the anti-Buddhist movement of the early Meiji period.
In the storm of haibutsu kishaku, many Buddha statues were sold or burned.
It is said that even the five-story pagoda of Kofuku-ji was put up for sale in the era of haibutsu kishaku.
en.notes: 廃仏毀釈 literally means "to abolish Buddhism (廃仏) and destroy Shakyamuni (毀釈)", where 釈 stands for 釈迦. It denotes the movement at the beginning of the Meiji period that, after the separation of Shinto and Buddhism in 1868, led to the destruction of countless temples, statues and scriptures. Typical: 廃仏毀釈の嵐, 廃仏毀釈で失われた. A historical technical term, rare outside historical writing.

examples[].german: The teaching that all things are impermanent is a fundamental idea of Buddhism.
Seeing the cherry blossoms fall so quickly, I feel the impermanence of the world.
The Hojoki strongly expresses Kamo no Chomei's view of impermanence.
en.notes: 無常 is the fundamental Buddhist insight that nothing lasts and everything changes. As a noun and な/の-adjective: 人生の無常, 世の無常を感じる. Very common is 無常観 "view of impermanence", a central motif of classical literature such as 平家物語 and 方丈記. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 無情 "heartless, unfeeling".

examples[].german: Reaching the state of non-self is the core of Buddhist practice.
In the fire, he rescued the child without a thought for himself.
As I concentrated on playing, I had entered a state of complete self-forgetfulness.
en.notes: 無我 has two levels: in Buddhism the doctrine of non-self, according to which there is no permanent ego; in everyday speech the state of complete self-forgetfulness. The latter occurs above all in 無我夢中 "totally absorbed, without thinking" (無我夢中で走った) and 無我の境地 "state of self-forgetfulness", for example in athletes or musicians. It coincides only partly with "selflessness" in the sense of unselfishness (無私, 利他).

examples[].german: Japan is a state based on indirect democracy.
In a representative democracy, the people take part in politics through representatives they elect.
In countries with large populations, it is common to adopt representative democracy.
en.notes: 間接民主制 is "indirect" or "representative democracy": the people elect representatives who decide in parliament. Equivalent are 代議制 and 議会制民主主義; the counterpart is 直接民主制. Typical are 間接民主制を採る/基本とする. The word belongs to the language of politics, law and textbooks; in conversation one rather says 選挙で代表を選ぶ仕組み.

examples[].german: The Heart Sutra teaches that form is emptiness.
The "emptiness" of Buddhism does not mean that nothing exists at all.
His punch cut through thin air.
en.notes: Read くう, 空 denotes in Buddhism "emptiness": all things have no independent, fixed essence, as known from 色即是空 in the Heart Sutra. Outside religion, くう stands for "nothingness, into the void": 空を切る "to strike at thin air", 空に帰する "to come to nothing". Do not confuse it with そら "sky" and から "empty (container)", which are written with the same character.

examples[].german: "... there is a sound of the impermanence of all things" is the opening of the Tale of the Heike.
For a once-glorious, famous restaurant to close, truly, nothing lasts.
The park where I played as a child was gone, and I felt the impermanence of all things.
en.notes: 諸行無常 is a yojijukugo: 諸行 "all conditioned things" and 無常 "without permanence": nothing stays as it is. It is a principle of Buddhism and, through the famous opening of the 平家物語 (祇園精舎の鐘の声、諸行無常の響きあり), familiar to all Japanese. In everyday speech it is said with a sigh when something beautiful passes or the mighty fall: まさに諸行無常だ, 諸行無常を感じる.

examples[].german: "Form is emptiness" is the central teaching of the Heart Sutra.
I copied out the sutra while chanting, "Form is emptiness, emptiness is form."
Since encountering the idea of "form is emptiness", my attachment to things has faded a little.
en.notes: 色即是空 comes from the Heart Sutra (般若心経): 色 "form, everything perceptible to the senses", 即是 "is precisely", 空 "emptiness": all phenomena have no fixed inherent nature. Immediately following is 空即是色 "emptiness is form"; the two are often quoted together. Note: 色 does not mean "color" here and is read しき. Outside religious or philosophical conversation it appears almost only as a quotation.

en.meaning: reliance on another's power; Amida's vow
examples[].german: In Jodo Shinshu, the teaching of relying on Amida's power is at the center.
The championship depends on the other teams' results, so it's out of our hands.
Stop depending entirely on your friends for your homework.
en.notes: 他力本願 is made up of 他力 "another's power", meaning the power of Amida, and 本願 "original vow", Amida's promise to save all beings. In 浄土真宗 it means relying entirely on this vow instead of on one's own effort (自力). Colloquially it is mostly used disparagingly for "relying on others, doing nothing oneself" (他力本願な態度), a usage that Buddhist circles criticize as a misunderstanding. In sports it is used soberly: one depends on the results of others.

examples[].german: The Zen school emphasizes enlightenment through one's own effort.
Three months after the fracture, I was finally able to walk on my own again.
The stranded climber came down the mountain under his own power.
en.notes: 自力 means "one's own strength": managing something without outside help. In everyday speech it is very common with で: 自力で歩く, 自力で解決する, 自力で脱出する; in sports 自力優勝 "winning the championship under one's own power". In Buddhism it denotes the path to enlightenment through one's own practice, as in Zen; the opposite is 他力. Do not confuse it with 実力 "actual ability" and 自立 "independence".

en.meaning: another's power; the power of Buddha
examples[].german: The Jodo school teaches salvation through the power of Buddha.
The question of self-power or other-power was a major theme in Japanese Buddhism.
Shinran taught that one should abandon one's own power and entrust everything to other-power.
en.notes: 他力 is "another's power, help from outside". In Buddhism, above all in 浄土宗 and 浄土真宗, it denotes the saving power of Amida Buddha, to whom the believer entrusts himself, as opposed to 自力, one's own practice. In everyday speech it appears almost only in contrast to 自力 or in 他力本願; for "help from others" one otherwise says 人の助け.

en.meaning: nenbutsu; invocation of the Buddha's name
examples[].german: It is believed that by reciting the nenbutsu "Namu Amida Butsu" one can be reborn in paradise.
Every morning my grandmother recites the nenbutsu in front of the household altar.
No matter how much you warn him, it's like preaching to a horse's ear.
en.notes: 念仏 is, in Pure Land Buddhism, the invocation 南無阿弥陀仏; one says 念仏を唱える, more rarely 念仏する. Very common is the proverb 馬の耳に念仏 "casting pearls before swine, preaching to deaf ears". Also found is 念仏のように繰り返す "to repeat like a prayer wheel". For reciting sutras in general one says お経を読む／あげる.

examples[].german: In the Shingon school it is taught that by reciting mantras one can become one with the Buddha.
It has been believed that reciting the Komyo Shingon erases the sins of the dead.
Kukai spread the esoteric Buddhism he had learned in Tang China to Japan as the Shingon school.
en.notes: 真言 is the "true word", the translation of mantra: short sacred formulas in Sino-Japanese rendering of the Sanskrit sounds, which are recited (真言を唱える).
