At the same time it is the short form for the school 真言宗 founded by 空海, centered on 高野山. The loanword マントラ is used rather in the context of yoga or Hinduism; related is 陀羅尼, a longer incantation.

examples[].german: A mandala is a visual representation of the Buddhist view of the cosmos.
A brightly colored mandala was hanging in the main hall of the temple.
Recently, mandala art has become popular as a coloring book for adults.
en.notes: 曼荼羅 is a mandala: a mostly circular-square diagram that shows Buddhas and deities in a fixed arrangement and represents the cosmos or enlightenment. In Shingon, the 胎蔵界曼荼羅 and the 金剛界曼荼羅, together the 両界曼荼羅, are central. It is often also written in kana (まんだら, マンダラ) or as 曼陀羅. Figuratively it stands for a colorful, many-layered overall picture.

examples[].german: At New Year, the talisman on the household altar is replaced with a new one.
My grandfather puts water and rice on the household altar every morning and presses his hands together.
In a judo dojo, people bow to the Shinto altar before practice.
en.notes: 神棚 is a small Shinto household altar in the form of a shelf, usually mounted high on a wall, on which one sets up お札 from shrines and offers rice, salt, water and 榊 branches. Its counterpart is the Buddhist 仏壇 for the ancestors; many traditional households have both. Typical: 神棚を祀る, 神棚に手を合わせる, 神棚にお供えする. One also finds a 神棚 in shops, companies and dojos.

examples[].german: The realization of universal suffrage was essential to the development of democracy.
The first election with universal male suffrage in Japan was held in 1928.
At that time women had no right to vote, so it could not be called true universal suffrage.
en.notes: 普通選挙 is an election in which the right to vote is not tied to property, tax payments or education; the opposite term is 制限選挙. In Japan it was introduced for men aged 25 and over with the 普通選挙法 in 1925; women received the right to vote only in 1945. Abbreviated, one says 普選, e.g. in 普選運動. The word occurs mainly in history and political science.

examples[].german: When reciting sutras, one strikes the wooden fish to keep the rhythm.
For some reason, I get sleepy when I hear the poku-poku of the wooden fish.
It is said that the mokugyo is shaped like a fish because fish never close their eyes, day or night.
en.notes: 木魚 is a hollow, round wooden instrument with carved fish scales that is struck with a padded mallet during sutra recitation to set the beat (木魚を叩く). The fish shape is meant to admonish vigilance, since according to old belief fish never close their eyes. It is common above all in Zen and in 浄土宗, but not in 浄土真宗. The tapping sound is rendered onomatopoeically as ポクポク.

examples[].german: On New Year's Eve, the year-end bell is rung in the bell tower.
The roof of the old bell tower was damaged by the typhoon.
In European towns, you can see the church bell tower from far away.
en.notes: 鐘楼 is the bell tower or bell house of a temple, in which the large bronze bell hangs; in Japan usually an open pavilion with a roof. The bell is struck with a beam: 鐘を撞く（つく）. More colloquial is 鐘つき堂; 鐘楼 sounds technical and written and is also used for church towers (教会の鐘楼). Do not confuse it with the character 鍾.

examples[].german: The main gate of this temple was built in the Muromachi period.
Passing through the temple gate, a quiet precinct spread out before me.
Large guardian statues stand on both sides of the temple gate.
en.notes: 山門 is the main gate of a Buddhist temple. The name comes from the fact that temples were formerly located in the mountains and to this day bear a "mountain name" (山号). Typical are 山門をくぐる "to pass through the gate" and 山門の仁王像. At Zen temples the main gate is often written 三門; for Shinto shrines one says 鳥居 or 楼門, not 山門.

examples[].german: The magnificent layout of the temple complex is a feature of this temple.
In Nara, temple complexes more than a thousand years old still stand today.
Most of the temple complex was destroyed in the fire.
en.notes: 伽藍 is a short form of the Sanskrit word for "monastery complex" and denotes a large Buddhist temple with its halls. Fixed phrases are 伽藍配置 "arrangement of the temple buildings" and 七堂伽藍 "complete complex with seven halls". The word is art-historical and written; in everyday speech one simply says お寺. The word がらんどう "completely empty, hollow" is traced back to 伽藍堂.

examples[].german: Walking through the cloister, you can admire the wall paintings.
The corridors of Itsukushima Shrine extend out over the sea.
Even on rainy days, if you take the covered corridor, you can get to the main hall without getting wet.
en.notes: 回廊 is a roofed passage that runs around a building or a courtyard, at temples, shrines, palaces and monasteries ("cloister"). One goes 回廊を歩く／巡る. The ordinary hallway in a house or school is 廊下, a connecting passage between two buildings 渡り廊下. In politics and business 回廊 also stands for a "corridor", e.g. 経済回廊.

examples[].german: Numerous buildings stand in a row on the temple grounds.
The present temple buildings were rebuilt in the Edo period.
Many temple halls collapsed in the great earthquake.
en.notes: 堂宇 is a literary word for temple buildings or halls; 堂 is the hall, 宇 the roof. It appears almost only in descriptions of temple complexes, in travel guides and in historical texts, often in the plural: 数多くの堂宇, 堂宇が建ち並ぶ. In speech one rather says お堂 or simply 建物.

en.meaning: halo; nimbus of a Buddha statue
examples[].german: The halo of a Buddha statue symbolizes the light of the Buddha's wisdom.
A flame pattern is finely carved into the halo of this Buddha statue.
For the repair, only the halo was removed from the statue itself.
en.notes: 光背 is the sculpted aureole or mandorla behind a Buddha figure, a technical word of art history that refers to the physical component of the statue. For the glow of light in a figurative sense, one says 後光, for example 後光が差す "to be surrounded by a halo". For Christian images of saints one rather speaks of 光輪.

examples[].german: The lotus is regarded as a symbol of Buddhism because it blooms pure out of the mud.
Amida Buddha sits on a lotus pedestal.
I scooped up the ramen broth with the ceramic spoon and drank it.
en.notes: 蓮華 is the lotus blossom as a Buddhist symbol; the plant itself is called 蓮（はす）in everyday speech. Buddha figures sit on a lotus pedestal, 蓮華座. In daily life one meets the word mostly in kana: れんげ is the ceramic spoon for soup and ramen (short for 散り蓮華), and れんげ草 is the Chinese milk vetch, a spring flower in rice fields.

examples[].german: The monk put on a kesa and conducted the memorial service.
I slung my bag diagonally across my shoulder and rode my bicycle.
As the saying goes, if you hate the monk you hate even his robe; he dislikes every product of that company.
en.notes: 袈裟 is the outer garment of Buddhist monks, draped over the left shoulder; one says 袈裟をまとう／掛ける. Derived from it is 袈裟懸け "diagonally over one shoulder", e.g. for a shoulder bag. Well known is the proverb 坊主憎けりゃ袈裟まで憎い: if you hate someone, you hate everything connected with them.

examples[].german: The early-morning alms round is part of the training at a Zen temple.
A trainee monk was collecting alms in front of the station.
In Thailand, monks go out on their alms round every morning.
en.notes: 托鉢 is the alms round of Buddhist monks, who receive food or money in their bowl (鉢); as a する-verb: 托鉢する, also 托鉢に出る／回る and 托鉢僧. In Japan one sees mainly Zen monks with large straw hats. The offering of laypeople is called 布施 or お布施; 托鉢 is the monk's side, 布施 that of the giver.

examples[].german: Under the proportional representation system, even small parties can win seats.
He lost in his district but was revived through proportional representation.
In proportional representation for the House of Representatives, you write the name of a party on the ballot.
en.notes: 比例代表 is proportional representation, where seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote; often shortened to 比例 or 比例区. In the Japanese lower house, it is combined with single-member districts (小選挙区比例代表並立制): someone who loses in the district can still get into parliament via the party list (比例で復活当選). Typical: 比例代表制, 比例名簿, 比例代表で当選する.

examples[].german: Shojin cuisine is a vegetarian cuisine based on Buddhist precepts.
I will strive even harder so as not to bring shame on the title of yokozuna.
He devoted himself to daily practice and finally won the championship.
en.notes: 精進 has two uses. Religiously, it is ascetic practice, above all abstaining from meat: 精進料理 "Buddhist vegetarian cuisine", 精進落とし "the first normal meal after the mourning period". Far more common today is 精進する "to devote oneself wholeheartedly to something", mostly with に: 芸に精進する. Typical of solemn resolutions is 一層精進いたします, for example in acceptance speeches of sumo wrestlers; 努力する is the neutral equivalent.

examples[].german: A shimenawa rope marks a sacred boundary.
This mountain was once a women-excluding sacred zone, and women could not enter.
The hero set up a barrier and kept the yokai from getting in.
en.notes: 結界 is originally a Buddhist term for a delimited sacred area into which disturbances may not intrude; Shinto ropes such as 注連縄 also mark such a boundary. Historically important is 女人結界, the ban on women entering sacred mountains. In manga, anime and games, 結界 is the magical protective barrier: 結界を張る "to put up a barrier", 結界を破る "to break through it".

examples[].german: The pilgrimage to the 88 sacred sites of Shikoku is an ancient pilgrim route.
Osorezan is known as one of Japan's foremost sacred sites.
My mother is visiting the sacred sites of the 33-temple Saigoku route little by little.
en.notes: 霊場 is a sacred site, above all a Buddhist temple or holy mountain as a pilgrimage destination. Such sites are often linked into numbered circuits, such as 四国八十八箇所 or 西国三十三所; visiting them is called 霊場巡り. The more general word 聖地 also covers sites of other religions and, jokingly, filming locations of anime; 霊場, by contrast, stays religious.

examples[].german: Pilgrims dress in white garments and visit the holy sites.
After retiring, my father walked the Camino de Santiago in Spain.
More and more fans are making pilgrimages to towns that served as settings for anime.
en.notes: 巡礼 is a pilgrimage to several holy places, and also the pilgrim himself (usually 巡礼者). As a する-verb it takes を for the places visited: 聖地を巡礼する. Fixed phrases are 巡礼の旅 and 聖地巡礼, the latter today also used jokingly for fan trips to anime locations. 参拝, by contrast, is the single visit to a shrine or temple, 遍路 specifically the Shikoku pilgrimage.

en.meaning: pilgrimage (to the 88 temples of Shikoku); pilgrim
examples[].german: The culture of offering hospitality to pilgrims survives on Shikoku.
My mother set out alone on the Shikoku pilgrimage.
There is a small rest area along the pilgrim trail.
en.notes: 遍路 denotes the pilgrimage to the 88 temples of Shikoku and also the pilgrim; in everyday speech almost always politely お遍路 or お遍路さん. One says お遍路に出る／お遍路を回る, and the pilgrim path is called 遍路道. The hospitality offered to pilgrims by locals is called お接待. For pilgrimages in general one uses 巡礼.

examples[].german: The mystical aspects of religious experience cannot be fully explained by science.
Drawn to the mysteries of the universe, I became an astronomer.
The lake wrapped in mist had a mysterious beauty.
en.notes: 神秘 is the enigmatic, mysterious thing that exceeds human understanding. Common in 生命の神秘, 宇宙の神秘 and 神秘に包まれる; as an adjective one mostly uses 神秘的な "mysterious, mystical". 秘密, by contrast, is a secret that people deliberately conceal, 謎 an unsolved riddle. 神秘主義 is "mysticism".

examples[].german: The saint's miracles became an occasion for the spread of the faith.
The car was totaled, but the driver miraculously escaped unharmed.
If we don't give up until the end, a miracle might happen.
en.notes: 奇跡 is a miracle, in the religious as well as the everyday sense. Typical: 奇跡が起きる／起こる, 奇跡的に助かる "to be saved as if by a miracle", 奇跡の生還 "miraculous survival". In religious texts the spelling 奇蹟 is also found. 不思議 is only "strange, mysterious", without the sense of a supernatural event.

examples[].german: The prophet bore the mission of conveying God's revelation to the people.
She believed that dream to be a revelation from God.
For me, who was undecided, my teacher's single remark was like a revelation.
en.notes: 啓示 is divine revelation, mostly in 神の啓示 and 啓示を受ける. Figuratively it stands for a sudden, decisive inspiration, often in a comparison: 天の啓示のように. For ordinary ideas one says ひらめき. Beware of homophones: 掲示 "notice posted" and 刑事 "detective" are also read けいじ.

examples[].german: The salvation of all sentient beings is the fundamental ideal of Mahayana Buddhism.
The government decided on special measures to relieve the disaster victims.
Public funds were injected to bail out the troubled bank.
en.notes: 救済 means "salvation" religiously, but is just as often used in a secular sense for help that frees people or companies from distress: 被災者の救済, 救済措置, 救済策, 企業を救済する. 救助, by contrast, is the immediate rescue from danger (e.g. from rubble), 救援 the relief supplies from outside. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を救済する.

examples[].german: The expectation of the coming of a savior is common to many religions.
The new player became the savior of the team.
People from the Salvation Army were soliciting donations in front of the station.
en.notes: 救世 "saving the world" hardly occurs on its own, but almost only in compounds: 救世主 "savior, messiah", figuratively also "rescuer in need", for example for a player who saves a team, and 救世軍 "Salvation Army". In Buddhist names it is read くせ, e.g. 救世観音.

examples[].german: Under the single-member district system, one candidate is elected from each district.
In single-member districts, a small margin of votes can sometimes decide victory or defeat.
The House of Representatives uses a parallel system of single-member districts and proportional representation.
en.notes: 小選挙区 is an electoral district in which only one seat is awarded; the candidate with the most votes wins (小選挙区制). The opposites are 中選挙区 and 大選挙区 with several seats. Since 1996, the lower house has been elected under the 小選挙区比例代表並立制. Typical: 小選挙区で当選する/敗れる, 小選挙区に立候補する. The seat won is rather called 小選挙区の議席.

en.meaning: next life; the world to come
examples[].german: I accumulate good deeds in the hope of happiness in the next life.
I want to meet you again in the next life too.
In Buddhism, it is believed that one's deeds in this life determine the next life.
en.notes: 来世 is, in the Buddhist worldview, the next life after rebirth, in the series 前世・現世・来世. あの世, by contrast, rather means the afterlife as the place of the dead. In everyday speech 来世 also appears romantically or jokingly: 来世でまた会おう, 来世に期待する "maybe it'll work out in the next life".

examples[].german: A faith that seeks this-worldly benefits is characteristic of the Japanese view of religion.
Some people believe that suffering in this life will be rewarded in the next.
This picture scroll depicts the boundary between this world and the world after death.
en.notes: 現世 is "this world, this life" as opposed to 前世 and 来世. The reading varies: on its own mostly げんせ, in Buddhist phrases げんぜ, especially in 現世利益（げんぜりやく） "this-worldly benefit", that is, prayers for health, success or wealth. In ordinary speech one more commonly says この世.

examples[].german: It is believed that karmic connections from past lives influence the present life.
Maybe those two are bound together by a tie from a past life.
To have such bad luck... did I do something terrible in a past life?
en.notes: 前世（ぜんせ） is the earlier life before the present existence, part of the series 前世・現世・来世. Typical: 前世の記憶, 前世からの縁, 前世で何か悪いことをしたのかな (jokingly when having bad luck). The reading ぜんせい, by contrast, means "former ages". The word is common in everyday conversations about fate and spirituality.

examples[].german: Belief in vengeful spirits is part of Japanese folk religion.
The Tenmangu shrine was built to appease the vengeful spirit of Sugawara no Michizane.
Rumor has it that a vengeful spirit haunts that mansion.
en.notes: 怨霊 is the ghost of a person who died with a grudge and takes revenge: 怨（うら）み "grudge" + 霊. Typical are 怨霊のたたり "curse of a vengeful spirit" and 怨霊を鎮める. Famous are, for example, the spirits of 菅原道真 and 平将門. 幽霊 is "ghost" in general, 悪霊 an evil spirit that does not necessarily come from a dead person.

en.meaning: honored spirit; spirit of the dead
examples[].german: The Goryo cult serves to pacify the spirits of those who met an unjust death.
The Gion Festival began originally as a goryo-e ceremony to quell epidemics.
There are several shrines in Kyoto called Goryo Shrine.
en.notes: 御霊（ごりょう） is above all a term of religious history: the spirit of a person who died a violent or unjust death and must be pacified through worship, hence 御霊信仰 and 御霊会. The same characters are read みたま when speaking reverently of the soul of a deceased person. On condolence envelopes one finds 御霊前, read ごれいぜん.

en.meaning: pacification of the dead; repose of souls
examples[].german: A ceremony to repose the souls of the war dead is held every year.
At the end of the ceremony, Mozart's Requiem was performed.
Facing the sea, people offered a prayer for the repose of the souls of the dead.
en.notes: 鎮魂 is the pacification of the souls of the deceased, especially of war and disaster victims: 鎮魂の祈り, 鎮魂の碑. 鎮魂歌 is the "requiem". For memorial services one usually says 慰霊祭, for Buddhist memorial masses 供養; 鎮魂 sounds more solemn and literary.

examples[].german: Rituals of purification by fire are found in many cultures.
This device purifies river water and makes it drinkable.
Listening to the beautiful singing voice, I felt as though my heart had been cleansed.
en.notes: 浄化 is "purification, cleansing", religious but above all technical and figurative: 水を浄化する, 浄化槽 "septic tank", 政界の浄化 "cleansing of politics". In everyday speech one says 心が浄化される when music or a sight "washes the soul clean". 掃除 is mere cleaning, 洗浄 washing with water; ritual purification in Shinto is called お清め or お祓い.

en.meaning: attaining buddhahood in this very body
examples[].german: The teaching of attaining buddhahood in this very body is the core of Shingon esoteric Buddhism.
Kukai systematically expounded the idea of sokushin jobutsu.
Sokushin jobutsu is different from sokushinbutsu, the mummified monks.
en.notes: 即身成仏 is a four-character term from Buddhist doctrine: 即身 "in this very body" + 成仏 "to become a Buddha", that is, attaining enlightenment already in this life instead of only after countless rebirths. It is the core teaching of the Shingon Buddhism founded by 空海. Do not confuse it with 即身仏, the self-mummified monks found, for example, in Yamagata. 成仏 on its own also means "to rest in peace" in everyday speech.

examples[].german: The history of the martyrdom of the Christians is deeply engraved in Nagasaki.
Many believers died as martyrs rather than renounce their faith.
He is still revered by people as a martyr.
en.notes: 殉教 means to die for one's faith; as an intransitive する-verb: 殉教する, and the martyr is called 殉教者. In Japan one thinks above all of the persecuted Christians of the Edo period. Similarly built are 殉職 "to die in the line of duty" (police, fire department) and 殉死 "to follow one's lord in death"; only 殉教 is religious.

examples[].german: Sects regarded as heretical by the orthodox were suppressed.
His theory was regarded as heterodox in the academic world of the time.
He is called the maverick of the gaming industry.
en.notes: 異端 is a doctrine or person that deviates from the recognized doctrinal opinion (正統): 異端の説, 異端者, 異端視する, 異端審問 "Inquisition". The word is also used in a secular sense: 異端とされる理論 in science, 異端児 for an outsider or maverick in an industry. More neutral for "unusual" are 型破り or 変わり者.

examples[].german: The dispute over the orthodox interpretation of the doctrine continues.
He alone is the legitimate heir of the royal house.
At this restaurant you can eat classic Neapolitan pizza.
en.notes: 正統 denotes the rightful, handed-down line: religiously orthodoxy (opposite 異端), politically the legitimate succession: 正統な後継者, 正統性. 正統派 also means "classic, in the traditional style" (正統派のピザ, 正統派の美人). Beware of the homophone 正当 "justified, lawful" in 正当な理由 or 正当防衛, which has nothing to do with tradition.

examples[].german: The advance of secularization is considered one cause of the turn away from religion.
I want to be free from worldly desires such as fame and money.
Turkey was founded as a state upholding secularism.
en.notes: 世俗 is the "world" as opposed to the religious or spiritual: worldly things, ordinary customs and desires. Common are 世俗的な "worldly, profane", 世俗化 "secularization" and 世俗主義 "secularism, laicism". 俗世 similarly means the worldly life that one leaves as a monk; for society in everyday life one says 世間.

en.meaning: holy orders; priesthood; sacred calling (e.g. teaching)
examples[].german: A high standard of ethics is demanded of those who hold clerical office.
Teaching used to be called a sacred calling.
Her older brother is a clergyman at a church.
en.notes: 聖職 is the clerical office; clergy are called 聖職者, and taking up an office is 聖職に就く. In addition, 聖職 denotes a profession regarded as a special, almost sacred calling, above all that of the teacher: 教師は聖職だ is a well-known formula, today often discussed critically. For the pastor himself one says concretely 牧師, 神父 or 僧侶.

examples[].german: Entering the sacred precinct is strictly prohibited.
For fiscal rehabilitation, no budget item is sacrosanct.
The study was my father's sanctuary, and we children could not enter.
en.notes: 聖域 is first of all a holy precinct that one may not simply enter. Figuratively it denotes an area exempt from criticism or cuts; famous is the slogan 聖域なき構造改革 "structural reform without sacred cows"; one says 〜に聖域はない. Casually it can also mean a private retreat: 父の書斎は聖域だ.

examples[].german: Some monks leave the secular world and train in the mountains.
Staying at an onsen inn deep in the mountains, you can forget the worries of the secular world.
Leaving home to become a monk means cutting one's ties with the secular world.
en.notes: 俗世 is the ordinary world shaped by desires and worries, which one leaves behind as a monk. Typical: 俗世を離れる／捨てる, 俗世の煩わしさ. More common and somewhat more colloquial is the longer form 俗世間. 世俗 stresses the worldly as a quality (世俗的), 俗世 the place from which one withdraws.

en.meaning: entering the monastic life; renunciation of the world
examples[].german: He became a monk and entered the Buddhist priesthood while still young.
After losing her husband, she renounced the world and became a nun.
A monk who has renounced the world lives in a temple, apart from his family.
en.notes: 出家 means to leave family life and become a monk or nun; as an intransitive する-verb: 出家する, often with 仏門に入る or 尼になる. It also denotes the monk himself. The opposite is 在家 "layperson"; returning to secular life is called 還俗.

examples[].german: Lay followers too are actively involved in running the temple.
Many people study the Buddhist path as laypeople without becoming monks.
Jodo Shinshu spread mainly among lay believers.
en.notes: 在家 is the Buddhist layperson who leads a normal family life, as opposed to the 出家. It mostly appears attributively: 在家信者, 在家仏教, 在家のまま. The reading is ざいけ; the rare meaning "farmhouse in the country" plays hardly any role in present-day Japanese.

examples[].german: The tablet is enshrined on the household altar in remembrance of the deceased.
When the fire broke out, my grandmother first of all fled with the ancestral tablets.
The deceased's posthumous Buddhist name is written on the memorial tablet.
en.notes: 位牌 is the lacquered wooden tablet bearing the Buddhist posthumous name (戒名) and the date of death, which stands in the household altar (仏壇) and is venerated on behalf of the deceased. After the funeral one first uses a plain wooden tablet (白木の位牌), and after 49 days a permanent one. Typical: 位牌を安置する, 位牌に手を合わせる.

examples[].german: The sotoba set up in the graveyard are for the memorial rites of the deceased.
For the memorial service on the sixth anniversary of the death, I asked the temple for one sotoba.
When the wind blew, the sotoba behind the grave rattled.
en.notes: 卒塔婆 goes back to the Sanskrit word for "stupa". In present-day Japan it almost always means the narrow wooden slats with Sanskrit characters and the posthumous name that are set up behind the grave at memorial services or at Obon: 卒塔婆を立てる. Short forms include 塔婆; the spelling 卒都婆 also occurs.

en.meaning: prajna, transcendent wisdom; Hannya mask (jealous demoness)
examples[].german: One overcomes worldly desires with the wisdom of prajna.
Every morning my grandfather recites the Heart Sutra in front of the household altar.
When I came home after forgetting our appointment, my wife had a face like a hannya.
en.notes: 般若 is the Buddhist wisdom that leads to enlightenment; best known is the Heart Sutra 般若心経. In everyday life, however, one often thinks of the 般若 mask of Noh theater: a horned demoness embodying female jealousy and rage. Hence one says jokingly 般若のような顔 for a frighteningly angry face.

en.meaning: top leader; head of state or government; leadership
examples[].german: Leaders of various countries attended the international conference.
A Japan-US summit meeting was held in Tokyo.
The company's top executives explained the new management policy.
en.notes: 首脳 are the top representatives of a state or organization: in politics the heads of state and government, in companies the top management. Very common: 首脳会談 ("summit meeting"), 首脳会議, 日米首脳, 各国首脳, 首脳陣 ("leadership team"). Unlike 元首, which formally means the head of state, 首脳 also includes prime ministers and chancellors.

examples[].german: An arms embargo was imposed.
After the outbreak of the disease, an import ban on beef continued for three years.
The negotiations came together, and the oil embargo was finally lifted.
en.notes: 禁輸 is the formal word for an embargo, i.e. a state ban on the export or import of certain goods. It mostly appears in fixed combinations such as 禁輸措置 "embargo measure", 武器禁輸 "arms embargo" or 石油禁輸 "oil embargo"; typical verbs are 禁輸措置を発動する "to impose" and 禁輸を解除する "to lift". More neutral and concrete are 輸出禁止 "export ban" and 輸入禁止 "import ban". Newspaper and political language.

en.meaning: samadhi, deep absorption; (〜三昧) indulging in something fully
examples[].german: Through zazen one aims to enter the state of samadhi.
On days off I spend from morning till night absorbed in reading.
Since winning the lottery, he has been living a life of pure luxury.
en.notes: 三昧 is originally meditative absorption (samadhi): 三昧の境地. Much more common today is its use as a suffix with the voiced initial ざんまい: 読書三昧, ゲーム三昧, 贅沢三昧, "to give oneself entirely to something, to one's heart's content". Often there is an undertone of enjoyment or mild criticism of excess.

examples[].german: The abbot's sermons contain teachings useful in daily life.
After the memorial service, the monk gave a short sermon.
At that temple, a sermon gathering that anyone can attend is held once a month.
en.notes: 法話 is a Buddhist sermon, usually an easy-to-understand talk by a temple priest after a ceremony or at a lecture evening (法話会). One says 法話を聞く／する. The old word 説教 also meant "sermon" but in everyday speech mainly means "a lecture, a telling-off"; for religious addresses 法話 is therefore the unambiguous choice.

examples[].german: Zen dialogue is meant to test the depth of a disciple's enlightenment.
At the reception desk, it turned into a back-and-forth over whether we could go in or not.
The guard threw me out without any discussion.
en.notes: 問答 is an exchange of questions and answers, especially the teaching dialogue in Zen (禅問答). Figuratively, 禅問答 also means "an incomprehensible conversation in which people talk past each other". Very common are 押し問答 "stubborn back-and-forth" and 問答無用 "no discussion!"; 一問一答 is a question-and-answer format.

examples[].german: Koans encourage an experience of enlightenment beyond logic.
"The sound of one hand" is one of the best-known koans.
The trainee monk kept pondering the koan his master gave him for days.
en.notes: 公案 is a paradoxical task that the Zen master gives the student to meditate on, such as 隻手の声 "the sound of one hand". It is meant to break through logical thinking; one says 公案を与える, 公案に取り組む. The Rinzai school in particular works with koans, while the Soto school relies more on pure sitting (只管打坐).

examples[].german: The teaching of Zen values direct experience beyond words.
I tried seated meditation at a Zen temple in Kyoto.
Steve Jobs was deeply interested in Zen.
en.notes: 禅 is both meditation (dhyana) and the Zen school of Buddhism. On its own it mostly stands in 禅の教え／思想／精神; more common are compounds: 禅宗 "Zen school", 禅寺 "Zen temple", 禅僧, 座禅 "seated meditation", 禅問答. Via the West, the word is now also returning as a lifestyle term for calm and simplicity.

examples[].german: The practices of esoteric Buddhism are passed from master to disciple through secret transmission.
Mt. Koya is known as the sacred site of Shingon esoteric Buddhism.
At esoteric temples, people burn a goma fire and offer prayers.
en.notes: 密教 is esoteric Buddhism, whose teachings and rituals are passed on only through direct initiation from master to student. In Japan these are above all Shingon Buddhism (東密) and parts of the Tendai school (台密); typical are mandalas, mantras and the fire ritual 護摩. The counterpart is 顕教, the publicly accessible teaching.

examples[].german: Exoteric Buddhism is characterized by teachings open to everyone.
Kukai discussed Buddhism by dividing it into exoteric and esoteric.
At the great temples of the Middle Ages, both exoteric and esoteric teachings were studied.
en.notes: 顕教 denotes the "revealed" teaching of Buddhism, accessible to all in texts and sermons. The word exists almost only as the counterpart of 密教, coined by 空海 to stress the superiority of the esoteric teaching; hence often in pairs: 顕教と密教, 顕密. A technical term of religious history, practically unused in everyday speech.

en.meaning: the Latter Day of the Law; the age of decline
examples[].german: The spread of mappo thought made Pure Land faith flourish.
People of the Heian period believed that the age of decline began in 1052.
With one incident after another, some lament that we are living in a degenerate age.
en.notes: 末法 is the last of the three ages after the Buddha's death (正法・像法・末法), in which the teaching still exists but no one attains enlightenment anymore. In Japan it was believed to have begun in 1052; the 末法思想 promoted the Amida faith in the Pure Land. Figuratively 末法の世 means "degenerate times", like the everyday lament 世も末だ.

examples[].german: In Buddhism, it is permitted to use skillful means to lead people to the truth.
They say a lie can be an expedient, so I didn't tell my sick grandmother the truth.
That promise was nothing more than an expedient to get through the moment.
en.notes: 方便 is in Buddhism the "skillful means" by which the Buddha adapts the teaching to the understanding of his listeners. In everyday speech it means "a means to an end, a stopgap", often with a slightly apologetic tone: 一時の方便, 〜するための方便にすぎない. Very well known is the proverb 嘘も方便 "even a lie can be useful".

examples[].german: The missionaries came all the way to the distant East to spread the gospel.
This new drug was a great boon for patients suffering from intractable diseases.
The Gospels record the life and teachings of Jesus.
en.notes: 福音 is the Christian gospel (福音を伝える／宣べ伝える); the four Gospels are called 福音書. In a secular sense it stands for "good news", especially an innovation that is a blessing for a particular group: 〜にとって福音となる, for example a new drug for patients. Somewhat elevated; in everyday speech one otherwise says いい知らせ.

examples[].german: Relief supplies were delivered to the disaster area.
After the earthquake, there was a shortage of supplies such as water and food.
Daily necessities are carried to the island by ship.
en.notes: 物資 refers to goods and materials as supplies, i.e. what is distributed, transported or stored - not the individual product in a shop (for that, 商品). Typical are 救援物資 or 支援物資 "relief supplies", 生活物資 "daily necessities" and 軍事物資 "military supplies". Common verbs: 物資を届ける/輸送する, 物資が不足する. Unlike 資源 "(natural) resources", 物資 means goods that are already available and transportable.

examples[].german: Holy Communion is one of the most important ceremonies of Christianity.
I received Communion at the Sunday service.
In Communion, the bread and wine represent the body and blood of Christ.
en.notes: 聖餐 is the Christian Lord's Supper with bread and wine; the celebration is called 聖餐式, and taking part is 聖餐にあずかる. The term is mainly Protestant; in the Catholic Church one speaks rather of 聖体拝領 or the ミサ. The historical "Last Supper" is 最後の晩餐. Do not confuse it with the homophones 清算 "settlement of accounts" and 精算 "fare adjustment".

examples[].german: Nature worship is an element common to primitive religions around the world.
Idol worship is forbidden in Islam.
He worships that writer like a god.
en.notes: 崇拝 is deep veneration up to adoration, religious as well as secular; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を崇拝する. Fixed compounds are 偶像崇拝 "idolatry", 祖先崇拝 "ancestor worship", 自然崇拝, 英雄崇拝. Applied to persons it is much stronger than 尊敬 "respect", almost deification.

examples[].german: Some religions forbid the worship of idols.
After the war, that politician was set up as an idol of the nation.
Ancient wooden idols are on display at the museum.
en.notes: 偶像 denotes an image or statue venerated as a deity and appears above all in 偶像崇拝 "idolatry, image worship". Figuratively an 偶像 is a person who is blindly revered; 偶像化する means "to turn into an idol, glorify". For pop idols one now almost always says アイドル; 偶像 sounds stiff and literary for that.

examples[].german: Japan's religious culture has a polytheistic character.
Ancient Greece was a polytheistic world in which each god had its own role.
In class we discussed the difference between monotheism and polytheism.
en.notes: 多神教 is the technical term for "polytheism"; the opposite is 一神教. With 的 it becomes adjectival: 多神教的な世界観 "polytheistic worldview". In connection with Japan the catchphrase 八百万の神 "the eight million gods" of Shinto often comes up, regarded as a typical example of 多神教. The word belongs to religious studies, history and factual texts.

examples[].german: The tradition of monotheism begins with Judaism.
Both Christianity and Islam are classified as monotheistic.
In monotheistic cultural spheres, God is regarded as the one absolute being.
en.notes: 一神教 "monotheism" denotes the belief in a single God; the opposite is 多神教. Typical 一神教 named are ユダヤ教, キリスト教 and イスラム教. Adjectivally: 一神教的な価値観 "monotheistic values". Note the reading いっしんきょう with small っ, not いちしんきょう.

examples[].german: Pantheistic elements can be seen in the Japanese view of nature.
Spinoza advocated a pantheism summed up as "God is nature".
The influence of pantheism can be seen in Goethe's works.
en.notes: 汎神論 "pantheism" is the philosophical doctrine that God and nature, or the universe, are one. 汎 means "all-encompassing" (cf. 汎用 "general-purpose"), 論 "doctrine, theory". It is associated above all with Spinoza (スピノザの汎神論); adjectivally 汎神論的. Do not confuse it with 多神教: 汎神論 is a worldview, not a religion with many gods.

examples[].german: Cultivating self-discipline is one of the aims of sports education.
In Zen training, self-conquest is valued above all else.
To overcome temptation, a spirit of self-restraint is needed.
en.notes: 克己 "self-conquest" (literally "to defeat oneself") is a literary, somewhat old-fashioned moral word. It mostly appears in combinations such as 克己心 "self-control" or 克己の精神 and in the Confucian phrase 克己復礼. As a verb, 克己する is rare; in everyday speech one rather says 自分に勝つ or 我慢する. Note the reading こっき with small っ.

examples[].german: Autonomous citizens support the foundation of a democratic society.
Stress can disrupt the autonomic nervous system.
To foster autonomy in children, it is important to let them decide for themselves.
en.notes: 自律 means "self-determination, autonomy": governing oneself by one's own rules, without external compulsion. Beware of the identically read 自立 "independence, standing on one's own feet" (経済的に自立する): 自律 concerns self-control, 自立 independence from others. Common are 自律的, 自律神経 "autonomic nervous system" and, in technology, 自律型ロボット "autonomous robot". As a する-verb it is rare.

en.meaning: to enlighten; to open someone's eyes
examples[].german: The Enlightenment thinkers regarded it as their mission to free the people from ignorance.
My professor's lecture opened my eyes.
en.notes: 啓く is a rare, elevated spelling of ひらく in the sense of "to enlighten, open someone's eyes". It is alive almost only in the fixed phrase 蒙を啓く "to free someone from ignorance", from which 啓蒙 "Enlightenment" also derives. For "to open a new era" or "to open up land" one writes 開く or 拓く (新しい時代を拓く), not 啓く. JMdict marks the word as obsolete; one should recognize it in texts but hardly needs it actively.

examples[].german: During the war, a food rationing system was in effect.
This film is distributed by a major company.
At the shelter, one rice ball was handed out to each person.
en.notes: 配給 has two main meanings: the allotment of scarce goods (rationing, 食料の配給, 配給制) and, in the film business, distribution (映画を配給する, 配給会社 "film distributor"). As a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を配給する. For ordinary handing out, one says 配る in everyday life; 配布 is the distribution of flyers or documents, 配達 is delivery. The rationing sense sounds of wartime and postwar times or of emergencies.

examples[].german: This scandal shook the foundations of the government.
A world-shaking discovery was born in a small laboratory.
My friend's betrayal shook my trust in people to the core.
en.notes: 揺るがす "to shake, throw into disarray" is transitive (Xを揺るがす) and mostly used figuratively: 政権を揺るがす, 世界を揺るがす大事件, 信頼を揺るがす. For the literal shaking of an object one rather says 揺らす or 揺さぶる. The intransitive counterpart 揺るぐ occurs almost only in the negative: 揺るがない決意, 揺るぎない自信 "unshakable".

en.meaning: to eat away at; to undermine
examples[].german: Corruption is eating away at the foundations of society.
Years of overwork gradually ruined his body.
Bullying deeply gnaws at a child's heart.
en.notes: 蝕む originally means "to be eaten away by worms" (cf. 虫歯), but today it is used almost only figuratively: illness, stress or corruption slowly "eat away at, undermine" something from within. Typical are 病が体を蝕む, 心を蝕む, 社会を蝕む, often in the progressive 蝕んでいる or the passive 蝕まれる. It sounds literary and is often written in kana むしばむ. In contrast to 損なう, it stresses the creeping, unnoticed process.

examples[].german: History warns us not to repeat the same mistakes.
I remind myself not to become complacent after a single success.
The father sternly admonished his son, who had lied.
en.notes: 戒める means "to admonish, warn (against something)"; patterns: 人を戒める or 〜ないよう戒める. Very common is the reflexive use 自らを戒める "to call oneself to order". It sounds more serious and more written than 注意する; while 叱る is mere scolding, 戒める stresses the lesson for the future. The noun 戒め means "admonition, lesson", e.g. 〜を戒めとする.

en.meaning: to refrain; to be careful about
examples[].german: In public places, one should be careful about one's words and actions.
On my doctor's advice, I decided to refrain from alcohol for a while.
Please refrain from private conversation during the exam.
en.notes: 慎む means "to restrain oneself, hold back, exercise caution"; the object is what one reins in or refrains from: 言葉を慎む, 酒を慎む, 外出を慎む. In rules and announcements it is often 〜は慎んでください. Do not confuse it with 謹む (also つつしむ) "to be respectful", which occurs mainly in 謹んで "respectfully". The noun 慎み stands for "restraint, decorum" (慎みのある人).

examples[].german: Religion shows a path of forgiveness for those who repent of their sins.
Lord, please forgive us our sins.
To celebrate the accession of the new king, many prisoners were pardoned.
en.notes: 赦す is a special spelling of ゆるす for forgiving guilt and sin or pardoning offenders (cf. 恩赦 "amnesty", 赦免 "pardon"). In everyday writing - also for "to permit" - one writes 許す; 赦す seems solemn, religious or literary. Typical are 罪を赦す, 人を赦す and the passive 赦される.

examples[].german: The hanami culture of admiring cherry blossoms is a hallmark of the Japanese spring.
We ate moon-viewing dumplings while admiring the harvest moon.
For my grandmother, nothing is a greater pleasure than enjoying the flowers in the garden.
en.notes: 愛でる is an elevated, poetic word for "to take pleasure in something beautiful, to gaze on lovingly". Typical objects are nature and the seasons: 花を愛でる, 月を愛でる, 紅葉を愛でる; more rarely also children or animals in the sense of "to caress". In everyday speech one says 楽しむ, 眺める or かわいがる instead.

en.meaning: to indulge in; to amuse oneself
examples[].german: The Heian aristocrats amused themselves exchanging waka poems.
During the break, the students were absorbed in chatting.
After the banquet, my colleagues amused themselves with karaoke until late at night.
en.notes: 興じる "to amuse oneself, be wholly absorbed in a pastime" is intransitive and takes に: 遊びに興じる, 雑談に興じる, トランプに興じる. It sounds literary and mostly describes from the outside how people give themselves over to an entertainment. The variant 興ずる is synonymous and even more elevated. In everyday speech one says 楽しむ (transitive with を) or 夢中になる.

en.meaning: to govern; to administer; to be in charge of
examples[].german: The independence of the courts, which exercise the judicial power, must be guaranteed.
The hippocampus is the part of the brain that governs memory.
In Greek mythology, Poseidon is regarded as the god who rules the sea.
en.notes: 司る means "to be in charge of something, to direct or govern something", often with institutions, organs or gods as the subject: 司法を司る, 記憶を司る脳の部位, 海を司る神. It is transitive (〜を司る) and has no intransitive partner. The word is literary; in everyday speech one says 担当する or 管理する. It is often written in kana つかさどる.

examples[].german: The scandal greatly damaged trust in the organization.
An extreme diet may harm your health.
I overslept and missed my usual bus.
en.notes: 損なう "to damage, impair" is transitive and mostly takes abstract or health-related objects: 健康を損なう, 信頼を損なう, 機嫌を損なう, 美観を損なう. The ichidan variant 損ねる is synonymous. As a suffix on the ます-stem, 〜損なう means "to miss, fail to do": 見損なう, 言い損なう, 乗り損なう. Unlike 壊す (to destroy physically), 損なう describes rather a loss of value.

examples[].german: Building a framework for international cooperation has become an urgent task.
To foster trust among employees, we hold regular social gatherings.
We want to build momentum across the whole region to support child-rearing.
en.notes: 醸成 literally means "brewing, fermenting" (醸 as in 醸造), but is used almost only figuratively: to let a mood or relationship gradually "come into being, mature". Typical objects are 雰囲気を醸成する, 信頼関係を醸成する, 機運を醸成する "to create a favorable climate". It is a word of politics, business and newspapers. Related is the more common 醸し出す "to give off (an atmosphere)".

examples[].german: Applicants are being recruited for public housing.
Horse racing and boat racing are called publicly run gambling.
In this town, the municipal bus runs only once an hour.
en.notes: 公営 means "operated by the public sector", usually by a municipality or prefecture, and almost always stands as a modifier before a noun: 公営住宅 "public housing", 公営ギャンブル (horse, boat and bicycle racing), 公営バス, 公営プール. The counterparts are 民営 "privately operated" and 国営 "operated by the central government"; 市営, 都営 or 県営 name the specific level of operator. Formal administrative vocabulary.

en.meaning: to fall into; to sink into
examples[].german: International aid is being called for to help countries that have fallen into an economic crisis.
The sudden power outage threw the hall into panic.
After failing the exam, he fell into a deep state of self-loathing.
en.notes: 陥る means "to fall into a bad state" and takes に: 危機に陥る, パニックに陥る, 自己嫌悪に陥る, ジレンマに陥る, 罠に陥る. It is intransitive; its transitive partner 陥れる means "to plunge someone into, to entrap" (人を罠に陥れる). Compared with the everyday 落ちる or 〜になる, 陥る sounds literary and stresses that one gets into the state unintentionally.

en.meaning: to devote oneself to; to do one's utmost
examples[].german: She devoted her whole life to social welfare.
The doctors did their best, but the patient could not be saved.
He knows every alley of this town inside out.
en.notes: 尽くす has two main uses: transitive "to exhaust, to bring to bear fully" (全力を尽くす, ベストを尽くす, 手を尽くす "to try every means") and, with に, "to devote oneself (to someone or something), to serve" (社会に尽くす, 家族に尽くす). As a suffix on the ます-stem, 〜尽くす means "to do completely, thoroughly": 食べ尽くす, 知り尽くす. The intransitive counterpart is 尽きる "to run out" (力が尽きる).

en.meaning: to look good; to stand out effectively
examples[].german: The gold leaf, set off by the autumn sunlight, radiates solemn beauty.
The red torii stands out beautifully against the snowy landscape.
This tie looks great with a navy suit, doesn't it?
en.notes: 映える "to shine, to look good against a background" is intransitive; the background or light takes に: 夕日に映える, 青空に映える, 雪に映える. You can also simply say 〜がよく映える "looks great". As a suffix it becomes 〜映え (ばえ): 見映え "appearance", インスタ映え "Instagram-worthy". Do not confuse it with the identically read 生える "to grow (hair, grass)".

en.meaning: to come back to life; to be revived
examples[].german: After restoration, the old mural was revived in vivid colors.
Looking at old photographs, memories of my childhood came back.
Ten years after the earthquake, the town has made a remarkable recovery.
en.notes: 甦る is an alternative spelling of よみがえる; today 蘇る is more common, and the kana spelling is also usual. It is intransitive: something "comes back to life, is revived" (死者が甦る, 街が甦る), and very often it is about memories: 記憶が甦る "the memory comes back". "To revive" as an action is expressed with the causative 甦らせる; 復活する is the more matter-of-fact Sino-Japanese word.

examples[].german: Sublime art leads the human spirit to greater heights.
As someone working in medicine, you must never forget the noble mission of saving lives.
The sight of Mt. Fuji at dawn can only be called sublime.
en.notes: 崇高 "sublime, noble" is a literary な-adjective for ideals and feelings that rise above the everyday: 崇高な理想, 崇高な使命, 崇高な精神. In aesthetics, 崇高 is also the technical term for "the sublime". It does not fit colloquial "great, awesome"; for that, use 素晴らしい or 立派. Do not confuse it with 高尚 "refined, cultured (taste)".

examples[].german: He offered a prayer with a solemn expression.
The graduation ceremony was held in a solemn atmosphere.
The government stated that it takes the election result very seriously.
en.notes: 厳粛 is a な-adjective meaning "solemnly serious, dignified": 厳粛な雰囲気, 厳粛な儀式, 式は厳粛に執り行われた. It can also mean "undeniable, to be taken seriously": 厳粛な事実, 結果を厳粛に受け止める. Unlike 真剣 "earnest (in an activity)", 厳粛 describes a dignified mood or attitude; 厳格, by contrast, means "strict (about rules)".

examples[].german: Devout believers come to worship every morning.
My grandmother is a devout Buddhist and never fails to put her hands together before the family altar morning and evening.
When I entered the cathedral, I naturally felt reverent.
en.notes: 敬虔 "devout, reverent" is a な-adjective that almost always stands before nouns for people or attitudes: 敬虔な信者, 敬虔なクリスチャン, 敬虔な祈り, 敬虔な気持ち. It is literary; in conversation one says 信心深い. Note: 敬虔 (けいけん) sounds exactly like 経験 "experience"; only context tells them apart.

examples[].german: People in ancient times revered the sun as a god.
He revered that painter as his lifelong teacher.
The villagers revere the large tree on the mountain as a sacred tree.
en.notes: 崇める "to revere, to worship" is transitive and often takes として or と: 神として崇める, 師と崇める "to revere as a master". It is used for gods, but also for people one holds in exceptionally high regard; the passive 崇められる is common. The Sino-Japanese 崇拝する is related. Compared with 尊敬する "to respect", 崇める sounds almost religiously exalted.

en.meaning: to cherish; to show loving compassion
examples[].german: Cherishing all living things is a teaching of Buddhism.
The mother held her newborn baby tenderly.
My grandfather raised the trees in the garden lovingly, as if they were his own children.
en.notes: 慈しむ "to care for lovingly, to love tenderly" is transitive and elevated; it describes a gentle, caring love, usually toward the small or weak: 子を慈しむ, 生き物を慈しむ, 自然を慈しむ. The noun 慈しみ "kindness, compassion" is common, e.g. in 慈しみの心. In everyday speech one says かわいがる or 大切にする; 慈悲 is the Buddhist term for "mercy".

en.meaning: to fear with reverence; to stand in awe
examples[].german: A heart that reveres the power of nature is the origin of faith.
People in the past feared thunder as the wrath of the gods.
The village elders frowned at the behavior that showed no fear even of the gods.
en.notes: 畏れる is the spelling of おそれる for reverent awe before something overpowering or sacred: 神を畏れる, 自然を畏れる. For ordinary fear, one writes 恐れる (失敗を恐れる). Related are 畏れ多い "too great an honor" and 畏敬 "reverence" (畏敬の念). It is transitive with を and sounds elevated.

examples[].german: The privatization of the postal service was a major political issue.
Japanese National Railways was privatized in 1987 and became JR.
There are many voices opposed to privatizing the water supply.
en.notes: 民営化 is the transfer of state or public enterprises into private hands; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を民営化する, passive 〜が民営化される. Well-known cases in Japan are the national railways (国鉄 → JR, 1987) and the post (郵政民営化). The opposite is 国有化 "nationalization"; the result is called 民営 "privately operated", as opposed to 公営 and 国営. Language of political and economic news.

en.meaning: to atone for; to make amends for
examples[].german: He devoted himself to ascetic practice to atone for his sins.
He tried to spend the rest of his life atoning for the mistakes of his youth.
In Christianity, it is taught that Jesus atoned for the sins of humankind.
en.notes: 贖う "to atone for, to make amends for" is transitive: 罪を贖う, 過ちを贖う. The means of atonement takes で or をもって: 命をもって罪を贖う. The word is elevated and often has a religious ring; the related 贖罪 means "atonement, (Christian) redemption". In everyday speech 償う is more usual; in older texts あがなう also means "to buy" and is then written 購う.

examples[].german: We should listen to the voices of the oppressed.
In that country, ethnic minorities have been oppressed for a long time.
Although she was mistreated by her stepmother, the heroine of the story never lost her kindness.
en.notes: 虐げる "to oppress, to treat cruelly" is transitive and is especially often used in the passive: 虐げられた人々 "the oppressed", 虐げられた民族. It describes lasting oppression of the weaker by the more powerful. For everyday bullying one says いじめる, for abuse in the legal sense 虐待する; 虐げる is literary and emotionally colored.

examples[].german: Disregarding basic human rights is unacceptable.
You must not neglect your family because of work alone.
An accident occurred as a result of putting profit first and neglecting safety.
en.notes: 蔑ろ "disrespect, disregard" occurs practically only in the phrase 〜を蔑ろにする "to disregard, to neglect, to trample on something": 規則を蔑ろにする, 家族を蔑ろにする, 安全を蔑ろにする. It is mostly written in kana, ないがしろ, because the kanji 蔑 (cf. 軽蔑 "contempt") is difficult. Unlike 無視する, it stresses treating something that is actually important as unimportant.

en.meaning: to take into account; to look back on
examples[].german: A society that cares only about its own interests and pays no heed to others is not healthy.
Disregarding the danger, he jumped into the river and saved the child.
Looking back on these ten years, I feel I have been supported by many people.
en.notes: 顧みる has two main meanings: "to look back (on the past)" (過去を顧みる) and "to heed, to take into consideration", the latter mostly negated: 家庭を顧みない "to neglect one's family", 危険を顧みず "regardless of the danger". Do not confuse it with 省みる "to reflect on oneself, to self-examine" (自らを省みる). The word is literary; in conversation one says 振り返る or 気にする respectively.

en.meaning: to regard as; to consider as
examples[].german: Silence may be regarded as consent in some cases.
If you do not submit by the deadline, you will be considered to have withdrawn.
He is regarded as the leading authority in this field.
en.notes: 見做す "to regard as, to consider as, (legally) to deem" appears in the pattern XをYと見做す, very often in the passive: Yと見做される. It is typical of rules, contracts and legal texts, e.g. 期限内に連絡がない場合は辞退と見做す. It is mostly written in kana, みなす. Unlike 考える or 思う, it expresses a (often formal) classification, not a personal opinion.

examples[].german: The style of The Tale of Genji is elegant and beautiful.
The refined melodies of gagaku drifted through the shrine grounds.
The court dance is characterized by slow, elegant movements.
en.notes: 典雅 "classically elegant, refined and dignified" is a rare, literary な-adjective. 典 points to the classical and exemplary, 雅 to courtly elegance (cf. 雅やか, 優雅). It describes mainly style, music and court art: 典雅な文体, 典雅な舞, 典雅な調べ. In everyday use 優雅 is far more common.

examples[].german: Sake with a mellow, aromatic flavor is brewed all over the country.
When I swirled the glass, the wine's rich aroma spread.
This coffee, made from dark-roasted beans, offers a rich, full-bodied taste.
en.notes: 芳醇 describes a full, mature aroma or flavor, especially in alcoholic drinks: 芳醇な香り, 芳醇な味わいの日本酒 or ワイン. Coffee, cheese or fruit can also be 芳醇. It is a word of gourmet and advertising language; in conversation one says 香りがいい or コクがある instead. The identically read 豊潤 "rich, abundant" is sometimes used synonymously, but it relates less to aroma.

examples[].german: One marvels at the maki-e technique, refined to the utmost.
This paper is based on a meticulous analysis of the data.
The inside of a mechanical watch is densely packed with exquisite parts.
en.notes: 精緻 "extremely fine, precise, worked out down to the detail" is a な-adjective and noun of the written language. It describes craftsmanship (精緻な細工), but equally intellectual constructs: 精緻な分析, 精緻な理論. The phrase 精緻を極める "to be of the highest delicacy" is common. Compared with 細かい or 精密, 精緻 stresses artful, well-considered fineness.

examples[].german: The magnificent castle architecture symbolizes the power of its time.
Tourists were breathless at the magnificent Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
The sunrise seen from the summit was magnificent beyond words.
en.notes: 壮麗 "magnificent, grand and majestic" is a な-adjective for large, impressive buildings and scenes: 壮麗な宮殿, 壮麗な大聖堂, 壮麗な景色. 壮 stands for greatness and strength, 麗 for beauty. Unlike 豪華 (luxurious, expensively furnished), 壮麗 stresses grandeur and dignity; 壮大 relates more to vast scale or plans.

examples[].german: The essence of Japanese beauty is condensed in the simple appearance of a tea room.
We held the wedding simply, with family only.
The city is pushing ahead with the simplification of administrative procedures.
en.notes: 簡素 "plain, simple, without anything superfluous" is a な-adjective with a positive ring: 簡素な暮らし, 簡素な式, 簡素なデザイン. 簡素化 "simplification" is very common, especially for administrative procedures (手続きの簡素化). Unlike 質素 ("frugal, thrifty" in lifestyle), 簡素 stresses reduction to the essentials; 簡単, by contrast, means "easy, uncomplicated".

examples[].german: I was captivated by the graceful movements of Japanese dance.
The graceful curve of the neck makes this vase beautiful.
A swan glides gracefully across the surface of the lake.
en.notes: 優美 "graceful, elegant" is a な-adjective for the delicate, soft beauty of movements, shapes and lines: 優美な動き, 優美な曲線, 優美な姿. It is literary; the similar 優雅 relates more to a cultivated, relaxed way of life (優雅な暮らし). For people, everyday speech prefers 上品 or きれい.

examples[].german: Momoyama culture is known for its gorgeous, resplendent decoration.
On our anniversary, we enjoyed a luxurious dinner at a hotel.
This film is the talk of the town for its star-studded cast.
en.notes: 豪華 "luxurious, gorgeous, lavish" is a な-adjective for anything that shows a lot of money and effort: 豪華な料理, 豪華なホテル, 豪華客船. It often stands directly before nouns: 豪華賞品, 豪華キャスト "all-star cast". The intensified form 豪華絢爛 means "magnificent and dazzling". Unlike 贅沢, 豪華 usually sounds admiring, not disapproving.

examples[].german: Staying in a tranquil mountain temple, one forgets the secular world.
Bashō's haiku express a state of tranquil solitude.
I gazed alone at the quiet, moss-covered garden.
en.notes: 閑寂 "quiet, secluded and peaceful" is a rare, literary な-adjective for a calm, slightly lonely mood far from the bustle of the world: 閑寂な山寺, 閑寂な庭. In aesthetics it is often used to explain わび・さび. In ordinary usage one says 静か or 閑静 (閑静な住宅街 "quiet residential area"); 静寂 is the more common word for "silence".

examples[].german: The solemn sound of the bell echoed across the temple grounds.
The ceremony opened with a stately performance by the orchestra.
The principal read the address in a solemn tone.
en.notes: 荘重 "solemn, dignified and weighty" is a な-adjective for sounds, ceremonies and speech: 荘重な音楽, 荘重な儀式, 荘重な口調. It resembles 厳粛 (a serious, solemn mood) and 荘厳 (そうごん, sublime and splendid, often for temples and churches); 荘重 stresses the weighty, measured quality. A literary word.

examples[].german: A simple, pure white flower was displayed in the tea room.
For an interview, it is safest to go in neat, simple clothing.
She has a neat, unaffected air and is liked by everyone.
en.notes: 清楚 "simple, pure and neat" describes a well-groomed, unobtrusive beauty without ostentation. It most often refers to women, their clothing and their aura: 清楚な女性, 清楚な服装, 清楚系 (a fashion style). Flowers such as white lilies are also considered 清楚. Opposites are 派手 "flashy" or 華やか; 上品 "elegant" is more general.

examples[].german: I was fascinated by the gorgeous world of the Heian picture scrolls.
On the Noh stage, an actor in a gorgeous costume dances quietly.
The great hall of the palace was adorned with sumptuous chandeliers.
en.notes: 絢爛 "gorgeous, splendid, dazzling" is a たる-adjective of the written language: attributive 絢爛たる, adverbial 絢爛と. It appears most often in the four-character compound 豪華絢爛 "sumptuous and splendid", which can also take な (豪華絢爛な衣装). It describes art, costumes and festivals, but also a flowery style (絢爛たる文体). In everyday speech one says 華やか.

examples[].german: The lonely mountain village scenery is the subject of haiku.
Before payday, dinner is a dreary affair of nothing but cup noodles.
I have finally gotten used to the lonely life of living alone at my post away from my family.
en.notes: 侘しい "dreary, lonely, shabby" is an い-adjective combining loneliness and bleakness: わびしい一人暮らし, わびしい食事, わびしい冬の景色. It is mostly written in kana. Unlike 寂しい (loneliness, longing for others), 侘しい also stresses the meager, joyless nature of the situation. Related is the aesthetic ideal 侘び (わび), which interprets plain austerity positively.

examples[].german: He took on social reform with unshakable conviction.
She built an unshakable position as a top athlete through her ability.
Years of dealings have created an unshakable relationship of trust between the two companies.
en.notes: 揺るぎない "unshakable, rock-solid" is an い-adjective made of 揺るぎ "wavering" + ない. It stands before abstract nouns: 揺るぎない信念, 揺るぎない自信, 揺るぎない地位. 揺るぎのない and the verbal 揺るがない mean the same. It sounds elevated and positive; in everyday speech one also says 強い or しっかりした.

examples[].german: Persistent awareness-raising activities are needed to wipe out deep-rooted prejudice.
The conflict between the two countries is historically deep-rooted.
Out of a deep-seated distrust of his boss, he decided to change jobs.
en.notes: 根深い "deep-rooted, deep-seated" is an い-adjective for problems, feelings and attitudes that have settled in for a long time and are hard to eliminate: 根深い問題, 根深い対立, 根深い不信感, 根深い差別. It is almost always negative in tone. For positive "firmly established" things such as popularity or traditions, one says 根強い (根強い人気) or 根付いている instead.

examples[].german: The management of the park was entrusted to a designated manager.
This library has introduced the designated manager system.
The city chose a local NPO as the designated manager of the gymnasium.
en.notes: 指定管理者 is a technical term of Japanese local government law: a company, NPO or similar body commissioned by the municipality to operate a public facility such as a library, gymnasium or park. The system is called 指定管理者制度 (since 2003). Typical: 〜を指定管理者に選定する, 指定管理者が運営する. One reads the word on signs and in tender notices; in conversation one rather says 民間の会社が運営している.

examples[].german: All life is equally precious.
Many precious lives were lost in the accident.
Hearing the sacred teachings at the temple, I felt cleansed.
en.notes: 尊い has two readings: たっとい and the now more usual とうとい; たっとい sounds older and more elevated. It means "precious, irreplaceable" (尊い命, 尊い犠牲) and "venerable, sacred" (尊い教え). Traditionally 尊い is written for "worthy of reverence" and 貴い for "valuable", but in modern usage the two are mixed. Compared with 大切 or 貴重, 尊い is more solemn and has a moral-religious coloring; the related verb 尊ぶ means "to revere, to esteem highly".

examples[].german: Awe toward great nature is the origin of religion.
The disciples held deep reverence for their master.
When I look up at the star-filled sky, I feel awe toward the universe.
en.notes: 畏敬 "awe" combines dread (畏) and esteem (敬). It almost always appears in the phrase 畏敬の念 "a feeling of awe": 〜に畏敬の念を抱く or 覚える. As a verb, 畏敬する is rarer. The object is nature, deities or outstanding people; compared with 尊敬 "respect", it carries a sense of dread before something overpowering.

examples[].german: This mountain has been revered as a sacred place since ancient times.
In India, the cow is regarded as a sacred animal.
A vote in an election is a sacred right of the citizens.
en.notes: 神聖 "holy, inviolable" is a な-adjective and noun: 神聖な場所, 神聖な儀式, 神聖な義務. Figuratively, things that must not be violated, such as a right or a duty, are also called 神聖. 神聖視する means "to regard as sacred", 神聖さ "sacredness". Unlike the literary 聖なる (attributive only: 聖なる夜), 神聖 is the neutral standard word.

en.meaning: high and low (social rank); noble and humble
examples[].german: The view that there is no high or low among occupations is spreading.
Many people visited the temple to worship, regardless of rank.
Under the Edo-period class system, whether one was of high or low status was determined by birth.
en.notes: 貴賤 "high and low" denotes the contrast between noble and humble social rank. It is alive mainly in set phrases: 職業に貴賤なし "no occupation is inferior" and 貴賤を問わず "regardless of rank". It is literary and sounds somewhat archaic; otherwise today one speaks rather of 身分 or 地位.

en.meaning: rise and fall; prosperity and decline
examples[].german: Rise and fall is the way of the world.
This port town has repeatedly gone through rise and fall along with trade.
The overgrown garden of the old mansion tells of the rise and fall of the family.
en.notes: 栄枯 "flourishing and withering" stands figuratively for the rise and fall of families, cities or empires. On its own it is rare; it almost always appears in the four-character compound 栄枯盛衰 "rise and fall, the ups and downs of fortune". Typical frames are 栄枯盛衰は世の習い and 栄枯盛衰を繰り返す. The word is literary and has a reflective, historical tone.

examples[].german: I am deeply concerned that social division is advancing.
The government regards the rapid spread of infections as a worrying situation.
Voices of concern are being raised by educators about children reading less.
en.notes: 憂慮 "serious concern" is a literary noun and する-verb (transitive: 事態を憂慮する). It is typical of politics, diplomacy and news: 深く憂慮している, 憂慮すべき事態 "a worrying situation". In everyday speech one says 心配する; 懸念 is similarly formal, but relates more to a concrete fear.

examples[].german: Concern about the decline of traditional culture is growing.
Experts fear a worsening of the economy.
This bird is designated as an endangered species.
en.notes: 危惧 is a serious, well-founded "apprehension" and belongs to written and news language. Typical are 〜に対する危惧, 危惧を抱く and 危惧が高まる; as a transitive する-verb it is 〜を危惧する or 〜ではないかと危惧する. Well known is 絶滅危惧種 "endangered species". In everyday speech one says 心配 or 不安 instead.

examples[].german: The worry I had back then turned out to be unfounded.
Your worry is nothing but needless anxiety.
I thought it might be canceled because of rain, but the worry was for nothing.
en.notes: 杞憂 refers to a worry that turns out in retrospect to be "unfounded"; the word goes back to a Chinese story about a man from the state of 杞 who feared that the sky might fall. The set phrase is 杞憂に終わる "to prove unfounded", also 〜は杞憂だった and 杞憂にすぎない. It sounds educated; in everyday speech one says 心配しすぎ or 取り越し苦労 instead.

examples[].german: A vigorous spirit of inquiry supports the development of society.
My son has a hearty appetite and eats three bowls of rice.
Curious children want to touch everything.
en.notes: 旺盛 describes a drive or power that is "bursting with energy": appetite, curiosity, drive to act, demand. Very often it is used as a suffix without な: 食欲旺盛, 好奇心旺盛, 元気旺盛; predicative 食欲が旺盛だ, attributive 旺盛な需要. It always needs such a related word: 好奇心旺盛な人 is natural, a bare 旺盛な人 is not. Neutral to literary.

examples[].german: Fresh sensibility overflows in the works of young artists.
Tomatoes picked in the morning are juicy and sweet.
After the rain, the young leaves shine fresh and dewy.
en.notes: みずみずしい means "fresh, juicy, full of life" and is mostly written in kana; 瑞々しい is the kanji spelling. Concretely it stands for fruit, vegetables, skin or leaves that look plump and moist (みずみずしいトマト, みずみずしい肌); figuratively for the youthful freshness of feeling and expression (瑞々しい感性, 瑞々しい文体). Unlike 新鮮, it stresses less that something is new or freshly harvested than the juicy, lively impression.

examples[].german: He captivated the audience with his skillful speaking.
Using smooth words, he deceived an old man and took his money.
The craftsman weaves the bamboo with deft hands.
en.notes: 巧み is a な-adjective for "skillful, adroit" and stresses artful technique: 巧みな話術, 巧みな手つき, adverbial 巧みに操る or 巧みに利用する. Compared with 上手, it is more literary and can also mean "cunning, crafty", as in 巧みな嘘 or 言葉巧みに騙す. As a noun ("craftsmanship") it is rare today.

examples[].german: I was moved by the clumsy but heartfelt performance.
It is a poor piece of writing, but I would be glad if you would read it to the end.
I explained as hard as I could in my clumsy Japanese.
en.notes: つたない means "unskilled, clumsy" and sounds more elevated than 下手. Typical is the humble use for one's own performance: 拙い文章ですが, 拙い日本語で失礼します. The same kanji 拙い is also read まずい ("unfavorable, bad"), so つたない is often written in kana. Related is 稚拙 "childishly clumsy".

examples[].german: Coarse behavior is not tolerated in social settings.
He looks rough, but is actually a very kind person.
The protagonist of the novel shocks readers with his crude language.
en.notes: 粗野 is a な-adjective and noun meaning "uncouth, coarse" in behavior, manner or speech: 粗野な振る舞い, 粗野な言葉遣い, 粗野な男. It criticizes a lack of refinement; unlike 乱暴, it is not about violence or recklessness. Antonyms are 上品 or 洗練された. Rather literary.

examples[].german: The barbarity of war must be passed on to future generations.
Trying to solve problems with violence is a barbaric way of doing things.
People in the past often regarded cultures different from their own as barbaric.
en.notes: 野蛮 is a な-adjective and noun meaning "uncivilized, barbaric": 野蛮な行為, 野蛮な考え, 野蛮人; the noun 野蛮さ denotes barbarity itself. It judges something as crude and uncultured. 乱暴 refers more to rough, violent behavior in an individual case, 残酷 to "cruel". Note: calling people or cultures 野蛮 sounds derogatory.

examples[].german: Faced with an unprecedented crisis, the international community united.
The earthquake caused unprecedented damage.
It became a topic of conversation when the prime minister misread 「未曾有」 as 「みぞうゆう」.
en.notes: 未曾有 literally means "never having been before" (未だ曾て有らず) and almost always stands attributively with の: 未曾有の危機, 未曾有の大災害, 未曾有の事態. It sounds much weightier than 前例のない or 初めての and is typical of news and speeches about disasters. The reading みぞう is a well-known trap; the incorrect reading みぞうゆう once made headlines.

examples[].german: The devastation of the land by the war was too terrible to look at.
With no one living there anymore, the village fell into ruin.
The prolonged recession caused people's hearts to become hardened.
en.notes: 荒廃 denotes the state in which land, buildings or towns are "devastated, fallen into ruin"; as an intransitive する-verb: 町が荒廃する, often attributive 荒廃した土地. Figuratively one speaks of 人心の荒廃 or 教育の荒廃, moral decay. Literary; in everyday speech one says 荒れる (荒れた庭) instead.

examples[].german: The number of young people aiming to revive declining traditional performing arts is increasing.
He devoted his life to restoring his fallen family.
After the war, the temple was rebuilt through donations from local people.
en.notes: 再興 means "to revive" something that has declined, or its revival: a family, a country, an art or a temple. It can be used both transitively (家を再興する) and intransitively (国が再興する). Unlike 復興 (reconstruction after war or disaster, 震災復興), 再興 stresses the revival of institutions and traditions; 復活 is more general and everyday. Literary, often historical (お家再興).

examples[].german: The reconstruction work on the burned-down castle has been completed.
Please tell me how to restore deleted files.
The appearance of the dinosaur was reconstructed from the excavated bones.
en.notes: 復元 means to return something to its "original state": buildings, fossils, paintings, but also data. It is mostly transitive (城を復元する, passive 復元される); the result is called e.g. 復元図 or 復元模型. In IT it means "to restore" (ファイルを復元する). Distinctions: 復旧 is putting infrastructure back into operation (電車が復旧する), 修復 is the repair of damaged things.

examples[].german: One learns the techniques of the time by copying old murals.
An art student is copying a Monet painting at the museum.
He is good at impersonating the voices of celebrities.
en.notes: 模写 is the exact copying of an original by hand, above all with paintings and calligraphy: 名画を模写する, 模写を通じて学ぶ. In addition, 声帯模写 and 形態模写 denote the imitation of voices or gestures as an entertainment art. Unlike コピー (mechanical), 模写 is handwork; 複製 is reproduction in general, 模倣 imitation of style or ideas.

en.meaning: great cause; higher purpose; moral ideal
examples[].german: A war without a just cause cannot win the support of the international community.
They risked their lives for the great cause of national independence.
If taxes are to be raised, a reasonable justification is needed.
en.notes: 大義 is the "great, morally justified purpose" one serves, originally the duty toward one's lord and state. Typical: 大義のために戦う, 大義を掲げる. Very common is 大義名分 "official justification", often critical in the sense of "pretext": 大義名分が立たない. Do not confuse it with the identically read 大儀 "tiresome, burdensome". Literary and elevated.

examples[].german: An administrative sanction was imposed on the offending business.
For drunk driving, he received an administrative sanction of license revocation, separate from the criminal penalty.
The prefecture issued an administrative order suspending business at the restaurant that caused food poisoning.
en.notes: 行政処分 is a binding measure by an authority toward a person or company, in everyday life above all sanctions such as business suspension, license revocation or, for traffic violations, 免許停止. Typical verbs: 行政処分を下す/行う/受ける. It is to be distinguished from the criminal 刑事処分; both can occur in parallel for the same violation. A non-binding recommendation by an authority, by contrast, is called 行政指導.

examples[].german: The conduct of sensible citizens keeps society healthy.
To say something like that, I doubt his good sense.
In the end, I would like to leave the judgment to the good sense of the readers.
en.notes: 良識 is the "sound judgment" of a decent, reasonable person: not mere knowledge, but a morally balanced judgment. Typical: 良識ある市民, 良識ある大人, 良識に訴える, 良識に欠ける and 良識を疑う "to doubt someone's good sense". Related is 常識 ("social norms, common knowledge"); 良識 is more elevated and stresses the ethical. The upper house is traditionally called 良識の府.

examples[].german: We need young people with the spirit to face difficulties.
With the resolve to rebuild the company by his own efforts, he took up the post of president.
One does not sense in recent politicians the spirit to shoulder the nation.
en.notes: 気概 is the "strength of will" not to be beaten by difficulties: backbone and fighting spirit. Typical: 気概を持つ, 気概がある/ない, 〜する気概, 〜という気概で. Compared with 意欲 ("motivation"), 気概 stresses steadfastness against resistance; 根性 is more colloquial. Elevated, often used in speeches and editorials.

examples[].german: He approaches his work with the pride of a craftsman.
His pride as a professional did not allow him to cut corners.
Though they lost, they kept their dignity as champions to the end.
en.notes: 矜持 is the "pride and self-respect" that grow out of skill or position and that one does not want to betray: 職人としての矜持, 矜持を持つ, 矜持を保つ, 矜持が許さない. The original reading is きんじ; today きょうじ is generally used. Compared with プライド or 誇り, it is clearly literary and has nothing arrogant about it (unlike 高慢).

examples[].german: The prophet received a divine revelation and conveyed the word of God to the people.
The idea struck me suddenly like an inspiration from above.
The composer is said to have felt that melody was a divine inspiration.
en.notes: 天啓 is a "revelation" from heaven or God in the religious sense: 天啓を受ける, 天啓が下る. Figuratively it denotes a sudden inspiration that seems to come from above: 天啓のようにひらめく. For an ordinary good idea, one says ひらめき or 思いつき; 啓示 is the more matter-of-fact word for religious revelation (神の啓示). Literary.

examples[].german: They light a goma fire and pray for the fulfillment of all wishes.
The worshippers wrote their wishes on goma sticks and offered them.
Goma fire ceremonies are held every day at Naritasan.
en.notes: 護摩 is the fire ritual of esoteric Buddhism (above all Shingon and Tendai), in which wooden sticks (護摩木) bearing wishes are burned in the fire, usually before 不動明王. The accompanying verb is 焚く: 護摩を焚く; the ritual is also called 護摩祈祷. Do not confuse it with the identically read 胡麻 "sesame" - the idiom ごまをする "to flatter" refers to sesame.

examples[].german: The ritual rebuilding of Ise Shrine is carried out once every twenty years.
Many worshippers visited the new shrine buildings after the relocation of the deity.
At Izumo Taisha, too, a sengu is held about every sixty years.
en.notes: 遷宮 denotes the transfer of the deity of a Shinto shrine to a newly built or renewed sanctuary. Best known is the 式年遷宮 of Ise Shrine, in which the shrine buildings are rebuilt every twenty years; Izumo Taisha also holds a 遷宮. A technical term from Shinto, mostly used as a noun (遷宮が行われる, 遷宮祭), rarely as an intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: At the festival, they carry the portable shrine and parade through the town.
The children carried a small mikoshi and shouted "Wasshoi!".
He was hoisted up as his faction's figurehead and ran in the party leadership election.
en.notes: 神輿 is the "portable shrine" in which the deity is carried through the neighborhood at a festival; one says 神輿を担ぐ, 神輿が出る, 神輿が町を練り歩く. In everyday speech the polite form お神輿 is very common, and it is often written in kana as みこし. Figuratively, 神輿を担ぐ means to put someone at the top as a figurehead and support them.

examples[].german: In the Edo period there were popular religious organizations such as the Ise-kō and Fuji-kō.
The villagers formed a kō and put aside a little money every month.
In this area, meetings of the nenbutsu-kō continue to this day.
en.notes: 講 historically denotes an association of believers who, for example, saved money together to finance pilgrimages; as a suffix it follows the pilgrimage destination or the venerated deity: 伊勢講, 富士講, 念仏講. Originally it was a Buddhist teaching assembly (the kanji as in 講義, 講話); later also a mutual savings and credit association such as 頼母子講. One says 講を組む. Today it is used mainly in history and folklore studies.

examples[].german: The Emperor is positioned as the one who presides over the state rituals.
Earthenware used in ancient rituals was excavated from this site.
It was the custom for the eldest son to take over the ancestral rites.
en.notes: 祭祀 is the formal word for "cult, ritual worship" of gods and ancestors: 祭祀を行う, 祭祀を司る, 宮中祭祀 (rites at the imperial court). Unlike 祭り ("festival"), it denotes the religious act itself, not the folk festival. It is a technical term in religious studies, archaeology (祭祀遺跡) and law (祭祀財産, e.g. the grave and household altar in inheritance law).

examples[].german: The discussion went around in circles like a Zen dialogue.
The trainee monk aimed for enlightenment through Zen dialogues with his master.
I inquired at the government office, but only got cryptic, noncommittal answers.
en.notes: 禅問答 is originally the question-and-answer exchange between a Zen master and a disciple intended to lead to enlightenment (cf. 公案). In everyday speech it is mostly used pejoratively for a conversation in which questions and answers talk past each other or remain incomprehensible: まるで禅問答だ, 禅問答のようなやり取り. The figurative meaning is much more common today than the religious one.

examples[].german: The ministry issued administrative guidance to the company.
The firm received administrative guidance from the Consumer Affairs Agency regarding inappropriate advertising.
Administrative guidance has no legal force.
en.notes: 行政指導 consists of recommendations, admonitions or instructions from an authority that are not legally binding but traditionally have great influence on companies in Japan. Typical: 行政指導を行う/受ける, 行政指導に従う. In contrast to 行政処分, a binding administrative act, it is formally based on voluntariness; but those who do not comply often risk a later 行政処分. Technical language from administration and business news.

examples[].german: Saving all sentient beings is the vow of a bodhisattva.
It is taught that the Buddha pours out compassion equally on all living beings.
In his sermon, the head priest spoke about the suffering of sentient beings.
en.notes: 衆生 is a Buddhist term for "all living beings" who suffer in the cycle of rebirth and are to be saved. Set phrases are 一切衆生, 衆生を救う (衆生済度) and 衆生の苦しみ. Note that the reading is しゅじょう. Unlike 大衆 ("the broad masses"), it is a religious term that also includes animals, and it occurs almost only in Buddhist texts and sermons.

examples[].german: This work skillfully weaves in satire of those in power.
This manga sharply satirizes the corruption of politicians.
Satire of the state of society is often seen in the senryū of the Edo period.
