en.notes: 諷刺 is "satire": abuses or the powerful are criticized in a witty, indirect way. Today 風刺 is the usual spelling; 諷刺 is the older one. Typical: 社会を諷刺する, 〜への諷刺, 諷刺画 (caricature), 諷刺が効いている. Unlike 皮肉 ("irony, sarcasm", also in personal conversation), 諷刺 is usually aimed at society or politics and is an artistic form.

examples[].german: The comical acting in kyōgen drew laughter from the audience.
His desperate attempt to make excuses was rather ridiculous.
The children laughed loudly at the clown's comical gestures.
en.notes: 滑稽 is a な-adjective meaning "comical, droll" (滑稽な仕草, 滑稽な話), but also "ridiculous" in a derogatory sense: 必死に言い訳する姿は滑稽だった. Unlike おもしろい, it does not mean "interesting" but only "provoking laughter", and like ばかばかしい it can express mockery. The genre 滑稽本 (comic prose fiction) comes from the Edo period. Neutral to literary.

examples[].german: The predators at the top of the food chain are declining.
The marine food chain begins with plankton.
Harmful substances accumulate in the human body through the food chain, too.
en.notes: 食物連鎖 is the "food chain" in ecology; here 食物 is read しょくもつ, not たべもの. Typical are 食物連鎖の頂点 "top of the food chain", 食物連鎖の上位/下位 and 食物連鎖を通じて, for example when pollutants accumulate (生物濃縮). A matter-of-fact technical term from biology and environmental reports.

examples[].german: Eye color is determined by heredity.
It seems the father's height has been passed on to the son.
Since this disease can be hereditary, the family also had themselves tested.
en.notes: 遺伝 is the biological "inheritance" of traits. As an intransitive する-verb, the trait takes が and the recipient takes に: 父の体質が子に遺伝する. Common derivatives are 遺伝子 "gene", 遺伝的 "genetic" and 隔世遺伝 "skipping a generation (atavism)". For inheriting property, one says 相続 instead, and for taking over in general 受け継ぐ.

en.meaning: core; cell nucleus; atomic nucleus; nuclear weapons
examples[].german: The cell nucleus contains DNA.
He is the player who forms the core of the team.
A rally calling for the abolition of nuclear weapons was held.
en.notes: 核 is generally the "core": in biology the cell nucleus (細胞の核, 細胞核), in physics the atomic nucleus (原子核). Very often it stands as short for nuclear weapons: 核兵器, 核実験, 核の脅威, 核なき世界; a nuclear power plant, by contrast, is 原子力発電所. Figuratively it denotes the central core of a group or matter, as in チームの核となる選手. For the core of fruit, everyday speech prefers 種 or 芯.

examples[].german: Proteins are indispensable as building blocks of the body.
After exercise, it is good to take in a bit more protein.
Soybeans are rich in plant protein.
en.notes: 蛋白質 is "protein". The kanji 蛋白 have become rare; today it is mostly written たんぱく質 or タンパク質. Typical are たんぱく質を摂る, 良質なたんぱく質 and 動物性/植物性たんぱく質. Colloquially and in the fitness world, one also says プロテイン, but this often means the powder.

examples[].german: Carbohydrates are important as a source of energy.
Since I am on a diet, I cut back on carbohydrates in the evening.
The ramen and fried rice set is nothing but carbohydrates.
en.notes: 炭水化物 is the nutrient "carbohydrate" (literally "carbon-water compound"). In everyday speech it also simply refers to rice, bread and noodles: 炭水化物を控える, 炭水化物抜きダイエット. In diet contexts, 糖質 ("digestible carbohydrates") is at least as widespread, e.g. 糖質制限. Matter-of-fact, known from nutrition science and daily life alike.

examples[].german: Excessive intake of fat has a negative effect on health.
This product is low in fat and also modest in calories.
At my health checkup, I was told I have dyslipidemia.
en.notes: 脂質 is the technical term "lipid, fat" from nutrition science and biochemistry and appears, for example, in nutrition labels alongside たんぱく質 and 炭水化物. In everyday speech one says 脂肪 (fat in food and body fat), 油 (oil) or 脂 (animal fat) instead. Common in medicine is 脂質異常症 "dyslipidemia (lipid metabolism disorder)".

examples[].german: Fungi contribute to the ecosystem as decomposers.
Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus called Trichophyton.
Antibiotics work against bacteria, but not against fungi.
en.notes: 真菌 is the biological and medical technical term for "fungi" in the sense of the kingdom of organisms, including yeasts and molds. In everyday speech one says きのこ for edible mushrooms and カビ for mold. Important is the distinction from 細菌 "bacteria"; 菌 alone usually means germs in general. Medically: 真菌感染症, 抗真菌薬.

examples[].german: Deregulation is being tried out in the National Strategic Special Zone.
The town was designated a "doburoku special zone", allowing farmers to brew their own rice wine.
Shenzhen is one of China's first special economic zones.
en.notes: 特区 is a short form for various special zones: in Japan it mainly means 構造改革特区 and 国家戦略特区, in which regulations are loosened on a trial basis; for China, 経済特区 "special economic zone". Typical: 〜を特区に指定する, 特区で〜を認める. Less often, 特区 is also short for 特別区, the wards of Tokyo; for Hong Kong and Macau, the full form 特別行政区 is more common. A word from political and business news.

examples[].german: Lichens are used as indicators of air pollution.
Lichens are organisms formed by a symbiosis of fungi and algae.
Lichens are clinging densely to the surface of the rock.
en.notes: 地衣類 are "lichens", that is, communities of fungi and algae or cyanobacteria; 類 denotes the group of organisms. In everyday speech lichens are often simply called コケ, although biologically they are not mosses (コケ植物). A technical term from biology and environmental science.

examples[].german: Conifers are distributed mainly in cold regions.
Conifers such as sugi and hinoki are used as building material.
Vast coniferous forests spread across Hokkaidō.
en.notes: 針葉樹 literally means "needle-leaf tree", that is, a conifer such as 杉, 檜 or 松; the forest is called 針葉樹林. The counterpart is 広葉樹 "broadleaf tree". The classification by leaf shape is independent of 常緑樹/落葉樹: most conifers are evergreen, but the larch (カラマツ) sheds its needles. Matter-of-fact, from biology and forestry.

examples[].german: Deciduous trees shed their leaves in autumn.
If you plant a deciduous tree in the garden, it provides shade in summer and lets the sun through in winter.
The larch is a conifer, but unusually it is also deciduous.
en.notes: 落葉樹 is a "deciduous tree"; here 落葉 is read らくよう, not おちば. The counterpart is 常緑樹 "evergreen tree". This classification concerns leaf shedding and is independent of 針葉樹/広葉樹 - hence expressions like 落葉広葉樹林 "deciduous broadleaf forest". Matter-of-fact, from biology and horticulture.

examples[].german: Evergreen trees keep green leaves all year round.
Evergreen trees, which provide privacy all year round, are suitable for hedges.
There are many evergreen trees, such as camphor trees, in shrine forests.
en.notes: 常緑樹 is an "evergreen tree" (常 "always", 緑 "green") that bears leaves all year, such as 松, 杉, クスノキ or ツバキ. The counterpart is 落葉樹. There are evergreen conifers and broadleaf trees (常緑広葉樹). In horticulture it is often recommended for hedges and privacy screens. Matter-of-fact.

examples[].german: They cleared wasteland overgrown with shrubs for cultivation.
Low shrubs continued on both sides of the road.
The rabbit quickly hid in a thicket of shrubs.
en.notes: 灌木 is a "shrub, bush", a low woody plant without a distinct main trunk. Since 灌 is not a jōyō kanji, it is also written かん木; in modern botany the usual word is 低木 (opposite 高木). Typical are 灌木林 "scrubland" and 灌木の茂み "thicket". Rather literary; in everyday speech one says 茂み or 低い木.

examples[].german: Herbaceous plants, unlike woody plants, do not become woody.
A variety of herbaceous plants grow in this marsh.
Bamboo looks like a tree, but is sometimes classified as herbaceous.
en.notes: 草本 is the botanical term for "herbaceous plants" whose stems do not become woody; the opposite is 木本 "woody plant". It mostly appears in 草本植物 or in 多年生草本 "perennial herb". In everyday speech one simply says 草. A purely technical term from botany and plant science.

examples[].german: I planted tulip bulbs in autumn.
After the flowers are finished, dig up the bulbs and let them dry.
I am growing a hyacinth bulb in water culture.
en.notes: 球根 is the "flower bulb" or "tuber" as a storage organ of plants such as tulip, hyacinth or dahlia; one says 球根を植える, 球根を掘り上げる, 球根植物. Note: the kitchen onion is 玉ねぎ, not 球根. Neutral, used above all in horticulture.

examples[].german: Moisture and a suitable temperature are necessary for seeds to germinate.
Dandelion seeds are carried far by the wind.
Seeds of crops from all over the world are preserved at this facility.
en.notes: 種子 is the technical word for "seed"; in everyday speech one says 種 (たね). It appears in biology, agriculture and specialist texts: 種子の発芽, 種子を散布する, 種子植物 "seed plant". Note: in place names such as 種子島 it is read たね.

examples[].german: Many people suffer from hay fever in spring.
There is a lot of pollen in the air today, so you should wear a mask.
Honeybees carry pollen from flower to flower.
en.notes: 花粉 is "pollen". In everyday life it appears mainly in 花粉症 "hay fever", which is very widespread in Japan because of cedar pollen (スギ花粉). Typical phrases: 花粉が飛ぶ, 花粉の飛散量, 花粉を運ぶ (of insects). Neutral.

en.meaning: decentralization; devolution of powers to local government
examples[].german: Powers of local governments were expanded by the decentralization reform.
To advance decentralization, the transfer of tax sources is indispensable.
Japan was long a centralized country, but calls for decentralization are growing louder.
en.notes: 地方分権 refers to the shift of powers and financial resources from the central government to prefectures and municipalities; the opposite is 中央集権 "centralism". Typical combinations: 地方分権を進める/推進する, 地方分権改革. Related is 地方自治 "local self-government": that is the principle, while 地方分権 is rather the process or the political demand. Language of politics and administration.

examples[].german: Honeybees play an important role in pollination.
Greenhouse strawberries are sometimes pollinated by hand.
Flowers that are not pollinated drop off without bearing fruit.
en.notes: 受粉 is "pollination"; as an intransitive する-verb it is 花が受粉する. Someone who pollinates actively uses the causative 受粉させる, for example in 人工受粉 "artificial pollination"; there is also 自家受粉 "self-pollination". Do not confuse it with 受精 "fertilization", which occurs only after pollination. Matter-of-fact.

examples[].german: Germination was confirmed one week after the seeds were sown.
These seeds do not germinate unless the temperature reaches twenty degrees or more.
Germinated brown rice is said to be easier to digest than ordinary brown rice.
en.notes: 発芽 is "germination"; as an intransitive する-verb: 種が発芽する. Typical are 発芽率 "germination rate", 発芽条件 and 発芽玄米 "germinated brown rice". In everyday speech one mostly says 芽が出る; 発芽 sounds factual and scientific.

examples[].german: The flowering time of cherry blossoms is getting earlier every year.
The Meteorological Agency announced the blooming of the cherry blossoms in Tokyo.
Her talent blossomed all at once after she studied abroad.
en.notes: 開花 is the "blooming" of flowers; as an intransitive する-verb: 桜が開花する. Very well known are 開花宣言 (the official announcement of the start of cherry blossom season) and 開花予想; 満開, by contrast, denotes full bloom. Figuratively it means "to come into full development": 才能が開花する, 文化が開花する. In everyday speech, for flowers one prefers 咲く.

examples[].german: When pollination is successful, fruit sets.
Years of research finally bore fruit in the development of a new drug.
The players' efforts bore fruit in the form of a championship.
en.notes: 結実 means "to set fruit" in botany; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜が結実する. At least as common is the figurative meaning "to bear fruit, to pay off": 努力が結実する, 長年の研究が〜として結実する. In conversation one says 実を結ぶ instead, which uses the same image. Literary.

examples[].german: The fall of leaves in autumn creates beautiful scenery.
The ginkgo turns yellow in autumn and then sheds its leaves.
If drought continues, some trees shed their leaves even in summer.
en.notes: 落葉 in the reading らくよう denotes "leaf fall, shedding of leaves" as a process and as an intransitive する-verb: 木が落葉する. For the fallen leaves themselves, everyday speech mostly uses 落ち葉 (おちば); らくよう sounds factual to technical. Attributively it appears in 落葉樹 "deciduous tree" and 落葉広葉樹.

examples[].german: Many trees died because of the drought.
The pines on the mountain are dying off one after another because of pest damage.
The potted plant with root rot died just like that.
en.notes: 枯死 is the matter-of-fact word for the "dying off" of plants, especially trees; as an intransitive する-verb: 木が枯死する. It appears in reports on drought, pests or environmental damage, e.g. 松枯れによる枯死. In everyday speech one simply says 枯れる; 枯死 is not used for people and animals. Literary.

examples[].german: Valuable plant communities remain in this region.
A large colony of skunk cabbage spreads across the marsh.
To protect the alpine plant communities, entering off the hiking trails is prohibited.
en.notes: 群落 is, in botany and ecology, a "plant community" or a dense "stand" of one species at a site: 植物群落, ミズバショウの群落, 高山植物の群落. Related is 群生 "to grow in groups" (群生する). The older meaning "a group of villages" is rare today. Technical, frequent in nature conservation texts.

examples[].german: Vegetation changes greatly depending on altitude.
After a forest fire, it takes decades for the vegetation to recover.
This island is known for its unique vegetation.
en.notes: 植生 is the "vegetation" of an area as a whole, that is, which plants grow there and how they are distributed. Typical: 植生が豊か, 植生が変化する, 植生の回復, 植生図 "vegetation map". Unlike 植物 (individual plants or plants in general), 植生 describes the plant cover of a landscape. Technical, in geography and ecology.

examples[].german: The stand of trees along the coast functions as a windbreak forest.
After passing through the belt of woods, the view suddenly opened up.
This park has a large woodland and is well suited to bird-watching.
en.notes: 樹林 is a matter-of-fact, rather technical term for a stand of trees or a piece of woodland, as found in ecology, urban planning or hiking guides; in everyday speech one simply says 林 or 森. It is very common in compounds such as 針葉樹林 "coniferous forest", 広葉樹林 "broadleaf forest" or 樹林帯 "forest belt" (in mountain descriptions). The related 森林 denotes forest rather as an area or a resource (森林破壊 "deforestation"), while 樹林 emphasizes the stock of trees as a vegetation type.

examples[].german: This bird enters its breeding season in spring.
The rainy season is very humid, so mold spreads easily.
The zoo succeeded in breeding pandas.
en.notes: 繁殖 is the multiplication or reproduction of animals, plants and microorganisms; as an intransitive する-verb: カビが繁殖する "mold spreads", 細菌が繁殖する. Typical compounds are 繁殖期 "breeding season, mating season", 繁殖力 "reproductive capacity" and 人工繁殖 "captive breeding". It is not used for humans. Distinguish 増殖, which describes rather the multiplication of cells or viruses (細胞が増殖する), and 生殖, reproduction as a biological function (生殖器).

en.meaning: regional system (proposed merger of prefectures into larger regions)
examples[].german: Debate is under way over the introduction of the regional system.
With a regional system, the prefecture might disappear as a unit.
Many governors are cautious about the regional system.
en.notes: 道州制 is a reform plan, discussed for decades but never implemented, to combine the 47 prefectures into a few large regions (about 9 to 13, depending on the draft) to be called 道 or 州 - modeled on 北海道. The regions are to receive far-reaching self-government; this recalls a federal state, but it would not be true federalism. Typical: 道州制を導入する, 道州制の是非. A purely political technical term.

examples[].german: Owls prey on small animals at night.
In an ecosystem, the balance between predators and prey is maintained.
Praying mantises sometimes prey even on insects larger than themselves.
en.notes: 捕食 means that an animal catches and eats another as prey; as a transitive する-verb: 獲物を捕食する. The word belongs to biology and nature documentaries; in everyday speech one says 食べる, 襲う or 狩る instead. Important derivatives are 捕食者 "predator" and its counterpart 被食者 "prey animal". Do not confuse it with 補食 "supplementary meal, snack", which is read the same.

examples[].german: Parasites take nutrients from their host.
This fungus grows by parasitizing the roots of other plants.
He doesn't work and lives off his parents.
en.notes: 寄生 denotes the life of one organism at the expense of another; as an intransitive する-verb, the host takes に: 腸に寄生する "to parasitize the intestine". Common derivatives are 寄生虫 "parasite" and 寄生植物. Figuratively and pejoratively, 寄生する also describes people who live off others (親に寄生する "to sponge off one's parents"); the host is called 宿主.

examples[].german: Insect mimicry is an astonishing product of evolution.
Stick insects mimic twigs to protect themselves from enemies.
Words like 「キラキラ」 and 「ドキドキ」 are called mimetic words (gitaigo).
en.notes: 擬態 is the mimicry or camouflage of living things that imitate something else; as an intransitive する-verb, the model takes に: 木の枝に擬態する "to mimic a twig". The word is biological and technical; in everyday speech one says 隠れる or 化ける. Also well known is 擬態語, the mimetic words describing states, such as キラキラ, in contrast to 擬音語 or 擬声語, which imitate actual sounds.

examples[].german: Bears use almost no energy during hibernation.
In spring, the bears wake up from hibernation.
The plan is in a dormant state due to a lack of budget.
en.notes: 冬眠 is the hibernation of animals; as an intransitive する-verb: クマが冬眠する. Typical combinations are 冬眠中, 冬眠に入る and 冬眠から覚める or 目覚める. Figuratively, one speaks of 冬眠状態 when a project or company is temporarily idle. Distinguish 休眠 "dormancy" (seeds, 休眠口座 "dormant account") and the more everyday 冬ごもり "staying holed up in winter".

examples[].german: Migratory birds travel long distances according to the season.
Swallows migrate south in autumn.
Just as it started to rain, a friend's car happened by - it was exactly what I needed.
en.notes: 渡り is the nominalization of 渡る "to cross over"; in nature it denotes above all bird migration: 渡りをする, 渡りの季節, 渡り鳥 "migratory bird" (figuratively also someone who constantly changes jobs). It also stands for "crossing, connection", as in 渡り廊下 "covered connecting corridor". Set phrases are 渡りに船 "exactly what one needs" and 渡りをつける "to establish contact".

examples[].german: Habitats of wild animals are being lost due to urban development.
This wetland is known as a habitat of the red-crowned crane.
The habitat of pandas is limited to mountainous areas of China.
en.notes: 生息地 is the habitat of an animal species; the underlying 生息する "to live (in the wild), to occur" is used only for animals and plants (この川にはサケが生息している). Typical combinations are 生息地を守る, 生息地が失われる and 生息地の破壊. For humans one says 居住地, and for the origin of plants 原産地. The variant 棲息地 with the character 棲 is rarer.

examples[].german: Conserving biodiversity is a global challenge.
The increase of invasive species is threatening local biodiversity.
Coral reefs are places with extremely rich biodiversity.
en.notes: 生物多様性 is the technical term for biodiversity and appears mainly in environmental policy, science and the news. Typical combinations are 生物多様性の保全 "conservation of biodiversity", 生物多様性が失われる and 生物多様性が豊か or 高い. Also well known is the 生物多様性条約 "Convention on Biological Diversity". It can also be shortened to 多様性 when the context is clear.

examples[].german: Organisms with an active metabolism tend to have shorter lifespans.
Exercise boosts your metabolism and also improves the condition of your skin.
By actively promoting young people, we aim to renew the organization.
en.notes: 新陳代謝 literally means "replacing the old with the new" and in everyday speech stands mainly for the body's metabolism: 新陳代謝がいい・活発だ・悪い, 新陳代謝を高める. In technical texts one usually says just 代謝 (基礎代謝 "basal metabolic rate"). As a four-character compound it also denotes the renewal of organizations, for example 組織の新陳代謝を図る "to bring fresh blood into the company".

examples[].german: The pattern of the bark helps in identifying the tree species.
Cinnamon is a spice made from the bark of a certain kind of tree.
Deer eat the bark in winter, and trees are dying as a result.
en.notes: 樹皮 is tree bark in a technical or written sense (botany, forestry, spices, medicinal remedies); in everyday speech one says 木の皮. Typical combinations are 樹皮を剥ぐ "to peel off the bark" and 樹皮から作られる. Do not confuse it with 樹液 "tree sap" or 樹冠 "tree crown", which contain the same character 樹.

examples[].german: By counting the annual rings, one can tell the age of a tree.
The rings of a long life are carved into my grandfather's face.
It was a profound performance, of a kind only a veteran actor with years behind him can give.
en.notes: 年輪 are the annual rings of a tree: 年輪を数える, 年輪が刻まれる. Figuratively it stands for life experience gathered over the years, especially in 年輪を重ねる "to mature with years and experience" or 年輪を感じさせる "to bear witness to long experience". This figurative use is appreciative and elevated in style.

en.meaning: head of a local government (mayor, governor); chief; emir
examples[].german: The head of the local government held a dialogue meeting with residents.
In the unified local elections, the heads of many municipalities changed.
The capital of the United Arab Emirates is Abu Dhabi.
en.notes: 首長 in Japan is above all the collective term for the elected heads of local governments: the 知事 of prefectures and the 市長, 町長 and 村長 of municipalities. In general, it means the "head" of an organization and also "emir", e.g. in アラブ首長国連邦 "United Arab Emirates". Because しゅちょう sounds exactly like 主張 "assertion", officials and journalists often say くびちょう. Formal administrative and media language.

examples[].german: Bamboo spreads and multiplies underground by rhizomes.
The edible part of ginger is not a root but a rhizome.
If the rhizomes remain, weeds keep growing back no matter how many times you pull them out.
en.notes: 根茎 is the botanical technical term for a rhizome, that is, a shoot growing underground that looks like a root. In more general usage one mostly says 地下茎 "underground stem". Well-known examples are ginger, bamboo and the lotus root レンコン, which botanically is not a true root. In herbal medicine, 根茎 often turns up among medicinal drugs.

examples[].german: Rhinoceros beetles have a habit of gathering at tree sap.
Maple syrup is made by boiling down the sap of maple trees.
Natural rubber is made from the sap of the rubber tree.
en.notes: 樹液 is the sap that oozes out of or flows within trees. Typical are 樹液が出る・にじむ, 樹液を吸う (of insects) and 樹液に集まる; in Japan it immediately brings to mind beetles gathering in summer at oozing oaks. Maple syrup and natural rubber are also obtained from 樹液. The juice of fruit, by contrast, is 果汁.

examples[].german: Chlorophyll is a pigment that absorbs light energy.
In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down and the leaves turn red and yellow.
Plant leaves look green because of chlorophyll.
en.notes: 葉緑素 is the green leaf pigment chlorophyll and the usual word in school lessons; in technical texts one also reads クロロフィル. Do not confuse it with 葉緑体 "chloroplast", the cell organelle in which 葉緑素 is located. Typical contexts are 光合成 "photosynthesis" and autumn coloring, in which 葉緑素 is broken down.

examples[].german: Fern plants reproduce by spores.
Mold spores float in the air.
Spores are released from the underside of a mushroom cap.
en.notes: 胞子 are the spores of ferns, mosses, fungi and mold. Typical combinations are 胞子で増える "to multiply by spores", 胞子を飛ばす and 胞子が放出される. In contrast, flowering plants reproduce by 種子 or 種 "seeds". In the household the word is met mainly with mold: カビの胞子.

examples[].german: Pollination takes place when pollen adheres to the pistil.
In science class, we observed the pistil and stamens of a flower.
In this variety the pistil has degenerated, so it bears no fruit.
en.notes: 雌蕊 is the pistil of a flower, the female organ on whose stigma 柱頭 the pollen lands. The character 蕊 is rare, so it is usually written めしべ or 雌しべ; in technical texts the Sino-Japanese reading しずい also occurs. The counterpart is 雄蕊 or おしべ "stamen"; both words are learned together in biology class.

examples[].german: Pollen released from the stamens is carried by the wind.
A morning glory flower has five stamens.
If pollen from a lily's stamens gets on your clothes, it hardly comes off.
en.notes: 雄蕊 is the stamen, the male organ of the flower, at whose tip pollen is produced in the anther 葯. Since 蕊 is rare, in everyday writing it is おしべ or 雄しべ; in technical language there is also the reading ゆうずい. The counterpart is 雌蕊 or めしべ "pistil".

examples[].german: The calyx has the role of protecting the petals.
The green cap of a strawberry is actually the calyx.
Even after the cherry blossoms have fallen, the calyxes remain on the branches.
en.notes: 萼 is the calyx, that is, the mostly green leaves that enclose the bud and sit beneath the petals. The character is rare, so it is often written in kana as がく. The individual sepal is more precisely called 萼片. A well-known everyday example is the green "cap" of the strawberry, called へた in daily speech. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 額 "frame, amount".

examples[].german: The color of petals exists to attract insects.
Cherry blossoms have five petals.
In field guides, plants are distinguished by the number and shape of their petals.
en.notes: 花弁 is the botanical or literary term for petal; in everyday speech one almost always says 花びら. Counting uses 枚: 花弁が五枚ある. In botany one distinguishes 合弁花 (fused petals) and 離弁花 (free petals). The reading はなびら for 花弁 also occurs in texts.

examples[].german: Seeds are contained within the fruit.
I made fruit liqueur using ume fruits.
The fruits of the reform need to reach the entire population.
en.notes: 果実 is fruit in the botanical or formal sense; when one means fruit as food, one says 果物, and the fruit on the plant is called 実 in everyday speech (実がなる). 果実 often appears in compounds such as 果実酒 "fruit liqueur" and on labels. In elevated language it also stands figuratively for "fruits, yield": 改革の果実 "the fruits of the reform".

examples[].german: The canopy of the tropical rainforest blocks sunlight.
This tree has a widely spreading crown and creates cool shade in summer.
The crowns of the street trees were pruned so that they would not touch the power lines.
en.notes: 樹冠 is the crown of a tree, that is, the entire area of branches and leaves; the word belongs to forestry, ecology and landscape care. For the closed canopy of a whole forest, one also says 林冠 in technical language. In everyday speech one speaks rather of 木のてっぺん or 枝葉. Typical combinations: 樹冠が広がる, 樹冠を剪定する.

examples[].german: The new governor called for reforms in his inaugural speech.
The prefectural governor election will be held next month.
The governor announced at a press conference that the budget for disaster preparedness would be increased.
en.notes: 知事 is the directly elected governor of a prefecture: Tokyo has a 都知事, Hokkaido a 道知事, Osaka and Kyoto each a 府知事, all the others a 県知事. With a name one says 〇〇知事. Typical combinations: 知事選 "gubernatorial election", 知事に就任する, 知事が〜を表明する. At the municipal level the counterpart is 市長 or 町長; the umbrella term for both is 首長.

examples[].german: The understory of the forest grows on little light.
Because there are too many deer, the understory of the forest has been almost entirely eaten away.
When the understory is lost, soil is easily washed away by rain.
en.notes: 下層植生 is a technical term from forestry and ecology for the plants that grow beneath the forest canopy: shrubs, grasses and young trees. It is composed of 下層 "lower layer" and 植生 "vegetation". In everyday speech one says 下草 instead. In Japan the word is often used in connection with wildlife damage and erosion: 下層植生が衰退する, 下層植生が失われる.

examples[].german: Leaf mold supplies plants with abundant nutrients.
Mixing leaf mold into potting soil improves drainage.
Fallen leaves pile up on the forest floor and become leaf mold over many years.
en.notes: 腐葉土 is leaf mold or leaf humus made from rotted leaves and is used mainly in gardening: 腐葉土を混ぜる, 腐葉土を敷く. In Japan you buy it by the bag at a home improvement store. More general is 堆肥 "compost", which can also consist of manure or kitchen waste; the soil-science term for humus is 腐植.

examples[].german: A network of fungal hyphae connects the trees with one another.
The real body of a mushroom is the hyphae spreading underground.
I could see the white hyphae of the mold growing on the bread.
en.notes: 菌糸 is the individual fungal hypha, a fine thread of which fungi and mold consist; the whole mesh is more precisely called 菌糸体 "mycelium". The visible mushroom is only the fruiting body 子実体, the actual organism is the underground 菌糸. Typical combinations are 菌糸が伸びる and 菌糸が広がる.

examples[].german: Butterfly larvae grow by eating leaves.
Rhinoceros beetle larvae spend nearly a year in the soil.
On a summer night, a cicada nymph climbed a tree and began to molt into an adult.
en.notes: 幼虫 is the larva of insects, that is, the stage after hatching from the egg; the counterpart is 成虫 "adult insect", and in many species 蛹 "pupa" lies in between. In everyday speech certain larvae are also called イモムシ "caterpillar", 毛虫 "hairy caterpillar" or ウジ "maggot". For frogs or fish, one speaks technically rather of 幼生 or 稚魚.

examples[].german: Inside the pupa, the larva metamorphoses into an adult.
The larva pupated on the underside of a leaf.
A butterfly that has just emerged from the pupa dries its wings for a while.
en.notes: 蛹 is the pupa of an insect, the resting stage between 幼虫 and 成虫. Since the character is rare, it is mostly written さなぎ or サナギ. Typical combinations are 蛹になる "to pupate" and 蛹から羽化する "to emerge from the pupa". Figuratively, さなぎから蝶へ stands for the transformation of a person, for example from an unremarkable girl to a self-confident woman.

examples[].german: Frogs undergo metamorphosis from larva to adult.
Butterflies undergo complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Being called a 「変態！」 ("pervert!") made him turn bright red.
en.notes: 変態 denotes metamorphosis in biology, for example from tadpole to frog; as an intransitive する-verb: 変態する. One distinguishes 完全変態 (with a pupal stage, e.g. butterfly) and 不完全変態 (without a pupa, e.g. grasshopper). Note: in everyday speech 変態 mostly means "pervert, perverted" (short for 変態性欲), so one should use it carefully outside biological contexts. For "transformation" in the general sense, one prefers 変身 or 変化.

examples[].german: Snakes shed their skin regularly as they grow.
Crabs grow by molting repeatedly.
The company transformed itself from a small town factory into a world-class enterprise.
en.notes: 脱皮 is the molting of snakes, insects or crustaceans; as an intransitive する-verb: ヘビが脱皮する. The shed skin is called 抜け殻. Figuratively, 脱皮 means "to break away from the old, to reach a new stage", often in 〜から脱皮する or 〜への脱皮を遂げる, for example when a company or an artist renews itself fundamentally. This figurative use is common in newspapers and speeches.

examples[].german: Insects detect smells with their antennae.
Ants exchange information with their companions by touching antennae.
There are eyes at the tips of a snail's long tentacles.
en.notes: 触角 are the antennae of insects, crustaceans or snails, with which they feel and smell: 触角を動かす, 触角で感じる. Do not confuse it with 触手 "tentacle" (jellyfish, octopuses) or with アンテナ, the technical term for an antenna, which is also used figuratively (アンテナを張る "to keep one's antennae out"). 触角 itself is hardly used figuratively.

examples[].german: Crustaceans are an important component of marine ecosystems.
Because of a crustacean allergy, I cannot eat shrimp or crab.
This soup contains crustaceans.
en.notes: 甲殻類 is the animal group of crustaceans, that is, shrimp, crabs, lobsters and woodlice; literally "shell-armor class". In everyday life the word is met mainly on menus and food labels, especially in 甲殻類アレルギー "crustacean allergy". Clams and squid do not belong to it; they are 軟体動物.

examples[].german: Shellfish and squid are classified as mollusks.
Octopuses are said to be particularly intelligent among mollusks.
Mollusks have no bones, but many protect their bodies with a shell.
en.notes: 軟体動物 is the zoological term for mollusks such as clams, snails, squid and octopuses; literally "soft-bodied animals". In everyday speech the individual animals are simply called 貝, イカ or タコ; the collective term appears mainly in school textbooks, aquariums and nonfiction books. Contrasts are 節足動物 "arthropods" and 脊椎動物 "vertebrates".

examples[].german: The bill was put to a vote in the plenary session.
The bill was passed in committee and will be sent to tomorrow's plenary session.
The prime minister answered questions from the opposition in the plenary session of the House of Councillors.
en.notes: 本会議 is the full assembly of a parliament (衆議院, 参議院 or a local assembly), as opposed to the committees (委員会). The usual procedure: a bill is deliberated in 委員会 and then voted on in 本会議. Typical: 本会議で可決する/採決する, 本会議に上程する, 衆院本会議. A technical word of parliamentary reporting.

examples[].german: Fish, amphibians and reptiles are all vertebrates.
Most animals on Earth are invertebrates; vertebrates are only a tiny fraction.
In biology class, we learned about vertebrates divided into five groups.
en.notes: 脊椎動物 are vertebrates, that is, animals with a backbone; 脊椎 is the technical word for the spinal column, while everyday speech says 背骨. The counterpart is 無脊椎動物 "invertebrates". In school lessons, 脊椎動物 are divided into five classes: 魚類, 両生類, 爬虫類, 鳥類 and 哺乳類.

examples[].german: Whales are mammals that live in the sea.
The platypus is a rare mammal that lays eggs.
Bats are the only mammals that can fly.
en.notes: 哺乳類 is the class of mammals, literally "the class that nourishes with milk" (哺乳 "to nurse"). An individual mammal is also called 哺乳動物. In textbooks and newspapers the spelling ほ乳類 is often seen, because 哺 was long not among the standard characters. Typical are statements like 〜は哺乳類である or 〜は哺乳類の仲間だ.

examples[].german: Reptiles are cold-blooded animals whose body temperature depends on the external environment.
More and more people keep reptiles as pets.
Dinosaurs have long been considered relatives of reptiles.
en.notes: 爬虫類 is the class of reptiles, that is, snakes, lizards, turtles and crocodiles; 爬 means "to crawl". In textbooks one often reads は虫類, because 爬 is not a standard character. In everyday life the word is met, for example, with pets (爬虫類を飼う) or in zoos. Do not confuse it with 両生類 "amphibians", which include frogs and newts.

examples[].german: Amphibians can live both in water and on land.
The skin of amphibians is thin and sensitive to dryness.
Because of environmental pollution, amphibians are declining all over the world.
en.notes: 両生類 are amphibians such as frogs, toads, newts and salamanders; literally "animals that live on both sides", that is, in water and on land. The larvae mostly live in water, the adult animals often on land. The older spelling is 両棲類. Do not confuse it with 爬虫類 "reptiles"; amphibians have moist, scaleless skin.

examples[].german: Insects and spiders belong to the arthropods.
Shrimp and crabs are also arthropods, like insects.
Arthropods make up the majority of animal species.
en.notes: 節足動物 are arthropods, literally "animals with jointed legs" (節 "joint, segment", 足 "leg"). They include insects, spiders, centipedes and crustaceans (甲殻類). The word is zoological and technical and appears mainly in school textbooks and nonfiction; typical frames are 〜は節足動物に属する and 節足動物の仲間.

examples[].german: Sea urchins and starfish are typical examples of echinoderms.
The body of most echinoderms spreads out in five directions like a star.
The sea cucumber, too, though it looks different, is a kind of echinoderm.
en.notes: 棘皮動物 are echinoderms such as sea urchins, starfish, sea cucumbers and sea lilies; 棘 means "thorn, spine", 皮 "skin". The word is purely zoological and appears almost only in textbooks, aquariums and nonfiction. In everyday speech the animals are simply called ウニ, ヒトデ or ナマコ.

examples[].german: Ecological findings are indispensable for environmental conservation.
I am majoring in ecology at university.
Ecologists have been investigating the decline of fish in this lake for years.
en.notes: 生態学 is ecology as a science, that is, the study of the relationships between living things and their environment; the researcher is called 生態学者. The loanword エコロジー can mean the same, but often stands for environmental awareness in general (エコ). 生態学, by contrast, denotes only the discipline: 生態学を専攻する, 生態学的な視点.

examples[].german: The invasion of non-native species threatens the survival of native species.
The American crayfish is a non-native species brought to Japan.
Releasing pets you can no longer keep into a river causes non-native species to spread.
en.notes: 外来種 is a non-native species introduced by humans, the opposite of 在来種 "native species". Not every 外来種 is harmful; for the problematic ones one speaks more precisely of 侵略的外来種 "invasive species", and in Japan there are legally designated 特定外来生物. 外来生物 is also often used as an umbrella term. Typical are 外来種が増える・広がる and 外来種を駆除する.

examples[].german: Measures to protect native species are urgently needed.
Native species in the lake have declined because of the introduced black bass.
In this region, traditional native varieties of soybeans are still cultivated today.
en.notes: 在来種 is a native species, one originally occurring in an area, the opposite of 外来種. In agriculture it also denotes old, regional varieties or breeds (在来種の大豆, 在来種の馬), in contrast to modern cultivars. Distinguish 固有種: a 在来種 may also occur elsewhere, whereas a 固有種 lives only in this area.

examples[].german: The opposition submitted a motion to end deliberations.
At the shareholders' meeting, a shareholder moved to replace the chair.
The amendment motion was rejected, with few in favor.
en.notes: 動議 is a formal motion made during a meeting (parliament, shareholders' meeting, club meeting), on which deliberation or a vote then takes place. Typical: 動議を提出する/出す, 動議が可決/否決される, 緊急動議 "emergency motion", 修正動議 "motion to amend". Unlike the general 提案 "proposal" or 議案 "agenda item", 動議 is a procedural or substantive motion made from within the ongoing meeting.

examples[].german: Many endemic species live on the Galápagos Islands.
The Amami rabbit is an endemic species that lives only on Amami-Ōshima and Tokunoshima.
Because islands are cut off from the outside, many endemic species are found there.
en.notes: 固有種 is an endemic species that occurs only in a particular area, for example on an island: 日本の固有種, 〜にしかいない固有種. Isolated islands such as the Galápagos, Okinawa or the Ogasawara Islands are known for many 固有種. Distinguish 在来種, which means only "native" and may also occur elsewhere.

examples[].german: Natural selection is the main mechanism of evolution.
Darwin held that living things evolve through natural selection.
Overuse of antibiotics promotes the natural selection of resistant bacteria.
en.notes: 自然選択 is natural selection in Darwin's sense, the technical term in biology and textbooks. Synonymous and more common in everyday speech is 自然淘汰, which is also used figuratively for companies or products that disappear from the market. The counterpart is 人為選択 "artificial selection" through breeding. Typical: 自然選択によって進化する, 自然選択が働く.

examples[].german: A food web shows more complex relationships than a food chain.
If one species goes extinct, the whole food web is affected.
In the marine food web, plankton forms an important foundation.
en.notes: 食物網 is the food web, that is, the network of all feeding relationships in an ecosystem; 網 means "net". It is usually explained in contrast to the better-known 食物連鎖 "food chain", which shows only a linear sequence. The word is technical and appears in biology textbooks and environmental texts.

examples[].german: Decomposers break organic matter down into inorganic matter.
Fallen leaves return to the soil thanks to decomposers such as fungi and bacteria.
Earthworms play an important role as decomposers in the soil.
en.notes: 分解者 is, in ecology, the decomposer, that is, organisms such as fungi, bacteria or earthworms that break down dead organic material. Together with 生産者 "producer" and 消費者 "consumer" it forms the basic concepts of the ecosystem in school lessons. Outside biology, 分解者 is hardly used; the related verb is 分解する "to decompose, to break down".

examples[].german: Plants are the main producers in an ecosystem.
At the supermarket, I bought vegetables with the producer's name and photo attached.
In the sea, phytoplankton is the main producer.
en.notes: 生産者 means in everyday speech "producer, maker", especially farmers and fishers: 生産者の顔が見える野菜 "vegetables whose producer you know". In ecology it denotes the producers, that is, plants and algae that make organic substances through photosynthesis; 消費者 and 分解者 belong with it. For industrial manufacturers one usually says メーカー or 製造業者.

examples[].german: Herbivores are classified as primary consumers.
Carnivores that eat herbivores are secondary consumers.
With price increases continuing, consumers are keeping a tight grip on their wallets.
en.notes: 消費者 in everyday speech is above all the "consumer": 消費者物価 "consumer prices", 消費者庁 "Consumer Affairs Agency", 消費者の声. In ecology it denotes animals that feed on other living things; herbivores are 一次消費者, carnivores 二次消費者, and so on. The counterpart is 生産者, to which 分解者 is added.

examples[].german: Legumes carry out nitrogen fixation with the help of root nodule bacteria.
Plants cannot use the nitrogen in the air as it is, so nitrogen fixation is necessary.
Milk vetch is planted in rice paddies to enrich the soil through nitrogen fixation.
en.notes: 窒素固定 is nitrogen fixation, that is, the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into a form usable by plants. Typical frames: 〜による窒素固定 or 窒素固定を行う. It is well known in legumes (マメ科) and their root nodule bacteria 根粒菌, which is why clover or vetch is planted to improve the soil. The word is technical (biology, agriculture, chemistry).

examples[].german: Photoperiodism controls the flowering time of plants.
With electric-light chrysanthemums, photoperiodism is exploited: they are lit at night to delay flowering.
It is thought that photoperiodism is also involved in the timing of bird migration.
en.notes: 光周性 is photoperiodism, that is, the response of plants and animals to day length (光 "light", 周 "period"). In botany one distinguishes 短日植物 "short-day plants" such as chrysanthemums and 長日植物 "long-day plants". The word is purely technical; typical are 光周性を示す and 光周性を利用する, for example in horticulture.

examples[].german: Plants transpire water through the stomata of their leaves.
On hot summer days, the amount of transpiration from the leaves increases.
If you cover a potted plant with a plastic bag, the transpired water collects on the inside of the bag.
en.notes: 蒸散 is a technical term of botany for the release of water vapor through the plant surface, above all through the 気孔. As an intransitive する-verb, the water takes が: 水分が蒸散する; with the plant as the agent, the causative form 水分を蒸散させる is used. It differs from the general 蒸発 "evaporation" (puddles, laundry) in that it is used practically only for plants. Typical compounds: 蒸散作用, 蒸散量.

examples[].german: The opening and closing of stomata regulates gas exchange.
When it is dry, plants close their stomata to prevent water loss.
Looking at the underside of a leaf under a microscope, you can observe many stomata.
en.notes: 気孔 denotes in botany the stomata of leaves, through which gas exchange and 蒸散 take place; one says 気孔が開く／閉じる and 気孔の開閉. In materials engineering it also stands for gas pores in metal or ceramics. Do not confuse it with the homophone 気候 "climate" - in conversation the context usually settles it. The skin pores of humans, by contrast, are 毛穴.

examples[].german: The bill was passed with a supplementary resolution attached.
The committee adopted a supplementary resolution calling for consideration of privacy.
A supplementary resolution is not legally binding.
en.notes: 附帯決議 is a resolution that a parliamentary committee passes together with the adoption of a law, to record concerns, interpretive guidance or demands to the government. It is not legally binding, but carries political weight. Typical: 附帯決議を付す/付ける, 附帯決議を採択する. The spelling 付帯決議 is just as common; 附帯 is the traditional official form.

examples[].german: Vascular bundles transport water and nutrients within the plant body.
Mosses have no vascular bundles.
If you stain a cross-section of a stem, you can see that the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring.
en.notes: 維管束 is the vascular bundle of vascular plants; it consists of the water-conducting 道管（導管） and the nutrient-conducting 師管. The word occurs almost only in biology class and technical texts, for example in 維管束植物 "vascular plants" as opposed to mosses, which have no vascular bundles. By the arrangement of the vascular bundles in the stem, one distinguishes 単子葉類 (scattered) and 双子葉類 (in a ring).

examples[].german: Sieve tubes transport the products of photosynthesis throughout the plant.
Vessels carry water, and sieve tubes carry nutrients.
Aphids insert their mouthparts into the sieve tubes and suck the sap.
en.notes: 師管 is the sieve tube, that is, the conducting tissue that transports the sugars formed in photosynthesis (養分) from the leaves to roots, fruits and other plant parts. The counterpart is the 道管（導管）, which conducts water from bottom to top; together the two form the 維管束. The whole phloem is strictly called 師部, but in school contexts it is often equated with 師管. Older texts write 篩管 (篩 = "sieve").

examples[].german: Vessels carry water absorbed from the roots upward.
City gas is delivered to each household through underground pipes.
Saliva is secreted into the mouth through ducts.
en.notes: 導管 generally means "conduit, pipe" for liquids or gases (ガス導管) and, in anatomy, the excretory duct of a gland. In botany it is the water-conducting vessel in the wood, which transports water and minerals from the roots upward. Today's Japanese school textbooks mostly write 道管 for this (same reading); 導管 is found in older and more general texts. The counterpart is the 師管, which conducts nutrients.

examples[].german: Herbivores feed mainly on plants.
Giraffes are herbivores and eat the leaves of tall trees.
It is said that there are now more young men who are rather reserved when it comes to romance.
en.notes: 草食 means "to feed on plants" and usually stands as a modifier before a noun: 草食動物 "herbivore", 草食恐竜, or with 性: 草食性の魚. As a する-verb (草食する) it is rare. Colloquially, 草食系（男子） became popular for reserved men who show little initiative in romance; the opposite is 肉食系. The biological counterparts are 肉食 and 雑食.

examples[].german: Carnivores have sharp fangs and claws.
It was only in the Meiji era that meat eating spread in Japan, too.
Most sharks are carnivores and attack fish and seals.
en.notes: 肉食 has two uses: for humans, "eating meat, a meat diet" (肉食を控える, 肉食文化); for animals, "carnivorous", mostly as a modifier: 肉食動物, 肉食獣, 肉食性. Opposites are 草食 and, for human diet, 菜食 "vegetarian diet". Colloquially, 肉食系 refers to people who are active and bold in romance. The reading にくじき occurs only in the Buddhist expression 肉食妻帯.

examples[].german: Bears are omnivorous and eat both fruit and fish.
Humans are omnivores and can digest both meat and vegetables.
My taste in music is omnivorous; I listen to everything from enka to jazz.
en.notes: 雑食 means "to feed on both plants and animals, to eat everything"; typical are 雑食性, 雑食動物 and 〜は雑食だ. Opposites are 草食 and 肉食. It is also said loosely of people with broad tastes, for example in reading or music: 読書は雑食です "I read widely". Distinguish 悪食, eating unusual or disgusting things.

examples[].german: Male lions have a vast territory.
Cats chase away cats that enter their territory.
There is a strong sense of turf between departments, so cooperation makes little progress.
en.notes: 縄張り originally means marking off an area with a rope; today it mainly means the "territory" of an animal: 縄張りを持つ, 縄張りを守る, 縄張り争い. Figuratively it denotes the sphere of responsibility or influence of people, often pejoratively for turf-mindedness in government offices and companies, or a gang's area: 縄張り意識が強い. It is also written 縄張 or, in games and magazines, ナワバリ.

examples[].german: Salmon travel around the sea and then return to the river where they were born to spawn.
Tuna are fish that migrate across the wide ocean.
This garden is a strolling garden that you enjoy by walking around the pond.
en.notes: 回遊 denotes above all the regular migrations of fish and marine animals for spawning or foraging: 海を回遊する, 回遊魚 (e.g. tuna, bonito). For salmon swimming up the river, one says 遡上, and for migratory birds 渡り. The original meaning "tour, round trip" lives on in 回遊式庭園 (strolling garden with a circuit path) and in urban planning (回遊性 "inviting to stroll around").

examples[].german: Sea turtles come ashore on the sandy beach to lay eggs.
At this river, you can see salmon spawning in autumn.
Let's avoid fishing for fish in their spawning season.
en.notes: 産卵 is the technical word for "laying eggs" or "spawning" in fish, birds, insects and reptiles: 産卵する, 産卵期, 産卵場所. In everyday speech, for example with chickens, one rather says 卵を産む; 産卵 sounds factual and is used in nature documentaries and the news. For mammals, one says 出産 "giving birth" instead.

examples[].german: It takes about three weeks for the eggs to hatch.
Salmon fry are raised by artificial hatching and released into the river in spring.
The newly hatched chicks are begging their parent birds for food.
en.notes: 孵化 means "to hatch" (intransitive: 卵が孵化する, ヒナが孵化する) or "to incubate, to hatch out" (especially artificially: 卵を孵化させる, 人工孵化). Since 孵 is not a jōyō kanji, newspapers and textbooks mostly write ふ化. In everyday speech one often says more simply 卵がかえる. Distinguish 羽化, the emergence of an insect from the pupa.

examples[].german: The opposition tried to delay the vote with ox-walk tactics.
The opposition lawmakers adopted ox-walk tactics and took hours to cast their votes.
In the recent Diet, ox-walk tactics are hardly seen anymore.
en.notes: 牛歩戦術 literally means "ox-walk tactics": in roll-call votes in the Japanese parliament, opposition lawmakers walk extremely slowly to the ballot box in order to drag out the vote. Typical: 牛歩戦術をとる, 牛歩戦術で抵抗する. Comparable is the filibuster (フィリバスター), which, however, works with long speeches. 牛歩 alone means "very slow progress". A political technical term, in news and commentary.

examples[].german: Ladybugs are natural enemies of aphids.
Because there are no natural enemies on this island, the introduced rats have multiplied rapidly.
With my stubbornly wavy hair, humidity is my arch-enemy.
en.notes: 天敵 is the "natural enemy" of a species, one that eats or parasitizes it: AはBの天敵だ, 天敵がいない. In agriculture, one speaks of 天敵を利用した害虫駆除 (biological pest control). Colloquially and jokingly, it also denotes a person or thing one simply cannot get along with: 彼は私の天敵だ "He is my arch-enemy". The general word for "enemy" is 敵.

examples[].german: Prey animals have defense mechanisms to escape from predators.
The numbers of predators and prey rise and fall, influencing each other.
Zebras reduce their danger as prey animals by living in herds.
en.notes: 被食者 is the ecological technical term for the animal that is eaten (被 = "to suffer", 食 = "to eat") and forms a pair with 捕食者 "predator"; the relationship is called 捕食・被食の関係 or 食う・食われるの関係. The word occurs almost only in biology textbooks and technical texts. In everyday speech one says 獲物 "prey" (from the hunter's viewpoint) or paraphrases with 食べられる側.

examples[].german: The presence of predators maintains the balance of the ecosystem.
Since wolves went extinct, deer no longer have any predators.
Orcas are known as apex predators of the sea.
en.notes: 捕食者 is the "predator" in ecology, that is, an animal that catches and eats other animals; the related verb is 捕食する. The counterpart is 被食者. The word is technical; in everyday speech one rather says 肉食動物 or names the animal specifically. A set combination is 頂点捕食者 "apex predator" for animals at the top of the food chain.

examples[].german: Deposition at the river mouth forms a delta.
Strata deposited over a long period are clearly visible on the cliff.
Sediment is accumulating at the bottom of the dam, and the water storage capacity is decreasing.
en.notes: 堆積 means that something piles up or is deposited; in geology it is "sedimentation": 土砂が堆積する, 堆積物, 堆積岩, 堆積作用. It is mostly intransitive with が; the counterpart in the geological cycle is 浸食 "erosion". For snow, dust or garbage it sounds literary (ごみが堆積する); in everyday speech one says 積もる or たまる. Do not confuse it with the homophone 体積 "volume".

examples[].german: Erosion of the coast by waves is progressing.
River water eroded the rock over a long time, creating a deep valley.
To prevent erosion of the sandy beach, wave-dissipating blocks were placed offshore.
en.notes: 浸食 is "erosion" or "wearing away" by water, waves or wind: 波が海岸を浸食する, 浸食が進む, 浸食作用. It is used as a noun and as a transitive する-verb; the affected rock takes the passive: 岩が浸食される. Equally common is the spelling 侵食, which also stands for the figurative "encroachment, spreading" (市場を侵食する "to eat into market share"). The counterpart in the geological cycle is 堆積.

examples[].german: Rocks weather over a long period of time.
A memorial service is held every year so that the memory of the earthquake disaster does not fade.
The old stone statue is so weathered that the expression on its face can hardly be made out.
en.notes: 風化 is first of all the "weathering" of rock by wind, rain and temperature changes: 岩石が風化する, 風化が進む. Very common in news and speeches is the figurative meaning: memories or lessons from disasters and wars "fade" with time, e.g. 震災の記憶を風化させてはならない. The verb is intransitive; "to let something fall into oblivion" is 風化させる. In chemistry it also denotes the efflorescence of crystals.

examples[].german: Soil quality greatly affects the growth of crops.
Soil contamination was found at the former factory site.
Workplaces with strict hierarchy easily become breeding grounds for power harassment.
en.notes: 土壌 is the technical term for "soil, earth" as a material and habitat, for example in agriculture and environmental protection: 土壌汚染, 土壌改良, 肥沃な土壌. In everyday speech one simply says 土 "earth"; 地面, by contrast, is the ground surface one stands on. Figuratively, 土壌 means "breeding ground" for a development: 不正を生む土壌, 才能が育つ土壌.

examples[].german: The Earth's crust is the outermost layer of the planet.
In this region, the mountains are gradually being uplifted by crustal movement.
As a result of the election, a seismic shift occurred in the political world.
en.notes: 地殻 is the "Earth's crust", the outermost solid layer of the Earth above the マントル. Typical compounds are 地殻変動 "crustal movement, tectonic change" as well as 大陸地殻 and 海洋地殻. The word is technical (geology, earthquake reports). Figuratively, 地殻変動 is also used for fundamental upheavals in politics or the economy. Beware of the homophones 知覚 "perception" and 近く "vicinity".

examples[].german: Convection in the mantle causes the movement of the plates.
The Earth's interior is divided into three layers: crust, mantle and core.
Magma is formed when part of the mantle melts.
en.notes: マントル is, in geology, the "Earth's mantle" between the 地殻 and the 核 "core"; typical compounds are マントル対流 "mantle convection" and 上部マントル／下部マントル. This loanword from English is written only in katakana. It does not refer to a "mantle" as a garment; for that one says コート, and for a cloak マント. Rarely it also stands for the mantle of a gas lamp (ガスマントル).

examples[].german: The rocks of this region contain a variety of minerals.
Rock crystal is a crystal of the mineral quartz.
The country is rich in mineral resources, which make up most of its exports.
en.notes: 鉱物 is a "mineral" in the geological sense, that is, a naturally occurring crystalline substance such as quartz or feldspar: 鉱物を含む, 鉱物資源, 鉱物標本. To be distinguished from ミネラル, which in Japanese stands almost only for mineral nutrients in food and water (ミネラルウォーター). 鉱石, by contrast, is "ore", that is, rock from which metal is extracted, and 岩石 is rock, which consists of minerals.

examples[].german: The ruling party pushed the bill through with a forced vote.
The ruling party forced a vote on the bill in committee.
In protest against the forced vote, opposition lawmakers crowded around the committee chairman's seat.
en.notes: 強行採決 is a vote that the majority pushes through despite protest and without sufficient deliberation - a critical term used mainly by the opposition and the media; the government side mostly avoids it. Typical: 〜を強行採決する, 強行採決に踏み切る, 法案を強行採決で可決する. Neutral is 採決 "vote"; 強行 means "to push through by force".

examples[].german: Compost can be made from household food waste.
If you collect fallen leaves and turn them into compost, you get good soil.
Before spring planting, I dug compost into the field.
en.notes: 堆肥 is "compost" made from rotted plant remains, kitchen waste or manure: 堆肥を作る, 堆肥にする, 堆肥を畑にすき込む. It is one of the organic fertilizers; the general term for fertilizer is 肥料, and artificial fertilizer is called 化学肥料. In everyday speech one also hears the loanword コンポスト, which can also refer to the composter itself.

examples[].german: Weeds grew rampant and the garden became overgrown.
In the tropical rainforest, a great variety of plants grow luxuriantly.
When the water temperature rises, algae proliferate in the lake and the water quality deteriorates.
en.notes: 繁茂 describes lush, dense plant growth: 草木が繁茂する, 藻が繁茂する, 雑草の繁茂. It is an intransitive する-verb and sounds literary; in conversation one tends to say 生い茂る or 草がぼうぼうに生える. It often has a negative connotation (weeds, algae), but can also neutrally describe dense vegetation. For the multiplication of animals, on the other hand, one says 繁殖, and for thriving businesses 繁盛.

examples[].german: This flower grows wild in the mountainous regions of Japan.
This area is known as a natural habitat of the Asian skunk cabbage.
I harvested the myoga ginger that had grown on its own in the garden.
en.notes: 自生 means that a plant grows in a place by itself, that is, wild and without cultivation by humans: 〜に自生する, 自生地, 自生種. It mostly appears in the form 自生している or attributively as 自生の植物. The opposite is 栽培 "cultivation". It differs from 野生 in that 自生 is used only for plants, whereas 野生 is also used for animals (野生動物).

examples[].german: The hill where lavender grows in masses has become a tourist attraction.
This mountain slope is famous as a growing site of dogtooth violets.
In the breeding season, black-tailed gulls gather in colonies on these rocks.
en.notes: 群生 means that plants of one species grow close together in large numbers: 〜が群生する, 〜の群生地. It is also used for animals that live in herds or colonies; in that case the spelling 群棲 is also common. In contrast to 繁茂 "to grow luxuriantly", 群生 emphasizes the gathering of many specimens in one place, not the vigor of growth. 群生地 often appears on information signs in nature reserves.

examples[].german: The branching of the phylogenetic tree shows the differentiation of species.
The road forks in two just ahead.
The branches of the plum tree branch out finely and bear many flowers.
en.notes: 枝分かれ literally means "to split into branches" and is used for trees, rivers, roads, family trees or veins: 道が枝分かれする, 川が二つに枝分かれする. It is an intransitive する-verb; more formal and technical is 分岐（する）, and the fork point is called 分岐点. Figuratively, 枝分かれ also describes how languages, species or fields of study develop from a common origin.

examples[].german: Strong typhoon winds caused fruit to fall one after another in the orchards.
If the summer drought continues, more apples drop prematurely.
Fallen mandarin oranges are shipped as raw material for juice.
en.notes: 落果 is a technical term from fruit growing and agriculture for the premature falling of fruit from the tree (due to storms, drought or natural thinning), and also for the fallen fruit itself: 落果する, 落果が相次ぐ, 落果防止. It is very common in damage reports after typhoons. In everyday speech one says 実が落ちる. Do not confuse it with the homophones 落下 "falling down" and 落花 "falling blossoms".

examples[].german: Epiphytes grow on other trees.
Many orchids are epiphytes that anchor their roots on tree trunks.
Unlike parasitic plants, epiphytes do not take nutrients from their host.
en.notes: 着生植物 are "epiphytes", that is, plants that grow on other plants (mostly tree trunks and branches) or on rocks without taking nutrients from them; many orchids, ferns and bromeliads belong here. 着生 means "to attach oneself and grow" (〜に着生する). The difference from 寄生植物 "parasitic plant", which takes nutrients from its host, is important. The word is technical, but also appears in connection with houseplants and horticulture.

examples[].german: Succulents store water in their leaves.
Succulents need little watering, so they are easy to grow even for busy people.
Succulents often suffer root rot from too much watering.
en.notes: 多肉植物 are "succulents", that is, plants with thick, fleshy leaves, stems or roots in which they store water (多肉 = "much flesh"). Cacti (サボテン) belong to them botanically, but in Japanese they are often named separately: サボテンと多肉植物. The word is well known in everyday life because succulents are popular houseplants; among enthusiasts one says simply 多肉.

examples[].german: Carnivorous plants catch insects to obtain nutrients.
The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant that catches insects by snapping its leaves shut at lightning speed.
Many carnivorous plants grow in nutrient-poor wetlands.
en.notes: 食虫植物 are "carnivorous plants" (literally "insect-eating plants") that catch and digest insects and other small animals to obtain nitrogen, e.g. ハエトリグサ (Venus flytrap), ウツボカズラ (pitcher plant) or モウセンゴケ (sundew). Typical verbs are 虫を捕らえる／捕まえる and 消化する. The word is common both in textbooks and in everyday life (garden centers, children's nonfiction books).

examples[].german: This cedar is estimated to be over three thousand years old.
Counting the annual rings showed that this tree is about 120 years old.
A camphor tree several hundred years old stands on the shrine grounds.
en.notes: 樹齢 is the "age of a tree" and usually comes directly before a statement of age: 樹齢千年の杉, 樹齢は約三百年, 樹齢百年を超える. It is determined by the 年輪 "annual rings" (年輪を数える). For people and animals one uses 年齢, for buildings 築年数. Particularly old trees at shrines are often described with their 樹齢 on a sign.

examples[].german: The struggle for hegemony among the great powers is intensifying.
Britain once held supremacy over the seas.
Companies are battling fiercely for supremacy in the smartphone market.
en.notes: 覇権 is the supremacy of a state or actor over others. Typical combinations: 覇権を握る ("to hold supremacy"), 覇権を争う, 覇権争い, 覇権国家, 覇権主義 ("hegemonism"). Besides world politics, it is often used for markets and sports, e.g. 市場の覇権 or 覇権奪回 ("winning back the title"). The same kanji 覇 is in 制覇 ("victory, conquest of a title").

examples[].german: A regent carried out the affairs of state in place of the young emperor.
Prince Shotoku is said to have governed as regent for Empress Suiko.
In the Heian period, the Fujiwara clan monopolized the positions of regent and chief advisor.
en.notes: 摂政 is a regent who rules for a minor or incapacitated ruler, and also the regency itself. In Japanese history, 摂政 was the office for a child on the throne, 関白 that for an adult emperor; the Fujiwara family thus dominated the Heian period (摂関政治). Even today the Imperial Household Law provides for a 摂政; most recently Crown Prince Hirohito was regent in 1921-1926. Do not confuse it with the identically read 殺生 ("killing of living beings").

en.meaning: political party subsidies; public funding for parties
examples[].german: Monitoring of how public party funding is used is being demanded.
The Communist Party refuses to accept public party funding.
Public party funding is calculated at 250 yen per citizen.
en.notes: 政党助成金 is the state subsidy to political parties under the 政党助成法 of 1995, financed from tax money (calculated as 250 yen per inhabitant). The official legal term is 政党交付金; 政党助成金 is the designation common in the media and in debates. Typical: 政党助成金を受け取る, 政党助成金の使い道. The Communist Party fundamentally refuses to accept it.

examples[].german: One must beware of branches falling in strong winds.
Because branches might fall from the old cherry trees in the park, the area around them was closed off.
A thick layer of fallen leaves and branches lies on the forest floor.
en.notes: 落枝 is a rare technical term from forestry, ecology and tree care for branches that break off or fall from a tree, or for the fallen branches themselves. It is found in warning notices from parks and road authorities (落枝に注意) and in ecological texts together with 落葉 as part of the forest litter. In everyday speech one says 枝が落ちる, 落ちた枝 or 枯れ枝. 落石 "rockfall" is formed analogously.

examples[].german: A fallen tree was blocking the hiking trail.
Because of the typhoon, a fallen tree landed on a power line and caused a power outage.
Young trees are growing from a moss-covered fallen log.
en.notes: 倒木 is a tree that has fallen over, for example after a storm, under snow load or from old age: 倒木が道を塞ぐ, 倒木の撤去, 倒木の被害. It is a noun; the falling over itself is described with 木が倒れる. It is very common in typhoon news and in notices for hikers. In ecology, 倒木更新 is used when young trees germinate on a decaying trunk.

examples[].german: A wide variety of fungi live on the forest floor.
When trees are thinned out, light reaches the forest floor and flowers can grow.
In early spring, many flowers bloom on the forest floor before the leaves come out on the trees.
en.notes: 林床 is a technical term of forestry and vegetation science for the "forest floor" as a habitat, that is, the ground layer beneath the tree crowns with leaf litter, mosses, herbs and fungi: 林床植物, 林床に光が差し込む. It occurs mainly in ecological texts and nature guides. In everyday speech one says 森の地面 or 林の中の地面. The low vegetation on the forest floor is called 下草.

examples[].german: Coral reefs are important habitats for marine life.
Because of rising sea temperatures, coral bleaching is progressing on Okinawa's reefs.
I enjoyed snorkeling in the sea over the coral reef.
en.notes: 珊瑚礁 is a "coral reef"; 礁 means "reef, underwater rock". Since 珊瑚 is not a jōyō kanji, newspapers and school textbooks usually write サンゴ礁. Typical expressions are 珊瑚礁が広がる, 珊瑚礁の白化 "coral bleaching" and 珊瑚礁を保護する. The individual coral or the material is called 珊瑚／サンゴ.

examples[].german: The tides are caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and the sun.
Research on power generation using tides is progressing.
Before going fishing, I checked the tide table for the time of high tide.
en.notes: 潮汐 is the scientific term for the tides, that is, ebb and flow as a whole. It appears mainly in technical texts and compounds: 潮汐力, 潮汐発電, 潮汐表. In everyday speech one says 潮の満ち引き, 干満 or simply 潮; high tide is called 満潮, low tide 干潮.

examples[].german: At high tide, the sandy beach is covered by seawater.
When the tide comes in, the road to this island sinks into the sea.
Today's high tide is around three in the afternoon.
en.notes: 満潮 is the "high tide" or high-water level of the sea; its counterpart is 干潮 "low tide". Typical expressions are 満潮時, 満潮になる, 満潮を迎える; tide tables call it 満潮時刻. A synonym is 満ち潮, which emphasizes more the rising of the water. Do not confuse it with 高潮 "storm surge", a dangerous rise in sea level caused by typhoons.

examples[].german: Many people enjoy shellfish gathering at low tide.
At low tide, you can see small fish and crabs left behind among the rocks.
The water level dropped due to the low tide, and the boat could no longer leave the harbor.
en.notes: 干潮 is the "low tide" or low-water level; its counterpart is 満潮. Typical are 干潮時, 干潮になる and 干潮の時刻. Tidal flats exposed at low tide are called 干潟, and the shellfish gathering at low tide that is popular in Japan is 潮干狩り. A synonym is 引き潮, which emphasizes more the receding of the water.

examples[].german: Warm ocean currents make the coastal climate milder.
In the waters off Japan, the warm Kuroshio and the cold Oyashio meet.
A letter in a bottle rode the ocean current and drifted ashore in a distant country.
en.notes: 海流 is a large-scale, steady "ocean current", e.g. the warm 黒潮 (日本海流) and the cold 親潮 (千島海流). A distinction is made between 暖流 and 寒流; typical are 海流に乗る and 海流に流される. Small-scale currents along the coast, on the other hand, are called 潮流 (tidal current) or, in everyday speech, 潮の流れ; the dangerous rip current at a swimming beach is 離岸流.

examples[].german: Many unknown organisms still live in the deep sea.
Some deep-sea fish emit light by themselves.
An unmanned probe surveyed the deep sea at a depth of 6,000 meters.
en.notes: 深海 is the "deep sea", usually from about 200 meters down, where hardly any sunlight reaches. It is often used as a modifier: 深海魚, 深海生物, 深海探査, 深海の水圧. The opposite is 浅海, or in everyday speech 浅い海. The word is neutral and, thanks to aquariums and nature documentaries, also familiar in everyday life.

examples[].german: The spring water at the foot of the mountain is pure and suitable for drinking.
In this town, tofu making using spring water thrives.
A large amount of groundwater gushed in during tunnel construction, and work was interrupted.
en.notes: 湧水 is water that wells up out of the ground by itself, that is, "spring water" or a spring: 湧水地, 湧水群, 湧水を汲む. It sounds literary and often appears on signs and in travel guides; in everyday speech one says 湧き水. More generally, "spring" is 泉, and a hot spring is 温泉. In construction, 湧水 also refers to groundwater seeping in, for example during tunnel work.

examples[].german: A financial report was submitted pursuant to the Political Funds Control Act.
Lawmakers who failed to report income from fundraising parties were criticized.
It was reported that he used political funds for private trips.
en.notes: 政治資金 is all money for political activity: donations, party dues, proceeds from fundraising events (政治資金パーティー) and state subsidies. Income and expenditure are regulated by the 政治資金規正法; a 政治資金収支報告書 must be filed each year. News often concerns scandals such as 政治資金の不記載 or 裏金. A single donation is called 献金.

examples[].german: River water sinks under the gravel, flows on as subsurface water, and wells up again downstream.
This sake brewery uses the subsurface flow from Mt. Fuji as brewing water.
The city's water supply pumps up the river's subsurface flow through wells and uses it.
en.notes: 伏流水 is water that flows through gravel and sand beneath a riverbed or alluvial fan, that is, a river that in places "goes underground" (伏 = "to hide"). The related verb is 伏流する, and typical is 伏流水が湧き出る. It is popular as drinking water or in sake breweries and is emphasized in advertising (富士山の伏流水). General groundwater is called 地下水; 伏流水 is a special case of it that is closely tied to a river.

examples[].german: I found the underground water vein and dug a well.
The tunnel construction cut off a water vein, and the wells in the surrounding area dried up.
It has not been scientifically proven that dowsing can locate water veins.
en.notes: 水脈 is an underground "water vein", that is, a watercourse in the ground that one looks for when building a well: 水脈を探す, 水脈に当たる, 水脈を掘り当てる. The second meaning "navigable channel, waterway" is rare. More general is 地下水; a well is called 井戸. In literary language, 水脈 occasionally also stands for a hidden, continuing current or tradition.

examples[].german: Excessive pumping of groundwater causes land subsidence.
The tap water in this town comes from groundwater, so it tastes very good.
The groundwater in the surrounding area was contaminated by the factory's wastewater.
en.notes: 地下水 is water in the soil beneath the earth's surface. Typical combinations: 地下水を汲み上げる "to extract groundwater", 地下水が湧く, 地下水汚染, 地下水位. Different from these are 湧き水 (spring water emerging at the surface) and 井戸水 (well water). The word is neutral and appears in environmental topics, the news and everyday life.

examples[].german: The thawing of permafrost releases methane gas.
The carcass of a mammoth was found in the Siberian permafrost.
Houses built on permafrost are tilting because the ground is thawing.
en.notes: 永久凍土 is "permafrost", that is, ground that stays frozen continuously for at least two years, for example in Siberia, Alaska or Canada. The word is composed of 永久 "permanent" and 凍土 "frozen ground". In news about climate change, 永久凍土が溶ける／融解する in particular is common, because methane and carbon dioxide are released in the process. Further compounds are 永久凍土層 and 永久凍土地帯.

examples[].german: Sedimentary rocks are formed over long periods of time.
Fossils are often found in sedimentary rock.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from accumulated corals and shells.
en.notes: 堆積岩 is "sedimentary rock", which forms when sand, mud, gravel or the remains of living things settle (堆積) and become consolidated. Examples are 砂岩 (sandstone), 泥岩 (mudstone), 礫岩 (conglomerate) and 石灰岩 (limestone). Together with 火成岩 and 変成岩, it makes up the three main groups of rocks. Typical of 堆積岩 are stratification (地層) and the occurrence of 化石.

examples[].german: Granite is a typical igneous rock.
Igneous rocks are formed when magma cools and solidifies.
Igneous rocks are divided into volcanic rocks and plutonic rocks according to how they cooled.
en.notes: 火成岩 is "igneous rock", that is, rock formed from solidified magma. A distinction is made between 火山岩 (solidified quickly at the surface, e.g. 玄武岩 "basalt", 安山岩 "andesite") and 深成岩 (solidified slowly at depth, e.g. 花崗岩 "granite"). Together with 堆積岩 and 変成岩, it makes up the three main groups of rocks. The word belongs to geography and geology classes.

examples[].german: Marble is a metamorphic rock that changed from limestone.
Metamorphic rocks are formed when rock is transformed by high temperature and pressure.
Metamorphic rocks formed by plate subduction are widely distributed in this region.
en.notes: 変成岩 is "metamorphic rock", that is, rock that has been transformed by high pressure and high temperature inside the Earth without melting; the process is called 変成作用. Well-known examples are 大理石 (marble from limestone) and 片麻岩 (gneiss). Be careful with the spelling: 変成 "transformation" is not to be confused with the identically read 編成 "organization, formation" and 変性 "denaturation".

examples[].german: After heavy snowfall, the risk of avalanches rises.
Two people were caught in an avalanche outside the ski area and are missing.
The moment the sale began, customers poured into the store in a rush.
en.notes: 雪崩 is an "avalanche"; typical expressions are 雪崩が起きる／発生する, 雪崩に巻き込まれる, 雪崩注意報 as well as 表層雪崩 and 全層雪崩. The reading なだれ is a special reading (熟字訓) and must be learned as a whole. Figuratively, 雪崩 stands for a mass of people or things suddenly rushing in: 雪崩を打って "in droves, all at once", 雪崩現象 "avalanche effect".

examples[].german: From the summit, I could take in the whole town at a glance.
If you look at this bird's-eye view map, you can clearly see the layout of the castle town.
This book gives a broad overview of modern Japanese history.
en.notes: 鳥瞰 means "to look over from above from a bird's-eye perspective" (literally "to look down like a bird") and is a transitive する-verb: 町を鳥瞰する. It is common in compounds: 鳥瞰図 "bird's-eye view picture, panoramic map", 鳥瞰的な視点. Figuratively, it means to gain a general overview of a topic, for example in book titles such as 〜史を鳥瞰する. The word is literary; a synonym that is more common today is 俯瞰.

examples[].german: Climate change is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity.
Because of climate change, heavy rain and extreme heat are increasing in many places.
As a measure against climate change, the government is promoting the introduction of renewable energy.
en.notes: 気候変動 is "climate change" and the standard word in politics, science and the media: 気候変動対策, 気候変動の影響, 気候変動に関する政府間パネル (IPCC). Alongside it, 地球温暖化 "global warming" is common, which refers more narrowly to the temperature rise only; 気候危機 "climate crisis" emphasizes urgency. The word is a noun; as a verb one says 気候が変動する.

examples[].german: A politician and a company executive were arrested in the bribery case.
There is suspicion that bribery was involved in the bidding for public works.
To prevent bribery, civil servants must not accept gifts from companies.
en.notes: 贈収賄 combines 贈賄 "bribery" (giving money) and 収賄 "taking bribes" (accepting money) and refers to the bribery case as a whole. Typical: 贈収賄事件, 贈収賄の疑いで逮捕される; the individual offenses are called 贈賄罪 and 収賄罪. The bribe itself is 賄賂 (賄賂を贈る/受け取る), colloquially 袖の下. Language of lawyers and the news.

examples[].german: The increase in carbon dioxide is strengthening the greenhouse effect.
The government announced a target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half.
Because of a strong greenhouse effect, the surface of Venus is extremely hot.
en.notes: 温室効果 is the technical term for the "greenhouse effect" and is usually followed by の and another noun: 温室効果の仕組み. It is most often encountered in the compound 温室効果ガス "greenhouse gas", as in 温室効果ガスを削減する "to reduce greenhouse gases". The consequence, global warming, is called 地球温暖化; the two terms are often confused, but denote cause and effect. Register: news, school, technical texts.

examples[].german: Emission standards for harmful substances were tightened.
Harmful substances were detected in imported toys.
Tobacco smoke contains many harmful substances.
en.notes: 有害物質 refers generally to "harmful substances", that is, substances that damage health or the environment. Typical are 有害物質を含む "to contain harmful substances", 有害物質が検出される "harmful substances are detected" and 有害物質を排出する. 有害 means "harmful" in the broad sense, whereas 有毒 means "poisonous" more narrowly; 有毒物質 is therefore a stronger expression. Typical of official language, news and product warnings.

examples[].german: Selecting a final disposal site for radioactive waste is proving difficult.
The plan is to bury high-level radioactive waste deep underground.
Radioactive waste from hospitals is also strictly controlled.
en.notes: 放射性廃棄物 is the official expression for "radioactive waste" from nuclear power plants, medicine and research. A distinction is made between 高レベル and 低レベル放射性廃棄物; typical expressions are 放射性廃棄物を処分する "to dispose of", 地下に埋める and 最終処分場 "final repository". In the media and in everyday speech one also hears the colloquial 核のごみ "nuclear garbage". Register: news, politics, technical texts.

examples[].german: The cost of solar power generation is falling every year.
When we built our house, we installed solar power generation on the roof.
On cloudy days, the output of solar power generation drops sharply.
en.notes: 太陽光発電 is "power generation using sunlight", that is, photovoltaics. Typical are 太陽光発電を導入する "to install photovoltaics" and 太陽光発電のパネル; the modules themselves are usually called ソーラーパネル or 太陽光パネル.
