en.notes: 痩せ地 (often also written やせ地) is nutrient-poor, infertile soil. In everyday speech people mostly say 痩せた土地; for soil to "become depleted" it is 土地が痩せる. The opposite is 肥沃な土地; to improve soil is 土を肥やす. Typical: 痩せ地でも育つ, 痩せ地を耕す. Neutral to literary.

examples[].german: Soil on which volcanic ash has accumulated is fertile.
The flooding of the Nile brought fertile land to the river basin.
Thanks to continuously adding compost, the soil of the field has become fertile.
en.notes: 肥沃 is a な-adjective (also a noun) for fertile, nutrient-rich soil: 肥沃な土地／土壌／平野, 土地が肥沃になる. It is used almost only for land and soil, not for people or ideas. Opposites are 不毛 and 痩せた. For fertile animals or people, one does not say 肥沃 but 繁殖力が強い or 子宝に恵まれる. Literary.

examples[].german: The land became barren through years of overcultivation.
Even in the barren land of the desert, a few plants grow.
Let's stop this fruitless argument already.
en.notes: 不毛 literally means "without growth": 不毛の地／不毛な土地 is infertile, barren land. Very common is the figurative use for something fruitless without result: 不毛な議論, 不毛な争い. It stands as a な-adjective or with の before nouns. The opposite in the literal sense is 肥沃; in the figurative sense 有意義 or 実りある fit. Literary, but common.

examples[].german: The degradation of forests is leading to a decline in ecosystem services.
My smartphone's battery has deteriorated, and the charge runs out quickly.
UV rays degraded the plastic, and it cracked.
en.notes: 劣化 is the deterioration of quality or performance through age, use or environmental influences; as an intransitive する-verb: バッテリーが劣化する, 経年劣化 "age-related wear". For situations or health people say 悪化, and for aging buildings and facilities 老朽化. Colloquially, 劣化 is used disparagingly of celebrities who "look worse"; that is impolite. Transitive: 劣化させる.

examples[].german: The court commissioned an expert to give an opinion.
After retirement, my father keeps working at the same company as a contract employee.
A contract doctor visits the nursing home twice a month.
en.notes: 嘱託 has two meanings: formally entrusting someone with a task, especially authorities or courts commissioning experts (〜に鑑定を嘱託する), and, in working life, employment on a contract basis outside the regular staff, often as continued employment after retirement: 嘱託社員, 嘱託として働く, 嘱託医. In the first meaning it is a transitive する-verb. Related: 委託 "entrusting work to companies, outsourcing", 依頼 "request, commission" in general.

examples[].german: Tests to evaluate the ecotoxicity of new chemical substances are mandatory.
This pesticide has low toxicity to humans but high ecotoxicity to fish.
In the laboratory, they use water fleas to examine the ecotoxicity of wastewater.
en.notes: 生態毒性 is ecotoxicity, that is, the harmful effect of a substance on organisms in the environment such as fish, water fleas or algae, as opposed to toxicity to humans (ヒトへの毒性). Typical: 生態毒性を評価する, 生態毒性試験, 生態毒性が高い／低い. Technical language of chemicals law and environmental toxicology.

examples[].german: A rare species of butterfly lives in this forest.
Poaching and illegal trade in rare species show no sign of ending.
A rare species was found at the planned development site, and construction was temporarily suspended.
en.notes: 希少種 (also 稀少種) is a rare animal or plant species with a small population or range. It overlaps with 絶滅危惧種 "endangered species" but is broader: a species can be rare without being acutely threatened. Legally protected species are called 希少野生動植物種. Typical: 希少種を保護する, 希少種が生息する. Technical and media language.

examples[].german: This fish is designated as a near-threatened species.
If habitat loss continues, it may be upgraded from near-threatened to threatened.
I was surprised to learn that this butterfly I saw in my garden is a near-threatened species.
en.notes: 準絶滅危惧種 is the Red List category "near threatened" (NT): the species is not yet acutely endangered but could move up into a threat category if conditions change. 準 means "quasi, preliminary stage"; the actual threat levels are called 絶滅危惧Ⅰ類 and 絶滅危惧Ⅱ類. Typical combinations are 〜に指定される, 〜に選定される and レッドリストで〜に分類される. In official lists often only 準絶滅危惧 appears without 種; the expression belongs to the language of nature conservation, officialdom and the news.

examples[].german: Thanks to conservation efforts, the population is gradually recovering.
In this lake, culling is carried out to reduce the population of invasive fish.
The survey team estimated the number of deer using drones.
en.notes: 個体数 is in biology and ecology the number of individual animals or plants in a population, that is, the "population size". Typical are 個体数が増える・減る・回復する and 個体数を調査する・推定する・管理する. For humans people say 人口; 生息数 is a close synonym for wild animals in an area, and 頭数 counts mainly large animals and livestock. 個体 alone denotes the single organism as a specimen.

examples[].german: Seeds enter a dormant state under conditions unsuitable for growth.
Accounts that have not been used for more than ten years may be treated as dormant accounts.
This club has been dormant for a while because of a lack of members.
en.notes: 休眠 is the resting phase of seeds, buds, insects (diapause) or spores in which metabolism almost stands still; as an intransitive する-verb: 種子が休眠する. Fixed phrases are 休眠状態に入る, 休眠から覚める and 休眠打破 "breaking of dormancy". Figuratively it means "dormant, inactive": 休眠口座 "dormant account", 休眠会社 "dormant company", 休眠中のプロジェクト. The hibernation of animals, by contrast, is 冬眠, and ordinary sleep 睡眠.

examples[].german: Changes in day length control the flowering of plants.
When the day length shortens in autumn, birds begin preparing for migration.
Chrysanthemum farmers adjust the day length with electric lights to shift the shipping season.
en.notes: 日長 in the reading にっちょう is a technical word from biology and agriculture for the length of the light part of the day, to which plants and animals respond. Typical compounds are 日長反応 "photoperiodism" as well as 短日植物 and 長日植物 "short-day and long-day plants". In everyday speech people rather say 昼の長さ; 日照時間, by contrast, means the actual hours of sunshine. Not to be confused with ひなが (usually written 日永), a poetic word for the long days of spring.

examples[].german: The sunflower is a typical plant that shows heliotropism.
That potted plants on the windowsill lean toward the light is due to the heliotropism of plants.
The people around her are always encouraged by her sunny cheerfulness.
en.notes: 向日性 literally means "the property of turning toward the sun" and is the traditional botanical term for heliotropism; the opposite is 背日性. In modern biology people usually speak more generally of 光屈性 (phototropism). Typical is 向日性を示す or 向日性がある. Occasionally the word is transferred to people in a literary way: 向日性の人 is someone with a "sunny", life-affirming nature.

examples[].german: Plant roots grow downward by gravitropism.
The stem bends toward the direction of the light, showing positive phototropism.
The difference between tropism and nastic movement lies in whether it relates to the direction of the stimulus.
en.notes: 屈性 is the technical term for tropism, a directed growth movement of plants toward or away from a stimulus. It mostly appears in compounds: 光屈性 (phototropism), 重力屈性 (gravitropism, older 屈地性), 接触屈性, 水分屈性. Toward the stimulus is 正の屈性, away from the stimulus 負の屈性. To be distinguished from 傾性 (nasty), in which the direction of movement does not depend on the direction of the stimulus, such as tulips opening in warmth.

examples[].german: Salt marshes form a unique ecosystem of the coastal zone.
Land reclamation in Tokyo Bay destroyed many of the former salt marshes.
At high tide, this salt marsh is submerged in seawater.
en.notes: 塩性湿地 ("salty wetland") is the salt marsh: a flat coastal wetland that is flooded by seawater at high tide and covered with salt-tolerant plants (塩生植物) such as アッケシソウ or ヨシ. To be distinguished are 干潟 (tidal flat, mostly unvegetated), 湿原 (moor, fresh water) and 汽水域 (brackish zone). The word belongs to the technical language of ecology and nature conservation; typical combinations are 塩性湿地が広がる, 塩性湿地を保全する, 塩性湿地が失われる.

examples[].german: Riparian forests have the function of weakening the force of the water during floods.
The shade of the riparian forest keeps the river's water temperature from rising and serves as a home for fish.
During river improvement work, there was debate over how much of the riparian forest should be cut down.
en.notes: 河畔林 is the forest that grows on river banks and in floodplains, typically with willows (ヤナギ) and alders (ハンノキ). 河畔 is the written-language word for "river bank"; in everyday speech people say 川沿い or 川辺; forest along mountain streams is called 渓畔林. The word appears mainly in ecology, hydraulic engineering and nature conservation: 河畔林を保全する, 河畔林を伐採する, 河畔林が魚のすみかになる.

examples[].german: Applications for issuance of the My Number card are increasing.
A copy of the residence certificate can be issued at the counter of the city hall.
The state granted subsidies to the municipalities.
en.notes: 交付 is the official issuing or handing over of documents or funds by an authority: 証明書/免許証を交付する, 交付金 "allocations, grants", 地方交付税 "local allocation tax (fiscal equalization for municipalities)". Transitive する-verb; from the citizen's perspective 交付を受ける. Distinction: 発行 is publishing or issuing in general (also magazines, tickets), 配布 is distributing to many people; 交付 stresses the official handover by the authorities.

examples[].german: Waterside ecosystems support many species.
Accidents near the water increase during summer vacation, so please be careful.
On the weekend, I caught crayfish with my kids at a park by the water.
en.notes: 水辺 is quite generally "at the water", that is, the area at the edge of rivers, lakes, ponds or the sea. It is neutral and appears both in everyday speech and in texts: 水辺で遊ぶ, 水辺の生き物, 水辺の公園, 水辺の事故. More specific are 川辺 (river bank), 海辺 (seashore), 浜辺 (beach) and 岸 (the shore as a line). In warnings about swimming accidents, 水辺 is the usual word.

examples[].german: Mangrove forests are indispensable for conserving coastal ecosystems.
Mangrove forests, also called mangroves, spread out at the river mouths of Iriomote Island.
Many mangrove forests were cut down to make shrimp farming ponds.
en.notes: 紅樹林 is a rare, scholarly-sounding word for the mangrove forest; 紅樹 ("red tree") denotes the mangrove after its reddish wood or bark. In present-day Japanese people almost always say マングローブ林 or simply マングローブ; 紅樹林 appears rather in technical texts, older writings or Chinese contexts. In Japan, mangroves grow mainly in Okinawa, Iriomote and Amami.

examples[].german: The sea of clouds we looked down on from the summit was a fantastic sight.
Takeda Castle ruins are famous for appearing to float on a sea of clouds on early autumn mornings.
Outside the airplane window, a sea of clouds spread as far as the eye could see.
en.notes: 雲海 is the "sea of clouds" seen from above, for example from a mountain summit or from an airplane: the cloud cover lies like a sea beneath you. Typical are 雲海が広がる, 雲海を見下ろす and 雲海に浮かぶ (e.g. 雲海に浮かぶ城, "castle above the clouds"). It often forms on cool autumn mornings in valley basins. Someone standing in the mist themselves speaks of 霧, not 雲海.

examples[].german: In the mountains in the depth of winter, rime ice covers the trees in white.
With the morning chill, rime ice bloomed on the trees of the highlands.
If you want to see rime ice, the best time is an early morning when it is clear and the wind is light.
en.notes: 霧氷 is the umbrella term for ice deposits that form on trees and objects in frost from fog or cloud droplets or water vapor; this includes 樹氷 (soft rime), 粗氷 (hard rime) and 樹霜 (hoar frost on twigs). People say 霧氷がつく, 霧氷ができる and, poetically, 霧氷が咲く. To be distinguished are 霜, frost on the ground and on surfaces, and 霜柱, ice needles in the soil.

examples[].german: The rime-covered trees of Zao are a winter specialty that draws tourists.
When we got off the ropeway, giant rime-covered trees stood in rows right before our eyes.
Because of the warm winter, the growth of the rime-covered trees is delayed this year.
en.notes: 樹氷 is rime ice that freezes onto trees when supercooled fog droplets are carried by the wind against branches; it is a form of 霧氷. Famous are the completely iced-over firs of Zao, Hakkoda or Moriyoshi, which are also called スノーモンスター ("snow monsters"). Typical are 樹氷原, 樹氷ツアー, 樹氷のライトアップ and 樹氷が成長する. As a tourism word, it is much more common than 霧氷.

examples[].german: Snowmelt water flows into rivers and causes spring flooding.
On winter mornings, snow-melting agent is often spread on the roads.
In towns in snow country, water comes out of the snow-melting devices on the roads.
en.notes: 融雪 is the melting of snow or the melted snow; the everyday word for it is 雪解け. 融雪 sounds technical and appears mainly in the news, weather reports and compounds: 融雪水 "meltwater", 融雪剤 "de-icing salt, snow-melting agent", 融雪装置 "snow-melting system" (such as water nozzles in roads in snowy regions) and 融雪洪水 "snowmelt flood". As a verb people do not say 融雪する but 雪が解ける.

examples[].german: On a winter morning, frost columns stood in the soil of the field.
On the way to school, the children enjoy crunching through the needle ice.
So that the seedlings would not be pushed up by frost columns, I covered the base of the plants with straw.
en.notes: 霜柱 are the fine ice needles that grow from damp soil on cold nights and lift the topmost layer of earth. The fixed phrase is 霜柱が立つ; if you step on them, you hear a crunch (ザクザク). They are dreaded in gardening and farming because 霜柱 pushes seedlings up. Not to be confused with 霜 (frost on surfaces) and つらら (icicles); in haiku, 霜柱 is a winter seasonal word.

examples[].german: Icing on the power lines caused the blackout.
To prevent icing on the main wings, de-icing fluid was sprayed before departure.
The landing of the quadruple jump broke down, and the skater fell.
en.notes: 着氷 is the freezing of ice onto objects, above all on aircraft wings, ships and power lines; as a する-verb: 翼に着氷する. The weather service issues an icing advisory 着氷注意報 when there is danger. In sports reporting, 着氷 also means the landing of a jump in figure skating: 着氷が乱れる, ジャンプを着氷する. Not to be confused with 結氷 ("freezing over" of bodies of water) and 凍結 ("freezing", also of roads).

en.meaning: freezing over; ice formation on water
examples[].german: The lake froze over in the severe cold.
When the lake freezes over completely, smelt fishing begins.
This harbor freezes over during winter, so ships cannot leave.
en.notes: 結氷 means that an ice cover forms on a body of water: 湖が結氷する "the lake freezes over". It is an intransitive する-verb with the body of water as subject and sounds matter-of-fact and written, for example in weather reports; in conversation people say 凍る or 氷が張る. Common combinations are 全面結氷 "completely frozen over" and 結氷期 "freezing period". The opposite, the breaking up of the ice, is 解氷.

examples[].german: The ice breakup of rivers begins with the rise in temperature in spring.
When the ice on the lake melts, the smelt fishing season ends too.
As the ice thaws in the Arctic Ocean, new shipping routes are attracting attention.
en.notes: 解氷 is the thawing or breaking up of the ice cover of rivers, lakes and seas in spring; as an intransitive する-verb: 湖が解氷する. The counterpart is 結氷 ("freezing over"); the season is called 解氷期. For the thawing of frozen food people say 解凍, for physical melting 融解, and for melting snow 雪解け. The word is rather literary and appears in weather and environmental reports.

examples[].german: The government issued a proclamation of martial law.
That country declared war on its neighbor.
The new president's remarks were taken as a declaration of war against a rival company.
en.notes: 布告 is an official "proclamation" or "decree" by which a government announces something publicly: 戒厳令を布告する "to proclaim martial law". It is most often met in 宣戦布告 "declaration of war" (宣戦を布告する), which is also used figuratively for an open "challenge" in everyday life or business. Historically, early Meiji laws were called 太政官布告. For the promulgation of new laws today, one says 公布; general announcements are 発表.

examples[].german: Issuance of a visa can take several weeks.
I can't depart until the embassy issues the visa.
Because of a system failure, the issuance of passports was temporarily suspended.
en.notes: 発給 is the official term for an authority issuing a document to a person, especially visas, passports and permits: ビザを発給する, 旅券の発給, often in the passive ビザが発給される. The more general 発行 is used for anything that is issued (tickets, magazines, shares, receipts); 発給 fits only where an office hands a document to an applicant. Typical of news, consulates and forms.

examples[].german: The drift ice of the Sea of Okhotsk is a signature sight of winter in Hokkaido.
In Abashiri, you can ride an icebreaker and see the drift ice up close.
This year the drift ice reached the shore a week later than usual.
en.notes: 流氷 is ice drifting on the sea, that is, ice floes and pack ice. In Japan, one thinks immediately of the Sea of Okhotsk off Hokkaido (Abashiri, Monbetsu, Shiretoko), where the ice reaches the coast every winter: 流氷が接岸する, 流氷初日, 流氷観光砕氷船. An iceberg that breaks off a glacier, by contrast, is called 氷山; 海氷 is the general technical term for sea ice.

examples[].german: Roads with packed snow are slippery and dangerous.
It feels great to ski down the groomed slope first thing in the morning.
The mountain pass road has a packed-snow surface, so winter tires are required.
en.notes: 圧雪 is compressed, packed snow as well as the compacting of snow; as a transitive する-verb: コースを圧雪する. In traffic reports, 圧雪路面 stands for a snow-covered, packed road surface; at ski resorts 圧雪バーン stands for a groomed slope (opposite 非圧雪, powder snow); the snow groomer is called 圧雪車. To be distinguished are 新雪 ("fresh snow") and 根雪 (snow cover that stays on the ground).

examples[].german: Consumption of luxury goods like coffee and tobacco is rising year by year.
In the survey, respondents were asked in detail about their food preferences.
This wine is made on the sweet side to suit Japanese tastes.
en.notes: 嗜好 is a preference (often in taste), especially for food, drink and luxury items such as coffee, tobacco and alcohol; the word is literary and sounds objective. Typical are 嗜好品 ("luxury foods and drinks" such as coffee, tobacco, alcohol), 消費者の嗜好, 嗜好に合う and 嗜好が変化する. In everyday speech people say 好み. Beware of the homophones 志向 ("orientation", e.g. 健康志向), 思考 ("thinking") and 試行 ("trial").

examples[].german: There are almost no entertainment facilities in this area.
In the old days, the radio was one of the few forms of entertainment in households.
This movie is pure entertainment that you can enjoy without thinking about anything difficult.
en.notes: 娯楽 is entertainment or amusement as a category, that is, what one does to pass the time for relaxation. Typical are 娯楽施設, 娯楽番組, 娯楽映画・娯楽作品, 娯楽が少ない and 〜を娯楽として楽しむ. The word sounds somewhat factual and general; a personal hobby is 趣味, outdoor leisure activities are more often レジャー, and for show business one now often says エンターテインメント.

examples[].german: It is important to spend your leisure time meaningfully.
He uses his free time in retirement to attend a pottery class.
Shorter working hours have given people more leisure time.
en.notes: 余暇 is the free time left over after work and duties; the word is literary and often appears in statistics, advice books and official documents. Typical are 余暇を過ごす・楽しむ・活用する and 余暇活動. In everyday speech people tend to say 暇, 自由な時間 or 休みの日; 暇 can also have the negative sense "having nothing to do", which 余暇 does not.

examples[].german: To kill time, I looked into a secondhand bookshop.
This puzzle is a good way to pass the time on long trips.
Until the meeting started, I killed time reading the newspaper in the lobby.
en.notes: 暇つぶし is a pastime that bridges waiting time or boredom; the word is colloquial and very common. Typical frames are 暇つぶしに〜する, 暇つぶしをする and 〜はいい暇つぶしになる; as a verb phrase one says 暇をつぶす. Pejoratively it can also mean "waste of time": ただの暇つぶしにすぎない. Compared with the neutral 気晴らし ("diversion, recreation"), 暇つぶし stresses that one actually has nothing better to do.

examples[].german: I like strolling through the old town on days off.
Around the hotel, a promenade has been laid out that goes all the way around the lakeshore.
The rain had stopped, so I took a short stroll through the nearby forest.
en.notes: 散策 is a leisurely walk in which one enjoys the surroundings, for example in old towns, parks or by lakes; as a する-verb with を for the area walked through: 旧市街を散策する. It sounds more refined than 散歩 and is typical of travel guides and tourism texts (散策路, 散策コース, 町並み散策). For the daily walk or walking the dog, one says 散歩; even more literary is 逍遥.

examples[].german: He composed poems while strolling through the garden.
The philosopher walked along the path by the river, lost in thought.
Aristotle's school is called the Peripatetic school because lectures were given while walking.
en.notes: 逍遥 is a literary word for aimless, unhurried wandering, often lost in thought; as a する-verb with を for the place: 庭園を逍遥する. It is hardly heard in spoken Japanese, where people say 散歩 or, more formally, 散策. It is known from 逍遥学派, the "Peripatetic school" of Aristotle, and from the pen name of the writer 坪内逍遥.

examples[].german: I bought a ceramic chopstick rest as a souvenir.
When you put your chopsticks down during a meal, place them on the chopstick rest, not across the bowl.
There was no chopstick rest, so I folded the chopstick wrapper to use instead.
en.notes: 箸置き is the small rest on which you lay the tips of your chopsticks so that they do not touch the table; one says 箸を箸置きに置く. They come in ceramic, glass or wood, often with seasonal motifs, and are a popular souvenir. Distinguish 箸立て (a container for chopsticks standing upright) and 箸袋 (the paper wrapper), from which one folds a makeshift 箸置き in a restaurant if necessary.

examples[].german: I laid out floor cushions in the guest room and welcomed the guests.
Please, use a floor cushion.
When the yokozuna lost, floor cushions flew from the spectator seats.
en.notes: 座布団 is the flat, usually rectangular floor cushion on which one kneels or sits on tatami; it is counted with 枚. Typical are 座布団を敷く・出す・すすめる and 座布団に座る; a guest is first offered a 座布団, and it is considered rude to step on one. Well known are the flying 座布団 at sumo when a yokozuna loses. A Western cushion for a sofa or chair is called クッション.

examples[].german: Approval to establish the nursery was granted.
It takes a long time before a new drug is approved by the state.
This daycare is unlicensed, so it receives little in subsidies.
en.notes: 認可 is the official approval by which an authority legally accepts an application: 認可を受ける/得る, 認可が下りる, 国が〜を認可する. The everyday 許可 is any kind of permission ("may I?"), 承認 is more the consent or approval of a body or person. Common in fixed expressions such as 認可保育園 and its counterpart 認可外/無認可 ("without official approval").

examples[].german: Packing for the move took as many as three days.
Next month I will be moving close to my company.
Spring is moving season, so it is hard to book a moving company.
en.notes: 引越し is the move of a home or office; as a する-verb: 引越しする, and as a verb also 引っ越す (東京に引っ越す, 〜から〜へ引っ越す). The most common spelling is 引っ越し; 引越し without the small っ is seen mainly in company names and advertising (引越し業者, 引越センター). Typical are 引越しの準備, 引越し祝い and 引越しそば. Officially, a change of residence is called 転居, and the relocation of a company or office 移転.

en.meaning: seasonal change of clothes; makeover; new look
examples[].german: June is the season for changing into summer clothes.
At the weekend I switched over my wardrobe and put the winter clothes away in the closet.
The bookstore in front of the station has been remodeled into a shop with a café attached.
en.notes: 衣替え is the seasonal change of clothing: one puts away the summer or winter clothes and takes out the others. Traditionally, school and work uniforms switch to summer wear on June 1 and to winter wear on October 1. One says 衣替えをする. Figuratively, 衣替え also means "makeover, new look", for example when a shop is refurbished: 〜に衣替えする. Older spelling: 更衣.

examples[].german: Sharing the housework keeps a marriage harmonious.
Since we both work, we do the housework all at once on the weekend.
Due to family circumstances, I will take the day off today.
en.notes: 家事 is housework, that is, cooking, cleaning, laundry and the like: 家事をする, 家事を分担する, 家事と育児, 家事代行 ("housekeeping service"). In formal excuses, 家事 also means "family matters": 家事の都合により. Individual tasks have their own words, such as 炊事 (cooking) and 洗濯 (laundry). Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 火事 ("fire").

examples[].german: The equipment in the kitchen area is aging.
At camp, the cooking-duty person got up early and cooked the rice.
My mother handled cooking, laundry and cleaning all by herself.
en.notes: 炊事 is cooking and kitchen work as a household duty, often in the list 炊事・洗濯・掃除. Typical are 炊事場 (cooking area at campsites or in communal lodgings), 炊事当番 ("kitchen duty") and 炊事をする. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned or factual; for cooking as an activity or a dish one says 料理, and for cooking for oneself 自炊.

examples[].german: My grandmother was good at sewing and made anything for us.
In home economics class, we made an apron using sewing tools.
I'm bad at sewing - I can't even sew on a button properly.
en.notes: 裁縫 is sewing as a skill, by hand or by machine: 裁縫が得意・苦手, 裁縫道具, 裁縫箱. At school one learns it in the subject 家庭科. The verb itself is 縫う ("to sew"); 手芸 is the umbrella term for handicrafts such as knitting and embroidery, and 洋裁 and 和裁 are the tailoring of Western and Japanese clothing respectively.

examples[].german: Few people these days darn socks.
In the evening my mother often did mending.
The fishermen were busy mending their nets at the harbor.
en.notes: 繕い is mending and patching, above all of clothing, socks or nets; it is the noun of the transitive godan verb 繕う (穴を繕う). Common is 繕い物 ("mending, things to be mended"). The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned; today people mostly say 直す, 修理 or, for clothes, お直し. 繕う also has the figurative meaning "to keep up appearances": 体裁を繕う.

examples[].german: If you prepare side dishes in advance on the weekend, weekdays are easier.
Kinpira burdock keeps well, so it is perfect as a make-ahead side dish.
I put make-ahead side dishes in clean containers and try to finish them within three or four days.
en.notes: 常備菜 ("side dishes always kept in stock") are side dishes cooked in larger quantities and kept in the refrigerator for several days, such as きんぴら, ひじきの煮物, 煮豆 or pickles. One says 常備菜を作る or 常備菜を作り置きする. 作り置き is the more colloquial word and stresses cooking in advance, whereas 常備菜 stresses the long-keeping side dish itself. The word is common in cookbooks and household advice books.

examples[].german: I keep a stock of non-perishable food in case of disasters.
Umeboshi and pickles are traditional preserved foods.
In regions with long winters, it is customary to prepare preserved food in autumn.
en.notes: 保存食 is food that keeps for a long time through drying, pickling, smoking or canning, such as 梅干し, 漬物, 干物 or 缶詰. Typical are 保存食を作る, 保存食を備蓄する and 昔ながらの保存食. Supplies meant specifically for disasters are called 非常食; 保存食 is broader and also covers traditional food storage.

examples[].german: My father looks forward to his evening drink every night.
After seeing my health checkup results, I cut my evening drink down to one bottle of beer.
Tonight's accompaniments for the evening drink are chilled tofu and edamame.
en.notes: 晩酌 is the little glass of beer or sake one drinks at home with dinner; as a する-verb: 晩酌する. Typical are 晩酌を楽しむ, 毎晩の晩酌 and 晩酌のお供 (snacks to go with it). Distinguish drinking out (飲みに行く) and 寝酒, the nightcap before going to bed. The modern, more casual word for drinking at home is 家飲み.

examples[].german: We obtained certification to an international standard.
Two-factor authentication is required to log in.
When I wear a mask, face authentication doesn't work well.
en.notes: 認証 has two fields of use: in business and administration, certification by an inspection body (ISO認証を取得する); in IT, the authentication of a user (二段階認証, 顔認証, 指紋認証, 認証コード). In both cases a body or system confirms that something is genuine or conforms to a standard. Not to be confused with 証明 ("proof, evidence") or 確認 ("checking" in the general sense).

en.meaning: snack to go with drinks; appetizer for sake
examples[].german: Edamame is the perfect accompaniment to sake.
Using old stories as our topic, I drank with an old friend until late at night.
This place has a good selection of small dishes that go well with sake.
en.notes: 肴 is anything one eats with alcohol, such as nibbles or small dishes; the set phrase is 酒の肴. The word arose from 酒 + 菜 ("side dish") and is homophonous with 魚 ("fish"), which often leads to confusion. Figuratively, 肴 is also a topic of conversation or a performance that livens up a drinking party: 〜を肴に飲む. Colloquially, for snacks to go with drinks, people tend to say つまみ.

examples[].german: I put the teacup on its saucer and serve it to the guest.
When drinking tea, don't lift the saucer along with it; hold only the teacup.
My grandmother carefully keeps lacquered tea saucers for guests.
en.notes: 茶托 is the small stand of wood, lacquer or metal on which a Japanese teacup (湯呑み) is served. When serving guests, including in the office, 茶托に載せて出す is considered polite; but one drinks only from the cup and does not lift the 茶托 along with it. For coffee cups one says ソーサー, for glass coasters コースター.

examples[].german: Water heated in a clay kettle tastes mellow.
In autumn, at a fine restaurant, I enjoyed matsutake mushroom soup steamed in a small clay teapot.
My grandmother brewed plenty of hōjicha for me in a clay teapot.
en.notes: 土瓶 is an earthenware pot with a bail handle (つる) over the lid, in which one brews tea such as ほうじ茶 or 番茶 or, in the past, decocted medicinal herbs. Well known is the dish 土瓶蒸し, a soup steamed in a small pot, usually with matsutake. Distinguish 急須 (a small teapot with a side handle for green tea) and やかん (a kettle for boiling water).

examples[].german: A mosquito coil is indispensable on summer nights.
We lit a mosquito coil on the veranda and enjoyed the evening cool.
When I smell mosquito coils, I remember the summer vacations of my childhood.
en.notes: 蚊取り線香 is the green incense coil against mosquitoes that one lights in summer: 蚊取り線香をつける or 蚊取り線香をたく. In Japan its smell is regarded as the typical scent of summer; the coil often sits in a pig-shaped holder (蚊遣り豚). Electric versions are called 電子蚊取り. Literally: "mosquito-catching incense stick".

en.meaning: dining tray; small meal table; counter for bowls of rice and pairs of chopsticks
examples[].german: In the ryokan room, a tray meal was brought to each person.
Would you like another bowl of rice?
When you have finished eating, please take the trays back to the kitchen.
en.notes: 膳 is the small individual table or tray, often with legs, on which each guest is served at traditional meals; usually one says politely お膳: お膳を運ぶ, お膳を下げる. As a counter, 膳 counts bowls of rice (ご飯一膳) and pairs of chopsticks (箸一膳). Related are 食膳 ("dining table, meal") and the expression 据え膳 ("a meal set out and ready", figuratively: an opportunity offered on a plate).

examples[].german: A paulownia chest is ideal for storing kimono.
I put my winter sweaters away in the drawer of the chest.
My grandmother didn't trust banks and hid her cash at the back of the chest of drawers.
en.notes: 箪笥 is the traditional piece of furniture with drawers for clothing, so more a "chest of drawers"; it is almost always written たんす or タンス. In compounds it becomes だんす: 洋服だんす "wardrobe", 茶だんす "dish cabinet". Clothes are put away with 箪笥にしまう; also well known is たんす預金 "cash hoarded at home". A built-in closet, by contrast, is called 押し入れ or クローゼット.

examples[].german: It is hard to set up a household of your own at a young age.
Since getting married, she has suddenly started to look domesticated.
Our club is a big group, with over a hundred members.
en.notes: 所帯 is the household as a unit of living and economy and sounds down-to-earth. Important phrases: 所帯を持つ ("to set up a household of one's own", usually through marriage), 所帯持ち ("married, with a family"), 所帯じみる ("to look worn down by domestic life") and 大所帯 ("large group, large operation"). In statistics and official language, 世帯 is used instead.

en.meaning: taking care of one's health; rest and recuperation; protective covering (construction, moving)
examples[].german: I have a cold, so I am trying to take care of myself.
Before the move, the movers covered the corridor walls with protective material.
As the saying goes, "a doctor doesn't look after his own health": the doctor himself collapsed from overwork.
en.notes: 養生 first means taking care of one's health and resting after an illness: 養生する, 養生に努める, and in letters ご養生ください. The opposite is 不養生, known from the proverb 医者の不養生 ("doctors take the least care of themselves"). On construction sites and when moving, 養生 means covering with protective material: 床を養生する, 養生テープ, 養生シート; for concrete, letting it cure. For recovery under medical supervision, people tend to say 療養.

examples[].german: He is convalescing at a hot spring resort.
On the doctor's orders, I have to recuperate at home for two weeks.
The department head is reportedly taking leave for a while to recover from an illness.
en.notes: 療養 is recovery, usually lengthy, under medical treatment; as an intransitive する-verb: 療養する. Typical are 療養中, 自宅療養, 病気療養のため, 療養生活 and 療養所 ("sanatorium"). Distinguish 治療 (the treatment itself), 静養 (recovery through rest, without illness) and 養生 (general health care, more everyday). 療養 sounds objective and is often used in official announcements.

examples[].german: I attended the wake and remembered the deceased.
I can't attend the funeral service because of work, so I decided to go to the wake.
After losing the game, the locker room felt just like a wake.
en.notes: 通夜 is the wake held on the evening before the funeral; usually one says お通夜: お通夜に行く・参列する・伺う. Originally people kept watch over the deceased all night; today the ceremony usually lasts one to two hours in the evening, and afterwards there is often 通夜振る舞い, a meal for the mourners. On the following day come the 葬儀 and the 告別式. Figuratively, お通夜のよう describes a gloomy, silent mood.

examples[].german: There is a duty to carry out one's official duties faithfully.
We have to carry out the mission with limited personnel.
She saw the difficult plan through to the end.
en.notes: 遂行 is formal and stresses that an assigned task is actually carried out to the end: 任務を遂行する, 職務を遂行する, 計画を遂行する, also 業務遂行能力. 実行 means "putting into action" in general, 実施 means "carrying out (a measure, event)"; 遂行 sounds like duty and responsibility. In everyday conversation one says やり遂げる instead.

examples[].german: The funeral service was held for close relatives only.
After the funeral service, we saw the coffin off.
I have to wear a black tie to tomorrow's funeral service.
en.notes: 告別式 is the farewell ceremony at which relatives and acquaintances take leave of the deceased; it usually takes place on the day after the 通夜 and is often combined with the religious part as 葬儀・告別式. Typical are 告別式に参列する, 告別式が執り行われる and 近親者のみで. In everyday speech people say 葬式, formally 葬儀; a later memorial gathering is called お別れの会 or 偲ぶ会.

en.meaning: seventh day after death; memorial service on the seventh day
examples[].german: We held the memorial service for the seventh day after the death.
Out of consideration for relatives living far away, we held the seventh-day service on the same day as the funeral.
Once the seventh day after my grandmother's death had passed, the family finally calmed down a little.
en.notes: 初七日 is, in Buddhist mourning practice, the seventh day after death (the day of death counts) and the service held on that day; the standard reading is しょなのか, but one also hears しょなぬか. One says 初七日の法要を営む or 行う. Today the service is often held on the day of the burial itself (繰り上げ初七日), so that relatives do not have to travel again. Further memorial days follow up to the 四十九日; the word belongs to ceremonial vocabulary.

en.meaning: courtesy calls; round of greeting visits
examples[].german: I visited the neighbors for New Year courtesy calls.
After moving in, it is common to make courtesy calls on the neighbors on both sides and the units above and below.
As the new person in charge, I made courtesy calls on our business partners.
en.notes: 挨拶回り is going around to several people or places to introduce oneself or say goodbye. Typical occasions: after a move, to the neighbors (often with a small gift); at the start of the year, to business partners (年始の挨拶回り); on taking up a post or being transferred. One says 挨拶回りをする or 挨拶回りに行く; often あいさつ回り is written half in kana.

en.meaning: knowledge; basic rules; code of conduct
examples[].german: I always check the basic rules of disaster preparedness.
She has some training in judo, so she stayed calm even in an emergency.
On my first day at the company, I was handed a booklet setting out guidelines for new employees.
en.notes: 心得 has several meanings: "knowledge, mastery" of a skill (茶道の心得がある, "to know one's way around the tea ceremony"), "basic rules, rules of conduct" (防災の心得, 新入社員の心得) and "inner attitude". Placed after a title, 〜心得 denotes an acting rank, e.g. 課長心得. The underlying verb is the ichidan verb 心得る ("to understand, to know"), known from 心得ました.

examples[].german: The tea ceremony is popular as a cultured pursuit for adults.
Not talking loudly in public is part of good manners for a working adult.
He is skilled in calligraphy and writes even all his New Year cards with a brush.
en.notes: 嗜み is usually written in kana as たしなみ and denotes, on the one hand, cultivated skill in the arts (茶道・書道のたしなみがある), and on the other, good manners, restraint and propriety (大人のたしなみ, 社会人としてのたしなみ). Related is 身だしなみ ("neat appearance"). The verb 嗜む (godan, transitive) means "to pursue something with connoisseurship, to enjoy in moderation": お酒を嗜む, 俳句を嗜む.

examples[].german: The atmosphere of the old townscape soothes the heart.
The inn still preserves the look it had when it was founded.
Everyone was spellbound by her dignified bearing in a kimono.
en.notes: 佇まい is the calm overall appearance or aura of a place, building or person. Typical are 町の佇まい, 静かな佇まい, 落ち着いた佇まい and, for people, 凛とした佇まい. It derives from 佇む ("to stand still") and sounds elevated and literary; often it is written in kana as たたずまい. More neutral are 雰囲気 ("atmosphere") and 外観 ("outward appearance").

en.meaning: seasonal feature; typical sign of the season
examples[].german: Fireworks festivals are a hallmark of summer.
The calls of the roasted sweet potato vendors are a familiar feature of winter.
The holiday homecoming rush is reported in the news every year as a fixture of the year's end.
en.notes: 風物詩 is something typical of a particular season that makes it palpable: a sight, sound, event or food. It almost always appears in the frame 〜は夏の風物詩だ or 冬の風物詩として親しまれている. Literally it is a "poem about scenery and the seasons" (meaning 2, rare today). Distinguish 名物 ("local specialty") and 季語 (the seasonal word in haiku).

examples[].german: One senses the seasons through annual events.
I teach my children Japan's annual events such as Setsubun and Hinamatsuri.
The big year-end cleaning has become an annual ritual in our home.
en.notes: 年中行事 are the festivals and customs that recur every year at the same time, such as 正月, 節分, ひな祭り or お盆; one speaks of 日本の年中行事 or 宮中の年中行事. Figuratively it also denotes something that reliably repeats every year, often slightly ironically: 〜はもう年中行事になっている. Mind the reading: ねんちゅう, not ねんじゅう as in 年中 "all year round".

examples[].german: The festival is held in accordance with local customs.
It took time until I got used to the customs of the family I married into.
We should try new ways instead of being bound by old conventions.
en.notes: しきたり are handed-down rules and practices of a family, place or industry that one is expected to observe: しきたりに従う／しきたりを守る／しきたりを破る, 古いしきたり, 家のしきたり. Compared with 習慣 "habit" (also personal) and 風習 "folk custom", しきたり stresses the binding character, often with an overtone of narrowness. The word is usually written in kana; 仕来り is rare.

examples[].german: Old customs remain in this village.
In our family, it is the custom to go together for the first shrine visit of the year at New Year.
In this company, it is customary for new employees to introduce themselves at their first morning meeting.
en.notes: 慣わし (also 習わし) is a custom that has long been practiced. Typical is the frame 〜のが慣わしだ or 〜のが慣わしになっている "it is the custom that ...", and also 古くからの慣わし. Compared with しきたり, 慣わし sounds less binding and more descriptive; compared with 習慣, more refined and slightly literary. The set phrase 世の習い means "the way of the world".

examples[].german: A lawsuit was filed demanding performance of the contract.
The prime minister is being urged to fulfill the campaign pledges he made in the election.
The company did not pay by the deadline and fell into default.
en.notes: 履行 is the legal term for fulfilling an obligation: 契約を履行する, 義務を履行する, 約束・公約を履行する. The opposite is 不履行, especially 債務不履行 ("non-performance, breach of obligation"). 実行 is general "carrying out", whereas 履行 stresses that one renders a performance that is owed. Sounds very formal, typical in contracts, court judgments and political commentary.

examples[].german: The shop's closing time is approaching.
That's all for today's class.
He was silent at first, but in the end he got angry.
en.notes: しまい means "end, finish" and belongs to the verb 仕舞う "to finish; to put away". In daily life one hears mainly おしまい "that's it, it's over" (これでおしまい) and しまいには "in the end, finally", mostly for an unpleasant escalation. In compounds it becomes じまい: 店じまい "closing time; closing down a business", 〜ずじまい "ended up not doing". It is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: I tidy up properly before going home.
Not only is he always late, it has now come to the point where he stays away from work without notice.
This child does nothing but play pranks; he is really unmanageable.
en.notes: 始末 has several important uses. As a transitive する-verb it means "to deal with, get rid of, dispose of": ゴミを始末する, 後始末 "cleaning up afterwards". 〜始末だ describes a bad final outcome: 〜する始末だ "and in the end it came to the point where ..."; 始末に負えない and 始末が悪い mean "unmanageable, hard to handle". 始末書 is a written letter of apology at the workplace; the meaning "thrift" (始末する, 始末屋) is rather old-fashioned.

examples[].german: It is hard to make ends meet on a small income.
I squeeze out time between work and childcare to study for a qualification.
My mother was good at managing the household budget and put a little aside every month.
en.notes: やりくり is skillful management of scarce resources in order to somehow get by. Typical are 家計のやりくり, 少ない収入でやりくりする and, figuratively, 時間をやりくりする "to squeeze time out of a busy schedule"; someone who is good at it is やりくり上手. Compared with 節約 "saving", やりくり stresses juggling limited resources, not the saving itself. It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: Thanks to my thrifty wife, our savings have grown.
To save money for the trip, I am cutting back on eating out and living frugally.
If you take frugality too far, people will think you are just stingy.
en.notes: 倹約 is deliberate thrift in one's own spending; as a する-verb: 食費を倹約する or simply 倹約して暮らす. A thrifty person is a 倹約家. The more everyday 節約 can also be applied to time, electricity or water, whereas 倹約 is used almost only for money and way of life and sounds somewhat more refined. Excessive thrift is pejoratively called けち.

examples[].german: There is happiness even in a simple life.
Even after becoming company president, my grandfather preferred plain clothing.
We held the wedding simply, with family only.
en.notes: 質素 is a な-adjective for a deliberately simple, modest way of life without luxury: 質素な暮らし／食事／服装, 質素に暮らす. It usually has a positive overtone of frugality and contentment; the opposite is 贅沢. 簡素, by contrast, stresses leaving out the superfluous in forms and procedures (簡素な手続き), and 地味 the unobtrusive in appearance.

examples[].german: He is a lazy person, and his room is always messy.
During the long holiday weekend I spent my time letting my stubble grow.
I am bad at writing letters, so I often end up replying late even to New Year cards.
en.notes: 無精 (also 不精) is the unwillingness to bother with everyday matters; it is used as a noun and as a な-adjective. Compounds are very common: 無精ひげ "stubble (from not bothering to shave)", 筆無精 "bad at writing letters", 出不精 "homebody", 無精者 "lazybones". Compared with the formal 怠惰 "idleness", 無精 is everyday and refers more to small lapses of care than to fundamental laziness.

en.meaning: to run; to conduct; to carry on
examples[].german: We have been running a ryokan since my grandfather's generation.
A person cannot lead a social life alone.
We held the memorial service for the second anniversary of my father's death at the temple.
en.notes: 営む is a transitive, slightly elevated verb with three uses: to run a business (店・旅館・農業を営む), to lead a life (生活を営む, 社会生活を営む) and to hold a religious ceremony (法要を営む). Compared with 経営する, 営む stresses less the management than the day-to-day running, often of a family business; in conversation one simply says 店をやっている. The related noun is 営み "activity, doings".

en.meaning: to make; to prepare; (money) to raise; (excuse) to invent
examples[].german: My mother lovingly made a lunch box for me.
To raise the money for the trip, I save a little every month.
Every time he is late, he comes up with a plausible excuse.
en.notes: こしらえる is a somewhat old-fashioned, colloquial word for "to make, to put together" and is mostly written in kana; the kanji 拵える is rare. Compared with the neutral 作る, it sounds like handiwork and effort: 弁当をこしらえる, 料理をこしらえる. By extension it also means "to raise money" (金をこしらえる) or "to think something up" (言い訳をこしらえる). Transitive with を, with no intransitive counterpart.

en.meaning: to be soothed; to soften; to relax
examples[].german: When I see a cat sleeping, my heart softens.
His joke lightened the mood of the meeting a little.
The flowers by the window brighten the atmosphere of the hospital room.
en.notes: 和む is intransitive: the heart, mood or atmosphere becomes gentle and relaxed, usually because of something lovable. Typical are 心が和む, 気持ちが和む and 場が和む. The transitive counterpart is the causative form 和ませる: 冗談で場を和ませる "to lighten the mood with a joke". Related are 和やか "harmonious, friendly" and 和らぐ, which is used more for easing pain or cold.

en.meaning: to acknowledge efforts; to show appreciation
examples[].german: I reward myself for a hard day's work by enjoying an evening drink.
The president thanked each employee for their efforts.
After the tournament, the coach acknowledged the players with warm words.
en.notes: ねぎらう means to thank someone for their trouble and acknowledge it; the set phrase is 〜の労をねぎらう. It comes from equals or superiors (boss to employee, coach to player); toward superiors it sounds presumptuous, and one says お礼を言う or 感謝する instead. Newer but very common is 自分をねぎらう "to treat oneself". Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: An evacuation order was issued.
The government declared a state of emergency nationwide.
The current personnel transfers will be officially announced as effective April 1.
en.notes: 発令 means that an authority officially announces an order, warning or personnel decision: 避難指示・警報・緊急事態宣言が発令される, mostly in the passive. In companies and agencies it also stands for the formal announcement of transfers and appointments: 人事異動が四月一日付で発令される. Lifting is called 解除 (警報が解除される). 発表 is neutral "announce"; 発令 always has the character of an official command.

examples[].german: Putting up with the cold, I went out for an early-morning walk.
I am embarrassed to ask, but could you lend me a little money?
The two met in secret, avoiding other people's eyes.
en.notes: 忍ぶ has two meanings. "To endure, to bear": 寒さを忍ぶ, 恥を忍んで "swallowing one's shame", 見るに忍びない "cannot bear to look". "To hide oneself, to do secretly": 人目を忍ぶ "to hide from others' eyes", 忍び込む "to sneak in". Do not confuse it with the identically read 偲ぶ "to recall with longing, to remember fondly". The word is rather elevated and occurs mainly in set phrases.

examples[].german: She finishes the cooking efficiently.
Although she is new, she handles the reception work efficiently.
Thanks to the paramedics' efficient response, the injured were taken to the hospital right away.
en.notes: 手際よい describes someone carrying out a task quickly, in an orderly way and without unnecessary steps; the adverb 手際よく (手際よく片付ける) is the most common form. Alongside it are the separated forms 手際がよい／手際のよい and the opposite 手際が悪い. 器用 refers more to manual dexterity in general, 要領がいい to a knack for organizing work cleverly (sometimes conveniently). Also written 手際良い.

examples[].german: I live in a quiet residential area.
Although this hotel is close to the station, the surroundings are surprisingly quiet.
After retirement, I want to build a house in a quiet place on the outskirts.
en.notes: 閑静 is a な-adjective for a pleasantly quiet area secluded from noise. It is used almost only for residential areas and places, especially in 閑静な住宅街, a standard formula in real estate ads. For people or sounds one says 静か; 静寂 is the stillness itself, のどか peaceful rural calm. The word sounds somewhat elevated and literary.

examples[].german: He offered to resign to take responsibility.
After the scandal came to light, the mayor was forced to resign.
The cabinet resigned en masse, and a new prime minister was chosen.
en.notes: 辞職 is resignation from an office or position, above all for civil servants, politicians and executives; as an intransitive する-verb: 辞職する. Typical are 辞職を申し出る, 辞職に追い込まれる, 引責辞職 "resignation to take responsibility" and 内閣総辞職. 辞任 refers to a particular post (会長を辞任する), 退職 to leaving employment in general, including retirement; in everyday speech people say 辞める.

en.meaning: temporary leave of absence from work
examples[].german: I took half a year off work to recover from an illness.
The employee on leave will return to the workplace next month.
I can't decide whether to take leave to care for my parent or to resign.
en.notes: 休職 is a temporary leave in which the employment relationship continues, for example because of illness, caregiving or study; as an intransitive する-verb: 休職する. Common are 休職中, 休職届 and the return, 復職. Do not confuse it with 休暇 "vacation", 休業 "business closure" or the legally regulated 育児休業 "childcare leave", nor with 退職, the final departure.

examples[].german: I was promoted from section chief to department head.
The team won the championship this season and secured promotion to the top league.
In recognition of its results, the sales office was upgraded to a branch.
en.notes: 昇格 is advancement to a higher level or status; as an intransitive する-verb: 課長に昇格する, causative 昇格させる. It applies not only to people but also to teams (一部リーグに昇格) and organizations (支店に昇格). 昇進, by contrast, refers only to a person's advancement to a higher post. The opposite is 降格.

examples[].german: The transfer with promotion to headquarters was decided, so we held a celebration.
Department head, congratulations on your promotion and transfer.
I thought the transfer to the provinces was a demotion, but it was actually a promotion.
en.notes: 栄転 is a transfer that is at the same time a promotion; as an intransitive する-verb: 本社に栄転する. The opposite is 左遷 "demotion by transfer". Because it expresses recognition, it is used mainly politely about others: ご栄転おめでとうございます. About oneself one speaks more modestly of 異動 or 転勤.

examples[].german: The new principal gave an address on taking office.
He took up his post as head of the Osaka branch in April.
Right after taking up his post, the new ambassador paid a courtesy call on the prime minister.
en.notes: 着任 is arriving at the new place of duty and taking up a new post, typical of teachers, civil servants, diplomats and branch managers; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜に着任する, 〜として着任する. Common are 着任の挨拶 and 着任早々 "right after taking up one's post"; the counterpart is 離任. 赴任 stresses the journey or move to the place of duty, 就任 the assumption of an office, as in 社長に就任する.

examples[].german: We commissioned an expert to carry out the survey.
A university professor was appointed as a member of the city council.
After receiving the letter of appointment, I formally began my activities as a counselor.
en.notes: 委嘱 is a formal word for entrusting a task or an office to someone outside one's own organization: XにYを委嘱する, passive 〜に委嘱される. Typical are 委員を委嘱する, 委嘱状 "letter of appointment" and 委嘱を受ける. 委託 refers more to outsourcing business to companies, 依頼 to a general request, 任命 to an appointment within a hierarchy.

examples[].german: We won the construction work on a contract basis.
We signed a contract with the builder, and the construction of the house began.
He is not a company employee but does system development work on a contract basis.
en.notes: 請負 is undertaking work for payment against an agreed result, that is, a contract for work from the contractor's point of view. Typical are 請負契約, 請負業者, 請負工事 and 請負で働く; the related verb is 請け負う. The spelling 請け負い also occurs. Unlike 派遣 "temporary agency work", under 請負 one does not work under the instructions of the client.

examples[].german: He was awarded a decoration in recognition of his many years of service.
The recipients of the spring decorations were announced in the newspaper.
My grandfather was delighted to hear the news of his decoration.
en.notes: 叙勲 is the state conferment of an order or decoration; in Japan especially the semiannual honors 春の叙勲 and 秋の叙勲. From the honoree's point of view one says 叙勲を受ける or 受章する; the decoration itself is called 勲章. A very formal word from news and ceremonies, hardly used in everyday life.

examples[].german: Payments to subcontractors are delayed.
Large manufacturers outsource the production of parts to small and medium-sized firms.
Our company has worked for years as a subcontractor for a major construction company.
en.notes: 下請 (usually written 下請け) is a subcontract, or the subcontractor who takes over part of the work from the main contractor 元請. Typical are 下請けに出す "to subcontract out", 下請け企業／下請け業者 and 下請けとして働く; one level further down is 孫請け. The word often carries an overtone of dependence, for example in 下請けいじめ "bullying of suppliers".

examples[].german: The main contractor manages the construction as a whole.
Payment from the main contractor to the subcontractors was delayed, which became a problem.
This time, as prime contractor, we received the construction order directly from the city.
en.notes: 元請 (also 元請け) is the main contractor who receives the order directly from the client (発注者) and passes parts of it on to 下請け. The word comes mainly from the construction and IT industries: 元請業者, 元請会社, 元請として受注する. The counterpart is 下請け, and one level below that is 孫請け.

examples[].german: The new factory is scheduled to start operating next month.
Because demand for electricity rises in summer, the power plants are running at full capacity.
The new accounting system goes live in October.
en.notes: 稼働 (also 稼動) means that machines, plants or systems are in operation; mostly intransitive: 工場が稼働する, 稼働中, 24時間稼働. For putting something into operation one usually uses 稼働させる; フル稼働 means "running at full capacity", 稼働率 "utilization rate", and in IT 本番稼働 "going live". 運転 refers to operating a machine, 作動 to the functioning of a mechanism; 操業 means the operation of a factory as a whole.

examples[].german: It is dangerous to continue operating with aging equipment.
Because of the typhoon, the factory suspended operations for two days.
Because of the decline in orders, we were forced to reduce operating hours.
en.notes: 操業 is the ongoing operation of a factory, mine or fishing business as an economic activity; as an intransitive する-verb: 工場が操業する. Typical are 操業を開始する／停止する／再開する, 操業中 and 操業短縮 "short-time work, production cutback". 稼働 refers more to individual machines and plants. Note: the identically read 創業 means "founding".

examples[].german: I work under a commission-based pay system.
In real estate sales, commission is paid according to sales.
The Bank of Japan once lowered the official discount rate to stimulate the economy.
en.notes: 歩合 has two meanings. In the working world it is the sales-based commission: 歩合制 "commission system", 歩合給, 完全歩合制 "pure commission basis". In general it denotes a ratio or percentage, today mainly in set terms such as 公定歩合 "discount rate (of the central bank)". For fees one says 手数料, for everyday ratios 割合.

examples[].german: This year's bonus was increased thanks to strong results.
Our company pays a bonus twice a year, in June and December.
Because of worsening results, the winter bonus will be skipped.
en.notes: 賞与 is the formal word for the bonus payment that in Japan is usually paid twice a year (summer and winter) in addition to the monthly salary. It appears in employment contracts, job ads and on pay slips: 賞与を支給する, 賞与年2回, 冬季賞与. In conversation people say ボーナス. The monthly salary is called 給与, allowances 手当.

examples[].german: Companies with excellent employee benefits are very popular.
This company has generous benefits, such as housing allowance and an employee cafeteria.
When choosing where to change jobs, it is better to check the benefits as well as the salary.
en.notes: 福利厚生 covers all benefits an employer provides beyond salary, such as housing allowance, a cafeteria, recreation facilities, or subsidies for leisure and further education. Typical are 福利厚生が充実している／手厚い, 福利厚生費 and 福利厚生施設. In job hunting it is an important criterion alongside 給与. The word belongs to the language of personnel departments and job ads.

examples[].german: A draft revision of the work rules is being discussed between labor and management.
I checked the work rules to see whether side jobs are permitted.
An employee received disciplinary action for violating the work rules.
en.notes: 就業規則 are the work rules issued by the employer, setting out working hours, leave, pay and discipline; in Japan they are mandatory from ten employees under the 労働基準法. Typical phrases are 就業規則に定める, 就業規則に違反する, 就業規則を変更する. 社内規定 is the more general umbrella term for internal regulations. Technical language of personnel management and labor law.

examples[].german: Labor-management negotiations are proving difficult.
Both labor and management compromised and agreed on a pay raise.
Maintaining good labor-management relations contributes to the stability of the company.
en.notes: 労使 combines employees (労働者) and employers (使用者) as the two parties to labor relations. It appears almost always in compounds: 労使交渉 "collective bargaining", 労使関係, 労使協定, 労使紛争, 労使双方, 労使間. The word is typical of news and labor law; in conversation people tend to say 会社と組合 or the like.

examples[].german: They resolved to strike, demanding better working conditions.
Legally, a strike is called "dōmei higyō".
Even in prewar Japan, strikes by workers occurred repeatedly.
en.notes: 罷業 is the formal, legal word for "strike"; in law it is called 同盟罷業. Typical are 罷業に踏み切る "to go on strike" and 罷業権 "right to strike". In everyday life and in the news today, people almost always say ストライキ or, shortened, スト; 罷業 is met mainly in legal texts and historical accounts. 怠業, by contrast, denotes deliberate slowdown.

examples[].german: The debtor repaid the full amount.
Because the borrower couldn't pay, the guarantor paid off the debt.
After the due date has passed, late-payment damages are incurred.
en.notes: 弁済 is the legal technical term for settling a debt: 債務を弁済する, 全額を弁済する, 弁済期 ("due date"), 代位弁済 (payment by a third party, such as a guarantor). In everyday speech, for loans one says 返済 ("repayment") or simply 返す. 弁済 is found in contracts, court proceedings and bank documents.

examples[].german: I am in a position to oversee the whole project.
She oversees sales for the whole Asia region.
We consolidate the views of each department and decide on the final policy.
en.notes: 統括 means to bring several parts or departments together and manage them as a whole; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を統括する. Common are 統括責任者, 統括部長 and 統括本部. Do not confuse it with 総括 "to take stock, to evaluate as a whole" (一年を総括する). 管理 is more general, "management, administration", and 監督 "supervision".

examples[].german: The committee put forward a reform proposal.
The expert group compiled recommendations to the government on countering the declining birthrate.
A proposal by younger employees led to the introduction of a work-from-home system.
en.notes: 提言 is a well-founded proposal, usually made by experts or bodies to politicians, authorities or the public; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を提言する, 政府に提言する. Common are 提言をまとめる, 政策提言 and 〜への提言. 提案 is the general "proposal" in any situation, 助言 advice to a person, 進言 advice to a superior. 提言 sounds formal and public.

examples[].german: The workers protested with slowdown tactics.
Unlike a strike, in a slowdown work continues, but efficiency is deliberately lowered.
The word "saboru" (to skip work) comes from the French "sabotage", which means a slowdown.
en.notes: 怠業 is an industrial action in which employees keep working but deliberately slowly or carelessly, that is, a go-slow; the loanword サボタージュ fits here, from which the colloquial サボる "to skip work, to slack off" is derived. Typical are 怠業戦術 and 怠業する. In a 罷業 or ストライキ, by contrast, work is stopped entirely. The word is formal and legal.

examples[].german: He holds the posts of department head and section chief at the same time.
Due to a labor shortage, the store manager also handles accounting.
With so many concurrent duties, every job ends up half done.
en.notes: 兼務 means to perform another function at the same time in addition to one's own post; as a transitive する-verb: AとBを兼務する, 〜も兼務する. Nearly synonymous is 兼任, which is somewhat more common for official posts. The opposite is 専任 "exclusively in charge"; 兼業, by contrast, means a side occupation outside the company.

examples[].german: It is necessary to assign a dedicated person in charge.
As a full-time lecturer at the university, she teaches classes every day.
I will be in charge of quality control exclusively rather than as a side duty.
en.notes: 専任 means being exclusively or full-time responsible for a particular task; mostly attributive with の: 専任の担当者, 専任スタッフ. At universities, 専任講師 is a permanent lecturer post, as opposed to 非常勤 "part-time lecturer". The opposite is 兼任 or 兼務; in job ads, 専任 often stands for a full-time position without side duties.

examples[].german: A forceful executive turned the company around.
Right after taking office, the new president took decisive action and disposed of unprofitable divisions one after another.
He is known in the industry as a formidable lawyer.
en.notes: 辣腕 is exceptional drive and assertiveness, especially in business, politics and law. Fixed is 辣腕を振るう "to act with a firm hand", plus 辣腕家 and, attributively, 辣腕の経営者／辣腕弁護士. Through 辣 "sharp, biting" it suggests toughness and can easily shade into ruthlessness. 敏腕 is more positive, "capable, able", and 手腕 is neutral, "ability". Literary and journalistic.

examples[].german: His negotiating skill is highly valued.
It will be a season in which the new manager's ability is put to the test.
She showed her management skill and turned around a loss-making shop.
en.notes: 手腕 is ability proven in practice, especially in leading, negotiating and managing. Typical are 手腕を発揮する, 手腕を振るう, 手腕が問われる "to have to prove one's abilities", as well as 経営手腕 and 政治手腕. For manual skill, people tend to say 腕前 or 器用; 辣腕 and 敏腕 stress particular sharpness or efficiency. The word is literary; in conversation 腕 is enough.

examples[].german: Spurred on by my superior's stern encouragement, I pulled myself together.
During the game, the coach shouted at the players from the bench to drive them on.
Without my mentor's stern urging, I would probably have given up my research partway.
en.notes: 叱咤 means to shout at someone loudly, but usually with the aim of driving them on. The most common form is the four-character phrase 叱咤激励 "to spur on with stern words"; as a transitive する-verb: 選手を叱咤する. Compared with 叱責 "formal reprimand", 叱咤 carries a note of encouragement, and compared with 激励 "encouragement", a note of sternness. Literary.

examples[].german: I made a mistake and was reprimanded by my boss.
The minister was sharply rebuked by the prime minister for his inappropriate remark.
Scolding subordinates in front of others is counterproductive.
en.notes: 叱責 is a serious, formal reprimand by superiors or an authority; as a transitive する-verb often in the passive: 上司から叱責される, 叱責を受ける, 厳しく叱責する. In everyday speech people say 叱る or, colloquially, 怒られる. Unlike 叱咤, 叱責 contains no encouragement; 譴責 is a formal disciplinary punishment.

examples[].german: The insurance company exercised its right of recourse against the perpetrator.
The company claimed reimbursement of part of the damage from the employee who caused the accident.
A guarantor can claim back from the principal debtor the amount he paid.
en.notes: 求償 is a legal technical term: someone who has paid for another claims the amount back from that person. Typical are 求償権 ("right of recourse") and 〜に求償する ("to seek recourse against someone"), for instance an insurer against the party causing the damage, or a guarantor against the principal debtor. Unlike 請求 ("demand" in general), 求償 presupposes that one has already paid in place of another.

examples[].german: A personnel appraisal is carried out every half year.
The results of the personnel appraisal are reflected in raises and bonuses.
In discussion with my superior, I filled in my self-assessment on the appraisal form.
en.notes: 考課 is the evaluation of employees' work performance and occurs almost only in 人事考課 "personnel appraisal" and 考課表 "appraisal form". The result feeds into promotion, 昇給 and 賞与. 評価 is the general word for "evaluation", 査定 the rating (also of prices). Beware of identically read words such as 効果 "effect" or 硬貨 "coin".

examples[].german: Negotiations with the business partner are taking time.
Negotiations with the Ministry of Finance over the budget are continuing.
After repeated rounds of negotiation, the terms were finally settled.
en.notes: 折衝 is negotiation in which interests are weighed and compromises are fought for, especially between organizations, authorities or states; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜と折衝する. Typical are 折衝を重ねる, 予算折衝 and 事務レベルの折衝. 交渉 is the general word for "negotiation"; 折衝 sounds more formal and stresses the tough back and forth.

examples[].german: We made inquiries with the relevant offices and gathered information.
I checked my account balance at the ATM.
We contacted the applicant's previous employer to ask about his work history.
en.notes: 照会 is an official inquiry to verify facts with a responsible body; as a transitive する-verb: 〜に…を照会する. Typical are 残高照会 "balance inquiry", 在庫照会, 身元照会 and, in IT, a database query. In everyday speech people say 問い合わせ. Do not confuse it with the identically read 紹介 "introduction, recommendation".

en.meaning: accepting a commission; undertaking on commission
examples[].german: We carry out contract work in research and development.
Our company has been commissioned by the city to run the library.
The former mayor was arrested on suspicion of accepting a bribe in return for a requested favor.
en.notes: 受託 is the acceptance of a commission or custody by the commissioned side; the counterpart on the client's side is 委託. As a transitive する-verb: 業務を受託する. Common are 受託業務, 受託開発 "contract development", 受託者 and, in law, 受託収賄 "bribery (accepting a bribe on request)". Formal business and legal language.

examples[].german: The acceptance inspection of the delivered goods has been completed.
Payment will be made at the end of the following month after acceptance inspection.
When I inspected the parts that arrived, the quantity did not match the order.
en.notes: 検収 is the inspection and formal acceptance of delivered goods or services by the buyer; payment usually follows only after that. As a transitive する-verb: 納品物を検収する; typical are 検収書, 検収日 and 検収後に支払う. 検品 means only the inspection of goods, 納品 the delivery itself. A technical word from purchasing, accounting and IT projects.

examples[].german: We digitize and manage the customer register.
City hall issues residence certificates based on the basic resident register.
I registered the newly purchased computer in the equipment ledger.
en.notes: 台帳 is an official or company master record in which data are entered continuously: 顧客台帳, 固定資産台帳, 土地台帳, 住民基本台帳 "resident register". Typical verbs are 台帳に記入する／登録する and 台帳で管理する. 帳簿 are the account books of bookkeeping, 名簿 a list of names. The secondary meaning "theater script" is rare.

examples[].german: We started drawing up the medium-term business plan.
The government has formulated a new disaster prevention plan.
The company is currently drawing up guidelines for the use of AI.
en.notes: 策定 is the drawing up and binding establishment of plans, guidelines or strategies by authorities and organizations; as a transitive する-verb: 計画を策定する. Typical are 方針・指針・基準の策定, 策定に着手する and 策定中. 立案 is the earlier phase of drafting, 作成 the mere creation of documents, 制定 the enactment of laws. Formal official and business language.

examples[].german: I was entrusted with planning the new project.
Young staff members took the lead in drawing up a tourism promotion plan.
In drafting policy, it is essential to reflect voices from the field.
en.notes: 立案 is the drafting of a plan or concept; as a transitive する-verb: 計画を立案する. Common are 企画立案, 政策立案, 立案者 and 法案を立案する "to draft a bill". 立案 stands for the conceptual phase, 策定 for working out up to the binding decision; in everyday speech people simply say 計画を立てる.

examples[].german: His name came up as the originator of the new system.
I submitted the draft proposal to the section chief and am waiting for approval.
This draft ordinance was drawn up by young staff members.
en.notes: 起案 denotes the drafting of a document, usually official or in-house, which is then passed on for approval (決裁); transitive: 計画を起案する. Typical in government and company jargon are 起案書 "approval request document" and 起案者 "drafter, originator". 起草 is used more for drafting legal and contract texts or speeches, while 立案 stresses the planning itself. In everyday speech people simply say 案を作る or 企画書を書く.

examples[].german: From next month we will start the construction work in earnest.
I haven't started the new research yet.
The police have begun an investigation into the corruption case.
en.notes: 着手 means "to take something in hand, to begin something"; the undertaking takes に: 工事に着手する, 改革に着手する. It sounds more formal than 取りかかる or 始める and is typical of construction projects, reforms, investigations and larger projects. The negative 〜にはまだ着手していない "have not yet started" is common. In lawyers' jargon there is 着手金 "retainer paid at the start of a case".

examples[].german: The mutual claims were offset against each other and settled.
My salary went up, but it was canceled out by rising prices.
The good and bad points canceled each other out, and the evaluation was average.
en.notes: 相殺 is read そうさい (not さつ). Legally it is the set-off of mutual claims: 債権を相殺する. In everyday use it means that two effects cancel each other out, mostly in the passive: 〜が〜で相殺される, 効果が相殺される. Similar is 帳消しになる ("to be wiped out, nullified"), which sounds more colloquial.

examples[].german: The project collapsed due to lack of funds.
The redevelopment plan was derailed by the opposition movement.
The negotiations broke down partway and no agreement was reached.
en.notes: 頓挫 describes an ongoing undertaking suddenly getting stuck or failing because of an obstacle; intransitive: 計画が頓挫する, the cause takes で or によって. Subjects are plans, projects and negotiations, not people. For a person who fails at something and gives up, people tend to say 挫折する; 中断 is a neutral "interruption". The word is literary and frequent in the news.

examples[].german: Many people are drawn to his warm personality.
In interviews, not only ability but also personality is assessed.
Her sincere character can be sensed from the wording of her letter.
en.notes: 人柄 is a person's character as it comes across to others in dealings, and it is used almost always positively: 人柄がいい, 温かい人柄, 誠実な人柄. 性格 describes inner qualities neutrally, including negative ones, and 人格 the moral personality as a whole. About third parties one politely says お人柄. Typical are 人柄が出る or 人柄がにじみ出る "the character shows".

examples[].german: With his artistic temperament, he lives freely and without restraint.
My older brother has a mild temperament and rarely gets angry.
Differences in temperament are said to show from childhood.
en.notes: 気質 denotes a person's or group's innate temperament or typical nature: 穏やかな気質, 日本人の気質, 県民気質. After occupational or period terms it is often read かたぎ (職人気質, 昔気質) and then means the typical "type" of such people; for 芸術家気質 both readings are common. 性格 is the general word for "character", and 気性 stresses temperament in the sense of hot-tempered or gentle (気性が荒い).

examples[].german: His qualities as a leader are being called into question.
What qualities do you think a leader needs?
She is blessed with the qualities of a researcher.
en.notes: 資質 are the innate or developed qualities that make someone suited to a role; typical is 〜としての資質 (指導者としての資質) as well as 資質がある, 資質に恵まれる and 資質が問われる "one's suitability is questioned". 素質 means more the innate talent for a particular skill (音楽の素質), 才能 "talent" itself. 資質 sounds objective to formal and is often found in connection with leadership, occupation and responsibility.

examples[].german: I want to become a person of great caliber.
He lacks the caliber to become company president.
My grandmother is said to have been the most beautiful girl in the village in her youth.
en.notes: 器量 has two main meanings: appearance, especially a woman's face (器量よし "pretty", 器量がいい), which is old-fashioned today and slightly delicate; and a person's "caliber", that is, ability and stature to fill a role (器量が大きい, 〜だけの器量がない). In the second meaning, 器 "caliber" is closely related (社長の器ではない). 度量, by contrast, means specifically generosity and tolerance toward others.

examples[].german: I was fortunate to have a broad-minded boss.
Being able to laugh off and forgive other people's mistakes is proof of a generous nature.
Without the largeness of mind to accept criticism, an organization cannot grow.
en.notes: 度量 is the inner breadth to accept other opinions and mistakes: 度量が広い or 度量が大きい "big-hearted", 度量が狭い "petty" (cf. 狭量). A relative clause often precedes it: 批判を受け入れる度量. 器量 means more ability and caliber, while 寛容 is the more abstract "tolerance" as an attitude. The meaning "measures of length and volume" is met practically only in 度量衡 "weights and measures".

examples[].german: I will never repeat that foolish mistake.
Nothing is as foolish as war.
It was foolish of me to believe such a rumor.
en.notes: 愚か is a な-adjective: 愚かな行為, 愚かだった. It sounds more serious and literary than the colloquial バカ and evaluates actions and decisions rather than intelligence; a "fool" is an 愚か者. The same word gives rise to the pattern 〜はおろか "let alone", which is usually written in kana (漢字はおろかひらがなも読めない).

examples[].german: Wise judgment is required.
For now, it is wise not to push yourself and to rest.
A typhoon was approaching, so postponing the trip was a wise choice.
en.notes: 賢明 evaluates a decision or course of action as sensible and wise: 賢明な判断, 賢明な選択, 〜のが賢明だ "it is advisable to ...". So it describes actions rather than a person's intelligence (for which 聡明 or 頭がいい). Do not confuse it with the identically read 懸命 "earnest, with all one's might" (懸命に働く, 一生懸命).

examples[].german: She is intelligent and always gives apt opinions.
My grandmother is still sharp in her eighties, and her memory has not declined.
A discerning reader will notice this contradiction right away.
en.notes: 聡明 praises a person as clever, sharp and capable of judgment, a mixture of intelligence and wisdom. It is literary and respectful and is often found in descriptions of people: 聡明な女性, 聡明な顔立ち. 賢明, by contrast, evaluates an action (賢明な判断), and 利発 the alertness of a child; colloquially people say 頭がいい or 賢い.

examples[].german: He is a bright child who learns anything right away.
A boy with bright-looking eyes asked me a question.
Your daughter is really bright, isn't she?
en.notes: 利発 describes almost exclusively children or young people who grasp things quickly and answer cleverly: 利発な子, 利発そうな顔. It is a somewhat elevated, slightly old-fashioned compliment; in everyday speech people tend to say 賢い or 頭がいい. For adults, 聡明 or 有能 is used instead.

examples[].german: We commemorate the day the new constitution was promulgated.
The law takes effect one year after the date of promulgation.
The city promulgated a new ordinance banning smoking on the streets from next month.
en.notes: 公布 is the official "promulgation" of a law, constitution or ordinance, in Japan by publication in the official gazette 官報. It is mostly used in the passive: 法律が公布される. It is almost always thought of together with 施行 "coming into force": a law is first 公布 and takes effect at a later date. The Meiji Constitution, by contrast, was called 発布; 布告 is a more general proclamation, 発表 an ordinary announcement.

examples[].german: The minister stated that he would deal with the matter appropriately.
When I complained, the store manager only answered, "We will see what we can do."
The residents urged the city to take prompt action on the noise problem.
en.notes: 善処 means to handle a matter appropriately and take suitable measures: 善処する, 善処いたします, 善処を求める. The reply 善処します from politicians or companies is famous for being polite but noncommittal: one promises to take care of it without committing to anything. Very formal; in everyday speech one says 対応する or 何とかする instead.

examples[].german: He can be insensitive to other people's feelings.
He is so dense that he has no idea she likes him.
With age you become less sensitive to heat, so you need to watch out for heatstroke.
en.notes: 鈍感 means that someone barely perceives stimuli, moods or other people's feelings; the object takes に: 人の気持ちに鈍感だ, 痛みに鈍感. The opposite is 敏感. It is usually a reproach, but as a buzzword, 鈍感力 "thick-skinned strength", it is also positive. Colloquially people also say 鈍い (彼は鈍いね).

examples[].german: She reacts sensitively to changes in her surroundings.
I have sensitive skin, so I am careful in choosing cosmetics.
Young people are quick to pick up on trends.
en.notes: 敏感 means reacting quickly and strongly to stimuli or changes; the object takes に: 音に敏感, 流行に敏感, adverbially 敏感に反応する. It is usually neutral to positive ("perceptive, attentive"); when the sensitivity is excessive or pathological, people say 過敏 (神経過敏). Opposite: 鈍感. Set expression: 敏感肌 "sensitive skin".
