examples[].german: People won't follow you if you think in a narrow-minded way.
A boss who can't forgive even small mistakes by his subordinates is narrow-minded.
He was criticized as narrow-minded for excluding differing opinions.
en.notes: 狭量 describes someone who gives others little leeway and does not tolerate differing opinions or mistakes: 狭量な考え方, 狭量な上司. It is literary; the opposite is 度量が広い or 寛大. In conversation people tend to say 心が狭い or 器が小さい.

examples[].german: When a mild-mannered man like him gets angry, it must be something serious.
The new homeroom teacher has a gentle personality and is popular with the students.
The lawmaker, known for his mildness, raised his voice, which was unusual.
en.notes: 温厚 describes a calm, friendly nature that does not easily fly into anger: 温厚な性格, 温厚な人柄, 温厚篤実 "gentle and sincere". It is used of adults and sounds appreciative and somewhat elevated. 穏やか is broader (also weather, sea), and 優しい stresses kindness toward others.

examples[].german: I was hurt by her cold attitude.
The government was criticized for being indifferent to the disaster victims.
He is indifferent to politics and doesn't even go to vote.
en.notes: 冷淡 means "cool, indifferent" toward people or things; the object takes に or に対して: 弱者に冷淡だ. It ranges from mere lack of interest (政治に冷淡) to heartlessness (冷淡な態度). Colloquially people say 冷たい; 冷酷 is stronger and means cruel harshness, 無関心 only lack of interest.

examples[].german: An insincere attitude hurts the other person.
Making only excuses without apologizing is insincere.
The company's reputation suffered from its insincere handling of customers.
en.notes: 不誠実 is the negation of 誠実 "sincere, conscientious" and criticizes behavior that does not take trust or obligations seriously: 不誠実な態度, 不誠実な対応, 〜のは不誠実だ. It is common in complaints about companies, in the media and in relationships (also "unfaithful"). 嘘つき stresses outright lying, 不誠実 rather a lack of seriousness and responsibility.

examples[].german: His arrogant way of speaking made me angry.
The customer got angry at the clerk's haughty attitude and left.
He has become arrogant since being promoted.
en.notes: 横柄 describes a condescending, impolite manner, above all in tone and bearing: 横柄な態度, 横柄な口のきき方, 横柄に振る舞う. 傲慢 denotes rather the inner arrogance, and 偉そう is the colloquial equivalent. It is typical in criticism of superiors, officials, staff or customers.

examples[].german: You should state your opinion confidently without being servile.
No matter what was said to him, he just wore a servile smile.
After a string of failures, he has become completely self-abasing.
en.notes: 卑屈 describes someone who humbles himself needlessly and behaves obsequiously toward others: 卑屈になる, 卑屈な態度, 卑屈な笑い. Unlike the positive 謙虚 "humble", 卑屈 carries an overtone of contempt or lack of self-esteem. The admonition 卑屈になるな "don't belittle yourself" is common.

examples[].german: He is respected by those around him for his noble character.
He is an upright politician who never once accepted a bribe.
The hero of the story is a noble knight who never lies.
en.notes: 高潔 praises a person as morally spotless and noble-minded, free of self-interest: 高潔な人格, 高潔な人物, 高潔な精神. It is literary and elevated, typical of obituaries, biographies and literature. More everyday are 立派 or 誠実; the four-character phrase 清廉潔白 stresses specifically incorruptibility.

examples[].german: An honest character leads to trust in business.
My father worked diligently at the same company for forty years.
An honest-looking young man showed me the way.
en.notes: 実直 describes an honest, conscientious person without show or tricks who does his work steadily: 実直な人柄, 実直に働く. It sounds appreciative but somewhat old-fashioned and appears in the four-character phrase 謹厳実直 "strict and upright". 誠実 stresses sincerity toward others, and 真面目 is the everyday word for "serious, diligent".

examples[].german: The party submitted a written statement to the court.
In consultation with my lawyer, I summarized the course of the accident in a written statement.
The victim's written statement was admitted as evidence.
en.notes: 陳述書 is, in Japanese civil procedure, a written account of the facts from the standpoint of a party or witness, submitted to the court: 陳述書を作成する・提出する. Unlike a sworn affidavit, it is not made under oath; the sworn statement is called 宣誓供述書. 陳述 alone is a statement (oral or written) before the court, whereas 供述 is the statement of a suspect or witness to the police or public prosecutor.

examples[].german: He is so dutiful that he always comes at the appointed time.
She dutifully sends me a New Year card every year.
Coming back to return the umbrella he borrowed; what a conscientious person.
en.notes: 律儀 describes someone who keeps promises, duties and manners precisely, even in small matters: 律儀な人, 律儀に約束を守る, 律儀にお礼を言う. It is also written 律義 and is usually appreciative, but can easily sound slightly ironic, like "overly punctilious". 几帳面, by contrast, stresses order and precision in work style, and 義理堅い a sense of obligation for favors received.

examples[].german: Rough behavior makes the people around you uncomfortable.
Some people become violent when they drink.
The suspect reportedly had been noted for rough words and behavior before.
en.notes: 粗暴 describes coarse, inconsiderate to violent behavior of people: 粗暴な振る舞い, 粗暴な言動, 粗暴になる. It is literary and frequent in news and police reports (粗暴犯 "violent offense, violent offender"). The everyday word is 乱暴, which can also refer to the handling of things (乱暴な運転, 乱暴に扱う).

examples[].german: My father was a man of few words, but I learned a lot from watching him.
A taciturn craftsman speaks through his work.
He is always quiet in meetings, but when he does speak, he is sharp.
en.notes: 寡黙 describes a person who speaks little, often with a positive undertone of seriousness and inner calm: 寡黙な父, 寡黙な職人. It is more literary than 無口, which sounds neutral to slightly negative; colloquially people also say 口数が少ない. The character 寡 means "few", as in 寡占 "oligopoly".

examples[].german: He captured the audience's hearts with an eloquent speech.
He is usually quiet, but when the talk turns to his favorite movies, he becomes eloquent.
This photograph eloquently shows how terrible the accident was.
en.notes: 雄弁 is persuasive, stirring oratory: 雄弁な演説, 雄弁に語る, 雄弁家 "good speaker". Very common is the figurative use 〜が…を雄弁に物語る "something speaks volumes", also of photos, figures or traces. Well known is the proverb 雄弁は銀、沈黙は金. 多弁, by contrast, means merely "talking a lot", and 口がうまい is rather pejorative, "smooth at talking people into things".

examples[].german: Talkative people sometimes lose people's trust.
When I get nervous, I end up talking too much.
The usually quiet man was unusually talkative that evening.
en.notes: 多弁 simply means "talking a lot" and is literary; depending on context it sounds neutral, "talkative", or slightly pejorative, "chatty": 多弁な人, 多弁になる. The opposite is 寡黙. 雄弁, by contrast, praises the persuasive power of a speech, and in everyday speech people simply say おしゃべり for "talkative". The botanical meanings ("many-petaled") play no role in everyday life.

examples[].german: He is thoughtful and doesn't act rashly.
The more thoughtful a person is, the less quickly they draw conclusions.
Thanks to her thoughtful advice, we were able to avoid trouble.
en.notes: 思慮深い (from 思慮 "consideration" and 深い) describes someone who considers the consequences and shows regard for others before acting or speaking; as an い-adjective also adverbial: 思慮深く行動する. The opposite is 思慮が浅い or 軽率. 慎重 stresses caution in acting, 思慮深い the depth of reflection. The word is elevated and sounds appreciative.

examples[].german: Deal with it calmly without losing your temper.
My father is short-tempered and quickly raises his voice.
They say impatience does no good, so let's calm down and talk it over.
en.notes: 短気 means that someone quickly loses patience and flares up: 短気な人, 父は短気だ. Set expressions are 短気を起こす "to lose one's temper" and the proverb 短気は損気 "impatience brings only harm". The opposite is 気が長い; colloquially people also say 怒りっぽい or すぐキレる. Do not confuse it with the identically read 短期 "short-term".

examples[].german: Her brave bearing was impressive.
Although she had just lost her husband, she remained composed throughout the funeral.
My mother, in the hospital, smiled bravely and said, "I'm fine."
en.notes: 気丈 describes someone who keeps their composure in pain, grief or crisis and does not let themselves be beaten down; typical are 気丈に振る舞う and 気丈な母. It is often used of women, older people or the bereaved and implies that the person is suffering inwardly. 勇敢 means courage in danger or battle, 気が強い rather assertiveness, which can also come across negatively.

examples[].german: You shouldn't be obstinate; you should respond flexibly.
Once he has objected, he digs in and won't give way.
We missed the moment to apologize, and both of us stubbornly held our ground.
en.notes: 意固地 means defiant stubbornness, often arising from wounded pride; it almost always appears as 意固地になる "to dig in one's heels, to become obstinate". It is also written 依怙地. 頑固 is the general "stubborn" as a character trait, 強情 stresses insisting on one's own will; a related phrase is 意地を張る.

examples[].german: Don't be stubborn; do as you're told.
This child is headstrong; once he says something, he won't listen.
He never admitted his fault to the end and kept on being stubborn.
en.notes: 強情 describes someone who persistently sticks to their opinion or will even when in the wrong; set phrase: 強情を張る "to be stubborn". It is typical of children or of quarrels. 頑固 is the more general "stubborn" and can also praise loyalty to principle (頑固な職人), 意固地 stresses defiance born of hurt feelings.

examples[].german: The lawyer drew up a preparatory brief and submitted it to the court.
Please submit the brief by the next hearing date.
I read the opposing party's brief and thought about the content of a rebuttal.
en.notes: 準備書面 is, in civil procedure, the brief in which a party sets out its claims and counterarguments before the oral hearing: 準備書面を作成する・提出する, 第一準備書面, 第二準備書面 etc. The complaint is called 訴状, the first reply to the complaint 答弁書; all further briefs are 準備書面. A pure technical term from law firms and courts.

examples[].german: We should be tolerant of diverse values.
My parents were lenient about curfew.
Let's be tolerant and listen to the other person to the end.
en.notes: 寛容 means tolerating other views, mistakes or ways of life instead of condemning them strictly; the object takes に or に対して: 多様性に寛容な社会. It often appears in abstract contexts (society, religion, politics) as 寛容な, 寛容さ, 寛容の精神, with the opposite 不寛容. 寛大 stresses generosity in forgiving or punishing (寛大な処置), 度量 personal big-heartedness.

examples[].german: He is often taken for a cantankerous old man, but he is actually kind.
The owner is a cranky character, but the ramen he makes is superb.
He is pigheaded and accepts nothing other than his own way.
en.notes: 偏屈 describes an obstinate, eccentric person who does not adapt and has trouble getting along with others: 偏屈な老人, 偏屈者. Unlike 頑固, which means stubbornness about a matter, 偏屈 stresses the loner-like, twisted nature as a whole; similar are へそ曲がり and ひねくれ者. The phrase 偏屈だが根は優しい "cranky but kind at heart" is common.

examples[].german: He has a gentle manner and is liked by everyone.
Her manner is refined and suggests a good upbringing.
The man at the reception desk guided me with a polite manner.
en.notes: 物腰 is the way someone speaks and moves, that is, their manner in dealing with others; it almost always appears with an adjective: 物腰が柔らかい, 物腰の丁寧な人, 上品な物腰. 態度 is more neutral and can also be negative (態度が悪い), whereas 物腰 is mostly used in praise. For purely physical agility, people say 身のこなし.

examples[].german: A gentleman of dignified appearance came in.
He looks every bit the artist.
My old teacher, whom I met after a long time, had gone completely gray and looked changed.
en.notes: 風貌 denotes a person's whole outward appearance (face, bearing, aura), especially when it reveals something about their nature: 〜らしい風貌, 威厳のある風貌, 〜な風貌をしている. The word is literary. 容姿 refers to figure and beauty, 顔つき to the face, and 外見 is the neutral "outward appearance".

en.meaning: trace of a face; vestige; remembered image
examples[].german: Sometimes I see my mother's features in my daughter.
Traces of the old days still remain in this town.
When I met her at the class reunion, nothing remained of the girl she used to be.
en.notes: 面影 is the image of a face or place as one remembers it, and the traces of it still visible today: 〜の面影がある, 面影が残る, 面影をしのぶ. For people it is often about resemblance (父の面影がある "has something of one's father"), for places 昔の面影. 名残 is similar, but denotes rather remnants of a past era or event, not facial features.

examples[].german: He went into the meeting with a stern look.
The exam candidates waited for the exam to start with tense expressions.
The doctor announced the test results with a grave expression.
en.notes: 面持ち is the facial expression as a mirror of one's emotional state and almost always appears in the form 〜な面持ちで + action: 緊張した面持ちで, 不安そうな面持ちで, 神妙な面持ちで. The word is literary and frequent in news and narratives. In everyday speech people say 表情 or simply 顔.

examples[].german: With age, he has acquired dignity.
The long-established inn has a dignity born of its long history.
Though a rookie, his pitching already has the air of an ace.
en.notes: 風格 is a dignified, assured aura that arises from experience, skill or age: in people, but also in buildings, cities or handwriting: 風格がある, 風格が備わる, 風格が漂う, 王者の風格. 品格, by contrast, stresses moral decency and refinement, and 威厳 an authority that commands respect.

examples[].german: I try to behave with dignity.
This remark calls into question his dignity as a politician.
This tea bowl has a quiet elegance.
en.notes: 品格 is dignity and refinement that come from decency and character: 品格がある, 品格に欠ける, 〜としての品格が問われる. Things such as works of art or language can also have 品格; in sumo, the 品格 of a yokozuna is regularly debated. The everyday counterpart is 品 (品がある, 上品), and 風格 stresses more aura and assuredness.

examples[].german: He is a professor who maintains his dignity yet is approachable.
To keep up his dignity as a father, he forced himself to act strict.
The portrait of the king was full of majesty.
en.notes: 威厳 is a dignified bearing that inspires respect or even awe: 威厳がある, 威厳を保つ, 威厳に満ちた, 威厳を損なう. It is typical of rulers, judges, fathers or teachers. 風格 means assured class through experience, 品格 moral refinement; 権威, by contrast, is "authority" in the sense of power or professional standing (その分野の権威).

examples[].german: Many people can't say what they really feel because they worry about appearances.
Please put your report into proper form before submitting it.
I'm fed up with politicians who only say nice-sounding things and do nothing.
en.notes: 体裁 has several meanings: the impression one makes outwardly (体裁を気にする, 体裁が悪い "embarrassing", 体裁を繕う "to keep up appearances"), the formal layout of a document (体裁を整える) and pleasant-sounding, empty words (体裁のいいことを言う). 世間体 stresses specifically one's reputation in society, 見た目 is the plain "looks".

examples[].german: An objection was raised against the opposing party's evidence.
"Are there any objections to this proposal?" "No objections!"
The manager protested the umpire's call.
en.notes: 異議 is an objection or dissent against a decision or proposal: 異議を申し立てる ("to lodge an objection"), 異議を唱える ("to raise objections"), 異議申し立て. In meetings one asks 異議はありませんか and replies curtly 異議なし. Beware of the homophones 意義 ("meaning, significance") and 異義 ("a different meaning").

examples[].german: Vain people worry about how others judge them.
The reason he buys only brand-name goods is probably vanity.
Some people lie about their income to satisfy their vanity.
en.notes: 虚栄心 (from 虚栄 "vain glory" and 心) is the need to appear better than one is in front of others: 虚栄心が強い, 虚栄心を満たす, 〜は虚栄心からだ. The word is always negative. 自尊心, by contrast, is one's own self-respect, which can be quite justified; the colloquial 見栄 (見栄を張る) denotes the showing off itself.

examples[].german: We should avoid words that hurt someone's self-esteem.
He is very proud and finds it hard to ask others for help.
To build children's self-esteem, it is important to praise small successes.
en.notes: 自尊心 is the sense of one's own worth and dignity, "self-respect" or "pride" depending on context: 自尊心が強い, 自尊心を傷つける, 自尊心をくすぐる "to flatter someone". Colloquially people usually say プライド (プライドが高い). In psychology, "self-esteem" is also called 自己肯定感 or 自尊感情; 虚栄心, by contrast, is vanity before others.

examples[].german: I was moved by his spirit.
I was struck by the shop owner's determination to protect the local store even at a loss.
What matters is the spirit of never giving up until the end.
en.notes: 心意気 is the spirited, often selfless attitude with which someone takes on a matter: 〜という心意気, 心意気に感じる, 心意気に打たれる, 職人の心意気. It is appreciative, emotional and somewhat old-fashioned (江戸っ子の心意気). 意気込み is the eagerness before a concrete task, 決意 the sober resolution.

examples[].german: There is a proverb: kindness to others comes back to you in the end.
Show no mercy to the enemy.
When I was in trouble while traveling, a stranger's kindness touched me deeply.
en.notes: 情け is compassion and kindness toward others: 情けをかける "to show mercy", 人の情け, 情け容赦なく "mercilessly". The proverb 情けは人の為ならず is often wrongly understood as "pity spoils the other person"; it means "kindness comes back to oneself". Do not confuse it with the adjective 情けない "pitiful, shameful". 同情 is more matter-of-fact "sympathy", 哀れみ more condescending "pity".

examples[].german: It is painful to be looked at with pitying eyes.
He looked at me with eyes that seemed to beg for pity.
Feeling pity for the abandoned puppy, I took it home.
en.notes: 哀れみ (also 憐れみ) is pity for someone in a pitiable situation; it is the noun of the verb 哀れむ. Typical are 哀れみを感じる, 哀れみを乞う and 哀れみの目. Because it carries a gap between the one who pities and the one pitied, those affected often find it insulting; 同情 is more neutral, 思いやり warmer.

examples[].german: It is unacceptable to hurl contemptuous words at someone.
He looked down at the other person with scorn.
Remarks that disparaged immigrants drew heavy criticism.
en.notes: 侮蔑 is open contempt with which one belittles someone; as a transitive する-verb 〜を侮蔑する, but more often in 侮蔑的な, 侮蔑の目, 侮蔑のまなざし, 侮蔑を込めて. It is literary and strong. 軽蔑 is the more general word for "contempt" and is also common in everyday speech; 侮辱 denotes the concrete "insult" through words or deeds.

examples[].german: He was deeply indignant at the injustice.
The residents are outraged at the city's unilateral decision.
An angry customer shouted for the manager to be called.
en.notes: 憤慨 is indignation at something one considers unjust or outrageous; as a する-verb, the cause takes に or に対して: 不正に憤慨する. It denotes a morally grounded, visible agitation, not mere annoyance (腹が立つ, 怒る). 憤り is the more elevated noun for the feeling itself.

examples[].german: I feel indignation at the unfairness of society.
The victim's family openly showed their outrage at the verdict.
He could not contain his anger and banged on the desk.
en.notes: 憤り is anger or indignation at injustice; it is the noun of the verb 憤る. Typical are 〜に対する憤りを感じる, 憤りを覚える, 憤りをあらわにする and 憤りを抑える. The word is elevated and frequent in news and statements. 怒り is the general word for "anger", 憤慨 the state of being indignant as a する-verb.

examples[].german: There is a supplier with whom we have a close relationship from years of trading.
I have been on friendly terms with the company president for a long time.
The owner of a shop I frequent specially arranged a seat for us.
en.notes: 懇意 denotes a close, friendly relationship, often in a business setting too. It almost always appears in set phrases: 懇意にする "to cultivate good relations", 懇意にしている店 "a place where one is well known", 懇意な間柄 "close relationship". It sounds more elevated and somewhat more distant than 親しい or 仲がいい. Do not confuse it with 好意 "affection" or 厚意 "kindness, favor".

examples[].german: Since moving, I have drifted apart from old friends.
I've been so busy with work that I've completely lost touch with my parents' home.
At my grandfather's funeral, I met again after a long time the relatives I had been distant from.
en.notes: 疎遠 describes contact and closeness fading over time, usually without a quarrel, simply through distance or changed circumstances. Typical: (〜と)疎遠になる "to lose touch", 疎遠な関係, 疎遠だった親戚. The opposite is 親密 or 懇意. Unlike 不仲 or 確執, it carries no hostility.

examples[].german: The defendant raised the defense of the statute of limitations.
The defendant argued, "I have already paid the price."
He silently obeyed his boss's instructions without so much as objecting.
en.notes: 抗弁 has two uses. Legally it is the defendant's plea that blocks or excludes the claim: 時効の抗弁, 同時履行の抗弁, 抗弁を主張する. In general, 〜に抗弁する means to talk back to someone (often a superior) and justify oneself. 反論 is a neutral "counterargument"; 抗弁 sounds more formal and like defending oneself against an accusation.

examples[].german: The feud between the brothers has lasted for many years.
A rift between the manager and a key player was reported.
Overcoming his conflict with his father, he decided to take over the family business.
en.notes: 確執 is a deep-seated, long-lasting conflict between persons or groups in which both sides stubbornly stick to their position. Typical: 〜との確執, 〜の間に確執がある/生じる, 確執が深まる, 確執を乗り越える. The word is literary and popular in press reports about families, politicians or sports clubs; in everyday speech people tend to say 仲が悪い or もめている. Unlike 喧嘩, it does not mean a single quarrel but a lasting rift.

examples[].german: They came to be at odds over a trivial matter.
The two countries were hostile for many years but finally reconciled.
Two factions within the company are at odds, and meetings get nowhere.
en.notes: 反目 means that two sides stand against each other with hostility and cannot stand one another. As an intransitive する-verb: AとBが反目する, 〜と反目する, very often 反目し合う "to feud with each other"; as a noun: 両派の反目. It is literary and stresses mutual aversion, whereas 確執 denotes the entrenched conflict and 対立 neutrally the opposing positions.

examples[].german: I want to repay those to whom I am indebted.
I owe him a debt of gratitude for helping me when I was young.
Feeling indebted to my company, I turned down the job offer.
en.notes: 恩義 is the moral obligation that arises from kindness received. Typical: (〜に)恩義がある "to be indebted to someone", 恩義を感じる, 恩義に報いる "to repay a debt of gratitude", 恩義を忘れる. 恩 alone is the benefit itself (恩を返す, 恩返し), while 恩義 stresses more the resulting duty. The word is serious and somewhat old-fashioned; one who disregards it is called 恩知らず "ungrateful".

examples[].german: I will never forget my feeling of gratitude toward my teacher.
To repay the community's kindness, he donated part of his fortune to a school.
With gratitude in her heart, she carried on her mentor's research.
en.notes: 報恩 means repaying kindness received (報いる + 恩). It is literary and often has a moral or religious coloring, for example in 報恩感謝 or the Buddhist 報恩講. In everyday speech people say 恩返し(をする) or 恩に報いる instead. The opposite is 忘恩 "ingratitude".

examples[].german: There is a strange destiny behind the two people's meeting.
The long-awaited showdown between old rivals was decided after extra time.
A drunk picked a fight with me at the station for no reason, which was quite unpleasant.
en.notes: 因縁 comes from Buddhism (因 "cause" and 縁 "condition") and denotes a fateful connection: 不思議な因縁, 浅からぬ因縁 "a deep connection", 因縁の対決 "showdown between old rivals". Also very common is 因縁をつける "to pick a fight under a pretext, to accost someone". The word sounds heavier and often gloomier than 縁 (ご縁がある), which is friendly and everyday.

examples[].german: Criticism of hiring through connections is growing.
He found a job in Tokyo by relying on his connections.
I have no connections whatsoever in this area.
en.notes: 縁故 denotes personal connections through kinship, marriage or acquaintance, especially when used for advantage. Typical: 縁故採用 "hiring through connections", 縁故を頼る "to rely on one's connections", 縁故のある土地. In everyday speech コネ is more common and more casual; 縁故 is neutral-formal, but in 縁故採用 it is usually meant critically.

examples[].german: I humbly ask for your continued friendship.
We sincerely thank you for your especially kind goodwill as always.
The two families have maintained friendly relations for three generations.
en.notes: 交誼 is a very formal word for friendly relations and occurs almost only in letters, greeting cards and speeches, usually with the prefix ご: 平素のご交誼に感謝申し上げます, 今後とも変わらぬご交誼のほどお願い申し上げます. There is also 交誼を結ぶ "to form friendly relations". In conversation people say お付き合い or 親交 instead; the identically read 厚誼 "cordial friendship" appears in the same formulas.

examples[].german: He and I have known each other since our student days.
The many acquaintances I made while studying abroad are my treasure.
Although we had only just met, we hit it off as if we had been friends for a hundred years.
en.notes: 知己 is an elevated word, originally "one who truly knows (知) me (己)", that is, a confidant who understands one. It also simply means "acquaintance": 知己を得る "to make someone's acquaintance". Well known is 百年の知己 "as if one had known each other for a hundred years", for instant familiarity. In everyday speech people say 知り合い or 親友; 知己 sounds literary.

examples[].german: It is a life blessed with trustworthy friends.
At the graduation ceremony, the principal told the students to cherish their bonds with their companions.
Mourning the death of his friend, he wrote a poem.
en.notes: 朋友 is a literary, somewhat old-fashioned word for "friend, companion" found almost only in written texts, speeches or poems. Both characters mean "friend"; 朋 originally meant fellow students under the same teacher. In everyday speech people use 友人, 友達 or 仲間.

examples[].german: We support compatriots living overseas.
After the news of the disaster, donations were collected from compatriots around the world.
In his speech, the president addressed the people as "fellow countrymen".
en.notes: 同胞 denotes people of the same nation or country, that is, "compatriots", often with an emotional undertone of solidarity: 在外同胞 "compatriots abroad", 同胞を救う. Originally it means "siblings from the same womb"; in this meaning and poetically it is also read はらから. More neutral are 同国人 or 同郷の人 "people from the same home region".

examples[].german: If you are dissatisfied with the judgment, you can appeal.
The appeal deadline passed, so the judgment became final.
The prosecution announced that it would give up on appealing.
en.notes: 上訴 is the umbrella term for legal remedies against a judgment that is not yet final. In detail one distinguishes 控訴 (appeal to the next instance), 上告 (final appeal to the Supreme Court) and 抗告 (complaint against rulings). In the news one mostly reads the specific 控訴 or 上告; 上訴 is used when all forms are meant: 上訴する, 上訴権, 上訴期間.

examples[].german: We pay tribute to the achievements of our predecessors.
As a pioneer in this field, she has guided young researchers.
In the mountains, it is safest to follow an experienced guide.
en.notes: 先達 is someone who walked a path first and leads others on it: a pioneer or experienced predecessor in a field. Typical: 先達の教え/知恵/功績, 〜の先達として. It is elevated and respectful; in everyday speech people say 先輩 or 先人. Originally it denotes the leader of pilgrim groups in Shugendō; besides せんだつ, the reading せんだち is also common.

examples[].german: Nothing is as painful as parting from a blood relative.
For sixty years he kept searching for the relatives from whom he had been separated by the war.
My grandmother is my only blood relative.
en.notes: 肉親 denotes the closest blood relatives (parents, children, siblings) and stresses the physical and emotional bond: 肉親の情, 肉親を亡くす, 唯一の肉親. It is narrower than 親戚 or 親類 (relatives in general) and warmer than the legal 親族. It is often met in serious contexts such as death, illness or separation.

examples[].german: Free of family ties, he travels the world unencumbered.
He had many dependents, so he could not easily change jobs.
As a monk without family ties, he lived quietly in a mountain temple.
en.notes: 係累 are dependents one has to provide for, and in a wider sense everything that binds and restricts one. It mostly appears negated or as a burden: 係累がない "unattached, without family", 係累が多い, 係累に縛られる. It is literary; in everyday speech people say 家族 or 扶養家族, and for social obligations rather しがらみ.

examples[].german: We held a social gathering to deepen friendship.
A barbecue event was planned to help the new employees get to know each other.
We went to a hot spring on the neighborhood association's social trip.
en.notes: 親睦 is friendly togetherness in a group, such as among colleagues, neighbors or club members. It almost always appears in set combinations: 親睦を深める/図る, 親睦会 "social gathering", 親睦旅行, 親睦団体. It sounds more formal than 仲良くなる and refers to the group atmosphere, not to a single close friendship like 親交.

examples[].german: He is known as a person with a wide circle of acquaintances.
Many famous people appear in the writer's memoir of his associates.
As a student, he socialized actively with international students.
en.notes: 交遊 denotes sociable contact with friends and acquaintances: going out, meeting and doing things together. Typical: 〜と交遊がある, 交遊範囲が広い, 交遊録 "memoir of associates". The identically read 交友 means rather the friendship or the friends themselves (交友関係 is the more common spelling); 交遊 stresses doing things together. Both are literary; in conversation people say 付き合い.

examples[].german: I am grateful for her attentive thoughtfulness.
Saying "please don't trouble yourself", he declined the tea.
He is thoughtful, so people rely on him at work.
en.notes: 気遣い is attentive consideration, thinking ahead about the needs of others, a highly valued trait in Japanese. Typical: 細やかな気遣い, 気遣いができる人, 〜への気遣い. Very common are the polite formulas お気遣いありがとうございます and お気遣いなく "please don't go to any trouble". The verb is 気遣う "to worry about someone"; 配慮 is more formal and matter-of-fact, 心配 stresses the worry itself.

examples[].german: We must not forget compassion for the sick.
When her husband came home tired, his wife spoke kind words to him.
We aim to build a town where consideration for the elderly can be felt.
en.notes: 労り (mostly いたわり in kana) is compassionate care toward the weak, sick, elderly or exhausted: one shows consideration and spares them. Typical: いたわりの気持ち/言葉, 〜へのいたわり. The verb is 労る/いたわる "to go easy on, to look after" (体をいたわる). Unlike 気遣い, which means general attentiveness, いたわり puts the foreground on sympathy for someone in a difficult situation.

examples[].german: I wrote a thank-you letter to my beloved teacher.
The deceased was revered and loved by the people of the area.
The employees held deep respect and affection for the president.
en.notes: 敬愛 combines respect (敬) and affection (愛): one looks up to someone and is fond of them at the same time. Typical as an attributive する-verb: 敬愛する先生/作家, and also 〜を敬愛する, 〜から敬愛される, 敬愛の念を抱く. The word is elevated; 尊敬 stresses only esteem, 親愛 only affection (親愛なる〜 "Dear ..." in letters).

examples[].german: Respecting one's elders is an important form of courtesy.
Respect for the Aged Day is a day to honor older people and celebrate longevity.
The people of this village have revered the mountain god since long ago.
en.notes: 敬う means to esteem and honor someone, above all elders, parents, teachers, gods or ancestors: 年長者を敬う, 神仏を敬う. It describes a basic attitude or duty rather than a personal feeling; 尊敬する is more everyday and expresses personal admiration (尊敬する人 "role model"). As a noun one usually uses 敬意 "respect" (敬意を払う/表する).

examples[].german: I spoke to the child gently, as if to reason with him.
The teacher counseled the student who had lied on the importance of being honest.
My mother told me not to overdo it, so I extended my hospital stay by a day.
en.notes: 諭す means calmly and reasonably making someone understand what they are doing wrong or what is right, typically from parents, teachers or elders toward younger people. Construction: 人を諭す, 人に〜と諭す or 〜ように諭す. Unlike 叱る "to scold", the tone is gentle; 説得する "to persuade" aims at a decision, 諭す at insight. Intensified: 教え諭す.

en.meaning: destruction (of documents); cancellation (of a contract); reversal (of a judgment)
examples[].german: The Supreme Court reversed the original judgment.
Please destroy documents containing personal information with a shredder.
The other country unilaterally abrogated the treaty.
en.notes: 破棄 means to destroy something or declare it invalid. Common in everyday use is the destruction of documents and data (書類を破棄する); also the unilateral cancellation of contracts, engagements and agreements (条約を破棄する, 婚約破棄). Legally it denotes the reversal of a judgment by the higher court (原判決を破棄する, 破棄差し戻し). Not to be confused with 廃棄 ("disposing of" waste or goods).

examples[].german: I was reprimanded for my rude attitude.
My mother scolded my younger brother for looking at his phone during the meal.
The chairman calmly rebuked the committee member who had become emotional.
en.notes: 窘める (mostly たしなめる in kana) means to reprimand someone calmly but clearly for inappropriate behavior or words, more a brief rebuke than a lecture. Typical: 〜を(やんわりと)たしなめる, 軽率な発言をたしなめる. It is milder than 叱る and also occurs among equals or toward elders. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 嗜む "to devote oneself to something, to enjoy in moderation".

examples[].german: It was hard to calm her down when she was angry.
I gently soothed the child, who was afraid of the thunder.
en.notes: 人を宥める means to calm or soothe someone, for example when they are angry or frightened. This transitive ichidan verb forms 宥めます・宥めて・宥めない. The kana spelling なだめる is common. Unlike 宥す（ゆるす, to forgive）, it is about the person's feelings, not about forgiving a fault.

en.meaning: to protect; to stand up for
examples[].german: It is only natural to protect the weak.
Favoring his injured right foot, he ran all the way to the finish.
She covered for her friend and lied to the teacher.
en.notes: 庇う (mostly かばう in kana) means to protect someone from attacks, criticism or punishment by standing in front of them, also in the negative sense of "covering for": 部下をかばう, 犯人をかばう. It is also used for body parts: 痛めた足をかばって歩く "to walk favoring the injured leg". Unlike 守る, which generally means "to protect, to keep" (約束を守る), かばう stresses partisan advocacy for someone.

examples[].german: It takes courage to admonish a friend for his mistakes.
The retainer, at the risk of his life, remonstrated with his lord about his reckless plan.
Not a single executive was able to remonstrate with the president about his arbitrary decisions.
en.notes: 諫める means to advise against a mistake and admonish someone, above all a superior, traditionally the lord, today for example the boss or parents: 主君を諫める, 社長の独断を諫める. This is the difference from 諭す and たしなめる, which mostly go from top to bottom. The word is elevated; there is also the spelling 諌める and the noun 諫言 "admonition to a superior".

examples[].german: I will do my very best to repay the kindness I was shown.
In recognition of the employees' efforts, the company paid a special bonus.
We got one back in the final inning, but we still lost the game.
en.notes: 報いる means to respond appropriately to kindness, expectations or effort that one has received. The recipient takes に: 恩に報いる, 期待に報いる, 努力に報いる. The passive form 報われる "to pay off, to be rewarded" is very common (努力が報われた). In the sense of "to strike back" it appears almost only in 一矢を報いる "to land a counterblow"; the noun 報い often means "deserved punishment" (当然の報い).

en.meaning: to become attached, to grow tame
examples[].german: The child quickly became attached to the teacher.
Our cat is shy around strangers and doesn't warm up to guests easily.
The dog I rescued has finally taken to me.
en.notes: 懐く (usually written なつく in kana) means that a child or animal gains trust and becomes affectionate: 〜に懐く, 犬が懐く. The subject is almost always the child or animal that turns to someone. The transitive counterpart is 懐ける "to tame, to win over"; related is 人懐っこい "friendly, sociable". Do not confuse it with 懐かしい "nostalgic", which uses the same kanji.

examples[].german: I'll be careful that my support for him doesn't end up doing more harm than good.
The teacher always favors that one student.
I took a friend to my favorite sushi restaurant.
en.notes: 贔屓 (often written ひいき in kana) means to favor or support someone. As a する-verb: 〜をひいきする; pejorative えこひいき "unfair favoritism". Positive uses: ひいきの店/チーム "regular haunt, favorite team", ご贔屓に "thank you for your continued patronage" (shopkeeper to customers), ひいき目に見ても "even looking at it favorably". 判官びいき is sympathy for the underdog; 贔屓の引き倒し means harming someone by supporting them too much.

examples[].german: We celebrated quietly, with family only.
There has been a death in my family, so I will take tomorrow off.
The company was criticized for trying to cover up a scandal among its own people.
en.notes: 身内 are one's own relatives, and in a wider sense members of one's own company or group, "our people" as opposed to outsiders. Typical: 身内だけで (式を挙げる/葬儀を行う), 身内の恥, 身内びいき "nepotism". As a polite explanation, 身内に不幸がありまして "there has been a death in the family" is a set phrase. Unlike 親戚 "relatives", 身内 stresses belonging to the close circle.

examples[].german: I worry about appearances and can't say what I really think.
I hid from my parents that I had lost my job, because it looked bad.
I want to value my own happiness more than what people think.
en.notes: 世間体 is the impression one makes in the eyes of society (世間), that is, what neighbors, relatives or colleagues might think. Typical: 世間体を気にする, 世間体が悪い "it looks bad", 世間体を繕う. Unlike 評判 "reputation" or 体面 "dignity, prestige", it is about social conformity and fear of gossip, so the word often sounds critical.

examples[].german: He is overextending himself to keep up appearances.
Because it concerned the honor of the nation, the government responded cautiously.
My grandfather, who values the family's honor, strongly opposed the divorce.
en.notes: 体面 is the outward dignity and prestige that a person, family or institution wants to maintain in front of others: 体面を保つ/重んじる, 体面を傷つける, 体面にかかわる. It is more formal than メンツ "face" and stresses one's own dignity, whereas 世間体 refers to the opinion of other people. Do not confuse it with the identically read 対面 "meeting, face-to-face encounter".

examples[].german: One must comply with a final judgment.
To overturn a final judgment, the only option is to request a retrial.
On the basis of the final judgment, the opposing party's assets were seized.
en.notes: 確定判決 is a judgment against which no ordinary appeal (控訴, 上告) is possible any more, that is, one that has become "final and binding". As a verb one says 判決が確定する ("the judgment becomes final"). A 確定判決 can only be challenged through a retrial (再審) and is the basis for enforcement, e.g. 確定判決に基づく強制執行. Technical language from law and the news.

examples[].german: He lost face and was left without standing.
I couldn't keep my promise; I am truly ashamed.
By scoring the winning goal, he upheld his honor as the team's ace.
en.notes: 面目 is "face" in the sense of honor and standing in front of others. Typical: 面目を失う/潰す "to lose face / to embarrass someone", 面目が立つ, 面目を保つ, 面目丸つぶれ. Very common is 面目ない "I am ashamed, I am terribly sorry" as an apology. The reading めんもく is also used, especially in 面目躍如 "living up to one's reputation, in one's element" and 面目一新.

en.meaning: sense of honor, sense of shame
examples[].german: Conduct without any sense of shame is unacceptable.
Above all else, politicians are required to have a sense of integrity.
The lawmaker was forced to resign over his shameless behavior.
en.notes: 廉恥 is the sense of decency and honor, that is, the ability to feel ashamed of wrongdoing (廉 "honest, upright" + 恥 "shame"). On its own it is very rare; it appears almost only in 廉恥心 and above all in its opposite 破廉恥 "shameless, scandalous" (破廉恥な行為). It is literary and morally weighty; in everyday speech one says 恥を知る "to have a sense of shame" or 恥知らず "shameless".

examples[].german: My face turned bright red from embarrassment.
To sing in front of people, you have to throw away your self-consciousness.
People who put on makeup on the train are sometimes criticized for having no sense of shame.
en.notes: 羞恥心 is a sense of shame in the sense of embarrassment and self-consciousness, for example when one feels exposed: 羞恥心がある/ない, 羞恥心を感じる, 羞恥心を捨てる. Unlike 廉恥心, the moral shame over wrongdoing, this is about awkwardness and shyness. In everyday speech one usually says 恥ずかしい; 羞恥心 is a factual, descriptive word.

examples[].german: It looks pathetic when someone can't accept the inevitable.
He won't admit it even when confronted with the evidence; he just can't accept defeat.
The audience applauded him for admitting defeat gracefully and without hesitation.
en.notes: 往生際 is literally "the moment of dying" (往生 "rebirth in paradise; death" + 際 "moment"). Today it is used almost only in 往生際が悪い "unable to give up, refusing to admit defeat", for example when someone makes excuses despite a clear loss. Less often in a positive sense: 往生際がいい "to yield gracefully". The expression is colloquial and reproachful, and is often directed at someone: 往生際が悪いぞ.

examples[].german: I'll cut off my lingering attachments and start a new life.
I still haven't gotten over the lover I broke up with.
I have no attachment to this town, so a transfer doesn't bother me.
en.notes: 未練 is the inability to let go: one still clings to a person, thing or possibility even though it is over. Typical: 〜に未練がある/ない, 未練が残る, 未練を断ち切る; as an adjective 未練がましい "pitifully clinging" and colloquially 未練たらたら. Especially common after breakups. 後悔 is regret over one's own actions, whereas 未練 is wistful clinging.

examples[].german: These are days of anguish over anxiety about the future.
It is a novel that carefully portrays the protagonist's anguish.
After long inner torment, he gave up the path of medicine.
en.notes: 懊悩 is a strongly literary word for tormenting inner brooding and mental anguish. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に懊悩する; as a noun: 懊悩の日々, 懊悩の末に. It is much stronger and more literary than 悩む or 苦悩 and is found mainly in novels, biographies and essays.

examples[].german: He decided immediately, without hesitation.
After hesitating for a while, she told the truth.
He wavered for nearly a year over whether to change jobs.
en.notes: 逡巡 is the literary word for "hesitation, wavering", an indecisive back and forth before acting. As an intransitive する-verb it typically appears in しばらく逡巡した末に "after hesitating for a while" and 逡巡することなく "without hesitation". In everyday speech one says ためらう or 迷う; 躊躇 is a similarly formal synonym, but 逡巡 stresses more the irresolute shrinking back. Common in novels, speeches and commentary.

examples[].german: You should ask for help without hesitating.
Without a moment's hesitation, he jumped into the river.
When I saw the price, I hesitated to buy it.
en.notes: 躊躇 is hesitation before an action because one is unsure or has misgivings. Typical: 〜するのを躊躇する, 躊躇なく/躊躇せずに "without hesitating", 一瞬の躊躇もなく. The same kanji also write the verb 躊躇う (ためらう) "to hesitate"; in conversation ためらう is more common, while ちゅうちょ sounds more formal. 迷う stresses wavering between options, 躊躇 stresses shrinking back from acting.

examples[].german: If one is too suspicious, human relationships break down.
Driven by suspicion, he secretly looked at his wife's phone.
Out of suspicion, the dictator purged his close associates one after another.
en.notes: 猜疑心 is deep-seated distrust of people: one assumes bad intentions on their part. Typical: 猜疑心が強い, 猜疑心に駆られる "to be driven by suspicion", 猜疑心を抱く. 疑い is neutral doubt about a matter; 猜疑心 is a trait of character or a feeling toward others and often involves envy or jealousy. The word is literary.

examples[].german: They eye each other with suspicion.
He is very distrustful and doesn't trust even close friends.
Driven by suspicion, the king even kept his loyal retainers at a distance.
en.notes: 猜疑 is suspicious distrust: one attributes bad intentions to others without real grounds, often out of jealousy or envy. On its own it is rare, and it almost always occurs in fixed combinations such as 猜疑心 "distrust" (猜疑心が強い "very distrustful"), 猜疑の目で見る "to view with suspicion" or 猜疑に駆られる "to be driven by suspicion". More neutral are 疑い and 疑念 "doubt"; 猜疑 always has a negative, almost pathological nuance. Literary.

examples[].german: The court granted an injunction to halt publication.
The residents applied for an injunction demanding that the construction be stopped.
After the injunction was ordered, the concert was canceled.
en.notes: 仮処分 is a provisional court order that secures a state of affairs before the main proceedings are decided, for example a ban on sale, construction or publication. Typical phrases: 仮処分を申し立てる ("to apply for"), 仮処分を認める/決定する, 〜差し止めの仮処分. While 仮差押え secures monetary claims by seizing assets, 仮処分 concerns other rights and conditions.

examples[].german: It was a scene that stirred pity.
More than anything, he hated being looked at with pity.
Wallowing in self-pity won't change anything.
en.notes: 憐憫 is pity or compassion for someone who is doing badly, often from a position of superiority. Typical: 憐憫の情 (を催す/を抱く), 憐憫の目で見る, 自己憐憫 "self-pity". It is literary; in everyday speech one says 同情 or かわいそうに思う. The person being pitied often finds 憐憫 condescending, much like 哀れみ.

examples[].german: It is important to approach people without hostility.
He openly showed his hostility toward his rival.
The stray cat glared at us with hostile eyes.
en.notes: 敵意 is a hostile attitude toward someone. Typical: 敵意を抱く/持つ, 敵意をむき出しにする "to be openly hostile", 敵意のこもった目, 〜に敵意を向ける. The word is neutral and common; 悪意 means ill intent (even without an adversary), and 反感 is more of an aversion or resentment.

examples[].german: The culture of the organization needs to be changed from the ground up.
I am the type who can't drink alcohol.
This medicine didn't agree with me, and I broke out in a rash.
en.notes: 体質 is first of all one's physical constitution: アレルギー体質, 太りやすい体質, 体質に合う/合わない "to agree / not agree with one's body", 体質改善. Figuratively it denotes the deeply rooted character of an organization or industry, usually critically: 古い体質, 隠蔽体質 "culture of cover-ups". Unlike 性格 "personality" or 体格 "build", it concerns innate or ingrained tendencies.

examples[].german: He rides a spirited horse with skill.
My grandmother had a frank, easygoing nature and was liked by everyone.
He has a rough temper and shouts right away.
en.notes: 気性 is the innate temperament of a person or animal, above all how easily it gets excited: 気性が激しい/荒い "fiery, hot-tempered", 気性がさっぱりしている "easygoing, straightforward", 負けず嫌いの気性. Unlike 性格, the whole personality, 気性 stresses the basic emotional nature. 気質 (きしつ) is similar but sounds more objective.

examples[].german: He is respected as a man of backbone.
The plucky reporter did not bow to pressure and reported the truth.
The department head lamented that young people these days lack backbone.
en.notes: 気骨 (きこつ) is inner firmness: the courage to hold to one's convictions and not bow to the powerful or to pressure. Typical: 気骨のある人物/政治家, 気骨を示す. It is appreciative and somewhat elevated. Note: read きぼね, the same spelling means "mental strain", as in 気骨が折れる "to be nerve-racking".

examples[].german: With a magnanimous attitude, he forgave his subordinate's mistake.
The president stayed calm and listened to everyone's opinion.
Grandfather just laughed good-naturedly even at his grandchildren's pranks.
en.notes: 鷹揚 describes a generous, composed attitude that does not get worked up over trifles; originally the proud, calm circling of a hawk (鷹). As a な-adjective: 鷹揚な態度/人柄, 鷹揚に構える "to stay calm and unbothered", 鷹揚にうなずく. It sounds elevated and is often used of older people or superiors. Similar are 寛大 "magnanimous" and おおらか "easygoing, big-hearted"; do not confuse it with the identically read 応用 "application".

examples[].german: I was appalled by his shameless behavior.
He had the nerve to come to borrow money again without having repaid his debt.
After such a blunder, how can he carry himself with such brazenness?
en.notes: 厚顔 literally means "thick face" and denotes brazenness: someone feels no shame even though they have every reason to. Most common in the four-character compound 厚顔無恥 "shameless and brazen"; also 厚顔にも "to have the nerve to ..." and 厚顔な態度. It is literary and sharply reproachful; in everyday speech one says 図々しい or 厚かましい.

examples[].german: He applies himself to his work with a commendable attitude.
My son, commendably, offered on his own to wash the dishes.
Having been scolded, he put on a contrite face, but whether he truly regrets it is doubtful.
en.notes: 殊勝 praises an attitude as admirable and well-behaved, especially in younger people or in someone from whom one wouldn't have expected it: 殊勝な心がけ, 殊勝にも "commendably". Because it easily praises from above, it is not used for superiors. Irony often resonates: 殊勝な顔をする "to put on a contrite look", which may not be genuine. More neutral are 感心な or 立派な.

examples[].german: You can't do this job unless you have thick nerves.
Even after being scolded that much, he calmly shows up late again. What a nerve.
Even after the great earthquake, she brazenly kept her shop open.
en.notes: 図太い describes someone who cannot be thrown off balance by anything and does not shrink even from embarrassing situations, "strong-nerved" or "brazen" depending on context. Typical: 図太い神経, 神経が図太い, 図太く生きる. It sounds positive when it refers to resilience and negative when it refers to impudence; 図々しい, by contrast, is clearly negative, "pushy, cheeky". The opposite is 繊細 "sensitive" or 気が小さい "timid".

en.meaning: very serious, overly earnest, deadly serious
examples[].german: His overly earnest nature works against him, and he is inflexible.
My joke was taken completely seriously, and I was at a loss.
Being so conscientious, he has never missed a deadline.
en.notes: 生真面目 means "through and through serious and conscientious"; 生 stresses "unadulterated, pure" here. It can be meant appreciatively (生真面目な人柄), but often carries the nuance "too serious, humorless, inflexible": 生真面目すぎる, 生真面目に受け取る "to take something far too seriously". 真面目 alone is neutral-positive "diligent, serious"; 生真面目 intensifies it to the point of excess.

examples[].german: The creditor had the debtor's assets provisionally attached.
My bank account was provisionally attached, and I can no longer withdraw money.
Since our business partner seemed about to go bankrupt, we applied to the court for a provisional attachment.
en.notes: 仮差押え is the provisional seizure of a debtor's assets so that a monetary claim remains secured until judgment: 仮差押えを申し立てる, 口座を仮差押えする, in the passive 仮差押えされる. The final seizure after a judgment is called 差し押さえ. In statutes it is often written without okurigana as 仮差押.

examples[].german: You must not fall into a pessimistic way of thinking.
Since his heartbreak, he has become thoroughly world-weary.
A world-weary atmosphere hangs over that poet's works.
en.notes: 厭世的 means "world-weary, tired of life": one is weary of the world and of living (厭 "to loathe" + 世 "world"). Typical: 厭世的な考え/気分/作家, 厭世的になる. It is stronger and more existential than 悲観的 "pessimistic" about an outcome, and sounds literary; related are 厭世観 "pessimistic view of the world, Weltschmerz" and 厭世主義.

examples[].german: Thanks to his optimistic nature, he overcame the difficulties.
"Oh, it'll work out somehow," he says; he is always optimistic.
If you think about things too optimistically, your preparation gets sloppy.
en.notes: 楽天的 is a な-adjective that describes above all a temperament: someone who worries little and trusts that everything will work out (楽天的な性格, 楽天的に考える). The close synonym 楽観的 refers more to the assessment of a concrete situation (楽観的な見通し "optimistic outlook"). Such a person is a 楽天家; the opposite is 悲観的 "pessimistic". Depending on context, 楽天的 can also sound slightly critical in the sense of "carefree".

examples[].german: I'm introverted and bad at appearing in front of people.
My son is introverted and often reads alone on his days off.
Introverted people tend to prefer small gatherings to big drinking parties.
en.notes: 内向的 is a な-adjective for an inward-turned personality: 内向的な性格, 内向的な人. The opposite is 外向的 "extroverted". In everyday speech, for "shy" one tends to say 内気 or 人見知り; 内向的 sounds somewhat more objective, almost psychological, and is not necessarily negative. Figuratively it can also describe an "inward-looking" policy or attitude (内向的な政策).

examples[].german: She is sociable and makes friends quickly.
In the interview, I emphasized my outgoing personality.
The older brother is sociable, but the younger one is shy around strangers.
en.notes: 社交的 is a な-adjective for someone who likes being among people and makes contacts easily: 社交的な人, 社交的な性格. Close in meaning is 外向的 "extroverted"; the everyday opposite is often 人見知り "shy around strangers". Do not confuse it with 社交辞令, which means "polite formula, empty compliment". In job applications and self-descriptions, 社交的 is a common positive trait.

examples[].german: You must not drown in fleeting pleasures.
It is a novel about a young man who lives for the moment without thinking about the future.
His fleeting romances never last long.
en.notes: 刹那 is a Buddhist term for "the shortest instant". 刹那的 describes an attitude aimed only at the moment with no thought for the future, or things that last only briefly: 刹那的な快楽 "fleeting pleasures", 刹那的に生きる "to live for the moment". The word is rather literary and usually has a critical or melancholy coloring. More neutral for "transient" are 一時的 or はかない.

examples[].german: I take my hat off to such devoted care.
She continued to support her sick husband devotedly.
There are volunteers who work selflessly for the children of the community.
en.notes: 献身的 ("self-giving", from 献身 "devotion, self-sacrifice") describes selfless commitment to other people or a cause. Typically adverbial: 献身的に支える, 献身的に尽くす, 献身的に看病する; attributive 献身的な介護, 献身的な努力. Unlike 一生懸命, which only expresses great effort, 献身的 stresses sacrifice for the benefit of others. The tone is appreciative and rather elevated.

examples[].german: Selfish behavior loses the trust of those around you.
Everyone was appalled at his selfish attitude of thinking only of his own profit.
"The Selfish Gene" became a worldwide bestseller.
en.notes: 利己的 ("intent on one's own benefit") is the objective, literary word for egoistic behavior: 利己的な考え, 利己的な行動, 利己主義 "egoism". Colloquially one rather says わがまま (willful, capricious) or 自己中 (short for 自己中心的 "self-centered"). The opposite is 利他的 "altruistic". Well known is the book title 利己的な遺伝子 ("The Selfish Gene").

examples[].german: I take part in volunteer activities in an altruistic spirit.
Altruistic behavior can sometimes be seen in animals too.
He is known as an altruistic business owner who thinks of others more than his own gain.
en.notes: 利他的 ("benefiting others") is the counterpart of 利己的 and means "altruistic, selfless": 利他的な行動, 利他的な精神, 利他主義 "altruism". It is a rather literary word from ethics, biology and economic philosophy. In everyday speech, selfless people are rather described with 思いやりがある or 人のために尽くす.

examples[].german: A calculating way of dealing with people doesn't last.
It is rumored that she married him for calculated reasons.
People who approach others out of calculation are quickly seen through.
en.notes: 打算 is weighing advantages and disadvantages for oneself; 打算的 therefore means "calculating" and is clearly pejorative: 打算的な人, 打算的な結婚, 打算的に動く. Colloquially 計算高い means the same. The base word also appears in expressions like 打算が働く "calculation is at work" or 打算抜きで "without ulterior motives".

examples[].german: He has a cleanliness obsession and avoids eating out.
He is scrupulous about money and doesn't tolerate even a one-yen discrepancy.
Our germophobic mother makes us wash our hands as soon as we get home.
en.notes: 潔癖 is a noun and な-adjective with two meanings: excessive cleanliness (潔癖な人, very commonly 潔癖症 "obsessive cleanliness", colloquially also used for "cleaning mania") and moral integrity that tolerates no dishonesty (金銭に潔癖だ). In the second sense it is praising, in the first often slightly mocking. Close in meaning to the second sense are 清廉 and 生真面目.

examples[].german: Ratification of a treaty requires the Diet's approval.
That country has not yet ratified the agreement.
The required number of countries ratified, and the treaty finally came into force.
en.notes: 批准 is the "ratification" of an international treaty by the state, in Japan after the consent of the parliament 国会. Typical: 条約を批准する, 批准書 "instrument of ratification", 批准書を交換する. The order matters: first a treaty is signed by representatives (調印・署名), then ratified, and only then does it enter into force (発効). In everyday life the word practically never occurs.

en.meaning: main action; the merits (of a case)
examples[].german: After the injunction, the main action was filed.
The suit was dismissed before it reached examination of the merits.
In its judgment on the merits, the court rejected the plaintiff's claim.
en.notes: 本案 denotes, in procedural law, the main issue, that is, the actual matter in dispute on which a decision is made on the merits: 本案訴訟 ("main action", as opposed to 仮処分), 本案審理, 本案判決. If a suit is dismissed already on formal grounds without reaching the merits, this is called 却下; dismissal on the merits is called 棄却. In parliament and meetings, 本案 can also mean "the present bill" (本案に賛成).

examples[].german: Stingy people easily lose friends.
My grandfather was famous as a miser and never wasted even a sheet of paper.
It is sometimes said that the richer people are, the stingier they are.
en.notes: 吝嗇 is a very literary word for stinginess, as a noun and な-adjective (吝嗇な人); the miser is called 吝嗇家. In everyday speech one almost always says けち (けちな人, けちる) instead. 吝嗇 is found mainly in literature, essays and character descriptions, and sounds detached and judgmental compared with けち. The kanji are rare and often given furigana.

examples[].german: There are people who start trouble over trivial matters.
There was a row among the siblings over how to divide the inheritance.
A minor squabble arose over the seating order at the meeting.
en.notes: 悶着 is a quarrel or hassle, usually over rather small but unpleasant matters: 悶着を起こす "to cause trouble", 悶着が起きる. Very common is the form 一悶着 (ひともんちゃく): 一悶着ある/起きる "there is a to-do, a row". Close in meaning are もめごと and the colloquial トラブル; 喧嘩 is more direct and can also be physical.

examples[].german: Friction between departments is hampering operations.
The introduction of the new system created friction with the veteran employees.
Quite a few households suffer from friction between daughter-in-law and mother-in-law.
en.notes: 軋轢 (literally the "grinding" of wheels, cf. 軋む) denotes friction and tension between people or groups: 軋轢が生じる, 軋轢を生む, 軋轢を避ける, 〜との軋轢. It is a literary word from news and specialist texts. 摩擦 can be used similarly (貿易摩擦), but is more general and also physical; 対立 is open opposition, whereas 軋轢 is more smoldering discord.

en.meaning: to be fed up, to be daunted
examples[].german: I am fed up with his bragging.
Having to listen to the same lecture every day, I really got sick of it.
I'm worn down by the muggy summer heat every year.
en.notes: 辟易 is almost always used as a する-verb: 〜に辟易する "to be sick of something, to be unable to bear something any longer", often in the state 辟易している. Typical triggers are long speeches, bragging, heat or smells. It is more literary and stronger than うんざりする, which is more usual in conversation. The older sense "to recoil, to shrink back" is rare today.

examples[].german: He is dejected because he failed the exam.
The players couldn't hide their disappointment when they heard the result.
There's no need to be so discouraged over a single failure.
en.notes: 落胆 (literally "the gallbladder falls") is deep disappointment and dejection after a failure; as an intransitive する-verb: 落胆する, 結果に落胆する. Set phrase: 落胆の色を隠せない "cannot hide one's disappointment". In conversation one usually says がっかりする; 落胆 is more literary and sounds heavier. 失望 stresses more that expectations of someone were disappointed.

examples[].german: He recovered from the depths of despondency.
After his business failed, he returned to his hometown in despair.
What supported me through those dark days was my friends' encouragement.
en.notes: 失意 is the state of deep disappointment when hopes have failed; it is a literary noun, not a する-verb. Typical phrases: 失意のどん底 "the depths of despair", 失意のうちに "in deep disappointment", 失意の日々. The opposite concept is 得意 in the sense of "success, elation" (得意の絶頂). Compared with 落胆, 失意 describes more a longer-lasting phase of life.

examples[].german: I let out a cry of admiration at the craftsman's skill.
The tourists involuntarily marveled at the magnificent sunset.
If you use too many exclamation marks at the end of sentences, your writing looks childish.
en.notes: 感嘆 is astonished admiration that is often voiced aloud: 感嘆の声を上げる/漏らす, 〜に感嘆する. It is more elevated than 感心する (to be impressed, to appreciate) and more spontaneous than 感動 (inner emotion). Grammatically important is 感嘆符 "exclamation mark"; 感嘆文 is an exclamatory sentence.

en.meaning: remnant, lingering trace, reluctance to part
examples[].german: I'm reluctant to part, but this is where we say goodbye.
In this town, traces of the Edo period can still be seen today.
Even after the graduation ceremony, the students were reluctant to part and didn't go home for a long time.
en.notes: 名残 has two main meanings: traces or remnants of something past (昔の名残, 江戸時代の名残, 夏の名残) and the wistful feeling at parting (名残を惜しむ "to be reluctant to part"). The adjective 名残惜しい "hard to part" is very common. For purely material remains one rather says 跡 or 痕跡; 名残 always has a nostalgic undertone.

examples[].german: Many young people are devoted to his ideas.
In my youth, I was completely enthralled by a certain philosopher.
He admires his master so much that he has even come to talk like him.
en.notes: 心酔 means being completely captivated by a person or their ideas: 〜に心酔する, often as a state 心酔している. Typical objects are teachers, thinkers, artists or ideologies. 夢中になる is more everyday and also used for hobbies; 傾倒 stresses more intellectual devotion, 崇拝 worship. 心酔 can point slightly critically to a lack of distance.

examples[].german: I keep luggage I don't use in the storeroom.
Old photo albums turned up from the storeroom at my grandmother's house.
This room has no window, so it is labeled as a storeroom on the floor plan.
en.notes: 納戸 is a windowless storage room in a Japanese house, traditionally for clothing, household goods and dishes. On present-day floor plans, 納戸 (or "S" for サービスルーム) stands for a room that does not count as living space because it lacks windows. To be distinguished from 押し入れ (a wall closet for futons) and 物置 (a shed, storage place). As a color name (納戸色) it denotes a muted gray-blue.

en.meaning: prima facie showing (lower standard of proof)
examples[].german: An application for an injunction requires a prima facie showing of the right.
The applicant submitted photos and e-mails as materials to substantiate the claim.
This procedure doesn't require full proof; a prima facie showing is enough.
en.notes: 疎明 is a procedural-law term: the judge only has to be convinced that an assertion is probably true, not that it is proven with certainty. This is sufficient especially in urgent proceedings such as 仮処分 and 仮差押え. Typical: 疎明する, 疎明資料 ("materials substantiating the claim"), 〜の疎明が必要だ. The opposite is 証明 ("full proof"). Older spelling: 疏明.

examples[].german: Keeping dishcloths clean is the basis of hygiene management.
I dried the washed dishes with a dishcloth and put them back on the shelf.
Could you wipe the table with the table cloth?
en.notes: 布巾 is a clean cloth for the kitchen and table: for drying dishes or wiping the table (台布巾). Typical: 布巾で拭く, 布巾を絞る, 布巾を煮沸する. For dirty jobs such as floors, one uses 雑巾 instead; mixing the two up would be a real faux pas in Japan. タオル is a towel for the body.

examples[].german: I wipe and polish the floor with a rag.
Please wring out the rag well before wiping the windows.
In elementary school, it is customary to bring one rag at the start of the new term.
en.notes: 雑巾 is the cleaning rag for floors, windows and furniture, often sewn from old towels. Typical: 雑巾で拭く, 雑巾を絞る, 雑巾がけ "wiping the floor on your knees with a rag" - in Japanese schools a daily cleaning task for the pupils. For dishes and dining tables one never uses a 雑巾, but a 布巾.

examples[].german: I sweep the entrance with a broom and dustpan.
I put the trash collected in the dustpan into the garbage bag.
I swept the broken glass into the dustpan with the broom and threw it away.
en.notes: 塵取り ("dust-taker") is the dustpan; in everyday life it is almost always written in kana: ちりとり. It usually appears together with the broom: ほうきとちりとり. Typical: ちりとりに集める, ちりとりで取る. 塵 means "dust" and also appears in 塵も積もれば山となる "many a little makes a mickle".

examples[].german: I sweep fallen leaves with a bamboo broom.
A witch flies through the sky on a broom.
We swept the classroom floor with a broom and then arranged the desks.
en.notes: 箒 is the broom; the kanji is rare, and in everyday writing it is almost always written ほうき. The related verb is 掃く "to sweep": ほうきで掃く. In compounds the initial sound is voiced: 竹箒 (たけぼうき) "bamboo broom". A vacuum cleaner is called 掃除機; ほうき and ちりとり are often mentioned as a pair. A well-known image: the witch flying on a broom.

examples[].german: I fill a washtub with water and do the laundry.
When I called to inquire, I got passed from one department to another.
In the summer garden, the children are playing in the water in a tub.
en.notes: 盥 is a shallow tub or basin, formerly used for washing clothes and bathing small children; today it is usually written たらい. Typical: たらいに水を張る. The idiom たらい回し（にする/される） is important: passing a person or a matter from office to office without anyone feeling responsible, for example at government offices or hospitals.

en.meaning: deficit, loss; missing part, damage (to parts)
examples[].german: Due to the aging of the equipment, some parts have been damaged.
This term, we posted a loss of 30 million yen.
If part of the gene is missing, one is more prone to this disease.
en.notes: 欠損 covers two areas: in accounting, a deficit or loss (欠損を出す, 欠損金, 欠損を補う), and otherwise the partial absence or damage of something, e.g. 歯の欠損, 遺伝子の欠損, 部品の欠損. As an intransitive する-verb: 一部が欠損している. It is a technical word; in general business one usually says 赤字 or 損失 for losses.

examples[].german: I spend my days off almost entirely reading.
Lately I've stopped cooking for myself and it's convenience-store bento all the time.
The rumor going around is that he will be the next president.
en.notes: 専ら is mostly written in kana: もっぱら. It means that one does almost exclusively or predominantly one thing: 休日はもっぱら読書, 最近はもっぱら電車通勤だ. Compared with 主に "mainly", もっぱら sounds stronger and somewhat elevated. Set phrase: もっぱらの噂 "what everyone is talking about".

examples[].german: The success is entirely thanks to all of you.
This accident was due solely to our lack of checking.
We sincerely ask for your continued support.
en.notes: 偏に (usually ひとえに) is an elevated adverb meaning "solely, wholly". Typical in thank-you speeches and apologies: ひとえに皆様のおかげです, ひとえに私の不徳の致すところです. In formal requests it strengthens sincerity: ひとえにお願い申し上げます. In everyday speech one says simply ただ or 全く. Do not confuse it with 一重 "single, single-layered", which is read the same.

examples[].german: There is no need to deliberately make the problem bigger.
This winter the cold is especially severe.
He made a point of emphasizing his own achievements.
en.notes: 殊更 (usually ことさら, also ことさらに) has two meanings: "deliberately, ostentatiously", often critical when something is artificially emphasized (ことさら強調する, ことさら騒ぎ立てる), and "especially, particularly" (今年の夏はことさら暑い). In the first sense, わざと is the everyday word, in the second 特に; ことさら sounds more elevated in each case.

examples[].german: I should have met in person and talked after all.
Just as the forecast said, it did start raining in the afternoon.
I've eaten at many restaurants, but my mother's cooking is still the best.
en.notes: 矢張り is practically never written with kanji, but as やはり, colloquially やっぱり (very casually やっぱ). It expresses that an expectation is confirmed ("as expected"), that after reflection one comes to a conclusion ("after all, in the end"), or that something stays the same ("as before, likewise"). Typical: やはりそうだったか, やっぱりやめた "I'll skip it after all".

en.meaning: involvement (in a crime); joint liability; guilt by association
examples[].german: The election was invalidated under the guilt-by-association system for election violations.
The former minister was arrested for being implicated in the corruption case.
In the past, a criminal's family members were sometimes punished along with him.
en.notes: 連座 means to be drawn into a crime or scandal and held jointly responsible for it: 〜に連座する, 汚職事件に連座して逮捕される. Well known is the 連座制 in election law: if close aides of a candidate commit election offenses, the candidate's election can be invalidated. Historically it also refers to the joint punishment of relatives (guilt by association). It differs from an actual accomplice (共犯) in that one is implicated through one's connection to the act.

examples[].german: The long winter has finally come to an end.
I finally passed the exam on my third attempt.
The medicine is taking effect, and the fever has finally started to come down.
en.notes: 漸く (usually ようやく) means "finally" after a long wait or effort, and can also mean "gradually" or "barely". やっと is more emotional and colloquial and stresses relief; ようやく sounds more factual and fits well in news and reports. ついに stresses the culmination or final result, even with negative things.

en.meaning: moreover; besides; in addition; and yet
examples[].german: The quality is good, and what's more, the price is reasonable.
It started to rain. And on top of that, I don't have an umbrella.
He was warned many times, and yet he repeated the same mistake.
en.notes: しかも adds a second, often intensifying piece of information: "and what's more, on top of that" - in positive as well as negative contexts. Similar are それに (more colloquial, often when listing reasons) and その上 (somewhat more formal). More rarely it means "and yet" when the second contradicts the first. It is almost always written in kana; the kanji spelling 然も is obsolete and can also be read さも.

examples[].german: Among Japanese dishes, I like sushi in particular.
She is good at languages, and her English in particular is excellent.
This region is known especially for its beautiful autumn leaves.
en.notes: 取り分け as an adverb is mostly written in kana: とりわけ "especially, above all". It singles out one element from a group and is somewhat more elevated than 特に; 中でも is similar. There is also the noun 取り分け "portioning" from the verb 取り分ける "to divide food onto plates"; in that meaning it is usually written with kanji.

examples[].german: He slowly opened his mouth and began to speak.
The president rose unhurriedly and looked out of the window.
He slowly took a letter out of his pocket.
en.notes: 徐に (usually おもむろに) originally means "slowly, in a measured way, without haste" and often introduces a significant action: おもむろに立ち上がる, おもむろに口を開く. Many Japanese people today wrongly use it in the sense of "suddenly"; this counts as a mistake in exams and careful writing. Opposites: いきなり, 突然.

examples[].german: I am determined not to give up even if I fail.
Even if it rains, the match will take place as scheduled.
Even as a joke, you must not say such a thing.
en.notes: 仮令 is nowadays almost only written in kana: たとえ. It introduces a concessive clause and almost always occurs with 〜ても/〜でも: たとえ失敗しても "even if I fail", たとえ冗談でも "even if it's only a joke". The sentence remains grammatical without たとえ, but たとえ strengthens the "even if". Do not confuse it with the noun 例え "comparison, simile" (verb 例える).

examples[].german: He works without even eating properly.
I was so busy last night that I hardly slept.
Don't complain when you haven't even looked into it properly.
en.notes: 碌に (usually ろくに) always occurs with a negative and means "not properly, hardly decently": ろくに寝ていない, ろくに知らない. The tone is colloquial and often reproachful (ろくに調べもしないで). Related are ろくな + negative (ろくなことがない "nothing good") and ろくでもない "good-for-nothing, lousy". More neutral is あまり〜ない or 十分に〜ない.

examples[].german: You must not spend your days aimlessly.
If you drive without paying attention, you easily cause an accident.
Studying without a goal, just going through the motions, you hardly retain anything.
en.notes: 漫然と describes doing something without goal, concentration or intention: 漫然と過ごす, 漫然と眺める, 漫然と運転する. Attributively one says 漫然とした (漫然とした日々). It is literary and almost always critical, for example in admonitions or accident reports. Similar but more colloquial is ぼんやり; なんとなく stresses more the lack of a clear reason.

examples[].german: We are proceeding with the procedure quietly and steadily.
Despite voices of opposition, the plan was carried forward undeterred.
The ceremony was held solemnly, with the bereaved family looking on.
en.notes: 粛々と originally means "quietly and solemnly" (式が粛々と行われる). Today it is heard mainly in politics and administration: 粛々と進める "to continue calmly and according to plan, without fuss". This formula is sometimes criticized because it suggests that opposition is simply being ignored. Attributively: 粛々とした雰囲気. Similar but more neutral is 淡々と.

examples[].german: He stated the facts impassively.
Without changing her expression, she calmly gets her work done.
The film depicts a family's daily life in a plain, understated way.
en.notes: 淡々と describes composed, matter-of-fact behavior without visible emotion: 淡々と語る, 淡々と仕事をこなす. Attributively: 淡々とした口調, 淡々とした文章. Depending on context, it sounds appreciative (calm, objective) or somewhat cold. Originally 淡々 also means "plain, light", for example of taste (淡々とした味). Do not confuse it with 堂々と "confidently, with dignity".

examples[].german: He confronts injustice with a resolute attitude.
One should firmly refuse unreasonable demands.
The minister answered firmly even the reporters' tough questions.
en.notes: 毅然と describes a firm, unyielding attitude, especially in the face of pressure or injustice. Most common is the form 毅然とした態度 "a resolute attitude"; adverbially 毅然と断る, 毅然として答える. The word sounds elevated and appreciative and is typical of politics, schools and corporate ethics. Similar but more neutral is きっぱり（と）, which mainly stresses clear words.

examples[].german: It was reported that the accomplice is on the run.
The police are investigating, also keeping the possibility of an accomplice in view.
"Don't tell Mom. Now you're an accomplice too."
en.notes: 共犯 refers to the commission of a crime jointly by several persons; the person involved is the 共犯者. Legally 共犯 covers the co-perpetrator (共同正犯), the instigator (教唆犯) and the accessory (従犯). The principal offender or mastermind is called 主犯. Colloquially it is used jokingly for someone in on a small secret: これで君も共犯だ.

en.meaning: to reverse, to retract; to flutter
examples[].german: I can't go back on a decision once it has been made.
In court, he retracted his earlier testimony.
With her skirt flying, she ran up the stairs.
en.notes: 翻す is transitive (〜を翻す); the intransitive partner is 翻る "to flutter, to turn over". Mainly used figuratively: to reverse an opinion, statement or decision – 前言を翻す, 証言を翻す, 決定を翻す; 反旗を翻す means "to rise up, to rebel". Concretely: 身を翻す "to whirl around in a flash", to make a skirt or flag flutter (旗を翻す).

examples[].german: No matter how many times his dreams were crushed, he got back up.
I sprained my ankle on the stairs.
It was an opening goal that took the wind out of the opposing team's sails.
en.notes: 挫く (often くじく) is transitive and has two meanings: to sprain a joint (足首を挫く) and to break another's courage or momentum (意欲を挫く, 出鼻を挫く "to stop someone right at the start"). The intransitive partner is 挫ける "to lose heart": 何度失敗しても挫けない. The noun 挫折 "failure, setback" contains the same kanji.

examples[].german: One should refrain from remarks that make fun of others.
Young people's new way of speaking often becomes a target of ridicule in the media.
The policy was derided as "handing out money indiscriminately".
en.notes: 揶揄 is the literary word for mockery or mocking criticism, as a transitive する-verb: 〜を揶揄する. Very typical is the passive form with a quotation: 「〜」と揶揄される "to be derisively called ...". In everyday speech one says からかう, which is sometimes even written with the same kanji, 揶揄う. 揶揄 often targets politics, society or public figures.

examples[].german: With this sorry state of affairs, it is only natural to lose trust.
Billed as a title favorite, yet knocked out in the first round – what a disgrace!
My room is a total mess, and even I find it a sorry state.
en.notes: 体たらく denotes a shameful, pitiful state and is always pejorative. Typical are exclamatory frames such as この体たらく, 何という体たらくだ or 〜とはひどい体たらくだ, as a reproach to others or as self-criticism. Neutral words for "state" are 状態 or 有様; 有様 can also be negative but is less harsh.

examples[].german: I'm angry at myself over this disappointing result.
I always rely on my junior to help me, and as a senior I feel pathetic.
The fans raised angry voices over the team's feeble performance.
en.notes: 不甲斐ない (also ふがいない) is an い-adjective for someone who falls short of expectations and shows themselves to be pitiful and spineless. Often as self-reproach: 自分が不甲斐ない, 不甲斐ない思いをする; or as criticism: 不甲斐ない結果, 不甲斐ない戦いぶり. It contains 甲斐 "worth, reward", so literally "without worth". Similar is 情けない, which means "pathetic, shameful" more generally.

examples[].german: I admired the sight of her working diligently.
She looked after her hospitalized mother devotedly.
My husband, in an apron, is busily moving around the kitchen.
en.notes: 甲斐甲斐しい (usually かいがいしい) describes someone who works or cares for others nimbly, eagerly and devotedly. Most often adverbial: かいがいしく世話をする, かいがいしく働く. The word has a warm, appreciative tone and is often used for nursing, housework or hosts. Do not confuse it with 不甲斐ない, which, despite the shared 甲斐, expresses the opposite.

en.meaning: brave, plucky (in the face of adversity)
examples[].german: I was moved to tears by the sight of the child doing their best so bravely.
I was deeply touched by the girl's plucky effort doing the housework to help her mother.
I found a flower blooming bravely in a crack in the asphalt.
