examples[].german: At the start of the year, the prime minister delivered the policy speech.
In his policy address, the governor made child-rearing support a priority.
The opposition criticized the policy speech for lacking concrete measures.
en.notes: 施政方針 refers to the guidelines of the government's work and usually appears in 施政方針演説 ("policy speech"), which the prime minister gives at the start of the ordinary Diet session in January. Governors and mayors also present their 施政方針 at the start of the fiscal year. Not to be confused with 所信表明演説, the policy speech of a new prime minister or at the start of an extraordinary session. Typical verbs: 施政方針を示す・述べる・掲げる; purely press and political language.

en.meaning: whether one likes it or not; inevitably
examples[].german: I was made to take part whether I liked it or not.
As you get older, your physical strength inevitably declines.
The transfer was decided, and the family had no choice but to move.
en.notes: 否応 means "yes or no"; 否応なく thus means "without being able to say yes or no", that is, "whether one wants to or not, inevitably". It often appears with the passive, the causative-passive or 〜ことになる: 否応なく参加させられる. 否応なしに means the same, and before nouns 否応なしの. Unlike 無理やり (someone forces actively), it stresses the inescapability of circumstances.

en.meaning: as a result; in the end
examples[].german: In the end it was the right decision.
What I did with good intentions ended up hurting him.
Thanks to the train being late, I ended up noticing that I had forgotten something.
en.notes: 結果的に describes how something "turned out in the end", often differently from what was intended or without having been planned. It differs from その結果 "as a result of that", which links a logical consequence, and from the more colloquial 結局 "after all, in the end". It is typical in retrospectives: 結果的に良かった, 結果的に〜してしまった.

examples[].german: To put it bluntly, it was a failure.
This figure shows plainly how serious the problem is.
We have little time, so please explain just the essentials briefly.
en.notes: 端的に is the adverbial form of 端的 and means "to the point, frankly". Very common is 端的に言えば・言うと "in short", similar to 要するに but more matter-of-fact. With verbs such as 示す・表す it means "clearly, unmistakably": the matter shows itself directly and without detour. Unlike 簡単に "simply", it is not about ease but about directness.

examples[].german: We will eliminate the bad habits root and branch.
We were burgled, and everything of value was taken.
The typhoon uprooted the tree in the garden.
en.notes: 根こそぎ literally means "pulled out by the roots" and is used both concretely (trees, plants) and figuratively "completely, root and branch". Typical combinations are 根こそぎ奪う・盗まれる・持っていかれる, often in connection with theft or destruction. As a noun it appears in 根こそぎにする "to eradicate". Compared with すべて or 全部, it stresses thoroughness and usually a loss.

examples[].german: He consented, though reluctantly.
The child reluctantly started his homework.
Asked by his boss, he reluctantly took on the overtime.
en.notes: 渋々 (from 渋い "astringent") describes doing something "reluctantly, out of necessity", usually after being asked or pressed to do so. Typical with verbs of consenting: 渋々承知する・従う・引き受ける, strengthened also as 渋々ながら. Compared with いやいや the aversion is weaker; one yields more in resignation. Often written in kana as しぶしぶ.

examples[].german: He remains perfectly composed.
A large eagle soared leisurely in the sky.
Although he was about to be late for the game, he was calmly drinking coffee.
en.notes: 悠然と describes a calm, unshakable composure, often precisely when others get flustered: "unhurriedly, leisurely". Typical are 悠然と構える "to wait calmly", 悠然と歩く and 悠然と空を舞う. Before nouns the literary form 悠然たる態度 is used. It sounds more elevated than 落ち着いて and, unlike のんびり, has no connotation of sluggishness.

en.meaning: to detest; to feel disgust for
examples[].german: He detests violence.
He detested dishonesty more than anything else.
Disgusted with my own weakness, I spent a sleepless night.
en.notes: 嫌悪する means "to detest, to reject deeply" and is clearly stronger and more formal than 嫌う or 嫌がる. It is transitive: 暴力を嫌悪する. More common than the verb is the noun in fixed combinations: 嫌悪感を抱く・覚える "to feel revulsion", 自己嫌悪 "self-loathing, dissatisfaction with oneself". The reading is けんお, not けんあく.

en.meaning: to run around busily; to make every effort
examples[].german: He is working hard to raise funds.
He ran around trying to get a job for his friend.
Since the disaster, city employees have been busy running the evacuation shelters.
en.notes: 奔走する literally means "to run about" and means "to work tirelessly for something, to pull out all the stops". The goal takes に: 資金集めに奔走する, 問題の解決に奔走する, or 〜のために. It is literary and sounds appreciative, similar to 尽力する; the everyday word 走り回る, by contrast, tends to be meant literally.

examples[].german: The government intervened in the market.
It is not good for parents to intervene too much in their children's quarrels.
The United Nations has decided to intervene in the conflict.
en.notes: 介入する means "to intervene" and is intransitive: what is intervened in takes に (市場に介入する, 紛争に介入する). Typical compounds are 軍事介入 and 為替介入 "currency market intervention". Compared with 干渉する "to interfere", which is clearly negative, 介入 sounds more matter-of-fact; colloquially one says 口を出す.

examples[].german: We respect universal values.
Love is a timeless, universal theme.
This law holds universally.
en.notes: 普遍的な means "universal", that is, valid for all people, times and cases. Typical are 普遍的な真理・価値・テーマ; the opposite is 特殊な or 個別的な. Unlike 一般的な "common, widespread", it is not about frequency but about exceptionless validity. Adverbially: 普遍的に成り立つ; the related noun is 普遍性.

examples[].german: The new prime minister delivered a policy speech in the Diet.
The new company president stated his views before all employees.
The newly elected student council president called for zero bullying in a short statement of her views.
en.notes: 所信表明 is the public presentation of one's own convictions and plans (所信 "conviction, intention" + 表明 "declaration"). In politics it is mostly 所信表明演説 by a new prime minister or at the start of an extraordinary Diet session, in contrast to the 施政方針演説 of the ordinary session in January. Outside politics it is also said of the inaugural speech of a new company president, chairperson or candidate. Verb: 所信表明を行う or 所信を表明する.

examples[].german: We are plagued by a chronic labor shortage.
This company constantly has a lot of overtime.
We need a permanent system, not a temporary measure.
en.notes: 恒常的な means "constant, permanent" and describes a state that does not pass; the opposite is 一時的な. It is often used with problems: 恒常的な人手不足・赤字, adverbially 恒常的に残業が多い. Similar is 慢性的な "chronic", which sounds even more negative; 恒久的な "designed to last" instead stresses a deliberately lasting arrangement (恒久的な平和).

en.meaning: direct; clear and to the point
examples[].german: I make an effort to express myself directly.
To his question, she gave a clear answer in a single word.
This incident is a telling example of the flaws in the system.
en.notes: 端的な is the attributive form of 端的 and means "direct, clear and to the point". Typical are 端的な表現・答え・説明 and 端的な例 "a clear, typical example". More common than the な-form, however, is the adverb 端的に (端的に言えば). It praises brevity and clarity; rude directness is more likely described with 率直な or ぶっきらぼうな.

examples[].german: I have a troublesome problem.
To make matters worse, I lost the key on Sunday night.
During my university days I stayed at my uncle's house for two years.
en.notes: 厄介な means "troublesome, knotty, burdensome" for things or people that cause you trouble: 厄介な問題・客・病気. Compared with 面倒な "cumbersome", it stresses that the matter is hard to resolve and becomes a burden. Also common are 厄介なことに "unfortunately, to make matters worse" and the noun in 〜に厄介になる "to stay with someone, to be a burden to someone" (e.g. to live with relatives).

examples[].german: Vulnerable infrastructure is a challenge.
This system has weak security.
Small and medium-sized companies with a weak management base are easily affected by recessions.
en.notes: 脆弱な means "weak, susceptible, vulnerable" and mostly describes structures and systems: 脆弱な地盤・インフラ・経営基盤. In IT the noun 脆弱性 "vulnerability" is very common. It sounds technical and formal; in everyday speech people say 弱い, and もろい for physically fragile things. The reading is ぜいじゃく; in newspapers it is also written ぜい弱.

examples[].german: I agree wholeheartedly.
The locals welcomed the construction of the new station with open arms.
I can't give that proposal my wholehearted support.
en.notes: 諸手を挙げて literally means "with both hands raised" and means "unreservedly, without restriction". It almost always stands before 賛成する or 歓迎する. The negation is very common: 諸手を挙げて賛成はできない "cannot agree without reservation", hinting at concerns. Also written もろ手を挙げて.

en.meaning: to bring into relief; to highlight
examples[].german: The survey highlighted the problem.
This novel brings the loneliness of postwar youth into sharp relief.
The recent disaster highlighted the challenges in supporting the elderly.
en.notes: 浮き彫り is actually a "relief" (sculpture); 浮き彫りにする means figuratively "to make stand out clearly, to expose", above all for problems and hidden conditions: 問題・課題・実態を浮き彫りにする. The intransitive counterpart is 浮き彫りになる "to come clearly to light". Compared with 明らかにする, it sounds more vivid and is often used in reports and newspapers.

en.meaning: good and bad mixed together; wheat and chaff
examples[].german: The information is a mix of good and bad.
Online reviews are a mix of good and bad, so you shouldn't swallow them whole.
The submitted works were of very mixed quality, and the judging took a long time.
en.notes: 玉石混淆 is made up of 玉 "gem", 石 "ordinary stone" and 混淆 "mixture": valuable and worthless things lie jumbled together. It describes sets of information, works or applicants whose quality varies widely: 〜は玉石混淆だ, 玉石混淆の情報. Grammatically it is a noun (with だ, の, で). Often also written 玉石混交.

en.meaning: to an onlooker; from the outside
examples[].german: To an onlooker, he seems happy.
It looks like an easy job from the outside, but it is actually quite hard.
The two got along so badly that even bystanders could tell.
en.notes: 傍目 (はため, often also written はた目) is the view of an outsider; 傍目に, usually 傍目には, means "from the outside, to outsiders" and almost always introduces a contrast with reality: 傍目には幸せそうに見えるが…. Similar are 外から見ると and はたから見ると. With the reading おかめ, 傍目 appears in the proverb 傍目八目 "onlookers see more than the players". Neutral to slightly literary.

examples[].german: A National Security Council was established.
The government approved a new national security strategy by Cabinet decision.
Cyberattacks are a serious threat to national security.
en.notes: 国家安全保障 is composed of 国家 "state" and 安全保障 "security (guarantee)". In running text one usually says simply 安全保障 or the abbreviation 安保 (日米安保 "Japan-U.S. security alliance"); the long form appears mainly in proper names such as 国家安全保障会議 and 国家安全保障戦略 and in 国家安全保障上の脅威. Not to be confused with 治安, which is internal public safety (crime), whereas 安全保障 is protection against external threats.

examples[].german: He has the strength to bounce back from adversity.
The goalkeeper deflected the shot.
A white wall reflects sunlight, so the room is bright.
en.notes: 跳ね返す is transitive and concretely means "to make bounce back, to ward off, to reflect" (ボール・光を跳ね返す), figuratively "to overcome, to not let get one down": 逆境・圧力・プレッシャーを跳ね返す. The intransitive counterpart is 跳ね返る "to rebound, to spring back" (ボールが壁に跳ね返る). In sports it is the typical verb for a save or a rebound.

examples[].german: She has both intelligence and beauty.
This car combines good fuel economy with fun driving.
Leaders are expected to be people who combine decisiveness and compassion.
en.notes: 兼ね備える means "to possess at the same time, to combine in oneself", usually two positive qualities: AとBを兼ね備える, often as 兼ね備えている or before nouns 〜を兼ね備えた人物. It is praising and rather literary. Not to be confused with 兼ねる, which expresses a double function (趣味と実益を兼ねる "to combine hobby and benefit", 会議室を兼ねる).

en.meaning: to emerge; to come to light
examples[].german: New facts have emerged.
The submarine slowly rose to the surface of the sea.
The illuminated castle stands out sharply against the night sky.
en.notes: 浮かび上がる is intransitive and literally means "to rise to the surface" (水面に浮かび上がる). Figuratively it means "to come to light, to emerge" (新たな事実・容疑者が浮かび上がる) or "to stand out clearly" against a background (夜空に浮かび上がる). The simple 浮かぶ, by contrast, means "to float, to drift" or "to come to mind". The transitive form is 浮かび上がらせる; close in meaning is 浮き彫りになる.

en.meaning: to reach an agreement; to settle
examples[].german: The negotiations were settled.
The wage negotiations were settled at 3 percent.
The two countries' trade talks aim for a settlement within the year.
en.notes: 妥結する means "to reach an agreement (after negotiations), to come to a conclusion" and is intransitive: the subject is the negotiations themselves (交渉が妥結する). The result takes で: 3パーセントで妥結する. It is a word from news, business and politics, often also as a noun (妥結を目指す). Unlike 妥協する "to make concessions", it describes the successful conclusion, not the giving way.

en.meaning: to be devoted to; to be deeply attracted to
examples[].german: I am devoted to his ideas.
In my student days I was an ardent admirer of Dostoevsky.
In her later years she became deeply devoted to Buddhism.
en.notes: 傾倒する literally means "to lean" and means "to devote oneself enthusiastically to (a person, doctrine or art), to be an ardent follower". The target takes に: 思想・作家・宗教に傾倒する, often reinforced by 深く. Unlike 熱中する "to be absorbed in an activity", it is about intellectual veneration; 心酔する is even more rapturous. Literary.

examples[].german: The ideal and reality are far apart.
The two people's opinions were far apart, and the discussion went nowhere.
I live in a town far away from my hometown.
en.notes: 隔たる is intransitive and means "to be distant", spatially, temporally or figuratively with opinions and ideas: 意見が大きく隔たる, 理想と現実が隔たる. It mostly appears in the form 隔たっている or attributively 隔たった. The transitive counterpart is 隔てる "to separate" (川を隔てて). Very common is the noun 隔たり "distance, gap" (意見の隔たり).

examples[].german: He hinted at his resignation.
She subtly hinted that she is thinking of changing jobs.
In the letter, the culprit had hinted at the next crime.
en.notes: ほのめかす is transitive and means "to hint, to let on" without saying it openly: 辞任・引退・関与をほのめかす, also 〜ことをほのめかす. それとなく often stands before it. It is more neutral than the colloquial 匂わせる and more everyday than the abstract 暗示する. Mostly written in kana; the kanji 仄めかす are rare.

en.meaning: to spin one's wheels; to be futile
examples[].german: My efforts are spinning their wheels.
The tires spun on the snowy road and the car stopped moving.
I was too keen on the first day, and my feelings just went to waste.
en.notes: 空回りする literally means "to turn idly" (engine, wheels: タイヤが空回りする) and figuratively "to run in vain, to achieve nothing". Typical are 努力・議論が空回りする and 気持ちが空回りする, when someone is overeager but has no effect. It is intransitive and rather colloquial-neutral. Compared with 無駄になる, it stresses the frantic effort without result.

en.meaning: to stumble; to trip; to hit a snag
examples[].german: I stumbled at the very first stage.
I tripped on a step and almost fell.
Many children get stuck on fractions in math.
en.notes: つまずく is intransitive and concretely means "to trip": the obstacle is marked with に (石・段差につまずく). Figuratively it means "to fail, to get stuck"; then the point is marked with で (最初の段階で・分数でつまずく). Unlike 転ぶ "to fall down", it refers only to catching one's foot. Usually written in kana; the kanji 躓く are difficult and rare.

en.meaning: to mesh; to be in sync
examples[].german: The discussion isn't meshing.
If the gears don't mesh well, the machine won't run.
Today the offense and defense meshed well, and we won easily.
en.notes: 噛み合う concretely means "to mesh" (gears, teeth) and is intransitive: 歯車が噛み合う. Figuratively it says that conversations or parts "fit together"; especially common is the negation 議論・話が噛み合わない "to talk past each other". In sports: 攻守が噛み合う "offense and defense work in harmony". The transitive form is 噛み合わせる; also written かみ合う.

examples[].german: Allowing the exercise of the right of collective self-defense sparked debate.
In 2014, the government permitted a limited exercise of the right of collective self-defense.
The UN Charter recognizes both the right of individual and collective self-defense.
en.notes: 集団的自衛権 is the right to come to the military aid of an attacked ally even if one's own country is not attacked; the counterpart is 個別的自衛権 "right of individual self-defense". Fixed combinations: 集団的自衛権を行使する, 〜の行使を容認する and 行使容認 "permitting the exercise". In Japan the term is politically highly controversial because of Article 9 and appears almost only in the news and constitutional debates.

examples[].german: Clichéd expressions should be avoided.
I'm tired of hearing such stale excuses.
Technology advances so fast that products quickly become obsolete.
en.notes: 陳腐な means "hackneyed, banal, outdated" and criticizes expressions, ideas or stories you have heard too often: 陳腐な表現・言い訳・セリフ. It is sharper than ありきたりな "ordinary"; 古臭い stresses the old-fashioned more. In business, 陳腐化 means the "becoming obsolete, obsolescence" of products and technology.

en.meaning: to try everything; to exhaust all means
examples[].german: We did everything we could, but he couldn't be saved.
I searched by every possible means, but the cat was not found.
The company tried every possible measure and avoided bankruptcy.
en.notes: 手を尽くす means "to exhaust all means, to leave nothing untried", literally "to use up one's hands (means)". It is reinforced by あらゆる手を尽くす or 八方手を尽くす "to try everything in every direction". Very often a disappointing result follows with が or けれど. Similar are 全力を尽くす "to give it everything" and 最善を尽くす "to do one's best", which however stress effort rather than means.

examples[].german: I face it with a resolute attitude.
Unreasonable demands require a firm response.
She answered the reporters' questions, too, with a resolute expression.
en.notes: 毅然とした is the attributive form of 毅然 and describes a "resolute, unbending" attitude, especially toward pressure or unjust demands: 毅然とした態度・対応・表情. Adverbially it is 毅然と(して)断る; literary 毅然たる. Similar is 断固とした, which stresses the firm decision more, whereas 毅然 emphasizes dignified, calm steadfastness.

examples[].german: We were enveloped in a solemn atmosphere.
The majestic sound of the pipe organ echoed in the cathedral.
The ceremony was conducted with solemnity.
en.notes: 荘厳な (そうごん) means "sublime, solemn, majestic" and describes buildings, music, ceremonies or an atmosphere that inspires awe: 荘厳な寺院・音楽・儀式. Close in meaning is 厳か (おごそか), which stresses solemn stillness more; 壮大な refers to sheer size. The reading しょうごん denotes the adorning of temples in Buddhism and is a different word.

en.meaning: to form the core; to be fundamental
examples[].german: Education forms the foundation of society.
Mutual trust is exactly what forms the core of this team.
Popular sovereignty is one of the principles that form the core of the constitution.
en.notes: 根幹 literally means "root and trunk", hence "core, foundation"; 根幹を成す (often also 根幹をなす) means "to form the foundation of something". What it is the foundation of comes before it with の: 社会・憲法・計画の根幹を成す. Related expressions are 根幹にかかわる "to concern the fundamentals" and 根幹を揺るがす "to shake to the foundations". Compared with 基礎 or 土台, it sounds more elevated and stresses the essential.

en.meaning: to expose to the light of day; to bring to light
examples[].german: He exposed the wrongdoing to the light of day.
The reporter's investigation brought the politician's corruption to light.
The whistleblower resolved to expose the company's cover-up.
en.notes: 白日 is "bright daylight", 下(もと) "under"; 白日の下に晒す thus means "to drag into broad daylight, to expose publicly". It almost always concerns hidden wrongdoing: 不正・汚職・隠蔽を白日の下に晒す. Very common is the passive 白日の下に晒される "to come to light". The verb is often written in kana as さらす; the expression is literary and typical of the press and factual texts.

en.meaning: on the other hand; turning it around
examples[].german: Let us now look at the situation in Japan.
Other people's faults are easy to see. What about my own?
When I was young, my parents' advice was annoying. Looking back, that was affection.
en.notes: 翻って is the て-form of 翻る "to turn around" and introduces a change of perspective: "if one turns the other way, on the other hand". It mostly stands at the beginning of a sentence after a statement about others, and you turn your gaze to yourself or your own country: 翻って日本は・自分は…, or 翻って考えると. It is literary, typical of essays and speeches, and does not simply mean "on the contrary" (それに反して).

examples[].german: Serious symptoms have appeared.
The patient's critical condition has continued since the accident.
This drug has rare but serious side effects.
en.notes: 重篤な is a medical technical term for "severe, life-threatening": 重篤な症状・副作用・患者, 重篤な状態 "critical condition". It is stronger and more formal than 重い or 重症の and appears above all in news, drug information leaflets and hospital reports. For serious errors or crimes one does not say 重篤 but 重大な. The related verb is 重篤化する "to worsen to a life-threatening state".

examples[].german: He proposed an unconventional idea.
He always shows up in outlandish clothes.
The building has an eccentric design and has become a landmark of the city.
en.notes: 奇抜な means "unconventional, original, strikingly unusual": 奇抜なアイデア・デザイン・服装・発想. Depending on context it is praise ("original") or mild criticism ("flashy"). 斬新な "innovative" is clearly positive, 突飛な "wild, far-fetched" rather negative, and 奇妙な simply means "strange".

examples[].german: Theory and practice have diverged.
The poll results diverged greatly from the actual election results.
Politics must not become detached from the sentiments of the people.
en.notes: 乖離する means "to diverge, to deviate" and is intransitive: AとBが乖離する or AがBから乖離する. Even more common than the verb is the noun: 理想と現実の乖離, 〜との乖離が大きい. It is a formal word from business, politics and science; in everyday speech people say ずれる or かけ離れる. Also written かい離.

examples[].german: The exclusively defense-oriented policy is the foundation of postwar Japan's security policy.
Whether possessing a counterstrike capability violates the exclusively defense-oriented policy became the point of contention.
He argued that the Self-Defense Forces should adhere strictly to an exclusively defensive posture.
en.notes: 専守防衛 (専ら守る "defend exclusively") is the principle of Japanese security policy of using military force only after an attack and only to the minimum necessary extent. Typical combinations: 専守防衛の原則・方針, 専守防衛に徹する "to adhere strictly to it", 専守防衛を逸脱する "to deviate from the principle". A term from politics and the press, often discussed together with 集団的自衛権 or 反撃能力.

en.meaning: to accompany; to go along with
examples[].german: Rights come with duties.
There are many procedures that go with moving, which is hard work.
Along with the earthquake, power outages occurred in various places.
en.notes: 付随する means "to go along with something, to be connected with it" and is intransitive: AにBが付随する "B goes along with A". Typical are 〜に付随する問題・業務・手続き and 〜に付随して起こる. Close in meaning and more everyday is 伴う (〜に伴って); 付随 sounds more formal and stresses that B is a side phenomenon of A.

examples[].german: He made a remark that provoked the other party.
You must not rise to cheap provocations.
The neighboring country provoked surrounding countries with a missile launch.
en.notes: 挑発する means "to provoke, to challenge" and is transitive: 相手を挑発する. Very common are the noun in 挑発に乗る "to take the bait" and the adjective 挑発的な "provocative" (also for revealing clothes). In politics it denotes military saber-rattling. Unlike 挑戦する "to take on a challenge", with 挑発 you want to trigger a reaction in the other person.

examples[].german: We will distribute the commemorative volume to those concerned.
I distributed my own manga at a doujinshi fair.
This shrine distributes amulets and talismans.
en.notes: 頒布する means "to distribute, to hand out (to many people)", free of charge or for a fee, and is transitive. It is used above all for printed matter and special items: 記念誌を頒布する; shrines hand out amulets (お守り) this way, and at doujinshi fairs people deliberately say 頒布 instead of 販売. For working documents in everyday life 配布する or 配る is usual; 頒布 sounds official and formal.

examples[].german: The impact spread to other industries.
A movement that started in one class spread to the whole school.
Hosting the Olympics brings a large ripple effect to the regional economy.
en.notes: 波及する literally means "to spread like waves" and means "to spill over, to have an effect on". It is intransitive; the target takes に: 影響が他の業界に波及する. Very common is 波及効果 "ripple effect, multiplier effect". Compared with the general 広がる, it stresses the chain reaction from a starting point; typical of business and news.

examples[].german: I stand by my convictions.
The bullet pierced the window glass.
A large river runs through the center of the town.
en.notes: 貫く is transitive and has three uses: "to pierce, to penetrate" (弾丸が壁を貫く), "to run through" (町を貫いて流れる川) and figuratively "to stick to something to the end" (信念・意志・独身を貫く). In the figurative sense it is stronger than 通す and stresses steadfastness against resistance. The compound 貫き通す "to persevere unwaveringly" is also common.

en.meaning: to make progress; to go well
examples[].german: The work is progressing well.
Studying goes well in a quiet library.
Because of the heat, the work isn't progressing at all.
en.notes: はかどる is intransitive and means "to progress well"; the subject is the work itself: 仕事・勉強・作業がはかどる. The negation はかどらない "isn't making progress" is very common. Compared with 進む, it stresses swift, efficient progress; the noun 進捗 is the formal word for "progress". Mostly written in kana; the kanji 捗る are rare.

examples[].german: The facts cannot be covered up.
Thick clouds were hiding the summit.
She masked her anxiety with a smile.
en.notes: 覆い隠す is transitive and combines 覆う "to cover" with 隠す "to hide": "to conceal completely, to shroud". Concretely, clouds or cloths hide something (雲が山頂を覆い隠す); figuratively one conceals facts or feelings (事実・不安を覆い隠す). It is stronger and more vivid than the simple 隠す and sounds rather literary.

en.meaning: to learn the hard way; to realize painfully
examples[].german: I painfully realized my own powerlessness.
Studying abroad made me painfully aware of how thick the language barrier is.
This time I'll teach you a lesson!
en.notes: 思い知る means to painfully grasp something, usually unpleasant, through your own experience; the object takes を: 無力さを思い知る, 〜ことを思い知る. Very common is the passive 思い知らされる "to be painfully made to realize". The causative 思い知らせてやる is a threat: "I'll show you!". Neutral noticing is 気づく; 痛感する is a more formal synonym.

examples[].german: The new way of thinking has permeated society.
Rainwater seeps into the ground.
The new rules have not yet taken hold within the company.
en.notes: 浸透する is intransitive and describes how ideas, rules, products or also liquids gradually penetrate something: 社会に浸透する, 水が土に浸透する. The destination takes に, the thing penetrating takes が. For the spread of devices or technology one says 普及する rather, in everyday speech simply 広まる. Often negated: まだ浸透していない "has not yet caught on".

examples[].german: The problem has started to surface.
The effects of the declining birthrate are becoming apparent in the regions.
The survey allowed us to bring hidden needs to the surface.
en.notes: 顕在化する is a literary word for problems, risks or needs that were hidden until now and become visible: 問題が顕在化する. The opposite is 潜在化 or 潜在的 "latent". Transitively the causative 〜を顕在化させる "to make visible" is used. Typical of news, reports and business texts; in everyday speech people say 表に出る or はっきりしてくる.

examples[].german: The constitution prohibits the use of force as a means of settling international disputes.
The two countries agreed to avoid the use of force and seek a diplomatic solution.
The UN Security Council adopted a resolution authorizing the use of force.
en.notes: 武力行使 (武力 "military force" + 行使 "exercise") refers to the use of armed forces, usually between states; for violence between individuals one says 暴力. Typical: 武力行使に踏み切る "to resort to force", 武力行使を辞さない "not to rule out force", 武力行使を容認する. Article 9 of the Constitution speaks of 武力による威嚇又は武力の行使; as a verb one mostly uses 武力を行使する.

examples[].german: The discussion converged on one conclusion.
Light converges to a single point at the lens.
The industry's technologies are gradually converging in the same direction.
en.notes: 収斂する is an elevated, often technical word for "to converge, to be bundled": opinions or developments 〜に収斂する, light is focused at one point. In biology there is 収斂進化 "convergent evolution", in cosmetics 収れん化粧水 "astringent toner". Often also written 収れん. In everyday speech people say まとまる; for mathematical convergence 収束 is usual today.

examples[].german: He received scathing criticism.
She made a cutting remark to her boss.
That defeat became a severe blow for the team.
en.notes: 痛烈な describes criticism, mockery or blows that hit especially hard: 痛烈な批判, 痛烈な皮肉, 痛烈な一撃. Adverbial: 痛烈に批判する "to criticize sharply". 厳しい is more general "strict, harsh"; 辛辣 stresses more the biting, spiteful tongue of a person. Rather literary and typical of news and reviews.

examples[].german: He listed plausible-sounding reasons.
He lies with a straight face.
The internet is flooded with plausible-sounding false rumors.
en.notes: もっともらしい is almost always written in kana; 尤もらしい is rare. It means "plausible-sounding" and often has a suspicious undertone: something sounds reasonable but perhaps is not (もっともらしい理由, もっともらしい嘘). To be distinguished from もっともな "truly justified" (もっともな意見). もっともらしい顔 means "a serious, weighty expression".

examples[].german: We aim for smooth communication.
The meeting went smoothly.
We made a manual to ensure a smooth handover.
en.notes: 円滑な means "smooth" for processes, relationships and communication: 円滑な人間関係, 円滑な取引. Very often adverbial: 円滑に進む, 円滑に行う, 円滑に運営する. It is more formal than the loanword スムーズ, which is mostly used in everyday speech. Typical of business language and official texts.

examples[].german: The effect was noticeably apparent.
Since I started taking the medicine, the symptoms have improved markedly.
Young people turning away from television is progressing markedly.
en.notes: 顕著に is the adverbial form of 顕著な "conspicuous, marked": 顕著に表れる, 顕著に改善する, 顕著な差. It is literary and typical of reports, statistics and science. A close synonym is 著しく, which stresses the extent more; in everyday speech people say はっきり or 目立って.

examples[].german: I remember it vaguely.
The shape of the mountain was faintly visible beyond the fog.
The overall picture of the plan has started to become dimly visible.
en.notes: 朧げに (often おぼろげに in kana) describes that something is perceived or remembered only vaguely: おぼろげに覚えている, 朧げに見える. It comes from 朧 "haze, veil", as in 朧月 "hazy moon". More everyday and broader is ぼんやり; うっすら stresses "very faintly, ever so slightly". Sounds somewhat literary.

en.meaning: to put on a bold front; to bluff
examples[].german: He put on a brave front and pretended to be fine.
The weaker the dog, the more it bluffs and barks.
Don't put on a brave front; if you're in trouble, honestly ask for help.
en.notes: 虚勢 is "empty strength, bluff", 張る "to stretch, to put on display": 虚勢を張る thus means to feign strength or courage although you are actually weak or afraid. It is not boasting about achievements (that would be 自慢する or 大口をたたく). Similar is 見栄を張る, which however concerns vanity and status symbols more; colloquially one says 強がる. The verb 張る conjugates normally (張って, 張らずに).

examples[].german: The momentum for reform is growing.
Momentum for environmental protection is growing in the region.
Ahead of the election, momentum for a change of government suddenly surged.
en.notes: 機運 is the favorable mood or momentum for a change; 〜の機運が高まる means "the readiness for … grows, … gains momentum". Typical are 改革の機運, 政権交代の機運, 〜への機運. Transitively one says 機運を高める "to foster the mood for something". It is a word of news and written language; the variant 気運 also occurs.

en.meaning: to be at a loss; to not know what to do
examples[].german: I stood there at a loss.
I lost my wallet and was at a loss in an unfamiliar town.
He suddenly lost his job and is at his wits' end.
en.notes: 途方 means "way, means", 暮れる "to come to an end" like the day: you no longer know a way and stand completely at a loss. Often with the cause in て-form: 財布をなくして途方に暮れる, or with どうしていいか分からず. 困る is more general, 戸惑う more a brief confusion. Not to be confused with 途方もない "tremendous, absurd".

en.meaning: to not know what to do with; to be unable to handle
examples[].german: I have time on my hands.
The mother was exhausted, unable to cope with her energetic children.
She didn't know what to do with her pent-up anger.
en.notes: 持て余す is transitive: you have something you can't cope with or don't know what to do with. Typical are 暇・時間を持て余す "to have time on one's hands, not to know what to do out of boredom", 子どもを持て余す "to be overwhelmed by one's child" and 感情・怒りを持て余す. Similar is 手に負えない "unmanageable", which however takes no object with を.

examples[].german: The Constitution of Japan does not recognize the right of belligerency.
Scholars are divided over the interpretation of the right of belligerency.
Under international law, the right of belligerency also includes the right to stop and search enemy ships.
en.notes: 交戦権 (交戦 "to engage in combat" + 権 "right") appears almost only in constitutional debate: Article 9, paragraph 2 reads 国の交戦権は、これを認めない. It is disputed whether this means the right to wage war at all, or the rights of a belligerent under international law, such as occupation or the search of enemy ships. Verbs: 交戦権を認める・否認する; strictly legal written language.

examples[].german: It is so exquisite that it could be mistaken for the real thing.
It was a cherry blossom flurry that looked just like snow.
That is unmistakably his handwriting.
en.notes: 見紛う is literary and means "to mistake A for B, to confuse". Typical are 〜と見紛うほど／ばかり "so much that one could take it for …" and the fixed expression 見紛うことなき／見紛うはずもない "unmistakable". In everyday speech people say 見間違える. Besides みまがう there is the older reading みまごう.

en.meaning: to cover up; to suppress; to stub out (a cigarette)
examples[].german: He tried to cover up the scandal.
He stubbed out his cigarette in the ashtray.
I was asked to cover up my boss's mistake, but I refused.
en.notes: 揉み消す (often もみ消す) has two meanings: literally to put out a cigarette or embers by rubbing (たばこを揉み消す), figuratively to cover up a scandal, mistake or evidence (事件を揉み消す). The figurative meaning is more common and sounds like abuse of power. Similar is 隠蔽する, more formal and legalistic; putting something out with the foot, by contrast, is 踏み消す.

examples[].german: I earnestly wish for peace.
We sincerely ask for everyone's cooperation.
We earnestly pray for your recovery as soon as possible.
en.notes: 切に is a formal adverb that almost only appears with verbs of wishing and requesting: 切に願う, 切に望む, 切に祈る, 切にお願い申し上げます. It expresses deep, sincere urgency and suits speeches, letters and official appeals. In everyday speech people say 心から or 本当に.

en.meaning: to have a prospect; to become foreseeable
examples[].german: A prospect of resolution has finally emerged.
There is no prospect of when train service will resume.
With no prospect of repayment, only the debt kept growing.
en.notes: 見通し is "outlook, forecast"; 〜の見通しが立つ means that it can be foreseen when or how something will succeed. Very common in the negative: 見通しが立たない "not yet foreseeable", for example with train cancellations or disasters. Transitively one says 見通しを立てる "to make a forecast". A close synonym is めどが立つ.

en.meaning: to get out of hand; to be unmanageable
examples[].german: The situation got out of hand.
The children started making a racket, and the classroom got out of control.
There are too many opinions, and the meeting can't be brought under control.
en.notes: 収拾 is "getting a situation back under control"; 収拾がつかない means that chaos can no longer be put in order. Very common is 収拾がつかなくなる "to get out of control". Transitively one says 事態を収拾する or 収拾をつける. Not to be confused with the identically read 収集 "collecting".

en.meaning: to feel vindicated; to feel satisfied
examples[].german: His apology satisfied me.
The fans felt vindicated when the cocky rival lost.
I said everything I wanted to say and felt a bit better.
en.notes: 溜飲 is actually sour reflux; when it "goes down", the pressure is gone. 溜飲を下げる therefore means that pent-up anger or frustration dissipates and you feel satisfaction, often because someone gets their just punishment or you are proven right. It is not actively venting steam (that would be 鬱憤を晴らす). Intransitive also 溜飲が下がる; the mixed form 溜飲を晴らす is considered wrong.

examples[].german: A new trend is sweeping the world.
That Japanese car once swept the American market.
The mounted army swept over Europe in no time.
en.notes: 席巻する originally means "to roll up a mat" and means to conquer a territory or market by storm: 世界を席巻する, 市場を席巻する. It is transitive with を and literary; the original spelling is 席捲. More neutral are 支配する or, for fashions, 流行する.

examples[].german: On the whole, it can be called a success.
This year's new employees are generally serious.
Winters in this region are generally mild.
en.notes: 概して is a literary adverb for "by and large, as a rule" and introduces a generalization: 概して言えば, 概して〜傾向がある. In conversation people rather say 全体的に, 一般的に or だいたい. It sounds matter-of-fact and judging, and suits reports, evaluations and essays.

en.meaning: to be rooted in; to be grounded in
examples[].german: We carry out activities rooted in the community.
This festival is rooted in agricultural culture.
His prejudice is rooted in experiences from his childhood.
en.notes: 根ざす (also 根差す) is intransitive and means "to be rooted in something": 〜に根ざす. Very common attributively: 地域に根ざした活動 "regionally anchored activities", 生活に根ざした文化. 基づく stresses more a factual basis (データに基づく), 根付く the taking root of something new.

examples[].german: Something is stirring in the darkness.
When I moved the stone, many insects were squirming about.
Behind the scenes of politics, various schemes are stirring.
en.notes: 蠢く describes a slow, crawling writhing of small creatures such as worms, insects or larvae, usually with an eerie or disgusting undertone. Figuratively one speaks of people or forces acting in secret: 裏で蠢く勢力 "forces at work in the background". Intransitive, mostly in the form 蠢いている; the difficult kanji is often replaced by kana うごめく. Compared with 動く "to move" and うようよする "to swarm", 蠢く stresses the sluggish, uncanny stirring; rather literary.

examples[].german: The Three Non-Nuclear Principles are regarded as one of Japan's national policies.
The Three Non-Nuclear Principles are the principles of not possessing, not producing, and not allowing the introduction of nuclear weapons.
The prime minister indicated that he would uphold the Three Non-Nuclear Principles.
en.notes: 非核三原則 (非核 "nuclear-free" + 三原則 "three principles") are the principles formulated in 1967 by Prime Minister 佐藤栄作: 持たず、作らず、持ち込ませず, that is, neither to possess nuclear weapons, nor to produce them, nor to allow their introduction. Typical verbs: 堅持する "to hold fast to", 見直す "to review". In debates about nuclear deterrence, the third point, 持ち込ませず, is usually the disputed one. A term from politics and the press.

en.meaning: to turn out to be needless worry
examples[].german: The worry turned out to be unfounded.
I was worried about rain, but it was needless, and the day was brilliantly clear.
I hope my anxiety turns out to be unfounded.
en.notes: 杞憂 goes back to a man from the ancient state of 杞 who feared the sky might fall: a completely unnecessary worry. 杞憂に終わる means that a fear turns out in hindsight to be unfounded, that is, a relieved, positive outcome. Typical: 心配は杞憂に終わった; as a hope 杞憂に終わればいいが. Elevated style.

en.meaning: to be worthwhile; to be worth it
examples[].german: My effort was worth it.
Waiting paid off, and we got to see a wonderful sunrise.
If he doesn't listen no matter how often I say it, there's no point in warning him.
en.notes: 甲斐 is the "reward, effect" of an effort; typical is Vた甲斐がある "it was worth doing …", negated 甲斐がない "it's no use". Often written in kana as かいがある. As a suffix it becomes -がい: 生きがい "purpose in life", やりがい "fulfillment in work". More elevated and emphatic is 〜甲斐あって without が.

en.meaning: support; basis; something to rely on
examples[].german: I find an emotional anchor.
What is this judgment based on?
For immigrants who had left their homeland, the church was an important mainstay.
en.notes: 拠り所 (also よりどころ) is that on which one relies: emotionally as 心の拠り所 "support, comfort", factually as the basis of a judgment or theory (判断の拠り所). Often in 〜を拠り所とする／にする. 根拠 refers more to evidence and proof, 支え to concrete support from people.

en.meaning: barking up the wrong tree; misdirected
examples[].german: That criticism is misdirected.
It's misplaced to complain to me.
Asking him for financial advice is totally barking up the wrong tree.
en.notes: 門 here is the gate of a house: お門違い literally means "ringing the wrong house's bell". It is used when criticism, resentment or a request is directed at the wrong person: 〜に文句を言うのはお門違いだ, お門違いの批判. Similar are 見当違い "off the mark" and 筋違い "out of place, not responsible". Mostly predicative with だ／です or attributive with の.

en.meaning: to come undone (seam); to fray; to burst open (blossoms)
examples[].german: The plan that had looked perfect began to unravel.
The cuff of the shirt has come unstitched.
The cherry buds have begun to open.
en.notes: 綻びる (mostly in kana ほころびる) is intransitive and has three images: a seam comes apart (袖口がほころびる), buds open (つぼみがほころびる), and figuratively a plan or system develops cracks (計画が綻びる). The face "opening" into a smile is usually 顔がほころぶ, with the equivalent godan form 綻ぶ. The noun 綻び means "a seam that has come apart, a weak point".

examples[].german: One should not criticize indiscriminately.
Please don't give out personal information to strangers carelessly.
Taking medicine indiscriminately is bad for your body.
en.notes: 無闇に is mostly written in kana as むやみに and means "thoughtlessly, indiscriminately, without good reason", often in warnings: むやみに〜しない, むやみに触らないでください. It also means "excessively". Intensified: むやみやたらに. Similar is やたらに, which is more colloquial and stresses the excess more.

en.meaning: to play a part in; to shoulder a share
examples[].german: I played a part in the success.
Our company, too, plays a part in promoting tourism in the town.
I want the younger generation, too, to take on a part of passing down traditional culture.
en.notes: 一端 (いったん) is "one part, one end" and not to be confused with the identically read 一旦 "once, for the time being". 〜の一端を担う means to share part of the responsibility or work for something bigger: 成功の一端を担う, 地域医療の一端を担う. It sounds modest and formal and is typical of speeches, company profiles and applications. More general is 役割を果たす.

examples[].german: A response plan for emergencies was drawn up.
You should stockpile food and water in preparation for an emergency.
A contingency in Taiwan is an issue that directly affects Japan's security as well.
en.notes: 有事 (literally "there is an incident") refers to an emergency, above all war or armed conflict; the opposite is 平時 "peacetime, normal state". Typical: 有事の際, 有事に備える, 有事法制 "emergency legislation" and as a suffix in 台湾有事 or 朝鮮半島有事. The word sounds formal; in everyday speech one says いざという時 or 緊急時 instead.

examples[].german: It's on me today.
My senior treated me to lunch.
I've eaten nothing but fine cuisine and have become thoroughly spoiled.
en.notes: 奢る (mostly in kana おごる) today mainly means "to treat someone, to pick up the bill": 今日は私がおごる, 先輩におごってもらう. It also means "to live in luxury, to be pampered", for example 口が奢る "to have a pampered palate". "To be arrogant", by contrast, is written 驕る (驕る平家は久しからず). The counterpart when being treated is ごちそうになる or ごちそうさま.

en.meaning: to cancel out; to wipe out (a debt); to offset
examples[].german: One mistake wiped out all the effort.
My friend wrote off my debt.
The goal in the second half made up for the mistake in the first half.
en.notes: 帳消し is originally the striking of a debt from the account book. 〜を帳消しにする therefore means "to cancel a debt" and figuratively "to nullify, to offset": a mistake can undo all the effort, but a success can also make up for an earlier mistake. Intransitively one says 帳消しになる. Neutral and common in sports and business reports.

examples[].german: I am filled with deep shame.
The minister spoke of his deep regret at having betrayed the public's trust.
We lost the match through poor preparation, and as manager I feel deeply ashamed.
en.notes: 忸怩たる is an elevated たる-form and appears almost only in 忸怩たる思い（がある／だ）: deep shame over one's own failure. Typical of politicians, managers and coaches who admit responsibility. It is often wrongly used in the sense of "annoying, frustrating" (悔しい); correct is shame about oneself. More everyday are 恥ずかしい or 情けない.

en.meaning: to put a brake on; to curb
examples[].german: We will curb environmental destruction.
The government intervened in the market to halt the weakening yen.
I put a brake on myself so as not to eat too many sweets.
en.notes: 歯止め is a brake block; 〜に歯止めをかける means to halt a negative development: 少子化・物価高・円安に歯止めをかける. Intransitively one says 歯止めがかかる, negated 歯止めがかからない／きかない "cannot be stopped". Typical of politics and business, but also of self-discipline.

en.meaning: to save face; to enhance one's reputation
examples[].german: I did myself credit with excellent results.
He performed well on a big stage for the first time and greatly enhanced his reputation.
I closed the negotiations and was able to do myself honor as the person in charge.
en.notes: 面目 is "honor, reputation, face"; 面目を施す means to gain honor and raise your reputation through an achievement. To be distinguished from this are 面目を保つ "to save face", 面目を失う／面目丸つぶれ "to lose face" and 面目ない "to be ashamed". For this expression the reading めんぼく is more traditional, but めんもく is also widespread. Elevated style.

en.meaning: to be indignant; to be outraged
examples[].german: I was indignant at the injustice.
The residents are outraged at the city's unilateral decision.
The clerk was inwardly furious at the rude customer's attitude.
en.notes: 憤慨する denotes indignant outrage, usually at injustice or insolent behavior: 〜に憤慨する, 〜に対して憤慨する. It is more formal than 怒る and stresses moral indignation; 激怒する is violent rage, 腹を立てる everyday annoyance. Common in reports on the reactions of citizens or those affected.

examples[].german: I have incurred the president's wrath.
A careless remark provoked the manager's fury, and he was dropped from the game.
I always keep to my curfew so as not to provoke my father's wrath.
en.notes: 逆鱗 is the scale growing in the wrong direction on a dragon's throat; whoever touches it is killed. 〜の逆鱗に触れる thus means to throw a superior or powerful person into violent rage: 社長の逆鱗に触れる, 父の逆鱗に触れる. It is not used for one's own anger and, strictly speaking, not toward equals or subordinates. Elevated expression.

en.meaning: to spur each other on; to improve through friendly rivalry
examples[].german: I grow by pushing each other to improve with my peers.
The two have spurred each other on as rivals.
In our laboratory we value an environment in which students can improve each other.
en.notes: 切磋琢磨 comes from the image of cutting and polishing bone, ivory and jade: you grind each other into shape. 切磋琢磨する means to spur each other on and improve in friendly rivalry, typically 〜と切磋琢磨する, 互いに切磋琢磨する. It is positive and popular in school, sports and corporate mission statements; pure competition would be 競い合う.

examples[].german: When you are in love, even pockmarks look like dimples.
Finding even her short temper cute is truly a case of love is blind.
After three years of marriage, the time when love was blind is long gone.
en.notes: 痘痕 are pockmarks, 靨 dimples: to those in love even pockmarks look like dimples, hence "love is blind". The proverb is almost always written in kana as あばたもえくぼ and used with だ or の (あばたもえくぼの時期). It is colloquial and jocular and mostly comments on other people's infatuation.

examples[].german: The evacuation of Japanese nationals from the conflict zone was carried out.
The local Japanese embassy is urging Japanese residents to be careful.
No harm to Japanese nationals has been confirmed in the accident.
en.notes: 邦人 refers to Japanese nationals, especially abroad, and is typical of news and official language: 在留邦人 "Japanese residing abroad", 邦人保護, 邦人の安否確認. In everyday speech one simply says 日本人. Not to be confused with the homophone 法人 "legal entity". The character 邦 ("one's own country") is also found in 邦画 "Japanese film" and 邦楽 "Japanese music".

examples[].german: The situation is gradually improving.
The new system is scheduled to be introduced step by step from next fiscal year.
Temperatures are expected to rise gradually toward the afternoon.
en.notes: 漸次 is a literary adverb for "step by step, little by little", typical of official language, weather forecasts and technical texts: 漸次導入する, 漸次改善される. In everyday speech people say 徐々に, 次第に or だんだん. Not to be confused with 暫時 "for a short while". As an adjective: 漸次的な変化.

en.meaning: to wield one's formidable skill; to take decisive action
examples[].german: He exercised his formidable abilities as an executive.
He, who had wielded great skill as a prosecutor, later became a politician.
The minister took decisive action and boldly cut wasteful budgets.
en.notes: 辣腕 is "sharp, assertive ability", 振るう "to wield, to use": 辣腕を振るう means to take energetic and sometimes ruthless action with great skill. Typical of managers, politicians, lawyers or prosecutors; also 辣腕の弁護士, 辣腕家. More neutral is 手腕を発揮する; 辣腕 sounds of toughness and sharpness.

examples[].german: The audience watched with bated breath.
The family waited with bated breath for the announcement of the exam results.
The venue was wrapped in a hushed silence.
en.notes: 固唾 (かたず, not かたつば) is the saliva that gathers in the mouth from tension; 固唾を飲む means to swallow it, that is, to wait tensely with bated breath. Almost always 固唾を飲んで見守る／待つ; also written 固唾をのむ. It is about tense expectation, not fright (that would be 息をのむ).

examples[].german: He is a young man with a promising future.
The company has high hopes for her as the next department head.
Although he had been tipped for a bright future, he was forced to retire due to injury.
en.notes: 嘱望する means to place great hopes in a person's future. Almost always in the passive: 将来を嘱望される, 前途を嘱望された若手 "promising". It is formal and typical of reports on talents in sports, art and science. More general and everyday is 期待する.

examples[].german: The media publicized it on a large scale.
The drug was touted as a miracle new medicine, but its effect was limited.
The government is eagerly trumpeting the results of its economic policy.
en.notes: 喧伝する means to make something known loudly and everywhere; often with a critical undertone that there is more noise than substance behind it. Typical: 大々的に喧伝する, 〜だと喧伝される "to be touted as …". 宣伝する is neutral advertising, 吹聴する stresses boastful spreading of the word. Literary, common in commentaries and criticism.

examples[].german: Performance has improved dramatically.
The new smartphone is far easier to use than the previous model.
Since studying abroad, his Japanese has improved remarkably.
en.notes: 格段に stresses a clear qualitative leap in a comparison, usually for the better: 格段に向上する, 格段に使いやすい, 格段に上達する. As a noun: 格段の差, 格段の進歩. 大幅に fits numbers and quantities better, はるかに is more general; in everyday speech people say ずっと.

examples[].german: The two positions are sharply divided.
I draw a clear distinction between public and private.
With the river as the boundary, the scenery of the town differs sharply.
en.notes: 截然と is a very elevated adverb for a sharp, unambiguous separation: 截然と分かれる, 截然と区別する, 截然と異なる. 截 means "to cut off", so the image is a clean cut. The reading さいぜん is also rare. In everyday speech people say はっきり or 明確に.

examples[].german: The participants were all equally surprised.
It is difficult to apply the same system uniformly nationwide.
The extent of the damage is not uniform and varies by region.
en.notes: 一様に means "all equally, without difference" and mostly describes that many people react the same way or that something is uniform: 一様に驚く, 一様に〜を適用する. The negation 一様ではない "is different, not uniform" is very common. 一律に stresses a uniform rule (一律千円), 同様に "likewise" a comparison.

examples[].german: He lavished praise.
The grandfather spends money unstintingly on his grandchildren.
My senior generously shared his knowledge with the juniors.
en.notes: 惜しみなく comes from 惜しむ "to be stingy, to regret" + なく: "without stinting". It is used with giving, praising and supporting: 惜しみなく与える, 惜しみなく協力する, 称賛を惜しみなく送る. Attributively it is 惜しみない: 惜しみない拍手. Positive and slightly elevated.

en.meaning: cannot bring oneself to; cannot bear
examples[].german: It was a sight too painful to watch.
I can't bear to throw away the desk I've used for years.
I hate to refuse, but I can't take it on this time.
en.notes: 忍びない (from 忍ぶ "to endure") expresses that you "cannot bring yourself" to do something out of compassion or regret. Typical patterns are dictionary-form verb + に忍びない (見るに忍びない "cannot bear to watch", 聞くに忍びない) and 〜のは忍びない (捨てるのは忍びない). It sounds elevated; in everyday speech people say 見ていられない or 〜のはかわいそう. 耐えられない, by contrast, means general inability to endure, e.g. pain or heat.

examples[].german: Overseas diplomatic missions handle passport renewal services.
If a child is born abroad, you submit the birth notification to the nearest overseas mission.
In response to the worsening security situation, the government strengthened security at its overseas missions.
en.notes: 在外公館 is the collective term for Japan's missions abroad: 大使館 "embassy", 総領事館 "consulate general" and permanent missions to international organizations. A word of official and press language; in everyday speech one names them specifically as 大使館 or 領事館. There, for example, passports are issued and births registered, and Japanese living abroad can vote there (在外公館投票).

examples[].german: I feel awe toward nature.
Seeing Mt. Fuji up close for the first time, I couldn't help feeling awe.
All the disciples held their strict master in awe.
en.notes: 畏敬 combines 畏 "reverent fear" and 敬 "respect"; 畏敬の念 is the "feeling of awe", and 抱く (read いだく here) means "to harbor". The object takes に or に対して: 自然に畏敬の念を抱く. Instead of 抱く one also says 畏敬の念を覚える or 持つ. Unlike 尊敬 ("respect for a person"), 畏敬 contains a reverence before something sublime such as nature, deities or great masters; 畏怖 stresses fear more. Elevated written language.

examples[].german: He speaks in an overbearing manner.
The customer kept complaining to the clerk in a domineering way.
Some people suddenly become overbearing when they gain a higher position.
en.notes: 居丈高 describes a domineering, intimidating manner of treating others "from above"; literally, sitting up tall (居丈 "sitting height") to look down at the other person. Typical are 居丈高な態度, 居丈高に言う／命じる and 居丈高になる. It is more aggressive than 偉そう and close to 高圧的 and 横柄; 傲慢 denotes more the character trait, 居丈高 the concrete behavior. Also written 威丈高.

examples[].german: The outcome of the war was decided.
Independent voters will decide the outcome of this election.
The outcome of the negotiations remains unclear.
en.notes: 帰趨 is the "outcome" of a matter or the direction it is heading, above all with wars, elections, negotiations or trials. Fixed combinations are 勝敗の帰趨, 帰趨を決する ("to decide the outcome"), 帰趨を見守る and 帰趨が注目される. The word belongs to written and news language; in everyday speech people say 結果 or 行方. Unlike 結果, 帰趨 usually stresses a still open course whose end one awaits with suspense.

en.meaning: to evoke; to be reminiscent of
examples[].german: That scenery is reminiscent of my hometown.
Her singing voice evokes a great singer of bygone days.
My son's way of laughing recalled my late father.
en.notes: 彷彿 means "standing vividly before the eyes, strikingly similar"; 彷彿とさせる means "to vividly remind of, to make one think of involuntarily". The pattern is A が B を彷彿とさせる, where A and B are strikingly similar. The short form 彷彿させる is equally common; without the causative one says 〜が彷彿とする or 目に彷彿と浮かぶ. Compared with 思い出させる it is literary and stresses strong similarity; very common in reviews and travel reports.

en.meaning: to open the way; to make a start
examples[].german: He opened the way for negotiations.
This discovery opened the door to the development of a new drug.
His one remark opened the way to resolving the long-standing conflict.
en.notes: 端緒 is the "first approach, starting point" (originally read たんしょ, today mostly たんちょ); 端緒を開く means "to take the first step, to pave the way for something". The pattern is 〜の端緒を開く, e.g. 解決の端緒を開く or 交渉の端緒を開く. Related are 端緒をつかむ ("to find a first clue", e.g. in investigations) and 〜の端緒となる. Literary; in everyday speech people say きっかけを作る or 道を開く.

examples[].german: A desolate, silent space stretches out.
The temple grounds were utterly silent and lonely at night.
In the village where no one lives anymore, old houses stand in a row, forlorn and silent.
en.notes: 寂然 describes a stillness that seems at once lonely and abandoned, for example in a deserted temple or an abandoned village. As an adverb, 寂然と mostly stands with verbs such as 静まり返る, 佇む or 立ち並ぶ; attributively one says 寂然とした + noun, elevated also 寂然たる. The word is purely literary; in everyday speech people say ひっそり(と) or しんと. The Buddhist reading じゃくねん appears above all in religious texts.

examples[].german: I apologize for the impertinent request, but could I ask you to write me a letter of recommendation?
Asking someone you've just met about their annual income is rude.
The man stared at my face rudely.
en.notes: 不躾 literally means "without 躾 (upbringing, good manners)", hence "tactless, boorish, impertinent". Typical are 不躾な質問／お願い and 不躾にじろじろ見る. Very common is the modest cushioning phrase 不躾なお願いで恐縮ですが or 不躾ながら, with which one introduces a direct request or question and apologizes in advance for the imposition. Compared with 失礼, 不躾 aims more at a lack of upbringing; 無礼 is sharper.

en.meaning: to be wholly absorbed in; to spare no effort
examples[].german: He is meticulous in his preparations.
Students facing exams are working hard on their final push.
Ahead of opening, the shop owner was fully occupied with preparing the food.
en.notes: 余念 means "other thoughts"; 余念がない therefore means "to think of nothing else but …", "to be completely absorbed in something". The target always takes に: 準備に余念がない, 練習に余念がない. It mostly describes others (athletes, merchants, examinees) in an appreciative tone; about oneself it sounds unusual. Similar are 〜に専念する and 〜に没頭する; 余念がない is, however, a fixed adjectival predicate and typical of news and reports.

en.meaning: to burst forth; to break the dam
examples[].german: She began to speak as if a dam had broken.
The moment she saw her mother's face, she burst into tears.
When the regulations were relaxed, new companies poured in as if a dam had burst.
en.notes: 堰 is a weir or dam; 堰を切る literally means "to open the weir", so that the dammed-up water shoots out. It almost always appears as 堰を切ったように ("as if a dam had broken") before verbs such as 泣き出す, 話し出す or 押し寄せる: something held back for a long time (tears, words, people, inquiries) suddenly bursts forth. Intransitively one also says 堰が切れる. Despite its -iru ending, 切る is a godan verb (切った).

examples[].german: It was protested that the statement amounted to interference in internal affairs.
Meddling in another country's elections is clearly interference in its internal affairs.
The country rejected criticism of its human rights situation as interference in its internal affairs.
en.notes: 内政干渉 (内政 "domestic affairs" + 干渉 "interference") is almost always used as an accusation: 内政干渉だ, 内政干渉に当たる, 内政干渉として反発する・退ける. The counter-principle is called 内政不干渉 "non-interference". Occasionally it is jokingly transferred to everyday life, when someone meddles in family or team matters. Basically a word from diplomacy and the press.

examples[].german: I admire his keen insight.
To have seen through the future potential of this technology ten years ago is truly his sharp eye.
The president is known as a man with a keen eye for talent.
en.notes: 慧眼 is a "sharp, penetrating eye" for the essence of things, especially the ability to judge people or developments correctly at an early stage. Typical are 慧眼の持ち主, 慧眼の士, 慧眼に感服する and さすがの慧眼だ. It is a praising word of written language and is said almost only about others. Similar are 炯眼 (same reading, "piercing gaze"), 洞察力 ("insight") and 先見の明 ("foresight").

examples[].german: He is placed in a pitiable situation.
The pitiable state of the refugees who escaped the flames of war was reported.
The once powerful man met a miserable end.
en.notes: 憫然 means "pitiable, wretched": a condition that arouses pity (憫 = "pity"). The たる-form stands attributively before nouns such as 姿, 有様, 状況 or 最期; there are also 憫然な and adverbial 憫然と. The word is very literary; in everyday speech people say 哀れな, 気の毒な or 不憫な, the latter above all for children and animals.

en.meaning: to be the beginning; to mark the start
examples[].german: This research marked the beginning of a new field.
This novel is the work that started Japanese detective fiction.
The small cafe he opened became the first step in the revival of the shopping street.
en.notes: 嚆矢 was originally a "whistling arrow" shot in ancient China as a signal for the start of a battle; from this came "beginning, first case" of a development. 〜の嚆矢となる means "to form the beginning of …, to be the first …". Equally common is 〜を嚆矢とする ("to begin with …"), e.g. in historical accounts. Very literary and typical of specialist and historical texts; in everyday speech people say 始まり or 先駆け.

en.meaning: to take a bird's-eye view; to survey
examples[].german: A perspective that surveys the whole is needed.
From the observation deck you can overlook the whole town.
When I stepped back and viewed the situation from above, the cause of the problem became visible.
en.notes: 俯瞰 means "to look down from above, to view from a bird's-eye perspective" (俯 "to bend down", 瞰 "to look down"). Literally: 山頂から町を俯瞰する; today even more common figuratively: 全体を俯瞰する, 状況を俯瞰的に見る ("to view the big picture with distance"). A transitive する-verb with を. Compared with 見下ろす ("to look down", also "to look down on"), it is more matter-of-fact and elevated; compared with 見渡す, it stresses the overview from above. Related: 俯瞰図 ("bird's-eye view diagram").

en.meaning: to maintain one's pride; to keep one's dignity
examples[].german: I keep my dignity at all times.
Even when business was hard, the shop kept its pride as a long-established store.
Even after losing his position, he maintained his dignity to the end.
en.notes: 矜持 is "pride, self-respect" in the dignified sense: the awareness of one's own worth that keeps you from degrading yourself. 矜持を保つ means "to preserve one's dignity"; related are 矜持を持つ, 〜としての矜持 (職人としての矜持) and 矜持が許さない. The original reading is きんじ, today きょうじ is usual. Unlike プライド or 自尊心, which can also mean vanity or touchiness, 矜持 is positive and elevated.

examples[].german: The prose is obscure and hard to read.
His paper is so obscure that even specialists struggle to understand it.
Please avoid obscure expressions and write in words anyone can understand.
en.notes: 晦渋 describes texts, ways of expression or lines of thought that are "dark, convoluted and hard to access" (晦 "dark", 渋 "halting"). Typical combinations are 晦渋な文章, 晦渋な表現, 晦渋な文体 and 晦渋で読みにくい. Compared with the more common 難解 ("hard to understand"), 晦渋 stresses the unclear, twisting presentation and sounds more critical and literary. The opposite is 平易 ("easy to understand").

en.meaning: to meet by chance; to run into
examples[].german: I unexpectedly ran into an old friend.
On a trip in Paris, I met my former teacher by chance for the first time in twenty years.
An encounter with a single book changed his life greatly.
en.notes: 邂逅 is a "chance, often fateful encounter", especially an unexpected reunion after a long time. The other party takes と: 旧友と邂逅する; the nominal use 〜との邂逅 or 運命的な邂逅 is also common. The word is literary and elevated; in everyday speech people say 偶然会う, 出会う or 巡り合う. A formative encounter with a book, an idea or an artwork can also be a 邂逅.

examples[].german: International cooperation based on multilateralism is considered important.
As the "our own country first" stance spreads, the significance of multilateralism is being questioned.
The leaders confirmed in a joint statement that they would uphold multilateralism.
en.notes: 多国間主義 (多国間 "among many countries" + 主義 "-ism") stands for the approach of solving problems together within frameworks such as the UN or the WTO. Opposite concepts are 単独行動主義 "unilateralism" and, as a slogan, 自国第一主義 "our own country first". A word from diplomacy and editorials; typical combinations: 多国間主義を堅持する・推進する, 多国間主義に基づく.

examples[].german: I explained by elaborating on that theory.
Expanding on the teacher's words, effort beats talent.
These survey results can probably be extended to other regions as well.
en.notes: 敷衍 means to "elaborate" a thought or "think it further": to explain a brief statement with examples or to transfer a principle to other cases. Typical are 〜を敷衍して説明する, 敷衍して言えば ("taken further, this means …") and 〜を〜に敷衍する ("to extend to …"). Compared with 説明する it is academic and literary; 詳述する stresses detail, 敷衍する the widening of the thought. Also written 敷延.

en.meaning: to boil; to seethe; to burn with passion
examples[].german: Anger seethed in his chest.
The water in the pot is boiling vigorously.
Ahead of the final, the players' blood was boiling.
en.notes: 滾る first describes water that boils bubbling or foams as a torrent (湯が滾る, 滾る激流). Figuratively it stands for surging emotions: 血が滾る ("the blood is stirred"), 闘志が滾る, 怒りが滾る. It is intransitive; "to bring to a boil, to stoke" is 滾らせる (闘志を滾らせる). Compared with 沸く／沸騰する it is more vivid and literary; mostly written in kana (たぎる).

examples[].german: I closed my umbrella before entering the shop.
I walked to the station, hunching my shoulders against the cold wind.
The child ate a sour pickled plum and puckered his mouth.
en.notes: 窄める means "to make narrower, to draw together" and occurs almost only in fixed combinations: 傘を窄める ("to close the umbrella"), 肩を窄める ("to hunch the shoulders, to make oneself small", from cold or embarrassment) and 口を窄める ("to purse the lips, to pucker the mouth"). It is transitive with を; intransitive counterparts are 窄まる and 窄む ("to become narrower"). Mostly written in kana (すぼめる). Shrugging the shoulders, by contrast, is 肩をすくめる.

examples[].german: He brags, "Nobody can beat me."
Even when confronted with the evidence, he brazenly said, "I don't know what you mean."
The man who had claimed "I'm not interested in money" was actually hiding a large sum.
en.notes: 嘯く today almost always appears with a quotation: 「…」と嘯く. It means to announce something brazenly or boastfully, often with feigned indifference ("to make a show of saying"), or to brazenly pretend ignorance (「知らない」と嘯く). The tone is always critical of the speaker. Unlike 自慢する ("to boast about something", with を), 嘯く takes no direct object such as 実力を. Literary and mostly written in kana; the old meanings "to recite to oneself" and "to howl (of animals)" are rare.

en.meaning: to be impatient; to be eager
examples[].german: I feel impatient ahead of departure.
Holding back my eager feelings, I first took a deep breath.
Young men carried away by hot-bloodedness made a reckless plan.
en.notes: 逸る describes a feeling that runs ahead: you are impatient, excited or hasty. Typical are 気が逸る, 心が逸る, 逸る気持ちを抑える and 血気に逸る ("to be carried away by youthful impetuosity", rather negative). It is intransitive and mostly written in kana; not to be confused with the identically sounding 流行る ("to be in fashion, to be rampant"). 焦る, by contrast, stresses nervousness and time pressure more.

examples[].german: A case of child abduction was reported.
"If you don't come home before dark, a kidnapper will take you," my grandmother often said.
In the story, the princess is abducted by bandits.
en.notes: 拐かす means "to abduct or carry off someone by force or trickery", traditionally above all children or young women. It sounds archaic and appears in tales, historical novels and fairy tales, often in the passive (人さらいに拐かされる). In news and everyday speech people say 誘拐する or さらう. Transitive with を; mostly written in kana (かどわかす).

examples[].german: One should refrain from slandering others.
He was denounced by the world as a traitor.
Such a decision will not escape the charge of irresponsibility.
en.notes: 謗る means "to revile, to disparage, to run someone down" and is transitive with を: 人を謗る, 陰で謗る. It is literary and mostly written in kana; in everyday speech people say 悪口を言う or 非難する, and 中傷する for targeted defamation. Very common is the noun 謗り in the fixed phrase 〜の謗りを免れない ("cannot escape the charge of …").

examples[].german: Kneading bread dough well makes it tasty.
A child is throwing a tantrum in the toy section.
He always quibbles to refuse troublesome jobs.
en.notes: 捏ねる first means "to knead" (パン生地を捏ねる, 粘土を捏ねる). Figuratively it appears in fixed phrases for persistent, useless arguing: 駄々を捏ねる ("to whine, to throw a tantrum", especially of children) and 理屈／屁理屈を捏ねる ("to split hairs"). Transitive with を, mostly written in kana (こねる). The similar 練る also means "to knead", but also "to work out (a plan)" -- one does not say 計画を捏ねる.

en.meaning: to pierce; to hit the mark
examples[].german: There is a proverb that dripping water wears away stone.
The workers drilled through the hard bedrock and pushed the tunnel forward.
His criticism hits upon the essence of human nature.
en.notes: 穿つ literally means "to bore a hole, to pierce" (岩を穿つ), known from the proverb 雨垂れ石を穿つ ("constant dripping wears away the stone"). Figuratively it means "to hit the core, to grasp shrewdly": 穿った見方 is actually a "pertinent, penetrating view". In present-day usage, however, 穿った見方をする is often used in the sense of "to look at with suspicion, in a biased way", which is considered a misuse. Literary; transitive with を.

examples[].german: A bilateral trade agreement was concluded.
The two leaders agreed to improve bilateral relations.
This problem should be discussed not bilaterally but in an international framework.
en.notes: 二国間 is used attributively with の (二国間の協定) or directly in compounds: 二国間関係, 二国間協議, 二国間会談. Adverbially one says 二国間で話し合う. The counterpart is 多国間 "multilateral"; when naming the two countries concretely, one says, e.g., 日米間 or 日中間. A word of diplomatic and business language.

en.meaning: to eat (of animals); to graze; to gnaw
examples[].german: A horse is grazing on the pasture.
A little bird is pecking at the persimmons in the garden.
For thirty years he drew a state salary as a civil servant.
en.notes: 食む is a literary word for the eating of animals, especially grazing and pecking (草を食む, 木の実を食む); for people one says 食べる. In the fixed phrase 禄を食む it means "to be on the payroll, to draw a salary" (originally from the feudal lord), today for example for civil servants. Transitive with を; mostly written in kana (はむ). Not to be confused with 蝕む (むしばむ, "to eat away, to undermine").

en.meaning: to creak; to squeak; to grate
examples[].german: The old floorboards creak with every step.
I woke in the middle of the night to the sound of a creaking door.
Over trade issues, relations between the two countries are starting to strain.
en.notes: 軋む describes the creaking, squeaking or grating of wood, doors, wheels or joints (床が軋む, ドアが軋む); the onomatopoeia ぎしぎし fits it. Figuratively one says 関係が軋む for relationships in which things "grate"; the noun 軋み and the related 軋轢 ("friction, tension") are used in this sense. Intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 軋ませる. Mostly written in kana (きしむ).

en.meaning: to smolder; to smoke; to languish
examples[].german: Discontent is smoldering among the employees.
The campfire I thought I had put out was still smoldering.
Although he has talent, he keeps languishing in the countryside.
en.notes: 燻る first means "to smolder, to smoke without really burning" (焚き火が燻る). Figuratively it stands for conflicts or discontent that keep smoldering beneath the surface (不満が燻る, 火種が燻る), and for people who despite abilities make no progress and "languish" (地方で燻っている). Intransitive, mostly in kana (くすぶる). With the same kanji there are いぶる ("to smoke") and the transitive 燻す (いぶす, "to smoke-cure").

examples[].german: He hid the fugitive in his home.
My son was secretly keeping the kitten he had picked up in his room, without telling his parents.
An acquaintance was arrested on suspicion of harboring the culprit.
en.notes: 匿う means "to hide and protect someone (secretly), to give shelter", mostly to the persecuted, fugitives or animals. The object takes を, the place に: 逃亡者を自宅に匿う. Unlike 隠す, which is also used for things, 匿う refers almost only to people or animals one takes under protection. Legally, aiding an offender is 犯人蔵匿. Mostly written in kana (かくまう).

examples[].german: I used a technique that blurs the background of the photo.
Blending eyeshadow with your finger gives a natural finish.
To the reporters' questions, the minister answered while keeping the crucial points vague.
en.notes: 暈す means "to blur, to let contours fade softly", for example in painting, photography or make-up (背景を暈す, アイシャドウを暈す). Figuratively it means "to deliberately keep something vague, to beat around the bush": 話を暈す, 答えを暈す, 肝心な点を暈す. Transitive with を; the intransitive counterpart is 暈ける (ぼける, "to become blurred"). Almost always written in kana (ぼかす).

en.meaning: to assign; to allot; to apply (to)
examples[].german: I assigned work to the new employee.
What was allotted to us was a small room without windows.
I held a cold towel against my bruised knee.
en.notes: 宛てがう has three uses: "to assign, to allot" (仕事を宛てがう), "to give (someone something), to provide" and "to apply to something, to hold against" (傷口にタオルを宛てがう). With allotting there is often an implication that the recipient has no say, especially in the passive 宛てがわれた部屋 ("the room assigned to one"). Transitive; mostly written in kana (あてがう). More neutral are 割り当てる and 与える.

en.meaning: to diminish; to dampen; to slice off
examples[].german: Repeated failures dampened his motivation.
I sliced bamboo at an angle to make a vessel for arranging flowers.
His needless remark spoiled the fun of the otherwise good banquet.
en.notes: 削ぐ concretely means "to cut off at a slant, to shave, to peel thinly" (竹を削ぐ, 鰹節を削ぐ). More common is the figurative use "to diminish, to dampen": 意欲を削ぐ, 興を削ぐ ("to spoil the mood"), 勢力を削ぐ ("to curtail power"). Transitive with を. Compared with 削る (けずる, "to plane, to cut down", also 予算を削る), 削ぐ stresses the slanting cut or the weakening of strength and motivation. Also written 殺ぐ.

examples[].german: I crouched by the roadside with a stomachache.
The scolded boy was crouching in the corner of the room, crying.
In the snow, a cat was crouching with its body curled up.
en.notes: 蹲る means "to crouch, to squat hunched over", mostly from pain, fear, cold or exhaustion. The place takes に: 道端に蹲る, 部屋の隅に蹲る; animals such as cats also "crouch" this way. Unlike しゃがむ ("to squat down", neutral), 蹲る stresses making oneself small and curling up. Intransitive; mostly written in kana (うずくまる).

en.meaning: to wilt; to weaken; to lose heart
examples[].german: After a long hospital stay, my legs have become completely weak.
Rejection notices arrived again and again, and my spirit almost flagged.
A work email arriving on Sunday killed my mood at once.
en.notes: 萎える means that strength or tension slackens: limbs become weak (足が萎える, e.g. after long bed rest), courage and willpower flag (気力が萎える). For wilting plants one more often says 萎れる (しおれる). Colloquially 萎える is very common today in the sense of "to lose the desire, to be turned off" (それは萎える). Intransitive. Legs that have fallen asleep after sitting seiza, by contrast, are 足がしびれる.

en.meaning: to graze; to flit across the mind; to steal
examples[].german: The bullet grazed his cheek.
Suddenly an ominous feeling flashed through my mind.
The man slipped past the clerk's eyes and put the goods in his pocket.
en.notes: 掠める means at its core "to touch lightly in passing, to graze" (弾が頬を掠める). From this develop two common uses: a thought or feeling "flits past" (不安が頭を掠める, 笑みが口元を掠める), and "to take something unnoticed", especially in 〜の目を掠めて ("unnoticed by …") and 掠め取る. Transitive with を; mostly written in kana (かすめる). Not to be confused with 掠れる (かすれる, "to become hoarse, to fade").

examples[].german: A department in charge of external affairs was newly established.
As the university's external liaison, he is advancing cooperation with companies.
As an international lawyer, I handle contract negotiations with foreign companies.
en.notes: 渉外 (literally "to negotiate with the outside") refers to an organization's contact with the outside, for example with authorities, business partners, customers or foreign bodies. Typical: 渉外担当 "liaison officer", 渉外部, 渉外事務, in banks 渉外係 for field-service client managers and 渉外弁護士 for lawyers with cross-border cases. Not the same as 外交 "diplomacy between states" or 広報 "public relations". Homophones: 生涯, 障害.

examples[].german: I am panting after running up the slope.
Many small and medium-sized companies are struggling under the prolonged recession.
The child who had a fever was gasping painfully.
en.notes: 喘ぐ first means "to gasp, to struggle for breath", for example after exertion or in illness. At N1 level the figurative meaning "to suffer under something, to groan" is particularly important, with に for the burden: 不況に喘ぐ "to groan under the recession", 重税に喘ぐ, 貧困に喘ぐ. For plain breathlessness people usually say 息が切れる in everyday speech; 喘ぐ is more vivid and literary. Intransitive godan verb; news likes to use it for companies and regions in distress.

examples[].german: He kept greedily pursuing power.
The hungry children ate the bread as if devouring it.
It was a holiday, so I ended up idly sleeping until past noon.
en.notes: 貪る means "to crave greedily" and is transitive with を: 権力を貪る, 利益を貪る. In fixed combinations it also means "to indulge oneself extensively in something": 惰眠を貪る ("to sleep lazily"), 本を貪るように読む ("to devour books").
