Concretely it can mean "to devour greedily" with food, mostly as 貪るように食べる. Literary and mostly written in kana; the related adjective is 貪欲 ("greedy").

en.meaning: to open; to bloom; to break into a smile; to come undone (seam)
examples[].german: When spring comes, the plum buds open.
Seeing his grandchild's face, the grandfather's face broke into a smile.
The cuff of the worn-out shirt has come unstitched.
en.notes: 綻ぶ describes how something closed opens slightly: buds "open" (蕾が綻ぶ, a typical spring image), a face "brightens into a smile" (顔が綻ぶ, 口元が綻ぶ) and seams "come undone" (袖口が綻ぶ). Intransitive; transitively one says 顔を綻ばせる. There also exists the equivalent ichidan form 綻びる; the noun 綻び also stands for weak points in plans or systems. Mostly written in kana (ほころぶ).

examples[].german: Luckily, he escaped the disaster.
With the bank's support, the company narrowly avoided bankruptcy.
The manager will probably not escape responsibility for this misjudgment.
en.notes: 免れる means "to escape a danger or burden": 災難を免れる, 倒産を免れる, 責任を免れる. Very common is the negated form 〜を免れない ("… is unavoidable"): 批判は免れない, 〜の謗りを免れない. The traditional reading is まぬかれる; in present-day Japanese まぬがれる is at least as widespread. The object takes を. Literary; in everyday speech people say 助かる or 避けられる.

en.meaning: to falsify; to lie; to pretend
examples[].german: He entered by falsifying his identity.
I want to stop living by deceiving myself.
She put her honest feelings into a letter.
en.notes: 偽る means "to give out something false, to falsify" and is transitive with を: 身分を偽る, 年齢を偽る, 経歴を偽る, 自分を偽る ("to put on a pretense"). The fixed phrase 偽らざる + noun (偽らざる気持ち, 偽らざる本音) means "sincere, unvarnished". Compared with 嘘をつく ("to lie", general), 偽る stresses the falsifying of a specific fact; 騙す is "to deceive someone", 偽造する "to forge documents". Neutral to literary.

examples[].german: She pitied the unfortunate people.
If people are going to pity me, I'd rather struggle on alone.
He just feels sorry for his own circumstances and does nothing.
en.notes: 憐れむ means "to pity, to take pity" and is transitive with を: 不幸な人を憐れむ, 自分を憐れむ ("to feel sorry for oneself"). Often a gradient is implied -- one looks down on someone weaker -- which is why 憐れむような目で見られる ("being looked at with pitying eyes") is felt as insulting. More neutral is 同情する ("to sympathize"). Also written 哀れむ; the noun is 憐れみ ("pity, mercy").

examples[].german: The subordinate remonstrated with the boss over his reckless behavior.
The retainer remonstrated with his lord at the risk of his life.
The daughter gently admonished her father for drinking too much.
en.notes: 諌める means to point out someone's faults and urge them to turn back -- traditionally to a superior such as a lord, boss or parents: 主君を諌める, 上司の暴走を諌める. The person takes を, and the misbehavior also takes を (〜の〜を諌める). Compared with 注意する or たしなめる ("to reprimand", more toward equals or inferiors), 諌める stresses the respectful, often courageous intervention from below; 戒める means generally "to warn, to admonish", also oneself. The correct spelling is actually 諫める.

examples[].german: I deeply apologized for my rude remark.
I apologized by phone to the other party for being late for the appointment.
He went around apologizing, house by house, to the neighbors he had troubled.
en.notes: 詫びる means "to apologize (formally)". The reason is marked with を (遅刻を詫びる, 非礼を詫びる), the person with に (先方に詫びる). It is more formal and more literary than 謝る; especially common is the noun in お詫びする, お詫び申し上げます and 詫びを入れる ("to formally ask for forgiveness"). Typical of business letters, official statements and novels.

en.meaning: to regret; to repent; to rue
examples[].german: I still regret the mistakes of my youth.
The defendant stated in court that he deeply regretted his crime.
"Those who repent of their sins will be saved," the pastor said.
en.notes: 悔いる means "to regret" in a serious, moral sense: 過ちを悔いる, 罪を悔いる. It is more literary and weightier than 後悔する, which also fits everyday trifles. Common related words are the noun 悔い (悔いが残る "regret remains", 悔いのない人生 "a life without regret") and the compound 悔い改める ("to repent and mend one's ways", also in a religious sense). Transitive with を.

en.meaning: to haunt; to bring a curse; to take its toll
examples[].german: His unhealthy lifestyle took its toll and he fell ill.
In the village it is believed that anyone who destroys this shrine will be cursed.
The early mistakes came back to haunt them, and the team lost the match.
en.notes: 祟る originally means that gods, spirits or the dead bring misfortune upon people (祟り "curse, punishment of the spirits"; passive 祟られる). In everyday speech the figurative use is much more common: something done earlier "comes back to bite" and leads to bad consequences, in the pattern 〜が祟って (無理が祟って, 寝不足が祟って, 不摂生が祟って). Intransitive. Similar but more neutral is 〜のせいで.

examples[].german: Members of the Diet have immunity from arrest during the session.
The immunity of legislators from arrest exists to prevent unjust suppression by the government.
Because they can be arrested even during a session with the Diet's consent, immunity from arrest is not absolute.
en.notes: 不逮捕特権 (不逮捕 "non-arrest" + 特権 "privilege"): Under Article 50 of the Constitution, members of the Diet may be arrested during the session only with the consent of their chamber (逮捕許諾); diplomats also enjoy 不逮捕特権. To be distinguished from 免責特権 (Article 51), which exempts legislators from liability for speeches and votes in the Diet. Typical: 不逮捕特権を有する・持つ; legal technical language.

en.meaning: to scream; to shout; to bawl
examples[].german: A drunk is shouting in the street.
The child is lying on the floor, crying and wailing.
When things do not go his way, he immediately starts yelling wildly.
en.notes: 喚く means "to scream or shout loudly and without restraint", often in a way others find annoying. Typical forms are 大声で喚く, 泣き喚く ("to cry and wail") and 喚き散らす ("to rant and rave"). Compared with 叫ぶ ("to cry out, shout", neutral) and 怒鳴る ("to shout at someone"), 喚く stresses chaotic, uncontrolled noise. Intransitive, pejorative, usually written in kana (わめく).

en.meaning: to steer into; to induce; to manoeuvre into
examples[].german: I maneuvered him into resigning.
It is hard to get children to study of their own accord.
The culprit steered things so that the police suspected someone else.
en.notes: 仕向ける means "to (cleverly) get someone to do something", mostly in the pattern 〜を／〜に…ように仕向ける. It often carries a sense of steering or manipulation: you do not give a direct order but create circumstances in which the other person seems to act on their own. Compared with the direct causative (させる) and 促す ("to prompt, urge"), it is more indirect and can sound negative. In trade, 仕向け also means "shipment" (仕向け地 "destination").

en.meaning: to incite; to egg on; to stoke
examples[].german: Those around him fanned his anger.
I lit the wood stove with rolled-up newspaper.
Egged on by a friend, he went to confront the company president directly.
en.notes: 焚きつける literally means "to light or kindle a fire" (ストーブを焚きつける; the noun 焚きつけ is "kindling"). Figuratively it means "to egg someone on, to incite" so that they do something: 〜を焚きつけて…させる, often in the passive 〜に焚きつけられる. Similar are 煽る ("to fan, stir up", also for moods and media) and けしかける ("to set on someone"). Also written 焚き付ける; neutral to slightly colloquial.

en.meaning: to start (a fight); to launch an attack; to set a trap
examples[].german: The enemy started the fight first.
I set a mousetrap in the kitchen.
There was a report that a bomb had been planted at the station.
en.notes: 仕掛ける is transitive and has two main uses: to "start" a conflict (戦い・喧嘩・攻撃を仕掛ける), often with 〜てくる when the opponent attacks on their own initiative, and to secretly "set up, plant" something (罠・爆弾・隠しカメラを仕掛ける). Unlike neutral 始める, it always implies intent or cunning. The noun 仕掛け means "mechanism, trick, device".

en.meaning: to go against; to disobey; to turn one's back on
examples[].german: He went against his parents' expectations.
The soldier disobeyed his superior's order and went back to help his comrades.
Acts that violate the law cannot be forgiven, whatever the reason.
en.notes: 背く is intransitive and takes に: 命令に背く "to disobey an order", 法に背く "to violate the law", 期待に背く "to disappoint expectations". Compared with 逆らう ("to defy", more toward people and forces), 背く stresses the breaking of a duty or loyalty and sounds more literary; 反する is the plain "to be contrary to". The transitive counterpart 背ける means "to turn away" (顔を背ける).

en.meaning: to cover up; to fudge; to deceive
examples[].german: He fudged the expense records and used the money privately.
When asked an awkward question, he always laughs it off.
I lied about my age and applied for a part-time job.
en.notes: ごまかす is almost always written in kana; 誤魔化す is an ateji spelling. It means "to fudge, cheat" with figures and information (年齢・数字・経費をごまかす) and "to gloss over, wriggle out" with questions or mistakes (話をごまかす, 笑ってごまかす). Unlike 騙す, which tricks a person directly, ごまかす is mostly about obscuring facts. The noun ごまかし means "swindle, evasion".

en.meaning: to patch up appearances; to gloss over
examples[].german: I tried to cover up the failure, but it was useless.
She hurriedly put on a smile and smoothed over the moment.
That company thinks only of keeping up appearances.
en.notes: 取り繕う means to cover up a mistake or an embarrassing situation in a makeshift way so that everything seems fine on the outside. Typical combinations are その場を取り繕う "to somehow smooth over the situation", 体裁を取り繕う "to keep up appearances" and 失敗を取り繕う. The original meaning "to mend, patch" is rare today. Transitive with を; unlike 言い繕う, the covering up is done not only with words but also through behavior.

en.meaning: to escape; to flee from; to evade
examples[].german: I narrowly escaped the disaster.
He keeps making excuses in an attempt to evade responsibility.
Escaping the bustle of the city, I moved to a village in the mountains.
en.notes: 逃れる is intransitive and takes から or を: 危険から逃れる, 責任を逃れる. It is more formal and abstract than 逃げる, which describes physical flight; typical objects are responsibility, punishment, pursuit or fate. Related are 言い逃れ "excuse" and 免れる ("to be spared"). Transitive relatives are 逃す/逃がす "to miss; to let escape".

en.meaning: to overlook; to let pass; to turn a blind eye to
examples[].german: We cannot just let this problem pass.
While proofreading, I overlooked a small typo.
It would be a waste to let the chance in front of you slip by like that.
en.notes: 見過ごす is transitive and has two nuances: to "overlook" something unintentionally (like 見落とす) and to knowingly "let it pass, stand by and do nothing" (like 見逃す). The second nuance often appears in the negative: 見過ごすわけにはいかない "we cannot just look the other way". With みすみす you stress that one lets an opportunity slip by with open eyes.

en.meaning: to deceive; to beguile; to lure
examples[].german: A swindler deceived an old man and took his money.
In folktales, foxes often bewitch people.
Taken in by sweet words, she handed over all her savings.
en.notes: たぶらかす is mostly written in kana and sounds archaic to literary. It means "to bewitch, lead astray", often with fine words or seduction, and is typical of foxes and tanuki in folktales (狐に誑かされる). Neutral 騙す is the everyday word for "to deceive". It often appears in the passive: 甘い言葉に誑かされる.

examples[].german: Legislators' immunity for their statements is guaranteed.
In the personal bankruptcy procedure, the discharge of his debts was granted.
The terms of use of this app contain a long disclaimer.
en.notes: 免責 (免 "to exempt" + 責 "responsibility") is exemption from liability or obligations. Common compounds: 免責事項 "disclaimer", 免責条項 "exemption clause", 免責特権 "immunity (indemnity)" of legislators and, in insolvency law, 免責決定 "discharge of debts". Typical is 〜の免責が認められる; as a する-verb (免責する, mostly 免責される) it is rather legal; in everyday speech one says 責任を負わない.

en.meaning: to set on; to incite; to egg on
examples[].german: I set the dog on the suspicious person and drove him away.
Egged on by my friends, I plucked up the courage to confess to her.
Behind the scenes he incited his associates to spread bad rumors about his rival.
en.notes: けしかける is mostly written in kana. It means to "set" a dog on someone (犬を嗾ける) and, figuratively, to "egg someone on" to do something: 人を嗾けて〜させる. The passive is very common: 友達に嗾けられて. Related are 唆す ("to tempt into something bad", rather covert) and 煽る ("to fan", often a crowd or mood).

examples[].german: The horse neighed loudly.
From a distant ranch came the sound of a horse neighing.
When the jockey pulled hard on the reins, the horse neighed high and reared up.
en.notes: 嘶く is intransitive and used practically only for horses (occasionally donkeys); the subject takes が or は. The noun is 嘶き "neigh", the onomatopoeia is ヒヒーン. Other animal sounds have their own verbs: dogs 吠える, birds and insects generally 鳴く. The word belongs to written, narrative language; the kanji is rare, so it is also found in kana as いななく.

en.meaning: to melt; to turn creamy; to melt away
examples[].german: The chocolate melts in your mouth.
When I baked it in the oven, the cheese melted nicely.
Whispered to in a sweet voice, her heart almost melted.
en.notes: とろける is mostly written in kana. Unlike the general 溶ける ("to melt, dissolve"), とろける describes a soft, creamy melting and sounds pleasant, which is why it is popular in advertising: 口の中でとろける, とろけるチーズ. Figuratively it means "to melt, be enraptured": 心がとろける, とろけるような笑顔. The transitive counterpart 蕩かす is rare.

examples[].german: An ear-piercing scream rang out.
Suddenly a thunderclap tore through the stillness of the night.
When the players appeared, deafening cheers rose up.
en.notes: つんざく is mostly written in kana and is a literary, transitive verb. It appears almost always in the set phrase 耳をつんざく(ような) "deafening", for screams, explosions or cheers. Besides that, a sound or flash "tears through" silence, air or darkness: 静寂・空気・闇を劈く. In everyday speech one says すごい音 or 耳が痛いほどの音 instead.

en.meaning: to gouge out; to hollow out; to cut deep
examples[].german: His words cut deep into my heart.
I gouged the sprouts out of the potato with a knife.
This film sharply exposes the darkness of modern society.
en.notes: えぐる is mostly written in kana and is transitive. Literally it means "to gouge, hollow out" (potato eyes, a hole in the ground), often as 抉り取る. Figuratively it can "wound deeply" emotionally (心を抉る) or, in journalism and criticism, "ruthlessly expose" a problem (社会の闇・問題の核心を抉る). Not to be confused with the colloquial adjective えぐい.

en.meaning: to twist; to wring; to screw
examples[].german: I wrung out the wet towel.
I twisted off the stuck jar lid with all my strength.
When stretching, you slowly twist your upper body to the left and right.
en.notes: ねじる is mostly written in kana or as 捻じる; the kanji 捩る can also be read よじる ("to writhe") or もじる ("to parody"). It is transitive and means to "turn, twist" something around its own axis: 蓋をねじる, 体をねじる, タオルをねじって絞る. Similar is ひねる, which means more a short, small twist (蛇口をひねる). The intransitive counterpart is ねじれる "to get twisted"; related is ねじ "screw".

en.meaning: to lean on; to sit heavily (in the stomach)
examples[].german: He leaned against the wall and rested.
I ate too much fried food last night, and now my stomach feels heavy.
On the train, the person next to me fell asleep and leaned on my shoulder.
en.notes: もたれる has two meanings: to lean one's body against something (壁にもたれる, いすの背にもたれる) and, relating to the stomach, "to sit heavily in the stomach" (胃がもたれる, whence the noun 胃もたれ). The kanji 凭れる is rare; it is almost always written もたれる. Close in meaning is 寄りかかる, which stresses putting one's weight on something more and can also mean "to depend on someone" figuratively. Intransitive; the support is marked with に.

examples[].german: An attitude of sucking up to one's boss is not liked.
A newspaper that fawns on those in power cannot be trusted.
He stayed true to his own music without pandering to trends.
en.notes: おもねる is intransitive, takes に and belongs to written, critical language: 権力に阿る "to toady to those in power", 大衆に阿る "to tell the public what it wants to hear". In everyday speech one says 媚びる, ご機嫌を取る or へつらう instead. It often appears negated as praise: 流行に阿らない "not to pander, to stay unwavering".

en.meaning: to freeze (with fear); to be paralyzed with fear
examples[].german: My legs froze with fear and I could not move.
At the sudden loud noise, she stood rooted to the spot.
Stared at sharply by the interviewer, I felt myself shrink.
en.notes: すくむ is intransitive and describes freezing up from fear, shock or awe. Typical phrases are 足が竦む ("to get weak knees, be unable to go on"), 身が竦む ("to be as if paralyzed") and the compound 立ち竦む "to stand rooted to the spot". The transitive counterpart 竦める appears mainly in 首・肩を竦める "to pull in one's head, shrug one's shoulders". Usually written in kana.

en.meaning: to obey respectfully; to be formal/stiff; to sit properly
examples[].german: I sat formally in front of the customer.
"Please reserve the meeting room." "Certainly."
We are friends, so you do not need to be so formal.
en.notes: かしこまる is mostly written in kana. It is most often met as かしこまりました, the humble polite formula "certainly, understood" in customer service and toward superiors (more polite than 分かりました). Otherwise it describes stiff, formal-respectful behavior or sitting: 畏まって座る, 畏まった席 "a formal occasion", そんなに畏まらないで "don't be so formal".

en.meaning: appearance (before a court/authority); turning oneself in
examples[].german: The defendant appeared in court.
The day after the incident, the suspect turned himself in at the police station.
A notice arrived from the tax office requiring me to appear in person.
en.notes: 出頭 means to appear in person, on order, before a court, the police or an authority: 裁判所に出頭する, 出頭を命じる・求める, 出頭命令. The second important meaning is "to turn oneself in": 警察に出頭する. Legally to be distinguished from this is 自首, voluntary surrender before the crime or the culprit is known, which mitigates punishment; someone who is already wanted merely "turns himself in" (出頭). Intransitive する-verb, the place takes に.

en.meaning: to tremble; to quake; to shudder
examples[].german: I shuddered at the horrifying sight.
The family trembled with fear at the threatening phone call from the culprit.
The night before the exam results, he trembled with anxiety and could not sleep.
en.notes: おののく is intransitive and literary; it means "to tremble, quake" with fear, excitement or cold and typically appears as 恐怖に慄く or 不安に慄く. The kanji 慄く and 戦く are equivalent spellings of the same word, but it is often written in kana. The 慄 also appears in 戦慄 "shudder, horror". Neutral 震える is the everyday word; おののく stresses inner shock.

examples[].german: The children are romping in the park.
On her first trip abroad, my mother was as excited as a child.
They played around too much during the day, and everyone fell asleep in the car on the way back.
en.notes: はしゃぐ is almost always written in kana; 燥ぐ is rare. It is intransitive and describes exuberant, loud joy, typically in children; for adults often with 子供のように. Common is はしゃぎすぎる "to overdo the frolicking". 騒ぐ stresses the noise, 浮かれる the elevated, slightly frivolous mood.

en.meaning: to tremble with fear; to shudder
examples[].german: My whole body trembled from the cold and fear.
Facing the enemy's huge army, the soldiers trembled.
People trembled in fear at the violent shaking.
en.notes: 戦く is the same word as 慄く: intransitive, literary, "to tremble, quake" with fear or excitement. The compound 恐れ戦く "to tremble in fear" is very common. Because 戦 is otherwise read たたかう or いくさ (戦いた could also be misread as たたかった), the word is often written in kana. The everyday word is 震える.

examples[].german: The newcomer made an overstepping remark and was warned by a senior colleague.
I apologize for overstepping.
I left the tea steeping and it brewed too long and became bitter.
en.notes: 出過ぎる is intransitive. Figuratively it means "to take too much upon oneself, be forward", above all in the set phrases 出過ぎた真似をする and 出過ぎたことを言う, often in apologies to superiors. More colloquial is 出しゃばる. Literally it means "to stick out too far" or, with tea, "to steep too long, get too strong".

en.meaning: to refrain from; to hold back; to jot down
examples[].german: I am cutting back on alcohol for my health.
Just in case, please make a note of your reservation number.
With an important exam tomorrow, he has been restless since morning.
en.notes: 控える is mostly transitive: 〜を控える means "to refrain from, abstain from something" (飲酒・外出・発言を控える); as a polite prohibition you often read 撮影はお控えください. Second, it means "to note down" (番号を控える). Third, 〜を…に控える expresses an "upcoming event": 試験を明日に控える "to have the exam tomorrow ahead of one". Related are 控えめ "restrained, modest" and 控え室 "waiting room".

en.meaning: to rebel; to revolt; to mutiny
examples[].german: The vassal rebelled against his lord.
Part of the army rose against the government and occupied the capital.
He was called a traitor who had turned against his homeland.
en.notes: 叛く is a special spelling of 背く with the same meaning and grammar (〜に叛く). The kanji 叛 ("rebellion", as in 謀叛 and 叛乱) stresses open revolt against a ruler, a government or the fatherland. In modern texts 背く is the standard spelling; 叛く appears mainly in historical and literary texts.

en.meaning: to admonish; to reprimand; to rebuke
examples[].german: I admonished a junior colleague who was behaving rudely.
A mother quietly scolded her child for making noise on the train.
"That's going too far," a friend chided me.
en.notes: たしなめる is mostly written in kana and is transitive (人を嗜める). It denotes a calm, often gentle "admonishing, rebuking", typically by elders or superiors. 叱る is stronger and angrier, 注意する more neutral. Not to be confused with 嗜む ("to be versed in something, to enjoy in moderation"), which has the same kanji.

examples[].german: He forgave his friend's mistake.
The king pardoned the offender and set him free.
en.notes: 宥す means to treat a mistake or guilt with leniency. The rare spelling stresses the forgiving; in everyday writing 許す is usual, and for a remission of punishment also 赦す. Not to be confused with 宥める (なだめる, "to soothe"). Typical are 人を宥す and 罪を宥す. Transitive godan verb in す: 宥します・宥して・宥さない.

en.meaning: to flutter; to wave; to reverse
examples[].german: The flag is fluttering in the wind.
No matter how many times they tried to persuade him, his resolve did not change.
Looking at it the other way round, at the current state of Japan, there are still many challenges.
en.notes: 翻る is intransitive: flags, skirts or coats "flutter, wave" (旗が風に翻る), things "turn over", and opinions or decisions "suddenly change". The te-form 翻って serves in texts as a transition: "looking at it the other way round, on the other hand ...". The transitive counterpart 翻す appears in 前言を翻す "to take back one's words" and 反旗を翻す "to raise the banner of revolt".

en.meaning: to be covered in; to be smeared with
examples[].german: He came home covered in mud.
After working in the field all day, he was soaked in sweat from head to toe.
He finally escaped from a life buried in debt.
en.notes: まみれる is intransitive and takes に: 泥に塗れる, 汗に塗れる "to be covered all over". Much more common is the suffix form 〜まみれ in kana: 泥まみれ, 血まみれ, 借金まみれ. Unlike 〜だらけ ("full of ...", also for many individual things such as 間違いだらけ), 〜まみれ stresses being smeared on the surface or, figuratively, being completely sunk in something. Set phrase: 一敗地に塗れる "to suffer a crushing defeat".

examples[].german: The witness received a summons from the court.
The Diet summoned those involved in the scandal as witnesses.
In the game, I summoned a powerful monster.
en.notes: 召喚 means to formally call someone in, above all to summon them in court or in parliament: 証人を召喚する, 召喚に応じる, 召喚状 "summons (document)". Transitive する-verb; from the summoned person's perspective it is in the passive: 裁判所に召喚される. From fantasy and games one knows the second meaning, "to summon (a creature)" (召喚魔法, 召喚獣). Not to be confused with the homophone 召還 "to recall (an ambassador)": 大使を召還する.

en.meaning: to dodge; to evade; to sidestep
examples[].german: He skillfully dodged his opponent's attack.
The minister parried the reporter's tough question with a smile.
A bicycle suddenly shot out, but I dodged it instantly.
en.notes: かわす is mostly written in kana and is transitive: to physically "dodge" an attack or obstacle (攻撃を躱す, 身を躱す) and figuratively to "deftly fend off" questions or criticism (質問・追及を躱す). Similar is 避ける, which means "to avoid" more generally. Not to be confused with the homophone 交わす "to exchange" (言葉・約束を交わす).

en.meaning: to gloss over with words; to make excuses
examples[].german: He tried to talk his way out of it but was seen through.
No matter how much he glossed over the reason for being late, it did not work on his boss.
The minister tried to smooth over his gaffe but only drew more criticism.
en.notes: 言い繕う means to gloss over a mistake or an omission with words, that is, with excuses or clever explanations. Typical are 失敗をうまく言い繕う and その場を言い繕う. It is the verbal variant of 取り繕う; similar, but aimed more at talking one's way out or deceiving, are 言い逃れる "to talk one's way out" and ごまかす. Transitive godan verb, rather literary and slightly pejorative.

en.meaning: to be intimidated; to lose one's nerve
examples[].german: You must not be daunted in the face of difficulties.
Not intimidated by the huge audience, she sang with composure.
When he realized his opponent was a big man, he completely lost his nerve.
en.notes: 怖じける is intransitive and literary; it means "to be intimidated, lose courage" in the face of a person or situation (〜に怖じける, 〜を前にして怖じける). More often heard is 怖気づく with the same meaning. Related are 怖気 "fear" and 物怖じ "timidity" (物怖じしない "fearless"). It often appears negated: 〜に怖じけることなく.

en.meaning: to spread; to run rampant; to proliferate
examples[].german: False information is rampant on the internet.
While we were away, weeds overran the whole garden.
Old customs and corruption were rife in the government office.
en.notes: はびこる is mostly written in kana and is intransitive (〜に蔓延る). Literally weeds "run riot"; figuratively unwanted things such as corruption, violence, prejudice or false information "are rampant, spread". The word always has a negative coloring, unlike neutral 広がる. Read with the same kanji, 蔓延 (まんえん) means "spread", above all of diseases.

en.meaning: to plan; to scheme; to have in mind
examples[].german: He was secretly plotting revenge.
That company is aiming to expand into the Asian market.
I schemed to make a quick profit but failed miserably.
en.notes: 目論む is transitive and means "to plan, have in mind", usually with an air of ambition or calculation: 復讐・進出・一儲けを目論む, or 〜ようと目論む. Clearly more negative is 企む "to hatch a plot"; 計画する is neutral. The noun 目論見 is very common: 目論見通り "as planned", 目論見が外れる "the plan does not work out".

en.meaning: to laugh scornfully; to laugh at; to ridicule
examples[].german: Laughing scornfully at other people's misfortune is a shameful act.
The people around him ridiculed his dream as reckless.
When I failed, he just snorted at me.
en.notes: 嗤う is the same verb as 笑う; the spelling with 嗤 fixes it to "to deride, to ridicule" and is literary. In this meaning it is transitive (人・夢・失敗を嗤う). Typical is 鼻で嗤う "to laugh contemptuously". In everyday texts one usually writes 笑う and recognizes the mockery from the context; an unambiguous word is 嘲笑う "to jeer at".

examples[].german: I tripped on a stone and fell.
I tripped on a step in the dark corridor and scraped my knee.
The new business stumbled in its first year.
en.notes: けつまずく is mostly written in kana and is a colloquially intensified form of つまずく; the 蹴 ("to kick") stresses that one catches one's foot on something. It is intransitive and takes に: 石に蹴躓く. Figuratively it can mean "to falter, fail" like つまずく, though for failures 躓く is more usual.

en.meaning: to torment; to plague; to haunt
examples[].german: I am tormented by guilt.
She has been plagued for years by headaches of unknown cause.
At night, anxiety about the future tormented him.
en.notes: 苛む is transitive but appears almost always in the passive: 罪悪感・不安・後悔・痛みに苛まれる "to be tormented by ...". It is literary and describes lasting mental or physical torment; intensified also 責め苛む. More neutral is 苦しめる; 悩む, by contrast, is intransitive and refers to one's own brooding.

en.meaning: to have made to order; to order
examples[].german: I visited a tailor to have a suit made.
I had a kimono made for the wedding.
Today's weather is just right for a picnic.
en.notes: あつらえる is transitive and means to "have something made" to one's own wishes, above all clothing, kimono, shoes or furniture (スーツを誂える). General ordering is 注文する; nowadays one also says オーダーメイドで作る. The phrase お誂え向き "tailor-made for, ideal for" is common: ピクニックにお誂え向きの天気.

examples[].german: Several lawmakers were arrested in a corruption case.
The mayor resigned after being accused of involvement in corruption.
Ethics rules for public servants have been tightened to prevent corruption.
en.notes: 汚職 is corruption by public officials, i.e. bribery and abuse of office by politicians and civil servants. Typical: 汚職事件, 汚職に手を染める ("to get involved in corruption"), 汚職で逮捕される, 汚職を摘発する. The bribe itself is 賄賂, and legally one speaks of 贈収賄; 腐敗, by contrast, means the general moral decay of a system.

examples[].german: A warrant for compulsory appearance was issued against the witness who did not appear.
A defendant who does not respond to a summons without good reason may be brought in by force.
A defendant who has been brought in by force is released within 24 hours unless detention is ordered.
en.notes: 勾引 is a technical term of the Code of Criminal Procedure: the court has a defendant or witness who fails to obey a summons (召喚) without good reason brought in by force; the document is called 勾引状. Unlike 逮捕 "arrest", it serves only to bring the person before the court; afterward 勾留 "pretrial detention" may follow. Mostly in the passive: 勾引される. In newspapers the substitute spelling 拘引 is also found.

en.meaning: to play dumb; to feign ignorance
examples[].german: Even when questioned, he played dumb and did not answer.
When asked "You snuck a bite, didn't you?", my younger brother played innocent: "What do you mean?"
I love the deadpan charm of that comedian.
en.notes: とぼける is mostly written in kana and is intransitive. Its main meaning is "to play dumb, act clueless", for example when caught; a synonym is しらばくれる. As とぼけた + noun it also describes a dry, quirky humor (とぼけた味, とぼけた顔). Note: the same kanji are also read ぼける ("to go senile") and ほうける.

examples[].german: The smoke made me choke and I could not stop coughing.
I ate my rice in a hurry and ended up choking.
When I entered the room, there was a stifling smell of perfume.
en.notes: むせる is mostly written in kana and is intransitive. One chokes on food or drink, or gets an urge to cough from smoke, dust or a strong smell: 煙に噎せる, 煙で噎せる. The intensified form 噎せ返る is also used figuratively: 噎せ返るような暑さ・香り "stifling, overpowering". 咳き込む stresses the coughing fit itself.

en.meaning: to be bulky; to take up space
examples[].german: Winter clothes are bulky, so storing them is a problem.
Let's pick souvenirs that are not bulky.
Paper dictionaries are bulky, so I take an electronic dictionary when traveling.
en.notes: かさばる is mostly written in kana and is intransitive: luggage, clothes or books "are bulky, take up a lot of room". It is about volume (嵩), not necessarily weight; for weight one says 重い. Not to be confused with 嵩む "to mount up", which applies above all to costs: 費用が嵩む.

en.meaning: to become excited; to be worked up; to rise
examples[].german: I was so keyed up before the match that I could not sleep.
My emotions ran high and I involuntarily raised my voice.
The moment the title was decided, the players' emotions surged all at once.
en.notes: 昂ぶる is intransitive and is used with 気持ち・感情・神経が as the subject: feelings "rise, come to a boil". The spelling 高ぶる is more common and also carries the second meaning "to be haughty" (驕り高ぶる). More neutral is 興奮する; 昂ぶる sounds somewhat more literary and stresses inner tension.

en.meaning: to peer; to watch for; to wait for
examples[].german: He is waiting for his chance.
Watching my boss's expression, I broached the subject.
Deep anguish can be glimpsed in his writing.
en.notes: 窺う is mostly written in kana and is transitive. It means "to watch secretly" (中の様子を窺う), "to lie in wait" (機会・チャンスを窺う), appears in the set phrase 顔色を窺う "to gauge someone's mood", and as 〜が窺える "can be discerned". Not to be confused with the homophone humble 伺う "to ask; to visit".

en.meaning: to concern; to be connected with; to get involved
examples[].german: It is a serious problem that involves life and death.
You had better not get involved with people like that.
He has been involved in this research for many years.
en.notes: 拘わる is a rare spelling of 関わる, which is standard today; the kanji 拘 is otherwise mostly read こだわる (拘る) or in にも拘らず. The verb is intransitive: 〜に関わる "to concern, to have to do with, to be involved in" (命に関わる "life-threatening", 事件に関わる), and 〜と関わる "to get involved with someone". The related noun is 関わり "relationship, connection".

examples[].german: A trifling sum will not change anything.
My contribution is negligible.
The difference between the two is slight and hardly noticeable.
en.notes: 微々たる is the attributive form of the たる-adjective 微々 and stands only before nouns: 微々たる金額・差・量・変化. As a predicate one says 微々たるものだ. Compared with neutral わずか it sounds more literary and stresses that something hardly counts; it is often used modestly for one's own contribution (私の力など微々たるものです).

examples[].german: His hateful attitude made me angry.
In court, the defendant glared hatefully at the prosecutor.
The actor who played the drama's villain with convincing odiousness became a talking point.
en.notes: 憎々しい is an i-adjective describing people, faces, tone of voice or behavior that "arouse hatred, seem repulsive": 憎々しい態度・口調・顔. It is stronger and more serious than 憎らしい, which can also be playful (憎らしいほど上手). The form 憎々しげに, by contrast, describes someone looking or speaking spitefully themselves.

examples[].german: The mountain lit by the morning sun looked divine.
In the dim main hall, the Buddha statue shone with a sacred glow.
The bride in her white dress was so beautiful she seemed divine.
en.notes: 神々しい is an i-adjective for a sublime, almost divine radiance that inspires awe: the rising sun, sacred mountains, shrines, Buddha statues or an otherworldly beautiful appearance. Typical are 神々しく輝く and 神々しいほど美しい. Related is 厳か "solemn", which rather describes a ceremony or atmosphere.

examples[].german: An ominous atmosphere enveloped the area.
The sky was stained an ominous red.
Sinister legends remain about that old mansion.
en.notes: 禍々しい is an i-adjective from 禍 "calamity" and means "ominous, threatening, foreboding misfortune". It is literary and popular in novels, horror and fantasy: 禍々しい雰囲気・気配・色・言い伝え. 不吉 is the more matter-of-fact "inauspicious", 不気味 stresses the eerie more.

examples[].german: A faint scent of flowers drifted over.
This tea has a subtle sweetness.
At the time, I harbored a faint affection for her.
en.notes: ほのか is a na-adjective and is mostly written in kana. It describes delicate, barely perceptible but pleasant impressions: ほのかな香り・甘み・光, ほのかな恋心 "a faint affection"; adverbial ほのかに. Compared with かすか ("barely perceptible", neutral, also for sounds and memories), ほのか has a soft, positive ring.

examples[].german: I heard a faint sound from far away.
I faintly remember my childhood.
He did not give up the slim hope that there were survivors.
en.notes: かすか is a na-adjective and is mostly written in kana. It means "faint, barely perceptible" and suits sounds, light, smells, memories and hopes: かすかな音, かすかに覚えている, かすかな望み. Unlike ほのか, which sounds delicate and pleasant, かすか is neutral and stresses the edge of perceptibility.

examples[].german: A tranquil pastoral landscape stretches out.
In the peaceful spring sunshine, a cat is napping.
Unlike in the city, time flows leisurely on this island.
en.notes: のどか is a na-adjective and is mostly written in kana. It describes a peaceful, leisurely mood, typical of rural landscapes and mild spring weather: のどかな田園風景, のどかな春の日. Adverbial のどかに means "leisurely". 静か means only "quiet, calm", 穏やか "gentle, even-tempered" and also suits people and the sea.

examples[].german: He looks dashing in his uniform.
He was a young man with finely set eyebrows.
Her profile as she drew the bow in hakama was gallant.
en.notes: 凛々しい is an i-adjective that praises a resolute, dignified and energetic appearance, often of young men but also of women: 凛々しい顔立ち・眉・姿, 制服姿が凛々しい. Related is 凛とした "taut, dignified". Colloquially one says かっこいい; 勇ましい stresses courage and fighting spirit.

examples[].german: The fresh look of the new employees is heartwarming.
The newlyweds still looked fresh and shy.
She looked fresh and endearing, nervous on stage for the first time.
en.notes: 初々しい is an i-adjective that affectionately describes the freshness and awkwardness of newcomers: new employees, first-year students, newlyweds or first love. It is meant positively, unlike 未熟 "immature". 若々しい, by contrast, means "youthful, vital" and is often used for older people who look young.

examples[].german: I was suddenly treated in a cold, distant manner.
Ever since their quarrel, the conversation between the two has been somehow stiff.
Don't use polite language with me, it feels so distant.
en.notes: よそよそしい is an i-adjective from よそ "strange, elsewhere" and describes cool, distant behavior, mostly in someone who is actually close to you: よそよそしい態度・口調. Typical is the switch from familiarity to distance, for instance after a quarrel. 冷たい is harsher, 他人行儀 stresses exaggerated formality as among strangers.

examples[].german: A fierce cry rang out.
The tiger in the cage was glaring at us with ferocious eyes.
To steal someone's property and then complain about it, what a nerve.
en.notes: 猛々しい is an i-adjective and literary. It means "wild, fierce, belligerent" and suits predators, warriors, glances or cries. The second meaning "brazen, impudent" survives mainly in the saying 盗人猛々しい: the one in the wrong also acts boldly and demandingly. 勇ましい is the positive "brave", 荒々しい "rough, violent".

examples[].german: Rough waves crashed against the quay.
Angry, he slammed the door violently.
I was moved by the rugged nature of Hokkaido.
en.notes: 荒々しい describes something raw, untamed and violent: forces of nature (荒々しい波, 荒々しい岩肌), but also behavior and speech (荒々しい口調, 荒々しくドアを閉める). Compared with the base word 荒い "rough, fierce", the doubling stresses the wild, unrestrained impression and sounds somewhat more literary. For landscapes or people it can also mean appreciatively "untamed, powerful" (荒々しい自然).

examples[].german: I was moved by the story of a beautiful friendship.
An actress of graceful appearance appeared on stage.
"I trust you are in good spirits," the butler greeted.
en.notes: 麗しい is an elevated, rather literary word for "beautiful, graceful". It describes on the one hand looks, voice or bearing (麗しい姿, 見目麗しい) and on the other heartwarming relationships (麗しい友情, 麗しい師弟愛). In everyday speech it sounds solemn or slightly ironic; neutrally one says 美しい or きれい. The set phrase ご機嫌麗しゅう is an old-fashioned polite greeting formula.

examples[].german: I love my child so much I can hardly bear it.
The sleeping face of the cat is adorable.
The ordinary days of my school years now seem precious to me.
en.notes: 愛おしい expresses a tender, almost painful feeling of affection: one wants to protect and hold on to someone or something. Typical for children, partners, pets or past times (愛おしい日々), intensified with 〜てたまらない: 愛おしくてたまらない. Compared with かわいい it is deeper and more emotional; unlike 愛くるしい "cute to look at", it describes one's own feeling, not the appearance. The older secondary meaning "pitiable" is rare today; いとおしい is often written in kana.

examples[].german: The lawyer met with the suspect at the detention center.
Contact with his family was banned on the grounds of a risk of destroying evidence.
The Pope received the ambassadors of various countries in audience at the Vatican.
en.notes: 接見 has two uses: formally, the reception of a visitor by a high-ranking person (an audience), and in criminal proceedings, the conversation of a detained person with a lawyer or relatives: 弁護士と接見する, 接見交通権, 接見禁止. Mind the direction: 接見 is said from the side of the receiving, higher-ranking person; someone who is admitted to a high-ranking person has a 謁見. In general language, visiting someone in prison is called 面会. Intransitive する-verb with と.

examples[].german: I was captivated by the adorable puppy.
The baby's charming smile soothed the whole family.
A line formed at the zoo to see the pandas' adorable gestures.
en.notes: 愛くるしい describes a disarming, childlike cuteness, above all in babies, small children and animals: 愛くるしい笑顔, 愛くるしい目, 愛くるしいしぐさ. It is somewhat more elevated and expressive than かわいい and sounds natural in narratives or advertising copy. Unlike 愛おしい, which expresses one's own tender affection, 愛くるしい describes outward appearance. For adults it fits only a childlike, sweet face or smile.

examples[].german: I found a mushroom with a poisonous-looking color.
Garish neon lights lit up the night town.
She spoke venomously ill of her former colleague.
en.notes: 毒々しい first means "poisonous-looking", for example mushrooms or insects with warning colors, and from there extends to anything that looks garish, obtrusive or repulsive: 毒々しい色, 毒々しい化粧 "overdone makeup", 毒々しい看板. For words or attitude it means "spiteful, vicious" (毒々しい言葉). The word is always negative; for neutral bright colors one uses 鮮やか, and for "garish, flashy" also けばけばしい.

examples[].german: I entered a ruin with an eerie atmosphere.
The title on the movie poster was written in creepy lettering.
The incident was reported in a lurid way, but in reality it was a mere accident.
en.notes: おどろおどろしい describes an eerie, ghastly effect, as known from horror films and ghost stories: おどろおどろしい雰囲気, おどろおどろしい音楽, おどろおどろしいタイトル. It is almost always written in hiragana. It often implies that something is deliberately staged in an exaggeratedly gloomy way (hence also "overblown, sensational"). More neutral are 不気味 and 気味が悪い "creepy"; 怖い describes more one's own feeling of fear.

examples[].german: I can't believe such a ridiculous story.
It's absurd to spend a whole hour getting here for a five-minute meeting.
The answer was ridiculously simple.
en.notes: 馬鹿馬鹿しい calls something "ridiculous, absurd, foolish" and mostly expresses annoyance or contempt: 馬鹿馬鹿しい話, 馬鹿馬鹿しくてやっていられない "so silly I won't go along with it". It judges a matter or situation, not a person; of a person one rather says 馬鹿だ. In everyday writing it is mostly in hiragana (ばかばかしい). With 〜ほど it also means "ridiculously (easy/cheap)": 馬鹿馬鹿しいほど簡単.

examples[].german: Fresh vegetables are lined up at the market.
The leaves wet with morning dew glisten freshly.
It is a novel in which the fresh sensibility of its teenage author shines.
en.notes: みずみずしい means "fresh, juicy, full of life". Concretely it stands for fruit, vegetables and leaves (みずみずしいトマト), figuratively for young skin, youthful radiance or a fresh, unspoiled sensibility (みずみずしい感性, みずみずしい文章). It is mostly written in hiragana; as kanji, 瑞々しい is more usual than 水々しい. Compared with 新鮮 "fresh (not old)", it stresses juiciness, elasticity and vitality.

examples[].german: He looks youthful for his age.
My grandmother is still youthful in her seventies and goes to the gym every day.
What is your secret to staying so young?
en.notes: 若々しい describes someone who looks youthful - usually someone who is actually no longer young. That is why it is a typical compliment for older people: いつまでも若々しい, 年齢の割に若々しい. It refers to appearance, voice, movements or attitude of mind. 若い, by contrast, merely states actual young age; with truly young people, 若々しい at most stresses freshness and vigor (若々しい声).

examples[].german: Graphic footage of the accident scene was broadcast.
The vivid testimony of a war survivor silenced the hall.
He had a fresh surgical scar on his arm.
en.notes: 生々しい means "raw, unvarnished, as if experienced firsthand". It describes depictions, memories and reports so graphic and immediate that they almost hurt: 生々しい映像, 生々しい証言, 記憶がまだ生々しい. Second, it means "still fresh" for wounds or traces: 生々しい傷跡. Unlike リアル or 鮮やか "lively, vivid", it usually has an unpleasant, shocking undertone.

examples[].german: The sight of the injured child was heartbreaking.
The bandage wrapped around his arm is painful to look at.
Watching her force herself to act cheerful was painful.
en.notes: 痛々しい is said when a sight is so pitiable that it hurts oneself: 痛々しい姿, 包帯が痛々しい, 見ていて痛々しい. It describes the observer's impression, not one's own pain (for that, 痛い). Unlike 痛ましい, which judges tragic events such as accidents, it concerns the visible suffering or condition of a person. Colloquially it is also used for desperately trying behavior that is cringeworthy (cf. the slang イタい).

examples[].german: He read out the declaration in a solemn tone.
A heavy atmosphere hung over the meeting room.
The doctor nodded gravely and began explaining the test results.
en.notes: 重々しい describes a heavy, weighty effect of voice, bearing or atmosphere: 重々しい口調, 重々しい雰囲気, 重々しくうなずく. Depending on context it sounds "dignified, solemn" or "oppressive, weighing"; for objects also "massive-looking" (重々しい扉). Not to be confused with 重苦しい "heavy, oppressive", which is clearly negative. Its counterpart in behavior is 軽々しい "frivolous".

examples[].german: You should not make promises lightly.
You should not suspect people rashly without proof.
The minister's careless remark developed into an international issue.
en.notes: 軽々しい means "frivolous, thoughtless" and criticizes words or actions without sufficient consideration. It most often stands adverbially in admonitions: 軽々しく口にする, 軽々しく約束する, 軽々しく判断すべきではない. Not to be confused with 軽々と (かるがると) "effortlessly, with ease", which is positive: 重い荷物を軽々と持ち上げる. The opposite in behavior is 慎重 "cautious, careful".

examples[].german: While awaiting trial, the defendant is held in a detention center.
Death-row inmates are held in a detention center rather than a prison.
The lawyer went to the detention center almost every day and met with his client.
en.notes: 拘置所 is the state facility for detainees whose judgment is not yet final; in Japan, prisoners sentenced to death are also held there. The counterpart is 刑務所 "prison" for convicted prisoners serving sentences. To be distinguished from this is 留置場 "police holding cell" at the police station, where arrested persons are held first. Typical: 拘置所に収容される, 東京拘置所.

examples[].german: I carefully climbed the steep mountain path.
When my father read the letter, his face suddenly turned stern.
The road to the championship is still rugged.
en.notes: 険しい literally means "steep, rugged, hard to reach": 険しい山, 険しい坂道, 険しい崖. Figuratively it describes a dark, tense facial expression (険しい顔, 険しい目つき) as well as an arduous road or a serious situation (険しい道のり, 前途は険しい). Unlike 急 "steep (slope)", 険しい always carries a sense of danger and hardship. A 険しい顔 is a momentary expression of anger or worry, whereas 厳しい describes more a strict attitude or person.

examples[].german: It was a pleasing result: everyone passed.
I am very pleased to be able to welcome you all here today.
The welcome news arrived that an athlete from the local area had won a gold medal.
en.notes: 喜ばしい judges an event or a piece of news as "pleasing, welcome": 喜ばしい知らせ, 喜ばしい結果, 〜は誠に喜ばしい. It is rather formal and typical of speeches, addresses and newspaper style. For one's own joy in daily life one says 嬉しい; 喜ばしい expresses a more general, objective assessment. The opposite is 嘆かわしい "deplorable".

examples[].german: The decline in young people's morals is deplorable.
It is deplorable that so many politicians lie casually in public.
Scribbling graffiti on cultural properties is truly deplorable.
en.notes: 嘆かわしい (from 嘆く "to lament, sigh") expresses that a state of affairs is morally regrettable or outrageous: 嘆かわしい事態, 嘆かわしい風潮, 〜とは嘆かわしい. It is formal and critical and often sounds a bit preachy, typical of editorials, commentaries and older speakers lamenting social ills. It does not fit personal regret over one's own bad luck; for that one uses 残念 or 悔しい.

examples[].german: The graduation ceremony is a day of glory.
Standing on the stage of the glittering award ceremony, he was a little nervous.
Praised in front of so many people, I felt both proud and uneasy.
en.notes: 晴れがましい describes the glory and festivity of a special occasion at which one is oneself the center of attention: 晴れがましい舞台, 晴れがましい日, 晴れがましい気持ち "proud and elated". Related is 晴れ "festive" as in 晴れ着 "formal clothes" and 晴れ舞台 "big moment". Depending on context it also expresses the embarrassed feeling of standing in the limelight (晴れがましくて落ち着かない). Slightly elevated; in daily life one rather says 誇らしい or 華やか.

examples[].german: He has a brilliant career.
The new singer made a dazzling debut.
He played a brilliant role as a member of the Japan national team.
en.notes: 華々しい means "glorious, spectacular, sensational" and describes successes, appearances and careers that attract much attention: 華々しい活躍, 華々しいデビュー, 華々しい経歴. It often stands adverbially: 華々しく登場する. Compared with 華やか "gorgeous, colorful", which describes more the outward appearance, 華々しい stresses achievement and effect. In 華々しく散る "to fall gloriously" it stands for a glorious end.

examples[].german: I drank water from a clear spring.
The girl's pure singing voice echoed through the church.
He has a pure heart and does not know what it is to doubt people.
en.notes: 清らか is a na-adjective for "pure, clear, unsullied". Concretely it describes clear water and clean air (清らかな流れ, 清らかな空気), figuratively a pure, innocent soul or love (清らかな心, 清らかな愛). It sounds poetic and elevated; in daily speech one says きれい or 澄んだ for water. Compared with 清潔 "clean, hygienic", it is not about hygiene but about purity in an aesthetic or moral sense.

examples[].german: The report of the tragic accident pained my heart.
We will thoroughly implement safety measures so that such a tragic accident never happens again.
The whole town was wrapped in sorrow over the heartbreaking incident in which a young life was taken.
en.notes: 痛ましい judges an event as "tragic, heartrending", especially accidents, crimes and disasters with victims: 痛ましい事故, 痛ましい事件, 痛ましい犠牲. It is typical of news and official statements (このような痛ましい事故が二度と起きないよう…). Unlike 痛々しい, which describes the pitiable sight of a person, it concerns the event as a whole. Similar but more drastic is 悲惨 "dreadful, disastrous".

examples[].german: I cannot keep up with the rapidly changing world.
With a move and a job change at the same time, it was a hectic month.
The game turned into a scoring duel, and the lead changed hands dizzyingly.
en.notes: 目紛しい (literally something like "so that everything spins before one's eyes") describes changes or sequences that follow each other so fast that one can hardly keep up: 目紛しい変化, 目紛しく変わる, 目紛しい一日. It is almost always written in hiragana (めまぐるしい); the kanji spelling is rare. Unlike 忙しい "busy", it describes not one's own workload but the rapid pace of events; 急速 "rapid" is more matter-of-fact and less emotional.

examples[].german: He gave orders to his subordinates in a domineering manner.
A customer was complaining to the shop assistant in an overbearing way.
Even if the other side comes on overbearing, let's respond calmly.
en.notes: 居丈高 describes an overbearing, intimidating manner in which someone barks at others from above: 居丈高な態度, 居丈高に命令する, 居丈高に出る. The image is of sitting up tall to look down on others; it is also written 威丈高. It is a rather literary, clearly critical word; in daily speech one says 偉そう or 上から目線. Closely related is 高飛車, which particularly stresses the imperious tone that tolerates no contradiction.

examples[].german: Improving treatment in correctional facilities is being called for.
I take my child to the dentist to have his teeth straightened.
I had my eyesight corrected with LASIK surgery.
en.notes: 矯正 means to straighten something crooked or faulty: 歯列矯正 "orthodontic treatment", 視力矯正, 姿勢を矯正する. In the penal system it stands for the rehabilitation of offenders: 矯正施設 (prisons, juvenile training schools), 矯正教育. Unlike 修正 "correction of a text or plan" and 訂正 "correction of an error", 矯正 concerns bodies, habits or behavior. Not to be confused with the homophone 強制 "compulsion"; transitive する-verb (〜を矯正する).

examples[].german: Everyone resented his high-handed way of talking.
When I came on strong with the business partner, the negotiations broke down.
She is beautiful, but she has a haughty side that makes her hard to approach.
en.notes: 高飛車 comes from 将棋 (Japanese chess): the rook (飛車) is moved far forward to put pressure on offensively. From this arises the meaning "imperious, from above": 高飛車な態度, 高飛車な物言い, 高飛車に出る "to come on strong, to use pressure". It stresses that someone forces their will on others; 居丈高 stresses more the intimidating, bombastic manner. Colloquially it is now also used for snooty, arrogant people.

examples[].german: This may be presumptuous of me, but let me say a word.
I realize it is presumptuous, but could you please check the figures in this document once more?
I was scolded for speaking out of turn, being only a newcomer.
en.notes: 差し出がましい describes behavior in which one meddles unasked in other people's affairs or oversteps one's role: 差し出がましい口をきく, 差し出がましいことを言う. It is very often used as a humble introduction before advice or an objection to a superior: 差し出がましいようですが…, 差し出がましいとは存じますが… "forgive me for interfering". Related is お節介 "intrusive helpfulness", which is more colloquial; 差し出がましい sounds more formal.

examples[].german: This is a photograph that conveys the tragic reality of war.
The village fell into a terrible situation because of the heavy rain.
The result of yesterday's math test was dismal.
en.notes: 悲惨 (な) describes conditions or events so bad that they arouse pity and horror: 悲惨な事故, 悲惨な現実, 悲惨な状況, 戦争の悲惨さ. In everyday speech it is also used in exaggeration for personal mishaps: テストの結果が悲惨だった "disastrous". Unlike 悲しい "sad", it does not denote a feeling but the objective severity of the situation; 凄惨 and 無惨 stress the gruesome sight even more.

examples[].german: The police rushed to the gruesome crime scene.
The survivor quietly recounted the horrific experience of that time.
The battlefield was horrific in the extreme.
en.notes: 凄惨 (な) means "gruesome, ghastly" and describes scenes full of blood and violence: 凄惨な事件, 凄惨な現場, 凄惨な光景, 凄惨を極める. It is a literary word, typical of news, court reports and war accounts. Compared with 悲惨 "tragic, wretched", the emphasis is on the dreadful, often bloody sight; it is not used for everyday mishaps.

examples[].german: He came through the fierce competition.
The fighting between the two armies grew more ferocious day by day.
The crew spent a year in the harsh environment of Antarctica.
en.notes: 苛烈 (な) means "mercilessly harsh, extremely intense" and stands for competition, fighting or conditions that know no mercy: 苛烈な競争, 苛烈な戦い, 苛烈な環境, 苛烈を極める. It is literary and occurs in business and sports reports or historical texts. Similar is 熾烈 "fierce", used above all for competitions; 苛烈 additionally stresses harshness and mercilessness.

examples[].german: We won after a fierce battle.
She compiled her harrowing days of fighting illness into a book.
As children, my brother and I had epic fights every day.
en.notes: 壮絶 (な) describes something that exceeds all measures in intensity and drama: 壮絶な戦い, 壮絶な最期, 壮絶な人生, 壮絶な体験. Originally it carries admiration for courage and greatness ("heroic"); today it mainly stresses the extreme, shattering scale, for instance in battles, illness or blows of fate. Colloquially also in exaggeration: 壮絶な兄弟げんか. Compared with 凄絶, which highlights the gruesome, 壮絶 sounds more like heroic grandeur.

examples[].german: A hideous power struggle unfolded.
Drunk, he exposed the ugly true nature of humanity.
The hideous building erected in front of the station ruins the scenery.
en.notes: 醜悪 (な) means "repulsively ugly", outwardly but above all morally: 醜悪な争い, 醜悪な本性, 醜悪な姿をさらす. It is a literary, sharply judgmental word expressing contempt. For merely unattractive looks one rather says 醜い or 見苦しい; 醜悪 denotes something downright revolting, such as greed, intrigue or hypocrisy.

examples[].german: The gloomy sky dampened my mood.
He wore a gloomy expression throughout the meeting.
The novel is set in a gloomy port town.
en.notes: 陰鬱 (な) describes a gloomy, oppressive mood that weighs heavily on the mind: 陰鬱な天気, 陰鬱な表情, 陰鬱な雰囲気. It is rather literary; in everyday speech one says 暗い, どんよりした or 憂うつ. Compared with 憂鬱 "depressed", which mainly denotes one's own mood, 陰鬱 rather describes the atmosphere of weather, places or faces.

examples[].german: Cherry blossoms stood out on a hazy moonlit night.
The outline of the mountain could be seen dimly beyond the fog.
I can now only vaguely recall my grandfather's face from my childhood.
en.notes: 朧 (おぼろ) describes something blurred and shadowy, especially light in the haze of spring: 朧月 "hazy moon", 朧月夜 "spring night with a misty moon", a classic motif of poetry. As a na-adjective it stands for indistinct outlines or memories (おぼろに見える), mostly in hiragana. In everyday speech the derivative おぼろげ (おぼろげな記憶, おぼろげに覚えている) is much more common. As a noun, おぼろ in cooking also denotes seasoned, finely shredded flakes of fish or meat.

examples[].german: He is a person indifferent to honors.
His detached attitude toward winning and losing instead earned the trust of those around him.
In his later years my grandfather lived quietly, free of desire and ambition.
en.notes: 恬淡 describes a person who does not cling to fame, money or success and is not thrown off balance by them. Typical are 〜に恬淡としている, 名利に恬淡 "indifferent to fame and profit" and the phrase 無欲恬淡 "selfless and content". It is mostly used with と/たる (恬淡とした人, 恬淡と生きる) and is an elevated, literary compliment. Similar but closer to daily speech is 淡白 "easygoing, not intense".

examples[].german: After the judgment became final, the convict was sent to prison.
His incarceration was postponed for health reasons.
I write a letter every month to my brother, who is in prison.
en.notes: 収監 refers to being committed to a detention facility, usually after a final judgment: 刑務所に収監される, 収監中, 収監を免れる. Compared with 逮捕 "arrest" and 勾留 "pretrial detention", 収監 marks the start of imprisonment or the imprisonment itself; the opposite is 釈放 or 出所. Almost always passive or from the authorities' viewpoint (〜を収監する); a word of press language; neutrally one says 刑務所に入る.

examples[].german: A spotted cat is sunning itself.
In early spring, snow still remains in patches on the mountains.
I forgot to apply sunscreen and my skin got tanned unevenly.
en.notes: まだら means "spotted, mottled, uneven" and is mostly written in hiragana: まだら模様, まだらの犬, まだらに日焼けする. It describes natural patterns in animals and plants as well as unwanted unevenness, for instance in color or snow (雪がまだらに残る). The kanji 斑 has other readings: ぶち "piebald (animal coat)" and むら "unevenness" (色むら); which one is meant depends on context.

examples[].german: A gruesome sight spread out before me.
After the typhoon, his proud garden was in a pitiful state.
The favored team was miserably defeated in the first match.
en.notes: 無惨 (な) has two sides: "cruel, merciless" with regard to a deed (無惨に殺される), but above all "gruesome, pitifully mangled" for the result of destruction: 無惨な姿, 無惨な光景, 見るも無惨 "a wretched sight". Figuratively also for defeats: 無惨な敗北, 無惨にも敗れる. It is also written 無残. Compared with 悲惨 "tragic, wretched (situation)", 無惨 highlights the shocking state of what has been destroyed.

examples[].german: The exam result was dismal.
After the earthquake, the town was in a dreadful state.
After great pains, the new product was finally completed.
en.notes: 惨憺 is a たる-adjective and appears almost only in two set patterns: 惨憺たる "disastrous, wretched" (惨憺たる結果, 惨憺たる有様, 惨憺たるものだった) and 苦心惨憺 "with the greatest effort". In the first sense it judges results or conditions as completely failed or devastating; in the second it describes laborious effort. It is literary and in conversation sounds elevated or humorously exaggerated.

examples[].german: A severe judgment was handed down.
My grandfather was strict with himself and with others.
Strict precepts are observed in that monastery.
en.notes: 峻厳 (な) means "relentlessly strict, tolerating no leniency" and refers to attitudes, judgments, rules or personalities: 峻厳な態度, 峻厳な裁き, 峻厳な規律. The first kanji 峻 "steep, rugged" gives the word a lofty, unapproachable hardness. It is very literary; in daily speech one says 厳しい or 厳格. Compared with 峻烈, which rather stresses the sharpness of criticism or attacks, 峻厳 denotes a lasting, principled strictness.

examples[].german: He came under severe criticism.
The critic panned the film in scathing words.
The opposition parties pursued the government's response relentlessly.
en.notes: 峻烈 (な) means "sharp, cutting, relentless" and is used above all for criticism, attacks or commentary: 峻烈な批判, 峻烈な論調, 峻烈を極める. It is a literary word from the press, scholarship and literature. Compared with the more common 痛烈 "biting, scathing", 峻烈 sounds more elevated and stresses uncompromising severity; 峻厳 denotes a strict attitude rather than an attack.

examples[].german: It is the story of a warlord who met a harrowing end.
The two boxers staged a fierce slugfest.
I was speechless at the disaster victim's harrowing account.
en.notes: 凄絶 (な) means "terribly intense, ghastly-extreme" and describes fights, death scenes or experiences whose harshness takes your breath away: 凄絶な戦い, 凄絶な最期, 凄絶な体験. It is literary and occurs mainly in narratives, historical accounts and reports. Compared with the similar-sounding 壮絶, which stresses heroic grandeur, 凄絶 highlights the gruesome, terrible; 凄惨 relates more to a bloody sight.

examples[].german: If I may be so presumptuous, let me state my opinion.
If I may be so bold, I will lead the toast.
It may be considered presumptuous for a newcomer to give his opinion to the company president.
en.notes: 僭越 means "presumptuous, taking something upon oneself that is not one's place". It almost always appears in the humble introductory formula 僭越ながら "if I may take the liberty", with which one downplays one's role in speeches, toasts or remarks; similar are 僭越ですが or 僭越至極. As criticism of others (僭越な振る舞い) it is rarer and very formal. Related is 差し出がましい, which refers more to interfering in other people's affairs.

examples[].german: Though it may be overly fussy of me, let me give you one piece of advice.
I say this out of concern, but please be sure to read the contract thoroughly.
Even though I knew my senior's words came from concern, they felt a little nagging.
en.notes: 老婆心 (literally "the heart of an old woman") denotes a perhaps exaggerated but well-meaning solicitude. It almost always appears in the humble introduction 老婆心ながら "even if I may be worrying too much" before unsolicited advice, mostly to younger people; likewise 老婆心から言うと. It is a noun and is used regardless of the speaker's gender. Related is お節介, which sounds more negative and criticizes the interference itself.

examples[].german: Because of his pushy personality, he is disliked by those around him.
I did not want to be thought pushy, so I stayed quiet in the meeting.
"Stop butting in, you busybody!" my older sister scolded me.
en.notes: 出しゃばり is the noun for the verb 出しゃばる "to push oneself forward, to meddle unasked" and denotes both this behavior and the person: 出しゃばりな人, あの出しゃばり. It is colloquial and clearly pejorative; often in hiragana (でしゃばり). Typical are 出しゃばりだと思われる and 出しゃばったまねをする. Compared with お節介, which means too much solicitude, 出しゃばり stresses pushing oneself into the foreground; 差し出がましい is the formal equivalent.

examples[].german: In idle hours, I wrote in my diary.
On a rainy day, to pass the time, I looked through old albums.
To ease the boredom of my hospital stay, a friend brought me books.
en.notes: 徒然 (usually つれづれ in kana) denotes the state of having nothing to do: leisure, boredom, time passing quietly. The opening of the classic essay 徒然草 is famous: つれづれなるままに "in idle hours, as things come to mind". Today the word sounds literary and slightly nostalgic: 雨の日のつれづれに, 老後のつれづれを慰める, つれづれ日記. In everyday speech one says 暇 or 退屈; つれづれ has a more poetic, pleasantly melancholy ring.

examples[].german: Support for reintegration into society after release from prison is important.
He finished his sentence and was released last month.
The article does not state the source of the information.
en.notes: 出所 has two main meanings: in the penal system "release from custody" as an intransitive する-verb (刑務所から出所する, 出所後), and "origin, source" (情報の出所, 出所不明). In the meaning "source" one also reads it colloquially as でどころ (うわさの出どころ). The opposite of release is 入所 or 収監; officially one also speaks of 釈放, and the older 出獄 is hardly used any more.

examples[].german: The participants each stated their opinions.
Even siblings each have different personalities.
The two live in Tokyo and Osaka respectively.
en.notes: 夫々 is a rare kanji spelling of それぞれ "each, individually"; today it is almost always written in kana, occasionally 其々. As a noun it takes の before nouns (それぞれの意見), as an adverb it stands directly before the predicate (それぞれ違う), also in the sense of "respectively". Compared with 各自 "each individual" (people only), それぞれ can also refer to things; 各々 is more formal. 夫 stands here for the demonstrative それ, a spelling from kanbun; on its own it is read おっと "husband".

examples[].german: Each person should fulfill his or her own role.
Please prepare your own lunch individually.
The participants freely expressed their respective opinions.
en.notes: 各々 (often おのおの in kana) means "each individual, respectively" and is a more elevated, somewhat more formal equivalent of それぞれ. It appears as a noun (各々が, 各々の意見) or adverbially (各々準備する). It is typical in announcements and instructions to a group: 昼食は各々でご用意ください. In everyday speech それぞれ is much more common; the archaic meaning "you" (addressing several people) is known almost only from samurai dramas.

examples[].german: Plans often do not go as scheduled.
First impressions are often unreliable.
Major accidents often arise from an accumulation of small mistakes.
en.notes: 往々にして means "often, not infrequently" and describes a general tendency, usually an undesirable one: 〜は往々にして〜するものだ, 往々にしてある. It is literary and sounds like experience or analysis. Unlike よく or しばしば, it does not refer to concrete repeated events but to what experience shows often happens; similar is とかく "to tend to".

en.meaning: tending to; often; all sorts of
examples[].german: People tend to love gossip.
When busy, meals tend to get neglected.
All sorts of rumors surround that politician.
en.notes: とかく (兎角, usually in kana) has several uses. The most common is "to tend to, easily": 人はとかく〜しがちだ, often combined with 〜がち or 〜やすい. Second, "all sorts of (negative things)": とかくの噂がある "there are all sorts of rumors", and "this and that" in とかくするうちに. Rarely also "anyway" (like とにかく). The kanji 兎角 are an ateji spelling (literally "hare's horn").

en.meaning: how; in what way; however much
examples[].german: How to solve the problem is what matters.
Falling ill made me realize how important health is.
However talented a person is, there is a limit to what one can do alone.
en.notes: いかに (如何に, usually in kana) is the elevated counterpart of どのように and どれほど. It has three main meanings: "how, in what way" (いかにして解決するか), "how much" (いかに大切かがわかる) and, with 〜ても, "however much": いかに努力しても. It is typical of speeches, essays and nonfiction. Not to be confused with いかにも "really, quite typical".

examples[].german: It is extremely regrettable, but the plan has been cancelled.
Noise in the middle of the night is a great nuisance.
Though very brief, with this I will conclude my greeting.
en.notes: 甚だ is a formal degree adverb for "extremely, highly" and almost always stands before negatively evaluative words: 甚だ遺憾, 甚だ迷惑, 甚だ疑問だ, 甚だ残念. In speeches and letters it also serves as a humble formula: 甚だ簡単ではございますが "though only very briefly". In everyday speech one says とても or 非常に. Derived from it is the adjective 甚だしい "excessive, glaring" (勘違いも甚だしい).

en.meaning: by all means; necessarily; ought to
examples[].german: Students ought by all means to devote themselves to their studies.
Those who are politicians should by all means listen to the voice of the people.
Researchers should, without exception, handle data honestly.
en.notes: 須く (すべからく) comes from kanbun and is linked with べし or べきだ: 〜はすべからく〜べきだ "should by all means, naturally has to ...". It is an elevated, didactic word in speeches, editorials and essays; usually written in kana. Common, but wrong by the traditional view, is its use in the sense of すべて "all, without exception" (若者はすべからくスマホ中毒だ); JMdict lists this meaning as a secondary one, but learners should avoid it.

examples[].german: It was a scene as if I were dreaming.
He presented someone else's idea as if he had thought of it himself.
The article reported the rumor as if it were fact.
en.notes: あたかも (恰も, usually in kana) introduces a comparison and means "just as if". It is almost always combined with 〜ように, 〜かのように or 〜ごとく: あたかも〜かのように振る舞う "to act as if". It is more literary than まるで, which is usual in conversation. A rare second use is "right at that time" (時あたかも…), almost only in literary texts.

en.meaning: and thus also; ultimately; by extension
examples[].german: Individual effort leads to the development of society as a whole.
Protecting employees' health ultimately benefits the company as well.
This incident damaged his credibility and, by extension, the reputation of the whole company.
en.notes: ひいては (延いては, usually in kana) means "and thus ultimately also, by extension" and links a closer effect with a larger, further-reaching one: AがB、ひいてはCにつながる. Typical is the escalation from small to large: 個人、ひいては社会 "the individual and thus also society". It is literary and occurs in speeches, essays and reports. Unlike さらに "moreover", it does not simply add something but shows a chain of consequences.

en.meaning: for a while; for a moment; briefly
examples[].german: I was lost in meditation for a while.
"Please wait a moment," an announcement played.
I was entranced by the beautiful sunset for a while.
en.notes: しばし is an elevated, slightly literary word for "for a while, for a moment"; in daily speech one mostly says しばらく. It is almost always written in kana; the kanji form 暫し is rare. Typical are set phrases such as しばしお待ちください (polite announcement), しばしの間 "for a short time", しばしの別れ "a temporary parting" and しばし沈黙する. Unlike しばらく, it never means "not for a long time" (しばらくぶり).

examples[].german: Parole was granted because of exemplary behavior.
While on parole, he committed another crime and was returned to prison.
Under current law, parole is called "karishakuhō".
en.notes: 仮出獄 (仮 "provisional" + 出獄 "release from prison") is the conditional early release of a prisoner. This is the older statutory term; since the penal reform of the mid-2000s, the law calls it 仮釈放, and the press and everyday speech today almost only use 仮釈放. Typical: 仮出獄が認められる・許可される, 仮出獄中. The word is found mainly in older texts and novels.

en.meaning: finally; at long last; more and more
examples[].german: The new school term finally starts tomorrow.
As night fell, the rain grew heavier and heavier.
If it comes down to it, I intend to consult my parents.
en.notes: いよいよ (mostly in kana, rarely 愈々) has two main meanings. 1. "Finally, the time has come" - for an event one has been eagerly awaiting that is now imminent: いよいよ明日だ. Unlike とうとう and ついに, which more often describe a result that has already occurred after a long time, いよいよ stresses tense anticipation. 2. "More and more" for intensification: いよいよ激しくなる (≈ ますます). The phrase いよいよとなったら means "when it gets serious".

examples[].german: This problem is not only an economic one.
Environmental destruction is not just one country's problem but a challenge for all humankind.
His achievements extended not only to the academic world but to society as a whole.
en.notes: ただに is a literary, almost archaic adverb and stands practically only in negating or extending frames: ただに〜のみならず "not only ... but also" or ただに〜だけではない. It reinforces the statement that something goes beyond the named domain. It is mostly written in kana; 啻に is very rare. In normal speech it corresponds to 単に〜だけでなく or ただ〜だけでなく.

examples[].german: I happened to pass by and ran into an old friend.
I happened to be at home yesterday, so I was able to receive the package.
Winning this time was just a matter of luck.
en.notes: たまたま (almost always in kana) means "by chance, as luck would have it" and stresses that something happened without intention or plan. The frame たまたま〜だけだ "it was merely a coincidence" is common, often to downplay success. 偶然 means something similar, but can also be a noun (偶然の一致); たまたま is only an adverb and sounds somewhat more colloquial. The meaning "occasionally" is rare; for that one normally says たまに.

examples[].german: All of his plans failed.
Every one of my proposals was rejected.
The typhoon ruined all the crops in the fields.
en.notes: ことごとく (usually in kana, also 悉く) means "all, without exception" and is more literary than すべて or 全部. It typically stands directly before the verb and is especially often used with negative results: ことごとく失敗する, ことごとく却下される, ことごとく外れる. This makes it sound emphatic, often frustrated. As a noun with の it is rare.

examples[].german: Appropriate measures should be taken.
It would be better to consult the appropriate agency about this matter.
The company ought to apologize.
en.notes: しかるべき (usually in kana) is not an adverb but an attributive word standing before nouns (連体詞): "appropriate, due" or "competent". Typical are しかるべき処置 "appropriate measures", しかるべき機関 "the competent authority" and しかるべき人 "a suitable person". Predicatively it stands in the pattern 〜てしかるべきだ "it would only be right and fair that ...". The adverbial form is しかるべく "in an appropriate manner". Register: formal, administrative and business language.

examples[].german: His whereabouts remain completely unknown.
The fate of the crashed aircraft is still unknown.
The reason the ancient civilization perished remains entirely unknown.
en.notes: 杳として is a literary expression from 杳 "dark, distant, unfathomable" and stands practically only before negated verbs of knowing: 杳として知れない, 杳として分からない, 杳としてつかめない. A typical subject is the unknown whereabouts of people, ships or aircraft (行方は杳として知れない) or an unsolved mystery. It is found in news and novels, not in conversation, where one says まったく分からない.

examples[].german: He took a firm stand against the wrongdoing.
She firmly refused the unreasonable demand.
The prime minister answered resolutely even the reporter's tough questions.
en.notes: 毅然 describes a firm, unyielding attitude, especially toward pressure, injustice or outrageous demands. It is used like a たる-adjective: attributive 毅然とした態度 (the most common combination) or 毅然たる, adverbial 毅然と(して) 断る / 対応する. Similar is 断固, which stresses the determination of an action; colloquially one says きっぱり. Register: elevated, common in politics and news.

examples[].german: He remained composed even in a critical situation.
My grandfather was a man who stayed calm whatever happened.
Even as those around him fussed, the manager sat on the bench looking unruffled.
en.notes: 泰然 means "calm, not to be rattled by anything" and praises a masterful inner calm, especially in crises. Typical are 泰然と構える "to wait calmly", 泰然としている and 泰然とした態度; intensified in the four-character word 泰然自若. Compared with 冷静 (level-headed, cool) and 落ち着いた (calm), 泰然 sounds dignified and elevated. Grammatically a たる-adjective with adverbial 泰然と.

examples[].german: He lives detached from worldly affairs.
Not taking part in factional struggles, he maintained an aloof position.
While everyone around her chased trends, she alone stayed above it all.
en.notes: 超然 describes someone who "stands above things" and is not touched by worldly worries, strife or fashions. Typical are 〜から超然としている "to keep aloof from ..., to stand above ..." and 超然とした態度. Depending on context it sounds positive (masterful, unswayed) or negative (aloof, indifferent). Not to be confused with 超越する "to transcend", which is a true verb with を.

examples[].german: The hall fell solemnly silent.
Standing before the memorial, everyone felt a reverent mood.
Learning of the hardships of those who came before, I solemnly straightened myself.
en.notes: 粛然 describes a solemn, serious silence or reverence that arises in the face of something dignified or tragic. Typical are 粛然とする, 粛然と静まり返る "to fall solemnly silent" and the phrase 粛然と襟を正す "to adopt a reverent posture, collect oneself inwardly". Related is the more common 厳粛 "solemn, grave" (厳粛な式典). 粛然 is literary and occurs mainly in reports and literature.

examples[].german: Protection of intellectual property rights is being strengthened internationally.
Care is needed not to infringe other companies' intellectual property rights.
Patent rights and copyrights are a kind of intellectual property right.
en.notes: 知的財産権 is the umbrella term for rights in intellectual creations: 特許権 "patent right", 著作権 "copyright", 商標権 "trademark right", 意匠権 "design right" etc. In business and the media it is often shortened to 知財 (知財戦略, 知財部). Typical combinations: 知的財産権を侵害する "to infringe", 〜の保護, 〜を取得する. Technical language from law and business.

examples[].german: I was stunned by the unexpected turn of events.
Everyone was dumbfounded by his utterly outrageous remark.
Seeing the amount on the invoice, I was too stunned to speak.
en.notes: 唖然 means "speechless, flabbergasted" from astonishment or disbelief, usually at something unbelievable or outrageous. It almost always stands as 唖然とする or 唖然として言葉も出ない. Since 唖 is not a jōyō kanji, the spelling あ然 is often seen. To distinguish: 呆然 is "stunned, absent-minded", 愕然 "shocked by a bitter realization", あきれる "aghast, disgusted" (more colloquial).

examples[].german: I was appalled to learn the facts.
I was shocked when I saw the results of my health checkup.
Visiting my hometown for the first time in a long while, I was appalled at how much it had changed.
en.notes: 愕然 describes the shock when one suddenly recognizes something alarming or bitter, such as a truth, a bad diagnosis or great decay. It almost always stands as 愕然とする, often with the trigger in te-form or with に: 〜を知って愕然とする, その変わりように愕然とする. Unlike 唖然 (speechless with astonishment), 愕然 puts the accent on shock and consternation. Elevated written language, but also understood in conversation.

examples[].german: I shuddered at the terrible story.
I shuddered to learn that one wrong step would have caused a major accident.
Before the documentary photographs of the battlefield, I felt a shudder of horror.
