en.notes: 慄然 means "shuddering, frozen in horror" and is a literary expression. Typical are 慄然とする and attributive 慄然たる思い "a feeling of horror". It is often triggered by the belated realization of a danger or by cruel facts. In conversation one says ぞっとする or 背筋が寒くなる instead.

examples[].german: Having received the notice of failure, he dejectedly went home.
The players who lost the match hung their heads in dejection.
The scolded younger brother returned to his room looking dejected.
en.notes: 悄然 describes visible dejection: drooping shoulders, bowed head, quietly slinking away. Typical are 悄然と帰る, 悄然とうなだれる, 悄然と肩を落とす and 悄然とした様子. It is the elevated, literary counterpart of しょんぼり. Not to be confused with 騒然 "tumultuous" or 粛然 "solemnly silent".

en.meaning: astonishment; gaping in amazement; to stare wide-eyed
examples[].german: There has been remarkable technological progress.
Everyone marveled at how much he had improved.
The newcomer achieved results worthy of admiration.
en.notes: 瞠目 literally means "to open one's eyes wide" and denotes looking on in astonishment. It is a noun or intransitive する-verb: 〜に瞠目する "to marvel at something". It most often stands in the set phrases 瞠目すべき "remarkable, astonishing" and 瞠目に値する "deserves admiration", for achievements, progress or results. Very literary; in daily speech one says 目を見張る.

examples[].german: I agonized over a problem with no answer.
Days of agonizing over whether to go on to higher education or get a job continued.
The young protagonist's anguish is the central theme of this novel.
en.notes: 煩悶 is a literary word for tormenting inner struggle when one finds no way out, for example over life decisions, matters of conscience or lovesickness. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に煩悶する or 〜で煩悶する; as a noun, for example 煩悶の日々 or 青年の煩悶. Compared with the everyday 悩む/悩み it sounds literary and more intense, like 苦悩. It has nothing to do with "anxiety" in the sense of fear.

examples[].german: At the graduation ceremony I was immersed in deep emotion.
Visiting my alma mater for the first time in twenty years, I was filled with deep feeling.
At his retirement press conference, he said, "I am overcome with emotion."
en.notes: 感慨 is a deep, reflective emotion, mostly when looking back on the past: farewells, reunions, the end of a phase of life. Common combinations are 感慨にふける / 感慨に浸る "to sink into memories and feelings", 感慨深い "moving" and the four-character word 感慨無量 "overwhelmed with emotion". Unlike 感動, which means spontaneous being moved by something beautiful, 感慨 always involves reflection on times gone by.

examples[].german: We should keep passing down the sorrow of war.
A drama depicting the pathos of middle-aged salarymen became a talking point.
There is somehow a note of sorrow in his singing voice.
en.notes: 悲哀 is a literary word for deep sadness and the suffering that belongs to a particular situation. It mostly stands in the pattern 〜の悲哀: 人生の悲哀, 戦争の悲哀, and, often slightly ironically, 中間管理職の悲哀 "the woes of middle management". Other combinations are 悲哀を感じる and 悲哀が漂う. In daily speech one says 悲しみ; 悲哀 sounds literary and more like a general mood than a concrete loss.

examples[].german: We registered the product's design as an industrial design.
The shop displays furniture that craftsmen have made with great ingenuity.
The company was sued for allegedly infringing a competitor's design right.
en.notes: 意匠 means, on the one hand, the aesthetic form of a product, and in law the "registered design": 意匠権 "design right", 意匠登録 "design registration". On the other hand, in elevated language it stands for an artful design or idea, above all in the fixed phrase 意匠を凝らす "to design with great ingenuity". In everyday speech one mostly says デザイン for design; 意匠 sounds technical or literary.

examples[].german: He put on a bewildered expression at the sudden question.
Employees are baffled by the sudden policy change.
The police, too, could not hide their bewilderment at the suspect's contradictory explanation.
en.notes: 困惑 denotes perplexity and embarrassment when one does not know how to react. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に困惑する; as a noun often in 困惑の表情, 困惑を隠せない, 困惑した様子. It is more formal than 困る and describes the inner state more; 戸惑う stresses hesitation at something unfamiliar. Typical of news and reports on the reactions of those affected.

examples[].german: Residents panicked when the earthquake struck.
When his lie was pointed out, he was visibly flustered.
Following the sharp drop in stock prices, panic selling spread through the market.
en.notes: 狼狽 denotes suddenly losing one's composure: one does not know what to do and appears frantic or caught out. As an intransitive する-verb: 狼狽する, often with the trigger marked by に; intensified in the four-character word 周章狼狽. The same kanji are also used for the verb うろたえる (狼狽える), which is more everyday. In stock-market language there is 狼狽売り "panic selling".

examples[].german: A cursed doll imbued with a vengeful grudge was found.
To settle a long-held grudge, he swore revenge.
It is said that the grudge of a murdered samurai remains in this mansion.
en.notes: 怨念 is a deep-seated, long-nursed grudge, often with a desire for retribution. Typical are 怨念を抱く, 怨念がこもる/込められる and 怨念を晴らす. It appears especially often in connection with ghosts and curses: the grudge of a dead person that clings to a place. In daily speech one says 恨み; 怨念 sounds darker, heavier and more literary.

examples[].german: Deep melancholy dwelt in her eyes.
An autumn dusk has a somehow melancholic touch.
He was gazing out the window with a pensive expression.
en.notes: 愁い is a quiet, melancholic sadness or wistfulness. Typical are 愁いを帯びる "to have a melancholic cast", 愁いを含んだ表情 and 愁いに沈む. The meaning "worry, apprehension" is usually written 憂い, for example in 後顧の憂い or 備えあれば憂いなし. The word is literary; in daily speech one says 悲しみ or 心配.

en.meaning: wailing; bitter weeping; sobbing in despair
examples[].german: The bereaved family's wailing echoed through the hall.
On hearing the news of her son's death, the mother broke down sobbing on the spot.
I was moved by the scene near the end of the novel in which the protagonist wails in grief.
en.notes: 慟哭 is loud, despairing weeping out of the deepest pain, typically at a death or immeasurable loss. As an intransitive する-verb: 慟哭する; as a noun, for example 遺族の慟哭. It is much stronger than 泣く or 号泣 ("to weep loudly") and belongs to elevated written language, such as reports or literature.

examples[].german: He flew into a rage when insulted.
Fans enraged by the referee's call threw objects onto the field.
He has a hot-tempered nature and immediately raises his voice.
en.notes: 激昂 denotes violent agitation, especially flaring anger. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に激昂する "to fly into a rage over something", 激昂した群衆. Besides げきこう, the reading げっこう is also common. Compared with 激怒 (to be very angry), 激昂 stresses the visible welling up of emotions; 逆上 is going completely berserk. Register: literary, common in news.

examples[].german: I was entranced by the beautiful music.
At the moment of the goal, the player looked up at the sky with a rapturous expression.
Sawako Ariyoshi's "Kokotsu no Hito" is a novel depicting the care of an elderly person with dementia.
en.notes: 恍惚 is a state of rapture in which one is completely captivated by something beautiful or overwhelming and forgets everything else. Typical are 恍惚とする, 恍惚とした表情, 恍惚の表情 and 恍惚感. Related is 陶酔, which stresses more the "intoxication" with something. The second meaning "senile confusion" is obsolete today and known mainly through Sawako Ariyoshi's novel 『恍惚の人』; today one says 認知症. Register: literary, elevated.

examples[].german: You must not become intoxicated with your own success.
The audience was enraptured by the pianist's performance.
His speech was so self-indulgent that I could not bear to listen.
en.notes: 陶酔 means "to be intoxicated, completely carried away", by music, art, a mood or even by oneself. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に陶酔する. Very common is 自己陶酔 "narcissism, self-congratulation", which sounds negative; also 陶酔感 and 陶酔しきった表情. Unlike 心酔 (admiration for a person or doctrine), 陶酔 is about a pleasurable state of intoxication. The literal sense "drunk on alcohol" is rare in modern Japanese.

examples[].german: He did not yield even to the derision of those around him.
His invention was at first met with public ridicule.
An attitude of mocking other people's failures is not acceptable.
en.notes: 嘲笑 is contemptuous laughing at someone, scorn and ridicule. As a transitive する-verb: 人を嘲笑する; as a noun often in 嘲笑を浴びる "to be laughed at", 嘲笑の的になる "to become the target of ridicule" and 周囲の嘲笑. The same kanji also stand for the native verb あざ笑う. To distinguish are 冷笑 (a cold, condescending smile) and 苦笑 (a wry smile); in daily speech one rather says ばかにする or 笑い者にする.

examples[].german: Left-wing parties asserted workers' rights.
In his student days, he took part in the left-wing movement.
He plays left field in the game.
en.notes: 左翼 means "left wing, the Left", especially for socialist and communist currents: 左翼政党, 左翼運動, 新左翼 "New Left", 左翼的. 左派 sounds more neutral; in internet slang サヨク is used pejoratively. Like 右翼, it also has the meanings "left field" in baseball (colloquially レフト, the player 左翼手) and "left wing" of a troop.

examples[].german: The price agreement between companies violated the Antimonopoly Act.
A major telecommunications company underwent an on-site inspection on suspicion of violating the Antimonopoly Act.
Forcing business partners into unjustified price cuts is prohibited under the Antimonopoly Act.
en.notes: 独占禁止法 is the usual name of Japan's competition law (officially 私的独占の禁止及び公正取引の確保に関する法律), often abbreviated in the news to 独禁法. It prohibits monopolization, cartels (カルテル, 談合) and the abuse of a dominant market position; the authority responsible is the 公正取引委員会. Typical: 独占禁止法に違反する, 独占禁止法違反の疑い.

examples[].german: Voices of wrath rose against the injustice.
Fudo Myoo is said to drive out evil with a wrathful countenance.
On learning of the betrayal, the king burned with fury.
en.notes: 忿怒 (ふんぬ) is violent anger, very literary. The usual modern spelling is 憤怒 (ふんぬ or ふんど); 忿怒 appears mainly in a Buddhist context, for example in the 忿怒の形相 "wrathful countenance" of guardian deities such as 不動明王. Typical are 忿怒に燃える and 忿怒の声. In daily speech one says 怒り or 激怒.

examples[].german: I let out a sob, overcome with emotion.
On the phone, my mother spoke while holding back sobs.
During the funeral, sobbing could be heard from all around the hall.
en.notes: 嗚咽 is choked, suppressed sobbing in which one can barely hold back the tears. Typical are 嗚咽を漏らす "a sob escapes someone", 嗚咽をこらえる and 嗚咽する (intransitive). Unlike 慟哭 (loud, despairing wailing), 嗚咽 is rather quiet; in daily speech it corresponds to すすり泣き. Register: literary, in reports and novels.

examples[].german: I escaped the clamor of the city and moved to the countryside.
On the night of the festival, the town was wrapped in bustle.
As if the daytime hubbub had never been, the area in front of the station was hushed late at night.
en.notes: 喧噪 denotes loud bustle, noise and commotion, typically of a big city or a crowd. The more common spelling today is 喧騒. Typical are 都会の喧噪, 喧噪を離れる/逃れる and 喧噪に包まれる. Unlike 騒音 (disturbing noise, for example from machines), 喧噪 means the lively, restless soundscape of a place. Register: literary.

examples[].german: I felt a sense of desolation in the autumn dusk.
The deserted winter seashore was a desolate landscape.
After my friends left, only a feeling of emptiness remained in the room.
en.notes: 寂寥 is a deep, quiet loneliness and desolation, often of a landscape or mood. Most common is 寂寥感 "a feeling of emptiness and loneliness"; as a たる-adjective also 寂寥とした風景 / 寂寥たる. The word is purely literary; in daily speech one says 寂しさ. Unlike 孤独 (being alone, having no ties), 寂寥 rather describes the bleak atmosphere.

examples[].german: The negotiations fell into a deadlock.
To break the deadlock, the leaders of the two countries met directly.
Japanese is classified as an agglutinative language.
en.notes: 膠着 denotes a standstill in which neither side makes progress; most often in the set expression 膠着状態: 膠着状態に陥る "to get stuck", 膠着状態が続く, 膠着状態を打開する "to break the deadlock". 膠 means "glue", and the basic meaning "sticking" lives on in technical terms like 膠着語 "agglutinative language". The verb 膠着する is intransitive. Compared with 停滞 "stagnation" (growth, progress), 膠着 stresses the stalemate between opponents; news language.

examples[].german: A sense of weariness hung over the long meeting.
If fever or general fatigue persists, please consult a doctor.
Five years into their marriage, the two had reached a stale period.
en.notes: 倦怠 means languor and weariness. It most often appears in two compounds: 倦怠感 "listlessness", a typical symptom in medical texts (全身の倦怠感), and 倦怠期 "a phase of routine and boredom" in a relationship. Standing alone or as a する-verb, 倦怠 is rare. In daily speech one says だるい or 疲れ for tiredness.

en.meaning: self-confidence; pride in one's ability; self-assurance
examples[].german: I have pride as a professional.
He is confident that he has the best skills in the industry.
The craftsmen take pride in having supported this town's development.
en.notes: 自負 is justified pride in one's own ability or achievements, that is, healthy self-confidence. Typical are 〜としての自負がある, 自負心 and the pattern 〜と自負する "to be convinced that ...". Unlike うぬぼれ or 慢心, 自負 is not inherently pejorative; it sounds like professional honor. Related is プライド, which is more common in daily speech.

examples[].german: Becoming complacent about his success, he neglected his effort.
Though called a title favorite, they kept practicing without getting cocky.
Years of monopoly had bred complacency in that company.
en.notes: 慢心 is arrogance and complacency, especially after a success, which leads one to become careless. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に慢心する, 慢心せずに; as a noun 慢心が生まれる, 慢心を戒める. In contrast to 自負 (justified pride), 慢心 is always negative; similar are おごり and 油断 (carelessness).

examples[].german: Excessive self-deprecation can sometimes backfire.
There is no need to put yourself down so much.
Modesty and self-abasement seem similar but differ.
en.notes: 卑下 means to belittle and diminish oneself. As a transitive する-verb: 自分を卑下する; often with criticism: 卑下しすぎる, 卑下することはない "you don't have to make yourself so small". The difference from 謙遜 is important: 謙遜 is appropriate, polite modesty, whereas 卑下 is exaggerated, often uncomfortable self-abasement. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced ひげ "beard" (髭).

examples[].german: Judgment that is well considered is needed.
His thoughtless remark hurt many people.
Though young, she is a person of discretion and good sense.
en.notes: 思慮 is careful, circumspect thinking before one acts or speaks. It appears almost only in set combinations: 思慮深い "prudent", 思慮が浅い "rash", 思慮に欠ける "thoughtless" and 思慮分別 "prudence and discernment". As a verb 思慮する it is rare. To distinguish are 考慮 "to take into consideration" (を考慮する) and 配慮 "consideration for others".

examples[].german: The Fair Trade Commission launched an investigation into the cartel.
The Fair Trade Commission indicated that it would approve the merger.
The Fair Trade Commission issued a cease-and-desist order to a major convenience store chain.
en.notes: 公正取引委員会 is Japan's antitrust and competition authority, which oversees compliance with the 独占禁止法; in the news mostly 公取委, colloquially also 公取. Typical actions: 立ち入り検査 "on-site inspection", 排除措置命令 "cease-and-desist order", 課徴金納付命令 "surcharge payment order" and the review of mergers (合併審査). The name literally means "Fair Trade Commission".

examples[].german: You should have the good sense expected of an adult.
Even though he was drunk, it was senseless behavior.
At about what age do children come to tell right from wrong?
en.notes: 分別 (ふんべつ) is reason and judgment, especially the ability of an adult to tell right from wrong. Typical are 分別がある, 分別のある大人, 分別がつく "to become sensible", 善悪の分別 and the opposite 無分別. Note: with the reading ぶんべつ, the same kanji means "separating, sorting", for example ゴミの分別 "waste separation". Related is 思慮分別.

examples[].german: The ability to sense the subtleties of people's hearts is needed.
Rakugo skillfully depicts the subtleties of human feeling.
He is a veteran legislator well versed in the subtleties of politics.
en.notes: 機微 denotes the fine, hard-to-grasp stirrings and connections that one perceives only with intuition. Typical are 人情の機微 "the subtle stirrings of the human heart", 心の機微, 機微に触れる and 機微に通じる "to be versed in the subtleties". It is mostly about feelings or interpersonal and political relations, not technical details (for those, 細部 or ニュアンス). Register: elevated, literary.

en.meaning: quick wit; presence of mind; tact
examples[].german: Using quick wit, he overcame the crisis.
A shop assistant thoughtfully lent me an umbrella.
She is quick-witted, so she is suited to customer service.
en.notes: 機転 is the ability to do the right thing in a situation in a flash. It stands almost always in two expressions: 機転が利く "to be quick-witted, resourceful" and 機転を利かせる "to show presence of mind". Similar is 気が利く, which refers more to attentiveness to others' needs, as well as 臨機応変 "flexible according to the situation". The spelling 気転 is rarer.

en.meaning: the essentials; knack; the way of doing something
examples[].german: He is someone who quickly gets the hang of a job.
His explanation was so muddled that I couldn't tell what he wanted to say.
My little brother is shrewd, so it is always me who gets scolded.
en.notes: 要領 has two meanings. 1. "The essentials, the gist": 要領を得ない "muddled, not to the point", 要領よく説明する; also "guidelines" in 募集要領 or 学習指導要領. 2. "Knack, the trick of it": 要領をつかむ "to get the hang of it". 要領がいい means "skillful, efficient", but can also mean, pejoratively, "cunning, shrewd about one's own advantage"; the opposite is 要領が悪い "clumsy, inefficient".

examples[].german: She is a manager with great business acumen.
By her own resourcefulness alone, she grew a small shop into a large company.
Even without funds, a way opens up depending on one's resourcefulness.
en.notes: 才覚 is practical skill and resourcefulness, especially in achieving something with few means or doing business. Typical are 才覚がある, 商売の才覚, 自分の才覚一つで "purely by one's own ability and resourcefulness" and 才覚次第. Unlike 才能 (talent in general) and 才知 (intelligence), 才覚 stresses practical, often commercial instinct. The meaning "to raise money" (金を才覚する) is obsolete.

examples[].german: I marveled at her wit.
He had drawn attention early on as a young man full of talent and intelligence.
He was a leader who excelled not only in intellect but also in character.
en.notes: 才知 (also 才智) denotes talent and intelligence together, that is, a bright, agile mind. Typical are 才知に富む "witty and clever", 才知にたける and 才知あふれる. The word is elevated and rather literary; in daily speech one says 頭がいい or 賢い. Unlike 才覚 (practical resourcefulness), 才知 stresses intellectual brilliance.

examples[].german: He ruined his health from repeated worries.
My mother became quite haggard from the strain of caring for my father.
I apologize for causing you concern.
en.notes: 心労 is mental strain from continuing worries, which can wear one down physically. Typical are 心労が重なる, 心労がたたる "the worries take their toll", 心労で倒れる and, politely, ご心労をおかけする "to cause someone worry". In daily speech one says ストレス or 気苦労; 心労 sounds more serious and formal. Similar is 心痛, which rather means grief and heartache.

examples[].german: Employees are worn out by long working hours.
Rural economies are thoroughly exhausted by the prolonged recession.
It will take a long time to rebuild a country exhausted by war.
en.notes: 疲弊 denotes deep, wearing exhaustion from long strain, in people as well as in organizations, regions or national economies (地方経済の疲弊, 財政の疲弊). As an intransitive する-verb: 〜で疲弊する, 疲弊しきる. Compared with 疲労 (physical tiredness), 疲弊 stresses the drained state after long overload. Register: literary, common in news.

examples[].german: It is a job that is mentally very draining.
The heat sapped a lot of my strength.
Please request consumables such as copy paper from the general affairs section.
en.notes: 消耗 is the using up and wearing out of strength, material or resources. It can be used transitively (体力を消耗する "to use up one's strength") and intransitively (体力が消耗する). Common compounds are 消耗品 "consumables" and 消耗戦 "war of attrition". The traditional reading is しょうこう; today しょうもう is standard. Compared with 消費 (consumption, using up in general), 消耗 stresses wearing out and being drained.

examples[].german: There is a danger that groundwater will dry up.
It is said that resources such as oil will eventually be exhausted.
Constantly chased by deadlines, my ideas have run dry.
en.notes: 枯渇 means "to dry up" (springs, groundwater) and figuratively "to run out, be exhausted" for resources, funds or even ideas and talent. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜が枯渇する; as a noun, for example 資源の枯渇 and 財源の枯渇. In daily speech one says 尽きる or なくなる; 枯渇 is typical of news and specialist texts.

examples[].german: The deadline for the final tax return is March 15.
Do you have anything to declare at customs?
He underreported his income and was hit with additional taxes.
en.notes: 申告 is the obligatory declaration or statement to an authority: 確定申告 "income tax return", 税関で申告する "to declare at customs", 所得を申告する. As a する-verb it is transitive (〜を申告する). 自己申告 means "self-declaration", 過少申告 "underreporting". Unlike 届け出 "notification (e.g. of moving, a birth)", 申告 mostly concerns taxes, customs and other declarations required by law.

examples[].german: The wear on the tires is progressing.
After years of use, the gears are completely worn.
Working at a harsh site, I felt my spirit being worn down.
en.notes: 摩耗 (also 磨耗) is wear caused by friction, a typical term in engineering and the automotive field: タイヤの摩耗, ブレーキパッドの摩耗, 部品が摩耗する (intransitive する-verb). Figuratively one also speaks of 心が摩耗する "to be worn down inside". The native counterpart is すり減る; 劣化, by contrast, means general aging and loss of quality.

examples[].german: The company went bankrupt due to the collapse of its management.
The couple's marriage fell apart in just three years.
Your theory has already broken down at the stage of its premises.
en.notes: 破綻 denotes the collapse of something that previously worked: companies and finances (経営破綻, 財政破綻), relationships (結婚生活が破綻する) or arguments (論理が破綻している "the logic falls apart"). As an intransitive する-verb: 〜が破綻する. Unlike 倒産, which means only the insolvency of a company, 破綻 is much broader in use. Register: literary, common in business news.

examples[].german: The economic slump is dragging on.
The cabinet's approval rating is stuck at around thirty percent.
That team has been languishing in the lower ranks of the league for years.
en.notes: 低迷 describes economy, stock prices, sales or performance staying at a low level for a long time without recovering. Typical are 景気の低迷, 低迷が続く/長引く and, as an intransitive する-verb, 株価が低迷している or 支持率が低迷する; in sports, 下位に低迷する means "to be stuck in the bottom of the table". While 不振 mainly stresses bad results or performance, 低迷 underlines the sluggish persistence. The original meaning "hanging low (of clouds)" is literary. News and written language.

examples[].german: We analyzed the cause of the sales slump.
My loss of appetite continued, so I had it checked at the hospital.
The ace fell into a slump, and the team lost consecutive games.
en.notes: 不振 means that something is going badly or not delivering the expected performance. It mostly stands in compounds: 業績不振 "poor business results", 売り上げ不振, 食欲不振 "loss of appetite", 打撃不振 "batting slump (baseball)". Set combinations are 不振に陥る "to fall into a crisis/slump", 不振が続く and 不振から抜け出す/脱する; there is no する-verb. Unlike 低迷 (lasting persistence at a low level), 不振 stresses the weak showing. Not to be confused with the identically read 不審 "suspicious".

examples[].german: The tourism industry is booming.
After the announcement of the new product, the stock market was buoyant.
Thanks to the redevelopment, the area in front of the station has regained its former liveliness.
en.notes: 活況 refers to lively business and brisk demand in a market, an industry or a district. The fixed, written-style phrase is 活況を呈する "to show lively activity, to boom"; also 活況に沸く, 活況を取り戻す and attributively 活況な市場. Its opposites are 不振, 低迷 and 閑散. 好況 means a good economy in general, while 活況 is more the visibly busy bustle. It is not used for people.

examples[].german: The end of the year is the busy season, and overtime increases.
For moving companies, March is the busiest time of the year.
The workload became extremely heavy, and I had to keep working on days off.
en.notes: 繁忙 means "swamped with work, very busy" and belongs to business and administrative language; in everyday speech people simply say 忙しい. The most common form is the compound 繁忙期 "peak season, rush period", with its counterpart 閑散期. There are also 繁忙な時期/業務 and, in written style, 繁忙を極める "to be extremely busy". Do not confuse it with 繁盛 "to do well, to flourish (of a business)": 繁忙 describes the workload, not the success.

examples[].german: The shopping street is empty and quiet on weekdays.
Airline tickets get cheaper in the off season.
When the game ended, the area around the stadium suddenly became deserted.
en.notes: 閑散 describes places or businesses where there should be activity but hardly anyone is around: "deserted, dead quiet, slack". It mostly appears with と: 閑散としている, 閑散とした街. In a business context, 閑散期 "off season" is the counterpart to 繁忙期, and 閑散な取引 means "sluggish trading". Unlike 静か (simply quiet), 閑散 carries a sense of emptiness and desertion. Rather literary.

examples[].german: Finances became so tight that budget cuts were unavoidable.
Because of the intense heat, electricity supply and demand are extremely tight.
With the rapid rise in infections, hospital beds became scarce.
en.notes: 逼迫 means that something is reaching its limit and is under heavy pressure, especially finances and supply: 財政が逼迫する, 電力需給が逼迫する, 医療の逼迫 "overload of the healthcare system". It is an intransitive する-verb used with が; attributively 逼迫した状況/情勢 "tense situation". Since 逼 is not a Jōyō kanji, newspapers often write ひっ迫. 不足 means a mere lack, while 逼迫 means a threatening scarcity; 切迫 emphasizes urgency in terms of time.

examples[].german: Vitamin deficiency affects health.
At high altitudes, oxygen is easily lacking.
During the war, supplies ran short and people depended on rationing.
en.notes: 欠乏 refers to a serious lack of something vital such as nutrients, oxygen, food or goods: ビタミン欠乏, 欠乏症 "deficiency disease", 酸素欠乏 (short: 酸欠). As an intransitive する-verb: 物資が欠乏する. 不足 is the neutral everyday word (人手不足, 睡眠不足); 欠乏 sounds stronger and more technical; 欠如 denotes the absence of abstract qualities (常識の欠如).

examples[].german: Food ran out at the time of the disaster.
The popular item is completely sold out; new stock arrives next month.
Young engineers are practically nonexistent in this industry.
en.notes: 払底 literally means "to sweep (払) out down to the bottom (底)": a supply is completely used up. It is an intransitive する-verb: 在庫が払底する; figuratively also 人材が払底している "there are hardly any capable people left". The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned; in everyday speech people say 底をつく, 品切れになる or 切らす. It is much stronger than 不足.

examples[].german: The National Tax Bureau's investigation division conducted an inquiry into tax evasion.
The International Atomic Energy Agency inspected the nuclear facilities.
A surprise fire department inspection found deficiencies in the emergency exits.
en.notes: 査察 is an official inspection of whether regulations are being observed: 国税局の査察部 "tax investigation division" (colloquially マルサ), 核査察 "nuclear inspection" by the IAEA, 消防査察 "fire inspection". Typical: 査察に入る, 査察を受ける, 抜き打ち査察 "surprise inspection". Unlike 視察 "an inspection tour for information", 査察 has the character of control or investigation; 監査 is the audit of accounts and management.

examples[].german: The coastline is being eroded by waves.
Cheap smartphone providers are eating into the market share of the big carriers.
With working from home, work began to encroach on my private life.
en.notes: 侵食 refers to gradual intrusion and eating away. In geography it is erosion by water or wind (波の侵食, 川が谷を侵食する); for water erosion the spelling 浸食 is also found. Figuratively: 市場シェアを侵食する "to take away market share" or 仕事が私生活を侵食する. It is a transitive する-verb (AがBを侵食する) and often appears in the passive: 〜に侵食される. 侵略, by contrast, is an active, violent invasion.

en.meaning: under the umbrella of; subsidiary status; sphere of influence
examples[].german: More and more small and medium-sized companies are coming under the umbrella of large corporations.
The union is affiliated with a nationwide organization.
Through acquisitions, the company brought three hotel chains under its umbrella.
en.notes: 傘下 literally means "under the umbrella" and refers to belonging to a higher-level organization such as a corporate group or an umbrella association. Typical patterns are Aの傘下に入る "to come under A", 傘下に収める "to bring under one's wing, to acquire", 傘下にある, as well as 傘下の企業/団体 and 傘下企業 "group subsidiary". It has nothing to do with "patronage" in the sense of sponsorship; that would be 後援 or 主催. Business and news language.

examples[].german: I checked whether there were any errors in the accounting.
Excuse me, could we have the check, please?
I have been put in charge of the treasury for the neighborhood association.
en.notes: 会計 has two main uses. Technically it is accounting: 会計処理, 会計年度, 公認会計士 "certified public accountant". In daily life it is paying at a restaurant or shop: お会計お願いします "the check, please", お会計は二千円です. In clubs and associations, 会計 also refers to the treasurer. 経理 is accounting as a department in companies, お勘定 an older alternative for the bill, レジ the register as a place.

en.meaning: journal entry; bookkeeping entry; account classification
examples[].german: I do the daily journal entries in the accounting department.
I do not know how to record this transaction.
You first enter it in the journal and then post it to the general ledger.
en.notes: 仕訳 is the journal entry of double-entry bookkeeping: each transaction is split into 借方 "debit" and 貸方 "credit". One says 仕訳する or, in jargon, 仕訳を切る "to make a journal entry"; the journal is called 仕訳帳. For general sorting (parcels, garbage) one usually writes 仕分け; the spelling 仕訳 is standard for bookkeeping. Transitive する-verb.

examples[].german: The case is being investigated by the police station with jurisdiction.
Please submit your tax return documents to the tax office with jurisdiction.
Crime dramas often depict conflict between headquarters and the local station.
en.notes: 所轄 refers to the jurisdiction of an authority over a certain area or subject matter, and above all to the specific office in charge: 所轄の警察署, 所轄の税務署, 所轄官庁. In police and crime-drama language, 所轄 on its own means the local station as opposed to the 本庁 (prefectural police headquarters). 管轄 is the more general word for area of jurisdiction (管轄区域); 所轄 stresses who is actually responsible. Administrative language.

examples[].german: He lightened the mood with a witty reply.
Using his quick wit, he skillfully deflected the reporter's nasty question.
The charm of this novel lies in its witty dialogue.
en.notes: 機知 is quick, clever wit: the ability to make a smart, often humorous remark at just the right moment. It almost always appears in 機知に富む "witty" (機知に富んだ会話) or 機知を働かせる. Compared with ユーモア "humor" and 冗談 "joke", 機知 emphasizes intelligence and spontaneity; the loanword ウィット is synonymous. For practical presence of mind in action, 機転 is more usual (機転が利く). Elevated, mostly complimentary.

examples[].german: I had been worried, but in the end it was needless worry.
My mother is always worrying needlessly.
The worry about rain turned out to be groundless, and the sports day was held under clear skies.
en.notes: 取り越し苦労 literally means "advance trouble" (取り越す "to anticipate"): one worries in advance about things that then never happen. Typical is the retrospective 取り越し苦労だった or 取り越し苦労に終わった "the worry was unfounded", as well as 取り越し苦労をする. Neutral and suitable for everyday use; the literary synonym is 杞憂, and colloquially one also says 心配しすぎ.

examples[].german: He is still basking in the afterglow of the concert.
The resonance of the bell kept ringing for a long time.
It was a novel with an open ending that stays with you.
en.notes: 余韻 is first of all the lingering resonance of a sound (鐘の余韻), and then the pleasant afterglow of an experience: 余韻に浸る "to bask in the afterglow", 余韻が残る, 余韻を楽しむ. In literary criticism, 余韻のある文章 means a suggestive text that lingers. The connotation is positive; for negative aftereffects one uses 余波 or 後遺症. Slightly elevated.

examples[].german: The repercussions of the financial crisis spread around the world.
Because of the aftereffects of the typhoon, the sea is still rough.
As a result of the weak yen, the prices of imported goods have risen.
en.notes: 余波 literally means the waves that remain after a storm, and figuratively the (mostly negative) aftereffects of an event. Typical: 〜の余波を受ける "to be hit by the consequences of", 余波が及ぶ/広がる, 〜の余波で "as a result of". With weather, 台風の余波 is still almost literal. 影響 is neutral and general, 余韻 the positive afterglow of an experience. News language.

examples[].german: There was a backlash against the radical reforms.
As a reaction to my diet, I ended up overeating.
When you fire a gun, you feel a strong shock in your shoulder from the recoil.
en.notes: 反動 is the counter-movement that follows a strong movement: physically the recoil (銃の反動), in everyday life the swing of a pendulum back, often as 〜の反動で "as a reaction to": ダイエットの反動で食べすぎる. In politics, 反動 or 反動的 means "reactionary" (反動勢力). Unlike 反発 (active rejection, resistance), 反動 is an almost inevitable counter-reaction; 反応 is the neutral response to a stimulus.

examples[].german: The Japan Coast Guard boarded and inspected a suspicious vessel.
A labor standards inspector went to the factory on an inspection and investigated the reality of long working hours.
Boarding and searching on the high seas is strictly limited by international law.
en.notes: 臨検 (臨む "to go to the spot" + 検 "to inspect") is an official inspection directly on site with a right of entry, for example the search of a ship at sea by the coast guard or navy, or the visit by a labor standards inspector to a workplace (労働基準監督官の臨検). Typical: 臨検を行う, 臨検に入る, 船舶を臨検する. A pure technical term from law and administration; more general are 立ち入り検査 or 査察.

examples[].german: Public resistance to the new policy is strong.
Magnets with the same poles repel each other.
Reversing the previous day's sharp drop, stock prices rebounded strongly.
en.notes: 反発 is above all resistance or rejection against something: 〜に反発する, 〜への反発, 反発を招く/買う "to provoke resentment", 反発を強める. Physically it means "to repel each other" (磁石が反発し合う), and on the stock market "to rebound after a decline" (株価が反発する). Intransitive する-verb. 反抗 is rebellion against authority (反抗期), 反対 is a matter-of-fact opposing position, and 反動 is the inevitable counter-reaction.

examples[].german: Risk aversion is hindering investment.
The defense filed a motion to recuse the judge.
During the war, some young men fled abroad to evade conscription.
en.notes: 忌避 means to deliberately avoid something or evade it out of aversion or fear: 徴兵忌避 "draft evasion", リスク忌避 "risk aversion", 責任を忌避する. In law, 忌避 is the challenge of a judge for bias (裁判官の忌避を申し立てる). There is also 忌避剤 "repellent". 回避 is the neutral "to avoid, to sidestep" (危険を回避する); 忌避 sounds more like inner revulsion. Very literary.

examples[].german: Escaping from reality will not solve the problem.
Before exams, I always end up escaping into cleaning my room.
Defying their families' opposition, the two ran away together.
en.notes: 逃避 is fleeing from something unpleasant, mostly in a psychological sense: 現実逃避 "escape from reality", 〜から逃避する, 〜に逃避する "to take refuge in something". 逃避行 is flight into the unknown, typically by a pair of lovers. In economics there is 資本逃避 "capital flight". For the physical flight of a culprit one says 逃走, for escaping from danger 脱出. Intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: My reverence for my former teacher has not changed in the slightest, even now.
The disciples revered their master from the bottom of their hearts.
In the area, many people still revere that doctor today.
en.notes: 敬慕 combines respect (敬) with heartfelt affection (慕): one reveres someone and feels inwardly attached to them. Typical are 敬慕の念を抱く and 〜を敬慕する; objects are teachers, masters, parents or great figures. The word is very literary. 尊敬 is the normal everyday expression for respect, 崇拝 a stronger, idealizing worship, and 思慕 yearning affection.

examples[].german: He went abroad to study with a longing for Paris.
As a boy, he had a strong yearning for the big city.
A yearning for Western culture was common to the writers of the Meiji era.
en.notes: 憧憬 is the literary counterpart of 憧れ: longing and infatuation for something idealized, often distant or unattainable. Typical are 〜への憧憬, 憧憬を抱く and 憧憬の念. The usual reading is どうけい; the original reading しょうけい is also considered correct. In everyday speech one says 憧れ/憧れる. 渇望, by contrast, is a burning desire for something one lacks.

examples[].german: People who longed for freedom rose up.
His acting oozed a craving to be recognized.
Her desire for victory drove her to hard training.
en.notes: 渇望 literally means "to thirst for" (渇 = thirst) and refers to a burning desire for something one lacks: freedom, peace, love, recognition, victory. It is a transitive する-verb (〜を渇望する); as a noun it appears with 〜への渇望 or 渇望感. It is stronger than 切望 and 熱望 and sounds literary. 憧憬 is more of an infatuated longing for an ideal.

examples[].german: Winning the championship had been a long-cherished wish.
The bridge that the locals had longed for was finally completed.
The atomic bomb survivors continue to appeal for the abolition of nuclear weapons as their dearest wish.
en.notes: 悲願 is a long-cherished, fervent wish that often comes true only after many setbacks; originally it denotes the Buddhist vow to save all beings. Typical are 長年の悲願, 悲願の初優勝, 悲願を達成する/果たす, 悲願がかなう. It carries emotional weight and often concerns a community (team, region, nation). 念願 is lighter and more personal (念願のマイホーム). Common in sports and news language.

examples[].german: He realized his long-cherished wish of owning a home.
My dream is coming true: from next month I will be working in Paris.
After retirement, he finally set out on the long-awaited pilgrimage around Shikoku.
en.notes: 念願 is a heartfelt wish held for a long time. It most often appears attributively as 念願の + noun (念願のマイホーム, 念願の一人暮らし) or in 念願がかなう / 念願かなって "the wish came true" and 念願を果たす. As a する-verb it is rare. Compared with 悲願, 念願 is lighter, more personal and suited to everyday use; 夢 is the simplest everyday word.

examples[].german: A grudge remains between the two families.
Because of the brawl last time, the match between the two teams is called a grudge match.
The forced merger left lasting resentment among the employees.
en.notes: 遺恨 is a grudge that remains for a long time after an incident (遺 "to leave behind", 恨 "grudge"). Typical are 遺恨が残る, 遺恨を残す, 〜に遺恨を抱く and 遺恨を晴らす "to take revenge for an old grudge". In sports, 遺恨試合 is a match with a bad history. The everyday word is 恨み; わだかまり is a quieter, unspoken ill feeling. Literary.

examples[].german: He looked back on the decision of that day with deep remorse.
In his later years he was tormented by remorse over the mistakes of his youth.
The defendant shed tears of remorse in court.
en.notes: 悔恨 is deep, tormenting remorse over one's own actions. It is very literary and appears mainly in fixed combinations: 悔恨の念, 悔恨の涙, 悔恨にさいなまれる "to be tormented by remorse". In everyday speech one says 後悔. 痛恨 refers more to the bitter pain over a single mistake (痛恨のミス), 遺憾 to formal regret over a matter.

en.meaning: administrative appeal procedure (review of administrative dispositions)
examples[].german: If you are dissatisfied with a disposition, you can request an administrative appeal review.
An administrative appeal is cheaper than a lawsuit, and the procedure is simpler.
With the amendment of the Administrative Appeal Act, the period for requesting review was extended to three months.
en.notes: 行政不服審査 is the procedure in which citizens object to an administrative act (処分) to the administration itself, without going to court; the counterpart is the 行政訴訟 "administrative lawsuit". The legal basis is the 行政不服審査法; the usual form of the application is called 審査請求. A technical term from administration and law, found in official notices and agency guides.

examples[].german: He lost the game because of a regrettable error.
This scandal is deeply regrettable, and we sincerely apologize.
It was painful that I had mistaken the deadline by one day.
en.notes: 痛恨 refers to the bitter pain over something one deeply regrets, usually one's own mistake or a missed chance. It is most often used attributively: 痛恨のミス/エラー/一打 "a costly, bitter error" (sports reports). In official apologies, 痛恨の極み "utterly regrettable" is used. Unlike 悔恨 (lasting inner remorse), 痛恨 refers to a concrete, painful event.

examples[].german: The present situation is truly regrettable.
The government expressed regret over the neighboring country's actions.
In the final, she showed her full ability.
en.notes: 遺憾 formally expresses that something is regrettable or unsatisfactory; it is the language of government offices, companies and diplomacy: 誠に遺憾である, 遺憾に思う, 遺憾の意を表する "to express regret", 遺憾ながら "regrettably". Important: 遺憾 is not an apology but only regret, which is why it is often criticized as an evasive formula. The fixed phrase 遺憾なく, however, means "fully": 実力を遺憾なく発揮する. In everyday speech one says 残念.

examples[].german: He felt anger, but restrained himself.
It is hard to teach children self-control.
The UN called on both countries to exercise the utmost restraint.
en.notes: 自制 is the ability to keep one's own feelings and desires in check. As a する-verb it often stands without an object (怒りを感じたが自制した); 自制心 "self-control" and 自制が利かない "cannot control oneself" are also common. In diplomacy, 自制を求める/促す means "to call for restraint". 自粛, by contrast, is voluntary abstention from certain activities, and 我慢 is enduring or putting up with something.

examples[].german: To prevent the spread of infection, people refrained from going out.
In response to the scandal, the actor decided to voluntarily suspend his entertainment activities for a while.
Because it was right after the earthquake, the fireworks at the festival were called off.
en.notes: 自粛 means voluntarily refraining from or limiting something, often out of consideration or under social pressure. Typical are 外出自粛, 営業自粛, 自粛要請 "request for self-restraint" (Covid era), 活動を自粛する after a scandal, and cancelling festive events after disasters. Transitive する-verb: 〜を自粛する, often in the passive. 自制 is inner self-control, and 遠慮 is polite reserve in dealing with others.

examples[].german: The city was reduced to ruins by the war.
Deep in the mountains there is a hotel that has become a ruin.
My hobby is going out on weekends to take photos of ruins.
en.notes: 廃墟 are abandoned, decayed buildings or entire places: 廃墟と化す "to turn into ruins", 廃墟になる, 廃墟となった工場. Today there are also hobbies such as 廃墟探索 "urban exploration". 遺跡, by contrast, denotes archaeological or historical sites, 残骸 the debris and wreckage of something destroyed, and 跡 the spot where something used to stand.

examples[].german: The wreckage of the crashed airplane was found.
Pieces of wrecked cars were scattered at the accident site.
The morning after the party, the remains of snack bags and empty cans were left in the room.
en.notes: 残骸 are the destroyed remains of something that was once whole: wreckage of airplanes and cars, rubble of a building, and figuratively also 夢の残骸 (literary). Typical: 機体の残骸, 残骸が散乱する, 残骸を回収する. 廃墟 is an abandoned building that is still standing, 瓦礫 is the rubble after a collapse, and 破片 means individual splinters. Also used jokingly for the leftovers of a party.

examples[].german: Relics of the feudal era still remain in society.
Residues such as burnt remains had collected in the filter.
In his words, one could not feel even a remnant of his former passion.
en.notes: 残滓 originally means "sediment, residue" (滓 = かす) and is used mainly figuratively for leftovers of an outdated era or way of thinking: 封建制の残滓, 植民地主義の残滓. The word is very literary; ざんし is the established reading, and the original reading is さんし. In engineering and chemistry it denotes concrete residues. 名残 sounds wistful and positive, while 痕跡 means neutral traces.

examples[].german: Traces of the culprit were left at the scene.
There are traces on Mars showing that water once flowed there.
The old streetscape preserves traces of the time when it was a post town.
en.notes: 痕跡 are traces proving that something existed or happened. Typical are 痕跡を残す/消す/とどめる, 痕跡がある and 痕跡もなく "without a trace". It is used in criminology, archaeology and science (痕跡器官 "vestigial organ"). 跡 is the general everyday word (足跡, 傷跡), while 形跡 emphasizes signs that someone has done something (侵入した形跡).

examples[].german: A request for review was filed against the denial of permission.
To obtain a patent, you must file a request for examination within three years of filing the application.
I could not accept the decision to deny my pension, so I filed a request for review.
en.notes: 審査請求 is the formal request for review, above all the appeal against an administrative act under the 行政不服審査法 (〜に対して審査請求をする). In patent law, 出願審査請求 is the request for substantive examination of a patent application. Typical: 審査請求を行う・する, 審査請求が棄却される "is rejected". To be distinguished from a mere 申請 "application (for a benefit)": 審査請求 is directed against a decision already made or requests an examination.

examples[].german: A shift from declining industries to new growth fields is necessary.
The once-thriving coal-mining town went into decline with the change in energy policy.
The setting sun streaming in through the window dyed the room red.
en.notes: 斜陽 literally means the evening sun shining in at a slant, but in current usage it mostly means decline: 斜陽産業 "declining industry", 斜陽化する "to go into decline". The figurative meaning became popular through Dazai Osamu's novel 『斜陽』 (1947) about an impoverished noble family, hence also 斜陽族. The literal meaning is literary; in everyday speech one says 夕日.

en.meaning: to run rampant; to proliferate; to take over
examples[].german: In the area where criminal organizations run rampant, public safety deteriorated rapidly.
Malicious scam operators are rampant on the internet.
In the Warring States period, rival warlords ran rampant in every region.
en.notes: 跋扈 means that bad actors run rampant unhindered and spread themselves around. The subject is mostly people or groups: 悪徳業者/犯罪組織/詐欺師が跋扈する; intensified in the yojijukugo 跳梁跋扈. It is an intransitive する-verb, strongly negative and very literary; because of the difficult kanji it is often written ばっこ. For abuses themselves, 横行 fits better (不正が横行する), and for diseases or vices 蔓延.

examples[].german: They parted without the resentment in their hearts being resolved.
Talking it over made the bad feeling between the two disappear.
I no longer hold any grudge about what happened back then.
en.notes: わだかまり is an unspoken ill feeling or unresolved unease that remains in the heart or between people. It is almost always written in kana; 蟠り is rare. Typical: わだかまりが残る/ある, わだかまりが解ける/消える, わだかまりを捨てる and わだかまりなく "without reservation, without resentment". It is quieter than 遺恨 or 恨み: more of a thorn than open enmity. The related verb 蟠る means "to lodge itself, to be stuck".

examples[].german: Everyday dissatisfaction built up and exploded.
The residents' anger, which had been building up for years, finally turned into a protest movement.
I let off the pent-up stress by jogging on weekends.
en.notes: 鬱積 describes how negative feelings such as dissatisfaction, anger or stress accumulate over a long time, often until they burst out: 不満が鬱積する, 鬱積した怒り, 鬱積を晴らす. Intransitive する-verb with が; in newspapers also written うっ積. 鬱屈 emphasizes the depressed, inhibited state of mind, while 蓄積 is neutral accumulation (疲労の蓄積, データの蓄積). Literary.

en.meaning: revenge (for a defeat); redeeming a humiliation; getting even
examples[].german: He got his revenge for the previous defeat.
This year we take on the opponent who beat us in last year's final, determined to get revenge.
I retook the exam I had failed once and brilliantly redeemed myself.
en.notes: 雪辱 literally means "to wash away (雪ぐ) a disgrace (辱)": one makes up for an earlier defeat with a later success. Fixed phrases are 雪辱を果たす "to take revenge", 雪辱を期す "to be firmly determined to get revenge" and 雪辱戦 "rematch"; 雪辱を晴らす is considered a mistake (confusion with 屈辱を晴らす). It concerns sports, competitions or exams, not revenge on persons; for that there are 報復 or 復讐.

examples[].german: It is important to break the chain of retaliation.
In response to the US tariff increase, the other country imposed retaliatory tariffs.
The employee who had blown the whistle was punished by the company with a retaliatory transfer.
en.notes: 報復 is retaliation for harm suffered, especially between states and organizations or in conflicts: 報復攻撃, 報復措置, 報復関税 "retaliatory tariffs", 〜に報復する, 報復の連鎖. In companies, 報復人事 refers to a punitive transfer as an act of revenge. Intransitive する-verb with に. 復讐 is personal, emotional revenge, and 仕返し is the colloquial "to get back at".

examples[].german: The minister is carrying out his duties at the official residence.
The mayor met a visitor in his office.
The office hours of our firm are from 9:00 to 17:00 on weekdays.
en.notes: 執務 (執る "to carry out" + 務 "duty") is the performance of official business, especially by officeholders, agencies and law offices: 執務室 "office room", 執務時間 "office hours", 執務中. As an intransitive する-verb: 官邸で執務する. Compared with 勤務 "duty, work (for an employer)" and 業務 "business activity", 執務 is more formal and related to public offices.

en.meaning: many difficulties ahead; a rocky road ahead
examples[].german: The reform faces many difficulties ahead, but he will not give up.
The new government is a minority government and got off to a difficult start.
On the opening day, no customers came because of heavy rain, a start that hinted at hardships to come.
en.notes: 前途多難 is composed of 前途 "the road ahead, the future" and 多難 "many difficulties": an undertaking still faces many obstacles. Typical patterns are 前途多難だ, 前途多難な船出 "difficult start" and 前途多難が予想される. The opposite is 前途洋々 "bright prospects". Frequent in news and speeches; in everyday speech also slightly jokingly about one's own plans.

examples[].german: The whole team was demoralized by the losing streak.
The father silently watched over his son, who was dejected after failing his first-choice school.
After receiving harsh criticism in the presentation, he left the meeting room dejected.
en.notes: 意気消沈 combines 意気 "spirit, fighting spirit" with 消沈 "to die out, to sink": one has lost all courage after a failure. It is an intransitive する-verb: 意気消沈する, 意気消沈した様子. Its opposites are 意気揚々 and 意気軒昂. In everyday speech one more often says 落ち込む or しょんぼりする; 意気消沈 sounds somewhat more elevated and is often used in reports.

en.meaning: covered in wounds; battered all over; badly battered
examples[].german: Even though he was battered all over, he completed the project.
After fierce fighting, the soldiers returned covered in wounds.
After a series of scandals, the cabinet is badly battered by criticism.
en.notes: 満身創痍 is a yojijukugo made of 満身 "the whole body" and 創痍 "wounds", literally "wounded all over the body". Figuratively it describes someone badly battered by criticism, setbacks or overwork, such as a cabinet after scandals or an athlete with many injuries. It is used predicatively (満身創痍だ), adverbially (満身創痍で戦う) and attributively (満身創痍の状態). Elevated, popular in news and sports reports.

en.meaning: keeping at a distance; shunning; (baseball) intentional walk
examples[].german: There is a tendency to avoid difficult topics.
Tough, dirty and dangerous jobs tend to be shunned by young people.
The manager instructed the pitcher to intentionally walk the cleanup hitter.
en.notes: 敬遠 literally means "to respect and keep at a distance": one politely keeps one's distance from someone without really liking them. Today it mostly simply means "to avoid something unpleasant, to shy away from something": 〜を敬遠する, 若者に敬遠される職業, 敬遠されがち. In baseball, 敬遠 is the intentional walk, in which a strong batter is sent to base. So politeness is not the core of the meaning; 避ける is the neutral everyday word.

examples[].german: He is extremely busy and has no time to rest.
I apologize for troubling you when you are so busy, but I ask you to please check this.
The company president was absent from the ceremony because of a busy schedule.
en.notes: 多忙 is the formal equivalent of 忙しい. It is very common in business letters and e-mails: ご多忙のところ/ご多忙中恐れ入りますが "I am sorry to trouble you when you are so busy". Other patterns are 多忙を極める "to be extremely busy", 多忙な毎日 and 多忙のため欠席する. 繁忙 refers more to periods and workload (繁忙期), 多忙 to people.

en.meaning: outsider's view; how it looks from outside
examples[].german: From the outside, they look happy.
It was obvious even to an onlooker that he was depressed.
Wear the clothes you like without worrying about what others think.
en.notes: 傍目 is the view of an outsider, that is, how something looks to others. Typical are 傍目には/傍目から見ると "seen from the outside", 傍目にも分かる "obvious even to outsiders" and 傍目を気にする "to worry about what others think". Often also written はた目. Note: in the proverb 傍目八目 "onlookers see more than the players", 傍目 is read おかめ. 人目, by contrast, emphasizes being seen in public.

examples[].german: The economic stagnation is dragging on.
After the losing streak, a mood of stagnation hangs over the team.
With the arrival of the new department head, vitality returned to the sluggish workplace.
en.notes: 沈滞 refers to a state without momentum or movement: the economy, a market, an organization or a mood is as if paralyzed. Typical are 沈滞ムード, 沈滞した空気/雰囲気 and 沈滞する (intransitive). 停滞 emphasizes the stalling of progress (景気の停滞, 前線が停滞する), and 低迷 staying at a low level; 沈滞 highlights the lack of drive. Opposite: 活気. Literary.

examples[].german: Even the port town that once flourished is quiet now.
In the Edo period, Nihonbashi was at its most prosperous, as merchants gathered there from all over the country.
The novel opens with a description of the bustling prosperity of prewar Shanghai.
en.notes: 殷賑 is a very elevated, almost archaic word for the lively, prosperous bustle of a city or trading place. It occurs almost only in the fixed phrase 殷賑を極める "to be at the height of prosperity" and in forms such as 殷賑ぶり. It is found in historical accounts and literature; in present-day usage one says にぎわい, 繁栄 or 活況.

examples[].german: We support families who have fallen into financial distress.
After the war, the nation's finances were in extreme straits.
Citing the hardship of his livelihood, he applied for an exemption from tuition fees.
en.notes: 窮迫 is an extremely hard-pressed situation, especially financially: 財政が窮迫する "the finances are at their end", 経済的窮迫, 生活の窮迫. It serves as a noun or an intransitive する-verb and is very formal, typical of official documents, history books and newspapers. Similar is 困窮 "hardship, poverty" (more the living circumstances of people); 逼迫 denotes a shortage and is also used for resources (医療の逼迫). In everyday speech one says お金に困る.

examples[].german: Repressed feelings show in the work of art.
After failing the entrance exam, he spent his days in gloom.
Unable to say what he wanted to say, his feelings grew more pent up inside.
en.notes: 鬱屈 describes a depressed state of mind in which feelings find no outlet and one feels inwardly inhibited and closed off. Typical are 鬱屈した感情/思い/日々 and 鬱屈する (intransitive). 鬱積 emphasizes the building up until an outburst, while 鬱屈 is more the depressed, closed-off mood itself. Literary; common in novels and reviews about characters or artists.

examples[].german: Stale policies cannot cope with today's challenges.
The ending of that movie was so hackneyed that I was disappointed.
Technology advances so fast that last year's products are already obsolete.
en.notes: 陳腐 (陳 "old" + 腐 "rotten") is a な-adjective for things that have become worn out and uninteresting through frequent use: 陳腐な表現 "hackneyed phrase", 陳腐なセリフ, 陳腐な発想. 陳腐化 means "becoming obsolete", for example of technology or products. Unlike 古い (merely "old"), 陳腐 always carries a negative judgment: banal, clichéd, without originality. Literary, frequent in reviews and commentary.

examples[].german: He warns himself not to repeat the same mistake.
I say this as a warning to myself as well: getting into a panic right before the deadline is not a good idea.
I wrote this failure down in my planner as a reminder to myself.
en.notes: 自戒 is "self-admonition", that is, a conscious warning to oneself not to repeat a mistake. As an intransitive する-verb: 自戒する; very common are 自戒を込めて "also as a reminder to myself" (typical in columns and blogs) and 自戒の念. The word is literary; in everyday speech one more often says 反省する "to reflect on oneself, to regret" or 自分を戒める. 自制, by contrast, means "self-control".

examples[].german: His years of research bore fruit, and he fulfilled his long-cherished wish.
With his selection for the national team, his heart's desire was finally fulfilled.
That my students have turned out well is, for me as a teacher, the true fulfillment.
en.notes: 本懐 is the "long-cherished wish", what one has always hoped for from the bottom of one's heart. It almost always appears in the fixed phrase 本懐を遂げる "to fulfill one's heart's desire, to achieve one's goal" or predicatively: 〜こそ本懐だ "that is exactly my true fulfillment" (also 男子の本懐). The word sounds elevated and somewhat archaic; more neutral are 念願, 宿願, 悲願 (a fervent wish, often unfulfilled for a long time) or 本望.

examples[].german: "Direct blood relatives" are blood relatives in a straight line, such as grandparents, parents, children and grandchildren.
In Japan, cousins may marry, but blood relatives within the third degree, such as an uncle and a niece, may not.
For the inheritance procedure, I looked up my late father's blood relatives in the family register.
en.notes: 血族 is a technical term from law and ethnology for "blood relatives, blood relationship". In family law it is contrasted with 姻族 "relatives by marriage"; together they form the 親族 "kinship". A distinction is made between 直系血族 (direct line: parents, children, grandchildren) and 傍系血族 (collateral line: siblings, cousins). In everyday speech one more often says 血のつながった家族, 血縁 or 身内.

examples[].german: I was diagnosed with intrinsic asthma.
Let us divide the reasons for the defeat into internal and external causes.
The real internal cause of the worsening business results was the management's poor decisions.
en.notes: 内因 is the "internal cause" of a process; its counterpart is 外因 "external cause", and the two often appear as a pair: 内因と外因. In medicine it forms 内因性 "endogenous, intrinsic" (内因性うつ病, 内因性ぜんそく). The word is technical or analytical; in everyday speech 原因 or 内部の原因 is enough. Do not confuse it with 要因 "factor".

examples[].german: I research Kampo medicinal formulas.
This shop is said to have a family formula handed down since the Edo period.
Based on a formula recorded in old documents, they reproduced a historical medicine.
en.notes: 薬方 is the "medicinal formula", that is, the composition and preparation instructions of a remedy. The word is found mainly in connection with Kampo (漢方) and historical remedies: 家伝の薬方 "handed-down family formula", 古い薬方. For a doctor's prescription today one says 処方, and for the prescription form 処方箋; 方 here, as in 処方, means "prescription, recipe".

examples[].german: If residual assets remain when the company is liquidated, they are distributed to the shareholders.
For the remaining term of the contract, the fee is refunded on a daily pro rata basis.
It was decided that the remainder of the budget would be carried over to the next fiscal year.
en.notes: 残余 means "remainder, remnant" and belongs to official, legal and financial language. It mostly stands before another noun or with の: 残余財産 "residual assets (after liquidation)", 残余期間 "remaining term", 予算の残余. In everyday speech one says 残り or 余り; the balance of an account, however, is called 残高.

examples[].german: Below, we have listed all the relevant laws and regulations.
Obey the traffic regulations and drive safely.
The factory was ordered to suspend operations for violating environmental regulations.
en.notes: 法規 is a collective term for "laws and ordinances", that is, all legally binding rules in a field: 交通法規, 関連法規, 環境法規. Typical are 法規を守る and 法規に違反する. 法律, by contrast, means a single law passed by parliament, 規則 means rather rules and house rules; 法令 is an almost synonymous official word.

examples[].german: The employees here seem more optimistic than those at the Osaka branch.
This company has about 500 employees.
All workers at this factory must wear a helmet while working.
en.notes: 従業 means "employment, working in a business", but appears almost only in compounds: 従業員 "employees, staff", 従業者 "persons employed" (official language), 従業員数. The verb 従業する exists but is rare; one says 働く, 勤務する or 〜に従事する "to be engaged in a field" instead. Watch the pronunciation: 従業 じゅうぎょう has a long う, whereas 授業 じゅぎょう "class, lesson" does not.

examples[].german: That is just an empty threat. Don't worry about it.
The company did not yield to the threat and notified the police.
A business partner threatened us, saying they would terminate the contract.
en.notes: 脅し is the noun of 脅す "to threaten, to intimidate" and means "threat, intimidation". Typical combinations: 脅しをかける "to apply pressure, to threaten", 脅しに屈する "to yield to a threat", ただの脅し "an empty threat", 脅し文句. The legal and formal word is 脅迫 (脅迫状 "threatening letter"), while 威嚇 means a threatening gesture or a warning shot. Rarely, a scarecrow is also meant (鳥脅し); おどし is often written in kana.

examples[].german: This music is very rhythmic.
The waves are breaking on the shore in a steady rhythm.
The audience was captivated by the dancers' rhythmic movements.
en.notes: 律動的 is a な-adjective meaning "rhythmic, in a regular beat", formed from 律動 "rhythm, rhythmic movement". It is used for music, movements, waves or the heartbeat: 律動的な動き, 律動的に響く. It sounds literary and somewhat elevated; in conversation one usually says リズミカル(な) or リズムがいい.

examples[].german: The leak of classified information caused a security problem.
This document contains company secrets, so it must not be taken out.
We signed a confidentiality agreement with our business partner.
en.notes: 機密 means "secrets" of states, agencies or companies, that is, strictly confidential information: 機密情報, 機密文書, 国家機密, 企業機密. Typical verbs are 機密を漏らす/守る; 機密保持契約 is a confidentiality agreement (NDA). 秘密 is more general and also personal ("my secret"), 極秘 means "top secret", 内密 "privately, discreetly".

examples[].german: I have collected famous sayings of great figures of the world.
As a child, I liked reading biographies of great figures.
Hideyo Noguchi is a great local figure that Fukushima Prefecture takes pride in.
en.notes: 偉人 refers to a "great person", usually a historical figure who deserves admiration for achievements or character: 歴史上の偉人, 郷土の偉人, 偉人伝 "biographies of great figures" (a classic children's book genre). Do not confuse it with 偉い人, which colloquially simply means "big shots, superiors", often slightly ironically. 有名人 is a "celebrity", 英雄 a "hero".

examples[].german: What is the greatest invention in the whole of human history?
I only understood my mother's greatness once I became a parent myself.
He broke the records of his great predecessors one after another.
en.notes: 偉大 is a な-adjective: "great, grand, eminent" in terms of rank and achievement, never of physical size (for that, 大きい). Typical: 偉大な人物, 偉大な業績, 偉大な発明; the noun "greatness" is 偉大さ (母の偉大さ). It sounds solemn and admiring; 偉い is more everyday and can also mean "of high standing", and 立派 means "admirable, fine".

en.meaning: great; admirable; of high standing; (colloq.) terrible, exhausting
examples[].german: Is the company president really that important?
You changed clothes all by yourself? Good for you!
Trains stopped because of heavy snow, and it turned into a huge mess.
en.notes: 偉い has several faces. As praise it means "great, commendable", especially toward children or juniors (偉いね！); toward superiors it sounds condescending. Second, it means "of high standing, important": 偉い人 "big shots", 偉そうにする "to act important". Colloquially and mostly in kana, えらい also means "terrible, severe" (えらいことになった) and in the Kansai dialect "exhausting" (= しんどい) or adverbially "very" (えらい暑い).

examples[].german: Could I have the check, please?
When I counted the money in the register, it was a thousand yen short.
I also factored in the traffic jam time and left early.
en.notes: 勘定 means "bill, payment" and also "calculation, counting". In a restaurant one says お勘定をお願いします (today just as often お会計); 勘定する means "to count (money), to calculate". Important phrases: 勘定に入れる "to factor in, to take into account", 損得勘定 "cost-benefit thinking", 勘定が合う "the accounts add up", and in bookkeeping 勘定科目 "account". 勘定高い describes a "calculating" person.

en.meaning: (honorific) to summon; to wear; to be pleased by; to take (age, a cold)
examples[].german: Your older sister has been called to God.
Is this kimono to your liking?
Please give up your seat to elderly people.
en.notes: 召す is a respectful verb (尊敬語) and never refers to oneself. Today it lives mainly in fixed phrases: お気に召す "to be to one's liking" (お気に召しましたか), お年を召した方 "elderly people", 着物をお召しになる "to wear", 風邪を召す "to catch a cold" and 神に召される, a Christian euphemism for "to die". The common 召し上がる "to eat, to drink" is derived from it. The basic meaning "to call, to summon to oneself" is rare today.

en.meaning: to arouse; to evoke; to stir up (attention, awareness)
examples[].german: That politician is skilled at stirring up public opinion.
The Japan Meteorological Agency is calling attention to heavy rain.
This advertisement is designed to arouse consumers' desire to buy.
en.notes: 喚起する means to awaken attention, awareness or feelings in others. Fixed combinations are 注意を喚起する "to urge caution" (in official notices often shortened to 注意喚起), 世論を喚起する, 関心を喚起する and 記憶を喚起する. Transitive with を; the object is always something mental, never a person. Do not confuse it with the identically read 換気 "ventilation". Formal, typical of news, administration and advertising.

examples[].german: I am from Ehime Prefecture.
Ehime Prefecture is famous as a mandarin-growing region.
During the summer vacation, I went to Dogo Onsen in Ehime Prefecture.
en.notes: 愛媛県 is a prefecture in the northwest of the island of Shikoku, with 松山市 as its capital. It is known for mandarin oranges (みかん, いよかん), the hot spring resort 道後温泉 and the towels from 今治. The reading is irregular: 愛 is read え here. In conversation people often simply say 愛媛.

examples[].german: She turned a smile full of loving kindness toward me.
The statue of the Virgin Mary bears an expression of gentle loving kindness.
The director raised the orphaned children with great tenderness.
en.notes: 慈愛 is "kind, caring love", as parents show to their child or a deity to humankind, that is, affection from above rather than romantic love. Typical is 慈愛に満ちた (目・まなざし・笑顔), plus 慈愛深い and 慈愛の心. The word is literary; in everyday speech one says 愛情 or 優しさ. The Buddhist term 慈悲, by contrast, emphasizes "compassion".

en.meaning: to soak; to dip; to steep
examples[].german: Why are you soaking the vegetables in water?
I dipped a towel in cold water and put it on my forehead.
It feels good to soak tired feet in hot water.
en.notes: 浸す is transitive: "to immerse, to soak, to drench", with the pattern XをYに浸す (タオルを水に浸す). The intransitive partner is 浸る "to be immersed", often figurative: 思い出に浸る "to indulge in memories". For comparison: つける means a brief dipping (しょうゆにつける), 漬ける a longer soaking or pickling (漬物).

en.meaning: center of a whirlpool; in the midst of (scandal, dispute)
examples[].german: He is in the thick of a divorce scandal.
The minister at the center of the controversy finally held a press conference.
Without realizing it, she had been drawn into the middle of a factional struggle within the company.
en.notes: 渦中 literally means "in the whirlpool", but is used almost only figuratively: "in the middle of a scandal, dispute or turmoil". Very typical for news is 渦中の人 "the person at the center of the scandal", plus 騒動・論争の渦中にいる and 渦中に巻き込まれる "to get dragged in". Neutral "in the middle of something" without a scandal connotation is 最中 or 真っただ中.

en.meaning: middle of the road; political center
examples[].german: A new party advocating a centrist line was formed.
As a result of the election, a center-right coalition government was born.
Buddhism teaches the middle way, which avoids both extremes.
en.notes: 中道 in politics is the "center" between left and right: 中道路線 "centrist course", 中道政党, 中道左派 "center-left", 中道右派 "center-right". In Buddhism it denotes the "middle way" that avoids extremes. In elevated style it can also mean "halfway" (中道にして倒れる), but today one mostly says 途中 or 道半ば for that. Do not confuse it with 中立 "neutral, impartial".

examples[].german: The Whistleblower Protection Act was amended and the scope of protection was expanded.
Upon learning of wrongdoing within the company, he reported it to an external contact point.
It is prohibited to dismiss an employee on the grounds of a whistleblower report.
en.notes: 公益通報 is the legal term for reporting violations of the law in one's own company or agency, that is, whistleblowing; the basis is the 公益通報者保護法 "Whistleblower Protection Act". In everyday speech and the press one mostly says 内部告発. Typical: 公益通報窓口 "reporting desk", 公益通報者 "whistleblower", 公益通報を受ける. 通報 alone means "report (to the police/an authority)", e.g. 警察に通報する.

examples[].german: This lotion keeps your skin moisturized.
Since I planted flowers in the garden, my daily life has become richer.
Thanks to the rain, moisture returned to the dry earth.
en.notes: 潤い is the noun of 潤う "to become moist; to profit" and literally means "moisture", especially of skin, hair and soil: 肌の潤い, 潤いを保つ, 潤いを与える (typical of cosmetics advertising). Figuratively it stands for "enrichment, joy in life": 生活に潤いを与える, 潤いのある暮らし. Unpleasant humidity in the air, by contrast, is 湿気; the transitive partner of the verb is 潤す.

examples[].german: We have run out of laundry detergent.
Using too much laundry powder causes residue to be left in the clothes.
In the old days, people washed clothes by hand in a tub with dissolved laundry powder.
en.notes: 洗濯粉 is "laundry powder", i.e. powdered detergent. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned; today one usually says 洗剤 or 洗濯洗剤 and distinguishes 粉末洗剤 "powder" from 液体洗剤 "liquid detergent". Typical: 洗濯粉を入れる, 洗濯粉が切れる "to run out".

examples[].german: I am going to pick up my dress shirt from the cleaner's.
In the past, this shopping street had as many as three laundries.
You should not wash suits yourself but take them to the cleaner's.
en.notes: 洗濯屋 is the "laundry, dry cleaner's", a shop that washes clothes for payment; politely also 洗濯屋さん. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned: today one usually says クリーニング屋 or クリーニング店, and a self-service laundromat is called コインランドリー. Typical: 洗濯屋に出す "to take to the cleaner's".

examples[].german: I wear a mask to deal with the dryness.
The air is dry in winter, so please be careful with open flames.
When I dried the laundry in the dryer, my sweater shrank.
en.notes: 乾燥 means "dryness" and, as a する-verb, "to be/become dry" or "to dry". Intransitive: 空気が乾燥している, 肌が乾燥する; the transitive meaning is usually expressed with 乾燥させる (木材を乾燥させる). Common compounds: 乾燥肌, 乾燥機 "dryer", 乾燥剤, 乾燥注意報. In everyday speech, for laundry one more often says 乾く/乾かす; 無味乾燥 means "dry, boring".

examples[].german: Please throw empty bottles away here.
I put flowers in an empty bottle and decorated the table with it.
I wash empty jam jars and use them as seasoning containers.
en.notes: 空き瓶 is an "empty bottle" or "empty jar" (e.g. a jam jar). In waste sorting it belongs to the 資源ごみ (recyclables), alongside 空き缶 "empty cans" and ペットボトル. It is also often written 空きびん or 空きビン. The prefix 空き "empty, vacant" is also known from 空き家 and 空き地.

examples[].german: The man threw a Molotov cocktail.
Some of the demonstrators hurled Molotov cocktails at the police.
In the student movement around 1970, Molotov cocktails were sometimes used.
en.notes: 火炎瓶 is a "Molotov cocktail, incendiary device", a bottle filled with gasoline with a wick. The word appears mainly in news about riots and attacks as well as in reports on the student movement of the 1960s/70s. Typical: 火炎瓶を投げる・投げ込む・投げつける. Occasionally it is also written 火焔瓶.

examples[].german: I bottle maple syrup.
I received jam in a jar that my grandmother made.
I bought bottled and canned food for emergencies.
en.notes: 瓶詰 (usually written 瓶詰め) refers to filling bottles or jars and, above all, the result, that is, food in a jar: ジャムの瓶詰め, 瓶詰めのピクルス. As a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を瓶詰めにする or 瓶詰めする. For metal cans one says 缶詰, and for drinks in plastic bottles ペットボトル入り. In everyday speech the noun is much more common than the verb form.

examples[].german: Farmland stretches across this area.
Japan's cultivated land area is shrinking year by year.
People cleared the forest and created new farmland.
en.notes: 耕地 is "arable land, cultivated area" and is used mainly in statistics, geography and administration: 耕地面積 "cultivated area", 耕地を広げる, 耕地整理. More general for agricultural land (also in the legal sense) is 農地; in everyday speech one says 田畑 or simply 畑 or 田んぼ. Fields no longer being farmed are called 耕作放棄地.

examples[].german: A permit is required to cultivate this land.
Because of the aging population, the number of rice paddies that are no longer cultivated is increasing.
He quit his company and now farms a rented field by himself.
en.notes: 耕作 means "tilling the soil, farming"; as a transitive する-verb, the land is its object: 土地・畑を耕作する "to till, to farm land". Common are 耕作地, 耕作面積 and 耕作放棄地 "abandoned farmland". The everyday verb for "to plow, to dig up" is 耕す; for growing specific plants one says 栽培する (トマトを栽培する), not 耕作する.

examples[].german: In the past, even in this village, farming was done with the help of oxen.
In the Yayoi period, farming centered on rice cultivation spread.
It is said that farming peoples and hunting peoples differ in their way of thinking.
en.notes: 農耕 refers to "farming" as a human way of life and culture, often in a historical or ethnological context: 農耕が始まる, 農耕社会, 農耕文化, 農耕民族 (in contrast to 狩猟民族 "hunting peoples" and 遊牧民族 "nomads"), 農耕馬. For today's branch of the economy or the occupation one says 農業; "He is a farmer" is therefore 農業をしている, not 農耕をしている.

examples[].german: The worker filed a lawsuit on the grounds of unfair dismissal.
The court recognized the dismissal as unfair, and I was able to return to my workplace.
Dismissal on the grounds of pregnancy constitutes unfair dismissal.
en.notes: 不当解雇 (不当 "unjustified" + 解雇 "dismissal") is a dismissal without objectively justified reason, which is invalid under Japanese labor law. Typical: 不当解雇で訴える, 不当解雇に当たる, 不当解雇が認められる. Colloquially one says クビ for dismissal; technical terms for other kinds of dismissal are 整理解雇 "redundancy dismissal" and 懲戒解雇 "disciplinary dismissal".

examples[].german: This is a really clever child.
He was known as a merchant with a keen nose for profit.
Even in old age, my grandmother has sharp hearing and immediately notices even small sounds.
en.notes: 聡い means "clever, quick-witted" and "sharp, sensitive (of the senses)"; it sounds literary and is often written in kana as さとい. Fixed combinations: 利に聡い "mindful of one's advantage, business-savvy", 耳聡い "to have sharp ears, to catch everything" and the related 目ざとい "sharp-eyed". In everyday speech one says 賢い or 頭がいい; more formal is the な-adjective 聡明.

examples[].german: Why won't you either confirm or deny it?
Rewrite the following affirmative sentence as a negative sentence.
To nurture children's self-esteem, praising them is the first important step.
en.notes: 肯定 is "affirmation, agreement" and the opposite of 否定 "negation". As a transitive する-verb: 事実を肯定する "to confirm a fact"; fixed is 肯定も否定もしない "neither to confirm nor to deny". Important derivatives are 肯定的(な) "positive, affirmative", 肯定文 "affirmative sentence" in grammar and 自己肯定感 "self-esteem". The word is rather formal; in conversation one often says 認める or そうだと言う.

examples[].german: I want to get rid of the fat on my thighs.
At my health checkup, I was told I have a lot of visceral fat.
For my health, I choose low-fat milk.
en.notes: 脂肪 is "fat" as a substance in the body and in food, rather factual or medical: 体脂肪, 内臓脂肪 "visceral fat", 皮下脂肪, 脂肪がつく "to put on fat", 脂肪を落とす "to lose fat", 低脂肪 "low-fat". In everyday cooking one speaks of あぶら (油 for liquid oil, 脂 for solid fat), and for meat the fatty part is 脂身.

examples[].german: I encased this in transparent resin.
This spoon is made of resin, so it will not break even if dropped.
Resin is oozing out of the pine trunk.
en.notes: 樹脂 is "resin": natural tree resin (天然樹脂, e.g. 松やに) and above all synthetic resin or plastic (合成樹脂). Very common in product descriptions: 樹脂製 "made of plastic", アクリル樹脂, エポキシ樹脂. In everyday speech, plastic objects are usually called プラスチック; 樹脂 sounds more technical. Used with の or as a first element: 樹脂の部品, 樹脂加工.

examples[].german: I've never heard that surname before.
My surname changed when I got married.
In Japan, when writing a name, the surname is written first.
en.notes: 苗字 is the "family name, surname"; there is also the spelling 名字, which is more usual in school textbooks and government offices. In Japanese, the 苗字 comes before the given name (下の名前). Typical: 苗字が変わる (e.g. through marriage), 珍しい苗字, 苗字で呼ぶ. On forms, the more formal 姓 (姓・名) or 氏名 for the full name appears; 名前 can mean the full name or only the given name.

examples[].german: What is the meaning of the lotus flower in the language of flowers?
On a summer morning, lotus flowers were blooming in the temple pond.
Renkon is a vegetable in which you eat the underground stem of the lotus.
en.notes: 蓮 (はす, often also written in kana はす or ハス) is the "lotus". Its edible root is called 蓮根 (れんこん). In Buddhism the lotus is a symbol of purity, because it grows from the mud and yet blooms clean; one speaks of 蓮の花, 蓮の葉 and 蓮池. Do not confuse it with 睡蓮 "water lily", whose leaves lie flat on the water, whereas lotus leaves rise above it.

en.meaning: lotus flower; porcelain soup spoon; Chinese milk vetch
examples[].german: The Buddha statue sits on a pedestal in the shape of a lotus flower.
I scooped up the ramen broth with a ceramic spoon and drank it.
In spring, Chinese milk vetch blooms all over the rice paddies.
