en.notes: れんげ (usually written 蓮華, more rarely 蓮花) originally means "lotus flower"; in this meaning it is mainly Buddhist-literary (蓮華座 "lotus seat" of a Buddha statue). The plant in the pond is called 蓮 or 蓮の花 in everyday speech. Today れんげ is mostly encountered in kana in two shortened meanings: as a ceramic spoon for ramen and soups (short for 散り蓮華) and as れんげ草, the Chinese milk vetch that colors rice paddies pink in spring.

examples[].german: She remained faithful to the very end.
In old novels, the faithful wife is often depicted as the ideal woman.
The word "teisetsu" is hardly used anymore today.
en.notes: 貞節 means "marital fidelity, chastity", traditionally a woman's fidelity to her husband. Typical: 貞節を守る・貫く and, as a な-adjective, 貞節な妻. The word belongs to old moral vocabulary and is found today mainly in literature and history. 貞操 emphasizes specifically sexual chastity, and the literary 操 (みさお) is almost synonymous; for couples today one more often speaks of 浮気しない or 誠実.

examples[].german: That man took her virginity.
Some lament that young people today have lax moral standards about chastity.
A chastity belt from medieval Europe was on display at the museum.
en.notes: 貞操 refers to "chastity, sexual fidelity". Typical combinations: 貞操を守る, 貞操を奪う (a euphemism for "to deflower, to rape"), 貞操観念 "moral attitudes in sexual matters" (貞操観念が低い・ない) and 貞操帯 "chastity belt". The word sounds old-fashioned; only 貞操観念 is still common in conversation today. 貞節 is broader and means fidelity in marriage as a whole.

examples[].german: My wife was unfaithful, so we got divorced.
She demanded compensation on the grounds of her partner's infidelity.
Suspected of infidelity, he desperately denied it.
en.notes: 不貞 means "infidelity, adultery". Typical: 不貞を働く "to commit adultery" and above all the legal term 不貞行為, which counts as a ground for divorce in divorce law; adjectivally 不貞な妻・夫. In everyday speech one says 浮気 or (for married people) 不倫. Caution: the same characters appear in 不貞腐れる (ふてくされる) "to sulk" and 不貞寝 (ふてね), which have nothing to do with infidelity.

examples[].german: A corrective recommendation was issued to the company that violated the Labor Standards Act.
The Labor Standards Act stipulates that daily working hours are in principle limited to eight hours.
The Labor Standards Act also applies to part-time workers.
en.notes: 労働基準法 is Japan's central labor protection law and sets minimum standards such as working hours, overtime premiums, leave and notice periods for dismissal. Abbreviated 労基法; the supervising authority is the 労働基準監督署 (colloquially 労基). Typical: 労働基準法に違反する, 労働基準法違反, 〜が適用される. Together with the 労働組合法 and the 労働関係調整法 it forms the 労働三法.

examples[].german: She was placed under house arrest.
After the coup, the president was placed under house arrest by the military.
The writer was practically confined to a hotel until the deadline.
en.notes: 軟禁 is "house arrest": a person is not locked up but may not leave a place (usually their own residence) and has no free contact. Typical: 自宅軟禁, 軟禁される, 軟禁状態. To be distinguished are 監禁 "unlawful confinement" (usually by criminals) and 拘束・拘禁 "detention". The word appears mainly in news about political prisoners, and jokingly also in a figurative sense.

examples[].german: This magnificent building is the president's private residence.
The prime minister spent the weekend at his private residence in Tokyo.
Reporters had been crowding in front of the minister's private residence since morning.
en.notes: 私邸 is the "private residence" of a public figure (politician, head of state, nobility), as opposed to the official 官邸 or 公邸. The word is typical of news: 首相が私邸に戻る, 私邸で静養する. For ordinary people one says 自宅 or 家.

en.meaning: official residence (office building of a head of government)
examples[].german: I took part in a tour of the prime minister's official residence.
An emergency cabinet meeting was held at the prime minister's office.
This policy was driven by the prime minister's office.
en.notes: 官邸 is the "official seat" of a high official, above all 首相官邸, the building where the prime minister works. In political language, 官邸 often stands for the prime minister and his staff: 官邸主導 "led by the prime minister's office". Distinguish: 官邸 = official and working seat, 公邸 = official residence, 私邸 = private residence.

examples[].german: The president's official residence was attacked by unknown persons.
After finishing work at the official office, the prime minister returned to the adjacent official residence.
A party for guests from many countries was held at the ambassador's residence.
en.notes: 公邸 is the "official residence" that an office-holder lives in at the state's expense: 首相公邸, 知事公邸, 大使公邸 (an ambassador's residence, often used for receptions). In Japan a distinction is made between 首相官邸 (workplace) and the neighboring 首相公邸 (living quarters); one's own private home is called 私邸.

examples[].german: This mansion is famous for being haunted.
After his business success, he built a large mansion on a hill.
The mansion of a Meiji-era businessman is now open to the public as an art museum.
en.notes: 邸宅 is a "large, stately residence, mansion". Typical are 豪華な邸宅, 大邸宅 and 邸宅を構える "to set up an estate"; the word sounds elevated and is found in reports, real estate ads and travel guides. 豪邸 is more colloquial ("palatial villa"), 屋敷 emphasizes the traditional estate with grounds, and 住宅 and 家 are neutral.

en.meaning: inside a residence; on the grounds of an estate
examples[].german: This is a photo from inside the estate.
Someone broke into the minister's residence, and the police are investigating.
The grounds have a Japanese garden where you can enjoy different flowers in every season.
en.notes: 邸内 means "within an estate", that is, the buildings and grounds of a stately residence (邸). Typical are 邸内に侵入する, 邸内を案内する and 邸内の庭園. The word is literary; for an ordinary house one says 家の中, and for premises in general 敷地内.

en.meaning: suburbs; outskirts; environs of a city
examples[].german: I live in the suburbs of Tokyo.
On weekends, I often make a day trip to a hot spring in the area around the city.
Farms in the environs of Osaka ship fresh vegetables to the urban area.
en.notes: 近郊 is the "nearby surroundings, environs" of a city, usually after a place name: 東京近郊, 大阪近郊, or generally 都市近郊, 近郊農業. The word emphasizes proximity to the big city. 郊外, by contrast, means the "city edge, suburb" as opposed to the city center (郊外に住む); 近所 is the immediate neighborhood.

examples[].german: Today, the county (gun) is mostly used only as part of place names.
My grandfather's address is Karuizawa Town, Kitasaku County, Nagano Prefecture.
A county in the United States is an administrative unit below the state.
en.notes: 郡 is a "county, district"; in Japan it is a unit within a prefecture that groups several small towns (町) and villages (村). As an administrative body, the 郡 was abolished as early as the 1920s and today lives on almost only in addresses: 〇〇県△△郡□□町. As a suffix it comes directly after the name (北佐久郡). It is also used as a translation for territorial units of other countries, e.g. the American county.

examples[].german: You need to give an official explanation of this.
After the scandal, the company president faced questions at a press conference.
The opposition demanded a sufficient explanation from the government.
en.notes: 釈明 is a "justification, clarifying statement" with which one explains one's position after criticism or a misunderstanding. Typical: 釈明する, 釈明を求める, 釈明に追われる, 釈明会見 "press conference to explain oneself"; it is a word of news and official language. 説明 is a neutral "explanation", 弁解 and 言い訳 sound like "excuse", and 弁明 is a formal synonym (e.g. in court).

examples[].german: In that case, please add annotations.
In classics class, we read The Tale of Genji with the help of the annotations.
I stated the source of the data in the graph in the note below.
en.notes: 注釈 is a "note, explanation" on a text, a table or a work: 注釈を付ける・加える, 注釈付きの本, 注釈書 "commentary" on classics. Short footnotes are called 注 or 脚注, a supplement 補足; a personal remark in conversation is more of a コメント. As a verb 注釈する is rare; one usually says 注釈を付ける.

examples[].german: The labor union held collective bargaining demanding a pay raise.
The company side did not agree to collective bargaining.
In the spring wage negotiations, a base pay increase was agreed on.
en.notes: 団体交渉 is negotiation between a labor union and the employer over wages and working conditions, abbreviated 団交. The right to it (団体交渉権) belongs under Article 28 of the Constitution to the 労働三権, alongside 団結権 and 団体行動権. Typical: 団体交渉を行う・申し入れる, 団体交渉に応じる, 団体交渉を拒否する. The employer may not refuse without a valid reason.

examples[].german: When someone bows to you, it is polite to bow back.
I passed the department head in the hallway and gave him a slight bow.
He opened someone else's refrigerator without any hesitation.
en.notes: 会釈 is a "slight bow, a greeting nod" of about 15 degrees, for example when passing each other or in an elevator; deeper ones are 敬礼 and 最敬礼. Typical: 軽く会釈する, 会釈を返す, 会釈を交わす; the verb is intransitive (〜に会釈する). The second meaning "consideration" survives only in 遠慮会釈もなく "without any consideration, unabashedly".

examples[].german: That had always nagged at me in a corner of my heart.
Please keep this in the back of your mind.
The two lived quietly in an obscure corner of the big city.
en.notes: 片隅 is a "corner, nook", usually an inconspicuous, out-of-the-way place: 部屋の片隅, 都会の片隅で暮らす. Figuratively very common: 心の片隅に "in a corner of the heart" and 頭の片隅に置いておく "to keep in the back of one's mind". 隅 is the neutral (inside) "corner", whereas 角 (かど) is the protruding corner of a street or table.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to darken the four corners of a photo.
I put stones on the four corners of the sheet so that it would not blow away.
Please line up the four corners of the documents neatly and then fasten them with a clip.
en.notes: 四隅 refers to the four corners of a rectangular surface: 部屋の四隅, 紙の四隅, 写真の四隅. Typical phrases are 四隅をそろえる "to line the corners up flush" and 四隅を押さえる "to hold down all four corners". For a single inside corner one says 隅, for a protruding outer edge 角. Rarely (more in literary writing) 四隅 also stands for the four intercardinal directions.

en.meaning: every nook and cranny; every corner
examples[].german: Today I cleaned every corner of my room.
Please read through the contract in every detail before you sign.
He knows every nook and cranny of this town.
en.notes: 隅々 means "every corner, down to the last nook" and almost always appears as 隅々まで before a verb: 隅々まで掃除する, 隅々まで探す, 隅々まで目を通す "to read everything carefully". It can be used spatially or figuratively (町の隅々まで知っている, 全国の隅々に行き渡る). A synonym, somewhat more colloquial, is 隅から隅まで. The repetition mark 々 is read like 隅 here, with rendaku: すみずみ.

examples[].german: I washed my sweater in hot water and it shrank.
Because I do the laundry all at once on the weekend, laundry piles up during the week.
I went to a hot spring for the first time in a while and really recharged.
en.notes: 洗濯する means "to do laundry" and is used only for clothing and textiles: 服を洗濯する or simply 洗濯をする. For hands, dishes or vegetables one says 洗う, for the car 洗車する. Important words are 洗濯物 "the laundry" (洗濯物を干す / たたむ) and 洗濯機. Figuratively, 命の洗濯 means "to really relax, to recharge one's soul".

examples[].german: My grandfather was born in the year the Great Depression broke out.
In 1929, stock prices in New York collapsed, and the Great Depression began.
As a result of the Great Depression, Japan's farming villages also fell into serious depression.
en.notes: 世界恐慌 usually means the Great Depression beginning in 1929 (1929年の世界恐慌), but can also refer in general to a worldwide depression. The usual verbs are 世界恐慌が起こる / 起きる / 始まる; 世界恐慌の影響で "as a result of the Great Depression". 恐慌 alone is a severe economic crisis with panic, whereas 不況 is merely a recession or slump. The 2008 financial crisis, by contrast, is usually called リーマン・ショック or 金融危機.

examples[].german: How do you roast coffee beans?
If you lightly roast sesame seeds in a frying pan, they smell better.
For the bean-throwing at Setsubun, roasted soybeans are used.
en.notes: 煎る (also written 炒る) means "to roast in a pan without oil", for example coffee beans, sesame, soybeans or tea (ほうじ茶). For coffee and tea 煎る is usual, for sesame often 炒る. Not to be confused with 炒める "to stir-fry in oil" and 焼く "to bake, to grill". Note: 煎る is a godan verb (煎って, 煎らない) and sounds like いる "to be" or 要る "to need" - context decides.

en.meaning: adultery; affair; to have an affair
examples[].german: It seems that my wife is having an affair.
After his affair was reported, the actor left the show.
The fact that he had been having an affair with his boss became known throughout the company.
en.notes: 不倫 is an extramarital affair, that is, adultery: 不倫する, 不倫をする, 〜と不倫関係にある, 不倫相手 "affair partner". For celebrities it is a perennial topic of the gossip press (不倫報道, 不倫騒動). 浮気 is broader and more colloquial, also covering unfaithfulness in a relationship without marriage; 姦通 is an obsolete legal term. A nominal adjective 不倫な is possible but rare.

en.meaning: right to strike; right of dispute
examples[].german: Workers' right to strike is guaranteed by the Constitution.
Japanese public employees are not granted the right to strike.
The union exercised its right to strike and went on strike.
en.notes: 争議権 (争議 "labor dispute" + 権 "right") is the workers' right to take industrial action, above all to strike; in the constitutional context one also speaks of 団体行動権. Colloquially it is called スト権. Typical: 争議権を行使する, 争議権が認められる・制限される. In Japan, public employees (公務員) have no right to strike. Related: 労働争議 "labor dispute".

examples[].german: If you are bound by fixed ideas, your way of looking at things becomes narrow-minded.
He is narrow-minded and never accepts opinions different from his own.
Narrow-minded nationalism is fueling conflict between countries.
en.notes: 偏狭 is a な-adjective meaning "narrow-minded, intolerant": 偏狭な考え, 偏狭な人, 偏狭なナショナリズム. It is literary and sounds clearly more critical than the everyday 心が狭い; closely related is 狭量. 頑固, by contrast, means "stubborn", not necessarily intolerant. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 辺境 "border region, remote area".

en.meaning: to hint at; to suggest; hint; suggestion
examples[].german: Messi seems to have made a comment hinting at a transfer.
The results of this survey suggest that lack of sleep can cause obesity.
The professor's lecture was full of insights, and I learned a lot.
en.notes: 示唆する means "to hint at, to suggest, to point to something" and is typical of news and science: 〜を示唆する, 〜ことを示唆している. Fixed phrases are 示唆に富む "insightful, thought-provoking" and 示唆を与える / 得る. ほのめかす is more of a deliberate, veiled hint by a person, whereas 指摘する is an explicit pointing out. In everyday speech one says more simply 〜を感じさせる or ヒントになる.

examples[].german: I took a photo of Sakurajima sending up a plume of smoke.
An ash plume rose from the crater and reached a height of 3,000 meters.
Because of the ash plume, many flights were canceled.
en.notes: 噴煙 is the cloud of smoke and ash that a volcano emits. Fixed combinations are 噴煙を上げる (with the volcano as subject), 噴煙が上がる and 噴煙が〜メートルに達する; typical of news and weather reports. Ordinary smoke is simply 煙, and the ash that falls down is called 火山灰. For the eruption itself one says 噴火.

examples[].german: Please show me how to spray tear gas.
The rocket fired its engines and flew off into space.
A defect was found in this car's fuel injection system.
en.notes: 噴射 is the targeted ejection of gas, liquid or fuel under pressure; as a する-verb it is transitive: ガスを噴射する, スプレーを噴射する. Technical combinations are 燃料噴射 "fuel injection", ジェット噴射 "jet stream" and 逆噴射 "thrust reversal". 噴出, by contrast, describes more an uncontrolled gushing out (mostly intransitive), and 発射 the firing of a rocket or bullet.

examples[].german: Let's meet at the fountain over there.
In summer, children play in the water in the park's fountain.
At night, the fountain is lit up in time with the music.
en.notes: 噴水 is a fountain or water jet, for example in a park or on a plaza. Typical are 噴水がある, 噴水の前で待ち合わせる and 噴水が上がる "the fountain shoots up". A natural spring, by contrast, is called 泉 or 湧き水, and a drinking fountain 水飲み場. The expression is neutral and everyday.

en.meaning: to gush out; to erupt; eruption
examples[].german: Is it true that gas is gushing out of black holes?
After the earthquake, water gushed out of cracks in the road.
Dissatisfaction with the new system burst out all at once among the employees.
en.notes: 噴出する means "to gush out, to spout" of gas, water, lava or oil and is mostly intransitive: 〜から〜が噴出する. Figuratively one often says 不満が噴出する or 問題が噴出する "to burst forth in large numbers". The transitive use (火山が溶岩を噴出する) is rarer. The word is literary; in everyday speech one says 噴き出す, which can also mean "to burst out laughing". 噴射, by contrast, emphasizes targeted technical ejection.

examples[].german: After talking it over with my wife, we decided to take in an orphan.
Many children became orphans because of the war.
He lost his parents at a young age and grew up as an orphan in an institution.
en.notes: 孤児 is an orphan, that is, a child without parents; the word is rather formal and often appears in compounds such as 戦争孤児 or 震災孤児. The older 孤児院 "orphanage" is now officially called 児童養護施設. In everyday speech people prefer to paraphrase: 親のいない子; みなしご is outdated. Figuratively 孤児 can also refer to an outsider without support.

examples[].german: I am currently writing a novel set on a remote island.
Heavy snow made the roads impassable, and the village became cut off from the outside world.
Many rare birds live on the remote islands far out at sea.
en.notes: 孤島 is a remote, solitary island; the fixed phrase 絶海の孤島 means an island far out in the open sea. Very common is the image 陸の孤島 "island on the mainland" for a place cut off from the outside world, such as a village after severe weather or a district without a rail connection. 無人島, by contrast, emphasizes that nobody lives there. The word is rather literary.

examples[].german: At our company, there is a Christmas party every year as a tradition.
The fireworks display at the summer festival is a regular event in this town.
Traveling with the family at the end of the year has become a tradition in our home.
en.notes: 恒例 refers to something that takes place regularly, usually every year, and has become a fixed custom: 毎年恒例の〜, 恒例行事, 〜が恒例となっている. It emphasizes regular recurrence, not age like 伝統 "tradition". 慣例 is a (often formal) custom, 習慣 a personal habit. Frequent in announcements: 新春恒例, 夏の恒例イベント.

examples[].german: Dismissal on the grounds of union activity constitutes an unfair labor practice.
The union petitioned the Labor Relations Commission for relief, arguing that the refusal of collective bargaining was an unfair labor practice.
Making non-membership in a union a condition of hiring is also an unfair labor practice.
en.notes: 不当労働行為 is a technical term from the 労働組合法: anti-union actions by the employer, such as discrimination because of union work, refusal of 団体交渉 or interference in the union. Those affected can apply for relief (救済を申し立てる) to the 労働委員会 "Labor Relations Commission". Typical: 不当労働行為に当たる. This does not mean every violation of labor law; violations of working hour rules are 労働基準法違反.

examples[].german: I pray for lasting peace.
We need a permanent measure, not an emergency fix.
The preamble of the Constitution of Japan contains the words "desiring lasting peace".
en.notes: 恒久 means "permanence, durability" and is used adjectivally as 恒久の or, more often, 恒久的な: 恒久の平和, 恒久的な対策 "a permanent solution". The opposite is 一時的 or 暫定的. 永久 and 永遠 mean more "eternal", whereas 恒久 means "designed to last"; it is literary and typical of politics and administration. Well known is the phrase 恒久の平和を念願し from the preamble of the Japanese Constitution.

examples[].german: I had no desire to study and was just going to university out of habit.
I canceled several subscriptions that I was only continuing out of inertia.
On the downhill slope, I did not pedal and just coasted.
en.notes: 惰性 is above all "the force of habit, the rut": 惰性で〜する means to simply keep doing something without real motivation (惰性で続ける, 惰性で通う). It usually sounds negative. Literally it also means physical inertia, for example when a vehicle coasts without power (惰性で走る); in physics, though, one rather says 慣性. 怠惰, by contrast, is laziness as a character trait.

examples[].german: Proudly bragging about your own affair - that's unbelievable.
Please be sure to try our ramen, the specialty of the house.
He is always bragging about his son's grades.
en.notes: 自慢する means "to boast, to brag" about something: 〜を自慢する, 自慢話 "bragging", 自慢げに "boastfully". Positive is 自慢の〜 "my pride and joy": 自慢の息子, 当店自慢のラーメン. 自慢じゃないけど introduces a bit of self-presentation in a modest-ironic way. 誇る is more formal and neutral-positive ("to be proud of"), 威張る means "to throw one's weight around".

examples[].german: I fired that waitress because her movements were so sluggish.
The government's sluggish response is drawing criticism.
As a side effect of the medicine, movements may become slow.
en.notes: 緩慢 is a な-adjective for "slow, sluggish, ponderous", above all for movements and reactions: 動作が緩慢だ, 緩慢な動き. Second, it means "lax, hesitant" in the actions of government offices: 緩慢な対応. It is literary and also common in medicine; colloquially one says のろい, and neutrally ゆっくり (without negative connotation). Do not confuse it with 怠慢 "negligence, neglect of duty".

examples[].german: The scene in that movie where the two leads exchange a sweet embrace was very beautiful.
The parent and child who met again at the airport embraced tightly.
When the title was decided, the manager and players hugged and rejoiced together.
en.notes: 抱擁 is an embrace and belongs to written and literary language: 抱擁する, 抱擁を交わす "to embrace each other", 熱い抱擁. In everyday speech one says 抱きしめる, 抱き合う or ハグする. The する-verb is transitive (子どもを抱擁する) but is often used without an object for mutual embracing. Typical of novels, film descriptions and reports on reunions.

en.meaning: to field (a candidate); to install (into a position)
examples[].german: The opposition plans to field a unified candidate in the next election.
The party fielded a well-known TV personality as its candidate.
The retainers installed the young prince as ruler in order to seize power themselves.
en.notes: 擁立する means "to put someone forward (for office), to install someone in a post", above all in politics: 候補者を擁立する, 〜を党首に擁立する, 独自候補の擁立. Historically it means to install someone as ruler (幼い王子を擁立する). So it is more than mere 支持 "support": the group actively puts the person forward. 推薦する means "to recommend", 立候補する "to run for office oneself".

en.meaning: to have; to possess (population, members, talent)
examples[].german: Kanagawa Prefecture has a larger population than Chiba Prefecture.
This team has several players of national-team caliber.
Tokyo is a major city with a population of about 14 million.
en.notes: 擁する is literary and today mostly means "to have, to possess", especially with residents, members or talent: 人口百万を擁する都市, 優秀な選手を擁するチーム. The original meaning "to embrace" is rare (for that, 抱擁する), and "to lead, to support" survives in 擁立. In everyday speech one says 〜がいる / 〜がある or 抱える instead. It conjugates like a する-verb: 擁して, 擁した, 擁している.

examples[].german: We are planning an exhibition commemorating the 50th anniversary of his death.
Many of Van Gogh's works came to be highly regarded only after his death.
After the author's death, unpublished manuscripts were found in his study.
en.notes: 没後 means "after death" and is used for well-known figures such as artists, writers or rulers, especially at anniversaries: 没後百年, 没後〜年記念展. The counterpart is 生誕〜年 "...years since birth". The general word, also used in daily life, is 死後; 没後 sounds literary and respectful. As an adverb: 没後に評価される "to be recognized posthumously".

en.meaning: death in war; to die in war
examples[].german: Many war dead rest here.
Every year on August 15, the National Memorial Service for the War Dead is held.
My grandfather's older brother is said to have died in the war on an island in the South Pacific.
en.notes: 戦没 means "to fall in war, to perish in war" and occurs almost only in compounds: 戦没者 "war dead, fallen", 戦没者慰霊碑 "war memorial", 全国戦没者追悼式 (the memorial service on August 15). The verb 戦没する is rare and solemn; 戦死する is more usual. 戦没 also covers civilians and soldiers who died of illness or hunger during the war, whereas 戦死 covers only death in combat.

examples[].german: There was someone who predicted the sinking of the Titanic.
A fishing boat sank in the storm, but the entire crew was rescued.
At yesterday's drinking party, he passed out early.
en.notes: 沈没する means "to sink, to go under" and is intransitive: 船が沈没する. It is used for ships; sinking in general (also of the sun) is 沈む, actively sinking a ship is 撃沈する, and running aground is 座礁する. Colloquially 沈没 also means "to pass out dead drunk" (飲み会で沈没する) or, among backpackers, "to get stuck somewhere". Well known is the novel title 日本沈没.

examples[].german: The territorial dispute was referred to the International Court of Justice.
The International Court of Justice is located in The Hague, the Netherlands.
The International Court of Justice found Japan's research whaling to be in violation of the convention.
en.notes: 国際司法裁判所 (ICJ) is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, based in The Hague, and decides disputes between states, for example over borders or treaties. Not to be confused with the 国際刑事裁判所, which prosecutes individuals for international crimes. Typical: 国際司法裁判所に提訴する・付託する, 〜の判決. 司法 means "administration of justice".

examples[].german: If I leave now, I think I can arrive before sunset.
In the mountains the temperature drops sharply after sunset, so let's take a jacket.
Today's sunset is at 5:12 p.m.
en.notes: 日没 is sunset as a point in time and sounds somewhat formal or technical: 日没前, 日没後, 日没時刻, 日没までに. In everyday speech one also says 日の入り (opposite: 日の出) or 日暮れ; 夕日 is the setting sun itself or its light. 日没 is typical in weather forecasts, hiking guides and regulations (日没後は立ち入り禁止).

examples[].german: Do you really think Japan is in decline?
Because of the postwar land reform, many landlords were ruined.
『斜陽』 is a novel depicting a noble family in decline.
en.notes: 没落する means "to fall, to go to ruin, to lose one's rank", mostly of families, social classes, empires or companies: 没落した貴族, 名家が没落する, 帝国の没落. It is intransitive and literary. 衰退 is a gradual decline (e.g. of an industry), 破産 financial bankruptcy; 没落 emphasizes the fall from a formerly high position.

en.meaning: to be buried; to be submerged; to be lost in obscurity
examples[].german: I had double-eyelid suture surgery done through plastic surgery.
Several houses were buried by the landslide.
In large organizations, an individual's talent can easily get lost.
en.notes: 埋没する literally means "to be buried, to be covered" (土砂に埋没する) and figuratively "to sink into obscurity, to go unnoticed": 才能が埋没する, 個性が埋没する. More rarely it means "to immerse oneself in something" (研究に埋没する), for which 没頭する is usually used. In medicine there is 埋没法 or 埋没手術 for eyelid fold surgery with sutures, and 埋没歯 "impacted tooth". It is literary and intransitive.

examples[].german: Bears are appearing in large numbers all over Japan.
In this area, raccoon dogs show up at night.
A suspicious person has been hanging around the station area, so please be careful.
en.notes: 出没する means "to turn up (again and again), to be seen prowling", literally "to appear and disappear". It is used for animals or unwanted persons: クマが出没する, 不審者が出没する; the place is marked with に. Very well known are warning signs such as クマ出没注意 or 痴漢出没注意. For a one-time appearance one says 現れる; 出没 emphasizes repeated, unpredictable appearances.

examples[].german: My uncle is a hunter.
This restaurant serves venison shot by a local hunter.
In winter, the hunters head into the mountains to hunt.
en.notes: 猟師 is a hunter, especially someone who hunts professionally or traditionally: 猟に出る, 猟銃, 猟師が仕留める "to bring down". Caution: 漁師 "fisherman" is also read りょうし - only the kanji differs (猟 with the animal radical, 漁 with the water radical). In official usage it is 狩猟者, colloquially also ハンター. The traditional mountain hunters of northern Japan are called マタギ.

examples[].german: Hunting this bird is prohibited.
You need a license to hunt.
Humans lived by hunting and gathering for a long time.
en.notes: 狩猟 is hunting as an activity, often in a legal or scientific context: 狩猟免許 "hunting license", 狩猟期間 "hunting season", 狩猟禁止, 狩猟採集 "hunting and gathering". The verb 狩猟する is rather formal; in everyday speech one says 狩りをする or 猟をする. For the person one says 猟師 or 狩猟者.

examples[].german: It is generally said that hunting dogs bark a lot.
My grandfather goes into the mountains every morning with his hunting dog.
The beagle is a breed originally developed as a hunting dog for rabbit hunting.
en.notes: 猟犬 is a hunting dog, that is, a dog bred or trained for hunting: 猟犬を連れる, 猟犬として飼う. Many well-known breeds such as the beagle or retriever were originally 猟犬. Figuratively 猟犬 can also refer to a tenacious pursuer, such as an investigator (権力の猟犬). The general 犬 or 飼い犬 does not have this function; a police sniffer dog is called 警察犬.

en.meaning: origin; birthplace (of a custom, sport, etc.)
examples[].german: Dekopon is a mandarin variety that originated in Japan.
Judo originated in Japan and is now practiced all over the world.
The Yellow River basin is regarded as the cradle of Chinese civilization.
en.notes: 発祥 means "origin, emergence" and is mostly used as a noun: 〜発祥の地 "birthplace of ...", 日本発祥の〜 "originating in Japan". As a する-verb it is intransitive: 〜で発祥した. 起源 is more general and scientific (生命の起源), 由来 explains the origin of a name, and 原産 the native region of plants and animals. 発祥 fits especially culture, sports, foods and civilizations.

examples[].german: The police are trying to cover up their own scandal.
The company president resigned, taking responsibility for an employee's misconduct.
Scandals involving players have been occurring one after another at that baseball club recently.
en.notes: 不祥事 refers to embarrassing, reputation-damaging misconduct within an organization, such as embezzlement, data falsification or harassment. Typical are 不祥事を起こす, 不祥事が相次ぐ, 不祥事を隠蔽する and 不祥事の責任を取って辞任する. Unlike スキャンダル, which often concerns the private lives of celebrities, 不祥事 is mostly used for companies, government offices, the police and sports clubs. Neutral to formal, a typical news word.

examples[].german: We have ample food reserves.
Many people in the world are still suffering from food shortages.
Food and water were delivered to the disaster area by helicopter.
en.notes: 食糧 refers to food as a supply good, especially staples such as rice and wheat: 食糧不足, 食糧危機, 食糧援助, 食糧を備蓄する. 食料 is more general and covers all foodstuffs including meat and vegetables (食料品店). In politics and disaster management one often reads 食糧; the difference is fluid, however, and authorities today mostly write 食料 (食料自給率).

examples[].german: A suspect in war crimes was indicted by the International Criminal Court.
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the president of a country.
Unlike the International Court of Justice, which handles disputes between states, the International Criminal Court tries the crimes of individuals.
en.notes: 国際刑事裁判所 (ICC) is a permanent court in The Hague that prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. In contrast, the 国際司法裁判所 decides disputes between states. Typical: 国際刑事裁判所に起訴される, 〜が逮捕状を出す. 刑事 here means "criminal" (cf. 刑事裁判 "criminal trial").

en.meaning: to swell; to bulge; to sulk
examples[].german: I ate too much and my stomach is swollen tight.
When you grill rice cake, it puffs up.
When she is scolded, my daughter immediately starts to sulk.
en.notes: 膨れる is intransitive and means "to swell, to puff up": お腹が膨れる, 餅が膨れる, 費用が膨れる (intensified: 膨れ上がる). The transitive counterpart is 膨らます / 膨らませる. 膨らむ is very similar but sounds more neutral and is also used positively (夢が膨らむ, つぼみが膨らむ). Second meaning: "to sulk", mostly in kana: ふくれる, ふくれっ面.

examples[].german: The universe is expanding.
Metal expands when heat is applied.
Ballooning defense spending is putting pressure on the nation's finances.
en.notes: 膨張 is the technical word for expanding and growing, mainly in physics (熱膨張, 気体が膨張する) and astronomy (宇宙の膨張), and figuratively also for budgets, cities or populations: 予算が膨張する "the budget balloons". As a する-verb it is intransitive; the opposite is 収縮. The older spelling 膨脹 is still found in specialist texts. In everyday speech, for balloons, bellies or dough one more often says 膨らむ.

examples[].german: After a bath, I enjoy the scent of aroma oil.
I put a new air freshener in the toilet.
The roses in the garden give off a sweet fragrance.
en.notes: 芳香 is a pleasant scent, a fragrance, and sounds literary: 芳香を放つ "to give off a fragrance", 甘い芳香. Very everyday, however, is the compound 芳香剤 "room fragrance, air freshener"; in chemistry 芳香族 means "aromatic". Otherwise in everyday speech one says 香り or いい匂い; 臭い is a bad smell. Do not confuse it with the identically read 方向 "direction".

examples[].german: The scent of plum blossoms is wonderfully fragrant in this season, isn't it?
Since sales are not good, we decided to review our sales strategy.
Since the surgery, my father's health has not been very good.
en.notes: 芳しい has two meanings. Literally "fragrant, sweet-smelling" it is literary (芳しい花の香り); for the roasted aroma of coffee or grilled food, 香ばしい (こうばしい) is used instead. Much more common is the figurative meaning "good, favorable", almost always negated: 芳しくない "not good, unsatisfactory" for results, reputation or health (成績が芳しくない, 芳しくない評判).

examples[].german: My son lacks drive even though he is young.
The new captain has spirit and is leading the team firmly.
The interviewer said, "I would like you to show more drive."
en.notes: 覇気 is drive, vigor and ambition with which someone wants to achieve something. It almost always appears in 覇気がある / 覇気がない or 覇気のない顔 / 声. やる気 is more everyday and means motivation for a concrete task, 野心 is ambition with an often negative connotation, and 意欲 is neutral drive. Manga fans know the word from One Piece as "Haki".

examples[].german: Our school's baseball team won the autumn league.
This team's goal is to win the national championship.
I have already conquered every ramen shop in front of the station.
en.notes: 制覇する means "to conquer, to dominate" and, in sports, "to take the title, to win a tournament": 〜を制覇する, 全国制覇, 世界制覇. Unlike 優勝する, 制覇 emphasizes complete dominance and sounds more forceful. Used casually it also means "to tick everything off, to try them all": 駅前のラーメン屋を全店制覇した. Winning titles in succession is 連覇.

examples[].german: Those guys are last year's champions of this tournament.
The one who ultimately came out on top in the Warring States period was Tokugawa Ieyasu.
This year's marathon winner was an unknown university student.
en.notes: 覇者 was originally a ruler who rules by power and force, as opposed to the virtuous 王者. Today it mostly means "winner, title holder" of a competition: 大会の覇者, 前年度の覇者 "defending champion", 世界の覇者. It sounds somewhat elevated and is often used in sports reports; more neutral are 優勝者 and 王者 or チャンピオン.

en.meaning: consecutive titles; title defense; winning back-to-back
examples[].german: Has there ever been a high school that won Koshien three times in a row?
She finally achieved her fifth consecutive title at this tournament.
The champion team lost in the final and missed out on a repeat title.
en.notes: 連覇 means "consecutive title wins" and often appears with a number: 二連覇, 三連覇, 大会五連覇. Typical combinations are 連覇を達成する, 連覇を狙う and 連覇を逃す "to miss out on defending the title". As a する-verb, the competition can take を (甲子園を三連覇する). It is a term from sports and competitions; a single win is 優勝 or 制覇.

examples[].german: I ordered just one piece of the finest fatty tuna.
He has consistently opposed the plan from the very beginning.
My daughter attends an integrated middle and high school.
en.notes: 一貫 has several meanings. The most important is "consistency, coherence": 一貫して "throughout, consistently", 一貫した態度, 一貫性 "consistency", 中高一貫校 "school with integrated middle and high school". In a sushi restaurant, 貫 is the counter for nigiri pieces: 一貫, 二貫. The old unit of weight 貫 (about 3.75 kg) now appears only in set expressions.

en.meaning: penetration; to pierce; to go through
examples[].german: The wire in my bra protected me from the bullet penetrating.
After years of construction work, the tunnel was finally broken through.
The nail went through the board and sticks out on the back.
en.notes: 貫通する means "to penetrate, to pierce, to go all the way through" and can be intransitive (弾丸が貫通する) or transitive (弾丸が壁を貫通する). Typical subjects are bullets, nails and tunnels: トンネルが貫通する refers to the breakthrough in tunnel construction. The native verb 貫く is similar but is also used figuratively (信念を貫く); 貫通, by contrast, stays concrete and sounds technical.

examples[].german: The application procedure for refugee recognition was simplified.
Japan is criticized for its low refugee recognition rate.
He was not recognized as a refugee, but was permitted to stay on humanitarian grounds.
en.notes: 難民認定 is the official recognition as a refugee under the Geneva Refugee Convention; in Japan the immigration authority (入管) decides. Typical: 難民認定を申請する, 難民認定される, 難民認定率 "recognition rate". Those who are rejected can still receive a residence permit on humanitarian grounds (在留特別許可). Political asylum in the narrow sense is called 亡命; in the Japanese procedure, 難民認定 is the technical term.

en.meaning: to carry through; to see through to the end; accomplishment
examples[].german: It was hard, but we were able to carry out the plan we all decided on.
I will stay true to my original resolve and keep going without giving up until the end.
The labor union pushed its wage demand through to the end.
en.notes: 貫徹する means "to carry through to the end" a plan, a demand or a will: 計画を貫徹する, 要求を貫徹する. Very well known is the four-character phrase 初志貫徹 "to stay true to one's original resolve". It sounds formal and determined; more everyday are やり遂げる and 貫く. Do not confuse it with the identically read slang word 完徹 "to pull an all-nighter".

en.meaning: all-out rush; crash job; hasty work
examples[].german: We built the doghouse in a rush job.
To make it in time for the opening ceremony, the venue was finished at breakneck speed.
I crammed the night before the exam, but I hardly remember anything.
en.notes: 突貫 was originally a charge with battle cries (obsolete, military). Today it appears almost only in 突貫工事 "construction work at breakneck speed" and, figuratively, for any rushed effort under time pressure: 突貫で仕上げる, 突貫作業. It often implies that quality may suffer. As a する-verb (突貫する) it is rare.

en.meaning: treatment; handling (of a person); terms of employment
examples[].german: We have to think about how to deal with the employee who committed misconduct.
Improvement of care workers' pay and working conditions is strongly demanded.
Not receiving treatment commensurate with his abilities, he decided to change jobs.
en.notes: 処遇 is the treatment of a person by an organization - above all status, pay and working conditions, but also the decision on how to deal with someone (e.g. after misconduct). Common are 処遇改善 "improvement of pay and conditions" and 処遇を決める / 検討する. 待遇 is very similar but more everyday (待遇がいい会社); 処分 is disciplinary punishment. As a verb 処遇する is rare.

en.meaning: encounter; to run into; to come across
examples[].german: I witnessed a terrible traffic accident.
I encountered a wild bear on a mountain path.
I ran into unexpected trouble while traveling abroad.
en.notes: 遭遇する means "to encounter (unexpectedly), to come across, to run into" and takes に: 事故に遭遇する, トラブルに遭遇する, クマに遭遇する. It is mostly about unplanned, often unpleasant or unusual encounters; also well known is 未知との遭遇 ("Close Encounters"). It sounds more formal than 出会う or 出くわす; for misfortune alone one also says 遭う. 遭遇 does not fit arranged meetings.

en.meaning: treatment; working conditions; pay and benefits
examples[].german: Thanks to this card, I was able to enjoy VIP treatment.
This company pays well and gives a lot of time off, so I am satisfied with the conditions.
The part-time workers are demanding improved working conditions.
en.notes: 待遇 has two main meanings: the way one treats or receives someone (VIP待遇, 特別待遇, 客の待遇), and the working conditions including pay at a company (待遇がいい会社, 待遇改善を求める). In job ads, 待遇 stands for salary and benefits. As a verb 待遇する is rare; one rather says 扱う or もてなす. Counterparts are 冷遇 "poor treatment" and 厚遇 "very good treatment".

examples[].german: Aren't the elderly being favored a bit too much?
This company gives preference to people who can speak English.
Under the new system, households raising children are given preferential tax treatment.
en.notes: 優遇する means "to give preferential, especially good treatment": 高齢者を優遇する, 経験者を優遇する. It is very common in job ads (経験者優遇 "experienced applicants preferred") and in tax and official language: 税制上の優遇措置 "tax incentives", 優遇金利 "preferential interest rate". The opposite is 冷遇 "to treat poorly"; 厚遇 is very similar but emphasizes generous pay or hospitality. Transitive with を, often in the passive 優遇される.

examples[].german: He is capable, so why is he being treated so poorly?
Because he had defied his boss, he was sidelined at a provincial branch.
The painter was neglected during his lifetime but highly appreciated after his death.
en.notes: 冷遇 means to treat someone coolly, dismissively or below their worth - for example an employee who is passed over or sidelined despite performance. It most often appears in the passive: 会社で冷遇される "to be treated poorly at the company". The opposites are 厚遇 and 優遇 "preferential treatment". The word is rather literary; in conversation one also says 冷たくされる or 冷たい扱いを受ける.

examples[].german: Don't blame your misfortune on your circumstances.
She grew up in disadvantaged circumstances, yet became a doctor.
Talking with people in the same situation makes me feel better.
en.notes: 境遇 refers to the circumstances of life into which one is born or has fallen - family, background, economic situation. Typical are 恵まれた境遇 "privileged circumstances", 恵まれない境遇, 苦しい境遇 and 同じ境遇の人 "people in the same situation". Unlike 環境 "surroundings, environment", 境遇 refers to one's personal lot; 状況, by contrast, is a momentary situation. Rather elevated, but also common in conversation.

en.meaning: to suffer; to meet with; to encounter (misfortune)
examples[].german: Have you ever experienced blatant racial discrimination?
On the way home I was suddenly caught in the rain and got soaked.
My grandmother almost fell victim to a scam over the phone.
en.notes: 遭う means "to experience (something unpleasant), to get caught in something" and takes に: 事故に遭う, 雨に遭う, 詐欺に遭う, ひどい目に遭う "to go through something terrible". It is a special spelling of 会う: for meeting people one writes 会う, for accidents, bad weather and crimes 遭う. In everyday writing it is often simply written in hiragana あう. The verb is intransitive and has no transitive counterpart.

en.meaning: mishap in the mountains or at sea; distress; to be stranded
examples[].german: We nearly got into serious trouble.
The mountain climbers who got into distress in the winter mountains were rescued after three days.
A fishing boat got into distress in the storm, and the Japan Coast Guard is searching for it.
en.notes: 遭難 means to get into mortal danger or have an accident in the mountains or at sea - through bad weather, avalanches, shipwreck, or because one has lost one's way. Typical: 山で遭難する, 冬山で遭難した登山者, 遭難者 "victim, person in distress", 遭難信号 "distress signal". For traffic accidents one says 事故; 遭難 emphasizes that one is stranded and must be rescued. Intransitive する-verb, with the subject marked by が.

examples[].german: Illegal residents were deported.
The prolonged detention of foreigners who refuse deportation has become a problem.
He was deported and cannot enter Japan for five years.
en.notes: 強制送還 (強制 "compulsion" + 送還 "sending back") is the forced removal of foreigners to their home country. Legally the procedure is called 退去強制; 強制送還 is the expression usual in the press and everyday speech. Mostly passive: 強制送還される; typical combinations: 不法滞在で強制送還される, 強制送還を拒む. When someone leaves voluntarily after a violation, one speaks of 出国命令.

examples[].german: When was Japan in isolation?
Triggered by Perry's arrival, Japan ended its isolation and opened the country.
Not hiring a single foreigner - this company is practically in a state of isolation.
en.notes: 鎖国 refers to a country's closure to the outside, above all Japan's isolation policy under the Tokugawa shogunate (c. 1639-1854). Typical phrases: 鎖国政策, 鎖国を解く, 鎖国していた時代. The opposite is 開国 "opening of the country". Figuratively it is also used to criticize present-day insularity, e.g. 鎖国状態 or 鎖国的な考え方.

examples[].german: The bank collapsed, and my deposits were frozen.
Part of the expressway is closed because of an accident.
To catch the culprit, the police sealed off all the station exits.
en.notes: 封鎖 means to completely block an access, an area or assets: 道路を封鎖する, 港を封鎖する "to blockade a port", 現場が封鎖される, 預金封鎖 "freezing of bank deposits". Unlike 閉鎖 "closure (of a facility)", 封鎖 emphasizes the sealing off, often by police, military or authorities. Also common are 都市封鎖 "lockdown" (often ロックダウン) and 経済封鎖 "economic blockade".

examples[].german: This pool will be closed at the end of this month.
With the flu spreading, my son's class was closed.
That village is closed-minded, and outsiders are hardly accepted.
en.notes: 閉鎖 is the usually longer-term or final closure of a facility or an access: 工場を閉鎖する, 店舗の閉鎖, 学級閉鎖 "closure of a school class (e.g. because of the flu)". For the daily closing of a shop one says 閉める or 閉店; 閉鎖 sounds official. The adjective 閉鎖的 means "closed, insular" (閉鎖的な村). Compare 封鎖 "sealing off, blockade".

examples[].german: First of all, we need to break this negative chain.
It is said that humans are at the top of the food chain.
One company's bankruptcy set off a chain reaction, and its business partners went under one after another.
en.notes: 連鎖 is a chain of connected things or events in which one triggers the next. Frequent in compounds: 連鎖反応 "chain reaction", 食物連鎖 "food chain", 連鎖倒産 "chain bankruptcies", 負の連鎖 "vicious cycle". As a verb 連鎖する is intransitive. For a physical metal chain one says 鎖 or チェーン, not 連鎖.

examples[].german: I hear the road over there caved in because of the earthquake.
A water main burst and the road collapsed, and a car fell into the hole.
He fell and hit his head hard, and his skull was depressed.
en.notes: 陥没 refers to a surface sinking or caving in downward: 道路が陥没する, 地面の陥没, 陥没骨折 "depressed fracture". It is an intransitive する-verb with the ground or road as the subject (with が). Unlike 崩壊 or 倒壊 "collapse of a building", 陥没 is about sagging into the depths. Typical of news and technical texts.

en.meaning: fall (of a fortress or city); capitulation; dropping from the top
examples[].german: Why do you think Toyota fell from the number one spot in the world?
After fierce attacks, the castle finally fell.
After being asked many times, my father finally gave in too.
en.notes: 陥落 has several meanings: the fall of a fortress or city (首都が陥落する, 城が陥落した), the drop from a top position (首位から陥落する) and, more rarely, the sinking of the ground. Colloquially it also means "to let oneself be persuaded, to give in". It is intransitive; transitively one says 攻め落とす "to capture". Rather news, history and sports language.

examples[].german: Consumers have pointed out safety defects in this product.
A defect was found in the brakes, so the cars are going to be recalled.
Rain leaking into a brand-new house - that's a defective house.
en.notes: 欠陥 is a fundamental, often dangerous flaw in a product, building, system or plan: 欠陥商品, 欠陥住宅, 制度の欠陥, 欠陥が見つかる. It is stronger than 欠点 "weakness, drawback" and more technical than ミス. Applied to people, 欠陥 sounds very disparaging (人格的な欠陥). Related: 不具合 "malfunction, glitch", which sounds milder.

examples[].german: By default, entering your name, date of birth and e-mail address is required.
A driver's license is required for this job.
If you climb in the mountains in winter, cold-weather gear is a must.
en.notes: 必須 means "absolutely necessary, mandatory". It is most often used predicatively (〜が必須だ) or with の before a noun: 必須の条件, 必須科目 "required subject", 必須項目 "required field" in forms; the form 必須な is rarer. It is stronger than 必要 "necessary": one cannot do without it. Reading ひっす, not ひつす; the opposite is 任意 "optional".

examples[].german: Akane quickly wiped away her tears.
Please blanch the spinach briefly in hot water.
When I opened the window, a cold breeze suddenly blew in.
en.notes: さっと describes a quick, deft action (さっと拭く, さっと片付ける, さっと茹でる "to blanch briefly") or a wind or rain that suddenly sets in (風がさっと吹く). The kanji spelling 颯と is rare and literary; さっと is normally written in hiragana. Similar is すっと "quietly, smoothly"; さっと stresses speed and lightness. In recipes, さっと means "just briefly".

examples[].german: I remember playing cat's cradle as a child.
My grandma taught me how to make the Tokyo Tower with string.
On rainy days, we played cat's cradle with friends in the classroom.
en.notes: あやとり is the string game in which a loop of knotted string is used to form figures between the fingers, played alone or by two people taking turns. You say あやとりをする or あやとりで遊ぶ; well-known figures include 東京タワー and ほうき "broom". The word is usually written in hiragana; 綾取り is the rarer kanji spelling. 綾 means "pattern", 取り means "taking".

examples[].german: Conservative forces called for the preservation of traditional values.
In the election, conservatives and progressives fought fiercely.
Due to elevator maintenance inspection, please use the stairs today.
en.notes: 保守 has two separate meanings. Politically it is "conservatism": 保守派, 保守政党, 保守系, 保守的 "conservative", with the opposite 革新 "progressive". Technically 保守 means "maintenance, upkeep" of facilities and systems: 保守点検, 保守管理, システムを保守する; here it is a transitive する-verb and corresponds to the loanword メンテナンス. 維持 is more general "maintaining".

examples[].german: The immigration control system was strengthened.
The Immigration Bureau was reorganized in 2019 into the Immigration Services Agency.
Because of the sharp rise in tourists, immigration control is short of staff.
en.notes: 入国管理 refers to the state control and administration of foreigners' entry and stay; the agency is called 入管 for short (officially 出入国在留管理庁 since 2019, previously 入国管理局). The actual passport check at the airport is called 入国審査, the customs check 税関. Typical: 入国管理体制, 入国管理の厳格化. A word of administrative and press language.

examples[].german: I'm not really a fan of shiso.
Green shiso leaves are laid under the sashimi.
Red shiso is used to dye umeboshi red.
en.notes: しそ is the herb perilla (shiso), whose aromatic leaves are common in Japanese cooking: green 青じそ with sashimi, tempura and noodles, and red 赤じそ for coloring umeboshi and for drinks. しそ is usually written in hiragana; 紫蘇 is seen more on labels. In supermarkets the green leaves are often called 大葉. The flavor is strong, so not everyone likes it.

examples[].german: My son is suffering from a skin disease.
The dog keeps scratching itself, so it may have a skin disease.
This skin disease isn't contagious, so please don't worry.
en.notes: 皮膚病 is the general term for skin diseases such as eczema, fungal infections or atopic dermatitis. Typical are 皮膚病にかかる, the more formal 皮膚病を患う, and 皮膚病が治る. In conversation people often say 皮膚の病気 too; the medical specialty is 皮膚科 "dermatology". The word is also used for pets: 犬の皮膚病.

examples[].german: There's foundation on your collar.
The wind was cold, so I kept my neck warm with a scarf.
Before the interview, I straightened my collar in the mirror.
en.notes: 襟元 is the area around the collar, i.e. the front of the neck, meaning both the clothing there and the skin beneath it. Typical: 襟元を正す "to straighten one's collar" (also figuratively "to pull oneself together"), 襟元が寒い, 襟元が汚れる. The collar alone as a part of a garment is called 襟 or カラー; 襟元 emphasizes the spot on the body. Neutral to slightly formal.

examples[].german: The girl wearing the pink scarf is my little sister.
Every winter, my grandmother knitted me a woolen scarf.
In old photos, my mother is wearing a fox-fur stole.
en.notes: 襟巻き is a scarf wrapped around the neck to keep warm. The word sounds a little old-fashioned today; in everyday speech people mostly say マフラー, and スカーフ or ストール for thin fashion scarves. Typical: 襟巻きをする, 襟巻きを巻く. A fur collar can also be called this, e.g. 狐の襟巻き "fox-fur stole". The spelling 襟巻 without き also occurs.

examples[].german: These are tomatoes that Grandma grew with devoted care.
This tea bowl was made by a craftsman with great devotion.
The roses I had raised with such care were all knocked down by the typhoon.
en.notes: 丹誠 means sincere, tireless effort and care. It almost always appears in the fixed phrase 丹誠を込める or 丹誠込めて "with one's whole heart", e.g. when raising vegetables and flowers or in craftwork. Today the spelling 丹精 is much more common; 丹誠 seems somewhat old-fashioned. Do not confuse it with 丹念 "careful, thorough", which describes the precise way of working.

examples[].german: The skilled dyer dyed each piece one by one with great care.
The detective examined the scene thoroughly and found a tiny piece of evidence.
Her paper is written on the basis of carefully collected materials.
en.notes: 丹念 is a な-adjective for a very careful, thorough way of working in which nothing is left out. It mostly appears adverbially: 丹念に調べる, 丹念に磨く, 丹念に読む. Similar are 念入り "thorough" and 丁寧 "careful, polite"; 丹念 sounds somewhat more elevated and stresses patient attention to detail. The related noun is 丹誠 "devoted effort".

examples[].german: Excessive packaging is a waste of paper.
Getting angry just because you were told off a little - that is an overreaction.
Parents' excessive expectations can become a burden for children.
en.notes: 過剰 means "too much, beyond the necessary measure" and is used as a noun, as a な-adjective and above all in compounds: 過剰包装, 過剰反応 "overreaction", 自信過剰 "overconfidence", 人員過剰. Before nouns it appears as 過剰な: 過剰な期待. The opposite is 不足 "shortage". Unlike 余剰 "surplus, remainder", 過剰 is clearly negative in tone.

examples[].german: I bought stocks with surplus funds.
To reduce surplus staff, the company called for early retirement.
Surplus electricity from solar power can be sold to the power company.
en.notes: 余剰 is a surplus, i.e. what is left over after needs are met. It almost always stands before another noun: 余剰資金, 余剰人員 "surplus staff", 余剰電力, 余剰生産物, or with の (余剰の米). There is no な-form. Unlike 過剰 "too much", 余剰 is factual and neutral and typical of economics and administration; in everyday speech people simply say 余り or 余分.

examples[].german: Land was expropriated for road construction.
Because of opposition from residents, the forced expropriation of land for the airport made slow progress.
The city expropriated the land and paid compensation to the owner.
en.notes: 収用 is the sovereign expropriation, especially of land for public projects against compensation (補償): 土地収用法, 土地を収用する, 強制収用. Transitive する-verb, often passive. Important is the homophone 収容 "to accommodate, house" (prisoners, injured people, refugees): 病院に収容される. In short: 収用 takes away property, 収容 puts people or things somewhere.

examples[].german: I once taught English in Pyongyang.
The news showed scenes of the streets of Pyongyang.
In the Sino-Japanese War, there was a major battle at Pyongyang.
en.notes: 平壌 is the capital of North Korea. Today it is read ピョンヤン; in the news this reading often appears as furigana, or the katakana spelling is used directly. The Sino-Japanese reading へいじょう appears only in historical contexts, such as the 平壌の戦い (へいじょうのたたかい) in the First Sino-Japanese War. Typical are 平壌市内 and 平壌からの報道.

examples[].german: This is the famous Supreme Commander, Marshal MacArthur.
Tōgō Heihachirō was later given the title of marshal.
Napoleon appointed many of his subordinates marshals.
en.notes: 元帥 is the highest military rank, e.g. "field marshal" in the army and "fleet admiral" in the navy (陸軍元帥, 海軍元帥). It is used like a title after the name: マッカーサー元帥, 東郷元帥. This rank no longer exists in Japan today, so the word appears mainly in historical texts and for foreign armies. Do not confuse it with 将軍 "general, shogun" or 総帥 "head of an organization".

en.meaning: supreme commander; leader; head of a conglomerate
examples[].german: That was an instruction directly from the head of the whole group.
In his thirties, he became the head of a huge corporate group.
The supreme commander of the enemy army offered to surrender.
en.notes: 総帥 is the supreme head of a large organization who directs everything: originally the commander-in-chief of an army, today mainly the head of a conglomerate or corporate group (グループの総帥, 財閥の総帥). It sounds weighty and is typical of business journalism. For an ordinary company head, people say 社長; 元帥, on the other hand, is a military rank. Hitler's title "Führer" is 総統 in Japanese, not 総帥.

examples[].german: Today at school, I learned about the Emperor's supreme command authority.
At that time, it was stipulated that the Emperor exercised supreme command over the army and navy.
The president holds supreme command of the military.
en.notes: 統帥 is military supreme command, i.e. the highest authority to command the armed forces. It is known mainly from history: under the Meiji Constitution, the 統帥権 "right of supreme command" lay with the Emperor, and the dispute over its independence from the government strengthened the military's influence. The word is formal and today appears almost only in historical or political texts. Compare 総帥 "head": that is the person, whereas 統帥 is the authority to command.

examples[].german: Please drive slowly near residential areas and schools.
Because of the heavy rain, trains are running at reduced speed.
When there is a slow-down sign, you must drive at a speed at which you can stop immediately.
en.notes: 徐行 means moving so slowly that you can stop immediately at any time. It is mainly traffic language: signs show 徐行, announcements and driving instructors say 徐行してください. Trains, too, run 徐行運転 during construction work or heavy rain. For pedestrians one does not say 徐行, but ゆっくり歩く. An intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: After the second term began, my grades gradually started to rise.
I've gradually gotten used to the new job.
After the operation, my father's strength is gradually recovering.
en.notes: 徐々 almost always appears as the adverb 徐々に "gradually, little by little": 徐々に慣れる, 徐々に回復する, 徐々に増える. It sounds somewhat more literary than だんだん and stresses a steady, slow change; 次第に is similar but even more formal. In conversation, だんだん or 少しずつ are more common. The forms 徐々と and 徐々たる are obsolete.

examples[].german: I want to avoid bringing about a disaster.
The driver falling asleep caused a terrible disaster.
Thanks to the smoke detector, a tragedy could be prevented.
en.notes: 惨事 is a terrible event with many victims or great destruction, such as a serious accident, fire or attack. The intensified form 大惨事 is very common: 大惨事になる, 大惨事を招く. Typical verbs are 起こる, 招く "to bring about" and 防ぐ "to prevent". Unlike 災害 "(natural) disaster", 惨事 stresses the gruesome occurrence; 惨状, on the other hand, is the terrible sight afterwards.

examples[].german: Japan was crushed at the World Cup.
The ruling party suffered a crushing defeat in this election, and the prime minister resigned.
I challenged my little brother at a game but lost 0 to 10.
en.notes: 惨敗 is a crushing, humiliating defeat, in sports, elections or exams. Typical: 〜に惨敗する "to lose by a landslide to ...", 選挙で惨敗する, and the formal 惨敗を喫する. The usual reading is ざんぱい; さんぱい also occurs. The opposite is 圧勝 "overwhelming victory"; an ordinary loss is 負ける or 敗北.

examples[].german: I cannot forget the devastation of the Great East Japan Earthquake.
The reporter told the world about the appalling conditions in the war zone.
The morning after the typhoon, the farmers were left speechless at the sight of their devastated fields.
en.notes: 惨状 is the horrific condition or sight after a disaster, war or accident: 被災地の惨状, 惨状を目の当たりにする "to see the misery with one's own eyes", 惨状を訴える. While 惨事 is the terrible event itself, 惨状 describes the situation one finds afterwards. The word is literary and typical of reports and news.

examples[].german: I performed magic tricks at the birthday party.
The groom's friend played the guitar at the wedding reception.
The singer performed her new song for the first time at the concert.
en.notes: 披露 means to show or perform something in front of others, or to announce it officially: 手品を披露する, 歌を披露する, 新作を披露する, 腕前を披露する "to show one's skill". Well known is 結婚披露宴 "wedding reception", where the couple is introduced to the guests. Unlike 発表 "announcement, presentation", 披露 often carries a sense of proudly showing off. Transitive する-verb with を.

examples[].german: Land use zones were designated under the City Planning Act.
The redevelopment in front of the station is proceeding in line with the city's urban plan.
I major in urban planning at university.
en.notes: 都市計画 is urban planning as a field and also the concrete plan of a municipality adopted by the authorities. Typical combinations: 都市計画を策定する "to draw up an urban plan", 都市計画決定 "plan decision", 都市計画道路 "planned (not yet built) road" and the 都市計画法 "City Planning Act". For community-oriented, rather informal urban development, one says まちづくり instead. Register: administrative and technical language.

en.meaning: to get caught; to be stuck between
examples[].german: You have asparagus stuck in your teeth.
My bag got caught in the train door.
Caught between my mother and my wife, I get no peace of mind any day.
en.notes: 挟まる means "to get between things, to be caught": 歯に何かが挟まる, ドアに指が挟まる. It is intransitive, with が for the thing caught and に for the place; the transitive partner is 挟む "to pinch, to put in between" (パンにハムを挟む). Figuratively, one can also be stuck between two parties: 母と妻の間に挟まる, often in the sense of an unpleasant mediator role (cf. 板挟み). A neutral everyday word.

en.meaning: to set; to install; to place (in a post)
examples[].german: I'm thinking of installing this machine in the factory soon.
The founder installed his son as the next president.
I intend to settle down and seriously commit to studying Japanese.
en.notes: 据える means to place something heavy or important firmly in a certain spot: 機械を据える, 墓石を据える. Figuratively, it means to install someone in a position (社長に据える "to make someone president") or to fix one's gaze firmly on something. Common phrases: 腰を据える "to settle down and devote oneself seriously and lastingly to something" and 腹を据える "to make up one's mind firmly". The intransitive counterpart is 据わる (目が据わる "to have a fixed stare").

examples[].german: At the motor show, each manufacturer unveiled cars equipped with the latest engines.
This smartphone is equipped with a high-performance camera.
An observation satellite was loaded onto the rocket and launched.
en.notes: 搭載 originally means to load cargo onto a ship or aircraft; today it mainly means to equip a device or vehicle with a function or component: カメラ機能を搭載する, ミサイルを搭載した艦. Typical patterns are X に Y を搭載する and Y 搭載の X "X equipped with Y" (AI搭載のスマホ). It sounds technical and is very common in advertising and news; in everyday speech people also say 付いている.

examples[].german: Let's make flowers bloom on the dead tree.
The city cut down a dead tree that looked about to fall in the typhoon.
In the winter park, bare trees that had shed their leaves stood in a row.
en.notes: 枯れ木 is a dead tree or a bare tree without leaves. Well known is the phrase 枯れ木に花を咲かせる from the fairy tale 花咲かじいさん, in which an old man makes dead trees bloom; figuratively it means "to revive something lost". The proverb 枯れ木も山の賑わい means "even something insignificant is better than nothing". The related verb is 枯れる "to wither, die".

en.meaning: to let wither; to kill (plants); to make hoarse
examples[].german: I watered the cactus too much and it died.
I sprayed weed killer and killed the weeds in the garden.
The cheering squad encouraged the players until their voices were hoarse.
en.notes: 枯らす is the transitive counterpart of 枯れる: you let plants die, usually by accident and therefore often in the form 枯らしてしまう. Typical: 植物を枯らす, 水やりを忘れて枯らす, 除草剤で雑草を枯らす. Rarely it also means "to let wood season". Figuratively, people say 声を枯らす "to shout oneself hoarse" (also written 嗄らす).

examples[].german: The soup is boiling and bubbling away.
Once the water boils, please add the pasta.
That remark set off a heated debate online.
en.notes: 沸騰 means "to boil, to come to a boil" and is the somewhat more formal word for 沸く: お湯が沸騰する, 沸騰したお湯. Figuratively it describes a heated mood (議論が沸騰する, 人気が沸騰する) or sharply rising prices (地価の沸騰). It is intransitive; transitively, say お湯を沸かす or 沸騰させる. Common in recipes: 沸騰したら火を弱める.

examples[].german: This incident will probably prompt the industry to clean up its own act.
Rivers have a self-purifying capacity, but it can't keep up if pollution is too heavy.
After a string of scandals, the organization's capacity for self-purification is being questioned.
en.notes: 自浄 is the ability to cleanse oneself by one's own power. It almost always appears in the compounds 自浄作用 "self-purifying action" (of rivers, the sea or the body) and 自浄能力: 川の自浄作用, 組織の自浄能力が問われる. Figuratively it concerns organizations that are supposed to remove abuses themselves. As a verb, 自浄する is rare; the word is formal and typical of news and commentary.

examples[].german: In India, the left hand is regarded as unclean, and people eat with the right hand.
Before entering a shrine, you cleanse your hands and mouth to wash away impurity.
My grandmother always called the toilet "gofujō".
en.notes: 不浄 means "unclean" in a religious or ritual sense and is used as a noun or with の/な: 不浄の手, 不浄なもの, 不浄を清める. In Shintō and Buddhism, the contrast 清浄 "pure" - 不浄 plays a large role. The polite, old-fashioned term ご不浄 means "toilet". For everyday dirt, say 汚い, not 不浄.

examples[].german: I was almost talked into buying a 300,000 yen water purifier.
The tap water in this town is river water that has been cleaned at a water purification plant.
When making tea, I use purified water instead of tap water.
en.notes: 浄水 is purified, clean water, mostly in the context of water treatment. It is common in compounds: 浄水器 "water filter", 浄水場 "water purification plant", 浄水処理 "water treatment". In everyday speech, for drinking water people tend to say きれいな水 or 水道水; 浄水 sounds technical. The opposite is 汚水 "sewage".

examples[].german: How do you clean your electric kettle?
For a wound from a fall, first rinse it well with water.
A man was arrested on suspicion of laundering money obtained through crime.
en.notes: 洗浄 is thorough cleaning with water or a cleaning agent, especially of devices, wounds and organs: 傷口を洗浄する, 胃洗浄 "stomach pumping", 洗浄剤 "cleaning agent", 温水洗浄便座 "bidet toilet seat". It sounds more technical than 洗う, which usually suffices in everyday speech. Figuratively there is 資金洗浄 "money laundering" (often マネーロンダリング). Transitive する-verb with を.

examples[].german: Why are mosquito coils spiral-shaped?
A large whirlpool has formed in the middle of the river, and it's dangerous.
I bought my daughter a candy with a swirl pattern.
en.notes: 渦巻き refers to a whirlpool or eddy of water and, in an extended sense, to any spiral shape: 渦巻き模様, 渦巻き状, 渦巻きパン. For whirlpools in the sea, people often simply say 渦 (鳴門の渦潮). The verb 渦巻く means "to swirl" and is also used figuratively: 不満が渦巻く "discontent is seething". The spelling 渦巻 also occurs alongside 渦巻き.

examples[].german: The food at this restaurant is a taste for connoisseurs.
His paintings are so skilled that you'd hardly think he's an amateur.
This is difficult work even for professionals.
en.notes: 玄人 is someone who masters a field professionally and with great skill, a pro or connoisseur. The counterpart is 素人 "layperson, amateur". Typical: 玄人はだし "(an amateur) so good that even professionals are astonished", 玄人好み "something for connoisseurs", 玄人向け. In the past, 玄人 also referred to women of the pleasure trade. In everyday speech, プロ is more common today.

examples[].german: I spilled coffee on my manuscript.
It doesn't look like my manuscript will be ready by the deadline.
I practiced so that I could give my speech without looking at the script.
en.notes: 原稿 is a manuscript or text that is to be published, read aloud or printed: 小説の原稿, 原稿を書く, 原稿の締め切り "deadline". The script of a speech or presentation is also called 原稿 (スピーチの原稿, 原稿を読み上げる). The classic Japanese writing paper with squares is called 原稿用紙. The fee for it is called 原稿料 or, in short, 稿料.

examples[].german: I posted photos of my dog on Facebook.
Inappropriate posts will be deleted by the administrators.
My grandfather used to send haiku to the newspaper.
en.notes: 投稿 was originally the sending of a contribution to a newspaper, magazine or radio program (新聞に投稿する, 投稿欄 "readers' letters column"); today it mainly means posting on social networks: SNSに写真を投稿する. As a する-verb it is transitive with を, and the destination is marked with に. The noun also refers to the post itself (投稿を削除する "to delete a post"). Colloquially, people also say アップする; 投稿 is the neutral standard word, also on buttons in apps.

examples[].german: It wasn't much, but I received a fee for my manuscript.
The fee for the essay I wrote for the magazine has been transferred.
In my younger days, I couldn't live on writing fees alone.
en.notes: 稿料 is the fee for a published text, such as an article, a column or a novel. The longer form 原稿料 is more common; 稿料 sounds terser and somewhat technical (publishing industry). Payment is often per manuscript page or per character: 一枚あたりの稿料. For royalties from book sales, on the other hand, people say 印税.

examples[].german: In theory, 45 degrees south latitude is said to be the midpoint between the South Pole and the equator.
Sydney is located at about 34 degrees south latitude.
If you mix up south and north latitude, you end up in a completely different place on the map.
en.notes: 南緯 is south latitude, i.e. how far a place lies south of the equator. Degrees are given with 度: 南緯30度, 南緯35度線. The counterpart is 北緯 "north latitude"; lines of longitude are called 東経 and 西経. The general term is 緯度 "latitude". Typical of geography, seafaring and the news.

examples[].german: Enoshima and the Greek island of Crete are at the same north latitude.
The Korean Peninsula is divided into north and south along the 38th parallel.
Tokyo is located at around 35 degrees north latitude and 139 degrees east longitude.
en.notes: 北緯 is north latitude, i.e. how far a place lies north of the equator: 北緯35度, 北緯38度線 "the 38th parallel" (the dividing line between North and South Korea). The counterpart is 南緯; together with 東経 "east longitude" it is used to give positions: 北緯35度、東経139度. Japan lies roughly between 20 and 45 degrees north latitude.

examples[].german: The parallel of latitude at 0 degrees is called the equator.
The horizontal lines on a map are parallels of latitude, and the vertical lines are meridians.
All parallels of latitude are drawn parallel to the equator.
en.notes: 緯線 are the parallels of latitude, i.e. the imaginary lines parallel to the equator on globes and maps. The counterpart is 経線 "meridians, lines of longitude"; together they are called 経緯線. Latitude as a numerical value is 緯度. The word belongs to geography and cartography; in everyday speech people more often say 〜度線, e.g. 38度線.

examples[].german: I use a synthetic-fiber broom for sweeping.
Clothes made of synthetic fiber easily build up static electricity in winter.
This shirt is synthetic, so it dries right away after washing.
en.notes: 化繊 is the short form of 化学繊維 "chemical fiber" and covers both fully synthetic fibers (合成繊維, short 合繊, e.g. polyester, nylon) and regenerated fibers such as viscose (レーヨン). The opposite is 天然繊維 such as 綿, 麻, ウール or 絹. In daily life it appears mainly on labels and in expressions like 化繊のシャツ, 化繊混 "with a synthetic fiber blend"; typical properties people talk about are 静電気 and quick drying.

examples[].german: With crude oil and naphtha prices down, the price of synthetic fibers is falling as well.
Polyester and nylon are typical synthetic fibers.
This factory produces synthetic yarn for clothing.
en.notes: 合繊 is the short form of 合成繊維 "synthetic fiber", i.e. fully synthetic fibers made from petroleum such as ポリエステル, ナイロン or アクリル. It is narrower than 化繊, which also includes regenerated fibers such as viscose. The word belongs more to business news and the technical language of the textile industry (合繊メーカー, 合繊の糸); in everyday speech people mostly say 化繊 or name the material directly.

examples[].german: A corrective order was issued for the building that violated the Building Standards Act.
With the 1981 amendment of the Building Standards Act, seismic standards became considerably stricter.
This extension requires a confirmation application under the Building Standards Act.
en.notes: 建築基準法 is Japan's central building law (1950). It sets minimum standards for earthquake safety, fire protection and building density (建ぺい率, 容積率). Typical combinations: 建築基準法に違反する／適合する, 建築基準法上の〜 "under the Building Standards Act", 建築基準法の改正. Among specialists also abbreviated 建基法; register: legal and technical language.

examples[].german: My mother kept nodding "uh-huh, uh-huh" as she listened.
The students nodded emphatically at the teacher's explanation.
When I asked, "Are you coming along?", my daughter nodded silently.
en.notes: うなずく means "to nod", usually as a sign of agreement or that one is listening: 黙ってうなずく, 大きくうなずく. The usual kanji spelling is 頷く; 肯く is a variant form, and in everyday writing people mostly use うなずく. The verb is intransitive; what one nods to is marked with に: 彼の意見にうなずく. Shaking the head to say no is 首を横に振る.

examples[].german: Don't sit around cross-legged in a place like this; get started on your work quickly.
If sitting formally on your knees is hard, cross-legged is fine too.
If you rest on your popularity, customers will quickly drift away.
en.notes: 胡座 is almost always written in kana, あぐら; the kanji are rarely seen. The accompanying verb is かく: あぐらをかく "to sit cross-legged". The counterpart is the formal kneeling position 正座; on casual occasions the host often says どうぞ、あぐらで. Figuratively, 〜にあぐらをかく means "to rest on one's laurels", e.g. on success or position, without making further effort.

examples[].german: I'm just not good with the fat on meat.
This steak has little fat and tastes light.
Please trim the fat from the pork before stir-frying it.
en.notes: 脂身 is the fatty part of meat, i.e. the fat edge and layers of fat, as opposed to 赤身 "lean meat". People say 脂身が多い・少ない, 脂身を取る・取り除く, 脂身が苦手. The kanji 脂 stands for animal or solid fat, 油 for liquid oil; hence also 脂がのった魚 "fatty, rich fish". With fish, however, people tend to say トロ or 脂, not 脂身.

examples[].german: This road hasn't been paved yet.
Starting next month, work to repave the road in front of the station will begin.
Beyond the village, an unpaved mountain road continued.
en.notes: 舗装 refers to surfacing a road or path with asphalt, concrete or paving stones, mostly asphalt. As a transitive する-verb (道路を舗装する), it very often appears in the passive or attributively: 舗装された道, 舗装道路; unpaved roads are called 未舗装の道 or 砂利道. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 包装 "packaging" (ほうそう).

en.meaning: head store; main shop; original shop
examples[].german: I always buy baby supplies at Akachan Honpo.
The shop sign says in large letters "Original Takoyaki Honpo".
I hear this Japanese sweet can only be bought at the main shop in Kyoto.
en.notes: 本舗 is the original shop of a manufacturer or retailer selling a particular product, and appears almost only as part of company and shop names: ○○本舗. It sounds traditional and advertises authenticity, similar to 元祖 "original"; for this reason modern chains also like to use the word. In ordinary speech, the main store of a chain is 本店, and a long-established shop is 老舗.

examples[].german: The navy's ships are short of crew.
A Maritime Self-Defense Force vessel entered port for resupply.
More than twenty naval vessels from various countries took part in the joint exercise.
en.notes: 艦艇 is a collective term for all ships of a navy, from large warships (艦) to small boats (艇), and belongs to the language of news and the military. It is counted with 隻. More specific are 軍艦 "warship", 戦艦 "battleship", 護衛艦 "destroyer" (of the Japanese Self-Defense Forces) and 潜水艦 "submarine". Beware of homophones: 首相官邸 "official residence" and 鑑定 "expert appraisal" are also read かんてい.

examples[].german: I made a big win at the boat races.
Going to the boat racing track on weekends is my father's only pleasure.
Part of the revenue from boat racing becomes funding for local governments.
en.notes: 競艇 is Japanese motorboat racing, on which one may bet under state license; like 競馬 (horse racing), 競輪 (track cycling) and オートレース, it is one of the 公営競技. For some years the official name has been ボートレース, but in everyday speech people still say 競艇. Related are 競艇場 "racecourse", 競艇選手 and 舟券 "betting slip". People say 競艇をする in the sense of "to bet on boat races".

examples[].german: I raised this bonsai from a sapling.
To commemorate our child's birth, we planted a cherry sapling in the garden.
At the tree-planting festival, each participant planted one sapling.
en.notes: 苗木 is a young tree or shrub for planting out, i.e. a "sapling, young plant" for woody plants. For vegetables, flowers and rice, people simply say 苗 (トマトの苗, 稲の苗). Typical verbs are 苗木を植える and 苗木を育てる; in spring there are 苗木市 "sapling markets" in many places. Someone who grows from seed says 種から育てる.

examples[].german: Today I made a strawberry seedbed with my husband.
I transplanted the tomato seedlings grown in the seedbed to the field.
I water every morning so the soil in the seedbed doesn't dry out.
en.notes: 苗床 is a seedbed in which seedlings are raised before being transplanted (植え替える) to the field or garden bed. So it is not the final vegetable bed, which is called 畑 or 花壇. Figuratively, 苗床 can also mean "breeding ground, hotbed"; for negative things such as crime, however, 温床 is the usual expression.

examples[].german: When it comes to the Tokugawa family crest, the "three-leaf hollyhock" is the most famous.
At Kyoto's Aoi Festival, the people in the procession wear hollyhock leaves.
Around the rainy season, hollyhocks begin to bloom by the roadside.
en.notes: 葵 refers to plants of the mallow family, in daily life mainly the hollyhock 立葵; in culture, however, the wild ginger フタバアオイ is usually meant, whose heart-shaped leaves appear in the Tokugawa crest (三つ葉葵, 葵の御紋) and at Kyoto's 葵祭.
