As a single word, 葵 is seen today mainly in these fixed expressions and as a popular given name (あおい). Note: ひまわり "sunflower" is written 向日葵, but botanically it does not belong here.

examples[].german: Environmental impact assessment is mandatory for large-scale developments.
An environmental impact assessment was carried out before the construction of the wind power plant.
The content of the environmental impact statement was explained at the residents' briefing.
en.notes: 環境影響評価 is the official term for environmental impact assessment, regulated in the 環境影響評価法 (1997). In the media and everyday speech one mostly says 環境アセスメント or briefly アセス. Typical combinations: 環境影響評価を実施する／行う, 環境影響評価の対象となる, 環境影響評価書 "environmental impact statement". Register: administrative and technical language.

examples[].german: This picture shows the scene at the time of the Mongol invasion.
The blue mark on a baby's bottom is called a Mongolian spot.
The Mongol cavalry armies ruled a wide area of the Eurasian continent.
en.notes: 蒙古 is the older designation for Mongolia and the Mongols, adopted from Chinese; the present-day state is called モンゴル (国). The word is alive mainly in historical terms such as 蒙古襲来 "the Mongol invasions of Japan (1274 and 1281)", also called 元寇, and in 蒙古斑 "Mongolian spot" on babies. Since 蒙 actually means "ignorant", the spelling is sometimes perceived as derogatory and replaced by モンゴル in neutral texts.

examples[].german: If you say the Nanjing Massacre was fabricated, please explain the evidence.
In the civil war, many civilians were massacred.
That film depicts a massacre that took place in a village.
en.notes: 虐殺 is the cruel, mostly mass killing of defenseless people, i.e. "massacre, slaughter". As a transitive する-verb, it is mostly used in the passive: 住民が虐殺された. Common combinations are 大虐殺, 大量虐殺 (also ジェノサイド) and 虐殺事件. More neutral for individual killings is 殺害, and more elevated and literary is 殺戮. The word belongs to history, politics and the news.

examples[].german: Children who have been abused often develop very low self-esteem.
Abusing pets is a crime.
A tip from a neighbor brought the child abuse to light.
en.notes: 虐待 is the continued mistreatment of a weaker person who cannot defend themselves. Typical are 児童虐待, 動物虐待, 高齢者虐待; people say 虐待を受ける "to be abused" or, as a transitive する-verb, 子どもを虐待する. To be distinguished from it are いじめ "bullying" among equals, DV "domestic violence" between partners and パワハラ at the workplace.

examples[].german: This is an extremely brutal crime.
This film has many cruel scenes, so it can't be shown to children.
This museum was created to convey the brutality of war to later generations.
en.notes: 残虐 is a な-adjective for acts that are deliberately cruel and inhuman: 残虐な犯行, 残虐な行為, 残虐な事件; the related noun is 残虐さ or 残虐性. It is narrower and stronger than 残酷, which also applies to a cruel fate or harsh truths (残酷な運命). 残忍 describes more the cold-hearted nature of a person. Register: news and written language.

examples[].german: Those people committed every atrocity imaginable.
The people could no longer bear the king's tyranny and rose up.
Under the brutal dictator, the people were deprived of freedom.
en.notes: 暴虐 refers to rough, cruel tyrannical rule, especially by rulers or occupiers, and can be used as a noun (王の暴虐) or as a な-adjective (暴虐な支配者). The fixed phrase 暴虐の限りを尽くす means "to commit every conceivable cruelty". The word is literary and historical; for a domineering boss in daily life, people say 横暴. Related is 残虐, which stresses the cruelty of individual acts.

examples[].german: That teacher is said to have married a former student.
She is a Japanese-language teacher at a prefectural high school.
I'm studying at university to obtain a primary school teaching license.
en.notes: 教諭 is the official job title for licensed teaching staff at schools: 小学校教諭, 高校教諭, 養護教諭 "school nurse". It is found in news (男性教諭), documents and résumés, never as a form of address; in conversation people say 先生. More general are 教師 (teacher as a profession) and 教員 (teaching staff, administrative language); at universities, teaching staff are called 教授 or 講師.

examples[].german: He succeeded in business and returned to his hometown in glory.
In autumn, the mountains are adorned with brocade-like autumn leaves.
Brocade woven with gold thread is used in this obi.
en.notes: 錦 is a splendid silk fabric patterned with gold and colored threads, i.e. brocade. More common than the fabric itself is the figurative use for something colorfully beautiful: 紅葉の錦 "brocade of autumn leaves", 錦鯉 "koi", 錦絵 "color woodblock print". The fixed phrase 故郷に錦を飾る means "to return home as a success", and 錦の御旗 (the imperial brocade banner) stands for an unassailable justification. Elevated, literary.

examples[].german: I released koi into the pond in my garden.
Niigata Prefecture is famous as a koi-producing region.
Some koi are traded for tens of millions of yen per fish.
en.notes: 錦鯉 is the koi, the colorfully bred ornamental carp; 錦 means "brocade". In biology it is written ニシキゴイ, and colloquially also 色鯉. Well-known varieties are 紅白 and 大正三色; Niigata Prefecture is regarded as the region of origin. Plain 鯉, on the other hand, usually means the dark edible or wild carp (真鯉). They are kept in a pond (池で飼う) and released into it (池に放つ).

examples[].german: This sushi restaurant has Japanese-style decorations placed throughout the interior.
Buildings from the Edo period remain in many places in this town.
In his paper, his own original touches can be seen throughout.
en.notes: 随所 means "in many places, scattered everywhere" and is used almost only adverbially: 随所に・随所で, often with 見られる, ある or 感じられる, and in reference to a whole: 町の随所に, 作品の随所に. It is written language; in conversation people say あちこちに or いたるところに. It usually does not mean "really everywhere" but that something turns up at many points within a space or text.

examples[].german: You did something quite bold, didn't you?
Your Japanese has gotten really good!
We walked quite a distance to the station.
en.notes: 随分 expresses that something clearly exceeds what was expected, often with a touch of surprise: ずいぶん寒いですね "it's pretty cold", ずいぶん待ちました "I waited a long time". It stands before adjectives, verbs and time or quantity expressions; ずいぶんと is equivalent. Compared with とても, ずいぶん sounds more subjective, and said about a person it can be reproachful: ずいぶんですね "that's rather harsh of you". Usually written in kana as ずいぶん.

examples[].german: I applied to the municipality for the issuance of a disaster victim certificate.
My house was half destroyed in the earthquake, so I went to city hall to get a disaster certificate.
A disaster victim certificate is required to receive the support payment.
en.notes: 罹災証明 is the municipality's official certificate of damage to a dwelling from an earthquake, flood, fire etc.; the degree of damage (全壊, 半壊 etc.) is determined in it. It is a prerequisite for relief payments, tax relief and emergency housing. One mostly speaks of the document, 罹災証明書; since 罹 is not a Jōyō kanji, authorities often write り災証明. 罹災 is the official word for "affected by a disaster"; in everyday speech one says 被災.

examples[].german: With overwhelming strength, this company let no other firm catch up.
When the big players cut prices, the small and medium-sized manufacturers immediately followed suit.
The government is criticized for merely following America's policy.
en.notes: 追随 means "to follow someone, to do as they do", often with the undertone of uncritical imitation: 〜に追随する, 対米追随 "following the US lead". Very common is the phrase 他の追随を許さない "to be unrivaled, to allow no competition" (in the sense of "catching up, drawing level"). It is an intransitive する-verb of written and business language. Similar, but with an undertone of flattery, is 追従.

examples[].german: Why are stock prices surging like this?
Because of the surge in crude oil prices, gasoline costs have gone up.
Vegetable prices have soared, and the household budget is tight.
en.notes: 高騰 is a sharp rise in prices and is used as an intransitive する-verb with prices, rates and costs as the subject: 物価・地価・原油価格が高騰する, 〜の高騰が続く. The word says nothing about speed; for a sudden jump use 急騰, and for an extreme rise that gets out of control use 暴騰. The opposite is 下落 or 暴落. Homophones are 口頭 "oral" and 高等 "higher".

examples[].german: Housing prices are skyrocketing.
After rumors of a takeover spread, the company's stock price skyrocketed in a single day.
In years of poor harvest, the price of rice has also skyrocketed.
en.notes: 暴騰 is the strongest of the words for price rises: an extreme, abrupt rise felt to be out of control. Like 高騰 and 急騰, it is an intransitive する-verb with prices as the subject (株価が暴騰する). It belongs mainly in stock market and business reports. The opposite 暴落 "price crash" is much more common than 暴騰 itself.

examples[].german: The dollar is surging again.
Following the announcement of a new product, the company's stock price surged.
When the news of the earthquake broke, the price of gold surged.
en.notes: 急騰 is a sudden, steep rise in prices or rates within a short time; it is an intransitive する-verb (株価が急騰する) and the counterpart of 急落 "sudden plunge". Unlike 高騰, which refers to a high rise in general, 急騰 stresses the speed; 暴騰 is even more extreme. Typical of stock market and foreign exchange reports.

examples[].german: The nishikigoi was bred from the red carp.
In the carp streamer song, the big black carp is the father and the small red carps are the children.
In the temple pond, red carp were swimming leisurely.
en.notes: 緋鯉 is a red to golden-colored carp; 緋 means "scarlet" (as in 緋色), and 鯉 becomes ごい through rendaku. It is regarded as a forerunner of the colorful 錦鯉. It is best known from the children's song "こいのぼり": the big black 真鯉 is the father, and the small 緋鯉 are the children; on carp streamers, the red carp therefore hangs below the black one.

examples[].german: I had a tattoo of a black carp done on my back.
The big black carp at the very top of the carp streamers is called magoi.
What I caught in the river was a dark-colored magoi.
en.notes: 真鯉 is the ordinary, dark-colored carp, as opposed to the colored 緋鯉 and 錦鯉; 真 here means "genuine, original", and 鯉 becomes ごい through rendaku. The word is best known from the carp streamers for Children's Day: the topmost big black carp is the 真鯉 and stands for the father. It does not mean the Chinese "black amur", which is called アオウオ in Japanese.

examples[].german: The king appeared riding his prized steed.
The sight of the fine horse galloping across the grassland was truly beautiful.
The warlord obtained a steed said to run a thousand ri a day.
en.notes: 駿馬 is a swift, noble horse and belongs to literary, historical or poetic language; besides しゅんめ, the reading しゅんば is also used. In daily life people say 速い馬 or 名馬 "famous, excellent horse". The opposite word is 駑馬 "nag". The character 駿 also appears in given names (駿) and, in the sense of "outstanding", in 俊才.

examples[].german: This ball is soft, so it can be used indoors too.
After the rain, the soil on the playing field has become soft.
For my grandmother, I cooked the rice a bit softer.
en.notes: 軟らかい is a spelling variant of やわらかい that, following the official recommendation, is chosen for the opposite of 硬い "hard, firm": 軟らかい土, 軟らかいご飯, 軟らかいボール. For softness in the sense of supple, gentle or flexible, one writes 柔らかい (柔らかい毛布, 柔らかい表情, 頭が柔らかい). In everyday life, 柔らかい is overall much more common; the character 軟 is known from 軟式, 軟水 and 柔軟.

examples[].german: A claim for state compensation was filed over the administration's unlawful act.
Former patients sued the state for state compensation.
Based on the State Redress Act, the court ordered the prefecture to pay about 5 million yen.
en.notes: 国家賠償 is the liability of the state and public bodies for damage unlawfully caused by public officials (国家賠償法, Art. 17 of the Constitution). Typical: 国家賠償を求める, 国家賠償請求訴訟 (short 国賠訴訟). To be distinguished from 損失補償: 賠償 compensates damage caused unlawfully, 補償 compensates for lawful interventions. Rarely also "war reparations" (for that, 戦争賠償 is more usual).

examples[].german: It's my first time at a public bathhouse.
We had no bath at home when I was a kid, so I went to the bathhouse every evening.
Recently, the neighborhood bathhouses are disappearing one after another.
en.notes: 風呂屋 is the colloquial, somewhat old-fashioned term for a public bathhouse; the neutral word is 銭湯. People say 風呂屋に行く or 風呂屋に通う. It is set apart from 温泉 (hot spring) and modern スーパー銭湯 by its simple neighborhood atmosphere. JMdict also lists the meaning "bathhouse operator", which is hardly used anymore.

examples[].german: I'm taking a course on medical ethics.
At university, I majored in ethics in the philosophy department.
Kant is an extremely important philosopher in the history of ethics.
en.notes: 倫理学 is ethics as an academic discipline, a branch of philosophy (哲学). To be distinguished from it are 倫理, morality or ethical norms themselves (企業倫理, 倫理観), and 道徳, everyday morality (also a school subject). Typical are 倫理学を専攻する, 倫理学の講義 and hyphenated ethics such as 生命倫理学 "bioethics" and 応用倫理学 "applied ethics".

examples[].german: Our company was chosen as one of the most ethical companies in the world.
Many people think animal testing raises ethical problems.
Even if it's not a problem legally, it's an act that is ethically unacceptable.
en.notes: 倫理的 is a な-adjective meaning "ethical, morally acceptable": 倫理的な問題, 倫理的な判断, adverbially 倫理的に問題がある. It is often contrasted with the legal: 法的には問題ないが、倫理的には.... 道徳的 emphasizes personal morality in everyday life more; the opposite is 非倫理的 "unethical".

examples[].german: You have a really biased way of thinking, you know.
I'm worried about an unbalanced diet, so I try to eat extra vegetables.
Because the respondents' ages are skewed, please treat this result as a rough guide only.
en.notes: 偏り is the noun for the intransitive verb 偏る "to be one-sided, to lean to one side" and refers to any kind of skew or imbalance: 栄養の偏り, 考え方の偏り, データの偏り. Typical frames are 〜に偏りがある・偏りが見られる and 偏りなく "evenly". For prejudice against people, 偏見 is the usual word, and for one-sided reporting 偏向.

examples[].german: Only the king may wear this crown.
The top part of 「花」 is called the "grass radical".
Because I stood her up, she is thoroughly annoyed.
en.notes: 冠 is primarily the crown or the traditional headgear of court officials and Shintō priests; for a royal crown, 王冠 is the more common word. In addition, 冠 denotes the kanji component at the top: 草冠 (くさかんむり), うかんむり. Colloquially, お冠 means "annoyed, in a bad mood". In the media, 冠 also denotes the sponsor's name in the title of a program or tournament (冠番組, 冠大会).

examples[].german: He fell in love and gave up the crown.
At the coronation, the crown was placed on the new king's head.
As a child, I collected the bottle caps from juice bottles.
en.notes: 王冠 is the crown of a king or queen, also as a symbol of royal dignity: 王冠を戴く, 王冠を捨てる "to renounce the throne". A second, everyday meaning is the crown cap of a bottle (ビールの王冠). More general and also used for court headwear is 冠; for victory in competitions people tend to speak of タイトル or 三冠 "Triple Crown".

examples[].german: He distinguished himself in both offense and defense.
The wrestler who defeated the yokozuna was awarded the Outstanding Performance Prize.
The rookie hit the game-turning decisive hit in the ninth inning.
en.notes: 殊勲 is an outstanding achievement or special merit, originally in war, today mainly in sports. Fixed combinations are 殊勲を立てる "to distinguish oneself by special service", 殊勲打 "decisive hit" in baseball, and 殊勲賞, the sumō prize for victories over yokozuna or ōzeki. More general is 功績 "merits", colloquially 手柄.

examples[].german: Why did you decline the decoration?
My grandfather received a decoration in recognition of his many years of service.
This scar is my badge of honor from the match where I gave it my all.
en.notes: 勲章 is a state decoration for merit, such as the 文化勲章 "Order of Culture". People say 勲章を授与する "to confer" and 勲章を受ける; receiving it is 受章 (not 受賞, which is for prizes), and the conferral as a whole is 叙勲. Figuratively, a scar or trace of hard work is jokingly called 名誉の勲章 "badge of honor". Sports medals, by contrast, are called メダル.

examples[].german: Could you also supply those goods to us wholesale?
This farm supplies vegetables wholesale to the local supermarkets.
Filleting a fish into three pieces is harder than I thought.
en.notes: 卸す means above all "to sell wholesale to retailers": 小売店に商品を卸す; related are 卸売り, 卸問屋 and 卸値. In the kitchen, おろす also means "to grate" (大根をおろす) and "to fillet a fish" (三枚におろす); for these one usually writes kana or 下ろす. Not to be confused with 下ろす "to take down, to withdraw money" and 降ろす "to let off".

examples[].german: Just compensation was paid for the expropriation of the land.
Compensation was paid to residents displaced by the road widening.
If you are going to ask businesses to close, you should consider compensation as part of the package.
en.notes: 損失補償 is the compensation the public authorities pay for lawful interventions that demand a special sacrifice from individuals, for instance with expropriation (土地収用) for road building (Art. 29 of the Constitution: 正当な補償). Typical: 損失補償を行う／受ける／求める. To be distinguished from 損害賠償 or 国家賠償, the damages for unlawful action. During the coronavirus period, 損失補償 for officially ordered business closures was much discussed.

examples[].german: I was able to buy it at the wholesale price.
Wholesale vegetable prices rose, and the prices in supermarkets went up too.
The retail price can be nearly double the wholesale price.
en.notes: 卸値 is the wholesale price, i.e. the price at which wholesalers sell to retailers. The contrasting terms are 小売価格 "retail price" and 定価 "list price"; from the retailer's point of view, the purchase price is 仕入れ値 and the manufacturing cost is 原価. Typical: 卸値で買う, 卸値が上がる・下がる.

examples[].german: I'm thinking of selling my autobiography as an e-book.
A retired actor published his autobiography.
Reading his autobiography, you can tell his life was full of hardship.
en.notes: 自叙伝 is an autobiography, i.e. one's own life story; the shorter 自伝 means the same and is more common in daily life. If someone else's life is described, it is 伝記, and for memories of particular periods people say 回顧録 "memoirs". Typical: 自叙伝を書く・出版する.

examples[].german: When I was a student, I was always doing stupid things.
There's no way something that silly could happen!
Forgetting your wallet at home, you really are a fool.
en.notes: 阿呆 "fool, idiot; stupid" is practically always written in kana, あほ or アホ; the full reading あほう sounds old-fashioned. It is typical of the Kansai region, where アホ comes across as teasing and friendly, while バカ sounds harsher there; in Tokyo it is the reverse. As a noun and な-adjective: アホなこと, アホみたい. Toward strangers it is rude and should be avoided.

en.meaning: to go senile; to be dazed; to play the fool
examples[].german: That comedian is really good at playing the fool.
Recently my grandfather seems to be getting a bit forgetful, and I'm worried.
Maybe my head is foggy from lack of sleep; I keep making the same mistake.
en.notes: 呆ける is mostly written in kana, ぼける, and is intransitive: "to become forgetful or senile with age", "to be mentally absent" and, in a manzai comedy duo, "to play the fool"; this role is called ボケ, and its counterpart ツッコミ. For dementia, ぼける is now regarded as slangy and insensitive; the neutral phrase is 認知症になる. Note: in 遊び呆ける, 呆ける is read ほうける, and for blurry photos ぼける is written with 暈ける.

examples[].german: All the wrongdoing he had been committing came to light.
This disaster exposed the weakness of the town's disaster-prevention system.
In the final, the team ended up exposing its lack of experience.
en.notes: 露呈 means that something hidden, mostly negative, comes out into the open: 弱点・問題点・矛盾・経験不足が露呈する. It is mainly intransitive, but can also be transitive with the party concerned as the subject: チームは弱さを露呈した "the team revealed its weakness". Unlike 暴露, where someone deliberately reveals something, 露呈 happens more by itself; 発覚 stresses the discovery of misdeeds. Colloquially people say バレる.

examples[].german: T-Points will be presented to blogs with many visitors.
Everyone who answers the survey will receive a small gift.
I presented one copy of my published book to the teacher who had helped me.
en.notes: 進呈 is the polite, slightly humble "presenting" of a gift from the giver's point of view. Today it appears mainly in advertising and campaigns: もれなく粗品を進呈, プレゼント進呈, ポイント進呈. More solemn and used for public ceremonies is 贈呈; in conversation people simply say 差し上げる or プレゼントする.

examples[].german: I presented a bouquet to my friend who played the lead role.
The winning team was presented with a trophy and prize money.
At the graduation ceremony, the graduates presented a commemorative gift to the school.
en.notes: 贈呈 is the formal presentation of a gift, prize or souvenir, typically at ceremonies: 花束贈呈, 記念品を贈呈する, 贈呈式. Compared with 進呈, it is more official and public. For donations to institutions people say 寄贈 (図書館に本を寄贈する), and for conferral by an authority 授与 (賞・学位を授与する).

examples[].german: Methods of infant feeding and care are changing greatly.
A panda mother carefully raises her newborn cubs one at a time.
Because the mother abandoned its care, the baby elephant was hand-reared by the keepers.
en.notes: 哺育 is the suckling and rearing of young, especially in animals, and belongs to the language of biology, zoos and specialist literature: 子を哺育する, 人工哺育 "bottle-rearing". The identically sounding 保育 "childcare" (保育園) is a different word; human breastfeeding is 授乳, and child-rearing in general is 育児. 哺 is known from 哺乳類 "mammals".

en.meaning: to spout out; to burst out
examples[].german: The anger I had been bottling up burst out all at once.
Bright red lava is spewing from the crater.
The moment I stepped outside, sweat poured out of my whole body.
en.notes: 噴き出す is intransitive and describes liquid, gas or lava shooting out under pressure: 温泉・溶岩・汗が噴き出す; figuratively also pent-up feelings or problems: 不満が噴き出す. For "to burst out laughing" it is usually written 吹き出す, and 吹き出す is often used as a variant in other cases too. The base verb is 噴く "to spew, to spray".

examples[].german: I spent my early childhood in an orphanage.
After the war, many war orphans were taken in by orphanages.
The protagonist of the novel is a girl who grew up in an orphanage.
en.notes: 孤児院 "orphanage" is an older term; in Japan, such facilities have officially been called 児童養護施設 since 1947 and also take in children whose parents are still alive. Today 孤児院 is used mainly in historical contexts, for facilities abroad or in novels. Related are 孤児 "orphan" and 戦災孤児 "war orphans".

examples[].german: Ministries were merged and abolished through administrative reform.
The new governor made administrative reform his top priority.
In the name of administrative reform, the number of staff was drastically cut.
en.notes: 行政改革 refers to the reform of public administration: merging agencies, cutting staff, more efficient procedures. In headlines often shortened to 行革. Typical combinations: 行政改革を進める／断行する, 行政改革担当大臣. To be distinguished from 規制改革 (reform of regulations) and 構造改革 (restructuring of entire economic and social structures). Register: political and media language.

examples[].german: Once upon a time, there was a priest who loved mizuame (malt syrup).
At the memorial service, the temple priest chanted the sutras for us.
Ikkyū-san, famous for his witty tales, was a priest of the Muromachi period.
en.notes: 和尚 is a Buddhist monk or priest, especially the head of a temple; in daily life people say respectfully 和尚さん or お坊さん. More official for the temple head is 住職, and for clergy in general 僧侶. Depending on the school, the word is also read わじょう (Shingon) or かしょう (Tendai). In folktales and anecdotes, the 和尚 is a stock character.

examples[].german: You have such refined hobbies.
What he said was far too highbrow, and I didn't understand it at all.
Not only high art, but manga and anime too are legitimate culture.
en.notes: 高尚 describes interests, art, topics or conversations as intellectually elevated and cultured: 高尚な趣味, 高尚な話題, 高尚な文学. It is a な-adjective and sounds elevated; often there is an undertone of irony or distance, as in 高尚すぎて分からない "too highbrow to understand". The opposite is 低俗 "vulgar, lowbrow". For a noble character, 高潔 or 気高い is more usual.

examples[].german: That's a story that has nothing to do with ordinary people like me.
With prices rising, the lives of ordinary people have become even harder.
This is a down-to-earth restaurant, and the prices are reasonable too.
en.notes: 庶民 are the common people, as opposed to the rich, the nobility or the powerful: 庶民の暮らし, 庶民感覚, 庶民の味. It is often used self-ironically: 私たち庶民には.... The derivative 庶民的 means "popular, down-to-earth, affordable" (庶民的な店). Related are 大衆 "the broad masses" and 一般人; 市民, on the other hand, stresses the role of citizen.

examples[].german: I'm going to be assigned to the General Affairs Section soon.
General affairs work includes managing supplies and sorting mail.
Please ask the person in charge of general affairs to book the meeting room.
en.notes: 庶務 refers to general administrative tasks not assigned to a specialist department: office supplies, mail, room bookings, documents. Typical are 庶務課, 庶務係 and 庶務担当. 総務 is the broader, higher-level area of "general affairs" (総務部), and 事務 is office work in general. The word is company and government language.

examples[].german: After retirement, I'd like to live a leisurely life in the countryside.
Even without running, you'll easily make the last train.
A large hawk is soaring leisurely through the sky.
en.notes: 悠々 (also 悠悠) describes calm, unhurried doing, and it mostly stands as 悠々と before the verb: 悠々と暮らす, 悠々と空を飛ぶ. Also very common is the meaning "with ease, with plenty of room to spare": 悠々間に合う "to make it easily in time", 悠々勝つ. Fixed phrase: 悠々自適 "a carefree, self-directed life (in retirement)". Unlike のんびり, 悠々 sounds more elevated and stresses composed calm.

examples[].german: Amid the timeless wonders of nature, I thought a great deal about life.
China has a history stretching back through the ages.
Over countless ages, the river carved out this deep valley.
en.notes: 悠久 means "eternal, continuing since time immemorial" and is an elevated, literary word. It almost always appears attributively with の: 悠久の歴史, 悠久の時, 悠久の大自然; the form 悠久な is possible but much rarer. It is typical in travel prose, speeches and texts about history and nature. In daily life people tend to say 永遠 "eternal" or 長い歴史.

examples[].german: We don't have time to talk so leisurely.
The deadline is tomorrow, yet he is taking it easy.
My grandfather is a person who speaks in an unhurried way.
en.notes: 悠長 means "leisurely, without hurry", but mostly has a critical undertone: one takes too much time although the situation is pressing. Very typical: 悠長なことを言っている場合ではない "this is no time to be talking so leisurely" and 悠長に構える "to wait calmly and composedly". Neutrally, it can describe a deliberate way of speaking (悠長な話し方). のんびり, by contrast, is mostly positive or neutral.

examples[].german: I sincerely apologize for saying such nonsense earlier.
Swimming in the sea on a typhoon day is the height of folly.
We must never repeat the same folly again.
en.notes: 愚 "folly, stupidity" is a written-language word that appears mainly in fixed expressions: 愚の骨頂 "the height of folly", 愚を犯す "to commit a folly", 同じ愚を繰り返す, 愚にもつかない "nonsensical, silly". The adjective "foolish" in present-day Japanese is normally 愚か(な); 愚な is rare and archaic. As a prefix, 愚 is used in humble language for one's own things: 愚見 "my humble opinion", 愚息 "my (unworthy) son".

examples[].german: I'm going to kidnap the president's son.
Cases of children being kidnapped are occurring one after another.
The kidnapper demanded a ransom.
en.notes: 誘拐する is transitive: 人を誘拐する "to kidnap someone", very often in the passive: 子どもが誘拐される. Related are 誘拐犯 "kidnapper", 誘拐事件 and 身代金 "ransom". For political or state abductions, 拉致 is used more, and for hijackings of aircraft ハイジャック. The word is neutral to news language.

examples[].german: A moderate lawmaker presented a compromise proposal.
He is known as a person of moderate views.
The government chose a more moderate reform plan.
en.notes: 穏健 is a な-adjective for "moderate, level-headed" and describes above all opinions, programs and political groups: 穏健な意見, 穏健な路線, 穏健派 "the moderates", as opposed to 強硬派 "hardliners" or 過激派 "radicals". For a calm temperament or mild weather, one says 穏やか instead, for a gentle character 温和. The word is elevated and typical of news and commentary.

examples[].german: The Regulatory Reform Council proposed measures to foster new industries.
The government is pushing regulatory reform toward lifting the ban on ridesharing.
Industry groups strongly oppose regulatory reform in the medical field.
en.notes: 規制改革 is the revision of government regulations to enable competition and new business models. It overlaps with 規制緩和 "deregulation, relaxation", but is broader and can also include new rules. Typical: 規制改革を推進する, 〜分野の規制改革, the government panel 規制改革推進会議. Register: political and business language.

examples[].german: The fruit of the ginkgo is called ginnan, and eating too much of it causes symptoms of poisoning.
In autumn, ginkgo leaves turn yellow.
A row of ginkgo trees continues in front of the university's main gate.
en.notes: 銀杏 read いちょう is the ginkgo tree; in everyday writing it is mostly written in kana (イチョウ, いちょう). The same characters read ぎんなん refer to the edible ginkgo nuts - a common source of confusion. Typical are 銀杏並木 "ginkgo avenue" and the yellow autumn foliage (銀杏の葉が黄色く色づく). The tree is, for example, a symbol of the city of Tokyo.

examples[].german: I'm growing tomatoes in my garden.
Tea cultivation is thriving in this region.
I only buy organically grown vegetables.
en.notes: 栽培 refers to the deliberate growing of plants, as a transitive する-verb: 野菜を栽培する. Common in compounds: 有機栽培 "organic farming", 水耕栽培 "hydroponics", 栽培が盛んだ "cultivation is widespread". More general and everyday is 育てる; for fish farming people say 養殖, and for keeping animals 飼育.

examples[].german: Please write your answer in the blank.
Please don't submit it with the blanks left empty.
Items that don't apply can be left blank.
en.notes: 空欄 is an empty field in a form, test or table. Typical: 空欄に記入する / 書き込む "to fill in the blank field", 空欄を埋める "to fill in the gaps", 空欄のまま "left blank". 空白 is more general (an empty spot, also figuratively: 記憶の空白), and 余白 is the free margin of a page.

examples[].german: My signature ran outside the box; is that okay?
The precautions are written in small print in the margin.
I jotted "needs checking" in the margin.
en.notes: 欄外 refers to the area outside a designated field or text block, i.e. the margin of a page or form. Typical: 欄外に書く / はみ出す, 欄外の注 "marginal note, footnote". Unlike 余白 "free margin, blank space", 欄外 stresses that something stands outside the actual field. It is a noun and is used with に or の.

examples[].german: There were many casualties in that plane crash.
We observed a moment of silence for the earthquake victims.
He too was a victim of bullying.
en.notes: 犠牲者 are victims, especially fatalities of accidents, disasters or wars: 犠牲者が出る, 犠牲者を悼む. Figuratively also for people who suffer from something (いじめの犠牲者). For those harmed by crimes or damage, who have often survived, 被害者 is the usual word; 死傷者 covers dead and injured. Related: 犠牲になる "to fall victim".

examples[].german: I'm sterilizing the baby bottle with boiling water.
The baby is drinking milk from a bottle.
The baby dislikes the bottle and won't drink.
en.notes: 哺乳瓶 is the baby bottle; also often written ほ乳瓶 or ほ乳びん. One drinks from it with で: 哺乳瓶でミルクを飲む; ミルク here usually means infant formula (粉ミルク), as opposed to 母乳 "breast milk". Typical collocations are 哺乳瓶を消毒する and 哺乳瓶を嫌がる "to refuse the bottle". The 哺乳 is also found in 哺乳類 "mammals".

examples[].german: Continuing such a pointless debate is a waste of time.
The speech was nothing but a string of empty words.
I was made to rewrite the report, which had little substance, over and over.
en.notes: 空疎 means "hollow, empty of content" and criticizes speeches, arguments or texts without substance: 空疎な議論, 空疎な言葉, 内容が空疎だ. It is written language and judgmental. Beware of confusion with 空虚: that describes more an inner emptiness or meaninglessness (空虚な気持ち), whereas 空疎 refers to lacking content. More neutral are 中身がない or 内容が薄い.

examples[].german: We had been evacuated to the countryside to avoid air raids.
During the war, children were sent to rural temples in a group evacuation.
My grandmother experienced the end of the war at her evacuation site.
en.notes: 疎開 refers above all to the evacuation of city dwellers to the countryside during World War II: 田舎へ疎開する, 学童疎開 / 集団疎開 "school-children's evacuation", 疎開先 "evacuation destination". For fleeing acute danger such as earthquakes or tsunami, people today say 避難. As a する-verb it is mostly intransitive, with へ/に for the destination; the military sense "to disperse troops" is rare.

examples[].german: I can't communicate with him at all.
We set up regular meetings to improve communication between bosses and subordinates.
Even though we didn't share a language, we managed to communicate somehow with gestures.
en.notes: 疎通 occurs almost only in the compound 意思疎通 or 意思の疎通 "mutual understanding": 意思疎通ができる, 意思の疎通を図る "to promote mutual understanding", 意思疎通が取れない. It sounds more formal than コミュニケーション or 話が通じる and is typical of the working world, nursing care and newspapers. The sense "unobstructed flow through" is technical and rare.

examples[].german: It's lively during the day, but at night foot traffic becomes sparse.
It was a weekday afternoon, so there were few customers.
Trees grow sparsely on the mountain slope.
en.notes: 疎ら "sparse, scattered" is mostly written in kana: まばら. It describes things or people that are widely spread out and unevenly distributed: 人通りがまばら, 客がまばら, まばらな拍手 "sparse applause", 木がまばらに生えている. Unlike 少ない, まばら stresses the loose, gappy distribution. Opposite: 密集した "densely packed".

examples[].german: Structural reform of the economy was made a pillar of the growth strategy.
The Koizumi cabinet advanced postal privatization under the banner of "structural reform without sacred cows".
The struggling company closed two factories as part of restructuring.
en.notes: 構造改革 means the thorough overhaul of economic or social structures; well known is the slogan 聖域なき構造改革 of the Koizumi government (2001-2006). At company level it means "restructuring" and is often a euphemism for plant closures and job cuts. Typical: 構造改革を断行する／進める, 構造改革特区. Broader than 行政改革 or 規制改革.

examples[].german: My younger sister has a mental illness.
People with heart conditions cannot ride this attraction.
In winter, the number of patients with respiratory diseases increases.
en.notes: 疾患 is the medical technical term for a disease, usually tied to an organ or area: 心疾患, 精神疾患, 呼吸器疾患, 心臓に疾患がある. In daily life people say 病気; 疾病, by contrast, is the administrative and statistical term (insurance, laws). 疾患を抱える "to suffer from a condition" is a common phrase.

examples[].german: The boy was sprinting at full speed through the station concourse.
A motorcycle raced off along the highway at night.
A horse galloping across the grassland is a beautiful sight.
en.notes: 疾走 is a written-language word for "to race, to run or drive at full speed". It is intransitive; the route is marked with を: 道を疾走する. Very common is 全力疾走 "to sprint with all one's strength". It suits people, animals and vehicles and feels more dynamic than 走る or 駆ける; colloquially people tend to say ダッシュする.

examples[].german: Cancer, acute myocardial infarction and stroke are called the three major diseases.
We are working on disease prevention and early detection.
The World Health Organization sets the international classification of diseases.
en.notes: 疾病 is the official or statistical umbrella term for diseases and appears in laws, insurance and statistics: 三大疾病, 疾病保険, 国際疾病分類 "ICD", 疾病の予防. In conversation people say 病気. 疾患, by contrast, is the clinical term for a specific organ disease (心疾患). The reading is しっぺい, not しつびょう.

en.meaning: tone-deafness; tone-deaf person; having no sense of (...)
examples[].german: I'm tone-deaf, so I'm bad at karaoke.
I have a terrible sense of direction and get lost easily.
I taught my father, who is hopeless with machines, how to use a smartphone.
en.notes: 音痴 first of all means "tone-deaf, singing off-key": 私は音痴だ, 音痴なので歌が苦手. As a suffix it denotes a lack of feel for a field: 方向音痴 "having no sense of direction", 機械音痴 "technically inept", 運動音痴 "unathletic". It is colloquial and often used self-ironically; said about others, it can be hurtful.

examples[].german: My grandmother's dementia has started.
The illness once called "chihō-shō" is now called "ninchi-shō".
In older medical books, the term "senile dementia" is often used.
en.notes: 痴呆 used to be the usual term for dementia (痴呆症, 老人性痴呆). Because it sounds derogatory ("idiocy"), it was officially replaced by 認知症 in 2004; today, 認知症 should be used in conversation and in texts. 痴呆 is still encountered in older books, quotations and some technical terms. It is a noun.

examples[].german: We arrested a groper this morning.
If you are groped on the train, please shout out loudly.
As a measure against gropers, there are women-only cars on the morning trains.
en.notes: 痴漢 refers to a man who sexually harasses women, above all by groping them on crowded trains, and also to the act itself (痴漢行為). Typical: 痴漢に遭う "to be groped", 痴漢をする, 痴漢対策, 痴漢冤罪 "false accusation of groping". More general is セクハラ for harassment at the workplace; 変質者 means a pervert in general.

examples[].german: Thousands of bottles of nail polish were lined up in the cupboard in no order at all.
Unplanned development of the suburbs has become a problem.
After the government collapsed, the country fell into a state of disorder.
en.notes: 無秩序 means "without order, chaotic" and works as a な-adjective or noun: 無秩序な開発 "unplanned development", 無秩序に並ぶ, 無秩序状態. It sounds factual and written, and often refers to society, urban planning or systems; for an untidy room people tend to say 散らかっている or ごちゃごちゃ. The opposite is 秩序正しい. Similar is 混乱 "confusion", which, however, describes more a process.

examples[].german: Silence, please.
The presiding judge called for order: "Silence!"
The ceremony venue was wrapped in a solemn, hushed atmosphere.
en.notes: 静粛 means "quiet and orderly" and is used almost only in formal requests: 静粛に願います / 静粛にお願いします at ceremonies, exams or in court; the judge calls 静粛に！ "Order in the court!". In daily life people simply say 静かに. 静粛 stresses appropriate, dignified silence, not merely the absence of noise.

examples[].german: He intends to starve them out by siege.
The siege dragged on, and the provisions inside the castle were running out.
As fuel for my exam studying, my mother made me onigiri.
en.notes: 兵糧 is the provisions of an army, a historical word from the time of the samurai wars. Well known is 兵糧攻め "siege by starvation": the enemy's supply is cut off. Another expression: 兵糧が尽きる "the provisions run out". Today it is also used jokingly for food during strenuous work; neutrally, people say 食料.

en.meaning: consolidation and abolition; merging and closing
examples[].german: Due to the declining birthrate, the consolidation of elementary schools is progressing.
The bank plans to merge or close about 30 branches by next year.
Because the hospitals were consolidated, there is no longer an emergency outpatient department nearby.
en.notes: 統廃合 combines 統合 "merging" and 廃止 "abolishing": facilities are brought together, with some closed altogether. Typical for schools, hospitals, bank branches and agencies: 〜の統廃合が進む, 〜を統廃合する (transitive する-verb). To be distinguished from 合併 "merger" (of companies or municipalities) and 統合 "integration" without closures. Register: administrative and news language.

examples[].german: I wiped the fingerprints off the doorknob clean.
The culprit's fingerprints were detected at the scene.
I unlock my smartphone with fingerprint authentication.
en.notes: 指紋 is the fingerprint. Typical combinations: 指紋を採る "to take fingerprints", 指紋が検出される, 指紋を拭き取る, 指紋認証 "fingerprint recognition". A fingerprint as a smudge on glass or a screen is also called 指紋 (画面に指紋がつく). For footprints people say 足跡.

examples[].german: The minister's careless remark caused a stir.
When I threw a stone into the pond, ripples spread over the water's surface.
The ruling sent big ripples through the industry.
en.notes: 波紋 are first of all the rings that spread across water (水面に波紋が広がる). Much more common is the figurative sense "repercussions, unrest", especially in the news: 発言が波紋を呼ぶ / 波紋を広げる "to make waves", 波紋が広がる. Unlike the neutral 影響 or the often positive 反響, 波紋 usually indicates controversy and agitation.

examples[].german: This is the royal family's coat of arms.
The chrysanthemum crest is the symbol of the Imperial Household.
A lion crest is depicted on the shield.
en.notes: 紋章 is a coat of arms or official emblem, for example of a royal house, noble family, state or city: 王家の紋章, 菊の紋章 (the crest of the Japanese Imperial House). The traditional Japanese family crest is usually called 家紋 or simply 紋; a school badge is 校章. 紋章 sounds somewhat more formal and is often used for European heraldry.

examples[].german: My family home is in Ibaraki Prefecture.
The prefectural capital of Ibaraki is Mito.
Ibaraki Prefecture is famous as a production area for natto.
en.notes: 茨城県 is a prefecture in the Kantō region northeast of Tokyo, with the capital 水戸. The correct reading is いばらき - the widespread pronunciation いばらぎ is considered wrong and annoys many locals. The prefecture is known for 納豆, the research city 筑波 (つくば) and the garden 偕楽園. The character 茨 means "thorn bush".

examples[].german: A tragedy took place in a mountain lodge cut off from the outside world.
In summer, we stay at the mountain villa as a family.
We held our seminar's training camp at the university's mountain lodge.
en.notes: 山荘 is a house or country residence in the mountains, often as a holiday home or as part of accommodation names (〜山荘). Unlike 山小屋, the simple hut for mountaineers, 山荘 sounds more comfortable and upscale. 別荘 is a holiday home in general, whether by the sea or in the mountains. In detective stories, 閉ざされた山荘 "the mountain lodge cut off from the outside world" is a classic motif.

examples[].german: I'm planning to sell my holiday home this spring.
He owns a holiday home in Karuizawa.
That guy is living in his "villa" now. I mean prison, of course.
en.notes: 別荘 is a holiday home or villa as a second residence, for example in resort areas such as 軽井沢: 別荘を持つ, 別荘を建てる, 別荘地 "vacation home area". Colloquially and jokingly, 別荘 also refers to prison ("to be at the holiday home" = to be locked up). A rented holiday home is often called 貸別荘; a house in the mountains can also be called 山荘.

examples[].german: Let's limit today's karaoke to Showa-era songs.
My grandfather still often hums old popular songs.
Many ancient songs are contained in the Kojiki.
en.notes: 歌謡 is an umbrella term for sung songs and mostly appears in compounds: 歌謡曲 "Japanese pop song (esp. of the Shōwa era)", 昭和歌謡, 歌謡番組 "music program", 古代歌謡 "ancient Japanese songs". On its own it sounds rather formal; in everyday speech one says 歌 or 曲. Cf. 民謡 "folk song" and 童謡 "children's song".

examples[].german: I learned a new children's song at kindergarten.
"Akatonbo" is one of Japan's most representative children's songs.
My mother often sang children's songs to me before bedtime.
en.notes: 童謡 are children's songs, especially the songs composed for children since the Taishō period, like 「赤とんぼ」 or 「ふるさと」: 童謡を歌う, 童謡を習う. Traditional play songs with no known composer are called わらべうた, and lullabies 子守歌. For songs at kindergarten, people in daily life also simply say 子どもの歌.

en.meaning: to carry through; to stick to
examples[].german: He stuck to his convictions to the very end.
My aunt remained single all her life, by choice.
The arrow that was shot pierced right through the thick board.
en.notes: 貫き通す intensifies 貫く: to "consistently carry something through to the end". Typical objects with を: 信念 / 意志 / 主張 / 沈黙を貫き通す, 生涯独身を貫き通す. It stresses steadfastness against opposition and sounds somewhat elevated. The literal sense "to pierce all the way through" (矢が板を貫き通す) is rarer. There is no intransitive partner; 貫く is likewise transitive.

examples[].german: There is a possibility that you may be asked to pay compensation.
The court ordered the company to pay 100 million yen in damages.
Heavy reparations were imposed on the defeated nations.
en.notes: 賠償金 is money paid as compensation for damages, as well as reparations between states: 賠償金を払う / 請求する / 受け取る, 損害賠償金. Related: 慰謝料 "compensation for emotional distress" and 補償金 "compensation" for losses caused lawfully (e.g. expropriation). 賠償 presupposes fault or unlawful damage.

examples[].german: The wide-area union handles affairs that span multiple municipalities.
The Kansai Wide-Area Union promotes cooperation among the prefectures in disaster prevention and tourism.
Medical insurance for people aged 75 and over is run by wide-area unions at the prefectural level.
en.notes: 広域連合 is a legal form under local government law (地方自治法): prefectures, cities and towns join together to carry out supra-local tasks jointly. Well-known examples are the 後期高齢者医療広域連合 (health insurance for people aged 75 and over) and the 関西広域連合. To be distinguished from the 一部事務組合, a special-purpose association for individual tasks such as waste disposal. 広域 means "wide-area, supra-regional"; register: administrative language.

examples[].german: Theory only has meaning when it is put into practice.
I practice the money-saving techniques I learned from the book every day.
In this course, you can learn practical English conversation.
en.notes: 実践 means "to put into practice" and is also common as a transitive する-verb: 教えを実践する, 学んだことを実践する. Fixed pairs and phrases: 理論と実践, 実践に移す, 実践的な "practical". Beware the homophone: 実戦 (じっせん) is "real combat, the real thing". 実行 stresses carrying out a plan, 実践 living by principles or knowledge.

examples[].german: This Japanese black beef steak is a gem that the chef takes special pride in.
This tea bowl is a superb piece from the Edo period.
As a souvenir, I chose a fine piece made by a local craftsman.
en.notes: 逸品 is an "exquisite, outstanding piece" - a work of art, a craft product or, in gastronomy, a special dish: シェフ自慢の逸品, 江戸時代の逸品. Beware the homophone: 一品 (いっぴん) means only "one item, one dish" (一品料理). 絶品 stresses the superlative (often for taste), 傑作 is the masterpiece of an artist.

examples[].german: This advertisement is said to be truly outstanding.
Her work stood out even among the submitted entries.
I was fooled by the brilliant trick until the very end.
en.notes: 秀逸 "excellent, outstanding" is an evaluative, rather written word for works, ideas, phrasings or achievements: 秀逸な作品, 秀逸なアイデア, 秀逸なキャッチコピー. For people and their abilities, 優秀 is more usual (優秀な学生). In daily life, 秀逸 sounds slightly appreciative and elevated; more neutral are 優れた or すばらしい.

en.meaning: to turn away; to divert; to miss
examples[].german: She quickly looked away.
Don't change the subject; answer me properly.
The catcher let the ball get past, and the runner scored.
en.notes: 逸らす (mostly in kana: そらす) is transitive: 目 / 顔を逸らす "to avert one's gaze", 話を逸らす "to change the subject", 注意 / 気を逸らす "to distract". In sports also "to let (the ball) through, to miss". The intransitive partner is 逸れる "to deviate": 話が逸れる, 台風が逸れる. Do not confuse it with 反らす "to bend backward" (胸を反らす).

examples[].german: The best preferential interest rate applies to this home loan.
Members can exchange foreign currency at the best preferential rate.
In gratitude for your many years of business with us, we have prepared our best terms for you.
en.notes: 最優遇 is the "most favorable preferential treatment" and occurs almost only in banking and business language: 最優遇金利 "preferential interest rate, prime rate", 最優遇レート "best exchange rate", 最優遇の条件. It is hardly used as a する-verb; "to give someone preferential treatment" is 優遇する. In trade between states, people say 最恵国待遇 "most-favored-nation treatment".

examples[].german: The fans of both teams kept up an exchange of jeers.
He retorted to the reporter's harsh question with sarcasm.
Retaliatory tariffs went back and forth between the two countries, and trade friction deepened.
en.notes: 応酬 is a back and forth of words, blows or measures in which each side reacts to the other: 非難の応酬 "mutual accusations", やじの応酬, 報復関税の応酬. As a する-verb it means "to retort, to respond", usually with で for the means: 皮肉で応酬する. Typical in reports on politics, sports and diplomacy; formal. In conversation, people tend to say 言い合い or やり合う.

examples[].german: They are being forced into unfairly harsh labor.
In the harsh environment of the desert, he survived for three days.
The grueling schedule went on, and I ended up ruining my health.
en.notes: 過酷 describes conditions that are harsh beyond what is reasonable: 過酷な労働 / 環境 / 条件 / スケジュール, 過酷な運命. 苛酷 is read the same and stresses more the cruel treatment by someone; today both are often used interchangeably. 厳しい is the neutral everyday word, and 残酷 means "cruel" toward living beings.

examples[].german: Is it all right to let black companies that work their employees to the bone go unchecked like this?
Maybe it's because I overuse my eyes at the computer, but my eyesight has gotten worse.
Because I overworked my knees when I was young, I can't run now.
en.notes: 酷使 means "to use ruthlessly, to overtax" and is transitive: 労働者を酷使する, 体 / 目 / 喉を酷使する, 機械を酷使する. It stresses overloading the object, not financial gain; economic exploitation in the narrow sense is 搾取. With body parts, it is completely everyday.

examples[].german: The contents of all three books are strikingly similar.
The man captured on the security camera closely resembled the wanted suspect.
It was pointed out that the design of the new product closely resembles another company's product.
en.notes: 酷似 means "to be strikingly similar" and is an intransitive する-verb, mostly in the form 〜に酷似している or AとBが酷似している. It is written language and typical of news about plagiarism, counterfeits or descriptions of suspects. In daily life people say よく似ている or そっくりだ.

examples[].german: Everything she cooked tasted terrible.
Don't say such awful things.
I caught a terrible cold and missed school for a week.
en.notes: ひどい is mostly written in kana and means "terrible, bad" (ひどい味, ひどい風邪, ひどい雨) as well as "mean, cruel" toward people: ひどいことを言う, ひどい人. As an exclamation, ひどい！ means "How mean!". The adverb form ひどく intensifies: ひどく疲れた. More generally "bad" is 悪い; ひどい is emotionally stronger.

examples[].german: Wasteful spending was cut through the program review.
In the program review, the budget for the supercomputer also became a subject of debate.
That subsidy was judged "to be abolished" in the program review.
en.notes: 事業仕分け is a procedure in which public programs are reviewed in open session and classified as "continue", "cut" or "abolish". It became known in 2009-2010 under the DPJ government; 仕分け literally means "sorting". Typical: 事業仕分けの対象になる, 事業仕分けで「廃止」と判定される. Today it is carried out mainly by municipalities; register: political and media language.

examples[].german: This summer, the scorching heat continued.
In this extreme heat, please refrain from outdoor work as much as possible.
In this season of scorching heat, how are you?
en.notes: 酷暑 is "extreme, oppressive summer heat" and a written-language word. It appears in news, warnings and letter style: 酷暑の候 as a seasonal greeting in July/August. In weather reports, 猛暑 (猛暑日 from 35 °C) is even more common; in daily life people simply say すごく暑い. Opposite: 酷寒 "bitter cold".

examples[].german: I was forced into an extremely cruel decision.
You must not treat animals cruelly.
This film has brutal scenes, so I can't show it to children.
en.notes: 残酷 means "cruel, brutal" and describes actions, depictions or circumstances that inflict suffering: 残酷な仕打ち, 残酷なシーン, 動物を残酷に扱う, 残酷な現実. 冷酷, by contrast, stresses the coldness of a person, and 残忍 deliberate, bestial cruelty. 過酷 describes harsh conditions, not cruelty.

examples[].german: I always thought you were a cold-hearted person.
The company callously fired a sick employee.
With a cold expression, he said, "Don't come anymore."
en.notes: 冷酷 means "cold-hearted, merciless" and stresses a lack of compassion: 冷酷な人, 冷酷な表情, 冷酷にも〜する "to do something coldly". Unlike 残酷, which describes the cruel act or situation, 冷酷 characterizes more the person and their attitude. Weaker and more everyday is 冷たい.

examples[].german: If I worried about every scathing review, I couldn't write anything.
The new film was panned by the critics.
My boss tore my proposal apart, and I was completely crushed.
en.notes: 酷評 is devastating criticism, a "scathing review"; as a transitive する-verb it is very often used in the passive: 評論家に酷評される. Typical of reviews of films, books, restaurants or work results. Opposite: 絶賛 "effusive praise". More neutral is 批判 "criticism", and weaker is 辛口の評価.

examples[].german: The sickle just slipped out of my hand.
My grandfather is cutting the grass in the garden with a sickle.
When I fished for information with a leading question, he readily told the truth.
en.notes: 鎌 is the sickle, used to cut grass or rice: 鎌で草を刈る, 草刈り鎌; a large scythe is called 大鎌. Important is the idiom 鎌をかける "to ask someone a leading question, to fish for information". Do not confuse it with the homophone 釜 "kettle, pot". The character is also found in the place name 鎌倉.

examples[].german: What on earth is on display in that exhibition room?
Old swords were lined up in rows in the museum's exhibition room.
You can view the new products in the showroom on the first floor.
en.notes: 陳列室 is a room in which goods or exhibits are displayed; 陳列 means "to put on display" (商品を陳列する). The word sounds a bit old-fashioned and formal: for car dealerships or furniture, people today mostly say ショールーム, and in museums more often 展示室. 陳列室 is still encountered in older buildings, museums and texts.

examples[].german: Taut, glowing skin is an essential condition for a woman to be popular.
For this job, a driver's license is a mandatory requirement.
Peace is an essential condition for economic development.
en.notes: 必須条件 is an "indispensable prerequisite": 〜が必須条件だ, 〜の必須条件. Common in job advertisements (応募の必須条件, as opposed to 歓迎条件 "desirable") and in arguments. 必須 (ひっす) means "mandatory, indispensable". In logic, people speak of 必要条件 "necessary condition" and 十分条件 "sufficient condition".

examples[].german: How did our conspiracy come to light?
When the wrongdoing came to light, the company president was forced to resign.
Lies are bound to come out sooner or later.
en.notes: 露顕 means "to come to light, to be exposed" - of conspiracies, lies or misdeeds that someone wanted to hide. It is intransitive: 悪事が露顕する. Today the spelling 露見 is much more common; in the news 発覚 is often used, and colloquially ばれる. The tone is written to dramatic.

examples[].german: This picture symbolizes the conscious and unconscious mind of human beings.
The effects of the declining birthrate are becoming apparent in rural areas.
The role of marketing is to bring latent demand to the surface.
en.notes: 顕在 refers to something that lies openly in view and is the opposite of 潜在 "latent, hidden". On its own it is rare; typical are compounds such as 顕在化する "to come to the surface, to become visible" (問題が顕在化する), 顕在的 "manifest" and 顕在意識 "waking consciousness". The word belongs to written and technical style (economics, sociology, psychology); in daily life people tend to say 表に出る or はっきりする.

en.meaning: public commendation; to honor publicly; to recognize
examples[].german: The commendation ceremony will be held at the civic hall tomorrow.
The city erected a monument honoring a great figure from the area.
Her many years of volunteer work were publicly recognized.
en.notes: 顕彰 means to honor and make known someone's merits or good deeds publicly; transitive with を: 功績を顕彰する, in the passive 〜が顕彰される. Typical are 顕彰式, 顕彰碑 "memorial stone" and 顕彰制度. Unlike the more everyday 表彰 "to commend with a certificate or prize", 顕彰 stresses public recognition, often also of deceased or historical figures. Very formal, mainly in official and press language.

examples[].german: Public comments were solicited on the new draft ordinance.
I also submitted a public comment on the draft regulation.
More than 2,000 comments were received in the public comment period of one month.
en.notes: パブリックコメント is the official consultation procedure (意見公募手続) in which authorities publish drafts of regulations and anyone can comment on them. The word means both the procedure and the individual comment; colloquially it is shortened to パブコメ. Typical: パブリックコメントを募集する／実施する, パブコメを出す／提出する, パブリックコメントに寄せられた意見.

examples[].german: I'm against whaling.
Japan resumed commercial whaling in 2019.
This town once flourished thanks to whaling.
en.notes: 捕鯨 is whaling as an activity or industry. Common combinations: 商業捕鯨 "commercial whaling", 調査捕鯨 "research whaling", 捕鯨船, 捕鯨問題, 捕鯨に反対する／賛成する. It is normally not used as a する-verb; the actual catching is 鯨を捕る. The word is neutral but appears mainly in news and debates.

examples[].german: I know a good whale meat restaurant.
Whale meat was often served in school lunches in the Showa era.
Whale meat consumption is falling year by year.
en.notes: 鯨肉 is the Sino-Japanese reading for "whale meat" and sounds factual and written (statistics, labels, reports). In conversation people mostly say 鯨の肉 or くじら肉. Common are 鯨肉の消費, 鯨肉を食べる, 鯨肉の竜田揚げ. Older Japanese people still know whale meat from school lunches in the postwar period.

examples[].german: The sky was dyed madder red by the sunset, and it was very beautiful.
She was wearing a madder-red kimono.
This cloth was dyed madder red with madder root.
en.notes: 茜色 is a deep, warm red named after the dye plant 茜 "madder". The word is literary and poetic and describes above all the evening sky: 夕焼けで空が茜色に染まる, 茜色の空; related is 茜空. Grammatically, it takes の before nouns and に with 染まる／染める. In daily life, people simply say 赤 or 真っ赤 for red.

examples[].german: On Sunday, I went to Nishiki Market in Kyoto.
Nishiki Market is called "Kyoto's kitchen".
At Nishiki Market, I snacked my way along on pickles and yuba.
en.notes: 錦市場 is a covered market street about 400 meters long in central Kyoto, known as "Kyoto's kitchen" (京の台所). There you find tsukemono, yuba, fish, sweets and kitchen knives; today it is also popular with tourists for 食べ歩き. Watch the reading: 市場 as a concrete marketplace is read いちば, while しじょう means the market in the economic sense (株式市場).

examples[].german: They say bad causes bring bad results, right? It's a well-deserved retribution.
As the saying goes, evil causes evil effects: whoever deceives others will eventually be deceived himself.
Buddhism teaches that evil causes bring evil results and good causes bring good results.
en.notes: 悪因悪果 is a Buddhist-influenced four-character expression: 悪因 "bad cause" and 悪果 "bad fruit" - evil deeds have evil consequences. The counterpart is 善因善果; more general and more common is 因果応報, and 自業自得 stresses more "you brought it on yourself". Typical frames: 悪因悪果というように..., まさに悪因悪果だ. Written to didactic; in conversation, rather ironic and quoting.

examples[].german: This is designed so that it forms a scalene triangle when seen from above.
Solve the following inequality.
The symbols "<" and ">" are called inequality signs.
en.notes: 不等 "inequality" occurs almost only in mathematical-technical compounds: 不等式 "inequality", 不等号 "inequality sign", 不等辺三角形 "scalene triangle". As an independent word it is rare. Do not confuse it with the identically read, much more common 不当 "unjust, unlawful" (不当な扱い, 不当解雇).

examples[].german: When I was little, my stepfather always gave me piggyback rides.
I didn't get along with my stepfather, my mother's new husband, at first.
I wrote "stepfather" in the relationship field of the form.
en.notes: 継父 is the formal word for "stepfather", i.e. the mother's husband who is not the biological father; the counterpart is 継母 (けいぼ). It appears in documents, reports and literature. In conversation people tend to say 義理の父, 母の再婚相手 or simply お父さん; 義父 is ambiguous because it also means "father-in-law".

en.meaning: vividly portrayed; living up to one's name
examples[].german: Show that guy what a real champion is made of!
The veteran player scored the winning goal and played up to his reputation.
In this novel, the author's personality comes through vividly.
en.notes: 躍如 "vivid, standing out clearly" occurs almost exclusively in the fixed phrase 面目躍如 "to fully live up to one's reputation, to show oneself at one's best" (面目 is also read めんぼく). Forms: 面目躍如たる活躍, 面目躍如だ, 面目躍如の一打; rarer is 躍如として "vividly". The word is written language and typical of sports reports and reviews.

examples[].german: Before my period, my emotional swings inevitably become intense.
This course has a lot of ups and downs and is tough by bicycle.
My grandfather lived a life full of ups and downs.
en.notes: 起伏 literally means "rising and falling": on the one hand, undulations in terrain (起伏の多い道, 起伏に富んだ地形), on the other the ups and downs of emotions or life stories (感情の起伏が激しい, 起伏の多い人生). It is mostly used as a noun; the intransitive 起伏する (起伏する丘陵) is written language. A similar, more casual word for life phases is 浮き沈み.

en.meaning: to lay face down; to lower (eyes); to withhold
examples[].german: Why did you keep it secret that your brother is a criminal?
She lowered her eyes shyly.
I put the half-read book face down on the table.
en.notes: 伏せる is a transitive Ichidan verb with several meanings: to lay something face down (本を伏せる, カードを伏せる), to lower one's gaze (目を伏せる), to lie flat (床に身を伏せる) and to keep something secret (名前を伏せる, 事実を伏せる). For a dog, 伏せ！ means "Down!". The literary counterpart 伏す is intransitive; "to lie ill in bed" is 病に臥せる (also written 伏せる).

examples[].german: The ombudsman system contributes to improving administrative transparency.
A citizens' ombudsman group investigated how legislators spent their political activity funds.
Not satisfied with the ward's response, I filed a complaint with the ombudsman.
en.notes: オンブズマン comes from Swedish and has two uses in Japan: the official ombudsperson of a municipality who examines citizens' complaints about the administration (行政オンブズマン), and above all citizens' groups called 市民オンブズマン that monitor public spending, request the release of information and file lawsuits. Typical: オンブズマンに苦情を申し立てる, オンブズマン制度. Gender-neutral also オンブズパーソン.

examples[].german: I'll make them surrender, no matter what.
In August 1945, Japan surrendered to the Allied Powers.
The castle withstood a three-month siege but finally surrendered.
en.notes: 降伏 means "to capitulate, to surrender", mainly in a military sense: 敵に降伏する (the opponent takes に), 無条件降伏 "unconditional surrender", 降伏を勧告する "to call on someone to surrender". It is an intransitive する-verb; to force someone to give up is 降伏させる. The synonym 降参 is also used jokingly in daily life (降参だ "I give up"), while 降伏 stays serious and formal. Do not confuse it with the identically read 幸福 "happiness".

examples[].german: The police tracked down the suspect's hideout.
The incubation period of this virus is about one week.
In the Edo period, Christians went into hiding and kept their faith.
en.notes: 潜伏 has two main meanings: to stay hidden or go underground (犯人が〜に潜伏する, 潜伏先 "hideout") and, in medicine, incubation or latency (潜伏期間 "incubation period", ウイルスが体内に潜伏する). It is an intransitive する-verb with に for the place. Undercover investigations, on the other hand, are called 潜入捜査 - 潜入 is "to infiltrate, to sneak in".

examples[].german: We were attacked from ambush.
The title favorite lost in the first round to an unexpected underdog.
The biggest unforeseen obstacle to the plan was the weak yen.
en.notes: 伏兵 literally means "hidden soldiers", i.e. an ambush (伏兵を置く, 伏兵に襲われる). Figuratively it refers to an unexpected opponent or unforeseen obstacle, especially in sports and elections: 思わぬ伏兵, 伏兵に足をすくわれる "to be tripped up by an underdog". The act of lying in wait itself is 待ち伏せ.

examples[].german: I just stood by and watched the bullying.
This is no time to stay silent and look on any longer.
The government merely looked on at the situation and took no measures at all.
en.notes: 傍観 means to merely watch something without intervening - almost always with a critical undertone. Transitive with を: 事態を傍観する, often reinforced by ただ／黙って. Common are 傍観者 "onlooker, bystander" and 傍観している場合ではない "we must not stand idly by". By contrast, 見守る is benevolent watching and 見物 is watching for pleasure.

examples[].german: The police may intercept communications for criminal investigations.
The military intercepted the enemy's radio.
My father's hobby is listening in on ships' radio communications with his amateur radio.
en.notes: 傍受 refers to listening in on or intercepting radio and communication signals not addressed to oneself: 無線を傍受する, 通信傍受, 通信傍受法. It is a neutral, technical-official term and also includes legal interception by authorities. 盗聴, by contrast, is secret eavesdropping with bugs and sounds clearly negative or illegal.

examples[].german: There was a woman who was my type, so I couldn't help staring at her.
He stared fixedly at the screen and didn't move.
The cat is staring fixedly at a spot outside the window.
en.notes: 凝視 means to stare at something for a long time and with concentration; transitive with を: 画面を凝視する, 一点を凝視する. The word is written language and sounds intense. In conversation people mostly say じっと見つめる; 注視 stresses attentive observation (e.g. of a situation), and じろじろ見る rude scrutinizing.

en.meaning: to get stiff; to be absorbed in; to be elaborate
examples[].german: It can't be helped that your shoulders and neck get stiff from desk work.
Recently, my father has been really into coffee.
This cake looks really elaborate.
en.notes: 凝る is intransitive and has three main meanings: muscles get stiff (肩が凝る, noun 肩こり), one gets passionately absorbed in something (〜に凝る, 凝り性 "perfectionist"), and something is elaborately made (凝った料理, 凝ったデザイン). The transitive counterpart is 凝らす: 工夫を凝らす "to devise something ingenious", 目を凝らす "to look closely".

en.meaning: to adhere to (a doctrine); firm belief
examples[].german: I think all Japanese citizens should believe in Shinto.
He is a firm believer in free-market economics.
That thinker still has many followers today.
en.notes: 信奉 means to believe in a doctrine, ideology or person and follow it; transitive with を: 市場原理を信奉する, 〜主義を信奉する. 信奉者 "follower" belongs here. Unlike 信仰 (religious faith, 神を信仰する), 信奉 refers more to doctrines and schools of thought; 信じる is the general everyday word. Written language.

en.meaning: service (to a master); apprenticeship as a live-in servant
examples[].german: "Orei-bōkō" means working for a set period after graduation at the hospital that paid your scholarship.
In the Edo period, many children were sent into service at merchant houses.
The self-sacrificing way of working for one's company is already outdated.
en.notes: 奉公 used to refer mainly to service as a servant or apprentice living in the master's house: 奉公に出る／出される, 丁稚奉公, 奉公人. The second meaning is service to one's lord or the public, for example in the Kamakura feudal relationship ご恩と奉公 or in 滅私奉公 "selfless devotion". Today it appears mostly in historical contexts or fixed expressions such as お礼奉公 (working in return for training or a scholarship). Intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: Rice cultivation spread across many regions in the Yayoi period.
I saw Yayoi pottery at the museum.
"Yayoi" is the old name for the third month of the lunar calendar.
en.notes: 弥生 has two meanings: the Yayoi period (roughly 300 BC to 300 AD by the classical dating; recent research places the start earlier), when wet-rice farming and metal tools spread, named after the Tokyo district 弥生, where the first 弥生土器 were found in 1884. It is preceded by the 縄文時代 and followed by the 古墳時代. 弥生 is also the poetic name of the third month in the old calendar and a woman's given name. The reading やよい is an irregular reading.

examples[].german: As e-government is promoted, administrative procedures are increasingly moving online.
Estonia is known as a leader in e-government.
Many kinds of applications can be made online from the e-government portal site.
en.notes: 電子政府 refers to digitized administration in which citizens handle applications and inquiries online; the central portal is called e-Gov. Typical: 電子政府の推進／実現, 電子政府ランキング. For the municipal level one says 電子自治体; newer texts prefer デジタル・ガバメント or 行政のデジタル化 (since 2021 with the デジタル庁). Register: administrative and media language.

examples[].german: I expressed my condolences and observed a moment of silence.
We respectfully offer our deepest condolences.
The whole country mourned the hero's death.
en.notes: 哀悼 is grief over a deceased person and sympathy with the bereaved. It almost always appears in the fixed phrase 哀悼の意を表する／示す, especially 謹んで哀悼の意を表します "we offer our sincere condolences". As a transitive する-verb (故人の死を哀悼する) it is rarer. 追悼 refers more to shared remembrance and memorial events; personally, one says お悔やみ.

examples[].german: Why don't we all hold a memorial concert for him?
A ceremony was held to honor the victims of the earthquake.
The TV station broadcast a tribute program for the late actor.
en.notes: 追悼 means to remember a deceased person and mourn him or her; transitive with を: 犠牲者を追悼する. Very common as a modifier: 追悼式 "memorial service", 追悼集会, 追悼番組, 追悼コンサート, 追悼文. Compared with 哀悼 (the feeling of grief, mostly in 哀悼の意), 追悼 stresses active, often public remembrance.

examples[].german: Many amusing characters appear in this anime.
He is a truly fun person.
Last night I had a merry drink with old friends.
en.notes: 愉快 is a な-adjective meaning "cheerful, pleasant, amusing" and often describes people, conversations or moods: 愉快な人, 愉快な仲間, 愉快に過ごす. It sounds somewhat more elevated than 楽しい and emphasizes the cheering quality. Very common is the negative 不愉快 "unpleasant, annoying" (不愉快な思いをする). 痛快, by contrast, is "wonderfully liberating, thrilling".

examples[].german: Young patriotic samurai, rise up now!
Many patriots concerned for their country appeared at the end of the Edo period.
Driven by concern for his country, he wrote a letter to the newspaper.
en.notes: 憂国 is composed of 憂える "to worry" and 国 "country": deep concern for the future of one's own country. Typical are 憂国の士／憂国の志士 "concerned patriot" and 憂国の情. The word is literary, sounds pathetic and is often nationalistically tinged; Mishima's story 『憂国』 is well known. Unlike 愛国 "love of country", 憂国 stresses worry.

examples[].german: A trace of anxiety crossed my heart.
On graduation day, I felt a touch of loneliness.
A slight doubt remained about his explanation.
en.notes: 一抹 literally means "one brush stroke" and is used almost only as 一抹の + feeling, meaning "a touch, a trace of": 一抹の不安, 一抹の寂しさ, 一抹の疑問. These are mostly quiet, negative feelings that one 覚える／感じる or that 残る. The word is written language; in everyday speech one says ちょっと不安 or 少し寂しい.

examples[].german: Inconvenient opinions were suppressed at the meeting.
The dictator eliminated his opponents one after another.
The scandal wiped him out of show business.
en.notes: 抹殺 is a strong transitive する-verb: to eliminate people or groups (反対派を抹殺する), to suppress or silence opinions or facts (意見を抹殺する) and, more rarely, to strike out something written. The passive 社会的に抹殺される "to be socially destroyed" is common. Unlike 抹消 "to delete (an entry)", 抹殺 means violent or complete eradication.

examples[].german: He was removed from the first-team roster because of an injury.
To scrap a car, you need to go through the deregistration procedure.
After you leave the membership, all personal data will be deleted.
en.notes: 抹消 means to officially and completely delete or strike out an entry or record: 登録を抹消する, 名簿から抹消する, データを抹消する. It is typical of official language, e.g. 抹消登録 "deregistration of a vehicle"; in baseball, 一軍登録を抹消される means "to be dropped from the top-team roster". More everyday are 消す and, for computer files, 削除.

en.meaning: to install; to set in place
examples[].german: I'm planning to install a cupboard here.
A new machine was installed at the factory.
The air conditioner installation work will be done in the afternoon.
en.notes: 据え付ける is transitive and means to firmly install a heavy device or piece of furniture in its place: 機械を据え付ける, エアコンを据え付ける, 金庫を据え付ける. The noun 据え付け often appears in 据え付け工事. More general is 取り付ける "to attach, fit" (also small parts); 設置する is the formal word for facilities. The base verb 据える "to set firmly" is known from 腰を据える.

examples[].german: On New Year's Day, I go to the first shrine visit of the year with my family.
It is common to write "元旦" as the date on New Year's cards.
Having to work from New Year's Day on -- what bad luck.
en.notes: 元旦 is New Year's Day; strictly speaking, 旦 means "morning, sunrise", so it refers to the morning of January 1, whereas 元日 covers the whole day. In everyday speech both are mostly used the same way. On New Year's cards (年賀状) you simply write 元旦 as the date; "1月1日元旦" or 元旦の朝 are considered redundant.

examples[].german: The My Number system aims at unified management of social security and taxes.
When I started a part-time job, I submitted my My Number to the company.
With a My Number card, you can get a copy of your residence certificate at a convenience store.
en.notes: マイナンバー is the twelve-digit personal identification number assigned to all residents of Japan since 2016 (社会保障・税番号制度). To be distinguished: マイナンバー is the number itself, マイナンバーカード (short マイナカード) the ID card with photo and chip, which also serves, for example, as a health insurance card (マイナ保険証). Typical: マイナンバーを提出する／記入する, マイナンバー制度.

en.meaning: to prosper; to do good business; prosperity
examples[].german: I prayed at a shrine for my business to prosper.
The ramen shop in front of the station is always full of customers and doing great.
It struggled at first, but thanks to word of mouth the shop gradually flourished.
en.notes: 繁盛 means that a business, restaurant or place has many customers and thrives: 店が繁盛する, 繁盛している店, 商売繁盛 "good business" as a wish found at shrines and on lucky charms. It is an intransitive する-verb with が; the spelling 繁昌 also exists. Compared with 繁栄 "prosperity, flourishing" (of a country, a city), 繁盛 is more concrete and relates to trade and customers. Neutral, everyday.

examples[].german: Are you from Tochigi Prefecture?
Nikkō Tōshōgū Shrine is in Tochigi Prefecture.
Tochigi produces the most strawberries in all of Japan.
en.notes: 栃木県 is a prefecture in the Kantō region north of Tokyo, with the capital 宇都宮, which is known for gyoza. Also well known are 日光 with the Tōshōgū Shrine, the highlands of 那須 and strawberries (とちおとめ). The character 栃 "horse chestnut" is a kanji created in Japan; in conversation people often say just 栃木.

examples[].german: The cleaning agent is under the sink.
Mixing chlorine-based and acidic cleaners is dangerous.
My grandmother soaks her dentures in cleaning solution every night.
en.notes: 洗浄剤 is a cleaning agent and sounds somewhat more technical than the everyday word 洗剤 (dish and laundry detergent). It is found mainly on product labels: トイレ用洗浄剤, パイプ洗浄剤, 入れ歯洗浄剤. 洗浄 is the formal word for "cleaning, washing" (洗浄する), and the suffix 剤 means "agent" as in 薬剤 or 漂白剤. The warning 混ぜるな危険 "do not mix, dangerous" on chlorine-based products is well known.

examples[].german: I'm looking for an actress with an oval face and a distinctive presence.
Beautiful women in ukiyo-e are often depicted with oval faces.
They say my grandmother was a famous beauty in her youth, with a fair-skinned oval face.
en.notes: 瓜実顔 is an oval, slightly elongated face, named after the shape of a melon seed (瓜実); fair skin often goes with it. It was regarded as a beauty ideal for women, especially in the Edo period, and is known from ukiyo-e portraits of women. The word is literary to old-fashioned; today people tend to say 卵形の顔 or 面長, and the opposite is 丸顔.

examples[].german: Cavities do not heal on their own.
It takes about three months for the wound to heal completely.
Human beings are naturally endowed with self-healing power.
en.notes: 治癒 is healing as a result; intransitive: 病気／傷が治癒する. Common are 自然治癒 "natural healing", 治癒力 "healing power" and 完全に治癒する. The word is medical and formal; in everyday speech one says 治る. Not to be confused with 治療 "treatment" and the transitive 治す "to cure (something)".

examples[].german: Poor-quality gasoline shortens the life of a car.
The wallet I bought online was shoddy goods.
Inferior counterfeit goods are in circulation on the market.
en.notes: 粗悪 is a な-adjective for inferior, poorly made goods and materials: 粗悪な商品, 粗悪な材料, especially often 粗悪品 "shoddy goods". For poor living or working conditions, 劣悪 is used instead (劣悪な環境). The word is written language; in everyday speech one says 質が悪い or 安物.

examples[].german: This site updates the ranking of cumulative downloads of popular apps every day.
The series' cumulative circulation has surpassed 100 million copies.
Adding up this year's sales, they exceeded last year's.
en.notes: 累計 is the total accumulated up to a point in time: 累計発行部数, 累計販売台数, 累計で100万人. It often stands directly before counters or with で; as a transitive する-verb (売上を累計する) it is rarer. 合計 is simply the sum of several items, while 累計 stresses adding up over time.

examples[].german: He was promoted step by step to department head at a young age.
Japan's income tax is progressive.
Electricity charges are tiered: the more you use, the higher the unit price.
en.notes: 累進 means "to rise step by step". Today it appears mainly in the second meaning "to increase progressively": 累進課税 "progressive taxation", 累進税率, 累進制. The meaning "to be promoted step by step" (部長に累進する) is written language and rather dated; normally one says 昇進する. Intransitive する-verb.

examples[].german: What do you think about the Japanese government accumulating a huge amount of government bonds?
The company's accumulated deficit reached one billion yen.
In soccer, you get suspended when yellow cards accumulate.
en.notes: 累積 is accumulation, mostly of undesirable things: 赤字が累積する, 累積赤字, 累積債務, 疲労の累積. It can be used intransitively (〜が累積する) and transitively (〜を累積する) and often stands as a modifier before nouns. 蓄積 is more general and can also be positive (知識の蓄積); 累計, on the other hand, is the accumulated total as a number.

examples[].german: They really showed the pride of an old established firm.
I bought yōkan at a 300-year-old traditional Japanese confectionery shop.
This inn is a famous long-established one even in Kyoto.
en.notes: 老舗 is a traditional shop or company that has existed for generations; the reading しにせ is an irregular reading (rarely also ろうほ). Typical are 老舗旅館, 老舗の和菓子屋, 創業百年の老舗; figuratively also 老舗メーカー or 老舗ブランド for long-established firms in any industry. With 老舗の意地／看板 one stresses pride and reputation.
