examples[].german: The administration's negligence led to the spread of the damage.
The security guard's neglect of duty was identified as the cause of the accident.
Failing to check was clearly my negligence. I am sorry.
en.notes: 怠慢 is the neglect of duties that one really ought to fulfill; as a noun and as a な-adjective (怠慢な態度). Typical: 職務怠慢 "dereliction of duty", 行政の怠慢, 怠慢だと批判される, in sports 怠慢プレー "lackluster play". Related to the verb 怠る "to neglect". To be distinguished from 怠惰 "laziness" as a trait; 怠慢 always criticizes a concrete omission. Register: formal, judgmental.

examples[].german: This is terrible. A prisoner of war has escaped!
My grandfather was taken prisoner in Siberia during the war.
The two countries agreed to a prisoner exchange.
en.notes: 捕虜 is a soldier or person captured in war: 捕虜になる "to be taken prisoner", 捕虜にする, 捕虜収容所, 捕虜交換. Also used figuratively in literary language: 恋の捕虜 "captive of love". To be distinguished are 人質 "hostage" and 囚人 "prisoner (in jail)".

examples[].german: Does this product also fall under the campaign?
Please circle the applicable items.
There were no results matching the search criteria.
en.notes: 該当 means "to apply to something, to fall under something"; intransitive with に: 条件に該当する, 対象に該当する. Typical of forms and official language: 該当する項目, 該当者, 該当箇所, 該当なし. In everyday speech one says 当てはまる. Not to be confused with the identically read 街頭 "street" (街頭演説).

examples[].german: When the company president entertained a foreign dignitary, I accompanied him as an interpreter.
We welcomed the minister in the VIP room at the airport.
Members of the royal family watched the match from the VIP seats.
en.notes: 貴賓 is a high-ranking, distinguished guest. On its own the word is rare; it mostly appears in 貴賓室 "VIP room" and 貴賓席 "VIP box". Related words: 来賓 "invited guest at a ceremony", 国賓 "state guest", 賓客 "honored guest". Very formal.

examples[].german: The American president visited Japan as a state guest.
A banquet was held at the Imperial Palace in honor of the state guest.
He was treated like a state guest.
en.notes: 国賓 is a state guest officially invited by the government, usually a head of state, who is received with the highest honors. Typical: 国賓として来日する, 国賓待遇, 国賓級; a 宮中晩餐会 is held for state guests. One step below is 公賓 "official guest". Figuratively, 国賓のような扱い is used for royal treatment.

en.meaning: invited guest; guest of honor (at ceremonies)
examples[].german: Thank you very much to everyone, including our guests of honor, for attending despite your busy schedules.
At the graduation ceremony, the mayor, as a guest of honor, gave a congratulatory address.
The guest-of-honor seats are on the right side of the stage.
en.notes: 来賓 are the specially invited guests at celebrations and ceremonies, such as school festivals, weddings or openings. Typical are ご来賓の皆様, 来賓席, 来賓祝辞 and 来賓のあいさつ. For customers or private visitors, one says お客様 or 客 instead. Formal, especially in speeches.

examples[].german: We entertained the foreign guest of honor with first-class Japanese cuisine.
The king was welcomed with great pomp as a guest of honor.
This is a special room for receiving distinguished guests.
en.notes: 賓客 is an important guest received with honors (more rarely also read ひんかく). Typical: 賓客として迎える, 賓客をもてなす. The word is written language and elevated. By comparison: 国賓 is the official state guest, 来賓 the invited guest at a celebration, and 貴賓 occurs mainly in 貴賓室／貴賓席.

en.meaning: husband; master of the house; (address) sir
examples[].german: My husband is away on a business trip all week.
The husband next door is said to be a good cook.
"I'll give you a good price, sir," called the shop owner.
en.notes: 旦那 today means mainly "husband" in familiar speech: うちの旦那 for one's own husband, 旦那さん／旦那様 for another person's husband. More formal are 夫 or 主人. Originally 旦那 was the master of the house or a patron (from the Sanskrit word for "alms"); merchants still jokingly address male customers as 旦那. It also refers to a geisha's patron.

examples[].german: The outline looked blurred through my tears.
Let's choose a hairstyle that suits the shape of your face.
As the investigation progressed, the outline of the case began to emerge.
en.notes: 輪郭 is the outline or contour of a shape, especially 顔の輪郭 and 輪郭線 in drawing. Figuratively it refers to the basic features of a matter: 計画の輪郭, 事件の輪郭が見えてくる／はっきりする. For a written overview, one says 概要 instead; シルエット is the dark silhouette.

examples[].german: The police took three days to put down the demonstrators.
The government troops put down the rebellion by force.
The fire was brought under control after about two hours.
en.notes: 鎮圧 means to bring a rebellion, unrest or a fire under control by force or with determination; transitive with を: 反乱を鎮圧する, 暴動を武力で鎮圧する, passive 鎮圧される. For firefighters, 鎮圧 means "under control", before the final 鎮火 "extinguished". Unlike 弾圧 "oppression (of people, opinions)", 鎮圧 is directed against a specific event.

examples[].german: His company brought industry heavyweights onto its board one after another.
She is known as a leading figure in the culinary world.
The party's heavyweights supported the new president.
en.notes: 重鎮 is an influential, respected leading figure in a field, usually an older, experienced person: 業界の重鎮, 政界の重鎮, 党の重鎮, 文壇の重鎮. The word is respectful and written language. More casual is 大物 "big shot"; 第一人者 stresses a top professional position.

examples[].german: Radical claims risk causing social division.
An extremist organization issued a statement claiming responsibility.
After the surgery, please refrain from strenuous exercise for a while.
en.notes: 過激 is a な-adjective for "radical, extreme": 過激な思想, 過激な発言, 過激派 "extremists". It can also mean "excessively strenuous", e.g. 過激な運動 "overly hard exercise", and in the media "drastic, offensive" (過激な表現, 過激なシーン). 極端 more neutrally means "extreme, one-sided", 激しい "intense"; the opposite in politics is 穏健.

examples[].german: A public official was indicted on charges of malfeasance in office.
After a series of corruption cases such as bribery, trust in the city government was shaken.
Malfeasance by public officials should be severely punished.
en.notes: 瀆職 literally means "to defile one's office": official misconduct by civil servants, especially bribery and abuse of power. The word is outdated and survives mainly in criminal law as 瀆職罪 (collective term for 職権濫用罪, 収賄罪 etc.); in the news today one says 汚職. Since 瀆 is not a Jōyō kanji, one also sees 涜職. Register: very formal, legal.

examples[].german: I had the doctor give me a painkiller injection.
I had a terrible headache, so I took a painkiller.
The painkiller may be wearing off, as the wound has started to hurt again.
en.notes: 鎮痛剤 is the technical word for "painkiller", as used on package inserts and by doctors; in everyday speech one mostly says 痛み止め. Tablets are taken with 飲む; injected, it is 注射する. Typical are 鎮痛剤が効く "the painkiller works" and 鎮痛剤が切れる "the effect wears off". To be distinguished: 解熱剤 "fever reducer" and 麻酔 "anesthesia" -- a 鎮痛剤 only relieves pain, it does not numb.

examples[].german: I was shown what being a professional truly means.
It is said that the essence of the tea ceremony lies in the spirit of hospitality.
He devoted his whole life to mastering the essence of the martial arts.
en.notes: 神髄 (also written 真髄) is the innermost core, the true "essence" of an art, teaching or skill -- an elevated, rather written word. Typical expressions: 〜の神髄を極める "to master the essence of ... to the fullest", 〜の神髄に触れる "to come into contact with the essence of ...", 神髄を見せる. Unlike the neutral 本質 "essence, nature of a thing", admiration resonates: it means the highest that a master attains.

examples[].german: My spinal cord was injured in the accident.
Pulling your hand back when you touch something hot is a spinal reflex.
Many people rebut by reflex without reading the article properly.
en.notes: 脊髄 is the "spinal cord" in the vertebral canal -- not the spine itself, which is 背骨 or, technically, 脊椎 or 脊柱. Common compounds: 脊髄損傷 "spinal cord injury" and 脊髄反射 "spinal reflex"; the latter is also used colloquially for thoughtless, reflexive reactions, especially on the internet. Not to be confused with 骨髄 "bone marrow" (骨髄移植).

examples[].german: My absolute favorite dish is deep-fried pufferfish.
Kids are happy when I put karaage in their bento.
At the izakaya, we ordered beer and karaage first of all.
en.notes: 唐揚げ is a deep-fried dish in which marinated pieces are lightly coated in flour or potato starch and fried; without further specification it almost always means chicken (鶏の唐揚げ), but there are also タコの唐揚げ and フグの唐揚げ. Spellings: 唐揚げ, から揚げ, 空揚げ. Unlike 天ぷら, it has no liquid batter, and unlike フライ, no breading. Popular in bento, at izakaya and as home cooking.

examples[].german: They are said to have chosen mass suicide rather than surrender to the enemy.
After World War I, the idea of national self-determination spread.
The officer took his own life that very night when he learned of the defeat.
en.notes: 自決 has two meanings: politically "self-determination", especially in 民族自決 "the right of peoples to self-determination", and "taking one's own life", especially out of a sense of honor or to avoid capture (集団自決 in the Battle of Okinawa in 1945). The second use is a historical, formal expression; neutrally one speaks of 自殺. The verb 自決する almost always refers to suicide, while self-determination appears as a noun. Serious, written register.

examples[].german: I think everyone was jealous of his extraordinary talent.
Since she was little, she showed extraordinary talent for music.
The manager immediately recognized this rookie player's exceptional ability.
en.notes: 非凡 ("not ordinary") is the elevated counterpart of 平凡 and praises outstanding talent. It almost always stands attributively with な before words like 才能, 能力, センス: 非凡な才能 "extraordinary talent"; as a noun 非凡さ. Predicatively (〜は非凡だ) it is rarer. In conversation one says すごい or 並外れた rather; not to be confused with 非常 "emergency; extremely".

examples[].german: I was bored with my ordinary daily life.
I was born and raised in an ordinary family.
The idea is not bad, but it is a little too ordinary.
en.notes: 平凡 means "ordinary, everyday, with nothing special": 平凡な人生, 平凡な毎日, 平凡なサラリーマン. Unlike the neutral 普通 "normal, usual", 平凡 stresses the lack of brilliance and can be slightly derogatory ("unimaginative"). Often, however, it is also meant positively, as quiet, modest happiness: 平凡が一番. Opposite: 非凡; much more derogatory is 凡庸.

examples[].german: He was a mediocre man, but he was full of love.
The critic dismissed the novel as a "mediocre work".
With mediocre leadership, this crisis cannot be overcome.
en.notes: 凡庸 "mediocre, without special talent" is elevated and clearly more derogatory than 平凡. While 平凡 rather describes a quiet, unremarkable life, 凡庸 judges abilities or achievements: 凡庸な作品, 凡庸な政治家, 凡庸な才能. Typical in reviews and commentary; in conversation ありきたり or 大したことない would be more usual. Opposite: 非凡, 卓越した.

en.meaning: breach of trust; embezzlement by a fiduciary
examples[].german: A company executive was arrested for aggravated breach of trust.
The former president is accused of breach of trust for having had an acquaintance's company granted an unsecured loan.
Breach of trust that betrays customers' confidence is unacceptable.
en.notes: 背任 is the criminal offense of breach of trust: someone who manages another's affairs (e.g. a director or an employee) acts for his own or another's benefit against his duties and thereby harms the principal. For directors the aggravated 特別背任 applies. To be distinguished from 横領 "embezzlement", the appropriation of another's property. Typical: 背任罪, 背任の疑いで逮捕される, 背任行為. Register: legal, news language.

examples[].german: He was the only son of a kimono merchant.
This department store was originally a kimono shop from the Edo period.
My grandmother chose the kimono for my coming-of-age ceremony at the kimono shop.
en.notes: 呉服 refers to fabrics for Japanese clothing, especially kimono fabrics, and in a wider sense the kimono as merchandise. It is most often found in 呉服屋 or 呉服店 "kimono shop"; large department stores such as 三越 or 大丸 started out as 呉服店. Western clothing, by contrast, is 洋服, and fabric in general is 生地 or 布. The name recalls the ancient Chinese state 呉, from which the art of weaving came.

examples[].german: Today is the auspicious day of the birth of the Crown Prince.
On this festive day, I offer my heartfelt congratulations.
My grandparents chose a lucky day to move into the new house.
en.notes: 嘉日 "auspicious, festive day" is very elevated and archaic; it is found in celebratory speeches, congratulatory formulas and older texts. 嘉 means "good, happy". More common are 吉日 (きちじつ, e.g. in the letter date 〇月吉日) and the identically read 佳日 "beautiful day". Beware of the homophone 過日 "the other day, a few days ago".

examples[].german: My dream is to run my own theater company someday.
She has led a haiku circle for twenty years.
The head of this theater company writes the plays and directs them himself.
en.notes: 主宰 means to lead a group as its founder and head -- typical of theater companies, haiku circles, study groups or art schools: 劇団を主宰する. The person himself or herself is also called 主宰 (劇団の主宰). Not to be confused with the identically read 主催 "to host an event" (イベントを主催する). For companies one says 経営する, for meetings 司会する or 議長を務める.

examples[].german: The baby's crying broke the silence.
On the snowy night, the town was wrapped in silence.
In the stillness of the forest, only the birds could be heard.
en.notes: 静寂 is the deep, solemn "stillness" of a place -- elevated and literary. Fixed expressions: 静寂を破る "to break the silence", 静寂に包まれる "to be wrapped in silence", 夜の静寂. In poetry it is also read しじま. In everyday speech one says 静けさ or simply 静か; 沈黙, by contrast, means the "silence" of people.

examples[].german: The captain's death was by no means in vain.
He was promoted to captain at the age of twenty-eight.
"Understood, Captain Tanaka!"
en.notes: 大尉 is an officer rank: "captain" in the army, "lieutenant" in the navy. The company-grade ranks rise 少尉 < 中尉 < 大尉, followed by 少佐 and so on. The Japan Self-Defense Forces officially call this rank 一尉; 大尉 is therefore found mainly in historical texts, in foreign armies and in films. As a form of address it follows the name: 田中大尉.

examples[].german: My great-grandfather was a second lieutenant in the former Imperial Japanese Army.
After graduating from military academy, he was commissioned as a second lieutenant.
The hero of the film was a young naval ensign.
en.notes: 少尉 is the lowest officer rank, "second lieutenant" (in the navy "ensign"). Above it come 中尉 "first lieutenant" and 大尉 "captain", then 少佐, 中佐 and 大佐. The Japan Self-Defense Forces use different rank names (三尉), so 少尉 is found mainly in historical texts, in foreign armies, in films and in anime. As a form of address, the rank is attached to the name: 山田少尉.

examples[].german: Our army's first lieutenant was abducted by the enemy and executed.
My grandfather was a first lieutenant in the navy during the war.
It took two years to be promoted from second lieutenant to first lieutenant.
en.notes: 中尉 is the "first lieutenant" (navy: "lieutenant junior grade"), the middle lieutenant rank between 少尉 "second lieutenant" and 大尉 "captain". In today's Self-Defense Forces the rank is called 二尉, so 中尉 belongs to historical and foreign military contexts. Note: read the same as 注意 "caution, attention".

examples[].german: She is beautiful and also smart, but she has a bad personality.
I'm thinking up dishes that are cheap and at the same time nutritious.
No matter how many times you fail, it is important to keep challenging yourself all the same.
en.notes: なおかつ connects two qualities or conditions that are met at the same time: "and in addition, and at the same time" -- 安くて、なおかつ美味しい. It also means "and yet, all the same", often strengthened as それでもなおかつ. Mostly written in kana; 尚且つ seems old-fashioned. It is somewhat more formal than そして or しかも, though しかも stresses an escalation, while なおかつ stresses that both points are met at once.

examples[].german: Sophisticated fraud methods have become a social problem.
My grandmother almost fell for a phone scam.
The photo and the real thing are completely different. This is a scam!
en.notes: 詐欺 is fraud in everyday life as well as in criminal law (詐欺罪). Typical: 詐欺に遭う／引っかかる "to fall victim to fraud", 詐欺を働く "to commit fraud", 詐欺師 "fraudster", 特殊詐欺 or オレオレ詐欺 (phone scam impersonating a relative). Colloquially one expresses indignation about a misleading product with こんなの詐欺だ. The related verb is だます; ぺてん and いかさま are more slangy.

examples[].german: What's good about the udon here is this simple, unpretentious flavor.
In the old downtown area, down-to-earth shopping streets still remain today.
The new minister is popular for his down-to-earth personality.
en.notes: 庶民的 means "down-to-earth, unpretentious, affordable for ordinary people" and is mostly positive: 庶民的な店, 庶民的な味, 庶民的な値段, 庶民的な雰囲気. For people it means "approachable, without airs": 庶民的な政治家. Opposite: 高級, 上品, 貴族的. 庶民 alone is "the common people"; with 的 it becomes a な-adjective.

examples[].german: In my school days, I played cello in the strings club.
Tonight I'm going to hear a Mozart string quartet.
The strings sound in this film's music is very beautiful.
en.notes: 弦楽 is music for stringed instruments (violin, viola, cello, double bass) and mostly appears in compounds: 弦楽四重奏 "string quartet", 弦楽合奏 "string ensemble", 弦楽部 "strings club" at schools. 弦楽器 means "stringed instrument" more generally and also includes guitar or koto. Counterpart: 管楽 "wind music". On its own as an object (弦楽をやる) it sounds unusual; one rather says バイオリンを習う.

examples[].german: My body feels sluggish because of the high fever from the flu.
I worked on my feet all day, so my legs feel heavy.
On Monday mornings, I really don't feel like going to work.
en.notes: だるい describes a physical feeling of heaviness and lethargy, for example with fever, exhaustion or heat: 体がだるい, 足がだるい. The kanji spelling 怠い is rare; it is almost always written in kana (怠 is known from 怠ける "to be lazy"). Colloquially, especially among younger people, だるい also means "tiresome, not in the mood": 学校だるい. Unlike 疲れた, だるい stresses a diffuse malaise; the noun is だるさ.

examples[].german: He is the laziest person in the company, but he has the best results.
I don't want to be seen as lazy, so I come to the office early every morning.
"You lazybones! How long are you going to sleep?"
en.notes: 怠け者 is a "lazybones", someone who shirks work - clearly derogatory. It comes from the verb 怠ける "to be idle, to shirk". More colloquial are ぐうたら or 面倒くさがり. In katakana, ナマケモノ refers to the sloth. A well-known proverb: 怠け者の節句働き "lazybones work on holidays of all days".

examples[].german: The two bowed reverently before the altar.
The butler presented the letter with a respectful gesture.
The winner received the certificate with a respectful attitude.
en.notes: 恭しい describes reverent, solemnly respectful behavior, especially toward gods, superiors or sacred things. It mostly appears adverbially: 恭しく頭を下げる, 恭しく差し出す, 恭しく受け取る. The word is written language and elevated; in everyday speech one says 丁寧に or 礼儀正しく. Unlike 丁寧 "careful, polite", 恭しい stresses reverence and an often ceremonial gesture.

examples[].german: You seem quite delighted.
Grandfather was delighted to receive a present from his grandchild.
The cat is sprawled out in the sun with a thoroughly contented look.
en.notes: 満悦 "great pleasure, satisfaction" almost always appears as ご満悦: ご満悦だ, ご満悦の様子, ご満悦の表情. It is often said slightly ironically about someone visibly pleased with themselves and the world -- also about children or pets. The verb form 満悦する is rare and written language. Neutral alternatives would be 大満足 or とても喜んでいる.

examples[].german: There is already no pulse.
The nurse measured my blood pressure and pulse.
After running, my pulse rose to 150 per minute.
en.notes: 脈拍 is the "pulse" or pulse rate -- factual and medical, for example at the doctor's or on measuring devices. Typical: 脈拍を測る, 脈拍が速い, 脈拍が乱れる, 脈拍数. In everyday speech one usually says the shorter 脈: 脈をとる "to take the pulse". Similar is 心拍 "heartbeat" (心拍数 on fitness watches).

en.meaning: to squeeze; to milk; to extort (money)
examples[].german: May I squeeze lemon over the fried chicken?
At the ranch, I had the experience of milking a cow.
In the past, feudal lords extorted heavy taxes from the peasants.
en.notes: 搾る means to press liquid out by pressure: レモンを搾る, 牛の乳を搾る "to milk", 油を搾る "to press oil". Figuratively it means "to exploit, to extort", e.g. 税金を搾り取る (cf. 搾取). The identically read 絞る is used for wringing out (タオルを絞る), narrowing down (候補を絞る), turning down (音量を絞る) and 知恵を絞る; 搾る is used only when juice, milk, oil or money is extracted. Transitive godan verb; noun 搾り, as in 一番搾り.

examples[].german: I tried milking at a ranch.
On this ranch, cows are milked by machine twice a day.
Since returning to work, I pump milk during my breaks.
en.notes: 搾乳 is the "milking" of cows, goats and so on -- a technical agricultural word (搾乳機 "milking machine", 搾乳体験). It also refers to pumping breast milk (搾乳器 "breast pump"). Colloquially one says 乳を搾る or 乳搾り. As a verb it is used with or without an object: 牛を搾乳する, 一日二回搾乳する.

examples[].german: Today's high temperature is twenty-five degrees Celsius.
Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.
In America, temperature is expressed in Fahrenheit, not Celsius.
en.notes: 摂氏 means "Celsius"; it goes back to the Chinese transcription of the name Celsius. It comes before the number: 摂氏二十五度, symbol ℃. In everyday speech it is usually omitted and one simply says 二十五度, because Celsius is the standard in Japan; 摂氏 serves mainly to distinguish from 華氏 "Fahrenheit" and in factual, scientific texts.

examples[].german: Perjury in court is punished as a serious crime.
The witness was indicted for perjury.
In a Diet witness examination, one is first told that perjury is punishable.
en.notes: 偽証 is the deliberately false statement of a person testifying as a witness under oath (宣誓); punishable as 偽証罪, also in witness examinations in parliament (証人喚問). As a する-verb: 偽証する. Lying in general is 嘘をつく; 虚偽の証言 is the paraphrase. Register: legal, news language.

examples[].german: No one can defy the laws of nature.
She believes that everything happens by the providence of God.
Parents wanting to protect their children is probably a law of life.
en.notes: 摂理 refers on the one hand to the ordering regularity of nature -- 自然の摂理 "the course of nature, natural law" -- and on the other, in a religious sense, to divine "providence" (神の摂理). The word is elevated; typical verbs are 逆らう and 従う. Unlike 法則, a scientifically formulated law, 摂理 means an inescapable, larger order, such as that of coming into being and passing away.

examples[].german: "If you go by reason alone, you will clash with others" is a famous passage from Sōseki's "Kusamakura".
Wisdom, benevolence and courage are the three virtues prized in Confucianism.
We must gather the wisdom of humankind and take on this difficult problem.
en.notes: 智 (ち) "wisdom, intelligence" is elevated and rare as a single word; today 知 is mostly written instead. It is known from 智・仁・勇, the three Confucian virtues "wisdom, benevolence, courage", and from the opening of Natsume Sōseki's 草枕: 智に働けば角が立つ "if you go by reason alone, you will clash with others". The character appears more often in compounds such as 機智 "wit, quick-wittedness" and 叡智 "profound wisdom"; in Buddhism it refers to higher knowledge.

examples[].german: The old man was gathering brushwood in the mountains.
In the old days, people heated bathwater by burning brushwood collected in the mountains.
Our Shiba Inu loves walks.
en.notes: 柴 means "brushwood", thin branches and undergrowth that people used to collect in the mountains as firewood. It is known from the beginning of the fairy tale 桃太郎: おじいさんは山へ柴刈りに -- 柴刈り is thus "gathering brushwood", not "mowing the lawn"; that would be 芝刈り with the identically read 芝 "lawn". Today the character appears mainly in 柴犬 "Shiba Inu" and in family names such as 柴田.

examples[].german: Nikka is not a Shiba but a Jindo dog.
Shibas are loyal to their owners but can also be quite stubborn.
Every morning, a neighbor walks his Shiba.
en.notes: 柴犬 is a small Japanese dog breed with pricked ears and a curled tail, protected since 1936 as a 天然記念物 "natural monument". Besides しばいぬ, the reading しばけん is also heard; in conversation it is often shortened to 柴 or affectionately 柴ちゃん. Other Japanese breeds include 秋田犬 and 甲斐犬. Shibas are considered loyal but independent and stubborn; they became internationally known through the "Doge" meme. Neutral.

examples[].german: I'll give you a grace period of three days.
The situation is serious, and not a moment can be spared.
The defendant was sentenced to two years in prison, suspended for three years.
en.notes: 猶予 is a "grace period, postponement" granted to someone: 猶予を与える, 猶予をもらう, 一週間の猶予. Fixed expressions are 一刻の猶予もない "there is not a second to spare", 執行猶予 "suspension of sentence on probation" and 支払いを猶予する "to defer payment". The word is elevated to official; in everyday speech one rather says 待ってもらう or 延期.

examples[].german: You must not neglect the basics.
I was so absorbed in work that I neglected my family.
Even if club activities are busy, studying must not fall by the wayside.
en.notes: おろそか "negligent, neglected" appears almost always in the phrase 〜をおろそかにする "to neglect something" or 〜がおろそかになる "to fall by the wayside", often as an admonition: 基本をおろそかにしてはいけない. Typical objects are 勉強, 仕事, 家庭, 健康. Mostly written in kana. Caution: the same kanji are also read おろか (〜はおろか "let alone"), and 愚か "foolish" is a different word. The matching verb is 怠る.

en.meaning: poor sense of direction; person with no sense of direction
examples[].german: I have no sense of direction and get lost right away.
Because I have no sense of direction, I can't go out without a map app.
So that I, with my poor sense of direction, wouldn't get lost, he came to meet me at the station.
en.notes: 方向音痴 is colloquial and humorous -- literally something like "direction-tone-deaf", after 音痴 "tone-deaf, singing off-key". It refers to a lack of sense of direction and also to the person: 私は方向音痴だ "I have zero sense of direction". Following the same pattern there are 運動音痴 "unathletic" and 機械音痴 "bad with machines". The opposite is expressed with 方向感覚がいい.

examples[].german: Someone knocked over the gravestone.
My grandfather's name and year of death are carved into the gravestone.
Reading old epitaphs tells you about the lives of people of that time.
en.notes: 墓碑 is the "gravestone" or grave marker with an inscription -- a written-language word. In everyday speech one says 墓石 or simply お墓. Common are 墓碑銘 "epitaph, grave inscription" and 墓碑に刻む "to carve into the gravestone". Related are 石碑 "memorial stone" and 記念碑 "monument", which, however, do not stand on graves.

examples[].german: These are the characters that were carved into the stone monument.
At the village entrance stands a memorial stone telling of a past flood.
This memorial stone was erected over a thousand years ago.
en.notes: 石碑 is a "memorial stone, stone monument" with a carved inscription, for example commemorating events, people or poems (句碑, 歌碑). Typical: 石碑を建てる, 石碑に刻む, 石碑に刻まれた文字. 記念碑 stresses the commemorative purpose and can also be made of metal; 墓碑 is specifically the gravestone.

examples[].german: What kind of monument is this?
In the center of the park, there is a memorial to those who died in the war.
To commemorate the 100th anniversary of its founding, a monument was erected in the schoolyard.
en.notes: 記念碑 is a "monument, memorial stone" that commemorates an event or a person: 平和記念碑, 戦没者の記念碑, 記念碑を建てる. The word is factual and neutral. 石碑 stresses stone and inscription; 銅像 is a statue. Figuratively, 記念碑的 means "groundbreaking, epoch-making": 記念碑的な作品.

en.meaning: criminal complaint (by a third party); exposure; denunciation
examples[].german: A citizens' group filed a complaint against the company's illegal acts.
A whistleblower from among the employees brought the data falsification to light.
This film exposes the misery of war.
en.notes: 告発 has two uses: legally, the criminal complaint filed by third parties (刑事告発), whereas the victim himself files a 告訴; and in general, the public denunciation of abuses, e.g. 内部告発 "whistleblowing" or a film that 告発する something. Construction: 〜を告発する. Note: indictment by the public prosecutor is called 起訴, not 告発. Register: formal, news language.

examples[].german: This soup contains five kinds of grain.
Japan depends on imports for much of its grain.
Because of the drought, grain prices have risen worldwide.
en.notes: 穀物 is the umbrella term for "grain" such as rice, wheat, barley, corn and millet - matter-of-fact, used in economics, agriculture and nutrition: 穀物の輸入, 穀物価格, 穀物を栽培する. 穀類 is almost synonymous, but more technical (nutrition science, food groups). 五穀 are the "five grains" in set phrases such as 五穀豊穣 "abundant harvest".

examples[].german: I try to eat grains at every meal.
Let's eat grains, legumes and vegetables in a balanced way.
In this region, grains such as rice and wheat are mainly cultivated.
en.notes: 穀類 "grains, cereals" is a technical collective term, typical in nutrition science and food statistics, often alongside 豆類, 野菜類 or 魚介類. In content it largely coincides with 穀物; 類 stresses the group as a category. In everyday speech people tend to talk concretely about ご飯, パン or 麺.

examples[].german: My grandfather ran a small rice shop in town.
For some time after the war, the state controlled the distribution of rice.
Our company's main business is the import and export of rice.
en.notes: 米穀 is an official and economic word for "rice" as a grain and trade commodity. It is mainly found in compounds such as 米穀店 "rice shop" or in expressions such as 米穀の流通 "rice distribution". In everyday speech one simply says 米 or お米. Beware of the homophone 米国 "USA".

examples[].german: The cause of death was suffocation due to strangulation of the neck.
At New Year, there are many accidents in which people suffocate on rice cakes stuck in the throat.
In this workplace full of rules, I feel like I'm suffocating.
en.notes: 窒息 is "suffocation, asphyxiation" -- medical and factual: 窒息する, 窒息死 "death by suffocation", 餅をのどに詰まらせて窒息する. Figuratively it describes an oppressive atmosphere: 窒息しそうな職場. In everyday speech one says 息が詰まる (also figuratively); むせる, by contrast, only means "to choke, cough".

examples[].german: Driven into a corner, the culprit finally gave himself away.
After a string of scandals, the government is in a tight spot.
With a friend's help, I somehow managed to get out of the predicament.
en.notes: 窮地 is a "dire situation, tight spot". Fixed expressions: 窮地に陥る "to get into a tight spot", 窮地に追い込まれる or 窮地に立たされる "to be driven into a corner", 窮地を脱する "to get out of a predicament", 窮地を救う "to rescue from distress". Elevated, common in the news. 窮状, by contrast, means the wretched condition itself (poverty, distress), 窮地 the cornered position.

examples[].german: Tight underwear is not good for the body.
The economy seat on the plane was cramped, and I couldn't sleep well.
The school rules are strict, so school life feels stifling.
en.notes: 窮屈 first means "tight, cramped" in terms of space (窮屈な靴, 窮屈な席), and figuratively "stiff, unfree, constricting" when rules or surroundings leave no room: 窮屈な規則, 窮屈な思いをする "to feel confined, uncomfortable". Also financially: 予算が窮屈だ "the budget is tight". Unlike 狭い, which only describes size, 窮屈 stresses the unpleasant feeling of being confined.

en.meaning: poverty; hardship; to be in distress
examples[].german: My parents were living in poverty, but I couldn't afford to help them either.
The city announced it would strengthen support for people in financial hardship.
At the sudden question, the minister seemed at a loss for an answer.
en.notes: 困窮 refers to great material "distress, poverty" -- elevated, typical in the news and official language: 生活に困窮する "to live in great hardship", 生活困窮者 "people in need". It can also mean being greatly at a loss over something: 返答に困窮する. In everyday speech one rather says 生活が苦しい or お金に困っている; 貧困 is "poverty" as a social condition.

examples[].german: I appealed to the government office about my plight, but it wasn't heard.
Many volunteers gathered because they couldn't bear to watch the plight of the disaster area.
News reports on the plight of farmers continue.
en.notes: 窮状 is a "plight, predicament" -- mostly economic or social hardship that one describes to others. Fixed combinations: 窮状を訴える "to appeal about one's plight", 窮状を見かねる "to be unable to bear watching the plight", 窮状を救う. Elevated, common in the media and petitions. 窮地 stresses the hopeless position, 窮状 the condition itself.

examples[].german: He was a paragon of the English gentleman.
The men's clothing department is on the third floor.
Opening the door for a woman -- he's a true gentleman.
en.notes: 紳士 is a "gentleman" -- a man with good manners and education: 紳士的な態度 "gentlemanly", 英国紳士, 紳士協定 "gentlemen's agreement". In department stores, 紳士 means "men's": 紳士服, 紳士靴, 紳士用; the counterpart is 婦人 "women's". The address 紳士淑女の皆様 "ladies and gentlemen" sounds ceremonial.

examples[].german: The sewing was done with this sewing machine.
This shirt is carefully sewn and lasts a long time.
Many sewing factories have moved to countries with low labor costs.
en.notes: 縫製 is the commercial, mostly machine "sewing, garment manufacturing" of clothing -- a technical word of the textile industry: 縫製工場 "sewing factory", 縫製工程, 縫製が丁寧だ "neatly made". For sewing at home, one says 縫う or 裁縫. 縫製 often describes the construction quality of a finished garment.

examples[].german: A drug smuggling ring was busted.
The National Tax Agency exposed a major company's tax evasion.
A shop operating without a license was raided by the police.
en.notes: 摘発 means that authorities such as the police, customs or tax investigators uncover violations of the law and take action against them, something like a "raid" or "bust". Mostly in the passive: 〜が摘発される; also 一斉摘発 "mass crackdown", 摘発件数. To be distinguished: 告発 is a complaint by citizens, 検挙 the police identifying and apprehending an offender, 逮捕 the arrest. Register: news and official language.

examples[].german: My uncle often boasted that it was imported brandy.
In the past, things were prized simply for being imported.
An imported fountain pen is carefully stored in my grandfather's study.
en.notes: 舶来 "brought by ship" means "imported, from abroad" and sounds old-fashioned today, with a touch of luxury and admiration for Western goods: 舶来品, 舶来の時計, 舶来のウイスキー. It almost always appears with の or as part of 舶来品. In neutral, modern speech one says 輸入品 or 外国製; the opposite is 国産.

examples[].german: A list of the 100 best unforgettable Showa-era kayōkyoku has been released.
My father is always humming old kayōkyoku in the car.
Recently, Showa-era kayōkyoku have been gaining popularity among young people.
en.notes: 歌謡曲 refers to the Japanese pop music of the Shōwa era -- catchy popular songs with orchestral accompaniment, sung by stars such as 美空ひばり. Today the word sounds nostalgic (昭和歌謡); current pop music is called J-POP, the sentimental ballad form 演歌. In general, 歌謡曲 can also simply mean "popular song".

examples[].german: So this is also an agency under the direct control of the government?
This new business will be pursued as a project directly under the president.
In the Edo period, Nagasaki was land under the direct administration of the shogunate.
en.notes: 直轄 means to administer or place something "directly under" oneself without an intermediate authority: 国が直轄する, 政府直轄の機関, 直轄地 "directly administered territory". Often attributive with の: 社長直轄のプロジェクト "directly under the president", 国の直轄事業. Official and business language; the opposite is 委託 "commissioning, outsourcing".

en.meaning: far away; distant; long ago; far more
examples[].german: The sound of the bell resounded far into the distance.
The dinosaurs went extinct very long ago.
The exam was far harder than I had expected.
en.notes: はるか means "far away" in terms of space (はるか遠く, はるか彼方) and "long ago, a long time back" in terms of time (はるか昔). Very common is はるかに in comparisons: "far more, by far" -- 予想よりはるかに難しい. Mostly written in kana; the kanji 遥か or 遙か seem literary. In comparisons, ずっと is the more spoken alternative.

examples[].german: I don't mind even if it's unpaid.
He tutors the neighborhood children for free.
The work of a board member is unpaid, but it is rewarding.
en.notes: 無報酬 "without payment, unpaid" is factual and mostly appears with で or の: 無報酬で働く, 無報酬で引き受ける, 無報酬の仕事. Unlike 無料 "free of charge" (from the customer's point of view), 無報酬 means that someone receives no fee for their work. Colloquially and often with a complaint, one says ただ働き.

examples[].german: Isn't that a bit anachronistic?
After repeated trial and error, the new product was finally completed.
A contract in which there was a mistake about an important point can be rescinded.
en.notes: 錯誤 "error, mistake, deviation" is an elevated word that, on its own, appears mainly in legal and technical language (in civil law, the "mistake" in a declaration of intent). In everyday speech it is found almost only in fixed compounds: 試行錯誤 "trial and error" and 時代錯誤 "anachronism, out of step with the times". For ordinary mistakes, one says 間違い, ミス or 誤り.

examples[].german: I was overcome by the illusion that it was somehow mine.
The two lines are the same length, but they look different because of an optical illusion.
When the train next to yours starts moving, you sometimes mistake it for your own train moving.
en.notes: 錯覚 is on the one hand a "sensory illusion" (目の錯覚 "optical illusion"), on the other a "false impression" in which one takes something to be true: 〜と錯覚する, 〜ような錯覚に陥る or 錯覚に襲われる "to have the feeling as if ...". Unlike 勘違い (an everyday misunderstanding) or 幻覚 "hallucination", 錯覚 means a misperception of something that is actually there.

examples[].german: He seemed to be delirious from the effects of the medication.
Right after the accident, she fell into a state of delirium.
My father, delirious with a high fever, was shouting things that made no sense.
en.notes: 錯乱 refers to a severe state of mental confusion in which someone can no longer think or act clearly -- for instance through shock, high fever, drugs or medication. Typical are 錯乱状態に陥る "to fall into a state of confusion" and the compound 精神錯乱 "mental derangement"; as an intransitive する-verb: 錯乱する. Unlike 混乱, which can also apply to situations, traffic or thoughts in everyday life ("to be in disarray"), 錯乱 refers only to the state of mind and sounds much more dramatic.

examples[].german: Various emotions were intermingled and we couldn't reach a conclusion.
Torn between hope and anxiety, I waited for the exam results.
Right after the earthquake, information was conflicting and the full extent of the damage couldn't be grasped.
en.notes: 交錯 means that several things cross or intertwine, creating a jumble. Very common are 感情が交錯する "to have mixed feelings", 期待と不安が交錯する and 情報が交錯する "conflicting reports come in"; concretely also for lines, rays of light or paths that cross. It is an intransitive する-verb (〜が交錯する) and rather written language. 混在 stresses only the coexistence, 混乱 the resulting confusion.

examples[].german: His novels depict twisted forms of love.
Making money has become the goal, and means and ends are inverted.
Sexual perversion is one of the subjects of psychiatric research.
en.notes: 倒錯 literally means "reversed and muddled": something is turned upside down, especially values, feelings or sexual behavior. Most common are 性的倒錯 "sexual perversion" and the attributive form 倒錯した (倒錯した愛情, 倒錯した世界). In the sense of "inversion" one says, for example, 価値観が倒錯している or 手段と目的が倒錯している; in everyday speech 本末転倒 or 逆転 are more common for this. The word is written language and sounds technical or literary.

examples[].german: The serial thief was apprehended.
The clearance rate for theft cases in this area is falling year by year.
Speeding cars were caught one after another on the expressway.
en.notes: 検挙 is a police technical term: an offender is identified and proceedings are initiated, with or without arrest. 検挙 is therefore broader than 逮捕 "arrest". Typical: 〜が検挙される, 検挙率 "clearance rate", 検挙件数, also with traffic violations (スピード違反で検挙される). Register: official and news language.

examples[].german: Have you ever visited Yasukuni Shrine?
The prime minister's visit to Yasukuni Shrine drew strong criticism from neighboring countries.
Whether the cherry blossoms have bloomed in Tokyo is judged by the reference tree at Yasukuni Shrine.
en.notes: 靖国神社 is a Shinto shrine in Tokyo (Chiyoda ward, near 九段下) that enshrines the souls of those who died for Japan -- since 1978 also convicted Class A war criminals. Visits by politicians, especially the prime minister (首相の靖国参拝), are therefore sensitive both domestically and diplomatically; the debate is called 靖国問題 for short. For a shrine visit with prayer, one says に参拝する. The reference tree by which the start of the cherry blossom season in Tokyo is announced also stands there.

en.meaning: to get tired of; to grow weary of
examples[].german: I'm just starting to get bored with my new partner.
The same lunch box every day - you really do get sick of it eventually.
I'm sick of hearing that story already.
en.notes: 飽きる means to lose interest in something through repetition or too much of it; the object takes に: ゲームに飽きる. Attached to a verb stem, it forms compounds such as 見飽きる "to have seen enough", 聞き飽きる or 食べ飽きる. 退屈, by contrast, describes boredom because nothing is going on, whereas 飽きる presupposes that one has already had something (too) often. Related are 飽きっぽい "easily bored, fickle" and 飽きが来る "to grow tired of something".

examples[].german: Japan changed greatly from the food shortages of the postwar period to an era of plenty.
Behind the abundance, huge amounts of still-edible food are being thrown away.
People in the past warned against overeating and recommended eating until 80 percent full.
en.notes: 飽食 means to eat one's fill and, figuratively, a state in which food is available in abundance. It is most often found in 飽食の時代 "the age of plenty" as a socially critical catchphrase, often together with topics such as food waste (食品ロス). As a verb (飽食する) it is rare and written language; in everyday speech one says お腹いっぱい食べる. The counterpart is 飢餓 "hunger, famine".

examples[].german: A butterfly fluttered in through the window.
Children are chasing butterflies in the park.
Let's tie your shoelaces firmly in a bow.
en.notes: 蝶々 is a softer, more affectionate form of 蝶 "butterfly"; in speech it is often shortened to ちょうちょ, for example in the children's song 「ちょうちょう」. In factual texts and in biology, 蝶 or katakana チョウ is more common; 蝶々 is used in everyday speech and with children. A fixed combination is 蝶々結び "bow" (on shoelaces or gift ribbon). Moths, by contrast, are 蛾.

examples[].german: Thank you very much for using our company's service this time.
Regarding the details, our person in charge will contact you again.
Our company is currently recruiting engineers.
en.notes: 弊社 is the humble (謙譲) term for one's own company when speaking to customers and business partners, in emails as well as in conversation. The other party's company is then 御社 (spoken) or 貴社 (written). 当社 is neutral and appears in press releases or terms and conditions, for example; among colleagues one simply says うちの会社. Typical is its combination with humble forms: 弊社の担当者からご連絡いたします.

examples[].german: On Sunday, I'm planning to walk the Kumano Kodo and go see Nachi Falls.
Nachi Falls is counted as one of Japan's three most famous waterfalls.
Standing in front of Nachi Falls, I was overwhelmed by the spray and the roar.
en.notes: The 那智の滝 is in Wakayama Prefecture in the Kumano area and, at about 133 m, has the greatest drop of any single-tier waterfall in Japan. Together with 華厳の滝 and 袋田の滝, it is counted among the 日本三名瀑 ("Japan's three most famous waterfalls"). The waterfall itself is worshipped as a deity at the shrine 飛瀧神社 and, together with the pilgrimage route 熊野古道, is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site in the Kii Mountains. Typical: 那智の滝を見に行く, 那智の滝に参拝する.

examples[].german: We must not let our bloodline die out.
He carries on the bloodline of a distinguished samurai family.
Because there was no heir, that family's bloodline came to an end.
en.notes: 血脈 refers to blood kinship or the line of descent of a family; it is written language and elevated. Typical are 血脈を受け継ぐ "to carry on the bloodline" and 血脈が絶える "the line dies out". In everyday speech one rather says 血筋 or 血統 (the latter also for breeding animals); the meaning "blood vessel" is obsolete, and today 血管 is used for it. In Buddhism the word is read けちみゃく and means the transmission of the teaching from master to disciple.

examples[].german: Clownfish live in symbiosis with sea anemones.
Ever since my child saw that movie, he has loved clownfish.
When I went snorkeling in the sea off Okinawa, I found a clownfish.
en.notes: 熊之実 is the clownfish or anemonefish, which lives in symbiosis with sea anemones (イソギンチャク). The kanji spelling is a rare ateji; like most animal and fish names, the word is almost always written in katakana in everyday use: クマノミ. The fish is known mainly from aquariums and from "Finding Nemo" -- Nemo himself is a カクレクマノミ ("false clownfish").

en.meaning: rank; better or worse; A and B
examples[].german: Both are so well done that it's hard to say which is better.
There is no difference in ability between the two who made it to the finals.
I wrote 甲 and 乙 the wrong way around in the contract.
en.notes: 甲 and 乙 are the first two of the ten heavenly stems and therefore stand for "first and second" or "better and worse". 甲乙 almost always appears in 甲乙つけがたい "it is hard to say which is better" (praise for two equally good things) and 甲乙ない / 甲乙なし "equal in value". In contracts, 甲 and 乙 denote the contracting parties ("Party A/B"); 甲乙 together then means both parties. The word is written language; in conversation one rather says どっちもいい.

examples[].german: When felling a forest, prior notification is required.
Because of illegal deforestation, tropical rainforests keep shrinking.
The roadside trees were cut down for road-widening work.
en.notes: 伐採 is the technical or official word for felling trees and clearing forests: 木を伐採する, 森林伐採, 違法伐採 "illegal logging". It is transitive (を); in the passive the tree becomes the subject: 木が伐採された. In everyday speech one says more simply 木を切る or 切り倒す. To be distinguished are 間伐 "thinning" and 開墾 "clearing land for cultivation".

examples[].german: The company told me my pay would be cut by 30 percent.
The manager who overlooked his subordinate's misconduct received a pay-cut penalty.
The pitcher took a significant pay cut because of poor performance.
en.notes: 減俸 is a reduction in salary, usually for a limited period and as a disciplinary penalty, e.g. for civil servants or after a company scandal: 減俸処分, 減俸10%（3か月）. It often stands as a noun or in the passive: 減俸になる/となる, 減俸処分を受ける, 減俸される. In contract negotiations of professional baseball players, too, one often reads of 減俸. 減給 is the more general word for a pay cut; the opposite is 昇給 "raise".

examples[].german: This player was offered an exceptional annual salary, but turned it down and stayed with his team.
Our company has an annual salary system, so the monthly pay is almost always the same.
In the salary negotiations for next season, he won a significant raise.
en.notes: 年俸 is the salary fixed by contract for a whole year, typical of professional athletes, executives and companies with a 年俸制 ("annual salary system"). To be distinguished from it are 年収, the actual annual income from all sources, and 月給, the monthly salary. Typical combinations: 年俸〇億円, 年俸交渉, 年俸がアップする/ダウンする, 年俸で契約する. Note the reading ねんぽう.

examples[].german: Our company uses a special technique to make resin relief printing plates directly at low cost.
In printmaking class, I learned that woodblock printing is a kind of relief printing.
I had our wedding invitations printed by traditional letterpress.
en.notes: 凸版 is a printing form in which the printing areas are raised -- relief printing, as with woodblock prints, stamps or classic letterpress (活版印刷). The counterparts are 凹版 "intaglio", 平版 "planographic printing (offset)" and 孔版 "stencil printing". The word is technical and is found mainly in 凸版印刷 and in art classes. It is also known through the name of the large printing company 凸版印刷 (now TOPPAN).

examples[].german: You have distinct facial features.
The road has many bumps, so it's hard to ride a bicycle.
This foundation makes unevenness in the skin less noticeable.
en.notes: 凹凸 refers to unevenness of a surface -- raised and sunken parts -- and is a noun, not an adjective: 凹凸がある, 凹凸のある道, 肌の凹凸. Figuratively it can also mean inequality or disparity, for example between regions. The synonymous でこぼこ (written 凸凹, with the characters in reverse order) is colloquial and more vivid, while 凹凸 is more written and technical. With faces, 凹凸のはっきりした顔 describes pronounced, sculpted features.

examples[].german: I'm being blackmailed by the yakuza over my affair.
The man was arrested on suspicion of extortion.
He extorted money from his classmates.
en.notes: 恐喝 is extorting money or valuables through threats and also the legal term (恐喝罪 "extortion"). Transitive with を for the victim: 人を恐喝する; very common in the passive 恐喝される or in police reports: 恐喝の容疑で逮捕. 脅迫 is more general "threat, intimidation", without it having to involve money. Colloquially one says ゆする, and among teenagers カツアゲ.

examples[].german: Ōoka Tadasuke served as Edo's town magistrate under the eighth shogun, Yoshimune.
In period dramas, scenes of the magistrate judging villains often appear.
When it comes to hot pot, my father always becomes the pot magistrate.
en.notes: 奉行 was the title of high administrative officials from the Kamakura to the Edo period. Particularly well known are the three offices of the Edo period (三奉行): 寺社奉行 for temples and shrines, 町奉行 for administration, police and jurisdiction in Edo, and 勘定奉行 for finances. In period dramas (時代劇), お奉行様 is the stern judge. Jokingly, 鍋奉行 today is someone who takes charge when eating hot pot.

examples[].german: I sent flowers to express my condolences.
Since I couldn't attend the funeral, I conveyed my condolences by condolence telegram.
Condolences poured in one after another from leaders around the world.
en.notes: 弔意 is the formal word for sympathy at someone's death and appears almost only in fixed combinations: 弔意を表す "to express condolences", 弔意を伝える, 謹んで弔意を表します. It appears in the news, official letters and condolence telegrams (弔電). In conversation one says お悔やみ申し上げます instead; 哀悼の意 is similarly elevated.

examples[].german: Who will read the eulogy?
He gave the eulogy on behalf of the friends.
Many people shed tears at the eulogy read at our beloved teacher's funeral.
en.notes: 弔辞 is the address to the deceased given at the funeral or farewell ceremony (告別式), usually by a close friend or a representative of a company or association. One says 弔辞を読む (the speech is traditionally read from a sheet), 弔辞を述べる or 弔辞を捧げる. Not to be confused with 弔電 "condolence telegram" and 弔意 "condolences"; the word is formal.

examples[].german: First of all, it is important to break that vicious circle.
I fell into a vicious circle: lack of sleep led to more mistakes, and working overtime meant even less sleep.
The vicious circle of rising prices, falling consumption and a still weaker economy continues.
en.notes: 悪循環 is a vicious circle in which cause and effect worsen each other. Typical verbs are 悪循環に陥る "to fall into a vicious circle", 悪循環を断ち切る "to break the vicious circle" and 悪循環が続く. The content is often placed in front with 〜という悪循環. The opposite is 好循環 "virtuous circle".

examples[].german: The Public Safety Commission decided policy on maintaining public order.
Driver's licenses are issued by the prefectural Public Safety Commissions.
The public security police are monitoring the movements of extremists.
en.notes: 公安 means "public safety and order" and appears mainly in fixed agency names: 公安委員会 (the oversight commission of the police, which e.g. issues driver's licenses), 国家公安委員会, 公安条例. As an abbreviation it stands for 公安警察 "security police" or 公安調査庁 (domestic intelligence agency). The general security situation, by contrast, is 治安 (治安がいい), not 公安. Register: official and news language.

examples[].german: Our clinic has five cardiovascular specialists.
My chest pain wouldn't stop, so I went to see a cardiologist.
High blood pressure is a major cause of cardiovascular disease.
en.notes: 循環器 is the medical collective term for the organs of blood circulation, that is, the heart and vessels. In everyday life it appears mainly in medical specialties and names of diseases: 循環器内科 "cardiology", 循環器専門医, 循環器疾患 "cardiovascular diseases". Formed analogously are 消化器 "digestive organs" and 呼吸器 "respiratory organs". The underlying word is 循環 "circulation".

examples[].german: We have really lost a precious person.
So close! I would have passed with one more point.
I'm so absorbed in my research that even the time to sleep feels precious.
en.notes: 惜しい expresses regret that something valuable is being lost or was narrowly missed. As an exclamation, 惜しい！ means "so close!"; 惜しい人を亡くす means "to lose a valued person". In the sense "too precious to give up" it takes が: 命が惜しい, 時間が惜しい, 捨てるのは惜しい. 残念 is general regret, whereas 惜しい presupposes that something good was almost achieved or is too good to waste - close to もったいない.

examples[].german: This video is unpleasant to watch.
We sincerely apologize for causing you an unpleasant experience this time.
Everyone was upset by his rude behavior.
en.notes: 不愉快 describes an unpleasant, irritating feeling, usually triggered by the behavior of others -- more "annoyed, put out" than "physically uncomfortable". Typical are 不愉快な思いをする/させる, 不愉快に思う and 不愉快な態度; it is a な-adjective. 不快 is similar but also covers physical discomfort (不快感, 不快指数); colloquially one simply says 嫌な気分 or むかつく.

examples[].german: She was looking at us with a melancholy expression.
Being prepared means no worries.
He harbored deep concern for the future of the country.
en.notes: 憂い is an elevated word for sorrow, melancholy and worry about the future; it is the noun for 憂う/憂える. Typical are 憂いを帯びた顔 "a melancholy expression", 後顧の憂い "worry about what one leaves behind" and the proverb 備えあれば憂いなし "preparedness means no worries". For rather sad moods, 愁い is also written. In everyday speech one says 心配 or 悩み.

examples[].german: He was reporting fearlessly in all parts of the world.
The young players boldly challenged the powerhouse team.
The firefighter dashed boldly into the burning building.
en.notes: 果敢 describes resolute, bold action despite risk or difficulty. It mostly appears adverbially with に (果敢に挑む, 果敢に攻める) or attributively (果敢な攻撃, 果敢な挑戦). Fixed combinations are 勇猛果敢 "brave and fearless" and 積極果敢. 勇敢 stresses bravery, 大胆 boldness (also in the sense of audacious); 果敢 highlights resolve in action and is rather written language, for example in sports reports.

en.meaning: to dare to do; to carry out boldly
examples[].german: Do you really intend to go through with this operation?
In the middle of the storm, the rescue team went ahead with a nighttime search.
The company dared to make a drastic price cut that defied industry conventions.
en.notes: 敢行 means to resolutely carry something out despite risk, resistance or poor conditions: 作戦を敢行する, 値下げを敢行する, 夜間の捜索を敢行する. It is transitive (を) and written language, typical of the news and reports. 実行 is neutral "to carry out", 決行 stresses sticking to the plan (雨天決行 "held even in rain"), 強行 pushing through against resistance, often with a negative connotation.

examples[].german: She boldly stood up against her company's wrongdoing.
The small country resolutely resisted the pressure of the great power.
While no one objected in the meeting, he fearlessly voiced his objection.
en.notes: 敢然 describes a fearless, resolute approach against danger or resistance. It almost always appears adverbially as 敢然と, especially with 立ち向かう, 戦う, 挑む or 抗議する; the form 敢然たる (敢然たる態度) is rare and very much written language. 果敢 is a な-adjective with a similar meaning (果敢に挑む); 敢然と stresses more the fearless confrontation. Not to be confused with the identically read 完全 "complete".

examples[].german: I think they fought bravely against the title favorite.
A wrestler who had just been promoted to the top division received the Fighting Spirit Prize.
We narrowly lost, but I want to praise the players' valiant effort.
en.notes: 敢闘 means "to fight bravely, to give a good account of oneself" and is used mainly in sports, often as praise for a narrow defeat: よく敢闘した. Best known is 敢闘賞, the Fighting Spirit Prize in sumo, and also 敢闘精神 "fighting spirit". It is an intransitive する-verb and rather written language; in everyday speech one says よく頑張った. 奮闘 is similar but stresses the effort, 健闘 the good performance.

examples[].german: In the parking lot, I practiced figure-eight turns on my motorcycle.
A helicopter has been circling overhead for a while.
A black kite was circling high in the sky, drawing rings.
en.notes: 旋回 refers to circling or a turn, especially of airplanes, helicopters, birds and ships: 上空を旋回する (を marks the space of movement), 左旋回, 急旋回, 旋回半径. Machine parts that swivel around an axis also 旋回する. Figuratively, 大旋回 stands for a U-turn in politics. In everyday speech, for cars one rather says 曲がる or Uターンする; 回転, by contrast, means turning on one's own axis.

examples[].german: Right before the pirates' eyes, the whirlwind turned into a storm.
The new singer's debut song created a sensation in the music world.
A small whirlwind arose on the schoolyard and kicked up dust.
en.notes: 旋風 literally means a whirlwind; in everyday speech one rather says つむじ風 for it, and a tornado is 竜巻. Much more common is the figurative meaning "sensation, stir", almost always in 旋風を巻き起こす "to create a sensation", for example of newcomers in sports, music or politics. Compounds such as 〇〇旋風 ("the XY craze") are also popular in headlines. The word is rather written language.

examples[].german: The Self-Defense Forces were dispatched for disaster relief operations.
My older brother joined the Self-Defense Forces after graduating from high school.
How to position the Self-Defense Forces in the Constitution has been a point of debate for many years.
en.notes: 自衛隊 is the official name of Japan's armed forces; because of Article 9 of the Constitution, the word 軍 "army" is avoided. There are three branches: 陸上自衛隊 (short 陸自), 海上自衛隊 and 航空自衛隊; a member is called 自衛官. Typical: 自衛隊を派遣する, 自衛隊に入る／入隊する, 災害派遣. Register: neutral, also used in everyday speech.

examples[].german: The maple leaves have started to change color, too.
A maple leaf is depicted on the Canadian flag.
My grandfather planted a small maple tree in the garden.
en.notes: 楓 is the maple tree. In everyday speech, for maple -- especially the Japanese maple with red autumn leaves -- one often says もみじ (紅葉); 紅葉 read こうよう, by contrast, means autumn leaf coloring in general. 楓 sounds somewhat more botanical or elevated and is also a popular girl's name. Typical: 楓の葉, 楓の木, 楓が色づく; maple syrup is メープルシロップ.

examples[].german: I often use maple sugar instead of sugar when cooking.
Maple sugar is made by boiling down the sap of the sugar maple.
As a souvenir from my trip to Canada, I bought maple sugar candies.
en.notes: 楓糖 is maple sugar, obtained by boiling down the sap of the sugar maple (サトウカエデ). The word is rare and written language; in everyday speech and on packaging it is almost always メープルシュガー, and the syrup is メープルシロップ. Its components are 楓 "maple" (かえで, also もみじ for the red autumn leaves) and 糖 "sugar".

examples[].german: How often do you clean the aquarium?
We keep the goldfish that my child scooped up at the summer festival in an aquarium.
I inspected the water tank on the roof of the apartment building.
en.notes: 水槽 is generally a water container or tank -- from an aquarium for fish to a water tank on the roof (受水槽, 高架水槽) or a fire-fighting water tank (防火水槽). Typical are 水槽で金魚を飼う, 水槽の水を替える, 熱帯魚の水槽. Note: 水族館 is the aquarium as an institution, 水槽 only the tank itself.

examples[].german: Did you know that Japan provides yen loans to many countries?
The government extended a loan for the construction of a bridge.
The leaders of the two countries signed a new loan agreement.
en.notes: 借款 is a loan, especially between states or from one state to another country; private loans are called ローン, 融資 or 借金. Most common is 円借款 "yen loan", with which Japan finances infrastructure as part of development aid. Typical combinations: 借款を供与する "to extend a loan", 借款協定, 借款を返済する. The word belongs to economic and political language.

examples[].german: An oolong tea without ice, please.
I came by car, so I'll have an oolong tea.
Oolong tea goes well with greasy food.
en.notes: 烏龍茶 is Chinese oolong tea, a semi-fermented tea. The kanji spelling can be seen on the menus of Chinese restaurants, for example; otherwise it is almost always written ウーロン茶. In Japan it is mostly drunk cold from bottles or cans, and in izakaya it is the standard drink for anyone who doesn't drink alcohol; mixed with shōchū it is called ウーロンハイ. Ordering: ウーロン茶をください, ウーロン茶を一つ.

examples[].german: An elderly blind man lives alone in that house.
In the Edo period, many blind people made their living from acupuncture and massage.
Today, the expression "visually impaired person" is more common than 盲人.
en.notes: 盲人 means "blind person". The word is outdated today and felt to be insensitive; in official language and the media one says 視覚障害者, in everyday speech 目の不自由な人. It is still found in historical texts, in literature and in older designations. A common mistake is confusing it with 盲点 "blind spot" or 盲目 "blindness".

examples[].german: The criminal exploited a blind spot in the investigation.
I see -- I hadn't thought of that at all.
The human eye has a blind spot, but normally the brain compensates for that area.
en.notes: 盲点 is first of all the blind spot on the retina, but much more often, figuratively, a point that one overlooks or a gap in a system: 盲点を突く "to exploit a weak point", 盲点になる, 法の盲点 "loophole in the law". The exclamation それは盲点だった means "I hadn't thought of that at all!". Note: the blind spot while driving a car is called 死角, not 盲点.

examples[].german: We have a blind dog.
They say love is blind, and she cannot see his flaws at all.
It is dangerous to follow the boss's instructions blindly.
en.notes: 盲目 literally means "blindness, blind" and takes の: 盲目のピアニスト. More common is the figurative meaning "blind, uncritical", especially in the proverb 恋は盲目 "love is blind" and in the form 盲目的 (盲目的に信じる, 盲目的な愛). For physical blindness the word is considered somewhat sensitive; more neutral are 目が見えない or 視覚障害. Note: 盲目な as a な-adjective is rare; one says 盲目的な.

examples[].german: Can color blindness be cured?
My father is slightly color-blind and has trouble telling red and green apart.
These days, people mostly say "color vision deficiency" rather than 色盲.
en.notes: 色盲 is the traditional term for color blindness or color vision deficiency. The word is considered outdated and discriminatory today; in medicine and in schools one says 色覚異常, and more recently also 色覚多様性. Typical: 赤緑色盲 "red-green color blindness". It is a noun, even though it is often used like a quality (父は色盲だ).

examples[].german: Apparently, putting coarse salt in the bath is good for the body.
Before grilling, sprinkle the fish with coarse salt and let it sit for a while.
We made a small mound of coarse salt at the shop entrance for good luck.
en.notes: 粗塩 (also written 荒塩) is coarse, little-refined salt with residual moisture and minerals, often from seawater. It is used for seasoning and salting (魚に粗塩をふる), but also ritually: for 盛り塩 at the entrance of shops or for purification after a funeral (お清め). The counterpart is 精製塩 or 食卓塩 "refined table salt". Note the reading: あらじお with a voiced じ.

examples[].german: Acts of inciting crowds are prohibited by law.
He was arrested on suspicion of inciting a riot online.
The audience was thrilled by the inflammatory speech.
en.notes: 扇動 means "incitement, agitation" of crowds; also written 煽動. Patterns: 群衆を扇動する, 人々を暴動に扇動する, plus 扇動者 "agitator" and 扇動的な演説 "inflammatory speech". Colloquially one says 煽る for it. そそのかす, by contrast, is inciting a single person to something bad. Do not confuse it with the identically read 先導 "to lead the way, guide".

examples[].german: Whether nuclear weapons function as a deterrent is being debated.
Installing security cameras acts as a deterrent to crime.
The government intends to strengthen deterrence through cooperation with allies.
en.notes: 抑止力 is the ability to keep someone from an action through the threat of countermeasures. In security policy: 核抑止力, 抑止力を高める／強化する, 抑止力として機能する. Also outside the military: punishments or security cameras are a 犯罪の抑止力. The verb for it is 抑止する; to be distinguished from 抑制 "containment, restraint" without the idea of deterrence. Register: formal.

examples[].german: It's handy to have one black suit and one dark navy suit.
That school's uniform is a dark navy blazer.
The evening sky gradually turned a deep dark blue.
en.notes: 濃紺 is a very dark navy blue, darker than 紺 or 紺色. It mostly stands with の before clothing: 濃紺のスーツ, 濃紺の制服, 濃紺のブレザー -- the classic color for business suits and school uniforms. Related color words are 藍色 "indigo" and 群青 "ultramarine"; 紺 alone is more everyday.

en.meaning: to cover comprehensively; to include everything
examples[].german: This guidebook covers almost all the restaurants in the city.
I bought a workbook that covers the entire exam scope.
I started writing my paper after comprehensively surveying past research.
en.notes: 網羅 means to capture something completely and without gaps -- literally "to catch with a net". It is typical of reference works, lists and exam material: 〜を網羅する, 〜を網羅した辞書, 網羅的に調べる "to investigate exhaustively". It is transitive (を) and written language. For "to master a subject" one does not say 網羅 but 把握する or 覚える; 含む, on the other hand, is only "to contain", without a claim to completeness.

examples[].german: At first glance, it looks like a meaningless string of characters.
In the report, don't just list data, but also write your own analysis.
His speech was a string of technical terms and was very hard to understand.
en.notes: 羅列 is a mere lining up of things, usually with a slightly derogatory tone: without order, connection or message. Typical are 文字の羅列, 数字の羅列, 専門用語の羅列 and 事実を羅列する "to merely list facts". Neutral are 列挙 "to enumerate" or 並べる; 羅列 is used more in criticism of texts, speeches or data.

examples[].german: He was the compass of my life.
In the old days, sailors navigated the open oceans relying on the compass.
The compass is one of the three great inventions of the Renaissance, alongside gunpowder and letterpress printing.
en.notes: 羅針盤 is the (ship's) compass; in everyday speech one mostly says コンパス (also for the drawing compass) or 方位磁針/方位磁石. The word sounds historical or elevated and is often used figuratively: 人生の羅針盤 "a compass/guiding principle for life". Together with 火薬 and 活版印刷, the 羅針盤 is counted among the three great inventions of the Renaissance.

examples[].german: On the ultrasound, I could see the fetus stretching and drawing in its legs.
Drinking alcohol during pregnancy has a bad effect on the fetus.
When can you tell the baby's sex?
en.notes: 胎児 is the child in the womb, that is, a fetus or embryo; the word is medical and factual. Typical are 胎児の成長, 胎児に影響する, 胎児の性別 and 胎児期. In conversation one says, more affectionately, お腹の赤ちゃん. After birth one speaks of 新生児 "newborn"; 胎児 is a noun.

examples[].german: It seems she is refusing to have an abortion.
Japan's Penal Code still contains a provision on the crime of abortion.
In the past, abortion was prohibited by law in many countries.
en.notes: 堕胎 is the traditional, legal and written-language word for abortion and has a negative, morally judgmental tone; the Japanese Penal Code still contains the offense 堕胎罪. In medicine and the media, people say neutrally 人工妊娠中絶 or, for short, 中絶, and colloquially 子どもをおろす. As a verb, 堕胎する is possible but rare.

examples[].german: It was confirmed that the mare had conceived successfully.
At the museum, I saw da Vinci's "Annunciation".
Conception is said to be most likely around the day of ovulation.
en.notes: 受胎 is conception, that is, the beginning of a pregnancy; the word is medical or elevated and is also used for animals. Typical are 受胎する, 受胎しやすい時期, 受胎調節 "contraception" and the Christian motif 受胎告知 "the Annunciation". In everyday speech one says 妊娠する "to become pregnant"; 受精 is the biological fertilization of the egg cell.

examples[].german: I had my appendix removed in surgery.
When I was a child, I was in the hospital for a week with appendicitis.
What is commonly called "mōchō" is medically called appendicitis.
en.notes: 盲腸 is anatomically the cecum (caecum). Colloquially, however, it usually means the appendix and above all appendicitis: 盲腸になる "to get appendicitis", 盲腸の手術. Medically correct terms for these are 虫垂 and 虫垂炎. It is a noun.

examples[].german: Colon cancer was found.
E. coli was detected in the well water.
Next week I'm scheduled for a colonoscopy.
en.notes: 大腸 is the large intestine; its counterpart is 小腸 "small intestine", and 腸 alone means the intestines in general. Common compounds are 大腸がん "colon cancer", 大腸菌 "E. coli" and 大腸内視鏡検査 "colonoscopy". It is a medical, factual noun that nevertheless often occurs in everyday life (screening, hygiene).

examples[].german: A treaty on nuclear disarmament was concluded.
After the end of the Cold War, disarmament progressed in many countries.
He appealed that disarmament, not an arms race, is the path to peace.
en.notes: 軍縮 is the short form of 軍備縮小 "arms reduction, disarmament". Typical: 核軍縮, 軍縮条約, 軍縮会議, 軍縮を進める, 軍縮交渉. The opposite is 軍拡 (軍備拡張) "arms buildup", as in 軍拡競争 "arms race". To be distinguished from 不拡散, which aims to prevent the transfer of weapons to new states. Register: political and news language.

examples[].german: Your job is to nip the budding love between the two of them.
The first signs of democracy can be seen in the thought of this era.
In spring, new branches sprout from the tree stump.
en.notes: 萌芽 literally means the sprouting of buds and shoots, and figuratively the first beginnings of a development. The figurative meaning clearly predominates: 〜の萌芽 (近代科学の萌芽, 恋の萌芽), 萌芽が見られる, 萌芽期 "initial phase". It is written language; in everyday speech one says 芽生え or 芽生える. For germinating seeds 発芽 is more usual; 萌芽 is used in botany more for buds and stump sprouts.

examples[].german: She suddenly lost her balance and fell over.
He has an excellent sense of balance and is even good at tightrope walking.
A chemical reaction eventually reaches a state of equilibrium.
en.notes: 平衡 is equilibrium in the physical, bodily and chemical sense: 平衡を保つ/失う, 平衡感覚 "sense of balance", 平衡状態, 化学平衡. In everyday speech one mostly says バランス; 均衡 refers more to a balance of forces or in economics and politics (需要と供給の均衡). Beware of the homophones 平行 "parallel", 並行 "simultaneous" and 閉口 "to be speechless".

examples[].german: We were attacked by pirates in the middle of the voyage.
You must not buy pirated DVDs.
As a child, I loved adventure novels with pirates.
en.notes: 海賊 is a "pirate, sea robber". One is attacked by pirates: 海賊に襲われる. Common compounds are 海賊船 "pirate ship", 海賊行為 "piracy" and especially 海賊版 "pirated copy" (illegally copied DVDs, software, books). The counterpart on land is 山賊 "mountain bandit"; generally, robbers are 盗賊.

examples[].german: They say bandits used to appear on this mountain pass.
The traveler was attacked by bandits and robbed of all his belongings.
The sanzoku-yaki at this restaurant is a specialty.
en.notes: 山賊 are "bandits, highwaymen" who rob travelers in the mountains -- a word found mainly in history, fairy tales and adventure stories. Typical: 山賊が出る "bandits are active", 山賊に襲われる. The counterpart at sea is 海賊, and the more general word is 盗賊. 山賊焼き is a dish from Nagano (fried chicken) and shares only the name with robbers.

examples[].german: This time I'll track down the robbers' hideout!
"Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves" is a famous story.
The castle was attacked by robbers, and its treasures were stolen.
en.notes: 盗賊 means "robbers, thieves", often as a gang -- a rather archaic, narrative word known from fairy tales, period dramas and titles such as 『アリババと四十人の盗賊』. For today's burglar or pickpocket, one says 泥棒, 空き巣 or スリ; in the news 窃盗犯 or 強盗. 盗賊団 is a "gang of robbers".

en.meaning: state guest house; guesthouse for state guests
examples[].german: I was invited to the State Guest House.
The State Guest House in Akasaka is sometimes open to the public.
The summit meeting was held at the Kyoto State Guest House.
en.notes: 迎賓館 is a "guest house for state guests" in which foreign heads of state are received and accommodated. Usually what is meant is the 迎賓館 in Akasaka (Tokyo) or the 京都迎賓館; both can be visited at certain times. For an ordinary guest house, one says ゲストハウス; for a reception hall in hotels, rather ロビー or 宴会場.

examples[].german: Even just once, I wanted to try caviar.
Say that one more time, if you dare!
Even if you tell me so much all at once, I can't remember it.
en.notes: 一遍 is a colloquial variant of 一度 or 一回 "once" and is usually written in kana as いっぺん: もういっぺん "once more". いっぺんに means "all at once, in one go". As a suffix, 一遍 means "only, exclusively", as in 通り一遍 "superficial, pro forma". Not to be confused with the identically read 一変 "complete change".

examples[].german: No matter how many times I watch this movie, I cry.
How many times do I have to tell you?
I've been to Kyoto countless times already.
en.notes: 何遍 is the colloquial counterpart of 何度 or 何回 "how often, how many times". Typical are 何遍も "many times, over and over", 何遍でも "as often as you like" and reproachful questions such as 何遍言ったらわかるの？. With 〜ても it expresses "no matter how often". In written or polite texts, one prefers 何度.

examples[].german: Michael has an interesting romantic history.
In his youth, he traveled through many lands and trained himself along the way.
Her career history is truly varied.
en.notes: 遍歴 originally means "wandering" from place to place (諸国を遍歴する "to travel through many lands"); today, figuratively, it mostly means a sequence of varied experiences: 恋愛遍歴 "love life, past relationships", 職業遍歴 "career path with many stations". It stresses the many and the changeable; a straightforward life history is rather 経歴 or 履歴. Written and elevated.

en.meaning: to interrupt; to block; to shield
examples[].german: It is rude to interrupt someone.
A tall building blocks the sunlight.
A fallen tree blocked our way.
en.notes: 遮る means "to interrupt, to block, to shield" and is transitive with を: 話を遮る "to cut someone off", 視界を遮る "to block the view", 光や風を遮る "to keep out light or wind", 行く手を遮る "to block the way". There is no intransitive counterpart; the passive 遮られる is used. Despite its ending in -いる, it is a godan verb. For stopping a process, one rather says 中断する.

examples[].german: All countries are required to comply with the nuclear nonproliferation treaty.
Japan continues its diplomatic efforts in both disarmament and nonproliferation.
Export controls were tightened toward the nonproliferation of weapons of mass destruction.
en.notes: 不拡散 means "nonproliferation" (拡散 "proliferation" with the negating 不) and appears almost always in combinations such as 核不拡散, 核不拡散条約 (NPT, "Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons") or 大量破壊兵器の不拡散. Frequently in the pair 軍縮・不拡散: 軍縮 reduces existing arsenals, 不拡散 prevents further states or groups from acquiring weapons. Register: technical and diplomatic language.

examples[].german: Access to the website was blocked.
The crossing gate at the railroad crossing came down.
These curtains block almost all of the light from outside.
en.notes: 遮断 is the "cutting off, shielding, interrupting" of a flow or a connection, transitive as 遮断する or passive 遮断される: 交通を遮断する, 電源を遮断する, 光や音を遮断する, 外部との連絡を遮断する. It is technical and factual; for interrupting a conversation, one says 遮る, not 遮断. 遮断機 is the crossing gate at a railroad crossing.

examples[].german: I make bread using my own homemade yeast.
Beer is made by yeast converting sugar into alcohol.
This bakery uses only wild yeast.
en.notes: 酵母 is "yeast" as a microorganism and technical term, for example in 酵母菌, 天然酵母 "natural leaven/wild yeast" and ビール酵母 "brewer's yeast". In everyday cooking, baker's yeast is mostly called イースト or ドライイースト. The process that yeast brings about is 発酵 "fermentation".

examples[].german: Please tell me how to stop fermentation while keeping the wine's sweetness.
Natto is made by fermenting soybeans.
Wait an hour until the bread dough has fermented sufficiently.
en.notes: 発酵 is "fermentation". As a する-verb it is intransitive (生地が発酵する "the dough rises"); for letting something ferment, one says 発酵させる. Important words are 発酵食品 "fermented foods" (味噌, 納豆, ヨーグルト) and 発酵茶. The older spelling 醗酵 still occurs. The opposite is spoilage: 腐敗 or 腐る.

examples[].german: I toured a beer brewery.
Sake has been brewed at this brewery since the Edo period.
Soy sauce is brewed from soybeans and wheat.
en.notes: 醸造 is "brewing" through fermentation, that is, the production of beer, sake, wine, soy sauce, miso or vinegar; transitive: 日本酒を醸造する. The brewery itself is 醸造所, and for sake also 酒蔵. Important is the contrast between 醸造酒 (beer, wine, sake) and 蒸留酒 (whisky, shochu): whisky is distilled in a 蒸留所, not brewed. The base verb 醸す is literary.

examples[].german: For now, let's wait for Father's anger to subside.
It was only when the police arrived that the riot subsided.
After I took the medicine, the pain eased a little.
en.notes: 鎮まる is intransitive: unrest, anger, pain or agitation "subsides, calms down", e.g. 怒りが鎮まる, 暴動が鎮まる, 痛みが鎮まる. The transitive counterpart is 鎮める "to soothe, to suppress". The identically read 静まる is used more for noise and sounds that fall silent (会場が静まる). In everyday speech one often says 収まる as well.

examples[].german: Internet censorship is practiced in this country.
During the war, even letters were censored.
Some scenes of that film were cut by the censors.
en.notes: 検閲 is above all state "censorship" of the press, mail, films or the internet; transitive: 手紙を検閲する, mostly passive 検閲される. Common are ネット検閲, 検閲制度 and 自己検閲 "self-censorship". The second meaning, "inspection" (military), is rare; for ordinary checks, one says 検査 or 点検. Voluntary restraint by the media is rather 自主規制.

examples[].german: That manager is good at boosting the players' morale.
The king's speech fired up the soldiers.
I psyched myself up and ran all the way to the end.
en.notes: 鼓舞 means "to fire up, to encourage, to rouse", literally "to drum and dance". It is written language and typically occurs with 士気を鼓舞する "to raise morale" or 人々を鼓舞する; also 自らを鼓舞する "to psych oneself up". In everyday speech one says 励ます (to comfort/encourage an individual) or 盛り上げる; 激励 is the formal giving of encouragement.
