The official weather forecast is 予報 (天気予報); 予想 is the expectation itself. 予測 is similar but more data-based and technical, while 期待 is a hopeful expectation.

examples[].german: You shouldn't make baseless speculations.
The company president's sudden resignation gave rise to various speculations.
Let's stop speculating this and that before we know the facts.
en.notes: 憶測 (also written 臆測) is a "conjecture, speculation" without a secure basis and usually has a critical undertone. The verb 憶測する exists, but the noun is more common in set phrases: 憶測を呼ぶ ("to give rise to speculation"), 憶測が飛び交う ("speculation is rife"), 憶測で物を言う ("to talk without any basis"). More neutral are 推測 ("guess, inference") and 予想. Typical of news and written language.

en.meaning: to presuppose; to take as a premise
examples[].german: This discussion presupposes the agreement of everyone.
This price assumes a two-year contract.
I am going out with him with a view to marriage.
en.notes: 前提とする means "to presuppose, to proceed from ...": 〜を前提とする, adverbially 〜を前提として or shortened 〜を前提に. Well known is 結婚を前提に付き合う ("to be together with serious intent to marry"); 〜ことが前提だ means "the prerequisite is that ...". The expression is neutral to formal and common in contracts, discussions and business language. 条件 is an explicitly stated "condition", whereas 前提 is the basis on which something tacitly builds.

en.meaning: to see through; to foresee; to look out over
examples[].german: He had foreseen how things would develop in the future.
My mother saw right through all my lies.
From the top of this hill, you can look out over the whole town.
en.notes: 見通す literally means "to look far over, to see through", figuratively "to look ahead, to foresee" and "to see through (someone)": 将来を見通す, 相手の心を見通す. The noun 見通し is even more common in daily life: 見通しが立たない ("to be unforeseeable"), 見通しが甘い ("to be too optimistic in one's outlook"), 見通しのいい道 ("a road with good visibility"). Compared with 予想する, 見通す stresses a wide view over a whole development; 見抜く is "to see through, to expose" in the sense of recognizing deception.

examples[].german: I applied for a passport renewal.
I applied to the university for a scholarship, but I haven't heard back yet.
When you apply for paid leave, please tell your supervisor at least a week in advance.
en.notes: 申請する means "to apply (to an authority or institution)": ビザを申請する, 奨学金を申請する, 〜に…を申請する. The form is called 申請書, the procedure 申請手続き. Unlike 申し込む ("to sign up, to apply", e.g. for courses or events), 申請 is formal and is examined and approved (許可, 受理). 申告する, by contrast, means "to declare", for example at customs or for taxes.

examples[].german: Every March, one has to file a tax return.
I have nothing to declare at customs.
Because he did not report his side-job income, he later had to pay taxes.
en.notes: 申告する means to "declare, report" something to an authority that one is obliged to: 所得を申告する, 税関で申告する. Best known is 確定申告 ("income tax return"), which in Japan is filed from mid-February to mid-March. At customs, the question is 申告するものはありますか ("Do you have anything to declare?"). Unlike 申請する ("to apply for"), you do not ask for anything but communicate facts; 届け出る is the more general "to report (officially)".

examples[].german: After moving, you need to report your change of address.
My wallet was stolen, so I reported it to the police right away.
If you are absent because of illness, please notify the school.
en.notes: 届け出る means to officially "report, notify, register" something with an office: 警察に届け出る, 市役所に出生を届け出る. The office takes に, the reported matter を. The related noun 届け出 or 届 appears in 婚姻届 ("marriage registration") or 欠席届 ("notice of absence"). 届ける alone means "to deliver, to bring", but also "to hand in (lost property)": 落とし物を交番に届ける.

examples[].german: Please submit your report by the deadline.
After submitting my resume, I noticed a mistake.
The government submitted a new bill to the Diet.
en.notes: 提出する means "to submit, hand in, present" and is used for documents, homework, applications or evidence: 宿題を提出する, 書類を役所に提出する. Typical are 提出期限 ("submission deadline") and 〜までに提出する. In parliament it means "to introduce a bill": 法案を提出する. More colloquial is 出す ("to hand in"); 申請する, on the other hand, refers to the application itself, not to handing in papers.

en.meaning: to accept (a document); to receive officially
examples[].german: The application was formally accepted.
I submitted my resignation to the department head, but he won't accept it.
Because required documents were missing, the application was not accepted.
en.notes: 受理する means to officially "accept, receive" a submitted document and thereby take it up for processing: 申請を受理する, 辞表を受理する ("to accept a resignation letter"). It is a formal official and business word and is usually in the passive: 書類が受理された. Important: 受理 only means that something was formally accepted; no decision on approval (許可, 認可) has been made yet. The opposite is 却下 ("rejection") or 不受理.

examples[].german: The new drug was finally approved.
The establishment of the new university was approved by the state.
I want to put my child in a licensed daycare center, but there are no openings.
en.notes: 認可する means that an authority officially "approves, permits, licenses" something: 国が設立を認可する, 認可を受ける/得る. Typical compounds are 認可保育園 ("state-licensed daycare") and 無認可 ("unlicensed"). Compared with 許可する ("to allow", also in everyday use), 認可 is an administrative term for companies, schools, products or fees. For medicines, 承認 is usually used in technical contexts.

examples[].german: She remarried and is living happily.
My father remarried five years after my mother died.
My new spouse has two children in elementary school.
en.notes: 再婚 is "remarriage"; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜と再婚する. The new partner is called 再婚相手. The counterpart is 初婚 ("first marriage"), e.g. in statistics. The word is neutral and is used both after divorce and after being widowed.

examples[].german: His proposal was rejected at the meeting.
My visa application was rejected, so I gave up the trip.
"Let's make it a three-day weekend." "Rejected!"
en.notes: 却下する means to "reject, dismiss" an application, proposal or demand: 申請を却下する, 提案が却下される, mostly in the passive. It is formal but is also used jokingly in everyday life (却下! "Rejected!"). In court, 却下 means dismissal on formal grounds without examining the merits, whereas 棄却 is dismissal after examining the merits. More general and less official is 断る ("to decline, to refuse").

examples[].german: The court dismissed the lawsuit.
The High Court dismissed the defendant's appeal.
As a result of analyzing the data, the initial hypothesis was rejected.
en.notes: 棄却する is a legal technical term: a court dismisses a lawsuit, appeal or motion as unfounded after examining the merits: 訴えを棄却する, 控訴が棄却される. By contrast, 却下 refers to dismissal as inadmissible on formal grounds. Outside law, the word appears in statistics: 仮説を棄却する ("to reject a hypothesis"). In everyday life it practically appears only in the news.

examples[].german: The plaintiff withdrew the lawsuit.
Because there was a lot of opposition, I decided to withdraw my proposal.
Since I had found a job, I withdrew my scholarship application.
en.notes: 取り下げる means to "withdraw" of one's own accord something one has submitted or put forward oneself: 訴えを取り下げる, 申請を取り下げる, 提案を取り下げる. Unlike 却下される (being rejected by the other side), the action here comes from the applicant themselves. The noun is 取り下げ. For taking back a statement or promise, 撤回する is more fitting.

examples[].german: A new student ID card has been issued.
Excuse me, could you issue a receipt?
This magazine is published once a month.
en.notes: 発行する means "to issue, publish" and is used for printed matter (雑誌を発行する), documents (証明書・パスポートを発行する), banknotes, shares and tickets. In everyday speech you often hear 領収書を発行する ("to issue a receipt") or パスワードを再発行する. 発行 stresses that an authority officially produces and issues something; 交付 stresses handing it over to a person, 発給 the official issuing of passports and visas. 発行部数 is the "circulation."

examples[].german: A driver's license was issued.
My Number cards are issued at the city hall counter.
The city granted a subsidy for moving expenses.
en.notes: 交付する is an official word for the formal "handing over, issuing" of documents or funds by an authority: 免許証を交付する, 補助金を交付する. From the recipient's viewpoint it usually appears in the passive (〜が交付される) or as 交付を受ける. At counters you often read 交付窓口 ("issuing counter"). Compared with 発行 (creating and issuing), the focus is on handing over to the entitled person; in everyday speech one simply says 渡す or もらう.

examples[].german: Visas are issued at the embassy.
Issuing a passport usually takes about a week.
That country temporarily suspended the issuance of visas to tourists.
en.notes: 発給する is an official expression for the "issuing" of passports, visas or permits by an authority: ビザを発給する, 旅券の発給. It appears almost only in administrative texts, on embassy websites and in the news, mostly in the passive. Compared with the broader 発行 (also for magazines, receipts, etc.), 発給 is limited to such papers; in everyday speech people often simply say ビザが出る or ビザが下りる.

en.meaning: to renew; to update; to break (a record)
examples[].german: I went to the police station to renew my driver's license.
If your address changes, please update your registration information.
She broke the Japanese marathon record.
en.notes: 更新する means "to renew, to extend, to update", translated differently depending on the object: 契約・免許を更新する ("to renew"), 情報・ページを更新する ("to update"), 記録を更新する ("to break a record"). In IT it is the standard word for "update" or "reload" (ページを更新する); アップデート is also widespread. In contrast to 新しくする ("to make new"), 更新 usually means continuing something existing in a new version. Often in the passive: 世界記録が更新された.

examples[].german: A restart is required to enable the new settings.
For safety, please enable two-factor authentication.
Expired points cannot be reactivated.
en.notes: 有効にする means "to make valid, to activate, to make effective" and is the standard word for "to enable, to turn on" above all in IT instructions: 機能を有効にする, 設定を有効にする. Opposite: 無効にする ("to disable"). Grammatically it is the na-adjective 有効 + にする ("to make into ..."); as a state one says 有効になっている. On its own, 有効 means "valid" (このチケットは三日間有効だ) or "effective" (有効な方法).

examples[].german: I invalidated the old password.
There were too many notifications, so I disabled notifications for this app.
If you lose your card, contact the bank right away and have it canceled.
en.notes: 無効にする means "to make invalid, to nullify, to disable": パスワードを無効にする, 契約を無効にする. In software menus it is the counterpart of 有効にする ("to enable"). Grammatically: na-adjective 無効 ("invalid, ineffective") + にする; the state is called 無効になる ("to become invalid"), for example with expired coupons. Note: 無効 (むこう) sounds exactly like 向こう ("over there, the other side").

en.meaning: to enforce; to put into effect
examples[].german: The new law will take effect next month.
This regulation has not been changed even once since it came into force.
The government is making preparations for the enforcement of the law.
en.notes: 施行する means to put a law or ordinance into effect: 法律を施行する, 〜から施行される. It mostly appears in the passive with a time expression; the noun occurs in 施行日 ("effective date"). To distinguish it from 試行 ("trial run"), jurists sometimes read it せこう. Distinguish it from 実施 ("to carry out", e.g. surveys, exams) and 制定 ("to enact"): a law is first 制定 and then 施行. Very formal, typical of news and official texts.

examples[].german: An event for married people was held.
I circled "married" in the "married/unmarried" box of the questionnaire.
This survey was conducted on married male employees.
en.notes: 既婚 ("married") almost never stands alone but in compounds or with の: 既婚者, 既婚の女性, 既婚・未婚. It is a formal, often statistical or official expression. In conversation, people say 結婚している. Antonyms are 未婚 ("never married") and 独身 ("unattached").

examples[].german: The international student was exempted from tuition fees.
Those who hold JLPT N2 are exempt from the written exam.
If income is low, one may be exempted from paying insurance premiums.
en.notes: 免除する means to exempt someone from an obligation, fee or exam, or to waive it for them: 授業料を免除する, 試験を免除する. In the passive, the person takes は and the waived item takes を, or the item is the subject with が: 学生は授業料を免除された / 授業料が免除された. Common compounds: 授業料免除, 免除申請, 一部免除 ("partial exemption"). It is formal; unlike 許す ("to forgive, allow"), it concerns a regulated, official exception.

examples[].german: To convert hiragana into kanji.
Please convert these documents to PDF before sending them.
Because of a conversion error, a strange kanji got into the email.
en.notes: 変換する means "to convert, to transform" and refers to changing from one form into another: AをBに変換する. In everyday life it is met mainly on the computer: ひらがなを漢字に変換する (kanji conversion while typing), ファイルをPDFに変換する, 変換ミス ("error in kanji conversion"). In technology it is used e.g. as 電気を熱に変換する. Unlike 変更する ("to change") and 変える ("to alter"), the content stays the same and only the form changes.

examples[].german: I changed the schedule of the meeting.
Because of the rain, the venue of the game has been changed.
We are told to change our passwords every three months.
en.notes: 変更する means "to change, alter" - above all plans, dates, settings and rules: 予定を変更する, パスワードを変更する. In announcements, 〜が変更になりました ("has been changed") often appears. Compared with 変える, it is more factual and formal; unlike 変換 ("to convert the form") and 改正 ("to amend a law"), it is the general word for changes to something that has been fixed. Common compounds: 変更点 ("change"), 予定変更, 住所変更.

examples[].german: A national referendum is required to amend the constitution.
The law was revised, and people now become adults at eighteen.
We amended the club's rules so that new members can also vote.
en.notes: 改正する means to formally "amend, revise" laws, regulations or rules: 法律を改正する, 憲法改正, 〜の一部を改正する. It belongs to legal and news language; the objects are almost always norms. To be distinguished are the two かいてい words 改定 ("to reset prices, rates") and 改訂 ("to revise texts, books"). 改革 is a more comprehensive "reform" of systems.

examples[].german: Fees will be revised from next month.
The company revised its salary regulations in April.
The minimum wage was revised, and the hourly wage went up by 50 yen.
en.notes: 改定する means to revise established values such as prices, fees, wages or sets of rules: 料金を改定する, 運賃改定, 価格改定のお知らせ. In company announcements it is often the neutral way of saying a price increase. Do not confuse it with the identically read 改訂 ("to revise texts", e.g. textbooks) and with 改正 ("to amend laws"). Very formal, typical of notices, official letters and news.

examples[].german: The textbook was revised for the first time in ten years.
This dictionary was revised with new words added.
We have revised the manual, so please use the new edition.
en.notes: 改訂する means to revise the content of an existing text - a book, dictionary, manual, curriculum - and bring out a new edition: 教科書を改訂する, 辞書の改訂版 ("revised edition"). The character 訂 ("to correct") points to the written word, as in 訂正. Do not confuse it with the identically read 改定 ("to revise prices, fees") and with 改正 ("to amend laws"). The word is formal and typical of publishers and educational institutions.

examples[].german: It is necessary to correct the unfair system.
The government announced policies to reduce the gap between rural areas and cities.
After being told it had too much overtime, the company changed how its employees work.
en.notes: 是正する means to correct or remedy a problem or inequality: 格差を是正する, 不平等を是正する, 長時間労働の是正. The object is almost always a social or organizational problem, not an individual mistake - for typos or calculation errors one says 訂正する or 直す. The word is formal and typical of politics, administration and news; authorities issue, for example, a 是正勧告 ("recommendation to rectify").

examples[].german: I go to the dentist to have my teeth straightened.
I stretch every day to correct my bad posture.
It is said that forcibly correcting left-handedness is not good.
en.notes: 矯正する means to deliberately "correct, straighten" something crooked or a bad habit: 歯並びを矯正する, 姿勢を矯正する, 視力を矯正する ("to correct poor eyesight", e.g. with glasses). Well known is 歯列矯正 ("orthodontic treatment, braces"). Unlike 是正 (social ills) and 訂正 (errors in texts), 矯正 mostly concerns the body or behavior. In the justice system it also refers to the rehabilitation of offenders.

examples[].german: I adjusted the brightness of the photo.
This camera has an image stabilization function.
The government drew up a supplementary budget for disaster countermeasures.
en.notes: 補正する means to "correct, readjust" values or deviations by supplementing or compensating: 明るさを補正する, 誤差を補正する. It is common in technology and photography (手ぶれ補正 "image stabilization", 色補正 "color correction") and in budget politics: 補正予算 ("supplementary budget"). Unlike 修正 ("to correct, to change"), 補正 stresses adjusting to a target value.

examples[].german: I adjusted my schedule and attended the meeting.
I adjusted the height of the chair to make the screen easier to see.
The date and time of next week's meeting is currently being arranged.
en.notes: 調整する means "to adjust, to set, to coordinate", both technically and organizationally: 音量・温度を調整する ("to adjust"), 日程を調整する ("to coordinate schedules"), 意見を調整する ("to bring opinions into line"). In the business world, 調整中 ("being arranged") is a common answer, often also an evasive one. Unlike 調節 (technically regulating amounts or degrees, e.g. 温度調節), 調整 also includes coordinating between people.

examples[].german: The rate of unmarried people is rising.
She raised her child alone as an unmarried mother.
It is no longer unusual for people in their forties to be unmarried.
en.notes: 未婚 means "(still) never married" and is used with の or in compounds: 未婚の母, 未婚率, 未婚化, 未婚者. Unlike 独身 ("unattached, single"), which also includes divorced people, 未婚 refers only to people who have never been married. Rather formal and common in statistics or news.

examples[].german: It took time to adapt to the new environment.
This plant can adapt even to cold climates.
Companies that cannot adapt to changing times will not survive.
en.notes: 適応する means "to adapt" to an environment or situation and is intransitive: 環境に適応する, 変化に適応する. Typical are 適応力 ("adaptability") and, in psychology, 適応障害 ("adjustment disorder"). Unlike 慣れる ("to get used to"), it sounds more factual and stresses active adjustment. Do not confuse it with 適用 ("to apply a rule") and 対応 ("to respond to something").

examples[].german: It is important to deal with problems calmly.
We talked as a family about how to handle things when an earthquake occurs.
The person in charge will deal with complaints from customers.
en.notes: 対処する means to respond appropriately to a problem or situation: "to deal with, handle, take measures": 問題に対処する, トラブルに対処する. The problem takes に; typical adverbs are 冷静に, 迅速に, 適切に. It is neutral to formal. 対応する is similar but broader (also "to serve customers, correspond to"), whereas 対処 specifically means coping with a difficulty; 処理する stresses working through tasks or data.

en.meaning: to process; to handle; to deal with
examples[].german: I processed a large amount of data in a short time.
I have to deal with all the accumulated emails today.
This factory treats the dirty water until it is clean before releasing it into the river.
en.notes: 処理する means to "handle, deal with, process" things or tasks: 仕事を処理する, データを処理する, ゴミを処理する ("to dispose of or treat garbage"). In IT, 処理 is "processing, operation" (処理速度, 処理中). Unlike 対処する (reacting to a problem), the focus is on working through something in a matter-of-fact way; 処分する, on the other hand, means "to get rid of, dispose of" or "to punish." The word is neutral and very common in offices, administration and technology.

en.meaning: to dispose of; to deal with; to punish
examples[].german: I decided to get rid of the old furniture.
Please dispose of broken appliances according to the city's rules.
The company disciplined the employee who leaked information.
en.notes: 処分する first means "to get rid of, dispose of, sell off": 古い家具を処分する, 不用品を処分する. Second, it means "to punish, take disciplinary action against": 社員を処分する, 停学処分 ("temporary suspension from school"), 懲戒処分 ("disciplinary action"). Unlike 捨てる ("to throw away"), 処分 is more neutral and also includes selling or giving away. With animals it is a euphemism for "to kill, put down".

examples[].german: Expired food was disposed of.
Please dispose of documents with personal information in a shredder.
Before we discard the old computer, let's erase the data completely.
en.notes: 廃棄する means to officially dispose of or destroy something unusable or superfluous - typically food, files, old appliances or industrial waste: 書類を廃棄する. The word is factual-formal and sounds like a company or authority; in everyday speech people mostly just say 捨てる "to throw away". Common derivations are 廃棄物 "waste" and 食品廃棄 "food waste". In reports the passive 廃棄される often appears.

examples[].german: The government retracted its statement.
In response to residents' opposition, the city withdrew its construction plan.
I take back what I said just now. I went too far.
en.notes: 撤回する means to officially "take back, withdraw" a statement, application or decision already made: 発言を撤回する, 前言を撤回する, 処分を撤回する. It is formal and typical of politics, law and company announcements; the retraction is often demanded: 撤回を求める. Unlike 取り消す (generally "to undo, to cancel", also reservations), 撤回 stresses withdrawing a position one has taken.

examples[].german: Unnecessary regulations should be abolished.
The two countries agreed to eliminate tariffs on imported goods.
At this company the dress code was abolished, and people can now work in casual clothes.
en.notes: 撤廃する means to completely "abolish" or "lift" existing rules, systems or restrictions: 規制を撤廃する, 関税を撤廃する, 差別を撤廃する. It is a formal word from politics, business and the news. Unlike 撤回 (taking back a statement or decision), 撤廃 is directed against existing institutions. Similar is 廃止する "to abolish"; 緩和する, by contrast, only means "to relax, to ease".

en.meaning: to compile; to put together; to broker
examples[].german: I compiled the opinions of each department and reported them.
Please collect the names of those who wish to participate by Friday.
The company president stepped in and brought the contract between the two firms to a conclusion.
en.notes: 取りまとめる means to "collect and combine into a whole" scattered opinions, data or documents: 意見を取りまとめる, 報告書を取りまとめる. A second meaning is to "bring to a conclusion" negotiations or a deal: 契約を取りまとめる. Compared with plain まとめる it sounds more formal and stresses the coordinating role; typical in the office and in the news. The noun 取りまとめ is also common, e.g. 取りまとめ役 "coordinator".

examples[].german: It is dangerous to make definitive claims without evidence.
The police concluded that the fire was arson.
At this point, we cannot say definitively which is correct.
en.notes: 断定する means to "declare" something as established with certainty or to "determine definitively", often in the pattern Xを〜と断定する: 警察は事故と断定した. Common is the negative 断定できない "cannot be said with certainty". Unlike 主張する ("to assert, to advocate one's opinion"), it concerns a final judgment. In grammar, 断定 denotes the definite form of statement with だ or である.

en.meaning: to be convinced; to be confident
examples[].german: I am convinced of his innocence.
The moment the goal was scored, we were certain of victory.
Honestly, I'm not confident that this method is right.
en.notes: 確信する means "to be firmly convinced" that something is true or will happen. Typical patterns are Xを確信する (勝利を確信する) and 〜と確信する; for the ongoing state 確信している is usual. As a noun: 確信がある/ない "to be sure / not sure", 確信を持つ. 信じる is simple "to believe"; 確信 stresses certainty. Do not confuse it with the homophone 革新 "innovation".

examples[].german: I like reading romance novels.
My parents did not have an arranged marriage but a love marriage.
I'm so busy with work right now that romance is out of the question.
en.notes: 恋愛 refers to romantic love as a relationship or topic, in a rather matter-of-fact way: 恋愛小説, 恋愛結婚 (love marriage, as opposed to お見合い結婚), 恋愛感情, 恋愛中. As an intransitive する-verb (恋愛する) it is less common than 付き合う. The feeling of being in love itself is more 恋 (恋をする), all-embracing love 愛.

en.meaning: to realize; to perceive; to attain enlightenment
examples[].german: I realized my mistake and reflected on it deeply.
Seeing his expression, I realized it was already too late.
I put on a smile so that the other person wouldn't sense that I was nervous.
en.notes: 悟る means to inwardly "realize" or "grasp" something unspoken or deeper: 自分の過ちを悟る, 〜と悟る, 死期を悟る. It sounds more literary than 気づく "to notice" or 分かる "to understand" and stresses a sudden, often painful insight. In the passive, 悟られる means "to be seen through": 相手に悟られないように "so that the other person doesn't notice". In Buddhism, 悟りを開く means "to attain enlightenment".

examples[].german: Silence may be regarded as consent.
If you are absent three times without notice, you will be regarded as having left the club.
He is regarded as the team's key player.
en.notes: 見なす means "to regard as, consider as" and appears in the pattern AをBと見なす; the passive AはBと見なされる is very common. It expresses a judgment or a (often rule-based) determination, even when it does not fully match reality: 欠席と見なす "to treat as absent". It is often written entirely in kana (みなす). Compared with 考える or 思う, it is more formal and sounds like a rule or assessment.

examples[].german: The organization was restructured to improve efficiency.
From next fiscal year, the bus routes are scheduled to be extensively reorganized.
Because of the declining birthrate, it was decided to reorganize the elementary schools in the city.
en.notes: 再編する means to "reorganize" or "restructure" organizations, structures or networks: 組織を再編する, 路線を再編する. It is a formal word from business, politics and administration and often appears as a noun in combinations such as 業界再編 "industry restructuring" or 再編成. Unlike 改革 "reform", it is about regrouping, merging or splitting parts. In the news, the passive 再編される is common.

en.meaning: to ease; to relax; to alleviate
examples[].german: Entry restrictions were eased.
This medicine has the effect of alleviating pain.
Thanks to the new road, the traffic jam in front of the station has eased considerably.
en.notes: 緩和する means to "ease" or "alleviate" restrictions, tensions or burdens: 規制を緩和する, 渋滞を緩和する, 痛みを緩和する, 緊張を緩和する. It is used transitively (Xを緩和する); the passive 緩和される is especially common. The word is formal and typical of news, politics and medicine. For rules, the opposite is 強化する "to tighten"; 撤廃する goes further and abolishes them completely.

examples[].german: This road is closed to traffic because of construction.
The road ahead is one-way, so you can't enter from here.
In Japan, cars drive on the left side of the road.
en.notes: 通行 denotes the "passing" of people or vehicles at a point, i.e. passage or transit. Common combinations: 通行止め "road closure," 通行人 "passerby," 一方通行 "one-way street," 左側通行 "left-hand traffic," 通行料 "toll." As an intransitive する-verb, the route takes を: 左側を通行する. Compared with 交通 (traffic and transport in general, 交通事故), 通行 means concretely walking or driving through.

examples[].german: Pedestrians, please use the crosswalk.
On Sundays, Ginza becomes a pedestrian zone.
An accident occurred at the intersection in which a car hit a pedestrian.
en.notes: 歩行者 is the formal expression for "pedestrian" and is typical of traffic signs, traffic rules and accident reports; in conversation people more often say 歩いている人. Important combinations: 歩行者天国 "temporarily car-free pedestrian zone", 歩行者優先 "pedestrians have priority", 歩行者用信号 "pedestrian signal". Opposites are 運転者 or ドライバー and 自転車.

examples[].german: The automobile industry supports Japan's economy.
On rainy days I go to the station by car.
en.notes: 自動車 is the formal term for a car or motor vehicle. In conversation the shorter 車 is often used instead. In 自動車産業 the noun stands before 産業 and means the automobile industry. In 自動車で行く, で marks the means of transport used.

examples[].german: Passenger car sales are increasing.
A passenger car and a motorcycle collided at the intersection.
This parking lot is for passenger cars only; trucks cannot park here.
en.notes: 乗用車 is the technical term for "passenger car" as opposed to commercial vehicles such as トラック or バス. It is found in statistics, news and accident reports; in everyday speech people simply say 車 or 自動車. It is counted with 台. Combinations: 軽乗用車 "kei car", 普通乗用車 "regular passenger car", 乗用車専用 "passenger cars only".

examples[].german: The truck carried the cargo to the factory.
Because of the weight limit, large trucks cannot cross this bridge.
A locomotive was pulling a long line of freight cars.
en.notes: 貨物車 is a factual, technical collective term for vehicles that carry goods (貨物). On the road it means trucks (formally 貨物自動車), for example in statistics as the opposite of 乗用車; on the railway it denotes a freight car, for which the shorter 貨車 is usually used. In everyday speech people almost always say トラック for a truck.

examples[].german: A large truck is driving on the expressway.
I rented a small truck for the move.
My father is a long-distance truck driver.
en.notes: トラック is the normal everyday word for "truck, lorry"; the driver is called トラック運転手 or ドライバー. It is counted with 台; sizes: 軽トラック (short 軽トラ) "small truck", 大型トラック "heavy truck". Note: a homonym トラック means "track" in a stadium (陸上のトラック) or a "track" on a CD; context clarifies the meaning. Formal counterparts are 貨物車 or 貨物自動車.

examples[].german: I had an unrequited love in high school.
I finally confessed to the senior I'd had a crush on for so long.
In the end, that love ended as unrequited.
en.notes: 片思い (literally "one-sided thinking of someone") is "unrequited love", when the other person does not know or share the feelings. Typical: 〜に片思いする／している, 片思いの相手, 片思いのまま終わる. The opposite is 両思い ("mutual love"). Neutral to colloquial, very common in daily life.

examples[].german: The police car was chasing the criminal.
Several police cars with sirens blaring passed by.
At night, police cars patrol this area.
en.notes: パトカー is the common short form of パトロールカー "patrol car, police car". Typical combinations: パトカーが出動する, パトカーに追われる, パトカーが巡回する; the siren is called サイレン. It is counted with 台. Related vehicles are 救急車 "ambulance" and 消防車 "fire engine"; the police motorcycle is called 白バイ.

examples[].german: It takes two and a half hours to Osaka by limited express train.
Many trains were cancelled because of the heavy snow.
I took an overnight train and arrived in Hokkaido in the morning.
en.notes: 列車 is the more formal, railway-technical term for "train" as a scheduled train service, typical in announcements, timetables and the news: 普通列車, 特急列車, 夜行列車, 列車が遅れる. In everyday speech people mostly say 電車, especially for local transport; 汽車 is outdated. A single car is 車両. Trains are counted with 本.

examples[].german: By Shinkansen, it takes about two hours from Tokyo to Kyoto.
I reserved a reserved seat on the Shinkansen in advance.
Now that the Shinkansen runs all the way to Kyushu, it has become very convenient.
en.notes: 新幹線 is Japan's high-speed railway; the word denotes both the line (東海道新幹線) and the individual train. You travel with で (新幹線で行く) and board with に (新幹線に乗る). The train types have names such as のぞみ, ひかり or こだま. For tickets, a distinction is made between 指定席 "reserved seat" and 自由席 "non-reserved seat".

examples[].german: You can get to the airport by monorail.
You can see the sea well from the monorail window.
The city is planning to build a monorail as a measure against traffic congestion.
en.notes: モノレール is a "monorail"; well known in Japan are, for example, the 東京モノレール to Haneda Airport and the line in Naha on Okinawa. Grammatically it is treated like 電車: モノレールで行く, モノレールに乗る. In urban planning it is considered a space-saving means of transport because it runs above the streets.

examples[].german: A helicopter was dispatched for the rescue.
Several helicopters are flying overhead.
On the trip, I rode in a helicopter and enjoyed the night view from above.
en.notes: ヘリコプター means "helicopter"; colloquially often shortened to ヘリ, e.g. ドクターヘリ "rescue helicopter". Typical combinations: ヘリコプターが出動する/飛ぶ/着陸する, ヘリコプターで運ぶ. It is counted formally with 機, in everyday speech also with 台. The landing site is called ヘリポート.

examples[].german: A large ship came into the harbor.
It takes an hour to get to the island by boat.
As soon as I get on a boat, I feel sick.
en.notes: 船 is the general word for ship and boat: 船に乗る, 船で行く, 船が港に着く; 船酔い is "seasickness". Small rowing boats are often called ボート, and 舟 (same reading) is written for small, simple boats. In compounds 船 is read せん: 客船 "passenger ship", 漁船 "fishing boat".

examples[].german: We crossed to the island by ferry.
We took the ferry with our car to Hokkaido.
Because of the typhoon, all ferry services are canceled today.
en.notes: フェリー is a "ferry" that carries people and often also cars; in Japan it connects islands with the main islands, sometimes overnight. Typical: フェリーで渡る, フェリーに乗る, フェリー乗り場 "ferry terminal", カーフェリー "car ferry". More general is 船 "ship"; a small boat is ボート.

en.meaning: sea route; shipping route; air route
examples[].german: This route runs every day.
To avoid the storm, the ship changed its course.
Ridership fell, and the ferry route to that island was discontinued.
en.notes: 航路 is the fixed route of ships or aircraft: 定期航路 "regular service", 国際航路, 航路を変更する. It is used mainly for shipping; for flight routes, 空路 or 路線 is more common. The matching verb is 運航する "(of ships/flights) to operate". The word is formal and typical of news and travel information.

examples[].german: Sending goods by air is expensive.
The prime minister left for Washington by air this morning.
Because the roads were impassable, relief supplies were delivered by air.
en.notes: 空路 means "air route" or flight path and is often used adverbially in the sense of "by air, by plane": 空路で帰国する; in the news also without で: 空路パリへ向かう. It is formal; in everyday speech people say 飛行機で. Counterparts are 陸路 "land route" and 海路 "sea route".

examples[].german: We crossed the border overland.
The flight was canceled, so I decided to go back overland.
Travelers in the past took many days to reach Edo overland.
en.notes: 陸路 means "land route", that is, travel or transport over land (road, rail) as opposed to 海路 and 空路. It usually stands adverbially with で: 陸路で移動する, 陸路で国境を越える. The word is formal and typical of the news, history and travel reports; in everyday speech people say 車で or 電車で more often.

examples[].german: I'm down because I got my heart broken.
I comforted my friend, who had just been dumped, all night.
The pain of lost love will surely be healed by time.
en.notes: 失恋 refers to the failure of a love, being rejected or left, and as an intransitive する-verb (失恋する) means "to be turned down, to be heartbroken". Typical: 失恋の痛み, 失恋から立ち直る, 失恋した友達を慰める. Unlike 片思い (love that is not yet returned), 失恋 stands for the painful end. Neutral, common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: Supplies were transported by sea.
There is no bridge to the island, so it can only be reached by sea.
As the saying goes, "good weather comes to those who wait at sea" - let's wait calmly for our chance.
en.notes: 海路 means "sea route", i.e. travel or transport by ship: 海路で運ぶ, 海路を行く. It is formal and rather literary; in everyday speech one says 船で. For a concrete shipping line, 航路 is more common. Well known is the proverb 待てば海路の日和あり "if you wait, there will be fair weather for sailing", i.e. "patience pays off". Counterparts: 陸路, 空路.

examples[].german: The expressway was congested, so we took the ordinary roads.
We left the expressway and drove about an hour on regular roads.
If you use the regular roads there is no toll, but it takes twice as long.
en.notes: 一般道 (short for 一般道路) refers to any normal, toll-free road as opposed to the 高速道路 "expressway". So it is not only the "country road" outside towns but also includes city streets. Typical: 一般道を走る, 一般道で行く, 高速を降りて一般道に入る. The word often appears in car navigation systems, traffic reports and route planning.

examples[].german: I filled up at the gas station.
We're low on gas, so let's stop at a gas station.
Is there a gas station near here?
en.notes: ガソリンスタンド is a Japanese-coined word (wasei eigo) for "gas station"; for short one also says スタンド. To fill up is ガソリンを入れる in everyday speech, 給油する in more formal speech. At self-service stations the sign says セルフ; at others the staff fill up for you. You stop by with に寄る: ガソリンスタンドに寄る.

examples[].german: I paid the toll at the expressway toll gate.
Congestion stretches for five kilometers before the toll gate.
With ETC, you can pass through the toll gate without stopping.
en.notes: 料金所 is the "toll gate" on expressways and toll roads, where you pay the 通行料. Today people mostly drive through with the electronic ETC system; there are separate ETCレーン next to the 一般レーン. Traffic jams often form before the 料金所 (料金所付近で渋滞). Not to be confused with 料金 alone, "fee, price".

examples[].german: We took a break and ate at the service area.
Let's stop at the next service area for the restroom.
This service area is popular because you can buy local specialties there.
en.notes: サービスエリア (abbreviated SA) is a large "rest stop" on Japanese expressways with restaurants, shops, restrooms and often a gas station. Smaller rest areas are called パーキングエリア (PA). Many service areas sell regional specialties and are themselves a popular excursion destination. Typical: サービスエリアで休憩する, サービスエリアに寄る.

examples[].german: I want to lead a life that values harmony with nature.
This building blends well with the surrounding scenery.
I try to eat a balanced diet.
en.notes: 調和 means "harmony" between different elements: 自然との調和, 色の調和. As an intransitive する-verb, AがBと調和する means "to harmonize with B, blend in". Very common is 調和のとれた "balanced, harmonious" (調和のとれた食事). The word is rather abstract and elevated; for concord within a group one rather says 和 or 協調.

examples[].german: It is important to maintain social order.
Even after the disaster, people queued up in an orderly way.
The demonstration turned violent, and order in the town was disrupted.
en.notes: 秩序 is the "order" of a system or society: 社会の秩序, 秩序を守る/保つ/乱す, 秩序が回復する. It is formal and common in politics and news; 治安, by contrast, refers specifically to public safety. Adverbially, 秩序正しく means "in an orderly, disciplined way". For tidiness in a room, one does not say 秩序 but 片付いている or 整理されている.

examples[].german: After the coup, the country fell into a state of chaos.
The meeting was chaotic because opinions did not come together.
The future economy is murky and hard to predict.
en.notes: 混沌 is a literary word for "chaos, complete disorder" and is usually used as a たる-adjective: 混沌とした状況, 混沌としている. It also describes uncertainty: 先行きが混沌としている "the future is completely open". 混乱 stresses confusion caused by a specific event (事故で交通が混乱する); in everyday speech people often say カオス or ごちゃごちゃ. As a noun: 混沌の時代.

examples[].german: We divorced because of infidelity.
My boyfriend's cheating came out and we had a huge fight.
I usually buy bread from this shop, but today I cheated a little and bought it from the shop next door.
en.notes: 浮気 is "cheating, infidelity" in a relationship, whether married or not: 浮気する, 浮気がばれる, 浮気相手. 不倫 is narrower and refers to an affair in which at least one party is married. As a な-adjective or in 浮気性 it means "fickle, unfaithful". Colloquially also jokingly for "trying something different" instead of one's usual brand.

examples[].german: Everyone's opinions coincided.
The fingerprints at the scene matched the suspect's.
Being born on the same day - what an amazing coincidence.
en.notes: 一致 means "agreement, match"; as an intransitive する-verb: 意見が一致する, AがBと一致する, 指紋が一致する. Important phrases are 全員一致で "unanimously," 偶然の一致 "coincidence" and 言行一致 "words and deeds agree." The opposite is 不一致 or the verb 食い違う. The word is neutral and ranges from everyday speech to the news.

examples[].german: There is a difference in the views of the two parties.
Please check once more that there are no discrepancies in the contents of the application form.
His testimony differs from the facts.
en.notes: 相違 means "difference, discrepancy" between opinions, statements or facts and is formal: 意見の相違, 見解の相違, 事実と相違する. Set phrases are 〜に相違ない "without doubt" (the written variant of 違いない) and, on forms, 上記の通り相違ありません "The above information is correct". In everyday speech people say 違い; 差異 stresses measurable differences.

examples[].german: It is important to understand cultural differences.
No significant difference was seen between the results of the two groups.
Depending on the region, there are various differences in dialects.
en.notes: 差異 is a literary word for "difference, discrepancy", especially for objectively ascertainable, often measurable deviations: 〜の間に差異がある, 大きな差異は見られない, 文化的な差異. In everyday speech one says 違い or 差. 相違 stresses rather that statements or opinions do not agree; for social inequality 格差 is more usual.

examples[].german: These two cases have many similarities.
Please beware of imitation products.
A design resembling a competitor's product became a problem.
en.notes: 類似 means "similarity"; as a する-verb, AがBに類似する, attributively often 類似した or 類似の. Common compounds are 類似点 "similarity, common point" and 類似品 "similar product, imitation". The word is formal and typical of reports, law and product notices (類似品にご注意ください); in everyday speech one says 似ている.

examples[].german: We are investigating whether these two incidents are related.
I read several books related to environmental issues.
Related articles are displayed below this article.
en.notes: 関連 denotes a factual "connection, relation": AとBの関連, Xに関連がある. As a する-verb, Xに関連する means "to be related to X," often attributively: 関連する資料. Very common as a first element: 関連会社 "affiliated company," 関連記事 "related articles," 関連商品. The nearly synonymous 関係 also covers human relationships; 関連 is more factual.

examples[].german: The causal relationship between smoking and lung cancer has been proven.
Whether there was a causal link between the accident and the road's design was disputed in court.
That he, who had done nothing but deceive people, was finally deceived himself is karmic retribution.
en.notes: 因果 means "cause and effect" and today occurs mainly in 因果関係 "causal relationship", for example in science and law. From Buddhism comes the meaning "karma, fate", known from 因果応報 "every deed meets its reward". As an adjective, 因果な "unfortunate" is old-fashioned and literary. 因果 on its own is rare; for simple reasons people say 原因 and 結果.

examples[].german: I investigated the correlation between temperature and electricity consumption.
It turned out that there is a correlation between sleep time and grades.
Even if there is a correlation, it does not necessarily mean there is a causal relationship.
en.notes: 相関 means "correlation, interrelation" and is a technical word from statistics and science: AとBの相関, 相関がある/ない, 相関関係, 正の相関/負の相関. As a する-verb (AとBが相関する) it is rarer. Important: 相関関係 is not the same as 因果関係 "causal relationship", a frequent reminder in technical texts.

examples[].german: The social isolation of elderly people is becoming a problem.
Heavy snow made the roads unusable, and the mountain village was cut off.
I've just changed schools and I'm worried about being isolated in the class.
en.notes: 孤立 means "isolation", i.e. being cut off from others - socially, politically or spatially. As an intransitive する-verb: クラスで孤立する, 国際的に孤立する, 大雪で村が孤立する. Common are 社会的孤立 and 孤立感 "feeling of isolation". Distinction: 孤独 is the inner feeling of loneliness, 孤立 the objective situation of having no connection to others.

examples[].german: I made a donation to show solidarity with the disaster area.
Even one person's mistake becomes joint responsibility of the whole team.
When I rented an apartment, I was told that I needed a joint guarantor.
en.notes: 連帯 means "solidarity", a group standing together: 連帯を示す, 連帯感 "sense of solidarity", 〜と連帯する. Important in law and everyday life are 連帯責任 "joint liability, collective responsibility" and 連帯保証人 "joint guarantor", who is required for rental contracts, for example. The word is formal; 団結 stresses banding together, 協力 practical cooperation.

examples[].german: International cooperation is indispensable.
He is very capable but lacks cooperativeness.
The countries acted in concert and lowered interest rates.
en.notes: 協調 means "cooperation, coordination" in the sense of mutual consideration in order to avoid conflict: 国際協調, 労使協調, 他国と協調する. Important in working life is 協調性 "teamwork ability" (協調性がある/に欠ける). Compared with 協力 (concrete helping out), 協調 stresses the harmonious coordination of interests. Not to be confused with the homophone 強調 "emphasis".

examples[].german: It is important to give children affection.
My mother made me a packed lunch with lots of love every morning.
My father has trouble expressing his love for the family in words.
en.notes: 愛情 is "affection, love" as a warm feeling toward family, children, animals or partners - broader than romantic 恋愛. Typical combinations: 愛情を注ぐ ("to give love"), 愛情を込めて ("with love"), 愛情たっぷり, 愛情表現. It is a noun; as a verb one uses 愛する or かわいがる.

examples[].german: We want to build a society of multicultural coexistence.
Clownfish and sea anemones live in symbiosis.
Let's think about town planning in which humans and wild animals can live together.
en.notes: 共生 means "living together, coexistence" and, in biology, "symbiosis". Typical are 自然との共生, 多文化共生 "multicultural coexistence" and AとBが共生する. The word is formal and common in discussions of the environment, integration and politics. 共存 "coexistence" stresses more the mere existing side by side, 共生 the mutual living together. Not to be confused with the homophone 強制 "compulsion".

examples[].german: I analyze the culprit's state of mind.
It's consumer psychology that people want to buy when prices drop.
Before exams, the psychological pressure is great.
en.notes: 心理 denotes the "mental state, way of thinking" of a person or group: 犯人の心理, 消費者心理, 群集心理 "mass psychology." Very common are 心理的な "psychological" (心理的な負担) and 心理状態 "state of mind." The science is 心理学; 心理 alone mostly means the state of mind, not the discipline. 精神 refers more to spirit and mental health.

examples[].german: I'm majoring in psychology at university.
According to psychologists, people form a first impression within a few seconds.
Knowledge of psychology is also useful in marketing.
en.notes: 心理学 is the science of "psychology": 心理学を学ぶ/専攻する, 心理学者 "psychologist". Subfields are called, for example, 社会心理学, 発達心理学 or 臨床心理学. To be distinguished are 心理 (a person's psyche, state of mind) and 精神科 (psychiatry as a medical specialty). The word is neutral to academic.

examples[].german: I consulted a psychiatrist.
I hadn't been able to sleep for days, so I saw a psychiatrist.
My older sister works as a nurse in the psychiatry department of a university hospital.
en.notes: 精神科 is the medical specialty or hospital department of "psychiatry": 精神科に通う "to be in psychiatric treatment", 精神科医 "psychiatrist", 精神科を受診する. Because 精神科 sounds off-putting to some, many practices call themselves 心療内科 (psychosomatic medicine) or メンタルクリニック. To be distinguished from 心理学 (the science) and カウンセラー (a counselor without a medical license).

examples[].german: He has become depressed and is taking time off work.
The number of people who develop depression from work stress is increasing.
Because the days are short in winter, some people become a bit depressed.
en.notes: 鬱 stands for "depression, low spirits" and, because of the very complex kanji, is usually written in kana (うつ). The medical diagnosis is called うつ病 (鬱病); うつになる means "to become depressed", うつっぽい "somewhat depressed". Even more common in everyday speech is 憂鬱 "gloomy, melancholy" (月曜日は憂鬱だ). The counterpart 躁 is found in 躁うつ病 "bipolar disorder".

examples[].german: I feel like I'm about to be crushed by the burden of responsibility.
Under the pressure of the nation's expectations, he won the gold medal.
The new company president is bearing up under the pressure of rebuilding the company.
en.notes: 重圧 means heavy, above all psychological "pressure, burden" that weighs on someone: 責任の重圧, 期待の重圧, 重圧に耐える, 重圧に負ける, 重圧がかかる. It is more formal and stronger than プレッシャー, which is more common in everyday speech. Literally "heavy pressure", it is used today almost only figuratively, typically in sports and business reports.

examples[].german: I received a request for a translation.
We decided to commission an expert to do the investigation.
I'm sorry, but we cannot accept your request this time.
en.notes: 依頼 means "request, commission": you officially ask someone to take care of something. Patterns: Person に Thing を依頼する, 依頼を受ける/断る, 依頼人 "client." It is more formal than 頼む and typical in business correspondence (ご依頼ありがとうございます). 要請 is an even more official request, mostly from authorities; 注文 is an order for goods.

examples[].german: We requested support from the government.
At the request of the prefecture, the Self-Defense Forces were dispatched to the disaster area.
The city is asking residents to cooperate in saving electricity.
en.notes: 要請 is a formal "request" or "call", mostly from or to institutions: 政府に支援を要請する, 〜の要請を受けて, 協力を要請する. It sounds more official and urgent than 依頼, but is less binding than 命令 "order" or 要求 "demand". Typical in news (出動要請, 協力要請); it is not used among friends.

examples[].german: We have great expectations of the new employees.
The film wasn't as interesting as I had expected.
I apologize for not meeting your expectations.
en.notes: 期待 is hopeful "expectation": you expect something good. Typical are 期待する (transitive with を, also 〜に期待する "to pin hopes on someone"), 期待を寄せる/かける "to place expectations," 期待に応える "to live up to expectations" and 期待外れ "disappointing." Before nouns, 期待の〜 means "promising" (期待の新人). A neutral prediction without hope is 予想, by contrast.

examples[].german: The bill is being deliberated in the Diet.
At the shareholders' meeting, all the proposals were approved by a majority.
The mayor submitted the new budget proposal to the city council.
en.notes: 議案 is a motion or bill on which an assembly (parliament, city council, shareholders' meeting) decides. Typical verbs: 議案を提出する "to submit", 審議する "to deliberate", 可決する "to pass", 否決する "to reject". 法案 is narrower, only a draft law; 議題 is merely the topic on the agenda, which is not necessarily voted on. A formal word from politics and administration.

examples[].german: She was elected as a member of the Diet.
I consulted our local city council member about the road problem.
The legislator resigned, taking responsibility for the scandal.
en.notes: 議員 is an elected member of a representative body, at all levels: 国会議員, 衆議院議員, 市議会議員. Typical: 議員に当選する ("to be elected"), 議員を辞職する, 議員バッジ. As a form of address or title it follows the name: 山田議員. For members of a club or committee, 会員 or 委員 is used instead.

examples[].german: Their friendship has lasted for many years.
While practicing in the same club, a friendship grew between the two.
Sometimes a friendship is ruined over lending and borrowing money.
en.notes: 友情 is "friendship" as a feeling or relationship, not the person (that would be 友達／友人). Typical: 友情が芽生える ("a friendship develops"), 友情を深める, 友情が壊れる, 友情と恋愛. Neutral, often in stories, speeches and films; in conversation one also says 仲がいい.

examples[].german: I prepared a draft of the contract.
The secretary wrote the draft of the president's speech.
The draft of the constitution was revised many times.
en.notes: 草案 is the first written draft of an official text, such as a contract, law, speech or charter. One says 草案を作成する/練る/まとめる and 草案を修正する. For everyday things like an essay or letter draft, people say 下書き instead; 原案 stresses the original proposal that is put up for deliberation. A rather formal written word.

examples[].german: It was approved as the original draft stood.
The committee made several amendments to the original proposal.
The original concept for this anime was thought up by a famous novelist.
en.notes: 原案 is the original proposal, that is, the plan or draft put forward for deliberation before changes are added. Typical: 原案どおり/原案のまま可決される "to be passed unchanged", 原案に修正を加える "to amend the draft". For films and manga, 原案 appears in the credits for the "original idea" on which the work is based. Unlike 草案, the focus is on "original" as opposed to the amended version.

examples[].german: To think of a plan for solving the problem.
I put together a proposal for improving operations and submitted it to the department head.
The city announced a concrete plan to increase tourists.
en.notes: 方案 is a worked-out plan or proposal for how to tackle a problem. The word is rather rare and literary, mostly in compounds such as 改善方案 or 解決方案. In normal Japanese, people say much more often 方策 "measure", 対策 "countermeasure" or simply 案. Not to be confused with 法案 (same reading) "bill".

examples[].german: Please let me think about this matter.
After examining it from various angles, we decided to cancel the plan.
I'm considering moving, so I'm going around looking at properties.
en.notes: 検討 is the thorough examination and weighing of a matter before deciding; 検討する is transitive (〜を検討する). Common: 検討中 "under consideration," 検討の余地がある "there is room for discussion," 検討した結果 "after examination." In business conversations, 前向きに検討します is often a polite, evasive refusal. Not to be confused with the identically sounding 見当 "guess, estimate."

examples[].german: I passed the document screening.
I was made to wait a full thirty minutes at immigration control at the airport.
My loan application was not approved, so I gave up on the car.
en.notes: 審査 is the formal examination of whether a person or thing meets certain criteria, for example for applications, loans, competitions or entry into a country. Typical: 審査を受ける, 審査に通る/合格する, 審査に落ちる, 入国審査, 書類審査, 審査員 "judge, jury". 検査, by contrast, is a technical or medical examination, 試験 a test with questions.

examples[].german: Deliberations were held in the committee.
The bill is scheduled to be deliberated in the Diet from next week.
The proposal was passed without sufficient deliberation.
en.notes: 審議 is the detailed deliberation of a body on a motion or bill before it votes. Typical: 法案を審議する, 審議が行われる, 審議中, 審議会 "advisory council". Compared with 議論 "discussion" and 検討 "examination", 審議 is clearly limited to official bodies such as parliament, committees or councils. A formal word from politics and news.

examples[].german: Bonus assessments are carried out.
Before selling my old car, I had it appraised.
The insurance company assessed the amount of damage from the accident.
en.notes: 査定 is an examining evaluation of a value or performance, especially as a sum of money: used cars, real estate, insurance damages or the performance review of employees (人事査定, ボーナスの査定). One says 査定する, 査定を受ける, 査定額 "appraised value". 鑑定, by contrast, is an expert opinion on authenticity, and 評価 is general evaluation.

examples[].german: I asked an expert to appraise the artwork.
The result of the DNA test showed that the two are parent and child.
When I had my grandmother's ring appraised, it turned out to be a real diamond.
en.notes: 鑑定 is the expert assessment by a specialist: the authenticity and value of artworks or gemstones, but also DNA-鑑定, 筆跡鑑定 "handwriting analysis" and 精神鑑定 "psychiatric evaluation" in court. Typical: 鑑定を依頼する, 鑑定してもらう, 鑑定書 "certificate of authenticity". For a mere valuation (car, house), 査定 is more usual.

examples[].german: He objected to the referee's call.
I was relieved when I got an A rating for my first-choice school on the mock exam.
After checking the video, the call was overturned.
en.notes: 判定 is the decision made according to set criteria about who has won or into which grade something falls: referee rulings, 判定勝ち "win on points", exam ratings such as A判定 on mock exams, or 合否判定 "pass/fail decision". 判断, by contrast, is one's own judgment in everyday life, 判決 a court judgment. One says 判定する, 判定が出る, 判定に従う.

examples[].german: This product has received quality certification.
My father's injury was recognized as an industrial accident.
I study every day for the Japanese certification exam.
en.notes: 認定 is official recognition by an authority or organization that something meets a condition. Typical: 〜と認定する/される (労災と認定される "to be recognized as a work accident"), 認定を受ける, 認定試験, 世界遺産に認定される. Unlike 認める (generally "to recognize, to admit"), 認定 is official and formal; 資格 is the qualification itself.

examples[].german: I cherish family bonds.
After the earthquake, the bonds within the community grew stronger.
Having gotten through the hard training together, the team's bond has deepened.
en.notes: 絆 is the emotional "bond" between people, e.g. in a family, team or neighborhood: 家族の絆, 絆が深まる／強まる, 絆を深める. After the 2011 earthquake it became a key word for solidarity (Kanji of the Year 2011). The original meaning "fetter, leash" is rare today. Positive and somewhat sentimental; occasionally also written in kana as きずな.

examples[].german: Please assemble at the designated place.
I booked a reserved seat on the Shinkansen.
You can specify the date and time for the delivery of your package.
en.notes: 指定 means to explicitly specify or designate something: place, time, person or category. Very common as the participle 指定された〜 "specified, given" and in compounds such as 指定席 "reserved seat", 日時指定 "specified date and time", 指定校. One says 〜を指定する or 〜に指定される (国宝に指定される "to be designated a national treasure"). More general is 決める; 選ぶ stresses the selection.

examples[].german: A new department head was appointed.
The prime minister appointed her foreign minister.
Because of the minister's scandal, the prime minister's responsibility for the appointment is being questioned.
en.notes: 任命 is the official appointment to an office by a higher authority: 〜を〜に任命する, in the passive 〜に任命される. Typical contexts are ministers, ambassadors, judges or leadership posts. 任命責任 is the responsibility of the person who made the appointment. 指名 is the naming of a person, 選任 stresses selection plus installation, and 任命 the formal act.

examples[].german: The selection of committee members was carried out.
New directors were elected at the shareholders' meeting.
The defendant appointed a lawyer himself.
en.notes: 選任 means to select someone and install them in a function, typical in legal and corporate language: 取締役を選任する "to appoint directors", 弁護人を選任する "to appoint defense counsel", 選任される. It is more formal and rarer than 選ぶ; 任命 stresses appointment by a higher authority, 選任 more the choice by a body or a party.

examples[].german: I received a scholarship on my professor's recommendation.
I would like to recommend him as a candidate for leader.
I had my former boss write me a letter of recommendation.
en.notes: 推薦 is the recommendation of a person or thing to third parties, often of an official nature: 〜を〜に推薦する "to recommend someone for something," 推薦状 "letter of recommendation," 推薦入試 "admission by recommendation." For everyday tips ("Try this"), people more often use 勧める or おすすめ. 推薦 sounds more formal and binding.

examples[].german: He was nominated as project leader.
In class I was suddenly called on by the teacher and couldn't answer.
The man is wanted by the police on suspicion of murder.
en.notes: 指名 means to name or select a particular person by name: 〜を〜に指名する, in the passive 〜に指名される. It is also used when a teacher calls on someone in class (先生に指名される), when one requests a particular hairdresser at a salon (指名料), and in 指名手配 "wanted notice". Compared with 任命 (formal appointment), 指名 is the mere naming.

examples[].german: A young employee was picked to be department head.
A newcomer actress was chosen for the lead role in the film.
The coach selected a high school student for the national team.
en.notes: 抜擢 means to pick someone out of many candidates for an important role, often surprisingly and bypassing the usual order. Mostly in the passive: 〜に抜擢される (部長に抜擢される, 主役に抜擢される). It stresses the special distinction, whereas 昇進 is normal promotion and 任命 is formal appointment. The kanji 擢 is rare; in the media 抜てき is also written.

examples[].german: I changed the arrangement of the furniture.
Security guards were posted at the entrance of the event venue.
From April, I will be assigned to the sales department.
en.notes: 配置 is the planned arrangement of things or people at particular places: furniture, keyboards, personnel, police or troops. One says 〜を配置する, 〜に配置される, 配置を変える, 人員配置 and 配置転換 "transfer, reassignment". 配置 stresses distribution in space or in an organization; 並べる is only "to line up in a row".

en.meaning: taking up a new post (away from home)
examples[].german: From next month, I will take up a post abroad.
My father lives in Osaka alone because of a job transfer, without the family.
I have finally gotten used to life at my new posting.
en.notes: 赴任 means to move to a new place of work because of a transfer and take up the job there; 赴任する is intransitive with に (海外に赴任する). Very common: 単身赴任 "to be transferred to another place without one's family", 赴任先 "place of posting", 海外赴任. 転勤 is the transfer itself, while 赴任 stresses going there and taking up the post. The counterpart is 帰任.

examples[].german: I returned to my post after finishing a three-year assignment.
I am scheduled to return to the Tokyo headquarters next spring.
Since returning, I have been working in a new department, making use of my overseas experience.
en.notes: 帰任 is the return to one's original workplace, usually to the head office or one's home country after a posting; 帰任する is intransitive (本社に帰任する). It is the counterpart of 赴任 and belongs to company and official language. 帰国 is generally "returning home to one's country", while 帰任 stresses returning to the old post.

examples[].german: We outsource the work to an outside party.
The city has entrusted the management of the park to a private company.
The artist's works are sold on consignment at a gallery.
en.notes: 委託 means to entrust a task or goods to another company or person by contract: 〜を〜に委託する (業務を外部に委託する). Common in 業務委託 "commissioned work, outsourcing", 委託販売 "consignment sale" and 委託先 "contractor". 依頼 is the general "to ask, commission", and 外注 stresses outsourcing to external providers.

examples[].german: I found a job through an acquaintance's introduction.
This is something I heard from an acquaintance, but that store is reportedly closing next month.
He is less a friend than a professional acquaintance.
en.notes: 知人 is an "acquaintance", someone you know without being close friends. It is the more formal counterpart of 知り合い and sounds natural in news, business contexts and polite speech: 知人の紹介, 知人から聞いた話. 友人 ("friend", formal) and 親友 ("close friend") express more closeness.

examples[].german: I outsourced the design work.
To reduce outsourcing costs, we decided to do the system development in-house.
We outsource translation, so it takes a little time.
en.notes: 外注 is giving work to outside companies, that is, "outsourcing": 〜を外注する or 外注に出す. Related are 外注先 "external contractor" and 外注費 "outsourcing costs". The opposite is 内製 "in-house production". 委託 is more formal and also common in the public sector; 外注 sounds like everyday business and cost accounting.

examples[].german: I asked a subcontractor to do the work.
We are a small factory working as a subcontractor for a major automaker.
Demanding unreasonable price cuts from subcontractors is a problem.
en.notes: 下請け refers both to the subcontract and to the company that carries it out ("subcontractor"). Typical: 下請け業者, 下請け会社, 大手の下請けをする, 下請けに出す. In Japan there are frequent reports of 下請けいじめ, the pressure big companies put on small suppliers. The counterpart is 元請け "main contractor"; in administrative texts 下請 without け is also written.

examples[].german: The main contractor handles overall management.
Our company gets almost all its work from the main contractor.
It was decided that the prime contractor also bears responsibility for the accident.
en.notes: 元請け is the main contractor, who receives the order directly from the client or customer and passes parts of it on to 下請け. Typical: 元請け会社, 元請け業者, 元請けから仕事をもらう. The word is used mainly in the construction, IT and manufacturing industries. Counterpart: 下請け "subcontractor", and below it also 孫請け "sub-subcontractor".

examples[].german: I took part in the bidding for a public works project.
I tried bidding on an old camera in an online auction.
Irregularities surrounding the bidding were discovered, and the person in charge was arrested.
en.notes: 入札 is submitting a bid, whether in a public tender (公共事業の入札, 競争入札) or at an auction, also online. 入札する is intransitive; the object takes に: 入札に参加する, オークションに入札する. The one who wins the bid has 落札した. A formal word from business and administration, but familiar in everyday life through online auctions.

examples[].german: We won the bid with the lowest price.
I managed to win the game I wanted at an auction.
A painting by a famous artist sold at auction for one billion yen.
en.notes: 落札 is the successful bid: you win the contract in a tender or win something at an auction. 落札する is transitive (絵を落札する), and often 〜円で落札される "to be sold for ... yen". Related: 落札者 "winning bidder" and 落札価格 "winning price". The preceding step is 入札 "to place a bid".

en.meaning: conclusion of a treaty or contract
examples[].german: A treaty was concluded between the two countries.
We have concluded a sales contract with a new business partner.
As a result of labor-management negotiations, a new agreement was concluded.
en.notes: 締結 is the formal conclusion of a contract or agreement: 契約を締結する, 条約が締結される, 協定の締結. The word belongs to legal, business and news language; in everyday speech people say the simpler 契約を結ぶ. In engineering, 締結 also means joining parts with screws, but learners rarely need this.

examples[].german: I canceled my mobile phone contract.
Before moving, I applied to cancel my internet service.
If you cancel a fixed-term deposit midway, you will receive less interest.
en.notes: 解約 is the termination of an ongoing contract, such as for a phone, internet, insurance, subscription or account: 〜を解約する, 解約を申し込む, 解約手数料 "cancellation fee". A one-time booking, by contrast, is canceled with 予約をキャンセルする or 取り消す. 解除 is legally the rescission of a contract, often unilaterally because of breach of contract.

examples[].german: The alarm was lifted.
I unlock my smartphone with my fingerprint.
Because the other party did not keep the agreement, we cancelled the contract.
en.notes: 解除 means to lift an existing state, restriction or bond: 警報が解除される "the warning is lifted", 規制を解除する, ロックを解除する "to unlock", 契約を解除する "to withdraw from a contract". Often used in the passive in news reports. In the contract context, 解除 is usually unilateral and legal, whereas 解約 is the ordinary cancellation of a subscription or contract.

examples[].german: Please cancel the reservation.
There is a cancellation fee for cancellations the day before.
For drunk driving, he received the penalty of license revocation.
en.notes: 取消 is the noun of 取り消す "to revoke, to cancel". The spelling without り appears mainly in forms, official texts and on buttons (取消, 取消料, 免許取消); in regular text 取り消し is usually written. It is used for reservations, orders, permits and statements (発言の取り消し). In everyday speech people also simply say キャンセル for bookings.

examples[].german: It was a defective product, so I asked for a refund.
The concert was canceled, and the ticket price was refunded in full.
If you are not satisfied, we will refund your money.
en.notes: 返金 is the repayment of money already paid, typically in shopping or for canceled events: 返金する, 返金を求める, 返金に応じる "to agree to a refund", 全額返金 "full refund". 返済, by contrast, is repaying a loan, and 払い戻し is a similar, somewhat more official word for refunds (e.g. for train tickets).

examples[].german: I talked to my best friend about my worries.
She has been my best friend since elementary school.
I was betrayed by someone I thought was my best friend.
en.notes: 親友 is a "close, trusted friend" or "best friend" - clearly more than 友達 or 友人. One usually has only a few: 一番の親友, 小学校からの親友, 親友に打ち明ける. Do not confuse with 親戚 ("relatives"). Neutral and very common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I returned the book to the library.
Please return the rental car with a full tank.
After the return deadline passes, a late fee is charged.
en.notes: 返却 is the return of something borrowed or entrusted to the place you got it from: books, rental cars, loaned equipment, graded exams. Typical: 〜を返却する, 返却期限 "return deadline", 返却口 "return slot". 返す is the everyday word; 返却 sounds more formal and often appears on signs and in rules.

examples[].german: There are three unpaid invoices.
I demanded the unpaid overtime pay from the company.
If rent stays unpaid for two months, you will be asked to move out.
en.notes: 未払い means "not yet paid" and is mostly used attributively with の (未払いの請求書) or predicatively (家賃が未払いだ). Well-known phrases are 未払い金 "outstanding amount" and 未払い残業代 "unpaid overtime". The prefix 未 "not yet" is also found in 未定, 未完成. In forms, 未払 without い is also written.

examples[].german: I received a reminder about the delivery.
I urged my friend to give back the money I lent.
I am sorry if this seems like a reminder, but I am awaiting your reply.
en.notes: 催促 is repeatedly urging someone to finally do something that is due: payment, delivery, a reply. One says 〜を催促する (返事を催促する), 〜に催促される, 催促の電話/メール. 督促 is the formal, often written reminder (督促状); 催促 is more general and also common in private life. 促す, by contrast, is more neutral, "to encourage, to urge".

examples[].german: Please make the payment by the end of the month.
Can I pay by card?
Paying the monthly rent is hard.
en.notes: 支払い is payment, the noun of the verb 支払う. Typical are 支払いをする／済ませる "to pay" and 支払いが遅れる "to be late with payment"; in a shop people politely ask お支払いはどうなさいますか "How would you like to pay?" In forms and compounds, the spelling without い is common: 支払方法, 支払期限. In compounds, the short 払い is also used (前払い "advance payment," 後払い).

examples[].german: The deadline for paying taxes is near.
You can also pay your pension insurance premiums at a convenience store.
I lost my payment slip, so I asked the city hall to reissue it.
en.notes: 納付 is paying money to the state or public bodies: taxes, pension contributions, fees. Typical: 税金を納付する, 納付期限 "payment deadline", 納付書 "payment slip". It is an official word; in everyday speech people say 払う, and for taxes also 納める. 納入 can additionally mean "delivery of goods", whereas 納付 concerns only money (and documents).

examples[].german: Delivery of the products is delayed.
Please pay the tuition fees by the end of April.
This company supplies parts to automobile manufacturers.
en.notes: 納入 has two meanings: paying fees (授業料の納入) and delivering goods to a buyer (部品を納入する, 納入業者 "supplier"). In business language it usually means delivery to companies or government offices. 納品 is almost synonymous for goods; 納付 refers only to payments to public bodies.

examples[].german: Tax collection has been stepped up.
The club fee of 1,000 yen is collected every month.
Income tax is withheld directly from salary.
en.notes: 徴収 is the collecting of money by an authorized body: taxes, fees, membership dues. Typical: 〜を徴収する, 会費を徴収する, 源泉徴収 "withholding tax". It is the recipient's perspective; the payer 納める or 納付する. 集める is the neutral everyday word for "to collect".

examples[].german: You are taxed according to your income.
The government decided to impose a new tax on imported goods.
This allowance is not subject to taxation.
en.notes: 課税 is taxation, that is, imposing a tax; the thing taxed takes に: 所得に課税する, 輸入品に課税される. Common compounds: 課税対象 "taxable", 非課税 "tax-free", 課税所得. From the citizen's point of view, the counterpart is 納税 "paying taxes". A formal word from administration and the news.

examples[].german: I worked out ways to lower costs.
To reduce inventory, we sold at below cost.
The cost of one bowl of this ramen is said to be about 200 yen.
en.notes: 原価 is the cost price of a product, that is, purchase or production cost without profit. Typical: 原価を下げる, 原価計算, 原価率 "cost ratio" and 原価割れ "below cost" (selling at a loss). Opposites are 売値/販売価格 "selling price" and 定価 "list price". 実費 is the actual cost incurred for a service.

examples[].german: The list price of this book is a thousand yen.
I bought a coat at 30 percent off the list price in the sale.
If you search online, you may be able to buy it for less than the list price.
en.notes: 定価 is the regular selling price set by the manufacturer or publisher, e.g. the price printed on books. Typical: 定価で買う, 定価の三割引き "30% off list price", 定価より安い. 原価 is the cost price, and 値段/価格 is price in general. In discount promotions, the 定価 is often crossed out with the sale price next to it.

examples[].german: I'm looking for a marriage partner.
When you talk, think about the other person's feelings.
Our opponent in the final is last year's champion team.
en.notes: 相手 is "the other party", that is, the other person in a relationship or action - depending on context partner, conversation partner or opponent: 結婚相手, 話し相手, 相談相手, 対戦相手, 相手チーム. Important expressions: 〜の相手をする ("to look after someone, to play with someone"), 相手にしない ("not to take seriously, to ignore"), 相手の気持ちを考える. Neutral and very common.

examples[].german: I negotiated and got a discount.
Just before closing time I bought a marked-down bento at the supermarket.
I'm buying several at once - could you give me a little discount?
en.notes: 値引き is a reduction of the price, usually by the seller: 値引きする, 値引きしてもらう, 〜円値引き. In supermarkets, 値引きシール mark reduced goods. Similar are 割引 (a percentage discount, more fixed by rule, e.g. 学生割引) and, colloquially, まける "to knock down the price". 値下げ is a general price cut, whereas 値引き is more of a discount in an individual case.

examples[].german: Everything is half price before closing time.
Admission for elementary school children and under is half price.
The company paid half of the moving expenses.
en.notes: 半額 is "half the amount", above all half price: 半額になる, 半額で買う, 半額セール, 子どもは半額. For fares and admission, it means "half fare". The more general word for "half" is 半分; 半額 refers only to sums of money. A discount of 50% is also called 五割引き.

examples[].german: Admission is free.
If you buy 5,000 yen or more, shipping is free.
This app is free to use, but it has a lot of ads.
en.notes: 無料 means "free of charge, no fee" and is used as a noun with だ/です or with の: 無料の駐車場, 入場無料, 送料無料 "free shipping", 無料で使える. The opposite is 有料. Colloquially one also says ただ (often written タダ), which sounds more casual; on signs and in advertising, however, it is almost always 無料.

examples[].german: This parking lot is paid.
Plastic bags cost extra. Would you like one?
If we take the toll road, we'll arrive an hour earlier.
en.notes: 有料 means "subject to a fee, paid" and is used with だ/です or with の: 有料の駐車場, 有料道路 "toll road", 有料会員, 有料になる. The opposite is 無料. Since 2020, for example, plastic bags in stores in Japan are 有料 (レジ袋の有料化). It says only that something costs money, not how much.

examples[].german: Travel expenses are reimbursed at actual cost.
Participation is free, but we charge for the materials at cost.
300 yen in actual costs is incurred for mailing the documents.
en.notes: 実費 is the cost actually incurred, without markup or profit, e.g. for travel, materials or postage. Typical: 実費で支給する "to reimburse at actual cost", 実費負担, 材料費は実費. Do not confuse with 自費 "at one's own expense": 実費 is about the amount, 自費 is about who pays.

examples[].german: This treatment is at your own expense.
I attended the seminar at my own expense, not as company training.
My grandfather published his own poetry collection through self-publishing.
en.notes: 自費 means that you pay for something out of your own pocket, without a company, the state or insurance: 自費で留学する, 自費出版 "self-publishing", 自費診療 "treatment not covered by health insurance". Typical are 自費で〜する and 自費になる. Opposites are 公費 "public funds" and 経費 "company expenses"; 実費, by contrast, concerns the actual amount of the costs.

examples[].german: The research is funded by public money.
It became a problem that a lawmaker had taken a family trip at public expense.
This vaccination is available at public expense.
en.notes: 公費 is public funds, that is, money from the state or local government derived from taxes: 公費で賄う "to cover from public funds", 公費負担, 公費の無駄遣い "waste of taxpayer money". The counterpart is 私費 or 自費 "at one's own expense". The word is formal and common in news about budgets, health and politicians' scandals.

examples[].german: The burden of medical expenses is heavy.
Working at a computer for hours strains the eyes.
The customer bears the shipping costs for returns.
en.notes: 負担 is on the one hand a "load, burden" (体に負担がかかる, 負担が大きい, 負担になる), and on the other the assuming of costs or responsibility: 〜を負担する (費用を負担する). In business texts the polite form is 送料はお客様のご負担となります. 分担, by contrast, is the dividing of a load among several people.

examples[].german: We split the costs and paid.
Since we both work, we share the housework as a couple.
Let's tackle the preparation of the presentation with a clear division of tasks.
en.notes: 分担 means dividing work, costs or responsibility among several people, each taking a share: 〜を分担する, 家事を分担する, 役割分担 "division of roles", 分担して〜する. In contrast to 負担 (bearing a burden), 分担 emphasizes the dividing; 割り勘 specifically means splitting the bill in a restaurant.

examples[].german: I invested in the new company.
Three companies jointly invested and built a new hotel.
You need to report the progress of the business to the investors.
en.notes: 出資 means to put money or capital into a company or project and thereby become a partner or backer. As a する-verb, the target takes に: 新会社に出資する; the amount can take を: 一億円を出資する. Typical compounds are 出資者 "backer", 出資金 "capital contribution" and 共同出資 "joint investment". Unlike 投資, which generally means "to invest money to make a profit" (e.g. in stocks), 出資 stresses participation in the capital of a specific undertaking.

examples[].german: She is always on my side.
When we siblings fight, Mom always takes my little brother's side.
On the day itself, even the weather was on our side, and the sports day was a great success.
en.notes: 味方 is an "ally" or someone who is on one's own side; the opposite is 敵. Very common: 〜の味方だ, 〜の味方をする ("to take someone's side"), 味方につける ("to win over to one's side"), 正義の味方. As an intransitive する-verb (〜に味方する) also figuratively: 天気が味方する ("the weather is on one's side"). Do not confuse with the homophone 見方 ("way of looking").

examples[].german: I applied for a research grant.
The city subsidizes part of the rent for households raising children.
This film was produced with a grant from a cultural foundation.
