en.notes: 助成 is financial support for projects, research or particular groups from the state, local governments or foundations. It is a word of administrative and application language and appears above all in 助成金 "grant, subsidy", 〜の助成を受ける "to receive funding" and 〜を助成する "to subsidize". 補助 is more general ("support, aid", also 補助金), while 援助 means rather help for people or countries in need. In everyday conversation, one mostly hears 助成金 or simply 補助金.

examples[].german: There are subsidies from the government.
The child practices riding a bicycle with training wheels.
The caregiver helps the elderly patient eat.
en.notes: 補助 means "support, help" in the sense of a supplement: one helps where someone or something is not sufficient alone. Financially it appears in 補助金 "subsidy, grant"; it also appears in many compounds meaning "auxiliary, additional": 補助輪 "training wheels", 補助席 "fold-down seat", 補助的な役割 "supporting role". As a suru-verb it is transitive: 〜を補助する. 助成 is narrower, limited to public funding, while 援助 emphasizes help for the needy.

en.meaning: to take a stance; to hold ready; to set up (shop, house)
examples[].german: To take the correct stance in martial arts.
He opened a small shop at the station.
I waited for the bird to take off with my camera at the ready.
en.notes: 構える has several uses: taking a posture or fighting stance (剣を構える, 正しく構える), holding something ready to fire or shoot (カメラを構える, 銃を構える), and setting up a business or house (店を構える, 家を構える). Intransitively it means "to tense up, to become formal": そんなに構えないで "don't be so stiff". The noun 構え is "posture, stance", 心構え "mental attitude". Do not confuse with 構う "to care about, to mind" (構わない).

en.meaning: to put in order; to arrange
examples[].german: I tidied up my appearance and then went out.
Before the competition I want to get into top physical shape.
I took a deep breath, calmed my breathing, and then began to speak.
en.notes: 整える means "to put in order, to bring into a clean, balanced state": 身だしなみを整える, 髪を整える, 部屋を整える. It is just as common for conditions and circumstances: 体調を整える "to get oneself in good shape", 息を整える "to calm one's breathing", 環境を整える "to create the conditions", 準備を整える. The intransitive partner is 整う (準備が整う). The spelling 調える, by contrast, is preferred for "to procure, to put together" and for seasoning food (味を調える).

en.meaning: to prepare; to procure; to season (味を〜)
examples[].german: To make travel preparations.
Finally, season with salt and pepper.
I somehow managed to raise the money for the wedding.
en.notes: 調える is a spelling of ととのえる that, according to official recommendation, stands for "to procure and put together what is needed" and "to bring into the desired state": 旅行の支度を調える, 費用を調える "to raise the money", 味を調える "to season", 縁談を調える "to arrange a marriage". For "to put in order" (髪, 服装, 体調) one writes 整える instead, which is much more common overall in daily life. The intransitive partner is 調う (準備が調う).

examples[].german: The king ruled the country peacefully.
He is the village head who has governed this village for many years.
My mother managed the large family skillfully.
en.notes: 治める means "to rule, to administer, to govern": 国を治める, 領地を治める, 家を治める "to run a household". It sounds elevated and is mostly said of rulers, governments or heads of families. The intransitive partner is 治まる (騒ぎが治まる, 痛みが治まる). Beware of the similarly read verbs: 収める "to put away, to achieve" (also recommended for "to settle a dispute": 争いを収める), 納める "to pay, to deliver", 修める "to study, to master".

en.meaning: to put away; to achieve (a result); to capture (in a photo)
examples[].german: He achieved good results at the tournament.
I captured the beautiful scenery in a photo.
Please put all the documents on this shelf.
en.notes: 収める basically means "to bring something into its place": 棚に収める "to put on the shelf," 写真に収める "to capture in a photo," 全集に収める "to include in a collection." It is very common with success and results: 成功を収める, 勝利を収める, 好成績を収める "to do well." "To settle, calm down" is also written this way: 騒ぎを収める. The intransitive partner is 収まる (箱に収まる, 騒ぎが収まる). Distinguish it from 納める "to pay, deliver" and 治める "to rule."

examples[].german: I pay my taxes properly.
I delivered the ordered parts to the factory by the due date.
I dedicated an old amulet to the shrine.
en.notes: 納める mainly means "to hand over money to an institution" (税金を納める, 授業料を納める, 会費を納める) and "to deliver goods" (商品を納める, 期日までに納める). In addition, one brings offerings or old good-luck charms to a shrine: お守りを神社に納める. As a suffix it means "to do for the last time, to wrap up": 仕事納め. The intransitive partner is 納まる. In everyday speech people also say 払う for taxes, but 納める sounds more correct and official.

examples[].german: I studied law at university.
He mastered cooking techniques in France.
I have decided not to marry until I finish my studies.
en.notes: 修める means "to study a subject thoroughly and master it" or "to complete an education": 学問を修める, 法学を修める, 学業を修める. It is more elevated than 勉強する or 学ぶ and stresses successful completion. A second, more literary use is 身を修める "to perfect one's conduct". Not to be confused with the identically read 治める "to rule", 収める "to put away, to achieve" and 納める "to pay".

examples[].german: I am always working to make improvements.
Holding back her tears, she tried to keep smiling.
Our store strives to protect our customers' personal information.
en.notes: 努める means "to make every effort to do something". The goal takes に (改善に努める, 安全の確保に努める) or comes as a clause with 〜よう(に)努める or 〜ようと努める. It is more formal than 頑張る or 努力する and typical of company and official language: 〜に努めております. Not to be confused with 務める "to serve in a post" (司会を務める) and 勤める "to be employed" (会社に勤める).

examples[].german: Sometimes it is necessary to forgive an enemy.
If you make an enemy of that person, you'll be in trouble.
Sweets late at night are the enemy of any diet.
en.notes: 敵 is the "enemy, opponent"; the opposite is 味方. Typical: 敵に回す ("to make an enemy of someone"), 敵を作る, 敵チーム. Figuratively, 〜の敵 means "enemy of something, bad for": ダイエットの敵, 女性の敵. More neutral than 敵 is 相手 or ライバル for sports opponents. In expressions such as 目の敵, the kanji is read かたき.

en.meaning: to be employed; to work for
examples[].german: I work for a bank.
My older sister starts working at a hospital next month.
en.notes: 勤める describes an employment relationship. The company or institution stands before に in the usual construction: 銀行に勤める means to work for a bank. 勤めている describes existing employment, while 勤め始める names the start. It is an ichidan verb: つとめます and つとめて. 努める, by contrast, means to make an effort.

en.meaning: to serve as; to act in the role of
examples[].german: I was asked to be the master of ceremonies.
She played the lead role in a film for the first time.
My father has served as head of the neighborhood association for ten years.
en.notes: 務める means "to take on or fill a role or post" and takes を: 司会を務める "to host", 議長を務める, 主役を務める "to play the lead role", 通訳を務める. It stresses the task, not the workplace: for "to work at a company", say 会社に勤める. 努める, in turn, means "to strive". The noun 務め means "duty, task".

examples[].german: He accomplished great things.
With the strength of the whole team, we finally won the championship.
Even if it's impossible alone, with companions it should be possible to accomplish.
en.notes: 成し遂げる means "to carry a great, difficult task through to success": 偉業を成し遂げる, 改革を成し遂げる, 優勝を成し遂げる. It sounds weighty and praising; for everyday tasks, やり遂げる "to see through to the end" or 終える is more fitting. 達成する stresses reaching a set goal or number (目標を達成する). The potential form 成し遂げられる is common.

examples[].german: The meeting lasted three hours.
The construction work is scheduled to continue for two years.
The damage from the heavy rain extended over a wide area of the prefecture.
en.notes: 亘る means "to extend (in time or space) over something" and appears almost always in the pattern 〜にわたって / 〜にわたる: 三時間にわたって, 長期にわたる工事, 全国にわたる調査. The kanji spelling 亘る is rare; today this word is mostly written in kana (わたる). The identically read 渡る means "to cross" (橋を渡る). The expression is rather written and typical of news and reports.

en.meaning: to step over; to straddle; to span; to cross (borders)
examples[].german: I stepped over the puddle and walked on.
Don't you ever set foot in this house again!
We were told to refrain from traveling across prefectures.
en.notes: 跨ぐ means "to step over something in one stride": 水たまりを跨ぐ, 敷居を跨ぐ "to cross the threshold" (二度と敷居をまたぐな "never darken my door again"). Figuratively it means "to extend across a boundary": 県をまたぐ移動, 年をまたぐ "to carry over the new year", 川をまたぐ橋. It is mostly written in kana (またぐ). Unlike 越える, it stresses spanning from one side to the other.

examples[].german: Sales exceeded the target.
Days when the temperature exceeds thirty-five degrees continue.
His songs are loved across the ages.
en.notes: 超える is used for exceeding a number, limit or standard: 目標を超える, 三十五度を超える, 限界を超える, 想像を超える. "To go beyond, transcend" is also written this way: 時代を超える, 国境を超えた友情. For physically crossing mountains, rivers or borders, 越える is written instead (山を越える). 上回る is more factual and limited to numbers in comparison.

examples[].german: I crossed the mountain and went to the neighboring village.
Migratory birds fly over the sea to the southern countries.
I hear that the patient's condition has finally passed the critical point.
en.notes: 越える is the spatial crossing of something that lies in the way: 山を越える, 国境を越える, 海を越える. Figuratively it stands for getting through a critical phase: 峠を越える "to be over the hump." For numbers and limits, 超える is written (三十度を超える). Related are 越す (年を越す "to see in the new year") and 乗り越える "to overcome" (困難を乗り越える).

examples[].german: The results exceeded expectations.
The number of tourists this year is clearly above last year's.
The yes votes narrowly prevailed, and the motion was passed.
en.notes: 上回る means "to be above something (numerically), to exceed" and is used mainly with statistics, results and forecasts: 予想を上回る, 前年を上回る, 平均を大きく上回る. It is factual and typical of news and business reports. Its opposite is 下回る. 超える is broader and emphasizes crossing a limit, while 勝る/優る means qualitative superiority.

en.meaning: to fall below; to be less than
examples[].german: This year's sales fell below last year's.
Because the number of applicants fell short of capacity, additional recruitment will be held.
My test score unfortunately fell below the average.
en.notes: 下回る means "to be below, to fall short of" (in numbers): 前年を下回る, 平均を下回る, 予想を下回る. Like its counterpart 上回る, it is factual and typical of statistics, surveys and business news. For falling below a threshold on the stock market, one also hears 割る or 割り込む. The standard of comparison takes を.

examples[].german: He is superior to the other players in skill.
There is no greater treasure than health.
The ramen here is every bit as good as that of famous shops.
en.notes: 優る means "to be better than, to be superior to" and appears in the pattern AはBに優る. The usual spelling is 勝る; 優る is a rarer variant. Fixed expressions are 〜に優るとも劣らない "is not inferior to ..." and 〜に優るものはない "there is nothing better than ...". Do not confuse with 優れる (すぐれる) "to be outstanding", which does not need a direct comparison with に. The tone is rather written.

examples[].german: You must not cause trouble for others.
You shouldn't worry too much about what other people think.
People often say we look alike, but we are complete strangers.
en.notes: 他人 are "other people" in contrast to oneself, often with the undertone "not belonging to the family, strangers": 他人に迷惑をかける, 他人の目を気にする. 赤の他人 means "a total stranger", 他人事 (ひとごと／たにんごと) "someone else's business, which does not concern one". More neutral in daily life is 他の人 or simply 人 (人の物を取る). For a "stranger" on the street, one rather says 知らない人.

examples[].german: She excels at mathematics.
People who excel in one skill are often successful in other fields too.
He excels at languages and can speak five languages.
en.notes: 秀でる means "to stand out clearly in a field" and takes に: 数学に秀でる, 語学に秀でる, 一芸に秀でる "to excel in one thing". It mostly appears as 秀でている or attributively as 秀でた. It sounds elevated and written; in conversation people say 優れている or 得意だ more often. Related is 抜きん出る, which stresses more the distance from others.

examples[].german: He stands out among his peers.
Her work stood out from the other entries.
This company is an outstanding presence in its industry thanks to its technological strength.
en.notes: 抜きん出る means "to stand clearly apart from others, to stand out", literally something like "to step forward pulled out". Typical are 〜の中で抜きん出る, 〜より抜きん出る and attributively 抜きん出た才能 / 抜きん出た存在. It stresses a large gap to the competition, like the phrase 群を抜く. It is also written 抜きんでる; the tone is rather written, and in conversation people often say ずば抜けている.

examples[].german: A tall mountain towered before my eyes.
A new high-rise apartment building towers in front of the station.
The sight of Fuji rising above the clouds was truly beautiful.
en.notes: そびえる describes how tall mountains or buildings rise majestically into the sky. It is almost always used in a state: 〜がそびえている, attributively そびえる山, or as the compound そびえ立つ. The place is marked with に: 町の中心に高いビルがそびえる. The word sounds descriptive and literary and is usually written in kana, since the kanji 聳 is not among the Jōyō kanji.

examples[].german: A skyscraper towers up.
The castle stands on a hill above the town.
In the distance you can see the peaks of the Alps rising up.
en.notes: 聳える is the kanji spelling of そびえる "to tower, to rise high", said of mountains, towers and high-rise buildings. Since 聳 is not a Jōyō kanji, this form is seen mainly in literature and elevated texts; in daily life it is usually written そびえる. Grammatically it is almost always used in a state (聳えている) or attributively (聳える塔), often also as 聳え立つ. The place is marked with に.

en.meaning: to lean; to tilt; to decline
examples[].german: The sun has begun to sink toward the west.
After the earthquake, the old house tilts slightly.
My father's company is faltering because of the recession.
en.notes: 傾く first means "to lean, to stand crooked" (家が傾く, 船が傾く). Of the sun and moon one says 日が傾く "the sun is sinking". Figuratively it means "to fall into crisis" (会社が傾く, 経営が傾く) and "to tend toward an opinion" (賛成に傾く, 気持ちが傾く). The transitive counterpart is 傾ける: 首を傾ける, 耳を傾ける "to listen attentively". 偏る, by contrast, stresses a one-sided distribution.

en.meaning: to be biased; to be lopsided; to be unbalanced
examples[].german: I am eating an unbalanced diet.
Please load the luggage so that it does not lean to one side.
If you read only online news, your information tends to be one-sided.
en.notes: 偏る means "to be distributed one-sidedly, to concentrate too much on one side". Very common are 栄養が偏る "to eat a one-sided diet", 偏った考え方 "biased way of thinking" and 〜に偏る "to be concentrated in ..." (人口が都市に偏る). The noun is 偏り. Unlike 傾く, which describes a visible tilt, 偏る usually concerns unequal distribution or lack of neutrality. The opposite is バランスがとれている.

en.meaning: to deviate; to stray; to veer off
examples[].german: The conversation strayed from the main topic.
The ball veered off to the right of the goal.
The typhoon veered east, so we were able to depart as planned.
en.notes: 逸れる means "to deviate from the intended direction": 話が本題から逸れる "to stray from the topic", 弾が逸れる "to miss the target", 台風が逸れる "the typhoon turns away", 道から逸れる. It is mostly written in kana (それる). The transitive counterpart is 逸らす: 目を逸らす "to look away", 話を逸らす "to change the subject". 外れる, by contrast, stresses missing the mark or coming off, not the movement to the side.

en.meaning: to miss; to come off; to be excluded
examples[].german: The weather forecast was wrong.
One of the buttons on your shirt is undone.
Because of an injury, he was dropped from the national team.
en.notes: 外れる has three main meanings: "to come off, to no longer be in place" (ボタンが外れる, 眼鏡が外れる), "to miss, not to come true" (予想が外れる, 天気予報が外れる, 宝くじが外れる "to draw a blank") and "to be excluded, to deviate" (メンバーから外れる, 道理に外れる). The transitive counterpart is 外す (眼鏡を外す, 席を外す). The opposite of 外れる in the sense of "to be wrong" is 当たる.

en.meaning: to go mad; to go wrong; to be thrown off
examples[].german: The plan went awry.
This clock is a bit off and is five minutes fast.
When he was young, he went wild over gambling and lost his fortune.
en.notes: 狂う originally means "to lose one's mind" (気が狂う), but in everyday speech it is mainly used for things that get out of sync: 時計が狂う "the clock is running wrong," 予定が狂う / 計画が狂う "the plan gets thrown off," 調子が狂う "to get out of rhythm." With に it means "to be crazy about something": ギャンブルに狂う. The transitive counterpart is 狂わせる. Applied to people, 狂う is drastic; be careful when using it in conversation about persons.

en.meaning: to fall into disorder; to be disturbed
examples[].german: My daily rhythm is out of order.
Because of the heavy snowfall, train service was disrupted.
The wind messed up my hair.
en.notes: 乱れる means "to fall out of order", both outwardly and inwardly: 髪が乱れる "the hair is tousled", 列が乱れる, 生活のリズムが乱れる, ダイヤが乱れる "the train timetable is disrupted", 心が乱れる "to be inwardly agitated". The transitive counterpart is 乱す (秩序を乱す "to disturb the order"). 狂う emphasizes more the malfunctioning of a mechanism or plan, 荒れる the wild and rough.

examples[].german: The young man took part in community service activities.
He is a polite, refreshing young man.
My grandfather spent his youth in Brazil.
en.notes: 青年 is a "young man" or "young person" roughly between the end of school and the late twenties; it usually refers to men. The word sounds somewhat literary or elevated: 好青年 ("likable young man"), 青年時代, 青年海外協力隊. More neutral and gender-independent is 若者; younger boys are called 少年.

en.meaning: to become rough; to run wild; to become chapped
examples[].german: The sea is rough because of the typhoon.
In winter the air is dry, and hands easily become chapped.
No one has lived there for a long time, so the garden has become completely overgrown.
en.notes: 荒れる means "to become rough, wild" and has several set uses: weather and sea (海が荒れる, 天気が荒れる), neglected places (荒れた庭 "overgrown garden"), skin (手が荒れる, 肌荒れ "rough or chapped skin") and people or situations that get out of control (クラスが荒れる, 会議が荒れる). The transitive counterpart is 荒らす "to ravage, to rummage through" (泥棒が部屋を荒らす). 乱れる, by contrast, is more "to get into disorder".

examples[].german: He is groaning in pain.
I heard someone groaning from the next room.
At the accident scene, injured people lay on the ground, groaning.
en.notes: 呻く means "to groan or moan in pain or torment". Typical are 痛みに呻く / 痛みで呻く and the noun うめき声 "groan". The word is mostly written in kana (うめく) because the kanji 呻 is not a Jōyō kanji. うなる describes more a deep rumble or growl (also of animals and engines), and 叫ぶ a loud scream. The tone is descriptive, often in narratives and reports.

examples[].german: My voice is trembling from nervousness.
My body shivered from the cold and wouldn't stop.
When I saw the news that I had passed, my hands trembled with joy.
en.notes: ふるえる (kanji 震える) means "to tremble, shake." The cause takes で: 寒さで震える, 緊張で声が震える, 怒りで手が震える. It describes involuntary, fine trembling of the body, voice or hands, but also the shaking of objects (窓ガラスが震える). 揺れる, by contrast, means a larger swaying (地震で建物が揺れる). The transitive counterpart is 震わせる (声を震わせる). Written in kana it looks softer; there is no difference in meaning.

examples[].german: The dog is afraid of the thunder.
The residents live in fear of the earthquakes that occur almost every night.
The child looked at me with frightened eyes.
en.notes: 怯える means "to be frightened, to be (continually) afraid"; the trigger is marked with に: 雷に怯える, 将来への不安に怯える. The attributive form 怯えた目 / 怯えた顔 is common. Unlike 怖がる, which describes visible fearful behavior, and 恐れる, which means "to fear" in a factual-formal way, 怯える emphasizes an inner, often lasting trembling with fear. The word is also written in kana (おびえる).

en.meaning: to be scared; to be startled
examples[].german: I calmed the child who was afraid of the dark.
He worked in constant fear of being fired at any moment.
Startled by the noise, the cat hid under the bed.
en.notes: おびえる is the kana spelling of 怯える "to be scared, to be frightened" and is often written this way in daily life. The trigger is marked with に (暗闇におびえる, 物音におびえる); with 〜かとおびえる one expresses what one constantly fears. 怖がる describes more the visible showing of fear, 恐れる the formal "to fear". Related is びくびくする "to flinch fearfully".

en.meaning: to be intimidated; to shrink; to atrophy
examples[].german: I get intimidated in front of my boss.
If you scold children too harshly, they become intimidated.
Muscles that aren't used gradually atrophy.
en.notes: 萎縮する literally means "to wither, to shrink" and, medically, "to atrophy" (筋肉が萎縮する). In everyday life it is used mainly figuratively: one is intimidated by pressure or authority and no longer dares to do anything (上司の前で萎縮する, 失敗を恐れて萎縮する). The economy or activities can also "slacken" (消費が萎縮する). Newspapers often write 委縮; 縮こまる is the physical, more colloquial cowering.

examples[].german: I was intimidated by the harsh criticism.
If regulations are too strong, there is a risk that corporate activity will be stifled.
Don't be intimidated by the fear of failure; just go for it.
en.notes: 委縮する is a substitute spelling of 萎縮する, used mainly by newspapers because 萎 was for a long time not among the Jōyō kanji. Meaning and use are the same: "to shrink" and, figuratively, "to be intimidated, to slacken". Typical are 批判を受けて委縮する, 経済活動が委縮する and the admonition 委縮せずに "without being intimidated". In books and technical texts, 萎縮 predominates again today.

en.meaning: to cower; to huddle up; to shrink back
examples[].german: It's cold, so I'm huddled up in my futon.
The newcomer who had been yelled at was cowering in a corner of the room.
In the interview, don't shrink back; speak confidently.
en.notes: 縮こまる means "to make oneself small, to cower", from cold (寒さで縮こまる) or from fear and shyness (隅で縮こまる). It describes a visible bodily posture and, figuratively, also timid behavior: 縮こまらずに堂々と. 縮む, by contrast, means "to shrink" (セーターが縮む), and 丸まる "to curl up round". The more literary 萎縮する describes more the inner state.

en.meaning: to curl up; to become rounded; to hunch
examples[].german: The cat is curled up on the sofa.
When I use the computer for a long time, my back gets rounded.
The edges of the old poster are curling, so I can't hang it up properly.
en.notes: 丸まる means "to become round, to curl up": 猫が丸まって寝る, 背中が丸まる "to get a hunched back", 紙の端が丸まる "to curl". The transitive counterpart is 丸める (紙を丸める "to crumple paper", 背中を丸める). Not to be confused with the identically read adverb 丸々 (丸々一日 "a whole day", 丸々と太った "plump").

en.meaning: to stoop; to bend down; to crouch
examples[].german: I stooped to get through the low entrance.
I bent down to pick up the dropped wallet.
My back hurts, so bending down is painful.
en.notes: 屈む means "to bend down, to lean forward, to crouch" and is mostly written in kana (かがむ). Typical: 屈んで拾う "to bend down and pick up", 低い入口で屈む. しゃがむ is crouching fully with bent knees, whereas かがむ stresses more the bending forward of the upper body. The transitive counterpart is 屈める (身を屈める, 腰を屈める).

examples[].german: After reaching middle age, I started paying attention to my health.
I'm bothered by my middle-age spread, so I decided to run every morning.
The culprit was reportedly a middle-aged man.
en.notes: 中年 is the "middle period of life", roughly from the early forties to the mid-fifties, and also refers to people of this age: 中年の男性, 中年になる. Well-known expressions are 中年太り ("middle-age spread") and 中高年 ("middle-aged and older people"). The word is neutral but can sound slightly unflattering; something like 四十代の方 is more polite.

en.meaning: to hang one's head; to look down
examples[].german: I was so embarrassed that I hung my head.
She was scolded by the teacher and stood there silently with her head bowed.
I was walking with my eyes on the ground and bumped into a utility pole.
en.notes: 俯く (usually written in kana, うつむく) means "to lower one's head, to look down", often out of shame, sadness, guilt or shyness. The verb is intransitive and takes no object; the everyday synonym is 下を向く, and the opposite is 顔を上げる or 上を向く. Common expressions are うつむいたまま "with one's head bowed" and うつむき加減に "head slightly lowered".

examples[].german: He hangs his head after losing the match.
Scolded by the teacher, he stood there in silence with his head bowed.
When she saw the result that she had failed, she hung her head in disappointment.
en.notes: うなだれる means "to hang one's head" - out of disappointment, shame or dejection. Typical: 負けてうなだれる, 叱られてうなだれる, がっくりとうなだれる. The kanji spelling 項垂れる is rare. うつむく means, more neutrally, "to look down" (also out of shyness), whereas うなだれる always expresses dejection. It is a descriptive word, common in narrative writing and sports reports.

en.meaning: to freeze; to stand rooted to the spot
examples[].german: I froze in the face of the sudden event.
A big bear suddenly appeared in front of me, and I stood frozen with fear.
Standing before his house burned down in the fire, all he could do was stand there, stunned.
en.notes: 立ちすくむ means "to stand rooted to the spot out of shock or bewilderment". The cause is marked with に or で: 突然の出来事に立ちすくむ, 恐怖で立ちすくむ; その場に立ちすくむ is also common. It is composed of 立つ and すくむ "to freeze" (足がすくむ "one's legs give way"). Unlike たたずむ, which describes standing still calmly and voluntarily, 立ちすくむ is always involuntary.

examples[].german: I stood lingering at the lakeshore.
In front of the station, a woman stood quietly in the rain.
Deep in the forest, a small shrine stands quietly, hidden from view.
en.notes: たたずむ (kanji 佇む) means "to stand quietly in one place and linger", often pensively or melancholically. The place is marked with に: 湖のほとりにたたずむ, 雨の中にたたずむ. Buildings or trees that stand calmly and inconspicuously in a place can also "たたずむ": 森の奥にたたずむ寺. The word is literary and descriptive. 立ち止まる only means "to stop (walking)", and 立ちすくむ "to freeze in shock". The noun たたずまい means "aura, appearance".

examples[].german: The children are running across the field.
The sight of a horse galloping across the grassland is beautiful.
He ran up the stairs in one go.
en.notes: 駆ける means "to run, to gallop", but sounds more dashing and literary than the everyday 走る. It is used of people, horses and animals running across an expanse (野原を駆ける, 草原を駆ける); the route is marked with を. It is very productive in compounds: 駆け足, 駆け上がる "to run up", 駆け寄る, 駆け付ける, 駆け回る, 駆け抜ける. There is no transitive counterpart.

en.meaning: to run up to; to rush over to
examples[].german: I ran over to the person who had collapsed.
When the child spotted its mother, it ran up to her happily.
The teammates all rushed up at once to the athlete who had reached the finish line.
en.notes: 駆け寄る means "to run up to someone or something", i.e. to run quickly over a short distance toward a nearby target. The target is marked with に or 〜のそばに: 倒れた人に駆け寄る, 母親に駆け寄る. 駆け付ける, by contrast, stresses hurrying to a place from farther away in response to news (現場に駆け付ける). The verb often shows joy, concern or readiness to help.

en.meaning: to rush to the scene; to hurry over
examples[].german: When I heard the news of the accident, I rushed over.
After receiving the report, the police rushed to the scene immediately.
A friend came all the way from far away to our wedding.
en.notes: 駆け付ける means "to come hurriedly to a place (in response to news)". The destination is marked with に or へ: 現場に駆け付ける, 病院に駆け付ける. It stresses urgency or readiness to help, so it suits police, firefighters and relatives, but also friends who travel specially (結婚式に駆け付けてくれた). It is often written 駆けつける. 駆け寄る, by contrast, is running up to something over a short distance.

en.meaning: to fly about; to run about
examples[].german: A butterfly is flying around the flowers.
The children are running around the park energetically.
He is rushing around all over the place every day for sales work.
en.notes: 飛び回る literally means "to fly around" (蝶が飛び回る), but also "to jump around, to romp" (子どもが飛び回る) and, figuratively, "to travel a lot, to be constantly on the go": 営業で飛び回る, 世界中を飛び回る. The area covered is marked with を. Related formations are 走り回る "to run around" and 駆け回る. The tone is neutral and everyday.

en.meaning: to crawl up; to claw one's way up
examples[].german: I clawed my way up from rock bottom.
The puppy that had fallen into a hole climbed back out by itself.
Climbing up from last place, the team finally won the championship.
en.notes: 這い上がる literally means "to crawl up, to pull oneself up" (穴から這い上がる). At least as common is the figurative meaning "to work one's way back up from a bad situation": どん底から這い上がる, 最下位から這い上がる. The starting point is marked with から. It is also written はい上がる. 這う alone means "to crawl, to creep".

examples[].german: The baby is crawling around on the floor.
Cockroaches were crawling around in the kitchen, and it made my skin crawl.
I crawled around on the floor looking for the contact lens I had dropped.
en.notes: 這い回る means "to crawl around, to creep about" and is used for babies, insects and animals, but also for people searching for something on the floor. The surface is marked with を: 床を這い回る. With insects such as cockroaches it often carries a sense of disgust. The base verb is 這う "to crawl"; the kana spelling はい回る is also common.

examples[].german: A cabinet meeting was held.
In the new cabinet, the number of female ministers has increased to five.
The prime minister appointed a young lawmaker as a cabinet minister.
en.notes: 閣僚 denotes the members of a cabinet (内閣), i.e. the ministers including the head of government, often as a group. It is a formal news word; for a single minister people more often say 大臣 in everyday speech. Typical: 閣僚に起用する ("to appoint to the cabinet"), 閣僚会議, 閣僚の顔ぶれ ("composition of the cabinet"), 女性閣僚.

examples[].german: There are educational programs for small children.
Please keep medicine out of the reach of small children.
Recently, many parents have their children learn English from early childhood.
en.notes: 幼児 is a "small child" of roughly one to six years, i.e. before starting school. Distinctions: 乳児 ("baby", under one year), 児童 ("schoolchild"). The word is factual and appears in notices, medicine and education: 幼児教育, 幼児向け, 乳幼児. In conversation one tends to say 小さい子 or 子ども.

examples[].german: I writhed in stomach pain.
In the hospital ward I have seen patients writhing in intense pain many times.
The fish that had been caught was thrashing about on the boat.
en.notes: のたうつ means "to writhe, to twist (in pain)" and is almost always written in kana. The compound のたうち回る "to roll about writhing" is especially common: 激痛でのたうち回る. It describes violent, uncontrolled movements of people or animals (snakes, caught fish). The tone is drastic and descriptive; in conversation, for mild pain one is more likely to say 痛くて動けない.

examples[].german: I struggle to get out of debt.
The child, who nearly drowned, flailed desperately in the water.
The patient writhed in severe pain.
en.notes: もがく is an intransitive verb and first describes physical flailing and writhing, for example in water or from pain (もがき苦しむ "to writhe in agony"). Figuratively it means "to struggle desperately", typically in the pattern 〜しようともがく. It is almost always written in kana. The closely related あがく emphasizes more the futile thrashing in a hopeless situation (悪あがき).

examples[].german: I intend to keep struggling until the end.
Struggling now won't change the result.
The dog that had fallen into the water was desperately paddling to get up onto the shore.
en.notes: あがく is intransitive and literally means "to paw the ground with one's feet, to kick about"; it is mostly used figuratively for a desperate, often futile struggle against a hopeless situation: 今さらあがいても無駄だ. The noun 悪あがき "pointless flailing, refusing to give up" is very common. The kanji spelling 足掻く is rare; kana is normal. Compared with もがく, あがく sounds more strongly "in vain".

examples[].german: I was ready to clutch at any straw.
My grandmother walked slowly, leaning on her cane.
In the end I prayed to pass, turning even to the gods in my desperation.
en.notes: すがる is the usual kana spelling of 縋る. It takes に and means "to cling to something, to lean on something" (杖にすがる) or, figuratively, "to rely desperately on someone, to implore". Set phrases: 藁にもすがる "to clutch at any straw" and 神にもすがる思い "praying to all the gods in one's distress". Unlike 頼る, すがる suggests dependence and having no way out.

en.meaning: to rely on; to depend on
examples[].german: When I'm in trouble, I turn to my friends.
If you rely too much on map apps, you won't be able to remember the way.
When I entered university, I went up to Tokyo relying on my uncle.
en.notes: 頼る means "to rely on someone or something, to depend on help" and mostly takes に: 親に頼る, 薬に頼る, 〜に頼りすぎる. With を it means "to use someone as a point of contact," e.g. 知人を頼って上京する "to go to Tokyo and stay with an acquaintance." Not to be confused with 頼む "to ask, commission." Related are 頼りになる "reliable" and 頼りない "unreliable."

en.meaning: to take over; to carry on
examples[].german: I took over the duties from my predecessor.
Before my transfer, I have to hand my work over to my successor.
My older brother took over our father's shop and became the second-generation owner.
en.notes: 引き継ぐ is transitive: 〜から〜を引き継ぐ "to take over from someone" (duties, a post, a business) or 〜に〜を引き継ぐ "to hand over to someone". It is typical of the working world; the noun 引き継ぎ is the "handover" at a job change or the end of a shift. In contrast, 受け継ぐ is used more for inherited traditions, talents or traits.

examples[].german: I inherited my grandfather's technique.
This festival is a tradition that has been handed down for over three hundred years.
The daughter inherited her mother's cheerful nature.
en.notes: 受け継ぐ is transitive (〜を受け継ぐ) and means "to inherit, to carry on" in the sense of traditions, techniques, character traits or the will of a deceased person. Very common in the passive: 代々受け継がれてきた伝統 "a tradition handed down from generation to generation". For the legal inheritance of property one says 相続する, for handing over work duties 引き継ぐ.

examples[].german: Please don't place excessive expectations on me.
Employees should not be given an excessive burden.
He overestimates his own abilities.
en.notes: 過大な is a rather written-language な-adjective meaning "too large, excessive", typically with abstract nouns: 過大な期待, 過大な負担, 過大な要求. The compound 過大評価(する) "to overestimate" is very common. The opposite is 過小. In everyday speech one often says simply 大きすぎる; 過度な stresses exceeding a limit in actions (過度な飲酒).

examples[].german: The damage must not be underestimated.
Because we had estimated the costs too low, the budget ran short.
She tends to underestimate her own ability.
en.notes: 過小 means "too small, too little" and is the counterpart of 過大. As the attributive form 過小な it is rather rare; typical are 過小に評価する / 過小に見積もる and above all the compound 過小評価(する) "to underestimate". It is written-language; in everyday speech people also say 甘く見る or 小さく見積もる.

examples[].german: The boy is playing soccer.
My father spent his boyhood in the countryside.
Every time I see news about juvenile crime, it pains my heart.
en.notes: 少年 is a "boy" roughly from school age to adolescence and sounds somewhat literary or narrative; in daily life one says 男の子. Typical: 少年時代, 少年野球, 少年漫画. In law (少年法, 少年犯罪), 少年 refers to all minors regardless of gender. The female counterpart is 少女.

examples[].german: Moderate exercise is good for your health.
Let's take an appropriate break between tasks.
I keep the room at a suitable humidity with a humidifier.
en.notes: 適度な describes the right, moderate amount: neither too much nor too little. Typical: 適度な運動, 適度な休憩, 適度な湿度, and adverbial 適度に (適度に体を動かす). 適切, by contrast, means "fitting, appropriate to the matter" (a measure, a choice of words), not "in the right amount". Be careful with 適当: in colloquial speech it often sounds like "sloppy, any old way".

examples[].german: Please respond appropriately.
It is difficult to choose the right words depending on the situation.
Thanks to the doctor's appropriate treatment, my father recovered quickly.
en.notes: 適切な means "suitable, appropriate, proper" and judges whether something fits the situation: 適切な対応, 適切な処置, 適切な表現, adverbial 適切に管理する. Opposite: 不適切 (不適切な発言). Unlike 適度, it is not about quantity. 適当 has the same basic meaning, but in speech it is often used pejoratively for "sloppy", so 適切 is the safe choice in formal contexts.

examples[].german: I think it is a reasonable decision.
For this quality, I think that price is reasonable.
For the time being, it would probably be reasonable to postpone the plan.
en.notes: 妥当な means "appropriate, justifiable, objectively warranted" and evaluates judgments, prices or conclusions: 妥当な判断, 妥当な金額, 〜とするのが妥当だ "it is reasonable to assume that ...". It is rather formal and typical of discussions and reports. The noun 妥当性 means "appropriateness, validity". 適切 stresses fitting the situation, 妥当 the reasonableness of a judgment.

examples[].german: I solved the problem in a rational way.
He is the type who thinks about everything rationally.
Cutting down on pointless meetings is a reasonable decision.
en.notes: 合理的な means "rational, reasonable, expedient" - without waste and based on reason: 合理的な方法, 合理的に考える, 合理的な判断. Opposite: 非合理的. Related is 合理化 "rationalization" (also in the sense of job cuts). 論理的, by contrast, stresses the logical consistency of an argument, 合理的 the practical reasonableness.

examples[].german: Please explain it logically.
Her writing is logical and easy to understand.
Let's not get emotional, but discuss it logically.
en.notes: 論理的な means "logical, consistent" and describes thinking, speaking and texts: 論理的に考える, 論理的に説明する, 論理的思考. Opposite: 非論理的; as a contrast, 感情的 "emotional" is common. Unlike 合理的 ("practically reasonable, efficient"), it is about a coherent structure of thought. Not to be confused with 理論的 "theoretical".

examples[].german: It is based on scientific evidence.
That health method has not been scientifically proven.
The claim that blood type determines personality is not scientific.
en.notes: 科学的な means "scientific" in the sense of "based on science and evidence": 科学的な根拠, 科学的に証明する, 科学的な方法. Opposite: 非科学的 (e.g. about superstition). In everyday speech it often appears negated: 科学的ではない. The noun 科学 refers mainly to the natural sciences; for "academic" in general, 学術的 is more usual.

examples[].german: I organized my knowledge systematically.
If you want to study grammar systematically, I recommend this textbook.
We have a systematic training program for new employees.
en.notes: 体系的な means "systematic, brought into an ordered overall system" and concerns mainly knowledge and learning: 体系的に学ぶ, 体系的に整理する, 体系的な知識. The base word is 体系 "system, structure". 組織的, by contrast, refers to the coordinated action of a group, and 計画的 to proceeding according to a plan.

examples[].german: Organized crime is increasing.
The company needs to tackle this as an organization.
After the earthquake, volunteers supported the disaster area in an organized way.
en.notes: 組織的な means "organized, coordinated, carried out by an organization": 組織的な犯罪 "organized crime", 組織的な支援, 組織的に取り組む "to tackle together as an organization". It stresses that not individuals but a group acts in a planned way. 体系的, by contrast, means ordered knowledge, and 計画的 acting according to a plan.

examples[].german: I am studying according to a plan.
I save money according to a plan every month.
The police regard this as a premeditated crime.
en.notes: 計画的な means "planned, according to plan": 計画的に貯金する, 計画的に勉強する. For crimes, 計画的な犯行 means "premeditated, planned act" as opposed to a spontaneous one (衝動的な犯行). Everyday opposite: 無計画 "unplanned". Often used adverbially with に.

examples[].german: To ease the regulations step by step.
The new system is scheduled to be introduced in stages.
I made a step-by-step practice menu for beginners.
en.notes: 段階的な means "step by step, in stages": 段階的に導入する, 段階的に引き上げる, 段階的な廃止. Typical of politics, administration and companies. Unlike 徐々に or 次第に ("gradually", smoothly), 段階的 stresses clearly separated steps. Base word: 段階 "step, phase".

examples[].german: The girl is playing in the park.
My older sister has loved shojo manga since long ago.
The protagonist of this novel is a twelve-year-old girl.
en.notes: 少女 is a "girl" roughly from school age to the teens and sounds somewhat literary, written or factual; in daily life one says 女の子. Typical are 少女漫画 ("manga for girls"), 少女時代 and news language such as 十歳の少女. The male counterpart is 少年.

examples[].german: A partial correction is necessary.
I partly agree with his opinion.
The novel is partly based on a true story.
en.notes: 部分的な means "partial": 部分的な修正, 部分的に賛成する "to agree in part", 部分的には正しい. Opposite: 全面的. In everyday speech 一部 is also often used (一部を修正する); 部分的 sounds somewhat more objective. Mostly adverbial with に or attributive with な.

examples[].german: A comprehensive review is being called for.
The company president fully supports this plan.
From next year, smoking will be banned throughout the station premises.
en.notes: 全面的な means "comprehensive, complete, across the board": 全面的に支持する, 全面的に協力する, 全面禁煙・全面的な見直し. Opposite: 部分的. It is used mainly adverbially with に and sounds more formal than 全部 or すっかり. Typical of the news, politics and official statements.

examples[].german: I carried out a thorough investigation.
At the end of the year I cleaned the whole house thoroughly.
Before the exam, I reviewed my weak areas thoroughly.
en.notes: 徹底的な means "thorough, down to the last detail": 徹底的に調べる, 徹底的に掃除する, 徹底的な調査. The base word is 徹底 (徹底する "to carry out consistently", 徹底した管理). It is stronger than よく or しっかり and stresses that nothing is left out. Mostly adverbial with に.

examples[].german: Fundamental reform is necessary.
Fundamental measures are being demanded to deal with the problem of the declining birthrate.
To reduce the deficit, there is no choice but to rethink the management from the ground up.
en.notes: 抜本的な literally means "pulling out the root", i.e. "fundamental, going to the root". Typical combinations: 抜本的な改革, 抜本的な対策, 抜本的に見直す. It belongs to the language of politics and business and sounds more formal than 根本的, which means something similar, "basic, from the ground up". "Radical" in the sense of extreme, by contrast, is 過激.

examples[].german: Please give a concrete example.
Could you explain it a little more concretely?
The specific travel schedule has not been decided yet.
en.notes: 具体的な means "concrete, tangible": 具体的な例, 具体的な計画, 具体的に説明する. Very common in requests for clarification: もう少し具体的に言ってください. Opposite: 抽象的. Related words: 具体例 "concrete example", 具体化 "concretization, making concrete".

examples[].german: I would like to avoid abstract discussions.
His explanation is so abstract that I can hardly understand it.
Abstract paintings give a different impression depending on the viewer.
en.notes: 抽象的な means "abstract" and is the opposite of 具体的. It is often used critically for vague, hard-to-grasp statements: 説明が抽象的すぎる. In art one speaks of 抽象画 "abstract painting" or 抽象的な絵. Base word: 抽象 "abstraction".

examples[].german: In theory it is possible, but carrying it out is difficult.
Both theoretical research and experiments are necessary.
The teacher explained the phenomenon to us theoretically.
en.notes: 理論的な means "theoretical, based on theory": 理論的な研究, 理論的に説明する. Very common is 理論的には "theoretically (but not in practice)", equivalent to 理論上は. The counterpart is 実践的 or 実際的. Do not confuse it with 論理的 "logical" - the two words have the same kanji in reverse order.

examples[].german: To acquire practical skills.
In this course you mainly learn practical conversation.
Not only theory but also practical experience is important.
en.notes: 実践的な means "practice-oriented, practically applicable" and describes knowledge, skills and teaching: 実践的なスキル, 実践的な英語, 実践的な訓練. The counterpart is 理論的. 実用的, by contrast, means "practical, useful" for objects (実用的なカバン). Base word: 実践 "practice, putting into action" (実践する "to put into practice").

examples[].german: Let's set more realistic goals.
Realistically speaking, finishing it within this year is difficult.
Rather than chase his dream, he chose a realistic path.
en.notes: 現実的な means "realistic, true to reality": 現実的な目標, 現実的な案, 現実的に考える "to think realistically". It can also mean "sober, pragmatic" as a character trait (彼は現実的な人だ). Opposite: 非現実的 or 理想的 in the sense of "idealistic". Base word: 現実 "reality".

examples[].german: That plan is unrealistic.
Losing ten kilos in a month is an unrealistic goal.
An unreal scene like something out of a movie spread out before my eyes.
en.notes: 非現実的な is the negation of 現実的 with the prefix 非 "non-". Usually it means "unrealistic, not feasible" (非現実的な計画, 非現実的な目標); but it can also mean "unreal, dreamlike", for example for landscapes or experiences. Similar: 現実離れした "detached from reality".

examples[].german: In Japan, you become an adult at eighteen.
On Coming of Age Day, I wore a furisode kimono and took photos with my family.
The children have all grown up and left home.
en.notes: 成人 is the "adult" in the legal or formal sense and, as an intransitive する-verb, "to come of age, to grow up" (子どもが成人する). In daily life one usually says 大人. Since 2022, the age of majority in Japan is 18; drinking and smoking, however, remain allowed only from 20. Well known are 成人式 and the holiday 成人の日 in January.

examples[].german: She always has an optimistic way of thinking.
Experts take an optimistic view of the economic recovery.
If you think about it that optimistically, you'll get into trouble later.
en.notes: 楽観的な means "optimistic" and describes a view of future developments: 楽観的な見方, 楽観的に考える, 見通しは楽観的だ. Opposite: 悲観的. The verb 楽観する or 楽観視する means "to view confidently", often negated: 楽観できない. 楽天的 describes more a fundamentally carefree nature.

examples[].german: Please don't be too pessimistic.
He is pessimistic about his own future.
According to the survey, more and more people are pessimistic about the economic outlook.
en.notes: 悲観的な means "pessimistic, gloomy": 悲観的な見方, 悲観的になる, 将来に悲観的だ. Opposite: 楽観的. The verb 悲観する means "to see things black, to despair" (将来を悲観する). Often found in advice: そんなに悲観的にならないで.

examples[].german: I will state my opinion from a neutral standpoint.
Reporters should report in a neutral manner.
When friends quarrel, I want to take neither side and stay neutral.
en.notes: 中立的な means "neutral, impartial": 中立的な立場, 中立的な態度, 中立的に報道する. The base word is 中立 "neutrality", which also stands alone (中立を守る, 中立国 "neutral country"). In everyday speech one also says どちらの味方もしない "to take neither side". 公平 stresses more "just, fair".

examples[].german: I feel a vague sense of unease.
I'm thinking vaguely about the future.
It's hard to answer such a vague question.
en.notes: 漠然 is a たる-adjective: attributively 漠然とした "vague, blurry" (漠然とした不安, 漠然としたイメージ), adverbially 漠然と (漠然と考える "to think only vaguely"). It describes something indefinite, without clear outlines. 曖昧, by contrast, means "ambiguous, unclear" - for example an evasive answer. Used mainly in written Japanese.

examples[].german: The outlook is uncertain.
The flow of political funds is criticized as opaque.
Please put it in an opaque bag so that the contents can't be seen.
en.notes: 不透明な literally means "opaque, not see-through" (不透明な袋, 不透明なガラス), and figuratively "unclear, impenetrable". Very common in the news: 先行き不透明 "uncertain prospects", 不透明な資金の流れ "opaque flows of money". Opposite: 透明. For unclarity in statements, 曖昧 fits better.

examples[].german: I use a clear glass cup.
The sea in Okinawa is so clear that you can see all the way to the bottom.
The election procedures should be more transparent.
en.notes: 透明な means "see-through, clear" for glass, water or film (透明なガラス, 透明な水). Figuratively it means "transparent, traceable" for procedures and flows of money; for this, the noun 透明性 "transparency" is very common. Opposite: 不透明. 透明人間 is the "invisible man".

examples[].german: Clear evidence was found.
It is obvious that he is lying.
This is a clear violation of the rules.
en.notes: 明白な means "evident, unambiguous, undeniable" and sounds more formal than the everyday 明らか: 明白な事実, 明白な証拠, 明白な違反, 〜のは明白だ. Typical of reports, courts and discussions. In conversation, people mostly say はっきりしている or 明らかだ.

examples[].german: He achieved remarkable results.
Recently, it has become clear that young people are reading less and less.
With this medicine, a marked effect was seen especially in elderly people.
en.notes: 顕著な means "strikingly evident, conspicuous, marked" and describes measurable differences, tendencies or effects: 顕著な効果, 顕著な傾向, 〜が顕著になる / 顕著に表れる. It is a formal word of reports and news; in everyday speech, 目立つ or はっきりした is more usual. Praise in the sense of "excellent" is expressed rather by 優れた.

examples[].german: The problem has become apparent.
We should pay attention not only to customers' manifest needs but also to their latent needs.
More than the risks that are visible, I fear the risks that nobody can see yet.
en.notes: 顕在的な is a technical word ("manifest, coming out into the open") and the counterpart of 潜在的 "latent". It appears mainly in marketing and specialist texts, e.g. 顕在的なニーズ "expressed, conscious needs" as opposed to 潜在的なニーズ. Much more common is the verb 顕在化する "to come to light, to become visible" (問題が顕在化する); 顕在的になる sounds unnatural.

examples[].german: Don't overlook latent risks.
I think she has latent ability.
With the aging of society, there is large potential demand for this product.
en.notes: 潜在的な means "latent, potential, present beneath the surface": 潜在的なリスク, 潜在的な需要, 潜在的な能力. It describes something that already exists but is not yet visible or effective. The counterpart is 顕在的. Related words: 潜在能力 "hidden potential", 潜在意識 "subconscious".

examples[].german: Drinking by minors is prohibited by law.
If a minor wants to take a part-time job, parental consent is required.
The suspect in the case was a minor, so the name was not made public.
en.notes: 未成年 means "underage" or "minor" (also 未成年者) and is the legal, formal term; it is combined with の: 未成年の子ども, 未成年の飲酒. Since 2022, people under 18 in Japan count as 未成年; alcohol and cigarettes are nevertheless allowed only from 20 (二十歳未満). The opposite is 成人.

examples[].german: This is a typical example.
He is a typical Japanese office worker.
This is a typical pattern common in fraud.
en.notes: 典型的な means "typical, a textbook example of something": 典型的な例, 典型的な日本人, 典型的なパターン. It is often also used with a slightly critical tone when something fits a cliché. 代表的, by contrast, means "representative, especially well known" (代表的な料理). Base word: 典型 "type, model example".

examples[].german: This building is a symbolic presence of its era.
That incident symbolically expresses the changes of the times.
At the opening ceremony there were several symbolic moments expressing the wish for peace.
en.notes: 象徴的な means "symbolic, emblematic, rich in symbolism": 象徴的な存在, 象徴的な出来事, 〜を象徴的に表す. The base word is 象徴 "symbol" (平和の象徴, 象徴する "to symbolize"). It describes something that stands in for a larger idea or era; in the sense of "purely formal, just for show", it is hardly used.

examples[].german: Special techniques are required.
Except in special cases, returns are not possible.
The door of this room can only be opened with a special key.
en.notes: 特殊な means "special, particular, of an unusual kind" and stresses that something deviates from the normal: 特殊な技術, 特殊なケース, 特殊な素材. 特別, by contrast, means "special, extra" in the sense of special treatment or appreciation (特別な日, 特別に許可する). Opposite of 特殊: 一般的 or 普通.

examples[].german: He is a person with a unique talent.
This region is known for its peculiar climate.
The case was widely covered in the newspaper as an unusual individual case.
en.notes: 特異な means "peculiar, unique, out of the ordinary": 特異な才能, 特異な性格, 特異な事件. It is a written-language word and stresses the unusual, not necessarily in a positive sense. Well-known compounds: 特異体質 "special (allergic) constitution", 特異点 "singularity". Note: it is read the same as 得意 "good at something, strong point".

examples[].german: The unusual heat continues.
I woke up in the middle of the night because of a strange noise.
The examination found nothing in particular wrong.
en.notes: 異常な means "abnormal, unusual, not normal": 異常な暑さ, 異常な音, 異常気象 "abnormal weather". As a noun it appears in medical findings: 異常なし "no abnormalities", 異常が見つかる. Opposite: 正常. Compared with 珍しい ("rare"), 異常 sounds like a malfunction or danger.

examples[].german: The system is operating normally.
In the health checkup, my blood pressure was normal.
The trains that had been delayed by the accident returned to normal service by the evening.
en.notes: 正常な means "normal, proper, functioning" in the sense of a fault-free state: 正常に動作する, 正常な値, 正常に戻る. Opposite: 異常. 普通, by contrast, means "ordinary, average", and 通常 "usually". 正常 suits technology, medicine and processes, not people in the sense of "average".

examples[].german: The regular business hours are from nine to six.
Normally, a reply takes about three days.
In this sale, you can buy it for half the regular price.
en.notes: 通常 means "usual, normal, regular" and is more formal than いつも or 普通. Attributively it takes の: 通常の営業時間, 通常の料金. Adverbially it means "normally": 通常、〜です. Other patterns: 通常通り "as usual", 通常は. Typical of business language, notices and announcements.

examples[].german: I want to be able to hold everyday conversations.
She jogs regularly as part of her daily routine.
In this area, power outages happen as a matter of routine.
en.notes: 日常的な means "everyday, regular, commonplace": 日常的な会話, 日常的に使う, 日常的に起きる. It can mean neutrally "part of everyday life" or critically "occurring constantly" (暴力が日常的に行われる). Base word: 日常 "everyday life" (日常生活). Opposite: 非日常的.

examples[].german: Travel gives us extraordinary experiences.
I spent a time away from everyday life at a luxury hotel.
After the earthquake, life in an evacuation shelter continued for a while in a state of emergency.
en.notes: 非日常的な means "out of the ordinary, beyond everyday life" and is the opposite of 日常的. In advertising for travel, hotels and theme parks it is positive ("special, exciting"), often as a noun: 非日常を味わう "to experience something extraordinary". In other contexts it can also describe a burdensome state of emergency.

examples[].german: Children's individuality should be respected.
She always wears distinctive clothes.
I want to create a workplace where each employee's individuality can be put to good use.
en.notes: 個性 is "individuality", i.e. what distinguishes a person or thing from others. Typical: 個性を尊重する, 個性を生かす／伸ばす, 個性が強い; the adjective 個性的な means "original, distinctive". 性格, by contrast, is "character" in the sense of temperament (性格がいい／明るい). Positive to neutral, very common in education and advertising.

examples[].german: My everyday efforts have borne fruit.
As thanks for everything she does for me day to day, I gave my mother flowers.
It is important to prepare for disasters in everyday life.
en.notes: 日頃 is a noun/adverb meaning "usually, constantly, in daily life". With の it stands before nouns: 日頃の努力, 日頃の感謝, 日頃の行い "everyday behavior". Very common is 日頃から "already in daily life, always" (日頃から備える). Also typical in thank-you formulas: 日頃より大変お世話になっております. Intensified: 常日頃.

examples[].german: I value my everyday life.
Please don't come in a suit today, but in your regular clothes.
I couldn't show my usual strength in the exam.
en.notes: 普段 refers to the normal, everyday state as opposed to special occasions; as an attribute it takes の: 普段の生活, 普段の服, 普段の自分. Adverbially one says 普段は "normally" or 普段から "already in daily life, constantly". Compared with いつも, 普段 stresses the contrast with an exceptional situation: 普段は静かな町 "a town that is normally quiet". 普段着 means "everyday clothes"; the more matter-of-fact 日常 sounds more written.

examples[].german: The traditional summer festival was held.
At the end of the year, the annual year-end party is held.
Going to the first shrine visit of the year as a family is a tradition in our house.
en.notes: 恒例 refers to something that recurs regularly as a fixed custom or tradition, mostly annually: 恒例の行事, 毎年恒例の花火大会. Typical are 毎年恒例の and 〜が恒例になっている "has become a tradition". Unlike 定例 (officially fixed dates such as meetings), 恒例 sounds like custom and anticipation. Slightly elevated, but common in the news and in daily life.

examples[].german: The regular meeting is held every Monday.
The minister announced the new policy at his regular press conference.
This month's regular meeting has been changed to next Wednesday.
en.notes: 定例 means "taking place regularly according to a fixed schedule" and concerns mainly official or business appointments: 定例会議, 定例会見, 定例の打ち合わせ. The counterpart is 臨時 "unscheduled" (臨時会議). Unlike 恒例, which sounds like custom and tradition, 定例 is sober and official. It is often used as a prefix directly before the noun without の.

examples[].german: An extraordinary day off was set.
On the day of the fireworks festival, extra trains will run.
I had some unexpected extra income this month, so we ate out as a family.
en.notes: 臨時 refers to something that is set up additionally or temporarily on a special occasion rather than according to schedule: 臨時休業 "closed unexpectedly", 臨時列車 "special train", 臨時ニュース "news flash", 臨時収入 "unexpected extra income". Opposites are 定例 and 定期 "regular". For fixed-term work one says 臨時職員; as a prefix, 臨時 often stands without の.

examples[].german: An urgent message came in.
In an emergency, please call this number.
Because of an urgent meeting, the department head canceled his business trip.
en.notes: 緊急 means "urgent, acute, emergency" and describes a situation that demands immediate action: 緊急の用事, 緊急事態 "state of emergency", 緊急連絡先 "emergency contact", 緊急地震速報 "earthquake early warning". Compared with the everyday 急ぎの "in a hurry", 緊急 is more serious and more formal; 至急 "immediately" appears more in requests (至急ご連絡ください). As a prefix, 緊急 often stands without の.

examples[].german: An immediate response is required.
At the scene of an accident, a split-second decision can sometimes save lives.
She was invited, but she declined immediately.
en.notes: 即座 means "on the spot, immediately". Most common is the adverbial form 即座に (即座に答える, 即座に断る); attributively with の it sounds written: 即座の判断, 即座の対応. Close in meaning are すぐ (everyday), 直ちに (formal, in instructions) and 即時 (technical, e.g. 即時払い). 即座 stresses that the reaction occurs at that very moment without any hesitation.

examples[].german: Urgent measures are necessary.
Could you please reply to me promptly about this matter?
Residents are demanding urgent repair of the old bridge.
en.notes: 早急 means "urgent, as soon as possible" and appears mainly in formal texts about measures and solutions: 早急な対策, 早急な対応, adverbial 早急に検討する. The reading さっきゅう is the traditional one; そうきゅう is now also widespread and accepted. Unlike 迅速 (which praises the actual speed of an execution), 早急 expresses that something must be done in a hurry.

examples[].german: Thank you for your prompt response.
Thanks to the fire brigade's swift action, the fire was put out quickly.
The goods I ordered arrived quickly, which was a great help.
en.notes: 迅速 means "swift and prompt" with regard to actions and procedures, not physical speed: 迅速な対応, 迅速な処理, 迅速に行動する. It is a formal word from business and official language; in everyday speech one says すばやい or 早い. Unlike 急速 (rapid change or development), 迅速 praises the speed of a deliberately carried-out response.

examples[].german: I am amazed at the rapid development of technology.
With the spread of the Internet, information now spreads rapidly.
Rapid population aging is progressing in this region.
en.notes: 急速 describes a very fast change or development: 急速な発展, 急速な成長, 急速に広がる, 急速に冷える. It typically appears with processes such as growth, spread or change, not with the actions of people - for those, 迅速 is used. Neutral to slightly formal; 急激, by contrast, stresses a sudden, often undesirable change (急激な変化).

examples[].german: This city has a lot of charm.
The best appeal of this job is that you get to meet people from many countries.
I was drawn to his kind smile.
en.notes: 魅力 is "charm, appeal, attraction" of people, places or things: 〜に魅力を感じる, 〜の魅力, 魅力がある. The adjective 魅力的な ("attractive, appealing") is very common. Unlike かっこいい／かわいい, 魅力 refers not only to appearance but to the overall impression. Neutral, equally common in advertising and conversation.

examples[].german: He is steadily producing results.
The construction work is progressing steadily as scheduled.
In language learning, steady daily effort is important.
en.notes: 着実 means "steady, step by step and reliable": progress is made not in leaps but surely. Often adverbial: 着実に進む, 着実に成果を上げる, 着実に力をつける. Unlike 堅実 (cautious, low-risk, solid), 着実 puts the emphasis on even progress. In everyday conversation, similarly, one says こつこつ "persistently, bit by bit".

examples[].german: The company has earned trust with its sound management policy.
She is a sensible person who doesn't waste money.
He has been saving money sensibly since he was young.
en.notes: 堅実 means "solid, sensible, low-risk" and praises an attitude that relies on safety rather than speculation: 堅実な経営, 堅実な生活, 堅実な人, 堅実に貯金する. In contrast to 着実 (even progress), 堅実 stresses reliability and caution. It is mostly positive, but can also carry a hint of "a bit tame, without risk-taking".

examples[].german: I am carrying out two tasks at the same time.
The moment the door opened, the children ran out.
I am glad to graduate, but at the same time I feel a little sad.
en.notes: 同時に means "at the same time" and has three uses: As an adverb it describes simultaneous events (二つのことを同時にする); after a verb, with と同時に, it means "at the same moment as ..." (ベルが鳴ると同時に). After adjectives or at the start of a sentence it means "at the same time, on the other hand": うれしいと同時に寂しい. In conversation one also says いっぺんに; 一斉に, by contrast, means "all at once".

examples[].german: We will respond in order.
The items you ordered will be shipped one after another as soon as they arrive in stock.
The new system will be introduced to each branch in turn from next month.
en.notes: 順次 means "one after another, in order, step by step" and is typical of formal announcements by companies and authorities: 順次発送いたします "will be shipped gradually", 順次対応いたします. It usually stands directly before the verb without a particle. In everyday speech one says 順番に or 一つずつ instead; 順次 stresses less a fixed order than working through things step by step.

examples[].german: I will call the names in order.
The restroom is crowded, so please line up in order.
The siblings decided to take turns using the game.
en.notes: 順番に means "in order, one after another" and is the everyday form: 順番に並ぶ, 順番に話す, 順番に使う. The noun 順番 means "order, turn": 順番を待つ "to wait for one's turn", 私の順番だ "it's my turn". More formal and more written is 順次; 交代で, by contrast, emphasizes taking over from one another in an activity.

examples[].german: I arranged red and blue alternately.
Skewer meat and vegetables alternately and grill them.
Since it was a long drive, my father and I took turns driving.
en.notes: 交互に means "alternately" in the sense of a regular switching between two (or more) things: AとBを交互に並べる, 左右の足を交互に出す. Compared with 順番に (in order, several participants) and 交代で (taking turns at an activity), 交互に stresses the A-B-A-B pattern. Neutral style, also in instructions and recipes.

examples[].german: It is important to help each other.
The two looked at each other and laughed.
The team members grew by competing with one another.
en.notes: 互いに means "mutually, each other" and often appears with verbs in 〜合う: 互いに助け合う, 互いに理解し合う. In conversation one more often says お互いに or お互い (お互い様 "we're in the same boat"); the bare 互いに seems somewhat more written. The formal synonym 相互に belongs more in specialist texts and contracts.

examples[].german: We share information with one another.
The two countries agreed to cooperate economically with each other.
Temperature and humidity influence each other.
en.notes: 相互に means "reciprocally, mutually" and is the formal, written counterpart of 互いに. It appears in contracts, reports and specialist texts: 相互に協力する, 相互に影響し合う; as a prefix in compounds such as 相互理解 "mutual understanding" or 相互作用 "interaction". In conversation, お互いに sounds more natural.

examples[].german: Please have lunch on your own.
It was decided that each person will bear their own travel costs.
Please look after your own valuables.
en.notes: 各自 means "each individual, each for themselves" and is used mainly in instructions to a group: 各自で準備する, 昼食は各自でお願いします "please arrange lunch yourselves", 各自の責任. It stands as a noun with の or adverbially, often with で. Similar are それぞれ (more neutral, also for things) and 一人一人 (stresses the individual person); 各自 sounds like an administrative or school instruction.

examples[].german: We will respond to you individually.
The sweets are individually wrapped, one by one.
The teacher talked with each student individually about their grades.
en.notes: 個別に means "individually, separately" - each case or person is dealt with on its own: 個別に対応する, 個別に相談する, 個別に包装する. The counterpart is まとめて or, formally, 一括して "collectively, all at once". As a prefix, 個別 forms compounds such as 個別指導 "one-on-one instruction" or 個別面談 "individual meeting". Neutral to formal, common in business language.

examples[].german: Single-person households are increasing.
The head of household's name is written on the residence certificate.
The electricity cost per household went up compared to last year.
en.notes: 世帯 is the "household" as a statistical or administrative unit (people who live and manage finances together): 世帯主 ("head of household"), 一人世帯, 共働き世帯, 一世帯あたり. For family life at home people say 家庭, for the people 家族. Do not confuse it with 所帯 (しょたい, "one's own household", more colloquial).

examples[].german: Overall, it was a good result.
This room is done in light colors overall.
The report is well written overall, but the conclusion is weak.
en.notes: 全体的に means "overall, by and large" and sums up a general impression: 全体的に見ると, 全体的に良い, 全体的に暗い色. A qualification often follows: 全体的にはいいが、細かいミスがある. The counterpart is 部分的に "partially". Close in meaning is the somewhat more formal 全般的に; in conversation one also says だいたい.

examples[].german: It needs to be corrected in part.
I think his opinion is correct in part.
The typhoon partially damaged the roof.
en.notes: 部分的に means "partially, in places" and restricts a statement to one part: 部分的に修正する, 部分的に正しい, 部分的に壊れる. The counterpart is 全体的に. In everyday speech one often says 一部 (一部だけ, 一部の人); 部分的に is somewhat more objective and typical of reports, evaluations and instructions.

examples[].german: Heavy rain is falling locally.
This medicine is applied locally to the painful area.
The earthquake damage was concentrated in localized areas.
en.notes: 局所的に means "locally, in a limited area" and comes from technical and news language: in weather reports (局所的に激しい雨 "locally heavy rain") and in medicine (局所的に痛む, 局所麻酔 "local anesthesia"). In everyday speech one more often says ところどころ or 一部の地域で. Compared with 部分的に, 局所的に refers to a spatially narrowly limited area.

examples[].german: We need to change our way of thinking fundamentally.
It will take time to solve this problem at its root.
The opinions of the two differ fundamentally.
en.notes: 根本的に means "fundamentally, from the ground up" and aims at the root (根本) of a matter: 根本的に見直す, 根本的に解決する, 根本的に違う. Typical is the contrast with superficial fixes: 一時的な対策ではなく根本的な解決. Close in meaning is 抜本的 (more formal, mainly for reforms); 本質的に, by contrast, describes the essence of a thing, not the extent of a change.

examples[].german: These two problems are essentially the same.
Human beings are by nature social creatures.
His proposal does not solve the essential problem.
en.notes: 本質的に means "in essence, basically" and refers to the actual nature (本質) of a thing, regardless of external differences: 本質的に同じ, 本質的に異なる, 本質的な問題 "the real problem". The counterpart is 表面的に "superficially". It sounds matter-of-fact to academic; it differs from 根本的に in that it describes the essence, not the extent of a change.

examples[].german: I only understand it superficially.
On the surface, those two seem to get along well.
Mere superficial measures cannot prevent accidents.
en.notes: 表面的に means "superficially, only in outward appearance": 表面的に理解する, 表面的には仲がいい "on the surface they get along well". It often appears with は or しか and hints that things look different underneath. The counterpart is 本質的に or 深く. Close in meaning, but more colloquial and more disparaging, is うわべだけ.

examples[].german: We exchanged formal greetings.
The meeting was only held as a formality, and nothing was decided.
There is an interview before you join the company, but it's just a formality, so don't worry.
en.notes: 形式的に means "purely formally, for form's sake": something is done because it is a rule or custom, without real substance - 形式的に確認する, 形式的な手続き, 形式的な挨拶. It often has a slightly critical undertone ("just pro forma"). The counterpart is 実質的に "in substance". For "formal" in the sense of etiquette, one says 改まった or フォーマルな.

examples[].german: In practice, he fulfills the role of leader.
This service is effectively free if you use points.
My salary went up, but prices also went up, so in real terms nothing has changed.
en.notes: 実質的に means "in substance, in fact, effectively" and contrasts the actual state with the formal one: 実質的に無料, 実質的には部長が決めている. The counterpart is 形式的に or 名目上. Very close is 事実上, which stresses more "de facto, although not official". Often with は for emphasis: 実質的には.

examples[].german: He announced his de facto retirement.
This plan was effectively canceled due to a lack of budget.
It is practically impossible to reach the venue at this time.
en.notes: 事実上 means "de facto, in fact, practically": something holds in reality even if it has not been declared officially. Adverbially it stands without a particle (事実上不可能だ), attributively with の (事実上の引退, 事実上のトップ). Very close is 実質的に; 事実上 sounds like news and written language. In everyday speech one more often says ほとんど or 実際には.

examples[].german: He is president in name only and has no real power.
Officially it was training, but in reality it was just a sightseeing trip.
He is nothing more than a nominal representative.
en.notes: 名目上 means "nominally, in name only": a title or purpose exists officially but does not correspond to reality. Typical is the contrast with 実際は or 実権: 名目上は社長だが実権はない. Attributively it takes の (名目上の代表), adverbially often は. The counterpart is 実質的に or 事実上; related is 建前上, which refers more to the official stance than to the title.

examples[].german: Let's observe good manners in public places.
On the day, please use public transportation.
I pay public utility bills such as electricity and gas by card.
en.notes: 公共 means "public, serving the general public" and almost always appears with の or as the first part of a compound: 公共の場, 公共施設, 公共交通機関, 公共料金 (fees for electricity, gas, water). 公共の福祉 is the "public welfare". Similar is 公衆 in 公衆トイレ／公衆電話; the noun "the public" is rather 公 (おおやけ) or 世間.

en.meaning: officially; as a matter of form
examples[].german: In principle I agree, but in my heart I am opposed.
Officially, overtime is prohibited at this company.
In principle anyone can take part, but in reality only members come.
en.notes: 建前上 means "officially, on the face of it" and refers to 建前, the publicly held stance, as opposed to 本音 "one's true intention". Typical is the contrast 建前上は〜だが、本音は〜 or 実際は〜. It is often used with a slightly critical tone when rules or statements apply only formally. Closely related are 表向きは and 名目上 (which refers more to titles or purposes).

examples[].german: As a rule, we are closed on Mondays.
Sale items cannot, as a rule, be returned.
As a rule, reports must be created on a computer, not by hand.
en.notes: 原則として means "in principle, as a rule" and announces a rule to which exceptions may exist: 原則として〜とする, 原則として認めない. A note on the exception with ただし often follows. Equivalent are 原則的に and, short, 原則 (原則、返品不可). Matter-of-fact and formal, typical of rules, notices and terms and conditions; in conversation one says 基本的に more often.

examples[].german: I will allow it as an exception this time.
This winter was exceptionally warm.
Except for exceptional cases such as illness, absence is not accepted.
en.notes: 例外的に means "as an exception" and is used when a rule is departed from: 例外的に認める, 例外的に許可する, often with 今回は. It can also mean "exceptionally, unusually": 例外的に暖かい冬. In conversation 特別に or 今回だけ sounds more natural; 例外的に is more matter-of-fact and stresses that a rule exists. Attributively: 例外的な措置 "exceptional measure", 例外的なケース.

examples[].german: I was given a special discount.
Since today is your birthday, we have specially prepared a cake.
I don't have any particular favorite food, but there is nothing I dislike either.
en.notes: 特別に means "specially, extra, as an exception" and sets something apart from the norm: 特別に許可する, 特別に作ってもらう, 特別に安くする. It often implies that it is a favor (今日だけ特別に). Negated, it means "not particularly": 特別に好きなわけではない. Unlike 特に ("above all", singling out from a group), 特別に describes special treatment.

examples[].german: This year was an especially hot summer.
Among this author's works, I especially like the early short stories.
In winter there are few tourists in Kyōto, and mornings in particular are quiet.
en.notes: 殊に means "especially, above all" and is a written-language variant of 特に. It stands before adjectives or highlights one element: 殊に暑い, 殊に印象的だった. In conversation 特に sounds more natural; 殊に is found in essays, speeches and literature, often also in kana (ことに). Do not confuse with 〜ことに after adjectives (残念なことに "regrettably"), which is a different pattern.

examples[].german: Of Japanese food, I especially like sushi.
This winter was particularly harsh.
In class he stands out above all in mathematics.
en.notes: とりわけ means "particularly, above all" and singles out one element from a group; it is slightly more elevated than 特に but also common in conversation. It is usually written in kana (取り分け as a noun means "portioning out food"). Typical: 中でもとりわけ, とりわけ〜が好きだ, 今年はとりわけ寒い. Synonymous but more written is 殊に.

examples[].german: Among the many issues, education is especially important.
He had a deep interest in art, especially music.
Relations with Asian countries, especially China, are becoming important.
en.notes: なかんずく means "above all, most especially" and is a very literary, archaic word (derived from 中に就く). It appears almost only in speeches, essays and elevated texts and is written in kana; typical is the form A、なかんずくB "A, especially B". In normal conversation it is replaced by 中でも, 特に or とりわけ. For learners it is enough to recognize the word when reading.

examples[].german: Health is more important than anything else.
I'm glad to see that you are well.
On the trip, I'm looking forward above all to the local food.
en.notes: 何より means "more than anything else, above all": 何より大切だ, 何より嬉しい; 何よりも strengthens it further. As an expression it means "the best, the nicest thing": お元気そうで何よりです "I'm glad to see you are well" is a very common polite phrase. Unlike 特に, 何より does not single something out from a named group but places something above everything else. Neutral; usual in conversation as well as in letters.

examples[].german: I meant to save money, but my expenses actually went up.
I tried to apologize to her, but she ended up apologizing to me instead.
Conversely, this means that now is our chance.
en.notes: 逆に means "conversely, on the contrary" and marks that a result or viewpoint runs counter to what was expected: 逆に〜になった, 逆に言えば "put the other way". In conversation 逆に is used very often, partly almost as a filler (逆にいいかも "maybe even better"). かえって is similar when an action brings about the opposite; 反対に means more the opposite direction or side.

en.meaning: on the contrary; the other way around
examples[].german: Contrary to expectations, sales rose.
The child is wearing the shoes on the wrong feet.
This is a product that sells well in summer but, on the other hand, hardly sells at all in winter.
en.notes: 反対に means "conversely, on the contrary, the opposite way": 予想とは反対に "contrary to expectations". It can mean literally a direction or side (靴を左右反対に履く "to put the shoes on the wrong way round") or express a contrast between two statements. 逆に is more common in conversation and stresses more the surprising reversal. Note: the noun 反対 also means "opposition, objection" (〜に反対する).

examples[].german: In contrast to his older brother, the younger brother is quiet.
In contrast to the growing populations of cities, the populations of farming villages are declining.
The white walls and black furniture make a beautiful contrast.
en.notes: 対照的に means "in contrast, completely differently" and sets two things with clearly opposite characteristics against each other: AとはBは対照的に〜, 対照的な性格. It stresses the visible contrast, not a reversal of expectation (for which 逆に is used). Neutral to slightly written; in conversation one often says 〜とは違って or それに比べて.

examples[].german: Ironically, his advice turned out to be right.
The rule made for safety ironically became the cause of an accident.
The doctor who took such care of his health ironically collapsed from overwork.
en.notes: 皮肉にも means "ironically" and comments that a result paradoxically contradicts what was expected or intended. It usually stands at the beginning of the sentence or before the predicate: 皮肉にも〜結果になった. The noun 皮肉 means "irony, sarcasm" (皮肉を言う "to make snide remarks"); 皮肉な結果 is "an ironic result". Slightly elevated, common in narratives and reports.

examples[].german: He was deliberately hiding information.
The designer deliberately leaves a lot of white space.
The referee judged that the player collided intentionally.
en.notes: 意図的に means "intentionally, deliberately, on purpose" and stresses that a plan or aim lies behind an action: 意図的に隠す, 意図的に避ける, 意図的なミス. In conversation one mostly says わざと, which often has a negative flavor. The counterpart is 無意識に or うっかり. 意図的に is matter-of-fact and appears in reports, news and analyses, also neutrally for conscious design decisions.

examples[].german: I sighed without realizing it.
When I'm thinking, I unconsciously touch my hair.
Since I take this road every day, I had reached the station without noticing.
en.notes: 無意識に means "unconsciously, involuntarily, without thinking": 無意識に手が動く, 無意識に口に出す. In conversation 思わず ("involuntarily", for sudden reactions) and つい ("out of habit, inadvertently") are more common; 無意識に stresses that one does not notice it at all. The counterpart is 意識的に or 意図的に. Also very common is 無意識のうちに "without realizing it".

examples[].german: The employees worked overtime of their own accord.
The parents are pleased that their child now studies on their own initiative.
After the disaster, many young people took part in volunteer work of their own accord.
