en.notes: 自発的に means "on one's own initiative, voluntarily, of one's own accord": 自発的に参加する, 自発的に勉強する. It stresses inner motivation without external prompting. In conversation one often says 自分から or 進んで; 自主的に is very similar but stresses more personal responsibility and self-organization. The counterpart is 強制的に "by force".

examples[].german: They were forcibly evicted.
The computer froze, so I forcibly turned off the power.
In my school days, everyone was forced to join a club.
en.notes: 強制的に means "compulsorily, against the will of those concerned": 強制的に退去させる, 強制的に終了する (e.g. to force-quit a program). Often with passive or causative forms: 強制的に〜させられる. The counterpart is 自発的に or 任意で "voluntarily". Matter-of-fact to formal; in conversation one also says 無理やり (more emotional, "by force").

examples[].german: The game was cancelled because the weather worsened.
Departure of the airplane is delayed due to bad weather.
This year we were blessed with good weather, and the rice grew well.
en.notes: 天候 means "weather, weather conditions" and denotes the weather situation over a certain period, mostly in factual contexts: 天候不順 "unsettled weather," 悪天候 "bad weather," 天候に恵まれる "to be blessed with good weather." In everyday speech people mostly say 天気; 天候 sounds more formal and appears in news, announcements, and in agriculture or air traffic. 気候, by contrast, is the long-term climate of a region.

examples[].german: In the bitter cold, the workers kept working in silence.
In the coldest season, temperatures fall to minus twenty degrees.
In this bitterly cold season, how are you all?
en.notes: 厳寒 means "severe cold, bitter cold" and is a written-language word from news, literature and letters: 厳寒の地, 厳寒期 "the coldest time of the year", 厳寒の候 as a formal letter opening in midwinter. In everyday speech one says 厳しい寒さ or simply すごく寒い instead. The counterpart is 酷暑 or 猛暑 "scorching heat".

examples[].german: In the dry season, water shortage becomes a serious problem.
If you travel to this country, I recommend the dry season.
When the dry season begins, the river almost completely dries up.
en.notes: 乾季 means "dry season" and refers mainly to tropical and subtropical regions with a clear alternation between rainy and dry seasons; the counterpart is 雨季. There is also the equally pronounced spelling 乾期, which occurs more in specialist texts. Typical: 乾季に入る "the dry season begins", 乾季には〜. For dry air in the Japanese winter, by contrast, one speaks of 乾燥.

examples[].german: The cabinet resigned en masse.
According to the latest survey, the cabinet's approval rating fell below 30 percent.
The prime minister announced a cabinet reshuffle in the fall.
en.notes: 内閣 is the cabinet, i.e. the prime minister with his ministers as a government body; often named after the head of government (〇〇内閣). Typical: 内閣を組織する (= 組閣する), 内閣改造 ("cabinet reshuffle"), 内閣支持率 ("approval rating"), 内閣が総辞職する. Unlike 政権 ("governmental power"), 内閣 refers to the concrete body.

examples[].german: Revitalizing the regions is a challenge.
Tomorrow it will probably snow in the Kanto region.
It has already been ten years since I came to Tokyo from the provinces.
en.notes: 地方 has two main meanings: 1. a larger "region" of a country (関東地方, 東北地方, especially in weather reports); 2. "the provinces" in contrast to the capital or the big cities (地方出身, 地方都市, 地方から上京する). 田舎 is more emotional and means rather "rural, in the countryside". The reading じかた is a different word.

examples[].german: The rainy season in Southeast Asia begins in June.
During the rainy season, heavy rain falls every afternoon.
Before the rainy season began, I had the roof repaired.
en.notes: 雨季 means "rainy season" in the general, geographical sense, e.g. in Southeast Asia or Africa; the counterpart is 乾季. For the Japanese rainy season in early summer, one almost always uses 梅雨 (つゆ). The spelling 雨期 is equivalent. Typical: 雨季に入る "the rainy season begins", 雨季の間, 雨季が終わる.

examples[].german: Heavy rain fell in various places due to the influence of the rainy-season front.
I hear a cold front will pass through tonight and temperatures will drop sharply.
The cherry blossom front is expected to reach the Tohoku region this weekend.
en.notes: 前線 in weather language is the "front" between two air masses: 寒冷前線 "cold front", 温暖前線 "warm front" and above all 梅雨前線, the rainy-season front in early summer. Typical are 前線が停滞する "the front stalls" and 前線が通過する "the front passes through". Outside weather it means "front line, the very front" (前線の兵士) and figuratively "on the front line" (営業の最前線). 桜前線, the line of cherry blossoms moving from south to north, is also a fixed term.

examples[].german: The arrival of the cold wave caused disruptions to transportation.
In the strongest cold wave of the year, the water pipes froze.
Hokkaido is being hit by a record-breaking cold wave.
en.notes: 寒波 is a "cold wave", a spell of very cold air lasting several days, a typical word from weather reports and news. Common combinations are 寒波が到来する／襲来する "a cold wave arrives", 寒波に見舞われる "to be hit by a cold wave" and 最強寒波 "the strongest cold wave". The summer counterpart is 熱波 "heat wave"; for a single cold day one says 寒い日 or 冷え込み.

examples[].german: I was deeply impressed by his speech.
This novel deeply moved many readers.
I was deeply impressed by the enthusiasm of the volunteers.
en.notes: 感銘 refers to a deep, lasting impression that moves one, usually through speeches, books, works or exemplary behavior. The standard combination is 〜に感銘を受ける "to be deeply impressed by something", more rarely 感銘を与える "to impress deeply"; as a する-verb: 〜に感銘する. It is more elevated and lasting than 感動 "emotion, being moved", which describes more spontaneous feelings. For a mere "first impression", 印象 is used, not 感銘.

examples[].german: Nothing is born from hatred.
The war left deep hatred between the countries.
Posts online that stir up hatred against particular groups have become a problem.
en.notes: 憎悪 is strong, deep-seated "hatred" and a heavy written-language word often found in news, politics and literature: 憎悪犯罪 "hate crime", 憎悪の連鎖 "chain of hatred", 〜に憎悪を抱く "to harbor hatred toward someone". In everyday speech one says 憎しみ or the verb 憎む instead. Unlike 嫌悪 "disgust" (rejection, aversion), 憎悪 stresses active hostility toward someone.

examples[].german: He has a strong aversion to violence.
I took my frustration out on a friend and ended up despising myself.
Many citizens expressed disgust at the politicians' lies.
en.notes: 嫌悪 is "disgust, aversion, revulsion", a strong inner rejection. Very common is the form 嫌悪感 "feeling of aversion": 嫌悪感を抱く／覚える, 〜に嫌悪感を示す. Also well known is 自己嫌悪 "self-loathing", e.g. 自己嫌悪に陥る. The word is rather elevated; in everyday speech one says 嫌だ or 大嫌い. Unlike 憎悪 "hatred", 嫌悪 aims more at rejection than at hostility.

examples[].german: I felt intense shame when I failed in front of others.
Talking loudly on the phone on the train - don't they have any sense of shame?
To improve in a foreign language, you first have to throw away your shame.
en.notes: 羞恥 is an elevated word for "shame" and occurs almost only in compounds, above all 羞恥心 "sense of shame": 羞恥心がない "to be shameless", 羞恥心を捨てる "to cast off one's shame", 羞恥心を覚える. In everyday speech, for embarrassment one mostly says 恥ずかしい or 恥. Unlike 屈辱 "humiliation", which is inflicted from outside, 羞恥 is one's own feeling of being ashamed.

examples[].german: I can never forget that humiliation.
The team suffered the humiliation of losing 0-5 to a weaker opponent.
Being scolded in front of everyone was humiliating.
en.notes: 屈辱 is "humiliation, disgrace", the feeling of having one's pride injured, for example by a defeat or belittlement. Typical combinations: 屈辱を味わう "to suffer humiliation", 屈辱を受ける, 屈辱を晴らす "to wipe out the disgrace" and the adjective 屈辱的な "humiliating". In sports, 屈辱の敗戦 "humiliating defeat" is a fixed expression. Unlike 恥 or 羞恥 (one's own shame), 屈辱 stresses the affront inflicted from outside.

examples[].german: No matter how many times you fail, you must not despair.
After losing all his fortune, he stood at the brink of despair.
Three goals behind one minute before the end - a victory is practically hopeless.
en.notes: 絶望 is "despair, hopelessness" and is used as a noun and as an intransitive suru-verb: 将来に絶望する "to despair of the future", 絶望に陥る "to fall into despair". With の or 的 come descriptions such as 絶望の淵 "the brink of despair" and 絶望的な状況 "a hopeless situation". The opposite is 希望 "hope"; weaker discouragement is expressed more with がっかりする or 落ち込む.

examples[].german: My fear of the dark has continued since childhood.
The building shook violently in the earthquake, and I was so terrified I couldn't even make a sound.
I'm afraid of heights, so I can't ride the Ferris wheel.
en.notes: 恐怖 is "fear, dread, terror" in a strong sense, mostly of something concretely threatening. Typical are 恐怖を感じる／覚える, 恐怖に襲われる "to be seized by fear," 〜に対する恐怖 and 〜恐怖症 "-phobia" (高所恐怖症). It is stronger and more formal than 怖さ or the adjective 怖い; 不安, by contrast, is diffuse worry, and 心配 is concern about something. As a genre it is ホラー or 恐怖映画.

examples[].german: I deepened my interaction with the people of the community.
Because of the typhoon, power outages continue in some areas.
Even the same dish is seasoned differently depending on the region.
en.notes: 地域 is an "area, district" with shared characteristics, often in the sense of a local community: 地域社会, 地域の住民, 地域活動, 地域によって異なる. Unlike 地方 (large region or provinces), 地域 is flexible in size and can even mean a residential neighborhood. 地元 stresses "one's own home area".

examples[].german: I felt irritated by the train delay.
No matter how many times he explained, he wasn't understood, and the department head could not hide his irritation.
Frustration with the government, which is slow with countermeasures, is growing among citizens.
en.notes: 苛立ち is the noun of the verb 苛立つ "to become irritated" and means "irritation, impatience, frustration" when something does not go as wished. Typical: 苛立ちを感じる／覚える, 苛立ちを隠せない "cannot hide one's irritation", 〜への苛立ちが募る "irritation about ... grows". It is very often written in kana (いらだち, いら立ち). Colloquially one says イライラ; 怒り "anger" is stronger and more open.

examples[].german: Many writers suffered from the sense of emptiness after the war.
After achieving a big goal, I was for some reason overcome by a feeling of emptiness.
A nihilistic worldview hangs over his works.
en.notes: 虚無 means "nothingness, emptiness, void" and is a literary-philosophical word. In everyday life it appears mainly as 虚無感 "feeling of emptiness and meaninglessness" (虚無感に襲われる) and in 虚無主義 "nihilism" (also ニヒリズム). It does not describe mere boredom like 退屈, but the feeling that everything is meaningless; 空しい／虚しい is the matching adjective.

examples[].german: When my best friend moved away, I was overcome by a sense of loss.
I can't recover from the sense of loss after losing my mother.
Not a few people carry a strong sense of loss after retirement.
en.notes: 喪失感 is the "feeling of loss", the emptiness that remains when a person, a relationship or something important is lost. Typical are 喪失感に襲われる "to be overwhelmed by a sense of loss", 喪失感を抱える, 喪失感から立ち直る "to recover from the loss". For pets one speaks of ペットロス. 喪失 alone (記憶喪失 "memory loss", 自信喪失) is the objective loss; -感 turns it into the feeling.

examples[].german: The guilt of having told a lie never went away.
Eating cake in the middle of the night makes me feel guilty.
I took a day off work and caused trouble for my colleagues, and I felt guilty.
en.notes: 罪悪感 is the "feeling of guilt", also over small things such as snacking or declining. Typical combinations: 罪悪感を抱く／覚える, 罪悪感がある, 罪悪感にさいなまれる "to be tormented by guilt"; colloquially also 罪悪感なしで食べられる "can eat without a guilty conscience". Not to be confused with 罪 "crime, sin" itself; for legal guilt one says 有罪.

examples[].german: I replaced the old window frame with a new one.
In winter, condensation collects on the window frame and mold easily grows.
The cat is sitting in the window frame looking outside.
en.notes: 窓枠 is the "window frame", i.e. the fixed frame around the glass pane or the window opening. Typical in the context of renovation and housing: 窓枠を交換する, 窓枠に結露がたまる "condensation collects on the window frame", 窓枠にもたれる "to lean on the window frame". The sill on which one puts something is called 窓辺 or 出窓; 枠 alone is generally "frame, border".

examples[].german: Recently I get headaches frequently.
Accidents happen frequently at this intersection.
We are in frequent contact with our overseas business partners by e-mail.
en.notes: 頻繁に is the adverbial form of the な-adjective 頻繁 and means "frequently, at short intervals", often with the undertone that it happens conspicuously or annoyingly often. It is more formal than よく or しょっちゅう and likes to appear in reports, news and explanations: 頻繁に起こる, 頻繁に連絡を取る. Attributively one says 頻繁な＋noun (頻繁な出張). Neutral "often" in conversation is mostly よく.

examples[].german: I exercise regularly for my health.
The elevator is inspected regularly, once a month.
Let's back up important data regularly.
en.notes: 定期的に means "regularly, at fixed intervals" and stresses a scheduled rhythm, e.g. for checks, maintenance or meetings: 定期的に点検する, 定期的に健康診断を受ける. Attributively: 定期的な＋noun. Related are 定期 (定期券 "commuter pass", 定期便 "scheduled service"). The opposite is 不定期に "irregularly"; よく or 頻繁に only say "often", without a fixed beat.

examples[].german: This event is held irregularly.
This blog is updated irregularly.
That shop closes at irregular times, so it's better to check before you go.
en.notes: 不定期に means "irregularly, without a fixed date" and is the counterpart of 定期的に. It describes events that recur but not according to a schedule: 不定期に開催される, 不定期に更新する. Attributively one says 不定期の＋noun (不定期のイベント, 不定期便). For "irregular" in the sense of an unhealthy daily rhythm, 不規則 is used instead (不規則な生活).

examples[].german: If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us at any time.
We are recruiting part-time staff on an ongoing basis.
We will announce the latest service information on our website as it becomes available.
en.notes: 随時 means "at any time, as needed, on an ongoing basis" and is typical of announcements, authorities and business language: 随時受け付ける "to accept at any time", 随時募集中 "recruiting continuously", 随時更新 "updated continuously". Unlike いつでも, it sounds formal and matter-of-fact. It differs from 常時 "constantly, throughout" in that 随時 means "whenever necessary", not uninterruptedly.

examples[].german: This service is available at all times.
A nurse is on standby at all times at this facility.
Please wear a helmet at all times inside the factory.
en.notes: 常時 means "constantly, continuously, at all times" and stresses that a state exists without interruption. It is a formal word from technology, administration and notice signs: 常時接続 "always-on connection", 常時監視 "constant monitoring", 常時点灯 "permanently lit"; also attributively with の (常時の警戒). In everyday speech one says いつも or ずっと instead. Compared with 随時 "as needed", 常時 means "without interruption".

examples[].german: The local government is calling for waste separation.
Child-raising support differs depending on the municipality.
After moving, you have to complete the change-of-address procedure with the new municipality.
en.notes: 自治体 is a "municipality" or "local authority" - cities, towns and prefectures as administrative bodies (in full 地方自治体). Typical: 各自治体, 自治体によって異なる, 自治体の支援. The term is factual and appears mainly in news and official documents; in everyday speech one speaks more concretely of 市役所 or 区役所.

examples[].german: He kept silent throughout the entire meeting.
The game went at the Japanese team's pace from start to finish.
At the press conference, the company president did nothing but make excuses.
en.notes: 終始 means adverbially "from beginning to end, the whole time" and describes consistent behavior during an event: 終始笑顔だった, 試合は終始リードした. It is somewhat more formal than ずっと. As a suru-verb, 〜に終始する means "to be limited to ..., to consist only of ...", often critically: 言い訳に終始する "to do nothing but make excuses". Also fixed is 終始一貫 "consistent from beginning to end".

en.meaning: for a while; for some time
examples[].german: Please wait a moment.
Let's take a break for a while and then start again.
Mr. Tanaka, it's been a while! How have you been?
en.notes: 暫く refers to an indefinite, usually manageable span of time: しばらくお待ちください "please wait a moment", しばらく休む "to take a break for a while", しばらくの間 "temporarily, for the time being". In しばらくぶり or the greeting しばらくですね, however, it is about a long time: "long time no see". Compared with ちょっと, しばらく sounds somewhat more formal and often means a longer duration. Almost always written in kana as しばらく; the kanji 暫く is rare.

examples[].german: The new system will apply from next month onward.
From 6 p.m. onward, please use this entrance.
Since moving to Tokyo, I have not been back to my hometown even once.
en.notes: 以降 follows a time expression directly and means "from, since, onward"; the stated point in time is included: 来月以降, 午後6時以降, 2000年以降. After verbs it takes the て-form: 入社して以降. It is more formal than から and stresses the whole period that follows. Similar is 以後 (more "after that, from now on"); 以前 is the counterpart "before, earlier". Grammatically 以降 is a noun or suffix, not a free adverb.

examples[].german: It is a restaurant you can't get into without booking in advance.
If you will be absent, please let us know in advance.
Before the interview, I looked up the company beforehand.
en.notes: 事前に means "in advance, beforehand", i.e. before a particular event, and sounds more matter-of-fact and formal than 前もって or あらかじめ. Common: 事前に予約する, 事前に連絡する, 事前に申し込む. Attributively: 事前の＋noun (事前の準備, 事前説明会). The counterpart is 事後に "afterward"; 直前に, by contrast, means "immediately before".

examples[].german: It's too late to report after the fact.
In urgent cases, you may apply after the fact.
The department head is troubled because his subordinates only ever report to him after the fact.
en.notes: 事後に means "afterward, after the fact", i.e. only after the event, and is the counterpart of 事前に. It is a formal word from work and administration; much more common than the form with に are compounds such as 事後報告 "report after the fact", 事後承諾 "approval after the fact" and 事後処理 "follow-up handling". In everyday speech one often simply says 後で or あとから.

examples[].german: Just before departure, I noticed I had forgotten something.
They say that looking at your smartphone right before going to bed makes your sleep shallower.
It was only right before the exam that I hurriedly started studying.
en.notes: 直前に means "immediately before, just before" and usually follows a noun with の or the dictionary form of a verb: 出発の直前に, 寝る直前に. It stresses a very short interval, unlike 事前に "in advance" (with planning) or 前に in general. Attributively: 直前の＋noun (直前のキャンセル). The counterpart is 直後に "immediately after". 直前 can also mean "right in front of" spatially.

examples[].german: A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the earthquake.
It started to rain just after I left the house.
It's not good to do intense exercise right after a meal.
en.notes: 直後に means "immediately after, right after" and follows a noun with の or the た-form of a verb: 地震の直後に, 家を出た直後に. It stresses that almost no time lies in between, more tightly than 後で or その後. Attributively: 直後の＋noun. The counterpart is 直前に "immediately before"; 事後に, by contrast, means only "after the event" without closeness.

examples[].german: The phone rang in the middle of the meal.
I suddenly felt sick in the middle of the exam.
Just as I was in the middle of preparing for the move, a friend came to visit.
en.notes: 最中に means "in the middle of, right while" and follows a noun with の or the ている-form: 食事の最中に, 話している最中に. It stresses the peak of an ongoing action, often when something unexpected intervenes; therefore it hardly appears with deliberate actions of one's own in the main clause. 間に "during" is weaker and more neutral; intensified, one says 真っ最中. The reading もなか, by contrast, denotes a sweet.

en.meaning: on the way; partway; in the middle
examples[].german: I fell asleep in the middle of the movie.
On my way to work, I saw a traffic accident.
I try not to give up halfway on something once I've started it.
en.notes: 途中で has two main meanings: spatially "on the way" (駅へ行く途中で) and temporally "in the middle, before the end" (話の途中で). Very common is 途中でやめる／あきらめる "to stop/give up halfway". With で it is used for events and actions; for a fixed place along the way, one says 途中に (途中にコンビニがある). Compared with 最中に, 途中で emphasizes more that something is not yet finished.

examples[].german: The system is temporarily suspended.
After I took the medicine, the pain subsided temporarily.
Because of construction work, this road will be temporarily closed to traffic.
en.notes: 一時的に is the adverbial form of the な-adjective 一時的 and means "temporarily, for a short time", with the expectation that the state will end again. Typical in announcements and explanations: 一時的に停止する, 一時的に閉鎖する, 痛みが一時的に治まる. Attributively: 一時的な＋noun (一時的な措置). Similar is the adverb 一時 ("for a time"); opposites are 永久に and 恒久的に "permanently".

examples[].german: I took part in a school event.
New Year is one of the most important annual events in Japan.
December has many company events, so I'm busy every weekend.
en.notes: 行事 is an "event" (usually regular, traditional or organized): 学校行事 (sports day, school trip), 年中行事 ("annual events and customs"), 行事に参加する, 行事を行う. イベント sounds more casual and commercial, 祭り is a "festival" with processions and stalls. Neutral; very common in school and community calendars.

examples[].german: I hope this beautiful scenery remains forever.
Data that has been deleted once cannot be restored, ever.
This membership card is valid permanently.
en.notes: 永久に means "forever, eternally, permanently". It sounds more matter-of-fact than the more emotional 永遠に and is typical in technology, law and administration: 永久に保存する, 永久に有効, and in compounds such as 永久歯 "permanent tooth" and 永久凍土 "permafrost". In love songs or vows one hears 永遠に more often. Opposite: 一時的に "temporarily".

examples[].german: My grandfather continued his research throughout his life.
I will never forget my teacher's words that day as long as I live.
She remained single all her life and devoted herself to creating her works.
en.notes: 生涯 is first of all a noun "life, lifetime" (生涯を閉じる "to end one's life", 〜の生涯), but it is also used adverbially for "all one's life": 生涯忘れない, 生涯独身を通す. Common are 生涯にわたって "throughout one's life" and compounds such as 生涯学習 "lifelong learning". 生涯 is more formal than 一生, which is more usual in conversation.

examples[].german: Okinawa has a warm climate all year round.
Those two are always fighting, yet somehow they never break up.
The supermarket in front of the station is open every day of the year, which is convenient.
en.notes: 年中 has two uses: literally "all year round" (年中暖かい, 年中無休 "open all year without a rest day") and colloquially "constantly, all the time," often with a slightly complaining tone: 年中忙しい, 年中けんかしている. In the second sense it resembles しょっちゅう or いつも. Not to be confused with 年中行事 "annual events"; the reading ねんちゅう refers to the middle kindergarten class.

en.meaning: to confer; to grant; to impart
examples[].german: The university conferred an honorary doctorate on him.
After years of training, the master passed on his secret technique to his disciple.
My grandmother gave me a lot of life wisdom to take along on my way.
en.notes: 授ける is an elevated transitive verb: someone of higher standing "confers, grants" something (〜に〜を授ける), such as titles, prizes or honors (学位を授ける), or "imparts" knowledge and skills (知恵を授ける, 技を授ける). The intransitive counterpart is 授かる "to be conferred, to be blessed with", very common in 子どもを授かる. In daily life one naturally says あげる or 与える for "to give".

en.meaning: to give out of pity; to bless with
examples[].german: I gave food to people in need.
Someone approached me in front of the station: "Could you spare some change?"
On the day itself we were lucky with the weather, and the sports festival was a great success.
en.notes: 恵む means "to give something out of pity, to give alms" (〜に〜を恵む) and has a condescending undertone; 恵んでもらう can therefore feel humiliating. Much more common is the passive 恵まれる "to be blessed with, to be fortunate in": 天気に恵まれる, 才能に恵まれる, 恵まれた環境. Related are the noun 恵み "blessing, bounty" (自然の恵み) and お恵み.

en.meaning: to dedicate; to devote; to sacrifice
examples[].german: She dedicated her life to medical research.
At the start of the ceremony, a moment of silence was observed for the victims.
I dedicate this song to my mother in heaven.
en.notes: 捧げる means "to offer, to dedicate, to devote" and has a solemn, reverent tone (〜に〜を捧げる). Typical: 人生を〜に捧げる "to dedicate one's life to ...", 祈りを捧げる "to offer a prayer", 黙とうを捧げる "to observe a moment of silence", 花を捧げる. Originally it means "to hold up with both hands". Unlike 供える (placing offerings on an altar), 捧げる emphasizes devotion; for mere "to give" one says あげる.

en.meaning: to mourn; to hold a memorial service
examples[].german: We gathered to mourn our deceased friend.
A memorial monument was erected to mourn the souls of those who died in the war.
At Obon, a memorial service for the ancestors is held at the temple.
en.notes: 弔う means "to mourn a dead person" and above all "to hold a mourning or memorial ceremony for them", i.e. the ritual act after a death: 死者を弔う, 霊を弔う, 先祖を弔う. By contrast, 悼む is inner mourning and 偲ぶ is fond remembrance. Related words: 弔問 "condolence visit", 弔辞 "funeral address". The word is elevated and rather written.

examples[].german: The people deeply mourned the deaths of the victims.
Mourning the sudden death of their mentor, many former students attended the funeral.
Fans around the world are mourning the actor's all-too-early death.
en.notes: 悼む means "to mourn, to lament" and describes the inner pain over a death; the object is usually 死 or the deceased: 〜の死を悼む. It is very formal and often appears in obituaries, news and expressions of condolence (哀悼の意を表す). Not to be confused with the identically sounding 痛む "to hurt" and 傷む "to get damaged". Compared with 弔う (holding mourning rites), 悼む is the feeling itself.

examples[].german: A memorial gathering for the deceased was held.
I opened the old photo album and remembered my late grandmother.
Old houses remain on this street that call to mind the Edo period.
en.notes: 偲ぶ means "to remember wistfully, to commemorate", mostly the deceased or the past: 故人を偲ぶ, 昔を偲ぶ. Set expressions are 〜を偲ぶ会 "memorial gathering" and the causative form 〜を偲ばせる "to make one recall ..." (昔の面影を偲ばせる町並み). Unlike 思い出す, it is elevated and emotionally colored. Not to be confused with 忍ぶ "to endure, to hide", which is read the same.

examples[].german: Everyone praised his courageous action.
After the match, the players of both teams praised each other's good fight.
A memorial hall was built in honor of the scientist's achievements.
en.notes: 称える means "to extol, to praise, to honor" and is used for public, ceremonial praise of achievements or deeds: 功績を称える, 健闘を称える, 勇気を称える. Also common is 称え合う "to honor one another". Other spellings are 讃える and 賛える. In everyday life one praises with 褒める, which suits children or small things; 称える, by contrast, sounds elevated.

examples[].german: It is important to observe table manners.
On the train, please set your mobile phone to silent mode.
Throwing trash on the street is bad manners.
en.notes: マナー means "manners, etiquette" in public: マナーを守る, マナーが悪い, マナー違反, テーブルマナー. マナーモード is the silent/vibrate mode of a mobile phone. Related: 礼儀 ("politeness, decorum", more of an attitude), 行儀 (behavior, especially of children: 行儀が悪い). The English word "manner" in the sense of "way" does not correspond to マナー.

en.meaning: to enshrine; to worship as a deity
examples[].german: The god of learning is enshrined in this shrine.
In this village, the mountain god has been worshipped since ancient times.
A talisman from the local shrine is enshrined on the household altar.
en.notes: 祀る means "to worship as a deity, to enshrine in a shrine" and is very often used in the passive: 〜に〜が祀られている "... is enshrined in ...". Objects are gods, ancestors or deified people (菅原道真を祀る神社). The spelling 祭る is also common; 祭り "festival" comes from it. For the act of praying itself, one says 拝む or お参りする.

en.meaning: to pray to; to worship; to put one's hands together
examples[].german: I went to the beach to pay my respects to the first sunrise of the year.
Every morning my grandmother puts her hands together and prays in front of the household Buddhist altar.
Even just once, I'd like to get to see real aurora.
en.notes: 拝む first means "to pray with folded hands, to bow reverently" (仏像を拝む, 手を合わせて拝む). Figuratively it means "to beg earnestly" (この通り拝むから "I'm begging you") and, modestly or jokingly, "to get to see": 初日の出を拝む, 一度でいいから拝んでみたい. The elevated compound 拝見する "to look at" (謙譲語, humble) comes from the same root. For visiting a shrine itself, one says 参拝する or お参りする.

en.meaning: to visit a shrine or temple to pray
examples[].german: At New Year, we visited the shrine as a family.
At a shrine, it is common to pray with "two bows, two claps, one bow".
On weekends, many tourists visit this temple to pray.
en.notes: 参拝する means "to visit a shrine or temple in order to pray there"; the place is marked with に: 神社に参拝する. It is the more formal word for お参りする, which is heard more often in daily life. The first shrine visit of the new year is called 初詣; someone who merely tours a temple without praying does 拝観. Typical combinations: 参拝客 "visitors", 参拝の作法 "etiquette when visiting".

en.meaning: to offer; to present as an offering
examples[].german: I offered flowers and fruit at the household Buddhist altar.
At the equinox week, we go to the grave to offer incense and flowers.
Many bouquets had been laid at the scene of the accident.
en.notes: 供える means "to present as an offering", i.e. to place flowers, food or incense before gods, Buddha or the deceased: 仏壇に花を供える, お墓に線香を供える. The related noun is お供え "offering". Beware of the identically read 備える "to prepare, to equip" (地震に備える). Unlike 捧げる, 供える stresses the concrete setting down of offerings.

examples[].german: The autumn leaves beautifully color the mountains.
Colorful dishes adorned the party table.
Her songs colored the Japanese music scene of the 80s.
en.notes: 彩る means "to color, to decorate with color" and is mostly used figuratively: nature, flowers or lights "adorn" a place (紅葉が山を彩る), dishes get color (料理を彩る). Figuratively it means "to shape, to enrich": 歴史を彩った人物, 青春を彩る思い出. It is an elevated, rather written word; the noun 彩り means "coloring, a touch of color" (彩りを添える). In everyday speech one often says 飾る.

examples[].german: I moisturized my dry skin with cream.
After walking the mountain path, I quenched my thirst with cold spring water.
The increase in tourists is enriching the local economy.
en.notes: 潤す literally means "to moisten, to wet" (のどを潤す "to wet one's throat", 肌を潤す) and figuratively "to enrich, to bring profit": 地域経済を潤す, 心を潤す. The intransitive counterpart is 潤う "to become moist; to profit" (観光で町が潤う). Related is the noun 潤い "moisture; enrichment" (生活に潤いを与える). For skin and cosmetics one also hears 保湿する.

en.meaning: to soften; to ease; to alleviate
examples[].german: I listened to music to ease the tension.
This medicine relieves pain.
His joke lightened the gloomy mood in the meeting.
en.notes: 和らげる means "to soften, to ease, to relax" and is used with pain, tension, atmosphere or expressions: 痛みを和らげる, 緊張を和らげる, 雰囲気を和らげる, 表現を和らげる "to express oneself more mildly". The intransitive counterpart is 和らぐ "to subside, to become milder" (寒さが和らぐ). Similar but more specialized is 緩和する (more technical: 規制を緩和する). The word is neutral to slightly elevated.

en.meaning: to calm; to soothe; to suppress
examples[].german: I took a deep breath to calm my anger.
The police were dispatched and finally quelled the riot.
People in the old days held festivals to try to appease the wrath of the gods.
en.notes: 鎮める means "to calm, to soothe" and for unrest "to put down, to bring under control": 怒りを鎮める, 気持ちを鎮める, 暴動を鎮める, 痛みを鎮める; in a religious sense also to appease spirits or gods (霊を鎮める). The intransitive counterpart is 鎮まる. Beware of the identically read verbs: 静める "to bring to quiet, to make still" (partly overlapping) and 沈める "to sink".

examples[].german: Although there are many people in Tokyo, it is well organized.
In the library shelves, the books are lined up neatly.
She always presents her opinion clearly and logically structured.
en.notes: 整然 describes something "well-ordered, systematic, neatly lined up" and is a たる-adjective: it is almost always used as 整然と (adverbially: 整然と並ぶ) or 整然とした + noun (整然とした街並み). Typical for rows, rooms, crowds or arguments (理路整然と話す "to speak in a logically coherent way"). The opposite is 雑然 "untidy, in disorder". In daily life, for a tidy room one says きちんと or 片付いている instead.

examples[].german: If you accept an exception to the rules even once, you will set a bad precedent.
In this textbook, hard-to-understand sentences are given as bad examples.
That company's response is often cited as a bad example of crisis management.
en.notes: 悪例 means "bad example" and above all "bad precedent", i.e. something that others might later imitate as an unfavorable model. Typical are 悪例を残す／作る "to set a bad precedent" and 悪例として挙げる "to cite as a negative example". The word is written-language; in conversation one says 悪い例. The counterpart is 好例 "good example"; similar is 悪しき前例.

examples[].german: Let's follow the rules and play safely.
At our house, we made a rule not to play video games after ten at night.
I explained the rules of soccer to my son.
en.notes: ルール is a "rule" in games, sports or daily life: ルールを守る／破る, ルールを決める, ルール違反. It sounds more casual than 規則 (a formal regulation, e.g. 学校の規則) and is similar to 決まり. For laws one says 法律, for social norms rather 規範 or 常識.

en.meaning: to damage; to harm; to injure
examples[].german: I damaged my skin by exposing it to the strong sunlight.
I badly damaged my hair by repeatedly getting perms and color.
I packed too much and damaged the suitcase.
en.notes: 傷める means "to damage, to harm, to injure (a body part)", often unintentionally through wrong treatment: 髪を傷める, 肌を傷める, 家具を傷める. The intransitive counterpart is 傷む "to get damaged, to spoil" (果物が傷む). For aching body parts one mostly writes 痛める (腰を痛める, 心を痛める); for skin and hair both spellings are common. For deliberate destruction one says 壊す more often.

examples[].german: Many precious lives were lost in the disaster.
In the past, only people of high rank were allowed to pass through this gate.
What I learned from my mistakes is a valuable treasure to me.
en.notes: 貴い means "precious, valuable" as well as "noble, exalted, distinguished" and is an elevated, rather written word. It is read the same as 尊い (also たっとい); the rule of thumb is: 貴い for value and rank (貴い身分, 貴い資料), 尊い for the venerable and sacred (尊い犠牲) - in practice the two are mixed, especially with 命. In daily life one usually says 大切 or 貴重.

en.meaning: unagi donburi (rice bowl topped with grilled eel)
examples[].german: "Take care, and keep in touch once in a while." "Of course. Actually, let's go eat unagi donburi sometime soon." "Sounds good." "Great. I'll get in touch again." "Yes, see you."
Many people eat unagi donburi on the Day of the Ox in midsummer.
Unagi donburi is expensive, so I only eat it on special days.
en.notes: うなぎ丼 is a bowl of rice topped with grilled eel (蒲焼) glazed with sweet sauce (タレ). In everyday speech it is mostly shortened to うな丼. It should be distinguished from うな重, which is served in a lacquered box (重箱) and is considered finer. Traditionally, eel is eaten in midsummer on 土用の丑の日 for strength. 丼 on its own is read どんぶり, but in many compounds it is shortened to -どん (牛丼, 天丼).

examples[].german: There is nothing as delicious as oyakodon.
I made oyakodon for lunch.
The oyakodon at this restaurant is delicious because the egg is so runny.
en.notes: 親子丼 literally means "parent-and-child bowl": chicken (parent) and egg (child) are cooked with onions in a sweetish broth and served on rice. Colloquially it is often shortened and read おやこどん. Related dishes are 他人丼 ("stranger bowl" with beef or pork and egg), カツ丼 and 牛丼. One orders it with 親子丼をください or 親子丼にします.

examples[].german: The man spat out the candy he had been sucking.
The factory chimney is belching black smoke.
After I got all my complaints off my chest to my friend, I felt a little better.
en.notes: 吐き出す (from 吐く "to expel, to vomit" + 出す "out") stresses that something comes entirely out of the mouth or the inside: spitting out food (ガムを吐き出す), expelling smoke or air (煙を吐き出す) and, figuratively, getting rid of pent-up feelings (不満を吐き出す, 本音を吐き出す). The verb is transitive with を. For "to throw up", one rather says simply 吐く or, politely, 戻す.

examples[].german: Those guys are sunbathing without a care while we're hard at work.
I never want to lose to them, of all people.
Those guys are here again. Watch out.
en.notes: 奴ら is the plural of 奴 "fellow, guy" and means, pejoratively, "those guys over there". It is rude, colloquial and rather masculine; one hears it mainly in crime stories, manga or among friends when talking about opponents or unpleasant people. It is often written in kana (やつら, ヤツら). Neutrally one says 彼ら or あの人たち, politely あの方々.

examples[].german: I seem to have left my lipstick in my pocket, and it melted in the dryer.
Before going out, she put on red lipstick.
Lipstick got on the glass.
en.notes: 口紅 (literally "mouth red") is lipstick. Typical combinations are 口紅を塗る or 口紅をつける "to apply", 口紅を落とす "to remove" and 口紅がつく "to rub off" (e.g. on a glass). In modern daily life and in advertising one often says リップ or リップスティック; 口紅 sounds a bit more classic. リップクリーム, by contrast, is lip balm.

examples[].german: These slippers are my recommendation.
On my teacher's advice, I decided to take the JLPT.
Let's first ask the server for their recommendation and then order.
en.notes: すすめ is the noun of すすめる. With 薦め one recommends a person or thing (a product, a candidate; cf. 推薦), with 勧め one advises an action: 医者の勧めで "on the doctor's advice". In practice it is mostly polite with お and often in hiragana: おすすめ, 今日のおすすめ, おすすめは何ですか. Do not confuse with 進める "to advance, to move forward", which is read the same.

en.meaning: work, employment; duty, task (usually written 務め)
examples[].german: Where do you work?
My mother goes out to work, so she isn't home during the day.
Protecting children is a parent's duty.
en.notes: 勤め is work as an employee, a regular job: 勤めに出る "to go to work, to be employed," 勤め先 "place of work," 会社勤め "to be a company employee"; the verb for it is 勤める (会社に勤める). In the meaning "duty, task, role," 務め is written: 親の務め, 務めを果たす "to fulfill one's duty" (verb 務める "to serve as ..."). 仕事 is more general and means any work or activity. お勤め can also refer to a Buddhist service.

examples[].german: My father holds a patent for an electromagnetic field generator, but I'm not sure what it's for.
When a current flows, an electromagnetic field arises around it.
Strong electromagnetic fields can affect precision instruments.
en.notes: 電磁場 is composed of 電磁 "electromagnetic" and 場 "field" and is a technical term from physics and engineering. In standards and official texts one also reads 電磁界 (でんじかい). Separately, the electric field is 電場 and the magnetic field 磁場. In everyday speech one more often speaks of 電磁波 "electromagnetic waves", for example with mobile phones or microwaves.

examples[].german: We should follow the norms of society.
The company established a new code of conduct for its employees.
It is sometimes said that young people's awareness of norms is declining.
en.notes: 規範 is a "norm, standard" for correct behavior, mostly in abstract or official contexts: 社会規範, 行動規範 ("code of conduct"), 規範意識 ("awareness of norms"), 規範に従う. It is considerably more formal than ルール or 決まり and appears mainly in texts on society, law and corporate governance. 基準 is more a measurable "standard".

examples[].german: I have only read The Tale of Genji as a manga.
The Tale of Genji was written by Murasaki Shikibu.
In classical Japanese class at high school, we read a part of The Tale of Genji.
en.notes: 源氏物語 is the famous court novel of the Heian period, written around the year 1000 by the court lady 紫式部; it tells of the life and love affairs of the "shining prince" 光源氏. 物語 means "tale". Japanese students read excerpts in 古文 class; many know it, however, through 現代語訳 (translations into modern Japanese) or manga versions.

examples[].german: "Good morning. What can I get you?" "The usual, please." "Certainly. Beer and edamame, correct?" "That's right."
In summer, it's beer and edamame, after all.
I boiled edamame in salted water and had it as a snack to go with drinks.
en.notes: 枝豆 literally means "branch bean": unripe green soybeans, which used to be sold with the branch. They are boiled in salted water (塩ゆで) and the beans are squeezed out of the pod (さや). In Japan they are the classic snack with beer in an 居酒屋, especially in summer. Ripe, dried soybeans, by contrast, are called 大豆.

examples[].german: I always use my mother's maiden name as a password.
Even after marriage, I use my maiden name at work.
After the divorce, I went back to my maiden name.
en.notes: 旧姓 (旧 "former" + 姓 "family name") is the family name before a change of name, usually the birth name of a married woman. Typical are 旧姓は〜です, 旧姓を使う (continuing to use the old name at work, 旧姓使用) and 旧姓に戻る after a divorce. The word is neutral and often appears on forms and identity documents.

examples[].german: Please do not use my full name.
Please write your full name accurately in kanji on the application form.
I had the stroke count of my name checked by a name-divination reading.
en.notes: 姓名 combines 姓 "family name" and 名 "given name" into the full name. It is formal and written-language; on forms 氏名 is more common, and in conversation one simply says 名前 or フルネーム. Also well known is 姓名判断, name divination based on the stroke count of the kanji.

examples[].german: If you don't tuck in your shirt, customers may not take you seriously.
You must not underestimate the weather in the mountains.
I had taken the exam lightly and couldn't even solve half of it.
en.notes: 甘く見る (甘い "sweet, lenient" + 見る) means "to underestimate, to not take seriously": 〜を甘く見る. Very common as a warning: 〜を甘く見てはいけない or 甘く見ないほうがいい. In the passive, 甘く見られる means "to not be taken seriously". Similar are colloquial なめる and written 侮る (あなどる); 甘く考える, by contrast, stresses "to think too optimistically".

examples[].german: I have a sweet tooth and can't resist cake.
My father prefers drinking, but my mother has quite a sweet tooth.
For my friend with a sweet tooth, I bought a souvenir at the cake shop in front of the station.
en.notes: 甘党 (literally "party of the sweet") is someone who likes eating sweets. Traditionally it is the opposite of 辛党, a person who prefers drinking alcohol; a 甘党 thus prefers cake to sake. Typical are 私は甘党です, かなりの甘党 and the phrase 甘いものに目がない "cannot resist sweets".

examples[].german: The boss bumped his head on the corner of the desk and got a lump.
I asked the owner of the sushi restaurant for today's recommendation.
His grandfather was an admiral in the navy.
en.notes: 大将 is originally the highest officer rank, "general" or, in the navy, "admiral" (陸軍大将, 海軍大将). In everyday life, though, you hear it much more often as a colloquial form of address for the boss or owner of a small eatery, especially at a sushi restaurant: 大将、いつもの！ ("Boss, the usual!") In team competitions (kendō, jūdō), the last fighter of a team is also called 大将. お山の大将 mockingly refers to someone who plays the "king of the hill".

examples[].german: Neither of the two team captains was particularly strong.
She was chosen as captain of the volleyball club.
As captain, it is not easy to hold the team together.
en.notes: 主将 is the captain of a sports team, especially in school and university clubs (野球部の主将, 主将に選ばれる); the vice-captain is called 副主将. In professional sports and in everyday speech, people usually say キャプテン. The older meaning "commander-in-chief" is found only in historical texts. Not to be confused with 部長, the organizational head of a club.

examples[].german: The skaters are complaining about the Japan Skating Federation.
The League of Nations was founded after the First World War.
Our university's karate club is a member of the student federation.
en.notes: 連盟 is a league or federation in which organizations, clubs or states join together, e.g. 日本スケート連盟 or, historically, 国際連盟 "League of Nations". One joins with 連盟に加盟する. Similar are 協会 "association, society" (日本サッカー協会), 連合 "union" (国際連合 = the UN) and 同盟 "alliance" between states. The word is rather formal and often appears in organization names.

examples[].german: Disparities between the strata of society are a problem.
The folder hierarchy is so deep that I can't find the file.
In this survey, we compared life satisfaction by income bracket.
en.notes: 階層 means "layer, level" in a hierarchy: social (社会階層, 所得階層, 階層間の格差) or structural, for example in organizations and computer folders (フォルダの階層, 組織の階層). For individual population groups, people often use just the suffix 〜層 (富裕層, 若年層). Matter-of-fact, more in texts and technical language.

examples[].german: Do you know whether there is a lost-and-found office at this airport?
I filed a loss report for my wallet with the police.
If you lose any documents, please report it to the person in charge immediately.
en.notes: 遺失 is an official word for the "loss" of objects. It is found almost only in compounds such as 遺失物 "lost item, lost property", 遺失物取扱所 "lost-and-found office" and 遺失届 "loss report" filed with the police. The verb 遺失する appears only in official texts; in everyday speech people say なくす or 落とす, and lost property is called 落とし物 or 忘れ物.

examples[].german: It is unclear why the culprit licked the lips of the corpse.
A man who had gone missing in the mountains was found dead.
Before the funeral, the family said their last goodbye to the deceased.
en.notes: 遺体 is the respectful word for a person's dead body and is used in the news and at funerals (遺体が見つかる, 遺体で発見される "to be found dead", polite ご遺体). 死体, by contrast, is matter-of-fact and sounds cold when referring to relatives; it is also used for animals. 遺骨 are the bones or the ashes after cremation.

examples[].german: I had stubborn stains removed from my teeth at a dentist in Nara.
In the parks of Nara, many deer walk around freely.
On the school trip we went to Nara and Kyoto.
en.notes: 奈良 refers both to the city 奈良市 and to Nara Prefecture 奈良県 in the Kansai region. From 710 to 784, Nara was Japan's capital as 平城京, hence the name of the 奈良時代. It is known for the Great Buddha at 東大寺 and the tame deer (鹿) of 奈良公園. Together with Kyoto, it is a classic destination for school trips.

examples[].german: There is a manga boom in Kanagawa Prefecture.
The capital of Kanagawa Prefecture is Yokohama.
I commute by train from Kanagawa Prefecture to my company in Tokyo.
en.notes: 神奈川県 is in the Kantō region, directly southwest of Tokyo; the prefectural capital (県庁所在地) is 横浜市. Well-known places include 鎌倉 with its Great Buddha and the hot-spring area 箱根. Many residents commute to Tokyo every day. In conversation people often say just 神奈川, for example 神奈川に住んでいます.

examples[].german: She carefully plucks the rose petals one by one by hand.
The children picked flowers in the field and gave them to their mother.
You should nip that problem in the bud before it gets bigger.
en.notes: 摘む means "to pick with the fingertips", for example flowers, herbs, tea leaves or strawberries (花を摘む, 茶を摘む, いちご摘み). The second meaning "to snip off, to trim" is found in the expression 芽を摘む "to nip in the bud" (悪の芽を摘む, also negative: 才能の芽を摘む). Note: the same kanji is also used for つまむ "to pinch with the fingers", which is usually written in kana. For fruit from a tree, people tend to say 採る or もぐ.

examples[].german: Would you mind if I pointed out your mistakes?
My boss pointed out a mistake in the report to me.
Experts point out that the consequences of global warming are serious.
en.notes: 指摘 means "to point something out, to point out (mistakes, problems)" and is mostly used as a suru-verb: ミスを指摘する, 〜と指摘する "to point out that ...". In the passive, 指摘される means "to have something pointed out to one", often unpleasantly. In business language ご指摘ありがとうございます is a fixed phrase of thanks for corrections. Unlike 注意する, 指摘 contains no admonition, only the naming of the problem.

en.meaning: to expose; to bust; to crack down on
examples[].german: I'm a police officer, but I've never had the chance to bust a drug trafficking ring.
The police raided an illegal casino and arrested the operator.
The company was exposed for tax evasion.
en.notes: 摘発する means that the authorities uncover crimes or abuses and take action against them: 警察が密売組織を摘発する, 脱税で摘発される. It is a typical news word. 逮捕 is the arrest of a person, 取り締まる is ongoing control and enforcement, 暴く is the general "to reveal secrets"; when an insider reports wrongdoing, people say 内部告発.

examples[].german: Before using the nuclear weapon, be sure to read the operating instructions in the manual.
We aim to rid the world of nuclear weapons.
It is said that there are currently nine countries that possess nuclear weapons.
en.notes: 核兵器 are atomic or nuclear weapons; 核 means "nucleus, core". Typical combinations: 核兵器を保有する "to possess", 核兵器の廃絶 "abolition", 核兵器を持たない国. Japan upholds the 非核三原則 "three non-nuclear principles". 原爆 refers specifically to the atomic bomb (e.g. Hiroshima). Note: 核家族 means "nuclear family" and has nothing to do with weapons.

examples[].german: The country conducted a nuclear test, ignoring the opposition of the international community.
As a result of the nuclear test, residents of the surrounding area suffered health damage.
Calls for a total ban on nuclear tests are growing louder.
en.notes: 核実験 is a test of nuclear weapons. People say 核実験を行う or 核実験を実施する; in the news you also read 地下核実験 "underground nuclear test" and 核実験の禁止. The word belongs to political and news language. The more general word is 実験 "experiment"; 核 as a prefix forms further terms such as 核兵器 and 核戦争.

examples[].german: I wonder if there were things like pacifiers in the Jōmon period, too.
The people of the Jōmon period lived by hunting and gathering nuts.
At the museum, I saw Jōmon pottery decorated with cord patterns.
en.notes: 縄文 literally means "cord pattern" (縄 "rope" + 文 "pattern") - the pattern pressed into early pottery. Named after it are 縄文土器 "Jōmon pottery" and above all the prehistoric 縄文時代 (approx. 14,000-1,000 BC), when people lived by hunting and gathering. The word appears almost only in such compounds (縄文人, 縄文文化). The Jōmon period is followed by the 弥生時代 with wet-rice farming.

examples[].german: Please show your ID.
In the Edo period there was a strict class system.
Lounging around on a weekday afternoon - must be nice!
en.notes: 身分 is a person's "standing, status" - historically a fixed social rank (身分制度, 身分の違い), today mainly "identity, status": 身分証明書 ("ID"), 身分を隠す, 学生という身分. Ironically one says いいご身分だね ("Must be nice for you"). In contrast to 地位 (a position one has worked for), 身分 emphasizes the ascribed or legal status.

examples[].german: I saw a car crash into a mobile blood donation bus.
I went to donate blood at the blood donation center in front of the station.
People with low body weight sometimes cannot donate blood.
en.notes: 献血 (献 "to offer" + 血 "blood") is blood donation; as an intransitive する-verb: 献血する, 献血に行く. Blood is donated at a 献血ルーム or in the mobile 献血車. To be distinguished from it are 輸血 "blood transfusion" (receiving blood) and 採血 "drawing blood" for tests. Formed similarly is 献金 "monetary donation".

examples[].german: We have received so many donations from all of you.
The lawmaker had accepted illegal donations from companies.
He donates money to the church every month.
en.notes: 献金 is a monetary donation, above all to political parties or politicians (政治献金, 企業献金) as well as to churches or religious groups. As a する-verb: 〜に献金する. For general donations to charities, people usually say 寄付 in everyday speech; 募金 is the collecting of donations (e.g. on the street). Formed similarly is 献血 "blood donation".

examples[].german: I want to become a doctor in Japan, so I'm studying medical terminology now.
In Japan, insurance covers part of the medical expenses.
Thanks to advances in medical care, average life expectancy has increased.
en.notes: 医療 denotes medical care as a field or system and often serves as a modifier in compounds: 医療費 "medical expenses," 医療機関 "medical institution," 医療保険, 医療ミス "medical error," 医療従事者 "medical personnel." The concrete treatment of a disease is 治療, medicine as a science 医学. You say 医療を受ける "to receive medical care."

en.meaning: to succeed; to take over; to inherit
examples[].german: In Japan, the eldest son usually succeeds to the family.
I'm still undecided about whether to take over my father's shop.
The prince succeeded to the throne at the age of twenty.
en.notes: 継ぐ mainly means "to succeed, to take over": 家業を継ぐ "to take over the family business", 父の跡を継ぐ, 王位を継ぐ. For the legal inheriting of money or property, people say 相続する instead; traditions or traits are "inherited" with 受け継ぐ, and a task is taken over with 引き継ぐ. Less often, 継ぐ means "to patch" or "to add on". Not to be confused with 注ぐ "to pour", which is read the same way.

examples[].german: I studied the Meiji Restoration at school, but I don't remember anything except the name.
With the Meiji Restoration, Japan began its path to a modern nation.
In the election, the Ishin candidate won.
en.notes: 維新 means "renewal, fundamental reform", but it almost always stands for the 明治維新, the Meiji Restoration of 1868, through which Japan modernized. Derived from this, politicians use the word as a slogan for reforms, and as an abbreviation 維新 refers to the party 日本維新の会. A similar word for revolution is 革命, which, however, emphasizes a violent overthrow.

en.meaning: to dance; to whirl; to flutter
examples[].german: There was an extreme amount of dust whirling around in my friend's room and it was awful, so I tried to imagine they were beautiful petals. But that didn't work.
Cherry blossom petals whirl in the wind.
At the shrine festival, the girls performed a traditional dance.
en.notes: 舞う means, on the one hand, "to dance" in the sense of the traditional, circling Japanese dance (舞を舞う); for modern dances one says 踊る. More common is the meaning "to whirl through the air, to flutter": 花びらが舞う, 雪が舞う, ほこりが舞う, 鳥が空を舞う. The verb is intransitive. Many compounds are built on it: 舞い上がる "to whirl up", 舞い散る "to flutter down", 舞い込む "to flutter in".

examples[].german: I'm super broke right now. I've run out of sugar and can't even afford to buy more.
An extremely large typhoon is approaching.
I was examined with ultrasound at the hospital.
en.notes: As a prefix before Sino-Japanese nouns, 超 means "over-, ultra-, super-": 超大型 "extremely large", 超高速, 超音波 "ultrasound", 超特急. Colloquially, especially among young people, it is used like a degree adverb before adjectives and verbs: 超おいしい, 超貧乏, often also in katakana チョー - this replaces とても or すごく and is out of place in formal situations. In news reports it also follows numbers: 1万人超 "over 10,000 people".

examples[].german: By the way, have I ever told you about my supernatural power?
Do you believe in supernatural phenomena that science cannot explain?
This movie is the story of a boy who fights supernatural beings.
en.notes: 超自然的 (超 "super-" + 自然 "nature" + 的) is a な-adjective: 超自然的な力, 超自然的な現象, 超自然的な存在. It sounds rather matter-of-fact to literary and appears in discussions of religion, the occult or fantasy. In everyday speech people often just say 不思議な; for paranormal phenomena there is also 超常現象.

examples[].german: My panda robot can fly through the sky at supersonic speed, you know.
The Concorde was a passenger aircraft that crossed the Atlantic at supersonic speed.
When a fighter jet flies at supersonic speed, a loud noise reaches the ground.
en.notes: 超音速 is composed of 超 "super-" and 音速 "speed of sound". Typical is 超音速で飛ぶ as well as compounds such as 超音速機 or 超音速旅客機 (e.g. the Concorde). Speed is given in マッハ. The counterpart "subsonic" is 亜音速. The word is technical, but also appears in the news and in science fiction.

examples[].german: If you weren't that stupid, I could explain to you just how stupid you are.
Stop making fun of people.
The man next door is a doting father; every time we meet, he shows me pictures of his daughter.
en.notes: 馬鹿 is mostly written in kana (ばか, バカ) and is a noun and a な-adjective: "idiot" or "stupid, silly" (馬鹿なこと, 馬鹿みたい). How insulting it is depends on tone and region; in Kansai, ばか is often felt to be harsher than アホ. Important phrases: 〜を馬鹿にする "to make fun of someone," 馬鹿馬鹿しい "ridiculous." As a suffix it denotes someone who is crazy about something, e.g. 親馬鹿 "doting parents."

examples[].german: People of high social standing gathered.
Through years of effort, he built a firm position in the industry.
Movements aiming to improve the status of women are spreading.
en.notes: 地位 is the "standing, position" of a person in society or an organization: 社会的地位, 地位が高い, 地位を築く, 地位を失う, 女性の地位向上. Unlike 身分 (ascribed, legal status), 地位 is usually acquired. 立場, by contrast, means the "standpoint" or the situation from which one acts. Neutral to formal.

examples[].german: In Kagoshima Prefecture, I drove on the bumpiest road I have ever driven on.
Sakurajima in Kagoshima Prefecture is an active volcano that is still erupting today.
Yakushima is an island in Kagoshima Prefecture.
en.notes: 鹿児島県 is the southernmost prefecture of the island of Kyūshū; its capital is 鹿児島市. Its landmark is the active volcano 桜島 directly across from the city. The prefecture also includes islands such as 屋久島 and 奄美大島. It is known for sweet potato shōchū (芋焼酎) and black pork (黒豚). In conversation people often say just 鹿児島.

examples[].german: Sorry for asking for your approval only after the fact.
For minors, the consent of the parents is required.
She accepted his marriage proposal.
en.notes: 承諾 is formal consent to a request or proposal: 〜の承諾を得る "to obtain consent", 〜を承諾する "to consent", 親の承諾, 承諾書 "consent form". 事後承諾 means asking for consent only afterwards. Similar: 了承 "to take note of and accept" (ご了承ください), 承知 "understood, agreed" (承知しました) and 同意 "agreement with an opinion".

examples[].german: Kōichi reluctantly accepted becoming president of the United States.
In 1945, Japan accepted the Potsdam Declaration.
He accepted the job offer from Company A.
en.notes: 受諾 is the formal acceptance of an offer, a demand or an appointment: 申し出を受諾する, 就任を受諾する. Historically well known is ポツダム宣言の受諾 (1945). The word is literary and appears in diplomacy, politics and business. In everyday speech people say 受け入れる or 引き受ける; 承諾 emphasizes more the consenting to a request.

examples[].german: Please obtain the administrator's permission beforehand.
To use this photo, the copyright holder's permission is required.
Please agree to the license agreement before installing the software.
en.notes: 許諾 is permission or authorization, above all in the legal sense for copyright and usage rights: 著作権者の許諾を得る, 無断で使わず許諾を取る, 使用許諾契約 "license agreement". General official permits are called 許可; 承諾 is consent to a request. The word is formal and is found mainly in contracts and business texts.

en.meaning: yes or no; acceptance or refusal
examples[].german: "Please let us know whether this is acceptable or not" is a phrase often used in business letters and e-mails.
Regarding your request, please let us know your answer, whether you accept or decline, by the end of this month.
Whether the contract will be renewed will be notified to you in writing.
en.notes: 諾否 (諾 "yes" + 否 "no") means "acceptance or refusal" and is a very formal written word, typical in business letters: 諾否をお知らせください, 諾否をご回答ください. In conversation, people simply ask whether someone accepts or not. Formed similarly are 可否 "whether possible or approved", 賛否 "pros and cons" and 出欠 "attendance or absence".

examples[].german: Haven't you ever once thought of giving up?
I have no idea about this riddle at all. I give up, so tell me the answer.
The enemy soldiers raised a white flag and surrendered.
en.notes: 降参する means "to surrender, to capitulate" and is intransitive: 敵に降参する. In everyday life it is often used jokingly for "I give up!", for example with riddles, games or arguments (もう降参！). The formal, military word for capitulation is 降伏; 諦める, by contrast, means "to give up a plan". Similarly colloquial is 参った "I'm beaten".

examples[].german: Could you exchange these for shoes one size larger?
At the airport I changed yen into euros.
Let's open the window and air out the room.
en.notes: 換える means "to exchange for something of equal value, to convert": X を Y に換える, e.g. 円をドルに換える, 空気を換える "to ventilate". There are also identically read spellings: 変える "to change" and 替える "to replace with something new" (電池を替える). 換える and 替える overlap considerably; 換える emphasizes the exchange. The kanji is also in 交換 "exchange" and 乗り換える "to transfer". The intransitive partner is 換わる.

examples[].german: How many beds does this hospital have?
As the number of infected people rose, hospital beds in the city ran short.
My grandfather wrote a letter to his family from his sickbed.
en.notes: 病床 is the "sickbed" and is used in two contexts: officially for the bed capacity of hospitals (病床数, 病床が足りない, 病床がひっ迫する) and in literary use for the time of illness (病床にある "to be bedridden", 病床で書いた手紙). In everyday speech, people simply say ベッド for the bed itself.

examples[].german: My uncle is the principal of this school.
During summer vacation I stayed at my uncle's house in the countryside.
My uncle is my father's brother, three years younger.
en.notes: 叔父 is the younger brother of a parent (or the husband of a younger aunt); the older brother is written 伯父, and both are read おじ. With 叔父 you talk about your own uncle; other people's uncles are called おじさん or おじさま, and when addressed directly he is likewise called おじさん. Note: おじさん also means "middle-aged man" in general.

examples[].german: Greater efficiency in administration is being called for.
The administration was criticized for responding slowly during the disaster.
The nation's power is divided into three: legislative, executive and judicial.
en.notes: 行政 is the executive power of the state and public administration as a whole. In the separation of powers (三権分立) it stands beside 立法 ("legislation") and 司法 ("judiciary"). In daily use it often means "the authorities": 行政の対応, 行政サービス, 地方行政, 行政機関. For the office of an individual company, people do not say 行政 but 管理 or 事務.

examples[].german: I don't have the authority to decide this matter.
The new department head was given the authority to decide the budget.
You don't have permission to edit this file.
en.notes: 権限 is the "authority" a person has by virtue of office, role or system: 権限がある／ない, 権限を与える, 権限を持つ, 管理者権限 (administrator rights on a computer). Do not confuse it with 権利 (a person's "right, entitlement") and 権力 ("power" over others). Matter-of-fact, common in work and administration.

examples[].german: My aunt is a school teacher.
My aunt is my mother's younger sister and is a very good cook.
Until I entered university, I went to school from my aunt's house.
en.notes: 叔母 is the younger sister of a parent (or the wife of a younger uncle); the older sister is written 伯母, and both are read おば. 叔母 is used for your own aunt; other people's aunts are called おばさん or おばさま, and she is addressed directly as おばさん. Not to be confused with おばあさん "grandmother, old woman" (long あ).

en.meaning: to well up; to gush; to arise (feeling, idea)
examples[].german: Oh, so water springs up around here.
As I listened to the story, I became interested in that job.
Even though I heard that I passed, it still doesn't feel real.
en.notes: 湧く is intransitive and first means "to well up, to gush" (水が湧く, 温泉が湧く). Very common is the figurative meaning "to arise" for feelings and ideas: 興味が湧く, 勇気が湧く, アイデアが湧く, 実感が湧かない "cannot yet take it in". Vermin can also "appear" (虫が湧く). Not to be confused with 沸く "to boil" (お湯が沸く) or "to get excited" (会場が沸く), which is read the same way.

examples[].german: The day before yesterday I went to my junior high school class reunion.
A class reunion was held for the first time in ten years since graduation.
A letter asking for a donation arrived from my university's alumni association.
en.notes: 同窓会 refers both to the alumni association of a school or university and to the gathering of alumni, that is, the class or year reunion. 同窓 literally means "same window" and means "having studied at the same school". Typical: 同窓会を開く, 同窓会に出る, 中学の同窓会. A reunion of just one class is also called クラス会.

examples[].german: The X-ray images showed nothing unusual.
To be safe, we will take an X-ray of your chest.
My wrist hurt after the fall, so I had it X-rayed at the hospital.
en.notes: レントゲン comes from the name of the physicist Röntgen and in daily life refers to the X-ray examination or image: レントゲンを撮る "to have an X-ray taken", レントゲン写真, 胸部レントゲン. In technical texts one says X線 (エックスせん). Less often it is the physical unit roentgen.

examples[].german: Do you have a regular dentist?
At the company dental checkup, a cavity was found in my teeth.
My older sister works as a dental hygienist.
en.notes: 歯科 is dentistry as a field or department and often appears in compounds: 歯科医 "dentist", 歯科医院 "dental clinic", 歯科検診 "dental checkup", 歯科衛生士 "dental hygienist", 小児歯科 "pediatric dentistry". In conversation one usually says 歯医者 or 歯医者さん instead of 歯科医. Note: it is read the same as the particle しか "only".

examples[].german: Hey, you shut up!
"Who are you, you bastard?!" the soldier shouted.
In manga, villains often use the word 「貴様」.
en.notes: 貴様 originally consisted of 貴 "noble" and 様 and used to be a polite form of address. Today it is an extremely rude, aggressive form of "you" that you hear almost only in anime, manga, war movies or in heated arguments among men. In real life you should not use it. Less extreme, but still rude, are お前 and てめえ; neutrally, people address others by name.

examples[].german: My brother is a shameless liar. He said he had no idea what I was talking about, but he was the one who ate all my bacon.
Taking credit for someone else's work - that is really the height of shamelessness.
Many people were angry at the shameless remark that ridiculed the victims.
en.notes: 恥知らず (恥 "shame" + 知らず "not knowing") means "shameless" or "shameless person". It is a noun and a な-adjective: 恥知らずな行為, 恥知らずな発言, also 恥知らずの嘘つき; as an insult: この恥知らず！ The expression 恥知らずにもほどがある means "that is the height of shamelessness". Somewhat milder are 図々しい "brazen" and 厚かましい "impudent".

examples[].german: For Japanese students suffering under exam hell, studying on the train is perfectly normal.
The exam hell continues until March - travel is out of the question.
I finally escaped the exam hell, and I want to spend the spring break in a totally relaxed way.
en.notes: 試験地獄 refers to the enormous pressure surrounding entrance exams (入試) for high school and university in Japan, often in connection with cram schools (塾) and studying late into the night. Typical combinations are 試験地獄に苦しむ, 試験地獄を経験する or 試験地獄から抜け出す. The word comes from the press and social criticism; related is 受験戦争 "exam war"; students also use it jokingly for their own exam period.

examples[].german: When I took this medicine, I didn't get seasick.
I got terribly seasick on the ferry.
People who get seasick easily should sit around the middle of the ship.
en.notes: 船酔い means "seasickness"; as an intransitive する-verb, 船酔いする means "to get seasick". Formed in parallel are 車酔い "carsickness" and the umbrella term 乗り物酔い "motion sickness"; pills against it are called 酔い止め. 酔う alone usually means "to get drunk", but 船に酔う also means "to get seasick". Typical are 船酔いしやすい and ひどく船酔いする.

examples[].german: The girlfriend made her boyfriend cook kimchi hot pot.
On cold days, the whole family gathers around a yosenabe hot pot.
I'd like to try authentic chanko nabe near a sumo stable.
en.notes: 〜鍋 is attached to a noun and denotes a stew-type dish cooked at the table in a shared pot: キムチ鍋, 寄せ鍋, もつ鍋, ちゃんこ鍋, 豆乳鍋. Unlike in many compounds, the reading usually stays なべ (寄せ鍋 = よせなべ). On its own, 鍋 stands for "pot, pan" or, for short, the dish: 今夜は鍋にしよう. Typical is 鍋を囲む "to sit around the pot together," especially in winter.

examples[].german: He is an authority in that field.
This is the most prestigious prize in the literary world.
The incident greatly damaged the government's authority.
en.notes: 権威 has two meanings: 1. the "authority, prestige" of an institution or thing (権威がある, 権威を失う, 権威のある賞); 2. a person as an "authority, expert" in a field (〜の権威). 権威主義 means "authoritarianism". To be distinguished from 権限 ("authority to act") and 権力 ("power"). Rather formal.

examples[].german: If you pay in cash, we will give you a 5 percent discount.
You can also buy this computer in installments.
The rent is already two months overdue.
en.notes: 払い is the noun form of 払う. On its own, people usually say 支払い for "payment"; 払い appears mainly as a suffix, in which case it takes a voiced initial, 〜ばらい: 現金払い, カード払い, 分割払い, 一括払い, 前払い, 後払い. On its own it occurs in fixed expressions, for example 払いがいい "pays well, generous" or 家賃の払いが遅れる. Further, rarer meanings are "sweeping away" (厄払い) and the trailing brush stroke when writing kanji.

examples[].german: I bought this oil painting at a flea market for 1,500 yen.
After retiring, my father started learning oil painting.
I took my time looking at oil paintings by a famous painter at the museum.
en.notes: 油絵 is an oil painting or oil painting as a technique. One says 油絵を描く (かく or えがく) and 油絵を習う; the paints are called 油絵の具. Contrasting terms are 水彩画 "watercolor" and 日本画 "Japanese-style painting". In catalogs and museums the more formal 油彩 or 油彩画 is often used.

examples[].german: The other day at school lunch, a student for some reason pulled a bottle of sweet vinegar out of his desk.
When I put sweet-and-sour sauce on fried chicken, the kids eat really well.
If you pickle daikon radish in sweet vinegar, it becomes a refreshing side dish.
en.notes: 甘酢 is vinegar sweetened with sugar, the base of many sweet-and-sour dishes. Typical are 甘酢漬け (vegetables pickled in sweet vinegar, e.g. ginger served with sushi) and 甘酢あんかけ (topped with a thickened sweet-and-sour sauce). Note the voiced initial: 酢 = す, but 甘酢 = あまず. Related seasoning mixtures are 三杯酢 and 合わせ酢.

en.meaning: to tear; to rip; to break
examples[].german: The seat of my pants always rips first - I wonder why.
The paper bag tore and the apples rolled onto the road.
After his long-held dream was shattered, he didn't feel like doing anything for a while.
en.notes: 破れる is intransitive: cloth, paper or nets tear or get a hole (袋が破れる, ズボンが破れる); the transitive counterpart is 破る "to tear". Figuratively, it means that plans, dreams or negotiations fail (夢が破れる, 交渉が破れる). Not to be confused with 割れる (glass, plates break), 壊れる (a device breaks down) and 敗れる "to lose (in a competition)", which is read the same way.

en.meaning: letter of introduction; letter of recommendation; (medical) referral letter
examples[].german: You need a referral letter from a doctor to make an appointment at this hospital.
Professor, could you write me a letter of introduction to the professor at my host university?
I visited a new business partner with a letter of introduction from the company president.
en.notes: 紹介状 is a letter with which you introduce or recommend someone to a third person. In everyday life it is encountered above all as a medical referral: large hospitals require a 紹介状 from the family doctor (病院への紹介状). Typical are 紹介状を書く/書いてもらう and 紹介状を持って行く. For job applications, the formal letter of recommendation is rather 推薦状.

examples[].german: He asked that waitress three times whether this restaurant has soup, and each time she said no. She was baffled.
The basics of a Japanese meal are rice, soup and side dishes.
On cold days you feel like drinking something hot and soupy.
en.notes: 汁物 is the umbrella term for soups as part of a Japanese meal, such as 味噌汁, お吸い物 or 豚汁; in the classic menu 一汁三菜, exactly one 汁物 is included. Western soups are usually called スープ. In Japanese, you "drink" soup: 汁物を飲む. The word sounds rather matter-of-fact (menu, cookbook, cafeteria); in conversation people usually name 味噌汁 or スープ directly.

examples[].german: My heart was pounding when a drunk picked a fight with me last night.
The last train on Friday is full of drunks.
A drunk was sleeping on the station platform, so I called a station attendant.
en.notes: 酔っ払い is the colloquial, slightly derogatory word for a drunk person; it comes from the verb 酔っ払う "to get drunk". For the state, people say 酔っ払っている rather than 酔っ払いだ. Typical: 酔っ払いに絡まれる "to be hassled by a drunk". News reports use more formal words like 泥酔者; writing it in kana (よっぱらい) is also common.

examples[].german: I have a hangover and a leg cramp too. Today is the worst.
I drank too much and had a hangover, so I couldn't concentrate in the morning meeting.
I hear that drinking lots of water helps with a hangover.
en.notes: 二日酔い literally means "drunkenness on the second day", that is, the hangover after too much alcohol. One says 二日酔いになる or simply 二日酔いだ; as a reason it takes 二日酔いで (二日酔いで頭が痛い). Not to be confused with 悪酔い (feeling sick while drinking itself) and 酔い止め, which is a remedy for motion sickness.

examples[].german: How long have you been working at this gas station?
Let's fill up the tank at the expressway gas station and then set off.
Because of the typhoon, long lines formed at the gas stations in the city.
en.notes: 給油所 is the formal word for "gas station", formed from 給油 "refueling" and 所 "place". In everyday speech people almost always say ガソリンスタンド or simply スタンド; 給油所 is found on signs, in the news and in official texts, and also for airplanes or ships. The related verb is 給油する "to refuel"; 満タンにする means "to fill up the tank".

examples[].german: She has great influence in the media.
That country is gradually losing its influence in the international community.
The teacher's words have a strong influence on the children.
en.notes: 影響力 is the ability to affect others - "influence" in the sense of power or weight of a person, company or country. Typical are 影響力がある／大きい／強い, 影響力を持つ, 影響力を失う and 〜に対する影響力. In contrast to 影響, which denotes the concrete effect itself (天気の影響で遅れる), 影響力 means the potential to exert influence. Factual-neutral, common in media, politics and business.

examples[].german: Although she landed a perfect triple axel, her score barely rose.
The frog hopped with a splash into the pond.
I tried to jump over the puddle, but failed and my shoes got wet.
en.notes: 跳ぶ emphasizes jumping off the ground with the legs: "to jump, to hop", whereas 飛ぶ means "to fly". In everyday writing 飛ぶ is often also used for jumping, but in sports terms 跳 appears: 縄跳び, 跳び箱, 走り高跳び. With を it takes the obstacle or the jump itself (溝を跳ぶ, トリプルアクセルを跳ぶ); 跳び越える means "to jump over". Related is 跳ねる "to hop, to splash".

examples[].german: In what year of Showa were you born?
This coffee shop still has a Showa-era atmosphere, and somehow it's calming.
"Women should stay at home" - that way of thinking is a bit Showa, isn't it?
en.notes: 昭和 is the era name (元号) of Emperor Hirohito, 1926 to 1989, between 大正 and 平成. Years are given as 昭和〇〇年, especially for birth dates on forms (昭和何年生まれ). In colloquial speech, 昭和 also stands for "old-fashioned, nostalgic": 昭和っぽい, 昭和な考え方, 昭和レトロ.

examples[].german: I know that fisherman. He's my brother-in-law.
My grandfather went out to sea every morning as a fisherman for fifty years.
At the harbor, the fishermen start preparing their nets early in the morning.
en.notes: 漁師 is the fisherman as an occupation. Note the reading りょう for 漁 - in most other words it is read ぎょ (漁業, 漁船). 猟師 "hunter" is pronounced the same, so context helps in conversation. Related terms are 漁師町 "fishing village" and 漁師料理; in statistics and administration, the term is rather 漁業者 or 漁民.

examples[].german: My fishing boat was stolen last night.
Because a typhoon is approaching, all the fishing boats in the harbor took shelter.
Even before sunrise, many fishing boats set out from the harbor.
en.notes: 漁船 is a fishing boat or fishing vessel; 漁 is read ぎょ here, unlike in 漁師 (りょうし). A boat for recreational anglers, by contrast, is called 釣り船. Typical are 漁船が出港する/港に戻る and 漁船で漁に出る. As counters, 隻 is used for larger ships and 艘 for small boats.

en.meaning: to atone for; to make up for; to compensate
examples[].german: I'm tired of atoning for my past mistakes.
He spent ten years in prison and paid for his crime.
I caused the company a loss through my own mistake, and I don't know how to make up for it.
en.notes: 償う is transitive and means "to make amends, to atone, to compensate": 罪を償う "to pay for a crime", 過ちを償う, 損害を償う. The noun is 償い (罪の償い). Actually paying for a damaged object is rather 弁償する, legal compensation for damages is 賠償. The word is rather elevated and sounds serious.

examples[].german: While filming, I accidentally tore a fisherman's net and had to replace it.
Of course I will replace the plate I broke.
If you lose a library book, you have to replace it.
en.notes: 弁償 means to make up concretely, with money or a replacement, for damage one has caused: 割った皿を弁償する, なくした本を弁償する. As a suru-verb it is transitive (〜を弁償する). In contrast, 賠償 is legal compensation on a larger scale (損害賠償), 補償 is compensation for losses, e.g. by the state or a company, and 償う is the general, also moral, "to make amends".

examples[].german: The prisoner was released after serving a fifteen-year term, but he had nowhere to go.
He has finished his sentence and plans to return to society next month.
Because of his good behavior in prison, his sentence was shortened by a year.
en.notes: 刑期 is the duration of a prison sentence, that is, the time in custody, not the punishment itself (that would be 刑 or 刑罰). Typical combinations are 刑期を終える, 刑期を務める, 刑期が短縮される and 刑期満了 "end of the prison term". The word belongs to legal and news language.

examples[].german: The court sentenced the defendant to life imprisonment.
In that country, the death penalty was abolished and the heaviest punishment became life imprisonment.
Japan currently has no life imprisonment without parole.
en.notes: 終身刑 is a life sentence; people say 終身刑を言い渡される "to be sentenced to life imprisonment" or 終身刑に処される. Japanese criminal law formally has 無期懲役, in which release on parole is possible; 終身刑 therefore often refers to sentences abroad or explicitly to imprisonment without release. The word belongs to legal and news language, often in contrast to 死刑 "death penalty".

examples[].german: My distrust of my wife just keeps growing.
The more days passed without news, the greater the worry became.
In front of the station, donations are being solicited for the earthquake areas.
