en.notes: 募る has two uses. Intransitively, feelings keep growing: 不安が募る, 不満が募る, 思いが募る, often with 〜ばかり or 〜一方. Transitively it means "to recruit, to collect (donations, participants)": 寄付を募る, 参加者を募る - close in meaning to 募集する, but more elevated. Both meanings are rather written-language.

examples[].german: Tofugu is still looking for bloggers.
I saw the "part-time help wanted" sign and called right away.
The city is recruiting participants for next year's marathon.
en.notes: 募集 means that a company or organization publicly seeks people or submissions: 社員を募集する, アルバイト募集, 参加者募集中, 作品を募集する. A person who responds to such a call 応募する; the conditions of the call are called 募集要項. 募集 is more neutral and everyday than the elevated 募る.

examples[].german: We decided to settle it by majority vote.
The accident left a large number of injured.
Supporters were in the majority, and the plan was approved.
en.notes: 多数 means "a large number, many" and, as the opposite of 少数, "the majority". Attributively it takes の (多数の人々, 多数の応募), but it can also be used adverbially: 応募が多数寄せられた. Fixed combinations are 多数決 ("majority vote") and 多数派 ("majority faction"). It sounds factual and literary; in everyday speech one mostly says たくさん or 多くの, and for "more than half" more precisely 過半数.

examples[].german: You can get the application form at the court.
I saw the job advertisement and applied to the company.
Over a thousand entries were received for the photo contest.
en.notes: 応募 is the response to a call for applicants (募集): one applies for a job or takes part in a contest or prize draw, with the pattern 〜に応募する. Common compounds are 応募者, 応募用紙, 応募締め切り. Signing up for courses or events in general is more 申し込む.

en.meaning: to take (charge, a post, a pen); to carry out; to hold (office)
examples[].german: We want you to take charge of this project.
For the first time in a long while, I took up my pen and wrote a letter to my old teacher.
My grandfather taught at a high school for thirty years.
en.notes: 執る is one of the many spellings of とる and stands for taking on and carrying out a task: 指揮を執る "to take command", 筆を執る "to take up the pen", 事務を執る, 教鞭を執る "to work as a teacher". For ordinary taking, people write 取る, for photos 撮る, for catching 捕る, and for adopting/hiring 採る. The word feels literary and occurs almost only in these fixed combinations.

examples[].german: It's been a while since he hit a double. Usually he hits home runs.
In the bottom of the ninth, Tanaka's triple tied the game.
He hit as many as thirty home runs this season.
en.notes: 塁打 is, in baseball, a hit with which the batter reaches one or more bases. On its own it is rarely used; it mostly appears in compounds: 二塁打 "double", 三塁打 "triple", 本塁打 "home run" (colloquially ホームラン). A simple hit is called ヒット in everyday speech; in statistics, 塁打数 is the total number of bases reached.

examples[].german: That first-base umpire was farting like crazy during the game.
The first-base umpire immediately called him safe.
In professional baseball, there are three base umpires in addition to the home plate umpire.
en.notes: 塁審 is the umpire at a base in baseball (塁 "base", 審 from 審判 "umpire"). The home plate umpire behind the catcher is called 球審 (also 主審). Depending on position, people say 一塁塁審, 二塁塁審, 三塁塁審; the call is called 判定 (アウト・セーフと判定する). The word belongs to sports terminology; generally people say 審判.

en.meaning: to suffer from; to be ill with
examples[].german: My mother may be suffering from dementia.
My father has suffered from diabetes for many years.
He had heart trouble when he was young and gave up sports.
en.notes: 患う means "to suffer from an (usually serious or long-lasting) illness" and takes を: 病気を患う, 心臓を患う; often in the form 患っている. For colds and harmless illnesses, people say 〜にかかる or 〜になる instead. The word is literary and elevated; related are 長患い "long illness" and 煩う "to worry, to be troubled", which has the same reading.

examples[].german: I hear a man died because a hospital, understaffed and in chaos, refused to take an emergency patient, but that's not only the hospital's fault, is it?
Emergency patients were brought in one after another in the middle of the night, and the doctors had no time to rest.
Because of an emergency patient, the start of consultations is delayed.
en.notes: 急患 is the short form of 急病患者 and refers to an emergency patient who must be treated immediately. Typical are 急患を受け入れる "to admit an emergency patient", 急患を断る and 急患が運ばれる. The word comes from hospital routine and news language; 救急患者 means the same, and the emergency room is called 救急外来 or 急患センター.

examples[].german: Because my mother became ill, I decided to return to my country.
I had forgotten something, so I went back home.
The section chief will be back at three o'clock.
en.notes: 戻る means "to return to a place or state where one has been before": 席に戻る, 会社に戻る, 元に戻る "to become as before again". 帰る, by contrast, means returning to where one belongs (home, one's homeland). That is why in the office one says 三時に戻ります when one is only away briefly. The transitive partner is 戻す "to put back, to return".

en.meaning: to face; to come from the opposite direction
examples[].german: I completely failed to notice the oncoming motorcycle.
This road is narrow, so be careful when passing oncoming cars.
The headlights of the oncoming car were so bright that I couldn't see ahead for a moment.
en.notes: 対向 means "to face each other, to come from the opposite direction" and is used above all in road traffic: 対向車 "oncoming traffic", 対向車線 "oncoming lane"; as a verb mostly attributive, as in 対向するバイク. Note: 対抗する is read the same way but means "to compete, to match, to put up resistance". The word is rather technical and written; in conversation people often say 向こうから来る車.

examples[].german: The students were forced into all-out resistance against authority.
Even when the capital was surrounded, the country's army kept resisting to the end.
The residents oppose the construction of the factory and are prepared to resist to the bitter end.
en.notes: 抗戦 is resistance against an attack, originally in the military sense: 抗戦を続ける, 最後まで抗戦する. Figuratively it is used in politics and disputes, above all in 徹底抗戦 "resistance to the utmost". General resistance is 抵抗; 交戦, which is read the same way, means "battle between two sides". Register: written, news language.

examples[].german: The Japan Meteorological Agency says the rainy season will begin in early June.
I'm planning to move early next month, so I'm busy packing right now.
The product you ordered is scheduled to be delivered in early March.
en.notes: 上旬 is the first third of the month, that is, the 1st to the 10th day; 中旬 (11th-20th) and 下旬 (21st to the end of the month) belong with it. People say 六月上旬 or 六月の上旬 and use it with に for time expressions. The word is typical for business letters, weather reports and announcements; colloquially people say 月の初め or 初めごろ instead.

examples[].german: Minority opinions should also be respected.
An ethnic minority lives in this village.
Only a very small number of people opposed it.
en.notes: 少数 means "a small number, few" and is the counterpart of 多数. Common combinations are 少数意見 ("minority opinion"), 少数派 ("minority, minority faction") and 少数民族 ("ethnic minority"); attributively it takes の: ごく少数の人. Note: 小数 with 小 is the "decimal number" in mathematics - same reading, different meaning.

examples[].german: I plan to return to Japan in late April and come back to the US again in early June.
Even in late August, the severe heat continues.
The deadline for the report is the end of this month.
en.notes: 下旬 is the last third of the month, from the 21st day to the end of the month; counterparts are 上旬 and 中旬. Note the reading げ for 下 (not した or か). People say 四月下旬 or 四月の下旬, and as a point in time with に. It is common in planning, news and weather reports; colloquially also 月末ごろ or 終わりごろ.

examples[].german: The due date is mid-November.
This year the cherry blossoms did not reach full bloom until mid-April.
The meeting has been postponed to the middle of next month.
en.notes: 中旬 is the middle third of the month, the 11th to the 20th day, between 上旬 and 下旬. It appears in patterns like 十一月中旬 or 十一月の中旬 and with に as a time expression. Typical for dates in business, news and weather reports; in conversation people also say 半ばごろ or 真ん中ごろ.

examples[].german: We traced the source of the infection to a flock of ducks in Taiwan.
Last summer I traveled to Taiwan with my family.
I can't forget the xiaolongbao I ate at a night market in Taiwan.
en.notes: 台湾 is the Japanese name for Taiwan; the character 湾 means "bay". Common derivations are 台湾人, 台湾料理, 台湾茶 and 台湾旅行. In everyday use the word is politically neutral; official documents sometimes use 中華民国. Because of its proximity and good food, Taiwan is a very popular travel destination for Japanese people.

examples[].german: Her one remark made his anger explode.
Gas exploded at the factory, and several people were injured.
That new game has been selling explosively since just after its release.
en.notes: 爆発 is an explosion; as a する-verb it is intransitive (ガスが爆発する), and transitively it is used as 爆発させる. Figuratively, feelings or dissatisfaction explode: 怒りが爆発する, 不満が爆発する. Very common is 爆発的 "explosive," as in 爆発的な人気 or 爆発的に売れる. Distinction: 破裂 is bursting (tire, balloon, pipe).

examples[].german: I knew that dismantling a bomb was dangerous, but I was really curious.
A suspicious package was found at the airport, and since it might be a bomb, everyone was evacuated.
The minister's bombshell remark caused an uproar in the Diet.
en.notes: 爆弾 is a bomb; typical combinations are 爆弾を仕掛ける "to plant a bomb", 爆弾が爆発する, 時限爆弾 "time bomb" and 原子爆弾 (short 原爆). Figuratively, 爆弾発言 stands for a "bombshell" in the sense of a shocking remark, and 〜に爆弾を抱える means to have a latent problem, such as a vulnerable knee in athletes.

examples[].german: Do you have any good April Fools' ideas that would make Mom and Dad burst out laughing?
At the host's joke, the whole hall was filled with roaring laughter.
I really cracked up at the animal video I watched yesterday.
en.notes: 爆笑 originally refers to the roaring laughter of a whole group (会場が爆笑する, 爆笑に包まれる). Colloquially it is also said when a single person bursts out laughing (この動画、爆笑した). Common forms are 大爆笑, 爆笑を誘う and 爆笑させる "to make roar with laughter". As a する-verb, it is intransitive.

examples[].german: A suicide bombing occurred in front of the station, and many people were killed.
I said something unnecessary and totally shot myself in the foot.
In that game, you blow yourself up if you hit a bomb you placed yourself.
en.notes: 自爆 literally means "to blow oneself up": in the news for suicide attacks (自爆テロ) or for weapons and machines that destroy themselves (自爆装置). Colloquially it is very common in a figurative sense: to harm oneself through one's own words or actions, to "score an own goal" (余計なことを言って自爆した). As a する-verb, it is intransitive.

examples[].german: The chocolate factory was reduced to pieces by the bombing.
This town was bombed several times during the war.
When my grandmother hears the sound of a bomber, she still remembers the war.
en.notes: 爆撃 is bombardment from the air by aircraft; people say 〜を爆撃する or, in the passive, 爆撃を受ける/爆撃される. The aircraft for it is called 爆撃機. Synonymous and frequent in the news is 空爆; shelling with artillery, by contrast, is 砲撃, and a general attack is 攻撃.

en.meaning: to bounce; to spring; to become lively
examples[].german: The ball bounced off the ground and fell into the lake.
I chatted late into the night with a friend I hadn't seen in a long time.
Because the service was so good, I gave a generous tip.
en.notes: 弾む is intransitive in its basic sense: a ball bounces or rebounds (ボールが弾む). Figuratively, something becomes lively: 話が弾む "the conversation gets going", 声が弾む, 心が弾む. 息が弾む means "to be out of breath", and transitively チップを弾む means "to give a generous tip". The causative form 弾ませる appears e.g. in 声を弾ませる; similar is 跳ねる "to hop".

examples[].german: I dodged the rain of bullets very skillfully.
Bullet marks from the war remained on the wall of the old building.
On the weekend I went to Seoul on a whirlwind two-day, one-night trip.
en.notes: 弾丸 is a projectile or rifle bullet; in everyday speech people also say 弾 (たま) or 銃弾. Typical are 弾丸が当たる, 弾丸をよける and 弾丸の跡. Figuratively it stands for extreme speed: 弾丸ツアー is a "whirlwind trip" with a very tight schedule, 弾丸のような速さ "as fast as a bullet".

en.meaning: majority; absolute majority; more than half
examples[].german: The bill passed with a majority vote.
That party won a majority in the election.
More than half of the respondents said they were satisfied with their current lives.
en.notes: 過半数 is "more than half", i.e. an absolute majority - in contrast to 多数, which only means "the larger number". Typical expressions are 過半数を占める ("to hold the majority"), 過半数を超える, 過半数に達する／届かない and 過半数の賛成. The word is factual and appears mainly in elections, votes and surveys.

examples[].german: This afternoon I intend to submit my report on the hearing ability of blind people.
As people get older, their hearing for high-pitched sounds tends to decline.
I also had a hearing test at my health checkup.
en.notes: 聴力 is the ability to hear, that is, the measurable capacity to hear. Typical are 聴力が落ちる/低下する, 聴力を失う and 聴力検査 "hearing test". Parallel to it is 視力 "eyesight". 聴覚, by contrast, refers to the sense of hearing as such (聴覚障害).

examples[].german: Maybe the phone is broken. It's strange that there hasn't been a single call from a listener.
I want to make a play that deaf people and hearing people can enjoy together.
Recently, more and more hearing people are learning sign language.
en.notes: 聴者 means "listener" (of a broadcast, for example), but it is rare in this meaning; more usual are 聴取者, リスナー or 聞き手. Today 聴者 is encountered above all as the opposite of ろう者 "deaf person" and refers to hearing people, for example in texts about sign language (手話). The word is literary or technical.

examples[].german: Mori-kun, do you listen to Western music?
If I listen to classical music before going to bed, I sleep well.
The students listened attentively to the professor's lecture.
en.notes: 聴く emphasizes attentive, conscious listening, especially to music, radio, lectures or other people's concerns (音楽を聴く, 講演を聴く, 話をじっくり聴く). 聞く is the general word for "to hear" and also for "to ask"; for "to ask" one never writes 聴く. In practice, 聞く is possible in all cases, while 聴く seems more deliberate and is very common with music.

examples[].german: Someone planted a bug in Tofugu's office, but we don't know who did it or why.
He suspects that his phone is being tapped.
Eavesdropping on other people's conversations is a crime.
en.notes: 盗聴 means "secret listening" (literally "to steal" + "to hear") and, as a する-verb, is transitive: 電話を盗聴する, passive 盗聴される. The listening device, the "bug", is called 盗聴器; you plant it with 仕掛ける. To be distinguished are 盗み聞き(する) and 立ち聞き for everyday eavesdropping at a door or wall, and 傍受 for the interception of radio communications by authorities. Formed similarly: 盗撮 "secret filming".

examples[].german: There was no trace of a crime in the room, but the police suspected it was a murder case.
In preparation for the audit, system operations need to be kept traceable.
When we checked the evidence trail of the transactions, we found irregularities.
en.notes: 証跡 is a trace that serves as proof of something. In everyday speech people say 証拠 "evidence" or 痕跡 "trace" instead; 証跡 is encountered today above all in IT, auditing and accounting, for example 監査証跡 "audit trail" or 操作の証跡を残す "to keep a traceable record of operations". The word is literary and technical.

examples[].german: That guy apparently spent quite a lot of money on his girlfriend.
She is always considerate of the people around her.
In an interview, you should be careful about your choice of words.
en.notes: 遣う is an alternative spelling of 使う that is used mainly for immaterial things and money: 気を遣う "to be considerate", 心遣い "thoughtfulness", 言葉遣い "choice of words", 金遣い "way of handling money", お小遣い "pocket money". For tools, devices and methods, 使う is written. With money (お金を遣う) both spellings are possible, 使う being more common.

examples[].german: All of these children are fighting illness.
The workers fought the company for a wage increase.
I kept studying for the exam to the end while fighting off sleepiness.
en.notes: 闘う means "to fight" in the sense of a tenacious struggle against difficulties: 病気と闘う, 貧困と闘う, 眠気と闘う, also in labor disputes (会社と闘う). 戦う, by contrast, is the usual word for war and competition (敵と戦う, 試合で戦う). The opponent takes と; the noun is 闘い.

examples[].german: The combat robot burned with fighting spirit.
Ahead of the final, the players are burning with fighting spirit.
Even after losing in the first round, his fighting spirit did not weaken in the slightest.
en.notes: 闘志 is fighting spirit or the will to fight, especially in sports and in challenges. Typical combinations are 闘志を燃やす "to burn with fighting spirit", 闘志がわく, 闘志満々 and 闘志をむき出しにする. Related are 闘争心 (combativeness, rather aggressive) and the more everyday やる気 and 意欲 "motivation".

examples[].german: Before the race, each camp began its final adjustments.
As the election approaches, the fight between the two camps is getting fiercer.
During the Cold War, the world was divided into two camps, East and West.
en.notes: 陣営 originally refers to a military camp; today it mainly means a "camp" of supporters: in politics and election campaigns (与党陣営, 〇〇陣営), in the Cold War (東側陣営) or in sports, for example the team around a racehorse or a boxer. Typical are 両陣営, 各陣営 and 相手陣営. For a tent camp or holiday camp, people do not say 陣営 but キャンプ.

examples[].german: Although perfume was banned at school, that boy always wore a sweet-smelling perfume and told the teachers it was his natural underarm smell.
I gave my girlfriend perfume for her birthday.
The smell of perfume in the elevator was so strong that I felt sick.
en.notes: 香水 is perfume. You put it on with 香水をつける (not 着る); too much of it is 香水をつけすぎる. The scent is called 香水の香り or 香水の匂い, though 匂い can also sound negative. Lighter scents are called コロン or オーデコロン; in Japan, strong perfume in the office or in restaurants is often considered impolite.

examples[].german: Dialogue is indispensable for solving problems.
The mayor set up an opportunity for direct dialogue with residents.
It is said that conversation between parents and children is decreasing.
en.notes: 対話 is a conversation with genuine exchange, especially a "dialogue" between parties with different viewpoints. Typical are 〜と対話する, 対話を重ねる, 対話を通じて and 対話の場を設ける. Unlike 会話, which means any everyday conversation, 対話 sounds more serious and aims at mutual understanding; 会談, by contrast, is an official meeting of high-ranking representatives. Common in politics, education and diplomacy.

examples[].german: Signs of an economic recovery are gradually becoming visible.
Getting tired easily could be a sign of illness, so you should get checked once.
The volcano is monitored 24 hours a day in order to detect signs of an eruption.
en.notes: 兆候 is a sign that something is developing or about to occur: 景気回復の兆候, 病気の兆候; in medicine it is also written 徴候. Typical are 兆候が見られる/現れる/ある. 前兆, by contrast, emphasizes the omen shortly before an event (often negative), 症状 is an actually present disease symptom, and 兆し (きざし) is a softer, often positive "sign" (春の兆し).

examples[].german: These clouds and this wind are a portent of a storm.
There is a story that animals become restless as a warning sign of a big earthquake.
My grandmother often said that a lot of crows cawing is a bad omen.
en.notes: 前兆 is an omen or harbinger that immediately precedes a particular event: 地震の前兆, 嵐の前兆, 病気の前兆. Often it concerns ominous things (不吉な前兆 "bad omen"), but also neutrally: 前兆現象. In contrast to 兆候 (sign of a development), with 前兆 it is clear what it points to; more elevated and literary is 予兆.

en.meaning: to face; to overlook; to attend; to approach (a situation)
examples[].german: Tofugu's headquarters is located in Oregon, a state in the northwestern United States facing the Pacific Ocean.
The players went into the final well prepared.
Before you go into the interview, let's research the company thoroughly.
en.notes: 臨む is an intransitive verb with に and has two main meanings: spatially "to face, to look out onto" (海に臨むホテル) and "to face a situation, to take part in something" (試合に臨む, 面接に臨む, 本番に臨む). The form 〜に臨んで means "on the occasion of, in the face of". Not to be confused with 望む "to wish, to hope for" (transitive with を), which is read the same way. The tone is written to elevated; in everyday speech people rather say 〜に向かう or 〜を受ける.

examples[].german: Many Japanese students experience going to a seaside school camp in summer.
In the coastal area of Tokyo, large parks and exhibition halls stand side by side.
This area has developed as a coastal industrial zone.
en.notes: 臨海 means "located by the sea, coastal" and almost always appears as the first element of a compound or with の: 臨海部 "coastal area", 臨海公園, 臨海工業地帯 "coastal industrial zone". 臨海学校 is a summer school camp at the sea where students learn, among other things, to swim. The word is matter-of-fact and official; in everyday speech people say 海辺 or 海の近く, and for "along the coast" also 沿岸.

examples[].german: Because of the typhoon, school was closed temporarily.
At the end of the year, we are recruiting temporary part-time workers.
On the day of the fireworks festival, special trains will run.
en.notes: 臨時 refers to something that is not regular but set up for a special occasion or temporarily. It usually appears with の or directly before a noun: 臨時休業 "closed on short notice", 臨時列車 "special train", 臨時ニュース, 臨時収入 "unexpected extra income", 臨時のアルバイト. The opposite is 定期 or 定例. In contrast to 一時的 (limited in time), 臨時 emphasizes what is outside the schedule.

examples[].german: I quit smoking after being hospitalized.
The Olympics led to an increase in tourists from overseas.
This accident prompted a review of safety measures.
en.notes: 契機 is the "occasion, trigger" for a change. Typical patterns: 〜を契機に(して) / 〜を契機として "on the occasion of, triggered by" and 〜が契機となる "to become the trigger". Synonymous, but colloquial, is きっかけ; 契機 sounds written and suits reports, news and essays. It differs from 機会 "opportunity" in that it emphasizes the turning point or trigger of a development.

en.meaning: to hoist; to hold up; to put forward (a goal)
examples[].german: James set himself a new goal: to take his pencil sharpening to the next level.
On national holidays, some families fly the national flag in front of the gate.
The winner held the trophy high in the air.
en.notes: 掲げる literally means "to hold up, to hoist, to hang up": 旗を掲げる, 看板を掲げる, トロフィーを掲げる. Very common is the figurative meaning "to put a goal, ideal or slogan on one's banner": 目標を掲げる, スローガンを掲げる, 公約を掲げる. It is transitive with を and has no intransitive partner. Unlike 上げる, 掲げる emphasizes that something is made visible to everyone.

examples[].german: When there is blank space on a notice about a restaurant's temporary closure, Aya scribbles on it.
The exam results will be posted on the bulletin board next week.
According to the notice at the station, the time of the last train seems to have changed.
en.notes: 掲示 is a public "notice" or the "posting" of an announcement, for example at a school, station or city hall. As a する-verb it is transitive (お知らせを掲示する), very often in the passive: 掲示板に掲示される. 掲示板 is the "bulletin board" and on the internet also a "forum." Colloquially, a pasted slip of paper is 張り紙; 掲載, by contrast, is publication in a newspaper, magazine or on the web.

examples[].german: The article in this month's issue is very interesting, isn't it?
My letter to the editor was printed in the newspaper.
Republishing photos from this website without permission is prohibited.
en.notes: 掲載 is the "printing, publishing" of a text, photo or advertisement in a newspaper, magazine or on a website. Typical: 新聞に掲載される, 記事を掲載する, 無断掲載禁止 "printing without permission prohibited", 〜号掲載の記事. Publishing a whole book, by contrast, is 出版 or 刊行; a notice posted on a wall is 掲示. As a suru-verb 掲載 is transitive, often in the passive.

examples[].german: The man came to a place with a view of the hotel room in order to snipe at the politician.
An incident occurred in which the president was shot at during a speech.
He received sniper training in the military.
en.notes: 狙撃 is composed of 狙う "to aim" and 撃つ "to shoot" and refers to an aimed shot from ambush or from a distance, typically at a specific person. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を狙撃する, in the news mostly in the passive: 〜が狙撃される. The shooter is called 狙撃手 or スナイパー. The word belongs to news and military vocabulary; the general "to shoot" is 撃つ.

examples[].german: Many shops closed because of the recession.
The recession continues and salaries hardly go up.
Why the gloomy face since the morning? What's wrong?
en.notes: 不景気 refers to a poor economic situation, a "slump" or "recession"; the opposite is 好景気. It is used as a noun (不景気が続く, 不景気のせいで) and as a な-adjective (不景気な世の中). In conversation people also simply say 景気が悪い; the more technical word for a deep crisis is 不況. Figuratively, 不景気な顔 means a "gloomy face".

en.meaning: to bury; to inter; to cover up
examples[].german: I'm worried that the truth about the incident might be covered up.
My grandfather was laid to rest in the family grave in his hometown.
The scandal ended his political career.
en.notes: 葬る first means "to bury, to inter" (墓に葬る), but today it is especially common figuratively, "to cover up, to sweep under the rug": 真相が闇に葬られる "the truth is covered up". Also "to finish off, to get out of the way": 政治生命が葬られる. Mostly in the passive; 葬り去る strengthens it. The neutral word for "to bury" is 埋める, the formal burial is 埋葬する.

examples[].german: The cremation system does not stop automatically. The person in charge checks the condition of the bones through a small window and stops it when he thinks it's done.
In Japan, almost all of the deceased are cremated.
After the funeral, the family headed to the crematorium together.
en.notes: 火葬 is "burial by fire, cremation"; as a transitive する-verb it is mostly used in the passive: 火葬される. The counterpart is 土葬 "burial in the ground", and the place is called 火葬場 "crematorium". In Japan, cremation is practically the rule; afterward the relatives use chopsticks to place the bones in the urn (骨壺). The word is matter-of-fact and neutral and belongs to the word field around 葬式 "funeral".

examples[].german: This park is known locally as a hotbed of crime, so you'd better stay away.
It was pointed out that old customs have become a breeding ground for wrongdoing.
A damp kitchen easily becomes a breeding ground for mold and bacteria.
en.notes: 温床 literally means "hotbed" (a heated bed for seedlings), but it is used almost only figuratively: "breeding ground, hotbed" for something negative. Fixed patterns: 〜の温床になる / 〜の温床となる, for example 犯罪の温床, 不正の温床, 細菌の温床. It is not used for positive developments. The tone is rather written, as in newspaper reports.

examples[].german: The elasticity of my skin is declining.
The cushions of this sofa are just right in their springiness.
Shouldn't the rules be applied a bit more flexibly?
en.notes: 弾力 is the "elasticity, resilience" of a material or body: 弾力がある, 弾力が失われる, 肌の弾力, ゴムの弾力. Figuratively it means "flexibility", above all in 弾力的 "flexible, adaptable" (規則を弾力的に運用する). The technical term in physics is 弾性; for a person's mental flexibility one rather says 柔軟.

en.meaning: skewered and grilled food; grilled skewers
examples[].german: Lately I'm hooked on grilled kale skewers.
At the izakaya, we ordered a few grilled skewers.
I bought a grilled squid skewer at a food stall at the festival.
en.notes: 串焼き is anything grilled on a skewer (串): meat, fish, vegetables. It is counted with 本 (串焼きを三本). 焼き鳥 is the best-known subgroup (chicken), while 串カツ and 串揚げ are deep-fried skewers. Typical places are 居酒屋 and festival stalls (屋台).

en.meaning: being held in one's arms; carrying
examples[].german: Big sister, pick me up!
Shopping with a baby in your arms is exhausting.
Our cat doesn't like being picked up.
en.notes: 抱っこ is the child-language or familiar word for "to pick up, to hold in one's arms", especially with babies, small children and pets: 赤ちゃんを抱っこする. Children simply call out 抱っこ！ or 抱っこして！ "Pick me up!". The neutral verb is 抱く (also figuratively: 夢を抱く). Carrying piggyback on the back is おんぶ; the baby carrier is called 抱っこひも.

examples[].german: Saliva helps digest food.
When you are nervous, less saliva is produced.
I took a virus test using saliva.
en.notes: 唾液 is the matter-of-fact, medical word for "saliva" and appears in biology, medicine and health reports: 唾液が出る, 唾液の分泌, 唾液検査, 唾液腺 "salivary gland". In everyday speech people say つば; saliva running out, for example while sleeping, is よだれ.

examples[].german: He was so nervous that he could hardly swallow his saliva.
Spitting on the street is bad manners.
My grandfather wets his finger with spit and turns the newspaper page.
en.notes: 唾 (つば) is the everyday word for "spit, saliva"; the technical counterpart is 唾液. Typical expressions: 唾を吐く "to spit", 唾を飲み込む "to swallow", 生唾を飲む "to lick one's lips" (from greed or tension). Idiomatically, 唾をつける (つばをつけておく) also means "to reserve something for oneself, to stake a claim". It is often written in kana つば.

en.meaning: to be crushed; to go bankrupt; to fall through
examples[].german: The bread was squashed in my bag.
The bookstore in front of the station went out of business last year.
I sang so much at karaoke that my voice gave out.
en.notes: 潰れる is intransitive and means "to be crushed, to be flattened" (箱が潰れる). It is also very common in a figurative sense: businesses "go bankrupt" (会社が潰れる), plans "fall through" (予定が潰れる), the voice "gives out" (声が潰れる) and time "is used up" (休みが潰れる). The transitive partner is 潰す "to crush, to ruin", also 時間を潰す "to kill time".

examples[].german: This company focuses on foreign trade.
The government decided to review its foreign policy.
It is difficult to explain internal company problems to the outside.
en.notes: 対外 means "toward the outside, toward foreign countries" and almost always stands before another noun: 対外政策 "foreign policy", 対外貿易, 対外関係, 対外援助. The derivation 対外的 (に/な) means more generally "outwardly", for example toward the public or other companies. The opposite is 対内 "inward". Freely with の (対外のビジネス) it sounds unnatural; people use the compounds.

examples[].german: The boom continued and the unemployment rate fell.
Thanks to the good economy, my bonus increased from last year.
Japan was in the midst of a boom at that time.
en.notes: 好景気 is a good economic situation, a "boom" or "prosperity", the opposite of 不景気. Typical are 好景気が続く, 好景気に沸く ("to be swept up in a boom") and 好景気の波に乗る. In conversation one usually simply says 景気がいい; 好景気 sounds more factual and often appears in news and business texts.

examples[].german: The culprit planted a time bomb at the station.
On Mondays, first period is math.
This law is a time-limited law for five years.
en.notes: 時限 has two meanings: at school and university the "class period" (一時限目 "first period", synonymous with the more casual 一時間目) and, generally, a "time limit". The second meaning is found in compounds such as 時限爆弾 "time bomb" and 時限立法 "sunset law, time-limited legislation". A deadline by which something must be done, by contrast, is 期限.

en.meaning: to put back; to restore; to return
examples[].german: "I wish I hadn't said such a terrible thing to him." "I know. But what's been said can't be taken back."
Please put the books you've finished reading back in their original place.
Rehydrate the dried shiitake in water before using them in cooking.
en.notes: 戻す is transitive: "to put something back in its place, return it to its former state" (元の場所に戻す, 元に戻す, 時計の針を戻す). In cooking it means "to soak, rehydrate" (乾物を水で戻す), and colloquially also "to vomit." The intransitive partner is 戻る "to return." For giving something back to a person, 返す is more usual (本を返す).

examples[].german: More than 300 people applied for a position at that trading company, but apparently no one was hired.
My father works at a trading company and often travels abroad on business.
After graduating, I want to get a job at a trading company and make use of my English.
en.notes: 貿易会社 is a company for import and export. Note the voicing: かいしゃ becomes がいしゃ in the compound (ぼうえきがいしゃ). Large Japanese trading houses that operate in many industries are called 商社 or 総合商社; 貿易会社 is the more general, matter-of-fact term and is also used for smaller firms.

examples[].german: She was one of my best friends when I lived in Nara Prefecture, but since I moved to Osaka we have been drifting apart.
In Nara Prefecture there are many old temples and shrines.
Nara is one of the prefectures that does not border the sea.
en.notes: 奈良県 is in the 近畿 (Kansai) region; the administrative seat is 奈良市. The prefecture is known for the ancient capital 平城京 of the 奈良時代 (710-794), the 東大寺 with the Great Buddha and the tame deer in 奈良公園. 奈良 alone can mean the city or the prefecture; with 県 it is unambiguous. Nara is one of the prefectures without a sea coast.

examples[].german: Please change from the Chuo Line to the Yamanote Line at Shinjuku Station and come as far as Ueno Station.
I will transfer to the subway at the next station.
It was cheaper, so I switched to a new mobile carrier.
en.notes: 乗り換える means "to transfer": the transfer station takes で, the new line に, the old one から: 新宿で山手線に乗り換える. The noun 乗り換え is "transfer" (乗り換えが便利だ). Figuratively it means "to switch", for example to another provider: 新しい携帯会社に乗り換える. It is built from 乗る "to board" and 換える "to exchange".

examples[].german: My daughter loves Okinawa so much that I have no idea when she will come back.
Okinawa is warm all year round, and the sea is very beautiful.
During summer vacation, we traveled to Okinawa with the family.
en.notes: 沖縄 is Japan's southernmost prefecture (沖縄県), a subtropical island chain, and also the name of its main island (沖縄本島). Until the 19th century, the Kingdom of 琉球 stood here, and its culture lives on in music, cuisine (沖縄料理) and dialect. You go "to Okinawa" with へ or に: 沖縄へ行く.

examples[].german: Fluorescent lights didn't exist yet at the time of the Meiji Restoration, right?
With the Meiji Restoration, Japan set out on the path to becoming a modern nation.
More than 150 years have passed since the Meiji Restoration.
en.notes: 明治維新 refers to the political upheaval around 1868 in which the Tokugawa shogunate ended, power formally returned to the emperor and Japan modernized rapidly. 維新 means "renewal"; the word appears almost only in historical contexts, for example 明治維新の頃, 明治維新以後. The period before is called 江戸時代, the period after 明治時代.

examples[].german: For this ball, I intend to wear a dress in a brighter color than last time.
With the power of magic, Cinderella went to the prince's ball.
In Vienna, many balls are held when winter comes.
en.notes: 舞踏会 is a formal Western-style "ball" with ballroom dancing, as known from fairy tales or Vienna: 舞踏会に招かれる, 舞踏会を開く, 仮面舞踏会 "masked ball". The word sounds elegant to old-fashioned; a casual dance event is rather a ダンスパーティー. 舞踏 alone can also refer to the dance style Butoh; traditional Japanese dance is called 日本舞踊.

examples[].german: This year's grades were good overall.
The economy is recovering across the board.
As a general trend, young people are reading newspapers less and less.
en.notes: 全般的 means "overall, on the whole, across the board", that is, relating to all parts of an area: 全般的に良い, 全般的な傾向. It is a な-adjective; adverbially 全般的に. Not to be confused with 一般的 "generally common, typical": statements like "dogs generally fear cats" require 一般的に. The base word 全般 is used as a suffix: 生活全般 "everyday life as a whole".

examples[].german: Koichi asked Viet to open the window, but Viet refused Koichi's request.
I have a small favor to ask - will you help me?
Now that I'm lost, the map on my phone is my only salvation.
en.notes: 頼み is the noun of 頼む and means, on the one hand, "request, favor": 頼みがある, 頼みを聞く "to grant a request", 頼みを断る. On the other hand it means "reliance, hope", above all in 頼みの綱 "last resort". In conversation お願い sounds more polite and is more common; the formal, business word is 依頼.

examples[].german: This country's economic growth is remarkable.
You've really grown since I last saw you.
Through this work, I was able to grow greatly as a person.
en.notes: 成長 is the growing and maturing of living things - children, animals, but also personal development - as well as the growth of companies and economies. As an intransitive する-verb: 子どもが成長する, 会社が成長する; typical compounds are 経済成長 and 成長率. Unlike 発展 ("development, upswing"), 成長 stresses getting bigger and more mature; for plants, 生長 is also written in technical language.

examples[].german: If you had been a bit more patient, you could have found out who the client was.
A lawyer must protect the secrets of his client.
The client asked the detective to investigate her husband's infidelity.
en.notes: 依頼人 is the "client, person who commissions", that is, someone who gives a task to a professional, typically a lawyer (弁護士), detective (探偵) or real estate agent. Synonymous, but somewhat more neutral, is 依頼者. In business, people rather say 顧客, お客様 or クライアント for customers. Note the reading いらいにん, not "-じん".

examples[].german: This is absurd beyond all limits!!!
It's ridiculous to fight over something like this.
I queued for a whole hour and then it was sold out - that's too ridiculous to put up with.
en.notes: 馬鹿らしい is an い-adjective meaning "ridiculous, absurd, not worth the effort"; it often expresses annoyance or resignation: 〜なんて馬鹿らしい, 馬鹿らしくてやってられない "this is too stupid for me". Stronger and more emotional is 馬鹿馬鹿しい; くだらない emphasizes "worthless, silly". It is often written in kana too (ばからしい). Colloquial; use with caution in polite speech.

examples[].german: I wonder what the essentials are for a newborn.
Smartphones are now a daily necessity.
Before going camping, I made a list of the essentials.
en.notes: 必需品 are "indispensable things" that you cannot do without: 生活必需品 "daily necessities" (food, hygiene products), 旅行の必需品, 〜にとっての必需品. In contrast to 日用品 "household goods", 必需品 emphasizes indispensability. In conversation people often simply say 必要なもの or 欠かせないもの.

examples[].german: Elderly people face difficult problems regarding employment.
I gave up my seat to an elderly person on the train.
The number of elderly people living alone is increasing in this town.
en.notes: 高齢者 is the matter-of-fact, official term for "elderly people, seniors" (in statistics usually from age 65): 高齢者福祉, 一人暮らしの高齢者, 高齢者向け. In personal conversation, お年寄り sounds friendlier; 老人 can come across as blunt to derogatory. Related are 高齢 "advanced age" and 高齢化 "population aging".

examples[].german: Could you explain how the old-age pension system in Japan works?
My grandfather retired from work because of old age.
We feed our old dog soft food.
en.notes: 老齢 means "advanced age, old age" and is written and official. It appears above all in compounds such as 老齢年金 "old-age pension" and 老齢化, as well as with の or as a reason: 老齢の犬, 老齢のため. Today 高齢 is much more common (高齢者, 高齢化); 老齢 sounds a bit more old-fashioned and emphasizes aging itself.

examples[].german: Is it all right if I put my bag down here?
If you like, please have a seat here.
The teacher said, "Very well. Then let's begin."
en.notes: 宜しい is the polite, formal equivalent of いい/よい "good, all right". It is typical in questions asking for permission: ～てもよろしいですか "may I ...?", and in よろしければ "if you like". From the mouth of a superior, よろしい alone means "Good, agreed". Not to be confused with よろしく(お願いします), the adverb form in the greeting formula. Mostly written in kana as よろしい.

en.meaning: to turn (pages); to reel in (thread); to shuffle (cards)
examples[].german: Oops. Sorry. I'm bad at shuffling cards.
Turning the pages of the dictionary, he looked up the meaning of the word.
My grandmother was reeling thread on a spinning wheel.
en.notes: 繰る is a rare, rather written verb for repeated hand movements: "to turn" pages (ページを繰る, in everyday speech rather めくる), "to wind up" thread (糸を繰る), "to shuffle" playing cards (トランプを繰る) and "to count off" days. It lives on mainly in compounds: 繰り返す, 繰り上げる, 繰り越す. Caution: 繰る is a godan verb (繰って, 繰らない) and should not be confused with 来る (来て, 来ない).

examples[].german: One of my New Year's resolutions this year is to use contraception properly.
I consulted a doctor about contraception methods.
We had our pet cat spayed.
en.notes: 避妊 is "contraception"; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 避妊する "to use contraception", often with を: 避妊をする. Typical compounds: 避妊具 "contraceptive", 避妊薬 or ピル, 避妊手術 "sterilization" (for pets, for females; for males people say 去勢). Matter-of-fact medical tone, as in sex education and counseling.

examples[].german: She took a urine pregnancy test, and the doctor told her she is pregnant.
You must not drink alcohol during pregnancy.
My wife is pregnant; our child will be born next spring.
en.notes: 妊娠する means "to become pregnant"; the state "to be pregnant" is expressed with 妊娠している. Typical expressions: 妊娠中 "during pregnancy", 妊娠三か月 "in the third month", 妊娠検査. The verb is intransitive; the mother is marked with が/は. In daily life one also says 子どもができる or, politely and indirectly, おめでた.

examples[].german: I found a temporary job as a counselor for pregnant women.
The priority seats on trains are seats for pregnant women and elderly people.
At the prenatal checkup, I heard the baby's heartbeat.
en.notes: 妊婦 means "pregnant woman, expectant mother". In conversation people usually say the polite 妊婦さん. Common combinations: 妊婦健診 "prenatal checkup", 妊婦用, 妊婦や高齢者 (e.g. on signs at priority seats). In official language you also find 妊産婦 "pregnant women and women who have recently given birth".

examples[].german: Bureaucrats are involved in drafting policy.
For twenty years after graduating from university, he worked as an official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
That government office's handling is thoroughly bureaucratic.
en.notes: 官僚 are the senior ministry officials who prepare and implement policy in the ministries, not every civil servant. The general term for state employees is 公務員. The word often has a critical undertone, especially in 官僚的 ("bureaucratic, stiff") and 官僚主義. Typical: 財務省の官僚, エリート官僚, 官僚出身の政治家.

examples[].german: Asia's economic development is remarkable.
This town developed greatly after the railway opened.
A small quarrel developed into big trouble.
en.notes: 発展 means "development, upswing" toward a larger, higher or more prosperous state: 経済が発展する, 町が発展する, 発展途上国 ("developing country"). It also describes how a situation develops further: 〜に発展する ("to grow into ..."). It is an intransitive する-verb; "to develop something" (product, technology) is 開発する. Next to 成長 (getting bigger and more mature), 発展 stresses expansion and progress.

en.meaning: to match; to coincide; to agree
examples[].german: The fingerprints left on the fake bacon matched Mami's.
After discussion, their opinions finally coincided.
The password you entered does not match.
en.notes: 一致する means "to agree, coincide" and is intransitive: AとBが一致する or AはBと一致する. Common with opinions (意見が一致する), data, fingerprints or passwords (パスワードが一致しません). Set expressions: 全会一致 "unanimous," 一致団結 "to stand united," 偶然の一致 "coincidence." In everyday speech, for small things people often simply say 合う.

examples[].german: I think everyone is more or less interested in the big news in today's morning paper.
Every morning I read the morning paper over coffee.
That incident will probably appear in tomorrow's morning edition.
en.notes: 朝刊 is the "morning edition" of a daily newspaper; the counterpart is 夕刊 "evening edition". In Japan, many newspapers are subscribed to as a package of 朝刊 and 夕刊 and delivered to the door in the morning. Typical: 朝刊を読む, 朝刊に載る "to appear in the morning paper", 今日の朝刊. The character 刊 means "publication, edition".

examples[].german: The monthly magazine "Bacon" reported, as an April Fools' joke, that "the Nobel Bacon Prize was awarded to Mami."
I buy a monthly cooking magazine every month.
This magazine is reportedly changing from weekly to monthly next year.
en.notes: 月刊 means "published monthly" and usually stands before a noun: 月刊誌 "monthly magazine", 月刊『〜』 as part of a title. It belongs to the series 日刊 (daily), 週刊 (weekly), 季刊 (quarterly) and 年刊 (annual). On its own it appears, for example, in 週刊から月刊に変わる "to change from weekly to monthly".

examples[].german: The evening edition of every newspaper reported the stock market crash on the front page.
My father makes a habit of reading the evening paper on the train ride home.
Recently, more and more newspaper companies are no longer publishing an evening edition.
en.notes: 夕刊 is the "evening edition" of a daily newspaper, delivered in the afternoon; the counterpart is 朝刊. Many regional newspapers have by now discontinued their 夕刊. There are also independent tabloids sold at kiosks as 夕刊紙. Typical: 夕刊に載る, 夕刊で報じる.

examples[].german: Mami asked Aya whether she wanted to put out a bacon magazine together.
The publisher brings out numerous specialist books every year.
A new dictionary is due to come out next month.
en.notes: 刊行する means "to publish, to issue" books, magazines or series and is transitive: 雑誌を刊行する, often in the passive: 〜が刊行される. The word sounds formal and is a publishing term; more general is 出版する, and for newspapers and ID documents also 発行する. Related: 創刊 "first issue, founding", 廃刊 "discontinuation", 刊行物 "publication".

examples[].german: Aya's illustration of a pug was chosen as the mascot character of a daily newspaper.
This newspaper is not published daily but once a week.
I bought a daily sports newspaper at the station kiosk.
en.notes: 日刊 means "published daily" and almost always stands before a noun: 日刊紙 "daily newspaper", 日刊誌. It forms a series with 週刊 (weekly), 月刊 (monthly) and 季刊 (quarterly). For the newspaper itself, people simply say 新聞 in everyday speech; 日刊 only emphasizes the publication rhythm.

examples[].german: The graduation ceremony began with a performance by the brass band club.
At the shrine festival, gagaku music was resounding.
I'm looking for handbells to use for the music at church. Do you have any?
en.notes: 奏楽 is an elevated word for "musical performance", especially at ceremonies, church services and formal events: 式典の奏楽, オルガンの奏楽, 雅楽の奏楽. In everyday speech, "to play music" is 演奏 or 演奏する; 奏楽 is heard more in program booklets and announcements. Also well known is the concert hall 旧東京音楽学校奏楽堂 in Ueno.

examples[].german: I thought your wife would be accompanying you today.
Minors must be accompanied by a guardian.
I'm looking for a hotel where you can stay with a pet.
en.notes: 同伴する means "to accompany" or "to bring someone along". It occurs in two patterns: Xに同伴する "to accompany X" and Xを同伴する "to take X along". Typical in rules and invitations: 保護者同伴 "only with a guardian", 夫人同伴, ペット同伴可, 同伴者 "accompanying person". Formal; in conversation people say 一緒に行く/来る or 連れて行く, and for looking after someone 付き添う.

examples[].german: The United States annexed Texas in 1845.
The country annexed part of its neighboring country by force.
In class, we learned about the annexation of Korea in 1910.
en.notes: 併合 means "annexation, incorporation": a state or territory is merged into another, mostly unilaterally (領土を併合する). Historically well known is 韓国併合 (1910). For the merger of companies or municipalities on an equal footing, people say 合併 instead. The word is written and belongs to political and historical vocabulary.

examples[].german: "What kind of person is your wife?" "She's the type who does everything energetically."
I met Mr. Tanaka's wife at the station.
en.notes: 奥さん is a respectful term for another person's wife; it can also address a married woman directly. おくさん is the hiragana spelling with the same reading. When talking about one's own wife, 妻 is the usual neutral term. The first dialogue is phrased very casually with おまえ and だよ; this form of address does not automatically suit polite conversation with strangers.

examples[].german: I keep a record of my monthly income and expenses.
This month my budget ended up in the red.
Japan's trade balance turned to a surplus for the first time in three months.
en.notes: 収支 is composed of 収 ("income") and 支 ("expenditure") and means the comparison of both, i.e. the balance or financial position. Typical are 収支が合う ("to balance out"), 収支のバランス, 収支が赤字／黒字になる and 貿易収支 ("trade balance"). It is matter-of-fact and used for private households as well as companies and states; in daily life people also simply say 収入と支出.

examples[].german: Is there anything you would stake your life on?
He is staking his career as an athlete on this match.
A reward of one million yen was offered for the arrest of the criminal.
en.notes: 懸ける is the kanji spelling of かける for "to stake, to put on the line" with serious things: 命を懸ける, 人生を懸ける, 選手生命を懸ける, as well as "to offer (a reward)": 賞金を懸ける. For gambling and betting one writes 賭ける, and for all everyday meanings ("to hang, to call") 掛ける or kana. The intransitive partner is 懸かる: 命が懸かっている "it is a matter of life and death". Related: 命懸け "at the risk of one's life".

en.meaning: earnest; with all one's might; diligent
examples[].german: My foot was stuck in the mud and I tried with all my might to pull it out, but I couldn't.
The rescue team is searching desperately for the missing people.
Thanks to the doctors' tireless treatment, he was saved.
en.notes: 懸命 is a な-adjective meaning "with all one's strength, earnestly"; mostly adverbial 懸命に (懸命に探す) or attributive 懸命な努力. 懸命 alone sounds written and like news language; in everyday speech people almost always use 一生懸命. Similar, but with desperation, is 必死. Not to be confused with 賢明 "wise, prudent" (賢明な判断), which is read the same way.

en.meaning: to handle; to treat; to deal in
examples[].german: Being treated like a total stranger by my husband's child from a previous marriage builds up a lot of stress.
This shop deals in imported foods.
It breaks easily, so please handle it carefully.
en.notes: 扱う is transitive and versatile: to "treat" people (子ども扱いする, 〜のように扱う, 〜として扱う), to "handle" objects (丁寧に扱う), to "operate" machines, to "carry, stock" goods (この店では〜を扱っている) and to "deal with" topics (問題を扱う). The noun 扱い appears in 扱いにくい "hard to handle"; more formal is 取り扱う (取扱説明書 "instruction manual").

examples[].german: Which country do you think has the best crime deterrence model?
Some people claim that nuclear weapons act as a deterrent to war.
Installing security cameras leads to deterring crime.
en.notes: 抑止 means "deterrence, containment", that is, preventing something in advance by deterring the act. Frequent in compounds: 抑止力 "deterrent effect" (also military: 核の抑止力), 犯罪抑止, 抑止効果. Related are 防止 "prevention" (more general) and 抑制 "restraint, suppression" of a process that is already under way. Written, from politics and law.

examples[].german: This software renders graphics very fast.
It is said that children's drawings reflect their state of mind.
I draw illustrations with a drawing app on my tablet.
en.notes: 描画 is a matter-of-fact, technical word for "drawing, depiction". It is found in psychology and art education (子どもの描画) and above all in IT, where it means "displaying, rendering": 描画ソフト, 描画速度, 描画アプリ. In everyday speech people say 絵 or 絵を描く; a sketch is called デッサン or スケッチ.

examples[].german: After a while, James came back with a disc under his arm and told us he had found a UFO.
I do the discus throw in the track and field club.
I saw something like a glowing disc in the night sky.
en.notes: 円盤 is a flat, round disc. In sports, the discus is 円盤 and the discus throw is 円盤投げ. It very often stands for UFOs: 空飛ぶ円盤 "flying saucer". In the anime and fan scene, 円盤 is also a casual word for DVDs and Blu-rays (アニメの円盤が売れる). For slices in everyday life, such as of lemons, people say 輪切り instead, and for data media otherwise ディスク.

examples[].german: Do you know the provisional name of this shopping mall under construction?
The new station is being planned under the provisional name "Central Station".
We decided to provisionally call this project "Plan A" for the time being.
en.notes: 仮称 is a "provisional name", for example for buildings, stations or projects before their official naming. On plans and in announcements it is often in parentheses: （仮称）〜駅. As a する-verb: 〜を「…」と仮称する "to provisionally call ...". The opposite is 正式名称; an unofficial, commonly used name, by contrast, is 通称.

examples[].german: This horror movie was filmed from a first-person perspective.
Japanese has many first-person pronouns, such as 「私」, 「僕」 and 「俺」.
This novel is written in the first person of the protagonist.
en.notes: 一人称 is the grammatical "first person"; 二人称 and 三人称 belong with it. In Japanese, 一人称 often also means the words one uses to refer to oneself (私, 僕, 俺, うち etc.), whose choice reveals a lot about gender, age and situation. In literature, film and games it stands for the "first-person perspective": 一人称視点, 一人称小説.

examples[].german: "May I join you?" "Not at all, I don't mind. Please have a seat."
On Sundays I cook together with my family.
en.notes: 一緒 is a noun often used with に to mean "together": 家族と一緒に料理をする. と marks the person one does something with. The polite form ご一緒する means to join someone or to do something together. The word is therefore not inflected like an ordinary i-adjective.

examples[].german: I secretly record conversations with my IC recorder.
Please keep this to yourself, okay?
I started a part-time job without my parents' knowledge.
en.notes: 内緒 means "secret" in the sense of "something others should not know" and is rather colloquial and familiar. Typical patterns: 内緒にする "to keep secret", 〜に内緒で "without the knowledge of ..., secretly", 内緒の話 / 内緒話 "confidential talk". 秘密 is more neutral and is also used for serious or official secrets (企業秘密), whereas 内緒 is more for private trifles among friends and in the family. Grammatically it is a noun (with の or で), not an adjective; it is often also written in kana ないしょ.

examples[].german: According to the financial results, a profit was made.
March is the closing period, so the accounting department is very busy.
That company will announce its quarterly results tomorrow.
en.notes: 決算 is the closing of the books at the end of an accounting period and the resulting business result. Common are 決算期 ("closing period"), 決算発表 ("announcement of financial results"), 四半期決算 ("quarterly results") and 決算書 ("annual financial statements"). As a する-verb it is rare; it mostly stands as a noun. Compared with the more general 会計 ("accounting, bill"), 決算 specifically denotes the period-end closing.

examples[].german: Some bolts in this tunnel have started to loosen.
Maybe because the tension eased after the exam, I caught a cold.
Since the beginning of March, the cold is finally easing.
en.notes: 緩む is intransitive: something "loosens" by itself, e.g. ねじ / ボルト / 結び目が緩む. The transitive counterpart is 緩める (ベルトを緩める "to loosen the belt"), the related adjective is 緩い "loose, lax". Figuratively one says 気が緩む "the tension eases, one becomes careless", 寒さが緩む "the cold eases" or 規制が緩む "rules are relaxed". The form 緩んでくる is typical for a gradual easing.

examples[].german: I'm planning to give a watch for Father's Day.
Everyone gave a bouquet to the senior who was graduating.
A big round of applause from the venue was given to the winning team.
en.notes: 贈る means "to give as a gift, to present (ceremonially)" and is to be distinguished from the identically read 送る "to send": 贈る stresses the gift or the honor, 送る the shipping. Pattern: 人に物を贈る, plus the noun 贈り物 "gift." Figuratively also 拍手を贈る "to give applause," 言葉を贈る "to offer words of farewell/encouragement" or 賞を贈る "to award a prize." In everyday speech, for gifts among friends people often simply say あげる or プレゼントする.

examples[].german: My little brother is so good-natured that he helped criminals escape and was arrested for it.
The perpetrator is said to be still on the run.
The suspect fled abroad the day after the crime.
en.notes: 逃亡 is an escape in which someone gets away or goes into hiding for good, such as a perpetrator, prisoner or soldier; as a suru-verb it is intransitive: 海外へ逃亡する, 逃亡中の犯人 "the fugitive perpetrator", 逃亡者 "fugitive". The word is written-language and typical of news reports. 逃走, by contrast, emphasizes more the running away from the scene of the crime, and in daily life one simply says 逃げる.

examples[].german: The missing English teacher returned safely, although his feet had frostbite.
The mountain climbers who had been in distress all returned alive after three days.
The runner made it home and tied the game.
en.notes: 生還 means "to return alive" from great mortal danger, for example after a mountain accident, an accident or from war; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 無事に生還する, 奇跡の生還 "miraculous rescue", 生還者 "survivor". It is written and typical for the news. 帰還 is the more neutral "return" (e.g. of astronauts), and 生き残る means "to survive" without the aspect of coming home. In baseball, 生還 also means that a runner reaches home plate and scores.

examples[].german: Okinawa was returned from the US to Japan in 1972.
The museum returned the stolen artwork to its original owner.
When I moved out, part of my deposit was refunded to me.
en.notes: 返還 is the formal return of something that is due to someone, such as territories, cultural property, deposits or fees: 〜を〜に返還する, very often in the passive 返還される. The word is written-language and typical of politics, law and administration. In daily life one says 返す; for borrowed items (books, rental cars) 返却 is usual, for money also 返金.

examples[].german: At first I tried yudofu just out of curiosity, and then I came to love it.
On a cold night, warming up with yudofu is the best.
Near Nanzen-ji temple in Kyoto, we ate the famous yudofu.
en.notes: 湯豆腐 is a simple winter dish: tofu is warmed in a pot (often 土鍋) with kombu broth and then dipped in ponzu or soy sauce with 薬味 such as spring onions. It is especially well known from Kyoto, for example around the temple 南禅寺. The counterpart is 冷奴, cold tofu in summer. People say 湯豆腐を食べる or 湯豆腐で温まる.

examples[].german: This security app is available for both Android OS and iOS.
Please enter your name and address here.
The president, the vice president and the department heads attended the meeting.
en.notes: 及び is a written-language conjunction "and, as well as" that connects nouns - typical of forms, laws, contracts and official notices. With three or more items it comes before the last one: A、B及びC. In conversation one says と or や instead. Even more formal is 並びに, which connects whole groups. Often also written in kana as および; not to be confused with the verb 及ぶ "to extend to".

en.meaning: to step in; to intrude; to delve deeper
examples[].german: I think my roommate intrudes too much on my privacy.
The police stormed the apartment where the culprit was hiding.
For this problem we need a discussion that goes one step deeper.
en.notes: 踏み込む literally means "to step into": 〜に踏み込む (to enter an area, to intrude on foreign terrain), 警察が〜に踏み込む "the police storm ...". With を it means "to press down (a pedal)": アクセルを踏み込む. Figuratively it stands for "to intrude too far into private matters" (プライバシーに踏み込む) or "to get to the bottom of a matter more deeply": 踏み込んだ議論 "a more in-depth discussion", 一歩踏み込む "to go one step further".

examples[].german: The number of participants in this event is expected to exceed ten thousand.
This summer there were many days when the temperature exceeded thirty-five degrees.
The repair costs went far over the budget.
en.notes: 超す means "to exceed (a number, limit, measure)" and almost always takes を: 三十五度を超す, 予算を超す, 一万人を超す. It is equivalent to the more common 超える, but sounds somewhat more like written and news language. Distinguish it from the identically read 越す: 越す is used for crossing physically (山を越す), getting through a season (冬を越す) and for 引っ越す "to move house." For "to go too far," 度を越す is usually written.

examples[].german: Cumin is one of the spices indispensable in Indian curry.
This dish is strongly seasoned and a little spicy.
In the past, spices such as pepper were very expensive in Europe.
en.notes: 香辛料 are spices in the narrower sense, i.e. pepper, cinnamon, cumin, chili and the like; the word is rather written-language, in daily life one mostly says スパイス. To be distinguished from it are 調味料 "seasonings" such as salt, sugar, soy sauce or miso, and 薬味 for fresh condiments such as ginger or spring onions. Typical: 香辛料が効いている "to be strongly spiced", 香辛料を使う / 加える.

examples[].german: His assets amount to several hundred million yen.
I am managing my assets for retirement.
Employees are the company's greatest asset.
en.notes: 資産 refers to wealth and assets, i.e. everything with monetary value such as cash, real estate or stocks. Typical are 資産を持つ／築く／運用する ("to invest"), 資産家 ("wealthy person") and 資産価値; the counterpart on the balance sheet is 負債 ("liabilities"). Unlike 財産, which tends to mean personal possessions and inheritance, 資産 sounds business-economic. Figuratively also: 社員は会社の資産だ.

examples[].german: The profession of hunter is an extremely deep one.
The tea ceremony is a world that gets deeper the more you know about it.
The village is located deep in the mountains.
en.notes: 奥深い is mostly used figuratively: a field, an art or a taste is "profound, multifaceted" and you always discover something new (奥深い世界, 奥深い味). In conversation, 奥が深い is heard more often for this. Literally it means "located deep inside", for example 山の奥深いところ, 奥深い森. It is an い-adjective: 奥深く, 奥深さ.

examples[].german: It was so boring that I started yawning.
I yawned loudly during the meeting and was warned by the department head.
I took a photo of a cat yawning sleepily.
en.notes: 欠伸 "yawn" is almost always written in kana あくび. Typical combinations: あくびが出る "to feel a yawn coming", あくびをする "to yawn", あくびをかみ殺す "to stifle a yawn", 生あくび "a suppressed yawn". As a する-verb it is intransitive; the only object with を is あくび itself (大きなあくびをする).

examples[].german: We have lightly pickled cucumbers.
My grandmother makes rice-bran pickles every day.
Even if you cram the night before an exam, you forget it right away.
en.notes: 〜漬け is a suffix (with rendaku づけ) for "something pickled in": ぬか漬け (in rice bran), 浅漬け (lightly pickled), 醤油漬け, 梅酒漬け; on its own, pickled vegetables are called 漬物. Figuratively it means "completely immersed in something, excessively dependent on something": 勉強漬け "nothing but studying", 薬漬け "stuffed with medication". Very common is 一夜漬け "last-minute studying, cramming overnight". The related verb is 漬ける "to pickle".

examples[].german: Deep down inside, I chuckled to myself.
Deep in her heart, she still cannot forget him.
Childhood memories that had been sleeping deep in my memory suddenly came back.
en.notes: 奥底 refers to the "deepest depth" of something and is used almost only figuratively: 心の奥底 "in the depths of one's heart", 記憶の奥底 "in the depths of memory", 奥底に眠る "to lie dormant deep inside". It emphasizes feelings or thoughts that one does not show outwardly. Similar, but more adverbial, is 心の底から "from the bottom of one's heart". Literally (海の奥底) it is rare.

examples[].german: The injury on my knee hurts so much that I can't even sleep.
I fell and scraped my knee.
After continuing to kneel in seiza, my knees started to hurt.
en.notes: 膝頭 is the front of the knee with the kneecap, that is, the spot you fall or kneel on. In everyday speech people often simply say 膝 or, colloquially, 膝の皿; the medical term for the kneecap as a bone is 膝蓋骨. Typical: 膝頭をすりむく "to scrape one's knee", 膝頭が痛い, 膝頭をぶつける.

examples[].german: I was bitten on the hand by a dog.
Chew your food well.
I stumbled over my words several times during the important presentation.
en.notes: 噛む means "to bite" (犬に噛まれる, very common in the passive) and "to chew" (よく噛んで食べる, ガムを噛む). Colloquially it also means "to misspeak, to stumble over words": 発表で噛んでしまった. It is mostly written in kana as かむ. Not to be confused with 鼻をかむ "to blow one's nose", which sounds the same but is a different word.

examples[].german: I can sing the Japanese national anthem perfectly.
A perfect person exists nowhere.
She is a perfectionist and lets not the slightest mistake slip through.
en.notes: 完璧 is a na-adjective: 完璧な仕事, 完璧に覚える, 完璧だ. It emphasizes "flawless, without any mistake", whereas 完全 rather means "complete, without gaps" (完全に忘れた "completely forgot"). Common are 完璧主義 "perfectionism" and 完璧主義者. Watch out when writing: the second character is 璧 (jade disc), not 壁 (wall).

examples[].german: Kiyomizu-dera in Kyoto is a temple with a long history.
She comes from a family of distinguished lineage.
We had someone from the shrine tell us about the history of this festival.
en.notes: 由緒 is the long, venerable history or origin of a place, a family or a custom. It almost always appears in fixed combinations: 由緒ある寺 / 旅館 "steeped in tradition", 由緒正しい家柄 "of distinguished family". The word is elevated; 歴史 is the general "history", and 由来 refers to the origin of a name or thing.

examples[].german: Oh, I can see the Milky Way!
According to the Tanabata legend, Orihime and Hikoboshi are separated by the Milky Way.
Where there is a lot of city light, you can hardly see the Milky Way.
en.notes: 天の川 is the everyday and poetic name of the Milky Way, literally "river of heaven". It is closely tied to the 七夕 festival: 織姫 and 彦星 are separated by the 天の川 and may meet only once a year. In astronomy, people also speak of 天の川銀河 or generally of 銀河 "galaxy". Typical: 天の川が見える, 天の川を見上げる.

examples[].german: First, let's start by roasting the soybeans until golden brown.
If you lightly roast the sesame seeds, they smell better.
For the bean-throwing at Setsubun, roasted soybeans are used.
en.notes: 炒る means "to roast without oil", for example ごま, 豆 or coffee beans (also written 煎る). To be distinguished from it is 炒める "to stir-fry with oil" (野菜を炒める). Although it ends in -iru, 炒る is a godan verb: 炒って, 炒らない. Because of the many homophones (居る, 要る, 射る), it is often written in kana いる, and 炒った豆 "roasted beans" is a common form.

examples[].german: Funds are needed to start a business.
We raised funds for the film's production through crowdfunding.
Due to a lack of funds, the plan was canceled.
en.notes: 資金 are funds that are available or needed for a specific purpose - for a company, a project or privately. Typical are 資金を集める, 資金を調達する ("to procure"), 資金が足りない, 資金不足 and compounds such as 結婚資金 or 開業資金. Unlike 資産 (existing wealth), 資金 denotes money that is to be deployed; 資本 is capital in the economic sense.

en.meaning: to eat (rough); to devour; to consume
examples[].german: I didn't have time to eat lunch.
This car is big, so it guzzles a lot of gas.
I slept with the window open and got my leg bitten by a mosquito.
en.notes: 食う is the rough variant of 食べる "to eat" (飯を食う), used mainly by men; in polite speech it is avoided. It also has many figurative meanings: 時間を食う / ガソリンを食う "to take up a lot of time / gas," 蚊に食われる "to be bitten by mosquitoes," 食っていく "to get by, earn a living." Set phrases are 食うか食われるか "eat or be eaten" and 一杯食わされる "to be tricked."

en.meaning: first installment; first round (of a series or campaign)
examples[].german: The first product of our collaboration with WaniKani is a WaniKani figure!
As the first round of the campaign, all products will be 20 percent off.
This movie is the first installment of the series, and a sequel will be released next year.
en.notes: 第一弾 refers to the first part of a planned series - a campaign, product line, film series or sequence of events. 弾 originally means "projectile" and here serves as a counter for stages: 第二弾, 第三弾, 最終弾. Typical is 〜の第一弾として. The word is very widespread in advertising, press releases and media. For the first date of a regular event, people rather say 第一回, and for the first section of a work 第一部.

examples[].german: That concert was held in prayer for the recovery after the Great East Japan Earthquake.
At the end of the ceremony, everyone prayed together for world peace.
Wishing you all good health and happiness - cheers!
en.notes: 祈念 is a solemn "praying, fervently wishing" and is encountered above all in ceremonies, speeches and letters: 平和を祈念する, 復興祈念, and as a closing formula ご健康とご多幸を祈念いたします. Not to be confused with 記念 "keepsake, commemoration" (記念日, 記念写真), which is read the same way. In everyday speech people say 祈る; 祈願 is asking for something specific at a shrine or temple (合格祈願).

en.meaning: to be bewildered; to be at a loss; to be led astray
examples[].german: Even at my age, I still get bewildered by trivial things.
When the fire broke out, people fled in a panic through the smoke.
Don't be led astray by sweet words; judge for yourself.
en.notes: 惑う means "to be uncertain, confused, not to know what to do" and also "to be led astray"; on its own it is rather written to literary. In everyday speech people mostly say 迷う or 戸惑う, and for "to be deceived" the passive of 惑わす is usual (〜に惑わされる). 惑う is very common in compounds such as 逃げ惑う "to flee in panic in all directions" and 思い惑う. Also well known is the Confucius quote 四十にして惑わず, hence 不惑 "forty years old".

examples[].german: It's hard to decide which scent to wear. Every morning I spend at least an hour on it.
The flowers in the garden smell nice.
The aroma of freshly brewed coffee woke me up.
en.notes: 香り is a pleasant scent, for example of flowers, coffee, tea or perfume: いい香りがする, 香りが漂う, 香りを楽しむ. 匂い is more neutral and can smell good or bad, and 臭い (also read におい) stands for a stench. The spelling 薫り is literary and used for a figurative "atmosphere." 香りを付ける refers to applying a fragrance.

examples[].german: "ゲッツー" (from "get two") is Japanese-coined English meaning a double play.
In the tight situation, the shortstop pulled off a brilliant double play.
The cleanup hitter grounded into a double play and wasted the chance.
en.notes: 併殺 is the technical term for the double play in baseball, in which two players are out in a single play. It is typical of sports reports; in conversation people mostly say ゲッツー or ダブルプレー. Important combinations: 併殺打 "a hit that leads to a double play", 併殺打に倒れる (from the batter's point of view), 併殺に打ち取る / 併殺を決める (from the defense's point of view). As a する-verb it is transitive.

examples[].german: The news that his father had chosen his younger brother as heir was a heavy blow to him.
Although it is a long-established ryokan, they say no successor can be found.
There were times when it was a matter of course for the eldest son to take over the family estate.
en.notes: 跡継ぎ is the successor who takes over a family business, a shop, a farm or "the house" (家); the spelling 後継ぎ is also common. Typical: 跡継ぎがいない, 〜の跡継ぎになる, 跡継ぎに選ぶ. 後継者 is more formal and is also usual for offices and positions, 相続人 is the legal "heir" to property. The related verb is 跡を継ぐ.

examples[].german: I'm jumping rope while listening to FM802.
When I was a child, I often played jump rope during recess.
Boxers train with jump rope every day.
en.notes: 縄跳び refers both to the jump rope and to jumping rope itself: 縄跳びをする "to jump rope", 縄跳びで遊ぶ, 縄跳びを買う. Well-known variants are 二重跳び "double under" and 大縄跳び, in which several children jump over a long rope swung by two people. It is often also written in kana なわとび, especially in children's texts.

examples[].german: That guy applied to be a lifeguard at the municipal pool only because he can see girls in bikinis there.
I entered a photo contest and actually won a prize.
I took part in a prize draw by postcard where you can win a new product.
en.notes: 応募する means "to apply in response to a call, to take part, to send in an entry" and takes に: 仕事に応募する, コンテストに応募する, 懸賞に応募する. It is the response to a 募集 "call for applicants, recruitment" from the other side. Derived are 応募者 "applicant", 応募用紙 and 応募締め切り. 申し込む is more general, "to sign up, to apply for" (courses, trips), whereas 応募 presupposes that someone is looking for applicants or entries.

examples[].german: I can't wait to see his 200th home run today.
In the bottom of the ninth, he hit a game-turning home run.
The player who hits the most home runs in a season becomes the home run king.
en.notes: 本塁打 is the official, written expression for the home run and is typical of newspapers and statistics; in conversation people say ホームラン. 本塁 is "home plate", 打 is the "hit". Typical: 本塁打を打つ / 放つ, 満塁本塁打 "grand slam", 本塁打王 "home run king". It is counted with 本: 二百本目の本塁打.

examples[].german: I used a low-interest loan.
Banks are increasing lending to small and medium-sized businesses.
I asked city hall about the loan program for students.
en.notes: 貸付 is the lending of money from the creditor's point of view, i.e. "loan, extension of credit"; the counterpart from the debtor's point of view is 借入. It is a technical word of banking and administrative language: 貸付金, 貸付制度, 貸付を受ける ("to receive a loan"), as a verb 〜に貸し付ける. In everyday speech one says rather ローン or お金を貸す. The spelling varies between 貸付, 貸付け and 貸し付け.

examples[].german: Excuse me, I no longer need my Suica, so I'd like to get the balance refunded...
Because the concert was canceled, the ticket price was refunded.
In the case of defective goods, we will refund the full price.
en.notes: 払い戻す means "to refund (money)" and is transitive: the subject is the one who pays out (company, railway, organizer): チケット代を払い戻す. From the customer's point of view, people say 払い戻してもらう or 払い戻しを受ける; very common is the noun 払い戻し "refund" (払い戻し窓口, 払い戻し手続き). The tone is matter-of-fact and administrative; in everyday speech people often say 返金する. General returning is 返す.

en.meaning: way of speaking; choice of words; wording
examples[].german: That person is very polite in the way he speaks.
In an interview, you should watch your language.
My son's way of speaking has become rough lately, and I'm worried.
en.notes: 言葉遣い is the way someone speaks, especially with regard to politeness and tone: 言葉遣いが丁寧だ / 乱暴だ / 悪い, 言葉遣いに気をつける "to watch one's language". So it is less about the choice of individual words (for that rather 言葉選び or 表現) than about register and manners. The suffix 〜遣い is read with rendaku づかい, as in 小遣い or 無駄遣い.

examples[].german: How much allowance do you give your child per month?
My husband's allowance is 30,000 yen a month.
When I was a university student, I earned some pocket money by tutoring.
en.notes: 小遣い is money at one's free disposal and is mostly used with お as お小遣い. It applies not only to children: the monthly "allowance" a husband gets from the family budget is also called this. Typical: 小遣いをもらう / あげる / 渡す, 小遣い稼ぎ "earning a bit on the side", 小遣い帳 "pocket money notebook". It is read with rendaku こづかい.

en.meaning: bulletin board; notice board; online forum
examples[].german: This bulletin board belongs to the school.
The exam results will be posted on the bulletin board tomorrow morning.
Bad reviews of that shop had been posted on an online forum.
en.notes: 掲示板 is the bulletin board or notice board in schools, train stations or residential complexes: 掲示板に貼る / 貼り出す "to post", 掲示板を見る. Just as often it refers to an online forum (ネットの掲示板) where you write posts (書き込む). A single notice is called 掲示 or お知らせ.

examples[].german: He is a computer geek, but he is good-looking, and he's looking for a girlfriend right now. How about it, want to meet him?
A sign saying "Part-time help wanted" was posted at the entrance of the convenience store.
This club is currently recruiting new members.
en.notes: 募集中 is composed of 募集 "call for applicants, recruitment" and 〜中 "currently in progress" and means "currently recruiting, applications welcome". Typical on notices: アルバイト募集中, 会員募集中, 参加者募集中; also with an object: 新しいメンバーを募集中です. Jokingly and colloquially one says 彼女募集中 / 彼氏募集中 "looking for a partner". A person who responds to it 応募する.

examples[].german: I didn't know which way was the way back.
So that we could find our way back, we marked the trees as we went.
The way back was downhill, so it was much easier than the way there.
en.notes: 戻り道 is the way back to the starting point, for example after a hike or a detour. In everyday speech, 帰り道 "way home" is much more common; 戻り道 emphasizes returning to a place where one was before. The counterpart is 行き / 行きの道 "way there". Figuratively: もう戻り道はない "there is no turning back".

examples[].german: You can solve this problem by resetting the computer to factory settings, but without a backup you can't recover the lost data.
I rested well during the holidays and got my strength back.
Regaining lost trust is not easy.
en.notes: 取り戻す means "to get back, to regain" and takes を. Besides objects or money (盗まれたお金を取り戻す), it is very often used abstractly: 自信 / 元気 / 落ち着き / 信頼を取り戻す, 遅れを取り戻す "to make up for a delay". 取り返す is similar but emphasizes more the active retrieving of something taken away; the expression 取り返しがつかない "irreparable" exists only with 取り返す.

examples[].german: My house is insured against fire, but what happens if someone drops an atomic bomb and my house burns down as a result? Will I still get the insurance money?
On August 6, 1945, an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.
On the school trip we visited the Atomic Bomb Dome and learned how terrible the atomic bomb is.
en.notes: 原子爆弾 is the atomic bomb; in daily life and the news it is almost always abbreviated to 原爆 (原爆ドーム, 原爆の日). Typical are 原子爆弾を落とす / 投下する and the passive 原子爆弾が投下された. The umbrella term is 核兵器 "nuclear weapons", the hydrogen bomb is called 水素爆弾 or 水爆. The word is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: The moment I found bear tracks in the snow, I tightly gripped the knife in my pocket.
The police followed the culprit's footprints toward the hill behind the house.
The waves washed away the children's small footprints left on the beach.
en.notes: 足跡（あしあと）are footprints of people or animals: 足跡が残る, 足跡を見つける, 足跡をたどる "to follow the tracks". On social networks it also refers to the list of profile visitors (足跡機能). In the figurative sense "to leave traces, achievements" (歴史に足跡を残す), the same spelling is often read そくせき and is then literary.

en.meaning: to aim at; to target; to eye; to go for
examples[].german: Just a warning: it looks like he's after your position.
This year we're going for the title, so we keep practicing every day.
Beware of pickpockets who target tourists' wallets.
en.notes: 狙う takes を and means "to aim at" (的を狙う), "to have one's eye on something or someone" (財布を狙う, ポジションを狙う) and "to aim for deliberately" (優勝を狙う). In contrast to 目指す "to aim for a goal", 狙う sounds more strategic and can also express a dishonest intention. The related noun is 狙い "aim, objective" (狙いを定める "to take aim").

examples[].german: The deadline for repaying the loan is approaching.
For capital investment, we borrowed 50 million yen from the bank.
The company's borrowings are decreasing year by year.
en.notes: 借入 refers to taking up money, i.e. "borrowing" from the debtor's point of view - the counterpart of 貸付. Typical are 借入金 ("borrowed funds, loans payable"), 借入額, 借入を返済する and as a verb 銀行から借り入れる. It belongs to business and banking language; in everyday speech one says お金を借りる or ローンを組む. The spelling varies: 借入, 借入れ, 借り入れ.
