examples[].german: The doorbell rang while he was on the toilet, and he rushed to the door without wiping himself.
I pressed the doorbell at the front door, but nobody came out.
When I rang the bell at the front desk, a staff member came right away.
en.notes: 呼び鈴 is a bell with which you call someone, above all the doorbell: 呼び鈴を鳴らす / 押す, 呼び鈴が鳴る. It sounds somewhat old-fashioned; today, for the front door, people mostly say インターホン or チャイム. The desk bell at a reception can also be called 呼び鈴; in restaurants people rather speak of a 呼び出しボタン.

examples[].german: I plan to go and see my parents in Gifu later in the week.
Shirakawa-gō in Gifu Prefecture is famous for its gasshō-style houses.
In summer, you can see ukai, Gifu's specialty cormorant fishing, on the Nagara River.
en.notes: 岐阜 is both the prefecture (岐阜県) and its capital (岐阜市) in the 中部地方 region of central Japan. Well known are the World Heritage site 白川郷 with its houses in 合掌造り style, the old town of 高山 and the cormorant fishing 鵜飼い on the river 長良川. The character 阜 appears almost only in this name and is one of the few place-name kanji on the school list.

examples[].german: Which industry in the US is flourishing the most right now?
In the Edo period, kabuki reached its heyday.
The mining town that once flourished now has hardly anyone living there.
en.notes: 隆盛 is the heyday or boom of a culture, industry, religion or house; the word is written. It almost always appears in fixed expressions: 隆盛を極める "to reach its peak", 隆盛を誇る "to be in full bloom", 〜の隆盛. 繁栄 emphasizes the prosperity of states or cities, 繁盛 the good business of a shop, and in everyday speech people say 盛んだ. It is used practically only as a noun.

examples[].german: I always use Aya's illustrations as my wallpaper.
Before moving, I replaced the wallpaper in the room.
I changed my computer's wallpaper to a family photo.
en.notes: 壁紙 is the wallpaper on a wall (壁紙を貼る, 壁紙を張り替える) and likewise the background image on a computer or smartphone (壁紙にする, 壁紙を変える). For the lock screen of a mobile phone, people also colloquially say 待ち受け. The reading has rendaku: かべがみ.

examples[].german: That shogi player has his own private practice room in this building.
Mr. Fujii became a professional shogi player at the age of fourteen.
Shogi professionals sometimes keep thinking for hours in a single game.
en.notes: 棋士 is a professional shogi or go player; 棋 stands for board games as in 将棋 and 棋院. Depending on context, people say 将棋の棋士 or 囲碁の棋士, plus プロ棋士 and 女流棋士 "female professional player". Hobby players are not called 棋士 but rather 将棋ファン or 愛好家. Not to be confused with 騎士 "knight", which is read the same way.

examples[].german: I come to this go hall every Monday and practice go.
The Nihon Ki-in is the organization that professional go players belong to.
I watched the title match held at the Ki-in on the internet.
en.notes: 棋院 is a go association or go hall where games are played and tournaments held. The best known is the 日本棋院 in Tokyo, the association of professional go players; besides it there is the 関西棋院. For shogi, the corresponding institutions are called 将棋会館 and 日本将棋連盟. A small public go club in the neighborhood is rather called 碁会所.

examples[].german: My eyesight is bad in only one eye.
The luggage is heavy; I can't carry it with one hand.
en.notes: 片〜 here refers to one part of a pair: 片目 is one eye, 片手 one hand. It stands directly before the component in question, without の. In the first example, the limited eyesight affects only one eye; in the second, one hand is not enough for carrying. The character 〜 is an unspoken placeholder mark. This card practices the prefix かた and not the other readings ひら or へん for a piece or component.

examples[].german: He lifted the heavy bag of rice with one hand, effortlessly.
He was reading the newspaper with a coffee in one hand.
Operating a smartphone with one hand while driving is dangerous.
en.notes: 片手 means "one hand" as opposed to 両手 "both hands": 片手で持つ, 片手に〜を持つ. Very idiomatic is 〜を片手に "with ... in hand" (コーヒーを片手に, 地図を片手に). Derived from it is 片手間 "on the side" (片手間にできる仕事). The word is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: When interest rates rise, the burden of mortgages increases.
The central bank announced it would lower interest rates.
I compared which bank has the lowest interest rate.
en.notes: 金利 is the interest rate or, in general, the level of interest, i.e. how high the interest is in percent. Typical are 金利が上がる／下がる, 金利を引き上げる／引き下げる, 低金利, 高金利 and 住宅ローンの金利. In contrast to 利子 and 利息, which mean the concrete amount of interest paid or received, 金利 refers more to the rate. Common in economic news and conversations at the bank.

examples[].german: With my broken Japanese, I somehow managed to get my passport reissued.
My one-year-old daughter has started saying "mama" in her baby talk.
On the trip I could somehow communicate even in broken English.
en.notes: 片言 is broken, halting speech, as spoken by foreigners with little knowledge or by small children: 片言の日本語 / 英語, 片言で話す. For small children it means the first incomplete words (片言を話し始める). It is a noun, mostly used with の or で, not an adjective.

examples[].german: I know hiragana, but I haven't fully learned katakana yet.
Foreigners' names are normally written in katakana.
The manual has so many katakana words that it seems hard for my grandfather to read.
en.notes: 片仮名 is the angular syllabary used mainly for loanwords, foreign names, onomatopoeia and for emphasis. The word itself is usually written in kana: カタカナ. The counterpart is 平仮名 / ひらがな. Typical: 片仮名で書く, 片仮名語 "words in katakana, loanwords".

examples[].german: Let me know when you get back from your parents' house in Gunma Prefecture.
Kusatsu Onsen in Gunma Prefecture is one of Japan's leading hot spring resorts.
You can get to Gunma Prefecture from Tokyo in about an hour by Shinkansen.
en.notes: 群馬県 is a landlocked prefecture in the 関東 region northwest of Tokyo; its capital is 前橋市. Well known are the hot springs of 草津温泉 and the silk mill 富岡製糸場 (World Heritage site). In conversation people often say just 群馬; the suffix 〜県 makes clear that the prefecture is meant.

examples[].german: The crowd burst into laughter when the little boy started imitating Justin Bieber.
After the fireworks, the crowd streamed to the station all at once.
Out of mass psychology, people sometimes do things they would never otherwise do.
en.notes: 群集 is a large gathering, above all a crowd of people; for people, however, the spelling 群衆 (same reading) is much more common. 群集 is usual in 群集心理 "mass psychology" and in biology (community). As a する-verb it is intransitive, "to crowd together, to swarm". In daily life one rather says 人込み "crowd, crush" or 人だかり "gathering of people".

examples[].german: "I'm right above you," said the hermit from atop a cloud.
My grandfather, who lives alone deep in the mountains, is just like a hermit.
It is said that hermit immortals live on mist.
en.notes: 仙人 comes from Taoism: a sage who lives in seclusion in the mountains, possesses supernatural powers and does not age - often depicted as an old man with a white beard riding on clouds. Figuratively, someone who lives far from worldly desires and money is called 仙人: 仙人のような生活. A hermit without magical connotation is called 世捨て人. Well known is the saying that 仙人 live on mist (霞を食べて生きる).

examples[].german: Right behind the grave, narcissus flowers were blooming.
Many narcissus were blooming on the winter coast and smelled lovely.
Narcissus bulbs are poisonous, so please don't let your pets eat them.
en.notes: 水仙 is the narcissus; in Japan it is mainly the white-and-yellow tazetta that blooms in winter to early spring, often in large fields on the coast. People say 水仙が咲く, 水仙の花 and 水仙の香り. The trumpet daffodil with its large trumpet is called ラッパ水仙. In biology and gardening texts the plant is often written in katakana as スイセン; in everyday speech and literature 水仙 is usual.

examples[].german: I will buy a map before I go to Sendai.
Sendai is famous for its beef tongue, so please be sure to try it.
From Tokyo to Sendai it takes about an hour and a half by Shinkansen.
en.notes: 仙台 is the largest city of the 東北 region and the capital of 宮城県. The city has the nickname 杜の都 "City of Trees" and is known for grilled beef tongue (牛タン) and the star festival 仙台七夕. In conversation one simply says 仙台; officially the city is called 仙台市; with directional particles: 仙台に行く, 仙台から来た, 仙台出身.

examples[].german: Could you refill the printer paper before you leave?
Because someone quit, we have to fill a part-time position.
When goods on the shelf run low, please restock immediately.
en.notes: 補充 means to fill up something missing or used up to the intended amount or number again: 紙を補充する, 在庫を補充する, 人員を補充する (to fill staff positions). Transitive with を. To be distinguished is 補給: this is the ongoing supply of something that is consumed, e.g. 水分補給 or 燃料補給. 補足, by contrast, is a supplementary explanation of what has been said.

examples[].german: I'll hand you the certificate the next time we meet.
After studying the tea ceremony for ten years, I finally received my certificate.
To work with hazardous materials, a national license is required.
en.notes: 免状 is a somewhat old-fashioned, formal term for a certificate confirming an authorization or rank. Today it is heard mainly in traditional arts (茶道や華道の免状, 師範の免状) and for some state qualification certificates. For a driver's license, people say 免許証, for a graduation certificate 卒業証書, and for general certificates 証明書. Typical: 免状をもらう, 免状を取る, 免状を渡す.

examples[].german: Sorry. There's really no way I can pick you up at the airport on the same day. I wish you had told me a bit earlier.
Hello? Is anyone there?
Commuting two hours a day on a packed train - I've had enough of that.
en.notes: 御免 is almost always written in kana: ごめん is the casual apology among friends and in the family, ごめんなさい is more polite, and toward superiors people say すみません or 申し訳ありません. ごめんください is called out at someone else's front door to make oneself noticed. In addition, 〜はごめんだ expresses that one absolutely does not want something (anymore): "I've had enough of it". The kanji spelling 御免 is seen today mainly in expressions like 天下御免.

examples[].german: The interest on savings deposits is very low.
This scholarship can be borrowed interest-free.
Debt accrues interest every month, so it's better to pay it back early.
en.notes: 利子 is the "interest" you receive on savings or pay on borrowed money - i.e. the concrete amount. Typical are 利子がつく, 利子を払う, 利子が高い／低い and 無利子 ("interest-free"). Nearly identical in meaning is 利息, which appears more often in contracts and at banks; 金利, by contrast, means the interest rate. Figuratively people also say 利子をつけて返す "to pay back with interest".

examples[].german: My grandfather was exempted from military service because of his heart disease.
Students with outstanding grades have their tuition fees waived completely.
We decided to exempt applicants with work experience from the introductory training.
en.notes: 免除 means exemption from a duty, payment or exam: 授業料を免除する, 兵役が免除される, 試験の一部が免除になる. It is very often used in the passive, with the exempted person as the topic: 〜は…を免除される. It fits only duties and burdens, not release from captivity (that would be 解放). For tax exemption there is the separate word 免税. Register: official, formal.

en.meaning: out of range; no signal; outside (a range)
examples[].german: Oh no! My brother said he'd call my phone, but there's no signal here.
Once you go into the mountains, your smartphone quickly loses signal.
Last time he was third, but this time he fell out of the top ten.
en.notes: 圏外 literally means "outside the range". In everyday life it appears mainly on the mobile phone display: ここは圏外だ, 圏外になる "no network". It also means "outside the ranking or reach": ランキング圏外, 優勝圏外, 台風の圏外. The opposite is 圏内 (圏内に入る). Colloquially, people say of a person 恋愛対象の圏外 "out of the question as a partner".

examples[].german: I never thought of Singapore as an English-speaking country.
I'd like to study abroad at a university in an English-speaking country.
In the English-speaking world, you say your first name first and your family name after.
en.notes: 英語圏 is the English-speaking sphere, that is, all countries in which English is the main language. The suffix 〜圏 forms many such words: フランス語圏, イスラム圏, 首都圏 (Greater Tokyo), 経済圏. Typical are 英語圏の国, 英語圏に留学する, 英語圏出身の人. Neutral, also common in newspapers and job applications.

en.meaning: Antarctica; Antarctic region; Antarctic Circle area
examples[].german: Are there other animals besides penguins in Antarctica?
Once you enter the Antarctic Circle area, the sun does not set all day in summer.
The research vessel advanced toward Antarctica, breaking through the ice.
en.notes: 南極圏 is, strictly speaking, the area south of the Antarctic Circle, and in a wider sense the Antarctic region. In everyday speech people usually just say 南極; the continent itself is called 南極大陸. The counterpart is 北極圏 (the Arctic). Typical: 南極圏に入る, 南極圏の動物, 南極圏の観測.

examples[].german: What brings you to Saitama Prefecture?
I commute by train every day from Saitama Prefecture to my company in Tokyo.
The capital of Saitama Prefecture is Saitama City, which is written in hiragana.
en.notes: 埼玉県 is the prefecture directly north of Tokyo in the 関東 region. Many residents commute to Tokyo, so it is regarded as a typical bedroom-community region. The prefectural capital is written in hiragana: さいたま市. In conversation, people usually drop 県 (埼玉に住んでいる), and the residents are called 埼玉県民.

examples[].german: I'm eating while watching a movie.
Oh no, I forgot to cook the rice!
"Dinner's ready!" "Okay, I'm coming!"
en.notes: 御飯 first means "cooked rice" and, by extension, "meal, food": 朝ご飯, 昼ご飯, 晩ご飯, ご飯ですよ "the meal is ready". Today it is mostly written ご飯 or ごはん; the kanji form 御飯 is rare. Uncooked rice is 米, and in a Western-style restaurant it is often ライス; 飯 (めし) is the rough, masculine variant. To cook rice is ご飯を炊く.

examples[].german: Have you already gone up to the third floor and seen the new rooms?
I hear the president watched yesterday's game on TV.
Professor, have you ever seen this photo?
en.notes: 御覧になる is the respectful form (尊敬語) of 見る and is used for the seeing of other, higher-ranking people; today it is mostly written ご覧になる. For one's own seeing, the humble form 拝見する is used. Very common is the request ご覧ください "please take a look". 御覧になられる is a double honorific and is considered incorrect. Casually toward children or younger people: 〜てごらん "try ...".

en.meaning: to refuse; to reject; to decline
examples[].german: My family doctor refused to let me have a colorectal cancer screening.
He refused to answer the questions until the end.
The island is surrounded by high cliffs, as if refusing anyone who approaches.
en.notes: 拒む is a written, rather strong "to refuse, to reject": 要求を拒む, 〜ことを拒む, 〜のを拒む. In everyday speech people rather say 断る, which also covers polite declining; 拒否する is the formal Sino-Japanese variant, 拒絶する even more abrupt. The second meaning is "to bar, to turn away": 人の侵入を拒む, 人を拒む険しい山.

examples[].german: He was called a coward because he had refused to go to the battlefield.
I blocked calls from unknown numbers.
The union rejected the company's proposal.
en.notes: 拒否 is a clear, formal rejection or refusal: 要求を拒否する, 〜することを拒否する. Common compounds are 拒否権 "right of veto", 着信拒否 "call blocking", 登校拒否 "school refusal" and 拒否反応 "rejection reaction". In conversation 断る is softer and more usual; 拒む is the native Japanese verb with a similar meaning, 拒絶 is even sharper.

examples[].german: My friend has much larger rice fields.
In autumn, the rice fields turn golden all around.
From the train window, rice fields stretching endlessly could be seen.
en.notes: 稲田 is a rice field in which rice (稲) grows. The word sounds rather literary or descriptive, for example in descriptions of landscapes; in everyday speech people say 田んぼ, and in a technical register 水田. As a family name, 稲田 is likewise read いなだ. Typical: 稲田が広がる, 一面の稲田.

examples[].german: When inflation progresses, life becomes harder.
This year's inflation rate exceeded three percent.
The government began subsidizing electricity costs as an anti-inflation measure.
en.notes: インフレ is the short form of インフレーション, "inflation"; the opposite is デフレ. Typical are インフレが進む, インフレが起こる, インフレ率 and インフレ対策. It describes the general rise in the price level; for individual price increases, people say 値上がり or 物価の上昇. Neutral, common in news and daily life.

examples[].german: He is absorbed in rice farming.
Because this region is rich in water, rice farming has been thriving here since long ago.
It is said that rice farming spread across Japan in the Yayoi period.
en.notes: 稲作 is wet-rice cultivation as an industry or agricultural technique: 稲作が盛んな地域, 稲作農家, 稲作文化, 稲作に適した気候. It sounds matter-of-fact and often appears in textbooks, the news and history texts. Colloquially people say 米作り; agriculture in general is 農業.

en.meaning: to hand over; to give up; to yield
examples[].german: He let me have an old novel that is out of print.
I gave up my seat to an elderly person on the train.
Neither team gave an inch, and the game went into extra time.
en.notes: 譲る means to leave something of one's own to someone else: AをBに譲る. Set phrases are 席を譲る "to offer one's seat," 道を譲る "to yield the right of way" and 一歩も譲らない "not to give an inch." Selling between private individuals is also 譲る (in ads: 譲ります), and handing down property is 財産を譲る. Mutual yielding is 譲り合う; unlike あげる, 譲る stresses that you give something up.

examples[].german: The principal doesn't want to hand over his power to anyone else.
The transfer of authority from the state to local governments is being pushed forward.
The company president plans to transfer management rights to his son next year.
en.notes: 移譲 is the formal transfer of rights, authority or property to someone else: 権限を移譲する, 地方への権限移譲, 経営権の移譲. It belongs to administrative, political and business language. Similar is 委譲 (same reading, transfer of authority to subordinates); 譲渡 emphasizes the sale or assignment of property. Beware of the similar-sounding 以上 and 異常.

examples[].german: When I found the classic car I had been looking for all this time, which went out of production in the 60s, my heart leapt with joy.
When I think that my dream trip to Paris starts tomorrow, my heart leaps.
The word "champion" stood out in huge letters on the front page of the newspaper.
en.notes: 躍る means "to jump, to leap" and is used mostly figuratively: 胸が躍る, 心が躍る "one's heart leaps" with joy or anticipation. Headlines also "leap out at the reader" (見出しに〜の文字が躍る), and fish leap (魚が躍る). Do not confuse it with the identically read 踊る "to dance". The verb is intransitive.

en.meaning: active role; success in one's work
examples[].german: In this industry, women's active contribution stands out.
He is now doing well in America as a professional baseball player.
I wish you every success in your new workplace.
en.notes: 活躍 means to be active and successful in a role and to distinguish oneself, not merely "to take part". It is mostly an intransitive する-verb: 〜で活躍する, 〜として活躍する. Common are 大活躍, 活躍の場 and the letter formula ご活躍をお祈りします "I wish you continued success". Mere participation, by contrast, is 参加.

examples[].german: This class aims to improve the students' jumping ability.
The high jump and the long jump count as jumping events.
Frogs leap far using their hind legs.
en.notes: 跳躍 is a technical, written-language word for "jump, to jump", used above all in sports: 跳躍力 "jumping power", 跳躍種目 "jumping events". In everyday speech one says ジャンプ or 跳ぶ. It differs from the similar 飛躍 in that 跳躍 means the physical jump, whereas 飛躍 usually means, figuratively, a leap forward or a leap in thought.

en.meaning: execution by firing squad; shooting dead
examples[].german: There was a sad incident in which a dog was shot dead by its owner.
The soldiers who had staged the rebellion were captured and shot.
During the war, spies were sentenced to death by firing squad if they were caught.
en.notes: 銃殺 means "to shoot dead", especially as an execution (銃殺刑 "death by firing squad"). It is mostly used in the passive: 〜に銃殺される. In police reports about the shooting of a criminal or an animal, 射殺 is often used; 撃つ is the neutral "to shoot". The word belongs in news, historical and crime contexts.

examples[].german: Could you wait a moment? I have to go and get my bullets.
The soldier was hit in the chest by a bullet and collapsed.
Several bullet marks remained on the wall at the scene.
en.notes: 銃弾 is a bullet fired from a firearm. Typical combinations: 銃弾を受ける "to be hit", 銃弾に倒れる "to be killed by a bullet", 銃弾が当たる, 銃弾の跡 "bullet hole". 弾丸 is more general, and in casual speech people simply say 弾 (たま). The register is that of news and narrative.

examples[].german: It took some time, but we were finally able to find the pistol that was used as the weapon in the crime.
The police officer wore a pistol at his waist.
In Westerns, there are often scenes where a gunslinger draws his gun in a flash.
en.notes: 短銃 is a short handgun, that is, a pistol or revolver. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned and literary; today the news usually says 拳銃, and colloquially ピストル. The opposite is long guns such as ライフル or 猟銃. Typical: 短銃を持つ, 短銃を抜く, 短銃で撃つ.

examples[].german: "Well then, let's move on to the next item on the agenda." "Wait a moment, please. Before we go on, shall we take a ten-minute break?"
This application form has far too many fields that have to be filled in.
This dictionary contains about 100,000 entries.
en.notes: 項目 is a single item in a list or outline: an agenda item, an entry, a form field, a heading; in a dictionary also "entry, headword". Typical: 項目を追加する, チェック項目, 入力項目, 調査項目; as a counter 5項目. The related term 事項 refers more to the matter or content (注意事項), whereas 項目 is the unit of an outline.

examples[].german: Politicians should listen to the voice of the people.
Becoming a politician has been my dream since I was a child.
Another politician's gaffe is in the news.
en.notes: 政治家 is the general word for a politician, whether an elected member of parliament or a minister. The component 家 denotes, as in 作家 or 画家, a person with an occupation or role. Typical: 政治家になる, 政治家を目指す, 若手政治家, 政治家の失言. A specific elected member of a parliament is, more precisely, 議員; derogatory is 政治屋.

examples[].german: It is difficult to escape deflation.
Japan has suffered from deflation for a long time.
If deflation continues, it becomes hard for companies to raise salaries.
en.notes: デフレ is the short form of デフレーション, "deflation", i.e. a sustained decline in the general price level - the opposite of インフレ. Typical are デフレが続く, デフレから脱却する ("to overcome deflation") and デフレ経済. In Japan the word is closely associated with the decades after the bursting of the bubble economy; a downward spiral is called デフレスパイラル.

examples[].german: Please fill in the required items on the form and send it to us by mail.
I'll send out the decisions from the meeting by e-mail later.
Please read the notes carefully before the exam.
en.notes: 事項 refers to individual matters or points, above all in formal texts such as forms, contracts and minutes. It appears almost always in compounds: 必要事項 "required items", 注意事項 "notes", 決定事項 "decisions", 連絡事項 "announcements", 禁止事項. In contrast to 項目 (an item in a list outline), 事項 means the content; the more general, softer word is 事柄.

examples[].german: For details, please check the attached application guidelines.
I downloaded the entrance exam information from the university website.
Before you apply, please read the guidelines carefully and check the requirements.
en.notes: 要項 means the essential points and conditions of an undertaking, usually in the form of an official information sheet: 募集要項 "call for applications, application requirements", 入試要項 "entrance exam information", 応募要項, 実施要項. One reads, distributes or publishes it (要項を確認する, 要項を配布する). Do not confuse it with the identically read 要綱 (outline of a law or program); 要点 simply means the key points.

examples[].german: We need to deal with the steel shortage as quickly as possible.
A special earthquake-resistant steel is used in this building.
Because of the rise in steel prices, the production costs of cars have gone up.
en.notes: 鋼材 is steel as a material in processed form, such as beams, sheets or pipes for construction and industry. Typical: 鋼材価格, 建築用鋼材, 鋼材不足, 鋼材メーカー. The component 鋼 means "steel" (read はがね when alone); the industry is called 鉄鋼業. Technical vocabulary, frequent in business news.

examples[].german: If you cut wages, the workers at the steelworks might go on strike.
This town has prospered from the steel industry since the Meiji era.
Technology for making steel by recycling scrap iron is attracting attention.
en.notes: 製鋼 is the production of steel. The word appears almost only in compounds and technical texts: 製鋼所 "steelworks", 製鋼業, 製鋼会社, 製鋼技術; as the verb 製鋼する it is rare. It must be distinguished from 製鉄, the production of pig iron from ore. Beware of words that sound the same, such as 成功 "success" and 精巧 "elaborate, finely made".

examples[].german: Why do prisoners wear striped clothes?
In the film, the prisoners were planning an escape from the prison.
That island was once used as a place to send prisoners.
en.notes: 囚人 is a prisoner in jail. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned or narrative and often occurs in films, novels and historical contexts (囚人服, 囚人を収容する). Officially, one nowadays speaks of 受刑者 (convicted inmate); prisoners of war are 捕虜, and suspects before the verdict are 容疑者.

examples[].german: A condemned prisoner climbs these stairs and heads for the gallows.
The Minister of Justice ordered the execution of the condemned prisoner.
He wrote a book about a death-row inmate who keeps protesting his innocence.
en.notes: 死刑囚 is a person sentenced to death who is waiting for the sentence to be carried out, that is, a death-row inmate. The suffix 〜囚 denotes prisoners (女囚, 未決囚). Typical combinations: 死刑判決を受ける, 死刑を執行する, 死刑囚の再審. Legal news vocabulary.

examples[].german: Who were the substitutes again?
Please keep the copy of the application form in a safe place.
The performers waited in the waiting room until the actual performance.
en.notes: 控え is the noun of 控える ("to hold back, to stand by, to note down") and has several meanings. "Reserve, substitute": 控えの選手, 控えに回る. "Copy, record": 領収書の控え, お客様控え, 控えを取る. And "waiting": 控え室 "waiting room, dressing room". Do not confuse it with 控えめ "modest, moderate".

examples[].german: There is still no news of my father's whereabouts.
Because of the typhoon, many houses are still without power.
The economy has recovered, but the unemployment rate remains high.
en.notes: 依然 means "still, as before" and usually appears as 依然として before the predicate: 依然として不明だ. In the news the short form 依然 also occurs (依然高い, 依然、〜が続いている). The word is written-style; in conversation one says まだ or 相変わらず. Beware: the identically read 以前 means "earlier, before". A well-known expression: 旧態依然 "unchanged and outdated".

examples[].german: I shaved my eyebrows only three hours ago, but they already look like they are about to join up again.
My older sister carefully draws on her eyebrows in front of the mirror every morning.
When he is in trouble, his eyebrows always slant downward in the shape of 八.
en.notes: 眉毛 are the eyebrows; shorter and somewhat more elevated is 眉 (まゆ). Typical: 眉毛を描く "to draw in", 眉毛を整える, 眉毛を抜く, 太い眉毛. In fixed expressions, 眉 is usually used: 眉をひそめる "to frown". Do not confuse it with まつげ "eyelashes".

examples[].german: This address seems to be wrong.
Please make out the receipt to the company name.
Writing all the New Year's cards' addresses by hand is a lot of work.
en.notes: 宛名 is the name of the recipient, usually together with the address on envelopes: 宛名を書く, 宛名書き, 宛名ラベル. On receipts, too, the customer name entered is called 宛名 (領収書の宛名). It must be distinguished from 宛先 (destination address, also for e-mails), 住所 (residential address) and 差出人 (sender).

examples[].german: The corporate tax was lowered.
This service is for corporations, not individuals.
As the business had grown, I turned it from a sole proprietorship into a corporation.
en.notes: 法人 is a "legal entity" - an organization such as a company, association or foundation that can act legally like a person; the opposite term is 個人. Common in compounds: 法人税 ("corporate tax"), 法人化 ("incorporation"), 法人向け ("for business customers"), NPO法人 and 学校法人. Technical and administrative language; in everyday speech one speaks rather of 会社 or 企業.

examples[].german: He comes from a family of distinguished lineage.
This inn is a venerable lodging that has existed since the Edo period.
Kyoto has many venerable temples and shrines.
en.notes: 由緒正しい is composed of 由緒 "origin, history" and 正しい "correct, proper": "of venerable, documented origin". It describes families, temples, shrines, inns or objects with a long, respected tradition: 由緒正しい家柄, 由緒正しい神社. 由緒ある means the same. Elevated style, sometimes also used slightly ironically.

examples[].german: Mr. and Mrs. Fugu both live in Kagawa Prefecture, but they are living apart.
Speaking of Kagawa Prefecture, it's of course Sanuki udon, isn't it?
Kagawa Prefecture is the prefecture with the smallest area in Japan.
en.notes: 香川県 lies in the northeast of the island of 四国; the seat of government is 高松市. It is the smallest prefecture of Japan by area. It is famous for 讃岐うどん (讃岐 is the old name of the province) and therefore jokingly calls itself うどん県. 香川 alone can also be a family name; with 県 the prefecture is clearly meant.

en.meaning: leap; rapid progress; leap in thought
examples[].german: He likes conspiracy theories, but his logic often makes big leaps.
With the spread of the internet, communication technology has advanced by leaps and bounds.
After winning this tournament, she made her leap onto the world stage.
en.notes: 飛躍 is almost always used figuratively: as great progress (飛躍的に進歩する, 飛躍を遂げる), as a leap onto a bigger stage (世界へ飛躍する) and as a leap in thought (論理の飛躍, 話が飛躍する). The adverb 飛躍的に "by leaps and bounds, dramatically" is very common. For the physical jump, one uses 跳躍 or ジャンプ. Intransitive する-verb.

en.meaning: please (asking for goodwill: よろしくお願いします); give one's regards (よろしく伝える); good, appropriate
examples[].german: Please give my regards to your mother.
Nice to meet you, I'm Tanaka. Please treat me kindly.
I will send the materials, so please check them.
en.notes: よろしく expresses a request for goodwill and can hardly be translated literally. Most often it appears in よろしくお願いします: at introductions "Nice to meet you," in requests "Thank you in advance," at the end of emails; among friends, short よろしく！／よろしくね. 〜によろしく伝えてください means "Please give my regards to ...". The old meaning "appropriate, good" survives in よろしくやる "to manage skillfully." Almost always written in kana; 宜しく is rare and formal.

examples[].german: Excuse me for interrupting, but it seems your wife has gotten stuck in the elevator.
Please give my best regards to your wife as well.
I hear the president's wife used to be a pianist.
en.notes: 奥様 is the very polite term for another person's wife, for example that of the person you are talking to or of a superior; slightly less formal is 奥さん. It is never used for one's own wife; for that, 妻 or 家内 are used. 奥様 also serves as a form of address for a married lady, for example by sales staff ("madam").

en.meaning: to be at stake; to depend on; (気に〜) to weigh on one's mind
examples[].german: I am worried about whether he is safe.
The championship is at stake in this match.
A large reward is offered for the arrest of the criminal.
en.notes: 懸かる is a kanji spelling of かかる for certain meanings: "to be at stake, to depend on" (命が懸かっている, 優勝が懸かった試合), "to be offered" for rewards (賞金が懸かる) and "to hang in the sky" (月が懸かる). "To be worried" results only from the expression 気に懸かる, which is mostly written 気にかかる. In everyday writing the verb is mostly written in kana; the transitive counterpart is 懸ける (命を懸ける).

examples[].german: Right after I was told to be careful with the wine glasses, I promptly broke one.
I was treated so badly by the staff that I will never go to that shop again.
Even though I'm already twenty, my parents still treat me like a child.
en.notes: 扱い is the noun of 扱う and means both the handling of things (機械の扱い, 扱いに注意する, 扱いやすい) and the treatment of people (ひどい扱いを受ける). As a suffix it means "to treat as": 子ども扱いする, 犯人扱いされる. The more formal variant, e.g. on labels and in instruction manuals, is 取り扱い (取扱説明書).

en.meaning: to handle; to deal with; to carry (goods)
examples[].german: I will deal with this topic in the next article.
In our shop we also carry a wide selection of foreign wines.
This chemical is dangerous, please handle it with care.
en.notes: 取り扱う is the more formal variant of 扱う and is transitive with を. It means "to handle, to operate" (機械を取り扱う, 慎重に取り扱う), "to deal with" topics or cases (問題を取り扱う) and in commerce "to carry, to offer" (当店では〜を取り扱っております). The noun 取り扱い appears on labels such as 取扱注意 "handle with care, fragile"; an instruction manual is called 取扱説明書.

examples[].german: The shareholders' meeting will be held next month.
With the shareholder benefit, you get meal vouchers.
The company decided to increase dividends to shareholders.
en.notes: 株主 is a "shareholder", i.e. someone who owns shares (株) in a stock company. Common combinations are 株主総会 ("general meeting"), 大株主 ("major shareholder"), 株主優待 ("shareholder benefits" - vouchers or gifts that are popular in Japan) and 株主への配当 ("dividend"). Factual vocabulary from business and finance; the shares themselves are called 株 or 株式.

examples[].german: They try to whisper, but their voices are so loud that I can hear everything.
When we were whispering to each other in class, we were reprimanded by the teacher.
The two seemed to be discussing something confidential in a corner of the room.
en.notes: 内緒話 is a confidential conversation that others should not hear, often quiet or whispered: 内緒話をする. It is based on 内緒 "secret" (内緒にする, 内緒で, often in kana ないしょ). For the whispering itself one says ひそひそ話; 秘密 is the more neutral, more serious word for "secret". Colloquial.

examples[].german: Please feel free to loosen your tie.
Please reduce your speed before the curve.
You must not let up until the exam is over.
en.notes: 緩める is transitive (〜を緩める) and means "to loosen, to release": ネクタイ, ベルト, ねじを緩める. Figuratively: スピードを緩める "to slow down", 気を緩める "to let one's guard down", 規制を緩める "to relax regulations", 手を緩める "to ease off". The intransitive counterpart is 緩む, the adjective 緩い, the opposite 締める.

examples[].german: This is a gift for my mother.
I am choosing a gift for a wedding celebration.
This watch is a precious gift from my grandfather.
en.notes: 贈り物 is a gift with a somewhat formal or ceremonial ring, for example for weddings, birthdays or seasonal gifts; in everyday speech one mostly says プレゼント. The related verb is 贈る "to give (ceremonially)", in everyday speech あげる. A souvenir from a trip, by contrast, is お土産. Note: 送る "to send" sounds the same but is written differently.

examples[].german: To stop young people from leaving Okinawa, the prefecture is trying to create new jobs.
Okinawa Prefecture is the southernmost prefecture in Japan.
Many American military bases are concentrated in Okinawa Prefecture.
en.notes: 沖縄県 is the southernmost prefecture of Japan and consists of many subtropical islands; the capital is 那覇市. Until the 19th century the area was the Kingdom of 琉球, and after the war it was under American administration until 1972. In conversation people usually say just 沖縄; from there, Japan's main islands are often called 本土.

examples[].german: In some countries this might be called a "present", but in this country it is "bribery".
The president of a construction company was arrested on suspicion of bribing city employees.
Both the side that gives the bribe and the side that takes it are held criminally liable.
en.notes: 贈賄 is active bribery, that is, giving a bribe; accepting one is 収賄, and both together are 贈収賄 (贈収賄事件). The bribe itself is 賄賂. Typical in the news: 贈賄の疑いで逮捕される, 贈賄罪. Legal and journalistic vocabulary.

examples[].german: The fugitive met a sick child during his flight and decided to turn himself in to the police.
The police are searching for the fugitive who escaped abroad.
Even helping a fugitive can make one criminally liable.
en.notes: 逃亡者 is someone who flees from the police, the justice system or from captivity, i.e. a fugitive or escapee. The word has nothing to do with war or economic refugees; these are called 難民 or 避難民. Related are 逃亡 "flight" (逃亡中, 国外逃亡) and 逃走. Typical in news reports and crime stories.

examples[].german: Why don't you ask the teacher who supervises the club whether you can skip club activities tomorrow?
The company consulted its legal adviser about the legal problem.
Even after retiring from the company, my father goes in once a week as an adviser.
en.notes: 顧問 is an adviser with a fixed function in an organization: 顧問弁護士 "(company) legal adviser", 技術顧問, 会社の顧問 (often former executives). At schools, the 顧問 (顧問の先生) is the teacher who supervises a club (部活). It must be distinguished from コンサルタント (an external consultant paid a fee) and 相談役.

examples[].german: What boring memoirs.
The former prime minister published memoirs looking back on his time as a politician.
My grandfather compiled his wartime experiences into memoirs.
en.notes: 回顧録 is composed of 回顧 "retrospection" and 録 "record" and means memoirs, especially of politicians, executives or witnesses of an era. Typical: 回顧録を書く, 回顧録を出版する, 回顧録にまとめる. Similar are 回想録 and 自伝 "autobiography"; 回顧録 sounds the most formal of these.

en.meaning: posting (to a place); stationing; residence abroad on assignment
examples[].german: My father was stationed in Singapore for three years for work.
It has been decided that I will be posted to London from next month.
The police officer at the village police box remembers the faces of all the residents.
en.notes: 駐在 means that someone is sent by a company, agency or state to a place for a longer period, usually abroad, and works there: ロンドンに駐在する, 海外駐在. The posted employee is called 駐在員 "expat". Distinctions: 滞在 is any stay (also private or short), 赴任 stresses taking up a post, and for troops one says 駐留. In addition, 駐在所 is a rural police box in which the officer also lives; he is colloquially called 駐在さん.

examples[].german: I opened an account at a securities firm.
The Tokyo Stock Exchange is the largest exchange in Japan.
Please keep your insurance policy safe.
en.notes: 証券 refers to "securities" such as stocks and bonds as well as, in general, certificates of rights, e.g. 保険証券 ("insurance policy"). It is most often encountered in 証券会社 ("securities firm, broker"), 証券取引所 ("stock exchange") and 証券口座 ("brokerage account"). It is technical vocabulary of the financial world; for concrete instruments one mostly says 株 or 債券.

examples[].german: After the war, Allied occupation forces were stationed in Japan.
Many residents around the bases of the stationed troops suffer from noise.
The government is demanding the withdrawal of the stationed troops.
en.notes: 駐留軍 are troops stationed in a foreign country for a longer period, usually on the basis of an agreement, such as the US forces in Japan (在日米軍). The related verb is 駐留する "to be stationed": 米軍が沖縄に駐留する. The word is neutral and belongs to news and historical language; 占領軍 "occupation army", by contrast, stresses the occupation. 駐在 is not used for troops but for people such as company employees or diplomats.

examples[].german: He is known as the person who championed that movement.
This plan was started at the mayor's initiative.
An organization that champions environmental protection is demanding a new law.
en.notes: 主唱 means to be the first, or in a leading position, to publicly advocate an idea, doctrine or movement and to promote it: 〜を主唱する. It is a written-language, rather rare word; the person is called 主唱者. The phrase 〜の主唱で means "on the initiative of ...". In everyday speech one says 提唱する ("to propose, to advocate") or 主張する/訴える instead.

examples[].german: "Furusato" is a long-loved school song from the Ministry of Education's song collection.
My grandmother still often sings the school songs she learned as a child.
In elementary schools before the war, music class was called "shōka".
en.notes: 唱歌 today refers above all to the simple, often nostalgic songs sung in schools since the Meiji era, especially the 文部省唱歌 such as 「ふるさと」 or 「春が来た」; often in the pair 童謡・唱歌. Until 1941, the school subject of music was also called 唱歌. For "singing" in general one says 歌う or, technically, 歌唱, and for choral singing 合唱.

examples[].german: Even though I have hay fever, I have to sing a solo at the recital.
At the graduation ceremony, she sang the school song as a solo.
In the second part of the concert, there was a solo by a famous soprano.
en.notes: 独唱 is singing alone, that is, a "vocal solo"; the opposites are 合唱 "choral singing" and 重唱 "ensemble singing (duet, trio ...)". As a する-verb it takes the song as its object (国歌を独唱する) or none. An instrumental solo is 独奏 (ピアノ独奏); in everyday speech, ソロ is often used for both. The soloist is 独唱者.

examples[].german: To show everyone your singing talent, may I post this video on Facebook?
For the choir competition, we received singing lessons from a professional teacher.
The national anthem was sung at the opening ceremony.
en.notes: 歌唱 is the technical, rather written-language word for "singing" and appears above all in compounds: 歌唱力 "vocal ability", 歌唱指導 "singing lessons", 歌唱法 "singing technique". As the verb 歌唱する it occurs almost only in official contexts (国歌を歌唱する); in everyday speech one simply says 歌う. Do not confuse: 唱歌 are school songs, 合唱 is choral singing, 独唱 is a vocal solo.

examples[].german: The choir members all sing hand in hand.
My daughter sings in a local children's choir.
The Vienna Boys' Choir gives concerts in Japan.
en.notes: 合唱団 is an organized choir as a group - a school, amateur or children's choir; one joins it (合唱団に入る) or is a member (合唱団員). 合唱 alone, by contrast, refers to the activity "choral singing" (合唱する, 合唱コンクール). For pop backing vocals one rather says コーラス, a church choir is called 聖歌隊.

en.meaning: filial piety; devotion and care for one's parents
examples[].german: I would like to do more for my parents, but I just don't have the time.
With my first salary I took my parents on an onsen trip to repay them.
There is a proverb: "When you want to be good to your parents, they are no longer there."
en.notes: 孝行 is the Confucian-influenced virtue of showing gratitude to one's parents and caring for them. In everyday speech it appears almost always as 親孝行 (親孝行する, 親孝行な息子); the opposite is 親不孝. It is used as a する-verb (親に孝行する) and as a な-adjective (孝行な娘), and can figuratively express care for others as well, e.g. 女房孝行 "doing something nice for one's wife".

en.meaning: lack of filial piety; ingratitude toward one's parents
examples[].german: I never want to commit the kind of unfilial act that makes my parents sad.
It is said that dying before one's parents is the greatest unfilial act.
I haven't gone home for a long time and have done nothing but neglect my parents.
en.notes: 不孝 is the opposite of 孝行: behavior by which one hurts one's parents, worries them or neglects them. On its own it sounds rather written; in everyday speech people almost always say 親不孝 (親不孝な息子, 親不孝をする). Do not confuse it with the identically read 不幸 "misfortune, death in the family" - only the kanji distinguishes the two. As a な-adjective: 不孝な子.

examples[].german: He is an exceptionally talented man who became a professor in his twenties.
Gifted students from all over the country gather at this cram school.
She is said to be the most gifted person in the company.
en.notes: 俊才 (also written 駿才) refers to a person of outstanding ability and quick comprehension, an "exceptional talent". It is a complimentary, written-language word for biographies, newspaper articles or speeches: 〜の俊才, 俊才が集まる. Close synonyms are 秀才 ("very bright mind, model student", more everyday) and 天才 ("genius", innate exceptional gift); for the education of gifted children one says 英才教育.

examples[].german: Government bonds are considered safe bonds.
When interest rates rise, bond prices fall.
The company issued bonds to raise funds.
en.notes: 債券 is a "bond" or "debenture": a security with which the state or companies borrow money and pay interest for it. Subtypes are 国債 ("government bond") and 社債 ("corporate bond"); typical verbs are 債券を発行する and 債券を買う. Not to be confused with the identically read 債権 ("claim, receivable"), the counterpart of 債務 ("debt"). Technical vocabulary of the financial world.

examples[].german: We farm part-time: my father works at a company on weekdays and in the rice field on weekends.
Recently more and more companies allow their employees to have side jobs.
He is both a writer and a part-time lecturer at a university.
en.notes: 兼業 means to carry on another gainful activity besides one's main occupation or to pursue two activities in parallel: AとBを兼業する. Well known is 兼業農家 "part-time farmer" as opposed to 専業農家; likewise 兼業主婦 vs. 専業主婦. In the working world it often appears next to 副業 "side job"; 副業 emphasizes the subordinate extra income, 兼業 more the simultaneous practice of two occupations (兼業禁止 in an employment contract).

examples[].german: This meal is a brunch.
This umbrella is meant for both sun and rain, so you can also use it as a parasol.
Because the apartment is small, my living room doubles as a study.
en.notes: 兼用 means to use one thing for two or more purposes: AをBと兼用する, or as a suffix A・B兼用: 男女兼用 "unisex", 晴雨兼用 "for sun and rain", 朝昼兼用 "breakfast and lunch in one". Before nouns it takes の (兼用のかばん). Distinctions: 兼業 concerns occupations, 兼任 offices, and 共用 emphasizes shared use by several people.

examples[].german: When you have finished using the agent, be sure to put it back on its original shelf.
At the pharmacy, the pharmacist explained to me how to take the medicine.
I sprayed an agent to keep insects away on the field.
en.notes: 薬剤 is a technical word for medicines and chemical agents of all kinds - medications, but also pesticides, disinfectants or bleaches. It sounds more technical than 薬 and is found mainly in medicine, agriculture and on product labels; well known is 薬剤師 "pharmacist". For chemicals in a laboratory one says 薬品 instead. Grammatically it is a noun.

examples[].german: This bread contains no preservatives, so please eat it soon.
I am looking for cosmetics without preservatives.
I applied preservative to the wooden posts so that they would not rot.
en.notes: 防腐剤 literally means "agent against rot" (防 "prevent", 腐 "rot", 剤 "agent"). It refers to preservatives in food and cosmetics, but also to wood preservatives; on labels one often reads 防腐剤不使用 or 防腐剤無添加. In food law the official term is 保存料; 防腐剤 is the more general everyday term. Disinfectants for wounds are nowadays rather called 消毒薬.

examples[].german: This detergent removes greasy dirt well.
I bought painkiller tablets at the pharmacy.
If you are bitten by a snake, you need to be given an antidote injection immediately.
en.notes: 〜剤 is a Sino-Japanese suffix for "agent, preparation" and is attached to a kanji word that indicates purpose or form: 洗剤 "detergent", 解毒剤 "antidote", 防腐剤 "preservative", 接着剤 "adhesive", 錠剤 "tablet", 消毒剤 "disinfectant". It cannot be used freely but forms fixed compounds that sound factual and technical. It is not a particle but a noun suffix.

examples[].german: Many people are jogging along the inner moat of the Imperial Palace.
After the Winter Campaign, not only the outer moat but even the inner moat of Osaka Castle was filled in.
Cherry blossom petals are floating on the surface of the inner moat.
en.notes: 内堀 is the inner castle moat, which directly surrounds the core areas of a Japanese castle (本丸 etc.); its counterpart is 外堀 "outer moat". Today the word is known mainly from historic castles and from the Imperial Palace in Tokyo, along whose moats runs the street 内堀通り. 堀 is an artificially dug water-filled ditch; for castle moats the spelling 濠 is also found.

examples[].german: Let's first persuade the people around him and so lay the groundwork before we talk to the president.
You can still see the outer moat of Edo Castle today around Iidabashi and Ichigaya.
To protect against enemy attacks, an outer moat was dug around the castle.
en.notes: 外堀 is the outer castle moat, which surrounds the entire castle complex including the outer districts; the 内堀 lies inside it. Very common is the expression 外堀を埋める "to first work on the surroundings in order to make a goal unavoidable" - after Osaka Castle, whose moats were filled in before the final attack. In Tokyo, remains of the Edo outer moat can still be seen between 飯田橋 and 四ツ谷.

examples[].german: We walked side by side along the canal.
In the Edo period, many canals were dug to transport goods.
In Kyoto there is a big street called Horikawa-dori.
en.notes: 堀川 is a watercourse dug by people, that is, a canal, usually built in the Edo period for shipping and the transport of goods. As a generic word it is rather rare and sounds historical; today it is encountered mainly as a place, river or family name (京都の堀川通, 名古屋の堀川). For canals in the modern sense, one says 運河 or 水路.

examples[].german: The weather forecast was wrong, and it started raining while I was on patrol.
In this district, police officers patrol at night.
A free shuttle bus runs between the station and the hospital.
en.notes: 巡回 means to visit several places in turn along a set route: to go on patrol (警備員が巡回する), rounds in a hospital or traveling exhibitions (巡回展). As a modifier: 巡回バス "circuit bus, shuttle bus". It is an intransitive する-verb; the area covered takes を (校内を巡回する). Related are パトロール (almost synonymous for the police) and the native Japanese 見回る.

examples[].german: I asked the police officer at the police box the way to the station.
He was promoted from patrolman to police sergeant.
Several police officers had already arrived at the scene of the incident.
en.notes: 巡査 is the lowest rank of the Japanese police, roughly "patrolman, police constable"; above it follow 巡査長, 巡査部長, 警部補 and so on. The word sounds official; colloquially one says おまわりさん, neutrally 警察官, or for short 警官. Officers of this rank typically work in a 交番 or on patrol.

examples[].german: Banknotes with a new design were issued.
This vending machine does not accept 10,000-yen bills.
At the airport I exchanged my banknotes for local currency.
en.notes: 紙幣 is the official, rather written word for "banknote, bill"; in everyday speech one mostly says お札. The counterpart is 硬貨 ("coins"). Typical are 紙幣を発行する, 新紙幣, 一万円紙幣 and 紙幣を両替する. On machines, in announcements and in the news one reads 紙幣, while in conversation one says rather 千円札 or 一万円札.

examples[].german: There is something I am a little wary of.
During the summit, the police stepped up security at stations and airports.
Our cat is very wary of strangers.
en.notes: 警戒 is attentive watchfulness against a danger or person: 〜を警戒する "to be on guard against ..., to be wary of ...", 警戒を強める/緩める, 警戒心が強い "to be distrustful". It is typical of news and severe weather warnings (土砂災害に警戒してください, 警戒レベル). In contrast to 注意 ("attention, care", general), 警戒 emphasizes a concrete threat; 用心 is the more everyday "caution". Grammatically it is a noun or suru-verb, not an adjective.

examples[].german: I dropped the commemorative coin down the drain.
In the heavy rain the street drainage could not keep up, and the water overflowed.
The washing machine's drain hose came loose, and the floor was flooded.
en.notes: 排水 refers to draining or pumping away water or wastewater: 排水溝 "drainage ditch, gutter", 排水口 "drain (in a basin)", 排水管 "drainpipe"; as a suru-verb: 水を排水する. The counterpart is 給水 "water supply"; 下水 is the wastewater or the sewer system itself. In technical language 排水量 also means the "displacement" of a ship.

examples[].german: To turn on the mobile phone, you need to hold down the power button for five seconds.
I left my phone somewhere.
Please carry your passport with you at all times during the trip.
en.notes: 携帯 originally means "to carry on one's person, to bring along": 傘を携帯する, 携帯用 "portable, for taking along", 携帯食. In everyday speech it is mainly the short form of 携帯電話 "mobile phone", often also written ケータイ. For smartphones one nowadays mostly says スマホ; 携帯 remains the general word for the mobile phone (携帯の番号). The verb 携帯する sounds formal and often appears in regulations and notices.

examples[].german: I suffer from irritable bowel syndrome.
He reacts hypersensitively as soon as anyone says something to him.
My skin is so sensitive that I can't use soap containing fragrance.
en.notes: 過敏 means "oversensitive", physically as well as mentally: 過敏な肌, 神経過敏, 〜に過敏に反応する. It is frequent in medical terms such as 過敏症 "hypersensitivity, allergy" or 過敏性腸症候群 "irritable bowel syndrome". In contrast to 敏感 ("sensitive, perceptive", neutral to positive), 過敏 is always negative: too much reaction. Grammatically a な-adjective or noun.

examples[].german: Waitresses are supposed to move briskly, but she is incredibly slow.
The cat caught the mouse with a nimble movement.
Even when trouble occurred, she responded quickly and sensibly.
en.notes: 機敏 is a na-adjective for "quick, nimble, quick to react" and describes both physical agility and quick, clever reaction: 機敏な動き, 機敏に動く, 機敏に対応する. It sounds somewhat more written than the everyday 素早い; すばしこい suits small animals and children better. Do not confuse it with 敏感 "sensitive". The opposite is 鈍い "sluggish, slow".

examples[].german: That dog's keen sense of smell has caught many drug dealers.
With his sharp mind, he immediately understood the heart of the problem.
This sensor reacts sensitively to changes in temperature.
en.notes: 鋭敏 refers to sharp, fine perception (鋭敏な嗅覚, 聴覚が鋭敏だ) and, figuratively, an alert, sharp mind (鋭敏な頭脳). It is written-language and elevated; in everyday speech people say 鋭い or 敏感 instead. In contrast to 過敏 ("oversensitive", negative), 鋭敏 is positive to neutral; even measuring instruments can 鋭敏に反応する (react sensitively).

examples[].german: The culprit slashed passersby with a sharp blade.
Broken glass is sharp, so please do not touch it with bare hands.
With a razor-sharp analysis, she pointed out the problems in the discussion.
en.notes: 鋭利 describes a sharp edge or point; 鋭利な刃物 "a sharp object, a sharp blade" is practically a set phrase in police and news reports. The word is written-language; in everyday speech people say 鋭い or, for knives, よく切れる. Figuratively it can also describe a razor-sharp mind or a sharp analysis, but 鋭い is more common for that. Grammatically a な-adjective.

en.meaning: new and powerful; up-and-coming; rising talent
examples[].german: The company decided to purchase the most up-to-date computers.
This year's literature prize was won by an up-and-coming young author in his twenties.
In the final, a veteran player will face a newcomer.
en.notes: 新鋭 refers to something new that is at the same time especially capable: for people "up-and-coming, rising talent" (新鋭作家, 期待の新鋭), for machines and equipment "new and high-performance". Very common is the intensified form 最新鋭 "state-of-the-art, up to date" (最新鋭の設備). In contrast to the neutral 新人 "newcomer", 新鋭 is complimentary; the counterpart for people is ベテラン. Before nouns it is usually used with の.

examples[].german: I persuaded him to lay a carpet in his room.
Before going to bed, I laid out the futon in the Japanese-style room.
In the Meiji era, Japan's first railway was laid between Shinbashi and Yokohama.
en.notes: 敷く means to spread something flat over a surface or put it underneath: 布団を敷く "to lay out the futon", カーペットを敷く, 座布団を敷く. Figuratively: 線路を敷く "to lay tracks", 体制/戒厳令を敷く "to put a system/martial law in place"; idiomatically 尻に敷く "to have (a husband) under one's thumb". For the futon, the opposite is 布団を畳む/上げる. There is no separate intransitive counterpart; one uses 敷いてある or the passive 敷かれる.

examples[].german: There is an old manor house on the hill.
In Kanazawa, samurai residences from the Edo period are still preserved today.
The haunted house at the amusement park was so scary that I left in the middle.
en.notes: 屋敷 is a large residential house together with its grounds, an "estate, mansion"; for the house of a distinguished family often with the polite お: お屋敷. Fixed compounds are 武家屋敷 "samurai residence", 屋敷町 "villa district", お化け屋敷 "haunted house" and ゴミ屋敷 "hoarder house". For an ordinary house one says 家 or 住宅; 邸宅 is an even more elevated word for a mansion.

examples[].german: I opened a new bank account.
The rent is debited from my account on the 27th of every month.
Please tell me the account number for the salary transfer.
en.notes: 口座 is an "account", above all 銀行口座; also 証券口座 ("brokerage account"). Typical verbs are 口座を開く／開設する／作る, 口座に振り込む ("to transfer to an account"), 口座から引き落とす ("to debit") and 口座を解約する ("to close"). The account number is 口座番号, the account holder 口座名義. Not to be confused with the identically read 講座 ("course, lecture series").

examples[].german: A cricket is chirping somewhere in the tatami room.
At the izakaya, I was asked, "Would you prefer a table seat or a tatami room?"
I showed the guest into the tatami room and served tea.
en.notes: 座敷 is a room covered with tatami, traditionally the good reception room of a Japanese house into which guests are shown (座敷に通す). In restaurants, (お)座敷 denotes the tatami area where one sits without shoes at a low table, as opposed to テーブル席. 和室 is the neutral general term for a Japanese-style room. For geisha, お座敷 also means the banquet to which they are called (お座敷がかかる).

examples[].german: This certificate is awarded to Mr. Kōichi Nakamura in recognition of his outstanding achievements.
On the addressee line of the notice was written "Ms. Hanako Tanaka".
en.notes: 〜殿 is a formal form of address after a name, for example on certificates or in official and business letters. The reading here is どの: 中村コウイチ殿. It is not a general recommendation for every personal form of address; the appropriate form depends on the letter and its institutional use. The sign 〜 is an unspoken placeholder. This card practices the address suffix and not 殿・との in the sense of "lord" or "prince".

examples[].german: To pass the time, I drew a handsome feudal lord.
In the Edo period, the lords commuted every year alternately between Edo and their own domains.
This shop just waits for customers to come - doing business like a lord of the manor.
en.notes: 殿様 is the respectful term for a feudal lord (大名) of the Edo period or, generally, a high-ranking lord; in samurai dramas he is addressed as 殿 or 殿様. Figuratively it refers to an unworldly, spoiled man who is used to being waited on; hence 殿様商売 "doing business without customer orientation". Above the 殿様 stood the 将軍 "shogun".

examples[].german: The number two batter laid down a sacrifice hit and moved the runner to second base.
To score one run, the manager gave the sign for a sacrifice hit.
He holds the season record for sacrifice hits.
en.notes: 犠打 is a baseball technical term for the "sacrifice hit": the batter is deliberately put out so that a runner can advance or score. It includes 犠牲バント (sacrifice bunt) and 犠牲フライ (sacrifice fly, 犠飛 for short). In sports reports it is 犠打を決める "to successfully lay down a sacrifice hit". The word is technical and written; fans usually just say 送りバント.

examples[].german: If you play the game today, you can get twice as many coins as usual.
The athlete won a gold medal at the Olympic Games.
The new party won ten seats in the election.
en.notes: 獲得 means to win something through effort or in competition: メダル/賞/議席/権利を獲得する, ポイント獲得, 顧客獲得 "customer acquisition". It is more written-language than 手に入れる or もらう and typical of news, sports and business. In contrast to 取得 ("to acquire" licenses, qualifications, data), 獲得 emphasizes winning against competition.

examples[].german: The wild boar that had been ravaging the fields was captured with a trap.
In this sea, the catch quota for tuna is limited.
It took a full three hours to recapture the escaped monkey.
en.notes: 捕獲 is the capturing or taking of animals - game, fish, whales, escaped zoo animals: クマを捕獲する, わなで捕獲する, 捕獲量 "catch volume". It is a factual word from official, news and technical language; in daily life one says 捕まえる. For the arrest of people one does not use 捕獲 but 逮捕; prisoners of war are called 捕虜.

examples[].german: The lion hides in the grass and lies motionless in wait for its prey.
The catch from today's fishing was only three small sticklebacks.
Fraud gangs target elderly people who live alone.
en.notes: 獲物 is the animal that is or is to be taken in hunting or fishing: 獲物を狙う/追う/捕らえる. Figuratively it also refers to victims that swindlers or criminals have targeted (〜を獲物にする), as well as captured things. The reading is えもの. For spoils of war one rather says 戦利品, for the catch when angling also 釣果 (technical).

examples[].german: How often do you vacuum your house?
This word is used very frequently, so be sure to learn it.
I feel that earthquakes have been occurring more often recently.
en.notes: 頻度 is the "frequency" with which something occurs. It is combined with 高い/低い rather than 多い/少ない: 頻度が高い "frequent", 使用頻度, 高頻度. With で it gives the rate: 週に一回の頻度で "once a week". In conversation people usually just ask どのくらい or 何回; 頻度 sounds more factual. Related are 頻繁 "frequent" (な-adjective) and 回数 "number of times".

examples[].german: Everyone is under more and more stress because of the repeated earthquakes.
Accidents occur frequently at this intersection.
Recently, system troubles keep happening, and I can't get any work done.
en.notes: 頻発 means that something - usually undesirable - occurs repeatedly and in clusters: 事故/事件/地震/トラブルが頻発する. It is an intransitive する-verb, and the event takes が; before nouns: 頻発する地震. Typical of the news; in conversation people say よく起きる or しょっちゅう起きる instead. 多発 is almost synonymous but stresses the large number (事故多発地帯), while 頻発 stresses the dense succession.

examples[].german: Most fish reproduce by laying eggs.
In biology class, we learned how plants reproduce.
This chemical may affect the reproductive ability of animals.
en.notes: 生殖 is the biological technical term for "reproduction": 有性生殖/無性生殖 "sexual/asexual reproduction", 生殖器 "reproductive organs", 生殖能力 "reproductive ability". It is factual and scientific and sounds stiff in everyday speech. 繁殖, by contrast, means the multiplication of a population (ペットを繁殖させる, カビが繁殖する); for humans, everyday speech uses 出産 or 子供を作る.

examples[].german: The transfer fee is 300 yen.
A fee applies to cancellations made the day before.
I paid the real estate company a fee equal to one month's rent.
en.notes: 手数料 is a "fee" for a service or processing, for example for bank transfers and cancellations, and in brokerage also a "commission". Typical are 手数料がかかる, 手数料を払う／取る, 手数料無料, 振込手数料 and キャンセル手数料. Unlike 料金 (generally "price, rate") and 費用 ("costs"), 手数料 specifically means the charge for processing effort. Neutral and very common in daily life.

examples[].german: The money deposited at the bank gradually grows with interest.
These bacteria multiply rapidly in warm places.
The goldfish in the pond have multiplied, and it is gradually getting crowded.
en.notes: 殖える is a special spelling of ふえる for "to multiply" through reproduction or growth - for living things, bacteria or assets and interest. For a general increase (人口, 仕事, 体重) one writes 増える, and today 増える is often used even for multiplication. The verb is intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 殖やす (財産を殖やす). Related are 繁殖 "reproduction" and 養殖 "farming, cultivation".

en.meaning: weak; feeble; flimsy (grounds); weak-willed (意志薄弱)
examples[].german: Your brother told me that you are too weak-willed to break up with me, although you actually want to.
Because the evidence was too thin, the court dismissed the suit.
Unfortunately, it must be said that this claim stands on weak ground.
en.notes: 薄弱 means "weak, thin, standing on weak ground" and is combined mainly with abstract things: 根拠が薄弱だ "the grounds are thin", 証拠が薄弱, 理由が薄弱. Applied to people it appears almost only in the fixed combination 意志薄弱 "weak-willed". It is written-language; in conversation one rather says 弱い or 根拠が乏しい. For physical weakness one does not use 薄弱 but 虚弱 or 弱い.

examples[].german: He is heartless, and I have no idea whose side he is on.
Abandoning a friend in need - how heartless.
If you never get in touch after moving away, people will think you are heartless.
en.notes: 薄情 is a na-adjective for "heartless, cold-hearted, disloyal" - above all for a lack of compassion or loyalty toward people close to one (friends, family, ex-partners). Often used as a reproach: 薄情だ, 薄情な人, 薄情者. 冷たい is more everyday; 冷酷 sounds much harsher ("cruelly cold"). The opposite is 情に厚い or 人情がある.

examples[].german: You fainted from the blast wave of an explosion.
His sudden announcement of resignation was a great shock for the fans.
This case is shockproof, so nothing happens if the smartphone is dropped.
en.notes: 衝撃 is both a physical shock or impact (衝撃に強い "shock-resistant", 衝撃を吸収する) and a mental shock (衝撃を受ける, 衝撃を与える, 衝撃的な "shocking"). In contrast to ショック, which in daily life mainly means the mental shock, 衝撃 sounds more factual and stronger and is typical of news and headlines (衝撃の事実).

examples[].german: When I was given the honor of working at Tofugu, I was so thrilled by the offer that I was at a loss for words.
He was crowned with the highest honor, the Nobel Prize.
The People's Honor Award is presented to people who have given hope to the nation.
en.notes: 栄誉 is an honor or distinction publicly conferred, and it sounds formal. Typical combinations: 栄誉に輝く "to be honored with a distinction", 栄誉を受ける/得る, 栄誉ある賞; well known is the 国民栄誉賞. It should be distinguished from 名誉 "personal honor, good reputation" (名誉を傷つける, 名誉教授) and 光栄 for one's own feeling "it is an honor for me" (光栄です).

examples[].german: I hope to get a reward for my hard work.
As a reward for a perfect score on the test, my mother bought me a cake.
After a tiring week, I treated myself to expensive chocolate.
en.notes: 褒美 is a reward for good performance or good behavior and almost always appears with the polite ご: ご褒美. Typical are ご褒美をもらう/あげる and 〜のご褒美に "as a reward for ...". Very popular is 自分へのご褒美 "a treat for oneself". The word sounds personal and warm; official prizes are called 賞 or 賞品, payment for work 報酬.

examples[].german: When she tried to go up on stage to receive her award, she tripped on the stairs.
The high school student who had saved a life received a commendation from the city.
The state honors people who have contributed to society over many years.
en.notes: 褒賞 is an official reward or commendation for meritorious deeds, granted by the state, authorities or organizations; as a する-verb: 人を褒賞する "to honor someone". In contrast to the personal, everyday ご褒美, 褒賞 is formal and official. Beware: the identically read 褒章 refers to the state medals of honor (紫綬褒章 etc.), whereas 褒賞 means the reward or prize in general.

en.meaning: to show through; to be see-through
examples[].german: If you hold a silver scratch card over a glowing light bulb, you can sometimes see through the silver part to what is written underneath.
This shirt is white and thin, so the underwear shows through.
The morning light shows through the curtain.
en.notes: 透ける is intransitive: something is so thin or clear that you can see what is behind or beneath it. The form 透けて見える "to show through, to shimmer through" is very common; for clothing: 下着が透ける. Figuratively: 本音が透けて見える "one's true intentions show through". The transitive counterpart is 透かす ("to hold up against the light, to let show through"); related are 透明 and, colloquially, スケスケ "completely see-through".

examples[].german: The invisible man dried himself thoroughly with a bath towel.
The water of this lake is so clear that you can see all the way to the bottom.
The government is required to be transparent about how it spends money.
en.notes: 透明 means "see-through, clear": 透明なガラス, 透明の袋, 無色透明 "colorless and clear"; before nouns with な or の. Figuratively it stands for traceability, above all as 透明性 "transparency" in politics and business. 透明人間 is "the invisible man". Distinction: 透ける is the verb "to show through", and 半透明 means "translucent, cloudy".

examples[].german: It seems that the people in the house next door clean their windows with newspaper.
In the middle of the night, a loud noise could be heard from the house next door.
The fire spread to the neighboring house as well.
en.notes: 隣家 is the "neighboring house" in written, factual language - typical for news, police reports or literature (隣家に燃え移る). In everyday speech people almost always say 隣の家, or お隣(さん) for the neighbors themselves. Grammatically it is a noun that takes の before other nouns (隣家の住人).

examples[].german: Trust was built through many years of business dealings.
Once trust is lost, it is hard to win back.
You shouldn't trust what that person says too much.
en.notes: 信用 is trust in the reliability of a person or company and the good reputation one earns through it; in finance also "credit(worthiness)", e.g. in 信用取引 or 信用金庫. As a transitive する-verb: 人を信用する, 彼の話は信用できない; also typical are 信用を得る／失う／築く. Unlike 信頼, which expresses a deeper reliance, 信用 stresses credibility based on past experience.

examples[].german: The government values its relations with neighboring countries.
If you make noise until late at night, you disturb the residents nearby.
Before the construction work, an information session was held for the neighborhood.
en.notes: 近隣 refers to the nearby surroundings or the neighborhood of a place and usually takes の before nouns: 近隣の住民 "nearby residents", 近隣諸国 "neighboring states", 近隣トラブル "neighborhood dispute". It is factual and formal (authorities, news, notices); in conversation people say 近所 instead. 隣国, by contrast, means a single, directly adjacent country.

examples[].german: This picture on the wall is very tasteful. Who painted it?
In this garden, an old stone lantern lends the whole an elegant touch.
His letter was written in a cultivated, elegant language.
en.notes: 雅致 refers to a fine, cultivated elegance with artistic taste, especially in works of art, gardens, handwriting or texts: 雅致がある, 雅致に富む, 雅致を添える. It is a rare, elevated literary word. In daily life one rather says 上品, 趣がある or 風情がある; related is 優雅 "graceful, elegant".

examples[].german: As soon as they have a child, they will surely tell us about it with joy.
The children were running around in the snow gleefully.
He started talking enthusiastically about the new game.
en.notes: 嬉々 (also written 喜々 or 嬉嬉) describes visible, exuberant joy and appears almost only in the fixed form 嬉々として "joyfully, with enthusiasm" before a verb: 嬉々として働く/話す/遊ぶ. It is written-literary; in conversation people say 喜んで or 楽しそうに. It sometimes sounds slightly ironic when someone does something questionable with enthusiasm.

examples[].german: I fell off my bicycle and my knee hurts.
As a child, I always had a plaster on my knee.
A hole has opened up in the knee of my pants.
en.notes: 膝小僧 is a colloquial, affectionate word for the round front of the knee, that is, the area of the kneecap - literally something like "knee boy". It is used above all for children and minor injuries: 膝小僧をすりむく "to scrape one's knee". The anatomical technical term for the kneecap is 膝蓋骨; in general people simply say 膝.

examples[].german: A fairy lives inside this tulip flower.
Tinker Bell is the famous fairy from "Peter Pan".
On stage, she danced lightly, just like a fairy.
en.notes: 妖精 refers to fairies, elves and similar small nature spirits from European fairy tales and fantasy, e.g. 森の妖精 "forest fairy" or 花の妖精 "flower elf". Figuratively, 妖精のような describes a delicate, almost unreal appearance, for example in dancers or figure skaters. Japanese ghosts and spooks, by contrast, are called 妖怪 or お化け; angels are 天使.

examples[].german: She has a bewitching beauty.
In the rain-soaked night city, the neon lights glowed mysteriously.
The eyes of the woman in the picture have a bewitching charm that draws in the viewer.
en.notes: 妖しい describes a mysterious, almost uncanny power of attraction: 妖しい美しさ, 妖しい魅力, 妖しく光る. It is a literary word and sounds seductive and dark. Note: the identically read 怪しい means "suspicious, doubtful" (怪しい人, 天気が怪しい); in everyday speech this one is almost always meant, while 妖しい appears mainly in novels, song lyrics and descriptions of atmosphere.

examples[].german: Please do not take this together with alcohol, as the effect will be weakened.
The ice melted, and the juice has become watered down.
As time passes since the accident, people's sense of crisis is fading.
en.notes: 薄まる is intransitive: something becomes thinner or weaker by itself, e.g. 味が薄まる, 色が薄まる, 効果が薄まる. The transitive counterpart is 薄める "to dilute" (水で薄める). For fading memories or feelings people usually say 薄れる (記憶が薄れる), whereas 薄まる is used more for liquids, concentrations and effects.

examples[].german: Where did you buy that rolling pin?
Roll the cookie dough out thin with the rolling pin.
I didn't have a rolling pin, so I used a wine bottle instead.
en.notes: 麺棒 is the rolling pin used to roll out dough: 生地を麺棒でのばす. Beware of the identically read 綿棒 "cotton swab" - in writing the two are easy to tell apart, while in conversation only the context helps. In everyday life it is used mainly for baking and for making うどん or そば at home.

examples[].german: I've been dying for Chinese noodles all day.
Chinese noodles are used for ramen and yakisoba.
I bought fresh Chinese noodles at the supermarket and made cold ramen at home.
en.notes: 中華麺 are the yellowish, firm wheat noodles used for ラーメン, 焼きそば and 冷やし中華; their color and firmness come from alkaline water (かんすい). They can be distinguished from Japanese noodles such as うどん and そば. The word appears mainly on packaging and in recipes; when ordering a meal, one simply says ラーメン or 中華そば.

examples[].german: I have an important business meeting this afternoon.
After talking it over many times, the deal was finally settled.
I'm going on a business trip to Osaka next week for a business meeting.
en.notes: 商談 is a "business talk" or negotiation about buying, selling or cooperation. Typical are 商談がある, 商談をする, 商談に行く, 商談がまとまる ("to come to a conclusion") and 商談が成立する. In contrast to 交渉 (any kind of negotiation) and 会議 ("meeting"), 商談 always refers to a concrete deal with a customer or partner. Neutral business language.

en.meaning: noodle dipping sauce; noodle soup base
examples[].german: This noodle sauce is the best!
I dipped cold somen noodles in mentsuyu and ate them.
This mentsuyu is a concentrate, so please dilute it with water at a ratio of 1:3 before use.
en.notes: 麺つゆ is a ready-made seasoning sauce made from dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar, usually written in kana as めんつゆ. You dip cold noodles such as そうめん or ざるそば into it, or dilute it as a soup for hot noodles; many households also use it as an all-purpose seasoning for 煮物 or egg dishes. Concentrated types (濃縮タイプ) must be diluted with water.

examples[].german: All of the abduction victims have returned safely.
The man was arrested on suspicion of abducting a woman in a car.
Resolving the abduction issue is an important task for the Japanese government.
en.notes: 拉致 means to take someone away by force; as a transitive する-verb: 人を拉致する, often in the passive 拉致される. In Japan the word is closely associated with the abductions of Japanese citizens by North Korea (拉致問題, 拉致被害者). 誘拐, by contrast, is kidnapping in the criminal sense, often of a child and with a ransom demand. Register: news and formal language.

en.meaning: to become known; to come out into the world
examples[].german: It's like a dream that my work is going to be published.
With this debut novel, she became known all at once.
When smartphones first came out, they were still expensive and rare.
en.notes: 世に出る literally means "to go out into the world": a person becomes known and makes a name for themselves (この作品で世に出た), or a work or product reaches the public (新製品が世に出る). The transitive counterpart is 世に出す "to bring out, to make known". The expression sounds somewhat elevated; in everyday speech people also say 有名になる or 発売される.

examples[].german: In his last years, my grandfather became so frail that he could no longer get out of bed.
As a child I had a weak constitution and often missed school.
Various nursing-care services are available for frail elderly people.
en.notes: 虚弱 describes a weak, susceptible physical constitution; mostly as a な-adjective (虚弱な子ども) or in the fixed expression 虚弱体質. It refers to the body, not to character or willpower - for that people say 意志が弱い. In everyday speech 体が弱い sounds more natural; 虚弱 is more formal and typical of medical or nursing-care texts.

examples[].german: I am in Hong Kong on a business trip in the first half of the week.
Hong Kong's night view is called the "million-dollar night view".
As a child, I was crazy about the action scenes in Hong Kong movies.
en.notes: 香港 is pronounced ホンコン - the reading comes from Cantonese and does not follow the Japanese kanji readings. In texts the kanji spelling is usually used; in katakana it appears rarely. Common combinations are 香港ドル, 香港映画 and 香港国際空港; as a place, like other cities, it takes に (香港にいる) or で (香港で働く).

examples[].german: Nakamura insisted that he would go to the funeral alone.
I took time off work and attended my grandmother's funeral.
At the wishes of the deceased, the funeral was held with family only.
en.notes: 葬儀 is the formal word for a funeral or memorial service; in everyday speech people usually say お葬式. Typical are 葬儀に参列する "to attend a funeral", 葬儀を行う, and compounds such as 葬儀場 and 葬儀社. The actual farewell ceremony is called 告別式, and the wake on the evening before お通夜.

en.meaning: to flock; to gather in a group
examples[].german: Why do delinquent teenagers in Japan tend to hang around in groups in front of convenience stores?
Pigeons are flocking around the pond in the park.
He doesn't like going along with the crowd and always acts alone.
en.notes: 群れる is intransitive: people or animals gather in groups (鳥が群れる, 子どもたちが群れている). For people it often has a derogatory touch of "following the herd, forming cliques" (人と群れるのが嫌い). The noun is 群れ "flock, herd"; 群がる, by contrast, stresses converging on a target (蟻が砂糖に群がる).

examples[].german: By what time do we have to be back on the bus from the restroom? There is a long line, and I'm worried about being late.
Excuse me, where is the restroom?
I'll go to the restroom quickly before the meeting starts.
en.notes: おてあらい is the polite, neutral word for toilet and is almost always written お手洗い; the spelling 御手洗 is rare and is easily read as みたらし (e.g. みたらし団子) or みたらい (purification basin at a shrine). お手洗い is more polite than トイレ and fits well when asking for directions in shops or restaurants. Formal and indirect is also 化粧室.

examples[].german: Do I need to change trains to get to Gifu Prefecture?
Gifu Prefecture is an inland prefecture with no access to the sea.
During summer vacation, I visited Shirakawa-go in Gifu Prefecture.
en.notes: 岐阜県 is an inland prefecture in the 中部 region with no sea access; its capital is 岐阜市. It is known for cormorant fishing (鵜飼) on the 長良川 river and for the World Heritage village 白川郷.
