As with all prefectures, 県 can be dropped when it is clear that the region is meant (岐阜に住んでいる); 岐阜 alone can, however, also refer to the city.

examples[].german: The number of employed people in the country has risen compared with the previous year.
The proportion of non-regular employees is rising year by year.
Talks on wages continue between the employer side and the union.
en.notes: 雇用者 is ambiguous: in statistics and economic news it usually refers to employees, i.e. workers (雇用者数, 非正規雇用者). In other texts it can also mean the employer, often clarified by 雇用者側 "employer side". Anyone who clearly means the employer should rather say 雇用主 or 雇い主; one's own boss is called 社長 or 上司 in conversation.

examples[].german: It is important to gain the people's support.
I support that opinion.
The new mayor's approval rating exceeds 60 percent.
en.notes: 支持 mainly means to support or back a person, party or opinion; as a transitive する-verb with を: 〇〇党を支持する. Common are 支持を得る, 支持を集める, 支持率 ("approval rating") and 支持者 ("supporter"). In technical texts 支持 also means "to prop up, bear"; in daily life people say 支える for that. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 指示 ("instruction").

examples[].german: Paying taxes is a duty of citizens.
The deadline for paying taxes is the end of this month.
Through hometown tax donations, I received local specialties.
en.notes: 納税 is the payment of taxes to the state or municipality, i.e. "tax payment"; as a する-verb 納税する. Typical are 納税者 ("taxpayer"), 納税の義務, 納税期限 and ふるさと納税 - a Japanese system in which one donates to municipalities and can deduct this from taxes. It is official and factual; in everyday speech one mostly says 税金を払う.

examples[].german: The ground is covered with broken glass, so please be careful.
I cut my finger on a shard of the broken plate.
Pieces of the car were scattered over the scene of the accident.
en.notes: 破片 is a fragment or splinter of something broken: ガラスの破片 "glass shards", 皿の破片, 爆弾の破片. Typical are 破片が飛び散る "fragments fly about" and 破片だらけ. The colloquial かけら is similar but is also used figuratively (良心のかけらもない); 破片 stays concrete and sounds somewhat more factual.

examples[].german: Sorry. This T-shirt in size M is sold out.
Sorry I'm late.
I'm sorry, I already have something on that day...
en.notes: ごめんなさい is a personal apology used among friends, in the family or toward children; even more casual are ごめん and ごめんね. Toward superiors or customers it sounds too familiar; there one says すみません or 申し訳ありません. Unlike すみません, it is not used to thank someone or to get their attention, but it is often used for a friendly refusal ("I'm sorry, but ..."). It is almost always written in kana; the kanji 御免なさい is rarely seen.

examples[].german: Tomorrow, after visiting the family grave, I might drop by the social welfare facility.
I study social welfare at university.
As society ages, the costs of social welfare keep rising.
en.notes: 社会福祉 is the state and societal care for people who need support, such as the elderly, people with disabilities or children. Common in compounds: 社会福祉施設 "social welfare facility", 社会福祉士 "certified social worker", 社会福祉協議会. 社会保障 is broader and also includes pensions and health insurance; 福祉 alone is the shortened form (福祉の仕事). Register: formal, administrative.

examples[].german: I once decorated my pistol with flashy sequins.
The culprit is on the run with a pistol.
In Japan, it is prohibited by law for ordinary people to own a handgun.
en.notes: 拳銃 is the handgun in general, that is, a pistol or revolver; colloquially people also say ピストル. 銃 is the general term for firearms, and 鉄砲 sounds old-fashioned. Typical combinations: 拳銃を持つ, 拳銃を撃つ, 拳銃を向ける; it is counted with 丁. The word occurs mainly in crime-story and news contexts.

examples[].german: Maybe you meant it kindly, but I didn't want you to lie.
She is a kind, considerate person.
Offering your seat to elderly people is a small act of consideration.
en.notes: 思い遣り (usually written 思いやり) is the ability to put oneself in others' place and to act considerately. Typical: 思いやりがある/ない, 思いやりのある人, 思いやりに欠ける. It comes from the verb 思いやる "to think of someone, to sympathize". Unlike 同情 "pity", it stresses not regret but kind consideration in action.

examples[].german: I'm not talking about atomic bombs.
On August 6, 1945, an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.
On the school trip we visited the Atomic Bomb Museum in Nagasaki.
en.notes: 原爆 is the short form of 原子爆弾 "atomic bomb" and in Japan is almost always connected with Hiroshima and Nagasaki: 原爆が投下される, 原爆ドーム, 原爆資料館. Survivors are called 被爆者. For nuclear weapons in general one says 核兵器; 原爆 refers to the concrete bomb or the historical bombings.

examples[].german: I often see foreigners at Shibuya Station.
The scramble crossing in Shibuya is always full of people.
Tomorrow I'm meeting a friend in front of the Hachiko statue in Shibuya.
en.notes: 渋谷 is a ward (渋谷区) and a large business and entertainment district in Tokyo, known for youth culture, fashion and the スクランブル交差点 crossing. 渋谷駅 is one of the busiest stations; the statue ハチ公 in front of it is a classic meeting place (ハチ公前で待ち合わせ). As usual with places: 渋谷で遊ぶ, 渋谷に行く.

examples[].german: I forgot to charge my phone, so it ran out of battery and the alarm didn't ring.
At this cafe you can charge your smartphone for free.
This weekend I plan to recharge my batteries at a hot spring.
en.notes: 充電する means "to charge" (a battery, a device) and is transitive: スマホを充電する; also, neutrally and intransitively, 充電が切れる "the battery is dead", 充電が終わる. Related are 充電器 "charger" and 充電中. Figuratively it means "to recharge one's batteries" (温泉で充電する, 充電期間). The technical opposite is 放電 "discharge".

en.meaning: ability to provide; reliability as a breadwinner
examples[].german: I really can't understand how that good-for-nothing managed to win her heart back.
Right now, I don't have what it takes to support a family.
My mother often told me to marry someone who is able to provide for a family.
en.notes: 甲斐性 is the ability to provide energetically for oneself and others, especially to earn enough money to live on. It appears almost only in 甲斐性がある/ない and in the derogatory 甲斐性なし "good-for-nothing, loser" - classically about husbands who cannot support their family. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned and colloquial; do not confuse it with やりがい or 生きがい, which also contain 甲斐.

examples[].german: She is proud of how beautiful the backs of her hands are.
A mosquito bit me on the back of my hand, and it itches terribly.
He wiped the sweat from his forehead with the back of his hand.
en.notes: 手の甲 is the back of the hand; 甲 here refers to the curved upper side. The counterpart is 手のひら "palm"; analogously, the top of the foot is 足の甲. Typical contexts: 手の甲を刺される, 手の甲で汗をぬぐう, 手の甲にキスをする. One does not say 手の甲を持っている but describes it directly (手の甲がきれい).

examples[].german: We are taking legal tax-saving measures.
Apparently you can save on taxes if you take out this insurance.
I consulted a tax accountant about ways to save on taxes.
en.notes: 節税 means reducing the tax burden by legal means - "saving on taxes". It is meant neutrally to positively, in contrast to 脱税 ("tax evasion"), which is illegal. Typical combinations are 節税する, 節税対策, 節税効果 and 節税になる. The word follows the pattern of 節約 and 節電 ("saving electricity"), in which 節 means "to allocate sparingly".

en.meaning: sense of purpose; feeling that something is worthwhile
examples[].german: This job is very rewarding because I can be useful to someone.
The salary isn't high, but I find my work meaningful every day.
If I change jobs, I want to do more fulfilling work.
en.notes: やり甲斐 (usually written やりがい) is the feeling that an activity is worthwhile and makes sense. Fixed patterns: やりがいがある, やりがいを感じる, やりがいのある仕事. It is formed from the stem of the verb やる and 〜甲斐 "worth, reward", as in 生きがい "purpose in life" or 教えがい "it is worth teaching". Especially common in the work context and in job interviews.

examples[].german: I jumped for joy.
An unknown rookie suddenly shot up to the top.
When my younger brother heard that he had passed, he jumped up with joy.
en.notes: 躍り means "leap, hop" and hardly occurs on its own; it is encountered mainly in compounds such as 小躍り "jump for joy" (小躍りして喜ぶ), 躍り出る "to leap forward, to burst into the lead" and 躍り上がる "to jump up". Do not confuse it with the identically read 踊り "dance". Related is the verb 躍る, for instance in 胸が躍る "one's heart leaps with excitement".

en.meaning: to devote oneself to; to stick to
examples[].german: In today's meeting I want to confine myself entirely to listening.
The rescue team searched for the missing all night long.
After his active career, he supported the team exclusively behind the scenes.
en.notes: 徹する means to confine oneself fully and consistently to one role or attitude: 聞き役に徹する "to only listen", 裏方に徹する "to work entirely in the background", 守りに徹する. With time expressions, 夜を徹して means "all night long". The verb is intransitive and takes に; in contrast to 専念する, it emphasizes deliberately doing nothing else. Register: elevated, written and in speeches.

en.meaning: to stay up all night; all-nighter
examples[].german: It's just like her to study English all night long.
I wrote my report all night yesterday, so I'm dying to sleep.
Rather than pulling an all-nighter, it is more efficient to go to bed early and study in the morning.
en.notes: 徹夜 means not sleeping all night, e.g. in order to study or work: 徹夜する, 徹夜で勉強する, 徹夜明け "after a night without sleep". A night shift at work, by contrast, is 夜勤, and simply staying up late is 夜更かし. 徹夜 is a noun or a する-verb, not an adverb; the adverbial "all night long" only arises with で.

examples[].german: A thorough investigation was carried out into the cause of the accident.
The company instructed all employees to strictly enforce the handling of personal information.
At the end of the year, I cleaned my room thoroughly.
en.notes: 徹底 means thoroughness and complete, gap-free enforcement. As a する-verb it is both transitive (ルールを徹底する "to enforce a rule consistently") and intransitive (指示が徹底していない "instructions are not being consistently followed"). Very common are 徹底した + noun (徹底した調査), the adjective 徹底的な/徹底的に "thorough, through and through", and 周知徹底 "making sure everyone knows". Register: neutral to formal, typical of business and official language.

en.meaning: shallows; shallow part of a river
examples[].german: The river is shallow around here, so I'm sure your feet will reach the bottom.
Takase boats were built with flat bottoms so that they could carry cargo even on shallow rivers.
Mori Ogai's "Takasebune" often appears in Japanese school textbooks.
en.notes: 高瀬 refers to a flat, shallow stretch of a river; today the word is rare and is encountered mainly in 高瀬舟, a flat river boat for freight, and in place names such as the 高瀬川 in Kyoto. It is well known through Mori Ogai's story "高瀬舟". For "shallow spot", everyday speech uses 浅瀬 or simply 浅い所.

examples[].german: I read the news about the clearing of rubble on the internet.
Bicycles left abandoned in front of the station are removed by the city.
Work to take down the old signboard has begun.
en.notes: 撤去 means the removal or dismantling of objects and installations: 看板を撤去する, 放置自転車の撤去, 瓦礫の撤去. It is transitive and often appears in the passive (撤去される). Do not confuse it with 撤回 "withdrawal (of a statement)" and 撤退 "retreat"; 除去 refers more to the removal of substances (汚れの除去). Register: formal, the language of authorities and news.

examples[].german: Sorry. I take back what I said.
The minister retracted the controversial remark and apologized.
In response to a backlash from customers, the company withdrew the price increase.
en.notes: 撤回 is the withdrawal of a statement, decision or demand: 発言を撤回する, 決定を撤回する, 撤回を求める. It is transitive and sounds formal; in everyday speech people also say 取り消す. The set phrase 前言撤回 "I take back what I said" is also used jokingly in conversation. Do not confuse it with 撤去 "removal of objects".

examples[].german: I have never been ashamed of that troop withdrawal.
Following the ceasefire agreement, both countries withdrew their troops from the border area.
The government announced a policy of withdrawing all units by next year.
en.notes: 撤兵 is the withdrawal of troops from a region: 〜から撤兵する. It is intransitive; the opposite is 派兵 "to dispatch troops" or 出兵. 撤退 is more general and refers to any retreat, including in business (市場から撤退する). 撤兵 belongs to the political-military language of news and history.

examples[].german: I was moved by how wonderful the wording of your poem is.
In haiku, the choice of each individual word greatly affects the impression of the work.
My teacher carefully corrected the wording of my composition one item at a time.
en.notes: 措辞 is an elevated, literary word for word choice and phrasing in a text, especially in poems, haiku and essays. One speaks of 措辞が巧みだ or 措辞が適切だ. In everyday speech people say 言葉遣い, 言い回し or 表現 instead; 措辞 appears almost only in literary criticism and haiku reviews.

examples[].german: I looked for job listings on the internet.
The convenience store in front of the station is advertising for part-timers.
Because of labor shortages, the number of job openings is increasing.
en.notes: 求人 is an employer's search for workers, i.e. a "job opening, job advertisement". Typical are 求人を出す, 求人広告, 求人情報, 求人サイト and 有効求人倍率 ("ratio of job openings to applicants"). The counterpart from the job seekers' point of view is 求職 ("job hunting"). Neutral, very common in advertisements and economic news.

en.meaning: to be based on; to be caused by
examples[].german: Thanks to everyone's support, I was able to succeed. As a token of my gratitude, I would like to give you some bacon.
The road closure is caused by last night's heavy rain.
This idea stems from past experience.
en.notes: 拠る is read よる here and means to be based on something or to be caused by something. The basis or cause stands before に; によって often names it in a full sentence. よる is usually written in hiragana. For an origin or cause, the rarer spelling 因る is also found. 拠って is the て-form of the godan verb; the identically read words 寄る and 夜 have other meanings.

examples[].german: We will move our production base overseas.
That band is based in Osaka and performs from there.
Using a hotel in Kyoto as our base, we toured the sightseeing spots in the area.
en.notes: 拠点 is a base or location from which one is active: 〜を拠点に(して)活動する, 拠点を置く, 拠点を移す. Common in business (生産拠点, 営業拠点) and the military (戦略的拠点). 本拠地 stresses the headquarters, e.g. of a sports club, and 基地 is above all a military or technical base.

examples[].german: Why do Japanese people keep bowing all the time?
When you meet your teacher, bow properly.
In a job interview, you bow lightly before entering the room.
en.notes: What is meant is the bow, which is practically always used with the polite prefix as お辞儀 (お辞儀をする); 辞儀 without お is obsolete. Depending on depth, one distinguishes 会釈 (a slight nod), 敬礼 and 最敬礼 (a deep bow). Typical are 深くお辞儀をする, 軽くお辞儀をする and the onomatopoeic ペコペコお辞儀する "to keep bowing subserviently".

examples[].german: Working in an orchard is rather boring.
We planted fruit trees such as apples and mandarins in the garden.
This region has a mild climate, and fruit growing is thriving.
en.notes: 果樹 is a fruit tree; the word is rather technical or written and appears mainly in 果樹園 "orchard, fruit plantation" and 果樹栽培 "fruit growing". For the fruit itself, people say 果物 or, technically, 果実. In everyday speech people often say something concrete like りんごの木 or みかんの木 instead of 果樹.

examples[].german: To commemorate our wedding, my husband and I planted a sugar maple in the garden.
Every spring, local volunteers plant trees in the mountains.
To commemorate graduation, a cherry tree was planted in the schoolyard.
en.notes: 植樹 is the (usually ceremonial or organized) planting of trees, for example as 記念植樹 or at a 植樹祭 and reforestation campaigns. As a する-verb it takes the tree species as its object (桜を植樹する); 木を植樹する is redundant, since 樹 already means "tree". In everyday speech people simply say 木を植える; 植樹 sounds more formal.

examples[].german: My parents neglected me, and I grew up in a children's home.
Because the debts were so high, my brother renounced the inheritance.
Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution stipulates the renunciation of war.
en.notes: 放棄 means to consciously give up or waive a right, duty or thing: 権利を放棄する, 相続を放棄する, 試合を放棄する, 責任放棄. Well known is 戦争の放棄 in Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution, as well as 育児放棄 "child neglect". It is transitive and formal; 諦める rather expresses the inner giving up of a wish, 捨てる the throwing away.

examples[].german: A couple in matching T-shirts with a fierce tiger face printed on them is walking arm in arm right in front of me.
A tiger cub was born at the zoo.
When my father drinks too much, he gets drunk and starts singing at the top of his voice.
en.notes: 虎 is the tiger; in zoos and biological texts it is often written in katakana トラ. The kanji appears in sayings such as 虎の威を借る狐 "the fox who borrows the tiger's might" (to throw one's weight around with borrowed authority). Colloquially, 虎 also means "a drunk": 虎になる "to get uninhibitedly drunk". Do not confuse it with 寅, the tiger of the zodiac (寅年).

examples[].german: She tasted a bite of my honey pudding.
When I have a sore throat, I drink black tea with honey.
You must not give honey to babies under one year old.
en.notes: 蜂蜜 is honey, composed of 蜂 "bee" and 蜜 "nectar, honey". It is mostly written in kana as はちみつ or ハチミツ; the kanji are seen more on labels of traditional products. Typical are 蜂蜜を塗る (on bread), 蜂蜜を入れる (in tea) and compounds like 蜂蜜レモン.

examples[].german: Several Maritime Self-Defense Force ships were lined up in the harbor.
On the anniversary, the naval ships were opened to the public.
More than twenty naval ships from various countries took part in this exercise.
en.notes: 艦船 is a collective term for warships and other ships of a navy; it is mostly used in a plural sense, as in 艦船が停泊する or 十隻の艦船. It is counted with 隻. A single warship is more often called 軍艦 or 艦, and a formation 艦隊. The word belongs to news and military language.

examples[].german: I had expected stronger resistance from the enemy fleet, so I feel somewhat let down.
The base of the US Seventh Fleet is in Yokosuka.
The admiral set sail leading a large fleet.
en.notes: 艦隊 is a fleet of warships, that is, a formation under common command: 艦隊を率いる, 太平洋艦隊, 連合艦隊. For civilian groups of ships, such as convoys or fishing fleets, people say 船団 instead. The word appears in history, news and also in science fiction (宇宙艦隊).

examples[].german: There is a pay raise once a year.
Business results were good this year, so everyone got a raise.
I decided to talk with my boss to ask for a raise.
en.notes: 昇給 is a "pay raise" for an employee, usually as part of regular adjustments; the opposite is 減給 ("pay cut"). Typical are 昇給がある, 昇給する, 定期昇給 and 昇給率. In contrast to 昇進 ("promotion"), it is only about money, not position; the general wage increase in collective bargaining is called 賃上げ or ベースアップ. Neutral language of the working world.

examples[].german: I plan to open a specialty shop for warship model kits.
When a foreign warship entered the port, there was great excitement in the town.
Gunkan-maki with salmon roe are so called because their shape resembles a warship.
en.notes: 軍艦 is the general word for a warship. A battleship in the narrower sense is called 戦艦, an aircraft carrier 空母; several warships together are 艦船 or, as a formation, 艦隊. The word is also known from sushi cuisine: 軍艦巻き are rice morsels wrapped in nori whose shape is reminiscent of a warship.

examples[].german: I probably lost my other earring in that submarine.
A submarine can stay submerged in the sea for a long time.
When I was a child, I once built a submarine model kit.
en.notes: 潜水艦 is the submarine (潜水 "diving" + 艦 "warship"). The character 艦 marks military ships, cf. 軍艦, 戦艦, 艦隊. Smaller civilian diving vessels for research or tourism are more often called 潜水艇 or 潜水調査船. Matching verbs: 潜る or 潜航する "to dive" and 浮上する "to surface".

examples[].german: That aircraft carrier suddenly disappeared from view.
Aircraft carriers are often called "kuubo" for short.
Fighter planes took off one after another from the deck of the aircraft carrier.
en.notes: 航空母艦 is the full, formal name for an aircraft carrier; in the news and in conversation the short form 空母 is almost always used. Typical combinations are 空母の甲板 "flight deck", 原子力空母 and 空母打撃群. The word is composed of 航空 "aviation" and 母艦 "mother ship".

examples[].german: Nuclear-powered submarines are sometimes called "gensen" for short.
Every time an American nuclear submarine makes a port call, protesting citizens gather.
A nuclear submarine can stay submerged and operate for a long time without refueling.
en.notes: 原潜 is the abbreviation of 原子力潜水艦 "nuclear submarine" and is used mainly in the news and in headlines (原潜が寄港する, 米原潜). Conventional submarines are simply called 潜水艦. Similar abbreviations with 原 are 原発 "nuclear power plant" and 原爆 "atomic bomb".

examples[].german: My sister got her diving license this summer.
He can dive for over two minutes holding his breath.
The ama divers dive without equipment and gather shellfish.
en.notes: 潜水 is diving underwater, as an intransitive suru-verb 潜水する. It sounds more factual than the everyday verb 潜る and often appears in compounds: 潜水艦 "submarine", 潜水士 "professional diver", 潜水服 "diving suit". For recreational sport diving one mostly says ダイビング or スキューバダイビング.

examples[].german: It's often said that dreams reflect our subconscious, isn't it?
Experiences from childhood remain in the subconscious even in adulthood.
This advertisement is designed to appeal to consumers' subconscious.
en.notes: 潜在意識 is the subconscious, that is, the layer of consciousness that is not directly accessible to us: 潜在意識に働きかける, 潜在意識の中に残る. 潜在 means "hidden, latent", cf. 潜在能力 "hidden abilities" and 潜在的な. Largely synonymous but shaped by psychoanalysis is 無意識 "the unconscious". The word is a noun and belongs to the vocabulary of psychology and self-help.

examples[].german: My father pretended he was going to hit me with his fist.
Because I had been mischievous, Grandpa gave me a knuckle rap.
He clenched his fist and held back his anger.
en.notes: 拳骨 (usually written げんこつ) is the clenched fist, above all as a means of hitting. Typical are げんこつを食らわせる/落とす "to give a knuckle rap" and げんこつをもらう "to get a knuckle rap" - classically the punishment from a father or teacher. The neutral word for fist is 拳 (こぶし); げんこつ sounds colloquial and somewhat old-fashioned.

examples[].german: What is the difference between carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide?
Diamonds consist of nothing but carbon.
Many countries in the world are aiming for a climate-neutral society.
en.notes: 炭素 is the chemical element carbon (C). It is most often encountered in compounds like 二酸化炭素 "carbon dioxide" and 一酸化炭素 "carbon monoxide" as well as in environmental terms like 脱炭素 "decarbonization" and 炭素税 "carbon tax". 炭 alone, by contrast, is charcoal. In daily life カーボン is also used, e.g. for materials.

examples[].german: These days, plowing fields without machines is a waste of time.
Heavy rain made the river overflow, and the fields were flooded.
My grandfather carefully looks after the fields inherited from his ancestors.
en.notes: 田畑 combines rice paddies (田) and dry fields (畑) and refers to the farmland of a farmer or of an area; the reading たはた is common, and でんぱた also occurs. Typical are 田畑を耕す, 田畑が荒れる and 田畑を手放す. The word sounds somewhat written; in conversation people say 田んぼ or 畑 instead.

examples[].german: He was held responsible for the failure and demoted.
That team performed poorly and was relegated to the second division.
He could not accept the demotion and quit the company.
en.notes: 降格 is a lowering to a lower level: at work a "demotion", in sports "relegation" to a lower league. It is used both transitively and intransitively: 部長を降格させる／降格する, 課長に降格される, チームが二部に降格する. The opposite is 昇格 ("promotion to a higher rank"); related is 昇進 ("promotion"). Factual, common in company and sports news.

examples[].german: That building will soon be surrounded by the police.
The enemy army besieged the castle and waited for the food supplies to run out.
The culprit slipped through the police cordon and escaped.
en.notes: 包囲する means "to encircle, surround, besiege" and is transitive: 〜を包囲する. The passive 〜に包囲される ("to be surrounded by ...") is very common, for example in police operations; historically it refers to the siege of a castle or city. 包囲網 is the "dragnet" or encirclement. In everyday speech people say 囲む or 取り囲む instead; 包囲 sounds like news and military language.

en.meaning: humanity and justice; code of honor; duty
examples[].german: There is no honor among thieves.
My grandfather was a man who valued honor and decency, and he always repaid favors he had received.
Before going independent, I paid my respects to the president of my former company.
en.notes: 仁義 originally refers to the Confucian virtues 仁 "humanity" and 義 "justice"; today it mostly means the code of honor or the duty of decency among people, especially in the world of the yakuza. Typical are 仁義を重んじる ("to value honor and decency") and 仁義なき ("without honor"). 仁義を切る is originally the formal greeting among yakuza, and colloquially also "to inform someone beforehand as a matter of courtesy". The word sounds old-fashioned and somewhat rough.

examples[].german: When I worked in the mine, I constantly had back pain.
This town was once prosperous thanks to its copper mine.
In a mining accident, workers were trapped underground.
en.notes: 鉱山 is a mine in which ores or minerals are extracted; specific kinds are called 金山, 銀山 or 銅山, a coal mine by contrast 炭鉱. Typical are 鉱山で働く, 鉱山を開発する and 鉱山事故 "mining accident". Be careful when listening: 高山 ("high mountain") is also read こうざん. A military explosive mine is not 鉱山 but 地雷.

examples[].german: Any ore he touches turns to gold.
Iron ore has been mined in this area since long ago.
At the museum, I saw samples of rare ores.
en.notes: 鉱石 is "ore", that is, rock from which a metal is extracted; compounds are 鉄鉱石 "iron ore" and 金鉱石 "gold ore". Typical verbs are 鉱石を採掘する ("to mine") and 鉱石が採れる ("to be obtained"). It should be distinguished from the scientific term 鉱物 "mineral" and from the gemstone 宝石, even though in everyday speech 鉱石 sometimes loosely refers to pretty crystals.

examples[].german: Hmm. It's really a shame that this coal mine is going to close.
In his youth, my grandfather worked in a coal mine in Kyushu.
Yubari, which once flourished as a coal-mining town, now focuses on tourism.
en.notes: 炭鉱 is a coal mine (炭 "coal" + 鉱 "mine, ore"); ore mines in general are 鉱山. The spelling 炭坑 properly refers to the shaft but is often used with the same meaning. Typical are 炭鉱で働く, 炭鉱の町 and 閉山 ("closure of a mine"); miners are called 炭鉱労働者 or, older, 炭鉱夫. In Japan the word is associated with the decline of towns such as Yubari or those in Kyushu.

examples[].german: I mined a lot of iron ore in Minecraft.
Australia is one of the world's leading exporters of iron ore.
It is said that high-quality iron ore lies buried in this mountain.
en.notes: 鉄鉱 means "iron ore" but on its own occurs rather in technical texts; in normal usage people almost always say 鉄鉱石. Typical are 鉄鉱石を輸入する, 鉄鉱石を採掘する and 鉄鉱山 ("iron ore mine"). Do not confuse it with the identically read 鉄鋼 てっこう "iron and steel", as in 鉄鋼業 "steel industry" - that is the processed product, not the raw material.

examples[].german: My father asked me if I knew what the 11th day after the summer solstice is called, and I proudly answered "hage-sho", but it seems that means "bald-head symptom". He laughed and told me the correct answer is "hangesho".
The summer solstice is the day with the longest daylight of the year.
In Scandinavia, a big festival is held on the day of the summer solstice.
en.notes: 夏至 is the summer solstice around June 21, the day with the longest daylight. Note the unusual reading げし (夏 read as げ). The counterpart is 冬至 (とうじ), on which people in Japan traditionally take a yuzu bath and eat pumpkin; the equinoxes are called 春分 and 秋分. 夏至 is one of the 二十四節気 and falls in the middle of the rainy season in Japan.

examples[].german: Why do they say in Japan that it is good to eat pumpkin on the winter solstice?
The winter solstice is the day with the shortest daylight of the year.
On the night of the winter solstice, it is customary to take a bath with yuzu.
en.notes: 冬至 is the winter solstice around December 22, the day with the shortest daylight; the counterpart is 夏至 げし "summer solstice". It is usually used as 冬至の日 or 冬至には. In Japan, people traditionally eat pumpkin (かぼちゃ) on this day and take a yuzu bath (ゆず湯). Do not confuse it with the identically read 当時 "at that time".

examples[].german: If this continues, a deficit is inevitable.
Experts believe that a tax increase will inevitably worsen the economy.
With the key players gone, the team is bound to struggle.
en.notes: 必至 means "inevitable, certain to occur" and is usually used predicatively as 〜は必至だ, almost always for undesirable developments: 値上げは必至, 苦戦は必至. It belongs to written and news language. Beware of two common mix-ups: 必死 (same reading) means "desperate, with all one's might", and 必須 ひっす means "indispensable, mandatory" - 必至 is wrong for "necessary".

examples[].german: He may be a smart man who graduated at the top of his class from a prestigious university, but he is obviously a white supremacist, and I dislike that about him.
Putting our customers' safety first is our company's supreme imperative.
Time spent with my family is the greatest joy for me.
en.notes: 至上 means "the highest, supreme" and is usually used attributively as 至上の〜 (至上の喜び "greatest joy") or in compounds: 至上命令 "supreme imperative" and 〜至上主義 "the ideology of putting X above everything" (利益至上主義, 学歴至上主義, 白人至上主義). The latter usually sound critical. Do not confuse it with the homophones 史上 "in history" (史上初) and 市場 "market".

examples[].german: The minimum wage was raised.
The gender wage gap is still large.
The labor union demanded a wage increase from the company.
en.notes: 賃金 is pay for work in the general, factual sense, "wages". Typical are 最低賃金 ("minimum wage"), 賃金を引き上げる, 賃金格差 ("wage gap") and the short form 賃上げ ("wage increase"). In daily life, people talk about their own income more as 給料 or 給与; 賃金 sounds like statistics, labor law and unions. For hourly or monthly pay there are 時給 and 月給.

examples[].german: Since I heard an explanation made in good faith, I decided to hear her side this time.
If you made a mistake, you should first apologize sincerely.
I can't sense any sincerity in the company's response.
en.notes: 誠意 is "sincerity, good faith", especially as an attitude shown in apologies, negotiations or complaints: 誠意を持って謝る, 誠意を見せる, 誠意ある対応. A typical reproach is 誠意が感じられない. The character trait "sincere, honest", by contrast, is expressed with the な-adjective 誠実. 誠意のこもった〜 means "carried by sincerity".

examples[].german: Looking back now, Hachiko was a good dog with absolute loyalty.
The knights swore loyalty to the king.
The days when employees were required to show loyalty to the company are over.
en.notes: 忠誠 is "loyalty, allegiance" toward a lord, state or organization. Typical phrases are 〜に忠誠を誓う ("to swear loyalty to ..."), 〜への忠誠 and 忠誠心 ("loyalty" as an attitude). The な-adjective 忠実, by contrast, means "faithful, conscientious, true" (原文に忠実な翻訳). Do not confuse it with the homophones 中世 "Middle Ages" and 中性 "neutral".

examples[].german: Visiting my hometown is a waste of time and money.
After retiring, I want to return to my hometown and grow vegetables.
My mother back home sends me apples every year.
en.notes: 郷里 is the hometown or region one comes from; it sounds somewhat elevated and written-language. Typical are 郷里に帰る, 郷里の両親 and 郷里を離れる. In daily life one rather says 地元, 田舎 or 故郷 (ふるさと), and for the parental home 実家. Returning to one's hometown is called 帰郷.

examples[].german: Like most gamblers, she believed she had a gift for it, but in the end she lost everything in a game of poker and had to return to her hometown.
When I returned to my hometown for the first time in ten years, the area in front of the station had completely changed.
After graduating from university, he returned to his hometown and took over the family business.
en.notes: 帰郷する means "to return to one's home region" and is intransitive; it is usually used without a destination, otherwise with に. It sounds somewhat written and can mean a visit or a permanent return. For the holiday visit to one's parents at New Year or Obon, 帰省 is the usual word; moving back to one's hometown is colloquially also 地元に戻る. The noun on its own means "homecoming".

examples[].german: This computer virus infects thousands of computers when the clock strikes midnight on New Year's Eve.
The burglar broke a window and broke into the house.
Entry by anyone other than authorized persons is prohibited.
en.notes: 侵入 is unauthorized or forcible entry; as an intransitive する-verb, the target takes に: 家に侵入する, システムに侵入する. Common compounds are 不法侵入 "trespassing" and 侵入者 "intruder". Beware of words read the same: 進入 is vehicles entering (車両進入禁止), and 浸入 is water seeping in. 侵略 refers to the military invasion of a country.

en.meaning: to violate; to invade; to affect (disease)
examples[].german: Many people are angry that their privacy was violated.
An aircraft of unknown origin violated the airspace.
The examination revealed that his body was affected by cancer.
en.notes: 侵す means "to invade foreign territory, to violate rights" and is transitive: 領空を侵す, プライバシーを侵す, 権利を侵す; often in the passive (〜を侵される). For diseases, 〜に侵される "to be afflicted by" is used. One must separate it from two verbs read the same: 犯す "to commit a crime, to make a mistake, to break a rule" and 冒す "to take a risk" (危険を冒す).

examples[].german: My uncle was arrested for falsifying the labels on his company's products and is currently in prison.
A sham marriage for a visa was discovered, and both were arrested.
The soldiers camouflaged the tank with branches.
en.notes: 偽装 is "camouflage, pretense, concealment"; 偽装する is transitive (〜を偽装する). In the news it appears in compounds such as 産地偽装 ("false labeling of origin"), 偽装結婚 ("sham marriage") or 偽装工作 ("cover-up maneuver"), and militarily for camouflage. Distinctions: 偽造 is the forging of an object (money, a passport), and 変装 is the disguising of a person.

examples[].german: Two kinds of counterfeit money started circulating in Tokyo on the same day.
A man was arrested on suspicion of forging a passport.
He forged his superior's signature and submitted the documents.
en.notes: 偽造 is the forging of objects, especially money and documents: 紙幣を偽造する, パスポートの偽造, 偽造カード, 偽造品. It is transitive and is often used in the passive or attributively (偽造された書類). Distinctions: 偽装 is disguise or the feigning of facts, 改ざん is the subsequent altering of existing data. Counterfeit brand goods are usually called 偽物 in daily life.

examples[].german: You're joking, right?
You must not lie to children.
He does nothing but lie, so I can't believe him anymore.
en.notes: 嘘 is a lie; "to lie" is 嘘をつく (not 嘘を言う as the standard), a liar is 嘘つき. As an exclamation うそ！ or 嘘でしょう？ it colloquially means "Really? No way!" and is not an accusation. The word is often written in kana as うそ.

examples[].german: The hourly wage for this part-time job is 1,000 yen.
At night, the hourly wage goes up by 25 percent.
The hourly wage is low, but the work is easy, so I keep at it.
en.notes: 時給 is the wage per hour, "hourly wage", typical for アルバイト and パート. Common expressions are 時給千円, 時給がいい／高い, 時給が上がる and 時給で働く. Besides this there are 日給 ("daily wage"), 月給 ("monthly salary") and 年収 ("annual income"). Everyday word, omnipresent in job ads.

examples[].german: Usopp is a liar.
"A liar will also steal," my mother often told me as a child.
If you constantly break promises, people will think you are a liar.
en.notes: 嘘吐き is "liar", derived from 嘘をつく "to lie"; it is almost always written 嘘つき or うそつき, the kanji 吐き are rare. It can be used directly as an insult (この嘘つき!) and often appears in 〜は嘘つきだ. Well known is the proverb 嘘つきは泥棒の始まり ("a liar will also steal"). The word is direct and derogatory; more cautiously one paraphrases with 嘘をつく人.

examples[].german: It's amazing that he could talk at just six months old!
It rained really hard last night, didn't it?
Your Japanese is really very good!
en.notes: すごい is almost always written in kana and expresses a high degree, positive or negative: すごい人 "an impressive person", すごい雨 "heavy rain". As a reaction, すごい！ or すごいですね is very common. Before adjectives, standard language uses the adverb form すごく (すごく上手); すごい きれい is casual. More formal is 素晴らしい "wonderful".

en.meaning: quarrel, fight; to quarrel, to fight (けんかする)
examples[].german: Don't fight!
I had a fight with my girlfriend yesterday.
As a child, I often fought with my younger brother.
en.notes: 喧嘩 is a quarrel, ranging from a war of words to a brawl; as a verb 喧嘩する means "to quarrel, to fight", the person takes と: 友達と喧嘩する, 喧嘩になる "it comes to a fight". Typical are 兄弟喧嘩 and 夫婦喧嘩, a purely verbal quarrel is 口喧嘩, and to make up again is 仲直りする. Because of the difficult kanji, it is mostly written けんか or ケンカ.

examples[].german: "Ah, so noisy! Shut up!"
The construction noise is so loud that I can't sleep even at night.
My father was a man who was particular about how one spoke.
en.notes: やかましい is usually written in kana and first means "noisy, unpleasantly loud", similar to the more common うるさい; as an exclamation (ああ、やかましい!) it is rude. Second, it means "strict, fussy": 〜にやかましい ("to be fussy about ..."), 口やかましい ("constantly nagging"). As with うるさい, annoyance or nuisance is always implied; neutral "loud" is 大きい音, or にぎやか for cheerful bustle.

examples[].german: Why do you think Tofugu made such great strides this year?
The opposition made major gains in this election.
With the hit of its new product, the company jumped to third place in the industry.
en.notes: 躍進 is a big leap forward, a rapid rise in rank or importance. As an intransitive する-verb it is often used with a destination (業界三位に躍進する), and as a noun in 大躍進を遂げる. Typical contexts are elections, sports and business. 進歩, by contrast, means gradual progress, and 発展 development and growth in general.

examples[].german: Aya's latest illustration of the Tofugu characters is full of dynamism.
The audience was greatly excited by the sight of the players moving energetically on the field.
In spring, you feel the pulse of life in nature.
en.notes: 躍動 refers to powerful, lively movement, the pulsing of energy (躍 "jump" + 動 "move"). The word is written-language and typical of sports reports, art criticism and advertising: 躍動する選手, 生命の躍動, 躍動感あふれる "full of dynamism". As a する-verb it is intransitive. In everyday speech people say 生き生きとした or ダイナミックな instead. Do not confuse it with 活躍 "to distinguish oneself, to work successfully".

examples[].german: I didn't know that it would count as illegal dumping.
Old home appliances had been dumped in the mountains.
Dumping hazardous substances into the ocean is banned by international treaty.
en.notes: 投棄 is the careless throwing away or dumping of things, usually waste; it almost always appears in 不法投棄 ("illegal dumping"), ゴミの投棄 or 海洋投棄 ("ocean dumping"). The word belongs to official and news language; in everyday speech people simply say 捨てる. 廃棄, by contrast, is orderly disposal or decommissioning, and 放棄 is giving up a right or plan.

en.meaning: to rush in; to dash into
examples[].german: I tried to dash onto the last train, but the door closed right in front of me.
It suddenly started to rain, so I dashed into a nearby convenience store.
Having dropped his wallet, he rushed into the police box in a panic.
en.notes: 駆け込む means "to run in, to rush in" and is intransitive: 〜に駆け込む. It often implies hurrying to find shelter or help (交番に駆け込む, 病院に駆け込む). The noun 駆け込み appears in set expressions such as 駆け込み乗車 ("boarding at the last second", expressly prohibited in stations) and 駆け込み需要 ("last-minute demand" before a price increase). Distinctions: 飛び込む "to jump into", 駆け出す "to start running".

en.meaning: to start running; to dash out
examples[].german: When I asked him a question, he suddenly ran off.
When the light turned green, the children all started running at once.
It started to rain, so I ran off toward the station.
en.notes: 駆け出す means "to start running, to suddenly break into a run" or "to run out" (駆ける "run" + 〜出す "begin; out"): 家から駆け出す. It is intransitive and used mainly for people and animals; the neutral 走り出す also suits vehicles. The noun 駆け出し "beginner, newcomer" is very common: 駆け出しの記者 "a rookie journalist".

en.meaning: unfilial child; ungrateful son or daughter
examples[].german: My mother called me an "unfilial child".
Not even coming home for your parents' funeral - what an unfilial child.
I didn't go home for years - I was truly an unfilial child.
en.notes: 不孝者 is someone who neglects their duties toward their parents (孝 "filial piety"). Today one mostly hears 親不孝者 or 親不孝 (親不孝をする); the opposite is 親孝行. The word is used as a reproach or in self-criticism and sounds somewhat old-fashioned. Do not confuse it with the identically read 不幸 "misfortune".

examples[].german: I used my paid leave to go on a trip.
I have twenty days of paid leave a year.
Before resigning, I used up all my remaining paid leave.
en.notes: 有給 first means "paid, with continued pay" (有給の仕事, 有給休暇); in everyday speech it is the common short form of 有給休暇 ("paid leave"). Typical are 有給を取る, 有給を使う and 有給を消化する ("to use up the remaining leave"). The opposite is 無給 ("unpaid"). One also reads 有休 - same reading, different character - with the same meaning "paid leave".

en.meaning: lack of filial piety; unfilial child
examples[].german: It's already too late, but I was truly an unfilial son.
It is said that dying before your parents is the greatest unfilial act.
Making your parents worry by not getting in touch is unfilial.
en.notes: 親不孝 is the opposite of 親孝行: the behavior of a child who does not honor their parents and causes them worry or grief; it also refers to the ungrateful child themselves (親不孝者). It is used as a noun, as a な-adjective (親不孝な息子) and as a する-verb (親不孝をする). A well-known idea is that dying before one's parents is the greatest 親不孝. "Disrespect" in general would be 失礼 or 無礼 instead.

examples[].german: "May I borrow your cell phone?" "Yes, go ahead."
Please turn off your mobile phone during class.
In Japan, talking on a mobile phone on the train is considered bad manners.
en.notes: 携帯電話 is the mobile phone; in everyday speech it is almost always shortened to 携帯 or ケータイ, for smartphones people say スマホ, and for older flip phones ガラケー. Typical are 携帯電話の電源を切る, 携帯電話で話す and 携帯電話を充電する. 携帯 on its own originally means "to carry with oneself" (携帯する, 携帯用). The full form sounds rather formal, for example in announcements and house rules.

examples[].german: Until recently, 3D printers were state-of-the-art machines.
That hospital is equipped with state-of-the-art medical devices.
State-of-the-art robots have been introduced in the factory.
en.notes: 最新鋭 is composed of 最新 "newest" and 鋭 "sharp, elite" and means "state-of-the-art, at the latest technical level". It is almost always used attributively as 最新鋭の〜 with machines, weapons, facilities and devices (最新鋭の戦闘機, 最新鋭の設備). For fashion, news or software versions, people simply say 最新; 最新鋭 stresses top technical performance.

examples[].german: Could you explain to me what the baseball terms sacrifice fly and sacrifice bunt mean?
They took a one-run lead in the third inning on a sacrifice fly.
In the ninth inning, he hit a sacrifice fly to tie the game.
en.notes: 犠飛 is the short form of 犠牲フライ, the "sacrifice fly" in baseball: the batter is put out but allows a runner to score. The short form appears mainly in sports reports and statistics (犠飛で一点); in speech people usually say 犠牲フライ. The counterpart is 犠打 or 犠牲バント "sacrifice bunt".

examples[].german: This is the girls' changing room, which has opaque windows.
The economic outlook remains uncertain.
It is criticized that how the political funds are used is not transparent.
en.notes: 不透明 literally means "opaque, cloudy" (glass, liquids, plastic), the opposite of 透明. Very common is the figurative use in news and business: 先行きが不透明 ("the outlook is uncertain") or 不透明なお金の流れ ("opaque money flows"). Fittingly, "transparency" is 透明性. As a な-adjective: 不透明な〜, 不透明だ.

examples[].german: I remember the Lunar New Year of ten years ago in detail.
She records the events of each day in detail in her diary.
The film depicts the misery of war in minute detail.
en.notes: 克明 means "exact, down to the smallest detail" and is mostly used adverbially: 克明に記録する, 克明に描く, 克明に覚えている. Attributively it appears as 克明な記録 or 克明な描写. It sounds written; in everyday speech people say 詳しく or 細かく. 鮮明, by contrast, stresses the clarity and vividness of a memory or image, not the completeness of its details.

examples[].german: I was too excited when I arrived in Japan, wasn't I?
The plane arrived at Narita thirty minutes behind schedule.
When the package arrives, please check the contents right away.
en.notes: 到着 is "arrival"; as an intransitive する-verb the destination takes に: 東京に到着する. It is the formal counterpart of 着く and appears in announcements, timetables and e-mails (到着時刻, 到着予定, 到着ロビー). Shipments also "arrive": 荷物が到着する. The opposite is 出発; 到達, on the other hand, means "to reach a goal or level".

examples[].german: Do you have these binoculars in black?
My hobby is watching wild birds with binoculars.
It's handy to bring binoculars to concerts.
en.notes: 双眼鏡 means binoculars, literally "double-eye glass". It is used with で: 双眼鏡で見る, 双眼鏡でのぞく; it is counted with 台 or simply 一つ. Related words with 鏡 are 望遠鏡 "telescope", 顕微鏡 "microscope" and 眼鏡 "glasses". Typical places of use are bird-watching, concerts, stadiums and theaters.

examples[].german: There is an old woman at the nursing home who apparently has memory loss, and she is really funny.
After the accident, he completely lost his self-confidence.
If you repeat violations, you may lose your qualification.
en.notes: 喪失 is the formal counterpart of 失う, but only for abstract things: 記憶喪失 "memory loss", 自信喪失, 資格喪失, 戦意喪失. As a する-verb it is transitive (自信を喪失する). 喪失感 is the "feeling of emptiness after a loss". For lost objects, people say なくす or, formally, 紛失.

examples[].german: I think this forecast is quite solid.
She keeps secrets well, so you can tell her a secret without worry.
This wood is hard, and working it takes a long time.
en.notes: 堅い describes a solid or reliable quality and can express that a result is considered certain. For a person, 口が堅い describes someone who keeps secrets to themselves. 堅い木 refers to the hardness of wood. 硬い often emphasizes material hardness, 固い often firm cohesion; the spellings overlap but are not equally common in every compound. The i-adjective forms 堅く and 堅くない.

examples[].german: I plan to take my summer vacation in August.
I took a week off to coincide with my wife's delivery.
After the long vacation, I can hardly concentrate on work.
en.notes: 休暇 is time off from work or duty that is officially taken - "vacation, leave". Typical are 休暇を取る, 休暇をもらう, 夏季休暇, 育児休暇 ("parental leave") and 有給休暇. Unlike 休み (general word for days off, breaks, holidays) and 休日 ("day off"), 休暇 sounds more formal and refers mainly to leave taken from an employer. School vacations are called 夏休み and so on.

examples[].german: Why did you put this sentence in parentheses?
I tied the old newspapers with string and put them out for recycling.
I had taken the exam lightly, thinking it would be easy, and then couldn't do anything.
en.notes: くくる is usually written in kana and is transitive: 〜を…でくくる ("to tie ... together with ..."), e.g. 新聞をひもでくくる, or to put text in brackets (括弧でくくる). Important expressions: 高をくくる ("to underestimate something"), 腹をくくる ("to steel oneself for the worst") and 一くくりにする ("to lump together"). 結ぶ, by contrast, means "to knot", and 縛る "to bind, to tie up".

en.meaning: lump sum; all at once; bundling
examples[].german: I'm wondering whether to pay for the computer in one go or in installments.
You can download multiple files at once.
Applications are accepted collectively by the department in charge.
en.notes: 一括 means "to put everything together and handle it at once". It is mostly used adverbially as 一括で or 一括して: 一括で支払う "to pay in a lump sum", ファイルを一括してダウンロードする. Important compounds are 一括払い (opposite 分割払い "installment payment"), 一括購入 and 一括処理. Do not confuse with 一くくりにする "to lump together" and 統一 "to unify".

examples[].german: We want people who have the ability to grasp things comprehensively.
At the end of the fiscal year, a meeting was held to review the year's activities.
After the game, the manager summed up: "Defense remains an issue."
en.notes: 総括 means "to sum up and take stock, to evaluate in retrospect": 一年間の活動を総括する, 選挙結果を総括する. It is transitive and belongs to the language of companies, politics and sports. 総括的 means "comprehensive, overall", 総括責任者 "person with overall responsibility". Shortening a text, by contrast, is 要約する, and in everyday speech people say まとめる.

examples[].german: When reading the left bracket, you simply say "kakko", but when reading the right bracket, you say "kakko-tojiru".
Write the answer inside the parentheses.
Please put the spoken parts of the conversation in corner brackets.
en.notes: 括弧 is the bracket or parenthesis and is often written in kana as かっこ. There are 丸括弧 （）, 角括弧 ［］ and the Japanese quotation marks かぎ括弧 「」. Typical are 括弧に入れる and 括弧でくくる ("to put in brackets"); when dictating, people say かっこ and かっことじ. Note: かっこいい "cool" comes from 格好 and has nothing to do with 括弧.

examples[].german: The father ordered his son to draw an arc.
You draw a circular arc using a compass.
The length of an arc can be calculated from the radius and the central angle.
en.notes: 円弧 is the "circular arc" (円 "circle" + 弧 "arc"), a technical term from geometry and engineering: 円弧を描く, 円弧の長さ. For trajectories and movements, people normally say just 弧: ボールが弧を描く. The word has nothing to do with the bow as a weapon (弓) or the structure (アーチ).

examples[].german: One of the protesters threw a Molotov cocktail to provoke the police.
Don't let yourself be provoked by your opponent.
She answered the reporters' questions with a provocative attitude.
en.notes: 挑発 is "provocation"; 挑発する is transitive: 相手を挑発する. Very common is 挑発に乗る ("to rise to the bait"), plus 挑発的な態度 and 挑発行為 (e.g. in a military context). 挑発的 can also mean "provocative" for clothing. Do not confuse it with 挑戦 "challenge, attempt", which sounds positive.

examples[].german: Kumaman is a middle-aged widower who digs for gold in the family business.
The children played on the beach and dug a big hole.
In autumn, we dig up sweet potatoes in the field.
en.notes: 掘る is transitive and means "to dig, to dig up": 穴を掘る, 井戸を掘る, トンネルを掘る, 芋を掘る, 金を掘る ("to prospect for gold"). Important derivatives are 掘り出す ("to dig out"), 掘り下げる ("to delve deeper into a topic") and 掘り出し物 ("bargain, find"). Do not confuse it with the identically read 彫る "to carve, to engrave, to tattoo".

examples[].german: He's your father, so you should interpret it charitably. For example, as him breaking your vintage Baccarat glass because his grip strength has weakened with age.
Grip strength was measured at the fitness test.
He has such a strong grip that he can crush an apple with one hand.
en.notes: 握力 is grip or hand strength (握る "to grip" + 力 "strength"). Typical combinations are 握力が強い・弱い, 握力が落ちる ("grip strength declines") and 握力を測る. In Japanese schools it is measured in kilograms with a 握力計 in the 体力テスト; in medicine it is considered an indicator of aging. Muscle strength in general is 筋力.

examples[].german: Don't rock the canoe!
My mother shook me awake from my sleep.
The incident shook the whole country.
en.notes: 揺る ("to shake, to rock", transitive) is rare as an independent verb and sounds archaic; it is alive mainly in compounds such as 揺りかご ("cradle"), 揺り起こす ("to shake awake") and 揺り動かす ("to shake, to rouse"). In everyday speech, "to rock, to shake" is 揺らす or 揺する, and intransitive "to wobble, to sway" is 揺れる. Also related are 揺るがす ("to shake") and 揺るぎない ("unshakable").

examples[].german: I've been looking for an important document in my study all day today, but I still haven't found it.
On his days off, my father always shuts himself in his study and reads.
In our new house, I want to build a small study.
en.notes: 書斎 is the home work or study room, classically with a desk and bookshelves. Typical are 書斎にこもる ("to retreat into one's study") and 書斎で仕事をする. An office outside the home is 事務所 or オフィス, a child's study room is 勉強部屋; today one also simply says 仕事部屋.

examples[].german: Working hours are from nine in the morning to five in the evening.
My older brother works at a trading company in Tokyo.
I work from home two days a week.
en.notes: 勤務 refers to regular work at a company or government office - "duty, work". As an intransitive する-verb: 〜に勤務する ("to be employed at ..."), e.g. 銀行に勤務している. Typical compounds are 勤務時間, 勤務先 ("place of work"), 夜間勤務 and 在宅勤務 ("working from home"). It sounds more formal than 働く or 勤める and often appears in resumes, forms and employment contracts.

examples[].german: We are just arriving at the funeral hall.
The wake will be held at the funeral hall near the station.
The city funeral hall is in the same building as the crematorium.
en.notes: 斎場 is a hall for funeral ceremonies such as the 通夜 ("wake") and 告別式 ("farewell ceremony"), often with an attached crematorium (火葬場). 葬儀場 and the more modern セレモニーホール mean the same. The meaning "place of a religious ceremony" is rare. The word sounds factual and formal and appears in funeral notices.

examples[].german: Please note that these price settings are provisional.
Because of the typhoon, trains are running on a provisional timetable.
As of this moment, the provisional ranking is third place.
en.notes: 暫定 means "provisional, until a final decision is made". It is used attributively as 暫定の〜, adverbially as 暫定的に, or in compounds such as 暫定政権 ("interim government"), 暫定予算 and 暫定順位 ("provisional ranking"). The tone is official. 一時的, by contrast, stresses only the temporal limit, and 仮 ("temporary") is closer to everyday speech.

examples[].german: The Axis powers fought against the Allies during World War II.
The prime minister positioned the Japan-US alliance as the pivot of diplomacy.
The phrase "axis of evil" was used by the US president in 2002.
en.notes: 枢軸 literally means "axis, pivot", but is used almost only figuratively: the center of power or the linchpin of a policy. Historically, 枢軸国 refers to the "Axis powers" of World War II, with 連合国 "the Allies" as the counterpart; also well known is 悪の枢軸 "axis of evil". The word is written-language; 中枢 stresses the inner core, and 軸 is the neutral "axis".

examples[].german: How could that stimulate her central nervous system?
Even at a young age, he became a pillar of the company.
Tokyo is the political and economic center of Japan.
en.notes: 中枢 is the central control point or load-bearing core of a system or organization: 政府の中枢, 会社の中枢を担う "to play a central role in a company". In medicine it stands for the central nervous system: 中枢神経 as opposed to 末梢神経 "peripheral nervous system". The word is written-language; in daily life one says 中心.

examples[].german: I thought something was wrong with the car, and sure enough, a defect was found in the central axle of the wheel.
He is active as a core member of the team.
The core of the lineup, batters three through five, couldn't get a single hit today.
en.notes: 中軸 is literally the "central axis" of a wheel or machine, but more often figuratively the "key figure" or "core" of a group: チームの中軸, 中軸を担う. In baseball, 中軸打線 denotes the batters numbered three to five, the heart of the batting order. 中心 and 中核 are similar; 中枢 is used more for organizations and systems.

examples[].german: Each country has its own national character, and I think we should all respect that in each other.
Being punctual may simply be a Japanese characteristic.
A country's character also shows in the seasoning of its dishes.
en.notes: 国柄 appears almost always with the polite prefix as お国柄: the character, mentality and customs of a country or even a region. Typical are お国柄が出る ("the character shows") and お国柄の違い. 国民性 is the more analytical term "national character", 土地柄 the character of a locality, and 人柄 the character of a person.

examples[].german: What do you think is most important for a smooth conversation in English?
So that the meeting runs smoothly, I'm distributing the materials in advance.
The switchover to the new system went smoothly.
en.notes: 円滑 means "smooth, without friction" and is a formal na-adjective, typical of business and official language: 円滑に進める, 円滑に進む, 円滑な人間関係, 円滑なコミュニケーション. In daily life one mostly says スムーズに or 順調に. 円滑 emphasizes that processes or relationships function without friction and conflict.

examples[].german: Last summer, I went bass fishing in Hachirogata in Akita Prefecture.
The place name Niigata contains the character for "lagoon".
Many migratory birds gather on the tidal flat at low tide.
en.notes: 潟 is a lagoon or a bay cut off from the sea, also a tidal flat area. On its own the word is rare; it is encountered mainly in place names such as 新潟 or 八郎潟 (read がた) and in the word 干潟 ひがた "tidal flat, Wadden Sea". For an ordinary lake people say 湖, and for a bay 湾 or 入り江.

examples[].german: When the teacher was explaining how to focus the microscope, I was absent-minded.
In this election, economic policy has become the biggest focus.
This book focuses on how women lived after the war.
en.notes: 焦点 is the optical "focal point": 焦点を合わせる ("to bring into focus"), 焦点が合う; colloquially people say ピント for this. Very common is the figurative use as "key point, center of attention": 〜に焦点を当てる ("to focus on ..."), 焦点を絞る ("to narrow down"), 〜が焦点となる ("to be the central issue"). The word is a noun.

examples[].german: My mom said that by stirring constantly, you can keep the bottom of the pot from burning.
I grilled the fish too long, and the skin got burned completely black.
I left the iron on the shirt, and it got scorched.
en.notes: 焦げる is intransitive: the food itself "burns" or "gets charred" - 魚が焦げる, 鍋の底が焦げる. The transitive counterpart is 焦がす ("to let burn"): パンを焦がしてしまった. Fabric can also 焦げる from heat (iron, cigarette). Related are 焦げ目 ("browned or burned spot") and 焦げ臭い ("to smell burnt"); for a suntan, by contrast, people say 日に焼ける.

examples[].german: The results of the opinion poll were announced.
In response to strong public opposition, the government reviewed the plan.
One young person's social media post moved public opinion.
en.notes: 世論 is public opinion, i.e. what the population as a whole thinks. There are two readings: せろん and よろん; on television and in daily life よろん is in fact more common today. Originally よろん was written 輿論 ("well-founded public view") and せろん 世論 ("popular sentiment"), but the distinction has disappeared. Typical: 世論調査 ("opinion poll"), 世論の反発, 世論を動かす.

examples[].german: I was assigned to the sales department.
This supermarket is open 24 hours a day.
I checked the business hours over New Year on the website.
en.notes: 営業 has two main meanings: the business operation of a shop or company (営業中 "open", 営業時間 "business hours", 24時間営業) and "sales" or customer acquisition (営業部, 営業の仕事, 営業に回る). As a する-verb it usually takes no object: 店が営業している. Unlike 販売 (the "sale" of a product), 営業 covers the whole of customer care and acquisition. Neutral, very common in the workplace.

en.meaning: to distract oneself; to dispel (boredom, sorrow); to gloss over
examples[].german: To dispel my bad mood, I listened to my favorite music at high volume.
In the hospital, I read every day to pass the time.
He covered up his embarrassment with laughter.
en.notes: 紛らす means to "dispel" unpleasant feelings or boredom, or to "distract oneself" from them: 気を紛らす, 退屈を紛らす, 寂しさを酒で紛らす - the means takes で. It also means "to gloss over, to cover up": 照れを笑いで紛らす. The variant 紛らわす is nowadays even more common and has the same meaning. Intransitive is 紛れる ("to be distracted, to get lost in"): 気が紛れる.

examples[].german: I don't want to complicate this problem any further.
The discussion over the budget got out of hand, and the meeting went on until late at night.
The residents' briefing session became chaotic as objection followed objection.
en.notes: 紛糾 describes a meeting, negotiation or debate "getting out of hand" - it becomes tangled and contentious: 会議が紛糾する, 議論が紛糾した. It is intransitive; someone who complicates a matter 紛糾させる it. The word is typical of news and formal reports; in everyday speech people say もめる or ややこしくなる. Unlike 混乱 ("disorder, confusion"), 紛糾 always contains an aspect of dispute or conflict.

examples[].german: I may look like an ordinary man now, but I was once a sumo grand champion.
He rose to yokozuna already in his twenties.
The curry at this shop is truly the number one among curries.
en.notes: 横綱 is the highest rank in sumo, the "grand champion". One is promoted to it (横綱に昇進する); below it stands the rank 大関. Originally 横綱 is the thick rope that the yokozuna wears around his waist when entering the ring ceremonially. Figuratively it means "the best of its kind, number one", often in the pattern 〇〇界の横綱 for a restaurant, a product or a company.

examples[].german: Is tug of war as popular in America as it is in Japan?
In the tug of war at the sports day, the red team beat the white team.
The tug of war between the two prefectures over the site of the new airport continues.
en.notes: 綱引き is "tug of war", a classic of the Japanese school sports day (運動会): 綱引きをする, 綱引きで勝つ. Figuratively it denotes a "contest of strength, jockeying" between two parties, for example in politics or business: 与党と野党の綱引き, 主導権をめぐる綱引き. 綱 is a thick, strong rope; an ordinary rope is called ロープ or 縄.

examples[].german: A major earthquake paralyzed the transportation network of the Tokyo metropolitan area.
This town has a well-developed transportation network, so you can live without a car.
In the run-up to the Olympics, the city's transportation network was improved.
en.notes: 交通網 is the entire "transportation network" of a region, consisting of rail, bus and roads. The suffix 網 ("net") forms many such words: 通信網, 鉄道網, 道路網. Typical combinations are 交通網が発達している ("to be well developed"), 交通網を整備する ("to build up") and 交通網が麻痺する ("to be paralyzed"). The word belongs rather to written and news language; in conversation people often simply say 交通の便がいい.

examples[].german: The moment the typhoon hit the island directly, all communications networks were cut off.
We are advancing measures so that the communications network can be maintained even during disasters.
In this country, the communications network extends even to remote mountain villages.
en.notes: 通信網 is the "communications or telecommunications network" made up of telephone, mobile and internet connections. Like 交通網, it belongs to the vocabulary of news and technology: 通信網が途絶える ("to go down"), 通信網を整備する ("to build up"), 通信網が広がる. In everyday speech people mostly say ネットワーク or describe concretely that 電話がつながらない. 網 originally means "net", as in a fishing net.

examples[].german: That hepatitis A patient is starved for love and is always trying to get the attention of the doctors and nurses.
Before traveling abroad, I got vaccinated against hepatitis B.
If you drink too much alcohol, you can also get hepatitis.
en.notes: 肝炎 is inflammation of the liver, hepatitis (肝 from 肝臓 "liver" + 炎 "inflammation"). One distinguishes A型肝炎, B型肝炎, C型肝炎 as well as ウイルス性肝炎 and アルコール性肝炎. To fall ill is 肝炎になる or 肝炎にかかる. Formed on the same pattern are 胃炎 "gastritis", 腸炎 and 皮膚炎. The word belongs to medical terminology but is widely known.

examples[].german: The email from Toshiba's customer center arrived completely garbled.
This refrigerator is a Toshiba product.
Toshiba is one of Japan's leading electronics manufacturers.
en.notes: 東芝 is the Japanese technology company Toshiba, headquartered in Tokyo. The name came from the merger of 東京電気 and 芝浦製作所. The company is known for home appliances, semiconductors and energy technology; "made by Toshiba" is 東芝製. In its logo the name is written in Latin letters as TOSHIBA, but in text it is usually written with kanji.

examples[].german: We planted lawn grass in part of the garden and turned it into a playground for the kids.
The rainy season makes lawn grass grow quickly, so you need to mow it often.
The lawn grass on the golf course is maintained by specialist craftsmen.
en.notes: 芝草 refers to the grass itself that a lawn is made of: "lawn grass". It is much rarer than 芝生 (the lawn area) or simply 芝, and appears more in texts about gardening, parks or golf courses. Typical combinations: 芝草を植える, 芝草が伸びる, 芝草を刈る. In everyday speech people almost always say 芝 or 芝生.

examples[].german: Sales of this product are going well.
Tickets will go on sale from next Monday.
This shop sells locally grown vegetables.
en.notes: 販売 is the sale of goods, mostly from the seller's point of view and in a business context. As a transitive する-verb: 商品を販売する; typical are 販売店, 自動販売機, 通信販売 ("mail order", short 通販) and 販売中. Do not confuse with 発売 ("market launch, start of sales"): 新製品を発売する, but 店で販売する. In daily life one rather says 売る; 販売 is more matter-of-fact and appears on signs and in the news.

examples[].german: The station attendant told me that when taking a bicycle on the train you're required to use a carrying bag, but I wonder if I couldn't use a garbage bag instead.
Please put burnable trash in the designated garbage bag and put it out.
The garbage bag is full, so tie it up for me.
en.notes: ゴミ袋 (also written ごみ袋) is a garbage bag or trash sack; here 袋 is read with a voiced initial, ぶくろ. In many Japanese municipalities, waste has to be sorted by type (燃えるゴミ, 燃えないゴミ) and disposed of in prescribed, sometimes paid, bags (指定のゴミ袋). Typical combinations are ゴミ袋に入れる, ゴミ袋を出す "put out" and 口を縛る "tie up". General plastic bags are called ビニール袋 or ポリ袋.

en.meaning: filial piety; love and care for one's parents
examples[].german: I'd like to do something to show my parents how grateful I am.
With my first paycheck, I took my parents on an onsen trip to repay them.
Mrs. Tanaka's daughter is really devoted to her parents, isn't she?
en.notes: 親孝行 means taking good care of one's own parents and making them happy: "filial piety, duty toward one's parents". As a する-verb: 親孝行する or 親孝行をする; as a な-adjective: 親孝行な息子 ("a son who is good to his parents"). The opposite is 親不孝. The proverb 親孝行したい時に親はなし warns that parents are often no longer alive by the time you finally want to thank them.

en.meaning: to burst out laughing; to spurt out; to gush out
examples[].german: When he saw my new hairstyle, that guy burst out laughing with a snort. How rude, right?
Water gushed out forcefully from the burst water pipe.
The moment I stepped outside, sweat broke out from the heat.
en.notes: 吹き出す has two main uses: liquid, gas or sweat "shoots out, gushes forth" (水が吹き出す, 汗が吹き出す), in which sense it is often also written 噴き出す. It also means someone suddenly "bursts out" laughing, often with プッと or 思わず: 思わず吹き出した. Compared with 笑い出す ("to start laughing"), 吹き出す is more involuntary and sudden. The trigger is usually in a subordinate clause such as 〜を見て.

en.meaning: to blow in; to instill; to record (on tape)
examples[].german: Our house is so rundown that wind and rain blow in every time a storm comes.
I left a message on the answering machine.
Who put such a lie into the child's head?
en.notes: 吹き込む has several meanings: intransitive "to blow in" of wind, rain or snow (窓から雨が吹き込む); transitive "to blow into" (風船に息を吹き込む, figuratively 新しい命を吹き込む), "to instill, whisper into someone's mind" (子どもに変な考えを吹き込む) and "to record, speak onto a recording" (留守番電話にメッセージを吹き込む). The target is marked with に in each case. Do not confuse it with 吹き出す ("to shoot out; to burst out laughing").

examples[].german: What do you find appealing about whistling?
When my father is in a good mood, he whistles while he cooks.
My grandmother often told me that if you whistle at night, snakes will come out.
en.notes: 口笛を吹く is the set phrase for "to whistle" with the mouth; 口笛 alone is whistling or a whistle sound. 吹く is used here as with wind instruments (笛を吹く, トランペットを吹く). For a referee's whistle, you say 笛を吹く or ホイッスルを鳴らす. In Japan there is a superstition that whistling at night attracts snakes or thieves.

examples[].german: This miso soup is too salty. Could you dilute it a little?
Please dilute this detergent ten times with water before use.
I thinned the paint with water to get a pale sky color.
en.notes: 薄める is transitive: you "dilute" a liquid, usually with water: 水で薄める, 十倍に薄める. Colors or flavors are also "weakened" this way, and figuratively impressions or statements too (印象を薄める). The intransitive counterpart is 薄まる ("to become thinner, weaker"). 薄める concerns concentration and strength; "to cut thinner" in the sense of thickness is instead 薄く切る or 薄くする.

en.meaning: to blow away; to sweep away; to dispel
examples[].german: Let's go to the party and blow away your gloom.
The typhoon's strong wind blew the roof tiles off.
His bright smile dispelled everyone's tension.
en.notes: 吹き飛ばす (吹く + 飛ばす) is transitive: wind or an explosion blows something away, often in the passive: 屋根が吹き飛ばされる. The intransitive counterpart is 吹き飛ぶ (帽子が吹き飛ぶ). Figuratively it means "to dispel, blow away" feelings and moods: 不安を吹き飛ばす, 暑さを吹き飛ばす, 疲れを吹き飛ばす – a popular expression in advertising and everyday speech.

examples[].german: This actor is popular with everyone.
This movie is quite violent and therefore not suitable for everyone.
These ramen taste simple and go over well with everyone.
en.notes: 万人 (ばんにん) means "all people, everyone" and sounds somewhat elevated. Common are 万人向け "suitable for everyone" and 万人受けする "to go over well with everyone". The reading まんにん also occurs in this meaning, but is mainly usual when counting: 一万人 (いちまんにん), 十万人 "ten thousand, a hundred thousand people". In daily life one otherwise simply says みんな or 誰にでも.

examples[].german: We can't let that criminal get away.
The fish I caught was small, so I let it go back into the river.
While I was hesitating, I let a precious chance slip away.
en.notes: 逃がす is the transitive counterpart of 逃げる: you let an animal or a person go "free" or "escape" – 鳥を逃がす, 犯人を逃がす. Secondly it means "to miss, let slip": チャンスを逃がす. In this second sense, the identically written 逃す (のがす) is more common and somewhat more literary. Proverb: 逃がした魚は大きい ("the fish that got away was always the biggest").

examples[].german: She is petite but full of energy.
I can't believe he can carry such heavy luggage with his small build.
My grandmother liked best to wear kimono with small patterns.
en.notes: 小柄 describes a person with a "small, petite build": 小柄な女性, 小柄な体. It is more tactful than 背が低い because it refers to the whole figure and not just the height. The opposite is 大柄 "large and strongly built". For fabrics and kimono, 小柄 also means "small pattern", then usually with の: 小柄の着物.

en.meaning: placing an order; order (to a supplier)
examples[].german: Please hurry with the order for the parts.
We outsourced the creation of the website to an external company.
Because of an ordering mistake, a hundred extra items arrived.
en.notes: 発注 means placing an order or commission with a supplier or service provider. As a transitive する-verb: 部品を発注する, 〜に…を発注する. The counterpart from the supplier's point of view is 受注 ("receipt of orders"); compounds are 発注書 ("purchase order") and 発注ミス. As a private customer one says 注文する; 発注 is business language for purchasing materials or services.

examples[].german: Her hands were so white they were almost transparent.
The sea in Okinawa is clear all the way to the bottom, so you can see the fish well.
The whole hall listened intently to her clear singing voice.
en.notes: 透き通る is intransitive and means "to be transparent, clear", for example of water, glass or skin: 透き通った海, 透き通るような肌. Before nouns, 透き通った or 透き通るような is usually used. Figuratively it also describes a "bright, clear" voice: 透き通った声. 透明な ("transparent") is more matter-of-fact; the spelling 透きとおる also occurs.

examples[].german: I hope the pickled cucumbers turn out delicious.
This napa cabbage is well pickled and goes great with rice.
The heavy rain left the rice paddies submerged in water.
en.notes: 漬かる is intransitive: vegetables in salt, vinegar or rice bran are well "pickled, steeped": よく漬かった白菜. The transitive counterpart is 漬ける ("to pickle"): 野菜を漬ける, and 漬物 comes from it as well. In the sense of "to be submerged, stand in water" or "to get into the bath" (お風呂に浸かる), 浸かる is usually written; both spellings belong to the same word.

examples[].german: This is the first time I'm eating salmon ramen!
There is a delicious ramen restaurant near the station.
en.notes: ラーメン here refers to the Chinese-influenced noodles or the noodle dish in soup. 鮭ラーメン denotes a variant with salmon; ラーメン屋 a shop that serves ramen. The usual spelling is katakana; the rare form 拉麺 is kept as a search alias. The same katakana form can denote a frame in construction engineering; this other meaning does not belong to this card.

examples[].german: The use of insecticides is strictly prohibited on this farm.
A cockroach appeared, so I hurriedly sprayed it with insecticide.
When using insecticide, please open the window and ventilate.
en.notes: 殺虫剤 is an agent for killing insects (殺 "kill", 虫 "insect", 剤 "agent"). You spray it: 殺虫剤をまく, 殺虫剤をかける, 殺虫剤のスプレー. Distinguish it from 虫除け ("insect repellent", which only drives them away) and 農薬 ("agricultural chemicals" in general in farming). The suffix 〜剤 forms many names of agents such as 洗剤, 消毒剤 or 防腐剤.

examples[].german: I love kimchi fried rice.
I made fried rice from the leftovers in the fridge.
One set of ramen and fried rice, please.
en.notes: 炒飯 is fried rice in the Chinese style; the reading チャーハン comes from Chinese. It is usually written in katakana, and the kanji are seen mainly on the menus of Chinese restaurants. 炒 means "to stir-fry in a wok" (cf. 炒める). It is a classic in 中華料理店 and ラーメン屋, often as a set with ramen. Similar is 焼き飯, which is used regionally or in older speech for a comparable dish.

en.meaning: to be bustling; to be lively
examples[].german: On weekends the shopping mall is full of shoppers.
On the evening of the summer festival, the shrine was full of people in yukata.
This shopping street is said to have been much livelier in the past.
en.notes: 賑わう is intransitive: a place "is bustling, full of people". What fills it is marked with で: 観光客で賑わう, 買い物客で賑わう. Figuratively it also means "to flourish, to do good business" (店が賑わう). The related noun is 賑わい (賑わいを取り戻す "to come back to life"), the adjective 賑やか "lively". Unlike 混む, 賑わう emphasizes cheerful, positive liveliness, not unpleasant crowding.

examples[].german: That guy is really boring. He talks about nothing but the modern legends surrounding Gunkanjima.
Gunkanjima is an uninhabited island in Nagasaki Prefecture and is a World Heritage site.
On a guided tour, I looked at the old apartment blocks that still stand on Gunkanjima.
en.notes: 軍艦島 is the nickname of the island 端島 off Nagasaki: with its sea walls and concrete buildings, its silhouette is reminiscent of a "warship" (軍艦). Coal was mined there until 1974; today it is an uninhabited island of ruins and part of the UNESCO World Heritage. The name is always read ぐんかんじま, not ぐんかんとう. Typical: 軍艦島に上陸する, 軍艦島ツアーに参加する.

examples[].german: That guy bragged to me about his fake Gucci wallet.
The bag I bought cheaply online was a fake.
Even experts find it hard to judge whether this painting is genuine or fake.
en.notes: 偽物 is a "fake, imitation" – the opposite of 本物 ("genuine, the real thing"). Before nouns, 偽物の is used: 偽物のブランドバッグ, 偽物の絵. Being palmed off a fake is 偽物をつかまされる. When a person is meant ("impostor, a false ..."), 偽者 with the same reading is usually written. More formal are 偽造品 and 模造品; counterfeit money is 偽札.

examples[].german: May I open this package at midnight?
The package from my mother contained homemade sweets.
She was holding a bundle wrapped in a furoshiki cloth carefully in her arms.
en.notes: 包み is the noun of 包む ("to wrap") and refers to something wrapped up: a package or bundle in paper or cloth. You open it with 包みを開ける or 包みをほどく. For postal parcels one rather says 小包 or 荷物. 包み紙 is "wrapping paper", and as a counter it appears in 一包み ("one package"). The polite form お包み also refers to a monetary gift wrapped in paper.

examples[].german: My boyfriend's surname is the unusual name 「御手洗」.
I wrote a bizarre answer on the test and the whole class laughed at me.
Programs compiling baseball's funniest plays are popular every year.
en.notes: 珍〜 is a Sino-Japanese prefix meaning "strange, curious, unusual", often with a humorous tone: 珍名 ("curious name"), 珍事件 ("strange incident"), 珍回答 ("bizarre answer"), 珍プレー ("funny play"). In the positive sense of "rare and precious" it appears in 珍味 and 珍品. As an independent word, you say 珍しい ("rare") or 変な ("strange") instead.

examples[].german: We won a large order.
This furniture is made to order, so it takes two months to arrive.
The construction company won the contract for the new airport.
en.notes: 受注 is the acceptance or receipt of an order from the point of view of the supplier or manufacturer - the counterpart of 発注. As a transitive する-verb: 工事を受注する; typical compounds are 受注生産 ("production to order"), 受注額 and 大型受注 ("large order"). Business language, common in economic reports and in the B2B field.

examples[].german: I have gout and know I shouldn't drink beer, but a friend gave me delicacies that go well with beer, so I can't resist just for today.
At this shop you can taste delicacies from all over the country.
Caviar is known as one of the world's three great delicacies.
en.notes: 珍味 is a rare, special "delicacy". It often means regional specialties or small, often salty bites to go with alcohol, such as イカの塩辛 or からすみ: 酒の珍味, 北海道の珍味. Also well known is 世界三大珍味 (caviar, foie gras, truffles). Unlike ごちそう ("feast, fine food"), 珍味 emphasizes the rarity and unusualness of the taste.

examples[].german: The two sides could not agree, and the talks broke down.
The labor-management negotiations over wages broke down, and the union went on strike.
The summit ended in a breakdown without reaching an agreement.
en.notes: 決裂 means that negotiations or talks "fail, are broken off" because no agreement can be reached: 交渉が決裂する, 会談が決裂した, 決裂に終わる. It is intransitive; the subject is almost always 交渉, 話し合い or 会談, not people. Typical of news language. For the failure of a relationship or a company, 別れる and 破綻する respectively are more fitting.

examples[].german: On the train I was suddenly seized by severe abdominal pain.
Recently, cases of bears attacking people near mountains have been increasing.
A powerful typhoon struck Kyushu last night.
en.notes: 襲う is transitive: people, animals or forces of nature "attack, assault, strike": クマが人を襲う, 台風が九州を襲う. Very common is the passive 〜に襲われる, also for sudden feelings and conditions: 不安に襲われる, 眠気に襲われる, 激しい腹痛に襲われる. The Sino-Japanese 襲撃する is more formal and only for targeted attacks; 攻撃する is more general and also used figuratively.

examples[].german: A police car was attacked by a motorcycle gang.
