An armed group raided the village in the middle of the night.
A report came in that the embassy had been attacked.
en.notes: 襲撃 is a targeted, often surprise "raid, attack" on people, vehicles or buildings: 村を襲撃する, 襲撃を受ける, 襲撃事件. As a suru-verb it is transitive; the passive 襲撃される is very common. It sounds more formal and more brutal than 襲う and is typical of news reports. 攻撃, by contrast, is the general term for "attack", also in sports or as criticism.

examples[].german: We did not anticipate the enemy's surprise attack.
Before dawn, the unit launched a surprise attack on the enemy base.
Our players could not cope with the opposing team's surprise tactics.
en.notes: 奇襲 is a "surprise attack" (奇 "unexpected", 襲 "attack"). Typical combinations: 奇襲をかける, 奇襲攻撃, 奇襲作戦, 奇襲を受ける. Originally military, it is also used figuratively in sports, games or business when someone catches others off guard with an unexpected tactic. As a する-verb it is transitive: 敵を奇襲する.

examples[].german: When I looked up at the sky, an air raid was just about to begin.
My grandmother reportedly experienced an air raid in Tokyo as a child.
When the air-raid siren sounded, people hurriedly fled underground.
en.notes: 空襲 is an "air raid" with airplanes and bombs. In Japan the word is closely associated with World War II, for example 東京大空襲 (the great air raid on Tokyo in 1945). Typical are 空襲を受ける, 空襲に遭う, 空襲で焼ける and 空襲警報 ("air-raid warning"). The verb form 空襲する is possible but rare; it is usually used as a noun. More general is 爆撃 ("bombing").

examples[].german: Pac-Man turned on the monsters chasing him and started eating them.
The team was under pressure in the first half, but turned to a counterattack in the second.
Stories in which a bullied protagonist hits back are gaining popularity.
en.notes: 逆襲 is a "counterattack" by someone who had been on the defensive or seemed to be at a disadvantage. Typical are 逆襲に転じる ("to switch to a counterattack"), 逆襲に出る and 〜の逆襲 in film or book titles. As a verb you can say 敵を逆襲する. 反撃 is more neutral and mainly military or sporting; 仕返し is a personal "revenge, payback" in everyday life.

examples[].german: Long-distance flights will become tiring for me as I age.
How far is it from the station to the hotel?
Recently I've been keeping a bit of distance from him.
en.notes: 距離 is the spatial "distance" between two points: 駅までの距離, 距離が遠い/近い, 長距離・短距離. Figuratively it refers to the inner "distance" between people: 距離を置く "to keep one's distance", 距離が縮まる "to grow closer", 距離感. For spacing between things in a row, 間隔 fits better, for differences in numbers 差.

examples[].german: I was quite surprised at how blunt she was.
When I asked for overtime, my coworker made a frown quite openly.
The film has many explicit scenes, so it can't be shown to children.
en.notes: 露骨 describes something that is shown "openly, bluntly", usually with a negative note: 露骨に嫌な顔をする, 露骨な態度, 露骨な差別. As a na-adjective: 露骨な, adverbially 露骨に. For depictions it can also mean "crude, offensive": 露骨な表現. Unlike 率直 ("frank, sincere"), which is positive, 露骨 criticizes a lack of tact.

examples[].german: All the accessories I bought at that street stall broke right away.
On the night of the festival, stalls were lined up in a row along the approach to the shrine.
On weekends, secondhand-book stalls appear in this square.
en.notes: 露店 is a "street stall" in the open air, for example at festivals or markets: 露店が並ぶ, 露店を出す, 露店で買う. In conversation people often say 屋台 (especially for food stalls) or 出店. Do not confuse it with 露天 ("open air") as in 露天風呂 – same reading, different kanji. Vendors who sell this way are called 露天商 or 露店商.

examples[].german: Your ordered goods will be delivered within three days.
I entered the delivery address incorrectly.
For purchases of 5,000 yen or more, shipping is free.
en.notes: 配送 means delivering goods to the respective recipients - "delivery, shipping". As a transitive する-verb: 商品を配送する; typical are 配送料 ("shipping fee"), 配送先 ("delivery address"), 配送センター and 配送無料. Compared to 配達 (delivery by a courier to the door, e.g. 新聞配達), 配送 sounds like logistics; 発送, on the other hand, is the sending off. Very common in online retail.

examples[].german: I thought it over and decided to refrain from wearing a dress that shows so much skin.
Because of the road work, the underground water pipe is exposed.
Since the drama became a hit, the actor has been appearing on TV more.
en.notes: 露出 means that something hidden "lies open, is exposed" or is shown. It often concerns skin: 肌の露出, 露出が多い服 ("revealing clothing"), 露出度. Pipes, rock or roots can also 露出する. In relation to media it means "presence, appearances": テレビへの露出が増える; in photography it is "exposure". The verb is usually intransitive, transitive only in phrases like 肌を露出する.

examples[].german: Has the pastor already left the church today?
My father is a pastor at a church in a small town.
At the wedding, the two vowed eternal love before the pastor.
en.notes: 牧師 is a Protestant "pastor, minister". For Catholic priests one says 神父, for Buddhist monks 僧侶 or お坊さん, for Shinto priests 神主. The 牧 ("to tend") alludes to the image of the shepherd. In conversation one says 牧師さん or addresses him as 先生. Typical: 教会の牧師, 牧師になる, 牧師の説教.

examples[].german: In Hokkaido, pastureland stretches as far as the eye can see.
On this pasture, cattle graze only during the summer.
In the future I want to take over my father's pasture and raise cattle.
en.notes: 牧野 (ぼくや) is "grazing land" where livestock graze – a rather literary, technical word from agriculture and geography. In everyday speech people usually say 牧場 (ぼくじょう, "pasture, ranch, farm with livestock") or 放牧地. Caution: as a family name 牧野 is read まきの, e.g. the botanist 牧野富太郎.

examples[].german: Because of the days of sub-zero temperatures, all the pasture grass has been killed.
The cows are leisurely eating the grass.
To prepare for winter, we cut the pasture grass and let it dry.
en.notes: 牧草 is "pasture grass, forage grass" that livestock eat or that is harvested as hay. Typical: 牧草を食べる, 牧草を刈る, 牧草地 ("pasture, meadow"). Dried, it is called 干し草. Unlike 芝 or 芝生 (lawn for looking at and walking on), 牧草 serves as fodder.

examples[].german: How many New Year's cards should we print this year?
Could you print a hundred copies of this poster for us?
This print shop prints a hundred thousand copies of newspapers in a single night.
en.notes: 刷る is transitive and means "to print": 年賀状を刷る, ポスターを百枚刷る. It is a godan verb (刷って, 刷らない) and sounds like する ("to do") or 擦る ("to rub"), so it is almost always written with kanji. In everyday speech and among printers, 印刷する is usually said; 刷る is shorter and typical of print shops, woodblock printing and compounds like 刷り上がる ("to be finished printing") or 増刷 ("reprint").

examples[].german: He was once a cheerful young man.
She has a cheerful nature and is liked by all her colleagues.
We have transparent prices, so you can drink without worry.
en.notes: 明朗 has two meanings: "cheerful, bright" as a character trait (明朗な性格, often in the four-character word 明朗快活) and "clear, transparent, honest" (明朗会計 "transparent, fair billing", 明朗な政治). It is written-language and often appears in references or job advertisements; in conversation one rather says 明るい. As a na-adjective: 明朗な, 明朗だ.

examples[].german: I came here to bring you good news.
Good news arrived from my son that he got into university.
The fall in train fares is good news for commuters.
en.notes: 朗報 is "good, welcome news" and sounds more refined than いい知らせ. Typical: 朗報が届く, 朗報を伝える, 朗報を待つ, 〜にとって朗報だ. Common in the media and advertising, for example when something is advantageous for a target group. The opposite is 悲報 ("sad news"), which is also used jokingly on the internet.

en.meaning: tidal current; current; trend (of the times)
examples[].german: Rowing the boat against the rough current is not easy, but it's the only way to get back to the cottage.
The current in this strait is fast, and there are many shipping accidents.
For a company to survive, it needs the ability to read the trends of the times.
en.notes: 潮流 literally means the "tidal current" in the sea: 潮流が速い, 潮流に逆らう. Even more often it is used figuratively for the "trend, current" of an era: 時代の潮流, 世界の潮流に乗る/逆らう. In this sense it is more refined than トレンド or 流れ and typical of newspapers and speeches. In everyday speech, for the ocean current people tend to say 潮の流れ.

examples[].german: I found a super cute teddy bear, so I bought it on the spot.
He answered the president's proposal right away.
When I sent the email, a reply came right away.
en.notes: 即 is a short prefix or adverb meaning "immediately, on the spot". As a prefix it forms fixed words such as 即答, 即決 or 即死 and colloquial coinages like 即買い or 即レス. As a free-standing adverb (即返事が来た), 即 sounds casual and informal; neutral expressions are すぐ or すぐに, formal ones 直ちに or 即座に. Do not confuse it with the literary conjunction 即ち "namely".

examples[].german: Please don't expect immediate results.
She answered the interviewer's question without hesitation.
When I made an unreasonable request, I was refused on the spot.
en.notes: 即座 is used almost only adverbially as 即座に ("immediately, on the spot"): 即座に答える, 即座に断る, 即座に反応する. Less often it appears attributively as 即座の (即座の判断, 即座の対応). It stresses a reaction without any hesitation and is somewhat more formal than すぐに; even more formal is ただちに. For technical processes, 即時 is preferred.

examples[].german: Raw material prices are soaring.
I have an allergy, so I check the ingredients carefully before buying.
This factory imports its raw materials from abroad.
en.notes: 原材料 covers the starting materials from which a product is made: raw materials and ingredients. On food packaging 原材料名 stands for the "list of ingredients". Typical are 原材料費, 原材料の価格 and 原材料を輸入する. Related are 原料 (the basic material, e.g. 石油を原料とする) and 材料 ("material, ingredient" in a broader sense); 原材料 combines both and is factual-business.

examples[].german: He tried to surf on a tidal bore, but unfortunately he died instantly.
The driver of the car that collided with the truck died instantly.
If he hadn't been wearing a helmet, he might have died on the spot.
en.notes: 即死 means "to be dead on the spot, instant death" and appears almost only in reports about accidents, attacks or disasters. As an intransitive する-verb: 運転手は即死した, often also as a noun: 即死だった. The neutral news word for "death" is 死亡; the counterpart for survivors is 重傷を負う "to be seriously injured". The tone is matter-of-fact and harsh, typical of police and press language.

examples[].german: We ship this rotisserie grill on the same day we receive your order.
The election votes were counted on the same day, and the result was mostly clear by evening.
This room is vacant, so you can move in right away.
en.notes: 即日 means "on the very same day" and usually stands without a particle before a Sino-Japanese verbal noun: 即日発送 ("shipping on the day of ordering"), 即日開票 ("vote count on election day"), 即日入居可 ("available for immediate move-in"). Typical of business and official language. More neutral is 当日 ("on that day"); in conversation people say その日のうちに.

examples[].german: Let me show you a way to relieve eye strain right away.
This headache medicine is fast-acting; it starts working about ten minutes after you take it.
Some fertilizers act immediately, and others act slowly.
en.notes: 即効 is an "immediate effect", especially of medicines and remedies: 即効性がある, 即効薬. Colloquially 即効で is also used as "immediately, lightning fast"; for this, 速攻 (same reading, literally "lightning attack" in sports) is often written. The opposite is 遅効性 ("slow-acting"). Very common in advertising and advice guides: 即効で効く, 即効ダイエット.

examples[].german: We built a low hedge on the boundary with the neighbor's house.
I chatted with the neighbor over the fence for a while.
Researchers are collaborating across the boundaries of their fields.
en.notes: 垣根 is an enclosure made of plants, bamboo or wood around a house and garden – a "hedge, fence": 垣根を作る, 垣根越しに話す. A wall of stone or concrete is called 塀, a metal fence フェンス. Figuratively, 垣根 means a "barrier, divide" between groups or fields: 分野の垣根を越える, 垣根を取り払う.

examples[].german: Around the castle, the tall stone walls of old still remain today.
Part of the stone wall collapsed in the earthquake.
A cat is taking a pleasant nap on top of the old stone wall.
en.notes: 石垣 is a "stone wall" stacked from natural stones, often without mortar. Typical are the mighty castle walls (城の石垣) and the retaining walls of terraced fields. You say 石垣を積む ("to stack") and 石垣が崩れる ("to collapse"). A smooth wall around a property is more often called 塀. As a place name, the island 石垣島 in Okinawa is well known.

en.meaning: pitching power; ball speed and force
examples[].german: As spring and the baseball season approach, that pitcher's pitching power keeps increasing.
Even in the ninth inning, the force of his pitches did not drop at all.
His speed isn't that great, but he's a pitcher whose balls have real power.
en.notes: 球威 is a baseball term for the "power, punch" of a pitch – how heavy and forceful the ball feels when it reaches the batter. Typical: 球威がある, 球威が落ちる/衰える, 球威が増す. It is not the same as 球速 (the measurable speed in km/h): a pitcher can throw fast and still have little 球威. The word appears mainly in sports reports.

examples[].german: It says that unopened products can be returned at any time, but what if the contents are broken after opening, or I don't like the product?
You must not open letters addressed to other people without permission.
After opening, please refrigerate and consume soon.
en.notes: 開封 means to "open" something sealed or closed – letters, packages, products: 手紙を開封する, 開封後. Typical on packaging: 開封後はお早めにお召し上がりください ("consume soon after opening"). The opposite term is 未開封 ("unopened"); 開封済み means "already opened". In everyday speech people just say 開ける; 開封 is more matter-of-fact and formal.

examples[].german: I signed the contract and put it in an envelope, but I haven't mailed the sealed letter yet.
Please send the application form in a sealed envelope, not on a postcard.
An important letter arrived from the bank, so I opened it right away.
en.notes: 封書 is a letter in a sealed envelope – the postal term as opposed to the open postcard はがき. Typical are 封書で送る and 封書が届く; government offices, banks and companies deliberately send important notices as 封書. The envelope itself is 封筒, and the letter as content is generally 手紙. The word is rather matter-of-fact and written; in everyday speech people usually just say 手紙.

examples[].german: Today in history class we learned about feudalism.
In a feudal society, the class one was born into determined one's occupation.
Our company has such a strict hierarchy that it's as if we still lived under feudalism.
en.notes: 封建主義 refers to feudalism as a social order, in Japan mainly the period from the Kamakura to the Edo period. Closely related are 封建制度 ("feudal system") and 封建時代 ("feudal era"). In daily life one hears more often the adjective 封建的, with which one pejoratively criticizes rigid hierarchies and old-fashioned ways of thinking, e.g. 封建的な考え方. The word belongs to history, politics and social criticism.

examples[].german: Do I need to declare the compensation I receive from the insurance company to the tax office?
In the divorce, the husband was required to pay his wife compensation.
The accident victim demanded compensation from the other driver.
en.notes: 慰謝 actually means "consolation, comfort", but today it appears almost only in 慰謝料: money as compensation for emotional suffering, i.e. "compensation for pain and suffering" or damages in cases of divorce, accidents or defamation. Typical are 慰謝料を請求する, 慰謝料を支払う and 慰謝料をもらう. An older spelling is 慰藉. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 医者 "doctor".

examples[].german: We source automobile parts from abroad.
After replacing the broken part, it worked again.
Since it's an old model, apparently you can't get the parts anymore.
en.notes: 部品 are the individual parts from which a machine, device or vehicle is assembled - "component, spare part". Typical are 部品を交換する, 部品を組み立てる, 自動車部品, 交換部品 and 部品メーカー. In contrast to 部分 ("part of a whole" in general), 部品 always means a physical component. Neutral, from technology and industry, but also in everyday life for repairs.

examples[].german: Every Sunday we visit a nursing home with therapy dogs.
The prime minister visited the earthquake-stricken area and encouraged the people in the shelters.
The children wrote get-well letters to the patients in the hospital.
en.notes: 慰問する means to visit people in a difficult situation in order to comfort and cheer them up – for example the sick, seniors, disaster victims or soldiers. It is transitive: 被災地を慰問する, 病院を慰問する. Compounds like 慰問団, 慰問品 and 慰問の手紙 are common. Unlike 見舞い, which one does privately for acquaintances, 慰問 sounds more official and is often said of groups, celebrities or the imperial couple.

examples[].german: At my company there's a mandatory recreational trip every year.
For the employees' recreation, the company planned a trip to a hot spring.
An entertainment event was held at the nursing home, and local children sang songs.
en.notes: 慰安 means "recreation, diversion" and almost always appears in compounds: 慰安旅行 is the classic company outing, 慰安会 an entertainment event for employees or seniors. The reason is given as 社員の慰安のために. Caution: 慰安婦 refers to the women forced into prostitution during World War II and is a politically sensitive word. For personal relaxation, everyday speech prefers 息抜き or 気分転換.

examples[].german: On October 22, we are planning a social gathering with the residents of the apartment building.
The mayor held a discussion with local young people and heard their opinions about the town's future.
After the meeting, we had time for a relaxed chat with the teachers.
en.notes: 懇話 is a refined word for an informal, friendly conversation. On its own it is rare; almost always it appears in 懇話会 "discussion group, social gathering", for example of government offices, associations or property managers with residents. In everyday speech people say 雑談 or おしゃべり instead. Similarly built is 懇談会, which sounds somewhat more official (e.g. a talk between parents and teachers).

examples[].german: Through parties with all-you-can-drink, I deepened my friendship with my teammates.
After the academic conference, a social gathering was held at the hotel.
Won't you join the get-together for new employees?
en.notes: 懇親 refers to friendly, sociable interaction to get to know each other better. It almost always appears in fixed combinations: 懇親会 "social gathering, get-together" after conferences or in companies, and 懇親を深める "to deepen relations". It is not used for "friendship" in general – for that, people say 友情 or 親しさ. The tone is formal; 懇親会 is the usual term on invitations.

examples[].german: Last week, the mayor held informal talks with people of various occupations.
Next week there is a parent-teacher meeting at school.
The company president chatted informally with the new employees over lunch.
en.notes: 懇談 is a relaxed, open conversation, often between groups that otherwise do not talk directly. As an intransitive する-verb, the partner takes と: 市民と懇談する. Very common is 懇談会, e.g. 保護者懇談会 ("parents' meeting") or 三者懇談 (teacher, parents and student). Unlike 会議 ("meeting, conference"), it is not about decisions; unlike 雑談 ("chatting"), it has an official setting.

en.meaning: to learn one's lesson; to be put off by experience
examples[].german: You've been turned down by her three times already and still haven't learned your lesson?
Wiser after the last failure, I started the preparations earlier this time.
No matter how many times you warn him, he is incorrigible and keeps coming late.
en.notes: 懲りる means to have become wise through a bad experience and not want to repeat something. The cause is marked with に: 失敗に懲りる. Very common are the negatives まだ懲りていない ("still hasn't learned") and 懲りずに ("incorrigibly, yet again") as well as 懲り懲りだ ("to be sick and tired of it"). It is intransitive; "to teach someone a lesson" is 懲らしめる.

examples[].german: Violators will be punished.
The lawmaker who made a problematic remark in the Diet was disciplined.
As punishment, the player was suspended for three games.
en.notes: 懲罰 is a disciplinary punishment within an organization, such as in parliament, in prison, in the military or in sports. It is mostly used as a noun: 懲罰を受ける, 懲罰を与える, 懲罰として; also 懲罰委員会 and 懲罰動議. The general word for "to punish" is 罰する or 処罰する; legal penalties are called 刑罰. The word is formal and appears mainly in news and regulations.

examples[].german: The students all looked at the thermometer at the same time.
When the bell signaling the end of the exam rang, all the examinees put down their pens at once.
Because of the approaching typhoon, all elementary and junior high schools in the city were closed.
en.notes: 一斉 is almost always used as the adverb 一斉に: many people or things do the same thing at the same time, as if on command. Unlike 同時に, which can link just two events, 一斉に emphasizes the large number. As a prefix it forms compounds like 一斉休校, 一斉送信 ("mass mailing") and 一斉検挙 ("roundup, sweep"). The word is neutral and common in the news as well as in daily life.

examples[].german: I found a place with really delicious okonomiyaki. Want to go together sometime?
Even with delicious food, I try not to eat too much.
en.notes: 旨い here means "delicious" and can also be written うまい. The meaning "skillful" belongs to the card 上手い. As an i-adjective, 旨い stands directly before a noun and forms, for example, 旨くない and 旨かった. In the first example, めっちゃ is a colloquial intensifier; 行かへん？ is a form from Kansai speech and serves here as an invitation, similar to the standard 一緒に行かない？. After 店 the object marker を is omitted in casual conversation. In the second example, でも means "even with"; 〜ないようにしています describes a behavior kept up deliberately. For the meaning "delicious", 甘い with the reading うまい is also attested. Without such a reading hint, 甘い is usually read あまい and then means "sweet". For this card, うまい remains the reading; the spelling 旨い or the kana form うまい makes the intended meaning easier to recognize.

examples[].german: The barber over there with the gentle smile is actually the boss of the pimps in this area.
Grandfather always watches over his grandchildren with a gentle expression.
The new principal has a gentle personality and is popular with the students too.
en.notes: 柔和 (reading にゅうわ, not じゅうわ) describes a gentle, mild nature or appearance. As a な-adjective, it typically goes with 顔, 表情, 笑み and 人柄: 柔和な笑顔. It does not fit soft things or materials; for that, use 柔らかい. Compared with 優しい and 穏やか, 柔和 sounds more literary and emphasizes the friendly expression one shows outwardly.

examples[].german: The finished products are stored in the warehouse.
Before shipping, we inspect the finished products one by one.
I'm bad at assembling things, so I bought an already assembled shelf.
en.notes: 完成品 is a completely manufactured product, a "finished product", as opposed to 部品, 半製品 ("semi-finished product") or 原材料. Typical are 完成品を出荷する, 完成品を検査する and 完成品の在庫. For furniture or models it also contrasts with 組み立て式 or キット and then means "already assembled". Factual, from production and trade.

examples[].german: Have you ever walked barefoot through a marshy rice paddy?
The marshy paddies around here drain poorly, so even rice planting is a struggle.
In the past, in marshy paddies where machines couldn't go, people reportedly harvested rice standing waist-deep in mud.
en.notes: 沼田 is a technical term from agriculture for a poorly drained, deeply muddy rice field in which one sinks in above the knees; a technical term with the same meaning is 湿田. In everyday language it is rare – far more often you meet 沼田 as a family name or as a city in Gunma Prefecture. For a normal rice field, people say 田んぼ.

examples[].german: This yellow-flowering plant grows in marshland.
There is a large marshland in this area, which many migratory birds visit in winter.
The marshes were filled in for development, and rare animals disappeared.
en.notes: 沼沢 refers to swamp and bog land, i.e. areas with ponds and wet ground. It is a written technical word from geography and biology and usually appears in 沼沢地 ("marshland"). In everyday speech people tend to say 沼 ("pond, marsh"), 湿地 ("wetland") or 湿原 ("moor", e.g. 尾瀬). It is encountered more often in texts on nature conservation and plant or bird species.

examples[].german: Who could believe that that clan will remain secure forever?
Just because you got a job at a big company doesn't mean you're secure for life.
Thanks to the new technology, the company's management is stable for the time being.
en.notes: 安泰 describes a secure, stable state with no danger of decline – of states, companies, families, positions or one's own future: 国家の安泰, 会社は安泰だ, 一生安泰. As a な-adjective or noun, it is mostly used predicatively with だ or in 安泰とは限らない. It differs from 安全 (protection from a concrete danger) and 平和 (peace, no war). In conversation, これで老後も安泰だ sounds half jocular.

examples[].german: They are trying to destroy Japan through media manipulation.
Oda Nobunaga destroyed many feudal houses.
I know several people who ruined themselves through gambling.
en.notes: 滅ぼす is transitive: to "destroy, to bring to ruin" something or someone, typically 国を滅ぼす or 敵を滅ぼす. The intransitive partner is 滅びる "to perish, to go extinct" (ローマ帝国が滅びた). Figuratively 身を滅ぼす means "to ruin oneself", e.g. through gambling or alcohol. Unlike 壊す (to break things), 滅ぼす is about states, peoples, species or entire existences; the tone is rather written and dramatic.

examples[].german: If this supervolcano erupted, we probably wouldn't escape destruction.
The Taira clan perished in the Battle of Dan-no-ura.
I'm writing a term paper on the fall of the Roman Empire.
en.notes: 滅亡 is the final downfall of a state, dynasty, clan, civilization or humanity: 帝国の滅亡, 人類の滅亡. As an intransitive suru-verb: 国が滅亡する. The native Japanese verb for it is 滅びる, transitive 滅ぼす ("to destroy"). For the extinction of animal species one uses 絶滅 instead. Also typical are 滅亡を免れる and 滅亡に追い込まれる.

examples[].german: The city was destroyed by the atomic bomb.
The seaside town suffered devastating damage in the great earthquake.
After a long investigation, the police wiped out the criminal organization.
en.notes: 壊滅 is complete destruction, after which practically nothing is left – for example through war, earthquake or tsunami. It is intransitive: 町が壊滅する; "to annihilate something" is 壊滅させる. Very common is the adjective 壊滅的: 壊滅的な被害 ("devastating damage"), colloquially also exaggerated as in 数学の成績が壊滅的だ. Unlike 滅亡 (the fall of a state), 壊滅 emphasizes the degree of destruction; unlike 破壊, it does not emphasize the act of destroying.

examples[].german: I happened to see my boyfriend peeing on the street, and I was completely disillusioned.
When I met the writer I admired, he was so rude that I was disillusioned.
Many young people have become disillusioned with politics and no longer go to vote.
en.notes: 幻滅 is the disillusionment felt when an idealized image shatters: you suddenly see the disappointing reality of a person or thing. The cause takes に: 政治に幻滅する; to disillusion someone is 幻滅させる. It is stronger than がっかりする, which covers any kind of disappointment, and applies above all to people one admired or loved. Very common in conversation as 幻滅した.

examples[].german: When you catch a cold, eat nourishing food such as soybeans or apples.
This soup is rich in nourishment and is good for a body that is just recovering from illness.
This energy drink says 「滋養強壮」 on it.
en.notes: 滋養 means the nutritional value, the strengthening effect of food. Typical phrases are 滋養のある食べ物, 滋養に富む and 滋養をつける. Very well known is 滋養強壮 ("strengthening and invigoration"), which appears on the labels of energy drinks and tonics. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned; in everyday speech people usually say 栄養. A single nutrient, on the other hand, is called 栄養素.

examples[].german: I read in this morning's paper that the steel company is planning to build the world's largest blast furnace.
In a blast furnace, iron is made using iron ore and coke.
For environmental reasons, a growing number of steelworks are switching from blast furnaces to electric furnaces.
en.notes: 高炉 is the blast furnace in which pig iron is produced from iron ore and coke. The word comes from industrial and business news; 高炉メーカー are the large integrated steel companies. A more general term, also understood in everyday life, is 溶鉱炉. In contrast stands 電炉 ("electric arc furnace"), which melts scrap and is considered more climate-friendly.

examples[].german: My kid wet his pants, so I washed them and am drying them in front of the fireplace now.
On winter nights, our family sat around the fireplace and talked.
When we arrived at the mountain hut, we first put firewood in the fireplace and lit it.
en.notes: 暖炉 is an open fireplace of the Western kind, in which wood is burned. Typical phrases are 暖炉に火をつける, 暖炉に薪を入れる and 暖炉を囲む ("to gather around the fireplace"). In Japanese homes it is rare and seems romantic and European; heating is usually done with a ストーブ or エアコン. The traditional open hearth in a farmhouse is called 囲炉裏.

examples[].german: We received a complaint from a customer.
The customer at the next table complained that the food was cold.
The new employees received training in handling complaints.
en.notes: The Japanese クレーム comes from the English "claim", but mostly means "complaint", especially from customers. Typical are クレームをつける ("to complain, to make a claim"), クレームが来る／入る, クレーム対応 ("complaint handling") and クレーマー for habitual complainers. More factual is 苦情; toward the customer themselves one politely says ご指摘 or ご意見. A loanword from French with the same spelling means "cream" (in sweets).

examples[].german: Why did they try to hide that the reactor core had melted?
The cooling system stopped, so a core meltdown occurred.
The workers constantly monitor the temperature of the reactor core.
en.notes: 炉心 is the core of a nuclear reactor, where the fuel assemblies sit. The word appears almost only in connection with nuclear power, especially in 炉心溶融 ("core meltdown", also メルトダウン) and 炉心損傷. It belongs to technical language and to news about power plant accidents. The reactor as a whole is called 原子炉.

examples[].german: Some people warned the government about building nuclear reactors.
The reactor shut down automatically when it detected the earthquake tremors.
It takes decades to decommission an aging reactor.
en.notes: 原子炉 is the nuclear reactor itself; the whole power plant is called 原子力発電所, 原発 for short. Typical phrases are 原子炉を停止する, 原子炉が稼働する and 再稼働 ("restart"). The final shutdown is called 廃炉, literally "to abolish the reactor". The word is technical and matter-of-fact and appears mainly in the news and energy debates.

examples[].german: May I ask for the URL of your blog?
I asked the department head for permission regarding my vacation dates.
Mr. Tanaka from the sales department phones his regular customers every month to ask after their well-being.
en.notes: 伺い is the noun form of the humble verb 伺う ("to ask; to visit") and almost always appears with お. お伺いを立てる means to ask a superior for permission or instructions. The meaning "visit" is contained in ご機嫌伺い ("courtesy visit, or a call to ask how someone is doing"), and in 進退伺い the formal offer to resign. お伺いする as a verb is strictly speaking considered double politeness, but is completely normal in business.

examples[].german: When I arrived at the airport, fans were crowded there - that really surprised me.
Ants are swarming over the candy that fell on the ground.
Customers crowded at the entrance to the clearance sale.
en.notes: 群がる is intransitive and describes many people or animals "crowding, flocking, swarming" at one spot. The target is marked with に: 砂糖に蟻が群がる, スターにファンが群がる. Compared with the neutral 集まる "to gather", 群がる emphasizes the dense, often disorderly mass and sounds vivid, sometimes slightly derogatory. Related is the noun 群れ "herd, swarm".

examples[].german: The lighter I threw hit the TV, and the LCD screen cracked.
I dropped my smartphone and the screen cracked.
The calculator's display is getting faint, so I'll change the battery.
en.notes: 液晶 is the liquid crystal or the liquid crystal display (LCD). Common in 液晶画面, 液晶テレビ and 液晶ディスプレイ. Colloquially, 液晶 alone often stands for a device's display: スマホの液晶が割れた. Newer technology is called 有機EL (OLED). The word is technical but familiar in daily life.

examples[].german: This crystal comes in three sizes: large, medium and small.
The fortune teller peered into the crystal ball and talked about my future.
Yamanashi Prefecture has long been known as a source of rock crystal.
en.notes: 水晶 is rock crystal or quartz as a mineral, literally "water crystal". Well known are 水晶玉 (the fortune-teller's "crystal ball") and the quartz in watches. "Crystal" in the general chemical sense, on the other hand, is 結晶, and crystal glass is クリスタル. In anatomy, 水晶体 is the lens of the eye.

examples[].german: You say I farted? That's a false accusation.
He was falsely accused of shoplifting and taken to the store's office.
Ten years later the real culprit was finally found, and the man was cleared of the false charge.
en.notes: 濡れ衣 literally means "wet garment" and figuratively means a false accusation. The fixed phrases are 濡れ衣を着せる ("to pin something on someone"), 濡れ衣を着せられる ("to be wrongly accused") and 濡れ衣を晴らす or 濡れ衣が晴れる ("to be cleared of false suspicion"). In conversation you retort with それは濡れ衣だ. For a legal miscarriage of justice, people say 冤罪.

examples[].german: Vietnamese coffee was very sweet. I was surprised!
Yesterday's exam was really hard.
I've been busy with work lately and am really exhausted.
en.notes: すごく is the adverbial form of すごい and means "very, totally, insanely"; it stands before adjectives and verbs: すごく暑い, すごく疲れた. It is colloquial – in formal texts, とても or 非常に is used. The kanji spelling 凄く is rare; normally すごく is written in kana. In conversation you often hear すごい美味しい instead of すごく美味しい, but this is considered non-standard. For emphasis people also say すっごく.

examples[].german: The fried chicken is ready!
If the oil temperature is low, the tempura won't fry up crisp.
On a windy day, a kite is flying high in the sky.
en.notes: 揚がる is the intransitive counterpart of 揚げる ("to deep-fry") and means that something is finished frying: 天ぷらが揚がる, カラッと揚がる ("to turn out nicely crisp"). With the same spelling, kites and fireworks also rise into the air: 凧が揚がる, 花火が揚がる. For the general "to rise, go up", 上がる is written instead. When cooking, you often hear 揚がったよ as a signal that the food is ready.

examples[].german: It's thanks to my father's help.
For this survey, we asked the local people for their assistance.
He spared no effort in helping his friend start a business.
en.notes: 助力 is support given to someone in an undertaking. It is formal and often used as a noun: 助力を求める, 助力を得る, 助力を惜しまない ("to support with all one's strength"), politely ご助力. As a する-verb it is intransitive: 〜に助力する. Unlike 協力 ("cooperation"), here one side helps the other; 援助 means more financial or material aid, 手伝い everyday help.

examples[].german: We are looking for a new supplier.
We were notified of a price increase by our supplier.
After we changed suppliers, costs fell by ten percent.
en.notes: 仕入先 is the "supplier" from which a business buys goods or materials for resale or processing - from 仕入れる ("to purchase, to source") and 先 ("counterpart, address"). Related is 取引先 ("business partner" in general); the counterpart is 販売先 ("buyer"). Typical are 仕入先を探す／変える and 仕入先との交渉. The spelling varies between 仕入先 and 仕入れ先; business language.

examples[].german: He watches the live broadcast of the Oscars while sinking into the sofa.
An enemy submarine sank the transport ship.
The champion floored the challenger in the third round.
en.notes: 沈める is the transitive counterpart of 沈む "to sink, to go down": 船を沈める "to sink a ship". Figuratively 身を沈める means "to sink (deep) into an armchair", and in boxing 相手をマットに沈める "to send the opponent to the canvas". Do not confuse with the same-sounding 静める/鎮める "to calm, to soothe" (気持ちを静める, 痛みを鎮める).

examples[].german: That phone strap is so gross that I feel sick just thinking about it.
As a souvenir, I bought a phone strap with the local mascot.
These days, far fewer people attach a strap to their phone.
en.notes: 携帯ストラップ is a small charm on a loop that is hung on a cell phone – often with figures, good-luck charms or souvenir motifs like ご当地キャラ. In the days of flip phones it was extremely widespread; today smartphones mostly have no strap hole anymore, and you see phone neck straps (ショルダーストラップ) more often. You say ストラップを付ける, and in conversation also simply ストラップ.

examples[].german: The philosopher held his beret firmly as he walked through the strong wind.
Socrates is a famous philosopher of ancient Greece.
When my father gets drunk, he starts talking about life like a philosopher.
en.notes: 哲学者 is a philosopher, formed from 哲学 ("philosophy") and the person suffix 者 as in 学者 or 科学者. Typical are ギリシャの哲学者 or 有名な哲学者. For a general "thinker", people tend to say 思想家. Jokingly, someone who likes to ponder life is also called 哲学者みたい.

examples[].german: My sister is anorexic, and in mourning clothes she looked even thinner.
The funeral was sudden, so I rented mourning clothes.
For the wake, it is said to be acceptable to go in plain clothes rather than mourning clothes.
en.notes: 喪服 is the black mourning clothing for funerals and memorial services; 喪 means "mourning" as in 喪中 (the mourning period during which one does not send New Year's cards). You say 喪服を着る; in stores it is also called ブラックフォーマル. For the wake お通夜, it is traditionally considered appropriate to also appear in plain, dark clothing, since 喪服 here can seem as if one had expected the death.

examples[].german: The arm-wrestling challenger crushed an apple with his right hand to show off his grip strength.
The champion knocked out the challenger in the third round.
On this quiz show, new contestants go after the prize money every week.
en.notes: 挑戦者 is the challenger, especially in sports, title fights and quiz shows; the opposite is the チャンピオン or the 王者. Note: 挑戦 does not mean "challenge" in the sense of a difficult task (that is 課題), but "to dare something, to try one's hand at something": 新しいことに挑戦する. Therefore 挑戦者 generally refers to someone who takes on a test or a record.

examples[].german: Fried donuts, fried bananas, fried dumplings... I just love fried food.
Kitsune udon has sweetly simmered fried tofu on top.
For lunch, I ate soba with kakiage (mixed vegetable fritters).
en.notes: 揚げ is the noun form of 揚げる ("to deep-fry"). As a prefix it means "fried": 揚げパン, 揚げ出し豆腐; as a suffix it forms dish names such as 唐揚げ, かき揚げ and 竜田揚げ. On its own, 揚げ (or お揚げ, especially in western Japan) stands for 油揚げ, fried tofu, for example in きつねうどん. Fried foods in general are called 揚げ物.

examples[].german: The angry Koichi pounded the desk with his clenched fist.
This racket has a thick grip and is easy to hold.
At the sushi restaurant, I ordered one serving of nigiri.
en.notes: 握り is the noun form of 握る ("to grasp, hold tightly") and has several meanings: the grip of an object (ラケットの握り), the way of gripping, a handful (一握りの米, figuratively ほんの一握りの人 "just a handful of people") and short for 握り寿司. It is also contained in 握り拳 ("fist") and おにぎり. For door handles, people tend to say 取っ手 or ノブ.

examples[].german: My uncle apparently shook a tree with a beehive in it because he had never been stung by a bee and wanted to know what it was like.
No matter how much I shook his shoulder, my younger brother didn't wake up.
The mother held the baby in her arms and slowly rocked her body.
en.notes: 揺する means to move something back and forth with the hand or body: 木を揺する, 肩を揺する, 体を揺する. It is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 揺れる ("to sway"). 揺らす is almost synonymous, 揺さぶる sounds more violent and is also used figuratively (心を揺さぶる). Written in kana, ゆする also means "to blackmail". Nervous jiggling of the leg is called 貧乏揺すり.

examples[].german: My kid had been really looking forward to the sleepover at kindergarten, but caught a cold and I've just given him antibiotics. So unfortunately he will have to miss tonight.
This weekend, we're going to a hot spring with an overnight stay.
I have an overnight shift tonight, so I can't go home.
en.notes: 泊まり is the noun form of 泊まる ("to stay overnight"). Very common is 泊まりで ("with an overnight stay") as opposed to 日帰り ("day trip"). お泊まり sounds childlike or friendly, as in お泊まり会 ("sleepover"). In work contexts, 泊まり also means night duty: 今日は泊まりだ. Guests who stay overnight are called 泊まり客.

examples[].german: I'm building a slide for my nephew's birthday, but I'm running a little behind schedule.
My daughter played on the playground slide, going down again and again.
In midsummer, the slide had gotten so hot that I almost got burned.
en.notes: 滑り台 is the slide on a playground, formed from 滑る ("to slide") and 台 ("stand, platform"). You say 滑り台を滑る or 滑り台で遊ぶ; it is also often written すべり台. Other playground equipment includes ブランコ ("swing"), ジャングルジム and 砂場 ("sandbox"). In technical language, it also refers to the slipway from which a ship is launched.

examples[].german: Popular sovereignty is the foundation of democracy.
The government strongly protested that the other country's actions were a violation of sovereignty.
Japan regained its sovereignty in 1952.
en.notes: 主権 is supreme state authority, i.e. the sovereignty of a state. Important combinations: 国民主権 ("popular sovereignty", a basic principle of the Japanese constitution), 主権国家 ("sovereign state"), 主権を侵害する ("to violate sovereignty"), 主権を回復する. The word belongs to political and legal written language. Do not confuse it with 主導権 ("leadership role, initiative").

examples[].german: We purchased goods at the wholesale price.
Every morning we buy fresh fish at the wholesale market.
My father runs a wholesale company for foodstuffs.
en.notes: 卸売 is the sale of goods in large quantities to dealers instead of to end customers - "wholesale"; the counterpart is 小売 ("retail"). Typical are 卸売業者 ("wholesaler"), 卸売市場 ("wholesale market") and 卸売価格. The related verb is 卸す ("to sell to dealers"); for short one also says 卸, e.g. in 卸値. Spellings: 卸売 and 卸売り.

examples[].german: I always burn my toast completely black.
I was so absorbed in the conversation that I burned the pot.
I scorched the shirt while ironing.
en.notes: 焦がす means to accidentally let something burn or to scorch it: パンを焦がす, 鍋を焦がす, アイロンでシャツを焦がす. It is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 焦げる ("to burn"), and the result is called 焦げ. Deliberate browning is described with 焦げ目をつける. Figuratively, 胸を焦がす means to be consumed by longing or love.

en.meaning: to blend in; to get lost among; to be distracted
examples[].german: The fever medicine got mixed in with the other medicines, and I no longer know which is which.
The culprit disappeared into the crowd and escaped.
When I listen to music, it takes my mind off things a bit.
en.notes: 紛れる means to get lost in a crowd or to mix in with other things so that one can no longer tell it apart: 書類に紛れる, 人込みに紛れる. From this come figurative meanings: acting under cover of something (闇に紛れて逃げる), being distracted (気が紛れる) and forgetting something in the midst of something else (忙しさに紛れて). It is intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 紛らす or 紛らわす (気を紛らわす).

examples[].german: That old screen door is really gross.
The screen door is torn, and mosquitoes are coming in.
On summer nights, it's cool to sleep with the window open and only the screen closed.
en.notes: 網戸 is the insect screen in front of windows and balcony doors, installed in almost every Japanese home; usually it is a sliding screen door. Typical are 網戸を閉める, 網戸が破れる and 網戸にする – opening the window and leaving only the screen closed. The word is composed of 網 ("net") and 戸 ("door").

examples[].german: That guy is just a youngster who has never been tossed about by the rough waves of society.
The Sea of Japan in winter is famous for its rough waves.
The company weathered the rough waves of the recession and kept growing.
en.notes: 荒波 literally means rough, raging waves on a stormy sea. Equally common is the figurative meaning "hardships, adversities of life", especially in 社会の荒波に揉まれる ("to have to prove oneself in the harsh working world"), 時代の荒波 and 荒波を乗り越える. The word has a slightly literary ring and appears in speeches and newspaper texts.

examples[].german: What is the best way to find dinosaur fossils?
My son loves dinosaurs and knows all their names.
Dinosaurs are thought to have gone extinct about 66 million years ago.
en.notes: 恐竜 literally means "terrible dragon" (恐 "fear", 竜 "dragon") and refers to dinosaurs. Typical combinations are 恐竜の化石, 恐竜の骨 and 恐竜が絶滅する. For mythical dragons, people say 竜 or ドラゴン instead. Well known in Japan is the dinosaur museum in Fukui Prefecture, where many fossils have been found.

en.meaning: unrelated to; having nothing to do with; without kin
examples[].german: This country road is free of traffic jams.
A life of luxury has nothing to do with me.
As the number of elderly people living alone grows, the "society without ties" has become a problem.
en.notes: 無縁 means "without connection to, having nothing to do with". Typical are AはBと無縁だ or Aには無縁だ: 私には贅沢など無縁だ. Also common is 無縁の: 争いとは無縁の生活. A second meaning is "without relatives", e.g. 無縁仏 (a dead person with no surviving relatives) and 無縁社会 ("society without ties", with isolated, lonely people). The word is neutral to literary.

en.meaning: marriage proposal (via a go-between); marriage talks
examples[].german: You're seriously offering me a match with a man who has at most a high school diploma? What are you thinking?!
A match was proposed for our daughter, but she herself is not particularly taken with it.
The marriage came about through a relative's mediation, and the wedding will be next spring.
en.notes: 縁談 is a marriage proposal made through intermediaries, i.e. the talks about a possible marriage that parents, relatives or acquaintances arrange - often in connection with お見合い. Typical are 縁談を持ち込む, 縁談がまとまる ("to be settled"), 縁談を断る and 縁談が破談になる. A personal marriage proposal from man to woman, by contrast, is called プロポーズ. The word sounds traditional.

examples[].german: Everyone wants to choose an auspicious day for their wedding.
When I drew a fortune slip at the New Year's shrine visit, it was 「吉」.
It's not yet clear whether this decision will turn out lucky or unlucky.
en.notes: 吉 (read きち on its own) means "good luck, good omen" and is met mainly on おみくじ, the fortune slips at shrines; the grades run roughly from 大吉 through 中吉, 小吉, 吉 and 末吉 down to 凶, though the order varies from shrine to shrine. The phrase 吉と出るか凶と出るか asks whether something will turn out lucky or unlucky. In compounds it is often read きつ or きっ: 不吉, 吉報. 吉日 ("lucky day") is read きちじつ.

examples[].german: I had such an ominous dream that I worried about you, so I called.
Some say it brings bad luck if a black cat crosses your path.
In Japan, the number four is considered unlucky because it sounds the same as the word for "death".
en.notes: 不吉 means "ominous, bringing bad luck" and is a na-adjective used with 予感, 夢, 数字 or 前兆: 不吉な予感がする. Colloquially the same is often said with 縁起が悪い; 不吉 sounds more serious and somewhat more literary. Well-known examples from Japan are the numbers 4 and 9, whose pronunciation recalls 死 ("death") and 苦 ("suffering").

examples[].german: Brandishing a knife, the man said to me in a low voice, "Come here."
When using bladed tools, please don't let children come near.
You cannot bring knives onto an airplane.
en.notes: 刃物 is the general term for all objects with a blade – knives, kitchen knives (包丁), scissors, razors. In the news, 刃物を持った男 is the typical phrasing for a knife attacker. Other combinations are 刃物を研ぐ ("to sharpen") and 刃物を扱う. The blade itself is called 刃 (は); Seki in Gifu is known as the town of cutlery (刃物の町).

examples[].german: The number of retail stores is decreasing.
It is being sold at 20 percent below the manufacturer's suggested retail price.
He has worked in the retail industry since graduating from university.
en.notes: 小売 is selling in small quantities directly to end consumers - "retail", the counterpart of 卸売. Typical are 小売店 ("retail store"), 小売業, 小売価格 and メーカー希望小売価格 ("manufacturer's suggested retail price"). The reading is こうり from こ＋うり, so no long o; also written 小売り. Matter-of-fact business language.

en.meaning: blade edge; tip of the blade
examples[].german: Holding the blade against my neck, he asked me what it feels like to have everyone always flatter you.
The tip of my kitchen knife chipped, so I bought a new one.
Using the tip of the knife, I carefully removed the fish bones.
en.notes: 刃先 is the cutting edge or the front tip of a blade, i.e. the part with which one actually cuts or stabs. Typical are 包丁の刃先, ナイフの刃先 and 刃先が欠ける ("to chip, break off"). With 刃先を当てる you hold the blade against something. Unlike 刃 ("blade" in general) and 刃物 ("edged tool"), 刃先 refers only to this front part.

examples[].german: I was embarrassed when my mother came to pick me up in a pink van.
In spring, the riverside is full of pink flowers.
Her cheeks flushed pink with embarrassment.
en.notes: 桃色 is the color of peach blossoms, i.e. a light pink – not the orange-yellow of a peach fruit. As a color noun it takes の or に: 桃色の花, 頬が桃色に染まる. In everyday speech people usually say ピンク; 桃色 (also もも色) sounds more traditional and poetic. In the past it also had the secondary meaning "erotic, amorous" (桃色遊戯), which is now obsolete.

examples[].german: That scene in the movie is always a mystery to me.
The mystery of the case remains unsolved to this day.
She is a very mysterious person; no one knows her real age.
en.notes: 謎 is a riddle or secret, something inexplicable: 謎を解く ("to solve a mystery"), 謎が解ける, 謎に包まれる ("to be shrouded in mystery"). As 謎の before a noun it means "mysterious, enigmatic": 謎の人物, 謎の死. The children's guessing game is called なぞなぞ. Colloquially, young people also use 謎 for "strange, incomprehensible": それ、謎すぎる.

examples[].german: All children probably like playing riddle games.
When I gave my daughter a riddle, she answered right away.
The riddle 「パンはパンでも食べられないパンはなあに？」 is famous.
en.notes: 謎々 is a wordplay riddle of the kind asked of children, often with a witty punchline: 「パンはパンでも食べられないパンは？」 Typical are 謎々を出す "to pose a riddle" and 謎々を解く／に答える "to solve". The word is usually written in kana: なぞなぞ. Do not confuse it with 謎 "secret, mystery" (謎の人物) or with クイズ "quiz" or パズル "puzzle, brainteaser".

examples[].german: Someone suddenly tapped my shoulder in the dark room, and I screamed involuntarily.
The concert hall was filled with the screams of the fans.
I'm not good with thrill rides like roller coasters.
en.notes: 絶叫 is a piercing scream let out at the top of one's lungs, usually from fear, shock or extreme excitement. As an intransitive する-verb, the exclamation takes と: 「助けて！」と絶叫する. It is much stronger than 叫ぶ "to shout, scream"; 悲鳴 is more a cry of fear or pain, 歓声 a cheer. Well known is 絶叫マシン for roller coasters and other thrill rides.

examples[].german: I'll let you know later how many we caught.
I caught a big fish in the river.
Be careful of shops that lure customers with cheap prices.
en.notes: 釣る means "to catch (with a rod)": 魚を釣る. "To go fishing" is mostly said with the noun: 釣りに行く, 釣りをする. The potential/intransitive form 釣れる means "to bite, to let itself be caught": 今日はよく釣れる. Figuratively 釣る means "to lure, to entice": 安い値段で客を釣る.

examples[].german: I wanted to have blond hair, so I bleached my hair with Coca-Cola.
Right after entering university, he dyed his hair blond.
A blond girl asked me for directions at the station.
en.notes: 金髪 refers to blond or golden hair, whether natural or dyed. As an attribute it takes の (金髪の女性); to dye is 髪を金髪に染める, "to turn blond" is 金髪になる. Hair dyed brown is 茶髪; the loanword ブロンド sounds more like natural blond. Grammatically 金髪 is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: "What are you doing right now?" "I'm just styling my hair."
There was a hair in the soup.
Lately my hair has been falling out easily, and I'm worried.
en.notes: 髪の毛 is the everyday word for hair on the head and also for a single hair (髪の毛が一本). It is somewhat more colloquial and concrete than 髪, which is used more for the hairstyle as a whole (髪を切る). 毛 alone refers to hair in general, including body hair or animal fur. Typical: 髪の毛が抜ける "hair falls out", 髪の毛をセットする "to style one's hair".

examples[].german: You have a Beatles-style hairstyle.
When I took the plunge and changed my hairstyle, everyone noticed right away.
What hairstyle should I wear to the interview?
en.notes: 髪型 is the hairstyle; the spelling 髪形 is also found. Typical are 髪型を変える "to change one's hairstyle", 短い髪型にする "to get a short hairstyle" and 髪型が似合う "the hairstyle suits one". At the hair salon you often hear the loanword ヘアスタイル as well. Grammatically 髪型 is a simple noun, not an expression.

examples[].german: The cannon boomed, and the man passed away, leaving three children behind.
A cannon from the Edo period is on display at the castle entrance.
The new foreign player is expected to be the team's big slugger.
en.notes: 大砲 is a cannon or heavy artillery piece; you say 大砲を撃つ "to fire a cannon" and count guns with 門 (大砲一門). Smaller firearms are 銃 or 鉄砲. In baseball, 大砲 colloquially refers to a home-run hitter who stands for a team's batting power.

examples[].german: Buying directly from a wholesaler makes it cheaper.
Many wholesalers of dolls and toys are gathered in Asakusabashi.
I thought I could memorize it all in one day, but it wasn't that easy.
en.notes: 問屋 means a "wholesaler" or wholesale business that buys goods from the manufacturer and resells them to retailers; more neutral and modern are 卸売業者 or simply 卸. Typical combinations are 問屋から仕入れる "to buy from a wholesaler" and 問屋街 "wholesale district". Very well known is the idiom そうは問屋が卸さない "it won't be that easy" - literally "the wholesaler won't supply on those terms".

en.meaning: tears of emotion; tears of joy
examples[].german: When do you think people choke up with tears of emotion?
The moment the victory was decided, the manager shed tears of emotion.
The final scene of this movie was truly a tearjerker.
en.notes: 感涙 are tears shed from emotion, gratitude or overwhelming joy – not from sorrow. The word is elevated and literary; fixed phrases are 感涙を流す and 感涙にむせぶ "to sob with emotion". Colloquially people say 感動して泣く or 嬉し涙. Informally, 感涙もの means "beautiful enough to make you cry".

examples[].german: My father works at a canned peach factory.
Please throw empty cans into this trash bin.
On the way home, I bought two cans of coffee at the convenience store.
en.notes: 缶 is a can or tin and appears in many compounds: 缶ビール, 缶コーヒー, 空き缶 "empty can", 缶切り "can opener", 缶詰 "canned food". For beverage cans one usually counts with 本, but 缶 itself can also be a counter (ビール3缶). Glass bottles, by contrast, are called 瓶 (びん), plastic bottles ペットボトル.

examples[].german: They're making a fortune selling delicious canned coffee.
On cold mornings, I buy a hot canned coffee from a vending machine.
Canned coffee is too sweet, so I rarely drink it.
en.notes: 缶コーヒー is sweetened or black coffee in a can, as bought everywhere in Japan from vending machines (自動販売機, 自販機 for short) and at convenience stores – hot (ホット) in winter, cold (アイス) in summer. It is a typical everyday drink for commuters and workers. It is counted with 〜本: 缶コーヒーを一本買う. Similarly formed are 缶ビール and 缶ジュース.

examples[].german: I've come to pick you up, my little princess.
Once upon a time, a beautiful princess lived in a certain country.
My daughter loves having her picture taken in a princess dress.
en.notes: 姫様 "princess" is almost always used with the polite prefix お: お姫様. It is the word of fairy tales and the world of children, and also used affectionately for little girls; the official term for daughters of a royal house is 王女, or for the Japanese imperial family 皇女. Also well known is お姫様抱っこ, carrying someone in one's arms "like a bride".

examples[].german: I was thinking about whether light is a particle or a wave and couldn't sleep last night.
The grain of this photo is coarse, so it becomes blurry when enlarged.
When fine particles in the air get into the lungs, they have a bad effect on health.
en.notes: 粒子 is a technical word for a particle or fine grain: in physics (素粒子 "elementary particle", 光の粒子), for fine dust in the air and in photography (粒子が粗い "coarse-grained"). In everyday speech, for grains people tend to say 粒 (つぶ). Note: the grammatical "particle" is not called 粒子 but 助詞.

examples[].german: The violent thunderstorm this morning caused a power outage, so I can't use the internet right now.
According to the weather forecast, there will be thunderstorms from the afternoon.
The open-air concert was canceled because of a sudden thunderstorm.
en.notes: 雷雨 is a thunderstorm with rain – literally "thunder and rain". The word belongs more to the language of weather reports and news: 雷雨になる, 激しい雷雨, 雷雨注意報. In conversation people often simply say 雷が鳴って雨が降る; a short summer shower in the afternoon is 夕立. 雷 alone means "thunder, lightning".

examples[].german: When I opened the package, there was a homing torpedo inside.
The torpedo fired from the submarine hit the enemy ship.
The battleship was hit by a torpedo and sank within just a few minutes.
en.notes: 魚雷 is a torpedo, literally "fish mine". Typical combinations: 魚雷を発射する "to fire a torpedo", 魚雷が命中する "a torpedo hits", 魚雷を受ける "to be hit by a torpedo". Related words with 雷 in the sense of "explosive device" are 機雷 "naval mine" and 地雷 "land mine". The word appears mainly in history, news and war films.

examples[].german: If a giant tornado hit this area, what would happen to the control tower?
The pilot landed following the control tower's instructions.
You can see the control tower well from the airport's observation deck.
en.notes: 管制塔 is an airport's control tower, from which air traffic is directed. 管制 means "control, direction" (航空管制 "air traffic control"), and the air traffic controllers are called 管制官. Typical: 管制塔の指示に従う "to follow the tower's instructions". For a playmaker in sports in the figurative sense, people say 司令塔 instead, not 管制塔.

examples[].german: What did you like about the Eiffel Tower?
If I go to Paris, I want to climb the Eiffel Tower.
We had a great view of the Eiffel Tower from the hotel room.
en.notes: エッフェル塔 is the name of the Parisian landmark; 塔 (とう) means "tower" and is attached to the proper name, as in ピサの斜塔. For 東京タワー, on the other hand, the English タワー is used. Typical are エッフェル塔に登る "to climb the Eiffel Tower" and エッフェル塔が見える "the Eiffel Tower is visible". The spelling mixes katakana for the name with the kanji 塔.

examples[].german: We signed a contract with an overseas agent.
I booked a tour to Hokkaido at a travel agency.
My older brother works at an advertising agency.
en.notes: 代理店 is a company that sells products or arranges services on behalf of another firm: "agency, agent, authorized dealer". It is most often encountered in compounds such as 旅行代理店 "travel agency", 広告代理店 "advertising agency" and 保険代理店 "insurance agency"; a 正規代理店 is an "authorized dealer". 代理店 stresses that one is not the manufacturer or provider oneself; in everyday speech one often simply says 旅行会社 for the travel agency.

en.meaning: to let get away; to fail to catch
examples[].german: Don't you think pretending you couldn't catch the criminal is a bit overdoing it?
The police let the culprit slip away at the last moment.
I let a precious chance slip away, and I'm really frustrated.
en.notes: 取り逃がす means to let someone or something you had almost caught get away: 犯人を取り逃がす "to let the culprit escape", figuratively also チャンスを取り逃がす "to miss a chance". It is transitive (〜を取り逃がす); the one who escapes is described with 逃げる. Unlike 逃がす "to set free" (intentionally), 取り逃がす emphasizes unintentional failure; 逃す (のがす) is the general "to miss".

examples[].german: "Well, it's about time to go to bed." My grandfather said this to me every night when I was a child.
I laid an old blanket in the cat's bed for it.
When we arrive at the campsite, let's first secure a place to sleep.
en.notes: 寝床 is the place to sleep, that is, a bed or a laid-out futon, of any kind. Typical phrases: 寝床に入る "to go to bed", more elevated 寝床に就く, and 寝床を作る "to prepare the sleeping place". In everyday speech people usually just say ベッド or 布団; 寝床 sounds somewhat old-fashioned or is used for animals (犬の寝床). Do not confuse it with 寝室 "bedroom".

examples[].german: It seems like a pretty secure job, so I'm thinking of studying to become a funeral director.
He isn't flashy, but he supports the team with his solid play.
This time I didn't take risks and chose a solid investment.
en.notes: 手堅い describes something solid, low-risk and dependable: 手堅い仕事 "a secure job", 手堅い投資 "a solid investment", 手堅いプレー "solid, error-free play". Adverbially: 手堅く勝つ "to win safely". Closely related is 堅実 "solid, conscientious"; 安全 rather means freedom from danger, and 確実 certainty. Applied to people, it praises a careful, reliable way of working.

examples[].german: My car was broken into last night and my Mac was stolen.
Wild boars ravaged the field, and almost all the vegetables are gone.
Someone is trolling our online forum, and it's a real problem.
en.notes: 荒らす means "to ravage, to cause damage": イノシシが畑を荒らす "wild boars ravage the field". Also "to break in, to plunder" - hence nouns like 車上荒らし "car break-in" or 事務所荒らし "office burglary". Colloquially, 荒らす on the internet means "to troll, to spam" (掲示板を荒らす), a troll is called 荒らし. It is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 荒れる (海が荒れる, 肌が荒れる).

examples[].german: One sun is one-tenth of a shaku, about 3.03 centimeters.
"Issun-bōshi" is a folktale about a boy who is only one sun tall.
They say you can't see even an inch ahead, so you'd better save up a little money.
en.notes: 寸 is an old Japanese unit of length: one-tenth of a 尺, about 3.03 cm. Today it is met mainly in fixed words and sayings: 一寸法師 (the "inch-high" boy from the fairy tale), 一寸先は闇 "the future is uncertain", 寸前 "just before" and 寸法 "measurements". In traditional crafts, such as with carpenters, measurements are still made in 寸 and 尺. Note: 一寸 can also be read as ateji for ちょっと.

en.meaning: on the verge of; just before
examples[].german: My company is on the verge of bankruptcy.
I somehow managed to get on the train just before the doors closed.
I fell just before the finish line and missed out on the victory.
en.notes: 寸前 means "immediately before, just before" and often emphasizes that something (usually negative) almost happened. It stands after nouns as a suffix (破産寸前, 倒産寸前) or after the dictionary form of a verb (閉まる寸前に). More neutral and temporal is 直前 "right before"; 寸前 sounds more dramatic, like "hanging in the balance". Grammatically it is a noun, not a particle.

examples[].german: Even though I took a direct lightning strike, I miraculously escaped unharmed.
Due to a lightning strike, train service is currently suspended.
Yesterday an accident caused by lightning occurred at a golf course.
en.notes: 落雷 is a lightning strike. The word is rather literary and typical of news and announcements (落雷のため運転見合わせ, 落雷による停電); in conversation people say 雷が落ちる. As an intransitive する-verb, 落雷する is possible but rare. To be struck by lightning is 雷に打たれる.

examples[].german: I've been given the chance to take on a part of a big project.
Volunteers are the ones who play a part in the area's disaster prevention activities.
Japan's automobile industry has played its part in economic growth.
en.notes: 一翼 literally means "one wing", but it is used almost only figuratively in the fixed phrase 〜の一翼を担う: "to take on a part (of a task), to play a role". The expression is elevated and typical of speeches, corporate texts and news. Related in meaning but more everyday are 役割を果たす and 一部を担当する.

examples[].german: The positions between second base and shortstop and in left and right field are still open.
The eagle spread both wings wide and took off.
This airplane has one engine on each wing.
en.notes: 両翼 means "both wings": of birds and airplanes, but also the two flanks of an army or the side wings of a building. In baseball, 両翼 means the left and right outfield (両翼100メートルの球場). The counterpart is 片翼 "one wing". Typical: 両翼を広げる "to spread the wings".

examples[].german: Lately I've been eating string cheese every morning.
The lightning split the big tree right in two.
I wouldn't tell that secret for anything.
en.notes: 裂ける is intransitive and means "to rip open, split (along a line or fiber)": 木が裂ける, 布が裂ける, 地面が裂ける. The transitive counterpart is 裂く (intensified 引き裂く). Paper or clothing getting holes is more 破れる; glass or dishes 割れる. Well known is the idiom 口が裂けても言えない "I won't say it at any price".

examples[].german: Next year a new branch will be opened in Osaka.
My father is going to be transferred to the Fukuoka branch next month.
The place where I opened my account was the branch in front of the station.
en.notes: 支店 is the "branch, branch office" of a company, especially at banks, department stores and trading firms; the counterpart is 本店 "main store" or 本社 "headquarters". Typical are 支店を開く/出す "to open a branch", 支店長 "branch manager" and 〜支店に転勤する "to be transferred to the ... branch". 支社, by contrast, is more of a regional office with administrative functions, and 店舗 simply a single retail store.

examples[].german: The Big Dipper is made up of seven stars.
If you use the Big Dipper as a guide, it's easy to find the North Star.
I could clearly see the Big Dipper in the spring night sky.
en.notes: 北斗七星 is the Big Dipper – literally "the seven stars of the northern dipper" (北斗). It belongs to the constellation おおぐま座 "Great Bear". A typical remark is that with its help one can find the North Star 北極星. The word is neutral and appears in school, astronomy and mythology.

examples[].german: An 18-liter can is used to store things such as detergent and oil.
Cooking oil for commercial use is often sold in 18-liter cans.
In a corner of the factory, many empty 18-liter cans were stacked.
en.notes: 一斗缶 is a square tin can with a capacity of 18 liters. 斗 is an old unit of volume (10 升, about 18 l) that today lives on practically only in this word. 一斗缶 are used for wholesale cooking oil, paint, solvents or kerosene. Note the reading with gemination: いっとかん.

examples[].german: A lot of sediment has accumulated on the riverbed.
Heavy rain caused a landslide, and the road became impassable.
Trucks are carrying soil away from the construction site.
en.notes: 土砂 means "earth and sand", i.e. loose soil, rubble and sediment. It is very common in disaster reports: 土砂崩れ "landslide", 土砂災害 "landslide and debris flow disaster". At construction sites people speak of 土砂を運ぶ／積む. The word 土砂降り "downpour" is written with the same characters, but is a figurative exception.

examples[].german: The more options you have for the future, the better.
Choose the correct answer from the following four options.
In the current situation, declining is not an option.
en.notes: 選択肢 are the possibilities available to choose from – originally the answer options in multiple-choice questions, today quite generally "option". Typical: 選択肢が多い／限られる, 選択肢から選ぶ and 〜という選択肢はない "... is out of the question". 選択, on the other hand, is the act of choosing itself. In business language, オプション is also used.

examples[].german: That star is about four light-years from Earth.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.
His skill is light-years ahead of mine.
en.notes: 光年 is a unit of length in astronomy: the distance light travels in a year – so not a time span, even though 年 is in it. It stands directly after numbers (4光年, 何光年) and is usually used with 離れている or 先. In an exaggerated figurative sense people also say 何光年も先を行っている "to be light-years ahead". Grammatically 光年 is a noun or counter unit, not a particle.

examples[].german: Anti-nuclear activists believe that abolishing nuclear weapons is achievable.
Education is indispensable for eradicating discrimination from the world.
With no one left to carry on, that distinguished family died out.
en.notes: 廃絶 transitively means "to abolish completely, eliminate"; it is a formal word, used above all in 核兵器の廃絶 or 核廃絶 "nuclear disarmament" and 差別の廃絶. Intransitively it can also mean "to die out, become extinct" (家が廃絶する). To distinguish: 廃止 "to abolish" (laws, institutions), 撤廃 "to repeal" (rules, tariffs), 根絶 "to eradicate" (diseases).

en.meaning: to let stay overnight; to put up
examples[].german: I don't like letting strangers stay at my place.
I let a friend who had missed the last train stay at my place for the night.
A typhoon was coming, so we left the boat moored in the harbor.
en.notes: 泊める is the transitive counterpart of 泊まる: to let someone stay overnight at one's home, to put someone up. Typical: 友達を家に泊める, 一晩泊めてもらう "to be allowed to stay overnight at someone's place". Less often it also means "to anchor a ship" (船を港に泊める). Do not confuse it with the identically read 止める "to stop" and 停める "to park".

examples[].german: If I manage to tear that couple apart, I'll let you know.
In her anger, she tore the letter to shreds.
A family torn apart by the war was reunited after fifty years.
en.notes: 引き裂く is an intensified form of 裂く: to tear something apart by force (手紙を引き裂く, びりびりに引き裂く). Figuratively it means to tear people apart by force: 二人の仲を引き裂く, 戦争で引き裂かれた家族. The intransitive counterpart is 裂ける. For simply tearing paper, people also say 破る in everyday speech.

examples[].german: They had no idea that they could attack Titans from the air.
An armed group raided a police station.
A plan was devised to raid the enemy base before dawn.
en.notes: 襲撃する means "to raid, to carry out an attack", usually by surprise and targeted at a place or person: 基地を襲撃する, 襲撃を受ける "to be attacked". The word is written-language and typical of news and war reports. More general is 攻撃 "attack" (also in sports); the native verb 襲う sounds more everyday and is also used for animals or forces of nature.

examples[].german: In Japan, long commutes to school or work are quite common.
My girlfriend and I are in a long-distance relationship between Tokyo and Osaka right now.
Long-distance driving is tiring, so we took several breaks on the way.
en.notes: 遠距離 means "a great distance, long haul" and usually appears as the first element of compounds: 遠距離通勤 "long commute", 遠距離恋愛 (short 遠恋) "long-distance relationship", 遠距離バス. As an attribute, の is used: 遠距離の運転. The opposite is 近距離; 長距離 emphasizes more the length of a route (長距離走 "long-distance run"). Grammatically it is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: I launched a new business.
Due to the recession, the company scaled back its overseas operations.
The city increased its budget for child-rearing support programs.
en.notes: 事業 refers to a larger-scale business or social undertaking: "business, line of business, project". Typical are 事業を始める/立ち上げる/拡大する, 事業に失敗する and compounds such as 事業部 "business division", 公共事業 "public works" and 慈善事業 "charity work". Unlike 仕事 "work, job", 事業 does not mean an individual's activity but a whole undertaking of a company, agency or organization; 企業, by contrast, is the enterprise as a firm.

examples[].german: Taxi drivers generally dislike short-distance rides, don't they?
For short distances, a bicycle is faster than the train.
That photo was taken from a fairly close distance.
en.notes: 近距離 is the "short distance, close range". It often appears in compounds like 近距離乗車 "short ride" or 近距離通勤, and with から／で: 近距離から撮影する. For "from the very closest range" there is 至近距離. The opposite is 遠距離; 短距離, on the other hand, emphasizes the shortness of a route (短距離走 "sprint").

examples[].german: She was a sprinter in high school.
For short distances, the Shinkansen is more convenient than the airplane.
This drone can only fly short distances.
en.notes: 短距離 means "short distance" and is the opposite of 長距離. In sports it appears in 短距離走 "sprint" and 短距離選手 "sprinter", in transport in 短距離便 "short-haul flight", in the military in 短距離ミサイル. For "near, a short way" in everyday speech, people tend to say 近い; 短距離 sounds matter-of-fact and technical, and often stands as a compound or with の before nouns.

en.meaning: entry into the family register; registering a marriage
examples[].german: We plan to register our marriage before the wedding ceremony.
A popular actor announced that he had registered his marriage with a non-celebrity woman.
The two registered their marriage last month and reportedly plan to hold a wedding ceremony next spring.
en.notes: 入籍 literally means "to enter into a family register (戸籍)". Colloquially and in celebrity news, it almost always means a legal marriage, i.e. filing the 婚姻届. Typical: 〜と入籍する, 入籍を発表する; synonymous and more casual is 籍を入れる. The wedding ceremony (結婚式) is separate and can take place before or after.

en.meaning: to perish; to fall; to go extinct
examples[].german: If the Earth is going to perish, why should I give up bacon?
Why the dinosaurs went extinct is still being researched today.
Even the flourishing ancient city eventually perished through war.
en.notes: 滅びる means "to perish, to go to ruin, to go extinct" and is used for empires, peoples, cultures, species or the world: 国が滅びる, 恐竜が滅びた. It is intransitive; transitively it is 滅ぼす "to destroy". There is also the synonymous godan form 滅ぶ. For the extinction of species in the technical sense, 絶滅 is usual.

examples[].german: Psychological rigidity is thought to hinder solving problems.
I was so nervous that my body froze and I couldn't speak.
The time of death was estimated from the state of rigor mortis.
en.notes: 硬直 is stiffening or becoming rigid: physically (体が硬直する from fear or tension, 死後硬直 "rigor mortis") and figuratively for rigid, inflexible structures (硬直した組織, 考え方が硬直している). For the development toward rigidity, people say 硬直化. As an intransitive する-verb it takes が. More everyday for muscles are 固まる or こわばる.

examples[].german: I get goose bumps just from hearing the name "cockroach".
It's cold, and I have goose bumps on my arms.
Hearing that singer's live voice gave me goose bumps.
en.notes: 鳥肌 is goose bumps – literally "bird skin". It almost always appears in the phrase 鳥肌が立つ "to get goose bumps". Originally it referred only to cold, fear or disgust; today it is also said for emotion and enthusiasm (鳥肌が立つほど感動した), which some language purists criticize as misuse. Informally, something thrilling is called 鳥肌もの "something that gives you goose bumps".

examples[].german: This towel is very soft and feels pleasant on the skin.
I'm looking for pajamas that feel good against the skin.
This sweater is scratchy and feels unpleasant.
en.notes: 肌触り is the feeling a material leaves on the skin: 肌触りがいい／悪い, 肌触りが柔らかい／滑らか. It is used above all for fabrics, clothing, towels and bedding. Related words are 手触り (when touching with the hand), 舌触り (in the mouth) and 歯ごたえ (when chewing). Rarely, it also refers to the way someone comes across to others.

examples[].german: The skin tone of the woman in this painting is really beautiful.
It's hard to choose a foundation that matches your own skin tone.
In today's crayons, the name 「うすだいだい」 is used instead of 「肌色」.
en.notes: 肌色 has two meanings: one's own skin color or skin tone (自分の肌色に合うファンデーション) and, as a color name, a light beige-orange. Because the color name is considered exclusionary, the colored pencil has mostly been called うすだいだい or ペールオレンジ since about 2000. For skin tone, people also say 肌の色. Grammatically 肌色 is a noun, not an adjective (肌色の).

examples[].german: The Pacific Ocean was crowded with small boats.
We rode in a small boat and slowly went down the river.
On the stormy sea, the small boat tossed like a leaf.
en.notes: 小舟 is a small boat or skiff, often rowed or sailed; you go with 小舟に乗る. The character 舟 stands for small, simple boats, whereas 船 refers to large ships. In modern everyday speech, for rowboats people tend to say ボート; 小舟 sounds somewhat literary and often appears in narratives and comparisons (木の葉のように揺れる小舟).

examples[].german: The bell rings twelve times at noon.
On New Year's Eve, we went to a nearby temple to ring the New Year's bell.
The church bells rang out, celebrating the couple's wedding.
en.notes: 鐘 is a large, usually hanging bell, as found in temples and churches. You say 鐘が鳴る "the bell rings", 鐘を鳴らす and, specifically for temple bells, 鐘をつく "to strike the bell". Small bells are called 鈴, electric bells ベル or チャイム. Do not confuse it with the identically read 金 "money".

en.meaning: type of industry; line of business
examples[].german: Companies from various industries took part.
In job hunting, I chose companies by job type rather than by industry.
Average salaries differ greatly by industry.
en.notes: 業種 is the "industry" in the sense of a category of types of business, such as retail, construction or restaurants. Typical are 業種別 "by industry", 異業種 "different industry" (異業種交流 "cross-industry exchange") and the question about the 業種 in job applications. 業界, in contrast, means the industry as the world of the companies active in it (IT業界), while 職種 denotes the type of work of the individual ("occupational group", e.g. sales or engineering).

examples[].german: Researchers are sounding the alarm about how fast the icebergs are melting.
Experts are warning about young people's smartphone addiction.
This accident can be called a wake-up call about lax safety management.
en.notes: 警鐘 is originally an alarm or fire bell; today it is used almost only figuratively as "warning, wake-up call". The fixed phrase is 〜に警鐘を鳴らす "to warn about something, to sound the alarm", often with experts or the media as the subject. The word is literary and typical of news and editorials. Read the same way are 継承 "succession" and 敬称 "title of address, honorific".

en.meaning: weapon (used in a crime); dangerous weapon
examples[].german: Shouting "Achoooo!", Koichi knocked the dangerous weapon out of Viet's hand.
The police found the weapon near the crime scene.
A car driven by a drunk driver is a weapon on wheels.
en.notes: 凶器 is a weapon in the sense of "weapon used in a crime, dangerous object", especially in crime and police reports: 凶器はナイフだった, 凶器が見つかる. Unlike 武器 (weapon in general, also in war or in games), 凶器 emphasizes use in an act of violence; everyday objects like a hammer also become a 凶器. Figuratively, 走る凶器 is said of a recklessly driven car.

examples[].german: The cause of the terrible virus that wiped out half of humanity was a watermelon filled with vodka.
Lack of sleep was the real cause of my skin problems.
The root cause of this incident is said to be the company's outdated culture.
en.notes: 元凶 refers to the real cause or main culprit of an evil – always with a negative tone: 事件の元凶, 不況の元凶. Compared with the neutral 原因 "cause", 元凶 sounds accusing, as if naming a guilty party. Typical pattern: 〜の元凶は…だ. The tone is rather literary (newspapers, commentary); in conversation it is often half-joking.

examples[].german: Everyone thought it would be impossible for that violent criminal to serve his sentence quietly in prison.
Violent crimes have been continuing lately, and it worries me.
The man had a fierce-looking face, but was actually a very kind person.
