en.notes: 凶悪 describes extremely brutal, heinous crimes or criminals. It is a な-adjective: 凶悪な事件, 凶悪な顔つき. Very common in the news are the compounds 凶悪犯 "violent criminal", 凶悪犯罪 and 凶悪事件. Related are 残酷 "cruel" (of an act) and 悪質 "malicious, vicious" (more for fraud or violations).

examples[].german: Next week I plan to be hunting in the mountains the whole time.
In autumn, our family goes out to view the autumn leaves.
In medieval Europe, many women fell victim to witch hunts.
en.notes: 狩り is hunting, the nominalization of 狩る: 狩りをする, 狩りに出かける. As a suffix with a voiced initial (〜狩り, がり) it also refers to gathering or picking in nature (いちご狩り, ぶどう狩り, 潮干狩り) and to admiring autumn foliage (紅葉狩り). Figuratively it stands for manhunts against people: 魔女狩り "witch hunt".

examples[].german: It's the first I've heard of hunters having a five-day work week.
In the story of Little Red Riding Hood, the hunter rescues the girl from the wolf's belly.
The hunter entered the forest early in the morning and waited motionless for his prey.
en.notes: 狩人 is a hunter; the reading かりゅうど (less often かりうど) is irregular and has to be learned. The word sounds archaic or literary and appears mainly in fairy tales, fantasy and songs. A real, professional hunter is nowadays called 猟師 (りょうし), and in games and advertising also ハンター.

examples[].german: We were getting along really well until just recently, but he suddenly became distant, and I have no idea why.
According to a survey announced recently, young people are spending less time reading.
Thank you very much for your kind help the other day.
en.notes: 先頃 means "recently, the other day" and refers to a specific point in the recent past. It is elevated and literary – typical of news, letters and speeches (先頃発表された調査). In conversation, people prefer 先日 or この間. Unlike 近頃 and この頃, which mean an ongoing period "lately", 先頃 designates a point in time.

examples[].german: Lately I've been working the night shift at a confectionery factory.
Young people these days apparently hardly read newspapers.
Lately I can hardly fall asleep at night, and it's troubling me.
en.notes: 近頃 means "lately, nowadays" and describes an ongoing state or habit of the present. It sounds somewhat more formal or old-fashioned than この頃 and 最近; the famous complaint is 近頃の若者は… "the youth of today ...". For a single recent event (moved last week), 最近 or 先日 fits better than 近頃.

examples[].german: That child is always alone, isn't he? He doesn't seem to have friends his own age, so I'm worried.
My daughter is gradually reaching the age where parents start to worry a little.
Middle schoolers are at the age when they want to rebel against their parents.
en.notes: 年頃 refers to an approximate age (同じ年頃の子ども "children of a similar age") and especially to the age at which one becomes adult or marriageable: 年頃の娘. With a preceding clause it means "the age when ...": 親に反抗したい年頃. For the exact age in years one uses 年齢 or 年 instead.

examples[].german: About when does Tofugu intend to enter the e-book market?
About when will the package arrive?
About when did you come to Japan?
en.notes: いつ頃 asks for an approximate point in time: "about when, around what time". It is softer and less pressing than a plain いつ because no exact answer is demanded – hence popular in business emails: いつ頃お届けできますか. It usually stands without a particle as an adverb; いつ頃に is also possible. It is often written in kana as いつごろ, and the answer correspondingly uses 〜頃 (三時頃).

examples[].german: The IT industry is growing rapidly.
He has worked in the publishing industry for twenty years.
That word is industry jargon, so ordinary people won't understand it.
en.notes: 業界 refers to an industry as the community of the companies and people active in it: "the industry, the scene". It usually follows the name of the industry: IT業界, 出版業界 "publishing", 芸能業界 "show business"; 業界トップ is the "industry leader". Also common are 業界用語 "industry jargon" and 業界人 "insider". In contrast to 業種, a factual classification category, 業界 sounds like a world of its own with rules and relationships.

examples[].german: Lately I've been adding crushed hazelnuts to my coffee to bring out the flavor.
It has suddenly gotten cold these days, hasn't it?
Children these days use smartphones from a young age.
en.notes: この頃 means "lately, these days" and describes an ongoing state or habit up to today; often written in kana as このごろ. It is more colloquial than 近頃 and similar to 最近, but does not fit single completed events (not: この頃結婚した). Note: その頃, by contrast, means "back then".

examples[].german: When I was young I didn't care about food, but now I do, since my doctor said I'm at risk of diabetes, and I always use less sugar than the recipe says.
My father reportedly traveled all over the world as a sailor when he was young.
Looking at a photo of my grandmother in her youth, I was surprised at how much she looks like me now.
en.notes: 若い頃 means "in one's younger days", "when one was young" and usually stands adverbially with は or に at the start of a sentence: 若い頃は…, 若い頃に…. Attributively with の: 若い頃の写真, 若い頃の夢. After nouns and adjectives, 頃 is read ころ here; ごろ, on the other hand, follows time expressions for "about" (3時ごろ). Similarly built is 子供の頃 "when one was a child"; 青春 by contrast emphasizes the emotional time of youth, and 若者 are "young people".

examples[].german: I asked Aya to draw an illustration dedicated to the souls of the dead.
At the year-end sale, all the shops lure customers with enormous business spirit.
Before the game, the coach urged the players to show fighting spirit.
en.notes: The reading こん is the Sino-Japanese reading of 魂 and occurs practically only in compounds: 霊魂 "soul", 商魂 "business spirit", 闘魂 "fighting spirit", 鎮魂 "repose of souls, memorial for the dead". As an independent word, 魂 is たましい "soul"; as a suffix after a noun it is usually read だましい (大和魂, 職人魂 "craftsman's spirit"). A free-standing word こん is not used in daily life. Fixed expression: 商魂たくましい "extremely business-minded".

examples[].german: I was quite surprised when I ran into my first love in Japan.
It looks like it will take quite a lot of time to finish this job.
It's quite a walk from the station, so you should take a taxi.
en.notes: かなり means "quite, considerably" - clearly more than expected or normal, but not extreme. It stands before adjectives and verbs (かなり難しい, かなり疲れた) and with の before nouns (かなりの時間, かなりの金額). The spelling 可也 is a rare ateji; it is almost always written in kana. By comparison: とても is stronger and more general, 相当 is similar but even more emphatic, and なかなか expresses "better than expected" and often has a positive ring.

examples[].german: The witch put a curse on the princess so that she could only hold cups upside down.
In the old castle, the legend of a curse laid on the royal family lives on.
Fans joke that a curse is the reason the team hasn't won a title in years.
en.notes: 呪い is a "curse": 呪いをかける "to lay a curse", 呪いが解ける / 呪いを解く "the curse is broken / to break a curse". The related verb is 呪う "to curse". The same kanji read まじない mean a harmless "charm, spell" (おまじない against pain or the like). Do not confuse it with the identically sounding adjective 鈍い（のろい）"slow, sluggish".

examples[].german: When is New Year according to the lunar calendar, anyway?
Some regions celebrate Tanabata by the old calendar.
In Japan, the switch from the old calendar to the new calendar took place in the Meiji period.
en.notes: 旧暦 is Japan's "old calendar", a lunisolar calendar that was replaced in 1873 by the Gregorian 新暦. You say 旧暦で数える, 旧暦の正月, 旧暦の7月. Some festivals such as お盆 or 七夕 are still celebrated regionally by the old calendar, or one month later. The purely lunar calendar is technically called 太陰暦 or 陰暦; the Western year count is 西暦.

examples[].german: In what year of the Western calendar did the Showa era end?
Please write your date of birth on the form in the Japanese calendar, not the Western one.
This temple is said to have been built around the year 800 AD.
en.notes: 西暦 is the Western (Christian) year count, as opposed to the Japanese 和暦 with era names such as 令和 or 平成. On forms you often have to choose whether to give the date in 西暦 or 和暦; you say 西暦2025年 or ask 西暦で何年ですか. "Before Christ" is 紀元前. In everyday conversation, 西暦 is usually omitted and people just say 2025年.

examples[].german: From our hotel room, we could take in a view of the beautiful blue sea.
This apartment building stands on high ground and has a wonderful view.
After the new building went up, the view from the room got worse.
en.notes: 眺望 is a literary word for "view, distant vista" and is used mainly as a noun: 眺望がいい, 眺望が開ける, 部屋からの眺望. It is typical in real-estate and tourism texts (眺望良好, 眺望抜群). As a する-verb (〜を眺望する "to overlook") it is rare and elevated. In everyday speech people tend to say 眺め, 景色 or 見晴らし; the related verb is 眺める.

examples[].german: You only live once! Come on! Let's go skydiving naked together. I think it'd be a great experience.
A man ran around the road naked and was taken into protective custody by the police.
At an onsen, it is the etiquette to enter the water completely naked.
en.notes: 全裸 means "stark naked, completely nude" and sounds more matter-of-fact than the colloquial 素っ裸 or the childish すっぽんぽん. Typical are 全裸で "naked" (adverbial) and 全裸の男 "a naked man", often in police reports (全裸で発見される). The counterpart is 半裸 "half-naked". The simple 裸 covers both and is the everyday word.

examples[].german: Eek! My dream just came true! The dream where a half-naked hunk drinking freshly brewed coffee says "good morning" the moment I wake up!
At the construction site, some people worked half-naked because of the heat.
At the festival, men carry the portable shrine through the town half-naked.
en.notes: 半裸 means "half-naked", usually "with a bare upper body". It is a noun and is used adverbially with で (半裸で働く) or attributively with の (半裸の男). The word sounds rather literary, as in news or descriptions; colloquially people say 上半身裸 or simply 裸. The counterpart for "completely naked" is 全裸.

examples[].german: Competition with other companies in the same industry is fierce.
At a gathering of people in the same line of business, we exchanged the latest industry information.
My wife and I are in the same line of work, so we understand each other's work worries well.
en.notes: 同業 means "same industry, same occupation" and is used almost only in compounds or with の/だ: 同業他社 "other companies in the same industry, competitors", 同業者 "colleague in the same industry or trade". It stresses the sameness of the trade, not cooperation; colleagues within the same company are 同僚 instead. The tone is factual and business-like.

examples[].german: Gross! I just saw a guy at that crosswalk over there wearing nothing but a sleeveless apron. Should I report him to the police?
I undressed the baby and put him in the bath.
When winter comes, the trees become completely bare.
en.notes: 裸 is a noun, not an adjective: 裸になる "to undress", 裸で寝る "to sleep naked", attributive 裸の王様 "the naked king". It also means "bare, uncovered" (裸の木) and figuratively "penniless" (裸一貫 "with nothing but oneself"). Related: 丸裸 "stark naked", 裸足（はだし）"barefoot", 半裸 "half-naked", 全裸 "completely naked".

examples[].german: She bets quite large sums of money on horse races.
I'll bet a thousand yen that he won't come on time.
He staked his life and founded this company.
en.notes: 賭ける means "to bet, wager": 〜に〜を賭ける (馬に1万円を賭ける). Figuratively it means "to put at stake": 命を賭ける, 人生を賭ける (here also written 懸ける). "I'd bet on that" is 賭けてもいい. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 掛ける "to hang", 駆ける "to run" and 欠ける "to be lacking". The related noun is 賭け "bet", gambling in general is 賭け事 or ギャンブル.

examples[].german: I won a bet against him.
I lost the bet and now have to pay for lunch.
Opening a shop with all my savings was a big gamble.
en.notes: 賭け is the noun of 賭ける: "bet" and, figuratively, "gamble, risk". Typical are 賭けをする, 賭けに勝つ / 賭けに負ける and 一か八かの賭け "an all-or-nothing gamble". With 大きな賭け one describes risky life decisions. Gambling as an activity is rather 賭け事 or ギャンブル, the stake 賭け金.

examples[].german: On my first day attending Keio Gijuku, I felt totally out of place.
The school opened by Fukuzawa Yukichi was later named Keio Gijuku.
A gijuku was originally a private school established for the good of society.
en.notes: 義塾 historically refers to a private school founded for the public good (義 "justice, public good" + 塾 "private school"). Today the word is encountered almost only in proper names, above all 慶應義塾 or 慶應義塾大学. For modern cram schools, people say 塾 or 学習塾, and for private schools in general 私立学校.

examples[].german: He had the worst memory of all the cram school students.
At this cram school, lessons are tailored to each individual student.
Students of Keio University call themselves jukusei.
en.notes: 塾生 is a student of a 塾, that is, a private tutoring or cram school; the word reflects the school's perspective (塾生募集 "students wanted"). In everyday speech people often simply say 塾に通っている子. For schoolchildren in general, 生徒 is used, for university students 学生. A special case: students of Keio University (慶應義塾) also call themselves 塾生.

examples[].german: Please stop tapping on the calculator. It's driving me crazy!
Please check with a calculator whether the calculation is correct.
Calculators are prohibited from being brought into this exam.
en.notes: 電卓 is the abbreviation of 電子式卓上計算機 and means the pocket or desktop calculator. You calculate with 電卓で計算する; 電卓を叩く / 電卓を打つ literally means "to tap on the calculator", figuratively "to crunch the numbers, work out the figures". 計算機 is the more general umbrella term. The calculator app on a phone is also often called 電卓.

examples[].german: I'll wash the dishes, so could you clean the table? Is that okay?
The family's favorite dishes were lined up on the dinner table.
I try to have the whole family sit around the table together once a week.
en.notes: 食卓 is the "dining table" and sounds somewhat more refined than テーブル. It is often figurative: 食卓を囲む "to eat together at the table", 食卓に並ぶ / 食卓に上る "to appear on the table", 家庭の食卓 "meals in families". It is a noun; attributively it takes の (食卓の上, 食卓の塩).

examples[].german: That table tennis sound is driving me crazy!
On the weekend, I played table tennis with friends and worked up a good sweat.
Onsen inns often have a table tennis table.
en.notes: 卓球 is "table tennis"; you say 卓球をする (not 遊ぶ). Related are 卓球台 "table tennis table", 卓球部 "table tennis club" and 卓球選手. ピンポン is colloquial and somewhat old-fashioned. In Japan, many onsen inns traditionally have a table tennis table, and "onsen ping-pong" is a well-known cliché.

examples[].german: I hope to find a job by polishing my Excel skills.
I try not to eat anything after brushing my teeth.
I had my shoes shined in front of the station, and now they sparkle like new.
en.notes: 磨き is the noun form of 磨く "to polish, clean". On its own it is rare; it mostly appears in compounds like 歯磨き "brushing teeth", 靴磨き "shoe shining" or in the phrase 〜に磨きをかける "to refine, improve further" (腕に磨きをかける, 技術に磨きがかかる). The range of meaning thus extends from literal polishing to honing skills.

examples[].german: Just because I'm homeless, people stare at me as if I were vermin - it really makes me angry.
There are loads of germs on your hands - wash them before eating.
We disinfect the wound so that no germs get in.
en.notes: ばい菌 is the everyday, often child-friendly word for "germs, bacteria": 手にばい菌がつく, 傷口からばい菌が入る. It is mostly written ばい菌 or バイ菌; the full kanji spelling 黴菌 is rare. In technical language one says 細菌 or 菌, for viruses ウイルス. Figuratively someone is ばい菌扱い, i.e. "treated like vermin".

examples[].german: The two banks merged.
It merged with the neighboring town and a new city was born.
Because the number of children decreased, the two elementary schools will be merged.
en.notes: 合併 is the "merger, consolidation" of companies, municipalities, schools and the like. As a する-verb it is used both intransitively (AとBが合併する, AがBと合併する) and transitively (AとBを合併する). Common are 吸収合併 "merger by absorption", 市町村合併 "municipal merger" and, in medicine, 合併症 "complication". 買収, by contrast, is a takeover by purchase; both together correspond to "M&A" (合併・買収).

examples[].german: I got an email asking whether the Tofugu stickers are sterile.
Surgery is performed in a sterile room.
Aseptically packaged rice can be stored for a long time at room temperature.
en.notes: 無菌 means "germ-free, sterile" and is used attributively with の or in compounds: 無菌室, 無菌状態, 無菌パック (aseptically packaged rice). It is not a な-adjective. Related words: 殺菌 "to kill germs", 除菌 "to remove germs" (advertising language), 滅菌 "to sterilize completely" (medical). Register: rather technical, from medicine and food technology.

examples[].german: She drove through the tunnel at high speed because she had heard there was an evil spirit there.
At that shrine, a ritual to drive away evil spirits is held every year.
In the movie, a girl becomes possessed by an evil spirit.
en.notes: 悪霊 is an "evil spirit" that harms people or possesses them. Typical: 悪霊に取りつかれる "to be possessed by an evil spirit", 悪霊を払う / 追い払う "to drive out", 悪霊払い "exorcism". A neutral spirit of a dead person is 幽霊 or 亡霊; 悪魔 is rather the Western "devil", 鬼 the Japanese demon.

examples[].german: She is a medium with a very strong sixth sense and can talk with people in the afterlife.
I have no sixth sense, so I've never seen a ghost.
The poet drew inspiration from the scenery on his travels and wrote a masterpiece.
en.notes: 霊感 today mostly means the ability to perceive the supernatural, such as ghosts: 霊感が強い, 霊感がある / ない. The older meaning "divine inspiration" is literary (霊感を得る); in everyday speech people say インスピレーション or ひらめき instead. 霊感商法 refers to fraud involving supposedly spiritual goods. A medium is called 霊能力者.

examples[].german: The ghost went on scaring people, undaunted.
There is a rumor that the ghosts of soldiers appear at the old battlefield.
You shouldn't stay trapped by the ghosts of the past forever.
en.notes: 亡霊 is the "spirit of a deceased person" and sounds gloomier and more literary than the everyday 幽霊 "ghost". Typical: 亡霊が出る / 現れる. Figurative use for something past that won't let go is common: 過去の亡霊, 軍国主義の亡霊 "the ghost of militarism". 悪霊, on the other hand, emphasizes the malice of the spirit.

examples[].german: My family took our dog to a pet cemetery.
My grandfather's grave is in a cemetery on the outskirts.
During Higan, the cemetery is crowded with people visiting graves.
en.notes: 霊園 is a large, park-like cemetery, often run by a city or privately, and frequently part of names (市営霊園, 〇〇霊園). 墓地 is the general word for "cemetery", also on temple grounds; 墓場 sounds colloquial and creepy; お墓 is the individual grave. You say 霊園にお墓を建てる and 霊園へ墓参りに行く.

examples[].german: My humidifier hasn't been working well lately.
The air is dry in winter, so I run the humidifier when I sleep.
If you don't change the water in the humidifier every day, it can cause mold.
en.notes: 加湿器 is a "humidifier" (加湿 "to humidify" + 器 "device"). You say 加湿器をつける / 消す or 加湿器を置く. The counterpart is 除湿機 "dehumidifier" – usually written with 機 here; related is 空気清浄機 "air purifier". In Japan, the humidifier runs mainly in the dry winter.

examples[].german: I sweated a lot in my sleep last night, so my bed feels kind of damp.
During the rainy season, laundry hardly dries and stays damp.
Because of the humid air, my hair won't stay in place.
en.notes: 湿る is intransitive: something becomes "damp, clammy", mostly in the state 湿っている: 洗濯物がまだ湿っている. Transitive counterparts are 湿らせる and 湿す "to dampen". Compared with 濡れる "to get wet", 湿る is weaker – only slightly damp. Figuratively it means "to be gloomy, listless", as in 湿った雰囲気 or, in baseball, 打線が湿る "the batting lineup is in a slump".

en.meaning: to marry into a family (of a woman)
examples[].german: Shortly after the wedding, my son's wife was still very reserved.
Since our daughter got married and moved out, the house has suddenly become quiet.
My older sister married into a farming family and now helps with the rice growing.
en.notes: 嫁ぐ is said of a woman: "to marry, to marry into a family". The destination takes に or へ: 農家に嫁ぐ, 遠くへ嫁ぐ. The word reflects the traditional idea that the bride moves into the husband's family, and sounds formal to somewhat old-fashioned; neutrally one says 結婚する, colloquially 嫁に行く. For a man who marries into the woman's family, one says 婿に入る. The verb is intransitive; "to marry off a daughter" is 娘を嫁がせる.

examples[].german: My grandmother told me that it is very dangerous to swim in a torrent.
In the snowmelt season, the mountain torrent swells and roars down the valley.
The current of the torrent is so strong that only experienced people can go down it by boat.
en.notes: 滝川 refers to a rushing river or mountain stream with rapids, literally "waterfall river". As a common noun it is rare and rather literary; in everyday speech one says 急流 "rapid current" or 渓流 "mountain stream". Much more often 滝川 appears as a family or place name (e.g. the city 滝川 in Hokkaidō).

examples[].german: The opposition parties opposed the bill.
The opposition parties sharply questioned the prime minister's remarks.
Unless the opposition parties cooperate, a change of government will be difficult.
en.notes: 野党 are the parties that do not take part in the government, i.e. the opposition; the counterpart is 与党. The 野 here stands for "outside of office", as in 下野する ("to lose power"). Typical contexts: 野党が政府を追及する, 野党第一党 ("largest opposition party"), 野党が反対する. 野党 can mean either a single party or the opposition as a whole.

examples[].german: A major company acquired the startup.
For the new road, the city bought up the surrounding land.
A lawmaker was arrested on suspicion of bribing voters in the election.
en.notes: 買収 has two meanings: economically the "takeover, buyout" of a company or land (企業買収, 土地を買収する), and negatively the "bribery" of people, e.g. in elections (有権者を買収する "to buy voters"). It is a transitive する-verb with を; in the passive it is 買収される "to be taken over / bribed". 合併, in contrast, is the merger into one company; the bribe money itself is called 賄賂.

examples[].german: Refusing that offer is sheer madness.
Madness dwelled in his eyes.
After watching the film about the madness of war, I was speechless.
en.notes: 狂気 is a noun meaning "madness" and sounds written or dramatic; attributively it takes の (狂気の目), not な. Set phrases are 狂気の沙汰 "sheer madness" and 狂気じみた "seemingly mad". The opposite is 正気 "being in one's right mind". Colloquially one more often says 正気じゃない, 頭がおかしい or クレイジー.

examples[].german: It looked like a phoenix flying high in the air.
The sight of a hawk gliding across the wide sky is truly beautiful.
You young people, fly out into the world and chase your dreams!
en.notes: 翔る is a poetic verb for "to fly high through the air, to soar". The space one flies through is marked with を: 大空を翔る, 天を翔る; also belonging here is 天翔る（あまかける）. In daily life one simply says 飛ぶ. 翔る is found mainly in literature, song lyrics, titles and slogans. Do not confuse with the similar-sounding 駆ける "to run", 掛ける and 賭ける.

examples[].german: My mother forbade my father from collecting tasteless dolls.
Making fun of other people's failures is in bad taste.
The room was full of gaudy gold furniture, and honestly I thought it was tasteless.
en.notes: 悪趣味 is a な-adjective or noun with two meanings: aesthetically "tasteless, kitschy" (悪趣味な服, 悪趣味な家具) and morally "tactless, nasty" for behavior (悪趣味な冗談, 悪趣味ないたずら). More casually one says 趣味が悪い. 下品 emphasizes "vulgar, coarse". Note: 趣味 here means "taste", not "hobby".

examples[].german: This wrapping paper has Braille on it.
I opened it carefully so as not to tear the wrapping paper of the present.
Please don't throw candy wrappers on the street.
en.notes: 包み紙 is "wrapping paper" (包む "to wrap" + 紙, with voicing to がみ): for gifts, but also for candies or the packaging in a department store. Typical: 包み紙を開ける / 破る / はがす. 包装紙 is more formal and businesslike; decorative gift wrap is often called ラッピングペーパー.

examples[].german: It's about time. Let's pull out.
If you're going to quit the company, now may be the right moment.
It is hard to judge the right time to retire.
en.notes: 潮時 originally means the time of ebb or flood tide; figuratively it means "the right moment", especially to end something or withdraw (引退の潮時, そろそろ潮時だ). Typical combinations: 潮時を見る "to pick the right moment", 潮時を逃す "to miss the right moment". Similar are 頃合い and タイミング; チャンス, by contrast, emphasizes an opportunity to begin something.

examples[].german: Where exactly does the Kuroshio flow?
Thanks to the influence of the Kuroshio, this region is relatively warm even in winter.
Bonito come to the waters near Japan riding the Kuroshio.
en.notes: 黒潮 is the warm ocean current that flows north from the south along Japan's Pacific coast; its cold counterpart from the north is the 親潮. 潮 here means "ocean current". One says 黒潮が流れる, 黒潮に乗る (fish, drifting objects) and 黒潮の影響. Another name is 日本海流.

en.meaning: to rub; to strike (a match); to lose (money) gambling
examples[].german: I struck a match and lit the candle.
I lost my whole salary on horse racing.
I fell and scraped my knee.
en.notes: 擦る（する）means "to rub, to strike", above all マッチを擦る "to strike a match", and colloquially "to lose money gambling" (競馬で給料を擦る, often written スる). The same kanji are also read こする; 目を擦る "to rub one's eyes" is always read こする. Compounds: 擦りむく "to scrape", 擦り傷 "scrape, abrasion". The intransitive counterpart is 擦れる（すれる）"to chafe, to rub against". Do not confuse with 掏る "to pick pockets" (財布をすられた).

examples[].german: That's a reasonable price.
This dictionary is a handy size and convenient to carry around.
Please tell me a hiking course suitable for beginners.
en.notes: 手頃 is a な-adjective: literally "fitting well in the hand", hence "handy" (手頃な大きさ) and "suitable, reasonable", especially for prices: 手頃な値段, 手頃な価格. In advertising, お手頃価格 "affordable price" is very common. Unlike 安い, 手頃 does not sound "cheap" but "reasonable, affordable". For abilities or difficulty it means "just right" (初心者に手頃なコース).

examples[].german: A pending trial is a great source of stress for the parties involved.
Please put the pending documents in the box on the right.
He spent more than half a year in custody awaiting trial, with no verdict issued.
en.notes: 未決 means "not yet decided, pending" and is used with の or in compounds: 未決の書類, 未決箱 (in-tray for pending items), opposite 既決. In criminal law it means "not yet sentenced": 未決囚 "prisoner awaiting trial", 未決勾留 "pretrial detention". The word is written and official; for everyday plans one says 未定 "not yet fixed". Note: a "draw" in sports is 引き分け.

examples[].german: I forbade my son from eating convenience store rice balls.
I went on the school excursion carrying the rice balls my mother made for me.
Which rice ball will you have, pickled plum or salmon?
en.notes: お握り is almost always written in kana as おにぎり; it comes from 握る "to form with the hand". One says おにぎりを握る / 作る, the filling is called 具 (梅干し, 鮭, ツナマヨ), and it is often wrapped in 海苔. A synonym is おむすび, which sounds somewhat softer or regional (usage differs between eastern and western Japan). Convenience-store onigiri and onigiri in a bento for outings are typical.

examples[].german: We established a subsidiary overseas.
After being acquired, the company became a subsidiary of a major manufacturer.
I was seconded to a subsidiary and appointed sales manager.
en.notes: 子会社 is a "subsidiary" that is majority-owned by another company, the 親会社. Typical are 子会社を設立する "to establish a subsidiary", 〜の子会社になる and 完全子会社 "wholly owned subsidiary". In the compound, 会社 becomes がいしゃ (voiced). In general, for companies of a group one also speaks of グループ会社 or 関連会社.

en.meaning: agedashi; lightly deep-fried and served in broth (esp. tofu)
examples[].german: This is delicious agedashi tofu, freshly made and piping hot.
When I go to an izakaya, I always order agedashi tofu.
Let's try making agedashi eggplant tonight.
en.notes: 揚げ出し refers to a method of preparation: ingredients are dusted with starch, briefly deep-fried and served in warm dashi broth. The word hardly stands alone; it is almost always 揚げ出し豆腐, more rarely 揚げ出しナス or 揚げ出し餅. It is a classic at izakaya. Do not confuse with 揚げ物 "fried foods" in general (tempura, karaage, etc.).

examples[].german: If you put AAA batteries into this doll and switch it on, it lets out a strange scream.
His songs give voice to the inner outcry of young people.
The outcry of the residents finally reached the government.
en.notes: 叫び is the noun of 叫ぶ "to shout". Concretely it appears in 叫びを上げる "to let out a cry", but for audible screaming one usually says 叫び声, or 悲鳴 for fear and pain. Very common is the figurative use as "outcry, cry for help": 心の叫び, 魂の叫び, 怒りの叫び, 住民の叫び. Munch's painting "The Scream" is 「叫び」 in Japanese.

examples[].german: Mami raised a scream while moving the bacon up and down.
I woke up in the middle of the night hearing a scream from outside.
Joyful-sounding screams echo from the roller coaster.
en.notes: 叫び声 is the concretely audible "scream" or "shouting": 叫び声を上げる, 叫び声が聞こえる, 叫び声が響く. Unlike 叫び, it is hardly used figuratively. A scream of fear or pain is specifically 悲鳴, cheering is 歓声; simply "loud voice" is 大声.

examples[].german: At this pace, I don't think we can finish picking the new tea shoots by evening.
When spring comes, new shoots begin to appear on the branches of the trees.
Deer have eaten the new shoots in our garden, which is a nuisance.
en.notes: 新芽 are "fresh shoots, young buds" in spring: 新芽が出る, 新芽が伸びる, 新芽を摘む. With tea, the first tender shoots are processed into 新茶 or 一番茶. More general is 芽 "sprout, bud"; a flower bud is つぼみ, young leaves 若葉. The verb 芽吹く describes sprouting.

examples[].german: When she finished the ink painting, she hung it on the wall at once and gazed at it.
Ink painting expresses mountains and rivers only through differences in the density of the ink.
An exhibition of Sesshū's ink paintings is being held at the art museum.
en.notes: 墨絵 is a picture painted only with black ink (墨), that is, "ink painting". The art-historical technical term is 水墨画; 墨絵 sounds somewhat more everyday and is also used for simple ink drawings. One says 墨絵を描く; attributively 墨絵の世界, 墨絵のような風景 "a landscape like an ink painting" (e.g. in mist). Famous master: 雪舟.

examples[].german: How much have you spent on that tattoo so far?
At some hot springs in Japan, people with tattoos are refused entry to the baths.
He has a dragon tattoo on his arm.
en.notes: 入れ墨 is a "tattoo"; one says 入れ墨を入れる or 入れ墨を彫る "to get a tattoo". Other spellings are 刺青 and 文身. The word is strongly associated with traditional Japanese tattooing and the yakuza milieu; for fashionable tattoos one more often says タトゥー. Many onsen, swimming pools and gyms still refuse entry to tattooed people.

examples[].german: It's not that I dislike him, but I felt that remark there was a bit inappropriate.
After hearing both sides' opinions, a reasonable conclusion should be reached.
In a public setting, it would be better to use somewhat more measured expressions.
en.notes: 穏当 is a written-language な-adjective: "appropriate, moderate, reasonable" in the sense of "not offensive, not provoking conflict". Typical: 穏当な判断, 穏当な処分, 穏当な表現; often negated: 穏当でない / 穏当を欠く "inappropriate". 妥当, by contrast, emphasizes "factually correct, justified"; 適当 is ambiguous ("suitable" or "sloppy"). The kanji 穏 means "calm, peaceful".

examples[].german: I hate living a peaceful, uneventful life.
After the incident, the town finally regained its calm.
Being able to spend peaceful days with my family is the greatest happiness of all.
en.notes: 平穏 means "calm, peaceful, without incident" and is a な-adjective or noun: 平穏な日々, 平穏に暮らす, 平穏を取り戻す "to regain calm". The doubled form 平穏無事 "calm and without incident" is very common. 平和 means rather "peace" as opposed to war, 穏やか the gentleness of weather or character. The opposite is 不穏.

examples[].german: Tonight's crescent moon gives off a somewhat ominous feeling.
It was reported that there is threatening activity near the border.
A vaguely tense atmosphere hung over the meeting room.
en.notes: 不穏 is a な-adjective for a situation in which unrest or danger is developing: 不穏な動き "threatening activity", 不穏な空気 "tense atmosphere", 不穏な情勢, 不穏な発言. It describes the situation, not one's own feeling; for that one says 不安. 物騒 means rather "unsafe, dangerous" (物騒な世の中). Opposite: 平穏.

examples[].german: The victim is believed to have been hit on the head with something like a blunt object.
The police are searching for the blunt object used as the weapon.
That dictionary is so thick it could pass as a blunt instrument.
en.notes: 鈍器 is a "blunt object" used as a weapon (hammer, stone, bottle) and appears almost only in crime news: 鈍器のようなもので殴られる "to be struck with something like a blunt object". Opposite: 刃物 "bladed weapon"; the weapon used in a crime in general is 凶器. Jokingly, very thick books are called 鈍器 or 鈍器本.

examples[].german: We have to follow the parent company's policy.
A new president was sent from the parent company.
The parent company of that baseball team is a railway company.
en.notes: 親会社 is the "parent company" that controls a subsidiary (子会社); the image of "parent and child" is literally present in the Japanese. Typical are 親会社の方針/意向 "the parent company's directives" and 親会社から出向する "to be seconded from the parent company". As with 子会社, 会社 is read がいしゃ here; for pure holding structures one speaks of 持株会社.

examples[].german: I don't feel like going out with the devil tonight.
I gave in to the devil's whisper and ate another piece of cake.
He is usually gentle, but when he gets angry he turns into a devil.
en.notes: 悪魔 is the "devil" or "demon" of Western belief (also Satan) and, in Buddhism, Māra. Figuratively: 悪魔のような人 "a devilish person", 悪魔のささやき "the voice of temptation", 悪魔的 "diabolical". 小悪魔 is a flirtatious, seductive woman. Japanese demons are rather called 鬼, evil spirits 悪霊.

examples[].german: Wow, are you learning a new A-rank spell? If it goes well, that'll be amazing!
The witch cast a spell on the prince and turned him into a frog.
"Thank you" is a magic word that makes people smile.
en.notes: 魔法 is "magic, sorcery, a spell" in fairy tales, fantasy and games: 魔法を使う "to use magic", 魔法をかける "to cast a spell", 魔法が解ける "the spell wears off". 魔法使い is "wizard, witch". To be distinguished from 手品 or マジック, i.e. magic tricks on stage. Figuratively: 魔法のような "as if by magic", 魔法の言葉 "magic word".

examples[].german: "Don't be picky! Study not only black magic but white magic properly too!" "Yeah, yeah. You always say the same thing." "It's one 'yes' only, right!"
That magician amazed the audience with tricks that seemed like sorcery.
In Europe long ago, people suspected of using sorcery were executed.
en.notes: 魔術 is "magic, sorcery" in the occult or fantasy sense: 黒魔術 "black magic", 白魔術（しろまじゅつ）"white magic", 魔術師 "magician, sorcerer". Secondly it refers to large stage illusions. More common and more child-friendly is 魔法 (fairy tales, games: 魔法使い, 魔法をかける); sleight-of-hand tricks are called 手品 or マジック. It is a noun; attributively it takes の (魔術の本).

examples[].german: "Can I say something?" "Of course." "Well... never mind." "Come on, confess!" "Um, actually, I'm a witch."
I read a picture book with a witch in it to the child.
I wrote a report on the history of European witch hunts.
en.notes: 魔女 is the "witch" of fairy tales, folklore and history: 魔女が出てくる話, 魔女のほうき, 魔女狩り "witch hunt" (also figuratively for public hunts for scapegoats). A male sorcerer is called 魔法使い or 魔術師. Colloquially, 美魔女 refers to a woman from about 40 who looks astonishingly young. Also well known is the Ghibli film 「魔女の宅急便」.

examples[].german: "Is the new dorm resident sexy?" "Yeah, he is. Fugu has already fallen for her."
Dorm residents must return by 11 p.m.
At this university, the dorm residents take turns on meal duty.
en.notes: 寮生 is someone who lives in a 寮, a dormitory of a school, university or company; at schools this corresponds to a "boarding student". Related: 寮生活 "dorm life" and 寮のルール. Someone who lives privately as a lodger is a 下宿生; a roommate is called ルームメイト or 同室の人.

examples[].german: Have you seen any good-looking guys in your ward?
After the surgery, my grandfather was transferred to the surgical ward.
Visiting hours are set in the pediatric ward.
en.notes: 病棟 refers to a ward or building wing of a hospital, often with the specialty in front: 外科病棟 "surgical ward", 小児病棟 "pediatric ward", 精神科病棟, 隔離病棟. One is placed in a ward, or transferred to one (病棟に移される). Do not confuse with 病室 "patient room" (a single room) and 病院 "hospital" (the whole institution).

examples[].german: I am a cat. As yet I have no name.
In the manga, a haughty cat said, "Leave it to me."
My older brother jokingly refers to himself as 吾輩.
en.notes: 吾輩 is an archaic, pompous first-person pronoun for men. It is famous through Natsume Sōseki's novel 吾輩は猫である "I Am a Cat", in which a cat calls himself this in a puffed-up, dignified manner. Today it is heard only jokingly or with arrogant characters in manga and anime; in daily life one says 私, 僕 or 俺. Occasionally also written 我輩.

examples[].german: It's a very novel idea, so I think the first proposal is better than the latter.
This building is attracting attention for its innovative design.
His novel's structure was innovative, and I never got bored until the end.
en.notes: 斬新 means "novel, original, innovative" and praises ideas, designs or concepts that break with the familiar: 斬新なデザイン, 斬新な発想. It is a な-adjective. Compared with 新しい ("new", purely temporal), 斬新 emphasizes surprising originality; similar but more matter-of-fact is 独創的. The tone is rather elevated and typical of reviews, presentations and advertising.

en.meaning: killing with a sword; cutting down
examples[].german: My favorite anime character got cut down.
In the late Edo period, many samurai were cut down on the streets of Kyoto.
The man was arrested on suspicion of slashing the victim to death with a blade.
en.notes: 斬殺 means to kill someone with a sword or blade. The word is written-language and appears in historical accounts, novels and police reports, mostly in the passive: 〜に斬殺される. Related formations: 刺殺 "to stab to death", 射殺 "to shoot dead", 殺害 "to murder" (general). In everyday speech one would more likely say 刀で切り殺す.

examples[].german: That samurai told me that if I couldn't say the tongue twister well, he would cut out my tongue.
The samurai cut down the enemy with a single stroke.
The critic sharply cut into the politician's remarks.
en.notes: 斬る is a special spelling of きる for striking with a sword or blade, especially for cutting people down. Typical in samurai films: 敵を斬る, 斬りかかる "to attack with a sword", 斬り合い "sword fight". Figuratively it means "to criticize sharply": 世相を斬る. For everyday cutting (paper, vegetables, hair) one always writes 切る. Despite the -iru ending, it is a godan verb.

examples[].german: The progress of science is remarkable.
My older brother says he wants to become a scientist in the future.
I went to the science museum with my child.
en.notes: 科学 is "science", especially the natural sciences and the scientific method; it includes 科学者, 科学的 and 科学技術. The school subject, by contrast, is 理科. Note: 化学 "chemistry" is read the same way, かがく; to avoid misunderstandings, people often say ばけがく for chemistry in conversation. Neutral, common in school and the news.

examples[].german: Half a century passed after that, and just when I had almost forgotten him, we met again by chance in a small bakery.
Time waits for no one.
This bridge took ten years to complete.
en.notes: 歳月 denotes a long span of time, "the years", and is elevated to written-language. Typical combinations: 歳月が流れる/経つ "years pass", 〜年の歳月をかける/要する "to take ... years", 長い歳月. Well known is the proverb 歳月人を待たず "Time waits for no one". Equivalent in meaning but a little less elevated is 年月 (としつき/ねんげつ).

examples[].german: I started learning Japanese in my thirties.
My daughter turns ten this year.
en.notes: 〜歳 follows a number to express an age. The pronunciation changes with some numbers: 一歳 is いっさい, 八歳 is はっさい and 二十歳 is usually はたち. For 十歳, both じっさい and じゅっさい are in use; the examples use じゅっさい. The sign 〜 only marks the place for the number. 歳・さい is a counter here and not the independent reading とし for "year" or "age".

examples[].german: How many carbonated soft drinks do you think you can drink in ten minutes?
This mint chewing gum has a refreshing feel and is perfect for staying awake.
In the midst of a stream of gloomy news, his sincere words were a breath of fresh air.
en.notes: 清涼 "cool and refreshing" appears almost only in compounds: 清涼飲料水 "soft drink", 清涼感 "refreshing feeling" (advertising language for mint, cosmetics), 清涼剤. Figuratively, 一服の清涼剤 is "a breath of fresh air, a welcome relief" in an oppressive situation. As a な-adjective (清涼な空気) it is rare and elevated; in daily life one says 爽やか or 涼しい.

examples[].german: When I opened the window, the beautiful sound of a piano drifted in along with a pleasant cool breeze.
In the evening, a cool breeze came blowing from the river.
Even in the severe heat, one can now feel a cool breeze in the mornings and evenings.
en.notes: 涼風 "cool breeze" is an elevated, literary word, often with a seasonal note (the end of summer). Typical: 涼風が吹く, 涼風を感じる, 涼風が立つ. The same spelling is also read すずかぜ, which sounds a little more poetic; this card teaches りょうふう. In daily life one simply says 涼しい風.

examples[].german: Stop aping others. It's embarrassing.
If you just ape other companies' products, customers won't choose you.
Even if you ape a famous singer, you won't develop a style of your own.
en.notes: 猿真似 is pejorative: thoughtless aping without understanding or contributing anything of one's own. Typical: 〜の猿真似をする, 〜の猿真似にすぎない "merely a cheap copy of ...". Neutral by contrast are 真似 "imitation" and the elevated 模倣. Criticizing someone this way directly sounds harsh.

examples[].german: Whether it's ten or twenty below zero, I'll do the washing up here.
This morning it dropped to five degrees below zero, and the roads were frozen.
In Hokkaido's winter, there are many days below zero even in the daytime.
en.notes: 零下 means "below zero (degrees)" and comes before the temperature: 零下10度 "minus 10 degrees". As an attribute with の: 零下の寒さ, 零下の日. In weather reports 氷点下 is more common today; colloquially one simply says マイナス5度. The counterpart "above zero" is 零上, but it is hardly used.

examples[].german: Around midnight, I saw her walking alone through town at a furious pace.
Ticket sales for this ticket start at midnight today.
After midnight, the trains stop running.
en.notes: 零時 is "zero o'clock" and means midnight in the 24-hour format (午前零時). 午後零時, by contrast, means 12 noon, which in daily life is usually called 正午 or 昼の12時. It is often written 0時 and pronounced れいじ. Typical in timetables and announcements: 零時ちょうど, 零時を過ぎる "to pass midnight". Colloquially one more often says 夜中の12時.

examples[].german: I couldn't understand at all about using the least common multiple as the common denominator, and I got zero on the exam.
I forgot to write my name, so the test was marked zero.
You're good at cooking, but when it comes to tidying up, you get a zero.
en.notes: 零点 mainly means "zero points" on tests: 零点を取る, テストが零点になる. In speech 0点 (れいてん or ぜろてん) is more common. Figuratively, 〜としては零点だ means "a complete zero, a total failure as ...". In technical language it also means "zero (root) of a function" (mathematics) or "freezing point", but these meanings are rare for learners.

examples[].german: I've improved a little since I started going to a go class.
My grandfather plays go with the neighbors every Sunday.
It became big news when a go AI beat a professional player.
en.notes: 囲碁 is the board game Go; for short one also says 碁. The matching verb is 打つ: 囲碁を打つ, 碁を打つ (colloquially also 囲碁をする). Related are 碁石 "stones", 碁盤 "board" and 棋士 "professional player". Do not confuse with 将棋 (Japanese chess), for which one says 指す.

examples[].german: This morning I caught the guy who was peeping into our go salon.
After retiring, my father started going to the go salon in front of the station.
At a go salon, even first-timers are introduced to an opponent of about the same strength.
en.notes: 碁会所 is an establishment where one pays a fee to play Go against other patrons; traditionally a meeting place for older men. Typical: 碁会所に通う "to go regularly to a go salon". Modern establishments often call themselves 囲碁サロン or 囲碁クラブ. A go course with lessons, by contrast, is a 囲碁教室.

examples[].german: We are observing the behavior of animals.
During summer vacation, I kept an observation diary of a morning glory.
He has sharp powers of observation and notices even small changes right away.
en.notes: 観察 is the careful, systematic "observing" of processes, e.g. in nature, in the lab or of people; as a する-verb it is transitive with を. Typical are 観察日記 "observation diary" (a classic school assignment), 観察力 "powers of observation" and, at the doctor's, 経過観察 "follow-up monitoring". 観測, by contrast, is used for measurements with instruments (weather, stars), 監視 for "surveillance" for control.

examples[].german: If you want to know about old Shanghai and the French Concession, he knows a lot about that.
In the latter half of the nineteenth century, several foreign concessions were created in Shanghai.
Many Western-style buildings of the former concessions still remain in Tianjin.
en.notes: 租界 is a historical term for the city districts administered by foreign powers in Chinese treaty ports (19th century to the 1940s). Typical: フランス租界, イギリス租界, 上海の共同租界, 旧租界. Related but different: 租借地 "leased territory", 植民地 "colony" and 居留地 for the foreigners' quarters in Japan (e.g. Yokohama).

examples[].german: The first thing you have to do is remove the air bubbles from the pottery clay.
After I put a protective film on my smartphone, air bubbles got in.
Small air bubbles keep rising one after another from the bottom of the aquarium.
en.notes: 気泡 is an (air) bubble in liquids or solid materials and sounds technical and matter-of-fact; in daily life one mostly says 泡. Typical: 気泡が入る/できる "bubbles form", 気泡を抜く/取り除く. Bubble wrap is 気泡緩衝材, colloquially プチプチ. Do not confuse with 水泡 "foam".

examples[].german: My browser crashed before I could save the data, so all my effort writing a long message came to nothing.
Because the tournament was canceled, the players' four years of effort came to nothing.
The waves hit the rocks and white foam spread out.
en.notes: 水泡 "foam, water bubble" is rare and literary in its literal meaning. Almost always it appears in the set phrase 水泡に帰す (帰す is read きす here) "to come to nothing, to be in vain": 努力が水泡に帰す. This is elevated; colloquially one says 水の泡になる. Do not confuse with 水疱 (same reading) "blister", in everyday speech 水ぶくれ.

examples[].german: Can I put the styrofoam in this bag? It has to be separated from the other trash, right?
Happoshu has lower taxes than beer, so it is cheaper too.
When you put this bath additive in hot water, it fizzes and releases carbon dioxide.
en.notes: 発泡 "foaming, formation of foam" is a technical word and mostly appears in compounds: 発泡スチロール "styrofoam", 発泡酒 (beer-like drink with little malt), 発泡性ワイン "sparkling wine", 発泡剤. As an intransitive verb 発泡する is rather technical; in daily life one says 泡が出る or 泡立つ.

examples[].german: Ever since I became a full-time housewife, it's as if I've been taken prisoner and confined in the kitchen.
The princess was confined in the castle tower for years.
After the coup, the former king was confined on a distant island.
en.notes: 幽閉 means to hold someone in a secluded place, cut off from the outside world, classically kings, princesses or deposed rulers: 塔に幽閉する, 〜に幽閉される. The word is written-language and sounds historical or fairy-tale-like. 監禁 is confinement as a crime (kidnapping), 投獄 is putting someone in prison; in daily life one says 閉じ込める.

examples[].german: On the day an alchemist tried and failed to turn lead into gold, rain was pouring outside.
In medieval Europe, many scholars were absorbed in the study of alchemy.
You should be careful of investment pitches like "alchemy" that make big money without capital.
en.notes: 錬金術 is alchemy, the attempt to turn base metals into gold; an alchemist is a 錬金術師. Figuratively it denotes (often critically) a method of making money out of nothing: 現代の錬金術, 〜は一種の錬金術だ. In this meaning it is often put in quotation marks.

examples[].german: Rice is our staple food, but that doesn't mean every Japanese person has seen beautiful golden ears of rice swaying in the wind.
In autumn, the ears of rice in the paddies ripen to a golden color.
An ear of rice that bows lower the more it ripens.
en.notes: 稲穂 is the ear of the rice plant (稲 + 穂). Typical: 稲穂が実る "the ears ripen", 稲穂が垂れる/揺れる, 黄金色の稲穂. Well known is the proverb 実るほど頭を垂れる稲穂かな: the riper the ear, the lower it bows - true greatness shows in humility. Distinguish 稲 (plant), 米 (grain) and ご飯 (cooked rice).

examples[].german: During the Roman imperial period, the emperor had his eye on the people of that village.
Russia's imperial rule came to an end with the revolution of 1917.
A building from the imperial era is now used as a museum.
en.notes: 帝政 is rule by an emperor as a form of government, i.e. "imperial rule, monarchy". Typical: ローマ帝政 "Roman imperial period" (as opposed to the republic), 帝政ロシア "Tsarist Russia", 帝政時代, 帝政が崩壊する. Opposites are 共和制 "republic" and 王政 "royal rule"; 帝国, by contrast, refers to the empire as a state.

en.meaning: to twinkle; to flicker; to blink
examples[].german: The surrounding scenery was covered in snow in an instant and turned pure white.
Stars are twinkling in the winter night sky.
The lights of a distant town flickered faintly in the fog.
en.notes: 瞬く mainly means "to twinkle, to flicker" of light: 星が瞬く, 明かりが瞬く. The meaning "to blink" also exists, but in daily life one says まばたきする for that. Very common is the set phrase 瞬く間に "in a flash, in no time". It is intransitive; 瞬く is occasionally also read しばたたく (to blink the eyes).

examples[].german: The moment you run into a spider web, you suddenly turn into a karate master.
The moment I opened the door, the cat dashed outside.
The camera superbly captured the moment the goal was scored.
en.notes: 瞬間 is a point in time, the "instant, moment". Very common after the past form: 〜た瞬間(に) "the moment when ...". Other combinations: 決定的瞬間 "the decisive moment", 瞬間的に "in a flash". 一瞬, by contrast, emphasizes the short duration ("for a moment"), whereas 瞬間 emphasizes the exact point in time.

examples[].german: A mathematical proof is required.
To prove who I was, I showed my passport.
She is trying to prove her innocence.
en.notes: 証明 means "proof, verification" - to show something to be true or correct, whether mathematically, scientifically or officially. As a transitive する-verb: 無実を証明する "to prove one's innocence", 本人であることを証明する "to prove one's identity". Very common are 証明書 "certificate" and 身分証明書 "ID card". 証拠, by contrast, is the "piece of evidence" itself with which one 証明する.

examples[].german: He said exactly what I wanted to say in an instant and straight to the point, and I was very impressed.
This app instantly translates the text in the photos you take.
While driving, a split-second decision can sometimes prevent an accident.
en.notes: 瞬時 "instant, split second" is more elevated than 一瞬 and appears almost always adverbially as 瞬時に "instantly, immediately" or attributively as 瞬時の判断 "split-second decision". Frequent in technical and news texts: 瞬時に計算する, 瞬時に反応する. In conversation, すぐに or 一瞬で sounds more natural.

examples[].german: Lining up masses of white chrysanthemums in front of someone's house is worse than a nuisance. After all, white chrysanthemums are flowers for mourning the dead in Japan. Do you understand what I mean?
I took a bouquet of white chrysanthemums when visiting the grave.
The funeral altar was decorated with many white chrysanthemums.
en.notes: 白菊 is the white chrysanthemum (also read しろぎく). In Japan it is the typical flower for funerals, graves and remembrance of the dead (お墓参り, 葬儀, お盆). For this reason, white chrysanthemums are not given to the sick or on happy occasions. The chrysanthemum in general (菊) is also a symbol of the imperial house.

examples[].german: I know that one in four people think advertising is exaggerated, but I don't think all of it is exaggerated advertising.
The company received a warning from the authorities for exaggerated advertising.
His stories are always exaggerated, so you should take them with a grain of salt.
en.notes: 誇大 means "exaggerated, inflated" and appears mainly in set compounds: 誇大広告 "exaggerated, misleading advertising", 誇大表現, 誇大妄想 "delusions of grandeur". As a な-adjective: 誇大な宣伝. The related 誇張 denotes the act of exaggerating (誇張する), whereas 誇大 describes the quality. In daily life one simply says 大げさ.

examples[].german: Don't blink, just keep looking at the picture.
The children followed the magic trick spellbound, without even blinking.
When you sit at a computer for a long time, you blink less and your eyes dry out more easily.
en.notes: 瞬き "blinking, blink of an eye" is usually written in hiragana まばたき; as an intransitive verb まばたきする. Typical: 瞬きもせずに見つめる "to stare without blinking", 瞬きする間に "in the blink of an eye". A deliberate wink, by contrast, is ウインク. Do not confuse with 瞬く (またたく) "to twinkle"; the same spelling 瞬き can also be read またたき "twinkling (of stars)".

examples[].german: "You won't catch me!" "Got you!" "Whoa! That was fast. It was over in a flash. But that's not fair of you. I'm just a kid, so go a bit easier on me."
For a moment, I didn't understand what had happened.
Mount Fuji was visible between the clouds for just an instant.
en.notes: 一瞬 is a very short moment and is used both as a noun and as an adverb: 一瞬、言葉を失った "for a moment I was speechless". Typical: 一瞬だけ, 一瞬のうちに/一瞬で "in no time", 一瞬の出来事. In contrast to 瞬間 (exact point in time, 〜た瞬間), 一瞬 emphasizes the shortness of the duration.

en.meaning: to be proud of; to boast
examples[].german: This short film is about the robotics industry that Japan is proud of in the world.
This temple can boast a history of over a thousand years.
He never boasts of his success and always remains modest.
en.notes: 誇る is transitive: Xを誇る "to be proud of X, to pride oneself on something". It is especially common for describing what distinguishes something: 世界一の高さを誇る, 長い歴史を誇る, 日本が世界に誇る技術. For personal pride one rather says 誇りに思う or 誇らしい in conversation. 自慢する is more colloquial and can sound like bragging. Noun: 誇り "pride".

examples[].german: The review said it was the best camera of all time, but that was a bit of an exaggeration.
He tends to exaggerate, so you'd better believe only half of what he says.
That's no exaggeration - we really did wait in line for three hours.
en.notes: 誇張 is exaggerating in presentation: 話を誇張する, 誇張した表現, 誇張して伝える. Common in denials: 誇張ではなく "it's no exaggeration". The word is somewhat formal; in daily life one says 大げさだ, オーバーだ or, in youth slang, 話を盛る.

examples[].german: All preparations for introducing the manor system are complete.
In the Heian period, nobles and temples and shrines held manors in various places.
On medieval European manors, peasants cultivated the fields for the lord.
en.notes: 庄園 is a variant of 荘園 (textbook spelling) and denotes a private landed estate or manorial lordship. In Japanese history (Nara to Muromachi periods), such estates belonged to nobles, temples and shrines; this is called the 荘園制度. The word is also used for medieval European manors. Purely a historical technical term.

examples[].german: Do everything to prevent this witness from testifying in court.
The police prevented the culprit's escape.
To prevent the winning goal, the goalkeeper threw himself desperately at the ball.
en.notes: 阻止 means to actively stop an action or plan before it succeeds: 侵入を阻止する, 計画を阻止する, 〜するのを阻止する. The word is formal and typical of news and sports. 防ぐ is more general ("to prevent, to ward off"); 阻害 means only "to hinder, to impede", not to prevent completely.

examples[].german: Drinks containing caffeine interfere with sleep.
Excessive regulation is hampering economic growth.
The language barrier is a factor hindering the promotion of foreign employees.
en.notes: 阻害 means "to hinder, to impede, to impair", mostly of developments and processes: 成長を阻害する, 発展を阻害する, 阻害要因 "inhibiting factor". Formal, typical of technical and newspaper texts; in everyday language 妨げる or 邪魔する. Unlike 阻止, something is not completely prevented. Do not confuse with the identically read 疎外 "alienation, exclusion".

examples[].german: I presented the research results at an international conference.
I'll be at a conference next week, so I'll be away from the lab.
He is a member of the Japanese Society of Psychology.
en.notes: 学会 has two closely connected meanings: the scientific "academic society" (e.g. 日本心理学会) and its "conference". Typical are 学会で発表する "to present at a conference", 学会に参加する/出る and 学会誌 "the society's journal". Not to be confused with the identically read 学界 "academic world"; 大会 is used more for sports or large events.

en.meaning: to fall silent; to keep quiet
examples[].german: What's wrong? Why are you so quiet?
Please don't use other people's things without asking.
When the teacher scolded them, the students suddenly fell silent.
en.notes: 黙る is intransitive: "to fall silent, to keep quiet"; the state is 黙っている. Very common is 黙って "without saying anything, without asking": 黙って帰る, 黙って使う. 黙れ "Shut up!" is rude; more polite is 静かにしてください. Related: 黙り込む "to lapse into silence", causative 黙らせる "to silence".

examples[].german: There was an awkward silence, and I reached for a salt shaker.
Even when asked by journalists, the minister kept silent.
After a long silence, the singer returned with a new album.
en.notes: 沈黙 is silence as a state: 沈黙が続く/流れる, 気まずい沈黙. Fixed combinations: 沈黙を守る "to maintain silence", 沈黙を破る "to break the silence". As a verb, 沈黙する is formal (news, literature); in daily life one says 黙る. Proverb: 沈黙は金 "silence is golden".

en.meaning: to ignore; to give the silent treatment
examples[].german: The police are turning a blind eye to many crimes in that area.
The residents' objections were ignored by the city.
The company kept ignoring the improvement proposals from its employees.
en.notes: 黙殺 means to deliberately pass over something and not react to it - literally "to kill by silence". Typical: 意見/要求/抗議を黙殺する, often in the passive 黙殺される. The word is formal and critical (press, politics). 無視する is the neutral everyday word, 見逃す means rather "to let slide".

examples[].german: Someone threw a piece of bread into the sumo ring.
Before entering the ring, the wrestler scattered salt.
If you don't discuss on the same footing, you end up talking past each other.
en.notes: 土俵 is the sumo ring of packed clay: 土俵に上がる "to enter the ring", 土俵を割る "to be pushed out of the ring". Figuratively it refers to the arena on which one measures oneself: 同じ土俵に立つ "to compete on equal terms", 土俵際 "at the edge, in a last-ditch situation". Traditionally women are not allowed to enter the ring.

examples[].german: Because it absorbs water well, I use cotton cloth as a dishcloth.
This factory has been weaving cotton cloth since long ago.
Please press lightly on the wound with a clean cotton cloth.
en.notes: 綿布 is cotton fabric or a cloth made of cotton. The word is matter-of-fact and written-language (textile industry, medicine, product descriptions); in daily life one says 綿の布, 木綿 or コットン. Do not confuse: 綿 read めん means the fiber in the fabric, read わた it means cotton wadding or raw cotton.

examples[].german: I have never built a bridge before.
Construction has begun on a new bridge across the river.
It was after the war that electric wires were strung to the village deep in the mountains.
en.notes: 架設 is a construction and engineering term for erecting something that spans or is laid out: 橋を架設する "to build a bridge", 電線/電話線を架設する "to lay lines". General building is 建設, installing equipment is 設置. Do not confuse with the identically read 仮設 "temporary" (仮設住宅).

examples[].german: At the library, you can find and borrow the books you need from the shelves yourself.
Old materials are stored on the bookshelves in the basement.
Bookshelves reaching to the ceiling lined the professor's office.
en.notes: 書架 is the written-language word for "bookshelf", typical in libraries and archives: 書架に並ぶ, 書架から本を取り出す, 開架 "open stacks" and 閉架 "closed stacks". At home one says 本棚; a casual chat about one's own IKEA shelf sounds unnatural with 書架.

examples[].german: The son of the family over there was in a traffic accident and was taken to the hospital on a stretcher, but apparently ended up in a persistent vegetative state.
The injured player was carried off the field on a stretcher.
Two paramedics lifted the stretcher and slid it into the ambulance.
en.notes: 担架 is the stretcher used to carry the injured: 担架で運ぶ/運ばれる, 担架に乗せる. A wheeled stretcher in a hospital is usually called ストレッチャー. Do not confuse with the same-sounding 短歌 (a poem form) and 啖呵 (in 啖呵を切る "to give someone a sharp piece of one's mind").

examples[].german: She is an unmistakable country girl.
This is an undeniable fact.
What appears in the photo is unmistakably my wallet.
en.notes: 紛れもない "unmistakable, undeniable" comes from 紛れる "to be mistaken for, to get lost": there is nothing it could be confused with. Typically attributive: 紛れもない事実/証拠, adverbial 紛れもなく "quite clearly, without doubt". Somewhat elevated; in conversation one often says 間違いなく or 明らかに.

examples[].german: Can you explain when and why the pupil constricts and dilates?
The doctor shone a light to check the patient's pupil response.
When eye drops are used for an examination, the pupils dilate and things look dazzling for a while.
en.notes: 瞳孔 is the medical term for the pupil: 瞳孔が開く/拡大する "to dilate", 瞳孔が縮む/収縮する "to constrict", 瞳孔反射. In daily life and literature one rather says 瞳 (ひとみ), which also stands poetically for "eyes".

examples[].german: I put liquid in the test tube and heated it.
I shook the test tube gently and mixed the two liquids.
Please heat it slowly so the test tube doesn't crack.
en.notes: 試験管 is the "test tube" in the laboratory or chemistry class, composed of 試験 "test, experiment" and 管 "tube". Typical verbs are 試験管に入れる/注ぐ, 試験管を振る "to shake" and 試験管を加熱する "to heat". 試験管ベビー is an older term for a child conceived by artificial insemination; today one says 体外受精. Not to be confused with the identically read 試験官 "examiner".

examples[].german: The skull specimen has two large eye sockets.
The toy skeleton is made so that the depths of its eye sockets glow red.
en.notes: 眼孔 is the eye socket in the skull. The word is rare and technical; in medicine 眼窩 (がんか) is more common, in daily life one speaks of 目のくぼみ. Do not confuse with the identically read 眼光 "gaze, gleam of the eyes" (鋭い眼光).

examples[].german: My husband is always working, begrudging every spare moment.
She studies for her certification, making use of every spare moment.
Busy days without a moment to spare continue.
en.notes: 寸暇 "a short moment of free time" (寸 = tiny, 暇 = free time) occurs almost only in the set phrase 寸暇を惜しんで〜: "to leave no spare minute unused, to use every minute to ...". Besides that, 寸暇もない "not to have even a spare minute". Elevated and written-language; the form 寸暇を惜しまず is a common mistake.

examples[].german: I received a cotton handkerchief as a present.
This shirt is cotton, so it's fine to wash it.
Please buy firm tofu at the supermarket.
en.notes: 木綿 is cotton as a fabric: 木綿のシャツ, 木綿のハンカチ. Today one often says コットン in everyday speech, and on labels 綿 (めん) appears: 綿100%. Also well known is 木綿豆腐 "firm tofu" as opposed to the soft 絹ごし豆腐. The cotton plant or cotton wool itself is more likely called 綿 (わた).

examples[].german: I bought a charm for the fulfillment of wishes at that shrine.
My long-held wish came true, and I was finally able to open my own shop.
Many wishes for passing exams were written on the ema plaques.
en.notes: 心願 is a fervent wish of the heart, especially a wish addressed to gods or Buddha. Very common is the set phrase 心願成就 "fulfillment of one's heartfelt wish" on amulets and votive plaques. Other combinations: 心願がかなう, 長年の心願. In daily life one says 願い; 念願 is a long-cherished wish without religious overtones.

examples[].german: In nineteenth-century Europe and America, a movement demanding the expansion of women's rights spread.
Hiratsuka Raichō is one of the figures representing the women's rights movement in Japan.
I wrote a report on the history of women's rights at university.
en.notes: 女権 "women's rights" is a somewhat old-fashioned, mainly historical term: 女権運動 "women's rights movement", 女権拡張 "expansion of women's rights". Today one mostly says 女性の権利 or 女性の人権. A "matriarchal society" is not called 女権社会 but 母系社会 or 女系社会.

examples[].german: Slips prevent skirts from rubbing against the skin.
The shoe chafes, and my heel hurts.
These jeans have worn thin and frayed at the knees.
en.notes: 擦れる is intransitive: two surfaces "rub against each other" (〜と擦れる, 〜に擦れる) or something "wears off, wears out": 袖口が擦れる. The transitive partner is 擦る (する) "to rub". Figuratively, 擦れた人 describes someone who has lost their naivety and become hardened; the opposite is 擦れていない "unspoiled". The word is often written in kana すれる.

examples[].german: Let's give three cheers for Koichi of Tofugu! Banzai! Banzai! Banzai!
When the election win was confirmed, supporters cheered "banzai" at the office.
Hearing the news that I had passed, I involuntarily shouted "banzai."
en.notes: 万歳 is the cheer "Hurrah! Hooray!", during which one throws both arms up. Typical: 万歳をする, 万歳三唱 "three cheers of banzai" at election wins and celebrations, 〜万歳 "Long live ...!". Colloquially 万歳(する) also means "to give up, to throw up one's hands" (like お手上げ). Read まんざい, by contrast, it is a traditional comedy performance at New Year.

examples[].german: I dampened a paper towel a little and wiped.
In a dry room, it helps to hang up a wet towel to humidify the air.
I was thirsty, so I moistened my mouth a little with water.
en.notes: 湿らせる is transitive: "to moisten something slightly", e.g. 布/タオルを湿らせる, 空気を湿らせる. The intransitive counterpart is 湿る "to become damp" (湿った服); equivalent in meaning but more elevated is 湿す. 濡らす means "to make wet" with more water, 湿らせる only a little.

examples[].german: This road is currently under crushed-stone paving work.
A lot of crushed stone is laid under the railway tracks.
I laid crushed stone in the parking lot to improve drainage.
en.notes: 砕石 is broken-up rock, i.e. crushed stone or gravel as used in road and rail construction: 砕石を敷く, 砕石舗装, 砕石場 "quarry". 砂利, by contrast, denotes natural, rather rounded gravel; in daily life both are often called 砂利. A technical word from construction.

examples[].german: My cousin fell and suffered a comminuted fracture of the left kneecap.
The collected plastic bottles are finely crushed by machine and recycled.
In the final, the team crushed the powerhouse 5-0.
en.notes: 粉砕 means "to grind, to smash": 機械で粉砕する, 粉砕骨折 "comminuted fracture". Figuratively, and more in sports and press language, 粉砕する means "to beat an opponent or plan crushingly": 強豪を粉砕する. Compared with the native 砕く, it is more formal and sounds like complete destruction.

en.meaning: to be persistent; to hold out; to be sticky
examples[].german: Wow! The salesman is still talking to my mother. How persistent!
If you stir natto well, it becomes even stickier.
We lost the game, but we fought to the end and didn't give up.
en.notes: 粘る has two meanings: literally "to be sticky, to be tough" (納豆が粘る), figuratively "to not give up, to stay at it stubbornly" (最後まで粘る). In the second sense one says e.g. 粘って交渉する or, jokingly, コーヒー一杯で三時間粘る "to sit for three hours over one coffee". Compared with 頑張る, 粘る emphasizes tenaciously holding out even when it seems hopeless. Related are 粘り強い "persevering" and ねばねば "sticky".

examples[].german: Are you thinking of buying clay?
The children played making animals out of clay.
The clay of this region is famous for being suited to pottery.
en.notes: 粘土 is both natural clay (粘土質の土, 陶芸用の粘土) and modeling clay for play and crafts (油粘土, 紙粘土). Typical: 粘土をこねる "to knead clay", 粘土で〜を作る. The 粘 is also in 粘る "to be sticky, to be tenacious".

examples[].german: Why are you keeping adhesive tape in your jewelry box?
This sticker has weak adhesion and peels off right away.
That person has been obsessively clinging to the same person online for years.
en.notes: 粘着 denotes the sticking or adhering of a substance to a surface and appears mainly in compounds: 粘着テープ "adhesive tape", 粘着力 "adhesive strength", 粘着シート "adhesive sheet". As an intransitive する-verb (〜に粘着する) it is rather technical; in daily life one says くっつく. Colloquially, especially on the internet, 粘着する means "to stalk someone persistently, to fixate on someone", and 粘着質 describes a clingy, resentful character.

examples[].german: My skin has been in bad shape since giving birth. Could you tell me the name of the cosmetic you recommended before?
Be sure to remove your makeup before going to bed.
She puts on makeup in ten minutes every morning and goes to work.
en.notes: 化粧 is "makeup, applying makeup"; 化粧する means "to put on makeup", the same as お化粧をする or the casual メイクする. Typical combinations: 化粧を落とす "to remove makeup", 化粧が濃い/薄い "heavily/lightly made up", 化粧品 "cosmetics", 化粧室 as a polite word for "restroom". Figuratively it means "beautification, coating", such as 雪化粧 "dusted with snow".

examples[].german: I was swindled out of money with a fake sales contract.
The man was arrested on suspicion of swindling cash from elderly people.
He had inflated expenses and defrauded the company of about one million yen.
en.notes: 詐取 is a legal, written-language term for obtaining money or goods by deception: 金を詐取する, often passive 詐取される. The general word for fraud as an offense is 詐欺; 詐取 emphasizes the result, namely the swindled loot. Typical in news: 〜を詐取した疑いで逮捕される. Colloquially one says だまし取る instead.

examples[].german: The gardener noticed right away that she was lying about her age, but said nothing.
It turned out that the employee had joined the company by misrepresenting his career history.
A man impersonating a police officer is reportedly going around visiting elderly people's homes.
en.notes: 詐称 means to give false information about oneself - about name, age, occupation or résumé: 年齢を詐称する, 経歴詐称 "falsified career history", 学歴詐称. It is a formal word, often with legal coloring, from the news. Unlike 詐取 (obtaining money by fraud), it is not about loot but about a feigned identity; in everyday speech one says 〜だと嘘をつく or 〜を名乗る.

examples[].german: My homestay father explained the Black Mist scandal to me at dinner today.
The public hopes that the dark dealings in the political world will be cleared up.
It is rumored that there are shady dealings between the mayor and a construction company.
en.notes: 黒い霧 literally means "black fog" but is used almost only figuratively: for corruption and dark dealings that remain hidden, especially in politics and sports. Typical are 政界の黒い霧 and 黒い霧を晴らす "to clear up the allegations". Well known is the 黒い霧事件, the match-fixing scandal in Japanese professional baseball around 1970. For real dense fog one says 濃い霧 or 濃霧.

examples[].german: At a charity auction, I won a wonderfully beautiful painting of mountains emerging from the morning mist.
When the morning mist cleared, a lake appeared before my eyes.
Riding a bicycle through the morning mist is a little dangerous.
en.notes: 朝霧 is the "morning mist" that forms over valleys, rivers and lakes on cool mornings and disappears with the sun. Typical: 朝霧がかかる "morning mist hangs", 朝霧が晴れる "the morning mist lifts". The word sounds poetic and often appears in landscape descriptions; in weather reports one says plainly 霧. The evening counterpart is 夕霧, light haze is もや.

examples[].german: He is a famous author of novels set in the pleasure quarters.
My grandmother reportedly worked as a geisha in Kyoto's geisha world when she was young.
In the past, venereal disease was called 花柳病.
en.notes: 花柳 (literally "flowers and willows") is an old-fashioned expression for the pleasure quarters with geisha and brothels. Today it survives almost only in compounds: 花柳界 "the geisha world" (still used for geisha districts such as in Kyōto), 花柳小説 "novels from the pleasure quarters" and the obsolete 花柳病 "venereal disease". The word is written-language and has a historical coloring.

examples[].german: You should visit Ise Shrine once.
In the Edo period, many people went on pilgrimages to Ise.
At the celebration, a magnificent Ise lobster was served.
en.notes: 伊勢 is the name of the old province in today's Mie Prefecture and of today's city 伊勢市. Best known is the 伊勢神宮, Japan's most important Shintō shrine; the traditional pilgrimage there is called お伊勢参り. The name is also in 伊勢エビ "spiny lobster" and in the bay 伊勢湾 "Ise Bay". The name is practically always written in kanji.

examples[].german: The periodic table lists 118 elements.
The element symbol for oxygen is O.
A Japanese research team discovered a new element.
en.notes: 元素 is the chemical "element", i.e. a basic substance such as 水素 "hydrogen" or 炭素 "carbon"; related are 元素記号 "element symbol" and 周期表 "periodic table". For "element" in the general sense of component or factor, one uses 要素 instead - a common mistake. The four elements of antiquity (earth, water, air, fire) are also called 四元素.

examples[].german: Datemaki is one of my favorite dishes among osechi cuisine.
These glasses are non-prescription fashion glasses.
I haven't lived in Japan for ten years for nothing.
en.notes: 伊達 means on the one hand "stylishness, elegance, flair" (伊達男 "dandy"), on the other hand "only for show, out of vanity": 伊達眼鏡 are glasses without a prescription worn only as an accessory. Very common is the phrase 伊達に〜ない "not for nothing, not merely for show": 伊達に年を取っていない "I haven't gotten older for nothing". As a name, 伊達 also stands for the lord's family (伊達政宗) and in the dish 伊達巻き.

examples[].german: I worked as an assistant in the Tofugu sales department.
From next month, I will be promoted to assistant section manager.
Assisting the president is an important job of a secretary.
en.notes: 補佐 means "support, assistance" and refers both to the activity (上司を補佐する "to support one's superior") and to the person. In job titles it is fixed: 課長補佐 "assistant section manager", 大統領補佐官 "presidential aide". Unlike the general 手伝う or 助ける, 補佐 is formal and implies a fixed supporting role under a leading person.

examples[].german: I'm looking forward to meeting the colonel.
He retired as a colonel in the U.S. Air Force.
The colonel in that film is a man who is very strict with his subordinates.
en.notes: 大佐 is the highest field-grade officer rank: "colonel" in the army and air force, "captain" in the navy. The series is 少佐 "major" → 中佐 "lieutenant colonel" → 大佐 "colonel". In today's Japan Self-Defense Forces the corresponding rank is called 一佐; 大佐 is therefore heard mainly with foreign armies, in history, films and anime. As a form of address it often stands alone: 大佐！

examples[].german: The major insisted on treating the colonel to a drink.
My grandfather was reportedly an army major during the war.
He was promoted to major at the young age of thirty-something.
en.notes: 少佐 is the lowest field-grade officer rank: "major" (army, air force) or "lieutenant commander" (navy). It ranks below 中佐 and 大佐; the characters 少・中・大 also order the ranks in 少尉, 中尉, 大尉. In the Self-Defense Forces the rank is called 三佐, so 少佐 appears mainly in historical or foreign contexts and in fiction.

examples[].german: The lieutenant colonel decided to oppose the move to Japan.
Lieutenant colonel is the rank one below colonel and one above major.
Command of the operation was entrusted to an experienced lieutenant colonel.
en.notes: 中佐 is the middle field-grade officer rank: "lieutenant colonel" in the army and air force, "commander" in the navy. It stands between 少佐 "major" and 大佐 "colonel". Like the other 佐 ranks, the word is mainly used today for foreign or historical armed forces; the Self-Defense Forces say 二佐.

examples[].german: Could you help me measure my chest with this tape measure?
Before buying a sofa, let's measure the width of the room with a tape measure.
When I pulled the tape measure out all the way, it wouldn't retract.
en.notes: 巻尺 is a roll-up tape measure, both the soft tailor's tape and the steel tape from the hardware store. One measures with it: 巻尺で測る. In daily life one mostly says メジャー; 巻尺 sounds somewhat old-fashioned or more technical. The 尺 is the old unit of length (about 30 cm), which can also be found in 尺度 "scale, yardstick".

examples[].german: I feel sorry for them, since they can barely afford food, clothing or shelter.
The sight of the puppy shivering in the rain was truly pitiful.
Trying to attract people's attention with such lies - what a pathetic person.
en.notes: 哀れ is, as a noun, "pity, pathos" and, as a na-adjective, "pitiful, wretched". Typical are 哀れに思う "to feel pity", 哀れな姿 "a miserable sight" and 哀れむ "to pity". Applied to people it can sound condescending (哀れな人 "a pathetic person"); more neutral is かわいそう. Classic is もののあわれ, the wistful sensitivity to the transience of things.

examples[].german: For some reason, I feel sorry for people who only drink as a social obligation.
A puppy was shivering in the rain, and I felt sorry for it.
If you talk like that, it's unfair to him.
en.notes: かわいそう expresses pity: "poor, pitiable, one feels sorry for someone". It is a na-adjective (かわいそうな犬); かわいそうに! means "You poor thing!", and 〜がかわいそう can also imply that something is unfair to someone. It is usually written in kana; 可哀想 and 可哀相 are ateji; despite the similar sound, it has nothing to do with かわいい "cute". 気の毒 is more distant and polite - toward superiors, かわいそう sounds condescending.

examples[].german: Even though the baby was wearing cotton mittens, he scratched his lower lip.
He bit his lower lip in frustration.
The "f" sound is made by lightly touching the upper teeth to the lower lip.
en.notes: 下唇 is the "lower lip"; its counterpart is 上唇 "upper lip", the base word 唇. Typical expressions: 下唇を噛む "to bite one's lower lip" (from anger, disappointment or embarrassment) and 下唇が腫れる "the lower lip swells". It is often heard in pronunciation lessons because Japanese has no sounds like "f" or "v" in which the upper teeth touch the 下唇.

examples[].german: When I'm tired, my upper lip often swells up.
My upper lip cracked from the cold, and it hurts every time I eat.
He has a habit of touching his upper lip with his finger when he is thinking.
en.notes: 上唇 is the upper lip; note the reading うわくちびる (not うえ〜), parallel to 下唇 したくちびる "lower lip". The う〜 prefix is also known from 上着 うわぎ. Typical combinations: 上唇が腫れる "the upper lip swells", 上唇を噛む. When no distinction is needed, one simply says 唇.

examples[].german: Communism had a major influence in the twentieth century.
The Cold War was a confrontation between capitalism and communism.
My grandfather was reportedly influenced by communist ideas when he was young.
en.notes: 共産主義 is communism as an ideology and economic order, literally "doctrine of common (共) property (産)".
