Related words: 共産党 ("Communist Party"), 共産主義者 ("communist"), 共産圏 ("Eastern Bloc"). 社会主義 ("socialism") is often mentioned as a preliminary stage or related current; the opposite is 資本主義. The word belongs to the domain of history, politics and news.

examples[].german: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Salt is not a mixture but a compound of sodium and chlorine.
A new compound was found in a certain plant.
en.notes: 化合物 is a chemical "compound" of two or more elements chemically bonded to one another (化合する "to combine chemically"). Antonyms are 単体 "pure substance of a single element" and 混合物 "mixture", whose components are merely mixed. Common are 有機化合物 "organic compound" and 炭素化合物. For "connection" in the sense of contact or link, one of course says 連絡 or 接続, not 化合物.

examples[].german: I'm calling to let you know that someone was climbing over the earthen wall of your house.
A long earthen wall continues around the old temple.
Part of the earthen wall collapsed in the earthquake.
en.notes: 土塀 is a wall of clay or earth, often with a small tiled roof, as seen around temples, old samurai residences and traditional houses. A wall or fence in general is 塀 (ブロック塀 "concrete block wall"); 土塀 emphasizes the material and has a historical feel. Typical combinations: 土塀が続く, 土塀が崩れる, 土塀に囲まれる.

examples[].german: I filmed the moment a military plane shot down a helicopter with my iPhone.
The military announced that it had shot down a drone near the border.
The passenger plane is believed to have been shot down by a missile.
en.notes: 撃墜 means "to shoot down (an aircraft)"; as a transitive する-verb: 戦闘機を撃墜する, passive 撃墜される. It applies only to targets in the air such as aircraft, drones or missiles; sinking a ship is 撃沈, shooting a person dead is 射殺. The word belongs to military and news language. For the crash itself one says 墜落.

examples[].german: Do you think the jet crashed due to human error?
Caught by a gust of wind, the drone fell into the river.
The cause of the crash is still unclear.
en.notes: 墜落 is a fall from a great height, typically of airplanes, helicopters or drones: 飛行機が墜落する, 墜落事故. It is an intransitive suru-verb. For people falling from buildings or stairs one rather uses 転落; 落下 is neutral for anything that falls down (落下物). 墜落 sounds dramatic and often appears in news reports.

examples[].german: I can only think that he lacks common sense.
The lack of safety awareness led to this accident.
The report was criticized for lacking specificity.
en.notes: 欠如 means that something necessary is completely missing, and is used above all for abstract qualities: 常識の欠如, 責任感が欠如している, 安全意識の欠如. For substances and supplies such as vitamins or water, one speaks instead of 欠乏 (ビタミン欠乏症) or 不足. 欠如 is written-language and often sounds critical. Grammatically: 〜が欠如する or 〜の欠如.

examples[].german: There is a reason for her sudden accusations of sexual harassment.
In the quiet night, a loud bang suddenly echoed.
The clear sky suddenly darkened, and it began to rain heavily.
en.notes: 突如 means "suddenly, abruptly" and is the written-language, somewhat dramatic variant of 突然. It is often used as 突如として. It is found in news, novels and reports about unexpected events; in casual conversation one rather says 突然 or 急に. Unlike 突然, 突如 is hardly used attributively (突然の雨, but not 突如の雨).

examples[].german: That old woman absolutely refuses to approve of gambling.
Folktales often feature a mysterious old woman living deep in the mountains.
If I may be a bit meddlesome, let me say just one thing.
en.notes: 老婆 is a written-language word for "old woman", as found in novels and fairy tales. About real persons it sounds distant to disrespectful; more polite are お年寄り, 高齢の女性 or おばあさん. The male counterpart is 老人 or 老翁. Fixed is 老婆心 "unsolicited, well-meant advice", often in 老婆心ながら "if I may be so bold as to say".

examples[].german: Over New Year I stay at my grandmother's house.
On the bus, I gave my seat to an elderly woman carrying luggage.
en.notes: おばあさん can mean a grandmother or an elderly woman. In kanji, a grandmother is usually written お祖母さん, an elderly woman お婆さん; the hiragana spelling is very common. When speaking about one's own grandmother to outsiders, one mostly says 祖母. An unknown elderly woman is better addressed by name or an appropriate form of address, depending on the situation. The long ああ distinguishes おばあさん from おばさん, aunt.

examples[].german: To tell the truth, I'm a collector of old coins and currency.
In the age of barter, money was not yet in use.
When prices rise, the value of money falls.
en.notes: 貨幣 is "money" as a means of payment in the economic sense, often specifically "coinage". It belongs to technical and written language: 貨幣経済, 貨幣価値, 記念貨幣. Distinguish 通貨 "currency" (円, ユーロ), 硬貨 "coin" and 紙幣 "banknote"; in everyday speech people simply say お金. Collectors speak of 古い貨幣 or 古銭.

examples[].german: I hated my mother, but my mother hated me just the same.
The feeling of hating war is shared by people all over the world.
There is a saying: "Hate the sin, not the sinner."
en.notes: 憎む means "to hate, to detest" and is a strong, rather written word for deep resentment against persons or things such as war and injustice: 〜を憎む. In daily life one mostly says 嫌い / 嫌う for dislike; 憎む expresses genuine hatred. Related are 憎い / 憎らしい "hateful" and 憎しみ "hatred". Well known is the proverb 罪を憎んで人を憎まず "Hate the sin, not the sinner".

examples[].german: In a chemistry experiment, we synthesized a new substance.
In high school, I was better at chemistry than physics.
Chemicals flowed from the factory into the river.
en.notes: 化学 is "chemistry" as a science and school subject; important compounds are 化学反応 "chemical reaction", 化学物質 "chemical substance" and 化学者 "chemist". Because it sounds exactly like 科学 "science", people in conversation often say ばけがく (from 化ける) to tell them apart. "Chemical" is usually rendered with 化学的 or 化学の.

examples[].german: Why don't we rest a bit in this mountain hut?
On holidays, many families relax by the riverside.
This park has long been a place of rest for the citizens.
en.notes: 憩う means "to rest, to take a break, to relax" and is an elevated, rather written verb. It is found in descriptions of peaceful scenes: 公園で家族が憩う. Much more common than the verb is the noun 憩い, especially 憩いの場 "place of relaxation" and 憩いのひととき. In conversation one says 休む, くつろぐ or 一休みする instead.

examples[].german: I'm really hot from wearing too many layers. Could you fan me a bit?
It was hot, so I fanned my face with a pencil board.
I fanned the charcoal fire with a fan to make it stronger.
en.notes: 扇ぐ means "to fan, to wave air toward": うちわで扇ぐ, 顔を扇ぐ. The tool takes で, the person or thing takes を: 子どもをうちわで扇ぐ. The identically read 仰ぐ means "to look up, to ask for advice" - do not confuse. For "to incite, to stir up" one mostly uses 煽る (あおる) today. 扇ぐ is often written in kana as あおぐ.

examples[].german: While I was waiting in front of the gate, someone cut in line.
At ten at night, the school gate is closed.
If you don't close the gate firmly, the dog will get out.
en.notes: 門扉 are the leaves or door of a gate, i.e. the movable part that one opens and closes: 門扉を開ける / 閉める. 門 alone is the whole gate, 扉 any door. The word is somewhat formal and appears with houses, schools and company grounds as well as in construction and real estate texts. Do not confuse with 門戸 in 門戸を開く "to open up, to grant access".

examples[].german: How about inserting Aya's illustration between these two paragraphs?
Please insert your card and enter your PIN.
The insert song of this drama is a big hit among young people.
en.notes: 挿入 means "to insert, to put in": to place something into an opening or between other parts. Typical are カードを挿入する, 文章に図を挿入する and, in a computer context, 挿入キー "Insert key". Fixed are 挿入歌 "song played in a film/series" and 挿入句 "parenthetical phrase". It is somewhat technical/formal; in daily life one often says 入れる or 差し込む.

examples[].german: You probably haven't noticed, but President Koichi has everything under control.
The military seized power in a coup.
The new department head began by first getting his subordinates firmly in hand.
en.notes: 掌握 means to hold something firmly "in the hand": to bring or keep power, organizations or people under control. Typical: 政権を掌握する "to seize the reins of government", 部下を掌握する "to have one's people in hand", 実権を掌握する. Do not confuse with 把握 "to grasp, to understand" (状況を把握する); 掌握 emphasizes control and leadership, not mere understanding. The word is formal and often appears in political and economic news.

examples[].german: Blood dripped from his forehead.
Drops are dripping from the leaves of the trees after the rain.
In early summer, the mountains, dripping with green, are very beautiful.
en.notes: 滴る means "to drip, to trickle": a liquid falls down in individual drops, e.g. 汗が滴る, 血が滴る, often as 滴り落ちる. It is intransitive and somewhat more literary than ぽたぽた落ちる or 垂れる. Figuratively it describes overflowing freshness or beauty, above all in 緑滴る "lush green, brimming with green" and 水も滴るいい男 "a stunningly handsome man".

examples[].german: There are water drops on the car window.
Many water droplets formed on the surface of the cold glass.
I can't sleep because the sound of water dripping from the faucet bothers me.
en.notes: 水滴 is a "water drop", especially drops that collect on surfaces (condensation) or fall: 水滴がつく, 水滴が落ちる. Similar in meaning is しずく (滴), which sounds softer and more poetic; 水滴 seems more matter-of-fact and is also used in technical texts. For raindrops one says 雨粒 or 雨のしずく.

examples[].german: I'm busy, but I do cook for myself properly. In fact, last night I made a vegetable stew called ratatouille.
Since I started living alone, I've begun cooking for myself to save money.
This inn has a kitchen, so you can cook for yourself too.
en.notes: 自炊 means "to cook for oneself, to prepare one's own meals" and is said mainly of people living alone and students, as opposed to 外食 "eating out" or コンビニ弁当. As an intransitive する-verb: 毎日自炊している. Accommodations with cooking facilities are advertised as 自炊可 or 自炊できる. More recently and colloquially, 自炊 also means "to scan one's own books" to read them as e-books.

examples[].german: As you'd expect from a veteran announcer, she answered the question in a very clear, easily audible voice.
His explanation was concise and clear.
For our customers' sake, please display the charges clearly.
en.notes: 明瞭 is a na-adjective meaning "clear, distinct, unambiguous", e.g. 明瞭な発音, 簡潔明瞭な説明 and 明瞭会計 "transparent accounting". The opposite is 不明瞭 "unclear". Compared with はっきり or 明らか, 明瞭 is more formal and is used mainly for pronunciation, explanations and differences; the adverbial form is 明瞭に.

examples[].german: When I bought a bento, they gave me two pairs of disposable chopsticks.
Splitting disposable chopsticks cleanly is surprisingly difficult.
For the environment, more and more people carry their own chopsticks instead of using disposable ones.
en.notes: 割り箸 are disposable chopsticks of wood or bamboo that are joined as a pair and snapped apart before eating: 割り箸を割る. One gets them at restaurants, snack shops and when buying a bento at a konbini. Chopsticks are counted with 膳 (一膳, 二膳). Reusable chopsticks are simply 箸, one's own brought along are マイ箸.

examples[].german: The laws of physics are the same everywhere in the universe.
I forgot the formula in the physics test.
Getting to the airport in thirty minutes from now is physically impossible.
en.notes: 物理 mainly denotes the subject "physics" (short for 物理学) and appears in compounds such as 物理法則 "physical law" and 物理学者 "physicist". 物理的 means "physical, material" and is often used figuratively: 物理的に無理 "simply impossible in practice" (e.g. in terms of time or space). For school subjects one simply says 物理, in science rather 物理学.

examples[].german: You have the longest torso I've ever seen.
Because the landing gear wouldn't come down, the plane made a belly landing.
The head and limbs of this doll can be removed from the torso.
en.notes: 胴体 is the torso, i.e. the body without head, arms and legs. Figuratively it is also the fuselage of an aircraft or the hull of a ship, known from 胴体着陸 "belly landing". 胴 alone also means "torso, waist" (胴回り "waist circumference"), 体 the whole body. For the human upper body in daily life one often says 上半身.

examples[].german: I tried buying rainbow-colored wasabi, but it tastes just like wasabi.
The soap bubbles are shining in rainbow colors in the sunlight.
I made a rainbow-colored cake for my daughter's birthday.
en.notes: 虹色 is "rainbow-colored, in all the colors of the rainbow" and is placed before nouns with の: 虹色の傘; adverbially with に: 虹色に光る "to shimmer in rainbow colors". Grammatically it is a noun, not an い- or な-adjective. Figuratively it stands for diversity and hope, e.g. 虹色の未来; the rainbow flag is usually called レインボーフラッグ. Similar: 七色 "seven-colored, colorful".

examples[].german: Didn't the department head's daughter want to become a singer, if I remember right?
How old is your daughter?
Miss, you dropped your handkerchief.
en.notes: お嬢さん is above all the polite term for someone else's daughter: 部長のお嬢さん, お嬢さんはおいくつですか. One's own daughter is called 娘. As a form of address for a young woman ("young lady") it sounds somewhat old-fashioned and is mostly used by older people. Even more polite is お嬢様, which can also mean "daughter of a good family"; the male counterpart is 息子さん.

examples[].german: If you don't want to get athlete's foot, you'd better not wear slippers barefoot.
The children were running around the beach barefoot.
His cooking skill rivals that of a professional.
en.notes: 裸足 means "barefoot" and is grammatically a noun: 裸足で歩く "to walk barefoot", 裸足の子ども "a barefoot child". Without socks but wearing shoes is 素足. As a suffix, usually written in kana, 〜はだし means "second to no professional": プロはだし. The kanji spelling 裸足 is a special reading (jukujikun).

examples[].german: Since my income isn't very high, I keep a household account book to review what I often spend money on and to save.
The end of the year is the best earning season for shops.
My older brother changed jobs to one with better pay.
en.notes: 稼ぎ is the noun of 稼ぐ "to earn" and denotes income from work: 稼ぎがいい / 少ない. It sounds more everyday than 収入 or 所得. Common compounds: 稼ぎ時 "peak season, best time to earn", 出稼ぎ "working away from home", 時間稼ぎ "playing for time". 稼ぎ手 is the main breadwinner of a family.

examples[].german: The lookout tower for deer hunting is now covered with a big blue tarp.
On the weekend, we went strawberry picking as a family.
When autumn comes, many people go to Kyoto to view the autumn leaves.
en.notes: 〜狩り (read がり as a suffix) first means "hunt" (鹿狩り "deer hunt"), but far more often "gathering, picking, enjoying" as a leisure activity: いちご狩り "strawberry picking", ぶどう狩り, 潮干狩り "shellfish gathering at low tide", 紅葉狩り "viewing autumn leaves". Figuratively it stands for hunting people: 魔女狩り "witch hunt". Read on its own, the word is 狩り (かり) "hunt".

examples[].german: "Why don't you brush your teeth?" "Because I like the taste of food lingering in my mouth. Is that wrong?"
I try to brush my teeth after every meal.
Did you brush your teeth properly before bed?
en.notes: 歯を磨く is the normal expression for "to brush one's teeth"; 磨く generally means "to polish, to shine". One never says 歯を洗う. Common frames: 寝る前に歯を磨く, 食後に歯を磨く. The noun 歯磨き "tooth brushing" also forms 歯磨きする, which means the same and is slightly more casual; the toothbrush is 歯ブラシ, toothpaste 歯磨き粉.

en.meaning: to clear (a liquid); to prick up (one's ears); to put on an air of indifference
examples[].german: When I listened closely, I could hear the sound of waves from far away.
No matter what is said to her, she keeps a composed, unruffled look.
Let the muddy water stand for a while to clear, then use only the water on top.
en.notes: 澄ます is the transitive counterpart of 澄む "to become clear" and has several meanings: "to make clear" (a liquid), 耳を澄ます "to prick up one's ears, listen closely", and, used intransitively, "to act indifferent, to put on airs", especially in 澄ました顔 / 澄まし顔. The meaning "to clear" is rare; 耳を澄ます is by far the most common. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 済ます "to get done, finish" (宿題を済ます).

examples[].german: But why did the hackers turn their attack on us?
After the accident, public criticism was aimed at the railway company.
For some reason, the department head's anger was directed at me.
en.notes: 矛先 is literally the tip of a spear (矛), but is used almost only figuratively: the target or thrust of an attack, criticism or anger. Set phrases: 批判の矛先, 矛先を向ける "to turn against someone", 矛先を変える / 転じる "to change the target", 矛先が向く "to come into the crosshairs". The word is neutral to written-language and frequent in the news.

examples[].german: Thanks to Mr. Date watching our child, I was able to shop without worry.
Thanks to everyone, I was able to graduate safely.
Because you were late, I missed the last train.
en.notes: おかげで expresses that a positive result is owed to someone or something: noun + のおかげで, verb + おかげで. It is mostly written in kana. For negative causes one uses せいで; ironically, however, おかげで can also stand for something negative ("thanks to you, I have..."). The polite phrase おかげさまで answers questions about one's well-being.

examples[].german: When I cleaned the dog's ear wax with a cotton swab, it was somehow sticky. Is that normal?
Sticky foods like natto and okra are said to be good for the body.
I stepped on gum, and the sole of my shoe is sticky.
en.notes: ねばねば is an onomatopoeic word for "sticky, viscous, stringy" and is almost always written in kana; 粘々 is rare. As a する-verb: 手がねばねばする; adnominally ねばねばした食べ物 or ねばねばの納豆. Compared with べたべた ("sticky-damp, greasy", e.g. of sweat or syrup), ねばねば describes a viscous, stringy mass like natto, okra or mucus. Related verb: 粘る.

examples[].german: Asphalt is gravel bound together with petroleum, you know.
White gravel is laid along the approach to the shrine.
Riding a bicycle on a gravel road makes it rattle and shake.
en.notes: 砂利 is "gravel, crushed stone": small stones of the kind laid on paths, parking lots, railway tracks and shrine grounds. Typical phrases are 砂利道 "gravel road" and 砂利を敷く "to spread gravel". Fine sand is 砂, larger stones 石. Colloquially and somewhat pejoratively, じゃり (usually in kana) can also mean "kid, brat".

examples[].german: How's your old man?
My old man used to be a carpenter.
The owner of that shop is taciturn, but his cooking is reliably good.
en.notes: 親父 is a familiar, rather masculine word for one's own father: "my old man". It is usually written in kana (おやじ / オヤジ). For someone else's father one says 親父さん or, neutrally, お父さん. It also means "middle-aged or older man" (often pejorative, e.g. オヤジギャグ "dad joke") and, as 親父さん, the owner of an eatery.

examples[].german: I crushed the cookies with a rolling pin until they were in pieces.
With that one remark, his dream was shattered.
My mother has always worried about the health of the family.
en.notes: 砕く means "to smash, to break up, to crush": 氷を砕く, 岩を砕く. Figuratively: to crush hopes or resistance (夢を打ち砕く), to take pains over something (心を砕く "to go to great pains") and to explain something in simplified form (砕いて説明する, more often 噛み砕く). The intransitive counterpart is 砕ける "to break", as in 砕けた言い方 "casual way of speaking".

examples[].german: While cooking rice, my younger sister grumbled to me that the household finances were in dire straits.
We have guests tonight, so I cooked five go of rice.
In Kansai, daikon is often simmered in a light seasoning.
en.notes: 炊く mainly means "to cook rice": ご飯を炊く, 炊飯器 "rice cooker", 炊き込みご飯. For cooking other food in liquid, standard Japanese says 煮る; in the Kansai dialect, however, 炊く is also used for vegetables or fish (大根を炊く). In the general sense of "to cook" one uses 料理する or 作る.

examples[].german: Behind their backs he calls customers "suckers", yet to their faces he bows and flatters them.
You don't know anything, yet you talk big.
I was told it's cheeky for a newcomer to go home on time every day.
en.notes: くせに connects two statements with reproach: "although ..., (shamelessly) ...". It is almost always written in kana and follows noun + の or a verb/adjective in plain form: 子どものくせに, 知らないくせに. Unlike the neutral のに, くせに expresses anger or contempt toward the person and is used only when both clauses have the same subject. Casual variant: くせして.

examples[].german: Is your country an imperialist state?
The latter half of the nineteenth century is called the age of imperialism.
In history class, I learned about the relationship between imperialism and colonial rule.
en.notes: 帝国主義 is "imperialism", the policy of extending power and rule over other countries. The word belongs to history and politics: 帝国主義の時代, 帝国主義国家, 反帝国主義. Closely connected are 植民地 "colony" and 植民地支配 "colonial rule". As an attribute, 帝国主義の or 帝国主義的な "imperialistic" is used.

examples[].german: Now that the station has an elevator, wheelchair users can use it with peace of mind.
My grandmother has been living in a wheelchair since she broke her leg.
If you'd like, shall I push your wheelchair?
en.notes: 車椅子 is the "wheelchair": 車椅子に乗る / 座る, 車椅子を押す "to push the wheelchair", 車椅子で生活する. Barrier-free facilities are called 車椅子対応, e.g. 車椅子対応トイレ. It is also written 車いす. The word is neutral and used equally in daily life, nursing care and transport.

en.meaning: edge of the sumo ring; brink
examples[].german: The wrestler dug in at the edge of the ring and flung his opponent with a last-ditch throw.
The negotiations somehow came together at the last moment.
Amid a string of problems, the company president is being driven to the brink.
en.notes: 土俵際 is literally the "edge of the sumo ring" (土俵 "ring" + 際 "edge"), where a wrestler is about to be pushed out: 土俵際で踏ん張る "to dig in at the edge of the ring". Figuratively it means "the last moment, on the verge of failure" and is popular in political and business news: 土俵際に追い込まれる "to be pushed into a corner". Similar is 瀬戸際 "on the brink of the abyss".

examples[].german: I recorded the measured values.
At the health checkup, my blood pressure reading was a little high.
The company announced numerical sales targets.
en.notes: 数値 is a concrete "numerical value, measured value", e.g. in measurements, examinations or statistics. Typical are 数値が高い/低い, 数値を測る/記録する, 数値目標 "quantitative target" and 数値化する "to express in numbers"; at a health checkup 検査の数値 means the "lab values". 数字, in contrast, is the digit or number in general, also in everyday use (数字に強い "good with numbers").

examples[].german: Getting that quiz answer right was just a fluke.
Winning once by a fluke doesn't mean it's real ability.
The answer I wrote at random turned out to be a lucky hit.
en.notes: まぐれ means "a lucky hit, a pure fluke" for a success that is not based on skill. It is almost always written in kana; the kanji 紛れ are normally read まぎれ (e.g. 腹立ち紛れ). Typical: ただのまぐれ, まぐれで勝つ, まぐれ当たり. For chance in the general sense one says 偶然; まぐれ is colloquial and always refers to lucky successes.

examples[].german: I called the police right after receiving a threatening phone call, but they didn't seem to want to deal with it.
The man was arrested on suspicion of threatening his former partner.
A threatening letter arrived at the company, and the event was cancelled.
en.notes: 脅迫 is threatening or coercing a person, also as a criminal offense: 〜を脅迫する, 脅迫状 "threatening letter", 脅迫電話 "threatening phone call", 脅迫罪. It is formal and legal; in everyday speech people say 脅す. Distinguish 恐喝 "extortion (for money)" and the identically pronounced 強迫 "compulsion" (強迫観念 "obsession").

examples[].german: If you don't keep your promises, nobody will take you seriously. Anyway, bring me that wizard you met the other day!
As a child, my dream was to become a wizard.
In this story, an evil wizard locks the princess in a tower.
en.notes: 魔法使い is a "wizard, magician", a person who commands real magic (魔法), as in fairy tales and fantasy. Witches are specifically 魔女. A stage magician, by contrast, is a 手品師 or マジシャン. The 使い comes from 使う "to use" and forms "someone who commands something", as in 猛獣使い "animal tamer".

en.meaning: bookkeeping entry; recording; signing the guest book
examples[].german: I was scolded by my boss because I forgot to make entries in the ledger.
I updated my passbook at the ATM to check whether my salary had come in.
Please sign in at the reception desk before entering the venue.
en.notes: 記帳 means "to enter something in a book" and has three typical uses: entering transactions in the account books (帳簿に記帳する), having account activity printed in the passbook (通帳に記帳する, at the ATM) and signing the guest book at occasions such as funerals or receptions (受付で記帳する). For "bookkeeping" as an activity, 簿記 or 経理 is more usual.

examples[].german: Sorry to interrupt, but I really want to ask you about your notepad.
When a good idea comes to me, I make a point of writing it in my notepad right away.
I drafted the email in Notepad on my computer.
en.notes: メモ帳 is a "notepad, memo book" for short notes: メモ帳に書く, メモ帳を持ち歩く. It is also the Japanese name of the Windows program "Notepad" and of note apps in general. A larger, bound notebook is more often ノート or 手帳 (pocket diary/planner); メモ alone is a single note.

examples[].german: I think it would be better to tidy up this phone book.
In the past, we used to look up shops' numbers in the telephone directory.
I deleted contacts I no longer use from my smartphone's phone book.
en.notes: 電話帳 is the printed "telephone directory" with names and numbers, e.g. 電話帳で調べる "to look up in the phone book". Today it often also means the contact list on a mobile phone (スマホの電話帳), also called 連絡先. The yellow pages were called タウンページ. The 帳 stands, as in 手帳 or 通帳, for a notebook for entries.

examples[].german: My shoulders were stiff, so I put on a pain-relief patch.
Please stick the stamp on the envelope.
en.notes: 貼る means to stick or attach something onto a surface. The object stands before を, the surface before に: 切手を封筒に貼る. It is a godan verb ending in る: 貼ります and 貼って. This spelling is especially suited to sticking something on; the related spelling 張る also appears in meanings such as stretching or setting up.

examples[].german: Why is it so amusing to you to humiliate me in front of everyone?
His conduct brings disgrace on the school's name.
An attitude that humiliates a defeated opponent is unacceptable for a sportsman.
en.notes: 辱める means "to humiliate, to dishonor, to bring shame upon" and is transitive: 人を辱める, 名誉を辱める, 家名を辱める. The word is written-language to elevated; in daily life one rather says 恥をかかせる "to embarrass someone". Often in the passive: 辱められる "to be humiliated". Note: in literature and news, 辱める is also a euphemism for sexual violence, so use it with care. Do not confuse with 恥じる "to be ashamed" (intransitive, one's own feeling).

examples[].german: Scolded in front of many people, he experienced great humiliation.
The players trained every day to wipe out the humiliation of last year's crushing defeat.
For him, there was no greater disgrace than being said to have betrayed his comrades.
en.notes: 恥辱 is a serious, publicly felt "disgrace, shame" and belongs to written language. Typical combinations: 恥辱を受ける, 恥辱を味わう, 恥辱に耐える, 恥辱を晴らす "to wipe out a disgrace". In daily life 恥 ("shame, embarrassment", 恥をかく) is enough. 屈辱 is the more common term for a "humiliation" suffered at the hands of others; 侮辱 is an active "insult".

examples[].german: The owner of that ramen shop always wore a faded cotton headband.
At the sports day, we split into red and white teams and wear headbands.
The exam takers tied on headbands reading 「必勝」 and tackled their last studying.
en.notes: 鉢巻 (usually written はちまき or 鉢巻き) is a cloth tied around the forehead. One says 鉢巻を締める or 鉢巻を巻く, in short also 鉢巻をする. It stands for determination: exam takers wear 必勝 headbands, at the school sports festival (運動会) there are red and white ones, craftsmen and cooks wear the twisted ねじり鉢巻. Note the verb: 締める (to tie, to tighten), not 絞める (to strangle).

examples[].german: This equation has three variables.
First, substitute 5 for the variable x.
I changed the variable names in the program to make them easier to understand.
en.notes: 変数 is the "variable" in mathematics, statistics and programming; the counterpart is 定数 "constant". Typical expressions are 変数に値を代入する "to assign / substitute a value to a variable" and, in programming, 変数を定義する/宣言する. In everyday speech, an unknown quantity is more often referred to as 未知数 ("still uncertain"); 変数 remains technical.

examples[].german: When fighting in the dark, it's best to see how your opponent moves and then decide what to do.
The power outage plunged the room into pitch darkness, and I looked for a flashlight.
As a child, I was afraid of the dark and slept with the light on.
en.notes: 暗闇 is concrete "darkness, the dark" as a place or state: 暗闇の中で, 暗闇に目が慣れる "eyes get used to the dark", 暗闇が怖い. Intensified: 真っ暗闇 "pitch dark". 闇 alone is more literary and often figurative (闇取引 "black-market dealing"), 暗さ denotes the degree of darkness. The corresponding adjective is 暗い.

examples[].german: I found a couple of coins that had fallen in the gap between the two vending machines.
Cold wind comes in through the gap in the window.
I memorize English words in my spare moments during the commute.
en.notes: 隙間 is a narrow "gap, crack, space" between two things: ドアの隙間, 〜と〜の隙間に, 隙間から光が漏れる. Compounds: 隙間風 "draft (through cracks)" and the modern 隙間時間 "small windows of free time". For an "opening, unguarded spot" one now rather uses 隙 alone (隙を見せる). 間 (あいだ) is more general "between", without the idea of a narrow gap.

examples[].german: I've been teaching myself Japanese for years, and now I'm hungry for Japanese conversation with someone.
During the war there was no food, and many people were starving.
That child may have been starved of parental affection.
en.notes: 飢える is intransitive and literally means "to starve, to suffer hunger" (飢えた子どもたち), which sounds rather written; for normal hunger one says お腹が空く. Very common is the figurative meaning with に: 愛情に飢える "to hunger for love", 知識に飢える, 刺激に飢える. The noun is 飢え (飢えに苦しむ), "to starve to death" is 飢え死にする or 餓死する.

examples[].german: The police believe the bedridden old man starved to death.
With days without rain continuing, many livestock starved to death.
"I'm hungry, I'm going to starve!" my younger brother shouted dramatically.
en.notes: 餓死 is "death by starvation"; as an intransitive する-verb 餓死する "to starve to death". The word sounds matter-of-fact to formal and is typical of news and reports (餓死者 "those who starved"). Colloquially one says 飢え死にする, and jokingly one likes to exaggerate with 餓死しそう "I'm about to starve". Cf. 飢える "to hunger" (without death).

examples[].german: This corn is livestock feed, not for human consumption.
In this region, livestock farming is the main industry.
My grandfather runs a livestock farm in Hokkaido.
en.notes: 畜産 refers to "animal husbandry" as an industry: keeping cattle, pigs and chickens to obtain meat, milk and eggs. Typical are 畜産業, 畜産農家, 畜産物 "animal products". Narrower terms: 酪農 "dairy farming", 養豚 "pig farming"; the animals themselves are 家畜. The tone is factual (business, government, school).

examples[].german: Are there any livestock unique to Japan?
The villagers make their living raising livestock such as cattle and pigs.
The dog is said to have been the first animal humans domesticated.
en.notes: 家畜 means "livestock, farm animals", animals that people keep for food or labor: 牛, 豚, 鶏, 馬. One says 家畜を飼う, 家畜の世話をする; 家畜化 is "domestication". Pets kept for pleasure are called ペット. The industry is 畜産. Figuratively 家畜 is pejorative ("treated like cattle", e.g. 社畜 "corporate drone").

examples[].german: You bastard! Why did you spill sriracha sauce all over my bed?!
Damn, I missed the last train again!
Damn it, I was one point away from passing.
en.notes: 畜生 is today mainly a coarse curse: "damn!, shoot!", usually written in kana as ちくしょう or, casually, ちきしょう. As an insult aimed at a person: この畜生め "you bastard". Originally it means "beast, animal" in the Buddhist sense (畜生道 "realm of animals"). The tone is rough and rather masculine; milder exclamations are くそ or しまった.

examples[].german: Thank you very much for your prompt and courteous handling of this matter.
Prompt provision of information is required during disasters.
We will ship the product you ordered promptly.
en.notes: 迅速 is a formal な-adjective for "rapid, swift, prompt", used above all in business language, government and news: 迅速な対応 "prompt handling", 迅速に処理する. The pairing 迅速かつ丁寧に "quickly and carefully" is typical. In everyday speech people say 速い or すぐ instead; 迅速 does not describe the speed of movements but quick action and response.

examples[].german: That jockey overslept on the day of his first G1 race.
Jockeys have to control their weight strictly.
The horse threw off its jockey and kept running on its own.
en.notes: 騎手 is a "rider", above all the professional jockey in horse racing (競馬). One says 騎手が乗る or 騎手を務める; a famous jockey is a 名騎手, a female jockey a 女性騎手. Someone who rides as a hobby does 乗馬; that person is then rather a 乗り手 and not a 騎手. The word is matter-of-fact and typical of sports reports.

examples[].german: Please draw the graph of this function.
Quadratic functions are learned in the ninth grade.
If you use an Excel function, you can get the total right away.
en.notes: 関数 is the mathematical "function" and, in programming or spreadsheets, a "function" as a calculation rule; formerly it was also written 函数. Typical are 一次関数 "linear function", 二次関数 "quadratic function" and 関数を呼び出す "to call a function". For "function" in the sense of a task or feature of a device, however, one says 機能 - a common mistake.

en.meaning: to run out; to be exhausted; to come to an end
examples[].german: The food stockpile finally ran out.
I had no end of things to talk about with a friend I hadn't seen in a long time.
The appeal of this restaurant comes down, above all, to how delicious the food is.
en.notes: 尽きる is intransitive: something "comes to an end, is exhausted": 食料が尽きる, 力が尽きる (力尽きる "to be at the end of one's strength"), 運が尽きる. In the negative it expresses abundance: 話が尽きない "there is no end to the conversation". With に, 〜に尽きる means "comes down to ..., nothing beats": この一言に尽きる. The transitive counterpart is 尽くす "to exhaust; to do one's utmost". In everyday speech, for supplies one often simply says なくなる or 切れる.

examples[].german: As president, I will do my utmost to improve our service.
Thanks to everyone's efforts, the event ended safely.
She has worked tirelessly for years for the education of local children.
en.notes: 尽力 is a formal する-verb: "to exert oneself with all one's strength" for something, usually for others or a cause: 〜に尽力する, 〜のために尽力する. Very common in thanks formulas: ご尽力いただき、ありがとうございます. Unlike 努力 ("to make an effort", often for one's own goals), 尽力 emphasizes service to a cause or to others; 協力 is "cooperation, assistance". Typical for speeches, business letters and news.

examples[].german: The teacher concluded that the student had a keen sense of color.
This painter's works are known for their bright, rich colors.
The demonstration had a strong political coloring.
en.notes: 色彩 is a refined, rather technical word for "color, coloring" as a whole, especially in art, design and description: 色彩豊か, 鮮やかな色彩, 色彩感覚 "sense of color". For a single color in everyday speech, one says 色. Figuratively 色彩 means "tinge, character": 政治的な色彩が強い.

examples[].german: I went to buy camouflage pants today, but couldn't find a single pair.
The soldiers were hiding in the forest in camouflage uniforms.
This vehicle is painted in camouflage so as not to stand out in the desert.
en.notes: 迷彩 is "camouflage" by color patterns, especially in the military: 迷彩服 "camouflage uniform", 迷彩を施す. In fashion, 迷彩柄 "camouflage pattern" is very common. For animals that adapt their color, one rather says 保護色 or 擬態; disguising a person is 変装.

examples[].german: I hear she is a wonderful watercolor painter.
On days off, I paint watercolors in a nearby park.
An exhibition of Meiji-era watercolors is being held at the art museum.
en.notes: 水彩画 is a "watercolor", a picture painted with watercolors; the verb is 描く (かく or えがく): 水彩画を描く. 水彩 alone denotes the technique or medium (水彩絵の具 "watercolor paints"), a 水彩画家 is a watercolor painter. The counterpart is 油絵 or, more formally, 油彩画 "oil painting".

examples[].german: I've gotten the knack of oil painting.
This work is painted in oil on canvas.
At art university, you study both watercolor and oil in the first year.
en.notes: 油彩 is the art-technical term for "oil painting" or oil paint as a technique; a single picture is a 油彩画. In daily life one says 油絵 far more often; the paints are 油絵の具. In catalogs and picture descriptions, キャンバスに油彩 "oil on canvas" typically appears. Counterpart: 水彩 "watercolor".

examples[].german: People speculate that the match was fixed.
Please stop speaking based on speculation.
The president's sudden resignation gave rise to various speculations.
en.notes: 憶測 (also 臆測) is a "conjecture, speculation" without secure basis and often sounds critical. Typical: 憶測を呼ぶ "to give rise to speculation", 憶測が飛び交う "speculation is flying around", 憶測で物を言う "to assert things at random"; as a verb 〜と憶測する. By contrast, 推測 is a reasoned "inference", 予想 a "forecast".

examples[].german: I read that water-soluble vitamin C is quickly excreted from the body, so our bodies can't store it.
Vitamin A is fat-soluble, but vitamin B is water-soluble.
This pen uses water-soluble ink, so it comes off easily with water.
en.notes: 水溶性 means "water-soluble" and is a technical word from chemistry, nutrition and product descriptions. It takes の before nouns (水溶性のビタミン) or stands directly in a compound: 水溶性食物繊維, 水溶性塗料. Opposites are 脂溶性 "fat-soluble" and 不溶性 "insoluble". The suffix 〜性 forms property words like 安全性 or 可能性.

examples[].german: This firefighter doll actually wears fire-resistant clothes and gloves.
I keep important documents in a fireproof safe.
This building has a fire-resistant structure, so fire is unlikely to spread even if one breaks out.
en.notes: 耐火 means "fireproof, fire-resistant" and almost always stands as the first element of compounds or with の: 耐火性 "fire resistance", 耐火金庫, 耐火構造, 耐火レンガ. To distinguish: 防火 "fire prevention" (防火扉), 耐熱 "heat-resistant" (e.g. tableware), 不燃 "non-combustible". The word is technical and matter-of-fact.

examples[].german: I learned how to solve quadratic equations.
Read the word problem and first try setting up an equation.
Scoring early and holding on to the lead is this team's winning formula.
en.notes: 方程式 is the mathematical "equation" with unknowns; typical verbs are 方程式を解く "to solve" and 方程式を立てる "to set up". Well-known types are 一次方程式 "linear equation", 二次方程式 "quadratic equation" and 連立方程式 "system of equations". Figuratively it means a proven "recipe for success", especially in sports: 勝利の方程式 "winning formula".

examples[].german: All the fish in the sea started dancing at once to the sound of the drum.
At the festival, we all danced the Bon dance together.
At the party, we danced to the music until morning.
en.notes: 踊る means "to dance" and is intransitive; however, the dance can appear as an object with を: 盆踊りを踊る, ワルツを踊る. To dance to music is 音楽に合わせて踊る. The noun 踊り tends to mean traditional dance, ダンス modern dance; ダンスをする is a synonym. The identically read 躍る appears in 胸が躍る "one's heart leaps with joy".

examples[].german: Chris? I passed him on the stair landing just now.
A flowerpot is placed on the stair landing.
The economy is said to have been in a plateau for the past few months.
en.notes: 踊り場 is mainly the "stair landing" today: 階段の踊り場で. The literal meaning "dance floor" is obsolete (one says ダンスフロア for that). In economic news, 踊り場 figuratively denotes a "phase of stagnation" after an upswing: 景気が踊り場にある "the economy is treading water".

examples[].german: I'm not especially smart, but when it counts, I'll show you I can do it properly.
Our dog is very clever and has learned a lot of words.
Buying in bulk during a sale is the smart way to shop.
en.notes: 賢い means "clever, bright, wise" and often praises practical cleverness as well: 賢い選択, 賢い買い物. For animals and children it also means "well-behaved, good" (especially Kansai: 賢くしてなさい). 頭がいい is the most neutral word for intelligence, 利口 is similar (お利口さん "good child"), while ずる賢い means "cunning". It conjugates as an い-adjective: 賢くない, 賢かった.

examples[].german: The sages of ancient Greece thought deeply about how people should live.
The saying 「急がば回れ」 is packed with the wisdom of sages of old.
Experts called "sages" were gathered from each country to discuss the world's problems.
en.notes: 賢人 is a "sage", a person of great wisdom and virtue. The word is elevated and appears mainly in history, philosophy and fixed expressions like 古代ギリシャの賢人, 七賢人 or 賢人会議 "council of sages". In daily life one rather says 賢い人 or 知恵のある人; 賢者 means the same but appears mainly in fantasy and games.

examples[].german: Our school has a history of a hundred glorious years.
The stars in the night sky gave off a quiet brilliance.
To uphold the team's glorious tradition, the players fought desperately.
en.notes: 光輝 is a very elevated, written-language word for "brilliance, radiance" and, figuratively, "glory". It appears almost only in set phrases: 光輝ある歴史 "glorious history", 光輝ある伝統, 光輝を放つ "to radiate brilliance". In daily life one says 輝き or 光. Do not confuse with the verb 光り輝く "to shine brightly".

examples[].german: For example, the luminance value of the sun is very high.
Lowering the screen brightness makes the battery last longer.
This monitor has high brightness, so it is easy to see even in a bright room.
en.notes: 輝度 is a technical term from physics and engineering: "luminance", i.e. how brightly a surface or light source shines. In daily life it is mostly encountered with screens: 画面の輝度を上げる／下げる, 高輝度LED. Colloquially one says 明るさ. To distinguish: 照度 "illuminance" (light falling on a surface) and 明度 "lightness of a color".

examples[].german: The use of cannabis is prohibited in this country.
A famous actor was arrested on suspicion of possessing cannabis.
In old Japan, cloth and rope were made from cannabis fibers.
en.notes: 大麻 denotes both the plant "hemp" (fibers for ropes and fabrics) and the drug "cannabis, marijuana". In Japan, possession is strictly prohibited, so the word often appears in the news: 大麻を所持する, 大麻取締法. Colloquially also マリファナ. The hemp fiber is technically also called 麻; the meaning "Shinto offering" is rare.

examples[].german: The room was lit only by the light of a small candle.
Please turn off the hallway light before you go to bed.
From the hilltop, the lights of the distant town looked beautiful.
en.notes: 灯り (also written 明かり) is the "light" of a lamp or candle, that is, a light source that you turn on: 灯りをつける／消す, 灯りがともる, 町の灯り "the lights of the town". The spelling 灯り emphasizes the lamp, 明かり rather the brightness (月明かり "moonlight"). 光 is "light" in the physical sense in general; in everyday life, for room lighting one often simply says 電気 (電気を消す).

examples[].german: Large numbers of moths are flying around each streetlight.
This road has few streetlights, and it's scary to walk alone at night.
When dusk fell, the streetlights along the street came on all at once.
en.notes: 街灯 is the "streetlight" along public roads: 街灯がつく／ともる, 街灯の下で, 街灯が少ない道. Pronounced the same but meant differently is 外灯 "outdoor light" on a house or building. 電灯 is generally "electric light", 信号 the "traffic light".

examples[].german: My wife never turns off the lights. I bet she doesn't even know there's a switch.
All the lights went out because of the power outage.
I bought a flashlight in advance in case of an earthquake.
en.notes: 電灯 is the electric light or lamp; the word sounds somewhat matter-of-fact to old-fashioned. In everyday speech one mostly says 電気: 電気をつける/消す, or 明かり, ライト. The compound 懐中電灯 "flashlight" is very common, and a street lamp is called 街灯.

examples[].german: Because winter dragged on, the cherry tree in our garden bloomed late this year.
This park also has late-blooming cherry varieties, so you can enjoy hanami until the end of April.
He is a late-blooming novelist who debuted at the age of forty.
en.notes: 遅咲き first means "blooming late", mostly with の: 遅咲きの桜, 遅咲きの品種. Figuratively it denotes people who succeed only late: 遅咲きの俳優, 遅咲きの才能 "late bloomer". The opposite is 早咲き. For the idea "great talents mature late" there is the proverb 大器晩成.

examples[].german: The former champion returned to the throne after three years.
The return of the lawmaker who lost in the last election has been decided.
Warm days continued, and azaleas were seen blooming again in autumn.
en.notes: 返り咲き is the noun of the verb 返り咲く and means a "return" to a former top position: 王座に返り咲く, 首位に返り咲く, 政権に返り咲く. It presupposes that one held that position before; a comeback in a game is 逆転. カムバック and 復帰 ("return after a break") are similar. Literally, 返り咲き also denotes the "second blooming" of a plant in the same season.

examples[].german: Ouch. Where are you looking? Don't walk while looking away!
The cause of the accident was the driver's inattention.
While I looked away for a moment, I lost sight of the child.
en.notes: 脇見 means "to look to the side, to avert one's gaze", mostly in the sense of inattention. The most important expression is 脇見運転 "distracted driving", a frequent accident cause in police reports. As an intransitive する-verb: 脇見しながら歩く. Equivalent in meaning, but more everyday and common especially toward children, is よそ見.

examples[].german: She keeps telling everyone she passed the audition, but it seems to be just a supporting role.
That actor shines more in supporting roles than in leads.
In this project, I intend to stick to a supporting role and back up the younger staff.
en.notes: 脇役 is the "supporting role" in film, theater or drama; the opposite is 主役 "lead role". One says 脇役を演じる, 脇役を務める. A very small part is 端役, extras are エキストラ. Figuratively, 脇役に徹する means "to deliberately stay in the background and support others".

examples[].german: The man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
The bank robbery ended in failure after the robber was noticed by a security guard.
In an interview, she said she had attempted suicide when she was young.
en.notes: 未遂 denotes an "attempted, uncompleted act", mostly a crime or suicide. It often appears as a suffix: 殺人未遂, 強盗未遂, 自殺未遂; the set phrase 未遂に終わる means "to remain at the attempt stage, to fail". In law the opposite is 既遂 "completed". For a general "attempt" in daily life, one says 試み or やってみること, not 未遂.

examples[].german: He is sociable and liked by everyone, so he was chosen as group leader.
In elementary school, we chose a group leader for each school lunch group.
As a factory team leader, I lead ten workers.
en.notes: 班長 is the "leader" of a 班, a small group: in Japanese schools the class groups (cleaning, lunch or project groups), in factories a work group, in the military or police a squad. One says 班長に選ばれる, 班長を務める. In offices, titles like 係長 or 主任 correspond; generally and in modern usage one often says リーダー.

examples[].german: Yesterday I spent the whole day applying plaster to the dry-construction wall.
Apply an appropriate amount to the affected area several times a day.
To prevent rust, a special oil is applied to the surface of the parts.
en.notes: 塗布 is a technical する-verb for "applying" an ointment, liquid or coating: 患部に塗布する, 表面に塗布する. It is found on package inserts, in instructions for use and in engineering (塗布剤). In daily life one simply says 塗る (薬を塗る, ペンキを塗る). Construction: 物を場所に塗布する.

examples[].german: I'm really sorry for being late. The painting of the bathroom wall took longer than expected.
The paint on the car has started to peel in places.
Next month, work to paint the exterior wall of the apartment building will begin.
en.notes: 塗装 is the "painting, lacquering" of surfaces such as walls, cars or buildings, and also the resulting layer of paint: 塗装がはげる "the paint peels off", 塗装工事, 再塗装. As a transitive する-verb: 壁を塗装する. It has nothing to do with painting in the artistic sense (絵を描く). In daily life one also says ペンキを塗る.

examples[].german: I dipped the brush in fluorescent paint.
This paint is water-based, so it has little odor and is easy to use indoors.
Please don't touch the door until the paint dries.
en.notes: 塗料 is the umbrella term for "paint, lacquer, coating material", i.e. paint for coating surfaces: 水性塗料, 油性塗料, 蛍光塗料, 塗料を塗る. In daily life, wall paint is often called ペンキ; paints for pictures are 絵の具. Color as a hue is 色.

examples[].german: I told you to draw a horizontal line, but it's a little slanted.
If you cut vegetables diagonally, the heat penetrates more easily.
The station is diagonally across from this intersection.
en.notes: 斜め means "slanted, diagonal, oblique" and is used as a noun, with の, or as an adverb with に: 斜めになる, 斜めに切る, 斜めの線. Location expressions: 斜め前, 斜め後ろ, 斜め向かい "diagonally opposite". Figuratively: ご機嫌斜め "in a bad mood", 斜めに構える "to take a cynical attitude", 斜め読み "skimming".

examples[].german: If you use this formula, you can calculate easily.
Please check the official website for detailed information.
The government has not yet announced it officially.
en.notes: 公式 has two important meanings: in mathematics and natural science the "formula" (公式を覚える/使う/当てはめる), and in everyday life "official" as a の-adjective, adverb with に or in compounds: 公式サイト "official website", 公式発表 "official announcement", 公式に認める. Today 公式 alone often also means a company's official social media account. Close in meaning is 正式 "formal, proper" (正式な契約); 公式 stresses the public, official side.

examples[].german: Our private road is a steep slope, so you need snow tires to get up to the top.
Tea fields spread across the entire mountain slope.
After the heavy rain, the slope collapsed and blocked the road.
en.notes: 斜面 is a "slanting surface, slope": 山の斜面, 急な斜面 (急斜面), 斜面を登る, 斜面が崩れる "a slope gives way". It describes the surface itself in a rather factual, geographical way. For a rising road or path, one says 坂 or 坂道; 傾斜 is the "incline", i.e. the degree of slant.

examples[].german: Why did you change the font of this word to italics?
Book titles are generally written in italics.
Please make the parts you want to emphasize bold or italic.
en.notes: 斜体 is "italic type" in typography: 斜体にする, 斜体で書く, 斜体の文字. Equivalent in meaning and very common in computer use is イタリック（体）. Related terms: 太字 "bold type", 下線 "underline". In mathematics, 斜体 also denotes a "skew field".

examples[].german: The moment the gong rang, the boxer punched his opponent in the jaw with all his might.
I was suddenly hit by a drunk and got injured.
After an argument, the two ended up in a fistfight.
en.notes: 殴る means "to hit (hard), to beat up", usually with a fist or an object: 人を殴る, 顔を殴る; passive 殴られる. Compounds: 殴り合い "brawl", 殴りかかる "to lash out at someone", 殴り付ける "to strike violently". 叩く is more neutral ("to knock, to hit, to clap", also drumming), ぶつ is colloquial, and 打つ is more "to hit" (a ball, a nail).

examples[].german: Suddenly, an unknown man struck me on the back of the head from behind.
The man was arrested on suspicion of beating a store clerk with a stick.
Marks of a heavy blow remained on the victim's head.
en.notes: 殴打 is the formal, legal-factual word for "hitting, beating" and appears mainly in news, police reports and court documents: 頭部を殴打する, 殴打される, 殴打事件. In conversation one uses 殴る instead. As a transitive する-verb: 人を棒で殴打する.

examples[].german: I was encouraged by my friend's support.
He was able to become president at a young age because he had a powerful backer.
That small country continues its assertive diplomacy with a major power as its backer.
en.notes: 後ろ盾 is literally the "shield at one's back" and denotes an influential "supporter, backing, patron": 〜の後ろ盾がある, 〜を後ろ盾にする, 〜の後ろ盾となる. It is mostly about power, money or influence (politics, companies, diplomacy). Emotional support in daily life is rather 支え or 応援; 味方 is an "ally".

en.meaning: to spill; to overflow; to fall out
examples[].german: I put too much water in the glass, and it spilled onto the table.
In the last scene of the movie, tears spilled out involuntarily.
Seeing a photo of her grandchild, a smile spread across the grandmother's face.
en.notes: 零れる is mostly written in kana (こぼれる) and is intransitive: liquid or grains "overflow, fall out, are spilled": 水がこぼれる, ご飯がこぼれる. The transitive counterpart is こぼす "to spill" (お茶をこぼす), which can also mean "to complain, to grumble" (愚痴をこぼす). Figuratively: 涙がこぼれる "tears well up", 笑みがこぼれる "a smile crosses one's face", 光がこぼれる "light filters through".

examples[].german: Oh, I'm out of staples.
Please staple the meeting materials at the top left.
The stack of documents was too thick, and the stapler wouldn't go through.
en.notes: ホッチキス (also ホチキス) is the common name for the "stapler" and goes back to a brand name; commercially it is officially called ステープラー. The staples are called ホッチキスの針 or 芯. Typical: ホッチキスで留める "to staple together", 針が切れる "to run out of staples".

examples[].german: Do you know how much the value of money has changed since then?
One ryo in the Edo period is said to be worth about 100,000 yen in today's money.
As inflation advances, the value of money falls.
en.notes: 貨幣価値 is the "value of money" in the sense of the purchasing power of money at a given time. It is typical when comparing prices across eras: 今の貨幣価値で, 当時の貨幣価値に換算すると. In economics: インフレで貨幣価値が下がる. Distinguish it from 為替レート "exchange rate" and 物価 "price level".

examples[].german: I read the manual, but it was so unclear that I'm a little worried about the new model's real capabilities.
The voice on the phone was indistinct, and I couldn't make out what was being said.
An audit was carried out on the grounds that there were unclear points in the accounts.
en.notes: 不明瞭 is a formal な-adjective for "indistinct, unclear, opaque": 不明瞭な発音, 説明が不明瞭だ, 会計が不明瞭 "opaque bookkeeping", 責任の所在が不明瞭. Opposite: 明瞭. In everyday speech people tend to say はっきりしない or 曖昧; 不明, by contrast, means "unknown" (原因不明).

examples[].german: I used to think that if I worked hard and persistently, I would be rewarded someday, but I was wrong.
This rice is sticky and very tasty.
The losing team showed tenacity at the end and caught up to tie the game.
en.notes: 粘り has two meanings: concretely "stickiness, viscosity" of foods or materials (納豆の粘り, 粘りのある米), and figuratively "staying power, tenacity" (粘りを見せる, 最後まで粘りを発揮する). It is the noun of the verb 粘る "to be sticky; to refuse to give up". The adjective 粘り強い "persistent" is very common. Similar: 根気 "patience", 忍耐 "endurance".

examples[].german: The capitalist economic system spread across the world.
In capitalist societies, the gap between rich and poor is said to widen easily.
In class we debated the differences between capitalism and socialism.
en.notes: 資本主義 is capitalism, i.e. an economic order based on private ownership of capital (資本) and market competition. Typical: 資本主義社会, 資本主義経済, 資本主義国. Related are 資本家 ("capitalist") and 資本金 ("capital stock"). Opposites are 共産主義 and 社会主義. The word belongs to the language of economics, history and news.

examples[].german: The magnet's magnetic force attracts iron.
This magnet has strong magnetic force, so be careful not to pinch your fingers.
The maglev train uses magnetic force to float and run.
en.notes: 磁力 is the "magnetic force" with which a 磁石 "magnet" attracts iron or repels other magnets. Typical are 磁力が強い/弱い, 磁力で引き寄せる/くっつく and 磁力線 "magnetic field lines". The magnetic field as a space is called 磁場 or 磁界, magnetism as a property 磁気 (磁気カード "magnetic card").

examples[].german: I was scolded by Grandma for lying.
In summer vacation, I'm going to visit my grandma's house in the countryside.
On the train, I gave my seat to an old lady carrying baggage.
en.notes: おばあちゃん (kanji 婆 rare) is the familiar form of address and term for "grandma", but also for older women in general. When talking to outsiders about one's own grandmother, 祖母 is more polite; おばあさん is more neutral. Addressing unfamiliar older women this way can seem condescending. Watch the vowel length: おばさん (short a) is "aunt, middle-aged woman".

examples[].german: Candidate Koichi was irritatingly calm before the presidential debate.
My little brother is always saying nasty things and getting on my nerves.
"Honestly, you're impossible," she said, laughing.
en.notes: 憎らしい describes a person or thing that provokes annoyance and dislike: "detestable, hateful, provoking". It is often weaker than "hateful": 憎らしいことを言う "to say nasty things", 憎らしいほど上手い "annoyingly good". Between close friends it can be teasing and affectionate (憎らしい人). The stronger 憎い expresses real hatred, whereas 心憎い means "admirably clever".

examples[].german: I was sure they hated each other.
He harbors intense hatred toward the criminal who took away his family.
War only breeds new hatred.
en.notes: 憎しみ is the noun of 憎む "to hate" and denotes deep "hatred": 憎しみを抱く, 憎しみが募る "hatred grows", 憎しみの連鎖 "cycle of hatred". The compound verb 憎しみ合う means "to hate each other". 恨み, by contrast, is a "grudge" over wrongs suffered; 嫌い is mere dislike.

examples[].german: It is the first time in my life that I have hated someone this much.
Even adding a handwritten letter to the gift - what an admirably thoughtful gesture!
en.notes: 憎い describes strong aversion to a person or thing. As an i-adjective it can stand directly before a noun or be completed with と: 憎いと思う. Used approvingly it also means "admirable", as if the skill were almost annoyingly good; context decides between praise and dislike. The unusual spelling 悪い with the reading にくい is attested in dictionaries. Ordinary 悪い "bad" is read わるい; for this card 憎い is the clear spelling. The suffix にくい "hard to do" is a different usage.

examples[].german: The concert tickets were by lottery, and I finally won after applying three times.
We will notify you of the drawing results by email next week.
Because there were so many applicants, it was decided that participants would be chosen by lottery.
en.notes: 抽選 is a "lottery, drawing"; as a する-verb "to draw lots". Typical: 抽選で当たる／外れる, 抽選に当たる, 抽選で決める, 抽選会. In Japan, sought-after concert tickets or apartments are often allocated by 抽選. More everyday are くじ and くじ引き "drawing lots"; 宝くじ is the "lottery" with purchased tickets.

examples[].german: While saying my wedding vows, I knew I was about to marry the wrong man.
He swore an oath never to drink alcohol again.
You cannot trust someone who breaks an oath once sworn so easily.
en.notes: 誓い is the noun of 誓う "to swear" and denotes a solemn oath or vow, often made to oneself, to God, or to a partner. Typical combinations: 誓いを立てる "to take an oath", 誓いを守る "to keep an oath", 誓いを破る "to break an oath", 結婚の誓い "wedding vow". An everyday promise is 約束; 誓い sounds much more solemn and serious. The formal, legal pledge is called 誓約.

examples[].german: This is the written pledge. You need to sign here and here.
When joining the company, I pledged not to leak company information to outsiders.
The athletes pledged to abide by the rules of the tournament.
en.notes: 誓約 is a formal, often legally binding pledge or declaration of commitment. It appears most often in 誓約書 "written pledge", which one signs when joining a company, signing a lease, or taking an exam. As a する-verb it is transitive with を, mostly in ～ことを誓約する "to pledge to do ...". Compared with the personal 誓い and the everyday 約束, 誓約 sounds official and literary.

examples[].german: The field may differ, but in terms of developing new markets, it's not much different from my previous job.
In the Meiji period, many people took part in the settlement of Hokkaido.
The sales department is focusing on cultivating new customers.
en.notes: 開拓 originally means "to clear and open up land" (荒れ地を開拓する, e.g. the settlement of Hokkaido). Today it is often used figuratively: 新しい市場を開拓する "to open up a new market", 顧客を開拓する "to win new customers". It is a transitive する-verb with を; 開拓者 "pioneer" is derived from it. Compared with 開発 (development of products or areas), 開拓 emphasizes stepping into uncharted territory.

examples[].german: The suspect is to be held at the Tokyo Detention House until the trial ends.
In Japan, prisoners sentenced to death are held in detention houses, not in prisons.
Long-term detention is criticized as a human rights issue.
en.notes: 拘置 is a legal term for holding suspects, defendants, or prisoners sentenced to death in a custodial facility, typically a 拘置所 "detention house". In the news it mostly appears in the passive: 拘置される "to be held in custody". The arrest itself is 逮捕, and actual prison sentences are served in a 刑務所. For police taking drunks or animals into protective care, one says 保護, not 拘置.

examples[].german: Yesterday was my fault. I'm really sorry. To make up for it, I'll cut the grass today.
The neighborhood people got together and cut the grass along the river.
With a brush cutter, even a large field is done in an hour.
en.notes: 草刈り means cutting grass and weeds, for example with a sickle (鎌) or a brush cutter (草刈り機), along roadsides, in fields, or in a garden; one says 草刈りをする. Neat lawn mowing, by contrast, is 芝刈り (lawn mower: 芝刈り機). Pulling weeds out by hand is 草取り or 草むしり. In residential neighborhoods, communal 草刈り is often a shared duty.

examples[].german: My parents are farmers who grow rice, so I have to help with the rice harvest this weekend.
I cut down the overgrown weeds with a sickle.
Before the problem grows bigger, one should nip evil in the bud early.
en.notes: 刈り取る is transitive and means "to mow, cut off, harvest": 稲を刈り取る "to harvest rice", 草を刈り取る "to mow grass". Compared with the simple 刈る, it stresses that something is cut off completely and removed; the noun is 刈り取り (稲の刈り取り). Figuratively one says 悪の芽を刈り取る "to nip evil in the bud". For harvesting fruit or vegetables, 収穫する or 取る is more usual.

examples[].german: He looks like a strong warrior of old, but he screamed when I accidentally pressed a blood blister on his foot.
Our school's motto is "simple and sturdy".
His handwriting is bold and forceful, just like his character.
en.notes: 剛健 is a literary word for strength and fortitude of body and spirit, with a touch of masculine austerity. Best known is the four-character expression 質実剛健 "simple, earnest, and robust", a popular school motto. As a な-adjective: 剛健な精神, 剛健な気風. For sturdy objects one says 頑丈, and for healthy and resilient people 丈夫 or 強健.

examples[].german: He is the only decent person in his family.
Reading is my only hobby.
The only way to get to this island is by boat.
en.notes: 唯一 means "only, sole" and stresses that there is exactly one. It takes の before nouns (唯一の趣味, 唯一の方法) or is used adverbially without a particle (唯一まともな人). Compared with ただ一つ or たった一つ, 唯一 sounds somewhat more refined. The reading is ゆいいつ, not ゆういつ. Intensified, 唯一無二 means "one of a kind, unparalleled".

examples[].german: I can't even explain materialism in my native language, so how could I explain it in a foreign language?
Marx's thought is based on materialism.
From a materialist standpoint, the mind too is merely a function of the brain.
en.notes: 唯物論 is philosophical materialism: the doctrine that everything is reducible to matter. Its opposite is 唯心論 "idealism"; well known are マルクスの唯物論 and 史的唯物論 "historical materialism", and an adherent is called 唯物論者. Materialism in the everyday sense of consumerism and a focus on possessions is 物質主義, not 唯物論. The word belongs to philosophical and academic contexts.

examples[].german: Whenever I see that flower bed, I always think of my mother.
Tulips were planted in the flower bed in front of the station.
Please do not enter the flower bed.
en.notes: 花壇 is a laid-out flower bed in gardens, parks, in front of schools or stations. One says 花壇に花を植える "to plant flowers in the bed" and 花壇の手入れをする "to tend the bed"; on signs you read 花壇に入らないでください. A vegetable bed is not a 花壇 but 畑 or 菜園; a large natural field of flowers is 花畑. For planters, one says プランター or 植木鉢.

examples[].german: That nun's face is always puffy when she wakes up.
At a convent in Kyoto, several nuns still continue their religious training.
She renounced the world at forty and became a nun.
en.notes: 尼僧 is the literary word for a Buddhist nun; in conversation 尼さん is more common. It can also refer to a Catholic nun, but 修道女 or シスター is more usual for that. A woman becomes a nun with 出家して尼僧になる; a nunnery is an 尼寺. The male counterpart is 僧 or 僧侶, colloquially お坊さん.

examples[].german: Some say shoplifters are mostly bored, lonely women, but a certain survey reportedly suggests men may shoplift more often than women.
On Sundays I mostly relax at home.
Enough with the jokes already.
en.notes: 大概 is used mainly as an adverb meaning "mostly, as a rule", being almost synonymous with 大抵 (たいてい) but sounding somewhat more colloquial. With の it stands before nouns: 大概の人 "most people". The phrase ～も大概にしろ "don't overdo ..." is important, e.g. 冗談も大概にしろ. Colloquially, あいつも大概だ means "that guy is pretty bad too".

examples[].german: Goldfish are freshwater fish, so you must not put salt in the tank.
The water of this lake is not fresh water but contains a little salt.
Only about three percent of the water on Earth is fresh water.
en.notes: 淡水 is the technical term for "fresh water", as opposed to 海水 "seawater"; in between lies 汽水 "brackish water". It is common in compounds: 淡水魚 "freshwater fish", 淡水湖 "freshwater lake". In everyday speech, non-salty water is more often called 真水 (まみず). Water that tastes "sweet" would instead be 甘い水.

examples[].german: The New Year's mochi soup should be about done cooking by now.
On New Year's morning, the whole family eats ozoni together.
How ozoni tastes is completely different from region to region.
en.notes: 雑煮 is the soup with mochi and vegetables that is traditionally eaten during the first days of the New Year, usually together with おせち料理. In daily speech people almost always say the polite お雑煮. Preparation varies greatly by region: in the Kantō area it is more often a clear broth with grilled square mochi, in the Kansai area often white miso with round mochi. Servings are counted with 杯.

examples[].german: The masked hero wore a tattered cape.
A masked man broke into the bank.
I was caught for speeding on the expressway by an unmarked police car.
en.notes: 覆面 is a mask or cloth that covers the face, as worn by robbers or wrestlers (覆面レスラー); one says 覆面をする or 覆面をかぶる. A surgical or face mask is マスク, a theater or carnival mask 仮面. In its second sense, 覆面〜 means "disguised, anonymous": 覆面パトカー "unmarked police car", 覆面調査 "mystery shopping", 覆面作家 "anonymous author".

examples[].german: This factory consumes a large amount of electric power.
In summer, power shortages are feared because of air-conditioner use.
This refrigerator consumes little power.
en.notes: 電力 is "electric energy, electricity" in the sense of supply and consumption, and in physics also the "electric power" in watts. Typical are 電力を消費する/供給する, 電力不足 "power shortage", 電力会社 "power company" and 消費電力 "power consumption" of a device. In everyday speech one mostly says simply 電気 for electricity (電気代 "electricity bill", 電気をつける); 電力 sounds more technical and belongs in news and business.

examples[].german: I broke out in a cold sweat when my canoe capsized in a swamp full of crocodiles.
A fishing boat capsized in strong winds, and three crew members were rescued.
They were arrested on suspicion of plotting to overthrow the government.
en.notes: 転覆 means "capsizing, overturning" of ships or vehicles, and is then intransitive: 船が転覆する, 列車が転覆する. Figuratively it is the "overthrow" of a government: 政府を転覆する, 政権の転覆を図る. The word is rather literary and typical of the news; in daily life one says ひっくり返る. It should be distinguished from 沈没 "sinking" and 脱線 "derailment".

en.meaning: to plot (evil); to scheme; to trick
examples[].german: Those guys are plotting a dramatic assassination in front of Michelangelo's David in Florence.
His subordinates secretly plotted the king's assassination.
Damn, I've been tricked!
en.notes: 謀る (はかる) means "to plan something evil, to scheme", e.g. 暗殺を謀る "to plot an assassination" or 謀反を謀る "to plot a rebellion"; in the passive, 謀られた means "I was tricked". The word is literary or sounds like a historical drama; in everyday speech people say 企む (たくらむ) instead. Do not confuse it with the identically read 図る "to aim at, attempt" (解決を図る) and 計る／測る／量る "to measure".

examples[].german: Could you stop my daughter? She is recklessly trying to do spy work.
Climbing a mountain in a storm like this is reckless.
I was told that starting a business without preparation is a reckless challenge.
en.notes: 無謀 describes an undertaking made without thought or regard for risk: "reckless, rash, ill-considered". Typical are 無謀な計画, 無謀な挑戦, 無謀運転 as well as 無謀にも～ "recklessly ...". Colloquially one often says 無茶; 軽率 refers more to thoughtless behavior in small matters. 大胆 "bold" is positive, whereas 無謀 is clearly critical.

examples[].german: He believes in a conspiracy theory that a secret society controls the world.
The minister was framed by a rival's plot and forced to resign.
The king's younger brother was plotting to seize the throne.
en.notes: 陰謀 is a secret intrigue or conspiracy with evil intent. Typical: 陰謀を企てる "to hatch a plot", 陰謀にはめられる "to be framed by a plot", 陰謀に巻き込まれる, 陰謀論 "conspiracy theory". Neutral planning is 計画; 策略 is a stratagem, 謀略 more of a political or military intrigue. The word is neutral to literary and frequent in politics and crime stories.

examples[].german: This anime airs every other week, and I like its opening and ending songs.
Recyclable waste is collected every other Wednesday.
My father goes to the hospital every other week.
en.notes: 隔週 means "every second week, every two weeks". It is used adverbially with で (隔週で開かれる) or without a particle before weekdays (隔週土曜日 "every second Saturday"), and attributively with の (隔週の会議). Colloquially one also says 一週おきに or 二週間に一回. Do not confuse it with 毎週 "every week" and 隔月 "every other month".

examples[].german: Contractions about as strong as period cramps started at intervals of 15 to 20 minutes, so I called the hospital to ask whether I should go now.
This bus runs at 15-minute intervals.
Please plant the seedlings 30 centimeters apart.
en.notes: 間隔 denotes the "interval" or "gap" between two things, in space or in time. Typical: 間隔をあける "to leave a gap", 一定の間隔で "at regular intervals", 15分間隔で "every 15 minutes" (for buses, for example). Compared with 距離 "distance", 間隔 stresses the space between recurring events or elements in a series. Do not confuse it with the identically read 感覚 "feeling, sense".

examples[].german: We have a Japanese culture class every other month, and this month we plan to pound mochi.
This magazine is published every other month.
Water bills are charged every other month.
en.notes: 隔月 means "every other month, every two months" and is used like 隔週: adverbially with で (隔月で発行される), attributively with の (隔月の会合). For magazines, a bimonthly issue is called 隔月刊. Colloquially one says 二か月に一回 or 一か月おき. In Japan, water bills, for example, are often issued 隔月.

examples[].german: In my apartment, the bathtub and the washroom are separated by just a single shower curtain.
There is a post office across the road.
The two met again after twenty years.
en.notes: 隔てる is transitive and means "to separate, partition off, have something in between": AとBを隔てる, 壁で隔てる. The て-form with space or time is very common: 道を隔てて "across the street", 十年の時を隔てて "after ten years". Its intransitive counterpart is 隔たる (二人の意見は大きく隔たっている), with the noun 隔たり "distance, gap". Compared with 分ける or 仕切る, 隔てる sounds a bit more literary and stresses the distance.

examples[].german: Due to the spread of swine flu, the expedition was canceled.
The team plans to travel to Europe for away games next month.
To see my favorite band's live show, I traveled all the way to Osaka.
en.notes: 遠征 originally meant a military campaign; today it usually refers to a long trip for a specific purpose: expeditions, away trips of sports teams (海外遠征, 遠征試合), or tours. Colloquially, fans also say ライブに遠征する when they travel far for a concert. As a する-verb it is intransitive and takes へ／に／まで: ヨーロッパへ遠征する. A pure research expedition into the unknown is more often 探検.

examples[].german: Your Majesty, with all due respect, weren't you scheduled to attend the meeting?
The Emperor visited the disaster-stricken area.
The British Queen was loved by her people for a long time.
en.notes: 陛下 is the highest honorific title for emperors, empresses, and reigning monarchs, and is placed after the title: 天皇陛下, 皇后陛下, 女王陛下. In direct address it stands alone: 陛下 "Your Majesty". Princes and princesses, by contrast, receive 殿下 "Highness", and heads of state or high officials formerly 閣下 "Excellency". Sentences about 陛下 normally use honorific language (訪問された, お言葉).

examples[].german: The household voltage in Japan is 100 volts.
When using it abroad, please check that the voltage matches.
The voltage suddenly dropped and the computer shut off.
en.notes: 電圧 is the electric "voltage", measured in ボルト "volts". Typical are 電圧が高い/低い, 電圧を上げる/下げる, 高電圧 "high voltage" and 電圧計 "voltmeter". For comparison: 電流 is the "current" (amperes), 電力 the "power" (watts). For "tension" in the sense of nervousness or suspense, however, one says 緊張 or ハラハラ; 電圧 is purely technical.

examples[].german: He is the director of the Museum of History and Folklore.
I'm majoring in folklore studies at university.
Young people are learning the dances in order to preserve the folk performing arts handed down in the village.
en.notes: 民俗 refers to traditional folk customs, practices and ways of life. The science of it, folklore studies, is 民俗学; other compounds are 民俗芸能 "folk arts, folk dances" and 民俗資料館 "local history museum". Beware of the homophone 民族 (みんぞく) "people, ethnic group": 民族衣装 "traditional costume", 少数民族 "ethnic minority". The word is neutral to technical.

examples[].german: There are mulberry fields all over my hometown.
In the past this area was covered with mulberry fields, and many families raised silkworms.
The map symbol for a mulberry field is no longer used today.
en.notes: 桑畑 is a field of mulberry trees (桑), whose leaves serve as feed for silkworms (蚕). Until the mid-20th century, 桑畑 shaped the landscape of many regions such as Nagano or Gunma, when silkworm farming (養蚕) was still important. Today the word appears mainly in stories about the past, in local histories, and in songs. 畑 generally means a dry field, as opposed to the rice paddy 田んぼ.

examples[].german: Fewer and fewer people wear pearls.
I'm planning to wear a pearl necklace to the wedding.
Mie Prefecture is famous for pearl cultivation.
en.notes: 真珠 is the pearl; in fashion and jewelry one often also says パール. Typical are 真珠のネックレス "pearl necklace", 真珠を身につける "to wear pearls" and 養殖真珠 "cultured pearl"; Ago Bay in Mie is famous for pearl farming. Pearls are counted with 粒. Also well known is 真珠湾 "Pearl Harbor".

examples[].german: As you get older, your physical strength inevitably declines.
The typhoon's strength weakened rapidly after landfall.
Even ten years after retiring, his popularity hasn't declined in the slightest.
en.notes: 衰える is intransitive and means "to decline, grow weaker, deteriorate". Typical subjects are strength and abilities (体力が衰える, 視力や記憶力が衰える), but also influence, popularity or forces of nature (人気が衰える, 台風の勢いが衰える). The noun 衰え appears in 体力の衰えを感じる. For fading flavor or falling quality, by contrast, one says 味が落ちる; 弱る is more everyday and rather physical.

en.meaning: senility; decline due to old age
examples[].german: When my mother died of old age, I didn't miss hearing my wife mutter to herself, "I'm glad that burden is gone."
My grandfather passed away peacefully at ninety-eight from old age.
In recent years, the proportion of deaths attributed to old age has been increasing.
en.notes: 老衰 denotes the frailty of old age, above all as a natural cause of death: 老衰で亡くなる, 死因は老衰. It is not a general word for growing older; the biological aging process is 老化. The word is neutral to formal and often appears in obituaries and statistics. As a する-verb (老衰する) it is rare.

examples[].german: This pumpkin pie tastes good fresh from the oven, but we recommend putting it in the refrigerator for a while before eating.
As the recommended environment for this software, at least 8 GB of memory is advised.
The government recommends vaccination for the elderly.
en.notes: 推奨 is an official or professional recommendation and sounds more formal than おすすめ or 勧める. Typical are ～を推奨する, ～することが推奨されている as well as 推奨環境 "recommended system requirements" and 推奨年齢. 推薦, by contrast, means to nominate a person or work for something (推薦状 "letter of recommendation"). 推奨 is found mainly in manuals, official texts, and technology.

examples[].german: Companies with terrible working conditions are often called "black companies" in Japan.
Dogs that had been kept in wretched conditions were taken into protective care.
Because cheap materials were used, the product quality has become poor.
en.notes: 劣悪 means "very bad, wretched" and refers above all to conditions and quality: 劣悪な環境, 劣悪な労働条件, 劣悪な品質. It is a strong, rather literary な-adjective, often in news about work, animal keeping, or housing conditions. For cheaply made goods one also says 粗悪; in daily life ひどい or 悪い is often enough.

examples[].german: That swindler was a bundle of inferiority complexes.
Because I was constantly compared with my older brother, I always felt inferior.
You don't need to feel inferior just because you can't speak English.
en.notes: 劣等感 is the feeling of being inferior to others, i.e. a "sense of inferiority, inferiority complex". Typical: 劣等感を持つ／抱く／感じる, ～に劣等感がある, 劣等感の塊 "full of inferiority feelings". The opposite is 優越感 "sense of superiority". Colloquially one often says コンプレックス, which in Japanese almost always has this meaning.

examples[].german: The secret to success is having a sharp intuition.
I didn't know the answer, so I picked by instinct, and it turned out right.
I hadn't driven for a while, so it took time to get my touch back.
en.notes: 勘 is intuitive sense, a "nose" for things or a gut feeling. Typical are 勘がいい／鋭い "to have good instincts", 勘が当たる／外れる "to be right／wrong", 勘で答える "to answer by gut feeling" and 勘を取り戻す "to get the feel for something back" after a break. The more literary 直感 emphasizes the sudden inspiration, 第六感 the "sixth sense". 勘 belongs to casual everyday vocabulary.

examples[].german: Come on, give me a break. I was busy today and I'm totally exhausted.
I'm sorry I was late, but please let me off just this once.
Please refrain from taking photographs inside the store.
en.notes: 勘弁 means "forbearance, pardon" and is used almost only as 勘弁する in fixed expressions. 勘弁してください means, depending on tone, "please forgive me" or "please spare me that"; もう勘弁してくれ is an exasperated "enough already". Someone who forgives says 今回だけは勘弁してやる. On signs, the polite ご勘弁ください means "we ask that you refrain from this". Compared with 許す it sounds more colloquial and pleading.

examples[].german: I adjusted the frequency of the radio waves.
The electrical frequency differs between eastern and western Japan.
I tuned the radio to the frequency and listened to my favorite program.
