en.notes: 周波数 is the "frequency" of an oscillation or wave, measured in ヘルツ "hertz". Typical are 周波数を合わせる "to tune (a radio) to a frequency", 周波数が高い/低い and 周波数帯 "frequency band". A Japanese peculiarity: the mains frequency is 50 Hz in eastern Japan and 60 Hz in western Japan. For "frequency" in the general sense of how often, however, one says 頻度 or 回数.

examples[].german: "Sorry, my mistake. I mistook you for someone else." "Who exactly did you mistake me for? Please. Tell me."
I mistakenly thought the meeting was tomorrow.
I mistakenly assumed she was being kind to me because she likes me.
en.notes: 勘違い is an error based on a false assumption: one takes something to be different from what it is. Typical: ～と勘違いする "to wrongly believe that ...", AをBと勘違いする "to mistake A for B", 日にちを勘違いする "to get the date wrong". 誤解, by contrast, is a misunderstanding between people, for example about intentions (誤解を招く). Colloquially, 勘違いしないで also means "don't get the wrong idea".

examples[].german: This is the queen's necklace.
Marie Antoinette was the queen consort of King Louis XVI of France.
When the king and queen waved, great applause broke out from the gathered crowd.
en.notes: 王妃 is the consort of a king, i.e. the queen as wife. A queen who reigns in her own right is called 女王, and the consort of an emperor 皇后. Typical in history and fairy tales: 王と王妃, マリー・アントワネット王妃. The word is neutral to literary.

examples[].german: Princess Diana was loved by people all over the world.
The Crown Princess visited a hospital.
en.notes: 〜妃 (ひ) is a suffix placed after the name of the consort of a prince or monarch, for example ダイアナ妃 "Princess Diana". It is also found in 王妃 "queen (consort)" and 皇太子妃 "Crown Princess"; in forms of address and honorific language it is extended to 妃殿下. When the character stands alone, it is read きさき. A princess by birth is called 王女 or 姫.

examples[].german: I overheard her grandmother grumble, "That child's shyness is pitiable."
He looked at me with a pitying look.
Just feeling sorry for yourself won't change anything.
en.notes: 哀れむ (also written 憐れむ) means "to pity, feel compassion for" and is transitive: 人を哀れむ, 自分を哀れむ. It sounds somewhat literary and can come across as condescending, especially in 哀れむような目で見る. More neutral are 同情する or かわいそうに思う. The noun is 哀れみ (哀れみをかける).

examples[].german: I want to make my restaurant a place of rest for busy salarymen.
This park has become a place of relaxation for the elderly in the neighborhood.
The coffee break between work is the only moment of relaxation for me.
en.notes: 憩い means "rest, relaxation, repose" and appears almost always in fixed combinations such as 憩いの場 "place of rest" or 憩いのひととき "moment of relaxation". It sounds elevated and friendly, typical of park descriptions or advertising copy. The verb 憩う is literary. In everyday speech, a break is 休憩, and relaxation is くつろぎ or リラックス.

examples[].german: I wondered why he was spending money so lavishly, and it turns out he was a swindler!
My grandmother was tricked by a swindler over the phone and had money taken from her.
He's such a smooth talker, he's just like a con man.
en.notes: 詐欺師 is a "swindler, con artist": 詐欺 means "fraud", and 〜師 denotes someone who practices something like a trade. Common is 詐欺師にだまされる "to be tricked by a swindler". For phone scams targeting seniors (振り込め詐欺, オレオレ詐欺) people usually speak of a 詐欺グループ or 犯人. Colloquially and somewhat old-fashioned there is also ペテン師.

examples[].german: It was my dream to experience the geisha world.
In her youth my grandmother worked as a geisha in the Kyoto hanamachi.
The geisha world has its own unique customs and vocabulary.
en.notes: 花柳界 literally means the "world of flowers and willows", an old image for geisha and courtesans. Today it mainly refers to the geisha world with its teahouses, for example in Kyoto's Gion; a synonym is 花街 (かがい／はなまち). Historically it also included pleasure quarters, but it is not the same as the modern sex industry (風俗). The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned.

examples[].german: The arrested man was suspected of trespassing in the rest area.
There is a rest area partway along the mountain path, so let's take a break there.
The rest area at the event venue was already full of people.
en.notes: 休憩所 is a place to rest: rest areas along hiking trails, rest areas in parks, at events, or in train stations. The reading is きゅうけいじょ, though きゅうけいしょ also occurs. On expressways one usually says specifically サービスエリア or パーキングエリア; a break room at a company is 休憩室. One says 休憩所で休む or 休憩所で一休みする.

examples[].german: Is the rice done?
As soon as the rice is done, let's make onigiri.
The rice cooker announced, "The rice is done."
en.notes: 炊ける is the intransitive counterpart of 炊く "to cook rice": ご飯が炊ける "the rice is cooked, is ready". The rice cooker accordingly announces ご飯が炊けました. In standard Japanese 炊く／炊ける is used almost only for rice; for things simmered in broth one says 煮える, and for things grilled or baked 焼ける.

en.meaning: to break into pieces; to shatter; to become informal
examples[].german: Suddenly the window glass shattered into pieces.
Big waves hit the rocks and broke.
When you talk with friends, it's fine to speak in a more casual way.
en.notes: 砕ける is intransitive and means "to break into pieces, shatter": ガラスが粉々に砕ける, 波が岩に当たって砕ける. Its transitive counterpart is 砕く "to smash, grind". Unlike 割れる (to crack, split), 砕ける stresses falling apart into many small pieces. The figurative sense "casual, informal" is very common: 砕けた言い方, 砕けた態度; also the saying 当たって砕けろ "just give it a try".

examples[].german: The color of light is determined by its wavelength.
Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light.
From the first time I met him, we were on the same wavelength.
en.notes: 波長 is the "wavelength" in physics, e.g. of light, sound or radio waves (波長が長い/短い). Very common is the figurative expression 波長が合う "to be on the same wavelength", i.e. to get along well; negated 波長が合わない. In this meaning it is colloquial and similar to 気が合う.

examples[].german: Have you already seen this company's published financial statements?
The election date was publicly announced in the official gazette.
Regarding the merger, the company placed a public notice in the newspaper.
en.notes: 公告 is an official or legally required public notice, for example 決算公告 "publication of annual accounts" or announcements in the official gazette (官報で公告する). As a する-verb it is transitive: ～を公告する, often passive 公告される. Beware of the homophone 広告 "advertisement". General announcements are more often called お知らせ, 告知, or 公表.

examples[].german: This music is very rhythmic.
The heart pumps blood at a steady rhythm.
The audience was captivated by the dancers' rhythmic movements.
en.notes: 律動 is a literary, technical word for "rhythm", for example in medicine, music theory, or literature: 心臓の律動, 律動的な動き. In daily life one almost always says リズム. Most common is the derivation 律動的 "rhythmic" as a な-adjective; the verb 律動する is rare.

en.meaning: to save up; to store; to accumulate
examples[].german: We're poor, but I intend to somehow save up for our child's education.
I stored up food in preparation for winter.
I want to build up strength while I'm young and someday become independent.
en.notes: 貯える means "to save up, lay in stores, store" and is transitive: お金を貯える, 食料を貯える. The spelling 蓄える is more common, especially for abstract things like 知識を蓄える, 力を蓄える, or ひげを蓄える "to grow a beard". For everyday saving of money one usually says 貯める; 貯える sounds more deliberate, as if setting something aside for later. The noun is 蓄え／貯え "savings, stock".

examples[].german: I have a cavalry battle (kibasen) practice for the sports day, so I have to get up early tomorrow.
At the festival, mounted warriors parade through town.
In London you often see mounted police officers.
en.notes: 騎馬 means "on horseback, mounted" and mostly appears as a modifier: 騎馬隊 "mounted troop", 騎馬警官 "mounted police officer", 騎馬民族 "equestrian people". Well known is 騎馬戦, a school sports game in which three children carry a "rider" who tries to capture opponents' headbands. Riding as a hobby or sport is 乗馬. The word sounds literary or historical.

examples[].german: That photo of the cavalryman somehow reminds me of my younger days.
In past wars, a cavalry charge often decided victory or defeat.
The cavalry appeared from beyond the hill.
en.notes: 騎兵 means "cavalry" or an individual "cavalryman", i.e. soldiers on horseback. Opposing terms are 歩兵 "infantry" and 砲兵 "artillery"; a unit is called 騎兵隊. The word belongs to military and historical topics and hardly occurs in daily life. 騎馬, by contrast, stresses riding or being mounted in general.

en.meaning: mulberry field (archaic); くわばらくわばら: God forbid!
examples[].german: Let's ask Kuwabara-san!
When it thundered, my grandmother would always chant "kuwabara, kuwabara".
God forbid! If you make that person angry, all hell will break loose.
en.notes: 桑原 literally means "mulberry field", but in this meaning it is obsolete; today one says 桑畑. 桑原 is known mainly as a family name and from the incantation くわばらくわばら (usually in kana), which was formerly recited during thunderstorms and is used today in the sense of "God forbid!" or "knock on wood" when one wants to escape a danger or unpleasantness. The formula sounds old-fashioned to jocular.

examples[].german: There's no way a crown princess would volunteer for the military.
The citizens welcomed the Crown Princess's visit with smiles.
The British Crown Princess took part in a charity event.
en.notes: 皇太子妃 is the wife of the crown prince (皇太子), i.e. the "crown princess" - in Japan, for example, 雅子さま until the accession to the throne in 2019. In the media she is respectfully called 皇太子妃殿下 or referred to with 〜さま. The wife of the present heir (皇嗣) is called 皇嗣妃. 皇太子妃 is also used for foreign royal families.

examples[].german: He's a cunning guy and a master at putting on an innocent act.
The cunning fox tricked the crow and took the cheese.
He is a crafty politician who is good at finding loopholes in the law.
en.notes: 悪賢い is an い-adjective made of 悪 "bad" and 賢い "clever": clever, but in a wicked, self-serving way, i.e. "cunning, crafty, sly". Very similar is ずる賢い, which sounds more everyday and stresses sneakiness. Related is 悪知恵が働く "to be crafty". Typical: 悪賢い男, 悪賢いやり方, and in fairy tales 悪賢いキツネ.

examples[].german: I was dazzled by the brilliance of the diamond.
When I see the sparkle in the children's eyes, I'm glad I became a teacher.
After retiring, she lost her former brilliance.
en.notes: 輝き is the noun of 輝く "to shine, gleam" and means "brilliance, radiance, sparkle". It is used for the glitter of gemstones or stars (ダイヤモンドの輝き, 星の輝き), but also figuratively: 目の輝き "the sparkle in one's eyes", かつての輝きを失う "to lose one's former brilliance". Typical verbs are 輝きを放つ, 輝きを増す, 輝きを失う. Mere light is 光, and surface shine is more like つや.

examples[].german: This crocodile ornament is in the way.
The crocodile at the zoo hardly moved all day.
The "wani" in the tale of the white hare of Inaba is said to mean sharks.
en.notes: 鰐 (わに) refers to crocodiles and alligators alike; in daily life it is almost always written ワニ in katakana, and the kanji is rare. Compounds include ワニ革 "crocodile leather" and ワニ口クリップ "alligator clip". In old Japanese, わに also meant "shark", for example in the tale of the white hare of Inaba.

examples[].german: The room temperature was set to 25 degrees.
When deep-frying tempura, pay attention to the temperature of the oil.
The window glass is fogged up because of the temperature difference between the room and outside.
en.notes: 温度 is "temperature" in general - of rooms, water, substances or devices; typical collocations are 温度が上がる/下がる, 温度を測る, 温度を設定する and 温度計 "thermometer". For the air temperature in the weather report one says 気温, for body temperature 体温 and for water 水温. 温度差 means "temperature difference", and figuratively also differing levels of enthusiasm among those involved.

examples[].german: The air is clear today, and you can see the Tateyama range clearly.
From the hotel window, I gazed at the snow-capped range.
My goal this year is to climb the highest peak of the range.
en.notes: 連峰 denotes a row of connected peaks seen as a chain, often with proper names: 立山連峰, 八ヶ岳連峰. Typical are expressions like 連峰を望む "to look out at the mountain range" or 雪をかぶった連峰. The word is literary and appears mainly in travel guides, weather reports, and the news. 山脈, by contrast, is the geographical term for a long mountain range (奥羽山脈); in daily life one simply says 山々.

examples[].german: He is good at persuading people.
This author is really skillful at writing dialogue.
I can't put it well, but something feels off.
en.notes: 巧い is the spelling of うまい in the sense of "skillful, adept"; the word is mostly written in kana, and 上手い is also common as a kanji spelling. For "delicious", 旨い or 美味い is used instead. Typical is 〜が巧い or 〜のが巧い (話すのが巧い), adverbially 巧く "well, as desired" (巧く言えない). 上手 is more neutral and polite; うまい sounds colloquial and is also used for one's own abilities.

examples[].german: A certain wicked wizard cleverly approached the woman, pretending it was by chance.
Fraud using sophisticated methods is increasing, so please be careful.
The jewel had been cleverly hidden at the bottom of the box.
en.notes: 巧妙 is a な-adjective for something cleverly devised and often carries a negative undertone of cunning or deception: 巧妙な手口 "a sophisticated scheme", 巧妙な嘘, 巧妙に隠す. The adverbial form is 巧妙に. For neutral skill one rather says 上手, for manual dexterity 器用. The word is rather literary and common in news about fraud and crime.

en.meaning: disturbance, hindrance; to disturb, to be in the way; (お邪魔する) to visit
examples[].german: Don't get in my way. I can do it by myself!
This box is in the way, so please take it outside.
Hello. Excuse me for coming in. (when entering someone's home)
en.notes: 邪魔 refers to something that disturbs or is in the way: 邪魔な荷物 "luggage that is in the way", 邪魔になる "to be a nuisance, to be a hindrance". As a する-verb, the thing disturbed takes を: 勉強の邪魔をする, 人の邪魔をしない. Very common is the polite formula お邪魔します when entering someone else's home (and お邪魔しました when leaving) - here it means "to visit". In everyday writing it is often written in kana as じゃま.

en.meaning: no good, useless, broken; futile; not allowed, can't
examples[].german: You absolutely must not go on a trip with a boy!
This computer is old now and no good anymore.
I practiced as hard as I could, but the match went badly anyway.
en.notes: 駄目 is a な-adjective with the basic sense "is no good, doesn't work": この傘はもうだめだ "the umbrella is done for", 私は料理がだめです "I can't cook". From this follows "not allowed": ～てはだめ / ～ちゃだめ "you must not ...", and on its own as an exclamation だめ！ "No! Stop that!". Also "futile, failed": 頑張ったけどだめだった. The word is colloquial-neutral and mostly written in kana as だめ (also ダメ); more politely one prohibits with いけません or ご遠慮ください.

en.meaning: abrupt; sudden; out of the blue
examples[].german: She suddenly asked me to repair her car.
I'm sorry to spring this on you, but I'll be leaving the company at the end of next month.
The movie's ending was so abrupt that I didn't really understand it.
en.notes: 唐突 describes something that comes without warning or connection, especially people's remarks and actions: 唐突な質問, 唐突に話題を変える. As a polite opener one says 唐突ですが… "Excuse me for bringing this up so abruptly". Unlike 突然, which fits any sudden event (突然雨が降り出した), 唐突 stresses the lack of transition; it is not used for natural events.

examples[].german: This novel is set at a court in medieval Europe.
Gagaku is music that was originally played at the imperial court.
In Beijing, I tasted the former imperial court cuisine.
en.notes: 宮廷 is the court of a monarch, as a place and as courtly society, mainly in historical or foreign contexts. It is common in compounds: 宮廷料理, 宮廷音楽, 宮廷画家. For the present Japanese imperial family one rather says 皇室, and for matters inside the Imperial Palace 宮中 (宮中晩餐会). The word is a pure noun and is placed before other nouns with の.

examples[].german: I went home without attending the award ceremony.
A man who saved a child drowning in the river was commended by the police.
The company honored an employee who had not taken a single day off in ten years.
en.notes: 表彰する means to officially honor someone for achievements or good deeds; the honor comes from an institution: 警察が市民を表彰する. Very common is the passive 表彰される, along with 表彰式 "award ceremony" and 表彰状 "certificate of commendation". For receiving a prize oneself, one says 受賞する, and everyday praise is 褒める. The word is neutral to formal and appears often in school, company, and news contexts.

examples[].german: A revised edition of this dictionary will be published next month.
Please use the revised edition, not the old textbook.
The revised edition of the manual corrects several errors.
en.notes: 改訂版 is the revised new edition of a book, dictionary, textbook or manual; 改訂 means the revision of the content of texts. Beware of the identically read 改定: that is the change of rules or prices (料金改定). Timetables are changed with 改正 (ダイヤ改正). Related terms are 新版, 増補版 "expanded edition" and 初版 "first edition".

examples[].german: The deeper the water, the higher the water pressure.
With a pressure cooker, meat becomes tender in a short time.
Because of pressure from above, the plan was canceled.
en.notes: 圧力 is, physically, "pressure" (force per area), as in 圧力鍋 "pressure cooker"; more specific terms are 気圧 "air pressure" and 水圧 "water pressure". Very common is the figurative meaning "political or social pressure": 圧力をかける "to exert pressure", 圧力を受ける "to be put under pressure", 政治的な圧力. For personal performance pressure or nervousness, people rather say プレッシャー (プレッシャーを感じる).

examples[].german: About how long until it's decided which stocks we'll recommend to customers?
Which brands of sake are popular?
My father always smokes the same brand of cigarettes.
en.notes: 銘柄 denotes a particular "brand, variety" of a product, especially for sake, rice, tea, tobacco, or beef (銘柄米, 銘柄牛). On the stock exchange, 銘柄 is a "security, issue", i.e. a single stock: 注目銘柄, 銘柄を選ぶ. For brands of companies, fashion, or electronics one rather says ブランド or メーカー; 銘柄 stresses the variety or designation of origin.

examples[].german: Participants, please each bring your own lunch.
The children each began drawing whatever they liked.
I divided the cake onto the individual plates.
en.notes: 銘々 means "each one for themselves" and is mostly written in kana, めいめい. It most often stands adverbially before the verb (めいめい好きな物を注文する) or before nouns with の (銘々の皿). Also well known is 銘々皿, small individual plates. それぞれ is more general and also applies to things; 各自 sounds like an instruction or rule (各自で持参すること).

examples[].german: One day my son suddenly started speaking Japanese fluently, as if a dam had burst inside him.
On this river, the amount of water is regulated by a weir.
The moment she saw her mother's face, she burst into tears.
en.notes: 堰 is a weir or small dam in a river or irrigation channel, used to regulate the amount of water; a large dam is called ダム. The word is most often met in the expression 堰を切ったように "as if a dam had burst": feelings, tears, or words suddenly pour out (堰を切ったように泣き出す). Related is the verb 堰き止める "to dam up".

examples[].german: When the mast broke and the yacht began to drift, I did get anxious.
The fishing boat drifted on the Pacific for three days before being safely rescued.
The discussion is not coming together, and the plan is still adrift.
en.notes: 漂流する is intransitive and describes a ship or person floating helplessly on the water: 海を漂流する, 海上を漂流する; also 漂流物 "flotsam". Figuratively it also means that a policy or project drifts aimlessly. 漂う is more general, "to float, drift" (also for scents), and 漂着 is the end of drifting, landing on a coast.

en.meaning: to drift ashore; to be washed up
examples[].german: Imagine an injured baby whale washing up on a sandy beach.
A large amount of trash from abroad has washed up on the coast.
The fishermen who were swept away by the storm drifted ashore on an uninhabited island a week later.
en.notes: 漂着する means to land on a coast or be washed up after drifting on the water; the place takes に: 島に漂着する. Common are 漂着物 and 漂着ごみ "washed-up trash". The word is literary; colloquially one says 流れ着く, and for animals thrown ashore by waves also 打ち上げられる.

en.meaning: change of mind; reversing one's decision
examples[].german: The company president urged the department head, who had said he would quit, to reconsider.
Persuaded by his teammates, he changed his mind and decided to keep playing.
Once she has decided, she hardly ever changes her mind.
en.notes: 翻意 is a formal word for reversing a decision one has made, especially an announced intention such as resignation or quitting. Typical are 翻意する, 翻意を促す "to urge someone to reconsider", and 翻意させる. It appears mainly in the news and reports; in daily life one says 気が変わる, 考えを変える, or 思い直す.

examples[].german: In this video, we trace the path of WaniKani from its birth to the present.
The exhibition lets you look back on the painter's fifty-year creative journey.
A shooting star traced a beautiful arc across the night sky.
en.notes: 軌跡 literally means "wheel track", but it is mostly used figuratively: the path a person or organization has traveled, typically 〜の軌跡をたどる or 〜の軌跡を振り返る. Concretely it also denotes the path of a moving object (ボールの軌跡) and, in mathematics, a locus. Do not confuse it with the identically read 奇跡 "miracle"; 足跡 rather stresses traces and achievements left behind.

examples[].german: Their Majesties the Emperor and Empress visited the disaster-stricken area.
In history class we learned about Joséphine, Napoleon's empress.
The Empress welcomed the foreign ambassador and his wife with a smile.
en.notes: 皇后 is the empress as consort of an emperor; in Japan respectfully 皇后陛下, and together with the Emperor 天皇皇后両陛下. An empress who rules in her own right is a 女帝, a queen is a 女王, and the consort of a king is an 王妃. The word belongs to the formal vocabulary of the news and history; when speaking about the Japanese Empress in the news, honorific forms are used.

examples[].german: Thinking that the trip starts tomorrow, I was so excited that I couldn't sleep for a long time.
At the goal just before the end of the match, the spectators jumped to their feet in excitement.
You seem a little worked up. First calm down and then speak.
en.notes: 興奮する is intransitive and means "to be excited, aroused", both positively and negatively: from joy, from anger, or physically aroused. Typical are 興奮して眠れない, 興奮を抑える, 興奮気味, and the causative 興奮させる. わくわくする is only joyful anticipation, and 熱狂 is the enthusiasm of a crowd. To calm someone down, one says 興奮しないで、落ち着いて.

en.meaning: rousing oneself; fresh fighting spirit; to rise to the occasion
examples[].german: A single remark from her spurred him on, and he began studying desperately for the entrance exam.
The team was far behind in the first half, but rallied in the second half and turned the game around.
In response to worsening business results, the president called on employees to rise to the occasion.
en.notes: 奮起 means to rouse oneself and gather fresh strength, often after a setback or a reprimand. As a する-verb it is intransitive (チームが奮起する); to spur someone on is 奮起させる, and to urge someone to rouse themselves is 奮起を促す. Compared with 頑張る, 奮起 is more formal and stresses the moment when someone takes up new fighting spirit; it is common in sports reports and speeches.

examples[].german: Food processing technology has advanced.
Eating only processed foods is not good for your health.
This photo is so heavily edited that I can't tell it's the person.
en.notes: 加工 is the "processing" of a raw material into a product; as a transitive する-verb: 木材を加工する "to process wood". Typical are 加工食品 "processed foods", 加工品, 金属加工 and, in daily life, 写真を加工する "to edit a photo" (加工アプリ). 処理 is more general "treatment, handling" (data, waste, tasks), while 加工 changes the form of a material or image.

examples[].german: There is always a line at the ramen shop "Sakura-tei" in front of the station.
Many rakugo performers have names with "-tei", such as "San'yūtei" or "Kokontei".
My father has worked for thirty years at the long-established Western-style restaurant "Midori-tei".
en.notes: 〜亭 is a suffix that originally means "pavilion, arbor" and today mainly forms names of restaurants and eateries (〇〇亭), especially traditional Japanese ones; an upscale Japanese restaurant is called 料亭. It also forms stage names of rakugo performers (三遊亭, 古今亭) and of some writers (二葉亭四迷). On its own as a word it is hardly used.

examples[].german: I was totally amazed at how fast Mami could eat bacon.
When I saw the amount on the bill, I was astounded.
Fans were shocked by the famous singer's sudden retirement announcement.
en.notes: 仰天する means "to be stunned with amazement", literally "to look up at the sky". The intensified expression びっくり仰天する is very common, rather colloquial and a bit humorous. In headlines, 仰天 stands for sensational news (仰天ニュース). 驚く is the neutral basic word, and 唖然とする describes speechless shock.

examples[].german: I wonder why my aunt didn't want to come to our wedding.
My aunt is five years older than my mother and has always doted on me.
During summer vacation, I stayed at my aunt's house in the countryside.
en.notes: 伯母 is an aunt who is older than one's own parent (the older sister of one's father or mother, or the wife of an older uncle). The younger aunt is written 叔母; both are read おば, and in conversation often simply おばさん. For other people's aunts one politely says おばさま or おばさん. The kanji spelling is needed mainly in writing.

examples[].german: I couldn't help laughing at the coincidence.
I ran into a friend from high school at the station by chance.
I don't think it's a coincidence that he took the same day off.
en.notes: 偶然 is a noun, a な-adjective and an adverb: 偶然の一致 "coincidental match", 偶然に・偶然 "by chance" (駅で偶然会った), 偶然にも "coincidentally". The opposite is 必然 "necessity". たまたま means almost the same, but is only an adverb and more colloquial. The phrase 偶然ではない "no coincidence" is also popular.

examples[].german: Undaunted by the dirty water, she swam in the Yodo River.
The Yodo River flows out of Lake Biwa and empties into Osaka Bay.
Every summer, a large fireworks festival is held on the Yodo River bank.
en.notes: 淀川 is the Yodo River in Kansai: it flows out of Lake Biwa, is called 瀬田川 and 宇治川 in its upper course, and empties into Osaka Bay in Osaka. 〜川 is read here with voiced がわ. The 淀 in the name means "still, stagnant water", as in the verb 淀む. In Osaka the river is known for its riverside meadows and the big summer fireworks.

examples[].german: In recent years the number of people visiting that burial mound has been increasing.
In Sakai there is the Daisen Kofun, Japan's largest burial mound.
A burial mound was discovered during construction, and the building work was temporarily halted.
en.notes: 古墳 are ancient burial mounds, especially from the 古墳時代 named after them (roughly the 3rd to 7th century). Famous are the keyhole-shaped 前方後円墳, such as the 大仙古墳 in Sakai. 墓 is an ordinary grave, and 墳墓 is the formal word for a burial site. In the news one often reads 古墳が見つかる, 古墳を発掘する.

examples[].german: You should definitely visit Tutankhamun's tomb.
In an excavation, a tomb thought to belong to a member of the royal family was found.
Desecrating tombs is severely punished by law.
en.notes: 墳墓 is a formal, literary word for a grave or burial site, mainly in archaeology, law, and elevated language; 墳墓の地 is the homeland where one's ancestors are buried. In daily life one says 墓 or お墓, and for a cemetery 墓地. For the ancient Japanese burial mounds there is the special word 古墳.

examples[].german: His older brother had a heart attack in the prime of life and died.
This disease is said to be common in men in their prime.
The town's kendo tournament has a youth division and a senior division.
en.notes: 壮年 is the time of full vigor in life, roughly from the thirties into the fifties, often as 壮年期 or 壮年層. Unlike 中年 "middle age", which sounds neutral to slightly negative, 壮年 stresses energy and capability. In sports, 壮年の部 denotes the older age class. The word is rather literary; counterparts are 青年 and 老年.

examples[].german: We're planning a send-off party for him on Friday. Are you available?
A send-off ceremony for the Olympic team members was held at city hall.
Before the overseas tour, the team gave local fans a victory in a send-off match.
en.notes: 壮行 is a ceremonious, encouraging send-off for someone setting out on a great undertaking, such as a competition, an overseas assignment, or an expedition. The word hardly stands alone; it is used almost only in 壮行会 "send-off party with good wishes" and 壮行試合 "send-off match". A 送別会, by contrast, bids farewell to someone who is leaving and not coming back (transfer, retirement).

examples[].german: This restaurant has a mini elevator for transporting meals and other small items.
At the construction site, materials are being transported by crane.
It's safer to ask a specialist company to move a piano.
en.notes: 運搬する is transitive and refers to carrying mostly heavy goods or materials from one place to another, by vehicle, machine or by hand: 資材を運搬する, 運搬費, 運搬車. 運送 is rather the commercial transport business (運送会社), and 輸送 is transport on a large scale by rail, ship or aircraft, also of people. In everyday speech one simply says 運ぶ.

examples[].german: The assembly of the parts is done by hand.
My older brother works in an automobile assembly plant.
Putting this bookshelf together took an hour.
en.notes: 組立 is the noun for 組み立てる "to assemble" and means "assembly, putting together", figuratively also "structure, composition" (文章の組み立て). The spelling without okurigana 組立 is seen mainly in technical terms and on signs such as 組立工場 "assembly plant" and 組立ライン; in running text and instructions one usually finds 組み立て (組み立て式の家具 "furniture you assemble yourself"). The related verb is transitive: 棚を組み立てる.

examples[].german: I dislocated my left shoulder during the transport work.
Three people injured in the accident were taken to the hospital by ambulance.
In the factory, parts are conveyed to the next process by conveyor belt.
en.notes: 搬送する is transitive and has two main meanings: transporting goods, for example in factories and warehouses (ベルトコンベヤーで搬送する), and taking sick or injured people to a hospital. The latter is very common in the news, almost always in the passive: 病院に搬送される, 救急搬送. In daily speech one says 運ぶ or 病院に運ばれる.

examples[].german: All works must be carried out by 7 p.m. on Sunday.
The moving company plans to carry out the furniture in the morning and bring it into the new home in the afternoon.
During the fire, museum staff carried out the most important works first.
en.notes: 搬出する means to carry heavy or valuable objects such as furniture, artworks, or equipment out of a building. Its counterpart is 搬入する "to carry in"; both are heard at moves, exhibitions, and events (搬入口, 搬出作業). In daily life one says 運び出す. The word is matter-of-fact and appears mainly in work instructions and technical language.

examples[].german: A polar bear was napping in a hollow in a tree when a lumberjack came by.
A cavity was found under the road, and it was closed to traffic.
As factories move overseas, the hollowing-out of domestic industry is advancing.
en.notes: 空洞 is a cavity inside something: 木の空洞, 地下の空洞; in medicine also cavities in the lung. Figuratively it means emptiness or lack of substance, and very common is 空洞化 "hollowing-out", such as 産業の空洞化 through the relocation of industry, or the desolation of city centers. 穴 is a hole in general, and a cave that one can walk into is a 洞窟.

examples[].german: I tripped in that cave and sprained my ankle.
In the cliffs along the coast there are many caves carved out by the waves.
Earthenware used by people in ancient times has been found in this cave.
en.notes: 洞穴 in the reading どうけつ is the literary, rather technical word for a natural cave, for example in geology and archaeology (洞穴遺跡). The same kanji are often read ほらあな in daily life. The most common word for "cave" is 洞窟; for an animal's hideout one says 巣穴.

examples[].german: All the people of that village died of the epidemic.
In the past, people prayed at shrines when an epidemic broke out.
In medieval Europe, a third of the population is said to have been lost to plague.
en.notes: 疫病 is a plague that spreads rapidly and sounds historical or literary: 疫病が流行る, 疫病で亡くなる. It can also be read やくびょう, as always in 疫病神 "bringer of bad luck". In modern news one mostly says 感染症, 伝染病, or パンデミック. Recently the formula 疫病退散 "drive away the plague" became well known again.

examples[].german: My heart aches every time I see photos of starving children.
The two who got lost in the mountains staved off hunger by eating nuts and berries.
During the war, my grandfather is said to have lived enduring hunger and cold.
en.notes: 飢え is the noun of 飢える and means serious hunger up to starvation, not just an empty stomach. Typical are 飢えに苦しむ, 飢えをしのぐ "to stave off hunger", and 飢え死に "death by starvation". Ordinary hunger is 空腹 or お腹が空く, and famine on a large scale is 飢餓. Figuratively the verb is mostly used: 愛情に飢える "to hunger for love".

examples[].german: I disliked my father's bento because he never considered the color scheme and everything was brown.
Adding tomatoes to a salad makes it more colorful.
Gardening as a hobby adds color to his life in retirement.
en.notes: 彩り is the noun of 彩る and means coloring and color coordination, especially when arranging food: 彩りがいい, 彩りを考える. Figuratively, 彩りを添える means "to add some color or brilliance", for example to life or a celebration. 色 is simply color, and 色合い is the shade; 彩り stresses the effect of the colors working together.

examples[].german: My buddy is in the middle of a fistfight at the club right now.
The argument escalated, and finally it came to blows.
A fight broke out between players during the match, and both were sent off.
en.notes: 殴り合い comes from 殴り合う "to hit each other" and denotes a brawl with fists. Typical are 殴り合いのけんか and 殴り合いになる "to come to blows". けんか is more general and can also be a verbal fight (口げんか), and 取っ組み合い is a scuffle with grappling and grabbing. The word is neutral to colloquial.

examples[].german: We ate an early lunch before the raid.
At the end of the movie, the hero storms the enemy's office all by himself.
A new company has barged into the budget smartphone market.
en.notes: 殴り込み is a violent raid on the headquarters of a rival group, typical of yakuza and action films; the set phrase is 殴り込みをかける. Figuratively it means forcing one's way vigorously into someone else's market or field: 業界に殴り込みをかける. The word is colloquial and sounds combative; more neutral are 襲撃 "attack" and 参入 "market entry".

examples[].german: I like clothes made of linen, but they're quite expensive.
In summer, linen sheets feel cool and pleasant.
In the old days, farming families made their work clothes from hemp cloth.
en.notes: 麻布 in the reading あさぬの is cloth made of hemp or linen; the same kanji are also read まふ, and as a place name in Tokyo they are read あざぶ (Azabu). In fashion today one usually just says 麻 (麻のシャツ) or リネン. The fabric is especially valued in summer because it is cool and breathable.

examples[].german: Many countries used to be colonies.
Buildings from the colonial era still remain in this town.
That country was under the colonial rule of a European country for about a hundred years.
en.notes: 植民地 is a colony, a territory ruled by a foreign power; literally "land (地) where people (民) are settled (植)". Typical: 植民地支配 ("colonial rule"), 植民地にする, 旧植民地, 植民地時代. The related verb is 植民地化する ("to colonize"). The rare meaning "Japanese settlement in Brazil" plays no role in normal usage.

examples[].german: Construction of a new bridge has begun.
A high-rise apartment building is under construction in front of the station.
Don't just complain; please offer constructive opinions.
en.notes: 建設 is the "construction" of large structures and facilities such as roads, bridges, dams or airports; as a transitive する-verb: ダムを建設する. Typical are 建設中 "under construction", 建設会社 "construction company" and 建設現場 "construction site". For individual buildings such as houses, one rather says 建築 or simply 建てる. Figuratively, 建設 also stands for "building up" something abstract, and 建設的 means "constructive".

examples[].german: My uncle is moping at home, depressed.
When the rain goes on for a long time, I somehow get gloomy.
Let's take a walk to shake off this gloomy mood.
en.notes: 鬱気 is a rare, literary word for a depressed, melancholy mood. It appears in expressions like 鬱気を晴らす "to dispel the gloomy mood" or 鬱気がたまる. In daily life one says far more often 憂鬱, 気が滅入る, or ふさぎ込む; the illness depression is called うつ病 and is not the same thing.

examples[].german: My uncle is a bank clerk.
My uncle is my father's older brother and farms in the countryside.
At New Year, relatives gather at my uncle's house.
en.notes: 伯父 is an uncle who is older than one's own parent (the older brother of one's father or mother, or the husband of an older aunt). The younger uncle is written 叔父; both are read おじ, and in conversation mostly おじさん. When speaking of other people's uncles, one politely says おじさま or おじさん. Do not confuse it with 祖父 おじいさん "grandfather", with a long い.

en.meaning: to be lit; to burn (of a light)
examples[].german: I saw a light come on in that room.
When the sun went down, the streetlights along the road all came on at once.
His words kindled a small flame of hope in my heart.
en.notes: 灯る is intransitive: a light, lamp, or candle comes on and burns (明かりが灯る, 街灯が灯る); also written 点る. Its transitive counterpart is 灯す "to light" (ろうそくを灯す). In daily life, for electric light one mostly says 電気がつく; 灯る sounds more atmospheric and literary. Figuratively: 心に希望の火が灯る.

en.meaning: to be cooked; to boil (of food)
examples[].german: Are the beans cooked through properly?
When the potatoes are cooked soft, please turn off the heat.
The meat in the pot isn't cooked yet, so wait a little longer.
en.notes: 煮える is intransitive: food becomes cooked in liquid (豆が煮える, よく煮えた); its transitive counterpart is 煮る "to simmer, cook". For water that boils one says 沸く, and for rice 炊ける. A well-known expression is はらわたが煮えくり返る "to seethe with rage". Typical are 煮えるまで待つ and まだ煮えていない "not cooked yet".

examples[].german: Please never go onto the tracks, no matter what.
I live near the railway tracks.
Heavy snow buried the tracks, and train service was suspended.
en.notes: 線路 is the track or rail line as a concrete place: 線路を渡る, 線路沿い, 線路に落ちる. Do not confuse it with 路線, the route as a transport connection (バス路線, 路線図); railway lines have names ending in 〜線 (山手線). Platforms are called ホーム. In announcements one often hears 線路内に人が立ち入ったため "because a person entered the tracks".

examples[].german: Certain conditions must be met.
Please keep the temperature constant.
The quality of his work is always consistent.
en.notes: 一定 means "fixed, constant, certain". Before nouns it appears as 一定の: 一定の条件, 一定の期間, and 一定の効果 means "a certain effect". Adverbially one says 一定に保つ "to keep constant", and as a state 一定している "is constant". Unlike 特定 "one very specific thing", 一定 refers to a fixed amount or a constant level.

examples[].german: Hasty judgments should be avoided.
I promised too casually and regretted it.
You shouldn't casually believe information on the internet.
en.notes: 安易 is a な-adjective and mostly meant critically: taken too lightly, without enough thought. Typical are 安易な考え, 安易な判断 and the adverbial 安易に〜する (安易に信じる). For neutral "easy, simple" one uses 簡単 or, formally, 容易; 安易, by contrast, criticizes the attitude of someone who takes the easy way out.

examples[].german: It has become somewhat warmer than this morning.
I felt somewhat reassured after hearing the explanation.
I put some of my income into savings every month.
en.notes: 幾分 means "somewhat, a little, to a certain degree" and often appears with changes and comparisons: 幾分よくなる, 幾分楽になる, 〜より幾分〜. It is somewhat more formal than 少し and similar to いくらか or やや. As a noun, 幾分か also means "a part" (収入の幾分か). Written in kana, いくぶん, it is also common.

en.meaning: to bring up; to start saying; to suggest
examples[].german: Who first brought up that proposal?
I couldn't bring myself to say the truth for a long time.
Once my father says he'll do something, he won't listen to anyone.
en.notes: 言い出す means to bring something up or to be the first to suggest it: 〜と言い出す "to suddenly say that ...", 誰が言い出したのか "who was it that brought it up". Very common is the negative potential 言い出せない "cannot bring oneself to say". 一度言い出したら聞かない describes stubborn people, and 言い出しっぺ is colloquial for "the one who suggested it". 話し出す, by contrast, only means "to begin talking".

en.meaning: to be in charge of; to take on
examples[].german: This year I'm in charge of the third-year classes.
I've been assigned to handle the reception.
Mr. Tanaka is in charge of deliveries in this district.
en.notes: 受け持つ means to be responsible for a task, a class, or an area: 〜を受け持つ. Typical in schools (三年生を受け持つ, 受け持ちの先生) and at the workplace. 担当する is the more common, matter-of-fact word at work, and 担任 specifically the homeroom teacher. 引き受ける stresses accepting a request, while 受け持つ stresses the ongoing area of responsibility.

examples[].german: Iron is used in many buildings.
They say to strike while the iron is hot, so try many challenges while you are young.
Liver contains a lot of iron.
en.notes: 鉄 is the metal "iron", in daily life often also meaning "steel" (鉄の扉, 鉄骨 "steel frame"). Common compounds are 鉄道 "railway", 地下鉄 "subway", 鉄分 "iron content (in food)" and 鉄棒 "horizontal bar". Well known is the proverb 鉄は熱いうちに打て "strike while the iron is hot". Colloquially, 〜鉄 also denotes railway fans, e.g. 撮り鉄 "train photographer".

examples[].german: The popular bread was sold out in the morning.
Let's reserve before the tickets sell out.
We are very sorry. That item is sold out.
en.notes: 売り切れる is intransitive: the goods are sold out (商品が売り切れる). The transitive 売り切る describes the seller who sells everything. The noun 売り切れ is very common (売り切れ次第終了 "while supplies last"). More formally one says 完売する; in shops one hears the polite 売り切れております.

examples[].german: If the weather is good, we'll eat outdoors.
This machine cannot be used outdoors.
The outdoor pool is open only during the summer.
en.notes: 屋外 means "outdoors, outside" and is the opposite of 屋内. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 外 and often appears in notices and compounds: 屋外プール, 屋外での使用, 屋外イベント. 野外 stresses open nature or events under the open sky (野外コンサート), and 戸外 is literary. With the place particle: 屋外で.

examples[].german: I increased the number of practice sessions.
There is a limit on the number of times you can use it.
If you buy a coupon book of bus tickets, it becomes a little cheaper.
en.notes: 回数 is the number of times something happens, not the duration. Typical are 回数が多い／少ない, 回数を増やす／減らす, 回数を重ねる "to do repeatedly" and 回数券 "book of tickets". 頻度 is more formal and denotes frequency per unit of time; counting uses the counter 〜回.

examples[].german: I consulted outside experts.
Please do not pass this information on to outsiders.
The exterior of the building is scheduled to be repainted next year.
en.notes: 外部 denotes the "outside" - spatially (建物の外部 "exterior of a building") and above all organizationally: everything outside a company, group, or system. Typical are 外部の人・外部の専門家 "outsiders", 外部に漏れる/漏らす "to leak", and 外部からの侵入 "intrusion from outside". The counterpart is 内部. In daily life one simply says 外 for "outside"; 外部 sounds matter-of-fact and suits business and official language.

examples[].german: The story is set in an imaginary town.
You must not report made-up figures.
If you receive an email with a fake invoice, please ignore it.
en.notes: 架空 means "merely invented, not really existing" and almost always stands with の before a noun: 架空の人物, 架空の町, 架空の話. In the news it often appears in connection with fraud: 架空請求 "fake billing, fraudulent demand for payment" or 架空の会社 "shell company". The opposite is 実在の "actually existing". Rare is the technical meaning "overhead, laid in the air" (架空線 "overhead line").

examples[].german: The library's loan period is two weeks.
Bicycle rentals are handled at the reception desk.
That book is currently checked out.
en.notes: 貸し出し is the noun of 貸し出す "to lend out" and is used above all for libraries, rental stations, and banks (loans). Common are 貸し出し期間 "loan period", 貸し出し中 "on loan", and 貸し出しを行う. On signs and cards the short spelling 貸出 without し is often used (貸出カード). The counterpart from the user's side is 借りる, and returning is 返却.

examples[].german: The train accelerated slowly.
Technological progress is accelerating.
The government intends to speed up the reforms.
en.notes: 加速 means "acceleration"; as a する-verb it is mostly intransitive: 車が加速する. Someone who actively speeds something up often says 〜を加速させる. Figuratively it is used for developments that become faster: 少子化が加速する, 改革を加速させる. The opposite is 減速 "slowing down"; the physics term "acceleration (quantity)" is 加速度.

examples[].german: What does this symbol represent?
I checked the map symbols.
Please include numbers and symbols in your password.
en.notes: 記号 is an agreed sign or symbol that stands for something: 地図記号, 元素記号, 発音記号, and for passwords the "special characters" besides letters and digits. One says 記号を付ける "to put a mark" and 〜を表す記号. 文字, by contrast, are written characters, 印 is a simple mark, and マーク is used in daily life for logos and labels.

en.meaning: closure (of a business); suspension of business
examples[].german: We will be closed tomorrow for repairs.
During the closure, please contact us by phone.
I took childcare leave to coincide with my wife's delivery.
en.notes: 休業 means that a shop, company, or school is temporarily not operating: 本日休業, 臨時休業 "unscheduled closure", 休業中. As a する-verb it is intransitive: 店が休業する. For employees there is 育児休業 "childcare leave" (short: 育休). To be distinguished: 定休日 is the regular closing day, 閉店 closing in the evening or for good, and 廃業 the final giving up of a business.

examples[].german: I got plenty of rest over the weekend.
I'm badly worn out, so I need rest.
The manager gave the players a week of rest.
en.notes: 休養 is a longer rest to regain strength or health: 休養を取る, 休養が必要だ, しばらく休養する. It sounds more serious than 休み and is often used for illness, exhaustion, or for athletes and celebrities. 休憩, by contrast, is a short break during work, and 休息 is "rest" in general.

examples[].german: Steel is harder and more durable than iron.
This kitchen knife is made of good steel, so it cuts well.
He has a will of steel.
en.notes: 鋼 (はがね) is "steel", i.e. iron hardened with carbon; the word sounds somewhat craftsmanlike or literary and appears, for example, with knives and swords. In industry and technology one mostly says 鋼鉄, 鉄鋼 (鉄鋼業 "steel industry") or スチール; in compounds 鋼 is read こう (鋼材 "steel material"). Figuratively it stands for hardness and strength: 鋼の意志 "iron will".

en.meaning: being sorry to trouble; feeling obliged; "excuse me"
examples[].german: I'm sorry to trouble you, but could you explain once more?
I am overwhelmed by the kind welcome you gave me.
I apologize for troubling you when you are so busy, but I would ask you to check this.
en.notes: 恐縮 expresses, in polite business language, that one feels indebted to someone or somewhat embarrassed. Most common is 恐縮ですが or お忙しいところ恐縮ですが as an introduction to a request ("Sorry to trouble you, but ..."). In response to praise or hospitality, one says 恐縮です or 恐縮しております ("That is too great an honor"). It is much more formal than すみません and belongs to humble language about oneself.

examples[].german: Complaints about the noise have been received.
I responded politely to the customer's complaint.
I complained to the store manager about the clerk's attitude.
en.notes: 苦情 is a complaint about noise, service, defects, and so on. Typical: 苦情を言う "to complain", 苦情が来る/寄せられる "complaints come in", 苦情に対応する "to handle complaints". In daily life one often hears the loanword クレーム for it; 文句 is colloquial grumbling and nagging. 苦情 sounds matter-of-fact and suits companies, authorities, and property managers.

examples[].german: Please write in the specified format.
Not only the form but also the content is important.
This exam will be conducted in interview format.
en.notes: 形式 is the outer form or prescribed format: 書類の形式, ファイル形式, 面接形式 "in the form of an interview". It often stands in contrast to content (内容): 形式だけ "only for form's sake", 形式的な挨拶 "a formal pleasantry". 形 is the concrete shape of a thing, and 様式 is more a style (architectural style, lifestyle). With で one states in what form something takes place.

examples[].german: We have strengthened security at the venue.
Security guards are checking the entrance.
In preparation for the prime minister's visit, many police officers are guarding the station.
en.notes: 警備 is guarding and securing places, buildings, or events against dangers: 〜を警備する (transitive), 警備を強化する, 警備に当たる. The people are called 警備員, and the companies 警備会社. 警護 is personal protection for a specific person, and 警戒 means "to be alert, on guard".

en.meaning: study visit; observing (rather than taking part)
examples[].german: In a school class, we toured a factory.
Those who wish to tour are asked to make a reservation.
I hurt my leg, so I'll just watch gym class today.
en.notes: 見学 is a visit to learn about something by watching: 工場見学, 社会科見学, 見学会, 〜を見学する. Unlike 見物 (looking at sights for pleasure) or 観光, the aim is learning and information. In school, 見学する also means to just watch in PE class instead of taking part.

examples[].german: We manage personal information with strict care.
After the accident, a thorough inspection was carried out.
Because I was late repeatedly, I received a stern warning from my boss.
en.notes: 厳重 is a な-adjective for measures that are strict and leave no gaps: 厳重な警備, 厳重なチェック, adverbially 厳重に管理する/注意する/抗議する. 厳重注意 is an official "stern warning". For strict people or teachers one says 厳しい; 厳重 describes the thoroughness of control and protection, not character.

examples[].german: The raw material of this paper is wood.
The price of raw materials is rising.
Plastic is mainly made from petroleum.
en.notes: 原料 is the raw material that is processed and transformed during manufacture: 石油を原料とする, 〜の原料は木だ. 材料, by contrast, are materials or ingredients that remain recognizable in the product (cooking ingredients, building materials). On food labels, 原材料 usually appears as the umbrella term. Typical is the phrase 〜を原料にして/として作る.

examples[].german: Please use public transportation.
Transportation is disrupted because of the snow.
Transportation in this town is inconvenient, so you need a car.
en.notes: 交通機関 are the means of transport as a system, above all trains, buses, airplanes, and ships. One almost always hears 公共交通機関 "public transportation", for example in directions. For disruptions one says 交通機関が乱れる/止まる. For individual vehicles in daily life one says 乗り物; 交通 alone is "traffic" in general.

examples[].german: The results of the survey were made public.
The company will announce its new plan next month.
The victims' names have not been made public.
en.notes: 公表 means that authorities, companies, or institutions officially make information public, often information not previously known: 結果を公表する, 名前は公表されていない, 公表を控える "to refrain from disclosure". 発表 is more general (also presentations, results in school), and 公開 means "to make accessible" (films, data, websites). It often appears in the passive in the news.

examples[].german: Do you have any idea where you lost the key?
I don't recognize that name.
I looked everywhere I could think of, but I couldn't find my wallet.
en.notes: 心当たり is an inkling of what something is about or where something might be, because something fitting comes to mind. Almost always with ある/ない: 〜に心当たりがある/ない, politely asked 心当たりはありませんか. 心当たりを探す means "to search everywhere one suspects it might be". Similar is the verb 思い当たる; 見当がつく rather means "to be able to make a rough estimate".

examples[].german: Copper is a metal that conducts electricity well.
He won a bronze medal at the Olympics.
A statue of a famous writer stands at the entrance of the park.
en.notes: 銅 is the metal "copper" (Cu), which conducts electricity and heat well. As a short form it stands for "bronze" in medals: 金・銀・銅, 銅メダル "bronze medal". Other compounds are 銅像 "bronze statue", 青銅 "bronze" and 銅線 "copper wire". In everyday life the word occurs mainly in these fixed combinations; on its own it is used more in technology and chemistry.

examples[].german: I prepared the materials for the meeting.
Preparing the application form takes time.
First create an account, then log in.
en.notes: 作成 is the creation of documents, plans, and data: 資料・書類・計画・報告書を作成する, and digitally アカウントやファイルを作成する. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 作る. Do not confuse it with 作製 (making concrete objects) or with 製作 and 制作 (production of goods and of artistic works, respectively). Often used as a noun: 〜の作成.

examples[].german: If you don't mind, please tell me your name.
There is no problem if you take tomorrow off.
If lack of sleep continues, it will interfere with your work.
en.notes: 差し支え is a "hindrance, problem" and appears mainly in polite set phrases: 差し支えなければ "if you don't mind", 〜ても差し支えありません "there is no objection to ...". With に one indicates what the disruption affects: 仕事に差し支えが出る. The verb for it is 差し支える "to be a hindrance". The phrases are more formal than 大丈夫 or 構いません.

examples[].german: Please bring writing materials on the day.
Everyone brings their own lunch.
Please bring your name seal and come to the counter.
en.notes: 持参 means "to bring along, take with one" and appears above all in notices, invitations, and forms: 〜を持参する, politely ご持参ください, 〜をご持参のうえ. In conversation one mostly says 持ってくる/持っていく. Common are 弁当持参 and 各自持参 "everyone brings their own".

examples[].german: Please explain by giving a real example.
This book contains many useful real-life examples.
Looking at real examples, you can clearly see the effect of this method.
en.notes: 実例 is an example from reality, not an invented one: 実例を挙げる/示す "to cite a concrete example". 例 is the general word, 具体例 stresses concreteness, and 事例 is used in reports and business for documented cases (成功事例). 実例 sounds somewhat literary.

examples[].german: This time we'll focus on safety.
Studying with set priorities is effective.
I intensively reviewed the grammar I'm weak at.
en.notes: 重点 is the point on which one places special weight: 〜に重点を置く "to put the emphasis on ...", 重点項目 "priority item". Very common is the adverb 重点的に "in a focused way, with emphasis". 重要 only means "important", while 重点 denotes a deliberately set priority.

examples[].german: There are many restaurants around the station.
The surrounding roads are congested because of construction.
I bought all the computer peripherals I needed.
en.notes: 周辺 is the area around a place, often as a suffix: 駅周辺, 東京周辺, 周辺地域, 周辺の道路. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 周り. 付近 stresses the immediate proximity, and 近所 is the neighborhood of one's own home. In IT, 周辺機器 means "peripheral devices".

en.meaning: going to work; attendance at work
examples[].german: I go to work at eight every morning.
I don't need to go to work tomorrow.
We were short-staffed, so I even worked on a day off this week.
en.notes: 出勤 means to show up for work or to be present at the workplace: 〜時に出勤する, 出勤時間, 休日出勤 "work on a day off". The opposite is 退勤. 通勤, by contrast, is commuting (the way there), and 出社 specifically means arriving at the company office. As a する-verb it is intransitive.

examples[].german: Please enter through the front entrance.
I faced the problem head-on.
There is a large bank directly in front of the station.
en.notes: 正面 is the front side or the spot directly opposite: 正面玄関 "main entrance", 駅の正面に "directly in front of the station", 真正面 "right opposite". 正面から also means "openly, directly" in a figurative sense: 問題に正面から向き合う. 前 is more general, and 向かい stresses "on the other side". 正面衝突 is a head-on collision.

examples[].german: I went to a shop that handles specialized books.
If it's an e-book, you can read it right away.
A popular blog was published as a book.
en.notes: 書籍 is the matter-of-fact, literary word for "books, publications" and appears above all in the book trade and in specialist contexts: 書籍売り場, 電子書籍 "e-book", 書籍化 "to be published as a book". In conversation one simply says 本. 図書 is the term used by libraries (図書館), and 著書 is the book of a specific author.

examples[].german: Please fill in your date of birth.
We will ask for your date of birth to verify your identity.
Using your date of birth as a password is dangerous.
en.notes: 生年月日 is the full date of birth with year, month, and day, and appears on forms, ID documents, and in identity checks. Note the reading: 月日 is read here as がっぴ, not つきひ. 誕生日, by contrast, is the yearly birthday that one celebrates. Typical: 生年月日を記入する/伺う.

examples[].german: Aluminum is light and easy to recycle.
Please dispose of aluminum cans and steel cans separately.
I wrapped the fish in aluminum foil and baked it in the oven.
en.notes: アルミ is the usual short form of アルミニウム "aluminum"; in everyday speech one hears almost only the short form. Typical compounds are アルミ缶 "aluminum can", アルミホイル "aluminum foil" and アルミサッシ "aluminum window frame". In waste sorting, people distinguish アルミ缶 and スチール缶 "steel can". In scientific texts the full form アルミニウム is more common.

examples[].german: I checked the ingredients before buying.
This medicine contains an ingredient that makes you drowsy.
The composition of hot spring water differs from place to place.
en.notes: 成分 are the components or ingredients of a substance: 有効成分 "active ingredient", 成分表示 "ingredient list", 〜成分が含まれている. It describes what something is chemically composed of; 原料, by contrast, is the raw material before processing, and 材料 is the material or ingredient used in making something.

en.meaning: coming into being; being concluded; taking effect
examples[].german: As a result of the talks, the contract was concluded.
Under these conditions, the deal will not go through.
A new law was passed in the Diet.
en.notes: 成立 means that something comes into being or becomes valid: 契約・取引・交渉が成立する, 法律が成立する "a law is passed". An argument or theory can also 成立する "hold up". The verb is intransitive; to bring something about actively is 成立させる. Do not confuse it with 設立 "to found an organization" (transitive).

examples[].german: I received an explanation of the job as a whole.
I'm interested in Japanese culture in general.
Sales were good overall this year.
en.notes: 全般 denotes a field in its entirety and mostly stands as a suffix: 仕事全般, 生活全般, 日本文化全般. Common are the adverb 全般的に "overall, on the whole" and the phrase 〜全般にわたって "covering the entire field of ...". 全体 stresses the whole as a unit, whereas 一般 means "general, common" or "the public".

examples[].german: Shipping is included in the price of the goods.
Please tell me the shipping cost overseas.
Shipping is free for purchases of 5,000 yen or more.
en.notes: 送料 is the shipping cost for parcels or letters, not the price of the goods. Typical phrases in online shopping: 送料無料 "free shipping", 送料込み "shipping included", 送料別 "shipping extra", 送料がかかる "shipping is charged". For postage on stamps one also says 郵便料金.

examples[].german: We have put in place a setup in which people can work safely.
We will start the business under a new structure.
The hospital accepts patients around the clock.
en.notes: 体制 is the organizational structure or system with which something is run: 体制を整える "to set up a structure", 新体制, 二十四時間体制 "around-the-clock system". Politically it also denotes the ruling system (反体制). Do not confuse it with the identically read 態勢 "readiness, posture" and 体勢 "body posture"; 制度, by contrast, are established rules and institutions.

examples[].german: Please adjust the room temperature.
I adjusted the height of the chair.
The button for adjusting the TV volume is broken.
en.notes: 調節 is regulating or adjusting a measurable quantity to the right level: 温度・音量・高さ・スピードを調節する, 体温調節. 調整 is similar but is used more for coordination between people, schedules, or opinions (日程を調整する). As a する-verb it is transitive with を.

examples[].german: I'd like to add one more order.
I added concrete examples to the explanation.
My baggage exceeded the weight limit, so I paid an additional fee.
en.notes: 追加 means to add something to what already exists: 〜に〜を追加する, 追加注文, 追加料金 "extra charge", 追加の説明. The Japanese verb 加える is more general, and 付け加える is used above all for remarks added afterward. 追加 sounds matter-of-fact and is very common in restaurants, online services, and offices.

examples[].german: Please don't leave luggage in the aisle.
I reserved an aisle seat.
The station and the airport are connected by an underground passage.
en.notes: 通路 is a passage or aisle through which one walks: in trains, airplanes, theaters, stores, or underground (地下通路). 通路側の席 is the aisle seat, as opposed to 窓側. 廊下 is specifically the corridor in houses and schools, and 通り is a street. On signs one often reads 通路に物を置かないでください.

examples[].german: The capacity of this room is ten people.
Applications were closed because the capacity was reached.
The elevator exceeded its capacity, and the buzzer sounded.
en.notes: 定員 is the set maximum number of people, for example in courses, vehicles, or elevators. Typical are 定員に達する "to be full", 定員を超える, 定員オーバー, and 定員になり次第締め切る "closing as soon as capacity is reached". Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 店員 "shop clerk". 定員割れ means that there are too few applicants.

examples[].german: This shop is closed on Wednesdays.
Let's check the closing day before we go out.
Many hair salons are closed on Mondays.
en.notes: 定休日 is the regularly recurring closing day of a shop or restaurant, for example 定休日は水曜日です or 月曜定休. A one-off, unscheduled closing day is called 臨時休業. 休日 is generally a day off, independent of any business.

examples[].german: The foundations of buildings are made of concrete.
This apartment building is reinforced concrete and resistant to earthquakes.
In summer, concrete roads get hot, so I walk the dog in the evening.
en.notes: コンクリート is "concrete"; typical combinations are コンクリートの建物/壁, 鉄筋コンクリート "reinforced concrete" and コンクリートを流す "to pour concrete". Colloquially it is shortened to コンクリ, and コンクリートジャングル figuratively stands for a big city dominated by concrete. Note: the adjective "concrete" (as opposed to abstract) is not コンクリート but 具体的.

en.meaning: the day (in question); the day itself
examples[].german: On the day, please gather by nine o'clock.
You can buy tickets even on the day itself.
On the day itself, it suddenly started raining, and the game was canceled.
en.notes: 当日 is "the day in question", i.e. the day on which a planned event takes place; it can also stand adverbially (当日は…). Typical: 当日券 "same-day ticket at the box office", 当日限り有効 "valid only on the day", 当日になって "when the day came". 今日 and 本日 refer to today, whereas 当日 refers to the day of the event, whenever that is.

examples[].german: My bicycle was stolen.
I lock up to prevent theft.
I filed a theft report with the police.
en.notes: 盗難 is a theft from the point of view of the victim and is not used with する. Typical: 〜が盗難に遭う "to be stolen", 盗難届 "theft report", 盗難防止, 盗難事件. The act itself is described with the verbs 盗む or 盗まれる; the thief is called 泥棒. 盗難 sounds matter-of-fact and is typical of the police, insurance, and the news.

examples[].german: I checked the contents of the box.
What's inside is more important than appearance.
It was a meeting that was only long, with no substance at all.
en.notes: 中身 is what is inside something: 箱・財布・かばんの中身. Figuratively it means "substance, content", as opposed to the exterior (見た目より中身). 中身がない means "empty, without substance". 内容 is the more matter-of-fact word for the content of texts, conversations or contracts; 中身 sounds more everyday and concrete.

examples[].german: Please confirm the date and time of the interview.
We will let you know the detailed date and time later.
You can specify the date and time of delivery.
en.notes: 日時 is the combination of date and time, for example for appointments, deliveries, and events: 日時を決める/指定する/変更する, 開催日時. 日付 is just the date, and 日程 is the schedule spanning several days. 日時 is matter-of-fact and typical of invitations and forms.

examples[].german: I buy daily necessities at a nearby store.
Before moving, I gathered the daily necessities I needed.
Prices have risen, and the prices of daily necessities have gone up as well.
en.notes: 日用品 are things one needs every day, such as soap, toothpaste, toilet paper, or detergent; in stores there is a 日用品売り場. Food is normally not included. Similar is 生活用品; 雑貨 are more small goods and decorative items. Note: do not confuse にちようひん with 日曜日.

examples[].german: Please summarize the author's opinion.
The author looks at this problem from a different angle.
The author worked for many years overseas as a journalist.
en.notes: 筆者 is the person who wrote the text at hand; very typical in reading comprehension questions (筆者の考え, 筆者が言いたいこと). In essays, authors also use 筆者 for themselves. 作者 is the creator of a literary or artistic work, 著者 the author of a book, and 作家 a professional writer.

examples[].german: I looked through the materials once.
The necessary tools are all there more or less.
I can cook the basics, but I'm not good at it.
en.notes: 一通り means "once through everything, on the whole", without going into depth: 一通り目を通す "to skim through once", 一通り説明する. As a noun with の: 一通りの知識 "basic knowledge"; 一通りできる means "to have mastered the essentials". Do not confuse it with 一通（いっつう）, the counter for a letter. Often also written in hiragana, ひととおり.

examples[].german: I looked for related literature in the library.
I included references at the end of the report.
According to old documents, this temple was built 800 years ago.
en.notes: 文献 are written sources, especially for research and academic work: 文献を調べる, 参考文献 "bibliography", 古い文献 "old writings". It is an academic word; in daily life one speaks of 本 or 資料. 資料 also includes data, photos, and documents, while 文献 covers only texts.

examples[].german: I showed the distribution of the population on a map.
This plant is distributed over a wide area.
Looking at the age distribution, you can see that there are many young users.
en.notes: 分布 is the distribution of something across space or in statistics: 人口分布, 年齢の分布, 分布図. As a する-verb it is intransitive with に: 〜が広い地域に分布している "is widely distributed", typical for plants and animals. For actively handing out things, one says 配る or 配布する instead.

examples[].german: I'm taking a train bound for Kyoto.
He is active in the field of music.
Opinions on this matter are coming in from all quarters.
en.notes: 方面 denotes a direction or area, mostly as a suffix: 京都方面行きの電車, 新宿方面. Figuratively it stands for a field or area of expertise: 音楽方面, その方面に詳しい, 各方面から "from all sides". 方向 is the pure direction, 方角 the compass direction, and 分野 the field in the narrower sense.

examples[].german: We should reduce the use of plastic.
Some plastic containers can't be used in the microwave.
Plastic waste that flows into the sea has become a problem.
en.notes: プラスチック is "plastic"; as an attribute it takes の: プラスチックの容器 "plastic container". Common are プラスチックごみ "plastic waste", 海洋プラスチック "marine plastic" and, in waste sorting, the short form プラ (プラごみ). A plastic bag, however, is not called プラスチック袋 but ビニール袋 or レジ袋.

examples[].german: People under eighteen years of age cannot enter.
There were fewer than a hundred participants.
Purchases under 1,000 yen do not earn points.
en.notes: 未満 means "less than" and excludes the stated value: 十八歳未満 means persons up to and including 17. 以下, by contrast, includes the value; the counterpart of 未満 is 以上 or 超 ("over, not including the value"). Typical in regulations, prices, and statistics: 〜未満の方, 千円未満.

examples[].german: This facility is run by a private company.
We will make use of private-sector experience in administration.
There is a folk remedy that says ginger is good for colds.
en.notes: 民間 denotes the non-governmental, private or civilian sphere as opposed to the state and authorities: 民間企業, 民間人 "civilian", 民間の経験, 民営化 "privatization". A second meaning is "popular, handed down among the people": 民間療法 "folk remedy", 民間信仰. Opposing terms are 公共, 官, or 国営.

examples[].german: We also accept documents by mail.
I mailed the application form yesterday.
We will mail the results to your home at a later date.
en.notes: 郵送 is sending by post: 書類を郵送する, 郵送で受け付ける, 郵送料. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 送る and stresses the postal route. 配送 is the delivery of goods (also by courier services), and 発送 is sending off in general. Typical in official and business texts, politely 郵送いたします.

examples[].german: I'll take spare batteries with me.
I prepared extra materials before the meeting.
It's a movie you can enjoy even without any background knowledge.
en.notes: 予備 denotes something kept ready for an emergency and mostly stands with の before a noun: 予備の電池, 予備の鍵. In fixed compounds it also means "preparatory, pre-": 予備知識 "background knowledge", 予備校 "cram school for entrance exams", 予備日 "backup date". Unlike 代わり ("substitute in place of something"), 予備 stresses that something extra is on hand in reserve.

examples[].german: Please fill in the name box.
You can leave empty boxes as they are.
Every morning I start reading the newspaper from the sports section.
en.notes: 欄 is a delimited area in forms, tables, or newspapers. In forms it means "box, field": 名前の欄に記入する, 空欄 "blank field", 備考欄 "remarks field". In newspapers and magazines it stands for a "column" or "section", often as a suffix: スポーツ欄, 投書欄. The meaning "railing" is rare in daily life; for that one says 手すり.

examples[].german: A trip was what got me started learning Japanese.
My life changed because of a small encounter.
I just can't find an opening to talk to her.
en.notes: きっかけ is the impulse or trigger through which something begins; mostly written in kana. Typical are 〜がきっかけで, 〜をきっかけに（して） "triggered by", and 〜のきっかけになる. With つかむ or 作る it means "to find/create an opportunity", for example to talk to someone. In contrast to 原因 ("cause", often negative), きっかけ is neutral and stresses the starting point of a development.

examples[].german: Please underline the parts you don't understand.
There are three places that need repair.
There are mistakes in three places in this text.
en.notes: 箇所 is a specific spot in a text, on an object, or at a location: 分からない箇所, 故障した箇所. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 所 and is typical of manuals, reports, and corrections. As a counter it follows numbers: 三箇所（さんかしょ）; in newspapers and on signs one often sees 3か所, 3カ所, or 3ヶ所 instead.

examples[].german: I somehow have no energy today.
The book I picked more or less at random was very interesting.
I vaguely understood what he wanted to say.
en.notes: 何となく describes a feeling or action without a clearly nameable reason: 何となく不安だ "vaguely uneasy", 何となく選ぶ "to choose on a whim". With 分かる it means "to understand roughly, vaguely". It is often written in kana (なんとなく). Similar, but more focused on the inexplicable, is なぜか "for some reason"; どことなく rather stresses an atmosphere that is hard to pin down.

en.meaning: at least; at the very least
examples[].german: At least tell me the reason.
Even if we're busy, let's at least eat breakfast.
If only I had at least one more day off!
en.notes: せめて expresses a minimum with which one is just barely satisfied: "at least, at the very least". It is often combined with だけでも, くらい, or with wish and request forms such as 〜てください, 〜たい, 〜ばいいのに. Unlike 少なくとも, which states a matter-of-fact lower limit, せめて sounds pleading or regretful. It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: Society is constantly changing.
I can hear the sound of cars continuously from outside the window.
He has continued to make efforts without ever stopping.
en.notes: 絶えず means "uninterruptedly, constantly" and comes from 絶える "to cease" with the negative ず. It feels somewhat more literary than いつも or ずっと and suits ongoing changes, noises, or efforts: 絶えず変化する, 絶えず努力する. Equivalent in meaning but even more formal is 常に; colloquially one rather says しょっちゅう or ずっと.

examples[].german: Glass is fitted in the windows.
A child broke the window glass with a ball.
This cup is made of glass, so please be careful.
en.notes: ガラス is glass as a material and is written in katakana (borrowed from Dutch). Typical are 窓ガラス "window pane", ガラス製 "made of glass" and ガラスが割れる. A drinking glass, on the other hand, is called コップ or, for wine and the like, グラス - ガラス refers only to the material. Neutral in tone.

en.meaning: to adopt; to incorporate; to take in
examples[].german: I introduced new methods into my lessons.
We made improvements by taking customers' opinions on board.
It looks like rain, so please bring the laundry in.
en.notes: 取り入れる has two main uses. Concretely it means "to bring in, gather in": 洗濯物を取り入れる "to bring in the laundry", 作物を取り入れる "to bring in the harvest". Figuratively it means "to adopt, introduce": 意見を取り入れる, 新しい技術を取り入れる, often with に for the target (授業に取り入れる). A synonym, but more formal, is 導入する; 受け入れる stresses accepting rather than incorporating.

examples[].german: Including tax, it comes to 1,000 yen.
Including the children, there are ten of us in all.
Including me, nobody knew about it.
en.notes: 含める is transitive: someone actively includes something in a group or total. Very common is the te-form 〜を含めて "including, inclusive of": 税金を含めて, 私を含めて. The intransitive counterpart 含む means "to contain" (この料金は税金を含む), and the passive 含まれる "to be included". For prices one also says 税込み for short.

en.meaning: to be in order; to be ready; to be prepared
examples[].german: The preparations for departure are complete.
We can start once the necessary conditions are in place.
This hospital is well equipped.
en.notes: 整う is intransitive: something is fully prepared or in good order. Typical are 準備が整う, 条件が整う, 設備が整っている "to be well equipped", and 整った顔 "regular features". The transitive counterpart is 整える (準備を整える, 服装を整える). Compared with できる or 終わる, 整う sounds somewhat more elevated and stresses that everything necessary is fully in place.

en.meaning: to drag on; to be prolonged
examples[].german: The meeting dragged on, so I got home late.
My cold is dragging on.
If the negotiations drag on, it will affect the plan.
en.notes: 長引く is intransitive and means that something lasts longer than expected or desired: 会議が長引く, 交渉が長引く, 風邪が長引く. It therefore usually has a negative nuance. There is no transitive counterpart in the narrow sense; someone who deliberately prolongs something 長引かせる (causative) it. More neutral is 長く続く.

en.meaning: to raise; to heighten; to enhance
examples[].german: I want to improve my conversation skills through practice.
It is an activity that raises awareness of safety.
Companies are investing in new technology to enhance their competitiveness.
en.notes: 高める is transitive: one deliberately raises quality, awareness, or ability, for example 能力を高める, 意識を高める, 効果を高める. The intransitive counterpart 高まる describes something increasing on its own (関心が高まる). For concrete heights and prices one rather says 上げる; 高める suits abstract values and sounds somewhat more elevated.

en.meaning: to aim for; to head for
examples[].german: I'm aiming to pass next year's exam.
We walked toward the summit of the mountain.
My older brother studies every day because he aims to become a doctor.
en.notes: 目指す takes its goal with を: 合格を目指す, 医者を目指す "to aim to become a doctor", 優勝を目指す. Spatially it means "to head for, make for": 頂上を目指して歩く. The form 〜を目指して often introduces a purpose. Unlike 狙う ("to aim at something", often strategic or sly), 目指す sounds positive and ambitious.

en.meaning: to apply; to fit (to); to assign
examples[].german: This rule cannot be applied to every case.
It is easier to understand if you apply it to an example.
You plug the numbers into the formula and calculate.
en.notes: 当てはめる is transitive: you apply a rule, pattern or formula to a case, or fit something in, mostly as X を Y に当てはめる. Its intransitive counterpart 当てはまる means "to apply, to fit" (この規則は例外にも当てはまる) and often appears in exercises: 当てはまる言葉を選びなさい. A more formal synonym is 適用する.

examples[].german: Sales of the new product are going well.
Sales change depending on the weather.
Products that sell poorly get marked down.
en.notes: 売れ行き describes how well a product sells, i.e. sales or demand. Typical uses are 売れ行きがいい・悪い, 売れ行きが好調だ・伸びる・落ちる. It refers to the trend, not to a total; for revenue in money, say 売り上げ. The word is equally common in business news and in everyday business.

examples[].german: I woke up at daybreak.
The rain continued until dawn.
The sky at dawn was very beautiful.
en.notes: 明け方 is the time just before and while it gets light; it is used with に (明け方に目が覚める) or まで (明け方まで続く). 夜明け has the same meaning but is more neutral in everyday speech; 早朝 refers more generally to early morning, including after sunrise. The counterpart in the evening is 夕方 or 日暮れ.

examples[].german: His face looked pale.
The pale light of the moon came in through the window.
You're so pale because you always stay at home.
en.notes: 青白い is an i-adjective made of 青 and 白 and has two uses: "pale, pallid" for an unhealthy complexion (青白い顔をしている) and "bluish white" for cold light such as moonlight or screen light. For turning pale suddenly from shock, 顔が青くなる or 真っ青になる are more usual. 顔色が悪い is also a neutral way to say "pale".

examples[].german: This engine has good fuel economy.
On cold mornings the engine hardly starts.
It was only in the afternoon that I finally got going.
en.notes: エンジン is the "engine" of cars, aircraft or ships, usually a combustion engine; electric motors are called モーター. Typical are エンジンをかける "to start the engine", エンジンを切る/止める "to turn off" and エンジンがかかる "to start". Figuratively エンジンがかかる means "to get going"; in IT there is also 検索エンジン "search engine".

examples[].german: I am sorry for being late.
I feel sorry for having caused trouble to everyone.
I am sorry to ask, but could I take tomorrow off?
en.notes: 申し訳ない expresses deep regret: "it is inexcusable, I am sorry". Towards superiors or customers, the polite forms 申し訳ありません or 申し訳ございません are used; 申し訳ないです is more colloquial, and 申し訳ない alone sounds familiar or like an inner thought. 申し訳ないんですが serves to introduce a request. It is much stronger than すみません and is also used to express thanks when you have put someone to trouble.

examples[].german: I checked next week's schedule.
Let's make a schedule that isn't unreasonable.
My schedule is packed this week, so I have no time to meet.
en.notes: スケジュール is a time plan or schedule. Typical combinations: スケジュールを立てる "to draw up", スケジュールを組む "to put together", スケジュールを確認する, スケジュールが詰まっている "to be fully booked". A single appointment is 予定; スケジュール means the overall planning across several appointments. In formal texts, 日程 is also used for this.

examples[].german: I interviewed the athlete.
I put the content of the interview together into an article.
I was interviewed by a TV station in front of the station.
