en.notes: インタビュー is questioning by the media or for a survey. The person asking says 〜にインタビューする or インタビューをする; the person being questioned says インタビューを受ける or インタビューに答える. For a job interview, Japanese does not use インタビュー but 面接.

examples[].german: I was sent a sample of the product.
You can't judge from just a small sample.
Sample dishes are lined up in front of the shop.
en.notes: サンプル is a sample or specimen, such as a free product sample (無料サンプル) or a random sample in statistics and research. In Japan it also refers to the plastic replicas of dishes displayed in front of restaurants (食品サンプル). For cosmetics or food samples in a shop, 試供品 or 試食 are also used; 見本 is the Japanese word for "sample, model".

examples[].german: A balance between work and rest is important.
I lost my balance and almost fell.
I cook meals with a balanced diet in mind.
en.notes: バランス is both physical balance (バランスを崩す "to lose one's balance") and balance in a figurative sense: 栄養のバランス, 仕事と生活のバランス. バランスを取る means "to keep one's balance, to balance out", バランスがいい "well balanced". The native Japanese equivalent is 釣り合い, but it is much rarer.

examples[].german: I choose books that suit my level.
This exam is at a fairly high level.
I played a match against world-class players.
en.notes: レベル means level, grade or standard: レベルが高い・低い, レベルが上がる, 自分のレベルに合う. As a suffix it forms expressions such as 世界レベル "world class" or 生活レベル "standard of living". For official grades and exams, 級 or 段階 are often used, and for water level 水位 is more usual. Colloquially, 〜レベル also expresses an extent: プロレベル "at a professional level".

examples[].german: Please show me the menu.
The menu changes with each season.
Please select a language from the menu on the screen.
en.notes: メニュー refers, in a restaurant, to the menu or the range of dishes offered. メニューを見せてください asks to be allowed to see the menu; メニューが変わる describes a change in the offerings. On a computer, a selection of functions can also be called メニュー. The place or the following verb shows which kind of selection is meant.

examples[].german: I am waiting in the hotel lobby.
There are chairs in the lobby that you can use freely.
The hospital lobby was full of people waiting for their examinations.
en.notes: ロビー is the entrance or waiting hall in hotels, hospitals, theaters or office buildings. One meets there (ロビーで待ち合わせる) or waits (ロビーで待つ). A smaller waiting room, for example at a doctor's, is called 待合室; the entrance area of an apartment building is more likely 玄関 or エントランス.

examples[].german: I put my luggage in a locker at the station.
I lost the locker key.
In the changing room at the pool, I put my clothes in a locker and changed.
en.notes: ロッカー is a lockable compartment or locker, for example at a station (コインロッカー "coin-operated locker"), at school, at a gym or in a changing room. You put something in (ロッカーに入れる) and lock it (ロッカーに鍵をかける). The homophone meaning "rock musician" is a separate, rarer word.

examples[].german: Electric cars run on a motor.
The washing machine's motor is broken and makes a strange noise.
As a child, I built a toy car powered by a motor.
en.notes: モーター is above all the "electric motor", which converts electrical energy into motion - in fans, washing machines, toys or electric cars. Combustion engines are mostly called エンジン in Japanese. In compounds such as モーターショー "motor show" and モータースポーツ "motorsport", モーター stands generally for motor vehicles; a power generator, on the other hand, is called 発電機.

examples[].german: I examined the patterns of mistakes.
I live following the same pattern every day.
The exam questions follow several set patterns.
en.notes: パターン is a recurring pattern, both in data and tasks (問題のパターン, 文型のパターン) and in behavior: いつものパターン "the usual routine", ワンパターン "always the same, unimaginative". For fabric patterns, 柄 or 模様 are more usual in everyday speech. Typical are 〜のパターンを覚える and 同じパターンで.

examples[].german: The refrigerator is completely empty.
I cleared away the empty boxes.
I was so nervous that my mind went blank.
en.notes: 空っぽ is an emphatic, spoken form of 空（から）"empty" and means "completely empty". It is used as a na-adjective or with の: 空っぽだ, 空っぽの箱, 空っぽになる. Figuratively, 頭が空っぽになる means "to have a blackout" or "to think of nothing". For rooms or seats that are unoccupied, 空いている is more fitting.

examples[].german: This street has a lot of foot traffic even at night.
I avoided roads with little foot traffic.
It was early in the morning, so there was hardly anyone about yet.
en.notes: 人通り refers to how many people pass along a street or place. It almost always appears with 多い・少ない: 人通りが多い "busy", 人通りの少ない道 "a little-used street". For crowds in a place, 人込み or 混雑 is used instead; 交通 refers to vehicles.

en.meaning: clothing, food and shelter; basic necessities
examples[].german: I record the costs of clothing, food and housing every month.
This organization supports the clothing, food and shelter of people who lost their homes in the disaster.
It is enough for me if I can live without worrying about clothing, food and housing.
en.notes: Summarizes the three areas of clothing, food and housing; the order in the Japanese word is fixed. Common are 衣食住に困る (to be unable to secure the basic necessities) and 衣食住を支える (to support the basic necessities). Especially common in texts about living conditions, household costs and social support.

examples[].german: Territorial disputes are a diplomatic issue.
Both countries claim that island as their own territory.
In the past, many countries tried to expand their territory through war.
en.notes: 領土 is the territory of a state, especially the land area over which a state has sovereignty. It is accompanied by 領海 ("territorial waters") and 領空 ("airspace"), together 領域. Typical: 領土問題 ("territorial dispute"), 領土を拡大する, 領土を主張する, 北方領土. For an area in the general sense, people say 地域 or 土地 instead.

examples[].german: Robots are working in the factory.
Since I bought a robot vacuum cleaner, cleaning has become much easier.
He is like a robot that only does what his boss says.
en.notes: ロボット means a "robot" - industrial robots (産業用ロボット), household appliances such as ロボット掃除機 "robot vacuum cleaner" or characters from anime and science fiction. Typical verbs are ロボットを作る/動かす/操作する. Figuratively and pejoratively, a person who only carries out orders is called a ロボット or 操り人形 "puppet". To be distinguished from this is AI or 人工知能, that is, software without a physical body.

examples[].german: This instrument is extremely precise.
The accuracy of weather forecasts is improving every year.
A large amount of data is used to improve the accuracy of machine translation.
en.notes: 精度 is the "precision, accuracy" of measurements, devices, machines or forecasts. Typical are 精度が高い/低い, 精度を上げる/高める and 高精度 "high-precision". Unlike 正確さ "correctness", which also applies to people and statements, 精度 is a technical term for measurable quality, e.g. 翻訳の精度 or 天気予報の精度. Not to be confused with the identically read 制度 "system, institution".

examples[].german: A new system was introduced.
Because of a system failure, the bank's ATMs could not be used.
It's my first time at this restaurant, so I don't quite understand how the ordering system works.
en.notes: システム means "system" - technical systems (IT, control) as well as organizational procedures. Typical are システムを導入する "to introduce", システムが止まる "to go down", システム障害 "system failure" and システムエンジニア. For social or legal systems (tax system, education system) one uses 制度 more often. In everyday life, システム is often used to explain how something works: この店のシステム "how things work in this shop".

examples[].german: A software update is necessary.
My older sister works at a software development company.
This software can be downloaded for free.
en.notes: ソフトウェア is "software"; in everyday speech it is almost always shortened to ソフト (ゲームソフト, 会計ソフト, ソフトを入れる "to install software"). Typical are ソフトウェアを更新する/アップデートする, ソフトウェア開発 and ソフトウェアエンジニア. The spelling ソフトウエア with a large エ also occurs; the counterpart is ハードウェア.

examples[].german: It stopped working due to a hardware failure.
This game doesn't run on old hardware.
She can design not only software but also hardware.
en.notes: ハードウェア is "hardware", i.e. the physical components of a computer or device; in everyday speech often shortened to ハード (ハードとソフト). Typical are ハードウェアの故障/性能 and ハードウェアを交換する. Note: ハード alone can also mean "hard, strenuous" (ハードな仕事 "a hard job"). A hardware store, on the other hand, is called ホームセンター.

examples[].german: I wrote a new program.
I received the concert program at the entrance.
New employees take part in a three-month training program.
en.notes: プログラム has several meanings: a "program" as the schedule of an event (コンサートのプログラム), the printed "program booklet" and the computer program. Typical are プログラムを書く/組む "to program", プログラムを実行する "to run" as well as 研修プログラム "training program". Programming as an activity is mostly called プログラミング; a television program, on the other hand, is 番組.

examples[].german: I downloaded a handy app.
With this app, you can instantly see where to transfer trains.
I ran out of storage, so I deleted apps I don't use.
en.notes: アプリ is the common short form of アプリケーション; in everyday speech one almost only says アプリ, especially for smartphone apps (スマホアプリ). Typical combinations: アプリをダウンロードする／インストールする (colloquially アプリを入れる), アプリを開く, アプリを更新する, アプリを削除する or, casually, アプリを消す. The long form アプリケーション sounds more technical and often refers to computer programs.

examples[].german: I saved the data to the cloud.
I share photos with my family on the cloud.
The company plans to switch to a cloud service from next year.
en.notes: クラウド refers in IT to the "cloud", i.e. storage and services on the internet: クラウドに保存する, クラウドにアップロードする, クラウド上のデータ, クラウドサービス. Note: the same katakana spelling also stands for English "crowd", e.g. in クラウドファンディング "crowdfunding". The cloud in the sky, in contrast, is always 雲.

examples[].german: We strengthened security measures.
Security in this building is strict, and you can't get in without an employee ID.
If a password is too simple, there is a security problem.
en.notes: セキュリティ means security in the sense of protection against attacks, theft or unauthorized access - for computers as well as for buildings. Typical: セキュリティ対策, セキュリティを強化する, セキュリティが厳しい／甘い, セキュリティ上の問題. For "safety" as harmlessness (traffic, food) one uses 安全, for national security 安全保障. The spelling セキュリティー with a long vowel is also common.

examples[].german: The computer was infected with a virus.
Influenza is a disease caused by a virus.
Let's wash our hands to prevent viruses from entering the body.
en.notes: ウイルス stands both for disease-causing agents and for computer viruses. Typical: ウイルスに感染する "to get infected", ウイルスを除去する／駆除する "to remove a virus", ウイルス対策ソフト. The spelling ウィルス with a small ィ is also common in everyday use, but ウイルス is the official and medical form. Bacteria, in contrast, are called 細菌 or simply 菌.

examples[].german: You need a passport to cross the border.
In Europe, you can easily cross borders by train.
Near the border, the armies of the two countries face each other.
en.notes: 国境 is the border between two states, normally read こっきょう. Typical: 国境を越える ("to cross the border"), 国境線, 国境付近, 国境なき医師団 ("Doctors Without Borders"). For borders within a country, e.g. between prefectures, one says 県境（けんざかい）; the old reading くにざかい referred to the historical provinces. In general, "border, limit" is 境 or 限界.

examples[].german: The video stalls because of insufficient bandwidth.
During the meeting, please refrain from downloading large files so that bandwidth is kept available.
This frequency band is used for mobile phones.
en.notes: 帯域 is a technical word: originally a "frequency band, range" (周波数帯域), in IT the short form of 帯域幅 "bandwidth". Typical: 帯域が不足する, 帯域が狭い／広い, 帯域を確保する, 帯域制限 "throttling". In everyday speech one rather says 回線速度 or 通信速度; 帯域 sounds technical.

examples[].german: In the mountains, there is no reception.
In the basement the signal was so weak that the call dropped.
Smartphones communicate with the base station using radio waves.
en.notes: 電波 technically means "radio waves", but in everyday life above all the mobile or Wi-Fi "reception": 電波が届く／届かない, 電波が弱い／悪い, 電波が入らない "no signal"; with no signal at all one is 圏外. Technically: 電波を発する, 電波を受信する. Colloquially and pejoratively, someone who talks confused nonsense is called 電波系 - one should know this meaning but use it carefully.

examples[].german: Virtual reality technology is attracting attention in the gaming industry.
With virtual reality, you can travel all over the world while staying at home.
At the medical school, they practice surgery in virtual reality.
en.notes: 仮想現実 is the Japanese translation of "virtual reality" and sounds technical or journalistic; in everyday speech one mostly says VR. 仮想 means "virtual, hypothetical" and is also found in 仮想通貨 "cryptocurrency". Typical: 仮想現実の世界, 仮想現実を体験する, 仮想現実の技術. To be distinguished from 拡張現実 "augmented reality", which only supplements the real environment.

examples[].german: Apps using augmented reality are popular.
With augmented reality technology, if you point your smartphone, you can see how furniture would look placed in your room.
The museum uses augmented reality to recreate what the town looked like in the past.
en.notes: 拡張現実 is "augmented reality": 拡張 means "expansion", so digital information is laid over the real environment. In contrast, 仮想現実 replaces reality completely. The word is technical-formal; in everyday speech one mostly says AR. Typical: 拡張現実を使ったアプリ, 拡張現実の技術, 拡張現実で再現する.

examples[].german: Demand for semiconductors is rising worldwide.
Because of the semiconductor shortage, my new car arrived a full six months late.
Silicon is a typical semiconductor material.
en.notes: 半導体 is the "semiconductor", literally "half-conductor", between 導体 "conductor" and 絶縁体 "insulator". In business news it often stands for computer chips in general: 半導体メーカー, 半導体産業, 半導体不足 "chip shortage". Colloquially, one also says チップ for the individual component.

examples[].german: Designing electronic circuits is complicated.
The light won't turn on; the circuit seems to be broken somewhere.
I can't understand that person's way of thinking at all.
en.notes: 回路 is a circuit: 電気回路, 電子回路, 集積回路 "integrated circuit"; 回路が切れる "to be interrupted". Figuratively, people speak of 思考回路 "thought pattern, way of thinking", often slightly mockingly. Do not confuse it with 回線, which means a line or connection (電話回線, インターネット回線).

examples[].german: I solder the components onto the circuit board.
My computer was broken, and when I took it in for repair, the whole board was replaced.
This factory manufactures circuit boards for smartphones.
en.notes: 基板 is the circuit board in electronic devices (プリント基板), in manufacturing also a "carrier material, substrate". Typical: 基板に部品をはんだ付けする, 基板を交換する. Beware of the identically read 基盤 "foundation, basis" (生活の基盤, 経営基盤) - a common writing mistake, even among native speakers.

examples[].german: The miniaturization of electronic devices is progressing.
Recently I read e-books more often than paper books.
An atom consists of a nucleus and electrons.
en.notes: 電子 is the "electron" in physics, but is used far more often as a modifier meaning "electronic, digital": 電子機器, 電子レンジ "microwave", 電子メール, 電子書籍 "e-book", 電子マネー. To be distinguished is 電気 "electricity, power", e.g. 電気製品 "electrical appliance". On its own, 電子 appears almost only in a scientific context.

examples[].german: A new device went on sale.
This service supports up to five devices with one account.
If you can't connect the device via Bluetooth, please restart it.
en.notes: デバイス is IT jargon for a (terminal) device such as a smartphone, tablet or PC, also for accessories and components. Typical: デバイスを接続する, 対応デバイス, 複数のデバイスで使う. In normal speech one rather says 機器, 端末 or simply 機械; デバイス sounds technical and appears mainly in manuals and advertising.

examples[].german: The temperature sensor detected an abnormality.
When someone approaches, the sensor reacts and the light turns on.
This wristwatch has a sensor and can measure heart rate.
en.notes: センサー is a "sensor". Typical: センサーが反応する, センサーが異常を検知する／感知する, センサー付きの照明, 人感センサー "motion detector", 温度センサー. In technical texts one also finds the spelling センサ without the long vowel.

examples[].german: My smartphone's battery runs out quickly.
I left the lights on and the car battery died.
This model has good battery life, so it's fine even if you don't charge it for a day.
en.notes: バッテリー is mainly the rechargeable battery in a phone, laptop or car; ordinary disposable batteries are called 電池 or 乾電池. Typical: バッテリーが切れる／なくなる "to be dead", バッテリーが減る, バッテリーの持ちがいい "lasts long". For a car, people say バッテリーが上がる for "the battery is dead". In baseball, バッテリー refers to the duo of pitcher and catcher.

examples[].german: I charge my smartphone before going to bed.
I forgot my charger, so I bought one at a convenience store.
Work was busy, so I plan to relax and recharge at home over the weekend.
en.notes: 充電 is electrical "charging"; as a する-verb it is transitive: スマホを充電する. Noun combinations: 充電が切れる "the battery is dead", 充電が少ない, 充電中, 充電器 "charger". Colloquially, 充電する also means "to recharge one's batteries", e.g. after stressful weeks. The opposite is 放電 "discharge"; not to be confused with 発電 "power generation".

examples[].german: The number of areas generating electricity with wind power has increased.
A new power plant is scheduled to be built nearby.
I bought a home generator in case of a power outage during a disaster.
en.notes: 発電 is "power generation"; as a する-verb the means takes で: 風力で発電する. Very common in compounds: 発電所 "power plant", 発電機 "generator", 火力発電, 水力発電, 原子力発電, 太陽光発電. Not to be confused with 充電 "charging" and 停電 "power outage"; 電力 denotes electricity as power or resource.

examples[].german: I installed solar panels on the roof.
Thanks to solar power generation, the electricity bill has become much cheaper.
Plants use sunlight to produce nutrients.
en.notes: 太陽光 is "sunlight" above all in the technical and energy-policy sense: 太陽光発電 "photovoltaics", 太陽光パネル "solar module", 太陽光エネルギー. For sunlight in everyday life, one rather says 日光 (直射日光を避ける), 日差し or speaks of the 日当たり of an apartment. In biology 太陽光 is usual in connection with photosynthesis.

examples[].german: Wind power is environmentally friendly.
Many wind turbines for wind power are lined up out at sea.
Wind power and hydropower are both renewable energy.
en.notes: 風力 is "wind power" and appears mostly in compounds such as 風力発電 "wind power generation" or 風力発電所 "wind farm"; 水力, 火力 and 原子力 are formed analogously. In weather reports for shipping, 風力 also denotes the "wind force" on the Beaufort scale (風力3). Wind speed in meters per second, on the other hand, is called 風速.

examples[].german: The disposal of industrial waste has become a problem.
Where to store radioactive waste is a major challenge.
To reduce waste, the factory reviewed its manufacturing process.
en.notes: 廃棄物 is the formal, official word for "waste, waste materials", especially from industry and technology: 産業廃棄物 (short 産廃), 放射性廃棄物, 廃棄物処理, 廃棄物を減らす. In daily life people say ごみ; the related verb is 廃棄する "to dispose of, discard".

examples[].german: The recycling rate of PET bottles has risen.
I sold furniture I no longer used to a secondhand shop.
This company recycles metals from collected smartphones.
en.notes: リサイクル is "recycling"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 空き缶をリサイクルする. Typical: リサイクル率, リサイクルに出す. Note: a リサイクルショップ is not a recycling center but a secondhand store for used furniture, appliances and clothing. Related are 再利用 "reuse" and 分別 "waste sorting".

examples[].german: Japan's manufacturing industry is globally competitive.
My father worked on the manufacturing floor for forty years.
A weak yen is a tailwind for the export-heavy manufacturing industry.
en.notes: 製造業 is composed of 製造 "manufacture" and 業 "industry" and denotes the "manufacturing industry" as an economic sector - a word from business news and statistics. An individual manufacturing company is called メーカー; 工業 is "industry" in the technical sense, 産業 the most general term. Typical: 製造業で働く, 製造業の現場.

examples[].german: Demand in the service industry is increasing.
In the service industry, you often can't take weekends off.
Since graduating from university, I've worked in the service industry, such as hotels, the whole time.
en.notes: サービス業 is the "service industry": restaurants, hotels, retail, hairdressers, etc. In formal statistical terms it roughly corresponds to 第三次産業 "tertiary sector". Typical: サービス業で働く／に勤める, サービス業の人手不足. Caution: サービス alone often means "free, on the house" in Japanese (これはサービスです).

examples[].german: You need to file an income tax return.
Households with low incomes receive support from the state.
The income gap between the city and the countryside has become a problem.
en.notes: 所得 is income in the economic and tax sense, strictly speaking revenue minus expenses or allowances. In daily life, for "what one earns" people usually say 収入 or 給料; 所得 sounds official. Typical: 所得税 ("income tax"), 所得が低い/高い, 低所得者, 所得格差 ("income disparity"), 国民所得.

examples[].german: The transportation industry is suffering from a labor shortage.
My older brother works at a transport company and decides truck delivery routes.
The government announced it would strengthen transportation safety measures.
en.notes: 運輸 refers to the "transport sector", i.e. the conveyance of people and goods as a branch of the economy; the word is formal and mostly appears in compounds: 運輸業, 運輸業界, 運輸会社. It is hardly used as a する-verb. For the concrete act of transporting, people use 輸送する or 運ぶ, for freight forwarders 運送 (運送会社); 交通 means traffic itself.

examples[].german: Greater logistics efficiency is being demanded.
The typhoon halted distribution, and goods disappeared from supermarket shelves.
With the growth of online shopping, the number of distribution centers is increasing.
en.notes: 物流 is "logistics", i.e. the physical flow of goods from production to the customer: 物流センター, 物流業界, 物流コスト, 物流が止まる／滞る. To be distinguished from 流通 "distribution", which also includes wholesale and retail, as well as 配送 "delivery" and 運送 "freight transport". Typical for business news.

examples[].german: The aviation industry has recovered after COVID.
Plane tickets are cheaper if you book early.
If you send this package by air mail, it arrives in three days.
en.notes: 航空 means "aviation" and appears almost only in compounds: 航空会社 "airline", 航空券 "plane ticket", 航空便 "air mail; flight", 航空機 (formal for "aircraft"), 航空業界. The airplane in daily life is 飛行機, "to fly" is 飛ぶ. On its own, 航空 is rare.

examples[].german: Japan's railways are punctual.
This town developed rapidly after the railway came through.
My little brother loves trains and goes out to photograph trains on his days off.
en.notes: 鉄道 is the "railway" as a transport system: 鉄道会社, 鉄道網, 鉄道が通る "a railway line runs through", 私鉄 "private railway". The individual train is called 電車 (electric) or 列車 in daily life, the track 線路. Railway fans are called 鉄道ファン, jokingly 鉄ちゃん.

examples[].german: Cargo is transported by large vessels.
A typhoon is approaching, so caution is needed when navigating ships.
Many ships enter and leave this port every day.
en.notes: 船舶 is the formal collective term for "ships, watercraft" and belongs in laws, news and technical texts: 船舶の航行, 船舶事故, 大型船舶. In daily life people simply say 船. The counter for larger ships is 隻, for small boats 艘.

examples[].german: Road repair work is being carried out.
The roads are frozen from the snow, so please drive carefully.
It's dangerous to suddenly run out onto the road.
en.notes: 道路 is the "road" as a traffic route, rather matter-of-fact and official: 道路工事, 道路標識, 高速道路, 道路が混む／渋滞する, 道路を渡る. 道 is more general ("path", also figuratively), 通り is a (busy) street, often with a name. Roadway and sidewalk are called 車道 and 歩道.

examples[].german: The tunnel through the mountain has been completed.
When you enter the tunnel, your phone loses reception.
We have finally emerged from the long tunnel of the recession.
en.notes: トンネル is the "tunnel": トンネルに入る, トンネルを抜ける "to come out through the tunnel", トンネルを掘る. Famous is the first sentence of Kawabata's "Snow Country": 国境の長いトンネルを抜けると雪国であった. Figuratively, 長いトンネルを抜ける stands for getting through a long, hard period. In baseball, トンネル(する) means letting a grounder go through one's legs.

examples[].german: This plant grows well even in the shade.
On the weekend, I went to the botanical garden and saw rare flowers.
Having a houseplant in the room calms the mind.
en.notes: 植物 is "plant" as a general, rather factual-scientific term, the counterpart of 動物. Typical: 植物を育てる, 植物園 "botanical garden", 観葉植物 "houseplant, foliage plant", 植物性 "plant-based". In daily life one speaks more concretely of 花, 草 or 木; 草花 are flowering plants.

examples[].german: The children like looking at the animals at the zoo.
I take care of the animals every morning.
en.notes: 動物 is an animal; the number is clear from the context. 動物を見る names animals as the thing being looked at. 動物の世話をする means to take care of animals. 動物園 is the zoo, as a compound word. どうぶつ contains a long o.

examples[].german: Many insects appear when summer comes.
As a child, I went insect collecting every day of the summer vacation.
A spider has eight legs, so it is not an insect.
en.notes: 昆虫 is an "insect" in the biological sense (six legs). In daily life people mostly say 虫, which also includes spiders, worms and other creepy-crawlies. Typical: 昆虫採集 "insect collecting" (a classic summer vacation hobby), 昆虫図鑑 "insect encyclopedia", 昆虫食 "insects as food".

examples[].german: Last night an incident occurred in front of the station.
The police solved the case within a week.
Please be careful not to get caught up in any criminal incident while traveling.
en.notes: 事件 is a conspicuous, usually negative event, especially a crime, a scandal or a criminal case: 殺人事件, 事件が起きる, 事件に巻き込まれる, 事件を解決する. 事故, by contrast, is an unintentional accident (交通事故), and 出来事 a neutral event. Historical incidents are also called 〇〇事件. In legal language, 事件 also means a legal case.

examples[].german: Microorganisms are not visible to the naked eye.
Natto and yogurt are made through the action of microorganisms.
Microorganisms in the soil break down fallen leaves.
en.notes: 微生物 is composed of 微 "tiny" and 生物 "living thing" and is the umbrella term for "microorganisms". More concrete are 細菌 "bacteria", 菌 "germ, fungus" and カビ "mold". Typical: 微生物の働き, 微生物が分解する, 微生物を利用する - especially in fermentation and environmental topics.

examples[].german: Many species live in the tropical rainforest.
Every year, large areas of tropical rainforest are lost.
The tropical rainforest is hot all year round, and it rains a lot.
en.notes: 熱帯雨林 consists of 熱帯 "tropics" and 雨林 "rainforest". The word is factual and appears in news, geography and environmental topics: アマゾンの熱帯雨林, 熱帯雨林の破壊, 熱帯雨林が失われる. ジャングル is the more casual, more adventurous word; 森林 is the general term for forest.

examples[].german: Horses are running across the wide grassland.
I spent a night on the Mongolian grassland and gazed at the starry sky.
I lay down on the grassy plain and looked up at the blue sky.
en.notes: 草原 is a wide area covered with grass - depending on context "meadow, grassland" or "steppe, savanna" (モンゴルの草原, アフリカの草原). 野原 is a simple, often smaller meadow or field in everyday life, 牧場 a pasture with livestock, 芝生 a lawn. Typical: 草原が広がる, 草原を走る.

examples[].german: Ocean pollution is a serious problem.
I went on to graduate school to study marine life.
International rules are needed to protect marine resources.
en.notes: 海洋 is the formal, scientific word for "sea, ocean" and appears almost always in compounds: 海洋汚染 "ocean pollution", 海洋生物, 海洋資源, 海洋性気候. In everyday speech one says 海; the great world oceans are also called 大洋 or 〜洋 (太平洋, 大西洋).

examples[].german: There are seven continents on Earth.
My dream is to cross the American continent by car.
It is said that, in ancient times, all the continents were connected as one.
en.notes: 大陸 is the "continent": アジア大陸, アメリカ大陸, 大陸を横断する. From a Japanese point of view, 大陸 on its own can also mean the Chinese mainland, from a British point of view continental Europe. The adjective 大陸的 describes something vast or a generous, easygoing manner. The opposite term is 島 "island".

examples[].german: Italy is a peninsula that juts into the Mediterranean.
On the weekend, I took a drive around the Izu Peninsula.
This peninsula is surrounded by sea on three sides, and the fish is delicious.
en.notes: 半島 is the "peninsula", literally "half island"; as a suffix with proper names: 伊豆半島, 能登半島, 朝鮮半島. Typical: 海に突き出た半島, 三方を海に囲まれた半島. 半島 alone as a designation for Korea is colloquial and can come across as derogatory - better avoided. A headland is called 岬.

examples[].german: The Alps mountain range crosses Europe.
From the airplane window, I could see a snow-capped mountain range.
In the middle of the Japanese archipelago, high mountain ranges run north to south.
en.notes: 山脈 is a "mountain range"; in names it serves as a suffix: ヒマラヤ山脈, アルプス山脈, 飛騨山脈. Typical: 山脈が連なる, 山脈が南北に走る "runs north to south". In contrast to 山々 "the mountains" or 山地 "mountainous area", 山脈 emphasizes the continuous chain. The Japanese high mountains are also called 日本アルプス.

examples[].german: The Kanto Plain is the largest plain in Japan.
Rice farming is thriving in the plains.
This plain was formed from soil carried by rivers.
en.notes: 平野 is a "plain, lowland", usually shaped by rivers; as a suffix with names: 関東平野, 濃尾平野. 平野部 denotes the flat parts of a country, as opposed to 山間部. To be distinguished are 盆地 "basin" (enclosed by mountains), 高原 "plateau" and 平地 "flat land" in general.

examples[].german: Because Kyoto lies in a basin, summers are hot and humid.
The Kofu Basin is famous as a production area for grapes and peaches.
Since it's a basin, fog often forms on winter mornings.
en.notes: 盆地 is a "basin" enclosed by mountains - 盆 means "tray", so the image is a flat bowl. Well-known examples: 京都盆地, 奈良盆地, 甲府盆地. Typical is the 盆地特有の気候: hot, humid summers, cold winters and frequent fog. In contrast, a 平野 is an open plain, usually toward the sea.

examples[].german: We test the water quality of rivers regularly.
There is a risk that rivers will overflow due to heavy rain.
On weekends, many people have barbecues on the riverbank.
en.notes: 河川 is the formal, official collective term for "rivers, running waters" and appears in official language, news and warnings: 河川の氾濫, 河川の水位, 一級河川. In daily life people simply say 川. A well-known compound is 河川敷, the riverside grounds between the river and the levee, where people exercise or barbecue.

examples[].german: The perpetrator was arrested.
The person responsible for the traffic accident apologized to the victim.
Perpetrators of bullying often don't realize the gravity of what they've done.
en.notes: 加害者 is the person who inflicts (加) harm (害) on another, i.e. a perpetrator or offender; the opposite is 被害者 ("victim, injured party"). It is used for crimes, bullying (いじめの加害者) and also for the person who caused a traffic accident, so it emphasizes the harming role, not necessarily a crime. 犯人, by contrast, specifically means the perpetrator of a crime. A factual, formal word from news and legal language.

examples[].german: A cold spring wells up in the mountains.
The traveler drank at a spring in the forest and rested a little.
My grandmother's stories are like a fountain of wisdom.
en.notes: 泉 is a natural "spring" from which water emerges: 泉が湧く "a spring wells up". The character is also found in 温泉 "hot spring". Figuratively, 泉 stands for an inexhaustible source: 知恵の泉, アイデアの泉. An artificial fountain is called 噴水, a draw well 井戸; 泉 is also a common name.

examples[].german: Glaciers are melting because of global warming.
In Switzerland, I took part in a tour to see a glacier.
This valley was carved by a glacier during the ice age.
en.notes: 氷河 is the "glacier": 氷河が溶ける, 氷河が後退する "retreats", 氷河期 "ice age", 氷河湖 "glacial lake". Not to be confused with 氷山 "iceberg" (氷山の一角 "the tip of the iceberg") and 流氷 "drift ice".

examples[].german: Japan's climate has four distinct seasons.
Because of climate change, heavy rain is becoming more frequent in many places.
The warm climate of Okinawa seems to suit me; I've felt better since I moved.
en.notes: 気候 is "climate," i.e. the long-term weather conditions of a region; the current weather is 天気, or more formally 天候. Typical: 温暖な気候, 気候変動 "climate change," 気候が穏やか. 気候が合う／合わない means that the climate agrees or disagrees with you.

examples[].german: Japan experienced severe pollution during its period of high growth.
Minamata disease is a pollution-caused disease that arose from factory wastewater.
People living near the airport suffer from noise pollution.
en.notes: 公害 denotes environmental damage caused by industry or traffic that harms the health of the population - air and water pollution, but also noise (騒音公害). Historically formative are the 四大公害病 of the growth years, such as 水俣病. The neutral, broader term for pollution is 汚染 or 環境汚染; private littering is not called 公害.

examples[].german: Car exhaust fumes are the cause of air pollution.
This car has a large engine displacement, so its fuel economy is poor.
If you block a computer's exhaust vent, heat builds up and can cause a malfunction.
en.notes: 排気 is the "discharge" of gas or air; the exhaust gas itself is called 排気ガス, abbreviated 排ガス. Other compounds: 排気口 "exhaust/ventilation opening" and 排気量 "engine displacement". To be distinguished are 換気 "ventilating" (letting in fresh air) and 排出 "discharge" in general, e.g. CO2の排出. As a する-verb, 排気する is rare.

examples[].german: This cosmetic product is made from natural ingredients.
This tuna is wild, not farmed.
She's a bit of an airhead and is always saying funny things.
en.notes: 天然 means "natural, formed by nature," as opposed to 人工 "artificial" or 養殖 "farmed." It is used with の or as a prefix: 天然の成分, 天然ガス, 天然資源, 天然水, 天然記念物. 自然, by contrast, means nature as scenery, or "natural" in the sense of unforced. In colloquial speech, a lovably naive person who is unintentionally funny is called 天然 or 天然ボケ.

examples[].german: Petroleum is a limited resource.
In winter I heat the room with a kerosene heater.
Japan imports most of its petroleum from the Middle East.
en.notes: 石油 is "petroleum" as a raw material: 石油製品, 石油会社, 石油危機 "oil crisis" (also オイルショック). In everyday life 石油 also means the heating kerosene for the 石油ストーブ, correctly 灯油. To be distinguished are 油 "oil" in general (also cooking oil), オイル and ガソリン "gasoline".

examples[].german: It is said that the use of coal should be reduced.
In the past, a lot of coal was mined in this town.
When winter came, my grandfather would heat the room with a coal stove.
en.notes: 石炭 is coal as a mineral resource and fuel. Typical combinations: 石炭を掘る / 採掘する ("to mine coal"), 石炭を燃やす, 石炭火力発電 ("coal-fired power generation"); together with 石油 and 天然ガス it is one of the 化石燃料 ("fossil fuels"). Charcoal for grilling, on the other hand, is 炭 or 木炭, not 石炭.

examples[].german: Natural gas has less impact on the environment than oil.
This country relies on imports for most of its natural gas.
This power plant uses natural gas as fuel.
en.notes: 天然ガス is "natural gas" (天然 "natural" + ガス) and is encountered mainly in news and texts about energy: 天然ガスを輸入する, 液化天然ガス ("liquefied natural gas, LNG"). In everyday speech, for the gas from the pipe one simply says ガス (ガス代, ガスコンロ); 都市ガス is city gas from the network, プロパンガス is bottled gas.

examples[].german: I make a point of carrying a reusable bag with me.
For the sake of the environment, I set the air conditioner's temperature a little higher.
This car is eco-friendly, but the price is too high.
en.notes: エコ is the short form of エコロジー and mostly appears as a prefix in compounds: エコバッグ ("reusable shopping bag"), エコカー, エコ活動. On its own it is used like a な-adjective: エコな生活, この車はエコだ. Often "economical" also resonates (エコモード). The word is casual and advertising language; in formal texts one rather says 環境に優しい or 環境に配慮した.

examples[].german: The ruling party won the election.
The ruling party holds a majority of seats in the Diet.
On this issue, opinions are divided even within the ruling party.
en.notes: 与党 is the ruling party or the parties of a governing coalition; the opposite is 野党. In the news both often appear as a pair: 与野党 ("government and opposition"). Typical: 与党が過半数を占める, 与党が議席を減らす, 連立与党 ("coalition parties"). 与 here means "to take part in" as in 関与.

examples[].german: The witness testified in court.
I was there, so I will be a witness.
The former company president was summoned to the Diet as a witness.
en.notes: 証人 is a witness who attests to something or gives testimony in court; the testimony itself is called 証言. Typical: 証人として出廷する, 証人になる, 証人喚問 (summoning of witnesses in the Diet). An eyewitness who has seen something is more precisely 目撃者. Do not confuse it with 保証人 ("guarantor"), who is needed for a rental contract, for example, or with the similar-sounding 商人 ("merchant").

examples[].german: Protection of the natural environment is called for.
The lost child was taken into protective custody by the police.
I put a film on to protect the screen.
en.notes: 保護 means "protection, preservation" and is frequent as a transitive する-verb: 〜を保護する. Typical are 自然保護, 環境保護, 個人情報の保護 and, in the passive, 警察に保護される ("to be taken into care"). Compared with the everyday 守る, 保護 is more formal and stresses care for something weak or endangered; 防ぐ, in contrast, means "to prevent, ward off". 生活保護 is welfare.

examples[].german: Rare species live in this region.
This kind of problem has happened before.
Humans, too, are merely one species of animal.
en.notes: 種 read しゅ is the biological "species" and, in a more formal register, generally "kind, sort": この種の問題 "problems of this kind". As a suffix it is found in 絶滅危惧種, 外来種 or 品種. Note: the same kanji read たね means "seed, pit" or "cause" (悩みの種). In daily life, for "sort" people more often say 種類 or タイプ.

examples[].german: The number of individuals of this species is declining year by year.
Even within the same species, size differs considerably from individual to individual.
The researchers numbered the captured individuals and released them.
en.notes: 個体 is a technical word from biology for a single living thing ("individual, specimen"), mostly for animals and plants. Common are 個体数 ("population size") and 個体差 ("individual differences", also for pets or products). For humans in everyday speech one says 個人. Not to be confused with the identically sounding 固体 ("solid body", cf. 固体・液体・気体).

examples[].german: I cracked the eggshell and took out the contents.
I picked up seashells on the beach.
He just can't seem to break out of his shell.
en.notes: 殻 is a hard outer covering: 卵の殻, ピーナッツの殻, カニの殻; in 貝殻 ("seashell") it is read voiced as がら. Soft peels of fruit or skin, on the other hand, are called 皮 (みかんの皮). Figuratively: 自分の殻に閉じこもる ("to retreat into one's shell"), 殻を破る ("to come out of one's shell, break one's limits"), もぬけの殻 ("empty, deserted").

examples[].german: More and more people oppose products made with animal fur.
My grandmother treasures her old fur coat.
Polar bears protect themselves from the cold with their thick fur.
en.notes: 毛皮 is fur or pelt with the hair, both as a material (毛皮のコート, 毛皮製品) and for the living animal in factual and documentary texts. To be distinguished: 革 ("leather", dehaired and tanned: 革の靴), 皮 ("skin" in general) and 毛 ("hair"). For the coat of pets, in everyday speech one rather says 毛 or 毛並み.

examples[].german: I exercise every day for my health.
My grandfather is ninety, but he is very healthy.
There is a health checkup at the company every year.
en.notes: 健康 is a noun and a な-adjective: 健康な人, 祖父は健康だ. Common combinations: 健康に気をつける, 健康を害する ("to harm one's health"), 健康に良い / 悪い, 健康診断 ("health checkup"). For "healthy" (food, lifestyle) one uses 健康的な. 元気 means more "lively, fit, in good spirits", 丈夫 "sturdy, robust"; 健康 describes the physical condition.

examples[].german: The doctor prescribed me medicine.
My younger sister says she wants to become a doctor.
en.notes: 医者 means a doctor, male or female. Politely, people often say お医者さん. 医者に…してもらう names the person from whom one receives an action. 医者になりたい expresses a career wish. In いしゃ, しゃ forms a single mora; there is no long vowel.

examples[].german: Please take the medicine according to your doctor's instructions.
He works as a doctor at a regional hospital.
I submitted the doctor's medical certificate to my company.
en.notes: 医師 is the official, formal word for "doctor": used in job descriptions, documents and the news (医師免許, 医師の診断書). In everyday speech people say 医者, politely お医者さん, and a doctor is addressed as 先生 - 医師 is never a form of address. Homophones such as 意思 / 意志 ("will, intention") are distinguished only by context.

examples[].german: I asked the pharmacist how to take the medicine.
My daughter is studying at the pharmacy faculty to become a pharmacist.
The pharmacist at the pharmacy told me this medicine would make me sleepy.
en.notes: 薬剤師 is the state-licensed "pharmacist", composed of 薬剤 ("medicine") and 師 ("professional") as in 医師 or 看護師. One meets them at a 薬局 ("pharmacy", where you fill a 処方箋) or at a ドラッグストア; so the place is called 薬局, the person 薬剤師. In conversation one politely says 薬剤師さん.

examples[].german: You should get a cancer screening once a year.
I had a regular checkup at the dentist.
During pregnancy, you need to have regular checkups.
en.notes: 検診 is an examination for a specific disease, a screening: がん検診, 歯科検診, 定期検診; the verb is 検診を受ける. To be distinguished are the identically read 健診 (short form of 健康診断, a general health checkup), 診察 (examination at a doctor's visit because of complaints) and 検査 (a test, e.g. a blood test).

examples[].german: This disease spreads from person to person.
Influenza spreads easily, so let's wear masks.
It is often said that yawning is contagious.
en.notes: 伝染 is transmission from person to person, as an intransitive する-verb: 病気が伝染する; 伝染病 is a "contagious disease". 感染, in contrast, denotes the infection of the individual organism (ウイルスに感染する) and is more common in modern medical language. Figuratively: あくびが伝染する. Colloquially one says うつる: 風邪がうつる, transitively 風邪をうつす.

examples[].german: Please wash your hands to prevent the growth of bacteria.
Bacteria and viruses differ in both size and nature.
I disinfected the wound so that bacteria wouldn't get in.
en.notes: 細菌 means "bacterium, bacteria" (same form for singular and plural) and is the factual, scientific word. In daily life one hears 菌 (大腸菌, 乳酸菌) or, childishly colloquial, ばい菌 ("germs"). Important is the difference from ウイルス: antibiotics (抗生物質) work against 細菌, not against viruses. Typical: 細菌が繁殖する / 増える, 細菌に感染する.

examples[].german: I have a terrible headache because of stress.
I've had a headache since this morning, so I took some medicine.
My son's career path is my latest headache.
en.notes: 頭痛 (ずつう) is a headache; you say 頭痛がする (not ある), 頭痛がひどい, plus 頭痛薬 ("headache pill") and 頭痛持ち ("someone who often has headaches"). In conversation 頭が痛い is more common, and it also means "to be a headache for (someone)" figuratively. 頭痛の種 ("a constant source of worry") is also figurative.

examples[].german: I got a stomachache from eating too many cold things.
Because of a stomachache, I will be absent today.
He complained of severe abdominal pain and was taken away in an ambulance.
en.notes: 腹痛 (ふくつう) is the Sino-Japanese, rather formal word for "stomachache": at the doctor's, in excuses, in the news. In everyday speech one says お腹が痛い; colloquially 腹痛 is also read はらいた. Typical: 腹痛がする, 腹痛を起こす, 腹痛を訴える ("to complain of stomach pain").

examples[].german: Because the bleeding was heavy, I called an ambulance.
I fell and bled a little from my knee.
The store is holding a closing-down sale with prices slashed below cost.
en.notes: 出血 means "bleeding"; as an intransitive する-verb: 出血する. Typical: 出血が止まる / 止まらない, 大量出血, 内出血 ("internal bleeding, bruise"). In everyday speech people usually just say 血が出る. In retail, 出血 figuratively means "selling at a loss": 出血大サービス ("prices below cost").

examples[].german: My throat is inflamed and it's hard to speak.
I got medicine from the doctor to reduce the inflammation.
My skin is inflamed from sunburn.
en.notes: 炎症 is the neutral medical word for "inflammation": 炎症が起きる (intransitive) or 炎症を起こす, 炎症を抑える ("to reduce inflammation"), 炎症がひどい. Specific inflammatory diseases are formed with the suffix 〜炎: 胃炎, 肺炎, 鼻炎, 皮膚炎. The visible swelling that goes with it is described with 腫れる.

examples[].german: There are voices calling for the abolition of the death penalty system.
The court sentenced the defendant to death.
In many European countries, the death penalty is no longer carried out.
en.notes: 死刑 is the death penalty, which still exists in Japan. Typical: 死刑判決 ("death sentence"), 死刑を言い渡す ("to sentence to death"), 死刑が執行される ("to be carried out"), 死刑制度, 死刑廃止 ("abolition of the death penalty"). A person sentenced to death is a 死刑囚. The word belongs to news and legal language.

examples[].german: I've suffered from asthma since childhood.
In the middle of the night I had an asthma attack and found it hard to breathe.
For the sake of our child with asthma, we don't smoke at home.
en.notes: 喘息 is "asthma"; because 喘 is a difficult kanji, it is often written ぜんそく or ぜん息. Typical are 喘息の発作 ("asthma attack"), 喘息持ち ("asthmatic"), 小児喘息 and 喘息に悩まされる. The symptoms are described with 咳, 息苦しい or the onomatopoeic ゼーゼーする.

examples[].german: I manage my diabetes through diet control.
My father has diabetes, so he cuts back on sweets.
At my health checkup, I was told that diabetes is suspected.
en.notes: 糖尿病 is "diabetes", literally "sugar-urine disease". Typical: 糖尿病になる, 糖尿病を患う (formal), 糖尿病の疑い, 糖尿病予備軍 ("at-risk group, prediabetics"); blood sugar is called 血糖値. It is one of the 生活習慣病 ("lifestyle diseases"); colloquially it is also shortened to 糖尿.

examples[].german: Too much salt can cause high blood pressure.
My grandmother takes medicine for high blood pressure every day.
At the health checkup, I was told my blood pressure was slightly high.
en.notes: 高血圧 is "high blood pressure" (高 + 血圧 "blood pressure"); the opposite is 低血圧, with which people in Japan often also explain being a poor morning person (低血圧で朝が弱い). Typical: 高血圧になる, 高血圧の薬, 高血圧気味 ("slightly elevated blood pressure"). In conversation one often simply says 血圧が高い.

examples[].german: Moderate exercise is important for preventing heart disease.
He continues to work despite having heart disease.
My grandfather once had surgery for heart disease.
en.notes: 心臓病 is the umbrella term "heart disease" (心臓 "heart" + 病 "disease"). Specific diagnoses are, for example, 心筋梗塞 ("heart attack") or 狭心症 ("angina pectoris"); technical texts also say 心疾患. Typical: 心臓病を抱える, 心臓病で亡くなる, 心臓病の予防. In everyday speech it is often simply 心臓が悪い.

examples[].german: If cancer is detected early, it can be treated.
My uncle died of lung cancer.
Smoking is said to increase the risk of cancer.
en.notes: がん ("cancer") is mostly written in hiragana or as ガン; the kanji 癌 is rare. As a suffix it forms types of cancer: 胃がん, 肺がん, 乳がん, plus がん検診 and 末期がん ("end-stage cancer"). Typical: がんになる, がんが見つかる, がんと診断される, がんで亡くなる. Figuratively, 〜のがん is the "cancer" or root problem of an organization.

examples[].german: A tumor was found in the examination, but it was benign.
The surgery to remove the tumor ended successfully.
Whether it is a malignant tumor can't be known without a detailed examination.
en.notes: 腫瘍 is the medical term for "tumor, growth" (腫 as in 腫れる "to swell"). A distinction is made between 良性腫瘍 ("benign") and 悪性腫瘍 ("malignant", i.e. がん). Typical: 腫瘍が見つかる / できる, 腫瘍を摘出する / 取り除く, 脳腫瘍. A harmless lump or pimple is called できもの in everyday speech.

examples[].german: It took three months for the fracture to heal completely.
This disease is said to be difficult to cure completely.
The injury has healed completely, so I will return to practice next week.
en.notes: 完治 ("complete cure") is an intransitive する-verb with the illness or injury as subject: 病気 / けがが完治する; transitively one says 完治させる. Compared with the everyday 治る it is more formal and stresses that nothing remains. 全快 is said more of the person ("fully healthy again"), 回復 is recovery in general, 治療 is treatment. Less often it is also read かんじ.

examples[].german: I suffer from chronic back pain.
I was diagnosed with chronic gastritis.
That company keeps running chronic deficits.
en.notes: 慢性 ("chronic") stands before disease names like a prefix (慢性胃炎, 慢性疲労) or with の: 慢性の病気. For problems outside medicine one uses the な-adjective 慢性的な: 慢性的な人手不足, 慢性的な渋滞. 慢性化する means "to become chronic"; the opposite is 急性 ("acute").

examples[].german: I was hospitalized for acute gastritis.
At a drinking party, a student got acute alcohol poisoning from chugging.
Once the acute symptoms subside, you should be able to be discharged.
en.notes: 急性 ("acute") describes an illness that occurs suddenly and severely and usually stands before the disease name: 急性胃腸炎, 急性アルコール中毒, 急性心不全, or with の: 急性の症状. The opposite is 慢性. For "acute" in the sense of "urgent", 急性 does not fit - for that one says 緊急 or 差し迫った.

examples[].german: The culprit was arrested at the scene.
The police arrested a man in his forties last night.
He shoplifted and was arrested in the act in front of the store.
en.notes: 逮捕 is arrest by the police; as a transitive する-verb: 警察が容疑者を逮捕する, often in the passive 逮捕される. Typical: 現行犯逮捕 ("arrest in the act"), 逮捕状 ("arrest warrant"). In the news, the arrested person is called 容疑者, not 犯人, as long as guilt has not been proven. In everyday speech one also says 捕まる/捕まえる.

examples[].german: The seriously ill patient was taken to the intensive care unit.
I was infected with COVID, but it didn't become severe.
My husband's love of games is already a severe case.
en.notes: 重症 denotes a severe course of illness: 重症患者, 重症になる, 重症化する ("to worsen"). Beware of the identically read 重傷 ("serious injury"), which is used for accidents: 重傷を負う. The opposite is 軽症. Jokingly, about a passion one says 〜はもう重症だ ("a hopeless case").

examples[].german: Fortunately it was only a mild case, so hospitalization is not necessary.
Most of the infected have mild symptoms and are resting at home.
Patients with mild symptoms, please first see a nearby clinic.
en.notes: 軽症 is a mild course of illness: 軽症で済む ("to get off lightly"), 軽症者, 軽症患者. The identically read 軽傷, in contrast, means "minor injury" (in accidents: 軽傷を負う). The opposite term is 重症; in between, hospitals speak of 中等症 ("moderate").

examples[].german: We had a physical examination at school, and I had grown five centimeters.
This job is physically very demanding.
He has great physical ability and quickly becomes good at any sport.
en.notes: 身体 read しんたい is the formal word for "body" and appears mainly in compounds: 身体検査, 身体測定, 身体能力, 身体障害, 身体的な. In everyday speech people say 体 (からだ); when 身体 stands alone in a text, it is often read からだ too (usually with furigana). 肉体 stresses the body as opposed to the mind, 人体 the human body in an anatomical sense.

examples[].german: The human brain is a very complex organ.
My grandfather collapsed due to a brain disease and is in the hospital.
I solve puzzles every day to train my brain.
en.notes: 脳 is the "brain" in the anatomical and scientific sense: 脳の病気, 脳卒中 ("stroke"), 脳死, 脳を鍛える, 脳トレ. For intelligence in everyday life one says 頭 (頭がいい), not 脳; 頭脳 ("brains, clever mind") is more elevated. Colloquially the brain is also called 脳みそ.

examples[].german: I put my hand on his forehead to check whether he had a fever.
Sweat ran down my forehead from the heat.
It's a garden the size of a cat's forehead, but I grow vegetables in it.
en.notes: 額 read ひたい is the "forehead"; the same kanji read がく means "picture frame" (額縁) or "amount" (金額) - context decides. Typical: 額に手を当てる, 額に汗をかく, 額に汗して働く ("to work by the sweat of one's brow"); 猫の額 denotes a tiny plot of land. In everyday speech, especially with children, people usually say おでこ.

examples[].german: She raised her eyebrows in surprise.
When he heard the story, he frowned in displeasure.
Every morning I draw on my eyebrows in front of the mirror.
en.notes: 眉 is the "eyebrow"; in everyday speech people mostly say 眉毛 (まゆげ), while 眉 alone appears mainly in set phrases and in cosmetics: 眉をひそめる ("to frown in disapproval"), 眉を寄せる, 眉を描く / 整える. The spot between the eyebrows is 眉間 (みけん); 眉唾 means "dubious, hard to believe".

examples[].german: I'm tired and my eyelids are getting heavy.
When I woke up in the morning, my eyelids were swollen.
When I close my eyes, the scenery of my hometown appears before my eyes.
en.notes: まぶた ("eyelid") is almost always written in kana (the kanji 瞼 / 目蓋 are rare). Typical: まぶたが重い ("to be sleepy"), まぶたが腫れる, 二重まぶた / 一重まぶた ("double / single eyelid", a common beauty topic). Figuratively: まぶたに浮かぶ ("to appear before one's mind's eye").

examples[].german: My heart is pounding after running.
Her kind words moved me deeply.
He stuck out his chest and presented his work proudly.
en.notes: 胸 is the "chest" (rib cage, also bosom) and, figuratively, the feeling "heart." Many expressions: 胸が痛む ("to feel sympathy, grief"), 胸がいっぱい ("overwhelmed"), 胸が熱くなる ("to be moved"), 胸がドキドキする, 胸を張る ("to carry oneself proudly"). The organ itself is 心臓, the abstract heart or mind 心.

examples[].german: I'm hungry, so I want to eat something.
His rude attitude made me angry.
I ate too much and my belly started to stick out, so I started a diet.
en.notes: 腹 is "belly," but it sounds more direct and rather masculine-casual compared with the neutral お腹 (おなか): 腹が減った vs. お腹が空いた. In many idioms only 腹 is possible: 腹が立つ ("to get angry"), 腹を立てる ("to lose one's temper"), 腹黒い ("devious"), 腹を割って話す ("to talk frankly"). Medically one says 腹部.

examples[].german: It is bad manners to rest your elbows on the table.
When I fell, I hit my elbow hard.
This chair has armrests and is comfortable.
en.notes: 肘 ("elbow") is also often written in kana as ひじ. Typical: 肘をつく ("to rest one's elbows", a table manners topic), 肘を曲げる / 伸ばす, 肘を打つ, テニス肘. 肘掛け is the "armrest". Not to be confused with the similar-sounding 膝 (ひざ, "knee").

examples[].german: The culprit has not been found yet.
In this mystery novel, you don't know who the culprit is until the end.
Who is the culprit who ate the pudding in the fridge?
en.notes: 犯人 is the perpetrator of a crime, often in the context of detective stories and investigations: 犯人を捕まえる, 犯人を探す, 犯人は誰だ. In news reports, a person who has been arrested but not yet convicted is called 容疑者; 犯人 presupposes that the crime is proven. 加害者, by contrast, emphasizes the role of harming a victim. Also used jokingly in everyday life: who ate the cake - 犯人は誰？

examples[].german: My wrist started to hurt from playing too much tennis.
I wear my watch on my right wrist.
When I fell and put my hand down, I twisted my wrist.
en.notes: 手首 is the "wrist" (手 "hand" + 首 "neck"), analogous to 足首 ("ankle"). Typical: 手首が痛い, 手首をひねる / くじく ("to sprain one's wrist"), 手首を回す, 手首をつかむ, 手首に時計をつける. 腕 is the whole arm, 手 the hand.

examples[].german: After the marathon, my legs are sore.
One leg of this table is wobbly.
She is a model and has long, slender legs.
en.notes: 脚 and 足 are both read あし: 足 is the foot and, in general, also the leg; 脚 refers more precisely to the leg from the hip to the ankle as well as the legs of furniture (机の脚). Hence 脚が長い, but 足が速い ("to run fast") or 足のサイズ. In everyday writing, 足 is often used for both. As a counter, 〜脚 (きゃく) is used to count chairs.

examples[].german: When I put on the new shoes, my heel started to hurt.
Wearing high-heeled shoes makes my feet tired.
In winter, heels easily become rough and dry.
en.notes: 踵 means "heel" and also the "heel" of a shoe or the heel of a sock; it is almost always written in kana as かかと. Typical: かかとが痛い, かかとの高い靴 ("high-heeled shoes"), 靴のかかとを踏む ("to step on the back of one's shoe"). In the elevated expression 踵を返す ("to turn on one's heel") the kanji is read きびす.

examples[].german: A balanced diet is important for keeping your internal organs healthy.
I remove the guts of the fish before grilling it.
He injured his internal organs in the accident and underwent emergency surgery.
en.notes: 内臓 refers to the internal organs as a whole ("viscera, entrails"), in medicine, biology and cooking: 内臓脂肪 ("visceral fat"), 内臓を取る ("to gut a fish"). A single organ is called 臓器 (臓器移植). A classic mix-up: the identically read 内蔵 means "built-in" (カメラ内蔵のスマホ).

examples[].german: Drinking too much alcohol is bad for the liver.
At my health checkup, I was told my liver values were high.
"Rebā" means the liver of cattle or chicken.
en.notes: 肝臓 is the "liver" as an organ. Typical: 肝臓を悪くする, 肝臓に負担をかける, 肝臓の数値 ("liver values"), 肝臓がん; because damage goes unnoticed for a long time, it is called 沈黙の臓器 ("silent organ"). As a food one says レバー. The older 肝 (きも) is found in expressions such as 肝に銘じる ("to take to heart") and 肝試し ("test of courage").

examples[].german: The kidney is an important organ that filters the blood.
My father has a kidney problem and receives dialysis three times a week.
I decided to donate one kidney to my mother.
en.notes: 腎臓 is the "kidney"; in technical terms often only 腎 appears: 腎不全 ("kidney failure"), 副腎 ("adrenal gland"). Typical: 腎臓が悪い, 腎臓病, 腎臓移植. Interesting: 肝心 ("crucial, essential") used to be written 肝腎 as well - liver and kidney as vital organs.

en.meaning: graduate school; master's and doctoral studies
examples[].german: I am doing research in linguistics at graduate school.
After I graduate from university, I intend to go on to graduate school.
I study English every day for the graduate school entrance exam.
en.notes: 大学院 is the level after the bachelor's degree in the 学部: 修士課程 ("master's") and 博士課程 ("doctorate"). Typical: 大学院に進む / 進学する, 大学院に入る, 大学院を修了する (formal "to complete" instead of 卒業). A student there is a 大学院生, or 院生 for short; the entrance exam is called 院試.

examples[].german: He belongs to the Faculty of Law.
I'm a third-year student in the Faculty of Economics.
Right after graduating from undergraduate studies, I went on to graduate school.
en.notes: 学部 is the "faculty" of a university and mostly stands as a suffix: 法学部, 経済学部, 医学部, 文学部. Below it is the 学科 ("department, program"). In contrast to 大学院, 学部 also denotes the bachelor's level: 学部生 ("undergraduate"), 学部時代. Typical: 〜学部に入る / 所属する, 〜学部の学生.

examples[].german: She is studying in the architecture department.
I belong to the English literature department of the Faculty of Letters.
I passed the written test for my driver's license on the first try.
en.notes: 学科 denotes at university the department or course of study below the faculty (学部): 文学部英文学科 "Faculty of Letters, Department of English Literature". In general it can also mean a subject of study or examination; well known is 学科試験 "written/theory exam" (e.g. for a driver's license) as opposed to 実技試験 "practical exam". Not to be confused with 専攻 "major, specialization" and 科目 "an individual subject of instruction or examination".

examples[].german: My major is international relations.
What did you major in at university?
I majored in economics, but now I do a completely different job.
en.notes: 専攻 is one's major or field of specialization in university studies. As a transitive する-verb it takes を: 経済学を専攻する "to major in economics"; the typical question is 専攻は何ですか. In contrast, 専門 is broader and also covers a professional field of expertise, while 学科 is the organizational department of a university. A minor is called 副専攻.

examples[].german: The fire truck arrived immediately.
My son says he wants to become a firefighter in the future.
The local volunteer fire corps is calling for fire prevention.
en.notes: 消防 denotes fire fighting and, in short, also the fire department as an institution. Mostly it appears in compounds: 消防車 ("fire truck"), 消防署 ("fire station"), 消防士 ("firefighter"), 消防団 ("volunteer fire corps"). The emergency number 119 connects to the fire department and ambulance (消防・救急). Extinguishing itself is called 消火する.

examples[].german: I signed up for an online course.
A cooking course is being held at the city cultural center.
From next month, I will be in charge of a public lecture series at the university.
en.notes: 講座 is a course or lecture series, often outside regular instruction: 市民講座 "community education course", 通信講座 "correspondence course", 英会話講座, 公開講座 "public lecture series". One signs up with に (講座に申し込む) and a course is held (講座が開かれる). Regular school instruction, on the other hand, is 授業, a single lecture 講義. At universities, 講座 also denotes a chair.

examples[].german: I went to a school for two weeks for my teaching practicum.
In home economics class, we made curry in cooking practice.
Nursing students must complete clinical training at a hospital.
en.notes: 実習 is practical exercise or a practicum as part of training, in which one applies something oneself: 教育実習 "teaching practicum", 調理実習 "cooking practice in class", 病院実習, 実習生 "trainee, intern". One says 実習を受ける or 実習する. An internship at a company for career orientation is rather called インターンシップ; mere practicing of a skill is 練習.

examples[].german: It takes two years to complete the program.
Those who have completed the training receive a certificate of completion.
After completing his master's program at graduate school, he got a job at a manufacturer.
en.notes: 修了 is the successful completion of a course, training program or stage of study: 課程を修了する, 研修を修了する, 修了証 "certificate of completion". For a master's degree one says 大学院を修了する, whereas 卒業 is used for school and bachelor's studies. Do not confuse it with the identically read 終了 "end, termination", which is used very generally for events, broadcasts or programs.

examples[].german: I'm majoring in environmental science in a master's program.
I'm going to study in England to get a master's degree.
Right now I'm under pressure from the deadline for my master's thesis.
en.notes: 修士 is the academic degree "master's" and appears almost only in compounds: 修士課程 "master's program", 修士号 "master's degree", 修士論文 "master's thesis" (colloquially 修論). The levels are 学士 "bachelor's", 修士 "master's", 博士 "doctorate". 修士 is not used as a form of address or title for a person; one says things like 修士の学生 or 修士課程の学生.

examples[].german: I have to decide on the topic of my doctoral dissertation.
My younger brother knows everything about insects - a real insect expert.
Dr. Yamanaka's research gave hope to many patients.
en.notes: 博士 has two readings: in official usage the doctorate is usually called はくし (博士号, 博士課程), while in everyday speech and as a title after names it is often はかせ: 山中博士. With はかせ one also jokingly refers to an expert who knows a lot about something: 虫博士, お天気博士. A doctor as a profession, on the other hand, is called 医者; so "doctor" in the sense of physician is not 博士.

examples[].german: Professor Tanaka's lectures are very easy to understand.
My father is a professor of economics at a university.
I received advice from my professor about the content of my paper.
en.notes: 教授 is a professor; after a name it serves as a title (田中教授), but in direct address you say 先生. Other ranks are 准教授 and 講師, and a professor emeritus is 名誉教授. As a する-verb, 教授 also means "to teach, instruct" in writing (書道を教授する), which is rare in everyday speech; people say 教える instead.

examples[].german: She was recently promoted to associate professor.
This lab is supervised by Associate Professor Sato.
It took ten years to go from associate professor to professor.
en.notes: 准教授 has been the official title since 2007 for the rank directly below 教授 and corresponds to "associate professor"; the earlier title was 助教授. Like 教授, it is used as a title after names (佐藤准教授), but in direct address one simply says 先生. Typical combinations are 准教授に昇進する and 准教授を務める.

examples[].german: A new lecturer will take over the English class.
He works as a part-time lecturer at a university.
A famous writer was invited as the speaker for the lecture event.
en.notes: 講師 is someone who gives courses or lectures: at a university a lecturer ranking below the 准教授, as a 非常勤講師 a part-time lecturer, as well as teachers at cram schools (塾の講師) and speakers at lecture events (講演会の講師). Unlike 教師, the general word for teacher, 講師 emphasizes giving courses. A 講師 is addressed as 先生.

examples[].german: The lab assistant helps with preparing the experiments.
Could you sit in the passenger seat and look at the map?
The magician picked one assistant from the audience.
en.notes: 助手 is an assistant or helper, e.g. of a professor, doctor or magician. The compound 助手席 "passenger seat" is very common. At universities, the rank 助手 has now largely been replaced by 助教. In the office people often say アシスタント too; 助手 sounds somewhat more classical and stresses the helping role beside a main person.

en.meaning: research lab; university research group; professor's office
examples[].german: I do experiments in the lab late every day.
In the afternoon I go to my professor's office with questions.
When you become a fourth-year student, you have to decide which research lab to join.
en.notes: At Japanese universities, 研究室 is not only a laboratory but also a professor's office and the whole research group around them - including in the humanities. Students join a 研究室 in a later year of study (研究室に入る) and write their graduation thesis there. With questions, one goes 先生の研究室に. A pure experiment room is more likely called 実験室 or ラボ.

en.meaning: emergency; first aid; emergency medical service
examples[].german: Please call an ambulance.
I ran a fever in the middle of the night and went to an emergency hospital.
Keeping a first-aid kit at home gives peace of mind.
en.notes: 救急 means first aid or emergency care and almost always appears in compounds: 救急車 ("ambulance"), 救急病院 ("emergency hospital"), 救急隊員 ("paramedic"), 救急箱 ("first-aid kit"), 救急外来 ("emergency room"). On its own it is rare. 緊急, by contrast, is generally "urgent, emergency" (緊急事態); 救急 refers specifically to medical help.

examples[].german: I have to hand in a report by next week.
I was writing a report all weekend.
I submitted the business trip report to the department manager.
en.notes: At university, レポート is above all the written paper you hand in for a course: レポートを書く, レポートを出す or, more formally, レポートを提出する, レポートの締め切り (report deadline). At work it can also be a (shorter) report, e.g. 出張のレポート; very formal business reports are more often 報告書. A scholarly thesis, on the other hand, is 論文, and on television レポート means an on-site report.

examples[].german: I study every day for the university entrance exam.
The results of the high school entrance exam will be announced next week.
This year's entrance exam questions were reportedly harder than last year's.
en.notes: 入試 is the common short form of 入学試験 "entrance examination". Typical are 大学入試, 高校入試, 推薦入試 "admission by recommendation" and 入試問題. One passes with 入試に合格する or colloquially 受かる; to fail is 入試に落ちる. Preparing for the exam is expressed with 入試に向けて勉強する or 受験勉強.

examples[].german: Art enriches people's hearts.
This dish is like a work of art.
He chose to live his life as an artist.
en.notes: 芸術 is "art" in the broad sense and includes not only painting but also music, theater, literature and film; visual art in the narrower sense is 美術. Common derivatives are 芸術家 "artist," 芸術作品 "work of art" and the adjective 芸術的な "artistic." In autumn people like to speak of 芸術の秋. Manual craftsmanship, on the other hand, is more often 技術 or 技.

examples[].german: In the Japanese literature class we read works by Natsume Soseki.
I study English literature at university.
My father loves literature, so we have lots of books at home.
en.notes: 文学 is literature as an art form and as a field of study: 日本文学, 英文学, 外国文学, 文学作品 "literary work", 文学部 "faculty of letters". A single novel is 小説, a single book 本; 文学 refers to the whole field. Do not confuse it with 文化 "culture" or 文法 "grammar", which share the same first kanji.

examples[].german: She is known for writing beautiful poems.
At the graduation ceremony, a student read aloud a poem he had written himself.
This collection of poems contains many spring poems.
en.notes: 詩 is a poem or poetry in general, especially modern or Western verse; traditional Japanese forms have their own names (俳句, 短歌), and Chinese poems are called 漢詩. You say 詩を書く or 詩を作る; the poet is 詩人, a volume of poems 詩集. Song lyrics are not called 詩 but 歌詞.

examples[].german: We staged a play at the school festival.
The children were delighted watching the puppet show.
My grandfather watches period dramas on TV every night.
en.notes: 劇 is a play or drama, often as a suffix in compounds: 人形劇 "puppet theater," 時代劇 "samurai drama," 劇団 "theater company." You say 劇を上演する or 劇を演じる. 演劇 refers more to theater as an art form; 芝居 is the more colloquial word for a play or stage performance and can also mean "pretense."

examples[].german: I'm majoring in theater at university.
In high school, I was in the drama club.
On the weekend I plan to go see a play with friends.
en.notes: 演劇 is theater as an art form and activity: 演劇を見る "to go to the theater", 演劇部 "drama club", 演劇を専攻する. A single play is rather called 劇 or 芝居, the building is a 劇場. In conversation 演劇 sounds somewhat factual; colloquially one also says 芝居を見に行く.

examples[].german: The actors gave a passionate performance on the stage.
The setting of this novel is Tokyo in the Meiji era.
Japanese athletes are doing well on the world stage.
en.notes: 舞台 is first of all the stage: 舞台に立つ "to stand on the stage," 舞台裏 "behind the scenes." Figuratively it denotes the setting of a story (物語の舞台は京都だ "the story is set in Kyōto") and an area of activity such as 世界の舞台 "the world stage." 舞台 can also mean the performance itself: 舞台を見に行く.

examples[].german: He is one of the most popular actors in Japan.
He came to Tokyo aiming to become an actor.
The actors' performances in this film were wonderful.
en.notes: 俳優 is the neutral word for an actor in film, television and theater; you become an actor with 俳優になる or work 俳優として. It is often associated with male actors and contrasted with 女優, but it can include women. 役者 sounds more traditional (e.g. Kabuki) and stresses the craft; a voice actor is 声優.

examples[].german: She has been active as an actress since she was young.
She won the Best Actress award for this film.
My daughter says she wants to become an actress in the future.
en.notes: 女優 is an actress; typical combinations are 女優になる, 女優として活躍する and 主演女優 "leading actress" (e.g. 主演女優賞). The male counterpart is 男優, but it is rarer because for men one usually just says 俳優. In newer texts the neutral 俳優 is increasingly used for women as well.

examples[].german: He puts effort into charitable work.
The proceeds of the concert will be donated to a charity.
After retiring, she continues charitable activities supporting children.
en.notes: 慈善 is charity, i.e. help for the needy out of compassion. It almost always stands as a modifier: 慈善事業 ("charitable work"), 慈善団体 ("charity organization"), 慈善活動, 慈善コンサート. The word is rather formal; in everyday life the loanword チャリティー is often heard. For a single donation, people say 寄付.

examples[].german: She plays the lead role in this drama.
My daughter is delighted to have been chosen for the lead in the school play.
Today's guest of honor is Mr. Tanaka, whose birthday it is.
en.notes: 主役 is the leading role or lead actor: 主役を演じる, 主役を務める, 主役に選ばれる; the opposite is 脇役 "supporting role". Figuratively it denotes the main person of an occasion: 今日の主役 is, for example, the birthday person. 主人公, in contrast, means the main character within a story, not the actor's role.

examples[].german: Many wonderful works are on display at the art museum.
I have read almost all of this author's works.
For our summer vacation homework, we are to freely create one work of our own.
en.notes: 作品 is a created work of art, literature, film or music, also by children or amateurs: 作品を発表する "to publish a work", 作品を展示する. An artist's best-known work is called 代表作. Industrially manufactured products, by contrast, are called 製品, and the similarly written 作物 (さくもつ) means "crops".

examples[].german: This film is said to be a masterpiece of the twentieth century.
I think this is his greatest work.
You put your wallet in the refrigerator? That's a riot!
en.notes: 傑作 is a masterpiece, an outstandingly successful work; 最高傑作 is an artist's best work. 名作, in contrast, means a recognized, famous work, often a classic. Colloquially and jokingly, 傑作 also describes something unintentionally funny: それは傑作だ "that's priceless".

examples[].german: I engage in creative activity with free imagination.
A new restaurant with creative cuisine opened in front of the station.
The story was not true; it was his invention.
en.notes: 創作 is the artistic creation of an original work of one's own (novel, film, music, etc.): 創作活動, 創作する, 創作料理 "creative (fusion) cuisine". It can also mean "invention, fiction", for instance when a story is not true: それは彼の創作だ. 創造 is more abstract ("creation, creativity"), 制作 stresses the practical production of a work.

examples[].german: Japanese people find beauty in nature.
This garden evokes a sense of typically Japanese beauty.
Standards of beauty change with the times.
en.notes: 美 is "beauty" as an abstract concept and sounds literary: 美を見出す, 美の基準, 美意識 "sense of beauty", 自然美 "natural beauty". In everyday speech people tend to say 美しさ or きれいさ instead. As a prefix, 美 forms words such as 美人, 美少年 or 美術.

examples[].german: An exhibition of contemporary art will be held next week.
I went to an exhibition at the art museum with a friend.
My daughter's picture was selected for the school exhibition.
en.notes: 展覧会 is an exhibition of works of art, photographs, pictures and the like: 展覧会が開かれる "an exhibition takes place", 展覧会を開く "to hold an exhibition", 展覧会を見に行く, 展覧会に出す "to exhibit a work". For product or trade fairs one more often says 展示会, and the museum itself is 美術館 or 博物館. On posters it is often abbreviated to 〜展, e.g. ピカソ展.

examples[].german: At the museum you can see dinosaur fossils.
The national museum is holding a special exhibition of old swords.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so please be careful.
en.notes: 博物館 is a museum of history, natural history, technology or ethnology: 国立博物館, 科学博物館. An art museum, on the other hand, is 美術館, and smaller collections are also called 資料館 or 記念館. You go to a museum with 博物館に行く and see exhibitions there (展示, 特別展); the closing day is 休館日.

examples[].german: A new theater has opened near the station.
The theatrical version of this anime will be released next month.
Please turn off your mobile phones inside the theater.
en.notes: 劇場 is the theater building or venue for plays, opera or musicals: 劇場で芝居を見る. A cinema, on the other hand, is 映画館, and theater as an art form is 演劇. Very common is 劇場版, the movie version of an anime or TV series. In announcements you hear 劇場内では… for rules of conduct in the hall.

examples[].german: Last week I went to a classical concert.
I managed to get tickets for my favorite singer's concert.
My daughter played the piano at the school concert.
en.notes: コンサート is a concert of any kind: コンサートに行く, コンサートがある, コンサートを開く, コンサートのチケット. For pop and rock performances, young people often say ライブ, while 演奏会 sounds more formal and is used mostly for classical music or school performances. The venue is marked with で: ホールでコンサートがある.

examples[].german: Shall we go see a ballet company's performance?
That musical will be performed in twenty cities nationwide.
Because of the typhoon, tonight's performance was canceled.
en.notes: 公演 is a public performance of theater, concert, ballet or musical: 公演を見に行く, 東京公演, 公演中止. As a transitive する-verb it often appears in the passive: 全国で公演される. Not to be confused with the identically read 講演 "lecture" and 公園 "park". 上演 stresses the staging of a particular play, 公演 the event in front of an audience.

examples[].german: I signed up for a group tour.
Groups of twenty or more people get a discount on the admission fee.
This citizens' group works on cleaning up the river.
en.notes: 団体 is on the one hand a group of people who do something together (団体旅行, 団体割引, 団体行動), and on the other an organization or association (市民団体, 宗教団体, 政治団体). In sports, 団体戦 ("team competition") is contrasted with 個人戦. グループ is more casual and everyday; 組織 stresses the internal structure of an organization.

examples[].german: The audience was moved and gave a standing ovation.
Fifty thousand spectators gathered for the final.
That film had so few viewers that it stopped showing soon after.
en.notes: 観客 are spectators who watch a performance, film or sports event on site: 観客席 "spectator seats," 観客数, 観客が集まる. TV viewers, on the other hand, are 視聴者, and listeners at lectures or concerts are often 聴衆; 観衆 is a large crowd of spectators, rather literary. Mere onlookers are 見物人 or 野次馬.

examples[].german: Her novel won a literary prize.
I got a prize in the essay contest.
This film was nominated for an award in three categories.
en.notes: 賞 is a prize or award; it often appears as a suffix: ノーベル賞, 文学賞, 一等賞, 新人賞. You receive a prize with 賞を取る, 賞をもらう or, formally, 賞を受ける or 受賞する. The material prize (the object) is 賞品, the prize money 賞金.

en.meaning: receiving an award; winning a prize
examples[].german: At the Nobel Prize ceremony, the laureates gave speeches.
Her novel won the Akutagawa Prize.
When I heard the news of the award, I couldn't believe it.
en.notes: 受賞 means to receive a prize or be honored: 〜賞を受賞する, 受賞者 "prize winner", 受賞作 "award-winning work". The award ceremony itself is called 授賞式 with the identically read 授賞 (授ける "to confer") - a common writing mistake. So 受賞 is the recipient's perspective, 授賞 that of the one conferring.

examples[].german: Did you learn any instrument when you were a child?
He can play any instrument.
I bought guitar strings at the music store in front of the station.
en.notes: 楽器 is the musical instrument. The matching verb depends on the instrument: 弾く for string and keyboard instruments, 吹く for wind instruments, 叩く for drums; neutral and suitable for all is 演奏する. To learn an instrument is 楽器を習う, a music store 楽器店 or 楽器屋.

examples[].german: She is a popular singer in Japan.
My childhood dream was to become a singer.
My grandmother often listens to songs by old enka singers.
en.notes: 歌手 is a singer, usually professional: 歌手になる, 人気歌手, 演歌歌手, オペラ歌手. The singer of a band is more likely called ボーカル. The word is gender-neutral; someone who simply likes to sing is not a 歌手 but 歌が上手な人 or 歌うのが好きな人.

examples[].german: I play the piano while looking at the sheet music.
I can't read music, so I learn pieces by ear and play them.
The sheet music for this piece can be downloaded for free on the internet.
en.notes: 楽譜 is sheet music or a musical score, including the full score of an orchestral piece. Typical are 楽譜を読む "to read music", 楽譜を見て弾く and 楽譜なしで弾く "to play from memory / by ear". A synonym, especially for the opened sheet itself, is 譜面; a single musical note is 音符.

examples[].german: Let's clap in rhythm.
He has a good sense of rhythm, so he dances well.
After many night shifts, my daily rhythm has been thrown off.
en.notes: リズム is rhythm in music, but also in life: リズムに合わせる "to follow the rhythm", リズムを取る "to keep the beat", リズム感 "sense of rhythm", 生活のリズム "daily rhythm". When everyday life gets disrupted, one says リズムが崩れる. The tempo of a piece, in contrast, is called テンポ.
