examples[].german: He plays the violin in an orchestra.
The community orchestra is recruiting members.
I went to a concert where film music was played live by an orchestra.
en.notes: オーケストラ is the orchestra; the formal Sino-Japanese word for it is 管弦楽団, in proper names often 〜交響楽団. One plays in an orchestra with で: オーケストラでバイオリンを弾く. Also typical are 市民オーケストラ "community orchestra" and オーケストラの生演奏 "live music by the orchestra".

examples[].german: A famous conductor conducted the concert.
When the conductor raised the baton, the performance began.
For the choral competition, I was chosen as our class's conductor.
en.notes: 指揮者 is above all the conductor of an orchestra or choir; the related verb is 指揮する (オーケストラを指揮する), and taking charge is 指揮を執る. In Japanese schools, each class chooses a 指揮者 for the choir competition. In a broader sense, 指揮者 can also denote a leader of an operation or troops; militarily, however, 指揮官 is more usual.

examples[].german: He is the chairman of the sports association.
I asked the tourist association to recommend some shops.
The Japan Football Association announced a new manager.
en.notes: 協会 refers to an association or federation that represents a field or a particular purpose, often with companies or persons as members: 日本サッカー協会, 観光協会. It is more formal and larger than a leisure "club" (クラブ, 同好会) and mostly appears in proper names; even the broadcaster NHK is officially called 日本放送協会. Do not confuse it with the identically read 教会 "church".

examples[].german: We won the gold prize at the school choral competition.
At the graduation ceremony, everyone sang the school song together.
My mother belongs to a local choir.
en.notes: 合唱 is singing together, i.e. choral singing; as a する-verb: 校歌を合唱する. The group itself is 合唱団 "choir", at schools 合唱部 "choir club"; the 合唱コンクール is very well known. When someone sings alone, it is called 独唱. Figuratively, 大合唱 refers to a loud chorus of voices, e.g. of frogs or protesters.

examples[].german: The pianist played a Bach piece solo.
At the end of the concert there was a violin solo.
Next month I will give my first piano recital.
en.notes: 独奏 is an instrumental solo; as a transitive する-verb: 曲を独奏する. A solo concert or recital is called 独奏会, e.g. ピアノ独奏会. A vocal solo, in contrast, is 独唱, playing together of several instruments 合奏. In everyday speech one often hears simply ソロ instead of 独奏.

examples[].german: I formed a band with friends and we play live.
I listened to a band's performance at the school festival.
The band of my wristwatch broke.
en.notes: バンド is above all a music group: バンドを組む "to form a band", バンドで演奏する. It also means a band or strap, e.g. 時計のバンド "watch strap", ヘアバンド or ゴムバンド "rubber band". A trouser belt is nowadays mostly called ベルト, and idol groups without instruments are rather called グループ.

examples[].german: Next month I'm going to a live show by my favorite band.
I hear my favorite singer is doing a livestream tonight.
At a small live music club, I heard a band I didn't know play.
en.notes: In modern Japanese, ライブ mainly means a live concert: ライブに行く "go to a live show", ライブをする "give a live show", ライブハウス "small live music club". As a modifier it means "live": ライブ配信 "livestream", ライブ中継 "live broadcast". For large, formal concerts (classical), コンサート or 演奏会 is more usual.

examples[].german: It was second place, but it was a wonderful match.
The Japanese team narrowly ended up in second place.
My younger brother took second place in a piano competition.
en.notes: 準優勝 is second place in a tournament or competition, i.e. "runner-up": 準優勝する, 準優勝に終わる "end up only second" (often with regret, e.g. with 惜しくも). Do not confuse it with 準決勝 "semifinal". The prefix 準 means "vice-, near-", and 優勝 is overall victory.

examples[].german: The final match will be held next Sunday.
Japan reached the final for the first time in three tournaments.
It was a rookie who scored the deciding goal at the end of the second half.
en.notes: 決勝 is the deciding round, i.e. the final of a competition; most often you hear 決勝戦 "final match" and 決勝に進む / 決勝に進出する "to advance to the final". Before it come 予選 "preliminary round" and 準決勝 "semifinal". 決勝点 is the deciding score, 決勝トーナメント the knockout round after the group stage.

en.meaning: preliminary round; qualifying round; preliminary selection
examples[].german: First we have to get through the preliminary round.
Unfortunately, I was eliminated in the preliminaries.
The ten people who passed the document-based preliminary selection can enter the main competition.
en.notes: 予選 is the preliminary round or qualifying stage of a contest: 予選を通過する / 突破する "get through the preliminaries", 予選で敗退する or, colloquially, 予選落ちする "be eliminated in the preliminaries". After it come 本選 or 決勝. In a wider sense 予選 also means a preliminary selection, e.g. for applications or competitions (書類予選).

examples[].german: I work out at the gym every morning.
New employees first undergo a month of training.
I train every day for the marathon.
en.notes: トレーニング is training, above all physical (筋肉トレーニング, short 筋トレ), but also job training; as an intransitive する-verb: ジムでトレーニングする. トレーニングを受ける is used for a training program. 練習, by contrast, is practicing a specific skill (piano, serve), and 研修 is in-house professional training.

examples[].german: There are many events at the Olympics.
She entered university as a track and field athlete.
The new stadium is ten minutes' walk from the station.
en.notes: 競技 is a sports competition or a sport in which people compete against each other: 陸上競技 "track and field," 競技場 "stadium, competition venue," 競技に出る / 参加する. The individual event within a competition is more precisely 種目, a single match 試合. As a する-verb, 競技する is rare.

examples[].german: The whole team fought together.
We formed a team for the new project.
Which team do you support?
en.notes: チーム is both the sports team and the team at work: チームを組む / 作る, チームに入る, チームワーク. For groups at school or in government offices one often says 班 or 組, for school clubs 部. To cheer on is チームを応援する.

examples[].german: The voter turnout was low.
It rained on Sunday, but I went to vote anyway.
We decided the theme for the school festival by a vote of the whole class.
en.notes: 投票 is the casting of a vote, i.e. the concrete act of voting with a ballot or a show of hands; 選挙, by contrast, is the election as a whole event. As an intransitive する-verb, the candidate or party takes に: 〇〇に投票する ("to vote for 〇〇"). Common: 投票に行く, 投票率 ("voter turnout"), 投票用紙, 期日前投票 ("early voting"). Also used outside politics, e.g. for votes in clubs or online polls.

examples[].german: I receive a scholarship from a foundation.
A foundation was established with my grandfather's estate.
This museum is run by a private foundation.
en.notes: 財団 is a foundation, i.e. an organization based on endowed assets that supports, for example, research, culture or scholarships. The legal form is called 財団法人 (e.g. 公益財団法人), as opposed to the membership-based association 社団法人. Typical phrases: 財団を設立する "to establish a foundation", 財団から援助を受ける. Not to be confused with 財閥, the large family conglomerates of the prewar era.

examples[].german: Next week we have a match against a strong team.
The opponent for the first round has been decided.
I played a head-to-head game online with friends.
en.notes: 対戦 means facing each other in a game or contest: 〜と対戦する "play against ...", 対戦相手 "opponent", 対戦成績 "head-to-head record". 対戦 is also common for video games (オンライン対戦). 試合 is the game as an event, and 対決 is an especially tense showdown.

examples[].german: The team won after a close game.
Her last shot led the team to victory.
The candidate who won the election thanked his supporters.
en.notes: 勝利 is victory and sounds more formal than 勝ち; typical of news and speeches: 勝利を収める "to achieve victory", 勝利する, 〜を勝利に導く "to lead to victory", 逆転勝利 "comeback victory". In everyday speech one simply says 勝つ or 勝った. The opposite is 敗北.

examples[].german: It is also important to learn from defeat.
He admitted defeat at the press conference.
After the 3-0 defeat, the players were speechless.
en.notes: 敗北 is defeat and sounds more formal than 負け: 敗北する, 敗北を認める "to admit defeat", in written language 敗北を喫する "to suffer a defeat", 敗北感 "feeling of defeat". In everyday speech people mostly say 負ける or 負けた. The opposite is 勝利.

examples[].german: A foul was called and it became a penalty kick.
In the boxing match, the opponent lost by disqualification.
I had to pay a fine for speeding.
en.notes: 反則 is a violation of the rules, especially in sports: 反則を取られる "have a foul called against you", 反則負け "loss by disqualification". As an intransitive する-verb: 反則する. Outside sports it also refers to minor violations of regulations, e.g. in road traffic (反則金 "fine"). Colloquially, people exclaim 反則だ when something is "unfairly" good: その笑顔は反則だ.

examples[].german: The media have a great influence on society.
The incident was covered by many media outlets.
Please save the photos on this storage medium.
en.notes: メディア refers mainly to the mass media (television, newspapers, the internet): メディアで取り上げられる "to be covered in the media", メディアに出る "to appear in the media", ソーシャルメディア "social media". In everyday speech the press is often also called マスコミ, which puts more emphasis on journalists and broadcasters as actors (マスコミに追われる). Technically, メディア also stands for storage media such as SD cards or DVDs (記録メディア).

examples[].german: That news was reported in last night's broadcast.
I couldn't hear the announcement at the station well.
The soccer match will be broadcast live on TV.
en.notes: 放送 is broadcasting or transmission via television and radio, but also any loudspeaker announcement: 駅の放送, 校内放送 (school announcement), 館内放送 (announcement inside a building). As a する-verb it is transitive: 試合を放送する, often in the passive 放送される; 生放送 means "live broadcast". A single broadcast as a program item ("last night's show") is usually 番組.

examples[].german: I listen to the news on the radio during my commute.
Please turn on the radio.
en.notes: ラジオ means the radio, or the medium. ラジオのニュース assigns the news to this medium. ラジオをつける means to turn on the radio. 通勤中に gives the time span during the commute. ラジオ has three short moras and is romanized rajio.

en.meaning: news gathering; research for a story
examples[].german: The reporter gathered information at the scene of the incident.
After a TV station covered us, the shop became famous.
To write her novel, the author researched a small port town.
en.notes: 取材 means collecting information on the spot for an article, a program or a book: "to research, report, conduct interviews". Typical: 〜を取材する (an event), 〜に取材する (to interview a person), 取材を受ける "to be interviewed", 取材に応じる "to agree to be interviewed". Unlike 調査 ("investigation, survey"), 取材 is always tied to reporting or writing work.

examples[].german: The minister answered questions at the press conference.
My father worked as a newspaper reporter for thirty years.
A large number of reporters had gathered at the scene of the accident.
en.notes: 記者 is a journalist or reporter who researches and writes news, especially for newspapers and news agencies: 新聞記者, 記者会見 "press conference," 記者クラブ "press club." For a TV reporter in front of the camera people often say レポーター, for freelance writers ジャーナリスト. As a job description: 新聞社で記者をしている.

examples[].german: I have worked for ten years as a magazine editor.
I edited my travel video and uploaded it online.
This file is read-only, so it can't be edited.
en.notes: 編集 is the editing and compiling of texts, books and magazines, today also of videos and files: 原稿を編集する, 動画を編集する "edit a video". Related words are 編集者 "editor", 編集部 "editorial department" and 編集長 "editor-in-chief". Unlike 修正 ("to correct"), 編集 also covers the selection, arrangement and structure of the material. As a する-verb it is transitive.

examples[].german: A government agency conducted an investigation.
Please use public transportation to get to the venue.
If it's about a loan, it's best to go to a financial institution first.
en.notes: 機関 denotes an institution or organization that fulfills a particular function in the state and society, and appears almost always in compounds: 政府機関 "government agency", 金融機関 "financial institution", 報道機関 "news organization", 教育機関, 公共交通機関 "public transportation". The older meaning "engine, machine" lives on in 機関車 "locomotive". Unlike 組織 (organization as a structure or association), 機関 stresses the role as an executing organ.

examples[].german: The publication of the new book is scheduled for next month.
She has worked at a publishing company since graduating from university.
My grandfather published a book summarizing his experiences at his own expense.
en.notes: 出版 is the publication of a book or magazine: 本を出版する, 〜から出版される "to be published by ...," 出版社 "publisher." In everyday speech, "to bring out a book" is often simply 本を出す. 発表, by contrast, is generally "to announce, present" (research results, plans), and 発行 stresses issuing (newspapers, ID cards, receipts).

examples[].german: The commercial featuring that actor is the talk of the town.
The result of the match will be announced after the commercial.
The company used a famous singer in the commercial for its new product.
en.notes: CM (pronounced シーエム) is the usual word for a TV or radio commercial, abbreviated from "commercial message". Typical uses: CMに出る "appear in a commercial", CMが流れる "a commercial is aired", CMの後で "after the commercial break". The spelled-out form is コマーシャル; for advertising in general (posters, print ads) one says 広告. In English, "CM" is not used in this sense; it is a typically Japanese abbreviation.

examples[].german: I watch the news on TV every morning.
Do you know this news?
en.notes: ニュース is a noun for news. テレビでニュースを見る names television as the medium. ニュースを知っていますか asks whether the content is already known. The small ュ in ニュー combines with ニ into one unit; the dash makes the u long: nyūsu.

examples[].german: Criticism of the government's response is growing.
The president's remarks were harshly criticized on social media.
Before criticizing others, you should reconsider your own behavior.
en.notes: 批判 is critical judgment, mostly in the sense of criticism of politics, people or decisions: 〜を批判する, 〜に対する批判, 批判を受ける / 批判を浴びる "to take criticism," 批判的な "critical." 非難 ("reproach, blame") is stronger and morally condemning; 批評, by contrast, is the expert review of art, films or literature. Colloquial grumbling is more often 文句を言う.

examples[].german: Plants absorb water through their roots.
Children absorb new knowledge rapidly.
That small company was absorbed by a large corporation.
en.notes: 吸収する means "to take in, absorb" and is transitive: 水分を吸収する, 衝撃を吸収する "to absorb shocks." Figuratively one takes in knowledge or culture (知識を吸収する), and in business a company is taken over by another (〜に吸収される, 吸収合併). Compared with 吸う ("to inhale, suck"), 吸収 is factual and rather literary.

en.meaning: to emit; to discharge; to excrete
examples[].german: The factory emits large amounts of carbon dioxide.
The body has a mechanism for expelling what it no longer needs.
In this city, the amount of garbage produced by households is decreasing.
en.notes: 排出する means "to emit, discharge, excrete" - of exhaust gases, pollutants and waste (二酸化炭素を排出する, 排出量 "amount of emissions") as well as of metabolic products in the body (体外に排出する). It is transitive but very often appears in the passive (排出される) and belongs to the factual vocabulary of environment and medicine. Do not confuse it with the identically read 輩出, which means "to produce (capable people)".

examples[].german: It is important to take in enough vitamins every day.
The doctor told me to cut down on my salt intake.
If you consume too much caffeine, you won't be able to sleep at night.
en.notes: 摂取する means "to take in (nutrients), to consume" and sounds medical and matter-of-fact; typical with nutrients and amounts: ビタミンを摂取する, 塩分の摂取量 "salt intake", 過剰摂取 "overdose, excessive consumption". In daily life one simply says 食べる, 飲む or 栄養をとる. Figuratively it can also mean "to absorb a foreign culture or knowledge" (外国の文化を摂取する), but this is literary.

examples[].german: Blood circulates through the body.
If money circulates well within society, the economy improves.
Let's open the window and let the air in the room circulate.
en.notes: 循環する means "to circulate, to go around in a cycle" and is intransitive: 血液が循環する; for "to circulate (something)" use 循環させる. It is common in compounds: 血液循環 "blood circulation", 悪循環 "vicious circle", 循環バス "loop bus line". 回転, by contrast, is rotation around an axis; 循環 means going around through a system and returning to the starting point.

examples[].german: Plans to supply electricity to this region are moving forward.
Because of the typhoon, the water supply has stopped in some areas.
This factory supplies parts to an automobile manufacturer.
en.notes: 供給する means "to supply, provide, make available" and is transitive, often in the pattern AにBを供給する: 地域に電力を供給する. The opposite is 需要 ("demand"), hence 需要と供給 "supply and demand." It is used for energy, water, raw materials or goods on a large scale; the delivery of a single package is 届ける or 配達する.

examples[].german: Japan consumes a large amount of energy.
If you run for thirty minutes, you burn about three hundred kilocalories.
This milk has a use-by date of today.
en.notes: 消費する means "to use up, consume" - energy, time, goods or calories: 電力を消費する, カロリーを消費する. Often in compounds: 消費者 "consumer," 消費税 "consumption tax," 消費期限 "use-by date" (as opposed to 賞味期限 "best-before date"). The word is value-neutral, while 浪費 stresses pointless wasting; the counterpart is 生産 ("production").

examples[].german: The constitution is the supreme law of the country.
Some say that this law violates the constitution.
May 3 is Constitution Memorial Day, and schools are closed.
en.notes: 憲法 is the constitution of a state; in Japan usually short for 日本国憲法. Typical combinations: 憲法で保障されている "guaranteed by the constitution", 憲法に違反する "to violate the constitution" (憲法違反), 憲法を改正する "to amend the constitution" (political slogan 憲法改正). Ordinary laws are called 法律, municipal regulations 条例. May 3 is the Japanese holiday 憲法記念日.

examples[].german: You must not waste time.
He always squanders his salary on gambling.
I think a meeting like this is a waste of time.
en.notes: 浪費する means "to waste, squander" and criticizes money, time or energy being spent pointlessly: お金を浪費する, 時間の浪費 "waste of time", 浪費家 "spendthrift". 無駄遣い is close in meaning but more everyday (especially for money: 無駄遣いする); 消費, by contrast, is the neutral "to consume". Opposite: 節約 ("saving, economizing").

en.meaning: to save up; to store; to accumulate
examples[].german: I save money for the future.
Squirrels store nuts in preparation for winter.
My grandfather wears a white beard.
en.notes: 蓄える means "to accumulate and keep for later": お金を蓄える "put money aside", 食料を蓄える "lay in provisions", 力を蓄える "gather strength". One can also 蓄える knowledge and experience (知識を蓄える), and ひげを蓄える means "to grow a beard, to wear a beard". For money, 貯める is more common in daily life; 蓄える sounds somewhat more elevated. The spelling 貯える is also in use; the noun 蓄え means "savings, stock".

examples[].german: This company manufactures electronic components.
This medicine is manufactured in a domestic factory.
The date of manufacture is written on the package.
en.notes: 製造する means "to manufacture, make" and refers to industrial production: 部品を製造する, 製造業 "manufacturing industry," 製造元 "manufacturer," 製造年月日 "date of manufacture." 生産 stresses production quantities (also in agriculture), and 作る is the everyday word. It is transitive; in the passive 〜で製造される means "is manufactured in ...".

examples[].german: Raw materials are processed to make products.
I edited the photo with an app and then posted it on social media.
Sausages and ham are made by processing meat.
en.notes: 加工する means "to process, work on": raw materials or foods are given a new form through processing: 木材を加工する, 加工食品 "processed food", 加工品. Today it is also very common for image editing: 写真を加工する "to edit, retouch a photo". Transitive. Do not confuse it with the identically read 下降 ("descent, decline").

examples[].german: We improved the product using new technology.
These strawberries have become sweeter through selective breeding.
Thanks to the improved engine, fuel efficiency is 20 percent better.
en.notes: 改良する means "to improve, refine" - above all products, technology, varieties or methods whose quality is raised by modifying them: 製品を改良する, 品種改良 "breeding of new varieties", 改良型 "improved version". 改善, by contrast, remedies bad conditions or problems (working conditions, health); with 改良 something concrete that already works is made even better. Transitive.

examples[].german: The working environment needs to be improved.
My symptoms have improved considerably since I started taking the medicine.
We will improve our service based on our customers' opinions.
en.notes: 改善する means "to improve, remedy problems": 環境を改善する, 生活習慣を改善する. It is used transitively (〜を改善する) and also intransitively (症状が改善する "the symptoms improve"). Compared with 改良 (developing products or technology further), 改善 targets bad conditions, processes or relationships; 改善点 are "points that should be improved." As "kaizen" it is also known as a philosophy of continuous improvement.

examples[].german: We will strengthen security measures.
Ahead of the tournament, we need to strengthen the team's defense.
At the end of the year, the police step up their crackdown on drunk driving.
en.notes: 強化する means "to strengthen, to reinforce, to tighten" and is transitive: 対策を強化する, 守備を強化する, 規制を強化する "tighten regulations" (opposite: 規制を緩和する). It sounds factual to formal and is typical of news, companies and sports; in daily life one says 強くする or 強める instead. The passive form 強化される describes something being strengthened. Common compounds: 強化合宿 "training camp", 強化ガラス "tempered glass".

examples[].german: The elderly population is increasing.
The number of foreign tourists increased by thirty percent over the previous year.
The increase in stress-related illnesses has become a problem.
en.notes: 増加する means "to increase, rise" (number, quantity) and is intransitive: 人口が増加する, 〜の増加 "increase in ...". It is the formal, statistical counterpart of 増える and often appears in news and reports; for "to raise" you need 増やす or 増加させる. Opposite: 減少. For prices and temperatures, 上昇 is more usual.

examples[].german: The birth rate is declining year by year.
The population of this town is on a downward trend.
More people shop online, and the shop's sales have decreased.
en.notes: 減少する means "to decrease, decline" and is intransitive: 人口が減少する, 売り上げが減少する. It is the formal equivalent of 減る and typical of statistics and news (〜の減少, 減少傾向にある "to be on the decline"). Transitive "to reduce" is 減らす or 減少させる; the opposite is 増加.

examples[].german: The temperature rose sharply.
Rising prices are making life hard.
The band's new song shot up to number three on the charts in one go.
en.notes: 上昇する means "to rise, go up" and is intransitive: 気温が上昇する, 物価が上昇する, 飛行機が上昇する. It describes an upward movement or value (temperature, prices, stock prices, rankings) and is more formal than 上がる. 増加, by contrast, is used for numbers and quantities. Opposite: 下降, for prices also 下落, for levels 低下.

examples[].german: Evidence was submitted in court.
The two companies will fight over the patent in court.
He took the stand in court as a witness.
en.notes: 法廷 is the courtroom, or the court as the place of a hearing. Typical: 法廷で争う "to fight in court", 法廷に立つ "to stand in court or to testify", 法廷に持ち込む "to bring to court". The court as an institution or building is 裁判所, and the proceedings themselves 裁判. 法廷 sounds formal and appears mainly in news, crime stories and legal dramas.

examples[].german: The plane began to descend gradually.
The economy has been in decline since last autumn.
In the second half of the season, the team's results went downhill.
en.notes: 下降する means "to descend, to go down" and is intransitive - for aircraft, but also for curves, values and performance: 飛行機が下降する, 景気が下降する, 下降線をたどる "be on a downward trend". Opposite: 上昇. For temperatures and abilities 低下 is more usual, for prices 下落. It is read the same as 加工 ("to process").

examples[].german: The exchange rate is fluctuating greatly.
Vegetable prices fluctuate greatly depending on the weather.
Because of the effects of climate change, heavy rain is increasing in many places.
en.notes: 変動する means "to fluctuate, change (greatly)" and is intransitive; typical of values that go up and down: 為替が変動する, 株価の変動, 価格変動. Unlike 変化 ("change" in general), 変動 stresses fluctuation and instability, mostly for prices, exchange rates and figures. Important compounds: 気候変動 "climate change", 変動相場制 "floating exchange rate system".

examples[].german: The patient's condition has stabilized.
Civil servants are popular because their income is stable.
The weather probably won't be settled over the weekend.
en.notes: 安定する means "to become/be stable, to stabilize" and is intransitive: 容態が安定する, 収入が安定している, 天気が安定する. Attributively 安定した is usual: 安定した生活 "a secure life"; the opposite is 不安定 "unstable, unsteady." Transitive "to stabilize something" is 安定させる.

examples[].german: Economic growth is stagnating.
With no leader, the project is stalled.
The seasonal rain front is stalling near Honshū, and the rain continues.
en.notes: 停滞する means "to stagnate, stall, make no progress" and is intransitive: 経済が停滞する, 議論が停滞する, in weather reports 前線が停滞する "a front stalls". It stresses that something that should be moving is stuck in place. For a traffic jam, one says 渋滞 instead; 低迷 describes rather a longer period at a low level (sales, stock prices).

examples[].german: The earth makes one rotation in twenty-four hours.
That person's mind works fast and comes up with an answer right away.
The blades of the electric fan stopped spinning.
en.notes: 回転する means "to turn, rotate" and is intransitive: 車輪が回転する, 地球が回転する; transitive is 回転させる or, in everyday speech, 回す (intransitive 回る). Figuratively: 頭の回転が速い "to think fast," 客の回転がいい "high customer turnover," 回転ずし "conveyor-belt sushi." Compared with 回る, 回転 sounds more technical and precise.

examples[].german: The building shook violently in the earthquake.
During the meeting, my smartphone vibrated in my pocket.
The washing machine vibrates so loudly that I can't sleep.
en.notes: 振動する means "to vibrate, oscillate" and is intransitive: 携帯が振動する, 振り子が振動する; as a noun 振動を感じる "to feel a tremor", 振動数 "frequency". 揺れる ("to sway, shake") is more everyday; 振動 sounds technical and refers to quick, repeated movements. For earthquakes the spelling 震動 is also found.

examples[].german: Metal expands when heat is applied.
The universe is thought to be still expanding.
The national budget is swelling year by year.
en.notes: 膨張する means "to expand, swell" and is intransitive: 金属が熱で膨張する, 宇宙が膨張する. Figuratively it is used for budgets, cities or costs that keep growing: 予算が膨張する, 都市の膨張. Opposite: 収縮. In everyday speech, for a balloon or for hopes, people tend to say 膨らむ; 膨張 is technical and literary.

examples[].german: Force is produced when muscles contract.
When it is cold, blood vessels contract and hands and feet get cold.
With the economy doing badly, the domestic market is shrinking.
en.notes: 収縮する means "to contract, to shrink" and is intransitive: 筋肉が収縮する, 血管が収縮する. It is the opposite of 膨張 and is also used in economics (市場が収縮する "the market shrinks"). For clothes that shrink in the wash, daily speech uses 縮む; 収縮 sounds technical (medicine, physics, economics).

examples[].german: Cells multiply by dividing.
Because of conflicting opinions, the party split into two.
Nuclear power generation uses the energy of nuclear fission.
en.notes: 分裂する means "to split, divide" and is intransitive: 細胞が分裂する (細胞分裂 "cell division"), 党が二つに分裂する, 意見が分裂する. It stresses the breaking apart of something that was a whole - often groups, parties or countries. For neutral "to separate" one uses 分ける or 分離; in physics: 核分裂 "nuclear fission".

examples[].german: Two cultures fused, and a new culture was born.
In this restaurant, Japanese and French cuisine are wonderfully blended.
The sun produces light through the nuclear fusion of hydrogen.
en.notes: 融合する means "to fuse, to merge" and is intransitive: AとBが融合する, 伝統と現代が融合する; the transitive form is 融合させる. In technical use: 核融合 "nuclear fusion", 細胞融合 "cell fusion". For the merger of companies one does not say 融合 but 合併. 融合 stresses that different elements fuse into a new unity.

examples[].german: The prosecution indicted the suspect.
The claims of the prosecution and the defense were very different.
The police sent the case materials to the prosecutors.
en.notes: 検察 is the public prosecutor's office as an authority (short for 検察庁), which investigates crimes and brings charges (起訴する). The individual person is a 検察官 or, colloquially, 検事. In trial reports, 検察側 "the prosecution (side)" is contrasted with 弁護側 "the defense". The police (警察) investigate first and then hand the case over to the 検察.

examples[].german: A new compound was synthesized in the laboratory.
This photo was made by compositing two images.
Synthetic voice is used for the announcements at the station.
en.notes: 合成する means "to put together, synthesize" and is transitive: chemically 化合物を合成する, 合成繊維 "synthetic fiber", 合成洗剤 "synthetic detergent"; for image and sound 写真を合成する "to make a photo composite", 合成音声 "synthetic voice". 合成 stresses artificial production from several parts; 加工, by contrast, is the processing of an existing material.

en.meaning: to take apart; to break down
examples[].german: I took the machine apart and investigated the cause.
Plastic hardly breaks down in nature.
As a child, I took toys apart and got scolded by my father.
en.notes: 分解する has two sides: transitive "to take apart, to disassemble" (時計を分解する) and intransitive or passive "to decompose, to be broken down" (プラスチックは分解されにくい, 微生物が落ち葉を分解する). The opposite of taking apart is 組み立てる ("to assemble"). In mathematics, 因数分解 means "factorization".

examples[].german: Sugar dissolves in water.
This medicine dissolves easily in water.
At the plant, old iron is melted at high temperature and reused.
en.notes: 溶解する means "to dissolve (in a liquid)" and also "to melt" (metals by heat). It is mostly intransitive: 砂糖が水に溶解する; in technology and industry it is also transitive: 鉄を溶解する "melt iron". The word is technical - in daily life one says 溶ける or 溶かす. Typical are 溶解度 "solubility" and 溶解炉 "melting furnace".

en.meaning: to evaporate; to vanish without a trace
examples[].german: Water evaporates from the heat of the sun.
The soup in the pot boiled away until only half was left.
A man in debt suddenly disappeared one day.
en.notes: 蒸発する means "to evaporate, to vaporize" and is intransitive: 水が蒸発する; the transitive form is 蒸発させる. Colloquially it also means "to disappear without a trace, to go into hiding" of people (夫が蒸発した). Unlike 沸騰 ("to boil"), 蒸発 can also happen at the surface of a liquid without boiling.

examples[].german: The lava cooled and solidified.
The blood in the wound clotted, and the bleeding stopped.
Water freezes at zero degrees and becomes ice.
en.notes: 凝固する means "to solidify, to become solid, to coagulate" and is intransitive; it is technical and used for liquids: 溶岩が凝固する, 血液が凝固する "blood clots", 凝固点 "freezing point". In daily life one says 固まる. The opposite (melting) is technically 融解.

examples[].german: Iron oxidizes in air and rusts.
Old oil has oxidized, so it is better not to use it.
If you leave a cut apple for a while, it oxidizes and turns brown.
en.notes: 酸化する means "to oxidize" and is intransitive: 鉄が酸化する, 油が酸化する ("to go rancid"); transitive 酸化させる, as a noun 酸化を防ぐ "to prevent oxidation". The chemical opposite is 還元 ("reduction"). For metals one says 錆びる ("to rust") in everyday speech; for foods such as cut apples, 酸化 is likewise used.

en.meaning: to give back; to let benefit; (chemistry) to reduce
examples[].german: We carried out an experiment to reduce oxidized metal.
The store returns part of its profits to customers as points.
I want to give the results of my research back to society.
en.notes: 還元する has two areas of use: in chemistry it means "to reduce" (to remove oxygen from a substance), the opposite of 酸化. In everyday life and business it means "to give back (profits, benefits), to let benefit", in the pattern AをBに還元する: 利益を社会に還元する, ポイント還元 "rebate in points". For "to reduce" in the sense of "to decrease", one does not say 還元 but 減らす or 削減する.

examples[].german: We will remove signs that were put up illegally.
Bicycles left in front of the station are removed by the city.
Right after the event ended, the stage was dismantled.
en.notes: 撤去する means "to remove, to dismantle, to clear away": something that was set up or built somewhere is taken away - 看板を撤去する, 放置自転車を撤去する, 古い建物を撤去する. It is transitive and in notices and news often appears in the passive (撤去される). 取り除く is more general; withdrawal from a market or of troops is usually expressed with 撤退.

en.meaning: to relocate; to move (an office, shop)
examples[].german: The head office will be relocated from Tokyo to Osaka.
The bakery I always used to go to has moved to the front of the station.
This technology is scheduled to be transferred to an overseas factory.
en.notes: 移転する means "to relocate, to move" - of companies, shops, government offices or institutions, not of private individuals (for that, 引っ越す). It can be transitive (本社を大阪に移転する) and intransitive (店が駅前に移転した); on notices you read 移転のお知らせ "notice of relocation". It also means "transfer", e.g. 技術移転 "technology transfer".

examples[].german: Construction to expand the airport terminal has begun.
There is a plan to widen the road in front of the station to reduce traffic jams.
I installed a translation extension in my browser.
en.notes: 拡張する means "to expand, to extend, to enlarge" and is transitive: 道路を拡張する, 事業を拡張する, 機能を拡張する. In IT: 拡張子 "file extension", 拡張機能 "extension, add-on". Similar is 拡大 ("to enlarge, to expand"), which can also be intransitive (被害が拡大する); 拡張 is used more for facilities, areas and functions.

examples[].german: The plaintiff demanded compensation for damages.
The court accepted the plaintiff's claim.
The victims of pollution became plaintiffs and sued the state.
en.notes: 原告 is the suing party in a civil or administrative lawsuit, the "plaintiff"; the opposing party is the 被告. Typical: 原告側 "the plaintiff's side", 原告の訴えを認める "to uphold the claim", 原告が勝訴する／敗訴する "to win/lose the case". For class actions people speak of the 原告団. In a criminal trial there is no 原告 - there the 検察 brings the charges.

examples[].german: The contract period was extended by one year.
The game ended in a tie and went into extra time.
I had the loan period for the book from the library extended.
en.notes: 延長する means "to extend, to lengthen" - in time (期間を延長する, 営業時間を延長する) and in space (線路を延長する). It is transitive; as nouns you know 延長戦 "extra time (sports)" and 延長コード "extension cord". Do not confuse it with 延期 ("to postpone"): 延長 makes something longer, 延期 moves an appointment to a later date. Opposite: 短縮.

examples[].german: A policy of shortening working hours was decided.
Thanks to the new road, the commute has been shortened by twenty minutes.
This shop has had shortened business hours since this month.
en.notes: 短縮する means "to shorten, cut short" and is transitive: 時間を短縮する, 距離を短縮する, 営業時間を短縮する "to shorten business hours". The abbreviation 時短 (from 時間短縮) is very common for saving time or shorter working hours. Opposite: 延長. 省略, by contrast, means "to omit, leave out".

examples[].german: Oil and water separate naturally.
A few minutes after launch, the booster separated from the rocket.
This device separates dirt from water.
en.notes: 分離する means "to separate, split off" and is used both transitively (AからBを分離する) and intransitively (油と水が分離する). It sounds factual and technical; well-known compounds are 政教分離 "separation of church and state" and 中央分離帯 "median strip". In everyday speech one says 分ける / 分かれる; 分裂, by contrast, stresses the breaking apart of a whole.

en.meaning: to become independent; to go independent
examples[].german: She became independent from her parents at twenty.
After working at a company for ten years, he went independent and opened his own shop.
That country became independent in the middle of the twentieth century.
en.notes: 独立する means "to become independent, to become self-employed" and is intransitive, mostly with から: 親から独立する "to stand on one's own feet," 会社を辞めて独立する "to quit one's company and go independent," 国が独立する. As a noun it appears in 独立記念日 "Independence Day" or 独立心 "spirit of independence." Close in meaning is 自立 ("to live self-reliantly"), which stresses personal maturity more.

examples[].german: The king ruled a vast territory.
He was gripped by fear and could not say anything.
That company dominates almost the whole domestic market.
en.notes: 支配する means "to rule, govern, control" and is transitive: 国を支配する, 市場を支配する. Figuratively also for feelings or moods that determine someone: 恐怖に支配される "to be gripped by fear." 支配人 is the "manager" of a hotel or cinema. Compared with 管理 ("to manage"), 支配 always has an aspect of power and rule.

examples[].german: Data needs to be managed securely.
I left the key with the apartment building's manager.
Before exams, it is important to take good care of your health.
en.notes: 管理する means "to manage, supervise, take care of" and is transitive: データを管理する, 建物を管理する, 健康を管理する. Very common are 管理人 "caretaker, building manager," 管理職 "managerial position" and 体調管理 "looking after one's health." 経営, by contrast, means "to run a company," and 支配 has an aspect of power; 管理 stresses order, control and upkeep.

examples[].german: He runs a nonprofit organization.
This site is run by an individual.
I've been put in charge of running the school festival and am busy with preparations every day.
en.notes: 運営する means "to run, organize, manage" - for institutions, events, websites or clubs: 学校を運営する, イベントの運営. It should be distinguished from 経営する, which stresses profit-oriented business management (会社・店を経営する), whereas 運営 refers to the practical operation and administration. Common are 運営側 "organizers, the operator side", 運営会社 and 運営費. Transitive with を, passive 運営される.

examples[].german: My father runs a restaurant.
My grandfather used to run a small bookstore in front of the station.
Running a hotel is harder than you would imagine.
en.notes: 経営する means to run and operate a company or business economically; the object takes を: 会社・店・ホテルを経営する. It mostly appears in the progressive form 経営している because it describes an ongoing state. For clubs, events or websites where profit is not the point, people more often say 運営する "to operate, organize," and for pure administration 管理する. Common derivatives are 経営者 "entrepreneur, manager" and 経営が苦しい "to be in financial difficulty."

en.meaning: to instruct; to coach; to guide
examples[].german: A senior employee coaches the new employees.
Professor Tanaka carefully guided me on how to write my graduation thesis.
Since I was coached by my trainer, my form has improved a lot.
en.notes: 指導する means to guide or supervise someone in a professional or academic way, typical for teachers, coaches, professors and experienced colleagues. The person being guided takes を (生徒を指導する), the content is often 〜の書き方を指導する or 〜について指導する. Compared with the everyday 教える "to teach," 指導 sounds more official and stresses longer-term supervision. Common words: 指導者 "instructor, leader," 指導教員 "thesis supervisor," 行政指導 "administrative guidance."

examples[].german: The defendant pleaded not guilty.
The court sentenced the defendant to three years.
A settlement was reached between the plaintiff and the defendant.
en.notes: 被告 is the sued or accused party. In a civil lawsuit it is the "defendant" (opposing party of the 原告); in a criminal trial the accused is legally called 被告人, which the media shorten to 被告 and attach to names like a title: 山田被告 "the defendant Yamada". Before the indictment, people speak of a 容疑者 "suspect". Typical: 被告側, 被告に判決を言い渡す.

en.meaning: to supervise; to oversee; to direct
examples[].german: He supervises the construction site.
Please enjoy fireworks only under adult supervision.
I have watched all the films directed by Akira Kurosawa.
en.notes: 監督する means "to supervise, oversee": work, people or processes are checked so that everything goes correctly (現場を監督する, 試験を監督する). The noun often appears in the phrase 〜の監督のもとで "under the supervision of." As a noun, 監督 also means "film director" or "manager/coach of a team," and 映画を監督する accordingly means "to direct a film." Compared with 指導する "to guide," the emphasis is on control, not on teaching.

en.meaning: to conduct; to command; to lead
examples[].german: She conducts the orchestra.
The fire chief on site directed the rescue operation.
The department head is personally leading the project.
en.notes: 指揮する means to lead a group and give it instructions: to conduct an orchestra, command troops or lead an operation (オーケストラを指揮する, 救助活動を指揮する). Very common is the set phrase 指揮を執る（とる） "to take charge." Derived from it are 指揮者 "conductor" and 指揮官 "commander." Unlike 指導する "to guide, teach," it is not about teaching but about command in a concrete situation.

examples[].german: The commanding officer ordered the soldiers to withdraw.
My father said "Go to bed early" in a commanding tone.
I hate being given orders by people, so I quit my company and went independent.
en.notes: 命令する means "to order": the person who receives the order takes に, the content takes を or appears as 〜ように／〜と (部下に待機するように命令する). The word is very direct and hierarchical; in the office people mostly say 指示する "to instruct," among equals 頼む. In the passive, 命令される often carries a note of resentment at being bossed around. In writing there is the synonym 命じる.

examples[].german: Soldiers must obey orders.
He is not the type to submit to whatever his boss says.
Dogs have a tendency to submit to the leader of the pack.
en.notes: 服従する means to submit unconditionally to an authority or an order; the thing obeyed takes に (命令に服従する). The word is rather literary and often carries a negative connotation of subjugation, e.g. in 絶対服従 "absolute obedience". For neutrally following rules or advice, daily speech uses 従う. Opposites are 反抗する "to rebel" and 抵抗する "to resist".

examples[].german: The citizens resisted the unjust law.
The culprit resisted fiercely when he was arrested.
Many employees feel resistance to the new way of doing things.
en.notes: 抵抗する means "to fight back, resist" violence, pressure or something imposed; the target takes に (権力に抵抗する). As a noun, 抵抗 also describes an inner reluctance: 〜に抵抗がある／抵抗を感じる "to have reservations about something." In physics, 抵抗 is electrical resistance. Compared with 反抗する, which is directed against authority figures such as parents, 抵抗 is more general and often physical.

examples[].german: Children in puberty sometimes rebel against their parents.
When I was in junior high school, I did nothing but defy my teachers.
My son is in his rebellious phase now and doesn't answer whatever I say.
en.notes: 反抗する means to rebel against an authority, typically children against parents, pupils against teachers or subordinates against superiors; the target takes に (親に反抗する). The word stresses defiant, often emotional behavior, as in 反抗的な態度 "rebellious attitude" and 反抗期 "defiant phase, rebellious phase." 抵抗する, by contrast, is the more general "to resist," and 反発する is more "to react with rejection."

examples[].german: The labor union negotiates with the company about wages.
I negotiated with the landlord to see if the move-out date could be pushed back a week.
When I negotiated the price at the flea market, I got it for a thousand yen less.
en.notes: 交渉する means "to negotiate": the negotiating partner takes と, the topic takes について or を (値段を交渉する). Success and failure are expressed with 交渉がまとまる "the negotiation reaches an agreement" and 交渉が決裂する "the negotiations break down". In everyday life you often meet 値段交渉 "price negotiation". Someone who does not negotiate personally but stands between two parties 仲介する "mediates".

en.meaning: to mediate; to act as intermediary
examples[].german: A real estate company brokers the sale.
A senior colleague acted as go-between, and I was able to talk to a researcher.
With the United Nations mediating, talks between the two countries began.
en.notes: 仲介する means to stand as an intermediary between two parties and bring them together, especially in business: 売買を仲介する, 不動産の仲介, 仲介手数料 "brokerage fee", 仲介業者 "broker". It can also mean arranging contacts or talks. When it is about the official settlement of a dispute, one says 調停する "to arbitrate"; 紹介する only means "to introduce", without an active role in what follows.

examples[].german: The court mediates the dispute between the two parties.
The government mediated the conflict between labor and management.
The divorce talks failed to reach an agreement, so they applied to the family court for mediation.
en.notes: 調停する means "to mediate": a neutral body such as a court, an authority or a state helps disputing parties agree on a compromise (紛争を調停する). The word is formal and often comes from law and politics, e.g. 離婚調停 "divorce mediation" or 調停が成立する "the mediation succeeds". In 仲裁, an arbitrator makes a binding decision; 仲介 is mediating in general, e.g. in business deals.

examples[].german: After years of conflict, the two countries reconciled.
After apologizing and talking it over, I made up with the friend I had quarreled with.
The trial ended with both sides reaching a settlement.
en.notes: 和解する means "to reconcile" or, legally, "to settle"; the partner takes と (友人と和解する). Among friends or children, 仲直りする sounds more natural in daily life; 和解 is more formal and is used for states, for families after a long dispute, or for court proceedings. Typical legal expressions are 和解が成立する "a settlement is reached" and 和解金 "settlement money".

examples[].german: This precedent will influence future trials.
The lawyer researched similar precedents.
There is no precedent yet for a case like this.
en.notes: 判例 are earlier court decisions that serve as a standard for later cases - "precedent" or "case law". Typical: 判例に従う "to follow case law", 判例を調べる, 最高裁の判例. A single verdict is a 判決; 判例 is a verdict in its function as a model. Precedents outside the judiciary ("this has never happened before") are called 前例.

examples[].german: Everyone cooperated for the success of the project.
The siblings worked together to prepare our mother's birthday party.
We ask for your cooperation with the questionnaire.
en.notes: 協力する means "to work together, to lend a hand." With と you work together with someone (地域と協力する), with に you contribute to something (調査に協力する "to take part in a survey"). Very common is the polite request ご協力をお願いします "We ask for your cooperation." Compared with 手伝う "to help," 協力 stresses the shared goal; 連携する emphasizes coordination between organizations more strongly.

examples[].german: The departments coordinate to deal with the problem.
The hospital and local clinics work hand in hand to support patients.
This app can be linked with the calendar on your smartphone.
en.notes: 連携する means that several parties coordinate their actions and work hand in hand; the partner takes と (警察と連携する), often as 連携して〜する. It is typical of government offices, departments, clinics or sports teams (連携プレー "teamwork play"). In IT it also means "to link, to sync": アプリと連携する. Compared with 協力する, 連携 stresses coordination between independent partners.

en.meaning: to form a partnership; to tie up
examples[].german: Our company formed a partnership with a foreign company.
This university has partnerships with three universities abroad.
At partner hotels, members can stay at discounted rates.
en.notes: 提携する means that companies or institutions enter a formal partnership; the partner takes と (海外企業と提携する). Typical words are 業務提携 "business alliance", 提携先 "partner company" and 提携ホテル "partner hotel". Unlike 協力する "to cooperate", 提携 presupposes a contractual agreement; for a real merger, one says 合併.

examples[].german: We are competing with other companies in the global market.
I competed with my older brother to see who could eat faster.
Is it really a good thing to be made to compete with everyone around you from childhood?
en.notes: 競争する means "to compete, to vie"; the opponent takes と (他社と競争する). It ranges from harmless rivalry among children to market competition; common are 競争が激しい "the competition is fierce", 競争相手 "competitor" and 競争率 "competition ratio". Not to be confused with the identically read 競走 "footrace". The verb 競う is similar but sounds somewhat more elevated.

en.meaning: to compete with; to stand up to
examples[].german: The shopping street started weekly sales to compete with the big supermarket.
At the sports festival, the inter-class relay is always the highlight.
I can't match him in strength, so I decided to use my head.
en.notes: 対抗する means to set oneself against an opponent or competitor and keep up with them; the counterpart takes に (大手に対抗する). It is less about mere rejection than about answering like with like, e.g. with countermeasures or a competition. Common are 対抗できる "to be able to compete with", 対抗策 "countermeasure" and 〜対抗 "competition between ..." as in クラス対抗. For rejecting a plan, one rather says 反対する.

examples[].german: The mountaineer conquered Mount Everest.
Ancient Rome conquered the countries around the Mediterranean one after another.
I feel as if I have finally conquered math, which I always struggled with.
en.notes: 征服する means "to conquer, subjugate" (国を征服する) and is used figuratively for conquering a mountain or a great challenge (エベレストを征服する). For difficulties or illnesses, 克服する "to overcome" is usually more natural; 征服 sounds more dramatic and is often jocular in everyday use. Do not confuse it with the identically read 制服 "uniform".

examples[].german: We collected donations to support the disaster-stricken area.
The government created a program to support families raising children.
I do volunteer work supporting the daily life of international students.
en.notes: 支援する means "to support", usually in an organized way and with money, materials or personnel: 被災地を支援する, 子育てを支援する. Typical words are 支援者 "supporter" and 支援物資 "relief supplies". 援助する stresses material or financial help from a stronger side, 応援する is "to cheer on" or personal support, and 手伝う is concrete help with a task.

en.meaning: to aid; to assist; to support
examples[].german: Developed countries give economic aid to developing countries.
While I attended university, my uncle supported my tuition.
This research receives financial support from the city.
en.notes: 援助する means "to give aid," above all material or financial, often from a stronger side to a weaker one: 途上国を援助する, 学費を援助する. The noun often appears in 援助を受ける "to receive aid" and 経済援助 "economic aid." 支援する is broader and can also mean organizational support; for spontaneous helping in everyday life people say 手伝う or 助ける.

examples[].german: The fire brigade rescued the residents from the fire.
A child who was drowning in the sea was rescued by a lifeguard.
A hiker who got lost on a snowy mountain was rescued by helicopter two days later.
en.notes: 救助する means to rescue people from acute danger to life, for example in fires, accidents or in the mountains; often in the passive 救助される. Typical words are 救助隊 "rescue team" and 人命救助 "life saving." 助ける is the general everyday word, 救う sounds more elevated and can also be figurative (心を救う), and 救出する stresses getting someone out of a trap or captivity.

en.meaning: to protect; to take into custody
examples[].german: There is a law that protects endangered species.
A lost child was taken into protective care by the police.
To protect your personal information, please change your password regularly.
en.notes: 保護する means "to protect" in the sense of preserving long-term or taking into care: 自然を保護する, 個人情報を保護する. The police 保護する lost children or drunk people, i.e. they take them into care. Important derivatives are 保護者 "guardian" and 自然保護 "nature conservation". 守る is the general everyday word (also "to keep a promise"), and 防ぐ means "to prevent, to ward off".

examples[].german: The city enacted a new ordinance.
In this ward, walking while smoking is prohibited by ordinance.
If you violate the ordinance, you have to pay a fine.
en.notes: 条例 is a bylaw or ordinance that a prefecture or municipality enacts itself - as opposed to the national law (法律). Typical verbs: 条例を制定する "to enact", 条例で禁止する, 条例に違反する. Well-known examples are 路上喫煙禁止条例 or 迷惑防止条例. The word is found mainly in news and on notice signs.

examples[].german: As a typhoon was approaching, we took shelter on high ground.
When the fire alarm sounds, please use the stairs to get outside.
Because floods made their homes uninhabitable, some people are still staying in the gymnasium.
en.notes: 避難する is intransitive and means "to move to safety, flee (from danger)": the place of refuge takes に／へ, the danger takes から (津波から高台へ避難する). To evacuate others, use the causative 住民を避難させる. Common words are 避難所 "evacuation shelter", 避難訓練 "evacuation drill" and 避難指示 "evacuation order". Do not confuse it with the identically read 非難 "criticism, reproach".

examples[].german: The prisoner escaped from the prison.
I noticed the fire and hurriedly escaped through the window.
Thanks to the hit new product, the company finally got out of the red.
en.notes: 脱出する means "to escape, free oneself from a bad situation"; the place one escapes from takes から (建物から脱出する). It is also used figuratively: 赤字から脱出する "to get out of the red", 不況から脱出する. 逃げる is the general "to flee, run away"; for prison breaks there is the specific 脱獄する. 脱出ゲーム "escape room game" is also well known.

examples[].german: A burglar broke into the house in the middle of the night.
Someone broke into the company's server and stole customer data.
Insects come into the room through the gaps.
en.notes: 侵入する means to enter a place or system without authorization or by force; the target takes に (家に侵入する, サーバーに侵入する). Typical words are 不法侵入 "trespassing" and 侵入者 "intruder". Do not confuse it with the identically read 進入する, which neutrally describes vehicles driving into an area; water seeping in is written 浸入. For the military invasion of whole countries, 侵略 is more usual.

en.meaning: to rush in; to plunge into
examples[].german: The police stormed into the building.
The two countries finally plunged into war.
The game went into extra time with the score tied.
en.notes: 突入する means to rush into something with force: police or troops 建物に突入する. Figuratively it means "to enter a new phase", often abruptly or unstoppably: 戦争に突入する, 延長戦に突入する, 夏休みに突入する. The destination always takes に. Compared with 入る "to go in", 突入 stresses speed and determination; 侵入する, by contrast, is stealthy, unauthorized intrusion.

en.meaning: to enter (a road, platform); to drive into
examples[].german: The train pulled into the platform.
Vehicles are prohibited from entering beyond this point.
At this intersection, watch out for cars entering from the right.
en.notes: 進入する is a neutral, rather technical word for vehicles, trains or aircraft entering an area; the destination takes に (交差点に進入する). You see it mainly on signs and in announcements, e.g. 進入禁止 "no entry" or 電車が進入します. Do not confuse it with the identically read 侵入する "to intrude without authorization". In daily life one simply says 入る.

examples[].german: The army withdrew from the front line.
Because sales did not grow, the company pulled out of the Japanese market.
As the weather worsened, the climbing party turned back just short of the summit.
en.notes: 撤退する means "to withdraw (in a planned and complete way)"; the place given up takes から (前線から撤退する). Besides the military, it is very common in business: 市場から撤退する "withdraw from the market", 事業から撤退する. In mountaineering or projects it also means "to abort and turn back". 後退する, by contrast, describes a gradual falling back, not a final giving up.

examples[].german: They fell back under enemy attack.
Exports are declining, and the economy is starting to slow down.
My father's hairline is receding more every year.
en.notes: 後退する means "to retreat, move backward" and is the opposite of 前進する. Figuratively it describes a decline, especially in economics: 景気が後退する "the economy slows down", 景気後退 "recession". It is intransitive; to set something back, one says 後退させる. Unlike 撤退する "to withdraw completely", 後退 refers to going back a certain distance. For cars, people mostly say バックする in everyday speech.

examples[].german: We overcome difficulties and move forward.
The soldiers advanced slowly through the snow.
After long discussions, the negotiations finally moved one step forward.
en.notes: 前進する means "to advance, move forward," literally as of troops or vehicles, and very often figuratively for progress: 交渉が一歩前進する "the negotiations move one step forward." The opposite is 後退する. In everyday speech, for physically walking forward people more often say 前に進む; 前進 sounds more formal or motivational, as in speeches. Related is 進歩する "to make progress (technology, skills)."

examples[].german: Sales broke through the 10 billion yen mark.
I got through the first-round exam and moved on to the interview.
The demonstrators broke through the police line.
en.notes: 突破する means "to break through": literally a barrier or defense (警察の列を突破する), figuratively to pass a limit or mark (売上が百億円を突破する, 入場者が百万人を突破する) or to clear a difficult hurdle (難関を突破する, 予選を突破する). The object takes を. For a new approach to a solution, one says 突破口 "breakthrough, starting point". With numbers, 超える is more neutral; 突破 sounds like a success announcement.

examples[].german: The climbing party reached the summit.
After a long discussion, we finally arrived at a conclusion.
It takes about seven months for the probe to reach Mars.
en.notes: 到達する means to reach a goal after a long way; the goal takes に (山頂に到達する, 結論に到達する). It is more formal than 着く and is also used abstractly for goals, levels or results. 達する is similar but typical for numbers and limits (気温が四十度に達する); 到着する is the arrival of people or vehicles.

examples[].german: That act was recognized as legal.
In some countries, that drug is legal.
I consulted a tax accountant about legal ways to reduce taxes.
en.notes: 合法 means "lawful, legal" and is used predicatively (合法だ／合法である) or as a na-adjective (合法な手段); 合法的に "in a legal way" is also very common. Opposites are 違法 and the stronger 非合法 "illegal, underground". In everyday speech people often say more simply 法律で認められている. The register is factual to formal.

examples[].german: A typhoon is approaching the Japanese archipelago.
The two cars came too close and nearly collided.
A stranger kept approaching me insistently, so I consulted the police.
en.notes: 接近する means "to approach" and is the formal counterpart of 近づく; the target takes に (台風が日本に接近する). It is often heard in news about typhoons, ships or aircraft, but also when someone approaches a person with intent. Figuratively it can mean that abilities or values are nearly equal (実力が接近している). From it comes 接近戦 "close combat; tight race".

examples[].german: That country withdrew from the international treaty.
Because of a conflict of opinion, several legislators left the party.
The injured player will be away from the team for a while.
en.notes: 離脱する means to detach oneself from an organization, an agreement or a group; the thing left takes から or を (条約から離脱する, 党を離脱する). In sports it also means that a player drops out due to injury (チームを離脱する). It is more formal than 抜ける or やめる; for clubs and companies one rather says 退会する or 退職する. A well-known example from the news is EU離脱 "withdrawal from the EU".

en.meaning: to join up; to merge; to flow together
examples[].german: Two rivers join here.
After work, I'll meet up with everyone in front of the station.
When merging onto the expressway, please speed up.
en.notes: 合流する first means "to flow together" of rivers, but it is very often used for people: joining a group later (友達と駅で合流する). In traffic it means "to merge" (高速道路に合流する), and signs read 合流注意. The partner takes と, the place one merges into takes に. The opposite is 分岐する "to branch off"; 集まる, by contrast, stresses many coming together.

examples[].german: The road forks into two here.
This line splits in two at the next station, so be careful not to take the wrong train.
That encounter became a turning point in my life.
en.notes: 分岐する means "to branch, to fork" of roads, railway lines or cables; the number of branches takes に (二つに分岐する). In daily life one usually just says 分かれる; 分岐 sounds more technical and appears in timetables, road maps and programming (条件分岐 "conditional branch"). Very common is 分岐点, literally "fork", figuratively a "turning point" in life. The opposite is 合流する.

examples[].german: Because of construction, we have to take a detour.
The expressway was closed due to an accident, so we took a detour via the regular roads.
Because of heavy rain, the buses are running on a detour.
en.notes: 迂回する means "to make a detour, to go around", usually because of construction, accidents or closures; the obstacle or route takes を (現場を迂回する). On signs you read 迂回路 "detour"; because the kanji is difficult, it is often written う回. In daily life, 遠回りする or 回り道する are more usual, and they are also used without external compulsion. Figuratively, 迂回 can also mean getting around rules or problems.

examples[].german: Pedestrians cross the road at the crosswalk.
My dream is to cross the Pacific Ocean by ship.
A child suddenly crossed the road, and I hurriedly hit the brakes.
en.notes: 横断する means "to cross over"; the object takes を (道路を横断する, 太平洋を横断する). In everyday life it is known mainly from 横断歩道 "crosswalk"; for simply crossing a street people otherwise usually say 渡る. With continents or oceans, 横断 denotes the east-west direction or the crossing; 縦断する, by contrast, is traveling through the length of something.

examples[].german: He traveled the length of Japan by bicycle.
A large typhoon passed across the whole length of the Japanese archipelago.
I set out on a journey crossing the American continent from north to south.
en.notes: 縦断する means to cross an area lengthwise, typically from north to south; the object takes を (日本を縦断する). It is used for trips, expeditions and especially for typhoons that sweep across the whole country (台風が列島を縦断する). The counterpart is 横断する "to cross sideways". The word is rather literary and often appears in news and travel reports.

examples[].german: A hawk is circling in the sky.
Before landing, the plane circled several times above the airport.
The ship made a wide turn to the right and headed for the port.
en.notes: 旋回する means "to circle, to turn in a curve" and is used mainly for aircraft, birds, helicopters and ships. The area circled over takes を (上空を旋回する), the direction takes に (右に旋回する). The word is technical and literary; in daily life one says 回る or 曲がる. 回転する, by contrast, is turning around one's own axis.

examples[].german: The plane landed safely.
Because of bad weather, the plane landed at a different airport.
The first time humans landed on the moon was in 1969.
en.notes: 着陸する means "to land" (aircraft, spacecraft); the landing place takes に (空港に着陸する, 月に着陸する). The opposite is 離陸する "to take off". Landing on water is 着水, ships docking is 着岸. For simply arriving at a destination, one says 到着する; 着陸 refers only to the actual moment of touching down.

examples[].german: The plane took off on schedule.
When a plane takes off, my ears sometimes hurt.
Because of fog, takeoff was delayed by an hour.
en.notes: 離陸する means "to take off" (aircraft); the departure airport takes から (成田から離陸する). The opposite is 着陸する "to land". For departure in the sense of the journey, one says 出発する; 離陸 refers only to the moment the aircraft leaves the ground. The native verb 飛び立つ is similar but sounds more narrative and also suits birds.

examples[].german: A new bill was deliberated in the assembly.
The city council approved the redevelopment plan for the area in front of the station.
The US Congress consists of two chambers.
en.notes: 議会 is the general word for an elected legislative assembly, from a city council to a country's parliament: 市議会, 県議会, イギリス議会. Japan's national parliament, however, is almost always called 国会. Typical collocations: 議会で審議する, 議会を解散する, 議会制民主主義. Its members are called 議員.

examples[].german: The illegal transaction was exposed.
Illegal parking in front of the station has become a problem.
Let's stop downloading movies illegally.
en.notes: 違法 means "against the law, illegal" and is used mostly as a na-adjective or in compounds: 違法な取引, 違法駐車 "illegal parking", 違法ダウンロード. The opposite is 合法. The similar 不法 ("unlawful") is tied to set combinations such as 不法侵入 or 不法滞在. To violate a specific rule is 〜に違反する, the noun for it is 違反.

en.meaning: to hold down; to secure; to grasp
examples[].german: I held my hat down with my hand so the wind wouldn't blow it away.
I've already reserved a room for next week's meeting.
Before the exam, let's at least make sure we have the key points down.
en.notes: 押さえる first means "to hold down or press with the hand" (帽子を押さえる, 傷口を押さえる). Figuratively it means "to secure something", such as a room or a date (会議室を押さえる), and "to grasp the essentials" (ポイントを押さえる). For suppressing feelings or keeping costs down, 抑える is usually written (怒りを抑える, 費用を抑える). There is no direct intransitive counterpart.

en.meaning: to hit; to strike; to knock
examples[].german: I knocked on the door and called the person inside.
Someone tapped me on the shoulder from behind.
The singer was heavily criticized online because of a casual remark.
en.notes: 叩く means "to hit, knock" with the flat of the hand or an object: ドアを叩く, 肩を叩く, 手を叩く "to clap," 太鼓を叩く "to drum." For punches with the fist or violence against people, 殴る is more usual. Figuratively, 叩く means "to criticize sharply," especially online: ネットで叩かれる. The word is also often written in kana as たたく.

en.meaning: to hit, to strike; to type
examples[].german: The batter hit the ball far.
You type messages on your smartphone fast, don't you!
I fell and hit my head, so I went to the hospital.
en.notes: 打つ means "to hit, to strike" with the hand or a tool: ボールを打つ, 釘を打つ; 頭を打つ is "to bump one's head". Also very common is "to type": メールを打つ, キーボードを打つ, and 注射を打つ "to give an injection". Repeated knocking or hitting is more 叩く, hitting with a fist 殴る; "to shoot" is read the same but written 撃つ.

examples[].german: The player kicked the ball hard.
My younger brother kicks off the futon in his sleep.
The company flatly rejected the union's demands.
en.notes: 蹴る means "to kick" (ボールを蹴る). Note: although it ends in -eru, it is a godan verb (蹴って, 蹴らない, not 蹴て). Figuratively it means "to flatly reject", e.g. an offer or a demand (要求を蹴る), which sounds rather blunt. Intensified forms are 蹴飛ばす "to kick away" and 蹴り "a kick" as a noun.

en.meaning: to sting; to pierce, to stab
examples[].german: I was bitten on the arm by a mosquito.
The criminal stabbed the man with a knife and fled.
For yakitori, you put the meat on skewers and grill it.
en.notes: 刺す means "to sting, to pierce" with something pointed (ナイフで刺す, 串に刺す) and is also used for insect stings, mostly in the passive: 蚊に刺される. The intransitive counterpart is 刺さる "to get stuck in" (とげが刺さる). Not to be confused with the identically read 指す "to point", 差す "to put up (an umbrella)" and 挿す "to insert (flowers)".

examples[].german: I tore the cloth in two with my hands.
I slit open the fish's belly with a kitchen knife and took out the innards.
There was someone who tried to drive the two of them apart.
en.notes: 裂く means "to tear (open), to slit", often along a fiber or line: 布を裂く, 魚の腹を裂く. Figuratively 仲を裂く means "to drive a couple or friends apart". The intransitive counterpart is 裂ける (服が裂ける). 破る is more general, "to tear up, to destroy" (paper, letters). Do not confuse it with the identically read 割く "to spare (time)": 時間を割く.

en.meaning: to tear; to break; to defeat
examples[].german: He got angry and tore up the letter.
My friend broke the promise and in the end didn't come.
In the final, they beat the previous champions and won their first title.
en.notes: 破る literally means "to tear, break" (紙を破る), but is very often figurative: 約束・ルールを破る "to break a promise / a rule," 記録を破る "to break a record," 相手チームを破る "to defeat the opposing team," 沈黙を破る "to break the silence." The intransitive counterpart is 破れる (紙が破れる, 夢が破れる). For tearing apart along a line, 裂く fits better.

examples[].german: I folded paper and made a crane.
I fell while skiing and broke my leg.
You must not break branches off the trees in the park.
en.notes: 折る has two basic meanings: "to fold, to bend" (紙を折る, 折り紙) and "to break, to snap off" (枝を折る, 足の骨を折る "to break one's leg"). The intransitive partner is 折れる: 枝が折れる "the branch breaks"; 骨が折れる also means "to be laborious" figuratively. Glass or plates, by contrast, are broken with 割る, and folding clothes or an umbrella is 畳む.

examples[].german: I bent my knees and crouched down.
I bent a wire to make a hanger.
No matter what anyone said to her, she did not change her mind.
en.notes: 曲げる means "to bend, to flex" (針金を曲げる, 膝を曲げる); the intransitive counterpart is 曲がる (道が曲がる). Figuratively it means "to distort" (事実を曲げる) and, often negated, "to abandon one's convictions" (自分の考えを曲げない "stick to one's opinion"). The idiom へそを曲げる means "to sulk, to get in a huff". 折る, by contrast, means "to snap, to fold, to break".

en.meaning: to get entangled; to be involved; to pick a fight with
examples[].german: The thread got tangled and could not be undone.
Apparently a lot of money is involved in this case.
A drunk customer was picking a fight with the clerk.
en.notes: 絡む is intransitive and means "to get tangled, entangled" (糸が絡む). Figuratively, 〜が絡む means "to be involved, to play a role" (お金が絡む問題) and 人に絡む means "to pick on someone, look for a fight", typical of drunk people. The transitive counterpart is 絡める "to entwine, coat" (ソースを絡める); 絡まる is a close synonym for physical tangling.

en.meaning: to sue; to complain of; to appeal
examples[].german: He decided to sue the company.
Because the child complained of a stomachache, I took him to the school infirmary.
Environmental groups are appealing for the need to protect the forest.
en.notes: 訴える has three main meanings: to sue someone (会社を訴える, 裁判所に訴える), to voice complaints or complain of something (腹痛を訴える, 不満を訴える), and to appeal to something or convey something urgently (平和を訴える, 感情に訴える). In a medical context, 〜を訴える is the usual wording for "to complain of ...". The noun is 訴え "lawsuit, appeal"; there is no intransitive counterpart, "to be sued" is the passive 訴えられる.

en.meaning: to bundle; to tie up; to lead
examples[].german: I tied my hair back with a hair elastic.
I bundled the old newspapers with string and put them out on recycling day.
He is the captain who leads the fifty club members.
en.notes: 束ねる is transitive: to gather something with を into a bundle, with the binding material marked by で (ひもで束ねる, ゴムで束ねる). Typical for hair, newspapers, letters, banknotes or flowers. Figuratively it means "to lead a group, hold it together": チームを束ねる, 組織を束ねる. Related is the noun 束 (たば) "bundle"; 結ぶ "to tie, knot", by contrast, stresses the knot itself.

en.meaning: to pile up; to stack; to repeat
examples[].german: I stacked the plates and put them away on the shelf.
After practicing over and over, I finally succeeded in the actual performance.
Even in her old age, my grandmother keeps going for a walk every morning.
en.notes: 重ねる is transitive: to lay or stack things on top of each other with を (皿を重ねる, 手を重ねる). The intransitive counterpart is 重なる "to lie on top of each other; to coincide" (予定が重なる). The figurative meaning "to repeat, to accumulate" is very common: 努力を重ねる, 失敗を重ねる, 年を重ねる ("to grow older", a gentle paraphrase). For piling things into a heap or loading, 積む is more usual.

examples[].german: I arranged the books neatly on the shelf.
Please set the plates side by side on the table.
en.notes: 並べる is a transitive ichidan verb: 並べます, 並べて. It means to arrange things in order or side by side. を marks the things, に the place. きれいに describes the neat arrangement. The intransitive 並ぶ, by contrast, means to stand in a line.

en.meaning: to flow; to stream; to play (music)
examples[].german: The river flows from the mountains to the sea.
Quiet jazz was playing in the shop.
Because of the rain, the game I had been looking forward to was called off.
en.notes: 流れる is intransitive: water, tears, time or music "flow, run"; the transitive counterpart is 流す (涙を流す, 音楽を流す). Typical are 川が流れる, 汗が流れる, 時間が流れる and 店内に音楽が流れる "music is playing in the shop." The stretch flowed through takes を (町の中を川が流れる). Colloquially, 計画・試合が流れる also means "to be cancelled, to fall through."

examples[].german: A child nearly drowned in the river.
After losing his job, he began to drown himself in drink.
If you see someone drowning in the sea, please notify a lifeguard right away.
en.notes: 溺れる is intransitive and describes being in danger of drowning or drowning in water; the place takes で (海で溺れる). You often hear 溺れそうになる "to nearly drown"; actual death is usually expressed with 溺れて死ぬ or 溺死する. Figuratively, 〜に溺れる means "to be addicted to something, to give oneself up to it": 酒に溺れる, 恋に溺れる - always with a negative connotation. Well-known proverb: 溺れる者は藁をもつかむ.

examples[].german: The tree fell over in the strong wind.
My father collapsed at work and was taken to the hospital.
I'm worried that the bookshelf will fall over during an earthquake.
en.notes: 倒れる is intransitive: something standing falls or tips over (木が倒れる, 本棚が倒れる), or a person collapses or becomes seriously ill (過労で倒れる). The transitive partner is 倒す "to knock over, to topple". Stumbling and falling while walking is more 転ぶ, and falling from above 落ちる; the cause takes で: 強風で倒れる.

en.meaning: to stick out; to thrust out; to hand over
examples[].german: A rock juts out from the cliff.
It is dangerous to stick your head out of a train window.
The shop clerk handed the shoplifter over to the police.
en.notes: 突き出す is transitive: to "stick out" a body part or object forward (窓から顔を突き出す, 口を突き出す "pout"). The intransitive counterpart is 突き出る "to protrude", but 〜が突き出している is also used for protruding things. A second fixed meaning is "to hand someone over (to the police)": 犯人を警察に突き出す. Do not confuse it with 差し出す "to hold out, to hand over".

en.meaning: to drive out; to kick out
examples[].german: I chased the cat out of the room.
Because I couldn't pay the rent, I was kicked out of the apartment.
I tried to push the unpleasant thoughts out of my head, but I couldn't fall asleep for a long time.
en.notes: 追い出す is transitive: to drive or throw a person or animal (を) out of a place; the place takes から or を (部屋から追い出す, 家を追い出す). Very common in the passive: アパートを追い出される "to be thrown out of one's apartment", チームから追い出される. The word stresses compulsion and unwillingness; its official, formal counterpart is 追放する "to banish, expel". Figuratively one can also drive thoughts out: 頭から追い出す.

en.meaning: to catch up with; to overtake
examples[].german: I ran and caught up with my friend.
There are too many orders, and production can't keep up.
I missed classes because I was in the hospital, so I want to catch up with everyone quickly.
en.notes: 追いつく is intransitive: whom or what you catch up with takes に (前の車に追いつく); also written 追い付く. Figuratively it means "to catch up, keep pace" in level, performance or demand: 先進国に追いつく, 生産が需要に追いつかない - especially often negated. The counterpart 追い越す "to overtake" is transitive and takes を. 間に合う, on the other hand, means "to be in time."

examples[].german: The criminal fled from the scene.
In case of fire, please escape outside immediately.
You can't just keep running away from unpleasant things.
en.notes: 逃げる is intransitive "to flee, to run away"; the starting point takes から (現場から逃げる), the destination へ/に (外へ逃げる). Animals also "run away": 犬が逃げた. Figuratively it means "to shirk, to evade": 問題から逃げる, 責任から逃げる. The transitive partner is 逃がす "to let escape, to set free", and 逃げ出す emphasizes suddenly running away.

examples[].german: The victim filed a criminal complaint against the culprit.
The victim later withdrew the complaint.
I'm still undecided about whether to file a complaint.
en.notes: 告訴 is the criminal complaint or petition that the victim (or their representative) files with the police or public prosecutor: 犯人を告訴する, 告訴を取り下げる "to withdraw the complaint". When an uninvolved third party reports an offense, it is called 告発. 起訴, by contrast, is the bringing of charges by the prosecutor, and a civil suit is usually expressed with 訴える or 提訴.

examples[].german: I missed an important chance.
The party dragged on, and I missed the last train.
I took notes so as not to miss anything of the teacher's explanation.
en.notes: 逃す is transitive and means above all "to miss an opportunity, let it slip": チャンスを逃す, 終電を逃す, 優勝を逃す. Attached to a verb stem, it means "to fail to ...": 聞き逃す "to fail to hear", 見逃す "to overlook". Distinguish it from 逃がす "to set free, let escape" (魚を逃がす). For means of transport 乗り遅れる is also common; 逃す stresses the loss.

examples[].german: The child hid behind a tree.
The moon went behind the clouds, and the surroundings suddenly became dark.
There are many hidden gem restaurants in this alley.
en.notes: 隠れる is intransitive: to hide or be hidden; the hiding place and the thing covering take に (木の後ろに隠れる, 雲に隠れる). The transitive counterpart is 隠す "to hide, conceal" (秘密を隠す). Attributively 隠れた means "hidden, unknown": 隠れた名店, 隠れた才能. The children's game of hide-and-seek is かくれんぼ.

examples[].german: The stars are shining in the night sky.
The children's eyes lit up when they saw the presents.
She was crowned with a gold medal at the Olympics.
en.notes: 輝く is intransitive: the sun, stars or gems "shine, sparkle" (星が夜空に輝く). Figuratively, eyes or faces shine with joy: 目が輝く, 喜びに輝く; the causative form 輝かせる appears in 目を輝かせる. A set phrase is 〜に輝く "to win a prize or title": 金メダルに輝く, 優勝に輝く. Compared with 光る ("to glow, flash"), 輝く sounds more positive and elevated.

en.meaning: to be reflected; to appear (on a screen); to look (to others)
examples[].german: The mountain is reflected in the lake.
The shopping street in our neighborhood appeared in yesterday's news.
His attitude seems to have come across as cold to the people around him.
en.notes: 映る is intransitive: something is reflected or appears on a surface or screen, and the place takes に: 鏡に顔が映る, テレビに映る, 画面が映らない "no picture". The transitive counterpart is 映す (鏡に姿を映す). Do not confuse it with 写る "to appear in a photo" (写真に写る) and 移る "to move, to shift". Figuratively, 〜の目に…と映る or 〜く映る means "to appear ... to someone".

examples[].german: I copied the content of the blackboard into my notebook.
You must not copy a friend's homework.
On my trip I took many pictures of beautiful scenery with my camera.
en.notes: 写す means "to copy, to transcribe": 黒板をノートに写す, 友達の宿題を写す; also "to photograph, to capture" (景色を写す), although in everyday speech 写真を撮る is said more often. The intransitive partner is 写る "to appear in, to be in a photo": 写真に写る. Not to be confused with the identically read 映す "to reflect, to project" (鏡に映す) and 移す "to move, to transfer".

examples[].german: The mirror reflects light.
The sunlight reflected off the snow was so dazzling that I couldn't keep my eyes open.
When the ball came flying, I shut my eyes reflexively.
