This town underwent great development in ten years.
Smartphones have undergone astonishing evolution.
en.notes: 遂げる is elevated and means "to accomplish, realize": 目的を遂げる, 思いを遂げる. Very often it describes reaching a result with nouns such as 発展/成長/進化/変化を遂げる "to undergo a development". In everyday speech the compound やり遂げる "to see through to the end" is more common; for goals one usually says 目標を達成する.

en.meaning: to perform; to apply; to add (decoration); to give (alms)
examples[].german: First aid was administered to the patient.
Beautiful carvings are applied to the walls of this temple.
To make the display easier to read, we incorporated various improvements.
en.notes: 施す is a formal verb meaning "to apply, carry out (a measure)": 治療/処置を施す, 対策を施す. It also means "to attach, provide with" (装飾/化粧/工夫を施す), often in the passive 〜が施されている. The older meaning "to give alms, donate" survives in 施しを受ける. In everyday speech one mostly says する or 行う.

examples[].german: A baby's skin is smooth.
He speaks Japanese fluently.
This pudding is very smooth and delicious.
en.notes: 滑らか is a な-adjective: smooth and without bumps (滑らかな肌, 滑らかな表面) or fluent and frictionless (滑らかに話す, 動きが滑らかだ). It is often written in hiragana too: なめらか. すべすべ describes pleasantly smooth skin, つるつる smooth, slippery surfaces; for fluent speaking of a foreign language, 流暢 is more formal.

examples[].german: These shoes are sturdy and last long.
My grandmother is still in robust health at ninety.
If you're putting in heavy books, you'd better use a sturdier bag.
en.notes: 丈夫 has two main meanings: for things "sturdy, durable" (丈夫な靴, 丈夫な袋), for people "healthy, strong", usually as 体が丈夫だ. The combination 丈夫で長持ちする "sturdy and long-lasting" is typical. The more massive 頑丈 rather stresses stability against great forces (頑丈な建物), while 丈夫 aims at durability in everyday use. Do not confuse it with 大丈夫 "all right".

examples[].german: A solid building can withstand even an earthquake.
This suitcase is built so solidly that it won't break even if you drop it.
He has the sturdy build typical of a rugby player.
en.notes: 頑丈 describes something that is massively built and withstands great stress: 頑丈な建物, 頑丈な金庫, 頑丈な鍵. For people it means a "strong, stocky" physique (頑丈な体). Unlike 丈夫, which rather expresses durability in use and health, 頑丈 stresses force and firmness. Adverbially: 頑丈に作られている "to be solidly built".

examples[].german: I attended the party wearing a gorgeous dress.
When I put up flowers, the room instantly became brighter and more festive.
The entertainment world looks glamorous, but in reality it is a harsh world.
en.notes: 華やか means "splendid, brilliant, colorful" and describes something that attracts attention and looks festive: 華やかなドレス, 華やかな雰囲気, 華やかな世界 (e.g. show business). Unlike 派手, which often sounds negative ("garish, flashy"), 華やか is positive. The opposite is 地味 "plain". Also typical: 会場が華やかになる "the hall becomes festive".

examples[].german: She always dresses plainly.
Data entry is unglamorous work, but it is very important.
Isn't this tie a bit too plain for me?
en.notes: 地味 means "plain, inconspicuous, understated" and is the opposite of 派手. It describes clothes and colors (地味な服, 地味な色), but also people who don't stand out, and tasks that are laborious and not very glamorous (地味な作業). Depending on context it sounds neutral to slightly negative ("boring, drab"); when meant positively one rather says 落ち着いた or シンプルな. Common: 地味だけど大切な仕事.

examples[].german: The person wearing a shirt in a flashy color stands out.
Since winning the lottery, he has been living an extravagant life.
I fell spectacularly on the snowy road.
en.notes: 派手 means "flashy, garish, showy" and is the opposite of 地味. It describes colors and clothes (派手な色, 派手な服) but also a lavish lifestyle (派手な生活, 派手にお金を使う). Criticism often resonates, in contrast to the positive 華やか. Adverbially 派手に means "spectacularly, dramatically": 派手に転ぶ "to fall spectacularly".

examples[].german: I long for the simple life in the countryside.
This is a naive question, but why do Japanese trains arrive on time?
This sweet has a simple, old-fashioned taste.
en.notes: 素朴 describes something simple and unadulterated, without sophistication: 素朴な暮らし "a simple life", 素朴な味 "an unpretentious taste", 素朴な人柄 "a simple, unspoiled character". Mostly positive and warm in connotation, unlike 地味, which rather means "inconspicuous, boring". Very common is 素朴な疑問 "a naive, very simple question".

examples[].german: She danced a waltz gracefully.
Swans are swimming gracefully on the lake.
After retirement, I want to live a leisurely life in Hawaii.
en.notes: 優雅 means "elegant, graceful" and describes movements and bearing (優雅に踊る, 優雅な仕草). A second important meaning is "leisurely, carefree, well-off": 優雅な生活, 優雅に暮らす - often said with slight envy or irony. Unlike 上品, which stresses good manners and taste, 優雅 puts the accent on ease and leisure.

examples[].german: I was impressed by her refined manners.
The Japanese sweets of this shop are modestly sweet and delicate in taste.
You should go to the interview in an elegant suit.
en.notes: 上品 means "refined, cultured, tasteful" and is used for manners (上品な振る舞い), speech (上品な言葉遣い), clothing and even the taste of food (上品な味 "delicate, subtly seasoned"). The opposite is 下品 "vulgar". Unlike 優雅, which stresses grace and leisure, 上品 puts good upbringing in the foreground.

examples[].german: We celebrated National Foundation Day.
Washington is regarded as one of the founding fathers of America.
Since the founding of the nation, this country has never fought a war.
en.notes: 建国 is the founding of a state: 建国する, 建国以来 "since the founding of the nation", 建国の父 "founding father". In Japan, February 11 is the holiday 建国記念の日 (colloquially also 建国記念日). 建国 applies only to states; companies or schools are 設立 or 創立.

examples[].german: You'd better refrain from vulgar jokes.
I was told that eating with your mouth open is vulgar.
A room that is all gold looks tasteless rather than luxurious.
en.notes: 下品 means "vulgar, coarse, tasteless" and is the opposite of 上品. It criticizes manners and speech (下品な冗談, 下品な言葉遣い, 下品な笑い方), but also clothing or design that looks cheap and pushy. It is a clear value judgment; toned down one says あまり上品じゃない.

examples[].german: The calm weather continues.
My father has a gentle temperament; I have never seen him angry.
The sea is calm today, so let's go fishing.
en.notes: 穏やか means "calm, peaceful, gentle" and describes weather and sea (穏やかな天気, 海が穏やかだ), character (穏やかな性格, 穏やかな人) and life circumstances (穏やかな日々). The opposite for the sea is 荒い. Unlike 静か "quiet, still", 穏やか is about the absence of agitation or violence. Fixed expression: 心中穏やかではない "to be inwardly agitated".

examples[].german: The sea is rough, so the ship can't go out.
He spends money recklessly and is always broke.
He had run up the stairs and was breathing hard.
en.notes: 荒い means "violent, wild, rough": 波が荒い / 海が荒い "the sea is stormy", 息が荒い "to breathe heavily", 言葉遣いが荒い "to have a rough way of speaking". With 遣い it forms expressions for immoderate handling: 金遣いが荒い "to be a spendthrift", 人使いが荒い "to drive people ruthlessly". Do not confuse it with the identically read 粗い "coarse, grainy" (粗い目, 粗い砂), which concerns structure and fineness.

examples[].german: I climbed a gentle slope.
The economy is recovering gradually.
This river flows gently, so even children can play in it safely.
en.notes: 緩やか means "gentle, gradual, leisurely". Spatially it describes slight slopes and curves (緩やかな坂, 緩やかなカーブ), in time a slow development: 緩やかに回復する "to recover gradually" - very common in economic news. It also means "loose, mild" for rules (緩やかな規制). The opposite is 急 "steep, abrupt". Compared with the more colloquial 緩い, 緩やか sounds more elevated and neutral to positive.

examples[].german: I was thrown by the sudden change of plans.
Something urgent has come up, so I'll leave early today.
The road ahead is steep, so please get off your bicycle and walk.
en.notes: 急 as a na-adjective has three core meanings: "sudden, unexpected" (急な予定変更, 急に雨が降り出す), "urgent" (急な用事) and "steep, sharp" (急な坂, 急なカーブ). Adverbially 急に "suddenly" is very common. The opposite for slopes is 緩やか. Note: 急いで "in a hurry" comes from the verb 急ぐ, not from 急な.

examples[].german: These pants are loose around the waist.
The dress code at our company is lax, so jeans are fine.
The screw has come loose, so please tighten it.
en.notes: 緩い means "loose, slack" for clothes, screws or knots (ズボンが緩い, ねじが緩い), "lax, lenient" for rules (ルールが緩い, 校則が緩い) and "gentle" for slopes (緩い坂). The opposite is きつい. It is more colloquial than 緩やか. Colloquially ゆるい also describes something relaxed and casual (ゆるいキャラ → ゆるキャラ).

examples[].german: These shoes are tight and hurt my feet.
Overtime every day is really tough.
Maybe the way I said it was a bit harsh. I'll apologize later.
en.notes: きつい is very versatile: "tight" for clothes and shoes (靴がきつい), "tough, demanding" for work or schedules (仕事がきつい, スケジュールがきつい), "sharp, harsh" for words and character (言い方がきつい, きつい性格) and "strong" for smells or alcohol. The opposite for clothing is 緩い. In everyday speech, きつい often replaces 大変 or 辛い as an honest "this is hard." Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: This medicine is bitter, but it works.
This coffee is too bitter for me to drink.
Failing at my first job is a bitter memory.
en.notes: 苦い describes the bitter taste of medicine, coffee or vegetables such as ゴーヤ. Figuratively it stands for painful experiences: 苦い経験, 苦い思い出, and 苦い顔をする means "to make a sour face". To be distinguished are 辛い "spicy", 酸っぱい "sour" and 渋い "astringent"; the same kanji is in 苦手 "to be bad at something, to dislike".

examples[].german: This lemon is very sour.
This milk smells a little sour, so you'd better not drink it.
My mother told me to clean up until she was blue in the face.
en.notes: 酸っぱい is the sour taste (レモン, 梅干し, 酢: lemon, pickled plum, vinegar) and also a sourish smell, e.g. of spoiled milk (酸っぱい匂いがする). The related noun is 酸味 "sour taste, acidity". Idiom: 口が酸っぱくなるほど言う "to repeat something until one is blue in the face". Mostly written with the kanji 酸っぱい; すっぱい in kana is also common.

en.meaning: astringent; tart; understated and refined; sour-faced
examples[].german: I like astringent tea.
That actor has become more and more cool and refined with age.
When I asked for a raise, the department manager made a sour face.
en.notes: 渋い first means "astringent, tart" (渋いお茶, 渋い柿). Figuratively it praises a restrained, mature style: 渋い色 "muted color", 渋い声 "distinctive, deep voice", 渋い趣味 "refined taste" - similar to "cool in a quiet way". It also appears in 渋い顔 "a sour face" and colloquially "stingy" (お金に渋い). Distinguish it from 苦い "bitter".

examples[].german: An excavation survey of the ruins was carried out.
Dinosaur fossils were excavated in this area.
She is a producer who is good at discovering young talent.
en.notes: 発掘 is the digging up of something hidden, especially archaeologically: 遺跡を発掘する, 発掘調査 "excavation", 化石が発掘される. Figuratively it means "to discover, unearth", especially of talent: 新人を発掘する "to discover new talent", 人材発掘. For ordinary digging, such as in a garden, people simply say 掘る.

examples[].german: The autumn leaves are vivid.
I still remember the day of my first trip abroad vividly.
The craftsman filleted the fish with brilliant skill.
en.notes: 鮮やか means "bright, vivid" for colors (鮮やかな色, 鮮やかな紅葉) and "vivid, clear" for memories (記憶に鮮やかに残る). A second important meaning is "masterly, brilliant" for skill: 鮮やかな手つき "deft hands", 鮮やかな逆転 "a brilliant turnaround". Unlike 派手, 鮮やか is always positive.

examples[].german: His reply was vague.
It's a childhood memory, so it's a bit hazy.
The meeting ended with responsibility left unclear.
en.notes: 曖昧 means "unclear, vague, ambiguous" and describes answers, attitudes and memories: 曖昧な返事, 曖昧な態度をとる, 記憶が曖昧だ. It is often a criticism of a lack of decisiveness; 曖昧にする means "to leave something unclear". The opposite is 明確 or 明瞭. Related, but more matter-of-fact, is はっきりしない "not clear".

examples[].german: Thanks to the clear explanation, I understood well.
Announcers have clear pronunciation and are easy to understand.
Please write the report simply and clearly.
en.notes: 明瞭 means "clear, distinct" and is rather literary or formal. It describes pronunciation and voice (発音が明瞭だ), explanations and accounts (明瞭な説明, 明瞭会計 "transparent pricing"). The fixed phrase 簡単明瞭 means "short and clear". The opposite is 不明瞭 or 曖昧. In daily life one usually says はっきりした or 分かりやすい.

examples[].german: Let's stop quarreling over trivial things.
A minor mistake can even lead to a major accident.
She immediately notices even slight changes.
en.notes: 些細 means "trivial, insignificant" and almost always stands before a noun: 些細なこと "a trifle", 些細なミス, 些細な違い. Typical is 些細なことで喧嘩する "to quarrel over trifles". It sounds somewhat more elevated than ちょっとした or 小さな; because of the rare kanji 些, it is often written in kana too: ささいな.

examples[].german: I analyzed an enormous amount of data.
To write my thesis, I have to read a vast amount of material.
Completing this dictionary took an enormous amount of time.
en.notes: 膨大 means "huge, enormous" and describes above all quantities and scale: 膨大な量, 膨大なデータ, 膨大な資料, 膨大な時間. It sounds factual to formal. The similar 莫大, by contrast, is preferred with money and damage (莫大な費用, 莫大な損害). In daily life one often says すごい量 or 大量.

examples[].german: This project costs an immense amount.
He inherited a huge fortune from his grandfather.
Farmers suffered immense damage from the typhoon.
en.notes: 莫大 means "immense, enormous" and is used above all with money, wealth and damage: 莫大な費用, 莫大な財産, 莫大な損害, 莫大な借金. Unlike 膨大, which describes quantity and scale (data, material), 莫大 stresses value or amount. It sounds formal and almost always stands attributively before a noun.

examples[].german: The relationship between the two of them is in a delicate state.
There is a subtle difference between these two words.
"How was the ramen at the new shop?" "Hmm, it was so-so."
en.notes: 微妙 originally means "fine, subtle": 微妙な違い "a subtle difference", 微妙な色合い. From this comes "delicate, tricky" (微妙な問題, 微妙な関係). In today's colloquial language, 微妙 is also a polite evasive answer for "well, not so good" or "hard to say": 「どう？」「うーん、微妙。」. It is worth knowing this nuance so as not to be misunderstood.

examples[].german: She has a sensitive heart.
Japanese food is said to be delicately seasoned.
This glasswork is very delicate, so please don't touch it.
en.notes: 繊細 means "fine, delicate" for things (繊細な指, 繊細な細工, 繊細な味) and "sensitive, tender-hearted" for people (繊細な性格, 繊細な心). For people it can be positive ("considerate") or slightly critical ("touchy, easily hurt"). Related is 敏感 "sensitive to stimuli", which concerns perception more; opposites are 大雑把 "rough" and 鈍感 "insensitive".

examples[].german: He proposed a bold plan.
The company president boldly restructured the loss-making departments.
This dress is open at the back - quite a daring design.
en.notes: 大胆 means "bold, daring, fearless" and describes plans, decisions, statements and designs: 大胆な計画, 大胆な発言, 大胆なデザイン. Adverbially: 大胆に挑戦する "to take something on boldly". It is mostly positive but can also mean "risque, cheeky". The opposite is 慎重 "cautious". Unlike 勇気がある, which stresses personal courage, 大胆 is about the unusual, risky nature of an action.

examples[].german: It is necessary to judge carefully.
On snowy days, please drive more carefully than usual.
He is a cautious person and doesn't reply right away.
en.notes: 慎重 means "cautious, careful, prudent" in the sense of thoroughly considered action. Very common adverbially: 慎重に判断する, 慎重に検討する, 慎重に運転する. Its counterparts are 大胆 or 軽率 "rash". Unlike 注意深い, which stresses attentiveness, 慎重 carries restraint before a decision; a 慎重派 is someone who "would rather wait and see".

examples[].german: The bill was voted down in the Diet.
The government plans to submit a new bill next month.
With so many voices against it, passage of the bill looks difficult.
en.notes: 法案 is a bill that has not yet been passed; after adoption it becomes a 法律. The path of a bill can be described with set verbs: 法案を提出する ("to introduce"), 審議する ("to deliberate"), 可決する ("to pass") or 否決する ("to reject"), and finally 法案が成立する ("to be enacted"). For the budget, people say 予算案 in the same way.

examples[].german: There was a new discovery in archaeological research.
Since childhood it has been my dream to become an archaeologist.
That earthenware is of great value archaeologically.
en.notes: 考古学 is archaeology, the study of the past through finds and excavations (発掘); literally something like "the study of investigating the old". The archaeologist is called 考古学者; typical combinations: 考古学を専攻する, 考古学の研究, 考古学的な発見. To be distinguished from 歴史学, the science of history based on written sources.

examples[].german: The result doesn't change even with a rough calculation.
I'll first explain the plan roughly and talk about the details later.
My older brother is easygoing and bad at tidying his room.
en.notes: 大雑把 means, for things, "rough, approximate, in broad strokes" (大雑把な計算, 大雑把に説明する "to explain roughly") and, for people, "careless, not fussy" (大雑把な性格). The opposite for character is 几帳面 "meticulous". The description of a person is usually slightly critical but can also mean good-naturedly "easygoing". More neutral for estimates are おおよそ or だいたい.

examples[].german: He is so orderly that his room is always clean.
My mother meticulously records her daily expenses in a household account book.
Mr. Tanaka is punctual and has never once been late.
en.notes: 几帳面 describes a person who is "orderly, conscientious, painstakingly exact": 几帳面な性格, 几帳面な人. One also says 時間に几帳面 "punctual" or 几帳面に記録する "to keep careful records". The opposite is 大雑把. It is predominantly positive; for exaggerated exactness one rather says 神経質 "fussy, nervous". The kanji 几 is rare, so it is often written in kana as きちょうめん.

examples[].german: It's better to apologize sincerely.
When you're praised, you should just be happy about it.
This child is obedient and listens well to the teacher.
en.notes: 素直 means "sincere, open, unaffected" and for children also "obedient, docile" (素直な子). Very common adverbially: 素直に謝る "to apologize honestly", 素直に喜ぶ "to be happy without reservation", 素直に言うと "to be honest". It means accepting or showing feelings or advice without defiance. The opposite is 素直じゃない or ひねくれた "twisted, contrary". Unlike 正直 "honest (not lying)", 素直 stresses the absence of inner resistance.

examples[].german: My grandfather is stubborn and doesn't change his opinion.
With this detergent, even stubborn kitchen stains come off quickly.
The owner of that ramen shop is stubborn and never changes his way of doing things.
en.notes: 頑固 means "stubborn, obstinate" and describes people who don't deviate from their opinion: 頑固な人, 頑固親父 "stubborn old man". Figuratively it stands for persistent things that are hard to remove: 頑固な汚れ "stubborn dirt", 頑固な肩こり. The similar 意地っ張り stresses defiance, 強情 willfulness; 頑固 sounds more neutral and can also suggest "principled".

examples[].german: One should forgive people with a generous heart.
Since it was his first failure, the company took lenient measures.
She is lenient with her subordinates' mistakes and always gives gentle advice.
en.notes: 寛大 means "magnanimous, lenient, tolerant" in dealing with other people's mistakes: 寛大な心, 寛大な処置 "lenient treatment, leniency", 寛大に許す. It does not mean generosity with money - for that, one says 気前がいい. The opposite is 厳しい or 厳格. The expression is rather elevated; in daily life one often says 心が広い "broad-minded".

examples[].german: His father was very strict.
In this factory, the temperature is strictly controlled.
That school is famous for having strict school rules.
en.notes: 厳格 means "strict, rigorous" and describes people (厳格な父親, 厳格な先生) as well as rules and their application (厳格な規則, 厳格に管理する). It sounds more formal and uncompromising than 厳しい, which is much more common in daily life and can also mean "harsh, difficult". 厳格 stresses the exact observance of principles without exceptions. Opposite: 寛大 or 緩い.

examples[].german: Diligent students are sure to succeed.
My grandfather worked diligently for forty years and supported the family.
His diligence was recognized, and he was chosen as leader.
en.notes: 勤勉 means "diligent, industrious" in the sense of steady, dutiful work: 勤勉な学生, 勤勉に働く. It is more elevated and character-oriented than the everyday 真面目 or よく頑張る. Common in attributions like 日本人は勤勉だ. The opposite is 怠惰 "lazy". The noun 勤勉さ means "diligence".

examples[].german: You must not lead an idle life.
I spent the summer vacation idly and haven't finished my homework.
His lack of success is due not to a lack of talent but to laziness.
en.notes: 怠惰 means "lazy, idle, inactive" and is literary and clearly judgmental: 怠惰な生活, 怠惰な性格, 怠惰に過ごす. In daily life one usually says 怠け者 "lazybones", だらしない "sloppy" or ごろごろする "to laze around" instead. The opposite is 勤勉. Related verb: 怠ける "to be lazy, to slack off".

examples[].german: One should approach work with a sincere attitude.
It is important to respond sincerely to complaints from customers.
As a spouse, I'd rather choose a sincere person than money.
en.notes: 誠実 means "sincere, honest, conscientious" and describes people and their behavior toward others: 誠実な人, 誠実な態度, 誠実に対応する "to respond responsibly". It stresses reliability and earnestness - important in business relationships, for example. Unlike 正直 "honest (not lying)" and 素直 "open, unaffected", 誠実 also includes fidelity and a sense of duty. Opposite: 不誠実.

examples[].german: I was disappointed by the insincere way they handled it.
I think it's insincere to break promises over and over.
The company's insincere attitude, refusing to explain the accident, was criticized.
en.notes: 不誠実 is the negation of 誠実 and means "insincere, unscrupulous, irresponsible". It criticizes above all how one treats others: 不誠実な対応 "a disingenuous response" (e.g. by a company to complaints), 不誠実な態度, 不誠実な人 (such as an unfaithful partner). It is a serious accusation, stronger than 適当 "lax, superficial".

examples[].german: He is praised as a national hero.
The athlete who won the gold medal was treated as a hero on returning to town.
Many people consider Napoleon a hero of France.
en.notes: 英雄 is a hero in the grand, often historical or national sense: 国民的英雄, 戦争の英雄, 英雄扱いされる "to be treated like a hero". In films, comics and daily life people tend to say ヒーロー; 英雄 sounds more solemn and literary. The word applies to men and women alike. Also well known is Beethoven's symphony 英雄 ("Eroica").

examples[].german: I was moved by the child's innocent eyes.
I'm not playing for a prize; I play purely because I love music.
This ring is made of pure gold.
en.notes: 純粋 means "pure, unmixed" for substances (純粋な金, 純粋な水) and "innocent, unspoiled, genuine" for people and motives (純粋な心, 純粋な気持ち). Also common as 純粋に "purely, simply": 純粋に楽しむ "simply enjoy". Applied to people it can sound positive or slightly naive. For purity in the sense of cleanliness, use 清潔 instead.

examples[].german: This problem is extremely complex.
The visa procedure was so complicated that I had to go to the government office several times.
When I heard that my best friend was moving far away, I had mixed feelings.
en.notes: 複雑 means "complicated, intricate" and describes problems, procedures and structures (複雑な問題, 手続きが複雑だ). Very common is 複雑な気持ち "mixed feelings", when you are happy and sad at the same time. The opposite is 単純 or 簡単. Unlike 難しい "difficult", 複雑 stresses that many parts interlock.

examples[].german: I got tired of the monotonous work.
The scenery on the expressway is so monotonous that you easily get sleepy while driving.
He speaks so monotonously that you fall asleep listening.
en.notes: 単調 means "monotonous, dull" and describes work, daily life, landscapes or sounds without variety: 単調な仕事, 単調な生活, 単調なリズム. It is mostly negative ("boring"). Unlike 退屈 "boring", which expresses the person's feeling, 単調 describes the thing itself. Opposite: 変化に富む "full of variety".

examples[].german: Diverse cultures coexist.
Many different opinions came up at the meeting, but no conclusion was reached.
Recently, ways of working are becoming more diverse, for example with working from home.
en.notes: 多様 means "diverse, of various kinds" and is a typical word in news and discussions of society: 多様な文化, 多様な意見, 多様な働き方. Related are 多様化 "diversification" and 多様性 "diversity". In everyday speech people more often say いろいろな or さまざまな; 多様 sounds objective and formal.

examples[].german: It is important to maintain uniform quality.
At this store, every item is sold for a flat 100 yen.
Mix the flour and sugar well until evenly blended.
en.notes: 均一 means "even, uniform" and describes quality, distribution and prices: 均一な品質, 均一に混ぜる "mix evenly". Very well known is 100円均一 (short: 百均) "100-yen flat price" for discount stores. The opposite is 不均一 or ばらばら. Unlike 平等 "equal in rights", 均一 refers to physical or numerical equality, not to fairness.

examples[].german: The paint job is uneven and the result is poor.
If the temperature inside the oven is uneven, the bread won't bake well.
There is a problem that the quality of medical services is uneven depending on the region.
en.notes: 不均一 is the opposite of 均一 and means "uneven, non-uniform". It is a rather technical word for color, thickness, temperature or distribution: 塗装が不均一, 温度が不均一, 色むらがあって不均一. In everyday speech people often say むらがある "to be uneven" or ばらばら. As a noun it also appears in technical texts (不均一性 "heterogeneity").

examples[].german: I bought fresh fish at the market.
Let's open the window and let in some fresh air.
When I had just come to Japan, everything felt new and exciting.
en.notes: 新鮮 means "fresh" for food (新鮮な魚, 新鮮な野菜) and air (新鮮な空気). Figuratively it means "new, refreshing, unjaded" for impressions and ideas: 新鮮な発想, 何もかもが新鮮に感じる. For freshly baked bread or something just made, people more often say できたて or 焼きたて; 新鮮 stresses the unspoiled state. Opposite for food: 古い or 腐った.

examples[].german: I drank warm soup and my body warmed up.
When I was down, I was saved by my teacher's kind words.
Please enjoy the food while it is warm.
en.notes: 温かい means "warm" for things you touch, eat or drink (温かいスープ, 温かい飲み物), and figuratively "heartfelt, warm-hearted" (温かい人, 温かい言葉, 温かい家庭). For warm air and weather, 暖かい is written instead (暖かい部屋, 暖かい春). Opposite: 冷たい (things, hearts) or 寒い (weather). Both spellings are read あたたかい; colloquially also あったかい.

examples[].german: The Roman emperor held enormous power.
The last emperor of the Qing was still a child.
That film depicts the life of a certain emperor.
en.notes: 皇帝 is an emperor, especially as the title of foreign rulers: ローマ皇帝, 中国の皇帝, 皇帝に即位する "to ascend the imperial throne". The Japanese emperor, by contrast, is called 天皇 (respectfully 天皇陛下), never 皇帝. The realm ruled by an emperor is a 帝国; a king is 王 or 国王.

examples[].german: I washed my face with cold water.
On hot days I want to drink cold tea.
en.notes: 冷たい is an i-adjective for something that feels cold. It stands directly before a noun: 冷たい水. 冷たくない and 冷たかった are the negative and past forms. 水で marks the water as the means of washing. For cold weather, 寒い is normally used.

examples[].german: I went home feeling miserable.
I failed in front of everyone and felt terribly humiliated.
The team suffered a pitiful 7-0 defeat.
en.notes: 惨め means "miserable, pitiful, wretched" and describes above all one's own feeling of humiliation or defeat: 惨めな気持ち, 惨めな思いをする "to feel miserable", 惨めな負け方 "a humiliating defeat". Unlike 哀れ, which expresses the pity of an observer, 惨め puts the shame and wretchedness of the situation in the foreground. Similar but weaker: 情けない "pathetic, shameful".

examples[].german: Tears came to my eyes when I saw his pitiful figure.
I felt sorry for the kitten shivering in the rain, so I took it home.
He, who could do nothing but keep lying, even seemed pitiful to me.
en.notes: 哀れ expresses an observer's pity: "pitiable, wretched" (哀れな姿, 哀れな老人), often in the phrase 哀れに思う "to feel pity". It can also sound contemptuous, "pathetic" (哀れな奴). The word is rather literary; in everyday speech people say かわいそう. Unlike 惨め, which stresses one's own feeling of wretchedness, 哀れ looks from the outside at the suffering of others. Classically related is もののあはれ "the pathos of the transience of things".

examples[].german: I miss the food from my hometown.
When it gets cold, I start craving hot pot dishes.
Half a year into studying abroad, I'm starting to miss my family.
en.notes: 恋しい means "missed, longed for": the thing missed is the subject with が, e.g. 故郷が恋しい "I miss my hometown", 母の料理が恋しい. With なる it expresses longing setting in: 冬になると鍋が恋しくなる. Unlike 懐かしい, which expresses wistful memory of the past, 恋しい means the wish to have the missed thing back now. Despite the kanji 恋 "love", it is by no means only about loved persons.

examples[].german: A suspicious person is lurking around the neighborhood.
The sky is looking threatening, so let's take an umbrella.
It's doubtful whether we'll meet the deadline.
en.notes: 怪しい is the everyday word for "suspicious, fishy": 怪しい人/動き/メール. But it also means "doubtful, uncertain" (間に合うかどうか怪しい), "shaky" for knowledge (私の英語は怪しい) and "threatening" for weather (空が怪しくなる). 疑わしい is more literary and aimed at statements and facts, 不審な is official (police, announcements). The related verb is 怪しむ "to become suspicious".

examples[].german: His testimony is doubtful.
The effect of that medicine is scientifically questionable.
If there is anything doubtful, please feel free to ask.
en.notes: 疑わしい is the adjective form of 疑う "to doubt, suspect" and refers to something whose truth or authenticity one must doubt: 疑わしい証言/データ/点. It sounds more objective and literary than the everyday 怪しい and is used more for claims, effects and results than for persons. Well known is the legal principle 疑わしきは罰せず "in doubt, in favor of the accused".

examples[].german: If you find a suspicious package, please report it.
A suspicious person was spotted near the school.
The clerk, who found his behavior strange, contacted the police.
en.notes: 不審 is a Sino-Japanese noun/な-adjective with an official ring: police, railways and schools warn about 不審な物/荷物 and 不審者 "suspicious person"; 挙動不審 means "suspicious behavior", 不審火 a fire of unclear cause. 不審に思う means "to find something strange, become suspicious". For a distrustful character, on the other hand, say 疑い深い; in everyday speech 怪しい mostly replaces the word.

examples[].german: I heard an eerie sound.
The hospital is quiet and creepy at night.
He wore an eerie smile.
en.notes: 不気味 describes an uncanny feeling whose cause one cannot quite pin down: 不気味な音/静けさ/笑み. Unlike 怖い, which expresses direct fear, 不気味 stresses the uneasy and ghostly; close in meaning are 気味が悪い and, intensified, 薄気味悪い. Not to be confused with 気持ち悪い, which rather means "disgusting, nauseating".

examples[].german: I saw news of a terrible accident.
Walking alone on a mountain path at night was frightening.
Rent in Tokyo is terribly high.
en.notes: 恐ろしい is somewhat more elevated than 怖い and often describes an objective threat: 恐ろしい事故/病気/事件. 怖い, by contrast, expresses the speaker's personal fear and is more colloquial. As an adverb, 恐ろしく "extremely, terribly" (恐ろしく高い) intensifies, as does 恐ろしいほど. The noun 恐ろしさ denotes the terribleness.

examples[].german: A heinous crime was reported.
Just imagining it is horrifying.
A large number of cockroaches were found in the corner of the room; it was a revolting sight.
en.notes: おぞましい combines horror with physical disgust: 想像するだけでおぞましい "just imagining it is horrifying". It is clearly stronger than 気持ち悪い or 嫌な and emotionally colored; 恐ろしい, by contrast, stresses fear. The word is almost always written in kana (the kanji 悍ましい is rare) and is often found in reports on crimes or in descriptions of revolting scenes.

examples[].german: The king ruled the country.
The lion is called the king of beasts.
Edison is known as the "king of inventors".
en.notes: 王 is the king or ruler. On its own it appears more in history books, fairy tales and news; in conversation one usually says 王様, and for real heads of state 国王. Queen is 女王, prince 王子. As a suffix, 王 denotes the best in a field: 発明王 "king of inventors", ホームラン王; 百獣の王 "king of beasts" is the lion.

examples[].german: I don't want to see an ugly quarrel.
As a child, I liked the story of "The Ugly Duckling".
I don't want to become an ugly adult who only thinks of his own profit.
en.notes: 醜い means "ugly" in appearance, but is very hurtful when applied to people; in everyday speech people more often say 見た目が悪い. More common is the figurative meaning "unsightly, shameful": 醜い争い/嫉妬, 醜い姿をさらす. Well known is the fairy tale 醜いアヒルの子 "The Ugly Duckling". Note: it is pronounced the same as 見にくい "hard to see"; the opposite is 美しい.

examples[].german: I was moved by the beautiful sunset.
She speaks beautiful Japanese.
I could hear the beautiful sound of a piano.
en.notes: 美しい is "beautiful" in an elevated, somewhat literary sense: 美しい景色, 美しい音楽, 美しい日本語, also 美しい心. In everyday conversation one usually says きれい; unlike きれい, however, 美しい never means "clean". The noun is 美しさ "beauty".

examples[].german: This puppy is very cute.
I gave my younger sister a cute doll.
en.notes: 可愛い is an i-adjective meaning cute or pretty. It can describe an animal, an object, or someone's appearance. It is often written in hiragana as かわいい; 可愛い is a common kanji spelling with an assigned reading. It needs no な before a noun: 可愛い人形. The ending is the vowel sequence ii; it is not shortened in kawaii. For food, "sweet" is 甘い instead.

examples[].german: He was wearing a sharp suit.
My older brother looks really cool when he's playing basketball.
I think people who can honestly admit their own mistakes are cool.
en.notes: Almost always written in kana: かっこいい (from 格好がいい); the kanji spelling 格好良い is rare, and in casual texts also カッコいい. It means "cool, good-looking, stylish" and fits appearance, things and also behavior. Like いい, it is conjugated via よ-: かっこよくない, かっこよかった. The opposite is かっこ悪い, colloquially ダサい. Colloquial; in formal texts people prefer 素敵な or スマートな.

en.meaning: to stand out; to be conspicuous
examples[].german: Her talent stands out among her peers.
The red flowers stand out against the white wall.
The cuisine of this region has distinctive characteristics.
en.notes: 際立つ is intransitive (〜が際立つ) and stresses that something stands out clearly from its surroundings through contrast, mostly in a positive sense and rather literary. Often attributive as 際立った特徴/才能 "distinctive, outstanding" or adverbial 際立って "remarkably". 目立つ is more neutral and often negative ("to stand out unpleasantly"). There is no transitive counterpart; "to highlight" is the causative 際立たせる (味を際立たせる).

en.meaning: to stand out; to be noticeable
examples[].german: If you wear red clothes, you stand out.
He doesn't like to stand out very much.
Lately, my gray hairs have become noticeable.
en.notes: 目立つ is intransitive: 〜が目立つ "something stands out". It is neutral, but often used for unwanted conspicuousness: 傷/ミス/白髪が目立つ. 目立たない means "inconspicuous", 目立ちたがり屋 is someone who likes to be the center of attention. Transitive "to make conspicuous" is the causative 目立たせる. Compared with 際立つ, 目立つ sounds more everyday and less laudatory.

examples[].german: I heard a terrific explosion.
The typhoon's violent winds knocked trees down.
His concentration is tremendous.
en.notes: 凄まじい describes an overwhelming, almost frightening intensity: 凄まじい音/風/勢い. Mostly negative ("terrible, fierce"), but also admiring ("tremendous"): 凄まじい集中力/人気. It is stronger and more literary than すごい and is often written in kana (すさまじい). 恐ろしい, by contrast, stresses fear, not force.

examples[].german: She has made remarkable progress.
Thanks to the rookie's remarkable performance, the team won the championship.
The progress in medical technology is remarkable.
en.notes: 目覚ましい is purely positive and is used above all for progress and achievement: 目覚ましい進歩/発展/成長/活躍. Typical is 目覚ましい成長を遂げる "to develop impressively". For beautiful things or skill, one rather uses 見事な. Despite the same kanji, it has nothing to do in meaning with 目覚まし時計 "alarm clock". Rather literary (news, speeches).

examples[].german: The cherry trees are in splendid full bloom.
He pulled off the difficult technique masterfully.
The plan failed completely.
en.notes: 見事 praises beauty or skill: 見事な桜/腕前, as an adverb 見事に "masterfully"; the exclamation お見事！ means "Bravo!". Ironically, 見事に also means "thoroughly, utterly": 見事に失敗した. 立派 praises rather dignity and decency, 素晴らしい is more general. Both the kanji and kana (みごと) spellings are common.

examples[].german: He has grown into a fine adult.
An impressive library was built in front of the station.
Using other people's things without permission is flat-out a crime.
en.notes: 立派 has several facets: "magnificent, imposing" for buildings and things (立派な家), "decent, respectable" for people and behavior (立派な人, 立派に育つ) and, as an intensifier, "downright, unmistakable" (それは立派な犯罪だ). Adverbial 立派に means "properly, impeccably". 偉い praises rather rank or achievement, 見事 skill and beauty.

examples[].german: The aristocrats led a luxurious life.
Aristocrats in the Heian period enjoyed composing waka poems.
My older brother is a carefree bachelor and spends his entire salary on his hobbies.
en.notes: 貴族 is the nobility or a noble, i.e. a privileged upper class by birth: ヨーロッパの貴族, 平安時代の貴族, 貴族社会. For the Japanese court nobility, 公家 is also common, and for the warrior class 武士. Figuratively, 〜貴族 describes people with a carefree, luxurious lifestyle, e.g. 独身貴族 "well-paid single who lives only for himself".

examples[].german: I learned about the achievements of a great scientist.
Only after she died did I realize how great my mother's presence had been.
The moon landing was a great step for mankind.
en.notes: 偉大 denotes greatness in the sense of historical importance and dignity: 偉大な人物/科学者/業績/指導者. It never refers to physical size (for that, 大きな, 巨大な). 偉い is the everyday word for "admirable" or "high-ranking" (and in 偉そう "arrogant"), whereas 偉大 sounds elevated and solemn. Predicative: 母の存在は偉大だった.

examples[].german: A magnificent view spread out before my eyes.
He made a grand plan to travel around the world.
This movie is a historical epic told on a grand scale.
en.notes: 壮大 stresses large scale and ambition: 壮大な景色/計画/夢/物語/スケール. Unlike 雄大, which is used almost only for nature, 壮大 also fits plans, music and films; sometimes ironic for overly big plans. 広大 denotes the vastness of an area, 巨大 the physical size of an object.

examples[].german: I gazed at the majestic mountain range.
I could see the majestic Mt. Fuji from the airplane window.
I was moved by the grand nature of Hokkaido.
en.notes: 雄大 is used almost exclusively for natural phenomena that impress through size and calm grandeur: 雄大な山/川/海/景色, especially 雄大な自然. For plans or stories one does not say 雄大, but 壮大. The word is descriptive and elevated, typical of travel reports and brochures.

examples[].german: A vast grassland stretches out.
That university has a vast campus.
The universe is vast, and there is still much we don't know.
en.notes: 広大 describes spatial vastness and extent: 広大な土地/敷地/草原/キャンパス, also 宇宙は広大だ. Not to be confused with 膨大, which denotes large quantities (膨大なデータ "huge amounts of data"), and with 巨大, which means the size of a single object. Rather literary; in everyday speech people often simply say 広い.

examples[].german: A huge building stands in the center of the city.
A huge typhoon is approaching Japan.
That giant corporation almost monopolizes the market.
en.notes: 巨大 stresses a size far above normal, for things (巨大なビル/岩) as well as for phenomena and organizations (巨大地震, 巨大企業). It often appears directly in compounds without な. 大きな is neutral, 巨大 emphatic; 広大 refers to areas, 膨大 to quantities. The verb 巨大化する means "to become huge".

examples[].german: I don't miss even the tiniest change.
Even tiny bits of dust can cause precision machines to break down.
Tiny earthquakes occur almost every day, but we hardly feel them.
en.notes: 微小 is a technical word for "microscopically small, tiny", typical in science and engineering: 微小な粒子/変化, 微小地震. It stands as 微小な or 微小の before a noun. In everyday speech people more often say ごく小さい or, for amounts and changes, わずかな. 微量, by contrast, denotes a tiny quantity, 極小 the utmost minimum.

examples[].german: An extremely small chip is embedded in the machine.
This camera is tiny and fits in your pocket.
The function reaches a local minimum at this point of the graph.
en.notes: 極小 (極 "extremely" + 小 "small") means "extremely small, minimal" and is technical and literary. Most often it appears as 極小の or directly in compounds such as 極小サイズ; 極小な is rarer. In mathematics, 極小 means a local minimum (counterpart 極大), whereas 最小 is the absolute minimum. In everyday speech people more often say ごく小さい or 超小型.

examples[].german: Life is finite, so we should live it with care.
The Earth's resources are limited.
My father runs a small limited company (yugen kaisha).
en.notes: 有限 means "limited, finite" and stands mostly predicatively (資源は有限だ) or as 有限の/有限な before nouns. In everyday speech people often say 限りがある. The opposite is 無限. 有限会社 is the legal form "limited company" (can no longer be newly founded since 2006). Not to be confused with the identically read 幽玄, a concept of aesthetics.

examples[].german: Samurai fought with swords.
In the Edo period, samurai made up less than one tenth of the population.
"A samurai does not go back on his word," said my father, and he kept his promise.
en.notes: 武士 denotes the Japanese warrior or samurai as a class, especially from the Heian to the Edo period. 武士 is the neutral, historical word; 侍 (often written サムライ) sounds more popular and is readily used for national teams (侍ジャパン). Typical: 武士道 "the way of the warrior", 武士の家に生まれる, and the saying 武士に二言はない "a samurai stands by his word".

examples[].german: This is nothing more than a temporary measure.
When I take the medicine, the pain subsides temporarily.
That popularity was only short-lived.
en.notes: 一時的 means "temporary, only for a short time": 一時的な措置/現象/ブーム, adverbial 一時的に (痛みが一時的に治まる). 暫定的, by contrast, stresses "provisional until a final arrangement", 臨時 "extraordinary, unscheduled". The opposites are 恒久的 and 永続的. Not to be confused with 一時 on its own, which can mean "for a while" or "one o'clock".

examples[].german: I want to bring about lasting peace.
That facility is not temporary; it is planned to be used permanently.
What we need is not temporary support but a permanent system.
en.notes: 恒久的 is formal and belongs to politics, law and administration: 恒久的な平和/対策/施設/制度, adverbial 恒久的に. It stresses lasting validity as opposed to 一時的 or 暫定的. 永久 sounds more like "eternal, for all time" (永久歯), 永続的 like "continuing". In everyday speech people say the simpler ずっと続く.

examples[].german: A provisional agreement was reached.
Until a new leader is decided, I will take charge on a provisional basis.
These are only provisional figures and may change later.
en.notes: 暫定的 means "provisional, until a final arrangement": 暫定的な合意/措置/数字, adverbial 暫定的に. Related are 暫定予算 "interim budget" and, in sports, 暫定1位 "provisionally first". 一時的 stresses only the short duration, not the later final solution; colloquially people often say 仮の (仮の予定). Typical of news and business language.

examples[].german: The final decision will be made next week.
I hesitated a lot, but in the end I bought the blue car.
The ultimate responsibility lies with the company president.
en.notes: 最終的 means "final, ultimate": 最終的な決定/結果/責任. Very common is the adverb 最終的に "finally, in the end", which neutrally describes the result of a process; 結局, by contrast, often sounds like "in the end after all (contrary to expectation)". 最後 only denotes the last position in a sequence.

examples[].german: A fundamental reform is necessary.
My way of thinking is fundamentally different from his.
We must clarify the root cause of the problem.
en.notes: 根本的 (根本 "root, foundation") means "from the ground up, fundamental": 根本的な原因/解決/改革/見直し, adverbial 根本的に違う/間違っている. 基本的, by contrast, means "basically, in principle", 本質的 "concerning the essence". Even more formal is 抜本的 (抜本的な改革 "radical reform").

examples[].german: We need to identify the essential problem.
The two methods are essentially the same.
Instead of petty details, let's have a more essential discussion.
en.notes: 本質的 (本質 "essence, core") means "essential, concerning the essence": 本質的な問題/違い/議論, adverbial 本質的に "essentially". 根本的 aims at origin and foundation, 実質的 at the actual effect as opposed to the name. The opposite is 表面的. Frequent in discussions, science and business.

examples[].german: A superficial understanding alone is not enough.
On the surface, the two seem to get along well.
With my colleagues I only have superficial relationships.
en.notes: 表面的 means "superficial, only on the outside" and is mostly meant critically: 表面的な理解/付き合い/変化. 表面的には means "on the surface, outwardly". For a superficial character people more often say 浅はかな or 薄っぺらい. The opposites are 本質的 and 根本的.

examples[].german: I got the formal greetings out of the way.
The interview is a mere formality; the hiring is almost decided.
The meeting was held only for form's sake, and nothing was decided.
en.notes: 形式的 mostly means "purely formal, only for form's sake" and is often critical: 形式的な挨拶/手続き/会議, 形式的なもの "a pure formality". It forms a pair with 実質的 "actual, in substance". For "formal, ceremonial" in clothing or occasions, people say フォーマルな, 正式な or 改まった instead.

examples[].german: The real leader is him.
The price is the same, but the amount has decreased, so in effect it's a price increase.
Prices are rising, so real salaries are falling.
en.notes: 実質的 means "actual, effective, in substance" as opposed to 名目 "in name only": 実質的なリーダー, 実質的には値上げ "effectively a price increase". In economics: 実質賃金 "real wage", 実質GDP. 本質的, by contrast, means "concerning the essence". It forms an opposing pair with 形式的.

examples[].german: One should judge based on objective facts, not subjective opinions.
How one perceives taste is something subjective.
This evaluation has become too subjective.
en.notes: 主観的 means "subjective, shaped by one's own view": 主観的な意見/評価/判断, adverbial 主観的に. It forms a fixed pair with 客観的. The noun 主観 often appears in the qualification あくまで私の主観ですが "this is just my personal view, but ...". Register neutral to objective-sounding.

examples[].german: Freedom of religion is guaranteed by the constitution.
My grandmother is deeply devout and visits the temple every morning.
Mt. Fuji has been an object of worship since ancient times.
en.notes: 信仰 is religious faith or the worship of gods or the sacred: 信仰を持つ, 信仰が厚い "to be deeply religious", 山岳信仰 "mountain worship"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 仏教を信仰する. Unlike 信じる or 信用 (to trust, to believe true), 信仰 is always religious or quasi-religious. Religion as an institution is 宗教.

examples[].german: I analyzed it based on objective data.
It is hard to view yourself objectively.
In court, objective evidence is given great weight.
en.notes: 客観的 (reading きゃっかん, not きゃくかん) means "objective, independent of personal feelings": 客観的なデータ/証拠/事実, especially common adverbially as 客観的に見る/判断する/評価する. The related noun is 客観性 "objectivity". The opposite is 主観的.

examples[].german: Happiness is a relative concept.
Because of the strong yen, imported goods have become relatively cheaper.
Grades at this school are determined by relative evaluation.
en.notes: 相対的 means "relative, in relation to something else": 相対的な概念/評価, adverbial 相対的に "relatively". The opposite is 絶対的; at school people distinguish 相対評価 and 絶対評価. In everyday speech, "relatively (cheap, etc.)" is mostly 比較的; 相対的 stresses the explicit comparison and sounds more objective.

examples[].german: Does absolute justice exist?
He has absolute confidence in his own judgment.
The president holds absolute power in that company.
en.notes: 絶対的 means "absolute, unlimited, unquestionable": 絶対的な権力/自信/存在, also 絶対的に不足している "absolutely insufficient". Not to be confused with the colloquial adverb 絶対(に) "definitely, without fail" (絶対に行く). The opposite is 相対的. Rather objective and formal.

examples[].german: Approach things with a positive attitude.
The department head received my proposal favorably.
In the survey, 70 percent gave affirmative answers.
en.notes: 肯定的 (肯定 "affirmation") means "approving, affirmative, evaluating positively": 肯定的な意見/回答/評価, adverbial 肯定的に受け止める. For an optimistic basic attitude, people in everyday speech more often say 前向き or ポジティブ. The opposite is 否定的; in grammar, the affirmative form is 肯定形.

examples[].german: I wish you wouldn't only voice negative opinions.
The experts are negative about the plan.
The experiment ended with a negative result.
en.notes: 否定的 means "dismissive, negative": 否定的な意見/見方/結果. Typical is 〜に否定的だ "to take a negative stance toward something". For a pessimistic attitude, people in everyday speech more often say ネガティブ or 後ろ向き. The related verb is 否定する "to deny, negate"; the opposite is 肯定的.

examples[].german: Active learning is called for.
We want to hire people who don't wait for instructions but can take the initiative.
I want to create an environment where children can play on their own initiative.
en.notes: 能動的 means "active, acting on one's own initiative" as opposed to 受動的: 能動的な学習/姿勢, adverbial 能動的に動く. In everyday speech 積極的 "proactive, enterprising" is much more common; 自主的 and 主体的 stress independence. In grammar, the active voice is 能動態. Rather formal (education, personnel).

examples[].german: You can't grow with a passive attitude.
Just watching TV passively won't improve your language skills much.
He is always passive in meetings and never speaks up on his own.
en.notes: 受動的 means "passive, merely reacting" as opposed to 能動的: 受動的な姿勢/学習, adverbial 受動的に見る. In everyday speech 消極的 "reserved, not taking initiative" is more common. In grammar, the passive is 受動態 or, in textbooks, 受身; 受動喫煙 is "passive smoking".

examples[].german: The original idea was appreciated.
Her works are all so original that you can tell right away they're hers.
This restaurant is famous for its original dishes combining Japanese and French cuisine.
en.notes: 独創的 (独創 "one's own creation") praises genuine originality: 独創的なアイデア/作品/発想; the noun is 独創性. 創造的 refers more to the general ability to create something new, whereas 独創的 stresses that something is unique and not imitated. Colloquially people also say ユニーク, which can also mean "odd".

examples[].german: An innovative technology was developed.
This company produces one innovative product after another.
At that time, the mayor drew attention with his reformist policies.
en.notes: 革新的 means "innovative, novel": 革新的な技術/製品/アイデア. In politics, 革新 stands for "reform-minded, progressive" as the counterpart to 保守 (革新的な政策). 画期的 stresses a single epoch-making breakthrough, 先進的 the lead over others. Typical of business, technology and news.

examples[].german: His way of thinking is conservative.
A conservative party won the election.
I want to invest my retirement funds conservatively.
en.notes: 保守的 means "conservative, holding on to the existing" in politics and values (保守的な政党/考え方), but also "cautious" for estimates and investments (保守的な見積もり). The opposite is 革新的 or 進歩的. Note: 保守 on its own also means "maintenance" in engineering (保守点検).

examples[].german: Many gods are worshipped in Japan.
Before the exam, I prayed to the gods at the shrine for success.
The way that clerk served me was simply amazing.
en.notes: 神 is a god or deity; in Shinto there are countless 神 (八百万の神), in Christianity it is the one God. In daily life one respectfully says 神様: 神様にお願いする. In youth slang, 神 also means "awesome, divine": 神対応 "superb service", この漫画は神. Do not confuse with the homophones 紙 "paper" and 髪 "hair".

examples[].german: A groundbreaking invention changed the world.
A groundbreaking cancer treatment was discovered.
That's a brilliant idea!
en.notes: 画期的 (reading かっき, not がき) means "groundbreaking, epoch-making", something that ushers in a new era: 画期的な発明/発見/治療法. In advertising and everyday speech it is also used exaggeratingly for "brilliant, handy" (画期的なアイデア). 革新的 stresses innovation in general.

examples[].german: Advanced medical technology was introduced.
This town is taking progressive initiatives in environmental protection.
That car is popular with young people for its modern design.
en.notes: 先進的 means "advanced, ahead of others": 先進的な技術/取り組み/デザイン. Related is 先進国 "developed country". 最先端 stresses the absolute cutting edge ("high-tech"), 進歩的 rather progressive ideas and views. The opposite is 後進的.

examples[].german: The outdated system needs to be improved.
This country was once said to be backward, but now it is developing rapidly.
That company is backward in terms of IT; it still uses fax machines.
en.notes: 後進的 means "backward, lagging behind" and is derogatory; for countries, people now say 発展途上国 or 途上国 instead of 後進国. In everyday speech people more often say 遅れている or 時代遅れ. Note: the noun 後進 on its own mostly means "younger generation, successors" (後進を育てる "to nurture the next generation"). The opposite is 先進的.

examples[].german: He never tells lies.
I will never forget this.
Please never let children take this medicine.
en.notes: 決して always occurs with a negation (〜ない, 〜ません, 〜ないでください) and strengthens it to "never, by no means": 決して忘れません. It sounds more serious and formal than 絶対に, which also occurs in affirmative sentences. In warnings, 決して〜ないでください is typical, and 決して悪くない means "not bad at all". It is often written in kana as けっして.

examples[].german: My homework is almost done.
I hardly slept yesterday.
Most of the students in the class come by bicycle.
en.notes: With an affirmative verb ほとんど means "almost, nearly" (ほとんど終わった), with a negation "hardly" (ほとんど寝ていない, ほとんど知らない). As a noun with の it means "most, the greater part": ほとんどの学生. It is almost always written in kana. だいたい is more approximate ("roughly, on the whole"), while ほとんど is closer to "completely".

examples[].german: I'm usually at home on weekends.
Most people know this method.
Raising three children alone is no small feat.
en.notes: 大抵 is mostly written in kana (たいてい). As an adverb it means "usually, as a rule" (週末はたいてい家にいる); as 大抵の + noun it means "most" (大抵の人). It lies between いつも "always" and よく "often"; ほとんど emphasizes quantity more. The fixed phrase 並大抵ではない means "no small matter, extraordinarily hard".

examples[].german: In the morning I usually drink coffee.
I usually go to work by train, but on rainy days I take the bus.
Most shops open at ten.
en.notes: たいてい describes a habit that holds in most cases: "usually, as a rule", so somewhat weaker than いつも and stronger than よく. With の before a noun it stands for "most": たいていの店, たいていの人. It is usually written in kana; the kanji spelling 大抵 is rare. Unlike ほとんど, たいてい is about frequency, not quantity.

examples[].german: It takes about thirty minutes from here.
After hearing the explanation, I roughly understood what the job involved.
Such a story is hardly believable at all.
en.notes: およそ (rarely 凡そ) means "approximately, about" and stands before numbers (およそ三十分) or with verbs (およそ分かる "to understand roughly"). It is somewhat more formal than だいたい; 約 stands only before numbers. With negation, およそ means "not at all" (およそ信じがたい). Variants: おおよそ, as a noun "outline."

examples[].german: There were about a hundred participants.
The meeting lasted about two hours.
The cost is planned to be about 30,000 yen.
en.notes: 約 stands as a prefix directly before numbers: 約百人, 約2時間. It is factual and literary (news, reports); in speech people often say 百人くらい or だいたい百人. Unlike およそ or だいたい, 約 cannot stand with verbs (not 約分かる). As a kanji it also occurs in 約束 "promise."

examples[].german: The work is almost complete.
I walk from the station to the company almost every day.
The two are almost the same height.
en.notes: ほぼ means "almost, nearly" (ほぼ完成, ほぼ毎日) or "roughly" in comparisons and quantities (ほぼ同じ, ほぼ半分). It is neutral to slightly literary and stresses that only a little is missing. ほとんど is similar, but can also stand as a noun (ほとんどの人) and means "hardly" with negation (ほとんどない); だいたい is more casual and means "by and large." Almost always written in kana; the kanji 略 and 粗 are very rare.

examples[].german: I put my hands together before the Buddha and prayed.
Ignorance is bliss - he still hasn't noticed anything.
Our late grandfather, too, must be watching over us as a buddha.
en.notes: 仏 denotes the Buddha or a Buddha statue; in daily life one respectfully says 仏様. Euphemistically, 仏 also stands for a deceased person (仏になる "to die"; in crime stories, police say 仏さん about the corpse). Idioms: 知らぬが仏 "ignorance is bliss", 仏の顔も三度まで "even Buddha's patience has limits". In compounds such as 仏教 or 仏像, 仏 is read ぶつ.

examples[].german: That's exactly right.
This is exactly the book I was looking for.
I arrived at the station just as the train was about to depart.
en.notes: まさに (rarely 正に) is an emphatic "exactly, truly": まさにその通り "exactly so," これこそまさに… "this is exactly ...". With 〜ようとする it means "just about to" (まさに出発しようとしていた). It sounds somewhat more formal than ちょうど or 本当に. Not to be confused with まさか "no way!"

examples[].german: It was truly an event one could call a miracle.
I think that's exactly right.
I arrived at the station just as the train was about to depart.
en.notes: まさに stresses that something applies exactly and without reservation: "exactly, truly, downright." Typical are まさに〜だ or まさに〜と言える (まさに奇跡だ) as well as the agreement まさにその通りです. With 〜ようとする or 〜ところ it means "just about to" (まさに出発しようとしていた). Mostly written in kana; 正に looks literary. Somewhat more elevated and emphatic than 本当に or ちょうど.

examples[].german: That is certainly a difficult problem.
This restaurant is indeed expensive, but the food is the best.
I have duly received the package.
en.notes: 確かに confirms a statement: "certainly, indeed, undoubtedly". Very common is the concessive use 確かに〜が/けど "it's true that ..., but": 確かに高いけど、品質はいい. As a short agreement, people say 確かに！ or 確かにそうですね "True!". To be distinguished from the na-adjective 確か (確かな情報 "reliable information") and from the sentence-initial 確か "if I remember correctly" (確か月曜日だった).

examples[].german: It was a truly wonderful performance.
The participants numbered over a thousand, no less.
His explanation was really easy to understand.
en.notes: 実に intensifies adjectives and judgments: "really, truly, extremely." It is weightier and more literary than 本当に or とても and sounds slightly stiff in everyday conversation; typical in speeches, reviews and commentary. Before numbers it expresses astonishment at the size: 実に千人 "no fewer than a thousand." Not to be confused with 実は "to be honest, actually."

examples[].german: Thank you very much indeed.
I sincerely apologize for the inconvenience.
I am very sorry to trouble you, but could you please fill this in here?
en.notes: 誠に is a very polite intensifying adverb: "sincerely, truly, deeply". It appears almost always in fixed polite formulas such as 誠にありがとうございます, 誠に申し訳ございません or 誠に恐れ入りますが; in business and in announcements it is standard. In casual conversation it sounds overly formal; there 本当に is enough. The kanji spelling 誠に is common, and the kana まことに is also widespread.

examples[].german: Let's take a break for now.
I forgot something, so I'll go back home for a moment.
Once you've made a promise, you should keep it.
en.notes: 一旦 has two main uses: "temporarily, for now" for an interruption after which things continue (一旦休憩する, 一旦家に帰る), and "once, as soon as" in conditional sentences with 〜たら/〜と/〜ば (一旦始めたら最後までやる). In the sense of "for the time being" it resembles とりあえず, but stresses the later continuation. Usually written in kana いったん; the kanji form looks more literary.

examples[].german: Once I decide something, I don't change it.
I know you're in the middle of work, but please save your data for now.
We'll take this matter back with us for now and consider it internally.
en.notes: いったん is the usual kana spelling of 一旦. It means, on the one hand, "for now, temporarily" (いったん保存する, いったん持ち帰る), and on the other, in conditional sentences, "once, as soon as": いったん〜たら/〜と/〜ば, often with the consequence that something can no longer be undone. In meetings, いったん持ち帰って検討します is a polite way to postpone a decision. Unlike とりあえず, it sounds more orderly and less provisional.

en.meaning: for now; first of all; anyway
examples[].german: A beer for now, please.
I decided the detailed schedule later and, for the time being, only reserved the venue.
Anyway, I'm glad everyone is safe.
en.notes: とりあえず means "for now, first of all": one deals with the nearest matter and postpones the rest, famous as とりあえずビール when ordering at an izakaya. It also means "at any rate, in any case" (とりあえず無事でよかった). With customers or superiors it can sound makeshift and unprepared; more formal are まず or ひとまず. Almost always in kana; 取りあえず is rare.

examples[].german: Let's start right away.
I bought new shoes, so I put them on and went out right away.
If I may, I'll get right to the main topic.
en.notes: さっそく means "immediately, right away, without hesitating" and describes a prompt reaction to something that came before: you receive something, learn something or are asked, and act at once. Typical: さっそく使ってみる and さっそくですが as a transition to the actual topic in meetings. Unlike すぐ, it has a positive coloring of eagerness; for urgent instructions, ただちに fits better. The kanji spelling 早速 is just as common.

examples[].german: I go to church every Sunday.
There is an old church in this town.
My older sister had her wedding in a church.
en.notes: 教会 is a Christian church, both the building and the congregation. To go regularly is 教会に通う, to get married in a church is 教会で結婚式を挙げる. For Buddhist temples one says 寺, for Shinto shrines 神社. The identically read 協会 means "association, society".

examples[].german: A problem occurred, so we responded immediately.
A tsunami warning has been issued. Please evacuate to high ground immediately.
This figure does not necessarily mean failure.
en.notes: ただちに means "immediately, without delay" and is formal: typical in instructions, announcements, news and regulations (ただちに避難してください). It is more urgent and stricter than すぐに; さっそく, on the other hand, stresses eager action in response to something pleasant. With negation, ただちに〜わけではない means "not immediately, not automatically" (ただちに健康に影響はない). The kanji spelling 直ちに is also common.

examples[].german: He answered the question immediately.
The proposal was turned down by the president on the spot.
If you feel an earthquake, immediately get under a desk.
en.notes: 即座に means "on the spot, promptly, without hesitation" - the reaction follows a trigger such as a question, a proposal or an event directly. It is somewhat more literary than すぐ(に); similar are 直ちに (formal, esp. in instructions) and その場で "on the spot". Before nouns it is 即座の: 即座の判断 "an immediate decision".

examples[].german: Thank you for your prompt reply.
I tried out the recipe you told me right away.
To get right to the point: I'd like to consult you about next month's event.
en.notes: 早速 is the kanji spelling of さっそく "immediately, promptly"; both forms are common, and in business emails 早速 is often seen. Set phrases are 早速のご返信ありがとうございます "thank you for your prompt reply" (with の before a noun) and 早速ですが as an introduction to the topic. It expresses a pleasantly quick reaction, not an obligation like ただちに.

examples[].german: Tomorrow is finally the day of the exam.
As night fell, the wind grew stronger and stronger.
If it really comes to that, I intend to consult my parents.
en.notes: いよいよ has two core meanings: "now at last, the time has come" for a long-awaited moment (いよいよ明日から夏休み) and "more and more, increasingly" for an intensification (雨がいよいよ激しくなる). In the first sense there is tension or anticipation, while やっと and ようやく stress relief after a long wait. いよいよとなったら means "when it gets serious, in an emergency". Almost always in kana.

en.meaning: all the more; even more so
examples[].german: If it rains, I want to go even less.
It's crowded even on ordinary days, so on holidays it's all the more so.
When I heard the reason, his effort seemed all the more admirable.
en.notes: なおさら means "all the more, even more so": a situation that already holds applies even more strongly under a further condition. Typical patterns are 〜ならなおさら, 〜たらなおさら and 〜はなおさらだ at the end of a sentence. With a negative it corresponds to "even less, all the less" (なおさら行きたくない). Unlike いっそう, which describes a mere increase, なおさら presupposes a comparison with a starting case. Do not confuse it with なお "furthermore, still"; the kanji 尚更 is rare.

examples[].german: The reality was far harsher than I had imagined.
Going by train is far faster than by car.
From the mountaintop, the sea could be seen far away.
en.notes: はるかに strengthens comparisons: "by far, far more", typical in the pattern A は B よりはるかに〜. It is stronger and somewhat more elevated than ずっと. Originally はるか means "far away", hence also spatially "in the distance" (はるかに海が見える) and temporally はるか昔 "long ago" (then without に). The kanji spelling 遥かに is possible, but kana predominates.

examples[].german: This restaurant is by far tastier.
He firmly opposed the plan.
Our team is far and away at the top of the league this season.
en.notes: 断然 has two uses: as an intensifier in comparisons, "by far, clearly" (こっちのほうが断然いい), very common in colloquial speech, and as an adverb of attitude, "resolutely, categorically" (断然反対する, 断然断る). In comparisons it resembles ずっと or はるかに but sounds more subjective and emphatic. With nouns: 断然トップ "far ahead at the top".

examples[].german: In the final, she was overwhelmingly strong.
This product is by far the most popular among young women.
Opinions in favor far outnumbered opinions against.
en.notes: 圧倒的に is the adverb form of the na-adjective 圧倒的 "overwhelming" and means "by an overwhelming margin, clearly". Common combinations: 圧倒的に多い, 圧倒的に強い, 圧倒的に有利だ; attributively 圧倒的な差 or 圧倒的な人気. It sounds stronger than 断然 or はるかに and is equally common in news, sports reports and colloquial speech.

examples[].german: It is very regrettable, but I will be absent.
This exam was extremely difficult.
Thank you for your cooperation; it was a great help.
en.notes: 非常に means "extremely, exceedingly" and sounds matter-of-fact to formal; it fits well in announcements, letters and reports. In casual conversation one rather uses とても or すごく. With a negation ("not very"), it is not 非常に but あまり〜ない that is used. 非常 alone means "emergency", as in 非常口 "emergency exit".

examples[].german: Considerable effort is needed.
He seems to be quite tired.
The winner will receive a prize worth 100,000 yen.
en.notes: 相当 as an adverb means "quite, considerably" and stresses a surprisingly high degree: 相当疲れている, 相当難しい. It is stronger than かなり and often sounds evaluative. As a na-adjective: 相当な努力 "considerable effort." There is also the noun and する-verb "to correspond to": 一万円相当の商品 "goods worth 10,000 yen," 〜に相当する "to be equivalent to ...".

examples[].german: The Bible is the most widely read book in the world.
The Bible says, "Love your neighbor."
There was a Bible in the drawer of the hotel room.
en.notes: 聖書 is the Bible; 旧約聖書 "Old Testament", 新約聖書 "New Testament". Typical: 聖書を読む, 聖書の言葉, 聖書に書かれている. An authoritative standard work of a field ("the cooks' bible"), on the other hand, is called バイブル. Holy scriptures of other religions are called 経典 or are referred to by name, such as コーラン.

examples[].german: There are some changes to the schedule.
This shop is slightly more expensive than the one in front of the station.
We are recruiting a few part-time workers.
en.notes: 若干 means "a little, some, a few" and is rather formal and literary: 若干の変更 "some changes", 若干名 "a few people" (in job ads). As an adverb it modifies adjectives and verbs: 若干高い "somewhat more expensive", 若干遅れる "to be slightly late". It sounds more businesslike than 少し or ちょっと; in youth slang, however, 若干 is also used casually for "a bit".

examples[].german: The temperature rose slightly.
The ball missed the goal by a narrow margin.
The door was open a crack, and light was leaking out.
en.notes: わずかに means "slightly, narrowly, only": it describes a very small amount or change (わずかに上がる, わずかに残る). For distances it means "narrowly" (わずかに届かなかった "just missed"). It is somewhat more literary than 少し or ちょっと and typical in news, reports and descriptions. The na-adjective わずか appears attributively: わずかな差, わずか三分 "only three minutes".

examples[].german: It's comparatively warm today.
This exam is said to be relatively easy.
On weekday daytimes the trains are relatively empty.
en.notes: 比較的 means "comparatively, relatively" and qualifies a statement against a tacitly assumed standard: 比較的安い, 比較的簡単だ. As an adverb it usually stands directly before adjectives or verbs without に; 比較的に is rarer. Attributively: 比較的新しい技術. It is neutral to slightly formal; colloquially people often say わりと or わりに.

examples[].german: This dish was surprisingly delicious.
When I tried it, it was surprisingly easy.
He seems taciturn, but he is surprisingly talkative.
en.notes: 意外と means "surprisingly, unexpectedly" and expresses that something is different (mostly better) than thought: 意外と簡単, 意外とおいしい. 意外に is synonymous and somewhat more neutral; 意外と is especially common in colloquial speech. The na-adjective 意外 appears predicatively or attributively: 意外な結果, それは意外だった. More elevated is 思いのほか.

examples[].german: It took unexpectedly long.
The meeting ended unexpectedly early.
My first solo trip was more fun than I expected.
en.notes: 思いのほか means "contrary to expectations, unexpectedly", literally "outside of what was thought". It is synonymous with 意外と, but more elevated and literary; in everyday conversation it sounds slightly literary. Often used with quantities and degrees: 思いのほか時間がかかる, 思いのほか早く終わる. The spelling 思いの外 is also common. Not to be confused with もってのほか "outrageous, completely unacceptable".

examples[].german: More people gathered than expected.
The new product sold better than expected, and the stock ran out.
The moving costs were more than expected.
en.notes: 予想以上に means "more than expected, beyond expectations" and is composed of 予想 "expectation, forecast" and 以上 "more than". It refers to quantities and degrees, positive as well as negative: 予想以上に売れる, 予想以上に難しい. Attributively one says 予想以上の結果, predicatively 予想以上だった. Close in meaning is 思った以上に, which sounds more colloquial; the opposite is expressed by 予想を下回る.

examples[].german: He behaved as if he knew nothing.
The sky that day was beautiful, as if painted.
He presented other people's opinions as if they were his own ideas.
en.notes: あたかも "as if, as though" opens a comparison that is completed with 〜ようだ/〜ように or 〜かのようだ/〜かのように: あたかも〜かのように振る舞う. It is literary and elevated; in conversation people more often say まるで. It often implies that appearances are deceptive (deception, pretense). Almost always in kana; 恰も is rare.

examples[].german: That's a very typical remark of his.
She was carrying a bag that looked really expensive.
"Is this your work?" "Indeed, it is."
en.notes: いかにも has three uses: before 〜らしい "typical, just like" (いかにも彼らしい), before 〜そうだ "evidently, obviously" (いかにも高そうな時計), and alone as formal agreement, "indeed, quite right". A slightly ironic or critical note often resonates (いかにも言い訳らしい). Almost always in kana; 如何にも is rare. Do not confuse it with いかに "how (much)".

en.meaning: (looking) just as if; with an air of
examples[].german: She laughed as if she were really enjoying herself.
He spoke as if he had thought of it himself.
My older brother replied with obvious reluctance.
en.notes: さも expresses that someone clearly puts something on display: "visibly, just as if". It almost always combines with 〜そうに/〜そうな or 〜かのように: さも嬉しそうに, さも知っているかのように話す. Often it implies that the impression is exaggerated or feigned; unlike あたかも, the focus is on a person's manner. Rather literary and written in kana.

examples[].german: It looks like it's going to rain.
The lights are off. It seems the shop has already closed.
Because I ran, I just barely made it to the last train.
en.notes: どうやら expresses a conclusion drawn from external signs: "apparently, it seems". It is almost always closed with 〜ようだ, 〜らしい or colloquially 〜みたいだ; 〜そうだ is also possible. Unlike たぶん or おそらく, the supposition rests on observation, not on a mere estimate. Second meaning: "somehow, with difficulty" (どうやら間に合った "just barely made it").

examples[].german: I offered a prayer for peace.
At the church there is prayer time every morning.
The thousand paper cranes carry the prayer that the person will get well soon.
en.notes: 祈り is a prayer or a heartfelt wish, the noun of 祈る "to pray, wish". Typical: 祈りを捧げる "to offer a prayer", 祈りを込める "to put a heartfelt wish into something", 平和への祈り. Unlike お願い (a simple request), 祈り has a solemn, religious or emotional ring. The polite お祈り also appears in rejection letters (ご活躍をお祈りいたします), hence the jargon お祈りメール for rejection emails in job hunting.

examples[].german: He probably won't come.
At this rate, the construction will probably continue until next month.
I think she probably already knows.
en.notes: おそらく means "probably, most likely" and is closed with a conjecture form: 〜だろう/〜でしょう, 〜と思う or 〜かもしれない. It is somewhat more formal and sounds more convinced than たぶん; typical in news, reports and cautious assessments. In contrast to どうやら, it does not need concrete signs. The kanji 恐らく is possible, kana is usual.

examples[].german: She will surely pass.
This is definitely his handwriting.
Please be sure to hand the documents to the person in question.
en.notes: 間違いなく means "without a doubt, absolutely certainly", literally "without error". As a sentence adverb it reinforces a supposition or fact (間違いなく成功する); as a manner adverb it means "without mistakes, properly" (間違いなく届ける). It is stronger than おそらく. Predicatively one says 〜に間違いない "there is no doubt that ...".

examples[].german: I sent it by registered mail so that it will surely arrive.
Because I practice every day, I'm steadily getting better.
If this continues, we will definitely miss the deadline.
en.notes: 確実に is the adverb form of the na-adjective 確実 "certain, reliable": "with certainty, reliably, steadily". It describes that something happens without risk or failure (確実に届ける, 確実に合格する) or advances step by step but surely (確実に上達している). Unlike 確かに, it does not confirm a statement but qualifies the action itself. Attributively: 確実な方法.

examples[].german: Of course I agree with the proposal.
This job requires not only English but also Chinese.
Of course, we leave the final decision to the president.
en.notes: 無論 means "of course, naturally" and is a literary, somewhat stiff synonym of もちろん. Common in enumerations: A は無論、B も "not only A, but naturally also B". In conversation it seems formal or old-fashioned; there people mostly say もちろん. The kana spelling むろん is also widespread.

en.meaning: needless to say; it goes without saying
examples[].german: It goes without saying that health is important.
Needless to say, safety takes priority above all else.
This shop is popular not only with locals, but also with tourists.
en.notes: 言うまでもなく means "of course, it goes without saying", literally "without needing to say it". As a sentence adverb it introduces a generally known fact; with nouns it forms A は言うまでもなく B も "not only A, but also B". Predicatively 〜のは言うまでもない stands at the end of a sentence. Slightly formal, typical in speeches, essays and news; in conversation people more often say もちろん.

examples[].german: I have always liked cooking.
According to the original plan, we were supposed to be back in three days.
I have nothing to lose, so let me just apply.
en.notes: もともと means "originally, from the beginning, by nature": もともと体が弱い, もともと東京の出身だ. Attributively it takes の: もともとの計画 "the original plan". There is also the expression だめでもともと (short だめもと) "you have nothing to lose". To be distinguished from the prefix 元 "former" (元社員): もともと emphasizes the initial state. Both kana and 元々 are common.

examples[].german: This land was originally a rice field.
He is quiet by nature.
This project was originally the president's idea.
en.notes: 元々 is the kanji spelling of もともと "originally, from the start, by nature"; the repetition mark 々 doubles 元. Both spellings are common. Typical are 元々は〜だった for the former state of a place or plan and 元々〜な性格 for a disposition. Not to be confused with the prefix 元 (もと) "former": 元首相 "ex-prime minister".

examples[].german: There used to be a large castle here.
I ran into a former colleague at the station by chance.
This typhoon caused unprecedented damage.
en.notes: かつて means "once, formerly" and is more elevated than 昔 or 以前; typical in narratives, history texts and news (かつての首都 "the former capital"). With a negative it means "never before": かつてない規模 "an unprecedented scale", いまだかつて〜ない "never before". The pronunciation かって is colloquial and considered incorrect.

examples[].german: Do you have any questions regarding this matter?
I read several books about environmental problems.
As for the fees, we will inform you by email at a later date.
en.notes: 〜に関して means "regarding, concerning, about" and names the topic at hand. It is more formal than 〜について and typical in business language, announcements and reports. Before nouns, 〜に関する (環境に関する調査) or 〜に関しての is used; with the topic marker, 〜に関しては "as for ...". In content it is mostly interchangeable with について, but for personal conversation topics に関して sounds stiff.

examples[].german: We deal politely with customers.
While the older sister is sociable, the younger one is quiet.
Many objections were raised against the government's decision.
en.notes: 〜に対して has two main meanings: "toward, to" for the target of an action or attitude (客に対して丁寧だ, 質問に対して答える) and "in contrast to" when comparing two things, after sentences with の (兄が背が高いのに対して、弟は低い). It also means "per, for each" in ratios (学生十人に対して先生一人). Before nouns: 〜に対する (政府に対する批判). Not to be confused with 〜について "about (a topic)".

examples[].german: During Obon, people visit their ancestors' graves.
I intend to take this secret to my grave.
My grandfather's grave is on a hill with a view of the sea.
en.notes: 墓 is the grave or burial place; politely お墓. A grave visit is called (お)墓参り, typically at お盆 and お彼岸. In Japan, graves are mostly family graves (〜家の墓), in which the urns are interred. Other words: 墓地 "cemetery", 墓石 "gravestone"; the saying 墓まで持っていく means "to take a secret to the grave".

examples[].german: Japan is leading the world in this field.
The entrance ceremony will be held in our school's gymnasium.
We think about the role of the family in modern society.
en.notes: 〜において is the formal counterpart of で and denotes place, time or field: "in, at, in the field of". Typical in announcements, official texts and technical language (会議室において, 現代社会において). Before nouns: 〜における (日本における教育). In everyday speech people simply say で; in conversation において sounds overly stiff.

en.meaning: based on; on the basis of
examples[].german: We judge based on the law.
Based on the survey results, we improved our service.
This is merely a forecast based on data.
en.notes: 〜に基づいて means "on the basis of, in accordance with" and names a binding basis such as data, laws, rules or facts. Before nouns: 〜に基づく or 〜に基づいた.
