Unlike 〜をもとに, which denotes source material for something new, に基づいて stresses conformity with a norm or body of data. Formal; typical in reports, administration and science. It comes from the verb 基づく "to be based on".

en.meaning: based on; using as a basis
examples[].german: It's a movie based on a true story.
I wrote a report based on the data I collected.
I made a new cake based on my grandmother's recipe.
en.notes: 〜をもとに means "on the basis of, starting from" and names the material or model from which something new arises (実話をもとにした映画, 資料をもとに報告書を書く). Before nouns: 〜をもとにした; variant 〜をもとにして. In contrast to 〜に基づいて, which stresses conformity with a norm, this is about source and inspiration. The kanji 元に or 基に are possible; kana is common.

examples[].german: I gather information through the internet.
It is warm on this island throughout the year.
I got to know her through a mutual friend.
en.notes: 〜を通じて has two meanings: "through, via, by means of" for a medium or intermediary (友人を通じて知り合う, ネットを通じて) and "throughout the whole ..." for a period of time (一年を通じて暖かい). It is somewhat more formal than the largely synonymous 〜を通して, which stresses conscious mediation more. Before nouns: 〜を通じての. It comes from the verb 通じる "to go through, to connect".

examples[].german: Customs differ depending on the culture.
The telephone was invented by Bell.
Many trains were suspended due to heavy rain.
en.notes: 〜によって has several functions: "depending on" for differences (人によって考え方が違う), "by" for the agent in the passive (ベルによって発明された), "by means of" for a means, and "due to" for a cause (事故によって遅れる). Before nouns: 〜による (地震による被害); in writing also 〜により. In the passive with persons, everyday speech mostly uses に; によって is used for creations, discoveries and official acts.

examples[].german: For me, that was a big challenge.
For foreigners, honorific language is difficult.
For the family, this house is a place of memories.
en.notes: 〜にとって means "for (someone), from the standpoint of" and stands before evaluations: 私にとって大切だ, 子どもにとって難しい. The predicate is a judgment (important, difficult, a challenge), not an action. For actions in favor of others use 〜のために (家族のために働く), for attitudes toward someone 〜に対して. With topic: 〜にとっては; before nouns: 〜にとっての.

examples[].german: Salary is determined according to ability.
Please add materials as needed.
Let's choose books suited to the child's age.
en.notes: 〜に応じて means "in accordance with, depending on, according to": something is adapted to a variable quantity (能力に応じて, 予算に応じて, 必要に応じて "as needed"). Unlike 〜によって, which merely states a difference, it stresses deliberate adjustment. Before nouns: 〜に応じた (年齢に応じた指導). It comes from the verb 応じる, which also means "to comply with a request" (依頼に応じる).

examples[].german: Living standards rose along with economic growth.
With the relocation of the store, the business hours will change.
The problems accompanying an aging society are becoming more serious year by year.
en.notes: 〜に伴って means "along with, accompanying, as a result of": one change brings another in its wake (人口の増加に伴って, 工事に伴って). It is literary and typical of news, reports and notices. Similar is 〜につれて, but that only expresses parallel, gradual developments; に伴って can also name a one-time event as the trigger (移転に伴って). Before nouns: 〜に伴う. It comes from the verb 伴う "to accompany, to bring with it".

examples[].german: Studying abroad made me like English.
Thanks to a TV program, the town became famous.
My illness was the trigger for quitting smoking.
en.notes: 〜をきっかけに means "triggered by, on the occasion of": an event gives the impetus to a new development (留学をきっかけに). Variants are 〜をきっかけにして and the more colloquial 〜がきっかけで. It is neutral and very common in everyday speech; the synonymous 〜を契機に is literary and formal. The noun きっかけ on its own means "occasion, trigger" (話すきっかけ).

en.meaning: on the occasion of; as a turning point
examples[].german: On the occasion of my marriage, I reviewed my lifestyle.
Since the earthquake disaster, interest in disaster prevention has risen.
With this merger as a starting point, the company expanded overseas.
en.notes: 〜を契機に means "on the occasion of, as a turning point" and is the literary counterpart of 〜をきっかけに. Typical in news, speeches and reports about social or personal turning points (震災を契機に, 就職を契機に). Variants: 〜を契機として, 〜を契機にして. In casual conversation it sounds stiff; there people say 〜がきっかけで.

examples[].german: It is said that a samurai's soul resides in his sword.
The craftsman puts his soul into every single piece.
She had a face as if her soul had left her from the shock.
en.notes: 魂 is the soul, which in traditional belief outlives death, and also spirit, vital force or devotion: 魂を込める "to put one's whole soul into it", 魂が抜けたよう "as if lifeless, completely absent-minded". As a suffix it denotes a typical mindset: 大和魂 "Japanese spirit", 職人魂 "craftsman's ethos". Compared with 心 (heart, feeling), 魂 sounds deeper and more solemn.

examples[].german: The result changes depending on how you do it.
Whether you can pass depends on your effort from now on.
Depending on the weather, tomorrow's barbecue might be canceled.
en.notes: 〜次第で means "depending on": the result depends decisively on N (天気次第で, 努力次第で). Predicatively: 〜次第だ "it depends on ..." (それはあなた次第だ). It stresses more strongly than 〜によって that N is the deciding factor. Caution: after a verb stem, 次第 means "as soon as" (分かり次第連絡します).

examples[].german: The school you advance to is determined by your grades.
Depending on the result of the negotiations, the plan may also be changed.
Regardless of the reason, lateness is not accepted.
en.notes: 〜いかんで means "depending on" and is a very formal, literary variant of 〜次第で. It stands directly after nouns or with の: 結果いかんで, 対応のいかんで. Related patterns are 〜いかんによっては "depending on ..., possibly" and 〜いかんにかかわらず or 〜いかんを問わず "regardless of". The kanji 如何 is possible, kana is usual; the pattern is often already counted as N1 level.

examples[].german: Anyone can participate regardless of age.
This app is used by many people regardless of whether at home or abroad.
You can apply regardless of whether you have experience.
en.notes: 〜を問わず means "regardless of, irrespective of" and often follows paired terms or categories: 年齢を問わず, 男女を問わず, 昼夜を問わず "day and night". It is formal and typical in job ads, invitations to tender and announcements. Similar are 〜にかかわらず and the more colloquial 〜に関係なく. It is the negative literary form of 問う "to ask, to take into consideration".

examples[].german: The match will be held regardless of the weather.
Anyone can apply regardless of age or experience.
Please reply by email, whether or not you will participate.
en.notes: 〜にかかわらず means "regardless of, no matter whether": the result applies equally to all cases. It follows nouns that contain a range (天候, 年齢, 性別, 経験の有無) or opposing pairs such as 行くか行かないかにかかわらず. Not to be confused with にもかかわらず "despite, although"! Typical for notices, invitations and formal announcements; mostly in kana, less often 関わらず or 拘らず.

examples[].german: Although he made an effort, he failed.
Despite the rain, many people gathered.
Thank you for coming despite your busy schedule.
en.notes: AにもかかわらずB means "despite A / although A": B happens contrary to expectation, often with surprise, regret or reproach. It attaches to nouns (雨にもかかわらず), and to verbs and adjectives in the plain form; with nouns and な-adjectives also 〜であるにもかかわらず. It is more formal than のに and also stands at the start of a sentence as それにもかかわらず. As a polite formula: お忙しいにもかかわらず "although you are so busy". Contrast: にかかわらず "regardless of".

examples[].german: Contrary to expectations, he won.
Contrary to his parents' expectations, he didn't go to university but became a singer.
Acts that violate the rules are prohibited.
en.notes: AにはんしてB means "contrary to A": the result contradicts an expectation (予想, 期待, 予報) or a will (本人の意志, 親の希望). Before nouns, 〜に反する or 〜に反した is used (規則に反する行為 "an act against the rules"). Not to be confused with 〜に対して "toward, in contrast to", which merely contrasts two things. Rather written and formal; in conversation people often say 予想と違って.

examples[].german: I walked along the river.
We reviewed the plan in line with the company's policy.
Please respond in accordance with the manual.
en.notes: 〜に沿って has two uses: spatially "along" (川に沿って, 線路に沿って) and abstractly "in line with, in accordance with" a guideline (方針に沿って, 計画に沿って, ご希望に沿って). Before nouns, 〜に沿った is used (マニュアルに沿った対応). Similar are 〜に基づいて "on the basis of" and 〜に従って "following", but に沿って stresses following a line or direction. The base verb is 沿う; not to be confused with 添う "to accompany".

examples[].german: There was a greeting before the opening.
A press conference was held ahead of the new product's release.
Before construction begins, we will hold an information session for local residents.
en.notes: 〜に先立って means "prior to, in the run-up to" an important, mostly official event and introduces a preparatory action. It follows event nouns (開会, 試合, 発売, 工事) or verbs in dictionary form (始めるに先立って). Before nouns: 〜に先立つ (試合に先立つ記者会見). Formal; in everyday speech people simply say 〜の前に. The verb 先立つ on its own means "to precede", also "to die before someone" (親に先立つ).

examples[].german: Let's just try it.
It's fine if you're late, but please come in any case.
Today it's just so hot that I don't feel like doing anything.
en.notes: とにかく sets details and concerns aside and turns attention to the essentials: "anyway, in any case, just" (とにかくやってみよう, とにかく来てください). In colloquial speech it also intensifies: とにかく暑い "just plain hot". With は, 〜はとにかく means "setting aside", for which 〜はともかく is more usual, however. Almost always in kana; the spelling 兎に角 is rare. Very common in conversation, somewhat more casual than ともかく.

examples[].german: Setting the reasons aside, the result is what matters.
It would be one thing for a child, but I can't believe an adult would do such a thing.
I don't know whether we'll make it in time, but let's set out anyway.
en.notes: On its own, ともかく means "anyway, be that as it may" (similar to とにかく, somewhat more formal). The most important pattern, however, is AはともかくB "setting A aside, apart from A": 味はともかく、値段は安い. Also 〜ならともかく "it would be one thing if ..., but ...". Extended also as 〜はともかくとして. Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: She is probably resting peacefully in heaven.
On weekends, this street becomes a pedestrian paradise.
A hot spring after work is pure heaven.
en.notes: 天国 is heaven or paradise in the religious sense, especially in Christianity: 天国へ行く, 天国の母. The physical sky, by contrast, is 空, and the Buddhist paradise is more 極楽. Figuratively, 天国 denotes a wonderful place or state (ここは天国だ) and, as a suffix, a place full of ...: 歩行者天国 "street temporarily closed to cars". Antonym: 地獄.

en.meaning: in any case; at any rate
examples[].german: In any case, please contact us early.
Whether by train or bus, either way it takes an hour.
The cause is still unknown, but in any case an investigation is necessary.
en.notes: いずれにしても "in any case, either way" draws, after several possibilities have been mentioned, the conclusion that holds in every case. Neutral to polite, frequent in conversation and emails; more formal are いずれにせよ and いずれにしろ, more casual どっちにしても. Not to be confused with いずれ on its own "someday, soon".

examples[].german: In any case, preparation is necessary.
It may be postponed, but in any case we will contact you as soon as it is decided.
The cause of the accident is under investigation, but in any case a review of safety measures is unavoidable.
en.notes: いずれにせよ means the same as いずれにしても "in any case, either way". せよ is the literary imperative of する, so the expression sounds more formal and appears mainly in reports, news, speeches and business emails; いずれにしろ lies in between. After open possibilities, it sums up what holds regardless.

examples[].german: If we're going anyway, let's enjoy ourselves.
Even if we go now, we won't make it in time anyway.
Nobody listens to what I say anyway.
en.notes: どうせ has two nuances: resigned "anyway, regardless (nothing will change)" - どうせ無理だ, どうせ私なんか - and "since ... anyway, might as well ..." with 〜なら or 〜のだから: どうせ行くなら楽しもう. The tone is colloquial and often pessimistic or defiant, unlike the neutral いずれにしても. Always in kana.

examples[].german: After all, human beings are not perfect.
A game is only a game after all. There's no need to take it seriously.
For an amateur like me, it was impossible from the start.
en.notes: 所詮 stresses that something is limited by its nature: "after all, ultimately just". Typical with 〜にすぎない, 〜でしかない, AはAだ or a negation (所詮無理だ). The tone is resigned or disparaging, stronger and more literary than どうせ; the neutral 結局, by contrast, only describes the outcome. Also in kana しょせん.

en.meaning: in the end; when all is said and done
examples[].german: In the end, you have no choice but to decide for yourself.
We discussed a lot, but ultimately it's a question of budget.
In the end, nobody knew what he was thinking.
en.notes: 結局のところ "in the end, bottom line" sums up the essentials after deliberation or discussion, often with 〜ということだ or 〜しかない. 結局 on its own rather describes how something turned out (結局行かなかった); 結局のところ sounds more summarizing and judgmental. Neutral to formal, also in essays; unlike 所詮, without a resigned undertone.

examples[].german: For example, Tokyo Tower is famous.
As for sports, I like, for example, tennis and soccer.
If, for example, it rains tomorrow, what will you do?
en.notes: 例えば introduces an example and is often combined with 〜など or, colloquially, 〜とか: 例えばテニスやサッカーなど. With 〜たら or 〜ば it means "suppose, let's say": 例えば雨が降ったら…. It is also often written in kana as たとえば; the noun 例 means "example".

examples[].german: What exactly should I do?
We will make operations more efficient. Specifically, we will halve the length of meetings.
In my previous job, I was specifically in charge of planning new products.
en.notes: 具体的には consists of the な-adjective 具体的 "concrete" + に + は and, after a general statement, introduces the specification: "specifically, in detail". Very frequent in presentations, reports and job interviews and as a follow-up question (具体的にはどういうことですか). Distinction: 例えば gives an example, つまり rephrases. Opposite: 抽象的.

examples[].german: It is convenient, but on the other hand there are also dangers.
He is strict at work, but kind to his subordinates.
The urban population is increasing. On the other hand, the population in rural areas keeps declining.
en.notes: 一方で connects two opposing sides: after a clause "while, on the one hand ... on the other" (便利な一方で危険もある), at the beginning of a sentence mostly as その一方で "on the other hand". Connection: verbs and い-adjectives in plain form, な-adjectives with な, nouns with である. Not to be confused with 〜一方だ "keeps getting more" (増える一方だ). More formal is 他方.

en.meaning: the other side; on the other hand
examples[].german: The city is convenient. On the other hand, it has little nature.
One side agreed, and the other opposed.
The new system reduces the burden on companies. On the other hand, procedures become more complicated for users.
en.notes: 他方 is, as a noun, "the other side, the other party", often in the pair 一方は…、他方は…, and as a conjunction "on the other hand" (also 他方で, 他方では). Very formal and literary - typical of essays, reports and news. In conversation one says 一方で or その一方で.

examples[].german: In Buddhism, it is said that those who do bad things fall into hell.
The crowded train every morning is like hell.
In Beppu, the "hell tour" of hot springs is popular.
en.notes: 地獄 is hell in the religious sense: 地獄に落ちる "to go to hell", 天国と地獄. Very common is the figurative use for an agonizing situation: 受験地獄 "exam hell", 通勤地獄, 地獄のような毎日. In spa towns such as Beppu, steaming hot springs are also called 地獄 (地獄めぐり). Proverb: 地獄で仏 "a savior in the hour of greatest need".

examples[].german: Last year was hot. Compared to that, this year is cool.
My older brother can do everything. Compared to him, I just keep failing.
Rents in Tokyo are high. By comparison, they are cheap in the countryside, but there are few jobs.
en.notes: それに比べて "compared to that" compares two things in degree or quality (more/less, better/worse), often with evaluation or self-criticism: それに比べて私は.... それに対して, by contrast, stresses pure opposition. In general also 〜に比べて or 〜と比べて after a noun. Neutral, in conversation and text.

examples[].german: Still, it really is hot today, isn't it?
It can't be helped that you're late. Even so, I wish you'd at least have contacted me.
Even so, why did she suddenly quit the company?
en.notes: それにしても acknowledges what came before and then qualifies it: "even so, even considering that" (遅れるのは仕方ない。それにしても...). In conversation it also introduces a spontaneous impression or astonishment: "but really, wow ..." - それにしても暑いですね. Mainly spoken; related to 〜にしても "even if".

en.meaning: on the contrary; far from it
examples[].german: I wasn't tired at all. On the contrary, I felt more energetic than before.
Even after taking the medicine, the fever didn't go down. On the contrary, it went up even more.
He didn't apologize. On the contrary, he started saying it was my fault.
en.notes: それどころか "on the contrary, even" mostly follows a negated statement and sets against it something that reverses the expectation or far exceeds it: Aない。それどころかB. Related is 〜どころか "far from ..." within a sentence. Distinction: そればかりか adds something in the same direction ("not only that, but also"). Neutral, spoken and written.

en.meaning: aside from that; setting that aside
examples[].german: Setting that aside, let's get to the main topic.
Yesterday's game was a close one, wasn't it? Anyway, about next week's trip ...
Joking aside, let's have a serious talk.
en.notes: それはさておき "setting that aside, be that as it may" ends a digression and leads back to the actual topic or deliberately changes the subject. さておく means "to leave aside"; as a pattern, 〜はさておき "setting ... aside" (冗談はさておき). Slightly formal; in casual conversation people more often say それはそうと or ところで. Unlike ちなみに, it does not add extra information.

examples[].german: Incidentally, my hobby is reading.
The meeting starts at three. By the way, the venue is on the second floor.
This cake is delicious, isn't it? Incidentally, I bought it at the shop in front of the station.
en.notes: ちなみに "incidentally, by the way" attaches additional information that fits thematically with what came before. ところで, by contrast, switches to a new topic, それはさておき returns to the main topic. Frequent in conversations, presentations and blogs; in official announcements なお is more common. Mostly in kana; the spelling 因みに is rare.

examples[].german: Furthermore, details will be announced at a later date.
Even now, many people remember that accident.
If it's close to the station, even better.
en.notes: なお has two main uses: at the beginning of a sentence in announcements and letters it introduces a supplementary note: "Also/Note: ..." (more formal than ちなみに). As an adverb it means "still, even more": 今もなお "even today", なお一層 "even more", それならなお良い "even better". Mostly in kana; 尚 is rare.

examples[].german: Participation is voluntary. However, prior registration is required.
You may take photos. However, please do not use a flash.
Admission is 1,000 yen for adults. However, elementary school children and younger are free.
en.notes: ただし introduces a restriction, condition or exception to a statement just made and usually stands at the beginning of a sentence: 〜。ただし、〜. Unlike しかし, which marks a general contrast, ただし does not cancel the previous statement but supplements it with a proviso. Typical for rules, price information and notices; in contracts also 但し, otherwise mostly kana. In conversation people more often say ただ or でも.

en.meaning: however; admittedly; justified; natural (もっともな意見)
examples[].german: He is excellent. Admittedly, he has flaws too.
If I were told something like that, it's only natural that he got angry.
What you say is perfectly reasonable.
en.notes: As a conjunction at the beginning of a sentence, もっとも qualifies what was said before: "however, admittedly" (… もっとも、欠点もある). As a na-adjective it means "justified, understandable, reasonable": もっともな意見, 怒るのももっともだ "no wonder he's angry"; to agree politely, people say ごもっともです. Not to be confused with the identically read 最も "most" (最も高い山). Mostly written in kana; the kanji spelling 尤も is rare.

examples[].german: The plan is good. However, carrying it out is difficult.
We are very grateful for your proposal. However, we will pass on it this time.
The economy is recovering. However, wages have hardly risen.
en.notes: しかしながら is the formal, literary variant of しかし "however, nevertheless". It appears in speeches, reports, essays and business letters, especially before refusals or qualifications; in everyday speech it seems stiff - there people say でも or けど. ところが additionally expresses an unexpected turn.

examples[].german: Even though I'm busy, health care is important.
Although it's spring, mornings and evenings are still cold.
I passed the exam. That said, I still can't relax.
en.notes: AとはいえB "A, but nevertheless B" acknowledges A and qualifies it: what one would expect from A does not quite apply. Connects to nouns and plain forms (春とはいえ, 忙しいとはいえ); at the beginning of a sentence as とはいえ、... "however". More written; in conversation people say とは言っても or そうは言っても. Equivalent to とはいうものの.

examples[].german: Those who commit a crime will be punished.
He was arrested for the crime of theft.
Innocent children became victims of the war.
en.notes: 罪 covers "crime, offense" (罪を犯す "to commit a crime", 〜の罪で逮捕される "to be arrested for ..."), "sin" in the religious sense, and "guilt" (罪を認める "to admit guilt", 罪のない "innocent"). As a na-adjective, 罪な means "cruel, thoughtless", often jokingly: 罪な人 "heartbreaker". 犯罪 is the factual term for crime, 罰 the punishment for it.

examples[].german: Although it's said to be easy, it takes time.
Although I've started a diet, I just can't give up sweets.
I'm going to study abroad from next month. That said, I haven't even decided where to live yet.
en.notes: A(と)はいうもののB "A, but ...": one concedes A, but reality looks different. ものの means "although". At the beginning of a sentence also とはいうものの、... or そうはいうものの "however". Same in content as とはいえ, somewhat more literary. It does not mean "although it is said" - it is about one's own concession.

examples[].german: He is busy. That doesn't mean he's allowed to break his promise.
My test score was bad. That doesn't mean you need to give up.
This shop is famous. That doesn't necessarily mean the food is good.
en.notes: だからといって stands at the beginning of a sentence, takes up the previous sentence as a reason and rejects an obvious conclusion: "just because ..., that doesn't mean ...". Typical sentence endings are 〜わけではない, 〜とは限らない, 〜必要はない or 〜てはいけない. Attached directly to a clause, the form is 〜からといって (高いからといって...); colloquially shortened to だからって.

en.meaning: but then again; on the other hand
examples[].german: I don't want to go. But I can't refuse either.
I don't like my current job. But I can't just quit right away either.
I'm cutting back on sweets. But not eating any at all is hard too.
en.notes: そうかといって "but on the other hand, not that either" shows that the obvious opposite reaction to A is likewise not possible or not good. A negation or 〜わけにもいかない usually follows. More common and shorter is かといって; the kanji spelling そうかと言って also occurs. Neutral, in conversation and text, fond of dilemmas.

examples[].german: He can speak English. Not only that, he can also speak French.
He was late for the appointment. Not only that, he didn't even apologize.
This medicine has no effect. What's more, it also has side effects.
en.notes: そればかりか "not only that, but even; furthermore" adds a further, often even stronger point in the same direction. The basic pattern is AばかりかBも "not only A, but also B". Distinction: それどころか reverses the expectation ("on the contrary"). More written; in conversation people say それに or しかも.

en.meaning: so to speak; as it were
examples[].german: He is, so to speak, the pillar of the team.
For my grandmother, this garden is, so to speak, life itself.
The internet is, so to speak, something like a modern library.
en.notes: 言わば "so to speak, as it were" introduces a figurative paraphrase or metaphor, often with 〜のようなものだ: 言わば第二の家だ. It comes from 言う plus the conditional ば ("if one were to say it") and is mostly written in kana as いわば. Not to be confused with いわゆる "so-called" (for established terms); つまり summarizes, and 例えば gives an example.

examples[].german: There was no train, so I had no choice but to take a taxi.
The game was canceled due to rain, so I reluctantly watched TV at home.
Since no one wanted to do it, I reluctantly took on the party preparations.
en.notes: 仕方なく is the adverbial form of 仕方ない and means "reluctantly, out of necessity, because there is no other way". It stands before an action one did not really want: 仕方なく〜した. Synonymous is 仕方なしに; more colloquial しょうがなく, more formal やむを得ず.

examples[].german: I paid the real estate brokerage fee.
I joined my current company through a friend's mediation.
This company brokers the buying and selling of used cars.
en.notes: 仲介 is "mediation" between two parties, especially in real estate (不動産の仲介, 仲介手数料 "brokerage fee", 仲介業者 "broker"), in trade and in negotiations. As a する-verb it is transitive: 売買を仲介する; "through the mediation of" is 〜の仲介で. Distinction: 紹介 "to introduce", 仲裁 "to arbitrate a dispute".

examples[].german: In the future, I want to live in a detached house.
I bought a used detached house in the suburbs.
A detached house is nice for having a garden, but the upkeep is hard work.
en.notes: 一戸建て is a freestanding single-family house as opposed to apartments in multi-unit buildings such as マンション or アパート. Typical combinations: 一戸建てを買う / 建てる, 新築の一戸建て, 中古の一戸建て. It is shortened to 戸建て, colloquially also 一軒家. Frequent in real estate ads and in talk about dream homes.

examples[].german: I moved into an apartment in front of the station.
You can see Mt. Fuji from the top floor of the high-rise apartment building.
I can't decide whether to buy a condo or keep renting.
en.notes: マンション is a false friend: it does not mean a mansion but a multi-story residential building of reinforced concrete or an apartment in one - rented (賃貸マンション) or owned (分譲マンション). アパート, by contrast, is a smaller, more simply built apartment building. Typical: マンションに住む, マンションの〜階, 高層マンション.

examples[].german: I am majoring in philosophy at university.
The company president has his own management philosophy.
"Why do people live?" - that's quite a philosophical question.
en.notes: 哲学 is philosophy as an academic discipline (哲学を専攻する, 西洋哲学, 哲学者) and, figuratively, a personal philosophy of life or work: 人生哲学, 経営哲学, 彼なりの哲学がある. In daily life, 哲学的 also stands for "profound, hard to answer": 哲学的な質問. The word was coined in the Meiji period as a translation of "philosophy".

examples[].german: I lived in an apartment when I was a student.
This apartment building has three floors.
en.notes: アパート can mean an apartment building or a single unit in it. アパートに住む describes where one lives. 三階建て gives the number of floors of a building (three). 学生の頃 refers to one's own student days. The dash in アパート makes the a after パ long: apāto.

examples[].german: I went to buy new furniture.
I'm looking for a furnished room.
As a precaution against earthquakes, I secured the furniture to the wall.
en.notes: 家具 is the collective term "furniture" (cabinet, table, bed, etc.); individual pieces are counted with 点 or つ. Important combinations: 家具付き "furnished", 家具を配置する "to arrange furniture", 家具を固定する (earthquake protection), 家具店. To distinguish: 家電 are electrical appliances, 道具 tools and utensils.

examples[].german: I bought a TV at an electronics retailer.
When moving, I disposed of my old appliances all at once.
Many recent home appliances can be operated with a smartphone.
en.notes: 家電 is the short form of 家庭用電気製品 and covers electric household appliances such as refrigerators, washing machines and rice cookers, but also TVs. Frequent: 家電量販店 "electronics superstore", 白物家電 "white goods", 生活家電. Distinction: 家具 means furniture; 電化製品 is a somewhat older umbrella term.

examples[].german: You can't get through winter without heating.
It's cold - may I turn on the heating?
This room is well heated and nice and warm.
en.notes: 暖房 is the heating of a room or the heating as a system: 暖房をつける/消す, 暖房を入れる, 暖房が効いている "it is well heated". The counterpart is 冷房 "cooling". The actual device is usually called エアコン, ヒーター or ストーブ; 暖房 emphasizes the function.

examples[].german: The air conditioning is too strong and it's cold.
It's hot, so let's turn on the air conditioning.
At night I turn off the air conditioning when I sleep.
en.notes: 冷房 is room cooling or the air conditioner in cooling mode: 冷房をつける/入れる/消す, 冷房が効いている "it is well cooled", 冷房が効きすぎる "too strongly cooled". The counterpart is 暖房. The device itself is usually called エアコン; 冷房 emphasizes the function and often appears on signs in trains and shops.

examples[].german: I dimmed the lighting in the room.
The stage lights went out, and the play began.
Warm-colored lighting suits a bedroom.
en.notes: 照明 denotes the lighting or lamps in a room (照明をつける / 消す, 照明を暗くする, 間接照明 "indirect lighting") as well as lighting technology in theater or film (舞台照明). In everyday speech, for switching on and off, people often simply say 電気をつける. As a する-verb "to illuminate" it is rare and rather technical.

examples[].german: I wash the sheets once a week.
At the hotel, they change the sheets every day.
Please put a sheet on the futon before you go to sleep.
en.notes: シーツ (from English "sheets") is the bed sheet, for both beds and futons. Typical verbs: シーツを替える "to change", 敷く "to lay on", 洗う; counted with 枚. For covers, on the other hand, people say カバー (布団カバー, 枕カバー).

examples[].german: Adding fabric softener makes towels fluffy.
The scent of the fabric softener was so strong that I felt sick.
I mistakenly bought fabric softener instead of detergent.
en.notes: 柔軟剤 is composed of 柔軟 "soft, supple" and 剤 "agent": "fabric softener". One says 柔軟剤を入れる / 使う; in Japan people often talk about 柔軟剤の香り "the scent of the softener". Not to be confused with 洗剤 "detergent"; both are put into the washing machine together.

examples[].german: You need a reservation to put out bulky waste.
I put the old sofa out as bulky waste.
Bulky waste is collected only once a month.
en.notes: 粗大ゴミ is bulky waste such as furniture, bicycles or large appliances. In Japan you usually have to register it beforehand and attach a paid sticker (粗大ゴミ処理券); it is then picked up on a set day. One says 粗大ゴミを出す or 〜を粗大ゴミに出す; in official texts it is often written 粗大ごみ. Jokingly it also refers to a retired husband sitting around uselessly.

examples[].german: In summer, the electricity bill goes up because of the air conditioner.
To save on electricity, I diligently switch off power I'm not using.
This month's electricity bill exceeded 10,000 yen.
en.notes: 電気代 is the electricity cost or electricity bill; 代 stands for the price of a service (cf. ガス代, 水道代). Typical: 電気代がかかる / 高い / 上がる, 電気代を払う / 節約する. In contracts and official texts, the more formal 電気料金 is used.

examples[].german: Medical ethics is being debated.
That experiment was criticized as ethically problematic.
Politicians are expected to have a high sense of ethics.
en.notes: 倫理 is ethics or morality as a system of rules for right action, often professional or social: 医療倫理, 企業倫理, 倫理に反する "to be unethical", 倫理的な問題, 倫理観 "moral values". In high school, 倫理 is also a school subject. Compared with 道徳 (morality as a personal virtue, also the school subject "moral education"), 倫理 sounds more abstract and is preferred for professional and scientific questions.

examples[].german: In winter, the gas bill piles up.
I pay the gas bill by credit card.
If you heat the bath every day, it costs quite a lot of gas.
en.notes: ガス代 is the gas cost or gas bill for cooking, hot water and heating (city gas or propane). Typical: ガス代がかかる / かさむ "to add up", ガス代を払う. Formally it is ガス料金. Colloquially ガス代 can also mean gasoline costs; for that, ガソリン代 is clearer.

examples[].german: The water bill is charged once every two months.
I shorten my showers to save on the water bill.
In this apartment, the water bill is included in the rent.
en.notes: 水道代 is the water cost or water bill; in Japan billing is usually every two months, often together with sewage (下水道). Formally it is 水道料金. Typical: 水道代を払う / 節約する, 水道代が家賃に含まれている.

examples[].german: I keep my food expenses to 30,000 yen a month.
I eat out a lot, so my food expenses are piling up.
Meals are also included in the dormitory rent.
en.notes: 食費 is household spending on food, i.e. groceries and meals overall; for dormitories also "board costs". Typical: 食費を抑える / 節約する / 切り詰める, 食費がかさむ. Distinction: 食事代 is the price of a single meal, 生活費 covers all living costs.

examples[].german: The company covers my transportation costs.
You bear your own transportation costs to the interview.
The accounting department reimbursed me for my business trip transportation costs.
en.notes: 交通費 are transportation or travel costs, above all commuting costs, which Japanese companies often reimburse (交通費支給, 交通費を負担する). For business trips: 交通費を精算する "to settle expenses". Distinction: 運賃 is a single fare, 旅費 the total travel costs including lodging.

examples[].german: I reviewed my communication costs and switched to a cheaper plan.
The company partly covers the internet costs for working from home.
Adding up the phones of the whole family, our communication costs come to 20,000 yen a month.
en.notes: 通信費 are the costs of communication, today mainly mobile phone and internet contracts, formerly also postage and landline. Typical in household budgets and saving tips: 通信費を見直す / 抑える / 節約する. For the mobile phone alone, people colloquially say スマホ代 or 携帯代.

examples[].german: I decided to cut back on entertainment expenses.
When I kept a household account book, my entertainment expenses were higher than I thought.
When I was a student, I could hardly spend any money on entertainment.
en.notes: 娯楽費 is composed of 娯楽 "entertainment, amusement" and 費 "cost" and denotes spending on leisure such as movies, games, hobbies and outings - a typical category in a household account book (家計簿). Related are 交際費 "social expenses" and 趣味にかけるお金. Typical: 娯楽費を削る / 抑える.

examples[].german: I budget 10,000 yen a month for miscellaneous expenses.
The move cost more in miscellaneous expenses than I expected.
Small purchases such as stationery are booked as miscellaneous expenses.
en.notes: 雑費 are "miscellaneous expenses, incidental costs" - small, varied items that fit no category of their own. 雑 means "mixed, various". Common in household account books, in bookkeeping (a "miscellaneous" account) and with moves or trips: 雑費がかかる.

examples[].german: I had a lot of expenses this month.
The car repair was a painful expense.
With one wedding after another, expenses are piling up.
en.notes: 出費 means expenses, especially noticeable or unexpected ones: 出費がかさむ "expenses pile up", 痛い出費 "a painful expense", 出費を抑える. Distinction: 支出 is the bookkeeping counterpart to 収入, 費用 the cost for a particular purpose. As a する-verb it is hardly used.

examples[].german: Stop wasting money.
After payday I always end up spending money needlessly.
Citizens are criticizing it as a waste of tax money.
en.notes: 無駄遣い is wasting money, also time or resources (時間の無駄遣い, 税金の無駄遣い). As a する-verb: 無駄遣いする, 無駄遣いをやめる. Opposite: 節約. More formal is 浪費. The spelling 無駄使い also occurs.

examples[].german: I go shopping on the supermarket's sale day.
Eggs were on sale at 100 yen a pack.
Sale items sell out quickly.
en.notes: 特売 is a special sale at reduced prices, typical in supermarkets: 特売日 "sale day", 特売品 "sale item", 本日の特売. One says 特売で買う / 特売になっている. Distinction: セール is more for clothing and department stores, 割引 is the discount itself, 安売り generally means "cheap sale".

examples[].german: You should act according to your conscience.
My conscience hurt because I had lied.
This shop gives large portions and its prices are fair, too.
en.notes: 良心 is the conscience, the inner voice for good and evil. Typical: 良心が痛む "to have a guilty conscience", 良心に従う "to follow one's conscience", formally 良心の呵責 "pangs of conscience". 良心的 means "conscientious, fair" and in everyday speech is often used for fair prices: 良心的な値段. Do not confuse it with the identically read 両親 "parents".

examples[].german: I bought clothes at the winter sale.
A half-price sale started today at the supermarket in front of the station.
Please note that sale items cannot be returned.
en.notes: セール is a sale at reduced prices. Typical are 夏のセール, 冬のセール, 半額セール or 期間限定セール; an item is セール中 or a セール品, and you buy something セールで ("at the sale"). "Sales" in the neutral sense, by contrast, is 販売; a clearance sale is 閉店セール or 在庫一掃セール.

examples[].german: With this coupon you get 10% off.
Please show the coupon screen on your smartphone when paying.
If you register as a new member, you will receive a coupon worth 500 yen.
en.notes: クーポン is a discount coupon or voucher, today often digital in an app (アプリのクーポン). You use it with 使う or 利用する, receive it with もらう, shops hand it out with 配る, and you show it at the register: クーポンを提示する. A gift certificate with a fixed cash value is rather called 商品券 or ギフト券; 割引券 is the Japanese word for a "discount ticket".

examples[].german: I had collected enough points, so I exchanged them for a product.
This report has three key points.
The cabinet's approval rating fell by 5 points from last time.
en.notes: ポイント has two main areas: in everyday life, the reward points of loyalty cards (ポイントが貯まる "points accumulate", ポイントを貯める, ポイントを使う, ポイントカード) and, figuratively, "the key point": 話のポイント, ここがポイントだ. It also stands for scoring points and percentage points in statistics (3ポイント上昇). For a point as a dot or for school grades, one says 点 instead.

examples[].german: Please be sure to keep the receipt.
Do you need the receipt? - No, thank you.
I collect receipts in order to keep a household account book.
en.notes: レシート is the machine-printed register receipt. You get it with もらう; at the register the staff ask 「レシートはいりますか」 or, more politely, 「レシートはご入用ですか」. For an official receipt, for example for expense reports with the company name, on the other hand, you ask for a 領収書 - this distinction matters in working life.

examples[].german: Will you be paying in cash?
This shop only accepts cash, so I withdrew money from the ATM.
He started helping the moment I said I'd give him pocket money - what a mercenary kid.
en.notes: 現金 is "cash" as opposed to cashless payment (キャッシュレス, カード). To pay cash is 現金で払う; 現金のみ is posted at shops that take only cash. As a な-adjective, 現金な also means "calculating, concerned only with one's own advantage": 現金な人, 現金なやつだ - colloquial and slightly mocking. In everyday speech, cash is also simply called お金 or キャッシュ.

examples[].german: Can I use a credit card?
If you pay by credit card, you earn points.
I lost my wallet, so I had my credit card blocked right away.
en.notes: クレジットカード is often shortened to カード in conversation: カードで払う, カードは使えますか. The means of payment takes で: クレジットカードで支払う. At the register you often hear the question about 一括払い ("in one payment") or 分割払い ("in installments"). To be distinguished are デビットカード and rechargeable IC cards such as Suica, which count as 電子マネー.

examples[].german: Recently I often pay with electronic money.
I topped up my electronic money at the convenience store.
My e-money balance was insufficient, so I was stopped at the ticket gate.
en.notes: 電子マネー in Japan mainly means prepaid electronic money on IC cards or in a smartphone, such as Suica, PASMO or nanaco. You top up with チャージする and pay with 電子マネーで払う, usually by briefly touching the reader (タッチ). The umbrella term for all cashless payment methods is キャッシュレス決済; QR code payments are mostly not counted as 電子マネー in the narrow sense.

examples[].german: Tickets can be purchased at the ticket machine.
To ride the Shinkansen, you need an express ticket in addition to the basic ticket.
May I see your tickets, please?
en.notes: 乗車券 is the official term for a ticket for train and bus; you read it on machines, signs and in announcements. In everyday speech people mostly simply say 切符. At JR, the 乗車券 covers only the basic fare - for express and Shinkansen trains you additionally need a 特急券. For flights it is 航空券, for concerts チケット.

examples[].german: I bought fresh ingredients at the market.
This restaurant is particular about local ingredients.
I made dinner with the ingredients left in the fridge.
en.notes: 食材 are foodstuffs as raw material for cooking, i.e. "ingredients" such as vegetables, meat or fish. Typical: 新鮮な食材, 地元の食材, 旬の食材, 食材を生かす "to bring out the ingredients". 材料 is more general and also appears in recipe lists for baking or crafts; 食品 means rather processed foods as goods, such as 冷凍食品.

examples[].german: Keep the basic seasonings on hand.
After adding all the seasonings, simmer for 10 minutes over low heat.
We do not use chemical seasonings in our dishes.
en.notes: 調味料 are seasonings in the broad sense: salt, sugar, soy sauce, miso, vinegar, mayonnaise, etc. The classic basic seasonings of Japanese cooking are remembered with さしすせそ (砂糖, 塩, 酢, 醤油, 味噌). Hot or aromatic spices such as pepper or cinnamon are more precisely called 香辛料 or スパイス. Typical: 調味料を加える, 調味料で味を調える; 化学調味料 are artificial flavor enhancers.

examples[].german: A new foreign minister was appointed.
The minister resigned, taking responsibility for his gaffe.
The finance minister explained the budget for the next fiscal year.
en.notes: 大臣 is a minister of cabinet rank; the portfolio comes before it: 外務大臣, 財務大臣, 文部科学大臣. The prime minister is officially called 内閣総理大臣. In headlines the short form with 相 is often used: 外相, 財務相. Typical: 大臣に就任する ("to take up the ministerial post"), 大臣を辞任する. As a form of address one says 〇〇大臣.

examples[].german: I fight for justice.
He has a strong sense of justice and can't stay silent when he sees bullying.
As a child, I admired defenders of justice.
en.notes: 正義 is justice in the moral sense, what is right: 正義のために戦う, 正義感が強い "to have a strong sense of justice", 正義の味方 "defender of justice" (typical for heroes in anime and children's series). Justice in the sense of fair distribution or treatment is more 公平 or 公正. The word sounds serious and is sometimes used ironically when someone thinks they are infallible.

examples[].german: I sprinkled pepper on the steak.
Season the meat with salt and pepper and grill it over high heat.
The soup tasted bland, so I added a little pepper.
en.notes: 胡椒 is mostly written in kana in everyday life (こしょう or コショウ); the kanji is seen more on packaging and menus. You sprinkle it with 振る or かける: 胡椒を振る. Very common is the pair 塩胡椒 "salt and pepper", also as a verb 塩胡椒する. Black pepper is 黒胡椒 or ブラックペッパー. Note: ピーマン is green bell pepper, not pepper.

examples[].german: I pour sauce over the fried noodles.
Tonkatsu is eaten with sauce and mustard.
I made the pasta sauce completely from scratch.
en.notes: ソース is "sauce" in general, but without further qualification in Japan it usually means the dark, savory Worcestershire-style sauce poured over とんかつ, お好み焼き or 焼きそば. Other sauces are named more precisely: トマトソース, ホワイトソース, デミグラスソース. You pour it on with かける or dip with つける. The same word is used for the "source" of information (ソースはどこ?), which is more internet jargon.

examples[].german: I make dashi from kelp and bonito flakes.
This miso soup is delicious, with a strong dashi flavor.
On busy days, I use instant dashi.
en.notes: だし (kanji 出汁, mostly in kana) is the Japanese basic stock made from 昆布, bonito flakes (鰹節) or dried sardines (煮干し). The set phrase is だしを取る "to extract stock"; instant powder is だしの素. だしが効いている means that the stock flavor comes through well. Western meat broth is rather called スープ or ブイヨン. Figuratively, 〜をだしにする means "to use someone or something as a pretext".

examples[].german: I thicken it with potato starch.
Karaage turns out crispy if you coat it in potato starch before frying.
Add the starch dissolved in water to the pot little by little.
en.notes: 片栗粉 is today practically always potato starch (originally it was made from the plant 片栗). It is used for thickening - 片栗粉でとろみをつける, usually as 水溶き片栗粉 "starch mixed with water" - and as a coating for crispy fried food such as 唐揚げ. Unlike wheat flour (小麦粉), it makes sauces translucent and glossy.

examples[].german: Put oil in the frying pan and fry.
Cleaning up after deep-fried dishes is hard work.
Stop idling around in a place like this and get back to work quickly.
en.notes: 油 is mainly liquid oil: cooking oil (サラダ油, ごま油, オリーブ油), but also machine oil. Solid animal fat is usually written 脂 (same reading), e.g. 脂身 or 脂がのった魚. In the kitchen, people say フライパンに油をひく ("to put oil in the pan") and 油で揚げる. Idioms: 油を売る "to loaf around," 火に油を注ぐ "to add fuel to the fire."

examples[].german: I spread butter on the toast.
There's no butter in the fridge.
en.notes: バター is butter. を marks it as the thing being spread; に marks the surface or food it is spread on. バターがない reports that there is none. The dash after タ lengthens the a: batā. 塗る is a godan verb with the form 塗った.

examples[].german: I piped fresh cream on top of the cake.
Whip the cream until stiff peaks form.
This pasta uses cream, so it tastes mild.
en.notes: 生クリーム is cream or whipping cream; 生 means "fresh, unprocessed" here. You whip it with 泡立てる, pipe it onto cakes with 絞る and stir it into sauces. In stores, real cream is distinguished from vegetable-based substitute cream, which is often sold as ホイップ. クリーム alone can also mean skin cream or custard (カスタードクリーム).

examples[].german: Egg yolk is used for carbonara.
Please separate the eggs into yolks and whites.
Mayonnaise is made from egg yolk, oil and vinegar.
en.notes: 卵黄 is the egg yolk in a rather technical or written register: in recipes, ingredient lists and nutrition texts. In everyday speech people mostly say 黄身; the counterpart is 卵白 or, colloquially, 白身. Typical: 卵黄と卵白に分ける "to separate yolk and white", 卵黄だけを使う.

examples[].german: Meringue is made by whipping egg whites.
Leftover egg whites can be frozen and stored.
I'm on a diet, so I made an omelet with only egg whites.
en.notes: 卵白 is the egg white in a technical or recipe register; colloquially people say 白身. Note: "egg white" in the sense of the nutrient is not 卵白 but たんぱく質 "protein". Typical: 卵白を泡立てる "to whip egg whites", 卵白だけを使う; the counterpart is 卵黄.

examples[].german: The distinction between good and evil is sometimes difficult.
Many people think violence is an absolute evil.
In this film, the protagonist fights an evil organization.
en.notes: 悪 is evil as an abstract principle, mostly in contrast to 善: 善と悪, 悪と戦う, 社会の悪 "social evil". In everyday speech, bad things are described with the adjective 悪い; 悪 on its own sounds abstract, philosophical or dramatic, as in films: 悪の組織 "villain organization". As a prefix it forms words such as 悪影響 "bad influence", 悪循環 "vicious circle", 悪人 "villain".

examples[].german: I eat yogurt for breakfast.
I like to eat plain yogurt with honey.
Yogurt is said to regulate the stomach.
en.notes: ヨーグルト is yogurt. Common combinations: プレーンヨーグルト "plain yogurt", 飲むヨーグルト "drinking yogurt", ヨーグルトにはちみつをかける. In Japan yogurt is strongly associated with health and digestion (乳酸菌, おなかの調子). You eat it with 食べる; only drinking yogurt is drunk with 飲む.

examples[].german: On cold days, I crave oden.
I bought oden with daikon and egg at the convenience store.
What's your favorite oden ingredient?
en.notes: おでん is a winter dish in which ingredients such as 大根, eggs, こんにゃく and fish products (ちくわ, はんぺん) simmer for a long time in a soy-seasoned だし. It is almost always written in hiragana. Typical are おでんを煮る, おでんの具 "the ingredients" and the おでん at the convenience store register, where you choose the pieces yourself. People like to eat it with からし (hot mustard).

examples[].german: I miss my mother's simmered dishes.
Simmered pumpkin is sweet and goes well with rice.
Simmered dishes taste better when left overnight, as the flavor soaks in.
en.notes: 煮物 are dishes simmered in a broth with soy sauce, sugar and mirin, such as 肉じゃが or かぼちゃの煮物 - a classic of home cooking, often associated with nostalgia. One says 煮物を作る; the related verb is 煮る "to simmer, stew", intransitive 煮える. The series 〜物 forms dish types by cooking method: 煮物, 焼き物, 炒め物, 揚げ物, 蒸し物.

examples[].german: I made a vegetable stir-fry.
The trick to stir-fries is to make them quickly over high heat.
This frying pan is light and easy to use for stir-frying.
en.notes: 炒め物 is a dish fried with little oil over high heat while constantly stirring, such as 野菜炒め or 肉野菜炒め. The verb is 炒める; unlike 焼く "to grill, pan-fry" (without much stirring) and 揚げる "to deep-fry", 炒める involves constant turning. Common are 炒め物をする and 炒め物に使う (e.g. of a frying pan or an oil).

examples[].german: Deep-fried food is high in calories.
When you deep-fry, the kitchen gets dirty with oil.
When I ate deep-fried food late at night, it sat heavily in my stomach.
en.notes: 揚げ物 are foods deep-fried in plenty of oil, such as 天ぷら, 唐揚げ, とんかつ or コロッケ. The verb is 揚げる "to deep-fry"; deep-fried without breading or batter is 素揚げ. Typical: 揚げ物をする "to deep-fry", 揚げ物を控える "to avoid fried food", 揚げ物で胃がもたれる "fried food sits heavily in the stomach". Not to be confused with 上げる "to raise" - same reading, different kanji.

examples[].german: Steamed dishes are healthy because they use no oil.
At the kaiseki meal, a steamed dish came out after the grilled dish.
You can make easy steamed dishes in the microwave, too.
en.notes: 蒸し物 are steamed dishes such as 茶碗蒸し, しゅうまい or steamed vegetables. The verb is 蒸す "to steam"; you cook in a 蒸し器 or a bamboo steamer (せいろ). In a Japanese banquet menu (会席料理), 蒸し物 is a course of its own. It always means the dish, not the cooking method - the latter is expressed with the verb: 蒸して作る.

examples[].german: Japanese cuisine is registered as an intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO.
For breakfast, would you like Japanese or Western food?
Japanese food is said to be low in calories and healthy.
en.notes: 和食 is traditional Japanese cuisine: rice, miso soup, fish, pickled vegetables and dishes with a delicate だし flavor. Contrasting terms are 洋食 ("Western cuisine") and 中華 ("Chinese cuisine"). 和食 is neutral and common in restaurants, cookbooks and media; 日本料理 sounds somewhat more formal and upscale. Typical: 和食の店, 和食派 ("someone who prefers Japanese food").

examples[].german: This restaurant specializes in Western-style food.
As a child, I always looked forward to going to a yoshoku restaurant with my family on Sundays.
My grandfather likes Japanese food better than Western food.
en.notes: 洋食 refers to Western dishes, but above all to the classics that have become established in Japan in a Japanized form, such as オムライス, ハンバーグ, エビフライ or カレーライス. A 洋食屋 is therefore a cozy restaurant with exactly such dishes, not a French restaurant. For genuine French or Italian cuisine, one rather says フランス料理 or イタリアン. Contrasting terms are 和食 and 中華.

examples[].german: Let's go eat Chinese for lunch today.
I ate steamed meat buns in Yokohama's Chinatown.
Of Japanese, Western and Chinese food, which do you like best?
en.notes: 中華 is, in everyday speech, the short form of 中華料理 "Chinese cuisine": 中華を食べる, 中華料理店, 町中華 (simple neighborhood Chinese restaurants). As a modifier it appears in 中華街 "Chinatown", 中華まん or 中華鍋 "wok". For the country China itself, people say 中国; 中華 in that sense appears only in fixed names such as 中華人民共和国.

examples[].german: I ordered a salad as a starter.
The course is served in the order of appetizer, soup, main dish and dessert.
The two of us shared an appetizer platter.
en.notes: 前菜 is the appetizer of a multi-course meal (コース料理), whether Western, Chinese or Japanese. Typical: 前菜の盛り合わせ "appetizer platter", 前菜に〜を頼む. It is usually followed by スープ, メイン or 主菜 and デザート. For small bites to go with drinks at a pub, people say つまみ instead, and for the starter automatically served at an izakaya, お通し.

examples[].german: Philosophers pursue the truth.
There is some truth in his opinion too.
I think "Haste makes waste" is a truth of life.
en.notes: 真理 is universally valid, often philosophical or scientific "truth": 真理を追究する／探究する, 永遠の真理, 普遍的な真理. For the truth about a concrete matter (what really happened) one says 真実, and in everyday speech simply 本当. The phrase 一面の真理 means "a grain of truth". The word sounds elevated and appears mainly in texts, speeches and discussions.

examples[].german: You can choose fish or meat as the main dish.
Let's have salted grilled salmon as today's main dish.
The school lunch menu is made with a balance of staple, main dish and side dishes in mind.
en.notes: 主菜 is the main dish of a meal, usually with meat, fish, egg or tofu as the protein source. The term comes from nutrition science and cookbooks and belongs to the meal pattern 一汁三菜 (rice, soup, one 主菜 and two 副菜); the rice itself is 主食, not 主菜. In restaurants people more often say メイン or メインディッシュ.

examples[].german: Side dishes are also important for a balanced meal.
Since the main dish is meat, I made the side dish mainly with vegetables.
It's handy to prepare a few side dishes in advance on the weekend.
en.notes: 副菜 is the small vegetable, bean or seaweed side dish to the 主菜, such as おひたし, salad or a small 煮物. The term comes from nutrition science and cookbooks; in everyday speech, for everything you eat with rice, people more often say おかず, and for the garnish on the same plate 付け合わせ. Rice counts as 主食, not as 副菜.

examples[].german: I ordered ice cream for dessert.
I'm full, but there's always room for dessert.
Shall I bring the dessert together with your coffee?
en.notes: デザート is the dessert after a meal, in restaurants often 食後のデザート. Typical: デザートを頼む, デザートにする and the saying デザートは別腹 "there's always room for dessert", literally "dessert goes into a different stomach". Sweets in general are rather called お菓子 or スイーツ, Japanese sweets 和菓子. "Desert" in Japanese is 砂漠, not デザート.

examples[].german: What would you like to drink?
It's hot, so I'll bring a cold drink.
en.notes: 飲み物 is the general word for a drink, whether hot or cold. 飲み物は何にしますか asks which choice one wants. In 飲み物を持って行く, by contrast, the drink is an object one takes along. The word is made up of "drink" and "thing"; the combination is used as a single noun.

examples[].german: There are many historic sites in this area.
I joined a tour of Kyoto's famous sights and historic sites.
I visited the historic sites of the town and learned about its history.
en.notes: 旧跡 is a place where something of historical importance happened or where traces of it remain. It most often appears in the fixed paired phrase 名所旧跡 ("famous sights and historic sites"), typical of travel guides and tourist brochures. The register is written; in conversation people tend to say 歴史のある場所. Archaeological excavation sites and ruins are called 遺跡.

examples[].german: Check-in is from three o'clock.
Please check in at the airport no later than two hours before departure.
I checked in as soon as I arrived at the hotel.
en.notes: チェックイン is checking in at a hotel or airport. As an intransitive する-verb, the destination takes に: ホテルにチェックインする. Typical: チェックインの手続き, チェックインカウンター, オンラインチェックイン. The counterpart is チェックアウト. For registering at events or doctor's offices, 受付 is more usual.

examples[].german: Please check out by eleven o'clock.
Even after check-out, the front desk can keep your luggage.
I checked out of the hotel at eight in the morning and headed for the station.
en.notes: チェックアウト is checking out of a hotel. As a する-verb, the place you leave takes を, as with 出る: ホテルをチェックアウトする. Typical: チェックアウトの時間, レイトチェックアウト ("late check-out"), フロントでチェックアウトする. The counterpart is チェックイン. In online shopping, however, the payment process is usually called 購入手続き.

examples[].german: I checked one large suitcase.
I put my clothes in the suitcase.
My suitcase didn't come out at the airport.
en.notes: スーツケース is the (usually hard-shell) travel or rolling suitcase: スーツケースに服を入れる, スーツケースを預ける "to check the suitcase", スーツケースを引く "to pull the suitcase". Synonymous terms you hear are キャリーケース or キャリーバッグ. A bag in general is かばん, a backpack リュック.

examples[].german: Please check the expiration date of your passport.
I lost my passport at the airport and had a terrible time.
I applied for a passport for my first trip abroad.
en.notes: パスポート is the passport; officially and on forms it is called 旅券. Typical combinations: パスポートを申請する ("to apply for"), パスポートを更新する ("to renew"), パスポートを提示する ("to show") and パスポートの有効期限 ("period of validity"). An ID in general is 身分証明書; in Japan, a driver's license (免許証) is often used for this.

examples[].german: Is there a direct flight to Tokyo?
Since there was no direct flight, I decided to transfer in Seoul.
Direct flights are expensive, but considering the time, they are easier.
en.notes: 直行便 is a direct flight without transfers; the opposite is 乗り継ぎ便 or 経由便 ("via ..."). Typical: 〜行きの直行便, 〜への直行便, 直行便で行く. The word can also refer to direct bus or ferry connections. It is based on 直行 ("to go directly"), which is also heard in everyday speech: 会社に直行する ("to go straight to the office").

examples[].german: You should judge by reason, not emotion.
I lost my composure in anger and shouted.
Humans are said to be animals possessing reason.
en.notes: 理性 is "reason" as the ability to judge objectively and thoughtfully, usually in contrast to 感情 ("emotion") or 本能 ("instinct"). Typical are 理性を失う ("to lose one's composure/reason"), 理性を保つ, 理性で判断する; the adjective is 理性的な. Do not confuse it with 理由 ("reason, cause") or 知性 ("intellect"). Rather literary, but also understood in conversation.

examples[].german: The seats in the Green Car are spacious and comfortable.
On business trips, the company pays the Green Car fare.
To ride the Green Car, you need a Green Car ticket in addition to your regular ticket.
en.notes: グリーン車 is the first-class car on JR; the name comes from the green marking these cars used to have, and today a green four-leaf-clover symbol marks them. You need a グリーン券 in addition to the 乗車券. The ordinary cars are called 普通車, with 自由席 and 指定席; some Shinkansen also have the even more luxurious グランクラス. Typical: グリーン車に乗る, グリーン車を予約する.

examples[].german: I hired a guide who speaks Japanese.
Thanks to the guide's explanations, I understood the history of the temple well.
When my friend came to Japan, I showed him around Tokyo.
en.notes: ガイド is above all a person who guides tourists (観光ガイド, ガイドさん, ガイド付きツアー); it can also mean a printed guide, usually explicitly ガイドブック. As a transitive する-verb: 町をガイドする ("to show someone around the town"). The general Japanese word for "to guide, to show, to give information" is 案内する, which is even more common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I received a commemorative gift at the graduation ceremony.
A commemorative gift was handed out to all participants of the marathon.
Everyone together gave a commemorative gift to our senior colleague who was retiring.
en.notes: 記念品 is a commemorative gift for an event, for example at graduation ceremonies, company anniversaries, farewells, or as a participation gift at events; it is usually presented: 記念品を贈る, 記念品をもらう, 記念品を配る. A souvenir brought back from a trip for other people is お土産 instead; a personal keepsake is more often called 思い出の品.

examples[].german: You must not be bound by old ideas.
He has no sense of time and is always late.
Realizing he could no longer escape, the culprit finally resigned himself to it.
en.notes: 観念 means "idea, notion, concept", especially in 固定観念 ("fixed idea, stereotype"). With の before it, it denotes a sense of something: 時間の観念がない ("to have no sense of time"), 金銭観念 ("attitude toward money"). As a する-verb, 観念する means "to resign oneself to one's fate, to give up": もう観念しろ! The word is rather literary; in everyday speech people usually say 考え or アイデア for "idea".

examples[].german: He advanced the discussion by clearly presenting his grounds.
The conclusion of this paper is interesting, but the supporting argument is weak.
Using statistical data as his basis, he argued for a review of the system.
en.notes: 論拠 is the foundation of an argument, that is, the evidence or reasons a claim rests on. It is literary and typical of essays, debates and specialist texts: 論拠を示す, 論拠が弱い, 〜を論拠に主張する. In conversation people say 根拠 ("basis, evidence") more often, which is also used outside of arguments (根拠のないうわさ). The claim itself is called 主張.

examples[].german: The motive for the crime is still unknown.
I was asked in the interview why I was applying and couldn't answer well.
My motivation for starting Japanese was that I liked anime.
en.notes: 動機 is the reason behind an action. Typical are 犯行の動機 ("motive for the crime") in the news and 志望動機 ("reason for applying") in interviews and application documents. One says 動機は〜だ, 〜が動機で, 不純な動機 ("impure motive"). "Motivation" in the sense of drive and willingness, by contrast, is やる気 or モチベーション. The homophone is 動悸 ("heart palpitations").

examples[].german: The aim of this policy is economic recovery.
I took careful aim and kicked the ball.
The new product became popular among young people, just as intended.
en.notes: 狙い is the noun of 狙う ("to aim, to have one's eye on something"). Concretely it is aiming with a weapon or ball (狙いを定める "to take careful aim"); figuratively it is the real intention behind a plan: 〜の狙いは…にある, 狙い通り ("as intended"). It often implies that the intention is strategic or hidden: 本当の狙いは何だ? More neutral are 目的 ("purpose") and 目標 ("goal, target").

examples[].german: We analyzed the opposing team's tactics.
From the second half, the coach changed tactics and strengthened the defense.
Even with the right strategy, you can't win if the tactics are wrong.
en.notes: 戦術 means tactics, i.e. concrete procedure in a particular situation - in war, sports, election campaigns or business. It must be distinguished from 戦略 ("strategy"), the overarching, long-term plan. Typical: 戦術を立てる, 戦術を変える, 戦術を練る, 選挙戦術. More colloquial is 作戦 ("plan, approach"), which is also used for private undertakings.

examples[].german: I acquired practical skills through vocational training.
To obtain this qualification, you must pass a written exam and a practical exam.
That craftsman has honed his skills over many years.
en.notes: 技能 is a practical skill acquired through practice, especially manual or occupational: 技能を身につける, 技能を磨く, 技能検定 ("skills test"), 技能実習生 ("technical intern"). 技術 stresses technique as knowledge and procedures, whereas 技能 means an individual's ability to carry something out in practice. In everyday speech you also hear スキル; 能力 is "ability" in general.

examples[].german: It is important to draw lessons from failure.
Drawing on the lessons of the earthquake, the town's disaster prevention plan was revised.
The moral of this old tale is that one must not lie.
en.notes: 教訓 is a lesson drawn from experience, often from mistakes or disasters. Typical: 〜から教訓を得る/学ぶ, 〜を教訓にする ("to take something as a lesson"), 教訓を生かす ("to make use of the lessons"). The moral of a story is also called 教訓. A "lesson" in the sense of a teaching unit in a textbook, by contrast, is 課 or レッスン.

examples[].german: I think about the meaning of human existence.
Do you think aliens really exist?
He is an indispensable presence for the team.
en.notes: 存在 means "existence, being" and, as an intransitive する-verb, "to exist": 〜が存在する is the formal equivalent of ある／いる. Also common is the meaning "a person with a certain role": 欠かせない存在, 大きな存在, 母のような存在. Other combinations: 存在を知る, 存在感 ("presence"), 存在意義 ("reason for being").

examples[].german: The final decision will be made next week.
The host city of the next Olympics has been decided.
We decided on a new policy at the meeting.
en.notes: 決定 is a (often official) decision or resolution, typical for organizations, committees and the news: 決定を下す ("to make a decision"), 正式に決定する, 決定事項. As a する-verb it is both transitive and intransitive: 方針を決定する / 開催地が決定した. For personal everyday decisions, people more often say 決める/決まる; 決心 is a person's inner resolve.

examples[].german: She made many sacrifices for her family.
I don't want to sacrifice time with my family for work.
Many people fell victim in that accident.
en.notes: 犠牲 is the sacrifice that one makes or that is demanded. Typical: 犠牲を払う ("to make sacrifices"), 〜を犠牲にする ("to sacrifice something"), 〜の犠牲になる ("to fall victim to something", often "to lose one's life"). People who die in accidents or disasters are called 犠牲者. The victim of a crime or damage who survives, by contrast, is 被害者.

examples[].german: Success can sometimes come at a high price.
Now I am paying the price for overdoing it when I was young.
In exchange for convenience, we hand over a great deal of personal information.
en.notes: 代償 is the "price" one pays for something, today mostly in a figurative sense: a sacrifice or disadvantage one must accept for a goal or because of a mistake. Typical: 代償を払う "to pay the price", 大きな代償 and 〜の代償として "as the price for ...". In its original meaning "compensation in kind" it is rare; for financial compensation, 補償 or 賠償 is used today. It is rather literary and common in news and commentary.

examples[].german: Appropriate compensation was paid to the victims.
The shop that closed because of construction work received compensation for lost sales.
This insurance also covers damage to luggage stolen during a trip.
en.notes: 補償 is compensation for damage or loss suffered, even when no one acted unlawfully, for example in cases of expropriation, construction work, or through insurance. Typical: 補償金, 損失を補償する, 補償を求める, 補償が出る. Read the same but different: 保証 "guarantee, surety" and 保障 "protection, security" (社会保障). For liability for fault, 賠償 is more often used.

examples[].german: The court ordered payment of compensation.
The company that caused the accident must compensate the residents for the damage.
I broke the camera I had borrowed and was asked to pay for the repairs.
en.notes: 賠償 is compensation that someone must pay because they are responsible for damage - mostly in a legal context. Set combinations: 損害賠償 "damages", 損害賠償を請求する "to claim damages", 賠償金, 賠償責任 "liability"; historically also 戦争賠償 "war reparations". Unlike 補償, 賠償 stresses the fault of the payer. As a する-verb it is transitive: 損害を賠償する.

examples[].german: The advantage of this method is that it is simple.
This car has the advantage of good fuel economy.
Living in a city has both advantages and disadvantages.
en.notes: 利点 is an "advantage" of a thing, method or situation, factual and neutral. Typical: 〜の利点は…ことだ, 〜という利点がある, 利点を生かす. For a person's strengths one rather says 長所 or 強み; colloquially 利点 is often replaced by メリット. Antonyms are 欠点, 難点 or デメリット.

examples[].german: This plan has several drawbacks.
His fault is that he isn't punctual.
There's no such thing as a person without flaws.
en.notes: 欠点 is a "weakness" or "shortcoming" - of people as well as of things, plans or products. Typical: 欠点がある, 欠点を直す, 欠点を補う, 欠点のない人はいない. 短所 is used almost only for character traits and usually appears in the pair 長所と短所; 欠陥, by contrast, is a (technical) defect, as in 欠陥商品. Rarely, 欠点 also means a failing grade in an exam.

examples[].german: I emphasized my strengths in the interview.
Everyone has strengths and weaknesses.
The merit of this camera is that it is light and easy to carry.
en.notes: 長所 is a "strength" or "merit", above all in a person's character; the opposite is 短所, often as the pair 長所と短所. A classic question in job interviews: あなたの長所は何ですか. Also typical are 長所を生かす and 長所を伸ばす. For things, 長所 is possible, but for methods or situations 利点 or メリット fits better; 強み stresses a competitive advantage.

examples[].german: I am working hard to overcome my weaknesses.
In the interview I was asked, "What is your weakness?"
Even a weakness can become a strength if you look at it differently.
en.notes: 短所 is a "weakness" in character or behavior, the opposite of 長所. It often appears in the pair 長所と短所 and is a typical job-interview question. Typical: 短所を直す, 短所を克服する, 短所を補う. For defects in things or plans, 欠点 is more usual; colloquially one also says 弱点 or ダメなところ.

examples[].german: Values differ from person to person.
I broke up with him because of differing values.
You shouldn't impose your own values on others.
en.notes: 価値観 are one's personal "values", i.e. what a person considers important in life. Very common in relationships: 価値観が合う／合わない, 価値観の違い (a classic reason for breaking up), 価値観を押し付ける ("to impose one's values"). In contrast to 価値 (the "value" of a thing), the focus here is a person's outlook. Neutral and very common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: The product was made by taking advantage of the properties of this material.
This metal has the property of being resistant to heat.
It is important to teach in a way that suits each child's individual characteristics.
en.notes: 特性 is a "characteristic property" that something has by nature, often of materials and technology, but also of people (for example, learning dispositions of children). Typical: 〜の特性を生かす, 〜という特性がある, 特性に合わせる. 特徴 is instead a conspicuous, distinguishing feature, and 性質 is general nature or constitution. Somewhat technical, less common in everyday conversation.

examples[].german: The properties of water change with temperature.
He is of a gentle nature and rarely gets angry.
Because of the nature of the problem, I cannot answer you right away.
en.notes: 性質 has two meanings: the nature of a thing (chemical properties, the nature of a problem) and the innate character of a person or animal. For a person's character, 性格 is more usual in everyday speech; 性質 sounds somewhat more fundamental here ("by nature"). Typical: 〜という性質がある, 性質が変わる, 問題の性質上 "because of the nature of the problem".

examples[].german: There is a big difference between the ideal and reality.
Her standards are so high that she just can't find anyone to marry.
He founded a company to realize his ideals.
en.notes: 理想 is the "ideal", often in contrast to 現実 "reality": 理想と現実. Typical: 理想の〜 "dream ..., ideal ..." (理想の家, 理想の相手), 理想が高い "to have high standards", 理想を実現する. The adjective is 理想的(な) "ideal". 夢 is more personal and emotional, whereas 理想 is more a standard of how something should be.

examples[].german: He still harbors illusions.
The idea that effort will always be rewarded may be an illusion.
The snow-covered town had a fantastical atmosphere.
en.notes: 幻想 is an "illusion", a beautiful but unrealistic notion. Typical: 〜に幻想を抱く "to have illusions about ...", 幻想が崩れる / 幻想を捨てる. The adjective 幻想的(な), on the other hand, is positive and means "fairy-tale-like, dreamlike" (幻想的な景色). By contrast, 空想 is harmless daydreaming and 妄想 is a delusion.

examples[].german: I like to immerse myself in a world of fantasy.
As a child, I often imagined myself flying through the sky.
Dragons are imaginary creatures.
en.notes: 空想 is a harmless "daydream", a fantasy about something that does not (yet) exist. As a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を空想する. Typical: 空想の世界, 空想にふける, 空想上の動物; 空想科学 used to be a word for science fiction. 想像 is more neutral and general, "to imagine"; 妄想 has a pathological or ridiculous connotation.

examples[].german: That is nothing but his delusion.
Because of his illness, he suffers from the delusion that someone is watching him.
I can't help fantasizing about what I would do if I won the lottery.
en.notes: 妄想 is a "delusion" or "figment of the imagination" that has nothing to do with reality. In medicine, for example, 被害妄想 "persecution delusion". Colloquially, especially among young people, 妄想(する) also refers self-ironically to uninhibitedly picturing wish scenarios. Distinction: 空想 is harmless daydreaming, 幻想 is a beautiful illusion. Typical: 〜にすぎない, 妄想にとらわれる.

examples[].german: It was a more difficult problem than I had imagined.
Please try to imagine yourself ten years from now.
I never imagined that he would become a teacher.
en.notes: 想像 is the general word for "imagination" and "to imagine something"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を想像する. Common: 想像以上 "more than expected," 想像通り, 想像がつく / 想像もつかない "can / cannot imagine," 想像力 "imagination." Not to be confused with the identically read 創造 "creation."

examples[].german: Art is born from the power of creation.
Many people believe that God created the world.
Our company aims at the creation of new value.
en.notes: 創造 is the "creating" of something completely new, also creation by God; as a する-verb it is transitive. It sounds elevated and often appears in art, religion and corporate mission statements: 創造力, 創造性, 創造的(な), 新しい価値の創造. In everyday speech people simply say 作る, and for artistic works 創作. The opposite is 破壊; beware of the homophone 想像 "imagination".

examples[].german: This novel took its inspiration from a true story.
The idea is interesting, but it seems difficult to realize.
The design of this chair is said to be inspired by bird feathers.
en.notes: 着想 is the original idea or basic thought from which a work, invention or plan arises. It is almost always found in the phrase 〜から／〜に着想を得る "to draw inspiration from ..." or as a subject: 着想が面白い / 着想がユニークだ. Rather literary; in everyday speech people say アイデア or 思いつき. 発想, by contrast, refers more to the way of thinking, how one comes up with ideas.

examples[].german: I am working out the concept for a new project.
A concept for urban development centered on the new station was announced.
From the initial concept to completion, this novel took five years.
en.notes: 構想 is an overall concept or design for a larger undertaking - a novel, an urban project, a political vision - before it is planned concretely. Typical: 構想を練る "to work out a concept", 構想を発表する, 構想段階 "conceptual stage", often as a suffix: 〜構想. 計画 is the more concrete plan with schedule and dates; 着想 is only the first idea.

examples[].german: I went to see a movie with my boyfriend/girlfriend.
In Japan, many people spend Christmas with their partner.
When I have a girlfriend/boyfriend, I want to go on a trip together.
en.notes: 恋人 is the neutral umbrella term for "partner in a romantic relationship" and applies to men and women alike. In conversation one usually says 彼氏 or 彼女; 恋人 sounds somewhat more written or romantic, but is often used in surveys and songs, for example. Typical: 恋人ができる, 恋人がいる, 恋人同士. It is not used for spouses.

examples[].german: Contrary to the forecast, it started to rain in the afternoon.
The exam result was better than expected.
Let's try guessing which team will win the championship.
en.notes: 予想 is the expectation or prediction of how something will turn out; as a する-verb it is transitive: 結果を予想する. Typical: 予想が当たる / 外れる, 予想通り, 予想以上, 予想外, 予想に反して "contrary to expectations". 予測 is more objective and data-based (経済予測), 予報 is specifically the weather forecast, and 予期 is more "to anticipate something" (予期せぬ出来事).

examples[].german: Japan faces the Pacific Ocean.
Tomorrow it will be sunny, mainly on the Pacific side.
My grandfather belongs to the generation that lived through the Pacific War.
en.notes: 太平洋 is the Pacific Ocean; literally something like "great peaceful ocean". Note: it is written with 太, not 大 as in 大西洋. Very common in Japan is the distinction between 太平洋側 (Pacific side) and 日本海側 (Sea of Japan side), above all in weather reports. Other combinations: 太平洋沿岸, 太平洋戦争 "Pacific War".

examples[].german: A sea voyage across the Atlantic is magnificent.
The Atlantic lies between Europe and the Americas.
Hurricanes form mainly over the Atlantic.
en.notes: 大西洋 is the Atlantic Ocean; literally "great western ocean" (西洋 = "the West, the Occident"). Unlike 太平洋, here it is written with 大, not 太, a common mix-up. Typical: 大西洋を横断する, 北大西洋, 大西洋岸. The other oceans are called 太平洋 and インド洋.

examples[].german: The ice of the Arctic is melting because of global warming.
If you find the North Star, you can tell which way is north.
Humans first reached the North Pole in the early twentieth century.
en.notes: 北極 refers both to the North Pole and to the Arctic as a region. For the exact point, one says 北極点; for the area also 北極圏 "Arctic Circle region", and for the sea 北極海. Other words: 北極星 "North Star" and ホッキョクグマ "polar bear" (usually in katakana). The counterpart is 南極.

examples[].german: Penguins live in Antarctica.
Most of the Antarctic continent is covered with thick ice.
A Japanese research team continues its research in Antarctica every year.
en.notes: 南極 refers to the South Pole and to Antarctica as a whole. More precise are 南極点 "South Pole (point)", 南極大陸 "Antarctic continent" and 南極海. Well known in Japan are the 南極観測隊 "Antarctic expeditions" and the station 昭和基地. The counterpart is 北極.

examples[].german: It is hot all year round near the equator.
The name of the country Ecuador means "equator".
When the ship crossed the equator, all the passengers celebrated together.
en.notes: 赤道 is the equator, literally "red road". Typical: 赤道付近 "near the equator", 赤道直下 "right on the equator", 赤道を越える. It divides the Earth into 北半球 and 南半球. In astronomy there is also the celestial equator (天の赤道).

examples[].german: Tokyo's latitude is about 35 degrees north.
The higher the latitude, the shorter the days in winter.
Hakodate and Rome lie at almost the same latitude.
en.notes: 緯度 is geographic latitude. It is given with 北緯 "north latitude" or 南緯 "south latitude"; the lines are called 緯線. Typical: 緯度が高い / 低い "high/low latitude", 同じ緯度にある. The counterpart is 経度 "longitude"; together one speaks of 緯度と経度 or 経緯度.

examples[].german: With longitude and latitude, you can pinpoint an exact position.
A difference of fifteen degrees of longitude makes a one-hour time difference.
Japan's standard time is based on the longitude of 135 degrees east.
en.notes: 経度 is geographic longitude. It is given as 東経 "east longitude" and 西経 "west longitude", measured from the prime meridian at Greenwich; the lines are called 経線. Japan's standard time is based on 東経135度 (Akashi). The counterpart is 緯度 "latitude".

examples[].german: The elevation of this mountain exceeds three thousand meters.
The higher the elevation, the lower the temperature.
This village is on a plateau at an elevation of 1,000 meters, so it is cool even in summer.
en.notes: 標高 is the height of a place above sea level, above all for mountains, passes and plateaus: 標高〇〇メートル, 標高が高い / 低い. 海抜 refers to the same measurement but is used more for low-lying land, coastal places and tsunami signs. 高度 is flight altitude or height in general, and 高さ is the height of an object itself.

examples[].german: This town is located at an elevation of five hundred meters.
A utility pole near the coast has a sign reading "3 m above sea level".
In the Netherlands, there is a lot of land at or below sea level.
en.notes: 海抜 is the "height above sea level", literally "rising above the sea". Its content is the same as 標高, but it is used especially for coasts and low-lying land - in Japan, signs such as 海抜3m stand along roads as tsunami warnings. Typical: 海抜〇〇メートル, 海抜ゼロメートル地帯 "area at or below sea level". For mountain peaks, 標高 is more usual.

examples[].german: Tokyo has a very high population density.
Hokkaido has a low population density, and rich nature remains.
In areas with a high population density, housing prices also tend to be high.
