en.meaning: to bury (one's face); to cover; to sink; to fill (densely) (会場を埋める)
examples[].german: The child buried his face in his mother's chest and began to cry.
Ten thousand spectators filled the concert venue.
He moved to this town resolved to spend the rest of his life here.
en.notes: A separate entry next to 埋める/うめる: うめる is the everyday word for "to bury, fill in", while うずめる sounds more expressive and appears mainly in 顔をうずめる, 骨をうずめる "to remain in one place for life" and 群衆が広場をうずめる. Because of the double reading, it is often written in kana. The intransitive counterpart is 埋まる/うずまる.

examples[].german: In Japanese companies, team harmony is valued.
The sum of three and five is eight.
en.notes: Peaceful togetherness (和を大切にする), in mathematics the sum (二つの数の和) and as a prefix "Japanese" (和食, 和室).

examples[].german: I looked up in a Japanese-English dictionary how to say 約束 in English.
This Japanese-English dictionary has many example sentences and is easy to use.
en.notes: Mostly for dictionaries: 和英辞典 (Japanese-English dictionary). Opposite: 英和.

en.meaning: to divide; to branch; to split
examples[].german: The road splits in two up ahead.
Experts' opinions are divided on that issue.
en.notes: Intransitive: 道が二つに分かれる, 意見が分かれる (opinions are divided). Do not confuse with 別れる (to part from someone).

examples[].german: I put miso soup into the bowl.
This bowl was precious to my grandmother.
en.notes: Lacquered wooden bowl for soup (お椀). Porcelain bowls are written 碗 (茶碗). Also a counter: 一椀.

en.meaning: ratio; rate; ten percent (1割 = 10%); allotment; (suffix) discount, diluted with
examples[].german: Everything is 20 percent off today.
About 80 percent of employees want to work from home.
Working this much for this salary isn't worth it.
en.notes: 割 denotes a ratio and above all tenths: 1割 = 10%, 3割 = 30%; this is how proportions (8割の人) and discounts (2割引き) are often expressed in Japan. The same word is in phrases like 割に合わない "not worth it" and 〜の割に "considering that ...". As a suffix on drinks, 〜割り means "diluted with" (水割り, お湯割り). The general word for "proportion, ratio" is 割合 (separate card).

examples[].german: The exam was comparatively easier than I expected.
It's fairly warm today.
en.notes: "Compared with what one expects": 割合に簡単だった. Similar: 割と, 比較的.

examples[].german: The child tore a page of the book.
I tore open the envelope and took out the letter.
en.notes: Transitive godan verb, more colloquial than 破る: 紙を破く.

examples[].german: I boiled water in the kettle and made tea.
The kettle whistled.
en.notes: A kettle for boiling water; mostly in kana, kanji 薬缶. やかんでお湯を沸かす.

examples[].german: This road is closed to traffic at night.
For night-time reception, please use the back entrance.
en.notes: Formal word for the night time, often on signs: 夜間工事 (night construction), 夜間の外出. Homophone: やかん (kettle).

examples[].german: I went from Tokyo to Osaka by night bus.
In the past, many people traveled by night train.
en.notes: Travel at night, especially 夜行バス (night bus) and 夜行列車. Also 夜行性 (nocturnal).

examples[].german: Chemicals used in the experiment must be returned to their designated place.
This factory produces medicines.
en.notes: Formal word for drugs and chemical substances: 医薬品, 化学薬品. In everyday speech one says 薬.

examples[].german: He is famous as a kabuki actor.
In this film, the actors' performances are wonderful.
en.notes: Especially for theater and kabuki; more general: 俳優. Idiom: 役者が一枚上 (to be a cut above someone).

examples[].german: I paid the rent to the landlord.
Before making a hole in the wall, I got the landlord's permission.
en.notes: The owner of a rental apartment or house; similar: 大家（おおや）. The reading いえぬし is rarer.

examples[].german: You must not trust strangers indiscriminately.
Lately I've been sleepy all the time.
en.notes: Adverb from やたら + に, also やたらと: やたらに物を買う. Critical, judgmental tone. The kanji 矢鱈 (ateji) is rare.

examples[].german: He's really a good guy.
Do you have these shoes in a slightly bigger size?
en.notes: Colloquial and often derogatory for a person (あいつは嫌な奴だ), but also for things: もっと安いやつ (a cheaper one). Usually written in kana.

en.meaning: to beat, to defeat; to get (something) done quickly
examples[].german: The hero defeated the villains.
Let's knock out the rest of the homework in an hour.
en.notes: Colloquial: to defeat an opponent (敵をやっつける) or to get a job done in haste (仕事をやっつける).

examples[].german: After class, I was called to the staff room by the teacher.
I had the person in charge paged at the reception desk.
en.notes: To call someone to oneself: 先生に呼び出される (to be summoned by the teacher); in IT also to call functions.

en.meaning: to call out to; to appeal to
examples[].german: A stranger called out to me from behind.
The city urged residents to use water sparingly.
en.notes: To call out to someone or to appeal to people to do something: 市民に節電を呼びかける. Noun: 呼びかけ (appeal).

en.meaning: to send (to me); to hand over (to me)
examples[].german: My son finally sent a letter.
Hand that pen over here.
en.notes: Colloquial: to send or give something toward the speaker (手紙をよこす). Kanji 寄越す.

examples[].german: I applied in February and attended classes from the following month.
It snowed last night, and by the following morning the garden had turned white.
en.notes: 翌（よく）combines with time expressions such as 月 or 朝 and denotes the next period after a stated point in time. 翌月 is therefore the month after the one mentioned, not automatically next month counted from today. In a narrative, 翌朝 refers to the morning after the evening described. The identically read よく meaning "often" or "well" is a different word. The accent of the whole compound cannot be derived from the prefix alone.

examples[].german: Wanting everything - how greedy you are!
Greedy people can never be satisfied.
en.notes: Someone who always wants more; also as a na-adjective: 欲張りな人. Verb: 欲張る.

examples[].german: Please turn right at the next intersection.
There is a bakery at the intersection.
en.notes: A place where two roads cross; similar: 交差点.

examples[].german: Plants absorb nutrients through their roots.
This soil is low in nutrients.
en.notes: Substances that living things, especially plants, need to grow: 土から養分を吸収する. Similar: 栄養.

examples[].german: This book has many difficult terms and is hard to read.
In the meeting, please use terms that everyone can understand.
en.notes: Words of a specialist field: 専門用語 (technical term), 医学用語.

examples[].german: I bought a tie at a clothing store in the shopping street.
My grandmother used to run a clothing store.
en.notes: A shop for Western-style clothing and accessories; somewhat old-fashioned, today more usually ブティック or 洋服店.

examples[].german: This refrigerator has a large capacity.
Please calculate the volume of the box.
en.notes: The capacity of a container or room: 容積を計算する. Similar: 体積 (volume of a solid body).

examples[].german: I boiled the eggs for eight minutes.
While the pasta boils, I make the sauce.
en.notes: To cook food in boiling water: 卵をゆでる, パスタをゆでる. Kanji 茹でる.

examples[].german: After the accident, the dog's whereabouts became unknown.
Attention is focused on how the election will turn out.
en.notes: Where someone or something has gone (行方がわからない) or how something develops (試合の行方). Special reading ゆくえ.

examples[].german: The sun setting into the sea was very beautiful.
Lit by the evening sun, the town was dyed red.
en.notes: The sun in the evening: 夕日が沈む (the sun sets). Opposite: 朝日.

examples[].german: I studied abroad for a year while I was a student.
Currently, ten thousand students are enrolled at this university.
en.notes: To be enrolled at a school or university: 在学中 (while enrolled), 在学証明書 (certificate of enrollment).

examples[].german: Please show your residence card at the ward office.
You must always carry your residence card.
en.notes: An ID card for foreigners living in Japan with a medium- to long-term visa; it must be carried at all times.

examples[].german: I really want to make this job a success.
Please be sure to take part next time.
en.notes: Emphatic form of ぜひ for requests and wishes made with force; also written 是非とも.

examples[].german: The former company president handed the documents over to the new president.
I compared the sales of the previous fiscal year with those of the current fiscal year.
en.notes: 前（ぜん）stands here before a job title or a time period. 前社長 denotes the previous or former company president, 前年度 the previous fiscal year. The prefix is attached directly to the following noun. For the spatial meaning "in front" one uses its own reading まえ.

en.meaning: front and back; before and after; about, around
examples[].german: Bicycles are parked in front of and behind the bus.
There look to be around twenty participants.
en.notes: Spatial (バスの前後), temporal (食事の前後) and, after numbers, approximate: 三十歳前後 (around thirty years old).

en.meaning: to know, to be acquainted with (humble); to think (humble)
examples[].german: We humbly hope to receive everyone's continued cooperation in the future.
In response to the reporters' questions, he stubbornly stuck to claiming he knew nothing.
en.notes: The literary ずる-form of the humble verb 存じる (separate card, N3): "to know" or "to think, to be of the opinion" from the speaker's standpoint. Today almost only in very formal letters and speeches (〜と存ずる次第です) and in the fixed phrase 知らぬ存ぜぬ "to feign ignorance", which contains the old negative 存ぜぬ. In normal polite Japanese, 存じます and 存じません are used.

examples[].german: The rise in medical costs has become a problem.
Demand rose, and goods ran short.
en.notes: Formal; as a verb 増大する: 費用が増大する. Opposite: 減少.

examples[].german: The number of customers fluctuates with the season.
I showed the changes in population in a graph.
en.notes: As a verb 増減する: to increase and decrease, to fluctuate.

examples[].german: This town is known for its shipbuilding.
My older brother works for a shipbuilding company.
en.notes: 造船所 (shipyard), 造船業 (shipbuilding industry).

examples[].german: I summarized the results in charts and tables.
Looking at this chart, you can see that the population is decreasing.
en.notes: Collective term for graphics and tables in reports: 図表を使って説明する.

examples[].german: I looked up the bird's name in the field guide.
My son looks at his dinosaur book every day.
en.notes: A book with many illustrations on one subject: 植物図鑑, 動物図鑑 - very popular with children in Japan.

examples[].german: I will be transferred to the Osaka branch effective April 1.
I have duly received your letter dated October 5.
Department head Tanaka retired as of today.
en.notes: 〜付け (づけ) follows a date and means "dated" or "effective from": 4月1日付けで異動, 10日付けの手紙, 本日付けで退職. Typical of official, business and newspaper language; often written only as 付 without okurigana. Not to be confused with 日付 (ひづけ, vocab-n3:3291) "date" and 〜漬け (づけ, vocab-n2:1532) "pickled in".

examples[].german: We calculated the area of figures such as triangles and circles.
If you fold this figure in half, the two halves overlap exactly.
en.notes: In mathematics: triangles, circles, etc. 図形の問題 = geometry problem.

examples[].german: This seat has already been reserved.
The membership fee has already been paid.
en.notes: Suffix for things that are completed: 支払い済み (paid), 予約済み (reserved), 確認済み (checked).

examples[].german: He is called the brains of the team.
This job requires a sharp mind.
en.notes: Often figurative: 頭脳明晰 (sharp-minded), チームの頭脳 (the brains of the team). The organ itself is usually called 脳.

en.meaning: hard to do (physically or emotionally; suffix)
examples[].german: The writing is faint, so this letter is hard to read.
Since this person has just helped me, it is hard to turn them down.
en.notes: づらい is attached to the stem before ます: 読みます → 読みづらい. It describes that an action is physically difficult or causes inner resistance. It is usually written in kana and conjugated like an i-adjective: 読みづらかった, 読みづらくない. In this meaning it is used with a verb stem, not as a free づらいな before a noun. 辛い／からい "spicy" and 辛い／つらい "painful, trying" are other readings.

examples[].german: Customers were lined up in a long row in front of the shop.
Old books are lined up in long rows on the shelf.
en.notes: Many things or people standing in an impressive line: ずらりと並ぶ. Also written ズラリ.

examples[].german: Please check the conditions.
I chose this room on the condition that the rent is cheap.
The pay is good, but the working conditions are too harsh.
en.notes: 条件 is a condition or prerequisite that must be met: 条件を満たす "to meet the conditions", 条件をつける "to set conditions". With 〜を条件に it means "on the condition that ...". Common compounds are 労働条件 "working conditions" and 応募条件 "application requirements". Do not confuse it with 状況, the overall situation.

examples[].german: The situation has changed.
The arrival time changes depending on road conditions.
Please explain in detail what the situation is now.
en.notes: 状況 refers to the overall situation, that is, how things currently stand around you: 状況が変わる, 状況を説明する, 状況を把握する "to grasp the situation". 状態, by contrast, is the condition of an individual person or thing (体の状態, 機械の状態). Common combinations are 現在の状況, 交通状況 and 〜な状況で "in a ... situation". The word is neutral and very common in the news as well as in the office.

examples[].german: Let's value the basics.
Using this sauce as a base, you can change it to your preferred taste.
At our company, there is basically no overtime.
en.notes: 基本 means the basics or fundamentals of something: 基本を学ぶ / 身につける "to learn the basics", 基本に戻る "to return to the basics". With 〜を基本にする it means "to take something as a basis". Very common is the adverb 基本的に "basically, in principle", which in conversation often leaves room for exceptions. 基礎 is similar but emphasizes the foundation on which one builds (基礎知識).

examples[].german: I analyze the data.
My computer broke and all the data disappeared.
Could you send me the photo data by email?
en.notes: データ (from English) means data and, in everyday use, also digital files: データを集める/分析する/保存する, データが消える, 写真のデータ. With mobile phones, データ often means the data volume (データ通信, データ量). As usual in Japanese, no plural is marked; singular and plural follow from the context.

examples[].german: It is a forceful way of doing things.
He tried to push the matter through by force.
A friend pushed me into going, so I went to karaoke.
en.notes: 強引 describes an approach that overrides others and pushes something through "by force": "pushy, overbearing" - not physical violence (that would be 暴力的). The adverb 強引に is very common: 強引に誘う, 強引に話を進める, 強引に決める. Also 強引なセールス ("pushy selling"). 無理やり is similar and more colloquial; 横暴 is stronger and means abuse of power.

examples[].german: It is a tyrannical attitude.
Because of a tyrannical boss, his subordinates quit one after another.
Many citizens opposed the government's high-handed decision.
en.notes: 横暴 refers to "tyrannical, arbitrary" behavior by someone who abuses their power: 横暴な上司, 横暴な態度, 権力の横暴. It is a noun and a na-adjective (横暴を許さない, 横暴に振る舞う). It is stronger than 強引 "pushy, forceful" and stresses abuse of power; 乱暴 refers more to rough, violent actions or language.

examples[].german: Let's stop the arrogant attitude.
After becoming successful, he became a bit arrogant.
It is arrogant to think that only you are right.
en.notes: 傲慢 ("arrogant, haughty") describes someone who considers themselves superior and treats others condescendingly: 傲慢な態度, 傲慢な人, 傲慢になる. It is a strong word close to the written language. In everyday speech people say 偉そう "acting important" instead; 生意気 "cheeky, impertinent" is used mainly for younger people or subordinates. The opposite is 謙虚 "modest".

examples[].german: A humble attitude is important.
He has remained humble even after becoming famous.
I try to listen to my seniors' opinions humbly.
en.notes: 謙虚 ("humble, modest") is a valued virtue: you do not put yourself in the foreground and you accept criticism openly. Typical: 謙虚な姿勢 / 態度, 謙虚に受け止める, 謙虚に学ぶ, 謙虚さを忘れない. 控えめ means more "reserved, understated", 遠慮 is holding back in a specific situation. The opposite is 傲慢.

examples[].german: He is a sincere person.
When handling customer complaints, it's important to respond sincerely.
Everyone puts their trust in his sincere character.
en.notes: 誠実 ("sincere, honest, faithful") describes people and actions that deal with others honestly and conscientiously: 誠実な人, 誠実な対応, 誠実に対応する, 誠実さ. 正直 only means "not lying", 真面目 "serious, dutiful"; 誠実 stresses sincerity toward others. The word is very popular in business language and in choosing a partner.

examples[].german: He is a diligent student.
Japanese people are often said to be diligent.
My grandfather worked diligently all his life and supported the family.
en.notes: 勤勉 ("diligent, hardworking") describes steady diligence in work or study and sounds rather formal and literary: 勤勉な学生, 勤勉に働く, 勤勉さ. Common in statements about national character (日本人は勤勉だ). In everyday speech one mostly says 真面目 or よく頑張る. The opposite is 怠惰 "lazy", colloquially 怠け者.

examples[].german: I live an idle life.
I spent the summer vacation idly.
His failure was caused not by lack of ability but by laziness.
en.notes: 怠惰 is a na-adjective and noun meaning "sluggish, lazy, idle" and sounds rather written or elevated: 怠惰な生活, 怠惰な性格, adverbially 怠惰に過ごす. In everyday speech people mostly use the verb 怠ける "to slack off", 怠け者 "lazybones" or だらしない. As a noun, 怠惰 names laziness itself, for example as a cause: 怠惰が原因だ.

examples[].german: I learn eagerly.
That player is hungry for victory.
I don't want to associate with people who are greedy for money.
en.notes: 貪欲 means "greedy", but today it is very often used positively for "hungry, eager, ambitious": 貪欲に学ぶ "to learn avidly", 勝利に貪欲だ "to be hungry for victory". The object of the greed is marked with に: 金に貪欲な人. It is morally negative only when it concerns money or possessions; colloquially 欲張り is also used for that. The word sounds somewhat elevated.

examples[].german: She has a pure heart like a child.
I don't care about winning or losing; I just want to enjoy soccer.
Pure water hardly conducts electricity.
en.notes: 純粋 has two main meanings: "pure, unmixed" for substances (純粋な水, 純粋な金) and "sincere, unspoiled" for people and feelings (純粋な心, 純粋な人), sometimes with an undertone of "naive". Adverbially, 純粋に means "simply, purely out of": 純粋に楽しみたい. For hygienically "clean", use 清潔 or きれい, not 純粋.

examples[].german: Seeing the children's innocent smiles lifts my spirits.
A puppy is playing innocently in the park.
He naively blurts out other people's secrets.
en.notes: 無邪気 (literally "without malice") describes above all children or childlike behavior: carefree, guileless, without ulterior motives, e.g. 無邪気な笑顔, 無邪気に遊ぶ. For adults it can also mean critically "thoughtless, naive": 無邪気に秘密を話す. 純粋 stresses inner purity more, 素直 openness and obedience.

examples[].german: Accurate information is necessary.
I looked up travel information on the Internet.
Please be careful in handling personal information.
en.notes: 情報 is "information" as an uncountable noun: 情報を集める/得る/調べる, 情報が入る, 最新情報, 個人情報 "personal data", 情報交換. For a concrete notice or announcement, お知らせ is rather said, and for news on TV ニュース. As a school subject, 情報 means "computer science".

examples[].german: The gloomy weather continues, and it even brings my mood down.
I don't want to live in a dismal basement room.
Don't make such a glum face; cheer up.
en.notes: 陰気 means "gloomy, dismal, oppressive" and describes people, faces, rooms or moods: 陰気な人, 陰気な部屋, 陰気な顔. The opposite is 陽気. In everyday speech, for people one more often simply says 暗い (暗い人); 陰気 sounds stronger and more negative. With weather it is possible (陰気な天気), but one mostly says どんよりした天気.

examples[].german: You are a cheerful person.
Cheerful music was playing at the party.
Today the weather feels like spring.
en.notes: 陽気 as a na-adjective means "cheerful, merry, lively": 陽気な人, 陽気な音楽, 陽気に歌う. The opposite is 陰気. As a noun it also means "weather, climate of a season", especially in phrases such as 春の陽気, 春らしい陽気 or いい陽気ですね. For people, 明るい is the more everyday, neutral word.

examples[].german: She speaks very elegantly.
This sweet is not too sugary and has a refined taste.
I went to the party in an elegant dress.
en.notes: 上品 means "refined, cultured, elegant" and refers to behavior, speech, clothing and also taste: 上品な話し方, 上品な人, 上品な味 ("delicate, subtle in taste"). The opposite is 下品. Unlike おしゃれ ("stylish, chic"), 上品 emphasizes restraint and good manners. Adverbial: 上品に食べる, 上品に笑う.

examples[].german: Let's stop the vulgar jokes.
I wish people would not use vulgar language on the train.
Flashy clothes that are covered in gold look a little tacky.
en.notes: 下品 means "vulgar, coarse, tasteless" and is used for speech, jokes, behavior and flashy clothing: 下品な冗談, 下品な言葉, 下品に笑う. The opposite is 上品. It is a clear, disparaging judgment about a lack of decency; for mere impoliteness one rather says 失礼. Also often used as an exclamation in speech: 下品だなあ.

en.meaning: refinement; polish; (洗練された) sophisticated, elegant
examples[].german: The furniture in this shop is popular for its sophisticated design.
Her clothes are always sophisticated.
I rewrote the text many times and polished it.
en.notes: 洗練 is actually a noun ("refinement, polish") and not a na-adjective: *洗練な is wrong. As an adjective, the passive form 洗練された or 洗練されている is used almost always: 洗練されたデザイン, 洗練された人. In the active you say 文章を洗練する or, more often, 洗練させる "to give a text the finishing touch". Related: 上品 "refined in manners", おしゃれ "fashionable".

examples[].german: That is a stylish kimono.
Thanks to the manager's tasteful gesture, a cake was brought out on my birthday.
My grandfather has always been a stylish man and always wore a hat.
en.notes: 粋 (いき) is an ideal of beauty from the Edo period: "chic, stylish" in a casual, unobtrusive way, e.g. 粋な着物, 粋な人. It can also mean "sensitive, considerate", especially in 粋な計らい "a nice, tactful gesture". The opposite is 野暮. Do not confuse it with the reading すい (粋 = "essence, the best", e.g. 技術の粋).

examples[].german: Asking such a thing is tactless.
I have an errand to run, so I'll go home a bit early today.
Disturbing the two when they are alone together would be really tactless.
en.notes: 野暮 is the opposite of 粋: "unrefined, tactless, uncool". Typical is 野暮なことを聞く/言う for questions or remarks that tact says to leave unsaid, often as a comment on oneself: 野暮なことは聞かないよ. Set expressions are 野暮用 ("a bothersome errand", used as a vague excuse) and 野暮ったい ("frumpy, dowdy" in appearance).

examples[].german: I feel the spirit of wabi.
In the tea ceremony, the spirit of wabi is cherished.
This old tea room has the beauty of wabi-sabi.
en.notes: 侘び is a concept of Japanese aesthetics: the quiet, plain, austere beauty that lies precisely in simplicity and imperfection. It is almost always heard in the pair 侘び寂び (often written わびさび) and in connection with the tea ceremony (茶道) and gardens. Not to be confused with お詫び ("apology"), which is read the same.

examples[].german: Wabi-sabi is a term expressing the Japanese sense of beauty.
The color of the old tea bowl has a patina created by long years.
In the old, moss-covered garden, I felt a quiet, aged beauty.
en.notes: 寂び (さび) denotes the beauty of age: patina, weathered surfaces and the quiet dignity of things that time has worked on. As a single word it is rare; it is met almost only in the pair 侘び寂び (わびさび). It is related to 寂しい ("lonely") and to 錆 ("rust"), which is read the same. JMdict lists the spelling 寂.

examples[].german: It is a town with charm.
Kyoto on a rainy day has its charm too, doesn't it?
With nothing but new buildings, this area has lost its charm.
en.notes: 風情 refers to the atmospheric, often traditional appeal of a place or scene. It almost always appears with ある/ない: 風情がある, 風情のある街, 風情がない. Unlike the neutral 雰囲気 "atmosphere", 風情 is always positive and aesthetic. As a suffix (〜風情) it means derogatorily "someone like ...", for example the humble 私風情; that is rather literary.

examples[].german: I will think about ways to achieve the goal.
In the countryside, cars are the main means of transportation.
If it is to win, he will stop at nothing.
en.notes: 手段 is the means by which one reaches a goal: 〜する手段, 交通手段 "means of transport", 連絡手段, 最後の手段 "last resort". The phrase 手段を選ばない means "to stop at nothing". Distinction: 方法 is the way or procedure of doing something; 手段 emphasizes the tool or route to an end.

examples[].german: It is a beautiful landscape.
I drew the scenery I could see from the window in a picture.
The morning station, full of hurrying people, is a familiar sight.
en.notes: 風景 means "landscape, scenery" but also covers everyday scenes in cities: 日常の風景, 朝の駅の風景. In art: 風景画 "landscape painting". 景色 is the more everyday word for a beautiful view in nature, 眺め stresses the view from a particular point, and 光景 is a scene or event that one observes.

examples[].german: It's a wonderful view, isn't it?
I reserved a room with a nice view.
A building went up next door, and the view got worse.
en.notes: 眺め is the noun of 眺める ("to look at, gaze into the distance") and means "view, outlook" from a certain location. Typical: 眺めがいい/悪い, 眺めのいい部屋, 山頂からの眺め. 景色 refers more to the scenery itself, while 眺め is the view you get from here.

examples[].german: This place is famous as a spot for spectacular autumn foliage views.
The breathtaking view from the summit left me speechless.
You can enjoy a spectacular view of the sea from the hotel's open-air bath.
en.notes: 絶景 (from 絶 "extremely" and 景 "view") is a breathtaking, exceptionally beautiful view. It is very common in travel magazines and advertising: 絶景スポット, 絶景を楽しむ, 〜からの絶景. As an exclamation before a view you simply say 絶景だ!. It is stronger than 景色 or 眺め and is used only for truly impressive sights.

examples[].german: It is a famous tourist destination.
During summer vacation, every tourist spot is crowded.
This village has recently become popular as a tourist destination.
en.notes: 観光地 is a place or area visited by tourists: 有名な観光地, 人気の観光地, 観光地として知られる. A single famous building or sight is more likely called 名所 or 観光スポット. Slightly derogatory is 観光地化する "to become overrun with tourism".

examples[].german: I bought souvenirs.
When I went to a friend's house, I brought a cake as a gift.
Please tell me stories from your trip.
en.notes: 土産 (special reading みやげ) is almost always used politely as お土産. It refers both to travel souvenirs bought for colleagues and family and to a gift for the host when visiting (then also 手土産). Typical: お土産を買う, 〜をお土産に持っていく. 土産話 are stories about the trip. An ordinary gift, by contrast, is プレゼント or 贈り物.

examples[].german: I stayed at a minshuku.
At a minshuku near the sea, I ate fresh fish dishes.
A minshuku is cheaper than a ryokan, but the toilet and bath are often shared.
en.notes: 民宿 is a family-run guesthouse, often in the countryside, by the sea or in ski areas. It is cheaper and simpler than a 旅館: bath and toilet are often shared, and the food often comes from the house's own kitchen or from the day's catch. One stays at one with 民宿に泊まる. ペンション, by contrast, is a pension in the Western style.

examples[].german: I am going on a day trip.
If it's Osaka, you can go and come back in a day by Shinkansen.
It was a one-day business trip, so I was very tired.
en.notes: 日帰り means "going and returning on the same day", that is, without an overnight stay. It often stands before nouns: 日帰り旅行, 日帰り温泉, 日帰り出張, or adverbially with で: 日帰りで行く. As an intransitive する-verb: 日帰りする, 日帰りできる. The counterpart is e.g. 一泊二日 ("two days, one night").

examples[].german: I will stay for two weeks.
How long do you plan to stay in Japan?
Please write the address of the hotel where you are staying.
en.notes: 滞在 is a "stay" in a place for a certain time, as an intransitive する-verb with に for the place: 日本に滞在する, ホテルに滞在する. Common compounds: 滞在期間, 滞在先 "accommodation during the stay", 長期滞在. 泊まる specifically means "to stay overnight" and 住む "to live permanently"; 滞在 lies in between and sounds somewhat more formal.

examples[].german: How much is the accommodation fee?
The meeting participants will stay at the hotel in front of the station.
Guests staying at our hotel get a free breakfast.
en.notes: 宿泊 is the formal word for "to stay overnight, accommodation" and is found mainly at hotels, travel agencies and on forms: ホテルに宿泊する, 宿泊施設, 宿泊客, 宿泊料/宿泊費. In conversation people mostly simply say 泊まる. In the polite language of hotels it is ご宿泊.

examples[].german: I will go through the boarding procedure.
Please show your boarding pass.
We will begin boarding shortly.
en.notes: 搭乗 is boarding an aircraft (more rarely a ship) and belongs to airport language: 搭乗券 "boarding pass", 搭乗口 "gate", 搭乗手続き "check-in", announcements such as ご搭乗の皆様. For trains, buses and cars you say 乗車, for ships also 乗船; in everyday speech simply 乗る.

examples[].german: We will introduce a new technique.
This director makes films with a very distinctive technique.
Recently there are more and more sales methods using the internet.
en.notes: 手法 is a method or technique, especially in work, research, art and business: 新しい手法, 研究手法, 販売手法, 独特な手法. It sounds more technical than the general 方法. 手段 is the means to an end, 技法 the craft-and-artistic technique. Typical verbs: 手法を使う/取り入れる/導入する.

examples[].german: I fill out the entry/exit card.
Passport control at the airport took a whole hour.
You can't complete the entry and exit procedures without a passport.
en.notes: 出入国 combines 出国 ("departure from a country") and 入国 ("entry into a country") and is an administrative word that occurs almost only in compounds: 出入国カード, 出入国審査 ("passport control"), 出入国管理. In conversation people usually speak of 出国 or 入国 separately, depending on what is meant.

examples[].german: The tour conductor will guide us.
The tour conductor warned me not to be late for the meeting time.
My older sister works as a tour conductor at a travel agency.
en.notes: 添乗員 accompanies a package or group tour (ツアー) from beginning to end and takes care of the schedule, hotels and organization. A ガイド (観光ガイド), by contrast, explains the sights on site. Colloquially you also hear ツアーコンダクター or, in short, ツアコン. The related verb is 添乗する "to accompany a trip".

en.meaning: to visit in a circuit; to go around
examples[].german: I visit shrines one after another.
Spring has come around again, and it is the cherry blossom season.
Residents are divided over the construction of the new station.
en.notes: 巡る is intransitive; を marks the route or the places visited: 名所を巡る, お寺を巡る ("to make a tour"). The noun 〜巡り (お寺巡り) fits with this. It also means "to come around again": 季節が巡る. The form 〜をめぐって ("concerning, centering on ...") is very common and is usually written in kana: 問題をめぐって議論する. 回る is the more everyday word for "to go around".

examples[].german: We trace history.
Map in hand, I followed the narrow path and finally reached the village.
Looking at old photos, I traced my childhood memories.
en.notes: 辿る is mostly written in kana (たどる) and is transitive: 道をたどる "to follow a path", 記憶をたどる "to trace back one's memory", 歴史をたどる. Figuratively it describes a development: 悪化の一途をたどる "to keep getting steadily worse". Related is たどり着く "to arrive after difficulty". 追う, by contrast, means "to chase, to pursue".

examples[].german: I wandered around the town.
I lost my way and wandered in the mountains all night.
After the accident, he hovered between life and death for three days.
en.notes: 彷徨う is almost always written in kana (さまよう) and means "to wander aimlessly". It is intransitive; を marks the area: 街をさまよう, 森の中をさまよう. Set phrase: 生死の境をさまよう "to hover between life and death". It sounds somewhat literary; in everyday speech people say うろうろする "to walk around" or 迷う "to get lost".

examples[].german: He is standing still on the lakeshore.
A small shrine stands quietly in the middle of the silent forest.
She stood alone in front of the station for a while.
en.notes: 佇む is a literary word for "to stand still, to linger (pensively)"; the place takes に: 湖畔に佇む, 駅の前に佇む. Mostly in the form 佇んでいる/佇んでいた. In travel writing it is also said of buildings: 森の中にひっそりと佇む神社. 立ち止まる, by contrast, is only "to stop (walking)", without the atmospheric note.

examples[].german: I am shivering from the cold.
I was nervous, and my voice trembled throughout the speech.
There was a noise so loud that the window glass shook.
en.notes: 震える ("to tremble, shake") is intransitive; the cause is expressed with で or in the て-form: 寒さで震える, 怖くて震える. Typical: 手が震える, 声が震える, 体が震える. The transitive counterpart is 震わせる (肩を震わせる). 揺れる, by contrast, means "to sway, wobble", for example in an earthquake or in a moving train.

en.meaning: to roar; to thunder; to resound
examples[].german: The thunder roared.
The sound of the airplane engines roared through the airport.
His name is known all over the world.
en.notes: 轟く describes a mighty, booming sound that can be heard far away: 雷が轟く, エンジン音が轟く. Figuratively it means "to be famous, to become widely known": 名が世界に轟く; the transitive counterpart is 名を轟かせる. The word is rather literary and dramatic. 響く is more neutral ("to resound, to echo"), 鳴る is simply "to sound".

en.meaning: to resound; to echo; to ring out
examples[].german: The sound of the temple bell echoed through the quiet night town.
The teacher's words struck a chord in my heart.
Staying up late affects your work the next day.
en.notes: 響く means "to echo, to resound, to ring out"; the space takes に: ホールに声が響く. Figuratively it means "to touch one's heart" (心に響く) and "to affect" (〜に響く): 睡眠不足が仕事に響く. The transitive counterpart is 響かせる. 鳴る means only "to sound" (bell, telephone), while 響く emphasizes the reverberation and the effect.

examples[].german: I will learn painting techniques.
This vessel is made with traditional techniques.
I am reading a book about techniques for writing novels.
en.notes: 技法 is a craft or artistic technique: 絵画の技法, 写真の技法, 伝統的な技法, 〜の技法を学ぶ. It is narrower than 手法 (a more general method, also in business and research) and more concrete than 技術 ("technique, technology, skill"). Rather written and technical.

examples[].german: He whispered in my ear.
In the library, my friend whispered, "Let's go home."
It is rumored that those two are going out.
en.notes: 囁く is often written in kana (ささやく) and means "to whisper", usually directed at someone: 耳元でささやく, 小声でささやく, 「…」とささやく. In the passive it means "to be rumored": 〜とささやかれている. The noun is ささやき. つぶやく, by contrast, is "to mutter to oneself", with no addressee.

examples[].german: He's muttering something.
"I'm tired," he muttered quietly.
I tweet about what happened that day on social media every day.
en.notes: 呟く (mostly written つぶやく) means "to murmur quietly to oneself", often with no listener: 独り言をつぶやく, 「…」とつぶやく. In contrast to ささやく "to whisper", one is not addressing anyone. Since Twitter, つぶやく also means "to post a message", and the noun つぶやき also "tweet". It can be used transitively (〜をつぶやく) or with と.

examples[].german: The dog is growling.
I was groaning all night with a stomachache.
This chef's cooking makes even gourmet customers marvel.
en.notes: 唸る describes deep, dull sounds: groaning with pain (痛みで唸る), growling of dogs (犬が唸る) and the hum of engines or wind. Figuratively it means "to marvel in admiration"; very common is the causative 唸らせる "to impress someone": 客を唸らせる料理. Loud barking, by contrast, is 吠える.

examples[].german: The dog is barking.
The neighbor's dog barks right away when it sees a stranger.
On the stormy night, the wind blew as if howling.
en.notes: 吠える is the barking of dogs, but also the roaring or howling of other animals. The one barked at is marked with に: 犬が知らない人に吠える. Figuratively it is said of howling wind or a roaring sea, and derogatorily of people who shout and scold loudly (負け犬の遠吠え). A deep growl, by contrast, is 唸る.

examples[].german: The birds are chirping.
Our cat meows when it gets hungry.
en.notes: 鳴く is an intransitive godan verb for animal sounds: 鳴きます, 鳴いて. Birds can chirp, cats meow; with が you name the animal. 鳴いている describes a sound being heard right now. The identically read spelling 泣く refers to human crying.

examples[].german: I have a cat.
Keeping dogs is not allowed in this apartment building.
My grandfather raises cows and chickens in the countryside.
en.notes: 飼う is transitive and means "to keep (an animal)": 猫を飼う, 犬を飼っている (mostly the ている form for the state). Related are 飼い主 ("owner") and 飼い犬. For children and plants you say 育てる, not 飼う. Watch out for the identically sounding 買う ("to buy"): ペットを買う means "to buy a pet".

examples[].german: I'm training the dog.
When I was a child, my parents' discipline was very strict.
Being able to greet people properly is proof of a good upbringing at home.
en.notes: 躾 is mostly written in kana (しつけ) and refers to training in good behavior and manners, for children as well as pets: 犬のしつけ, しつけが厳しい, しつけのいい子. The verb is しつける. 教育, by contrast, is education in the school sense. The kanji 躾 (身 + 美) is a character created in Japan.

examples[].german: I feed the fish.
I used earthworms as fishing bait.
Please don't feed the pigeons in the park.
en.notes: 餌 is "feed" for animals and "bait" in fishing. To feed is 餌をやる or, more politely, 餌をあげる (animal with に). Figuratively it stands for a lure: 餌に釣られる "to fall for a bait". Used for human food it is an insult. For pet food people also say ペットフード; the reading え occurs in 餌食 "prey".

examples[].german: There is a bird's nest.
Swallows built a nest above the entrance.
A spider web was spun in the corner of the room.
en.notes: 巣 is the nest or burrow of an animal: 鳥の巣, 蜂の巣, アリの巣, and also クモの巣 "spider web". Building a nest is 巣を作る, and a spider web is stretched: クモの巣が張る. Derived is 巣立つ "to fledge", also "to leave the parental home". Figuratively 巣 can be a "hideout, shelter".

examples[].german: A white feather had fallen.
The bird spread its wings and flew away.
A butterfly's wings are very thin.
en.notes: 羽 (はね) means both "feather" and "wing" (of birds and insects): 羽を広げる, 白い羽. 翼 (つばさ) is the larger, more poetic or technical "wing", for example of an airplane. For badminton shuttlecocks and rotor blades, 羽根 is often written. As a counter for birds, 羽 is read わ, with sound changes such as 三羽 (さんば).

examples[].german: What is your field of specialization?
She works in the medical field.
Mathematics is not my strong area.
en.notes: 分野 is a field of expertise or activity: 専門分野, 得意分野 "strength, specialty", 〜の分野で働く/活躍する, IT分野. It is the everyday word; 領域 sounds more formal and academic. 範囲, by contrast, means "scope, range" (for example 試験の範囲).

examples[].german: The fangs are sharp.
Elephants have long tusks.
The dog bared its fangs and growled.
en.notes: 牙 are the fangs of predators and the tusks of elephants or wild boars; ordinary teeth are 歯. Ivory is 象牙 (ぞうげ). The phrase 牙をむく "to bare one's fangs" is also used figuratively for "to show hostility".

examples[].german: A butterfly is flying.
A butterfly is resting on a flower in the garden.
I wore a bow tie to the wedding.
en.notes: 蝶 is "butterfly"; in everyday writing it often appears in kana (チョウ) or, in child language, as ちょうちょ. Moths, by contrast, are called 蛾 (が). Well-known expressions are 蝶ネクタイ ("bow tie") and 蝶よ花よと育てる ("to spoil a child greatly"). Butterflies land on flowers: 花にとまる.

examples[].german: I got stung by a bee.
I spread honey on bread and ate it.
Please watch out for bees when hiking in the mountains.
en.notes: 蜂 (はち) is the general term for bees, wasps and hornets. More specific are ミツバチ "honeybee" and スズメバチ "hornet"; in compounds はち becomes ばち. To be stung is 蜂に刺される, and honey is 蜂蜜. Idiom: 蜂の巣をつついたよう "like a stirred-up beehive".

examples[].german: Fireflies are glowing.
When June comes, many people come to this river to see fireflies.
When closing time comes, "Hotaru no Hikari" plays inside the store.
en.notes: 蛍 is the "firefly", often written in kana ほたる/ホタル. It is a symbol of early summer (June-July) on clean rivers; watching fireflies is called 蛍狩り. The song 蛍の光 (to the melody of "Auld Lang Syne") plays in many shops shortly before closing time. In words such as 蛍光灯 and 蛍光ペン the kanji is read けい.

examples[].german: Cicadas are chirping.
On summer vacation mornings, I wake up to the sound of cicadas.
When I was a child, I often caught cicadas in the park.
en.notes: 蝉 is the "cicada", often written in kana セミ. Its loud chirping (蝉が鳴く, 蝉の声) is the typical sound of high summer in Japan. Children like to catch cicadas in the park (蝉を捕まえる), and their empty larval shells are called 蝉の抜け殻. For the sound, as with all animals, the verb 鳴く is used.

examples[].german: I ate crab.
When winter comes, many people go to Hokkaido to eat crab.
A small crab was walking sideways on the sandy beach.
en.notes: 蟹 is the "crab" with claws; on menus it is mostly written カニ or かに. It is eaten as a delicacy especially in winter, for example from Hokkaido; in compounds かに becomes がに (毛ガニ, タラバガニ). Walking sideways is jokingly called カニ歩き. Shrimp and lobster, by contrast, are 海老.

examples[].german: I like shrimp tempura.
Shrimp is included in New Year's dishes in the hope of a long life.
Peeling the shells off shrimp is a hassle.
en.notes: 海老 covers prawns, shrimp and also lobsters or spiny lobsters (伊勢海老); it is often written in kana エビ. The spelling literally means "old person of the sea" because the curved back resembles an old person, which is why shrimp in the New Year's meal stand for a wish for a long life. Popular are 海老フライ and 海老の天ぷら. Crabs with claws, by contrast, are 蟹.

examples[].german: I eat squid sashimi.
I bought grilled squid at a stall at the festival.
The difference between squid and octopus is the number of legs.
en.notes: 烏賊 "squid, cuttlefish" is almost always written in kana in everyday life, as いか or イカ; the kanji is seen mainly on the menus of sushi restaurants. Typical combinations are いかの刺身, いか焼き (grilled squid at a festival stall) and イカリング (fried squid rings). Cuttlefish and squid are both called いか; the eight-armed octopus, by contrast, is たこ.

examples[].german: I like takoyaki.
I bought boiled octopus at the supermarket and put it in a salad.
I saw a big octopus at the aquarium.
en.notes: 蛸 "octopus" is normally written in kana: たこ or タコ. Best known is たこ焼き, batter balls with pieces of octopus from Osaka; in addition, ゆでだこ (boiled octopus) is eaten as sushi or in salads. Be careful when listening: the identically sounding 凧 (たこ) is a paper kite, and colloquially たこ is also used as an insult meaning "fool".

examples[].german: It is sea bream sashimi.
On celebration days we grill and eat sea bream.
Taiyaki has no fish in it.
en.notes: 鯛 is the red sea bream and, in Japan, the lucky fish par excellence, because たい is reminiscent of めでたい "auspicious". It is served at weddings, at New Year and at celebrations, often whole, salted and grilled (鯛の塩焼き) or as 鯛めし. It is usually written 鯛 or たい; the sweet たい焼き only has the shape of the fish and contains no fish.

examples[].german: I will take on a challenge in a new field.
This research spans both the fields of medicine and engineering.
Entering another country's territory without permission is not allowed.
en.notes: 領域 means on the one hand a field of expertise or research (研究領域, 新しい領域に挑戦する), on the other the sovereign territory of a state (land, sea and airspace together). It sounds more formal and academic than 分野. Common phrases: 〜の領域に入る/踏み込む "to venture into the realm of ...".

examples[].german: Tuna sushi is my favorite.
At the conveyor-belt sushi place, I ate as many as three plates of tuna.
I saw freshly caught tuna at the harbor.
en.notes: 鮪 "tuna" is mostly written in kana (まぐろ / マグロ); only in sushi restaurants is the kanji often used. By fat content one distinguishes 赤身 (lean red meat), 中トロ and 大トロ (very fatty belly meat). For canned tuna, by contrast, one says ツナ, as in ツナ缶; まぐろ means the fresh fish.

examples[].german: I eat salmon rice balls.
For breakfast I had grilled salmon and miso soup.
When autumn comes, salmon swim up the rivers.
en.notes: 鮭 "salmon" is also pronounced しゃけ, especially colloquially and in dishes such as 鮭おにぎり or 焼き鮭. Salted, grilled salmon is part of the classic Japanese breakfast. As a sushi topping, especially for farmed salmon, people mostly say サーモン. Caution: お酒 (さけ) "alcohol" sounds the same but differs in pitch accent.

examples[].german: I make dashi with bonito flakes.
In Kochi, I ate seared bonito.
From spring to early summer, bonito tastes especially good.
en.notes: 鰹 is the skipjack tuna (bonito), a close relative of tuna. Most important is its use as 鰹節 (かつおぶし): dried and shaved into flakes, it forms the base of many だし. Fresh, it is enjoyed as かつおのたたき, briefly seared on the outside. In everyday life it is often written かつお in kana; 初鰹, the first bonito of early summer, is regarded as a delicacy.

examples[].german: I make dashi.
I made stock with kelp and bonito flakes.
The udon at this restaurant has delicious broth.
en.notes: 出汁 is the Japanese basic stock, usually made from kombu and 鰹節, and is almost always written in kana: だし. The fixed combination is だしを取る "to extract a stock"; ready-made granules are called だしの素. Unlike スープ (Western soup) or 汁 (soup as a dish), だし is the base from which miso soup, noodle broths and simmered dishes are made.

examples[].german: I add mirin.
Teriyaki sauce is made from soy sauce, mirin and sugar.
We have run out of mirin, so I will go buy some at the supermarket.
en.notes: 味醂 "mirin" is sweet rice wine for cooking and is almost always written みりん. Together with しょうゆ, 砂糖 and 酒, it forms the base of many sauces, such as for 照り焼き or 煮物, and gives sweetness and gloss. It is not drunk; cheap substitutes with little alcohol are called みりん風調味料.

examples[].german: I add the condiments on the side.
For soba, scallions and wasabi are used as condiments.
Please add the condiments as you like.
en.notes: 薬味 are small, mostly fresh seasoning ingredients that are added to noodles, tofu or sashimi: chopped ねぎ, grated ginger, わさび, みょうが, 大葉 or 七味. So it is neither "spice" in general (スパイス, 香辛料) nor a seasoning such as soy sauce or salt (調味料). Typical are 薬味を添える, 薬味を入れる and, on menus, 薬味はお好みで.

examples[].german: I will order nigiri sushi.
At this restaurant, nigiri sushi comes two pieces per plate.
The chef made nigiri sushi for me right in front of my eyes.
en.notes: 握り寿司 is sushi in which a topping (ネタ) is placed on a hand-shaped ball of rice; the name comes from 握る "to form by hand, press". Note the voicing: すし becomes ずし in the compound, as in 巻き寿司 and ちらし寿司. In restaurants the pieces are counted with 〜貫 (一貫, 二貫); in everyday speech people often just say にぎり.

examples[].german: Let's make sushi rolls.
I put sushi rolls in the lunch box.
It is a custom to eat thick sushi rolls on Setsubun.
en.notes: 巻き寿司 is sushi rolled up with nori seaweed (海苔) and then cut into pieces; 巻く means "to wrap, roll". Thin rolls with one filling are called 細巻き (e.g. かっぱ巻き with cucumber), thick ones with many ingredients 太巻き. On 節分, in many regions people eat an uncut roll as 恵方巻き.

examples[].german: I eat toshikoshi soba (New Year's Eve noodles).
On hot days I feel like eating cold zaru soba.
I had lunch at a standing soba shop in the station.
en.notes: 蕎麦 "buckwheat noodles" is mostly written in kana (そば), but on restaurant signs you often see 蕎麦. They are eaten cold with a dipping sauce (ざるそば) or hot in broth (かけそば), and slurping is perfectly normal. On New Year's Eve people eat 年越しそば for a long life. Caution: 焼きそば are fried wheat noodles, and そば (側) "beside" is a different word.

examples[].german: I eat warm udon.
When you have a cold, soft udon is just right.
Kagawa is famous for its Sanuki udon.
en.notes: 饂飩 "udon" are thick wheat noodles; the difficult kanji is practically never used, and it is written うどん. Well-known varieties are きつねうどん (with sweetly simmered fried tofu), 天ぷらうどん and 讃岐うどん from Kagawa. Unlike そば (buckwheat), うどん are made of wheat flour and are thicker and softer; they are eaten hot or cold.

examples[].german: Let's think from a different perspective.
If you change your perspective, new ideas are born.
This novel is written from a dog's perspective.
en.notes: 視点 is the standpoint from which one views something: 〜の視点から, 視点を変える, 新しい視点, 子どもの視点. In narratives it also means "narrative perspective". Distinction: 観点 is more the viewpoint or criterion of an evaluation (経済の観点から); 立場 is one's own position or situation.

examples[].german: I will have Japanese sweets and matcha.
I bought Japanese sweets as a souvenir from Kyoto.
I like Japanese sweets better than Western sweets.
en.notes: 和菓子 are traditional Japanese sweets such as 大福, 羊羹 or 団子, often made from sweet bean paste (あんこ) and rice flour. The opposite is 洋菓子 "Western pastries" such as cakes or cookies; 和 here stands for "Japanese", as in 和食. 和菓子 is often served with green tea, especially at the tea ceremony, and many kinds are available only in a certain season.

examples[].german: I like matcha.
One matcha-flavored ice cream, please.
I learned how to whisk matcha at a tea ceremony class.
en.notes: 抹茶 is finely ground green tea that is not steeped but whisked into a froth with hot water; in the tea ceremony (茶道) this is called 抹茶を点てる. In everyday life it appears mainly as a flavor: 抹茶アイス, 抹茶ラテ, 抹茶味. Ordinary leaf green tea, by contrast, is 緑茶 or simply お茶.

examples[].german: I drink bancha.
Bancha has little caffeine, so you can drink it even in the evening.
At my grandmother's house, bancha is always served after meals.
en.notes: 番茶 is a simple, inexpensive green tea made from late, coarser leaves; it tastes mild and contains little caffeine. It is drunk as an everyday tea with meals, in contrast to the finer 煎茶 or the premium 玉露. Roasted, it is often made into ほうじ茶. In conversation people usually just say お茶; 番茶 is used when the type matters.

examples[].german: I drink shochu on the rocks.
On cold days, shochu with hot water is the best.
I received sweet potato shochu as a souvenir from Kagoshima.
en.notes: 焼酎 is a Japanese distilled liquor made from sweet potatoes (芋焼酎), barley (麦焼酎), rice or other ingredients. Unlike 日本酒, which is brewed, it is a clear spirit, usually around 25% alcohol. It is drunk ロックで (on the rocks), 水割り (with water), お湯割り (with hot water) or mixed as チューハイ; shochu from Kyushu is especially famous.

examples[].german: One glass of sake, please.
This sake tastes good chilled.
Sake is made from rice and water.
en.notes: 日本酒 is Japanese rice wine brewed from rice, known internationally as "sake". In Japanese, however, お酒 means any "alcoholic drink" in general; so those who specifically mean rice wine say 日本酒 (formally also 清酒). It is drunk chilled (冷酒), at room temperature or hot (熱燗); the amount is counted with 一杯 or 一合.

examples[].german: I warm up amazake and drink it.
At my New Year's shrine visit, I received amazake at the shrine.
This amazake contains no alcohol, so children can drink it too.
en.notes: 甘酒 is a sweet, thick drink made from fermented rice (with 麹) or from sake lees (酒粕). Despite 酒 in the name, the koji version contains no alcohol and is also given to children; the sake-lees version contains only a trace. Traditionally it is drunk warm at New Year or at shrines, and in summer chilled as a tonic drink.

examples[].german: I am planning this week's menu.
The school lunch menu was handed out.
I decided tonight's menu based on what was in the fridge.
en.notes: 献立 is the combination of dishes for a meal or a period, that is, the meal plan: 今日の献立, 一週間の献立, 給食の献立. Typical are 献立を考える and 献立を立てる "to draw up a menu plan". For the menu in a restaurant, by contrast, one says メニュー; 献立 sounds like the household, the school cafeteria or a cookbook.

en.meaning: season (best time for food); in season
examples[].german: I eat seasonal vegetables.
Pacific saury is in season in autumn.
If we talk about the actor of the moment, it would be him.
en.notes: 旬 is the best time for a food, when it is freshest and tastiest: 旬の野菜, 旬の魚, 今が旬だ "it is in season now". It is narrower than 季節 "season", because 旬 stresses the peak of flavor. Figuratively, currently popular people or topics are also called 旬, for example 旬のタレント.

examples[].german: These are vegetables direct from the producer.
Before buying meat, I check where it comes from.
Aomori is famous as an apple-producing region.
en.notes: 産地 is the place where something is produced or grown: 米の産地, ワインの産地, みかんの産地. On packaging you find 産地 or 原産地 "country of origin", and 産地直送 means "delivered directly from the producer". The word sounds mainly like agriculture, fish and regional specialties; for industrial products people rather speak of 製造国 or 生産地.

examples[].german: I buy organic vegetables.
This store sells organically grown coffee.
My grandfather does organic farming in his field.
en.notes: 有機 "organic" almost always stands as the first element before a noun: 有機野菜 "organic vegetables", 有機栽培 "organic cultivation", 有機農業. It is neither an い- nor a な-adjective: you don't say 有機な野菜 but 有機野菜 or, more rarely, 有機の野菜. In everyday speech you also often hear オーガニック for organic products; in chemistry the opposite is 無機 "inorganic".

examples[].german: From an economic point of view, it is important.
From the standpoint of safety, this road is closed to traffic at night.
The teacher evaluates essays from several viewpoints.
en.notes: 観点 is the viewpoint from which one judges something; almost always in the form 〜の観点から(見ると/考えると): 安全の観点から, 環境の観点から. It sounds more formal and analytical than 視点, which describes more one's own angle of view. Typical of reports, justifications and official statements.

examples[].german: It is a food without additives.
For my children's snacks, I choose ones with as few additives as possible.
When I looked at the label, it contained many additives.
en.notes: 添加物 are additives in food such as preservatives or colorings; the full term is 食品添加物. Typical expressions are 添加物が入っている, 添加物を避ける and 無添加 "additive-free", which is often printed large on packaging. The verb 添加する "to add" is technical; in everyday speech people simply say 入れる for ingredients.

examples[].german: Please check the best-before date.
This milk is past its best-before date.
Products close to their best-before date are discounted.
en.notes: 賞味期限 is the best-before date: until then a product is guaranteed to taste good, and afterwards it is often still edible. To be distinguished from it is 消費期限 "use-by date" for perishable goods such as meat or bento, after which you should not eat anything. Typical phrases are 賞味期限が切れる "to expire", 賞味期限切れ "expired" and 賞味期限が近い.

examples[].german: I buy frozen food.
I froze the leftover curry.
Please put the ice cream in the freezer.
en.notes: 冷凍 means "freezing, deep-freezing" and is common as a transitive する-verb: 肉を冷凍する, 残りを冷凍しておく. It often stands at the front of compounds such as 冷凍食品, 冷凍庫 "freezer" and 冷凍保存. The opposite is 解凍 "to thaw"; mere cooling in the refrigerator, by contrast, is 冷蔵 (冷蔵庫). When something freezes by itself, the intransitive 凍る is used.

examples[].german: I thaw the meat.
It is convenient to thaw frozen bread in the microwave.
Please unzip the downloaded file.
en.notes: 解凍 means "to thaw" and is very common as a transitive する-verb: 冷凍の肉を解凍する, 電子レンジで解凍する, 自然解凍 "letting it thaw at room temperature". The opposite is 冷凍 "to freeze". On a computer, 解凍 also means "to unpack a compressed file" (ZIPファイルを解凍する); the counterpart is 圧縮.

examples[].german: Please be careful about food poisoning.
In summer food spoils easily, so food poisoning increases.
I ate raw shellfish and got food poisoning.
en.notes: 食中毒 is food poisoning caused by bacteria, viruses or toxins in food. Typical are 食中毒になる "to get food poisoning", 食中毒を起こす (said of foods or restaurants) and 食中毒に気をつける. Especially in the humid summer, news and schools warn about it. The shorter 中毒 means "poisoning" in general, but also "addiction" (ゲーム中毒).

examples[].german: I stand in front of the class as a teacher.
My father taught at a high school for thirty years.
The teacher stepped down from the platform and came over to the students' seats.
en.notes: 教壇 is the raised platform at the front of the classroom on which the teacher stands; the desk on it is called 教卓. Very common is the figurative phrase 教壇に立つ "to teach as a teacher", e.g. 三十年間教壇に立つ, as well as 教壇を去る "to leave teaching". The word sounds somewhat elevated; in modern schools the platform itself often no longer exists.

examples[].german: I look it up in the dictionary.
I borrowed a Japanese dictionary from the library.
This dictionary contains many example sentences.
en.notes: 辞典 means "dictionary" and appears mainly in titles and fixed designations: 国語辞典 (Japanese dictionary), 英和辞典 (English-Japanese). In everyday speech, 辞書 is usually said; the same thing is meant. The identically pronounced 事典, on the other hand, is an encyclopedia of subjects (百科事典). To look something up is 辞典で調べる or 辞典を引く.

examples[].german: I looked it up in the encyclopedia.
The library has a twenty-volume encyclopedia.
My older brother knows everything; he is a walking encyclopedia.
en.notes: 百科事典 is an encyclopedia covering all fields of knowledge (百科 "a hundred subjects"). Typical is 百科事典で調べる "to look something up in the encyclopedia"; today it often also means online encyclopedias. Note the kanji: 事典 explains things, whereas 辞典 or 辞書 explains words. A person who knows everything is jokingly called 歩く百科事典 "walking encyclopedia".

examples[].german: I attend a lecture.
Professor Tanaka's lectures are always interesting.
I overslept and couldn't attend the morning lecture.
en.notes: 講義 is a lecture at a university or college. Students attend it with 講義を受ける or 講義に出る, and the lecturer gives it with 講義をする. In school, 授業 is used instead; a public talk before an audience is 講演. The word is neutral and very common in student life (講義ノート, 講義室).

examples[].german: I am taking part in the seminar.
Please solve the exercises at the back of the textbook.
A military exercise was held in the nearby sea.
en.notes: 演習 is a practical exercise for consolidating what has been learned, e.g. 演習問題 "practice problems". At universities it refers to a seminar or practice class as opposed to a lecture 講義, often in course names such as 英語演習. In the military, 演習 means maneuvers (軍事演習). For everyday "to practice" one more often says 練習する; 演習 sounds academic and formal.

examples[].german: Let's understand this concept.
In old Japan there was no concept of a "weekend".
The notion of happiness differs from person to person.
en.notes: 概念 is an abstract concept or idea: 〜という概念, 概念がない, 新しい概念, 時間の概念. It is a rather academic word; in everyday speech one often says 考え方 "way of thinking". Typical combinations: 概念を理解する, 概念が広がる, 〜の概念を変える.

examples[].german: I will graduate next year.
After I graduate from university, I want to work in Japan.
At the graduation ceremony, my parents took lots of photos.
en.notes: 卒業 is graduation from a school or university. Although the verb is intransitive, the institution that is left takes を: 大学を卒業する. Common compounds are 卒業式 "graduation ceremony" and 卒業生 "graduate". Figuratively it also means "to grow out of something" (マンガを卒業する) or leaving a group, for example when an idol leaves their band. Counterpart: 入学.

en.meaning: entering a school or university; admission
examples[].german: I entered university.
My younger brother will enter elementary school next April.
The entrance exam is in February.
en.notes: 入学 is entry into a school or university; the institution takes に: 小学校に入学する, 大学に入学する. Since the Japanese school year begins in April, the entrance ceremony 入学式 usually takes place then. Further compounds are 入学試験 (short 入試) "entrance exam" and 入学祝い "gift for starting school". Counterpart: 卒業.

examples[].german: I joined a club.
I have club activities today, so I will get home late.
In junior high, I played basketball in a club.
en.notes: 部活 is the short form of 部活動 and refers to club activities at junior high and high schools, such as サッカー部 or 吹奏楽部. You say 部活に入る "to join a club", 部活がある and 部活を休む; for a specific club usually 〜部に入る. A distinction is made between 運動部 (sports) and 文化部 (culture). The word is a very common, everyday student word.

examples[].german: We are preparing for the cultural festival.
At the cultural festival, I performed a play with my classmates.
I went to my younger sister's high school cultural festival.
en.notes: 文化祭 is a school's annual cultural festival, usually in autumn: classes run food stalls, perform plays or exhibit work, and outside visitors are welcome too. Typical are 文化祭の準備, 文化祭で劇をする and 文化祭に行く. At universities the festival is often called 学園祭 or 大学祭; the sporting counterpart is 体育祭.

examples[].german: I am looking forward to the sports festival.
I ran as the anchor in the relay at the sports festival.
Because of rain, the sports festival was postponed to next week.
en.notes: 体育祭 is the sports festival of a junior high or high school with races, relays and team games, often between teams such as 紅組 and 白組. In elementary schools the same event is usually called 運動会, a word that is also used for company or neighborhood events. Typical are 体育祭に出る, 体育祭のリレー and 体育祭が延期になる.

examples[].german: I went on a school outing.
Tomorrow's outing is to the zoo.
My mother made my lunch box for the outing.
en.notes: 遠足 is a day trip that a kindergarten or school makes with the whole class, for example to a park, a zoo or a hill. Set expressions are 遠足に行く and 遠足のお弁当; legendary is the rule that sweets for a 遠足 may cost no more than 300 yen. Unlike 修学旅行 (a multi-day class trip), a 遠足 lasts only one day; a private excursion is rather called ハイキング or お出かけ.

examples[].german: We are going to Kyoto on the school trip.
On the night of the school trip, I talked with my friends until late.
I bought yatsuhashi as a souvenir from the school trip.
en.notes: 修学旅行 is the multi-day class trip that Japanese schools usually take in the last year of elementary, junior high or senior high school; popular destinations are Kyoto, Nara and Okinawa. One says 修学旅行に行く and 修学旅行で〜へ行く. The word is firmly tied to school: a training trip for company employees is called 研修旅行, and a one-day school outing is an 遠足.

en.meaning: taking an exam; sitting an entrance exam
examples[].german: I am taking the university entrance exam.
Because of exam preparation, I stay up late every night.
Please make sure not to forget your exam admission ticket.
en.notes: 受験 means sitting an exam, especially an entrance exam for a school or university. As a する-verb, the school or exam takes を: 大学を受験する, 高校を受験する; for exams in general one also says 試験を受ける. Many compounds revolve around the dreaded exam period: 受験生 "exam candidate", 受験勉強, 受験票 "exam admission ticket".

examples[].german: I passed the exam.
I got into the university I wanted to go to.
This product has passed the safety inspection.
en.notes: 合格 is passing an exam and is very common as an intransitive する-verb: 試験に合格する, 大学に合格する "to be admitted to a university". The goal is marked with に, not を. It also applies to inspections and standards, for example 検査に合格する. The opposite is 不合格; the announcement of results is 合格発表, and you can congratulate with 合格おめでとう.

examples[].german: Unfortunately, I failed.
I was one point short and failed.
Parts that fail the inspection cannot be used.
en.notes: 不合格 is failing an exam or inspection. It is a pure noun without する: you say 不合格になる or 不合格だった, not 不合格する. In conversation, 試験に落ちる "to fail an exam" sounds more natural and personal; 不合格 appears more on notices and in objective reports. The opposite is 合格.

examples[].german: We will tour the manufacturing process.
Not only the result but also the process leading to it is important.
I keep photos of my child's growth process.
en.notes: 過程 is the course or process through which something comes about or develops: 製造過程, 成長の過程, 〜に至る過程. Typical is 〜の過程で "in the course of". 段階, by contrast, refers to a single stage within such a sequence; プロセス is the loanword with almost the same meaning. Watch out for homophones: かてい is also 家庭 "family, household" and 仮定 "assumption".

examples[].german: What is the definition of this word?
This survey defines people aged 65 and over as the elderly.
The definition of "success" differs for everyone.
en.notes: 定義 is a definition: 〜の定義, 定義がはっきりしない/あいまいだ. As a transitive する-verb the pattern is AをBと定義する "to define A as B". Typical in science, statistics and discussions about what exactly a word means; in everyday speech people often ask more simply 〜ってどういう意味？

examples[].german: I will take attendance.
The department head will also attend next week's meeting.
I attended a friend's wedding.
en.notes: 出席 is attendance at classes, meetings or celebrations; as an intransitive する-verb with に: 会議に出席する, 結婚式に出席する. 出席を取る means "to check attendance". In casual conversation people often simply say 出る (授業に出る); 出席 is more formal and polite and appears, for example, on invitation cards (ご出席). Opposite: 欠席.

examples[].german: I will be absent because of a cold.
Mr. Tanaka is absent from today's meeting.
If you have many absences, you can't get credit.
en.notes: 欠席 is being absent from classes, meetings or celebrations; as a する-verb, the missed event is marked with を: 授業を欠席する, 会議を欠席する, and the reason with で: 風邪で欠席する. For staying away from work, by contrast, people say 欠勤 or simply 休む. On reply cards to invitations you choose ご出席 or ご欠席; the opposite is 出席.

examples[].german: I will start maternity leave next month.
While Ms. Yamada is on maternity leave, I will take over her work.
After her maternity leave ended, my older sister returned to her workplace right away.
en.notes: 産休 is the short form of 産前産後休業, the statutory maternity leave before and after childbirth. Typical phrases are 産休に入る "to go on maternity leave", 産休を取る and 産休中. It is usually followed by 育休 (parental leave), which fathers can also take; in conversation the two are often mentioned together: 産休・育休.

examples[].german: I took parental leave.
My husband has also decided to take three months of parental leave.
I plan to end my parental leave next April and return to work.
en.notes: 育休 is the short form of 育児休業 "parental leave". You say 育休を取る, 育休中 and 育休から復帰する "to return from parental leave". Unlike 産休, which concerns only the mother around childbirth, both mothers and fathers can take 育休; fathers on parental leave are often called 男性の育休.

examples[].german: I work as a temp.
The government sent doctors to the region.
I registered with a temp agency and am looking for work.
en.notes: 派遣 originally means "to send out" and is then a transitive する-verb: 医者を被災地に派遣する. In working life it mainly stands for agency (temp) work: 派遣社員 "temp worker", 派遣会社 "temp agency" and, briefly, 派遣で働く. The opposite term in working life is 正社員 "regular employee".

examples[].german: I want to become a regular employee.
After working part-time for three years, I was finally hired as a regular employee.
This company is recruiting regular employees.
en.notes: 正社員 is a permanent full-time employee with an open-ended contract, social benefits and bonus. You say 正社員になる, 正社員として働く or 正社員として採用される. The opposites are 契約社員 (fixed-term), 派遣社員 (temp agency work) as well as パート and アルバイト; together these are called 非正規 "non-regular employees".

examples[].german: I started my own business.
My father is self-employed and runs a small bakery.
In the occupation field of the application form, I wrote "self-employed".
en.notes: 自営業 is self-employed work with one's own shop, business or practice, for example as a restaurant owner or craftsman. On forms, 自営業 appears as an occupation entry next to 会社員 or 学生. Typical are 自営業をしている, 自営業の家 and 実家は自営業です. In contrast to 起業 "founding a company", 自営業 stresses working independently as such, often on a small scale.

examples[].german: I am thinking about starting a business.
He started a company at 25 and made it grow.
To start a business, you first need funds.
en.notes: 起業 is founding one's own company; as an intransitive する-verb: 起業する, 大学を出てすぐ起業する. Related are 起業家 "founder, entrepreneur" and 起業資金. Caution, homophone: 企業 (きぎょう) means "enterprise, company" itself, whereas 起業 means the act of founding. More formal, especially for corporations, is 会社を設立する.

examples[].german: We established a stock corporation.
Thank you for calling. This is Sakura Co., Ltd.
Most Japanese companies are stock corporations.
en.notes: 株式会社 is the Japanese joint-stock company (K.K.), the most common legal form for companies. It stands before or after the name in a company name, e.g. 株式会社さくら or さくら商事株式会社, and is often abbreviated as (株). Note the voicing change: かいしゃ becomes がいしゃ. In conversation one simply says 会社; 株式会社 is heard mainly in formal contexts such as contracts, on business cards and on the phone.

examples[].german: The head office is in Tokyo.
Next month I will be transferred from the Osaka branch office to the head office.
In this matter we have to wait for the decision of the head office.
en.notes: 本社 is the head office or headquarters of a company: 本社は東京にある, 本社に転勤する, 本社ビル. Contrasting terms are 支社 (regional branch office) and 支店 (branch with customer traffic, e.g. for banks or shops). Less often, 本社 refers to the main shrine of a shrine complex, but in everyday use the meaning "headquarters" clearly dominates.

examples[].german: Let's talk on that premise.
We are going out together with a view to marriage.
For this job, it is a prerequisite that you can speak English.
en.notes: 前提 is a prerequisite or starting point that is tacitly taken for granted: 〜を前提に(して)/〜を前提として, 〜が前提だ, 大前提 "basic prerequisite". Well known is 結婚を前提に付き合う "to date with the intention of marrying". Distinction: 条件 are negotiated conditions, whereas 前提 is presupposed.

examples[].german: We have a branch office in Osaka.
Next year, we plan to set up a new branch office in Singapore.
I had an online meeting with the people at the branch office.
en.notes: 支社 is a branch office or subsidiary location of a company, usually responsible for a region: 大阪支社, 海外支社, 支社長. Compared with 支店 (a branch with customer traffic, e.g. a bank or shop), a 支社 is more of a regional administrative unit. The opposite is 本社 "head office"; you can be, for example, 支社に転勤する "transferred to a branch office".

examples[].german: I was transferred to a new department.
Excuse me, which department are you from?
Please submit this document to the department in charge.
en.notes: 部署 is the department or post to which one is assigned in a company or government agency. Typical are 部署に配属される "to be assigned to a department", 部署を異動する, 別の部署 and the question どちらの部署ですか. It is a general term for units such as 部, 課 or 係; for a specific one people usually give the name, such as 営業部 or 経理課.

examples[].german: There was a personnel reshuffle.
I have been assigned to be transferred to the sales department from next month.
I don't know anyone yet in the department I am transferred to.
en.notes: 異動 is a transfer within a company or government agency, i.e. a change of department or post. Typical are 人事異動 "personnel changes" and 〜に異動する or 〜に異動になる "to be transferred to ...". Do not confuse it with the identically read 移動 "movement, change of location". 転勤, by contrast, stresses a transfer to a different workplace, often with a move.

examples[].german: I am taking part in the training for new employees.
From next week, I will have three days of training in Tokyo.
A clerk with a name tag saying "in training" explained everything to me eagerly.
en.notes: 研修 is professional training or induction, especially for employees: 新人研修, 社員研修, 海外研修. One says 研修を受ける or 研修に参加する; a person who is currently being trained often wears a badge saying 研修中. Unlike トレーニング (more sports) or 練習 ("practice"), it concerns organized further education on the job; 実習, by contrast, emphasizes practical exercises, for example during studies.

examples[].german: There is a morning assembly.
Every morning at nine, we check the day's schedule at the morning meeting.
At the Monday assembly, the principal's talk was so long that I got tired.
en.notes: 朝礼 is the short assembly in the morning before work or school starts, at which announcements are made and the day's plan is discussed. One says 朝礼がある, 朝礼に出る and 朝礼で発表する. In schools 朝会 is also common; the short class meeting is called 朝の会 or ホームルーム. The word is neutral and common in both company and school life.

examples[].german: I enjoyed the year-end party.
This year's year-end party will be held at the izakaya in front of the station.
In December one year-end party followed another, and I drank a bit too much.
en.notes: 忘年会 literally means "gathering to forget the year": the year-end party in December, usually with colleagues, clubs or friends in an izakaya. Typical are 忘年会をする/やる, 忘年会を開く and 忘年会に出る. The counterpart in January is 新年会. The party is often followed by a 二次会.

examples[].german: I will take part in the New Year's party.
At the company's New Year's party, there was a bingo game.
I have already reserved the place for the New Year's party.
en.notes: 新年会 is the New Year's party held in January among colleagues, in clubs or in neighborhoods, so it is not the New Year's Eve party. One says 新年会を開く, 新年会をする and 新年会に参加する/出る. The counterpart is the 忘年会 in December. As with other 〜会 words, an organizing person often takes care of the venue and reservation.

examples[].german: We will hold a welcome party.
The welcome party for Mr. Tanaka, who just joined, is on Friday.
At the club's welcome party, I got to talk a lot with the seniors.
en.notes: 歓迎会 is a welcome party for new colleagues, students or guests. Typical: 〜さんの歓迎会, 歓迎会を開く/する, 新入生歓迎会 (often shortened to 新歓). The counterpart at a farewell is 送別会. It is based on 歓迎 "welcome, reception", which also occurs as the verb 歓迎する.

examples[].german: I will attend the farewell party.
At the farewell party for Mr. Yamada, who is being transferred, we gave him a bouquet.
We all held a farewell party for our friend who is going to study abroad.
en.notes: 送別会 is the farewell party for someone who is being transferred, retiring, moving away or going abroad. One says 〜さんの送別会, 送別会を開く and 送別会に出る/出席する; 出席する sounds more formal. The counterpart is 歓迎会. Often flowers or a gift are presented on such occasions.

examples[].german: Are you going to the after-party?
Let's go to karaoke for the second round.
At the after-party of the wedding, I saw friends from my university days for the first time in a long while.
en.notes: 二次会 is the second round of an evening: after the first party (一次会), people move on, often to a karaoke bar or another venue; after that a 三次会 can even follow. Typical are 二次会に行く and 二次会に参加する. At weddings, the 二次会 is the casual party after the official reception, to which more friends are also invited.

examples[].german: There is a contradiction.
What he says contradicts what he said before.
Saying "I want to lose weight" while eating cake is contradictory, you know.
en.notes: 矛盾 is a contradiction; literally "spear and shield", from the Chinese story of a merchant who boasted of a spear that nothing could withstand and a shield that nothing could pierce at the same time. Common are 矛盾がある and the intransitive する-verb: AがBと矛盾する "A contradicts B", 矛盾した態度 "contradictory behavior". It is not used for a person contradicting someone: that is 反論する or 言い返す.

examples[].german: Let's split the bill.
If the five of us split it, it is 2,000 yen per person.
I'll treat you today, so we don't need to split it.
en.notes: 割り勘 means that everyone present pays the bill in equal shares. Typical are 割り勘にする and 割り勘で払う. The opposite is おごる "to treat someone, to pay the bill". The word is an abbreviation of 割り前勘定 and is used very often in everyday life; occasionally the spelling 割勘 is also seen.

en.meaning: feast; treat; to treat someone (ごちそうする)
examples[].german: Thank you for the meal. (after eating)
Today it is my treat.
At New Year, lots of delicious dishes are laid out on the table.
en.notes: ご馳走 is, on the one hand, an especially good, plentiful meal: すごいごちそうですね "what a feast!" On the other hand, ごちそうする means "to invite someone (to a meal), to treat", where the host pays: 友達に昼ご飯をごちそうする; the one who is treated says ごちそうになる. Well known is the phrase ごちそうさまでした after a meal or as thanks for an invitation. It is mostly written in kana, ごちそう, more rarely also 御馳走.

examples[].german: Please introduce yourself.
In the first class, I introduced myself in Japanese.
In the interview, please first introduce yourself in about one minute.
en.notes: 自己紹介 is introducing oneself, for example in the first class, in a job interview or at a meeting. You say 自己紹介をする or simply 自己紹介する; politely you ask with 自己紹介をお願いします. Those who introduce other people use 紹介する (〜を〜に紹介する) instead. Typical phrases are 簡単に自己紹介する "to introduce oneself briefly" and 自己紹介が苦手だ.

examples[].german: I will check the roster.
My name is not on the class roster.
I made a directory for the new members.
en.notes: 名簿 is an official list of the names of members or participants: クラス名簿, 会員名簿, 社員名簿. Typical phrases are 名簿を作る, 名簿に載る "to be on the list" and 名簿から外す "to remove from the list". Unlike the general リスト or 一覧, a 名簿 always contains people, often with addresses or contact details.

examples[].german: I will prepare the minutes.
Who will take the minutes of today's meeting?
If you read the previous minutes, you can see what was decided.
en.notes: 議事録 are the minutes of a meeting or conference, recording the discussion and the decisions. Typical are 議事録を取る "to take minutes", 議事録を作成する/まとめる and 前回の議事録. More general is 記録 "record"; a private メモ is not an official 議事録. The word belongs to office and administrative language.

examples[].german: I will send the quotation.
Before moving, I got quotations from three companies.
Is the amount in this quotation tax included?
en.notes: 見積書 is a written offer with a cost estimate, for example from a moving company or a repair shop. It comes from 見積もる "to estimate"; in conversation people often say just 見積もり: 見積もりを取る/出す. Typical are 見積書を作成する, 見積書を送る and 見積書をもらう. Do not confuse it with 請求書 (invoice after the service) and 領収書 (receipt after payment).

examples[].german: I will issue the invoice.
The electricity bill has arrived.
Please transfer the invoiced amount by the end of the month.
en.notes: 請求書 is the invoice by which a payment is requested, for example from companies, or electricity or telephone providers. You say 請求書を発行する/送る, 請求書が届く and often pay by bank transfer (振り込む). To be distinguished from it are 領収書 (receipt for a payment already made) and, in a restaurant, お会計 "the bill, please". It is based on 請求する "to demand, bill".

examples[].german: A receipt, please.
This is a company expense, so please get a receipt.
When I got out of the taxi, I got a receipt from the driver.
en.notes: 領収書 is a formal receipt, often with the recipient's name and the purpose, which is needed, for example, for expense reports. The simple cash-register receipt is called レシート. Typical are 領収書をください, 領収書をもらう and 領収書を書く; there is also the spelling 領収証. By comparison: 請求書 demands a payment, 領収書 confirms it.

examples[].german: I put the proposal through the approval process.
To buy a new computer, you have to submit an approval request.
The proposal just isn't getting approved, so we can't start the project.
en.notes: 稟議 is the typically Japanese approval procedure in companies: a proposal (稟議書) circulates from office to office, and all responsible persons give their consent, often with their seal. Typical phrases are 稟議を上げる/回す "to put a proposal into circulation" and 稟議が通る "to be approved". The character 稟 is rare and occurs practically only in this word.
