It is purely office and business language.

examples[].german: The superior's approval is required.
The department head has given his approval, so construction will begin next month.
The president is away on a business trip, so I can't get the documents approved.
en.notes: 決裁 is the formal approval by a person with decision-making authority, e.g. a department head or managing director. Typical are 決裁をもらう/受ける, 決裁が下りる "the approval is granted" and 〜を決裁する. Note: the identically read 決済 means "payment, settlement" (e.g. カード決済) and is often confused with it. The word belongs to business and administrative language.

examples[].german: I will form a hypothesis and test it.
That hypothesis was proven correct by experiment.
This is still nothing more than a hypothesis.
en.notes: 仮説 is a scientific hypothesis: 仮説を立てる "to form a hypothesis", 仮説を検証する "to test", 仮説が正しい/証明される. Distinction: 仮定 is a mere assumption in a line of thought ("assuming that ..."), 推測 a conjecture. 仮説 belongs to research, business and analysis.

examples[].german: Please bring your seal.
Please put your seal here.
When I received the parcel, I signed instead of using a seal.
en.notes: 判子 is the personal name seal that is used in Japan instead of a signature on forms, contracts or for package deliveries. One says 判子を押す "to stamp"; often it is written just はんこ or ハンコ. The more formal word is 印鑑, especially for an officially registered seal. A stamp for pictures or dates, by contrast, is called スタンプ.

examples[].german: I will submit a notification.
Since I lost my wallet, I filed a report at the police box.
When you miss school, please submit an absence notice.
en.notes: 届け (often also written 届) is a written notification to an authority, school or company. It often appears as a suffix: 欠席届 "absence notice", 退職届 "resignation letter", 婚姻届 "marriage registration"; in such compounds the okurigana is usually omitted. Typical is 届けを出す. The related verb is 届ける "to submit, report", and the formal noun is 届け出.

examples[].german: I lost my passport.
If you lose your card, please contact us immediately.
Some of the meeting materials seem to be missing.
en.notes: 紛失 is the formal word for "loss" of objects and often appears on forms and in announcements: 紛失届, 紛失物. As a する-verb it can be used transitively (パスポートを紛失する) or intransitively (書類が紛失する). In everyday speech one usually says なくす or なくなる. It is not used for people or for abstract things such as trust.

examples[].german: I reported the found item.
Please write the date, time and place of the find on this form.
Items found at the station are handed over to the police.
en.notes: 拾得 is the official word for "finding (a lost item)" and appears almost only in forms, notices and police language: 拾得物 "found item", 拾得者 "finder", 拾得する. In everyday speech one simply says 拾う, and instead of 拾得物 mostly 落とし物. The counterpart on the loss side is 紛失 or 遺失.

examples[].german: I forgot something.
When you get off the train, please be careful not to leave anything behind.
Excuse me, you forgot something!
en.notes: 忘れ物 is an object that has been left behind, or the act of leaving something behind itself; "to leave something behind" is 忘れ物をする. Politely with お: お忘れ物ですよ "you forgot something", and on trains one hears お忘れ物のないようご注意ください. It should be distinguished from 落とし物: that is something lost along the way, whereas 忘れ物 is something one has left standing somewhere.

examples[].german: Has a black wallet been turned in as lost property?
I lost something on the train.
I took the item I found on the street to the police box.
en.notes: 落とし物 is an item that has been lost or dropped somewhere, that is, lost property from the point of view of the loser or the finder. Typical are 落とし物をする "to lose something", 落とし物を交番に届ける and 落とし物センター. To be distinguished from this is 忘れ物: something that you have left lying somewhere or forgotten. The related verb is 落とす "to drop, to lose".

examples[].german: Please be careful with your valuables.
We will keep your valuables at the front desk.
Before going into the pool, I put my valuables in a locker.
en.notes: 貴重品 are valuables such as a wallet, passport, jewelry or mobile phone. The word often appears on notices in hotels, baths and trains: 貴重品はお手元に, 貴重品ロッカー. Typical are 貴重品を預ける "to leave valuables in safekeeping" and 貴重品に気をつける. It is based on the adjective 貴重な "valuable, precious", which is also used for experiences (貴重な体験).

examples[].german: Please check your belongings.
I had my belongings inspected at the airport.
The police searched the man's belongings.
en.notes: 所持品 are the things someone carries with them; the word is formal and appears mainly in police, security and exam contexts: 所持品検査, 所持品を調べる. In everyday speech one says 持ち物, e.g. on packing lists for an outing. It is based on 所持する "to carry, possess".

examples[].german: I will check my baggage.
You can bring only one piece of baggage into the cabin.
I'm waiting at baggage claim for my suitcase to come out.
en.notes: 手荷物 is the luggage a traveler has with them. At the airport it includes both checked baggage (手荷物を預ける, 手荷物受取所 "baggage claim") and carry-on baggage; the latter is precisely called 機内持ち込み手荷物. In everyday speech people mostly simply say 荷物. The word is rather formal and often appears on signs and in announcements.

examples[].german: Let's pack.
I haven't finished packing for the move yet.
On the night before the trip, I packed in a hurry.
en.notes: 荷造り means "to pack up things, to pack luggage or boxes", for example before a trip or a move. Typical phrases are 荷造りをする, 引っ越しの荷造り and 旅行の荷造り. In everyday speech one also says 荷物をまとめる or パッキング. The opposite, unpacking after a move, is 荷ほどき. The spelling 荷作り is occasionally seen.

examples[].german: Theory and practice are different.
It is possible in theory, but difficult in reality.
This is a book that explains Einstein's theory in an easy-to-understand way.
en.notes: 理論 is a theory: 理論を立てる, 〜の理論, 理論的な. Often in contrast to practice: 理論と実践, 理論上は "theoretically". 理屈, by contrast, means "logic, reasoning" and often sounds derogatory (理屈を言う "to quibble"), and 説 is a doctrine or hypothesis.

examples[].german: I am getting ready to go out.
If you don't get ready quickly, you'll be late for school.
Have you finished packing for the trip yet?
en.notes: 支度 is everyday preparation, especially getting ready and preparing meals: 出かける支度, 食事の支度, 身支度 "getting dressed and groomed". One says 支度をする or, shortened, 支度する. 準備 is more general and more formal (also for projects and exams), and 用意 emphasizes making things available. 仕度 is a rarer spelling variant of the same word.

examples[].german: I get ready.
Get ready before the guests arrive.
I overslept, so I got ready in five minutes and left the house.
en.notes: 身支度 means "getting oneself ready": dressing, doing one's hair, putting on makeup, i.e. preparing one's appearance for going out. Typical are 身支度をする, 身支度を整える and 身支度を済ませる. 支度 or 準備 on their own mean general preparations (夕食の支度), and 着替える only changing clothes. The word is neutral to slightly written; in conversation people often simply say 準備する.

examples[].german: I will do the preparation in advance.
I did the preparation for cooking, such as cutting the vegetables, the day before.
I prepared thoroughly, so I was able to explain well in the meeting.
en.notes: 下準備 is the preliminary work done beforehand so that the actual work goes smoothly: in cooking cutting and marinating, at work gathering material. Typical are 下準備をする and 下準備をしておく; 〜ておく fits especially well because it is about preparing in advance. 準備 is the general term, whereas 下準備 stresses the basic first steps.

examples[].german: I will proceed in an organized way.
The arrangements were poor, so preparations took a long time.
Let's decide the arrangements for tomorrow's event by the end of today.
en.notes: 段取り is the planned sequence of work steps, i.e. how one organizes and prepares something. Typical phrases: 段取りがいい/悪い "well/badly organized", 段取りよく "in an efficiently planned way", 段取りをつける/決める "to set the procedures". In contrast to 手順 (the fixed order of a procedure), 段取り is about forward-looking planning; 手際, by contrast, describes skill in carrying something out.

examples[].german: I will arrange the hotel.
I have arranged a taxi for you, so please wait at the entrance.
That man is wanted nationwide.
en.notes: 手配 means "to organize, procure, arrange", e.g. a hotel, tickets, a taxi or staff: 〜を手配する, 〜の手配をする. It sounds more businesslike than 用意する or 準備する and stresses that one orders something from third parties or sets it in motion. A second meaning is a police manhunt, especially in 指名手配 "wanted (by the police)".

examples[].german: I cook skillfully.
Even though he is new, he works quite efficiently.
I was so clumsy that cleaning up took a full two hours.
en.notes: 手際 refers to the skill and efficiency with which someone gets a job done in practice. It almost always appears in fixed combinations: 手際がいい/悪い and adverbial 手際よく "quickly and skillfully". The opposite 不手際 means "clumsiness, oversight" and is often used in apologies. While 段取り concerns planning in advance, 手際 describes the execution itself.

examples[].german: I will check the procedure.
Please assemble it step by step according to the instructions.
I got one step wrong, so I have to start over from the beginning.
en.notes: 手順 is the fixed sequence of steps, i.e. the procedure: 手順を守る, 手順を確認する, 手順通りに "according to the procedure, step by step", 手順を間違える. Compared with 順番 ("order, whose turn it is"), 手順 refers to work steps. 段取り, by contrast, stresses the planning and organization of the whole.

examples[].german: I will show you a sample.
Replicas of the dishes are displayed in front of the restaurant.
He is always late and is a bad example.
en.notes: 見本 is a sample or specimen that shows what something looks like: 商品の見本, 料理の見本 (the plastic food displays in front of restaurants), 見本市 "trade fair". It also means "example, model case", as in いい見本 or 悪い見本. A model to imitate is rather 手本; in commerce people today often also say サンプル.

examples[].german: I write by looking at the teacher's model.
I took my senior colleague as a model and learned the job.
Parents have to set a good example for their children.
en.notes: 手本 is a model or template to imitate: originally a writing or drawing model, today also a person with exemplary behavior. Typical are 〜を手本にする "to take ... as a model", 手本を見せる and the polite everyday お手本. Unlike 見本 (sample, specimen), 手本 always carries the idea of imitation.

examples[].german: I will explain the basic principles.
Do you know the principle by which airplanes fly?
Prices are determined by market forces.
en.notes: 原理 is the fundamental principle by which something works: 〜の原理, 基本原理, 〜が動く原理, 市場原理 "market mechanism". Distinction: 原則 is a rule one adheres to (原則として), 法則 is an observed regularity (物理の法則). So 原理 explains the "why" of a mechanism.

examples[].german: I have circumstances and cannot go.
Please explain the circumstances of your delay.
The housing situation in Tokyo is quite tough.
en.notes: 事情 are the circumstances or background of a situation. Very common is the politely vague reason 事情があって "for certain reasons", with which one need not name private reasons; similar is 家庭の事情 "family reasons". Other phrases: 事情を説明する, 事情が変わる, and as a suffix 住宅事情 or 交通事情 "housing/traffic situation". 理由, by contrast, names the concrete reason directly.

examples[].german: It was a valuable experience.
In Kyoto, I tried wearing a kimono.
At this gym, you can try it out once for free.
en.notes: 体験 is a firsthand, direct experience you have had yourself: 〜を体験する, 体験談 "personal account", 無料体験 "free trial session", 職場体験 "work experience placement". 経験 is more general and also means accumulated experience and knowledge, e.g. 仕事の経験がある. For something one-off that you experienced yourself, 体験 fits better; for work experience, always 経験.

examples[].german: Please tell me your impressions.
We all discussed our impressions after watching the movie.
For summer vacation homework, I wrote a book report.
en.notes: 感想 are one's personal impressions and thoughts after an experience, for example after a film, book or event. Typical are 感想を言う/述べる/書く, 感想を聞かせてください and 読書感想文 "book report as a school essay". 意見, by contrast, is an opinion or statement on a question; 印象 is the impression something or someone makes.

examples[].german: It is a restaurant with a good reputation.
That movie is said to be boring.
The newly opened bakery in front of the station is the talk of the town.
en.notes: 評判 is the reputation or what people say about something: 評判がいい/悪い, 評判の店 "a shop everyone is talking about". With 〜と評判だ you convey the general assessment ("is reputed to be ..."), and 評判になる means "to become the talk of the town, become known". 噂 refers more to unconfirmed rumors about people, 人気 to popularity itself.

examples[].german: I am concerned about what other people think.
Meeting in a place like this, it's a small world, isn't it?
He is naive about the world and often gets deceived.
en.notes: 世間 is "the people, the world out there", i.e. society from the individual's point of view, especially as a judging public: 世間の目 "what people think", 世間体 "reputation, appearances". Other set expressions: 世間話 "small talk", 世間知らず "naive about the world", 世間は狭い "the world is small". 社会 is more abstract and objective, and 世論 means measurable public opinion.

examples[].german: We conducted an opinion poll.
Much of public opinion is against the new law.
The government changed its plan out of concern for public opinion.
en.notes: 世論 is the public opinion of the population on political or social issues; it is read よろん or せろん. Typical are 世論調査 "opinion poll", 世論が高まる and 世論を気にする. The word belongs mainly to news and politics. 世間, by contrast, generally means "the people" and their judgment in everyday life.

examples[].german: It is a recent trend.
The tendency to think that you don't need to marry early is spreading.
I have doubts about the tendency to think of everything in terms of money.
en.notes: 風潮 is a social current or tendency, often with a slightly critical undertone: 〜という風潮がある, 風潮が広がる, 社会の風潮. In contrast to 流行 (fashion, what is currently "in"), it is about ways of thinking and behaving; 傾向 is more neutral and is also used for data or individuals. The word is rather literary and common in commentaries or the news.

examples[].german: The food went bad.
The milk has gone bad and smells strange.
Don't get discouraged just because you failed once.
en.notes: 腐る is intransitive: food spoils or rots (牛乳が腐る), wood or metal decays. Figuratively it means "to lose heart, sulk" (腐るなよ) or "to be morally corrupt" (腐った政治). The transitive partner is 腐らせる "to let spoil". Well known is the proverb 腐っても鯛 "a sea bream is still a sea bream even when it has spoiled".

en.meaning: to wither; to shrivel; to deflate
examples[].german: The flower withered.
The balloon deflated and became small.
After losing the match, the dream of winning the title shriveled away.
en.notes: 萎む is mostly written in kana しぼむ and is intransitive: flowers wilt, a balloon or tire loses air, and in a figurative sense hopes or dreams fade (夢がしぼむ). 枯れる, by contrast, means that a plant dries out completely and dies; 縮む means "to shrink" (e.g. clothing). The transitive form is しぼませる.

en.meaning: to become accustomed; to blend in
examples[].german: I got used to the new environment.
These shoes have finally molded to my feet.
My little sister, who had transferred schools, quickly fit in with the class.
en.notes: 馴染む (often in kana なじむ) is intransitive and takes に: 新しい環境になじむ "to settle in", 職場になじむ. With things it means "to fit, to blend in": 靴が足になじむ, 化粧が肌になじむ. The noun なじみ appears in なじみの店 "regular haunt" and 幼なじみ "childhood friend". 慣れる emphasizes getting used to an activity, なじむ harmonious belonging.

examples[].german: I study the laws of physics.
Newton discovered the law of universal gravitation.
Apparently, popular shops follow a certain pattern.
en.notes: 法則 is a regularity, above all in nature and science: 自然の法則, 物理の法則, 万有引力の法則. Used loosely, it also refers to recurring patterns in everyday life (成功の法則). Do not confuse it with 法律 "law (legal)" and 規則 "regulation"; 原則 is a rule one adheres to, whereas 法則 is one that simply holds.

examples[].german: The flavor has soaked in.
The rainwater slowly seeps into the ground.
The habits from my childhood are ingrained in me.
en.notes: 染み込む is intransitive and means "to soak into, to seep into something": liquid or flavor penetrates deeply (味が染み込む, 雨が地面に染み込む). Figuratively, habits or experiences are said to "become second nature" (体に染み込む). Compared with 染みる, 〜込む emphasizes penetrating to the inside. The transitive form is 染み込ませる; it is also often written しみ込む.

en.meaning: to soak in; to sting; to touch
examples[].german: It is a song that touches the heart.
When I cut onions, my eyes sting.
Cold water makes my teeth hurt.
en.notes: 染みる is usually written in kana as しみる and is intransitive with に. It means "to seep in", but very often "to sting, burn": 目にしみる (onions, smoke), 傷にしみる, 歯にしみる (sensitive teeth). Figuratively it means "to touch the heart": 心にしみる, 身にしみる "to feel something keenly"; the spelling 沁みる is also seen for this. The noun 染み means "stain".

examples[].german: The writing blurred because of tears.
Blood is seeping out of the knee I fell on.
His love for his family showed through in his letter.
en.notes: 滲む (usually in kana as にじむ) is intransitive: ink or color bleeds, outlines blur, blood, sweat or tears seep out (額に汗がにじむ, 血がにじむ). Figuratively, a feeling shows indirectly in words or gestures, often as にじみ出る. Typical patterns are 〜で滲む for the cause and 〜に滲む for the place. Distinguish it from 染みる "to soak in, sting".

en.meaning: to glare at; to stare angrily
examples[].german: Please don't glare at me.
The teacher glared at the noisy students.
The police suspect that man is the culprit.
en.notes: 睨む (often in kana にらむ) is transitive: 〜をにらむ "to glare at someone, to look at them sternly"; intensified, にらみつける. With 〜とにらむ it means "to suspect, to have one's suspicions", for example with police or detectives. 見つめる, by contrast, is a neutral, attentive look without hostility. The phrase 上司ににらまれる means "to be on the boss's bad side".

en.meaning: to gaze at; to look at
examples[].german: I am gazing at the scenery.
I was vacantly looking outside from the train window.
I sat on a bench and watched the children play.
en.notes: 眺める is transitive (〜を眺める) and means "to look at calmly, let one's gaze wander", especially at landscapes, the sky or the goings-on outside. It can also mean to watch something idly from the outside. 見る is general, 見つめる is a concentrated stare, and 見渡す is surveying a wide area. The noun 眺め means "view": 眺めがいい.

en.meaning: to be spellbound; to gaze in admiration
examples[].german: I was captivated by the beautiful scenery.
I couldn't help being captivated by her smile.
I was so spellbound by the fireworks that I forgot to take photos.
en.notes: 見惚れる is intransitive: what one is spellbound by takes に - 景色に見惚れる, 笑顔に見惚れる. Typical are 思わず見惚れる and つい見惚れてしまう for an involuntary, admiring gaze. Unlike 見つめる ("to stare at", with を), 見惚れる emphasizes the fascination in which one forgets everything else. It is often written half in kana as 見とれる; the reading みほれる is rare.

examples[].german: I woke up at six in the morning.
I discovered a passion for music when I was in high school.
After the operation, the patient did not wake up for a long time.
en.notes: 目覚める means "to wake up", but sounds more elevated and literary than the everyday 目が覚める; "to get up" is 起きる, by contrast. Figuratively, 〜に目覚める means "to awaken to something, to discover something in oneself": 音楽に目覚める, 才能に目覚める. The verb is intransitive; "to wake someone" is 起こす, "to make someone awaken" is 目覚めさせる. Related are the noun 目覚め and 目覚まし時計 "alarm clock".

examples[].german: Please don't stay up late.
I stayed up late yesterday and am very sleepy today.
I hear that staying up late is bad for the skin.
en.notes: 夜更かし is staying up late at night, usually as an intransitive する-verb: 夜更かしする. It is not about going out or partying, but simply about going to bed late (e.g. because of games, studying, TV series). Someone who stays up all night says 徹夜する. The counterpart is 早寝早起き; it is also often written in a kana mix as 夜ふかし.

examples[].german: He is a late riser.
I overslept this morning and was late for work.
On Sunday I want to sleep in leisurely.
en.notes: 朝寝坊 refers above all to oversleeping or sleeping late in the morning: 朝寝坊する, often with the consequence 遅刻する. Shortened, one also says simply 寝坊する. It can also denote a person: 彼は朝寝坊だ "He is a late sleeper". The opposite is 早起き; 寝過ごす also means to oversleep, including riding past your stop on a train.

examples[].german: In principle, I agree.
In principle, our store does not accept returns.
"One person, one vote" is a basic principle of elections.
en.notes: 原則 is a principle or general rule. Very common is 原則として or 原則的に "in principle, as a rule", which hints at exceptions; in notices also simply 原則、… at the start of a sentence. Other combinations: 原則を守る, 基本原則. Distinction: 原理 explains how something works, 原則 lays down how one should act.

examples[].german: Jogging is my daily routine.
I make it a daily habit to write in my diary before going to bed.
Walking the dog is my father's daily task.
en.notes: 日課 is something that one does habitually every day. Typical patterns are 〜が日課だ, 〜のが日課です and 〜を日課にする ("to make something a daily habit"). Unlike 習慣 ("habit" in general, also bad ones), 日課 is a daily task that is consciously kept up. A daily plan with times, by contrast, is called スケジュール.

examples[].german: I take lessons.
As a child, I attended piano and swimming lessons.
Many people also start new lessons after becoming adults.
en.notes: 習い事 are courses or lessons outside school, especially hobbies and skills such as piano, swimming, calligraphy or ballet. You say 習い事をする, 習い事に通う or ask 何か習い事をしていますか. Tutoring in school subjects, by contrast, is 塾; teaching at school is 授業. The word is typical for children but is also used by adults.

examples[].german: I go to tea ceremony lessons every Saturday.
I train in kendo at the dojo every day.
Before the actual performance, the actors rehearsed over and over.
en.notes: 稽古 is practice in traditional arts and martial arts (tea ceremony, ikebana, kendo, sumo) as well as rehearsal in the theater. One says 稽古をする, 稽古に通う, 稽古を重ねる; 稽古をつける means "to teach, to train someone". The polite form お稽古 often stands for lessons in tea, flowers or piano. For ordinary practice in sports or music, 練習 is the neutral word.

examples[].german: After years of hard training, he became a full-fledged craftsman.
I trained at a temple for a week.
He is still in training, so he is not allowed to cook yet.
en.notes: 修行 is hard, demanding training: originally religious asceticism (お寺で修行する, 山で修行する), today also the strict apprenticeship in a craft or kitchen (修行を積む, 修行中). The similar 修業（しゅうぎょう） refers more to learning a trade; for craft apprenticeships both spellings are found. Compared with 練習 or 稽古, 修行 sounds much more serious and longer-term. As a する-verb it is usually used without an object: 〜で修行する.

examples[].german: I train my body.
I never skip my morning training.
In martial arts, it is said that training of mind and body is important.
en.notes: 鍛錬 (also 鍛練) is steeling body and mind through hard, persistent training; originally it meant forging metal. It sounds written and serious: 心身を鍛錬する, 日々の鍛錬, 鍛錬を怠らない. In everyday speech people prefer the verb 鍛える (体を鍛える) or トレーニングする. The word is typical in the context of martial arts and sports.

examples[].german: My Japanese has improved.
If you practice every day, you'll improve quickly.
She improves at tennis very quickly.
en.notes: 上達 is progress in a skill: X が上達する (intransitive), for example 日本語が上達する, ピアノが上達する. Common are 上達が早い and 上達のコツ. Colloquially people simply say うまくなる; 進歩 is more general (also technology, science), and 向上 stresses the rise of a level. 上達 doesn't fit health or a situation; there you say 良くなる or 改善する.

examples[].german: He is a skilled engineer.
This work requires skill.
Skilled craftsmen make them by hand one by one.
en.notes: 熟練 is skill acquired through long experience. It mostly stands attributively: 熟練した職人, 熟練の技, or in compounds such as 熟練者 and 熟練工. It sounds somewhat formal; colloquially such people are called ベテラン. In contrast to 上手 "skillful", 熟練 stresses the long practice behind it.

examples[].german: My cooking skills have improved.
His golf skills are at a professional level.
Today is a chance to show the guests my proud skills.
en.notes: 腕前 is concrete, showable skill in an activity such as cooking, golf or craftwork; 腕 ("arm") stands for skill here. Typical are 〜の腕前, 腕前が上がる, 腕前を見せる/披露する and 腕前はプロ並み. The shorter and more colloquial 腕 (腕がいい) also exists. 能力, by contrast, means abstract ability, and 技術 means technique.

examples[].german: My special skill is piano.
In the interview, I was asked, "What is your special skill?"
His special skill is remembering a song immediately after hearing it once.
en.notes: 特技 is a concrete ability that one can demonstrate, such as an instrument, a language or a trick. On a résumé and in job interviews, the classic question is about 趣味 and 特技 ("hobbies and special skills"). 趣味 is what you like to do, 得意 (な-adjective) means "to be good at" (ピアノが得意だ), and 才能 is more of an innate talent. The pattern 特技は〜です is typical.

examples[].german: He has an aptitude for sports.
The teacher said this child has what it takes to be a musician.
Not only aptitude but also effort is important.
en.notes: 素質 is an innate disposition or potential for something: 〜の素質がある/ない, 素質に恵まれる, 〜としての素質. Unlike 才能, which also means developed talent, 素質 emphasizes the predisposition that still has to be nurtured. Not to be confused with 性質 ("property, nature").

examples[].german: I will look at the population trend.
This year's sales are progressing smoothly.
Please check the temperature trend on the graph.
en.notes: 推移 is the development or change of something over time, typically for figures and statistics: 人口の推移, 売り上げの推移. As an intransitive する-verb: 順調に推移する, 高い水準で推移する. It is formal and belongs in reports and the news; the more general word is 変化, and for the course of a process, 経過.

examples[].german: He is a genius.
She is called a math genius.
To come up with an idea like this, you're a genius!
en.notes: 天才 is a genius or prodigy: 〜の天才 (数学の天才), 天才児, adjectivally 天才的な. Colloquially it is often used as exaggerated praise: お前、天才だな! In contrast, 秀才 is someone who achieves very good results through diligence; the opposite of 天才 is 凡人.

examples[].german: I am an ordinary person.
What do you think is the difference between a genius and an ordinary person?
As an ordinary person, I can't really understand his thinking.
en.notes: 凡人 is an ordinary person without special talent, often in contrast to 天才. It is often used humbly about oneself: 私のような凡人には.... The word sounds somewhat literary; neutrally one says 普通の人. 一般人, by contrast, means the "ordinary citizen" as opposed to celebrities or experts.

examples[].german: He is a master of cooking.
My grandfather was a master of kendo.
She is a master of saving money and puts away a lot every month.
en.notes: 達人 is someone who masters an art or skill brilliantly: 剣の達人, 料理の達人. Casually it is also used for everyday talents, such as 節約の達人 "master of thrift". 名人 sounds more like a title (e.g. in shogi), 専門家 is the specialist with expert knowledge, and プロ the professional who lives off it.

examples[].german: I take on a disciple.
I became an apprentice of a famous chef.
The master was very strict with his disciples.
en.notes: 弟子 is the pupil or apprentice of a master (師匠) in traditional arts, crafts, martial arts or religion. Typical are 弟子になる, 弟子入りする ("to become someone's apprentice") and 弟子を取る ("to take on a pupil"); the first and most important disciple is the 一番弟子. For pupils of a school, by contrast, one says 生徒 or 学生.

examples[].german: I learn from my master.
I asked a rakugo master to take me on as an apprentice.
Master, I look forward to working with you again today.
en.notes: 師匠 is the master or teacher in traditional arts, crafts, martial arts or rakugo; the counterpart is 弟子. It is also used as a form of address: 師匠! In sumo it denotes the stable master. 先生 is more general (teacher, doctor, lawyer), whereas 恩師 means a former teacher to whom one is grateful.

examples[].german: I am going to visit my former teacher.
At the wedding, my former teacher gave a speech for me.
I am who I am today thanks to my former teacher.
en.notes: 恩師 is a former teacher to whom one owes a great deal; the word expresses respect and gratitude. It is used about one's own former teachers, for example at class reunions, in wedding speeches or in thank-you notes: 恩師に会う, 恩師のおかげ. As a direct form of address, 先生 is used, not 恩師. 師匠, by contrast, is the master of an art.

examples[].german: At the end of the year, I go to greet our clients.
Mr. Tanaka from the sales department visits clients every day.
We can't afford to lose an important client.
en.notes: 得意先 is a business term for a company's regular customers, mostly in the B2B field. Typical are 得意先を回る "to make the rounds of clients", 得意先に挨拶に行く and, politely, お得意様. 取引先 is more general "business partner" (also suppliers), and 顧客 is the formal "customer". Regulars at shops or restaurants are rather called 常連(客).

examples[].german: I met an acquaintance.
We use the same station, so I know him by sight.
The culprit seems to have been an acquaintance of the victim.
en.notes: 顔見知り is someone you know by sight and perhaps greet, but are not really acquainted with. Typical are 顔見知りになる and 〜とは顔見知りだ. 知り合い is an acquaintance you have already talked to, and 友達 a friend. Do not confuse it with 人見知り "shyness toward strangers".

examples[].german: I go to my regular shop.
I am not very familiar with traditional Japanese music.
An actor familiar from TV was at the station.
en.notes: 馴染み (often written なじみ) means familiarity through frequent contact. 馴染みの店 is a regular haunt, 馴染みの客 a regular customer, 幼馴染み a friend from childhood. 〜に馴染みがある/ない means "to be familiar / not familiar with something", and お馴染み means "well-known, familiar" (お馴染みの曲). The verb 馴染む "to get used to, become familiar" belongs here.

examples[].german: I will explain to the residents.
I got a certificate of residence at the city hall.
Many residents are opposed to the new road plan.
en.notes: 住民 are the inhabitants of a certain area or place, above all in administrative and news contexts: 地域住民, 住民税, 住民票 "certificate of residence", 住民の反対. 市民 stresses the citizen of a city with rights, 国民 the people of a nation. 住人 is more the occupant of a specific house or apartment.

examples[].german: I am looking into market trends.
Please keep a close eye on the typhoon's movements.
Each company is paying attention to young people's spending trends.
en.notes: 動向 are the movements and developments of a group, a market or a situation: 市場の動向, 世論の動向, 台風の動向, 消費動向. Typical verbs: 動向を調べる/見守る, 動向に注目する/注意する. Formal, typical of news and business. 傾向, by contrast, is a lasting inclination or tendency.

examples[].german: We listen to the voices of the citizens.
The municipal pool is open every day during the summer.
I have been a citizen of Yokohama for ten years.
en.notes: 市民 first of all refers to the inhabitants of a city (市): 横浜市民, 市民プール, 市民会館. It is also used more generally for "citizen" in the political sense, for example 市民の声 or 市民運動. 国民, by contrast, are the nationals of a country, and 住民 the residents of a particular area or building. The word is neutral and common in administration and news.

examples[].german: It is a duty of the citizens.
May 5 is a national holiday.
The prime minister called on the people to cooperate.
en.notes: 国民 are the people or citizens of a country as a whole, typical in politics, law and the news: 国民の祝日 "national holiday", 国民健康保険, 国民性 "national character". In contrast, 民族 denotes an ethnic group, 市民 the citizens of a city and 住民 the residents of an area. In everyday speech people rather say 人々 or 日本人.

en.meaning: the masses; the general public; popular
examples[].german: Manga is part of Japan's popular culture.
Near the station there is an inexpensive and tasty casual restaurant.
This magazine is written in an easy-to-understand way for the general public.
en.notes: 大衆 is the broad masses, the general public, especially as consumers and a target audience. It most often appears in compounds: 大衆文化 ("popular culture"), 大衆食堂 ("simple, cheap eatery"), 大衆向け, and adjectival 大衆的な. 群衆, by contrast, is a concrete crowd of people in one place. On its own, 大衆 sounds somewhat sociological and literary.

examples[].german: A crowd has gathered.
The crying of a child could be heard from within the crowd.
The police called on the crowd to clear the way.
en.notes: 群衆 is a crowd of people that has physically gathered in one place: 群衆が集まる, 群衆の中, 群衆を押しのける. The word is rather literary and typical of the news; in everyday speech one says 人込み or 大勢の人. Unlike 大衆 ("the broad masses" as a social stratum), 群衆 always means a concrete crowd.

examples[].german: May I ask your age?
You can apply for this part-time job regardless of age.
Please write your name and age on the application form.
en.notes: 年齢 is the formal word for "age" and typically appears in forms, rules and statistics: 年齢制限, 年齢を問わず ("regardless of age"), 年齢層. In conversation one says 年（とし） more often, asks 何歳ですか, or politely おいくつですか. Asking directly about someone's 年齢 sounds somewhat official.

examples[].german: Gender does not matter.
Please enter your name, age and gender on the form.
We knew the baby's sex before it was born.
en.notes: 性別 is gender as a category, for example in forms, statistics and rules: 性別欄, 性別を問わず ("regardless of gender"), 性別による差別. In conversation people ask 男の子？女の子？ rather than about the 性別. For man/woman there are 男性 and 女性.

examples[].german: What is your blood type?
In Japan, many people tell fortunes by blood type.
They check your blood type before surgery.
en.notes: 血液型 is the blood type; the types are called A型, B型, O型 and AB型, and one asks 何型ですか. In Japan, blood type is a popular small-talk topic because many people believe it reveals character (血液型占い, 血液型性格診断). Medically it appears, for example, in 血液型を調べる.

examples[].german: What is your star sign?
In the winter night sky, you can see constellations such as Orion well.
I like watching the horoscope on TV in the morning.
en.notes: 星座 means both the constellation in the sky and the zodiac sign in astrology. Individual constellations/signs are formed with 〜座: オリオン座, しし座, おうし座; the question is 何座ですか. The horoscope by star sign is called 星座占い and often airs on morning TV in Japan.

examples[].german: That's a good omen, isn't it?
Please don't say such ominous things.
In Japan, four is considered an unlucky number because it sounds the same as "death".
en.notes: 縁起 refers to an omen of good or bad luck: 縁起がいい/悪い, 縁起物 "lucky charm", 縁起を担ぐ "to pay attention to good omens". The set phrase 縁起でもない wards off ominous words, as in "Don't tempt fate!". A second, written meaning is the origin story of a temple or shrine (寺の縁起). 運, by contrast, is luck itself.

examples[].german: That is a superstition.
There is a superstition that you must not cut your nails at night.
My grandmother still believes in old superstitions.
en.notes: 迷信 is superstition, that is, a belief without rational basis: 迷信を信じる, ただの迷信, 〜という迷信がある, 迷信深い ("superstitious"). Unlike 縁起 (a concrete sign of good or bad luck) and 言い伝え (tradition, not necessarily false), 迷信 dismisses the matter as unfounded.

examples[].german: We will proceed to the next stage.
This plan is still in the preparation stage.
At this stage, nothing has been decided yet.
en.notes: 段階 is a step or phase in a development: 次の段階に進む, 準備の段階, 最終段階. With 〜の段階で it means "at the stage of, at the time of": 今の段階では "at the present stage". The adverb 段階的に means "step by step". In contrast to 過程, the whole course of events, 段階 counts the individual sections; it also stands for gradations as in 五段階評価 "rating on a five-point scale".

examples[].german: I will follow the company's policy.
Our educational policy is to let children do what they like.
Next year's course of action was decided at the meeting.
en.notes: 方針 is the set course or guideline by which an organization or person acts: 方針を決める/立てる/変える, 会社の方針, 教育方針, 〜という方針だ. Note: the English word "policy" is a common translation, but 方針 means "course of action, guiding principle"; government policy is 政策.

examples[].german: There is an old legend.
According to legend, a dragon lives in this pond.
I told the children a legend I had heard from my grandfather.
en.notes: 言い伝え is something passed down orally from generation to generation: 昔からの言い伝え, 〜という言い伝えがある, 言い伝えによると. It can be a legend, a piece of folk wisdom or a folk belief. 伝説 is more of an embellished legend about places or heroes, and 迷信 a belief judged to be unfounded. The related verb is 言い伝える.

en.meaning: folk tale; old story; reminiscing about the past
examples[].german: I read Japanese folk tales.
"Momotaro" is a famous folk tale.
At the class reunion, we got caught up in reminiscing.
en.notes: 昔話 are, on the one hand, folk tales such as 桃太郎 or 浦島太郎, which begin with むかしむかし. On the other hand, it means telling about the past: 昔話をする, 昔話に花が咲く ("to indulge in reminiscences"). 童話 is more of a children's story (often written by an author), and 物語 means a story or tale in general.

examples[].german: It is a beautiful story.
This is the story of a boy who grew up in a small village.
"The Tale of Genji" was written more than a thousand years ago.
en.notes: 物語 is a story or tale, fictional or true: 〜の物語, 物語を書く/語る. Many classical works carry it in the title, for example 源氏物語 and 竹取物語. 話 is more general ("conversation, story"), ストーリー refers more to the plot, and 小説 to the novel. The verb 物語る figuratively means "to show clearly".

examples[].german: There is an old legend.
A legend of a mermaid remains about this lake.
He is still popular today as a legendary soccer player.
en.notes: 伝説 is a legend about places, heroes or events: 〜の伝説, 〜という伝説がある, 伝説が残る; 都市伝説 is the "urban legend". In modern use, 伝説の is also used for "legendary": 伝説の選手, 伝説のバンド. 言い伝え stresses oral tradition, and 神話 stresses myths of the gods.

examples[].german: I study Japanese mythology.
Many gods appear in Greek mythology.
The earthquake shattered this country's "myth of safety".
en.notes: 神話 is a myth or the mythology of a people: ギリシャ神話, 日本神話 (handed down in the 古事記, among others). Figuratively, 〜神話 denotes a widespread but unfounded belief, such as 安全神話 ("myth of safety"); typical is 神話が崩れる. Legends about people and places, by contrast, are called 伝説.

examples[].german: I like stories about yokai.
Kappa and tengu are famous yokai.
When I was a child, I was often told that yokai appear in the mountains at night.
en.notes: 妖怪 are supernatural beings of Japanese folklore, such as 河童, 天狗 or 雪女; you say 妖怪が出る. 幽霊, by contrast, is the ghost of a dead person, and お化け is the colloquial umbrella term for haunting creatures. Through manga and anime such as ゲゲゲの鬼太郎 or 妖怪ウォッチ, 妖怪 are also very present in pop culture.

examples[].german: Have you seen a ghost?
There is a rumor that this old inn is haunted.
He is a ghost member of the tennis club and never comes to practice.
en.notes: 幽霊 is the spirit of a dead person; in the Japanese image, in a white robe and without feet. Typical are 幽霊が出る ("it is haunted"), 幽霊を見る and 幽霊屋敷 ("haunted house"). Figuratively, 幽霊〜 stands for something that exists only on paper: 幽霊部員 (inactive club member), 幽霊会社 (shell company). 妖怪, by contrast, are legendary creatures, and お化け is the casual everyday word.

examples[].german: The oni comes on Setsubun.
In the game of tag, I'm "it" next.
When it comes to work, the department manager is demonically strict.
en.notes: 鬼 is the horned ogre of Japanese folklore, often red or blue, with an iron club and tiger-skin loincloth. At 節分, families throw beans and shout 鬼は外、福は内. In tag (鬼ごっこ) or hide-and-seek, the 鬼 is the chaser or seeker. Figuratively it stands for relentlessness: 鬼のように厳しい, 仕事の鬼, 鬼コーチ; in youth slang it is also an intensifier (鬼かわいい).

examples[].german: There is a legend of the tengu.
The tengu is a yokai with a red face and a long nose.
You shouldn't get conceited just because you won a game once.
en.notes: 天狗 is a mountain spirit of Japanese folklore with a red face, long nose, wings and a feather fan; a variant with a bird's beak is called 烏天狗. Because of the long nose (cf. 鼻が高い "to be proud"), 天狗 figuratively stands for arrogance: 天狗になる "to become conceited", often after a success. The word is usually written in kanji.

examples[].german: The kappa is a Japanese yokai.
It is said that kappa like cucumbers.
"Kappa no kawanagare" means that even masters sometimes make mistakes.
en.notes: 河童 is a water creature of rivers and ponds with a water-filled dish (皿) on its head, a beak and a shell; it is often also written カッパ. Because it supposedly loves cucumbers, the cucumber sushi roll is called かっぱ巻き. The proverb 河童の川流れ ("even a kappa is swept away by the river") means that even masters make mistakes.

examples[].german: I will think of a new strategy.
To win the match, the team made a strategy.
This company is pursuing a strategy that emphasizes overseas markets.
en.notes: 戦略 is a long-term strategy, originally military, today mainly in business, politics and sports: 戦略を立てる/練る, 経営戦略, 販売戦略, 戦略的な. Distinction: 戦術 is the concrete tactic in an individual case, 作戦 the plan for a particular operation (also used casually in daily life).

examples[].german: I will send the invoice.
I was charged 10,000 yen for the repair.
I forgot to claim my transportation costs from the company.
en.notes: 請求 is demanding money or a right; as a transitive する-verb: (人)に料金を請求する, passive 〜を請求される "to be billed". Very common are 請求書 "invoice", 請求額 and 損害賠償を請求する. 要求 is a more general "to demand", 依頼 a polite request; the receipt after payment is called 領収書.

examples[].german: I will check the delivery date.
The ordered goods will be delivered next Monday.
We will send the delivery note and the invoice together.
en.notes: 納品 is the delivery of ordered goods to a business customer; as a する-verb it is mostly transitive: 商品を納品する. Typical are 納品日, 納品書 "delivery note" and 期日までに納品する. 配達 is delivery (mail, parcels, pizza) to private individuals, and 出荷 shipping from a warehouse. The word clearly belongs to business language.

examples[].german: I bought shares.
My father runs a small joint-stock company.
Recently, the stock market has been moving sharply.
en.notes: 株式 is the share as a formal economic term: 株式市場, 株式投資, 株式を発行する. It is most often met in 株式会社 ("joint-stock company", read かぶしきがいしゃ), which appears in almost every company name. In everyday speech, shares are usually just 株: 株を買う.

examples[].german: I will submit the notification.
When you move, you need to file a notification at the city hall within 14 days.
I lost my wallet, so I filed a report with the police.
en.notes: 届出 (also 届け出) is an official notification to authorities, the police or an employer: 届出をする, 届出を提出する, 届出が必要だ. Certain notifications are named with the ending 〜届（とどけ）: 婚姻届, 出生届, 転居届. The verb is 届け出る. 申請, by contrast, is an application for permission, and 申込 a registration for something.

examples[].german: Please fill in the application form.
The application deadline is the 30th of this month.
You can sign up for this seminar online.
en.notes: 申込 is the application, sign-up or order for something. In running text one usually writes 申し込み; the short form 申込 appears mainly in compounds and forms: 申込書, 申込用紙, 申込締切. The verb is 申し込む (〜に申し込む). 申請 is an application to an authority, 応募 is applying for a job, competition or prize draw, and 予約 is a reservation.

examples[].german: Your boss's approval is required.
The plan was approved at the meeting.
The new drug was approved by the government.
en.notes: 承認 is formal approval by an authority or a superior: 承認を得る, 承認が下りる, 〜を承認する, passive 承認される. 許可 is permission to do something, and 賛成 agreement with an opinion. In addition, 承認 means "recognition", for example in 承認欲求 "need for recognition".

examples[].german: The proposal was rejected.
My visa application was rejected.
The court dismissed the lawsuit.
en.notes: 却下 is the formal rejection of an application, proposal or lawsuit by a competent body; mostly passive: 申請が却下される, 提案が却下される. The word is official or legal; in everyday speech people say 断る or 認められない. 拒否 is a firm refusal, and 不採用 a rejection in a job application.

examples[].german: The hiring has been decided.
My proposal was adopted at the meeting.
This company hires about thirty new employees every year.
en.notes: 採用 has two main meanings: "hiring" of personnel (社員を採用する, 採用試験, 採用が決まる "to get an offer") and "adoption, acceptance" of ideas, proposals or methods (案を採用する, 新しいシステムを採用する). It is a transitive する-verb; from the viewpoint of the applicant or the proposal one says 採用される, and a rejection is 不採用. The everyday 雇う "to employ" is more general; 採用 sounds more official and refers to the selection process.

examples[].german: I reserved the conference room.
Please set up the projector in the conference room.
Is the department head still in the conference room?
en.notes: 会議室 is the conference or meeting room in a company or government office. Typical are 会議室を予約する or, colloquially, 会議室を押さえる "to block the room"; meetings take place 会議室で. When there are several rooms, they are numbered: 第一会議室. The loanword ミーティングルーム is also common.

examples[].german: We concluded a business partnership.
Our company has a partnership with a Korean company.
At partner hotels, members can stay at discounted rates.
en.notes: 提携 refers to contractually regulated cooperation between companies, organizations or universities. Typical are 業務提携 "business partnership", 提携を結ぶ "to enter into a partnership" and 〜と提携する "to partner with ...". As a first element: 提携先 "partner company", 提携校 "partner school", 提携店 "partner shop". For personal cooperation in everyday life one rather says 協力; 提携 belongs to business and news language.

examples[].german: There are many challenges.
I want to finish my summer vacation assignment early.
Pronunciation is my challenge for the future.
en.notes: 課題 is a task to be solved or a challenge: 課題が多い/残る, 課題を解決する, 今後の課題 "what one must work on in the future". In school and university it also means "homework, assignment" (夏休みの課題, レポートの課題). Compared with 問題, 課題 sounds more constructive; 宿題 is homework in the narrower school sense.

examples[].german: It is a large-scale project.
The scale of this earthquake was large.
The company is small in scale, but the pay is good.
en.notes: 規模 means "scale, extent, magnitude" of projects, companies, events or disasters. Very common in compounds: 大規模 "large-scale", 小規模 "small-scale", 世界規模 "worldwide", attributively with な or の (大規模な工事, 世界規模の問題). Used freely, it appears with が大きい/小さい or 規模を拡大する "to expand". For the mere physical size of an object, one uses 大きさ or サイズ instead, not 規模.

examples[].german: I will have an examination.
There was a baggage inspection at the airport.
At the factory, all products are inspected before being sent to stores.
en.notes: 検査 is a systematic check or examination: in a hospital (血液検査 "blood test", 検査を受ける "to undergo an examination", 検査結果 "test result"), in a factory (製品を検査する) or at checks (荷物検査). It differs from the similar 試験 in that 試験 is usually an exam on knowledge or skills; 点検 is more the regular maintenance check of equipment, and 診察 the medical examination in the consulting room.

examples[].german: I got a prescription.
The doctor prescribed me cold medicine.
Please take all of the prescribed medicine.
en.notes: 処方 is the medical prescription of drugs: 医者が薬を処方する, from the patient's view 薬を処方してもらう or 処方される. The prescription as a document is called 処方箋; with it you pick up the medicine at the pharmacy (薬局). Over-the-counter drugs are called 市販の薬. In a broader sense, 処方 can also mean "formulation, formula"; a cooking recipe, by contrast, is レシピ.

examples[].german: I'm not feeling well.
It is easy to get sick when the seasons change.
Before a match, I am careful about managing my physical condition.
en.notes: 体調 is one's current physical condition. Typical: 体調がいい/悪い, 体調を崩す "to get sick, not feel well", 体調を整える "to get in shape", 体調管理 "taking care of one's health"; politely one asks 体調はいかがですか. In contrast to 健康 ("health" in general, long-term), 体調 describes the state on a particular day or in a phase; 具合 is more colloquial and can also refer to things.

examples[].german: Fatigue has built up.
Hot springs are said to be good for recovering from fatigue.
The cause of the accident is thought to be the driver's fatigue.
en.notes: 疲労 is the Sino-Japanese, rather factual word for "fatigue, exhaustion". Typical collocations: 疲労がたまる "to build up", 疲労がとれる "to go away", 疲労回復 "recovery" (often in ads for baths and drinks). In everyday speech one usually says 疲れ or 疲れた; 疲労 sounds medical, newsy or technical. Technically it also refers to material fatigue (金属疲労).

examples[].german: I pray for your speedy recovery.
The weather will improve from the afternoon.
After the surgery, my father is recovering well.
en.notes: 回復 means that a former good state returns: health (病気から回復する, 体力が回復する), but also weather (天気が回復する), the economy (景気の回復) or trust. It is mostly intransitive with が, but also transitive with を (信頼を回復する "to restore trust"). A polite get-well wish is 一日も早いご回復をお祈りしています. 治る refers specifically to the healing of an illness or wound, whereas 回復 is broader.

examples[].german: I give first aid.
I had my wound treated at the hospital.
The company immediately took appropriate measures.
en.notes: 処置 is the concrete measure with which one reacts to a situation. In the medical field: 応急処置 "first aid", 傷の処置 "wound care", 処置室 "treatment room". In general: 適切な処置をとる "to take appropriate measures". Similar are 対策 (countermeasure, often preventive) and 治療 (medical therapy over a longer period); 処置 stresses immediate action in an individual case.

examples[].german: The verdict has come out.
The court sentenced the man as guilty.
Because they could not accept the ruling, they decided to go to court again.
en.notes: 判決 is the judgment of a court. Typical: 判決が出る/下る "a verdict is handed down", 判決を言い渡す "to pronounce a verdict", 有罪判決 "guilty verdict", 無罪判決 "acquittal". It belongs to news and legal language. For a personal judgment or assessment in everyday life, one does not say 判決 but 判断 or 評価.

examples[].german: I follow the order.
I was ordered by my boss and went to work even on my day off.
"ike" is the imperative form of "iku".
en.notes: 命令 is an "order" from a higher authority: 命令する, 命令を出す, 命令に従う "to obey", 命令に背く "to defy". It sounds harsh and hierarchical (military, authorities, strict boss); in normal office life people rather say 指示 "instruction". In grammar the imperative is called 命令形 (行け, 食べろ), and in computer science 命令 is a program instruction.

examples[].german: Please follow the instructions.
On the department head's instructions, I remade the materials once more.
Please take the medicine exactly as the doctor instructed.
en.notes: 指示 is an "instruction", the neutral word in the office, at school and at the doctor's. Typical: 指示を出す "to give instructions", 指示に従う "to follow", 指示を受ける, 〜の指示で "on the instructions of", 医者の指示 "doctor's orders"; as a する-verb: 部下に〜するように指示する. Compared with 命令, 指示 sounds more matter-of-fact and less authoritative. In exams one often reads 指示に従って答えなさい "Answer according to the instructions".

examples[].german: The subjects of the survey are students.
This event is aimed at elementary school children.
This product is excluded from the sale.
en.notes: 対象 is the target or object at which something is directed: 調査の対象, 〜を対象に(した) "for, aimed at", 〜の対象になる, 対象外 "excluded". Very common in notices and offers (小学生を対象にしたイベント). Do not confuse it with the identically read 対照 "contrast" and 対称 "symmetry".

examples[].german: I ask for help.
When I was in college, I received financial support from my parents.
Japan provides food aid to many countries.
en.notes: 援助 is "help, support", mostly in material or financial form, often from states, organizations or parents: 経済的な援助, 資金援助, 援助を受ける, 〜に援助する. It sounds more formal than 手伝い (practical help) or 助け (help in general). 支援 is very similar but stresses supporting activities (reconstruction, projects), whereas with 援助 one thinks above all of money or goods.

examples[].german: Opinions are divided.
Parents and children are at odds over the new rules.
The confrontation between the two countries is deepening more and more.
en.notes: 対立 denotes an opposition or conflict between two sides whose opinions or interests are opposed: 意見が対立する, AとBが対立する, Aと対立する, 対立が深まる "to intensify". Attributively: 対立する意見, 対立関係. It describes a situation rather than a single quarrel; for a concrete quarrel one says 喧嘩 or 争い. Typical of politics, news and discussions.

examples[].german: I solved the problem.
That case has not been solved yet.
I can't find a good solution.
en.notes: 解決 is the "solution, settlement" of a problem or conflict. As a する-verb it is used both transitively (問題を解決する) and intransitively (問題が解決する). Typical: 解決策 "solution", 解決方法, 円満に解決する "to settle amicably", 事件が解決する "a case is solved". Caution: the solution of a math problem or exam question is called 答え or 解答, not 解決.

examples[].german: Patience is needed.
She listens to her patients patiently.
Studying a foreign language has built up my endurance.
en.notes: 忍耐 means "patience, perseverance" in the sense of enduring hardship or suffering. Typical: 忍耐が必要だ, 忍耐強い "patient, persevering", 忍耐力 "staying power". It sounds rather written and serious; in everyday speech people more often say 我慢 (to put up with something, hold back) or 辛抱. As a verb (忍耐する) it is rare.

examples[].german: I have a firm resolution.
He decided to quit the company and study abroad.
I wrote my New Year's resolutions in a notebook.
en.notes: 決意 is a firm "resolution", an inner, often emotionally charged determination. Typical: 〜ことを決意する, 決意を固める "to make up one's mind firmly", 固い決意, 決意表明 "statement of intent". The very similar 決心 is somewhat more everyday; 決意 sounds more solemn and stresses determination. 決定, by contrast, is a matter-of-fact decision, for example by a company or committee.

examples[].german: I stand by my convictions.
My father holds the conviction that one should live honestly.
No matter how much people opposed her, she did not give up her convictions.
en.notes: 信念 is a deep personal "conviction" that one acts on. Typical: 信念を持つ, 信念を貫く "to stand by one's convictions", 信念を曲げる "to give up one's convictions", 強い信念. Religious faith, by contrast, is 信仰. Compared with 意見 ("opinion"), 信念 is much stronger and more lasting; 自信 means "self-confidence".

examples[].german: I fell in front of people and was embarrassed.
Making mistakes is not a disgrace.
Please don't embarrass me in front of my subordinates.
en.notes: 恥 is the noun "shame, disgrace". The most important phrase is 恥をかく "to be embarrassed, lose face"; to embarrass someone is 恥をかかせる. Others: 〜は恥ではない "is no disgrace", 恥を知れ "Shame on you!" (very harsh). The related adjective 恥ずかしい "embarrassing, shy" is a separate word, as is the literary verb 恥じる "to feel ashamed".

examples[].german: He casts envious glances.
Her new car is the envy of everyone.
I saw off my friend who was going to study abroad with a feeling of envy.
en.notes: 羨望 is an elevated, written word for "envy" in the sense of admiring envy - you wish for what another person has. It is almost always in set phrases: 羨望の眼差し "envious, admiring looks", 羨望の的 "object of general envy". In everyday life people say うらやましい or うらやむ instead. Jealousy (e.g. in relationships) is called 嫉妬 or やきもち; 羨望 is less negative.

examples[].german: I feel nostalgia.
The old streetscape evokes nostalgia.
When I ate a dish from my hometown abroad, I felt homesick.
en.notes: 郷愁 is a literary word for "homesickness, nostalgia", the wistful longing for one's homeland or for times gone by. Typical: 郷愁を感じる, 郷愁を覚える, 郷愁を誘う "to evoke nostalgia" (for example an old street or a song). In everyday speech one rather says ホームシック (homesickness abroad) or 懐かしい "familiar, nostalgic". 郷愁 is met mainly in literature, song lyrics and arts-and-culture columns.

examples[].german: He harbors great ambitions.
His big ambition is to make his own company number one in the world.
The villain in the movie had the ambition to make the world his own.
en.notes: 野望 is a big, often boundless "ambition" - an ambitious plan, for example for power or wealth. It often has a slightly negative or dramatic coloring (villains in movies have 野望), but it can also be used with a wink for big dreams. Typical: 野望を抱く "to harbor", 野望を実現する, 野望を持つ. Neutral to positive alternatives are 夢 "dream", 目標 "goal" and 抱負 "resolution"; 野心 is very similar but puts more emphasis on the ambitious trait of character.

examples[].german: Weather forecasting is difficult.
Experts predict that prices will rise next year as well.
There's no predicting what children will do.
en.notes: 予測 is a prediction based on data or analysis: 〜と予測する (transitive する-verb), 予測が当たる/外れる, 予測がつかない "unpredictable". Distinction: 予想 is an everyday expectation or guess, 予報 specifically a weather forecast (天気予報). 予測 sounds more objective and scientific.

examples[].german: He/she is shaken.
She was quite upset by the sudden news.
Even when I was asked difficult questions in the interview, I tried not to show any agitation.
en.notes: 動揺 means to be thrown inwardly off balance: "shock, loss of composure, agitation". As an intransitive する-verb: 知らせを聞いて動揺する, also 動揺を隠す "to not let it show", 動揺を見せる. It can also refer to unrest in markets or in society. Compared with 驚く ("to be surprised"), 動揺 stresses that one loses one's composure; 慌てる describes more frantic, headless action.

examples[].german: I can feel myself getting anxious.
Out of sheer nervousness, I got an easy question wrong.
All my friends have found jobs, and I am gradually getting restless.
en.notes: 焦り is the noun of 焦る "to get nervous, to feel under pressure". It means the inner restlessness when time is short or when one is falling behind others: 焦りを感じる, 焦りが出る, 焦りから失敗する "to make mistakes out of nervousness". In everyday speech the verb is often used: 焦らないで "don't panic, take your time". Not to be confused with 焦げる "to burn (food)", which has the same kanji.

examples[].german: I can't hide my bewilderment.
When I first came to Japan, I felt bewildered by the differences in lifestyle customs.
When the plan suddenly changed, everyone looked perplexed.
en.notes: 戸惑い is the noun of 戸惑う "to be confused, at a loss": the feeling of not knowing how to react or behave, for example in a new environment or when something unexpected happens. Typical: 戸惑いを感じる, 戸惑いを隠せない, 戸惑いの表情. The verb is even more common: 習慣の違いに戸惑う. In contrast to 混乱 ("chaos, disorder"), 戸惑い is a mild, personal uncertainty; 迷う means more "to waver, to be unable to decide".

examples[].german: He has a composed attitude.
My grandfather seems to take a detached view of life.
Although he is only twenty, he is remarkably composed about everything.
en.notes: 達観 means looking at things with distance and composure - "to stand above things", also "broad vision". Mostly as a する-verb in the form 達観している "sees everything calmly" or 人生を達観する. It is often said of older, experienced people, sometimes slightly ironically also of young people (若いのに達観している). It is rather written; more everyday would be 落ち着いている "calm", while あきらめている "resigned" sounds negative.

examples[].german: I comforted my friend.
I comforted my son, who was crying after losing the game.
When I was feeling down, this song comforted me many times.
en.notes: 慰める means "to comfort": to lift up someone who is sad or disappointed. Construction: 人を慰める, 〜と言って慰める; passive 慰められる "to be comforted", also by things (音楽に慰められる). The noun is 慰め "comfort" (慰めの言葉). Unlike 励ます "to encourage" (looking ahead, giving strength), 慰める is directed at grief already suffered. There is no intransitive counterpart.

examples[].german: I encouraged him.
Before the exam, my teacher encouraged me by saying, "Don't worry, you can do it."
When I was ill, I was encouraged by letters from my friends.
en.notes: 励ます means "to encourage, cheer up": to give someone courage so that they keep going. Construction: 人を励ます, 〜と言って励ます; passive 励まされる "to be encouraged". The noun is 励まし (励ましの言葉). Related is the intransitive 励む "to strive diligently" (仕事に励む). Unlike 慰める (comforting after grief), 励ます looks forward; 応援する is "to cheer on, support", for example a team.

examples[].german: Let's make up.
Today I was finally able to make up with the friend I had quarreled with yesterday.
It looks like the two of them have already made up.
en.notes: 仲直り means to be reconciled again after a quarrel - literally "to set the relationship (仲) right again (直る)". As an intransitive する-verb: 〜と仲直りする, AとBが仲直りする. Typical of friends, couples, siblings and children; the word is colloquial and warm. For formal reconciliation, for example between countries or parties to a lawsuit, one rather says 和解. The opposite is 喧嘩する.

examples[].german: We had a quarrel.
I ended up in a quarrel with my wife over a trivial matter.
Quarrels between siblings are an everyday occurrence.
en.notes: 口喧嘩 is a quarrel with words only - as opposed to 喧嘩 in general, which can also be a physical fight. Typical: 口喧嘩をする, 〜と口喧嘩になる "it comes to a quarrel", 夫婦の口喧嘩. Because the kanji are difficult, it is often written 口げんか. The word is colloquial; more formal are 口論 or 言い争い.

examples[].german: You should not talk behind people's backs.
I happened to overhear a colleague badmouthing me behind my back.
She never talks behind other people's backs, so everyone trusts her.
en.notes: 陰口 is malicious talk about someone behind their back - literally "shadow mouth". Typical: 陰口を言う, very common colloquially 陰口をたたく, 〜の陰口, 陰口を言われる. Unlike 悪口 ("to run someone down", also directly to their face), 陰口 emphasizes that the person is not present. うわさ is more neutral, "rumor, gossip".

examples[].german: It was registered as a World Cultural Heritage site.
Many cultural heritage sites remain in Kyoto.
Local festivals, too, are cultural heritage that we want to pass on to the next generation.
en.notes: 文化遺産 is "cultural heritage": buildings, art and traditions handed down from earlier generations. Very common is 世界文化遺産 (UNESCO World Cultural Heritage), often shortened to 世界遺産, with 〜に登録される "to be registered as". Natural heritage is 自然遺産. 遺産 alone also means "inheritance" in the private sense (親の遺産).

examples[].german: I assume the worst case.
An evacuation drill assuming an earthquake was held.
I hadn't anticipated that this many people would come.
en.notes: 想定 is the mental playing through of a possible case: 〜を想定する, 最悪の場合を想定する, 〜を想定した訓練. Very common are 想定外 "unforeseen, not planned for" and 想定内 "within expectations". Distinction: 予想 is an expectation of what will probably happen; 想定 is the assumption of a scenario one prepares for.

examples[].german: The open-air bath feels great.
I soaked in the open-air bath while looking at the snow.
This hotel has rooms with a private open-air bath.
en.notes: 露天風呂 is a bath under the open sky, usually at a 温泉 or ryokan: 露天 means "open-air", 風呂 "bath". One says 露天風呂に入る "to bathe in the open-air bath", 露天風呂付きの部屋 "room with a private open-air bath", 貸切露天風呂 "open-air bath that can be reserved privately". The counterpart is 内風呂 or 内湯 "indoor bath". As usual at a 温泉, you wash beforehand and bathe without swimwear.

examples[].german: I went to a souvenir shop.
I bought sweets for my coworkers at the souvenir stand in the station.
Souvenirs at tourist spots are a little expensive.
en.notes: 土産物 are "souvenirs, gifts brought back" as merchandise, especially the products sold at tourist destinations. Typical: 土産物屋 "souvenir shop", 土産物売り場 "souvenir stand", 土産物を買う. In conversation one mostly says (お)土産; 土産物 sounds more matter-of-fact and more like goods in a shop. In Japan, people often bring back edible souvenirs such as お菓子 for coworkers and family from trips.

examples[].german: I will return to my home country next month.
During the summer vacation I made a short trip home and saw my family.
The day of my return home is getting closer, and I am feeling a little lonely.
en.notes: 帰国 means "to return to one's home country". As an intransitive する-verb: 帰国する, 〜から帰国する. Typical: 一時帰国 "short visit home", 帰国子女 "children who grew up abroad and have returned", 帰国の日. For trips home within Japan, one says 帰省 (to one's hometown) or simply 帰る. Leaving the country is 出国.

examples[].german: I am preparing for my trip overseas.
Depending on the destination, you need a visa.
The government is urging people to refrain from traveling to that country.
en.notes: 渡航 originally referred to a journey across the sea; today it is practically "travel abroad" in the official sense. It appears mainly in official texts: 渡航する, 海外渡航, 渡航先 "travel destination abroad", 渡航者, 渡航費 "travel costs". In everyday speech one says 海外旅行 or 海外に行く instead. Returning to one's own country is 帰国.

examples[].german: Please sign here.
Please read the contract carefully before signing.
People were collecting signatures in front of the station to protect the park.
en.notes: 署名 is a handwritten "signature". Typical: 署名する, 書類に署名する, 署名をもらう, 署名欄 "signature field", 署名を集める "to collect signatures". It is the word for contracts and forms; the everyday サイン is used for parcels, credit cards and autographs of stars. In Japan a seal is often added as well: 署名捺印 "signature and seal". Merely writing out the name is 記名.

examples[].german: Please affix your seal.
Please sign and seal the document and send it back.
I sealed the contract in two places.
en.notes: 捺印 is the placing of the personal name seal (印鑑, はんこ) on a document. Typical: 捺印する, 捺印をお願いします, 署名捺印 "signature and seal", 捺印欄. It is an official word that one reads on forms and in contracts; in conversation one usually says はんこを押す or 印鑑を押す. 押印 means practically the same and is more common in official language today.

examples[].german: I will hand in the report.
Please submit the application form at the counter by Friday.
I had forgotten the submission deadline for the homework.
en.notes: 提出 means "submitting, handing in" documents: homework, reports, applications, receipts. Transitive する-verb: 〜を〜に提出する (レポートを先生に提出する). Typical: 提出期限 "submission deadline", 提出物 "documents to be submitted", 書類を提出する. Among students one also hears simply 出す; 提出 sounds more official. 申請, by contrast, is the applying itself (ビザを申請する "to apply for a visa").

examples[].german: The deadline is next week.
I managed to make the deadline somehow.
The application deadline is five o'clock today.
en.notes: 締切 (often also written 締め切り) is the "deadline" - the last date for submission, registration or application. Typical: 締切に間に合う "to meet the deadline", 締切を過ぎる, 締切を延ばす "to extend", 締切日. The related verb is 締め切る "to close, to cut off" (受付を締め切る). For submission deadlines one also says 期限 (提出期限).

examples[].german: The meeting has been postponed.
Because of rain, the sports day was postponed to next week.
Could you postpone the business trip by a week?
en.notes: 延期 is the "postponing" of an appointment to a later date. As a transitive する-verb: 会議を延期する; for the event itself mostly 延期される or 延期になる. Typical: 〜まで延期する, 雨のため延期, 無期限延期 "postponed indefinitely". In contrast to 中止 ("cancellation", it does not take place), with 延期 the event is made up for later. Colloquially one also says 延ばす.

examples[].german: The game was canceled.
A typhoon is coming, so we are canceling tomorrow's trip.
Because it didn't agree with me, I stopped taking that medicine.
en.notes: 中止 means "cancellation" (a planned event does not take place) or "discontinuation, halt" (something ongoing is stopped). Typical: 中止になる "to be canceled", 中止する "to cancel", 雨天中止 "canceled in case of rain". In contrast to 延期 ("postponement"), nothing is made up later; 中断 is only a temporary interruption. For private appointments one says キャンセルする or やめる more often.

examples[].german: The economic outlook is bright.
This curve has poor visibility, so please be careful.
The new station is expected to be completed next year.
en.notes: 見通し (from 見通す "to see through, to survey") has three meanings: clear visibility (見通しがいい/悪い道), outlook or forecast (〜の見通しが立つ, 〜する見通しだ "is expected to", typical in news) and foresight (見通しが甘い "to be too optimistic in one's assessment"). Compared with 予測, 見通し sounds less technical.

examples[].german: We have resumed business.
The train that had been stopped by an accident resumed service an hour later.
Since the rain stopped, the game was resumed.
en.notes: 再開 means "resumption, reopening" after a pause or interruption. It can be used transitively (営業を再開する) and intransitively (試合が再開する); often also 再開される. Typical: 運転再開 "resumption of train service", 営業再開, 試合再開. Note: 再会 "reunion" with people (友達と再会する) is read the same way.

examples[].german: They say "persistence is power," so let's practice a little every day.
I am thinking about whether to renew this contract next year as well.
The investigation is still ongoing.
en.notes: 継続 means "continuation, carrying on" of something that is in progress. Transitive: 契約を継続する "to renew", 研究を継続する; intransitive: 〜が継続する. Typical: 継続中 "ongoing", 継続的に "continuously", 継続して "continuing to". Well known is the proverb 継続は力なり "persistence is power". Compared with the everyday 続ける/続く, 継続 sounds more formal (contracts, projects, memberships).

examples[].german: The work was interrupted.
The game was suspended for about thirty minutes because of heavy rain.
The phone rang, so I interrupted my meal.
en.notes: 中断 is an "interruption": something in progress is stopped temporarily and can continue later. Transitive: 作業を中断する; intransitive: 試合が中断する; also often passive 中断される. Typical: 一時中断, 雨で中断, 話を中断する "to interrupt the conversation". Unlike 中止 (definitive cancellation or abort), 中断 implies a continuation; resuming is then 再開.

examples[].german: The construction work has been completed.
When the registration is complete, you will receive an e-mail.
Have you already finished the paperwork for the move?
en.notes: 完了 means "completion, finishing" - something is fully done. As a する-verb it is intransitive (工事が完了する) and transitive (手続きを完了する). Very common on screens and in system messages: 登録完了 "registration complete", 送信完了, 準備完了. In conversation one mostly says 終わる; 完了 sounds matter-of-fact and official. In grammar, 完了 also denotes the perfect.

examples[].german: I will report on the progress.
Every Friday we check the progress of the project.
"How is the progress?" "We are a little behind schedule."
en.notes: 進捗 refers to the "progress" of a task or project and belongs mainly to business language. Typical: 進捗状況 "status of things", 進捗を報告する, 進捗を確認する, 進捗管理. In the office, colleagues like to ask briefly 進捗どうですか "How far along are you?". In contrast to 進歩 ("progress" of technology or abilities) and 上達 ("progress in learning"), 進捗 is only about how far a task has been completed.

examples[].german: I will check the operating status.
This bus runs twice an hour.
Because of heavy snow, train service has stopped.
en.notes: 運行 is the scheduled "operation" of buses, trains or ferries. Typical: 運行する, 運行状況 "current operating situation", 運行情報 "traffic information", 運行を見合わせる "to temporarily suspend service". For trains, announcements often use 運転 too (運転を見合わせる); for ships and aircraft 運航 (same reading) is mostly written. In astronomy, 運行 also refers to the movement of celestial bodies.

examples[].german: Please look at the timetable.
According to the timetable, the next bus is at 10:15.
Japanese trains mostly arrive on time, as per the timetable.
en.notes: 時刻表 is the "timetable" for trains, buses, ferries or flights, the list of departure and arrival times (時刻 "time of day, point in time" + 表 "table"). Typical: 時刻表を見る/調べる, 時刻表によると "according to the timetable", 時刻表どおり "on schedule". A class schedule at school, by contrast, is a 時間割, and a personal agenda is a スケジュール or 予定表.

examples[].german: We hold a disaster drill.
In case of an earthquake, I have prepared emergency supplies.
With the city's disaster prevention app, you can check the evacuation sites.
en.notes: 防災 means "disaster prevention, disaster preparedness" - measures against damage from earthquakes, typhoons, floods, etc. It appears almost always in compounds: 防災訓練 "disaster drill", 防災グッズ "emergency supplies", 防災の日 (September 1), 防災意識 "disaster awareness". Related are 災害 "disaster" and 避難 "evacuation". Because of frequent earthquakes, the topic is very present in Japan.

examples[].german: The river overflowed because of the torrential rain.
Because of the heavy rain last night, the trains stopped.
According to the weather forecast, there is a risk of torrential rain in Kyushu tomorrow.
en.notes: 豪雨 refers to very heavy rain, often lasting for hours, that can cause damage. The word belongs mainly to weather reports and news; in everyday speech one mostly says simply 大雨. Typical are 豪雨で〜 ("because of the heavy rain"), 豪雨による被害 and 豪雨に見舞われる. Fixed compounds: 集中豪雨 "localized torrential rain" and ゲリラ豪雨 "sudden downpour".

examples[].german: There is a rainbow out.
After the rain stopped, a big rainbow stretched across the sky.
In Japan, the rainbow is said to have seven colors.
en.notes: 虹 is the rainbow. One says 虹が出る ("a rainbow appears") or, somewhat more pictorially, 虹がかかる ("a rainbow arches across the sky"). In Japan traditionally seven colors (七色) are counted, hence also 虹色 "rainbow-colored, colorful". The word is almost always written with kanji; in children's books and song lyrics にじ is also used.

examples[].german: Demand is increasing.
In summer, demand for air conditioners rises.
Prices are determined by supply and demand.
en.notes: 需要 is (economic) demand and usually appears as the counterpart of 供給 "supply": 需要と供給. Typical are 需要が高い/多い, 需要が増える/減る and 〜の需要がある "there is demand for ...". For personal needs in daily life, people rather say 必要 or ニーズ; 需要 sounds like markets and economics. Do not confuse it with the identically read 重要 "important".

examples[].german: The dry spell continues.
Because of the drought, water for the rice paddies ran short.
This summer, vegetable prices have risen because of the drought.
en.notes: 日照り is a longer period without rain, especially in summer, that dries out fields and water supplies. Typical: 日照りが続く, 日照りで〜 ("because of the drought"), 日照り続き. In the news, 干ばつ or 水不足 is used more often. Not to be confused with 日照 (にっしょう), which means the duration of sunshine, e.g. 日照時間.

examples[].german: The extreme heat continues.
Because of the heat wave, air conditioner sales keep rising.
A day with temperatures above 35 degrees is called a 猛暑日.
en.notes: 猛暑 is extreme, oppressive summer heat, a word from weather reports and the news; in conversation one says more すごく暑い. Typical: 猛暑が続く, 記録的な猛暑, 猛暑のため〜. Meteorologically, a day with at least 35 degrees is called 猛暑日, with at least 30 degrees 真夏日. Synonymous but rarer is 酷暑.

examples[].german: The temperature has risen.
They say today's high will be 32 degrees.
It's cooler up on the mountain, so let's take a jacket.
en.notes: 気温 is the air temperature, as given in the weather report. You say 気温が高い/低い and 気温が上がる/下がる; also 最高気温 and 最低気温. Other temperatures use other words: 温度 in general (room, water, oven), 体温 "body temperature", 水温 "water temperature". Note: not 気温が暑い, but 気温が高い or simply 暑い.

examples[].german: Forestry is important.
Forestry has been thriving in this village since long ago.
The number of young people working in forestry is decreasing.
en.notes: 林業 is forestry, i.e. planting, tending and felling forests for timber. It belongs to the series 農業 "agriculture", 漁業 "fishing", 林業 and 鉱業 "mining". Typical: 林業が盛んだ ("forestry is significant"), 林業で働く, formally 林業に従事する. A matter-of-fact word, common in geography and the news.

examples[].german: This town developed through mining.
Australia is a country with a thriving mining industry.
Work in mining is said to be very dangerous.
en.notes: 鉱業 is mining as an industry: the extraction of ores, coal and other mineral resources (鉱物). Caution: it sounds exactly like 工業 "industry", so the meaning can only be recognized from context or the script. The mine itself is called 鉱山. Typical: 鉱業が盛んだ, 鉱業で発展する; rather matter-of-fact style (geography, economics).

examples[].german: Industry is well developed.
This area is an industrial zone, so there are many factories.
My older brother is studying machinery at a technical high school.
en.notes: 工業 is manufacturing industry, that is, the production of goods in factories. Typical compounds are 工業地帯 "industrial zone", 工業高校 "technical high school" and 重工業 "heavy industry". 産業 is broader and includes all branches of the economy, 商業 is commerce and 農業 is agriculture. A factual word from geography and economics.

examples[].german: This year's harvest is good.
In autumn, rice is harvested in the rice paddies.
The biggest gain from this trip was that I could talk with all kinds of people.
en.notes: 収穫 is the harvest - both the process and the yield. As a する-verb it is transitive: 米を収穫する, 野菜を収穫する. Figuratively it means the "gain, yield" of an experience: 〜が一番の収穫だった. In everyday speech, for fruit and vegetables one also simply says 取る/採る, for rice 稲刈り; 収穫 sounds somewhat more matter-of-fact. Also typical: 収穫期 and 収穫量.

examples[].german: I sow seeds.
These grapes are seedless, so they are easy to eat.
My son's grades are always a cause of worry.
en.notes: 種 (たね) is the seed of a plant and also the pit in fruit: 種をまく "to sow", 種のないぶどう. Figuratively it is the cause or source of something: 心配の種 "cause for worry", けんかの種, 話の種 "topic of conversation"; 手品の種 is the trick behind a magic act. In compounds the kanji is read しゅ (種類, 品種). まく is mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: I fertilize the plants.
When spring comes, let's spread fertilizer on the field.
We grew these vegetables without chemical fertilizer.
en.notes: 肥料 is fertilizer for plants and fields. In everyday speech one says 肥料をやる (garden, potted plants), more formally 肥料を与える, and 肥料をまく when spreading it on a field. Important compounds: 化学肥料 "chemical fertilizer" and 有機肥料 "organic fertilizer". The older word 肥やし mainly means manure and is also used figuratively (芸の肥やし "nourishment for one's art").

examples[].german: We will set up the irrigation system.
Since it rains little in this region, irrigation is indispensable for agriculture.
In the old days, people drew water from the river to irrigate the rice fields.
en.notes: 灌漑 is the artificial watering of fields via canals or pipes. Neither kanji is among the standard kanji (常用漢字), so it is often written in kana as かんがい. Typical: 灌漑設備, 灌漑用水, 灌漑農業; as a する-verb it is transitive (畑を灌漑する), but rather literary. In everyday speech it is paraphrased with 水を引く "to channel water in".

examples[].german: The supply is insufficient.
This power plant supplies electricity to the whole town.
After the earthquake, the water supply stopped.
en.notes: 供給 is supply in the economic sense, or provision and delivery; as a transitive する-verb: AにBを供給する "to supply A with B" (町に電気を供給する). The counterpart is 需要 "demand". Typical: 供給が足りない, 供給が止まる, 安定した供給. A special offer in a shop, however, is not 供給 but セール or 特売.

examples[].german: They keep cows on the ranch.
During summer vacation I went to a ranch in Hokkaido and ate ice cream.
