Horses are leisurely grazing in the wide pasture.
en.notes: 牧場 is an operation or area where livestock such as cows, horses or sheep are kept, that is, a livestock farm or pasture. For crop farming you say 農場 or 畑, not 牧場. Typical: 牧場で牛を飼う, 観光牧場 (a tourist farm with animals, milk and ice cream). The reading まきば is poetic and mainly refers to the green pasture.

examples[].german: I store it in the warehouse.
Please put away the desks we don't use in the storeroom.
Many warehouses stand in a row near the harbor.
en.notes: 倉庫 is a storage room, warehouse or storage hall, especially of companies, ports and shops. Typical: 倉庫に保管する, 倉庫にしまう, 倉庫から出す. The small storage shed by a house is rather 物置, a traditional storehouse 蔵. Not to be confused with 在庫 "stock, goods in inventory".

examples[].german: I conduct experiments at the research institute.
After graduating from university, my older brother has been working at a pharmaceutical research institute.
This institute researches earthquakes.
en.notes: 研究所 is a research institute or research laboratory as an institution, for example of companies, the state or at universities. There are two readings, けんきゅうじょ and けんきゅうしょ; which applies is decided by each institution itself. The individual lab room or professor's chair at a university is called 研究室 instead. Typical: 研究所で働く, 研究所に勤める, 〜の研究所.

examples[].german: I'm going to the embassy.
Please wait in front of the embassy.
en.notes: 大使館 is an embassy as an institution or a building. 大使館に行く names it as the destination of a visit. 大使館の前 describes a place in front of it; 前で待つ names it as a meeting point. たいしかん contains the vowel sequence ai, not a long a. 館 is read かん here.

examples[].german: I apply for a visa at the consulate.
I had lost my passport, so I contacted the consulate right away.
There is a Japanese consulate general in Munich.
en.notes: 領事館 is a consulate, the representation of a state in a city other than the capital; one turns to it for visas, passports or emergencies abroad. The embassy in the capital is called 大使館, a consulate general 総領事館, and the consul himself 領事. Typical: 領事館で申請する, 領事館に連絡する.

examples[].german: He went to prison.
After getting out of prison, it is not easy to find a job.
An old prison building was used for the filming of the movie.
en.notes: 刑務所 is the prison for convicted offenders. Typical: 刑務所に入る/入れられる, 刑務所に入っている ("to be in prison"), 刑務所から出る, formally 出所する. Suspects awaiting trial, by contrast, are held in a 拘置所, and arrested people first in the police cell 留置場. The old word 牢屋 sounds historical or colloquial.

examples[].german: I report it to the fire station.
The children toured the fire station and were allowed to ride in a fire engine.
There is a fire station near our house, so we often hear sirens at night too.
en.notes: 消防署 is the fire station, that is, the office and building of the fire department. The fire service as an organization is called 消防, the firefighter 消防士, the fire engine 消防車. In Japan, ambulances (救急車) also come from the 消防署; the emergency number for both is 119. Typical: 消防署に通報する, 消防署を見学する.

examples[].german: I take care of the procedures at the government office.
The government office is closed on weekends, so I have to go on a weekday.
The way that company handles things is pure bureaucratic red tape.
en.notes: 役所 is in general a government office or authority, in everyday life usually the city hall, where one handles registrations and applications. More concretely one says 市役所, 区役所, and in small municipalities 町役場/村役場. With お it is often ironic: お役所仕事 "red tape, bureaucratic sluggishness". Typical: 役所で手続きをする, 役所に行く, 役所に勤める.

examples[].german: I submit the notification at the ward office.
After moving, you have to change your address at the ward office.
The ward office is about ten minutes' walk from the station.
en.notes: 区役所 is the ward office, the administration of a city ward (区). Wards exist in the 23 wards of Tokyo and in large cities such as Osaka or Yokohama; elsewhere one goes to the 市役所. There one takes care of registering and re-registering residence, obtains the 住民票 "certificate of residence" and submits forms. Typical: 区役所に届出を出す, 区役所で手続きをする.

examples[].german: Let's value natural resources.
Japan is a country with few resources.
Please put out recyclable waste on Wednesday.
en.notes: 資源 refers to raw materials and resources: 天然資源, 地下資源, エネルギー資源. Typical are 資源が豊か/少ない, 資源を大切にする and 資源を無駄にする. In daily life the word is met in waste separation: 資源ごみ is recyclable waste such as bottles, cans and paper. Figuratively there is also 人的資源 "human resources".

examples[].german: The tuition is high.
I work part-time and pay my tuition myself.
Private schools cost more in fees than public ones.
en.notes: 学費 is the total cost of education at a school or university: tuition, school fees, often also materials. The actual teaching fee is, more precisely, 授業料. Typical: 学費が高い, 学費を払う, 学費がかかる, 学費を稼ぐ ("to earn one's way through school"); financial support for it is a 奨学金 "scholarship, student loan".

examples[].german: Environmental pollution is a problem.
The smoke from factories is a cause of environmental pollution.
Let's think about what we can do to prevent environmental pollution.
en.notes: 環境汚染 is composed of 環境 "environment" and 汚染 "pollution, contamination" and is a matter-of-fact word from the news and school textbooks. More concrete are 大気汚染 "air pollution", 水質汚染 "water pollution" and 土壌汚染 "soil contamination". Typical: 環境汚染を防ぐ, 環境汚染の原因, 環境汚染が進む. The older 公害 means environmental damage caused by industry that the population suffers from.

examples[].german: I sort out items that can be reused.
I wash this plastic bottle and reuse it.
I made a bag by reusing the fabric of an old kimono.
en.notes: 再利用 is using something again instead of throwing it away; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を再利用する. It overlaps with リサイクル (more recycling as raw material) and リユース (reuse in the same form); 再利用 covers both. Typical: 再利用できる, 再利用可能 (as a label), 紙を再利用する. It is neutral and common in notes on waste separation.

examples[].german: Customs duty will be charged.
The government lowered the tariff on imported beef.
When tariffs go up, foreign products also become more expensive.
en.notes: 関税 is customs duty, a levy on imported goods. Note: with the kanji swapped, 税関 means the customs authority or the customs inspection at the airport. Typical: 関税がかかる ("duty is charged"), 関税をかける ("to impose duty"), 関税を引き上げる/引き下げる. Opposite: 免税 "duty-free, tax-free". A matter-of-fact word from economics and the news, but also used when shopping online from abroad.

examples[].german: A guarantor is required.
This computer comes with a one-year warranty.
There is no guarantee that you will succeed with this method.
en.notes: 保証 is a guarantee or surety: the assurance that something will certainly happen, or that someone vouches for something. As a する-verb it is transitive: 品質を保証する. Typical: 保証が付いている, 保証期間, 保証書, 保証人 "guarantor" (e.g. for a rental contract), 〜という保証はない. Pronounced the same but different: 保障 "security, safeguarding" (社会保障, 安全保障) and 補償 "compensation".

examples[].german: I take childcare leave.
We share the childcare as a couple.
Balancing childcare and work is hard.
en.notes: 育児 is the care and raising of small children, especially in the baby and toddler years. It sounds more formal than the everyday 子育て; 教育, by contrast, means education and schooling. Typical: 育児をする, 育児休暇 (short 育休) "parental leave", 育児と仕事の両立 "balancing childcare and work". Not to be confused with the identically sounding 意気地 in 意気地なし "coward".

examples[].german: The number of dual-income households is increasing.
Since both of us work, my husband often makes dinner.
I intend to keep working even after getting married.
en.notes: 共働き means that both spouses are employed. It usually stands with の before nouns (共働きの家庭/夫婦/世帯) or with だ: うちは共働きだ; as a する-verb it is rarer. The counterpart is a household with a housewife or househusband (専業主婦/専業主夫). Neutral, common in conversations about family and childcare, and in statistics.

examples[].german: I started living alone.
Students who live alone have to cook and do laundry themselves.
My grandmother lives alone in the countryside, so I call her from time to time.
en.notes: 一人暮らし is living alone in one's own apartment, often by students, young professionals or elderly people. Through rendaku, 暮らし becomes ぐらし here. Typical: 一人暮らしをする/始める, 一人暮らしの学生, 一人暮らしのお年寄り; also written 独り暮らし. It is not the same as 独身 "single (unmarried)"; the opposite is, for example, 実家暮らし "living with one's parents".

examples[].german: I live with my parents.
After the wedding, it was decided that we would live with my husband's parents.
How many family members live with you?
en.notes: 同居 is living together under one roof, especially within the family, for example several generations. As an intransitive する-verb, the partner takes と: 両親と同居する. The counterpart is 別居, which also means spouses living apart. For unmarried couples one says 同棲, for shared housing ルームシェア. Forms ask about 同居している家族 "family members living in the household".

examples[].german: Let's think about the other person's position.
From a parent's standpoint, that decision is worrying.
In my position, I can't answer that question.
en.notes: 立場 literally means "the place where one stands": the position someone is in, either socially (教師という立場) or as a point of view (〜の立場から見ると). Fixed expressions are 相手の立場に立つ / 相手の立場になって考える "to put oneself in the other person's shoes" and 立場が弱い "to be in a weak position". In discussions, 立場 also denotes one's fundamental stance, whereas 意見 is a single opinion.

examples[].german: I will reduce energy consumption.
This refrigerator doesn't use much electricity.
I threw away the milk whose use-by date was yesterday.
en.notes: 消費 is consumption or use; as a transitive する-verb: 電気を消費する "to consume electricity". Fixed words are 消費者 "consumer", 消費税 "consumption tax" and 消費期限 "use-by date". The counterpart is 生産 "production". For "spending money" in daily life, people rather say お金を使う; 消費 sounds objective and economic.

examples[].german: I rearranged the room.
Since it is spring, I redecorated by changing the curtains to a bright color.
I hear the shop in front of the station will be closed for a week for a makeover.
en.notes: 模様替え literally means "pattern change": rearranging furniture or redecorating a room, also remodeling a shop. Typical: 部屋の模様替えをする, 模様替えする (transitive: 部屋を模様替えする), 季節の模様替え. Larger construction work is more often called 改装 or リフォーム. It is neutral and everyday.

examples[].german: The building is ten years old.
Rooms in older buildings are often cheaper in rent.
When looking for a room, I check the distance from the station and the age of the building.
en.notes: 築年数 is the number of years since a building was completed, a typical word from real estate and apartment listings. 築 means "built": 築十年 "built ten years ago", 新築 "newly built", 築浅 "only a few years old". Typical: 築年数が古い/新しい, also 築年数が浅い; when looking for an apartment 築年数を確認する.

examples[].german: It gets a lot of sunlight.
This flower does not grow well in places with poor sunlight.
A cat is taking a nap by the sunny window.
en.notes: 日当たり describes how much direct sun an apartment, a room or a spot gets. Almost always with いい/悪い: 日当たりがいい, 日当たりの悪い部屋; in listings 日当たり良好. Related: 日差し "sunbeams", 日なた "sunny spot", 日陰 "shade". A south-facing aspect (南向き) with good 日当たり is considered especially valuable in Japan.

examples[].german: The noise is terrible.
I live near the tracks, so I suffer from the noise of the trains.
Please don't make noise after 10 p.m.
en.notes: 騒音 is disturbing, unpleasant noise, for example from traffic, construction sites or neighbors; the neutral word for a sound is 音. Typical: 騒音がひどい, 騒音に悩む, 騒音を出す, 騒音問題, 騒音対策. 雑音, by contrast, means background noise or static. 騒音がうるさい is redundant; better is 騒音がひどい or simply 音がうるさい.

examples[].german: It is an area with good public order.
Japan is safe, so it is relatively safe to walk alone at night.
I hear this area has become less safe recently.
en.notes: 治安 is public security or the security situation in a country, city or neighborhood. One says 治安がいい/悪い (not 高い/低い), 治安が悪化する, 治安を守る. 安全, by contrast, generally means the safety of a thing or situation, and 防犯 means crime prevention. Common in apartment hunting and travel planning.

en.meaning: to make an effort; to keep in mind
examples[].german: I try to live a healthy lifestyle.
I try to go to bed early every day.
Please always try to speak to customers with a smile.
en.notes: 心掛ける means to firmly resolve something and consciously pay attention to it in daily life. It is transitive: 〜を心掛ける (健康的な生活を心掛ける) or 〜ように心掛ける (早く寝るように心掛ける); there is no 〜に心掛ける; for that one says 健康に気をつける. Often written in kana: 心がける; the noun 心掛け means "attitude, resolution". 気をつける stresses caution, 心掛ける conscious habit.

examples[].german: I overlooked an important point.
I had overlooked the email, so my reply was late.
It was written in small letters, so I simply overlooked it.
en.notes: 見落とす means to fail to notice something through inattention although one could have seen it. It is transitive: 〜を見落とす. The noun is 見落とし (見落としがないか確認する "to check that nothing was overlooked"). 見逃す, by contrast, stresses missing a chance or a broadcast, or deliberately letting something pass; 見過ごす rather means "to let something go by without acting".

en.meaning: to be thorough; to be attentive to detail
examples[].german: The service is thoroughly attentive.
This hotel is cleaned thoroughly, which is very pleasant.
With so many employees, the president's eye cannot always reach everywhere.
en.notes: 行き届く means that care or attention reaches into every corner. It is intransitive; the subject is the effort itself: サービスが行き届く, 掃除が行き届く, 目が行き届く, 気配りが行き届く. Mostly in the state form 行き届いている or attributively 行き届いたサービス. Negated, it serves as a polite apology formula: 行き届かない点もございますが. Also read ゆきとどく.

en.meaning: to make up one's mind; to take the plunge; to give up
examples[].german: I took the plunge and acted.
I summoned my courage and told her my feelings.
I just can't give up the dream I've had since childhood.
en.notes: 思い切る occurs almost always as 思い切って: "to take heart, to dare the step" - you overcome your hesitation and do something bold. Attributively: 思い切った決断 "a bold decision". The other meaning is transitive: 〜を思い切る "to give something up, to put something out of one's mind", often negated (夢を思い切れない). Not to be confused with 思い切り "with full force, to one's heart's content".

examples[].german: I will do the groundwork in advance.
You should lay the groundwork with the department head before the meeting.
Because there had not been enough groundwork, the new plan was opposed.
en.notes: 根回し literally means digging around the roots (根) of a tree before transplanting it. Figuratively, it is the informal coordination with everyone involved before a matter is officially discussed or decided, typical of Japanese companies and politics. Typical: 〜に根回しをする, 根回しをしておく, 根回しが足りない. Neutral to businesslike, sometimes with a slightly critical undertone ("backroom dealing").

examples[].german: I invest overseas.
My brother invested part of his bonus in stocks.
I think of studying English as an investment in myself.
en.notes: 投資 is an investment, and as a する-verb "to invest". What is invested in takes に (株に投資する, 海外に投資する), the amount or capital takes を. Figuratively it is also used for time and education: 自分への投資 "investment in oneself". Related is 投資家 "investor"; saving in a bank account, by contrast, is 貯金.

en.meaning: to be considerate; to go to trouble for others
examples[].german: Please don't go to any trouble.
Eating with my boss makes me tired because I have to be so attentive.
She is always considerate of the people around her.
en.notes: 気を遣う means to pay attention to the feelings and needs of others, to be considerate, to go to trouble. The person is marked with に: 周りの人に気を遣う. 気を遣わないでください is said politely when someone offers a gift or hospitality: "Please don't go to any trouble." Often also written 気を使う; noun: 気遣い. Not to be confused with 気をつける "to be careful" and 気にする "to worry about".

examples[].german: I want to repay their kindness.
I am working hard to repay my parents, who raised me.
"Tsuru no Ongaeshi" is an old folktale in which a crane that was helped shows its gratitude.
en.notes: 恩返し means to repay a kindness (恩) received, that is, to show gratitude. As an intransitive する-verb the person is marked with に: 両親に恩返しする. Unlike a one-time お礼, 恩返し sounds like a deep, often long-term debt of gratitude. Well known is the folktale 鶴の恩返し; the opposite is described by the saying 恩を仇で返す "to repay kindness with evil".

examples[].german: I give obligation chocolate.
I attended the wedding out of obligation.
He is my brother-in-law.
en.notes: 義理 is the social obligation one feels out of relationships, politeness or gratitude. Typical: 義理がある, 義理で〜する "to do out of obligation", 義理を欠く, 義理堅い "dutiful"; 義理チョコ is obligation chocolate for Valentine's Day. With の it denotes in-law relatives: 義理の母 "mother-in-law", 義理の兄 "brother-in-law". Often paired with 人情 (義理人情).

examples[].german: He/she is a warmhearted person.
The warmth of the old days remains in this town.
It is only human to want to help people in trouble.
en.notes: 人情 is humanity and warmth toward others. Typical: 人情に厚い "warmhearted", 人情味がある, 下町の人情 "the warmth of the old downtown districts". The second meaning is "human nature": 〜のが人情だ "it is only human to ...". Together with 義理 it forms the classic pair 義理人情. It is more general than 思いやり, which means concrete consideration.

examples[].german: He/she is a considerate person.
Consideration, thinking about the other person's feelings, is important.
Offering your seat to an elderly person on the train is a small act of consideration.
en.notes: 思いやり is the ability to put oneself in others' shoes and act considerately; it is the noun of 思いやる. Typical: 思いやりがある/ない, 思いやりのある人, 相手への思いやり. The second part is almost always written in kana. 気遣い puts more emphasis on concrete attentiveness in dealing with others, 優しさ on kindness in general.

examples[].german: It is rewarding work.
My hard studying paid off - I passed the exam.
Despite hurrying, I missed the train anyway.
en.notes: 甲斐 is the reward or point of an effort, that is, the result that makes an investment worthwhile. Typical: 〜た甲斐があった "it was worth it", 〜甲斐もなく "in vain despite all the effort". As a suffix it becomes がい: やり甲斐 "fulfillment in a task", 生き甲斐, 〜し甲斐がある. Often written in kana (かい/がい). As a proper name, 甲斐 is also an old province (today Yamanashi).

en.meaning: reason for living; something to live for
examples[].german: I found my reason for living.
For my grandmother, watching her grandchildren grow up is what makes life worth living.
Not a few people lose their purpose in life after retirement.
en.notes: 生き甲斐 is that for which one lives and which gives life meaning and joy. Typical: 〜が生き甲斐だ, 〜を生き甲斐にする, 生き甲斐を感じる/見つける/なくす. Often also written 生きがい. やり甲斐, by contrast, means the fulfillment in a particular job or task, and 目標 a concrete goal. The word is now also known in the West as a loanword.

examples[].german: He/she is a methodical person.
My father is very conscientious and keeps a diary every day.
Her room is always tidied meticulously.
en.notes: 几帳面 is a な-adjective for people who are careful, orderly and precise and reliably keep rules or deadlines. Typical: 几帳面な人/性格, 几帳面に片付ける, 几帳面に記録する. Opposite: 大雑把 or ずぼら. It is meant positively, unlike 神経質 "overly sensitive, fussy". The kanji 几 is rare; the word is also seen in kana (きちょうめん).

examples[].german: He/she is a careless sort of person who doesn't bother with details.
He is sloppy in his work and often makes mistakes.
Roughly speaking, the plan is divided into three stages.
en.notes: 大雑把 is a な-adjective with two sides: "rough, approximate" for estimates and explanations (大雑把に言うと "roughly speaking", 大雑把な計算) and "not fussy, sloppy" for people and work (大雑把な性格). For people it sounds slightly critical, but it is often also used self-ironically. Opposite: 几帳面 or 細かい. Often in kana: おおざっぱ.

examples[].german: He is good with his hands.
She is so skillful that she makes her own clothes.
My brother is good at doing anything, but I am clumsy.
en.notes: 器用 is a な-adjective: skillful with the hands (手先が器用だ), but also skillful in handling situations (器用に生きる "to get through life skillfully"). Adverbially: 器用に使う, 器用にこなす. Opposite: 不器用, which can also mean "socially awkward". 器用貧乏 is someone who can do many things a little but nothing properly. For skill in a particular subject, one more often says 上手 or 得意.

examples[].german: Earnings have increased.
We will donate all the proceeds of the event.
The new service is not yet generating revenue.
en.notes: 収益 are the earnings or revenue from a business activity, so it is a word of business and corporate language. Typical: 収益が上がる/増える, 収益を上げる, 収益が出る "to turn a profit". Distinction: 収入 is a person's income, 利益 the profit after deducting costs; 収益 is often used similarly to 利益 but sounds like a company or project.

examples[].german: Sorry for being clumsy.
I am clumsy with my hands, so I am bad at fine work.
My father is awkward, but he cares deeply about his family.
en.notes: 不器用 is a な-adjective (also a noun): 不器用な人, 手先が不器用だ "clumsy with the hands". It describes not only a lack of manual dexterity but also awkwardness in dealing with people or feelings: 生き方が不器用 "clumsy at life". The opposite is 器用; colloquially one also hears ぶきっちょ. Unlike 下手 "bad at a particular thing", 不器用 describes more a general trait of the person.

examples[].german: He/she has a timid personality.
Our cat is timid and hides immediately when guests come.
Since failing once, I have become timid about new things.
en.notes: 臆病 is a な-adjective: 臆病な人/性格, plus 臆病者 "coward". With 〜に臆病になる one expresses that one has become hesitant about something (恋愛に臆病になる). More colloquial and childlike are 怖がり "scaredy-cat" and 弱虫; antonyms are 勇敢 and 大胆. Despite the rare kanji 臆, the word is usually written in kanji.

examples[].german: It is a brave act.
The firefighters bravely went into the flames.
The heroes of old folktales are often brave young men.
en.notes: 勇敢 is a な-adjective with a praising, somewhat elevated tone: 勇敢な兵士/行動, adverbial 勇敢に戦う. It stresses bravery in the face of real danger and therefore suits news, stories and heroic deeds. In everyday speech one usually says 勇気がある "to have courage"; the opposite is 臆病.

examples[].german: He has a delicate sensibility.
The flavor of this dish is very delicate.
She is sensitive, so she gets hurt if you speak harshly.
en.notes: 繊細 has two sides: "fine, delicate" for things (繊細な指, 繊細な味, 繊細な模様) and "sensitive, delicate-minded" for people (繊細な人, 繊細な心). For people it is usually meant kindly, but it can also hint at "easily hurt"; the loanword デリケート is similar. 敏感, by contrast, means "reacting sensitively to stimuli" (肌が敏感).

examples[].german: It was a thoughtless remark.
You must not sign a contract rashly without checking carefully.
It is dangerous to post photos on social media thoughtlessly.
en.notes: 軽率 is a な-adjective: 軽率な発言/行動/判断, adverbial 軽率に決める. It criticizes that someone acted without thinking, and often appears in apologies (軽率でした "that was thoughtless of me") and in news about politicians' remarks. 不注意 stresses lack of attention, うっかり a one-time slip; 軽率 stresses lack of forethought. Opposite: 慎重.

examples[].german: Please say it honestly.
He is so honest that he can't tell a lie.
Honestly, I wasn't very happy with this present.
en.notes: 正直 is a な-adjective: 正直な人, 正直に話す/言う. Very common is the sentence opener 正直に言うと or just 正直、… "honestly", which introduces a frank, often uncomfortable opinion; the short 正直、… is colloquial. 素直 means more "unaffected, obedient, open-minded", not "truthful". Opposite: 不正直 or simply 嘘つき "liar".

examples[].german: You must not do anything sly.
Only my big brother gets a bigger piece of cake? That's not fair!
He is sly and always makes other people do the tedious work.
en.notes: ずるい is an い-adjective and is almost always written in kana; the kanji 狡い is rare. It means "unfair, cunning, sly" and is very common in everyday life, especially as an exclamation ずるい！ "That's not fair!" when someone gets an undeserved advantage. With the noun ずる one says ずるをする "to cheat". 卑怯 is stronger and means "cowardly and mean", 不公平 soberly "unfairly distributed".

examples[].german: He is a carefree person.
Even though the exam is tomorrow, my little brother is calmly playing video games.
After retirement, I want to live a carefree life in the countryside.
en.notes: 呑気 is mostly written in kana のんき. As a な-adjective (のんきな性格, のんきに暮らす) it can be positive, "relaxed, carefree", but often it is critical, "too carefree" - when someone doesn't worry although they should (この状況でよくそんなにのんきでいられるね). のんびり describes rather a leisurely pace or a relaxed situation, 気楽 the absence of burdens and obligations.

en.meaning: to jump in; to dive in
examples[].german: I jumped into the pool.
The child came rushing into the room, crying.
Right after graduating from university, I plunged into the IT world.
en.notes: 飛び込む is intransitive; the destination takes に: プールに飛び込む. Besides "to jump in" it also means "to rush in" (部屋に飛び込んでくる) and figuratively "to plunge into something" (新しい世界に飛び込む). The counterpart is 飛び出す ("to jump out, to rush out"). The noun 飛び込み denotes diving, but also spontaneous things such as 飛び込み営業 ("cold calling").

examples[].german: I went over budget.
What is your budget?
The travel budget is 50,000 yen per person.
en.notes: 予算 is a budget, both the national budget (国の予算) and a private budget for shopping or travel. Typical: 予算を立てる "to draw up a budget", 予算を超える, 予算が足りない, 予算内で "within the budget". In shops or at real estate agencies, staff politely ask ご予算はどのくらいですか.

examples[].german: The dog is running around the garden.
Because of the moving preparations, I ran around here and there all day.
The reporter ran all over town to gather information.
en.notes: 駆け回る is intransitive, but takes を for the area one runs through: 庭を駆け回る, 町中を駆け回る. Literally it means "to run around" (children, dogs), figuratively "to rush about, to be on the go a lot" when running errands (資金集めに駆け回る). In everyday speech 走り回る is the more common word for literal running around; 駆け回る sounds livelier and somewhat more literary.

examples[].german: The baby is crawling.
An insect was crawling over my foot, and I was startled.
I crawled forward through the narrow tunnel.
en.notes: 這う is intransitive; the path takes を (床を這う), the destination に or へ. It describes crawling on all fours or along the ground - babies, insects, snakes - and also plants that spread along walls (ツタが壁を這う). For crawling babies, children's talk also uses はいはい. The て-form is 這って (like 買う → 買って); do not confuse it with 入って from 入る.

examples[].german: My conviction is wavering.
A single remark from my teacher shook my resolve to study abroad.
The candle flame is flickering in the wind.
en.notes: 揺らぐ is intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 揺るがす "to shake". Physically it means "to sway, flicker" (炎が揺らぐ), but far more often it is used figuratively: 決心/自信/信頼が揺らぐ "to be shaken". Unlike 揺れる, the everyday word for shaking and swaying (地震で家が揺れる), 揺らぐ sounds more elevated and stresses that something actually firm becomes unstable. Negated: 揺らがない決意 "unshakable resolve".

en.meaning: to be dyed; to be tinged
examples[].german: The mountains were dyed red by the autumn leaves.
My white shirt got stained red by the wine.
Since coming to Tokyo, he has completely taken on the city lifestyle.
en.notes: 染まる is intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 染める "to dye" (髪を染める). The color and the cause take に or で (夕日に染まる, ワインで染まる), often also adverbial 赤く染まる. Figuratively it means "to be imbued with, influenced by something", often negatively: 悪に染まる "to go astray", 都会の色に染まる. For mere soiling one rather says 汚れる or シミになる.

en.meaning: to sprout; to bud; to awaken (feelings)
examples[].german: The snow has melted, and the plants have started to sprout.
As the two traveled together, a friendship budded between them.
After losing the match, the feeling "I want to get stronger" awoke in me.
en.notes: 芽生える is intransitive and literally means "to put out shoots, to sprout" (芽 "bud" + 生える "to grow"). That is why 芽が芽生える sounds redundant; for plants one says more simply 芽が出る. Much more common is the figurative use for feelings or attitudes that newly arise: 恋/友情/自覚/責任感が芽生える, often with 〜の間に or 〜の中に. The noun 芽生え "budding" is used in the same way.

en.meaning: to grow thick; to be overgrown
examples[].german: The grass is growing thick.
In summer, the leaves of the trees in the garden grow really dense.
Trees grow thick on both sides of the mountain path, so it is dark even in the daytime.
en.notes: 茂る is intransitive: 草/木/葉が茂る. It usually stands as a state, 茂っている "to be densely overgrown". Intensified, it is 生い茂る "to grow luxuriantly"; the noun 茂み means "thicket, undergrowth". Unlike 生える "to grow, to sprout" (also hair, teeth), 茂る emphasizes the density and abundance of plants and is not used for hair.

en.meaning: to become cloudy; to become muddy
examples[].german: The water is cloudy.
The air in the room was foul from the cigarette smoke.
When "hito" and "hito" follow each other, the sound becomes voiced, as in "hitobito".
en.notes: 濁る is intransitive; the opposite is 澄む. It describes cloudy water or polluted air (川の水が濁る), figuratively also hoarse voices, dull colors or an impure heart. In linguistics, 濁る means "to become voiced" - hence 濁音 (が, ざ ...) and 濁点 for the mark ゛. The transitive 濁す is known mainly from 言葉を濁す "to answer evasively".

examples[].german: The air is clear.
The water of this lake is so clear that you can see the bottom.
She sang in a clear voice.
en.notes: 澄む is intransitive and usually appears as the state 澄んでいる or attributively 澄んだ: 澄んだ空気/水/目/声. The opposite is 濁る. The transitive counterpart 澄ます is known from 耳を澄ます "to listen closely". Beware of the homophones: 住む "to live" and 済む "to be finished" are also read すむ.

en.meaning: to dress (salad); to toss with a dressing
examples[].german: I dress it with sesame.
I toss the vegetables with dressing and bring them to the table.
Please toss the boiled pasta well with the sauce.
en.notes: 和える is transitive: AをBで和える "to dress A with B" or AをBと和える "to toss A with B". It is a cooking term for mixing ingredients with a sauce, dressing or paste - typical for Japanese side dishes such as ごま和え or 白和え; the related noun is 和え物. Unlike the general 混ぜる "to mix", the ingredients stay in pieces and are only coated. Not to be confused with the identically sounding 会える "to be able to meet".

examples[].german: I knead the dough.
I kneaded clay and made a small plate.
My daughter is throwing a tantrum, saying she doesn't want to go home yet.
en.notes: こねる is transitive and is mostly written in kana (捏ねる). Literally it means "to knead": 生地/粘土をこねる; the milder 混ぜる means "to mix". Two set phrases are important: 駄々をこねる "to throw a tantrum, to be stubborn" (of children) and 理屈をこねる "to split hairs, to make up excuses".

examples[].german: Cost reduction is necessary.
The company decided to reduce overtime hours.
Next fiscal year, the budget will be cut by ten percent.
en.notes: 削減 is the deliberate cutting of quantities and expenses; as a transitive する-verb: 経費を削減する. Typical objects are コスト, 経費, 予算, 人員 and 残業時間; often also passive: 予算が削減される. The word sounds official and businesslike - in everyday speech one says 減らす. For lowering prices 下げる fits, not 削減.

examples[].german: I slurp my soba noodles.
It was so cold that I walked along sniffling.
My grandfather is sipping his hot tea in small sips.
en.notes: すする is transitive and is mostly written in kana (啜る). It means audible sucking in: 麺/そば/ラーメンをすする, お茶/スープをすする. In Japan, slurping noodles is not considered impolite but is normal. With 鼻をすする it means "to sniffle". More neutral is 飲む; 吸う means generally "to suck, to inhale".

examples[].german: I entertain the guests.
My grandmother treated us to her homemade cooking.
At this inn, the staff welcome guests with all their heart.
en.notes: もてなす is transitive and usually written in kana (持て成す): 客をもてなす, with the means marked by で (料理でもてなす). The noun もてなし, or politely おもてなし, stands for Japanese hospitality and has almost become a slogan. 接待する is the business "to entertain clients"; 招く refers only to the inviting itself.

en.meaning: to hold (an event); to feel (a sensation)
examples[].german: I will hold a party.
A concert for children was held at the city hall.
After taking the medicine, I suddenly felt drowsy.
en.notes: 催す is transitive and elevated or literary. Meaning 1: to host an event (会/宴/展覧会を催す), often in the passive 〜が催される in announcements and news; in everyday speech one rather says 開く, 行う or 開催する. Meaning 2: to feel a physical sensation: 眠気を催す "to feel drowsy", 吐き気を催す "to feel nauseous". The noun 催し(物) means "event".

en.meaning: to liven up; to get excited; to swell
examples[].german: The party livened up.
I met a friend after a long time, and we got caught up talking about old times.
Tree roots have made part of the sidewalk bulge up.
en.notes: 盛り上がる is intransitive; the transitive counterpart is 盛り上げる "to liven up" (場を盛り上げる). Most often it describes atmosphere: パーティー/試合/会話が盛り上がる, 〜の話で盛り上がる "to have a lively conversation about ...". Literally it means "to bulge, swell" (地面/筋肉が盛り上がる). The noun 盛り上がり "excitement, climax" is also common.

examples[].german: I am playing with the kitten.
The children are frolicking with the waves on the beach.
Two butterflies are flying around the flowers as if playing.
en.notes: 戯れる is intransitive and literary; the partner takes と (子犬と戯れる, 波と戯れる). In everyday speech one says 遊ぶ, or ふざける for fooling around. 戯れる sounds poetic and is gladly used for animals, children or nature scenes; it can also mean "to flirt, to dally". The noun 戯れ appears in phrases such as 戯れに "for fun, on a whim".

en.meaning: to relax; to make oneself at home
examples[].german: I am relaxing at home.
Please make yourself at home and take your time.
On weekends, I relax on the sofa and watch movies.
en.notes: くつろぐ is intransitive and mostly written in kana; 寛ぐ is seen more in texts. It means "to make oneself comfortable, to feel at home"; the place takes で (家/ソファでくつろぐ). Hosts say the set phrase どうぞおくつろぎください. Compared with リラックスする, くつろぐ emphasizes the cozy, informal atmosphere; 休む means merely "to rest, to take a break".

en.meaning: to soak in; to be immersed in
examples[].german: I soak in the hot spring.
Looking through the graduation album, I lost myself in memories.
After winning the game, the players basked in joy for a while.
en.notes: 浸る is intransitive; what one is immersed in is marked with に. Literally it means "to be immersed in liquid" (湯に浸る); for bathing, however, 浸かる (お風呂に浸かる) is more common in everyday speech. Much more common is the figurative sense: 思い出/喜び/感傷/幸せに浸る "to indulge in something, to give oneself up to a mood". The transitive counterpart is 浸す "to immerse, to soak".

examples[].german: I am absorbed in my work.
He forgot the time and became absorbed in reading.
Since retiring, my father has been devoting himself to his hobby, photography.
en.notes: 没頭 is a noun and is mostly used as an intransitive する-verb with に: 仕事/研究/読書に没頭する "to immerse oneself completely in something". It stresses that one forgets everything around oneself, and sounds somewhat more elevated. 夢中になる is more everyday and emotional (ゲームに夢中), 熱中する stresses enthusiasm, 集中する concentration for a certain time.

examples[].german: I tackle it with passion.
He pours his passion into music.
I feel that as I have gotten older, I have lost the passion of my youth.
en.notes: 情熱 is "passion, enthusiasm" for a thing or a person. Typical combinations: 情熱を持つ, 〜に情熱を注ぐ/燃やす, 情熱を失う; the な-adjective 情熱的 means "passionate" (情熱的な恋). 熱意 is more sober "zeal, commitment", やる気 colloquially "motivation". 情熱 sounds more emotional and somewhat more pathetic.

examples[].german: He is full of vitality.
Breakfast gives you energy for the day.
As more young people have moved in, vitality has returned to the town.
en.notes: 活力 is a somewhat elevated noun for life force and vigor - for people as well as for towns, companies or the economy (経済の活力). Common are 活力に満ちる, 活力を与える, 〜の活力になる and 活力源 "source of energy". In everyday speech about people one rather says 元気; エネルギー is the loanword, which is also used in the physical sense.

examples[].german: Income inequality is widening.
The gap between city and countryside has become a problem.
The gap in pay between men and women should be eliminated.
en.notes: 格差 is a gap or inequality between groups, usually with a social overtone: 所得格差, 地域格差, 男女の格差, 格差社会. Typical: 格差が広がる/縮まる, 格差をなくす. Neutral differences, for example in taste, are called 違い or 差; 格差 always implies a higher and a lower.

examples[].german: I study the history of ninja.
When I was a child, I wanted to become a ninja.
My little brother came into the room as quietly as a ninja.
en.notes: 忍者 refers to the spies and covert fighters of feudal Japan; the kanji 忍 means "to endure, to hide" (cf. 忍ぶ), and an older term is 忍び. Their techniques are called 忍術, and famous centers were 伊賀 and 甲賀. Today the word is encountered mainly in tourism, manga and comparisons like 忍者のように "as silent as a ninja".

examples[].german: I study the spirit of the samurai.
The samurai of old always carried two swords.
He played a samurai in a period drama.
en.notes: 侍 refers to the warrior class of old Japan; originally it meant "someone who serves (a lord)", from the old verb さぶらう "to serve, attend". In historiography, 武士 is the more neutral technical term; 侍 sounds more popular and romantic. In katakana, サムライ often stands for courage and discipline today, for example as the nickname of Japanese national teams. A samurai's sword is called 刀, and his code of honor 武士道.

examples[].german: It is the spirit of bushido.
Inazō Nitobe wrote a book called "Bushido" in English.
In bushido, honor was regarded as the most important thing of all.
en.notes: 武士道 is composed of 武士 "warrior, samurai" and 道 "way" and denotes the samurai code of honor with values such as loyalty, honor, courage and self-control. The term became internationally known mainly through 新渡戸稲造's English book of 1900. As in 柔道 or 茶道, 道 stands for a spiritual path; figuratively, in sports one speaks of 武士道精神 for fairness and self-discipline.

examples[].german: I toured the shogun's castle.
Tokugawa Ieyasu was the first shogun of the Edo shogunate.
That general won many battles.
en.notes: 将軍 generally means "general, military commander", but in the Japanese context it mostly means the shogun - short for 征夷大将軍, the military ruler who actually governed. His government is called 幕府 (江戸幕府), his family 将軍家. For officers of modern armies, rank titles like 大将 are used instead; 将軍 is heard today mainly in history, tourism and literature.

examples[].german: There was a daimyo's mansion.
In the Edo period, daimyo had to live in Edo every other year.
At this festival, a parade is held that reenacts a daimyo procession.
en.notes: 大名 were the feudal lords of Japan who governed their own territory (藩) under the 将軍. Well known are the 大名行列 "daimyo procession" and the 参勤交代 system, which forced them to reside in Edo regularly. Figuratively, 大名旅行 means "luxury trip", often ironic for expensive business trips. Not to be confused with 有名 "famous" or 題名 "title".

examples[].german: I saw Osaka Castle.
From the top of the castle you can see the whole town well.
I built a sandcastle on the beach with my child.
en.notes: 城 alone is read しろ (often politely お城), but in names it is じょう: 大阪城, 姫路城. It refers to Japanese castles with a main keep (天守閣) as well as European castles and palaces; an unfortified palace is called 宮殿 instead. Common combinations are 城を建てる, 城を攻める and 城下町 "castle town". Figuratively, 城 can also mean one's own little realm (この部屋は私の城だ).

examples[].german: Suits of armor are on display.
At the festival, people in armor walked through the town.
A real suit of armor is so heavy that you can't put it on alone.
en.notes: 甲冑 consists of 甲 "armor plate" and 冑 "helmet" and refers to the complete armor including the helmet, especially that of the samurai. The word is rather technical and is encountered in museums, exhibitions and history books; in everyday speech one mostly says 鎧 for the armor and 兜 for the helmet. For putting it on, one says 甲冑を着る or, in elevated style, 甲冑を身に着ける.

examples[].german: I forge a sword.
The samurai wore a sword at the waist.
At the end of the play, the hero quietly drew his sword.
en.notes: 刀 is the single-edged Japanese sword; 日本刀 emphasizes "Japanese sword" as opposed to foreign weapons. 剣 is the more general, often double-edged sword and appears in 剣道. Fixed verbs are 刀を差す "to wear (in the belt)", 刀を抜く "to draw" and 刀を鍛える "to forge"; a swordsmith is a 刀鍛冶. In compounds it is mostly read とう: 日本刀, 木刀 (竹刀 has the special reading しない).

examples[].german: I walk in zori sandals.
When wearing a kimono, it is usual to wear zori.
I took off my zori at the entrance and went into the temple.
en.notes: 草履 are flat, traditional thong sandals (originally made of straw, hence 草) that are worn with kimono or yukata, usually with 足袋 "split-toe socks". The verbs are 草履を履く and 草履を脱ぐ. To be distinguished from this is 下駄, the wooden sandal with ridges under the sole. Simple flip-flops are colloquially also called ゴム草履 or ビーチサンダル.

examples[].german: I walk through the noren.
If the noren is out in front of the shop, it is open for business.
When there is no reaction whatever you say, it is called "pushing against a noren".
en.notes: 暖簾 is mostly written in kana のれん and denotes the short, split cloth curtain at the entrance of shops, restaurants and bathhouses. Set expressions are のれんをくぐる "to enter (an establishment)" and のれんを出す/しまう "to open/close". Figuratively, のれん stands for the good reputation of a business (のれんを守る, のれん分け "a branch shop under the same name"). The proverb のれんに腕押し means "wasted effort, no reaction".

examples[].german: The economy is recovering.
How is business these days?
Business is bad, so we didn't get a bonus.
en.notes: 景気 is the state of the economy or the business cycle: 景気がいい/悪い, 景気が回復する, 景気が悪くなる. Among businesspeople, 景気はどうですか is a stock phrase for "How is business going?". A slump is 不景気 or, more formally, 不況. In 景気よく or 景気づけ, the secondary meaning "vigor, good spirits" comes through.

examples[].german: Paper lanterns are hung as decoration.
On the night of the summer festival, many red lanterns were lined up along the street.
After work, I had a drink at a red-lantern pub in front of the station.
en.notes: 提灯 is the foldable lantern of paper or silk over a bamboo frame; the reading ちょう for 提 is unusual. They are seen at festivals, at temples and in front of restaurants; 赤提灯 stands for a simple, inexpensive pub. Typical verbs are 提灯を飾る/下げる/ともす. Pejoratively, 提灯記事 means a "puff piece".

examples[].german: I decorate the alcove with flowers.
The room at the ryokan had a magnificent alcove.
The seat in front of the alcove is the best seat, where guests sit.
en.notes: 床の間 is the raised decorative alcove in a Japanese tatami room, in which a hanging scroll (掛け軸) is hung and flowers or ceramics are displayed. 床 is read とこ here, not ゆか "floor". The place in front of the alcove is considered the seat of honor (上座) for guests. Typical is 床の間に飾る "to display in the alcove".

examples[].german: I am growing bonsai.
My grandfather waters his bonsai every morning.
Bonsai are popular overseas now as well.
en.notes: 盆栽 is composed of 盆 "tray, shallow dish" and 栽 "to plant" and refers to artfully kept miniature trees in dishes. Typical verbs are 盆栽を育てる/手入れする and 盆栽に水をやる. In Japan it is traditionally regarded as a hobby of older people, but it is also known internationally. An ordinary potted plant is a 鉢植え, a garden plant 植木.

examples[].german: This is a lacquered bowl.
Wajima is a town famous for its lacquerware.
Please do not use lacquerware in the microwave.
en.notes: 漆器 is tableware and craft made with lacquer from the sap of the lacquer tree (漆); in everyday speech also called 塗り物. Typical pieces are お椀, お盆 and 重箱, well-known production places are 輪島 and 会津. Unlike 陶器 "earthenware" and 磁器 "porcelain", 漆器 usually consists of lacquered wood - which is why it does not belong in the microwave or dishwasher.

examples[].german: This town is famous for its pottery.
As a travel souvenir, I bought a ceramic plate.
In a Japanese course meal, a grilled dish comes after the sashimi.
en.notes: 焼き物 is above all "ceramics, pottery" as the umbrella term for 陶器 (earthenware) and 磁器 (porcelain). Well-known regional styles carry the suffix 〜焼, such as 有田焼 or 信楽焼. In Japanese cuisine, especially in a 懐石 menu, 焼き物 also denotes the course of grilled food, usually fish. On menus the spelling 焼物 is also seen.

examples[].german: I wipe the sweat with a tenugui.
At festivals, many people have a tenugui tied around their heads.
As a souvenir from Kyoto, I bought a tenugui with a pretty pattern.
en.notes: 手拭い (often てぬぐい) is a thin, printed cotton cloth about 90 cm long that is used as a hand towel, headscarf, sweatband or wrapping. Unlike the fluffy タオル, it dries quickly and has open, unhemmed edges. Typical are 手拭いで拭く and 頭に手拭いを巻く. Today it is also popular as a fashionable souvenir.

examples[].german: I wrap it in a furoshiki.
Recently, some people use a furoshiki instead of a shopping bag.
He is always boasting, so I only believe half of what he says.
en.notes: 風呂敷 is a square cloth for wrapping and carrying things; the name comes from the fact that it was once spread out (敷く) in the bathhouse (風呂). Typical are 風呂敷で包む and 風呂敷を広げる. Today it is experiencing a comeback as an environmentally friendly alternative to plastic bags. The idiom 大風呂敷を広げる means "to talk big, to boast".

examples[].german: I calculate with an abacus.
As a child, I went to a soroban class.
Whatever he does, he first calculates what's in it for him.
en.notes: 算盤 is mostly written in kana そろばん and denotes the Japanese abacus. Calculating with it is called そろばんをはじく; そろばん教室 are still popular classes for children today. Figuratively, そろばん stands for cost-benefit calculation: そろばんをはじく "to calculate one's advantage", そろばんが合わない "to not add up, not to be worth it".

examples[].german: Sitting in seiza is painful.
I sat in seiza for so long that my legs fell asleep.
In the tea ceremony, you drink the tea sitting in seiza.
en.notes: 正座 is the formal kneeling posture on tatami (knees together, buttocks on the heels) and is used as an intransitive する-verb: 正座する. It is regarded as a polite posture at ceremonies, in martial arts or on visits; if you sit like this for a long time, your legs fall asleep (足がしびれる). Hosts often say どうぞ足を崩してください "Please sit comfortably." Casual counterparts are あぐら "cross-legged sitting" and 横座り; not to be confused with 星座 "constellation".

examples[].german: I am learning table manners.
I was taught the proper etiquette for praying at a shrine.
My mother told me it is bad manners to talk while eating.
en.notes: 作法 refers to fixed, often traditional rules for correct behavior in a situation: 食事の作法, 茶道の作法, 礼儀作法 "rules of etiquette". Typical are 作法を守る/学ぶ and 作法に従う; the opposite 無作法 means "rude, impolite". In everyday speech one often simply says マナー (電車のマナー); 作法 sounds more traditional and emphasizes the correct sequence of actions. The reading is さほう, not さくほう.

examples[].german: The recession continues.
Because of the recession, many shops closed.
This job is said to be resistant to recessions.
en.notes: 不況 is a recession, a prolonged economic slump. Typical: 不況が続く, 不況の影響で, 不況に強い "recession-proof". More colloquial is 不景気; the opposite is 好況 or 景気がいい. 不況 always refers to the economy as a whole or an industry, never to one's own financial situation - for that one says お金がない.

examples[].german: I send a year-end gift.
Every year I send a year-end gift to my superior who has looked after me.
In December, department stores are crowded with customers choosing year-end gifts.
en.notes: 歳暮 appears almost always with the polite prefix as お歳暮: a gift sent in December to people to whom one feels indebted (superiors, relatives, teachers), as thanks for the past year. Typical are お歳暮を贈る and お歳暮をいただく. The summer counterpart is お中元. The meaning "end of the year" is rare and literary.

examples[].german: I will send a midsummer gift.
A business partner sent us beer as a midsummer gift.
Recently, more and more households no longer send midsummer gifts.
en.notes: 中元 appears in everyday life almost only as お中元: a summer gift sent, roughly from July to mid-August, to people to whom one is indebted. Originally 中元 refers to the 15th day of the 7th lunar month, which is connected with the お盆 festival. Popular gifts are beer, juices, noodles or sweets; the winter counterpart is お歳暮.

en.meaning: first shrine visit of the new year
examples[].german: I am going on the first shrine visit of the new year.
When I drew a fortune slip on the first shrine visit of the year, it was "great luck"!
On New Year's Day, Meiji Shrine is very crowded with people making their first visit of the year.
en.notes: 初詣 is the first visit to a Shinto shrine or Buddhist temple in the new year, usually within the first three days (三が日). The usual phrase is 初詣に行く; there one prays for the new year, draws a fortune slip (おみくじを引く) and buys charms (お守り). The spelling 初詣で also occurs. Famous shrines are extremely crowded at this time (初詣の人で混雑する).

examples[].german: Let's go leaf viewing.
On the weekend I went to Kyoto to see the autumn leaves.
When the leaf-viewing season comes, the roads into the mountains are crowded.
en.notes: 紅葉狩り is the viewing of the colorful autumn leaves in mountains, parks or temple gardens; 狩り ("hunt") is only figurative here, nothing is picked or collected. Typical is 紅葉狩りに行く／出かける, the counterpart to cherry blossom viewing 花見 in spring. 紅葉 alone is read こうよう ("autumn coloring") or もみじ ("maple, red leaves"); in the compound 紅葉狩り it is always もみじ.

examples[].german: I saw the Sapporo Snow Festival.
At the snow festival, many large snow sculptures are lined up.
Next February I plan to go to Hokkaido to see the snow festival.
en.notes: 雪祭り is a winter festival with large sculptures of snow and ice; the best known is the Sapporo snow festival in February, officially written さっぽろ雪まつり. As with many festival names, the spelling 雪まつり is very common. You say 雪祭りに行く or 雪祭りを見に行く; 夏祭り and 秋祭り are formed similarly.

examples[].german: It was a grand celebration.
Their wedding was held on a grand scale.
When the presentation ended, there was thunderous applause.
en.notes: 盛大 describes events that are celebrated big, lavishly and with many guests: 盛大な結婚式, 盛大なパーティー, adverbial 盛大に祝う／盛大に行われる. A fixed combination is 盛大な拍手 "thunderous applause". Colloquially and often jokingly, 盛大に also means "badly, thoroughly", e.g. 盛大に転ぶ. Not to be confused with 壮大, which stresses size and scale (landscape, plan).

examples[].german: It is a magnificent view.
He made a grand plan to travel around the world.
This film is a grand epic that depicts a hundred years of a family.
en.notes: 壮大 means "immense, grand" in the sense of great scale and sublime effect. Typical partners are 景色, 自然, 計画, 夢 and 物語: 壮大な計画, 壮大なスケール. Unlike 盛大 (a lavishly celebrated event), it is not about celebrating, and unlike 荘厳 not about solemnity, but about size and breadth. The word is somewhat literary, but common in travel writing and film or book reviews.

examples[].german: It is a solemn atmosphere.
The majestic sound of the organ resounded in the church.
The ceremony was held solemnly at the shrine.
en.notes: 荘厳 means "solemn, majestic" and describes a dignified, awe-inspiring mood, above all at temples, churches, ceremonies and sacred music: 荘厳な雰囲気, 荘厳な儀式, adverbial 荘厳に行われる. The word is written-language and elevated; in Buddhism the same spelling with the reading しょうごん is used for the adornment of temples. Distinction: 壮大 emphasizes grandeur, 盛大 splendor and many guests, 荘厳 dignity and reverence.

examples[].german: It is an elegant dance.
A swan is gliding gracefully across the lake.
When I retire, I want to live a leisurely life by the sea.
en.notes: 優雅 has two meanings: "elegant, graceful" for movements, bearing and clothing (優雅な踊り, 優雅に泳ぐ), and "carefree, leisurely" for a life without money worries (優雅な生活, 優雅に暮らす). In the second meaning it often sounds slightly envious or ironic, for example 平日に旅行なんて優雅だね. Related is 上品 ("refined, cultivated"), which describes more character, taste and manners.

examples[].german: It is a vivid color.
In autumn, the mountains turn vivid red and yellow.
He scored a goal with a brilliant shot.
en.notes: 鮮やか first describes bright, clear colors (鮮やかな赤, 色鮮やか) and also vivid memories (記憶に鮮やかに残る). Equally common is the meaning "skillful, brilliant" for a masterly performance: 鮮やかな手つき, 鮮やかなシュート, 鮮やかに解決する. For colors, 淡い is the opposite; 派手 ("flashy, showy") often sounds judgmental, whereas 鮮やか is positive.

examples[].german: The unemployment rate is rising.
The company went under, and my older brother lost his job.
While I was unemployed, I received unemployment insurance.
en.notes: 失業 is unemployment; as an intransitive する-verb, 失業する means "to become unemployed". Compounds: 失業者, 失業率, 失業保険 "unemployment insurance". Colloquially people also say 仕事がない or 無職; voluntarily quitting, on the other hand, is 仕事を辞める or 退職.

examples[].german: I like pale colors.
I bought a spring-like pale pink shirt.
I held a faint hope that I might pass.
en.notes: 淡い means "pale, delicate, light" for colors, light, taste and scent (淡い色, 淡いピンク, 淡い味) and sounds more elevated and poetic than the everyday word 薄い. Figuratively it describes weak, fleeting feelings: 淡い期待 "faint hope", 淡い恋 "tender, shy love". The opposite is 濃い; unlike 薄い, however, 淡い is never used for the thickness of objects (a thin book is 薄い本).

examples[].german: I like strong flavors.
This morning the trains were delayed because of dense fog.
My older brother has a heavy beard, so he has to shave every morning.
en.notes: 濃い is the opposite of 薄い and covers several areas: dark or strong colors (濃い青), strong taste or smell (味が濃い, 濃いコーヒー), dense consistency (濃い霧, 濃いスープ) and thick hair growth (眉が濃い, ひげが濃い). Figuratively it stands for high probability (可能性が濃い) and close relationships (濃い人間関係). 化粧が濃い means "wearing heavy makeup" and is meant rather critically.

examples[].german: There is a close relationship.
Diet and health are closely related.
During COVID, we were told to avoid situations of close contact with other people.
en.notes: 密接 means "close" in the sense of a tight connection or interaction between things and almost always appears in 密接な関係 or 密接に関係する／関わる／結びつく. For personal, warm closeness between people one rather says 親密. As a する-verb, 密接する means "to be close together"; this became well known through the COVID rule 三密 (密閉・密集・密接). The word is slightly literary and common in news and factual texts.

examples[].german: Fundamental reform is necessary.
The government announced drastic measures to reduce traffic accidents.
Because losses continued, the company fundamentally reviewed its management.
en.notes: 抜本的 means "fundamental, sweeping" and refers to measures that tackle a problem at its root (抜本 = "pulling out the root"). It is used almost only with words for reforms and measures: 抜本的な改革, 抜本的な対策, 抜本的な見直し, adverbially 抜本的に見直す／改める. The word belongs to the language of politics, economics and the news; in everyday speech one says more 根本的 or 根本から変える.

examples[].german: It is irrational behavior.
I think it is irrational to hold meetings until late every day.
When people become anxious, they tend to make irrational decisions.
en.notes: 非合理的 is the opposite of 合理的 ("rational, reasonable, efficient") and means "irrational, unreasonable" - both for thinking and behavior (非合理的な判断) and for inefficient rules and procedures (非合理的なルール). Synonymous and somewhat more common is 不合理; 非論理的, by contrast, stresses the lack of logical coherence. The prefix 非 negates, as in 非常識 or 非公式.

examples[].german: It is morally right.
Some conduct is morally questionable even if it violates no law.
It is the parents' role to teach children moral ways of thinking.
en.notes: 道徳的 means "moral, ethical" and judges actions by general social norms: 道徳的に正しい／問題がある, 道徳的な責任. 道徳 itself is also the name of the school subject "moral education". Closely related is 倫理的 ("ethical"), which is used more for professional ethics, medicine or philosophy; the opposite is 不道徳 ("immoral").

examples[].german: It is a solid building.
This castle stood on a mountain and was well defended.
She has a firm will and always sees through what she has decided.
en.notes: 堅固 means "firm, solid, hard to capture" and is a written-language word; typical are 堅固な城, 堅固な守り, 堅固な建物. Figuratively it describes an unshakable will: 意志が堅固, as a four-character word 意志堅固. In everyday speech, for sturdy objects one rather says 頑丈 or 丈夫; 堅固 sounds like fortress, defense and history.

examples[].german: It is a vulnerable system.
A vulnerability was found in this software, so please update it immediately.
Because the ground in this area is weak, earthquake damage tends to be large.
en.notes: 脆弱 means "weak, susceptible, vulnerable" and is a written-language word for structures, systems and foundations: 脆弱な地盤, 脆弱な経済基盤, 体制が脆弱だ. In IT, 脆弱性 is the technical term for a "security vulnerability". The character 脆 is known from 脆い ("brittle, fragile"). For people and objects in everyday speech, one more often says 弱い, 壊れやすい or 脆い.

examples[].german: It is nothing more than conjecture.
From his expression, I inferred that the exam results had been bad.
My guess was right: he really was planning to quit the company.
en.notes: 推測 is a conjecture derived from available clues; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を推測する, 〜と推測する, passive 〜と推測される (common in the news). Fixed combinations are 推測が当たる／外れる and 推測に過ぎない "is only a conjecture". 予想 refers more to future results, 推理 to logical deduction as in a detective story, and 想像 to free imagination.

examples[].german: I will push the project forward.
The government is promoting the use of renewable energy.
This engine gives the ship strong propulsion.
en.notes: 推進 means "to push forward, promote" and is used mainly for politics, projects and movements: 〜を推進する, 改革を推進する, 推進派 "proponents"; the passive 〜が推進されている is also common. The basic technical meaning is "propulsion" (推進力 "thrust"). The word is literary and typical of official and corporate language; in conversation one rather says 進める.

examples[].german: We need to increase employment.
The new factory created 300 jobs.
This company employs many foreigners.
en.notes: 雇用 is employment from the point of view of the employer or the labor market; as a transitive する-verb: 人を雇用する "to employ someone". In everyday speech 雇う is usually used instead. Typical: 雇用を生む/増やす/守る, 雇用契約, 正規雇用 and 非正規雇用. From the employee's point of view, starting a job is 就職する.

examples[].german: I will eliminate obstacles.
The police removed the demonstrators from the road.
The possibility of an accident cannot be ruled out either.
en.notes: 排除 means "to exclude, eliminate, remove", often forcefully or with force: 障害を排除する, 反対派を排除する, 警察がデモ隊を排除する. Very common is 可能性を排除する／排除できない "to rule out (be unable to rule out) a possibility". More neutral are 除く／取り除く; 除外 means "to take out of a list or evaluation" and sounds less harsh. A transitive する-verb, literary.

examples[].german: We will introduce a new system.
A new salary system is scheduled to be introduced from next year.
The opening part of this novel was so interesting that I read it in one go.
en.notes: 導入 means "to introduce" systems, technology, rules or devices: 〜を導入する, 制度を導入する, passive 〜が導入される. For introducing people one says 紹介 instead, not 導入. The second meaning is the "introduction" of a text, lecture or piece of music (導入部, 導入部分). The word is matter-of-fact and very common in business and the news.

examples[].german: We withdrew from the market.
The army withdrew from the front.
The rain got heavier, so we gave up on the summit and decided to turn back.
en.notes: 撤退 is an intransitive する-verb: 〜から撤退する "to withdraw from ...". Originally military (軍が撤退する), it is now often used for companies that give up a market or a line of business (海外から撤退する, 事業撤退). In mountaineering, too, one speaks of 撤退 when turning back before the summit. It should be distinguished from 撤去 ("to remove, to dismantle objects"), which is transitive.

examples[].german: We will merge the two departments.
We combined several apps into one to make them easier to use.
As the number of children declined, three of the town's elementary schools were merged.
en.notes: 統合 means "to bring together, unify" several parts into a whole: AとBを統合する, 〜を一つに統合する, passive 〜が統合される. Common are 経営統合 ("merger of two companies"), 学校の統合 and データの統合. 合併, by contrast, is the legal merger of companies or municipalities, and 統一 means "to unify" (rules, countries).

examples[].german: It is the principle of the separation of religion and state.
Water and oil separate right away even if you mix them.
A car hit the median strip on the expressway.
en.notes: 分離 means "to separate, become separated" and is both transitive (〜を分離する) and intransitive (〜が分離する), for example when water and oil separate. It is technical and literary: 政教分離 ("separation of state and religion"), 中央分離帯 ("median strip"). For sorting trash one says 分別, and for people separating 別れる or 別居.

examples[].german: We changed our policy.
Why don't we take a walk to change our mood?
If you change your way of thinking, the problem can be solved easily.
en.notes: 転換 means a fundamental switch or turn in direction or kind: 方針を転換する, 方向転換, 発想の転換 ("rethinking"), 転換期 ("turning point"). Especially everyday is 気分転換 "a change of pace to take your mind off things". As a する-verb it can be transitive (〜を転換する) and intransitive (〜に転換する). Not to be confused with 変換, for example when converting kana to kanji on a computer.

examples[].german: We build a relationship of trust.
The company built a new customer management system.
The researchers are working on constructing a new theory.
en.notes: 構築 means "to build up, to construct", mostly in the abstract sense: systems, networks, theories and relationships are built (システムを構築する, 信頼関係を構築する). For actual buildings, 建築 or 建設 are used instead. The word is matter-of-fact and written-language and very common in IT and business; in conversation 作る or 築く are often enough.

examples[].german: The economy collapsed.
An old bridge collapsed in the earthquake.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
en.notes: 崩壊 is an intransitive する-verb for the complete collapse of structures, systems and orders: 建物が崩壊する, 経済が崩壊する, バブル崩壊, 家庭崩壊, 学級崩壊 ("the class getting out of control"). In physics it denotes radioactive decay. The everyday word for things falling down is 崩れる; 崩壊 sounds more dramatic and final.

examples[].german: We will ensure safety.
I'll go early and save us a good seat.
It is difficult to secure time for studying every day.
en.notes: 確保 means "to secure something, make sure of it": you make sure that something necessary is reliably available: 席を確保する, 時間を確保する, 人材を確保する, 安全を確保する, 食料や水の確保. A transitive する-verb with を. In police reports, 身柄を確保する means "to arrest, take into custody". For merely obtaining something one says 手に入れる; 確保 stresses securing it.

examples[].german: I make full use of my abilities.
I was so nervous that I couldn't show my true ability in the match.
This medicine takes effect about thirty minutes after taking it.
en.notes: 発揮 means bringing an existing power or ability into play: 能力／実力／力を発揮する, リーダーシップを発揮する, 本領を発揮する "to show what one is made of". Things can also take effect: 薬が効果を発揮する. A transitive する-verb with を, often in the potential or negated: 実力を発揮できなかった. Not to be confused with 発表 ("to announce, to present").

examples[].german: Specialized knowledge is required.
I tried using the knowledge I gained from books in actual work.
He has extensive knowledge of history.
en.notes: 知識 is acquired knowledge: 知識がある / ない, 知識を得る, 知識を身につける "to acquire knowledge". Common combinations are 専門知識 "specialized knowledge", 基礎知識 "basic knowledge" and 〜に関する知識; someone who knows a lot has 豊富な知識. 知恵, by contrast, denotes practical wisdom and resourcefulness, and 情報 individual pieces of information.

examples[].german: Welfare services are well developed.
My older sister is studying social welfare at university.
This town focuses on the welfare of the elderly.
en.notes: 福祉 is welfare or social services, above all as a field of state and social support: 社会福祉, 老人福祉, 福祉施設, 福祉の仕事. Typical: 福祉が充実している "social services are well developed", 福祉に力を入れる. It is a factual word from politics and administration; personal well-being is rather 幸せ or 健康.

examples[].german: I make use of the resources.
I want to use my experience from studying abroad in my job.
I just can't memorize the conjugation of Japanese verbs.
en.notes: 活用 means "to make good use of, to put to use" - one gets something out of what is available: 経験を活用する, データを活用する, 〜を〜に活用する, 有効活用 "effective use". It sounds more active than 利用 ("to use") and is common in business and administration. In grammar, 活用 means "conjugation, inflection": 動詞の活用, 活用形; in this sense 活用する is intransitive (動詞が活用する).

examples[].german: We apply the new rules.
Health insurance does not cover this treatment.
The discount applies only to students.
en.notes: 適用 means to apply a rule, a law, an insurance or a rate to a case: 規則を適用する, 法律が適用される. The passive is very common: 保険が適用される "the insurance covers the costs", 割引が適用される "the discount applies". Distinctions: 応用 is the creative transfer of knowledge or technology to something new, 活用 the sensible use of resources; 適用 is the formal application of a rule.

examples[].german: I apply the theory.
Once you understand the basics, let's try the application problems next.
This technology is also applied in medicine.
en.notes: 応用 means applying basic knowledge, theories or techniques practically to something new: 理論を応用する, 〜を〜に応用する, passive 〜に応用されている. In compounds it stands for "applied" or "advanced": 応用化学, 応用問題 ("transfer problem"), 応用力 ("ability to transfer what has been learned"). The counterpart is 基本／基礎; 適用, by contrast, is the formal application of rules and laws.

examples[].german: The effects are spreading.
The recession in America spread to the whole world.
The Olympics bring a large ripple effect to the regional economy.
en.notes: 波及 describes how an effect spreads in waves (波 "wave" + 及 "to reach"): 影響が〜に波及する, 〜全体に波及する. A fixed combination is 波及効果 "ripple effect, spillover effect", mostly economic. It is an intransitive する-verb, and its subjects are effects, crises or unrest. It is written-language and typical of the news; in conversation one says more 広がる or 影響が出る.

examples[].german: The economy is stagnating.
The rainy-season front is stalled near Kyushu.
Since the leader quit, the project has been stalled.
en.notes: 停滞 means "standstill, stagnation": something that should move or develop does not progress: 経済が停滞する, 景気の停滞, 議論が停滞する, 作業が停滞する. In weather reports one hears 前線が停滞する and 停滞前線 ("stationary front"), for example in the rainy season. An intransitive する-verb. Not to be confused with 渋滞, which stands for traffic jams.

examples[].german: I avoid risks.
The driver swerved instantly and avoided an accident.
He keeps making statements that dodge responsibility.
en.notes: 回避 means "to avoid something undesirable, to avert it". Although dictionaries list it as intransitive, in practice it almost always takes を: 危険／リスク／事故を回避する, 責任を回避する ("to evade responsibility"). It is more matter-of-fact and formal than 避ける; also common are 回避策 ("workaround") and 衝突回避. In law, it refers to a judge's recusal of himself.

examples[].german: I will deal with the problem.
We discussed as a family what to do in an earthquake.
As a way to deal with a headache, I recommend first drinking water.
en.notes: 対処 means to respond appropriately to a problem or situation and cope with it. It is intransitive and takes に: 問題に対処する, 事態に対処する, 迅速に対処する; plus the noun 対処法 ("remedy, way of dealing with it"). Very similar is 対応, which is broader and also covers customer service or replying (お客様の対応); 対処 stresses solving a difficulty.

examples[].german: I will think of a new approach.
We cannot find an effective measure to stop the declining birthrate.
The company drew up a plan to increase sales.
en.notes: 方策 is a plan or measure for reaching a goal or solving a problem: 方策を考える／立てる, 有効な方策, 〜ための方策. In formal texts it appears as 方策を講じる "to take measures". The word is literary; in everyday speech one rather says 方法 or やり方, and for countermeasures against a specific problem 対策 is far more common.

examples[].german: It was an inappropriate remark.
This video contains inappropriate content.
Using medicine improperly can sometimes have bad effects on the body.
en.notes: 不適切 is the negation of 適切 ("appropriate, suitable") and means "inappropriate, unsuitable". Typical are 不適切な発言, 不適切な表現, 不適切な内容, 不適切な関係 and adverbially 不適切に使う. The word is matter-of-fact and formal and often appears in apologies, news and guidelines; in conversation one more often says よくない or ふさわしくない. The similar 不適当 stresses more "not suited for a purpose".

examples[].german: It is an apt remark.
The department head always gives clear, accurate instructions.
She answered the question briefly and precisely.
en.notes: 的確 means "accurate, exactly right" - something hits the target like an arrow (的 "target"): 的確な判断, 的確な指示, 的確なアドバイス, 的確に答える. While 正確 emphasizes that something is error-free and exact (正確な時間), 的確 emphasizes that it fits the situation and hits the heart of the matter. Besides てきかく, the reading てっかく is also possible; the tone is matter-of-fact and mostly praising.

examples[].german: I work in caregiving.
I quit my job to take care of my father.
My grandmother is cared for at home by her family.
en.notes: 介護 is the care and support of elderly, sick or disabled people in daily life (eating, bathing, moving about); as a transitive する-verb: 母を介護する. Compounds: 介護士, 介護施設, 親の介護. Distinction: 看護 is medical nursing (看護師 "nurse in a hospital"), 育児 is childcare.

examples[].german: I used to live here.
Your Japanese has gotten better than before.
Before I got married, I worked at a company in Tokyo.
en.notes: 以前 as an adverb or noun means "previously, before": 以前は〜, 以前の家, 以前より上手になった; it is somewhat more formal than 前 and usually refers to a nearer past than 昔. As a suffix it means "before, up to": 明治以前, 結婚する以前. The phrase それ以前の問題 means "an even more fundamental problem"; not to be confused with the similar-sounding 依然 ("still, as before").

examples[].german: I haven't seen him/her since graduation.
Ever since I came to Japan, I have written a diary in Japanese every day.
We met once last summer, but I haven't heard from him since then.
en.notes: 以来 means "since, ever since" and describes a state that continues from a point in the past up to now. It follows nouns (卒業以来, 去年以来), the て-form (日本に来て以来) or stands alone as それ以来. Unlike から or 以降, 以来 cannot refer to the future: "from next week" is 来週から or 来週以降. It is often followed by a negation or a continuing state (〜ていない, ずっと〜).

examples[].german: I will respond immediately.
A tsunami warning has been issued. Please evacuate to high ground immediately.
At this amount, there is no immediate effect on health.
en.notes: 直ちに means "immediately, without delay" and is the formal counterpart of すぐに. It is heard in announcements, warnings, laws and business language: 直ちに避難してください, 直ちに対応いたします. With a negation it means "not immediately, not automatically": 直ちに健康に影響が出るわけではない. 速やかに is similar but allows a bit more leeway ("promptly, without unnecessary delay").

examples[].german: Please vacate promptly.
Please submit the documents promptly.
Thanks to the company's prompt response, the problem was solved quickly.
en.notes: 速やかに is the adverbial form of the な-adjective 速やか and means "swiftly, promptly". It is formal and typically appears in requests and instructions from authorities, companies or schools: 速やかに提出してください, 速やかに退出する, as an adjective 速やかな対応. Compared with 直ちに ("immediately, without any delay"), it sounds somewhat less urgent; in conversation one simply says すぐ or 早めに.

examples[].german: I deliberately won't say it.
She deliberately chose the difficult path.
If I had to say something, I think it would be better a little shorter.
en.notes: あえて (rarely 敢えて) means "deliberately, on purpose": you do something although it is unnecessary, difficult or unexpected: あえて難しい道を選ぶ, あえて何も言わない. The phrase あえて言うなら／あえて言えば introduces an answer one gives reluctantly: "if I had to say something". With a negative it means "not necessarily, not especially" (あえて〜する必要はない). Unlike わざと ("on purpose", often with ill intent), あえて sounds considered and bold.

examples[].german: By the way, are you free tomorrow?
By the way, what happened with that trip you were talking about the other day?
Even if we hurry now, we won't make it anymore.
en.notes: ところで introduces a change of topic at the beginning of a sentence: "by the way, speaking of which". It signals that the new topic is unrelated to what came before; そういえば ("that reminds me"), by contrast, picks up on something that was said, and さて ("well then") sounds more like a transition in speeches. After the た-form, ところで has a different meaning: 〜たところで "even if ..., (it is no use)", e.g. 今さら謝ったところで遅い.

en.meaning: for the time being; for now
examples[].german: This is enough for now.
Let's just buy what we need for now.
Until I find a new job, I will live off my savings for the time being.
en.notes: 差し当たり (mostly written in kana as さしあたり) means "for the time being, for now, to begin with": one adopts a provisional solution until something final comes up. In spoken language the variant さしあたって is just as common. Close in meaning are とりあえず (more casual, very everyday) and 当面 (more formal, "for the foreseeable future").

en.meaning: with all one's might; as best one can
examples[].german: I will do my best.
I can barely make ends meet each month - saving is out of the question.
I was so nervous that all I could do was answer "yes".
en.notes: 精一杯 means "with all one's strength, as well as one can". As an adverb it stands before verbs like 頑張る, 生きる or やる; 精一杯頑張ります is a typical formula for introductions and promises. As a noun, 〜のが精一杯／〜で精一杯 expresses that one can just manage that much and no more: 生活するだけで精一杯. It is often also written 精いっぱい.

en.meaning: we're in the same boat; it's mutual
examples[].german: It is mutual.
"Thank you for helping me." "We help each other when in trouble."
We are both busy, so please don't worry about it.
en.notes: お互い様 is said when both sides are in the same situation or do each other favors - it takes away the other person's feeling of owing something. Typical is 困った時はお互い様 "when in need, we simply help each other" as a reply to thanks or an apology, and 〜のはお互い様 "that goes for both of us". It is friendly and very common among neighbors and coworkers; お互いに alone, by contrast, is just the adverb "mutually".

examples[].german: The declining birthrate has become a problem.
Because of the declining birthrate, the village elementary school closed.
The government announced new measures against the declining birthrate.
en.notes: 少子化 refers to the decrease in the number of children or the birthrate, a central social issue in Japan. It is often combined with 高齢化 to form 少子高齢化. Typical: 少子化が進む, 少子化対策 "measures against the declining birthrate". The suffix 化 expresses a change; the birthrate itself is 出生率.

en.meaning: thank you for your trouble (said to subordinates)
examples[].german: Thank you for your efforts.
I said to the delivery person, "Thank you for your trouble in this heat."
The department head said to the staff who had worked overtime, "Thank you for staying so late."
en.notes: ご苦労様（です／でした） thanks someone for their work or effort. Traditionally it is said by a person of higher rank to subordinates, or to service providers such as delivery people; toward superiors it is considered impolite, where one says お疲れ様です instead. With でした it is used after finished work, with です during ongoing work or on arrival. Also written ご苦労さま.

examples[].german: I am terribly sorry.
I am sorry to have kept you waiting.
We are sorry, but reception has already closed for today.
en.notes: 申し訳ございません is a very polite apology, more polite than 申し訳ありません and much more formal than すみません or ごめんなさい. It is heard mainly in customer service, in business e-mails and for serious mistakes, often intensified by 大変 or 誠に. With が it introduces a polite refusal (申し訳ございませんが、…); sometimes it also expresses thanks for the trouble one causes someone (お忙しいところ申し訳ございません).

examples[].german: Excuse me, but could you tell me your name?
"Shall I carry your luggage?" "That is very kind of you, thank you."
Excuse me, but please wait a moment.
en.notes: 恐れ入ります is a humble, polite formula with three functions: before a request or question as 恐れ入りますが "excuse me, but ...", as thanks for kindness ("that is very kind of you"), and as an apology for causing trouble. It is typical of business life, customer service and phone calls and sounds much more polite than すみませんが. After 恐れ入りますが there usually follows an equally polite request such as 〜ていただけますか.

examples[].german: Understood. I will deal with it right away.
"Please put these documents together by tomorrow." "Certainly, I will take care of it."
"Then I will come by at three o'clock." "Certainly. We will be expecting you."
en.notes: 承知しました is the polite past form of 承知する "to take note of, to agree" and the standard reply at work when one accepts an assignment or a piece of information. Toward superiors and customers it replaces the too casual わかりました; 了解しました is often considered inappropriate toward those of higher rank. Even humbler is 承知いたしました; in service and hospitality one mostly hears かしこまりました. Related: 承知しております "I am aware of that".

examples[].german: Certainly. Please wait a moment.
"Two coffees, please." "Certainly."
Understood, sir. I will have it ready by tomorrow.
en.notes: かしこまりました is the very polite, humble confirmation "Certainly, it will be done", typical for staff toward customers and, at work, toward superiors. It is more polite than わかりました and expresses not only understanding but also readiness to comply with the request. Among friends it would be out of place; there one says わかった or 了解. The kanji spelling 畏まりました is rare.

examples[].german: Please, go ahead and help yourself.
If you have any questions, please feel free to ask.
If you need anything, please don't hesitate to let us know.
en.notes: ご遠慮なく is the polite form of 遠慮なく "without reserve, freely" and tells the other person not to be shy: when offering food, when inviting questions or requests. Typical: ご遠慮なくどうぞ, ご遠慮なくお申し付けください, ご遠慮なくお召し上がりください. Not to be confused with ご遠慮ください, a polite prohibition ("please refrain from", e.g. 喫煙はご遠慮ください). About oneself one says it without ご: では、遠慮なくいただきます.

examples[].german: Please don't worry about it.
"Sorry I'm late." "Don't worry about it. I just got here too."
Don't dwell on the mistake - let's do our best next time.
en.notes: 気にしないで is the negative て-form of 気にする "to take something to heart, to worry about" and reassures someone who is apologizing or is upset about a mistake. Among friends 気にしないで(ね) is enough, politely 気にしないでください, very politely お気になさらないでください. 気にしないで usually refers to something that has already happened; 心配しないで comforts more with worries about the future. Similarly casual: 大丈夫だよ.
