examples[].german: I have looked at the materials.
Tickets, please.
Would you mind if I take a quick look at that photo?
en.notes: 拝見する is the humble form (謙譲語) of 見る and is used when one looks at or reads something that belongs to a person of higher status: 資料を拝見する, お手紙を拝見しました. The conductor says 切符を拝見します during a ticket check. For the actions of the other person it is wrong; there the honorific ご覧になる (ご覧ください) is used. A common request is 拝見してもよろしいですか "May I take a look?"

examples[].german: May I have your business card?
We have received many opinions from all of you.
Mom, give me that snack.
en.notes: As a する-verb, 頂戴する is the humble form of もらう as well as of 食べる/飲む: 名刺を頂戴する, ご意見を頂戴する, お電話を頂戴する. It sounds slightly more formal than いただく. There is also the familiar ちょうだい (mostly in kana) as a request "give me / please": それちょうだい, 見せてちょうだい - typical of children, parents and rather feminine speech, inappropriate toward superiors.

examples[].german: The teacher said so.
Excuse me, could you please say that once more?
You are quite right.
en.notes: 仰る is the honorific verb (尊敬語) for "to say" and is used only for statements by other, higher-status people; for oneself one says humble 申す. It is a special Godan verb: the ます-form is おっしゃいます (not おっしゃります). Common are 何とおっしゃいましたか "What did you say?" and おっしゃる通りです "You are quite right". It is almost always written in kana, おっしゃる; the kanji forms 仰る and 仰っしゃる are rare.

examples[].german: In Japan, the population is aging.
The village population is aging, and there are hardly any young people.
The declining birthrate and aging population is a major challenge for Japan.
en.notes: 高齢化 is aging, usually of the population or society; as an intransitive する-verb: 人口が高齢化する. Typical: 高齢化が進む, 高齢化社会, 少子高齢化. 高齢 is the polite word for "advanced age" (高齢者 "seniors"), and 化 denotes the change. The aging of an individual person is not 高齢化 but 年を取る.

examples[].german: The teacher taught me.
My department head gave me flowers for my birthday.
Thank you for coming from so far away.
en.notes: くださる is the honorific form (尊敬語) of くれる: a person of higher status gives something to the speaker or their side. As an auxiliary verb, ～てくださる expresses gratitude for a favor: 先生が教えてくださった. The ます-form is irregular (くださいます), and the request ください is actually its imperative. It is mostly written in kana, especially as an auxiliary verb; the kanji spelling 下さる is rarer. The counterpart from the recipient's point of view is humble いただく.

examples[].german: It is an honor to meet you.
I am scheduled to meet the company president next week.
Pleased to meet you. My name is Yamada.
en.notes: お目にかかる is the humble form (謙譲語) of 会う: one places oneself below the person one meets; that person is marked with に - 先生にお目にかかる. Fixed formulas: 初めてお目にかかります, お目にかかれてうれしいです/光栄です, またお目にかかれるのを楽しみにしております. Somewhat less formal is お会いする. For the other person's meeting, never use お目にかかる, but お会いになる. Not to be confused with お目にかける "to show (something)".

examples[].german: I am sorry to trouble you.
Sorry for the trouble, but please fill out this form.
Thank you for the trouble you took the other day.
en.notes: お手数 "trouble, bother" always means the effort one causes OTHERS and appears almost only in fixed politeness formulas: お手数をおかけします (apology or thanks in advance), お手数ですが… (introducing a request), お手数をおかけしました (thanks afterwards). The standard reading is おてすう; おてかず also occurs. ご迷惑をおかけします sounds similar but stresses real inconvenience rather than just extra work.

examples[].german: I apologize for the inconvenience.
Please set your mobile phone to silent mode so as not to disturb other customers.
If it's no trouble, shall I take you to the station?
en.notes: ご迷惑 is the polite 迷惑 "nuisance, inconvenience" and refers to the burden placed on others. Formulas: ご迷惑をおかけしました (apology), 〜のご迷惑になる "to disturb someone" (typical in announcements), ご迷惑でなければ "if it is not inconvenient for you". Without ご, 迷惑 is also a な-adjective: 迷惑な人 "annoying person", 迷惑メール "spam". お手数 is milder and means only extra effort.

examples[].german: I look forward to your guidance.
Thanks to my teacher's guidance, I was able to pass the exam.
I received strict guidance from the department manager.
en.notes: ご指導 is the respectful form of 指導 "guidance, supervision, coaching" and refers to instruction by teachers, superiors or trainers. Fixed phrases: ご指導よろしくお願いします (when starting a job or at the beginning of a course), ご指導いただく, ご指導のおかげで. In speeches one hears the stiff formula ご指導ご鞭撻のほど…. Whoever gives the guidance says it without ご: 新人を指導する. Unlike 説明 or 案内, it is about longer-term instruction.

examples[].german: We ask for your consideration.
Could you please give it favorable consideration?
Have you had a chance to consider the pricing plans?
en.notes: ご検討 is the polite 検討 "examination, consideration" and refers to the weighing up by customers or business partners. Typical in business e-mails: ご検討のほどよろしくお願いいたします, ご検討いただけますと幸いです, 前向きにご検討ください. One's own consideration is called without ご: 検討いたします. Caution: 検討します as a reply is often a polite refusal in Japanese.

examples[].german: Please bear with us.
Please note in advance that changes may be made without notice.
We will begin the work after we have received the customer's consent.
en.notes: ご了承 means "acknowledgment and acceptance" and appears almost always in one-sided notices: one announces a restriction and asks that it be accepted - ご了承ください, あらかじめご了承ください (on websites, signs, in announcements). It is more a polite notice than a real request for permission. Softer is ご理解ください "please understand". As a verb: 了承する "to consent", ご了承いただく.

examples[].german: Please check it.
Please check the attached file.
When getting off, please make sure you have not left anything behind.
en.notes: ご確認 is the polite 確認 "checking, verification". Note: it mostly means "to look over, to check", not "to confirm" in the sense of giving a commitment. Typical: ご確認ください, ご確認をお願いします, ご確認のうえ… "after you have checked", ご確認いただけますか. For one's own checking there is no ご: 確認いたします, 確認させていただきます. Very common in e-mails (添付ファイルをご確認ください) and announcements.

examples[].german: I look forward to hearing from you.
If you are going to be late, please let us know.
We will contact you later.
en.notes: ご連絡 is the polite 連絡 "contact, notification". A peculiarity: ご is used both for the other person's action (ご連絡ください, ご連絡お待ちしております) and in the humble pattern ご〜いたします for one's own: こちらからご連絡いたします. The person notified is marked with に: お客様にご連絡する. 連絡 includes calls, e-mails and messages; 連絡先 is the contact address.

examples[].german: I will report to you.
We have some happy news for all of you.
I will report the result of the meeting to the department manager tomorrow.
en.notes: ご報告 is the polite 報告 "report, notification". Since one usually reports to a superior oneself, it typically appears in the humble pattern ご報告いたします/ご報告します, with the recipient marked by に. In speeches and on social media, ご報告があります often announces private news (marriage, a baby). A written report is more often called 報告書 or レポート.

examples[].german: I listen to the opinions of the younger generation.
My father and I are of different generations, so we also think differently.
This song is loved across generations.
en.notes: 世代 is a generation: 若い世代, 親の世代, 次の世代, 同じ世代. Typical: 世代が違う, 世代を超えて "across generations", 世代交代 "generational change". Product generations are also counted this way: 第三世代. Distinction: 時代 is an era, not an age group.

examples[].german: I will guide you there.
We will send you information about our new products.
The invitation to the wedding has arrived.
en.notes: ご案内 is the polite 案内 with two main meanings: (1) to guide someone, to show the way - お席へご案内いたします; (2) notice, information, invitation - 新商品のご案内, 説明会のご案内 (often as a subject line). In announcements, ご案内いたします introduces a piece of information. As with ご連絡, ご is used in the humble pattern ご案内いたします for one's own action too. 案内所 is an information desk.

examples[].german: Have you decided on your order?
Let me repeat your order.
The item you ordered will be shipped tomorrow.
en.notes: ご注文 is the polite 注文 "order" and is used by staff for the customer's order. In a restaurant: ご注文はお決まりですか, ご注文は以上でよろしいですか, ご注文を繰り返します; in online shopping: ご注文ありがとうございます. The customer himself says it without ご: 注文をお願いします, 注文してもいいですか. A reservation, by contrast, is 予約.

examples[].german: I use public facilities.
This hotel has facilities such as a pool and a gym.
My grandmother has lived in a care facility since last year.
en.notes: 施設 denotes a facility as a building or installation with a specific purpose: 公共施設, スポーツ施設, 医療施設, 研究施設. On its own, 施設 can also mean a home (children's home or care home): 施設で育つ "to grow up in an institution". Distinction: 設備 is the technical equipment inside a building (air conditioning, piping), 施設 the facility as a whole. As a する-verb it is hardly used.

examples[].german: The facilities are complete.
This factory has replaced its old equipment.
Because of an equipment failure, the trains have stopped.
en.notes: 設備 is permanently installed technical equipment: heating, piping, machines, safety systems. Collocations: 設備が整う "to be well equipped", 設備投資 "investment in equipment", 設備の点検/故障. Distinctions: 施設 is the facility itself (building, complex), 設備 what is installed in it; 装置 is a single device, 備品 movable inventory such as furniture or office supplies.

examples[].german: Let's give a little.
In the negotiations, we made major concessions to the other side.
We cannot make any further concessions.
en.notes: 譲歩 means "concession, giving way" in negotiations and conflicts; you give way to someone with に: 相手に譲歩する. Typical: お互いに譲歩する, 譲歩を引き出す "to extract concessions", 一歩も譲歩しない. In everyday speech one says 譲る (to give up a seat or way); 妥協 "compromise" often carries the flavor of settling for less. In grammar, 譲歩 also denotes concessive clauses (〜ても).

examples[].german: Trade friction is occurring.
When you rub your hands, they become warm through friction.
There seems to be friction between the departments.
en.notes: 摩擦 literally means physical "friction" (摩擦が大きい, 摩擦熱) and figuratively "frictions, tensions" between people, groups or states: 貿易摩擦, 〜との間に摩擦が起きる/生じる. As a する-verb ("to rub") it is rare; in everyday speech one says こする. 対立 "confrontation" is stronger; 摩擦 rather suggests smaller, ongoing tensions.

examples[].german: We reached a reconciliation.
The brothers, who had been on bad terms for years, finally reconciled.
The lawsuit ended in a settlement.
en.notes: 和解 is reconciliation or an amicable agreement after a serious dispute; the partner is marked with と: 父と和解する. Legally it means "settlement": 和解が成立する, 和解金. For small everyday quarrels among friends, one prefers 仲直りする - 和解 sounds more formal and weighty. Fixed phrases: 和解に至る, 和解を図る.

examples[].german: That constitutes obstruction of business.
The noise from the construction next door is disturbing my sleep.
The signal is being jammed, so the TV has no picture.
en.notes: 妨害 is the (often deliberate) obstructing or disrupting of an activity: 〜を妨害する, 〜に妨害される. Common compounds: 業務妨害 (a criminal offense), 営業妨害, 睡眠妨害, 電波妨害. It sounds harsher and more formal than the everyday word 邪魔 ("to disturb, be in the way": 邪魔しないで); 妨害 often carries a sense of intent or illegality.

examples[].german: It is a violation of rights.
Using other people's photos without permission is copyright infringement.
That app may violate privacy.
en.notes: 侵害 is the violation of rights or protected spheres: 権利を侵害する, 人権侵害, 著作権侵害, プライバシーの侵害. The word is formal and typical of law, media and politics. Distinctions: 侵略 is a military invasion, 違反 the violation of a rule (交通違反) - 侵害 always concerns the rights or interests of a person or group.

examples[].german: I wish the town prosperity.
This port town prospered through trade in the Edo period.
The company's prosperity is thanks to the employees' efforts.
en.notes: 繁栄 "prosperity, flourishing" describes the thriving of cities, countries, companies or families over a longer period; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜で繁栄する. The opposite is 衰退 "decline". Unlike 繁盛 (a shop "doing well": 店が繁盛する), 繁栄 is thought of on a larger scale and is more formal. In speeches and greetings: ますますのご繁栄をお祈りします.

examples[].german: Environmental awareness is growing.
After the accident, he was unconscious for a while.
Recently I've been walking every day, mindful of my health.
en.notes: 意識 has two main meanings: consciousness in the medical sense (意識を失う "to lose consciousness", 意識が戻る "to regain consciousness") and awareness of something (環境意識, 意識が高まる). As a する-verb, 〜を意識する means "to pay attention to, to be aware of", for example 人の目を意識する "to be conscious of how one appears to others". 意識が高い describes someone with high awareness of issues, colloquially also used ironically.

examples[].german: The industry is in decline.
As young people decreased, the shopping street went into decline.
I am researching the decline of the Roman Empire.
en.notes: 衰退 "decline, decay" is a formal, intransitive する-verb for the slow weakening of industries, towns, cultures or states: 産業が衰退する, 地方の衰退. Opposites are 繁栄 and 発展. For waning physical strength, one says 衰える (体力が衰える), not 衰退; 衰弱 is physical exhaustion.

examples[].german: Technological innovation is advancing.
This company is releasing one innovative product after another.
The old system needs to be fundamentally renewed.
en.notes: 革新 means "innovation, fundamental renewal" and is formal: 技術革新, 革新的な "innovative", and as a transitive する-verb 制度を革新する. In politics, 革新 stands for "progressive, left-wing" as the counterpart to 保守 "conservative". 改革 "reform" stresses rebuilding existing systems, 革新 the completely new; in everyday speech one also hears イノベーション. Not to be confused with the identically read 確信 "conviction" and 核心 "core".

examples[].german: I took part in the ceremony.
The wedding was held at the shrine according to a traditional ritual.
Drinking coffee every morning is the ritual that starts my day.
en.notes: 儀式 is a formal ceremony or rite with a fixed procedure, often religious or traditional: 儀式を行う, 儀式に参加する/出席する. For concrete celebrations, 式 usually appears in compounds (結婚式, 卒業式, 入学式); 儀式 is the more general, somewhat more abstract term. Figuratively it can also denote a personal "ritual"; 儀式的 means "purely formal, ceremonial".

examples[].german: We will reexamine old customs.
The custom of pounding rice cakes at New Year remains in that region.
In this industry, it is customary to begin work on a verbal promise alone.
en.notes: 慣習 is a socially handed-down custom, a practice in a community, region or industry: 地域の慣習, 商慣習, 慣習に従う, 慣習を守る. Not to be confused with 習慣 (the same characters reversed), which mainly means personal habits (早起きの習慣). 風習 stresses more folk customs, 慣例 an established institutional practice. 慣習 is literary and formal.

examples[].german: I was looked at with contempt.
I despise people who lie.
He behaved in a way that looked down on poor people.
en.notes: 軽蔑 "contempt" is used as a transitive する-verb: 人を軽蔑する, passive 軽蔑される. Collocations: 軽蔑の目/まなざし, 軽蔑的な態度. Somewhat weaker and more everyday are 見下す "to look down on someone" and, colloquially, バカにする "to make fun of". Opposite: 尊敬 "respect, esteem".

examples[].german: I am driven by impatience.
As the deadline approached, my restlessness grew stronger.
After days without results, a look of agitation showed on his face.
en.notes: 焦燥 is a written-language word for tormenting impatience and inner unrest when something is not progressing or time is pressing. It usually appears as 焦燥感 "a feeling of restlessness" - 焦燥感に駆られる, 焦燥感を覚える - or in 焦燥の色 "signs of nervousness". In everyday speech one says 焦る "to get flustered, nervous" or イライラする "to be irritated" instead. It practically does not occur as a する-verb.

examples[].german: I feel gloomy.
Monday mornings are always depressing.
When it rains for days, I get gloomy.
en.notes: 憂鬱 describes a dejected, listless mood, often because of something coming up: 試験が憂鬱だ, 月曜日の朝は憂鬱. It is mostly used as a な-adjective (憂鬱な気分, 憂鬱になる), less often as a noun. In everyday speech it means "to feel down, not feel like doing anything" rather than clinical depression; that is called うつ病. Because of the difficult kanji it is often written ゆううつ or 憂うつ; casually one also says ブルーになる.

examples[].german: I feel lonely.
The loneliness of elderly people living alone has become a social problem.
He spent a lonely childhood.
en.notes: 孤独 "loneliness, solitude" describes the state of having no one close to you; as a noun (孤独を感じる, 孤独に耐える) and as a な-adjective (孤独な人, 孤独な生活). Compared with 寂しい (the subjective feeling of "feeling lonely"), 孤独 sounds more objective and serious. Well-known compounds: 孤独感, 孤独死 ("lonely death, dying alone unnoticed"). 一人 means only "alone", with no negative coloring.

examples[].german: I overcame the setback.
There is probably no one who has never experienced a setback.
I took up the guitar, but gave up after three months.
en.notes: 挫折 is a "setback" in which one loses courage, and as an intransitive する-verb "to fail, to give up". The thing one fails at is marked with に: 英語の勉強に挫折する; 計画が挫折する is also possible. Typical are 挫折を味わう, 挫折を乗り越える and 挫折感 ("feeling of failure"). Unlike 失敗 (a single failure), 挫折 stresses giving up and the discouragement afterwards.

examples[].german: He gracefully admitted defeat.
I was impressed by his upright attitude of making no excuses.
He took responsibility and resigned from the company without any fuss.
en.notes: 潔い praises someone who accepts a defeat, a mistake or responsibility without excuses, hesitation or clinging. Most often adverbial: 潔く負けを認める, 潔く謝る, 潔く諦める, 潔く身を引く. As an attribute: 潔い態度, 潔い決断. Negated, 潔くない means "unsporting, unable to let go". Unlike 正直 "honest", it is about the dignified, clean manner of accepting something.

examples[].german: Awareness of the problem is too weak.
On that point, our understandings seem to differ a little.
This camera automatically recognizes people's faces.
en.notes: 認識 is recognizing and understanding something, that is, how one assesses a situation: 問題を認識する, 認識が甘い "to underestimate the situation", 認識が違う "to see things somewhat differently". In technology it means "recognition": 顔認識, 音声認識. Distinction: 意識 is consciousness or awareness, 認識 is the factual grasping and comprehension; both sound rather literary.

examples[].german: I negotiate persistently.
She has a persevering nature and never gives up until the end.
As a result of continuing to practice persistently, I was able to win.
en.notes: 粘り強い is composed of 粘り "tenacity" and 強い and praises endurance: sticking with it even when it gets difficult. Typically adverbial: 粘り強く交渉する/説得する/取り組む; as an attribute 粘り強い性格. It is positive - in contrast to しつこい "annoyingly persistent" and 頑固 "stubborn". Related: 粘る "to hold out, not to let up" and 根気強い "patiently persevering".

examples[].german: Stop that cheeky attitude.
Don't talk back like that - you're only a child!
I wonder if people will think I'm cheeky if I voice my opinion to my seniors as a newcomer.
en.notes: 生意気 criticizes someone who takes too much liberty for their age or rank - typically said of children, juniors or subordinates: 生意気な子, 生意気な態度, 生意気を言う, 生意気だ. So it presupposes a hierarchy gap; about people of equal rank one rather says 偉そう "self-important" or 失礼. Sometimes it also sounds affectionately teasing: 生意気な弟.

examples[].german: That is an underhanded method.
Attacking from behind is cowardly!
It's unfair to blame others for your own mistakes.
en.notes: 卑怯 condemns unfair, cowardly behavior: sneaky tricks, shifting responsibility, dodging duty. Often as an indignant exclamation: 卑怯だ!. ずるい "unfair, mean" is more everyday and weaker and can also be jocular; 卑怯 is morally sharper. Collocations: 卑怯な手を使う, 卑怯なやり方, 卑怯者 "coward". Mere timidity, by contrast, is 臆病.

examples[].german: He laughs heartily.
He downed the beer in one hearty gulp.
The player hit a mighty home run.
en.notes: 豪快 describes a powerful, generous, carefree manner on a grand scale - mostly admiringly: 豪快に笑う, 豪快な性格, 豪快なホームラン, 豪快に飲む. There is something rough and unconstrained about it, but in a positive way. Distinctions: 大胆 stresses daring, 派手 a showy appearance, 豪華 the luxury and splendor of things.

examples[].german: Insidious bullying is unforgivable.
Talking badly about someone behind their back is an insidious way to behave.
Insidious harassment on the internet has become a problem.
en.notes: 陰湿 literally means "shady and damp", but today it is used almost only figuratively for insidious, covert malice: 陰湿ないじめ, 陰湿な嫌がらせ, 陰湿な性格. It means meanness that is practiced in secret and persistently. Open, crude violence, by contrast, is 乱暴; 意地悪 is more general and weaker. For damp, dark rooms, people in everyday speech rather say じめじめした.

examples[].german: He puts on airs.
I put on a show and bought expensive brand-name goods.
He is a show-off and always tries to make himself look bigger.
en.notes: 見栄 is the outward appearance one wants to keep up, and the vanity behind it. It appears almost always in 見栄を張る "to show off, to live beyond one's means"; also 見栄っ張り "show-off". 自慢する, by contrast, is open boasting in words, 見栄を張る the pretending through conduct or consumption. Not to be confused with 見栄え（みばえ）"good looks, impression" and 見得を切る (a kabuki pose, "to strike a pose, to act grandly").

examples[].german: He is a person of discernment.
He has deep insight into international affairs.
The remark made one doubt the expert's judgment.
en.notes: 見識 is judgment based on knowledge and experience, a well-founded outlook: 見識がある, 見識が高い, 見識を持つ, 見識を疑う. The word is formal and praising. Distinctions: 知識 is mere knowledge, 意見 an opinion; 見識 is the ability to assess things correctly. Not to be confused with 面識 "personal acquaintance" (面識がある).

examples[].german: Don't say mean things.
When I was a child, my older brother often teased me.
He asked a nasty question to embarrass the other person.
en.notes: 意地悪 means "mean, nasty" and describes small, deliberate acts of spite: 意地悪な人, 意地悪を言う, 意地悪をする/される. It is common among children and siblings and is often meant teasingly: 意地悪! Heavier are いじめ "bullying" and 陰湿 "insidious". 意地 alone means "stubbornness, pride" (意地を張る).

examples[].german: He is a good-natured person.
Since I'm so good-natured, I can't refuse when asked.
Believing such a story - that is naive beyond measure.
en.notes: お人好し describes someone so good-natured that he is easily taken advantage of or deceived. It is half praise, half criticism: お人好しすぎる, お人好しにもほどがある, お人好しな性格. As a noun also "good-natured person": 彼はお人好しだ. Purely positive are 優しい or 親切; 人がいい is similar and can also hint at "gullible".

examples[].german: Let's clear up the misunderstanding.
Please don't misunderstand. I'm not angry.
It's better to avoid phrasing that could cause misunderstanding.
en.notes: 誤解 is a misunderstanding or false notion; as a する-verb: 〜を誤解する "to misunderstand something/someone". Fixed combinations: 誤解を招く "to lead to misunderstandings", 誤解を解く "to clear up a misunderstanding", 誤解される "to be misunderstood". Compared with 勘違い (one's own error, more everyday), 誤解 mostly emphasizes a wrong picture of a person or statement.

en.meaning: to get complicated; to get worse
examples[].german: The problem got complicated.
The talks went sour and ended up in court.
My cold dragged on, and I missed school for a whole week.
en.notes: こじれる (usually in kana; the kanji 拗れる are rare) means that something gets "stuck, worse" and hard to resolve: relationships and negotiations (話がこじれる, 関係がこじれる) as well as lingering illnesses (風邪がこじれる). It is intransitive with が; the transitive counterpart is こじらせる "to aggravate, let drag on": 風邪をこじらせる. 複雑になる is more neutral; こじれる stresses that something has become deadlocked.

en.meaning: to fit in; to put on (a ring); to put on (gloves)
examples[].german: I put on the ring.
I fitted a new pane of glass into the window frame.
He set me up!
en.notes: はめる (mostly in kana, the kanji 嵌める is rare) means "to fit or slip something snugly into or onto something": 指輪/手袋をはめる "to put on", 窓枠にガラスをはめる "to fit in", ボタンをはめる "to button up". Transitive with を, the target with に; the intransitive counterpart is はまる "to fit in, to get stuck; to become hooked on something". Colloquially, はめる also means "to set up, to frame" (人をはめる, passive はめられる). For clothing in general, 着る/履く are used; はめる only for tight-fitting things such as rings or gloves.

en.meaning: to urge; to prompt; to promote
examples[].german: I urge participation.
The teacher urged the students to go home soon.
Moderate exercise promotes digestion.
en.notes: 促す is more formal than 勧める or 言う and has two uses: (1) to urge or prompt someone to do something: 人に〜するよう促す, 注意を促す "to call for caution", 参加を促す; (2) to promote or speed up a process: 成長/消化/発展を促す. Transitive with を, the person addressed with に. Common in news and official texts. 勧める is gentler ("to recommend"), 催促する "to press" (e.g. for payment).

examples[].german: It blocks progress.
Heavy snow blocked our way.
We managed to stop the opposing team's winning streak.
en.notes: 阻む is a literary verb for "to prevent, stop, stand in the way"; transitive with を: 行く手を阻む (fixed phrase), 侵入を阻む, 連勝を阻む. The subject is often an obstacle (snow, a wall) or an opponent. In everyday speech one says 止める or 邪魔する. 妨げる is similarly formal but stresses disrupting a process, 阻む rather blocking progress.

examples[].german: It endangers safety.
Global warming is threatening the lives of many animals.
A new company is threatening the industry leader's position.
en.notes: 脅かす（おびやかす）means "to threaten, endanger" and usually takes abstract objects: 平和/安全/生活/地位を脅かす. It is formal and common in the news; passive 脅かされる. Caution: the same kanji read おどかす mean "to startle, scare" (後ろから脅かす). 脅す（おどす）is "to threaten, intimidate" a person.

examples[].german: I endure the pain.
His slander is unbearable to listen to.
I endured the long hospital stay and was finally able to be discharged.
en.notes: 堪える（たえる）means "to endure, bear"; the thing endured takes に: 痛みに堪える, 寒さに堪える. In this sense the spelling 耐える is much more common today. 堪える remains common in fixed phrases such as 聞くに堪えない/見るに堪えない "unbearable to hear/see" and 〜に堪える "to be worth ...". Caution: read こらえる, the same kanji means "to hold back" (涙をこらえる), and read こたえる "to take its toll" (寒さが堪える). The everyday word is 我慢する.

examples[].german: There is no use regretting the past.
I still regret not having studied more back then.
Please accept my sincere condolences.
en.notes: 悔やむ means "to regret, to rue" with を: 失敗を悔やむ, 〜たことを悔やむ. It is somewhat more written than the everyday word 後悔する. 悔しい, by contrast, is the vexation over a defeat or injustice. From the meaning "to mourn" comes お悔やみ "condolences": お悔やみ申し上げます. Set phrase: 悔やんでも悔やみきれない "one cannot regret it enough".

en.meaning: to regret; to spare; to begrudge
examples[].german: We part only with reluctance.
He is someone who spares no effort.
Many fans lamented his retirement.
en.notes: 惜しむ has two sides: (1) to "be reluctant to give up, to be sparing with" something, mostly negated as praise: 努力を惜しまない "to spare no effort", 協力を惜しまない; (2) "to regret, mourn": 別れを惜しむ "to part with reluctance", 死を惜しむ, 名残を惜しむ. Transitive with を. Related is the adjective 惜しい "a pity, so close". 悔やむ, by contrast, means regret over one's own actions.

en.meaning: to envy; to be jealous of
examples[].german: He envies other people's success.
My colleagues were jealous of my promotion and spoke ill of me.
Envying others won't make you happy yourself.
en.notes: 妬む is resentful envy: you begrudge others their happiness: 人の成功を妬む, 人を妬む, passive 妬まれる. More neutral are うらやむ/うらやましい "to envy, want to have too" without resentment. 嫉妬する also covers jealousy in love; colloquially one says やきもちを焼く. Noun: 妬み (妬みを買う "to draw envy").

en.meaning: to neglect; to be remiss in
examples[].german: You must not neglect your studies.
Because the check was neglected, a major mistake occurred.
While driving, let's make sure never to stop paying attention to our surroundings.
en.notes: 怠る is transitive and takes を: 努力を怠る, 注意を怠る, 確認を怠る, 準備を怠る - one "fails to" do a duty or care that would actually be necessary. It sounds written to formal (reports, admonitions, safety notices). Related is 怠ける (same kanji, reading なまける): that means "to be lazy" in general, while 怠る emphasizes omitting a specific task; colloquially one says サボる.

examples[].german: Please don't be prejudiced.
Prejudice against foreigners still remains.
When I actually met them, I noticed my own prejudice.
en.notes: 偏見 is a prejudice, a one-sided, biased view. Typical: 偏見を持つ, 〜に対する偏見, 偏見をなくす, 偏見の目で見る. It is not a する-verb; "to be prejudiced" is expressed with 偏見がある or 偏見を持っている. Related: 先入観 is a (more neutral) preconceived notion, 差別 is the discrimination that can follow from prejudice.

examples[].german: I work hard at my studies.
The athletes are training hard for the tournament.
My father worked diligently until retirement.
en.notes: 励む is intransitive; what one strives at takes に: 勉強に励む, 練習に励む, 仕事に励む, 研究に励む. It sounds more elevated than the everyday 頑張る and likes to appear in speeches, letters and reports (日々練習に励んでおります). Not to be confused with 励ます (transitive, "to encourage someone"); the noun 励み means "incentive": 〜が励みになる.

examples[].german: I will go to the site.
The company president went to the factory himself and listened to the explanation.
On days off, I wander around town as the mood takes me.
en.notes: 赴く is an elevated, literary word for "to go somewhere (on duty, with a task)"; the destination takes に or へ: 現地に赴く, 現場へ赴く, 任地に赴く. In everyday speech one simply says 行く. Very common is the fixed phrase 気の赴くままに "entirely as the mood takes one", in which 赴く means "to give oneself over to an inclination".

examples[].german: My skin gets moisturized.
With more tourists, the town is prospering.
The first rain in a long time moistened the fields.
en.notes: 潤う is intransitive (〜が潤う); the transitive counterpart is 潤す: のどを潤す "to moisten the throat". Literally it means "to become moist" (肌が潤う, 雨で大地が潤う), typical of cosmetics ads. Figuratively it means "to flourish, benefit" (観光で町が潤う, 懐が潤う "to have more money in one's pocket") or "to be spiritually refreshed" (心が潤う). The noun 潤い appears in 潤いのある肌／生活.

examples[].german: The facts were reported in a distorted way.
After the earthquake, the door frame got slightly warped.
His face twisted with pain.
en.notes: 歪む is intransitive: something warps or bends out of its proper shape unintentionally (枠が歪む, 眼鏡が歪む, 痛みで顔が歪む). The transitive counterpart is the ichidan verb 歪める: 事実を歪める "to twist the facts". Figuratively, 歪んだ性格／考え means "twisted, warped character／way of thinking". Unlike 曲がる ("to bend, to turn", neutral), 歪む always stresses an undesirable deformation; the noun is 歪み.

en.meaning: to come back to life; to revive
examples[].german: The memory came back.
The old shopping street was revived by the efforts of young people.
When I watered them, the drooping flowers revived.
en.notes: 蘇る (also 甦る, often in kana よみがえる) is a godan verb although it ends in -eru: 蘇って, 蘇らない. It means "to come alive again" - of the dead, but also of towns, plants or traditions (町が蘇る). Very common is 記憶／思い出が蘇る: the memory comes back by itself, whereas with 思い出す one actively "remembers". More everyday is 生き返る, which also means "to feel reborn".

en.meaning: to fall out of use; to decline
examples[].german: Old customs died out.
Trendy clothes quickly go out of fashion.
Since the big supermarket opened, the shopping street in front of the station has been declining.
en.notes: 廃れる is intransitive and describes how something gradually falls out of use or decays by itself: 習慣／流行／言葉が廃れる, 町が廃れる. The opposite is 流行る "to be in fashion". Unlike 廃止する (to abolish deliberately), 廃れる happens without any decision; 衰える, on the other hand, stresses the loss of strength. The word sounds somewhat literary, but is common in the news and in conversation about urban development.

examples[].german: I cultivate human relationships.
I want to put the language skills I developed while studying abroad to use at work.
This shop preserves the craftsmanship it has built up over a hundred years.
en.notes: 培う is transitive and elevated; it means "to build up, to develop over a long time" and usually takes abstract objects: 経験／能力／技術／信頼関係を培う. Typical are relative clauses such as 〜で培った経験 or 長年培ってきた技術. Originally it means "to hill up plants with soil". More everyday are 育てる ("to raise") and 養う ("to nourish, to foster", also "to support a family").

examples[].german: I will cover the costs myself.
I pay my tuition with a part-time job.
Almost all of this town's electricity is supplied by solar power.
en.notes: 賄う is transitive: to "cover, defray" costs or needs, with the source marked by で: 生活費をアルバイトで賄う. In reports the passive is common: 税金で賄われている. A second sense is "to provide meals"; from it comes 賄い（まかない）, the staff meal in restaurants. Not to be confused with 補う ("to make up for a shortage") or 払う ("to pay"). According to the dictionary it is often in kana, but newspapers mostly use kanji.

examples[].german: Please don't stir up anxiety.
Fanned by the strong wind, the fire spread all at once.
On the expressway, I was scared when the car behind me tailgated me.
en.notes: 煽る is transitive and has a whole bundle of meanings. Literally: to fan a fire; often in the passive 強風に煽られる "to be caught by the wind / buffeted". Figuratively: to "stir up" feelings or conflicts (不安／危機感／対立を煽る) and to incite people. For some years now, 煽り運転 ("aggressive tailgating in road traffic") has been a major topic. It is often written in kana as あおる; for 酒をあおる "to knock back (a drink)" there is the kanji 呷る.

en.meaning: to instigate; to tempt; to incite
examples[].german: Egged on by bad friends, I skipped school.
He incited his younger brother to steal money from their parents.
Even if someone tempted you into it, you did it yourself.
en.notes: 唆す is transitive and means to "incite, tempt" someone to do something bad. Typical patterns are 人を唆して〜させる (with the causative) and, in the passive, 〜に唆されて "incited by ...". Unlike the neutral 誘う ("to invite, to urge"), 唆す is always negative; 煽る is aimed more at emotions or crowds. Mostly written in kana そそのかす.

examples[].german: Discrimination is bad.
She was discriminated against because she is a woman.
Education is important for eliminating racial discrimination.
en.notes: 差別 is discrimination, that is, unfair disadvantaging of people; as a transitive する-verb: 人を差別する, passive 差別される. Typical: 人種差別, 男女差別, 差別をなくす. The older neutral meaning "distinction" lives on in 差別化 "differentiation (of products)". For neutral distinctions, people otherwise say 区別: 公私を区別する.

examples[].german: You must not deceive people.
The criminal deceived the police and fled abroad.
To deceive the enemy, start with your own side.
en.notes: 欺く is the elevated, literary word for "to deceive, lead astray": 人／敵／世間を欺く, 警察の目を欺く. In everyday speech one says 騙す; 裏切る, by contrast, means "to betray, disappoint". Well known is the proverb 敵を欺くにはまず味方から. In literary use, 〜を欺く can also mean "to rival ...": 昼を欺く明るさ "bright as day".

en.meaning: to reflect on; to look back on
examples[].german: I reflect on my own behavior.
Before going to bed, I try to reflect on my day.
Especially after a failure, it is important to reflect on your own way of doing things.
en.notes: 省みる means "to reflect on oneself, critically examine one's behavior" and takes を, usually with 自分, 自ら or 我が身. The identically read 顧みる, by contrast, means "to look back" or "to have regard for" (家庭を顧みない, 危険を顧みず). Both are literary; in everyday speech one rather says 反省する or 振り返る.

examples[].german: I discern the truth.
It is hard to tell whether something is genuine or fake.
Let's observe the situation a little more closely before we decide.
en.notes: 見極める (見る + 極める) is transitive and means to "ascertain, get to the bottom of" something with certainty by looking closely: 真実／本質／原因を見極める, 状況を見極める. Often with an indirect question: 本物かどうかを見極める. The noun 見極め appears in 見極めが大切だ. Unlike 見分ける ("to distinguish") or 確かめる ("to verify"), 見極める stresses seeing through to the bottom, often before a decision.

examples[].german: Let's reduce disposable containers.
I use disposable contact lenses.
I don't want to work at a company that uses up its employees and throws them away.
en.notes: 使い捨て (使う + 捨てる) refers to things for single use. It stands directly before nouns (使い捨てカイロ, 使い捨てカメラ, 使い捨て容器) or with の (使い捨ての箸). Figuratively, 人を使い捨てにする means to exploit people and then drop them - often said about exploitative companies. The opposite is 繰り返し使える or 再利用.

examples[].german: I make a point of saving energy.
The new air conditioner has high energy-saving performance, and the electricity bill went down.
I'm tired, so today I'll work in energy-saving mode.
en.notes: 省エネ is the usual short form of 省エネルギー and mixes kanji with katakana. Typical are compounds like 省エネ家電, 省エネ住宅, 省エネ対策 and 省エネ性能. Compared with 節電 ("saving electricity"), 省エネ is more general and often stresses the efficiency of appliances. Colloquially, it is jokingly called 省エネ when someone spends only the bare minimum of their own effort.

examples[].german: We value natural resources.
Japan is a country with few natural resources.
That country is blessed with natural resources such as oil.
en.notes: 天然資源 (天然 "natural" + 資源 "resources") are raw materials and mineral resources such as oil, natural gas, ores, water or forest. Typical phrases: 天然資源が豊富／乏しい, 天然資源に恵まれる, 限りある天然資源. The word belongs to the news, geography and economics; in conversation one often says just 資源 (資源ごみ, 資源を大切に).

examples[].german: I look it up in the index.
This book has an index at the back, which is convenient.
The index is arranged in gojūon order.
en.notes: 索引 is the index or list of keywords at the end of a book; one looks things up in it with 索引で調べる or 索引を引く. Not to be confused with 目次 ("table of contents" at the beginning). In Japanese books, the index is usually arranged in 五十音順. In IT, for a database index one rather says インデックス.

examples[].german: Please look at the map legend.
Before using a dictionary, it is a good idea to read the explanatory notes.
The colors in the chart legend are hard to tell apart.
en.notes: 凡例 is read はんれい, not ぼんれい, although 凡 is otherwise mostly ぼん (平凡). It has two meanings: the "user's guide" at the beginning of a book or dictionary, which explains abbreviations and symbols, and the "legend" of a map or chart (地図／グラフの凡例). The word is technical and written, and is met mainly in dictionaries, atlases and presentations.

examples[].german: Please read the footnotes.
Please list the cited literature in the footnotes.
Technical terms are explained in footnotes.
en.notes: 脚注 (脚 "foot" + 注 "note") is the footnote at the bottom of the page; one says 脚注をつける／入れる and 脚注で説明する. More general are 注 or 注釈 ("annotation"); endnotes at the end of a chapter or book are called 後注 or 巻末注. The word belongs to academic and editorial vocabulary, for example in term papers.

examples[].german: I finish the draft.
The draft of the president's speech was made public.
After the writer's death, an unpublished manuscript was found.
en.notes: 草稿 is the first written draft of a text, such as a speech, a novel or a paper: 演説の草稿, 草稿を書く／仕上げる／練る. The word is elevated; in everyday speech one says 下書き (also for sketches and e-mail drafts). 原稿 is the (finished) manuscript for submission, 案 a draft plan or proposal.

examples[].german: This painting has value.
Old diaries have a value that cannot be measured in money.
That museum is worth visiting at least once.
en.notes: 価値 is the value of a thing, material or ideal: 価値がある / ない, 価値が上がる / 下がる. After a verb, 〜価値がある means "it is worth ...ing": 一度行く価値がある "worth a visit". Do not confuse it with 価格 or 値段, the concrete price in money. Well-known compounds are 価値観 "values" and 付加価値 "added value".

examples[].german: Gender equality is important.
We divided the cake equally among the three of us.
All people are equal under the law.
en.notes: 平等 means equality or equal rights and is used as a noun and as a な-adjective: 平等な社会, 平等に分ける "to divide fairly". Typical: 男女平等, 法の下の平等; the opposite is 不平等. Distinction: 公平 emphasizes fairness and impartiality; 平等 emphasizes equal treatment or equal rights for all.

examples[].german: I had my essay corrected.
The teacher corrects the students' reports every evening.
I used a service that reviews and revises résumés.
en.notes: 添削 (添 "to add" + 削 "to strike out") is the correcting and revising of a text by a more knowledgeable person, mostly a teacher: 作文／論文／答案を添削する, 添削してもらう. 通信添削 is a correspondence course with corrected assignments. To be distinguished are 訂正 ("to correct an error"), 修正 ("to change, to touch up") and 校正 ("proofreading" for typos).

examples[].german: I write the abstract of the paper.
Let's practice grasping the gist of a talk.
Please submit a summary of your presentation by next week.
en.notes: 要旨 is the core content of a text or talk, also the "abstract" of a scholarly paper: 論文の要旨, 発表要旨, 要旨をまとめる／つかむ. 要約, by contrast, is summarizing as an activity (要約する), 要点 are the individual key points, あらすじ the plot outline of a story. Beware of homophones: 用紙 "form", 容姿 "appearance", 養子 "adopted child".

examples[].german: I read a review of a new book.
In the newspaper's book review section, I found an interesting book.
He writes book reviews for a magazine every month.
en.notes: 書評 is a (usually published) book review in a newspaper or magazine: 書評を書く, 新聞の書評欄 "book review section". 感想, by contrast, are personal impressions (読書感想文 "book report" at school), and 批評 is criticism in general. User reviews on the internet are usually called レビュー.

examples[].german: I read Aesop's fables.
This fable has the lesson that you should not lie.
That film can also be understood as a parable of modern society.
en.notes: 寓話 is a fable or parable that conveys a lesson (教訓) in a story (often with animals); 寓 means "to put something in, to hint". Well known is イソップ寓話 "Aesop's fables"; the adjective 寓話的 means "parable-like". To be distinguished are 童話 ("children's tale"), 昔話 ("folk tale") and おとぎ話. The word is rather written.

examples[].german: I read Homer's epic.
The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest stories in the world.
This film is a grand epic depicting a family across three generations.
en.notes: 叙事詩 (叙事 "to narrate events" + 詩 "poem") is an epic that tells of the deeds of heroes or peoples, such as the works of Homer or the Epic of Gilgamesh. The counterpart is 叙情詩（抒情詩） "lyric poetry". Figuratively, big films or novels spanning generations are gladly called 壮大な叙事詩 "monumental epic". The word is literary and written.

examples[].german: I read between the lines.
Please widen the line spacing a little so it is easier to read.
It is said that with Japanese e-mails you need the ability to read between the lines.
en.notes: 行間 is literally the "line spacing" in a text: 行間を空ける／広げる／詰める, for example in Word documents. Much better known is the figurative phrase 行間を読む "to read between the lines", that is, to recognize unspoken intentions - an ability often expected in Japanese communication. The spacing between individual characters, by contrast, is called 字間.

examples[].german: The drain is clogged.
I clean the bathroom drain once a week.
Because of the heavy rain, water overflowed from the road drains.
en.notes: 排水溝 (排水 "drainage" + 溝 "ditch, channel") is a drainage channel, both at the roadside and in the bathroom or kitchen: 排水溝が詰まる, 排水溝を掃除する. The identically read 排水口 strictly denotes the drain opening (e.g. in a sink); in everyday use the two are often mixed up. Colloquially, a dirty ditch is called どぶ, and the sewage system 下水.

examples[].german: I clean the rain gutter.
Fallen leaves are clogging the gutter, and the water is overflowing.
The typhoon broke the rain gutter, so I asked for a repair.
en.notes: 雨樋 (雨 reads あま in compounds + 樋 とい → どい) is the rain gutter including the downspout. It is often written 雨どい or simply called 樋（とい）. Typical problems are 落ち葉が詰まる and 雨樋が外れる／壊れる after a storm or snow; one has it repaired (修理を頼む).

en.meaning: eaves; small roof over a window or door; visor
examples[].german: I shelter from the rain under the eaves.
I pulled down the brim of my cap to avoid the sunlight.
There is a small canopy above the window, so rain hardly gets in.
en.notes: 庇 is mostly written in kana ひさし. It is a small canopy over a window or door that protects from rain and sun (庇の下で雨宿りする), and also the "visor" of a cap (帽子のひさし). The roof overhang of the whole house is rather called 軒 or 軒先. Well known is the proverb 庇を貸して母屋を取られる - literally "to lend the canopy and lose the main house", i.e. "give them an inch and they take a mile".

examples[].german: That high-class restaurant is too intimidating for me.
Please enter the room without stepping on the threshold.
Never set foot over the threshold of this house again!
en.notes: 敷居 is the threshold with grooves for sliding doors (襖, 障子); the upper counterpart is called 鴨居. According to traditional etiquette, one does not step on the 敷居. Important are the idioms: 敷居をまたぐ "to enter a house" and 敷居が高い - originally "to be ashamed to visit someone" (because one owes them something), today mostly "hard to approach, intimidating", e.g. for expensive restaurants. Technically, しきい値 stands for "threshold value".

examples[].german: I will protect my rights.
When you turn 18, you have the right to vote in elections.
Since the product differed from the description, I should be entitled to get my money back.
en.notes: 権利 is a right in the legal sense, an entitlement: 〜する権利がある, 権利を守る/主張する/失う. The counterpart is 義務 "duty" (権利と義務). Combinations: 人権 "human rights", 選挙権 "right to vote". "To be right" in the sense of being correct, on the other hand, is 正しい, and "law" as a legal order is 法律 or 法.

examples[].german: I lean against the railing.
I peered down at the river from the bridge railing.
Please do not climb on the railing; it is dangerous.
en.notes: 欄干 is the railing on bridges, on the verandas of temples or on balconies of traditional buildings, often made of wood and with decorated posts. Typical are 橋の欄干, 欄干にもたれる and 欄干から川を見下ろす. For a modern handrail on stairs one says 手すり, for a fence 柵 or フェンス. The word sounds somewhat traditional and literary.

en.meaning: eaves; edge of the eaves; front of a house
examples[].german: I sheltered from the rain under the eaves.
I hung a wind chime from the eaves.
Vegetables are being sold cheaply in front of the farmhouses.
en.notes: 軒先 (軒 "eaves" + 先 "tip") is the front edge of the roof overhang and the area directly in front of it, so also "in front of the house". Typical phrases: 軒先で雨宿りする, 軒先に吊るす／干す, 軒先を借りる (to take brief shelter at someone's place) and 軒先で売る (selling in front of the house). 庇, by contrast, is a small canopy over a window or door, 玄関先 the area in front of the entrance.

examples[].german: It is a house with a tiled roof.
The typhoon blew off several tiles from the roof.
The karate teacher broke as many as ten roof tiles in front of us.
en.notes: 瓦 is the (usually fired) roof tile; it is counted with 枚. Common are 瓦屋根 "tiled roof", 瓦を葺く "to lay a roof", and damage after typhoons or earthquakes (瓦が落ちる／ずれる). 瓦割り is the breaking of tiles in karate. For wall and floor tiles, one does not say 瓦 but タイル.

examples[].german: The plastered wall is beautiful.
The white walls of Himeji Castle are coated with lime plaster.
I re-coated the walls of my room with plaster myself.
en.notes: 漆喰 is traditional lime plaster, with which the walls of storehouses (土蔵) and castles are plastered white - Himeji Castle is famous for it. One says 漆喰を塗る, 漆喰の壁, 漆喰で仕上げる. Modern cement mortar is called モルタル, wallpaper 壁紙. Today, 漆喰 is also popular with DIYers because of its moisture-regulating effect.

examples[].german: Thick beams are visible.
We threw a rope over the beam and made a swing.
We made a table from an old beam.
en.notes: 梁 is a horizontal supporting beam in the roof or under the ceiling; the vertical post is 柱. Typical are 天井の梁, 太い梁 and 梁がむき出しになっている ("exposed beams") in old houses or lofts. Beware of the homophone 針 "needle"; the context usually makes it clear.

examples[].german: I learn the fundamentals thoroughly.
Before building a house, you first do the foundation work.
I run every morning to build my basic physical fitness.
en.notes: 基礎 is both the structural foundation (建物の基礎, 基礎工事) and the basis of knowledge and skill (基礎知識, 基礎体力, 基礎から学ぶ, 基礎的な). Compared with 基本 ("basic rule, standard"), 基礎 emphasizes the base on which one builds; often both are interchangeable (基礎／基本を学ぶ). 土台 is more concrete and colloquial.

examples[].german: I bought some ceramics.
Ceramics break easily, so please wrap them in newspaper.
In my grandmother's kitchen there are many old ceramic bowls.
en.notes: 瀬戸物 originally meant ceramics from Seto (Aichi Prefecture) and became, especially in eastern Japan, the collective term for tableware made of ceramic and porcelain (in western Japan, 唐津物 was traditionally said). Today it sounds somewhat old-fashioned; neutral are 焼き物, 陶器 ("earthenware") and 磁器 ("porcelain"). Typical: 瀬戸物屋, 瀬戸物の茶わん, 瀬戸物が割れる.

examples[].german: I saw bunraku in Osaka.
In bunraku, one puppet is operated by three people.
Bunraku and kabuki have many plays based on the same stories.
en.notes: 文楽 is the traditional puppet theater (人形浄瑠璃) from Osaka, today a UNESCO World Heritage item. It combines three arts: the narrator (太夫), the shamisen music and the puppeteers, three of whom operate one puppet together. Alongside 歌舞伎 and 能, it is one of the great classical stage arts; the main theater is the 国立文楽劇場 in Osaka. One says 文楽を見る／鑑賞する.

examples[].german: I saw ukiyo-e at the museum.
Hokusai's ukiyo-e also influenced European painters.
I bought ukiyo-e postcards as a souvenir.
en.notes: 浮世絵 (浮世 "the fleeting, earthly world" + 絵 "picture") are the color woodblock prints of the Edo period with motifs from theater, pleasure quarters and landscapes. Famous artists (浮世絵師) are 葛飾北斎 and 歌川広重; their works influenced the European Impressionists. One says 浮世絵を見る／集める, 浮世絵展.

examples[].german: Let's fulfill our duties.
In Japan, education up to junior high school is compulsory.
When riding in a car, you are required to wear a seat belt.
en.notes: 義務 is a duty, especially a legal or moral one: 義務を果たす "to fulfill one's duty", 〜する義務がある, 〜が義務づけられている "is required". Fixed: 義務教育 "compulsory education", 納税の義務 "duty to pay taxes". The counterpart is 権利 "right". For personal tasks in daily life, people rather say 〜なければならない; 責任 is responsibility.

examples[].german: A golden folding screen is on display.
At weddings, the bride and groom sit in front of a gold folding screen.
I set up a folding screen and divided the room into two.
en.notes: 屏風 is a multi-panel folding screen, often artfully painted or covered with gold leaf; a pair is called 一双. One says 屏風を立てる／広げる. The golden 金屏風 still serves as a backdrop at weddings and press conferences. A simple one-panel room divider is called ついたて or パーティション.

examples[].german: I hang a scroll in the tokonoma.
I change the hanging scroll to suit the season.
The tea room's hanging scroll bore the character for "harmony".
en.notes: 掛け軸 (掛ける + 軸 "roll, shaft", also written 掛軸) is a hanging scroll with calligraphy or a painting. It is hung in the alcove 床の間 (掛け軸を掛ける／飾る) and changed according to the season or occasion, especially in the tea ceremony. It is traditionally counted with 幅（ふく）.

en.meaning: earthen floor; earth-floored area (at the entrance)
examples[].german: You take off your shoes on the earthen floor and then step up into the room.
In old farmhouses, people used to cook in the earthen-floored area.
Recently, houses with a spacious earthen-floored entrance area where you can park bicycles are popular.
en.notes: 土間 is an area without a wooden floor at ground level, formerly made of pounded clay and now often of concrete. In traditional farmhouses it served as kitchen and work space; you take off your shoes there and step up (上がる) onto the raised floor. The small area in today's 玄関 is a kind of 土間; modern houses with a large 土間 for bicycles or hobbies are popular again. Do not confuse it with "ground floor" (一階).

examples[].german: We renovated an old storehouse.
We toured a sake brewery and tasted sake.
Old kimonos turned up in the storehouse at my grandfather's house.
en.notes: 蔵 is a traditional fireproof storehouse with thick clay and lime walls (土蔵), in which rice, valuables or sake were stored. Important compounds: 酒蔵（さかぐら） "sake brewery", 蔵元 "brewery owner", 蔵造りの町 "town of storehouses". お蔵入り means figuratively "shelved, never released". A modern warehouse is 倉庫.

examples[].german: I warm myself at the hearth.
We grilled fish over the hearth and ate it.
My grandmother's old house still has an open hearth today.
en.notes: 囲炉裏 is the square hearth set into the floor of old farmhouses (古民家), used for heating and cooking; a kettle often hangs above it. Typical expressions are 囲炉裏を囲む ("to sit around the hearth") and 囲炉裏で魚を焼く. Today it is found mainly in old houses, country inns and restaurants. A Western fireplace is called 暖炉; 囲炉裏 is also often written in kana as いろり.

examples[].german: I purify my hands at the temizuya.
Before praying, you rinse your hands and mouth at the temizuya.
In the temizuya of this shrine, seasonal flowers are floated.
en.notes: 手水舎 is the roofed fountain with a water basin and ladles at the entrance of shrines and temples. Before praying, you cleanse your left hand, right hand and mouth there, taking the water from your hand and not drinking directly from the ladle. It is usually read ちょうずや, but also てみずや or ちょうずしゃ; the water itself is called 手水. Recently, 花手水 with floating blossoms have become popular.

examples[].german: I can see a red torii.
Let's bow lightly before passing through the torii.
Many torii stand in a row at Fushimi Inari Taisha.
en.notes: 鳥居 is the gate that marks the entrance to the sacred precinct of a Shinto shrine; Buddhist temples have a 門 or 山門 instead. One says 鳥居をくぐる "to pass through the torii" and bows briefly before it; the center of the path is regarded as the path of the gods. Famous are the 千本鳥居 at Fushimi Inari shrine. It is counted with 基.

examples[].german: There are guardian lion-dogs at the shrine entrance.
Of the komainu pair, one has its mouth open and the other has it closed.
The komainu at this shrine are known for their cute expressions.
en.notes: 狛犬 are the pairs of stone guardian figures ("lion-dogs") placed at the entrance of a Shinto shrine. Usually one figure has its mouth open and the other closed, after 阿吽 ("a" and "un", the beginning and the end). Although they are statues, besides 狛犬がある you also hear 狛犬がいる. At Inari shrines there are foxes (狐) instead of 狛犬, and in Okinawa the related シーサー.

examples[].german: I drew an omikuji.
When I drew a fortune slip on the first shrine visit of the year, it was "great luck".
A fortune slip with a bad result is tied to a tree at the shrine and left there.
en.notes: 御神籤 is almost always written in kana as おみくじ (rarely お神籤); it consists of the politeness prefix お, 神 "deity" and 籤 "lot". One says おみくじを引く. The results range from 大吉 ("great luck") through 吉, 中吉, 小吉, 末吉 to 凶 and 大凶. Unfavorable slips are often tied to a tree or rack at the shrine (結ぶ) instead of being taken home.

examples[].german: I throw in an offering coin.
Putting a five-yen coin in as an offering is meant to bring "good connections" (ご縁).
In front of the offering box, you bow twice and clap your hands twice.
en.notes: 賽銭 is the money thrown into the offering box (賽銭箱) when praying at a shrine or temple; politely it is usually お賽銭. Typical expressions are お賽銭を入れる／投げる. The five-yen coin is popular because 五円 sounds like ご縁 ("good connection, bond of fate"). Donations to monks for ceremonies, by contrast, are called お布施, and general donations 寄付.

examples[].german: The regulations have become stricter.
Because of the marathon event, traffic restrictions are in effect in front of the station.
The government regulates tobacco advertising.
en.notes: 規制 is regulation or restriction by laws and authorities; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を規制する. Typical: 規制が厳しい, 規制を緩める "to loosen", 規制を強化する "to tighten", 交通規制 "traffic restriction, road closure". Distinction: 規則 is a single rule or regulation, 制限 a limit such as 年齢制限 "age restriction".

examples[].german: I have a goshuin book.
After praying, I received a goshuin stamp.
Recently, collecting goshuin has become popular among young people.
en.notes: 御朱印 (often written ご朱印) is the red seal stamp with brush calligraphy that you receive at shrines and temples as proof of your visit. Politely, you say 御朱印をいただく, not 買う, even though you pay a small amount. They are collected in a 御朱印帳; the hobby 御朱印集め has been very popular for some years.

examples[].german: I ate shojin ryori.
No meat or fish is used at all in shojin ryori.
Shojin ryori is also popular with vegetarian foreign tourists.
en.notes: 精進料理 is Buddhist temple cuisine without meat and fish, traditionally also without strong-smelling ingredients such as leeks or garlic; typical are tofu, 湯葉 and ごま豆腐. 精進 originally means "ascetic practice, devotion" (精進する "to strive diligently"). It is eaten in temples or temple lodgings (宿坊); politely one says 精進料理をいただく.

examples[].german: Let's make some sencha.
Sencha tastes better when brewed with water that is not too hot.
Shizuoka is famous as a sencha-growing region.
en.notes: 煎茶 is ordinary Japanese leaf green tea made from steamed leaves, brewed with water that is not too hot (about 70-80 °C). In everyday speech people usually just say お茶 or 緑茶. It should be distinguished from 抹茶 (powdered tea), 玉露 (shade-grown top-grade tea), 番茶 (a plainer grade) and ほうじ茶 (roasted tea). "To make tea" is お茶を入れる, in formal writing with the kanji 淹れる.

examples[].german: I like the aroma of genmaicha.
Before bed, I often drink genmaicha, which is low in caffeine.
At the set-meal restaurant, warm genmaicha was served with the meal.
en.notes: 玄米茶 is composed of 玄米 "brown rice" and 茶 "tea": green tea (usually 番茶 or 煎茶) mixed with roasted rice grains, which gives it a nutty, toasty flavor. It is an inexpensive everyday tea with little caffeine and is often served free of charge in simple restaurants. Not to be confused with ほうじ茶 ("roasted green tea" without rice) or 抹茶 ("powdered tea"). One says 玄米茶を淹れる "to brew genmaicha".

examples[].german: Please pass the soy sauce dispenser.
The soy sauce dispenser was empty, so I refilled it.
I bought a soy sauce dispenser at the 100-yen shop that doesn't spill even when knocked over.
en.notes: 醤油差し is the small bottle or pitcher from which soy sauce is poured at the table; 差す here means "to pour in, to refill". It is found on every restaurant table and is also written しょうゆ差し or 醤油さし. Typical are 醤油差しを取る "to pass the soy sauce dispenser" and 醤油差しに醤油を入れる/足す "to refill". The sauce itself is just 醤油; the small dish for dipping is called 小皿.

examples[].german: I sprinkle shichimi on my udon.
I like to sprinkle plenty of shichimi on my gyudon.
If you can't handle spicy food, please use only a little shichimi.
en.notes: 七味 is the short form of 七味唐辛子, a spice blend of chili and six other ingredients such as sesame, sansho pepper and citrus peel. One sprinkles it with 七味をかける or 七味を振る over udon, soba, 牛丼 or yakitori. To be distinguished from it is 一味 (唐辛子), pure chili without other spices. The literal meaning "seven flavors" (sense 1) plays hardly any role in everyday life.

examples[].german: I make stock from kelp.
Which onigiri filling would you like, pickled plum or kelp?
I bought kelp as a souvenir from Hokkaido.
en.notes: 昆布 is edible seaweed (kelp), which when dried is the basis of Japanese stock: 昆布で出汁を取る "to make stock with kombu", often together with 鰹節. It is also eaten as an onigiri filling or as 佃煮. In compounds there is the reading こぶ, e.g. 昆布茶. Other seaweeds have their own names: わかめ, のり, ひじき; the umbrella term is 海藻.

examples[].german: I sprinkle bonito flakes on top.
On the hot okonomiyaki, the bonito flakes look like they are dancing.
If you make the stock from kombu and bonito, the miso soup tastes better.
en.notes: 鰹節 is boiled, smoked and rock-hard dried bonito; in everyday life it is almost always bought already shaved into flakes (削り節). Together with 昆布 it is the basis of 出汁: 鰹節で出汁を取る. It is also sprinkled over tofu, okonomiyaki or vegetables: 鰹節をかける/のせる. It is often written かつお節 or entirely in kana.

examples[].german: I make rice-bran pickles.
My grandmother stirs her pickling bran bed every day.
Rice bran is said to be good for the skin and has long been used for washing the face.
en.notes: 糠 is the bran that comes off when rice is polished, usually called 米ぬか and almost always written in kana. It is best known through ぬか漬け, vegetables pickled in a fermenting bran bed (ぬか床), which must be stirred every day. Set phrases are ぬか喜び "premature joy" and ぬかに釘 "futile, like a nail in bran".

examples[].german: I like sweets with bean paste.
Which do you like better, chunky or smooth bean paste?
At the Chinese restaurant, I ordered fried noodles with thick sauce.
en.notes: 餡 (mostly written あん) is above all the sweet paste made of red azuki beans; colloquially one says あんこ. A distinction is made between つぶあん "with whole beans" and こしあん "strained, smooth". More generally, あん also refers to the filling of dumplings (肉まんのあん) and a sauce thickened with starch, as in あんかけ. In kanji, the word is seen almost only on packaging.

examples[].german: Educational reform is necessary.
The new president thoroughly reformed the company's organization.
Thanks to work style reform, there is less overtime.
en.notes: 改革 is a fundamental reform of systems and organizations; as a transitive する-verb: 制度を改革する. Typical: 教育改革, 政治改革, 働き方改革 "reform of working styles", 改革を進める. Distinction: 改善 is a (gradual) improvement, 改正 is the amendment of a law, 革命 is a revolution.

examples[].german: I eat dango at the cherry blossom viewing.
I bought three skewers of mitarashi dango at the Japanese confectionery shop in front of the station.
The children are running in a tight pack, chasing the ball.
en.notes: 団子 are small round dumplings made of rice flour, often three or four on a skewer, e.g. みたらし団子 with sweet soy sauce or 三色団子 for cherry blossom season. The proverb 花より団子 "dumplings rather than blossoms" means that practical things matter more to someone than beauty. Figuratively, 団子 stands for something round or a dense clump: 団子になる "to bunch together", お団子ヘア "hair bun". Skewers are counted with 本.

examples[].german: I like strawberry daifuku.
At tea time, we shared a bean daifuku, half each.
Daifuku is soft, so elderly people should be careful not to choke on it.
en.notes: 大福 is the short form of 大福餅: soft mochi dough filled with sweet bean paste. Popular variants are いちご大福 with a whole strawberry and 豆大福 with beans in the dough. The literal meaning "great fortune" now occurs in everyday life practically only in names. Like all mochi sweets, 大福 is very chewy, which is why warnings about choking are issued, especially for older people.

examples[].german: Yokan goes well with matcha.
In summer, chilled mizu-yokan tastes great.
When I visit my grandfather's house, thickly sliced yokan is always served.
en.notes: 羊羹 is a firm, sliceable block of bean paste, agar and sugar, often also written ようかん. The classic is 練り羊羹; in summer one eats the softer, chilled 水羊羹. It is cut into slices (羊羹を切る) and served with green tea. Because it keeps for a long time, it is a popular gift and emergency food supply.

examples[].german: I bought onsen manju as a souvenir.
I served the guest tea and manju.
This manju has a thin skin and is generously filled with bean paste inside.
en.notes: 饅頭 is a small steamed or baked bun, in Japan mostly filled with sweet bean paste; politely one says お饅頭 and often writes まんじゅう. Almost every spa town sells 温泉饅頭 as a typical souvenir; there are also e.g. 栗饅頭. Savory Chinese variants are called 中華まん or 肉まん. The dough shell is called 皮, the filling あん.

examples[].german: I enjoy monaka together with tea.
The wafer shell of this monaka is nicely crisp and delicious.
Ice cream monaka is easy to eat because the wafer doesn't stick to your hands.
en.notes: With the reading もなか, 最中 is a sweet made of two crisp wafer shells of rice dough filled with bean paste. Note: the same kanji are much more often read さいちゅう and mean "in the middle of" (食事の最中に). That is why shops often write the sweet in kana as もなか. A modern variant is アイス最中 with ice cream instead of bean paste.

examples[].german: Konpeito has a star-like shape.
I received a jar of colorful konpeito as a souvenir.
Apparently it takes about two weeks to make konpeito.
en.notes: 金平糖 are small, colorful sugar balls with spiky bumps that look like stars. The word comes from Portuguese "confeito"; the kanji were chosen only for their sound (ateji), so it is usually written こんぺいとう or コンペイトウ. Making it by hand takes several weeks because sugar syrup is applied layer by layer. It is a traditional souvenir and gift.

examples[].german: Chilled kuzumochi is delicious in summer.
I ate the kuzumochi with soybean flour and dark syrup.
When it comes to souvenirs from Kawasaki Daishi Temple, kuzumochi is famous.
en.notes: 葛餅 is a translucent, soft and springy sweet, traditionally made from kudzu starch (葛粉), eaten with きな粉 "roasted soybean flour" and 黒蜜 "dark sugar syrup". In the Tokyo area a similar but cloudy kind made from fermented wheat starch is also called くず餅, known for example from Kawasaki. It is often eaten chilled in summer. The word is also written くず餅.

examples[].german: I reserved a kaiseki meal.
Dinner at the ryokan was a kaiseki meal using seasonal ingredients.
A kaiseki meal takes a long time because the dishes come out one at a time in order.
en.notes: 懐石料理 was originally the simple meal before the tea ceremony (茶懐石); today it usually means an upscale menu with many small, seasonal courses served one after another. It is eaten at ryokan or 料亭. Pronounced the same but written differently is 会席料理, a banquet menu in which alcohol is in the foreground; the two are often confused.

examples[].german: I went to a kappo restaurant.
We ate at a small counter-only kappo place, chatting with the chef.
My grandmother always stood in the kitchen wearing her white apron.
en.notes: 割烹 literally means "to cut and cook" and stands for the Japanese culinary art and for the restaurants that practice it. Typical is the chef who prepares food in front of the guests behind a counter (カウンター割烹); this is somewhat more casual than an exclusive 料亭. As a standalone word it is mostly heard in 割烹料理店 or in restaurant names. Also well known is 割烹着, the white apron with sleeves.

examples[].german: Let's have a drink at an izakaya.
The company drinking party was held at an izakaya in front of the station.
At an izakaya, once you sit down, a small dish called otoshi is served.
en.notes: 居酒屋 is a Japanese pub where you order many small dishes with beer, sake or highballs; it is the typical place for a 飲み会 with coworkers or friends. There is often 飲み放題 "all-you-can-drink", and when you sit down you get a starter that is charged for (お通し). Not to be confused with 酒屋, the liquor store. Colloquially, 飲み屋 is also used as a general term.

examples[].german: We will aim to improve the living environment.
The doctor told me to improve my lifestyle habits.
Since I started taking the new medicine, my symptoms have improved a little.
en.notes: 改善 is the improvement of a bad or inadequate state; as a する-verb it is both transitive (〜を改善する) and intransitive (状況が改善する "the situation improves"). Typical: 改善を図る, 改善点, 生活習慣を改善する. In daily life people often say more simply よくする/よくなる. Distinction: 改良 is the technical improvement of a product, 改革 a fundamental reform; as a loanword, "kaizen" denotes the Japanese management philosophy.

examples[].german: I ate ramen at a food stall.
At the summer festival, many stalls line up in front of the shrine.
At the school festival, my classmates and I set up a yakisoba stall.
en.notes: 屋台 is a small, often mobile sales stand, mainly for food: at festivals (祭りの屋台) or as a ramen or oden stall, for example in Fukuoka. Typical combinations are 屋台が並ぶ "stalls line up" and 屋台を出す "to set up a stall". At festivals, 屋台 can also refer to a decorated festival float. Figuratively, 屋台骨 is the "backbone" of a family or company.

examples[].german: The children are playing with pinwheels.
When the wind blew, the colorful pinwheels all began to turn at once.
I made a pinwheel from origami and gave it to my grandchild.
en.notes: With the reading かざぐるま, 風車 is above all the colorful pinwheel, a children's toy that spins in the wind: 風車が回る. The real windmill or wind turbine, by contrast, is mostly read ふうしゃ, e.g. オランダの風車 or 風力発電の風車. Pinwheels are seen at festivals and in temples; they are also made from origami.

examples[].german: People spin tops at New Year.
The top won't stop and just keeps spinning.
My grandfather taught me how to spin a top.
en.notes: 独楽 is a spinning top; the kanji spelling is rare, and こま or コマ are usual. One says こまを回す "to spin a top" and こまが回る "the top spins". こま回し is, together with 凧揚げ, one of the traditional New Year games. Homophones are 駒 "game piece (shogi)" and コマ "class period, single frame".

examples[].german: I fly a kite.
At New Year, I flew kites with the children by the riverbank.
The wind was so strong that the kite string broke.
en.notes: 凧 is the kite for flying. The fixed combination is 凧を揚げる (with 揚げる, not 上げる); the noun for it is 凧揚げ, a classic New Year game. It is often written たこ, but this can be confused with 蛸 "octopus". The string is called 凧の糸.

examples[].german: I bought a lucky bag at the department store.
A long line had formed already on the morning of New Year's Day to buy the popular lucky bags.
The contents of my lucky bag this year were a jackpot, and I feel like I got a good deal.
en.notes: 福袋 literally means "lucky bag": a sealed bag that shops offer mainly at the New Year sale (初売り) and whose contents are usually worth more than the price. One speaks of 福袋の中身 "contents" and of whether it was a 当たり "hit" or a はずれ "dud". For popular brands, customers line up early on January 1 (福袋に並ぶ).

en.meaning: New Year's Eve; turn of the year
examples[].german: I eat New Year's Eve soba.
This year I plan to spend the turn of the year with friends at a countdown event.
It's the first time in three years that I'm spending New Year's Eve with my family at my parents' house.
en.notes: 年越し means "to see in the new year", that is, passing into the new year on the night of 大晦日. The best-known term is 年越しそば, soba noodles eaten on New Year's Eve for a long life. One can say 年越しをする or express it with the verb 年を越す. The date December 31 itself is called 大晦日, the New Year days お正月.

examples[].german: I go home over the New Year holidays.
Please check our business hours over the year-end and New Year holidays on our website.
If you travel abroad over the year-end and New Year holidays, airfares are very high.
en.notes: 年末年始 is the period around the turn of the year, roughly from December 29 to January 3, when government offices and many companies close. One often reads it on notices: 年末年始の営業時間 "business hours over the holidays", 年末年始休業 "closure for the year-end and New Year holidays". As a time expression it is used with は or に. It is more general than お正月, which means only the New Year days.

examples[].german: I go back to my hometown for Obon.
Because of the holiday travel rush, the non-reserved seats on the Shinkansen were full.
This summer I was so busy with work that I couldn't go back to my parents' home.
en.notes: 帰省 is the trip home to one's hometown or parents' house (実家), typically at お盆 or 年末年始; as an intransitive する-verb: 実家に帰省する. The travel rush for it is called 帰省ラッシュ. To be distinguished are 帰宅 "to come home" (daily), 帰国 "to return to one's home country" and 里帰り, which especially stresses the visit to one's own parents after marriage.

examples[].german: I gave birth at my parents' home.
My wife has gone back to her parents' with the kids for about a week.
A painting that had gone abroad has come back to Japan for the first time in a hundred years.
en.notes: 里帰り is a return to one's parental home, originally mainly that of a married woman visiting her own parents (里 "home village, parental home"). Today it is best known as 里帰り出産: the woman moves in with her parents for a few weeks around the birth. As an intransitive する-verb: 実家に里帰りする. Figuratively it is also said of artworks that temporarily return to their country of origin. The more general, neutral word is 帰省.

en.meaning: travel stories; tales from a trip
examples[].german: Please tell me about your trip.
My sister, back from her trip, told stories about it throughout dinner.
Have a safe trip. I'm looking forward to hearing your stories.
en.notes: 土産話 are the stories one "brings back" from a trip like a souvenir (土産). Typical are 土産話をする "to tell about the trip", 土産話を聞かせる "to let someone hear (the stories)" and 土産話を楽しみにしている "to look forward to the travel stories", often as a farewell to someone going on a trip. It sounds warm and personal, not like a formal 旅行記 "travelogue".

examples[].german: I will adjust the schedule.
Please adjust the height of the chair.
The date of the meeting is currently being coordinated.
en.notes: 調整 means adjusting, coordinating or setting something so that it fits; it is a transitive する-verb. Typical: 日程/スケジュールを調整する "to coordinate dates", 温度を調整する, 意見を調整する. In the office you often hear 調整中 "currently being coordinated". Distinction: 調節 is rather the mechanical regulation of amount or degree (温度調節), while 調整 also includes coordination between people.

examples[].german: What is this region's specialty?
Aomori is known as a famous apple-producing area.
The station kiosk displayed lots of local specialties.
en.notes: 名産 is a product known for a region, usually food or crafts: 〜の名産, 名産品, 名産地 "famous production area". Similar is 特産 "specialty produced mainly there", which sounds more matter-of-fact. 名物 is broader and means anything a place is famous for, including dishes you eat on the spot, or even people.

examples[].german: I took a trip visiting secluded hot springs.
To get to that secluded hot spring, you have to walk a mountain path for an hour after getting out of the car.
Since it was featured on TV, more tourists have come to this secluded hot spring too.
en.notes: 秘湯, from 秘 "secret" and 湯 "hot water", is a remote, little-known hot spring, often deep in the mountains and hard to reach. Common are 秘湯巡り "tour of secluded hot springs", 山奥の秘湯 and 秘湯の宿. The general term is 温泉; touristy spa towns with many hotels are called 温泉街. The word has a romantic, advertising ring.

examples[].german: I stayed at a temple lodging.
At the temple lodging on Koyasan, vegetarian temple cuisine was served for dinner.
At a temple lodging, you can listen to sutra chanting with the monks early in the morning.
en.notes: 宿坊 is lodging in a Buddhist temple, originally for monks and pilgrims and now also for tourists. A stay usually includes 精進料理 "vegetarian temple cuisine" and taking part in the morning service (朝のお勤め). One says 宿坊に泊まる. The 宿坊 on 高野山 are particularly well known. An ordinary Japanese inn, by contrast, is a 旅館.

examples[].german: I strolled around the castle town.
Kanazawa once flourished as a large castle town.
Old samurai residences still remain in this castle town.
en.notes: 城下町 literally means "the town below the castle": a town that developed around a lord's castle in feudal times, e.g. 金沢, 松本 or 彦根. One speaks of 城下町の町並み "the townscape" and says 〜の城下町として栄えた "flourished as the castle town of ...". Similarly formed are 門前町 "temple town" and 宿場町 "post town".

en.meaning: temple town; town at a temple gate
examples[].german: I went shopping in the temple town.
The city of Nagano developed as a temple town around Zenko-ji.
Along the approach to the temple in the temple town, souvenir shops and dango shops line up.
en.notes: 門前町 is a town that arose in front of the gate (門前) of a large temple or shrine because pilgrims stayed overnight and shopped there; examples are 長野 at 善光寺 or 成田 at 新勝寺. The main street to the temple is called 参道 and is usually lined with souvenir shops and snack stands. 町 is read まち here. Comparable types of towns are 城下町 and 宿場町.

examples[].german: I toured an old post town.
In Tsumago, the townscape of an Edo-period post town is well preserved.
In post towns, there were many inns for travelers.
en.notes: 宿場町 is a historical post town on the major highways (街道) of the Edo period, where travelers stayed overnight and horses were changed; the station itself is called 宿場. Well-preserved examples are 妻籠 and 馬籠 on the 中山道. One speaks of 宿場町の町並み. Related town types are 城下町 and 門前町.

examples[].german: The scenery of the terraced rice fields is beautiful.
Countless small terraced fields continue in tiers up the mountain slope.
Because machines can hardly get in, growing rice on terraces takes a lot of work.
en.notes: 棚田, from 棚 "shelf, step" and 田 "rice field", are rice fields laid out in terraces on mountain slopes; a great many small terraces are also called 千枚田. They are regarded as a typical image of rural beauty, but are laborious to farm because machines can hardly get in. Common expressions are 棚田の風景, 棚田が続く and 棚田を守る.

examples[].german: We protect the nature of the satoyama.
On weekends, my family walked through the nearby satoyama and observed insects and birds.
Since people stopped looking after it, the satoyama has been becoming overgrown.
en.notes: 里山, from 里 "village" and 山 "mountain", is the landscape used by humans, consisting of groves, fields and ponds at the edge of villages, from which firewood and leaves were formerly gathered. Today the word is mainly a term from nature conservation and environmental education: 里山を守る, 里山の自然. The opposite term is 奥山 "untouched, deep mountain land". If the 里山 is no longer tended, one says 里山が荒れる "it becomes overgrown".

examples[].german: I walked through the gorge.
In autumn, this gorge is bustling with people coming to see the autumn leaves.
The suspension bridge over the gorge swayed a little, which was scary.
en.notes: 渓谷 is a valley with a river flowing through it, usually with steep slopes: a gorge. Popular are 紅葉の渓谷 in autumn, 渓谷沿いの遊歩道 "walking trail along the gorge" and the word 渓谷美 "beauty of the gorge". More general is 谷 "valley"; 峡谷 stresses a particularly narrow, deep gorge.

examples[].german: I crossed the mountain pass.
My fever is going down, so the worst of the illness seems to be over.
After a short rest at the teahouse on the pass, we went down the mountain.
en.notes: 峠 is the highest point of a road or path over a mountain, i.e. a pass; in names it appears as a suffix, e.g. 碓氷峠. One says 峠を越える "to cross the pass". Figuratively, 峠 means the critical peak: 峠を越す "the worst is over" (illness, heat, work), 今夜が峠だ "tonight is the critical point". The kanji is a Japanese creation made from 山, 上 and 下.

examples[].german: I will process the data.
I have to deal with these documents today.
This computer processes quickly.
en.notes: 処理 means to handle, take care of or dispose of something properly; a transitive する-verb. Typical: 仕事/書類を処理する, データ処理, ゴミ処理, 事故の処理. For computers it stands for "processing" (処理速度, 処理が速い). Distinction: 処分 is throwing away or a punishment, 対応 is responding to a situation or person.

examples[].german: The view from the cape is wonderful.
A white lighthouse stands at the tip of the cape.
