Cape Ashizuri is at the southernmost point of Shikoku.
en.notes: 岬 is a cape, a point of land jutting into the sea; in place names it appears as 〜岬, e.g. 足摺岬 or 宗谷岬. Typical expressions are 岬の先, 岬の灯台 and 岬からの眺め. A larger projection of land is a 半島 "peninsula". In many names 崎 alone is also used for a point of land.

examples[].german: There is a quiet inlet.
Fishing boats are lying quietly in the inlet.
The waves in the inlet are calm, so even children can swim safely.
en.notes: 入り江, from 入る and 江 "inlet", is a small bay reaching into the land, usually with calm water; also written 入江. Typical expressions are 静かな入り江 and 入り江に船が停まる. Larger bays are called 湾, e.g. in names such as 東京湾. The word sounds rather descriptive and scenic.

examples[].german: I took a walk in the wetland.
At Kushiro Marsh you can see red-crowned cranes.
Please walk on the wooden boardwalk so as not to damage the wetland plants.
en.notes: 湿原 is a wet grassland, a marsh or wetland with its own plant life; famous ones are 釧路湿原 in Hokkaido and 尾瀬. Visitors walk on wooden boardwalks there to protect the plants. The more general, rather technical word is 湿地 "wetland"; 沼 is a swamp or pond.

examples[].german: We protect the virgin forest.
A virgin beech forest spreads across the Shirakami Mountains.
Inside the virgin forest it is dark even in the daytime, and it is easy to lose your way.
en.notes: 原生林 is a forest untouched by humans, a primeval forest; well-known examples in Japan are the beech forest of 白神山地 and the forests of 屋久島. Typical are ブナの原生林, 原生林が広がる and 原生林を守る. The opposite term is 人工林 "planted forest"; forest in general is 森 or 森林.

examples[].german: I walked through the sea of trees at Mt. Fuji.
Seen from the mountaintop, a green sea of trees stretched as far as the eye could see.
There is a story that compasses don't work in the forest, but apparently they do work in reality.
en.notes: 樹海 literally means "sea of trees": a huge, dense forest that looks like a green sea from above. In everyday life one almost always thinks of the 青木ヶ原樹海 at the foot of Mt. Fuji. In general it describes wide expanses of forest, e.g. 緑の樹海が広がる. It is a rather figurative word; neutrally one says 森 or 森林.

examples[].german: The river overflowed.
The river may overflow because of the heavy rain, so please evacuate early.
The internet is flooded with false information.
en.notes: 氾濫 is a river overflowing its banks; as an intransitive する-verb: 川が氾濫する. In weather warnings one hears 氾濫のおそれ "risk of overflow". Figuratively, and mostly negatively, it stands for an oversupply: 情報が氾濫する "a flood of information". 洪水 rather means the flood as a disaster, 浸水 water entering buildings.

examples[].german: A landslide occurred because of heavy rain.
The road is closed because of a landslide.
After an earthquake, please be careful of landslides.
en.notes: 土砂崩れ, from 土砂 "earth and rubble" and 崩れる "to collapse", is a landslide, usually after heavy rain or earthquakes. One says 土砂崩れが起きる/起こる and 土砂崩れで道路が通行止めになる. Related are がけ崩れ "collapse of a steep slope", 山崩れ "mountain collapse" and 地すべり "slow sliding of a slope".

examples[].german: There was storm surge damage.
A typhoon is approaching, so please beware of storm surges near the coast.
A storm surge is caused not by an earthquake but by a typhoon's strong winds and low air pressure.
en.notes: 高潮 is a storm surge: the sea level rises due to the low air pressure and strong wind of a typhoon. Not to be confused with 津波, which is caused by earthquakes, and 満潮 "high tide". Typical expressions are 高潮の被害 and 高潮に注意する. With the reading こうちょう, the same kanji mean "climax", mostly in 最高潮.

examples[].german: A tornado occurred.
There were houses whose roofs were blown off by the tornado.
If a tornado advisory is issued, please go inside a sturdy building.
en.notes: 竜巻, from 竜 "dragon" and 巻く "to swirl", is a tornado or whirlwind; the image is a dragon rising to the sky. In the news it is 竜巻が発生する, and the weather service issues a 竜巻注意情報. A small whirlwind is つむじ風; a typhoon (台風) is a completely different, large-scale weather system.

examples[].german: I manage quality.
Let's manage our own health ourselves.
Please manage your passwords properly.
en.notes: 管理 is administration, supervision or control over things, buildings, money or people; a transitive する-verb. Typical: 健康管理, 品質管理, 時間を管理する, 管理人 "building manager, caretaker", 管理職 "managerial position". Distinction: 経営 is running a company as a business, 運営 the operation of an organization or event.

examples[].german: It has started to hail.
Large hailstones dented my car.
Even in summer, it can suddenly hail.
en.notes: 雹 is hail made of ice pellets of at least 5 mm; the kanji is rare and ひょう is usually written in kana. As with rain, the verb is 降る: 雹が降る. Smaller pellets are called あられ "graupel", and sleet is みぞれ. In Japan hail occurs mainly during thunderstorms in early summer and can damage cars and crops.

examples[].german: There is morning haze.
White haze hung over the lake, and it was very beautiful.
When the sun rose, the haze disappeared quickly.
en.notes: 靄 is light haze or mist through which one can still see fairly far; the kanji is rare and もや is usual. One says もやがかかる "haze hangs" and 朝もや "morning haze". Denser is 霧 "fog"; 霞 refers to poetic spring haze. Related is the onomatopoeic もやもや for an unclear, oppressive feeling.

examples[].german: This year we have a mild winter.
Because of the mild winter there is little snow, and all the ski resorts are in trouble.
According to the weather forecast, this winter will be mild.
en.notes: 暖冬 is an unusually mild winter and often appears in weather forecasts: 今年は暖冬になる "this year the winter will be mild". Typical consequences are 雪不足 "lack of snow" at ski resorts. The opposite is 厳冬 "severe winter"; for summer, the analogues are 冷夏 "cool summer" and 猛暑 "scorching summer".

examples[].german: The cool summer affected the crops.
The forecast says this year will have a cool summer.
Because of the cool summer, air conditioners and fans did not sell well.
en.notes: 冷夏 is a summer that turns out clearly cooler than normal; it is a factual term from weather reports and news, often in connection with poor harvests (冷夏で米が不作になる). Typical are 冷夏になる and 冷夏で/冷夏のせいで as a cause. Related weather terms are 暖冬 "mild winter" and 猛暑 "intense summer heat". In conversation people more often simply say 今年の夏は涼しい.

examples[].german: The early-summer rain continues.
I'm sorry that I sent the materials in a piecemeal fashion.
Outside the window, the early-summer rain was falling quietly.
en.notes: 五月雨 is the long-lasting rain of the early-summer rainy season; 五月 means the fifth month of the old lunar calendar, i.e. about June. The reading さみだれ is a special reading and cannot be derived from the individual kanji. The word itself is poetic (haiku, songs, literature); in everyday life one says 梅雨 or 梅雨の雨. Very common, however, is 五月雨式に "piecemeal, little by little", for example when sending documents in several installments in business emails.

examples[].german: I got caught in an evening shower.
A shower is probably coming, so let's bring in the laundry.
It gets a little cooler after an evening shower, doesn't it?
en.notes: 夕立 is a sudden, heavy rain shower on summer afternoons or evenings, often with thunder, that stops after a short time. Typical are 夕立が降る/来る and the adversative passive 夕立に降られる "to get caught in a shower". Unlike にわか雨 "shower" in general, 夕立 is tied to summer and the time of day; extreme downpours are nowadays often called ゲリラ豪雨 by the media.

examples[].german: A cold wintry wind is blowing.
Today the first kogarashi of the season blew in Tokyo.
I walked in the biting wind with my coat collar turned up.
en.notes: 木枯らし is the cold, dry north wind of late autumn and early winter that strips the trees bare (木 "tree" + 枯らす "make wither"). Typical is 木枯らしが吹く. The first such wind of the year is officially announced by the weather bureau in the Tokyo and Osaka areas as 木枯らし1号; it is regarded as a sign of the start of winter. Its spring counterpart is 春一番.

examples[].german: The first spring gale has blown.
The first spring gale was observed in the Kanto region yesterday.
The first spring gale knocked over my bicycle.
en.notes: 春一番 refers to the first strong, warm south wind of the year, which blows between the beginning of spring (立春, early February) and the spring equinox. The weather agency announces it officially (春一番が観測される); it is regarded as a harbinger of spring, but often brings violent gusts and dust, and afterwards it often turns cold again. Typical is 春一番が吹く; the autumn counterpart is 木枯らし1号.

examples[].german: The sunrise glow is beautiful.
I got up early and watched the dawn glow from the mountaintop.
My grandmother often said that a red dawn means rain.
en.notes: 朝焼け is the red or orange coloring of the sky at sunrise (朝 "morning" + 焼ける "glow"). Typical are 朝焼けがきれい, 朝焼けの空 and 空が朝焼けに染まる. It differs from the sunrise itself (日の出) in that it is about the color of the sky. An old weather saying goes: 朝焼けは雨、夕焼けは晴れ - red sky in the morning brings rain, red sky in the evening brings fine weather.

examples[].german: I saw the sunset glow.
The western sky is dyed deep red by the sunset glow.
The sunset is beautiful, so it will surely be sunny tomorrow.
en.notes: 夕焼け is the evening glow, the red coloring of the sky around sunset. Common combinations: 夕焼けがきれい, 真っ赤な夕焼け, 空が夕焼けに染まる and the children's song 夕焼け小焼け. The counterpart is 朝焼け "morning glow". It differs from 夕日 "evening sun" in that it means the colored sky, not the sun itself; according to the weather saying, an evening glow announces fine weather for the next day.

examples[].german: I run a company.
The students run the school festival themselves.
Running this website costs money.
en.notes: 運営 is the operation or management of an organization, facility or event; transitive する-verb: 〜を運営する. Typical: 店/学校/サイト/イベントを運営する, 運営会社, 運営費. Distinction: 経営 stresses the business management of a company, 運営 the practical organizing and keeping things running, also for clubs and volunteer work; 管理 is administering and supervising.

examples[].german: Heat haze is rising from the road.
Heat haze was shimmering over the field in midsummer.
Through the heat haze, distant buildings look distorted.
en.notes: 陽炎 is the shimmering of the air above hot ground, for example above asphalt in summer or on warm spring days. One says 陽炎が立つ or 陽炎が揺れる. The word sounds rather literary; in everyday speech the phenomenon is often described simply as 空気がゆらゆらしている. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced かげろう "mayfly" (蜉蝣), an image of transience.

examples[].german: Dragonflies are flying around.
In autumn, red dragonflies fly over the rice fields.
As a child, I had fun catching dragonflies with a net.
en.notes: 蜻蛉 is the dragonfly; in everyday writing it is almost always in kana (とんぼ or トンボ), and the kanji are seen mostly in literature. Caution: the same kanji can also be read かげろう "mayfly". Dragonflies are a typical autumn symbol in Japan, especially the red 赤とんぼ from the well-known children's song. The expression とんぼ返り means "an immediate return trip", e.g. a business trip without an overnight stay.

examples[].german: The crane is a symbol of longevity.
We folded a thousand paper cranes for our friend in the hospital.
The president's word of authority settled the conclusion of the meeting.
en.notes: 鶴 is the crane, in Japan above all the red-crowned crane (丹頂). Together with the turtle, it stands for long life and happiness: 鶴は千年、亀は万年. Well known are 折り鶴 "folded paper crane" and 千羽鶴, a thousand paper cranes strung together as a wish for recovery or peace. The phrase 鶴の一声 refers to the commanding word of an authority that ends a discussion immediately.

examples[].german: I feed the carp in the pond.
In May, carp streamers are flying everywhere.
The ornamental carp in this garden are said to be very expensive.
en.notes: 鯉 is the carp, in Japan above all as a colorful ornamental carp (錦鯉) in the ponds of gardens, temples and castles. For the children's festival on May 5, 鯉のぼり are hung up, carp streamers as a wish for strong, successful children. "To feed" is 餌をやる, more kindly also 餌をあげる. The similar-sounding 恋 "love" is often used for wordplay.

examples[].german: A sparrow is on the roof.
The bonus was a mere pittance.
In the morning, sparrows were chirping outside the window.
en.notes: 雀 is the sparrow, more precisely the tree sparrow found everywhere in Japan. Sparrows chirp (チュンチュン鳴く) and sit on roofs and power lines. The phrase 雀の涙 "a sparrow's tears" means "a tiny amount", e.g. 雀の涙ほどのボーナス. The word is often written in kana (すずめ/スズメ); the kanji is also found in 麻雀 "mahjong".

examples[].german: Crows are raiding the garbage.
When evening comes, the crows fly back to the mountains, cawing.
He always takes a very quick bath and comes out of the tub in five minutes.
en.notes: 烏 is the crow (also the raven); in everyday life it is almost always written カラス or からす. The kanji 烏 looks almost like 鳥 "bird" - it only lacks one stroke. In Japanese cities, crows are considered a pest that tear open garbage bags (ゴミを荒らす); their cawing is rendered as カーカー. The phrase 烏の行水 means "a very short bath".

examples[].german: I heard an owl in the forest.
Since owls are nocturnal, they sleep most of the day.
The owl is said to be lucky because its name sounds like "no hardship" (不苦労).
en.notes: 梟 is the owl, especially the Ural owl; in everyday writing it is usually フクロウ or ふくろう since the kanji is rare. Owls are nocturnal (夜行性) and are regarded as wise. Because ふくろう sounds like 不苦労 "without hardship", owl figures are popular good-luck charms in Japan. Their call is rendered as ホーホー.

examples[].german: A tanuki came into the garden.
Some people pretend to be asleep on the train because they don't want to give up their seat.
That department manager is quite a sly fox, so you'd better not believe everything he says.
en.notes: 狸 is the raccoon dog (tanuki), a wild animal native to Japan that appears in folklore as a shape-shifting trickster; clay figures with straw hats stand in front of many restaurants. Figuratively, 狸 refers to a cunning, crafty person, e.g. 古狸 or 狸親父. Well known are たぬき寝入り "pretending to be asleep" and たぬきうどん/たぬきそば with tempura crumbs. Often written in kana (たぬき/タヌキ).

examples[].german: I express my emotions.
I tried not to just unleash my anger on the other person.
I became emotional in the meeting and reflected on it afterwards.
en.notes: 感情 means feelings and emotions such as joy, anger or sadness: 感情を表す / 表現する, 感情を抑える "to suppress emotions", 感情的になる "to become emotional". 気持ち is more everyday and also covers mood or intention (感謝の気持ち); 感情 sounds more objective. 感想, on the other hand, is an impression or opinion about something experienced, and 感覚 is a sensory perception.

examples[].german: I receive the teacher's guidance.
Mr. Tanaka is in charge of training new employees.
The coach gently guides the children.
en.notes: 指導 is guidance, supervision or instruction by an experienced person such as a teacher, trainer or superior; a transitive する-verb: 学生を指導する. Typical: 指導を受ける, 〜の指導のもとで, 指導者, 生活指導. Distinction: 教える is "to teach" in general; 指導 sounds more formal and emphasizes the guiding, correcting role.

examples[].german: Wild boars are ravaging the fields.
If you meet a wild boar on a night road, don't provoke it and quietly move away.
I was born in the year of the boar.
en.notes: 猪 is the wild boar. In rural areas, wild boars cause great damage to fields (畑を荒らす), which is why fences and traps are set up. It is also one of the twelve zodiac animals (いのしし年), and 猪突猛進 means "to charge blindly ahead". In everyday life it is often written in kana (いのしし/イノシシ); as meat it is known from the stew ぼたん鍋.

examples[].german: There are deer in Nara Park.
When you hold deer crackers, lots of deer come over.
On mountain roads at night, deer sometimes jump out in front of the car.
en.notes: 鹿 covers both deer and roe; in everyday life Japanese does not distinguish here, and the Sika deer is usually meant. Famous are the freely roaming deer in Nara Park, which are fed with special crackers (鹿せんべい). The kanji is also found in 馬鹿 "fool". A fawn is called 子鹿 (こじか) - in compounds, しか often becomes じか.

examples[].german: Be careful of bears in the mountains.
A bear was sighted near here, so the mountain trail is closed.
I gave my daughter a teddy bear for her birthday.
en.notes: 熊 is the bear. In Japan, Asian black bears (ツキノワグマ) live on 本州 and brown bears (ヒグマ) on 北海道; bear sightings in forests and villages are a frequent news topic (熊が出る/出没する). Hikers therefore carry bear bells (熊よけの鈴). In compounds, くま often becomes ぐま (白熊 "polar bear"); a teddy bear is called 熊のぬいぐるみ.

examples[].german: Frogs are croaking in the rice paddy.
Like father, like son: his son also became a doctor.
On a rainy day, I found a small green frog in the garden.
en.notes: 蛙 is the frog (also the toad); it is usually written かえる or カエル. Frogs croak ケロケロ or ゲロゲロ, especially in rice paddies during the rainy season; the verb is 鳴く. Well-known expressions are 蛙の子は蛙 "the apple doesn't fall far from the tree" and 井の中の蛙 "a frog in a well" for someone with a narrow outlook. 帰る "to return" and 変える "to change" sound the same.

examples[].german: I found a spider web.
A big spider appeared in my room and I screamed without thinking.
As soon as the teacher came, the students scattered in all directions.
en.notes: 蜘蛛 is the spider; because of the difficult kanji it is usually written くも or クモ. The web is called 蜘蛛の巣, which also stands for cobwebs in old rooms; spinning a web is 巣を張る. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 雲 "cloud". The expression 蜘蛛の子を散らすように describes people suddenly running off in all directions.

examples[].german: The ants are forming a line.
Ants got into the kitchen, so I put the sugar away.
Security around the venue was so tight that not even an ant could have slipped out.
en.notes: 蟻 is the ant; it is usually written あり or アリ. Ants walk in columns (列を作る) and live in nests (蟻の巣). The fable アリとキリギリス "The Ant and the Grasshopper" about diligence and foresight is well known. The expression 蟻の這い出る隙もない describes a seamless cordon - not even an ant could get out.

examples[].german: I keep the books.
During the tax office audit, I showed the books for the past five years.
The figures in the books don't add up, so I'll calculate again.
en.notes: 帳簿 is the business ledger in which income, expenses or stock of goods are recorded - today often digital as well. The typical collocation is 帳簿をつける "to keep the books"; also 帳簿を確認する and 帳簿が合わない "the books don't add up". It sounds businesslike and matter-of-fact; the private household account book is 家計簿, and accounting as an activity or department is 経理.

examples[].german: I buy in new products.
Every morning I buy the fish for the restaurant at the market.
Because the purchase prices have risen, we will raise our prices from next month.
en.notes: 仕入れ is the purchase of goods or materials for resale or processing - that is, the business purchasing of a merchant, restaurant or company, not private shopping (買い物). The related transitive verb is 仕入れる (商品を仕入れる). Common compounds are 仕入れ先 "supplier" and 仕入れ値 "purchase price". Figuratively, one can also "pick up" information: 情報を仕入れる.

examples[].german: I buy at the wholesale price.
My father works in vegetable wholesale.
The Toyosu wholesale market is very lively from early in the morning.
en.notes: 卸売り is wholesale, i.e. selling large quantities to retailers rather than to end customers; the opposite is 小売り "retail". In compounds the り is usually dropped: 卸売業, 卸売市場 "wholesale market", 卸売価格. The related verb is 卸す "to supply to retailers" (商品を店に卸す); in everyday speech you also hear the short form 卸値 "wholesale price".

examples[].german: I will negotiate my salary.
I negotiated the price at the market and got it a bit cheaper.
The negotiations between the two companies have not yet been settled.
en.notes: 交渉 is a negotiation; as a する-verb: 〜と交渉する "to negotiate with someone", 値段を交渉する "to negotiate the price". Typical: 交渉がまとまる "to reach an agreement", 給料交渉, 値下げ交渉. Distinction: 相談 is a consultation or arrangement, 話し合い a discussion to reach agreement; 交渉 stresses bargaining over differing interests.

examples[].german: I work at a retail store.
The manufacturer's suggested retail price is 3,000 yen.
With the growth of online shopping, local retail is in a tough situation.
en.notes: 小売り is retail, the sale to end customers in small quantities; the counterpart is 卸売り "wholesale". In compounds it is usually written without り: 小売店 "retail shop", 小売業 "retail industry", 小売価格 "retail price". As a する-verb (小売りする) it means "to offer for retail sale", but it is rarer than the noun.

examples[].german: I analyze competing companies.
This product competes with products from a major manufacturer.
Two security programs conflicted with each other, and the PC stopped working.
en.notes: 競合 means that several parties compete for the same thing. In business language it appears mainly in 競合他社 "competing company" and 競合商品 "competing product"; short 競合 also simply means "the competition". As an intransitive する-verb one says 〜と競合する "to compete with ...", and technically it is also used for programs that interfere with each other. The more general, everyday word is 競争 "competition"; 競合 emphasizes the direct overlap of offers or interests.

examples[].german: I am conducting market research.
Before opening the new cafe, I did market research in the neighborhood.
The market research showed that the product is popular with young women.
en.notes: 市場調査 is market research, that is, the study of demand, customer wishes and competition, for example before launching a product. Note the reading: 市場 is read しじょう here, "market in the economic sense", not いちば "marketplace, market hall". Typical are 市場調査を行う/実施する/する and 市場調査の結果; in practice one also often hears マーケティングリサーチ or simply リサーチ.

examples[].german: I belong to the PR department.
The information about the event is in the city's bulletin.
Our press office handles inquiries from reporters.
en.notes: 広報 is public relations, that is, informing the public on the part of companies, public authorities or schools. Very common are 広報部/広報課 "PR department", 広報担当 "press officer" and 市の広報 "city bulletin". Compared with 宣伝 "advertising", 広報 is less about selling than about information and image; in company jargon one also says PR.

examples[].german: There was a personnel reshuffle.
Please consult HR about how to take time off.
Next week I have a performance review interview.
en.notes: 人事 in working life refers to personnel matters: hiring, transfers, promotions and evaluations. Common are 人事部 "personnel department", 人事異動 "transfer, reshuffle" and 人事評価 "employee evaluation"; one often simply says 人事 for the department (人事に相談する). Do not confuse it with 他人事 (ひとごと) "someone else's affair". The proverb 人事を尽くして天命を待つ uses the basic meaning "human effort".

examples[].german: Please contact the general affairs department.
If we run out of copy paper, please tell general affairs.
The company is small, so I handle general affairs and accounting by myself.
en.notes: 総務 is the general administration of a company or public office, which takes care of everything not assigned to a specialist department: office supplies, buildings, events, documents. Typical are 総務部/総務課 and, short, 総務 for the department (総務に聞く). In larger companies it is separate from 人事 "personnel" and 経理 "accounting"; in small businesses 総務 often handles everything together. At the national level there is the 総務省 "Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications".

examples[].german: I'll submit it to the accounting department.
We are looking for people with accounting experience.
She is in charge of accounting at the company.
en.notes: 経理 refers to the accounting or bookkeeping of a company: payments, receipts, settlements, salaries. It means both the activity (経理の仕事, 経理を担当する) and, short, the department (経理部, 経理に出す); receipts and expense reports typically go to 経理. Related are 会計 "accounting; the till" (also paying the bill at a restaurant) and 帳簿 "business ledgers".

examples[].german: I carry out product inspection work.
When I inspected the delivered goods, one box was missing.
All products are inspected before shipping.
en.notes: 検品 is the inspection of goods for quantity, damage or defects, for example on receipt in a warehouse or before shipping. As a する-verb it is transitive: 商品を検品する; also common are 検品作業 and 検品済み "inspected". Compared with 品質管理 "quality management", 検品 is the concrete checking step on an individual product; 点検, by contrast, is the inspection of machines or facilities.

examples[].german: I'm returning the defective product.
If the product is defective, we will exchange it for a new one free of charge.
This factory renewed its machines to reduce defective products.
en.notes: 不良品 is faulty or defective merchandise that does not meet quality requirements. Typical combinations are 不良品が出る "defective products turn up" and 不良品を交換する/返品する. 不良 alone means "bad, defective" and also appears in 体調不良 "feeling unwell" or colloquially for "delinquent". A product with a fundamental design flaw is more likely called 欠陥品.

examples[].german: Is a return possible?
The size didn't fit, so I returned the shoes I bought online.
Sale items cannot be returned, so please note this.
en.notes: 返品 is the return of purchased goods to the shop or supplier, but also the returned goods themselves. As a する-verb: 商品を返品する. In shops and online stores one reads 返品・交換 "returns and exchanges", 返品不可 "no returns" and 返品期限 "return deadline". Unlike the general 返す "to give back", 返品 applies only to purchased or delivered goods.

examples[].german: I ask for your cooperation.
Thank you for your cooperation with the survey.
We all worked together and tidied up the room.
en.notes: 協力 is cooperation or help; an intransitive する-verb with に or と: 〜に協力する "to take part in, to support", 〜と協力する "to work together with". The polite formulas ご協力をお願いします and ご協力ありがとうございます are heard in announcements and read on signs. Distinction: 手伝う is concrete help with an activity; 協力 sounds more formal and means working together toward a common goal.

examples[].german: I'd like to exchange it for another size.
I exchanged business cards with someone I met for the first time.
The remote control didn't work, so I tried replacing the batteries.
en.notes: 交換 means "exchange" in a broad sense: swapping things with each other (AとBを交換する), replacing something old with something new (電池を交換する) or exchanging in a shop (サイズ交換). Also common are 情報交換 "exchange of information", 名刺交換 "exchange of business cards" and 交換留学 "exchange study". When replacing parts one can also say 取り替える; 交換 sounds somewhat more formal and is the standard form on signs and in shops.

examples[].german: We will renovate the building.
The north exit is unavailable because of renovation work at the station.
The city renovated the old bridge and widened the sidewalk.
en.notes: 改修 is the repair and improvement of structures and facilities such as buildings, roads, bridges or riverbanks; typical are 〜を改修する and 改修工事 "renovation work". It sounds rather official and appears in notices and the news. For renovating a home one rather says リフォーム in everyday speech, for a simple repair 修理, and for remodeling a shop 改装.

examples[].german: We added an extension to our house.
We are expecting a child, so we plan to build on one more room.
This inn has been extended so many times that the inside is like a maze.
en.notes: 増築 is the extension of an existing building, for example by an additional room or floor: 家を増築する, 部屋を増築する. To be distinguished from it are 改築 "remodeling (without enlarging)", 新築 "new construction" and 建て替え "demolition and rebuilding". The compound 増改築 combines extension and remodeling.

examples[].german: The old building will be demolished.
The supermarket held a show where a whole tuna was cut up.
Finances became difficult, and it was decided to disband the team.
en.notes: 解体 means taking a whole apart into its parts: demolishing buildings (ビルを解体する, 解体工事), taking machines apart or cutting up a large fish (マグロの解体ショー). Figuratively it stands for the dissolution of organizations (組織の解体). For small things like appliances, 分解 is more common in daily life; 解体 sounds larger and more official. It is mostly transitive (〜を解体する), but intransitive use is also possible (組織が解体する).

examples[].german: Construction will start next month.
Construction of the new library is scheduled to start next spring.
The start of construction is delayed because of residents' opposition.
en.notes: 着工 denotes the start of construction work, i.e. groundbreaking. It is a formal word from construction and the news: 来月着工する, 工事に着工する; in reports one also reads 新しいビルを着工する. The counterpart is 竣工 or 完工 "completion"; in everyday speech one simply says 工事が始まる.

examples[].german: The building has been completed.
All employees attended the completion ceremony of the new company building.
This bridge was completed in 1964.
en.notes: 竣工 is the completion of a structure and a formal, written-language word from construction, press releases and news: ビルが竣工する, 竣工式 "completion ceremony". Its counterpart is 着工 "start of construction". 完工 and 落成 (落成式) mean the same; in daily life one simply says 完成する or ビルができる.

examples[].german: Please tell me the purpose of use.
This knife has a wide range of uses and is very handy for camping.
You should choose a computer according to how you will use it.
en.notes: 用途 is the purpose of use - what something is or can be used for. Typical are 用途が広い "widely usable", 用途に合わせて/応じて選ぶ "choose according to the purpose" and 多用途 "multi-purpose". It sounds factual (product descriptions, forms); in conversation one more often says 使い道. 目的, by contrast, is the goal of an action, not the use of an object.

examples[].german: It has a waterproof finish.
This smartphone is waterproof, so you can use it even in the bath.
In preparation for rainy days, I sprayed my shoes with waterproofing spray.
en.notes: 防水 means protection against water, or making something waterproof. It is mostly used attributively: 防水の時計 "waterproof watch", 防水スプレー "waterproofing spray", 防水加工 "waterproof treatment", or predicatively as in このスマホは防水だ. As a する-verb (屋根を防水する) it is technical. To distinguish: 防水 keeps water out completely, whereas 撥水 only makes it bead off ("water-repellent").

examples[].german: We installed insulation material.
This house is well insulated, so it is warm even in winter.
After we replaced the windows with insulating glass, the electricity bill went down.
en.notes: 断熱 is thermal insulation, preventing heat transfer through walls, windows or containers. It most often appears in compounds: 断熱材 "insulating material", 断熱性 "insulating property", 断熱効果, 断熱ガラス. Since older Japanese houses are often poorly insulated, 断熱性が高い is an important selling point. Related are 遮音 "sound insulation" and 保温 "keeping warm".

examples[].german: It's a wall with high sound insulation.
The noise from the next room bothers me, so I bought soundproof curtains.
This apartment has poor sound insulation, and you can clearly hear footsteps from upstairs.
en.notes: 遮音 is sound insulation, i.e. the shielding of noise (遮る "to shield" + 音 "sound"). It is a technical word from construction and housing, found mostly in 遮音性 "sound insulation", 遮音シート or 遮音カーテン. In everyday life 防音 "soundproofing" is better known (防音室); but when viewing apartments, 遮音性 is an important criterion.

examples[].german: I will coordinate with other departments.
The hospital and the school are working together to protect children's health.
This app can be linked with the calendar.
en.notes: 連携 is cooperation and coordination between organizations, departments or systems, mostly with と: 〜と連携する. Typical: 連携を取る, 連携を強める, 地域と連携する, アプリ連携 "app integration". Distinction: 協力 is general helping out; 連携 emphasizes that different parties coordinate and link their work; the word is rather formal and businesslike.

examples[].german: Please ventilate the room.
When cooking, please turn on the ventilation fan.
This room has small windows and poor ventilation.
en.notes: 換気 is the ventilation of a room, i.e. exchanging stale air for fresh. Typical are 換気する/換気をする, colloquially also 部屋を換気する, as well as 換気扇 "ventilation fan, extractor" and 換気が悪い "poorly ventilated". Compared with 窓を開ける, 換気 names the purpose; in everyday speech one also says 空気を入れ替える.

examples[].german: It's a room with good natural light.
It faces north, but there is a large window, so the natural light is sufficient.
We installed a skylight in the ceiling to brighten the hallway.
en.notes: 採光 is the admission of daylight into an interior (採る "to take in" + 光 "light"). It is a technical word from architecture and real-estate ads: 採光がよい, 採光窓, 採光を確保する. In everyday speech one more often talks about 日当たり "sunlight exposure" (日当たりがいい); 採光 means daylight in general, even without direct sun, for example with north-facing windows.

examples[].german: It's land with good drainage.
This sports field drains poorly, so it can't be used right after rain.
Please grow lavender in well-drained soil.
en.notes: 水はけ describes how well water drains away or soaks in, for example with soil, building plots, sports fields or drains: 水はけがいい/よい or 水はけが悪い. The all-kanji spelling 水捌け is rarely seen; the mixed form is usual. It is an important criterion for gardeners and when buying a plot; 排水, by contrast, is the technical word for drainage through pipes and drains.

examples[].german: The ground is solid.
The ground around here is weak, so it shakes easily in an earthquake.
Before building the house, we had a ground survey done.
en.notes: 地盤 is the natural ground on which one builds, i.e. the "building ground" or "subsoil". Its firmness is described with 地盤が固い／強い or 地盤が弱い／緩い; set phrases are 地盤沈下 "ground subsidence" and 地盤調査 "ground survey". Unlike 土台 (the "foundation" of concrete or stone that belongs to the building), 地盤 means the ground itself. Figuratively, it denotes a politician's power base in his constituency (選挙の地盤).

examples[].german: I'll clear the land and sell it.
The old house was torn down, and it became a vacant lot.
A new apartment building is said to be going up on the vacant lot near the station.
en.notes: 更地 is a plot with nothing (any longer) standing on it - usually after an old house has been demolished, so ready for building and free of structures. Typical are 更地にする "to clear a plot", 更地になる and 更地で売る. The everyday word 空き地, by contrast, means a "vacant, unused area" in general, for example where children play; 更地 is more a real-estate and construction term. 更 here has the sense of "new, fresh".

examples[].german: Land readjustment is being carried out in this area.
This residential area is divided into thirty lots in total.
I rent a plot in a community garden and grow vegetables.
en.notes: 区画 is a demarcated area: "lot", "building plot", "block". It also serves as a counter for plots of land (一区画、二区画). Fixed combinations are 区画整理 "land readjustment, reorganization of plots" and 〜を区画に分ける. As a する-verb (区画する "to demarcate, divide") it is rather literary. For administrative zones one says 区域, for sections of a text 部分 or 段落, not 区画.

examples[].german: Water is drawn to the rice paddies through the irrigation canal.
A fence was built so that children don't fall into the irrigation canal.
The water in the irrigation canal overflowed because of heavy rain.
en.notes: 用水路 is an artificially built canal or ditch that brings utility water (用水) for agriculture, industry or households - in Japan mostly narrow concrete ditches between rice fields. Water is led in with 水を引く. A shipping canal is a 運河, a drainage ditch a 排水路, and a natural river a 川. In the news the word often appears in connection with accidents and floods after heavy rain.

examples[].german: I walk along the embankment.
The river levee broke in the heavy rain, and the town was flooded.
Children are flying kites on top of the embankment.
en.notes: 堤防 is an earthen wall or dike along a river or coast that protects against floods. Typical phrases: 堤防を築く "to build an embankment", 堤防が切れる／決壊する "the embankment breaks". The grassy bank on which one takes walks is often called 土手 in everyday speech. A dam that impounds a lake is ダム, and a breakwater in a harbor is 防波堤.

examples[].german: The water level of the reservoir has dropped.
The reservoir is running low, and there are worries about a water shortage.
The town's tap water comes from a reservoir in the mountains.
en.notes: 貯水池 is an artificially built water store (貯水 "store water" + 池 "pond") for drinking water, agriculture or power generation. The structure itself is called ダム, and the lake dammed up behind it ダム湖 or simply 貯水池. Common accompanying words are 水位 "water level" and 貯水率 "fill level", which is reported in the news in summer during dry spells. A natural lake is a 湖.

examples[].german: We protect the water source.
The source of this river is in those mountains.
This town uses groundwater as its water source.
en.notes: 水源 is the origin of a river or the source of a water supply (river, lake, groundwater). Typical combinations: 水源地 "headwater area", 水源を守る／保護する, 〜を水源にする "to draw one's water from ...". A single spring from which water gushes is called 泉 or 湧き水, and a hot spring 温泉. The word is rather matter-of-fact and often appears in environmental and administrative texts.

examples[].german: The cultures are different.
The fee differs depending on the season.
The two have different opinions.
en.notes: 異なる is the literary, more formal counterpart of 違う "to be different": AとBは異なる, 〜によって異なる "differs depending on ...". It often appears in manuals, the news and texts, also attributively: 異なる意見. Unlike 違う, 異なる never means "to be wrong"; "That's not right" remains 違います. The verb is intransitive and has no transitive counterpart.

examples[].german: I take a walk on the promenade.
A walking path has been built along the river.
Cycling is prohibited on this walking path.
en.notes: 遊歩道 is a constructed footpath for strolling and enjoying the surroundings - along a river, in a park, on the coast or as a wooden walkway through a marsh. Cars are not allowed there, often not bicycles either. To be distinguished are 歩道 "sidewalk" beside a road and 登山道 or ハイキングコース for real mountain hiking trails. In daily life one also simply says 散歩道.

examples[].german: I look at the view from the observation deck.
It takes one minute by elevator to the tower's observation deck.
It's windy on the observation deck, so please bring a jacket.
en.notes: 展望台 is an observation platform on a mountain, tower or high-rise (展望 "view" + 台 "platform"). Typical: 展望台に上る／上がる and 展望台から〜を眺める／見下ろす. 展望 on its own is also used figuratively ("prospects, outlook", e.g. 将来の展望), whereas 展望台 is used only concretely. At airports one often speaks of 展望デッキ.

examples[].german: I can see the lighthouse.
A white lighthouse stands at the tip of the cape.
As the saying 「灯台下暗し」 goes, the glasses I was looking for were on the desk.
en.notes: 灯台 is the "lighthouse"; related are 灯台の光 and 灯台守 "lighthouse keeper". The idiom 灯台下暗し "it is dark under the lamp stand" means that one overlooks what is close at hand - originally the old oil-lamp stand (meaning 2) is meant, not the lighthouse. Do not confuse it with 東大 (same reading, short form for the University of Tokyo).

examples[].german: I board the ship from the pier.
In the evening, many people fish on the pier.
The typhoon destroyed the pier, so the boats cannot go out.
en.notes: 桟橋 is a pier or jetty that projects into the water and where ships and boats dock, from a large ferry pier to a small boat jetty on a lake. Typical: 船が桟橋に着く, 桟橋から船に乗る. Despite 橋, it does not mean a bridge across a river. Large reinforced harbor quays for cargo ships are rather called 埠頭 or 岸壁; the whole harbor is 港.

examples[].german: Containers are unloaded at the wharf.
A large passenger ship is moored at the pier.
The view of the harbor from the wharf at night is beautiful.
en.notes: 埠頭 is a paved harbor quay where large ships dock and are loaded or unloaded; it often appears in place names of port facilities (〜埠頭). The word is rather written and technical - in daily life one usually simply says 港. Unlike 桟橋 "jetty, pier" (which can also be small), 埠頭 is a large facility. Since 埠 is not a Jōyō kanji, government offices and newspapers often write ふ頭.

examples[].german: Ships are built at the shipyard.
My grandfather worked at a shipyard in Nagasaki.
I took part in a shipyard tour.
en.notes: 造船所 is the "shipyard" (造船 "shipbuilding" + 所 "place"). 造船 alone denotes shipbuilding as an industry (造船業). For building ships and other large things, 造る is written instead of 作る: 船を造る. 所 is read じょ here, as in 研究所; other words ending in 所 have しょ (製材所, 事務所), which has to be learned individually. A dry dock or repair dock is called ドック.

examples[].german: I toured a beer brewery.
This brewery makes soy sauce using traditional methods.
I tried wine made at a local winery.
en.notes: 醸造所 is the general, neutral term for an establishment that produces by fermentation (醸造): beer, sake, wine, but also soy sauce, miso and vinegar. In daily life more specific words are more common: 酒蔵 or 蔵元 for sake breweries, ブルワリー for beer breweries, ワイナリー for wineries. To tour one is 醸造所を見学する. 所 is read しょ here.

examples[].german: Timber is processed at the sawmill.
The smell of wood is coming from the sawmill.
My father works at a sawmill near the mountains.
en.notes: 製材 means sawing logs (丸太) into boards and beams; 製材所 is the "sawmill" that makes 木材 "lumber" from them. 所 is read しょ here, unlike in 造船所 (じょ) - such readings must be learned word by word. The word is neutral and matter-of-fact; in company names 〜製材所 is common.

examples[].german: Cast-iron pots are sturdy.
This town has long been famous as a production center for castings.
Nanbu ironware is a traditional casting from Iwate Prefecture.
en.notes: 鋳物 is a cast metal object (鋳る "to cast" + 物), i.e. castings or cast goods; the workshop is called 鋳物工場. The material cast iron is technically 鋳鉄, and a cast-iron pan is often simply called 鉄鍋 or 鉄のフライパン in everyday speech. The counterpart is 鍛造 "forged". Well-known cast goods are the iron kettles 南部鉄器 from Iwate.

examples[].german: I will judge based on the facts.
This movie is based on a true story.
In accordance with the rules, people who are late cannot participate.
en.notes: 基づく is almost always used as 〜に基づく / 〜に基づいて "based on, in accordance with": データに基づいて判断する, 法律に基づく. Attributively: 事実に基づいた話 or 事実に基づく話 "a story based on facts". The verb is intransitive and rather literary; in daily life people also say 〜をもとに(して).

examples[].german: We use a titanium alloy.
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.
The frame of this bicycle is made of an aluminum alloy and is very light.
en.notes: 合金 means "alloy". It mostly stands as the second element after the main metal: アルミ合金, チタン合金, 形状記憶合金 "shape-memory alloy". The composition is described with 〜と〜の合金. The word is technical, but appears often in product descriptions. The reading is ごうきん, not がっきん.

examples[].german: I dye with natural dyes.
In the past, dyes were made from plants.
Chemical dyes have beautiful colors, but you also need to consider their impact on the environment.
en.notes: 染料 is a dye used for dyeing (染める) textiles, yarn or leather; a distinction is made between 天然染料 and 合成染料 or 化学染料. To be distinguished from it are 顔料 "pigment" in paints and lacquers, 絵の具 "artist's paint" and ペンキ "house paint". For food, one speaks of 着色料, not 染料.

examples[].german: I tried indigo dyeing.
I bought an indigo-dyed handkerchief as a souvenir.
Tokushima has long been a place where indigo dyeing thrives.
en.notes: 藍染め is dyeing with indigo (藍) and also the fabric dyed this way; the typical deep blue color is called 藍色 and is regarded as "Japan blue". One says 藍染めのハンカチ, 藍染め体験 (a workshop for tourists) or, as a verb, 藍で染める. The spelling 藍染 without め also occurs. A well-known center is Tokushima Prefecture.

examples[].german: I saw traditional textiles.
Nishijin-ori is a famous woven textile from Kyoto.
In her youth, my grandmother worked in a textile mill.
en.notes: 織物 is woven cloth (織る "to weave" + 物), i.e. "woven fabric, textile". Knitted goods, by contrast, are 編み物, and fabric in general 布 or 生地. For well-known weaving traditions, 〜織 is used as a suffix, e.g. 西陣織 (Kyoto) or 博多織. The weaving mill as a business is 織物工場.

examples[].german: Embroidery is my hobby.
I embroidered my name on the handkerchief.
This dress has flower embroidery.
en.notes: 刺繍 is "embroidery"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜に〜を刺繍する "to embroider something on something". If a garment is embroidered, one says 刺繍が入っている or 刺繍入りの〜. As a hobby: 刺繍をする. Since 繍 is not a Jōyō kanji, the word is often seen in kana (ししゅう). Distinguish it from 縫う "to sew" and 編む "to knit".

examples[].german: I bought a piece of cloisonne work.
I gave my mother a cloisonne brooch as a present.
At the workshop I made a cloisonne pendant.
en.notes: 七宝焼き is enamel art, especially cloisonné: colored glass powder is applied to metal and fired (焼き). 七宝 "the seven treasures" comes from Buddhism and stands for precious colors. Despite 焼き, it is not ceramics - pottery is called 焼き物. It is often seen in brooches, pendants and vases; in workshops you can make 七宝焼き yourself (七宝焼きを作る).

examples[].german: The maki-e box is beautiful.
Maki-e is a technique of sprinkling gold or silver powder on lacquer to draw patterns.
I saw maki-e works from the Edo period at the museum.
en.notes: 蒔絵 is a Japanese lacquer art: gold or silver powder is sprinkled onto still-wet urushi lacquer (漆) (蒔く "sprinkle, sow" + 絵 "picture"). It is found on small boxes, bowls, writing boxes and other lacquerware (漆器). Typical are 蒔絵の箱 or 蒔絵を施す (written language, "to decorate with maki-e"). The word is a technical term of the decorative crafts.

examples[].german: I display paper-cut artworks.
I like making fine paper cuttings with a utility knife.
The children played making paper cuttings with colored paper.
en.notes: 切り絵 is a picture made of cut paper (切る + 絵), made with scissors or a utility knife - that is, a "paper cut". One says 切り絵を作る or 切り絵をする. Related are 切り紙 (folded paper in which patterns are cut), 折り紙 "paper folding" and 貼り絵 "collage". The spelling 切絵 without り also occurs.

examples[].german: I paint ink wash pictures.
Ink wash painting depicts mountains and rivers solely through the gradation of the ink.
A magnificent ink wash painting is drawn on the sliding doors of the temple.
en.notes: 水墨画 is ink painting using black ink (墨) and water (水), working only with gradations of light and dark. It came from China together with Zen Buddhism; the most famous Japanese master is 雪舟. A more everyday synonym is 墨絵. To paint is 水墨画を描く (かく or, more elevated, えがく).

examples[].german: I went to an exhibition of Japanese-style painting.
Nihonga uses mineral pigments called iwa-enogu.
My older sister is majoring in Japanese-style painting at art college.
en.notes: 日本画 is not simply "a picture from Japan" but a genre: painting in the traditional Japanese style with mineral pigments (岩絵の具) and glue on silk or washi. The term arose in the Meiji period as a counterpart to 洋画 "Western painting, oil painting" - 洋画 also means "foreign film". Artists are called 日本画家, exhibitions 日本画展.

examples[].german: It involves risks.
This operation involves some pain.
Heavy rain accompanying the typhoon stopped the trains.
en.notes: 伴う has two main patterns: 〜を伴う "to bring something with it, to be accompanied by something" (危険を伴う, 痛みを伴う) and 〜に伴って / 〜に伴い / 〜に伴う "along with, as a result of" (人口の増加に伴って). The word is literary and formal and common in news and official announcements. The meaning "to take someone along" (家族を伴って) is rarer.

examples[].german: I printed a print.
In art class at elementary school, we made woodblock prints.
Ukiyo-e are prints from the Edo period.
en.notes: 版画 is the general term for prints; more precisely one distinguishes 木版画 "woodblock print", 銅版画 "copperplate engraving, etching" and シルクスクリーン "silk screen". Typical verbs: 版を彫る "to carve the printing block" and 版画を刷る "to print" (刷る, not 擦る). The famous ukiyo-e are woodblock prints; in Japanese elementary schools, children often make their own woodblock prints in art class.

en.meaning: Buddhist statue; image of the Buddha
examples[].german: Old Buddhist statues are enshrined.
I saw a large Buddha statue at a temple in Nara.
Recently, the number of young people who love Buddhist statues is also increasing.
en.notes: 仏像 denotes the statue or image of a Buddha and, generally, of Buddhist figures such as Kannon or temple guardians. Respectful phrases are 仏像を拝む "to pray before a statue" and 仏像が安置されている "a statue is (reverently) enshrined". A "great Buddha" is 大仏; statues in general are 像 (銅像 "bronze statue"). Buddha statues are counted with 体.

examples[].german: There is a stone lantern in the garden.
When the stone lanterns are lit, the atmosphere of the garden changes.
Stone lanterns line the approach to the shrine.
en.notes: 石灯籠 is a stone lantern, as found at temples, shrines and in Japanese gardens. 灯籠 (とうろう) undergoes rendaku in the compound: いしどうろう. Originally they held votive lights; today they are mostly decoration. Do not confuse with 提灯 (portable paper lantern); 灯籠流し is the floating of lanterns on water at Obon.

examples[].german: I gaze at the dry landscape garden.
In a karesansui garden, the flow of water is represented by white sand.
The rock garden of Ryoanji is the representative karesansui.
en.notes: 枯山水 is the Japanese dry landscape garden without real water: stones, gravel or sand and moss represent mountains, islands and watercourses. Literally a "dried-up mountain-and-water landscape" (山水 = landscape). One mostly says 枯山水の庭; it is typical of Zen temples. The counterpart is the pond garden 池泉庭園. Reading かれさんすい - 枯 is not こ here.

examples[].german: I planted plants in the courtyard garden.
The old townhouses in Kyoto have small courtyard gardens.
Light and air come in through the small courtyard garden, so the house is bright.
en.notes: 坪庭 is a tiny garden enclosed by parts of a building in the interior of a house - typical of the narrow townhouses (町家) in Kyoto. 坪 is a unit of area of about 3.3 m² and emphasizes smallness. The garden brings light and air into the house. 中庭, by contrast, is any "inner courtyard", including a large one, for example in schools or hotels.

examples[].german: The moss-covered garden is beautiful.
Moss is growing on the shady north wall.
The stones around the pond are slippery with moss, so please be careful.
en.notes: 苔 is "moss" and, in general, moss-like growth. According to the dictionary it is often written in kana (こけ, コケ), but in garden and cultural contexts 苔 is usual. Moss "grows": 苔が生える; 苔むす means "to be moss-covered" and suggests venerable age (also in the national anthem: 苔のむすまで). In Japan moss is aesthetically appreciated, for example at the 苔寺 in Kyoto.

examples[].german: Hydrangeas bloom in the rainy season.
The color of hydrangea flowers changes to blue or pink depending on the soil.
Shall we go see the hydrangeas in Kamakura?
en.notes: 紫陽花 is the hydrangea. The kanji are a purely meaning-based spelling (熟字訓); in everyday life it is usually written あじさい or アジサイ. The hydrangea is the symbol of the June rainy season 梅雨, and many temples are famous hydrangea spots. Its flower color depends on the soil: rather blue in acidic soil, rather pink in alkaline soil.

examples[].german: Red spider lilies bloom in autumn.
Red spider lilies are poisonous, so let's wash our hands if we touch them.
The red spider lily is also called 「曼珠沙華」.
en.notes: 彼岸花 is the red spider lily, named after 彼岸, the week around the autumn equinox in which people visit graves - exactly when it blooms. Because it often grows at cemeteries and along the edges of rice fields and is poisonous, it is associated with death and is not suitable as a gift. A second, poetic name is 曼珠沙華.

examples[].german: The scent of osmanthus is drifting.
Osmanthus flowers are orange and very small.
Osmanthus-scented hand cream is popular.
en.notes: 金木犀 is the fragrant orange osmanthus, a shrub with tiny orange flowers that give off an intense sweet scent from late September to October - for many Japanese the epitome of the start of autumn. Typical: 金木犀の香りがする／漂う. It is often written in katakana (キンモクセイ). The white-flowering relative is called 銀木犀.

examples[].german: The camellias are in bloom.
Camellia oil is said to be good for the hair.
Because camellia flowers fall off whole, they are said to be unsuitable for hospital visits.
en.notes: 椿 is the Japanese camellia, which blooms red or white from winter into spring. Its flowers fall off whole, which recalls a falling head - for this reason one doesn't bring them to hospital visits. 山茶花 (さざんか) looks similar, but blooms earlier and loses its petals one by one. From the seeds one obtains 椿油, a traditional hair oil.

en.meaning: to reflect; to take into account; to incorporate
examples[].german: We will reflect everyone's opinions in the plan.
This novel reflects the society of that time.
I changed the settings, but they are not yet reflected on the screen.
en.notes: 反映 means that something is reflected in, or taken into account in, something else. Transitive: AをBに反映する / 反映させる "to incorporate A into B" (意見を計画に反映させる); very often passive: 〜に反映される "to be reflected in …". In an IT context it means "to apply (a change)": 変更が反映されない "the change is not applied". For the physical reflection of light, 反射 is usually used.

examples[].german: The wisteria trellis is magnificent.
In May, the wisteria blooms in purple.
The kanji for wisteria is also often used in family names, such as Satō and Itō.
en.notes: 藤 is the wisteria, a climbing plant with long, hanging purple flower clusters that blooms from late April to May. It is grown on a pergola, the 藤棚; the light purple color is called 藤色. In family names 藤 is mostly read とう (佐藤, 伊藤), and at the start of a word often ふじ (藤田). Do not confuse with 富士 (same reading, Mount Fuji).

examples[].german: I went to an iris garden.
On May 5th there is a custom of taking a sweet flag bath.
In June, irises bloom around the pond.
en.notes: 菖蒲 (しょうぶ) actually refers to the sweet flag, whose fragrant leaves are put into the bath water on Children's Day (May 5) (菖蒲湯). Colloquially, however, it mostly means the Japanese water iris 花菖蒲, which blooms in June in 菖蒲園. The same kanji read あやめ refer to yet another kind of iris. Because しょうぶ sounds like 尚武 "martial spirit", the plant is regarded as a good-luck symbol for boys.

examples[].german: I eat tsukimi dango, the rice dumplings for moon viewing.
On the night of the harvest moon, we all viewed the moon together.
I ordered tsukimi soba, soba with a raw egg as the "full moon".
en.notes: 月見 is the viewing of the autumn full moon, especially on the night of 十五夜 (the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, mid-September to early October), traditionally with 月見団子 and pampas grass. Politely and warmly one says お月見 and お月見をする. Figuratively, dishes with an egg as the "moon" are called 月見〜 (月見そば, 月見バーガー). Comparable formations are 花見 and 雪見.

examples[].german: We enjoy snow viewing from an open-air bath.
Sake drunk while looking at the snow is called 「雪見酒」.
From a Japanese-style room with a yukimi shoji, I enjoyed the snowy scenery of the garden.
en.notes: 雪見 is the enjoyable viewing of snow-covered landscapes, one of the classic seasonal pleasures alongside 花見 and 月見 (together 雪月花). One says 雪見をする and forms compounds like 雪見酒 "sake while viewing snow", 雪見風呂 or 雪見障子 (shoji with a glass window in the lower part). The word sounds traditional and poetic; in everyday speech one more often says 雪景色を楽しむ.

examples[].german: Let's go shellfish gathering.
We gathered lots of clams while shellfish gathering.
The shellfish-gathering season runs from spring to early summer.
en.notes: 潮干狩り is gathering shellfish at low tide: when the water recedes (潮が引く), people dig in the tidal flats for shellfish such as アサリ. The parts: 潮 "tide" + 干る "dry up" + 狩り "hunt" - as in いちご狩り or 紅葉狩り, 狩り stands for an outing pastime. Typical: 潮干狩りに行く／をする. The season is spring to early summer.

examples[].german: I catch insects with my children.
In the summer vacation, I went to the park with a butterfly net.
As a child I was crazy about catching insects and went to the woods every day.
en.notes: 虫取り is catching insects such as beetles, cicadas or dragonflies - a classic summer pastime of Japanese children. The equipment is a 虫取り網 "insect net" and a 虫かご "insect cage". One says 虫取りをする or 虫取りに行く; the spelling 虫捕り also occurs. In Japanese, 虫 also includes animals that are not insects, such as spiders.

en.meaning: wild vegetable gathering; foraging for edible wild plants
examples[].german: In spring I go foraging for wild vegetables.
I made the bracken I had gathered into tempura.
Every year there are accidents in which people who go into the mountains to gather wild plants get lost.
en.notes: 山菜 are edible wild plants from the mountains, such as fern shoots (ワラビ, ゼンマイ), butterbur buds (ふきのとう) or angelica-tree buds (タラの芽). 山菜採り is the gathering of these plants in spring. For picking plants one writes 採る instead of 取る. In the news one reads every year about gatherers who get lost or encounter bears.

examples[].german: I went fishing at a fishing pond.
At a fishing pond, even beginners can catch fish.
I had the fish I caught at the fishing pond grilled on the spot.
en.notes: 釣り堀 is a commercial fishing pond or tank stocked with fish, usually paid for by the hour (堀 = "ditch, pool"). Even beginners and children are sure to catch something there, and some facilities grill the catch right away. A fishing spot in the wild, by contrast, is called 釣り場. Typical: 釣り堀で釣る, 釣り堀に行く.

examples[].german: We did a test of courage.
On summer nights, the children hold a spooky test of courage in the temple graveyard.
In the test of courage I had to walk a dark path alone, and it was really scary.
en.notes: 肝試し is a nighttime test of courage in an eerie place such as a graveyard or an abandoned building - a typical summer pastime, often combined with ghost stories (怪談). 肝 "liver" is regarded as the seat of courage (cf. 肝が据わる "to be fearless"), and 試す means "to test". One says 肝試しをする or 肝試しに行く. For a test of courage without a spooky element, 度胸試し fits better.

examples[].german: I will apply the new rules.
Insurance applies to this treatment.
The student discount does not apply to this product.
en.notes: 適用 means to apply a rule, law or rate to a case: AをBに適用する; very often passive: 〜が適用される "applies, is in effect". Typical: 保険が適用される "is covered by insurance", 割引が適用される, 法律を適用する. Distinction: 応用 is the practical application of knowledge or technology, 使う is general using. Do not confuse it with 適応 "adaptation".

examples[].german: Today it's my treat.
A senior colleague treated me to yakiniku.
You always treat me and I feel bad, so let's split the bill today.
en.notes: おごり is a treat in which someone pays for others; the related verb is おごる (〜に〜をおごる "to treat someone to something"). Typical: 今日は私のおごり, 先輩のおごりで. The word is colloquial and suits friends or people younger than you; more polite are ごちそうする and ごちそうになる. It is mostly written in kana (kanji 奢り); do not confuse with 驕り "arrogance, haughtiness".

en.meaning: small gift to bring; souvenir brought to a host
examples[].german: I'll bring a small gift.
I was invited to a friend's house, so I bought a cake as a gift to bring.
What would be good as a gift to bring to a business partner?
en.notes: 手土産 is a small gift that one brings in person when visiting (手 "hand"), e.g. sweets or cake for hosts or business partners. お土産, by contrast, mainly means a souvenir from a trip. Typical: 手土産を持って行く, 手土産に〜を買う; more formally 手土産を持参する. When handing it over, one traditionally says modestly つまらないものですが.

examples[].german: I send a year-end gift.
The year-end gift section at the department store is always crowded.
A ham arrived from my uncle as a year-end gift.
en.notes: お歳暮 is the gift given in December to people to whom one felt indebted during the year - superiors, teachers, relatives, business partners. The summer counterpart is お中元. One says お歳暮を贈る (formally "to give") or お歳暮を送る ("to send", when shipped). Department stores have their own sections for it. 歳暮 without お also means "year-end" in writing.

examples[].german: I received a midsummer gift.
We sent midsummer gifts to our business partners.
At the department store I picked out a beer set as a midsummer gift.
en.notes: お中元 is the thank-you gift sent in summer (in the Tokyo area early to mid-July, in western Japan often until mid-August) to superiors, business partners, teachers or relatives; the winter counterpart is お歳暮. It is almost always said with the polite お: お中元を贈る, お中元を頂く, お中元のお礼を言う. Without お, 中元 appears mainly in business language such as 中元セール.

examples[].german: I prepare the money gift for the wedding.
I handed over the congratulatory money at the reception desk.
Etiquette says to put new bills in the congratulatory money.
en.notes: 祝儀 refers above all to a gift of money for a joyful occasion, especially a wedding; in daily life one almost always says ご祝儀. The money is put in a ご祝儀袋, and new bills are used if possible. In addition, ご祝儀 can also be a tip or a reward for artists and craftsmen. The counterpart for sad occasions is 不祝儀 or 香典.

examples[].german: I bought a condolence envelope.
At sad occasions, let's avoid flashy clothes.
The way of wrapping money differs between congratulatory and condolence occasions.
en.notes: 不祝儀 is literally a "non-celebration", i.e. a sad occasion, above all a funeral or memorial service - the opposite of 祝儀. The word is most often encountered in 不祝儀袋, the black-and-white envelope in which condolence money (香典) is handed over. It is a somewhat formal word from the area of etiquette; in conversation one more often says お葬式 or お通夜.

examples[].german: I'll bring condolence money.
At the wake, I handed the condolence money to the reception desk.
A return gift of tea arrived in thanks for the condolence money.
en.notes: 香典 is the money one brings to a wake (お通夜) or funeral; literally it was originally an offering for incense (香). It is put into a condolence envelope, and one says 香典を包む, 香典を渡す or 香典を供える; new banknotes are avoided here. The family later thanks the giver with a return gift, the 香典返し.

examples[].german: I attend the ceremony with prayer beads.
My grandmother always reads the sutras with prayer beads in her hand.
Because of the holidays, the cars are lined up bumper to bumper.
en.notes: 数珠 are the Buddhist prayer beads that one holds in the hand at funerals, memorial services and grave visits, or drapes over the folded hands when praying: 数珠を持つ, 数珠を手にかける. The reading じゅず is irregular and must be learned. Also very common is 数珠つなぎ "strung together like beads", for example for a long line of cars.

examples[].german: I received a posthumous Buddhist name.
I had a monk give my father a posthumous Buddhist name.
My grandfather's posthumous Buddhist name is carved on the grave.
en.notes: 戒名 is the Buddhist name that a monk gives to a deceased person; it is written on the memorial tablet (位牌) and on the gravestone. One says 戒名をつける or, politely, 戒名をつけていただく, and the family 戒名をもらう. Originally it was the name received on taking the Buddhist precepts (戒); in the Jodo Shinshu school it is called 法名.

examples[].german: I honor my ancestors at Urabon.
Urabon events are held at the temple.
Urabon is usually called 「お盆」.
en.notes: 盂蘭盆 is the full, Buddhist name of the festival of the dead that is simply called お盆 in everyday life; the word comes from Sanskrit (ullambana). It is encountered mainly in temple and written contexts, for example in 盂蘭盆会, the Obon memorial service. At Obon (mid-July or mid-August, depending on the region), the spirits of the ancestors are welcomed and sent off again; the difficult kanji are often also written as うら盆.

examples[].german: We will introduce a new system.
This store has introduced self-checkout registers.
School uniforms will be introduced from next year.
en.notes: 導入 means introducing or acquiring something new, such as a system, technology or procedure: 〜を導入する; passive 〜が導入される. Typical: システム/制度/機械を導入する, 導入費用. In texts and teaching, 導入 also means "introduction". Distinction: 紹介 is introducing a person or thing, 輸入 is importing goods.

examples[].german: I visit the graves at Obon.
On my grandfather's death anniversary, our family went to visit his grave.
Before the grave visit, I bought flowers and incense sticks.
en.notes: 墓参り is a visit to the family grave; politely and very commonly also お墓参り. One says 墓参りに行く or, as a する-verb, 墓参りする. Typical occasions are お盆, お彼岸, New Year and the death anniversary (命日); one cleans the grave, pours water over it, places flowers and lights incense sticks (線香をあげる).

examples[].german: We celebrated my father's 60th birthday.
It is traditional to give a red vest as a gift for the 60th birthday.
Even though my mother has turned sixty, she works energetically every day.
en.notes: 還暦 is the 60th birthday: after 60 years, the cycle of combinations of the zodiac and celestial stems (干支) is complete and one "returns to the starting calendar". One says 還暦を迎える and 還暦を祝う; traditionally one gives something red, such as a red ちゃんちゃんこ, as a sign of a new beginning. Further milestones are 古希 (70), 喜寿 (77) and 米寿 (88).

examples[].german: This year is an unlucky year for me.
Because it's an unlucky year, I had a purification ritual done at the shrine.
Between the accident and the illness, this year was like a real unlucky year.
en.notes: 厄年 are the years of life in which, according to old folk belief, one is especially prone to misfortune - by the traditional count (数え年), mainly 25 and 42 for men and 19 and 33 for women; the worst one is called 大厄, the year before 前厄, and the year after 後厄. Many people then have themselves purified at a shrine (厄払い, 厄除け). Loosely, 厄年 is also used for a year in which everything goes wrong.

examples[].german: We celebrate according to the old calendar.
According to the calendar it is already spring, but cold days continue.
In the old days, people looked at the calendar to decide when to plant rice.
en.notes: 暦 denotes the calendar as a system of timekeeping or almanac, for example with moon phases, lucky days and seasonal divisions; the everyday wall calendar is called カレンダー. Very typical is the phrase 暦の上では "according to the calendar", for example when it is already spring by the calendar but still cold. In compounds, 暦 is read れき: 旧暦, 西暦, 還暦.

en.meaning: the 24 solar terms; 24 divisions of the year
examples[].german: People in the past did their farm work according to the 24 solar terms.
Risshun and the summer solstice are among the 24 solar terms.
If the 24 solar terms are written on the calendar, you can feel the change of seasons.
en.notes: 二十四節気 divide the solar year into 24 sections of about 15 days each according to the position of the sun. Well-known names are 立春 ("start of spring"), 春分, 夏至, 秋分, 冬至 and 大寒. They originally served agriculture; today one encounters them in weather reports, calendars and seasonal greeting formulas in letters. A single section is called 節気.

en.meaning: doyo (hottest days of summer; period before a change of season)
examples[].german: On the Day of the Ox in the doyo period, we eat eel.
When doyo begins, the heat gets even harsher.
Every year my mother airs out her kimono in the summer doyo.
en.notes: 土用 are, by the old calendar, the roughly 18 days before the start of each season; today it almost always means the summer 土用 from about late July to early August, the hottest days of the year. Well known is 土用の丑の日, on which eel (うなぎ) is traditionally eaten. Other compounds are 土用干し (airing out clothes and books in high summer) and 土用波 (high waves in late summer).

en.meaning: equinox week; Higan (Buddhist); the other shore
examples[].german: I visit graves during the equinox week.
They do say: the heat and the cold last only until the equinox.
During the autumn Higan week, I made ohagi with my grandmother.
en.notes: 彼岸 in daily life means the week around the equinox in spring and autumn, when one visits graves and offers sweets such as おはぎ; one mostly says お彼岸. Literally it means "the other shore", in Buddhism the nirvana beyond this world. Well known is the proverb 暑さ寒さも彼岸まで: heat and cold last only until the equinox.

examples[].german: We'll hold the wedding on a taian day.
On a taian Saturday, wedding venues get booked up quickly.
I chose a taian day for the shop opening.
en.notes: 大安 is the luckiest of the six day types of the traditional calendar (六曜), which also include 仏滅 and 友引. On 大安 days people like to marry, open businesses or pick up a new car; the set phrase 大安吉日 stresses a particularly favorable day. One says 大安の日 or simply 大安に.

examples[].german: I avoid butsumetsu days.
Apparently wedding halls get cheaper on butsumetsu.
My grandmother disliked moving on a butsumetsu day.
en.notes: 仏滅 is the least favorable day in the six-part calendar cycle 六曜 and the opposite of 大安. People avoid it for weddings, moves or openings, which is why wedding halls often give discounts on 仏滅. Literally it means "Buddha's death", but the calendar custom actually has nothing to do with Buddhism.

examples[].german: I'll move on an auspicious day.
"The day you make up your mind is the lucky day" - let's start exercising from today.
On invitations, the date is written as 「十月吉日」.
en.notes: 吉日 (also read きちにち) is a day that promises good luck, often strengthened to 大安吉日. Very well known is the proverb 思い立ったが吉日: the day you decide to do something is the right day to start. In letters and invitations, "〇月吉日" is often written instead of an exact date, to leave the day of writing open.

examples[].german: I will convey my feelings of gratitude.
I wrote a letter full of gratitude to the friend who helped me.
I am truly grateful to my parents.
en.notes: 感謝 is gratitude. As a する-verb, the person takes に: 先生に感謝する "to be grateful to the teacher", and so does the occasion: ご協力に感謝します "we thank you for your cooperation". Fixed expressions are 感謝の気持ち, 感謝を込めて "with gratitude" and 感謝してもしきれない "one can never be grateful enough". In daily life people usually just say ありがとう; 感謝しています sounds more serious and more elevated.

examples[].german: We will conduct a survey.
We will hold an evacuation drill next month.
A double-points campaign is currently being held.
en.notes: 実施 means to officially carry out plans, measures, exams or campaigns: 〜を実施する; passive 〜が実施される. Typical: 調査/試験/訓練/キャンペーンを実施する, 実施中 "currently under way". It sounds formal and official; in daily life people say 行う or する. Distinction: 実行 emphasizes a person carrying out a plan or resolution, 実施 the regulated carrying out by an organization.

en.meaning: auspiciousness of a day (per the calendar)
examples[].german: I'll choose a day with good auspiciousness.
It is a beautiful, auspicious day today, and congratulations are truly in order.
My father cares about the auspiciousness of days and dislikes signing contracts on butsumetsu.
en.notes: 日柄 is the quality of luck or misfortune of a day as determined by the traditional calendar, i.e. whether it is, for example, a 大安 or a 仏滅. One says 日柄がいい/悪い or, politely, お日柄; especially well known is the set phrase 本日はお日柄もよく at the start of wedding speeches. Do not confuse it with 日付 (date).

examples[].german: It is a turning point in life.
We have reached the milestone of our 50th anniversary.
Let's review our goals at the turn of the fiscal year.
en.notes: 節目 is originally the knot in bamboo or wood; figuratively it is a break or milestone at which one stage ends and a new one begins. Typical are 人生の節目, 節目の年 and 〜周年という節目を迎える. Unlike 転機 (a turning point that changes something), 節目 emphasizes the marked section in a sequence, such as anniversaries, graduations or year changes.

examples[].german: I'm standing at a crossroads in life.
The company is now facing a major crossroads.
He wavered at that crossroads between further education and employment.
en.notes: 岐路 is literally a fork in the road, but it is used almost only figuratively: 岐路に立つ "to stand at a crossroads", 人生の岐路, 重大な岐路. The word sounds literary and elevated; in conversation one more often says 分かれ道. Unlike 瀬戸際 (on the verge of success or ruin), 岐路 is about the choice between different directions.

en.meaning: to get past the worst; to pass the peak
examples[].german: The illness has passed its peak.
The worst of the heat seems to be over at last.
The busy period is over the hump, so I should be able to take next week off.
en.notes: 峠 is a mountain pass; 峠を越える literally means "to cross the pass", figuratively "to have the worst behind one, to get past the peak". It is typical for illnesses (病気が峠を越える), heat, work peaks or crises; 峠を越す means the same. With 峠 alone one also says 今が峠だ "now is the most critical point".

en.meaning: to spur on; to accelerate; to step up
examples[].german: We will accelerate technological innovation.
The weak yen is further fueling the rise in prices.
With the new coach, the team's training has really picked up speed.
en.notes: 拍車 is the rider's spur; X に拍車をかける means "to spur X on, to accelerate or intensify X". It is often about developments that are already moving anyway, frequently negative ones: 少子化に拍車をかける, 物価高に拍車をかける. The intransitive form is 拍車がかかる "to gain momentum". The idiom is typical of news and written language.

en.meaning: to get on track; to get going; to take off
examples[].german: The business has gotten on track.
My new life has finally settled into a routine too.
First of all, it is important to get the new project on track.
en.notes: 軌道 is an orbit or a track; 軌道に乗る means "to get onto the track", figuratively "to get going, to run as planned". Typical subjects with が are 事業, 仕事, 計画 or 新しい生活. The transitive counterpart is 軌道に乗せる "to bring something on track"; literally, the expression can also refer to a satellite reaching orbit.

examples[].german: I'll arrange the funds.
I have to figure out how to pay the rent.
He is working out a way to get time off cleverly.
en.notes: 算段 means thinking up ways and means to manage something, especially to raise money. Typical are 金の算段, 算段をつける "to find a way" and, as a する-verb, 〜か算段する "to figure out how to ...". The word sounds a bit old-fashioned; close synonyms are 工面 (raising money) and 段取り (planning the sequence of steps), while 計画 is "plan" in general.

examples[].german: The prospect of completion has been established.
We aim to put the report together by around the end of next month.
There is no prospect yet of when train service will resume.
en.notes: 目処 is mostly written in kana めど (more rarely 目途) and denotes a foreseeable prospect or goal. The main patterns are めどが立つ/つく "to become foreseeable" (intransitive), めどを立てる/つける (transitive) and 〜をめどに "aiming at about ...", e.g. 月末をめどに. Unlike 見通し (forecast, outlook), めど emphasizes the tangible reference point as to when or how something will succeed.

examples[].german: I found a pretext.
He declined the drinking party on the pretext of feeling unwell.
I borrowed a book in order to create an excuse to meet her.
en.notes: 口実 is a pretext that one puts forward in order to do or avoid something. Typical patterns are 〜を口実に(して) "under the pretext of ..." and 口実を作る/見つける. Unlike 言い訳 (an excuse, a justification after the fact), 口実 is usually used in advance as a reason that is not the real one.

examples[].german: It is corroborated information.
Reporters write an article only after obtaining corroboration of the information.
No evidence was found to support his story.
en.notes: 裏付け is evidence that supports a statement or assumption, literally something applied from behind (裏). Common are 裏付けがある/ない, 裏付けを取る "to check and substantiate something" (press, police) and the verb 裏付ける "to substantiate". 証拠 is the proof itself, 根拠 the grounds; 裏付け emphasizes confirmation through facts or data.

examples[].german: We promote environmental protection.
The city is promoting a recycling campaign.
The company is pushing ahead with a plan to increase the number of women in management positions.
en.notes: 推進 means actively driving forward a project, policy or movement: 〜を推進する. Typical objects are 計画, 政策, 改革, 環境保護 and デジタル化. The word is formal and occurs mainly in politics, administration and companies. Distinction: 促進 stresses speeding up a process (成長を促進する), 推進 the active pushing forward of an undertaking; technically 推進 also means "propulsion" (ships, rockets).

examples[].german: A clue to the solution has been found.
Starting with talk about the weather, the conversation took off.
The police are trying to get a lead on the case.
en.notes: 糸口 is literally the end of a thread, where one begins to wind up a ball of yarn; figuratively a first starting point or hint. Typical are 解決の糸口, 事件の糸口 and 話の糸口 (a conversation opener), plus 糸口をつかむ/見つける/探る. 手がかり is more a concrete clue in a search, きっかけ a trigger; 糸口 stresses the first step with which a matter can be unraveled.

examples[].german: I will open a breakthrough in the negotiations.
I can't see a breakthrough that gets us out of the recession.
A remark by the newcomer became the breakthrough in the discussion.
en.notes: 突破口 is the opening or breach through which a breakthrough succeeds; originally military, today mostly figurative for negotiations, research or crises. Typical are 突破口を開く, 突破口を見つける and 〜の突破口になる. 突破 on its own is the breaking through itself (e.g. 予選突破), whereas 糸口 is rather a cautious first lead.

examples[].german: The company is on the brink of bankruptcy.
At the critical moment between winning and losing, he stayed calm.
en.notes: 瀬戸際 is literally the edge of a strait (瀬戸); figuratively the critical moment in which success or ruin is decided. Typical are 倒産の瀬戸際, 〜か〜かの瀬戸際 (生きるか死ぬかの瀬戸際) and 瀬戸際に立つ/立たされる. While 岐路 means a choice between paths, at 瀬戸際 one stands just before a fall.

en.meaning: being caught in the middle; dilemma
examples[].german: I'm caught in the middle.
Middle managers easily get caught between their bosses and their subordinates.
I'm in trouble, caught between my mother and my wife.
en.notes: 板挟み is literally "pinched between boards": one stands between two sides with conflicting demands and cannot satisfy either. Typical is AとBの板挟みになる or 板挟みにあう, for example between boss and staff or between mother and wife. For a pure decision dilemma without people involved, one more often says ジレンマ.

en.meaning: one's own domain; where one shines unrivaled
examples[].german: This field is his domain.
When it came to karaoke, it was once again the department head's show.
In the second half, it became the ace's show.
en.notes: 独壇場 is an area or situation in which someone shines without competition: 〜の独壇場だ, 〜の独壇場となる. The word was originally 独擅場 (どくせんじょう); through confusion of the character 擅 with 壇 ("stage"), the present form became established. It does not mean an economic monopoly (that would be 独占), but a stage that someone dominates alone.

examples[].german: We promote economic growth.
Moderate exercise aids digestion.
An event promoting cultural exchange between the two countries was held.
en.notes: 促進 means promoting or accelerating a process: 〜を促進する. Typical: 経済成長/販売/交流/消化を促進する, 販売促進 (short 販促) "sales promotion". It usually concerns processes that are already under way and are meant to become faster or stronger. Distinction: 推進 is the active pushing forward of a plan by people or organizations. The word is formal and common in business and medicine.
