en.meaning: reaping what you sow; getting what you deserve; your own fault
examples[].german: That's your own doing.
You overslept because you stayed up all night gaming - that's your own fault.
He didn't study and failed the exam, so all you can say is: he brought it on himself.
en.notes: 自業自得 is composed of 自業 "one's own deeds" and 自得 "receiving oneself" and comes from the Buddhist doctrine of karma: one reaps the consequences of one's own actions. Today it is used almost only negatively in the sense of "serves you right": 自業自得だ, 自業自得としか言えない. It sounds quite harsh and accusatory; a figurative synonym is 身から出た錆.

examples[].german: We understand each other without words.
Couples who have been together for a long time understand each other's feelings without words.
At work, it's better to say things clearly rather than rely on unspoken understanding.
en.notes: 以心伝心 literally means "to transmit heart to heart" and comes from Zen, where teaching passes from master to disciple without words. In everyday use it describes tacit understanding between people who are close: 以心伝心で分かる/通じる, 以心伝心の仲. It is not about telepathy but about familiarity; similar is 阿吽の呼吸 (perfectly synchronized timing).

en.meaning: once-in-a-lifetime encounter; every moment is unique
examples[].german: I cherish each unrepeatable encounter.
I think encounters while traveling are once-in-a-lifetime.
We treat our guests in the spirit of ichigo ichie.
en.notes: 一期一会 comes from the tea ceremony: 一期 (いちご) is "a lifetime", 一会 (いちえ) "one meeting" - every gathering is unique and should be conducted with full devotion. One says 一期一会を大切にする, 一期一会の出会い or 〜は一期一会だ. The readings いちご and え are unusual and must be learned; the expression is popular in hospitality, tourism and greetings.

en.meaning: so busy one would take any help; extremely busy
examples[].german: I'm so busy that I need any help I can get.
At the end of the year it's so busy that we'd welcome any helping hand.
On moving day, I really could have used any help.
en.notes: Literally: "I'd even like to borrow a cat's paws" - so much to do that even a cat would be welcome as help. Almost always with a degree expression: 猫の手も借りたいほど/くらい忙しい or 猫の手も借りたいくらいの忙しさ. The expression is colloquial and humorous; 借りたい inflects like an い-adjective (借りたかった).

examples[].german: We will keep costs in check.
This medicine has the effect of suppressing appetite.
The government is trying to curb the rise in prices.
en.notes: 抑制 means holding back, braking or suppressing something undesirable: 〜を抑制する. Typical: 物価の上昇/食欲/感情を抑制する, 抑制効果. The word is formal and literary; in everyday speech one says 抑える (コストを抑える, 気持ちを抑える). Distinction: 削減 is cutting in numerical terms, 抑制 is limiting or braking an increase.

en.meaning: to speak frankly; to open up
examples[].german: Let's talk openly with each other.
We need to have a frank talk once.
Over drinks with the department head, we were able to talk openly.
en.notes: In Japanese, 腹 (belly) stands for one's true intentions; 腹を割る literally means "to cut open the belly", that is, to lay one's real thoughts bare. It almost always appears as 腹を割って話す/話し合う or attributively as 腹を割った話. It emphasizes mutual openness in private; related are 本音で話す and the quite different 腹を括る (to prepare for the worst).

en.meaning: to acquire; to master; to wear (on one's body)
examples[].german: I acquire new skills.
I want them to learn proper manners while they are still children.
She always wears her grandmother's ring.
en.notes: 身につける literally means "to attach to the body" and has two meanings: to internalize skills, knowledge or habits (技術・マナーを身につける) and to wear clothes or jewelry on the body (for the latter also written 身に着ける). The intransitive counterpart is 身につく "to sink in, to stick": 習慣が身につく. Unlike 覚える, 身につける emphasizes that something truly becomes one's own ability.

examples[].german: I will point out the problem areas.
My boss pointed out a mistake in the materials.
Thank you for pointing that out. I will fix it right away.
en.notes: 指摘 means explicitly pointing out a mistake, a problem or an important point: 〜を指摘する, 〜と指摘する. Typical: 間違いを指摘する, 問題点を指摘する; passive: 〜に指摘される "to have something pointed out by someone". ご指摘ありがとうございます is a polite reaction to criticism. Distinction: 注意する is "to warn, to caution", 指す is literally pointing at something.

en.meaning: to throw cold water on; to dampen
examples[].german: Don't put a damper on the cheerful mood.
I don't want to be a killjoy, but I think the budget isn't enough for that plan.
The rain dampened the excitement of the festival.
en.notes: 水を差す literally means "to pour in water" (for example into hot water or sake), figuratively "to put a damper on, to disturb something". The target is marked with に: 雰囲気に水を差す, 話に水を差す, 二人の仲に水を差す (to drive a wedge between two people). Very common is the apologetic introduction 水を差すようで悪いけど before one raises an objection.

en.meaning: to make up one's mind; to be resolved
examples[].german: I take on the challenge with resolve.
I realized I couldn't escape anymore and resigned myself to it.
When I resolved that it was fine to fail, I felt relieved.
en.notes: 腹を括る literally means "to tie up the belly": one makes a firm decision and is prepared for the worst. It is mostly written 腹をくくる in kana; typical are 〜と腹をくくる and 腹をくくって〜する. Similar are 覚悟を決める and 腹を決める; do not confuse with 腹を割る (to speak openly).

examples[].german: I take part in a clinical trial.
New drugs are released only after their safety has been confirmed in clinical trials.
When I was a student, I once did a paid job as a clinical trial participant.
en.notes: 治験 is a clinical trial in which a new drug is tested on humans to obtain government approval. One says 治験に参加する, 治験を行う; the test drug is called 治験薬. 臨床試験 is the more general technical term for clinical research; in Japan one also knows the paid 治験のアルバイト for test subjects.

en.meaning: to consider; to examine; to look into
examples[].german: I will consider the proposal.
I am considering moving.
We will look into that matter positively within the company.
en.notes: 検討 means to examine and weigh something thoroughly before deciding: 〜を検討する, 〜するかどうか検討する. In business language, 前向きに検討します "we will consider it favorably" is very common, and often a polite way of not agreeing right away. Typical: 検討中, 再検討. Distinction: 考える is "to think" in general, 検査 a technical or medical examination.

examples[].german: I am receiving an IV drip.
I was severely dehydrated, so I got an IV drip at the hospital.
It takes about an hour until the drip is finished.
en.notes: 点滴 in daily life is the infusion (short for 点滴注射): 点滴を受ける, 点滴を打つ/打ってもらう, and as a する-verb also 点滴する. Typical for dehydration, exhaustion or in the hospital; the stand is called 点滴スタンド. The original meaning "falling drops of water" is still known from the proverb 点滴石を穿つ (constant dripping wears away the stone).

examples[].german: I have an examination in the morning.
The doctor examined the patient carefully.
Please hand in your patient card at the reception.
en.notes: 診察 is the medical examination or consultation: the patient says 診察を受ける, the doctor 患者を診察する. Related are 診察室 (examination room), 診察券 (patient card) and 診察時間 (consultation hours). 検査 are individual tests such as blood draws, 診断 is the resulting diagnosis, and 健康診断 the regular health checkup.

examples[].german: I sincerely wish you a speedy recovery.
After the operation, my grandfather is recovering well.
She recovered from the illness and returned to work.
en.notes: 快復 mainly means recovery from an illness; one says 病気から快復する or, in get-well wishes, ご快復をお祈りします. The far more common spelling 回復 has the same reading and covers all areas, including 景気の回復 or 体力の回復; newspapers usually write 回復 even for illnesses. 快復 therefore seems somewhat more elevated and is especially suited to polite letters.

examples[].german: I got the flu shot.
I checked my child's vaccination schedule.
Please get the necessary vaccinations before traveling abroad.
en.notes: 予防接種 is composed of 予防 "prevention" and 接種 "inoculation" and is the official, neutral term for vaccination. One says 予防接種を受ける, and for a child 予防接種を受けさせる; colloquially also ワクチンを打つ. Typically the disease is given with の: インフルエンザの予防接種.

examples[].german: I prevent lifestyle-related diseases.
Lack of exercise can cause lifestyle-related diseases.
My father is careful about lifestyle-related diseases such as diabetes.
en.notes: 生活習慣病 are diseases that depend strongly on diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol, such as diabetes, high blood pressure or lipid metabolism disorders. In 1996 the term replaced the older 成人病 "adult diseases" in order to emphasize the role of lifestyle. Typical are 生活習慣病を予防する, 生活習慣病になる and 生活習慣病のリスク; often in connection with メタボ.

examples[].german: I made an appointment for a comprehensive medical checkup.
Since I turned forty, I had a comprehensive checkup for the first time.
A small polyp was found in my stomach at the comprehensive checkup.
en.notes: 人間ドック is a comprehensive health checkup lasting half a day to two days; the name alludes to the dry dock in which ships are thoroughly overhauled. One says 人間ドックを受ける or 人間ドックに入る. Unlike the annual, legally required 健康診断, it is voluntary, more extensive and usually partly paid for by oneself.

examples[].german: I'm taking herbal medicine.
I tried herbal medicine to cure my sensitivity to cold.
Herbal medicine is bitter, but it seems to suit my body.
en.notes: 漢方薬 are medicines of traditional Chinese medicine (漢方) as developed further in Japan, usually mixtures of herbs and roots. Like all medicines, one "drinks" them: 漢方薬を飲む, not 食べる. Many kampo preparations are also prescribed by doctors in Japan; the counterpart is Western medicine (西洋医学の薬).

examples[].german: I am receiving acupuncture and moxibustion treatment.
My shoulder stiffness is severe, so I started going to an acupuncture clinic.
My older brother obtained his license as an acupuncturist.
en.notes: 鍼灸 combines 鍼 (acupuncture needle, also written 針) and 灸 (moxibustion, in daily life お灸). Typical words are 鍼灸院 (clinic), 鍼灸師 (state-certified acupuncturist) and 鍼灸治療; one goes there with 鍼灸院に通う. Also well known is the idiom お灸を据える "to teach someone a lesson".

examples[].german: I go for chiropractic treatment.
My back hurt, so I had my body misalignment corrected at a seitai clinic.
A new body-therapy clinic has opened near the station.
en.notes: 整体 is a manual body therapy meant to "put in order" posture, spine and pelvis; one goes to a 整体院 to see a 整体師. Typical are 整体に行く/通う and 整体で体のゆがみを直す. Unlike 鍼灸 or 接骨院, 整体 is not a state-recognized medical profession in Japan but a private healing method.

examples[].german: I had a shiatsu massage.
When you're tired, pressing the pressure points on your neck brings relief.
My grandfather runs a shiatsu shop in front of the station.
en.notes: 指圧 is the Japanese pressure massage in which specific points are pressed with the fingers and thumbs. Typical are 指圧を受ける "to receive a shiatsu treatment", 指圧師 "shiatsu therapist" and, as a transitive する-verb, ツボを指圧する "to press pressure points". Unlike マッサージ, which generally means kneading and rubbing, 指圧 emphasizes pressure on specific points; 指圧マッサージ is a common advertising term.

examples[].german: I will analyze the results.
Let's analyze the cause of the failure thoroughly.
Before job hunting, I did a self-analysis.
en.notes: 分析 means to break something into its components and examine it systematically: 〜を分析する. Typical: データ/結果/原因/市場を分析する, 分析結果, 自己分析 "self-analysis" (in job hunting). Distinction: 調査 is gathering information, 分析 is the subsequent evaluation, 検討 is weighing before a decision.

en.meaning: no smoking; non-smoking; to quit smoking
examples[].german: A non-smoking seat, please.
My father has quit smoking since last year.
Smoking is prohibited inside this restaurant.
en.notes: 禁煙 has two uses: as a notice or attribute meaning "smoking prohibited" (店内は禁煙です, 禁煙席, 全席禁煙) and as an intransitive する-verb meaning "to quit smoking" (去年から禁煙している, 禁煙中). The counterpart is 喫煙 "smoking" (喫煙席, 喫煙所). In conversation, for quitting you can also simply say タバコをやめる; 禁煙 sounds somewhat firmer and more determined.

en.meaning: giving up alcohol; abstinence from alcohol
examples[].german: I'm abstaining from alcohol for my health.
It has been three years since I gave up drinking.
The doctor advised me to give up drinking completely.
en.notes: 断酒 means giving up alcohol completely and permanently, and is often used in connection with alcohol dependence (断酒会 "self-help group for alcoholics"). As an intransitive する-verb: 断酒する, 断酒している, 断酒を続ける. The similar 禁酒 can also refer to temporary abstinence or a ban on alcohol; 断酒 emphasizes the final break. In daily life one usually simply says お酒をやめる.

examples[].german: Picky eating is not good.
My son is a terribly picky eater and hardly eats any vegetables.
Since I started living alone, I tend to eat an unbalanced diet.
en.notes: 偏食 refers to picky, one-sided eating: one eats only what one likes and leaves the rest - said especially often of children. Typical are 偏食がひどい, 偏食の子ども, 偏食を直す; as an intransitive する-verb 偏食する. More colloquial is 好き嫌いが多い "to have many food dislikes"; for the unbalanced diet itself one also says 栄養が偏る.

examples[].german: He collapsed from overwork.
Death from overwork is a major social problem in Japan.
I've been a bit overworked lately, so I'll take some time off.
en.notes: 過労 is exhaustion from too much work. Typical are 過労で倒れる "to collapse from overwork", 過労がたまる and 過労気味 "somewhat overworked"; well known is 過労死 "death from overwork". 過労 is not a する-verb; "to overwork oneself" is 働きすぎる or 無理をする. General tiredness is 疲労 or 疲れ.

examples[].german: I got burnout syndrome.
Now that the tournament is over, I feel completely burned out.
Many students burn out after entrance exams.
en.notes: 燃え尽き is the noun form of 燃え尽きる "to burn up completely; to burn out" (intransitive). For burnout it is almost always in the compound 燃え尽き症候群; besides that one says verbally 燃え尽きてしまう or 燃え尽きたような気分. It is also used for the emptiness after a big goal, for example for athletes after a tournament or students after entrance exams. The loanword バーンアウト is also in use.

examples[].german: My hay fever is bad.
I suddenly developed hay fever last year.
During hay fever season, I wear a mask when I go outside.
en.notes: 花粉症 is pollen allergy, in Japan mainly to cedar pollen (スギ花粉) in spring. One says 花粉症だ / 花粉症がある "to have hay fever", 花粉症になる "to develop hay fever" and 花粉症がつらい / ひどい. Typical symptoms are くしゃみ, 鼻水 and 目がかゆい. 花粉 on its own is "pollen" (花粉が飛ぶ, 花粉情報). Not a する-verb.

examples[].german: Please watch out for heatstroke.
Let's drink water frequently to prevent heatstroke.
During club practice, a student collapsed from heatstroke.
en.notes: 熱中症 is the umbrella term for heat-related illnesses, from heatstroke to heat exhaustion; in the Japanese summer one hears it daily in the news. Typical are 熱中症になる, 熱中症で倒れる / 運ばれる, 熱中症に注意 and 熱中症対策. The 中 here is in the sense of "being hit" (熱に中る) - the word has nothing to do with 熱中する "to be enthusiastic about something". The older 日射病 refers specifically to sunstroke.

examples[].german: I'll be careful not to get frostbite.
My toes got frostbitten while mountain climbing.
For mild frostbite, warm the area slowly with lukewarm water.
en.notes: 凍傷 is frostbite, i.e. tissue damage from severe cold. One says 凍傷になる or 凍傷にかかる, often with a body part: 指が凍傷になる. Milder, everyday cold damage is called しもやけ "chilblains". The word is neutral to medical and is encountered mainly in mountaineering, winter sports and cold snaps.

examples[].german: Please watch out for dehydration.
I had persistent diarrhea and became dehydrated.
Elderly people can become dehydrated even if they don't feel thirsty.
en.notes: 脱水症状 denotes the condition or symptoms of dehydration (脱水 "removal of water" + 症状 "symptom"). Typical are 脱水症状を起こす, 脱水症状になる and 脱水症状が出る, often in connection with heat, fever or diarrhea. 脱水 alone is also used for the spin cycle of a washing machine (脱水する). Neutral to medical.

examples[].german: You must not infringe copyright.
The copyright of this photo belongs to the photographer.
Old novels whose copyright has expired can be read for free.
en.notes: 著作権 is copyright (著作 "authoring, work" + 権 "right"). Typical collocations are 著作権を侵害する "to infringe copyright", 著作権侵害, 著作権がある / 切れる "to expire" and 著作権者 "rights holder"; on the internet one often reads 著作権フリー. Related legal terms are 特許 "patent" and 商標 "trademark". Legal, but also common in daily life.

examples[].german: I will compare the two proposals.
Compared with last year, there has been less rain this year.
Before buying, I compared prices online.
en.notes: 比較する means "to compare", mostly in the form AをBと比較する or AとBを比較する. Very common is the phrase 〜と比較して "in comparison with". In daily life people mostly use the native verb 比べる; 比較する sounds more objective and suits reports, statistics and price comparisons. Related: 比較的 "relatively, comparatively".

examples[].german: We registered the trademark.
This name is already a registered trademark of another company.
They used a similar logo and were sued for trademark infringement.
en.notes: 商標 is the trademark in the legal sense. Typical are 商標を登録する, 登録商標 "registered trademark (®)" and 商標権 "trademark right" (商標権を侵害する). For "brand" in the sense of image or label, one says ブランド in daily life, and ロゴ for the pictorial mark. The word belongs to business and legal language.

en.meaning: right to one's own image; portrait rights
examples[].german: Please be mindful of portrait rights.
Posting photos that show strangers' faces on social media can violate their portrait rights.
Photos of celebrities have portrait rights, so you can't just use them freely.
en.notes: 肖像権 is the right to one's own image (肖像 "likeness, portrait" + 権 "right"). Typical collocations are 肖像権を侵害する, 肖像権の侵害 and 肖像権に配慮する. The word comes up today mainly when it is about photos of other people on social networks. It is a legal term, but also used in daily life; related are 著作権 and プライバシー.

examples[].german: We protect personal information.
Customers' personal information leaked from the company.
Don't enter your personal information on suspicious websites.
en.notes: 個人情報 is personal data such as name, address or phone number. Typical are 個人情報を守る / 保護する, 個人情報が漏れる "data gets out", 個人情報の取り扱い "handling of personal data" and the law 個人情報保護法. More general is プライバシー "privacy". The word is neutral and constantly encountered on forms and websites.

examples[].german: I have a duty of confidentiality.
When I joined the company, I signed a confidentiality agreement.
Lawyers must observe their duty of confidentiality.
en.notes: 守秘義務 is the duty of confidentiality or secrecy (守秘 "to keep secrets" + 義務 "duty"), for example for doctors, lawyers, civil servants or employees. Typical are 守秘義務がある, 守秘義務を守る, 守秘義務に違反する and 守秘義務契約 "non-disclosure agreement". In conversation, 守秘義務があるので… serves as a polite reason why one may not say something. Formal, business and legal language.

examples[].german: The misconduct came to light through whistleblowing.
Following a whistleblower report from an employee, the company began an investigation.
There is a law to protect whistleblowers.
en.notes: 内部告発 is the exposure of wrongdoing by insiders (内部 "internal" + 告発 "accusation, exposure"). Typical are 内部告発で発覚する "to come to light through a whistleblower", 内部告発を受けて調査する and 内部告発者 "whistleblower"; occasionally also as a する-verb (不正を内部告発する). 告発 alone means "to file a criminal complaint" or "to denounce". News and business language.

examples[].german: Bid rigging is illegal.
The construction companies had colluded on bids for public works.
After the bid rigging came to light, the company president apologized.
en.notes: 談合 today is mainly the prohibited price-fixing, especially in public tenders (入札談合). Typical are 談合する (intransitive), 談合が発覚する, 談合に加わる and 官製談合 "collusion orchestrated by government agencies". The older meaning "consultation, discussion" is obsolete; for ordinary arrangements one says 打ち合わせ or 話し合い. News language.

examples[].german: The cozy ties between politicians and companies are a problem.
It came out that a police officer was in cahoots with the yakuza.
To prevent collusion between the government office and contractors, the people in charge are rotated regularly.
en.notes: 癒着 has two meanings: medically "adhesion" (e.g. after an operation) and figuratively an "improper, entangled connection" between politics, government offices and companies. In the second sense it is AとBの癒着 or, as an intransitive する-verb, Aと癒着する "to be in cahoots with A". The word is clearly negative and typical of the news.

en.meaning: amakudari; post-retirement placement of senior officials in private industry
examples[].german: Amakudari is being criticized.
A retired senior bureaucrat took a post at an industry association.
The government made new rules to restrict amakudari.
en.notes: 天下り literally means "descending from heaven" (天 + 下る), originally said of gods. Today it refers almost exclusively to the move of retired senior civil servants to well-paid posts in companies or associations within their former area of responsibility. Typical are 天下りする, 天下り先 "destination post" and 天下りを規制する; the word has a strongly critical tone. More rarely it denotes orders from above (天下り人事).

examples[].german: A slush fund scandal came to light.
That company was creating a slush fund in order not to pay taxes.
It was reported that under-the-table money was used to sign players.
en.notes: 裏金 is money that is managed covertly and outside the official books - a "slush fund" - and often also money for bribery (裏 "back side, hidden" + 金 "money"). Typical are 裏金を作る, 裏金を渡す and 裏金問題 / 裏金事件. Unlike 賄賂, the concrete bribe money given to a person, 裏金 emphasizes the hiding of the money. News language.

examples[].german: He accepted a bribe.
He tried to get the permit by handing a bribe to an official.
It is said that in this country nothing moves without bribes.
en.notes: 賄賂 is the bribe money or gift itself. Typical are 賄賂を贈る / 渡す "to bribe" and 賄賂を受け取る / もらう "to accept a bribe". The offenses are legally called 贈賄 "active bribery" and 収賄 "passive bribery (accepting bribes)". Because of the difficult kanji, the word is often written わいろ.

examples[].german: Please distinguish between the two.
It is important to separate work and private life.
They are twins, so I can't tell which is which.
en.notes: 区別する means "to distinguish, to tell apart": AとBを区別する or AをBと区別する. Very common are 区別がつく "one can tell them apart" and 区別がつかない "one cannot tell them apart". Do not confuse it with 差別 "discrimination", which means unfair disadvantaging of people. 見分ける, by contrast, emphasizes recognizing with the eyes.

examples[].german: We petitioned the mayor.
The residents petitioned the city to install a traffic light.
A local organization visited ministries in Tokyo to present its petitions.
en.notes: 陳情 means presenting a concern to a government office or politician and asking for a remedy, often in person (陳 "to state" + 情 "circumstances"). As a する-verb, the addressee takes に and the concern takes を: 市に信号の設置を陳情する; also 陳情書 and 陳情団. The more formal 請願 is a legally regulated, written petition procedure. Administrative and news language.

examples[].german: I submitted a written petition.
A citizens' group collected ten thousand signatures and petitioned the Diet.
The petition was adopted by the assembly.
en.notes: 請願 is a formal petition to parliament or authorities under fixed rules (請願権, 請願法), usually in writing and often with collected signatures (署名). Typical are 請願書を提出する, 〜に請願する and 請願を採択する "to adopt a petition". Compared with 陳情, the rather personal presenting of a concern, 請願 is the more official procedure. Very formal, written language.

en.meaning: the will of the people; public will
examples[].german: We reflect the will of the people.
The election result can be seen as an expression of the will of the people.
The prime minister decided to dissolve the Diet and ask the people for their verdict.
en.notes: 民意 is the will of the people as a political quantity. Typical are 民意を反映する "to reflect the will of the people", 民意を問う "to let the people decide" (for example through new elections), 民意に従う / 背く and 民意が示される. Similar is 世論 "public opinion", which refers more to polls and moods; 民意 sounds more fundamental. Political and news language.

examples[].german: A public hearing was held.
Residents voiced their opinions at the public hearing on the plans for the new airport.
A public hearing is planned in the Diet to hear experts' opinions on the budget.
en.notes: 公聴会 is a public hearing organized by parliament or government offices to hear the opinions of experts and citizens (公 "public" + 聴 "to listen" + 会 "meeting"). Typical are 公聴会を開く / 開催する, 公聴会が開かれる and 公聴会で意見を述べる. At a 説明会, by contrast, the authority itself explains its plans. Formal, administrative language.

en.meaning: reply (in a legislature or official proceedings); response to questions
examples[].german: I listened to the prime minister's reply.
The minister replied to the opposition's questions.
Vague answers continued, and the members got angry.
en.notes: 答弁 is the answer to questions in an official session, above all the government's reply to interpellations by members of parliament (国会答弁); in court also the defense's rebuttal. As an intransitive する-verb, the question takes に: 質問に答弁する; also 答弁に立つ, 答弁を求める and 答弁書. For ordinary answers in daily life one says 答え, 返事 or 回答. Political and news language.

examples[].german: The vote on the bill was held.
Then, let's take a vote on this proposal.
The ruling party forced the bill through a vote over the opposition's objections.
en.notes: 採決 is the formal vote on a motion or bill in a body. Typical are 採決を行う, 採決をとる, 採決に入る and 強行採決 "forced vote, ramming something through"; transitive also 法案を採決する. The result is 可決 "passed" or 否決 "rejected". For casting ballots in elections one says 投票, and for the principle of majority decision 多数決.

examples[].german: The bill was passed.
The budget proposal was passed by a majority vote.
At the class meeting, the cultural festival act was approved unanimously.
en.notes: 可決 is the adoption of a motion or bill by vote. It mostly appears in the passive: 法案が可決される; in the active it is 議会が法案を可決する. Typical are 賛成多数で可決 "adopted by a majority" and 全会一致で可決 "adopted unanimously". The opposite is 否決; the vote itself is called 採決.

examples[].german: The proposal was rejected.
The no-confidence motion against the cabinet was rejected by a majority.
In a referendum, the plan to build a dam was rejected.
en.notes: 否決 is the rejection of a motion or bill by a vote, the opposite of 可決. Mostly in the passive: 提案が否決される; also 反対多数で否決 and 不信任案が否決される "the no-confidence motion fails". In the active: 議会が案を否決する. For personally declining a request one says 断る instead.

examples[].german: The new law came into effect.
The amended law will come into effect on April 1 next year.
Ahead of the ordinance coming into effect, the city held briefing sessions.
en.notes: 施行 is the putting into force of a law or ordinance. It mostly appears in the passive: 法律が施行される "a law takes effect"; also 施行日 and 〜から施行. Legal professionals often read it せこう to distinguish it from 試行 "trial run" (しこう); not to be confused with 施工 "construction work". Administrative and news language.

examples[].german: The law was revised.
There was a timetable revision in March, and the train times changed.
Public opinion is divided on constitutional revision.
en.notes: 改正 is the official change of laws, rules, timetables or fares. Typical are 法律を改正する, 憲法改正, ダイヤ改正 "timetable change" and 料金改正 "fare revision" (often a euphemistic increase). Similar is 改定 "re-setting" of prices or rules; 修正 is the correction of a draft, 改善 the improvement of a condition. Formal.

examples[].german: I will classify the data.
The books in the library are classified by theme.
Tomatoes are often classified as vegetables.
en.notes: 分類する means "to classify, to sort into groups": AをBに分類する "to classify A into B". The passive 〜に分類される "is classified as …" is very common. In everyday speech one says more simply 分ける. For sorting trash, 分別（ぶんべつ） is used rather than 分類: ゴミの分別.

examples[].german: We will abolish the regulation.
Many countries agreed to the abolition of tariffs.
At this school, the rule on hair color was abolished.
en.notes: 撤廃 is the complete abolition of rules, restrictions or discrimination. Typical are 規制を撤廃する, 関税撤廃 "abolition of tariffs", 差別撤廃 and 制限を撤廃する. The more general 廃止 is also used for institutions, bus lines or laws; 撤回 is the withdrawal of a statement or plan. Formal, news language.

examples[].german: We will expand our services.
The city announced a plan to expand daycare centers.
Calls for expanded child-rearing support are growing.
en.notes: 拡充 means "to expand and improve" (拡 "enlarge" + 充 "fill up") - mostly of services, facilities, support programs or offerings. Typical are 制度を拡充する, 支援の拡充 and サービスを拡充する. 拡大 only stresses the enlargement of scope, 充実 only the fullness of content; 拡充 combines both. Formal, typical of authorities and companies.

examples[].german: It is a fusion of Eastern and Western cultures.
In this dish, Japanese and Italian cuisine blend well together.
The sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion.
en.notes: 融合 is the merging of different things into a unity. As an intransitive する-verb it is AとBが融合する, transitive AとBを融合させる; common are 文化の融合, 伝統と現代の融合 and 核融合 "nuclear fusion". Note: a company merger is not 融合 but 合併. Rather elevated, neutral style.

examples[].german: I take the environment into consideration.
Taking the weather into account, we postponed our departure by a day.
Salary is determined taking experience and ability into account.
en.notes: 考慮 is taking circumstances into account when making a decision. Typical are 〜を考慮する, 〜を考慮に入れる "to take into consideration", 〜を考慮して "taking ... into account" and 考慮の上 "after careful consideration". 配慮, by contrast, is consideration for the feelings or needs of others, and 検討 is examining a matter. Formal, rather written language.

examples[].german: I will decide the budget allocation.
Time allocation is important in exams.
In a marathon, if you pace yourself wrongly, you can't run to the end.
en.notes: 配分 is the distribution of something by shares: budget, profit, points, or also time and energy. Typical are 予算を配分する, 利益の配分, 時間配分 "time management" (e.g. in exams) and ペース配分 "pacing". 分配 is similar, but stresses dividing up profit or assets; 割り当て is the concrete assignment to people, 配る the physical handing out.

examples[].german: I assign the work.
The allotment per person is 5,000 yen.
The seat assigned to the newcomer was near the window.
en.notes: 割り当て is the allotment of tasks, shares or quantities, also in the sense of a quota (輸入割り当て "import quota"). It is the noun form of the transitive verb 割り当てる: 仕事を新人に割り当てる; passive 割り当てられた仕事. In official texts, 割当 often appears without okurigana. 分担, by contrast, stresses dividing something among each other.

en.meaning: originality and ingenuity; creativity and resourcefulness
examples[].german: I put in originality and ingenuity.
The children used a lot of ingenuity to build a robot out of cardboard boxes.
Even with a small budget, a good event is possible, depending on ingenuity.
en.notes: 創意工夫 is a yojijukugo from 創意 "original idea" and 工夫 "tinkering, clever solution": creative resourcefulness with which one makes something good out of little. Typical are 創意工夫を凝らす "to put a lot of ingenuity into it", 創意工夫する, 創意工夫が見られる and 創意工夫次第で "depending on ingenuity". Popular in schools, companies and competitions; neutral to slightly formal.

examples[].german: I play by improvisation.
At the wedding he recited an improvised poem.
In the improv theater class, I got used to speaking in front of people.
en.notes: 即興 is improvisation, that is, doing something off the cuff without preparation. Typical are 即興で演奏する / 歌う / 作る, 即興の詩, 即興演奏 and 即興劇 "improv theater". Colloquially, especially in acting, one also says アドリブ. Do not confuse with 即席 "instant, quickly prepared" (即席ラーメン).

examples[].german: I'll check the itinerary.
Because of the typhoon, we shortened the itinerary by one day.
A detailed itinerary arrived from the travel agency.
en.notes: 旅程 is the travel plan over several days with places and dates. Typical are 旅程を立てる / 組む, 旅程を変更する and 旅程表 "itinerary (document)". 行程 means more the route or stage to be covered, 日程 a schedule in general, also for appointments. 旅程 sounds somewhat written; in conversation one often says 旅行の予定 or スケジュール.

examples[].german: I respect the other person's opinion.
Even if our opinions differ, I want to respect the other person's choice.
In this country, individual freedom is respected.
en.notes: 尊重する means "to respect, to hold in regard" and mostly refers to abstract things: 意見を尊重する, 意思を尊重する, 人権を尊重する. It is transitive with を and sounds objective to formal; a common pattern is 〜の気持ちを尊重する "to take someone's feelings seriously". 尊敬する, by contrast, means to admire and revere a person (先生を尊敬する). The passive is 尊重される "to be respected".

examples[].german: I will identify the cause.
The police identified the culprit from security camera footage.
Please be careful, since your location can sometimes be identified from photos.
en.notes: 特定する means "to determine precisely, to pinpoint, to identify" - to find the one correct answer among several possibilities: 原因を特定する, 犯人を特定する, 場所を特定する. Typical for news, police and technology. As an adjective, 特定の means "certain, specific" (特定の人). Do not confuse it with 指定する "to designate, to specify".

en.meaning: itinerary; distance of a journey; stage
examples[].german: Today's journey is long.
It is a four-hour trek one way to the summit.
We completed the entire tour safely.
en.notes: 行程 is the distance or stage to be covered on a trip, hike or tour, often with a time or distance specified: 片道三時間の行程, 一日の行程, 全行程. 行程を終える and 行程を組む go with it. Do not confuse with the identically read 工程 "work step, manufacturing process". 旅程, by contrast, is the travel plan as a whole.

examples[].german: I get in line for immigration.
At immigration, I was asked the purpose of my stay.
After getting through immigration, customs is next.
en.notes: 入国審査 is the entry or passport control at an airport or port. Typical are 入国審査を受ける, 入国審査を通る / 通過する, 入国審査に並ぶ and 入国審査官 "immigration officer". The counterpart on departure is 出国審査; customs is separate, 税関, and the health inspection is 検疫. Neutral, travel language.

examples[].german: I shop at a duty-free store.
Foreign tourists can shop tax-free by showing their passport.
This product is not eligible for tax exemption.
en.notes: 免税 is exemption from taxes or customs duties. Typical are 免税店 "duty-free shop", 免税品, 免税手続き and 免税で買う; in Japanese shops, the "Tax-free" sign indicates the tax waiver for tourists. Do not confuse it with 減税 "tax cut" and 非課税 "not taxable by law". Neutral.

examples[].german: I will send money abroad.
Every month I send money to my family back home.
With a smartphone app, you can send money to friends instantly.
en.notes: 送金 is sending money to a person or place, often abroad or to family. The recipient takes に: 家族に送金する, 海外に送金する; also 送金手数料 and 海外送金. 振込 is a transfer to a specific bank account, for example for bills; regular support for children who are studying is called 仕送り.

en.meaning: bank transfer; payment into an account
examples[].german: I pay by bank transfer.
Salary is transferred on the 25th of every month.
The transfer fee is borne by the customer.
en.notes: 振込 is a transfer to a bank account, for example for bills or salary. The verb is the transitive 振り込む: お金を口座に振り込む. It is written 振込 (as on bank forms) or 振り込み; typical are 振込手数料, 振込先 "recipient account" and, politely, お振込み. Also well known is 振り込め詐欺, a fraud involving tricked transfers.

examples[].german: I pay by bank direct debit.
The electricity bill is debited from my account on the 27th of every month.
There wasn't enough balance, so the debit could not be made.
en.notes: 引き落とし is the automatic debit from a bank account, for example for electricity, rent or a credit card. The verb is the transitive 引き落とす; one mostly hears the passive 口座から引き落とされる. Typical are 引き落とし日, 自動引き落とし and 〜を引き落としにする "to pay by direct debit". With 振込, by contrast, one actively transfers the money oneself.

examples[].german: I put it into a time deposit.
A time deposit pays slightly higher interest than a regular account.
I suddenly needed money and closed my time deposit.
en.notes: 定期預金 is a time deposit: money placed for a fixed term, which earns somewhat more interest in return. Typical are 定期預金にする / 入れる / 預ける, 定期預金を解約する "to close" and 満期 "maturity"; often shortened to 定期. The account available at any time is called 普通預金. 貯金 means savings in general.

examples[].german: I took out a home loan.
We still have twenty years left on our home loan.
Interest rates rose, and repaying the mortgage has become hard.
en.notes: 住宅ローン is the loan for buying or building an apartment or house. Typical are 住宅ローンを組む "to take out", 住宅ローンを返す / 返済する "to repay" and 住宅ローンが残っている; in Japan 35-year loans (35年ローン) are common. In conversation one often says just ローン. 借金 means debt in general.

examples[].german: I filed my tax return.
Since I'm a freelancer, I have to file a tax return by March every year.
Because I had high medical expenses, I got some tax back through my tax return.
en.notes: 確定申告 is the annual income tax return filed with the tax office (税務署), due roughly from February 16 to March 15. Employees usually do not need it because the employer handles the 年末調整 "year-end tax adjustment"; it is required for self-employed people, side income, or to get a refund, e.g. for high medical expenses. Typical: 確定申告をする, 確定申告の時期, 確定申告で税金が戻る.

en.meaning: withholding tax; tax withheld at source
examples[].german: I received my withholding tax slip.
Income tax is withheld from my salary at the source.
About ten percent is withheld from the manuscript fee before it is transferred.
en.notes: 源泉徴収 is tax deduction at the source: the employer or client withholds the income tax directly from wages or fees and pays it to the government. Typical are 源泉徴収される and 源泉徴収票 "withholding tax slip", which one receives at the end of the year; colloquially also just 源泉. The topic is closely connected with 年末調整 and 確定申告. Administrative language.

en.meaning: to assume; to presuppose; to factor in
examples[].german: I will assume the worst case.
Assuming an earthquake, we held an evacuation drill.
I hadn't anticipated that this many people would come.
en.notes: 想定する means "to assume (a case), to proceed from, to factor in": one imagines a situation in advance in order to prepare for it: 〜を想定して準備する. Very common are 想定外 "unexpected, not planned for" and 想定内 "within expectations". 予想, by contrast, is the expectation of an outcome, and 仮定 a purely mental assumption.

examples[].german: I have three dependents.
My wife is covered as my dependent.
I am supporting my elderly parents.
en.notes: 扶養 is the official and tax term for the financial support of relatives; as a transitive する-verb: 家族を扶養する "to support one's family". It is very common in fixed combinations: 扶養家族 "dependent family members", 扶養控除 "dependent deduction" and 扶養に入る "to be covered as a dependent (of one's spouse) for insurance and tax purposes". In everyday conversation one rather says 養う or 面倒を見る; 扶養 sounds like forms, taxes and health insurance.

examples[].german: I will claim the medical expense deduction.
Social insurance premiums are deducted from your salary.
Is this expense eligible for a tax deduction?
en.notes: 控除 means the "deduction" of an amount, especially in tax and payroll matters. Typical are 控除を受ける "to claim a deduction" and the passive 給料から控除される "to be deducted from one's salary". Many fixed compounds: 基礎控除 "basic deduction", 扶養控除, 医療費控除. In everyday speech one rather says 引く or 差し引く for "to subtract"; 控除 is the technical term on pay slips and tax forms. Not to be confused with 控訴 "appeal (in court)".

examples[].german: The refund was transferred to my account.
If you file a tax return, you will get part of your taxes back.
Beware of scam calls about refunds.
en.notes: 還付 is the refund of money by a government office, above all of overpaid taxes: 税金が還付される, 還付を受ける, 還付金 "refund amount". For refunds in shops or for tickets one does not say 還付 but 返金 or 払い戻し. The word is formal and is encountered mainly with tax returns (確定申告) - and unfortunately also in scams (還付金詐欺) in which callers promise supposed refunds.

examples[].german: I am a member of a mutual aid association.
My house burned down in a fire, and I received the mutual-aid payout.
Mutual-aid premiums are often cheaper than insurance.
en.notes: 共済 literally means "helping together" and denotes mutual-benefit organizations run by cooperatives, unions or professional groups (e.g. for civil servants or farmers). In daily life this mostly means their insurance-like products: 共済に加入する "to join", 掛け金 "premium", 共済金 "benefit". Unlike 保険 (commercial insurance), 共済 is not profit-oriented and often cheaper. Do not confuse with the identically read 共催 "to co-host".

examples[].german: I save every month.
I'm investing regularly in an accumulation plan for my old age.
We're going on a graduation trip with the money the class saved up.
en.notes: 積立 (also written 積み立て) is the regular saving of money for a particular purpose; the related transitive verb is 積み立てる "to save up, set aside". Typical compounds: 積立預金 "savings plan", 積立金 "reserve fund", 積立投資 "fund savings plan". In compounds it is mostly written without okurigana (積立金), for the verb with it (積み立てる). 貯金 is saving in general or savings; 積立 emphasizes planned, repeated deposits.

examples[].german: I drew up a will.
My grandfather left the house to his grandchildren in his will.
"Take care of the family" were my father's last words.
en.notes: 遺言 is on the one hand a will, and on the other hand the "last wish" or last words of a dying person. Typical: 遺言を残す "to leave a will", 遺言書を書く/作成する, 遺言で〜を残す "to bequeath by will". The general reading is ゆいごん; lawyers say いごん. Do not confuse with 遺書 (a farewell letter, often before a suicide) and 遺産 "inheritance, estate".

examples[].german: Gift tax is levied.
I received a gift of land from my father.
To reduce inheritance tax, some people give their property to their children while still alive.
en.notes: 贈与 is the legal and tax term for the gift of property (money, land, shares): 贈与する, 贈与を受ける, 贈与税 "gift tax", 生前贈与 "gift during one's lifetime". For an ordinary present one says プレゼント or 贈り物, and for donations to organizations 寄付. 贈与 is thus encountered almost only in connection with inheritance, taxes and contracts.

examples[].german: I sold my watch at the pawnshop.
I was short of money, so I took my ring to the pawnshop.
If you don't repay the money by the deadline, the item becomes the pawnshop's.
en.notes: 質屋 is the pawnshop: 質 "pledge" (reading しち, not しつ) + 屋 "shop". One brings valuables and gets a loan for them: 〜を質に入れる or 質屋に入れる "to pawn". If one doesn't repay in time, the pledge is forfeited (質流れ). Many pawnshops today also buy items outright, so one can also "sell" something there. The word is somewhat old-fashioned; modern shops often advertise with 買取.

examples[].german: I took part in an antiques auction.
He couldn't pay the loan, and his house was put up for auction.
A painting by a famous artist was sold at auction for a high price.
en.notes: 競売 is an auction, especially a formal or court-ordered one: 競売にかける "to put up for auction", 競売にかけられる "to go under the hammer", 競売で落札する "to win at auction". In forced sales, lawyers also read the word けいばい. In daily life, especially online, one usually says オークション; at fish markets the auction is called せり. 競売 is rather written and news language.

examples[].german: Price fluctuations are severe.
Vegetable prices fluctuate greatly depending on the weather.
Cryptocurrencies carry the risk of price fluctuations, so caution is needed.
en.notes: 価格変動 is made up of 価格 "price" (formal) and 変動 "fluctuation, change", and is a term from economics and the news. Typical: 価格変動が大きい/激しい, 価格変動のリスク. For movement in one direction only, one says 値上がり (price rise) or 値下がり (price drop); the general price level is called 物価. In casual conversation one would rather say 値段がよく変わる.

examples[].german: It is difficult to predict the future.
Experts predict that prices will rise next year as well.
Children's behavior cannot be predicted.
en.notes: 予測する means "to predict, to forecast", usually on the basis of data or analysis: 売り上げを予測する, 〜と予測している. Often negated: 予測できない / 予測がつかない "unpredictable". 予想 is more general and also used for personal guesses (試合の結果を予想する); 予報 is specifically a weather forecast.

en.meaning: weak yen; depreciation of the yen
examples[].german: Imports have become more expensive because of the weak yen.
As the yen weakens, the number of tourists from abroad is increasing.
A weak yen is advantageous for export companies.
en.notes: 円安 literally means "yen cheap" and describes a weak yen relative to other currencies. Typical: 円安になる, 円安が進む "the yen weakens further", 円安の影響. The opposite is 円高. A weak yen makes imports and foreign travel more expensive, but helps export firms and lures tourists to Japan. The word is equally familiar in the news and in everyday conversation.

en.meaning: strong yen; appreciation of the yen
examples[].german: Because of the strong yen, overseas travel is getting cheaper.
The continued strong yen reduced the profits of export companies.
There was also an era of a strong yen, with one dollar at 80 yen.
en.notes: 円高 literally means "yen high": the yen is strong, and one yen buys a lot of foreign currency. Typical: 円高になる, 円高が進む, 円高が続く. The opposite is 円安. A strong yen makes foreign travel and imports cheaper, but hurts export firms. The word is heard constantly in business news, but also in daily life, for example when traveling or shopping online abroad.

examples[].german: Stock prices fell.
After the announcement of a new product, the company's stock price rose sharply.
I check stock prices in the news every morning.
en.notes: 株価 is the stock price (株 "share" + 価 "price"). It rises or falls: 株価が上がる/下がる, in the news 株価が上昇する/下落する, in a crash 株価が暴落する. The best-known index is the 日経平均株価. Do not confuse with 物価 "price level, cost of living"; 株 alone denotes the share or shares as an investment (株を買う).

examples[].german: I received dividends.
This company pays a dividend to its shareholders every year.
I won at the horse race, but the payout was small.
en.notes: 配当 first means "allotment", but in daily life mainly the dividend of a joint-stock company: 配当を出す "to pay a dividend", 配当を受け取る, 配当金, 高配当株 "high-dividend stock". At horse races and lotteries, 配当 is the payout per stake. For interest on savings one says 利息 or 利子, and for the distribution of resources in general 配分.

examples[].german: I filed for personal bankruptcy.
His debts grew from gambling, and he went bankrupt.
The company went under last year and entered bankruptcy proceedings.
en.notes: 破産 is bankruptcy or insolvency in the legal sense, for private individuals as well as firms; as an intransitive する-verb: 破産する "to go bankrupt". Important are 自己破産 "personal bankruptcy (self-filed)" and 破産手続き "bankruptcy proceedings". 倒産 is said only of companies and means economic failure in general; 破産 is the court procedure. Colloquially one also says つぶれる.

examples[].german: The debts are large.
The company went bankrupt with liabilities of about one billion yen.
A home loan is also a kind of liability.
en.notes: 負債 is the formal expression for debts or liabilities, typical in balance sheets, business news and bankruptcies: 負債を抱える "to carry debts", 負債総額 "total liabilities". In everyday life one almost always says 借金; 負債 sounds like bookkeeping and companies. Its counterpart on the balance sheet is 資産 "assets".

examples[].german: I collect the debt.
The creditors came to the company and demanded repayment.
The bank sold the claim on the loan it made to another company.
en.notes: 債権 is a claim, that is, the right to demand money or a service from someone: 債権を回収する "to collect a claim", 債権者 "creditor". The opposite is 債務 "liability, debt" or 債務者 "debtor". Note: the identically read 債券 means "bond, security" - that is a different word. Both are legal and financial technical terms.

examples[].german: I put up real estate as collateral.
Loans that can be borrowed without collateral have high interest rates.
This system guarantees the safety of users.
en.notes: 担保 is the security for a loan: 〜を担保に入れる / 担保にする "to put up as collateral", 〜を担保に借りる, 担保を取る (the bank demands security), 無担保 "without collateral". In business and government jargon, 担保する additionally means "to ensure, to guarantee": 安全を担保する. For a personal guarantee one says 保証, and for a pledge at a pawnshop 質.

examples[].german: I am behind on my rent.
When I was three months behind on the electricity bill, my power was cut off.
If you are behind on your taxes, you will be charged late fees.
en.notes: 滞納 means being in arrears on a payment that is due: rent, taxes, fees, insurance premiums. As a transitive する-verb: 家賃を滞納する; also 税金の滞納, 滞納者 "delinquent payer". The tone is formal and official; in everyday speech one would rather say 払うのが遅れる or まだ払っていない. 未払い only stresses that something is unpaid, whereas 滞納 stresses that the deadline has already passed.

examples[].german: A reminder notice arrived.
I got a phone call from the card company urging payment.
The city hall is urging people who haven't paid their taxes to pay.
en.notes: 督促 is a formal demand to fulfill an obligation - almost always a payment reminder from authorities, banks or companies: 支払いを督促する, 督促を受ける, 督促状 "reminder letter". The similar 催促 is more everyday and also common among private individuals (返事を催促する "to press for a reply"). 督促 sounds official and strict.

examples[].german: I will estimate the amount of damage.
This temple is estimated to have been built about 800 years ago.
The police estimate the man's age at about forty.
en.notes: 推定する means "to estimate, to presume (on the basis of evidence)". Typical in news and science, often in the passive: 〜と推定される "it is estimated that …", for example for age, damage or time. 推測 is rather a conjecture without firm grounds, and 見積もる is estimating costs (a cost estimate). Also well known is 推定無罪 "presumption of innocence".

examples[].german: My property was seized.
If you don't pay your taxes, your wages may be garnished.
The police seized the computer as evidence in the case.
en.notes: 差し押さえ is seizure or attachment by a court, tax office or police. The related transitive verb is 差し押さえる; those affected appear in the passive: 財産を差し押さえられる. Typical objects: 給料, 口座, 家, 証拠品. In official texts also written without okurigana as 差押え or 差押. A synonym from criminal matters is 押収 "seizure of evidence".

examples[].german: I filed a lawsuit.
The lawsuit has been going on for three years.
I would like to settle this by talking before it turns into a lawsuit.
en.notes: 訴訟 is a lawsuit or legal action in the legal sense: 訴訟を起こす "to bring a lawsuit", 訴訟に勝つ/負ける, 民事訴訟 "civil lawsuit". In conversation one would rather say 裁判 "trial" or the verb 訴える "to sue"; 訴訟 sounds like the news and a law firm. As a する-verb it is intransitive, but it is rarely used that way.

examples[].german: I filed an appeal.
The defendant, dissatisfied with the verdict, appealed.
On appeal, the first-instance judgment was overturned.
en.notes: 控訴 is the appeal against a first-instance judgment to a higher court; as an intransitive する-verb: 控訴する "to appeal". Typical: 判決を不服として控訴する, 控訴審 "appeal trial", 控訴を棄却する "to dismiss the appeal". The next stage to the Supreme Court is 上告; the umbrella term for both is 上訴. Do not confuse with 控除 "deduction, allowance".

examples[].german: The statute of limitations has run out.
The statute of limitations for murder has been abolished.
It's long past the statute of limitations, so I can say it: I'm the one who broke that vase.
en.notes: 時効 is the statute of limitations: 時効が成立する, 時効になる, 時効を迎える "to become time-barred"; 時効が成立した事件 "a time-barred case". Colloquially it is used jokingly in a figurative sense: もう時効だから言うけど "it's long past the statute of limitations, so I can say it" - with it one admits old secrets or mishaps. Unlike 期限 "deadline", 時効 emphasizes that a claim or prosecution lapses through the passage of time.

examples[].german: The matter was settled out of court.
An out-of-court settlement was reached with the other party in the traffic accident.
The insurance company conducted the settlement negotiations for me.
en.notes: 示談 is the out-of-court settlement between the parties, typically after traffic accidents or minor offenses: 示談にする, 示談が成立する, 示談で解決する/済ませる, 示談金 "settlement money", 示談交渉 (often conducted by the insurance company). As an intransitive する-verb: 相手と示談する. 和解 is the more general term for compromise/reconciliation and can also occur in court.

examples[].german: I am demanding damages.
Because of the construction noise, the residents demanded damages from the company.
The court ordered the company to pay 100 million yen in damages.
en.notes: 損害賠償 is made up of 損害 "damage" and 賠償 "compensation" and is the legal term for damages: 損害賠償を請求する/求める, 損害賠償を支払う, 損害賠償責任 "liability". When you break something in everyday life and pay for it, you say 弁償する. 慰謝料 is the portion for emotional suffering, and 補償 is compensation without fault of one's own (e.g. from the state).

examples[].german: I am researching elementary particle physics.
The electron is one of the elementary particles.
A Japanese person won the Nobel Prize for research on a particle called the neutrino.
en.notes: 素粒子 is a technical term of physics: 素 "basic, element" + 粒子 "particle". It refers to particles that cannot be broken down further, e.g. electron, quark or neutrino; the discipline is called 素粒子物理学. By comparison, 原子 "atom" and 分子 "molecule" are larger units, and 粒子 alone is any small particle (including dust). The word is encountered in science news and popular science texts.

examples[].german: Plants carry out photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis requires light, water and carbon dioxide.
In a room that gets no sunlight, this plant cannot photosynthesize and withers.
en.notes: 光合成 (光 "light" + 合成 "synthesis") is photosynthesis, a school term from biology. One says 光合成をする/行う or 光合成によって〜を作る; in the process plants take in 二酸化炭素 and release 酸素. Its counterpart in class is 呼吸 "respiration". The word is neutral and part of the basic vocabulary of natural science and environmental topics.

examples[].german: I discovered a dinosaur fossil.
We need to reduce fossil fuels such as oil and coal.
The coelacanth is called a "living fossil".
en.notes: 化石 is a fossil (literally "something turned to stone"): 化石が見つかる / 化石を発見する, 恐竜の化石. Important compounds are 化石燃料 "fossil fuels" and 生きた化石 "living fossil". In colloquial speech, completely outdated things or views are also jokingly called 化石. The meaning "to fossilize" as a する-verb is rare.

examples[].german: I will measure the temperature.
We measured the noise level in the room.
In April, height and weight are measured at school.
en.notes: 測定する means "to measure (with instruments)" and sounds technical: 温度・距離・騒音を測定する, 測定値 "measured value". In everyday speech one usually says 測る (length, temperature), 計る (time) or 量る (weight). At school there are 身体測定 (measuring height and weight) and 体力測定 (fitness test).

examples[].german: We are surveying the strata.
At this cliff you can see strata formed over tens of thousands of years.
Shell fossils were found in an old stratum.
en.notes: 地層 is a geological layer in the ground or rock, as seen on steep slopes or in excavation pits: 地層を観察する/調べる, 地層ができる, 地層が重なる. Fossils (化石) are often recovered from 地層. For any layer one says 層 in general, e.g. オゾン層; 断層, by contrast, is a fault, that is, a break between layers. A typical school and technical term.

examples[].german: I toured the limestone cave.
Inside the limestone cave, it is cool even in summer.
A limestone cave is formed by rainwater dissolving rock over a long time.
en.notes: 鍾乳洞 is a stalactite cave: 鍾乳 stands for the dripstones (鍾乳石 "stalactite"), 洞 for "cave". In Japan such caves are popular excursion destinations; one says 鍾乳洞を見学する/探検する, 鍾乳洞に入る. Since 鍾 is not an everyday character, signs often read しょうにゅう洞. A cave in general is called 洞窟 or 洞穴.

examples[].german: Lava is flowing.
When underground magma comes to the surface, it is called lava.
The black rocks on this island are lava that cooled and hardened.
en.notes: 溶岩 (溶 "melt" + 岩 "rock") is lava, i.e. molten rock at the surface; underground it is called マグマ. Typical: 溶岩が流れる/流れ出す, 溶岩流 "lava flow", 溶岩が冷えて固まる. Solidified lava forms entire landscapes in Japan, e.g. at Fuji or Sakurajima. A neutral word from geography and news about volcanic eruptions.

examples[].german: Volcanic ash fell.
Near Sakurajima, volcanic ash often gets on the laundry.
Flights were canceled because of the volcanic ash.
en.notes: 火山灰 is volcanic ash; note the reading with voicing (rendaku): かざん + はい → かざんばい. Typical: 火山灰が降る "ash rains down", 火山灰が積もる, 火山灰の影響で欠航する. In the news, ashfall is also called 降灰. In places like Kagoshima, volcanic ash is part of daily life - on cars, laundry and streets.

examples[].german: The geyser erupted.
This geyser shoots up hot water about every ten minutes.
I went to see the famous geysers in Iceland.
en.notes: 間欠泉 is a geyser: 間欠 "at intervals, periodically" + 泉 "spring". Typical verbs are 噴き出す and 噴き上げる; one says, for example, 〇分ごとにお湯を噴き上げる. Occasionally it is also written 間歇泉. An ordinary hot bath or thermal spring, by contrast, is an 温泉. The word is encountered mainly in travel and nature texts.

examples[].german: Please don't build your house on an active fault.
This earthquake was caused by a shift along a fault.
There is a gap in thinking between the generation of the parents and that of the children.
en.notes: 断層 in geology is a fault, that is, a break in the earth's crust along which rock layers shift against each other: 断層がずれる/動く. Particularly important in Japan is 活断層 "active fault", which can trigger earthquakes. In the figurative, written-language sense, 断層 means a "gap" between groups, such as 世代間の断層. Do not confuse with 地層 "stratum".

en.meaning: epicenter; hypocenter; focus of an earthquake
examples[].german: The focus of the earthquake was on the seabed.
The focus of the earthquake is about ten kilometers deep.
In towns near the epicenter, many houses were destroyed.
en.notes: 震源 is strictly speaking the earthquake's focus (hypocenter) inside the earth; the point directly above it on the surface is called 震央 "epicenter". In Japanese earthquake reports one constantly hears 震源は〇〇沖 "the focus is off the coast of ..." and 震源の深さは〇キロ. Figuratively, 震源 also denotes the origin of rumors or unrest (うわさの震源).

examples[].german: There was an earthquake of intensity 5.
Intensity 4 was recorded in Tokyo.
A quake has only one magnitude, but its intensity differs by location.
en.notes: 震度 is the shaking intensity on the Japanese scale (0 to 7, with 5弱/5強 and 6弱/6強) and indicates how strongly the ground shakes at a particular place. Typical: 震度〇を観測する, 最大震度, 震度〇の地震. The energy released by the quake itself, by contrast, is the マグニチュード: a quake has one magnitude, but at each place a different 震度. In the news, the numbers are mostly written in Arabic numerals.

examples[].german: Please watch out for aftershocks.
After the big earthquake, aftershocks continued for about a week.
I was afraid of aftershocks and couldn't sleep well last night.
en.notes: 余震 (余 "remaining, after-" + 震 "quake") are aftershocks following a larger earthquake. Typical: 余震が続く, 余震に注意する/警戒する, 大きな余震. The main shock is called 本震, a foreshock 前震. After strong quakes, authorities and media warn for days with 余震に注意してください.

examples[].german: Liquefaction occurred because of the earthquake.
On reclaimed land, the ground liquefies easily.
Before buying a house, I checked the risk of liquefaction.
en.notes: 液状化 (液状 "liquid state" + 化 "becoming") refers mainly to soil liquefaction during earthquakes: water-saturated, sandy ground loses its firmness, houses sink, and sand and water well up. As an intransitive する-verb: 地盤が液状化する; also 液状化現象 and 液状化が起きる. Reclaimed land (埋め立て地) is especially at risk.

examples[].german: I observe animals.
During summer vacation, I observed morning glories every day and wrote a diary.
I like observing people's behavior.
en.notes: 観察する means "to observe attentively", usually over a longer period, in order to learn or understand something: 植物・動物・様子を観察する. Japanese elementary school children often keep an observation diary (観察日記) during vacations. 観測 is scientific observation with measurements (weather, stars), 監視 is surveillance. Simply "looking at" is just 見る.

examples[].german: We carried out seismic retrofitting.
This building was built to old seismic standards.
When looking for a room, it's better to check the earthquake resistance too.
en.notes: 耐震 (耐 "to withstand" + 震 "quake") means "earthquake-proof" and almost always stands as a modifier before other nouns: 耐震構造 "earthquake-resistant construction", 耐震基準 "seismic building code", 耐震工事 "seismic retrofitting", 耐震性 "earthquake resistance". More rarely with の: 耐震の建物. Related are 免震 (base isolation, the building is decoupled from the ground) and 制震 (vibration damping). An important term when looking for housing and buying a house.

examples[].german: I went to the evacuation shelter.
A nearby elementary school serves as an evacuation shelter.
After the earthquake, I lived in an evacuation shelter for a month.
en.notes: 避難所 (避難 "evacuation, flight" + 所 "place", read here as じょ) is the emergency shelter where people live temporarily after a disaster, usually school gymnasiums or community centers. Typical: 避難所に避難する/行く, 避難所で生活する, 指定避難所 "designated shelter". To be distinguished from this is 避難場所, an open gathering place (park, square) where people only briefly get to safety.

examples[].german: I keep stockpiles of food.
Let's stock up on three days' worth of water for each family member.
The government decided to release rice from its stockpile onto the market.
en.notes: 備蓄 is the planned building up of supplies for emergencies; as a transitive する-verb: 食料/水を備蓄する. Also 備蓄品 "emergency supplies", 備蓄米 "government rice reserve", 石油の備蓄. In contrast to 買いだめ, the (often panicky) hoarding, 備蓄 sounds sensible and forward-looking. The word is slightly formal and typical of disaster prevention and politics.

examples[].german: We will send relief supplies.
The Self-Defense Forces headed to the disaster area for relief work.
Since the pitcher was hit hard, a relief pitcher came out.
en.notes: 救援 is organized help for people in need, especially after disasters: 救援物資 "relief supplies", 救援活動 "relief operation", 救援隊 "relief team", 救援に向かう/駆けつける. 救助, on the other hand, means the direct rescue of people from mortal danger (人命救助), and 支援 means "support" in general. In baseball, 救援投手 is the reliever who steps in for the starter.

examples[].german: I donated money for disaster victims.
Money for earthquake victims is being collected in front of the station.
The donations collected from all over the country were distributed to the victims.
en.notes: 義援金 is donation money for victims of disasters or accidents, which is distributed directly to those affected, e.g. through the Red Cross: 義援金を送る/寄付する/集める, 義援金が集まる. The original spelling is 義捐金. 寄付金 is the general term for donations; 募金 refers to the collecting itself (fundraising drive, collection box). The word is neutral-formal and appears in the news after every major earthquake.

examples[].german: I'm living in temporary housing.
We left the shelter and moved into temporary housing.
The walls of temporary housing are thin, and it's very cold in winter.
en.notes: 仮設住宅 (仮設 "provisionally built" + 住宅 "housing") is temporary housing built after disasters for people whose homes were destroyed. The usual sequence is 避難所 → 仮設住宅 → 復興住宅 (permanent housing). Typical: 仮設住宅に入居する/移る, 仮設住宅で暮らす; those affected often say just 仮設.

examples[].german: We clear the rubble.
A dog was rescued from under the rubble of a house that collapsed in the earthquake.
After the tsunami, the town was nothing but a heap of rubble.
en.notes: 瓦礫 (瓦 "roof tile" + 礫 "pebble") is rubble and debris, for example after earthquakes, tsunamis or demolition. Since 礫 is not a Jōyō kanji, it is mostly written がれき. Typical: がれきを撤去する/片付ける, がれきの山, がれきの下敷きになる "to be buried under rubble". Figuratively it also means "worthless junk", but that is rare.

examples[].german: We are searching for the missing persons.
A friend who went mountain climbing has gone missing.
My house key is missing, and I've been looking for it since morning.
en.notes: 行方不明 means "missing, lost, whereabouts unknown"; 行方 has the special reading ゆくえ "whereabouts". Typical: 行方不明になる, 行方不明者 "missing persons", 行方不明の子ども. A child who has lost their way, by contrast, is a 迷子. Jokingly it is also said of misplaced objects: 鍵が行方不明. In serious cases it is a word from police and disaster reports.

en.meaning: safety check; confirming that someone is safe
examples[].german: We are checking whether everyone is safe.
After the earthquake, I received an email from the company checking whether I was safe.
The phone lines were down, and I couldn't confirm whether my family was safe.
en.notes: 安否確認 means "checking whether someone is safe and well": 安否 = "whether someone is safe or not" (安 "safe", 否 "not"), 確認 = "confirmation". After earthquakes, companies and schools inquire by email or app (安否確認メール, 安否確認システム); one says 家族の安否確認をする or 家族の安否を確認する. 安否が分からない means "one doesn't know whether someone is alive".

en.meaning: stranded commuters; people unable to return home
examples[].german: Many commuters were stranded.
A hall near the station was opened for stranded commuters.
In case we can't get home, we keep water and food at the company.
en.notes: 帰宅困難者 (帰宅 "return home" + 困難 "difficulty" + 者 "person") are people who cannot get home after an earthquake or a breakdown of public transport. The word became well known through the millions of stranded commuters in Tokyo in March 2011. Typical: 帰宅困難者が出る/発生する, 帰宅困難者向けの施設. In the media one also reads the more colloquial 帰宅難民.

examples[].german: I'll test through an experiment whether the new method is effective.
In science class, we did an experiment using water.
As a result of experiments on mice, the effect of the drug was confirmed.
en.notes: 実験する means "to carry out an experiment, to experiment". It often appears as 実験をする, with で for the material or test subject (マウスで実験する), or as 〜かどうか実験する "to test whether ...". For simple trying out in daily life, 試す is rather said. Related: 実験室 "laboratory", 実験的 "experimental".

examples[].german: Lifelines were cut off.
After the earthquake, it took a week for utilities to be restored.
Before moving, let's take care of the utility procedures.
en.notes: In Japanese, ライフライン refers above all to vital basic services: electricity, gas and water, often also telephone, internet and transport. The disaster context is typical: ライフラインが止まる／寸断される "are cut off, are disrupted", ライフラインが復旧する "are restored". When moving, too, people talk about ライフラインの手続き (starting and stopping electricity, gas and water). The English meaning "rescue line" is rare; for that one says 命綱.

examples[].german: I'm researching robotics.
I want to major in robotics at university.
My brother uses his knowledge of robotics to build care robots.
en.notes: ロボット工学 is the technical term for "robotics" as a scientific and engineering discipline; 工学 means "engineering" (cf. 機械工学, 電子工学). Typical: ロボット工学を学ぶ／専攻する／研究する, ロボット工学の専門家. In specialist circles one also hears the loan form ロボティクス. The machines themselves are simply called ロボット; ロボット工学 always means the field of study.

examples[].german: Self-driving cars are increasing.
This subway is run automatically, so there is no driver.
If self-driving technology advances, even elderly people can go out with peace of mind.
en.notes: 自動運転 denotes automatic operation without human intervention, today above all "autonomous driving" of cars. Typical: 自動運転の車／自動運転車, 自動運転の技術, 自動運転で走る. 運転 means "driving, operating" here, so the word can also apply to trains and machines (自動運転の電車). The opposite is 手動運転; mere driver-assistance systems are called 運転支援.

examples[].german: I'm investing in cryptocurrency.
The price of cryptocurrencies can change greatly in a single day.
I saw in the news that a crypto exchange was hacked.
en.notes: 仮想通貨 ("virtual currency") is the word long customary in Japan for cryptocurrencies such as ビットコイン. Laws and authorities have officially used 暗号資産 since 2020, but 仮想通貨 is still very widespread in the media and daily life. Typical: 仮想通貨に投資する, 仮想通貨を買う／売る, 仮想通貨の取引所 "crypto exchange". Do not confuse with 電子マネー - that is ordinary yen balance on a card or in a smartphone.

examples[].german: Electronic payment is becoming widespread.
This shop doesn't accept electronic payment, so please pay in cash.
With smartphone payment, you can shop without taking out your wallet.
en.notes: 電子決済 is the umbrella term for cashless, electronic payment - by credit card, IC card such as Suica, or QR-code payment with a smartphone. 決済 is a rather formal word for "settling a payment"; in daily life one therefore often hears キャッシュレス決済 or simply キャッシュレス. Typical: 電子決済に対応している "accepts electronic payment", 電子決済で払う, 電子決済が普及する. The counterpart is 現金払い "cash payment".

examples[].german: I move the robot by remote control.
I can control the air conditioner remotely with my phone, so I can cool the room before I get home.
My computer was infected with a virus and was being remotely controlled by someone.
en.notes: 遠隔操作 means "remote control" of machines, robots or computers from a distance; 遠隔 means "distant" (cf. 遠隔授業 "distance learning"). As a transitive する-verb: ドローンを遠隔操作する; often instrumental with で: 遠隔操作で動かす. The device for remote operation of the TV, by contrast, is called リモコン, and in IT, for remote access, one also says リモート操作. A neutral, rather technical word.

examples[].german: I work from home.
At our company, you can work from home twice a week.
Since I started working from home, I no longer spend time commuting, and it's easier.
en.notes: 在宅勤務 literally means "duty at home" and is the neutral word for employees' home office. Typical: 在宅勤務をする, 在宅勤務になる, 週に二日在宅勤務する. Almost synonymous and very common in daily life are テレワーク and リモートワーク; 在宅勤務 sounds somewhat more official and explicitly means one's own home. Someone who works independently at home says rather 在宅で仕事をしている.

examples[].german: Staggered commuting is permitted.
I commute at off-peak hours to avoid crowded trains.
Starting next month, staggered commuting begins, and I will be allowed to arrive at the office at ten.
en.notes: 時差出勤 refers to a staggered work start: you travel to work earlier or later than rush hour in order to avoid crowded trains. 時差 is otherwise known as the "time difference" between time zones; here it means "offset in time", and 出勤 means "to go to work". Typical: 時差出勤をする／時差出勤する, 時差出勤を導入する, 時差出勤が認められる. Unlike フレックスタイム "flextime", usually only the start time is shifted and the working hours stay the same.

examples[].german: I started a side job.
Side jobs are prohibited at our company.
On weekends I do web design work on the side.
en.notes: 副業 is a secondary activity alongside one's main occupation (本業) - such as a side job, freelance assignments or a small online business. Typical: 副業をする／始める, 副業で稼ぐ, 副業が禁止されている／認められている; many Japanese companies long prohibited side jobs, and that is changing now. A student's part-time job, by contrast, is アルバイト, because 副業 presupposes a main occupation. Somewhat more casual and synonymous is サイドビジネス.

en.meaning: to quit a salaryman job (to go independent)
examples[].german: I quit my office job and started farming.
At fifty, my father quit his salaried job and opened a ramen shop.
I want to leave the salaried life, but I'm afraid of losing my income.
en.notes: 脱サラ is an abbreviation of 脱 "to break away from" and サラ(リーマン) "salaried employee": one quits a steady employee job to become self-employed, for example with a shop, a farm or one's own business. Almost always used as a する-verb: 脱サラして店を開く, 脱サラした人. The word is casual, but perfectly normal in conversation and the media. Merely switching to another company is 転職, not 脱サラ.

examples[].german: I proved my ability.
Do you have something that can prove your identity?
I proved by experiment that this theory is correct.
en.notes: 証明する means "to prove, to demonstrate" a fact, theory or ability: 〜ことを証明する, 力を証明する. It also means "to certify (officially)": 身分を証明する "to identify oneself", 証明書 "certificate, proof". Do not confuse it with 説明する "to explain" and the identically read 照明 "lighting".

examples[].german: I value work-life balance.
I work a lot of overtime and don't have a good work-life balance.
When changing jobs, I put work-life balance above salary.
en.notes: ワークライフバランス is the English loanword for the balance between work and private life; it is also written ワーク・ライフ・バランス. Typical: ワークライフバランスを大切にする／重視する, ワークライフバランスが取れている "is balanced", ワークライフバランスを改善する. The word often comes up together with 残業 "overtime" and 働き方改革 "work style reform". The Japanese equivalent 仕事と生活の調和 is found mainly in government texts.

examples[].german: I took childcare leave.
My husband has also decided to take three months of childcare leave.
When my childcare leave ends, I plan to return to the same department.
en.notes: 育児休暇 is parental leave for caring for a small child; colloquially it is almost always shortened to 育休. Legally it is actually called 育児休業, and in everyday life the two words are interchangeable. Typical: 育児休暇を取る／取得する, 育休中, 育休から復帰する "to return from parental leave". Maternity leave before and after the birth, by contrast, is called 産休.

examples[].german: The problem of children on daycare waiting lists is serious.
This city is building more daycare centers so that no child has to wait for a place.
My daughter ended up on the waiting list, so I can't go back to work.
en.notes: 待機児童 are children who are registered for a daycare center (保育園) but, due to lack of space, get no place and have to "wait" (待機). The word is known mainly from politics and the news, mostly as 待機児童問題. Typical: 待機児童が多い／減る, 待機児童をゼロにする, 待機児童になる. About one's own child one also says 待機児童になる or simply 保育園に入れない.

examples[].german: The aging of society is progressing.
Because of the low birthrate and aging population, there is a growing shortage of workers.
I have to write a report on the declining birthrate and aging population.
en.notes: 少子高齢化 combines two processes: 少子化 "falling birth numbers" and 高齢化 "aging of the population"; together it describes Japan's demographic change. Typical: 少子高齢化が進む, 少子高齢化社会, 少子高齢化による人手不足. It is a word from the news, politics and essays, but also fits conversations about society. The individual words 少子化 and 高齢化 likewise go with 進む.

examples[].german: The overcrowding of cities is a problem.
Next week my schedule is packed with meetings and a business trip.
The train timetable in Tokyo in the morning is extremely dense.
en.notes: 過密 means "too dense": too many people, buildings or appointments in too little space or too short a time. As a noun it often stands in contrast to 過疎 "depopulation" (都市の過密と地方の過疎); as a な-adjective mainly in 過密なスケジュール or 過密ダイヤ "tightly packed timetable". For a full train or shop, everyday speech uses 混んでいる or 混雑; 過密 is more matter-of-fact and sounds like planning, statistics and the news.

en.meaning: marginal village; village on the verge of extinction
examples[].german: We are revitalizing marginal villages.
The village where my grandmother lives has no young people and has become a marginal village.
In marginal villages, even the bus is gone and shopping is difficult.
en.notes: 限界集落 is a sociological term for villages in which more than half of the inhabitants are 65 or older, so that community life can hardly be maintained any more. It belongs to the topic area of 過疎 "depopulation" and 少子高齢化. Typical: 限界集落になる, 限界集落を活性化する／支援する. 集落 itself is a rather formal word for "settlement, hamlet"; the whole sounds factual and news-like.

examples[].german: I took part in the Community Revitalization Cooperator program.
We are revitalizing the region with dishes made from local vegetables.
To revitalize the region, vacant houses are rented cheaply to young people.
en.notes: 地域おこし is the revival of a region - through tourism, local products, events or the arrival of young people. おこし comes from 起こす "to awaken, to set in motion" and is usually written in hiragana. Well known is the government program 地域おこし協力隊, in which city dwellers move to the countryside for a few years. Almost synonymous are 町おこし (town) and 村おこし (village); more formal is 地域活性化.

examples[].german: We are holding a town revitalization event.
This town succeeded in revitalizing itself by becoming the setting of an anime.
To revitalize the town, the shopkeepers of the shopping street came up with a new local specialty dish.
en.notes: 町おこし means breathing new life into a town or community, e.g. with festivals, mascots (ゆるキャラ), regional specialties or anime settings. It is also written 町興し or まちおこし; おこし comes from 起こす. Typical: 町おこしをする, 町おこしのイベント, 町おこしに成功する. Compared with 地域おこし, the focus is smaller (one town instead of a whole region); for villages one says 村おこし.

examples[].german: We make use of tourism resources.
This prefecture is rich in tourism resources such as hot springs and the sea.
The old streetscape is also one of the important tourism assets.
en.notes: 観光資源 are all the things that can attract tourists: scenery, hot springs, temples, festivals or regional cuisine. 資源 actually means "resource, raw material", so the word sounds planning-oriented and economic and appears mainly with government offices, in the tourism industry and in the news. Typical: 観光資源を活用する／生かす, 観光資源が豊富だ, 豊かな観光資源. For individual sights one says 観光地 or 名所 in daily life.

examples[].german: It was registered as a World Heritage site.
In the summer vacation, I want to go to Yakushima, a World Heritage site.
Since it became a World Heritage site, the number of tourists has suddenly increased.
en.notes: 世界遺産 is a UNESCO World Heritage site and includes both cultural heritage (文化遺産) such as 姫路城 and natural heritage (自然遺産) such as 屋久島. Typical: 世界遺産に登録される "to be inscribed on the World Heritage List", 世界遺産に選ばれる, 世界遺産を訪ねる／巡る. Intangible heritage such as 和食 is not called 世界遺産 but 無形文化遺産. A neutral, very common word from travel guides and the news.

examples[].german: I discovered a new star.
The cancer was detected at an early stage in a health checkup.
When I travel, I always make new discoveries.
en.notes: 発見する means "to discover": to find something previously unknown (新しい星, 遺跡) or to detect something hidden (病気の早期発見 "early detection"). For everyday things such as lost keys, people say 見つける. 発明する, by contrast, is "to invent", that is, to create something new. As a noun: 新しい発見がある "to make a new discovery".

examples[].german: It was designated an intangible cultural property.
The traditional dance of this village is an intangible cultural property of the prefecture.
My grandfather passes on the techniques of an intangible cultural property to young craftsmen.
en.notes: 無形文化財 ("formless cultural property") is a term from Japanese cultural property protection for intangible cultural assets such as theater, music and craft techniques, e.g. 能, 歌舞伎 or lacquer art.
