A person recognized as a holder of an 重要無形文化財 is popularly called 人間国宝. Typical: 無形文化財に指定される, 県の無形文化財, 重要無形文化財. The UNESCO list, by contrast, is called 無形文化遺産; the counterpart for buildings and objects is 有形文化財.

examples[].german: I saw the work of a living national treasure.
That ceramic artist was certified as a living national treasure last year.
I learned how to dye kimono directly from a teacher who is a living national treasure.
en.notes: 人間国宝 ("living national treasure") is the popular name for persons whom the state has recognized as holders of an 重要無形文化財 - masters of, for example, pottery, dyeing, 能 or 歌舞伎. The official title is 重要無形文化財保持者, but in the news and daily life one almost always says 人間国宝. Typical: 人間国宝に認定される, 人間国宝の作品, 人間国宝の職人. It always refers to a person; an object or building is a 国宝.

en.meaning: scenic spot; place of scenic beauty
examples[].german: I visited a scenic spot.
This garden is designated as a Special Place of Scenic Beauty of the nation.
Kyoto has many scenic spots, and you can't see them all in one day.
en.notes: 名勝 is a place famous for its beautiful scenery; in cultural property protection it is also an official category (国の名勝, 特別名勝) for gardens, gorges or coastal landscapes. The word is rather literary and is encountered on signs, in guidebooks and in 名勝地. In conversation, one mostly says 名所 or 景色のいい所; 名所 is more general and also includes buildings or cherry-blossom spots (桜の名所), while 名勝 emphasizes the landscape.

examples[].german: I visited a historic site.
On the weekend, I took a bike tour of the town's historic sites.
This castle ruin is designated a national historic site.
en.notes: 史跡 is a historic site: a place where something historical happened or where remains of it are preserved, such as castle ruins, ancient burial mounds or battlefields. It is also an official category in cultural property protection (国の史跡, 特別史跡). Typical: 史跡を見学する, 史跡めぐり "tour of historic sites", 史跡に指定される. Unlike 名勝 (scenic beauty), it is about history; a building that is still standing is rather called 歴史的建造物.

examples[].german: I do community service activities.
I want to contribute to society through my work.
This company donates part of its sales and thus contributes to society.
en.notes: 社会貢献 is a "contribution to society" - through volunteer work, donations or the social engagement of companies (企業の社会貢献, roughly corresponding to CSR). Typical: 社会貢献をする, 社会貢献活動, 社会貢献につながる. As a verb one uses 貢献する with に: 社会に貢献する. The word is neutral to formal and often appears in job interviews, applications and corporate mission statements.

examples[].german: I will take part in community service.
On Sunday morning, I picked up trash in the neighborhood park as community service.
At our high school, there is community service once a year.
en.notes: 奉仕活動 is unpaid work for the community, such as picking up trash, park maintenance or helping at a nursing home. 奉仕 means "to serve" and sounds somewhat formal and traditional; you often hear it in schools, where students do 奉仕活動 as part of class, as well as in clubs and religious communities. In general usage, ボランティア and ボランティア活動 are more common and more casual. Typical: 奉仕活動に参加する, 奉仕活動をする, 地域の奉仕活動.

examples[].german: We are doing a fundraising drive on the street.
We collected donations in front of the station for people in trouble because of the earthquake.
I donated my change to the box next to the convenience store register.
en.notes: 募金 primarily means collecting donations (募 "to call for, to collect" + 金 "money"): 募金活動 "fundraising drive", 街頭募金 "street fundraising", 募金を集める, 募金箱 "donation box". Colloquially, however, 募金する is also used in the sense of "to donate (into a collection box)": おつりを募金する. Larger or formal donations to organizations are rather called 寄付 (寄付する). The word is heard very often especially after natural disasters.

examples[].german: I applied for public assistance.
I became unable to work because of illness, and I am receiving public assistance.
The number of people receiving public assistance is increasing year by year.
en.notes: 生活保護 is Japan's state social assistance, which secures a minimum standard of living for people without sufficient income. Typical: 生活保護を受ける "to receive public assistance", 生活保護を申請する, 生活保護費 "welfare benefits", 生活保護世帯. Unemployment benefit is something different (colloquially 失業保険, officially from 雇用保険), as is the pension (年金). The topic carries a certain stigma in Japan, so people tend to talk about it with restraint.

examples[].german: We protect the rights of people with disabilities.
Elevators in stations are important for people with disabilities and the elderly.
This company is focusing on employing people with disabilities.
en.notes: 障害者 is the standard word for "person with a disability" in laws, government offices and the news: 障害者手帳 "disability certificate", 障害者用トイレ, 身体障害者. Because the character 害 "harm" has a negative effect, many government offices and media write 障がい者, more rarely 障碍者. In polite conversation about a particular person, one prefers to say 障害のある方 or 体の不自由な方. 障害 alone can also mean "obstacle, disruption" (通信障害 "network outage").

examples[].german: I invented a new device.
It was a Japanese person who invented instant cup noodles.
When I was a child, I wanted to invent a machine that flies through the sky.
en.notes: 発明する means "to invent": to create technically something new that did not exist before: 機械・道具を発明する. Related: 発明品 "invention" and 発明家 "inventor". Opposite: 発見する "to discover" (to find something already present). 開発する is the planned development of products in companies.

examples[].german: Barrier-free facilities are increasing.
For my parents, we renovated the house to be barrier-free.
This hotel is barrier-free, so even wheelchair users can stay without worry.
en.notes: バリアフリー describes buildings, transportation or homes without obstacles for older people, wheelchair users or people with disabilities - that is, without steps, with ramps, elevators and wide doors. Grammatically it is a noun used adjectivally with の: バリアフリーの家／トイレ; also バリアフリー化 "barrier-free conversion" and バリアフリーにする. In daily life one also simply says 段差がない "without steps". A more broadly defined, related concept is ユニバーサルデザイン.

examples[].german: We incorporate universal design.
This station was built on the idea of universal design.
The ridges on shampoo bottles are also an example of universal design.
en.notes: ユニバーサルデザイン means design that is usable by everyone from the start, regardless of age, disability or language. By contrast, バリアフリー means removing existing obstacles for particular groups after the fact. The word is encountered with stations, public buildings and everyday products, often abbreviated as UD. Typical are ユニバーサルデザインを取り入れる and ユニバーサルデザインの〜.

examples[].german: I'm learning sign language.
The TV news comes with sign language interpretation.
I talked in sign language with a deaf friend.
en.notes: 手話 is "sign language". Typical are 手話で話す, 手話を使う and 手話を習う; the person who interprets is a 手話通訳者. Japanese Sign Language (日本手話) is a language in its own right with its own grammar; spelling with the fingers is called 指文字. General gestures while speaking, by contrast, are called ジェスチャー or 身振り手振り.

examples[].german: Please do not stand on the tactile paving.
The elevator buttons have braille on them.
After his eyesight got worse, my grandfather started learning braille.
en.notes: 点字 is braille, literally "dot script"; Japanese braille represents the kana, not the kanji. Typical: 点字を読む, 点字で書かれた本, 点字の案内. Very common is 点字ブロック: the yellow, ridged guide strips on sidewalks and station platforms, on which one should not stand or park bicycles. Of people, one politely says 目の不自由な方.

examples[].german: We aim for a multicultural society.
This town runs Japanese classes to promote multicultural coexistence.
As the number of foreign residents grows, multicultural coexistence has become a major issue.
en.notes: 多文化共生 means that people from different cultural and national backgrounds live together as equal members of one society. 共生 means "living together, coexistence" (in biology, "symbiosis"). The word is a buzzword in local politics and administration: 多文化共生社会, 多文化共生を進める／推進する, 多文化共生センター. In conversation it sounds official; casually, people tend to say 外国人と一緒に暮らす.

examples[].german: Intercultural understanding is important.
Studying abroad is a good opportunity to deepen your understanding of other cultures.
A training course on intercultural understanding was held for the new employees.
en.notes: 異文化理解 is the understanding of other, unfamiliar cultures: 異文化 "other culture" + 理解 "understanding". The word is typical of education, exchange programs and corporate training: 異文化理解を深める, 異文化理解の授業, 異文化理解に役立つ. Related terms are 異文化コミュニケーション "intercultural communication" and 異文化交流 "cultural exchange". It is rather formal and matter-of-fact; in casual conversation people say 外国の文化を理解する.

examples[].german: I became a naturalized Japanese citizen.
I hear the naturalization procedure takes about a year.
That athlete is originally from Brazil, but he was naturalized and now represents Japan.
en.notes: 帰化 is naturalization: a foreigner takes on the citizenship of a country. As an intransitive する-verb, the country is marked with に: 日本に帰化する; related are 帰化申請 "naturalization application" and 帰化を申請する. In principle, anyone who becomes naturalized in Japan has to give up their previous citizenship - this distinguishes it from 永住権, where one remains a foreign national. In biology, 帰化 also refers to naturalized plants and animals (帰化植物).

examples[].german: I am renewing my residence status.
To work in Japan after graduating, international students have to change their residence status.
Before I started my part-time job, my residence status was checked against my residence card.
en.notes: 在留資格 is a foreigner's residence status in Japan, that is, the legal category under which one may live in the country (e.g. 留学, 家族滞在, 永住者). In everyday speech people often just say ビザ, although strictly speaking a visa only concerns entry into the country. Typical: 在留資格を取得する／変更する, 在留資格の確認; officially one extends the 在留期間 "period of stay", but in daily life people also speak of 在留資格の更新. The status is shown on the 在留カード "residence card".

examples[].german: I obtained permanent residency.
Since I have lived in Japan for more than ten years, I am thinking of applying for permanent residency.
With permanent residency, you don't have to renew your visa.
en.notes: 永住権 is the right to reside permanently in a country without taking on its citizenship. In Japan, the official equivalent is the residence status 永住者; in everyday speech people say 永住権 or 永住ビザ. Typical: 永住権を取る／取得する, 永住権を申請する, 永住権が下りる "is granted". Unlike after a 帰化, you keep your own nationality, but you must still carry the 在留カード.

examples[].german: He asked for political asylum.
The writer went into exile in France during the war.
There was news that an athlete who had taken part in a tournament had defected abroad on the spot.
en.notes: 亡命 means fleeing one's own country for political or religious reasons and seeking protection abroad. As an intransitive する-verb, the destination country is marked with に or へ: アメリカに亡命する; also 亡命を求める "to ask for asylum", 亡命政府 "government in exile", 亡命者. The word comes from the news and from history and stresses the political flight of individuals. People who flee war or persecution in large numbers, on the other hand, are called 難民 "refugees".

en.meaning: to assert; to insist; to claim
examples[].german: I assert my own opinion.
At the meeting, she insisted that break times should be increased.
The man insisted to the end that he was not the culprit.
en.notes: 主張する means "to advocate an opinion emphatically, to claim". The content takes を (意見を主張する, 権利を主張する "to assert a right") or is quoted with と (無実だと主張する "to maintain one's innocence"). It is neutral but more forceful than 言う; for stubborn insistence one rather says 言い張る. The noun 主張 appears in 自己主張が強い "assertive, very sure of oneself".

examples[].german: We will develop a new product.
This company develops smartphone apps.
The area around the station was developed, and there are now many more tall buildings.
en.notes: 開発する means "to develop" (products, technology, software: 新製品・アプリを開発する) and "to develop (land), to exploit" (land, resources: 駅前を開発する, 都市開発). Related: 開発者 "developer" and 開発途上国 "developing country". Not to be confused with 発展する "to develop, to grow" (city, economy), which is intransitive.

examples[].german: They normalized diplomatic relations.
Japan and China established diplomatic relations in 1972.
Those two countries still have no diplomatic relations today.
en.notes: 国交 means the official diplomatic relations between two states; 国 "state" + 交 "intercourse, exchange". Fixed phrases: 国交を結ぶ "to establish", 国交を断絶する "to sever", 国交を回復する／正常化する "to restore / normalize", 国交がない. 国交 refers to the formal status; general relations between countries are called 関係 (日中関係), and cultural exchange 交流. A typical word from the news and history class.

examples[].german: We will impose economic sanctions.
The United Nations decided to impose new sanctions on that country.
The player who broke the rules received a severe penalty from the team.
en.notes: 制裁 is a punitive measure against someone who has broken rules. In the news it mostly concerns international politics: 経済制裁 "economic sanctions", 制裁を加える／科す "to impose", 制裁を解除する "to lift". It can also mean a punishment within a group, e.g. 社会的制裁 "social ostracism". For punishments by courts one says 刑罰, and for simple punishments in everyday life 罰. As a transitive する-verb (〜を制裁する) it is possible, but it mostly appears as a noun.

examples[].german: A ceasefire agreement was reached.
The two countries agreed to a three-day ceasefire.
The ceasefire was broken, and fighting started again.
en.notes: 停戦 is the cessation of hostilities, i.e. "ceasefire, truce". Typical: 停戦する, 停戦に合意する, 停戦合意, 停戦協定, 停戦を呼びかける, 停戦が破られる. A 停戦 is often provisional; the final end of a war is 終戦 (for Japan especially 1945) or a 平和条約 "peace treaty". The similar 休戦 sounds more like a pause for a limited time; in today's news 停戦 is more common.

examples[].german: They concluded a peace treaty.
Japan and Russia still do not have a peace treaty between them.
In history class, I learned about the peace treaty concluded after the war.
en.notes: 平和条約 is a peace treaty that officially ends a war between states. 条約 means "(international) treaty", as opposed to 契約 for private contracts. Typical: 平和条約を結ぶ／締結する, 平和条約に署名する. Well known are the サンフランシスコ平和条約 of 1951 and the peace treaty between Japan and Russia, which is still missing today. A 停戦, by contrast, is only a provisional ceasefire.

examples[].german: We promote international cooperation.
In the future I want to work in international cooperation.
The problem of global warming cannot be solved without international cooperation.
en.notes: 国際協力 is cooperation between countries, especially support for developing countries by the state, NGOs or volunteers. Typical: 国際協力を進める／推進する, 国際協力に関わる, 国際協力の仕事; the government agency JICA is called 国際協力機構. 協力 means "cooperation, help" and otherwise takes に: 調査に協力する. A neutral, somewhat formal word from politics, education and the working world.

examples[].german: We will provide development aid.
Thanks to Japanese development aid, a new bridge was built in this country.
We need to check whether the development aid money is really reaching the people who are truly in need.
en.notes: 開発援助 is "development aid": financial or technical support from richer countries for the economic and social development of poorer countries. Best known is 政府開発援助 (ODA), Japan's government development aid. Typical: 開発援助を行う, 開発援助を受ける, 開発援助の予算. 援助 alone means "help, support" more generally (経済援助, 食料援助), and 開発 here means the development of a country, not product development. A formal word from politics and the news.

examples[].german: We are promoting technology transfer.
When building a factory overseas, technology transfer can become an issue.
Research results from the university were transferred to a company, and a new product was born.
en.notes: 技術移転 refers to the passing on of technology and know-how, for example from industrialized to developing countries, from a company to a partner company abroad, or from universities to businesses. 移転 means "relocation, transfer" and is otherwise also used for moving an office (事務所を移転する). Typical: 技術移転を進める／行う, 海外への技術移転. A technical word from business and politics; in conversation one says more simply 技術を伝える／教える.

examples[].german: I earned the credits.
If I fail this course, I won't be able to graduate.
In Japan, the meter is used as the unit of length.
en.notes: 単位 has two main meanings: "unit of measurement" (長さの単位はメートル) and, at school or university, "credit". Typical for students: 単位を取る "to pass a course, earn credits", 単位を落とす "to fail", 単位が足りない "to not have enough credits". As a suffix, 〜単位 means "in units of, per ...": 千円単位, グループ単位で行動する. Not to be confused with 単語 "word, vocabulary item".

examples[].german: I decided on the topic of my graduation thesis.
There is only one week left until the thesis deadline.
In my graduation thesis, I researched the language of young people in Japan.
en.notes: 卒論 is the common abbreviation of 卒業論文, the thesis written at the end of a bachelor's degree (at Japanese universities usually in the fourth year). Typical: 卒論を書く, 卒論のテーマ, 卒論を提出する, 卒論発表 "presentation of the thesis". The short form is completely normal among students and instructors; official documents use 卒業論文. Master's theses are called 修士論文 (short: 修論), doctoral dissertations 博士論文.

examples[].german: I'm in the middle of job hunting.
I bought a black suit for job hunting.
Many people start job hunting in the winter of their third year.
en.notes: 就活 is the short form of 就職活動, the very rigidly structured job hunt that students go through in Japan before graduating: company information sessions, application forms (エントリーシート), tests and several interviews. Typical: 就活をする, 就活中, 就活生 "students job hunting", 就活スーツ. The short form is colloquial but used everywhere. Working people who change jobs, by contrast, do 転職活動; following the same pattern there is 婚活 "spouse hunting".

examples[].german: Smartphones have spread all over the world.
Electric cars are not yet sufficiently widespread.
The government is trying to spread the idea of recycling.
en.notes: 普及する means "to spread, to become generally common" - technology, products or ideas adopted by many people: スマホが普及する, 〜に普及している. It is mostly intransitive with が; to actively spread something is 普及させる. Related: 普及率 "penetration rate". 広まる also fits rumors, and 流行る short-lived trends.

examples[].german: I received an informal job offer.
I got an offer from my first-choice company.
Because of the poor economy, some students had their offers withdrawn.
en.notes: 内定 is a provisional, not yet official offer, above all a company's job offer to students who will start only after graduation, in April. Typical: 内定をもらう／取る, 内定が出る, 内定者, 内定式 "ceremony for future employees"; the opposite is 内定取り消し "withdrawal of the offer". The formal hiring is called 採用, and 内定 is the step before it. In principle it can be used for other provisional decisions as well (人事が内定する), but in daily life it is almost always in the 就活 context.

examples[].german: I was assigned to the sales department.
Once the training is over, the assignments will be announced.
I'm very happy to have been assigned to the department I wanted.
en.notes: 配属 is the assignment of a person to a department, post or unit, typically after being hired. Almost always in the passive: 営業部に配属される "to be assigned to the sales department"; in the active, the company says 新人を総務部に配属する. Other combinations: 配属先 "assigned unit", 配属が決まる. A later move to another department is called 異動, a transfer to another location 転勤.

examples[].german: I'm on secondment to a subsidiary.
The department head will be seconded to a business partner for two years starting next month.
The atmosphere at the company I'm seconded to is very good.
en.notes: 出向 is the temporary secondment of an employee to another company, usually a subsidiary or a business partner; the contract with the original employer remains in place. As an intransitive する-verb, the destination is marked with に: 子会社に出向する; the company one works for is called 出向先. To be distinguished from 転勤 ("transfer to another location of the same company"), 転職 ("job change") and 派遣 ("dispatch, temp work"). Not to be confused with the verb 出向く (でむく, "to go to a place").

examples[].german: I was transferred to a provincial branch as a demotion.
Because he opposed the president, he was sent down to a small branch office.
This isn't a promotion, it's a demotion.
en.notes: 左遷 is a transfer to a worse position or an unattractive place, in effect a punitive transfer. It is usually used in the passive from the point of view of the person affected: 地方に左遷される, 支店に左遷された. The opposite is 栄転 ("transfer with promotion"); neutral is 転勤, and a formal demotion in rank is called 降格. The word always sounds negative and is often used with pity or irony.

examples[].german: I will reach retirement age next year.
After retirement, my father grows vegetables in the garden every day.
The retirement age at this company is sixty-five.
en.notes: 定年 is the fixed age limit at which one leaves the company, and also the leaving itself. Typical are 定年を迎える, 定年になる, 定年退職する ("to retire") as well as 定年後 ("after retirement") and 定年延長 ("raising of the age limit"). 退職 is generally "to leave one's post" (also early), 引退 "to withdraw" (e.g. athletes); the pension as money is called 年金. The older spelling 停年 is only rarely seen now.

examples[].german: This is my calling.
For her, who loves playing with children, being a nursery teacher is a true calling.
I feel I have finally found my calling.
en.notes: 天職 is literally "the occupation given by heaven": work for which one is as if made. Typical are 〜は私の天職だ, 天職だと思う, 天職に出会う, 天職を見つける. Attention, homophone: 転職 (also てんしょく) means "job change" - in spoken language the context decides. Related is 生きがい ("reason for living"), which is not limited to a job.

examples[].german: I cherish the aesthetics of wabi-sabi.
When you enter an old tea room, you can feel wabi-sabi.
It is difficult to explain wabi-sabi to foreigners.
en.notes: 侘び寂び (often written in kana as わびさび) combines two aesthetic concepts: 侘び, plain, quiet simplicity and contentment with little, and 寂び, the beauty of age, patina and calm solitude. The word belongs to the world of the tea ceremony, gardens and haiku. Typical: 侘び寂びを感じる, 侘び寂びの世界, 侘び寂びがある. It is a rather abstract cultural concept that even Japanese people find hard to explain precisely.

examples[].german: I experienced the elegant culture of the court.
At festivals in Kyoto, you can see the elegant costumes of the Heian period.
The graceful sound of the koto calmed my heart.
en.notes: 雅 refers to the refined, courtly elegance of the old imperial court, especially of the Heian period and of Kyoto. It is mostly used as a な-adjective: 雅な衣装, 雅な音色; there is also 雅やか(な). More general words are 上品 ("refined, cultured") and 優雅 ("elegant, graceful", also for a luxurious lifestyle). The word sounds literary and is often used in advertising, names and descriptions of traditional culture.

examples[].german: It is a scenic view full of charm.
Gion at night is full of old-fashioned charm.
Lately he has been emotionally unstable and gets angry easily.
en.notes: 情緒 has two uses: first, the atmospheric charm or flair of a place, often nostalgic: 情緒がある, 情緒あふれる町, 下町情緒, 異国情緒. Second, in psychology, a person's emotional state: 情緒不安定 ("emotionally unstable"), 情緒教育. The original reading is じょうしょ; today じょうちょ is usual. 雰囲気 is neutral "atmosphere", whereas 情緒 sounds like poetic charm; for individual feelings one says 感情 or 気持ち.

examples[].german: Remarkable progress was made.
Over the past ten years, there has been a marked change in the town's population.
The temperature differences have been striking lately, so please take care of your health.
en.notes: 著しい is a literary い-adjective: a change or difference is "strikingly large, considerable". Typical: 著しい変化・成長・進歩・差. It evaluates only the degree, not whether something is good - 著しい低下 "a drastic decline" is also possible. Adverbial: 著しく. In conversation one tends to say すごい, 大きい or かなり.

examples[].german: It is a building with charm.
The garden on a rainy day has a different charm as well.
I have understood the content of your request.
en.notes: 趣 is mostly the quiet appeal or charm of something, often old and traditional: 趣がある, 趣のある建物, 違った趣. Very similar is 風情, while 情緒 rather means the flair of a place. In formal letters 趣 also means "gist, content" (ご依頼の趣, cf. 趣旨), and in literary language there is 趣を異にする ("to differ"). The kanji is known from 趣味 ("hobby").

examples[].german: She is a gracefully reserved woman.
The fact that he doesn't boast about his success is part of his modest charm.
I was moved by that inn's gracefully understated hospitality.
en.notes: 奥ゆかしい praises a discreet, modest reserve behind which one senses depth and refinement - in people, their behavior or an atmosphere. It is always positive and sounds somewhat elevated. 控えめ is neutral "restrained", 上品 "refined", 遠慮がち "hesitant, shy". The word is almost always written in kana; 奥床しい is rare.

examples[].german: She is a beloved presence.
When I look at the sleeping baby's face, I'm overcome with tenderness.
Ordinary days spent with family feel precious.
en.notes: いとおしい (also written 愛おしい) describes tender, protective affection for a loved person, a child or animal, but also for things and times (いとおしい日々). Typical is 〜がいとおしくてたまらない. It sounds emotional and somewhat literary; in everyday speech one more often says 可愛い or 大好き. Similar is 愛しい (いとしい); the older meaning "pitiable" is rare today.

examples[].german: It is a melancholy autumn dusk.
A wistful melody could be heard from somewhere.
The town after the festival has ended feels somehow melancholy.
en.notes: The prefix 物- means "somehow, vaguely" here (cf. 物寂しい, 物足りない): 物悲しい is a diffuse wistfulness without a concrete reason. It describes above all moods, sounds, landscapes and seasons, classically autumn. 悲しい is concrete sorrow, 寂しい loneliness. The word sounds somewhat literary, but also occurs in conversation.

examples[].german: It is a desolate landscape.
Autumn dusk feels somehow lonely, doesn't it?
After the children became independent, the house became lonely.
en.notes: もの寂しい is an い-adjective; the prefix もの〜 means "somehow, vaguely", as in もの悲しい or もの静か. It describes a wistful, desolate mood of landscapes, seasons, places or sounds, hardly the direct feeling of missing someone; for that one simply says 寂しい. It is also written 物寂しい or 物淋しい.

examples[].german: I felt empty.
I tried desperately to persuade them, but my efforts ended in vain.
After playing games all day, I somehow felt empty.
en.notes: 空しい (today often written 虚しい for feelings, same reading) has two main meanings: the feeling of inner emptiness (空しい気持ち, 空しくなる) and futility (空しい努力, 努力が空しく終わる). Adverbially: 空しく時間が過ぎる ("time passes uselessly"). 寂しい, by contrast, is "lonely", and 無駄 is the matter-of-fact "useless". The kanji 空 is read むな- here, not そら or から.

examples[].german: I find it off-putting.
In adolescence, one tends to find parents' warnings annoying.
I gradually came to find him, who contacted me over and over, annoying.
en.notes: 疎ましい expresses that someone or something is bothersome and one wants to keep one's distance; it is mostly about people and their behavior (親が疎ましい, 干渉が疎ましい). Typical are 疎ましく思う and 疎ましく感じる. Related are 疎む ("to shun") and 疎遠 ("estranged"). The word sounds rather written; in conversation one says うるさい, 面倒くさい or, casually, うざい.

examples[].german: He/She has a dignified bearing.
In a clear, firm voice, she answered, "No."
On winter mornings the air is crisp and clear, which feels good.
en.notes: 凛とした is the attributive form of the word 凛 (a と-adjective): 凛と + した. It describes an upright, dignified and clear presence - in posture, voice or appearance - and also cold, clear air (凛とした空気). In the predicate, one says 凛としている. Not to be confused with 凛々しい (りりしい, "gallant, brave"). The word is positive and somewhat elevated; 凜 is a variant of the kanji.

examples[].german: He is a shrewd negotiating partner.
She has lived tenaciously even in harsh circumstances.
I fell and hit my knee hard.
en.notes: したたか (mostly in kana) describes, as a な-adjective, someone who is tough, resilient and skillfully pursues their interests - depending on context admiring ("tough, clever") or pejorative ("cunning"). Typical: したたかな人, したたかに生きる. As an adverb it means "hard, thoroughly": 頭をしたたか打つ, したたかに酔う. ずるい is clearly negative "unfair, sly", 粘り強い positive "persistent".

examples[].german: I'll give a rough estimate.
Roughly calculated, the moving costs are about 200,000 yen.
I'll first give a rough estimate and let you know the exact amount later.
en.notes: 概算 is a rough calculation: 概算で "roughly calculated", 概算を出す, 概算見積もり; as a transitive する-verb: 費用を概算する. The counterpart is 精算 ("exact settlement"), e.g. with an advance payment and a later settlement. 見積もり is the cost estimate itself; in conversation people often simply say だいたい or ざっと. The word belongs to business and administrative language.

examples[].german: It had a remarkable effect.
Young people's turning away from reading has become pronounced.
This tendency is particularly pronounced in urban areas.
en.notes: 顕著 is a な-adjective of written and technical language: "clearly noticeable, pronounced". Typical: 顕著な効果・傾向・例, 〜が顕著だ, 〜が顕著に現れる. Close to 著しい, but 顕著 emphasizes clear visibility, 著しい the large extent. In conversation people rather say はっきりした or 目立つ.

examples[].german: I'm settling my travel expenses.
Since I had ridden past my stop, I used the fare adjustment machine in front of the ticket gate.
Please settle your business trip expenses by the end of the month.
en.notes: 精算 is the exact (after-the-fact) settling of accounts: 交通費を精算する ("to settle travel expenses"), 経費精算, at the station 乗り越し精算 ("paying the fare difference") at the 精算機, as well as paying at a parking garage. Beware of homophones: 清算 ("to clear up debts or the past", e.g. 過去を清算する) and 生産 ("production"). The counterpart is 概算 ("rough estimate").

examples[].german: I'll round off the odd amount.
It's 1,030 yen, but I'll throw in the odd amount, so 1,000 yen is fine.
I'll pay the leftover odd amount of the split bill.
en.notes: 端数 is the "odd" remainder below a round unit, such as the 30 yen in 1,030 yen. Typical are 端数を切り捨てる ("to round down"), 端数を切り上げる ("to round up") and 四捨五入する ("to round off in the usual way"). To be distinguished are お釣り ("change"), 残り ("remainder" in general) and 余り ("remainder" in division). A fraction in the mathematical sense, by contrast, is 分数.

examples[].german: It's off by one order of magnitude.
The PIN is a four-digit number.
I got the digits of the price wrong and put on a price tag that was far too high.
en.notes: 桁 is the place of a number: 三桁の数字 ("three-digit number"), 桁を間違える ("to get the number of digits wrong"). As a counter: 一桁 (ひとけた), 二桁 (ふたけた), 四桁 (よんけた). 桁が違う literally means "to have a different number of digits" and figuratively "to be on a completely different level"; related are 桁違い and 桁外れ ("extraordinary"). In construction, 桁 also means "girder, beam".

examples[].german: I am good at mental arithmetic.
I worked out the answer in my head without using a calculator.
When shopping, I calculate the total amount in my head.
en.notes: 暗算 is mental arithmetic; 暗 here stands for "without aids, in the head", as in 暗記 ("memorization"). Typical are 暗算が得意/苦手, 暗算で計算する, 暗算する. Counterparts are 筆算 ("written calculation") and 珠算 ("calculation with an abacus"). Beware of the homophone 安産 ("easy childbirth").

examples[].german: I'm learning abacus calculation.
I passed level 2 of the abacus certification exam.
In elementary school class, I studied abacus a little.
en.notes: 珠算 is the technical, somewhat formal term for calculating with an abacus; in everyday speech one usually simply says そろばん (そろばんを習う). 珠算 appears mainly in set expressions such as 珠算検定 ("abacus exam") or 珠算教室. Someone with good practice calculates in their head with an imagined abacus (珠算式暗算). To be distinguished from 暗算 ("mental arithmetic") and 筆算 ("written calculation").

examples[].german: He was arrested for embezzlement.
The accountant had embezzled 30 million yen of company money.
The department head denies the suspicion of embezzlement.
en.notes: 横領 is the misappropriation of money or goods that have been entrusted to one: 会社の金を横領する, 公金横領, legally 業務上横領. In contrast to 盗む/窃盗 ("theft" of someone else's property), one already legitimately holds the goods. Almost synonymous is 着服 ("pocketing"). Typical of news and legal language: 横領で逮捕される, 横領の疑い.

examples[].german: Tax evasion is a crime.
The company president had hidden sales and evaded taxes.
I don't want to evade taxes - please tell me legal ways to save on taxes.
en.notes: 脱税 is tax evasion, i.e. the illegal non-payment of taxes: 脱税する, 脱税で逮捕される, 脱税の疑い. The counterpart is the legal 節税 ("saving taxes"); more colloquial and vaguer is 税金逃れ. Taxes that have been declared but not paid are 滞納 ("payment arrears"). Typical of news and legal language.

en.meaning: window dressing of accounts; falsified financial statements
examples[].german: The falsification of the accounts came to light.
The company had falsified its financial statements for five years.
The president resigned to take responsibility for the accounting fraud.
en.notes: 粉飾決算 is made up of 粉飾 ("to make up, to gloss over") and 決算 ("annual financial statement"): the falsification or embellishment of the books. Typical: 粉飾決算をする, 粉飾決算が発覚する ("to come to light"), 粉飾決算の疑い; often just 粉飾 is said for short. 改竄 is the manipulation of documents or data in general, 脱税 is tax evasion. A technical term from business news.

examples[].german: Internal strife is occurring within the party.
Internal strife broke out in the company over the president's successor.
The band broke up because of internal conflict.
en.notes: 内紛 is a dispute within an organization - party, company, club or country: 内紛が起きる, 内紛が続く, 〜をめぐる内紛, 内紛に揺れる. To be distinguished from 内戦 ("civil war", armed) and the colloquial 内輪もめ ("squabbling among themselves", also in families). The word belongs to news language.

examples[].german: The secret was exposed.
A former employee exposed the company's wrongdoing on the internet.
A book exposing the actor's private life was published.
en.notes: 暴露 is the exposing or revealing of something that was supposed to stay hidden, often scandals or private matters: 秘密を暴露する, 不正を暴露する, 暴露本 ("tell-all book"), 暴露記事 ("exposé"). The neutral "to make public" is 公開, the intransitive "to come to light" is 発覚; colloquially one says ばらす ("to spill"). In technical language 暴露 also means "to be exposed" (放射線に暴露される). The kanji 暴 is read ばく here.

examples[].german: It's a delicate issue.
"How's this outfit?" "Hmm, it's kind of so-so."
Even if I leave now, it's iffy whether I'll make it to the meeting.
en.notes: 微妙 has several meanings: "fine, subtle" (微妙な違い "a subtle difference"), "delicate" (微妙な問題・立場) and "questionable, uncertain" (間に合うか微妙だ). Colloquially, 微妙 is also a polite evasive answer for "well, not so great": "どう？" - "うーん、微妙。". This avoids a direct no.

examples[].german: The facts were covered up.
The company had covered up the product's defects for years.
When the cover-up of the accident came to light, public anger spread.
en.notes: 隠蔽 is the deliberate covering up of mistakes, accidents or scandals, mostly by organizations: 事実を隠蔽する, 隠蔽工作 ("cover-up operation"), 組織的な隠蔽, 隠蔽体質 ("culture of covering things up"). 隠す is the general word for "to hide"; the opposites are 公表 ("to announce publicly") and 暴露 ("to expose"). Because 蔽 is not a Jōyō kanji, newspapers often write 隠ぺい.

examples[].german: The data was fabricated.
The reporter had made up interviews for his articles.
A police officer was arrested for allegedly fabricating evidence.
en.notes: 捏造 means to invent something non-existent and pass it off as true - data, evidence, quotations or stories: データを捏造する, 証拠の捏造, 記事の捏造. In contrast, 改竄 alters something that already exists, and 偽造 is the counterfeiting of documents or money (偽造パスポート). Because 捏 is not a Jōyō kanji, the press often writes ねつ造.

examples[].german: I falsified the documents.
After the falsification of inspection data came to light, the factory shut down.
The website was tampered with, and false information was displayed.
en.notes: 改竄 is the subsequent altering and falsifying of something that exists - documents, data, records, web pages: 書類を改竄する, データ改竄, 公文書改竄. 捏造, by contrast, invents something entirely new, and 偽造 imitates an original. Because 竄 is not a Jōyō kanji, in newspapers you almost always see 改ざん. It is typically combined with 発覚する ("to come to light").

examples[].german: The president was impeached.
The citizens' group sharply condemned the government's responsibility.
In Japan, impeachment trials are sometimes held to remove judges from office.
en.notes: 弾劾 is the public accusation of an official for misconduct; politically, it means impeachment proceedings: 大統領を弾劾する, 弾劾決議, 弾劾裁判 (in Japan against judges). 弾劾 is the proceeding or the accusation - the actual removal from office is called 罷免. In a broader sense it also means "to denounce sharply": 政府の責任を弾劾する; general criticism is 非難 or 批判. Very formal.

examples[].german: The minister was dismissed.
The prime minister dismissed the minister who had made problematic remarks.
No judge has ever been dismissed through a national review.
en.notes: 罷免 is the removal of an office holder by a higher authority, for example when the prime minister dismisses a minister: 首相が大臣を罷免する, 大臣が罷免される. Someone who leaves on their own resigns (辞任); the dismissal of ordinary employees is 解雇, a replacement in a post often euphemistically 更迭. A very formal word from politics and law; also in the constitution (公務員を選定し、罷免する権利).

examples[].german: The company president resigned.
The minister took responsibility and resigned.
She stepped down as captain for health reasons.
en.notes: 辞任 is the voluntary resignation from an office or post: 社長が辞任する; the office can take を (会長を辞任する). A set phrase is 責任を取って辞任する ("to take responsibility and resign"). To be distinguished from 辞職 ("to give up one's position", often for civil servants), 退職 ("to leave employment") and 罷免/解任 ("to be dismissed").

examples[].german: The cabinet resigned en masse.
Taking responsibility for the accident, the company's executives all resigned.
If the no-confidence motion passes, the cabinet must choose between mass resignation and dissolution.
en.notes: 総辞職 is the joint resignation of all members of a body; 総 means "entire". Most common is 内閣総辞職 or 内閣が総辞職する, but a board of directors can also choose 総辞職. After a successful no-confidence motion, the Japanese cabinet must either choose 総辞職 or dissolve the lower house (解散). Individual persons, on the other hand, resign with 辞任.

examples[].german: The assembly was dissolved.
Tomorrow we meet at the station at nine and plan to disperse at five.
My favorite band broke up last year.
en.notes: 解散 has three uses: a group disperses (at the end of an outing: ここで解散します, opposite 集合 "meeting point, assembly"), an organization or band disbands (バンドが解散する), and parliament is dissolved (衆議院を解散する, 衆議院が解散する). The word is both intransitive and transitive. For the end of a romantic relationship one does not say 解散, but 別れる.

examples[].german: A general election will be held.
Following the dissolution of the House of Representatives, each party began preparing for the general election.
The ruling party won a majority in the general election.
en.notes: 総選挙 in Japan is the election of all members of the lower house (衆議院), either after its dissolution or at the end of the term; the upper house election, by contrast, is called 参議院選挙. Typical: 総選挙が行われる, 総選挙で勝つ, 総選挙に立候補する. Colloquially, the word also refers to fan votes on idols or characters (人気投票).

examples[].german: Please keep your campaign pledges.
He pledged to lower the consumption tax and was elected.
The new mayor has hardly fulfilled any of his campaign pledges.
en.notes: 公約 is a publicly given promise, above all a politician's campaign promise: 公約を掲げる ("to put forward"), 公約を守る/果たす ("to keep"), 公約を破る ("to break"), 選挙公約. As a する-verb: 減税を公約する. A private promise is 約束; the whole election platform is often called マニフェスト.

examples[].german: Strictly speaking, that is different.
The quality of the medicine is strictly controlled.
There are no strict rules, so please feel free to write however you like.
en.notes: 厳密 is a な-adjective for "exact, precise, strict" in the sense of thorough precision: 厳密な検査, 厳密に管理する. Very common is 厳密に言えば／言うと "strictly speaking". 厳しい, by contrast, means "strict, harsh" toward people (厳しい先生), and 正確 simply "correct, accurate".

examples[].german: Voter turnout is low.
Turnout in this election fell below 50 percent.
What can be done to raise turnout among young people?
en.notes: 投票率 is the voter turnout; 率 means "rate, ratio". Typical: 投票率が高い/低い, 投票率が上がる/下がる, 投票率は〜パーセントだった. Not to be confused with 得票率 ("share of the vote" of a candidate) and 支持率 ("approval rating" in polls).

examples[].german: We aim to win the swing votes.
There are many swing voters in urban areas, so election results are hard to predict.
The swing voters made up their minds at the last minute, and the opposition candidate won.
en.notes: 浮動票 is made up of 浮動 ("to fluctuate, to drift") and 票 ("vote"): the votes of voters with no fixed party loyalty, who vote one way or another. Counterparts are 固定票 ("votes of loyal supporters") and 組織票 ("votes of organized groups"). Typical: 浮動票を集める/狙う/取り込む. The voter group itself is called 無党派層.

examples[].german: We will promote local self-government.
Local governments provide services close to residents' daily lives.
There is a saying, "Local self-government is a school of democracy."
en.notes: 地方自治 is the self-government of prefectures and municipalities vis-a-vis the central state (国). The bodies themselves are called 地方自治体 or, for short, 自治体 ("municipality"); the legal basis is the 地方自治法. Well known is the saying 地方自治は民主主義の学校. The word belongs to the language of politics, administration and school lessons (civics).

examples[].german: We will hold a local referendum.
A referendum was held on the merger of municipalities.
In the referendum, most votes were against building the airport.
en.notes: 住民投票 is a vote of the residents (住民) of a municipality or prefecture on a concrete issue, such as a merger of municipalities, a power plant or a military base - that is, a local referendum. A nationwide referendum (e.g. on a constitutional amendment) is called 国民投票; in an 選挙, people are elected. Typical: 住民投票を行う/実施する, 住民投票の結果, 反対多数.

examples[].german: I request the disclosure of information.
A citizens' group requested information disclosure regarding the city's expenditures.
Companies are being asked to disclose information more proactively.
en.notes: 情報公開 refers, on the one hand, to citizens' right to inspect government records (情報公開法, 情報公開請求 "request for access to records"), and on the other, generally to the disclosure of information by companies or organizations. Related are 公表 ("to announce") and 開示 ("to disclose", e.g. 情報開示 in the financial world); 暴露, by contrast, is an exposure against the will of those concerned.

examples[].german: We will protect freedom of the press.
According to reports, three people were injured in the accident.
The incident was widely covered on TV.
en.notes: 報道 is media coverage: 〜と報道する, 報道によると ("according to media reports"), 大きく報道される, 報道の自由 ("freedom of the press"), 報道陣 ("members of the press"), 報道番組 "news program". ニュース is the individual news item, 放送 the broadcast, 記事 the newspaper article. The word is neutral, but occurs mainly in news language.

examples[].german: I read the editorial.
My father works as an editorial writer for a newspaper.
In the Japanese test, I read an argumentative essay and summarized the author's opinion.
en.notes: 論説 is an argumentative opinion piece or commentary, in newspapers also the editorial; the author is called 論説委員 ("editorial writer"). In school lessons, 論説文 is the argumentative text type (as opposed to 物語文 and 説明文). 社説 is specifically the editorial in the newspaper's name, 記事 an article in general, コラム a column. An elevated, written word.

examples[].german: I skimmed the editorial.
Today's editorial sharply criticizes the government's economic policy.
The opinions in editorials differ quite a lot depending on the newspaper.
en.notes: 社説 is the editorial that expresses the official opinion of the newspaper (社 = publishing company) and is usually not signed. Typical: 〜新聞の社説, 社説で〜を批判する, 社説は〜と主張している. 論説 is the broader term for commentaries, コラム a column with a personal touch. Anyone who wants to know a newspaper's standpoint reads its 社説.

examples[].german: I only read the headlines.
A big headline reading 「首相辞任」 was on the front page of the newspaper.
Please add a heading to each chapter of the report.
en.notes: 見出し is the heading of an article or chapter, or the headline: 大きな見出し, 見出しを付ける, 見出しだけ読む. In a dictionary, 見出し(語) is the headword. タイトル and 題名 rather refer to the title of a whole work. Do not confuse it with the verb 見出す, which is read みいだす and means "to find, to discover".

examples[].german: We will hold a press conference.
At the press conference, the company president bowed deeply and apologized.
After the game, the manager agreed to a press conference.
en.notes: 記者会見 is a press conference: 記者会見を開く/行う, 記者会見で発表する/謝罪する, 緊急記者会見 "emergency press conference". It is often shortened to 会見 (会見に応じる "to face the press's questions"). A one-on-one interview is インタビュー. In Japan, the deep bow at an apology 会見 is a fixed part of the picture of scandals.

examples[].german: It is a reasonable price.
This time, I think it is reasonable to postpone the plan.
Let's think once more about whether that conclusion is valid.
en.notes: 妥当 is a na-adjective meaning "appropriate, reasonable, valid" - correct after weighing the circumstances: 妥当な判断・価格・結論, 〜とするのが妥当だ. It sounds matter-of-fact and suits business and discussion. Be careful with 適当: in everyday speech it often means "sloppy, half-hearted"; 適切 means "suitable, fitting".

examples[].german: A breaking news alert about an earthquake was issued.
In the middle of the drama, a news flash scrolled across the top of the screen.
The election results will be reported on TV right away.
en.notes: 速報 is a quick first report or news flash: ニュース速報 (the ticker on TV), 選挙速報, 速報値 ("preliminary value"), 緊急地震速報 ("earthquake early warning"). As a する-verb: 結果を速報する. News coverage in general is 報道; a printed extra edition is 号外.

examples[].german: The political controversy continues.
The film set off a major controversy over freedom of expression.
The two scholars argued about that theory for years.
en.notes: 論争 is a dispute carried on with arguments, often a public controversy: 論争が起きる/続く, 〜をめぐる論争, 論争を巻き起こす ("to spark"); as an intransitive する-verb: 〜と論争する. 議論 is a neutral "discussion", 口論 a personal verbal quarrel, 喧嘩 a fight or quarrel in general. Rather written language or news language.

examples[].german: We need to be careful about the manipulation of public opinion.
Manipulation of public opinion using social media has become a problem.
The government was criticized for having manipulated public opinion.
en.notes: 世論操作 is the deliberate influencing of public opinion, for example by governments, the media or bots on social networks: 世論操作をする, 〜による世論操作, 世論操作の疑い "suspicion of opinion manipulation". 世論 is read よろん or せろん, and 操作 means "to steer, to manipulate". Not to be confused with 世論調査 ("opinion poll"); similar are 情報操作 ("information manipulation") and プロパガンダ.

examples[].german: I criticize biased reporting.
Some viewers condemned the program as biased reporting.
I make a point of reading several newspapers so that I'm not fooled by biased reporting.
en.notes: 偏向報道 is made up of 偏向 ("one-sided orientation, bias") and 報道 ("news coverage"). The word almost always appears as an accusation in political debates: 〜は偏向報道だ, 偏向報道を批判する. It means distorted, partisan presentation - not necessarily false facts as with フェイクニュース. The opposite concept is 公平/中立な報道. Note the homophone: 変更 ("change") is also read へんこう.

examples[].german: I draw satirical cartoons.
This novel satirizes contemporary society.
That comedy show is funny because its political satire really hits the mark.
en.notes: 風刺 is satire: society, politics or well-known people are criticized through exaggeration and mockery. As a transitive する-verb, the target takes を: 政治を風刺する. Common compounds are 風刺画 "caricature" and 風刺漫画; a pointed satire "hits home": 風刺が効いている. Unlike 皮肉 ("irony, sarcastic remark"), which one makes toward individuals in daily life, 風刺 is a form of criticism in art, literature and the media.

examples[].german: I use figurative expressions.
"Life is a journey" is a metaphor.
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand because of its many metaphors.
en.notes: 比喩 is the umbrella term for figurative expressions of all kinds - metaphor, simile, parable. Typical: 比喩を使う, 比喩的な表現 and 比喩的に言えば "figuratively speaking". Technically, one distinguishes 直喩 (a comparison with ような／みたいな) from 隠喩 or 暗喩 (a metaphor without a comparison word). The word sounds somewhat elevated; in daily life people tend to say たとえ or 例える ("to compare, to use an analogy"). Because of the rare kanji 喩, the spelling 比ゆ is also seen.

examples[].german: This poet uses a lot of metaphors.
"She is the sun" is a metaphor, and "She is like the sun" is a simile.
Let's think about the meaning of the metaphor in the lyrics.
en.notes: 隠喩 is the metaphor in the narrower sense: an image without a comparison word like ような, for example 彼女は太陽だ. The counterpart is 直喩 ("simile", literally "direct comparison") with ような／みたいだ: 太陽のようだ. 隠喩 is a technical term from literature and language teaching and means the same as 暗喩; 隠 means "hidden". In everyday speech one talks more generally of 比喩.

examples[].german: This title contains a metaphor.
A metaphor is a way of comparing without using words like 「ような」.
It is said that a metaphor for war is hidden in his paintings.
en.notes: 暗喩 means "metaphor" and is a synonym of 隠喩: both denote an image without a comparison word (人生は旅だ), in contrast to 直喩 or 明喩 with ような. 暗 ("dark, concealed") and 明 ("bright, open") form the pair of opposites. The word belongs to literary criticism and teaching; typical are 暗喩を使う and 〜の暗喩 "a metaphor for ...". In everyday speech, 比喩 or たとえ is enough.

examples[].german: Waka poetry has many pivot words.
「まつ」 is a pivot word that plays on 「松」 and 「待つ」.
In classics class, I struggled to find the pivot words in this poem.
en.notes: 掛詞 is a stylistic device of classical poetry (waka): one sound-word carries two meanings at once, e.g. まつ as 松 "pine" and 待つ "to wait". One says 掛詞を使う or 〜と〜をかけた掛詞; the related verb is かける ("to combine two meanings"). The term belongs to literature lessons; an everyday wordplay or pun is called ダジャレ. It is also written 掛け詞.

examples[].german: The Manyoshu has many pillow words.
「ひさかたの」 is a pillow word that attaches to 「光」 or 「空」.
The epithet "genius" always comes attached to her name.
en.notes: 枕詞 are fixed epithets of classical poetry, mostly of five morae, placed before a particular word, such as あしひきの before 山 or たらちねの before 母. One says that a 枕詞 "attaches to" a word: 〜にかかる. Their original meaning is often unclear, so they are mostly not translated. In modern Japanese, 枕詞 figuratively denotes a standing epithet or a fixed introductory phrase: 「天才」という枕詞がつく.

examples[].german: This method is effective.
This ticket is valid for three days from the date of issue.
I'm studying English by making effective use of my commuting time.
en.notes: 有効 has two main meanings: "effective" (有効な方法, 時間を有効に使う "to use time wisely") and "valid" (チケットは三日間有効, 有効期限 "period of validity, expiration date"). The opposite is 無効. 効果的 emphasizes only effectiveness, not validity.

examples[].german: Please include a seasonal word.
"Cherry blossoms" is a spring seasonal word.
Which is the seasonal word in this haiku?
en.notes: 季語 are words that indicate the season in a haiku, e.g. 桜 for spring or 紅葉 for autumn. One says 春の季語, 季語を入れる and 季語が入っている; they are collected in seasonal word almanacs (歳時記). The assignment follows the traditional calendar, so for example 月 counts as an autumn word. The humorous 川柳, unlike 俳句, does not need a 季語.

examples[].german: The salaryman senryu are funny.
Unlike haiku, senryu don't need a seasonal word.
My grandfather submits senryu to the newspaper every week.
en.notes: 川柳 is a humorous short poem in the 5-7-5 pattern like the 俳句, but without a 季語 and mostly in everyday language. It pokes fun at human weaknesses, work and family life; competitions such as the サラリーマン川柳 are well known. Typical expressions are 川柳を作る／詠む and 川柳を投稿する. The name goes back to the Edo-period poet 柄井川柳.

en.meaning: Hyakunin Isshu (100 poems by 100 poets; card game)
examples[].german: I'm playing Hyakunin Isshu.
In junior high school, I memorized all of the Hyakunin Isshu.
The Hyakunin Isshu contains a lot of love poems.
en.notes: 百人一首 refers above all to the collection 小倉百人一首: one hundred waka by one hundred poets, compiled in the 13th century. It is also a card game (百人一首かるた), traditionally played at New Year: someone reads a poem aloud, and the players try to grab the card with the second half as fast as possible. One says 百人一首をする／で遊ぶ and 百人一首を覚える; as a competitive sport it is called 競技かるた.

examples[].german: I write letters on Japanese paper.
Washi is thin, yet strong and long-lasting.
The lamp made of washi paper was very beautiful.
en.notes: 和紙 is traditional Japanese paper made from plant fibers, such as those of the paper mulberry (楮). It is thin but tear-resistant and very durable, and is used for calligraphy, 障子 sliding doors, lanterns and handicrafts. The opposite is 洋紙 "Western paper"; the prefix 和 ("Japanese") is also familiar from 和食 and 和室. The handcrafted production (紙すき) is part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

examples[].german: I'm grinding ink.
During calligraphy class, I got ink on my clothes.
After eating squid ink pasta, my teeth turned black.
en.notes: 墨 is black ink, originally a solid ink stick that is ground with water on an 硯 (inkstone): 墨をする (also written 磨る or 擦る). Ready-made liquid ink is called 墨汁. 墨 also refers to the ink of squid and octopus, as in イカ墨. Well-known compounds are 水墨画 "ink wash painting" and 墨色 "ink black".

examples[].german: I grind ink on the inkstone.
After calligraphy, let's wash the inkstone clean.
My grandfather's inkstone is said to be more than a hundred years old.
en.notes: 硯 is the grinding stone on which one rubs an ink stick with a little water to make ink: 硯で墨をする. Together with 筆, 墨 and 紙, it is one of the "four treasures of the study" (文房四宝). Since 硯 is not a standard kanji (常用漢字), the word is often written すずり. A box for inkstone and writing utensils is called 硯箱.

examples[].german: I write characters with a brush.
I left my pencil case at home.
She loves writing and often sends me letters.
en.notes: 筆 is the brush for writing and painting; one says 筆で書く and counts with 本. Many derivatives relate to writing in general: 筆箱 "pencil case" (also for pencils), 筆者 "author", 筆まめ "diligent at writing", 筆が速い "to write quickly". Well known is the proverb 弘法も筆の誤り "Even masters make mistakes". A painting brush is more precisely called 絵筆.

examples[].german: I practice by writing on many sheets of calligraphy paper.
I'm going to a calligraphy class, so I bought calligraphy paper and ink.
Calligraphy paper is thin, so please put newspaper underneath.
en.notes: 半紙 is the standardized calligraphy paper (about 24 x 33 cm) that students practice on in 書道 class. It is thin and absorbent, so one puts a pad or newspaper underneath to keep the ink from soaking through. It is counted with 枚: 半紙を一枚. In daily life, 半紙 is practically always connected with 書道; ordinary writing paper is called 便箋 or simply 紙.

examples[].german: I stamp the document with a red seal.
I received a goshuin at the temple.
Every time I travel, I take my goshuin book and visit shrines.
en.notes: 朱印 is a seal impression stamped in red ink: 朱印を押す. Today it is mostly encountered as 御朱印: artistic stamps with brush writing that one receives for a donation at temples and shrines and collects in a 御朱印帳. For this one politely says 御朱印をいただく, not 買う. Historically there are the 朱印状, permits sealed in red by the shoguns.

examples[].german: I registered my registered seal at city hall.
When buying a house, you need your registered seal and a seal certificate.
My registered seal is important, so I keep it in a safe.
en.notes: 実印 is the personal seal registered at the city hall (印鑑登録). It is used for important contracts such as buying a house or a car and presented together with the 印鑑証明. It is distinguished from the 銀行印 deposited with the bank and the simple 認印 for everyday use. A seal in general is called 印鑑, colloquially はんこ.

examples[].german: This ticket is invalid.
Expired coupons become invalid.
I disabled notifications in the settings.
en.notes: 無効 means "invalid, void" - for tickets, contracts, coupons or votes (無効票): 無効になる "to become invalid". In IT, 無効にする means "to disable" (opposite 有効にする). For "ineffective", everyday speech tends to use 効果がない. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 向こう "over there".

examples[].german: An informal seal is fine.
I stamped my informal seal when receiving the package.
You can buy an informal seal even at a 100-yen shop.
en.notes: 認印 is a simple, unregistered name stamp for everyday purposes, such as signing for parcels or for internal forms. One says 認印を押す; on forms 認印可 "an ordinary stamp is acceptable" often appears. Self-inking stamps (シャチハタ) are nevertheless often not accepted for this. The counterpart is the officially registered 実印.

examples[].german: You stamp a seal after dipping it in the red ink pad.
The red ink pad was dry, so I couldn't stamp cleanly.
I went to the reception desk to borrow a red ink pad.
en.notes: 朱肉 is the red stamp ink, or the ink pad, with which one stamps a はんこ: 朱肉をつけて押す. Seals such as 実印 or 認印 are almost always stamped in red in Japan. For normal stamps with black or blue ink, one says スタンプ台 instead of 朱肉. A stamp with built-in ink (シャチハタ) does not need 朱肉.

examples[].german: I'll send it by registered mail.
When sending money, you must use cash registered mail.
A registered letter arrived, so I signed for it.
en.notes: 書留 is mail sent as registered mail: 書留で送る. Japan Post offers, among others, the normal 一般書留, the cheaper 簡易書留, and 現金書留, the only permitted way to send cash. Receipt is confirmed by signature or seal. The word comes from 書き留める "to note down, record": the item is registered.

examples[].german: Please check the address.
I sent the email to the wrong recipient.
The letter came back as addressee unknown.
en.notes: 宛先 is the destination address or the recipient of a shipment - for letters as well as for emails (メールの宛先). Typical are 宛先を書く, 宛先を間違える and 宛先不明 "addressee unknown". The recipient's name alone is more likely called 宛名; the counterpart is 差出人 "sender". 宛 also serves as a suffix: 田中様宛て "to Mr. Tanaka".

examples[].german: Please write the sender.
A letter arrived with no sender's name.
It's better not to open emails from unknown senders.
en.notes: 差出人 is the sender of a letter or parcel, the counterpart of 宛先 or 受取人. The word is rather formal and appears on forms and envelopes; in conversation one also says 送り主, and for emails 送信者. Typical are 差出人の住所 and 差出人不明. The underlying verb is 差し出す "to submit, to send off", hence also the spelling 差し出し人.

examples[].german: I'll check the date of the postmark.
The deadline is March 31; the postmark date counts.
My father carefully collects old stamps that still carry a postmark too.
en.notes: 消印 is the postmark that cancels the stamp (消す "to erase, to invalidate"). The key formula is 〇月〇日消印有効: for mailed submissions, the date of the postmark counts, not the date of receipt. You say 消印を押す; it is the post office that stamps, not the sender. Do not confuse it with personal seals such as 認印 or 実印.

en.meaning: notice of absence (delivery slip); out-of-office notice
examples[].german: There was a notice of absence in the mailbox.
I saw the notice and asked for redelivery.
I will set up an out-of-office reply for my email while I am on vacation.
en.notes: 不在通知 in everyday life is mainly the notification card that the post office or a delivery service drops in the mailbox when nobody was home; its official name is ご不在連絡票, abbreviated 不在票. It states how to request 再配達 ("redelivery"). In the office, the word also refers to the automatic out-of-office reply by email. Typical are 不在通知が入っている and 不在通知を設定する.

examples[].german: I'm having my mail forwarded.
Please forward this email to the department head.
When I'm out, I forward calls to my cell phone.
en.notes: 転送 means "forwarding": emails, calls or mail are sent on to another address. As a transitive する-verb: メールを上司に転送する, 電話を携帯に転送する. After a move, a 転居届 filed with the post office ensures that letters are forwarded for one year. To be distinguished from 送信 ("to send") and 返信 ("to reply"); in IT, 転送 also means "data transfer".

examples[].german: I'm specifying a delivery time.
When I was a student, I had a part-time job delivering newspapers.
The package will be delivered tomorrow morning.
en.notes: 配達 is the delivery of mail, packages, newspapers or food right to the front door. As a transitive する-verb: 荷物を配達する, passive 配達される. Important compounds are 新聞配達, 配達員 "delivery person" and 再配達 "redelivery". 配送 stresses more the whole transport route from the company, 宅配 delivery to the home; ordered food is also called 出前 or デリバリー.

en.meaning: specifying a date and time; requested delivery date and time
examples[].german: I'll send it with a specified date and time.
I'm not home on weekdays, so I specified Saturday morning for delivery.
This ticket is for a specified date and time, so you can't enter on any other day.
en.notes: 日時指定 is made up of 日時 "date and time" and 指定 "to specify" and mainly refers to choosing a delivery time when shipping something: 日時指定で送る, 日時指定をする. Admission tickets can also be 日時指定; they are then valid only for a certain day and time slot (日時指定券). Related patterns with 指定 are 時間指定 "requested time of day" and 指定席 "reserved seat".

examples[].german: Teamwork is indispensable.
For plants to grow, water and light are essential.
Smartphones have become something indispensable in life today.
en.notes: 不可欠 is composed of 不 "not", 可 "possible" and 欠 "to lack": "must not be missing, essential". Typical: 〜に不可欠だ, 〜にとって不可欠な, and the fixed combination 必要不可欠 "absolutely necessary". It is stronger and more formal than 必要; colloquially one says 欠かせない.

examples[].german: I'll ship it prepaid.
For returns for customer-side reasons, please pay the shipping yourself.
Please tick on the slip whether it is prepaid or cash on delivery.
en.notes: 元払い means that the sender pays the shipping costs when handing in the item - "postage paid, delivered free of charge". The opposite is 着払い (the recipient pays); with courier companies 発払い is also used. Typical uses are 元払いで発送する and 送料元払い. For returns, shops specify whether 元払い or 着払い applies.

examples[].german: I pack it carefully.
Before the move, I packed all my books into cardboard boxes.
The product was sloppily packed, and the box was crushed.
en.notes: 梱包 is the transport-safe packing of goods for shipping or moving, mostly in cardboard boxes with cushioning material. As a transitive する-verb: 商品を梱包する, 段ボールに梱包する. To be distinguished from 包装 ("wrapping, gift wrapping") and 荷造り ("packing one's things for a trip or a move"). Common compounds are 梱包材 "packing material" and 梱包作業.

examples[].german: I'm packing it into cardboard boxes.
I picked up twenty cardboard boxes for the move.
Please put cardboard boxes out on recyclables collection day.
en.notes: 段ボール is corrugated cardboard and, above all, the box made from it (more precisely 段ボール箱). The word mixes kanji and katakana: 段 "step" for the corrugated layer and ボール from English "board"; it is very often written entirely in katakana as ダンボール. Typical are 段ボールに詰める, 段ボールを組み立てる and 段ボールをつぶす. It is counted with 箱 or 個.

examples[].german: I'm wrapping it in cushioning material.
It's fragile, so please put in plenty of cushioning material.
The box was full of packing material, and the item itself was tiny.
en.notes: 緩衝材 is cushioning or filling material that protects goods in a package from impact, e.g. bubble wrap, paper or Styrofoam (発泡スチロール). 緩衝 means "to cushion, to buffer"; the word sounds somewhat technical and often appears in shipping instructions. Typical are 緩衝材で包む and 緩衝材を入れる／詰める. Bubble wrap is usually called プチプチ in daily life.

examples[].german: I'll issue a slip.
Please bring this order slip to the register when paying.
I wrote my address and name on the parcel delivery slip.
en.notes: 伝票 is a slip or voucher that records a transaction: in a restaurant the order slip you hand in at the register, with a courier the waybill (宅配便の伝票), in accounting a journal voucher. Typical uses are 伝票を書く and 伝票を切る "to issue a slip"; it is counted with 枚. Do not confuse it with 領収書 ("receipt") or レシート ("register receipt").

examples[].german: I'll prepare a waybill.
Please write the item name and the delivery address on the waybill.
Don't throw away the copy of the waybill until the package has arrived.
en.notes: 送り状 is the accompanying document of a shipment: the waybill or label with recipient and sender details, and in commerce also the delivery invoice. Courier companies often use 伝票 or 配送伝票 with the same meaning. Typical uses are 送り状を書く／作成する／貼る and 送り状の控え "the sender's copy". The word is rather businesslike.

examples[].german: Please tell me the tracking number.
With the tracking number, you can check where the package is now.
After shipping, we will notify you of the tracking number by email.
en.notes: 追跡番号 is the shipment number with which you can follow online where a package currently is (追跡 "to track"). Japanese delivery services often officially call it お問い合わせ番号 or 伝票番号. Typical are 追跡番号を教える／入力する and 追跡番号で調べる. The tracking itself is called 荷物を追跡する.

examples[].german: Popular products are currently out of stock.
The out-of-stock items are scheduled to arrive next week.
When I tried to assemble the furniture, one screw was missing.
en.notes: 欠品 means that an item is missing from or not in stock at a store or warehouse; it is a term from retail and logistics. Typical are 欠品中, 欠品している and 欠品が出る. From the customer's point of view, one tends to say 売り切れ ("sold out") or 在庫切れ. A second meaning is a missing part in a delivery, for example with furniture kits.

examples[].german: New products have arrived in stock.
This product is currently awaiting restock.
When it's back in stock, we'll let you know by email.
en.notes: 入荷 is the arrival of goods at a store or warehouse. Mostly intransitive: 商品が入荷する; from the store's point of view also transitive: 新商品を入荷する. On signs you often read 入荷待ち "awaiting restock", 再入荷 "back in stock" and 新入荷 "newly arrived". The counterpart is 出荷 "shipment, dispatch".

examples[].german: My health is good.
The refrigerator door was left open.
This used bicycle is in very good condition.
en.notes: 状態 is the state of something at a given time: 健康状態, 体の状態, 部屋の状態. After a verb in the た-form, 〜た状態 describes a state that continues after an action: ドアが開いた状態, 電気をつけた状態で寝る. Fitting expressions are 状態がいい / 悪い and 〜状態になる. 状況, by contrast, means the external overall situation, and 様子 more the visible appearance or behavior.

en.meaning: to evaluate; to assess; to appreciate
examples[].german: My work was appreciated.
I chose it by evaluating not only the price but also the ease of use.
The teacher thinks highly of the students' efforts.
en.notes: 評価する means "to evaluate, to assess" and, especially with 高く, "to appreciate, to value": 努力を高く評価する. The passive 評価される therefore often means "to receive recognition", not just "to be graded": 仕事が評価された. The noun 評価 stands for ratings and grades (評価が高い, 五段階評価), and on the internet also for customer reviews.

examples[].german: There are diverse opinions.
People with diverse cultures live in this town.
Ways of working have become more diverse.
en.notes: 多様 is a な-adjective for "diverse, varied" and sounds rather written: 多様な文化・価値観・働き方. Related: 多様化 "diversification", 多様性 "diversity" and the set phrase 多種多様 "of all kinds". In conversation one usually says いろいろな or さまざまな.

examples[].german: We ship today.
Because of the typhoon, vegetable shipments are delayed.
This factory ships 10,000 products a day.
en.notes: 出荷 is the shipping of goods from a manufacturer, farm or warehouse to retailers or customers. As a transitive する-verb: 商品を出荷する; in online shopping, 本日出荷 means "ships today". In contrast to 発送 ("to send off", also by private individuals), 出荷 sounds commercial and implies larger quantities. The counterpart is 入荷.

examples[].german: We do the stocktaking at the end of the month.
Because of stocktaking, we will open tomorrow only from the afternoon.
Once a year, I take stock of my own skills.
en.notes: 棚卸し is stocktaking: the stock of goods is counted and valued (literally "taking goods down from the shelf"). Typical uses are 棚卸しをする, 棚卸しのため休業 and 年末の棚卸し; in business texts it is also written without し: 棚卸. Figuratively one says キャリアの棚卸し "taking stock of one's career". The older meaning "picking at others' faults" (人の棚卸しをする) is rare.

examples[].german: Gourmet specialties ordered in from around the country are popular.
We don't have it in stock, so it will have to be a special order.
A special order takes about a week.
en.notes: 取り寄せ is ordering an item that is not in stock or that comes from another region; the related verb is 取り寄せる ("to have sent in, to order in"). In a shop you hear お取り寄せになります "We'll have to order that in". With お, お取り寄せ is also a trend word for regional specialties ordered online (お取り寄せグルメ). More general is 注文 "order".

examples[].german: I bought it by mail order.
Recently I often buy even clothes through online shopping.
When I watch TV shopping late at night, I end up wanting something.
en.notes: 通販 is the short form of 通信販売 "mail-order sales" and today mainly means online shopping. Typical are 通販で買う, ネット通販, 通販サイト and テレビ通販 "TV shopping". The word is neutral and everyday; the long form 通信販売 sounds more formal. For shopping on the internet, people also say ネットショッピング.

examples[].german: I'm going to the bank counter.
Please wait at counter number 3.
Mr. Tanaka will be the point of contact for this matter.
en.notes: 窓口 is the counter at a bank, post office, station or government office where you are served: 窓口に行く, 〇番の窓口. Figuratively it means "point of contact": 相談窓口 "consultation desk", 〜の窓口になる "to be in charge of ...". In both meanings the word is very common and neutral.

examples[].german: Please take a numbered ticket.
Please pay the fare in the column matching the number on your ticket.
The popular bakery hands out numbered tickets from 9 a.m.
en.notes: 整理券 is a numbered card that regulates the order: when there is a big crowd in front of shops or events (整理券を配る), or at counters. On many local buses you take a 整理券 when boarding; its number shows the fare on the display board. Typical are 整理券を取る／もらう and 整理券番号. A reusable numbered tag made of plastic is more often called 番号札.

examples[].german: Please wait until the number on your tag is called.
Please take your number tag and wait at your seat.
When I checked my coat, I was handed a number tag.
en.notes: 番号札 is a small tag or card with a number, e.g. a cloakroom tag, a waiting number at a counter or a pickup number at a restaurant. Unlike the 整理券, which is mostly made of paper, a 番号札 is often made of plastic or wood and is returned afterwards. 札 is read ふだ here ("sign, tablet"), not さつ as in banknotes. Typical are 番号札を取る／渡す／持つ.

examples[].german: I have no small change.
I dropped my coin purse.
Excuse me, I have a lot of coins - may I pay with them?
en.notes: 小銭 is small change, especially coins: 小銭がない, 小銭を出す, 小銭入れ "coin purse". In conversation people also say 細かいお金 or simply 細かいの. A second meaning is a small amount of money, as in 小銭を稼ぐ "to earn a little extra money". The official word for coin is 硬貨.

examples[].german: In 1,000-yen bills, please.
There wasn't a single bill in my wallet.
This vending machine doesn't accept 10,000-yen bills.
en.notes: 札 (さつ) is a banknote. On its own it is mostly used politely as お札, otherwise as a suffix: 千円札, 一万円札, 札束 "bundle of banknotes"; it is counted with 枚. Careful: with the reading ふだ, the same kanji means "sign, tablet", and お札 (おふだ) is a protective amulet from a shrine. The formal word for banknote is 紙幣.

examples[].german: I collect coins.
This machine only accepts coins.
It was decided to issue a commemorative coin for the Olympics.
en.notes: 硬貨 is the official, rather formal word for coin and the counterpart of 紙幣 "banknote". It appears on machines, in the news and among collectors: 記念硬貨 "commemorative coin", 硬貨投入口 "coin slot". In conversation people mostly say 小銭 or, specifically, 百円玉, 十円玉. Rarely, 硬貨 also means "hard currency".

examples[].german: Let's act carefully.
It's an important matter, so I will decide after thinking it over carefully.
It breaks easily, so please carry it carefully.
en.notes: 慎重 is a な-adjective meaning "careful, circumspect, deliberate": one acts or decides only after thorough consideration: 慎重に検討する, 慎重に選ぶ, 慎重な性格. The opposite is 軽率 "rash". 気をつける is more about watchfulness toward dangers, 丁寧 about care and politeness. Do not confuse it with the identically read 身長 "body height".

examples[].german: I put money into the piggy bank.
I save only 500-yen coins in my piggy bank.
The piggy bank was full, so I opened it.
en.notes: 貯金箱 is a piggy bank or coin bank into which you put coins: 貯金箱に入れる, 貯金箱にためる. The classic piggy bank is called 豚の貯金箱. 貯金 is everyday saving; bank deposits in the narrower sense are 預金. It is popular to collect only one particular coin in the 貯金箱, for example as 五百円玉貯金.

examples[].german: I'll have my passbook updated.
I got a passbook when I opened the account.
Recently, there are many online banks with no paper passbook.
en.notes: 通帳 is the passbook of a bank or post office in which deposits and withdrawals are recorded (預金通帳); it exists for ordinary checking accounts as well, not only for savings accounts. At the ATM you have it updated: 通帳記入 or 記帳. For transactions at the counter you traditionally need 通帳と印鑑. Many banks now offer accounts without a paper book (通帳なし, ネット通帳).

examples[].german: Please enter your PIN.
I entered my PIN wrong three times and now the card is blocked.
It's dangerous to use your birthday as your PIN.
en.notes: 暗証番号 is the secret number (PIN) for a bank card, credit card, locker or government card. Typical are 暗証番号を入力する／押す and 暗証番号を忘れる／間違える. Unlike パスワード, a 暗証番号 usually consists only of digits, often four. 暗証 is composed of 暗 "hidden" and 証 "proof".

examples[].german: I obtained a seal registration certificate.
You can get a seal registration certificate at city hall or a convenience store.
When I bought a car, I was told to submit two seal registration certificates.
en.notes: 印鑑証明 is the official certificate that a seal (実印) is registered with the municipality; the document is officially called 印鑑登録証明書. You need it for important contracts such as buying real estate or a car. Typical are 印鑑証明を取る／取得する and 印鑑証明が必要だ; it is counted with 通. You can have it issued at city hall or, with the マイナンバーカード, also at a コンビニ.

examples[].german: I need a certified copy of the family register.
When you get married, a new family register is created for the two of you.
Even if a foreigner marries a Japanese person, they cannot have a family register.
en.notes: 戸籍 is the Japanese family register, in which births, marriages, divorces and deaths of family members are recorded. For official procedures you need extracts: 戸籍謄本 (full copy) or 戸籍抄本 (partial extract). Typical are 戸籍に入る／入れる and 戸籍を移す. To be clearly distinguished from it is the 住民票 ("certificate of residence"); foreign nationals do not have their own 戸籍.

examples[].german: I'm going to pick up a certificate of residence.
After moving, you have to transfer your residence registration.
Nowadays you can even get a certificate of residence at a convenience store.
en.notes: 住民票 is the certificate of residence that you get at the 市役所 or 区役所; one says 住民票を取る or 住民票を取りに行く. Officially you receive a copy, the 住民票の写し, which serves as proof of residence for employers, banks or landlords. When you move to another municipality, you "transfer" your registration: 住民票を移す. Not to be confused with the 戸籍, the family register.

examples[].german: I'm submitting a moving-out notification.
Please file a moving-out notification at city hall before you move.
I hear you can also file a moving-out notification online.
en.notes: 転出届 is the notification you file before moving to another municipality at your current 市役所 or 区役所: 転出届を出す or, more formally, 転出届を提出する. You receive the 転出証明書 for it, which you need at your new place of residence for the 転入届. For a move within the same municipality, a 転居届 is enough instead. The 届 ("notification, report") is read どけ here.

examples[].german: I filed a moving-in notification.
You must file a moving-in notification within 14 days of moving.
When you file the moving-in notification, please bring your moving-out certificate.
en.notes: 転入届 is the registration at your new place of residence when you move in from another municipality; it must be filed at the 市役所 or 区役所 within 14 days of moving in. Typical: 転入届を出す / 提出する. You must bring the 転出証明書 from your old place of residence, which you received when filing the 転出届. For a move within the same city, people say 転居届.

examples[].german: We submitted our marriage registration.
The marriage registration form needs the signatures of two witnesses.
Many couples file their marriage registration on November 22.
en.notes: 婚姻届 is not a marriage certificate but the form with which you register a marriage at the municipal office. In Japan you are legally married as soon as the 婚姻届 is accepted; therefore 婚姻届を出す practically means "to get married officially" (colloquially also 入籍する). The form needs the signatures of both partners and of two witnesses (証人). Many people choose a special date for it.

examples[].german: I will submit the birth notification.
Since the baby's name was decided, my husband went to the ward office to submit the birth notification.
The birth notification must be submitted within 14 days of birth.
en.notes: 出生届 is the official registration of a birth, not a certificate; it is submitted to the 市役所 or 区役所 within 14 days after the birth: 出生届を出す / 提出する. On the same form, the doctor or midwife confirms the birth (出生証明書), and the parents enter the child's name. The standard reading is しゅっしょう, but in everyday speech you also hear しゅっせい.

examples[].german: That's a bold plan.
She boldly had her hair cut short.
A bold design using red and green is popular.
en.notes: 大胆 is a な-adjective for "bold, daring, fearless" (literally "big gall bladder", in the sense of great courage).
