It can praise (大胆なアイデア, 大胆なデザイン) or sound slightly critical, "audacious, reckless". Often adverbial: 大胆に変える. Opposite: 慎重 or 臆病. 勇敢, by contrast, is bravery in the face of danger.

en.meaning: power of attorney; letter of proxy
examples[].german: Please write a letter of proxy.
If a representative comes, a letter of proxy is required.
With my mother's letter of proxy, I took care of the procedures at the bank.
en.notes: 委任状 is a written authorization by which you commission someone to act in your place, for example at government offices or banks. Typical: 委任状を書く / 作成する, 委任状を持参する; the authorized person is called 代理人. The related verb is 委任する "to entrust, to delegate". Offices often require: 代理の場合は委任状が必要です.

examples[].german: I need a medical certificate.
Since I missed work, I had a doctor write me a medical certificate.
I sent the insurance company a medical certificate about my accident injuries.
en.notes: 診断書 is a medical certificate or report on an illness or injury. You have the doctor write it (医者に診断書を書いてもらう) and submit it to a company, school or insurance company (診断書を提出する). In Japan it usually costs money. Not to be confused with 処方箋, the prescription for medication.

examples[].german: I submitted a written apology.
I lost my company laptop and was made to write a written apology.
The department head told me that if I'm late again, I'll have to write a written apology.
en.notes: 始末書 is a written statement with an apology that an employee has to hand to a superior after a mistake or misconduct (e.g. lateness, loss of company property). Typical: 始末書を書く, 始末書を提出する and often the causative-passive 始末書を書かされる "to be made to write a written apology". A neutral report without an admission of guilt is called 報告書; at school, people tend to write a 反省文.

examples[].german: Please sign the written pledge.
When you lend money, it's better to have them write a written pledge.
I was made to write a pledge that I would never do it again.
en.notes: 念書 is a signed written assurance, mostly between private individuals, for example that one will repay borrowed money or will not do something again. You say 念書を書く (to write one yourself), 念書を取る (to have someone give you one) and 念書にサインする. More formal, and often a prepared form, is the 誓約書; a full contract is called 契約書.

examples[].german: I'm signing the written pledge.
When I joined the company, I submitted a pledge to keep secrets.
When I joined the gym, I signed a pledge stating that I'm responsible for any injury myself.
en.notes: 誓約書 is a written declaration of commitment in which you promise (誓う "to swear, to pledge") to follow certain rules, such as confidentiality when joining a company or a liability waiver at a gym. It is not an oath in court; usually it is a prepared form: 誓約書に署名する / サインする, 誓約書を提出する. Less formal private assurances are more often called 念書.

examples[].german: We exchanged a memorandum.
Before the formal contract, let's first draw up a memorandum.
My grandfather's notes were found in an old diary.
en.notes: 覚書 (also written 覚え書き) is, in business, a written agreement or declaration of intent that is less comprehensive than a contract (契約書); you say 覚書を交わす or 覚書を結ぶ. In diplomacy it means a memorandum. It can also mean personal notes, but in everyday life メモ is usually used for that.

examples[].german: The sound of the koto is beautiful.
My grandmother plays the koto for us at New Year.
I joined a koto club at university.
en.notes: 琴 is the traditional Japanese zither with usually 13 strings, which is plucked with finger picks. One "plays" it with 弾く: 琴を弾く; its sound is called 琴の音色. Technically the instrument is written 箏, but in daily life it is almost always written 琴. A Western harp, on the other hand, is called ハープ.

examples[].german: I want to learn the shamisen.
Tsugaru shamisen playing is very powerful.
At the festival, I danced to the shamisen.
en.notes: 三味線 is the three-stringed Japanese long-necked lute, played with a large plectrum (撥); one says 三味線を弾く. It accompanies kabuki, folk songs and festivals; particularly powerful is the 津軽三味線 style, in which the reading changes to じゃみせん. Colloquially, 三味線を弾く also means "to put on an act, to evade".

examples[].german: The sound of the shakuhachi echoes.
After retiring, my father began playing the shakuhachi.
I went to hear a concert of shakuhachi and koto together.
en.notes: 尺八 is the Japanese bamboo flute played held vertically; its name comes from its standard length 一尺八寸 (about 54 cm). It is played with 吹く: 尺八を吹く. It is typically played together with the 琴 and the 三味線. Note: in vulgar slang the word also has a sexual meaning, but in normal contexts everyone thinks of the instrument.

examples[].german: I saw a taiko performance.
At the summer festival, the children were beating the drum.
I'll personally vouch for the taste of this restaurant.
en.notes: 太鼓 is the (traditional Japanese) drum; you strike it with たたく: 太鼓をたたく. To set it clearly apart from Western instruments, 和太鼓 is used; a drum set is called ドラム. A well-known idiom is 太鼓判を押す "to guarantee something, to vouch for something" (literally "to press a big seal").

examples[].german: It is a groundbreaking invention.
This is a groundbreaking product that makes housework easier.
The arrival of the internet changed the way information is conveyed in a revolutionary way.
en.notes: 画期的 is a な-adjective for "groundbreaking, epoch-making" - 画期 literally means "to mark off an epoch". It is always positive and typical of technology, inventions and advertising: 画期的な発明・技術・商品. Adverbial 画期的に変わる "to change fundamentally". Stronger than 新しい, similar to 革命的.

examples[].german: I practice playing the flute.
The referee blew the whistle, and the game began.
From far away I can hear the flutes of the festival.
en.notes: 笛 is a general term for flutes and whistles: from the Japanese transverse flute at festivals to the referee's whistle. One blows it with 吹く: 笛を吹く; the sound is called 笛の音. The recorder at school is usually called リコーダー, and a whistle also ホイッスル. Whistling with the mouth is 口笛を吹く.

examples[].german: I can hear the sound of a bell.
I put a bell on the cat's collar.
When I climb in the mountains, I take a bear bell with me.
en.notes: 鈴 is a small, usually spherical bell with a ball inside, as seen at shrines, on cat collars or as a bear bell when hiking. Typical uses: 鈴が鳴る (intransitive), 鈴を鳴らす (transitive), 鈴をつける. A large temple bell is called 鐘, a doorbell ベル or チャイム. Onomatopoeically, a 鈴 sounds like チリンチリン.

examples[].german: I bought a silk scarf.
This kimono is made of silk.
Can you buy silken tofu at the supermarket?
en.notes: 絹 is silk as a material; before items of clothing it takes の: 絹のスカーフ, 絹のブラウス. When shopping, the loanword シルク is at least as common. Also well known is 絹ごし豆腐 "silken tofu", the especially delicate tofu in contrast to the firmer 木綿豆腐. Other materials are 綿 (cotton) and ウール or 毛 (wool).

examples[].german: Linen clothes are cool.
This tablecloth is made of linen.
In the old days, rope and cloth were made from hemp.
en.notes: 麻 refers both to the hemp plant and to fibers and fabrics such as linen or ramie; on clothing labels, 麻 stands for linen. Typical: 麻の服, 麻のシャツ, which are considered cool in summer. The drug cannabis, by contrast, is called 大麻; the character is also found in 麻薬 "narcotics". Linen as a fashion word is also リネン.

examples[].german: The cotton batting in my futon has gotten old and hard.
Stuffing is coming out of the stuffed toy.
I got cotton candy at the festival.
en.notes: 綿 with the reading わた means raw cotton, the cotton plant and above all stuffing, such as in a 布団 or stuffed toys; cotton candy is called 綿あめ or 綿菓子. For the fabric on clothing labels, the same character is read めん (綿100%), or people say 木綿 or コットン. A cotton shirt is therefore 綿 (めん) のシャツ, not わた.

examples[].german: I'm learning the technique of weaving cloth.
My grandmother used to weave the cloth for her kimonos herself.
In this region, carpets are still woven by hand.
en.notes: 織る means "to weave" and is transitive: 布を織る, 着物の生地を織る; the result is an 織物 ("woven fabric, textile"), the loom is called 機 (はた), hence also 機を織る. There is no intransitive counterpart. Not to be confused with the similar-sounding 折る "to fold, to break" or with 降りる "to get off". Figuratively: 織り込む "to weave in, to incorporate".

examples[].german: I train at the dojo.
When I was a child, I went to a karate dojo every week.
When entering the dojo, you always bow.
en.notes: 道場 is the training hall for martial arts such as 柔道, 剣道 or 空手; one says 道場に通う "to go to the dojo regularly" and 道場で稽古する "to train". One bows when entering and leaving (礼をする). An ordinary sports hall is called 体育館, a gym ジム. Originally, the word referred to a place of Buddhist practice.

examples[].german: I passed the third-dan exam.
He has a second dan in judo.
It took me five years to get my first dan.
en.notes: 段 here means the master grade (dan) in martial arts, Go or Shogi. The first grade is called 初段, not 一段; after that come 二段, 三段 and so on, and the student grades below it are called 級. One says 段を取る or 三段に合格する; "He has a 2nd dan in judo" is 柔道二段だ. In daily life, 段 also means "step, level", for example for stairs (階段) or shelves.

examples[].german: I cook rice in an iron pot.
Please wash the inner pot of the rice cooker.
He and I have shared the same pot of rice; we are very close.
en.notes: 釜 is a heavy (iron) pot, mainly for cooking rice, often politely お釜; the inner pot of a rice cooker is also called 釜 or 内釜, and the tea kettle in the tea ceremony 茶釜. A dish is 釜飯, rice cooked in a pot. For stews you use a 鍋, for water a やかん. Idiom: 同じ釜の飯を食う "to have lived and worked closely together".

examples[].german: I put water in the bucket.
I transfer the rice into the sushi tub and mix in vinegar.
At the onsen, I poured hot water over my body with a wooden bucket.
en.notes: 桶 is a tub or bucket, traditionally made of wood: 桶に水を入れる / くむ. Well known are the 寿司桶 for sushi rice, the 手桶 as a ladle bucket and the bath bucket at an onsen; the coffin is also called 棺桶. A modern bucket made of plastic or metal is usually called バケツ.

examples[].german: I will judge taking everything into account.
Taking everything into account, I think this proposal is the best.
The company evaluates the results of the exam and interview comprehensively.
en.notes: 総合的 means "comprehensive, holistic" - looking at all factors together. Very common: 総合的に判断する／評価する／見る "to judge all things considered". Without 的, 総合 appears in compounds such as 総合病院 "general hospital" or 総合大学 "comprehensive university". 全体的 describes more the overall impression ("on the whole").

examples[].german: I pound mochi with the pestle.
I raised the pestle and brought it down with all my strength.
They say a rabbit on the moon is pounding mochi with a pestle.
en.notes: 杵 is the large wooden mallet or pestle used to pound steamed rice into mochi in a 臼; you say 杵で餅をつく. In the traditional 餅つき at New Year, one person strikes with the 杵 while another turns the dough by hand. In Japan it is said that you can see a rabbit in the moon pounding mochi with a 杵.

examples[].german: We make mochi with a mortar and pestle.
Buckwheat flour is being ground with a stone mill.
Before pounding mochi, the mortar is warmed with hot water.
en.notes: 臼 is a mortar or millstone. For pounding mochi, a large 臼 made of wood or stone is used together with the pestle 杵: 臼と杵で餅をつく. A grindstone for flour or tea is called 石臼, and you grind (ひく) with it. The character is also found in 臼歯 (きゅうし) "molar", literally "mortar tooth".

examples[].german: I drink tea from a teacup.
I bought five teacups for guests.
The large teacups at the sushi restaurant have fish kanji written on them.
en.notes: 湯呑み is the handleless Japanese teacup for everyday green tea; it is the short form of 湯呑み茶碗 and is also written 湯飲み or 湯のみ. A cup with a handle is called カップ or マグカップ. Do not confuse it with 茶碗, which in everyday use mainly means the rice bowl (and in the tea ceremony also the matcha bowl).

examples[].german: I pour sake into the flask.
I ordered hot sake in a flask.
My father often wore turtleneck sweaters in the old days.
en.notes: 徳利 is the bulbous flask with a narrow neck in which sake is served (often warmed); you drink from it into small cups (お猪口). In restaurants one often orders with the synonym お銚子: お銚子を一本. Because of its shape, a turtleneck sweater is colloquially also called とっくり(のセーター), though today タートルネック is usual. The word is often written in kana.

examples[].german: I enjoy sake from a small cup.
Please bring two sake cups.
The strong wind turned my umbrella inside out.
en.notes: 猪口 is the small sake cup that you drink from together with the 徳利. It is almost always said politely as お猪口 and usually written in kana: おちょこ. A well-known expression is 傘がおちょこになる "the umbrella turns inside out (in the wind)", because it then looks like a small cup. For Western-style glasses, グラス is used.

examples[].german: I cut vegetables on the cutting board.
I disinfect the used cutting board with boiling water.
Before the operation, I felt completely at the mercy of fate.
en.notes: 俎板 is the cutting board in the kitchen; today it is almost always written まな板, and the spelling 俎板 is rare. You cut on it: まな板の上で切る. The idiom まな板の(上の)鯉 "a carp on the cutting board" describes someone who is at the mercy of fate and can do nothing more, for example before an operation or exam results.

examples[].german: I grate daikon radish with the grater.
If you don't wash the grater right after use, the dirt is hard to remove.
I bought a small grater at the 100-yen shop.
en.notes: おろし金 is the fine Japanese grater, used mainly to grate daikon radish, ginger or wasabi. The matching verb is おろす or すりおろす: 大根をおろす; the result is called 大根おろし. The 金 stands for the metal it is traditionally made of and is read がね in this word. A coarse grater for cheese or vegetables is more often called グレーター or スライサー.

examples[].german: This route is convenient.
I got a route map at the station.
The company greatly changed its management course.
en.notes: 路線 is the transport line or route of a train, bus or aircraft: 路線バス "local bus", 路線図 "route map", 新しい路線が開通する. An individual named railway line is designated with 〜線 (山手線). Figuratively, 路線 also means the "course" of an organization or policy: 路線を変更する, 改革路線.

examples[].german: The overhead wire snapped and the train stopped.
Because a balloon got caught in the overhead wire, service is suspended.
The overhead wire swayed in the strong wind and sparks flew.
en.notes: 架線 is the overhead wire above railway tracks; you mostly hear the word in announcements and news about disruptions: 架線トラブル, 架線が切れる, 架線に物が引っかかる. Note that there are homophones: 河川 "rivers", 化繊 "synthetic fiber" and 下線 "underline"; in railway jargon it is therefore often said がせん. General power lines are usually called 電線.

examples[].german: I bought a coupon ticket.
With a coupon booklet, you get 11 rides for the price of 10.
The coffee coupon booklet of this shop is a good deal.
en.notes: 回数券 is a booklet of tickets or multi-use card that usually gives a discount, typically eleven rides for the price of ten. It exists for buses and trains, but also for cafes, baths or classes. You say 回数券を買う / 使う; with IC cards such as Suica, paper 回数券 have become rarer. A monthly pass, by contrast, is called 定期券.

examples[].german: Please look at it objectively.
Please present objective data, not your own opinion.
I asked a friend for an objective opinion.
en.notes: 客観的 means "objective, impartial, unbiased": 客観的に見る／判断する, 客観的な事実・データ. The opposite is 主観的 "subjective". Related: 客観視する "to view something from a distance". The word sounds somewhat elevated, but is also common in everyday life, for example when asking for a neutral opinion.

examples[].german: I put the car in the garage.
This bus is going to the depot.
To buy a car, you need a garage certificate.
en.notes: 車庫 is a garage for a car, but also the depot for buses and trains: このバスは車庫行きです "goes to the depot". Typical: 車を車庫に入れる; parking into the garage is called 車庫入れ. In Japan you need a 車庫証明 (proof of parking space) to register a car. A parking lot or parking garage, by contrast, is called 駐車場; ガレージ is a synonym for a private garage.

examples[].german: I go through the underpass.
On rainy days it's convenient, because you can get to the station through the underground passage.
The underpass is dark and a little scary at night.
en.notes: 地下道 is an underground pedestrian passage or underpass, for example under a large road or between a station and buildings: 地下道を通る / 抜ける. Not to be confused with 地下街, the underground shopping arcade, and 地下鉄, the subway. Over the road, on the other hand, runs the pedestrian bridge 歩道橋.

examples[].german: I'm updating the database.
We manage all customer information in a database.
I looked for papers in the library's database.
en.notes: データベース is the database in IT, often abbreviated DB. Typical combinations: データベースを作る / 構築する, データベースを更新する, データベースで検索する, データベースに登録する. It is also used for collections of information in general, such as a library's literature database. The individual data are called データ.

examples[].german: The server went down.
Please save the files on the shared server.
We put a water dispenser in the office.
en.notes: サーバー is above all the server in IT; in technical texts it is often written サーバ without the long-vowel mark. Typical: サーバーがダウンする / 落ちる "the server goes down", サーバーに保存する / 接続する. In daily life you also encounter the word as ウォーターサーバー "water dispenser" and in sports for the server in tennis or volleyball.

examples[].german: I'm connecting to the network.
Because of a network failure, I can't send email.
To expand my professional network, I took part in a networking event.
en.notes: ネットワーク is a network, first of all a computer network: ネットワークに接続する / つなぐ, ネットワークの障害 "network failure". It can also refer to a network of people, stores or broadcasters: ネットワークを広げる "to expand one's network". The short form ネット, on the other hand, mostly means the internet.

examples[].german: I'm decoding the code.
On this website, data is sent encrypted.
When we were children, my friends and I had fun writing letters in code.
en.notes: 暗号 is a secret code or cipher, that is, an encrypted message: 暗号を解く / 解読する "to decipher", 暗号で書く. The process of encryption is called 暗号化 (暗号化する "to encrypt"). A login password is not called 暗号 but パスワード, and a PIN is 暗証番号.

examples[].german: I'm attaching the file.
I can't open the attachment, though.
Please attach a certificate of residence to the application form.
en.notes: 添付 means "to attach, to append" and is used as a transitive する-verb: メールにファイルを添付する; an attachment is called 添付ファイル. Documents are also attached to applications: 書類を添付する, formally 〜を添付の上、提出してください. If you put something in an envelope, people tend to say 同封する.

examples[].german: I received an email.
There are lots of unread emails in the inbox.
Because we're in the mountains, TV reception is poor.
en.notes: 受信 is the reception of messages or signals and is used as a transitive する-verb: メールを受信する. Common compounds: 受信箱 "inbox", 受信料 "broadcast reception fee", 受信状態 "reception quality". The counterpart is 送信 "sending". For physical things such as packages, people say 受け取る instead.

examples[].german: I'm sending an email.
I accidentally sent an unfinished email.
When you have finished typing, please press the send button.
en.notes: 送信 is the electronic sending of messages or data, as a transitive する-verb: メールを送信する; the button is called 送信ボタン. In conversation people usually just say 送る; 送信 is typical of on-screen text and technology. The counterpart is 受信; related are 返信 "reply" and 転送 "forwarding".

examples[].german: That is a subjective opinion.
Taste in flavor is a subjective matter.
We set criteria so that the evaluation would not be subjective.
en.notes: 主観的 means "subjective, colored by personal feeling": 主観的な意見・判断. Often slightly critical (主観的すぎる "too subjective"). Opposite: 客観的. Without 的 one often hears あくまで主観ですが "this is only my personal impression" as a modest introduction.

examples[].german: I will look through the documents.
Please be quiet in the library's reading room.
I cleared my browser's browsing history.
en.notes: 閲覧 means "to look through, to inspect" documents, books or web pages and is a formal transitive する-verb: 資料を閲覧する. Typical are 閲覧室 "reading room", 閲覧履歴 "browsing history" and 閲覧禁止 "no viewing allowed". In everyday speech one simply says 見る or 読む; 閲覧 sounds official or technical.

examples[].german: I'm starting up the computer.
My smartphone won't start anymore, and I'm in trouble.
As soon as I launch the app, ads appear.
en.notes: 起動 is the starting of computers, programs or machines. As a する-verb it is both transitive and intransitive: パソコンを起動する "to boot up the PC", but also パソコンが起動しない "the PC won't start". Restarting is 再起動する. Colloquially people also say 立ち上げる / 立ち上がる; a vehicle, on the other hand, is started with エンジンをかける.

examples[].german: I fish at the breakwater.
On typhoon days, waves sometimes go over the breakwater.
Our section chief always shields us.
en.notes: 防波堤 is a breakwater or mole that protects a harbor from waves (防ぐ "to ward off" + 波 "wave" + 堤 "embankment"). 防波堤で釣りをする is popular. A levee along rivers, by contrast, is called 堤防. Figuratively, a person can be 〜の防波堤になる, that is, shield others from attacks or criticism.

examples[].german: I walk along the canal.
Be careful not to fall into the irrigation ditch next to the rice field.
This town has had many canals since long ago, and goods were carried by boat.
en.notes: 水路 is a waterway in the broad sense: canal, ditch or water channel. Very common is 用水路 "irrigation ditch" next to rice fields. A large navigable canal is more often called 運河, a natural river 川. In swimming, 水路 also refers to a swimmer's lane (第3水路).

examples[].german: I took a walk through the bamboo grove.
The bamboo grove at Sagano in Kyoto is very popular with tourists.
In the bamboo grove behind the house, you can harvest bamboo shoots in spring.
en.notes: 竹林 is a bamboo grove or small bamboo wood. The Sino-Japanese reading ちくりん sounds somewhat more elevated; there is also the native reading たけばやし. The bamboo forest in 嵯峨野 near Kyoto is famous. In spring, young bamboo shoots (たけのこ) are harvested in the 竹林.

examples[].german: I look for insects in the copse.
There is a small copse behind our house.
When autumn comes, the trees in the copse turn red and yellow.
en.notes: 雑木林 is a small grove of various, mostly deciduous trees such as oaks, typical of the landscape at the edge of a village (里山). So it is not a large forest; for that one says 森 or 森林. The reading is ぞうき (as in 雑巾), not ざつ. Children like to look there in summer for beetles such as カブトムシ.

examples[].german: Rare birds live in the wetland.
I hear this area used to be a wetland.
Volunteers pick up trash to protect the wetland.
en.notes: 湿地 is an area with permanently wet, marshy ground - "wetland, marshland". Typical are 湿地帯 ("wetland, marsh area") and 湿地に生息する鳥. A marsh or pond with standing water is more often called 沼, a larger moorland landscape 湿原 (e.g. 釧路湿原). The word is factual and appears mainly with nature and environmental topics; for damp ground in daily life, people tend to describe it with じめじめした土地.

examples[].german: I'm exploring the cave.
It's pleasantly cool inside the cave even in summer.
People in ancient times are said to have lived in caves.
en.notes: 洞窟 is a natural cave in rock or a mountain. Typical combinations are 洞窟に入る, 洞窟を探検する and 洞窟の中は暗い／涼しい. The synonymous 洞穴（ほらあな） sounds somewhat more colloquial; a small hole or an animal's burrow is simply called 穴, a dug tunnel トンネル. The kanji 窟 is rare, but the word itself is common in travel guides and the news.

examples[].german: I trim the hedge.
The house is surrounded by a tall hedge.
A cat came out through a gap in the hedge.
en.notes: 生垣 (also written 生け垣) is a hedge of living shrubs that marks the boundary of a property - literally a "living fence". By contrast, 塀 is a wall or solid fence made of stone, concrete or wood, フェンス is a (metal) fence; 垣根 is the general term "enclosure". Typical uses are 生垣を刈り込む／手入れする ("to trim/maintain the hedge") and 生垣に囲まれた家.

en.meaning: ornamental transom above a door or partition
examples[].german: The carving on the transom is magnificent.
Light from the next room leaks through the transom.
When we repaired the old house, we kept only the transom.
en.notes: 欄間 is, in traditional Japanese houses, the open, often elaborately carved or latticed wooden panel between the lintel of the sliding doors (鴨居) and the ceiling. It lets light and air pass between two rooms and also serves as decoration; it roughly corresponds to a "transom window". Typical uses are 欄間の彫刻 ("carving on the ranma") and 欄間から光が入る. It is an architectural technical term that you mostly hear in connection with old houses, temples and ryokan.

examples[].german: It has gradually gotten colder.
Studying Japanese has gradually become fun.
The rain will gradually get stronger.
en.notes: 段々 means "gradually, step by step, more and more" and is mostly written in kana だんだん. Typical with verbs of change: だんだん〜くなる, 〜てくる／〜ていく. Spoken and neutral; more literary is 徐々に. どんどん, by contrast, emphasizes quick, rapid increase. As a noun, 段々 means "steps, terraces" (段々畑).

examples[].german: I close the storm shutters before the typhoon.
When I get up in the morning, the first thing I do is open the shutters.
In the middle of the night, the shutters were rattling in the wind.
en.notes: 雨戸 are sliding shutters made of wood or metal that are pulled across the outside of windows and glass sliding doors - as protection against storms, rain and burglars. You say 雨戸を閉める／開ける, and in bad weather also 雨戸を閉め切る ("to shut all the shutters tight"). Modern roller shutters are usually called シャッター; European hinged shutters are more often called よろい戸. Closing the 雨戸 before a typhoon is a typical precaution in Japan.

examples[].german: I put the dishes in the cupboard.
The sweets are on the top shelf of the kitchen cupboard.
When I tidied up the cupboard, some old canned food turned up.
en.notes: 戸棚 is a cupboard with doors and shelves, mainly for dishes, supplies or small items in the kitchen and living room; the dedicated dish cabinet is called 食器棚. For clothing, タンス or クローゼット is more usual, and for the built-in futon closet 押し入れ. Typical uses are 戸棚にしまう ("to put away in the cupboard"), 戸棚から出す and 戸棚の上の段.

examples[].german: I sweep the garden.
Could you sweep up the fallen leaves in front of the entrance?
I swept up the broken glass with a broom.
en.notes: 掃く means "to sweep with a broom (ほうき)". The object with を is either the place (庭を掃く, 床を掃く) or the dirt (落ち葉を掃く, ごみを掃き集める). Not to be confused with the identically read 履く ("to put on shoes/trousers") and 吐く ("to spit, to vomit"). Vacuuming is 掃除機をかける, wiping with a cloth 拭く; sweeping as a household chore is called 掃き掃除.

examples[].german: I wipe the table.
Please wipe off your sweat with this towel.
I dried the washed dishes with a dishcloth and put them back on the shelf.
en.notes: 拭く means "to wipe, to dry (with a cloth)". The object is the surface or what is being removed: テーブルを拭く, 汗を拭く, 涙を拭く; the means takes で (タオルで拭く, ふきんで拭く). Not to be confused with 掃く ("to sweep") and the identically read 吹く ("to blow"). For drying hands, people say 手を拭く; wet wiping can be specified as 水拭き, dry wiping as 乾拭き.

examples[].german: I fold the laundry.
I closed my umbrella before getting on the train.
My grandfather decided to close down the shop he had run for forty years.
en.notes: 畳む means "to fold up, to fold together, to close" - above all for fabric and larger things: 洗濯物を畳む, 布団を畳む, 傘を畳む ("to close an umbrella"). Paper, on the other hand, is mostly folded with 折る. Figuratively, 店を畳む means "to give up a business (for good)". The word is often written in kana as たたむ; the same kanji is in 畳 ("tatami").

en.meaning: to dry; to hang out to dry
examples[].german: I air out the futon.
It looks like rain, so let's hang the laundry inside.
He drained the beer in one go.
en.notes: 干す means "to hang or spread out to dry (in the sun or air)": 洗濯物を干す, 布団を干す; the place is marked with に (ベランダに干す). The intransitive "to become dry" is 乾く, and active drying, for example with a hair dryer, is 乾かす (髪を乾かす) - 干す emphasizes hanging or spreading out. Derived from it are 干物 ("dried fish") and 干し柿; as a verb suffix, 飲み干す means "to drink up completely".

examples[].german: The iron rusted.
I left the bicycle out in the rain and it has rusted.
To keep the kitchen knife from rusting, wipe it well after use.
en.notes: 錆びる means "to rust, to get rusty" and is intransitive: 鉄が錆びる, 自転車が錆びてしまった. The attributive form 錆びた ("rusty") is very common: 錆びた釘, 錆びたナイフ. The noun is 錆（さび）, for example 錆が出る／つく ("rust forms"). Both the verb and the noun are often written in kana (さびる, サビ); letting an object rust is expressed causatively with 錆びさせる.

examples[].german: I peel the apple.
I peeled a mandarin and gave it to the child.
Will you help me peel the potatoes?
en.notes: 剥く means "to peel, to remove the skin or shell". The object is either the fruit itself (みかんを剥く) or the peel (りんごの皮を剥く, ゆで卵の殻を剥く); it is mostly written in kana as むく. To be distinguished from 剥がす ("to peel off, to detach", e.g. a sticker) and the intransitive 剥ける ("to peel, to come off": 日焼けで皮が剥ける). Figuratively, 目を剥く means "to open one's eyes wide"; not to be confused with 向く ("to turn toward").

examples[].german: I turn the faucet.
I twisted my ankle on the stairs.
We all racked our brains, but no good idea came up.
en.notes: 捻る means "to turn, to twist (with the fingers)": 蛇口を捻る ("to turn on the faucet"), 体を捻る ("to twist the upper body"). For injuries, 足首を捻る means "to twist/sprain one's ankle" (medically 捻挫する). Fixed expressions are 頭を捻る ("to rack one's brains") and ひねった問題 ("a tricky, clever problem"). It is mostly written in kana; similar is ねじる ("to wring, to twist"), whereas 回す rather means "to turn around in a circle" (key, knob).

examples[].german: I scatter seeds.
It was hot, so I sprinkled water on the garden.
On Setsubun, people scatter beans while calling out "Demons out!"
en.notes: 撒く means "to scatter, to strew, to spray": 水を撒く ("to sprinkle water"), 餌を撒く, 節分に豆を撒く. "To sow" in the narrower sense is mostly written 蒔く (種を蒔く), in kana simply 種をまく. Other meanings are ビラを撒く ("to distribute flyers") and 尾行を撒く ("to shake off a pursuer"). Mostly written in kana as まく; not to be confused with 巻く ("to wind").

examples[].german: I am gradually recovering.
I have gradually gotten used to my new job.
I will gradually reduce the dose of the medicine.
en.notes: 徐々に means "gradually, step by step" and is somewhat more formal than だんだん. It is used for slow, steady changes: 徐々に回復する, 徐々に増える／減らす, 徐々に慣れる. The に is an integral part. Opposite: 急に or 急激に. Typical in reports, medicine and the news, but also in polite conversation.

en.meaning: to mow; to cut; to crop
examples[].german: I mow the lawn.
When autumn comes, the farmers harvest the rice.
During the summer vacation, my father cut my hair short.
en.notes: 刈る means "to cut, to mow, to shear (grass, hair, grain)": 芝生を刈る, 草を刈る, 稲を刈る ("to harvest rice"), 髪を短く刈る. For ordinary cutting with a knife or scissors, people say 切る; at the hairdresser it is 髪を切ってもらう, whereas 刈る is more "to shear short" (刈り上げ). Derived nouns are 草刈り and 稲刈り; not to be confused with the identically read 狩る ("to hunt").

examples[].german: I plow the field.
Before sowing, I till the soil thoroughly.
In the old days, rice paddies were plowed with oxen.
en.notes: 耕す means "to work the soil, to plow, to dig over" - whether with a plow, tractor or spade: 畑を耕す, 田んぼを耕す, 土を耕す. Related words are 耕作 ("farming") and 耕運機 ("power tiller"). The verb belongs to the vocabulary of agriculture and gardening; harvesting, by contrast, is 収穫する or, for grain, 刈る.

examples[].german: The cherry blossom buds are swelling.
The rose has many buds on it.
It was still a bud in the morning, but by evening the flower had opened.
en.notes: 蕾 is the flower bud; a leaf or shoot bud, by contrast, is called 芽. Typical combinations: 蕾がつく ("to form buds"), 蕾がふくらむ ("the buds swell"), 蕾が開く ("to bloom"), まだ蕾だ ("has not bloomed yet"). つぼみ is mostly written in kana. Figuratively it can refer to a promising young person, but that is rather literary.

en.meaning: vine; tendril; climbing plant; temple (of glasses)
examples[].german: The vine is creeping along the wall.
The morning glory vines have grown all the way to the window.
The temple of my glasses broke.
en.notes: 蔓 is the vine or climbing shoot of climbing and creeping plants such as morning glory, cucumber or grapevine. Typical uses are 蔓が伸びる, 蔓が絡まる ("to get tangled") and 蔓が壁を這う. It is mostly written つる in kana; the ivy plant itself is called 蔦（つた）. つる also refers to the temple (arm) of a pair of glasses (眼鏡のつる); do not confuse it with the identically read 鶴 ("crane").

en.meaning: graupel; arare (small toasted rice crackers made from mochi)
examples[].german: On the Sea of Japan side in winter, graupel often falls.
Graupel hits the window and makes a pattering sound.
I served soy sauce flavored arare with tea.
en.notes: あられ is "graupel": small, whitish ice pellets under about 5 mm in diameter. Larger hailstones are called 雹（ひょう）, sleet みぞれ; one says あられが降る. あられ is mostly written in kana; the kanji 霰 is rare. The same word denotes small toasted rice crackers made from mochi (e.g. ひなあられ for the Doll Festival) - in this meaning always in kana; in cooking, a fine dice cut is called あられ切り.

examples[].german: Thunder rang out.
We heard thunder in the distance, so we hurried down the mountain.
According to the weather forecast, tonight there will be heavy rain with thunder.
en.notes: 雷鳴 is the rumble of thunder, the thunderclap as a sound. It sounds literary and appears in news, weather reports and narratives (雷鳴が響く／轟く, 雷鳴を伴う雨). In everyday speech, 雷が鳴る or the onomatopoeia ゴロゴロ is used instead. Lightning is called 稲妻 or 稲光, and a thunderstorm in general 雷.

examples[].german: The tide has come in.
When the tide goes out, let's go look for shellfish.
The currents around here are fast, so please do not swim.
en.notes: 潮 means "tide, ocean current" and also "seawater". Typical: 潮が満ちる ("the tide comes in"), 潮が引く ("the water recedes, low tide"), 満ち潮／引き潮, 潮の流れ ("current"). Well-known compounds are 潮風 ("sea breeze") and 潮干狩り ("gathering shellfish at low tide"). Not to be confused with the identically read 塩 ("salt").

examples[].german: I walk along the water's edge.
The children are playing at the water's edge, splashing each other.
The day after the storm, there were many shells at the water's edge.
en.notes: 波打ち際 is the line on the beach where the waves run out - the "water's edge, strandline"; literally "the edge (際) where waves beat (波打つ)". Typical uses: 波打ち際を歩く, 波打ち際で遊ぶ. The beach in general is called 浜辺 or 砂浜, the coast 海岸; 波打ち際 refers precisely to the narrow wet strip.

examples[].german: I fish on the rocky shore.
In the summer vacation, our family played in the tide pools and found small crabs.
When I opened the window, it smelled of the sea.
en.notes: 磯 is a rocky coast or a rocky beach with stones and tide pools - in contrast to 砂浜 ("sandy beach"). Typical are 磯で釣る ("to fish on the rocky shore"), 磯遊び ("to look for crabs and shellfish in tide pools") and 磯の香り, the smell of the sea and seaweed. In the kitchen, it appears in names such as 磯辺焼き (mochi wrapped in nori).

examples[].german: I fan myself with an uchiwa.
I went out to the summer festival wearing a yukata and carrying an uchiwa.
They were handing out uchiwa advertising a shop in front of the station.
en.notes: 団扇 is a flat, non-folding round fan, usually made of paper or plastic on a bamboo frame; the folding fan is called 扇子（せんす）. One says うちわであおぐ ("to fan oneself"). It is almost always written うちわ in kana. In summer, promotional fans are handed out, and at concerts fans hold up homemade うちわ; not to be confused with 内輪 ("inner circle, internal").

examples[].german: The temperature dropped sharply.
Because of the weak yen, the price of imported goods rose sharply.
Losing weight rapidly is not good for the body.
en.notes: 急激に is the adverbial form of the な-adjective 急激 and means "abruptly and strongly, drastically". It is used for changes in numbers and states: 急激に増える／減る／上がる／下がる, also 急激な変化. 急に means only "suddenly" (starting without warning), and 急速に emphasizes the high speed of a development. Rather news and written language.

examples[].german: I lower the bamboo blind to block the sunlight.
When summer comes, they hang a bamboo blind on the veranda at my grandmother's house.
A cool breeze comes in through the bamboo blind.
en.notes: 簾 is a blind made of thin bamboo or reed slats that is hung outside windows or the veranda in summer: it blocks the sun but lets air through. Typical uses are すだれを下ろす／上げる and すだれを掛ける; it is usually written すだれ in kana. A larger reed screen that is leaned against a wall is called よしず; the bamboo mat for rolling sushi is called 巻きす.

examples[].german: I hang up the mosquito net.
As a child, I slept under a mosquito net in summer.
Even though it was an important matter, only I was left out.
en.notes: 蚊帳 is a large mosquito net that is traditionally hung from the corners of a room in summer so that you sleep under it on the futon. You say 蚊帳を吊る ("to hang up") and 蚊帳の中で寝る. The reading かや is a special reading. The idiom 蚊帳の外 ("left out, not in the loop") is very common: 私だけ蚊帳の外だった.

examples[].german: This program has high ratings.
The ratings of the final episode exceeded 30 percent.
Programs that can't get ratings end quickly.
en.notes: 視聴率 is the viewership rating of TV programs, given in percent. Typical: 視聴率が高い／低い, 視聴率を取る ("to get good ratings"), 視聴率が20パーセントを超える. 視聴者 are the viewers; for internet videos, people speak of 再生回数 ("view count") instead. The word belongs to the language of media and news.

examples[].german: We'll cover it live.
This program is broadcast live every Sunday morning.
During the live broadcast, a guest made a slip of the tongue.
en.notes: 生放送 is a live broadcast; 生 here means "raw, unedited, live", as in 生ビール. The opposite terms are 録画放送 and 収録 ("recording"). Typical: 生放送で, 生放送中, and as a する-verb 番組を生放送する. A live transmission from a location is called 生中継, a livestream on the internet 生配信.

examples[].german: I'm recording the program.
I recorded yesterday's soccer match, so let's watch it together.
The face of the culprit was captured on the security camera recording.
en.notes: 録画 is video recording, especially of TV programs or by cameras; 録画する = "to record". Pure sound recording is 録音. Typical: 番組を録画する, 録画予約 ("to schedule a recording"), 録画したドラマ. When you film yourself with a camera or phone, people tend to say 動画を撮る or 撮影する.

examples[].german: I'm watching a movie with subtitles.
I want to be able to understand English movies without subtitles.
I'm on the train, so I'm watching with the sound off and subtitles on.
en.notes: 字幕 are subtitles in film and television. At the cinema you choose between the 字幕版 ("subtitled version") and the 吹き替え版 ("dubbed version"). Typical: 字幕付き, 日本語字幕, 字幕を出す／消す ("to show/hide"), 字幕なしで分かる. The word is neutral and everyday.

examples[].german: I'm watching the dubbed version.
When I watch with children, dubbing is easier than subtitles.
That actor is always dubbed by the same voice actor.
en.notes: 吹き替え is the dubbing of a film or series into another language; the 吹き替え版 is the opposite of the 字幕版. The related verb is 吹き替える, and the dubbing actors are usually 声優. The spelling 吹替 also occurs. Less often, the word also refers to an actor's stunt double in dangerous scenes.

examples[].german: I am writing a screenplay.
This drama has a well-crafted script.
A screenplay for a new movie was written based on a famous novel.
en.notes: 脚本 is the screenplay or stage text as a literary work; the author is called 脚本家. Typical: 脚本を書く, 脚本がいい／よくできている, in the credits 脚本：〇〇. 台本, by contrast, rather means the working copy from which actors and presenters learn their lines; シナリオ is a loanword with a similar meaning.

examples[].german: I will memorize the script.
The host said something that was not in the script and made the venue laugh.
Even though it is called reality TV, apparently there is actually a script.
en.notes: 台本 is the text book or script that actors, presenters or announcers use at work - with dialogue and stage directions. Typical: 台本を覚える／読む, 台本通りに ("as in the script"), 台本にない ("not in the script, improvised"). In contrast to 脚本, which emphasizes the author's work, 台本 is the practical working material - also for shows and presentations.

examples[].german: I will change my costume.
Everyone made the costumes by hand for the play at the school festival.
My older sister's wedding dress was very beautiful.
en.notes: 衣装 is special, often striking clothing for performances or occasions - "costume, garb": 舞台衣装, 花嫁衣装 ("bridal gown"), ハロウィンの衣装. Everyday clothing, by contrast, is called 服 or 洋服, and clothing in general (formal) 衣服. Typical are 衣装を着る, 衣装を着替える ("to change costumes") and 衣装を用意する; the spelling 衣裳 also occurs.

en.meaning: to realize; to make come true
examples[].german: I want to make my dream come true.
The hope of living abroad as a family finally came true.
The plan for the new station was not realized because of budget problems.
en.notes: 実現する means "to realize" or "to become reality" and is used both transitively and intransitively: 夢を実現する "to realize a dream", 夢が実現する "a dream comes true". Typical objects are 夢, 希望, 計画, アイデア. For measurable goals such as sales figures, 達成する fits better. In everyday speech, for dreams one also says 夢をかなえる / 夢がかなう; 実現 sounds somewhat more objective.

examples[].german: Business performance improved markedly.
If lack of sleep continues, concentration declines markedly.
The two people's opinions differed markedly.
en.notes: 著しく is the adverbial form of 著しい: "considerably, strikingly strongly". It is used with verbs of change and with adjectives: 著しく向上する／低下する, 著しく異なる. It only evaluates the extent and can therefore be positive or negative. Literary; in conversation people rather say かなり, すごく or 大きく.

examples[].german: I'm preparing the stage sets.
For the school festival play, I was in charge of the stage sets.
As soon as the performance is over, the stage sets have to be cleared away right away.
en.notes: 大道具 are the large stage structures and scenery in the theater or TV studio - walls, houses, trees, stairs. The counterpart 小道具 are the small props that performers take in their hands. Typical: 大道具を組み立てる／運ぶ／片付ける, 大道具係 ("stage-set crew"). In short form, 大道具 can also refer to the stagehands themselves.

examples[].german: I'm gathering the props.
In this play, an old letter is an important prop.
I bought handy little camping gadgets at a 100-yen shop.
en.notes: 小道具 are the small props that performers use in theater, film or television - letters, cups, swords; in contrast to 大道具, the large sets. Typical: 小道具を揃える／用意する, 小道具係. In daily life, the word also refers to small practical aids or gadgets: 便利な小道具.

examples[].german: I toured backstage.
Backstage, the staff were running around busily.
This book describes in detail what went on behind the scenes at the Olympics.
en.notes: 舞台裏 is literally the area behind the stage ("backstage"). Equally common is the figurative meaning "behind the scenes", i.e. what stays hidden from the public: 政治の舞台裏, 舞台裏を明かす. The performers' dressing room, on the other hand, is called 楽屋; the loanword バックステージ is also in use.

examples[].german: I'm getting ready in the dressing room.
After the concert, I visited the dressing room and handed over a bouquet.
That's an inside joke, so the audience won't get it.
en.notes: 楽屋 is the lounge and changing room of performers behind the stage - the "artists' dressing room" (not the coat check for the audience, which is called クローク). Typical: 楽屋に入る, 楽屋を訪ねる, 楽屋見舞い (a gift for performers). 楽屋ネタ or 楽屋落ち is an inside joke that only insiders understand.

examples[].german: Applause rang out.
When the presentation was over, everyone applauded for me.
Let's give the winning team a big round of applause.
en.notes: 拍手 is clapping, applause; as an intransitive する-verb: 拍手する. The one who is applauded takes に: 選手に拍手する, 〜に拍手を送る ("to give applause to someone"). Other expressions are 大きな拍手が起こる and 拍手喝采 ("thunderous applause"). The ritual clapping of hands at a shrine is usually called 柏手（かしわで）.

examples[].german: The first act is about to begin.
When the curtain rose, the hall fell silent.
The Olympics came to a close after seventeen days.
en.notes: 幕 is first of all the "curtain" in the theater: 幕が上がる / 幕が開く ("the curtain rises"), 幕が下りる ("falls"). As a counter, it stands for acts: 第一幕, 三幕. Figuratively, 幕を開ける means "to begin" and 幕を閉じる "to come to an end", hence also 開幕 and 閉幕. In 君の出る幕じゃない, 幕 means "role, place": "This is none of your business"; it is also familiar from 字幕 ("subtitles").

examples[].german: The show was a success.
This movie grossed over 10 billion yen.
A pro wrestling event will be held in this town next month.
en.notes: 興行 is a commercial event for which admission is charged - theater, film, circus, sumo, boxing or wrestling - and also the event business itself. Typical are 興行収入 ("box-office revenue"), 興行成績 and 興行が成功する. The word sounds businesslike and appears mainly in the news; not to be confused with the identically read 工業 ("industry") and 鉱業 ("mining").

en.meaning: final day of a run; last day of a sumo tournament
examples[].german: The final day of the run has arrived.
The sumo tournament championship was decided only on the final day.
The tickets for the final performance sold out immediately.
en.notes: 千秋楽 is the last day of a run of performances in the theater or of a sumo tournament (場所); the counterpart is 初日 ("premiere, first day"). Typical: 千秋楽を迎える ("to reach the final day"), 千秋楽まで, 千秋楽のチケット. Among theater people it is shortened to 楽日 or 楽. The word comes from the world of the stage and sumo and is also often used in sports news.

examples[].german: I met my childhood friend.
He and I have been friends since kindergarten.
Marrying your childhood friend - it's just like a TV drama.
en.notes: 幼なじみ (also written 幼馴染) is someone you have known since early childhood - often the neighborhood child you grew up with; the word is used for both boys and girls. Typical: 幼なじみの〇〇, 〜とは幼なじみだ ("I grew up with ..."). An old friend from a later period is more likely 昔の友達 or 旧友; 幼なじみ stresses the shared childhood.

examples[].german: I asked someone to be our matchmaker.
At my parents' wedding, my father's boss reportedly served as the matchmaker.
Recently, almost all weddings are held without a matchmaker.
en.notes: 仲人 is the traditional marriage go-between - usually a respected married couple who arrange a 見合い and officially act as intermediaries at the wedding. Typical: 仲人を頼む, 仲人をする／務める, 仲人を立てる. The reading なこうど is irregular. Today, weddings with a 仲人 are rare; professional matchmaking is called 結婚相談所.

examples[].german: Approximately a thousand people took part.
It takes roughly ten minutes from the station to the venue.
I understood the general content of the talk.
en.notes: おおよそ means "approximately, about" with numbers and quantities: おおよそ千人, おおよそ十分. As a noun with の it means "the rough outline, the gist": おおよその内容, おおよその見当がつく "to have a rough idea". Mostly written in kana (rarely 大凡). およそ is synonymous but somewhat more common; in conversation だいたい is usually used.

examples[].german: I leave the key with the building manager.
Something is wrong with the water supply, so I contacted the caretaker.
The administrator of this site updates the articles every day.
en.notes: 管理人 is the person who looks after a building or facility – in apartment complexes (マンションの管理人) the "caretaker/building manager", who sits in the 管理人室; in conversation often politely 管理人さん. The word also applies to dormitories, campsites or websites (サイトの管理人 "operator, admin"). The owner or landlord, by contrast, is 大家（おおや）.

examples[].german: It is a well-ventilated house.
This room is poorly ventilated, so moisture easily builds up.
The new president says he wants to create a company with open communication.
en.notes: 風通し is the air circulation, the draft in a room or building; it is almost always said as 風通しがいい／悪い or attributively 風通しのいい部屋. Actively airing out is 換気（する）, by contrast. Figuratively, 風通しのいい職場 describes a work environment with open communication. Besides かぜとおし, there is also the reading かざとおし.

examples[].german: Condensation forms on the window.
On winter mornings, the windows get condensation and are soaking wet.
If you leave condensation alone, it causes mold.
en.notes: 結露 is condensation, when moisture settles on cold surfaces - a typical winter problem in Japanese homes. Typical uses: 窓に結露がつく, 結露が発生する, as an intransitive する-verb 窓が結露する, and 結露対策. Literally "bound dew" (露 = dew); moisture in general is 湿気. Untreated 結露 often leads to カビ.

examples[].german: Mold grew in the bathroom.
Mold grows easily during the rainy season, so be careful.
When I opened the closet, it smelled of mold.
en.notes: 黴 means "mold"; the kanji is very rare, and it is almost always written かび or カビ. Typical uses: カビが生える ("mold forms"), カビ臭い ("musty"), カビ取り ("mold remover"). In Japan mold appears especially in the rainy season (梅雨) and as a result of 結露; bacteria, by contrast, are called 細菌 or 菌.

examples[].german: I'm repairing the leak.
Water is leaking from the kitchen faucet.
Because of a leak in the apartment above, a stain formed on our ceiling.
en.notes: 水漏れ is a water leak: water comes out where it shouldn't - from pipes, faucets or through the ceiling. Typical: 水漏れする, 水漏れが起きる, 天井から水漏れする, 水漏れを修理する. When rain comes in through the roof, people say 雨漏り. The underlying verb is 漏れる ("to leak, to seep through").

examples[].german: I'm calculating the gross profit.
This product is cheap, but the gross profit is small.
Sales rose this month, but the gross margin fell.
en.notes: 粗利 is the gross profit: sales minus cost of goods. It is the business-language short form of 粗利益（あらりえき）; in accounting it is called 売上総利益. Typical: 粗利が出る／少ない, 粗利率 ("gross margin"), 粗利を計算する. To be distinguished from 売上 ("sales, revenue") and 純利益 ("net profit").

examples[].german: I will display the goods.
Please display the new products on the shelf near the entrance.
Many old tools were on display at the museum.
en.notes: 陳列 is the exhibiting and orderly laying out of goods or exhibits: 商品を陳列する, 陳列棚 ("display shelf"), 陳列ケース ("display case"). It sounds businesslike or literary; in everyday speech one rather says 並べる or 飾る. 展示 emphasizes showing something to be looked at (museum, trade fair), while 陳列 mainly means arranging goods for sale, but is also used for museum pieces.

examples[].german: May I try it on?
Where is the fitting room?
When I tried it on, the size was a little big.
en.notes: 試着 is trying on clothes in a store, mostly as a する-verb: 服を試着する, asked politely 試着してもいいですか. The fitting room is called 試着室, and staff respectfully say ご試着. For shoes, people tend to say 履いてみる, and in private settings for clothing also simply 着てみる. A sign saying 試着はご遠慮ください means that trying on is not allowed.

examples[].german: Please shorten the hem.
How many days does it take to hem these trousers?
I asked my mother to hem my skirt.
en.notes: 裾上げ is shortening trousers or skirts by sewing up the hem (裾 "hem, lower edge" + 上げ "to raise"). In clothing stores it is a common service: 裾上げをお願いします, 裾上げは無料です. As a する-verb: ズボンを裾上げする. The opposite, letting the hem out to lengthen, is called 裾出し; shortening sleeves or length in general is expressed with 丈を詰める.

examples[].german: I ordered a made-to-measure suit at a tailor's.
This coat is really well made, isn't it?
Tailoring a kimono takes about a month.
en.notes: 仕立て is the noun for 仕立てる "to tailor, to make (clothing)" and refers to the tailoring as well as the workmanship of a garment: 仕立てがいい "well cut and well made", 着物の仕立て. For custom-made clothing as opposed to ready-made goods (既製服), people today often say オーダーメイド. In a broader sense, 仕立て means "preparation, style", e.g. 和風仕立て "prepared in Japanese style" or 特別仕立ての列車 "special train".

en.meaning: at least; at the very least
examples[].german: It will take at least three days.
I don't know about the others, but I, at least, agree.
Let's open the window at least once a day to air out the room.
en.notes: 少なくとも means "at least" with quantities and times (少なくとも三日) and "at any rate, at least" as a qualification (少なくとも私は賛成だ "I, at least, am in favor"). In conversation you also hear 最低（でも）. せめて, by contrast, expresses a modest wish ("at least ..., please").

examples[].german: I take measurements.
Before buying furniture, please check the dimensions of the room.
The dimensions didn't match, so the shelf didn't fit.
en.notes: 寸法 are the exact dimensions of an object (length, width, height); the word goes back to the old unit of length 寸. Typical uses: 寸法を測る "to take measurements", 寸法が合わない "the dimensions don't match", 部屋の寸法, 寸法図. For clothing, サイズ is usually used in everyday speech; 寸法 sounds more exact and craft-technical. Colloquially, 寸法 can also mean "plan, intention" (〜という寸法だ "that's the plan"), but that is rarer.

examples[].german: I tie the obi.
The obi of my yukata came undone.
My younger brother got his black belt in karate.
en.notes: 帯 is the wide sash with which a kimono or yukata is tied: 帯を締める "to put on the obi", 帯を結ぶ for tying the knot. In addition, 帯 generally refers to bands and strips, such as the wrap-around band on books and CDs (本の帯) or the belt in martial arts: 黒帯 "black belt". A Western trouser belt, on the other hand, is called ベルト. As a suffix, it is read たい: 時間帯 "time period", 地帯 "zone".

examples[].german: I put on tabi.
With a kimono, you wear white tabi.
My grandfather wears rubber-soled tabi work shoes when gardening.
en.notes: 足袋 are traditional socks with a separate big toe, worn with kimono and 草履 or 下駄; with formal clothing they are white. As with socks and shoes, one says 履く, not 着る: 足袋を履く, 足袋を脱ぐ. Work shoes in tabi form with rubber soles are called 地下足袋. Modern toe socks, on the other hand, are called 五本指ソックス.

examples[].german: I put on a haori.
At the Coming of Age Day ceremony, he wore haori and hakama.
It was cold, so I threw a haori over my kimono.
en.notes: 羽織 is a short, front-open jacket worn over the kimono and fastened with cords (羽織紐). Together with the divided skirt, it forms the formal men's dress 羽織袴. You say 羽織を着る or 羽織を羽織る; the related verb 羽織る "to throw something on over" is also used for Western clothing: カーディガンを羽織る.

examples[].german: I used to live in a nagaya.
In the Edo period, many people lived in cramped nagaya.
In the nagaya, you could hear the neighbors' voices well.
en.notes: 長屋 is an elongated, mostly single-story wooden house divided into several narrow dwellings side by side - the typical rental housing of ordinary people in the Edo period. The word appears mainly in history, 落語 and samurai dramas (長屋暮らし, 長屋の住人). Modern row houses are more often called テラスハウス or タウンハウス, and rental apartments in general アパート.

examples[].german: There is a pub in the alley.
Many small shops line the alley in front of the station.
Please turn right at the next side street.
en.notes: 横丁 is a narrow side street branching off a main street (横 "side" + 丁 "block of street"); the spelling 横町 is equally common. Today the word often appears in the names of small pub and snack alleys such as 新宿の思い出横丁 and sounds nostalgic and folksy. Compared with 路地, a very narrow lane between houses, 横丁 stresses the branching off from the main street and the shops in it.

examples[].german: I walk through the alley.
When I went into a narrow alley, there was a quiet cafe.
The children are playing in the alley.
en.notes: 路地 is a narrow lane between houses, often so narrow that no car can pass: 路地に入る, 路地に迷い込む, 路地裏 "back alley". Compared with 横丁 (a side street with shops), 路地 sounds more like a residential area and something hidden. For an ordinary street, people say 道 or 通り. The garden in front of a tea house is read the same way but is mostly written 露地.

examples[].german: I cross the stepping stones.
The stepping stones in the garden are slippery on rainy days.
This year's Golden Week is a broken-up holiday stretch.
en.notes: 飛び石 are flat stepping stones placed with gaps in Japanese gardens or across streams, so that you walk from stone to stone: 飛び石を渡る, 飛び石の上を歩く. Figuratively the word describes things that are spread out with gaps; well known is 飛び石連休 "holidays with working days in between". Stones in general are called 石, a gravel path 砂利道.

examples[].german: There is a stone lantern in the garden.
Stone lanterns line the approach to the temple.
On the night of the summer festival, we floated lanterns down the river.
en.notes: 灯籠 is a traditional lantern in which a flame used to burn. In gardens and at shrines, it usually means stone lanterns, more precisely 石灯籠; there are also hanging metal lanterns (釣り灯籠) and paper lanterns that are floated on the water at 灯籠流し. The portable, collapsible paper lantern in front of shops and at festivals, on the other hand, is called 提灯. The word is often also written 灯ろう.

examples[].german: I purify my hands at the stone water basin.
There is a small stone water basin in front of the tea room.
Flowers were floating in the water of the stone basin.
en.notes: 手水鉢 is a water basin, usually of stone, for purifying the hands - in a tea garden (often set low) or at shrines and temples. The roofed washing place at a shrine entrance is called 手水舎; the 手水鉢 is the basin itself. 手水 is read ちょうず (contracted from てみず); typical verbs are 手を清める "to purify the hands" and 口をすすぐ "to rinse the mouth".

examples[].german: There are about ten people at most.
With a part-time job, you can earn at most 50,000 yen a month.
Even if you hurry now, you'll arrive five minutes earlier at best.
en.notes: せいぜい names an upper limit: "at most, at best", often with 〜ぐらい／程度 or 〜しか and a slightly disparaging tone ("that's all you can get"). In its second meaning, "as best as one can", せいぜい頑張って often sounds ironic or condescending. The kanji 精々 is rare. More neutral are 多くても or 最大で.

examples[].german: The sound of the shishi-odoshi echoes.
In the ryokan's garden, the shishi-odoshi quietly clacks.
The shishi-odoshi was originally a device for scaring away animals.
en.notes: 鹿威し is a bamboo tube that slowly fills with water, tips over, empties and, as it snaps back, strikes a stone with a bright clack. Originally it was meant to scare away wild animals such as deer (鹿) (威す "to frighten"); today it is a sound element in the Japanese garden. It is mostly written in kana: ししおどし. The sound is rendered onomatopoeically as カーン or コーン.

examples[].german: I learned how to put on a kimono.
On the morning of Coming of Age Day, I had my kimono put on at the beauty salon.
If it's a yukata, I can put it on by myself.
en.notes: 着付け is the proper putting on of a kimono or yukata, including tying the obi - a skill of its own that you learn in a 着付け教室. People often have it done professionally: 着付けをしてもらう, 美容院で着付けを頼む. For the ordinary putting on of Western clothing, 服を着る is used, not 着付け. The related verb is 着付ける.

examples[].german: I light the candle.
The power went out, so I lit candles.
I blew out the candles on the cake in one go.
en.notes: 蝋燭 is the candle; because the kanji are difficult, it is almost always written ろうそく or ロウソク. Typical uses: ろうそくに火をつける "to light", ろうそくを消す or 吹き消す "to blow out". キャンドル sounds modern and decorative (scented candle, candlelight dinner), whereas ろうそく is the neutral word, for example in a power outage, at the household altar (仏壇) or at a grave.

examples[].german: I burn incense in the incense burner.
It is said that if you bathe in the smoke of the large incense burner at the temple, you will become healthy.
I stood an incense stick in the incense burner on the household altar.
en.notes: 香炉 is a vessel made of metal or ceramic in which incense is burned - at the household altar (仏壇), at graves or in front of temples, where large bronze 香炉 stand and visitors waft the smoke toward themselves. The incense stick itself is called 線香, incense in general お香. Typical uses: 香炉に線香を立てる, お香を焚く.

examples[].german: I bought an amulet.
Before the entrance exam, my grandmother gave me an amulet for passing.
I have a traffic safety amulet on my car.
en.notes: 御守り is an amulet from a shrine or temple, usually a small cloth pouch that is meant to bring protection or luck in a particular area: 交通安全 (traffic), 合格 (exams), 安産 (childbirth). The spelling お守り is usual. One says お守りを買う, more reverently お守りを受ける, and carries them on a bag or key ring. Not to be confused with お守り read おもり "babysitting".

examples[].german: I drew an omikuji.
I got "great blessing" in the omikuji at my first shrine visit of the year!
A bad omikuji is tied to a tree at the shrine before going home.
en.notes: おみくじ are fortune slips that you draw at shrines and temples for a small donation, especially on the New Year visit 初詣. You say おみくじを引く; the result ranges from 大吉 ("great blessing") through 吉, 中吉, 小吉 and 末吉 to 凶 ("misfortune"). Bad slips are often tied to a tree or a rack at the shrine to leave the bad luck there. The word is almost always written in kana; 御籤 or 御神籤 are rare.

en.meaning: approach path (to a shrine or temple)
examples[].german: I walk along the approach path.
Souvenir shops line both sides of the approach.
It is said that the middle of the approach is the path of the gods.
en.notes: 参道 is the path that leads to the sanctuary of a shrine or temple, often lined with 鳥居, stone lanterns and shops (参道の店); 表参道 is the main approach. The middle of the 参道 is considered the path of the deity, so it is polite to walk at the edge. The word is related to 参る "to visit (a shrine)", as in お参り.

examples[].german: I pray at the worship hall.
In front of the worship hall, you bow twice and clap your hands twice.
The main hall is behind the worship hall.
en.notes: 拝殿 is the worship hall of a shrine (神社), in front of which visitors throw coins into the offertory box (賽銭箱), ring the bell and pray. Behind it lies the 本殿, in which the deity is enshrined and which is normally not entered. For Buddhist temples, 本堂 is used instead. Typical uses: 拝殿で手を合わせる, 拝殿の前でお参りする.

examples[].german: The main hall is not open to the public.
The main hall of this shrine is a national treasure.
The roof of the main hall was renewed last year.
en.notes: 本殿 is the main building of a shrine in which the deity or its symbol is enshrined. It usually lies behind the 拝殿 and is generally closed to visitors; prayers are made in front of the 拝殿. For the main hall of a Buddhist temple, 本堂 is used, not 本殿. It is common in descriptions such as 本殿は国宝に指定されている.

examples[].german: I can see the five-story pagoda.
The five-story pagoda of Horyuji is one of the oldest wooden towers in the world.
Five-story pagodas are said to hardly collapse even in earthquakes.
en.notes: 五重塔 is the five-story pagoda of a Buddhist temple; it is read ごじゅうのとう with an inserted の that is not written. Well-known examples stand in 京都 (東寺) and 奈良 (法隆寺). Correspondingly, a three-story pagoda is called 三重塔; for the floors of ordinary buildings, 階 is used instead (五階建て). 塔 alone means "tower".

examples[].german: It is somewhat difficult.
Tomorrow will be a somewhat cloudy day.
These trousers are a little big for me.
en.notes: やや means "somewhat, a little" and sounds objective to written, typical of weather reports (やや強い雨, 雲がやや多い) and of reports. In conversation, people mostly say ちょっと or 少し. Do not confuse it with ややこしい "complicated, tricky", which is a separate word.

examples[].german: The sound of the temple bell echoes.
The bell of this temple was cast 400 years ago.
During the war, many temple bells were collected as metal.
en.notes: 梵鐘 is the large bronze bell in the bell tower (鐘楼) of a Buddhist temple; it has no clapper but is struck from the outside with a wooden beam: 鐘をつく. In everyday speech, people usually just say お寺の鐘 or 鐘; 梵鐘 is the technical, written-language term (museums, cultural properties). Well known is the ringing on New Year's Eve, 除夜の鐘.

examples[].german: I climb the stone steps.
There are 300 stone steps up to the shrine.
We sat on the stone steps and looked at the view of the town.
en.notes: 石段 is a staircase of stone steps outdoors, typical on slopes and as the approach to shrines and temples: 石段を上る/登る, 石段を下りる. Staircases inside buildings are called 階段; 石段 emphasizes the material and the outdoor location. The steps are counted with 段: 三百段の石段.

examples[].german: I visited the Moss Temple.
The garden of the Moss Temple is said to be most beautiful after rain.
To tour the Moss Temple, you need to apply in advance.
en.notes: 苔寺 is the popular name of the temple 西芳寺 in 京都, whose garden is covered with over a hundred kinds of moss (苔 "moss" + 寺 "temple"). It is thus a proper name and not a general word; a moss garden in general is called 苔庭. In the compound, 寺 becomes voiced: てら → でら, as in 山寺. A visit is possible only with prior application.

examples[].german: The thatched roof is still preserved.
In Shirakawa-go there are many houses with thatched roofs.
Thatched roofs are said to be cool in summer and warm in winter.
en.notes: 茅葺き refers to a roof thatched with grasses such as Chinese silvergrass or reed (茅) (葺く "to roof"), as well as the thatching itself. It is mostly used attributively with の: 茅葺きの屋根, 茅葺きの家; the farmhouses of 白川郷 are famous. A roof made of rice straw is more precisely called 藁葺き, a tiled roof 瓦屋根. The kana spelling かやぶき is also common.

examples[].german: I turn the potter's wheel and make vessels.
In the pottery class, I used a potter's wheel for the first time.
On the potter's wheel, the shape of the clay keeps changing.
en.notes: 轆轤 is mainly the potter's wheel; since the kanji are very difficult, it is mostly written ろくろ. Typical uses: ろくろを回す "to turn the wheel", ろくろを挽く "to shape on the wheel", 電動ろくろ "electric potter's wheel". The word also refers to a lathe, as well as a winch or pulley. Pottery as an art and hobby is called 陶芸.

examples[].german: I fire pottery in the kiln.
This pizza is baked in a stone oven.
The tea bowl fresh out of the kiln is still hot.
en.notes: 窯 is a kiln, above all for pottery but also for charcoal or bricks; today it often appears in 窯焼きピザ "wood-fired oven pizza". Typical: 窯で焼く, 窯に入れる, 窯から出す. Not to be confused with the identically read 釜 "kettle, pot" (e.g. the inner pot of a rice cooker). In compounds it is often がま: 石窯 "stone oven", 登り窯 "climbing kiln".

examples[].german: I apply glaze.
The color of the glaze is quite different before and after firing.
A blue glaze was used for this plate.
en.notes: 釉薬 is the glaze that is applied to ceramics before the second firing and that melts into a glass-like layer during firing: 釉薬をかける (by dipping or pouring), 釉薬を塗る (with a brush). Synonymous, but older and without the difficult kanji, is うわぐすり. Sugar glaze on baked goods, by contrast, is called アイシング.

examples[].german: I'm learning dyeing with indigo.
Kyoto has many traditional dyeing workshops.
This cloth is dyed with natural materials.
en.notes: 染色 is the dyeing of fabrics, yarn or hair, and in biology the staining of samples; it is the technical Sino-Japanese word for 染める. In daily life people mostly say 染める or 〜染め (藍染め, 草木染め); 染色 is found in crafts, industry and science: 染色工場, 染色体 "chromosome". As a する-verb: 布を染色する, often in the passive 染色される. Dyeing hair at the hairdresser, on the other hand, is called カラー or 髪を染める.

examples[].german: I dye cloth with indigo.
I bought an indigo-dyed handkerchief as a souvenir.
The indigo yukata suits you very well.
en.notes: 藍 is the dye plant (Japanese indigo), the indigo dye obtained from it and its hue (藍色 "indigo blue"). It is most often encountered in 藍染め "indigo dyeing", a traditional craft, for example from 徳島. As a color, 藍色 is darker than 青 but lighter than 紺 "dark blue, navy". Well known is the proverb 青は藍より出でて藍より青し: the student surpasses the master.

examples[].german: I apply lip color.
My grandmother always puts on lipstick before going out.
Crimson flowers are blooming in the garden.
en.notes: 紅（べに） is a strong crimson, originally the dye obtained from safflower (紅花), and hence also rouge or lip color: 紅を差す "to apply red to the lips or cheeks", 口紅 "lipstick", 頬紅 "blush". The color is called 紅色; poetically, 紅 is also read くれない. The Sino-Japanese reading こう is in 紅茶 and 紅葉. In daily life, people otherwise mostly use 赤 or 真っ赤 for the color.

en.meaning: on the contrary; if anything; rather
examples[].german: It got worse instead.
I took a shortcut and ended up taking even more time.
When people go out of their way for me, I actually get more nervous.
en.notes: かえって expresses that an action brings about the opposite of what was expected: "on the contrary, all the more, instead". Typical after 〜たら／〜と／〜ので: 手伝ったら、かえって迷惑だった. Mostly written in kana (rarely 却って). 逆に is more general, "conversely", and むしろ means "rather, preferably" in comparisons and preferences.

examples[].german: I fold a crane from patterned paper.
Covered with chiyogami, an ordinary box becomes really cute.
I bought some beautiful chiyogami paper at the souvenir shop.
en.notes: 千代紙 is colorful paper with traditional patterns such as flowers, cranes or waves, used for folding, for paper dolls or for covering small boxes. 千代 "a thousand generations" alludes to the auspicious motifs. Plain-colored folding paper is simply called 折り紙; 和紙 is handmade Japanese paper in general.

examples[].german: I tie the mizuhiki.
For wedding gifts, you use a mizuhiki with a knot that cannot be untied.
A black-and-white mizuhiki is attached to the envelope for a funeral.
en.notes: 水引 are stiff decorative cords made of twisted, dyed paper that are tied around money envelopes and gifts. Color and knot carry meaning: red-white or gold-silver for joyful occasions, black-white for bereavements; the unbreakable knot 結び切り stands for occasions that should not be repeated (wedding, mourning), the bow 蝶結び for repeatable ones such as births. On many envelopes today the 水引 is only printed.

examples[].german: Please add a noshi.
I attached a noshi paper reading "Ochugen" to the summer gift.
The shop assistant asked me whether I wanted noshi on it.
en.notes: 熨斗 was originally a strip of dried abalone in folded paper that was enclosed with gifts as a good-luck sign; today it is mostly just a small symbol at the top right of the wrapping paper. In shops you hear のしをお付けしますか; this usually means のし紙, a sheet with a printed 水引 and the occasion (御祝, 御中元). For bereavements, no のし is used. The word is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: I put money in the celebration envelope.
For my friend's wedding, I bought a celebration envelope at a convenience store.
You write your own name on the front of the envelope.
en.notes: 祝儀袋 is the decorated envelope for gifts of money on joyful occasions, above all weddings; politely often ご祝儀袋. It bears red-and-white or gold-and-silver 水引, the occasion on the front (寿, 御祝) and below it the name of the giver. It should contain new, unfolded bills; the money itself is called ご祝儀. The counterpart for bereavements is the 不祝儀袋 or 香典袋.

examples[].german: I'm bringing a condolence envelope.
The funeral was so sudden that I bought a condolence envelope at a convenience store.
You should not put new bills in a condolence envelope.
en.notes: 不祝儀袋 is the envelope for money on occasions of mourning, above all for condolence money (香典) at funerals; in daily life, people mostly say 香典袋. It has black-and-white or silver 水引 and inscriptions such as 御霊前 or 御香典. 不祝儀 means "sad occasion" and is the opposite of 祝儀. Traditionally, you do not put new bills in it, so that it does not look as if you had expected the death.

examples[].german: I'm sending a summer greeting.
A summer greeting card arrived from my teacher.
In the second half of August, you send a late-summer greeting instead of a summer greeting.
en.notes: 暑中見舞い is a greeting card sent during the hottest time (roughly mid-July to early August) to friends, relatives and business partners to ask how they are doing. Typical: 暑中見舞いを出す/送る; the card begins with 暑中お見舞い申し上げます. After 立秋 (around August 8), people write 残暑見舞い instead. The counterpart at the turn of the year is the New Year's card 年賀状.

examples[].german: We are in mourning, so we won't send New Year's cards.
In November, I received a card from a friend saying his family is in mourning.
Let's avoid saying "congratulations" to people in mourning.
en.notes: 喪中 is the mourning period after the death of a close relative, usually about one year. During this time you refrain from celebrations and above all from New Year's greetings: instead of 年賀状, you send a 喪中はがき in November or early December announcing that you will not be sending New Year's cards. Greetings such as あけましておめでとう are also avoided toward those in mourning. In writing, it is 喪中につき "due to mourning".

en.meaning: New Year's Eve temple bells; bells of New Year's Eve
examples[].german: I listen to the New Year's Eve bells.
At a nearby temple, I was allowed to ring the New Year's Eve bell.
When the New Year's Eve bells begin to ring, the new year is almost here.
en.notes: 除夜の鐘 is the ringing of the temple bells on New Year's Eve night (除夜 "the last night of the year"): the bell is struck 108 times, corresponding to the 108 worldly desires (煩悩) in Buddhism. Typical uses: 除夜の鐘を聞く, 除夜の鐘が鳴る, 除夜の鐘をつく (to strike it yourself, possible for visitors at many temples). After that often follows the first shrine or temple visit of the year, 初詣.

en.meaning: kagami mochi; New Year's rice cake offering
examples[].german: I put up the kagami mochi.
On Kagami-biraki day, we turned the kagami mochi into oshiruko and ate it.
Recently, plastic kagami mochi are also often sold.
en.notes: 鏡餅 are two round rice cakes stacked on top of each other with a bitter orange (橙, today often a mandarin) on top, set up in the house at New Year as an offering for the New Year deity; the name comes from the round shape of old mirrors (鏡). You say 鏡餅を飾る or 鏡餅を供える. Around January 11, it is broken at the 鏡開き - not cut, since cutting is considered bad luck - and eaten, for example, in sweet bean soup (おしるこ).

examples[].german: I put up the kadomatsu.
A large kadomatsu stands at the entrance of the department store.
After January 7, we take down the kadomatsu.
en.notes: 門松 is the New Year decoration made of pine branches and bamboo stalks cut at an angle, set up in pairs on the left and right of the house entrance or in front of shops. It is regarded as a guide and a seat for the New Year deity (年神). It is put up in the second half of December and taken down again after the New Year period (松の内, until January 7 or 15 depending on the region). Typical uses: 門松を飾る, 門松を立てる.

examples[].german: He became famous in no time.
The new game sold out in no time on its release day.
I thought the sky had gone dark, and then it was immediately pouring.
en.notes: たちまち means "in an instant, in no time" and mostly describes, after the fact, how quickly something happened: たちまち売り切れる, たちまち有名になる. It sounds narrative and somewhat literary. Unlike すぐ, it cannot be used for requests or plans (not: たちまち来てください). 突然 emphasizes the unexpected, not the speed.

examples[].german: I hang up the shimenawa.
A shimenawa is tied around the large tree at the shrine.
The shimenawa of Izumo Taisha is famous for being enormous.
en.notes: 注連縄 is a twisted rope of rice straw that marks off a sacred area - at shrines, around sacred trees or rocks - and is often hung with zigzag paper strips (紙垂). At New Year, a small decorated version, 注連飾り, is hung on the front door to ward off evil. Because of the difficult kanji, it is mostly written しめ縄 or しめなわ. Typical uses: しめ縄を張る, しめ縄を飾る.

examples[].german: The carp streamers are swimming in the wind.
Since our son was born, we raised carp streamers in the garden.
Many carp streamers are displayed above the river.
en.notes: 鯉のぼり are carp-shaped wind socks made of cloth that are raised on a pole in spring until Children's Day (こどもの日, May 5) - traditionally for the health and success of sons, because the carp swims against the current. Classically a black carp for the father hangs at the top, below it a red one and smaller colored ones for the mother and children. You say 鯉のぼりを上げる/立てる, and the streamers "swim" in the wind: 鯉のぼりが泳ぐ. Also often written in kana: こいのぼり.

examples[].german: I'm displaying the samurai helmet.
On Children's Day, I folded a helmet out of newspaper.
I really had to admit defeat in the face of his knowledge.
en.notes: 兜 is the helmet of a samurai or warrior. Today it is encountered mainly on Children's Day: an ornamental helmet or armor (五月人形) is put on display, and a helmet is folded for children out of newspaper (新聞紙で兜を折る). Modern protective helmets for construction or cycling are called ヘルメット. Idiom: 兜を脱ぐ "to admit defeat"; カブトムシ (兜虫) is the rhinoceros beetle.

examples[].german: On Tanabata, we write wish strips.
The Tanabata festival in Sendai is held in August.
I hope the sky is clear on the night of Tanabata.
en.notes: 七夕 is the star festival on July 7 (in some regions in August). It goes back to the legend of the weaver 織姫 (Vega) and the cowherd 彦星 (Altair), who are allowed to meet only on this night across the Milky Way (天の川). People write wishes on 短冊 and hang them on bamboo branches (笹). The reading たなばた is a special reading of the whole word and cannot be derived from the individual kanji.

en.meaning: tanzaku; wish slip (Tanabata); long narrow strip of paper
examples[].german: I write a wish on the tanzaku.
The children hung their tanzaku on the bamboo.
Please cut the daikon radish into thin rectangular strips.
en.notes: 短冊 is a long, narrow strip of paper; today it is best known from the 七夕 festival, where wishes are written on it and it is hung on bamboo branches (短冊に願い事を書く, 短冊を笹に飾る). Traditionally, poems such as 俳句 or 短歌 are also written on sturdier 短冊. In the kitchen, 短冊切り means cutting vegetables into thin rectangular strips.

en.meaning: shoro nagashi; floating lanterns or boats for the spirits (Obon)
examples[].german: We float lanterns at the shoro nagashi.
At the Shoro Nagashi in Nagasaki, people pull large boats through the town.
The year my grandfather died, we held a shoro nagashi as a family.
en.notes: 精霊流し is a custom at the end of お盆: small boats or lanterns with offerings are set on a river or the sea to send off the returned souls of the deceased (精霊, read しょうろう here). Very similar is 灯籠流し, in which only paper lanterns are floated. In 長崎, by contrast, families pull large, decorated boats through the streets to the noise of fireworks during the 精霊流し. Typical uses: 精霊流しをする, 精霊流しが行われる.

examples[].german: I light the welcoming fire.
On the evening of the first day of Obon, we lit the welcoming fire in front of the entrance.
Since we live in an apartment, we use an electric lantern instead of a welcoming fire.
en.notes: 迎え火 is the small fire lit in front of the house or at the grave on the first evening of お盆 (usually on July 13 or August 13) so that the souls of the ancestors can find their way home. Traditionally, hemp stalks (おがら) are burned in a clay dish for this; you say 迎え火を焚く. The counterpart on the last evening is 送り火. The word comes from 迎える "to welcome".

examples[].german: We send off our ancestors with the send-off fire.
In Kyoto, the Gozan Okuribi is held on August 16.
Once the send-off fire was lit, Obon was over.
