en.notes: 送り火 is the fire on the last evening of お盆 with which the souls of the ancestors are sent back to the other world (送る "to see off"); it is the counterpart of 迎え火. Typical use: 送り火を焚く. The best known is the 五山送り火 in 京都 on August 16, in which huge characters such as 大 burn on the mountainsides (popularly also called 大文字焼き).

examples[].german: I'm going to try goldfish scooping.
At the summer festival, I played goldfish scooping and caught as many as three.
The paper scoop for goldfish scooping tore right away.
en.notes: 金魚すくい is the classic stall game at summer festivals (夏祭り, 縁日): you try to scoop goldfish out of a shallow tank into a small bowl with a thin paper scoop (ポイ). Typical expressions are 金魚すくいをする and 金魚すくいに挑戦する; you can usually take the fish you caught home in a plastic bag. Besides the kana spelling すくい, 金魚掬い is also seen, but in daily life 金魚すくい is usual.

examples[].german: I aim for the prizes at the shooting gallery.
As a child, I often played the shooting gallery at festivals.
I knocked down a box of sweets at the shooting gallery and got to keep it.
en.notes: 射的 now mainly refers to the shooting gallery at festivals (縁日, 夏祭り): you shoot with a cork gun (コルク銃) at small prizes (景品) and get to keep what falls down. You say 射的をする or 射的で景品を狙う/取る. The general meaning "target shooting, shooting practice" is rare; for shooting as a sport or in the military, 射撃 is used.

en.meaning: sometime; someday; which (of several, formal); いずれも: all, both; いずれにしても: in any case
examples[].german: You will find out sooner or later.
Let's talk at length again sometime.
In any case, please reply by tomorrow.
en.notes: As an adverb, いずれ means "sooner or later, someday" (いずれ分かる) and often appears in polite farewells: いずれまた "until we meet again sometime". いずれにしても／いずれにせよ means "in any case, at any rate". In written language it is also a pronoun, "which (of several)": いずれの場合も "in either case", いずれも "all, both" (いずれも人気の商品です). いつか is vaguer and sounds more like a wish; the kanji spelling 何れ is rare and is also read どれ.

examples[].german: I bought cotton candy.
At the festival, a child was walking around holding a huge cotton candy.
Cotton candy melts right away when you put it in your mouth.
en.notes: 綿飴 is cotton candy, as bought at festival stalls (屋台). The word is mostly written in kana (わたあめ); synonymous is 綿菓子 (わたがし), and depending on region and person, one or the other is more common. The name is made up of 綿 "cotton, fluff" and 飴 "candy, sweet", because of its cotton-like shape.

examples[].german: The yakisoba from the food stall is delicious.
At the end of the barbecue, we made yakisoba on the iron griddle.
On busy days, I get by with instant yakisoba for lunch.
en.notes: 焼きそば are fried wheat noodles with vegetables and meat, usually with a sweet-savory sauce (ソース焼きそば). Despite そば in the name, they have nothing to do with buckwheat noodles; そば here stands generally for Chinese noodles, as in 中華そば. They are typical at festival stalls (屋台) and barbecues; one says 焼きそばを作る or 焼く. There are also 塩焼きそば and the instant version カップ焼きそば.

examples[].german: I'm making takoyaki.
When I go to Osaka, I want to eat authentic takoyaki.
On the weekend, we had a takoyaki party at a friend's house.
en.notes: たこ焼き are batter balls with pieces of octopus (たこ), baked in a special pan with half-round hollows (たこ焼き器) and served with sauce, mayonnaise, 青のり and かつお節. They are considered a specialty of Osaka. One says たこ焼きを焼く or たこ焼きを作る; a party where people make them together is colloquially called たこパ. たこ is almost always written in kana, rarely 蛸焼き.

examples[].german: I'm eating shaved ice.
It was hot, so I ordered strawberry-flavored shaved ice.
When I ate the shaved ice in a hurry, I got a brain freeze.
en.notes: かき氷 is finely shaved ice over which sweet syrup is poured, such as strawberry (いちご), melon, or matcha with sweet beans (宇治金時). It is a typical summer snack at festival stalls and in cafes; a little flag with the character 氷 shows that it is sold. The word comes from かく "to scrape" and 氷, where こおり becomes ごおり in the compound. If you eat too fast, you get a brain freeze: 頭がキーンとする.

examples[].german: I make shiratama.
Roll the dough into balls and put them in hot water.
Shiratama on top of matcha ice cream tastes great.
en.notes: 白玉 are small, soft dumplings made of glutinous rice flour (白玉粉), which is kneaded with water, rolled into balls and boiled. They are eaten in sweets such as あんみつ or ぜんざい, with sweet bean paste or on ice cream; you say 白玉を作る or 白玉を丸める. Unlike だんご, which are often sold on a skewer, 白玉 are usually loose. The basic meaning "white gem, pearl" is literary and hardly used in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I make jelly with agar.
Agar is low in calories, so I often eat it when I'm on a diet.
I set fruit juice with agar and made a dessert.
en.notes: 寒天 is a gelling agent made from red algae (agar-agar), used in Japan for sweets such as ようかん, あんみつ or fruit jelly. Unlike ゼラチン, it is plant-based, sets firmer and does not melt at room temperature. Typical are 寒天で固める "to set with agar" and 粉寒天 "agar powder". The literal meaning "cold winter weather" is literary and rare.

examples[].german: Hojicha has a roasted aroma.
In the evening, I make a point of drinking hojicha because it is low in caffeine.
The hojicha latte at this cafe is very popular.
en.notes: 焙じ茶 is green tea (usually 番茶 or 煎茶) that has been roasted at high heat. This makes it brown, gives it a nutty, roasted fragrance (香ばしい) and leaves it with little caffeine and bitterness, which is why it is gladly drunk in the evening or given to children. Instead of the difficult character 焙, it is mostly written ほうじ茶; the related verb is 焙じる "to roast". In cafes, ほうじ茶ラテ is popular.

examples[].german: I crossed the suspension bridge.
This suspension bridge sways a lot when the wind blows.
I'm bad with heights, so my legs shook on the suspension bridge.
en.notes: 吊り橋 is a suspension bridge, from narrow rope bridges over gorges to large structures across straits. You say 吊り橋を渡る; that it sways is expressed with 揺れる. Other spellings are 吊橋 and つり橋. Also well known is the 吊り橋効果: a pounding heart from fear is easily interpreted as being in love.

examples[].german: You can see the sea from the cliff.
Along the coast, high cliffs continue for many kilometers.
It is dangerous near the cliff, so please do not go beyond the fence.
en.notes: 断崖 is a vertically dropping rock face, especially a sea cliff. The word is rather literary and appears in travel guides, news and crime novels; in everyday speech, simply 崖 (がけ) is usually used. A fixed combination is 断崖絶壁 "sheer, vertical cliff face". For a hopeless situation in the figurative sense, 崖っぷち is more often used.

examples[].german: The Tottori Sand Dunes are famous.
When I climbed to the top of the dune, I could see the Sea of Japan.
Dunes gradually change shape because of the wind.
en.notes: 砂丘 is a sand dune piled up by the wind, on coasts as well as in deserts. In Japan, one immediately thinks of the 鳥取砂丘, where you can ride camels and go sandboarding. Unlike 砂漠 "desert", 砂丘 refers only to the dune or dune area; a sandy beach, by contrast, is 砂浜.

en.meaning: only; merely; to the end; persistently
examples[].german: It is only my personal opinion.
This is only a plan, so it may change.
He never changed his opinion to the very end.
en.notes: あくまで (also あくまでも, rarely 飽くまで) has two uses: as a limitation, "only, merely" (あくまで個人の意見, あくまで予定です) - very often as a caveat - and "to the end, persistently" (あくまで反対する, あくまで戦う). In the first sense it resembles ただ／単に, but stresses that something should not be misunderstood.

examples[].german: It smells of sulfur.
This hot spring contains a lot of sulfur, so the water is cloudy white.
Near the volcano, you can see yellow sulfur on the ground.
en.notes: 硫黄 is the chemical element sulfur. In daily life it is encountered mainly in volcanic and onsen areas: 硫黄の匂い（におい）がする "it smells of sulfur" (strictly speaking of hydrogen sulfide, 硫化水素), and 硫黄泉 is a sulfur spring. The reading いおう is an irregular reading of the whole word and cannot be derived from the individual characters.

examples[].german: This is an onsen with source water flowing freely through the bath.
The source water here is as hot as 90 degrees, so it is cooled with water.
Taxes are withheld at source from my salary.
en.notes: 源泉 is the origin of a spring, in daily life above all the point where a hot spring emerges. On onsen signs you read 源泉掛け流し: the source water flows fresh into the bath and runs off without being circulated or treated; 源泉の温度 is the temperature at the source. Figuratively, 源泉 stands for a source of power or knowledge, which is more literary. Very common in daily life is 源泉徴収 "withholding at source (of income tax)".

examples[].german: I take off my clothes in the changing room.
In winter the changing room is cold, so I keep a heater there.
The onsen changing room has lockers with keys.
en.notes: 脱衣所 is the room for undressing and dressing in front of the bath: in a private house, the anteroom of the bathroom, often with a sink and washing machine; at a 銭湯, 温泉 or swimming pool, the changing room. One says 脱衣所で服を脱ぐ. The fitting room in a shop, on the other hand, is called 試着室, and the changing room in gyms or companies usually 更衣室. Synonymous is 脱衣場.

examples[].german: I pay at the bathhouse counter.
The old woman sitting at the attendant's seat welcomed us with a smile.
In today's bathhouses, many places have you check in at a front desk instead of an attendant's seat.
en.notes: 番台 is the raised seat of the attendant in a traditional public bath (銭湯), usually at the entrance between the men's and women's changing rooms. From there, the attendant collects the admission fee and keeps an eye on the changing rooms; one says 番台に座る or 番台で料金を払う. Many 銭湯 today have a reception desk (フロント) in the entrance area instead, so 番台 sounds nostalgic.

en.meaning: cherry blossom blizzard; falling cherry petals
examples[].german: Cherry blossom petals are swirling.
Amid the falling cherry petals, the new students walked into the school.
Let's go take photos while the falling cherry petals are still beautiful.
en.notes: 桜吹雪 describes cherry blossom petals swirling down in large numbers in the wind, as if it were snowing (吹雪 "snow flurry"). You say 桜吹雪が舞う or 桜吹雪の中を歩く; the image stands for the end of the cherry blossom season and is popular in songs, poems and advertising. 花吹雪 is almost synonymous, since 花 in such expressions usually means cherry blossoms.

en.meaning: blizzard of blossoms; falling flower petals
examples[].german: The falling blossoms are beautiful.
While I was walking through the park, a sudden wind blew and the petals swirled like snow.
The two took a commemorative photo amid the falling blossoms.
en.notes: 花吹雪 refers to flower petals swirling through the air like snowflakes; this almost always means cherry blossoms, so it is largely synonymous with 桜吹雪. Typical uses are 花吹雪が舞う and 花吹雪の中で. The word sounds poetic and is a spring word in haiku. Swirling paper confetti, by contrast, is called 紙吹雪.

en.meaning: fresh greenery; young green leaves (early summer)
examples[].german: The fresh greenery is dazzling.
May is the season of fresh greenery and perfect for hiking.
It feels great to cycle through the fresh greenery.
en.notes: 新緑 is the fresh, light-green foliage of trees in early summer, roughly from the end of April through May. It is a typical seasonal word in letters, travel brochures and weather reports: 新緑の季節, 新緑が美しい, 新緑がまぶしい. In autumn, 紅葉 is spoken of instead. 新緑 sounds somewhat more elevated than 若葉 "young leaves".

examples[].german: I sweep up the fallen leaves.
Fallen leaves have piled up on the park path.
The children were playing, gathering fallen leaves.
en.notes: 落葉 (おちば) are leaves that have fallen, i.e. leaf litter. In everyday life it is mostly written 落ち葉; typical are 落ち葉を掃く, 落ち葉を拾う and 落ち葉が積もる. The spelling 落葉 is also read らくよう and then means "leaf shedding", for example in 落葉樹 "deciduous tree". The colorful autumn foliage on the trees, by contrast, is called 紅葉.

examples[].german: Thunderheads are building up.
A huge thunderhead has risen in the blue summer sky.
I can see a thunderhead, so there may be a thunderstorm in the evening.
en.notes: 入道雲 is a towering thunderhead (cumulonimbus), such as forms on hot summer afternoons. The name compares the cloud to a bald-headed giant (入道). You say 入道雲が出る or 入道雲が湧く; it often heralds thunder (雷) and sudden downpours (夕立). The technical term is 積乱雲; 入道雲 is the everyday word and a typical summer image.

examples[].german: Icicles hang from the eaves.
It was so cold this morning that long icicles had formed on the roof.
Falling icicles are dangerous, so please do not walk underneath.
en.notes: 氷柱 (つらら) is an icicle, such as hangs from the edge of the roof (軒) in winter. The word is mostly written in kana; typical combinations are つららが下がる, つららが垂れる and つららができる. The spelling 氷柱 can also be read ひょうちゅう and then refers to an ice column, for example a large block of ice for cooling in summer.

en.meaning: in the first place; to begin with
examples[].german: What is the problem in the first place?
To begin with, it's your fault for forgetting the appointment.
The original cause of the accident was a lack of checking.
en.notes: そもそも goes back to the origin or basic premise: "in the first place, actually, from the outset". It often questions a premise and then sounds slightly accusatory (そもそもあなたが…). As a noun with の: そもそもの原因 "the real cause". 最初に, by contrast, only means "first" in a sequence.

examples[].german: There is haze in the air.
Beyond the haze, you can faintly see distant mountains.
The town seen from the window was wrapped in haze.
en.notes: 霞 is the milky haze that lies over the landscape especially in spring and makes the distance blur; one says 霞がかかる or 霞に包まれる. It is a classic spring word, while dense fog, especially in autumn, is called 霧. Related is the verb 霞む "to blur, to become hazy", also for the eyes: 目が霞む. The word is often written in kana and is also a given name.

examples[].german: The morning dew glitters.
Dew had settled during the night, and the car windows were wet.
When I went out into the garden early in the morning, there was dew on the leaves.
en.notes: 露 is dew, the water droplets that form at night on grass and leaves; one says 露が降りる "dew falls" and 葉に露がつく. Common is the compound 朝露 "morning dew". Not to be confused with the identically read 梅雨 (つゆ) "rainy season". Literarily, 露 also stands for tears or transience, and adverbially つゆ…ない means "not in the least", as in つゆ知らず "without the faintest idea".

examples[].german: The echo resounds in the mountains.
When I shouted "yahoo" on the summit, an echo came back.
The children's laughter echoed through the valley.
en.notes: 木霊 is an echo, especially in mountains and valleys; originally people believed a tree spirit (木の霊) was calling back. You say 木霊が返ってくる or, as a する-verb, 声が谷に木霊する "the voice echoes in the valley". It is mostly written こだま in kana; 山彦 (やまびこ) is synonymous, whereas エコー stands more for technical reverb. こだま is also the name of the Shinkansen that stops at every station.

examples[].german: The sound of the bell crickets makes you feel autumn.
When night came, bell crickets began to chirp in the garden.
My son keeps bell crickets during summer vacation.
en.notes: 鈴虫 is a species of cricket whose chirping is reminiscent of a fine little bell (鈴) and is usually rendered as "リーンリーン". Its song is considered a typical sound of autumn; some people keep the insects at home in a container in summer. You say 鈴虫が鳴く, and the sound is called 鈴虫の声 or 鈴虫の音色. Other well-known autumn singers are コオロギ and マツムシ, which chirp differently.

examples[].german: I found a praying mantis.
The praying mantis catches small insects with its forelegs and eats them.
My little brother put the praying mantis he caught in the park into a bug cage.
en.notes: 蟷螂 is the praying mantis. The difficult kanji are hardly seen in daily life; it is almost always written カマキリ or かまきり. The name is usually interpreted as 鎌切り "sickle cutter", because of the sickle-shaped catching legs (鎌). Typical uses are カマキリを捕まえる and カマキリが虫を食べる; it is a popular insect for children to catch.

examples[].german: I use a calabash as a water bottle.
The calabash we grew in the garden took on a funny shape.
Something I said as a joke coming true - that's truly a horse out of a gourd.
en.notes: 瓢箪 is the bottle gourd with its typical pinched shape, and also the dried vessel made from it, which used to serve as a water or sake bottle. It is mostly written ひょうたん in kana. Well known is the idiom 瓢箪から駒（が出る） "a horse comes out of the gourd": something said in jest unexpectedly becomes reality. A pond in this shape is called 瓢箪池.

examples[].german: I am growing morning glories.
When I got up early, the morning glories on the balcony were in bloom.
In elementary school, I kept an observation diary of morning glories during summer vacation.
en.notes: 朝顔 is the Japanese morning glory, a climbing plant whose funnel-shaped flowers open early in the morning and wilt by noon; hence the name "morning face". It is the classic summer plant: elementary school pupils often grow it as a school project and keep an observation diary (観察日記). Typical uses are 朝顔が咲く, 朝顔を育てる and 朝顔のつる "vine". Summer markets for morning glories (朝顔市) are also well known.

examples[].german: The sunflower faces the sun.
During the summer vacation, we went to see a field full of sunflowers.
She is a person with a bright smile like a sunflower.
en.notes: 向日葵 is the sunflower; the kanji literally mean "mallow that turns toward the sun", and the reading ひまわり applies only to the whole word. In daily life it is mostly written in kana as ひまわり. It is a symbol of summer and cheerfulness; a radiant smile is called ひまわりのような笑顔. Typical expressions are ひまわりが咲く, ひまわり畑 "sunflower field" and ひまわりの種 "sunflower seeds".

examples[].german: The bush clover sways in the autumn wind.
Lots of bush clover flowers were blooming in the temple garden.
Bush clover is one of the seven flowers of autumn.
en.notes: 萩 is bush clover, a shrub with small pink to purple pea-like flowers on long, arching branches that blooms in late summer and autumn. It is one of the seven plants of autumn (秋の七草) and appears often in classical poetry. The sweet おはぎ is named after it because the bean paste is reminiscent of its blossoms. 萩 is also the name of a city in Yamaguchi.

examples[].german: A field of silvergrass stretches out.
On moon-viewing day, we displayed silvergrass and dumplings.
In the autumn evening sun, the silvergrass plumes shone silver.
en.notes: 芒 is silvergrass (Miscanthus), a tall grass with silvery-white, feathery plumes that covers whole slopes and fields in autumn. It is one of the seven autumn flowers (秋の七草) and is displayed together with rice dumplings (月見団子) at the moon-viewing festival (お月見). It is almost always written すすき, more rarely 薄; typical uses are すすきが揺れる and すすきの穂. South American pampas grass, by contrast, is called パンパスグラス.

examples[].german: I achieved my goal.
By running a little every day, I reached my goal of one hundred kilometers a month.
The whole team worked together and was able to meet the sales target.
en.notes: 達成する means "to reach a goal", almost always with a clearly defined goal as the object: 目標を達成する, ノルマを達成する, 記録を達成する. From it comes 達成感 "sense of accomplishment, feeling of having done something". 実現する fits better for dreams and plans that become reality; 到達する means reaching a place or level. In the office you often hear the noun 目標達成.

examples[].german: The problem still remains.
The cause of the accident is still not known.
The economy has recovered, but the unemployment rate is still high.
en.notes: 依然として means "still, as before" and sounds written; it is typical of the news and reports, often with unchanged, mostly unpleasant conditions: 依然として続く, 依然として分からない. In conversation people say まだ or 相変わらず. Do not confuse it with the identically read 以前 "earlier, before".

examples[].german: Matsutake is a luxury ingredient.
When autumn comes, my mother makes matsutake rice for me.
Domestic matsutake is too expensive, and I can hardly ever buy it.
en.notes: 松茸 is a strongly fragrant edible mushroom that grows in pine forests (松) in autumn and can hardly be cultivated. For that reason it is regarded as an expensive delicacy and the epitome of the taste of autumn (秋の味覚). Typical dishes are 松茸ご飯 and 土瓶蒸し; people rave about the 松茸の香り. Domestic mushrooms are especially expensive, so imported ones are often bought.

examples[].german: I add wasabi on the side.
I used too much wasabi and it stung my nose.
Please make the sushi for the children without wasabi.
en.notes: 山葵 is wasabi, the hot Japanese horseradish, whose rhizome is served freshly grated (すりおろす) with sushi and sashimi. It is mostly written わさび or ワサビ; the kanji are rare. The paste from a tube often consists largely of ordinary horseradish. The sharp pungency is described with 鼻にツーンとくる; "without wasabi" is called わさび抜き or simply サビ抜き for sushi.

examples[].german: Yuzu smells good.
On the winter solstice, it is customary to take a yuzu bath.
If you add a little yuzu peel to the hot pot, it smells better.
en.notes: 柚子 is an aromatic, very sour citrus fruit. It is hardly eaten on its own but is used mainly as a seasoning with its peel and juice, for example in ゆずポン酢 or as 柚子胡椒, a spicy paste of yuzu peel and chili. On the day of the winter solstice (冬至), people traditionally take a 柚子湯, a bath with floating yuzu. ゆず is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: I grate ginger.
Let's have ginger pork for dinner tonight.
When I have a cold, I drink hot black tea with ginger.
en.notes: 生姜 is ginger. In Japanese cooking it is mostly used freshly grated (すりおろす) or finely chopped, for example in the popular 豚の生姜焼き (pork in ginger-soy sauce). Pickled pink ginger served with sushi is called ガリ, and red ginger served with yakisoba 紅しょうが. In daily life it is often written in kana as しょうが; since ginger is considered warming, people like to drink 生姜湯 when they have a cold.

examples[].german: Konnyaku is low in calories.
Of the oden ingredients, I like konnyaku best.
Konnyaku doesn't absorb flavor easily, so score it first.
en.notes: 蒟蒻 is a firm, gray or white jelly made from the tuber of the konjac plant (devil's tongue). It has hardly any flavor of its own and almost no calories, so it is regarded as a diet food; it is typical in おでん and simmered dishes. It is almost always written こんにゃく in kana. In noodle form it is called しらたき, and こんにゃくゼリー is a popular snack.

examples[].german: I eat somen in summer.
When the somen is boiled, rinse it right away with cold water.
During summer vacation, we had nagashi somen as a family, and it was fun.
en.notes: 素麺 are very thin wheat noodles that are eaten cold, mainly in summer: briefly boiled, rinsed with cold water and dipped in a cold sauce (めんつゆ). They are thinner than 冷や麦 and much thinner than うどん. A summer fun activity is 流しそうめん, in which the noodles glide with water through a bamboo channel and you catch them with chopsticks. It is mostly written そうめん in kana.

examples[].german: I'm pan-frying gyoza.
On the weekend, the whole family wrapped gyoza together.
One ramen and gyoza set, please.
en.notes: 餃子 are dumplings of Chinese origin, usually filled with ground meat, cabbage and garlic. In Japan they are eaten mainly pan-fried (焼き餃子), often as a side dish to ラーメン, and dipped in soy sauce with vinegar and chili oil (ラー油). There are also 水餃子 (boiled) and 揚げ餃子 (deep-fried). One says 餃子を包む for filling and folding and 餃子を焼く for frying; on menus it is often written ギョーザ.

en.meaning: tsukudani; food simmered in soy sauce
examples[].german: I put tsukudani on top of the rice.
I used kombu tsukudani as the filling for the rice balls.
Tsukudani keeps well, so it is just right as a souvenir.
en.notes: 佃煮 are small fish, seaweed, shellfish or vegetables that are simmered for a long time in soy sauce, sugar and mirin until they are salty-sweet and keep for a long time. They are eaten in small amounts with rice or as the filling of おにぎり; well-known kinds are 昆布の佃煮 and のりの佃煮. The name goes back to the island 佃島 in Tokyo, where fishermen made these preserves in the Edo period.

examples[].german: I make chawanmushi.
When I go to a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant, I always order chawanmushi.
Chawanmushi is hot, so eat carefully.
en.notes: 茶碗蒸し is a savory steamed egg custard served in a small cup with a lid. The egg mixture is thinned with dashi and contains pieces such as chicken, shrimp, shiitake or ginkgo nuts (銀杏). It is eaten warm with a spoon, for example as a side dish in a sushi restaurant; you say 茶碗蒸しを作る or 蒸す. Unlike a pudding, it is not sweet.

examples[].german: I make zosui after the hot pot.
When I had a cold, my mother made egg zosui for me.
I made a simple zosui with leftover rice.
en.notes: 雑炊 is a rice porridge made from already cooked rice that is briefly simmered in seasoned broth with egg, vegetables or fish. It is typical as the finish of a hot pot (鍋の締め): you add rice to the remaining broth and stir in an egg. お粥, by contrast, is cooked for a long time from raw rice and is plainer; おじや is largely synonymous with 雑炊. When you have a cold, you like to eat a light 雑炊.

examples[].german: I will visit tomorrow.
May I ask your name?
I have already heard about this from Mr. Tanaka.
en.notes: 伺う is humble language (謙譲語) and replaces 訪ねる "to visit" as well as 聞く "to ask" and "to hear" when the action concerns a respected person: 先生のお宅に伺う, お名前を伺う, お話を伺う. ちょっと伺いますが is a polite way to introduce a question. For simply going somewhere with no reference to the other person, 参る fits better, and 伺う is never used for the actions of others. Do not confuse it with 窺う "to peek, to wait for an opening".

examples[].german: I draw water with the well bucket.
In the old days, every house drew water with a bucket from the well.
As the saying goes "an autumn day drops like a well bucket", it is already dark outside.
en.notes: 釣瓶 is the draw bucket of a draw well (井戸), which is lowered into the well on a rope and pulled back up when full; you say 釣瓶で水を汲む. Since such wells hardly exist any more, the word is known today mainly from the saying 秋の日は釣瓶落とし: the autumn sun sinks as fast as a falling well bucket, so it gets dark quickly. The word sounds old-fashioned.

examples[].german: I warm myself at the brazier.
At my grandfather's house, the brazier was brought out every winter.
An old brazier was displayed in the ryokan room.
en.notes: 火鉢 is a portable charcoal brazier made of ceramic, metal or wood in which charcoal (炭) glows in ash. Before modern heating, people warmed their hands at it (火鉢に手をかざす) or heated water; 暖を取る is the fixed phrase for "to warm oneself". Today it is mostly seen only in old houses, ryokan or as decoration. What English calls a "hibachi" (a small grill) corresponds in Japanese more to a 七輪.

examples[].german: The light of the andon is soft.
At night, andon are lit in the corridor of the ryokan.
I bought a lantern-style light that suits a Japanese-style room.
en.notes: 行灯 is a traditional standing lantern: a wooden frame covered with paper in which an oil lamp used to burn. Today 行灯 serve as atmospheric lights in ryokan, restaurants or at festivals, usually electric. The reading あんどん is irregular. Hanging, collapsible paper lanterns, by contrast, are called 提灯 (ちょうちん); colloquially, the illuminated sign on taxi roofs is also called 行灯.

examples[].german: I hang a scroll in the tokonoma.
For New Year, we replaced the scroll with a new one.
At the museum, I saw a hanging scroll by a famous painter.
en.notes: 掛軸 is a hanging scroll with a painting or calligraphy that is hung in the alcove (床の間) of a Japanese room and changed according to the season or occasion. You say 掛軸を掛ける or 掛軸を飾る. The spelling 掛け軸 is also common; for short, people often say just 軸.

examples[].german: I divide the room with a partition.
In the shop, transparent partitions are placed between the tables.
When changing clothes, please use the area behind this screen.
en.notes: 衝立 is a freestanding, single-panel screen used to divide a room or shield an area from view, for example in a restaurant, office or reception. You say 衝立で仕切る or 衝立を立てる. Unlike the foldable 屏風, a 衝立 consists of a single panel on feet; modern partitions are often called パーティション.

examples[].german: I carry soil with the wheelbarrow.
At the construction site, I put cement in a wheelbarrow and carried it.
I loaded the fallen leaves from the garden into the wheelbarrow and pushed it around back.
en.notes: 猫車 is a one-wheeled wheelbarrow, as used on construction sites and in the garden. You say 猫車で運ぶ or 猫車を押す. 一輪車 is heard more often for it, but that also means "unicycle"; on construction sites people often say just ネコ. There are several explanations for the origin of the name, for example that the barrow can go along narrow paths where otherwise only a cat has room.

examples[].german: I play on stilts.
I practiced stilts in elementary school and can finally walk on them.
The higher the stilts, the harder it is to keep your balance.
en.notes: 竹馬 are stilts made of bamboo with footrests, a traditional children's toy that is often practiced in elementary schools. You say 竹馬に乗る "to walk on stilts" or 竹馬で歩く. Also well known is the expression 竹馬の友 "friend from childhood", in which the characters are read in the Sino-Japanese way as ちくば.

examples[].german: We play hanetsuki at New Year.
The person who loses at hanetsuki gets ink painted on their face.
These days, you rarely see children playing hanetsuki.
en.notes: 羽根つき is a traditional New Year's game, similar to badminton: you hit a feathered shuttlecock back and forth with a decorated wooden paddle (羽子板). Whoever lets the shuttlecock drop traditionally gets something painted on their face with ink (墨). One says 羽根つきをする; the spelling 羽根突き is also common. It is rarely played today, but splendid 羽子板 are still sold as good-luck charms.

examples[].german: We laughed while playing fukuwarai.
At New Year, I played fukuwarai with the children.
In fukuwarai, you place the parts of a face while blindfolded.
en.notes: 福笑い is made up of 福 "luck" and 笑い "laughter" and is a classic New Year's game: blindfolded (目隠しをして), you place eyes, nose, mouth and eyebrows on the outline of a face, usually a plump-cheeked おかめ figure. The crooked result causes laughter. One says 福笑いをする or 福笑いで遊ぶ; like かるた and 凧揚げ, it is one of the typical お正月の遊び.

examples[].german: We play sugoroku with the family.
I rolled the dice and moved my sugoroku piece forward three spaces.
"Back to square one" is an expression that comes from sugoroku.
en.notes: 双六 is a dice racing game similar to snakes and ladders: you roll the dice (サイコロを振る), move your piece forward (コマを進める) and want to be the first to get from the start (ふりだし) to the goal (あがり). It is mostly written in kana as すごろく and used to be a typical New Year game. The expression ふりだしに戻る "back to square one, to start over" comes from it. The old 盤双六, by contrast, was a backgammon-like board game.

examples[].german: My name is Tanaka.
My father sends his best regards.
As I said earlier, the meeting starts at three o'clock.
en.notes: 申す is the humble form of 言う and is used for one's own speech or that of one's own family or company: 田中と申します "my name is Tanaka", 父がよろしくと申しておりました. 申し上げる is even more deferential and is addressed directly to the respected person (お願い申し上げます). For the speech of superiors, one uses おっしゃる. The word is also often found in 申し訳ありません "I am very sorry".

examples[].german: I play shogi.
My grandfather plays shogi with a neighbor every evening.
Becoming a professional shogi player is very hard.
en.notes: 将棋 is Japanese chess with 駒 "pieces" that you may place back on the board yourself after capturing them. The typical verb is 指す: 将棋を指す; colloquially, 将棋をする also works. For Go, 碁を打つ is said instead. A professional player is called 棋士. Figuratively, 将棋倒し means that a crowd of people topples like dominoes.

examples[].german: I place a stone on the go board.
The streets of Kyoto are laid out like a go board grid.
There is an old wooden go board at my grandfather's house.
en.notes: 碁盤 is the game board for Go (囲碁), on which 19 x 19 lines are drawn; the stones are placed on the intersections (碁盤に石を置く / 打つ). The board for shogi, by contrast, is called 将棋盤. Very common is the figurative expression 碁盤の目のよう "like a checkerboard, grid-like", for example for the street network of Kyoto or Sapporo.

examples[].german: Go stones come in white and black.
The child dropped the go stones on the floor.
The teacher placed a go stone in the center of the board.
en.notes: 碁石 are the round playing pieces of the game of Go, black (黒石) and white (白石). When playing you say 石を打つ or 石を置く; in conversation, simply 石 is often enough. For counting, 〜個 or 〜目 (points on the board) is mostly used. Do not confuse it with 碁盤, the playing board.

examples[].german: We play mahjong.
My father likes playing mahjong with his friends on weekends.
The rules of mahjong are complicated, and it took me a long time to learn them.
en.notes: 麻雀 is read with the Chinese-derived reading マージャン and is therefore often written in katakana as well. One says 麻雀をする; among players 麻雀を打つ is common. It is played by four people with 牌 "tiles", often in a 雀荘 "mahjong parlor". In Japan the game is regarded as a rather adult hobby, often associated with betting.

examples[].german: Hanafuda is a traditional Japanese card game.
At New Year, I played hanafuda with relatives.
Each hanafuda card has the flower of a month painted on it.
en.notes: 花札 are Japanese flower cards: 48 cards in 12 suits, each standing for a month and showing its flower or plant (e.g., 桜 for March). A single card is called 札. You say 花札をする or 花札で遊ぶ; the best-known game played with them is こいこい. Incidentally, Nintendo started out as a maker of 花札.

examples[].german: I was shown a kamishibai.
The kindergarten teacher read a kamishibai story to the children.
In the old days, kamishibai storytellers reportedly came to the park by bicycle.
en.notes: 紙芝居 is a picture-story theater: the storyteller pulls large picture boards one after another out of a small wooden frame and reads the text on the back. In the past, 紙芝居屋さん came to squares by bicycle and sold sweets; today it is used mainly in kindergartens and libraries. Typical phrases are 紙芝居を読む, 紙芝居をする and 紙芝居を見せる.

examples[].german: The rakugo performer's stories are funny.
My grandfather reportedly wanted to become a rakugo storyteller when he was young.
A rakugo performer portrays all sorts of scenes with just a fan and a hand towel.
en.notes: 噺家 refers to a professional teller of comic stories, especially in 落語. The character 噺 "tale" is a kanji created in Japan (国字). In everyday speech and in the media, 落語家 is the more common term; 噺家 sounds more traditional and is often used by the performers themselves. A 噺家 appears in a 寄席 and works only with a fan (扇子) and a hand towel (手ぬぐい).

examples[].german: I went to a yose.
At a yose, I heard live rakugo for the first time.
Old yose theaters still remain in Asakusa.
en.notes: 寄席 is a small traditional entertainment theater in which 落語, 漫才, magic and other variety acts perform one after another. You say 寄席に行く, 寄席に通う and 寄席で落語を聞く. The reading よせ is irregular and has to be learned. Classic 寄席 exist mainly in Tokyo, for example in Asakusa or Ueno.

en.meaning: manzai; comic dialogue by two performers
examples[].german: I laughed while watching manzai.
The two have been a manzai duo since high school.
I am going to do a manzai routine with a friend at the school festival.
en.notes: 漫才 is a comic dialogue act for two: the ボケ says nonsense, and the ツッコミ corrects them with quick retorts. 漫才 thus means the performance, not the duo itself; the duo is called 漫才コンビ, and the performers 漫才師 or 芸人. One says 漫才をする and コンビを組む. The art form is especially associated with Osaka and the Kansai dialect.

examples[].german: He dances wearing a Noh mask.
When she is angry, her face becomes as stiff as a Noh mask.
I saw old Noh masks at the museum.
en.notes: 能面 is the wooden mask of Noh theater (能). You say 能面をつける or 能面をかける. Although the mask looks rigid, its expression seems to change depending on the tilt of the head. Figuratively, 能面のような顔 is an "expressionless, stony face", often with suppressed anger.

examples[].german: I perform a shimai dance.
Shimai is Noh danced without a mask or special costume.
My mother is learning shimai as a hobby.
en.notes: 仕舞 here is a short excerpt from a Nō play, danced without mask and costume, only in formal kimono with hakama, to the chanting of the chorus. The matching verb is 舞う: 仕舞を舞う. Note: the same spelling and reading also means "end, finish"; in that sense, however, it is nowadays usually written おしまい or 終い.

examples[].german: The joruri recitation is wonderful.
Puppet joruri is also called Bunraku.
Joruri is an art form in which a story is recited to shamisen accompaniment.
en.notes: 浄瑠璃 is a narrative art in which a reciter (太夫) performs a story in song, accompanied by the shamisen. It is best known as the accompaniment of puppet theater: 人形浄瑠璃, today mostly called 文楽. Typical expressions are 浄瑠璃を語る and 浄瑠璃の語り. The most important style is called 義太夫節.

examples[].german: The actor enters via the hanamichi.
He won his last match and gave himself a glorious send-off into retirement.
In sumo, the wrestlers walk to the ring along the hanamichi.
en.notes: 花道 is, in Kabuki, the raised walkway that leads from the edge of the stage through the audience and is used for spectacular entrances and exits; in sumo, too, the wrestlers' path to the ring is called this. Very common is the figurative meaning "glorious exit at the end of a career", especially in 引退の花道を飾る. Not to be confused with 華道 (かどう, flower arranging).

examples[].german: He strikes a dramatic pose.
When the Kabuki actor struck his mie, people in the audience called out to him.
The department head boasted, "I will make sure it succeeds."
en.notes: 見得 is the dramatic, briefly frozen pose of a Kabuki actor at a climax; the fixed verb for it is 切る: 見得を切る. Figuratively, 見得を切る or 大見得を切る means "to boast, to put oneself on show with confidence". Not to be confused with the identically read 見栄 "vanity, outward show", which is paired with 張る: 見栄を張る.

examples[].german: I was amazed by the quick change.
This sofa turns into a bed in no time when you unfold it.
The actor changed into a different costume in an instant.
en.notes: 早変わり is originally the lightning-fast costume and role change of a kabuki actor on an open stage. As an intransitive する-verb, it generally means "to transform into something in no time", with に: AがBに早変わりする. It is used, for example, to advertise convertible furniture or to describe a room that is suddenly used differently.

examples[].german: The sound of the sanshin is pleasant.
On my trip to Okinawa I tried playing the sanshin.
The sanshin is covered with snakeskin.
en.notes: 三線 is the three-stringed lute of Okinawa, whose body is traditionally covered with snakeskin; it is regarded as the predecessor of the shamisen (三味線). It is played by plucking: 三線を弾く. Its sound (音色) characterizes Okinawan folk music and is often associated with vacations and relaxation.

examples[].german: I play the shinobue.
At the summer festival, you can hear drums and bamboo flutes.
The shinobue is a bamboo flute that is held sideways.
en.notes: 篠笛 is a simple, bright-sounding transverse flute made of bamboo (篠竹). You say 篠笛を吹く. It is the typical melody instrument of festival music (祭囃子) and folk dance. Do not confuse it with the shakuhachi (尺八), which is held vertically; a flute in general is simply called 笛.

examples[].german: I listen to a biwa performance.
Lake Biwa is said to have gotten its name because its shape resembles a biwa.
In the old days, biwa priests recited stories while playing the biwa.
en.notes: 琵琶 is a pear-shaped lute with a short neck that is played with a large plectrum: 琵琶を弾く. In the Middle Ages, 琵琶法師, blind wandering monks, used it to recite the Tale of the Heike (平家物語). 琵琶湖 owes its name to the shape of the instrument. Read the same but written differently is 枇杷 "loquat" (fruit).

examples[].german: We offer a kagura dance to the gods.
On the evening of the autumn festival, I saw kagura at the shrine.
The sound of kagura flutes and drums echoed through the shrine.
en.notes: 神楽 is Shinto music with dance that is offered to the gods, often on a dedicated stage in the shrine (神楽殿). The typical verb is 奉納する "to dedicate as an offering"; as a spectator one says 神楽を見る. The polite form is also お神楽. Besides the court kagura there are many regional folk forms (里神楽), which are performed at shrine festivals.

examples[].german: I listened to court music.
Gagaku was playing at the wedding at the shrine.
Gagaku is music that has been played at the imperial court for over a thousand years.
en.notes: 雅楽 is the ceremonial court music of Japan, which has been cultivated at the imperial court for over a thousand years; typical instruments are 笙, 篳篥 and 龍笛. You say 雅楽を演奏する or 雅楽を聴く. In daily life, you mainly encounter it at weddings at a shrine (神前式) and at New Year ceremonies. 雅 means "elegant, courtly".

examples[].german: The lion dancers have come.
It is said that if the lion bites your head at New Year, you will stay healthy all year.
I saw a lion dance at the festival in Chinatown.
en.notes: 獅子舞 is the lion dance, in which one or two dancers dance under a cloth with a large wooden lion head. In Japan it is seen mainly at New Year and at festivals; it is said that if you let the lion bite your head (頭をかんでもらう), you will stay healthy for a year. 獅子 is the mythical lion; the real animal is called ライオン.

examples[].german: I carry the portable shrine.
On festival day, the people of the neighborhood walk along carrying the mikoshi and shouting "wasshoi".
With the people around him pushing him forward, he became chairman.
en.notes: 御輿 is the portable shrine in which the deity is carried through the streets at festivals; it is more often written 神輿 or simply みこし, politely お神輿. The fixed verb is 担ぐ "to carry on the shoulders", often with shouts like わっしょい. Figuratively, 御輿を担ぐ means "to build someone up as a figurehead"; a festival float with wheels, by contrast, is a 山車.

examples[].german: The float parades through the street.
The children are pulling the ropes and moving the float.
The festival float was decorated with beautiful dolls.
en.notes: 山車 is a decorated festival float that is pulled on ropes through the streets at shrine festivals: 山車を引く. The reading だし is irregular; regionally, such floats are also called 曳山 or 屋台. By contrast, a 御輿 is carried on the shoulders. Similar in sound but unrelated is 出汁 "broth".

examples[].german: I take part in the festival wearing a happi coat.
The shop assistants wore matching happi coats and sold their products.
Happi coats are popular with foreign tourists as souvenirs.
en.notes: 法被 is a short, straight-cut cotton jacket, often printed with the name or crest of a neighborhood, club or shop. It is worn at festivals when carrying the shrine, but also by salespeople at promotions and by sports fans. The verb is 着る or 羽織る "to throw on". The reading はっぴ is irregular.

examples[].german: I tie on the headband.
At the sports festival, teams are distinguished by red and white headbands.
The exam candidate is studying wearing a headband that says "certain victory".
en.notes: 鉢巻き is a cloth tied around the forehead, mostly written in kana as はちまき. You say 鉢巻きを締める or 鉢巻きをする. It stands for determination and effort: it is worn at the sports festival (運動会, red against white), at festivals, as a way of cheering someone on, or when studying for exams with an inscription such as 必勝 "certain victory". A cloth twisted into a rope is called ねじり鉢巻き.

examples[].german: I wear a loincloth at the festival.
The match tomorrow is important, so let's roll up our sleeves.
I don't like the kind of approach that takes credit for other people's work.
en.notes: 褌 is the traditional Japanese loincloth for men made from a long strip of fabric, mostly written in kana as ふんどし. The verb is 締める. Today it is seen mainly at festivals such as the 裸祭り. Idioms are common: 褌を締めてかかる "to get down to work in earnest" and 人の褌で相撲を取る "to seek one's own advantage with someone else's means". The belt of sumo wrestlers, by contrast, is called まわし.

examples[].german: I put on the hand guards.
Travelers in the old days walked wearing hand guards and leg wraps.
I paired white hand guards with the dance costume.
en.notes: 手甲 is a cloth protector for the back of the hand and the wrist that is held in place by a loop around the middle finger. It used to be worn by travelers and field workers; today it is seen in folk dances such as the 阿波踊り or in ninja costumes, often together with 脚絆. You say 手甲をはめる or つける. Do not confuse it with 手の甲 (てのこう) "back of the hand" or with the identically read 鉄鋼 "steel".

examples[].german: I wrap on the leg wraps.
Travelers in period dramas usually wear leg wraps and straw sandals.
In old photos, all the soldiers have leg wraps wound around their legs.
en.notes: 脚絆 are cloth gaiters that are wrapped around the lower leg to protect the legs when walking and to make them less tired. You say 脚絆を巻く or つける. They were part of the equipment of Edo-period travelers (often with 手甲 and 草鞋) and, as wrap puttees (巻脚絆), part of soldiers' uniforms. Today the word is mostly encountered in historical films and festival costumes.

examples[].german: In the old days, people traveled in straw sandals.
He holds two jobs at once, as an office worker and a writer.
A huge straw sandal was hung at the temple gate.
en.notes: 草鞋 are woven straw sandals that are tied around the ankle with cords; mostly written in kana as わらじ. The verb is 履く. The idiom 二足のわらじを履く "to hold two jobs at the same time" is important. Do not confuse it with 草履 (ぞうり), flat sandals without lacing, which are also worn with a kimono.

examples[].german: I look into the kaleidoscope.
When you turn the kaleidoscope, the pattern keeps changing.
During summer vacation, I made a paper kaleidoscope with my child.
en.notes: 万華鏡 is a kaleidoscope, literally something like "mirror of ten thousand flowers". You say 万華鏡をのぞく (覗く is often written in kana) and 万華鏡を回す. Figuratively, 万華鏡のような describes something colorful and constantly changing, such as colors, landscapes or feelings.

en.meaning: to be; to go; to come (honorific)
examples[].german: Is the president in?
I hear the teacher is going to Kyoto next week.
A customer has arrived.
en.notes: いらっしゃる is the honorific verb (尊敬語) for 行く, 来る and いる – it elevates the person who goes, comes or is present, never oneself. The ます-form is irregular: いらっしゃいます (not いらっしゃります); in the て-form, besides いらっしゃって, the shorter いらして is often heard. As an auxiliary verb it replaces ている: 読んでいらっしゃる "is reading". The humble counterparts for one's own side are 参る ("to go, to come") and おる ("to be"); the shop greeting いらっしゃいませ also comes from this verb.

examples[].german: I paint in the eye of the daruma.
After winning the election, the candidate painted in the daruma's other eye.
The children are making a snowman in the park.
en.notes: 達磨 is the round, usually red good-luck doll modeled on the monk Bodhidharma, usually written in kana as だるま. When making a wish, you paint in one eye (目を入れる), and when it comes true, the second - typically done, for example, after election victories. Because it rights itself again and again, it stands for 七転び八起き. Well-known derivatives are 雪だるま "snowman" and 火だるま "ablaze, engulfed in flames".

examples[].german: The train will arrive shortly.
The meeting will start shortly.
Soon after I came to Japan, I made friends.
en.notes: 間もなく means "soon, shortly" and is mostly written in kana as まもなく. It sounds more formal than もうすぐ and is typical of announcements: まもなく電車が参ります. After the て-form, 〜て間もなく means "shortly after ..."; 〜て間もない describes something that happened only a short time ago. Rarer is 〜する間もなく "without having time to do something".

examples[].german: No matter how many times I threw the darts, they didn't hit the dartboard, and in the end they were all misses.
I drew a lottery ticket, but it was a blank.
My grandmother's house is on the outskirts of town.
en.notes: 外れ is the noun of 外れる "to miss, to come off". It means, on the one hand, "blank, miss" - the opposite of 当たり, for example with lottery tickets or predictions - and on the other hand "edge, far end", especially in 町の外れ or 町外れ "outskirts of town". As a suffix it is very productive: 期待外れ "disappointing", 季節外れ "out of season", 的外れ "beside the point".

examples[].german: There are all kinds of people in the world.
Life isn't that easy, you know.
I want to do work that is useful to society.
en.notes: 世の中 means the world as the human society one lives in, with its rules and the spirit of the times - not the globe (世界). Typical phrases are 世の中は甘くない "life is no picnic", 世の中の役に立つ "to be useful to society" and 世の中が変わる. It sounds more everyday and emotional than the matter-of-fact 社会.

examples[].german: What an admirable child you have.
I was impressed by how good his Japanese is.
Making noise until late at night is not something I approve of much.
en.notes: 感心 expresses appreciative impressedness: 〜に感心する "to be impressed by something, to admire something". As a な-adjective, 感心な means "commendable", often said of children or younger people; toward superiors it comes across as condescending, where 感動 or 感銘を受ける fit better. In the negative, あまり感心しない means "not exactly approve of". Not to be confused with the identically read 関心 "interest" (〜に関心がある).

en.meaning: to give birth to; to lay (eggs)
examples[].german: I heard that she just had a baby last winter and is going to have another one this autumn.
This hen lays an egg every morning.
My sister gave birth to a healthy boy last month.
en.notes: 産む is transitive: 子どもを産む "to give birth to a child", 卵を産む "to lay eggs". The intransitive counterpart is 生まれる "to be born". For the figurative "to produce, to create", 生む is usually written: 誤解を生む, 新記録を生む; 産む is reserved for actual birth. More formal and medical is 出産する.

examples[].german: The boy was whistling happily.
My grandmother often told me that if you whistle at night, snakes will come.
He called the dog with a whistle.
en.notes: 口笛 is whistling with the lips; the verb is 吹く: 口笛を吹く, often written in kana as ふく. With で one can whistle something or call someone: 口笛で曲を吹く, 口笛で犬を呼ぶ. A whistle or a referee's whistle, on the other hand, is called 笛 or ホイッスル. A well-known superstition says that whistling at night attracts snakes.

examples[].german: The oldest participant at the party for movie lovers was, believe it or not, a hundred years old.
All participants, please wear a name tag.
This year's marathon had more than ten thousand participants.
en.notes: 参加者 are the "participants" in an event, course or competition, formed from 参加 + 者. Typical are 〜の参加者, 参加者を募集する and 参加者数. For people present at meetings or in class one rather says 出席者, for participants in competitions also 出場者, for visitors to an event 来場者. The word is neutral and sounds somewhat formal in announcements.

en.meaning: to throw into disorder; to disturb
examples[].german: Don't you realize that remarks like that are disturbing everyone's harmony?
Please don't break the line; line up in order.
The strong wind tousled her hair.
en.notes: 乱す is transitive and means "to throw into disorder, to disturb"; the intransitive counterpart is 乱れる "to become disordered". Typical objects are 列を乱す "to break ranks", 秩序を乱す "to disturb order", 和を乱す "to disturb harmony", 髪を乱す "to tousle hair" and 心を乱す "to unsettle". Unlike 邪魔する, it is less about obstruction than about destroying an order.

examples[].german: When I was told not to become friends with an alien, I wanted to even more.
Do you think aliens really exist?
He thinks in such a unique way that everyone calls him an alien.
en.notes: 宇宙人 refers to a being from another planet, "extraterrestrial", formed from 宇宙 "outer space" and 人. It is the normal everyday word; エイリアン sounds more like a science-fiction monster. Colloquially, a very eccentric person is also jokingly called 宇宙人: あの人は宇宙人みたいだ.

examples[].german: Please help yourself.
What would you like to drink?
Our teacher does not drink alcohol.
en.notes: 召し上がる is the honorific verb (尊敬語) for 食べる and 飲む; the food or drink takes を. It is used for guests, customers and superiors, never for oneself – for one's own eating one says humble いただく. The invitations どうぞ召し上がってください and, even more politely, お召し上がりください are very common, for example in restaurants or on packaging. 何を召し上がりますか is the polite version of 何を食べますか.

examples[].german: Because of the enemy's sudden attack, the inside of the spaceship was thrown into great confusion.
Through the window of the spaceship, the Earth looked blue.
In the future, we may be able to travel to the moon by spaceship.
en.notes: 宇宙船 is a "spaceship", especially a crewed vehicle for travel in space – in reality as in science fiction. One says 宇宙船に乗る and 宇宙船で〜へ行く. The launch rocket, by contrast, is called ロケット, a space station 宇宙ステーション, and a UFO (ユーフォー) is an unidentified flying object.

examples[].german: Amazon sent me two more pairs of footwear than I ordered.
Please take off your footwear in the entrance.
I collect Japanese footwear such as geta and zori.
en.notes: 履き物 (also 履物) is the umbrella term for everything worn on the feet: 靴, サンダル, 下駄, 草履 and so on. It sounds somewhat more formal than 靴 and often appears on signs: 履き物をお脱ぎください. Typical uses are 履き物を脱ぐ and 履き物をそろえる "to line up the shoes you took off neatly". The corresponding verb is 履く.

en.meaning: to be confused; to be thrown into disorder; to fall into chaos
examples[].german: Many users were confused by the sudden rule change.
The station was in total chaos because of the accident.
So much was explained to me at once that my head was in a muddle.
en.notes: 混乱する is intransitive and describes two things: a situation falls into disorder (駅が混乱する, 交通が混乱する), or a person is confused (頭が混乱する). The cause is marked with に or で: 急な変更に混乱する. Intensified, it is 大混乱. To confuse someone is 混乱させる. Not to be confused with 混雑 "crowding, congestion".

examples[].german: You can't use proper nouns in shiritori.
"Tokyo" and "Mt. Fuji" are proper nouns.
Japanese does not capitalize proper nouns, so they can sometimes be hard to recognize.
en.notes: 固有名詞 is the grammatical term for proper nouns such as names of people, places or companies; the counterpart is 普通名詞 "common noun". Since Japanese has no capitalization, proper nouns can only be recognized from context or from katakana and readings. In everyday life you hear the word, for example, in the rules of games like しりとり or when using a dictionary.

examples[].german: I know it's not my place to say, but I think you should leave the yakuza.
The police searched the office of the crime syndicate.
People connected to organized crime are refused entry to this shop.
en.notes: 暴力団 is the official term used by the police, in laws and in the news for yakuza organizations. Colloquially, ヤクザ is said; in contracts and on signs you also read 反社会的勢力 (short: 反社). Members are called 暴力団員. Typical expressions are 暴力団に入る and, for leaving, 暴力団から足を洗う.

examples[].german: The motorcycle gang admitted to running over the raccoon.
In the middle of the night I couldn't sleep because of the noise of a biker gang's motorcycles.
He was in a motorcycle gang when he was young, but now he works honestly.
en.notes: 暴走族 are youth motorcycle or car gangs who drive noisily and recklessly through the streets at night; formed from 暴走 "to race, to drive out of control" and 族 "tribe, group". Typical phrases: 暴走族に入る, 暴走族のバイク. The phenomenon was especially widespread in the 1970s and 80s; today the word is known mainly from the news and films.

examples[].german: Knock it off! You've made too many errors of judgment lately.
"Enough is enough!" the older brother yelled at his younger brother.
How many times do I have to say the same thing? Knock it off.
en.notes: いい加減にしろ is the rough imperative of いい加減にする "to let it be enough" and means "That's enough!, Stop it!". It sounds harsh and rather masculine; it is shouted in anger when someone keeps doing something over and over. Somewhat softer are いい加減にして (a request), いい加減にしなさい (parents to children) or いい加減にしてください. Not to be confused with the adjective いい加減な "careless, sloppy".

examples[].german: Humidity is a camera's worst enemy.
Even if we're in the lead, carelessness is the great enemy.
Lack of sleep is said to be the enemy of beauty.
en.notes: 大敵 is a "great, dangerous enemy". In everyday life it is almost always used figuratively in the pattern AはBの大敵: 湿気はカメラの大敵 "humidity is the enemy of any camera". Very well known is the proverb 油断大敵 "carelessness is the greatest enemy". For a personal rival, ライバル is used more often; an archenemy in the sense of a mortal enemy is 宿敵.

examples[].german: Koichi is invincible at shiritori.
That team hasn't lost once this year; it is an invincible team.
In the game, if you pick up this item, you become invincible for a while.
en.notes: 無敵 means "invincible, without an equal opponent" (literally "no enemy"). It is used predicatively with だ or attributively with の: 無敵のチーム; less often with な. In games, 無敵 also denotes the state of invulnerability: 無敵になる. Intensified there is 天下無敵 "invincible in the whole world". Merely undefeated so far, on the other hand, is 負けなし.

en.meaning: to be finished, to end; to get by (with)
examples[].german: I have just now finally finished my work.
I was wearing a seat belt, so I got off with a minor injury.
A friend drove me, so I did not have to take a taxi.
en.notes: 済む means "to be done, to be over", with the matter as the subject: 仕事が済む, 用事が済む; in contrast to 終わる, it emphasizes that something is checked off. Also important is the meaning "to get off lightly, to get by with something": 軽いけがで済む, and ～ずに済む or ～なくて済む "not to have to do something". The transitive counterpart is 済ませる or 済ます "to finish, to get done"; the apology すみません is originally the negated form of this verb. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 住む "to live".

examples[].german: That committee member has excellent judgment, doesn't he?
I was elected library committee member in my class.
More than half of the committee members opposed the plan.
en.notes: 委員 is a member of a committee; the committee itself is called 委員会, and its chairperson 委員長. At school one encounters the word constantly: 学級委員 "class representative", 図書委員 "library duty member", 保健委員 "health duty member". One is 委員に選ばれる "elected as a member". Not to be confused with 会員 "member of an association or club" or the general メンバー.

en.meaning: to be raised (a hand); to be named; to turn up (evidence)
examples[].german: When the teacher said that, many hands went up.
Mr. Tanaka's name has come up as a candidate for the next leader.
New evidence turned up, and the case was finally solved.
en.notes: 挙がる is the intransitive counterpart of 挙げる "to raise, to name": 手が挙がる "hands go up", 名前が挙がる "a name is mentioned / is under discussion", 例が挙がる "an example is given", 証拠が挙がる "evidence comes to light", 犯人が挙がる "the culprit is caught". For general upward movement (prices, stairs, temperature), 上がる is written; for raising hands, both spellings are seen, with 挙がる emphasizing the deliberate raising.

examples[].german: Was your high school uniform a sailor suit or a blazer?
At our company, the receptionists have to wear a uniform.
That police officer was not wearing a uniform, so I didn't notice.
en.notes: 制服 is a prescribed uniform, for example of schools, police, railway staff or companies: 制服を着る, 制服姿 "in uniform". The opposite is 私服 "civilian or casual clothes", e.g. 私服の警官 "plainclothes police officer". For sports jerseys one rather says ユニフォーム. Japanese school uniforms are typically セーラー服 "sailor suit" or ブレザー "blazer".

examples[].german: Well, but knowledge you learned under compulsion is quickly forgotten, isn't it?
Participation is not mandatory, so feel free to join as you like.
The app stopped responding, so I force-quit it.
en.notes: 強制 is "compulsion"; as a する-verb it means "to force someone to do something": 人に〜を強制する. Very common are the passive 強制される "to be forced" and the adverb 強制的に "forcibly". On a computer, 強制終了 means the forced termination of a program. Colloquially one rather says 無理やり〜させる; 強制 sounds matter-of-fact to official, often in 強制ではない "not obligatory".

examples[].german: Smoking is not permitted in this office.
My older brother works at a law office.
I'll bring the documents to the office tomorrow.
en.notes: 事務所 is an office as a workplace, often the whole office of a small company or firm: 弁護士事務所, 設計事務所, 芸能事務所 (talent agency). For the office in a large company, you also say オフィス, and for the administration in schools or buildings, 事務室. 会社, by contrast, is the company as an organization, not the room.

examples[].german: Making delicious mixed rice is your mission.
He accomplished the dangerous mission safely.
The astronauts are undergoing training for their next mission.
en.notes: 任務 is an officially assigned task, a mission - typical in the military, police, space travel or in games and films. Fixed phrases: 任務を果たす "to fulfill the mission", 任務を与える "to give an assignment", 任務に就く "to take up a post". For ordinary work one says 仕事, for a role (even an everyday one) 役目; 義務 is a duty. In everyday life, 任務 therefore often sounds jokingly solemn.

examples[].german: Taking everything together, I think this site is well made.
My father works at the general hospital in front of the station.
She came first in the class on the overall test score.
en.notes: 総合 means "summary, totality". As a verb, 総合する means "to sum up, to put together", especially in 総合すると "all in all" and 総合的に "comprehensively, holistically". It is very common as a prefix "overall, general": 総合病院 "general hospital", 総合大学 "comprehensive university", 総合点 "total score", 総合優勝 "overall victory". In contrast to 全体, 総合 emphasizes bringing different parts together.

examples[].german: Various incidents happened on this trip, but overall it was very enjoyable.
Looking at it overall, this year's sales were not bad.
My overall impression was of a bright and friendly town.
en.notes: 総体的 is a na-adjective meaning "overall, on the whole" and is mostly used adverbially: 総体的に(は), 総体的に見て. It sounds bookish; in everyday speech one rather says 全体的に or 全体として. Note: the identically pronounced 相対的 means "relative" - the opposite of 絶対的 - and is much more common. So pay close attention to the kanji when typing.

examples[].german: I heard a rumor that that company is finally opening a branch in Japan; is it true?
An information center for tourists has been set up inside the station.
This school has strict rules on how to use smartphones.
en.notes: 設ける is a formal transitive verb for "to set up, to create, to provide for": 支店を設ける "to open a branch", 窓口を設ける "to set up a contact point", ルールを設ける "to establish rules", 機会を設ける "to create an opportunity", 席を設ける "to arrange a meeting". In the passive, 〜が設けられている describes existing facilities. In everyday speech it often corresponds to 作る. Not to be confused with the similar-sounding 儲ける "to make money".

examples[].german: Starting next fiscal year, a public committee will be set up.
At the town's public market, you can buy fresh fish cheaply.
This gymnasium is a public facility of the city, so anyone can use it.
en.notes: 公設 means "established by the public sector (state, city, municipality)" and almost always appears with の or as a prefix: 公設市場 "municipal market", 公設の施設 "public facility", 公設秘書 "publicly paid secretary of a legislator". The opposite is 私設 "privately established". For public schools and hospitals, 公立 is used instead, and for "public" in the general sense 公共 (公共交通機関).

examples[].german: I am aware of it.
I am very sorry, but I do not know about that matter.
We would be grateful for your cooperation.
en.notes: 存じる is the humble verb (謙譲語) for 知る "to know" and 思う "to think". It is used almost only in fixed forms: 存じております "I know", 存じません "I am not aware of it" (more polite than 知りません), 〜と存じます "I think" in business letters. When one knows a respected person, one says 存じ上げております. The respectful counterpart for others is ご存じ: ご存じですか.

examples[].german: To start a new company, you need a certain amount of capital.
Foreign capital has come into this company.
In this job your body is your capital, so I make sure to sleep well.
en.notes: 資本 is "capital" in the economic sense. Common compounds are 資本金 ("capital stock"), 資本主義 ("capitalism") and 外国資本, shortened 外資 ("foreign capital"). For money for a specific purpose one rather says 資金, and colloquially for start-up money 元手. Very common is the expression 体が資本 ("health is the most important capital").

examples[].german: My father is from Okayama Prefecture.
Okayama Prefecture is famous for peaches and grapes.
In the summer vacation I traveled to Kurashiki in Okayama Prefecture.
en.notes: 岡山県 is a prefecture in the Chūgoku region of western Japan, with the capital 岡山市. It is known for the legend of 桃太郎, for peaches and muscat grapes, the garden 後楽園 and the old town of 倉敷; because of its sunny weather it calls itself 晴れの国. Typical combinations: 岡山県出身 "from Okayama", 岡山県の〜. Without 県, 岡山 often means the city.

examples[].german: Following is optional.
Please choose any number.
If you buy a car, you should also take out voluntary insurance.
en.notes: 任意 means "voluntary, optional, at one's own discretion" and is used with です, の or で: 参加は任意です, 任意の項目, 任意で提出する. On forms, 任意 is the opposite of 必須 "required field". In mathematics and technology, 任意の means "arbitrary" (任意の数). Fixed terms are 任意保険 "voluntary supplementary car insurance" and 任意同行 "voluntarily accompanying the police". The tone is matter-of-fact and official.

en.meaning: to check (at a checkpoint); to inspect
examples[].german: Look, the police are checking cars over there.
At night I was stopped at a drunk-driving checkpoint.
At the border, soldiers inspected the cars one by one.
en.notes: 検問 is a check at a roadblock, above all road or border control by police or military; the place is called 検問所 "checkpoint". As a verb: 警察が車を検問する, often also without an object (検問している). Typical is 飲酒検問 "drunk-driving checkpoint". For technical inspections one says 検査 or 点検, for everyday checking チェックする.

examples[].german: "I should have checked it properly myself." "Don't blame yourself so much. It's not your fault."
He was reproached by his boss for being late.
Blaming the person who failed won't solve the problem.
en.notes: 責める means "to reproach someone, to put the blame on someone": 人を責める, 〜のことで責める, often reflexive 自分を責める "to blame oneself". It is about blame, not about upbringing - for scolding by parents or teachers one says 叱る; 非難する is public, formal criticism. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 攻める "to attack" (sports, war).

en.meaning: to omit; to cut out; to save
examples[].german: I've been very busy lately, so I skip the trouble of cooking dinner and just get takeout.
Since I'm short on time, I will omit the detailed explanation.
Let's cut out waste and reduce costs.
en.notes: 省く is transitive and means "to omit, to save": 説明を省く "to omit the explanation", 手間を省く "to save oneself trouble", 無駄を省く "to cut out waste", politely 詳しいことは省きます. For abbreviating words one says 略す, for skipping a meal rather 抜く (朝ご飯を抜く), for excluding people 除く.

examples[].german: What are your thoughts, Professor, on the recent surge in young people living alone?
The number of foreign tourists has been rising sharply lately.
Because online shopping has surged, deliveries are delayed.
en.notes: 急増 means "abrupt increase"; as a verb it is mostly intransitive: 観光客が急増する, as a noun 〜の急増. The word belongs to the language of news and reports; in conversation one rather says 急に増える. The opposite is 急減 "sharp decline"; more neutral is 増加, even stronger 激増.

examples[].german: I will never accept a tax increase.
The government plans to raise the consumption tax next year.
Let's replace the refrigerator before the tax increase.
en.notes: 増税 is the "tax increase"; as a verb, the state raises taxes: 政府が増税する, often with the name of the tax: 消費税の増税 "increase of the consumption tax". The opposite is 減税 "tax cut". The word is typical of politics and news; in everyday speech one also says 税金が上がる.

examples[].german: I wish alcohol were tax-free.
In this country, books can be imported duty-free.
The residents of this island are said to have paid no taxes in the past.
en.notes: 無税 means "tax-free, duty-free" in the sense of "no tax at all is levied here"; it is used with の, で or だ: 無税の品, 無税で輸入する. More common in everyday life are 免税 "tax exemption" (免税店 "duty-free shop") and 非課税 "non-taxable" (非課税の収入). The opposite is 課税 "taxation".

examples[].german: In fact, even if an alien were mingling with the crowd, nobody would notice.
It looked nice in the photos, but when I actually went there, it was a small room.
In actual fact, nothing has been decided yet.
en.notes: 実際 is both a noun and an adverb. 実際に means "actually, in real life" (実際に見る "to see with one's own eyes"), 実際は / 実際には "in reality (however)" as opposed to expectation or theory, 実際の "actual, real". At the beginning of a sentence, 実際、… means "indeed, really" and confirms what was said. 本当に is more colloquial, 現実 means reality as the opposite of a dream.

examples[].german: I have looked at your photos.
May I see your ticket?
I have read your e-mail. I will reply right away.
en.notes: 拝見する is the humble verb (謙譲語) for "to look at, to read" when one looks at something that belongs to the person one is talking to or to a superior: お手紙を拝見しました, 切符を拝見します "your ticket, please". It is used only for one's own action, never for the other person's; for that one says honorific ご覧になる. In neutral language it corresponds to 見る or 読む. It is transitive with を.

examples[].german: When the confirmation screen appears, please enter your ID and password to log in.
Please check that the windows are closed before you go out.
Just to be sure, please let me confirm the time of tomorrow's meeting.
en.notes: 確認 is "confirmation, checking"; mostly used as a transitive する-verb: 〜を確認する "to check something, make sure". It is very common in polite formulas like ご確認ください "please check" and 念のため確認させてください "let me double-check to be safe". Compounds: 確認画面, 本人確認 "identity verification", 再確認. The Japanese verb 確かめる is somewhat more personal, チェックする more casual.

examples[].german: Complaining doesn't solve anything, so I make it a principle not to complain.
Japan is a democracy.
He is a perfectionist, so his work takes a very long time.
en.notes: 主義 is a noun meaning "principle, doctrine" and serves above all as a suffix for "-ism": 民主主義 "democracy", 資本主義 "capitalism", 個人主義 "individualism", 完璧主義 "perfectionism". Used personally: 〜ない主義だ "it is my principle not to ...", 主義を守る / 曲げる. Related are 信念 "conviction" and 方針 "course, guideline".

examples[].german: My older brother works at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology announced a new education policy.
Which ministry is in charge of this problem?
en.notes: 〜省 forms the names of the Japanese ministries: 外務省 ("Ministry of Foreign Affairs"), 財務省, 文部科学省, 厚生労働省. The minister is called 〜大臣 (外務大臣); ministries and agencies together are called 省庁, and subordinate offices end in 〜庁 (気象庁). In China, 省 also denotes a province (広東省). Not to be confused with the verb 省く ("to omit"), which uses the same kanji.

en.meaning: to make up for; to compensate
examples[].german: I plan to make up for the time I took off sick by working on my days off.
To make up for the deficit, the bonus was cancelled.
Sorry I couldn't keep my promise. I'll make it up to you next time.
en.notes: 埋め合わせる is transitive and means "to make up for, to compensate": to fill in absences, losses or a deficit with something else (〜を…で埋め合わせる). The noun 埋め合わせ is very common, especially toward people: この埋め合わせは必ずするよ "I'll definitely make it up to you". Related are 補う "to supplement" and 取り戻す "to take back, to make up for lost ground".

examples[].german: Today's lesson was on na-adjectives.
"Shizuka" is a na-adjective, so it becomes "shizuka na" before a noun.
In Japanese class at school, we learned the difference between i-adjectives and na-adjectives.
en.notes: 形容動詞 is the term of traditional Japanese school grammar for na-adjectives such as 静か or 便利; the i-adjectives are simply called 形容詞 there. In teaching Japanese as a foreign language, ナ形容詞 and イ形容詞 are mostly used. Literally it means "adjective-verb", because these words are conjugated like a predicate with だ/です.

en.meaning: real sense; actual feeling; to really feel
examples[].german: I'm finally starting to feel like a parent.
I still can't believe that we won.
Since I started living on my own, I have realized how much I appreciate my parents.
en.notes: 実感 is the "real, personal feeling" for something - that it is really so. Typical: 実感がわく "something becomes tangible", often negated: まだ実感がわかない "I still can't believe it"; 実感が持てる, 実感がこもる. As a transitive verb, 〜を実感する means "to feel something firsthand, to really notice". Simple 感じる is more general; 実感 emphasizes personal experience.

examples[].german: I sewed lace onto the fabric.
This shirt is made of thin fabric, so it's perfect for summer.
At the craft store, I bought fabric for curtains.
en.notes: 布地 is "fabric" as a material, especially for clothing, curtains or covers: 布地を選ぶ, 厚い布地, 布地が薄い. In sewing shops and fashion, 生地 is also often heard with the same meaning. 布 alone is more general, "cloth, piece of fabric". Type of weave: 綿の布地 "cotton fabric", ウールの布地 "wool fabric".

examples[].german: I can't eat something this mysterious.
In the middle of the night I heard a strange noise and was too scared to sleep.
A shady stranger called me over and over.
en.notes: 得体 "true nature, identity" occurs almost only in the fixed phrase 得体の知れない (also 得体が知れない): "unidentifiable, shady, eerie" - one doesn't know what or who it really is. It is used for things, noises and people: 得体の知れない男, 得体の知れない音. It is often also written in kana as えたい. On its own the word is hardly used.

examples[].german: Koichi is a man the whole world envies.
Stop just envying other people and make an effort yourself.
I felt a bit of envy at my friend's passing, but I said "congratulations" from the bottom of my heart.
en.notes: 羨む is transitive: 人を羨む "to envy someone", 人の成功を羨む "to envy someone's success". It sounds rather written; in conversation, the adjective 羨ましい is almost always used ("I envy you" = 羨ましいなあ). The expression 誰もが羨む〜 "enviable" is common. 妬む or 嫉妬する, by contrast, contain ill will. It is also often written in kana as うらやむ.

en.meaning: to be irritated; to feel on edge
examples[].german: That person is always on edge, isn't he?
The train just wouldn't come, and I got irritated.
When I'm hungry, I get irritated easily.
en.notes: 苛々する means "to be irritated, impatient, to get annoyed". It is written almost always in kana, often in katakana イライラ; the kanji 苛々 are rare. The trigger is marked with に: 〜にイライラする "to get worked up about ...". As a noun: イライラが溜まる "frustration builds up". 怒る means to get openly angry, whereas イライラ describes rather inner tension; むかつく is cruder.

en.meaning: to challenge; to take on a challenge
examples[].german: I will take on something new.
Without fearing failure, I tried baking bread for the first time.
A young player is going to challenge the champion.
en.notes: 挑戦する means "to dare to try something, to take on a challenge"; the target takes に: 新しいことに挑戦する, 世界記録に挑戦する. It can also mean to challenge a stronger opponent: チャンピオンに挑戦する. Unlike the English "challenge", 挑戦 does not mean a mere difficulty; for that one says 課題. The loanword チャレンジする is just as common in everyday speech and somewhat more casual.

examples[].german: Has the teacher already looked at these materials?
Please take a look at this picture here.
en.notes: ご覧になる is the honorific form of 見る. It is used for seeing or looking by a person one wants to show respect to, not for one's own action. The object takes を. The expression is conjugated via なる like a Godan verb: ご覧になりました, ご覧になってください. The meaning "to try something" after a te-form does not belong to these examples.

examples[].german: Drunk driving is a crime.
He was caught drunk driving and his license was revoked.
There's a drinking party tonight, so I'm going by train. Otherwise it would be drunk driving.
en.notes: 飲酒運転 is composed of 飲酒 "alcohol consumption" and 運転 "driving": "driving under the influence of alcohol". Typical: 飲酒運転をする, 飲酒運転で捕まる "to be caught drunk driving". In Japan the limit is practically zero, and even passengers who allow it are punished. The slogan is 飲んだら乗るな "If you drink, don't drive"; legally one also speaks of 酒気帯び運転.

examples[].german: Adults work and get money for it, right?
I received a watch from my older sister for my birthday.
For the parts you don't understand, it is good to have a senior colleague explain them to you.
en.notes: 貰う "to receive" is mostly written in kana, もらう. The giver takes に or から: 姉に/から時計をもらう. As an auxiliary verb, 〜てもらう means "to have someone do something for oneself, to get something done". The humble form is いただく. On direction: あげる "I give", くれる "someone gives to me", もらう "I receive" – the subject is always the recipient.

examples[].german: How awful, leaving without saying anything.
You must not leave the scene of an accident.
She bowed quietly and left the room.
en.notes: 立ち去る is intransitive and means "to move away, to go off" - usually for good and often without a word. The place left takes を: その場を立ち去る "to leave the place". The word is narrative and literary; in conversation one rather says 出ていく, 帰る or いなくなる. 去る alone is even more formal.

examples[].german: I hope this wish comes true someday.
My dream from childhood came true, and I became a pilot.
Unfortunately, that love went unrequited.
en.notes: 叶う is intransitive: 夢が叶う "a dream comes true", 願いが叶う, 恋が叶う "love is requited". The transitive counterpart is 叶える: 夢を叶える "to fulfill a dream". Not to be confused with 敵う "to be a match for someone" (彼には敵わない) and 適う "to meet, to suit" (目的に適う), which are pronounced the same.

examples[].german: They do say that autumn is the season of harvest.
The weather was good this year, so the rice harvest is good.
Studying abroad was a very fruitful experience.
en.notes: 実り is the noun of 実る "to ripen, to bear fruit" and denotes the ripening crop or the yield: 稲の実り, 実りの秋 "autumn as the harvest season" (fixed phrase). Figuratively, 実りの多い / 実りある means "productive, fruitful": 実りある話し合い, 実りの多い一年. 収穫, on the other hand, means rather the bringing in of the harvest or the "gain" from an experience.

examples[].german: I don't want to live anywhere but a newly built condominium.
I plan to build a new house next year.
I brought beautiful flowers as a housewarming gift for my friend's new home.
en.notes: 新築 means a new building; as an attributive, 新築の家 / 新築マンション "newly built". As a transitive verb, 家を新築する "to build a new house". The opposite in the housing market is 中古 "used, existing property"; 改築 is "rebuilding", リフォーム "renovation". 新築祝い "housewarming gift" is also common.

examples[].german: Marilyn's cat has a very fluffy tail.
The dog is wagging its tail happily.
The police have finally caught on to the culprit.
en.notes: 尻尾 is the tail of an animal and is often written in kana as しっぽ; the written-language word is 尾.
