Expressions: 尻尾を振る "to wag the tail" (figuratively also "to fawn"), 尻尾を出す "to give oneself away", 尻尾をつかむ "to catch on to someone". The end of things can also be called 尻尾, for example of a fish or bread.

examples[].german: I was so absorbed that I lost track of time.
Five years have already passed since I came to Japan.
As time passes, the pain will surely fade too.
en.notes: 経つ is intransitive and used only for time: 時間が経つ, 三年が経つ, 〜てから一年経つ "a year has passed since ...". 経てば "as time passes" is common. It is often also written in kana as たつ. Not to be confused with the homophones 立つ "to stand", 建つ "to be built" and 発つ "to depart". 過ぎる is similar but rather emphasizes passing a point in time.

examples[].german: We were able to receive valuable advice from someone experienced.
It says "experienced applicants preferred" - can I apply even without experience?
I would like to hear from someone who has studied abroad.
en.notes: 経験者 is a person with experience in a particular field or someone who has experienced something themselves: 留学経験者 "someone who has studied abroad", 〜の経験者. In job ads one reads 経験者優遇 "experienced applicants preferred" and, as the opposite, 未経験者歓迎 "career changers welcome". ベテラン, on the other hand, means someone with very long experience.

examples[].german: The roads are pretty congested at that time, aren't they?
The morning train is always crowded, and I can't get a seat.
It gets crowded on weekends, so let's go on a weekday.
en.notes: 混む is intransitive: the place or vehicle takes が/は, and for the state one usually uses 混んでいる: 電車が混んでいる "the train is crowded". It is also written 込む. The opposite is すいている "to be empty". More formal is 混雑する (station announcements); for car traffic jams one also says 渋滞する.

en.meaning: to grab; to seize; to grasp
examples[].german: I seized the chance.
The train shook, so I ended up grabbing the arm of a person nearby.
After practicing several times, I finally got the knack.
en.notes: 掴む (often つかむ) means "to grab, to grasp" (腕を掴む), figuratively "to seize, to obtain" (チャンスを掴む), "to grasp" (要点・コツを掴む "to get the hang of it") and "to win" (人の心を掴む). 握る is to hold firmly in the hand, 捕まえる to catch something that is fleeing. Intransitive partner: 掴まる "to hold on" (つり革に掴まる).

examples[].german: This review is quite well put together.
My father writes film reviews for the newspaper.
A well-known commentator on TV explained the election result.
en.notes: 評論 is an expert review or critical essay on literature, films, art or politics; its author is a 評論家 "critic, commentator". As a verb: 〜を評論する. It is an analysis, not necessarily negative - "criticism" in the sense of blame is 批判. Similar is 批評; casually, レビュー is used.

examples[].german: Darin was overwhelmed by the beauty of nature.
In the final, we were overwhelmed by the opposing team.
Her singing overwhelmed the other contestants.
en.notes: 圧倒する is transitive: 相手を圧倒する "to overpower the opponent, to be clearly superior". Very common is the passive 〜に圧倒される "to be overwhelmed by something" (beauty, size, presence). The adjective 圧倒的 "overwhelming" is also common: 圧倒的な勝利, 圧倒的に多い "by far the most". The tone is neutral to slightly formal.

examples[].german: In the days before dictionary apps existed, looking up kanji was hard.
Do you think aliens really exist?
There is no correct answer to this problem.
en.notes: 存在する is intransitive and the formal, abstract counterpart of ある/いる: 〜が存在する "there is, to exist". It suits questions of existence (宇宙人は存在するか), rules, problems or data. In everyday speech it sounds stiff - there one says ある/いる. The noun 存在 also means "presence, person of importance": 大きな存在, 存在感.

examples[].german: I was told sarcastically, "You can't even solve a quiz like this?"
She is always bragging and is a bit of an unpleasant person.
Saying "You're early today" to me when I'm late - what a nasty dig.
en.notes: 嫌味 is a pointed, spiteful remark or an unpleasant, affected manner. Typical: 嫌味を言う "to make snide remarks", 嫌味な人 "unpleasant, arrogant person", 嫌味っぽい "snide, condescending". Often in kana いやみ or イヤミ. 皮肉 is "irony", rather indirect and sometimes witty; 悪口 is badmouthing, usually behind someone's back.

examples[].german: Many proposals were made for crime prevention.
Convenience stores have security cameras installed.
I have my child carry a personal safety alarm.
en.notes: 防犯 means "crime prevention" and appears mainly as a prefix or with の: 防犯カメラ "security camera", 防犯ブザー "personal safety alarm", 防犯対策, 防犯のため. Similarly built are 防災 "disaster prevention" and 防火 "fire prevention". 警備 is guard duty, and 防止 is general prevention (事故防止).

examples[].german: I'm going to take a quick nap.
On Sunday afternoons, I like to take a nap on the sofa.
The cat is napping comfortably in the sun.
en.notes: 昼寝 is the midday nap; as an intransitive verb 昼寝する or 昼寝をする, often downplayed: ちょっと昼寝する. 居眠り, by contrast, is dozing off unintentionally (in class, on the train), and 仮眠 is a short nap, for example during a night shift. Do not confuse it with 寝坊 "oversleeping".

examples[].german: "Are you planning to work overtime today too?" "Um... well, I'm sleep-deprived today, so I'd rather leave early, if anything."
I was playing games until late yesterday, so I'm short on sleep.
If the lack of sleep continues, you make more mistakes at work.
en.notes: 寝不足 is "lack of sleep" and is used as a na-adjective or noun: 寝不足だ "to have slept too little", 寝不足で頭が痛い, 寝不足が続く. Toned down: 寝不足気味 "a bit sleep-deprived". More formal and medical is 睡眠不足; 徹夜 is an all-nighter.

en.meaning: to pass; to elapse (time); to exceed
examples[].german: Summer has passed, and mornings and evenings have become cool.
It is already ten minutes past the appointed time.
The train has just passed Tokyo Station.
en.notes: 過ぎる means "to pass, to go by" – spatially past a place, where the place then takes を (駅を過ぎる), and in time (夏が過ぎる, 約束の時間が過ぎる). In addition there is "to exceed": 四十歳を過ぎる. As a suffix on verb stems and adjectives, ～すぎる means "too much, too" (食べすぎる, 高すぎる) and is then mostly written in kana. The noun 過ぎ follows time expressions: 五時過ぎ "just after five". The transitive counterpart is 過ごす "to spend time".

examples[].german: I have never once had onions sting my eyes.
This summer was the hottest on record.
Forget the past and look ahead.
en.notes: 過去 is "the past" and forms a series with 現在 and 未来. Typical: 過去に "in the past, so far", 過去の〜 "past ...", 過去最高 "record high", 過去形 "past tense". Also one's personal, often undisclosed past: 暗い過去. 昔 is more colloquial and rather means more distant times, 以前 "before, previously".

en.meaning: penalty game (for the loser of a game)
examples[].german: The person who lost the game had to take a photo making a silly face as a penalty game.
As a penalty game, I was made to sing a song in front of everyone.
Working outside on such a hot day is like a penalty game.
en.notes: 罰ゲーム is the "penalty task" that the loser has to carry out in party games or TV shows, such as doing something embarrassing or eating something disgusting. Typical are 罰ゲームをする, 罰ゲームを受ける and 罰ゲームとして〜. Colloquially, anything unpleasant is called that: 〜なんて罰ゲームだ. Here 罰 is read ばつ; ばち in 罰が当たる, on the other hand, is divine punishment.

en.meaning: to hold in one's arms; to have (a problem)
examples[].german: I have many problems.
He headed to the station carrying a large piece of luggage in both arms.
Seeing the test results, I held my head in my hands.
en.notes: 抱える first means "to hold in the arms, to carry under the arm" (荷物を抱える); 頭を抱える means "to rack one's brains, to despair". Figuratively: "to have (problems, debts, worries), to be burdened with": 問題・借金・悩みを抱える. Also "to employ, to have to support" (社員を抱える). Do not confuse it with 抱く（だく）"to embrace" - same kanji, different reading.

examples[].german: How did this company come into being?
Last month a baby was born to my sister.
As a result of the election, this town got its first female mayor.
en.notes: 誕生 is "birth" and, as an intransitive verb, 誕生する "to be born, to come into being". For people it sounds solemn; in everyday speech one says 生まれる. It is very common for the emergence of things: 新しい会社 / 政権 / スターが誕生する. Well-known compounds are 誕生日 "birthday" and 誕生会 "birthday party".

examples[].german: Oh no, there's a missing character!
Before submitting, please check carefully for typos and omitted characters.
This book has many missing characters, so it is hard to read.
en.notes: 脱字 is an omitted character in a text. It mostly appears in the pair 誤字脱字 "typos and omitted characters", for example in 誤字脱字がないか確認する "to proofread for errors". 誤字 is a wrong character, 誤植 a printing error. The word belongs to written and office language.

examples[].german: That monk also has some American blood.
At the temple, a monk was reciting sutras.
We called a priest for my grandfather's funeral.
en.notes: 坊さん is a familiar but respectful term for a Buddhist monk or priest; the most common form heard is お坊さん. 坊主 alone can sound derogatory, while 僧 and 僧侶 are formal. Typical situations: funerals and memorial services (お坊さんを呼ぶ "to call a priest"), お経を読む "to recite sutras".

examples[].german: The baby finally went to sleep for me.
My mother showed me photos from when I was a baby.
A baby was crying the whole time on the train, and the mother was at a loss.
en.notes: 赤ん坊 refers to a baby or infant. In everyday speech, 赤ちゃん is much more common and sounds more affectionate and polite, especially when talking about someone else's baby; 赤ん坊 is more matter-of-fact and often appears in narratives and descriptions. Typical are 赤ん坊が泣く, 赤ん坊が生まれる and 赤ん坊のころ "as a baby". The literary 赤子 is dated.

examples[].german: Before becoming a monk, I shaved my head.
I started a diary, but it ended up lasting only three days.
Fishing today was a bust. I didn't catch a single fish.
en.notes: 坊主 means "Buddhist monk", but today often sounds disrespectful - politely one says お坊さん. Other meanings: shaved head (坊主頭, 坊主にする "to shave one's head"), familiarly "boy" (うちの坊主 "my boy") and, in fishing, "caught nothing". The expression 三日坊主 denotes someone who quickly gives up on their plans.

examples[].german: There should be a guide stationed at each venue.
I sent the same materials to each school.
en.notes: 各〜 stands before a noun and means "each individual" or "all respectively": 各会場 means every venue, 各学校 every school. It suits organizational announcements and the distribution of tasks or documents. No の stands before the noun. The sign 〜 marks the following element and is not pronounced; 各 is the spelling of the prefix.

examples[].german: This app has users all over the world.
This weekend, it will probably snow all around the country.
On my trip, I toured hot springs all over Japan.
en.notes: 各地 means "various places, everywhere (in an area)" and is a noun. Typical: 全国各地 "all over the country", 世界各地 "all over the world", 日本各地, 各地で "in many places", 各地の天気 in the weather report. The tone is factual (news, reports); in conversation, あちこち or いろいろな所 is more usual.

examples[].german: On your marks, get set, go!
I changed the position of the desk a little.
Nagano Prefecture is located almost in the center of Honshū.
en.notes: 位置 is the position or location of an object or place: 位置を変える ("to rearrange"), 位置を確認する ("to check the position"). As an intransitive する-verb, Xに位置する means "to be located in X" - typical of geography and rather written. For an arbitrary place, everyday speech uses 場所; social standing or standpoint is usually expressed with 地位 or 立場. Fixed: 位置について、用意、ドン！ as the starting command.

examples[].german: Roughly how much does moving cost in Japan?
Studying abroad costs quite a lot.
The company covered the repair costs.
en.notes: 費用 is the cost incurred for an undertaking: 費用がかかる ("it costs"), 費用を払う, 費用を負担する ("to bear the cost"). It sounds somewhat more businesslike than everyday speech and often appears in compounds such as 引っ越し費用 or 旅行費用. The price of a product is 値段, a fee for a service 料金, and for individual running costs one uses the suffix 〜代 (電気代, タクシー代).

examples[].german: I am being allowed to study Japanese at my company's expense.
He studied abroad at an American university at company expense.
Let's not waste company money.
en.notes: 社費 is costs borne by the company and almost always appears in the form 社費で "at company expense": 社費で留学する, 社費で研修に行く. The counterpart is 自費 ("at one's own expense"). Related is 経費 (business expenses), which is heard more often in the office, for example 経費で落とす "to charge to the company". Register: business language.

examples[].german: I support my family.
I supported the body of an elderly woman who was about to fall.
When times were hard, my friend's words supported me.
en.notes: 支える means physically "to support, to hold" (倒れないように支える) and figuratively "to support, to sustain" - emotionally, financially or as a foundation: 家族を支える, 経済を支える. The noun 支え means "support, backing" (心の支え). 助ける is "to help, to rescue", 手伝う "to help with a task", 応援する "to cheer on, to support". Often in the passive: 〜に支えられる.

examples[].german: The fall in land prices caused by the Chinese market crash won't stop.
Land prices in Tokyo are quite high even by global standards.
Since the station was built, land prices in this area have risen.
en.notes: 地価 is the price of land, not of buildings. Typical: 地価が上がる／下がる, 地価が高い, 地価の下落 ("fall in land prices"); the word belongs mainly to the news and economic topics. Not to be confused with 物価 (general price level) or 家賃 (rent) - and with the homophone 地下 ("underground, basement"), which you can tell apart only by the writing.

examples[].german: The momentum of criticism of that high school student's video has grown stronger again, hasn't it?
He flung the door open with force.
In the heat of drunkenness, I ended up confessing to her.
en.notes: 勢い is momentum, force or drive - of movements, but also of people, companies or trends. Common: 勢いがある ("energetic, on the rise"), 勢いよく ("vigorously, with force"), 勢いを増す, 勢いがつく. With 〜た勢いで one describes something done in a moment of excess, e.g. 酔った勢いで "in a drunken state". 力, on the other hand, is simply "strength", 元気 the liveliness of a person.

examples[].german: When you think of the world's two major powers, which countries come to mind?
The strength of the typhoon has gradually weakened.
That political party is expanding its influence among young people.
en.notes: 勢力 is the power or influence of groups, parties or states: 勢力を伸ばす／拡大する ("to gain influence"), 勢力争い ("power struggle"), 二大勢力 ("the two major powers"). In weather reports it refers to the strength of a typhoon: 台風の勢力が強い／弱まる. 勢い, by contrast, is the momentum of a movement, 権力 the governing power of the state, and 影響 means "influence" in the sense of "effect".

examples[].german: That store manager always takes a humble stance, so I like him.
If your posture is bad, your lower back will hurt.
That company is showing a proactive stance on environmental issues.
en.notes: 姿勢 is first of all body posture: 姿勢がいい／悪い, 姿勢を正す ("to sit/stand up straight"). Figuratively it means the stance or attitude toward a matter: 前向きな姿勢, 〜に対する姿勢. 低姿勢 means "a humble, reserved manner". 態度 describes more the concrete behavior toward others, and ポーズ a pose, for example for a photo.

examples[].german: When I take attendance for a large number of students, I sometimes skip one or two names.
Today we're going to the park in a big group.
en.notes: 大勢 refers to a large number of people. As a noun it connects with の: 大勢の生徒 "many students". It is not a general quantity expression for things. 出席を取る means to take attendance. 大勢で can describe an action as a joint undertaking of many people.

examples[].german: My parents work at a privately run nursing home.
In Japan, privately run railways are called "shitetsu".
This parking lot is privately run, so the fee is a bit high.
en.notes: 私営 means "privately operated", that is, run by private individuals or companies, in contrast to 公営, 国営, 市営 or 官営. It appears as a prefix (私営バス) or with の before a noun (私営の鉄道). In daily life, 民営 ("privately owned", cf. 民営化 "privatization") is heard more often, or 私鉄 for private railways. Note: 市営 ("municipal") is read しえい in the same way.

examples[].german: I live in municipal housing now.
In this town, seniors can ride the city buses for free.
I went to the municipal pool every day during summer vacation.
en.notes: 市営 means "run by the city" and mostly appears as a prefix: 市営バス, 市営地下鉄, 市営住宅 (municipal public housing), 市営プール; or with の: 市営の施設. In the same series are 国営, 県営, 町営 and, as the opposite, 私営 - which is read just the same, しえい. For municipal schools, hospitals or libraries, on the other hand, one says 市立 (市立図書館).

examples[].german: In the Meiji period, many government-run factories were built.
Please explain the difference between government-run and privately run.
en.notes: 官営 means "operated by the government" (官 = government office, 営 = to operate). Today it appears mainly in historical texts about the Meiji period, for example 官営工場 or 官営八幡製鉄所. For present-day state enterprises, 国営 is used, for public facilities in general 公営; the opposite is 民営 or 私営. Register: written, history and economics.

examples[].german: I jog every morning in a prefecture-run park.
Applications for prefectural housing start next month.
This baseball stadium is run by the prefecture, so the usage fee is cheap.
en.notes: 県営 means "operated by the prefecture" and appears mostly as a prefix or with の: 県営住宅, 県営球場, 県営の公園. It belongs to the series 国営 (national), 県営, 市営 (municipal), 町営 and 私営 (private). For schools and similar prefectural institutions, 県立 is used instead (県立高校).

examples[].german: The president's speech was very moving.
The US presidential election is held once every four years.
Japan has no president; it has a prime minister.
en.notes: 大統領 is the president of a state, such as the USA or France; 大統領選挙 is the presidential election. Other "presidents" have their own words: company president 社長, chairman 会長, university president 学長. Japan itself has no 大統領, but a prime minister (首相, 総理大臣). The shout よっ、大統領！ to a performer is an old-fashioned, joking compliment.

en.meaning: to support; to nurture; to cultivate
examples[].german: I support my family.
I run every day to build up my stamina.
Reading cultivates the power of thought.
en.notes: 養う means "to support (someone), to provide for their livelihood": 家族を養う, 妻と子供を養う. It is also used for developing abilities and qualities: 体力を養う, 想像力を養う, 考える力を養う - often in the passive 養われる. It is somewhat more elevated than 育てる "to raise"; keeping pets is 飼う. Also fixed is 英気を養う "to recharge one's energy".

examples[].german: In today's presentation, I will mainly take up three measures.
Do you have any good ideas?
As a measure against the declining birthrate, the government created a new system.
en.notes: 策 is a plan, measure or stratagem for solving a problem. On its own it appears in rather written expressions like 策を練る ("to devise a plan"), 策を講じる ("to take measures") or いい策がない. It is much more common in compounds: 対策 (countermeasure), 政策 (policy), 解決策 (solution). In everyday speech one rather says 方法, 手 (打つ手がない) or 作戦.

examples[].german: Last night I came up with a really good subtitle that fits my book perfectly.
I think the subtitle of this paper is a bit too long.
The film has the subtitle "The Last Summer".
en.notes: 副題 is the subtitle of a book, film or article, that is, the addition to the main title (題名, タイトル); サブタイトル is synonymous. Typical: 副題を付ける, 副題が付いている, 「〜」という副題. Note: the subtitles shown on screen in films are not called 副題 but 字幕. 見出し is a headline in a newspaper or text.

examples[].german: I think I was past twenty when I watched that match.
When you watch the same movie many times, you start to see expressions you didn't notice at first.
en.notes: 観る（みる）is used for watching films, performances or sporting events. What is watched takes を. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 観ます, 観て, 観た. 見る is the more general spelling for "to see"; the special spelling 観る is used for spectating and viewing. Even in this spelling the reading is みる.

examples[].german: I like the exterior of this apartment building.
It was a hotel that looked old on the outside but was very clean inside.
In Kyoto, there are even rules for the exterior color of buildings.
en.notes: 外観 is the outward appearance, especially of buildings and objects: 建物の外観, 外観がいい, 外観は古いが…. The counterpart is the interior (内装, 中). For people's looks, one says 外見 or, colloquially, 見た目. The word sounds somewhat matter-of-fact and written, e.g. in real estate or product descriptions.

examples[].german: Do you have any suggestions on how to improve public safety in this area?
This is a no-parking zone.
After the earthquake, this area was closed off to entry.
en.notes: 区域 is a delimited area or zone, often officially designated: 禁煙区域, 駐車禁止区域, 危険区域, 立ち入り禁止区域. 地域, by contrast, is a region or locality in the general sense, 地区 is a district or neighborhood, and 区 is the administrative ward of a large city (新宿区). Register: rather matter-of-fact; typical of signs and government offices.

examples[].german: After this one, I'm going to quit smoking for good.
I went outside and breathed in fresh air.
en.notes: 吸う is a transitive godan verb: 吸います, 吸って. It can mean breathing in air or smoking a cigarette; with を you name the air or tobacco. 吸うのをやめる ends the activity, and つもり names the intention. In sū the u is long; the negative form is 吸わない.

examples[].german: This plate looks like it has a crack, but it's designed that way on purpose!
I wonder if he lost on purpose.
I didn't do it on purpose. I'm really sorry.
en.notes: わざと means "on purpose, deliberately" and is almost always written in kana; the kanji 態と are rare. Very common is the apology わざとじゃない ("it wasn't on purpose"). Not to be confused with わざわざ ("specially, going out of one's way"), which stresses an effort made for someone. More formal are 故意に and 意図的に; わざとらしい means "affected, put on".

examples[].german: The company president committed a huge blunder and tried to cover it up, but that only backfired.
I made the blunder of being late to an important meeting.
The prime minister's blunder drew criticism from the public.
en.notes: 失態 is an embarrassing mistake or blunder, especially when someone in a position of responsibility damages their reputation. Fixed combinations: 失態を演じる, 失態を犯す, 大失態. More neutral and general is 失敗 ("failure, mistake"), ミス is a small mistake. The word sounds rather written and often appears in the news.

examples[].german: A New Year's card arrived from a friend on New Year's Day.
We are in mourning, so we are not sending New Year's cards this year.
Recently, fewer and fewer people write New Year's cards.
en.notes: 賀状 is a greeting card, almost always in the sense of a New Year's card; in everyday speech people usually say 年賀状 instead. They are sent at the end of the year so that they arrive on January 1: 賀状を出す, 賀状が届く. Anyone in a year of mourning (喪中) does not send them and instead sends a notice of mourning. For congratulations on other occasions, one says お祝いのカード or お祝いの手紙.

examples[].german: Nothing was impossible for the invincible Superman.
It is impossible to finish this work by tomorrow.
He is the man who made the impossible possible.
en.notes: 不可能 is a な-adjective and noun: 不可能なこと, 〜のは不可能だ, 不可能に近い ("nearly impossible"). The opposite is 可能. In conversation one often says the more casual 無理 or simply できない; 無理 can additionally mean "excessive, unreasonable". A well-known phrase: 不可能を可能にする ("to make the impossible possible").

examples[].german: I will build a relationship of trust.
The two of them built a happy home.
This castle was built four hundred years ago.
en.notes: 築く literally means "to build (walls, dikes, castles)": 城を築く, 石垣を築く. Much more common today is the figurative meaning: to build up relationships, trust, a fortune or a position step by step - 信頼関係を築く, 家庭を築く, 地位を築く, 財産を築く. For ordinary buildings, people say 建てる; 築く emphasizes that something is built up laboriously and lastingly.

examples[].german: What food do you really hate?
I can't stand bugs.
"I hate you!" my little sister said and left the room.
en.notes: 大嫌い is a な-adjective ("hated, can't stand at all"), not a verb: the thing one hates is marked with が - 私は虫が大嫌いだ. It is the intensification of 嫌い and the opposite of 大好き. In conversation it sounds emotional, often childish or defiant ("I hate you!"). The real verb for deep hatred is 憎む, which weighs much heavier.

en.meaning: to make fly; to blow away; to skip; to speed
examples[].german: Don't skip my turn!
My hat was blown off by the strong wind.
I drove too fast on the highway and got caught for speeding.
en.notes: 飛ばす is the transitive counterpart of 飛ぶ ("to fly") and first means "to make fly": 紙飛行機を飛ばす, often passive 風に帽子を飛ばされる. Other common meanings: "to skip, to leave out" (ページを飛ばす, 順番を飛ばす), "to speed" (車を飛ばす) and colloquially "to transfer (as a punishment)" (地方に飛ばされる). Also found are 冗談を飛ばす ("to crack jokes") and, in cooking, アルコールを飛ばす ("to cook off the alcohol").

examples[].german: You should check whether the door is properly locked.
I want to see with my own eyes whether the rumor is true.
Let's check the train times before we leave.
en.notes: 確かめる means "to make sure, to verify" - by looking, asking or trying: Xを確かめる or 〜かどうか確かめる. 確認する means the same but sounds more formal and is more usual in business. 調べる, on the other hand, means "to find out, to look up" when one doesn't yet know something. Fixed phrase: 自分の目で確かめる ("to see with one's own eyes"). Related is the adjective 確か ("certain").

en.meaning: to inspect; to examine; to test
examples[].german: My luggage was inspected at the airport.
In this factory, every product is inspected one by one.
Next week I'm going to have my stomach examined at the hospital.
en.notes: 検査する means "to check, examine, inspect by fixed criteria": 荷物を検査する, 製品を検査する. In medicine the patient usually says 検査を受ける (血液検査, 胃の検査); the doctor's examination in the consulting room, on the other hand, is called 診察. 調べる is more general ("to look into, to find out"), 試験 is an exam in the sense of a test. Register: neutral to formal.

examples[].german: I've been supporting that idol all along.
Let's all go and cheer at tomorrow's match!
Good luck with the new job. I'm rooting for you.
en.notes: 応援する means "to cheer on" (in sports: チームを応援する, 応援に行く) and "to support, to keep one's fingers crossed" - for a star or a friend, for example: 応援してるよ. Another meaning is "reinforcement, temporary help": 応援を頼む, 他の店から応援に来る. For formal, often financial help one says 支援, for concrete helping out 手伝う.

examples[].german: Please change your password.
The schedule of the meeting has changed.
Because of the rain, we are changing the venue of the match to the gymnasium.
en.notes: 変更 is a change of plans, data or settings; as a transitive する-verb: Xを変更する, AをBに変更する. Without an agent one likes to say 変更になる ("will be changed"), typical in announcements and notices. In everyday speech one rather says 変える (transitive) or 変わる (intransitive); 変更 sounds businesslike and matter-of-fact. Common: 予定の変更, パスワードの変更, 変更点.

examples[].german: When getting off, please be careful not to leave anything behind.
If you are getting off at the next stop, please press the stop button.
On this bus, please get off through the front door.
en.notes: 降車 is the official word for "getting off" a bus, train or taxi and is found mainly in announcements and on signs: 降車口, 降車ボタン, 降車の際は…. In everyday speech people simply say 降りる. The opposite is 乗車 ("boarding"). Intransitive: Xから降車する, Xで降車する. Homophones such as 校舎, 公社 or 後者 are told apart by their written form.

examples[].german: Please undress before bathing.
In the changing room of the hot spring, there are lockers for valuables.
Please put your removed clothes in the clothes basket.
en.notes: 脱衣 is the formal word for "to undress, to take off one's clothes" and appears mainly on signs and in compounds: 脱衣所 or 脱衣場 (changing room at a bath, onsen or sento), 脱衣かご (clothes basket). In everyday speech one says 服を脱ぐ. The opposite is 着衣. As a する-verb it is intransitive; the clothing is not named as an object.

examples[].german: The restroom is straight ahead and then on the left.
May I use your restroom?
en.notes: お手洗い is a polite word for the toilet. The お is part of the word here and is written with it: otearai. 真っすぐ行って左 gives directions: go straight and then left. 借りてもいいですか politely asks whether you may use the restroom. 御手洗い is an additional dictionary and search spelling of the same word おてあらい. Practice the usual spelling お手洗い first; the variant changes neither the reading nor the meaning.

en.meaning: to reside (as a foreigner); to stay
examples[].german: What do foreigners need when they stay in Japan?
You must always carry your residence card.
Before my period of stay ran out, I went through the renewal procedure.
en.notes: 在留する is an official word for the longer stay of foreigners in a country: Xに在留する. It appears in many official terms: 在留カード (residence card), 在留資格 (status of residence), 在留期間 (period of stay). For a temporary stay, such as on a trip or in a hotel, one says 滞在する; in everyday speech simply 住む. Register: administration, written.

examples[].german: It overturned conventional wisdom.
The court overturned the earlier ruling.
The weak team defied expectations and won the championship.
en.notes: 覆す means "to turn over, to tip over" and above all, figuratively, "to overturn, to throw out". Typical combinations: 常識を覆す "to turn conventional wisdom upside down", 判決を覆す "to overturn a verdict", 予想を覆す "to defy all predictions", 政権を覆す "to topple a government". The intransitive counterpart is 覆る (判決が覆る). For tipped-over objects, everyday speech tends to use ひっくり返す; 覆す sounds literary.

examples[].german: I don't like people who get into a bad mood easily.
My father has had a grumpy look on his face since the morning.
Because I was short on sleep, I was in a bad mood all day.
en.notes: 不機嫌 is a な-adjective and noun for "in a bad mood, grumpy": 不機嫌になる, 不機嫌な顔, 不機嫌そう. The opposite is 上機嫌 ("in the best of moods"); ご機嫌 denotes good mood or appears in the polite question ご機嫌いかがですか. 怒る, on the other hand, means "to get angry", イライラする "to be irritated, on edge". 不機嫌 describes rather a quiet, visible ill humor.

examples[].german: You can keep your clothes on.
Let's recycle clothes that we no longer wear.
Stains on clothing will come out if you wash them right away.
en.notes: 衣服 is a matter-of-fact, written word for "clothing" and appears in notices, at the doctor's, on labels or in texts. In everyday speech one says 服 or 洋服. 衣類 denotes clothing rather as a product category (衣類の売り場), and 衣食住 ("clothing, food, shelter") the basic needs. Counter: 着.

examples[].german: How much does this product cost?
Because of the bad weather, vegetable prices are rising.
I make a point of comparing prices online before buying.
en.notes: 価格 is the matter-of-fact word for "price" and appears above all in news, business texts and on price tags: 価格が上がる／下がる, 価格を比べる, 販売価格, 価格競争. In everyday conversation one mostly says 値段. To be distinguished are 物価 (general price level), 料金 (fee for services) and 費用 (cost of an undertaking).

examples[].german: If a stranger suddenly put a hand on your head, of course you would feel revulsion.
I have a strong aversion to violent scenes.
His discriminatory remarks caused disgust in many people.
en.notes: 嫌悪感 is a strong feeling of disgust or aversion toward a person, action or thing. Typical verbs: 嫌悪感を抱く, 嫌悪感を覚える, 嫌悪感がある; 嫌悪感を感じる is widespread but is considered stylistically awkward because of the doubling of 感. The word sounds rather written; in conversation one says 嫌だ, 気持ち悪い ("gross") or 大嫌い. 憎しみ, on the other hand, is "hatred".

examples[].german: I was told to stay home on standby, but I sneaked out and bought a hamburger at McDonald's.
Paramedics are on standby 24 hours a day.
Please wait in this room until it's your turn.
en.notes: 待機 means "to wait on standby, to be ready" until an assignment or instruction comes: 待機する, 待機中 (also "standby" for devices). Common compounds are 自宅待機 ("standby at home", also quarantine) and 待機児童 ("children on a daycare waiting list"). The general "to wait" is 待つ; 待機 sounds official and formal. Intransitive: Xで待機する.

examples[].german: Why can't you just say thank you honestly?
Thank you for helping me.
Teacher, thank you so much for the whole year.
en.notes: ありがとう is the casual "thank you" among friends and in the family; politely one says ありがとうございます, and with ありがとうございました one thanks for something already completed. It is almost always written in kana; the kanji 有り難う go back to 有り難い ("rare, precious"). Other ways to thank: どうも (short), すみません (thanks with a shade of apology) and 恐れ入ります (very polite).

en.meaning: to stick in; to pierce; to strike a chord
examples[].german: Those were words that struck me to the heart.
A fish bone got stuck in my throat.
The dart stuck in the center of the target.
en.notes: 刺さる is intransitive: something pointed pricks in and stays stuck - XがYに刺さる (とげが指に刺さる, 骨がのどに刺さる). The transitive counterpart is 刺す ("to stab, to sting", also of insects). Figuratively, 心に刺さる means "to cut deep, to hit hard"; in youth slang, 刺さる alone also means "hits exactly my taste".

examples[].german: Please tell me about the effects of alcohol.
I hear this medicine has few side effects.
Apparently, laughing has the effect of reducing stress.
en.notes: 作用 is an effect or function, especially in natural science and medicine: 〜作用がある, Xに作用する ("to act on X"). Well-known compounds are 副作用 ("side effect") and 反作用 ("reaction, counteraction"). 効果, by contrast, is desired effectiveness, and 影響 is influence; in everyday speech one simply says 効く ("to work, to take effect"). Register: matter-of-fact, technical.

examples[].german: The establishment of this public corporation required the cooperation of many people.
In the old days, Japan's telephones were run by the Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Public Corporation.
This housing complex is managed by the housing supply corporation.
en.notes: 公社 is a public-law corporation that runs a business on behalf of the state or a municipality. Historically well known are the three big 公社 (国鉄, 電電公社, 専売公社), which were privatized in the 1980s into JR, NTT and JT; today there still exist, for example, regional 住宅供給公社. 会社, on the other hand, is an ordinary company. Homophones such as 降車 or 校舎 are distinguished by the writing.

examples[].german: There is a plan to build a new school in this district.
My grandfather built this house thirty years ago.
A tall building was built in front of the station.
en.notes: 建てる means "to erect, to build a building": 家を建てる, ビルを建てる, 学校を建てる. The intransitive counterpart is 建つ: 駅前にビルが建った "a building has gone up in front of the station". Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 立てる "to set up, to stand up", which is also used for plans (計画を立てる) – in the first example both occur side by side. For things that are not structures, 作る is used.

examples[].german: Please do not obstruct traffic.
The noise from nearby construction is disturbing my sleep.
Using your smartphone too much gets in the way of studying.
en.notes: 妨げる means "to hinder, to disturb" and takes を: 交通を妨げる, 睡眠を妨げる. The word sounds written and formal and is typical for signs, news and regulations; in conversation 邪魔する is more usual. The noun 妨げ is very common in 〜の妨げになる "to be a hindrance to". Do not confuse it with 防ぐ ("to prevent, to ward off", e.g. accidents or illnesses).

examples[].german: Dad, I'm so proud now that you have become an architect.
In the future I want to become an architect and design my own house.
A famous architect designed this museum.
en.notes: 建築家 is the architect who designs buildings (設計する); the suffix 〜家, as in 作家 or 画家, marks an expert or artist. The officially certified professional title is 建築士 (e.g. 一級建築士), whereas 建築家 means more the creative, often well-known architect. A carpenter or construction craftsman is 大工.

examples[].german: The population of this town is currently about 50,000.
The current time is 3:15 p.m.
As of April 1, there are 200 members.
en.notes: 現在 means "the present, now, currently" and is the more formal equivalent of 今: adverbial at the beginning of a sentence (現在、…), attributive with の (現在の状況). After a date it means "as of": 4月1日現在 "as of April 1". 現代, on the other hand, means the present as an era ("today's age, the modern era"). Opposites: 過去 ("past"), 未来 ("future").

examples[].german: Hey, is that politician a conservative?
Conservatism is a way of thinking that values tradition and the current structure of society.
In class, we learned about the difference between conservatism and liberalism.
en.notes: 保守主義 is conservatism as a political outlook that wants to preserve tradition and the existing order (保守 = "to preserve", 主義 = "-ism"). Opposing concepts are 革新 ("reform, progressive") and 自由主義 ("liberalism"). For persons one says 保守派 or 保守主義者, as a quality 保守的 ("conservative"). Note: 保守 alone also means "maintenance" in IT. Register: written, politics and school.

examples[].german: The conversation went off topic.
There was an accident in which a train derailed because of heavy rain.
The teacher often goes off on tangents, but that is what makes it interesting.
en.notes: 脱線 literally means the "derailment" of a train (脱線する, 脱線事故) and, figuratively, straying from the topic: 話が脱線する. The verb is intransitive; "to take a conversation off topic" is 話を脱線させる. Similar is 話がそれる ("the conversation drifts off topic"). In the figurative sense it is an everyday word; in the literal sense it is typical of news reports.

examples[].german: How did you manage to escape?
A lion escaped from the zoo, causing a great uproar.
Our cat escapes as soon as a window is open.
en.notes: 脱走する means "to break out, to escape" from a place where one is held: Xから脱走する (刑務所, 軍隊, 動物園, 檻). It is also used jokingly for pets that slip away. 逃げる is the general "to flee, to run away", 逃亡 the flight from the law (more formal), 家出 running away from home. As a noun: 脱走に成功する.

en.meaning: local train; train stopping at every station
examples[].german: This local train has just passed through a tunnel.
The express doesn't stop there, so please take the local train.
I like to travel at a leisurely pace by local train.
en.notes: 各駅停車 is a train that stops at every station (各駅 = "every station", 停車 = "stop"). On display boards it is often shortened to 各停 or 普通. The opposite terms are the faster train types 快速, 急行 and 特急. Those in a hurry avoid it - those traveling at leisure gladly take it.

en.meaning: to finish; to make do with
examples[].german: I often get my shopping done online.
Finish your homework before you go out to play.
I was busy, so I made do with a single piece of bread for lunch.
en.notes: 済ます is the transitive counterpart of 済む ("to be finished"): Xを済ます "to get something done, to get something over with". With で it means "to make do with something, to get by with something": パン一つで済ます; 謝って済ます means "to dismiss it with an apology". The variant 済ませる (ichidan) means the same and is in fact more common in present-day usage. Not to be confused with 澄ます (耳を澄ます "to listen closely").

examples[].german: With this many people, wouldn't it be more economical to take a taxi?
For financial reasons, I had to quit university.
My parents raised me despite financial hardship.
en.notes: 経済的 is a な-adjective with two meanings: "economic, financial" (経済的な理由, 経済的に苦しい, 経済的に自立する) and "economical, cheap" (〜方が経済的だ). Adverbially: 経済的に. For "cheap" in the simple sense one says 安い; "to save" is 節約する. Register: neutral, also common in conversations about money.

en.meaning: to hold an election; to choose by election
examples[].german: In this club, the president is chosen by election every year.
I went to vote on Sunday.
Next month the mayoral election will be held.
en.notes: 選挙 is an election (political or in clubs); the verb form 選挙する is rare and sounds stiff. Common are 選挙がある／行われる, 選挙に行く ("to go to vote"), 選挙に出る ("to run as a candidate") and 選挙で選ぶ ("to choose by election"). The casting of the vote itself is 投票する, and "to vote for someone" in everyday speech is simply 選ぶ. Important words: 選挙権 (right to vote), 総選挙 (general election).

examples[].german: Let's avoid danger.
To avoid the crowds, I left early in the morning.
Recently she seems to be avoiding me.
en.notes: 避ける (さける) means "to avoid, to steer clear of", especially with situations, topics and people: 危険を避ける, 人混みを避ける, その話題を避ける, 彼は私を避けている. With 〜のを避ける an action is avoided; 避けられない means "unavoidable". The same kanji is also read よける - that means physically dodging (車をよける, 水たまりをよける) and is mostly written in kana. In notices, 〜は避けてください serves as a polite prohibition.

examples[].german: The factory halted production because it was short of parts.
Because of the earthquake, trains are temporarily stopped.
Because of repeated violations, his driver's license was suspended.
en.notes: 停止 means "stopping, standstill, suspension" and is both intransitive (Xが停止する "comes to a stop") and transitive (Xを停止する "to suspend, halt"). Common combinations: 一時停止 (stop sign; pause in videos), 生産停止, 営業停止, 運転免許の停止 (colloquially 免停). In everyday speech people say 止まる／止める; 中止, by contrast, means the cancellation of an event. Register: formal, used in technology and administration.

examples[].german: Didn't Kawasaki have a power outage?
The power was out all night because of the typhoon.
Let's get a flashlight ready in case of a power outage.
en.notes: 停電 is a power outage; as an intransitive する-verb: 停電する, likewise 停電になる. The place or building appears as the subject (町が停電する) or as a location with で. When the power comes back, one says 電気が戻る or, formally, 復旧する; 計画停電 is a planned power cut. For water, the counterpart is 断水.

examples[].german: Vampires are said to dislike garlic and crosses.
As a child, I couldn't sleep after watching a vampire movie.
Low pay and constant overtime - that's a real bloodsucker of a company.
en.notes: 吸血鬼 is the vampire (吸血 = "to suck blood", 鬼 = "demon"). In pop culture and games one often also reads バンパイア or ヴァンパイア. Figuratively it denotes a "bloodsucker", someone who exploits others. Related is 吸血 in words like 吸血昆虫 ("blood-sucking insects" such as mosquitoes).

examples[].german: I can't keep up with how fast young people absorb knowledge.
This towel absorbs water well.
Vitamin C helps the absorption of iron.
en.notes: 吸収 means "to take in, to soak up, to absorb" and, as a する-verb, is transitive: 水分を吸収する, 衝撃を吸収する, 知識を吸収する ("to absorb knowledge"). The passive or nominal form is very common: 栄養が体に吸収される, 鉄分の吸収. In business jargon, 吸収合併 stands for the takeover of one company by another. The everyday verb for "to suck, to inhale", on the other hand, is 吸う; 吸収 sounds more matter-of-fact and scientific.

examples[].german: This factory makes leather goods.
Is this wallet made of genuine leather or synthetic leather?
Please use a special cream to care for leather.
en.notes: 皮革 is the factual technical term for "leather, animal hide" and appears mainly in industry, trade and on labels: 皮革製品 ("leather goods"), 天然皮革 ("genuine leather"), 合成皮革 ("faux leather"). In everyday speech people almost always say 革: 革の靴, 革のかばん. 皮 is raw skin or peel (みかんの皮), 革 is tanned leather; 皮革 covers both.

examples[].german: I'm unemployed again.
My father retired and is now without a job.
The longer you are without a job, the harder it becomes to find employment.
en.notes: 無職 denotes the status "without an occupation, without employment" and is a noun that is used with の or だ: 無職の人, 今は無職だ, 無職になる. It also includes retirees or people who deliberately do not work, and often appears in forms and news reports (無職の男). 失業, on the other hand, emphasizes the loss of a job (失業中, 失業者), 求職中 the active job search. The opposite is 有職.

examples[].german: What occupation do you want to have when you grow up?
I wrote "company employee" in the occupation field of the document.
I think the teaching profession is tough.
en.notes: 職業 is the general, somewhat formal word for "occupation": in forms (職業欄), statistics and conversations about career choice. To take up a profession is 職業に就く (often in kana 職業につく). In everyday speech one rather asks お仕事は何ですか, not about the 職業. Useful derivations: 職業病 ("occupational disease") and 職業柄 ("owing to one's occupation"). Not to be confused with 職場 ("workplace").

examples[].german: I am not a teacher, but I am a school staff member.
A city hall employee taught me how to fill out the documents.
I had business with my teacher, so I went to the staff room.
en.notes: 職員 are the staff of an organization, above all of government offices, schools, hospitals and associations: 市役所の職員, 学校の職員, 職員室 ("staff room"), 職員会議 "staff meeting". For employees of a private company one rather says 社員, for workers in shops or factories 従業員, casually also スタッフ. 職員 can mean a single person or the personnel as a whole.

examples[].german: The man I met on the internet is in his thirties and has a job, but he is divorced and has a child.
The proportion of employed women is increasing year by year.
Please circle either "employed" or "unemployed" on the questionnaire.
en.notes: 有職 means "employed, gainfully employed" and is a written-language word from statistics and forms: 有職者, 有職率, 有職の女性, often in the pair 有職・無職. In conversation people say 働いている or 仕事をしている instead. The old meanings "learned" or "versed in court customs" (usually read ゆうそく, as in 有職故実) are obsolete.

examples[].german: I will tackle a new challenge.
The city is actively tackling environmental problems.
I am studying seriously every day for the exam.
en.notes: 取り組む means "to devote oneself seriously to a task, to tackle something" and takes に: 課題に取り組む, 環境問題に取り組む, 研究に取り組む. It stresses active, persistent commitment and is very common in school, work and politics; the noun 取り組み "initiative, effort" is just as widespread. Originally it means "to grapple with each other" (in sumo: 取組 "bout"). Not to be confused with 取り込む "to take in, to incorporate".

examples[].german: Do you know a good job-hunting site?
He is job hunting at the moment.
I registered for job seeking at Hello Work.
en.notes: 求職 is the search for work from the applicant's point of view: 求職中 ("looking for a job"), 求職者, 求職活動. The counterpart from the employer's point of view is 求人 ("job offer", 求人広告). As a する-verb, 求職する is rare; one rather says 求職活動をする or, quite everyday, 仕事を探す. For students, the job search is called 就活 (就職活動).

examples[].german: I work as a law teacher.
My older sister is an elementary school teacher.
I'm studying to become a Japanese teacher.
en.notes: 教師 refers to a teacher as an occupation and is used mainly descriptively: 教師をしている, 小学校の教師, 日本語教師, 家庭教師 ("private tutor"). 先生, by contrast, is a form of address and title (also for doctors or lawyers); about yourself you humbly say 教師です, not 先生です. Officially, teaching staff is called 教員, and university lecturers often 講師.

en.meaning: to break; to split; to divide; to dilute
examples[].german: Is the answer to "seven divided by two" three remainder one?
I accidentally broke a plate while washing up.
I drink whisky diluted with water.
en.notes: 割る is transitive (X を割る); the intransitive partner is 割れる (お皿が割れた). It means "to break" with glass, dishes and eggs (卵を割る), "to split" (薪を割る), in mathematics "to divide" (十割る二は五) and with drinks "to dilute" (水で割る, 水割り). It also means "to fall below": 1万円を割る. Unlike 壊す (to break devices) or 折る (to break a stick or bone), 割る is about shattering or dividing.

examples[].german: In a trial, it is necessary to judge as fairly as possible.
It is hard for people to judge people.
This case will be tried in court next month.
en.notes: 裁く means "to judge, to pass judgment" and is transitive: 人を裁く, 罪を裁く, 法で裁く. The passive 裁かれる ("to be put on trial") is very common. Related are 裁判 ("trial") and 裁判官 ("judge"). Not to be confused with the similar-sounding 捌く ("to handle skillfully, to fillet a fish") or 砂漠 ("desert").

examples[].german: The culprit fled but was caught in Kawasaki.
Kawasaki is a big city between Tokyo and Yokohama.
Please change trains at Kawasaki Station.
en.notes: 川崎 is a large industrial and residential city in Kanagawa Prefecture between Tokyo and Yokohama. The name is also a common family name (川崎さん) and appears in company names like 川崎重工. Literally: 川 "river" + 崎 "cape". 崎 is read さき or ざき depending on the name: 川崎 かわさき, but 宮崎 みやざき.

examples[].german: My surname is Nagasaki, so everyone calls me Naga-chan.
Nagasaki is famous as a port city.
On the school trip we visited the Peace Park in Nagasaki.
en.notes: 長崎 is a city and prefecture (長崎県) in the west of Kyushu. During Japan's seclusion, the port with the island 出島 was the only gateway for trade with the Netherlands; in 1945 the city was destroyed by an atomic bomb. Well known today are, among other things, ちゃんぽん and カステラ. 長崎 is also a family name.

en.meaning: to stretch; to pitch (a tent); to form (ice)
examples[].german: I was taught how to stretch a canvas over a frame.
Let's pitch the tent before it gets dark.
On a cold morning, ice had formed on the pond.
en.notes: The basic idea of 張る is "to stretch or spread something taut": ロープを張る, テントを張る ("to pitch a tent"), キャンバスを張る. Intransitively it describes a surface forming or something becoming taut or swollen: 池に氷が張る ("the pond freezes over"), 肩が張る ("stiff shoulders"), 値段が張る ("to be expensive"). Other phrases: 胸を張る ("to be proud"), 意地を張る ("to be stubborn"). For sticking paper on, you usually write 貼る (切手を貼る).

examples[].german: That actor is famous for his terrible attitude toward fans.
He won the best actor award for this film.
Three actors and two actresses appear in that stage play.
en.notes: 男優 is a male actor and is used above all in contrast to 女優 or in award names: 主演男優賞 ("best actor award"), 助演男優賞. In normal conversation, 俳優 is mostly used for actors, and for stage performers also 役者. Since 男優 alone is often associated with the adult film industry, 俳優 is the more neutral choice.

examples[].german: It's not acceptable for young people to sit boldly in the priority seats.
I want to put family before work.
Please give safety top priority.
en.notes: 優先 means "precedence, priority". As a する-verb it means "to prefer, to give priority": 仕事より家族を優先する. Common combinations are 優先的に ("as a priority"), 最優先 ("top priority"), 優先順位 "order of priority", 歩行者優先 "pedestrians first" and 優先席 (seats on trains for the elderly, pregnant women, etc.). 先に, by contrast, only means "first" in terms of time.

examples[].german: Today I'm visiting the Yamadas' house.
The package will be delivered to the Tanaka residence.
We'll spend the year-end at my wife's parents' house.
en.notes: 〜宅 follows names or terms for people and means "home, house of ...": 山田宅, 田中様宅, 友人宅, 知人宅, 両親宅. It sounds formal and written (delivery slips, news, polite conversation); in everyday speech one says 山田さんの家 or 山田さんのところ. Related are お宅 ("your home", also a polite "you"), 自宅 and 住宅.

examples[].german: I overcame the difficulties.
By practicing speaking in front of people repeatedly, I overcame my discomfort with it.
He overcame a serious illness and stood on the stage again.
en.notes: 克服する means "to overcome, to master" and takes を for a difficulty one defeats by one's own strength: 困難を克服する, 病気を克服する, 苦手意識 / 弱点を克服する. It sounds somewhat elevated and emphasizes long effort. In everyday speech, people often say 乗り越える, which also fits grief and crises ("to get over something"); 克服 fits weaknesses and illnesses better.

examples[].german: I overcame the difficulties.
The thief climbed over the wall and ran away.
Thanks to my family's support, I got through the hard times.
en.notes: 乗り越える literally means "to climb over something" (塀を乗り越える) and figuratively "to overcome, to get through": 困難を乗り越える, 壁を乗り越える, 悲しみを乗り越える. Although it is considered intransitive, the obstacle takes を, as with verbs of movement. Unlike 克服する, which is more literary and often used for weaknesses or illnesses, 乗り越える sounds more vivid and emotional; it often appears with みんなで or 力を合わせて.

examples[].german: I heard a voice calling for help from the toilet at home.
I'm working from home today.
Please send the documents to my home address.
en.notes: 自宅 is one's own home, usually in contrast to the workplace or being out and about: 自宅で仕事をする, 自宅待機, 自宅療養, 自宅の住所. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 家 or うち and is typical of forms, work contexts and news reports. For someone else's home, one politely says お宅. 住宅, by contrast, means residential buildings in general.

examples[].german: The houses in this area were fine even in that big earthquake.
Many new houses are going up near the station.
I took out a mortgage with a term of thirty-five years.
en.notes: 住宅 means residential buildings as a category, that is, "housing, living space", rather matter-of-fact: 住宅地, 住宅街 ("residential area"), 住宅ローン ("mortgage"), 公営住宅 ("public housing"), 住宅問題. For one's own home one does not say 住宅 but 家, うち or 自宅. Similarly formal is 住居, warmer-sounding is 住まい.

examples[].german: If you wait here, that tabby cat will surely show up again.
An hour after the appointed time, he finally showed up.
The effect appeared about thirty minutes after taking the medicine.
en.notes: 現れる means "to appear, to turn up, to become visible" and is intransitive: 犯人が現れる, 効果が現れる. The transitive counterpart is 現す (姿を現す "to show oneself"). For feelings or traits that show, one usually writes 表れる (気持ちが顔に表れる). Compared with 出る or 来る, 現れる stresses the sudden, often unexpected becoming visible.

examples[].german: With the live stream, I hope the fun atmosphere on site comes across.
The police headed to the scene of the accident right away.
My father works at a construction site.
en.notes: 現場 is the place where something actually happens or has happened: 事故現場 ("accident scene"), 犯行現場 ("crime scene"), 工事現場・建設現場 ("construction site"), 撮影現場 ("film set"). Figuratively it means practice on the ground as opposed to administration: 教育の現場, 現場の声 ("voices from the field"). 現地, on the other hand, denotes a region or country on site, for example when traveling (現地の人).

examples[].german: My nipples chafed during the marathon and bled.
I replaced the nipple of the baby bottle with a new one.
If you notice anything abnormal in your breast or nipples, please see a doctor early.
en.notes: 乳首 is the nipple in humans and animals (also "teat" in the latter) and also the nipple of a baby bottle (哺乳瓶の乳首). The reading ちくび is irregular; otherwise 乳 is read ちち or にゅう. The word is neutral-anatomical, but in everyday speech it is used rather discreetly; in medical texts 乳頭 is also used.

examples[].german: I have to finish this article on economics by the end of this month.
I'm majoring in economics at university.
Students in the faculty of economics also have to study mathematics.
en.notes: 経済学 is economics as a subject: 経済学を専攻する, 経済学部 ("faculty of economics"), 経済学者 ("economist"), マクロ経済学・ミクロ経済学. The ending 〜学 forms names of academic fields, as in 経営学 ("business administration") or 心理学. 経済 alone means the economy itself (日本の経済).

en.meaning: to cite; to raise; to hold (a ceremony)
examples[].german: If I started citing examples, there'd be no end to it.
We plan to hold our wedding ceremony next spring.
If you have a question, please raise your hand.
en.notes: 挙げる is the writing of あげる for "to cite, to name" (例を挙げる, 名前を挙げる), "to raise one's hand" (手を挙げる), "to hold a ceremony" (結婚式を挙げる) and "to muster" (全力を挙げる). For lifting in general, 上げる is used, for deep-frying or hoisting flags 揚げる. The verb is transitive; the intransitive partner is 挙がる (例や名前が挙がる). Colloquially, 犯人を挙げる also means "to arrest the culprit".

examples[].german: With this, every escape route has now been cut off.
For the sake of my health, I decided to give up alcohol.
He cut off contact with his family and lives alone.
en.notes: 断つ is transitive and means "to cut off, to break off", mostly in the figurative sense: 関係を断つ, 連絡を断つ, 退路を断つ. It also means "to renounce something": 酒を断つ, たばこを断つ. The passive 断たれる is common. Verbs that sound the same: 絶つ (命を絶つ, 消息を絶つ), 裁つ (to cut fabric); for concrete cutting in everyday life, one says 切る.

examples[].german: The moment came suddenly.
Suddenly, the lights went out.
I apologize for the sudden request.
en.notes: 突然 means "suddenly, unexpectedly". As an adverb it stands alone or with a comma: 突然泣き出す, 突然、電気が消えた. Before nouns, 突然の is used: 突然の雨, 突然の知らせ. Related are 急に (more colloquial, also for quick changes) and いきなり (abrupt, often with an unpleasant undertone); 突然 above all emphasizes the unexpected. Polite phrase: 突然のご連絡失礼します.

examples[].german: The changing room is over there.
I change into my uniform in the changing room and then start work.
The changing room of this pool has lockers.
en.notes: 更衣室 is the changing room in gyms, swimming pools, fitness studios or at the workplace, often separate as 男子更衣室・女子更衣室. 更衣 is a formal word for "changing clothes"; in everyday speech one says 着替える. Note: the fitting room in a clothing store is not called 更衣室 but 試着室.

en.meaning: to anticipate; to factor in; to count on
examples[].german: We anticipate an increase in sales.
I allowed for a traffic jam and left home an hour early.
I have confidence in your ability, so I'd like to ask you to take this job.
en.notes: 見込む means "to expect in advance, to factor in, to estimate" and belongs to the language of business and planning: 売上の増加を見込む, 渋滞を見込んで早めに出る. It also means "to have confidence in someone": 君を見込んで頼む. The noun 見込み "prospect, forecast" is very common (〜する見込みだ, 見込みがない). Unlike 期待する "to hope", 見込む is sober and calculating.

examples[].german: Huh, isn't it on the bookshelf?
I bought a new bookshelf.
en.notes: 本棚 is a bookshelf. 本棚に indicates where a sought item might be. 本棚を買う names the shelf as the thing bought. あれ can introduce a surprised question; ない？ asks here whether the thing sought is not there. 棚 is read だな in the compound word.

examples[].german: She always wears a purple vest over her uniform.
The evening sky was dyed a beautiful purple.
Your lips have turned purple from the cold.
en.notes: 紫色 means "purple, violet" and is a noun: before nouns 紫色の is used (紫色のベスト), as a result 紫色になる or 紫色に染まる. Unlike 赤い, 黄色い or 茶色い, there is no form 紫色い. 紫 alone means the same; lighter shades are called 薄紫. In fashion one also hears パープル; traditionally, purple was considered a noble color in Japan.

examples[].german: I aim to be an actor who can act with facial expressions.
That athlete gave a perfect performance at the Olympics.
She's crying, but that's surely an act.
en.notes: 演技 is the performance of actors, but also of athletes in disciplines like figure skating or gymnastics: 演技が上手い, 演技力, 迫真の演技. As a する-verb it is intransitive (舞台で演技する). Figuratively it means "play-acting, pretense": あれは演技だ ("that's just an act"). For music, on the other hand, one says 演奏, for the play itself 芝居 or 演劇.

examples[].german: The protagonist is played by a newcomer actor.
The theater company plans to perform a Shakespeare work next month.
He ended up playing an important role in those negotiations.
en.notes: 演ずる is the older, literary variant of 演じる and means the same: to play a role (役を演ずる), to perform a play, and figuratively to play a part in events (重要な役割を演ずる). In the dictionary form and in written texts you still often encounter 演ずる; most of the other forms today sound as for 演じる (演じて, 演じない, 演じた). Classical forms like 演ぜず or 演ぜられる sound very elevated. Also 失態を演ずる ("to make a fool of oneself") is a fixed phrase.

examples[].german: The variety show is next week! Let's do our best, everyone!
I listened to rakugo at a variety theater in Asakusa.
My grandfather loves variety programs on TV.
en.notes: 演芸 is popular stage entertainment such as 落語, 漫才, 手品 or 講談, so it means something closer to "variety acts, vaudeville" than to "performing arts" in general. Typical words: 演芸場 ("variety theater", cf. 寄席), 演芸会 (a "talent show" at schools or companies), 演芸番組. Broader is 芸能 (the entertainment industry, 芸能人); for theater one says 演劇, for high art 芸術.

examples[].german: Please tell me the running time of The Lion King.
Shakespeare's works are staged at this theater every year.
Please turn off your mobile phone during the performance.
en.notes: 上演 is the performance of a stage play, an opera or a musical; as a する-verb it is transitive (劇を上演する), often in the passive (作品が上演される). Films, by contrast, are shown with 上映, and music is 演奏. 公演 refers to a performance as an event (tour, guest performance). Typical: 上演中, 上演時間.

en.meaning: lines (of a script); spoken part; catchphrase
examples[].german: How can you memorize such long lines?
I was so nervous that I forgot my lines.
I can't say a line like "I love you" as if it were from a TV drama.
en.notes: 台詞 are the spoken lines in theater, film or manga: 台詞を覚える, 台詞を言う, 台詞を忘れる. The word is usually written in kana, せりふ or セリフ. Figuratively it also means a remark or a hackneyed phrase: それはこっちのせりふだ ("That's my line!"), ドラマみたいなせりふ.

en.meaning: to understand; to know; to be well versed in
examples[].german: Do you know who this gentleman is?
He knows very well how to handle customers.
You should know the precautions for climbing mountains.
en.notes: 心得る means "to know thoroughly, to understand what matters" and is almost always used as 心得ている: 扱い方を心得ている. The form AをBと心得る ("to regard A as B") sounds archaic and is familiar from samurai dramas. The noun 心得 refers to basic rules or knowledge (心得がある). The word is literary to elevated in register; in everyday speech people say 分かる or 知っている.

en.meaning: to be buried; to fill up; to be booked
examples[].german: The car was completely buried in snow because of the heavy snowfall.
My weekend schedule is already full.
The venue was filled with a large crowd of fans.
en.notes: 埋まる is intransitive and first means "to be buried, to be covered": 土に埋まる, 雪に埋まる. Very common is the sense "to fill up, to be taken": 席が埋まる, 予定が埋まる, 会場がファンで埋まる, 穴が埋まる. The transitive counterpart is 埋める (穴を埋める, 時間を埋める). The reading うずまる is a literary variant.

examples[].german: My older brother is not good at socializing, but being an optimist, he doesn't worry about it much himself.
His optimism sometimes helps me.
Optimism or pessimism - which are you closer to?
en.notes: 楽天主義 is "optimism" as an attitude to life or worldview and sounds rather formal; synonymous and more common is 楽観主義, the opposite is 悲観主義. An optimistic person is a 楽天家 or 楽天主義者, and 楽天的 serves as the adjective (楽天的な性格). In everyday speech one often says simply ポジティブ or 前向き.

en.meaning: to take into account; to base on
examples[].german: I will make a judgment based on the results.
Taking everyone's opinions into account, we will review the plan.
Measures that take last year's failure into account are necessary.
en.notes: 踏まえる means "to build on something, to take something into account" and appears almost always as 〜を踏まえて or attributively as 〜を踏まえた: 結果を踏まえて, 経験を踏まえた提案. It belongs to formal usage in meetings, reports and news. Unlike 〜に基づいて "on the basis of", 踏まえる stresses that one considers what is known and draws conclusions from it. The literal meaning "to step firmly" is rare.

examples[].german: This month I got a lot of money.
Yesterday I walked a lot.
en.notes: 沢山 refers to a large amount or number. Before a noun, 沢山の is common: 沢山の本. It can also be used as an adverb with an action: 沢山歩く "to walk a lot". It is often written in hiragana as たくさん. 金 is read かね in the sense of "money"; 手に入れる means "to get" or "to obtain".

examples[].german: Mom, I got 100 on my division test!
When I was in elementary school, I was bad at division.
Division answers sometimes come out with a remainder.
en.notes: 割り算 is division, one of the four basic arithmetic operations alongside 足し算, 引き算 and 掛け算. The actual calculating is expressed with the verb 割る: 10を2で割る ("to divide 10 by 2"); 割り算する is possible but less common. Related: 余り ("remainder") and 割り切れる ("to be divisible without remainder").

en.meaning: to fit in; to settle down
examples[].german: Did the hundred million yen fit in that suitcase?
The travel expenses stayed within the budget.
You'd better not go outside until the wind dies down.
en.notes: 収まる is intransitive and means "to fit in, to find room": 箱に収まる, 予算内に収まる, 写真に収まる ("to get into the photo"). It also means "to subside, to calm down": 騒ぎが収まる, 怒りが収まる; for pain and illness it is usually written 治まる (痛みが治まる). The transitive counterpart is 収める (箱に収める).

examples[].german: A new character will be added soon!
May I join the conversation too?
When consumption tax is added to the fee, it gets quite expensive.
en.notes: 加わる is intransitive: "to be added" (AにBが加わる), "to join, to take part" (仲間に加わる, 話に加わる) as well as "to increase, to be applied" (スピードが加わる, 力が加わる). The transitive counterpart is 加える (塩を加える "to add salt"). 参加する is more formal and means taking part in an event.

examples[].german: The inside of my nose is itchy.
The spot where the mosquito bit me is incredibly itchy.
During pollen season, my eyes itch unbearably.
en.notes: 痒い is an い-adjective and is usually written in kana (かゆい). The itchy spot is marked with が: 背中がかゆい. To scratch is 掻く (かゆいところを掻く), the itch itself かゆみ. Idiom: 痒い所に手が届く ("to think of everything, to be very attentive"), for example about good service.

examples[].german: The man worked at a gas station on the outskirts of town.
There is an old temple on the edge of town.
When I walked to the edge of town, rice fields stretched out ahead.
en.notes: 町外れ is the edge of a town, where the built-up area ends: 町外れに住む, 町外れの工場. 外れ comes from 外れる ("to deviate, to lie outside"); likewise there is 村外れ. 郊外, by contrast, refers more to the ring of suburbs around a large city (郊外に住む). 町外れ sounds slightly narrative and is often used in stories.

en.meaning: granted wish; to grant; to fulfill
examples[].german: I will definitely make this dream come true!
I became a doctor to fulfill my parents' wish.
The wizard granted the girl's wish.
en.notes: 叶える is transitive and means "to fulfill a wish or dream, to make it come true": 夢を叶える, 願いを叶える; often also in kana かなえる. The intransitive counterpart is 叶う (夢が叶う "the dream comes true"). For duties or promises, by contrast, one says 果たす (約束を果たす), for plans 実現する, for conditions 満たす.

examples[].german: A willingness to learn on one's own is important.
The company president went to the customer's house in person to apologize.
It is hard to admit one's own mistakes.
en.notes: 自ら means "oneself, personally, on one's own initiative" and sounds more literary and weighty than 自分で: 自ら学ぶ, 社長自ら ("the boss in person"). As a noun it takes の: 自らの手で, 自らの責任. Colloquially it corresponds roughly to 自分から. Not to be confused with 自ずから or 自ずと ("by itself, quite naturally").

examples[].german: I bought these rain boots at a surprisingly low price, but they weren't waterproofed.
The stock price hit a new low for the year.
Vegetables are being traded at low prices, and farmers are in trouble.
en.notes: 安値 is a low price or quotation, above all in trading and on the stock exchange: 安値で売る・買う, 最安値 ("lowest point, cheapest price"), 年初来安値. The opposite is 高値. 値 is read ね here ("price"). In everyday speech, for "cheap" one simply says 安い or 格安.

examples[].german: I always end up buying stocks when they're at a high.
The painting sold for a high price at auction.
Because there was little rain, cabbage is expensive right now.
en.notes: 高値 is a high price or quotation, especially in trading and on the stock exchange: 高値で売れる, 高値がつく, 最高値 ("record high, highest price"). The opposite is 安値. For "expensive" in everyday speech, 高い is enough. Not to be confused with the identically read 高嶺 (高嶺の花 "unattainable").

en.meaning: to make use of; to bring out
examples[].german: I will make use of my experience.
I am looking for a job where I can make use of my strengths.
This dish brings out the flavor of the vegetables.
en.notes: 活かす is a variant spelling of 生かす in the meaning "to make use of, to bring out": 経験を活かす, 特技を活かす, 素材の味を活かす. The spelling with 活 is often chosen when it is about putting abilities and resources to use; for "to keep alive" only 生かす is written. Unlike 利用する "to use", 活かす stresses that potential is fully realized. Typical is 〜を活かして "making use of ...".

examples[].german: Lead a more orderly life.
This school is famous for its strict discipline.
Players who do not follow the team's discipline cannot play in games.
en.notes: 規律 is "discipline" or "order" within a group such as a school, army, company or sports team. Typical are 規律を守る, 規律を乱す, 規律が厳しい and 規律正しい ("disciplined, regular", e.g. of a lifestyle). Concrete individual rules are more often called 規則 or ルール. Teaching children good manners, by contrast, is called しつけ.

examples[].german: What is the difference between this new product and that older model?
I don't really understand the difference between the two words.
My older sister and I are three years apart.
en.notes: 違い is the noun of 違う and means "difference": AとBの違い, 違いがある・ない, 違いが分かる, 大違い. With ages: 三つ違いの兄弟 ("siblings three years apart"). The meaning "mistake" is usually expressed with 間違い. Important grammar: 〜に違いない ("must surely be"). 差 emphasizes more a measurable gap (点数の差), and 相違 is formal.

examples[].german: Today is burnable garbage day, isn't it?
Please put kitchen waste out as burnable garbage.
Is plastic burnable or non-burnable garbage?
en.notes: 可燃ゴミ is a category of Japanese garbage sorting: kitchen waste, paper scraps and the like. Colloquially it is called 燃えるゴミ, and in some cities officially 燃やすゴミ. The counterparts are 不燃ゴミ ("non-burnable garbage"), 資源ゴミ ("recyclables") and 粗大ゴミ ("bulky waste"). To put out the garbage is ゴミを出す; the fixed collection day is 可燃ゴミの日.

en.meaning: to do business; to be open for business
examples[].german: Our cafe opens for business from today.
This shop is open until 10 p.m.
My father works in sales at a car company.
en.notes: 営業する means that a business is "open, in operation": 夜十時まで営業している, 営業中 ("open"), 営業時間, 本日の営業は終了しました. In addition, 営業 refers to sales: 営業部, 営業の仕事, 営業に回る. In conversation, people often simply say 開いている about shops; someone who runs a company as its owner 経営する it. It is mostly intransitive, with the business as the subject.

examples[].german: Japan has a lot of traditional culture.
My grandmother still makes miso in the traditional way.
This company traditionally has many male employees.
en.notes: 伝統的 is a な-adjective made from 伝統 ("tradition") and 〜的: 伝統的な料理, 伝統的な祭り; as an adverb 伝統的に ("traditionally, from time immemorial"). Warmer and more nostalgic is 昔ながらの (昔ながらの作り方). 古典的 means "classical", 保守的 "conservative" in the sense of an attitude.

examples[].german: I overslept and couldn't properly warm up my shoulder before the game.
I overslept and was late for school.
On days off I tend to oversleep.
en.notes: 寝坊する means "to sleep too long (unintentionally), to oversleep" and is intransitive. The classic apology: 寝坊して遅刻しました. 朝寝坊 emphasizes getting up late in the morning; a late sleeper is called 寝坊 or, affectionately, お寝坊さん. 寝過ごす means to miss something by sleeping (電車で寝過ごす "to sleep through one's station"), and 二度寝 "to fall asleep again".

examples[].german: Please change this adjective into the past tense.
The past tense of 「食べる」 is 「食べた」.
Learning the past tenses of English irregular verbs is hard.
en.notes: 過去形 is the grammatical term for "past tense": 〜の過去形, 過去形にする・に変える. Related terms are 現在形, 未来形, 否定形, 辞書形 and て形. In these grammar terms, 形 is read けい, not かたち or がた. In Japanese grammars the past tense is also called タ形.

examples[].german: My stomach hurts from eating too much.
I will arrive at the station a little after five.
My father is past sixty, but he runs every morning.
en.notes: 過ぎ is a suffix with two main meanings. After verb stems it means "too much": 食べ過ぎ, 飲み過ぎ, 働き過ぎ (often in kana すぎ, as a noun: 食べ過ぎに注意). After times of day or ages it means "past, over": 五時過ぎ, 昼過ぎ, 六十過ぎ. The related verb is 過ぎる (食べ過ぎる); colloquially a sentence often ends directly in すぎ: 高すぎ!

examples[].german: In junior high, I was a member of the baseball club's cheering squad.
The loud voices of the cheering squad echoed through the stadium.
If it's your dream, I'll be your cheerleader.
en.notes: 応援団 is an organized cheering squad, typical of Japanese schools and universities, for example at high school baseball (高校野球): groups in black uniforms with drums and chants, led by the 応援団長. This is something different from cheerleading (チアリーディング). Figuratively, supporters of a person are also called this. Verb: 応援する ("to cheer on, to support").

examples[].german: I'm in charge of Japanese language education at this company.
I'll connect you to the person in charge, so please wait a moment.
Who is in charge of preparing for next week's meeting?
en.notes: 担当 means "to be in charge of an area of work"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 日本語教育を担当する. Very common are 担当者 ("contact person, person in charge"), 担当の先生 and compounds like 営業担当. On the phone: 担当の者に代わります. 係 means a smaller, often temporary task (受付係), 責任 responsibility in the sense of liability.

en.meaning: to make use of; to bring out; to keep alive
examples[].german: I want a job that makes use of my talent.
I put the fish I caught in water and kept them alive.
I want to put what I learned at university to use in my work.
en.notes: 生かす is the transitive counterpart of 生きる "to live" and first means "to let live, to keep alive": 魚を生かしておく. In everyday life, however, "to make use of, to bring out" is far more common: 才能を生かす, 経験を仕事に生かす. In this meaning the spelling 活かす is also widespread, but 生かす is regarded as the standard spelling. The figurative opposite is 殺す: 才能を殺す "to let a talent go to waste".

examples[].german: The company made a large investment to develop a new product, but it ended in failure.
My grandfather died leaving a large debt.
She made a large donation to the hospital.
en.notes: 多額 refers exclusively to money and almost always appears as 多額の before a noun: 多額の借金, 多額の費用, 多額の寄付. It sounds formal and is typical of news and reports. The opposite is 少額. For large quantities of other things one says 大量 or 多量, in everyday speech simply たくさんのお金 or 大金.

examples[].german: The annual amount is a better deal than the monthly one.
The membership fee is 5,000 yen per year.
How much is the premium for this insurance per year?
en.notes: 年額 is the "annual amount" for fees, subscriptions, salaries or dues: 年額五千円, 年額で払う. The counterparts are 月額 ("monthly amount") and 日額; the total sum is 総額. In conversation people also often say 一年で or 年間. Related are 年収 ("annual income") and 年会費 ("annual membership fee").

examples[].german: How much is that per month?
You can use this app without limit for 500 yen a month.
Rent and management fees together come to 80,000 yen a month.
en.notes: 月額 is the monthly amount, especially for subscriptions, fees, rents and salaries: 月額料金 "monthly fee", 月額制 "monthly subscription model", 月額千円 "1,000 yen per month". With で it is often adverbial: 月額でいくら？ "How much per month?". Formed in parallel are 年額 "annual amount" and 日額 "daily rate". In conversation one also simply says 月に〜円 or 毎月〜円; 月額 sounds somewhat more matter-of-fact, as in contracts and price lists.

examples[].german: I chose the flat-rate plan.
This taxi takes you to the airport for a flat fare.
I use a flat-rate video streaming service.
en.notes: 定額 denotes a fixed, unchanging amount, no matter how much one uses: 定額制 "flat-rate model", 定額料金 "flat fee", 定額で〜 "at a fixed price". It is a noun and is used with の before nouns (定額のプラン). Not to be confused with 定価 "list price, regular price" and 月額 "monthly amount" - a subscription can be both 月額 and 定額. Typical of mobile plans, streaming and taxi rides to the airport.

examples[].german: Just in case, I'll check the remaining balance on my IC card.
The remaining balance on the loan is 500,000 yen.
Please pay the remaining balance next month.
en.notes: 残額 is the amount still remaining, for example with installments, bills or credit: 残額を支払う "to pay the remaining balance", ローンの残額 "outstanding loan balance". For an account balance and the credit on cards, 残高 is the usual word (預金残高, チャージ残高); 残額 puts more emphasis on what is left over or still open from a total sum. Colloquially one also says あと〜円残っている.

examples[].german: We are now getting started on making the prototype.
My father made this furniture all by himself.
It took three years to produce that film.
en.notes: 製作 is the making of concrete things such as furniture, machines, models or prototypes; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を製作する. For films and broadcasts it means "production" (映画製作). To distinguish: 制作 (same reading) is preferred for artistic works and programs, 製造 for industrial mass production in factories. Typical are 〜の製作に取りかかる "to begin making" and 製作費 "production costs".

examples[].german: This table looks wooden, but it's actually made of plastic.
Wooden toys are popular because they feel warm.
I put a wooden bench on the balcony.
en.notes: 木製 means "made of wood" and is used as a noun with の before the object (木製の机) or predicatively with です. It belongs to the series of 〜製 words for material: 鉄製 "made of iron", プラスチック製 "made of plastic", ガラス製 "made of glass". For buildings, on the other hand, one says 木造 (木造の家). In everyday speech 木でできた〜 is also common; 木製 sounds somewhat more matter-of-fact, for example in product descriptions.

examples[].german: Is this shawl made in Japan?
Japanese home appliances are said to be hard to break.
If you're buying souvenirs, you should check properly whether they are made in Japan.
en.notes: 日本製 means "made in Japan" and refers to products, not people - for persons one says 日本出身 or 日本人. It is used with の before nouns (日本製の車) or predicatively (これは日本製です). It is mostly read にほんせい, less often にっぽんせい. Formed likewise are 中国製, アメリカ製, 外国製; labels often say "Made in Japan" or 日本製.

examples[].german: Please don't assume the quality is bad just because it's made in China.
This smartphone is made in China, but it's very easy to use.
Most of the clothes in the store were made in China.
en.notes: 中国製 means "made in China" and describes goods, not people (for people: 中国出身, 中国人). It is used with の before nouns (中国製の服) or as a predicate with です. The pattern country + 製 is productive: 日本製, アメリカ製, ドイツ製; the general opposite is 外国製, or 国産 for "produced domestically". One encounters the word very often in conversations about quality and price.

examples[].german: Yesterday I had the shoulders of that American-made suit taken in.
This motorcycle is made in America and has a loud engine.
American-made refrigerators are too big to fit in our kitchen.
en.notes: アメリカ製 means "made in the USA" and is a compound of アメリカ and the suffix 〜製 "made in / of". It describes products and is used with の before nouns (アメリカ製の車) or predicatively with です. In newspapers and official texts one often reads 米国製 instead. For persons one does not use 〜製 but アメリカ出身 or アメリカ人.

examples[].german: It does not apply to everyone.
In the following questions, please circle the ones that apply.
I think this explanation also applies to young people in Japan.
en.notes: 当てはまる means "to apply, to fit, to be applicable" and takes に: この規則はすべての場合に当てはまる. Typical for questionnaires is 当てはまるものに丸をつけてください "circle what applies". The transitive counterpart is 当てはめる "to apply, to fit in" (公式に数字を当てはめる). It is often written in kana as well (あてはまる); that something physically fits (clothes, a key) is expressed with 合う or はまる instead.

examples[].german: We use delicious homemade bacon.
My mother's homemade umeboshi are a little salty.
All the bread in this shop is made in-house.
