en.notes: 自家製 means "made by oneself, homemade" and is used above all for food: made at home (自家製の梅干し) or made in-house at a restaurant (自家製パン, 自家製麺). It is a noun and is used with の before the object or as a predicate. 手作り, on the other hand, emphasizes "made by hand" and also suits gifts or clothing; on menus, 自家製 acts like a promise of quality.

examples[].german: Please put out non-burnable garbage on Tuesday.
I put out broken glasses on non-burnable garbage day.
May I put spray cans in the non-burnable garbage?
en.notes: 不燃ゴミ is the "non-burnable garbage" of Japanese garbage sorting: glass, ceramics, metal, small electrical appliances, etc. The counterpart is 可燃ゴミ or, colloquially, 燃えるゴミ; in everyday speech 不燃ゴミ is often also called 燃えないゴミ. Garbage is put out with 出す: 不燃ゴミを出す, 不燃ゴミの日. On municipal schedules 不燃ごみ is often written in hiragana; what exactly belongs to it is regulated by each municipality itself.

examples[].german: Have you already made plans for the next holiday?
Monday is a holiday, so it will be a three-day weekend.
This museum is open on holidays too.
en.notes: 祝日 is a statutory public holiday (国民の祝日), e.g. 文化の日 or 海の日. 休日 is the more general "day off" and includes weekends; the older 祭日 can still be heard in 祝祭日. Signs often say 土日祝 "Sat, Sun and holidays". When a holiday falls on a Sunday, there is a 振替休日 "substitute holiday". Typical: 祝日も営業, 月曜日が祝日で三連休.

examples[].german: I have absolutely no desire to buy a luxury wristwatch.
When I looked at my wristwatch, it was already past ten.
I received a wristwatch from my father for my birthday.
en.notes: 腕時計 is the wristwatch; through rendaku, とけい becomes どけい. One wears it with する, はめる or つける (腕時計をしている), and takes it off with 外す. If it runs fast or slow, one says 進んでいる or 遅れている. Other clocks: 置き時計 "table clock", 掛け時計 "wall clock", 目覚まし時計 "alarm clock"; in general, simply 時計 is often enough.

examples[].german: The feel of this stole is like silk.
The interview felt good, so I think it will probably be fine.
When you walk barefoot on the beach, the feel of the sand is pleasant.
en.notes: 感触 is first of all the feeling on touching, the tactile quality of a material: 感触がいい, さらさらした感触, 砂の感触. Figuratively it means the "impression" of how something went: 面接の感触はよかった "The interview felt good"; 手ごたえ is similar here. Not to be confused with 触覚 "sense of touch" as a sensory faculty; 手触り is a more everyday word specifically for the surface feel when handling something.

examples[].german: That article is in the May issue.
All the photos in this book were taken by the author.
This material is a compilation of articles that appeared in old newspapers.
en.notes: 所載 is a very literary, bibliographic word: "printed in, contained in" a magazine or book. It follows the source directly (五月号所載, 本書所載の写真) and stands before a noun with の. In ordinary usage people say 〜に掲載されている or 〜に載っている instead. 記載, by contrast, means "an entry or statement in a document".

examples[].german: It says here, "Bieto is a timid yakuza."
We will send the documents to the address entered on the application form.
Please use it in the way described in the instruction manual.
en.notes: 記載 is a written statement or entry in a document (form, contract, manual). As a する-verb it is transitive (住所を記載する), but mostly in the passive: 〜に記載されている "is written in ...". Typical: 記載事項 "entries, particulars", 記載漏れ "missing entry", 〜という記載がある. 記述 is a more detailed description, 掲載 is publication in a newspaper or on the web.

en.meaning: to be placed on; to fit on; to be published; to appear (in print)
examples[].german: What, there are eight apples? I wonder if they'll fit on this tray?
That word isn't in the dictionary.
Our shop was featured in a magazine.
en.notes: 載る is intransitive and has two main meanings: "to lie on something, to have room" (〜に載る, e.g. on a tray) and "to be printed, to appear" (新聞に載る, 辞書に載っていない). The transitive counterpart is 載せる "to put on; to publish". Not to be confused with 乗る "to board, to ride" - same reading, different kanji. In everyday writing 載る is often written in hiragana too.

examples[].german: This fashion is popular with young people.
When prices rise, life becomes especially hard for low-income households.
This cake has five layers.
en.notes: 〜層 is a suffix for a group or stratum of society: 若者層 "young people as a target group", 高齢者層, 富裕層 "the wealthy", 中間層, 支持層 "supporter base". It sounds matter-of-fact and is typical of marketing, media and statistics. Literally 層 means "layer, tier", hence also 五層のケーキ, 地層 "rock stratum" and オゾン層. On its own it is heard in 層が厚い "broad-based".

en.meaning: original model; prototype; archetype; basic pattern
examples[].german: Oh, so this is the original model of the Wanikani doll?
The archetype of this story is said to be an old folktale.
I make the basic pattern of the skirt out of paper first, and then cut the fabric.
en.notes: 原型 is the original model or template from which something was developed: 人形の原型, 物語の原型 "archetype of a story". In tailoring it is the basic pattern. Not to be confused with 原形 "original form" (原形をとどめない, 動詞の原形 "base form of a verb"). For technical prototypes, everyday speech rather says 試作品 or プロトタイプ.

examples[].german: That goes without saying.
"Will you help me?" "Of course!"
Being able to eat every day is not something to be taken for granted.
en.notes: 当たり前 means "obvious, natural, a matter of course" and is used as a な-adjective or with の: 当たり前のこと, 〜のは当たり前だ. In casual speech people answer with 当たり前だよ! or 当たり前じゃん "Of course!". It sounds more everyday and sometimes blunter than the literary 当然. It can also mean "ordinary, normal": 当たり前の生活 "a perfectly normal life".

en.meaning: Tokyo Metropolitan Government; Tokyo city hall
examples[].german: A 1995 Honda Civic was parked in front of the Metropolitan Government Building.
I could see Mt. Fuji from the observation deck of the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building.
My older sister works at the Tokyo Metropolitan Government.
en.notes: 都庁 is the short form of 東京都庁, the administration of Tokyo Prefecture, and at the same time denotes the building in Shinjuku. At its head is the 都知事. Correspondingly, the administrations of other prefectures are called 県庁, 府庁 or 道庁, and that of a city 市役所. The building's free observation decks are a popular destination for tourists.

examples[].german: A man was swindled out of 400,000 yen at a rip-off bar and had consulted the Metropolitan Police Department.
The Metropolitan Police Department is the police organization in charge of Tokyo.
In the drama, a detective of the Metropolitan Police Department solves the case.
en.notes: 警視庁 is the police of Tokyo Prefecture (Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department), headquartered in Kasumigaseki. All other prefectures have a 〜県警 or 道警/府警; 警視庁 exists only for Tokyo. Not to be confused with 警察庁, the national police agency, which coordinates the prefectural police but does not investigate itself. Typical in the news: 警視庁によると, 警視庁は〜を逮捕した.

examples[].german: Why is the National Police Agency making statements that seem to take the culprit's side?
The National Police Agency is the national organization that oversees the police across the country.
According to an announcement by the National Police Agency, traffic deaths decreased last year.
en.notes: 警察庁 is Japan's National Police Agency; it plans, coordinates and publishes statistics, while the actual police work lies with the prefectural police (〜県警, in Tokyo 警視庁). In the news often: 警察庁の発表によると, 警察庁長官. Mind the reading: けいさつちょう, not to be confused with 警視庁 (けいしちょう). "The police" in general is simply 警察.

examples[].german: We can't do anything that disregards the law.
I sent a message, but I keep being ignored.
It's dangerous to cross the road ignoring the traffic light.
en.notes: 無視する means "to ignore, to disregard" and is transitive: 人を無視する, 注意を無視する, 法律を無視する. Very common in the passive: 無視される "to be ignored". Fixed expressions are 信号無視 "running a red light / crossing on red" and 既読無視 "read but not answered" (in chat apps). Colloquially one also says スルーする; 見て見ぬふりをする means "to look the other way".

examples[].german: Hmm... I'd like a more visual design that appeals to consumers more.
Humans get much of their information through sight.
For people with visual impairments, there are Braille guides.
en.notes: 視覚 is the sense of sight as one of the five senses (五感): 視覚, 聴覚, 嗅覚, 味覚, 触覚. Visual acuity, on the other hand, is 視力. Common is the derivation 視覚的(な) "visual" (視覚的に分かりやすい). Other phrases: 視覚障害 "visual impairment", 視覚に訴える "to appeal to the eye". Beware of homophones: 資格 "qualification", 四角 "square", 死角 "blind spot".

examples[].german: I wear glasses not as a fashion statement but simply because I'm nearsighted.
Nearsightedness is increasing among children because they look at smartphones too much.
I'm severely nearsighted, so I can't see anything without glasses.
en.notes: 近視 is the medically neutral term for nearsightedness; colloquially one says 近眼 (きんがん, also ちかめ) or simply 目が悪い. One "is" nearsighted: 近視です, 強い近視 "severely nearsighted"; nearsightedness "progresses": 近視が進む. As an attribute it takes の: 近視の人, 近視用のメガネ. The opposite is 遠視 "farsightedness"; age-related farsightedness is 老眼.

examples[].german: I'm farsighted, so I need glasses.
It is important to detect farsightedness in children early.
People who are farsighted tire their eyes easily when reading nearby text.
en.notes: 遠視 is farsightedness: near objects are seen blurred. It is a noun (遠視です, 遠視の子ども, 遠視用のメガネ). The opposite is 近視. It is important to distinguish it from 老眼 "presbyopia", which comes with age; 遠視, by contrast, is a characteristic of the eye that already occurs in children. In everyday speech people more often say 近くが見えにくい.

examples[].german: Light is shining into the dark room.
I put a chair in a place where the sun shines in.
en.notes: 差す here means that light or sunlight shines into an area. It is an intransitive godan verb: 差します, 差して. With が you name the light, with に the lit area. 日が差す場所 refers to a place the sun shines on. 光が差している describes light currently coming in. In this sense of light, 射す／さす is also attested. This describes incoming light and is not 射る／いる "to shoot". The identically sounding spelling 注す, for pouring a liquid, belongs to a transitive verb.

examples[].german: Please check the parts before attaching the pipe.
Water is flowing through a thin pipe.
During my hospital stay, an IV tube was connected to my arm.
en.notes: 管 (くだ) is a pipe or tube, especially a thin one, e.g. on an IV stand. On its own it is mostly read くだ; in compounds it is read かん: 水道管, ガス管, 血管, 試験管. In everyday speech パイプ and チューブ are also very common. The expression くだを巻く means "to ramble on drunkenly".

examples[].german: My father was so angry that it looked like a blood vessel might burst.
When drawing blood, the nurse couldn't find the vein for a long time.
Lack of exercise can cause diseases of the blood vessels.
en.notes: 血管 is the blood vessel in general; more precisely one distinguishes 動脈 "artery", 静脈 "vein" and 毛細血管 "capillary". Typical: 血管が浮き出る "veins stand out", 血管が細い, 血管が詰まる "a vessel gets blocked". Figuratively, 血管が切れそう stands for extreme anger. The kanji 管 is read かん here, as in 水道管 or 試験管.

examples[].german: I will look for a person suited to this job.
I'm going to buy clothes appropriate for a wedding.
I think his attitude is not fitting for a teacher.
en.notes: ふさわしい means "suitable, appropriate, worthy" and takes に: この仕事にふさわしい人, 場にふさわしい服装. It is mostly written in kana; the kanji 相応しい are correct but rarer. Compared with 合う or 適切な, ふさわしい is more elevated and carries a judgment ("worthy of something"). The negative ふさわしくない means "unsuitable, inappropriate".

examples[].german: According to the weather forecast, it will snow heavily tomorrow.
The Meteorological Agency announced that there is a risk of heavy rain tomorrow.
Due to global warming, abnormal weather is increasing.
en.notes: 気象 is weather phenomena in the scientific or official sense and almost always occurs in compounds: 気象庁 "Meteorological Agency", 気象情報, 気象予報士 "meteorologist", 気象衛星, 異常気象 "extreme weather". In everyday speech one says 天気 ("how is the weather?") and 天気予報; 天候 means the weather over a period (天候不順). 気象 on its own in conversation sounds technical.

examples[].german: Just because I changed my mind, I canceled the order for a large quantity of donuts the day before.
These parts are made in large quantities at the factory.
After the heavy rain, a large amount of trash was washed down the river.
en.notes: 大量 means "large quantity" and is used attributively with の (大量のゴミ) or adverbially with に (大量に買う). In compounds it stands for "mass-": 大量生産, 大量消費. The opposite is 少量. In conversation たくさん or いっぱい sounds more casual; 大量 stresses a strikingly, often excessively large amount. The written 多量 is rarer.

examples[].german: Koichi wandered between life and death for a whole week.
This river forms the boundary between the two villages.
He has changed since that incident.
en.notes: 境 is the border or dividing line between two areas: 庭と道の境, 村の境. For national and prefectural borders one mostly uses 国境 (こっきょう) and 県境; 境界 is the more formal expression. Temporally, 〜を境に(して) means "from ... on, since ... (turning point)". Fixed phrase: 生死の境をさまよう "to hover between life and death".

examples[].german: I've decided to quit the cafe and start a new weapons export business.
The police took the weapon away from the man.
His greatest weapon is his bright smile.
en.notes: 武器 is a "weapon": 武器を持つ, 武器を捨てる, 武器の輸出. For military weapon systems 兵器 is usual (核兵器), for a weapon used in a crime 凶器. Very common is the figurative meaning "strength, trump card": 笑顔が彼の武器だ, 英語力を武器にする ("to score points with one's English skills").

examples[].german: I try to get high-quality protein at breakfast.
To get good-quality sleep, I don't look at my phone before bed.
This region is famous for producing high-quality rice.
en.notes: 良質 means "of good quality" and stands as a な- or の-adjective before nouns: 良質なタンパク質, 良質の米, 良質な睡眠. It sounds somewhat elevated and is typical of advertising, health and nutrition texts. In conversation one rather says 質のいい〜 or 品質がいい. Note: 悪質 is not simply the opposite, but means "malicious, fraudulent" (悪質な詐欺).

examples[].german: This can be called a distinctive quality of Japanese culture.
The characteristic of this material is that it is light and sturdy.
Education that makes use of each child's individual qualities is important.
en.notes: 特質 is a special, essential quality that sets something apart from other things; it sounds abstract and rather literary: 日本文化の特質, 素材の特質. The everyday word is 特徴 "feature", often for visible characteristics; 特色 emphasizes what is unmistakable (地域の特色), 性質 the inner nature. Typical pattern: 〜の特質を生かす "to make use of the special quality of ...".

examples[].german: Hmm, that is not an accurate description.
This question is a written-answer type, so please write your answer in sentences.
The textbook describes that war in detail.
en.notes: 記述 is a written description or account; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を記述する, often in the passive 〜に記述されている. It is well known from exams: 記述式 "free-response questions" as opposed to 選択式 "multiple choice". To distinguish: 記載 is a brief entry in forms, 説明 is an explanation, 描写 is a vivid depiction in literature.

examples[].german: For the reasons mentioned above, I have decided not to take part in this project.
As stated above, the application deadline is the end of March.
Looking at the table above, you can see that sales are increasing year by year.
en.notes: 上述 refers in texts to something already said further above: 上述の理由, 上述したように "as mentioned above". It is purely written language (reports, theses, official texts). Synonyms are 前述 and 先述; in forms and e-mails 上記 is more usual, and the counterpart is 下記 or 以下. In speech one says 先ほど言ったように instead.

examples[].german: Then I'll send it marked confidential.
The envelope says "personal", so please don't open it unless you are the addressee.
A confidential letter arrived from the bank.
en.notes: 親展 is a marking on envelopes: "personal, confidential - to be opened only by the addressee". It is written next to the address, or one sends something 親展で. Typical for letters from banks, government offices or with health data. For confidentiality in general (information, documents), people say 機密, 内密 or 秘密 instead.

examples[].german: It's Sunday, and yet it's open.
A sign saying "Open" is hanging on the door.
On my phone's map, I searched for a pharmacy nearby that is open.
en.notes: 営業中 means "open, in operation" and typically appears on signs at shops and restaurants; the counterpart is 準備中 "not yet open / being prepared" or 本日休業. In a sentence it is used with です or の (営業中の店). For opening hours one says 営業時間, and for "is open" in conversation often 開いている. 営業 alone also means "sales" (営業部).

examples[].german: Desirable results were obtained.
It is advisable to take the medicine after meals.
For this job, someone with experience is preferable.
en.notes: 望ましい means "desirable, preferable" and comes from 望む "to wish". Typical patterns are 〜ことが望ましい and 〜のが望ましい, often in rules, recommendations and job ads (経験者が望ましい "experience preferred"). It sounds factual and formal; in conversation one tends to say 〜たほうがいい. Not to be confused with 好ましい, which expresses more "likable, pleasant".

en.meaning: storage place; place to put things
examples[].german: I park my bicycle at the bicycle parking lot at Kawasaki Station.
We have so much luggage that there is nowhere to put it.
The garbage area is next to the entrance of the apartment building.
en.notes: 置き場 is a place where one puts or stores something, mostly in compounds: 自転車置き場, ゴミ置き場, 傘置き場, 資材置き場. Important expressions: 置き場に困る / 置き場がない "not to know where to put it". Figuratively, 身の置き場がない means "to feel out of place". The neutral general term for a storage room is 倉庫; 置き場 is more everyday and concrete.

examples[].german: That man with the broad, sturdy shoulders is this country's vice president.
Because the president was ill, the vice president attended the meeting in his place.
In the United States, the president and vice president are elected together.
en.notes: 副大統領 is the vice president of a state led by a 大統領 "president", such as the USA. The prefix 副〜 means "deputy, vice-": 副社長, 副会長, 副市長. For presidents of companies one says 社長, not 大統領. Typical: 副大統領に就任する "to take office", 副大統領候補.

examples[].german: Many tourists visit this town every year.
More English signs were added at the station for foreign tourists.
There were so many tourists that I couldn't take photos in peace.
en.notes: 観光客 are tourists, that is, visitors who come for sightseeing; 〜客 means "guest, customer" as in 乗客 "passenger". Typical: 観光客が訪れる, 観光客でにぎわう "crowded with tourists", 外国人観光客. 旅行者 is the more neutral "traveler" (also on business); 観光地 is the tourist destination. Too many tourists is called 観光公害 or オーバーツーリズム in the media.

en.meaning: to poke; to thrust; to prod; to hit (a weak point)
examples[].german: Could you stop poking me with your elbow?
My grandmother walks slowly with a cane.
His question hit the weak points of my explanation.
en.notes: 突く is transitive and means "to poke, to thrust, to prod" with a body part or an object: ヒジで突く, 棒で突く. One also supports oneself with it: 杖を突く "to walk with a cane", 手を突く. Figuratively, 弱点を突く means "to hit the weak point". Distinctions: 刺す is "to pierce with something pointed", つつく "to poke repeatedly". つく is often written in kana; homophones are 付く, 着く, 点く.

examples[].german: We burn fallen leaves and make roasted sweet potatoes.
I burned all the letters from my ex-lover.
He is burning with passion for his dream.
en.notes: 燃やす is transitive "to burn something" (ゴミを燃やす, 手紙を燃やす); the intransitive counterpart is 燃える "to burn" (燃えるゴミ). Figuratively it means "to kindle passion": 情熱を燃やす, 闘志を燃やす. Distinction: 焼く means "to fry, bake, grill" or "to burn down" (家を焼く); 燃やす stresses the burning itself.

examples[].german: What, this whole amount in cash!?
Since the trip was canceled, I got the full price refunded.
The company pays the transportation costs in full.
en.notes: 全額 is the full amount. It is often used adverbially before the verb without a particle: 全額払う, 全額返す; likewise 全額返金 "full refund" and 全額負担 "full coverage of costs". Counterparts are 一部 "a part" and 半額 "half price". 総額, on the other hand, is the total of several items (総額で十万円).

examples[].german: Koichi has a Tofugu tattoo on his left arm.
I fell and broke my left arm.
I always wear my wristwatch on my left arm.
en.notes: 左腕 is read ひだりうで in everyday speech, "left arm"; the counterpart is 右腕. In baseball it is read さわん and denotes a left-handed pitcher (左腕投手). 右腕 also figuratively means "right-hand man, closest confidant": 社長の右腕. For watches or injuries one says quite normally 左腕に〜 or 左腕を〜.

examples[].german: In Japan, it is rude to point at people.
A child pointed at the sky and shouted, "Airplane!"
The station attendant pointed at the clock and checked the departure time.
en.notes: 指差す means "to point at something with a finger" and is transitive: 〜を指差す. It is also written 指さす. More general is 指す "to point, to indicate" (also with clock hands: 時計の針が三時を指す). In Japan, it is considered impolite to point at people with a finger. Among railway staff, 指差し確認 "point and call" is well known as a safety check.

examples[].german: This morning I saw news about next-generation fuel vehicles.
We're about to run out of fuel, so let's stop at the next gas station.
Fuel costs went up, and airplane tickets became more expensive too.
en.notes: 燃料 is generally "fuel" for vehicles, heating or power plants; ガソリン is specifically gasoline. Typical phrases: 燃料を補給する "to refuel", 燃料が切れる "to run out of fuel", 燃料費/燃料代 "fuel costs", 化石燃料 "fossil fuels". On flight tickets, 燃油サーチャージ "fuel surcharge" often appears.

examples[].german: I have a lot of moles on both arms.
She was carrying an armful of flowers in both arms.
Stretch both arms upward and take a deep breath.
en.notes: 両腕 means "both arms"; the prefix 両〜 "both" is known from 両手, 両足, 両親. Typical phrases: 両腕を広げる "to spread one's arms", 両腕で抱える "to carry with both arms", 両腕を組む "to fold one's arms". The counterpart is 片腕 "one arm", which figuratively also means "right-hand man, closest associate". 腕 is the whole arm from the shoulder to the wrist.

examples[].german: There was a favorable change.
His cheerful personality is very likable.
Using a smartphone during class is not desirable.
en.notes: 好ましい means "pleasant, likable, welcome" and describes a positive impression: 好ましい人物, 好ましい変化. The negative 好ましくない "undesirable, frowned upon" is very common, for example for behavior: その態度は好ましくない. Compared with 望ましい ("desirable as a goal"), 好ましい stresses the assessment as pleasant. It is more formal than 好きな or いい.

examples[].german: What, you shipped whiskey from Japan in a container?!
Heavy snow is having a major impact on rail transport.
This package is going by ship, so it will take about a month.
en.notes: 輸送 is the "transport" of goods or people by vehicle, ship or aircraft, usually on a larger scale; as a transitive する-verb: X を輸送する. Typical are トラック輸送, 航空輸送, 輸送費 and 輸送に影響が出る. In everyday speech people simply say 運ぶ; 運送 emphasizes commercial carriage (運送会社 "freight company"). The word sounds matter-of-fact and is typical of news and logistics.

examples[].german: This item has no price sticker.
It's a present, so could you take off the price tag?
When I looked at the price tag, I was surprised that it was more expensive than I had thought.
en.notes: 値札 is the price tag on goods; 値 "price, value" + 札 "tag, slip" (read ふだ). Typical phrases: 値札が付いている, 値札を外す/取る "to remove the price tag" (e.g. for gifts), 値札を見る. The price itself is called 値段 or 価格; 値札シール is a price sticker.

examples[].german: No, no, short sleeves are way too early. Aren't you cold?
The summer uniform is a short-sleeved shirt.
It was getting hot, so I changed into short sleeves.
en.notes: 半袖 denotes short sleeves and is also short for a short-sleeved top: 半袖を着る, 半袖に着替える. Before nouns with の: 半袖のシャツ, 半袖のTシャツ. The counterpart is 長袖; sleeveless is ノースリーブ. Related: 袖 "sleeve", 七分袖 "three-quarter sleeve".

examples[].german: Should I wear long sleeves today?
It's cold at the top of the mountain, so please bring one long-sleeved top.
To avoid getting sunburned, I wear long-sleeved shirts even in summer.
en.notes: 長袖 means long sleeves and often also stands for a long-sleeved top: 長袖を着る, 長袖一枚. Before nouns with の: 長袖のシャツ. The counterpart is 半袖. Typical contexts are weather and seasons (朝晩は長袖が必要) as well as sun or mosquito protection in summer.

examples[].german: I am in Paris on official business right now.
You must not use an official car for private purposes.
The official languages of this country are English and French.
en.notes: 公用 means "official or governmental business" (公用で出張する) and "public/official use" in compounds: 公用車 "official car", 公用語 "official language". The opposite is 私用 "private" (私用で使う). For companies one rather says 社用 or 仕事で; 公用 sounds like a government office or an official function.

examples[].german: In this town, the school district is divided into three sections.
Fee categories differ depending on age.
I sorted the documents by content and put them in files.
en.notes: 区分 is the division into sections or categories according to fixed criteria; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を区分する. Typical in administration and fee schedules: 料金区分, 年齢区分, 区分けする (more everyday). To distinguish: 区別 is telling two things apart (公私を区別する), 分類 is systematic classification, e.g. in biology.

en.meaning: to be involved; to be concerned with
examples[].german: I know Viet is involved with a shady organization, but I still can't believe he was involved in that crime.
It's not a life-threatening illness, so please don't worry.
You'd better not get involved with that person.
en.notes: 係わる is a variant spelling of 関わる (today the usual spelling) and is intransitive. 〜に係わる means "to be involved in something" (事件に係わる) or "to affect something" (命に係わる "life-threatening"); 〜と係わる means "to have dealings with someone". Often negatively tinged: あの人と係わらないほうがいい. There is no direct transitive counterpart; similar is 関係する.

examples[].german: A new building is planned to be built there.
A large apartment building was built in front of the station.
It has been fifty years since this house was built.
en.notes: 建つ is intransitive and describes a building being erected or standing: ビルが建つ, 家が建った. The transitive partner is 建てる ("to build"): 家を建てる. Not to be confused with the homophone 立つ ("to stand, to stand up"), which is used for people, things or smoke - 建つ applies only to structures such as houses, towers or monuments. With 〜てから it expresses how long a building has been standing.

examples[].german: It is an honor to play in such a wonderful team.
It is an honor to meet you.
I feel greatly honored to receive such an award.
en.notes: 光栄 expresses that one feels honored and appears almost always in polite phrases: 〜て光栄です ("it is an honor to ..."), 光栄に思います ("I feel honored") or, formally, 身に余る光栄 ("an honor I hardly deserve"). It refers to one's own joy at an award or encounter, whereas 名誉 is honor in the sense of prestige and good reputation (名誉を守る). Grammatically it is a な-adjective or noun; typical in speeches, interviews and greetings.

examples[].german: I put my own fire safety tips into writing.
This building is equipped with fire doors.
For fire prevention, be sure to turn off the heater before going to bed.
en.notes: 防火 means "fire protection, fire prevention" and appears mainly in compounds: 防火扉 ("fire door"), 防火壁 ("firewall (wall)"), 防火対策 ("fire prevention measures"), 防火訓練 ("fire drill"). It is about preventing fires, in contrast to 消火 ("extinguishing a fire"). The more general term for disaster prevention is 防災. The word sounds rather matter-of-fact and official.

examples[].german: I will solve the problem.
As a result of talking it over, the trouble was resolved.
That case has not been solved yet.
en.notes: 解決する means to get a real problem, dispute or case out of the world. It is both transitive and intransitive: 問題を解決する "to solve a problem", 問題が解決する "a problem gets solved". A math or exam question, on the other hand, is "solved" with 解く (問題を解く). Also common are 解決策 "solution" and 解決に向けて "toward a solution".

examples[].german: There are unavoidable circumstances.
Because of the rain, the match was unavoidably canceled.
Lateness is not accepted except in unavoidable cases.
en.notes: やむを得ない means "unavoidable, cannot be changed", literally something like "one cannot stop it". Typical are やむを得ない事情 "unavoidable circumstances" and the adverbial form やむを得ず "out of necessity". It is more formal than 仕方がない or しょうがない and often appears in apologies and official notices: やむを得ない場合を除き …. The spelling 止むを得ない is less common.

en.meaning: receipt of delivery; acknowledgment of receipt
examples[].german: When the delivery is complete, please remember to get a receipt from the recipient.
Please sign the acknowledgment of receipt.
When you submit documents, you should get an acknowledgment of receipt.
en.notes: 受領書 is a business document confirming that goods or documents have arrived; 受領 is the formal word for "receipt". Typical are 受領書にサインする, 受領書を受け取る or 受領書を発行する. Not to be confused with 領収書, the receipt for a payment, or the till receipt レシート. In everyday speech one rather says 受け取り; 受領書 sounds written and businesslike.

en.meaning: to limit; to restrict; to be the best
examples[].german: As expected, there's nothing like Tofugu for studying Japanese.
Participants are limited to twenty.
Of all days, I forgot my umbrella today.
en.notes: 限る has three important uses: transitive "to limit" (人数を限る, often passive: 限られた時間), with に "to be restricted to something" (参加者は二十人に限る) and colloquially 〜に限る "there's nothing like ..." (夏はビールに限る). In addition there are fixed patterns: 〜に限って "of all things", 〜とは限らない "not necessarily" and 〜限り "as long as, as far as". Close in meaning is 制限する, which sounds more formal and technical.

examples[].german: Young people have unlimited potential.
I wonder whether the universe expands infinitely.
Time is not unlimited, so let's use it wisely.
en.notes: 無限 means "infinite, boundless" and is mostly used attributively with の (無限の可能性, 無限の宇宙) or adverbially as 無限に (無限に広がる). The form 無限な is rare. The opposite is 有限 ("finite, limited"). Similar, but more emotional and literary, is 限りない; 無制限, by contrast, means "without restriction" in the sense of rules (無制限に使える).

examples[].german: The glass pufferfish figurine fell off the table and broke.
Please put the eggs at the very top of the bag so that they don't break.
On that issue, the class's opinion split in two.
en.notes: 割れる is intransitive: something breaks or gets a crack, typically glass, plates, eggs or ice. The transitive counterpart is 割る "to break, to crack (an egg)". Figuratively, opinions or votes also split: 意見が割れる. To be distinguished are 壊れる (general "to break down", also for devices) and 折れる (for long things such as sticks or bones).

examples[].german: Tomorrow is a field trip, so I have to prepare a bento.
Have you finished preparing for the trip yet?
I will prepare the materials before the meeting.
en.notes: 準備する means "to prepare, to get ready" and is transitive: 資料を準備する. The form ～の準備をする is very common: 旅行の準備をする "to prepare for the trip". "To be ready" is 準備ができる: 準備ができました "Everything is ready". Closely related is 用意する, which emphasizes more the providing of concrete things, whereas 準備 also includes planning and organization.

en.meaning: to pull out; to leave out; to overtake
examples[].german: Could you leave out the wasabi?
I had a tooth pulled at the dentist.
Please be extremely careful when overtaking the car ahead.
en.notes: The basic meaning of 抜く is "to pull out": 歯を抜く, 草を抜く, 栓を抜く. From this follow "to leave out" (朝ご飯を抜く, ワサビを抜く; 手を抜く "to slack off") and "to overtake" (前の車を抜く, intensified 追い抜く). After a verb stem it means "to carry through to the end": やり抜く, 走り抜く. The intransitive partner is 抜ける ("to come out, to fall out"): 歯が抜ける, 力が抜ける.

en.meaning: to be caught; to hold on
examples[].german: A part-timer at our company hit someone and got arrested.
It will shake, so please hold on firmly to the strap.
On rainy days, it's hard to get a taxi.
en.notes: 捕まる is intransitive: 犯人が警察に捕まる ("the culprit is caught by the police"), and the agent takes に. Its transitive partner is 捕まえる ("to catch, to arrest"); more formal is 逮捕される. In the meanings "to hold on to" (つり革につかまる) and "to catch, to get hold of" (タクシーがつかまる, 電話で人がつかまらない), it is mostly written in kana. Colloquially it also means "to be held up by someone": 先輩につかまって帰れなかった.

examples[].german: My grandfather made me a model airplane.
A model of the old town is on display at the museum.
My older brother's hobby is collecting model trains.
en.notes: 模型 is a noun for a replica, usually scaled down: 模型飛行機 or 模型の飛行機, 鉄道模型 ("model railway"), 建築模型 ("architectural model"). Unlike the loanword モデル, which also means "fashion model", "role model" or "product model", 模型 always means a physical object. A plastic kit is colloquially called プラモデル.

examples[].german: After hearing about the bonus, I suddenly felt like studying.
The bonus is paid twice a year, in June and December.
The company is doing badly this year, so apparently there will be no bonus.
en.notes: 賞与金 is the formal expression for the bonus payment, which in Japan is usually paid twice a year (summer and winter). In contracts and on pay slips it is usually shortened to 賞与; in everyday speech one almost always says ボーナス. Not to be confused with 賞金, the prize money in competitions. Typical are 賞与金が出る ("there is a bonus") and 賞与金を支給する.

examples[].german: Depending on how words are used, political implications can arise.
It is difficult to read the implications of this text.
The phrase "I'll consider it" often carries the implication of a refusal.
en.notes: 含意 is a literary, rather academic word for the underlying, unspoken meaning of a statement: 政治的な含意, 言葉の含意を読み取る. In everyday speech people say ニュアンス, 言外の意味 or simply 意味 instead. 暗示, by contrast, emphasizes deliberate hinting. As a する-verb (含意する "to imply") it occurs mainly in logic and linguistics.

examples[].german: There are many negative opinions.
The president is negative about the plan.
He tends to see everything negatively.
en.notes: 否定的 is a な-adjective meaning "negative, dismissive": 否定的な意見, 否定的な態度, 〜に否定的だ "to take a negative view of something". The suffix 的 turns the noun 否定 "denial" into an adjective; the opposite is 肯定的. In conversation you often hear the loanword ネガティブ, which tends to describe a generally pessimistic attitude, while 否定的 refers to a negative stance toward a particular matter.

examples[].german: It's a sight I see almost every day, yet I never noticed it until then.
I'll never forget the sight of the sunrise seen from the top of the mountain.
Seeing the scene of the accident, I was at a loss for words.
en.notes: 光景 is a scene that one sees with one's own eyes, often with people and events in it: 信じられない光景, ほほえましい光景, 事故の光景. 景色 and 風景, on the other hand, denote mainly landscapes and views. 光景 can be beautiful as well as frightening and is often used with 目にする or 目に浮かぶ ("to come before one's eyes").

examples[].german: All the candidates were wearing glasses.
Before the election, I went to hear a candidate's speech.
We have to choose one from among the candidates who came to the interview.
en.notes: 候補者 is a person who is up for selection - above all in elections, but also on the shortlist for filling a position. 候補 alone can also mean things (候補地 "candidate site"). To run as a candidate is 立候補する. For applicants who apply for a job one mostly says 応募者; 候補者 sounds like a preselection.

examples[].german: The seasonal greeting changes depending on the month.
It is a Japanese custom to write a seasonal greeting at the start of a letter.
In business emails, the seasonal greeting is often omitted.
en.notes: 時候 is an elevated word for "season, seasonal weather" and today occurs almost only in 時候のあいさつ: the seasonal greeting at the start of a formal letter, such as 初夏の候 ("in the season of early summer"). In everyday speech people say 季節. In business emails this greeting is often shortened or left out entirely.

en.meaning: to care about; to mind; to pay attention to
examples[].german: Lately I'm so busy with work that I can't give my children any attention at all.
Do you mind if I smoke here?
Don't worry about me, please go ahead.
en.notes: 構う means "to care about something, to mind" and is often written in kana. It is most often encountered in the negative: ～てもかまいません "you may ..., it doesn't matter" and simply かまいません "no problem". 構わないで(ください) means "don't worry about me, don't go to any trouble". In the meaning "to pay attention to someone", the person takes を or に: 子供に構ってあげる; 構ってほしい means "to want attention".

examples[].german: My wife likes patterns with small flowers.
According to the weather forecast, it looks like rain tomorrow.
The details of the accident were reported on the news.
en.notes: 模様 first means a "pattern" on fabric or dishes: 花の模様, 水玉模様 ("polka-dot pattern"). It also refers to the "state, course" of an event (事故の模様) and, in news reports, to "appearance, signs that something seems so": 〜した模様です ("it appears that ... has ..."). In weather words it expresses a tendency: 雨模様 ("it looks like rain"). For the pattern of clothes and fabrics, 柄 is also used.

examples[].german: For some reason, a line had formed at the fresh fish counter of the supermarket.
This shop sells fresh fish brought in from the harbor every morning.
Fresh fish is best eaten on the day you buy it.
en.notes: 鮮魚 is a trade word for "fresh fish" and is found mainly on signs and in advertising: 鮮魚コーナー, 鮮魚店. In conversation, people more often say 新鮮な魚 or 生の魚. It refers to raw, unprocessed fish, not cooked or dried fish (干物).

examples[].german: The medicine has finally started to work.
This medicine works well against headaches.
The air conditioner in this room doesn't work very well.
en.notes: 効く means "to be effective, to help" and is intransitive: 薬が効く. What it works against is marked with に (頭痛に効く). It is also used for devices whose effect you can feel: エアコンが効く, 冷房が効きすぎる. The homophone 利く means "to function" in the sense of ability: 気が利く ("to be attentive"), ブレーキが利く; in everyday writing the two spellings are often mixed up. Do not confuse it with 聞く ("to hear").

examples[].german: I do not belong to an entertainment agency.
In high school, I belonged to the soccer club.
Your name and affiliation are written on the business card.
en.notes: 所属 means "affiliation" with an organization and, as a する-verb, is mostly used in the progressive form: 〜に所属している ("belongs to ..., is a member of ..."). As a noun, it stands for the department or organization one belongs to: 所属部署, 名前と所属, politely ご所属. 属する is more general and more literary (哺乳類に属する), 入る emphasizes joining.

examples[].german: I prefer women with a full-figured body over thin ones like models.
The woman in the painting is depicted with a voluptuous figure.
en.notes: 豊満 describes a full, voluptuous body, almost always a woman's: 豊満な体つき, 豊満な胸. The word has a sensual overtone and is rather literary; in conversation it can sound suggestive. Neutral and casual is ぽっちゃり ("plump"); 太っている ("fat") is judgmental. Grammatically it is a な-adjective.

examples[].german: Let's think positively.
In the survey, there were many positive opinions.
My parents were positive about my studying abroad.
en.notes: 肯定的 is a na-adjective: "affirmative, approving, positive". Typical are 肯定的な意見, 肯定的な評価 and 〜に肯定的だ "to be positive about something"; adverbially 肯定的に考える/捉える "to see positively". The opposite is 否定的. For an optimistic attitude, everyday speech prefers 前向き or ポジティブ; 肯定的 sounds more matter-of-fact and is typical for surveys, reports and discussions.

examples[].german: On a full-moon night, it is bright outside and you can walk even without lights.
Tonight is a full moon, so let's do moon viewing.
Three more days until the full moon.
en.notes: 満月 is the full moon, a noun that takes の attributively: 満月の夜. The other moon phases are 新月 ("new moon"), 半月 ("half moon") and 三日月 ("crescent moon"). For the traditional moon viewing in autumn (お月見), one speaks of 十五夜 or 中秋の名月. At full moon the sky is bright, so fewer stars are visible then.

examples[].german: If possible, I don't want to ride a packed bus.
The morning train is always packed.
The concert hall was full, and some people could not get in.
en.notes: 満員 means that a place or vehicle is filled with people to its capacity limit: 満員電車, 満員のバス, 会場は満員だ. 満員御礼 at sumo and in theaters means "sold out". For seats in a restaurant or aircraft, 満席 is more usual; for things and containers, いっぱい. 混む only means "to be crowded, busy", not necessarily full to the last place.

examples[].german: If I get full marks, the teacher gives me a flower stamp.
This hotel was perfect in both service and scenery.
I made a breakfast packed with nutrition.
en.notes: 満点 is the full score: 満点を取る, 百点満点 ("100 out of 100 points"); the opposite is 零点. Figuratively it means "perfect, completely" and is attached to nouns: 栄養満点 ("extremely nutritious"), 迫力満点 ("full of power"), サービス満点. 花丸 is the flower-shaped circle that Japanese teachers draw on especially good work.

examples[].german: First, let's check your own degree of obesity!
Obesity is the cause of many diseases.
I hear that obesity among children has been increasing lately.
en.notes: 肥満 is the medical, factual term for "obesity, being overweight": 肥満度 ("degree of obesity"), 肥満体, 子どもの肥満. In everyday speech people say 太っている or 太りすぎ; calling a person 肥満 directly sounds cold and impolite. The softened form is 肥満気味 ("a bit too heavy"). The form 肥満する is rare.

examples[].german: I only have the first volume of this manga.
Try reading it starting from the first volume.
If you fall here, it's all over.
en.notes: 一巻 with the counter 巻 means "volume 1" of a book or manga series (more formally 第一巻) or "one volume". For works in two or three volumes, people say 上巻・中巻・下巻 instead. The set phrase 一巻の終わり means "it's all over, the end". Not to be confused with the homophone 一貫 ("consistency, coherence").

examples[].german: This economics textbook has a first volume and a second volume.
The first volume was interesting, so I bought the second one right away.
I reserved the second volume at the library, but my turn hasn't come yet.
en.notes: 下巻 is the last volume of a multi-volume work: the second for two volumes (上巻・下巻), the third for three volumes (上巻・中巻・下巻). For longer, consecutively numbered series, people speak of 第二巻, 第三巻 and so on instead. Typical: 下巻を買う, 下巻が出る, 上下巻セット.

examples[].german: It was a light novel, so I could read the first volume in thirty minutes.
When you finish the first volume, I'll lend you the second.
This book is divided into a first volume and a second volume.
en.notes: 上巻 is the first volume of a work in two or three parts; its counterparts are 中巻 and 下巻. For consecutively numbered series, people say 第一巻 or 一巻. Typical combinations: 上巻を読み終わる, 上巻と下巻に分かれている, 上下巻 ("both volumes").

examples[].german: I'm happy that the second volume of the novel I was looking forward to has been released.
This series suddenly becomes interesting from the second volume.
I finished reading the two-volume novel in a week.
en.notes: 二巻 is made up of the number 二 and the counter 巻 for volumes. It means either "volume 2" (more formally 第二巻) or "two volumes" (全二巻 "in two volumes"). For works with exactly two volumes, people usually say 上巻・下巻 instead of 一巻・二巻. The counting goes いっかん, にかん, さんかん.

en.meaning: to search for; to look for
examples[].german: My grandmother, who has Alzheimer's disease, hasn't come home since yesterday. Could you help me look for her?
The police searched all night for the missing child.
I searched around the station for the wallet I dropped, but couldn't find it.
en.notes: 捜す and 探す are both read さがす. By the traditional rule, 捜す is used for something you have lost or that has disappeared (a missing person, a lost wallet), while 探す is used for something you want to have (仕事を探す, 部屋を探す). In practice, 探す is increasingly used for both; 捜す is typical of police work and the news (cf. 捜査, 捜索). The result of finding is expressed with 見つかる or 見つける.

examples[].german: The man was found strangled at his home.
The police believe the victim was strangled and are investigating.
In that novel, a woman is strangled in the first incident.
en.notes: 絞殺 is a technical term from police and news language for "strangulation, to strangle". As a する-verb it is almost always in the passive: 絞殺される, 絞殺された遺体. In conversation people say 首を絞めて殺す instead. Related words are 絞める ("to choke") and 殺害 ("killing").

examples[].german: A fundamental solution is needed.
The two of them think fundamentally differently.
They are investigating the root cause of the accident.
en.notes: 根本的 is a na-adjective: "fundamental, from the ground up", derived from 根本 "root, foundation". Common are 根本的な問題, 根本的な原因, 根本的な解決 and adverbially 根本的に違う/見直す. It emphasizes going to the root of a matter - as opposed to superficial or temporary solutions (表面的, 一時的). Similar, but not the same, is 基本的 "basically, in principle".

examples[].german: My father is enjoying his retired life.
At seventy, my grandfather left the shop to his son and retired.
Saying it is still too early to retire, my father is still working in the field.
en.notes: 隠居 means withdrawing from working and business life to live quietly, traditionally after handing over the business or the headship of the family to the next generation: 隠居する, 隠居生活. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned; ご隠居 is an elderly gentleman in retirement. More neutral are 退職 ("leaving a job") and 定年 ("retirement age"); 引退 is said for athletes or politicians.

examples[].german: The curtains designed by Aya were hung in the Tofugu office.
Please hang the photo on the wall.
en.notes: 掛ける here means "to hang" and is a transitive ichidan verb: 掛けます, 掛けて. With を you name the object hung, with に the place. 掛けられました is passive in the curtain sentence: the curtains were hung. The intransitive 掛かる, by contrast, describes the hanging object.

en.meaning: to exchange; to replace; to change
examples[].german: I exchanged dollars for yen at Narita Airport.
The light bulb in the room burned out, so I replaced it with a new one.
The manager substituted two players in the second half.
en.notes: 替える means "to exchange for something else, to switch": 電球を替える, ドルを円に替える ("to exchange into ..." with に). There are several spellings of the same reading: 変える ("to change, alter"), 換える ("to convert, swap"), 代える ("to replace, to use in place of"); 替える and 換える overlap strongly. The intransitive partner is 替わる. Common in compounds: 着替える, 取り替える, 両替.

examples[].german: Ernesto Che Guevara was a revolutionary from Argentina.
In his youth, he dreamed of becoming a revolutionary.
She is called a revolutionary of the culinary world.
en.notes: 革命家 is composed of 革命 ("revolution") and the suffix 家 for people who pursue an activity (cf. 政治家, 芸術家). It refers to people who lead a political overthrow, but is also used figuratively for innovators in a field: 料理界の革命家. The adjective "revolutionary" is 革命的な.

examples[].german: Wow, it's a small world. Who would have thought my friend from Nagasaki Prefecture was a friend of Koichi's friend.
Nagasaki Prefecture is in the west of Kyushu.
I traveled to an island in Nagasaki Prefecture during the summer vacation.
en.notes: 長崎県 is the prefecture in the west of Kyushu, with 長崎市 as its capital. A large part of it consists of islands (e.g. 五島列島, 対馬), and it is known for its history as the only trading port during the period of national isolation (出島) and for the atomic bombing in 1945. In conversation people often just say 長崎; with 県 it is clear that the whole prefecture is meant and not only the city.

en.meaning: to be called; to be summoned; to be invited
examples[].german: The alligator gar is also called the "Clavigator".
When your name is called, please come to the front.
I've been invited to a friend's wedding, so I'm going to Osaka next month.
en.notes: 呼ばれる is the passive of 呼ぶ and has several meanings: "to be called (named)" (〜と呼ばれる), "to be called out" (名前を呼ばれる), "to be invited" (結婚式に呼ばれる) and "to be summoned" (先生に呼ばれる). The agent is marked with に. For naming, 〜と呼ばれている is very common; in explanations 〜と言われる is also used.

en.meaning: to reveal; to show; to bring to light
examples[].german: Koichi has finally shown up at the concert venue!
Mt. Fuji appeared from between the clouds.
The culprit doesn't reveal his true identity easily.
en.notes: 現す means "to make visible, to bring to light" something that was previously hidden: 姿を現す ("to appear, show up"), 正体を現す ("to show one's true colors"). The intransitive partner is 現れる ("to appear"). Do not confuse it with 表す ("to express, represent": 気持ちを表す, 記号が表す) or 著す ("to write a book") - all are read あらわす.

examples[].german: Do you think ghosts really exist?
There is a cat in the garden.
en.notes: 居る is an intransitive ichidan verb for the presence of living things: 居ます, 居て. It is mostly written in hiragana as いる. With に you name the place, with が the person or animal. と思いますか asks for an opinion. For inanimate objects you normally use ある.

en.meaning: now (that it is too late); at this point
examples[].german: It's a problem if you tell me that at this point.
Even if you apologize now, it's already too late.
It's late to ask, but may I ask your name?
en.notes: 今更 expresses that something comes "now" although it is actually too late for it; mostly with reproach or resignation: 今更〜ても, 今更遅い, 今更言われても困る. Often written in kana (いまさら). Fixed phrases: 今更ながら ("admittedly late, but ..."), 今更聞けない ("what one no longer dares to ask at this point"). As a polite opener: 今更ですが ("it may be a bit late, but ...").

examples[].german: Let's avoid abstract expressions.
His explanation was too abstract, and I hardly understood it.
I saw abstract paintings at the museum.
en.notes: 抽象的 is a na-adjective: "abstract, not concrete". Typical are 抽象的な表現, 抽象的な説明 and 抽象的すぎてわからない. The opposite is 具体的 "concrete" - the pair is often heard when someone asks for examples: もっと具体的に説明してください. In art, abstract painting is 抽象画.

examples[].german: It's almost time to change into the season's clothes.
Coat the shrimp in batter and deep-fry it.
The monk was wearing a black robe and reciting a sutra.
en.notes: 衣 (ころも) is an old, elevated word for "clothing, garment". Today it appears mainly as a monk's robe (お坊さんの衣) and in the kitchen as batter or breading: 天ぷらの衣, 衣をつける. For everyday clothing people say 服 or 衣服. You know it as a component of 衣替え ("seasonal change of clothes"); in Sino-Japanese words it is read い (衣類, 衣食住).

examples[].german: When I looked around, I was surrounded by lots of investigators.
From the top of the mountain, you can see the whole town.
As far as the eye could see, the blue sea stretched out.
en.notes: 見渡す means "to survey, to let one's gaze sweep over something" and takes を: 辺りを見渡す, 町を見渡す. The fixed phrase 見渡す限り means "as far as the eye can see". 見回す emphasizes turning the head to look around, 眺める calm viewing. The potential form 見渡せる ("can be seen across") is common: 海が見渡せる部屋.

examples[].german: Please try to lead a regular life, going to bed and rising early.
The heart beats regularly.
The books are lined up neatly on the desk.
en.notes: 規則正しい is an い-adjective for "regular, orderly, following a fixed rhythm". The most typical combination is 規則正しい生活 ("a regular daily routine"); adverbially it is 規則正しく (規則正しく並ぶ). The opposite is 不規則な. 定期的, by contrast, emphasizes fixed time intervals (定期的に検査する), 几帳面 a person's conscientiousness.

examples[].german: The tutor leaned the whiteboard against the wall.
When I was a university student, I had a part-time job as a tutor for a junior high school student.
My son's grades dropped, so we decided to get him a tutor.
en.notes: 家庭教師 is a private teacher who comes to the students' home and usually teaches one-on-one. Typical: 家庭教師をつける ("to get a tutor"), 家庭教師をする ("to work as a tutor"), 家庭教師のアルバイト - a classic student job. By contrast, 塾 is a cram school where 講師 teach. Colloquially it is shortened to カテキョー.

examples[].german: My work hours are irregular.
If you keep living an irregular lifestyle, you will ruin your health.
"行く" is a verb with an irregular te-form.
en.notes: 不規則 is a な-adjective for "irregular, without a fixed rhythm": 不規則な生活, 勤務時間が不規則だ, 不規則に並ぶ. In grammar, irregular verbs are called 不規則動詞. Opposites are 規則正しい and 規則的. 不定期, by contrast, refers to something that does not take place at fixed intervals (不定期便).

en.meaning: to take down; to drop off; to unload
examples[].german: Help me unload the luggage.
Please drop me off at the next corner.
The president removed him as leader of the project.
en.notes: 降ろす is transitive and mainly means to bring people or cargo down from a vehicle or from above: 荷物を降ろす, 客を降ろす ("to drop passengers off"), as well as to remove someone from a post (リーダーから降ろす). The intransitive partner is 降りる. The homophone 下ろす means "to lower" (手を下ろす, シャッターを下ろす), to withdraw money (お金を下ろす) and to grate (大根を下ろす).

examples[].german: The response to this article was very large.
The voice echoed inside the tunnel.
The new product drew a big response right after its release.
en.notes: 反響 has two meanings: literally "echo, reverberation", as an intransitive する-verb (声が反響する), and figuratively the "response, reaction" of the public to something (記事への反響). Typical are 反響がある, 大きな反響, 反響を呼ぶ ("to find resonance"). 反応 is the more general "reaction"; 響く means "to resound, to ring".

examples[].german: It rained and the water level of the river rose.
With the arrival of spring, the sunlight has gradually grown stronger.
Because of the snow, the danger of accidents is increasing on the expressway.
en.notes: 増す means "to increase, to rise" and can be used both intransitively (水かさが増す, 危険が増す) and transitively (速度を増す, 強さを増す). It sounds more literary than the everyday words 増える (intransitive) and 増やす (transitive) and often appears with abstract quantities such as danger, difficulty or interest. Set phrase: いつにも増して ("more than ever").

examples[].german: Today my tutor taught me multiplication.
In second grade of elementary school, children learn the multiplication table.
Please do the multiplication first, and then the addition.
en.notes: 掛け算 is multiplication; the four basic arithmetic operations are 足し算, 引き算, 掛け算 and 割り算. The multiplication table is called 九九 and is memorized in Japan in second grade. "To multiply" is 掛ける: 三に四を掛ける. It is also often written かけ算; the mathematical technical term is 乗法.

examples[].german: Japan has many excellent engineers who are recognized around the world.
This new camera has particularly excellent performance in dark places.
My mother doesn't seem to be feeling well lately.
en.notes: 優れる means "to be outstanding, to be superior" and is almost never used in its dictionary form: predicatively as 優れている (性能が優れている), attributively as 優れた + noun (優れた技術). Comparison is expressed with より, the area of excellence with に (記憶力に優れる). In the negative, 気分が優れない or 体調が優れない means "not to feel well". 上手, by contrast, describes a person's skill at an activity.

examples[].german: We will improve the conventional method.
The new model is 30 percent lighter than before.
The meeting will be held on Monday as usual.
en.notes: 従来 means "up to now, so far" and with の "conventional, previous": 従来の方法, 従来の製品, 従来どおり "as before". It belongs to formal and written style, for example in business reports and product descriptions (従来より軽い "lighter than before"). In conversation one tends to say 今までの or これまでの. Although it is listed as an adverb, it is mostly used like a noun with の or より.

en.meaning: to grasp; to capture; to catch
examples[].german: Depending on the person, a glass filled halfway with water can be seen as either "only half" or "half already".
His explanation captures the essence of the problem well.
A security camera had captured the culprit's figure.
en.notes: 捉える means "to grasp, to capture", above all in the figurative sense: 本質を捉える ("to grasp the core"), 〜を〜と捉える ("to understand something as ..."), 前向きに捉える ("to see positively"). Cameras or radar also "capture" things: カメラが犯人の姿を捉える. The physical catching of animals or criminals is more often written 捕らえる. Related is the passive 捉われる ("to be caught up in something").

examples[].german: You'd better stop doing things that only hurt yourself.
The man was arrested after trying to strangle the other person.
I hear that long ago my grandmother used to wring the necks of the chickens she kept in the garden and cook them.
en.notes: 絞める means "to constrict the neck, to choke": 首を絞める. It is also used for slaughtering poultry (鶏を絞める). The idiom 自分で自分の首を絞める means "to harm oneself, to shoot oneself in the foot". Not to be confused with 締める ("to tighten": ネクタイ・ベルトを締める) and 閉める ("to close": ドアを閉める). The intransitive partner is 絞まる (首が絞まる).

examples[].german: Have you ever seen a werewolf?
We played the Werewolf game at a friend's house and it got lively.
In this movie, a werewolf attacks the village on a full-moon night.
en.notes: 人狼 is the "werewolf", a human who turns into a wolf. In everyday life the word is mostly found today in the party game 人狼ゲーム ("Werewolf", similar to "Mafia"), in which you have to find out who the 人狼 is. For the horror figure in films, 狼男 ("wolf man") is also very common; 人狼 sounds somewhat more literary or is the technical term in fantasy and games.

examples[].german: The illumination of Okayama Castle was really beautiful!
Okayama Castle is also called "Crow Castle" because of its black exterior.
After strolling through Korakuen, I walked to Okayama Castle.
en.notes: 岡山城 is the castle in the city of Okayama. Because of its black outer walls it has the nickname 烏城 ("Crow Castle"), in contrast to the white castle of Himeji. It stands right next to the famous garden 後楽園, so the two are often visited together. In castle names 城 is read as the suffix じょう (大阪城, 名古屋城); on its own it is read しろ.

examples[].german: Please take this medicine every 6 hours.
She gets prettier every time I see her.
For every 100 retweets, we will add one more gift!
en.notes: 〜ごとに comes after nouns and counters and means "every ..., per ...": 3時間ごとに "every three hours", クラスごとに "per class". After verbs it means "each time" and often stresses a progressive change (会うごとに, 回を重ねるごとに); in everyday speech たびに is more common for this. Be careful with おきに: 1日おきに means "every other day", whereas 1日ごとに means "every day". It is usually written in hiragana; the spelling 毎に is rarer (毎 alone as a prefix is read まい, as in 毎日).

examples[].german: It was just a fluke.
I got a perfect score on the test by sheer luck.
Once might be a fluke, but winning three times in a row is real ability.
en.notes: まぐれ is a "lucky hit" or "fluke" - a success that does not rest on skill. Typical are ただのまぐれ, まぐれで当たる/勝つ and the compound まぐれ当たり. It is often used modestly about one's own successes, but can also be said disparagingly about others. Unlike the neutral 偶然 ("coincidence"), まぐれ stresses that one had not really expected it; it is almost always written in hiragana and is rather colloquial.

en.meaning: active (in one's job or duty); still in service
examples[].german: Her father is an active professional wrestler.
My grandmother is 80, but she is still working.
My older brother got into a university in Tokyo straight out of high school.
en.notes: 現役 refers to someone who is "still active in service/profession": 現役の選手 "active player", 現役で働く "to still be working", 現役を引退する "to retire from active service". It is a noun that takes の before other nouns, not a true adjective. A second important meaning comes from the exam system: 現役で合格する means passing the university entrance exam directly after high school - the opposite is 浪人 (someone who repeats a year).

examples[].german: As expected, there are a lot of elderly people at this time of day.
I gave up my seat on the train to an elderly person.
This shop is popular with older customers.
en.notes: 年配 denotes "advanced age" and usually stands with の before people: 年配の人, politely 年配の方 or ご年配の方 "elderly ladies and gentlemen". It is a considerate, neutral expression; 老人 can sound blunt to impolite, and 高齢者 is the official term. There are also 同年配 "about the same age" and 50年配の男性 "a man around 50" (more written).

en.meaning: like; in the same way as
examples[].german: The sky is clear as if yesterday's typhoon had been a lie.
He speaks Japanese like a Japanese person.
Receiving the present, my father was delighted like a child.
en.notes: Noun + のように means "like ..." and describes how something happens: 子供のように喜ぶ "to be delighted like a child". Before a noun it becomes のような (夢のような話 "a story like a dream"). It can also introduce examples ("such as"). Colloquially people say みたいに. In this grammar 様 is usually written in hiragana; the kanji spelling の様に is rarer.

examples[].german: I think a country will prosper if it spends money on education.
This town used to flourish as a port town.
The area around the station is thriving, but a little further away it is quiet.
en.notes: 栄える is intransitive and means "to bloom, to thrive, to flourish" - mostly of countries, cities, industries or cultures: 町が栄える, 港町として栄えた. In the form 栄えている it also describes a lively place with many shops. The related 繁栄する is more formal, にぎわう rather emphasizes lively bustle. The opposite is 衰える ("to decline, to grow weaker").

en.meaning: from now on; in the future
examples[].german: I will keep making an effort from now on, too.
I will be careful so that nothing like this happens again.
We look forward to your continued support.
en.notes: 今後 means "from now on, in the future" and is more formal than これから. It stands alone as an adverb (今後気をつけます) or with の before nouns (今後の予定, 今後の課題). It is very common in apologies and business correspondence, e.g. 今後ともよろしくお願いいたします "we look forward to your continued support". Unlike 将来 "the (more distant) future", 今後 means the time from now onward.

examples[].german: This is a service exclusively for Lifetime members.
It's a limited-time menu, so let's go eat it early.
Participants are limited to university students.
en.notes: 限定 means "restriction to a certain group" and very often comes after nouns: 会員限定 "members only", 期間限定 "for a limited time only", 数量限定 "limited quantity", 限定品 "limited-edition item". As a する-verb it is transitive: 対象を大学生に限定する; in the passive 〜に限定されている. Unlike 制限 ("limit, restriction" as in 速度制限), 限定 means narrowing down to something specific.

examples[].german: I stopped watching Doraemon after the voice actor was replaced.
The homeroom teacher will change from April.
Excuse me, would you mind switching seats with me?
en.notes: 替わる is intransitive and means that something or someone "is exchanged, changes": 担当者が替わる "the person in charge changes", 席を替わる "to swap seats". The transitive counterpart is 替える ("to exchange"). 変わる ("to change, become different") and 代わる ("to take someone's place, substitute") are read the same way; 替わる and 代わる often overlap, e.g. when handing over the phone (電話を代わる).

en.meaning: to put on; to load; to publish
examples[].german: I'll leave this Tofugu doll up on that shelf.
I posted the shop's information on the website.
I carried the luggage on the roof of the car.
en.notes: 載せる is transitive: to "put/place something on something" (棚の上に載せる) or to "load" (荷物を車に載せる). Also very common is "to publish, to print": 記事を新聞に載せる, 写真をサイトに載せる. The intransitive counterpart is 載る ("to be on top of; to be printed"). For people you take along in a vehicle, write 乗せる (乗る/乗せる).

examples[].german: I went for an interview for a job at the Meteorological Agency.
According to the Meteorological Agency, there will be heavy rain tomorrow.
The Meteorological Agency issued a heavy snow warning.
en.notes: 気象庁 is the Japanese weather service (Japan Meteorological Agency), which issues weather forecasts, severe weather warnings and earthquake information. Typical in the news: 気象庁によると "according to the weather service", 気象庁が警報を出す/発表する. 気象 means "weather (phenomena)" in the technical sense, 庁 is a government "agency" as in 警察庁.

examples[].german: It might be better to reconsider this matter once more.
An error has occurred. Please try again after a while.
There was a mistake in the documents, so I submitted them again.
en.notes: 再度 means "again, once more" and is considerably more formal than もう一度. It is found mainly in business language, announcements and error messages: 再度ご確認ください, 再度お試しください. It usually stands as an adverb directly before the verb; as a noun it also takes の (再度の連絡). In casual conversation, もう一度 or また sounds more natural.

examples[].german: There are many young people around me, so I'm getting inspired too.
This shampoo is mild, so it can be used on children too.
My life is the same every day, and I lack stimulation.
en.notes: 刺激 is a "stimulus", both physical (肌への刺激, 刺激が強い "irritating, strong") and mental ("inspiration, spur"): 刺激を受ける "to be inspired", 刺激が足りない "there is a lack of variety". As a transitive する-verb: 食欲を刺激する "to stimulate the appetite". The na-adjective 刺激的 means "exciting, stimulating", often also "provocative".

examples[].german: Koichi intends to found Tohugu University before he dies.
This school was founded in the Meiji period.
Next month there is a party for the company's 50th anniversary.
en.notes: 創立 means "to found, founding" and is used above all for schools, universities, associations and long-established companies: 創立者, 創立記念日, 創立100周年. As a する-verb it is transitive, often in the passive: 〜年に創立された. 設立 is the sober, also legal term (会社を設立する), 創業 emphasizes the start of a business (創業100年の店).

examples[].german: I received words of encouragement from President Koichi.
The coach encouraged the players before the game.
Many messages of encouragement arrived from fans.
en.notes: 激励 is "encouragement, cheering on" and sounds more formal than 励ます or 応援する. Typical are 激励の言葉 "encouraging words", 激励会 "send-off party (before a tournament)" and the transitive する-verb: 選手を激励する. The fixed phrase 叱咤激励 means "to drive on with rebuke and encouragement". Grammatically it is a noun or する-verb, not an adjective.

examples[].german: The first impression apparently wasn't a very good one.
First impressions are very important in an interview.
My first impression of him was that he looked scary, but when I talked to him he was kind.
en.notes: 第一印象 is the "first impression" of a person or thing. Common combinations: 第一印象がいい/悪い, 第一印象で決まる "to depend on the first impression", 〜の第一印象は…だった. 第一 is the ordinal prefix "first" here; on its own 印象 means "impression" (印象に残る "to stay in one's memory").

examples[].german: Why do you discriminate?
You must not discriminate against people because of their nationality.
She was being discriminated against in the workplace because she was a woman.
en.notes: 差別する means "to discriminate against, to treat unequally and unfairly" and is transitive: 人を差別する, 国籍で/〜を理由に差別する. The passive 差別される and the noun 差別 in 人種差別 "racism" or 差別をなくす are very common. It must be clearly distinguished from the neutral 区別する ("to distinguish"): 区別 is factual, while 差別 always implies disadvantage.

en.meaning: for the time being; for now
examples[].german: For now, we will carry on as we are.
The shop will remain closed for the time being.
I will somehow manage my immediate living expenses with a part-time job.
en.notes: 当面 as an adverb means "for the time being, until further notice, for now": 当面は休業します, 当面の間. With の before nouns it means "current, pressing": 当面の課題, 当面の生活費. It is more formal than とりあえず or しばらく and is typical of announcements and news. Its use as a する-verb meaning "to face" is rare; people usually say 直面する instead.

examples[].german: Koichi has a habit of pushing up his glasses with his index finger.
She put her index finger to her mouth and said "Quiet."
I cut my index finger with a kitchen knife while cooking.
en.notes: 人差し指 is the "index finger", literally the finger with which one points at people (人を指す). The other fingers are called 親指, 中指, 薬指 and 小指. Typical: 人差し指で指す "to point with the index finger", 人差し指を口に当てる "to put the finger to one's lips". Pointing at people with a finger is considered impolite in Japan.

examples[].german: Let's review the te-form today.
Every evening I review the kanji I learned that day.
You should go over your notes once more before the test.
en.notes: 復習 is the review of material already learned; as a する-verb it is transitive: 漢字を復習する, or as a noun 復習をする. The counterpart is 予習 "preparation"; together one says 予習・復習. For repeating an action or statement in general, 繰り返す is used instead; 復習 applies only to studying. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 復讐 "revenge".

examples[].german: I prepare before class.
If you prepare in advance, you will understand the lesson much better.
The teacher said, "Please prepare the next lesson before coming."
en.notes: 予習 is preparing for the upcoming class, that is, studying new material in advance; as a する-verb: 次の課を予習する or 予習をする. It forms the pair 予習・復習 with 復習 "review". General preparation for a trip or event is 準備; 予習 applies only to study material. Typical of school and language courses, neutral in tone.

examples[].german: What a bizarre mystery that was.
The mysterious incident that occurred in the town was widely reported on TV.
This novel is a story in which a famous detective solves a mysterious case.
en.notes: 怪事件 is a "puzzling, eerie incident"; the prefix 怪 means "strange, mysterious" (cf. 怪談, 怪獣). The word sounds like a newspaper headline or a detective story: 怪事件が起きる, 怪事件を解決する. In everyday speech people say 不思議な事件 or 謎の事件 instead.

examples[].german: Are there any famous school ghost stories in America?
When summer comes, there are more ghost story programs on TV.
On the camping night, my uncle told us a scary ghost story.
en.notes: 怪談 are Japanese "ghost and horror stories". Traditionally they are told in summer, because the shivers are supposed to cool you down; well known are 学校の怪談 ("school ghost stories") and phrases like 怪談を話す/聞く or 怪談話. Careful when listening: 階段 ("stairs") is pronounced the same, which is often used for wordplay.

examples[].german: When the shop opened, everyone ran toward the sale items, each one trying to get there first.
Forgetting myself, I was painting absorbed in the picture.
When I came to my senses, it was already two in the morning.
en.notes: 我（われ） is an old, literary word for "I" or "oneself". Today it survives mainly in fixed phrases: 我を忘れる ("to forget oneself"), 我に返る ("to come to one's senses"), 我も我もと ("everyone wants to be first") and 我先に. The plural 我々 ("we") is common in speeches and texts. In the rough Kansai dialect, われ can also mean "you" in a derogatory way; 我が in 我が強い ("self-willed"), on the other hand, is read が.

examples[].german: I think you also bear indirect responsibility.
I heard that story indirectly from a friend.
This room has indirect lighting, so it has a calm atmosphere.
en.notes: 間接 ("indirectness") is the counterpart of 直接. On its own it is rarely used; people almost always say 間接的な/間接的に ("indirect, indirectly") or use it as a prefix in compounds such as 間接照明 ("indirect lighting"), 間接税 ("indirect tax") or 間接キス. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 関節 ("joint").

examples[].german: My mother has almost no knowledge about the stock market.
According to the news, the stock market fell sharply today.
The results of the election also affect the stock market.
en.notes: 株式市場 is the "stock market"; 株式 means "shares" (colloquially shortened to 株). The reading is important: in the abstract sense of "market", 市場 is read しじょう, whereas for a real market with stalls it is read いちば. Typical combinations: 株式市場が上がる/下がる, 株式市場に影響を与える, 株式市場が暴落する.

examples[].german: Ugh, this shirt somehow smells of sweat!
It's right after club activities, so I might smell a bit sweaty.
A packed train in summer smells of sweat and is awful.
en.notes: 汗臭い is an i-adjective: "smelling of sweat". The suffix 〜臭い ("smells of") also appears in 焦げ臭い ("smelling burnt") and 酒臭い ("smelling of alcohol"). It sounds direct and can be hurtful when said about a person; about clothes or rooms it is unproblematic. Forms: 汗臭くなる, 汗臭くて.

examples[].german: I began to hear the sound of the river.
A big river was flowing slowly.
We went down the river by boat to the sea.
en.notes: 河 means "river" like 川, but tends to refer to large, wide rivers and feels written or literary. In daily life you almost always write 川; 河 appears mainly in compounds such as 運河 ("canal"), 河口 ("river mouth"), 銀河 ("Milky Way") or 大河 ("great river"). For the Yellow River, 黄河 is read こうが.

examples[].german: You can't say that across the board.
You can't say categorically that games are bad.
Just because the price is high doesn't mean it is necessarily good.
en.notes: 一概に means "across the board, without distinction" and is almost always used with a negation: 一概には言えない "you can't say that so generally", 一概に悪いとは言えない. は is often inserted (一概には). Similar is 必ずしも〜ない; 一概に, however, stresses that one cannot lump all cases together. Neutral to formal and very common in discussions.

examples[].german: I would like to see the Panama Canal.
In Otaru, we took a walk along the canal.
Long ago, many boats carrying cargo passed through this canal.
en.notes: 運河 is an artificially constructed, navigable "canal" - such as パナマ運河 or スエズ運河; in Japan the 小樽運河 is well known. Typical are 運河沿い ("along the canal") and 運河を通る ("to pass through the canal"). A natural river is called 川, a small ditch or irrigation channel more often 水路. A television channel, by contrast, is called チャンネル.

examples[].german: "A tofu and fugu sandwich, please." "Same for me."
Shimonoseki is famous for its fugu dishes.
Fugu is poisonous, so only qualified people can prepare it.
en.notes: 河豚 is the "pufferfish" (fugu), an expensive delicacy eaten mainly in winter as ふぐ刺し (thinly sliced sashimi) or in hot pot. Since parts of the fish are highly poisonous (ふぐの毒), only chefs with a special license may prepare it. The kanji spelling is rare; people almost always write ふぐ or フグ. The city of Shimonoseki is known for pufferfish.

examples[].german: Is this burnable trash or non-burnable trash?
Help! The house next door is on fire!
Ahead of the final match, the players are fired up.
en.notes: 燃える is intransitive: "to burn, to be in flames" (家が燃える). The transitive counterpart is 燃やす ("to burn, to set alight"). In daily life it comes up constantly in garbage sorting: 燃えるゴミ ("burnable trash") and 燃えないゴミ. Figuratively it means "to be fired up": 試合に燃える, やる気に燃える. It differs from 焼ける ("to be roasted, to burn down") and 焦げる ("to scorch") in that real flames are involved.

examples[].german: A cigarette ignited the curtains and caused a fire.
Dry wood catches fire easily.
Charcoal doesn't catch fire easily, so it helps to use newspaper.
en.notes: 燃え付く (also 燃えつく) means "to catch fire, to ignite" and is intransitive: 木が燃え付く, 火がカーテンに燃え付く. The word is rather rare; in everyday speech people usually say 火がつく, 燃え移る ("to spread to something") or, in technical language, 引火する. It describes the moment when a material starts to burn.

examples[].german: I lost everything and ended up all alone.
My grandfather lives alone in the countryside.
He was talking to himself on the train.
en.notes: 独り stresses "being alone" (without company, often also lonely or unmarried), while 一人 mainly means the number "one person". Typical are 独りで暮らす, 独り暮らし (also 一人暮らし), 独り言 ("talking to oneself") and 独りぼっち ("all alone"). In modern Japanese, plain 一人 is often written for "alone" too; 独り feels somewhat more emotional. Grammatically it is a noun or adverb, not an adjective.

examples[].german: Sakura's cat has distinctive eyes, doesn't it.
Natto has a distinctive smell.
The kimono is a culture unique to Japan.
en.notes: 独特 means "distinctive, peculiar, unmistakable" and is used as a な-adjective or with の: 独特な味, 独特の雰囲気. It is not always praise - 独特なにおい can also mean that a smell takes some getting used to. 〜独特の means "typical of": 日本独特の文化. The related 特有 stresses more a feature that belongs only to one group; ユニーク is usually positive.

examples[].german: Superman showed up a few minutes after the monster.
Godzilla is the most famous kaiju in Japan.
My son loves playing with monster toys.
en.notes: 怪獣 are the giant monsters from Japanese films and series (kaiju) such as ゴジラ, often fought by heroes like ウルトラマン. Typical: 怪獣映画, 怪獣が現れる, 怪獣のおもちゃ. More general is 怪物 ("monster, creature"); 化け物 is rather a haunting creature or ghost. Children also use 怪獣 playfully for rough games (怪獣ごっこ).

examples[].german: My child's dream is to become a veterinarian.
My dog wasn't feeling well, so I took it to the vet.
The vet at the animal hospital was very kind.
en.notes: 獣医 is the "veterinarian"; the official job title is 獣医師, the field 獣医学. The practice is called 動物病院, but colloquially people also say 獣医に連れて行く. When addressing the vet directly, you say 獣医さん or simply 先生. The kanji 獣 means "animal, beast" (けもの).

examples[].german: The girl raised by wolves walked on all fours like a beast.
Many animals, including birds and beasts, live in this forest.
Among the beasts, many are active at night.
en.notes: 獣類 is a literary or technical collective term for "beasts, mammals", especially furry four-legged animals (獣, けもの). It appears in series such as 鳥類 ("birds") and 魚類 ("fish"). In modern biological usage people mostly say 哺乳類, in everyday speech simply 動物. Grammatically it is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: That man had eyes like a wild beast.
"Beauty and the Beast" is my favorite movie.
Long ago, this mountain had many wild beasts, and no one went out at night.
en.notes: 野獣 is a "wild animal, beast of prey, brute" and sounds dramatic or literary. It is often applied to people figuratively: 野獣のような目 "eyes like a beast of prey", i.e. brutal or wild. Well known is the title 美女と野獣 ("Beauty and the Beast"). For wild animals in a neutral, factual sense, people say 野生動物. Grammatically it is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: It is not necessarily correct.
Having money does not necessarily make you happy.
Expensive medicine does not necessarily work better.
en.notes: 必ずしも means "not necessarily" and is always combined with a negation, usually 〜とは限らない or 〜わけではない: 必ずしも正しいとは限らない. Without a negation it is wrong - do not confuse it with 必ず "certainly, without fail". It sounds somewhat more formal than いつも〜とは限らない and is very common in discussions and texts.

examples[].german: My younger brother was sulking, saying that nobody had wished him a happy birthday.
Happy birthday! I hope you have a wonderful year.
Yui, happy birthday! Here, this is a present.
en.notes: お誕生日おめでとう is the standard greeting "Happy birthday!". With friends and family people often say the shorter 誕生日おめでとう; toward superiors or in cards it becomes polite with ございます: お誕生日おめでとうございます. As a quotation it takes って/と: お誕生日おめでとうって言う. ハッピーバースデー is also common.

examples[].german: Oh, there's a vending machine over there!
I bought a cold tea from a vending machine.
This vending machine doesn't accept 1,000-yen bills.
en.notes: 自販機 is the common short form of 自動販売機 ("vending machine"). In Japan they stand almost everywhere, mainly for drinks: 自販機で買う, 自販機のジュース. Ticket machines, by contrast, are called 券売機, and cash machines ATM. The short form is usual in conversation; official texts tend to use 自動販売機.

en.meaning: to build; to make; to brew
