examples[].german: I like the heavy machinery used to build structures.
This bridge was built 100 years ago.
This sake brewery makes sake in the traditional way.
en.notes: 造る is a spelling variant of つくる for large, elaborate production: buildings, bridges, ships (橋を造る, 船を造る) as well as brewing alcohol (酒を造る). For everyday things like food or plans, you write 作る, and for artistic creation sometimes 創る. The verb is transitive and often appears in the passive: 〜年前に造られた.

examples[].german: My friend is studying landscape gardening in graduate school.
My father works at a landscaping company, building gardens.
I hear this park was designed by a famous landscape designer.
en.notes: 造園 is "garden and landscape design" as a profession or field. Typical are 造園業 ("landscape gardening business"), 造園会社 and 造園家 ("landscape architect"). Someone who tends gardens and prunes trees is called a 庭師; gardening as a hobby is called ガーデニング. The word belongs more to technical and professional language.

examples[].german: Impressive, isn't it? I converted the garage into a kid's room.
My older brother's hobby is modifying cars.
The prime minister plans to reshuffle the cabinet next month.
en.notes: 改造 means "to remodel, to reconfigure, to modify" and, as a する-verb, is transitive: XをYに改造する ("to convert X into Y"). Well-known compounds: 改造車 ("tuned car"), 内閣改造 ("cabinet reshuffle"); game modding is also called 改造. For renovating an apartment, people say リフォーム in everyday speech, for structural alterations 改築; 改良 means "to improve".

examples[].german: This lake is not a natural lake but a man-made one.
Android No. 18 who appears in the manga is very strong.
This table is made of artificial marble.
en.notes: 人造 means "artificial, made by humans" and usually stands as a prefix or with の before nouns: 人造湖 ("reservoir"), 人造大理石 ("artificial marble"), 人造人間 ("artificial human, android"). In everyday modern usage 人工 is much more common (人工知能, 人工衛星); 人造 seems somewhat old-fashioned or like science fiction. 腎臓 ("kidney") is pronounced the same.

examples[].german: There are many sake brewing companies in this town.
My grandfather's family has been in the sake brewing business for generations.
Clean water and delicious rice are essential for sake brewing.
en.notes: 酒造 means "brewing of sake" (and in general the production of alcoholic drinks) and appears almost only in compounds: 酒造会社, 酒造業, or as part of company names (〇〇酒造). The brewery building itself is called 酒蔵; as a verb one says 酒を造る. For beer, people rather speak of a ビール工場.

examples[].german: Kanae sometimes comes into the office doing a frenzied, crazy-looking dance.
The word "気違い" often appears in old novels, but today it is considered discriminatory.
In his youth, my father was so absorbed in fishing that he was called a fishing fanatic.
en.notes: Caution: 気違い is a derogatory, discriminatory expression (差別語) that is avoided in broadcasting and the press; one should only know it passively. It is often written in kana (きちがい, キチガイ). It means "madman" and, as a suffix, "-fanatic, -maniac" (釣り気違い, 野球気違い); today one neutrally says 〜マニア, 〜好き or 〜狂 instead. The derivation 気違いじみた means "seeming crazy, insane". For mental illnesses, 精神疾患 or 心の病 are appropriate.

examples[].german: Sorry, I mistook you for someone else.
"Are you Tanaka?" "No, you've got the wrong person."
From behind, he looked like my friend, so I mistook him for him and called out.
en.notes: 人違い is "mistaken identity": one takes someone for another person. Typical are 人違いをする and the apology 人違いでした, すみません; someone who is addressed wrongly answers 人違いですよ. To be distinguished from 勘違い ("misunderstanding, wrong assumption"), which is not limited to people.

examples[].german: Today I made a super embarrassing misreading.
Reading "雰囲気" as "ふいんき" is a common misreading.
I misread the map and got lost.
en.notes: 読み違い is a "reading error", e.g. a wrong kanji reading or a misread value. One says 読み違いをする; the variant 読み間違い is more common in everyday use (verbs: 読み間違える or 読み違える). Figuratively it can also mean a "misjudgment" of a situation (状況の読み違い).

en.meaning: to develop; to grow; to prosper
examples[].german: The economy is developing.
A small consultation developed into a plan for the whole town.
This town prospered as a port town in the past.
en.notes: 発展する is intransitive and describes the growth and unfolding of economies, cities, technology or culture: 経済が発展する, 町が発展する. With 〜に／〜へと発展する it means "to expand into something", often also negatively: 小さなけんかが大きな問題に発展する. Well known is 発展途上国 "developing country". By contrast, 進歩 emphasizes qualitative improvement (technology, skill), while 発展 is more about growth and spread.

examples[].german: Will it really succeed?
I wonder whether this method will really solve the problem.
I thought it might rain, and sure enough, it started raining in the afternoon.
en.notes: 果たして is mostly used in questions or doubts and strengthens the uncertainty: 果たして〜だろうか "I wonder whether … really …?". Less often it means "as expected, sure enough": 果たして雨になった. It sounds literary and elevated; in conversation one says 本当に〜かな instead. Do not confuse it with the て-form of 果たす "to fulfill" (約束を果たして).

examples[].german: As expected, hearing about something and seeing it are worlds apart.
Compared to last year, this year's sales are completely different.
If you think he's an easy opponent, you're greatly mistaken.
en.notes: 大違い is a colloquial, emphatic form of 違い: AとBでは大違いだ ("A and B are worlds apart"). Very common is the pattern 〜と思ったら大違いだ ("anyone who thinks that ... is gravely mistaken"), which shows the second meaning "big mistake". In a neutral style people more often say 全然違う or 大きな違いがある.

examples[].german: My younger brother has a dream of becoming an acupuncturist.
When her back hurts, my grandmother goes to an acupuncturist in the neighborhood.
I hear that many acupuncturists in the old days were blind.
en.notes: 針医 is an "acupuncturist", someone who treats with needles (はり). The word is rather old-fashioned; today people usually say はり師 or 鍼灸師 (acupuncture and moxibustion). For the acupuncture needle, the kanji 鍼 is often used instead of 針. Colloquially people simply say はりに行く ("to go for acupuncture").

examples[].german: I couldn't sleep, so I spent the night watching the second hand of the clock.
The second hand has stopped; maybe the battery has run out.
During the exam, the sound of the second hand seemed very loud.
en.notes: 秒針 is the "second hand" of a clock. The other hands are called 長針 ("minute hand", also 分針) and 短針 ("hour hand"); together they are 時計の針. Typical: 秒針が動く/止まる, 秒針の音 ("the ticking").

examples[].german: A worker found an old lead pipe inside the wall.
Lead pipes are bad for the body, so they are rarely used now.
We replaced the old lead water pipes with new pipes.
en.notes: 鉛管 is a "lead pipe". 鉛 is read えん in Sino-Japanese compounds (鉛筆, 鉛管, 鉛毒) but なまり ("lead") on its own. Lead pipes were formerly used for water supply and are now being replaced because of the health risk; the general term for water supply pipes is 水道管. The word is technical.

examples[].german: Pencils contain no lead, so there is no lead poisoning.
Edo-period face powder contained lead, and some people suffered from lead poisoning.
There are concerns about lead poisoning from old water pipes.
en.notes: 鉛毒 refers to the "poison in lead" or "lead poisoning". The word is literary and somewhat old-fashioned; for the illness, people mostly say 鉛中毒 today. 鉛 is read Sino-Japanese えん here. Historically well known are lead poisonings caused by lead-containing white makeup (おしろい) in the Edo period. Grammatically it is a noun, not an adjective.

en.meaning: to harm; to offend; to be bothersome
examples[].german: Sorry. If I offended you, I apologize.
If you overdo it, it will harm your health.
His arrogant way of speaking somehow gets on my nerves.
en.notes: 障る is intransitive and takes に: something "harms" or "disturbs" a person or thing. It appears almost always in fixed phrases: 気に障る ("to offend, to annoy, to rub someone the wrong way"), 体に障る ("to harm one's health") and 癪に障る ("to irritate"). Not to be confused with the identically read 触る ("to touch").

examples[].german: What kind of social security does Japan have?
The constitution guarantees the freedom of the people.
This company reliably secures its employees' livelihoods.
en.notes: 保障 means "to guarantee, to safeguard" - to protect a condition, rights or safety: 社会保障 ("social security"), 安全保障 ("security policy"), 憲法で保障された権利, 生活を保障する. Three homophones are often confused: 保証 ("guarantee, warranty, surety", as in 保証書, 保証人), 保障 ("safeguarding a condition") and 補償 ("compensation"). As a する-verb it is transitive.

examples[].german: I plan to spend the New Year holidays relaxing by myself.
I often spend weekends with my family.
The cold days continue; how are you getting along?
en.notes: 過ごす is transitive and means "to spend (time)": 休みを過ごす, 家族と過ごす, 楽しく過ごす. It is very common in polite phrases such as いかがお過ごしですか ("How have you been?", in letters) or 良いお年をお過ごしください. The intransitive counterpart is 過ぎる ("to pass": 時間が過ぎる). As a verb suffix, 〜過ごす means "to overlook, to miss" (見過ごす, 寝過ごす).

examples[].german: I was surprised that the smartphone was standing upright.
Draw a line perpendicular to this line.
The cliff is almost vertical, so climbing it is impossible.
en.notes: 垂直 means "perpendicular, vertical" and is used as a な-adjective or with の: 垂直に立つ, 垂直な壁, 垂直の線. In geometry, 〜に垂直 means "perpendicular to ...". The opposite is 水平 "horizontal". In everyday speech, for the direction "upright, lengthwise", people more often say 縦; 垂直 sounds more precise and technical.

en.meaning: to cool off; to enjoy the cool air
examples[].german: Shall we go somewhere to cool off a bit?
It's hot, so let's cool off a little in the shade of a tree.
In the evening, my grandfather sits on the veranda and enjoys the cool air.
en.notes: 涼む means "to cool off (in a cool place), to enjoy the cool air". The place takes で: 木陰で涼む, 川辺で涼む, 縁側で涼む. It is intransitive and always describes people, not things: food or tea cools down with 冷める, and one cools it actively with 冷ます. Related is the adjective 涼しい "pleasantly cool".

en.meaning: once again; anew; at another time
examples[].german: I would like to express my thanks once again.
I don't have time today, so I will visit again another time.
Falling ill made me realize anew how important health is.
en.notes: 改めて means "once more, again (on another occasion)" and also "expressly, specially": 改めて連絡します "I will contact you again", 改めてお礼を申し上げます. Also common is 改めて〜を感じる/実感する "to become aware of something anew". It comes from 改める "to renew, to change" and sounds more polite and formal than もう一度 or また.

examples[].german: That guy is as obedient as a dog.
As a child, I had a personality that was obedient to my parents.
Merely being obedient to your boss won't let you do good work.
en.notes: 従順 is a な-adjective meaning "obedient, docile"; whom one obeys is marked with に: 親に従順な子ども. For animals the word is positive, for people it can sound critical, "submissive". 素直, by contrast, means "honest, open to advice" and is almost always praise; 言いなり ("at someone's beck and call") is clearly negative. The word is slightly literary and related to the verb 従う.

examples[].german: I wonder how anyone can say such terrible things.
Why aren't you going to school today?
en.notes: 何故 is the interrogative adverb "why", read なぜ. It is often written in hiragana as なぜ. It asks for the reason of an action or state. なぜ…んだろう can express that you are wondering to yourself about a reason. In a direct question it is followed by, for example, ですか or the polite verb form with か.

examples[].german: The monster had almost no friends.
There is a legend that a monster lives in this lake.
Although that player is a high schooler, he's a monster who throws 160 km/h pitches.
en.notes: 怪物 is a "monster, creature" from legends, fairy tales and films: 怪物が現れる, 怪物の伝説. Figuratively it refers to people with almost uncanny strength or talent, especially in sports: 怪物投手 "phenomenal pitcher". モンスター is the loanword used in games and in phrases like モンスターペアレント; 化け物 sounds more ghostly and colloquial, and 妖怪 are Japanese folk spirits.

examples[].german: This is pretty much like a dictatorial regime, isn't it?
In that country, military dictatorship continued for a long time.
My department head is like a dictator who decides everything by himself.
en.notes: 独裁 is "sole rule, dictatorship". It mostly appears in compounds: 独裁者 "dictator", 独裁政権 "dictatorial regime", 独裁政治, 軍の独裁 "military dictatorship". Figuratively it is used to criticize bosses or leaders who decide everything alone: 社長の独裁. The opposite concept is 民主主義 "democracy"; the verb 独裁する is rare.

examples[].german: You dropped your fountain pen.
I'll write the letter with this fountain pen.
en.notes: 万年筆 is a fountain pen. The reading on this card is まんねんひつ. With を you name it as the object of an action, with で as the writing tool. 落とされましたよ is a respectful form here for "you dropped it". The first n closes まん; then ねん begins with another n.

examples[].german: Could you make the width here a little narrower?
Narrowing the search range makes it easier to find the information you want.
If you cling to a single idea, you end up narrowing your own outlook.
en.notes: 狭める means "to make narrower; to narrow down" and is transitive: 幅を狭める, 間隔を狭める, 範囲を狭める "to narrow the range", 視野を狭める "to narrow one's view". The intransitive partner is 狭まる "to become narrower" (道幅が狭まる). Opposites are 広げる / 広がる. For reducing a number, one does not use 狭める but 減らす.

examples[].german: I broke my right arm, so I can't work for a while.
My right arm started to hurt from playing too much tennis.
Mr. Tanaka has supported the company as the president's right-hand man.
en.notes: 右腕 is literally the "right arm" (counterpart 左腕). Very common is the figurative meaning "right-hand man, closest confidant": 社長の右腕として働く. In baseball, 右腕 in 右腕投手 "right-handed pitcher" is read うわん. For arms in general 腕 suffices; 右腕 stresses the side.

en.meaning: to scrape together (money, time); to manage to raise
examples[].german: I'm working hard at my part-time job to raise the money to go to university.
Even when I'm busy, I make time for thirty minutes of exercise every day.
The city doesn't have enough budget and is struggling to raise the repair costs for the bridge.
en.notes: 捻出する means to laboriously "raise, set aside" money or time although there is hardly anything left: 費用を捻出する, 時間を捻出する, 資金の捻出に苦労する. More rarely it also means "to work out" a plan or an idea. The word sounds rather written; in conversation people often say 時間を作る or お金を工面する. 稼ぐ, by contrast, is simply "to earn".

examples[].german: Let's wait and see for a while.
My younger brother has been acting strange lately, so I am worried.
He didn't seem to want to go home yet.
en.notes: 様子 describes how something or someone appears from the outside: "state, situation, appearance, behavior, sign". Fixed expressions are 様子を見る "to wait and see", 様子がおかしい "to behave strangely" and 〜様子だ "it seems that ..." (more written). 状態 is the objective, often technical condition, and 状況 the overall situation; 様子 emphasizes the visible impression.

examples[].german: The doorbell rang at two in the middle of the night.
I woke up many times during the night.
Please stop listening to loud music in the middle of the night.
en.notes: 夜中 refers to the time in the middle of the night, roughly from midnight until before dawn. It is usually used with に (夜中に目が覚める "to wake up at night") or attributively with の (夜中の二時). The general 夜 is "evening/night" without emphasis on the time of day; 真夜中 intensifies it to "dead of night", and 深夜 is the more factual, more written equivalent (深夜番組, 深夜料金).

examples[].german: Even greater effort is needed.
When night fell, the wind grew even stronger.
We will continue to strive even harder in the future.
en.notes: 一層 means "even more, all the more" and intensifies a comparison: 一層寒くなる, より一層努力する. With の it stands before nouns: 一層の努力 "even greater effort". It is more formal than もっと or さらに and is common in speeches and letters (今後より一層頑張ります). Do not confuse it with いっそ "might as well", which is usually written in kana; the meaning "one layer" is rare.

examples[].german: We'll take back the leftover stock, so could you sell it at your shop?
We decided to sell the leftover goods at half price before closing the store.
The clearance sale on remaining stock runs until this weekend.
en.notes: 残品 is the leftover, unsold merchandise of a shop - a word from trade and business language. Typical are 残品処分 "clearance of remaining stock", 残品セール and 残品を引き取る "to take back leftover goods". In everyday speech people more often say 売れ残り "unsold goods"; 在庫, by contrast, is the normal stock in storage without any negative overtone.

examples[].german: The one who has taken the glory of victory this time is the Red Team!
You must not keep clinging to past glory forever.
This school has a glorious history of a hundred years.
en.notes: 栄光 is "glory, splendor" in a solemn tone - typical of sports reports, speeches and school songs. Common combinations: 栄光をつかむ / 手にする, 栄光に輝く, 過去の栄光 "past glory", 栄光ある歴史. 名誉 is "honor", 名声 is "reputation, fame"; in daily life people speak more of 有名 or 人気 than of 栄光.

examples[].german: I'm worried whether they will really keep to the agreement.
My spouse and I made an arrangement about dividing the housework.
The two countries concluded an agreement on fisheries.
en.notes: 取り決め is an "agreement, arrangement" between two or more parties, often about rules or divisions: 取り決めをする / 結ぶ / 守る / 破る. The corresponding verb is 取り決める. 約束 is rather a personal promise, 契約 a legally binding contract, 決まり an existing rule. In official texts it is also written 取決め.

examples[].german: It helps to speed up the breakdown of alcohol.
When I was a child, I took a clock apart and couldn't put it back together.
Plastic doesn't easily break down in nature.
en.notes: 分解 means "to take apart, to disassemble" (machines, devices) and, in chemistry and biology, "to break down, to decompose". As a する-verb it is transitive (時計を分解する) and intransitive or passive (微生物によって分解される, アルコールが分解される). 解体 is used for buildings or large structures. Figuratively, 空中分解 "to break apart in mid-air" is also said of groups that fall apart.

examples[].german: These two lines are parallel.
The railroad runs parallel to the river.
The discussion lasted three hours, but remained at an impasse to the end.
en.notes: 平行 means "parallel" for lines and directions: 二つの線は平行だ, 〜と平行に走る. The phrase 平行線をたどる / 平行線のままだ means that a discussion reaches no agreement. Beware of the homophone 並行 "to proceed simultaneously" (二つの仕事を並行して進める) - in everyday writing, 並行 is usually used for simultaneity.

examples[].german: Being part of a group is not my style.
Whales are not fish; they belong to the mammals.
This island used to belong to another country.
en.notes: 属する means "to belong to" and takes に: グループに属する, 哺乳類に属する. It sounds matter-of-fact to written in register and is often used for categories and assignments. For membership in a company, club or team, 所属する is more usual, and in conversation simply 〜に入っている. It is conjugated as a special form of する: 属さない, 属して.

examples[].german: I hear this cafe is popular with older people.
I gave up my seat on the train to an elderly person.
He is a little older than me, but he is very easy to talk to.
en.notes: 年輩 (today more often written 年配) means "of advanced age" and is almost always used attributively with の: 年輩の方, 年輩の人 "older people". It is more polite and softer than 老人 or 年寄り and is well suited to speaking respectfully about seniors, often as ご年輩の方. With より it expresses "older than" (私より年輩), and 同年輩 means "of the same age".

examples[].german: My cousin's wedding is the month after next.
The move is planned for the month after next.
This ticket can be used until the month after next.
en.notes: 再来月 is "the month after next"; the prefix 再来 means "after the next" and also appears in 再来週 and 再来年. Like 来月, it can stand without a particle as a time expression (再来月引っ越します); a に after it is also heard in conversation. With の it connects to nouns (再来月の予定), and with まで it gives a deadline. In the opposite direction there are 先月 and 先々月 "the month before last".

examples[].german: The year after next, the economy will probably have improved, too.
The year after next I want to study abroad in Japan.
en.notes: 再来年 is the year after next year. 再来年には can emphasize this point in time as the limit of an expected development; でしょう marks a supposition. 再来年…したいです states a personal wish for that year. さ来年 is a mixed spelling of the same reading, for example in simplified texts; the full kanji spelling is 再来年. さらいねん contains no long vowels.

examples[].german: I want to be financially independent.
After I graduate from university, I intend to become independent of my parents.
Helping children become independent is also the role of parents.
en.notes: 自立 means "independence" in the sense of "standing on one's own feet", financially or in daily life: 経済的に自立する, 親から自立する. As a する-verb it is intransitive; what one breaks away from takes から. 独立, by contrast, means the independence of states or the step into professional self-employment (独立して店を開く). Related: 自立心 "drive for independence"; the opposite is 依存.

en.meaning: limited-edition sale; sale in limited quantity
examples[].german: I finally got my hands on the ice cream sold only in Kansai.
This cake is sold in a limited quantity of fifty a day.
It is sold only in winter, so let's buy it while we can.
en.notes: 限定販売 is a "sale in limited quantity, time or region" - not a special offer. You find it on advertising signs: 数量限定販売, 期間限定販売, 地域限定販売, 〜限定販売の商品; often only 限定 is said (期間限定, 関西限定). A cheap clearance sale, by contrast, is called 特売 or セール.

examples[].german: I'm a coward, so even though I want to talk back, I can't.
You can't even go apologize on your own - what a coward.
At first, everyone called the movie's protagonist a coward.
en.notes: 腰抜け comes from 腰が抜ける "to go weak at the knees from fright, to be unable to stand up" and is a derogatory insult for a "coward, wimp". It is colloquial and insulting if said to others. 臆病 describes the trait "timid" more neutrally, 弱虫 is the childish "scaredy-cat".

en.meaning: to fall out; to be missing; to leave; to pass through
examples[].german: A necessary particle is missing in this sentence.
Lately my hair has been falling out a lot, and it's a problem.
When we came out of the tunnel, the sea spread out before our eyes.
en.notes: 抜ける is intransitive; the transitive partner is 抜く. Basic meaning: something comes loose or is missing - 髪の毛が抜ける, 歯が抜ける, 名前が抜けている "is missing (from the list)". Further: to leave a group (会議を途中で抜ける, チームを抜ける) and to pass through something, with the place passed through marked by を (トンネルを抜ける). Also: 力が抜ける "to go limp", 疲れが抜けない "the fatigue won't go away".

examples[].german: The soldiers captured the enemy alive.
The police finally caught the culprit.
The cat caught a mouse in the garden.
en.notes: 捕らえる is transitive (〜を捕らえる) and means "to catch, to arrest, to take prisoner": 犯人を捕らえる, 獲物を捕らえる. It sounds more literary than the everyday 捕まえる; the corresponding intransitive everyday verb is 捕まる "to be caught". In the figurative meanings "to grasp, comprehend" (要点をとらえる) and "to captivate" (心をとらえる), people mostly write 捉える or kana.

en.meaning: to hang; to take (time); to cost
examples[].german: I want to hang the clock here, but I wonder if it will hang properly.
A picture is hanging on the wall.
It takes twenty minutes on foot from home to school.
Repairing this bicycle cost three thousand yen.
en.notes: 掛かる is also often written かかる. Besides "to hang", it means that something takes time or money: 時間がかかる, お金がかかる. A duration or an amount can stand directly before かかる. It is an intransitive godan verb: 掛かります, 掛かって. When hanging, the object takes が; 掛ける, by contrast, describes actively hanging something. 掛かっている describes the hanging state.

examples[].german: Is amnesia an incurable disease?
Lately I can't recall people's names right away. Maybe I have amnesia.
After the accident, he suffered temporary amnesia.
en.notes: 健忘症 is the medical term for "amnesia, memory disorder". Colloquially it is often used jokingly for forgetfulness: 最近健忘症気味だ. For memory loss after an accident (as in films), people mostly say 記憶喪失, for everyday forgetfulness 物忘れ; dementia is 認知症.

examples[].german: But your team is efficient, though not effective, isn't it.
Reading aloud is effective for memorizing words.
I want to use my limited budget effectively.
en.notes: 効果的 is a な-adjective: "effective, producing results" - 効果的な方法, 効果的に使う, 〜には〜が効果的だ. The point is that the desired result is achieved. 効率的, by contrast, means "efficient" (much result for little effort). For medicines people rather say 効く or 効果がある, for valid documents 有効.

examples[].german: Please tell me Mr. Hayashi's working hours.
Please refrain from private phone calls during working hours.
At this company, foreigners work under the same conditions as Japanese people.
en.notes: 就業 is a formal word for "work, employment" or "to take up work". It appears mainly in compounds from the working world and administration: 就業時間 "(contractual) working hours", 就業規則 "work rules", 就業中 "during work", 就業率 "employment rate". 就職, by contrast, is "to take up a job", especially after studies. As a verb, 就業する is official; in conversation one says 働く.

examples[].german: I hear Koichi is having a sushi roll party this Friday.
On Setsubun, our family ate sushi rolls.
When making sushi rolls, spread the rice thinly over the nori.
en.notes: 巻きずし (also 巻き寿司) is sushi in which rice and filling are rolled in nori or a thin omelet; すし becomes voiced to ずし in the compound. A distinction is made between thin 細巻き (e.g. かっぱ巻き with cucumber, 鉄火巻き with tuna) and thick 太巻き; on 節分 people eat the uncut 恵方巻き. Counterparts are 握りずし (nigiri) and 手巻きずし, which one rolls into a cone oneself.

examples[].german: No matter how many spring rolls I make, they keep getting stolen.
I'm going to fry spring rolls tonight, so could you help me?
I ordered fresh spring rolls at a Vietnamese restaurant.
en.notes: 春巻き is the "spring roll" of Chinese cuisine; in Japan it is usually fried and filled with glass noodles (春雨), pork and vegetables. It is also written 春巻. The thin dough sheets are called 春巻きの皮. 生春巻き is the Vietnamese, non-fried "summer roll". It is counted with 本.

examples[].german: Smartphone addiction is a problem.
Japan depends on imports for much of its energy.
He depends too much on his parents.
en.notes: 依存 means "dependence" and, as a する-verb, "to depend on": 〜に依存する, 輸入に依存する. As part of a word it denotes addictions: スマホ依存, ゲーム依存, アルコール依存症. Today the reading いぞん is standard; いそん is regarded as traditional. The opposite is 自立; for an everyday "to rely on" one rather says 頼る.

en.meaning: Go for it!; Hang in there!; Good luck!
examples[].german: Go, Japan! Don't lose, Japan!
Just a little more, hang in there!
The day before the exam, my mother sent me an email saying "Do your best".
en.notes: 頑張れ is the imperative of 頑張る and a cheer: "Go for it!, Hang in there!, Give it your all!". It is shouted to athletes, friends or younger people, often written in kana as がんばれ. Toward superiors one says 頑張ってください, among friends the softer 頑張って. For people who are already exhausted or down, 頑張れ can be felt as pressure.

examples[].german: You seem to have no worries at all, lucky you.
If something is troubling you, talk to me anytime.
My biggest problem is that I can't get up in the morning.
en.notes: 悩み is the noun form of 悩む and refers to a "worry, problem" that preoccupies one inwardly: 悩みがある, 悩みを抱える, 悩みを相談する, 悩みの種 "cause for worry". 心配 is more concern about something in the future or about someone, and 問題 is a factual problem. 悩み sounds more personal and emotional.

examples[].german: I gave in to the sweet temptation and ate the cake.
There are many temptations in the city, so be careful.
He tried to seduce her with sweet words.
en.notes: 誘惑 is "temptation, allurement" and, as a transitive する-verb, "to seduce" (人を誘惑する). Fixed phrases are 誘惑に負ける "to succumb to temptation", 誘惑に勝つ "to resist it" and 誘惑が多い. Unlike the neutral 誘う "to invite, to ask", 誘惑 always carries the undertone of luring someone into something unreasonable or immoral.

examples[].german: Mr. Shuto is good at discerning people's potential.
Parents can see through a child's lies right away.
She had seen through the other person's true feelings.
en.notes: 見抜く means "to see through, to recognize what is hidden": 嘘を見抜く, 本性を見抜く, 才能を見抜く, 相手の気持ちを見抜く. It is transitive and has no intransitive partner. 見破る stresses exposing a deception or disguise (変装を見破る), while 気づく is mere "noticing". 見抜く presupposes insight into people or sharp-mindedness.

examples[].german: I'm a fool, so I didn't notice. Thanks for telling me.
Going shopping after forgetting your wallet at home is a silly thing to do.
A photo was taken of my goofy face just after waking up.
en.notes: 間抜け comes from music and theater: someone who misses the right 間 ("timing") is clumsy. As a な-adjective it means "foolish, silly" (間抜けな顔, 間抜けな失敗), as a noun "fool" (この間抜け!). It is colloquial and insulting as a form of address. ばか is more general, あほ is typical of Kansai; it is also often written まぬけ or マヌケ.

en.meaning: to extract; to pull out; to pick out
examples[].german: Is there an Excel function that extracts only the month part of a date?
Pick out the important words from the text and write them in your notebook.
Please pull one card out of the box.
en.notes: 抜き出す means "to pull out of a set, to pick out, to extract": データを抜き出す, 必要な部分だけを抜き出す, 本文から言葉を抜き出す. It is transitive; the source takes から. 取り出す is the general "to take out" (from a pocket or refrigerator), 選ぶ is plain "to choose", 抽出する is the technical, formal variant "to extract".

examples[].german: My mother apologized for forgetting to bring my change of clothes.
I'm taking three days' worth of changes of clothes on the trip.
I'm changing right now, so wait a moment!
en.notes: 着替え is the noun form of 着替える and means both "changing clothes" and "a change of clothes": 着替えを持っていく, 着替えを用意する, 着替え中 "in the middle of changing". The verb is 服を着替える or simply 着替える (ichidan). For clothing in general, people say 服, for underwear 下着.

examples[].german: I intend to master the ultimate ramen before I die.
Being able to eat only meat or only fish for the rest of your life - that's an ultimate choice.
The ultimate goal of this research is to eliminate disease.
en.notes: 究極 means "ultimate, extreme, final" and almost always stands with の before a noun: 究極の選択 "a real dilemma", 究極の目的 "final goal", 究極の味. As an adverb, 究極的に "ultimately" is used; 究極な is uncommon. 最高 means "the best", 最終 "the last in a sequence".

en.meaning: no thank you; that's fine; that will do
examples[].german: "Would you like fries with that?" "No, thank you."
"Can I pay by card?" "Yes, card is fine."
Replying tomorrow is fine.
en.notes: 結構です works in two directions: as a polite refusal "No thank you, not necessary" (いいえ、結構です) and as approval "that's fine, that will do" (それで結構です, 明日で結構です). Without いいえ or context it can be ambiguous. As a refusal it sounds rather cool; 大丈夫です or いえ、けっこうです with thanks is friendlier. Do not confuse it with the adverb 結構 "quite".

en.meaning: please don't go to any trouble
examples[].german: I'll be leaving soon, so please don't trouble yourself.
"Would you like some coffee?" "Please, don't go to any trouble."
Please don't worry about me; go ahead and start eating.
en.notes: お構いなく is a polite phrase used by a guest when the host wants to offer tea or food: どうぞお構いなく "please don't go to any trouble". It comes from 構う "to care for someone, to bother about" plus negation. With 〜のことは you can say that you yourself need not be attended to: 私のことはお構いなく. At parting, the host modestly says 何のお構いもしませんで.

examples[].german: His speech won the sympathy of many people.
I really relate to the lyrics of this song.
I couldn't relate to the protagonist's feelings.
en.notes: 共感 means "empathy, agreement" in the sense of "feeling the same, being able to identify with something": 〜に共感する, 共感を得る/呼ぶ "to resonate". One feels with someone because one shares feelings or views. 同情, by contrast, is "pity" for someone in a worse situation. Very common for films, books, songs and in social media (共感できる "relatable").

examples[].german: What would you do if a large-scale earthquake hit the town where you live?
Large-scale construction work is being carried out in front of the station.
A large-scale power outage occurred in the city last night.
en.notes: 大規模 is a な-adjective: "large-scale, on a large scale" - 大規模な工事, 大規模な地震, 大規模に行う. In compounds the な drops: 大規模災害, 大規模停電. Opposites are 小規模 and 中規模. The word is typical of news and official texts; 大型, by contrast, describes the build or type (大型台風, 大型店).

examples[].german: Our company's project team has been made smaller in scale so that it can be nimble.
It's a small company, so I know the face and name of every employee.
This year's summer festival is planned to be held on a small scale.
en.notes: 小規模 ("small scale") is a な-adjective and noun: 小規模な会社, 小規模の店, adverbially 小規模に行う "to carry out on a small scale". The opposite is 大規模; 規模 alone means "scale, magnitude". The word is typical of news, business and administration; in casual conversation one often simply says 小さい. 小規模化 means "downsizing".

examples[].german: Then, Ms. Mori, please read the first section.
The first section of this text states the author's thoughts.
Two minutes after launch, the rocket's first stage was separated.
en.notes: 第一段 is made up of 第一 "first" and 段 "section, stage" and refers to the first section of a text or the first stage of, for example, a rocket. For paragraphs, 第一段落 is more common today; 第一段 is heard mostly in the classroom. A phase in a process is called 第一段階. Analogous: 第二段, 第三段.

examples[].german: What is this "mammography density"?
The salt concentration of seawater is about 3.5 percent.
If the carbon dioxide concentration in the room gets high, let's open a window.
en.notes: 濃度 is the "concentration, density" of a substance in a solution or in the air: 塩分濃度, アルコール濃度, 二酸化炭素の濃度. People say 濃度が高い / 低い; the adjectives 濃い and 薄い go with it. Watch out: "concentration" in the sense of attention is 集中. Physical density (mass per volume) and population density are called 密度.

examples[].german: Kishida's essay recounts her days with her mother in a wheelchair and her younger brother with Down syndrome.
Every spring, my eyes get itchy from hay fever.
Please watch out for heatstroke in summer.
en.notes: 〜症 is a suffix for diseases, syndromes and disorders and occurs only in fixed compounds: 花粉症 "hay fever", 熱中症 "heatstroke", 不眠症 "insomnia", 認知症 "dementia", 後遺症 "after-effects". The general word for illness is 病気, for symptom 症状. Many other disease names, by contrast, end in 〜病 (糖尿病 "diabetes"), without the two being freely interchangeable.

examples[].german: Yesterday I got only three hours of sleep.
Work has been busy lately, and my lack of sleep continues.
To get over a cold quickly, it is important to get enough sleep.
en.notes: 睡眠 is a noun for "sleep" and sounds factual to medical: 睡眠時間, 睡眠不足 "lack of sleep", 睡眠薬, 十分な睡眠をとる (with とる, not する). In everyday speech, sleeping is expressed with the verbs 寝る or 眠る; the noun 眠り is more general and also literary (深い眠り).

examples[].german: That designer presented fashion at the cutting edge of the times.
The tip of the needle is sharp, so please be careful.
State-of-the-art technology is used in this factory.
en.notes: 先端 is the "tip, outermost end" of an elongated object (針の先端, ペンの先端, 岬の先端) and, figuratively, the "leading edge, forefront" of a development: 時代の先端を行く, 最先端の技術 "cutting-edge technology" (very common). In everyday speech, for a fingertip or pen tip, people often simply say 先; the summit of a mountain is 頂上.

examples[].german: Quitting the company just because something unpleasant happened - you're being extreme, Mr. Takei!
Extreme dieting is not good for your body.
In winter, this town becomes extremely empty of people.
en.notes: 極端 is a な-adjective and noun for "extreme, exaggerated, radical": 極端な例, 極端な意見, adverbially 極端に寒い "extremely cold". It often sounds critical - one reproaches someone who exaggerates (極端だね). Unlike the neutral 非常に, 極端 judges the degree as unreasonable; 過激 rather means "radical, militant" in the political sense.

examples[].german: I wonder why that country suddenly concluded a peace and friendship treaty.
The two companies plan to conclude a business partnership agreement next month.
A trade agreement was concluded between the two countries.
en.notes: 締結する means "to formally conclude (a treaty, agreement)": 条約を締結する, 協定を締結する, 契約を締結する; often in the passive 締結される. The word belongs to the news, politics and law. In normal conversation people say 契約を結ぶ or 約束をする. Technically, 締結 can also refer to joining parts with screws.

examples[].german: I deeply sympathize with the victims' families.
Hearing his story, everyone felt sorry for him.
I don't need your pity. I want help.
en.notes: 同情 means "pity, compassion" for someone who is suffering or unlucky: 〜に同情する, 同情を集める. Unlike 共感 ("feeling with someone because one feels the same"), 同情 carries a sense of a gap; 同情なんかいらない "I don't need pity" shows that it can also come across as condescending. For condolences on a death one says お悔やみ.

en.meaning: to tighten; to turn off (a valve)
examples[].german: Did you properly turn off the gas valve?
Please tighten this screw.
en.notes: 締める is a transitive ichidan verb: 締めます, 締めて. It means tightening or securely closing, for example a tap or a screw. With を you name the thing affected. For simply closing a door, 閉める usually fits. 締めた？ casually asks about the completed action.

examples[].german: My stomach pain got so bad that I was hospitalized and spent a month in the hospital.
Because of stress-induced stomach pain, I can't sleep well at night.
This medicine works well for stomach pain and heartburn.
en.notes: 胃痛 is the factual, rather written word for "stomachache", for example at the doctor's or on package inserts: 胃痛がする, 胃痛に悩む, ストレスによる胃痛. In conversation people mostly say 胃が痛い, and for the belly in general お腹が痛い. Similarly formed are 頭痛 "headache" and 腹痛 "abdominal pain".

examples[].german: Just thinking about seppuku is painful.
In the Edo period, samurai sometimes committed seppuku to take responsibility.
Losing the president's important documents is a seppuku-worthy offense.
en.notes: 切腹 is the ritual suicide of samurai by cutting open the abdomen; the native Japanese paraphrase is 腹を切る. Abroad, "harakiri" is better known, while in Japan people say 切腹. Historically: 切腹を命じられる "to be sentenced to seppuku". Today it appears jokingly when a mistake seems unforgivable: 切腹ものだ.

examples[].german: You should call before you visit their house.
I visited a friend who lives in Kyoto.
Yesterday my former teacher came to see me at the company.
en.notes: 訪ねる means "to visit a person or place"; the destination takes を: 友達を訪ねる, 実家を訪ねる. When someone comes to visit one, one says 訪ねてくる and marks the place with に. In conversation, 遊びに行く or 会いに行く are more casual, and 訪問する is more formal. Note: the identically read 尋ねる means "to ask"; only the kanji distinguish the two.

examples[].german: During my last visit, did I do something that offended you?
The prime minister plans to visit the United States next week.
Tomorrow the teacher is coming for a home visit.
en.notes: 訪問 is a formal "visit" to a person, company or country: 訪問する (transitive: 会社を訪問する, アメリカを訪問する), 家庭訪問 "teacher's home visit", 公式訪問, 訪問者. Visits to websites are also called 訪問. In private settings people rather say 遊びに行く or 訪ねる; a visit to a sick person is 見舞い.

examples[].german: Our company chartered a whole plane and went to Bermuda.
Today is a private booking, so regular customers cannot use the facility.
I went early on a weekday morning, and I almost had the hot spring to myself.
en.notes: 貸し切り (from 貸す "to lend" and 切る "completely") means that a place or vehicle is reserved exclusively for one group: 貸し切りバス, 〜を貸し切りにする, the sign 本日貸し切り "private party today". Colloquially, 貸し切り状態 means that one has a place practically to oneself. The verb is 貸し切る; 予約 is an ordinary reservation.

en.meaning: to approach; to be imminent; to press
examples[].german: I pressed him to pay the money back, but he got away.
The deadline is approaching, so I can't sleep tonight.
A large typhoon is approaching Kyushu.
en.notes: 迫る has two main meanings. Intransitive: "to draw near, to be imminent" - 締め切りが迫る, 台風が迫る, 試験が目前に迫る; the destination takes に. Transitive: "to press, to force" someone to do something - 人に返事を迫る, 〜よう迫る, in the passive 決断を迫られる. Related is 迫力 "power, impact".

en.meaning: pressure; to press on; to strain
examples[].german: For some reason, since the weekend I've had a feeling of pressure on my chest.
Rising prices are straining household budgets.
Press firmly on the wound until the bleeding stops.
en.notes: 圧迫 means "to exert pressure, to compress", physically (胸を圧迫する, 傷口を圧迫して止血する) and figuratively "to burden, to constrict": 家計を圧迫する "to strain the household budget". The passive 圧迫される is common, as is the noun 圧迫感 "feeling of oppression" (e.g. in cramped rooms). 圧力 is pressure as a force or as leverage, プレッシャー is psychological pressure to perform.

examples[].german: His situation must be quite desperate.
I heard an urgent voice from the other end of the phone.
The deadline is pressing, so I have no choice but to work overtime.
en.notes: 切迫 describes a situation that is "pressing, acute, close to coming to a head". It mostly appears as 切迫している or attributively 切迫した: 切迫した状況, 切迫した声, 事態が切迫する; also the noun 切迫感. Medically: 切迫早産 "threatened premature birth". The verb 迫る is more neutral, "to approach"; 緊急 refers to an emergency.

examples[].german: I hear there are no lost-child announcements at Disneyland.
My child got lost in the department store, and I was really panicked.
I got lost in a town I'd never been to and asked someone the way to the station.
en.notes: 迷子 is a child or person who has gotten lost or lost their companions. The most important phrase is 迷子になる "to get lost", which adults also use jokingly about themselves. In a department store you hear 迷子のお知らせ "announcement about a lost child". The verb 道に迷う describes only losing one's way, whereas 迷子 describes the state as a person.

examples[].german: I feel anxious about the future.
I'm living alone for the first time and feel a little uneasy.
I'm so worried about my exam results that I can't sleep at night.
en.notes: 不安 means "unease, worry, anxiety" about something uncertain and is both a noun and a な-adjective: 将来が不安だ, 〜に不安を感じる, 不安になる, 不安な気持ち. Unlike 心配 ("to worry about something or someone", also about others), 不安 describes more of a diffuse, personal feeling of uncertainty; concrete fear is 怖い. The opposite is 安心.

examples[].german: Somewhere, a map of the maze is hidden.
The children are playing with a maze drawn on paper.
The old streets of this town are like a maze, and you get lost right away.
en.notes: 迷路 (迷う "to lose one's way" + 路 "road") is a "labyrinth, maze" - as a puzzle on paper, in an amusement park or in imagery: 迷路のような道 "winding alleys", 迷路に迷い込む. 迷宮 is more literary; 迷宮入り means "an unsolved criminal case". In medicine 迷路 also refers to the inner ear.

en.meaning: on the way; in the middle of (an activity)
examples[].german: Could you stop by the supermarket on the way and buy some tofu?
In the middle of work, I got a phone call.
en.notes: 途中 refers to a point on a route or in a process that is not yet finished. 途中で in the first example means "on the way"; 仕事の途中で means "in the middle of work". The noun connects with の for the named process and with で for the point in time of an action. Here it does not mean that the trip or work is already finished.

examples[].german: How do you intend to arrest him?
The police arrested the thief yesterday.
The man was arrested on the spot for drunk driving.
en.notes: 逮捕する means "to arrest, to detain" and is the official term for the police: 犯人を逮捕する. Especially common in the news is the passive 逮捕される; also 逮捕状 "arrest warrant" and 現行犯逮捕 "arrest in the act". In everyday speech people also say 捕まえる "to catch" or, intransitively, 捕まる "to be caught".

examples[].german: I don't like the way that guy talks.
You bastard, wait!
Tonight it's just us guys going out for a drink.
en.notes: 野郎 is rough, predominantly male colloquial speech. As a swear word it appears in この野郎! "You bastard!" or ばか野郎 "idiot"; in a more neutral but still casual sense it means "guy, fellow", e.g. 野郎ばかり "only men". You should never use it toward strangers, superiors or in polite situations; neutrally one says 男の人 or やつ.

examples[].german: I hear three pairs of socks are 500 yen! That's so cheap!
I wash my socks every night.
en.notes: 靴下 means socks. Pairs are counted with 足: 三足 is read さんそく. 三足で五百円 gives a total price for three pairs. だって reports a price heard from someone else here, and めっちゃ is a casual word for "very". 靴下を洗う names the socks as the thing being washed.

examples[].german: There is a famous shoe store in front of Mr. Takahashi's house.
I bought sneakers at the shoe store in front of the station.
The heel came off, so I had the shoe store repair it.
en.notes: 靴屋 is the "shoe store" or the "shoemaker"; 〜屋 forms shop names and occupational titles. With さん (靴屋さん) it sounds friendlier and can also mean the person. In department stores the section is called 靴売り場; modern shops often call themselves シューズショップ.

examples[].german: Koichi always comes in Pikachu rain boots on rainy days.
The snow was deep, so I went out wearing boots.
Rubber boots are indispensable when planting rice.
en.notes: 長靴 (with rendaku, ながぐつ) are tall boots, in daily life mainly "rubber boots" for rain, snow or field work. Shoes are put on with はく (履く): 長靴をはく. Fashionable leather boots are mostly called ブーツ; 靴 is the umbrella term for shoes.

examples[].german: That man was a bad influence on everyone.
Using your smartphone too much has a negative effect on your eyes.
Because of the unseasonable weather, the vegetable harvest is being adversely affected.
en.notes: 悪影響 is a "bad, negative influence". Typical combinations: 悪影響を与える / 及ぼす "to harm, to have a negative effect", 悪影響を受ける, 〜に悪影響が出る. It sounds more compact and somewhat more formal than 悪い影響. The counterpart is いい影響 or, formally, 好影響.

en.meaning: to retire; to live in seclusion
examples[].german: Because of my stomach ailment, I had to retire.
My father left the company to my older brother and lives in retirement in the countryside.
When I stop working, I want to lead a quiet retired life near the sea.
en.notes: 隠居する means "to withdraw from working life (or as head of a family) and live quietly". It sounds somewhat old-fashioned; common are 隠居生活 and 田舎で隠居する. ご隠居 is an old gentleman in retirement, known from rakugo stories. 引退 is withdrawal from sports or politics, 退職 leaving a company, 定年 the age limit.

examples[].german: "Where are you now?" "Huh, I'm in the living room now."
After dinner, the family watches TV in the living room.
Please show the guests into the living room.
en.notes: 居間 is the "living room" where the family spends time. The word sounds somewhat traditional; today people often say リビング. 茶の間 is the old-fashioned family room with a low table. 居間 is a homophone of 今 "now", which is used for wordplay.

examples[].german: I was nervous at the interview.
Don't be nervous - if you do it like you always do, you'll be fine.
Relations between the two countries are tense.
en.notes: 緊張 means "tension, nervousness" and as an intransitive する-verb "to be nervous, tense": 面接で緊張する, 緊張して手が震える. Someone who gets nervous easily is 緊張しやすい; tension eases with 緊張がほぐれる/とける. It can also refer to political tension (両国の関係が緊張している). Unlike 不安 ("worry about the uncertain"), 緊張 means the physical and mental tension in the moment.

examples[].german: That entertainer doesn't mention retirement at all.
I hear that player will retire at the end of this season.
Since retiring, my father tends the garden every day.
en.notes: 引退 refers to the final withdrawal from an active career, especially for athletes, artists and politicians; as an intransitive する-verb: 引退する, 現役を引退する, 〜から引退する. It is to be distinguished from 退職 "leaving employment" (e.g. 定年退職 "retirement at the mandatory age") and 辞任 "resignation from an office". Common combinations are 引退後 "after retirement" and 引退試合 "farewell match".

examples[].german: I don't have the courage to hand over the present in person.
The teacher handed each graduate their diploma personally.
Please hand this document to the staff member at the reception desk.
en.notes: 手渡す means "to hand something over personally, from hand to hand": 人に物を手渡す. In contrast to the general 渡す, it emphasizes that one hands it over directly oneself rather than sending it or passing it on through others. The noun 手渡し often stands adverbially: 手渡しでお願いします "please hand it over in person". A transitive godan verb with no intransitive partner.

examples[].german: In reality, there are loads of things that logic alone can't handle.
Even though I understand it in theory, I can't put it into practice easily.
My younger brother immediately comes up with arguments and doesn't try to help.
en.notes: 理屈 is the (often theoretical) reasoning or logic behind something: 理屈に合う "to be logical", 理屈では分かる "to understand in theory". It often sounds negative in the sense of "hair-splitting, excuse": 理屈を言う "to make excuses, to argue", 理屈っぽい "argumentative", 屁理屈 "quibbling". For logic as a subject or rigorous argumentation, one says 論理, for the mere reason 理由.

en.meaning: leaving it to someone; entrusting; chef's choice
examples[].german: Could I ask you to choose my hairstyle as you see fit?
I'll leave the details to Mr. Yamada.
Tonight I reserved the chef's choice course.
en.notes: お任せ is the polite noun form of 任せる "to leave to, to entrust" (人に仕事を任せる). As a phrase, お任せします means "I leave it to you", often said at the hairdresser or to craftsmen. In a restaurant, お任せ means the chef decides the menu (お任せコース). It is mostly used as a noun with で or as the humble お任せする.

en.meaning: to meet (expectations); to live up to; to take a toll
examples[].german: It is difficult to meet customers' diverse needs.
I want to live up to my parents' expectations, so I work hard every day.
This cold takes a toll on an aging body.
en.notes: 応える means "to respond to, to live up to an expectation" and takes に: 期待に応える, 要望に応える, 声援に応える. Do not confuse it with 答える "to answer (a question)" - same reading, but 応える responds to wishes, expectations or calls. A second meaning is "to take a toll, to be hard on" (寒さが体に応える), often written in kana こたえる here. It is an intransitive Ichidan verb.

examples[].german: Excuse me, could I have a wet wipe?
When I bought a bento at the convenience store, a wet wipe came with it.
It's handy to bring wet wipes on a picnic.
en.notes: お手拭き is a cloth for wiping the hands, today mostly a packaged wet wipe given in restaurants or with ready-made meals. The rolled warm or cold towel in a restaurant is usually called おしぼり; the two words overlap strongly in everyday use. The お is a fixed part of the word; without it (手拭き) it sounds unfamiliar. For packaged wipes people also say ウェットティッシュ.

en.meaning: to grow late (night, season); to advance
examples[].german: Autumn is deepening, and the mushroom season will soon be here.
While we were absorbed in conversation, the night grew late.
When the night grows late, this area becomes very quiet.
en.notes: 更ける describes the night or a season advancing: 夜が更ける "the night deepens, it gets late" is by far the most common combination, along with 秋が更ける "autumn wanes". Derived from it are 夜更け "late night" and 夜更かし "staying up late". Not to be confused with the identically read 老ける "to age" and 耽る "to indulge in". An intransitive ichidan verb.

examples[].german: I have never been abroad yet.
The cause of the accident is still not known.
Even though my older brother has turned forty, he is still single.
en.notes: いまだ is the written, somewhat formal counterpart of まだ and mostly occurs with a negative: いまだ〜ない "not yet, to this day". The form いまだに "still" also occurs in affirmative sentences (いまだに独身だ). Since 未だ can also be read まだ, the word is often written in kana. In conversation, まだ sounds more natural; いまだ(に) emphasizes that something continues for a surprisingly long time.

examples[].german: Why don't you try setting a somewhat more concrete standard for your goal?
The teacher explains the evaluation criteria at the start of the term.
This school even has detailed standards for how to wear the uniform.
en.notes: 規準 is a standard or norm by which one judges or acts: 規準を設ける, 評価の規準. The identically read and much more common 基準 means "standard, criterion"; 規準 stresses more a binding rule and appears mainly in education and administration (評価規準). When in doubt, people write 基準 in everyday life. The word is a pure noun and is connected with の (行動の規準).

examples[].german: However, the limit is 1,000,000 yen per person.
Even jokes have their limits.
I went over my card limit and couldn't make the payment.
en.notes: 限度 is a fixed or tolerable limit, a maximum: 限度額 "credit limit, maximum amount", 限度を超える "to exceed the limit", formal 〜を限度とする "up to a maximum of ...". Very common is ものには限度がある "everything has its limits". 限界, by contrast, means the limit of one's own strength or abilities (体力の限界).

examples[].german: I went through a lot of hardship.
My mother had a hard time raising us.
We worked hard to buy this house, so we treasure it.
en.notes: 苦労 means "hardship, toil, troubles" and as a する-verb "to struggle, to go through a lot": 仕事で苦労する, 〜のに苦労する, 苦労して〜 "with great effort ...". 苦労をかける means "to cause someone trouble". The phrase ご苦労さま is really directed at subordinates; to superiors it is better to say お疲れさまです. Compared with 努力 ("purposeful effort"), 苦労 emphasizes the hardship suffered.

examples[].german: From here you can see the whole town.
This is a full view of the island taken from an airplane.
There are many buildings, so you can't see the whole castle from in front of the station.
en.notes: 全景 is the overall view of a place, usually from a height or distance: 町の全景, 全景を見渡す, 全景を撮る. In everyday speech, for a beautiful view people more often say 景色 or 眺め; 全景 stresses that one sees the whole at once. Not to be confused with the identically read 前景 "foreground".

examples[].german: I'll try blurring the foreground a little.
In this painting, flowers are depicted in the foreground and mountains in the distance.
When taking a photo, putting something in the foreground gives it depth.
en.notes: 前景 is the foreground of a picture, photo or scene; antonyms are 背景 "background" as well as 中景 and 遠景. Typical are 前景に〜を置く/入れる and 前景をぼかす. The word belongs to the technical language of painting, photography and graphics; in everyday speech people often simply say 手前. Not to be confused with 全景 "full view".

examples[].german: Although the man staggered, he slowly started walking again.
I look forward to the day I visit this town again.
The game was interrupted by rain, but started again thirty minutes later.
en.notes: 再び is an adverb meaning "again, a second time"; it sounds more formal and more literary than また or もう一度. Typical in news, speeches and narratives: 再び訪れる, 再び始まる. In conversation people would mostly say また; 再び often stresses a return to an earlier state.

examples[].german: The sports day is not this week but the week after next.
I have an exam on Friday the week after next.
Please submit the report by the week after next.
en.notes: 再来週 is "the week after next", that is, in two weeks; formed with 再来 "after the next" like 再来月 and 再来年. As a time expression it usually stands without a particle, with の before weekdays (再来週の金曜日) and with までに for deadlines. The opposite direction is 先々週 "the week before last". The word is neutral and very common in everyday use.

examples[].german: Therefore, this medicine came to be known to people.
I think, therefore I am.
A is bigger than B, and B is bigger than C. Therefore, A is bigger than C.
en.notes: 故に (mostly ゆえに in kana) is a literary conjunction "consequently, therefore" that introduces a logical conclusion - typical in proofs, treatises and quotations like 我思う、故に我あり. In conversation people say だから or それで, in factual texts often したがって. The noun 故 also appears after a phrase as "because of": 若さゆえの失敗 "a mistake due to youthful recklessness".

examples[].german: There was a wire lying on the floor.
I fixed the fence boards with wire.
This hanger is made of wire.
en.notes: 針金 is thin metal wire, as used for crafts, tying or fastening: 針金で留める, 針金を曲げる; counter 本. For electrical cable, people say 電線 or コード, for thick steel cables ワイヤー. The word is made up of 針 "needle" and 金 "metal".

examples[].german: To insects, humans are giants too, aren't they.
Folktales often feature giants as big as mountains.
In yesterday's baseball game, the Giants won 3 to 2.
en.notes: 巨人 is a giant, literally a "huge person"; figuratively also an outstanding personality (文学界の巨人). In Japan, 巨人 very often stands for short for the baseball team the Yomiuri Giants. The adjective "huge" is 巨大な, not 巨人な.

en.meaning: to invite; to cause; to bring about
examples[].german: We plan to invite one hundred clients to this party.
One remark of his caused a big misunderstanding.
I was invited to a friend's wedding and will be giving a speech.
en.notes: 招く is transitive and first means "to invite (formally)": 人を〜に招く, passive 招かれる; it sounds more elevated than 呼ぶ or 誘う, and the related noun is 招待. Equally important is the meaning "to bring about, to cause", for mostly undesirable consequences: 誤解を招く "to cause misunderstandings", 事故を招く. 手招きする means "to beckon".

en.meaning: to master; to carry to the extreme; to reach the utmost
examples[].german: To master the way of kanji, Koichi went to Japan and attended a kanji dojo.
The airport at the year's end was extremely crowded.
Through years of practice, she mastered piano technique.
en.notes: 極める means "to go to the utmost": to fully master a path or an art (道を極める, 技術を極める) or to reach an extreme state (混雑を極める "to be extremely crowded", 多忙を極める "to be extremely busy"). For thorough research, 究める is also written. It is a transitive Ichidan verb with を; the intransitive partner is 極まる, and the adverb 極めて means "extremely".

en.meaning: to retreat; to step back; to step down
examples[].german: It's still too early to retire from active duty.
Let's step back one pace and look at the whole picture.
The enemy army withdrew toward the mountains.
en.notes: 退く means "to draw back, to withdraw", both spatially (一歩退く) and figuratively "to leave an office or active service" (現役を退く, 職を退く); the place left takes を. It sounds more formal than 下がる. The transitive partner is 退ける "to repel, to reject". Note: the same kanji read 退く (どく/のく) colloquially means "to make way".

examples[].german: Technology has advanced.
If you record your practice, you can tell how much you have improved.
Thanks to advances in medicine, many lives are being saved.
en.notes: 進歩する is intransitive and means that something becomes qualitatively better or more advanced: 技術が進歩する, 医学の進歩. It fits abstract fields well, as well as a person's general progress (少しずつ進歩している). For skills such as language or sports, people often say 上達する (日本語が上達する). 発展, by contrast, is more about growth and spread, for example of an economy or city.

examples[].german: I am torn between work and family.
I struggled for a long time over whether to give up my dream.
This film depicts conflict between parents and children.
en.notes: 葛藤 mainly denotes an inner conflict, being torn between two desires or duties: 心の葛藤, 〜と〜の間で葛藤する. It can also mean conflicts between people (親子の葛藤). The kanji stand for kudzu and wisteria - two climbing plants that entwine with each other. The word sounds literary; in conversation people often say 迷う or 悩む.

examples[].german: Please proceed following the arrows.
Please turn the lid in the direction of the arrow.
If you click the arrow at the top right of the screen, you move on to the next page.
en.notes: 矢印 is the arrow symbol on signs, maps and screens, from 矢 "arrow (weapon)" and 印 "mark". Typical are 矢印に沿って進む "to follow the arrows", 矢印の方向 and 矢印キー "arrow key". The real arrow for shooting is called 矢. Colloquially, 矢印が向く also means that someone's romantic interest is directed at a person.

examples[].german: Today at school I learned about series circuits and parallel circuits.
In this sentence, two nouns are joined in parallel with 「と」.
The new computer can process multiple tasks in parallel.
en.notes: 並列 means "to arrange side by side, on an equal footing" and is mainly a technical word: in electrical engineering 並列回路 "parallel circuit" (opposite 直列 "series"), in IT 並列処理 "parallel processing", in grammar the listing of coordinate elements with と or や. Not to be confused with 並行 "to run side by side at the same time" and 平行 "geometrically parallel". As a する-verb it is mostly passive: 並列される.

en.meaning: running in parallel; simultaneous; side by side
examples[].german: I'm not good at doing several things at once.
A river flows alongside the railway tracks.
Alongside my job, I study at graduate school in the evenings.
en.notes: 並行 means "to run side by side" and, figuratively, "to proceed simultaneously"; most often in the form 〜と並行して "parallel to, at the same time as". It is an intransitive する-verb. For geometrically parallel lines, people write 平行 (平行線), for parallel circuits 並列. In conversation, for simultaneous things people also say 同時に.

examples[].german: When is the deadline for the rhetoric report?
Rhetoric is a field of study that was born in ancient Greece.
After studying rhetoric at university, I became better at giving speeches.
en.notes: 修辞学 is rhetoric as a science, from 修辞 "rhetorical expression, figure of speech" and 学 "study". The word belongs to an academic context (university subject, literary studies). In daily life people more often hear レトリック, often disparagingly for clever but empty words; eloquence itself is called 話術 or 弁論.

examples[].german: I left my umbrella in the restaurant's umbrella stand and walked out without it.
Please put wet umbrellas in the umbrella stand at the entrance.
I found a stylish umbrella stand at a 100-yen shop.
en.notes: 傘立て is an umbrella stand, usually in the entrance area of homes, shops and restaurants. It is formed like 本立て "bookend" or ペン立て "pen holder" from a noun and 立て (from 立てる "to set upright"). Typical: 傘立てに傘を入れる/立てる. In shops there is often 傘袋 "umbrella bag" as an alternative for wet umbrellas.

examples[].german: My older sister works at a child guidance center.
About three hundred pupils attend this elementary school.
There is a children's book corner on the second floor of the library.
en.notes: 児童 is a formal, official word for children; in the school context it refers specifically to elementary school pupils, while junior and senior high school students are 生徒 and university students 学生. It appears mainly in compounds: 児童書 "children's book", 児童公園, 児童相談所 "child guidance center". In everyday speech people simply say 子ども.

examples[].german: I tried to speak in as calm a tone as possible.
Especially during an earthquake, please act calmly.
Let's calm down a little and think about it once more.
en.notes: 冷静 is a な-adjective for "calm, level-headed, with a cool head", especially in difficult situations: 冷静な判断, 冷静に行動する, 冷静になる "to calm down", 冷静さを失う "to lose one's composure". Unlike 冷たい "cold, unfriendly", 冷静 is positive. For simply calming down, people also say 落ち着く in daily life.

examples[].german: Our freezer is always full.
Please put the ice cream in the freezer.
I put ice made in the freezer into the juice.
en.notes: 冷凍庫 is the freezer compartment or freezer, from 冷凍 "deep-freezing" and 庫 "storehouse". Not to be confused with 冷蔵庫 "refrigerator". In Japanese refrigerators the freezer is usually a drawer, also called 冷凍室. Typical: 冷凍庫に入れる, 冷凍庫で凍らせる.

en.meaning: death from cold; to freeze to death
examples[].german: A mouse had frozen to death in the doghouse.
I got lost in the mountains in winter and almost froze to death.
In the past, quite a few people froze to death in the cold.
en.notes: 凍死 means dying of cold (凍 "to freeze" + 死 "death"); as an intransitive する-verb: 凍死する "to freeze to death". Typical in news: 凍死者 "people who froze to death", 凍死しそうになる. Not to be confused with 凍傷 "frostbite (on hands, feet)", in which one does not die. In conversation people jokingly say 凍死しそう for "I'm freezing to death".

examples[].german: My account has been frozen.
On winter mornings the roads freeze over, so please drive carefully.
The company decided to freeze hiring for next fiscal year.
en.notes: 凍結 has two uses: literally "to freeze, to ice over" as an intransitive する-verb (道路が凍結する, 水道管が凍結する) and figuratively "to freeze, to put on ice" as a transitive verb (資産を凍結する, 計画を凍結する), often passive: アカウントが凍結される "the account is suspended". In daily life, 凍る is more usual for water; food is frozen with 冷凍する, not with 凍結.

examples[].german: I savored the sense of accomplishment.
When I reached the summit of Mt. Fuji, I felt a tremendous sense of accomplishment.
This job is tough, but it is rewarding.
en.notes: 達成感 is the feeling of having accomplished something - a "sense of achievement". It is composed of 達成 "achievement" and 感 "feeling". Typical combinations: 達成感を味わう, 達成感を得る, 達成感がある. Unlike 満足感 "feeling of satisfaction", 達成感 stresses that a goal was reached through one's own effort; related is 充実感 "sense of fulfillment".

examples[].german: I got rid of everything I don't need.
Before moving, I disposed of the old furniture cheaply.
He broke the rules and received a suspension from school.
en.notes: 処分 means "to get rid of something unwanted": to dispose of it or sell it cheaply (古い家具を処分する, 処分セール). It sounds more matter-of-fact than 捨てる and includes selling. The second important meaning is "punishment, disciplinary action": 処分を受ける, 停学処分, 厳しい処分. Transitive する-verb with を.

examples[].german: With a new passport, the passport number should also be new.
Please check the passport's expiration date.
One photo is required for a passport application.
en.notes: 旅券 is the official term for the passport and is found mainly on forms, in laws and in official letters: 旅券番号, 旅券の申請, 一般旅券. In everyday speech one almost always says パスポート. The word is composed of 旅 "travel" and 券 "ticket, certificate".

examples[].german: Where can I buy advance tickets?
Advance tickets are 300 yen cheaper than tickets on the day.
It's a popular live show, so advance tickets sold out quickly.
en.notes: 前売り券 is an admission ticket bought in advance, from 前売り "advance sale" and 券 "ticket"; the counterpart is 当日券 "ticket sold on the day". Typical: 前売り券を買う/購入する, 前売り券が売り切れる. It is often written without り (前売券); colloquially it is also shortened to 前売り.

examples[].german: I'm really looking forward to working with a creative person like you.
This job requires creativity above all.
Drawing pictures helps develop children's creativity.
en.notes: 創造力 is the ability to create something new: 創造力がある, 創造力が豊かだ, 創造力を育てる/発揮する. Watch out: the identically read 想像力 means "imagination, fantasy" - 創造 means "to create", 想像 "to imagine". The corresponding adjective is 創造的な "creative"; casually people also say クリエイティブ.

examples[].german: In every era, there are many young people who want to take up creative work.
Let's think of a more creative solution.
This company values an environment where employees can work creatively.
en.notes: 創造的 is a な-adjective for "creative, inventive": 創造的な仕事, 創造的な発想, adverbially 創造的に考える. It sounds somewhat more formal than the loanword クリエイティブ, which is common in everyday speech. The opposite would be something like 模倣的 "imitative". Not to be confused with 想像的, which is hardly used.

examples[].german: I spent all my money on gambling.
Opening a new shop is a kind of gamble.
When he was young, my father ran up a huge debt through gambling.
en.notes: 博打 is gambling for money, often written ばくち in kana; it sounds somewhat old-fashioned and colloquial. Typical: 博打を打つ "to gamble", 博打で負ける. Figuratively it refers to a risky undertaking: それは一種の博打だ. In modern usage people mostly say ギャンブル, legally 賭博.

examples[].german: Every day I watch today's horoscope on the morning show and then go to school.
According to the horoscope, I apparently have good luck in love today.
I don't believe in horoscopes at all.
en.notes: 星占い is divination by star sign (星座), that is, astrology or a horoscope; 星座占い means the same. In Japan there are daily horoscopes on morning TV and in magazines: 今日の星占い, 星占いによると. Fortune-telling in general is 占い, and the fortune it predicts is 運勢.

examples[].german: Eel has long been popular as a wonder food for beating the summer heat.
Laughter is said to be the best medicine.
There is no miracle cure for a broken heart.
en.notes: 妙薬 is a "miracle cure", from 妙 "wonderful, mysterious" and 薬 "medicine". The word sounds literary and is mostly used figuratively: 〜の妙薬, 〜に効く妙薬, 何よりの妙薬 "the best remedy". A remedy for a specific illness is matter-of-factly called 特効薬.

examples[].german: Where is the women's clothing section?
There were many ladies in kimono at the venue.
I was examined at the gynecologist's in front of the station.
en.notes: 婦人 is an older, formal word for "lady, adult woman"; as a standalone word it is considered dated today, and people mostly say 女性. It lives on in compounds: 婦人服 "women's clothing", 婦人科 "gynecology", 婦人用. Politely, one speaks of a lady one doesn't know as ご婦人. Do not confuse it with 夫人 "wife" (〜夫人 "Mrs. 〜").

examples[].german: That child is still so young, poor thing.
When I was little, I often went to play at my grandmother's house.
My boss told me that my way of thinking is still immature.
en.notes: 幼い describes children at a very young age: 幼い子ども, 幼い頃 "when I was little". Figuratively it means "childish, immature" (考え方が幼い). For size, one says 小さい, for young adults 若い; 子どもっぽい is more colloquial and more derogatory than 幼い. i-adjective: 幼くて, 幼かった.

examples[].german: It was a fulfilling day.
This hotel is well equipped.
The city plans to expand its child-rearing support.
en.notes: 充実 means "fulfillment, fullness, good provision". As a する-verb it describes either a fulfilled, full life (充実した毎日, 毎日が充実している) or that something is rich and well developed (設備が充実している, 品ぞろえが充実している). "To expand" is expressed with 〜を充実させる. Related is 充実感 "sense of fulfillment"; satisfaction with a result, by contrast, is 満足.

examples[].german: "Childhood" is a novel Tolstoy wrote based on his own childhood.
My grandfather spent his childhood in the countryside of Hokkaido.
I still remember memories of my childhood clearly.
en.notes: 幼年時代 refers to early childhood, roughly up to school age; it sounds literary and appears in biographies and memoirs. Typical: 幼年時代を過ごす, 幼年時代の思い出. In conversation people more often say 子どもの頃 or 子ども時代; the following stage of life is called 少年時代.

examples[].german: Do you have a safe at home?
Important documents are kept in the safe.
During the night, money was stolen from the shop's safe.
en.notes: 金庫 is a safe or strongbox: 金庫にしまう, 金庫を開ける, 金庫破り "safecracker". The second meaning "treasury, financial institution" is found in names like 信用金庫 "credit association". A safe-deposit box at a bank, by contrast, is called 貸金庫, and a small coin locker コインロッカー.

examples[].german: She is the youngest prime minister in the history of Thailand's constitutional government.
Constitutionalism means conducting politics on the basis of the constitution.
In this country, constitutional government has continued for more than a hundred years.
en.notes: 憲政 is government based on a constitution, from 憲法 "constitution" and 政治 "politics". The word belongs to political, written language and appears mainly in set phrases such as 憲政史上 "in the history of constitutional government", 憲政の常道 "the normal course of constitutional government" or in the synonym 立憲政治. It hardly occurs in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I was somehow able to communicate with the Japanese people using gestures.
He makes big gestures when he talks.
A tourist who had lost his way asked for the station's location using gestures.
en.notes: 身振り is a movement of the body with which one expresses something, that is, gesture or gesticulation. Very common is the fixed phrase 身振り手振りで "with gestures, using hands and feet", for example when communicating without a shared language. Also typical are 身振りが大きい and 身振りで伝える. Synonymous but more casual is the loanword ジェスチャー.

examples[].german: Today, as an examiner, I interviewed ten applicants.
The department head plans to interview applicants for the part-time job this afternoon.
Since I live far away, it was decided that I can have my interview online.
en.notes: 面接する means "to conduct an interview or selection interview" from the point of view of the examining side: 応募者を面接する. The applicant, by contrast, says 面接を受ける "to go to an interview". Related are 面接官 "interviewer" and 面接試験 "oral selection exam". An interview with the media is called インタビュー, not 面接.

examples[].german: Don't move. If you don't stay still, I'll shoot!
The police officer shot the criminal in the leg.
At the sports day, the teacher fires a pistol to signal the start.
en.notes: 撃つ means "to shoot, to fire" with a firearm: 銃を撃つ, 人や動物を撃つ. The homophones 打つ "to hit, to type" and 討つ "to defeat, to avenge" are read the same; the spelling shows the meaning. Transitive Godan verb; the passive 撃たれる "to be shot" is common.

examples[].german: The server is under a cyberattack.
In soccer, the balance between attack and defense is important.
He fiercely attacked the department head's proposal at the meeting.
en.notes: 攻撃 is an attack - military, in sports or verbal: 攻撃する, 攻撃を受ける "to be attacked", サイバー攻撃. The opposite term is 守備 or 防御 "defense". Figuratively it stands for sharp criticism (人を攻撃する); the adjective 攻撃的 means "aggressive". The related verb 攻める is more everyday and especially common in sports.

en.meaning: to attack; to go on the offensive
examples[].german: Tomorrow we attack the enemy's castle!
In the second half, our team was attacking the whole time.
This design is quite daring.
en.notes: 攻める means "to attack, to go on the offensive": 城を攻める, 相手のゴールを攻める; the opposite is 守る. Careful: the homophone 責める means "to reproach, to blame". Colloquially 攻めている also means "to be bold, daring" (攻めたデザイン). Transitive Ichidan verb; the noun 攻め means "attack".

examples[].german: At the same time, the Soviet Union launched a counteroffensive.
When the enemy weakened, our side counterattacked all at once.
In history class, we learned about the Allied counteroffensive operations.
en.notes: 反攻 is a counterattack, especially the counteroffensive of a side that was previously inferior in war: 反攻を開始する, 反攻に出る, 反攻作戦. The word is military-historical and literary. For counterattacks in sports, quarrels or discussions, people almost always say 反撃. Not to be confused with the identically read 反抗 "resistance, defiance".

examples[].german: I am satisfied with the result.
I'm so busy that I don't even have enough time to sleep properly.
We will do our best so that our customers are satisfied.
en.notes: 満足 means "satisfaction" and as a する-verb "to be satisfied": 結果に満足する, 現状に満足している. As a な-adjective it also means "sufficient, proper" - mostly negated: 満足な食事もできない, 満足に〜できない "cannot even ... properly". The opposite is 不満. Common in business: 顧客満足 "customer satisfaction", 満足度 "degree of satisfaction".

examples[].german: Could you give me a ride to Yokohama?
I had lunch in Yokohama's Chinatown.
Yokohama is about thirty minutes from Tokyo by train.
en.notes: 横浜 is the port city south of Tokyo in Kanagawa Prefecture and, by population, the second-largest city in Japan. The characters mean roughly "sideways beach". Well known are 横浜港, the 中華街 "Chinatown" and みなとみらい; residents are called 横浜市民, colloquially also ハマっ子.

examples[].german: But I heard it can only be seen by people with a pure heart.
The water in this river is clear, and many fish swim in it.
Before elections, posters appear saying "Cast your honest vote."
en.notes: 清い means "clear, pure" of water or air and, figuratively, "pure, innocent" of heart and character: 清い水, 心の清い人, 清い交際 "platonic relationship". It sounds elevated and literary; in everyday speech people say きれい or 澄んだ. The classical attributive form 清き lives on in phrases such as 清き一票 "an honest vote (in elections)".

examples[].german: Please don't touch me with those dirty hands!
I don't want to use a dirty toilet.
Cooking without washing your hands is unsanitary.
en.notes: 不潔 is a な-adjective for "unhygienic, dirty" and stresses a lack of cleanliness that causes disgust: 不潔な手, 不潔なトイレ. The opposite is 清潔. General "dirty" is 汚い; 不潔 is stronger and can also mean morally "indecent, dirty" (不潔な金).

examples[].german: Thank you for the useful advice.
This book contains a lot of information useful for travel.
I want to make good use of my precious time off.
en.notes: 有益 is a な-adjective for "useful, profitable, instructive", often used for information, advice or time: 有益な情報, 有益なアドバイス, 時間を有益に使う. It sounds more formal than 役に立つ; 便利, by contrast, means "handy, convenient". Opposites are 無益 "useless" and 有害 "harmful".

examples[].german: I work at a public interest corporation.
This project is carried out for the public good.
The public interest should take priority over individual interests.
en.notes: 公益 is the public good, i.e. the benefit to the general public, from 公 "public" and 益 "benefit". The word is formal and often appears in compounds: 公益法人 "public interest corporation", 公益事業 "public utility". The opposite term is 私益 "self-interest"; in everyday speech people say 社会のため or 公共の利益.

examples[].german: Protecting the national interest is a diplomat's job, isn't it?
The prime minister stated, "We will put the national interest first."
Some say this policy goes against the national interest.
en.notes: 国益 is the "national interest" of a state and belongs to the language of politics, diplomacy and the news. Typical combinations are 国益を守る "to safeguard the national interest", 国益を損なう "to harm the national interest", 国益になる or 国益にかなう "to be in the national interest" and 国益に反する "to run counter to the national interest". The general 利益 means only "profit, benefit"; 国益 always refers to the state as a whole.

en.meaning: to move; to transfer; to shift
examples[].german: We are considering moving the office to Ginza.
From next month, we will finally put the plan into action.
I caught a cold from my child.
en.notes: 移す is transitive: you bring something from A to B, often in the pattern AからBに〜を移す (事務所を銀座に移す). Figuratively, 計画を実行に移す means "to put a plan into action" and 視線を移す "to shift one's gaze elsewhere". For passing on an illness (風邪をうつす) it is mostly written in kana. The intransitive partner is 移る "to move, to shift, to catch (an illness)"; do not confuse it with the homophones 写す "to copy, to photograph" and 映す "to reflect, to project".

examples[].german: For now, I have no plans to move to Japan.
After retirement, I'm thinking of moving to Okinawa.
In the past, many Japanese people emigrated to Brazil.
en.notes: 移住 means settling permanently in a different place, abroad or within the country (e.g. 地方への移住 "moving to the countryside"). As an intransitive する-verb the destination takes に: ブラジルに移住する; as a noun with への: 日本への移住.
