An ordinary change of residence is called 引っ越し; 移民 rather means "migrant(s)" or migration as a social phenomenon.

examples[].german: My husband is really childish.
A childish lie like that will be found out right away.
The content of this essay is a bit childish.
en.notes: 幼稚 is a な-adjective and sounds derogatory: it describes the behavior, thinking or work of adults as "childish, immature, primitive" (幼稚な考え, 幼稚なうそ). Neutrally, the kanji means "young child" only in words such as 幼稚園 "kindergarten". Colloquially milder is 子どもっぽい; 未熟 means more "not yet mature, inexperienced" without mockery.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to end my relationship with my partner.
After quitting the company, he cut off contact with everyone.
Accidents keep happening at this intersection.
en.notes: 絶つ is transitive and means to deliberately and definitively break something off: 関係を絶つ "to sever a relationship", 連絡を絶つ "to cut off contact", 消息を絶つ "to go missing". Very common is the fixed phrase 後を絶たない "does not stop, never ends". In the sense of "to give up something" (酒を断つ) and "to cut off", 断つ is usually written; the intransitive partner of 絶つ is 絶える "to cease, to die out".

examples[].german: I have a complaint.
Many employees are dissatisfied with their current salary.
The child had a dissatisfied look on his face.
en.notes: 不満 means "dissatisfaction, discontent" and is both a noun and a な-adjective: 〜に不満がある, 不満を言う "to complain", 不満そうな顔. The opposite is 満足. Unlike 文句 ("grumbling, a complaint" as spoken words), 不満 refers to the feeling itself; 不平 is similar but more literary (不平不満).

examples[].german: Mom, you don't need to worry. I can go to that sweet shop by myself.
I bought souvenirs at the sweet shop in front of the station.
When I was a child, my dream was to become a confectioner.
en.notes: お菓子屋 is a shop for sweets and pastries; in conversation people almost always add さん (お菓子屋さん), as in パン屋さん or 本屋さん. With 屋, the person who runs the shop can also be meant. More specific are 和菓子屋 for Japanese sweets and 駄菓子屋 for the nostalgic shop with cheap children's sweets; in written, business style it is 菓子店.

examples[].german: Isn't that shirt on backwards?
After I took the medicine, I actually felt worse.
The station is in the opposite direction.
en.notes: 逆 means "reversed, opposite, the contrary" and is used as a noun or な-adjective: 逆の方向 "the opposite direction", 順番が逆だ "the order is reversed". Very common is the adverb 逆に "on the contrary, conversely", in conversation often also as an introduction (逆に言えば). Unlike 反対, which also means "objection, being against", 逆 describes only the reversal; as a prefix it is found in 逆効果 or 逆転.

examples[].german: Isn't that counterproductive?
Scolding a child too much can sometimes backfire.
Drinking alcohol before bed has the opposite effect for sleep.
en.notes: 逆効果 is an effect that runs counter to the actual goal: "counterproductive, to backfire". Grammatically it is a noun and is usually used with だ or になる: 逆効果だ, 逆効果になる, with reference to something as 〜には逆効果. Do not confuse it with 副作用 "side effect" or 効果がない "ineffective" - with 逆効果, the measure makes things worse.

examples[].german: That politician often uses paradoxical expressions.
"Losing is winning" is a well-known paradox.
Paradoxically speaking, the more failures a person has, the closer they are to success.
en.notes: 逆説 is a "paradox": a statement that sounds contradictory but contains a truth, such as 負けるが勝ち "losing is winning". The derivation 逆説的な / 逆説的に "paradoxical, paradoxically" is common. Watch out: the identically read 逆接 is a grammatical term for adversative connections such as しかし or けれども. The word belongs more to written, elevated language.

examples[].german: Anyone who thinks that things will work out somehow if they just keep smiling is greatly mistaken.
If you think Japanese is easy, you're badly mistaken.
I made a big mistake in the calculation and had to redo everything.
en.notes: 大間違い is a "gross error" or "serious mistake"; 大 is read おお here, not だい. Very typical is the warning frame 〜と思ったら大間違いだ "anyone who thinks that ... is gravely mistaken", often also 〜と思っている人は大間違い. As a concrete mistake it takes する: 計算で大間違いをする. The neutral base word is 間違い; colloquially, for small mistakes, people also say ミス.

examples[].german: What is your postal code?
Please write the postal code before the address.
When you enter the postal code, the address appears automatically.
en.notes: 郵便番号 is the "postal code"; in Japan it has seven digits in the format 123-4567 and is written before the address with the symbol 〒. Typical are 郵便番号を書く / 入力する / 調べる. On forms, often only 〒 appears as the field label; you ask for the number with 郵便番号は何番ですか or, more politely, 郵便番号を教えていただけますか.

examples[].german: How did this book get into my little mailbox?
While I was traveling, the mailbox filled up with flyers.
I lost the key to my mailbox.
en.notes: 郵便箱 is a "mailbox", especially one's own box for incoming mail. In everyday Japanese, however, people usually say 郵便受け or simply ポスト; the red public mailbox for outgoing mail is almost always called ポスト. Typical are 郵便箱に入れる, 郵便箱をのぞく and 郵便箱がいっぱいになる.

examples[].german: Did you record Koichi's speech?
I recorded the content of the meeting on my smartphone.
This radio program is not recorded; it is live.
en.notes: 録音 is a "sound recording"; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を録音する "to record". For picture and video recordings, people say 録画 instead. Typical combinations are 録音を聞く / 再生する "to listen to / play back the recording" and 留守番電話に録音する "to leave a message on the answering machine". As the opposite of a live broadcast, 録音 also stands for "pre-recorded".

examples[].german: Are you playing army? Sounds fun. Let me join too.
I hear my grandfather was in the army when he was young.
That club is as strict as the military.
en.notes: 軍隊 refers to the army or armed forces as an organization and to the troops: 軍隊に入る "to join the military", 軍隊生活. Shorter, and in compounds, 軍 is used (陸軍, 海軍); an individual soldier is 兵士. Japan's own armed forces are officially called 自衛隊, not 軍隊. Figuratively, 軍隊みたい describes extremely strict drill.

examples[].german: This is a soldier ant, isn't it?
When my grandfather was young, he went to war as a soldier.
The children are playing with toy soldiers.
en.notes: 兵隊 means "soldiers, troops", especially ordinary soldiers; it sounds somewhat old-fashioned and colloquial. In news and formal texts people prefer 兵士, and for military personnel in general (including officers) 軍人. Children say 兵隊さん, and it appears in comparisons such as 兵隊アリ "soldier ant" or おもちゃの兵隊 "toy soldiers". Colloquially it can also mean a company's "lowly employee, foot soldier".

examples[].german: I will discern the essence of the problem.
I think human nature doesn't change.
The discussion is straying from the essence.
en.notes: 本質 means the "essence, core, true nature" of a thing: 問題の本質, 本質をつかむ, 本質から外れる. It is used above all in discussions, analyses and texts and sounds rather formal. In contrast to 表面 "surface" or 見た目 "appearance", 本質 means what makes a thing what it is at its innermost. The な-adjective 本質的 means "essential, fundamental".

examples[].german: It's finally been decided that I'm joining the band.
My older brother joined the Self-Defense Forces at eighteen.
Newly enlisted recruits undergo training from early every morning.
en.notes: 入隊 is "joining" a unit called 隊: the army, the Self-Defense Forces (自衛隊), but also a music corps (音楽隊) or fire brigade (消防隊). As an intransitive する-verb, the destination takes に: 自衛隊に入隊する; as a noun it takes への. The opposite is 除隊 or 退隊. For a company, school or club, people say 入社, 入学 and 入会 instead.

examples[].german: The shoes I bought at the weekend don't fit, and my heels hurt.
On rainy days, the knee I injured long ago aches.
My heart ached when I saw that news.
en.notes: 痛む is intransitive: the body part takes が (頭が痛む, 傷が痛む). It sounds somewhat more descriptive and literary than the everyday adjective 痛い and emphasizes lasting pain (ずきずき痛む). Figuratively, 胸が痛む / 心が痛む means "it pains me deeply". The transitive partner is 痛める "to injure oneself" (腰を痛める); for "to spoil, to be damaged" it is usually written 傷む.

examples[].german: I can't sleep without sleeping pills.
I had the doctor prescribe sleeping pills.
After taking sleeping pills, you must not drive a car.
en.notes: 睡眠薬 are "sleeping aids, sleeping pills"; 薬 is read やく in this compound. Like all medicines, you "take" them with 飲む: 睡眠薬を飲む. Doctors prescribe them (睡眠薬を出す / 処方する). Somewhat more colloquial is 眠り薬; in advertising and among doctors you also hear 睡眠導入剤 for mild agents.

examples[].german: Even though she knows I'm on a diet, Ms. Matsumoto always tempts me to go to the cake shop.
Beware of scams that lure people with sweet words.
Even though it was right before the exam, I gave in to the temptation of games.
en.notes: 誘惑する is transitive: one "seduces" or "tempts" someone (人を誘惑する), with bad intentions or also jokingly, as with sweets. The noun 誘惑 is very common in phrases such as 誘惑に負ける "to succumb to temptation", 誘惑に勝つ "to resist temptation" and 誘惑が多い. The neutral 誘う only means "to invite, to ask"; 誘惑 emphasizes the temptation to do something one should not actually do.

examples[].german: We can't do anything about it with our strength alone.
We need to discuss this problem once more.
We humans must take better care of nature.
en.notes: 我々 is a formal pronoun for "we". You hear it in speeches, lectures, company and newspaper texts, and in rather masculine, elevated language; in daily life people say 私たち, casually 僕ら or 俺たち. It often stands before a group designation: 我々人間 "we humans", 我々日本人. The mark 々 repeats the preceding kanji.

examples[].german: It is thought that there is no direct effect on health.
She always speaks in a direct way, so she is easily misunderstood.
It is not directly related, but it has an indirect influence.
en.notes: 直接的 is a な-adjective meaning "direct, immediate", mostly with abstract things: 直接的な原因, 直接的な影響, 直接的な言い方 "a direct, blunt way of speaking". The simple 直接 is a noun or adverb for concrete actions (直接会う, 直接話す). The opposite is 間接的 "indirect", often in contrast: 直接的には…、間接的には….

examples[].german: The lid doesn't seem to be closed properly, and sauce is dripping from the side.
This dog has droopy ears and is very cute.
The players who lost the game quietly bowed their heads.
en.notes: 垂れる is mostly intransitive and has two basic meanings: "to hang down" (耳が垂れた犬, 枝が垂れる) and "to drip, to run down" (ソースが垂れる, 鼻水が垂れる). The transitive partner is 垂らす "to let hang down, to let drip" (ロープを垂らす). Elevated and transitive is 頭を垂れる "to bow one's head"; pejoratively one says 文句を垂れる "to grumble". The barbecue sauce タレ is derived from the same verb.

examples[].german: Many wild animals live in this marshland.
Your feet sink in marshland, so be careful when walking.
This area used to be a swamp, but now it's a residential district.
en.notes: 沼地 is a "marshland", that is, wet, muddy land with swamps (沼 "swamp, pond" + 地 "land"). The technical word for wetlands in environmental and nature conservation texts is 湿地; 池 is a small pond, 湖 a lake. Typical contexts are nature, animals and local history (昔は沼地だった).

examples[].german: Somehow stop the enemy's advance!
This year's team continues its triumphant run.
"Attack on Titan" is a manga popular all over the world.
en.notes: 進撃 is the military "advance, thrust" against the enemy; as an intransitive する-verb: 敵地へ進撃する. Typical are 敵の進撃を止める / 阻む. In sports and news, 快進撃 "winning streak, triumphant run" is very common. The more general 攻撃 means "attack", the neutral 前進 "forward movement"; the word is also known from the manga title 進撃の巨人.

examples[].german: I'm doing an Instagram live on the beach right now.
In the evening, I took a walk on the beach with my dog.
Many pretty shells were lying on the beach.
en.notes: 浜辺 is the flat, mostly sandy shore by the sea and sounds somewhat vivid and narrative: 浜辺を歩く, 浜辺で遊ぶ. ビーチ is rather used for swimming beaches and leisure, 砂浜 emphasizes the sand, 海岸 is the coast in general, also rocky. For river banks one does not say 浜辺 but 川辺 or 岸.

examples[].german: Let's look at it from another angle.
He also has a gentle side.
Please write your name on the side of the box.
en.notes: 側面 literally means "side, lateral surface" (箱の側面, 建物の側面) and figuratively "aspect, side of a matter or person": 意外な側面, 経済的な側面, いろいろな側面から考える. In the figurative sense it is more formal than 面 or 部分. For the side next to something in everyday speech one says 横; 側面 means the surface or the aspect itself.

examples[].german: The reason is that tomorrow is the card's closing date.
I like cats. That's because they seem to live freely.
I'm against this plan. The reason is that it costs too much.
en.notes: なぜなら (mostly in kana) introduces, after a statement, a new sentence giving the reason and is almost always closed with 〜からだ / 〜からです: 〜。なぜなら、〜からです "..., because ...". It sounds somewhat formal and argumentative, suited to essays, speeches and discussions. In casual conversation people simply add 〜から or say なんでかというと.

examples[].german: I'll go move the car for a moment.
From Tokyo to Osaka, we travel by Shinkansen.
Please move this file to a different folder.
en.notes: 移動 is the "moving, relocating, traveling" from one place to another and can be used transitively (車を移動する "to move the car") as well as intransitively (会場へ移動する "to move to the venue"). Common are 移動中 "on the move" and 移動時間 "travel time"; on a computer it means "to move". Do not confuse it with the homophone 異動 "transfer (at work)"; moving house is 引っ越し.

en.meaning: to be complete; to be gathered; to match
examples[].german: It's the first time in five years that everyone is together.
Once all the necessary documents are ready, please submit them at the counter.
This supermarket has a good selection of vegetables.
en.notes: 揃う is intransitive and means "to be complete / all present" (全員が揃う, 書類が揃う), "to be well stocked" (品物が揃っている) or "to be even, in unison" (足並みが揃う). The transitive partner is 揃える "to complete, to align" (靴を揃える). The て-form 揃って means "all together" (家族揃って). It is often written in kana そろう.

examples[].german: The Halloween party lasted until late at night.
The phone rang late at night, and I was startled.
The town late at night was quiet, with almost no people or cars passing.
en.notes: 夜更け is "late, advanced night", for example after midnight, and sounds somewhat narrative and literary: 夜更けまで "until deep into the night", 夜更けに. It comes from 夜が更ける "the night wears on". Not to be confused with 夜更かし (する) "to stay up late". More matter-of-fact are 夜中 and 深夜.

examples[].german: That treaty will expire tomorrow.
This contract is not valid without a signature.
The effect of this insect repellent spray lasts about five hours.
en.notes: 効力 is "effectiveness" in the sense of legal validity (契約・法律の効力) or the potency of a remedy. Typical are 効力がある / を持つ "to be valid", 効力を失う "to become invalid" and 効力が切れる "the effect wears off". For the result of a measure, people more often say 効果; for medicines, 効き目 is more usual in everyday speech. The word sounds matter-of-fact and formal.

examples[].german: This is a major project aimed at rebuilding the nation.
The temple that collapsed in the earthquake was rebuilt over ten years.
The new president was entrusted with rebuilding the company.
en.notes: 再建 is the "reconstruction" of buildings (寺を再建する), but equally the "restructuring" of organizations and finances: 経営再建, 財政再建, 会社の再建. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を再建する, often in the passive 再建される. For the reconstruction of a whole region after a disaster, one rather says 復興; colloquially, "to rebuild" is also 建て直す. Note: the identically read 債権 means "claim (creditor's right)".

en.meaning: to take up (a post, position); to assume
examples[].german: Why do you want a job that pays a daily wage?
From April, Mr. Tanaka will take the post of section chief.
My grandfather goes to bed at nine every night.
en.notes: 就く is intransitive and takes に: you "take up" a job or position (仕事に就く, 職に就く, 社長の地位に就く). Set phrases are 床に就く "to go to bed" and 帰路に就く "to set off for home". With a company as the destination you don't say 会社に就く but 会社に入る or 就職する; the noun for taking office is 就任. It is also often simply written つく; do not confuse it with 付く "to stick" and 着く "to arrive".

examples[].german: It's okay. The sun will rise again.
The smoke of the bonfire slowly rises into the sky.
He rose to the position of department head at thirty.
en.notes: 昇る is intransitive and is used for things that rise on their own: 日が昇る "the sun rises", 煙が昇る, and for advancement in a career (地位に昇る). For stairs, slopes or numbers use 上る, and for climbing a mountain with effort 登る. The counterpart for the course of the sun is 日が沈む; figuratively 天にも昇る気持ち means "to be overjoyed".

en.meaning: to get angry; to be furious
examples[].german: I'm seriously furious. You're getting in the way of my practice!
Doesn't that clerk's attitude annoy you a bit?
Even when something makes me angry, I try not to get angry right away.
en.notes: 腹立つ is the colloquial short form of 腹が立つ "to get angry, to become furious"; in written or polite language the form with が is used. It describes inner anger, whereas 怒る expresses more the visible scolding. The cause is marked with に or stands as the subject: 彼の態度に腹が立つ, あの態度、腹立つ. The related adjective is 腹立たしい "irritating".

examples[].german: The daimyo ordered that low-ranking samurai to commit harakiri.
The harakiri scene in the period drama was a little scary.
The word "harakiri" is famous abroad, but in Japan people more often say "seppuku".
en.notes: 腹切り is the ritual suicide of samurai by cutting open the belly (腹 "belly" + 切り "cutting"). Abroad it is known as "harakiri", but in Japanese 腹切り sounds rather colloquial; in history books and formal language people say 切腹. Typical are 腹切りを命じる and 腹切りをする.

examples[].german: That is an interesting idea.
Children have a free way of thinking that adults lack.
If you change your way of thinking, you may be able to solve the problem quickly.
en.notes: 発想 means "idea, inspiration, way of thinking" - above all the way one comes up with something: 面白い発想, 自由な発想, 発想を変える "to rethink". The word emphasizes the creative approach; for a concrete idea, everyday speech often uses アイデア, and for a spontaneous notion 思いつき. Important compounds are 発想力 "inventiveness" and 発想の転換 "change of perspective".

examples[].german: The housewife made 30,000 yen on the stock market.
My mother has been a full-time housewife ever since she got married.
In this supermarket, many of the daytime customers are housewives.
en.notes: 主婦 is the "housewife" who runs the household. A distinction is made between 専業主婦 "full-time housewife" and 兼業主婦 "working housewife"; a househusband is the identically pronounced 主夫. The word is neutral and often appears in advertising and the media as a target group (主婦向け). When talking about someone else's wife, however, you use 奥さん.

examples[].german: I finally received a final notice.
When I didn't pay my rent, the landlord formally demanded payment.
If there is no reply by the deadline, we will send a formal demand in writing.
en.notes: 催告 is a legal technical term for a formal "demand" to fulfill an obligation, such as a payment (支払いの催告). As a transitive する-verb: 〜を催告する; the letter is called 催告書, the final demand 最終催告. In everyday speech, for payment reminders people more often say 督促 or simply 請求; 催告 is mainly encountered in contracts, official letters and legal texts.

examples[].german: I wonder what a golf tournament hosted by celebrities is like.
This fireworks festival is hosted by the city every year.
First, there will be a greeting from the organizer.
en.notes: 主催 means "hosting, organizing" - the person or organization itself is called 主催者 "organizer". Typical is 〜主催の + event (市主催の祭り) as well as 〜が主催する "to host, to organize". Related are 共催 "joint hosting", 後援 "patronage" and 協賛 "sponsorship". Not to be confused with the identically read 主宰 "to head (a group, magazine)".

examples[].german: Something came out of the completely collapsed building.
A house near the sea was completely destroyed by the typhoon.
The car was totaled in the accident, but the driver was unharmed.
en.notes: 全壊 means "complete destruction" of buildings or vehicles, for example by earthquake, typhoon or accident. As an intransitive する-verb: 家が全壊する (not with を). In damage reports it appears alongside 半壊 "partially destroyed" and 一部損壊 "damaged"; 倒壊 stresses collapsing. The identically read 全快 means "complete recovery".

examples[].german: Just now a news ticker said "London Bridge collapses in terror attack"! Is that true?
Many old houses collapsed in the big earthquake.
This building is in danger of collapse, so please do not approach.
en.notes: 倒壊 refers to the "collapse" of buildings, bridges or walls, mostly due to earthquakes or disasters. As an intransitive する-verb: 家が倒壊する; also typical is 倒壊のおそれがある "danger of collapse". In everyday speech people say 崩れる or 倒れる; 崩壊 is also used abstractly (経済の崩壊), while 全壊 stresses complete destruction. The word is typical of the news.

examples[].german: Clara is the only daughter of the Sesemann family.
After my only daughter got married, the house suddenly became quiet.
She is an only daughter, so she was raised very carefully by her parents.
en.notes: 一人娘 is the "only daughter" and usually means that the couple has only this one child at all. Correspondingly, the only son is 一人息子; "only child" in general is 一人っ子. The word often carries the undertone that the daughter is especially sheltered (一人娘を大切に育てる).

examples[].german: Zen Buddhism teaches emptying the mind and focusing on the present.
There are many Zen temples in Kyoto.
Zen Buddhism was transmitted from China to Japan in the Kamakura period.
en.notes: 禅宗 refers to Zen Buddhism as a school (宗 "school, sect", cf. 浄土宗). In Japan the most important branches are 臨済宗 and 曹洞宗, which came from China in the Kamakura period. In everyday speech people often say just 禅, for example in 座禅 "Zen meditation" or 禅寺 "Zen temple".

examples[].german: I've been put in charge of organizing the next banquet.
At the company banquet, the department head sang karaoke.
This inn has a banquet hall that holds a hundred people.
en.notes: 宴会 is a convivial meal with a lot of drinking in a group, typically at a company, club or ryokan; 忘年会, 新年会 and 歓迎会 are types of 宴会. Typical are 宴会を開く, 宴会に出る and 宴会の幹事 "organizer of the party"; the hall is called 宴会場. More casual is 飲み会, Western-influenced and often standing is パーティー.

examples[].german: You'd better stop dieting in an unhealthy way.
Eating only convenience store bento every day is unhealthy.
I keep up an unhealthy lifestyle of staying up until late at night.
en.notes: 不健康 is a な-adjective or noun meaning "unhealthy": 不健康な生活, 不健康な食事. In everyday speech people often simply say 体に悪い. Do not confuse it with 不健全 "morally questionable, unsound" (不健全な関係). The prefix 不 negates, as in 不便 or 不安.

examples[].german: My anger doesn't last more than three minutes.
The minister's irresponsible remark made the public's anger explode.
I held back my anger and tried to speak calmly.
en.notes: 怒り is the noun for 怒る and means "rage, anger, indignation". Typical combinations are 怒りを感じる, 怒りを抑える "to suppress anger", 怒りが爆発する "anger erupts" and 怒りを買う "to incur someone's wrath". It is read いかり, although the verb is usually おこる. It is somewhat more factual than 腹立ち, and often used in the news for public outrage (国民の怒り).

en.meaning: to focus on; to pay attention to
examples[].german: I focused on this point.
She is doing research focusing on children's sleeping hours.
One should pay attention not only to the price but also to the quality.
en.notes: 着目する means "to direct one's attention to something, to deliberately take an aspect into view" and takes に: この点に着目する, 〜に着目して研究する. It is literary and typical of analyses, reports and science. Unlike 注目する, which generally means "to pay/attract attention" (注目を集める), 着目 stresses the deliberate singling out of a specific point as a starting point.

examples[].german: Both my father and I are afraid of heights.
I have claustrophobia, so I'm not good with small elevators.
He has social phobia and is said to be very afraid of meeting people.
en.notes: 恐怖症 is a "phobia" (恐怖 "fear" + 症 "condition") and mostly appears as a suffix: 高所恐怖症 "fear of heights", 閉所恐怖症 "claustrophobia", 対人恐怖症 "social phobia". Colloquially it is also used jokingly (月曜日恐怖症). For a mere dislike people rather say 〜が苦手; 恐怖 alone is general "fear, dread".

examples[].german: This restaurant's sign is big and stands out well.
This ramen is our shop's signature dish.
Sorry, we're closed for today.
en.notes: 看板 is first of all a "sign, shop sign, billboard" (看板を出す / 掲げる). Figuratively it means the "showpiece" of a business: 看板メニュー "house specialty", 看板娘 "the shop's poster girl", and reputation (看板に傷がつく). In restaurants and bars, もう看板です means "we're closing now". A traffic sign, by contrast, is called 標識.

examples[].german: Japanese food is popular in the West too.
In the West, many people keep their shoes on even inside the house.
After the war, the Japanese diet rapidly became Westernized.
en.notes: 欧米 stands for "Europe and America" and thus for "the West" (欧 = Europe, 米 = America). Common are 欧米人 "Westerners", 欧米諸国 "Western countries" and 欧米化 "Westernization". The older, culturally colored 西洋 "the Occident" is often contrasted with 東洋 "the Orient"; 欧米 is the usual word in news and everyday speech.

examples[].german: The Edo period lasted about 260 years.
Edo is the old name of present-day Tokyo.
My grandfather says he himself is a true "Edokko".
en.notes: 江戸 is the old name of Tokyo, until the city was renamed 東京 in 1868. It is most often encountered in 江戸時代 "Edo period" (1603-1868) and 江戸幕府 "Tokugawa shogunate". A true Tokyoite whose family has lived there for generations proudly calls himself 江戸っ子; words like 江戸前 designate the traditional Tokyo style, for example with sushi.

en.meaning: to attach; to enclose; to garnish
examples[].german: If you garnish the ice cream with mint leaves, it looks a bit stylish.
I sent a short letter along with the birthday present.
Her singing added a touch of splendor to the party.
en.notes: 添える is transitive: AにBを添える means to put B with A as an accompaniment or supplement - a garnish to food, a letter with a gift, a helping hand (手を添える). Figuratively, 花を添える means "to add extra splendor". Unlike 加える or 足す ("to add, to mix in"), with 添える the added thing remains something separate standing alongside. The intransitive partner is 添う "to accompany, to snuggle up to".

examples[].german: My impression of Mr. Miyazaki when we first met was very strong.
The intense summer sunlight turned my skin bright red.
This cheese has a pungent smell.
en.notes: 強烈 is a な-adjective for a very strong, penetrating effect on the senses or the impression: 強烈な日差し, 強烈なにおい, 強烈な印象, 強烈なキャラ "quirky, striking personality". The neutral 強い is weaker; 激しい emphasizes violent movement or emotions, 猛烈 rather wild force and speed. Possible both positively and negatively.

examples[].german: He finished the work at a furious speed.
A violent typhoon is approaching Kyushu.
From a week before the exam, I studied like mad.
en.notes: 猛烈 is a な-adjective for wild, impetuous strength or speed: 猛烈な台風, 猛烈な暑さ, 猛烈なスピード. Adverbially, 猛烈に means "like crazy, with all one's might" (猛烈に反対する, 猛烈に勉強する). 強烈 refers more to sensory impressions and the impression made, 激しい is the more general "violent". In weather reports, 猛烈な is even an official level for typhoons and rain.

examples[].german: Passionate fans of the band filled the venue.
The players received an enthusiastic welcome from fans at the airport.
He wrote her a passionate love letter.
en.notes: 熱烈 is a な-adjective for glowing, passionate feelings: 熱烈なファン "ardent fan", 熱烈な歓迎 "enthusiastic welcome", 熱烈な恋, adverbially 熱烈に応援する. 熱心, by contrast, means "eager, dedicated" (熱心に勉強する) and describes diligence, not passion. 熱烈歓迎 is often seen as a set greeting on signs.

en.meaning: to pay attention to; to take note of
examples[].german: The whole world is watching.
Everyone, please look this way.
That new product is attracting attention among young people.
en.notes: 注目する means "to pay attention to, to follow closely" and takes に: 〜に注目する, 世界中が注目している. Very common expressions are 注目を集める/浴びる "to attract attention" and 注目の〜 "much-watched" (注目の新人). Teachers say to the class: こちらに注目してください. Compared with 着目する (focusing on one particular aspect), 注目する is more general; being careful about dangers is 注意する instead.

examples[].german: He studied like mad and passed the university entrance exam.
This summer, days of intense heat continue.
A car sped past right in front of me at breakneck speed.
en.notes: 猛〜 is a prefix meaning "fierce, extreme, wild" and intensifies the following noun: 猛勉強 "cramming", 猛練習 "hard training", 猛反対 "fierce opposition", 猛スピード "breakneck speed". Some formations are fixed words, such as 猛暑 "extreme heat" (in the weather report, 猛暑日 is a day of 35 °C or more). Many of them are used with する (猛勉強する, 猛反対する).

en.meaning: to abbreviate; to shorten; to omit
examples[].german: Young people in Japan are quick to shorten words and phrases.
"国際連合" is abbreviated to "国連".
We're short on time, so I'll skip the detailed explanation.
en.notes: 略す means "to abbreviate" and "to omit" and is transitive: 〜を略す. Very typical is the pattern AをBと略す ("to abbreviate A as B") and the form 略して "in short, abbreviated": 国際連合、略して国連. For leaving out parts (e.g. an explanation), 省略する or 省く is more common in everyday speech; 略す sounds somewhat more concise and literary. The related noun is 略 ("abbreviation"), cf. 略語.

examples[].german: In Japanese conversation, the default is to omit the grammatical subject unless it is needed.
"パーソナルコンピューター" is abbreviated and called "パソコン".
I don't have time, so I'll omit the detailed explanation.
en.notes: 省略 is "omission, abbreviation" and, as a transitive する-verb, "to leave out, to abbreviate": 説明を省略する, 主語を省略する. Typical are 省略形 "short form" and 以下省略 "rest omitted". More colloquial is the verb 略す (to abbreviate words), and 省く means "to leave out, to save" (手間を省く).

examples[].german: I'll draw a rough map from the station to my house and send it by email.
A rough map to the venue is on the back of the invitation.
Please explain the situation at the time of the accident with a sketch.
en.notes: 略図 is a simplified, rough drawing, usually a route sketch or location map that one makes quickly by hand. Typical are 略図をかく (描く/書く) and 〜までの略図 "a sketch to ...". A proper, scale city map is 地図; an artistic sketch is more often called スケッチ or 下絵, a floor plan 見取り図. On invitations one often finds 会場略図 "sketch map of the venue".

examples[].german: Could you at least tell me the outline of the meeting?
Now, I will explain the outline of the new plan.
The course of the incident is, in outline, as follows.
en.notes: 大略 is a formal, literary word for "outline, summary": 計画の大略, 大略を説明する. As an adverb it means "by and large, in essence", for example in reports: 大略次のとおりである. In everyday speech people instead say 概要, あらまし or simply だいたい or ざっと; 大略 therefore fits better in meetings, reports and polite requests.

examples[].german: I don't have any particular pain.
If you take this medicine, the pain will go away right away.
The pain in my heart from losing my friend didn't disappear easily.
en.notes: 痛み is the noun for 痛い and denotes physical as well as emotional "pain". Typical combinations: 痛みがある/ない, 痛みを感じる, 痛みが取れる ("the pain goes away"), 痛みに強い/弱い and 心の痛み. In daily life people usually just say 頭が痛い; 痛み sounds more factual and is common at the doctor's, for example. Note: the meaning "damage, wear" is usually written 傷み (cf. 傷む).

examples[].german: My headache is bad, so I took a painkiller.
I got a painkiller from the dentist.
The painkiller has started to work, and I feel a little better.
en.notes: 痛み止め (from 痛む "to ache" and 止める "to stop") is the everyday word for a painkiller; in technical language and on package inserts it is 鎮痛剤. Tablets are "taken" in Japanese with 飲む: 痛み止めを飲む. Also common are 痛み止めが効く "the painkiller works" and 痛み止めの注射 "painkilling injection".

examples[].german: Lately I can't sleep well because of stress.
The baby is sound asleep.
My grandfather rests at this temple.
en.notes: 眠る means "to sleep" in the sense of "actually being asleep". 寝る is broader and also means "to go to bed, to lie down" – one can be 寝ている and still not be able to 眠れる. Very common is the potential form 眠れない "cannot sleep"; "tired, sleepy", by contrast, is 眠い. In an elevated register 眠る also stands for the dead ("to rest") and for unused things (眠っている才能 "dormant talent").

examples[].german: Fairy tales often have stories in which a sleeping potion is used to put someone to sleep.
I took a sleeping pill before bed, so I didn't wake up once until morning.
It is dangerous to take alcohol and sleeping pills together.
en.notes: 眠り薬 is made up of 眠り ("sleep") and 薬, with くすり becoming ぐすり. It is the everyday, somewhat old-fashioned word for "sleeping drug"; in medicine and on package inserts it is called 睡眠薬 or 睡眠導入剤. One says 眠り薬を飲む; in fairy tales and crime stories, 眠り薬を使う or 〜に眠り薬を飲ませる ("to give someone a sleeping drug") also occurs.

examples[].german: Find the volume of this cube.
When water freezes, its volume increases.
This box is very light for its volume.
en.notes: 体積 is the spatial "volume" of a body in mathematics and physics: 体積を求める/計算する, 体積が増える/減る. To be distinguished from 容積 (capacity, the internal volume of a container), 容量 (capacity, also amount of data) and 面積 ("area"). "Loudness" is not 体積 but 音量 or ボリューム.

examples[].german: I recovered from my illness.
The weather improved in the afternoon, so we could play outside.
The economy is not recovering easily.
en.notes: 回復する means to return to an earlier good state. Usually intransitive with が: 体力・景気・天気が回復する; one recovers from an illness with から (病気から回復する). Transitive with を it means "to regain": 意識を回復する, 信用を回復する. Unlike 治る (the illness itself heals), 回復 usually focuses on the person, the strength or the situation.

examples[].german: I am hoping for good results.
I want to live up to my parents' expectations.
The movie wasn't as interesting as I had expected.
en.notes: 期待する means "to expect, to hope, to look forward to something" and has a positive tone: 良い結果を期待する, 〜に期待する "to count on someone". Set phrases are 期待に応える "to meet expectations", 期待を裏切る "to disappoint" and 期待外れ "disappointing". For a neutral forecast (including of negative things) use 予想する or 見込む; "to wait for someone" is 待つ.

examples[].german: My father is going to have emergency surgery.
In case of emergency, please call this number.
Something urgent has come up, so I'll go home early today.
en.notes: 緊急 means "urgent, emergency" and mostly appears as the first element of compounds: 緊急手術, 緊急事態, 緊急停止, 緊急地震速報. Attributively both 緊急の (緊急の場合 "in an emergency") and 緊急な (緊急な用事) are possible; also 緊急時. Related are 急 ("sudden, hurried": 急な用事), 至急 ("immediately", typical in office emails: 至急ご連絡ください) and 非常 ("emergency": 非常口 "emergency exit").

examples[].german: This seat belt tightens automatically.
The tie is tight and I can hardly breathe.
Since I started exercising every day, my body has become firmer.
en.notes: 締まる is intransitive: something "becomes tight, tightens up", such as a ねじ (screw), belt or ネクタイ (tie); the transitive counterpart is 締める (ベルトを締める). Figuratively it means "to become taut, toned" (体が締まる) or "to become tense, focused", often as 引き締まる (気が引き締まる). Do not confuse it with 閉まる "to close" (ドアが閉まる), which is read the same.

examples[].german: Where did you learn aerial navigation?
Sailors of old used celestial navigation, steering by the positions of the stars.
Today's airplanes fly using GPS-based navigation.
en.notes: 航法 is a technical term for the "navigation" of ships and aircraft, that is, the technique of determining position and course: 天文航法 ("celestial navigation"), 推測航法 ("dead reckoning"), 衛星航法. In everyday speech, for example when driving a car, people say ナビ or カーナビ, not 航法. Watch out for similar-sounding words: 広報 ("public relations"), 後方 ("rear").

examples[].german: This ship sails directly to Kobe Port.
Because of the typhoon, the ship went straight to its destination without calling at ports along the way.
There used to be daily direct flights connecting Tokyo and Naha.
en.notes: 直航 refers to a direct ship or flight connection without a stopover; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 〜に/へ直航する. Common is the compound 直航便 ("direct service, direct flight"). For flights, people mostly write 直行便 today; 直行 generally means "to go directly" (会社に直行する), whereas 直航 is limited to ship and air traffic and is more literary.

examples[].german: If you keep going straight along this highway, you'll eventually reach Kyoto.
In the old days, travelers walked along highways such as the Tokaido toward Edo.
Since his debut, he has kept running on the fast track to success.
en.notes: 街道 are above all the historic long-distance roads of the Edo period, such as the 五街道 with 東海道 and 中山道; many roads today still bear names like 甲州街道 or 日光街道. For ordinary city streets one says 道, 通り or 道路, for national highways 国道. Figuratively, 〜街道 stands for a "path" in life, especially 出世街道 ("career ladder, fast track to success").

examples[].german: When I had the doctor examine me, I was told it was just a cold.
Doctor, could you take a look at this wound, please?
This hospital sees patients even on Sundays.
en.notes: 診る is used only for medical examination: the subject is the doctor, the object the patient or a body part (患者を診る, 傷を診る, 脈を診る). From the patient's point of view, 医者に診てもらう is the standard form. Ordinary "to see" is 見る, "to nurse, to look after" is 看る (親を看る). More formal is 診察する; the kanji 診 is also in 診断 ("diagnosis").

en.meaning: to take on (a job); to undertake
examples[].german: Taking on this project is risky, but I'd like to take up the challenge.
I work freelance and take on translation jobs.
We just can't find a company that will take on this construction job.
en.notes: 請ける is a special spelling of うける for accepting jobs and contracts: 仕事を請ける, 注文を請ける, 工事を請ける. In all other meanings ("to receive", "to take an exam") one writes 受ける, and many write 受ける even for jobs. More common than the simple verb are the derivatives 請け負う ("to take on a contract"), 下請け ("subcontractor") and 元請け ("main contractor").

examples[].german: This isn't mine; it's a rental bicycle.
We played on the lake riding a rental boat.
Let's have the meeting in the rental meeting room in front of the station.
en.notes: 貸し〜 is a prefix from 貸す and denotes something lent or rented out for a fee - from the provider's point of view: 貸し自転車, 貸しボート, 貸し衣装, 貸し会議室. The okurigana し is often dropped on signs (貸自転車, 貸会議室). Today it competes with レンタル〜 (レンタサイクル). On its own, 貸し means "a favor someone owes you": 彼には貸しがある. Do not confuse it with 貸し切り ("exclusively rented").

examples[].german: I have no sense of direction and often get lost.
I got lost and was late for the appointment.
When you get lost in the mountains, it is better not to move around much.
en.notes: 道に迷う is the fixed expression for "to get lost, to lose one's way"; the particle に is fixed. On its own, 迷う means "to hesitate, to be undecided" (どちらにするか迷う). A lost child is 迷子 (迷子になる); colloquially adults also say 迷子になった. Someone who generally has no sense of direction is 方向音痴. Figuratively there is 人生の道に迷う ("to lose one's bearings in life").

examples[].german: Last year I went to South Korea.
I like Korean food.
en.notes: 韓国 here means South Korea. With に you name the country as a travel destination; 韓国の料理 links country and cuisine with の. The word is read かんこく and has no long vowels. 去年 names the past year; 好き marks a personal preference.

examples[].german: I demand a pay raise.
The customer demanded a refund from the store.
This job requires high language skills.
en.notes: 要求する means "to demand, to require" - often emphatically, as a right or condition: 賃上げを要求する, 〜に〜を要求する, 説明を要求する. It is much more demanding than 頼む or お願いする "to ask"; 求める is similar but more neutral. Often used in the passive: 〜が要求される "is required". As a noun: 要求に応じる "to comply with a demand".

examples[].german: This custom is often seen in both Japan and South Korea.
Soccer matches between Japan and Korea are always very exciting.
I looked up a Korean word in a Japanese-Korean dictionary.
en.notes: 日韓 is the short form for "Japan and (South) Korea" and almost always stands before a noun: 日韓関係, 日韓戦, 日韓両国, 日韓辞典 ("Japanese-Korean dictionary"). From the Japanese perspective, 日 comes first; in Korea, people say it the other way round, 韓日. 韓 refers to South Korea (韓国); for Japan-North Korea one says 日朝. Formed on the same pattern are 日米, 日中 and 日独.

examples[].german: It is difficult to explain odd numbers to a three-year-old child.
An odd number is a number that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2.
People in even-numbered seats, please move to the right; people in odd-numbered seats, please move to the left.
en.notes: 奇数 is the "odd number", the opposite is 偶数 ("even number"). Attributively it takes の: 奇数の日, 奇数の席, 奇数の月. The kanji 奇 also means "strange" (cf. 奇妙). Culturally, odd amounts are considered appropriate for wedding gifts in Japan because they cannot be "divided" - hence, for example, 3万円.

examples[].german: Do you know the TV program "Yo ni mo Kimyo na Monogatari"?
I woke up when I heard a strange sound in the middle of the night.
It's a curious story that the two of them had the same dream.
en.notes: 奇妙 is a な-adjective for "strange, odd" in the sense of hard to explain or slightly eerie: 奇妙な音, 奇妙な話, 奇妙な形. It sounds somewhat more literary than 変な or おかしな; 不思議な stresses more the wondrous and is neutral to positive. A common phrase: 奇妙なことに ("strangely enough").

examples[].german: "How can you say something so cold!" said Koichi in an angry voice.
The department head's words carried a note of anger.
He suppressed his anger and began to speak quietly.
en.notes: 怒気 is a literary word for the "anger" that can be felt in a voice, words or expression. Typical are 怒気を帯びる ("to be filled with anger"), 怒気を含んだ声 and 怒気を抑える. In spoken language people say 怒り or 腹が立つ; 激怒, by contrast, refers to a violent outburst of rage.

examples[].german: I'm hungry. Make me something.
After club activities I'm always starving.
Ah, I'm hungry. Let's go get some ramen or something.
en.notes: 腹が減った is the rough, mainly male way of saying "I'm hungry": 腹 "belly" is coarser than お腹, 減る means "to decrease", and the past tense describes the present state. Even more casual is 腹減った without が. Neutrally one says お腹が空いた, politely お腹が空きました; 腹が減った is inappropriate in polite situations.

examples[].german: It's been three years since I last visited here.
Every year, many tourists visit Kyoto.
The long winter ended, and spring finally arrived.
en.notes: 訪れる means "to visit, to call on" and sounds more elevated than 行く or 訪ねる; it is used mainly with places: 京都を訪れる, 現地を訪れる. For visits to people, 訪ねる is more usual. Intransitively it is used for times and events that "come, set in": 春が訪れる, チャンスが訪れる. The noun is 訪れ (春の訪れ).

examples[].german: There are rumors that he is being watched by the police.
This building is monitored by cameras 24 hours a day.
During the exam, the teacher monitored the students while walking around the classroom.
en.notes: 監視 is "surveillance, supervision"; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を監視する, passive 監視される. Common compounds are 監視カメラ, 監視員 (e.g. lifeguard) and 監視下. 見張る is a simpler word for "to keep watch", 観察 means "to observe" in the neutral or scientific sense, and 見守る is a benevolent "to watch over someone". 監視 often carries an undertone of control and distrust.

examples[].german: I think solicitation phone calls are a nuisance.
When you enter university, you get recruited by various clubs.
It is hard to turn down persistent insurance sales pitches.
en.notes: 勧誘 is recruiting people to join, buy or sign a contract, often with an intrusive undertone: 新聞の勧誘, 保険の勧誘, 宗教の勧誘, サークルの勧誘. Construction: 人を〜に勧誘する, passive 勧誘される. Advertising of products in the media, by contrast, is 広告 or 宣伝. The simple everyday word for "to invite, to ask" is 誘う.

examples[].german: I'm currently working at a factory as a trainee.
Three new trainees will join us starting next month.
While you are a trainee, you learn the work by following your seniors.
en.notes: 研修生 is someone who is going through a 研修 - training, orientation or further education - such as new employees at a company. In Japan it often also refers to foreign workers in training programs (外国人研修生, today mostly 技能実習生). An internship during university is more often called インターン; 新入社員 are simply "new employees". Typical: 研修生として働く, 研修生を受け入れる.

examples[].german: Spam emails keep coming one after another.
An important email was in the spam folder.
Please delete spam emails from people you don't know without opening them.
en.notes: 迷惑メール (迷惑 "nuisance" + メール) is the usual everyday word for spam; there is also スパムメール. Typical phrases are 迷惑メールフォルダ "spam folder", 迷惑メールに振り分けられる "to end up in spam" and 迷惑メール対策 "spam protection". On the same pattern, 迷惑電話 is formed for nuisance calls.

examples[].german: I emphasize the importance.
The president stressed that safety comes first.
I highlighted the important parts in red.
en.notes: 強調する means "to emphasize, to highlight", in speech as well as in writing: 重要性を強調する, 〜と強調する "to say emphatically that ...". Also visually: 赤い字で強調する, 太字で強調する. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 協調 "cooperation, coordination". Literally it means "strong tone".

examples[].german: I'm glad the housekeeper is sensible.
Both my parents work, so a housekeeper comes twice a week.
I work as a housekeeper, cooking and cleaning at the homes of elderly people.
en.notes: 家政婦 is a paid housekeeper or domestic helper who cleans, cooks and does laundry; people usually say 家政婦さん politely. Today 家事代行 ("housework service") and ハウスキーパー are also common, and お手伝いさん is somewhat old-fashioned. Do not confuse it with 主婦 ("housewife"), who runs her own household. Typical: 家政婦さんに来てもらう, 家政婦として働く.

examples[].german: If you make Dad angry, it's a hassle afterwards.
I meant it as a joke, but I ended up making her angry.
Please be careful with your words so you don't anger the customers.
en.notes: 怒らせる is the causative form of 怒る "to get angry" and means "to anger, to make someone furious": 人を怒らせる. Very common is 怒らせてしまう for accidentally angering someone. There is also the equivalent, somewhat more casual form 怒らす. Do not confuse it with 怒る in the sense of "to scold" (子どもを怒る) or the stricter 叱る.

examples[].german: Brown rice is good for the body.
Brown rice takes longer to cook than white rice.
Lately I've been trying to eat rice mixed with brown rice.
en.notes: 玄米 is unhulled "natural" or "whole-grain rice" from which only the husk has been removed; the opposite is 白米 or 精米 ("polished rice"). One says 玄米を炊く, and it is considered healthy but takes longer to cook. Also well known is 玄米茶, green tea with roasted rice. Cooked rice in general is ご飯, raw rice 米.

en.meaning: to drop by; to stop by
examples[].german: I plan to drop by the library on my way home from school.
I'm taking a photo, so please move a little closer to the middle.
If you are ever nearby, please do drop by our place, too.
en.notes: 寄る has two core meanings. First, "to drop by briefly, to stop on the way", with the destination marked by に: 帰りにスーパーに寄る; similar is 立ち寄る. Second, "to approach, to move to the side": もう少し右に寄ってください; 近寄る belongs here. The transitive counterpart is 寄せる "to move closer, to bring near". Do not confuse it with よる in ～によると "according to", which is written in kana.

examples[].german: If you have doubts, you should think about it a little longer.
Hearing his words, my hesitation disappeared.
She answered "I'll do it" with a face free of hesitation.
en.notes: 迷い is the noun for 迷う and denotes "doubt, indecision, hesitation" before a decision. Typical are 迷いがある/ない, 迷いが消える, 迷いを捨てる and attributively 迷いのない表情 ("without any hesitation"). ためらい stresses more the hesitation before an action, 疑い is "suspicion". In the Buddhist sense, 迷い also stands for "delusion".

examples[].german: Searching becomes difficult at night, so we plan to stop for now and resume early in the morning.
The police are searching for the missing child.
The police searched the man's house and found evidence.
en.notes: 捜索 is an organized "search" for missing persons or things (捜索隊, 捜索願を出す "to file a missing person report") and the police "search" of premises (家宅捜索). As a transitive する-verb: 人/場所を捜索する. In everyday speech one simply says 探す/捜す. Not to be confused with 検索 ("search" on the internet or in databases) and 捜査 ("police investigation").

examples[].german: I leave everything about this shop to your judgment.
I'll leave the details to you, so feel free to do as you like.
I've done all I can, so all that's left is to leave the rest to luck.
en.notes: 任す is a variant of the much more common 任せる (ichidan) with the same meaning "to leave, to entrust": AをBに任す. It sounds somewhat more colloquial or older; it is familiar mainly in forms such as 任しておけ ("Leave that to me!"). In neutral and polite contexts, it is better to use 任せる (お任せします, 任せてください).

examples[].german: There are few tonkatsu restaurants around here.
The day before the exam, I ate tonkatsu as a pun on "win" (katsu).
Sauce and cabbage go well with tonkatsu.
en.notes: 豚カツ is a breaded, deep-fried pork cutlet; it is mostly written とんかつ or トンカツ, and the mixed spelling 豚カツ is also common. カツ comes from "cutlet" and is found in カツ丼, カツカレー, ヒレカツ and ロースカツ. Before exams or competitions, people like to eat it as a pun on 勝つ ("to win"). A tonkatsu restaurant is called 豚カツ屋.

examples[].german: When my mother saw that, she flew into a rage.
The company president was furious at his subordinate's big mistake.
The player's rude remark enraged the fans.
en.notes: 激怒 is "raging anger" and, as an intransitive する-verb, "to be beside oneself with rage"; the cause takes に: 〜に激怒する. Causative: 〜を激怒させる ("to send someone into a rage"). It is clearly stronger than 怒る and typical of the news and reports; colloquially one more often says かんかんに怒る or ブチ切れる. The literary 怒気, by contrast, denotes anger that can be felt in the voice or expression.

en.meaning: to occur in succession; to follow one after another
examples[].german: That YouTuber kept making content, undeterred by the string of critical voices.
This year, big earthquakes have occurred one after another.
Reservations are coming in one after another for the new shop.
en.notes: 相次ぐ is intransitive and means "to follow one after another, to pile up"; the subject takes が: 事故が相次ぐ. Very common are the attributive form (相次ぐ批判, 相次ぐトラブル) and the te-form as the adverb 相次いで ("one after another"). The word is typical of the news; in daily life people more often say 次々に or 続けて. 続く is more general and stresses only continuation.

examples[].german: I reject that opinion.
The minister denied the rumor.
It is not good to dismiss other people's dreams out of hand.
en.notes: 否定する means "to deny, to dispute, to reject": うわさを否定する, 事実を否定する, 自分を否定する. It means to portray something as untrue or wrong - unlike 断る "to decline (a request)" or 反対する "to oppose". In the news, 〜を否定した often means "denied". The opposite is 肯定する; in grammar, 否定形 is the negative form.

examples[].german: The former prime minister held the same view.
The prime minister explained the new policy at a press conference.
Who do you think will be the next prime minister?
en.notes: 総理 is the short form of 内閣総理大臣, the Japanese "Prime Minister". Newspapers mostly use 首相, while on TV and in spoken language 総理 or 総理大臣 is often heard; the prime minister is also addressed directly as 総理. 元総理 is a "former prime minister". A head of state, by contrast, is called 大統領.

examples[].german: That samurai is famous for taking a very beautiful middle-level stance.
The company is showing a posture of readiness to fight it out in court.
There is an impressive-looking Japanese confectionery shop in front of the station.
en.notes: 構え is the noun of 構える. In martial arts and sports it is the "posture, basic stance": 構えをとる, 中段の構え, バットの構え. Figuratively, 〜構え means "readiness, determination" to do something, for example in the news: 争う構えを見せる. For buildings it means the "outward appearance, the facade" (立派な構えの店). The inner attitude is called 心構え.

examples[].german: I went to the Food Expo, "Shokuhaku" for short!
In 2025, a World Expo was held in Osaka.
The expo grounds were full of people even on weekdays.
en.notes: 博覧会 is a large public "exhibition, expo" on a theme, often with pavilions and many visitors; 万国博覧会 (short 万博) is the "World Expo". It is often abbreviated with 〜博 (食博, 花博). An art exhibition is called 展覧会, a product or trade fair 展示会 or 見本市. Typical: 博覧会が開かれる, 博覧会に行く.

examples[].german: There are many immigrants from Asia in the towns along the West Coast.
Recently, the number of people moving from cities to the countryside is increasing.
This village rents old houses cheaply to newcomers.
en.notes: 移住者 is someone who settles permanently in a new place - both abroad ("emigrant/immigrant") and within Japan, for example from the city to the countryside (地方移住, Iターン). The verb is 移住する. 移民 is narrower and more political and means migrants across state borders. Typical: 〜からの移住者, 移住者が増える, 移住者を受け入れる.

examples[].german: This town lacks greenery.
He has little experience, but he has plenty of motivation.
Japan, which is poor in resources, imports most of its oil.
en.notes: 乏しい is an い-adjective for "scarce, poor in, meager". It takes が (経験が乏しい) or に in the sense of "poor in" (資源に乏しい, 変化に乏しい). Typical related words are abstract: 経験, 知識, 資源, 想像力, 表情. It sounds more literary than 少ない or 足りない; opposites are 豊か and 豊富.

examples[].german: I forgot to chill the juice, so I'll put in some ice.
When you have a fever, it's good to cool your forehead.
Let's cool our heads a bit and then talk it over again.
en.notes: 冷やす is transitive: to actively "cool, make cold" something (ビールを冷やす, 冷蔵庫で冷やす); the intransitive counterpart is 冷える ("to get cold"). 冷ます, by contrast, means letting something hot cool down to a normal temperature (お茶を冷ます). Idiomatically: 頭を冷やす ("to get a cool head") and 肝を冷やす ("to get a fright").

examples[].german: Views on marriage vary from person to person.
My older sister married a friend last year.
en.notes: 結婚 is marriage or wedlock. 結婚する forms an intransitive する-verb. 人と結婚する names the partner with と. 結婚について means "about marriage"; 人によってさまざま describes differing personal views. The small っ in けっこん doubles the k.

examples[].german: I'm thinking of proposing soon.
He proposed to her many times, but was turned down each time.
At the end of the story, the prince proposes to the princess.
en.notes: 求婚 is the "marriage proposal"; as an intransitive する-verb the person takes に: 〜に求婚する. The word is formal or literary and appears mainly in novels, fairy tales and reports. In daily life people almost always say プロポーズする or, neutrally, 結婚を申し込む. Someone who asks for a hand in marriage is a 求婚者.

examples[].german: When are you going on your honeymoon?
We went to Hawaii for our honeymoon.
Work was busy, so our honeymoon took place one year after the wedding.
en.notes: 新婚旅行 is composed of 新婚 ("newly married") and 旅行 and means "honeymoon trip". One says 新婚旅行に行く or 新婚旅行で〜へ行く. The loanword ハネムーン is also common, especially in advertising and travel agencies. Newlyweds are colloquially called 新婚さん.

examples[].german: I decided to extend my return trip by one week.
Could you extend the deadline by three days?
There are plans to extend the subway to the airport.
en.notes: 延ばす is transitive and, with time and distances, means "to extend" or "to postpone": 予定を延ばす, 締め切りを延ばす, 寿命を延ばす, 路線を延ばす. For growth and stretching out the body, it is written 伸ばす (髪を伸ばす, 手を伸ばす, 才能を伸ばす). The intransitive counterpart is 延びる; the more formal word for "to postpone" is 延期する.

examples[].german: I affirm that idea.
In response to the question, he neither confirmed nor denied it.
I want to be able to accept myself even when I have failed.
en.notes: 肯定する means "to affirm, to acknowledge as correct, to approve": 意見を肯定する, 自分を肯定する. The opposite is 否定する; together they appear in 肯定も否定もしない "neither confirm nor deny". Also common is 自己肯定感 "self-esteem". For simple agreement in conversation, 賛成する is more usual; 肯定する is formal and abstract. In grammar, 肯定文 is an affirmative sentence.

examples[].german: I wonder how many times we've extended since we entered the karaoke place.
The game went into overtime with the score tied.
I completed the procedure to extend my visa's expiration date.
en.notes: 延長 is the "extension" of time or distance; as a する-verb it is mostly transitive: 期限を延長する, passive 延長される. In sports, 延長 (延長戦) is the "overtime" of a game. Other compounds: 延長コード ("extension cord"), 延長料金 (e.g. at karaoke). The opposite is 短縮; the native verb with a similar meaning is 延ばす.

examples[].german: Her voice is very pleasing to the ear, like the murmur of a brook.
When I asked him for a favor, he gladly accepted.
I took a walk by the sea, with the pleasant morning breeze blowing.
en.notes: 快い is an elevated い-adjective for "pleasant, soothing": 快い風, 快い眠り, 耳に快い. In everyday speech one rather says 気持ちいい or 心地よい. Very common is the adverb 快く ("willingly, gladly"): 快く引き受ける, 快く承知する. The kanji 快 is also found in 快適, 快感 and 不快.

examples[].german: Plucking the hair on my arm with tweezers feels satisfying.
I can't forget the pleasure of solving a difficult problem.
A shower after working up a sweat is truly delightful.
en.notes: 快感 is an intense "pleasant feeling, thrill", physical or as satisfaction after an achievement: 快感を覚える, 快感を味わう, 〜が快感になる. Depending on context, it can also denote sensual pleasure, so be careful with its use. 快適, by contrast, means "comfortable" (快適な部屋), and 喜び is general "joy".

examples[].german: If you take the rapid train, you'll reach your destination in 30 minutes.
The next rapid train does not stop at this station.
The player made use of his prized speed and ran straight to the goal.
en.notes: 快速 is, in rail transport, a "rapid service, rapid train" that skips smaller stations but usually costs no surcharge. Rough order: 普通/各駅停車 < 快速 < 急行 < 特急 (varying by railway company). In general, 快速 also means "high speed, swiftness", as in 快速船 or 快速を生かす. One says 快速に乗る, 快速電車.

examples[].german: The fabric of these clothes is rough and feels unpleasant.
Everyone felt uncomfortable at his rude attitude.
The rainy season is humid and unpleasant.
en.notes: 不快 is a な-adjective/noun meaning "unpleasant, discomfort, displeasure": 不快な音, 不快に感じる, 不快な思いをする. It is very common in polite apologies: ご不快な思いをおかけして申し訳ございません. It is more formal than 嫌な or 気持ち悪い; the opposites are 快適 and 愉快. Note: 深い ("deep") is read the same way.

examples[].german: That actress has been living in a hotel for half a year because of a film shoot.
Please refrain from taking photographs inside the building.
This photo was taken with a smartphone during a trip.
en.notes: 撮影 covers both photographing and filming, so "shooting, filming"; as a transitive する-verb: 写真/映画を撮影する. It is more formal than 撮る and often appears on signs: 撮影禁止 ("no photography"), 撮影中. Other compounds are 撮影所 ("film studio") and ロケ撮影 ("location shooting").

examples[].german: There's a lot of secret filming at that station, so you'd better be careful.
A man was arrested for secretly filming on the station stairs.
A camera for secret filming had been hidden in the hotel room.
en.notes: 盗撮 (盗 "steal" + 撮 "photograph") is secretly photographing or filming without consent, especially in a voyeuristic way on trains, stairs or in restrooms - a criminal offense in Japan (盗撮で逮捕される). As a transitive する-verb: 〜を盗撮する; also 盗撮カメラ. More neutral is 隠し撮り "secret shooting" (e.g. by paparazzi); the normal word for photographing is 撮影.

examples[].german: It's dangerous to diagnose your own symptoms.
I was diagnosed with influenza at the hospital.
I hear the doctor makes a diagnosis after looking at the test results.
en.notes: 診断する means "to diagnose": 医者が病気を診断する. Very common is the passive 〜と診断される "it is diagnosed as ..." (インフルエンザと診断された). 診察 is the medical examination, 診断 the judgment resulting from it; related are 診断書 "medical certificate" and 健康診断 "health checkup". Figuratively there are also 性格診断 "personality test" and the diagnosis of systems.

examples[].german: I'd like to try learning how to send signals with flags.
At the sports day, the children cheered by waving little flags.
When we reached the summit, we planted a flag as a memento.
en.notes: 旗 is the general word for "flag, banner"; typical verbs are 旗を振る ("to wave"), 旗を立てる ("to put up") and 旗を揚げる ("to hoist"). Compounds: 国旗 ("national flag"), 優勝旗 ("championship flag"), 白旗 ("white flag", 白旗を上げる "to surrender"). The loanword フラグ is used almost only figuratively (games, programming).

examples[].german: He criticized the policy.
That remark was criticized by many people online.
Don't just criticize other people's opinions; offer your own proposal too.
en.notes: 批判する means "to criticize" in the sense of a (often public) assessment of opinions, policies or actions; the thing criticized takes を: 政府を批判する. The passive 批判される "to be criticized" is especially common in the news. For personal grumbling about trivial things, 文句を言う fits better; for scolding by parents or superiors, 注意する or 叱る. The opposite in the sense of recognition is 評価する or 褒める.

en.meaning: to float; to drift; to be left over
examples[].german: Both watermelons and pumpkins float on water.
In my new class, I feel like I'm the only one who sticks out.
If I commute by bicycle, I save on transportation costs.
en.notes: 浮く is intransitive and means "to float on the surface, to drift, to hover" (水に浮く, 空中に浮く) - in contrast to 泳ぐ, active swimming; the opposite is 沈む. The transitive counterpart is 浮かべる ("to set afloat"); related is 浮かぶ ("to surface, to come to mind"). Colloquially, 浮いている means "to be out of place, not to fit in", and お金が浮く means "money is saved, is left over".

examples[].german: I'm thirsty, so go buy me some juice!
On hot days, try to drink water before you get thirsty.
Since childhood, he has always thirsted for his parents' love.
en.notes: 渇く is used almost exclusively in 喉が渇く ("to be thirsty, to get thirsty"); "I'm thirsty" is expressed with 喉が渇いた (past tense). Do not confuse it with the homophone 乾く ("to dry": 洗濯物が乾く). Literarily, 〜に渇く also means "to thirst for, to long for something" (愛に渇く). The related noun is 渇き.

examples[].german: The cause of the water leak was an old pipe.
Water is leaking from the ceiling, so I contacted the management company.
The water supply will be unavailable tomorrow morning due to a leak survey.
en.notes: 漏水 is the leaking of water from pipes, roofs or tanks - a rather technical term from building management, construction and waterworks. As an intransitive する-verb: 天井から漏水している. Typical compounds are 漏水事故 and 漏水調査. In everyday speech people usually simply say 水漏れ or 水が漏れる.

examples[].german: Gas is leaking from the collapsed building and it's dangerous, so stay away.
Because of an accident at the factory, harmful substances leaked into the river.
We regularly inspect the water pipes to check whether water is leaking.
en.notes: 漏出 is a technical, literary word for the escape of gas, liquids or radiation: ガスが漏出する. In everyday speech people say 漏れる (intransitive, ガスが漏れる) or 漏らす (transitive) instead; the leak itself is 漏れ. For the leaking of information, 漏えい (漏洩) is more usual (情報漏えい).

en.meaning: to feel embarrassed; to be shy
examples[].german: Oh, thank you. You're making me blush.
When he's praised, he gets embarrassed right away and his face turns red.
Don't be shy; try singing in front of everyone.
en.notes: 照れる is intransitive and describes a pleasantly embarrassed shyness, typically when one is praised or noticed: 褒められて照れる; as a reaction one says 照れるなあ oneself. Related are 照れくさい "embarrassing", 照れ屋 "shy person" and 照れ笑い "embarrassed laugh". 恥ずかしい is broader and can also express genuine shame over mistakes; 照れる cannot.

examples[].german: Does the publisher hold the publishing rights?
I hear a film company bought the rights to this novel.
Old works whose copyright has expired can be read online for free.
en.notes: 版権 refers to the right to publish and reproduce a work, i.e. mainly publishing and licensing rights: 版権を買う, 版権を持つ, 版権が切れる. The general legal term for "copyright" is today 著作権; 版権 is heard more in the publishing, film and anime world (版権イラスト = picture with licensed characters).

examples[].german: I heard that shop was robbed! But luckily nobody was hurt.
The bank robber was arrested yesterday.
Be careful not to be attacked by a robber on a night road.
en.notes: 強盗 denotes both the act (robbery by force or threat) and the perpetrator (robber). Typical: 強盗が入る (to break into a shop/house), 強盗に襲われる, 銀行強盗, 強盗事件. In contrast to 泥棒 ("thief", who steals secretly) and すり ("pickpocket"), 強盗 stresses the use of violence.

examples[].german: Doesn't that author's new work seem kind of plagiarized?
He was found to have plagiarized someone else's paper and ended up leaving the university.
People online are discussing whether that song is plagiarized.
en.notes: 盗作 is plagiarism, that is, taking over someone else's works as one's own; as a transitive する-verb: 論文を盗作する. Common are 盗作の疑い and 〜は盗作だ. Colloquially people say パクる or パクリ; the literary synonym is 剽窃. For theft of objects, 盗む is used instead.

examples[].german: Those guys make money by reselling stolen goods.
The police found a large quantity of stolen goods in the warehouse.
What happens if I unknowingly buy stolen goods?
en.notes: 盗品 are stolen objects, that is, stolen goods - a matter-of-fact term from police and news language. Typical: 盗品を売る, 盗品を買う, 盗品が見つかる. In everyday speech people often simply say 盗まれた物. Not to be confused with 盗作 ("plagiarism"), in which intellectual property is stolen.

examples[].german: I think this child needs psychological care right now.
Work is busy, and I'm more mentally tired than physically.
The accident was a great psychological shock for her.
en.notes: 精神的 is a な-adjective: 精神的な疲れ, 精神的なショック; adverbially 精神的に疲れる, 精神的に強い. It refers to the psyche and mind and is the counterpart of 肉体的 or 身体的 ("physical"). In conversation you also hear 気持ち的に or メンタル（が強い）; 精神的 sounds somewhat more factual.

examples[].german: There are various interpretations.
I interpreted his silence as "agreement".
How should this poem be interpreted?
en.notes: 解釈する means "to interpret": one understands a text, a law, a statement or behavior in a certain way, typically with 〜と解釈する ("to take as ...") or 〜に解釈する ("to interpret in a ... way"): 好意的に解釈する. The noun often appears in 解釈が分かれる "interpretations differ". Do not confuse it with 通訳する (to interpret orally) or 翻訳する (to translate) - 解釈 refers to interpreting the content.

examples[].german: My father is hospitalized with a mental illness.
In the past, prejudice against mental illness was very strong.
Recently, the word "精神疾患" is used more often than "精神病".
en.notes: 精神病 is an older collective term for mental illnesses, especially severe ones such as psychoses. Today the word is considered stigmatizing; in medicine and the media people rather say 精神疾患 or 心の病気, and 精神病院 has mostly become 精神科病院. Typical: 精神病を患う, 精神病と診断される.

examples[].german: Many Korean Americans live in my town.
He is known as a soothing-type actor.
en.notes: 〜系 is attached to an element and roughly denotes origin or affiliation: 韓国系 means "of Korean descent". Colloquially it also describes a type or aura, as in 癒し系 for people who have a calming effect. The sign 〜 is a placeholder and is not pronounced; 系 is the spelling of the attached element. This card does not teach an independent mathematical term.

examples[].german: Many Japanese Americans live in Los Angeles.
It is said that there are about two million people of Japanese descent in Brazil.
My older sister works at a Japanese company in Thailand.
en.notes: 日系 usually stands as a prefix before a noun: 日系アメリカ人, 日系ブラジル人 ("of Japanese descent"). 日系人 are people of Japanese ancestry living abroad. In addition, 日系企業 or 日系の会社 means a Japanese company or branch abroad, as opposed to 外資系 ("foreign-affiliated company" in Japan).

examples[].german: Where in the Milky Way is the solar system located?
The largest planet in the solar system is Jupiter.
Pluto is no longer counted as a planet of the solar system.
en.notes: 太陽系 is the solar system; 系 here means "system, group" as in 銀河系 ("Milky Way") or 生態系 ("ecosystem"). Typical combinations: 太陽系の惑星, 太陽系の外 or 太陽系外惑星 ("exoplanet"). The word belongs to school and scientific vocabulary, but is also well known in daily life.

examples[].german: I'd like to buy a book that summarizes economic theory systematically.
If you want to study grammar systematically, I recommend this textbook.
His knowledge is wide, but it isn't very systematic.
en.notes: 体系的 is a な-adjective for 体系 ("system, ordered whole"): 体系的な知識, 体系的に学ぶ, 体系的にまとめる. It stresses that knowledge or content is logically ordered and coherent. Similar is 系統的; 組織的, by contrast, refers more to organized action by groups (組織的な犯罪).

en.meaning: to die out; to cease; to break off
examples[].german: It is very much appreciated that electricity and water are supplied without interruption.
Laughter never stops in her house.
In this region, the people who speak this language have died out.
en.notes: 絶える is intransitive and means "to die out, to become extinct" (家系が絶える, 息が絶える = to die) as well as "to cease, to break off" (連絡が絶える). The negative is very common: 笑いが絶えない ("there is constant laughter"), 〜が絶えることなく, and the adverb 絶えず ("constantly"). The transitive counterpart is 絶やす (火を絶やさない). Not to be confused with 耐える ("to endure"), which is read the same.

examples[].german: The day after the sports festival, my whole body ached terribly.
The goods you ordered will be delivered the next day.
He started working the day after he arrived in Japan.
en.notes: 翌日 means "the following day" and refers to a reference point in a narrative or plan: 〜の翌日, 〜た翌日. For "tomorrow" counted from today, you say 明日; 翌日 sounds more matter-of-fact and is common in reports, schedules and delivery terms (翌日配送). 翌朝, 翌週, 翌月 and 翌年 belong to the same series.

en.meaning: following month; next month (after a given point)
examples[].german: I joined the company in April, and training began the following month.
What I charge to my card, I pay in one lump sum the following month.
The month after she got married, she was transferred overseas.
en.notes: 翌月 is "the month after" a stated point in time: 〜の翌月, 〜た翌月, 翌月に. From today's standpoint, by contrast, you say 来月 ("next month"). The word is typical in contracts and billing: 翌月払い, 翌月末. It is rarely also read よくつき.

examples[].german: When I woke up the next morning, I had a pounding hangover headache.
We left on an overnight bus and arrived in Osaka early the next morning.
Your luggage will be delivered to your room the next morning.
en.notes: 翌朝 is "the next morning" after an event mentioned in the narrative, and it often stands without a particle as a time adverb: 翌朝早く, 翌朝出発する. From today's standpoint you say 明日の朝 or, formally, 明朝. The reading よくちょう also occurs in formal language.

en.meaning: following year; next year (after a given point)
examples[].german: Mr. Hino started a business the year after he returned to Japan from America.
I failed the exam once, but took it again the following year and passed.
The two married in 2020, and their eldest son was born the following year.
en.notes: 翌年 is "the year after" a stated event: 〜の翌年, 〜た翌年に. From the current year, "next year" is 来年 instead. The word is typical in résumés, history and reports; the reading よくとし also occurs.

examples[].german: I understood the situation.
I still can't understand why he got angry.
There will be some inconvenience during construction; we ask for your understanding.
en.notes: 理解する is "to understand, to comprehend" in the sense of grasping content or having understanding for someone: 内容を理解する, 相手の気持ちを理解する. In everyday conversation people usually just say 分かる (with が), whereas 理解する takes its object with を and sounds more objective and a bit more formal. Set expressions: 理解できない "cannot comprehend", 理解が早い "quick to understand" and, in announcements, ご理解ください "we ask for your understanding".

examples[].german: I made a list of the Japanese words I want to learn.
A list of the prices is on the website.
I'll put the participants' names into a list and send it by email.
en.notes: 一覧 is an overview or list on which you can see everything at a glance: 一覧を作る, 一覧にする, 一覧表 ("overview table"). It often follows a noun: 料金一覧, 商品一覧, 参加者一覧. リスト is synonymous and a bit more casual. The basic meaning "to take a quick look" (一覧する) is rare and formal.

examples[].german: Please enjoy the show.
Has the president already looked at the materials?
Try tasting it. It's delicious.
en.notes: ご覧 is the respectful form for others' seeing: ご覧になる is the 尊敬語 of 見る, ご覧ください means "please look", ご覧のとおり "as you can see". With the て-form, 〜てごらん ("try ...") is a friendly request to children or younger people; here it is usually written in kana. For one's own seeing, one never uses ご覧 but 拝見する.

examples[].german: The spectator seats are already full.
The admission fee for this museum is 1,000 yen for adults.
Anyone can watch the practice game for free.
en.notes: 観覧 is watching events, sports, exhibitions or broadcasts as a spectator; as a transitive する-verb it is rather formal: 試合を観覧する. Frequent in compounds: 観覧席 ("stand, spectator seats"), 観覧料 ("admission fee"), 観覧無料, 観覧車 ("Ferris wheel"). 鑑賞, by contrast, emphasizes the enjoyment of art, 見学 a visit for learning.

examples[].german: When I grow up, I want to work to help poor people.
He was born into a poor family, but studied hard and became a doctor.
Even with money, I don't want to become a person who is poor in heart.
en.notes: 貧しい is an い-adjective meaning "poor, needy": 貧しい家, 貧しい国, 貧しい人々. It sounds more neutral and serious than 貧乏, which is colloquial and often self-deprecating. Figuratively, 貧しい also means "meager, lacking in something": 心が貧しい, 想像力が貧しい. The opposite is 豊か.

examples[].german: When I was a student I was poor all the time and ate nothing but cup ramen every day.
Sometimes a poor painter only becomes famous after he dies.
Being poor leaves no time to rest – I work even on days off.
en.notes: 貧乏 is a noun and a な-adjective: 貧乏な学生, 貧乏で…, 貧乏生活. It is more colloquial than 貧しい and is often said about one's own situation, often self-mockingly (貧乏学生). Fixed expressions are 貧乏暇なし ("the poor have no time to rest") and 貧乏ゆすり ("nervous leg jiggling").

examples[].german: I am considering purchasing new software.
You can purchase tickets from this site.
You should think carefully before buying a house.
en.notes: 購入 is the formal word for "purchase, to buy" and is commonly used as a transitive する-verb: 商品を購入する. You find it on websites, in shops and in contracts (購入手続き, ご購入ありがとうございます, 購入者); in conversation one usually just says 買う. 購買, by contrast, means buying as an economic activity (購買力) and 購読 subscribing to newspapers.

examples[].german: Let's develop a new marketing strategy based on this purchasing data.
I'll go buy some bread at the school store during lunch break.
Because of the weak yen, consumers' willingness to buy is falling.
en.notes: 購買 refers to buying as an economic activity and appears mainly in compounds: 購買力 "purchasing power", 購買意欲 "willingness to buy", 購買データ, 購買部 "purchasing department". For the actual purchase of a specific item, use 購入. In schools and universities, the small shop selling bread, drinks and stationery is called 購買 for short ("school store").

examples[].german: The number of subscribers to this online news site is increasing year by year.
My father subscribes to two newspapers.
I don't have time to read, so I decided to cancel my magazine subscription.
en.notes: 購読 means regularly receiving newspapers, magazines or newsletters; as a transitive する-verb: 新聞を購読する. Typical compounds are 定期購読 ("subscription"), 購読者 ("subscriber") and 購読料. For subscriptions in general (streaming, etc.) people tend to say サブスク, and for YouTube channels チャンネル登録.

examples[].german: Why did you draw the butterfly upside down?
That picture is hanging upside down.
He slipped and fell headfirst down the stairs.
en.notes: 逆さま means "upside down, inverted" and is a な-adjective or noun: 逆さまにする, 逆さまになる, 逆さまに置く. Intensified it is 真っ逆さま (真っ逆さまに落ちる = "to fall headfirst"). 逆 means "the opposite, reverse" in general, 裏返し "inside out" or "turned over (back side up)".

examples[].german: This amusement park is popular as a date spot.
When I was a child, my family went to the amusement park every summer vacation.
I'm too scared to ride the roller coaster at the amusement park.
en.notes: 遊園地 is an amusement park with rides such as ジェットコースター ("roller coaster") and 観覧車 ("Ferris wheel"). Large themed parks such as Disneyland are usually called テーマパーク; a simple 公園, by contrast, is a park without attractions. Typical: 遊園地に行く, 遊園地で遊ぶ.

examples[].german: I was convinced by the explanation.
I just can't accept this result.
After listening to the teacher, I finally understood and accepted it.
en.notes: 納得する means to accept something inwardly because it makes sense to you: "to be convinced, to be satisfied". Typical are 説明に納得する and, negated, 結果に納得できない; the object usually takes に. Unlike 理解する (purely understanding), 納得 emphasizes agreement - you can understand something without agreeing with it. Set expressions: 納得がいく／いかない "to make / not make sense to one", 納得のいく説明 "a convincing explanation".

examples[].german: Please choose the appropriate answer.
He always just says whatever.
Please, sit down wherever you like.
en.notes: 適当 has two very different meanings. In a factual sense, 適当な means "suitable, appropriate", for example in exam questions: 適当な答えを選びなさい. In everyday speech, however, the meaning "any old way, as one likes, carelessly" is much more common: 適当に座って "sit anywhere", 適当なことを言う "to say whatever comes to mind", 適当な人 "an unreliable person". Anyone who clearly means "appropriate" should rather choose 適切.

examples[].german: People have aptitudes and non-aptitudes.
This land is unsuitable for growing rice.
He was judged unsuitable for this job.
en.notes: 不適 means "unsuitable, inappropriate" and is a な-adjective or noun, mostly with に: 〜に不適だ, 〜には不適な. It sounds formal and literary. In everyday speech people more often say 向いていない or 不向き, and for inappropriate behavior 不適切. The compound 適不適 means "suitability or unsuitability".

examples[].german: I graduated from a fashion vocational school.
She works in Paris as a fashion designer.
At this museum you can learn about the history of clothing and accessories in the Edo period.
en.notes: 服飾 covers clothing together with accessories and appears mainly in compounds from fashion and training: 服飾デザイナー, 服飾専門学校, 服飾雑貨 ("fashion accessories"), 服飾史. In everyday speech, for clothes you say 服, 洋服 or ファッション; 服飾 sounds technical and written.

examples[].german: The lights on that truck were so sparkly and pretty!
When December comes, lights are put up on the trees in front of the station.
At night, the shop's illuminated signboard glows brightly.
