en.notes: 電飾 is decorative electric lighting, for example on buildings, trees or the gaudily decorated デコトラ trucks. Typical are 電飾看板 "illuminated sign" and 電飾を付ける. For seasonal light displays at Christmas or in winter, イルミネーション is mostly used today; 電飾 sounds a bit more technical.

examples[].german: A plan to attack the enemy base is under way.
Many people attack his statements online.
In the second half, the opposing team attacked fiercely.
en.notes: 攻撃する is transitive: 敵を攻撃する, 基地を攻撃する. Besides military attack, it is often used figuratively for sharp criticism (相手の意見を攻撃する) and, in sports, for offense (攻撃と守備). The opposite is 守る or 防御/守備. 襲う, by contrast, stresses a sudden assault on people or animals.

examples[].german: Oh, didn't we also meet earlier at the convenience store?
This is Tanaka, who called you earlier. Is Mr. Yamamoto in?
Please let me explain the earlier matter in a bit more detail.
en.notes: 先程 is the polite equivalent of さっき ("a while ago, just now") and is often written in kana: さきほど. It stands adverbially (先程お電話しました) or with の before nouns (先程の件). A typical polite formula: 先程は失礼しました. The counterpart for "later" is 後程 (のちほど).

examples[].german: His bureaucratic way of speaking irritated me a little.
The government office's handling was so bureaucratic that the procedure took a whole month.
As this company has grown, it has gradually become bureaucratic.
en.notes: 官僚的 is a な-adjective and almost always derogatory: rigid, formalistic, oriented toward regulations rather than people. Typical: 官僚的な対応, 官僚的な組織, 官僚的になる. It refers not only to government offices but also to large companies. The base word 官僚 refers to the (high-ranking) officials of the ministries.

examples[].german: I hear my grandfather was a prime minister long ago.
A new prime minister was elected in the Diet.
My childhood dream was to become prime minister.
en.notes: 総理大臣 is the Japanese prime minister; the official title is 内閣総理大臣. In everyday speech and in forms of address, people often say just 総理 (山田総理), and in news and newspapers 首相 is very common. Typical: 総理大臣になる, 総理大臣に選ばれる.

en.meaning: to move; to transfer; to spread (to)
examples[].german: From next month I will be moving to a new department.
I am wearing a mask so that I don't pass on my cold.
May I move to the seat by the window?
en.notes: 移る is intransitive and means "to change to another place or state", with the destination marked by に: 新しい部署に移る, 窓側の席に移る. The transitive counterpart is 移す "to relocate, to move". Illnesses and smells also "pass on": 風邪がうつる; in this meaning it is mostly written in kana. For moving house, 引っ越す is more usual in everyday speech.

en.meaning: to drip; to let hang down; to dribble
examples[].german: Finally, you drizzle on a little olive oil, like this.
The dog is drooling as it waits for its food.
I dangled a fishing line from the bridge and waited for fish.
en.notes: 垂らす is transitive and means, on the one hand, "to let drip, to drizzle" (油を垂らす, よだれを垂らす, 汗を垂らす), and on the other, "to let hang down" (釣り糸を垂らす, 髪を垂らす). The intransitive counterpart is 垂れる (水が垂れる, 枝が垂れる). For pouring larger amounts, people instead say 注ぐ or かける.

examples[].german: We agreed on the terms.
The two countries agreed on trade rules.
I came to an agreement with the landlord and got the rent lowered a little.
en.notes: 合意する means "to agree, to come to terms" - usually between parties, companies or states, and therefore rather formal. What one agrees on takes に (条件に合意する) or 〜について, with whom takes と (相手と合意する). Also common are 合意に達する／合意に至る "to reach an agreement" and 合意を得る "to obtain consent". In private everyday life one rather says 話がまとまる or 賛成する.

examples[].german: Our dog is afraid of thunder.
My daughter is scared of dark places and can't sleep alone.
You don't need to be that scared. This dog doesn't bite.
en.notes: 怖がる describes the visible fear of another person or an animal: 〜を怖がる. For one's own fear, people mostly say 怖い (私は犬が怖い), because 〜がる expresses an observation from the outside. Common are 怖がらないで and そんなに怖がらなくても大丈夫. Similar is 恐れる, which sounds more literary.

en.meaning: to be buried; to be covered; to remain undiscovered
examples[].german: Last night 30 cm of snow piled up, and my car got buried.
My desk is buried in papers, and I can't see the computer.
It's a waste that talent like his remains undiscovered.
en.notes: 埋もれる is intransitive and means "to be buried, covered": 雪に埋もれる, 書類に埋もれる. Figuratively it means "to remain undiscovered": 埋もれた才能, 歴史に埋もれる. The transitive counterpart is 埋める ("to bury, to fill"); close in meaning is 埋まる. The variant うずもれる is more literary.

en.meaning: back; behind a person; background (of events)
examples[].german: In horror movies, the pattern where something is standing behind you is the scariest!
I was startled when someone suddenly called my name from behind.
Apparently there is a large organization behind this incident.
en.notes: 背後 is a noun meaning "the space behind someone, the back": 背後に立つ, 背後から近づく. Figuratively it refers to what stands hidden behind something: 事件の背後, 背後関係, 背後にいる人物 ("mastermind"). It is more literary than 後ろ and often sounds tense or ominous. For the "background" of a picture, on the other hand, use 背景.

examples[].german: When I started living alone in my twenties, I awakened to the pleasure of eating junk food.
You shouldn't spend too much money for a moment's pleasure.
He only seeks pleasure and doesn't take his work seriously.
en.notes: 快楽 is sensual pleasure, lust or enjoyment, and often carries an overtone of hedonism or excess: 快楽を求める, 快楽に溺れる "to give oneself up to pleasure", 快楽主義 "hedonism". It does not fit everyday joy or fun; for those use 楽しみ or 喜び. The word sounds rather written and serious.

examples[].german: Life with air conditioning is comfortable.
The Shinkansen Green Car was very comfortable.
We are adjusting the temperature inside the building so that everyone can be comfortable.
en.notes: 快適 is a な-adjective meaning "pleasant, comfortable" with regard to surroundings and living conditions: 快適な部屋, 快適な旅, 快適に過ごす. It sounds somewhat more refined than 気持ちいい or 楽 and is typical of advertising and announcements. 便利 ("convenient"), by contrast, refers to usefulness, not to well-being.

examples[].german: I see, so that was the reason.
I see, so I just have to press this button.
Just as everyone says, it really is a good restaurant.
en.notes: 成程 is almost always written in kana: なるほど. As an interjection it shows that one has understood something and finds it convincing ("I see, I understand"). As an adverb it means "indeed, truly" (なるほどおいしい). Toward superiors, a bare なるほど can come across as somewhat condescending; more polite are そうなんですね or おっしゃるとおりです.

examples[].german: I'm weak against pushiness.
She is very pushy, so she's suited to a sales job.
With just one more push, the department head seems likely to agree too.
en.notes: 押し is the noun of 押す and means "push, thrust", but above all, figuratively, "assertiveness, forcefulness". Fixed expressions: 押しが強い ("pushy, assertive"), 押しに弱い ("has trouble saying no"), あと一押し ("just one more little push"). Do not confuse it with 推し ("favorite idol" in fan language), which is read the same.

examples[].german: Knead the ground meat just enough.
Beer that is chilled just right tastes best.
This room gets just the right amount of sunlight, and it feels pleasant.
en.notes: 程よく is the adverbial form of 程よい and means "just right, in the proper measure" - neither too much nor too little. It is often written in kana (ほどよく) and likes to appear in recipes and descriptions: 程よく冷えた, 程よく焼けた, 程よい甘さ. Similar but more general is ちょうどよく; 適当に, by contrast, can also mean "sloppily".

examples[].german: This perfume has no scent at all.
When I opened the front door, I could smell curry.
This shirt smells a bit of sweat, so please wash it.
en.notes: 匂う is intransitive: the thing that smells takes が (花が匂う, 部屋が匂う). Someone who deliberately smells something uses the transitive 嗅ぐ (匂いを嗅ぐ). For pleasant smells, people write 匂う, for unpleasant ones often 臭う (足が臭う). Figuratively, 何か匂う means "something smells fishy". More common than the verb in everyday speech is 〜の匂いがする.

examples[].german: It's good to wet your hair well before shampooing.
I walked in the rain and got my shoes wet.
I wet a towel with water and held it to my forehead.
en.notes: 濡らす is transitive: to make something wet, either on purpose or by accident (髪を濡らす, タオルを濡らす, 靴を濡らしてしまう). The intransitive counterpart is 濡れる (雨で服が濡れる). For "to moisten" slightly, you can also say 湿らせる; the opposite is 乾かす ("to dry").

examples[].german: I will deal with the problem.
This app also supports older models.
In this table, each number corresponds to a particular color.
en.notes: 対応する always takes に and has three main meanings: "to take care of something, to respond to something" (客・問題・変化に対応する, 対応が早い), "to correspond to something" (AはBに対応する) and, in technology, "to support, to be compatible" (古い機種にも対応している, 日本語対応). In everyday work the first meaning is the most common. 応じる, by contrast, stresses complying with a request or demand.

examples[].german: Let's compromise with each other.
When looking for a room, I compromised on the distance from the station.
That chef never compromises on flavor.
en.notes: 妥協する means "to make a compromise", often with the nuance that one departs from one's own standards: 〜で妥協する "to settle for ..." (この値段で妥協する), with whom takes と. Very common in the negative as an expression of uncompromising consistency: 妥協しない, 妥協を許さない "to tolerate no compromise". Related is 譲歩する, which stresses more one-sided giving way to the other party.

en.meaning: to move close; to push aside; to send in; to direct toward
examples[].german: I moved the toy up against the wall.
Please pull your car over to the left side of the road and stop.
The program received many opinions from viewers.
en.notes: 寄せる is transitive and in its basic sense means "to move up close to something, to push to the side": 〜を〜に寄せる (机を壁に寄せる, 車を左に寄せる). Figuratively it means "to send in, to submit" (意見を寄せる, 多くの声が寄せられる) and "to direct feelings toward" (関心を寄せる, 好意を寄せる). The intransitive counterpart is 寄る; 波が寄せる is a fixed intransitive use.

examples[].german: This amulet has the power to ward off misfortune.
The company rejected the union's demands.
In the final they beat last year's champions and won the title for the first time.
en.notes: 退ける (しりぞける) is transitive and formal: "to reject, turn down" (要求を退ける, 訴えを退ける) and "to repel, defeat" (敵を退ける, 相手チームを退ける). The intransitive counterpart is 退く (しりぞく, "to withdraw"). Note: the same kanji is also read どける/のける, and then means "to move aside" in colloquial speech.

examples[].german: Playing too many video games is bad for your eyes.
I hurt my lower back lifting a heavy package.
My mother has been very worried about my brother for a long time.
en.notes: 痛める is transitive: to injure a body part or harm it (腰を痛める, 喉を痛める, 目を痛める); 心を痛める means "to be deeply worried, distressed". The intransitive counterpart is 痛む ("to hurt"). Read the same are 傷める ("to damage", e.g. 髪を傷める) and 炒める ("to stir-fry") - mind the spelling.

examples[].german: How about putting up an iron fence there?
There is an iron fence around the pond in the park.
Climbing over the iron fence and going onto the tracks is very dangerous.
en.notes: 鉄柵 is an iron grille or iron fence, for example around parks, railway tracks or buildings. 柵 on its own is a general fence or barrier; in everyday speech people often say フェンス. Typical verbs: 鉄柵を設ける, 鉄柵で囲む, 鉄柵を乗り越える. The word is rather literary and technical.

examples[].german: More and more fields are being surrounded with electric fences.
To prevent damage from wild boars, we installed an electric fence around the field.
It's dangerous to touch the electric fence, so please be careful.
en.notes: 電気柵 is an electric fence, as used in Japan mainly in rural areas against wild boars, deer and monkeys. Typical: 電気柵を設置する, 電気柵を張る, 電気柵で囲む. Here 柵 is read さく; the reading しがらみ applies only to the standalone word ("ties, obligations").

examples[].german: Tonight's dinner at our house is fried shrimp.
Let me introduce our company's new product.
It's truly delightful to watch my child grow.
en.notes: 我が is a prenominal word meaning "my, our" that stands only directly before a noun. In everyday life it survives mainly in set phrases: 我が家 "our home", 我が子 "one's own child"; formally in speeches 我が社 "our company" and in politics and media 我が国 "our country". Freely formed, it sounds elevated or jokingly solemn; normally you say 私の or うちの.

examples[].german: This is a tonkotsu ramen shop.
If I go to Hakata, I want to try authentic tonkotsu ramen.
Tonkotsu ramen has a rich soup, so if you drink all of it you get thirsty.
en.notes: 豚骨ラーメン (often also written とんこつラーメン) is ramen with a cloudy, whitish broth made from long-simmered pork bones (豚骨). It comes from 九州, especially 博多 and 久留米, and is usually served with thin, firm noodles; extra noodles for a refill are called 替え玉. Other basic types are 醤油ラーメン, 味噌ラーメン and 塩ラーメン.

examples[].german: Somehow my joints are throbbing all over.
I have a fever and all my joints hurt. It might be the flu.
In his every word, I could feel his gratitude toward his family.
en.notes: 節々 are the joints of the whole body; almost always in 体の節々が痛い or 節々が痛む, typical of flu or sore muscles ("aching limbs"). Figuratively, 言葉の節々に means "in many individual points (of a speech)". Individual joints, by contrast, are called 関節.

examples[].german: I hear this hotel is 5,000 yen with a breakfast buffet included.
The lunch buffet is all-you-can-eat for 90 minutes.
Just because it's a buffet, don't take too much.
en.notes: バイキング in Japan means above all "self-service buffet" (朝食バイキング, ランチバイキング) - a Japanese coinage based on a hotel restaurant. The original meaning "Viking" exists as well. Synonymous but more upscale is ビュッフェ; 食べ放題 stresses "eat as much as you like".

en.meaning: to gather; to put in order; to make uniform
examples[].german: Oh no, I forgot to collect the documents for the meeting.
Line up the shoes you took off in the entryway properly.
Everyone said "Congratulations!" in unison.
en.notes: 揃える is transitive and has three core meanings: "to gather, to make complete" (書類を揃える, 道具を揃える), "to line up neatly" (靴を揃える) and "to make uniform, to match" (声を揃える, 長さを揃える, 足並みを揃える). The intransitive counterpart is 揃う (全員が揃う).

examples[].german: Let's give a little.
The company side made concessions, and salaries are going to rise.
On the price, I can't concede any further.
en.notes: 譲歩する means "to give way, to make a concession" - one grants the other side something in a negotiation or dispute. To whom takes に (相手に譲歩する), on which point takes 〜について. The word is rather formal and typical of negotiations, politics and business; in everyday life one often says 譲る ("to hand over, to give way"). Unlike 妥協する (both sides meet in the middle), 譲歩 stresses the accommodation of one side.

examples[].german: I ordered one commercial-grade griddle.
I cooked okonomiyaki on the griddle.
This story is a sure-fire joke that will definitely get laughs.
en.notes: 鉄板 is an iron or steel plate, in everyday life above all the hot griddle for お好み焼き or 鉄板焼き. Colloquially it means "a sure thing, guaranteed to succeed": 鉄板ネタ ("a joke that always works"), この組み合わせは鉄板だ. The phrase 鉄板の上で is typical in cooking.

examples[].german: To me, you are like the moon that lights up the black sea.
I walked while lighting the ground at my feet with a flashlight.
Considered in light of the rules, this act is problematic.
en.notes: 照らす is transitive: to cast light on something (月が海を照らす, ライトで足元を照らす). The intransitive counterpart is 照る (日が照る). In the set form 〜に照らして it means "in the light of, measured against": 法律に照らして, 経験に照らして - a literary expression.

examples[].german: I booked the plane ticket.
Around the end of the year, plane ticket prices get quite high.
I searched for a cheap plane ticket and compared options online for hours.
en.notes: 航空券 is the plane ticket that you buy or book: 航空券を予約する, 航空券を取る, 格安航空券, 往復航空券. In conversation people often just say チケット. The boarding pass you receive at check-in, by contrast, is 搭乗券. For train tickets use 切符 or 乗車券.

examples[].german: My stuffy nose is so bad that I can't sleep.
I have a terrible stuffy nose from a cold and can't smell anything.
Is there any medicine that works for a stuffy nose?
en.notes: 鼻詰まり (鼻 "nose" + 詰まる "to be blocked") is a stuffy nose as a complaint: 鼻詰まりがひどい, 鼻詰まりに効く薬. In conversation the condition is often described with the verb: 鼻が詰まっている. A runny nose, by contrast, is 鼻水が出る.

examples[].german: I brooded over my failure alone, and it only made me more anxious.
Don't dwell on it so much; why not talk to someone about it?
He said "I have something to tell you" with a troubled look.
en.notes: 思い詰める means to brood so long and one-sidedly over a matter that one sees no way out - stronger than 考える "to think" or 悩む "to worry". Typical are 一人で思い詰める, consolingly そんなに思い詰めないで and 思い詰めた顔 "a grimly troubled expression". 思い詰めて〜する often means taking a drastic step out of desperation. An object with を is possible, but the verb usually stands without one.

examples[].german: Secretly gazing at the person you like feels so youthful, doesn't it?
The baby is staring fixedly at my face.
It is also important to look squarely at your own weaknesses.
en.notes: 見詰める means to direct one's gaze at something long and intently: 〜をじっと見詰める. Unlike 見る "to see" or 眺める "to look at (leisurely)", it stresses intensity, but is not necessarily impolite - disapproving staring is more like じろじろ見る. Figuratively: 現実を見詰める "to face reality". In practice the word is usually written 見つめる.

examples[].german: That male dog was full of energy even as a puppy.
Our dog is a male, and his name is Taro.
Male dogs often mark utility poles during walks.
en.notes: 雄犬 is a male dog; 雄 (オス) marks the male sex in animals, while for humans you say 男. The counterpart is 雌犬 "female dog", which, however, also occurs as an insult for women. In conversation you more often hear オスの犬 or simply うちの犬はオスです.

en.meaning: to let die out; to exterminate
examples[].german: She never let her smile fade.
While camping, we made sure not to let the fire go out all night.
It is difficult to exterminate cockroaches completely.
en.notes: 絶やす is the transitive counterpart of 絶える "to cease, to die out". Very often used in the negative: 笑顔を絶やさない "to always keep a smile", 火を絶やさない "to not let the fire go out", 在庫を絶やさない "to never run out of stock". In the affirmative it means "to eradicate, to put an end to" (害虫を絶やす), intensified 根絶やしにする. Not to be confused with 耐える "to endure" (the same reading たえる as 絶える).

en.meaning: to be nervous; to be tense
examples[].german: It's common to be nervous before a match.
I was so nervous at the interview that I couldn't speak well.
Relations between the two countries are strained.
en.notes: 緊張する describes inner tension before exams, speeches or job interviews: 面接で緊張する, 緊張して手が震える. It is intransitive; the situation takes で or comes before as a time expression, not with を. The opposite is リラックスする or 緊張がほぐれる "the tension eases"; colloquially, あがる is also used for stage fright. Relations between countries can also be "tense": 関係が緊張する.

en.meaning: to move away; to be apart from
examples[].german: It is hard to be apart from my pet for a while.
When I started university, I left my parents' home and began living alone.
My apartment is a little way from the station.
en.notes: 離れる is intransitive and emphasizes distance or separation: the starting point takes から or を (駅から離れる, 親元を離れる "to leave one's parents' home"), the person one is separated from takes と (家族と離れて暮らす). As an attributive, 離れた describes a distant location: 駅から少し離れた所. The transitive counterpart is 離す (手を離す "to let go"). In contrast to 出る "to go out", the focus is on the distance that arises.

examples[].german: We promote international exchange.
While studying abroad, I wanted to interact more with local people.
With this app, you can interact with Japanese learners from all over the world.
en.notes: 交流する means "to interact, to keep in contact" between people, groups or countries; the partner is marked with と (地元の人と交流する). The noun is very common in compounds: 国際交流, 文化交流, 交流会 ("exchange meeting, mixer"). Unlike 交換する (exchanging things), the focus is on encounters and relationships, not objects. In electrical engineering, 交流 also means "alternating current".

examples[].german: This is fragile, so be careful!
I put a "Fragile" sticker on the package.
At the post office, I was asked, "Is there anything fragile inside?"
en.notes: 壊れ物 refers to fragile objects such as glass, tableware or electronics, especially in shipping: 壊れ物注意 "Caution, fragile" is on parcels, and at the post office counter you are asked whether there is any 壊れ物 inside. Formed from 壊れる "to break" + 物 "thing". It can also mean an already broken thing, but that is rare. As an adjective, "fragile" is 壊れやすい.

examples[].german: Payment has already been completed.
By the time I reached the station, the train had already left.
Many of you probably already know, but the fees will change from next month.
en.notes: 既に corresponds to もう "already", but is more written and formal: typical of news, business emails and announcements, while in casual speech you say もう. Unlike もう, it cannot mean "another" (もう一つ) or "soon" (もうすぐ). It is often used with 〜ている/〜ていた for a state that has already come about, and in the formula 既にご存じのとおり "as you already know". According to dictionaries, it is often written in kana as すでに.

examples[].german: It doesn't matter which, please try opening an existing file.
Even with the new app, you can use your existing data as is.
Let's value not only new customers but also existing customers.
en.notes: 既存 means "already existing, present" and almost always stands attributively with の: 既存のファイル, 既存のシステム, 既存の店舗. It is typical of business, technology and administration; the opposite is 新規 "new" (新規のお客様 vs. 既存のお客様 "existing customers"). Besides きそん, the reading きぞん is also common; in conversation people often simply say 今ある.

examples[].german: This matter has already been decided.
There is no need to discuss matters that have already been decided again.
I sorted the documents into the "decided" box and the "pending" box.
en.notes: 既決 is a formal official and legal word for "already decided, settled". It is a noun and takes の before other nouns (既決の事項 "matters already decided"), and it forms a pair with 未決 "undecided, pending" - for example on office filing trays. In criminal law it means "convicted with final effect" (既決囚). In everyday speech you say もう決まっている instead.

examples[].german: What do you usually do on weekends?
I usually commute by bus, but today I walked.
The party is fine with everyday clothes.
en.notes: 普段 refers to normal everyday life as opposed to special occasions. As an adverb it is mostly 普段は "usually", often with a contrast: 普段は…が、今日は…. Attributively it takes の (普段の生活 "everyday life"), and it also appears in 普段着 "everyday clothes" and 普段通り "as usual". Compared with いつも "always", 普段 stresses the normal case, which has exceptions. Occasionally it is written in kana as ふだん.

examples[].german: Who is the editor of this book?
The editor of this dictionary spent twenty years collecting words.
The cover shows the name of the editor, not the author.
en.notes: 編者 is the person who compiles texts by others into a book - for example dictionaries, anthologies or collected volumes; the title page then often has 〜編 "edited by". Distinguish it from 著者 "author" and from 編集者 "editor" as a job title at a publishing house. The word is rather literary; less often it is also read へんじゃ.

examples[].german: Did you see the foreign minister's speech at the UN yesterday?
The foreign minister plans to visit the United States next week.
The foreign ministers of the two countries held talks.
en.notes: 外務大臣 is the head of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs 外務省. In headlines and news it is often shortened to 外相; with a name it is, for example, 山田外務大臣. Other ministerial posts follow the same pattern: 財務大臣 "finance minister", 総理大臣 "prime minister". The word belongs to the neutral to formal language of politics and news.

examples[].german: It's raining, so shall we go to the underground mall?
The underground mall at Osaka Station is huge, and I often get lost.
Let's meet at a restaurant in the underground mall.
en.notes: 地下街 (地下 "underground" + 街 "street, district") is an underground shopping street with shops, restaurants and connecting passages, typically beneath large train stations in Osaka, Nagoya, Tokyo or Sapporo. You say 地下街に行く or 地下街を通る. A pure pedestrian tunnel, by contrast, is called 地下道, and the food section in the basement of a department store デパ地下.

examples[].german: Everyone except him took part in the meeting.
This shop is open every day except Sundays.
Please remove the seeds and then cut it into small pieces.
en.notes: 除く has two main meanings: "to exclude, to except" - very common as 〜を除いて/〜を除き "except, with the exception of" in opening hours and rules - and "to remove, to get rid of" (種を除く), for which 取り除く is often used in everyday speech. 〜を除いて is more formal than 〜以外. Do not confuse it with the identically read 覗く "to peek in".

examples[].german: Could you tell me the reason for the exclusion?
We excluded data that did not meet the conditions from the analysis.
Because of an injury, he was dropped from the national team.
en.notes: 除外 is the formal Sino-Japanese noun for 除く "to exclude": 〜を…から除外する "to exclude X from Y", passive 除外される. Typical in rules, statistics and contracts: 対象から除外する, 除外理由, 除外対象. In everyday speech 〜を除く or 外す is usually enough. The opposite is 含める "to include".

examples[].german: I think the quickest way is to ask him directly.
At the station a stranger asked me the way.
Excuse me, may I ask whether there is a post office near here?
en.notes: 尋ねる means "to ask, to inquire" and is somewhat more formal than 聞く. The person asked takes に, the thing asked about takes を: 駅員に道を尋ねる. お尋ねします very politely introduces a question. The secondary meaning "to search" survives in 尋ね人 "missing person being sought". Read the same but different is 訪ねる "to visit".

examples[].german: The police interrogated everyone involved.
The questioning of the witness will take place from the afternoon.
He underwent harsh interrogation for hours.
en.notes: 尋問 is the formal word for questioning by the police, a court or the military: 容疑者を尋問する, 尋問を受ける "to be interrogated"; in court one speaks of 証人尋問 "examination of witnesses". Questioning after an arrest is usually called 取り調べ, and a stop-and-question check on the street 職務質問. Do not use it for ordinary questions in daily life - use 質問する or 聞く for that. Older spelling: 訊問.

en.meaning: how much; no matter how much (with ～ても)
examples[].german: How much is this?
No matter how much I explain, he won't be convinced.
en.notes: いくら asks for an amount, especially the price; おいくらですか is a polite question. In いくら～ても it means "no matter how much / even if ...". It is usually written in hiragana. The identically pronounced イクラ means salmon roe and is a separate word.

examples[].german: How many apples are in this box?
How old is your child?
en.notes: いくつ asks for the number of things counted with the general counter ～つ. It also asks for age: おいくつですか is more polite than 何歳ですか. For people or special counters, you use, for example, 何人 or 何枚. The kana spelling is usual; the kanji spelling 幾つ is read the same way.

examples[].german: You got an A+ on the geometry test? That's great, well done!
The geometric pattern on this scarf is stylish.
Geometry developed greatly in ancient Greece.
en.notes: 幾何学 is geometry as a branch of mathematics, alongside 代数 "algebra"; in school lessons at lower levels, 図形 is used more often. In everyday life the word appears mainly in 幾何学模様 "geometric pattern" and 幾何学的 "geometric", for example in fashion, architecture or design. 幾何 alone can also mean "geometry".

examples[].german: She opened her own gallery.
There are many small galleries in Ginza.
I bought a painting I liked at the gallery.
en.notes: 画廊 is an art gallery, usually commercial, where pictures are exhibited and sold. Today ギャラリー is also often used; a large public art museum, by contrast, is called 美術館. Typical are 画廊を開く "to open a gallery" and 画廊で個展を開く "to hold a solo exhibition in a gallery". The word sounds a bit more refined than ギャラリー.

examples[].german: The water in that river has turned completely into muddy water.
A car splashed me with muddy water and my clothes got dirty.
The children were playing happily in the muddy puddles.
en.notes: 泥水 is cloudy, muddy water, for example after rain, in floods or in puddles. Typical combinations are 泥水をかけられる "to be splashed with muddy water" and 川が泥水になる. Figuratively, 泥水をすする "to slurp muddy water" stands for a life of poverty and hardship. The dictionary meaning "pleasure district" is obsolete and unimportant for learners.

examples[].german: Everyone marveled at his performance.
I can only marvel at that craftsman's skill.
His memory is worthy of admiration.
en.notes: 驚嘆 combines 驚く "to be surprised" with 嘆 "to sigh" and describes admiring amazement at something great - never fright. Construction: 〜に驚嘆する "to marvel at something"; set phrases are 驚嘆に値する "admirable" and 驚嘆の声を上げる. The word is literary; in conversation people say びっくりする or すごいと思う instead. Related is 感嘆 "admiration".

examples[].german: He sighed deeply when he saw the result.
Not a few people sigh over the current state of politics.
"We can't make it in time anymore," the department head said with a sigh.
en.notes: 嘆息 is a literary word for a sigh of grief, disappointment or resignation and can also mean "to lament". As a verb it is 嘆息する; set phrases are 嘆息を漏らす and 嘆息まじりに "with a sigh". In everyday speech you say ため息をつく - 嘆息をつく is not a common combination. Related is 嘆く "to grieve, to lament".

examples[].german: The exclamation mark is used to express strong emotion.
In business emails, it's better not to use exclamation marks much.
Her message was full of exclamation marks.
en.notes: 感嘆符 (感嘆 "exclamation, admiration" + 符 "mark") is the technical term for the exclamation mark ！. In daily life people mostly say エクスクラメーションマーク or, colloquially, ビックリマーク. The question mark is accordingly called 疑問符, colloquially はてなマーク. In formal Japanese texts, both are traditionally used sparingly.

examples[].german: We will merge the two departments.
Because there are fewer children, two elementary schools were merged.
The new app integrates email and calendar functions.
en.notes: 統合する means "to merge, to integrate": several organizations, systems or data are combined into one unit, e.g. 部署を統合する, 学校を統合する. Transitive with を; "to merge with ..." is 〜と統合する. Typical of business and administrative language (経営統合 "corporate merger"). Distinction: 統一する stresses uniformity, 合併する the legal merger of companies or municipalities.

examples[].german: I spread out the map I had found in the storehouse.
There is an old storehouse at my grandfather's house where old tools are kept.
The rice harvested in autumn is stored in the storehouse.
en.notes: 倉 is a traditional storehouse, especially for grain and goods. 蔵, which has the same reading くら, tends to mean a solid storehouse with thick clay walls and appears in 酒蔵 "sake brewery"; in everyday use the two are often used similarly. Modern warehouses are called 倉庫. Typical: 倉にしまう "to keep in the storehouse", 米を倉に入れる.

examples[].german: He is a descendant of an imperial branch family.
I want to protect the forest for our future descendants.
Living things employ various strategies in order to leave descendants.
en.notes: 子孫 covers all descendants across generations - children, grandchildren and beyond - and is therefore broader than 子供. Typical are 〜の子孫 "descendant of", 子孫を残す "to leave descendants" (also in biology) and 子孫に伝える "to pass on to posterity". The opposite is 先祖 or 祖先 "ancestors". The word is neutral, rather literary.

en.meaning: leaving the nest; fledging; becoming independent
examples[].german: The day has finally come for the children to leave the nest, and I feel a little sad.
In early summer, the swallow chicks reach the time to fledge.
Graduation is the step out into society.
en.notes: 巣立ち is the noun of 巣立つ: literally young birds leaving the nest (ひなの巣立ち), figuratively the step into independence - children move out, students graduate. Common in graduation speeches, greeting cards and parents' reports: 子供の巣立ち, 社会への巣立ち, 巣立ちの日. It sounds warm and somewhat literary; it means "fledging", not the biological "precocial" behavior of leaving the nest right after birth.

examples[].german: Even if you find a bee's nest, it's dangerous, so please don't go near it.
A big wasp nest had formed under the eaves, and we had a pest control company remove it.
After the announcement, the venue erupted in an uproar as if someone had poked a hornet's nest.
en.notes: ハチ (蜂) covers bees and wasps, so ハチの巣 is, depending on context, a beehive or honeycomb or - very often in everyday life - a wasp or hornet nest (スズメバチの巣). It is usually written with katakana ハチ, also 蜂の巣. Idioms: ハチの巣をつついたような騒ぎ "an uproar like a stirred-up wasp nest" and ハチの巣にする "to riddle with holes".

examples[].german: Oh, a spider web has formed!
The room that hadn't been used for a long time was full of cobwebs.
A spider web wet with morning dew was glittering.
en.notes: クモの巣 covers both the elaborate spider web in a garden and cobwebs in a dusty corner: クモの巣が張る/できる "a web forms", クモの巣を払う "to brush away cobwebs", クモの巣だらけ "full of cobwebs", クモの巣にかかる "to get caught in the web". Usually written with katakana クモ, also 蜘蛛の巣. Figuratively, クモの巣のように describes a dense network, for example of roads.

examples[].german: Never enter the off-limits danger zone.
Japan lies in an earthquake-prone zone.
This area is an industrial zone, so there are many trucks even at night.
en.notes: 地帯 denotes a larger area marked by a common characteristic and usually stands after another noun: 工業地帯 "industrial zone", 危険地帯 "danger zone", 安全地帯 "safety zone, traffic island", 山岳地帯 "mountain region". With a modifier it can also stand alone: 地震の多い地帯. Unlike 地域 "area, region" (general, also administrative) or 地区 "district", 地帯 emphasizes the extent as a zone or belt.

examples[].german: The diameter of this circle is 10 centimeters.
There was a hole about 3 meters in diameter in the road.
This pizza is as much as 30 centimeters across.
en.notes: 直径 is the diameter; half of it is 半径 "radius", and the circumference is 円周. Statements follow the pattern 〜の直径は〇センチです or 直径〇センチの〜 (直径5ミリのねじ). The word is used in mathematics as well as in everyday life - for pizzas, plates, tires or holes.

examples[].german: The radius of this circle is 10 centimeters.
There are as many as five convenience stores within a 1 km radius of my home.
Since my child was born, my range of movement has become much narrower.
en.notes: 半径 is the radius, i.e. half of 直径 "diameter". Besides geometry (円の半径) it is very common in location statements: 半径〇キロ以内 "within a radius of ... km", for example for delivery services or restricted zones. Figuratively there is 行動半径 "range of action, range of movement".

examples[].german: They work every day to save people.
The doctor saved the life of the child who had been in an accident.
When I was feeling down, a few words from a friend saved me.
en.notes: 救う means "to rescue, to free from distress": 命を救う, 人を危険から救う, 被災者を救う. The passive 〜に救われる "to be saved by ..., to find comfort through ..." is very common. Compared with 助ける "to help, to rescue", which is more everyday and broader, 救う sounds more serious - it concerns great danger, hardship or emotional suffering. Do not confuse it with the identically read 掬う "to scoop" (water, goldfish).

examples[].german: This was made by kneading wheat flour.
There are many dishes using wheat flour in this region.
Wheat flour got on my clothes and I turned all white.
en.notes: 麦粉 is flour made from 麦 "grain (wheat, barley)", usually wheat flour. In present-day everyday life, on packaging and in recipes, people almost always say 小麦粉; 麦粉 sounds somewhat old-fashioned or regional. "Flour, powder" in general is 粉; barley flour is, more precisely, 大麦粉.

examples[].german: We will expand the business.
If you enlarge the photo, you can see the faces well.
The damage from the fire is spreading more and more.
en.notes: 拡大する means "to enlarge, to expand" and is both transitive and intransitive: 事業を拡大する (to expand something) vs. 被害が拡大する (to spread). Typical in news and business: 感染の拡大, 市場の拡大; in everyday life also for enlarging pictures: 写真を拡大する, 拡大コピー. The opposite is 縮小する. For everyday "to get bigger" people often simply say 大きくなる or 広がる.

examples[].german: This is crayon turned into powder.
This medicine is a powder, so please take it with water.
Liquid is easier to use than powdered detergent.
en.notes: 粉状 means "in powder form, powdery" and is read ふんじょう or こなじょう. It stands as a noun with の (粉状の薬, 粉状の洗剤) or with に (粉状にする "to pulverize"). The word is rather technical and written (product descriptions, chemistry, medicine); in conversation people mostly say 粉の〜 or 粉末の〜. The kanji 状 forms many such shape words: 液状 "liquid", 球状 "spherical".

examples[].german: She is a vegetarian.
For my health, I eat vegetarian two days a week.
At this temple you can eat vegetarian shojin cuisine.
en.notes: 菜食 is a plant-based diet, a diet without meat. It is most common in 菜食主義 "vegetarianism" and 菜食主義者 "vegetarian", also 菜食にする "to eat vegetarian" or 菜食中心の食事. As a する-verb it is rare. In everyday life today ベジタリアン and ヴィーガン are more common; the opposite is 肉食.

examples[].german: The cargo was carried by truck.
A long freight train passed in the middle of the night.
This ship carries cargo, not people.
en.notes: 貨物 is freight or cargo transported by rail, ship, truck or plane, often in compounds: 貨物列車 "freight train", 貨物船 "cargo ship", 航空貨物 "air freight". The opposite is 旅客 "passengers". For private luggage or parcels you say 荷物; 貨物 is the business and technical term for goods in transport.

examples[].german: For some reason, my name was recorded in that army's records.
My grandfather was an army soldier during the war.
The army, navy and air force together are called the three services.
en.notes: 陸軍 is the army, i.e. the land forces, as opposed to 海軍 "navy" and 空軍 "air force"; the armed forces as a whole are called 軍隊 or 軍. For Japan it is used mainly historically (旧日本陸軍 until 1945); the present-day equivalent is called 陸上自衛隊. For other countries one says, for example, アメリカ陸軍.

examples[].german: The average price of a meal at that restaurant is 1,500 yen.
My test score was slightly higher than average.
On average, I sleep about six hours a day.
en.notes: 平均 is the average: 平均を出す "to calculate the average", 平均より上/下, 平均点 "average score", 平均気温, 平均価格. As a する-verb it is very common in 平均すると or 平均して "on average". The second meaning "balance" survives mainly in 平均台 "balance beam". Do not confuse it with 普通 "normal, ordinary", which is not meant statistically.

examples[].german: Please cut it so that the sizes are as even as possible.
The profits were divided equally among all the members.
Equal treatment of men and women is being demanded.
en.notes: 均等 means "evenly distributed, equal" - every part gets the same amount. As a な-adjective: 均等に分ける "to divide into equal parts", 均等な機会 "equal opportunity"; known from the law 男女雇用機会均等法. Unlike 平等 "equality (of rights, treatment)", 均等 stresses quantity and distribution; 平均, by contrast, is the statistical average.

examples[].german: She has a very well-proportioned figure.
The left-right symmetry of this building is very beautiful.
It is difficult to write well-balanced characters.
en.notes: 均整 denotes a harmonious relationship of the parts to one another, i.e. symmetry and balance. It almost always appears in the phrase 均整のとれた〜 "well-proportioned" (body, figure, building, face) or 均整がとれている. Do not confuse it with 均等 "evenly distributed"; in everyday speech similar things are often expressed with バランスがいい. The word is descriptive and somewhat elevated.

examples[].german: When I enter a cemetery, I somehow end up holding my breath.
At Obon, our family goes to the cemetery to visit the graves.
There is an old cemetery on the edge of town.
en.notes: 墓地 is a cemetery as a place with many graves; a single grave is (お)墓, and a grave visit is お墓参り. Large, park-like grounds are often called 霊園, and many cemeteries lie on temple grounds. In conversation people often simply say お墓 instead of 墓地; 墓地 sounds more matter-of-fact.

examples[].german: The tallest mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji.
On clear days you can see Mt. Fuji from here.
During summer vacation I climbed Mt. Fuji with friends.
en.notes: 富士山 is Japan's highest mountain at 3,776 m and a symbol of the country, a World Heritage Site since 2013. The さん here is the on-reading of 山 "mountain", not a polite suffix; "Fujiyama" is not used in Japanese. Typical are 富士山に登る "to climb Mt. Fuji" (season roughly July to September) and 富士山が見える.

examples[].german: The appeal of this website is its richly varied content.
This region is rich in natural resources.
His stories are always full of humor and entertaining.
en.notes: 富む means "to be rich in" and is almost always used with に: 〜に富む, 〜に富んでいる. Typical partners are abstract qualities: 変化に富む "full of variety", 経験に富む "experienced", 栄養に富む "nutritious", ユーモアに富む. Attributively often 〜に富んだ (変化に富んだ人生). The word is rather written; in conversation people say 〜が多い or 〜が豊富だ, and "wealthy" is usually expressed with お金持ち.

examples[].german: We will scale down the operation.
Please copy this page reduced in size.
As the population declines, the domestic market is shrinking.
en.notes: 縮小する means "to reduce, to scale down, to cut back", both transitive (規模を縮小する) and intransitive (市場が縮小する). It sounds matter-of-fact and suits business, administration and technology: 事業の縮小, 縮小コピー. The opposite is 拡大する. For quantities getting smaller, everyday speech prefers 減る／減らす; 縮小 emphasizes scope and extent.

examples[].german: The Maldives is a resort popular among the wealthy.
He was born into a wealthy family and grew up wanting for nothing.
The government decided to raise taxes on the wealthy.
en.notes: 富裕 is a written な-adjective and noun meaning "wealthy, rich". It is most often seen in 富裕層 "the wealthy, upper class", and also in 富裕な家庭 and 富裕国 "rich countries". In conversation people say 金持ち or お金持ち, somewhat more refined 裕福; the opposite is 貧困 or 貧しい.

examples[].german: Who is Tokugawa Ieyasu?
The Tokugawa shogunate lasted about 260 years.
Tokugawa Ieyasu is enshrined at Nikko Toshogu.
en.notes: 徳川 is the family name of the shogun dynasty that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1867. It appears almost always in compounds: 徳川家康 (founder of the shogunate), 徳川幕府 "Tokugawa shogunate", 徳川時代 "Tokugawa period" (= 江戸時代) and 徳川家 "the House of Tokugawa". The name is ubiquitous in history lessons, museums and historical dramas.

examples[].german: I've never been to Tokushima Prefecture, but I'd like to go someday.
Tokushima Prefecture is famous for the Awa Odori.
Tokushima Prefecture is on the eastern side of Shikoku.
en.notes: 徳島県 is a prefecture in the east of the island 四国 Shikoku, with 徳島市 as its capital. It is known for the Obon dance 阿波おどり (阿波 is the old province name) and the sea whirlpools of 鳴門. In conversation 県 is often dropped: 徳島に行く, 徳島出身.

examples[].german: Keeping a spirit of inquiry is the key to growth.
He spent his whole life investigating the mysteries of the universe.
In class, students choose their own topics and investigate them.
en.notes: 探究 means to get to the bottom of something in depth - truth, essence, causes: 真理を探究する, 〜の探究. 探究心 "spirit of inquiry, thirst for knowledge" is very common. Do not confuse it with the identically read 探求 "to search for something, to strive for" (幸福を探求する) or with 研究 "scientific research" as an activity. The word is elevated and literary and often appears in education and science.

examples[].german: Haven't you watched too many detective dramas?
She hired a detective to investigate her husband's affair.
As a child, my dream was to become a detective.
en.notes: 探偵 is a detective, usually a private detective; the agency is called 探偵事務所, and a master detective in novels 名探偵. Police investigators, by contrast, are called 刑事. Typical are 探偵を雇う "to hire a detective" and 探偵小説 "detective novel". As a する-verb ("to investigate secretly") it is rare; people prefer 調べる or 調査する.

examples[].german: When does the police conduct covert investigations?
The police had been secretly investigating that company since six months ago.
The secret investigation revealed the wrongdoing.
en.notes: 内偵 is covert preliminary investigation carried out before those concerned know about it - typical of the police, public prosecutors or tax authorities: 〜を内偵する, 内偵を進める, 内偵捜査. It is a news-language word and hardly occurs in everyday life. Do not confuse it with the identically read 内定 "informal job offer".

examples[].german: Sorry, I didn't mean to confuse you...
Be careful of ads that mislead people with sweet words.
If there are too many items on the menu, you end up confusing the customers.
en.notes: 迷わす is the causative form of 迷う "to get lost, to be undecided": to confuse, unsettle or tempt someone. There is also the regular causative form 迷わせる, which is more common in present-day Japanese; 迷わす sounds more concise and somewhat more literary. Typical are 人を迷わす and 心を迷わす. For deliberate deception, people more often say だます.

examples[].german: This event is organized by the city.
Next month the student council is hosting an international exchange party.
This tournament was held under the sponsorship of a newspaper company.
en.notes: 主催する means to put on an event as the main party responsible: 〜を主催する; as a noun phrase 〜主催の〜 (市主催のイベント) or 〜の主催で. On posters, 主催 "organizer", 共催 "co-organizer" and 後援 "patronage, support" are distinguished. Do not confuse it with the identically read 主宰 "to head, preside over" (e.g. a theater group). Neutral to formal.

en.meaning: to press (for); to remind; to dun
examples[].german: I can't forget the face of the gorilla begging for a banana.
The landlord pressed me for the rent.
I got no reply, so I sent another email to press for one.
en.notes: 催促する means to urge someone to do or deliver something that is due or expected - money, a reply, work: 返事を催促する, 支払いを催促する; passive 催促される "to be pressed". A written reminder is, more formally, 督促状. Because pressing directly seems impolite, it is often paraphrased in emails with お返事をお待ちしております. Compared with せかす "to hurry, to urge on", 催促 concerns something that one is owed.

examples[].german: No matter how many times he failed, he never gave up.
I had the same dream countless times.
That temple burned down many times, but each time it was rebuilt.
en.notes: 幾度 is the literary variant of 何度 "how often, how many times" and is also read いくたび. It mostly appears in fixed patterns: 幾度も "many times, again and again", 幾度となく "countless times", 幾度〜ても "no matter how often". As a genuine question ("How many times?") it sounds old-fashioned; in daily life people say 何度 or 何回.

examples[].german: We will eliminate obstacles.
The police removed the demonstrators from the road.
The possibility of an accident cannot yet be ruled out.
en.notes: 排除する means "to eliminate, to exclude, to remove" - something disturbing or undesirable is actively removed or kept away: 障害を排除する, 可能性を排除する "to rule out a possibility". It is transitive with を and sounds formal, typical of news, law and politics; with people it sounds harsh (反対意見を排除する "to shut out dissenting views"). For everyday removal one rather says 取り除く; merely leaving out or not counting is 除く.

examples[].german: I think that is probably true.
It will probably rain tomorrow.
This record will probably never be broken.
en.notes: 恐らく expresses a fairly confident conjecture and is almost always combined with だろう/でしょう or と思う. It is more formal and written than たぶん and is very common in news, reports and talks. Originally it carried a note of apprehension ("I fear"), but today it is mostly used neutrally. According to dictionaries, it is usually written in kana as おそらく.

examples[].german: She feels a strong fear of speaking in front of people.
There is a risk that the typhoon will make landfall.
In his youth he knew no fear.
en.notes: 恐れ has two uses: as a feeling, "fear, dread" (恐れを感じる, 恐れを抱く, 恐れを知らない "fearless"), which is rather literary - in everyday speech people say 怖さ or 不安. Very common is the pattern 〜おそれがある "there is a risk that ..." in news, weather reports and on warning signs, usually written in kana. It refers to undesirable possibilities; for neutral ones, say 可能性がある.

examples[].german: Won't you be my bodyguard?
A big bouncer stands at the entrance of that bar at night.
I live alone, so I keep a big dog as a sort of bodyguard.
en.notes: 用心棒 is someone hired for protection: a "bodyguard" or "bouncer", often with a slightly old-fashioned ring (known from samurai films such as Kurosawa's "Yojimbo"). Typical are 用心棒を雇う and 〜の用心棒をする. For personal protection officers of politicians or stars, ボディーガード is more usual today, and 警備員 for security staff in buildings. Also used jokingly: 用心棒代わりに犬を飼う "to keep a dog as a protector".

examples[].german: Wouldn't it be better to hold back on a showy dress?
For an interview, avoid flashy clothes and accessories.
The temple looks plain from the outside, but inside it is lavishly decorated.
en.notes: 華美 is a literary な-adjective meaning "gorgeous, splendid" - often with an undertone of "excessive, ostentatious". Typical in dress codes and rules: 華美な服装は避けること "avoid flashy clothing". Adverbially: 華美に飾る. More positive for "luxurious" is 豪華, and colloquially for "loud, flashy" people say 派手. In daily life 華美 is rarely heard, more in notices from schools and companies or at funerals.

en.meaning: to be extended; to be postponed
examples[].german: Because of construction, my usual running course got longer.
The meeting ran an hour over, and I missed my train.
Because of the typhoon, the departure was postponed to tomorrow.
en.notes: 延びる is intransitive: time, deadlines or distances "get extended", or something "gets postponed": 会議が延びる, 締め切りが延びる, 出発が明日に延びる. The transitive counterpart is 延ばす (締め切りを延ばす). Do not confuse it with the identically read 伸びる, which is for physical growth and stretching (背が伸びる, 髪が伸びる, ゴムが伸びる). For an official postponement, the more formal 延期になる is used.

examples[].german: Many politicians in our country are men.
The prime minister stated, "Our country's economy is recovering."
Our country is surrounded by sea on all sides.
en.notes: 我が国 (often also written わが国) means "our country" and belongs to the formal language of politicians, authorities, news and textbooks; 我が is an old possessive "our, my" as in 我が家. In conversation people simply say 日本 or 自分の国 or うちの国 instead. Typical: 我が国の経済, 我が国にとって. Foreigners, too, use it in speeches for their own country.

examples[].german: The new employee has plenty of experience.
This shop has an extensive menu, so I never get bored no matter how often I come.
Spinach is said to be rich in iron.
en.notes: 豊富 is a な-adjective meaning "abundant, plentiful" in quantity or choice: 豊富な経験, 豊富な知識, 種類が豊富だ, ビタミンが豊富だ ("rich in vitamins"). It sounds more matter-of-fact than たくさん or 多い. Distinction: 豊か describes prosperity or fullness in a broader sense (豊かな生活, 自然が豊かだ), while 豊富 describes a concrete, countable abundance of something. The thing something is rich in takes が.

examples[].german: I'm saving this money for my future self.
I save 30,000 yen every month for a trip.
If you shop with this card, you can accumulate points.
en.notes: 貯める is transitive and means "to save, to accumulate (money)": お金を貯める, ポイントを貯める. The intransitive counterpart is 貯まる (お金が貯まる "the money builds up"). The identically read 溜める is used for accumulating things in general (水を溜める, ストレスを溜める); in everyday writing, ためる is often simply written in kana. 貯金する stresses depositing money into an account, 節約する saving by spending less.

examples[].german: It has been a long time since I stopped eating bacon.
A letter suddenly arrived from a friend I hadn't seen in a long time.
It has long been said that the declining birthrate is a problem.
en.notes: 久しい is a literary い-adjective: "long (ago)". It appears almost always in the pattern 〜て久しい "it has been a long time since ..." (〜と言われて久しい "it has long been said that ...") or adverbially as 久しく "for a long time" (久しく会っていない). In conversation people say ずいぶん前から or 長い間 instead. Related is the everyday 久しぶり "after a long time".

en.meaning: to get to the bottom of; to investigate thoroughly
examples[].german: The police are investigating the cause of the accident.
The victims' families are demanding that the truth be established.
Scientists are trying to clarify the mechanism of this disease.
en.notes: 究明 means "to investigate thoroughly and clarify", especially causes, truth or scientific relationships: 原因を究明する, 真相究明, 原因究明を急ぐ. It is formal and typical of news and specialist texts. Distinctions: 調査 is investigation or survey in general, 研究 is research, 解明 is unraveling a mystery. For personal matters such as one's own weaknesses, 究明 does not fit.

examples[].german: We will abolish the old system.
Because there are few users, this bus route will be discontinued next year.
School uniforms were abolished at our school.
en.notes: 廃止する means "to abolish, to discontinue" and refers to institutions, rules, systems or services: 制度を廃止する, 路線を廃止する. Transitive with を; very common in the passive: このバスは来年廃止されます. It sounds official and factual. Distinction: 中止する is cancelling a single plan or event (試合が中止になる), 廃止 the permanent abolition of something existing.

examples[].german: The exam material is so hard that I'm about to give up.
The soldiers approached slowly, waving a white flag.
The president finally gave up too and called off the plan.
en.notes: 白旗 is the "white flag" as a sign of surrender. Most common is the phrase 白旗を上げる (also 揚げる) "to raise the white flag" - literally in war, figuratively in everyday life for "to give up, to admit defeat", for example with tasks that are too hard. Besides しろはた there is the reading はっき. Synonymous but more direct are 降参する and 諦める.

examples[].german: First, I plan to start by expanding my local network of contacts.
She has a wide network of contacts, so she's reliable when you're in trouble.
He went independent, making use of the connections he built at his previous company.
en.notes: 人脈 is a personal "network" of contacts, above all in working life: 人脈を広げる, 人脈を作る/築く, 人脈が広い, 人脈を生かす. The word is neutral to positive. コネ, by contrast, means "connections" that one exploits, often with an air of nepotism (コネで入社する). More general and softer is つながり "connection".

examples[].german: Is a door with a push button also called an automatic door?
This traffic light is the push-button type, so press the button and wait.
In an emergency, please use this push button to call a station attendant.
en.notes: 押しボタン is a "push button", especially on devices or installations that are operated by pressing a button. 押しボタン式 "push-button type" is very common: 押しボタン式信号 is a pedestrian-activated traffic light, and there are also emergency call buttons in stations or stop-request buttons on buses. In daily life people mostly say just ボタン; 押しボタン appears more on signs and notices.

examples[].german: He is a famous novelist, but sometimes he also self-publishes.
She published her first novel last year.
This book was published fifty years ago, yet it still sells well today.
en.notes: 出版する is transitive: to "publish" a book - 本を出版する, and in the passive 出版される "to come out". Important compounds are 自費出版 "self-publishing" and 出版社 "publishing house". For newspapers and magazines people tend to say 発行する, and for research results or music 発表する. In conversation you also hear simply 本を出す.

examples[].german: At that publisher, you have to show ID when entering the building.
My older brother edits a magazine at a publishing company.
I sent my manuscript to several publishers, but I haven't heard back from any of them.
en.notes: 出版社 is a "publisher" of books and magazines: 出版社に勤める, 出版社から本を出す, 大手出版社 "major publisher". Do not confuse it with 書店 or 本屋 "bookstore", where books are sold. A newspaper publisher is called 新聞社. The staff who work with the texts are 編集者 "editors".

examples[].german: You seem to think you're wonderful, but keep firmly in mind that you're just a poor person from a poor family.
A poor person like me can't afford such an expensive restaurant.
Old tales often feature poor people and rich people.
en.notes: 貧乏人 is a "poor person, poor wretch" and sounds blunt to derogatory. It is often used self-deprecatingly (僕みたいな貧乏人) or as an insult; neutrally one says 貧しい人, 生活が苦しい人 or 低所得者. The opposite is 金持ち; a well-known proverb is 貧乏人の子だくさん "the poor have many children".

examples[].german: I asked her father whether I could marry her and got his permission.
My older sister married a friend from her university days last year.
"Are you married?" "No, I'm still single."
en.notes: 結婚する means "to marry"; the person takes と, not を: 彼女と結婚する. 結婚している describes the state "to be married", 結婚した the event "got married". Related words: 結婚式 "wedding ceremony", 婚約 "engagement", 離婚 "divorce", 独身 "single". To congratulate, you say ご結婚おめでとうございます.

examples[].german: At this kindergarten, photography is prohibited at the children's performances.
Photography is prohibited inside the museum, so please put your camera away.
The entrance says "No photography," but someone was taking pictures.
en.notes: 撮影禁止 means "photographing (and filming) prohibited"; 撮影 covers photos as well as video. You see it mainly on signs in museums, temples, concerts or shops, and in a sentence mostly as 〜は撮影禁止です or 撮影禁止の場所. Variants are フラッシュ撮影禁止 and 撮影禁止区域. In speech, and more politely, you say 写真を撮らないでください.

examples[].german: "Koichi, did you forget anything?" "No." "Oh, wait a moment. I forgot to put the teriyaki salmon in your lunchbox." "What?! Mom, hurry up."
Let's make chicken teriyaki tonight.
At this shop, the teriyaki burger is the most popular.
en.notes: 照り焼き is a cooking method: meat or fish is glazed with a sweet sauce of soy sauce, mirin and sugar and fried or grilled until it shines (照り "gloss"). Typical are 鶏の照り焼き, ぶりの照り焼き and 照り焼きバーガー; "to prepare something as teriyaki" is 照り焼きにする. On menus you also see てりやき in kana.

examples[].german: That magazine is worth subscribing to.
We subscribe to two newspapers at home.
The price went up, so I decided to cancel my magazine subscription.
en.notes: 購読する means "to take, subscribe to (a newspaper or magazine)": 新聞を購読する, 定期購読 "subscription", 購読料 "subscription fee". The word is rather formal and typical for print media and newsletters. For YouTube channels people say チャンネル登録, and for online services in general 登録する. To cancel a subscription, say 購読をやめる or, more formally, 解約する.

examples[].german: We established a new company.
This university was founded a hundred years ago.
Together with friends, I founded a club that helps international students.
en.notes: 設立する means "to found, to establish" in an institutional sense: companies, associations, schools, foundations. Transitive with を, often in the passive or as a noun: 1950年に設立された, 会社の設立. In everyday speech one also simply says 作る; 創立 stresses the original founding (創立記念日), and 建設 is the building of structures - 設立 refers to the organization, not the building.

examples[].german: I remember that in some country a gorilla escaped and caused an uproar.
The children are making a big fuss about seeing snow for the first time.
I made a big fuss because I couldn't find my wallet, but it was in my bag.
en.notes: 大騒ぎ is a "great uproar, a big fuss": 大騒ぎになる "to cause an uproar", 大騒ぎする "to make a big fuss, to celebrate boisterously" (intransitive). Depending on context it can mean real excitement, exaggerated fuss or loud partying. Weaker is 騒ぎ; more serious and formal is 騒動 (for example for riots or scandals).

examples[].german: I summarized on my blog the order of the procedures after bidding on Yahoo Auctions.
The explanation was hard to follow because the order was reversed.
Please tell me in order what happened.
en.notes: 順序 is the "order" or "sequence" of steps: 順序が逆だ, 順序を守る, 順序よく並べる, 順序立てて説明する "to explain in order". It sounds somewhat more factual than 順番, which is used above all for "whose turn it is" (順番を待つ). For concrete work steps one also says 手順.

examples[].german: I'm well aware that I'm a weak-willed person.
Without anyone telling him to, he quit the company of his own will.
My father has a strong will and sees through whatever he has decided to the end.
en.notes: 意志 is the "will" in the sense of willpower and determination: 意志が強い/弱い, 強い意志, 自分の意志で "of one's own free will". Do not confuse it with the identically read 意思, which rather means "intention, wish" and appears in legal contexts (意思表示, 本人の意思を確認する). As a rule of thumb: 意志 = strength of will, 意思 = an opinion that one expresses.

examples[].german: What is your motivation for applying for this job?
I got into my first-choice university.
My younger brother is aiming for medical school and studies late every night.
en.notes: 志望 denotes the wish to aim for a particular school, university or profession: 〜を志望する, 第一志望 "first choice", 志望校 "preferred school", 志望動機 "motivation for applying". As a suffix, 〜志望 means "aspiring" (作家志望の若者). More general is 希望 "wish, hope"; actually submitting an application is 応募する.

examples[].german: Koichi is my benefactor. When I was drowning in bacon, he saved me.
You, who helped me back then, are the savior of my life.
The company president is my benefactor who hired me when I had no work.
en.notes: 恩人 is a person to whom one owes a great deal: a "benefactor", someone to whom one is indebted. 命の恩人 "life-saver" is very common. Typical: 〜は私の恩人だ, 恩人に恩返しする "to repay one's benefactor". Related are 恩 "debt of gratitude, favor" and 恩師 "revered former teacher".

examples[].german: I shall grant a reward to whoever captures that bacon thief.
The samurai who distinguished himself in battle received land as a reward.
Period dramas often feature retainers complaining that the reward is small.
en.notes: 恩賞 is a "reward" that a ruler or lord grants for meritorious service, for example land or money for achievements in war. The word is historical and today appears mainly in history books and samurai dramas: 恩賞を与える, 恩賞を受ける. For a reward in modern everyday life you say ご褒美, and for an offered cash prize 賞金 or 謝礼.

en.meaning: to gather; to pick; to hire; to adopt (a measure)
examples[].german: My father is a master at catching rhinoceros beetles.
I went and gathered mushrooms in the mountains at the weekend.
Our company plans to hire ten new employees this year.
en.notes: 採る is a special spelling of とる for "to gather, to pick" (キノコを採る, 虫を採る), "to hire (personnel)" (新人を採る) and "to choose (a measure, a method)" (この案を採る, 決を採る). In everyday writing 取る is often used instead. Other spellings: 捕る "to catch (animals)", 撮る "to photograph". Related nouns are 採用 "hiring, adoption" and 採集 "collecting".

examples[].german: These cherries are insanely delicious.
Yamagata Prefecture is famous as a cherry-growing region.
I put one cherry on top of the cake.
en.notes: さくらんぼ is the "cherry" as a fruit and is almost always written in kana; the spelling 桜んぼ is rare, and on packaging you often see サクランボ. Distinguish 桜, the cherry tree or cherry blossom. A well-known growing region is Yamagata Prefecture. In sweets and on menus you also see チェリー.

examples[].german: You come to the horse meat party with me, too. It's going to be a cool party.
In Kumamoto, horse meat sashimi is a local specialty.
When winter came, my grandfather would make hot pot with horse meat.
en.notes: 桜肉 is a traditional expression for horse meat (plainly 馬肉); the name is usually explained by the pink color of the meat. Well-known dishes are 馬刺し "raw horse meat" and 桜鍋 "horse meat stew", specialties for example in 熊本 or 長野. In a similarly euphemistic way, wild boar meat is called ぼたん and deer meat もみじ.

examples[].german: I saw a photo of myself at two or three years old, looking all grown up in a pale pink tuxedo.
Her cheeks were tinged pink from the cold.
I bought a spring-like cherry-pink sweater.
en.notes: 桜色 is the very delicate, pale pink of cherry blossoms. It stands attributively with の (桜色のセーター) or with に for changes (桜色に染まる "to turn pale pink") and sounds more poetic than ピンク. 桃色 is a stronger peach pink. 桜色 is also often used to describe rosy cheeks or lips.

examples[].german: Let's think of a countermeasure.
As a measure against the heat, I put a sunshade on the window.
I bought a Japanese-Language Proficiency Test prep book at the bookstore.
en.notes: 対策 is a targeted measure against a problem or in preparation for something. Typical are 対策を立てる "to plan measures" and 対策を取る "to take measures". As a suffix, 〜対策 names the problem being addressed: 暑さ対策, 地震対策, 風邪対策 - and 試験対策 means "exam preparation". A general plan with no problem behind it is, by contrast, 計画.

examples[].german: I will propose a new plan.
I suggested to my friends that we all go camping on the weekend.
The department head accepted my proposal.
en.notes: 提案する is transitive: you propose something with を, and the person addressed takes に. The content can also be quoted: 〜ようと提案する, 〜ことを提案する. As a noun, 提案 goes with 出す, 受け入れる or 断る. Unlike 勧める ("to recommend something to someone", for their benefit), 提案 puts an idea up for decision; it is neutral to businesslike.

examples[].german: I will set a goal.
I set an alarm for 6 o'clock every morning.
Please set a new password.
en.notes: 設定する means "to set, to configure": fixing goals, deadlines or rules (目標を設定する, 期限を設定する) and above all configuring devices and software (アラームを設定する, パスワードを設定する). The noun 設定 also means "settings" in a menu (設定を変更する) as well as the setting of a story (物語の設定). For simply setting an alarm clock, one also colloquially says セットする or 目覚ましをかける.

examples[].german: When you're waiting for the kitchen timer to ring, it feels like it goes on forever, doesn't it?
The two vowed eternal love in the church.
With this photo, the memories of that day will remain forever.
en.notes: 永遠 means "eternity" and is used mainly in two forms: adverbially 永遠に "forever, eternally" (永遠に続く, 永遠に忘れない) and attributively with の (永遠の愛, 永遠のテーマ). The form 永遠な is unusual. The word sounds solemn or romantic; in conversation people prefer ずっと or いつまでも. 永久 is more matter-of-fact and technical (永久歯 "permanent teeth").

examples[].german: How much liquid can I bring on board the plane?
Water changes into solid, liquid and gas depending on temperature.
For laundry I use liquid detergent rather than powder.
en.notes: 液体 is the technical term for "liquid" and, together with 固体 "solid" and 気体 "gas", forms the three states of matter. In everyday life it appears at airport security checks (液体の持ち込み) and in product names such as 液体洗剤 "liquid detergent" or 液体のり "liquid glue". As a suffix, often just 〜液 is used (消毒液, 洗浄液).

examples[].german: Work that involves using a computer easily strains the eyes.
He has an eye for people, so you can feel safe with anyone he chooses.
I had my eyes examined at the hospital.
en.notes: 眼 is a rarer spelling of め "eye"; in daily life you almost always write 目. 眼 seems technical or literary and often appears in medical contexts or when a "trained eye, judgment" is meant: 人を見る眼がある, 鋭い眼. In compounds the character is mostly read がん: 眼科 "ophthalmology", 眼球 "eyeball"; 眼鏡 is read めがね.

examples[].german: I searched everywhere for my left eyeball but could not find it.
When the surface of the eyeball dries out, the eyes tire easily.
The doctor used a light to examine the patient's eye movements.
en.notes: 眼球 is the medical-anatomical term for the "eyeball" (眼球運動 "eye movement", 眼球が乾く). In everyday speech people usually say 目玉, which is also found in 目玉焼き "fried egg" and 目玉商品 "loss leader". With の, 眼球 forms technical expressions such as 眼球の表面 or 眼球の動き.

examples[].german: Around when does presbyopia usually start?
My presbyopia has progressed lately, and small print has become hard to read.
My father wears reading glasses when he reads the newspaper.
en.notes: 老眼 is "age-related farsightedness" (presbyopia): with age, one sees worse up close. Typical: 老眼になる, 老眼が始まる/進む, and 老眼鏡 "reading glasses". Distinguish it from 近視 or 近眼 "nearsightedness" and 遠視 "farsightedness" (not age-related). Since the word alludes to age, people politely paraphrase it with 手元が見えにくい.

examples[].german: My family has an old sword that has been passed down through generations from our ancestors.
At Obon, my family goes to visit our ancestors' graves.
My ancestors apparently grew rice in this village in the Edo period.
en.notes: 先祖 are the "ancestors" of a family. Respectfully you say ご先祖様, especially in connection with お盆 and grave visits (お墓参り). Common is 先祖代々 "for generations" (先祖代々の土地). The synonym 祖先 sounds more objective and is also used biologically (人類の祖先 "ancestors of humankind"); for a single family 先祖 is more usual.

examples[].german: Is killing in self-defense legal?
To avoid becoming a victim of fraud, it is important for each person to protect themselves.
My older brother graduated from high school and joined the Self-Defense Forces.
en.notes: 自衛 means "self-defense, self-protection": 自衛のため, 自衛手段, 自衛する "to protect oneself" (also against fraud or infection). Well known is 自衛隊, Japan's "Self-Defense Forces". In criminal law, by contrast, self-defense is 正当防衛; national defense is 防衛 (防衛省).

examples[].german: I have multiple nicknames and accounts.
This question has multiple correct answers.
In English, an s is often added to make a noun plural.
en.notes: 複数 means "several, multiple" and usually stands before the noun with の: 複数の人, 複数のアカウント; adverbially 複数回 "several times". It sounds more objective than いくつかの or たくさん and is typical of forms, instructions and news (複数回答可 "multiple answers allowed"). In grammar, 複数形 is the "plural", the opposite is 単数 "singular".

examples[].german: I want to remove the noise from this audio file.
Static came onto the phone line, and I can't hear the other person's voice well.
Ignore the noise around you and keep going your own way.
en.notes: 雑音 is disturbing background noise: static on the radio or phone (雑音が入る), noise in recordings (雑音を消す). Figuratively it also means "chatter, unqualified criticism" from outside (周りの雑音). Distinction: 騒音 is loud, bothersome noise (traffic, construction), 物音 a single sound that one hears.

examples[].german: My grandfather's day begins at the public bathhouse.
My bath at home broke, so I went to the nearby public bathhouse.
At a public bathhouse, you must not put your towel in the bathtub.
en.notes: 銭湯 is a public bathhouse in a residential neighborhood that you go to for an entrance fee (銭 "coin", 湯 "hot water"): 銭湯に行く, 銭湯に入る. Unlike 温泉, it uses ordinary heated water, not a natural hot spring. Larger modern facilities with saunas are called スーパー銭湯. The rules include washing before bathing and not dipping the towel into the bath.

examples[].german: The brand has been established.
The new treatment has not yet been established.
At 30, he established his position as a writer.
en.notes: 確立する means "to establish firmly, to put on a secure foundation": 地位を確立する, 方法を確立する, 信頼関係を確立する. It is mostly transitive with を, but also occurs intransitively (制度が確立する). The word is formal and typical of business, science and news. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 確率 "probability".

examples[].german: He dumped me and I'm down, so I'm going to Paris on a trip to heal my broken heart.
Her friends gently comforted the heartbroken girl.
The players who lost the match returned home heartbroken.
en.notes: 傷心 is an elevated word for "heartbreak, deep sorrow", usually after a breakup or defeat. Typical are 傷心の〜 (傷心の彼女), 傷心のまま and 傷心旅行 "a trip to get over heartbreak". In conversation people more often say 落ち込む or 失恋してつらい. Grammatically 傷心 is a noun that modifies nouns with の.

examples[].german: It is said that the accident left three dead and more than two hundred injured.
All the injured were taken to a nearby hospital.
After the earthquake, doctors gathered and treated the injured.
en.notes: 傷者 means "injured person" and belongs to the language of news and reports. On its own it is rather rare; much more common are 負傷者 "injured person" and the compound 死傷者 "dead and injured". In everyday speech you say けが人. Typical are statements of numbers: 傷者は〜人にのぼる "the number of injured amounts to ...".

examples[].german: Our LDP is on fire this year. No one will call us the "Fool's Party" anymore.
The Liberal Democratic Party was formed in 1955.
In this election, the Liberal Democratic Party lost seats.
en.notes: 自民党 is the short form of 自由民主党, the "Liberal Democratic Party" (LDP), which has governed Japan almost continuously since its founding in 1955. Important related terms are 与党 "ruling party", 野党 "opposition" and 総裁 "party president". All party names are formed on the pattern 〜党.

examples[].german: The first thing I noticed was that he is a Communist Party member.
In China, the Communist Party has long been at the center of politics.
Japan also has a Communist Party, and it has members in the Diet.
en.notes: 共産党 is the "Communist Party", e.g. 日本共産党 or 中国共産党. A member is 共産党員, the ideology is 共産主義 "communism". In conversation party names are often shortened; 共産党 itself is already the usual short form of 日本共産党. Related terms: 政党 "political party", 与党 "ruling party", 野党 "opposition party".

examples[].german: I was deeply moved by the speech of a certain Republican Party member.
The number of members of that party is decreasing year by year.
If you become a party member, you can vote in the election for the party leader.
en.notes: 党員 is a "party member"; usually the party name comes before it with の or directly as a compound (共産党員, 自民党員). Typical: 党員になる, 党員数 "number of members", 党員集会. Distinctions: 議員 is an elected member of a legislature, 党首 is the party leader. Not every 党員 is a politician - it can be any ordinary member.

examples[].german: I feel that the Socialist Party's claims are not realistic.
When he was young, my grandfather supported the Socialist Party.
The Japan Socialist Party changed its name to the Social Democratic Party in 1996.
en.notes: 社会党 is a "Socialist Party". In Japan this usually means the former 日本社会党, for a long time the largest opposition party, which renamed itself 社会民主党 (short 社民党) in 1996. Foreign parties are also called this, for example the French 社会党. Related: 社会主義 "socialism", 野党 "opposition".

examples[].german: "Do you have an allergy to raw eggs?" "Not as far as I know."
In Japan, many people eat raw egg over rice.
Please store raw eggs in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 生卵 is a "raw egg" (生 "raw"). In Japan eggs are often eaten raw, for example as 卵かけご飯 (raw egg over rice) or as a dip for すき焼き. Counterparts are ゆで卵 "boiled egg", 半熟卵 "soft-boiled egg" and 温泉卵 "egg cooked at low temperature". Reading: なまたまご.

examples[].german: If you think I stole your boiled egg, you've got the wrong guy.
I ate two boiled eggs for breakfast.
The shell of the boiled egg won't peel off properly.
en.notes: ゆで卵 is an egg "boiled" in water, from ゆでる "to boil in water" (also written 茹で卵). Depending on cooking time, one distinguishes 固ゆで "hard-boiled" and 半熟 "soft-boiled, medium-boiled". Typical phrases: ゆで卵を作る, ゆで卵の殻をむく "to peel the boiled egg". A fried egg, by contrast, is called 目玉焼き.

examples[].german: Private chatter among employees is strictly prohibited.
Open flames are strictly prohibited at gas stations.
Street shoes are strictly prohibited in this room, so please take off your shoes.
en.notes: 厳禁 is a "strict prohibition" and clearly stronger than 禁止. It appears mainly on signs and in regulations, often directly after the prohibited thing: 火気厳禁 "open flames strictly prohibited", 土足厳禁 "no street shoes", 〜は厳禁です. As a verb, 厳禁する is rare; you mostly hear 〜は厳禁だ.

examples[].german: We often use this room for our secret meetings.
A weekly magazine reported a secret meeting between a popular actor and a singer.
The spy was secretly meeting a foreign official in the park at night.
en.notes: 密会 is a "secret meeting", often with the flavor of an affair or scandal: 〜と密会する, 密会が報じられる. It is typical of tabloids, crime stories and spy stories. As a する-verb it is intransitive; the person takes と. A neutral meeting is simply 会う or 会合, and a date is デート.

examples[].german: I accumulate knowledge.
We are analyzing data accumulated over many years.
After a succession of busy days, fatigue is building up.
en.notes: 蓄積する means "to accumulate, to pile up (gradually)", both transitive (データを蓄積する) and intransitive (疲労が蓄積する). Typical of factual texts about data, knowledge, experience, fatigue or pollutants. In everyday speech 溜める／溜まる sounds more natural: 疲れが溜まる. For money one says 貯める or 貯金する, not 蓄積する.

examples[].german: In every age, there are people who curry favor with their boss by informing on others, aiming for promotion.
Someone seems to have tipped off the police, and the culprit was caught immediately.
During the war, everyone was afraid of being reported by their neighbors, so no one said what they really thought.
en.notes: 密告 is secretly reporting someone's misconduct to the authorities or superiors: "denunciation, informing on someone". Typical: 警察に密告する, 〜を密告する, 密告される. The word mostly carries a negative flavor of betrayal. Neutral is 通報する "to report" (for example an accident), and childish and colloquial is 告げ口する "to tattle".

examples[].german: I was once offered a deal to smuggle drugs. Of course, I turned it down.
At the airport, a man who tried to smuggle in a rare animal was arrested.
I hear smuggling used to be rampant at this port in the past.
en.notes: 密輸 means "smuggling": 〜を密輸する, 麻薬の密輸, 密輸品 "contraband", 密輸業者 "smuggler". More precisely, one distinguishes 密輸入 "smuggling in" and 密輸出 "smuggling out". The word is typical of news and crime stories. As a する-verb it is transitive: what is smuggled takes を.

examples[].german: What is the most dangerous infectious disease in the world?
In the past, many people died of infectious diseases.
An infectious disease broke out in that village, and school was closed for a month.
en.notes: 伝染病 is a "contagious disease, epidemic": 伝染病が流行する/広がる, 伝染病にかかる. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned today; in medicine and official language people now mostly say 感染症 "infectious disease". The related verb is 伝染する "to be transmitted"; in everyday speech, for "to infect" people simply say うつる/うつす.

examples[].german: That incident left a big blemish on his career.
This loss is the biggest stain in the team's history.
We will never tolerate wrongdoing, so that it does not become a blemish on the company.
en.notes: 汚点 is a "blemish, stain on one's reputation" and is used almost only figuratively: 経歴の汚点, 歴史に汚点を残す, 〜の汚点となる. For a real stain on clothing, people say シミ or 汚れ in everyday speech. It is not synonymous with the internet slang 黒歴史, which means more an "embarrassing past" that one laughs about; 汚点 is more serious and sounds literary.

examples[].german: A cup ramen can't satisfy my craving for ramen.
People have a desire to be recognized by someone.
I work overtime every day, and my frustration is building up.
en.notes: 欲求 is a "need, desire", especially in the psychological sense: 欲求を満たす "to satisfy a need", 〜したいという欲求, 承認欲求 "need for recognition", 欲求不満 "frustration".
