It is used almost only as a noun; 欲求する is rare. Distinctions: 欲望 is stronger and rather negative, "lust, greed"; 欲 is colloquial "desire, greed".

examples[].german: Why do some Christians and Buddhists deny carnal desire as sinful?
A monk in training must renounce carnal desire.
That novel is about a man who gives in to carnal desire and loses everything.
en.notes: 肉欲 is "carnal desire, sensual lust" and comes from religious and literary language: 肉欲に溺れる "to indulge in carnal desire", 肉欲を断つ "to renounce it". More neutral and medical is 性欲 "sexual desire". The component 欲 "desire" also appears in 食欲 "appetite" and 物欲 "greed for possessions".

examples[].german: This winter was colder than usual and there was a lot of snow, but is the Earth really warming?
This region is blessed with a mild climate all year round.
After retirement, I want to live a relaxed life in a warm place.
en.notes: 温暖 describes almost only climate and regions: 温暖な気候, 温暖な地域. For a warm room, water or clothing, you say 暖かい or 温かい, not 温暖. The derivation 温暖化 "warming" is very common, especially 地球温暖化 "global warming", also as a する-verb 温暖化する. The opposite is 寒冷 "cold (climate)"; overall it belongs more to written and news language.

en.meaning: to hold within; to keep to oneself; to conceal
examples[].german: He is the type who keeps things inside, so I'm worried.
She finally wrote in a letter the feelings she had kept in her heart.
This child holds great potential.
en.notes: 秘める means "to keep something hidden within oneself, to keep to oneself" - usually feelings, intentions or abilities, not concrete objects. Typical are 胸に秘める / 心に秘める "to carry in one's heart" and 可能性を秘める "to hold potential", mostly as 秘めた + noun or 秘めている. To physically hide something is 隠す. The word sounds elevated to literary; related is 秘密 "secret".

examples[].german: This word is hard to translate.
Could you translate this letter into Japanese for me?
I tried translating the lyrics of my favorite English song myself.
en.notes: 訳す is the everyday verb for "to translate": X を Y に訳す "to translate X into Y", the source language takes から: 英語から日本語に訳す. 翻訳する means the same but sounds more formal and is preferred for professional translations; oral interpreting is 通訳する. The noun 訳 (やく) appears in 和訳 and 英訳; 訳 read わけ "reason" is a different word.

examples[].german: Do you know how to read the name of this book's translator?
Reading the translator's afterword helps you understand the work better.
Even for the same novel, the impression changes quite a lot depending on the translator.
en.notes: 訳者 is the translator of a particular work and appears mainly in books and reviews: 訳者あとがき "translator's afterword", 著者と訳者 "author and translator". In general, "someone who translates" is 翻訳者, as a profession 翻訳家; an interpreter is 通訳. In everyday conversation 訳者 sounds rather literary.

en.meaning: to be fulfilling; to be rich; to be well-equipped
examples[].german: I will enrich the content.
My summer vacation this year was really fulfilling.
This library has a rich selection of children's books.
en.notes: 充実する is intransitive and means "to be fulfilled, rich, well-equipped": 設備が充実している, 充実した一日. It mostly appears as 充実している or attributively as 充実した〜. To actively expand or enrich something, one uses the causative 充実させる (内容を充実させる). The noun 充実感 "sense of fulfillment" is also common.

examples[].german: Among Japanese words, some have no perfect English equivalent.
I looked in the dictionary for a translation word that fits this sentence.
This new technical term doesn't have a fixed translation yet.
en.notes: 訳語 is the individual word that corresponds to a foreign-language word in a translation - that is, the equivalent as in a dictionary, not the translation of a whole text (that is 訳 or 翻訳). Typical are 訳語を探す, 訳語を当てる "to choose an equivalent" and 適切な訳語 "a fitting equivalent". The word belongs more to technical and written language.

examples[].german: I can only translate from Japanese into English.
Could you translate this email into English?
I hear an English translation of that novel will be published next year.
en.notes: 英訳 is always translation into English, not from English - that would be 和訳. As a する-verb: X を英訳する; the source language takes から. As a noun it also denotes the result: 英訳版 "English edition". From school, one knows the exercise types 和文英訳 "Japanese -> English" and 英文和訳 "English -> Japanese".

examples[].german: Although there are a few small mistakes, I think you translated it into Japanese well.
Translate the following English sentences into Japanese.
This book doesn't have a Japanese translation yet, so I have no choice but to read it in English.
en.notes: 和訳 is translation into Japanese, usually from English; 和 stands for "Japan" here as in 和食. As a する-verb: X を和訳する. The counterpart is 英訳. For published translations of foreign books, 邦訳 is also used; 和訳 is known mainly from school and exams (英文和訳).

en.meaning: to let leak; to leak (a secret); to let slip (a complaint)
examples[].german: Even adults wet themselves sometimes.
Please don't tell anyone about this.
After the meeting, the department head voiced his dissatisfaction with the new plan.
en.notes: 漏らす is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 漏れる (水が漏れる "water leaks"). Besides "to let leak", its most important use is "to leak, blab": 秘密を漏らす, 情報を漏らす. It also means "to voice, let out": 不満を漏らす, ため息を漏らす; colloquially also "to wet oneself" (おしっこを漏らす). As a suffix, 〜漏らす means "to miss by oversight": 聞き漏らす.

en.meaning: to cross; to get through; to exceed; to move (house)
examples[].german: When we crossed the mountain, the sea came into view.
The tree in the garden got through the winter safely and bloomed in spring.
Next month, I'm going to move to an apartment near the station.
en.notes: 越す is transitive (〜を越す) and has several meanings: "to cross" (山を越す), "to get through" (冬を越す), "to exceed" (with numbers mostly written 超す: 30度を超す) and "to move house" (新しい家に越す, more often 引っ越す). The related 越える is used similarly with を and is somewhat more common in the sense of "to cross". As a respectful form one knows お越しください "please come".

en.meaning: to be giddy; to be carried away
examples[].german: Too many people are getting carried away over the Olympics.
I was elated about passing, and then I left my wallet on the train.
Carried away by the festival atmosphere, I ended up spending too much money.
en.notes: 浮かれる is intransitive and describes an exuberant, buoyant mood, often with the undertone that one becomes careless in the process. The trigger takes に: お祭りに浮かれる, 勝利に浮かれる; mostly as 浮かれている or 浮かれて. 浮かれ気分 is "high spirits". Unlike はしゃぐ (romping around noisily, often of children), it concerns more the inner mood; simply being happy is 喜ぶ.

en.meaning: to suit; to look good on
examples[].german: Glasses suit Koichi better than contact lenses.
That hat really suits you.
Clothes in flashy colors don't suit me.
en.notes: 似合う is intransitive: Person に clothing/hairstyle が似合う "something suits someone". For the current impression one usually says 似合っている / 似合ってる. Do not confuse it with 合う, which concerns fit (サイズが合う). The noun お似合い describes a well-matched couple (お似合いのカップル); 似合わない can also mean that a behavior does not suit someone.

examples[].german: A short man came stumbling out of the bar and threw up right in front of me.
I changed the height of the desk to match the child's height.
The grass in the garden has grown as tall as a person.
en.notes: 背丈 denotes a person's height or stature, more as a visible impression. The measured value in centimeters is 身長 (身長は170センチ); in everyday speech people usually just say 背 (背が高い). 背丈 often appears in comparisons: 背丈が同じくらい, 背丈ほどの草 "grass as tall as a person". It sounds somewhat more descriptive and literary than 背.

examples[].german: He showed his eagerness to win the gold medal.
Lately I've been losing my motivation for work.
Our company is recruiting motivated young people.
en.notes: 意欲 is the active will to do something: 〜への意欲, 〜に意欲を見せる / 燃やす. Common are 意欲がある / ない, 意欲的な "enthusiastic" and compounds like 学習意欲 "motivation to learn" or 購買意欲 "willingness to buy". Compared with the colloquial やる気, 意欲 sounds more formal and is often used in news, job ads and reports.

examples[].german: I've never seen such a tall hobbit.
My older brother is the tallest in the family.
Because I'm tall, I can see around me well even on a crowded train.
en.notes: 背が高い means "tall (in stature)" and is used for people and animals; buildings or mountains are simply 高い. Before a noun, が usually becomes の: 背の高い人. The opposite is 背が低い, and "to grow taller" is 背が伸びる. Colloquially you also hear 大きい, but 背が高い refers unambiguously to body height.

en.meaning: to be involved; to be connected
examples[].german: I am involved in this problem.
I don't really want to have anything to do with that person.
This is not a life-threatening illness, so please rest assured.
en.notes: 関わる means "to have to do with something, to be involved" and takes に: 事件に関わる, プロジェクトに関わる. With people, 〜と関わる means "to have dealings with": あの人とは関わらない方がいい. For serious matters, 命に関わる means "to be life-threatening". Unlike 携わる (to work professionally in a field), 関わる is broader and can also mean an unwanted entanglement; alternative spelling 係わる.

examples[].german: I need to start getting the New Year decorations ready soon.
I put ornaments on the Christmas tree with the kids.
He's called a department head, but it's only a nominal title, and he can't decide anything.
en.notes: 飾り is the noun of 飾る "to decorate" and means "ornament, decoration". It is common in compounds: 正月飾り, 髪飾り (かみかざり) "hair ornament", クリスマスの飾り; typical are 飾りをつける and 飾りを外す. Figuratively, (お)飾り means "mere façade": a position without real power is ただの飾り.

examples[].german: That woman is really unpretentious.
It's a plain room, but clean and calming.
The president's unpretentious way of speaking is popular with the employees.
en.notes: 飾り気 is the "inclination to adorn, affectation" and appears almost only negated: 飾り気のない / 飾り気がない "plain, unaffected, natural". This is mostly praise for people, their way of speaking or a simple style. The affirmative 飾り気がある is rare; someone who puts on airs is more likely 気取っている.

examples[].german: Please tell me about the games that are popular at schools these days.
On the weekend I went to a friend's house to hang out.
This is not play, it's work.
en.notes: 遊び is the noun of 遊ぶ and means "play, amusement, leisure activity": 子どもの遊び, 新しい遊び. Especially common is 遊びに行く/来る, which usually does not mean "to go to play" but "to visit someone for fun, to go out". As a contrast to work or seriousness it appears in これは遊びじゃない. Technically it also refers to the play (the free travel) of, for example, a steering wheel.

en.meaning: to glow; to flush; to feel feverish
examples[].german: My body is flushed with a high fever.
Being praised made me embarrassed, and my face flushed.
Even after getting out of the bath, my body is still glowing with heat.
en.notes: 火照る describes the face or body becoming hot and glowing - from fever, shame, alcohol or a hot bath: 顔が火照る, 体が火照る. It is intransitive and, despite the -eru ending, a godan verb (火照って, 火照らない). It is often written in kana (ほてる); the noun is 火照り, e.g. 顔の火照り. Plain 熱い only says "hot", without the feeling of flushing up.

examples[].german: I lost a button from my suit.
Tomorrow I'm going to work in a suit.
en.notes: 背広 is a business suit. 背広のボタン assigns the button to the suit; 背広を着る refers to putting on or wearing it. 着て行く means going to a place wearing this suit. The reading is せびろ, with a voiced b and short vowels.

examples[].german: This year's annual convention ended without incident.
I still have ten days of annual paid leave left.
He and I joined the company in the same year.
en.notes: 年次 stands before nouns and means "annual, yearly": 年次大会, 年次報告書, 年次有給休暇 (short 年休). Placed after a noun, it denotes the year of joining or graduation: 入社年次, 卒業年次 - important for hierarchy in Japanese companies. It is official and business language; in daily life people say 毎年 or 年に一度.

examples[].german: My four-year-old daughter imitates everything she sees, which is a problem.
Don't just imitate others; think for yourself.
Please stop such dangerous behavior.
en.notes: 真似 is "imitation"; you say X の真似をする or X を真似する "to copy X", and the plain verb for it is 真似る (まねる). ものまね is "impression" as a show act. With evaluative adjectives, 真似 means "behavior, act", almost always negative: 馬鹿な真似, 危ない真似をするな. It is often written in kana as まね.

examples[].german: For now, I've put up a simple tent.
This application uses a simplified procedure and is finished quickly.
It was an important document, so I sent it by simple registered mail.
en.notes: 簡易 means "simplified, makeshift" - a simpler version than the full-fledged one. It usually stands directly before nouns: 簡易テント, 簡易書留 "simple registered mail", 簡易検査; as an adjective 簡易な手続き or 簡易的な. Unlike 簡単 "easy, uncomplicated", 簡易 emphasizes the reduced equipment or scope. Rather written and official language.

examples[].german: About what time are you planning to take a walk?
I took a walk along the riverbank with my dog.
en.notes: 散歩する means "to take a walk". 散歩 alone is the noun "walk"; with する it becomes the verb, whose forms are, for example, 散歩します and 散歩した. A place can be given with で; for a route traversed, を is also used, as in 河原を散歩する. 犬を連れて means "with the dog" or "taking the dog along". The first question asks about the approximate time of a planned walk.

examples[].german: She pulled off the troublesome job well... except for one thing, that is.
This shop is open every day except Sundays.
Everyone except Mr. Tanaka agreed.
en.notes: 除いて is the て-form of 除く "to exclude" and forms the fixed phrase N を除いて "except, with the exception of". It sounds somewhat more formal than 以外: 日曜日以外 and 日曜日を除いて mean the same. In writing and on notices, 〜を除き is common; 〜を除けば means "if you exclude ...". The excluded part always takes を.

en.meaning: to be engaged in; to take part in
examples[].german: I am involved in education.
My father has worked in the newspaper business for thirty years.
More than a hundred people took part in developing this game.
en.notes: 携わる means "to be active in a field, to take part in something" and takes に: 教育に携わる, 映画の制作に携わる. It usually refers to professional or serious, longer-term activities and sounds somewhat elevated, typical in résumés and self-introductions. Unlike 関わる (generally "to be involved", also negatively), 携わる always means active participation. Mostly in the form 携わっている or 携わってきた.

examples[].german: If you lived next to a graveyard, a ghost might even knock on your door.
The graveyard at night is scary, and I can't walk there alone.
I intend to take this secret to my grave.
en.notes: 墓場 is a cemetery or burial ground, often with an eerie or figurative coloring, for example in ghost stories. The neutral, official words for cemetery are 墓地 or 霊園, and a single grave is (お)墓. Fixed phrases are 墓場まで持っていく "to take to the grave" and 揺りかごから墓場まで "from the cradle to the grave".

examples[].german: The actress denied that she was on a diet.
No one can deny that effort is important.
The negative form in Japanese is made with 「〜ない」.
en.notes: 否定 means "negation, denial"; as a する-verb: X を否定する "to deny, to dispute". 否定できない "undeniable" and 否定的な "negative, dismissive" are common. The opposite is 肯定 "affirmation". In grammar, 否定形 is the negative form. Declining a request, by contrast, is 断る, not 否定する.

examples[].german: I injured a tendon in my leg while jogging.
This movie has a complicated plot and is a bit hard to follow.
What you're saying makes sense.
en.notes: 筋 has many meanings, all going back to "line, strand". On the body it is a tendon or muscle strand (足の筋を痛める); in stories it is the plot (筋, あらすじ); in thinking it is logic: 筋が通る "to be coherent", 筋が通らない "illogical". 筋がいい means "talented", and in news 関係筋 denotes "informed sources". In the word 筋肉 "muscle", the kanji is read きん.

examples[].german: When was the Potsdam Declaration again?
The government declared a state of emergency.
My brother declared in front of the family that this year he would really quit smoking.
en.notes: 宣言 is a public, solemn declaration; as a する-verb: X を宣言する or 〜と宣言する. Typical in politics and history: 独立宣言, 緊急事態宣言, ポツダム宣言. In everyday life it is used half-jokingly for firm resolutions: 禁煙宣言, 〜すると宣言する. A mere "announcement" of results is 発表, and an official statement is 声明.

examples[].german: Unlike yours, our children obediently do what they're told.
This film was made faithfully to the original work.
Dogs are said to be animals loyal to their owners.
en.notes: 忠実 is a な-adjective: 〜に忠実な / 〜に忠実に. It means on the one hand "loyal, devoted" toward people (飼い主に忠実な犬), and on the other "faithful, exact" toward originals and rules: 原作に忠実, 基本に忠実, 忠実に再現する. 誠実, by contrast, is "sincere, honest" as a character trait. For faithfulness in a relationship, people tend to say 一途 or 浮気しない.

examples[].german: Don't take his warning lightly. It could cost you your life.
On the doctor's advice, I stopped drinking.
I'm telling you this as a friend: you'd better not get involved with that person.
en.notes: 忠告 is well-meant advice intended to warn someone about a mistake or danger - "advice, warning". As a する-verb: Person に忠告する, often with 〜ように or 〜ほうがいい. Typical are 忠告を聞く / 守る / 無視する. More neutral is アドバイス, more formal 助言; 注意 refers more to a concrete misbehavior in the moment.

examples[].german: Blood was spreading quietly across the floor of the dimly lit room.
The damage from the fire spread to the neighboring town.
The rumor spread throughout the school in no time.
en.notes: 拡がる is an alternative spelling of 広がる; the standard spelling in newspapers and textbooks is 広がる. 拡 stresses expansion of extent or scale (被害が拡がる, 感染が拡がる). The verb is intransitive: X が Y に/まで拡がる. The transitive counterpart is 拡げる or 広げる "to spread out, to expand".

examples[].german: How did you stretch your piercing holes that much?
Construction to widen the road in front of the station has begun.
This browser becomes even more convenient if you install extensions.
en.notes: 拡張 means "expansion, extension" of scope, area or functions; as a する-verb it is transitive: 道路を拡張する, 事業を拡張する. It is common in IT: 拡張機能 "extension, add-on", 拡張子 "file extension". Unlike 拡大 "to enlarge" (写真を拡大する), 拡張 is about widening a framework or capacity. Rather written, administrative and technical language.

en.meaning: to handle; to operate; to manipulate
examples[].german: There's a rumor that Kuma is the mastermind manipulating everyone behind the scenes.
She speaks five languages freely.
In puppet theater, the puppets are operated with strings.
en.notes: 操る is transitive and means "to steer skillfully": marionettes (人形を操る), vehicles (船を操る) or languages (英語を自由に操る "to have fluent command of"). Figuratively it means "to manipulate, pull the strings behind the scenes": 人を操る, 世論を操る. For the technical operation of machines, 操作する is more usual.

examples[].german: My older brother says that women should preserve their chastity until marriage.
She remained faithful to her late husband and never married again.
No matter how poor he was, he kept to his principles to the end.
en.notes: 操 is an old-fashioned, literary word for steadfastness and loyalty to principles or to a partner, traditionally especially a woman's chastity. Fixed phrases are 操を守る "to preserve one's fidelity/chastity" and 操を立てる "to remain faithful to someone". In modern daily life it sounds dated. The kanji otherwise occurs with the reading そう (体操, 操作); as a given name it is also read みさお.

en.meaning: to serve as both; to hold concurrently; (as 〜かねる) to be unable to
examples[].german: He serves as both president and chairman.
I walked to the bakery in front of the station, combining it with a stroll.
I am very sorry, but I am unable to answer that question.
en.notes: 兼ねる (transitive, with を) means that a person or thing fulfills two roles at once: 社長と会長を兼ねる, 趣味と実益を兼ねる; very common is 〜を兼ねて "at the same time as …" (散歩を兼ねて買い物に行く). After a verb stem, mostly in kana, 〜かねる means "can hardly, to find oneself unable to" - a polite refusal in business Japanese: お答えしかねます. Note: 〜かねない, by contrast, means "might well (do something bad)": 事故になりかねない.

en.meaning: to live; to make a living
examples[].german: He lives happily now, but, believe it or not, he has been through hardship.
Since entering university, I have been living alone in Tokyo.
It's hard to live on a pension alone.
en.notes: 暮らす is intransitive and means "to lead one's life, to spend one's daily life". The difference from 住む: 住む names the place of residence (東京に住む), 暮らす the way of living (幸せに暮らす, 一人で暮らす, 年金で暮らす); the place with 暮らす usually takes で. The noun is 暮らし "life, livelihood", e.g. 一人暮らし. As a suffix, 〜暮らす means "to spend the whole day doing ..." (泣き暮らす).

examples[].german: This gray charm drives away bad luck.
Gray clouds have covered the sky since morning.
All I do is work, and every day looks gray.
en.notes: 灰色 is "ash gray, gray" and is used as a noun with の: 灰色の雲, 灰色のスーツ. For clothing and fashion, グレー is at least as common; ねずみ色 is a more traditional word for gray. Figuratively, 灰色 stands for bleakness (灰色の毎日) and for unclarity or suspicion - a case that is neither black nor white.

examples[].german: I bought an ashtray just in case.
There are ashes left in the ashtray.
en.notes: 灰皿 is an ashtray. 灰皿を買う names it as the thing bought. 買っておきました describes the purchase as preparation; 念のため means "just in case". 灰皿に灰がある says what is in it. In はいざら, 皿 is read with voicing as ざら.

examples[].german: It is about time for the peaches to ripen.
These tomatoes are well ripened and very sweet.
I made a cake with overripe bananas.
en.notes: 熟れる is intransitive and means "to ripen" of fruit, vegetables or grain: 柿が熟れる, 熟れたトマト. Synonymous and more common is 熟す (じゅくす), which is also used figuratively (機が熟す "the time is ripe"). Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 売れる "to sell". With the reading なれる, 熟れる denotes fermented foods maturing - that is a different word.

examples[].german: I just learned that compound yesterday.
"学校" is a compound made of the two kanji "学" and "校".
Many English idioms cannot be guessed from the meanings of the individual words.
en.notes: 熟語 mainly denotes a word composed of several kanji: 二字熟語 like 学校, 四字熟語 like 一石二鳥. In English classes in Japan, 熟語 also means "set phrase, idiom" (e.g. look after). For Japanese idioms people more often say 慣用句; a single word is 単語.

examples[].german: I'm still inexperienced and there's a lot I don't understand, but I'll do my best.
My amateurish mistake caused trouble for all of you.
This tomato is still unripe and green.
en.notes: 未熟 is a な-adjective and noun: literally "unripe" for fruit, but much more often "inexperienced, not yet mature" for people and skills (未熟な運転, 技術が未熟だ). As a humble self-description people say 未熟者ですが、よろしくお願いします. 未熟児 is a premature baby. 幼い, by contrast, describes childlike behavior or young age.

examples[].german: I'm writing a paper on the differences between the mature female brain and the mature male brain.
You're an adult now, so I want you to respond maturely.
Japan's mobile phone market is already mature.
en.notes: 成熟 means "maturity" and as a する-verb is intransitive: 成熟する "to mature", mostly as 成熟した + noun or 成熟している. It is used for body and personality (成熟した大人), for fruit, and for society or markets (成熟した市場). In everyday speech, people say 熟す / 熟れる for fruit and 大人になる for people; the opposite is 未熟 "immature".

examples[].german: I'm terrified because my cervical cancer screening result was "abnormality found".
The guard made his rounds, but there was nothing unusual about the building.
The inspection found an abnormality in the engine.
en.notes: 異状 is a noun for a specific unusual condition, an irregularity or malfunction: 異状がある / ない, 異状なし "everything is fine". Do not confuse it with the identically read 異常, which as a な-adjective means "abnormal, extraordinary" more generally (異常な暑さ). 異状 typically appears in medical findings, inspection and police reports; in conversation people more often say どこかおかしい.

examples[].german: When I first heard about shared houses, I thought it was impossible for strangers of the opposite sex to live together.
I went to the movies, just the two of us, with a friend of the opposite sex.
Once they reach junior high school, many kids start becoming aware of the opposite sex.
en.notes: 異性 is "the opposite sex" from the viewpoint of the person in question; the counterpart is 同性 "the same sex". Typical are 異性の友達, 異性にもてる "to be popular with the opposite sex" and 異性を意識する. 異性同士 emphasizes mutuality. The word is neutral and used in conversation as well as in surveys.

examples[].german: Does this word have a homophone?
"科学" and "化学" are homophones, so they are hard to tell apart when speaking.
"異義" and "異議" are read the same but have different meanings.
en.notes: 異義 means "a different, divergent meaning" and appears almost only in 同音異義語 "homophone" (a word that sounds the same but has a different meaning), e.g. 橋 and 箸. On its own it is hardly used. Beware of the identically read 異議 "objection, protest" (異議あり！, 異議を唱える) - "a dissenting opinion" is also normally written this way today. Rather technical and written language.

en.meaning: to prepare for; to be equipped with
examples[].german: Let's prepare for disasters.
I'm going to bed early to prepare for tomorrow's exam.
The rooms in this hotel are equipped with a kitchen and a washing machine.
en.notes: 備える has two main meanings: "to prepare for" with に (災害に備える, 試験に備える) and "to be equipped with, to possess" with を (設備を備える, 才能を備える). In the first sense it is forward-looking: one takes precautions for a possible case, whereas 準備する means "to prepare" more generally and takes the thing prepared with を. Common forms: 〜に備えて "in case of ...", 〜を備えている "is equipped with". The intransitive counterpart 備わる means "to be provided, to be equipped".

examples[].german: The Emperor's Birthday is a national holiday.
His Majesty the Emperor visited the earthquake-stricken area.
In Japan, when the emperor changes, the era name changes too.
en.notes: 天皇 refers exclusively to the Japanese emperor; foreign emperors are called 皇帝 (ナポレオン皇帝). In respectful speech you say 天皇陛下 and use honorific forms such as 訪問される. Related words are 天皇誕生日 (national holiday), 皇室 "imperial house" and 上皇 "emperor emeritus". With each new emperor a new era (元号) such as 令和 begins.

examples[].german: I told His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince, "I hope it goes well."
The crown prince made an official visit to Europe.
The crown prince is the person who will become emperor next.
en.notes: 皇太子 is the crown prince, the designated heir to the Japanese emperor; in honorific language 皇太子殿下, and his wife is 皇太子妃. The word is also used for heirs of foreign monarchies (イギリスの皇太子). A prince who is not heir is called 王子 or, in the imperial house, 親王; the current heir bears the title 皇嗣. It belongs to news and formal language.

examples[].german: Trains sometimes make special stops at a station reserved for the imperial family.
The marriage of an imperial family member always becomes big news.
She married a commoner and left the status of imperial family member.
en.notes: 皇族 are the individual members of the Japanese imperial family (legally excluding the emperor himself). 皇室, by contrast, denotes the imperial house as an institution. For the royal houses of other countries, 王族 or 王室 is used. Typical are 皇族の方々, 皇族の身分 and 皇族専用 - mostly in news and formal language.

examples[].german: The Imperial Household has recently fallen into a rather difficult situation.
My mother always looks forward to news about the Imperial Household.
The Japanese Imperial Household and the British royal family have a long history of exchange.
en.notes: 皇室 is the Japanese imperial house as a whole, i.e. institution and family: 皇室の行事, 皇室典範 "Imperial Household Law". The individual members are 皇族. For foreign royal houses, 王室 is used (イギリス王室). The word belongs to formal news language, and reports about it use honorifics.

examples[].german: They say high-fructose glucose syrup is bad for you, don't they?
Fruit contains a lot of fructose.
Fructose tastes sweeter than sugar.
en.notes: 果糖 is fruit sugar (fructose), a technical word from nutrition and chemistry. On food labels you often read 果糖ぶどう糖液糖 or ぶどう糖果糖液糖 - glucose-fructose syrup, named according to which sugar predominates. ぶどう糖 is glucose, 砂糖 is table sugar and 糖分 in general is "sugar content".

examples[].german: As I said earlier, I'm an unsweetened-coffee person.
Could you buy me some unsweetened tea at the convenience store?
This yogurt is unsweetened, so I eat it with honey on top.
en.notes: 無糖 means "without added sugar, unsweetened" and appears mainly on drinks and foods: 無糖コーヒー, 無糖の紅茶, 無糖ヨーグルト. On labels there is the gradation 無糖 - 微糖 "slightly sweetened" - 加糖 "sweetened". It is a noun that takes の or, as a predicate, だ; in conversation people also say 砂糖なし, and for coffee ブラック.

examples[].german: There isn't much storage space in my room, so I need a bit of ingenuity.
I keep winter clothes I don't use stored in the closet.
This bed lets you store things underneath, so it's convenient.
en.notes: 収納 is the orderly stowing of objects: X を Y に収納する. As a noun it is common in apartment listings and furniture ads: 収納スペース, 収納ケース, 収納が多い部屋. In daily life, for "to put away", people rather say しまう or 片付ける. There is also the formal meaning "receipt of money" (収納代行 for payments).

examples[].german: I understand how hard it is for you. I have lung cancer too.
People who smoke have a higher risk of getting lung cancer.
My father had early-stage lung cancer found at a checkup and underwent surgery.
en.notes: 肺がん is lung cancer. がん is usually written in hiragana because the kanji 癌 is difficult; likewise 胃がん, 乳がん. Typical are 肺がんになる "to get lung cancer", 肺がんと診断される and 肺がんが見つかる. In technical texts 肺癌 is also used.

examples[].german: I'm being admitted to the hospital in three days for treatment of a lung disease.
In the past, many people died young of lung disease.
My grandfather apparently caught a lung disease in his youth and was hospitalized for a year.
en.notes: 肺病 is generally "lung disease", but in the past it was mainly a euphemism for tuberculosis (today 結核). The word therefore sounds somewhat old-fashioned; in modern texts and at the doctor's, people more often say 肺の病気 or, specifically, 肺炎, 肺がん. Typical are 肺病にかかる and 肺病の治療.

examples[].german: As it happens, my older sister was also an author of that book.
There was an autograph session by the author at the bookstore.
When citing a paper, write the author's name and the year of publication.
en.notes: 著者 is the writer of a particular book or document: この本の著者, 著者名, 著者のサイン会. 作家, by contrast, is the profession "writer", 作者 is the creator of a (often literary or artistic) work, and 筆者 is the writer of the text at hand - typical in reading-comprehension exercises. 著者 sounds matter-of-fact and written.

en.meaning: to supplement; to make up for
examples[].german: I will make up for the shortage.
When I don't eat enough vegetables, I supplement my nutrition with supplements.
I want to make up for my lack of experience with effort.
en.notes: 補う means "to supplement, to compensate, to make up for": something missing is added or a weakness is offset. Transitive with を: 不足を補う, 栄養を補う; the means is marked with で: 経験不足を努力で補う. Also typical is お互いの弱点を補い合う "to complement each other's weaknesses". Unlike 足す (simply adding, also in arithmetic), 補う emphasizes filling a gap.

examples[].german: She has at least fifty works to her name.
If you use photos from the internet without permission, it becomes a copyright issue.
Even after retiring, the teacher continues his writing activities.
en.notes: 著作 denotes the writing of books and the result, i.e. "(literary) work": 著作がある, 主な著作. As a する-verb it is rare; people prefer 本を書く or 執筆する. Compounds are very common: 著作権 "copyright", 著作物 "copyrighted work", 著作活動. A single book of one's own is usually called 著書.

en.meaning: to get stuffy and sweaty; to steam (rice)
examples[].german: These shoes are cute, but my feet get sweaty and smell.
Don't open the lid until the rice has finished steaming.
When I wear a helmet in summer, my head gets stuffy and sweaty.
en.notes: 蒸れる is intransitive and has two uses. In cooking it is the finishing steaming: ご飯が蒸れる (transitive: ご飯を蒸らす "to let it steam"). In daily life it describes damp heat under clothing or in closed rooms: 足が蒸れる, 頭が蒸れる. 蒸し暑い, by contrast, is "muggy" for weather, and "to sweat" proper is 汗をかく.

examples[].german: I got burned by the steam from the coffee maker.
In the past, steam locomotives ran on this line.
This iron smooths out wrinkles with steam.
en.notes: 蒸気 is "steam" in the physical-technical sense: water vapor coming out of machines, boilers or irons, and steam as motive power, e.g. in 蒸気機関車 ("steam locomotive", abbreviated SL). For the visible steam over hot food, tea or the bath, people usually say 湯気 in everyday speech; invisible water vapor in the air is 水蒸気. Typical combinations: 蒸気が出る, 蒸気でやけどする.

examples[].german: A Jizo statue stands at the entrance of the village.
Grandma puts her hands together before the Jizo statue every morning.
This Jizo is said to protect travelers' safety.
en.notes: 地蔵 is the bodhisattva Jizō, who is venerated in Japan as a protector of children and travelers, and above all the small stone statues by the roadside or at temples. In daily life people lovingly say お地蔵さん or お地蔵さま; the bare 地蔵 sounds matter-of-fact and often appears in compounds like 地蔵菩薩. It is typical that Jizō statues wear red bibs and that people put their hands together (手を合わせる) before them.

examples[].german: It's already completely spring attire, isn't it?
The cafe in front of the station has opened with a brand-new look.
Please come to the party in subdued attire.
en.notes: 装い is the elevated, somewhat literary word for outfit or appearance - from clothing to a place or shop. It is the noun of 装う ("to dress; to feign"). Typical are 春の装い ("spring wardrobe, spring attire") and the phrase 装いも新たに ("in a new guise"), for example at a reopening. In normal conversation about clothes, people rather say 服 or 服装.

examples[].german: The criminal disguised himself as a police officer and entered the bank.
That celebrity was disguised with a hat and sunglasses, but was recognized immediately.
He is so good at disguises that even his mother didn't recognize him.
en.notes: 変装 means "to disguise oneself, to go incognito" so as not to be recognized; as an intransitive する-verb, the role takes に: 警察官に変装する ("to disguise oneself as a police officer"). The means takes で: 帽子とサングラスで変装する. To be distinguished from this is 仮装, a costume for fun (Halloween, carnival, 仮装パーティー). Celebrities or detectives 変装する; children at a festival 仮装する.

examples[].german: I like him, but I don't really like his clothes.
What should I wear to the interview?
This company has no dress code.
en.notes: 服装 denotes all the clothing or outfit that someone wears, and is the usual word in rules and notices: 服装自由 ("no dress code"), 動きやすい服装 ("comfortable clothing"), 服装に気をつける. 服 rather means the individual garment ("I'm going to buy a 服"); 格好 is more colloquial and stresses overall appearance. You ask about the dress code with どんな服装で….

examples[].german: Delivery people, please come in through the back door.
The singer avoided reporters and left through the hotel's back door.
The backdoor admission was exposed and became big news.
en.notes: 裏口 is the rear entrance or back door of a building, the counterpart of 表口 or 正面玄関. You go 裏口から入る/出る, for example as a supplier or in order not to be seen. Figuratively, 裏口 means an improper route "through the back door", especially in 裏口入学 ("admission to a university through bribery or connections"). The front door itself is 玄関, and any door is ドア or 戸.

examples[].german: When I learned of her betrayal, everything went dark before my eyes.
The plan failed because of a comrade's betrayal.
This movie is interesting because of an unexpected betrayal at the end.
en.notes: 裏切り is the noun of 裏切る ("to betray; to disappoint expectations") and means "betrayal, breach of trust". Typical: 仲間の裏切り, 裏切りにあう ("to be betrayed"), 裏切りを許さない. A person who betrays is 裏切り者 ("traitor"). The verb is also used in a weaker sense: 期待を裏切る ("to disappoint expectations"), 予想を裏切る ("to turn out differently than expected").

examples[].german: The motorcycle ran on, weaving through the back streets.
There are more cheap, tasty restaurants on back streets than on main streets.
It's better not to walk alone on back streets at night.
en.notes: 裏通り is a side street, usually running parallel behind a main street (大通り, 表通り). It often carries the connotation that it is quieter and has hidden little shops, but is also less safe at night. You walk 裏通りを歩く/通る; a particularly narrow passage is more likely 路地. The opposite 表通り is the busy street frontage.

examples[].german: Snow covers the mountain.
At the scary scene, I covered my eyes with my hands without thinking.
The sky was covered with thick clouds all day today.
en.notes: 覆う means "to cover, to shroud" and is transitive with を: 雪が山を覆う, 手で顔を覆う. It often describes something completely covering a surface, and sounds somewhat more literary than かぶせる (to put something over) or 隠す (to hide). Often used in the passive: 〜に覆われる "to be covered with": 空が雲に覆われる. Figuratively: 目を覆う "to cover one's eyes, to look away (because something is terrible)".

examples[].german: Please write your name on the back of the paper.
The bicycle is parked behind the house.
There seems to be something behind that person's kindness.
en.notes: 裏 is the back or hidden side of something; the opposite is 表 "front": 紙の裏, 写真の裏. For buildings it means the rear area: 家の裏, 裏口 "back entrance". Unlike 後ろ, which is simply "behind" from the viewer's perspective, 裏 emphasizes the side facing away, often invisible. Figuratively it stands for ulterior motives: 裏がある "there is something behind it".

examples[].german: Everyone, did you realize this is probably the last time all ten singles at the Tofugu office will be together?
Students, there is one week left until the exam. Study hard.
I sincerely thank you all for your cooperation.
en.notes: 諸君 is a form of address to a group, used by a person of higher status toward equals or juniors - such as teachers, commanders or speakers: 学生諸君, 諸君！ It sounds old-fashioned, authoritative and rather masculine. It is inappropriate toward superiors or customers; neutrally and politely, say 皆さん.

examples[].german: Due to various circumstances, we will be closed today.
Japan is tackling this problem in cooperation with other countries.
When moving, various expenses arise in addition to the rent.
en.notes: 諸 is a Sino-Japanese prefix meaning "various, diverse, all" and stands before Kango nouns: 諸外国 ("foreign countries, other countries"), 諸問題, 諸事情 ("various circumstances"), 諸費用 ("miscellaneous expenses"), 諸君 ("gentlemen, everyone"). It feels written and formal and is common in notices, news and contracts. In conversation people say いろいろな or 様々な instead; 各, by contrast, stresses "each individual".

examples[].german: A friend of mine is looking for a rental apartment. Do you know of any good properties?
Which do you think is better, renting or owning a home?
My father decided to put the old house up for rent.
en.notes: 賃貸 means "leasing" or "for rent" and is almost always used attributively: 賃貸マンション, 賃貸のアパート, 賃貸物件 ("rental property"), 賃貸契約 ("lease contract"). The opposite terms are 持ち家 ("owned home") and 分譲 ("for sale"). The monthly rent itself is not called 賃貸 but 家賃. To rent something out is 賃貸に出す or simply 貸す.

examples[].german: Don't make a racket on my cargo ship!
Several large cargo ships are anchored in the port.
This car was shipped from Asia on a cargo ship.
en.notes: 貨物船 is a cargo ship, made up of 貨物 ("freight, goods") and 船. Counterparts are 客船 ("passenger ship") and 漁船 ("fishing boat"); more specific types are コンテナ船 and タンカー. Ships are counted with 隻 (何隻). Goods are 貨物船で運ぶ; a freight train is accordingly 貨物列車.

examples[].german: A 23-year-old new employee married an 82-year-old CEO, surprising everyone who worked with them.
I called out suddenly from behind and startled my friend.
Don't scare me! I thought my heart would stop.
en.notes: 驚かす is the transitive counterpart of 驚く "to be surprised, to be startled" and means "to surprise, to startle": 人を驚かす, 世間を驚かす "to cause a stir". Synonymous and somewhat more common in everyday speech is the causative form 驚かせる; more casually people say びっくりさせる. A typical exclamation is 驚かさないでよ！ "Don't startle me like that!"

examples[].german: "I've been up since four this morning." "No way! What on earth are you doing?" "Um... I'm giving the whole house a deep clean."
After putting away the luggage, I cleaned the floor of the shop.
en.notes: 掃除する means "to clean" or "to tidy up". The place cleaned takes を as its object: 家を掃除する, 床を掃除する. 大掃除する refers to a thorough, large-scale cleaning. In conversation, 掃除している and 起きている are shortened to 掃除してる and 起きてる; this shows the casual tone of the first example. In the second example, 〜てから orders the actions: first put things away, then clean the floor. Without する, 掃除 is a noun.

en.meaning: to separate; to keep apart; to let go
examples[].german: It's dangerous to take your eyes off a child while swimming!
A train is coming, so please don't let go of your child's hand.
Since it's a test, please line up the desks a little apart from each other.
en.notes: 離す is transitive and means "to separate, to move apart, to leave a distance" as well as "to let go": 机を離して並べる, 手を離す. The phrase 目を離す ("to take one's eyes off something, to not pay attention") is very common, mostly negated: 目を離さないで. The intransitive counterpart is 離れる ("to move away"). Do not confuse it with 話す ("to speak") and 放す ("to set free", e.g. 魚を川に放す), which are pronounced the same.

examples[].german: This lawsuit has become a quagmire.
After the rain, the path through the field turned into a mudhole.
He can't get out of the quagmire of debt.
en.notes: 泥沼 is literally a muddy swamp, but it is mostly used figuratively for a stuck, hopeless situation from which one can no longer escape. Typical are 泥沼化する ("to get bogged down, to turn into a mudslinging fight"), 泥沼の争い/離婚 and 〜の泥沼から抜け出す ("to get out of the quagmire of ..."). For a real wetland in nature, the more neutral 沼 or 湿地 is used.

examples[].german: She works as a magazine editor at a publishing company.
When I sent the manuscript to the editor, it came back with lots of corrections.
We are recruiting video editors.
en.notes: 編集者 is the person who edits books, magazines, newspapers or even videos - at a publishing house, an "editor". It consists of 編集 ("editing", 編集する) and 者. The head is 編集長 ("editor-in-chief"); among authors people often say 担当編集 or simply 編集さん. Whoever compiles a work is listed in the imprint as 編者.

en.meaning: to be active; to play an active role
examples[].german: He is active on the world stage.
The new player played a great part in the game.
This robot is playing an active role at disaster sites.
en.notes: 活躍する does not merely mean "to be active", but "to stand out, to work successfully": someone achieves something outstanding in a field. The field takes で, the role takes として: 世界で活躍する, 歌手として活躍する. Things can also 活躍する when they render useful service. Intensified, it is 大活躍. Mere "being active" without praise would be 活動する.

examples[].german: This house is always filled with the smiling faces of children.
The river overflowed because of the heavy rain.
The station was packed with tourists on the weekend.
en.notes: 溢れる means "to overflow": water spills over the banks (川があふれる), a place is overfull (駅は人であふれている), and figuratively one is "full of" a feeling or quality (自信にあふれる, 涙があふれる). It is intransitive; the content is marked with で or に (人であふれる, 元気にあふれる). It is mostly written in kana, あふれる. Related is こぼれる, which rather describes small amounts falling out or being spilled.

examples[].german: Wasn't the supermarket flyer left here?
I had a part-time job handing out event flyers in front of the station.
On Girls' Day, my mother makes chirashi sushi for me.
en.notes: ちらし is an advertising flyer or leaflet, the kind that lands in your mailbox, is inserted in the newspaper or is handed out on the street. The word is almost never written with kanji, but as チラシ or ちらし; typical verbs are 配る ("to distribute") and 入る ("to be inserted"). It comes from 散らす ("to scatter"). As a short form of ちらし寿司, it also denotes sushi rice with colorful toppings scattered over it.

examples[].german: It seems they were attacked by an armed group.
All the security guards at this bank are armed.
After the talks, the country agreed to disarmament.
en.notes: 武装 is "armament" and, as an intransitive する-verb, "to arm oneself"; the weapon takes で: 銃で武装する. Very common are the participle 武装した ("armed") and compounds like 武装勢力 ("armed group, militia") and 武装解除 ("disarmament"). The weapon itself is 武器. Figuratively people also say 理論で武装する ("to arm oneself with arguments").

examples[].german: Abnormal weather continues.
The test results showed nothing in particular wrong.
He is abnormally fond of cleanliness.
en.notes: 異常 is a noun and a な-adjective: "abnormal, unusual"; as a noun also "malfunction, abnormality". Typical are 異常がある/ない (for example in medical examinations or machines), 異常な + noun, the adverb 異常に ("unusually, excessively") and compounds like 異常気象 ("extreme weather"). The opposite is 正常. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 以上 ("more than; that's all").

examples[].german: My crotch itches terribly.
In soccer, the ball hit him in the groin, and he couldn't move for a while.
These pants are a little tight in the crotch.
en.notes: 股間 is the crotch or groin area between the thighs. The word is matter-of-fact and anatomical, but direct; you hear it, for example, in sports (股間にボールが当たる) or when discussing complaints. For the crotch of trousers, people rather say 股 (また) or 股下 ("inseam length"); medically more precise is 鼠径部 ("groin").

examples[].german: I think you're talking about farts, am I right?
A problem like this is nothing to me.
Stop making hair-splitting excuses and clean up quickly.
en.notes: 屁 is the vulgar word for "fart"; the neutral and child-friendly word is おなら. To fart is vulgarly 屁をこく or 屁をひる, neutrally おならをする. Figuratively, 屁 stands for something worthless: 屁でもない "a piece of cake, no problem at all", and 屁理屈 are "quibbles, far-fetched excuses".

examples[].german: That is not a quibble, it is a fact.
Stop making excuses with your hair-splitting and do your homework quickly.
No matter what you say, he makes quibbling arguments and won't apologize.
en.notes: 屁理屈 is composed of 屁 ("fart") and 理屈 ("logic, reasoning") and denotes quibbles or far-fetched arguments with which one tries to talk one's way out. Typical are 屁理屈を言う and 屁理屈をこねる ("to split hairs"); 屁理屈ばかり言う is a common reproach from parents to children. The word is colloquial and derogatory. A mere apology or excuse, by contrast, is 言い訳.

examples[].german: The Japanese-style taro salad at that izakaya is delicious.
Simmered taro is my grandmother's specialty.
When you peel taro, your hands can get itchy.
en.notes: 里芋 is the taro tuber, a typical autumn vegetable of Japanese cuisine with a sticky, soft (ねっとり) texture. It is eaten mainly braised as 煮物 or in soups such as 豚汁. It is often written in kana (さといも). When peeling, it can make the skin itch. Other "potatoes": じゃがいも ("potato"), さつまいも ("sweet potato"), 長芋 ("Chinese yam").

en.meaning: freeloader; sponger; to live at someone's place for free
examples[].german: If you're going to freeload, you should at least learn to cook.
Since graduating from university, I've been living off my uncle at his house.
As I'm just a freeloader, I can't complain much.
en.notes: 居候 is someone who lives and eats at others' places without paying for it, and, as an intransitive する-verb, living in that way: 友達の家に居候する. The word sounds rather self-deprecating or slightly disparaging, but not as harsh as "parasite". Typical is 居候の身 ("as someone who is only tolerated here"). Someone who pays regular rent is instead a 下宿人 or ルームメイト.

examples[].german: My child still has the habit of wiping his mouth with his sleeve.
He wiped the sweat from his forehead with a handkerchief.
Even after hearing the explanation, I couldn't shake my anxiety.
en.notes: 拭う means "to wipe away" and is somewhat more elevated than the everyday 拭く, which is written with the same kanji. Typical are 汗を拭う, 涙を拭う, 口を拭う; the means takes で (ハンカチで, 袖で). Figuratively it means "to get rid of a feeling or a stain", mostly negated: 不安を拭えない ("cannot shake the worry"), 汚名を拭う ("to clear one's name"). A table or a window, by contrast, is wiped with 拭く.

examples[].german: Danger lurks.
The culprit may still be hiding somewhere near here.
Behind convenient services, unexpected problems can also lurk.
en.notes: 潜む means "to hide, to lurk, to lie hidden" - intransitive, the place takes に: 草むらに潜む, 心の奥に潜む. Besides living beings keeping themselves hidden, it is often used abstractly for dangers, problems or feelings lying beneath the surface: 危険が潜んでいる. It sounds somewhat literary; in everyday speech "to hide" is usually 隠れる. The same kanji appears in 潜る "to dive".

en.meaning: to accumulate; to build up (money, points)
examples[].german: I have so many business trips that my miles really pile up quickly!
I saved a little every month and finally reached 100,000 yen.
If you shop with this card, you'll accumulate points.
en.notes: 貯まる is intransitive and means that money, savings or points accumulate: お金が貯まる, ポイントが貯まる, マイルが貯まる. The transitive counterpart is 貯める ("to save, to build up savings"). The identically pronounced 溜まる stands for things that pile up (often undesirably): dust, water, stress, work. It is also often simply written in kana as たまる.

examples[].german: I lost to my rival by a narrow margin and was really frustrated.
The election was undecided until the end, and the opposition won by a narrow margin.
The scores of first and second place were separated by only a hair.
en.notes: 僅差 is a narrow margin or slight difference, especially in competitions, elections and votes: 僅差で勝つ/負ける, 僅差の勝利. The first kanji is also in 僅か (わずか, "slight"). The word sounds more like news and sports reports; in conversation people also say ぎりぎりで勝った or ちょっとの差で負けた. The opposite is 大差 ("big margin").

examples[].german: "What do you do all the time?" "I practice impressions all day every day."
He is good at impressions of the teacher and makes everyone in the class laugh.
I did an impression of the department head at a drinking party, and he saw it himself.
en.notes: 物真似 is imitating the voice, way of speaking or gestures of a certain person or animal, mostly for entertainment: 先生の物真似をする, 物真似が上手だ. It is mostly written in kana (ものまね, モノマネ); professionals are called ものまね芸人. The more general 真似 (真似をする, 真似る) means any kind of copying or imitating, including in learning or imitating a style.

examples[].german: There is one lung on each side of the chest.
Cigarette smoke does great damage to the lungs.
In science class, we learned how the heart and lungs work.
en.notes: 肺臓 is the anatomical-medical term for the lung, comparable to 心臓 ("heart") or 腎臓 ("kidney"). In everyday life and in almost all compounds people simply say 肺: 肺炎 ("pneumonia"), 肺がん ("lung cancer"), 肺活量. 肺臓 appears mainly in textbooks, technical texts or lists of organs (内臓).

examples[].german: I spend summer vacation at my grandparents' house in the countryside.
I was raised by my grandparents when I was little.
On Respect for the Aged Day, I wrote a letter to my grandparents.
en.notes: 祖父母 is the collective word for "grandparents", from 祖父 ("grandfather") and 祖母 ("grandmother"). It is matter-of-fact and is used for one's own grandparents toward outsiders, in forms and in texts. In family conversation people say おじいちゃんとおばあちゃん; when speaking about someone else's grandparents one politely says おじいさまとおばあさま. A pair of great-grandparents is 曾祖父母.

en.meaning: pet owner; owner of an animal
examples[].german: Please clean up your dog's droppings during walks.
I found a lost cat, so I'm looking for its owner.
It's often said that pets resemble their owners.
en.notes: 飼い主 is the keeper or owner of an animal, formed from 飼う ("to keep an animal") and 主 ("master, owner"). It is used only for animals; the owner of an object is 持ち主, formally 所有者. Typical are 犬の飼い主, 飼い主を探す (for strays) and notices addressed to 飼い主. The kept animal itself is called 飼い犬 or 飼い猫.

en.meaning: to hurt; to wound; to damage
examples[].german: I may have scratched my contact lens.
His remark hurt me deeply.
A man who injured someone with a knife was arrested.
en.notes: 傷つける is transitive and has three meanings: to injure someone physically, to hurt someone emotionally (人を傷つける, プライドを傷つける), and to scratch or damage objects. The intransitive counterpart is 傷つく ("to get hurt, be offended; to get scratched"). In everyday speech it is most often used for feelings; for a physical injury people also say colloquially けがをさせる. Also written 傷付ける.

en.meaning: to throw away (carelessly); to fling away
examples[].german: When the alarm rang at six this morning, I ended up flinging the clock away.
Please stop throwing trash out of the car window.
He threw away his dream of becoming a singer and took over his parents' shop.
en.notes: 投げ捨てる combines 投げる ("to throw") and 捨てる ("to throw away") and means to fling something away carelessly or violently - for example trash out of a window or an object in anger. For the wild dumping of garbage, people also say ポイ捨て colloquially. Figuratively, one can also 投げ捨てる plans, dreams or pride ("to throw overboard"). For normal disposal, 捨てる is enough.

en.meaning: to put into (feeling, strength); to load (a gun)
examples[].german: I didn't have time to load the shotgun.
For my mother's birthday, I wrote her a letter with all my heart.
I pushed the door with all my strength, but it wouldn't open.
en.notes: 込める means "to put in, pack in" and is used mainly figuratively: putting feelings, effort or strength into something. Very common are 心を込めて ("with all one's heart"), 気持ちを込める, 願いを込める and 力を込める ("to put strength into"). Concretely it means "to load": 銃に弾を込める. Related are 〜込み ("included", e.g. 税込み) and the intransitive 込む.

en.meaning: to drift; to float; to hang in the air
examples[].german: Clouds are drifting in the sky.
A nice smell of curry drifted from the kitchen.
A heavy atmosphere hung in the meeting room.
en.notes: 漂う means "to drift, to float" (on water or in the air: 海に漂う, 空に漂う) and figuratively "to hang in the air" for smells and moods: いい香りが漂う, 緊張感が漂う. It is intransitive; the place takes に, the source of a smell takes から (〜から漂ってくる). The word sounds somewhat literary and is often used in descriptions. 浮かぶ, by contrast, means just "to float on the surface, to hover", without the aimless drifting.

en.meaning: suicide by jumping in front of a train
examples[].german: There was a suicide by jumping onto the tracks at the station, and the trains stopped for an hour.
More and more stations are installing platform doors to prevent suicides by jumping in front of trains.
According to the news, the number of train-jumping suicides decreased from last year.
en.notes: 飛び込み自殺 denotes suicide by jumping in front of an approaching train, formed from 飛び込み ("jumping in") and 自殺. The word is matter-of-fact and appears mainly in news and statistics. Train announcements use the euphemism 人身事故 ("accident involving a person") instead. Jumping from a building is 飛び降り自殺. It is a sensitive topic - in conversation it should be used carefully.

en.meaning: to write in; to fill in; to post (online)
examples[].german: You'd better fill in the application form quickly. The office closes in ten minutes.
Let's stop posting bad things about people on social media.
I wrote the important parts into my textbook.
en.notes: 書き込む means "to write in, to enter": into a form, in the margin of a book or in a calendar; the place takes に: 申込書に名前を書き込む. Today the meaning "to post online" (掲示板やSNSに書き込む) is very common; the noun 書き込み is then the post or comment. For formally filling in forms, 記入する is also used. In IT it additionally means "to write data".

examples[].german: I'm too scared to go into crowds.
I got separated from my child in the crowd at the festival.
Harajuku was incredibly crowded on the weekend.
en.notes: 人込み is a crowd or throng in a place, such as at a festival, in a station or in a shopping street. Today the spelling 人混み is actually more common. Typical are 人込みの中, 人込みを避ける, 人込みが苦手 ("to dislike crowds") and すごい人込みだ. That a place is full is expressed with 混む or 混雑する; 群衆 is a formal, rather written word for a crowd.

examples[].german: I wonder if I can get this stain out somehow.
A coffee stain got on my white shirt.
As I've gotten older, the spots on my face have increased.
en.notes: 染み is a stain that has soaked into fabric or paper, and is mostly written in kana (しみ, シミ). Typical are しみが付く/できる, しみを取る/抜く (しみ抜き = "stain removal"). It also denotes pigment spots or age spots on the skin. General dirt is 汚れ. The word comes from 染みる ("to soak in, to seep").

examples[].german: Somehow I managed to cram all my clothes into the suitcase.
The night before the exam, I crammed vocabulary into my head all at once.
The morning train is packed tight with people.
en.notes: 詰め込む means "to stuff in, to pack full": clothes into a suitcase, people into a train, appointments into a calendar. The container takes に: スーツケースに服を詰め込む. Figuratively it means "to cram, to drum knowledge in" (頭に詰め込む); 詰め込み教育 criticizes pure rote learning. The simple 詰める means "to fill, to pack" without the connotation of "too much".

examples[].german: There was a box on the counter with "Tips greatly welcome" written on it.
A party was held to welcome the new employees.
I was warmly welcomed by my homestay family.
en.notes: 歓迎 means "welcome, reception" and, as a transitive する-verb, "to welcome someone": 新入生を歓迎する; in the passive 温かく歓迎される. Common are 歓迎会 ("welcome party") and 大歓迎 ("heartily welcome, very much appreciated"), also for things: 初心者大歓迎. As a greeting formula at the door, one says ようこそ or いらっしゃいませ, not 歓迎.

examples[].german: I'm not interested in becoming personally close with customers.
I'm not very interested in sports.
I pretended not to be interested, but actually I was curious.
en.notes: 興味がない is the negative of 興味がある ("to be interested") and means "to have no interest"; the topic takes に: スポーツに興味がない. It is strengthened or softened with 全然 or あまり. Said directly to someone, it sounds rather blunt; more polite is 興味がありません or the evasive あまり詳しくなくて. For social topics, 関心がない sounds more matter-of-fact.

examples[].german: For now, it's fine if you just find the typos and omitted characters.
There is a typo in this document, so please correct it.
I had many wrong kanji on the test and lost points.
en.notes: 誤字 is a wrongly written character, i.e. a spelling or typing error; with kanji, for example a missing stroke or a similar but wrong character. The pair formula 誤字脱字 ("typos and omissions") is very common, e.g. in proofreading. Typical: 誤字がある, 誤字を直す. For errors in kanji conversion on the computer, 誤変換 is also used, and for pure typing mistakes, colloquially タイプミス.

examples[].german: Misuse of medicine can be life-threatening.
This word is often misused.
Misuse of honorific language is common even among Japanese people.
en.notes: 誤用 means "wrong usage, misuse" and emphasizes the mistake, not the intent; as a transitive する-verb: 言葉を誤用する. It is particularly common with language (言葉の誤用, 敬語の誤用) and with medicines or devices. Deliberate abuse, e.g. of drugs or power, is by contrast 乱用 (濫用) or 悪用.

examples[].german: I thought she was fluent in English, but that was a huge miscalculation.
It was a big miscalculation that hardly any customers came because of the rain.
I didn't expect so many people to come - it's a happy miscalculation.
en.notes: 誤算 is literally an arithmetic error, but is almost always used in the sense of "miscalculation, misjudgment": one expected something, and it turned out differently. Typical are 大きな誤算, とんだ誤算 ("a real blunder") and the positive うれしい誤算 ("a pleasant surprise"). For a real arithmetic error, people more often say 計算ミス or 計算違い in everyday speech.

en.meaning: to rot; to decay; to crumble
examples[].german: The old building is decaying.
In the forest there was a rotted wooden bridge.
His works do not fade even as times change.
en.notes: 朽ちる means "to rot, to decay, to become rotten" - above all wood and buildings that fall apart over time: 朽ちた木, 橋が朽ちる. It is intransitive and very often appears as 朽ちた〜 or 朽ちている; intensified it is 朽ち果てる "to decay completely". Figuratively and literarily: 朽ちることのない名声 "imperishable fame". For food one says 腐る instead, for metal さびる.

examples[].german: Your older brother is cool, but mine is lame.
My older brother got married last year and now lives in Osaka.
Senior Tanaka is dependable, like an older brother to everyone.
en.notes: 兄貴 is a familiar, rather male and colloquial word for one's older brother, both when talking about him and in direct address. Neutral are 兄 (one's own) and お兄さん; women use 兄貴 less often. It is also used for an admired older comrade or mentor - in clubs, among workers or even in the yakuza. The female counterpart is 姉貴.

en.meaning: surrender; to give up; to admit defeat
examples[].german: I haven't given up yet.
The enemy raised a white flag and surrendered.
I have no idea about this riddle. I give up!
en.notes: 降参 means "to surrender, to yield" and in everyday use mainly "to give up, to admit defeat"; it is intransitive, the opponent takes に: 敵に降参する. As an exclamation, 降参！ means "I give up!", for example at a riddle or game. For official military capitulation 降伏 is more usual; the neutral "to give up on something" is あきらめる.

examples[].german: "This gyudon is my treat." "Wow, thanks. Then I'll take you up on your offer."
I got lunch done quickly at the gyudon shop in front of the station.
Please make it a large gyudon with an egg.
en.notes: 牛丼 is a bowl of rice topped with thinly sliced beef and onions simmered in a sweetish soy sauce - the classic quick and cheap meal from chain restaurants called 牛丼屋. You order by size: 並盛り (regular) or 大盛り (large); popular extras are a raw egg (生卵) and pickled red ginger. The 丼 "bowl" is also in other rice dishes like 親子丼 or 天丼.

en.meaning: to vomit; to breathe out; to spit out
examples[].german: "Sorry I'm late. I felt a bit sick this morning and threw up." "It's okay. Better late than never."
Please take a deep breath and exhale slowly.
No matter how hard it was, he never once complained.
en.notes: 吐く mainly means "to vomit, to throw up"; colloquially also もどす. It also means "to breathe out, to emit" (息を吐く, 煙を吐く) and "to utter", mostly negative: 弱音を吐く ("to whine, to give in"). Note: in ため息をつく or うそをつく, the same kanji is read つく. Related is 吐き気 ("nausea").

en.meaning: to shorten; to narrow (a gap); to shrink
examples[].german: The distance between the two of them has gradually been narrowing.
In the second half, the point gap narrowed all at once.
With the new road, the commute got ten minutes shorter.
en.notes: 縮まる is intransitive and means that a distance, difference or span of time gets smaller: 距離が縮まる, 差が縮まる, 時間が縮まる. Figuratively, 二人の距離が縮まる means "to become closer". The transitive counterpart is 縮める ("to shorten"). For fabric that shrinks in the wash, people say 縮む; to cower in fear is 縮こまる.

examples[].german: I started studying Japanese out of impure motives.
This water contains many impurities.
Be careful of people who approach you with impure intentions.
en.notes: 不純 is a な-adjective with two uses: materially "impure, contaminated" (especially in 不純物, "impurity") and morally "dishonest, insincere", typically in 不純な動機 or 不純な目的. The opposite is 純粋 ("pure, sincere"). Regarding motives it often sounds half self-deprecating: 動機が不純だ ("my motives are not quite noble").

examples[].german: My new pure wool sweater is scratchy and itchy.
This coat is pure wool, so please don't wash it at home.
A pure wool blanket is warm, but it's expensive.
en.notes: 純毛 means "pure wool" (純 "pure" + 毛 "hair, wool") and appears mainly on labels and in product descriptions, mostly attributively: 純毛のセーター. In modern retail you more often read ウール100％. Sheep's wool as a material is 羊毛, blended fabric is 混紡. In conversation people often simply say ウールのセーター.

examples[].german: I want to make the text vertical.
Japanese newspapers and novels are mostly written vertically.
I decided to write the thank-you letter vertically.
en.notes: 縦書き is the traditional Japanese writing direction: characters from top to bottom, columns from right to left - this is how novels, newspapers and many manga are set. The counterpart is 横書き (horizontal, from left to right), which is usual in math books, emails and on the computer. Typical are 縦書きにする, 縦書きで書く and 縦書きの手紙; in 縦書き, numbers are mostly written with kanji numerals.

examples[].german: I want to measure the length and width of the wall - could you help me a bit?
This box is 30 centimeters both lengthwise and widthwise.
If you swap the rows and columns of the table, it becomes easier to read.
en.notes: 縦横 in the reading たてよこ very concretely denotes the two dimensions "vertical and horizontal", i.e. height or length and width: 縦横の長さ, 縦横30センチ. In tables it means rows and columns. The Sino-Japanese reading じゅうおう is a different word meaning "in all directions, freely" (縦横に走る道路, 縦横無尽). Individually: 縦 ("length, vertical"), 横 ("width, horizontal").

examples[].german: Today falls on a Jewish holy day.
In Christianity, Sunday is treated as a holy day and worship is held at church.
Quite a few believers take time off work on holy days.
en.notes: 聖日 denotes a religious "holy day", such as the Sabbath in Judaism or Sunday in Christianity (there also 主日). The word is literary and rather rare. Legal holidays, by contrast, are 祝日, and days off work in general are 休日. Typical are 〜の聖日 and 〜を聖日とする.

examples[].german: We reached an agreement.
A lot has happened, and that is how I came to be where I am now.
At this shop, everyone from children to adults can enjoy themselves.
en.notes: 至る means "to arrive at, to lead to" and takes に: 結論に至る, 合意に至る, 死に至る. It sounds literary and formal; in everyday speech people prefer 〜になる or 着く. Important patterns: 〜から〜に至るまで "from ... all the way to", 今に至る "up to the present", 至る所 "everywhere". Spatially it can also mean "(to) lead (to a place)", for example of roads.

examples[].german: This road leads to the holy land.
Koshien is called the sacred ground of high school baseball.
More and more fans are visiting towns featured in films on "pilgrimages".
en.notes: 聖地 is a holy place of a religion, e.g. エルサレム as the 聖地 of three religions; in this sense also "the Holy Land". Figuratively, the most important place of a sport or scene is called 〜の聖地 ("Mecca"), for example 甲子園 for school baseball. Colloquially, 聖地 also means the real-life settings of anime, films or novels; visiting them is called 聖地巡礼.

examples[].german: You shouldn't keep magnetic cards and magnets together.
These scissors are magnetized, so paper clips stick to them.
The magnetism of my commuter pass weakened, and I couldn't get through the ticket gate.
en.notes: 磁気 is magnetism as a physical property or force, not the magnet itself - that is 磁石. It is very often the first element of compounds: 磁気カード "magnetic card", 磁気テープ, 磁気嵐. To become magnetized is 磁気を帯びる. The field around a magnet is 磁場 or 磁界.

examples[].german: A compass points north because the Earth has a magnetic field.
Near a strong magnetic field, machines sometimes don't work properly.
This town has a mysterious aura that attracts artists.
en.notes: 磁場 is the magnetic field; in physics 磁界 is used synonymously. Typical are 地球の磁場, 強い磁場, 磁場が発生する. Figuratively, 磁場 denotes the aura or attractive force of a place or person. Do not confuse it with 磁気 "magnetism" and 磁石 "magnet".

examples[].german: How would you like your black tea prepared?
One black tea, please.
en.notes: 紅茶 is black tea. In especially polite language an お can precede it: お紅茶. おいれ致しましょうか offers to prepare the tea; it is a humble form for your own action. 紅茶をください orders the tea directly and politely. こうちゃ is written kōcha with a long o and a jointly pronounced ちゃ.

examples[].german: The missile was launched as scheduled.
The rocket was launched from Tanegashima at 10 a.m.
The police officer fired one shot into the sky.
en.notes: 発射する is transitive: 弾・ミサイル・ロケットを発射する "to fire, to shoot off, to launch"; in the news often in the passive 〜が発射された. For space rockets, 打ち上げる is also common, and for firearms in daily life simply 撃つ. Beware of the homophone 発車 "departure" of a train or bus: 電車が発車します.

examples[].german: So you were the mastermind after all. No wonder you seemed so practiced when you killed that woman.
There seems to be a mastermind pulling strings behind the scenes in this case.
That politician was long called the power broker of the political world.
en.notes: 黒幕 literally means "black curtain" (from kabuki theater), but today it is almost always used figuratively: the person who pulls the strings in the background without appearing themselves. Typical are 事件の黒幕, 黒幕がいる and 〜が黒幕だった - a favorite word in crime stories, political reports and conspiracy stories. It always has a negative coloring; a neutral organizer is called 中心人物 or まとめ役.

examples[].german: The president's estimated annual income is 50 million yen.
This temple is presumed to have been built about a thousand years ago.
The cause of the accident is, for now, nothing more than a presumption.
en.notes: 推定 is an estimate or assumption supported by data or indications. Very typical is the passive form 〜と推定される in news and reports, as well as its use as a first element: 推定年収, 推定年齢. Mere guessing is more 推測, a cost estimate is 見積もり, a forecast is 予想. In legal language 推定 stands for "presumption", e.g. 推定無罪 "presumption of innocence".

examples[].german: From the way the date was written, I deduced that the threatening letter was written by an American.
I like reading mystery novels before going to sleep.
Let's all try to deduce who the culprit is.
en.notes: 推理 is logical deduction from clues, especially in the manner of a detective: 〜と推理する, 推理が当たる/外れる. As a noun it also stands for the mystery genre: 推理小説, 推理ドラマ (loosely also ミステリー). Compared with 推測 "guess", 推理 emphasizes the logical train of thought; 推定 is a factual estimate based on data.

examples[].german: The damage extended over a wide area.
The meeting went on for five hours.
When it comes to cooking, I can't compare with my mother.
en.notes: 及ぶ means "to extend to, to reach, to amount to" and takes に: 被害が全国に及ぶ, 会議が三時間に及ぶ. It stresses that something reaches a (often large) extent or area. Negated, 〜に及ばない means "to not match" (彼には及ばない), and 〜には及ばない also means "to not be necessary". It is literary and formal and very common in news; the transitive counterpart is 及ぼす (影響を及ぼす "to exert influence").

examples[].german: For this model application, both self-nominations and nominations by others are accepted.
He became project leader by nominating himself.
Please write your reason for self-nomination on the application form.
en.notes: 自薦 means "to recommend or propose oneself", for example for a post, an election or a competition. The counterpart is 他薦 "nomination by others"; the set phrase 自薦・他薦は問いません "self-nominations and nominations by others both welcome" often appears in calls for applications. With で: 自薦で立候補する. The word is formal; casually people say 自分から手を挙げる.

examples[].german: He recommended this show to me, but I don't really like watching anime.
I was asked for a recommendation, so I recommended the shop in front of the station.
The department head recommended her as the next leader.
en.notes: 薦める means "to recommend (a person or thing as suitable)": AにBを薦める or BをCに薦める "to propose B for C (a position)". There are three すすめる spellings: 勧める "to advise, to offer" (お茶を勧める), 薦める "to recommend" and 進める "to advance". In practice, 勧める or kana is often used for recommendations too; the noun is おすすめ.

en.meaning: to demonstrate (an ability); to exert; to bring out
examples[].german: Who showed the most leadership in solving the problem?
I was nervous and couldn't show my true ability on the exam.
This medicine takes effect about thirty minutes after you take it.
en.notes: 発揮する means to bring an existing ability or effect fully into play. Typical objects: 実力/能力/才能/リーダーシップを発揮する, 効果を発揮する "to take effect". For merely showing or demonstrating, people use 見せる or 示す. It often appears negated in the potential: 実力を発揮できなかった "couldn't show what I'm capable of".

examples[].german: He invited me to go sailing along the coast with him on a yacht this Sunday.
Because of the typhoon, people in coastal areas need to watch out for high waves.
The people of this town have long made their living from coastal fishing.
en.notes: 沿岸 refers to the coast as the area along the sea, a lake or a river, including the near-shore waters: 沿岸部, 沿岸地域, 太平洋沿岸, 沿岸漁業, 沿岸警備隊. It is matter-of-fact and typical of news and weather reports. The beach or shore where you take a walk is more often called 海岸 or 海辺. Grammatically 沿岸 is a noun and takes の: 沿岸の町.

examples[].german: Why not try writing a monthly column about life in coastal areas?
China's coastal regions have more developed economies than its inland regions.
This fish can be caught in Japan's coastal waters all year round.
en.notes: 沿海 means the waters near the coast or the coastal region. The word is literary and much rarer than 沿岸; it appears most often in 沿海部 "coastal region" (often about China: 中国の沿海部) and 沿海州 "Primorye region". In everyday speech people mostly say 海の近く or 沿岸. 沿海 is a noun and is linked with の.

en.meaning: area along a rail line; along the line
examples[].german: My younger brother lives along the Keio line.
There are many universities along this line, so there are lots of apartments for students.
The railway company explained the construction work to residents along the line.
en.notes: 沿線 is not the railway track itself (that is 路線 or 線路), but the area along a train or bus line. Typical: 〜線沿線に住む "to live along the ... line", 沿線の住民, 沿線の観光地; the word is very common in apartment hunting and advertising. Along a road, by contrast, is 沿道, e.g. for spectators at a marathon.

en.meaning: to run along; to follow; to meet (wishes)
examples[].german: Along both banks of the river there is a beautiful row of cherry trees all the way.
We will proceed with the meeting following the materials distributed in advance.
I'm sorry that we could not meet your wishes.
en.notes: 沿う always takes に: 川に沿う "to run along the river". Most common is the て-form 〜に沿って "along ..." (道に沿って歩く) as well as figuratively "in accordance with, in line with": 方針に沿って, マニュアルに沿って. Very polite is ご期待に沿えるよう "in order to live up to your expectations", often negated as ご希望に沿えず申し訳ございません. Do not confuse it with the identically read 添う "to accompany, to stand by" (寄り添う).

examples[].german: The battle between the Genji and the Heike is well known in Japanese history.
The Tale of Genji is a story written about a thousand years ago by Murasaki Shikibu.
The name a hostess uses at the club is called a "genji-na".
en.notes: 源氏 has two meanings: historically the warrior nobility of the Minamoto, whose struggle against the Taira (平家/平氏) in the 源平合戦 led to the Kamakura shogunate; and in literature Prince Hikaru Genji (光源氏), the main character of the 源氏物語. Derived from this is 源氏名, originally the names of court ladies taken from chapters of the novel, today the stage name of hostesses. In modern daily life, 源氏 occurs almost only in these contexts.

examples[].german: When I go out, I unplug all the outlets to cut the power completely.
Even when I turn it on, the computer doesn't run.
At the cafe I looked for a seat where I could use a power outlet.
en.notes: 電源 is the power source or power supply of a device and in everyday use mainly its on/off state: 電源を入れる "to switch on", 電源を切る "to switch off", 電源が入らない "does not turn on", 電源ボタン. In cafes and trains, 電源 also refers to a usable power outlet; the outlet as a component is called コンセント. In announcements one often hears 携帯電話の電源をお切りください.

examples[].german: I'm worried about my friend who lives near the epicenter.
The epicenter was off the coast of Shizuoka Prefecture, and the magnitude was 5.8.
The epicenter of that rumor seems to be the next-door class.
en.notes: 震源地 is the place or area from which an earthquake originates. Technically, 震源 is the earthquake focus at depth; the news often says 震源は〜 and 震源の深さ "focal depth". Figuratively, 震源地 denotes the starting point of a rumor, scandal or trend: うわさの震源地. On strength: マグニチュード is the magnitude, 震度 the locally measured intensity.

examples[].german: Communication is indispensable.
I can't do without my coffee every morning.
He is an indispensable player for this team.
en.notes: 欠かせない is the negative potential form of 欠く "to lack, to omit" and literally means "cannot be left out" - that is, "indispensable, essential". It conjugates like an i-adjective (欠かせなかった). Typical pattern: AにBは欠かせない "B is indispensable for A", attributively 欠かせない存在. A synonym is the more formal 不可欠 (必要不可欠); 欠かせない sounds more vivid and also suits personal habits: 毎朝のコーヒーが欠かせない.

examples[].german: Until my child gets a bit older, full-time work seems a bit impossible.
This hospital has five full-time doctors.
From next month, I will work as a full-time employee instead of part-time.
en.notes: 常勤 means working regularly full time at one post; it usually takes の (常勤の医師, 常勤職員) or で (常勤で働く). The opposite is 非常勤 "part-time, on a non-regular basis", e.g. 非常勤講師 "part-time lecturer". It is more formal than フルタイム and typical of job ads, schools and hospitals; 正社員, by contrast, emphasizes the permanent employment contract.

examples[].german: I am asking, knowing that it is unreasonable.
"Please send me the materials by tomorrow." "Understood."
As you know, the fees go up from next month.
en.notes: 承知 means "knowledge" and "consent". In working life, 承知しました (even more politely 承知いたしました) is the standard answer "Understood, will do"; toward customers also かしこまりました. ご承知のとおり means "as you know", and 〜を承知で "although one knows ...". In the negative as a threat: 今度やったら承知しないぞ "I won't let you get away with it next time".

examples[].german: Having said that, Kuroda disappeared into the entertainment district.
Shinjuku's Kabukicho is the most famous entertainment district in Japan.
Walking alone in the entertainment district at night may be a little dangerous.
en.notes: 歓楽街 is an entertainment district with bars, clubs, hostess venues and often also red-light businesses; the word therefore has a slightly shady connotation. A lively downtown area with shops and restaurants is neutrally called 繁華街, a street full of pubs 飲み屋街. Typical are 〜の歓楽街 and 夜の歓楽街.

examples[].german: I went to play pachinko intending to win big, but I ended up losing a lot.
My friend who lost a lot on stocks reportedly quit investing.
If you miss this sale, you'll lose out big.
en.notes: 大損 is a heavy loss, usually of money; as a verb 大損する or 大損をする, the cause takes で: 株で大損する. The opposite is 大儲け "big profit". Colloquially, 大損だ is also used exaggeratedly for missed opportunities ("you're missing out a lot"). More neutral or formal are 大きな損失 and 損害.
