examples[].german: If a car is a total loss, the repair cost is often not paid in full by insurance.
After the accident, the car was judged a total loss.
The goods in the warehouse were a total loss in the fire.
en.notes: 全損 is a term from insurance and business: the complete loss or total damage of a vehicle, building or goods. Typical are 全損になる, 全損と判断される and 全損事故; the counterpart is 分損 "partial loss". In daily life, for cars people often say 廃車になる "has to be scrapped".

examples[].german: On Setsubun, we do the bean-throwing ritual with the family.
These coffee beans were imported from Brazil.
Beans are good for the body, so I try to eat a little every day.
en.notes: 豆 is the general term for legumes and their seeds - beans, peas and above all the soybean, from which 豆腐, 納豆 and 味噌 are made. In daily life you often hear the friendly-polite form お豆; coffee beans are コーヒー豆. Well known is the bean-throwing 豆まき at 節分 ("鬼は外、福は内"). As a prefix, 豆〜 means "mini-": 豆知識 "a little piece of trivia", 豆電球 "miniature light bulb".

examples[].german: Anko is made from azuki beans, but it has quite a lot of sugar.
On celebration days, we make sekihan with glutinous rice and azuki beans.
I bought an azuki-colored sweater.
en.notes: 小豆 is irregularly read あずき; compare 大豆 (だいず) "soybean". It refers to the small red bean from which sweet bean paste (あんこ) for Japanese sweets, お赤飯 and ぜんざい are made. The word is also often written in kana as あずき; 小豆色 is a dark reddish brown.

examples[].german: Don't get me wrong. I love Japanese food, but I just can't eat natto.
Mix natto well and then eat it over rice.
Natto is said to be good for you, but many people can't stand the smell.
en.notes: 納豆 is fermented soybeans with sticky strings (糸を引く) and a strong smell. You stir it well (よく混ぜる) and mostly eat it with mustard and soy sauce on rice (納豆ご飯), especially for breakfast. 納豆 is sold in small packs, counted with 〜パック. In eastern Japan (関東) it is traditionally more popular than in western Japan (関西).

examples[].german: I was trying to cut my dog's nails with the nail clippers, but I got distracted by my phone.
Where are the nail clippers?
Some people say it's bad luck to cut your nails at night.
en.notes: 爪切り denotes both the tool (nail clipper, nail scissors) and nail cutting itself: 爪切りをする. The corresponding verb is 爪を切る; 爪 includes fingernails and toenails as well as the claws of animals. The き stays unchanged, so it is not つめぎり.

examples[].german: The shogunate killed my entire family.
In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu established the shogunate in Edo.
The Edo shogunate restricted contact with foreign countries for a long time.
en.notes: 幕府 is the military government of a shogun (将軍) in premodern Japan. One distinguishes 鎌倉幕府, 室町幕府 and 江戸幕府 (also 徳川幕府). Typical phrases are 幕府を開く "to found a shogunate" and 幕府が倒れる "the shogunate falls"; the final phase of the Edo shogunate is called 幕末. A purely historical word from school lessons and historical dramas.

examples[].german: Enormous damage occurred.
The typhoon had a huge impact on agriculture.
The damage to the company from this mistake is enormous.
en.notes: 甚大 means "enormous, immense", but is used almost only for negative magnitudes: 甚大な被害, 甚大な損害, 影響が甚大だ. It is a な-adjective with a strongly literary, formal tone, typical of news about disasters and accidents. It does not fit positive size such as a great success; there people say 大きな, or 莫大な for sums of money.

examples[].german: I'll send someone to pick you up at the station.
I go to pick up my child at nursery school at six.
A car to pick you up has arrived in front of the hotel.
en.notes: 迎え is the nominal form of 迎える and means picking up or receiving a person. Most common: 〜を迎えに行く/来る "to go/come to pick up", 駅まで迎えに来て. Polite is お迎え (お迎えの車). The counterpart is 見送り "seeing off, escorting out"; 出迎え stresses going to meet someone upon arrival. お迎えが来る can also euphemistically mean "death is approaching".

examples[].german: This avocado, I only bought it yesterday and it's already gone bad.
Food spoils easily in summer, so please put it in the fridge early.
From overusing the hair dryer, my hair got quite damaged.
en.notes: 傷む is intransitive and means "to get damaged, to spoil": with food (野菜が傷む), hair (髪が傷む), houses or furniture (家が傷む). The transitive counterpart is 傷める (髪を傷める). Do not confuse it with the identically read 痛む "to hurt" (頭が痛む). For completely rotten food 腐る is stronger; 傷む means more "going off, no longer fresh".

examples[].german: I hear that salon specializes in slimming.
I often see ads for slimming salons in front of the station.
He was a tall, slender young man.
en.notes: 痩身 has two meanings: elevated and literary "slender body" (e.g. 長身痩身 "tall and slim") and "slimming, weight loss", especially in advertising and cosmetics: 痩身エステ, 痩身効果. In everyday speech people say やせる, ダイエット or スリムな体 instead. 痩身 is a noun; as a description it takes の, not な.

examples[].german: Koichi has a star-shaped mole on his crotch.
The crotch of my pants tore.
Up ahead, the road splits into two.
en.notes: 股 is the crotch, i.e. the area between the legs up to the inner side of the thighs; the thigh itself is 太もも. Important compounds are 股下 "inseam length (trousers)", 内股 "inner thigh" and 股関節 "hip joint". 二股 is a fork (道が二股に分かれる), and colloquially also "two-timing" in relationships: 二股をかける.

en.meaning: diving; jumping in; dropping in unannounced
examples[].german: Diving is prohibited in this pool.
The diver entered the water cleanly from the ten-meter platform.
We also politely handled walk-in customers without reservations.
en.notes: 飛び込み is the nominal form of 飛び込む and first denotes jumping into water; as a sport it is diving (高飛び込み "platform diving"). Figuratively it means showing up unannounced: 飛び込みの客 "walk-in customer", 飛び込み営業 "door-to-door cold calling", 飛び込みで参加する. At swimming pools, 飛び込み禁止 is often posted.

examples[].german: That guy is good at making money.
Money is important, but I don't work only to make money.
He tried to make money on stocks and lost instead.
en.notes: 金儲け means "making money, turning a profit" and is colloquial, often with a slightly negative ring ("money-grubbing"); 金儲け主義 criticizes pure profit-seeking. Typical are 金儲けがうまい, 金儲けのために and 金儲けをする/金儲けする. Neutral for "earning money" through work is お金を稼ぐ; the verb 儲ける stresses the profit.

examples[].german: Insurance premiums are calculated based on age and income.
It takes time to assess the amount of damage caused by the accident.
From next month, the method for calculating electricity charges will change.
en.notes: 算定する means to calculate or determine an amount or value according to fixed rules. It is formal and typical of administration, insurance and business: 保険料/税額/損害額を算定する, 算定方法, 算定基準; often in the passive 〜をもとに算定される. For simple arithmetic, 計算する is used, and for counting people 数える or 集計する.

en.meaning: to get hurt; to be hurt
examples[].german: Am I at the age where people call me "auntie"? That hurts.
A friend's remark hurt me very much.
When we moved, the new table got scratched.
en.notes: 傷つく is intransitive: someone or something gets hurt or damaged. Most often it concerns feelings (心が傷つく, 〜に傷つく "to be hurt by ...", 傷つきやすい "sensitive"), and also objects that get scratched. The transitive counterpart is 傷つける (人を傷つける). For physical injuries, people usually say けがをする in daily life. Also written 傷付く.

en.meaning: devoted to; single-minded; a single streak; a ray
examples[].german: Our eldest son is all about baseball. He has no interest in girls, either.
My father has devoted himself to bread-making for forty years and kept this shop going.
A single ray of light came in through the window into the dark room.
en.notes: 一筋 has two uses. Literally it denotes a single narrow streak: 一筋の光 "a ray of light", 一筋の涙 "a single tear", figuratively also 一筋の希望 "a glimmer of hope". After a noun, 〜一筋 means "wholly and exclusively devoted to ...": 野球一筋, 仕事一筋, この道一筋三十年 - usually appreciative, sometimes with a slight mockery of one-sidedness. Similar is 一途 "single-minded, devoted", which describes the person more (一途な人).

examples[].german: We quarreled over a trivial matter.
Even a small mistake can lead to a serious accident.
She worries right away even about trivial things.
en.notes: 些細 means "trivial, insignificant" and is a な-adjective: 些細なこと "a trifle", 些細なミス. It often appears in sentences stressing that something big arose from a small cause (些細なことで喧嘩する) or that one should not get upset over trifles. Synonyms are ちょっとした (more colloquial) and 小さな; 些細 sounds somewhat more elevated and is also written in kana as ささい.

en.meaning: to liven up; to build excitement
examples[].german: My friend is hilarious and good at livening up parties.
Let's all cheer together and get the game going!
The host skillfully livened up the conversation, so the gathering was enjoyable.
en.notes: 盛り上げる is transitive (〜を盛り上げる) and mostly means "to create atmosphere, to get something going": パーティーを盛り上げる, 会場を盛り上げる, 話を盛り上げる. The intransitive counterpart is 盛り上がる: パーティーが盛り上がった "the party really got going". The literal meaning "to heap up" (土を盛り上げる) is rare in daily life. Someone who is good at livening up a group is colloquially the 盛り上げ役.

examples[].german: He's not a traitor or anything. He's just a bit scatterbrained by nature.
There must be a traitor on this team.
Shouting "Traitor!", she left the room.
en.notes: 裏切り者 is someone who breaks trust: traitor, turncoat. It is composed of 裏切り (the noun of 裏切る "to betray, to deceive") and 者 "person". The word is strong and emotional and often comes up as an accusation or exclamation: 裏切り者！. It is used for friends, partners, groups or states; a spy, by contrast, is スパイ.

examples[].german: For various reasons, we have decided to temporarily close the shop for a while.
Well then, regarding tomorrow's meeting, I'm counting on you for all the various things.
The various procedures for the move are finally finished.
en.notes: 諸々 means "all sorts of, all the various things" and mostly stands with の before a noun: 諸々の事情 "various circumstances" (often as a polite reason without details), 諸々の手続き. It sounds somewhat more refined than 色々 or いろんな, but in the office it is also used casually as an adverb: 諸々よろしくお願いします. Often also written in kana as もろもろ.

examples[].german: Come on, please. It was obvious that you two were not compatible at all! You really shouldn't call that girl with the braid!
My daughter has her hair braided by my wife every morning.
If you braid long hair, it doesn't get in the way when you exercise.
en.notes: 三つ編み literally means "three-strand weave": a braid plaited from three strands. Typical are 髪を三つ編みにする "to braid one's hair" and 三つ編みの女の子 "a girl with a braid". An unbraided ponytail, by contrast, is ポニーテール; two braids on the left and right are also called おさげ. The word is likewise used for braided cords or braided bread loaves and is often written in kana as みつあみ.

en.meaning: to fit in; to settle into a place; to take a post; to be satisfied
examples[].german: I don't think they'll be satisfied just by being paid money.
All the luggage fit into this box.
Since last year he has been installed in the president's seat.
en.notes: 納まる is intransitive and means "to fit in, come to its place" (箱に納まる, 予算内に納まる), "to take up a position" (社長のいすに納まる), "to be paid" (税金が納まる) and "to be satisfied" (それでは彼が納まらない). For "to fit in", 収まる is usually written in everyday text; pain or unrest that subsides is 治まる. Transitive counterpart: 納める "to pay in, to store".

en.meaning: to be convinced; to understand and accept; consent
examples[].german: I'm convinced by his opinion.
After listening to the teacher's explanation, I finally understood and accepted it.
I simply cannot accept this result.
en.notes: 納得 means to inwardly understand and accept something after an explanation. Typical patterns are 〜に納得する, 納得できる/できない, 納得がいく/いかない "to be convinced/not convinced", and 納得させる "to convince". It is also used casually as an exclamation: なるほど、納得！ or 〜には納得だ. Compared with 理解 "to understand", 納得 stresses that you also agree.

examples[].german: Can you turn this sentence into a negative one?
The negative form of 「食べる」 is 「食べない」.
The polite negative form takes the form 「〜ません」.
en.notes: 否定形 is the grammatical term for the negative form of a verb or adjective, e.g. 行かない, 高くない, 静かじゃない. In Japanese classes for foreigners the plain form is often called ない形; the opposite is 肯定形 "affirmative form". A whole negative sentence is a 否定文. Typical: 〜を否定形にする "to put into the negative".

examples[].german: Technology has greatly changed people's lives.
I have already gotten completely used to life in the countryside.
Since I started living alone, I have started cooking for myself.
en.notes: 暮らし is the noun form of 暮らす and refers to everyday life, lifestyle, and also one's livelihood. Typical are 暮らしが楽/苦しい "to get by comfortably/barely", 田舎暮らし and 一人暮らし "living alone". Compared with 生活, 暮らし sounds softer and closer to daily life; 生活 is more matter-of-fact (生活費, 生活習慣). Life in the sense of a lifetime is 人生, and life as the opposite of death is 命.

en.meaning: to rehash; to bring up again
examples[].german: That again? Don't rehash something that's already over.
Please stop bringing up in meetings things that have already been decided.
I steamed a cooled manju again and ate it.
en.notes: 蒸し返す literally means "to steam again, to reheat" (蒸す + 返す), but is mostly used figuratively: to bring up a closed topic or an old quarrel again: 話/問題/昔のことを蒸し返す. It sounds reproachful and often appears in requests or negation: 蒸し返さないで. More neutral is 話を戻す "to return to the topic".

examples[].german: I keep in contact frequently.
Accidents happen frequently on this road.
Frequent changes to the schedule are a problem.
en.notes: 頻繁 means "frequent, at short intervals" and is a na-adjective mostly used adverbially as 頻繁に: 頻繁に連絡する, 頻繁に起こる; attributively: 頻繁な変更. It sounds more factual than よく or the colloquial しょっちゅう and stresses a conspicuously high frequency, often with a slightly critical undertone. Opposite: まれ or めったに〜ない.

en.meaning: to pretend; to pose as; to dress up
examples[].german: He had expected a promotion that didn't come, but he pretended to be unbothered and congratulated the employees who were promoted.
The culprit entered the shop posing as a customer.
People dressed up beautifully had gathered at the wedding.
en.notes: 装う has two meanings: in a literary sense "to dress, to adorn oneself" (美しく装う), and, more often, "to feign, to put on an appearance": 平気を装う "to act calm", 〜を装って "disguised as ..." (客/警察官を装って, typical in news about fraud). In everyday speech, "to pretend" is more commonly 〜ふりをする. The same kanji is used to write よそう "to dish up food" (ご飯をよそう), which is usually written in kana.

en.meaning: to be late; to fall behind
examples[].german: The train was thirty minutes late because of an accident.
I'm sorry for being late for our appointment.
Because I was absent for a month, I'm behind everyone else in my studies.
en.notes: 遅れる means "to be late, not to be on time"; the appointment or occasion takes に: 授業に遅れる, 約束の時間に遅れる. 遅刻する is narrower and means above all arriving late for school or work. Means of transport also run late (電車が遅れる), and clocks run slow (時計が遅れている). It also means "to fall behind": 勉強が遅れる, 流行に遅れる. The related adjective is 遅い, and the transitive 遅らせる means "to delay, to postpone".

examples[].german: The rabbit hutch was destroyed by fire.
Environmental destruction caused by human activity has become a major problem.
The culprit smashed the window and entered the house.
en.notes: 破壊 is violent, often complete destruction; as a する-verb it is mostly transitive (建物を破壊する) and very often used in the passive 〜によって破壊される. Typical compounds are 環境破壊, 自然破壊 and 破壊的 "destructive". Compared with the everyday word 壊す, 破壊する sounds heavier and more formal; opposites are 建設 "construction" and 創造 "creation".

examples[].german: The ship carrying a famous Edo-period sword was wrecked in a storm.
The morning after the storm, timber from the wrecked ship had washed up on the shore.
Many old tales are about being shipwrecked and reaching a deserted island.
en.notes: 破船 is a literary, rather archaic word for a shipwreck or the destroyed ship itself (wreck). It can be used as a する-verb: 嵐で破船する. Today people mostly say 難破 (難破する, 難破船) or speak of sinking: 沈没する. It is found mainly in novels, historical texts and stories.

examples[].german: A foul smell hung in the barracks, and it was hard even to breathe.
The soldiers slept and lived in an old barracks.
After the war, the barracks was used as a school building.
en.notes: 兵舎 is the building where soldiers are housed: barracks. The word is military and historical; for the Japanese Self-Defense Forces people rather speak of 隊舎, and the whole grounds are called 駐屯地 or 基地. 舎 means "building" as in 校舎 "school building", 庁舎 "government office building" and 宿舎 "lodging".

examples[].german: It seems lightning struck the government building.
The city hall's new building is scheduled to be completed next year.
You can pick up your residence certificate at the counter on the first floor of the government building.
en.notes: 庁舎 is the building of a government office: 市庁舎 "city hall building", 県庁舎, 合同庁舎. It is a formal word for the structure itself and often appears on signs, maps and in the news (新庁舎の建設). In everyday speech people usually say just 市役所, 区役所 or 県庁, meaning the office together with its building.

examples[].german: That lecturer showed up at the lecture hall in a limousine.
A famous author is going to give a lecture at the university next week.
Yesterday's lecture was so interesting that the time passed in no time.
en.notes: 講演 is a public talk before an audience, usually by experts or well-known figures: 講演をする/行う, 講演会, 講演者, 記念講演. A regular university lecture course is 講義, a political speech is 演説, and a speech in general is スピーチ. Beware of homophones: 公園 "park", 公演 "performance", and 後援 "support, sponsorship".

examples[].german: Delete that video without delay.
If a payment is delayed, an additional fee will be charged.
Due to heavy snow, delays are occurring in deliveries.
en.notes: 遅滞 denotes a delay or default, especially with obligations, payments and processes; it is a word of official, legal and business language. Very common is the set phrase 遅滞なく "without delay, promptly", typical in instructions and contracts. As an intransitive する-verb it takes が: 支払いが遅滞する "the payment falls into default". In everyday speech people say 遅れ or 遅れる instead.

examples[].german: With the police's intervention, the situation became even more complicated.
The government intervened in the market to stop the yen's decline.
You shouldn't interfere in other people's family problems.
en.notes: 介入 is intervention from outside in a matter (often unwelcome, or official). As an intransitive する-verb, the target takes に: 市場に介入する "to intervene in the market". Typical combinations are 軍事介入, 政府の介入 or 警察の介入. Close in meaning is 干渉 "interference", which sounds more negative; colloquially people say 口を出す "to butt in".

examples[].german: I think everyone should build their own grave themselves before they die.
Before getting to know others, it is important to first know yourself.
He believed in his own strength and fought to the end.
en.notes: 己 is a literary, archaic word for "oneself, one's own self"; in normal daily life people say 自分. It survives mainly in set phrases such as 己を知る "to know oneself", 己に勝つ "to overcome oneself" or 己の力 "one's own strength". As a form of address, おのれ is derogatory ("you there!"), and as an exclamation おのれ！ expresses anger, typical of samurai dramas and anime.

examples[].german: I want to contribute to society.
His goal contributed to the team's victory.
This research contributed greatly to solving environmental problems.
en.notes: 貢献する is intransitive; what one contributes to takes に: 社会に貢献する, 勝利に貢献する. As a noun, one says 〜への貢献 or 社会貢献. The word is rather formal and suggests a meaningful contribution toward a larger goal. In everyday speech, for "to be useful" people rather say 役に立つ; 協力する means "to cooperate, to help out".

examples[].german: A chance like this is rare.
With this medicine, headaches may occur in rare cases.
It is rare for ten centimeters of snow to pile up in Tokyo.
en.notes: 稀 (mostly written in kana, まれ) means "rare" and is a na-adjective: 稀なケース, 〜は稀だ. Adverbially, 稀に means "rarely, in rare cases": 稀に副作用が出る. It sounds somewhat more literary than めったに〜ない, which is more common in everyday speech. Fixed phrase: 稀に見る "exceptional, such as is rarely seen" (稀に見る才能). 珍しい, by contrast, emphasizes the unusual and surprising.

examples[].german: "The singer I like best is myself," he boasted with a self-satisfied smile.
In the interview, please start with a brief self-introduction.
If you climb a winter mountain alone, you do so at your own risk.
en.notes: 自己 means "the self" and almost never stands alone but appears in fixed compounds: 自己紹介 "self-introduction", 自己満足 "self-satisfaction", 自己責任 "personal responsibility", 自己中心的 "self-centered", 自己管理 "self-management". In daily speech, "I myself / oneself" is 自分, and after a person 自身 is used (彼自身 "he himself"). 自己 sounds objective and abstract, as in psychology and on forms.

examples[].german: If you scribble on Biet's face, it will cause trouble later.
My department head asked me to do a troublesome job.
In my university days, I was staying at my uncle's house, relying on his care.
en.notes: 厄介 is a な-adjective for something "troublesome, tricky" that causes effort and annoyance: 厄介な問題, 厄介な客. Common are 厄介なことになる "to get into trouble" and 厄介者 "a person who is a burden". A second meaning is "to depend on someone's care": 〜の家に厄介になる "to stay at someone's house". Similar is 面倒 "bothersome" (more everyday); 迷惑, by contrast, stresses the nuisance caused to others.

examples[].german: That species of sea turtle is in danger of extinction.
On summer nights, sea turtles come to the beach to lay eggs.
I swam with sea turtles in the sea off Okinawa.
en.notes: 海亀 is the sea turtle; in biology, zoos and the news it is usually written in katakana as ウミガメ. 亀 alone is the general term for turtles and tortoises, including land tortoises. Common combinations are 海亀の産卵 "egg-laying of sea turtles" and 海亀が卵を産む - a well-known summer event on beaches in Okinawa and Yakushima.

examples[].german: The two of them each offered the other their seat, saying "Please, sit down."
When you're in trouble, it's the same for all of us.
The team members cooperated with each other and made the project a success.
en.notes: 互い is mostly used with the polite prefix as お互い; without お it sounds more literary. As an adverb, お互いに / 互いに means "each other, mutually": 互いに助け合う; with の it forms attributive phrases like お互いの意見 "the opinions of both sides". The set phrase お互い様 means "it's the same for all of us, no need to thank me" and is a typical reply to thanks or an apology among equals.

examples[].german: Let's read the pages alternately.
It was a long trip, so my brother and I took turns driving.
Red and white flags are lined up alternately on both sides of the road.
en.notes: 交互 is almost always used adverbially as 交互に "alternately, in turns": AとBを交互に使う "to use A and B alternately"; attributively it stands as 交互の. It describes a regular alternation between two things or people. Similar are 代わる代わる "in turn (people one after another)", 交代で "in shifts, taking turns" and 順番に "in order".

examples[].german: The battery life of my phone has been getting shorter.
The average life expectancy of Japanese people is among the highest in the world.
A car suddenly darted out, and it took years off my life.
en.notes: 寿命 is the lifespan of living things and - very commonly - also of devices and objects: 電池の寿命 "battery life over the years", 電球の寿命. Typical are 寿命が長い／短い, 寿命が延びる and 平均寿命 "average life expectancy". 寿命が来る means a device is "at the end of its life"; the idiom 寿命が縮む ("one's lifespan shrinks") expresses a great shock.

examples[].german: My grandma always tells me, "Eating bananas leads to a long life."
Okinawa is known as a region of longevity.
This program is a long-running show that has continued for thirty years.
en.notes: 長寿 means "long life, longevity" and sounds somewhat more elevated than the everyday 長生き. Typical are 長寿の秘訣 "the secret of a long life", 長寿を祝う and 長寿国. Before nouns it also means "long-running": 長寿番組 is a TV program that has been on for decades. As a verb one does not say 長寿する but 長生きする.

examples[].german: All of us part-timers are planning to celebrate the manager's 77th birthday at a convenience store.
The whole family gathered to celebrate my grandfather's 77th birthday.
My mother turns 77 next year.
en.notes: 喜寿 is the 77th birthday, one of the traditional congratulatory birthdays for older people. The name comes from the cursive form of 喜 looking like 七十七. The series is 還暦 (60), 古希 (70), 喜寿 (77), 傘寿 (80), 米寿 (88) and 白寿 (99). Typical are 喜寿を迎える "to turn 77" and 喜寿のお祝い; the lucky color is purple.

examples[].german: I pray for the two of you to enjoy happiness and long life for years to come.
At New Year, we visited the shrine, wishing for our grandparents' happiness and longevity.
I decorated the entrance with a pot of pheasant's eye.
en.notes: 福寿 means "happiness and long life" and is an elevated, auspicious word for good wishes, New Year cards and inscriptions. It is not a celebration in itself, but something one wishes for someone: 福寿をお祈りします. It is best known in 福寿草 "pheasant's eye (Adonis)", a yellow New Year flower, and in the four-character word 福寿円満 "happiness, long life and harmony".

examples[].german: While I was sipping 100% orange juice through a straw, someone tapped me on the shoulder.
This juice contains only 10 percent fruit juice.
Squeeze the lemon and sprinkle a little of the juice over the fish.
en.notes: 果汁 is the juice from fruit. Because ジュース in Japanese can refer to any sweet soft drink, 果汁 on labels indicates the actual fruit content: 果汁100％ "100% juice". Typical combinations are 果汁を絞る "to squeeze out juice" and 果汁たっぷり "extra juicy". 汁 alone means more "broth, soup, liquid".

examples[].german: One-sided opinions are not good.
He did all the talking and didn't listen to me at all.
The company terminated my contract unilaterally.
en.notes: 一方的 means "one-sided" - coming from one side only, without regard for the other: 一方的な意見, 一方的に話す, 一方的に決める. As a na-adjective it takes な attributively and に adverbially. It is usually meant critically, when someone talks or decides over the heads of others; in sports 一方的な試合 is a "one-sided game". Opposite: 相互の or 双方向の.

en.meaning: in order to; for; because of
examples[].german: I wanted to sleep before my night shift, but I couldn't because the train noise was too loud.
I save money every month in order to buy a house.
The trains stopped because of the heavy snow.
en.notes: ために (usually written in kana, rarely 為に) has two main meanings. Purpose: after nouns with の or after the dictionary form of volitional verbs, "for, in order to": 家族のために, 家を買うために. Reason: after nouns with の or after past forms, "because of, as a result of": 大雪のために - this sounds written and formal; in conversation people say から or ので. With non-volitional verbs or potential forms, ように is usually used instead of ために.

examples[].german: That is an act of betrayal.
Let's stop disruptive behavior on the train.
I was deeply moved by the kind act of a stranger.
en.notes: 行為 is a single "act, deed", usually with a legal or moral evaluation: 違法行為 "illegal act", 迷惑行為 "nuisance behavior", 犯罪行為, 親切な行為. It sounds formal and is not used with する. 行動 is more general "behavior, action" (行動する), and 行い refers more to a person's moral conduct.

examples[].german: The night bus was temporarily suspended because of an accident that occurred in Kumamoto Prefecture.
Kumamoto Prefecture is in the middle of Kyushu and is famous for Mount Aso.
Kumamon is the mascot of Kumamoto Prefecture.
en.notes: 熊本県 is a prefecture in the middle of the island of Kyushu; its capital is 熊本市. Well known are Kumamoto Castle (熊本城), the volcano 阿蘇山 and the mascot くまモン. In conversation people often say just 熊本 when it is clear whether the city or the prefecture is meant; 県 is added to name the prefecture explicitly, for example in the news and in addresses.

examples[].german: He kept writing novels inside the prison.
Life inside the prison was harsh, with almost no freedom.
Violence inside the prison has become a major problem.
en.notes: 獄内 means "in prison, inside the prison" and is a rare, literary word, found mainly in historical texts and reports. It usually appears as 獄内で or attributively as 獄内の. The synonymous 獄中 is more common (獄中で書いた手紙); in modern everyday speech people simply say 刑務所の中 or 刑務所内.

examples[].german: The first time I went to prison, for some reason I felt a sense of relief.
He was imprisoned for three years for fraud.
The experience of having been in prison in his youth changed his life greatly.
en.notes: 入獄 means "to go to prison, to begin serving a prison sentence"; it is an intransitive する-verb from formal, somewhat old-fashioned written language. The opposite is 出獄 "to be released from prison". If someone is locked up, the transitive 投獄 is used in the passive: 投獄される. In everyday speech people more often say 刑務所に入る, in news 服役する "to serve a sentence".

examples[].german: On the day I was released from prison, I shoplifted and was arrested by the police again.
His mother was waiting in front of the gate for him, released after ten years.
After his release, he opened a small shop and worked diligently.
en.notes: 出獄 means "to be released from prison" and is an intransitive する-verb of written language; the opposite is 入獄. In today's news you mostly hear 出所 (出所する) or 釈放 (釈放される "to be set free"). Typical are time expressions such as 十年ぶりに出獄する or 出獄後 "after release".

examples[].german: His mother forced him to break out of prison.
Two prisoners escaped from the prison in the middle of the night.
If you jailbreak your smartphone, you will no longer be covered by the manufacturer's warranty.
en.notes: 脱獄 is a "prison break"; as an intransitive する-verb: 刑務所から脱獄する. The escapee is called 脱獄囚. More general is 脱走 "escape, desertion" (also from barracks or zoos). In IT language 脱獄 also means "jailbreak" of a smartphone or game console, and it is then used transitively: スマホを脱獄する.

en.meaning: to get drunk; to get motion sick; to be intoxicated
examples[].german: Everyone got seasick and was throwing up all over the place.
I drank too much beer yesterday and got completely drunk.
The whole audience was enchanted by her singing voice.
en.notes: 酔う is an intransitive godan verb with three meanings: "to get drunk" (酒に酔う), "to feel sick in vehicles" (車に酔う, 船に酔う; also 車酔い, 船酔い), and figuratively "to be intoxicated, carried away" (音楽に酔う). The state "to be drunk" is expressed by 酔っている; colloquial and stronger is 酔っ払う. The causative 酔わせる means "to make drunk".

examples[].german: I was completely plastered and had lost my sense of direction.
A drunken man was sleeping on the station platform.
Driving while dead drunk is very dangerous.
en.notes: 泥酔 is a state of total drunkenness in which one can hardly stand or remember anything - much stronger than 酔う or 酔っ払う. It sounds matter-of-fact to formal and often appears in news and police reports: 泥酔状態 "state of being dead drunk", 泥酔客, 泥酔した男性. As an intransitive する-verb it usually appears in the forms 泥酔している／泥酔した.

examples[].german: I came to like vinegared dishes once I became an adult.
I made a vinegared dish with cucumber and wakame.
A small vinegared dish came with the set meal.
en.notes: 酢の物 is a small Japanese dish whose ingredients are dressed in a vinegar mixture - typically cucumber, wakame seaweed or octopus. It is served as a side dish in a small bowl (小鉢), for example with a set menu. It is not the same as 漬物, which is pickled with salt, rice bran or miso. To prepare it is 酢の物を作る.

examples[].german: Mutual understanding is important.
The two countries promised to cooperate with each other.
These two problems are related to each other.
en.notes: 相互 means "mutual, reciprocal" and is actually a noun that mostly stands before other nouns: 相互理解, 相互関係, 相互作用; with の: 相互の信頼. The adverbial 相互に is also possible (相互に協力する). It sounds literary and matter-of-fact; in conversation one says お互い(に) instead. It is not used as a na-adjective with な.

examples[].german: Considering they were taken with a cheap camera, your photos of Lake Yamanaka came out really beautiful.
Lake Yamanaka is the largest of the Fuji Five Lakes.
During summer vacation, I went camping near Lake Yamanaka with friends.
en.notes: 山中湖 is the largest of the five Fuji lakes (富士五湖) in Yamanashi Prefecture, right at the foot of Mt. Fuji. It is a popular excursion spot with a view of the mountain, for camping and for training camps of school and university clubs. In lake names 湖 is read こ (山中湖, 琵琶湖), whereas the word on its own is みずうみ.

examples[].german: How about casting a statue of Koichi in bronze?
Bronze is made by mixing copper and tin.
I saw ancient Chinese bronze ware at the museum.
en.notes: 青銅 is bronze, an alloy of copper and tin; the name ("blue copper") comes from the greenish patina. The word sounds technical and historical: 青銅器 "bronze vessel", 青銅器時代 "Bronze Age". In everyday speech people often say ブロンズ. Note: the bronze medal is 銅メダル, not 青銅メダル, and a bronze statue is usually simply 銅像.

examples[].german: In Japan, copper mines are closing one after another.
The Ashio copper mine is known as the beginning of Japan's pollution problems.
My grandfather worked in a copper mine when he was young.
en.notes: 銅山 is a copper mine. In words for mines, 山 is read ざん or さん: 金山 (きんざん) "gold mine", 銀山 (ぎんざん) "silver mine", generally 鉱山 (こうざん) "mine"; a coal mine, by contrast, is 炭鉱. Closing a mine is 閉山 (閉山する). Historically well known is the 足尾銅山, the scene of Japan's first major environmental scandal.

examples[].german: Someone smashed the bronze statue to pieces.
In front of Shibuya Station there is a bronze statue of Hachiko.
A bronze statue of a famous author was erected in the town park.
en.notes: 銅像 is a statue (usually cast in bronze), typically of a person or an animal on a pedestal. One says 銅像を建てる "to erect a statue" or, in the passive, 銅像が建てられる. The general term is 像 "statue, image"; one made of stone is a 石像. Famous is the ハチ公の銅像 in Shibuya, a popular meeting spot (ハチ公前で待ち合わせ).

examples[].german: I'm sorry, but none of the oil fields belong to me.
There are many large oil fields in the Middle East.
A new oil field was discovered on the seabed.
en.notes: 油田 is an oil field, an area where petroleum is produced. The word is built like 炭田 "coalfield" and ガス田 "gas field": 田 here means "field, deposit". Typical combinations are 油田を発見する／開発する and 海底油田 "offshore oil field". The extracted oil is 原油 "crude oil", petroleum in general is 石油.

examples[].german: The price of crude oil keeps rising.
Japan relies on imports for almost all of its crude oil.
Crude oil prices fell, and gasoline became a little cheaper.
en.notes: 原油 is unprocessed crude oil as it comes out of the ground; 原 here means "raw, original" as in 原料. Products such as ガソリン "gasoline" and 灯油 "kerosene, heating oil" are obtained from it; 石油 is the umbrella term "petroleum". Common in business news: 原油価格 "crude oil price", 原油高 "high oil price", 原油を輸入する.

examples[].german: The refueling hose doesn't reach the car.
Let's refuel at a gas station before getting on the expressway.
The plane landed at an airport along the way to refuel.
en.notes: 給油 is the "refueling, filling up" of cars, planes or ships and can be used as a する-verb: 給油する. The word sounds somewhat formal; in conversation people often say ガソリンを入れる. Typical are セルフ給油 "self-service refueling", 給油口 "fuel filler opening" and 給油所 (= ガソリンスタンド). A second meaning is oiling machines.

examples[].german: Tomorrow I'm scheduled to get up at 4.
I get up at six every morning and go jogging.
At the training camp, wake-up time and bedtime are fixed.
en.notes: 起床 is the formal word for "getting up (out of bed)"; in everyday speech people say 起きる. It appears in schedules, dormitories, hospitals and in the military: 起床時間 "wake-up time", 6時起床 "getting up at 6". The counterpart is 就寝 "going to bed". 起床 means getting up, whereas 目覚める or 目が覚める means merely waking up.

en.meaning: to be full of spirit; to be eager
examples[].german: The children ran off to the sea, joyful and full of spirit.
He set off for the match full of eagerness, but lost in the first round.
Announcing it when it hasn't been decided yet was a bit of a rash move.
en.notes: 勇む means "to be full of spirit, to be in high spirits" and is used almost only adverbially in the て-form: 勇んで出かける "to set off full of zeal", especially in the set phrase 喜び勇んで "joyfully and full of vigor". Other forms such as 勇む必要はない are hardly used. Related is the noun 勇み足 "overeagerness, rash step" (originally a sumo foul).

en.meaning: to get dark; to end (day, year)
examples[].german: If you don't hurry, it will get dark.
In winter it is already dark by around five o'clock.
I had lost my way and was at a loss.
en.notes: 暮れる means "to get dark" and almost always has 日 as its subject: 日が暮れる. The opposite is 夜が明ける "dawn breaks". Figuratively a year can also come to an end (年が暮れる); hence 暮れ "year-end" and 夕暮れ "dusk". The fixed expression 途方に暮れる means "to be at a loss". Do not confuse it with the verb くれる "to give", which is written in kana.

examples[].german: Nothing lasts forever.
When children's baby teeth fall out, permanent teeth grow in.
This membership card can be used permanently.
en.notes: 永久 means "eternity; eternal, permanent". It is used as a noun and adjectivally, most often adverbially as 永久に "forever" and attributively with の or in compounds: 永久歯 "permanent teeth", 永久保存 "permanent storage". Compared with 永遠 (more poetic and emotional, 永遠の愛), 永久 sounds more factual and technical. In everyday speech people often say ずっと or いつまでも.

examples[].german: Why is there a polar bear here?
As Arctic ice shrinks, the lives of polar bears are becoming endangered.
If you go to Kagoshima, be sure to try the shaved ice "Shirokuma".
en.notes: 白熊 is the everyday name for the polar bear and is often written in kana (シロクマ, しろくま); the zoological name is ホッキョクグマ "North Pole bear". In Kagoshima, 白熊 is also a famous shaved-ice specialty with condensed milk and fruit. 熊 on its own is the bear in general.

examples[].german: Let's chat for a bit later.
Please don't chat with the person next to you during class.
Please don't tell this secret to anyone.
en.notes: 喋る is colloquial for "to talk, to chat, to blab" and is usually written in kana as しゃべる. Unlike the neutral 話す, it stresses casual, often voluminous talking; with を it can also mean "to blab out": 秘密を喋る. Related are お喋り "chat; chatterbox" and お喋りな人. In formal situations 話す is used.

examples[].german: What is the inseam on those jeans?
To have my pants hemmed, I had the clerk measure my inseam.
He is tall and has a long inseam, so it's hard to find pants that fit.
en.notes: 股下 is the inseam or inside leg length, measured from the crotch to the hem; the word appears mainly with trouser sizes and alterations. Typical are 股下を測る "to measure the inseam" and figures like 股下75センチ. The counterpart 股上 denotes the rise of trousers. Shortening trousers is called 裾上げ.

examples[].german: I took a selfie with my smartphone.
At tourist spots, many people use selfie sticks.
I got so absorbed in taking selfies that I almost fell on the station stairs.
en.notes: 自撮り (from 自分 + 撮る, with voiced ど) is the colloquial word for "selfie" and can be used as a する-verb: 自撮りする. Well known is 自撮り棒 "selfie stick". The loanword セルフィー also exists but is rarer. When you have others take your picture, you say 写真を撮ってもらう instead.

examples[].german: In case of rain, the fireworks festival is canceled.
The marathon is held rain or shine, so it will take place even if it rains.
I reserved a tennis court with a roof that can be used even in rainy weather.
en.notes: 雨天 is the formal word for "rainy weather" and appears mainly in announcements and notices: 雨天中止 "canceled in case of rain", 雨天決行 "held even in the rain", 雨天順延 "postponed to the next day in case of rain", 雨天の場合は… The opposite is 晴天. In conversation people simply say 雨の日 or 雨だったら.

examples[].german: Professionals really are different from amateurs!
Even as an amateur, I can tell this painting is good.
It's dangerous for amateurs to do electrical work.
en.notes: 素人 ("layperson, amateur, non-specialist") has an irregular reading: しろうと. The opposite is 玄人 (くろうと) "expert, pro"; today people often say プロ instead. Typical are 素人の私でも "even I as a layperson", 素人目には "to the eye of a layperson" and 素人っぽい "amateurish". Colloquially, ド素人 "total beginner" is an intensified (derogatory) form.

en.meaning: to be profitable; to make a profit
examples[].german: That company seems to be making a lot of profit lately.
This business isn't as profitable as I thought.
I made 100,000 yen on stocks.
en.notes: 儲かる is intransitive: a business or a person "yields profit, makes a profit" - 店が儲かる, 株で儲かる. The transitive counterpart is 儲ける "to earn (money), to make a profit": お金を儲ける. 稼ぐ, by contrast, emphasizes earning through one's own work. Often written in kana もうかる; well known is the Osaka greeting 儲かりまっか "How's business?".

examples[].german: My father is a scholar of psychology.
That person is a famous scholar.
Scholars are divided in their opinions on this issue.
en.notes: 学者 refers to a scholar or scientist, especially one doing research at a university, in both the humanities and the natural sciences. Fields are formed with 〜学者: 経済学者, 言語学者, 心理学者. 研究者 "researcher" is more neutral and modern, while 科学者 means specifically natural scientists. 学者肌 describes someone with a scholarly, theoretical temperament.

examples[].german: It took time to get it to the correct angle.
Let's take a photo from this angle.
If you think about it from a different angle, you might find another answer.
en.notes: 角度 is the "angle" in the geometric sense - 角度を測る "to measure an angle", 30度の角度 - and also the viewing angle of a camera or of consideration. Figuratively, 別の角度から見る／考える means "to look at or think about from a different angle". Distinguish it from 角 (かど) "corner"; 視点 and 観点 refer more to a "standpoint".

examples[].german: The plane is flying at an altitude of ten thousand meters.
As you climb a mountain, the temperature drops as the altitude rises.
This job requires advanced specialized knowledge.
en.notes: 高度 has two meanings. As a technical word it is the height above sea level or flight altitude: 高度一万メートル, 高度を上げる / 下げる; for the height of a building or a person's height, by contrast, people say 高さ or 身長. As a な-adjective, 高度 means "high-level, sophisticated": 高度な技術, 高度な知識. Also well known is 高度経済成長, Japan's rapid economic growth after the war.

examples[].german: It is a temporary phenomenon.
Trains are temporarily stopped because of heavy rain.
Taking medicine makes the pain disappear for a while, but it comes back.
en.notes: 一時的 means "temporary, for a time"; as a na-adjective it takes な attributively (一時的な現象) and に adverbially (一時的に止まる). Typical in announcements and news: 一時的に運転を見合わせる, 一時的な措置. Opposite: 恒常的 or 永久的. The base word 一時 (いちじ) means "for a while, temporarily", but also "one o'clock"; only with 〜的 does it become the adjective.

examples[].german: It began to rain just before departure.
Right before the exam, I suddenly became anxious.
A child ran out right in front of the car.
en.notes: 直前 means "immediately before" in time and "directly in front of" in space. It follows a noun with の or the dictionary form: 出発の直前に, 寝る直前に. 直前になって emphasizes "only at the last minute", 直前のキャンセル is a last-minute cancellation. The opposite is 直後 "immediately after"; 寸前 "on the verge of" usually stands before something negative (倒れる寸前).

examples[].german: I can't accept such an expensive present.
I ate a high-class meal.
A new luxury hotel opened in front of the station.
en.notes: 高級 means "high-quality, luxurious, upscale" and is used as a な-adjective (高級な料理) or directly before nouns in set combinations: 高級車, 高級ホテル, 高級品, 高級住宅街. 高級感がある means "looks classy". Distinguish it from 高価 "expensive, of high price": 高級 emphasizes class and quality. Less often it means "high-ranking" as in 高級官僚.

examples[].german: Please tell me about higher education in your country.
"高校" is a shortened form of "高等学校".
That's quite an advanced technique.
en.notes: 高等 means "higher, of a higher level" and occurs mainly in set compounds: 高等学校 (short 高校) "high school", 高等教育 "higher education", 高等裁判所 "high court", 高等動物 "higher animals". As a な-adjective it is rarer and means "sophisticated, advanced", e.g. 高等なテクニック. Do not confuse it with 高級 "luxurious" and 高度 "highly developed" (高度な技術).

examples[].german: There was a debate about the state of Japanese language education.
In elementary school, I memorized a lot of kanji in Japanese class.
I looked up the words I didn't know in a Japanese dictionary.
en.notes: 国語 is generally the "national language", but in Japan it mainly means the school subject "Japanese" for native speakers: 国語の授業, 国語の先生. For Japanese as a foreign language, 日本語 is used instead (日本語教育 vs. 国語教育). 国語辞典 is a monolingual Japanese dictionary. For one's own mother tongue there are 母語 and 母国語.

en.meaning: the person himself/herself; the person in question
examples[].german: Please ask the person directly for the details.
The applicant's own signature is required for the application.
Please show your ID card so we can verify your identity.
en.notes: 本人 is "the person in question himself/herself", as opposed to relatives, representatives or third parties: 本人に聞く "to ask the person directly", 本人以外 "other than the person himself/herself". Very common is 本人確認 "identity verification"; in shops and on the phone the polite ご本人様 is used. Unlike 自分 ("I myself / oneself"), 本人 always refers to a specific person meant in the context.

examples[].german: The teacher asked each person a question.
We value each individual's opinion.
If each person is careful, accidents should decrease.
en.notes: 一人一人 (also written 一人ひとり) stresses "each individual" of a group as an individual: 一人一人の意見, 一人一人に配る. It often sounds appreciative, for example in speeches: 一人一人が気をつける. それぞれ "respectively" can also refer to things, 各自 is the formal "each for himself/herself", and 一人ずつ stresses the order "one by one".

examples[].german: Finally, please say a few words.
She said nothing and wrote just one word.
In a word, this movie is the best.
en.notes: 一言 means "a word, a few words, a brief remark". Common phrases: 一言で言うと／言えば "in a word, in short", 一言も話さない "not to say a single word", 一言お願いします "please say a few words" (a request for a short speech) and 一言多い "always to say one word too many". The reading is ひとこと; いちごん appears only in fixed expressions such as 一言一句.

examples[].german: On a trip, you have new encounters.
Meeting my teacher changed my life.
Spring is the season of meetings and partings.
en.notes: 出会い is the noun of 出会う "to meet (by chance), to get to know" and often means a meaningful encounter: 〜との出会い, 運命の出会い "fateful encounter", 出会いを大切にする. 出会いがない colloquially means "I'm not meeting anyone (a partner)". In a romantic context it is sometimes written 出逢い. 春は出会いと別れの季節 is a set saying.

examples[].german: Please write your address here.
I handed the completed form in at the reception desk.
Please be sure to write your name with a ballpoint pen.
en.notes: 記入 is the entering of information into forms, lists or diaries; as a transitive する-verb: 住所を用紙に記入する. Typical are ご記入ください, 記入例 "filling-in example", 記入漏れ "missing entry" and 記入欄 "field to fill in". 書く is generally "to write", 入力 refers to digital input, and 記載 to something being listed (formally) in documents.

examples[].german: I set a fixed study time for each day.
I study new words together with example sentences.
This robot learns by itself and gets smarter and smarter.
en.notes: 学習 is more matter-of-fact and formal than 勉強 and is often used in school, pedagogy and technology: 学習時間, 学習者 "learner", 学習塾 "cram school", 生涯学習 "lifelong learning". It can also refer to the learning of animals or machines: 機械学習 "machine learning". 勉強 stresses laborious cramming, and 習う learning from a teacher.

examples[].german: It is a chronic problem.
Overtime is a constant at this company.
Hospitals in rural areas continue to suffer from a chronic shortage of doctors.
en.notes: 恒常的 means "constant, permanent, chronic" - something exists not just temporarily but as a lasting state. As a na-adjective: 恒常的な人手不足, adverbially 恒常的に残業する. It is literary and formal and occurs mainly in reports, business and administration; in conversation people say いつも or ずっと. Opposite: 一時的.

examples[].german: My hobby is reading.
I read for about thirty minutes before going to bed.
The number of people who read books on the train has decreased.
en.notes: 読書 is reading books as an activity or hobby; as an intransitive する-verb it is 読書する or 読書をする. It does not take an object with を: one says 本を読む, not ×本を読書する. Typical are 趣味は読書です, 読書の秋 ("autumn as the reading season") and 読書家 ("avid reader"). For reading newspapers, e-mails or signs, only 読む is used.

examples[].german: I studied abroad in order to learn languages.
She is good at languages.
This job requires strong language skills.
en.notes: 語学 refers to learning or studying (foreign) languages as a subject or skill, not the language itself - that is 言語 or 〜語. Common are 語学が得意だ ("to be good at languages"), 語学力 ("language skills"), 語学留学 ("language study abroad") and 語学学校 ("language school"). The scientific study of language is nowadays usually called 言語学.

examples[].german: When you go out, please close the windows.
The person in charge is out at the moment.
On typhoon days, please refrain from going out.
en.notes: 外出 is leaving one's home or office to go somewhere; as an intransitive する-verb: 外出する. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 出かける and is typical in notices, phone calls and office life: 外出中 ("currently out"), 外出先 ("where one is while out"), 外出を控える ("to refrain from unnecessary outings"). In conversation among friends, 出かける is more common.

examples[].german: I'll cook dinner after I get home.
It looks like I'll be getting home late today.
I stopped by the supermarket on the way home.
en.notes: 帰宅 is the return to one's own home; as an intransitive する-verb: 帰宅する. It is more matter-of-fact than 帰る and often appears in the news, at school and at work: 帰宅時間, 帰宅途中 ("on the way home"), 帰宅が遅くなる. It means only returning home - for returning to one's home country 帰国 is used, and for traveling to one's hometown 帰省.

examples[].german: There is a community meeting next week.
We talked about the new plan at the meeting.
I felt unwell and couldn't attend yesterday's meeting.
en.notes: 会合 is an arranged meeting of several people for an exchange or consultation, for example of neighbors, clubs or representatives. It sounds more formal than 集まり; 会議, by contrast, is a meeting with a fixed agenda, especially in companies. Typical are 会合を開く ("to hold a meeting"), 会合に出席する/参加する and 会合で話し合う.

examples[].german: Lunch starts at twelve.
I talked with a colleague while having lunch.
The company pays for lunch during the training.
en.notes: 昼食 is lunch in a matter-of-fact, written style - typical of schedules, menus and hotels. In daily life people say 昼ご飯, and casually also お昼 or ランチ. 昼食をとる goes especially well with 昼食; there are also 昼食会 and 昼食代. The parallel words are 朝食 and 夕食.

examples[].german: Let's meet in front of the station at noon.
Reception is open until noon.
After noon, the temperature rose even more.
en.notes: 正午 refers to exactly 12:00 noon, the boundary between 午前 and 午後. 昼, by contrast, means roughly the midday period or the whole daytime. The word is rather formal and appears in announcements, deadlines and the news: 正午に, 正午まで, 正午過ぎ, 正午のニュース.

examples[].german: I am planning a long trip.
This problem needs to be considered from a long-term perspective.
In the long summer vacation, I'm going to Hokkaido with my family.
en.notes: 長期 means "a long period" and is mostly used attributively: 長期の計画, or directly in compounds such as 長期休暇, 長期入院, 長期滞在. Its counterpart is 短期, with 中期 in between. As an adjective, 長期的な/長期的に ("long-term") is used; the duration itself is 長期間 ("over a long time").

en.meaning: junior high school; lower secondary school
examples[].german: I studied English in junior high school.
I met a friend from junior high school for the first time in a long while.
My son entered junior high school this April.
en.notes: 中学 is the usual short form of 中学校, the three-year Japanese junior high school (roughly grades 7-9). In conversation people almost always say 中学: 中学に入る, 中学の時, 中学の友達; the students are 中学生, and the grades are 中学一年 (short: 中一). It comes after 小学校 and before 高校.

examples[].german: Most of the work is finished.
Most of the participants were students.
In this area, most shops are open on Sundays too.
en.notes: 大部分 refers to by far the largest part of a whole, mostly in the patterns 〜の大部分は/が or 大部分の + noun. It is somewhat more matter-of-fact than ほとんど, which is more common in everyday speech and also works as an adverb before verbs (ほとんど終わった). 大半 is close in meaning but tends to stress "more than half".

examples[].german: I was unavoidably absent.
Because it rained so hard, we had no choice but to cancel the match.
I missed the last train and had no choice but to go home by taxi.
en.notes: やむを得ず means "out of necessity, whether one likes it or not" - one does something unwillingly because there is no other option. It consists of 止む "to stop" and the classical negative 得ず, literally something like "without being able to stop". It stands adverbially before the verb and sounds formal, often in apologies and notices: やむを得ず中止する. Related is the adjective form やむを得ない "unavoidable" (やむを得ない事情); colloquially one says しかたなく.

examples[].german: I spent most of my day off reading.
Most of the seats in the hall are already filled.
Most of my salary disappears into rent.
en.notes: 大半 literally means "big half", i.e. more than half up to almost all: 〜の大半, 大半が/は, 大半を占める "to make up the majority". It is somewhat more written in style than ほとんど and is close to 大部分, which tends to stress "almost all". As an adverb ("for the most part"), 大半 is rarer and rather written.

examples[].german: The two documents bear the same number.
I didn't realize it was the same person.
I conducted the experiment once more under the same conditions.
en.notes: 同一 means "one and the same, identical" and is the formal, written counterpart of 同じ. It usually appears as 同一の before a noun or in fixed combinations such as 同一人物 "the same person" and 同一視する "to equate". It is typical in forms, rules, science and the news; in conversation people say 同じ.

examples[].german: Rain is unfavorable for this team.
He didn't give up even under unfavorable conditions.
Is it a disadvantage in job hunting if you have no experience?
en.notes: 不利 is a な-adjective (also a noun) for an unfavorable, disadvantageous position in a competition or a decision; the opposite is 有利. Typical are 〜に不利だ "disadvantageous for someone", 不利になる, 不利な条件/立場. Not to be confused with 不便 "inconvenient": 不利 concerns chances and prospects of success.

examples[].german: The sun set beyond the horizon.
On a wide plain, you can see all the way to the horizon.
On a desert morning, the sun rose from the horizon.
en.notes: 地平線 is the horizon line where land and sky seem to touch. Over the sea, 水平線 is used. Typical are 地平線の向こう, 地平線まで続く "to stretch to the horizon" and 地平線から日が昇る/地平線に沈む. The word sounds somewhat descriptive and literary and suits wide plains, deserts and steppes.

examples[].german: Education is an important role of the state.
I learned about the relationship between the state and the individual.
My older sister passed the national exam and became a nurse.
en.notes: 国家 is the state as a political organization with a government and laws; in daily life, "country" is simply 国. It often appears in matter-of-fact compounds: 国家試験 "state examination", 国家公務員 "national civil servant", 国家予算 "national budget". For the population of a country, 国民 is used.

examples[].german: I tried every possible method.
People of all ages can take part.
This shop sells every kind of tea.
en.notes: あらゆる is a prenominal word (連体詞): it always stands directly before a noun, never with の and never as a predicate. It stresses "every conceivable kind of" and sounds more emphatic than すべての: あらゆる方法, あらゆる手段, あらゆる角度から. It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: This is not a mere mistake.
At first it was just a hobby.
That is nothing more than a rumor, so don't worry about it.
en.notes: 単なる is a prenominal word (連体詞) and stands directly before a noun: 単なる偶然, 単なるうわさ, 単なる間違い. It is often followed by 〜にすぎない "is nothing more than", or negated (単なる〜ではない). In daily speech the more casual ただの is used instead; the corresponding adverb is 単に "merely".

en.meaning: a kind of; a sort of
examples[].german: This is a kind of herb.
I think reading is also a kind of journey.
This tea has a certain unique fragrance.
en.notes: 一種 has two typical patterns: 〜の一種 assigns something to a group ("a kind of, a type of"), while 一種の + noun serves as a cautious paraphrase ("a sort of ..., in a way a ..."). There is also the set phrase 一種独特の "quite peculiar". For "kind, sort" as a counter, 種類 is used instead (三種類).

examples[].german: The whole family moved to the countryside.
The whole family runs that shop.
At New Year, the whole family gathers at my grandfather's house.
en.notes: 一家 is the whole family as a unit, or the household; it sounds somewhat more formal than 家族. Typical are 一家で "as a whole family", 一家そろって "the whole family together", 一家の主 "head of the family" and surname + 一家 (田中さん一家). With the names of groups, 〜一家 can also refer to a yakuza family.

en.meaning: any moment now; at any moment
examples[].german: It looks like it could rain at any moment.
The child looked about to burst into tears.
We crossed an old bridge that looked as if it might collapse at any moment.
en.notes: 今にも describes that something appears to be imminent, and it almost always occurs with 〜そうだ or 〜ばかりに: 今にも雨が降りそうだ, 今にも泣き出しそうな顔. It does not express intention – for "I'm going soon" one says すぐ行く or もうすぐ, not ×今にも行く. It is often about something threatening or emotionally charged.

examples[].german: Please wait a moment.
I add a little salt.
Excuse me, could I take a moment of your time?
en.notes: 少々 means "a little" or "a moment" and is the polite, formal equivalent of 少し or the casual ちょっと. The fixed phrase 少々お待ちください is very common in customer service and on the phone. In recipes, 塩少々 stands for "a pinch of salt"; 少々お時間をいただけますか is also typical of polite requests.

en.meaning: not at all; not a bit
examples[].german: I couldn't sleep at all last night.
Even after hearing the explanation, I don't understand at all.
Even after the long journey, he showed no sign of being tired.
en.notes: 少しも is always used with a negative and means "not a bit, not at all": 少しも〜ない. It is neutral to slightly formal; colloquially people say ちっとも, and quite generally also 全然 or 全く. Without a negative it is ungrammatical - for "a little" only 少し is used.

examples[].german: Please store food in a cool place.
This store also sells foreign foods.
On busy days I often use frozen food.
en.notes: 食品 is the factual collective term for food as products – typical in retail, on labels and in the news. In everyday speech one says 食べ物; 食料, by contrast, emphasizes food as a supply. Common compounds are 冷凍食品 ("frozen food"), 食品売り場 ("food department"), 健康食品 and 食品ロス ("food waste").

examples[].german: Old books remain in the library.
Through books, we can learn about life in the past.
Lots of difficult books are lined up in my grandfather's room.
en.notes: 書物 is an elevated, rather literary word for "book", especially for old, valuable or scholarly works. In daily life people say 本; 書籍 is the matter-of-fact term from publishing and the book trade. Typical are 古い書物, 書物を読む, 書物を通して "through books".

examples[].german: The temperature dropped sharply.
It is difficult to cope with abrupt changes.
Recently, the population of this town has been increasing rapidly.
en.notes: 急激 is a な-adjective for a change that is both sudden and strong: 急激に増える/減る/下がる, 急激な変化. It is used especially with numbers and developments such as temperature, prices or population. 急 is more general ("sudden"), 急速 stresses high speed, and 突然 only the unexpectedness of an event.

examples[].german: First, let's check the current situation.
Under the present circumstances, we need to change the plan.
He is not satisfied with his current salary and wants to change his situation.
en.notes: 現状 is the present state of a thing or situation, often in work, politics and the news. Typical are 現状を把握する "to grasp the situation", 現状に満足する, 現状維持 "maintaining the status quo" and 現状では "under the present circumstances". 状況 stresses more a developing situation, and 現在 only the point in time "now".

examples[].german: I heard the experts' views on this issue.
The two of them hold very different views.
The company announced its official position on the accident.
en.notes: 見解 is a considered, reasoned view, especially of experts, authorities or organizations. It is more formal than 意見 "opinion" and even more so than 考え. Typical are 見解を述べる/示す/発表する, 見解が分かれる "opinions are divided", 見解が一致する and 公式の見解 "official statement".

examples[].german: I picked three candidates for the travel destination.
He is a candidate for the next department head.
This team is a favorite to win the championship this year.
en.notes: 候補 is a person or thing that comes into question for an election or selection: 〜の候補, 候補に挙がる "to come into consideration", 候補に入れる. In elections 候補者 is mostly used, and "to run as a candidate" is 立候補する. In sports, 優勝候補 is the title favorite; travel destinations, dates or names can also be 候補.

examples[].german: I used my senior's opinion as a reference.
This material is helpful.
For your reference, I will also send you the materials from last year's presentation.
en.notes: 参考 is something you consult for orientation or as a point of reference. The main patterns are 〜を参考にする "to take something as a guide" and 〜が参考になる "to be helpful, informative"; politely and casually one says 参考までに "just for your information". Compounds are 参考書 "study guide, reference book" and 参考資料.

examples[].german: The situation was more serious than expected.
I will contact you if the situation changes.
Let's prepare early so that the worst doesn't happen.
en.notes: 事態 is a (mostly serious or escalating) state of affairs, especially in the news, politics and business: 事態が悪化する "the situation worsens", 最悪の事態, 緊急事態 "state of emergency", 事態を見守る. 状況 is more neutral and general; 状態 describes the condition of a person or thing (体の状態).

examples[].german: It looks easy at first glance, but it's difficult.
It looks like a quiet town at first glance, but it is very lively at night.
He looks scary at first glance, but he is actually a very kind person.
en.notes: 一見 (いっけん) as an adverb means "at first glance, apparently" and usually announces a contrast: 一見〜だが、実は…. As a noun or する-verb it means "a quick look, to glance at" - known from the proverb 百聞は一見にしかず "seeing once is better than hearing a hundred times". Not to be confused with 一見 in the reading いちげん "first-time customer without an introduction" (一見さんお断り).

examples[].german: The time has come to carry out the plan.
It is important not only to talk but to act.
When you press this button, the program is executed.
en.notes: 実行 means to actually put a plan or resolution into practice; as a transitive する-verb: 計画を実行する, passive 実行される. Typical are 実行に移す "to put into action" and 実行力 "ability to act". 実施 sounds more official (carrying out exams, measures), and 実現 means realizing a goal or dream. In IT, 実行 means "to run" (a program).

examples[].german: Actually, I'm going to be moving next month.
To be honest, I've already seen that movie.
Actually, I have a small favor to ask...
en.notes: 実は introduces information that the other person doesn't know yet: a confession, a surprise or a request ("I have to tell you something..."). Very typical is 実は、お願いがあるんですが… as a preparation for a request. 本当は, by contrast, stresses the contrast with reality ("actually I wanted to..."), and 実際 means "in practice, in fact".

examples[].german: I noticed a serious mistake.
This is an important decision that concerns the future.
I hear the president is going to make a major announcement to everyone.
en.notes: 重大 is a な-adjective for things with serious consequences: 重大な問題, 重大なミス, 重大な責任, 重大な決定. It stresses the weight of the consequences and often sounds serious or threatening. 重要, by contrast, is neutral "important" (重要な会議), while 深刻 describes a serious, worrying situation.

examples[].german: The work is progressing smoothly.
So far, the preparations are going well.
After the surgery, my father's recovery is going well.
en.notes: 順調 is a な-adjective for a problem-free course that goes as planned: 順調に進む/いく, 準備は順調だ, 順調な回復. It suits work, projects, recovery and business. Similar is スムーズ, which stresses the smoothness of a process; 予定通り means only "as planned".

examples[].german: The official reply will arrive next week.
The new name has been officially decided.
Please write the company's official name on the document.
en.notes: 正式 means "official, formally correct", i.e. in accordance with the prescribed procedure: 正式な返事, 正式に決まる/発表する, 正式名称 "full, official name". The opposite is 非公式 or 略式 "simplified". 公式 is close in meaning but tends to refer to what has been made public (公式サイト, 公式発表).

examples[].german: We chose the class representative.
I gave a greeting on behalf of the company.
Sushi is one of the dishes that represent Japan.
en.notes: 代表 is a representative or a representation; 〜を代表して means "on behalf of" (used as a transitive する-verb). The second important meaning: 〜を代表する + noun or 代表的な "typical, representative of", for example 日本を代表する料理. Other forms are 代表者, 代表選手 and 日本代表 "the national team".

examples[].german: There is a big park in the center of town.
I am studying Japanese with a focus on conversation.
She is always at the center of the class's conversation.
en.notes: 中心 is the central point in both the spatial and the figurative sense: 町の中心, 円の中心, 話題の中心. Very common is 〜を中心に(して) "centering on, around", plus 中心となる and the suffix 〜中心 (家族中心の生活). 真ん中 is the everyday word for the physical middle, while 中央 sounds more official (中央駅).

examples[].german: I wrote the events of the day in my diary.
I still remember that event today.
What was the happiest event of last year for you?
en.notes: 出来事 is something that has happened – neutral as to whether it is big or small, good or bad; often also written in kana, できごと. Typical are 今日の出来事, 不思議な出来事, 一番うれしかった出来事. 事件, by contrast, means an incident or crime, 事故 an accident, and 行事 and イベント a planned event.

examples[].german: Please answer the following questions.
I can't answer that question easily.
In class, we thought about the question "What is happiness?"
en.notes: 問い is a question in a written or reflective sense: exam questions (次の問いに答えなさい) or fundamental questions (〜という問い). For a question you ask a person, everyday speech uses 質問; 問題 is a problem to solve or an issue. The related verb is 問う "to ask, to question".

en.meaning: per year; a period of years
examples[].german: I read about a hundred books a year.
I lived in Japan for three years.
Many tourists come to this town throughout the year.
en.notes: 年間 has two uses: Alone before numbers or nouns it means "yearly, per year" (年間百冊, 年間計画, 年間を通して "all year round"). After a number, 〜年間 gives a duration: 三年間 "for three years", as opposed to 三年 as a mere year count. With eras, it stands for "during the period" (明治年間).

examples[].german: In short, you're against it?
I explained a lot, but in short, we don't have enough time.
In short, I just have to get all of this done by tomorrow, right?
en.notes: 要するに means "in short, in a word, basically" and sums up or boils down what came before, often with 〜ということだ at the end of the sentence. When used to sum up someone else's words ("So what you're saying is ..."), it can come across as impatient or blunt. Related: つまり (more neutral, also used to clarify) and 簡単に言うと (friendlier). It comes from 要する "to grasp the essentials".

examples[].german: This building was built in the 1980s.
People of a wide range of ages gathered.
I arranged the photos in chronological order and made an album.
en.notes: 年代 refers to a period of time. With a year number it stands for a decade: 1990年代 "the 1990s", 八十年代の音楽. For people, it means the age group: 同じ年代の人, 幅広い年代 - similar to 世代 "generation", which however stresses a shared formative background more. For historical eras such as the Edo period, 時代 is used. Set phrases are 年代順 "in chronological order" and 年代物 "old, valuable item".

examples[].german: Please write today's date on the document.
I got the date wrong by one day.
The work dragged on, and I got home around the time the date changed.
en.notes: 日付 is the calendar date, for example on documents, letters or receipts: 日付を書く/入れる, 日付順 "sorted by date". 日付が変わる means "to pass midnight". For the number of days or an appointed day, 日にち or 日数 is more common; it is sometimes written 日付け.

examples[].german: I wiped the surface of the desk clean.
You can't tell the real problem from the surface alone.
Those two seem to get along well on the surface.
en.notes: 表面 is the surface or outer side of an object (机の表面, 月の表面) and, figuratively, the outward appearance. Common are 表面上 "outwardly", 表面的な "superficial" and 表面化する "to come to the surface". The opposite is 内面, or 裏面 for paper; 表 refers more to the front side.

examples[].german: He is a trustworthy person.
I will introduce the characters who appear in the story.
Who is the person in the middle of this photo?
en.notes: 人物 is a person seen in terms of their role, importance or character; it sounds more matter-of-fact than 人. Typical are 登場人物 "characters in a story", 重要人物, 危険人物 and 写真の人物. As an evaluation, 〜な人物だ means "to be a ... kind of person"; 人間, by contrast, stresses the human being as a creature.

examples[].german: I spotted my friend at the station.
I was moved by the sight of the child studying so hard.
There were many people in kimono at the festival.
en.notes: 姿 is the visible figure or appearance, especially of people: 姿を見せる/現す ("to appear"), 姿を消す ("to disappear"), 姿が見えない, 後ろ姿 ("view from behind"). As a suffix, 〜姿 describes clothing: 着物姿, 制服姿. 形, by contrast, is the shape of objects, and 格好 is more one's get-up and clothing.

examples[].german: There is a price difference between the two products.
If you keep practicing, it will make a difference.
Yesterday's match was lost by one point.
en.notes: 差 is a measurable or clearly recognizable difference, often in numbers: 差がある, 差が出る/つく "to make a difference", 差が縮まる/開く "the gap narrows/widens", 〜点差で "by a margin of ... points". 違い is more general and refers to any kind of difference. Compounds are 時差 "time difference" and 温度差.

examples[].german: Please check the amount to be paid.
The amount turned out larger than expected.
The amount on the receipt was wrong, so I told the clerk.
en.notes: 金額 is a concrete sum of money, such as on bills, receipts or contracts: 金額を確認する, 金額が大きい, 合計金額 ("total amount"). 値段 is the price of a product, 料金 a fee for services, and 代金 the purchase price to be paid. お金 is the general word for money.

examples[].german: Taste preferences differ from person to person.
I chose clothes that suit my taste.
Please add lemon to your liking before eating.
en.notes: 好み is the noun of 好む and refers to preferences and taste: 〜の好み, 好みに合う "to suit someone's taste", 好みのタイプ "my type", 好みがうるさい "to be picky". Polite is お好みで "as you like", also known from お好み焼き. To state that you like something, 好きだ is otherwise used.

examples[].german: Please follow the school rules.
The rule here is to take off your shoes.
Taking a family walk on Sunday morning is our family's custom.
en.notes: 決まり is the noun of 決まる and refers to rules or fixed habits in daily life: 決まりを守る/破る, 〜する決まりだ "it is the rule that ...". It sounds more everyday than 規則; ルール is similarly casual. お決まりの means "usual, as always"; the phrase 決まりが悪い means "to feel embarrassed".

examples[].german: I maintain my health.
Maintaining an old house costs money.
This team has maintained first place for three years.
en.notes: 維持する is transitive and means to keep a state unchanged or to keep something in good repair: 健康・平和・体重・品質を維持する. Fixed words are 現状維持 "status quo" and 維持費 "maintenance costs". The Japanese verb 保つ is very similar but sounds more everyday (清潔を保つ). 続ける, by contrast, means to continue an action, not to preserve a state.

examples[].german: The test result is normal, that is, there is no problem.
He is my mother's younger brother, that is, my uncle.
My grandfather was born in 1945, that is, in the year the war ended.
en.notes: すなわち means "that is, namely" and equates two expressions, the second explaining or naming the first more precisely: A、すなわちB. It is literary and formal (specialist texts, speeches, reports); in conversation people usually say つまり. Grammatically it is a conjunction and does not stand alone at the start of a conversation but needs a preceding expression. It is almost always written in kana (kanji: 即ち).

examples[].german: I have a habit of touching my hair when I get nervous.
I want to fix my habit of speaking fast.
Once you eat this snack, you get hooked.
en.notes: 癖 is a mostly unconscious and often unwanted habit or quirk: 〜する癖がある, 癖を直す, 癖がつく, 口癖 "favorite phrase", 寝癖 "hair sticking up from sleep". 習慣, by contrast, is a conscious, neutral to positive habit. 癖になる means "to become addictive, to be unable to quit"; the word is often written in kana as くせ.

examples[].german: Let's help each other.
It is important to respect each other's opinions.
It's the same for both of us when we're in trouble, so please don't worry about it.
en.notes: お互い refers to "each other" or "both sides". As an adverb it usually appears as お互いに before a verb, often together with 〜合う: お互いに助け合う, お互いに話し合う. Before nouns it is お互いの: お互いの気持ち, お互いの意見. The set phrase お互い様 means "we're in the same boat, it's only natural". The form without お, 互いに, sounds more literary.

examples[].german: I felt sorry after hearing his story.
You came all this way and couldn't meet him - that was unfortunate for you.
I made a donation for the poor family who lost their home in a fire.
en.notes: 気の毒 is a な-adjective expressing sympathy for the misfortune of others: 気の毒な人, 気の毒に思う "to feel sorry for someone". To those affected, one politely says お気の毒に or それはお気の毒でしたね. Unlike かわいそう, which is more emotional and often used for children or animals, 気の毒 sounds more adult and distanced. 気の毒なことをした also means "I caused him trouble, and I'm sorry".

examples[].german: The dark road felt creepy.
A sound came from the empty house, and I got creeped out.
I thought it served him right when he, who had always laughed at others, failed.
en.notes: 気味 (きみ) means "feeling, sensation" and appears almost only in set phrases. Most common is 気味が悪い "eerie, creepy" (intensified: 不気味). Not to be confused with 気持ちが悪い, which tends to mean "disgusting" or "I feel sick". いい気味だ means, gloatingly, "serves him right". As a suffix, 〜気味 is read ぎみ and expresses a touch of something: 風邪気味 "slightly under the weather with a cold", 疲れ気味.

examples[].german: I received good news from a friend.
I am waiting for detailed information.
Maybe it was a premonition, but I suddenly wanted to call my grandmother.
en.notes: 知らせ is the noun of 知らせる "to notify" and means a piece of news that is passed on to someone: 知らせが届く, 知らせが入る, 知らせを受ける. It often comes with an evaluation: うれしい知らせ, 悲しい知らせ. The polite form お知らせ is used for official notices and announcements. Unlike ニュース (media reports), it concerns personal news. 虫の知らせ means "a premonition".

examples[].german: My long-held wish came true.
Everyone's wish is for their family's health.
Actually, I have a favor to ask...
en.notes: 願い is a wish or a request, the noun of 願う. Typical are 願いがかなう "a wish comes true", 願いをかなえる "to grant a wish" and 願いを込める "to put a wish into something". As a request to others, the polite form お願い is almost always used: お願いがあります. Compared with 希望 (more matter-of-fact, also "preference") and 望み (also "prospect, chance"), 願い sounds more personal and heartfelt.

examples[].german: I keep up moderate exercise for my health.
Please take breaks at appropriate intervals during work.
Let's enjoy alcohol in moderation.
en.notes: 適度 is a な-adjective for "the right measure, neither too much nor too little": 適度な運動, 適度な湿度, adverbially 適度に休む. It sounds matter-of-fact and often appears in health tips and instructions. The opposite is 過度 "excessive". Not to be confused with 適当, which also means "suitable" but colloquially often means "careless, half-hearted". In daily speech, ちょうどいい is also simply used.

examples[].german: This dish takes a lot of effort.
Using a tool saves you the trouble.
I'm sorry to trouble you when you're so busy.
en.notes: 手間 is the amount of time and effort something takes. Typical: 手間がかかる "to be laborious", 手間が省ける / 手間を省く "to save oneself work". 手間をかける means "to invest effort", but also "to cause someone trouble"; politely one apologizes with お手間を取らせてすみません. The verb 手間取る "to take longer than expected" is derived from it. 面倒 stresses more the annoying feeling, while 手間 is the objective effort.

examples[].german: The flow of this river is fast.
I will explain the flow of the work.
In line with the trends of the times, the way the shop does things has also changed.
en.notes: 流れ is the noun of 流れる and first means the current of water or air: 流れが速い, 川の流れ. Figuratively it stands for the course of a process (仕事の流れ, 話の流れ "flow of conversation") and for developments and trends (時代の流れ). 流れに乗る means "to go with the flow, to ride the momentum". For fashion trends in the narrower sense, 流行 is used instead.

examples[].german: The width of this road is three meters.
I want to broaden the range of my knowledge through reading.
This shop's wines come in a wide range of prices.
en.notes: 幅 is first the measurable width: 道の幅, 横幅, 幅が広い / 狭い. Figuratively it refers to range or leeway: 知識の幅を広げる, 値段の幅 "price range", 選択の幅 "range of choices". With 大 it forms 大幅 "drastic, considerable": 大幅に値上がりする. 広さ, by contrast, is an area, while 幅 is only the extent from side to side.

en.meaning: by and large; on the whole
examples[].german: I largely agree.
Tomorrow will be mostly sunny.
The project is progressing largely as planned.
en.notes: 概ね (usually in kana おおむね) means "by and large, mostly": something holds for the most part, with minor exceptions. It stands adverbially before a verb or adjective: おおむね良好, おおむね賛成. It sounds factual and formal (reports, weather forecasts, business language); in conversation people say だいたい or ほとんど instead. As a noun it rarely means "gist, main content".

examples[].german: The standard of living in this region is high.
We keep the quality of our products at a certain standard.
The research at this university is at a high level even by world standards.
en.notes: 水準 is a matter-of-fact, rather written word for "level, standard": 生活水準, 教育水準, 高い水準. Typical combinations are 水準が高い / 低い, 水準に達する "to reach the level" and 一定の水準に保つ. In conversation people mostly say レベル. Not to be confused with 基準, which refers to a yardstick or criterion by which something is measured.
