examples[].german: Between the train and the bus, I'd choose the former.
Of the two proposals, the former costs less.
In the meeting, opinions for a price increase and a price decrease came up, but I agree with the former.
en.notes: 前者 means "the former" and refers to the first of exactly two previously mentioned things or persons; its counterpart is 後者 "the latter". Both often appear in one sentence: 前者は…、後者は…. The word is matter-of-fact to written and typical of comparisons, discussions and reports. With more than two possibilities, 最初の is used instead.

examples[].german: I talked with my family about the future.
Let's all discuss the problem together.
Instead of fighting, you'd better talk it over properly.
en.notes: 話し合う is composed of 話す and 〜合う "mutually": you discuss something together in order to reach agreement. The partner is marked by と, the topic by を or について: 家族と将来について話し合う. The noun 話し合い means "discussion, talk". Unlike 相談する (asking someone for advice) and the more formal 議論する (to debate), 話し合う stresses an exchange between equals.

examples[].german: I finished my homework before going out.
I kept lunch simple.
Please go upstairs after you have paid at the register.
en.notes: 済ませる is transitive: you bring something to an end or get it done (宿題を済ませる, 支払いを済ませる, 用事を済ませる). The intransitive counterpart is 済む "to be done"; there is also the equivalent godan variant 済ます. With 簡単に, 安く or 〜で, it also means "to make do, to get by with little": 昼食をパンで済ませる. Compared with 終える, it stresses that an obligation has been ticked off.

en.meaning: to take up; to adopt; to take away
examples[].german: We took up environmental issues in class.
It was dangerous, so I took the scissors away from the child.
That incident was also covered prominently in the newspapers.
en.notes: 取り上げる has several meanings, which the context clarifies: to take up a topic (授業で問題を取り上げる), to accept a proposal (意見を取り上げる), to report on something in the media (新聞に取り上げられる, often in the passive) and to take something away from someone (子供からはさみを取り上げる). The person something is taken from is marked with から. Compared with 奪う "to rob", the taking away here suggests authority, for example by parents or teachers.

examples[].german: My mother smiled without saying anything.
The two of them are smiling in the photo.
When our eyes met, the baby gave a big smile.
en.notes: 微笑む is intransitive and means "to smile softly", without audible laughter. 笑う is more general and also includes laughing out loud. The person one smiles at is marked with に: 〜に微笑みかける. The noun is 微笑み "smile". The word sounds somewhat elevated and narrative; in daily life people often say にっこりする or にこにこする. In newspapers you also see ほほ笑む.

en.meaning: all at once; at the same time
examples[].german: You don't need to memorize everything at once.
The dishes we ordered were all brought out at once.
This elevator can carry up to ten people at a time.
en.notes: 一度に means "at once, in one go": several things happen together instead of one after another. Not to be confused with 一度 "once" (一度行ったことがある). 一気に, by contrast, stresses momentum and speed ("in one breath"), and 同時に exact simultaneity. 一度に often appears with quantities: 一度に十人まで, 一度にたくさん.

examples[].german: I started a company together with a friend.
Both of the methods are useful.
Along with the times, words also change.
en.notes: 共に is the more formal equivalent of 一緒に: 〜と共に "together with". In the form AとBは共に it means "both". After nouns or verbs, 〜と共に also expresses a parallel development: 時代と共に "with the times". In everyday speech it sounds stiff; in speeches, articles and grammar it is often written in kana as ともに.

examples[].german: Please eat plenty of vegetables.
We have plenty of time before departure.
I walked a full hour from the station.
en.notes: たっぷり means "plenty, more than enough" and is used for quantities, time and liquids: たっぷり食べる, 時間がたっぷりある, before nouns たっぷりの + noun. As a suffix it intensifies qualities: 自信たっぷり, 愛情たっぷり. Before numbers it means "a good, a full" (たっぷり一時間), and たっぷりした服 is loose-fitting clothing. Compared with 十分, it sounds more generous; compared with いっぱい, it is somewhat less colloquial.

examples[].german: Would you like something to drink?
If there are any problems, please let me know.
Is there anything you want for your birthday?
en.notes: 何か means "something, anything" and stands for an unspecified thing; the particles が and を often drop after it: 何か飲みますか. Do not confuse it with 何が "what?" as a real question word. Questions with 何か are first answered with yes or no. 何か can stand directly before a noun (何か質問, 何か飲み物). The negative is 何も…ない "nothing"; colloquially 何か becomes なんか.

examples[].german: Sales have increased substantially.
Trains are considerably delayed because of an accident.
We changed our travel plans drastically.
en.notes: 大幅に means "considerably, markedly, on a large scale" and is the adverbial form of the na-adjective 大幅 (literally "large width"). It typically goes with changes in numbers, plans or times: 大幅に増える／減る, 大幅に遅れる, 大幅に変更する; attributively it is 大幅な値下げ. It sounds factual (news, business). かなり or ずいぶん also mean "quite, very", but are not limited to changes.

examples[].german: Ask about anything you don't understand.
My younger brother eats anything.
Apparently that shop is going to close next month.
en.notes: 何でも means "everything, no matter what" and takes an affirmative verb: 何でも食べる. The counterpart 何も takes a negative ("nothing"). 何でもない means "it's nothing, no big deal". At the beginning of a sentence, 何でも also means "apparently, I hear" and is combined with 〜そうだ or 〜らしい. It is often written in kana, なんでも.

examples[].german: I pay for my own share.
I also made some for tomorrow.
At the hospital I got three days' worth of medicine.
en.notes: 分 (ぶん) is the share or portion that falls to someone or serves a purpose: 自分の分, 明日の分. As a suffix after quantities it means "enough for ...": 三人分, 三日分の薬. Other expressions are その分 "to that extent, correspondingly" and この分では "if things go on like this". Do not confuse it with 分 (ふん/ぷん) "minute" and with 部分 "part of a whole".

examples[].german: Please look at the following figure.
It is easy to understand if you explain using a diagram.
Could you draw me a map of the way to the station?
en.notes: 図 (ず) is an explanatory representation: figure, sketch, diagram. In textbooks and reports one reads 図1, 次の図, 図のように. Typical verbs are 図を見る, 図にかく and 図で示す. 絵, by contrast, is a picture of an artistic nature, and グラフ specifically a chart with data. 図 is also in 地図, 図形 and 図書館.

examples[].german: Please make three short sentences.
I don't understand the meaning of this sentence.
The last sentence of the e-mail sounds a bit rude.
en.notes: 文 (ぶん) is a single sentence in the grammatical sense: 文を作る, 文を書く, この文の意味. A coherent text of several sentences is a 文章, and an essay is a 作文. Many compounds contain 文: 例文 "example sentence", 文法 "grammar". In 文句 and 注文 the character is read もん. 言葉, by contrast, means "word" or language in general.

examples[].german: Please mark the correct answer.
The red mark shows the location of the entrance.
This is just a token of my gratitude.
en.notes: 印 (しるし) is a sign or mark: 印を付ける "to mark, to tick", 目印 "landmark", 矢印 "arrow". Figuratively it is a token of affection or thanks: 感謝の印, お礼の印; in this meaning it is often written in kana as しるし. Read as いん, 印 means "stamp, seal" (印鑑).

examples[].german: This fish can be eaten raw.
Please wash the raw vegetables well.
I heard my favorite singer's song live for the first time.
en.notes: 生 (なま) means "raw, uncooked" and in general "unprocessed, direct". Adverbially it appears as 生で (生で食べる, 生で聞く "to hear live"), before nouns as 生の or as a prefix: 生卵, 生ビール "draft beer", 生放送 "live broadcast", 生クリーム. 新鮮, by contrast, means "fresh" in the sense of not old. Other readings have other meanings, for example せい in 生活 or う in 生まれる.

examples[].german: There are footprints in the snow.
A ring from the glass remained on the desk.
This is the site of an old castle.
en.notes: 跡 (あと) is a visible trace that something has left behind: 足の跡 or 足跡 "footprint", 傷跡 "scar", コップの跡. It also refers to the site or remains of something past: 城跡 "castle ruins". Typical verbs are 跡が残る and 跡を残す. Not to be confused with the identically read 後 "after, later".

examples[].german: There is a hole in my sock.
I dug a hole to plant a tree.
Everyone is filling the gap left by Mr. Tanaka's resignation.
en.notes: 穴 is a hole or pit. Note the verb pair: 穴が開く "a hole appears" (intransitive) and 穴を開ける "to make a hole" (transitive); in the ground it is 穴を掘る. Figuratively 穴 refers to a gap, for example due to lack of staff or money: 穴を埋める "to fill the gap". 穴場 is a "hidden gem" that hardly anyone knows.

examples[].german: The waves are high today.
I fell asleep listening to the sound of the waves.
His mood fluctuates, so it is hard to find the right moment to talk to him.
en.notes: 波 is a wave on water: 波が高い / 荒い / 静か, 波の音. Figuratively it stands for fluctuations and movements: 気分に波がある "to be moody", 人の波 "stream of people", 時代の波. 波に乗る means "to ride the wave", that is, to take advantage of a trend. As a component it appears in 寒波 "cold wave" and 電波 "radio waves, reception".

examples[].german: Skin dries out easily in winter.
These clothes are gentle on the skin.
I went there and felt the cultural differences firsthand.
en.notes: 肌 is skin as a surface, especially in connection with care, appearance and sensation: 肌が乾燥する, 肌が荒れる, 肌に優しい. 皮膚 is the matter-of-fact, medical term, and 皮 the skin of animals or the peel of fruit. Figuratively 肌で感じる means "to experience firsthand", and 肌が合う "to get along well with someone". Related is 肌寒い "chilly, cool".

examples[].german: Viewed relatively, it is good.
Rents in this town are relatively cheap compared to Tokyo.
School grades are determined by relative evaluation.
en.notes: 相対的 means "relative, in proportion" - something is judged in comparison with other things, not on its own. As a na-adjective: 相対的な評価 "relative evaluation"; adverbially: 相対的に見ると "comparatively speaking", 相対的に安い "relatively cheap". The opposite is 絶対的. The word is factual and literary; in conversation one often says 比較的 or 〜と比べると.

examples[].german: Please wipe the screen with a soft cloth.
I made a bag out of this cloth.
A white cloth is laid over the desk.
en.notes: 布 is fabric as a material or a piece of cloth: 布で拭く, 布で作る, 布をかける. Something "made of fabric" is 布製. For yard goods used for sewing, 生地 is also used; specific cloths have their own words such as タオル, ハンカチ or 雑巾 "cleaning rag". In contrast to 紙 or ビニール, 布 stresses woven textile.

examples[].german: I collect empty bottles.
I put jam into a jar to preserve it.
Could you open the beer bottle for me?
en.notes: 瓶 is a container made of glass: a bottle (ビールの瓶, 瓶ビール) and also a screw-top jar (ジャムの瓶). Plastic bottles, by contrast, are called ペットボトル, and cans 缶; in waste separation one often reads びん・缶. Empty bottles are 空き瓶. The character is difficult and is often written in kana, びん. A vase is 花瓶 (かびん).

examples[].german: The soil became soft from the rain.
I put soil in the pot and plant flowers.
There is dirt on your shoes, so shake it off in the entrance.
en.notes: 土 (つち) is earth as a material: 土を入れる, 土が柔らかい, 土が付く. 地面, by contrast, refers to the surface of the ground, 土地 to a plot of land, and 泥 to wet mud. 土に返る means "to return to earth". As the abbreviation for Saturday (土曜日), the character is read ど, while in 土地 it is read と.

examples[].german: There is a big rock near the sea.
I sat on a rock and rested.
This mountain has many rocks, so it is hard to climb.
en.notes: 岩 is a rock or large boulder that cannot be lifted. 石 is a stone of handy size, 小石 a pebble, and 砂 sand. Common compounds are 岩場 "rocky terrain" and 岩山 "rocky mountain". One sits on a rock (岩に座る) or climbs it (岩に登る).

examples[].german: I saw cows at the ranch.
The cows are eating grass.
There are many farms around here that raise cattle.
en.notes: 牛 (うし) is the general term for cattle, whether cow, bull or ox. The meat is 牛肉 and milk 牛乳; in these words and in 牛丼 the character is read ぎゅう. Large animals are counted with 頭 (とう): 牛が三頭. Keeping or raising cattle is 牛を飼う or 牛を育てる.

examples[].german: When I was a child, I rode a horse once.
A horse is running across the wide grassland.
I got along with her from the very start.
en.notes: 馬 is the horse; riding is 馬に乗る, with に for the mount. Horses are counted like other large animals with 頭 (とう). In 競馬 "horse racing" the character is read ば. The idiom 馬が合う means "to get along well, to be on the same wavelength".

examples[].german: I keep a white rabbit.
The rabbit moved its ears.
In Japan, it is said that a rabbit pounds rice cakes on the moon.
en.notes: 兎 (うさぎ) does not distinguish between rabbit and hare; the wild hare is more precisely called 野うさぎ. The kanji is rare; usually it is written うさぎ or, especially in biology and at the zoo, ウサギ. Counting is nowadays mostly done with 匹, traditionally also with 羽. In the Japanese imagination, a rabbit pounds rice cakes on the moon.

examples[].german: I got back home before the storm came.
Many trees fell in the storm.
When the performance ended, the hall was engulfed in a storm of applause.
en.notes: 嵐 is a violent storm, usually with rain: 嵐が来る, 嵐がやむ, 嵐が去る. 台風 is specifically a typhoon, and 暴風雨 is the formal term for a storm with rain. Figuratively 嵐 stands for a violent outburst: 拍手の嵐 "thunderous applause", 批判の嵐 "a storm of criticism". The saying 嵐の前の静けさ corresponds to "the calm before the storm".

examples[].german: I wash my hands with soap lather.
Bubbles rose from the water.
The match was canceled because of rain, so all our practice came to nothing.
en.notes: 泡 covers foam and individual bubbles in liquids: 石鹸の泡, ビールの泡, 泡が立つ "it foams". Related verbs are 泡立つ "to foam" and 泡立てる "to whip", for example cream or egg whites. The idiom 水の泡になる means "to vanish into thin air, to have been in vain". It is also often written in kana as あわ.

examples[].german: Mix the powder into the water little by little.
White powder has fallen on the desk.
I'm making bread, so could you buy some flour?
en.notes: 粉 (こな) is any powdery substance, in a kitchen context often flour. More precisely, wheat flour is 小麦粉 (こむぎこ); in compounds the character is often read こ. Other words: 粉薬 "powdered medicine", 粉雪 "powder snow", 粉々 "to pieces". 粉末 is the more technical term, for example on packaging.

examples[].german: There is absolute trust.
In the past, the king held absolute power.
This team doesn't have an undisputed ace.
en.notes: 絶対的 means "absolute, unconditional" - something holds without comparison or restriction: 絶対的な権力, 絶対的な信頼, 絶対的な存在. As a na-adjective it is mostly used attributively with な. Unlike the adverb 絶対(に) "definitely, guaranteed", which is very common in everyday speech, 絶対的 describes a factual property. Opposite: 相対的.

examples[].german: Please breathe slowly.
After running, I caught my breath.
The two of them were perfectly in sync.
en.notes: 呼吸 is breathing and, as a する-verb, "to breathe"; it sounds more matter-of-fact and medical than 息 or 息をする. Typical are 呼吸を整える "to calm one's breathing", 呼吸が苦しい "to have difficulty breathing" and 深呼吸 "to take a deep breath". Figuratively 呼吸が合う means that people are perfectly in tune with each other.

examples[].german: Waiting a long time was torture for him.
The painkiller eased the pain.
The packed train every morning is unbearably painful for me.
en.notes: 苦痛 refers to physical or mental pain and distress. It sounds more formal than 痛み (concrete pain) or 苦しみ (suffering). It is often used with 〜にとって苦痛だ, 苦痛を感じる, 苦痛を和らげる. It also often describes things one finds unbearably annoying, such as long waits or crowded trains: 〜が苦痛だ.

examples[].german: It's hot, so I bought ice cream.
Please eat the ice cream before it melts.
Let's buy some ice cream at the convenience store and head home.
en.notes: アイスクリーム is ice cream; in daily life people almost always say just アイス, and アイス alone can also mean an ice pop. Soft-serve is ソフトクリーム, shaved ice with syrup かき氷. Flavors are named with 〜味: バニラ味のアイスクリーム. アイスクリームが溶ける means "the ice cream melts".

examples[].german: I put cheese on the bread and bake it.
This cheese has a strong salty taste.
When taking a photo, people say "はい、チーズ".
en.notes: チーズ is cheese. Typical combinations are チーズを載せる "to put cheese on top", チーズを溶かす, 粉チーズ "grated Parmesan" and チーズケーキ. When taking a photo, people say はい、チーズ so that everyone smiles. In Japanese supermarkets, sliced processed cheese (スライスチーズ) is especially common.

examples[].german: I made soup using vegetables.
The soup is hot, so please be careful.
On cold days, drinking warm soup warms the body.
en.notes: スープ refers mainly to Western soups such as コーンスープ or 野菜スープ, and also to the broth of ramen (ラーメンのスープ). Japanese soups like 味噌汁, by contrast, are called 汁 or お吸い物. In Japanese, soup is not eaten but drunk: スープを飲む. To cook it is スープを作る.

examples[].german: Can I pay by card?
I made a library card.
I wrote a birthday card and sent it to a friend.
en.notes: カード is a card in the broadest sense. カードで払う usually means by credit card (クレジットカード); also ポイントカード, 図書館のカード and 誕生日カード. For playing cards, people in daily life tend to say トランプ. Figuratively, カード also stands for a trump card in negotiations: 最後のカード.

examples[].german: The new office is close to the station.
Today I'm working at home, not at the office.
At noon, the restaurants in the office district get crowded.
en.notes: オフィス means office space or the office workplace and sounds modern; オフィス街 is a district of office towers. 事務所 is the classic word for an office, also for law firms or agencies. The daily commute is usually expressed with 会社に行く, not with オフィス. 職場 means "workplace" in general.

examples[].german: Please discuss it in groups of four.
I introduced myself to the people in my group.
Traveling as a group makes it cheaper.
en.notes: グループ is a group of people or things that belong together: グループで, グループに分かれる "to split into groups", グループを作る. Corporate groups (〜グループ) and chat groups are also called this. 団体 is more formal and refers to organized groups, as in 団体料金 "group rate". チーム stresses a shared goal, 仲間 personal bonds.

examples[].german: In this case, a reservation is required.
I put my glasses in the case.
I got a new case for my smartphone.
en.notes: ケース has two main meanings: a container or cover (眼鏡ケース, スマホのケース, ビール一ケース "a case of beer") and a case in the sense of a situation (よくあるケース, このようなケース). ケースバイケース means "it depends on the individual case". In the sense of "case", 場合 is more neutral and grammatically versatile (〜場合は); ケース sounds businesslike.

examples[].german: I made a travel plan.
I chose the plan that includes breakfast.
I switched my mobile phone rate plan to a cheaper one.
en.notes: プラン is a plan or project (旅行のプラン, プランを立てる) and often a selectable package or rate: 宿泊プラン, 料金プラン. 計画 is the more general, more serious word for planning, while 予定 is a fixed appointment or schedule. プラン sounds casual and is common in advertising and booking sites.

examples[].german: Economic stability is important.
I want to get a more secure job.
After the operation, my father's condition has finally stabilized.
en.notes: 安定 means "stability, steadiness" and is often used as an intransitive する-verb: 収入が安定している "income is stable". Attributively 安定した comes before nouns (安定した仕事 "a secure job"); the opposite is 不安定(な). To stabilize something is 安定させる. Do not confuse it with 安心 "relief, reassurance", which describes a feeling, while 安定 refers to the state of things, a situation or health.

examples[].german: Please use the microphone when you speak.
I checked the microphone before the presentation.
Once he picks up the microphone at karaoke, he hardly lets go.
en.notes: マイク is the usual short form of マイクロホン "microphone". Typical are マイクを使う, マイクを通して話す and マイクを持つ. When a microphone is switched off, one says マイクが入っていない. At karaoke and events the word is everywhere, and the long form is hardly ever heard.

examples[].german: I got the chance to work overseas.
Even if you fail, there's another chance.
The sale ends today, so if you're going to buy, now's your chance.
en.notes: チャンス is a favorable opportunity, often one you can seize or miss. Typical combinations: チャンスをつかむ "to seize a chance", チャンスを生かす "to make use of an opportunity", チャンスを逃す "to miss a chance" and 今がチャンスだ "now is the right moment". The Sino-Japanese 機会 is more neutral and formal and stands more for a plain "opportunity" without the overtone of luck or success.

examples[].german: It was dangerous, so I hit the brakes.
I repaired my bicycle's brakes.
The strong yen put the brakes on export growth.
en.notes: ブレーキ is the brake on a car, bicycle or train. "To brake" is ブレーキをかける or, with a view to the pedal, ブレーキを踏む; an emergency stop is 急ブレーキ. Intransitively one says ブレーキがかかる "the brake engages". Figuratively it means slowing down a development: 景気にブレーキがかかる "the economy is slowed down".

examples[].german: I rested on a park bench.
There was a lost item on the bench.
I sat on a bench at the station and waited for the next train.
en.notes: ベンチ is a bench, for example in a park, on a platform or at a bus stop - not a bank for money (that would be 銀行). One says ベンチに座る "to sit on the bench", but ベンチで休む "to rest on the bench". In sports, ベンチ is also the substitutes' or coaches' bench; ベンチ入り means "to make the game-day roster".

examples[].german: The child is throwing a ball.
The ball rolled onto the road.
For my birthday I got a new soccer ball.
en.notes: ボール is a ball for sports and play; typical are ボールを投げる "to throw", ボールを蹴る "to kick" and ボールを打つ "to hit". Compounds such as サッカーボール or テニスボール are very common. The bowl (dish) is mostly written ボウル, although both are pronounced the same; in baseball, ボール also means a pitch outside the strike zone.

examples[].german: I found a learning style that suits me.
This shop values the old style.
My older sister is tall and has a good figure.
en.notes: スタイル means, on the one hand, "style, manner" (生活スタイル, 学習スタイル, ヘアスタイル). On the other hand, スタイルがいい does not mean "stylish" but "to have a good figure", i.e. to be slim and well proportioned. For "fashionable, chic", おしゃれ is used instead.

examples[].german: I gave a short speech at the wedding.
I practiced the content of my speech many times.
I took second place in the Japanese speech contest.
en.notes: スピーチ is usually a short, prepared speech before an audience, such as at weddings, parties or in school; you say スピーチをする. 演説 is the formal, often political speech, and 発表 is more a talk or presentation of results. Also common are スピーチコンテスト and 結婚式のスピーチ.

examples[].german: Please knock before entering the room.
I knocked on the door, but there was no answer.
I heard a knocking sound in the middle of the night and woke up.
en.notes: ノック is knocking at a door; as a する-verb it takes を: ドアをノックする. The sound is ノックの音, and the knocking itself can be described onomatopoeically as トントン. In baseball, ノック also refers to hitting balls for fielding practice.

examples[].german: I bought three boards to build a shelf.
Please don't touch the broken sheet of glass.
It's an old house, so one of the floorboards has cracked.
en.notes: 板 is a flat board of wood, but also a plate of other material, such as ガラスの板 or 鉄の板. It is counted with 枚; typical verbs are 板を切る and 板を張る. A cutting board is called まな板 in daily life. The idiom 板につく means "to become accustomed to something", e.g. 制服姿が板についてきた.

examples[].german: You can see the sea from the top of the hill.
The children ran down the grassy hill.
On the weekend, my family went hiking to a nearby hill.
en.notes: 丘 is a gentle, rather low elevation; a real mountain is 山. Typical are 丘の上 "on top of the hill", 丘に登る "to climb a hill" and 丘を下りる. In place names and housing developments, 〜が丘 is very common. For a small rise in the terrain, 小高い丘 is also used.

examples[].german: The scene is in chaos.
There were so many explanations that my head got all muddled.
Heavy snow caused great chaos at the station.
en.notes: 混乱 is "confusion, disorder, chaos" and is mostly used as an intransitive する-verb: 現場が混乱する, 頭が混乱する "to be all mixed up in one's head". Someone who causes chaos does 混乱を招く or 混乱させる. It describes situations, processes or thoughts - for a messy room, people say 散らかっている instead. Mild uncertainty or hesitation is better expressed with 迷う.

examples[].german: My older sister is studying at an art university to become a painter.
This museum exhibits works by local painters.
During his lifetime, Van Gogh was not a very famous painter.
en.notes: 画家 is a fine-art painter, i.e. someone who paints pictures as art; someone who paints walls is a ペンキ屋 or 塗装工. Typical are 画家になる and 画家の作品. 芸術家 is the broader term "artist"; colloquially 絵描き is also used. For comic artists, 漫画家 is used, and for illustrators イラストレーター.

examples[].german: An economic crisis occurred.
This animal is in danger of extinction.
Everyone worked together and overcame the company's crisis.
en.notes: 危機 is a "crisis, critical situation" and often appears in compounds: 経済危機, 危機管理 "crisis management", 危機感 "sense of crisis". Typical are 危機に陥る "to fall into a crisis", 危機を乗り越える "to overcome a crisis" and 〜の危機にある "to be threatened by ..." (絶滅の危機). Unlike 危険 "danger", 危機 means a serious turning point; colloquially people often say ピンチ.

examples[].german: Let's prepare for disasters.
Japan is a country with many natural disasters such as earthquakes and typhoons.
In the event of a disaster, this school becomes an evacuation shelter.
en.notes: 災害 is a "disaster, (natural) calamity" such as an earthquake, typhoon or flood; 自然災害 stresses the natural origin. One says 災害が起きる, 災害に遭う "to be hit by a disaster" and 災害に備える "to prepare for disasters". Related are 防災 "disaster prevention" and 被災地 "disaster area". An ordinary accident is 事故, the resulting damage 被害.

examples[].german: The damage is spreading.
Many houses were damaged by the typhoon.
I fell victim to having my wallet stolen at the station.
en.notes: 被害 is the "damage" someone suffers - the character 被 marks the passive "to suffer". Typical are 被害を受ける "to suffer damage", 被害に遭う "to become a victim of ..." and 被害が出る/広がる. The injured person is 被害者 "victim", the perpetrator 加害者. Damage to an object in general (e.g. a scratch) is more 損害 or 傷; 被害 stresses that one was hit from outside (bad weather, theft, fraud).

examples[].german: Please judge for yourself.
You must not judge people by their looks alone.
Judging it to be dangerous, we called off the match.
en.notes: 判断する means to assess a situation and draw a conclusion from it. The object takes を, the result is quoted with と (危ないと判断する), and the basis takes で or から (見た目で判断する). Common expressions are 判断に迷う "to be undecided" and 判断がつかない "cannot judge". 決める is simply "to decide on something", whereas 判断 emphasizes weighing things up.

examples[].german: We are hurrying to restore the power.
The trains that had stopped because of an accident resumed an hour later.
It looks like it will still take time to restore the server.
en.notes: 復旧 means the "restoration" of infrastructure after a disruption: electricity, water, rail service, roads, computer systems. Mostly intransitive: 電車が復旧した "the trains are running again"; transitive use is rarer (システムを復旧する). Common are 復旧作業 "repair work" and 復旧の見込み "prospect of restoration". Distinction: 回復 for health or the economy, 復興 for the reconstruction of whole regions, 修理 for repairing an object.

examples[].german: Please respond promptly.
That clerk is very polite in dealing with customers.
This app does not support Japanese.
en.notes: 対応 has several meanings: above all "dealing with, response to, handling" - 〜に対応する "to respond to, to take care of", 客の対応 "customer service", 対応が早い/遅い. In technology, 〜に対応している means "supports ..., is compatible with" (日本語に対応). It also means "correspondence": AとBが対応する. In contrast to 対策 "countermeasure (preventive)", 対応 describes the reaction to a concrete situation.

examples[].german: We are heading in the right direction.
Excuse me, which direction is the station?
I have no sense of direction, so I often get lost.
en.notes: 方向 is "direction", both spatially and figuratively: 駅の方向 "toward the station", 正しい方向に進む "to go in the right direction". Set expressions are 方向を変える, 反対方向 and, colloquially, 方向音痴 "having no sense of direction". In everyday speech people often ask more briefly どっち? or use 〜の方; 方面 refers more to an area or a destination (新宿方面), 向き to the orientation of an object (窓の向き).

examples[].german: One hour per day is a rough guide.
Please use about a hundred grams of rice per person as a guide.
Could you tell me roughly how much the repair will cost?
en.notes: 目安 means "rough guide, benchmark, approximate orientation" - not a fixed rule but a yardstick for orientation. Typical: 〜が目安です, 〜を目安にする "to go by …", 料金の目安 "approximate price" and 目安がつく/立つ "to have a rough idea". Often found on packaging, in instructions and in price lists. A binding "standard", by contrast, is 基準.

examples[].german: I found a clue to the solution.
The police have not yet picked up any leads in the case.
This old photograph became a clue in the search for my grandfather's house.
en.notes: 手掛かり is a "clue, lead, trace" that leads to solving a riddle, case or problem; literally a "handhold" (also in climbing). Typical: 手掛かりを見つける/つかむ, 〜の手掛かりになる, 何の手掛かりもない. Very often also written 手がかり. A mere tip or piece of advice is rather ヒント; 手掛かり is more concrete, often in a detective or research context.

examples[].german: We are starting a new initiative.
This town is putting great effort into reducing waste.
In today's sumo, the Yokozuna's bout was the most exciting.
en.notes: 取り組み is the noun of 取り組む "to tackle (a task) seriously" and means "effort, initiative, measure". Typical: 〜への取り組み "commitment to ..." (環境問題への取り組み), 新しい取り組みを始める. Popular in corporate, school and government texts. In sumo, 取り組み also means "bout, match". 取組 without okurigana also appears in official texts.

examples[].german: We will create a new framework.
Let's first decide on the broad framework of the plan and then discuss the details.
Within the framework of the current law, that is not possible.
en.notes: 枠組み is literally a "structure made of frames" and usually means, figuratively, the "framework, basic structure" of a plan, system or agreement: 法律の枠組み, 〜の枠組みの中で "within the framework of ...", 枠組みを作る/決める. Concretely it can also be a wooden or metal frame. A single frame (picture, window, form field) is 枠; 枠組み emphasizes the overall construction.

examples[].german: There is a prospect of recovery.
The new station is expected to be completed next spring.
Sales were lower than expected.
en.notes: 見込み (from 見込む "to estimate, to expect") means "prospect, likelihood" and "forecast, expectation". Typical: 〜の見込みがある/ない "there is/is no prospect of ...", 見込みが外れる "the expectation does not come true", 卒業見込み "expected graduation". 見込みのある人 is someone "with potential". After verbs at the end of a sentence: 〜する見込みだ "it is expected that ..." - more factual than 予定 (firm plan).

en.meaning: to consist of; to hold; to be viable
examples[].german: Society is built on trust.
This committee consists of five members.
With so few customers, the business is not viable.
en.notes: 成り立つ is intransitive and has three core meanings: "to consist of" (〜から/で成り立つ), "to come into being, to hold" (契約が成り立つ, 理論が成り立つ) and "to be viable, to work" (商売が成り立たない "the business doesn't pay"). There is no transitive partner; one uses 成り立たせる. The noun 成り立ち means "origin, structure". In everyday speech, "to consist of" is often simply said 〜でできている.

en.meaning: course of events; how things turn out
examples[].german: I will watch how things develop.
As the conversation went, I ended up being in charge of organizing the party.
We didn't make detailed plans and decided to leave the trip to chance.
en.notes: 成り行き is the "course of things, progress, development" of a situation, often without deliberate planning. Typical: 成り行きを見守る "to wait and see how things develop", 成り行きに任せる "to let things take their course", 話の成り行きで "as the conversation went". 当然の成り行き is "the logical consequence". In stock-market jargon it also means "market order". For planned progress, people say 進行 or 経過 instead.

examples[].german: I will get a grip on the situation.
I still haven't grasped what my new job involves.
After the earthquake, the city has not yet been able to grasp the extent of the damage.
en.notes: 把握する is transitive and means to fully take in facts or a situation and keep them in view: 状況・内容・現状・人数を把握する. It is typical of the working world and the news, for example 被害の状況を把握する. Unlike 理解する (understanding the meaning or reasons), 把握 is about having an overview of the facts. In everyday conversation people tend to say 分かる.

en.meaning: side; vicinity; while (doing something else); alongside
examples[].german: I study alongside my job.
While working at a company, she writes novels.
The mother sat quietly beside her sleeping child.
en.notes: 傍ら is a noun with two uses: spatially "side, immediate vicinity" (〜の傍らに座る "to sit beside ...", literary) and above all 〜の傍ら / verb + 傍ら "alongside (a main activity), on the side": 会社に勤める傍ら小説を書く. This construction describes ongoing dual activities, not simultaneous actions like 〜ながら. Literary; in conversation one rather says 〜の横に or 〜しながら.

examples[].german: Let's set an example.
Senior students must be a model for the younger ones.
Model answers were handed out after the test.
en.notes: 模範 is a "model, pattern" that others should follow. Typical: 模範を示す "to set a good example", 〜の模範となる "to be a model for ...", 模範的な学生 "a model student", 模範解答 "model answer". Somewhat more formal than お手本 / 手本, which is more common in everyday life (for example in calligraphy). 見本, by contrast, is a "sample, specimen" of a product.

examples[].german: This is a typical example.
He works overtime every day - a typical salaryman.
This temple is said to be a classic example of old Japanese architecture.
en.notes: 典型 means "type, prime example" and is most often used as the na-adjective 典型的(な) "typical": 典型的な例, 典型的な日本人. As a noun it appears in 〜の典型だ "is a prime example of ...". Compared with いかにも〜らしい (colloquial "just so typical"), 典型 sounds objective and analytical. 代表的, by contrast, stresses "representative, best known".

examples[].german: The cherry blossom is a symbol of Japan.
The white dove symbolizes peace.
This old bridge is a structure that symbolizes the town's history.
en.notes: 象徴 is a "symbol, emblem" for something abstract: 平和の象徴 "symbol of peace". As a transitive する-verb: AがBを象徴する "A symbolizes B", often in the form 象徴している. The adjective 象徴的(な) means "symbolic, emblematic". For signs such as traffic signs or chemical symbols, one uses 記号 or マーク instead; 象徴 always refers to a meaning beyond the thing itself.

examples[].german: Please do not forget the original purpose.
Normally I would have the day off today, but sudden work came up.
His injury has healed, and he can now show his true ability.
en.notes: 本来 means "originally, properly, by nature" and is used as an adverb and as a noun with の: 本来の目的 "the original purpose", 本来の力 "one's true strength". 本来なら/本来は "normally, properly (it should be so)" often introduces a contrast with reality. In everyday speech もともと is often used; 元来 is more literary and refers more to innate characteristics.

examples[].german: He is by nature a serious person.
This region has always been one where rice farming flourishes.
Originally, this festival was meant to pray for a good harvest.
en.notes: 元来 means "by nature, originally, from the beginning" and is a pure adverb: 彼は元来まじめな人だ. It describes qualities that something or someone has always had. The tone is literary to elevated; in conversation one mostly says もともと. Unlike 本来, it hardly forms phrases with の and is not used for "actually it should ..." (本来なら).

examples[].german: I just didn't know.
This is not simply a matter of money.
I came to Japan not only for work but also because I was interested in the culture.
en.notes: 単に means "merely, simply, just" and is typically combined with だけ or にすぎない: 単に〜だけだ. The negation 単に〜ではない / 単に〜だけでなく "not merely ..., but also" is very common. It sounds somewhat more objective than ただ; in casual conversation people often say ただ〜だけ. Do not confuse it with 簡単に "easily (= simply)".

en.meaning: if pressed; if one must; insistently
examples[].german: If I had to say, the problem is here.
If you don't like it, you don't have to take part.
I like all kinds of food, but if I had to pick one, it would be ramen.
en.notes: 強いて comes from 強いる "to force" and means "with insistence, by force, necessarily". Most common is the fixed phrase 強いて言えば / 強いて挙げれば "if I had to say/name something", with which one hesitantly gives an answer although nothing in particular comes to mind. Also in 強いて〜する必要はない "you don't necessarily have to ...". Slightly elevated; in conversation it is often replaced by 無理に.

examples[].german: I can sense the signs of spring.
I sensed someone's presence from a room that should have been empty.
There are no signs of the rain stopping.
en.notes: 気配 (read けはい, not きはい) is a "sign, a feeling that something is there or coming" - something one senses rather than clearly sees. Typical: 人の気配がする "to sense that someone is there", 春の気配を感じる, 〜する気配がない "there are no signs that …". Do not confuse it with 気配り "attentiveness, consideration". 兆し is more literary and refers to the first sign of a change.

examples[].german: There are signs of recovery.
The plum blossoms are starting to bloom, and you can feel the signs of spring.
Signs of change have begun to appear in the two people's relationship.
en.notes: 兆し is a "sign, omen" - the first signal that something is changing, often for the better: 回復の兆し, 景気回復の兆しが見える, 春の兆し. Typical verbs: 兆しが見える/表れる. It sounds a bit more literary than 気配 and is often used in news. The related verb is 兆す "to announce itself" (rare). A clearly ominous sign is rather called 前兆.

examples[].german: Please respond appropriately.
This word is not appropriate here.
Please use the medicine appropriately, following the doctor's instructions.
en.notes: 適切 is a な-adjective: 適切な対応, 適切に使う; its negative is 不適切. It sounds objective and formal and often appears in instructions, official texts and at work. 適当 also actually means "suitable", but colloquially it is often used for "careless, any old way"; 適切 never has this negative undertone. ふさわしい emphasizes that something suits a person or an occasion.

examples[].german: There are concerns about safety.
There are concerns that the river will rise because of the heavy rain.
The president expressed concerns about the plan.
en.notes: 懸念 is "concern, apprehension" and sounds much more formal than 心配: it appears mainly in news, reports and business language. Typical: 〜への懸念 "concerns about ...", 懸念を示す/表明する "to voice concerns" and the passive 〜が懸念される "it is feared that ...". The verb 懸念する is transitive (〜を懸念する). In personal conversation people almost always say 心配する.

examples[].german: Consideration for the environment is necessary.
With the elderly in mind, an elevator was built at the station.
Thank you for always being so considerate.
en.notes: 配慮 is "consideration, thoughtful care" for people or concerns. Typical: 〜に配慮する "to take ... into consideration", 〜への配慮, 配慮が足りない "not enough consideration", polite ご配慮いただきありがとうございます. It sounds factual to formal; 気配り and 気遣い are more personal and everyday. Not to be confused with 遠慮 "restraint" - there one holds oneself back, whereas with 配慮 one thinks of others.

examples[].german: I came up with all sorts of ideas.
Even in a small room, you can make it feel spacious with some ingenuity.
I put thought into my cooking so that my children will eat vegetables.
en.notes: 工夫 (read くふう) means to "come up with" something clever, to work out a practical solution - and the result itself: "a trick, an idea". Typical: 工夫する, 工夫を凝らす "to put a lot of thought into ideas", 〜に工夫がある "… is well thought out", 工夫次第で "depending on what you come up with". Unlike 改善 "improvement", 工夫 emphasizes everyday creativity (cooking, saving, studying).

examples[].german: We took emergency measures.
The school decided to take strict measures against bullying.
There are special measures for people affected by the earthquake damage.
en.notes: 措置 is a "measure" taken by authorities, companies or schools and sounds official. Typical combinations: 措置を取る "to take measures", formal 措置を講じる, 緊急措置, 特別措置, 必要な措置. Compared with 対策 "countermeasure against a problem", 措置 stresses the concrete administrative action; 処置, by contrast, rather means treatment (medical) or immediate action in an individual case.

examples[].german: We will implement new measures.
The city has announced measures to support families raising children.
What measures could be considered to boost sales?
en.notes: 施策 is a planned "measure, program", above all by governments, municipalities or companies - used almost only in official, business and news language. Typical: 施策を実施する "to implement", 施策を打ち出す "to announce, to launch", 〜のための施策. The standard reading is しさく; せさく is sometimes heard but is considered less correct. More general is 政策 "policy (as a line of action)", more concrete 対策 "countermeasure".

examples[].german: We provide a service.
Please provide information about the incident.
This hotel offers breakfast free of charge.
en.notes: 提供 means "provision, offering, making available" of services, information, rooms or goods; as a transitive する-verb: 〜を提供する. Common in 情報提供, 無料で提供する and for donations: 臓器提供 "organ donation". On television 提供 also means "sponsorship" (この番組は〜の提供でお送りします). For personally offering something (for example help), one rather says 申し出る.

examples[].german: The spread of the internet is progressing.
Smartphones spread rapidly in about ten years.
The government is trying to promote electric cars.
en.notes: 普及 is the "spread" of technology, products, knowledge or habits in society. Mostly intransitive: スマホが普及する "smartphones spread"; transitively one says 普及させる (普及する with を is also possible). Typical: 普及率 "penetration rate", 〜の普及が進む. 普及 does not fit rumors or diseases - for those one says 広まる or 広がる; 浸透 emphasizes ideas penetrating deeply.

examples[].german: New ways of thinking are taking hold.
Rainwater slowly seeps into the ground.
It is not easy to get new rules to really take root among employees.
en.notes: 浸透 literally means the "seeping in" of a liquid (水が土に浸透する) and, figuratively, that ideas, rules or brands "take hold, become firmly rooted" deep in a group: 〜が社会に浸透する. It is intransitive; the transitive form is 浸透させる (ルールを社員に浸透させる). Unlike 普及 "spread (quantity, reach)", 浸透 emphasizes depth - that something is truly accepted.

examples[].german: We strive to promote health.
This medicine has the effect of promoting digestion.
The store held a discount sale to promote sales.
en.notes: 促進 is the "promotion, acceleration" of a process, transitive as 〜を促進する. Typical in administration, business and medicine: 販売促進 (short 販促) "sales promotion", 消化を促進する "to stimulate digestion", 〜の促進を図る. It sounds formal; in conversation one rather says 進める or 早める. 推進 stresses pushing a project forward, 促進 accelerating a development.

examples[].german: Curbing inflation is necessary.
This medicine works to suppress appetite.
He could not restrain his anger and ended up raising his voice.
en.notes: 抑制 means "curbing, suppression, inhibition" - something is kept under control so that it does not increase. Transitive: 〜を抑制する (物価上昇を抑制する, 食欲を抑制する, 感情を抑制する). Typical in business, medicine and psychology. In everyday speech one mostly says the simpler 抑える. The political suppression of people, by contrast, is 弾圧 or 抑圧.

examples[].german: This is an important issue.
It's an important document, so please don't lose it.
Continuing every day is the most important thing.
en.notes: 重要 is a な-adjective meaning "important, of great significance": 重要な会議, 重要な書類, 重要性 "importance". It is more objective and more formal than 大切 and 大事. 大切 often expresses personal, emotional appreciation: 大切な友達, not 重要な友達. In news and texts, 重要 is the usual choice, for example in 重要人物 "key person".

examples[].german: The easing of regulations is progressing.
This medicine relieves pain.
Since the new road was built, the congestion in front of the station has eased.
en.notes: 緩和 means "easing, relief, relaxation" of rules, pain, tension or traffic. It is both transitive and intransitive: 規制を緩和する "to relax regulations", 痛みが緩和される "the pain subsides". Fixed terms are 規制緩和 "deregulation", 金融緩和 "monetary easing", 緩和ケア "palliative care". In everyday speech people often say 和らげる/和らぐ or ゆるめる.

examples[].german: We will strengthen security.
The police have stepped up their night patrols.
Looking ahead to next year, I want to strengthen the team's defense.
en.notes: 強化 is "strengthening, reinforcement" and is mostly used as a transitive する-verb: X を強化する, passive 強化される. Typical are 対策を強化する, 警備を強化する, 規制を強化する, and compounds such as 強化ガラス "tempered glass" or 強化合宿 "intensive training camp". The opposite is 弱体化, or for rules 緩和 "relaxation". Compared with the general verb 強める, 強化 sounds matter-of-fact and suits organizations, systems and measures.

examples[].german: We aim to revitalize the regional economy.
To revitalize the shopping street, we hold an event every month.
It is said that eating breakfast activates the brain.
en.notes: 活性化 means "revitalization, activation": the economy, towns, organizations or brain cells are made lively again. With -化 it works as a する-verb, both transitive and intransitive: 町を活性化する / 経済が活性化する; often also 活性化させる. 地域の活性化 "revitalization of the region" and 〜の活性化を図る are very common. It is a typical word of politics and advertising; more personal is 元気にする.

examples[].german: We will optimize the process.
This website is optimized for smartphones.
After I optimized my PC settings, it started running faster.
en.notes: 最適化 means "optimization" (最適 "best suited" + 化) and is a typical technical term in IT, engineering and business administration: 〜を最適化する "to optimize", 〜に最適化された "tailored to ...", 検索エンジン最適化 "search engine optimization (SEO)". Unlike 改善 "improvement", it means bringing something to the best possible state for a given purpose. In everyday speech people say 一番いい形にする instead.

examples[].german: We will push forward with improving operational efficiency.
We installed new software and made accounting work more efficient.
I want to make housework more efficient and have more time for myself.
en.notes: 効率化 means "improving efficiency, streamlining": getting work done with less time and effort. Typical: 業務の効率化 "streamlining of operations", 〜を効率化する, 効率化を図る/進める. Popular in office and management language. The base word 効率 "efficiency" appears in 効率がいい/悪い; 効率的(な) means "efficient". Do not confuse it with 能率 "efficiency (of a person's work)".

examples[].german: Needs are diversifying.
Ways of working have become more varied recently, and more people work from home.
We discussed the diversification of young people's values.
en.notes: 多様化 means "diversification, becoming more varied" (多様 "diverse" + 化) and is mostly used intransitively: 価値観が多様化する "values become more diverse", ニーズの多様化. Often with 進む: 多様化が進む. It describes a social development; the result is called 多様性 "diversity". For deliberate spreading (e.g. of investments), people prefer 分散.

examples[].german: Internationalization is advancing.
English classes have increased as part of the university's internationalization.
This town, too, has become more international as the number of foreign residents has grown.
en.notes: 国際化 means "internationalization" of society, companies, universities or cities; intransitive 国際化が進む / 社会が国際化する, and also transitive 大学を国際化する. In Japan it has been a buzzword since the 1980s, often in the sense of "opening up to foreigners and other cultures". Related: グローバル化 "globalization", which refers more to worldwide economic interconnection.

examples[].german: The computerization of society is advancing.
In an information society, protecting personal data is very important.
With the digitalization of schools, every student was given a tablet.
en.notes: 情報化 refers to "informatization, digitalization" - the process by which computers and information networks permeate society and work. It occurs most often in fixed terms: 情報化社会 "information society", 情報化が進む, 学校の情報化. The word sounds somewhat dated (a buzzword of the 1980s/90s); today, for government offices and companies, people often speak of デジタル化 or DX.

examples[].german: The IT industry is growing.
The main industry of this town is tourism.
The automobile industry is thriving in Japan.
en.notes: 産業 is the general term for branches of the economy of all kinds, from agriculture to services; hence the many compounds such as 自動車産業, 観光産業 or IT産業. That an industry is strong in a region is expressed with 産業が盛んだ. Do not confuse it with 工業: 工業 means only manufacturing industry with factories, whereas 産業 covers every line of economic activity. The word is factual and typical of news, textbooks and economic topics.

examples[].german: It is a region where agriculture thrives.
My grandfather farms in the countryside.
More and more young people are quitting their jobs and taking up farming.
en.notes: 農業 is "agriculture" as an industry and an occupation. Typical: 農業をする/営む "to engage in farming", 農業が盛ん "agriculture flourishes", 農業で生活する. Related are 農家 "farm, farming family", 農民 "farmer (historical)" and 農作物 "agricultural products". The work in the field itself is 畑仕事 or 農作業.

examples[].german: It's a serious problem.
You have such a serious look on your face. What's the matter?
The water shortage is becoming serious in this region.
en.notes: 深刻 is a な-adjective for serious, worrying situations: 深刻な問題, 深刻な被害, 水不足が深刻になる. It also describes a grave expression or attitude: 深刻な顔, 深刻に考える. Do not confuse it with 真剣 ("serious, in earnest": 真剣に勉強する). 重大 emphasizes great consequence, as in 重大なミス.

examples[].german: Fishing is the main industry.
Many people on this island make their living from fishing.
The rising sea temperature is having a major impact on the fishing industry.
en.notes: 漁業 is "fishing" as an economic sector, including fish farming. Typical: 漁業が盛んな町, 漁業で生活する, 漁業関係者 "people working in the fishing industry". The fishermen themselves are 漁師, and the fishing port is 漁港. Angling as a hobby is 釣り. Note when reading: 漁 is read ぎょ here (but りょう in 漁師).

examples[].german: Commercial facilities are increasing.
Osaka has long been known as a commercial city.
My older brother graduated from a commercial high school and got a job at a bank.
en.notes: 商業 is "commerce, trade" as an economic sector - buying and selling goods. Typical in compounds: 商業施設 "commercial facility, shopping complex", 商業高校 "commercial high school", 商業地域. 商業的(な) means "commercial" (often slightly pejorative: 商業的な映画). The actual trade between countries is rather 貿易, and an individual's business 商売.

examples[].german: We will cut manufacturing costs.
This factory manufactures car parts.
The manufacturing date is written on the bread bag.
en.notes: 製造 is "manufacturing, production" on an industrial scale, transitive as 〜を製造する. Typical: 製造業 "manufacturing industry", 製造元 "manufacturer", 製造年月日 "date of manufacture", 製造コスト. The more general, everyday word is 作る; 生産 emphasizes the quantity produced (also in agriculture), 製作 the making of individual works (films, furniture).

examples[].german: We will improve the distribution system.
Counterfeit money is in circulation, so please be careful.
This room has small windows, and the air circulation is poor.
en.notes: 流通 means "circulation, distribution": goods travel from the manufacturer to the consumer (流通業 "distribution and logistics industry", 流通コスト), money is in circulation (お金が流通する). In its second meaning it is the "circulating" of air or water (空気の流通). As a する-verb it is intransitive: 〜が流通する "is in circulation, is traded". For the sale itself one says 販売.

examples[].german: We will enter a new market.
The Japanese stock market fell sharply today.
Let's do market research before launching the new product.
en.notes: 市場 has two readings: しじょう is the "market" in the economic sense (株式市場 "stock market", 市場調査 "market research", 市場に参入する "to enter a market"); いちば is a concrete market with stalls (魚市場 "fish market"). This card teaches しじょう. Typical: 市場が拡大する, 国内市場, 海外市場. A local market in everyday life is rather called いちば or マーケット.

examples[].german: I work for a large company.
Most Japanese companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
That company is famous for its eco-friendly products.
en.notes: 企業 is a "company, enterprise" as an economic organization and sounds more objective than 会社: 大企業 "large company", 中小企業 "small and medium-sized enterprises", 外資系企業 "foreign-owned company", 企業に就職する. In everyday speech people almost always say 会社 about their own firm; 企業 appears more in news, statistics and job applications. "To found a company" is 起業 (same reading!).

examples[].german: I run a company.
My uncle runs a small restaurant near the station.
With fewer customers, the shop's finances have become difficult.
en.notes: 経営 is the "management, running" of a company or business, transitive as 〜を経営する: 店を経営する "to run a shop". Typical: 経営者 "business owner, executive", 経営が苦しい "the business is struggling", 経営学 "business administration". For managing people or projects, people say 管理 or マネジメント; 運営 refers to running facilities, clubs or events.

examples[].german: We will reform the organization.
Working within a large organization can be hard at times.
They set up a volunteer organization.
en.notes: 組織 refers to an organization as an entity (company, club, party) and also to its structure: 組織の一員 "a member of the organization", 大きな組織 "a large organization", 組織的 "organized, systematic". As a する-verb, 組織する means "to form, to establish (a group)" - to "organize" an event, by contrast, is 企画する or 準備する. In biology 組織 also means "tissue" (筋肉の組織).

examples[].german: I work in the sales division.
This company plans to expand its IT division next year.
Her photo took first place in the landscape category of the contest.
en.notes: 部門 is a sub-unit of a larger whole - in companies a division or business area (営業部門, 技術部門). One's own department is usually called 部 or 課 in everyday speech (営業部, 総務課); 部門 sounds more general and formal and often groups several departments together. A second important use: category in competitions and awards, e.g. 小説部門で優勝する "to win in the novel category".

examples[].german: We train outstanding personnel.
There is a shortage of young talent in rural areas.
He is a valuable asset to our company.
en.notes: 人材 refers to people as a resource of an organization, usually with a view to their abilities: 優秀な人材 "highly qualified people", 人材を育てる "to train the next generation", 人材が不足している "there is a shortage of skilled people". Mostly used collectively, but it can also mean a single person: 彼は貴重な人材だ "he is a valuable asset". Unlike 人員 (staffing level, headcount), 人材 stresses quality; 人材派遣 is "temporary staffing, personnel placement".

examples[].german: Let's make our goals clear.
He did not answer the question clearly.
This company has no clear rules.
en.notes: 明確 is a な-adjective for things that are clearly outlined and unambiguously defined: 明確な目標, 明確な理由, 明確に答える. 明確にする means "to clarify, to define". It sounds formal. 明らか, by contrast, emphasizes that something is obvious (〜のは明らかだ); はっきり is the everyday word and also applies to seeing and hearing.

examples[].german: We will pay appropriate remuneration.
It's volunteer work, so I don't receive any pay.
The fee for the translation is 3,000 yen per page.
en.notes: 報酬 is the compensation for work or a service, usually in money: 報酬を払う／受け取る, 成功報酬 "success fee", 役員報酬 "executive compensation". It sounds more factual and formal than 給料 (regular salary of employees) and fits especially fees for commissions, freelance work and side jobs. Also non-material: 努力の報酬 "the reward of effort". For a reward given to children one rather says ご褒美.

examples[].german: I was transferred to Osaka.
Because of my father's job transfers, we moved many times when I was a child.
I want to work for a company with no transfers.
en.notes: 転勤 is a transfer within the same company to a different location, usually with a move. Typical: 〜に転勤になる "to be transferred to ..." (decided by the employer) or 〜へ転勤する; 転勤族 are families who move often because of transfers. Do not confuse it with 転職 "changing employers" and 異動 (moving to a different department, even without a change of location). If you go to the new place without your family, it is called 単身赴任.

examples[].german: I will take paid leave.
Next week I'm using paid leave to go to a hot spring.
I still have ten days of paid leave left this year.
en.notes: 有給休暇 is the legally guaranteed paid leave; in conversation people almost always say 有給 or 有休 for short. One says 有給休暇を取る／使う, to apply for it is 申請する, and 有給がまだ残っている means "I still have leave days left". In Japan it is often taken by the day rather than as a long vacation. General "time off, holidays" is 休み or 休暇.

examples[].german: Overtime pay is provided.
Our company has no housing allowance.
The teacher treated the injury right away.
en.notes: 手当 (also written 手当て) as a work term is an allowance in addition to the base salary: 残業手当 "overtime pay", 住宅手当 "housing allowance", 通勤手当 "commuting allowance", 児童手当 "child benefit". One says 手当が出る／つく "there is an allowance". The second common meaning is treating an injury: けがの手当をする "to treat a wound", 応急手当 "first aid".

en.meaning: to take up a post; to be posted (to a location)
examples[].german: I will be posted overseas.
My father will go to Nagoya on a solo assignment from next month.
The new teacher took up her post at this school in April.
en.notes: 赴任する means to travel to a new place of duty in order to take up a position there; the destination takes に or へ: 海外に赴任する. It stresses the change of location and is used mainly for company employees, teachers and diplomats: 赴任先 "new place of duty", 海外赴任 "overseas posting". 単身赴任 means going to the new location without one's family - very common in Japan. 転勤 is the transfer itself, 赴任 the going there and taking up the post.

examples[].german: The company president resigned.
The minister took responsibility for the problem and resigned.
She resigned as chairperson for health reasons.
en.notes: 辞任する means to step down voluntarily from an office or position of responsibility; the office takes を: 社長を辞任する, 大臣が辞任する. It is a word from the news and formal contexts, often in 責任を取って辞任する "to take responsibility and resign". An ordinary resignation as an employee is 仕事を辞める or 退職する in everyday speech; 辞退する, by contrast, means "to decline an offer, to give something up".

examples[].german: We will hire new employees.
I was hired by the company where I had the interview.
My proposal was adopted at the meeting.
en.notes: 採用する has two main meanings: to "hire" personnel (新卒を採用する, 採用試験 "hiring exam") and to "adopt, accept" ideas, proposals or methods (案を採用する). From the applicant's point of view one says the passive 採用される "to be hired"; the acceptance notice is 採用通知, the rejection 不採用. A more casual word for "to employ" is 雇う; the employer-side counterpart is 解雇する "to dismiss".

examples[].german: I was unfairly dismissed.
Because sales dropped, the company laid off fifty employees.
If you're late often, you might get fired, you know.
en.notes: 解雇する is dismissal by the employer, a formal and legal word: 社員を解雇する, 不当解雇 "unfair dismissal". Those affected say 解雇される; colloquially it is クビになる "to get the sack", and with job cuts also リストラされる. If you quit yourself, you say 辞める or 退職する, never 解雇する.

en.meaning: to entrust; to commission; to outsource
examples[].german: We will outsource it.
The city has outsourced garbage collection to a private company.
This store sells works that artists have placed on consignment.
en.notes: 委託する means handing over a task or goods to another company or person to carry out; the recipient takes に, the thing takes を: 清掃を外部の会社に委託する "to outsource the cleaning to an outside company". Common in business and administration: 業務委託 "commissioned work", 委託販売 "consignment sales". In everyday speech one rather says 頼む or 任せる; 委託 sounds businesslike and contractual.

examples[].german: We concluded a new contract.
I signed a contract for a new apartment.
The player signed a three-year contract with an American team.
en.notes: 契約する means to conclude a contract; the contract partner takes と, the object takes を: 会社と契約する, スマホを契約する. Equivalent but somewhat more formal is 契約を結ぶ; to cancel a contract is 解約する, to renew it 契約を更新する. Important compounds: 契約書 "contract document", 契約社員 "fixed-term employee".

examples[].german: I will take responsibility.
I will take responsibility for this job until the end.
The responsibility for the accident lies with me, since I was driving.
en.notes: 責任 is responsibility in the sense of duty and liability. The verbs are important: 責任を持つ "to take responsibility, to look after something responsibly", 責任を取る "to take the consequences" (often up to resigning) and 責任がある "to be responsible". 〜の責任だ means "it is ...'s fault". The feeling of being responsible, on the other hand, is 責任感.

examples[].german: It's a land rich in nature.
Compared with the past, life has become more prosperous.
She is very expressive, and it's fun to watch her.
en.notes: 豊か is a な-adjective with three main uses: abundance (自然が豊かな土地, 経験豊か), material prosperity of a society or a life (豊かな国, 生活が豊かになる) and richness of inner qualities (表情・想像力が豊か, 心が豊か). For "He is rich" one does not say 豊か but お金持ち. 豊か sounds positive and somewhat elevated.

examples[].german: We will deliver tomorrow.
We will deliver the ordered goods by Friday.
I delivered the design files to the client last week.
en.notes: 納品する means to deliver ordered goods or a finished work product to the customer; the recipient takes に: 取引先に商品を納品する. It is business language from trade and production and also applies to services such as software, designs or translations. Related are 納品書 "delivery note" and 納期 "delivery date". Delivering a parcel is 届ける or 配達する in everyday speech; the ordering side is 発注する.

en.meaning: to place an order; to commission
examples[].german: We ordered parts.
Stock is low, so please order a little more paper.
The city commissioned a local company to build the new bridge.
en.notes: 発注する means to place an order with a supplier or contractor, or to award a contract: 部品を工場に発注する. It is business language between companies and government offices; as a private customer in a shop or online, people say 注文する. The counterpart is 受注する "to receive an order"; 発注書 is the written order, 発注ミス an ordering error.

examples[].german: I will check the inventory.
I'm sorry, we no longer have this size in stock.
Because it's a popular product, it sold out online right away, too.
en.notes: 在庫 is the stock of goods in a warehouse or shop: 在庫がある／ない, 在庫を確認する, 在庫切れ "out of stock, sold out". In shops one often hears 在庫を確認してまいります "I will check the stock". Having too much stock is 在庫を抱える. For supplies at home one rather says 買い置き or ストック.

examples[].german: We will improve quality.
The price is a little high, but the quality is good.
The factory checks quality every day.
en.notes: 品質 is the quality of products or services: 品質がいい／高い, 品質管理 "quality control", 品質を保証する "to guarantee quality". It is more factual and narrower than 質, which generally means "quality, nature" (睡眠の質, 人の質); 品質 is not used for people. Typical is the contrast with price: 値段より品質.

examples[].german: The performance of the car has improved.
This computer is cheap but performs well.
I will compare the performance of the cameras before buying one.
en.notes: 性能 is the technical performance of machines and devices: 性能がいい／高い, 高性能 "high-performance", エンジンの性能. It is not used for people; personal abilities are 能力, and results at school or work 成績. Distinction from 機能: 機能 is what a device can do (functions), 性能 is how well it does it.

examples[].german: A new feature has been added.
This smartphone has many useful camera functions.
The new rule is not working properly yet.
en.notes: 機能 is the function of a device, system or organ: 便利な機能, 機能が多い, 機能を使う. As an intransitive する-verb, 機能する means "to function, to fulfill its role", especially for systems and rules: 制度がうまく機能していない. Whether a device simply runs is expressed in everyday speech more with 動く／動かない. Derived: 機能的 "functional, practical".

examples[].german: The area is very convenient, with the station close by.
We redesigned the app with user convenience in mind.
I value convenience over price, so I shop at convenience stores.
en.notes: 利便性 refers to how convenient and practical something is to use, and is a typical word in advertising, housing listings and reports: 利便性が高い, 利便性を高める, 交通の利便性 "good transport access". It is the formal noun for 便利; in conversation people usually just say 便利だ. For software it often corresponds to "usability".

examples[].german: It is a durable material.
This bag is light and also very durable.
We are examining the durability of the old bridge.
en.notes: 耐久性 is the ability of a material or product to withstand long use and stress: 耐久性がある／高い, 耐久性に優れる, 耐久性のある素材. It is used mainly in product descriptions, engineering and construction. In everyday speech people often simply say 丈夫だ "sturdy" or 長持ちする "to last long".

examples[].german: It is a highly reliable system.
Information from the internet should be checked for reliability before you use it.
This survey had few participants, so the reliability of its results is low.
en.notes: 信頼性 is the reliability or credibility of systems, products, data or sources: 信頼性が高い／低い, データの信頼性, 情報の信頼性を確かめる. It is the abstract noun of 信頼 "trust"; about people one says 信頼できる人 or 頼りになる人 instead. Related is 信用 "trust in someone's word, creditworthiness".

examples[].german: We will improve productivity.
If meetings are too long, productivity drops.
Since I started working from home, I feel my productivity has gone up.
en.notes: 生産性 is productivity, the ratio of output to the labor or time invested: 生産性が高い／低い, 生産性を上げる／向上させる. It comes from economics but is also used for personal work (今日は生産性が低い "I'm unproductive today"). Related is 効率 "efficiency", which stresses the economical use of resources; 生産 alone means "production".

examples[].german: I had a valuable experience.
Please leave valuables at the front desk.
Thank you for giving me your valuable time despite how busy you are.
en.notes: 貴重 is a な-adjective meaning "valuable, precious", mainly because something is rare or hard to obtain: 貴重な経験, 貴重な資料, 貴重なご意見. 貴重品 are "valuables". In polite thank-you phrases, one often says 貴重なお時間をいただき. 大切, by contrast, emphasizes personal value, and 高価 the high price.

examples[].german: We aim for a sustainable society.
For sustainable fishing, we take care not to catch too many fish.
The current way of doing things is not sustainable.
en.notes: 持続可能 means "sustainable" in the sense of "able to be maintained over the long term" and is a term of environmental, economic and social policy. As a な-adjective it usually stands before a noun: 持続可能な社会, 持続可能な開発目標 (the SDGs); predicatively it is 持続可能だ／持続可能ではない. The opposite is 持続不可能; the simple "to last" is 持続する or 続く.

examples[].german: We use renewable energy.
The sun and wind are renewable resources.
In this country, more than half of the electricity is produced from renewable energy.
en.notes: 再生可能 means "renewable" and appears almost only in fixed technical terms, above all 再生可能エネルギー (sun, wind, water), often shortened to 再エネ in the media. In this combination it stands directly before the noun without な; otherwise it is used as a な-adjective: 再生可能な資源. 再生 alone means "playback, recycling, regeneration" (動画を再生する "to play a video").

examples[].german: Global warming is serious.
As warming progresses, summers keep getting hotter.
To slow global warming, I try not to use the car much.
en.notes: 温暖化 is warming, almost always in the sense of climate warming: 地球温暖化 "global warming", 温暖化対策 "measures against global warming", 温暖化が進む "warming progresses", 温暖化を防ぐ "to prevent warming". The verb form 温暖化する is possible but rarer than these noun combinations. The broader term 気候変動 "climate change" also covers extreme weather.

examples[].german: We will reduce CO2 emissions.
This car produces few exhaust emissions.
That factory was discharging dirty water into the river.
en.notes: 排出 means to release or expel something to the outside - especially exhaust gases, pollutants and wastewater: CO2の排出量 "CO2 emissions", 排出ガス "exhaust gas". As a transitive する-verb: 工場が有害な物質を排出する. It is a word from environmental science, engineering and medicine (excretion from the body). Taking out the garbage is ごみを出す in everyday speech, not 排出する.

examples[].german: Water pollution is a problem.
We checked whether the vegetables from this region are contaminated.
In big cities there are days when air pollution is severe.
en.notes: 汚染 is the pollution or contamination of the environment, food or substances by harmful substances: 大気汚染 "air pollution", 水質汚染 "water pollution", 土壌汚染 "soil contamination". As a する-verb it mostly appears in the passive or as a state: 川が汚染される／汚染されている. For everyday dirt on clothes or in a room, people say 汚れる or 汚い; 汚染 presupposes harmful substances and danger.

examples[].german: We strive to conserve the natural environment.
Cutting down trees is prohibited in order to preserve this forest.
I am in charge of maintaining the machines at the factory.
en.notes: 保全 means keeping something in good condition and safeguarding it - above all nature and the environment (環境保全, 自然保全) as well as facilities and machines (設備の保全 "maintenance"). It is a formal word from administration, law and engineering; in everyday speech people say 守る or 大切にする. Distinctions: 保護 "protection" from a danger (also of animals and people), 保存 "storage, preservation" (data, food).

examples[].german: Let's protect the ecosystem.
Fish from other countries are destroying the ecosystem of this lake.
Global warming is also having a major impact on marine ecosystems.
en.notes: 生態系 is the ecosystem, the interplay of all living things and their environment in an area: 海の生態系, 生態系を守る／壊す, 生態系に影響を与える. Originally a technical term, it is very common in news and environmental topics. Applied to business and IT, people usually say エコシステム. Related is 生態 "way of life (of animals and plants)".

examples[].german: We protect endangered species.
The dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago.
Public telephones may soon die out.
en.notes: 絶滅 is the complete extinction of a species or group; as an intransitive する-verb: 恐竜が絶滅した. Common combinations are 絶滅危惧種 "endangered species", 絶滅の危機にある and 絶滅寸前 "on the verge of extinction". Figuratively also used jokingly for things that are disappearing (絶滅しそうな職業). To actively wipe out is 絶滅させる; for diseases or crime, people more often say 撲滅.

examples[].german: I study marine life.
It is still not known whether there is life on Mars.
In high school, biology class was my favorite.
en.notes: 生物 is the scientific, neutral umbrella term for all living things (animals, plants, microorganisms): 海の生物, 生物の多様性. In everyday speech people tend to say 生き物, which sounds warmer and more child-friendly. As a school subject, 生物 means "biology" (生物の授業). Note: read as なまもの, the same kanji mean "raw, perishable food".

examples[].german: The cells divide.
The human body is made up of tens of trillions of cells.
Lack of sleep is said to be bad for brain cells.
en.notes: 細胞 is the biological cell: 細胞が分裂する "cells divide", がん細胞 "cancer cell", 脳細胞 "brain cell". Other meanings of "cell" are not translated with 細胞: a prison cell is 独房, a spreadsheet cell セル, a battery cell 電池. Derogatory and colloquial, 単細胞 means "simple-minded, simple" (単細胞な人).

examples[].german: It's a huge building.
I caught a huge fish in the sea.
A huge typhoon is approaching Japan.
en.notes: 巨大 is a な-adjective for things far larger than normal: 巨大な建物, 巨大な魚. It usually comes before a noun and also forms compounds such as 巨大地震 or 巨大企業. It is stronger and more literary than 大きい／大きな. For quantities (data, costs, time), 膨大 is more common, since 巨大 mainly describes spatial size.

examples[].german: Genetic research is advancing.
No genetically modified soybeans are used in this tofu.
Genes are also involved in whether someone gets sick easily.
en.notes: 遺伝子 is the gene as the carrier of hereditary information: 遺伝子の研究, 遺伝子検査 "genetic test", 遺伝子組み換え食品 "genetically modified food" (on packages often 遺伝子組換え). To be distinguished from this is 遺伝 "heredity" (遺伝する "to be inherited"); "It runs in the family" is more 遺伝だ than 遺伝子だ. DNA is also called DNA in Japanese.

examples[].german: Let's boost our immune system.
Once you've had measles, you become immune.
My brother is used to strict bosses, so he is immune to being scolded.
en.notes: 免疫 is immunity, the body's defense against pathogens: 免疫がある／できる, 免疫力 "immune strength" (免疫力を高める, 免疫力が下がる). Figuratively, 〜に免疫がある means to be hardened against something, and 〜に免疫がない means to have no experience with something and therefore react sensitively. The vaccination itself is called 予防接種 or ワクチン.

examples[].german: I will get a doctor's diagnosis.
After the test, I was diagnosed with influenza.
There is a health checkup at the company every year.
en.notes: 診断 is a medical diagnosis or assessment: 医者が診断する, 〜と診断される "to be diagnosed with …", 健康診断 "health checkup" (mandatory every year at companies), 診断書 "medical certificate". The examination in the consulting room itself is 診察; 診断 is the judgment that follows from it. Figuratively also used for tests and analyses: 性格診断 "personality test".

examples[].german: I am receiving treatment.
I'm currently getting a cavity treated at the dentist.
This illness can be cured if treated early.
en.notes: 治療 is the medical treatment of an illness or injury: 治療を受ける "to be treated", 病気を治療する, 歯の治療 "dental treatment", 治療中 "under treatment". It refers to the treatment process; getting well itself is 治る, recovery 回復. Minor first-aid measures are more often called 手当て.

examples[].german: Disease prevention is important.
I wash my hands often to prevent colds.
My child will get vaccinated next week.
en.notes: 予防 is prevention of illness, accidents or damage: 病気を予防する, 予防接種 "vaccination", 風邪の予防. Very common are 〜の予防に "to prevent ..." (予防にマスクをする) and 〜の予防になる "helps prevent ...". Distinction: 防止 "prevention, stopping" is used more for accidents and acts (事故防止, 犯罪防止), 予防 mainly for health.

examples[].german: I will reduce my calorie intake.
On hot days, please drink fluids frequently.
Japanese people are said to have a high salt intake.
en.notes: 摂取 is the intake of nutrients, fluids or other substances into the body: 栄養を摂取する, 水分を摂取する, 塩分の摂取量 "salt intake". It is a factual word from medicine, nutritional counseling and package labels; in everyday speech people say 食べる, 飲む or 栄養をとる. Formally and figuratively it is also used for absorbing culture and knowledge (外国の文化を摂取する).

examples[].german: Let's build up our stamina.
As I get older, my physical strength has been declining.
This work is physically demanding.
en.notes: 体力 is physical strength and stamina, including resistance to illness: 体力がある／ない, 体力をつける "to build up fitness", 体力が落ちる "to lose physical strength", 体力的にきつい "physically demanding". Pure muscle strength is 力 or 筋力, mental strength 気力. Figuratively also for the financial strength of a company (企業の体力).

examples[].german: I want to become mentally stronger.
He is someone with a spirit of challenge.
The spirit of helping one another remains in this town.
en.notes: 精神 denotes the mind as opposed to the body (肉体) as well as inner attitude and mindset: 精神力 "willpower", チャレンジ精神 "spirit of enterprise", 助け合いの精神 "spirit of mutual help". The form 精神的(な) "mental, psychological" is very common (精神的に疲れる). For the everyday "heart, mind", people more often say 心; a "ghost" in the sense of a specter is 幽霊.

examples[].german: Relaxing is important.
Take a deep breath before the interview and relax.
On weekends I relax at home listening to music.
en.notes: リラックス means relaxation and is almost always used as an intransitive する-verb: リラックスする "to relax", リラックスして "nice and loose", リラックスできる場所 "a place to relax". Often used as encouragement before exams or performances: もっとリラックスして. Related are くつろぐ "to make oneself comfortable" (more at home) and 落ち着く "to calm down".

examples[].german: We will analyze an enormous amount of data.
This construction work will cost an enormous amount.
This library has an enormous number of books.
en.notes: 膨大 is a な-adjective for huge quantities or volumes: 膨大なデータ, 膨大な時間, 膨大な費用, 膨大な数の本. It almost always stands before the noun and sounds literary. For the spatial size of a single object, 巨大 is used (巨大な建物), not 膨大. In conversation it corresponds roughly to すごくたくさんの.

examples[].german: He is mentally strong.
Mental strength is important for athletes.
The company set up a consultation desk for mental health.
en.notes: メンタル is used in Japanese mainly as a noun for one's mental state and resilience: メンタルが強い／弱い "mentally strong/weak", メンタルの強さ "mental strength". As a first element it appears in メンタルヘルス "mental health" and メンタルケア. It sounds modern and rather colloquial; more formal are 精神的(な) or 心. The use as a な-adjective (メンタルな問題) is rarer.

examples[].german: I have chronic pain.
This hospital is chronically short of nurses.
There is chronic traffic congestion every morning on the road in front of the station.
en.notes: 慢性的 means "chronic" - medically for long-lasting complaints (慢性的な頭痛, 慢性的な疲れ) and figuratively for persistent problems: 慢性的な人手不足 "chronic staff shortage", 慢性的な渋滞. It is used as a な-adjective before nouns or adverbially as 慢性的に. The base word 慢性 appears without な before disease names (慢性胃炎); the opposite is 急性 "acute".

examples[].german: It is an innovative technology.
Thanks to her innovative idea, sales doubled.
That party is not conservative but holds progressive views.
en.notes: 革新的 means "innovative, groundbreaking" for technology, ideas and products (革新的な技術／アイデア) and politically "reform-minded, progressive" - the opposite is 保守的 "conservative". It is rather a word of written and media language; in conversation one often says 新しい, 画期的 "groundbreaking" or イノベーティブ. The noun 革新 means "innovation, reform" (技術革新).

examples[].german: We are doing cutting-edge research.
This university is famous for its cutting-edge medical technology.
A building with a futuristic design has been built in front of the station.
en.notes: 先端的 means "state-of-the-art, at the forefront of development", above all in research and technology. More common than 先端的, however, are 最先端 and 先端 in fixed combinations: 最先端の技術, 先端技術 "cutting-edge technology"; 先端的 sounds somewhat stiff and literary. 先端 itself originally means "tip, extreme end" (棒の先端). Related is 先進的 "progressive, advanced".

examples[].german: We will draw up a comprehensive plan.
The two countries reached a comprehensive agreement on the economy.
We need to think about the problems comprehensively, not one at a time.
en.notes: 包括的 means "comprehensive, all-encompassing" and belongs to administrative, legal and technical language: 包括的な計画, 包括的な合意 "comprehensive agreement", 包括的に検討する "to examine comprehensively". It stresses that many individual areas are covered together. In everyday speech people more often say 全体的(な) or 全部まとめて. It has nothing to do with "inclusion" in the social sense.

examples[].german: We will implement it step by step.
Train fares will rise in stages from next year.
For beginners, I made a training menu that builds up step by step.
