en.notes: 段階的 means "step by step, in stages" and is mostly used adverbially as 段階的に (段階的に進める／導入する／引き上げる) or attributively as 段階的な. It is typical for plans, reforms, price increases and relaxations in news and company announcements; in everyday speech one says 少しずつ or だんだん instead. 徐々に means "gradually" in a smooth transition, while 段階的に emphasizes clearly separate stages. The base word is 段階 "step, phase".

examples[].german: Continuous effort is necessary.
If you don't study Japanese continuously, you forget it quickly.
This company has supported the local elementary school for a long time.
en.notes: 継続的 means "continuous, ongoing", that is, carried on over a long period without interruption: 継続的な努力／支援, 継続的に運動する. The base word is 継続 "continuation" (継続する, proverb 継続は力なり "persistence is power"). In everyday speech one often says 続けて or ずっと. Distinctions: 連続 "directly in a row" (三日連続), 定期的 "regularly, at fixed intervals".

examples[].german: There are latent risks.
I think there is still a lot of untapped demand in this region.
She has latent talent, but she herself hasn't noticed.
en.notes: 潜在的 means "latent, potential": something is present but (not yet) visible or used. As a な-adjective: 潜在的なリスク／需要／能力, adverbially 潜在的に. Typical in business, medicine and psychology, e.g. 潜在的な顧客 "potential customers"; related is 潜在意識 "the subconscious". The counterpart is 顕在化する "to come to the surface". It is rather written and formal; in conversation people often simply say 〜可能性がある.

examples[].german: There is a fatal flaw.
I made a critical mistake at the end of the game.
If this illness isn't treated early, it can become fatal.
en.notes: 致命的 literally means "fatal" (cf. 致命傷 "fatal wound"), but is mostly used figuratively: a mistake or flaw that ruins everything - 致命的なミス, 致命的な欠陥, 致命的なダメージ. As a predicate it often goes with にとって: 〜にとって致命的だ "fatal for ...". Common in business, IT and sports. When real danger to life is meant in everyday speech, people more often say 命に関わる.

examples[].german: Conclusive evidence was found.
This photo captures the decisive moment.
There is a decisive difference between their ways of thinking.
en.notes: 決定的 means "decisive, conclusive, final": something that clearly settles a matter and leaves no more doubt. Fixed combinations: 決定的な証拠 "conclusive evidence", 決定的な瞬間 "the decisive moment", 決定的な違い "the fundamental difference". As a predicate: 敗北が決定的になった "defeat became all but certain". Distinction: 重要 only means "important", whereas 決定的 means "tipping the balance".

examples[].german: I will respond flexibly.
He thinks very flexibly.
I stretch every morning to keep my body supple.
en.notes: 柔軟 is a な-adjective for flexibility in thinking and acting (柔軟な考え方, 柔軟に対応する) and for the suppleness of the body (体が柔軟だ, 柔軟性). 柔軟剤 is "fabric softener". 柔らかい is the everyday word for "soft" to the touch; 柔軟 sounds more formal. The opposite in thinking is, for example, 頭が固い or 頑固.

examples[].german: It is a symbolic building.
This incident is emblematic of today's society.
He is the symbolic player of the team.
en.notes: 象徴的 means "symbolic, emblematic": something stands for a larger idea. It is derived from 象徴 "symbol" (鳩は平和の象徴だ). Typical: 象徴的な建物／出来事／存在; adverbial 象徴的に表す "to express symbolically". Often it carries a nuance of "telling, characteristic": an event shows a larger development in miniature. Neutral to literary, frequent in news and commentary.

examples[].german: It is a typical Japanese house.
That is a typical mistake beginners make.
He is a typical morning person and gets up at five every day.
en.notes: 典型的 means "typical, classic": something shows all the characteristics of a category and is a prime example. Common: 典型的な例, 典型的なパターン, 典型的な日本人. Often slightly critical or ironic: 典型的なミス "a typical mistake". Similar is 代表的 "representative, leading", which sounds more positive (代表的な料理); colloquially, "typical" is often expressed with 〜らしい or ありがち.

examples[].german: It was an impressive speech.
Her bright smile was very memorable.
The last scene of the film was the most memorable.
en.notes: 印象的 means "impressive, memorable": something leaves a strong, lasting impression (印象). Attributively: 印象的な場面／言葉／笑顔. As a predicate, 〜が印象的だった is a very typical phrase in storytelling: "What stuck with me especially was ...". Distinction: 印象がいい means "to make a good impression" (to seem likable), whereas 印象的 only means "memorable" and need not be positive.

examples[].german: That's an attractive proposal.
He has a very charming way of speaking.
This town has many old buildings and is very appealing.
en.notes: 魅力的 means "attractive, appealing, fascinating" and comes from 魅力 "charm, appeal". It suits people (魅力的な人) as well as places, offers and conditions (魅力的な提案／条件／町). For people it refers more to their aura than to mere looks; for "pretty" people say きれい or かっこいい. Alternative: 〜に魅力がある. In business it also serves as a polite lead-in to a refusal: 魅力的なお話ですが...

examples[].german: I am working on it with great motivation.
The new employee is very eager and asks questions about everything.
This is an ambitious work by a young director.
en.notes: 意欲的 means "motivated, engaged, ambitious" and comes from 意欲 "will, drive". Very common adverbially: 意欲的に取り組む／学ぶ "to approach something with enthusiasm". Attributively: 意欲的な学生, 意欲的な作品 "an ambitious work". Typical in reports, evaluations and applications; in casual conversation one rather says やる気がある. 積極的 is similar, but stresses active behavior, whereas 意欲的 stresses the inner drive.

examples[].german: I will submit the notification.
When you move, please report it to the city office within 14 days.
If you take time off from the company, prior notification is required.
en.notes: 届け出 is a formal notification to an authority, school or company, e.g. 出生届 "birth registration" or 転居届 "change-of-address notification". Typical: 届け出をする／出す／提出する, with the recipient marked by に: 市役所に届け出る. On forms the spelling 届出 without で is also common. Distinction: with 申請 you ask for approval, with 届け出 you merely report a fact. Handing in or reporting something to the police is 警察に届ける.

examples[].german: I shouted, "Help!"
The children are shouting at the top of their voices toward the sea.
Recently, the importance of environmental problems has been loudly stressed.
en.notes: 叫ぶ means "to shout, to cry out loudly" - at high volume and often with strong emotion. What is shouted usually appears as a quotation with と: 「助けて！」と叫ぶ; the direction with に向かって. Distinctions: 大声を出す "to raise one's voice" is neutral, 怒鳴る "to yell at" is angry, 呼ぶ is "to call someone". Figuratively, 〜を叫ぶ means "to demand loudly", often in the passive: 改革の必要性が叫ばれている. Noun: 叫び（声） "cry".

examples[].german: My family gathers around the dining table.
The town where I was born is surrounded by mountains.
Please circle the correct answer.
en.notes: 囲む means "to surround, to encircle" and is transitive: 〜を囲む. Typical: 食卓を囲む "to sit around the table together", 正しい答えを丸で囲む "to circle the correct answer" (the means takes で). The passive is very common: 山に囲まれた町 "a town surrounded by mountains", ファンに囲まれる "to be surrounded by fans". There is no separate intransitive counterpart; 囲まれる is used. Noun: 囲み "border, box".

examples[].german: I will fill the hole.
The dog buried a bone in the garden.
Fill in the blanks and complete the sentences.
en.notes: 埋める means "to bury; to fill up, to fill in" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 埋まる "to be buried; to fill up". Literally: 穴を埋める, 骨を土に埋める. Figuratively very common: 空欄を埋める "to fill in the blanks", 差を埋める "to close a gap", 会場を埋める "to fill the hall", 赤字を埋める "to cover a deficit". The reading うずめる exists but is elevated or literary.

examples[].german: I overtook the car in front.
My son has already overtaken me in height.
In the marathon, I passed three more runners at the end.
en.notes: 追い越す means "to overtake, to pass" and is transitive: 前の車を追い越す. It combines 追う "to chase" and 越す "to exceed". Figuratively it means to surpass someone, e.g. 背で父を追い越す "to grow taller than one's father". Distinction: 追いつく only means "to catch up, to draw level"; 追い越す goes beyond that. 追い抜く is almost synonymous and especially popular in sports. Traffic sign: 追い越し禁止 "no overtaking".

examples[].german: I will choose a reliable method.
If things continue like this, his passing is almost certain.
Please be sure to hand the documents to the person themselves.
en.notes: 確実 is a な-adjective with two main focuses: "reliable" (確実な方法) and "certain, settled" (合格はほぼ確実だ). As an adverb, 確実に means "definitely, reliably" or "steadily" (確実に上達している). The opposite is 不確実. 確か expresses more subjective certainty and, at the start of a sentence, means "if I remember correctly"; 安全 means "safe, harmless".

en.meaning: to hold in one's arms; to embrace
examples[].german: I held the baby in my arms.
She came home holding a big bouquet of flowers.
I took a photo holding the cat.
en.notes: 抱く（だく） means "to take in one's arms, to hold in one's arms" and is transitive: 赤ちゃんを抱く. Common are 抱きしめる "to hug tightly" and the childish 抱っこする. For feelings and hopes, the same character is usually read いだく (夢を抱く, 不安を抱く) - a different, literary reading. Caution: between adults, だく can also mean "to sleep with someone"; a friendly hug is therefore more often ハグする or 抱き合う. For birds: 卵を抱く "to brood".

examples[].german: I point at the map as I explain.
The clock hands are pointing exactly to twelve.
What does "それ" in this sentence refer to?
en.notes: 指す means "to point at; to refer to" and is transitive. Literally: 指で地図を指す, 時計の針が三時を指す. In class: 先生に指される "to be called on". Abstractly very common: AはBを指す "A refers to / means B" - 「これ」は何を指していますか. Also in shogi: 将棋を指す. Do not confuse it with the homophones 刺す "to stab" and 差す (傘を差す "to put up an umbrella"). 指差す stresses pointing with the finger.

examples[].german: I released the bird.
It's dangerous, so don't let go of my hand.
Dogs must not be let off the leash in the park.
en.notes: 放す means "to let go, to release" and is transitive. Typical: 鳥を空に放す, 魚を川に放す "to release", 犬を放す "to let a dog off the leash", 手を放す "to let go of a hand". Be careful with the spelling: 離す (also はなす) means "to separate, to create distance" (目を離す "to look away"); with 手をはなす both spellings are common. 話す "to speak" is a pure homophone. Related: 手放す "to part with, to give up".

examples[].german: The child is running wild.
A drunk man rampaged at the station, and the police came.
The cat thrashed wildly during the injection, which was quite a struggle.
en.notes: 暴れる means "to rampage, to run riot, to flail wildly" and is intransitive (subject with が). It fits people (酔っ払いが暴れる), animals (馬が暴れる) and children who struggle violently or romp around. In sports it can also be positive: 試合で大暴れする "to shine in a big way". Distinction: 騒ぐ only means "to be loud, to make noise"; 暴れる includes violent movement or violence. Related: 暴力 "violence".

examples[].german: Water is leaking.
The company's secrets leaked onto the internet.
Music can be heard leaking in from the next room.
en.notes: 漏れる means "to leak, to seep through, to escape" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 漏らす. It applies to liquids, gas, light and sounds: 水が漏れる, ガスが漏れる, 隣から声が漏れる. Figuratively: 情報が漏れる "information leaks" (cf. 情報漏れ). It also means "to be left out": リストから名前が漏れる. In everyday writing it is often written in kana もれる.

en.meaning: to crush; to squash; to ruin; to kill (time)
examples[].german: I kill time.
Please mash the boiled potatoes with a fork.
My father was bad at management and ran the shop into the ground.
en.notes: 潰す means "to crush, to squash; to ruin" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 潰れる ("to be crushed; to go bankrupt"). Concretely: 空き缶を潰す, じゃがいもを潰す. Very common expressions: 時間を潰す "to kill time", 会社を潰す "to ruin a company", 顔を潰す "to make someone lose face". Distinction: 壊す is generally "to break", while 潰す emphasizes flattening or completely destroying something. Often also written in kana, つぶす.

en.meaning: to savor; to taste; to experience
examples[].german: I savor the food.
For the first time, I tasted the bitterness of losing.
In Kyoto, I would like to take in Japanese culture at leisure.
en.notes: 味わう means "to taste, to savor, to enjoy" and is transitive. It emphasizes conscious, slow tasting: 料理をゆっくり味わう. Figuratively it means "to experience something intensely" - negative things too: 喜びを味わう, 悔しさを味わう, 苦しみを味わう. Unlike 食べる "to eat" and 楽しむ "to have fun", the focus is on conscious experience. Polite invitation: どうぞ味わってください. Noun: 味わい "flavor, charm".

en.meaning: to chop; to mince; to engrave
examples[].german: I chop the green onions.
I engrave my teacher's words in my heart and do my best every day.
The names of the two were carved into the tree trunk.
en.notes: 刻む means "to cut finely, to chop; to carve" and is transitive. In the kitchen: ネギ／キャベツを刻む "to chop finely" (cf. みじん切り "finely minced"). Engraving: 石に文字を刻む, 木に名前を刻む. Figuratively: 心に刻む "to engrave in one's memory", 時計が時を刻む "the clock ticks away the time", リズムを刻む. Distinction: 切る is generally "to cut", while 刻む means many small, even cuts or notches.

examples[].german: I pour the tea.
He puts a lot of effort into his children's education.
This river flows into the Pacific Ocean.
en.notes: 注ぐ（そそぐ） means "to pour" and is mostly transitive: カップにお茶を注ぐ, 花に水を注ぐ. Intransitive for rivers: 川が海に注ぐ "flows into the sea". Figuratively very common: 〜に力を注ぐ "to put a lot of effort into ...", 愛情を注ぐ, 注目が注がれる. When pouring drinks, the same characters are often read つぐ (ビールをつぐ) - つぐ is more everyday, そそぐ somewhat more elevated and the usual one for all figurative meanings.

examples[].german: I spilled some water.
The child spilled juice on the table.
My father is always complaining about work.
en.notes: 零す means "to spill, to scatter" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 零れる "to overflow, to fall out". It is almost always written in kana: こぼす. Typical: コーヒーをこぼす, ご飯をこぼす, 涙をこぼす "to shed tears". Second important meaning: 愚痴をこぼす "to grumble, to complain". Distinction: 落とす is "to drop" an object, while こぼす emphasizes sloshing out or scattering of liquid, crumbs, etc.

examples[].german: Please explain specifically.
Please give a concrete example.
The travel plans have not been decided in concrete terms yet.
en.notes: 具体的 is a な-adjective with -的: 具体的な例, 具体的に説明する. The opposite is 抽象的 "abstract". Related are 具体例 "concrete example" and 具体化する "to make concrete". The word is very common in school and at work when asking for details: もう少し具体的に言うと…

en.meaning: to tilt; to incline; to devote
examples[].german: I tilt the glass.
Everyone listened attentively to his story.
She is devoting her passion to her research.
en.notes: 傾ける means "to tilt, to hold at an angle, to tip" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 傾く "to lean, to stand crooked". Concretely: 首を傾ける "to tilt one's head to the side", 瓶を傾ける. Very common figuratively: 耳を傾ける "to listen attentively", 〜に情熱／力を傾ける "to pour one's energy into ...". グラスを傾ける can, in elevated style, also mean "to have a drink". Tilting one's head in doubt is usually 首をかしげる.

en.meaning: to break down; to destroy; to throw off balance; to break (money)
examples[].german: My health has worsened.
Excuse me, could you break a 10,000-yen bill for me?
Please sit comfortably and make yourself at ease.
en.notes: 崩す means "to bring down, to demolish; to throw out of balance" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 崩れる. Very common expressions: 体調を崩す "to fall ill", バランスを崩す "to lose one's balance", 一万円札を崩す "to break a 10,000-yen bill", 足を崩す "to sit comfortably" (out of the formal seiza position). Concretely: 壁を崩す, 山を崩す. Also: 字を崩して書く "to write in cursive style".

examples[].german: The building collapsed.
I hear the weather will turn bad from the afternoon.
My makeup smeared because of sweat.
en.notes: 崩れる means "to collapse, to fall apart; to lose shape" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 崩す. Concretely: 建物／崖が崩れる, cf. 土砂崩れ "landslide". Very common for weather: 天気が崩れる "the weather turns bad". Also: 化粧が崩れる "makeup smears", 形が崩れる, 計画が崩れる. Distinction: 壊れる is said of devices and objects, while 崩れる emphasizes the breakdown of a structure or order.

examples[].german: I gain experience.
We load the luggage onto the truck and then set off.
Books are stacked high on the desk.
en.notes: 積む means "to pile up, to load; to accumulate" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 積もる "to pile up" (snow, dust). Literally: 箱を積む "to stack boxes", トラックに荷物を積む "to load onto the truck" (destination with に). Figuratively: 経験を積む "to gain experience", 練習を積む "to practice a lot". The resulting state with 〜てある: 本が積んである. Compounds: 積み重ねる "to stack up, to build up step by step", 積み木 "building blocks".

examples[].german: Snow has piled up.
Because it hasn't been cleaned for a long time, dust has accumulated on the shelf.
We hadn't seen each other for a long time, so we had a lot to catch up on.
en.notes: 積もる means "to pile up, to settle" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 積む. Typical for snow and dust: 雪が積もる, ほこりが積もる. Figuratively: 積もる話 "a lot to talk about (after a long time)" and the proverb 塵も積もれば山となる "many a little makes a mickle". The rarer transitive meaning "to estimate" lives on mainly in 見積もる／見積もり "cost estimate".

examples[].german: The clothes shrank.
The gap with the first place has gradually narrowed.
I nearly got hit by a car, and it took years off my life.
en.notes: 縮む means "to shrink, to contract" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 縮める "to shorten". Typical: 洗濯で服が縮む "to shrink in the wash", 差が縮む "the gap narrows". Idiomatic after a scare: 寿命が縮む "it took years off my life". Opposite: 伸びる "to stretch, to become longer". The formal Sino-Japanese word for reduction is 縮小.

examples[].german: My hair has grown.
Sales grew greatly this year.
Eat quickly, or the ramen will get soggy.
en.notes: 伸びる means "to grow, to get longer, to stretch; to make progress" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 伸ばす. Used for hair, nails, body height (背が伸びる) and plants. Figuratively: 売り上げ／成績が伸びる "to rise, to improve". Colloquially: ラーメンが伸びる "the noodles get soggy". For extending or postponing in time, the spelling 延びる is used (会議が延びる, 締め切りが延びる).

examples[].german: I stretch out my hand.
Since entering university, I've been growing my hair out.
This teacher is good at developing his students' strengths.
en.notes: 伸ばす means "to stretch, to let grow longer; to develop" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 伸びる. Literally: 手を伸ばす "to stretch out one's hand", 髪を伸ばす "to grow one's hair out", 背筋を伸ばす "to straighten up". Figuratively: 才能／売り上げを伸ばす "to develop, to increase"; 足を伸ばす also means "to go a bit farther". For extending or postponing in time, the spelling 延ばす is mostly used (締め切りを延ばす).

examples[].german: I tie it with a string.
I bundled the old magazines together, tied them up, and put them out for disposal.
I don't like being bound by company rules.
en.notes: 縛る means "to tie, to bind, to tie up" and is transitive: 〜を紐／縄で縛る. Concretely: 古新聞を紐で縛る "to tie up old newspapers", 犯人を縛る. Figuratively very common in the passive: 規則に縛られる "to be bound by rules", 時間に縛られない生活 "a life not bound by time". Distinction: 結ぶ means "to knot, to tie together" (a bow, shoelaces), while 縛る means wrapping firmly to hold something together or immobilize it.

examples[].german: I will conclude a contract.
Let's tie our shoelaces tightly before we run.
This bridge connects the island with the town.
en.notes: 結ぶ means "to tie, to knot; to connect; to conclude" and is transitive. Literally: 靴ひも／リボンを結ぶ, 髪を結ぶ. Connecting: AとBを結ぶ, e.g. 東京と大阪を結ぶ新幹線. Concluding: 契約／条約を結ぶ. Other expressions: 実を結ぶ "to bear fruit" (also figuratively), 口を結ぶ "to press one's lips together". Opposite: ほどく "to untie". Distinction from 縛る: 結ぶ is knotting and linking, 縛る is tying up tightly.

examples[].german: Let's participate actively.
She proactively talks to everyone.
Our company is proactive about hiring foreigners.
en.notes: 積極的 is a な-adjective meaning "active on one's own initiative, proactive": 積極的に参加する, 積極的な性格. With に, 〜に積極的だ means "to be engaged in, open to something". It is usually meant positively and does not mean "aggressive". 熱心 emphasizes zeal, whereas 積極的 emphasizes that one takes the initiative oneself. The opposite is 消極的.

examples[].german: I solve the problem.
I want to clear up the misunderstanding quickly.
This puzzle is hard, and I just can't solve it.
en.notes: 解く means "to solve; to untie" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 解ける "to be solved, to come undone" (この問題は解けない). In everyday speech mainly for tasks with an answer: 問題／パズル／なぞを解く. Figuratively: 誤解を解く "to clear up a misunderstanding". For untying cords, ほどく is often read or written. Distinction: "solving" a problem in the sense of a difficulty is more 解決する.

examples[].german: I melt the butter.
Please dissolve the medicine in water and drink it.
The spring sunshine melts the snow little by little.
en.notes: 溶かす means "to melt, to dissolve" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 溶ける. It applies to solids through heat (バター／チョコレート／雪を溶かす) and to dissolving in a liquid, with the target marked by に: 砂糖をお湯に溶かす. For metal, 融かす is also seen in technical writing, but in everyday use 溶かす suffices. Do not confuse it with the homophone とかす "to comb" (髪をとかす, mostly in kana).

examples[].german: English is mixed into Japanese.
Gray hair has started to appear in my father's hair.
Snow has begun to mix with the rain.
en.notes: 混じる means "to mix, to be mixed in" and is intransitive: the added element takes が, the whole takes に - 日本語に英語が混じる, 髪に白髪が混じる. The transitive counterpart is 混ぜる "to mix". 混ざる is almost synonymous; 混じる often stresses that individual elements remain recognizable. For people, 交じる is usually written: 大人に交じって子どもも走る. As a suffix: 〜混じり (雨混じりの雪, 冗談混じりに).

examples[].german: I pack my things into the bag.
Excuse me, could you move over a little?
Let's work out the details at next week's meeting.
en.notes: 詰める means "to stuff in, to pack (full); to move closer together; to work out" and is transitive; the intransitive counterpart is 詰まる. Literally: カバンに荷物を詰める, 箱にお菓子を詰める (destination with に). Making room: もう少し詰めてください "Please move over a little". Abstractly: 話／細かい点を詰める "to sort out details". As an auxiliary: 思い詰める "to brood too much", 問い詰める "to press with questions". Related: 缶詰 "canned food".

en.meaning: to be clogged; to be packed; to be at a loss
examples[].german: The drainpipe is clogged.
My schedule is packed this week.
I was asked suddenly and was lost for an answer.
en.notes: 詰まる means "to be clogged; to be full; to be stuck" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 詰める. Clogging: 排水管／トイレが詰まる, 鼻が詰まる "stuffy nose". Full: 予定がぎっしり詰まっている, 思い出が詰まったアルバム. Getting stuck: 言葉／答えに詰まる "to be at a loss for an answer", 息が詰まる "to be unable to breathe; to feel suffocated". Related: 行き詰まる "to reach a dead end".

en.meaning: to paint; to spread; to apply
examples[].german: I am painting the wall.
I spread butter on bread and eat it.
I applied ointment to the wound.
en.notes: 塗る means "to apply a layer onto a surface": the material takes を, the surface takes に – 壁にペンキを塗る, パンにバターを塗る, 顔にクリームを塗る, 傷に薬を塗る. For painting a picture, 描く is used instead; 塗る is only painting over or spreading on. There is no intransitive counterpart; "is painted" is 塗ってある. Related are 塗り薬 "ointment" and the sign ペンキ塗りたて "wet paint".

examples[].german: I dry my hair.
I dried my rain-soaked shoes in front of the heater.
I always dry the laundry in the dryer.
en.notes: 乾かす means "to dry, to let dry" and is transitive: 〜を乾かす; the intransitive counterpart is 乾く "to become dry". Typical: 髪をドライヤーで乾かす, 洗濯物を乾かす, 濡れた靴を乾かす. Distinction: 干す means "to hang or lay out to dry" (in sun or wind), whereas 乾かす stresses the result of becoming dry, also with a hair dryer or tumble dryer. Do not confuse it with 渇く "to be thirsty" (喉が渇く).

examples[].german: The cherry blossoms have fallen.
When the TV is on, I get distracted and can't study.
When the festival ended, people dispersed, each to their own home.
en.notes: 散る means "to fall (off), to scatter" and is intransitive (subject with が); the transitive counterpart is 散らす. Classic for blossoms and leaves: 桜が散る - strongly associated with transience. Also: 人々が散っていく "to disperse", 火花が散る "sparks fly" and, very common, 気が散る "to be distracted". Distinction: 落ちる is the general "to fall down", whereas 散る means many pieces scattering. Note: despite the -iru ending, it is a godan verb.

examples[].german: My efforts paid off.
The weather was good this year, so the rice ripened well.
My long unrequited love has finally come true.
en.notes: 実る means "to bear fruit, to ripen; to pay off" and is intransitive (subject with が); it comes from 実 "fruit". Literally: 稲が実る, リンゴが実る. Figuratively very common: 努力が実る "effort pays off", 恋が実る "love is returned". Well-known proverb: 実るほど頭を垂れる稲穂かな - the riper the ear of rice, the lower it bows (humility). Similar, somewhat more formal: 実を結ぶ.

examples[].german: A sprout has come out.
Please don't eat the sprouts of potatoes.
He worked hard for ten years, but his big break never came.
en.notes: 芽 is the "sprout, shoot, bud" - the first thing that grows from a seed or branch. Typical verbs: 芽が出る／芽を出す "to sprout, to bud", plus 新芽 "young shoot". Figuratively: 才能の芽 "the seeds of talent", 悪の芽を摘む "to nip evil in the bud", 芽が出ない "to not make a breakthrough" (especially artists, athletes). Distinction: つぼみ is the flower bud shortly before blooming. Homophone: 目 "eye".

examples[].german: A passive attitude is not good.
He is always passive in meetings and hardly speaks up.
The government is reluctant about that plan.
en.notes: 消極的 is a な-adjective for a lack of initiative or a hesitant attitude: 消極的な態度, 消極的な性格. 〜に消極的だ means "to be reluctant, not very willing toward something". It is usually a negative evaluation. A quiet character alone is more likely 大人しい, shyness 恥ずかしがり屋. The opposite is 積極的.

examples[].german: The tree's roots are deep.
He has a sharp tongue, but at heart he is a kind person.
Are you still holding a grudge about that old matter?
en.notes: 根 is the "root" - literally of plants (木の根, 根を張る "to put down roots") and on the body (歯の根). Figuratively: 問題の根は深い "the problem runs deep", 根に持つ "to hold a grudge", 根はいい人 "a good person at heart". In compounds it is often read こん: 大根 "daikon radish", 根気 "perseverance". Colloquially, people also say 根っこ for plant roots.

examples[].german: It is a tree with a thick trunk.
The children are pressing their ears against the tree trunk.
The typhoon knocked a tree down, and the trunk broke in two.
en.notes: 幹 is the "tree trunk" - the main part of a tree between the roots (根) and the branches (枝). Typical: 太い幹, 幹が太い. As a standalone word it is almost always literal; the figurative meaning "core, main part" is found mainly in compounds: 幹線道路 "main road", 新幹線 "Shinkansen" (literally "new trunk line"), 幹事 "organizer (e.g. of a party)", 根幹 "foundation".

examples[].german: Let's protect the forests.
About two thirds of Japan's land area is forest.
On weekends, I go hiking to take a forest bath.
en.notes: 森林 "forest, woodland" is a Sino-Japanese word made of 森 and 林 and is typical of news, statistics and environmental topics: 森林破壊 "deforestation", 森林資源, 森林浴 "forest bathing". In everyday speech one usually says 森 (a large, dense forest) or 林 (a small wood, grove). 森林 refers more to forest as an area or ecosystem. About two thirds of Japan is forested.

examples[].german: I went to see the waterfall.
After running, sweat poured off me like a waterfall.
This waterfall is nearly a hundred meters high.
en.notes: 滝 is a "waterfall"; famous waterfalls have it in their names, such as 華厳の滝. Typical: 滝を見に行く, 滝が落ちる. Figuratively: 滝のような汗／雨 "sweat or rain in torrents". In a religious context there is 滝に打たれる "to stand under a waterfall for purification". The Sino-Japanese word 瀑布 is purely literary.

examples[].german: There is a deep valley.
Looking down into the valley from the bridge, I felt a little scared.
Life has its ups and downs.
en.notes: 谷 is a "valley" or "gorge" - a depression between mountains, often with a river: 深い谷, 谷底 "valley floor", 谷川 "mountain stream". The opposite is 山. Figuratively: 山あり谷ありの人生 "a life with ups and downs", 景気の谷 "an economic trough". Common in place names and family names, where it is sometimes read や (渋谷). A wide basin surrounded by mountains, by contrast, is a 盆地.

examples[].german: Please be careful of the cliff.
After the heavy rain, there was a landslide near the road.
If we lose, we have nothing left - it's a match with our backs to the wall.
en.notes: 崖 is a "cliff, steep face" - an almost vertical wall of rock or earth. Typical: 崖から落ちる, 崖の上／下, 崖崩れ "landslide" (common in bad-weather news). Figuratively: 崖っぷち "on the brink of the abyss", e.g. 崖っぷちのチーム "a team with its back to the wall". Distinction: 坂 is a walkable slope, 崖 is almost vertical and dangerous; 断崖 is the literary "sheer cliff".

examples[].german: We crossed the desert.
In the desert, the temperature difference between day and night is very large.
Deserts are spreading because of global warming.
en.notes: 砂漠 is a "desert", made of 砂 "sand" and 漠 "vast, barren". Typical: サハラ砂漠, 砂漠を横断する, 砂漠化 "desertification". Figuratively: 都会の砂漠 "the big city as a desert" (loneliness). The older spelling 沙漠 is still occasionally seen. Do not confuse it with 砂浜 "sandy beach" and 砂場 "sandbox".

examples[].german: There are many volcanoes in Japan.
The volcano erupted, and ash fell on the town.
Do you know that Mt. Fuji is also a volcano?
en.notes: 火山 is a "volcano", from 火 "fire" and 山 "mountain". Typical: 火山が噴火する "to erupt", 活火山 "active volcano", 火山灰 "volcanic ash". Japan lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire and has over a hundred active volcanoes; 富士山 is one of them. The country's many 温泉 "hot springs" are also due to volcanism. Neutral, used in everyday speech as well as in the news.

examples[].german: The volcano erupted.
Because of the eruption, flights were canceled.
Mt. Fuji last erupted in 1707.
en.notes: 噴火 is the eruption of a volcano. As an intransitive する-verb, the volcano is the subject with が: 火山が噴火する. Common compounds are 大噴火 "huge eruption", 噴火警報 "eruption warning" and 噴火口 "crater". For the outbreak of diseases, fire or conflict, 噴火 is not used; one says, for example, 発生する or 起こる.

examples[].german: A tsunami warning was issued.
There is no danger of a tsunami from this earthquake.
A tsunami may come, so please flee to high ground.
en.notes: 津波 (literally "harbor wave") is the word that was adopted into other languages as "tsunami". Typical are 津波が来る／押し寄せる, 津波警報 "tsunami warning" and the weaker 津波注意報 "tsunami advisory". After every earthquake, the news says 津波の心配はありません "there is no danger of a tsunami". Ordinary high waves during a storm are called 高波 or 大波 instead.

examples[].german: Let's work efficiently.
To use my time efficiently, I make a plan every morning.
This method is efficient, but it costs a little money.
en.notes: 効率的 is a な-adjective formed with -的 from 効率 "efficiency": 効率的な方法, 効率的に働く. The opposite is 非効率的. In conversation one also very often hears 効率がいい／悪い. 便利, by contrast, means "handy, convenient" and does not refer to the ratio of effort to result.

examples[].german: The flood caused damage.
The river overflowed in the heavy rain, and the town was flooded.
Modern people live in a flood of information.
en.notes: 洪水 is a flood, mostly because a river overflows its banks after heavy rain. Typical: 洪水が起きる, 町が洪水になる, with the cause marked by で: 洪水で家が流された. In the news one often hears 浸水 "being under water" (houses, streets) alongside it. Figuratively, 〜の洪水 means a flood of something, e.g. 情報の洪水 "information overload" or 車の洪水.

examples[].german: The drought continues.
Vegetable prices rose because of the drought.
That country suffered a severe drought last year.
en.notes: 干ばつ is a long dry period in which rain fails to come and fields dry out. It is originally written 旱魃; because these kanji are not everyday kanji, newspapers write the mixed form 干ばつ. Typical: 干ばつが続く, 干ばつが起きる, 干ばつの被害, 干ばつに苦しむ. For merely dry weather, everyday speech uses 雨が降らない or 水不足 "water shortage".

examples[].german: Please check the evacuation site.
Because a typhoon was coming, we took shelter in a nearby elementary school.
At the company, there is an evacuation drill once a year.
en.notes: 避難 is moving to a safe place to escape danger, especially in disasters. As an intransitive する-verb the destination takes に or へ: 学校に避難する "to take shelter in the school". Important compounds: 避難所 "emergency shelter", 避難場所 "assembly point", 避難訓練 "evacuation drill", 避難指示 "evacuation order". Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 非難 "criticism, blame".

examples[].german: The rescue team has arrived.
A person who got lost in the mountains was rescued by helicopter.
A man rescued a child who was drowning in the sea.
en.notes: 救助 is the rescue of people from acute danger, for example in accidents, at sea or after disasters. As a transitive する-verb: 人を救助する; from the viewpoint of those affected, usually in the passive: 救助される "to be rescued". Compounds: 救助隊 "rescue team", 人命救助 "life-saving"; 救助を求める means "to call for help". In everyday speech people say the simpler 助ける; 救助 sounds like an official operation and news reports. Do not confuse it with 救急 "emergency" as in 救急車.

examples[].german: We prevent crime.
Crime has been increasing in this town recently.
Using someone else's password without permission is a crime.
en.notes: 犯罪 is the general term for criminal acts, often as a social phenomenon. Typical: 犯罪を犯す "to commit a crime", 犯罪を防ぐ, 犯罪が増える／減る, 犯罪に巻き込まれる "to get caught up in a crime"; the perpetrator is 犯罪者. For a specific individual case, people usually say 事件, and 罪 is more "guilt, sin" in the moral sense.

examples[].german: The suspect was arrested.
The police released a photo of the suspect's face.
The suspect is reported to have said, "I was in financial trouble."
en.notes: 容疑者 is a person suspected of a crime who is under police investigation - a typical news word. In reports it even stands like a title directly after the name: 山田容疑者. Typical: 容疑者を逮捕する, 容疑者が逃げる, 容疑者が容疑を認める "the suspect confesses". After indictment, the same person is called 被告 "defendant"; 犯人, by contrast, is the actual perpetrator.

examples[].german: We help the victims.
Victims of fraud are often elderly people.
We spoke with the family of the accident victim.
en.notes: 被害者 is someone who has suffered harm or wrong: a victim of crime, fraud, accidents or disasters. The opposite is 加害者 "perpetrator, offender". The underlying word is 被害 "damage": 被害に遭う "to become a victim", 被害を受ける. For fatalities in disasters, people more often say 犠牲者; 被害者 stresses the harm suffered, not necessarily death.

examples[].german: I agree with that proposal.
"How about ramen tonight?" "Sounds good!"
My father did not approve of my studying abroad.
en.notes: 賛成 means to agree with a proposal or an opinion. What one is in favor of takes に: 〜に賛成する, 〜に賛成です. The opposite is 反対: 賛成ですか、反対ですか "Are you for or against?" In casual conversation, a short 賛成！ "Count me in!" is enough. 賛成 is the neutral everyday word, also used in votes; 同意 "consent" sounds more formal and contractual.

examples[].german: We will find a compromise.
When looking for a home, I compromised on the distance from the station.
That chef never compromises on the taste of his food.
en.notes: 妥協 means giving way and meeting in the middle to reach an agreement. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜と妥協する "to compromise with someone", 〜で妥協する "to settle for something". Fixed expression: 妥協点 "common ground". 妥協 often sounds slightly negative in the sense of "making concessions"; 妥協しない "to make no compromises" is therefore praise for high standards.

examples[].german: I will apply for a visa.
I'd like to apply for paid leave. What should I do?
Please submit the application form at the counter of City Hall.
en.notes: 申請 is an official application to an authority, company or institution, on which a decision is then made. As a transitive する-verb: ビザを申請する, with the recipient marked by に: 市役所に申請する. Compounds: 申請書 "application form", 申請中 "application in progress". For registrations to courses or events, one says 申し込み, and for applying for a job 応募 - 申請 is the formal application for permission or benefits.

examples[].german: The education system will change.
I used the childcare leave system and took three months off.
From next year, a work-from-home system will be introduced at the company.
en.notes: 制度 is an institutional system or official arrangement, such as 教育制度, 社会保障制度 or 育児休暇の制度. Typical are 制度を導入する "to introduce", 制度を利用する "to use" and 制度が変わる. A single rule is 規則 or ルール; 仕組み describes more the mechanism of how something works. The word is neutral but especially common in the news and official language.

examples[].german: Please make a rational judgment.
This room is small, but the storage is designed efficiently.
His explanation was rational and everyone was convinced.
en.notes: 合理的 is a な-adjective and means "reasonable, rationally justified" (合理的な判断, 合理的な説明), but also "efficient, without waste" (合理的な設計). Related is 合理化 "rationalization"; the opposite is 不合理. 論理的, by contrast, refers to the logic of an argument, 合理的 more to practical reason and efficiency.

examples[].german: I got permission.
Please do not enter this room without permission.
The school does not allow part-time jobs.
en.notes: 許可 is permission or official approval. Typical: 許可をもらう／得る "to receive", 許可を出す "to grant", 許可を求める "to ask for permission", 〜を許可する; "without permission" is 許可なく or 無断で. Compounds: 許可証 "permit", 営業許可 "business license". The opposite is 禁止. Between friends 許可 sounds very formal – there one simply asks いい？

examples[].german: Photography is prohibited.
Playing ball games is prohibited in this park.
From this month, the company has banned smoking inside the building.
en.notes: 禁止 is an explicit prohibition. On signs it usually comes without a particle after what is prohibited: 駐車禁止, 立入禁止, 撮影禁止, 喫煙禁止. As a verb: 〜を禁止する, often in the passive 〜は禁止されている. The opposite is 許可. In conversation, prohibitions are phrased more softly with 〜てはいけません or 〜ないでください; 禁止 sounds official and strict.

examples[].german: There is a speed limit.
This plan has no limit on data usage.
The doctor told me to limit my salt intake.
en.notes: 制限 is a limitation of quantity, time, age or speed. Typical: 制限がある, 制限を設ける, 〜を制限する; compounds: 速度制限, 年齢制限, 制限時間 "time limit", 無制限 "unlimited". Distinction: 禁止 forbids something entirely, 制限 allows it only up to a limit. The personal limit of endurance ("I'm at my limit") is 限界 instead.

examples[].german: I committed a traffic violation.
I paid a fine for speeding.
Using a dictionary during the exam is against the rules.
en.notes: 違反 is a violation of rules, laws or contracts. What is violated takes に: 法律に違反する, ルールに違反する. Very common as compounds: 交通違反, スピード違反, 駐車違反, 契約違反, ルール違反; colloquially: それ、ルール違反だよ "That's against the rules!" 違反 refers to rule-breaking; serious offenses are called 犯罪.

examples[].german: I will receive punishment.
Whoever loses the game has to sing a song as a penalty.
As punishment for forgetting my homework, I was made to clean the classroom.
en.notes: 罰 is a punishment as a consequence of misbehavior, especially in upbringing, games or in the moral sense. Typical: 罰を受ける "to be punished", 罰を与える "to punish", 〜の罰として "as punishment for ..."; the verb is 罰する. 罰ゲーム is the forfeit for the loser of a game, and in 罰が当たる "to suffer divine retribution" it is read ばち. Fines are 罰金, judicial punishments 刑.

examples[].german: I build trust.
He is highly trusted by his boss.
It is hard to regain trust once it has been lost.
en.notes: 信頼 is trust based on experience - one relies on someone. Typical: 信頼を得る "to gain trust", 信頼を築く "to build", 信頼を失う "to lose", 〜を信頼する, 信頼できる人, 信頼関係 "relationship of trust". The similar 信用 stresses credibility and creditworthiness (often in business), and 信じる is the general "to believe".

examples[].german: I respect my teacher.
The person I respect is my father.
Being able to help people in need right away - I admire that.
en.notes: 尊敬 is high regard for someone because of their character or achievements. As a transitive する-verb it mostly appears in the ている-form: 先生を尊敬している. Very typical is 尊敬する人 "role model", a classic question in job interviews. In grammar, 尊敬語 denotes respectful honorific language. The opposite is 軽蔑 "contempt".

examples[].german: I feel jealousy.
She gets jealous just from him talking to other girls.
I hate that I get envious of my colleague's success.
en.notes: 嫉妬 is jealousy or resentful envy. As a する-verb the person or thing takes に: 〜に嫉妬する "to be jealous/envious of someone"; also 嫉妬心 and 嫉妬深い "very jealous". For jealousy in relationships one colloquially often says やきもちを焼く. うらやましい, by contrast, is harmless, benevolent envy ("enviable"); 嫉妬 sounds stronger and more negative.

examples[].german: I hold a grudge.
I have nothing against him, but I cannot forgive what happened this time.
You shouldn't do anything that would make others resent you.
en.notes: 恨み is deep-seated resentment toward someone who has wronged you - longer-lasting than acute anger (怒り). Typical: 恨みを持つ／抱く "to hold a grudge", 〜に恨みがある, 恨みを買う "to incur someone's resentment", 恨みを晴らす "to take revenge". The related verb is 恨む. Jokingly one says 食べ物の恨みは恐ろしい: someone who takes your food will never be forgiven.

examples[].german: I regret it.
I regret not having studied more when I was a student.
It is better to do something and regret it than not to do it and regret it.
en.notes: 後悔 is regret about something one did or failed to do. As a する-verb: 〜を後悔する, often with こと: 言ったことを後悔している. In everyday speech the same feeling is expressed with 〜ばよかった (もっと勉強すればよかった). Proverb: 後悔先に立たず "it is no use crying over spilt milk". 後悔 does not fit regretful apologies to others - for that people say 残念です or 申し訳ありません.

examples[].german: It was an unexpected result.
I was surprised that he is good at cooking.
This restaurant is cheap, yet surprisingly tasty, isn't it?
en.notes: 意外 is a な-adjective for things that differ from what was expected: 意外な結果, 〜なんて意外だ. Very common in conversation is the adverb 意外と／意外に "surprisingly, actually quite": 意外とおいしい. The surprise can be positive or negative. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 以外 "except". Similar is 予想外 "unforeseen".

en.meaning: to become impatient; to get flustered
examples[].german: Please don't get impatient.
I ran short of time during the exam and got flustered.
I realized on the train that my wallet was gone and I really panicked.
en.notes: 焦る describes inner restlessness and hurry when time is short or something threatens to go wrong. It is intransitive and takes no object: 時間がなくて焦る. Very common as soothing advice: 焦らないで, 焦らなくていいよ "no rush, take it easy". Colloquially it can also mean a brief scare: 財布がなくて焦った. Distinction: 急ぐ is the outward act of hurrying, 焦る is the feeling; the noun is 焦り.

examples[].german: Please don't shout.
As a child, I was yelled at by my father for misbehaving.
A customer was yelling at a clerk in the shop, and I was startled.
en.notes: 怒鳴る means to shout at someone loudly and angrily. The person shouted at is marked with に: 部下に怒鳴る; from the victim's perspective, the passive: 父に怒鳴られた. Distinction: 叫ぶ is generally "to scream, to cry out" (also from fear or joy), 怒る is "to get angry, to scold" without necessarily being loud; 怒鳴る is always loud and aggressive. Intensified: 怒鳴りつける.

en.meaning: to be appalled; to be amazed
examples[].german: I was appalled.
I was so appalled by his excuse that I could say nothing.
When my mother saw the messy room, she gave me an exasperated look.
en.notes: 呆れる expresses stunned amazement, almost always with criticism: one is dumbfounded, fed up, or can only shake one's head at someone's behavior. The trigger is marked with に: 彼の態度に呆れる. Typical: 呆れて物が言えない "I am at a loss for words", 呆れた顔 "an exasperated look". Often written in kana (あきれる). Unlike the neutral 驚く, 呆れる carries disapproval; do not confuse it with 飽きる "to get tired of".

examples[].german: I feel miserable.
I failed in front of everyone and felt utterly humiliated.
Waiting alone in the rain without an umbrella, I felt pathetic.
en.notes: 惨め is a na-adjective for a wretched, miserable state that arouses pity or shame. Typical: 惨めな気持ち, 惨めな思いをする "to feel miserable and humiliated", 惨めな生活, 自分が惨めになる. Often there is a sense of humiliation in front of others; 悲しい, by contrast, is simply "sad", and 可哀想 is "pitiable" from an observer's point of view. Frequently also written in kana: みじめ.

examples[].german: I felt empty.
I prepared so hard, and then the match was cancelled, so it all feels pointless.
If I spend the whole day playing games, I feel empty in the evening.
en.notes: 虚しい describes a feeling of inner emptiness and meaninglessness, for example when effort was in vain or something has no real substance. Typical: 虚しい気持ち, 虚しくなる, 努力が虚しく終わる. The adverbial form 虚しく means "in vain": 声が虚しく響く. It is also written 空しい or in kana むなしい. Unlike 寂しい "lonely" (longing for people), 虚しい is about emptiness and futility.

examples[].german: He is a reliable person.
Even though he is new, he can solve everything by himself, which is reassuring.
When my son said, "I'll protect you," he seemed really strong to me.
en.notes: 頼もしい describes someone you can rely on and who gives you a sense of security. It is mostly praise: 頼もしいね！, 頼もしい味方 "a strong ally". It is also used for younger people who grow beyond themselves: 頼もしく成長した. Almost synonymous, but more everyday, is 頼りになる; 信頼できる emphasizes trustworthiness, while 頼もしい emphasizes strength and support in difficult situations.

examples[].german: I feel proud.
My daughter won the tournament, and I was very proud.
He proudly showed me his new car.
en.notes: 誇らしい expresses the feeling of being proud - of one's own achievement or that of people close to one. Typical: 誇らしい気持ち, 誇らしく思う, and with 〜げ: 誇らしげに "with a proud look". Related are 誇り "pride" (誇りに思う) and 誇る "to boast of". In present-day usage 誇らしい is positive; the meaning "arrogant" given in dictionaries is rare, and for that people say 偉そう.

examples[].german: I devote myself to my studies.
Economics is a discipline that also considers the human mind.
University is not only for preparing for a job, but a place for scholarship.
en.notes: 学問 denotes serious, scholarly learning and erudition as well as an academic discipline. Typical: 学問に励む "to devote oneself to study", 学問の自由 "academic freedom", 学問的な "scholarly". It sounds more elevated and abstract than 勉強 (studying, e.g. for exams); 科学 means science as a method, especially the natural sciences.

examples[].german: I will carry out an experiment.
In science class we did an experiment with water.
I hear the experiment with the new drug was successful.
en.notes: 実験 is a scientific or practical experiment. Typical: 実験をする／行う, 〜を実験する, 実験に成功する／失敗する, 実験室 "laboratory", 実験結果, 動物実験. Figuratively it is also used for trial projects: 実験的な試み. Do not confuse it with 試験 "exam, test" (school, quality control).

examples[].german: I am writing a paper.
I still haven't decided on the topic of my graduation thesis.
My professor's paper was published in a well-known journal.
en.notes: 論文 is an academic work: a journal article, graduation thesis or doctoral dissertation. Typical: 論文を書く, 論文を発表する "to publish, to present", 論文を提出する; 卒業論文 (short 卒論) "graduation thesis", 博士論文 "doctoral dissertation". A school essay, by contrast, is 作文, and a shorter seminar paper or assignment is レポート.

examples[].german: The problem is obvious.
The investigation revealed the cause of the accident.
It is obvious that he is lying.
en.notes: 明らか is a な-adjective for facts that are obvious and undeniable: 〜のは明らかだ, 明らかに間違っている. Very common in the news are 明らかになる "to come to light" and 明らかにする "to reveal, to clarify". 明確, by contrast, emphasizes that something is precisely defined (明確な目標); in everyday speech people often just say はっきりしている.

examples[].german: Educational background doesn't matter.
Please write your highest level of education on your résumé.
Japan is sometimes said to be a society that values educational credentials.
en.notes: 学歴 is a person's school and academic history, especially their highest qualification. Typical: 学歴が高い, 学歴社会 "credentialist society", 最終学歴 "highest level of education" (on a résumé), 学歴より実力 "ability counts more than diplomas". Do not confuse it with 経歴 "career history" and 資格 "qualification, certificate".

examples[].german: I obtained a qualification.
To work as a nurse, you need a national license.
People who don't keep their promises have no right to complain.
en.notes: 資格 is a formal qualification or entitlement: a certificate, a license or the prerequisite for something. Typical: 資格を取る "to obtain", 資格がある／ない, 資格試験 "qualification exam", 受験資格 "eligibility to take an exam". Also moral: 君に文句を言う資格はない "You have no right to complain". Official permits such as a driver's license are called 免許 instead.

examples[].german: I was dismissed.
As business deteriorated, the company laid off a hundred employees.
You can't dismiss employees without a reason.
en.notes: 解雇 is dismissal by the employer - a formal word from contracts, news and labor law. From the viewpoint of those affected, usually in the passive: 会社に解雇される. Compounds: 不当解雇 "unfair dismissal", 解雇通知 "notice of dismissal". Colloquially people say クビになる "to get fired"; if you quit yourself, it is 辞める or, formally, 退職する.

examples[].german: My salary has gone up.
Salary is transferred on the 25th of every month.
You should check your pay slip carefully.
en.notes: 給与 is pay for work, a formal word from contracts, pay slips and job ads; compounds include 給与明細 "pay slip" and 給与振込 "salary transfer". In conversation one usually says 給料 (給料日 "payday"); 月給 is monthly salary, 時給 hourly wage. The second meaning, "granting, provision" (as a verb 給与する), is rare.

examples[].german: I have a new proposal.
I proposed a new project to the department head.
At a friend's suggestion, we're going camping on the weekend.
en.notes: 提案 is a proposal, especially in meetings and at work. Typical: 提案する, 提案を出す, 提案を受け入れる／断る, 人に提案する; 提案書 is a written proposal. In a meeting you announce: 一つ提案があるんですが.... For spontaneous private suggestions, 〜しようよ or 〜はどう？ usually suffices; 提案 sounds somewhat more formal.

examples[].german: I'm drawing up a plan.
Our class is planning what to do at the school festival.
My proposal was approved at the meeting.
en.notes: 企画 is the planning and conceiving of a project, event or product, and also the plan itself. Typical: 企画を立てる "to develop a plan", 企画書 "project proposal", 企画が通る "to be approved", 〜を企画する; 企画部 is the planning department. In contrast to 計画 (a general plan, e.g. a travel plan), 企画 stands for a creative idea, such as for an event, a show or a campaign.

examples[].german: There was a big loss.
Because of this accident, the company incurred a loss of about 100 million yen.
That player's injury is a big loss for the team.
en.notes: 損失 is a loss, usually financial; it is a formal word from business and the news. Typical: 損失が出る, 損失を出す, 損失を受ける, 〜円の損失. Figuratively it is also used for irreplaceable losses: チームにとって大きな損失だ. The opposite is 利益 "profit". In everyday speech people say the simpler 損 (損をした "I lost out").

examples[].german: I'm getting a loan from the bank.
The bank lent 300 million yen for the new factory.
I applied for a loan, but was turned down.
en.notes: 融資 is financing or a loan granted by a bank or institution; it is a technical term from business and finance. Watch the perspective: the bank 融資する "grants a loan", the customer 融資を受ける "receives" or 融資を申し込む "applies for" it. In everyday speech people more often use ローン for loans, and 借りる／貸す for private lending; debts are called 借金.

examples[].german: I'm handling the inheritance procedures.
My father inherited my grandfather's house.
Because the inheritance tax was so high, we decided to sell the land.
en.notes: 相続 is legal succession: inheriting assets (or debts) after a death. As a transitive する-verb: 財産を相続する, from whom with から. Compounds: 相続税 "inheritance tax", 相続人 "heir", 遺産相続 "settlement of an estate". For taking over tradition, a business or an office, people more often say 継ぐ／受け継ぐ (家業を継ぐ); 相続 has a legal flavor.

examples[].german: It's a wonderful invention.
It was Bell who invented the telephone.
As a child, I wanted to invent a machine that would do my homework for me.
en.notes: 発明 is the invention of something new that did not exist before. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を発明する; plus 発明家 "inventor" and 発明品 "invention (an object)". The distinction from 発見 is important: one 発見する something that already existed (an element, a planet), but 発明する something newly created (the telephone). Proverb: 必要は発明の母 "necessity is the mother of invention".

examples[].german: It is developing rapidly.
Smartphones spread rapidly.
Some people cannot keep up with the rapid changes in society.
en.notes: 急速 is a な-adjective for fast change or development over time, not for speed of movement: 急速に発展する／広まる／増える, 急速な変化. A fast car is 速い, not 急速. 急 emphasizes suddenness (急に雨が降る), whereas 急速 emphasizes the high pace of a development. The word sounds literary and is typical of the news; compare also 急速冷凍 "flash freezing".

examples[].german: There was a new discovery.
Dinosaur bones were discovered in Hokkaido.
Because the fire was discovered early, there was no major damage.
en.notes: 発見 is discovering or finding something that already existed but was unknown or hidden. As a transitive する-verb: 〜を発見する; in the news often passive: 〜が発見される. In everyday life also for small revelations: 新しい発見がある. Compared with 見つける, 発見 sounds more formal; 発明, by contrast, means inventing something new.

examples[].german: The Industrial Revolution took place.
The French Revolution began in 1789.
Smartphones have revolutionized our lives.
en.notes: 革命 is a revolution, either political (フランス革命) or figuratively a fundamental upheaval: 産業革命, IT革命. Typical: 革命が起きる／起こる, 〜に革命を起こす "to revolutionize ...", 革命的な "revolutionary" (also in advertising). Gradual reforms, by contrast, are 改革, and general change is 変化.

examples[].german: Technology is evolving.
Birds are thought to have evolved from dinosaurs.
The characters in this game evolve when they level up.
en.notes: 進化 is biological evolution and, figuratively, further development toward something more advanced. As an intransitive する-verb: 〜が進化する; related is 進化論 "theory of evolution". Very common about technology and products: スマホは年々進化している. Distinctions: 進歩 "progress" (技術の進歩), 発展 "development, growth" (city, economy); the opposite is 退化. Do not confuse it with the identically read 深化 "deepening".

examples[].german: I opened the shoji.
The cat made a hole in the shoji paper.
At the end of the year, our family re-papers the shoji.
en.notes: 障子 is the traditional sliding door or window made of a fine wooden lattice covered with translucent Japanese paper that lets light in. Typical: 障子を開ける／閉める, 障子を張り替える "to re-paper" (often before New Year), 障子に穴を開ける (children, cats). Proverb: 壁に耳あり障子に目あり "walls have ears". The opaque counterpart that divides rooms is 襖.

examples[].german: Please close the fusuma.
The futons are stored in the closet behind the fusuma.
If you take out the fusuma, two rooms become one large room.
en.notes: 襖 is an opaque sliding door made of a wooden frame covered with thick paper or cloth. It separates rooms or closes off the closet (押し入れ). Typical: 襖を開ける／閉める, 襖を外す "to take out" (to join two rooms), 襖絵 "paintings on sliding doors" in temples. The kanji is rare, so it is often written in kana as ふすま. Unlike 障子, 襖 lets no light through.

examples[].german: I drink tea on the veranda.
My grandmother often sat on the veranda looking at the garden.
The cat is sleeping contentedly on the veranda.
en.notes: 縁側 is the narrow, roofed wooden walkway on the outside of traditional Japanese houses, between the rooms and the garden. People sit there, drink tea, look at the garden or bask in the sun: 縁側に座る, 縁側でひなたぼっこする. The word evokes images of cozy life at the grandparents' house in the countryside. In the kitchen, えんがわ also refers to the fin-edge meat of flatfish, for example in sushi.

examples[].german: Please don't run in the hallway.
There are two chairs in the hallway.
en.notes: 廊下 is a hallway or corridor. In 廊下を走る, を marks the path traversed, not a direct object of running. 廊下に names the place where something is. 走らないでください asks you not to run there. ろうか is written rōka with a long o.

examples[].german: Smoke is coming out of the chimney.
Public baths in the old days had tall chimneys.
The children believe that Santa comes down the chimney.
en.notes: 煙突 is a chimney on houses, factories, public baths (銭湯) or ships. Typical: 煙突から煙が出る／上がる, 工場の煙突, 高い煙突. Since Japanese homes rarely have fireplaces, 煙突 is seen mainly at 銭湯 and factories. A well-known image from Christmas stories: Santa comes through the 煙突.

examples[].german: We built a fence.
A cat is walking along the top of the wall.
In an earthquake, it is dangerous near concrete block walls.
en.notes: 塀 is a solid enclosure around a property: a wall of stone, concrete or concrete blocks, or a solid wooden fence. Typical: 塀を作る, 高い塀, 塀に囲まれた家, ブロック塀, 塀を乗り越える. Distinctions: 壁 is the wall of a building or room, 垣根 a hedge or light fence, フェンス a mesh or wire fence. Cats like to stroll along 塀の上 (the top of a wall).

examples[].german: I put the tools away in the shed.
We set up a small tool shed in the garden.
We use the unused room as a storeroom.
en.notes: 物置 is a room or small shed where you keep things you do not need at the moment: tools, garden equipment, seasonal items. Typical are 物置にしまう "to put away in the storeroom" and 物置に入れる; a room used as a junk room is called 物置部屋. To be distinguished from 倉庫 "warehouse, storehouse" (larger, often commercial) and 押し入れ, the closet in a Japanese room for futons.

examples[].german: It's not a simple problem.
This machine has a simple mechanism, so it is hard to break.
He is simple-minded, so he's in a good mood right away when you praise him.
en.notes: 単純 is a な-adjective meaning "simply built, not complex" (opposite 複雑): 単純な仕組み, 単純作業, 単純ミス "careless mistake". Applied to people it means "naive, simple-minded" and sounds slightly mocking. 簡単, by contrast, means "easy to do": 簡単な問題 is an easy task, 単純な問題 an uncomplicated matter. For plain design, one positively says シンプル.

examples[].german: It's an apartment building five years old.
How old is this apartment building?
The house was built in 1990, but it's very clean inside.
en.notes: 築 appears almost only in fixed patterns about the age of a building: 築五年 "five years old" (before the number) or 1990年築 "built in 1990" (after the year). You mostly encounter it in housing listings and at viewings; the question about the building's age is 築何年ですか. Related are 築年数 "age of the building", 築浅 "nearly new, only a few years old" and 新築 "newly built". For people or things, one never says 築, but 〜歳 or 〜年前の.

examples[].german: I'm sending it in for repair.
I repaired the bicycle brakes myself.
The air conditioner repair is said to cost about 10,000 yen.
en.notes: 修理 is the repair of devices, vehicles or machines; as a transitive する-verb: 車を修理する. Very common are 修理に出す "to send in for repair", 修理中 "under repair" and 修理代 "repair costs". In everyday speech people often simply say 直す; 修繕 is more formal and used more for buildings or clothing, and 修正 means "correction" of texts or data, not repair.

examples[].german: Under construction.
The construction next door is so noisy that I can't sleep.
This road is closed because of road construction.
en.notes: 工事 refers to construction or installation work of all kinds: 道路工事 "road construction", 水道工事, 配線工事. Typical are 工事中 "under construction, due to construction work", 工事が始まる/終わる and 工事現場 "construction site". Compared with 建築 (erecting buildings, also "architecture") and 建設 (large projects such as bridges or dams), 工事 means the actual work on site, with noise and barricades.

examples[].german: I design a building.
I assembled the machine while looking at the blueprint.
Before getting married, the two of us thought about our future life plans.
en.notes: 設計 is the technical planning and construction design of buildings, machines or systems; as a transitive する-verb: 家を設計する. It includes 設計図 "blueprint, construction drawing" and 設計士 "designer, architect". Unlike デザイン, which refers more to appearance, 設計 is about structure and function. Figuratively people also speak of 人生設計 or 生活設計 "life planning".

examples[].german: Japanese architecture is beautiful.
My older brother is studying architecture at university.
Construction of a new hotel is progressing in front of the station.
en.notes: 建築 means both the erecting of buildings and architecture as a field and style: 建築を学ぶ, 木造建築 "wooden construction", 建築家 "architect", 建築物 "structure". As a する-verb it is transitive (家を建築する) but sounds formal; in everyday speech people say 家を建てる. 建設 is used more for infrastructure such as roads or dams, 工事 for the construction work itself.

examples[].german: I use laboratory equipment.
I'm starting to live alone, so I got together some cooking utensils.
I replaced the ceiling light with a new one.
en.notes: 器具 is a collective word for tools and instruments, mostly in compounds: 実験器具 "laboratory equipment", 調理器具 "cooking utensils", 医療器具, 照明器具 "lighting fixtures", 運動器具 "exercise equipment". On its own, it sounds somewhat matter-of-fact. 道具 is the general word for tool, 機械 is a (often motorized) machine, and 装置 is a larger technical installation.

examples[].german: The safety device was activated.
This old apartment has no heating system.
The stage set in that play was very beautiful.
en.notes: 装置 is a technical device or installation that fulfills a particular function: 安全装置 "safety device", 暖房装置 "heating system", 防犯装置 "anti-theft device". Typical verbs are 装置が作動する "to activate, to kick in" and 装置を取り付ける "to install". In the theater, 舞台装置 means "stage set". 機械 stresses the machine itself, 器具 rather smaller hand tools, 設備 the entire equipment of a building.

examples[].german: I operate the machine.
My father is bad with technology and can't even use a smartphone properly.
In this factory the machines run twenty-four hours a day.
en.notes: 機械 is a machine, especially one with a motor or mechanism: 機械を動かす/止める, 機械が故障する. Colloquially, 機械に弱い means "to be bad with technology" and 機械的 "mechanical, without thinking". Beware of the identically read 機会 "opportunity". For smaller devices you tend to use 器具, for household appliances 家電, and for large installations 装置.

examples[].german: I'll check the wiring.
The wiring behind the TV is a tangled mess.
Because it's an old house, electrical rewiring work is needed.
en.notes: 配線 is electrical wiring or cable routing, in house installations as well as behind a TV or computer. Typical are 配線工事 "electrical installation work", 配線図 "wiring diagram" and 配線を確認する/つなぐ. As a する-verb (配線する) it means "to wire". A single cable is called コード or ケーブル; 配線 refers to the whole system.

examples[].german: We'll go by expressway.
The expressway has expensive tolls, so let's take the regular roads.
We'll get off the expressway at the next interchange.
en.notes: 高速道路 is a highway or expressway; in Japan it almost always charges tolls. In everyday speech people say 高速 for short: 高速に乗る "to get on the expressway", 高速を降りる "to get off", 高速料金 "expressway toll". In contrast, the ordinary road is often called 下の道 or 一般道. Entrances and exits are called インター.

examples[].german: Let's find a topic we have in common.
We got to know each other through a mutual friend.
This problem is common to many countries.
en.notes: 共通 is mostly used with の before nouns: 共通の話題, 共通の友達, 共通の趣味. As a する-verb, AはBに共通する means "A is common to B"; 共通している describes the state. Common words are 共通点 "common point" and 共通語 "common language". The form 共通な is rare.

examples[].german: I reserved a seat.
Because of the consecutive holidays, the reserved seats on the Shinkansen were already full.
All seats at this concert are reserved.
en.notes: 指定席 is a reserved seat, above all on the Shinkansen and long-distance trains, but also at concerts and sports events. One says 指定席を取る or 指定席を予約する; the ticket is called 指定席券. The counterpart is 自由席 "non-reserved seat". 全席指定 means "all seats reserved / only with a seat ticket".

examples[].german: I'll sit in an unreserved seat.
The unreserved cars are cars 1 to 3.
The unreserved section was crowded, and I had to stand all the way to Tokyo.
en.notes: 自由席 is an unreserved seat, especially on the Shinkansen: in the 自由席 cars (自由席車両) you may sit anywhere you like, but have no guarantee of a seat. Typical are 自由席に座る, 自由席で行く and announcements like 自由席は一号車から三号車です. The counterpart is 指定席. Caution: "a free seat" in the sense of "unoccupied" is 空いている席 or 空席, not 自由席.

examples[].german: How much is the fare?
I hear train fares will go up from next month.
A child's fare is half the adult fare.
en.notes: 運賃 is the fare in public transport (train, bus, taxi, plane) and, in freight transport, the shipping cost. Typical are 運賃を払う, 運賃が上がる "fares rise" and 片道運賃 "one-way fare". 料金 is more general "fee, price" (also for electricity or admission), and 交通費 is the total "travel expenses", such as those reimbursed by an employer.

examples[].german: The passengers get off.
There were two hundred passengers on that plane.
Morning trains are always full of passengers.
en.notes: 乗客 are the passengers on a train, bus, plane or ship. The word is objective and typical of news and announcements: 乗客を乗せる "to pick up passengers", 乗客が乗る/降りる, 乗客数 "number of passengers". Staff address passengers directly as お客様. 旅客 is even more formal and appears in compounds such as 旅客機 "passenger aircraft".

examples[].german: The train is delayed.
For my company, I got a delay certificate at the station.
Because of heavy snow, many flights are delayed.
en.notes: 遅延 is the formal word for "delay" and typical of train announcements, airport boards and official letters; as an intransitive する-verb: 電車が遅延する. In everyday life, 遅延証明書, the delay certificate you present at work, is important. In conversation people usually say 遅れ or 遅れる: 電車が十分遅れた. In IT, 遅延 also means "latency".

examples[].german: Trains are stopped because of a passenger accident.
Because of a passenger accident, trains are running thirty minutes late.
There was an accident involving a car and a bicycle at the intersection, with injuries.
en.notes: 人身事故 is an accident involving personal injury (injured or dead), as opposed to 物損事故 "accident with property damage only". In road traffic it is a legal term; on the railways it is heard constantly in announcements like 人身事故の影響で..., often with a suicide behind it. Typical are 人身事故が起きる/発生する and 人身事故で電車が止まる.

examples[].german: The suspension of service continues.
Because of the typhoon, Shinkansen service has been suspended.
During the suspension of service, I waited at the station for a whole hour.
en.notes: 運転見合わせ is the temporary suspension of train or bus service, for example because of an accident, storm or earthquake; it comes from 運転を見合わせる "to hold off operation for the time being". Typical in announcements and on display boards: 運転見合わせ中, 〜線は運転見合わせとなっています. Unlike 運休 "cancellation (of a train)", it stresses that service will resume later (運転再開).

en.meaning: substitute transport (ticket valid on other lines)
examples[].german: I use the substitute transport.
Substitute transport is currently being offered on the subway.
When you use substitute transport, please show your ticket at the ticket gate.
en.notes: 振替輸送 is substitute transport during a service disruption: your own ticket is then also valid on other lines or companies, at no extra charge. Typical phrases are 振替輸送を行う "to offer substitute transport" (railway company) and 振替輸送を利用する "to use it" (passenger); at the counter you often get a 振替乗車票 for it. You hear the word almost only in train announcements, together with 運転見合わせ or 人身事故.

examples[].german: I show my ticket to the conductor.
From the conductor's announcement, I learned the name of the next station.
I had left my umbrella on the train, so I asked the conductor.
en.notes: 車掌 is the train conductor who operates the doors, makes announcements and checks tickets; politely one says 車掌さん. The train driver, by contrast, is 運転士, and station staff are 駅員. On many Japanese local trains there is no 車掌 any more (ワンマン運転), but on the Shinkansen there is.

examples[].german: I pilot the airplane.
Flying a drone is harder than I thought.
She really has her husband wrapped around her finger, doesn't she?
en.notes: 操縦 is the operation of vehicles that require special skills: airplane, ship, helicopter, drone, robot. As a transitive する-verb: 飛行機を操縦する; the pilot is called 操縦士, the cockpit 操縦席. For a car or train you say 運転する, for operating devices 操作する. Figuratively, 操縦 also means to steer someone skillfully: 夫をうまく操縦する.

en.meaning: to obey; to follow; to comply
examples[].german: Please follow the rules.
Please follow the guidance and go to the venue on the second floor.
As I get older, my physical strength has declined.
en.notes: 従う is intransitive; what one follows takes に: ルール・指示・命令に従う, 親に従う. 守る (ルールを守る, with を) emphasizes keeping to something, whereas 従う emphasizes following and submitting. In instructions, 案内に従って means "following the signs". As N3 grammar, 〜に従って means "as ..., the more ..." or "with increasing ...".

examples[].german: The cars collided.
A bicycle hit a utility pole, and the rider was injured.
I ended up clashing with my department head over an opinion in the meeting.
en.notes: 衝突 is a violent collision of vehicles or objects; as an intransitive する-verb: AとBが衝突する or AがBに衝突する. Common are 正面衝突 "head-on collision" and 衝突事故. Figuratively it means "conflict, quarrel": 意見が衝突する. In everyday speech, ぶつかる is used for lighter cases; 衝突 sounds like the news or a serious matter.

examples[].german: Please call an ambulance.
My grandmother was taken to the hospital by ambulance.
An ambulance was coming through, so I pulled my car over to the side of the road.
en.notes: 救急車 is the ambulance; in Japan it is called on the number 119. Typical are 救急車を呼ぶ, 救急車で運ばれる "to be taken by ambulance" and 救急車が来る. The emergency medical team is 救急隊, the emergency room 救急外来. Do not confuse it with 消防車 "fire engine", which also comes via 119.

examples[].german: The fire engine has arrived.
There was a fire in the neighborhood, and several fire engines came.
My son loves his toy fire engine.
en.notes: 消防車 is the fire engine; the fire station is called 消防署, the firefighter 消防士. Typical phrases are 消防車が来る/出動する "to turn out" and 消防車のサイレン. In Japan you call the fire department at 119, the same number as for an ambulance. The fire itself is 火事, and "to extinguish" is 消す or, formally, 消火する.

examples[].german: I notified the police.
The police came immediately after the report.
If you find a suspicious piece of luggage, please report it to the station staff immediately.
en.notes: 通報 is a report to authorities such as the police or fire department, often in emergencies or cases of suspicion: 警察に通報する, 110番通報, 消防に通報する. The authority 通報を受ける "receives the report"; the person who reports is the 通報者. Unlike 報告 (a report, e.g. to a superior) and 連絡 (letting someone know in general), 通報 always goes to a competent body. A formal criminal complaint, on the other hand, is 被害届 or 告訴.

examples[].german: I witnessed the accident.
The police are looking for witnesses to the incident.
A bear has reportedly been sighted in the mountains near here.
en.notes: 目撃 means to see an event by chance with one's own eyes, usually an accident, a crime or something unusual; as a transitive する-verb: 事故を目撃する. Very common are 目撃者 "eyewitness" and 目撃情報 "witness reports, sighting information". In the passive it describes sightings: クマが目撃された. For ordinary seeing or deliberate observing, use 見る or 観察する respectively.

examples[].german: I gave first aid.
A station employee gave first aid until the ambulance arrived.
As a stopgap, I taped up the broken window.
en.notes: 応急処置 is an emergency measure taken before the actual treatment or repair: for injured people "first aid", for objects a "temporary repair". People say 応急処置をする, 応急処置を受ける and 応急処置として… "as a stopgap". For first aid given to people 応急手当 is also common; a first-aid course is called 救命講習.

examples[].german: I put on a bandage.
Please change the bandage every day so that the wound stays clean.
It took two weeks until the bandage came off.
en.notes: 包帯 is a bandage made of gauze; the typical verb is 巻く: 包帯を巻く "to apply a bandage", also 包帯を替える "to change" and 包帯を取る "to take off". A small adhesive plaster, by contrast, is 絆創膏 (mostly written ばんそうこう), and a gauze pad is ガーゼ. The older spelling 繃帯 is still occasionally found.

examples[].german: I was in the hospital for a week.
My grandmother is in the hospital right now.
I have to be hospitalized for an operation on my leg.
en.notes: 入院 is admission to or a stay in the hospital; as an intransitive する-verb one says 病院に入院する or simply 入院する. That someone is currently in the hospital is expressed with 入院している or 入院中. When a doctor sends someone to the hospital, it is 入院させる. The opposite is 退院 "discharge"; someone who only goes for outpatient treatment does 通院.

examples[].german: I will be discharged next week.
My father was discharged from the hospital safely yesterday.
When you get out of the hospital, let's go on a trip together.
en.notes: 退院 is discharge from the hospital; as an intransitive する-verb: 退院する, with the hospital as the starting point marked by を: 病院を退院する. It is the counterpart of 入院. Typical expressions are 無事に退院する "to be discharged safely" and the congratulation 退院おめでとう(ございます). For leaving a school or company, other words are used (卒業, 退職); 退院 applies only to hospitals.

examples[].german: I go to the doctor every week as an outpatient.
Even after being discharged, I go to the hospital once a month.
Because of my hospital visits, I go home early every Wednesday.
en.notes: 通院 means to go to a hospital or clinic regularly for treatment, i.e. to be treated as an outpatient; as an intransitive する-verb with に: 病院に通院する, often simply 通院している. Its counterpart is 入院 "to be admitted to hospital", followed by 退院. Common are 通院中 "under medical treatment" and 週に一回通院する. For a single doctor's visit, one says 病院に行く or 診察を受ける instead.

en.meaning: to respond to; to comply with; to meet
examples[].german: I will comply with the request.
Thank you for agreeing to the interview.
The fee changes depending on the number of people.
en.notes: 応じる is intransitive; what one responds to takes に: 要求・質問・誘い・インタビューに応じる. It means "to comply with a request, to agree" and sounds rather formal; plain "to answer" is 答える. Very common is 〜に応じて "depending on, in accordance with": 人数に応じて料金が変わる. The literary variant is 応ずる.

examples[].german: I got a prescription.
On the way home from the hospital, I took the prescription to the pharmacy.
You can't buy this medicine without a prescription.
en.notes: 処方箋 is the doctor's prescription. In Japan the clinic issues it (処方箋を出す), and you bring it to the pharmacy (薬局に処方箋を出す/持って行く); pharmacies that fill prescriptions advertise 処方箋受付. Prescription-only medicines can only be bought 処方箋があれば. A cooking recipe, by contrast, is レシピ. Figuratively, 処方箋 is also used for "cure-all, solution".

examples[].german: Are there any side effects?
This medicine can cause drowsiness as a side effect.
If side effects occur, please consult your doctor immediately.
en.notes: 副作用 is the side effect of a medicine or vaccination. Typical phrases are 副作用がある, 副作用が出る "side effects appear" and 〜の副作用で眠くなる. Figuratively, it also refers to negative side effects of a measure. Its counterpart, the desired effect, is 効果 or 効き目.

examples[].german: I have a pollen allergy.
Excuse me, I'm allergic to shrimp.
My younger brother is allergic to math, apparently; just seeing numbers puts him off.
en.notes: アレルギー is an allergy, usually with the trigger in front: 花粉アレルギー, 卵アレルギー, 猫アレルギー. You say 〜アレルギーがある or 〜にアレルギーがある; the reaction is アレルギー反応, an allergic predisposition アレルギー体質. Colloquially it also stands for a strong aversion: 数学アレルギー. Hay fever is usually just called 花粉症.

examples[].german: I got vaccinated.
I had my child vaccinated against the flu.
The second shot is scheduled for next month.
en.notes: 接種 is the administering of a vaccine; as a transitive する-verb: ワクチンを接種する. The everyday word for "vaccination" is 予防接種 (予防接種を受ける), colloquially also ワクチンを打つ. On its own, 接種 appears more in official texts and the news, e.g. 接種券 "vaccination voucher" or 二回目の接種 "second dose".

examples[].german: I will get a health checkup.
At my company, there is a health checkup once a year.
At the health checkup, I was told that my blood pressure is a little high.
en.notes: 健康診断 is the general health examination, which in Japan is usually organized annually by the employer for employees. Typical is 健康診断を受ける; abbreviated, one often says 健診, and the more comprehensive version is called 人間ドック. Results are in the 健康診断の結果, for example for 血圧 or 体重. An examination because of specific complaints is 診察.

examples[].german: I'm taking my pulse.
I was so nervous before the interview that my pulse sped up.
If she messages you every day, you might have a chance.
en.notes: 脈 is mainly the pulse: 脈を測る "to measure the pulse", 脈を取る "to take the pulse", 脈が速い/遅い. Colloquially, 脈がある means "there is hope", especially in love ("he/she is interested"), and 脈がない means the opposite. In compounds 脈 stands for veins and chains: 動脈 "artery", 山脈 "mountain range". 脈拍 is the more technical word for the pulse rate.

examples[].german: I broke my leg.
I fell while skiing and broke my arm.
It took three months for the fracture to heal completely.
en.notes: 骨折 is a bone fracture. As a する-verb, the body part takes を: 足を骨折する "to break one's leg", 腕を骨折した. Synonymous but more everyday is 骨が折れる "a bone breaks"; careful, 骨が折れる also means "to be laborious" figuratively. Also typical are 骨折が治る and ギプス "cast".

examples[].german: I got burned.
I burned my hand with hot water.
I got into stocks and got badly burned.
en.notes: やけど is a burn or scald; it is mostly written in kana, and the kanji 火傷 is seen more in texts. Typical are やけどをする, 手にやけどをする and 舌をやけどする "to burn one's tongue". Figuratively, やけど(を)する means "to burn one's fingers", for example with stocks or risky relationships; 大やけど is a severe burn or a big loss.

examples[].german: The wound has healed.
The new car already has a scratch.
Emotional wounds from childhood do not disappear easily.
en.notes: 傷 is a wound, cut or scrape, but also a scratch on objects and, figuratively, emotional pain. Typical are 傷が治る, 傷が残る "a scar remains", 傷がつく "to get scratched" and 心の傷. Related verbs: 傷つく "to get hurt" and 傷つける "to hurt". けが refers to the accident or injury as a whole, 傷 to the concrete spot.

examples[].german: My foot is swollen.
I was bitten by a mosquito and my arm swelled up red.
I cried too much yesterday and my eyes got puffy.
en.notes: 腫れる is intransitive: a body part swells, usually from inflammation, a blow or an insect bite: 足が腫れる, 目が腫れる. It is often used in the form 腫れている "is swollen" and with 赤く: 赤く腫れる. The noun 腫れ appears in 腫れが引く "the swelling goes down". Do not confuse it with the identically read 晴れる "to clear up (weather)". A transitive counterpart exists only in expressions like 目を泣き腫らす "to cry one's eyes red".

examples[].german: Tax is included.
This juice contains a lot of vitamin C.
