This song is popular in Asian countries, including Japan.
en.notes: 含む is transitive; the whole is the subject and the component takes を: このジュースはビタミンを含む. 〜を含む + noun means "including, among them". The passive is very common: 料金に税金が含まれている. Do not confuse it with 含める (ichidan), which expresses actively including: 私を含めて五人. In the sense of "to hold in the mouth", one says 水を口に含む.

en.meaning: to go numb; to tingle; to be thrilled
examples[].german: My foot has gone numb.
My fingertips are numb from the cold, and I can't write well.
That guitarist's performance really blew me away.
en.notes: しびれる is intransitive and mostly written in kana. The basic meaning is "to go numb, to fall asleep" of limbs, typically after sitting a long time in seiza: 正座で足がしびれる. It also describes tingling from electricity or cold (指先がしびれる). Colloquially, 〜にしびれる means "to be captivated by something": あの演奏にはしびれた. The noun しびれ appears in しびれが取れる "the numbness goes away".

examples[].german: I feel dizzy.
I got dizzy from the heat and collapsed.
I've had severe dizziness since this morning, so I'm taking the day off work.
en.notes: めまい is dizziness; mostly in kana, since the kanji 眩暈 (also 目眩) are hard and rather literary. The fixed pattern is めまいがする "I feel dizzy"; for severe dizziness one says めまいを起こす. The brief dizziness when standing up quickly is 立ちくらみ. For nausea, which often comes with it, 吐き気 is used.

examples[].german: I feel nauseous.
I got carsick on the mountain road and started to feel nauseous.
I got anti-nausea medicine at the hospital.
en.notes: 吐き気 is nausea, literally "the feeling of having to vomit". The standard pattern is 吐き気がする; formally it is 吐き気を催す. A remedy against it is 吐き気止め. In conversation, people often simply say 気持ち悪い, which can also mean "disgusting". For motion sickness, one hears 酔う: バスに酔う.

examples[].german: The diarrhea is continuing.
I drank the water on my trip and got diarrhea.
Excuse me, do you have any anti-diarrhea medicine?
en.notes: 下痢 is diarrhea, a plain, factual word used at the doctor's or the pharmacy: 下痢をする, 下痢が続く, 下痢止め "anti-diarrhea medicine". As a する-verb it is intransitive. In everyday speech it is often put more politely as お腹を壊す "to upset one's stomach" or お腹が緩い. The opposite is 便秘.

examples[].german: I'm having trouble with constipation.
If you don't eat much vegetables, you tend to get constipated.
Lately I've been a little constipated.
en.notes: 便秘 is constipation. Typical phrases are 便秘になる, 便秘が続く, 便秘で困る and 便秘気味 "slightly constipated". The word is matter-of-fact and is used openly even in advertising for yogurt or tea; as an intransitive する-verb (便秘する) it is rarer. The opposite is 下痢, a remedy is called 便秘薬.

examples[].german: I suffer from insomnia.
I developed insomnia from work stress.
It may not be just lack of sleep, but insomnia.
en.notes: 不眠症 is insomnia as a (chronic) disorder, i.e. more than one bad night. Typical phrases are 不眠症になる, 不眠症に悩む "to suffer from insomnia" and 不眠症の治療. Someone who has simply slept too little is 寝不足; "cannot fall asleep" is 眠れない or 寝つけない.

examples[].german: I have no appetite.
After exercising a lot, I got an appetite.
Autumn is such a good season for food that it is called the "autumn of appetite".
en.notes: 食欲 is the appetite for food. Typical are 食欲がある/ない, 食欲が出る "to get an appetite" and 食欲が落ちる "the appetite decreases". The well-known expression is 食欲の秋 "autumn, the season of good eating". Physical hunger, by contrast, is お腹が空く, and a craving for something specific is 〜が食べたい.

examples[].german: I'm on a diet.
I want to lose three kilos by summer, so I started a diet.
My sister, who succeeded in dieting, runs every morning.
en.notes: ダイエット in Japanese almost always means "losing weight", not a medical diet. You say ダイエットする, ダイエット中 "I'm dieting right now", ダイエットに成功する/失敗する. It also includes exercise for weight loss. A medically prescribed diet is called 食事制限 or 食事療法.

examples[].german: My joints hurt.
When it gets cold, my knee joints start to hurt.
Stop cracking your finger joints.
en.notes: 関節 is the joint. Typical phrases are 関節が痛む/痛い, 膝の関節, 指の関節を鳴らす "to crack one's knuckles" and 関節が柔らかい "flexible". Medically you hear 関節炎 "arthritis" and 関節痛 "joint pain", e.g. as a flu symptom. The bone itself is 骨, the muscle 筋肉.

examples[].german: An organ transplant was carried out.
On the back of the driver's license there is a field for stating your wishes about organ donation.
Drinking too much alcohol puts a heavy burden on the organs.
en.notes: 臓器 are the internal organs such as heart, liver or kidneys, mainly in a medical context. Most often you encounter 臓器移植 "organ transplant" and 臓器提供 "organ donation". 内臓 is the more general word for "internal organs, entrails"; 器官 is the biological umbrella term for organs by function (e.g. 感覚器官 "sense organs"). Individual organs often end in 臓: 心臓, 肝臓, 腎臓.

examples[].german: I will show the results.
This graph shows the change in population.
He showed strong interest in the new plan.
en.notes: 示す is transitive and means "to show, to point out, to indicate", especially for data, examples, directions and attitudes: グラフが変化を示す, 例を示す, 関心・態度を示す, 矢印が示す方向. It sounds more literary than 見せる, which is used for physically showing something (写真を見せる). So you do not show a photo with 示す.

examples[].german: Antibodies have formed.
I had measles in the past, so I should have antibodies.
Just to be safe, I had an antibody test at the hospital.
en.notes: 抗体 is the antibody that the immune system forms against a pathogen. Typical phrases are 抗体ができる "antibodies form", 抗体がある and 抗体検査 "antibody test". The word is technical but entered everyday language through vaccinations. Its counterpart, the triggering foreign substance, is 抗原 "antigen"; the immune system itself is 免疫.

examples[].german: We prevent infection.
I caught a virus.
The flu is spreading in the school.
en.notes: 感染 is medical infection or contagion. As an intransitive する-verb, the pathogen takes に: ウイルスに感染する "to be infected with a virus". Common compounds are 感染症 "infectious disease", 感染者 "infected person" and 感染拡大 "spread of infection"; computer viruses also "infect" a computer. In everyday speech, for colds people more often say うつる/うつす: 風邪がうつった.

examples[].german: I was put in quarantine.
Patients with a fever are isolated in a separate room.
He lives as if cut off from society.
en.notes: 隔離 means to separate someone or something from others, especially the sick to prevent infection. As a transitive する-verb: AをBから隔離する; very common in the passive 隔離される. Well-known words are 自主隔離 "self-isolation" and 隔離病棟 "isolation ward". Official quarantine on entry to a country is actually 検疫, but in everyday speech people also say 隔離 for that.

examples[].german: Please disinfect your hands.
I disinfected the wound from the fall.
Disinfectant is placed at the entrance of the shop.
en.notes: 消毒 is disinfecting, that is, killing germs with alcohol, heat or chemicals. As a transitive する-verb: 手を消毒する, 傷口を消毒する. Common are 消毒液 "disinfectant" and アルコール消毒. 殺菌 is the more technical "sterilizing, killing of germs", and 除菌 appears mainly in advertising for cleaning products.

examples[].german: I pay attention to hygiene.
This restaurant has strict hygiene control.
Let's always keep the kitchen hygienic.
en.notes: 衛生 means hygiene and health protection, but mostly appears in compounds: 衛生的 "hygienic" (な-adjective), 不衛生 "unhygienic", 衛生管理 "hygiene control", 公衆衛生 "public health", 衛生面 "in terms of hygiene". For everyday "clean" people more often say 清潔 or きれい. Do not confuse it with the identically read 衛星 "satellite".

examples[].german: Oxygen is needed.
The oxygen is thin at the top of high mountains.
The paramedics put an oxygen mask on the patient.
en.notes: 酸素 is oxygen; literally "acid element", following the same pattern as 水素 "hydrogen", 窒素 "nitrogen" and 炭素 "carbon". Typical phrases are 酸素が薄い "the oxygen is thin" (high-altitude air), 酸素不足 "lack of oxygen", 酸素マスク and 酸素ボンベ "oxygen cylinder". For thin mountain air, people also simply say 空気が薄い in everyday speech.

examples[].german: We reduce CO2.
Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen.
The CO2 coming from cars has become a problem.
en.notes: 二酸化炭素 is carbon dioxide, literally "carbon dioxide" (二 "two", 酸化 "oxide", 炭素 "carbon"). In environmental news it appears with 出す/排出する "to emit" and 減らす/削減する "to reduce"; it is often simply written CO2 (pronounced シーオーツー) or grouped under 温室効果ガス "greenhouse gases". In biology class: plants take in 二酸化炭素 and release 酸素.

examples[].german: Hydrogen energy is attracting attention.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
The number of cars that run on hydrogen is gradually increasing.
en.notes: 水素 is hydrogen, literally "water element". Outside chemistry class, it is heard mainly in connection with energy: 水素エネルギー, 水素自動車 "hydrogen car", 燃料電池 "fuel cell". Do not confuse it with 水 "water" itself: water consists of 水素 and 酸素. 水素水 "hydrogen water" is an advertising term for beverages.

examples[].german: It contains harmful substances.
This substance does not dissolve in water.
Some people say we have become materially rich but poor in spirit.
en.notes: 物質 is "substance, matter" in the scientific sense, typically in 化学物質 "chemical" and 有害物質 "harmful substance". To be distinguished from 材料 "material (for making things)" and the everyday 物 "thing". The adjective 物質的 "material" is often contrasted with 精神的 "mental, spiritual". Reading with small っ: ぶっしつ.

examples[].german: I will look into recent trends.
When I'm tired, I tend to want to eat sweet things.
The population of this town is on the decline.
en.notes: 傾向 is a recognizable tendency or inclination. Very common is 〜傾向がある "to tend to" after a verb, and 〜傾向にある "to be in the process of ...": 増える傾向にある. In reports you read 最近の傾向 or 〜の傾向が見られる. Unlike ブーム or 流行 ("boom, fad"), 傾向 is sober and descriptive and can also refer to personal quirks; an observed tendency is not an exceptionless rule.

examples[].german: Please give me a chance.
The typhoon caused great damage to agriculture.
Please do not feed the pigeons in the park.
en.notes: 与える is transitive: AにBを与える. Toward people it sounds formal or condescending; in conversation, people rather say あげる／くれる. Very common with abstract objects: 影響・被害・印象・ショック・チャンスを与える. Signs often read えさを与えないでください "Please do not feed (the animals)".

examples[].german: Atoms are extremely small.
A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
There is a nuclear power plant near this town.
en.notes: 原子 is the atom; 分子 is the molecule, which consists of 原子. Very common is the compound 原子力 "nuclear power", e.g. 原子力発電所 (abbreviated 原発) "nuclear power plant"; 原子爆弾 is shortened to 原爆. Do not confuse it with the identically read 原始 "primitive, primeval" (原始時代 "primeval age").

examples[].german: A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
The higher the temperature, the faster the air molecules move.
In a fraction, the upper number is called the numerator and the lower number the denominator.
en.notes: 分子 is the "molecule" in chemistry; its building blocks are called 原子 ("atom"). In mathematics, 分子 is the "numerator" of a fraction; the denominator is 分母. In written language it also refers to "elements" of a group, usually pejoratively, as in 不満分子 ("discontented elements"). Which meaning is intended is clear from the context.

examples[].german: The moon's gravity is small.
Inside a spacecraft, you hardly feel gravity.
The apple falls from the tree because of gravity.
en.notes: 重力 is gravity, literally "weight force". There is also 引力 "attractive force" (more general, e.g. 万有引力 "law of universal gravitation", also the moon's pull on the tides). 無重力 means "weightlessness". Typical combinations: 重力がある/小さい, 重力を感じる, 重力に逆らう "to defy gravity".

examples[].german: It sticks to the magnet.
I fastened the note to the fridge with a magnet.
In the mountains, I used a compass to determine the direction.
en.notes: 磁石 is a magnet; things stick to it with に: 磁石にくっつく/つく. Refrigerator magnets are also called マグネット. The secondary meaning "compass" is preserved today mostly in 方位磁石; otherwise one says コンパス. Magnetic force is 磁力, and the magnetic field 磁場 or 磁界.

examples[].german: I do research in the laboratory.
You have to wear a white coat in the laboratory.
Chemistry class is held in the laboratory.
en.notes: 実験室 is a room for experiments, i.e. a laboratory (実験 "experiment" + 室 "room"). At schools, the science room is usually 理科室. 研究室 at universities often means a professor's research group or their office, not just the lab room; colloquially and in companies you also hear ラボ.

examples[].german: I observe with a microscope.
You can't see cells without a microscope.
In science class, I looked through a microscope for the first time.
en.notes: 顕微鏡 is a microscope. One "peers into" it (顕微鏡をのぞく) or observes with it (顕微鏡で見る/観察する). The character 鏡 "mirror, lens" links it with 望遠鏡 "telescope", 双眼鏡 "binoculars" and 眼鏡 "glasses". 電子顕微鏡 is the electron microscope.

examples[].german: I look at the stars through a telescope.
When I looked through the telescope, I could see the craters of the moon.
For my birthday, my father bought me a telescope.
en.notes: 望遠鏡 is a telescope or spyglass, literally "mirror for looking into the distance". You look through it (望遠鏡をのぞく) or view something with it (望遠鏡で見る). The astronomical telescope is more precisely called 天体望遠鏡; binoculars with two eyepieces, by contrast, are 双眼鏡.

examples[].german: I want to go into space.
Becoming an astronaut has been my dream since childhood.
I wonder how far the universe extends.
en.notes: 宇宙 covers both "outer space" and "the universe". One goes 宇宙へ/に行く; common compounds are 宇宙飛行士 "astronaut", 宇宙人 "alien", 宇宙ステーション and 宇宙開発 "space development". 空, by contrast, is the visible sky, and 天 is the heavens in a religious or poetic sense.

examples[].german: There are eight planets in the solar system.
The Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun.
The brightest planet in the night sky is Venus.
en.notes: 惑星 is a planet, literally a "wandering star" (惑 "confused, to wander"). Its counterparts are 恒星 "fixed star" and 衛星 "moon, satellite". The planets are called 水星, 金星, 火星, 木星, 土星 etc.; 星 alone is any star in the sky. Rarely, 惑星 also refers to a "dark horse with a chance of winning" in sports.

en.meaning: to demand; to request; to seek
examples[].german: Please don't demand too much perfection.
I asked the clerk for an explanation, but he didn't answer anything.
He moved to Tokyo in search of work.
en.notes: 求める means "to want, to seek, to demand" and takes を: 助けを求める, 意見を求める. The person asked takes に: 店員に説明を求める. Unlike 探す (to search for something concrete), 求める aims more at abstract things such as help, peace, work or solutions and sounds somewhat more formal. The passive 求められる means "to be expected"; in shops, polite お求め means "purchase" (お求めやすい価格).

examples[].german: An artificial satellite was launched.
The moon is the Earth's only satellite.
I watched an overseas soccer match on satellite broadcasting.
en.notes: 衛星 is a natural moon of a planet, but in everyday use it is mostly short for 人工衛星 "artificial satellite". Common compounds: 気象衛星 "weather satellite", 衛星写真 "satellite image", 衛星放送 "satellite broadcasting", 衛星都市 "satellite city". Satellites are 打ち上げる "launched". Read the same as 衛生 "hygiene"; only context tells them apart.

examples[].german: The Milky Way is beautiful.
On a summer night, I could see the Milky Way clearly on the mountain.
There are countless galaxies in the universe.
en.notes: 銀河, literally "silver river", refers to the Milky Way and, in general, a galaxy. For the Milky Way visible in the night sky, people usually say 天の川 in everyday speech, especially around the Tanabata festival. Our own galaxy is technically called 銀河系. In names and titles, 銀河 sounds romantic and poetic.

examples[].german: The satellite is circling the Earth in orbit.
The new shop's business has finally got on track.
The plan needs a course correction.
en.notes: 軌道 is an orbit or flight path (衛星が軌道を回る), and technically also the track of a railway. The figurative use is very common: 軌道に乗る "to get going, to take off well" (business, project) and 軌道修正 "course correction". For ordinary railway tracks, people say 線路 in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I imitate the teacher's pronunciation.
Children imitate everything their parents do.
I tried painting in imitation of a famous painter's picture.
en.notes: 真似る is transitive: 〜を真似る "to imitate something/someone", e.g. pronunciation, style or behavior. In conversation, the form with the noun 真似 is even more common: 〜の真似をする; ものまね is imitation as an entertainment act. It is often written in kana, まねる. The verb 学ぶ historically goes back to まねぶ "to imitate".

en.meaning: to act spoiled; to be clingy; to take advantage of someone's kindness
examples[].german: The child is acting spoiled with its mother.
Well then, if I may take you up on your kind offer, I'll leave first.
The cat snuggled up and climbed onto my lap.
en.notes: 甘える is intransitive; the person one leans on takes に: 母親に甘える "to snuggle up to one's mother, to let oneself be pampered". Second meaning: to accept someone's kindness, as in the polite phrase お言葉に甘えて "since you kindly offer". The transitive counterpart 甘やかす means "to pamper, to spoil someone"; a clingy child is an 甘えん坊.

en.meaning: to be lazy; to slack off
examples[].german: Don't slack off and study.
He does nothing but slack off at work.
If you skip practice for one day, it's hard to make up for it.
en.notes: 怠ける means "to be lazy, to shirk"; it can be used intransitively or with an object: 仕事を怠ける, 勉強を怠ける. A lazybones is a 怠け者. With the same kanji there is the more formal 怠る (おこたる) "to neglect, to fail to do" (注意を怠る); colloquially, for skipping or loafing, one says サボる.

en.meaning: to act important; to throw one's weight around
examples[].german: Please don't act so high and mighty.
The department head is always lording it over his subordinates.
Just because you came in first, there is no need to be arrogant.
en.notes: 威張る means "to act important, to play the big boss" - a condescending, domineering manner, not boasting about something. The people one lords it over are marked with に: 部下に威張る. For "to boast about something", one says 〜を自慢する; similar to 威張る is 偉そうにする. Often written in kana: いばる.

examples[].german: I won't betray my friends.
I was betrayed by a colleague I had trusted.
That movie exceeded my expectations in a good way.
en.notes: 裏切る is transitive: 友達を裏切る "to betray a friend", in the passive 〜に裏切られる "to be betrayed by someone". Also very common is 期待を裏切る "to disappoint expectations"; with いい意味で "in a good sense" it means that something exceeds expectations. The noun is 裏切り, a traitor is a 裏切り者.

en.meaning: to watch over; to keep an eye on; to follow closely
examples[].german: I watch over the children.
Everyone is following the outcome of the game with bated breath.
My parents always supported my dream with warm encouragement.
en.notes: 見守る is transitive and describes protective, benevolent watching without intervening: 子供を見守る, 温かく見守る "to look on warmly, to support lovingly". In the news, 今後の動きを見守る means "to follow further developments attentively". Unlike 見張る "to guard, to keep watch" or 監視する "to monitor", it carries no distrust.

en.meaning: to overlook; to miss; to let slide
examples[].german: I missed an important scene.
I'll let it go just this once.
I can't afford to miss this chance.
en.notes: 見逃す is transitive and has three main meanings: to miss or overlook something (場面を見逃す), to deliberately let a mistake pass (今回は見逃す "to turn a blind eye this time") and to let an opportunity slip (チャンスを見逃す). 見落とす stresses the accidental overlooking of a detail, 見過ごす the tolerating of something. Online replays of TV programs are called 見逃し配信.

en.meaning: to recognize; to admit; to approve
examples[].german: I admit my mistake.
My parents approved of our marriage.
His efforts were also recognized by the company.
en.notes: 認める is transitive and has several meanings: "to admit" (間違い・罪を認める), "to permit, to approve" (結婚・入学を認める) and "to recognize, to appreciate", often in the passive (努力・才能が認められる). In reports it also means "to find, to detect": 異常は認められない. With と it expresses an assessment: 本物と認める. 許す, by contrast, means "to forgive" or "to allow" and sounds more personal.

en.meaning: to gaze at; to fix one's eyes on; to stare
examples[].german: I gazed at her.
He was silently looking out the window.
On a solo trip, I took a fresh look at myself.
en.notes: 見つめる is transitive: 〜を見つめる "to gaze at, to fix one's eyes on something". It describes a long, intense and often emotional gaze, as opposed to じろじろ見る "to stare rudely" or にらむ "to glare". Figuratively: 現実を見つめる "to face reality", 自分を見つめ直す "to reexamine oneself". The kanji form 見詰める is rare.

en.meaning: to catch sight of; to see by chance
examples[].german: I saw a friend at the station.
Recently, you often see foreign tourists around here.
I often see this cat; I wonder whose it is.
en.notes: 見かける means to see someone or something by chance and fleetingly, without making contact: 駅で友達を見かけた. With よく it expresses that you come across something often. By contrast, 会う means a real meeting and 見つける "to find after searching". Kanji form 見掛ける; the noun 見かけ means "appearance, outward look".

en.meaning: to think of; to come up with
examples[].german: I came up with a good idea.
I can't think of anything to give as a present.
I write down whatever comes to mind right away.
en.notes: 思いつく means that an idea or solution suddenly occurs to you. The idea can take を or が: いい考えを/が思いつく. In the negative: 何も思いつかない "nothing comes to mind". The noun 思いつき is a spontaneous idea, often pejorative (思いつきで決める "to decide on a whim"). Do not confuse it with 思い出す "to remember"; similar is アイデアが浮かぶ.

examples[].german: I was convinced that it was right.
I was sure it was Sunday today and overslept.
That's just your assumption.
en.notes: 思い込む means to be firmly convinced of something - mostly wrongly: 〜と思い込む "to wrongly assume, to talk oneself into". The noun 思い込み means "delusion, preconception", e.g. 思い込みが激しい "full of preconceptions, stubborn in one's assumptions". Neutral "to believe" is 信じる; a mere misunderstanding is 勘違い.

examples[].german: I will cancel the reservation.
I take back my remark from a moment ago.
His license was revoked for drunk driving.
en.notes: 取り消す is transitive: to annul something already decided - a reservation, an order, a statement (発言を取り消す) or a permit. In everyday speech, for bookings one often says キャンセルする; 取り消す sounds somewhat more formal and also fits words and licenses (免許を取り消される "to have one's license revoked"). The noun is 取り消し.

examples[].german: Please handle with care.
Please read the instruction manual carefully before use.
I'm sorry, but our store does not carry this product.
en.notes: 取り扱い is the noun of 取り扱う "to handle, to deal with, to carry (goods)". Typical are 取り扱いに注意 "handle with care", 取り扱い説明書 (short 取説) "instruction manual" and, in shops, 〜の取り扱いがある/ない "to (not) have something in stock". On signs and parcels it is often written without okurigana: 取扱注意, 取扱説明書.

examples[].german: The color combination is lovely.
The pairings for the tournament have been decided.
Please make the password a combination of numbers and letters.
en.notes: 組み合わせ is a combination of two or more things: AとBの組み合わせ, 色の組み合わせ. In sports it refers to the pairings of a tournament (試合の組み合わせ). The verb is 組み合わせる "to combine". Do not confuse it with 組合 (くみあい) "union, cooperative".

en.meaning: to interfere; to affect; to cause trouble
examples[].german: If you don't mind, please tell me.
If I drink until late, it will affect tomorrow's work.
The pain is not so bad that it interferes with daily life.
en.notes: 差し支える is intransitive: something has an adverse effect, with に for the affected area: 仕事に差し支える "to affect work". Most often you meet the noun 差し支え in polite formulas: 差し支えなければ "if you don't mind", 〜ても差し支えありません "there is no objection to ...-ing" (a formal version of 〜てもかまいません).

examples[].german: Thank you for your inquiry.
For details, please inquire by phone.
I still haven't received a reply to the inquiry I sent last week.
en.notes: 問い合わせ is an inquiry to a company or office to obtain information. In business Japanese it is almost always with お: お問い合わせください "please contact us", 問い合わせ先 "contact address", お問い合わせフォーム. The verb is 問い合わせる: 〜に〜を問い合わせる. 質問, by contrast, is any question, e.g. in class.

examples[].german: Please ask at the reception desk.
Applications are accepted until the end of this month.
When you arrive at the hospital, please first check in at reception.
en.notes: 受け付け is on the one hand the reception or check-in desk in companies, clinics or offices, and on the other hand the acceptance of applications or registrations (受付時間, 受付中, 受付終了). For the counter and on signs, the spelling without okurigana, 受付, is the most common. The verb is 受け付ける "to accept, to receive"; at a hotel the front desk is usually フロント.

en.meaning: to state; to express; to mention
examples[].german: Please state your opinion.
At the press conference, the Prime Minister stated the future policy.
As stated in the previous chapter, this problem has two causes.
en.notes: 述べる is transitive and means "to state, to set out" in formal situations: in speeches, essays, meetings and the news. Typical are 意見・理由・感想を述べる and, in texts, 〜と述べた "stated that ..." or 前に述べたように "as stated above". For ordinary speech, use 言う or 話す.

examples[].german: I met an acquaintance.
I got this job through an acquaintance's introduction.
He is just an acquaintance rather than a friend.
en.notes: 知り合い is an acquaintance, someone you know without being close friends; as opposed to 友達. The verb 知り合う means "to get to know each other" (〜と知り合う), 知り合いになる "to become acquainted". In formal language one says 知人. Typical is 知り合いの紹介 "an introduction through an acquaintance".

examples[].german: The relatives gathered.
During summer vacation, I stayed at a relative's house in the countryside.
He and I are distant relatives.
en.notes: 親戚 are the relatives outside the immediate family (家族), such as uncles, aunts and cousins. Traditionally they gather at New Year, Obon, weddings and 法事. 遠い親戚 means "distant relative", 親戚付き合い "contact with the relatives". 親類 is a more formal synonym.

examples[].german: My son's wife is a kind person.
My sister is marrying into a farming family next month.
My wife is really good at cooking.
en.notes: 嫁 is traditionally the bride or the daughter-in-law from the viewpoint of the husband's family: 息子の嫁. 嫁に行く (or 嫁ぐ) means "to marry into a family", 花嫁 is the bride. Colloquially - especially in western Japan - men say うちの嫁 for their own wife; some consider this old-fashioned. The neutral word is 妻, and for someone else's wife 奥さん.

examples[].german: My daughter's husband is a good person.
The bridegroom entered with a nervous expression.
He was adopted into his wife's family and uses her family's surname.
en.notes: 婿 is the son-in-law (娘の婿, also 娘婿) and the bridegroom (花婿; formal 新郎). 婿養子 is a man who marries into his wife's family and takes on its family name; 婿入り is the marrying-in itself. The counterpart is 嫁.

examples[].german: I get along well with my mother-in-law.
It is often said that the relationship between a daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law is difficult.
On weekends I take the kids to my mother-in-law's house.
en.notes: 姑 is traditionally the husband's mother from the wife's point of view; the father-in-law is 舅 (しゅうと). The word is closely tied to the cliché of the 嫁姑問題 "conflict between daughter-in-law and mother-in-law". Today 姑 sounds somewhat old-fashioned; more neutral are 義母 (ぎぼ) and, as a form of address, お義母さん.

examples[].german: I am an only child.
Since I'm an only child, I wanted siblings when I was little.
Recently, families with only one child are increasing.
en.notes: 一人っ子 is an only child. The ending っ子 marks children or people of a certain kind: 末っ子 "youngest child", 江戸っ子 "native Tokyoite", 都会っ子 "city kid". To be distinguished are 一人娘 "only daughter" and 一人息子 "only son". Typical: 一人っ子の家庭 "one-child family".

examples[].german: He is the eldest son.
My father took over the family home as the eldest son.
Our eldest son starts elementary school this year.
en.notes: 長男 is the eldest son – even if he is the only one. It belongs to the series 長男, 次男, 三男 or 長女, 次女 and is used objectively for birth order, also on forms. 兄, by contrast, means "older brother" from the speaker's point of view. Traditionally the 長男 inherits the family home (家を継ぐ).

examples[].german: My second son entered university.
I am the second of three brothers.
The eldest son took over the family home, and the second son works in Tokyo.
en.notes: 次男 is the second son (次 "next"). In official documents it is also written 二男, likewise read じなん. The female counterparts are 長女 and 次女; the third son is 三男. It is used to describe birth order among siblings: 三人兄弟の次男.

examples[].german: The youngest child is very clingy.
I am the youngest of five siblings.
Being the youngest, I grew up doted on by the whole family.
en.notes: 末っ子 is the youngest child of a family (末 "end" + っ子). Youngest children are said to be 甘えん坊 "clingy, affectionate" and to be pampered by everyone (かわいがられる). It applies to boys and girls alike; contrasting terms are 長男/長女 and 一人っ子.

examples[].german: The reception starts at six.
After the ceremony, a wedding reception was held at the hotel.
I was asked to give a speech at a friend's wedding reception.
en.notes: 披露宴 is the reception with food and speeches, usually after the wedding ceremony itself (結婚式); in full 結婚披露宴. 披露 means "to announce publicly, to present" - the couple is presented to friends and relatives. Typical: 披露宴を開く/行う, 披露宴に招待される; guests bring ご祝儀, and often a more casual party, the 二次会, follows.

examples[].german: I fulfilled my role.
To keep his promise, he came to Japan once more.
The team won the championship for the first time.
en.notes: 果たす is transitive and means to carry out a task or duty or to achieve a goal: 役割・責任・義務・約束・目的を果たす. In sports news it often appears as 優勝を果たす "to win the title". For a promise, 約束を守る is more everyday, while 約束を果たす sounds weightier. As a second element, 〜果たす means "completely": お金を使い果たす.

examples[].german: I will attend the memorial service.
The relatives gathered for the first time in a long while at my grandfather's memorial service.
There is a memorial service next Saturday, so I can't come.
en.notes: 法事 is a Buddhist memorial service for the deceased, held on fixed dates such as the 49th day (四十九日) or the anniversaries 一周忌 and 三回忌. A monk recites sutras, after which the relatives eat together. Typical: 法事がある, 法事に出る/出席する; more formal is 法要. The funeral itself is called 葬式.

examples[].german: I will wear a kimono to the coming-of-age ceremony.
In many towns, the coming-of-age ceremony is held on Coming-of-Age Day.
At the coming-of-age ceremony, I saw my junior high classmates for the first time in a long while.
en.notes: 成人式 is the ceremony for young adults organized by local municipalities, usually on or around the holiday 成人の日 in January. Women traditionally wear a 振袖, men a suit or hakama. Since 2022 people in Japan are adults at 18, but most municipalities still celebrate twenty-year-olds, often under the name 二十歳の集い.

examples[].german: I go back to my parents' home for New Year.
Until what date are the New Year holidays?
It is a custom to eat osechi dishes at New Year.
en.notes: 正月 is the New Year season, especially the first three days (三が日), when many Japanese visit family, go to shrines and eat special dishes. In daily life people mostly say the polite お正月; typical are 正月休み "New Year holidays" and 正月に実家に帰る. January 1st itself is 元日 or 元旦; 新年 is more the "new year" in greetings and formal texts (新年あけましておめでとうございます).

examples[].german: I received New Year's money.
I gave my nephew 5,000 yen as a New Year's gift.
I am going to buy a new game with my New Year's money.
en.notes: お年玉 is the money that children receive at New Year from parents, grandparents and relatives, usually in a small decorated envelope (ポチ袋). The typical verbs are お年玉をもらう and (to someone) お年玉をあげる; the お is firmly part of the word, and 年玉 alone is practically never said. Figuratively, companies also call New Year offers お年玉キャンペーン, and お年玉付き年賀はがき are New Year's cards with a lottery number.

examples[].german: We display the dolls for the Girls' Day festival.
On Girls' Day, our family eats chirashi sushi.
Our daughter was born, and this year is her first Girls' Day.
en.notes: 雛祭り is the Girls' Day or Doll Festival on March 3 (also 桃の節句). Families with daughters set up ひな人形 or お雛様 on a tiered platform and wish the girls health and happiness; people eat things like ちらし寿司 and ひなあられ. It is often written partly in kana as ひな祭り. The dolls are set up with 飾る and put away soon afterward - otherwise, it is said, the daughter will marry late.

examples[].german: We display carp streamers for Boys' Day.
On Boys' Day, people eat kashiwa mochi.
Boys' Day is now a public holiday called "Children's Day".
en.notes: 端午の節句 is the traditional festival for boys on May 5; 端午 originally meant the first "horse day" of the fifth month, and 節句 is a seasonal festival. Today the day is a public holiday for all children, こどもの日. Typical are carp streamers (鯉のぼりを飾る/揚げる), samurai helmets (兜) and 柏餅. The expression is somewhat traditional; in daily life people usually just say こどもの日.

examples[].german: Lightning flashed.
A bolt of lightning ran across the night sky.
He ran to the finish line as fast as lightning.
en.notes: 稲妻 is the visible bolt of lightning; literally "rice spouse", from the old belief that lightning makes the rice ripen. Typical: 稲妻が光る or 稲妻が走る "a bolt of lightning flashes". 雷, by contrast, refers to the whole thunderstorm phenomenon and especially the thunder (雷が鳴る); in daily life people often say 雷 or 稲光 instead of 稲妻. Figuratively, 稲妻のように means "lightning-fast". Slightly elevated, vivid style.

examples[].german: Thunder is rumbling.
Lightning struck a tree nearby.
Because I hadn't done my homework, my father exploded at me.
en.notes: 雷 is the thunderstorm as a whole – thunder and lightning. Thunder "rumbles" with 雷が鳴る, a lightning strike is 雷が落ちる; the pure flash of light is more often called 稲妻 or 稲光. Figuratively, 雷 is an angry outburst: 父の雷が落ちる "Father blew up". Children often say 雷さま affectionately; 雷雨 is a thunderstorm with rain.

examples[].german: I can't see ahead because of the fog.
There was thick fog in the morning, but it cleared by noon.
Because of the fog, the flight's departure is delayed.
en.notes: 霧 is fog. It "forms" with 霧が出る or 霧がかかる, is dense with 霧が濃い and clears with 霧が晴れる. As a cause, 霧で or, more formally, 霧のため is used. Light haze is もや, the milky spring haze かすみ. 霧 is also found in 霧雨 "drizzle" and 霧吹き "spray bottle" (in the sense of "spray mist").

examples[].german: Frost has formed.
A lot of frost has built up inside the freezer.
Let's harvest the vegetables before the frost comes.
en.notes: 霜 is rime or ground frost. The fixed phrase is 霜が降りる "frost forms" - not 降る as with rain. Related are 初霜 "first frost", 霜柱 "needle ice in the ground" and 霜焼け "chilblains". Ice in the freezer is also 霜 (霜がつく). Poetically, 霜 can refer to gray hair. For below-zero cold in general, 氷点下 is used more.

examples[].german: A problem has arisen.
A misunderstanding arose between the two of them.
If there is a change to the schedule, please contact us immediately.
en.notes: 生じる is mostly intransitive and means "to arise, to occur": 問題・誤解・疑問・差が生じる. It is the formal, written counterpart of 起こる or 出る and often appears in business e-mails and reports (変更が生じた場合). Transitively, "to cause", it is rare and literary. The variant 生ずる is even more formal.

examples[].german: I can't go outside because of the snowstorm.
The weather in the mountains suddenly changed, and it turned into a snowstorm.
In the park, I saw a shower of cherry blossom petals.
en.notes: 吹雪 is a snowstorm, that is, snow with strong wind; literally "blowing snow". Typical: 吹雪になる, 吹雪が続く, intensified 猛吹雪. Pure heavy snowfall without wind is 大雪. Figuratively, one speaks of 花吹雪 when cherry blossom petals swirl through the air like snow. The related verb 吹雪く "to storm and snow" is rare.

examples[].german: The humidity is high.
Today's humidity is as high as 80 percent.
The air is dry in winter, so I use a humidifier.
en.notes: 湿度 is the measured humidity of the air, usually in percent: 湿度が高い/低い, 湿度は80パーセント. For felt dampness or moisture indoors, one says 湿気 (湿気が多い, 湿気でカビが生える). The counterpart to temperature is 気温, together in weather reports: 気温と湿度. A neutral, somewhat technical term.

examples[].german: The atmospheric pressure is dropping.
Changes in air pressure sometimes give me a headache.
The air pressure is low at the top of the mountain, so snack bags puff up.
en.notes: 気圧 is atmospheric pressure: 気圧が高い/低い, 気圧が下がる/上がる. High- and low-pressure areas are 高気圧 and 低気圧; 低気圧 often stands for bad weather in everyday speech. In Japan, it is common to attribute headaches or tiredness to 気圧の変化. As a unit ("atmosphere"), 気圧 appears in physics, e.g. 1気圧.

examples[].german: I watch the weather forecast.
According to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.
Today the weather forecast was wrong; it was sunny all day.
en.notes: 天気予報 is the weather forecast on TV, radio or in an app. You watch or hear it (天気予報を見る/聞く) and usually report its content with 天気予報によると…そうです or 天気予報では…. When the forecast is right, you say 天気予報が当たる; when it is wrong, 天気予報が外れる. In conversation it is often shortened to 予報.

examples[].german: Tomorrow's forecast is rain.
According to the weather forecast, it will snow from the afternoon.
Today the forecast was wrong; it was sunny all day.
en.notes: 予報 is an official forecast, above all in 天気予報 "weather forecast". Typical: 予報によると…, 予報が当たる "the forecast is right", 予報が外れる "the forecast is wrong". As a する-verb (〜を予報する) it sounds technical. To distinguish: 予想 is a general expectation or guess (試合の予想), 予測 a calculated prediction (経済の予測).

examples[].german: The sunlight is strong.
I went for a walk in the warm spring sunshine.
Please wear a hat to avoid the sun.
en.notes: 日差し is direct incoming sunlight, as you feel it on your skin: 日差しが強い, 日差しがまぶしい, 日差しを浴びる "to bask in the sun", 日差しを避ける. Often also written 陽射し. 日光 is more neutral or technical "sunlight", 日当たり describes how sunny a home is (日当たりがいい), and 日なた is a sunny spot.

examples[].german: Let's rest in the shade of the trees.
I like reading on a bench in the shade of the trees.
I parked the car in the shade of a tree.
en.notes: 木陰 is the shade under a tree, a pleasantly cool place: 木陰で休む, 木陰に入る, 木陰のベンチ. The more general "shade, where the sun doesn't reach" is 日陰 (e.g. behind buildings). 影, by contrast, is the silhouette that an object casts. 木陰 sounds slightly picturesque but is quite common in everyday use.

examples[].german: The gentle breeze feels good.
When I opened the window, a gentle breeze came in.
At the beach, I read a book with a light breeze blowing past me.
en.notes: そよ風 is a gentle, pleasant breeze; related to the sound-symbolic そよそよ "blowing softly". Typical: そよ風が吹く, そよ風が気持ちいい, そよ風に吹かれる "to let the breeze blow over oneself". The word has a positive, slightly poetic ring. 微風 is the literary equivalent, while strong wind is 強風.

examples[].german: It's muggy today, isn't it?
Japanese summers are so muggy that I can't sleep well even at night.
Having the meeting in the muggy room was tough.
en.notes: 蒸し暑い means "muggy", literally "steaming hot" - the typical weather of the Japanese summer and rainy season. A popular small-talk phrase is 蒸し暑いですね. Merely hot is 暑い; じめじめ describes damp, clammy wetness, 暑苦しい an oppressive, stuffy heat (also figuratively: overbearing). As an i-adjective: 蒸し暑くて, 蒸し暑かった.

examples[].german: It's chilly this morning.
It gets chilly at night, so you had better take a jacket.
On rainy days, it feels a bit chilly even in spring.
en.notes: 肌寒い describes a slight, unpleasant coolness felt on the skin - typical for mornings and evenings in spring or autumn and on rainy days. It is weaker than 寒い and, unlike 涼しい "pleasantly cool", slightly negative. Common: 肌寒い朝, 肌寒く感じる, 少し肌寒い. In winter, with real cold, one does not say 肌寒い but 寒い.

en.meaning: to exert (influence); to have an effect
examples[].german: It has a great influence.
Cigarettes have a bad effect on health.
This earthquake caused damage over a wide area.
en.notes: 及ぼす is transitive and appears almost always in the combination Xに影響・被害・害を及ぼす "to affect X, to harm X". It is literary and typical of the news. The intransitive counterpart is 及ぶ "to reach, to extend": 被害が広い地域に及ぶ. 与える (影響を与える) is nearly synonymous, but 及ぼす emphasizes reaching out to something.

examples[].german: The weather is mild.
My grandfather is a very gentle person and has never gotten angry.
After retirement, I want to live a quiet life in the countryside.
en.notes: 穏やか is a な-adjective for anything calm without violent swings: weather and sea (穏やかな天気, 海が穏やかだ), character (穏やかな人 "gentle person") and way of life (穏やかに暮らす). In the second sense it means "moderate, peaceful": 穏やかに話し合う; 穏やかではない means "disturbing, worrying". 静か, by contrast, emphasizes silence above all, i.e. little noise.

examples[].german: It is a gross misunderstanding.
The damage caused by the typhoon was enormous.
Thinking you are the best - what an extreme misjudgment.
en.notes: 甚だしい means "to an extreme degree" and is used almost always with something negative: 甚だしい誤解, 被害が甚だしい, 甚だしい違い. The pattern 〜も甚だしい is common as a sharp rebuke: 勘違いも甚だしい "what a gross misjudgment", 非常識も甚だしい. The style is literary to formal; in conversation one says ひどい or すごい instead. The related adverb is 甚だ "extremely".

examples[].german: The continuing rain is gloomy.
My bangs have grown so long that they're annoying, so I'm going to get them cut.
Being asked the same thing over and over felt irritating.
en.notes: 鬱陶しい is usually written in kana as うっとうしい. It describes, on the one hand, what is gloomy and oppressive (梅雨の鬱陶しい天気, 気分が鬱陶しい) and, on the other, what gets on one's nerves: 前髪が鬱陶しい, ハエが鬱陶しい. Said about people (あの人、鬱陶しい) it is rather rude. 煩わしい aims more at tedious procedures, うるさい at noise or pushiness.

examples[].german: It's a tedious procedure.
Many people find socializing with the neighbors troublesome.
The smartphone notifications were bothersome, so I turned them off.
en.notes: 煩わしい means "annoying, laborious", especially for cumbersome procedures and obligations: 煩わしい手続き, 人間関係が煩わしい, 近所付き合いが煩わしい. It sounds more matter-of-fact and somewhat more refined than the colloquial 面倒くさい; 鬱陶しい, by contrast, is more emotional "irritating". Related is the verb 煩わす, e.g. in the polite phrase お手を煩わせてすみません "sorry to trouble you".

examples[].german: It's a refreshing morning.
The air up on the mountain is refreshing, isn't it?
All my exams are over, and I feel refreshed.
en.notes: 清々しい describes a clear, pure freshness that revives body and mind: 清々しい朝, 清々しい空気, and the liberated feeling after work is done (清々しい気分). People or their behavior can also come across as 清々しい, for example an open smile. さわやか is similar, but more everyday and broader (also taste, weather); 清々しい puts more emphasis on clarity and purity. Often written in kana as すがすがしい.

examples[].german: The atmosphere is awkward.
Since we fought, things have become awkward between him and me.
I ran into my ex in the elevator, and it was awkward.
en.notes: 気まずい describes the unpleasant, tense mood between people: 気まずい雰囲気, 気まずい沈黙, (〜と) 気まずくなる "to become estranged from someone". So it concerns the relationship, not personal shame - for one's own embarrassment, one says 恥ずかしい. Typical after quarrels, embarrassing encounters or when nobody says anything.

examples[].german: Thank you for the quick response.
The cat caught the mouse in a flash.
Thanks to the driver's quick decision, the accident ended without serious injuries.
en.notes: 素早い means "nimble, swift" and describes quick movements or prompt reactions: 素早い動き, 素早い判断, 素早い対応; very often adverbial 素早く (素早く逃げる). 速い is generally "fast" (speed), 早い "early". A relative is すばしこい "nimble, agile", mostly for small animals or children. In business emails: 素早いご対応ありがとうございます.

examples[].german: The reaction is slow.
I've had a dull pain in my head since this morning.
He is so dense that he doesn't notice her feelings at all.
en.notes: 鈍い is the opposite of 鋭い and has several meanings: blunt (鈍い刃), dull (鈍い痛み, 鈍い音), sluggish (動きが鈍い, 反応が鈍い) and slow on the uptake, especially in matters of feeling (彼は鈍い). For people, 鈍感 "insensitive" is also common. Note: the same kanji is read のろい "slow, sluggish"; にぶい is the standard reading.

examples[].german: He has a sharp look in his eyes.
Cat claws are sharp, so please be careful.
My mother has sharp instincts; if I lie, she finds out right away.
en.notes: 鋭い first means "sharp, pointed" for blades and claws (鋭いナイフ, 鋭い爪). Figuratively it stands for sharpness in expression - 鋭い痛み "stabbing pain", 鋭い批判, 鋭い質問, 鋭い目つき - and for a keen mind: 勘が鋭い "to have good instincts", 鋭い観察. The opposite is 鈍い. For food in the sense of "spicy", 辛い is used instead.

examples[].german: It is a coarse cloth.
The image in this photo is coarse, and I can hardly see the face.
He works fast, but he is a bit sloppy.
en.notes: 粗い means "coarse" in the sense of coarse-grained or loosely woven: 粒が粗い, 目が粗い布, 画像が粗い "pixelated"; figuratively also "sloppy" (仕事が粗い). Beware of the identically read 荒い "rough, violent": 波が荒い, 言葉遣いが荒い, 金遣いが荒い. Rule of thumb: 粗い = not fine, 荒い = wild, rough. The opposite of 粗い is 細かい.

en.meaning: to occupy; to account for; to make up
examples[].german: It makes up half of the whole.
At this company, women account for sixty percent of the employees.
Japanese athletes took the top three places.
en.notes: 占める is transitive and describes above all proportions: 全体の半分を占める, 六割を占める "to account for sixty percent". It also stands for taking positions: 上位を占める, 多数を占める. The word is typical of statistics and the news. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 閉める "to close" and 締める "to tighten".

examples[].german: She has lovely smooth skin.
He speaks Japanese fluently.
This pudding is so smooth that it melts in your mouth right away.
en.notes: 滑らか is a な-adjective and is often written in kana as なめらか. It describes smooth, even surfaces and textures (滑らかな肌, 滑らかなクリーム) as well as flowing processes: 滑らかに話す "to speak fluently", 動きが滑らか. Note: the same kanji is in 滑る "to slip". In everyday speech, for smooth-running processes people also say スムーズ, and for a smooth feel the onomatopoeic すべすべ.

examples[].german: It's a brittle material.
Bones become brittle with age.
She is soft-hearted and cries right away at movies.
en.notes: 脆い, mostly in kana もろい, means "brittle, easily broken": 脆いガラス, 骨が脆くなる, 地盤が脆い. Figuratively it stands for emotional softness, especially in compounds: 涙もろい "easily moved to tears", 情にもろい "easily touched". In everyday speech, for objects people often just say 壊れやすい; 弱い is generally "weak".

examples[].german: I gave a vague reply.
It was in my childhood, so my memory is hazy.
Please don't leave important issues unresolved.
en.notes: 曖昧 is a na-adjective for the unclear or ambiguous: 曖昧な返事, 曖昧な態度, 記憶が曖昧 "hazy memory"; 曖昧にする means "to deliberately leave something open". Often written in kana, あいまい. In conversation, はっきりしない is equivalent. 漠然, by contrast, describes a diffuse overall picture without clear contours (漠然とした不安), not an evasive statement.

examples[].german: Please give me your frank opinion.
To be frank, I am against that plan.
She is a frank person, so she says everything clearly.
en.notes: 率直 means "open, candid, direct" and is positive: 率直な意見, 率直な感想, 率直に話す. The fixed phrase 率直に言うと / 率直に言って introduces an open, often critical statement ("frankly speaking"). 正直, by contrast, emphasizes honesty in the sense of "not lying"; はっきり is more everyday and describes only clarity. Neutral to polite, common in meetings.

examples[].german: I have a simple question.
This sweet has a simple flavor and makes me nostalgic.
The villagers were simple and kind.
en.notes: 素朴 describes what is simple and unaffected, with a positive undertone: 素朴な味 "simple, honest flavor", 素朴な人柄, 素朴な村. The set phrase 素朴な疑問 is a naive, very basic question that one simply asks oneself. 単純, by contrast, can mean "simplistic" in a negative sense, 質素 means "frugal, modest" (lifestyle), and シンプル stresses plain design.

examples[].german: It will cost a fortune.
He inherited a huge fortune from his parents.
The earthquake caused enormous damage.
en.notes: 莫大 refers to huge amounts, above all of money, costs, damage or data: 莫大な費用, 莫大な財産, 莫大な借金, 莫大な損害. For physical size (a huge building), 巨大 is used instead. The word almost always stands attributively with な before the noun and sounds matter-of-fact to written-language; in conversation people often say すごい額 or ものすごく.

examples[].german: It's an obvious fact.
It's obvious that he is lying.
This is a clear violation of the rules.
en.notes: 明白 means "evident, unmistakable" and sounds formal, for example in reports, debates or in court: 明白な事実, 明白な証拠, 明白なルール違反, 〜ことは明白だ. In everyday speech people usually say 明らか or, colloquially, はっきりしている. The opposite would be 曖昧 or 不明.

examples[].german: Steady effort bore fruit.
I memorize vocabulary steadily every day.
He isn't flashy, but he is someone who works steadily.
en.notes: 地道 praises persistent, unspectacular work step by step: 地道な努力, 地道な作業, 地道に続ける/働く. It has an appreciative tone - someone works without show, but reliably. Similar is こつこつ "bit by bit"; 着実 emphasizes sure progress. The opposite would be 派手 "flashy" or quick success.

examples[].german: It can be made easily.
You can easily edit photos on a smartphone.
For lunch I kept it simple with a sandwich.
en.notes: 手軽 means "without much effort, uncomplicated, inexpensive" and refers to effort, time or cost: 手軽に作れる, 手軽な料理, 手軽な値段; in advertising often お手軽. To be distinguished from 気軽, which describes the inner threshold ("relaxed, without hesitation"). So: 手軽に作れる料理 (little effort), but 気軽に聞いてください (without reserve).

examples[].german: Please feel free to ask.
She is a senior colleague you can talk to casually.
You can go into this cafe easily, even alone.
en.notes: 気軽 means "carefree, without reserve" and describes the inner attitude: 気軽に話しかける, 気軽に参加する. Very common is the polite service phrase お気軽にどうぞ / お気軽にお問い合わせください "feel free to contact us any time". Do not confuse it with 手軽, which refers to little effort or a low price (手軽な料理).

examples[].german: Let's behave politely.
He acted as if nothing had happened.
On festival days, we treat our neighbors to food.
en.notes: 振る舞う means "to behave" and needs an expression of manner: 礼儀正しく振る舞う, 大人らしく振る舞う, 何もなかったかのように振る舞う. Used transitively it means "to treat someone (to food or drink)": 客に料理を振る舞う. The noun 振る舞い means "behavior, conduct". 行動する, by contrast, means "to act, to take action". It is also often written in kana.

examples[].german: I stood there stunned.
When I found out I'd failed the exam, I was dumbfounded.
The family's house had burned down, and they had stunned looks on their faces.
en.notes: 呆然 describes the state of being paralyzed with shock or surprise. It is not used with な but with と: 呆然とする, 呆然と立ち尽くす, 呆然と見つめる, attributively 呆然とした顔. The spelling 茫然 is equivalent and often used interchangeably; 呆然 stresses the shock more. Slightly literary; in conversation people often say びっくりして何も言えなかった.

examples[].german: I'm gazing absent-mindedly outside.
After the sudden breakup, he was in a state of complete daze.
I didn't know what to do and was standing there in a daze.
en.notes: 茫然 is a spelling variant of 呆然 with the same reading; the kanji 茫 originally means "vast, boundless". Therefore 茫然 rather stresses the empty, absent-minded staring into space when everything slips away. It is used with と: 茫然とする, 茫然と眺める. The set phrase 茫然自失 means "completely stunned, beside oneself". More literary.

examples[].german: I have a vague sense of anxiety.
I've only thought about the future in vague terms so far.
The question is so vague that I don't know how to answer.
en.notes: 漠然 describes something indefinite without clear contours. It is used with と: 漠然とした不安 "diffuse anxiety", 漠然としたイメージ, 漠然と考える "to think about it only vaguely". Unlike 曖昧, which often means an evasive, ambiguous statement, 漠然 simply lacks concreteness: a feeling or plan is still blurry.

examples[].german: Clean up quickly.
Let's finish work quickly and go for a drink.
As soon as the meeting ended, he left right away.
en.notes: さっさと means "promptly, without dawdling" and is colloquial. It often appears in commands with a slightly impatient tone (さっさとしなさい "Hurry up!") or describes someone doing something quickly and without consideration: さっさと帰る "to make oneself scarce quickly". 早く is neutral, すぐ emphasizes "immediately", and てきぱき praises efficient work.

examples[].german: I opened the door quietly.
She's feeling down, so let's leave her alone for a while.
I laid the baby gently in bed so as not to wake it.
en.notes: そっと means "quietly, gently" (そっとドアを閉める, そっと置く) and "secretly, unnoticed" (そっと教える). Very common is そっとしておく "to leave someone alone", for example when someone is sad. こっそり stresses concealment more strongly, often with a guilty conscience; 静かに refers only to volume.

examples[].german: I waited without moving.
Hold still for the injection, okay?
He looked me in the face fixedly, without saying a word.
en.notes: じっと describes someone not moving (じっとする, じっと座る), looking at something fixedly or doing something intensely (じっと見つめる, じっと考える), or enduring patiently (じっと我慢する). With children you often hear じっとしていなさい "Hold still!". Not to be confused with ずっと "the whole time" - じっと stresses motionlessness, not duration.

examples[].german: My eyes are spinning.
I got lost and kept walking around in circles in the same place.
I wrapped a bandage around the injured leg several times.
en.notes: ぐるぐる is onomatopoeic for repeated turning or circling: ぐるぐる回る, 同じところをぐるぐる歩く "to walk in circles", 目がぐるぐる回る "to feel dizzy". It also describes wrapping something around several times: 包帯をぐるぐる巻く, ぐるぐる巻き. Thoughts can also go ぐるぐる round in one's head. くるくる is lighter and faster, ぐるっと means "once all the way around".

en.meaning: to stroll; to dangle; to loaf around
examples[].german: I strolled around the town.
She was sitting on the chair, swinging her legs.
Since graduating from university, he has been idling around without working.
en.notes: ぶらぶら is onomatopoeic and has three main meanings: to stroll aimlessly (街をぶらぶら歩く, ぶらぶらする), to dangle (足をぶらぶらさせる) and to hang around idly, for example without a job (毎日ぶらぶらしている). Related is the verb ぶらつく "to wander about". うろうろ, by contrast, describes restless, searching wandering, often with a suspicious connotation.

examples[].german: It was unexpectedly easy.
The place looks plain, but the ramen here is surprisingly good.
I was worried, but he got used to the new job surprisingly quickly.
en.notes: 案外 expresses mild surprise when something is different from what was expected (usually better); it usually stands adverbially before an adjective: 案外簡単だった, 案外おいしい. Very similar is 意外と; 案外 sounds a bit more casual and conversational. 思ったより says the same in a completely neutral way. As a な-adjective (案外な結果) it is rarer.

examples[].german: Everyone stood up at the same time.
When the light turned green, all the cars set off at once.
It got warm, and the cherry trees all began to bloom at once.
en.notes: 一斉に means "all at the same time, all at once" and presupposes that many people or things do the same thing at the same moment: 一斉に立ち上がる, 一斉に咲く. 同時に, by contrast, can also concern two things or a single actor, and いっぺんに stresses "everything at once instead of one after another". As a noun, 一斉 appears in compounds such as 一斉送信 ("mass email") or 一斉休校 ("nationwide school closure").

en.meaning: to be blessed with; to be fortunate to have
examples[].german: We were blessed with good weather.
I am really happy to be blessed with good friends.
This country is blessed with resources such as oil.
en.notes: 恵まれる is intransitive; what one is blessed with is marked with に: 天気・才能・友達・資源に恵まれる. Formally it is the passive of 恵む, but it is used as a verb in its own right. 恵まれた環境／家庭 means "a privileged environment/family", and 恵まれない子どもたち means "underprivileged children". It often expresses gratitude for good fortune that one had no control over.

examples[].german: He is a good singer by nature.
I have been physically weak since birth.
Her hair is naturally brown; she doesn't dye it.
en.notes: 生まれつき means "from birth, by nature". Adverbially it stands before the statement (生まれつき体が弱い), as an attribute with の (生まれつきの才能, 生まれつきの髪の色). It is often used to explain that something is not chosen or trained, e.g. hair color. More elevated is 生まれながら(に); 天性 stresses a special talent.

examples[].german: Thanks to you, I was saved.
Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass the exam.
Thanks to taking the medicine, my fever went down.
en.notes: おかげで names a cause with a positive result: Nのおかげで, Vたおかげで ("thanks to"). Alone at the beginning of a sentence it means "Thanks to you/that ...". Related is the set phrase おかげさまで "I'm fine, thank you" as an answer to questions about one's well-being. For negative causes one uses せいで; but ironically おかげで can also assign blame (君のおかげで遅刻したよ).

examples[].german: I was late because of the rain.
I was late for the train because I overslept.
I couldn't sleep at all last night because of the noise from the construction next door.
en.notes: せいで names a cause with a negative result and often assigns blame: Nのせいで, Vたせいで ("because of, it's the fault of"). The counterpart for positive results is おかげで. Related are 〜のせいにする "to blame someone" (人のせいにする) and 〜せいか "perhaps because". The underlying noun せい (rarely written 所為) means "fault, consequence".

examples[].german: Therefore, a change is necessary.
This region gets little rain. Therefore, water is precious.
The application period ended today. Therefore, we cannot accept any applications after this.
en.notes: 従って (mostly written in kana as したがって) is a conjunction at the beginning of a sentence: "therefore, consequently". It sounds literary and formal - typical in reports, announcements and arguments; in conversation people say だから or なので instead. Not to be confused with the て-form of the verb 従う: 〜に従って means "in accordance with" (指示に従って) or "as ..., the more ..." (年を取るに従って).

examples[].german: I will explain in even more detail.
Tomorrow the temperature is expected to drop even further.
This shop is cheap. Moreover, it's conveniently close to the station.
en.notes: さらに intensifies something already there: "even (more), still further" before verbs and adjectives (さらに寒くなる, さらに詳しく). At the beginning of a sentence it acts as a conjunction "moreover, in addition" and adds another argument. Compared with the colloquial もっと, さらに sounds more objective and somewhat more literary. Mostly written in kana; the kanji spelling 更に is rarer.

examples[].german: Incidentally, we will contact you with details at a later date.
Even though I took medicine, my fever still won't go down.
If it's close to the station, all the better.
en.notes: なお has two main uses. As a conjunction at the start of a sentence (なお、…) it introduces an additional note in announcements, emails and notices: "incidentally, in addition, note:". As an adverb it means "still" or "even more": なおいい "all the better", なお一層 "even more strongly". In everyday speech people more often say まだ for "still". Almost always in kana; related is なおさら "all the more".

examples[].german: He is my mother's younger brother, that is, my uncle.
No reply means, in other words, that they are against it.
The game will take place next Saturday, namely on October 15.
en.notes: すなわち equates two expressions: "that is, namely, in other words". It stands between what has been said and its explanation or clarification (A、すなわちB) and sounds written and objective, typical of textbooks, reports and speeches. In conversation, つまり is used instead. Without preceding content, it cannot simply open a sentence. Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: I'll say it anyway, if you'll allow me.
He deliberately chose the difficult path.
If I had to say something, the color is perhaps a little plain.
en.notes: あえて means to do something deliberately although it seems unnecessary, risky or unusual: "deliberately, on purpose, despite reservations". Typical are あえて言うなら "if I had to say something" and あえて〜ない "not necessarily, not particularly". Unlike わざと (often negative, with malicious intent) and わざわざ (going out of one's way), あえて stresses a considered decision. Mostly in kana.

examples[].german: I barely made it in time.
I only just passed the exam.
He was in an accident, but narrowly survived.
en.notes: かろうじて means "just barely, by a narrow margin": the result was achieved, but only very narrowly (間に合う, 合格する, 助かる). It sounds somewhat more literary than ぎりぎり, which is used colloquially mainly for time limits, and stresses the narrowness more than やっと, which stresses the long wait. Mostly in kana; the kanji 辛 is read unusually here.

examples[].german: I'll prepare in advance.
If you cannot participate, please let us know beforehand.
Since the restaurant is popular, I reserved a table in advance.
en.notes: あらかじめ means "in advance, beforehand" and often appears with 〜ておく (あらかじめ準備しておく) or in polite requests such as あらかじめご了承ください "we ask for your understanding in advance". It sounds more formal than 前もって; in business language 事前に is also very common. Mostly written in kana. Unlike 前に, あらかじめ does not designate a point in time but stresses preparation before an event.

examples[].german: It's a mysterious phenomenon.
A rare phenomenon occurred in which a ring of light could be seen in the sky.
The movie was a huge hit and became a social phenomenon.
en.notes: 現象 is an observable occurrence in nature or society: 自然現象, 社会現象. Typical are 現象が起きる / 起こる and 現象が見られる. The word describes what happens, not why; the cause is 原因. 社会現象 is also used for a huge hype, for example when a film captivates all of Japan. Do not confuse it with the identically read 減少 "decrease, decline".

examples[].german: In Japan, it is common to take off your shoes when entering a house.
In general, women live longer than men.
This is a very common name, so there are many people with the same name.
en.notes: 一般的 is a な-adjective meaning "usual, widespread". Typical patterns are 〜のが一般的だ "it is common that ...", 一般的に（言えば）"in general" and 一般的な + noun "ordinary, common". The noun 一般 appears in 一般の人 "the general public, laypeople". 普通 is the more everyday word for "normal".

examples[].german: I rarely catch a cold.
My father rarely gets angry.
You don't get a chance like this every day.
en.notes: めったに always goes with a negative: めったに〜ない "rarely, hardly ever". It is stronger than あまり〜ない and stresses that something happens only exceptionally. Fixed phrase: めったにない "rare, once in a lifetime" (めったにないチャンス). Without negation, めったな means "rash, careless" (めったなことを言うな). Both the kanji 滅多 and kana are common.

en.meaning: by no means; no way (with negative)
examples[].german: It's absolutely impossible.
I can't possibly finish this amount of work in one day.
I can't possibly understand his feelings.
en.notes: 到底 intensifies an impossibility and is used with a negative or with words such as 無理, できない: "by no means, not by any stretch". It expresses that something objectively cannot be managed, whereas 決して〜ない rather stresses a will or a prohibition. とても〜ない is similar but more colloquial. Both kanji and kana are common; the tone is somewhat elevated.

examples[].german: I've hardly slept.
I took the exam without studying properly.
I was so busy that I couldn't even eat lunch properly.
en.notes: ろくに is always used with a negative and means "not properly, hardly decently": ろくに寝ていない, ろくに勉強しない. It sounds colloquial and often reproachful or complaining, because something was not done to the necessary degree. Related is ろくな + noun + ない "no decent ..." (ろくなことがない). ほとんど〜ない is more neutral. Almost always in kana.

examples[].german: The phone keeps ringing.
He kept looking at his watch.
A friend keeps recommending that movie to me.
en.notes: しきりに describes something that repeats conspicuously often: "constantly, over and over" (しきりに時計を見る, 電話がしきりに鳴る). It can also express an insistent attitude: しきりに勧める "to recommend eagerly". It sounds somewhat more descriptive and literary than 何度も or the colloquial しょっちゅう. Almost always in kana; the kanji 頻りに is rare.

examples[].german: I'll do my best.
At most about twenty participants will come.
Even on foot, it's ten minutes to the station at most.
en.notes: せいぜい has two meanings. Mostly it means "at most, at best" and judges a quantity as rather small, often with ぐらい, 程度 or だろう (せいぜい20人ぐらい). It also means "as well as one can": せいぜい頑張ります. Said by others, せいぜい頑張って can sound condescending or ironic. A more neutral word for "maximum" is 多くても. Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: That's so typically Japanese, isn't it?
He looks really sleepy.
That's a typical answer for him.
en.notes: いかにも says that something looks exactly as one would expect: "truly, typical, decidedly". Typical combinations are いかにも〜らしい "typical of" and いかにも〜そう "looks just like". On its own as an answer, いかにも means "indeed, exactly", but sounds old-fashioned. Unlike 本当に, いかにも stresses the outward impression. Mostly in kana.

examples[].german: With a casual remark, I ended up hurting her.
When I glanced out the window without thinking, it was snowing.
On the TV I had turned on without thinking, an interesting program was on.
en.notes: 何気なく, the adverbial form of 何気ない, means "without particular intention, just like that, casually": 何気なく窓の外を見る, 何気なく言った一言. Unlike うっかり (by mistake, with an error), it stresses only the lack of intention; なんとなく means more "for no clear reason, somehow". The form 何気に "actually quite" is youth slang. Mostly written with kanji.

examples[].german: It takes a little time.
If it's only light rain, the game will be held.
I can speak a little English.
en.notes: 多少 as an adverb means "somewhat, a little, to a certain degree" and sounds more objective and polite than 少し or ちょっと, for example in announcements: 多少時間がかかります. With の it stands before nouns: 多少の雨, 多少の違い. As a noun it means "quantity, much or little", e.g. 金額の多少にかかわらず "regardless of the amount". Always written with kanji.

examples[].german: Prices have risen substantially.
The train is running considerably late.
A sale with big price cuts has started.
en.notes: 大幅 describes large changes in quantities and values: "considerable, drastic". Adverbially it appears as 大幅に before verbs such as 増える, 減る, 上がる, 遅れる, 変更する; before nouns as 大幅な (大幅な値下げ). For a general increase in qualities people use かなり or ずいぶん, not 大幅. Opposite: 小幅 "slight". Typical of the news and business language.

examples[].german: I enjoyed it a great deal.
I agree with that opinion wholeheartedly.
I think this experience will be very useful in the future.
en.notes: 大いに means "very much, to a great extent, to one's heart's content" and mainly intensifies verbs: 大いに楽しむ, 大いに期待する, 大いに賛成する, 大いに役に立つ. Before adjectives, you normally use とても or 非常に, not 大いに. The tone is somewhat elevated and emphatic, typical of speeches and invitations such as 大いに飲みましょう. Always written with kanji.

examples[].german: I actually went and tried it.
Seeing it in person was much prettier than seeing it in photos.
I want to hear the impressions of people who actually use this app.
en.notes: 実際に contrasts real experience or reality with theory, imagination or hearsay: 実際に行ってみる, 実際に使ってみる. 実際は／実際には means "in reality, though" and contradicts an expectation; 実際の + noun means "real, actual". Unlike 本当に, 実際に is not an intensifier: "really pretty" is 本当にきれい, not 実際にきれい.

examples[].german: In fact, it is succeeding.
This medicine works well. In fact, I got better in a week myself.
That intersection is dangerous. In fact, there was an accident there last month, too.
en.notes: 現に cites a concrete, actually existing fact as evidence for a claim: "actually, as you can see". The typical sequence is claim → 現に + example. 実際に is more general, and 実は rather introduces a revelation ("to tell the truth"). The tone is matter-of-fact, but it is as common in conversation as in texts.

en.meaning: certain; sure; if I remember correctly
examples[].german: If I remember correctly, the deadline is tomorrow.
If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Tanaka is from Osaka.
Is that reliable information?
en.notes: As an adverb at the beginning of a sentence, 確か means "if I remember correctly, as far as I know" and marks a statement as not entirely certain; often ～と思います, ～はずです or a past form follows. As a な-adjective, on the other hand, it means "certain, reliable": 確かな情報, 確かな腕. Do not confuse it with 確かに "indeed, truly", which confirms a statement (確かにそうですね). In casual conversation the adverb is often followed by a short pause: 確か、….

examples[].german: I secretly made a plan.
She was secretly in love with him.
The weekend nap is my little secret pleasure.
en.notes: 密か is a na-adjective for "secret, quietly" and is mostly used as ひそかに (ひそかに計画する, ひそかに好きだ). Before nouns it appears as ひそかな: ひそかな楽しみ "little secret pleasure", ひそかな夢. It describes a quiet, inconspicuous hiding of feelings or plans; こっそり is more colloquial and stresses the furtiveness of an action. Both kana and kanji are common.

examples[].german: He/She grew up healthy.
We wish your child a healthy and strong upbringing.
My grandfather is ninety now and still lives in good health.
en.notes: 健やか means "healthy, robust, in good health" and sounds elevated and warm. It is typical for children (健やかに育つ, 健やかな成長) as well as in congratulations and greeting formulas. In everyday speech people say 元気 or 健康 instead; 健康 is the neutral noun "health". 健やか stresses a healthy, undisturbed thriving of body and mind.

examples[].german: What a fresh, pleasant morning.
He is always smiling and has a refreshingly pleasant manner.
This tea has a refreshing scent of mint.
en.notes: 爽やか describes something pleasantly fresh without sultriness or heaviness: dry, clear weather (especially in autumn and spring), fresh scents and flavors (ミントの爽やかな香り) and likable, open people (爽やかな笑顔, 爽やかな青年). 涼しい, by contrast, refers only to pleasantly cool temperature. Written with kanji or in kana as さわやか.

examples[].german: There is a harmonious atmosphere.
The meeting went along in a friendly atmosphere.
We enjoyed our meal in a pleasant family atmosphere.
en.notes: 和やか describes the friendly, relaxed mood among people: 和やかな雰囲気, 和やかに話す, 会議が和やかに進む. It thus characterizes a situation or group, not the temperament of an individual; for that people use 穏やか "calm, gentle", which also applies to weather and sea. Typical of reports on meetings, celebrations and family meals.

examples[].german: It's a glamorous party.
She always wears colorful, elegant clothes.
The entertainment industry looks glamorous, but it is actually a tough world.
en.notes: 華やか means "splendid, brilliant, colorful" and is positive: 華やかなパーティー, 華やかな服, 華やかな世界. Unlike 派手 (flashy, conspicuous, often critical), 華やか praises the effect; 豪華 stresses luxury and high cost more. It can also describe a heyday: 華やかな時代 "glorious era". The kanji 華 means "blossom, splendor".

examples[].german: It's a gentle slope.
The economy is recovering gradually.
This school's rules are lenient.
en.notes: 緩やか means "gentle, gradual, loose": a gentle slope or a shallow curve (緩やかな坂, 緩やかなカーブ), a slow change (景気が緩やかに回復する) or mild rules (規則が緩やか). It sounds more matter-of-fact and more literary than the everyday word 緩い, which stands for example for shoes that are too loose or lax controls. Very common in the news.

examples[].german: We will respond promptly.
In the event of an earthquake, evacuate the building immediately.
Please submit the documents promptly.
en.notes: 速やか means "without delay, promptly" and appears almost always as 速やかに in formal announcements, instructions and business texts: 速やかに避難してください, 速やかに対応いたします. In daily life, people say すぐに or 早く instead. It stresses acting without hesitation, not necessarily high speed; for speed, 速い is used.

examples[].german: We lost by a narrow margin.
There are only three days left until the deadline.
Only a tiny amount of my savings is left.
en.notes: わずか means "slight, little, narrow": わずかな差, わずかなお金. Before numbers it means "only, merely" and often goes with しか or だけ: わずか三日しかない. In shops you read 残りわずか "only a few left in stock". It sounds somewhat more elevated than 少し or ちょっと and stresses how small the amount is. Mostly written in kana.

en.meaning: in the end; after all; eventually
examples[].german: In the end, I didn't go.
I agonized over many things, but in the end I bought it at my usual shop.
So, what is it that you want to say?
en.notes: 結局 sums up the result after some back and forth, often with an outcome different from what was planned: 結局行かなかった. At the start of a sentence it also means "when all is said and done, in the final analysis" (結局は自分次第); 結局、何が言いたいの? impatiently asks for the point. ついに／とうとう, by contrast, emphasize the long-awaited occurrence, and 最後に means "lastly" in a sequence.

examples[].german: He made a sarcastic remark.
Ironically, it never rains on the days I go out with an umbrella.
His compliment sounded sarcastic.
en.notes: 皮肉 means "irony, sarcasm, a pointed remark"; literally "skin and flesh", that is, something that only scratches the surface. Typical are 皮肉を言う "to make snide remarks", 皮肉っぽい "sounding sarcastic" and the verb 皮肉る. As a na-adjective it describes ironic coincidences: 皮肉な結果, 皮肉なことに "ironically". Unlike 冗談 (a joke), 皮肉 always contains a hidden reproach.

examples[].german: Thank you for all your help.
Every morning I take care of the dog.
Mind your own business!
en.notes: 世話 is "care, looking after, help". One takes care of someone with 〜の世話をする (犬の世話をする); receiving help is 世話になる. From this come the fixed polite formulas お世話になりました "thank you for everything" at parting and お世話になっております as the standard greeting in business e-mails. 余計なお世話 means "mind your own business", and 世話を焼く "to fuss (too much) over someone".

examples[].german: Behave yourself!
It's bad manners to rest your elbows on the table while eating.
That child is very well-behaved.
en.notes: 行儀 refers to a person's behavior, especially in daily life and at the table: 行儀がいい／悪い, 行儀よくする. With children, people like to say お行儀. マナー, by contrast, means the rules of etiquette in particular situations, and 礼儀 respectful politeness toward others. 他人行儀 means "formal and distant, as with strangers".

examples[].german: That is thoughtless behavior.
Calling at two in the morning is just not done!
I was told it's inappropriate to go to a wedding in a white dress.
en.notes: 非常識 means "without common sense, out of line, outrageous" and is a な-adjective or noun: 非常識な人, 非常識な時間, 〜なんて非常識だ. It is a clear criticism of behavior that violates generally expected social rules. 失礼, by contrast, stresses rudeness toward a specific person. Opposite: 常識的, 常識がある.

examples[].german: Please observe the rules of etiquette.
On the train, please set your mobile phone to silent mode.
He has bad table manners.
en.notes: マナー refers to the rules of etiquette in particular situations: 食事のマナー, ビジネスマナー, 電車のマナー. Typical are マナーを守る "to follow the rules", マナーが悪い and マナー違反 "violation of etiquette". マナーモード is the silent mode of a mobile phone. Unlike English "manner", it never means "way of doing something". 行儀 is more personal behavior.

examples[].german: I apologize for the trouble.
If you make noise late at night, you disturb the neighbors.
I get lots of spam emails every day, and it's a nuisance.
en.notes: 迷惑 is "nuisance, inconvenience, burden on others". Central are 迷惑をかける "to be a burden to someone" (politely ご迷惑をおかけしました) and 〜の迷惑になる "to disturb others". As a な-adjective: 迷惑な人, 迷惑な話. 迷惑する means "to be bothered, to suffer from" (騒音に迷惑している). 迷惑メール is spam email. 邪魔, by contrast, means "to be in the way, to hinder".

examples[].german: Please don't hold back.
Please refrain from smoking here.
Sorry, I'll pass on the drinking party today.
en.notes: 遠慮 is the typically Japanese restraint out of consideration for others. 遠慮しないでください and 遠慮なく… invite someone to help themselves or speak up without hesitation. On signs and announcements, ご遠慮ください is a polite form of prohibition ("Please refrain from this"). With 遠慮しておきます one kindly declines an offer or invitation; the thing one gives up can take を or は.

examples[].german: You are being too modest.
In Japan, it is normal to be modest when praised.
He is modest and hardly talks about his achievements.
en.notes: 謙遜 is modestly playing down one's own accomplishments, especially in response to praise: 謙遜する, 謙遜して〜と言う. When someone is praised and deflects it, one politely replies ご謙遜を "You are too modest". 謙虚 (na-adjective), by contrast, describes a modest character in general. In Japan, deflecting praise is considered normal politeness.

examples[].german: I'll wait patiently.
Just a little more patience, so hang in there.
It hurts a bit, but bear with it for a moment, okay?
en.notes: 辛抱 is patiently enduring an unpleasant situation over some time: 辛抱する, 辛抱強い "patient, persevering", もう少しの辛抱だ "just hang on a little longer". 我慢 is more common and stresses suppressing wishes or pain in the moment; 忍耐 is more literary. 辛抱 sounds warm and encouraging, often toward children.

examples[].german: It's a job that requires perseverance.
I kept practicing patiently and got good at it.
I have no perseverance, so I can't stick with anything I do.
en.notes: 根気 is the perseverance to keep going calmly with a tedious or lengthy task: 根気がある／ない, 根気よく続ける, 根気強い, 根気のいる仕事. 辛抱 stresses enduring unpleasant things, 根性 rather fighting spirit and grit. 根気 suits patient detail work such as practicing, studying or crafting in particular.

en.meaning: on the other hand; while; one side
examples[].german: Work is busy. On the other hand, it is rewarding.
While prices rise, salaries do not.
Recently, my work has been increasing more and more.
en.notes: 一方 has three important uses: at the start of a sentence (一方、／一方で) it introduces the other side, "on the other hand, in contrast". After a clause, 〜一方（で）means "while, at the same time". After the dictionary form, 〜一方だ means "it just keeps ...ing", mostly for negative developments (増える一方だ). As a noun it means "one side, one of the two" (一方の意見). It is rather literary; in conversation people often say でも.

examples[].german: I study with concentration.
It's so noisy that I can't concentrate on my work.
In Japan, the population is concentrated in Tokyo.
en.notes: 集中 is "concentration" in two senses. Mental: 〜に集中する "to concentrate on something", 集中して勉強する, 集中力 "ability to concentrate". Spatial: people, buildings or power cluster in one place (人口が都市に集中する). Transitive with を: 意識を集中する. 集中豪雨 is a localized heavy downpour.

examples[].german: Please don't let your guard down.
I let my guard down for a moment, and my wallet was stolen.
Even if the opponent is weak, you must not be careless.
en.notes: 油断 means letting one's vigilance slip because one feels too safe: 油断する, ちょっと油断したら…, 油断は禁物 "one must not become careless". The proverb 油断大敵 means "carelessness is the greatest enemy". 不注意, by contrast, emphasizes a specific careless mistake; 油断 is rather an attitude of carefree complacency.

examples[].german: I have steeled myself.
I'll take on the challenge, prepared to fail.
If you study abroad, you should be prepared for hardship.
