en.notes: 覚悟 is the inner readiness to take on something hard or negative: 覚悟を決める "to make up one's mind to face it", 覚悟はできている, 〜は覚悟している "to be prepared for something", 〜覚悟で "at the risk of". 決心 and 決意 mean more the decision to do something; 覚悟 stresses accepting possible consequences.

examples[].german: He took on the world record.
A young athlete challenged the champion to a match.
Taking on Mt. Fuji in winter is dangerous.
en.notes: 挑む means "to venture at something difficult" or "to challenge someone". With a task it takes に: 記録に挑む, 冬山に挑む, 難問に挑む. With a person, the opponent takes に and the fight takes を: 相手に勝負を挑む. The word sounds elevated and often appears in news and sports reports; in everyday speech people usually say 挑戦する. 挑戦に挑む would be redundant.

examples[].german: I overcame the difficulties.
She overcame her illness and returned to work.
To overcome my weakness in math, I practice every day.
en.notes: 克服 is overcoming a difficulty or weakness: 困難を克服する, 病気を克服する, 苦手を克服する. It is a transitive する-verb with を and sounds somewhat more formal than the synonymous 乗り越える. Typical of reports about illness, crises, fears and academic weaknesses.

examples[].german: I achieved my goal.
When I reached the summit of the mountain, I felt a great sense of accomplishment.
I can't go home until I meet my quota.
en.notes: 達成 means "achieving, fulfilling" a goal or target: 目標を達成する, 記録を達成する, ノルマを達成する. For arriving at a place, by contrast, one uses 着く or 到着する. Common is 達成感 "sense of accomplishment, feeling of having achieved something". 実現 rather means "to realize" (a dream, a plan).

examples[].german: He left behind great achievements.
His contributions to environmental protection were recognized, and he received an award.
The success of this project is an achievement of the whole team.
en.notes: 功績 is a recognized, significant contribution to a community or a field: 功績を残す, 功績を上げる, 功績が認められる, 功績をたたえる. It is formal and often appears in speeches, obituaries and award citations. 業績 refers more to measurable results (company results, scholarly achievements), and 手柄 is colloquial "credit, laurels".

examples[].german: It's an honorable award.
I was chosen as a representative and feel very honored.
My reputation was damaged by a false article.
en.notes: 名誉 means "honor" in the sense of distinction (名誉ある賞, 名誉に思う) and "good reputation" (名誉を傷つける, 名誉を回復する). As a prefix it means "honorary": 名誉教授, 名誉市民. For the modest thank-you formula "It is an honor for me" people usually say 光栄です. 名誉 can also be used as a na-adjective: 名誉なこと.

examples[].german: I am proud of Japanese culture.
My son won, and I'm proud of him.
His words hurt my pride.
en.notes: 誇り is positive pride in something valuable: 〜に誇りを持つ, 〜を誇りに思う, 誇りを傷つける. The verb is 誇る, the adjective 誇らしい "proud, feeling proud". プライド is often used for sensitive pride or ego (プライドが高い). Note: ほこり in kana usually means 埃 "dust", so 誇り is almost always written with kanji.

examples[].german: Spring will come soon.
The rain eventually turned to snow.
It was a small shop, but before long it became known across the country.
en.notes: やがて describes that something occurs "after a while, in time" in the natural course of time, without anyone helping it along: やがて春が来る, やがて雪に変わる. It is rather narrative and literary and is almost always written in kana. When talking about one's own plans in conversation, people say もうすぐ or すぐ; いずれ means "someday".

examples[].german: Please have confidence.
I'm confident about cooking.
After failing the exam, I lost my confidence.
en.notes: 自信 is confidence in one's own abilities: 自信がある／ない, 〜に自信がある "to be confident in something", 自信を持つ, 自信をなくす, 自信満々 "full of confidence", 自信過剰 "overconfident". Beware of the identically read 地震 "earthquake". 自身 (oneself, 私自身) is also a homophone.

examples[].german: Please have courage.
His words gave me courage.
Going abroad alone takes courage.
en.notes: 勇気 is "courage": 勇気を出す "to muster courage", 勇気がある, 〜には勇気がいる "it takes courage to do that". Typically Japanese are 勇気をもらう "to be encouraged" and 勇気を与える "to give courage", often about athletes or artists; there is also the verb 勇気づける. 勇敢 (な-adjective) describes brave, valiant action, and 度胸 more nerve.

examples[].german: I'm absorbed in the game.
I was so absorbed in reading the book that suddenly it was morning.
The children are chasing insects, completely absorbed.
en.notes: 夢中 means to be completely absorbed in something: 〜に夢中だ／夢中になる "to be enthusiastic about, absorbed in, crazy about" (ゲームに夢中, 彼女に夢中). 夢中で describes acting oblivious to oneself, without thinking of anything else. Intensified: 無我夢中 "completely oblivious to oneself". 熱中 is more matter-of-fact; 夢中 stresses more strongly forgetting one's surroundings. Grammatically a な-adjective or noun.

examples[].german: He is studying diligently.
Mr. Tanaka is a person who is dedicated to his work.
The children were listening to the teacher with rapt attention.
en.notes: 熱心 is a な-adjective: 熱心な学生 "a diligent student", adverbially 熱心に勉強する "to study diligently". What one is dedicated to takes に: 仕事に熱心だ; as a compound 教育熱心な親 "parents who place great value on education". In contrast to 一生懸命 (with all one's might, often in a concrete situation), 熱心 describes more a lasting attitude of interest and commitment. Almost always written in kanji.

examples[].german: I'm thinking about it seriously.
He began to speak with a serious look.
I don't want a fling; I want a serious relationship.
en.notes: 真剣 describes a serious, fully concentrated attitude in a situation: 真剣に考える, 真剣な顔, 真剣に付き合う. まじめ, by contrast, is a character trait ("diligent, conscientious"), and 本気 stresses that something is meant seriously and is not a joke. Literally, 真剣 is a "real sword" instead of a practice sword; hence 真剣勝負 "a life-and-death fight, a serious contest".

examples[].german: The management is sound.
He isn't flashy, but he's a dependable player.
I don't invest; I save steadily instead.
en.notes: 堅実 means "solid, reliable, without risk": 堅実な経営, 堅実な生き方, 堅実に貯金する. It praises a cautious, down-to-earth way that is not spectacular but reaches its goal safely. 着実, by contrast, stresses steady, step-by-step progress, and 確実 the certainty of a result. Typical of descriptions of business and people.

examples[].german: There is a legitimate reason.
I demanded proper pay for the work I had done.
I think his claim is justified.
en.notes: 正当 means "justified, legitimate, proper" and mostly stands before nouns: 正当な理由, 正当な権利, 正当な評価, 正当な給料. 正当化する means "to justify", 正当防衛 "self-defense". Do not confuse it with the homophone 正統 "orthodox, legitimate (succession)". 妥当 rather means "appropriate, plausible".

examples[].german: We will make a fair judgment.
Elections must be conducted fairly.
I don't think the referee's call was impartial.
en.notes: 公正 means "just, impartial" in the sense of correct and free of favoritism; as a な-adjective: 公正な判断, 公正な選挙, 公正な裁判. The similar word 公平, by contrast, stresses equal treatment of everyone ("everybody gets the same"). 公正 sounds objective to formal and often appears in fixed terms such as 公正取引委員会 (Fair Trade Commission); adverbially it is 公正に扱う "to treat fairly".

examples[].german: It's a relationship between equals.
Even as a newcomer, you can voice your opinion on equal terms in meetings.
The two companies merged as equal partners.
en.notes: 対等 describes equality of rank between persons or parties: "on an equal footing, with equal rights". Typical are 対等な関係, 対等な立場 and adverbial 対等に話す／対等に扱う; it is also possible with の (対等の条件). Unlike 同じ "same, identical", 対等 is about status and power, not appearance or quantity. The opposite would be something like 上下関係 "hierarchy".

examples[].german: She is a capable professional.
She is a competent secretary and is highly trusted by the president.
The more capable a person is, the better they are at delegating work.
en.notes: 有能 means "capable, competent" and evaluates how well someone does their work; mostly a な-adjective before people: 有能な社員, 有能な秘書, 有能な人材. It sounds somewhat more objective and literary than できる人 or 仕事ができる, which you hear more often in daily life. The opposite is 無能; for outstanding performance in school or exams, 優秀 fits better.

en.meaning: rather; if anything; on the contrary
examples[].german: This one is rather better.
I can't stand the summer heat; if anything, I prefer winter.
Far from getting angry, he was actually happy.
en.notes: むしろ compares two possibilities and says that the second is more accurate, often contrary to expectation: AよりむしろB, むしろ〜ほうがいい. With 〜どころか it means "quite the opposite". かえって, by contrast, emphasizes that a result runs counter to the intention (手伝ったらかえって邪魔になった). It is mostly written in kana and sounds somewhat elevated; in conversation people also say どちらかというと.

examples[].german: He is an incompetent boss.
I couldn't do anything and grew sick of my own incompetence.
The newspaper harshly criticized the government as incompetent.
en.notes: 無能 means "incapable, incompetent" and is a harsh, derogatory judgment of a person: 無能な上司, 無能な政治家. Said to someone's face it is very insulting; in everyday speech people prefer to paraphrase with 仕事ができない or 頼りない. It can also be used self-critically (自分の無能さ "one's own incompetence"). Opposite: 有能.

examples[].german: He is an outstanding student.
He graduated from university with excellent grades.
This work received an excellence award at the contest.
en.notes: 優秀 means "outstanding, excellent" and praises performance and talent, especially in pupils, students and employees: 優秀な学生, 優秀な成績, 優秀な人材. Products or works can also be 優秀 (優秀賞 "award for outstanding achievement"). Unlike 有能 ("competent on the job"), 優秀 sounds like top performance and intelligence; colloquially people often say 頭がいい or すごくできる.

en.meaning: to be inferior; to fall short of
examples[].german: This product is inferior in quality to those of other companies.
I'm physically inferior to the young players, but I'm not beaten in experience.
It's cheap, but the taste is no worse than expensive restaurants.
en.notes: 劣る is intransitive and means "to be worse than, to be inferior"; the point of comparison takes より or に, the area で or が: AはBより品質が劣る, 体力で劣る. It is rather objective and written; in conversation people more often say 負けている or よくない. The counterpart is 勝る; the fixed phrase 勝るとも劣らない means "is in no way inferior". Very often negated: 劣らない "not inferior".

en.meaning: to be superior to; to surpass
examples[].german: Nothing is better than health.
The ramen at this shop tastes at least as good as that of famous shops.
It's inferior in looks, but this one is superior in performance.
en.notes: 勝る (まさる) is intransitive and means "to be superior, to surpass"; the comparison is made with に or より: 健康に勝るものはない "nothing surpasses health". Do not confuse it with 勝つ (かつ) "to win": 勝る describes a lasting advantage in quality or ability, not the result of a competition. Because 勝って can be read both as かって and as まさって, 勝る is mostly seen in the dictionary form or in fixed phrases such as 勝るとも劣らない "at least equal". It sounds elevated.

en.meaning: to be comparable to; to rival
examples[].german: Her ability rivals that of professionals.
The price of that watch is equivalent to three months of my salary.
I don't think any other scenery rivals this town's night view.
en.notes: 匹敵する is intransitive and means "to be equal to, to be able to measure up to"; the object of comparison always takes に: プロに匹敵する実力, 一年分の給料に匹敵する金額. It is mostly about abilities, sizes or amounts that equal something known, often something higher. It sounds matter-of-fact to literary; in conversation people more often say 〜と同じくらい or 〜に負けない. Negated (匹敵するものはない) it means "incomparable".

examples[].german: We will expand the business.
The text is small, so please enlarge the display.
The damage from the typhoon is spreading further.
en.notes: 拡大 means "expansion, widening" and also "enlargement" (optical). As a する-verb it is transitive (事業を拡大する, 画面を拡大する) and intransitive (被害が拡大する "the damage spreads"). Typical are 拡大コピー "enlarged copy" and 感染拡大 "spread of an infection". Opposite: 縮小; in daily life, for pictures people also simply say 大きくする.

examples[].german: We will scale down the operation.
Please copy this map reduced to A4 size.
As the population declines, the domestic market is shrinking.
en.notes: 縮小 means "reduction, scaling down, cutback": 規模を縮小する, 予算を縮小する, 縮小コピー. Like 拡大, it is both transitive and intransitive (市場が縮小する "the market shrinks"). For money and quantities in general, 削減 "cut" often fits too; for clothes that have shrunk, one says 縮む instead. Opposite: 拡大.

examples[].german: The population is increasing.
The number of foreign tourists rose by 20 percent from last year.
Recently, the increase in online shopping stands out.
en.notes: 増加 is the objective word for "increase, rise" in numbers and quantities: 人口の増加, 観光客が増加する. As a する-verb it is almost always used intransitively with が, like the everyday word 増える; but 増加 sounds like statistics, news and reports. Often with numbers: 前年より10％増加した. Opposite: 減少.

examples[].german: The birth rate is declining.
This village's population has halved in the past ten years.
The number of traffic accidents is on a downward trend.
en.notes: 減少 is the formal word for "decrease, decline": 人口の減少, 売り上げが減少する. As a する-verb it is mostly intransitive with が, corresponding to the everyday word 減る. Typical in the news and statistics, often with percentages or 〜傾向 ("tendency"): 減少傾向にある. Opposite: 増加.

examples[].german: The temperature is rising.
Salaries can't keep up with the rise in prices.
After takeoff, the plane climbed slowly.
en.notes: 上昇 means "rise, ascent" and is used intransitively with が: 気温が上昇する, 物価が上昇する. It describes values, rates and temperatures, but also upward movement (飛行機が上昇する). In everyday speech people say 上がる instead; 上昇 sounds like weather reports and economic news. Opposite: 下降, for values also 低下.

examples[].german: Even if I fail, I will start over.
Supposing you won the lottery, what would you do?
Let's tentatively set the meeting day for Friday.
en.notes: 仮に introduces a purely hypothetical assumption and usually stands at the start of a sentence together with 〜ても, 〜としても, 〜たら or 〜とすれば: 仮にそうだとしても "even if that were so". Compared with the everyday もし, 仮に sounds more objective and stresses "just for the sake of argument". The second meaning is "provisionally, temporarily": 仮に決めておく "to set provisionally" (cf. 仮の "provisional").

examples[].german: Stock prices are falling.
When the plane descended below the clouds, the town came into view.
That team's popularity has been on the decline for the past few years.
en.notes: 下降 means "descent, falling" and is intransitive: 飛行機が下降する, 成績が下降する. It describes both downward movement and falling values; it is the counterpart of 上昇. For prices and rates, the news often uses 下落, and for performance and quality rather 低下. Typical is 下降線をたどる "to be on the decline".

examples[].german: Currency fluctuations are severe.
Vegetable prices fluctuate greatly depending on the weather.
In this job my income fluctuates from month to month, so I'm a little worried.
en.notes: 変動 refers to fluctuations and changes of values that go up and down: 為替の変動, 価格が変動する, 気温の変動. As a する-verb it is intransitive. In contrast to the general 変化 "change", 変動 stresses the fluctuation of numbers, prices or conditions, often in economics and nature (地殻変動). Often with 激しい or 大きい.

examples[].german: The weather is unsettled.
The Wi-Fi is unstable here and often drops.
With part-time jobs alone, the income is unstable.
en.notes: 不安定 is a な-adjective for "unstable, unsteady, shaky": 天気が不安定だ, 不安定な仕事, 気持ちが不安定になる. It fits weather, situations, income, connections (電波が不安定) and feelings. Not to be confused with 不安 "worry, unease": 不安定 describes a state that easily tips over, 不安 a feeling. Opposite: 安定した.

examples[].german: We maintain the balance of supply and demand.
In the 20th minute of the second half, a goal broke the balance of the match.
When the balance of power between the great powers collapses, the danger of war rises.
en.notes: 均衡 means "equilibrium" between forces or quantities and is a rather formal word from economics, politics and sports: 需要と供給の均衡, 力の均衡. Typical verbs are 均衡を保つ "to maintain the balance" and 均衡が崩れる／均衡を破る "the balance tips / is broken", for example when the first goal is scored in a match. In everyday speech people mostly say バランス.

examples[].german: We export from Japan.
This company exports cars to Asian countries.
Exports of Japanese rice are gradually increasing.
en.notes: 輸出 means "export"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 車を輸出する, 海外へ輸出する. The destination country takes に／へ, the country of origin takes から. Common compounds are 輸出品 "export goods" and 輸出国 "exporting country". Opposite: 輸入; together they are called 輸出入 "imports and exports".

examples[].german: We import from overseas.
Japan relies on imports for most of its oil.
In this shop you can buy imported sweets and wine.
en.notes: 輸入 means "import"; as a する-verb it is transitive: 石油を輸入する, 海外から輸入する. Common are 輸入品 "imported goods" and 輸入食品; in supermarkets one often reads 〜産 for the place of origin (アメリカ産). 輸入 can also refer to ideas or culture (文化の輸入). Opposite: 輸出.

examples[].german: Prices are rising.
Prices are high in Tokyo, so life there is hard.
Prices are low in this country, so it's easy to travel.
en.notes: 物価 is the general price level, that is, the overall cost of living, not the price of a single item (that is 値段 or 価格). Typical: 物価が高い／安い, 物価が上がる, 物価の上昇. It is used to compare cities and countries (東京は物価が高い). For rising prices in the news you also hear 物価高.

examples[].german: I'll exchange into foreign currency.
In many European countries, a common currency, the euro, is used.
Japan's currency unit is the yen.
en.notes: 通貨 is the "currency" as the system or means of payment of a country: 日本の通貨は円です, 外国の通貨, 共通通貨 "common currency". In daily life when exchanging money, people often simply say お金 or 外貨 "foreign currency"; 通貨 sounds more objective and belongs to economics and the news. Also well known is 仮想通貨 "cryptocurrency".

en.meaning: foreign exchange; exchange rate; money order
examples[].german: I will check the exchange rate.
Because of exchange rates, the prices of imported goods have risen.
In the past, people often sent money by postal money order.
en.notes: 為替 has an irregular reading (かわせ) and means "currency exchange" or "money order". It is most often encountered in 為替レート／為替相場 "exchange rate" and 外国為替 "foreign exchange"; in the news one hears, for example, 為替が円安に動く. The older meaning "money order" lives on in 郵便為替. On its own, 為替 rarely stands for the rate itself - for that one usually says レート.

examples[].german: I'm withdrawing my savings.
I deposit part of my salary in the bank every month.
I checked my account balance at the ATM.
en.notes: 預金 is money deposited at a bank: "bank deposit, savings". Typical are 預金する "to deposit", 預金を引き出す "to withdraw" and 普通預金／定期預金 "checking / time deposit account". The everyday word 貯金 means "savings" in general (also in a piggy bank) and is used at the post office; 預金 is the bank's technical term. An account is called 口座.

examples[].german: Let's meet and talk in person.
Please hand the documents directly to the person in charge.
The direct cause of the accident is not yet known.
en.notes: 直接 is used as an adverb without に directly before the verb: 直接会う, 直接話す, 直接渡す. Before nouns it is connected with の: 直接の原因 "direct cause", 直接の関係はない. The opposite is 間接 or 間接的; the na-adjective form is 直接的. 直接会って話す means "to talk in person (not by mail or phone)"; for a trip without a detour, 直行する is rather said.

examples[].german: The company went bankrupt.
Because of the recession, several small factories in town went under.
The company was on the brink of bankruptcy but was saved by a hit new product.
en.notes: 倒産 is the bankruptcy of a company; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 会社が倒産する. For private individuals and as a legal term, 破産 ("personal bankruptcy, insolvency") is used. Typical are 倒産寸前 "on the verge of collapse" and 倒産の危機. Colloquially one also says 会社がつぶれる.

examples[].german: We keep running in the red.
We went on a trip this month, so the household budget is in the red.
My teacher corrected my composition in red ink.
en.notes: 赤字 literally means "red characters" and stands for "deficit, loss, being in the red": 赤字になる, 赤字が続く, 赤字経営. It applies to companies, government budgets and also one's own wallet (今月は赤字だ). Opposite: 黒字. In another meaning, 赤字 also means "corrections in red" (赤字を入れる "to correct").

examples[].german: We have turned a profit.
The new shop became profitable six months after opening.
We reduced eating out this month, so the household budget is slightly in the black.
en.notes: 黒字 literally means "black characters" and stands for "profit, surplus, being in the black": 黒字になる, 黒字に転換する "to return to profit", 黒字を出す. It applies to companies, the government budget (貿易黒字 "trade surplus") and the private household. Opposite: 赤字. For the concrete amount of profit, people more often say 利益 or もうけ.

examples[].german: We will meet the delivery date.
At this rate we won't make the delivery date, so I'll work overtime today.
Because parts didn't arrive, the customer let us extend the delivery date by a week.
en.notes: 納期 is the agreed delivery or submission date for goods and orders, more rarely also for payments. Typical in working life: 納期を守る "to meet the deadline", 納期に間に合う／間に合わない, 納期が遅れる, 納期を延ばす. Unlike the general 締め切り ("submission deadline", e.g. for applications or papers), 納期 concerns delivery to a customer.

examples[].german: I will contact the customer.
Please be very careful in managing customer information.
This company surveys customer satisfaction every year.
en.notes: 顧客 is the business term for "customer, clientele", especially for regular customers and customer data: 顧客情報, 顧客満足度, 顧客リスト. In direct contact you never address customers as 顧客, but say お客様; in daily life it is 客 or お客さん. So 顧客 is an objective word from reports, marketing and company internals.

examples[].german: I'm meeting a business partner.
Our company has had dealings with that bank for many years.
The criminal offered the police a deal.
en.notes: 取引 (also written 取り引き) is a "deal, trade, transaction" between companies or persons. Typical are 取引先 "business partner", 取引がある "to have business dealings", 〜と取引する and 取引を始める／やめる. In crime stories and politics, 取引 can also mean a "deal" or horse-trading (取引に応じる). It is not used for simply buying something in a shop.

examples[].german: They monopolize the market.
My younger brother hogs the TV all day, so I can't watch the program I want.
This magazine carries an exclusive interview with that actor.
en.notes: 独占 means "monopoly, sole possession": 市場を独占する. Besides the economic meaning, it is often used jokingly in everyday speech for "to claim for oneself alone": テレビを独占する, 部屋を独占する. Common compounds are 独占インタビュー "exclusive interview" and 独占販売 "exclusive sales rights". As a する-verb it is transitive with を.

examples[].german: We will display the goods.
I'm sorry, this item is sold out.
At convenience stores, new products come out almost every week.
en.notes: 商品 is the "goods" offered for sale: 商品を並べる, 新商品, 人気商品, 商品券 "gift certificate". Unlike 製品 ("product", from the manufacturer's viewpoint), 商品 stresses sale to customers. 品物 is more general, "thing, article", also without a trade connection. In shops you hear sentences like この商品は売り切れです.

examples[].german: We obtained a patent.
We have already applied for a patent on this technology.
Two companies are fighting in court over a patent.
en.notes: 特許 is a "patent" on an invention. Typical: 特許を取る／取得する "to obtain a patent", 特許を申請する "to apply for", 特許を持つ. Whoever violates a patent commits 特許侵害. In an older meaning, 特許 also means "special permission, license"; in present-day usage, however, it almost always means the patent.

examples[].german: We are developing a new product.
My older brother develops apps at a game company.
Development has progressed in this area, and the old forest has disappeared.
en.notes: 開発 means "development" of products, technology or software (新製品を開発する, アプリの開発) and also "development" of land or resources (土地の開発, 都市開発). As a する-verb it is transitive with を. A person's development or a child's growth, by contrast, is not called 開発 but 成長 or 発達. Common: 開発者, 研究開発.

examples[].german: I conveyed it indirectly.
He often expresses himself indirectly, so he is hard to understand.
The weak yen also has an indirect effect on our daily lives.
en.notes: 間接的 is a na-adjective formed with 〜的: 間接的な表現 "indirect expression", adverbially 間接的に伝える/影響する. Opposite: 直接的, or simply 直接. For a message deliberately put tactfully or in a roundabout way, 遠回しに is also common in conversation; 間接的 sounds more matter-of-fact and is also used for effects and causes (間接的な原因).

examples[].german: I'll talk about the outlook for the future.
From the observation deck you can see the whole town.
In the interview, the company president spoke about the prospects for next year.
en.notes: 展望 literally means "wide view" (展望台 "observation deck", 展望が開ける) and figuratively "prospect, outlook" for the future: 将来の展望, 今後の展望. In the figurative meaning it sounds rather formal and often appears in speeches, interviews and reports. For the plain view from a window, people say 眺め or 景色 in everyday speech.

examples[].german: We'll increase efficiency.
You study more efficiently in the morning than late at night.
This old air conditioner is not energy efficient.
en.notes: 効率 is "efficiency", the ratio of effort to result. Typical are 効率がいい／悪い, 効率を上げる, 効率よく勉強する and the な-adjective 効率的. 効率 concerns ways of working, machines and energy (エネルギー効率). Do not confuse it with 効果 "effect": 効果 asks whether something works, 効率 how economically it works.

examples[].german: We'll look into the actual situation on site.
That rule doesn't fit the actual situation at schools.
I was surprised to learn what care work is really like.
en.notes: 実情 is the "actual state of affairs", how things really are, often in contrast to expectations or official statements: 現場の実情, 実情に合わない規則. It sounds matter-of-fact and appears in reports, news and discussions. The similar 実態 rather stresses the (often hidden) reality of a problem; 事情, by contrast, are a person's "circumstances, reasons".

examples[].german: We will verify the hypothesis.
An experiment was conducted to verify the effect of the new drug.
After the accident, the police were conducting an on-site investigation.
en.notes: 検証 means "verification, proof": you check with data or experiments whether something is true or works (仮説を検証する, 効果を検証する). As a する-verb it is transitive with を. Unlike 確認 ("to take a quick look, to make sure"), 検証 is a thorough, often scientific or official check; for accidents one speaks of 現場検証 "on-site inspection" by the police.

examples[].german: We will analyze the data.
I watched the video of the lost game and analyzed the causes.
Before job hunting, it's good to do a self-analysis.
en.notes: 分析 is "analysis": breaking something down into its components and examining it closely. As a する-verb it is transitive: データを分析する, 原因を分析する. Common are 分析結果 and 自己分析 "self-analysis" (for job hunting). Unlike 調べる ("to look up, to investigate", very general), 分析 stresses systematic evaluation.

examples[].german: We received a high evaluation.
The department head thinks highly of his efforts.
This restaurant doesn't have very good ratings online.
en.notes: 評価 means "evaluation, assessment" and also "appreciation": 評価が高い／低い, 高く評価する "to value highly", 評価を受ける. As a する-verb it is transitive with を. It is used for grades, performance reviews at work, online ratings (星の評価) and reviews. With 高い or 高く, praise usually resonates; 評判, by contrast, is the "reputation" among people.

examples[].german: It's an important indicator.
The unemployment rate is one of the indicators for judging the economy.
Blood pressure is an important indicator of one's health.
en.notes: 指標 is an "indicator, benchmark value" from which you can read a state or a development: 経済の指標, 健康の指標, 〜の指標になる. It sounds objective and occurs in economics, medicine and statistics. Unlike 目標 ("goal"), an 指標 only shows where you stand; a "standard" for judging is more 基準.

examples[].german: The results are contrasting.
In contrast to her cheerful older sister, the younger sister is very quiet.
I compared the translation with the original and looked for errors.
en.notes: 対照 means "juxtaposition, comparison, contrast". Very common is the な-adjective 対照的 "contrasting" (対照的な性格); as a する-verb it means "to compare side by side" (原文と訳文を対照する). Note, the same reading たいしょう: 対象 "object, target group" (子ども対象) and 対称 "symmetry" (左右対称) are different words.

examples[].german: We will check the consistency.
His explanation is not consistent with what he said before.
Please reconcile the figures in the two documents.
en.notes: 整合性 is "consistency, freedom from contradiction" - whether parts, data or statements fit together: データの整合性, 説明に整合性がない, 整合性を取る "to bring into agreement". The word is objective and typical of offices, IT and law. In conversation people say more simply つじつまが合う／合わない or 矛盾している "contradictory".

examples[].german: We found a compromise.
The labor union and the company are still looking for common ground.
Opinions were divided about the travel destination, but we settled on a compromise: a seaside town with hot springs.
en.notes: 妥協点 is the point where both sides can meet: "compromise solution, common ground". Typical: 妥協点を探る／見つける, 妥協点に達する. The base word 妥協 ("compromise, concession") can also sound negative (妥協しない "to make no concessions"), whereas 妥協点 is neutral to positive. Common in negotiations, politics and everyday disputes.

examples[].german: It is the most important problem.
Mt. Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.
The coldest time of the year is February.
en.notes: 最も forms the superlative before adjectives: 最も高い山, 最も重要な問題. It is the formal, written counterpart of 一番; in conversation, 一番 is mostly said. The frame of comparison is marked by で or の中で: 日本で最も…. Do not confuse it with もっと "more" and with the identically sounding もっとも (尤も) "however, understandably", which is mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: We reached an agreement.
The two countries agreed on trade rules.
Selling the house requires the agreement of the whole family.
en.notes: 合意 is an "agreement, accord" between two or more parties: 合意に達する, 合意を得る, 〜と合意する (intransitive, partner with と, content with で or に). It sounds formal and belongs to contracts, politics and negotiations. In everyday speech people more often say 話がまとまる or 意見が一致する. 同意, by contrast, is one side's consent to a proposal.

examples[].german: I will make the right decision.
Judging from the color of the sky, it looks like rain this afternoon.
Whether you go or not, I leave to your judgment.
en.notes: 判断 is "judgment, assessment": you assess a situation and decide what is right. Typical: 判断する, 判断を誤る "to misjudge", 〜から判断すると "judging from ...", 判断に迷う, 自分で判断する. Unlike 決定 ("official decision") and 決断 ("bold resolution"), 判断 stresses weighing and assessing.

examples[].german: I made a big decision.
I decided to quit my job and study abroad.
A leader needs the ability to decide quickly.
en.notes: 決断 is a "resolution", especially a difficult or courageous one, after long hesitation: 決断する, 決断を下す, 大きな決断, 決断力 "decisiveness". Compared with 決める (everyday, also for trifles) and 判断 (matter-of-fact weighing), 決断 stresses determination. For trifles like lunch, 決断 would be exaggerated or jocular.

examples[].german: It's a difficult choice.
Please choose the correct answer from the following four options.
When choosing a university, you should also think about the tuition.
en.notes: 選択 is the "choice, selection" between possibilities: 選択する, 選択肢 "option, answer choice", 正しい選択, 選択を迫られる. It sounds somewhat more objective than the everyday verb 選ぶ. Note: 洗濯 "doing laundry" is also read せんたく - the kanji differ. For elections in the political sense, 選挙 is used.

en.meaning: to turn out; to be established
examples[].german: The cause has been established.
The investigation revealed that the data was wrong.
The identity of the person who died in the accident has not yet been established.
en.notes: 判明 means "to turn out, to become clear" and is intransitive: 原因が判明する, 身元が判明する. Something unknown becomes known through investigation. The word is typical of the news and reports; in conversation people say 分かる instead. The difference from 解明 (transitive, "to clear up"): with 解明 someone actively clears something up, with 判明 it simply becomes known.

examples[].german: We will solve the mystery.
Scientists are working on elucidating the cause of this disease.
The police are trying to uncover the truth of the case.
en.notes: 解明 means "elucidation, deciphering" of something mysterious or unknown: 謎を解明する, 原因を解明する, 真相の解明. As a する-verb it is transitive with を; someone (researchers, the police) clears it up actively. The word sounds objective and often appears in science and crime reports. When something becomes known "on its own", 判明する fits better.

examples[].german: I'll get a grasp of the situation.
The new leader still doesn't know the names of the team members.
You should keep a proper grasp of how much you spend every month.
en.notes: 把握 means "to grasp, to have a handle on, to have an overview": 状況を把握する, 内容を把握する, 全体を把握している. As a する-verb it is transitive with を. It is less about deep understanding (理解) than about knowing the facts and the current state. Typical for work and organization; in conversation people also say 分かっている or つかむ.

examples[].german: We value the company's philosophy.
This school upholds the principle of "freedom and responsibility".
The principle of that law is good, but in reality it is difficult.
en.notes: 理念 refers to the fundamental idea or guiding principle by which an organization or a person wants to act - especially common in 企業理念 "corporate philosophy" and 経営理念 "management philosophy". Typical combinations are 理念を掲げる "to adopt a principle as one's banner" and 理念に基づく "to be based on a principle". Unlike 考え "thought" or 思想 "worldview, ideology", 理念 sounds formal and goal-oriented; 理想, by contrast, means "ideal, vision".

examples[].german: We will classify the data.
The books in the library are classified by theme.
Tomatoes are mostly classified as vegetables.
en.notes: 分類 is dividing things into groups according to fixed characteristics; as a transitive する-verb: AをBに分類する "to classify A into B". The passive is very common: 〜に分類される "is classified as …". For trash sorting in daily life, one says rather 分別 (ぶんべつ) or simply 分ける; 分類 sounds more matter-of-fact and systematic, for instance in science, libraries or data processing.

examples[].german: I can't tell them apart.
I want to clearly separate work and private life.
Please separate garbage into burnable and non-burnable before putting it out.
en.notes: 区別 is distinguishing or telling two things apart: AとBを区別する or AとBの区別がつく/つかない "to be able (or not) to tell A and B apart"; 区別がつかない in particular is the most everyday form. 差別 looks similar but means "discrimination" - mixing them up is embarrassing. 区別 is value-neutral and only says that one recognizes or makes a difference.

examples[].german: Please tell me the scope of the test.
I keep exercising within a range that isn't too much for me.
Tomorrow it will rain over a wide area.
en.notes: 範囲 is the range or extent within which something applies: テストの範囲 "exam material", 予算の範囲 "budget limits". Typical are 範囲内 / 範囲外 and 〜の範囲で "within the scope of"; 無理のない範囲で means "as far as possible without overdoing it". It is also used spatially: 広い範囲で雨が降る "it rains over a wide area". A field of expertise or knowledge is rather 分野.

examples[].german: It is an extremely difficult problem.
In that region, it rains extremely rarely.
According to the doctor, the chance that the operation will succeed is extremely high.
en.notes: 極めて is a formal intensifying adverb ("extremely, highly"), stronger than とても and more formal than 非常に. It stands before adjectives and na-adjectives, as in 極めて重要, 極めて危険, 極めてまれ, and is typical of news, reports and technical texts. For everyday feelings it sounds stiff (instead of 極めておいしい one says すごくおいしい). It comes from the verb 極める "to push to the utmost".

examples[].german: It's a culture unique to Japan.
This fish has a distinctive smell.
A sudden rise in fever is a symptom characteristic of this illness.
en.notes: 特有 means "peculiar to a certain thing only, characteristic of". It almost always appears as 〜特有の + noun or 〜に特有の: 日本特有の習慣, この病気に特有の症状. It is often about smells, tastes, symptoms or peculiarities that one recognizes at once: 特有のにおい. Similar is 独特 "peculiar, unique", which stresses the unusual more strongly; 固有 rather means something that belongs to a thing by nature.

examples[].german: Each country has its own problems.
"Tokyo" is a proper noun.
There are many animals unique to this island.
en.notes: 固有 describes something that is inherent to a thing by nature or has been from the beginning: 〜固有の文化, 日本固有の植物 "plants native only to Japan". Fixed terms are 固有名詞 "proper noun" and 固有種 "endemic species". Compared with 特有 "characteristic of", 固有 stresses original belonging; as an adjective it almost always takes の, and the tone is matter-of-fact and rather literary.

examples[].german: We developed our own method.
He paints in his own unique style.
This is the result of the newspaper's own investigation.
en.notes: 独自 means "one's own, developed independently of others" and hence also "original, distinctive". It mostly stands as 独自の + noun (独自の方法, 独自のスタイル) or adverbially as 独自に "independently, on one's own": 独自に調査する. In contrast to 特有 "characteristic of", 独自 stresses that something was created by oneself and not adopted; 独特 "peculiar" rather describes the special character.

examples[].german: We will hear both sides' opinions.
Both parties agreed, and the contract was concluded.
Both sides were to blame for the accident.
en.notes: 双方 means "both sides, both parties" and is used above all for counterparts who deal with each other - negotiating partners, parties to a dispute, contract partners: 双方の合意, 双方が納得する. In daily life, for "both" people more often say 両方 (for things) or 二人とも (for people); 双方 sounds formal and often appears in the news and business language. Related is 双方向 "two-way, interactive".

examples[].german: It's a general opinion.
This garden is open to the public only on weekends.
Please explain it so that even laypeople can understand.
en.notes: 一般 means "general, common" and also refers to "the general public, ordinary people". As a noun it takes の: 一般の人 "ordinary people, laypeople (not experts or celebrities)", 一般公開 "open to the public". As an adjective people use 一般的な "generally common, widespread", as an adverb 一般に or 一般的に "in general"; a bare 一般な does not exist. Opposites are 特殊 "special" and 専門 "specialized".

examples[].german: It has universal value.
Love is a universal theme of literature.
This way of thinking is universally valid in every country.
en.notes: 普遍 means "universally valid, applicable everywhere and at all times". It almost always appears as 普遍的な + noun or 普遍的に: 普遍的な価値, 普遍的なテーマ. The tone is elevated and typical of essays, philosophy and art criticism. Compared with 一般的 "generally common", 普遍的 is stronger: it holds for all people and cultures without exception; the opposite is 特殊.

examples[].german: Special technology is required.
My company has somewhat special circumstances, so we work on Saturdays too.
The special-effects makeup in this movie is amazing.
en.notes: 特殊 means "special, particular, unusual" in the sense of "different from the normal": 特殊な技術, 特殊な事情, 特殊メイク "special-effects makeup". It is a na-adjective and often sounds matter-of-fact or technical. Unlike 特別 "special (mostly positive, preferential)", 特殊 is value-neutral and can also mean "unusual, hard to handle". Antonyms are 一般 and 普通.

examples[].german: Please explain concretely.
Could you give one concrete example?
The travel plans are not yet concretely decided.
en.notes: 具体 alone means "concreteness" and hardly occurs on its own; it is learned almost always as 具体的な "concrete" and 具体的に "concretely, in detail". Typical are 具体的に説明する, 具体的な例 and the compound 具体例 "concrete example". The opposite is 抽象的 "abstract". A bare 具体な is wrong - the adjective always needs 的.

examples[].german: It is an abstract concept.
Your explanation is too abstract, and I don't really understand it.
I saw abstract paintings at the museum.
en.notes: 抽象 means "abstraction"; in everyday speech it appears almost only as 抽象的な "abstract" or 抽象的に. It is often used to criticize statements that are too vague: 説明が抽象的すぎる. Fixed terms are 抽象画 "abstract painting" and 抽象化する "to abstract". The opposite is 具体的 "concrete".

examples[].german: I judge objectively.
It's hard to see oneself objectively.
Let's talk based on objective data.
en.notes: 客観 means "objectivity" and is used almost only as 客観的な "objective" or 客観的に "objectively, factually": 客観的に見る, 客観的なデータ, 客観的な事実. The counterpart is 主観 or 主観的 "subjective". Watch the pronunciation: きゃっかん with a double consonant.

examples[].german: The problem is becoming more and more serious.
After listening to the explanation, I understood even less.
The more you practice, the better you will get.
en.notes: ますます (rarely 益々) describes that an already existing state intensifies further; typically with 〜くなる/〜になる and 〜ている/〜てきた. With a negative it means "less and less": ますます分からなくなる. Compared with だんだん ("gradually", a neutral change), ますます emphasizes the increase. In letters and speeches there is the formula ますますのご活躍をお祈りします.

examples[].german: It's a subjective opinion.
This is strictly my own view, but the ramen here is the best.
Evaluations should be decided by data, not by subjective impressions.
en.notes: 主観 is "subjectivity", that is, one's own personal view. It mostly appears as 主観的な "subjective" or as a noun as in 主観で判断する "to judge by one's own feelings"; 私の主観ですが… is a polite introduction to a personal opinion. The counterpart is 客観 or 客観的. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 習慣 "habit".

examples[].german: It's a relative evaluation.
Compared with Tokyo, rents in this town are relatively cheap.
Einstein is famous for the theory of relativity.
en.notes: 相対 means "relativity"; it is used almost always as 相対的な "relative" or 相対的に "comparatively, by comparison": 相対的に安い. The counterpart is 絶対 or 絶対的 "absolute". Fixed expressions are 相対評価 "relative evaluation (compared with others)" and 相対性理論 "theory of relativity". The tone is matter-of-fact and rather literary.

examples[].german: We'll definitely make it in time.
Please don't tell this to anyone under any circumstances.
The president has absolute power in the company.
en.notes: 絶対 is above all an adverb: 絶対(に) "definitely, without fail", in a negative sentence "under no circumstances": 絶対に行かない. With の or as 絶対的な it means "absolute": 絶対の自信, 絶対的な権力. Colloquially, 絶対 without に is very often used as a strong affirmation; in formal texts this seems too emotional, and 必ず or 確実に is better there. The opposite of 絶対的 is 相対的.

examples[].german: It is a rational way of thinking.
Let's carry out the work in a more rational way.
I think that rule is unreasonable.
en.notes: 合理 means "rationality" and is used practically only in derived forms: 合理的な "rational, reasonable, efficient" and 合理化 "rationalization". 合理的 often means less "logical" than "practical, without unnecessary effort": 合理的なやり方. The opposite is 不合理 "unreasonable, absurd".

examples[].german: I think logically.
His argument doesn't hold together.
Please write the report with a logical structure.
en.notes: 論理 is "logic", that is, the consistent connection of thoughts. As an adjective one uses 論理的な "logical", as an adverb 論理的に: 論理的に考える, 論理的な文章. The noun alone is also common: 論理が通らない "that is not coherent", 論理の飛躍 "leap in logic". For "logical!" in the sense of "of course", one does not say 論理 but 当然 or もちろん.

examples[].german: I study systematically.
This company's salary structure is hard to understand.
Japanese honorific language forms a system of its own.
en.notes: 体系 is an ordered whole made of interrelated parts, that is, a "system" in the sense of an organization of knowledge or rules: 法体系 "legal system", 給与体系 "pay structure". Very common is 体系的な / 体系的に "systematic(ally)". For technical systems one usually says システム, and for institutional arrangements 制度.

examples[].german: It plays an important role.
Let's divide up the roles within the team and prepare.
The role of the father in the family has also changed.
en.notes: 役割 is the "role" or "task" that someone or something takes on in a given context. The most typical combination is 役割を果たす "to play a role, to fulfill a function"; also 役割を分担する "to divide tasks" and 役割分担 "division of tasks". For a theater or film role, one says 役 instead; 役目 is similar to 役割, but stresses duty more.

examples[].german: I will explain the course of events of the incident.
I heard how the two came to marry.
First, let me briefly explain how things have gone so far.
en.notes: 経緯 refers to the course of events, i.e. how a situation came about - the sequence of events with their circumstances: 事件の経緯, これまでの経緯を説明する. It is formal and typical of reports, apologies and the news. The same spelling is also read いきさつ, which sounds a bit more colloquial. The meaning "longitude and latitude" plays hardly any role in daily life.

examples[].german: We have entered a new phase.
The game has entered a crucial phase.
Even in the difficult situation, he stayed calm.
en.notes: 局面 comes from board games such as 囲碁 or 将棋, where it means the "position"; figuratively it means the "situation, phase, stage" of a development. Typical are 新たな局面を迎える "to enter a new phase", 重要な局面 "crucial moment" and 難しい局面 "difficult situation". Unlike 状況 "situation (in general)", 局面 stresses a particular segment within a course of events; the tone is rather formal, as in the news and sports reports.

examples[].german: I've reached a turning point in my life.
My illness became a turning point for reconsidering my lifestyle.
The success of this new product became a turning point for the company.
en.notes: 転機 is a "turning point" at which life or a development changes fundamentally. It almost always appears in 転機を迎える "to be at a turning point", 転機になる / 転機となる "to become a turning point" or 人生の転機. It is often used in retrospect and sounds rather positive. Not to be confused with the identically read 天気 "weather"; 転換, by contrast, means "switch, change of course" as a process.

examples[].german: I have gradually gotten used to it.
In the evening, the sky gradually grew dark.
After I took the medicine, the fever gradually went down.
en.notes: 次第に describes a slow, steady change and is used with verbs of change such as 慣れる, 暗くなる, 下がる, often with 〜てくる/〜ていく. It sounds somewhat more literary than the everyday だんだん; it does not fit one-off, intentional actions. Do not confuse it with the suffix 〜次第: 着き次第 "as soon as I arrive", 天気次第 "depending on the weather".

examples[].german: Social transformation is advancing.
The Internet has brought great change to our lives.
For the company to survive, the organization needs to be transformed.
en.notes: 変革 refers to a far-reaching restructuring of structures, in society, organizations or thinking: 社会の変革, 組織の変革, 変革をもたらす "to bring about an upheaval". 改革 "reform" usually means the deliberate improvement of a system (政治改革), 変革 rather the fundamental reshaping as a whole; 変化 is simply "change". The tone is formal; as a する-verb (変革する) it occurs less often than the noun.

examples[].german: We study historical changes.
In this museum you can see how clothing in Japan has changed.
The meanings of words have also changed with the times.
en.notes: 変遷 describes how something has changed step by step over a longer period, the historical change seen in retrospect: 時代の変遷, 言葉の変遷, ファッションの変遷. It is a written-language word, typical of history books, exhibitions and specialist texts; as a する-verb it is intransitive (〜が変遷する). Unlike 変化 "change", 変遷 stresses the succession of several stages; 変革, by contrast, means a deliberately brought-about upheaval.

examples[].german: I'm investigating the origin of the word.
The origin of life is still not well understood.
This sport is said to have originated in England.
en.notes: 起源 is the "origin" in the sense of the very first beginning from which something arose: 生命の起源, 言葉の起源, 〜に起源がある. It sounds scientific and is used for big questions of history, biology or culture. 由来 is similar, but tends to tell the origin story of a name or custom; 原因 is the "cause" of an event. Note: read the same as 機嫌 "mood" and 期限 "deadline".

examples[].german: Please tell me the origin of the name.
"Pan" (bread) is a word derived from Portuguese.
This cosmetic is made with plant-derived ingredients.
en.notes: 由来 is the origin or the story of how something came about, above all of names, words, customs and festivals: 名前の由来, 地名の由来. As an intransitive する-verb, 〜に由来する means "to go back to ..., to derive from ...". 〜由来の is also common, e.g. 植物由来の "of plant origin". Compared with 起源 "origin, the very first beginning", 由来 tends to tell why something has its name or is the way it is.

examples[].german: It was registered as a World Heritage site.
We siblings divided our grandfather's inheritance.
This festival is an important cultural heritage of the town.
en.notes: 遺産 is, first, the "inheritance" in the legal sense, i.e. the estate of a deceased person: 遺産を相続する "to receive an inheritance", 遺産相続. Second, it means "heritage, legacy" in the cultural sense: 文化遺産, 世界遺産 "World Heritage". For inheriting as an action, 相続する is used; 遺産 is what is left behind. 財産, by contrast, means "assets, property" in general.

examples[].german: I'm going to see ancient ruins.
Old ruins were discovered during construction work.
Machu Picchu is one of the most famous ruins in the world.
en.notes: 遺跡 are "ruins, historical archaeological sites", places where remains of earlier buildings or settlements are preserved: 古代の遺跡, 遺跡を発掘する "to excavate a site". It usually refers to an archaeological place; individual finds are called 遺物, an officially protected historic site 史跡. Do not confuse it with 遺産 "heritage" and 奇跡 "miracle".

examples[].german: I'm learning about ancient civilizations.
Egyptian civilization arose near the Nile.
Even as civilization advances, people's worries hardly change.
en.notes: 文明 is "civilization", above all the technical and material level of development of a society: 古代文明, 文明が発達する, 文明社会. 文化 "culture" tends to stress art, customs and spiritual values, 文明 technology, cities and organization. Fixed terms are 四大文明 "the four great early civilizations" and 文明開化, the modernization of Japan in the 明治時代.

examples[].german: There are various ethnic groups.
At the festival, people dance in traditional costume.
More than fifty ethnic minorities live in China.
en.notes: 民族 is a group of people with a shared language, culture and history: "people, ethnic group". 少数民族 "ethnic minority", 多民族国家 "multi-ethnic state", 民族衣装 "traditional costume". It is not the same as 国民 "nation, citizens" or 人種 "race" (by physical characteristics). Beware of the similar-sounding 民俗 "folk customs, folklore".

examples[].german: The number of immigrants is increasing.
My grandfather emigrated to Brazil when he was young.
The debate about immigration policy continues.
en.notes: 移民 means both emigration or immigration as a process and the person, the "migrant". As an intransitive する-verb: ブラジルに移民する "to emigrate to Brazil"; also typical are 移民政策 "immigration policy" and 移民を受け入れる "to accept immigrants". For an ordinary move abroad, people more often say 海外に移住する; 移民 sounds like permanent migration and is a word from politics and history. Unlike 難民 "refugee", migration is usually voluntary.

examples[].german: We will accept refugees.
Many people became refugees because of the war.
On the day of the earthquake, the station was full of stranded commuters.
en.notes: 難民 is a "refugee" - someone who had to leave their homeland because of war, persecution or disasters: 難民を受け入れる, 難民キャンプ, 難民申請 "asylum application". Unlike 移民 "migrant", the flight is involuntary. In the media, 〜難民 also forms words for people stuck somewhere or unable to get something: 帰宅難民 "stranded commuters", 買い物難民 "people without access to shopping".

examples[].german: I will think about the composition of the team.
This book is composed of three chapters.
The application form has a field for writing the family composition.
en.notes: 構成 refers to how a whole is put together from its parts: 家族構成, チームの構成, 文章の構成, 番組の構成. As a transitive する-verb it mostly appears in the passive: AはBで構成されている "A consists of B". Unlike 構造 (fixed inner structure, for example of a building), 構成 is about the arrangement or selection of elements, which can be planned and changed.

examples[].german: We will strengthen diplomatic relations.
My older brother works abroad as a diplomat.
This problem should be solved through diplomacy.
en.notes: 外交 is "diplomacy", i.e. a state's relations with other states: 外交関係, 外交政策, 外交問題, 外交官 "diplomat". In the business world it also refers to outside sales, e.g. in 外交員 "outside sales representative (e.g. in insurance)". Careful: the identically read 外向的 means "extroverted" and has nothing to do with diplomacy.

examples[].german: A peace treaty was concluded.
Japan has not yet joined that treaty.
In history class we learned about the unequal treaties.
en.notes: 条約 is a "treaty, agreement" between states or international organizations: 条約を結ぶ "to conclude a treaty", 条約に加盟する "to join a treaty", 平和条約. For contracts between persons or companies one uses 契約 "contract"; 約束 is a personal "promise, appointment". 条約 belongs to the language of politics, history and the news.

examples[].german: We will resolve the conflict.
Conflict has continued in that region for a long time.
A dispute over land arose with the neighboring company.
en.notes: 紛争 is a "conflict" or "dispute", usually between groups, states or parties and often over a longer period: 国際紛争, 地域紛争, 民族紛争, 紛争地域 "conflict zone". Typical are 紛争が起きる, 紛争が続く and 紛争を解決する. For a private quarrel between two people, people more often say けんか or もめごと; 戦争 is open "war", whereas 紛争 also covers smaller armed or legal disputes.

examples[].german: Peace negotiations have begun.
The two countries finally agreed to peace.
The United Nations is working toward achieving a peace settlement.
en.notes: 和平 refers to "peace" as the result of negotiations, i.e. the end of a war or conflict: 和平交渉 "peace negotiations", 和平合意 "peace agreement", 和平が実現する. By contrast, 平和 is the general state of peace, as in 平和を願う "to wish for peace". 和平 is a word of news and political language.

examples[].german: The country's security is very important.
The Security Council held an emergency meeting.
In this election, security policy is also a big issue.
en.notes: 安全保障 refers to (above all national) "security" and the policy meant to ensure it - defense, alliances, crisis preparedness. It often appears in compounds: 安全保障政策 "security policy", 安全保障理事会 "(UN) Security Council", 日米安全保障条約, abbreviated 安保 "Japan-US Security Treaty". For everyday safety (road traffic, food), one says only 安全; 保障 alone means "guarantee, safeguard", as in 社会保障 "social security".

examples[].german: We treat everyone fairly.
We divided the cake fairly among the three of us.
That teacher is fair to everyone.
en.notes: 公平 means "fair, just, impartial" - everyone is treated equally, without favoritism: 公平な判断, 公平に分ける. It is a な-adjective, adverbially 公平に. The opposite 不公平 "unfair" is very common in daily life: それは不公平だ! 平等 "equality" stresses equal rights or shares, 公平 impartial treatment, and 公正 "just, correct" adherence to rules.

examples[].german: We respect diversity.
This forest is rich in biodiversity.
Our company values diversity in nationality and age.
en.notes: 多様性 is "diversity", the coexistence of many different species, people or opinions: 生物の多様性 or 生物多様性 "biodiversity", 文化の多様性, 多様性を認める / 尊重する. It is the noun of 多様な "diverse", formed with the suffix 性 "-ness, -ity". The word is matter-of-fact and frequent in politics, education and companies; there the loanword ダイバーシティ is also widespread.

examples[].german: We coexist with nature.
In this town, old buildings and new skyscrapers coexist.
It is not easy for wild animals and humans to coexist.
en.notes: 共存 means "coexistence", the peaceful side-by-side existence of different groups, living things or objects: AとBが共存する, 〜と共存する, 人間と自然の共存. The reading きょうぞん is usual; きょうそん is also correct. Similar is 共生 "living together, symbiosis", which stresses mutual dependence more strongly.

examples[].german: I contribute to society.
His goal contributed to the team's victory.
I would like to contribute to the development of your company.
en.notes: 貢献 is a "contribution" to a goal or to the well-being of others; as an intransitive する-verb: 〜に貢献する "to contribute to ...". Typical are 社会に貢献する, チームの勝利に貢献する, 社会貢献 "contribution to society" and 大きな貢献をする. Unlike 寄付 "donation (money, goods)", 貢献 is any contribution through work, knowledge or effort. The tone is positive and rather formal, often in job applications and speeches.

examples[].german: I will examine the structure of the building.
Japanese and English differ quite a lot in sentence structure.
This house is built to withstand earthquakes.
en.notes: 構造 is the internal structure or construction of something: 建物の構造, 文の構造 "sentence structure", 社会の構造, 体の構造. Common patterns are 〜な構造になっている and 構造上 "structurally". Distinction: 構成 emphasizes the composition from parts, 仕組み rather how something works. 構造 is not a する-verb.

examples[].german: I serve the community.
The students cleaned the park on the weekend as community service.
Today we have prepared a large number of special-offer items for our customers.
en.notes: 奉仕 is selfless "service" for others or the community; as an intransitive する-verb with に: 社会に奉仕する, plus 奉仕活動 "community service". In everyday speech today people mostly say ボランティア for voluntary work; 奉仕 sounds older, more solemn or religious. In retail, 奉仕 also means "special offer", for example in 奉仕品 "bargain goods".

examples[].german: I made a donation.
We are collecting donations for the earthquake victims.
I donated books I no longer read to the library.
en.notes: 寄付 is a "donation" of money or goods to an organization or for a good cause: 寄付をする, 寄付を集める "to collect donations", 寄付金. As a transitive する-verb: 学校に本を寄付する "to donate books to the school". In laws and at government offices, the spelling 寄附 is also found. 募金 refers specifically to collecting donation money, often on the street, while 貢献 is a general "contribution".

examples[].german: He/She goes to daycare.
My older sister works as a nursery teacher.
This town lacks childcare places, and many parents are in trouble.
en.notes: 保育 is the care and upbringing of small children as it takes place in daycare: 保育園 / 保育所 "daycare center", 保育士 "childcare worker", 保育料 "daycare fee". 保育園 (care for children of working parents, from infancy) differs from 幼稚園 "kindergarten (educational institution from age three)". As a する-verb, 保育する is rather technical; in everyday speech people say 子どもの面倒を見る or 子どもを預ける.

examples[].german: Depopulation is progressing.
My grandmother lives alone in a depopulated village.
In depopulated areas there are few buses, which is inconvenient.
en.notes: 過疎 means "too sparse a population, depopulation", above all of rural areas from which young people move to the cities. Typical are 過疎化 "depopulation (as a process)", 過疎化が進む, 過疎地 / 過疎地域 "depopulated region" and 過疎の村. The opposite is 過密 "overcrowding, concentration". The word belongs to the news and social studies; in conversation people also simply say 人が減っている.

examples[].german: Urbanization is progressing.
Because of urbanization, the rice fields around here have almost all disappeared.
In urbanized areas, summer temperatures rise more easily.
en.notes: 都市化 is "urbanization", formed from 都市 "city" and the suffix 化 "-ization, becoming something". Typical are 都市化が進む, 急速な都市化 and the intransitive 〜が都市化する. It is the counterpart to 過疎化 "depopulation" in the countryside. The tone is objective, typical of geography and the news.

examples[].german: I want to eliminate poverty.
There are still many people in the world suffering from poverty.
Child poverty is a big problem in Japan, too.
en.notes: 貧困 is "poverty" as a social problem: 貧困問題, 貧困をなくす, 子どもの貧困, 貧困層 "poor segment of the population". An individual person is described in everyday speech more often with 貧乏 "poor, broke" (貧乏な学生); 貧困 is matter-of-fact and appears in the news, politics and statistics. Figuratively it can also mean "lack", for example 発想の貧困 "poverty of ideas".

examples[].german: They are suffering from hunger.
Many children around the world still face hunger today.
This organization works to end hunger.
en.notes: 飢餓 means "hunger, famine" in the serious sense - prolonged lack of food, often as a global problem: 飢餓に苦しむ, 飢餓をなくす, 飢餓状態. For ordinary hunger in daily life, people say お腹がすいた; 飢餓 would be far too strong for that. Related is 飢饉 "famine (due to crop failure)". 飢餓 is a written word from the news and the language of aid organizations.

examples[].german: We will support the disaster area.
There is a program that supports international students in their daily lives.
We thank you all from the bottom of our hearts for your support.
en.notes: 支援 is organized, often material or financial support from the state, companies or groups: 〜を支援する, 支援を受ける, 支援金, 被災地支援. In thank-you formulas it takes ご: ご支援に感謝いたします. For cheering on or morally supporting a team, one says 応援; for personally helping with a task, 手伝う; 援助 stresses mainly financial and material aid. Rather formal, typical of the news and government offices.

examples[].german: Reconstruction is progressing.
Ten years after the earthquake, the town has almost completely recovered.
Many volunteers gathered for the reconstruction of the region.
en.notes: 復興 is the rebuilding of a whole area, a town, the economy or culture after a war or disaster: 復興が進む, 町が復興する, 震災からの復興, 復興支援. Mostly intransitive (町が復興する), more rarely transitive (町を復興する). For repairing individual things one says 修理, for the restoration of a building 修復, for rebuilding a house or company 再建; 回復 is recovery of health or the economy.

examples[].german: This video has exceeded one million views.
When you press the button, the music plays.
This notebook is made of recycled paper.
en.notes: In everyday speech today, 再生 mostly means playing video or sound: 動画を再生する, 再生ボタン, 再生回数 ("view count"), opposite 停止. It also stands for reuse (再生紙 "recycled paper", 再生プラスチック; in speech more often リサイクル) and for biological regeneration (細胞が再生する). It can be used transitively (〜を再生する) and intransitively or passively (音楽が再生される).

examples[].german: I will explain the mechanism of this machine.
This door is set up so that it opens when you hold a card up to it.
I don't really understand the Japanese election system.
en.notes: 仕組み (also written しくみ) describes how something works or is set up: 機械の仕組み, 社会の仕組み, 選挙の仕組み. Very common is 〜仕組みになっている "is set up so that ...". Unlike 構造 (physical structure), it is about processes and mechanisms. The related verb 仕組む, by contrast, mostly means "to scheme, to engineer".

examples[].german: The blood is circulating.
Let's open the window and let the air in the room circulate.
I want to escape from the vicious circle of lack of sleep and stress.
en.notes: 循環 is a cycle in which something keeps returning to its starting point: 血液が循環する, 空気・水・お金の循環. As a する-verb it is intransitive; to make something circulate, the causative 循環させる is used. Common compounds are 悪循環 "vicious circle", 好循環 "virtuous circle" and 循環バス "loop bus". For simple turning or flowing in daily life, one says rather 回る or 流れる.

examples[].german: Food past its best-before date is discarded.
Please delete the data before disposing of the old computer.
Waste from the factory polluted the river.
en.notes: 廃棄 is the official, often systematic disposal of things no longer needed: food, documents, devices, chemicals. Typical are 〜を廃棄する, 廃棄される, 廃棄物 "waste (industrial)" and 食品廃棄. In everyday life one simply throws garbage away (ゴミを捨てる); 廃棄 sounds official, or like a company and regulations. Rather formal and literary.

examples[].german: Let's save water.
To save money, I make my own lunch every day.
If you take the subway, you can save time.
en.notes: 節約 means to be sparing with something and use less: お金・電気・水・時間を節約する, 節約のために, 節約家 "thrifty person". Not to be confused with 貯金: 節約 means spending less, 貯金 (お金を貯める) putting money aside. 倹約 is similar, but stresses a frugal lifestyle and sounds more elevated. Opposite: 浪費 or, colloquially, 無駄遣い.

examples[].german: I wasted time.
She squanders her salary on brand-name goods.
To prevent wasting electricity, let's turn off the lights in unused rooms.
en.notes: 浪費 is the pointless wasting of money, time or energy: 時間を浪費する, 〜に給料を浪費する ("to squander one's pay on something"), 浪費家 "spendthrift". It sounds somewhat more elevated and critical than the everyday 無駄遣い (お金を無駄遣いする), which is more common in conversation. The opposite is 節約. For food that gets thrown away, people more often say 無駄にする or 食品ロス.

examples[].german: I have time to spare.
I'm short on money this month, so I'll take the trip next month.
Even though the exam is tomorrow, he looks completely relaxed.
en.notes: 余裕 is, first, the leeway that is left over: 時間・お金・スペースに余裕がある/ない, 余裕を持って "with a buffer" (余裕を持って家を出る). Second, it refers to inner composure: 余裕のある人, 余裕の表情. Colloquially, 余裕! or 余裕で合格した means "easy, a piece of cake". ゆとり is similar, but refers more to relaxed living conditions (ゆとりのある生活).

examples[].german: I've reached my limit.
I can't take any more! Let me rest a moment.
There are limits to what one can do alone.
en.notes: 限界 is the utmost limit of strength, ability or capacity: 限界に達する, 限界を超える, 〜には限界がある, 体力の限界. Colloquially, もう限界! means "I can't take it anymore!". Not to be confused with 制限 (an imposed restriction, e.g. 速度制限), 限度 (permissible maximum, 限度額) and 境界 or 国境 for spatial borders between regions or countries.

examples[].german: The risk is high.
This medicine carries a risk of side effects.
Experts point out the risk of a major earthquake.
en.notes: The suffix 〜性 forms abstract nouns; 危険性 is the risk, or degree of danger, that something bad will happen: 〜する危険性がある/高い, 〜の危険性を指摘する. 危険 alone is the danger itself and also a な-adjective (危険な場所). In conversation people more often say 危ない or リスク; 危険性 sounds objective and is typical of the news, reports and package inserts.

examples[].german: I feel the necessity.
In the meeting, we discussed the need for a new system.
At this stage, apparently no surgery is necessary.
en.notes: 必要性 is necessity as an abstract topic that one talks about or judges: 〜の必要性を感じる/認める/訴える, 必要性について話し合う. In simple sentences, 必要 or 〜必要がある is enough: 行く必要がある is more natural than 行く必要性がある. Formal, typical of discussions, reports and justifications.

examples[].german: I will analyze the elements of success.
This movie has elements of both romance and mystery.
In cooking, not only taste but also appearance is an important element.
en.notes: 要素 is a component or element that belongs to a whole: 重要な要素, 〜の要素がある "has something of ...". Unlike 要因 (a factor that causes a result), 要素 is more an "ingredient" of the whole. In IT it also denotes elements of an array or a list. Neutral to slightly formal.

examples[].german: I'm financially independent.
After ten years, he quit the company he worked for, went independent and opened a cafe.
America became independent from Britain in 1776.
en.notes: 独立 means independence and is used as an intransitive する-verb with から: 親から独立する, イギリスから独立する. It covers countries (独立国, 独立記念日), people (経済的に独立する) and work: 会社を辞めて独立する "to quit a company and go independent". 独立した部屋 is a separate room. 自立 is similar, but stresses getting by without outside help.

examples[].german: I want to be freed from constraints.
My boyfriend is so controlling that I can't even meet my friends freely.
I became a freelancer because I hated being bound by company rules.
en.notes: 束縛 is a fetter in the figurative sense: constraints that take away someone's freedom. Transitive 人を束縛する, very often passive 〜に束縛される, and 束縛から解放される "to be freed from constraints". Colloquially, 束縛が強い/束縛する彼氏 describes a controlling, jealous partner. 制限, by contrast, is a matter-of-fact limitation, and 拘束 is rather detention in the legal sense.

examples[].german: I was freed from stress.
Three days later, all the hostages were released.
At least on weekends, I want to forget about work and set myself free.
en.notes: 解放 is freeing from compulsion, oppression or burden: 人質を解放する, 〜から解放される. The passive very often expresses relief: 仕事・試験・ストレスから解放される. Beware of the homophone: 開放 (also かいほう) means "to open up, to make accessible" (窓を開放する, 校庭を開放する). The opposite of 解放 is 束縛 or 拘束.

examples[].german: There are time constraints.
Because of budget constraints, we had to scale down the plan.
There is a character limit, so please summarize what you want to say briefly.
en.notes: 制約 are circumstances or conditions that restrict one's room to act: 時間・予算・スペースの制約, 制約がある, 制約を受ける. 制限, by contrast, is an explicitly set limit (年齢制限, 速度制限); 制約 sounds more abstract and describes the situation rather than a rule. Do not confuse it with the homophones 誓約 "pledge" and 製薬 "pharmaceuticals". Rather formal.

examples[].german: We will overcome the obstacle.
There are more and more stations that are easy to use for people with disabilities, too.
Because of a system failure, the trains have stopped.
en.notes: 障害 has three main areas: an "obstacle" (障害を乗り越える), a technical "disruption" (システム障害, 通信障害) and a "disability" or "disorder" in the medical sense (障害者, 睡眠障害). A person with a disability is 障害のある人; because 害 means "harm", government offices and media often write 障がい. A physical obstacle in the way is usually called 障害物. In everyday speech, for minor things that get in the way, 邪魔 is more common.

examples[].german: I maintain my health.
The upkeep costs of this old house are high.
Keeping first place is harder than becoming first.
en.notes: 維持 means to keep a state as it is: 健康・体重・平和・関係を維持する, 現状維持 "status quo". 維持費 are the ongoing upkeep costs. The native verb 保つ is similar, but sounds less official. 保存 is the keeping of things or data, 整備 the practical maintenance of machines.

examples[].german: We will carry out the plan.
Next month, we will conduct a survey of all employees.
In case of rain, the sports festival will be held the next day.
en.notes: 実施 is the official carrying out of plans, surveys, exams, campaigns or rules: 〜を実施する, very often passive 〜が実施される and on notices 実施中. In conversation people mostly say やる or 行う. 実行 stresses the actual action of a person (計画を実行する), 実現 the coming true of a goal or dream.

examples[].german: I realized my dream.
The long-held plan finally came true.
The idea is good, but I think it will be hard to realize.
en.notes: 実現 means that a dream, plan or wish becomes reality. It can be transitive (夢を実現する) and intransitive (夢が実現する); also common are 実現可能 "feasible" and 実現は難しい. More emotional and more frequent in daily life is 夢が叶う/夢を叶える. 実施, by contrast, is the formal carrying out of a program.

examples[].german: We reached the goal.
The temperature reached 40 degrees.
The discussion went on for three hours but did not reach a conclusion.
en.notes: 達する means "to reach" and takes に: 目標に達する, 40度に達する, 結論に達する. It is used for numbers, amounts, levels, places and stages and sounds written or formal; in conversation people say 届く, 着く or 〜になる instead. It is an irregular する-verb: 達して, 達した, negative 達しない. Close in meaning is the likewise elevated 至る.

examples[].german: I will explain the characteristics of Japanese.
Please tell me the characteristics of the culprit.
The feature of this town is that it has many old buildings.
en.notes: 特徴 is a conspicuous, distinguishing feature: 〜の特徴は…ことだ, 特徴がある, 特徴的な. It can be neutral, for example in descriptions of persons (犯人の特徴). The identically read 特長, by contrast, means "strength, merit" and is positive; 特色 emphasizes the distinctive character of a region or institution.

examples[].german: Please give me an estimate.
I got quotes from three companies and compared them.
The moving cost was 20,000 yen more than the estimate.
en.notes: 見積もり is the noun of 見積もる "to estimate, to appraise" and mainly refers to a cost estimate: 見積もりを取る (to obtain), 見積もりを出す (to prepare), 見積もりを依頼する; the written quotation is called 見積書. It also means "estimate" in general: 見積もりが甘い "to have estimated too optimistically". The spellings 見積もり, 見積り and 見積 all occur.

examples[].german: I weigh the pros and cons.
I helped my friend move without thinking about my own advantage.
If you choose a job based only on advantage, you may regret it later.
en.notes: 損得 consists of 損 "loss" and 得 "gain" and means personal advantage or disadvantage: 損得を考える, 損得勘定 "cost-benefit calculation". 損得抜きで means "without thinking of one's own advantage, selflessly". 利害, by contrast, is the constellation of interests of different parties, and 損益 is accounting profit and loss.

examples[].german: I have a conflict of interest with that company, so I cannot take part in the review.
The interests of the two countries coincided, and an agreement was concluded.
Negotiations in which interests conflict are hard to settle.
en.notes: 利害 are the interests, that is, the benefit and harm, of the parties involved: 利害が一致する "interests coincide", 利害が対立する "interests clash", 利害関係 "interest relationship, conflict of interest", 利害関係者 "stakeholder". Typical of business, politics and law and rather formal. 損得, by contrast, is the personal calculation of whether one gains or loses.

examples[].german: Negative effects are appearing.
The harmful effects of overusing smartphones are becoming a problem.
Rules that are too strict can even produce harmful side effects.
en.notes: 弊害 is a harmful side effect of a system, rule, technology or habit: 〜による弊害, 弊害が出る/生じる, 弊害をもたらす. It usually presupposes that the thing itself is useful but has negative consequences. Written and objective; in daily life people more often say 悪影響 or 害. 副作用 are side effects of medicines, but are also used figuratively.

examples[].german: The pay gap between men and women needs to be corrected.
The problems pointed out in the inspection were corrected immediately.
To curb excessive working hours, the company banned overtime.
en.notes: 是正 means bringing something wrong or unjust into the right state: inequalities, abuses, violations (格差・不公平・長時間労働を是正する, 是正措置, 是正勧告). It is an official word from politics, administration and business. For correcting errors in text or speech, one says 訂正; for revising a draft, 修正; for general improvement, 改善.

en.meaning: by all means; right and wrong
examples[].german: Please do come by all means.
When you come to Japan, be sure to visit Kyoto.
"Would you like to go for a drink together sometime?" "I'd love to!"
en.notes: 是非 as an adverb means "by all means, definitely" and strengthens wishes, requests and invitations: ぜひ来てください, ぜひ行きたいです. It therefore appears with ～てください, ～たい or ～てほしい, not in mere suppositions (for those use きっと) or statements of fact (use 必ず). As a short reply, ぜひ！ means "I'd love to!". As a noun, 是非 means "right and wrong, pros and cons" (written language); the adverb is usually written in kana as ぜひ in daily life.

examples[].german: How are you feeling?
Would you like some tea?
en.notes: いかが is the polite equivalent of どう: ご気分はいかがですか asks about someone's condition; お茶はいかがですか offers tea. The kana spelling is usual. In いかがなものか there is a tone of doubt or polite criticism; here it does not simply mean "how". The kanji can also be read differently, for example 如何に（いかに）.

examples[].german: I humbly ask for your kind consideration.
We apologize for the inconvenience during construction and humbly ask for your understanding.
Please forgive me for my late reply.
en.notes: 何卒 is a very formal "please" that makes a request especially humble and earnest. It appears almost only in business letters, emails, notices and speeches, mostly before よろしくお願い申し上げます or ご〜ください (何卒ご理解ください). It is clearly more formal than どうか or どうぞ and seems out of place in casual conversation. Often also written in kana: なにとぞ.

en.meaning: to be very sorry; to be much obliged (polite); to be impressed
examples[].german: Excuse me, may I ask your name?
Thank you so much for going out of your way to come despite your busy schedule.
I was amazed at the depth of his knowledge.
en.notes: 恐れ入る is a very polite verb that appears almost only as 恐れ入ります. As 恐れ入りますが it introduces a request in customer service and business, and is more formal than すみませんが; for one's own mistake, by contrast, one says 申し訳ありません. On its own, 恐れ入ります can also express thanks for someone's trouble ("much obliged"). With に, 〜には恐れ入った means "to take one's hat off to ...", sometimes also ironically "I'm speechless".

examples[].german: The key to success is hard work.
Several causes can be considered for the accident.
We are investigating the factors behind the drop in sales.
en.notes: 要因 is a (main) factor that contributes to a result: 〜の要因, 主な要因, 〜が要因となる. It sounds more analytical than 原因: 原因 is the direct cause (for example of an accident), 要因 is one of several contributing factors. Typical of reports, news and analyses; compare also 要素 "component".

en.meaning: to receive (humble); to eat, to drink (humble)
examples[].german: I would like to hear your opinion.
I received a letter from my teacher.
Well then, I will eat while it is still warm.
en.notes: 頂く is the humble counterpart (謙譲語) of もらう: 先生に本を頂きました "I received a book from my teacher"; the giver takes に or から. At the same time it is the polite word for "to eat, to drink", hence いただきます before a meal. As an auxiliary verb, ～ていただく means that someone kindly does something for one: 教えていただけますか "could you show me?" It is mostly written in kana, いただく, especially as an auxiliary verb; 戴く is a rare variant.

examples[].german: I will give you a present.
I gave the customer the new catalog.
I would like to give my teacher a souvenir from my trip.
en.notes: 差し上げる is the humble form (謙譲語) of あげる: the speaker or their side gives something to a person of higher status – 先生にお土産を差し上げる. The recipient takes に, the gift takes を. As an auxiliary verb, ～て差し上げる "to do for someone" sounds slightly condescending when said directly to the other person; better then is お持ちします instead of 持って差し上げます. The basic meaning "to lift up" is rare today. The counterpart for the direction toward the speaker is くださる.

examples[].german: I will take your order.
I have received your message. I will pass it on to the person in charge.
I have long heard your name.
en.notes: 承る is a humble verb (謙譲語) used by staff when speaking to customers. It replaces 受ける/引き受ける (to receive an order, reservation or message: ご予約を承ります, かしこまりました、承りました) and 聞く (to hear, to learn: お名前は承っております). It is used only for one's own action, never for the customer's. Do not confuse it with 承知する "to understand, to agree" (承知しました).

examples[].german: I will guide you.
I will prepare the materials for next week's meeting.
Pleased to meet you, my name is Yamada. I look forward to working with you.
en.notes: 致す is the humble form (謙譲語) of する and describes only one's own actions or those of one's own side. The pattern お/ご＋noun＋いたします is especially common: ご案内いたします, お送りいたします.
