Fixed polite formulas are 失礼いたします and よろしくお願いいたします. It is mostly written in kana; the kanji spelling 致します is seen mainly in business letters and e-mails. For the actions of others, honorific なさる is used.

examples[].german: Communication has been cut off.
To save on data charges, I use Wi-Fi at home.
I'm studying English through a university correspondence course.
en.notes: 通信 is the transmission of information over lines, radio or a network, today mostly data traffic: 通信環境, 通信速度, 通信料金, 通信制限 "throttling"; 通信が切れる/途絶える. In older words it stands for "by mail": 通信教育 "distance learning", 通信販売 or 通販 "mail order". For communication between people, one does not say 通信 but コミュニケーション or 連絡.

examples[].german: The line is congested.
I had a fiber-optic line installed in my new apartment.
The connection dropped during the online meeting.
en.notes: 回線 is the technical line for telephone or internet: 電話回線, 光回線 "fiber-optic connection", 回線速度. Typical verbs: 回線が混む ("to be congested"), 回線がつながる, 回線が切れる, 回線を引く ("to have a line installed"). 接続, by contrast, denotes the process or state of connecting, and ケーブル or コード the physical cable.

examples[].german: I connect to the internet.
This train connects with the express at the next station.
Please connect the printer to the computer.
en.notes: 接続 is connecting or hooking up: intransitive インターネットに接続する ("to connect"), transitive プリンターをパソコンに接続する ("to hook up"). In rail travel it means "connection": 特急に接続する, 接続駅. In grammar there is 接続詞 "conjunction". In everyday speech, one often simply says つなぐ/つながる; 接続 sounds more technical.

examples[].german: I operate the terminal.
The clerk keyed the order into the terminal.
Please set a password on all devices, such as company PCs and smartphones.
en.notes: 端末 (literally "outermost end") is short for 端末装置, a device at the end of a network: smartphone, tablet, PC, point-of-sale or ordering device, ticket machine. Typical are 携帯端末, 情報端末, 端末代 "device cost" when buying a phone. A technical, objective word from companies, government offices and contracts; in conversation people more often say スマホ, パソコン, 機械 or デバイス.

examples[].german: Please touch the screen.
The screen cracked, so I sent my smartphone in for repair.
Suddenly an error message appeared on the screen.
en.notes: 画面 is the screen surface and what is seen on it: テレビ・スマホの画面, 画面に表示される/映る, 画面をタッチする, ホーム画面, 画面が割れる ("the display cracked"). The device itself is more モニター or ディスプレイ, the cinema screen スクリーン. 画面 also refers to the frame of an image in a film or painting.

examples[].german: I'll print the documents.
I printed the New Year's cards with the printer at home.
The ink has run out, so I can't print.
en.notes: 印刷 is printing, both on a printer and at a print shop: 〜を印刷する, 印刷できない, カラー印刷, 両面印刷, 印刷物, 印刷所. In the office you also hear プリントする or プリントアウト; the noun プリント, however, mostly means a worksheet or handout. Photocopying is コピー (formally 複写), not 印刷.

examples[].german: I will look into the background of the incident.
We took a photo with Mt. Fuji in the background.
Behind this problem lies a labor shortage.
en.notes: 背景 is on the one hand the visible background of a picture or stage (〜を背景に写真を撮る), on the other the background of an event: 事件の背景, 〜の背景には…がある "behind ... lies ...". For a person's personal career one does not say 背景 but 経歴; for photos, バック is also common colloquially.

examples[].german: I copy the documents.
Unauthorized copying of these materials is prohibited.
The application form is a carbon-copy type, so please press firmly when writing.
en.notes: 複写 is the formal, written word for copying or duplicating. It is found on notices (無断複写を禁じます "unauthorized duplication prohibited"), in 複写機 "copier" and 複写式 "form with carbon copy". In conversation, one almost always says コピーする. 写す is copying by hand, and 複製 is reproducing works of art or keys.

examples[].german: I'll save the file.
After opening, please store in the refrigerator.
This temple has been carefully preserved in its original form.
en.notes: 保存 means keeping something in good condition for later: food (冷蔵保存, 冷凍保存, 保存料 "preservative"), buildings and cultural properties (保存される), and data (ファイルを保存する, 上書き保存). 保管 is the safe keeping of objects or documents, 維持 the maintaining of a state.

examples[].german: I deleted the data.
Rude comments were deleted.
Please delete the last paragraph of the text.
en.notes: 削除 is deleting or striking from data, texts or lists: データ・メール・コメントを削除する, 削除される, 削除キー. It sounds technical or formal. The everyday 消す is broader (also wiping a blackboard, turning off a light), 取り消す means "to cancel, to take back", and 削る "to shave off, to cut down".

examples[].german: I'll update the software.
I have to renew my passport next month.
He broke the marathon world record.
en.notes: 更新 means renewing or updating: extending contracts, IDs and visas (契約・免許・パスポートを更新する), updating software and websites (ブログを更新する, ページが更新される) and breaking records (記録を更新する). Both transitive and intransitive are possible. 延長, by contrast, is simply the extension of a deadline or duration.

examples[].german: Please enter your password.
My job is to enter sales data into the computer every day.
I'm still not used to typing Japanese on a smartphone.
en.notes: 入力 is the input of data into a device: 〜を〜に入力する, 入力欄 "input field", 入力ミス, 音声入力. The opposite is 出力. For filling in a paper form by hand, one says 記入, not 入力. Colloquially, typing is also 打つ (メールを打つ).

examples[].german: We output the data.
Please export the report as a PDF and send it by email.
This engine has a high output.
en.notes: 出力 is the output of data to a screen, printer or file: データを出力する, PDFで出力する, プリンターに出力する ("to print out"). It also refers to the power of engines, speakers or power plants: 出力が大きい, 最大出力. The opposite is 入力; for plain printing, 印刷 is more common.

examples[].german: I'll convert it into kanji.
I want to convert this video to MP4.
Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity.
en.notes: 変換 means converting something into another form: 〜を〜に変換する. Very common in everyday IT: かな漢字変換 and the 変換キー of the keyboard, 変換ミス (wrong kanji from the input aid), converting file formats. Also in technology: 光を電気に変換する. 変化, by contrast, is a change of its own accord, 交換 an exchange, 換算 the conversion of units and 両替 currency exchange.

examples[].german: I'll search on the internet.
For words I don't know, I look them up in a dictionary app.
When I searched for "Tokyo ramen", many shops came up.
en.notes: 検索 is searching for information in a database, a dictionary or on the internet: 〜を検索する, 〜で検索する (search term or tool), 検索エンジン, 検索結果. Colloquially also ググる. For searching for lost things or people, one says 探す, for investigating in general 調べる; so you cannot 検索する a lost key.

examples[].german: I'm registering as a member.
If you save the phone number, the name will be displayed.
Mt. Fuji was registered as a World Heritage Site in 2013.
en.notes: 登録 is the official entering into a list, register or database: 会員登録, ユーザー登録, 〜に登録する (to register with something), 〜を登録する (to save a number, card or name). On YouTube, チャンネル登録 means "to subscribe", and 世界遺産に登録される means "to be designated a World Heritage Site". 申し込む is "to apply, sign up for", and registering your residence is called 転入届.

examples[].german: I'm changing the settings.
I set the alarm for six o'clock.
This movie is set in a future Tokyo.
en.notes: 設定 means, on the one hand, setting or configuring devices and programs: 〜を〜に設定する, 初期設定, 設定画面, パスワードを設定する. On the other hand, it refers to the starting situation of a story: 〜という設定 "set in ..., the premise is ...". Goals or deadlines are also set this way (目標を設定する). 設置, by contrast, is the physical setting up or installing.

examples[].german: It meets the standard.
I don't choose products based on price alone.
The criteria for whether a room is clean differ from person to person.
en.notes: 基準 is a yardstick or criterion against which something is measured: 基準を満たす "to meet the standard", 基準に合う, 基準を決める. 〜を基準にする means "to take something as a yardstick". Common compounds are 安全基準 "safety standard" and 判断基準 "decision criterion". 基本, by contrast, means "foundation, basis" and is not a measured value.

examples[].german: We will expand the business overseas.
The plot of this drama moves so fast that you can't look away.
The match took an unexpected turn.
en.notes: 展開 means, first, the development of events: 話の展開, 意外な展開, 展開が速い. Second, the expansion of an activity: 事業を展開する, 全国展開. As a する-verb it is both transitive (〜を展開する) and intransitive (話が展開する). In IT it means "to unpack/extract" (ファイルを展開する), and in mathematics "to expand" (an expression).

examples[].german: Please tell me how to operate it.
This machine is easy to operate; even children can use it.
He manipulated the data to make the results look good.
en.notes: 操作 is the operation of machines and devices: 機械・パソコン・スマホを操作する, 操作方法, 操作ミス, 遠隔操作. Secondly, it means manipulation for one's own advantage: データ操作, 情報操作. Vehicles, by contrast, are driven with 運転する. Beware of the homophone: 捜査 (also そうさ) is a police investigation.

examples[].german: The elevator has broken down.
This vending machine is out of order.
My car broke down, so I was late for work.
en.notes: 故障 refers to a technical failure of machines, devices or vehicles; as an intransitive する-verb: エレベーターが故障する. On signs you read 故障中 "out of order". 壊れる is more general and also covers mechanical breaking (glass, toys), whereas 故障 stresses that something no longer works. For people, 故障 is used only in sports for injuries (膝の故障); otherwise you say けが.

examples[].german: We will restore the building.
There is software that repairs corrupted data.
After the fight, it took a long time to mend the relationship between the two.
en.notes: 修復 means bringing something damaged back to its original state: historic buildings and works of art (文化財の修復), damaged data, and also relationships (関係を修復する "to mend"). For everyday repairs of devices, one says 修理; for restoring power, trains or networks after outages, 復旧; for rebuilding whole regions, 復興.

examples[].german: I took my car in for inspection.
Every morning, the driver checks the bus's brakes.
Today the elevator is undergoing maintenance, so please use the stairs.
en.notes: 点検 is a thorough check in which every part is examined for faults and safety: 車・機械・設備を点検する, 定期点検, 安全点検, 点検中. Taking a car in for inspection is 点検に出す. 検査 is a test or examination (also medical), 確認 a confirmation, 整備 the maintenance work itself; チェック is the casual equivalent.

examples[].german: We will develop the roads.
Airplanes are always serviced before departure.
It is important to create an environment in which it is easy to raise children.
en.notes: 整備 has two main meanings. First, the maintenance of vehicles and machines: 車・飛行機の整備, 整備士 "mechanic", 整備不良. Second, the development and organization of infrastructure or framework conditions: 道路・環境・制度を整備する. 点検 is the inspection beforehand, 修理 is the repair after a defect, and 手入れ is everyday care of a garden or tools.

examples[].german: Artificial intelligence is advancing.
I translated the text using AI.
Some people worry that AI might take their jobs in the future.
en.notes: 人工知能 is the full technical term for "artificial intelligence"; in the news, advertising and daily life people mostly say AI for short (pronounced エーアイ). 人工 means "artificial, man-made" (cf. 人工衛星 "satellite"), 知能 "intelligence" (cf. 知能テスト). Typical combinations: 人工知能を活用する "to use AI", 人工知能が発達する／進歩する, 人工知能に仕事を奪われる "to have one's job taken by AI".

examples[].german: We are automating the work processes.
Many tasks are automated at the factory.
Since I automated the monthly invoice preparation, things have become much easier.
en.notes: 自動化 "automation" is a noun with the suffix 〜化 "-ization" (cf. 機械化, 国際化) and is mostly used as a transitive する-verb: 作業を自動化する "to automate a workflow". For the result you say 自動化される or 自動化が進む "automation is progressing". Do not confuse it with 自動 "automatic" on its own, which usually stands before nouns: 自動ドア, 自動販売機.

examples[].german: I set this printer as the default.
He speaks not standard Japanese but the Kansai dialect.
This child's height is a little above average.
en.notes: 標準 means "standard, norm" in the sense of the usual or average: 標準的な "average, normal", 標準より高い "above average". Frequent in compounds: 標準語 "standard language", 標準体重 "standard weight", 標準サイズ; for devices and software, 標準で means "as standard" and 標準に設定する "to set as the default". To be distinguished from 基準 "benchmark, criterion (for judging)" and 規格 "technical standard".

examples[].german: We comply with international standards.
This plug doesn't conform to the Japanese standard, so it can't be used.
I bought non-standard vegetables cheaply.
en.notes: 規格 is a fixed technical standard for the size, shape or quality of products: 国際規格, 日本工業規格, 規格に合う／合わない "to conform / not conform to the standard". Common in everyday speech is 規格外 "outside the standard", for example for crooked vegetables sold more cheaply, or jokingly for people with extraordinary abilities. Do not confuse it with the identically read 企画 "planning, project"; 標準 is more general "standard, average".

examples[].german: We will check the specifications.
This watch is waterproof, so you can use it in the bath too.
The specifications were changed at the customer's request.
en.notes: 仕様 refers to the fixed design or technical specification of a product: 仕様書 "specification document, requirements document", 仕様を変更する "to change the specification". 〜仕様 is often used as a suffix meaning "version, model" (防水仕様 "waterproof model", 日本仕様), and それは仕様です means jokingly "that's by design, not a bug". The old meaning "means, way" lives on in 仕様がない, which today is usually written しょうがない. Do not confuse it with the identically read 使用 "use".

examples[].german: I will present the results of my research.
The results of daily practice showed, and we won the match.
I tried a new method, but it didn't produce much result.
en.notes: 成果 is the positive result of an effort, the "fruit of one's work": 成果を上げる/出す, 成果が出る, 研究成果. Unlike 結果, which is neutral and can also turn out badly, 成果 is always a success; 成果がない means "without yield". Compare 実績 "proven track record".

examples[].german: We use natural materials.
What material is this shirt made of?
This dish brings out the natural flavor of the ingredients.
en.notes: 素材 is the raw material something is made of, especially for clothing, furniture and cooking: 天然素材, 素材の味を生かす "to bring out the natural flavor of the ingredients". On the Internet, 素材 also means freely usable raw material such as images, music or icons (フリー素材). Compared with 材料 "material, ingredients" (general, also in recipes), 素材 stresses the quality of the raw material; 原料 is the industrial raw material.

examples[].german: These are clothes made of natural fibers.
Burdock root contains a lot of dietary fiber.
This town once prospered thanks to the textile industry.
en.notes: 繊維 means fibers, both textile fibers (天然繊維, 化学繊維, 繊維工業 "textile industry") and dietary fiber in nutrition: 食物繊維 "dietary fiber", 繊維が多い野菜. In everyday life, you meet the word most often in 食物繊維 on food packaging. For finished fabric, one says 布 or 生地, not 繊維.

examples[].german: We process metal.
I have a metal allergy, so I can't wear cheap earrings.
At airport security I was told to take the metal objects out of my pockets.
en.notes: 金属 is the general term "metal"; individual metals have their own words such as 鉄 "iron", 銅 "copper", 銀 "silver". Typical: 金属製の "made of metal", 金属アレルギー "metal allergy", 貴金属 "precious metal", and 金属ごみ in waste sorting. 金 on its own means "gold" or, as お金, "money", not "metal".

examples[].german: Japanese pottery is famous.
Ceramic cups break easily if you drop them.
On the weekend, I bought plates at a pottery fair.
en.notes: 陶器 is earthenware or pottery made of clay, fired at a relatively low temperature, and looks rather thick and warm; the harder, thinner porcelain is called 磁器. As a general term for ceramic tableware, one says 陶磁器 or simply 焼き物 (well-known kinds: 有田焼, 益子焼). Typical: 陶器の皿 "ceramic plate", 陶器市 "pottery fair".

examples[].german: It is a lacquered bowl.
Lacquerware becomes more beautiful the longer you use it.
I touched a lacquer tree in the mountains and got a rash on my hand.
en.notes: 漆 is the traditional East Asian lacquer made from the sap of the lacquer tree, which is also called 漆 (often written in kana うるし). Lacquered objects are called 漆器 "lacquerware"; 漆塗り "coated with Japanese lacquer" describes bowls, chopsticks or trays (e.g. 輪島塗). The fresh sap irritates the skin: 漆にかぶれる "to get a rash from the lacquer tree". For modern lacquer or paint you say ペンキ or ニス, not 漆.

examples[].german: I attend a pottery class.
On a trip I tried pottery and made my own rice bowl.
My grandfather took up pottery after retiring.
en.notes: 陶芸 is the art of pottery as an activity or hobby, i.e. shaping and firing ceramics; the product itself is called 陶器 or 焼き物. Typical combinations: 陶芸教室 "pottery class", 陶芸家 "ceramic artist", 陶芸体験 "try-it-yourself pottery" (a popular offering for tourists). As a verb you say 陶芸をする or, more concretely, 器を作る, ろくろを回す "to turn the potter's wheel".

examples[].german: I enjoy ikebana.
In high school, I was in the ikebana club.
My mother has been studying ikebana for over twenty years.
en.notes: 華道 is the art of flower arranging as a "way" (道) with schools and rules, like 茶道 "tea ceremony" and 書道 "calligraphy". In everyday speech one usually says 生け花 or いけばな (いけばなを習う); 華道 sounds more formal and emphasizes discipline: 華道部 "ikebana club", 華道の先生, 華道の流派 "ikebana school". A single flower arrangement is 生け花, not 華道.

examples[].german: I train my mind through martial arts.
In Japanese junior high schools, students learn martial arts in physical education class.
It is said that martial arts begin and end with a bow.
en.notes: 武道 is the collective term for the Japanese martial arts as a "way" with mental training, e.g. 柔道, 剣道, 空手, 合気道, 弓道. Compared with 格闘技 "combat sports" (boxing etc.), 武道 stresses etiquette, discipline and character building; a well-known saying is 武道は礼に始まり礼に終わる "martial arts begin and end with a bow". Typical: 武道を習う, 武道館 "martial arts hall". The identically read ぶどう "grapes" exists, but it is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: I am practicing kyudo.
I worked hard for three years in the kyudo club at high school.
In kyudo, correct posture is more important than hitting the target.
en.notes: 弓道 is traditional Japanese archery with the long bow 弓 and counts as one of the 武道; posture, breathing and concentration matter more than the number of hits. Olympic sport archery, by contrast, is called アーチェリー. Typical: 弓道部 (a popular school club), 弓道場 "kyudo range", 弓を引く "to draw the bow", 的に当たる "to hit the target".

examples[].german: I saw Kabuki.
In Kabuki, female roles are also played by male actors.
If you're watching Kabuki for the first time, it's a good idea to rent an earphone guide.
en.notes: 歌舞伎 is the traditional popular theater of the Edo period, with magnificent costumes, striking makeup and exclusively male performers; female roles are played by 女形. Typical: 歌舞伎を観る／見る (観る stresses watching performances), 歌舞伎座 (the theater in Ginza), 歌舞伎役者 "Kabuki actor". The kanji 歌 "song", 舞 "dance", 伎 "skill" were assigned afterward to the old verb かぶく "to behave eccentrically".

examples[].german: This company has an outstanding track record.
I just joined the company, so I don't have a track record yet.
He built up a track record and became a section manager.
en.notes: 実績 means results actually achieved and verifiable, a track record: 実績がある/ない, 実績を積む, 実績を上げる, 販売実績. Typical in business and job applications. 成果 is the result of a specific effort, and 業績 is a company's business performance or scholarly achievements.

examples[].german: I am going to listen to rakugo.
A rakugo performer plays many different roles all by himself.
Recently there are also people who perform rakugo in English.
en.notes: 落語 is traditional comic storytelling: a single 落語家 sits on a cushion in a kimono and, with only a fan and a hand towel, plays all the characters of a story that ends with a punch line (落ち／オチ), which is also where the name comes from. You usually say 落語を聞く, even though you also watch, and you experience it live in a 寄席 "variety theater". Do not confuse it with 漫才, comedy performed as a duo.

examples[].german: I saw a Noh performance.
In Noh, the actors perform wearing masks.
As they say, a skilled hawk hides its talons.
en.notes: 能 as a stage form is the classical Japanese masked theater with slow, stylized movements, singing and music; it is often performed together with the comic 狂言 under the name 能楽. Typical: 能を観る, 能面 "Noh mask", 能舞台 "Noh stage". Otherwise 能 means "ability, talent" and appears almost only in compounds (能力, 才能, 可能) or in the proverb 能ある鷹は爪を隠す "a capable hawk hides its talons", said of skilled people who don't boast.

examples[].german: Kyogen is entertaining.
Between two Noh plays, a short kyogen is performed.
They say the incident was staged by a man in need of money.
en.notes: 狂言 is the classical comic stage form performed between the serious 能 plays; in old colloquial language, short dialogues show everyday scenes with masters, servants and farmers. Typical: 狂言を観る, 狂言師 "kyogen performer". Outside the theater, 狂言 means "staged deception, a put-up job", especially in 狂言強盗 "faked robbery" or 狂言誘拐 "faked kidnapping".

examples[].german: I want to become a voice actor.
The main character of this anime is voiced by a famous voice actor.
I watched a foreign film dubbed by Japanese voice actors.
en.notes: 声優 are voice actors for anime, video games, radio dramas and dubbed versions of foreign films; in Japan they are often stars with their own fans, concerts and radio shows. Typical: 声優になる, 人気声優, 声優を目指す "to aim to become a voice actor", 〜の声を担当する "to voice ...". The dubbing itself is called 吹き替え; a narrator in documentaries is more likely a ナレーター.

examples[].german: I'm going to the exhibition.
A trade show for new products will be held in Tokyo next month.
An exhibition of children's pictures is being held in the lobby of the city hall.
en.notes: 展示会 is an exhibition where things are shown, especially products at trade and sales fairs (新製品の展示会) or collections and works by amateurs. For art exhibitions, one more often says 展覧会 or, in short, 〜展 (ピカソ展); 展示会 sounds more matter-of-fact. Typical: 展示会を開く／開催する, 展示会に出展する "to exhibit at a trade show"; the verb 展示する "to exhibit" is transitive.

examples[].german: I saw the painter's solo exhibition.
A friend of mine is holding his first solo exhibition in Ginza next month.
My dream is to hold a solo exhibition of my own photographs someday.
en.notes: 個展 is the short form of 個人展覧会 and means a solo exhibition showing only the works of a single artist; the counterpart is グループ展. Typical: 個展を開く "to hold a solo exhibition", 初個展 "first solo exhibition". Caution: the identically read 古典 "classic, classical literature" exists.

examples[].german: I am looking at sculptures.
There is a large sculpture in the middle of the park.
In art class, I carved a wooden board using a carving knife.
en.notes: 彫刻 is both the work, "sculpture, carving", and the activity, "sculpting, engraving", and can be used as a する-verb: 木に模様を彫刻する. Typical: 彫刻家 "sculptor", 石の彫刻, 彫刻刀 "carving knife" (familiar from art class). For the action itself, everyday speech mostly uses the simple verb 彫る "to carve, to engrave"; 彫刻 sounds more artistic.

examples[].german: Painting is my hobby.
This museum has many Western paintings.
My mother takes oil painting lessons at a painting class every week.
en.notes: 絵画 is the formal, objective word for "painting" as an art form; in everyday speech you simply say 絵: 絵を描く, 絵が好き. You encounter 絵画 in museums, catalogs and résumés: 西洋絵画, 日本の絵画, 絵画教室, 絵画展. Paintings are counted with 〜点 or 〜枚.

examples[].german: I am composing music.
For this song, she wrote both the lyrics and the music all by herself.
I hear Mozart began composing at the age of five.
en.notes: 作曲 is the composing of music; as a する-verb: 曲を作曲する or simply 作曲する. For songs, a clear distinction is made between 作曲 "music", 作詞 "lyrics" and 編曲 "arrangement", as also written in song credits (作詞・作曲). The composer is called 作曲家; colloquially one also says 曲を作る.

examples[].german: I play the piano.
At the restaurant we ate while listening to live jazz.
When the performance ended, loud applause rose from the hall.
en.notes: 演奏 is the playing of a musical instrument, especially before an audience or at a higher level; as a transitive する-verb: ピアノを演奏する. In everyday speech, for individual instruments you say ピアノを弾く, 笛を吹く, 太鼓をたたく rather than this; 演奏 sounds more formal and fits all instruments. Typical: 演奏会 "concert", 生演奏 "live music", 演奏者 "musician, performer".

examples[].german: The company's business results improved.
Because performance worsened, bonuses were reduced.
The professor left great achievements in the field of medicine.
en.notes: 業績 refers above all to the business performance of a company: 業績が上がる/伸びる/悪化する, 業績不振 "poor business performance". It also refers to the lasting accomplishments of a person, especially in science: 業績を残す, 研究業績. Unlike 実績 (verifiable track record), the emphasis here is on the overall result or life's work.

examples[].german: I conduct the orchestra.
At the scene of the fire, the captain commanded the firefighters.
At the choir contest, I was chosen as our class's conductor.
en.notes: 指揮 means "leadership, command" over a group and, specifically in music, "conducting". As a transitive する-verb: オーケストラを指揮する, 部隊を指揮する. Typical: 指揮者 "conductor", 〜の指揮で／〜の指揮のもとで "under the direction of ...", 指揮を執る "to take command". For everyday work instructions in the office you say 指示する "to give instructions" instead.

examples[].german: It is a beautiful melody.
This piece begins with a quiet piano melody.
In a choir, the sopranos sing the main melody.
en.notes: 旋律 is the elevated, technical word for "melody"; in everyday speech people mostly say メロディー. You find it in music class, in reviews and in literature: 美しい旋律, 旋律を奏でる "to play a melody", 主旋律 "main melody". Do not confuse it with the identically read 戦慄 "shudder, horror".

examples[].german: I play a chord.
On the piano, the left hand plays chords and the right hand plays the melody.
Discord is arising within the team.
en.notes: 和音 is a "chord" in music theory, that is, several tones sounding at the same time; 和 stands here for "harmony", not for "Japanese". Among musicians one often hears the loanword コード (コードを押さえる "to play a chord"), while 和音 is the term from school lessons and theory (三和音 "triad"). 不協和音 "dissonance" is also used figuratively for "discord, disagreements" in a group.

en.meaning: beat; rhythm; the moment (〜た拍子に)
examples[].german: I keep time.
A waltz is a piece in triple time.
As I stood up, I hit my head on the desk.
en.notes: 拍子 is "time signature, meter" in music (三拍子 "triple time", 四拍子 "quadruple time") and "rhythm": 手で拍子を取る "to keep time with one's hands". Also very common is 〜た拍子に "just at the moment when ...", usually with an unintended consequence: 転んだ拍子に眼鏡が落ちた. Related is 拍子抜け "letdown because things turned out to be milder than expected"; identically read but different is 表紙 "book cover".

examples[].german: I compose haiku.
A haiku normally includes a seasonal word.
In class, we wrote haiku on the theme of summer.
en.notes: 俳句 is the shortest Japanese poem, with 5-7-5 morae, which traditionally contains a seasonal word (季語); famous poets are 松尾芭蕉 and 小林一茶. The typical verb is 詠む "to compose (a poem)", in daily speech also 俳句を作る; it is counted with 〜句 (一句詠む). A similarly structured but humorous poem without a seasonal word is called 川柳.

examples[].german: I composed a tanka.
A tanka consists of 31 syllables in the pattern 5-7-5-7-7.
My grandmother's tanka was published in the newspaper.
en.notes: 短歌 is the classical Japanese verse form with 5-7-5-7-7, that is, 31 morae, and thus longer than the 俳句; a seasonal word is not required. The form is already attested in the ancient collection 万葉集 and is still cultivated today in newspaper columns and contests. The verb is the same as for 俳句: 短歌を詠む or 作る; they are counted with 〜首 (一首).

examples[].german: I am reading an essay.
"The Pillow Book" is one of the oldest essay works in Japan.
Reading a writer's essays tells you a lot about their daily life.
en.notes: 随筆 is a freely written prose form in which the author records personal experiences, thoughts and observations; literally "following the brush" (随 "to follow", 筆 "brush"). Classic examples are 枕草子 and 徒然草. Today, in everyday speech people usually say エッセイ; 随筆 sounds more literary. A scholarly paper, by contrast, is 論文.

examples[].german: Let's use polite language.
With people you meet for the first time, it is better to speak politely.
"desu" and "masu" are polite language.
en.notes: 丁寧語 is the polite language with です／ます (and ございます), which makes the tone polite toward strangers, customers and superiors without elevating anyone or humbling oneself. It is one of the three main types of 敬語 alongside 尊敬語 and 謙譲語; sometimes 美化語 (お茶, ご飯) is counted as well. The counterpart is plain speech, 普通体, or colloquially タメ口.

examples[].german: I am learning how to use honorific language.
"irassharu" is the honorific form of "iru".
When talking to customers about the president of your own company, you must not use honorific language.
en.notes: 尊敬語 is honorific language: it elevates the actions of other people (customers, superiors, teachers), e.g. いらっしゃる instead of いる／行く／来る, 召し上がる instead of 食べる, おっしゃる instead of 言う, or regularly with お〜になる and 〜られる. Important: for your own actions, and toward outsiders also for your own company, you never use 尊敬語 but 謙譲語.

examples[].german: I spoke in humble language.
"ukagau" is the humble form of "iku" and "kiku".
In job interviews, they also look at whether you can use humble language correctly.
en.notes: 謙譲語 is humble language: you present your own actions (or those of your own group) modestly and thereby indirectly elevate the other person, e.g. 参る／伺う instead of 行く, いただく instead of もらう／食べる, 申す instead of 言う, regularly with お〜する. A typical mistake is to use 謙譲語 for the actions of others (wrong: 先生が申しました, right: 先生がおっしゃいました); there 尊敬語 belongs.

examples[].german: I will get a grip on the actual state of affairs.
The survey revealed the reality of long working hours.
Unlike the advertisement, the reality of that company was terrible.
en.notes: 実態 is the actual state of affairs, often in contrast to appearance, advertising or official statements: 実態を調査する/把握する, 〜の実態が明らかになる. Typical of news and reports. Not to be confused with the identically pronounced 実体 "substance, essence"; 現状 is simply "the current situation".

examples[].german: I want to increase my vocabulary.
She has a rich vocabulary and explains things very clearly.
Before the exam, I practiced a lot of vocabulary questions.
en.notes: 語彙 is the vocabulary of a person or language as a whole, not an individual word (that would be 単語 or 言葉). Typical: 語彙が豊富だ "to have a rich vocabulary", 語彙が少ない, 語彙を増やす, 語彙力 "vocabulary skills" (jokingly also 語彙力がない, when one is so excited that one can't find words). Because the kanji 彙 is rare, the spelling 語い is also seen.

examples[].german: I conjugate the verb.
In Japanese, the verb comes at the end of the sentence.
Is this verb intransitive or transitive?
en.notes: 動詞 is the part of speech "verb". In Japanese classes a distinction is made between 五段動詞 (group 1, e.g. 書く), 一段動詞 (group 2, e.g. 食べる) and the irregular する and 来る; also 自動詞 "intransitive verb" and 他動詞 "transitive verb". Typical: 動詞を活用する "to conjugate a verb", 動詞のて形 "the te-form of a verb". The identically read 同志 "comrade" exists.

examples[].german: I am learning the adjectives.
"Kirei" ends in "i", but it is not an i-adjective.
Using plenty of adjectives makes a text vivid.
en.notes: In Japanese school grammar, 形容詞 is the adjective ending in 〜い (高い, 新しい), which itself conjugates (高くない, 高かった). In classes for Japanese as a foreign language, people distinguish い形容詞 and な形容詞; the latter is called 形容動詞 in native Japanese grammar (静かだ, きれいだ). Typical: 形容詞を活用する, 形容詞の過去形 "past form of the adjective".

examples[].german: There are many nouns.
With "koto" you can use a verb like a noun.
Japanese nouns normally have no plural form.
en.notes: 名詞 is the part of speech "noun", e.g. 本, 学校, 自由. Japanese nouns have neither articles nor grammatical gender and mostly no plural; they are linked with の (日本の車). Typical: 固有名詞 "proper noun", 名詞化 "nominalization" (with の or こと). Caution: the identically read 名刺 "business card" exists.

examples[].german: I use adverbs correctly.
"Hayaku" is an adverb formed from the adjective "hayai".
Changing the position of an adverb can slightly change the meaning of a sentence.
en.notes: 副詞 is the part of speech "adverb", which modifies verbs, adjectives or whole sentences: とても, ゆっくり, もう, たぶん. Many adverbs are formed from adjectives: 早い → 早く, 静か → 静かに. Some require a particular sentence ending, e.g. 全然 with negation, たぶん with でしょう, まるで with ようだ.

examples[].german: I connect sentences with conjunctions.
「しかし」 is a conjunction often used in essays.
Too many conjunctions make a text hard to read.
en.notes: 接続詞 are sentence-connecting words that in Japanese usually stand at the beginning of the new sentence: しかし, だから, それに, ところで. Particles such as から, けど, のに, which connect clauses directly, are grammatically called 接続助詞, not 接続詞. In writing, pay attention to style: しかし is literary and formal, でも is more spoken.

examples[].german: Let's learn idioms.
「顔が広い」 is an idiom meaning that one knows many people.
If you use idioms skillfully, your Japanese sounds natural.
en.notes: 慣用句 is a fixed expression whose meaning does not follow from its individual words, for example 顔が広い "to know many people", 手を焼く "to have a hard time with something", 猫の手も借りたい "to be extremely busy". Many 慣用句 contain body parts such as 目, 口, 手, 足, 腹. To be distinguished are ことわざ "proverb", which expresses a piece of life wisdom, and 四字熟語 "four-kanji expression".

examples[].german: Please tell me some Japanese proverbs.
There is a proverb "Even monkeys fall from trees".
As the proverb says, haste makes waste.
en.notes: 諺 is a proverb expressing a general piece of life wisdom or a lesson, e.g. 猿も木から落ちる "even monkeys fall from trees", meaning "even experts make mistakes". The kanji 諺 is rare; ことわざ is usually written in kana. Typical frames: 〜という諺がある, 諺にもあるように "as the proverb says". Unlike an 慣用句 "idiom", a 諺 is a whole statement with a lesson.

examples[].german: I am studying four-character idioms.
"isseki nicho" is a four-character idiom meaning to gain two benefits from one action.
My favorite four-character idiom is "ichigo ichie".
en.notes: 四字熟語 are fixed expressions made of four kanji, often of Chinese origin, that sum up a lesson or situation concisely: 一石二鳥 "kill two birds with one stone", 一期一会 "every encounter is unique", 自業自得 "you reap what you sow". They are often used in speeches, essays and as life mottos and sound educated. 熟語 on its own refers to any kanji compound of two or more characters.

examples[].german: Let's accept reality.
I realized once I became a working adult that dreams and reality are different.
That plan is interesting, but it isn't very realistic.
en.notes: 現実 is "reality", often in contrast to 夢 or 理想: 夢と現実. Typical combinations are 現実を受け入れる, 現実を見る and 現実から逃げる; escapism is 現実逃避. The adjective 現実的な means "realistic", 非現実的な "unrealistic". To be distinguished are 事実 ("a fact") and the adverb 実際に ("actually").

examples[].german: I correct the error.
There was an error in our recent notice. We apologize.
It is hard to admit an error in your own judgment.
en.notes: 誤り is the written, more formal word for "mistake, error", especially in texts, data and official notices: 記載に誤りがある "the entry contains an error", 誤りを訂正する, 誤りを認める. In conversation people mostly say 間違い. The related verb is 誤る "to err"; do not confuse it with the identically read 謝る "to apologize".

examples[].german: I corrected the typo.
Let me correct my earlier statement.
When you correct a document, draw two lines through it and put your seal next to it.
en.notes: 訂正 is correcting wrong information in texts, documents or statements; as a transitive する-verb: 誤字を訂正する, 発言を訂正する. Typical: 訂正印 "correction seal", 訂正してお詫びします "we correct this and apologize" (newspapers, news). Compared with 修正 "revision, touching up (plans, data, images)", 訂正 stresses setting an error right; in everyday speech one simply says 直す.

examples[].german: I'll give a supplementary explanation.
Let me add a little to the explanation just given.
For detailed data, please see the supplementary materials.
en.notes: 補足 is an addition to something already said or written, supplying missing points; as a transitive する-verb: 説明を補足する. Very common in meetings: 補足させていただきます "may I add something briefly", 補足説明, 補足資料. Compared with 追加 "adding (things, quantities)", 補足 refers to information and explanations.

examples[].german: I will summarize the content.
Please summarize this article in 200 characters or less.
I summarized what was discussed in the meeting and sent it by email.
en.notes: 要約 is summarizing the essentials of a text, talk or conversation in shorter form; as a transitive する-verb: 記事を要約する. Typical: 〜字以内で要約する "to summarize in no more than ... characters" (a common exam task), 要約文. Compared with まとめ (more everyday), 要約 is more objective; 概要 is more of a brief overview of a matter. The identically read ようやく "finally" exists.

examples[].german: I will explain the outline.
The project overview is summarized in this document.
The outline of the incident was reported on the news.
en.notes: 概要 is the rough overview of the essential points of a plan, project, event or text: 計画の概要, 事件の概要, 概要を説明する. In documents it often appears as a heading meaning "overview", and in academic papers it stands for the abstract. Unlike 要約 "summary of an existing text", 概要 describes the basic outline of a matter; the counterpart is 詳細 "details".

examples[].german: We will let you know the details.
Please see the website for details.
The details of the accident are not yet known.
en.notes: 詳細 refers to the "details" of a matter and sounds matter-of-fact and formal; typical in announcements and business: 詳細をお知らせします, 詳細はホームページをご覧ください, 事故の詳細. It also works as a na-adjective or adverb: 詳細な説明, 詳細に調べる. In everyday speech one more often says 詳しい ("detailed, thorough") or 詳しく. The counterpart is 概略 or 概要 ("rough overview").

examples[].german: I'll explain the outline.
I summarized the outline of the plan on one sheet of paper.
I'll talk about the details later, but first just listen to the outline.
en.notes: 概略 is the "rough outline" or "main points" of a plan, project or event, the counterpart to 詳細. It is a rather literary word; typical are 概略を説明する, 計画の概略, 概略図 ("overview sketch"). In business documents 概要 is even more common; in conversation one usually says だいたいの内容 or あらまし. A summary of the most important points would rather be 要点.

examples[].german: I will sum up the main points.
I don't have much time, so please tell me only the main points.
The teacher's talk has clear main points and is easy to understand.
en.notes: 要点 is the "main point", i.e. the essential content of a speech, text or explanation. Typical combinations: 要点をまとめる "to summarize the main points", 要点を押さえる "to grasp the essentials", 要点だけ話す, 話の要点. In casual conversation people often say ポイント. 核心 is narrower and means the actual core of a problem, whereas 概略 is the rough overall overview.

examples[].german: I am getting to the heart of the problem.
His question hit the core of the matter.
She won't touch on the core of the story.
en.notes: 核心 is the innermost "core" of a matter, especially of a problem or question. Set phrases: 核心に迫る "to get closer to the core", 核心を突く "to hit the nail on the head", 核心に触れる "to touch on the core", 問題の核心. For a spatial center you don't use 核心 but 中心. 要点 refers more to the most important points of a presentation, while 核心 is the decisive thing around which everything revolves.

examples[].german: I study the quintessence of Japanese culture.
This dish is packed with the essence of Japanese cuisine.
My teacher spent thirty years mastering the essence of the tea ceremony.
en.notes: 真髄 (also written 神髄) is the "quintessence", the innermost essence of an art, doctrine or culture. It is an elevated, rather written-language word and almost always appears with の: 日本文化の真髄, 茶道の真髄. Typical verbs are 学ぶ, 味わう, 極める ("to master completely"). 本質 is the more neutral, analytical word for "essence"; 核心 means the core of a problem, not of an art.

examples[].german: Please confirm the facts.
This movie is a story based on fact.
He admitted the fact that he had lied.
en.notes: 事実 is a fact: 事実を確認する/認める, 事実に基づく, 〜という事実. 事実上 means "in fact, de facto". At the start of a sentence, 事実、… can also be adverbial, meaning "in fact". 真実 "truth" sounds more emotional and is often opposed to lies, whereas 事実 is sober and objective.

examples[].german: I'll explain the purpose.
I took part because I support the aims of this group.
He said something to the effect that "more time off is needed."
en.notes: 趣旨 is the "point and purpose", or the aim, of an event, plan or statement. Typical: 会の趣旨を説明する, 趣旨に賛同する "to support the aim", 〜という趣旨の発言 "a statement to the effect that ...". The word is formal and often appears in speeches and writing. 目的 is the general word for "goal", 意図 a person's individual intention.

examples[].german: The intention doesn't come across.
I didn't understand what he was getting at with his question.
I didn't intend to hurt anyone.
en.notes: 意図 is the conscious "intention" behind an action or statement; as a する-verb it is transitive: 〜を意図する. Common are 意図が伝わる "the intention comes across", 質問の意図, 〜する意図はない and the adjective 意図的 ("intentional"). In everyday speech intentions are mostly expressed with つもり (傷つけるつもりはなかった); 意図 sounds more matter-of-fact and analytical. 趣旨, by contrast, is the purpose of a thing, not of a person.

examples[].german: He has high aspirations.
He never gave up his resolve to become a doctor.
I started a company with like-minded friends.
en.notes: 志 is a lofty, firmly held life goal or "resolution", often with an idealistic overtone: 志を持つ, 志を立てる "to set oneself a goal", 高い志, 志を果たす, 同じ志を持つ仲間 "like-minded companions". The related verb is 志す (医者を志す). More rarely, お志 means a "kind gesture" or a thank-you gift. 夢 is more general and less serious, 目標 a concrete, measurable goal.

examples[].german: I have a strong desire.
I hear she doesn't have much desire to get married.
Everyone has the desire to "become famous".
en.notes: 願望 is a (often inner, deep-seated) "wish" or longing. Typical: 願望がある, 強い願望, 〜たいという願望, and compounds such as 結婚願望 "desire to marry" or 変身願望. 希望 is more neutral and often refers to concrete plans (希望の大学), while 願い sounds softer and more personal. 願望 is often used in psychological or analytical contexts.

examples[].german: I long for Japan.
I was very happy to talk with the senior student I admire.
When I was a child, being a pilot was my dream job.
en.notes: 憧れ is a rapturous "longing" or admiration for something unattainable or for a role model. Very common is 憧れの + noun: 憧れの先輩, 憧れの職業 "dream job". The verb 憧れる is intransitive and takes に: 日本に憧れる. Expressions: 憧れを抱く, 憧れの的. Unlike 羨ましい "envious", 憧れ is purely positive; 尊敬, by contrast, stresses sober respect.

examples[].german: Please don't cling to the past.
He has a strong attachment to money.
If you're too fixated on winning or losing, the game stops being fun.
en.notes: 執着 is a compulsive "clinging" to something, usually negative: 〜に執着する (intransitive する-verb with に), 強い執着がある, 執着心. Typical objects are money, power, the past or an ex-partner. In contrast, こだわる can also be positive ("to care about": 素材にこだわる). A rarer reading is しゅうじゃく.

examples[].german: I am indifferent to politics.
He takes an indifferent attitude toward the people around him.
Not a few parents are indifferent to their children's studies.
en.notes: 無関心 ("indifference, lack of interest") is a noun and a na-adjective: 〜に無関心だ, 無関心な態度, 政治的無関心. The counterpart is 関心がある "to be interested". In everyday speech people often simply say 興味がない; 無関心 sounds more objective and often critical, for example when it concerns politics, the environment or fellow human beings.

examples[].german: I am very curious.
Out of curiosity, I opened that box.
I want to value children's curiosity.
en.notes: 好奇心 is "curiosity" as a trait or driving force. Typical: 好奇心が強い, 好奇心が旺盛だ "to be very eager to learn", 好奇心から "out of curiosity", 好奇心をくすぐる "to arouse curiosity". The word is mostly positive; by contrast 好奇の目 "curious, staring looks" is derogatory. For "I'm eager to see / interested" people say 興味がある or 気になる in everyday speech.

examples[].german: I seek the truth.
He traveled all over the world in search of his ideal taste.
There is no end to the pursuit of knowledge.
en.notes: 探求 is the "search and striving" for something desirable (knowledge, truth, flavor, happiness); as a transitive する-verb: 〜を探求する. Note: the identically read 探究 stresses scientific investigation and getting to the bottom of things (学問の探究, 真理の探究); 探求 stresses the searching. The similar 追求 means "to strive for" (利益を追求する). The word is rather literary.

examples[].german: I pursue happiness.
A company must not pursue only profit.
This camera was made with a thorough pursuit of ease of use.
en.notes: 追求 is the persistent "pursuit of" a goal or ideal; as a transitive する-verb: 利益を追求する, 幸福を追求する, 理想を追求する. Beware of the homophones: 追及 means "to hold accountable, press for answers" (責任を追及する), and 追究 "to investigate thoroughly" (真理を追究する). 追求 sounds objective and is often used in business and advertising (品質を追求する).

examples[].german: Please show your grounds.
That is a groundless rumor.
What are you basing that on?
en.notes: 根拠 is the basis on which a claim or opinion rests: 根拠がある/ない, 根拠を示す, 〜を根拠に, 根拠のない噂 "groundless rumor". 証拠, by contrast, proves a fact (for example a crime), and 理由 is simply "reason". Typical in discussions and argumentation.

examples[].german: He has an expression full of anguish.
He agonized for a long time over whether to choose his family or his work.
That novel depicts the anguish of young people.
en.notes: 苦悩 is deep mental "suffering" or inner struggle; the word is literary and often appears in novels, biographies and the news. Typical: 苦悩する (intransitive), 苦悩に満ちた表情, 苦悩の日々, 若者の苦悩. In everyday speech people say 悩む or 悩み; 苦しみ is more general and can also be physical, whereas 苦悩 is always mental.

examples[].german: I was relieved.
When I heard that everyone was safe, I breathed a sigh of relief.
A look of relief appeared on the face of my son, who had passed the exam.
en.notes: 安堵 is the "relief" felt when a worry disappears; as an intransitive する-verb: 安堵する. Typical combinations: 安堵の表情, 安堵のため息をつく "to breathe a sigh of relief", with 胸をなで下ろす as an idiomatic parallel. The word is literary and often appears in the news; in conversation people say ほっとする or 安心する.

examples[].german: I was moved.
I was so moved by that movie that tears came out.
The players' performance moved many people.
en.notes: 感動 is the state of being "touched and moved" by something beautiful or great; as an intransitive する-verb: 映画に感動する. Common are 感動を与える "to move (someone)", 感動的な "moving", and 感動して泣く. Distinctions: 感心 means "to be impressed" by someone's skill or behavior (偉いと思う "thinking it admirable"), and 感激 stresses overflowing joy or gratitude.

examples[].german: He incurred resentment.
Many people resent his arrogant way of speaking.
If you force your opinion on people, you'll just provoke resentment.
en.notes: 反感 is an "aversion" or resentment toward a person or their behavior. The most important phrase is 反感を買う "to make oneself unpopular, to draw resentment"; also 反感を持つ / 抱く "to feel an aversion" and 反感を持たれる. 反対, by contrast, is matter-of-fact opposition to an opinion, and 嫌い is simply "not liking".

en.meaning: to underestimate; to look down on
examples[].german: You must not underestimate your opponent.
The ramen at this shop is cheap, but its taste is not to be underestimated.
I underestimated the mountain weather and had a terrible time.
en.notes: 侮る means "to underestimate, to belittle" and is transitive: 相手を侮る. The negated potential form is very common: 侮れない ("not to be underestimated"), often praising something unassuming. In warnings you get 〜を侮ってはいけない. Colloquially one says 甘く見る or なめる; 見下す emphasizes looking down on people, while 侮る is more about underestimating opponents, dangers or things.

en.meaning: to despise; to look down on
examples[].german: You must not despise people.
She looked at the poor people with a contemptuous look.
It is wrong to look down on people because of their education.
en.notes: 蔑む means "to despise, to look down on someone" and is transitive: 人を蔑む. It is literary and written-style and is often written in kana (さげすむ); typical are 蔑むような目で見る and the noun 蔑み. In conversation people more often say 見下す or バカにする; 軽蔑する is the more neutral Sino-Japanese word. 侮る, by contrast, emphasizes underestimating.

en.meaning: to adore; to look up to
examples[].german: I look up to my teacher.
Tanaka is kind, so the juniors look up to him.
The puppy adores its mother and follows her everywhere.
en.notes: 慕う means to "revere" someone full of affection and respect, or to long for them; transitive: 先生を慕う. The passive is very common: 部下に慕われる上司 "a boss who is looked up to by his subordinates". It can also mean "to follow someone devotedly" (母を慕ってついて行く). 尊敬する stresses sober esteem, 憧れる rapturous admiration from afar; 慕う contains personal warmth.

examples[].german: It was a fleeting dream.
It is said that cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they are fleeting.
Even the faint hope of winning the championship vanished in the final match.
en.notes: 儚い describes something "transient, fleeting": life, dreams, cherry blossoms, love. It has a poetic, wistful undertone and is mostly written in kana (はかない). Second meaning: "vague, faint" for hopes (儚い望み). Typical are 儚く消える and 人の命は儚い. Unlike 短い "short", 儚い stresses the wistfulness about passing away.

examples[].german: Looking at my beloved child's sleeping face, I forget my tiredness.
I wrote a letter to a loved one who lives far away.
I find the newborn puppy unbearably endearing.
en.notes: 愛しい expresses tender love for a person (or an animal): "dear, beloved, precious". It sounds emotional and poetic and is found mainly in songs, novels and letters (愛しい人, 愛しいわが子). In modern Japanese the variant 愛おしい (いとおしい) is more common. In everyday speech, for children or animals people say かわいい, and for a partner 大好きな人.

examples[].german: I am frustrated that I lost.
I missed passing by just one point, and it is really frustrating.
I was so frustrated that I could not sleep that night.
en.notes: くやしい is the bitter feeling after a defeat, a mistake or an injustice: "it really rankles". The spelling 口惜しい is rare and archaic; today it is almost always written 悔しい. If 口惜しい is read くちおしい, it is a literary word for "regrettable". Typical: 負けて悔しい, 悔しくて泣く. 残念 is a more neutral regret, without the anger at oneself or others.

examples[].german: There is no evidence.
The police are collecting evidence at the scene.
Laughing a lot is proof that you're doing well.
en.notes: 証拠 is proof, especially in the legal sense: 証拠がある/ない, 証拠を集める/残す/隠す, 動かぬ証拠 "irrefutable evidence". In everyday use, 〜のは…証拠だ means "is a sign that ...". Distinction: 根拠 is the justification of an opinion, 証拠 is what proves a fact.

examples[].german: It's a little unsatisfying.
This soup is bland; something is missing.
This exercise might not be challenging enough for advanced learners.
en.notes: 物足りない describes the feeling that "something is missing", not that the quantity is objectively insufficient (that would be 足りない). Typical: 何か物足りない, 味が物足りない "too bland", 〜には物足りない "not demanding enough for ...". It is used for food, explanations, performances or experiences and sounds milder than 不満 "dissatisfaction".

examples[].german: He is an unreliable person.
The new leader is still young and a bit unreliable.
All I got back was an unconvincing reply: "Probably fine..."
en.notes: 頼りない literally means "without anything to rely on": a person or thing seems weak, unsure and not very trustworthy. Typical: 頼りない人, 頼りない返事, 頼りなさそうに見える. The opposite is 頼もしい "reliable, inspiring confidence". Unlike 信用できない ("not trustworthy", moral), 頼りない implies no dishonesty, only a lack of strength or competence.

examples[].german: He is a reliable ally.
It's reassuring if you come along with me.
There was an experienced senior colleague, so I felt reassured.
en.notes: 心強い describes the reassuring feeling of having support: "encouraging, reassuring". Typical: 〜がいてくれて心強い, 心強い味方, 心強く思う. The opposite is 心細い "uneasy, forlorn". 頼もしい describes a person rather as reliable and capable, whereas 心強い describes one's own feeling of security which this person evokes.

examples[].german: I feel uneasy being alone.
I got lost in an unfamiliar town and felt forlorn.
My wallet is rather thin, so I'll skip eating out today.
en.notes: 心細い is the "uneasy, forlorn" feeling when one is alone or without support: 一人で心細い, 心細くなる. Figuratively it also describes scarce supplies: 残りのお金が心細い. The opposite is 心強い. 寂しい stresses loneliness and longing for company, 不安 general worry; 心細い combines both with helplessness.

en.meaning: reluctant to part; sorry to leave
examples[].german: I am sorry to leave, but it is time to say goodbye.
When I think that this wonderful trip ends today, I hate to part.
She kept waving again and again, as if she did not want to leave.
en.notes: 名残惜しい is composed of 名残 ("lingering trace, memory") and 惜しい ("a pity"): you part only reluctantly from a person, a place or a good time. A classic polite farewell formula is 名残惜しいですが、そろそろ… at the end of parties and speeches. The form 名残惜しそうに describes someone who is visibly reluctant to leave. 寂しい is more general and not tied to parting.

examples[].german: Thank you very much for those kind words.
If you could help me, I would be really grateful.
On cold days, a cup of warm tea is a blessing.
en.notes: ありがたい (usually in kana; 有り難い is rare) describes something that you feel as a blessing: "welcome, a blessing, something to be grateful for". So it refers to the thing or help, not to the grateful person (that would be 感謝している). Typical: 〜てもらえるとありがたい ("I would be grateful if ..."), ありがたいことに ("fortunately"), ありがたく受け取る. ありがとう is derived from it.

examples[].german: It was an anticlimactic ending.
The favored team lost easily in the first round.
The summer vacation I'd been looking forward to ended all too quickly.
en.notes: あっけない (mostly in kana; 呆気ない is rare) describes something that is over "disappointingly quickly" or without drama: an ending, a victory, a defeat, the holidays. Very common is the adverb あっけなく: あっけなく負ける "to lose without a fight", あっけなく終わる. Related is あっけにとられる "to be dumbfounded". 物足りない stresses that something is missing, あっけない the shortness.

examples[].german: That is shameful behavior.
Making excuses after losing is unseemly.
I apologize for letting you see me in such an unpresentable state.
en.notes: 見苦しい literally means "painful to look at": behavior or appearance is "unsightly, embarrassing, undignified". Typical: 見苦しい言い訳, 見苦しい負け方. In the polite formula お見苦しいところをお見せしました, one apologizes for having shown oneself in a messy or embarrassing state. Colloquially one says みっともない; 醜い rather means physical ugliness.

examples[].german: This is a brazen request, but...
Cutting in line like that - what a brazen person!
He had the nerve to eat my bento without asking.
en.notes: 図々しい ("brazen, cheeky, impudent") describes someone who takes or demands without consideration. It sounds more colloquial and sharper than the nearly synonymous 厚かましい. Typical: 図々しい人, 図々しい頼み, 図々しくも ("had the cheek to ..."). 図々しいお願いですが is heard as a modest opening to a request, but 厚かましいお願いですが is more common.

examples[].german: Please prepare the materials.
I'll hand out the materials before the meeting.
I gathered materials at the library for my graduation thesis.
en.notes: 資料 are documents or materials collected for a purpose: handouts in meetings (会議の資料), sources for research, informational material. Typical verbs: 資料を作る/配る/集める/準備する. Distinctions: 書類 are forms and official papers to fill out or submit, 材料 are raw materials or ingredients, and データ is raw data.

examples[].german: This is an impudent request, but...
We have only met once, and he asks to borrow money - how shameless.
I knew it was presumptuous, but I asked my teacher for a letter of recommendation.
en.notes: 厚かましい ("shameless, brazen", literally something like "thick-skinned") describes someone who asks for favors without shame. It is almost synonymous with 図々しい but sounds somewhat more composed. The modest opening 厚かましいお願いですが ("it is presumptuous of me, but ...") is very common, with which one makes oneself small. Related is 面の皮が厚い ("to be thick-skinned").

examples[].german: That is a despicable act.
Deceiving friends for money is despicable.
I felt ashamed of myself for trying to take the biggest piece of cake.
en.notes: 浅ましい condemns behavior as "base, despicable, wretched", usually because greed or self-interest lies behind it: 浅ましい行為, 浅ましい考え. It can also be used self-critically (自分が浅ましく思える). The word is strongly judgmental and rather literary. 情けない stresses pitifulness or weakness, ずるい unfairness, 浅ましい moral lowness.

examples[].german: It is noisy next door.
The classroom was noisy, so the teacher gave a warning.
Lately the world has been rather unsettled.
en.notes: 騒がしい describes an environment as "noisy, restless" because of voices and commotion: 教室が騒がしい, 隣が騒がしい. Figuratively it means "unsettled, turbulent" (世の中が騒がしい). うるさい is more subjective and expresses annoyance (also about people), にぎやか is positive ("bustling, lively"). Related are 騒ぐ ("to make noise") and 騒ぎ ("uproar").

examples[].german: There was a dangerous incident.
This area is unsafe at night, so you had better not walk alone.
The world has become quite a dangerous place lately, hasn't it.
en.notes: 物騒 is a na-adjective for an "unsafe, dangerous" situation in which crime or violence is a threat: 物騒な世の中, 物騒な事件, この辺は夜物騒だ. Objects or talk can also be 物騒 (物騒なものを持ち歩く, 物騒な話). 危ない and 危険 are more general (also accidents, illnesses), while 物騒 refers mainly to crime and unrest.

examples[].german: Let's settle it peacefully.
We settled the trouble with the neighbor amicably through discussion.
As a company, we would like to keep the disciplinary action as lenient as possible.
en.notes: 穏便 is a な-adjective meaning "amicable, without fuss", that is, without quarrel, scandal or legal action. It almost always appears adverbially as 穏便に with 済ませる, 解決する or 収める, or attributively in 穏便な方法 and 穏便な処分. Not to be confused with 穏やか, which describes a calm nature or mild weather. The word sounds somewhat formal and is typical when you want to settle a conflict discreetly.

examples[].german: It's a harmonious family.
The problem was settled amicably through discussion.
She left the company on good terms.
en.notes: 円満 ("round and full") describes relationships and solutions as "harmonious, peaceful, amicable". Typical: 円満な家庭, 夫婦円満, 円満に解決する "to settle amicably", 円満退社 "to leave the company on good terms". It refers to relationships without conflict; for a calm environment or a gentle character one more often says 穏やか.

examples[].german: Let's have a generous heart.
The teacher was lenient with the students who came late.
Thanks to the president's lenient decision, he did not have to quit the company.
en.notes: 寛大 means "magnanimous, forgiving, tolerant": generous in the sense of forgiving, not in the sense of being free with money (that would be 気前がいい). Typical: 寛大な心, 寛大な処置 "lenient treatment", 〜に寛大だ "to be lenient toward ...". In everyday speech people often say 心が広い; 寛大 sounds somewhat more formal.

examples[].german: He is a strict father.
This school has strict rules, and even dyeing your hair is prohibited.
Personal information is managed strictly.
en.notes: 厳格 ("strict, rigorous") describes people, rules and procedures that tolerate no exceptions: 厳格な父親, 厳格な規則, 厳格に管理する. It is more formal and objective than the everyday word 厳しい, which is also used for weather, situations or criticism (厳しい寒さ, not 厳格). The opposite is 寛大 "lenient".

examples[].german: He is an obedient child.
You had better just apologize honestly.
When you are praised, you can simply be happy.
en.notes: 素直 describes an open, unpretentious character: "obedient" for children (素直な子), but above all "honest about one's own feelings, not stubborn". The adverb 素直に is very common: 素直に謝る, 素直に喜ぶ, 素直になれない ("cannot bring oneself to be honest"). 正直 means "not lying", whereas 素直 means "without stubbornness and pretense". For straight hair one also says 素直な髪.

examples[].german: He's a stubborn old man.
My father is stubborn; once he decides something, he never changes his mind.
This detergent removes even stubborn stains cleanly.
en.notes: 頑固 ("stubborn, headstrong") describes people who do not change their opinion: 頑固な人, 頑固おやじ "stubborn old coot", 頑固に拒む. It can also be used appreciatively for loyalty to principles. Figuratively it means "persistent": 頑固な汚れ "stubborn stain", 頑固な肩こり. 強情 is similar but even more negative; 意地っ張り stresses defiance out of pride.

examples[].german: Oh, I forgot my wallet!
Ah, it's Mr. Tanaka. Hello!
en.notes: A short exclamation of surprise or of suddenly remembering something; the small っ represents the abrupt cutoff. Longer and calmer: ああ.

examples[].german: I lost my key and searched all over the house.
In spring, cherry blossoms bloom everywhere.
en.notes: Various places: あちこちに (in many places), あちこち探す (to search everywhere). More formal: あちらこちら.

examples[].german: A mother's love is very deep.
This song is about love for one's family.
I cooked for the children with a lot of love.
en.notes: 愛 is deep, often selfless love (母の愛, 家族への愛) and sounds rather solemn or literary in everyday life; in conversation one usually says 好き. 恋, by contrast, is romantic love. The verb "to love" is 愛する (its own card); あい written with the kanji 藍 means "indigo".

examples[].german: Unfortunately, my father is out right now.
Unfortunately, it rained on the day of the trip.
en.notes: Polite expression of regret when something is inconvenient: あいにく雨だった. As a reply: あいにく… (Sorry, but ...). Kanji 生憎 is rare.

examples[].german: I have a little free time this afternoon.
I called to ask whether the hotel had any vacancies.
en.notes: 空き refers to a free space, a vacant room or free time. 空きがある reports an available opening; at a hotel it is used to ask about a vacant room. 今日の午後は空きがある means one has free time in the afternoon. The dictionary variant 明き has the same reading あき; 秋 "autumn" and 飽き "weariness" are different words.

examples[].german: I made a small bag from the leftover fabric.
If you divide ten by three, the remainder is one.
en.notes: Noun from 余る (to be left over). The identically pronounced adverb あまり ("not very", used with negation) is a separate entry and is usually written in hiragana. In mathematics: 割り算の余り "remainder of a division".

examples[].german: I don't like natto very much.
Don't push yourself too hard.
en.notes: Colloquial form of あまり. With a negative: あんまり好きじゃない (not very much). Without a negative: "too much, excessively": あんまり食べると太るよ.

en.meaning: so much; such (about something distant or past)
examples[].german: Even though we practiced so much, we lost the match.
I had never had such a fun trip before.
en.notes: Series こんなに・そんなに・あんなに・どんなに. あんなに refers to something both people know or that lies in the past: あんなに練習したのに.

examples[].german: I uploaded my travel photos to the internet.
The file is too large, so I can't upload it.
en.notes: As a verb with する: 写真をアップロードする. Colloquially often shortened to アップする.

en.meaning: flaw, defect, weak point; fish scraps (head and bones left after filleting)
examples[].german: He is always just nitpicking at other people's faults.
I made miso soup from the sea bream scraps.
This plan has too many weak points to be carried out right away.
en.notes: Usually written in kana (あら, for fish often アラ); 粗 is the kanji spelling. Typical are 粗を探す and 粗探し "to nitpick, to look for faults" and 魚のアラ "head and bones after filleting", which are used for soup or braised dishes. Do not confuse with the interjection あら "oh!" (its own card, a different word) and the adjective 粗い "coarse".

examples[].german: His harsh words are a sign of his expectations.
This behavior may be an expression of anxiety.
en.notes: A visible expression of an inner attitude, mostly 〜の現れ (a sign of ...). Verb: 現れる.

examples[].german: One day, I found a strange bird in the forest.
Someone recommended this book to me.
en.notes: Prenominal word (連体詞), usually in kana: ある日 (one day), ある人 (someone). A typical opening of fairy tales and stories. Not to be confused with the verb ある (there is).

examples[].german: When I look at old photo albums, I remember my childhood.
My favorite singer's new album has come out.
en.notes: Photo album (卒業アルバム = the school's graduation album) and music album.

examples[].german: Please apply by email or by phone.
Perhaps what he says is right.
en.notes: Written-language "or" (everyday: または, か). As an adverb also "perhaps": あるいは本当かもしれない. Kanji 或いは is rare.

examples[].german: In the following equation, find the value of x.
This old painting is said to be worth over a million yen.
I recorded the values obtained in the experiment in my notebook.
en.notes: A literary word for "value" or "price"; in everyday speech people say 値段 (ねだん) for price and 価値 (かち) for value. Especially common in mathematics and science: xの値を求めなさい "find the value of x". In compounds 値 is usually read ね or ち (値上げ, 数値); related is the verb 値する "to be worth" (一読に値する).

en.meaning: overwhelming; overpowering (圧倒される: to be overwhelmed)
examples[].german: I was overwhelmed by the opposing team's intensity and couldn't play well.
The election ended in an overwhelming victory for the ruling party.
I was overwhelmed by the size of Mt. Fuji, seen up close for the first time.
en.notes: The noun form of the card 圧倒する; the noun alone is rare and mostly appears as 圧倒される "to be overwhelmed" (by impressions, strength) or as the adjective 圧倒的な/圧倒的に "overwhelming, by a landslide". Typical: 迫力に圧倒される, 圧倒的な勝利, 圧倒的多数.

examples[].german: The ball went outside the line and was out.
Being a whole hour late to the meeting is really unacceptable.
en.notes: In sports "out" (ball out of bounds, baseball out). Colloquially also "not okay, too late": それはアウトだ. Opposite: セーフ.

examples[].german: I replied on the spot.
His joke lightened the mood.
en.notes: On its own, mostly in set phrases: その場で (on the spot), 場を和ませる (to lighten the mood), 場に合う (to suit the occasion). In compounds as 〜場 (駐車場, 会場).

examples[].german: If you treat food carelessly, you'll be punished by the gods.
I told nothing but lies, so I got what I deserved.
Being this happy, I'm afraid I'll be punished.
en.notes: ばち is the punishment from gods or Buddhas for bad behavior and appears almost always in the phrase 罰が当たる "to receive one's just punishment", often also written バチが当たる. 罰当たり means "sacrilegious, impious". The card 罰/ばつ, by contrast, means a punishment imposed by humans (罰を受ける, 罰ゲーム); in sentences with 当たる the kanji is always read ばち.

examples[].german: I bought a new bag.
I put my wallet in the bag.
en.notes: General term for handbags, shoulder bags or shopping bags; compounds: ハンドバッグ, エコバッグ. A backpack is called リュック.

examples[].german: My daughter has been learning the violin since she was five.
He is good at playing the violin.
en.notes: Also written ヴァイオリン. "To play the violin": バイオリンを弾く（ひく）.

en.meaning: East Asian rainy season; rain of that season (reading ばいう)
examples[].german: During the rainy season, laundry is slow to dry.
Because the rainy season dragged on, the growth of the crops in the fields was delayed.
The rain of the rainy season quietly wet the window.
en.notes: ばいう is, besides つゆ, a reading for the East Asian rainy season. It appears e.g. in weather descriptions and in 梅雨前線（ばいうぜんせん, rainy-season front）. 梅雨の時期 denotes this period; 梅雨が長引く describes a rainy season lasting longer than expected. The word can also denote the rain during this season, e.g. in a description of a landscape. The vowels a, i and u remain three morae.

examples[].german: We transported our moving belongings in a van.
A delivery van is parked in front of the shop.
en.notes: バン is the loanword "van": a box van or small truck for goods and tools, often used for business (配達用のバン, 営業用のバン). For large trucks one says トラック (its own card), for station wagons and minivans rather ワゴン. Do not confuse with 晩 "evening" and 番 "number"; バン as the sound of a bang is a different word.

en.meaning: by chance (run into); with a thud; abruptly (stop)
examples[].german: I ran into an old friend at the station by chance.
Exhausted, I flopped onto the bed.
en.notes: Common: ばったり会う (to run into by chance). Also for suddenly falling over (ばったり倒れる) or stopping abruptly (客がばったり来なくなった).

examples[].german: The pants are too big, so I wear a belt.
The belt in the factory suddenly stopped.
en.notes: A belt on clothing (ベルトを締める), also a strap or conveyor belt in machines. Seat belt: シートベルト.

examples[].german: We watched the wedding video with the whole family.
I filmed my child's sports day on video.
en.notes: Today mostly a video recording; formerly also a videocassette or VCR. For clips on the Internet, 動画（どうが）is often used.

examples[].german: I'm taking the 3 p.m. flight to Osaka.
I will send you the documents by tomorrow's mail.
en.notes: A transport connection, especially a flight: 午後の便, 次の便, 直行便 (direct flight). Also a shipping method: 船便 (sea mail), 航空便 (air mail). Homophone: 瓶 (bottle).

examples[].german: I asked the waiter for water.
The hotel bellboy carried my luggage to the room.
en.notes: Today mainly waiter or hotel bellboy; "boy" is mostly found only in compounds (ボーイフレンド, カウボーイ).

examples[].german: We went boating on the pond.
The two of us rowed a boat to the island.
en.notes: A small boat, especially a rowboat: ボートをこぐ (to row). Large ships are called 船.

examples[].german: The dog came running with a wooden stick in its mouth.
After walking all day, my legs were stiff as sticks.
en.notes: Pole, stick: 木の棒, 鉄の棒. Also a straight line (棒を引く). Idiom: 足が棒になる (legs become stiff from walking).

en.meaning: un-, non- (prefix, e.g. 不器用, 不気味, 不用心)
examples[].german: My little brother is clumsy and has trouble even sewing on buttons.
An old hospital at night is somehow eerie.
Going out without locking up is careless.
en.notes: A negating prefix in the reading ぶ, only in a few fixed words: 不器用 "clumsy", 不気味 "eerie", 不用心 "careless, insecure", 不細工 "clumsy, ugly". Most words with 不, by contrast, are read ふ (不便, 不安, 不足); which reading applies must be learned word by word. The same syllable ぶ is also written 無 (無事, 無礼); see also 非〜（ひ） "non-".

en.meaning: one tenth of the next higher unit: one percent (3割5分 = 35%), 0.1 degree for body temperature (counter)
examples[].german: When I took my temperature, it was 37.5 degrees.
That player's batting average is .320.
I think the chances of winning or losing are fifty-fifty.
en.notes: 〜分（ぶ）denotes one tenth of the next higher unit: after 割 (10%) it is one percent, e.g. 打率三割二分 "batting average .320"; after 度 it is a tenth of a degree for a fever (三十七度五分). Fixed expressions are 五分五分 "fifty-fifty" and 九分九厘 "almost certain". Do not confuse with 〜分/ふん "minute" and 分/ぶん "share" (their own cards).

examples[].german: Despite the typhoon, everyone arrived home safely.
It has been a long time since I last contacted you; how are you?
The clerks in that shop are a bit unfriendly.
en.notes: A rarer reading of the negating prefix 無, only in fixed words such as 無事 "safe and sound", 無礼 "rude", 無愛想 "unfriendly", 無精 "lazy", 無難 "safe, unobjectionable" and ご無沙汰 "long silence (not keeping in touch)". The normal, productive reading is む (無理, 無料, 無意味); which applies must be learned word by word. Comparable to the prefixes 非〜 and 不〜, where 不 is also read ぶ in some words (不気味, 不用心).

en.meaning: manner, style (suffix, e.g. 話しぶり); for the first time in ... (e.g. 3年ぶり)
examples[].german: I returned to my hometown for the first time in ten years.
His calm way of speaking reassured everyone.
The department head was praising the new employee's work style.
en.notes: 〜ぶり has two main meanings: after verb stems and nouns "manner, way" (話しぶり, 仕事ぶり, 暮らしぶり), and after time expressions "for the first time in ..." (三年ぶり, 久しぶり - its own card). With に it becomes adverbial: 五年ぶりに会った. It is almost always written in kana; the kanji form 振り is rare and easily confused with ふり "pretending".

examples[].german: I write about my daily cooking on my blog.
I read about life in Japan on that blog.
en.notes: "To write a blog": ブログを書く. A post is called 記事（きじ）.

en.meaning: to hit, to strike (someone); to give (a speech)
examples[].german: My little brother suddenly hit me on the head.
No matter how angry you are, you must not hit a child.
The department head gave a speech for a whole hour at the meeting.
en.notes: Colloquial "to hit (someone)", typical in the speech of children and parents (ぶたないで!). Mostly written in kana, because 打つ is normally read うつ (its own card, much broader in meaning: to hit, type, inject, etc.). The more neutral word for "to hit, to knock" is たたく. Ironically, 演説をぶつ means "to hold forth with a big speech".

en.meaning: tea, tea plant; brown (short for 茶色)
examples[].german: Shizuoka is famous as a tea-growing region.
A person in a brown coat was waiting in front of the station.
In Kyoto, I experienced a tea ceremony for the first time.
en.notes: Bare form of お茶 (vocab-n5:119). On its own, 茶 sounds written or terse; in conversation one says お茶. Common in compounds and fixed expressions: 茶色 "brown", 紅茶 "black tea", 茶の湯 "tea ceremony", 茶畑 "tea plantation". As a short form, 茶 also stands for the color brown, e.g. 茶のコート "brown coat".

examples[].german: The focus of this research is children's sleep time.
Focusing on young customers led to the shop's success.
His points of focus are always different from other people's and interesting.
en.notes: 着目 means to direct one's attention deliberately to a particular point, often as the starting point of an analysis: 着目点 "point of focus", 〜への着目. The verb form is on the card 着目する (〜に着目する). Unlike 注目, which also refers to the attention of many people (注目を集める), 着目 is active and analytical and appears mainly in reports and specialist texts.

examples[].german: I got a call from my mother during the meeting.
Please turn down the ringtone.
en.notes: Display on a mobile phone: 着信あり (call received). Ringtone: 着信音. Opposite: 発信 (outgoing call, sending).

examples[].german: My grandfather was born and raised in this land.
Dead leaves danced in the wind and quietly fell to the ground.
en.notes: Literary word for "earth, ground" and "place": 天と地 (heaven and earth), 約束の地 (the promised land). Very common in compounds: 土地, 地下, 地元, 目的地.

examples[].german: The light is off, so he must already be asleep.
After practicing that much, he is sure to pass.
en.notes: After a sentence, mostly as ～に違いない: the speaker's strong conviction. More literary than きっと～だろう. Polite: 違いありません.

examples[].german: The accumulation of fatigue caused the accident.
His years of accumulated experience are his greatest strength.
This system automatically accumulates and analyzes data.
en.notes: 蓄積 is the gradual accumulation of something over a longer period, often with の: 疲労の蓄積 "accumulated exhaustion", 知識の蓄積, データの蓄積. The verb form "to accumulate" is on the card 蓄積する. For money, people say 貯金 or 貯蓄 instead; 蓄積 sounds matter-of-fact and suits science, technology and economics.

examples[].german: Dolphins are said to be highly intelligent animals.
This test measures children's intelligence.
en.notes: Mental capacity, often thought of as measurable: 知能指数 (IQ), 人工知能 (artificial intelligence). For everyday "smart", 頭がいい is more usual.

examples[].german: According to the Meteorological Agency, there will be heavy rain tomorrow.
My father works at the prefectural office.
The Agency for Cultural Affairs focuses on preserving old buildings.
en.notes: 庁 mostly appears as a suffix in names of government agencies: 気象庁 "Meteorological Agency", 警察庁, 都庁 and 県庁 "prefectural government" (all with their own cards), and also 文化庁. A 庁 is often a subordinate agency, whereas 省 is a ministry; for municipal administration people say 役所 or 役場. On its own, 庁 appears almost only in newspaper language (同庁 "the said agency", 庁内). Homophones such as 蝶 "butterfly" and 兆 "trillion" are different words.

examples[].german: After climbing for three hours, we finally reached the summit.
The view from the summit was wonderful.
en.notes: The summit of a mountain; figuratively also the highest level (頂上会談 = summit meeting). Similar: 山頂.

en.meaning: among, out of; during; in the middle of (suffix)
examples[].german: Three out of ten people were absent.
During the summer vacation, I went to the library every day.
This road is closed because of ongoing construction.
en.notes: ちゅう is used here as a suffix. 十人中 means "out of ten people", 夏休み中 "during the summer vacation" and 工事中 "under construction / while construction work is going on". The suffix attaches directly to the noun. It can indicate an ongoing process; 一日中（いちにちじゅう）, on the other hand, emphasizes the whole day.

examples[].german: Difficult words come with a note.
For details, see the note at the bottom of the page.
en.notes: An explanatory note in books and texts: 注を付ける, ※注. More detailed: 注釈, 脚注 (footnote).

examples[].german: The new smartphone is drawing attention from around the world.
She is the most closely watched newcomer singer this year.
Everyone, may I have your attention, please!
en.notes: Noun for 注目する (vocab-n3:279). Typical combinations: 注目を集める "to attract attention", 注目を浴びる "to be in the spotlight", 注目の的 "center of attention" and, attributively, 注目の新人 "closely watched newcomer". Unlike 注意 "caution, heed (of danger)", 注目 means looking with interest.

examples[].german: Parking is prohibited here.
I parked the car in front of the shop.
en.notes: Leaving a vehicle standing, as a verb 駐車する: 駐車禁止 (no parking), 駐車場 (parking lot). Similar sounding: 注射 (injection).

examples[].german: The plan was perfect. But it did not work out.
He is still young. But he has plenty of experience.
en.notes: A written-language, somewhat harsh conjunction (newspapers, novels, male speech). Polite: ですが; everyday: でも, けど.

en.meaning: big, large size; large- (prefix, e.g. 大問題, 大成功)
examples[].german: Which coffee size would you like, large or small?
Yesterday's party was a great success.
Large can serve as small, so let's buy the big box.
en.notes: Counterpart of 中 "medium" (vocab-n5:correction:chu-medium) and 小 "small": sizes are given as 大・中・小. As a prefix, だい- intensifies mainly Sino-Japanese nouns: 大問題 "big problem", 大成功 "great success", 大事件 "major incident". Before native Japanese words it is usually おお- (大雨, 大きい). Homophones: 台 "stand", 〜代 "fee", 題 "title".

en.meaning: ordinal prefix: the n-th (prefix, e.g. 第一, 第三章)
examples[].german: World War II ended in 1945.
Please read Chapter 3 of the textbook before class.
The 10th tournament will be held in Osaka.
en.notes: A prefix placed before a number that turns it into an ordinal: 第一回, 第二次世界大戦, 第三章.
