examples[].german: That comes to 3,000 yen in total.
How much does it come to altogether?
Please add up the test scores.
en.notes: 合計 is the total sum: 合計で三千円 "3,000 yen in total", 合計金額. As a する-verb it is transitive: 点数を合計する "to add up the points". In conversation one often simply says 全部で; on receipts it appears as 合計 or, short, 計, and the subtotal is 小計.

examples[].german: He calculates quickly.
I made a mistake in the calculation.
Let's make a plan that also takes rainy days into account.
en.notes: 計算 is calculating or a calculation: 計算が速い／得意, 計算を間違える "to miscalculate", 計算ミス; as a する-verb it is transitive (費用を計算する). Figuratively it means "taking into account, calculation": 計算に入れる "to factor in", 計算通り "as planned", 計算高い "calculating". A pocket calculator is usually called 電卓.

examples[].german: My father is a former soldier.
My grandfather was a soldier.
Members of the Self-Defense Forces are called "Jieikan", not "soldiers".
en.notes: 軍人 is a member of the armed forces, whether officer or soldier, usually as an occupation; 元軍人 "former soldier". Ordinary soldiers are called 兵士 or 兵隊. Members of the Japanese Self-Defense Forces (自衛隊) are officially called not 軍人 but 自衛官.

examples[].german: I heard that my grandfather was a navy man.
A navy ship entered the harbor.
There is a US Navy base near this town.
en.notes: 海軍 is a noun: "navy, naval forces"; related are 陸軍 "army" and 空軍 "air force". One says 海軍に入る, 海軍の基地, アメリカ海軍. Japan itself officially has no 海軍, but the 海上自衛隊 "Maritime Self-Defense Force"; 海軍 therefore appears mainly for foreign armed forces and in history.

examples[].german: Please! Help me!
I have a favor to ask.
I couldn't turn down my friend's request.
en.notes: お願い is the polite form of 願い "wish, request": お願いがあります "I have a favor to ask", お願いを聞く "to grant a request", お願いを断る "to turn down". As a verb: お願いする (humble, X を Y にお願いする), and in the set phrase お願いします "please". On its own, as an exclamation, お願い！ is a casual, urgent plea among close friends.

examples[].german: This restaurant seems to have an all-you-can-drink option.
Let's go with the all-you-can-drink plan.
The all-you-can-drink option is limited to two hours.
en.notes: 飲み放題 means "drink as much as you want" for a fixed price, typical in izakaya and at company parties, usually with a time limit (2時間飲み放題). One says 飲み放題がある, 飲み放題付きのコース, 飲み放題にする. The suffix ～放題 "as much as one likes" also appears in 食べ放題 and 言いたい放題 "saying whatever one wants".

examples[].german: Please give an example.
I'll explain using examples.
en.notes: 例 means "example" here. 例を挙げる is the fixed phrase for "to give / cite an example"; 例を使う means "to use an example". The reading is れい, written rei. The other dictionary meanings, "precedent" or "custom", are not used in these sentences.

examples[].german: Breakfast at this hotel is all-you-can-eat.
That restaurant is popular for its all-you-can-eat deal.
Just because it's all-you-can-eat, don't eat too much!
en.notes: 食べ放題 is an offer where you can eat as much as you like for a fixed price, often with a time limit (90分食べ放題) and for particular dishes: 焼肉食べ放題, ケーキ食べ放題. A buffet is also called バイキング in Japan. As in 飲み放題, ～放題 means "as much as one likes".

examples[].german: That man is a murderer.
Murder cannot be justified.
In the movie, a woman screamed, "Murderer!"
en.notes: 人殺し is the native Japanese word for "murder" and "murderer" and sounds direct and emotional, for example as an accusation or a scream 「人殺し！」. In news and legal language, 殺人 "murder" (殺人事件) and 殺人犯 or 殺人者 "murderer" are used. The underlying verb is 殺す "to kill".

examples[].german: This murderer is a famous serial killer.
The murderer was arrested.
In that novel, you don't find out who the murderer is until the end.
en.notes: 殺人者 is a formal, rather literary word for "murderer". In news and criminal law, 殺人犯 (convicted or wanted murderer) or 犯人 "culprit" is heard more often; 殺人 alone is the act (殺人事件 "murder case"). Colloquially and emotionally, 人殺し is used.

examples[].german: This rubber band is very durable.
I bundled the documents together with a rubber band.
Excuse me, could I have a rubber band?
en.notes: 輪ゴム is a rubber band: 輪 "ring" plus ゴム "rubber" (from Dutch). Typical are 輪ゴムで留める "to fasten with a rubber band" and 輪ゴムで束ねる "to bundle with a rubber band"; it is usually counted with 本 or 個. A hair tie, by contrast, is a ヘアゴム, and an eraser is a 消しゴム.

examples[].german: Where will you practice?
I practice the piano every day.
en.notes: 練習する means to practice a skill through repetition. What is practiced can be named with を: ピアノを練習する. どこで asks about the place; the first example can refer to a planned practice location. 毎日練習しています, by contrast, describes a regular habit. The forms 練習します, 練習した and 練習して show how する changes; 練習 alone is the noun "practice".

examples[].german: An unusual incident occurred that year.
If an incident occurs, please contact us immediately.
Old records describe the unusual events of that year.
en.notes: 変事 is a rare, literary word for an unusual, disturbing event or misfortune, for example in chronicles or formal texts. Caution: it sounds exactly like the very common 返事 "reply". In everyday speech one says 事件, 事故, 異変 or 大変なこと instead.

examples[].german: Sorry, the data is syncing right now, so wait a moment.
The data is syncing.
"Syncing" is displayed on the phone screen.
en.notes: 同期中 is made up of 同期 "synchronization" and the suffix ～中（ちゅう）"in progress", like 会議中 or 電話中; it is seen mostly as a status display on phones and computers (同期中です, 同期中…). Note: 同期 also means "same year group" (会社の同期 "colleague who joined the company in the same year"). The verb is 同期する "to synchronize".

examples[].german: The costs rise in proportion to that.
Results come in proportion to effort.
In math class I learned about direct and inverse proportion.
en.notes: 比例 is proportionality; as an intransitive する-verb it takes に: X に比例する "to be proportional to X", adverbially X に比例して "in proportion to X". The opposite is 反比例 "inversely proportional". 割合 and 比率, on the other hand, denote a concrete ratio or share. In politics, 比例 is short for 比例代表 "proportional representation".

en.meaning: to be solved; to come undone
examples[].german: If Maria were here, she'd solve a math problem like this in five seconds. It's a piece of cake for her.
I was able to solve this problem.
Your shoelace is untied.
en.notes: 解ける is intransitive: a problem "gets solved" or "can be solved" (問題が解ける); the transitive counterpart is 解く (問題を解く). Since the potential form of 解く is also 解ける, 問題が解けた covers both readings: "I was able to solve the problem". Other meanings: ひもが解ける "to come loose, to come undone", 誤解が解ける "a misunderstanding gets cleared up". Do not confuse it with 溶ける "to melt, to dissolve".

examples[].german: This dish is very delicious.
Thank you for cooking me a delicious meal.
en.notes: 美味しい is an i-adjective for good taste: 美味しくない, 美味しかった. It comes directly before a noun: 美味しい料理. It is often written in hiragana as おいしい. 作ってくれてありがとう thanks someone for having cooked for you. In oishii there is no gap inside the word; desu stays separate.

en.meaning: at least; or more; the above; that's all
examples[].german: That concludes it.
It is aimed at people aged 18 and over.
Please pay attention to the points above.
en.notes: 以上 after a number includes that number: 十八歳以上 means "from age 18", that is, including exactly 18. Here it is a nominal postposition. As a closing formula, 以上で終わります means "That concludes it". "More than 18" without including the limit would be wrong in this numerical use. Before a noun, 以上の also refers to the points mentioned earlier.

examples[].german: Understood. I'll do it right away.
"We meet at nine tomorrow, OK?" "Got it!"
Let's start after obtaining the president's approval.
en.notes: 了解 means "understanding, consent"; 了解しました is the usual acknowledgment "Understood, will do". Toward superiors and customers, 承知しました or かしこまりました is considered more polite, as 了解 seems too casual to some. Among friends, 了解！ is enough (in chats even りょ). Formal usage: 了解を得る "to obtain approval".

examples[].german: It's better to make the foundation as sturdy as possible.
This desk is built sturdily.
My father has a robust body and rarely catches a cold.
en.notes: 頑丈 is a な-adjective for massive, solid things and strong bodies: 頑丈な箱, 頑丈な体, 頑丈にできている "solidly built". 丈夫 also means "durable", but is also used for health (体が丈夫) and sounds less hefty; 頑丈 emphasizes heavy, stable construction. Opposite: 壊れやすい "fragile".

en.meaning: to look over again; to prove someone wrong
examples[].german: It's a good idea to get into the habit of going over your test again at the end.
I checked the report once more.
Someday I want to show up the people who looked down on me.
en.notes: 見返す takes を and mostly means "to look through once more": to review notes, photos or an exam before handing it in. Unlike 見直す, which tends to mean "to review and improve" or "to reassess", 見返す is simply looking at it again. A second common meaning is "to show someone": a person who was underestimated wants to prove the others wrong through success, typically as 見返してやる. It can also mean "to look back, to stare back" (相手の顔を見返す).

en.meaning: to fire; to release; to emit
examples[].german: I heard that this player hits some really big home runs.
I shot the arrow.
In the dark room, the clock was giving off a blue light.
en.notes: 放つ is rather elevated and literary; it appears in sports reports, news and literature: 矢を放つ "to shoot an arrow", ホームランを放つ "to hit a home run", 光を放つ "to emit light", 火を放つ "to set fire". In everyday speech, 放す is usually used for "to release" (魚を川に放す) and 撃つ for "to shoot". The passive 放たれる is also common (矢が放たれた).

examples[].german: Oh no! The lunch break starts in five minutes.
I take a walk during the lunch break.
At this company the lunch break is from twelve to one.
en.notes: 昼休み is the lunch break at school, office or factory. As a time expression it takes に (昼休みに散歩する) or から/まで for the period. You say 昼休みを取る "to take a lunch break" and 昼休み中 "during the lunch break". Distinguish it from 昼ご飯 or, colloquially, お昼 (the lunch meal itself) and from 休憩, any short break.

examples[].german: This 24-hour supermarket opened last year.
I went to Japan last year.
Thank you very much for all your support over the past year.
en.notes: 昨年 is the formal equivalent of 去年 "last year". It appears in business letters, news, speeches and especially in New Year greetings (昨年は大変お世話になりました). In ordinary conversation people almost always say 去年. Like other time words, it is used adverbially without a particle (昨年オープンした) or with の before a noun (昨年の夏).

en.meaning: to take off; to remove; to miss
examples[].german: Wow, you look like a different person without your mask.
I took off my glasses.
Mr. Tanaka is away from his desk at the moment.
en.notes: 外す is transitive (X を外す); the intransitive partner is 外れる (ボタンが外れる, 予報が外れる). It means "to take off, to detach" things that are fastened: メガネ・マスク・時計・ボタンを外す. Clothes and shoes, on the other hand, are taken off with 脱ぐ. Other common uses: 席を外す "to be away from one's seat for a moment" (typical on the phone in an office), 的を外す "to miss the target", メンバーから外す "to drop from the team".

examples[].german: What? That's news to me.
It's news to me that he was married.
Huh, there's a test next week? That's the first I've heard of it.
en.notes: 初耳 means "to hear something for the first time" and almost always stands as a predicate: それは初耳です / 初耳だ is the typical surprised reaction to a piece of news. Often a sentence with なんて or とは precedes: 彼が結婚していたなんて初耳だ. It refers to information, not a sound; for music or noises, 初めて聞く is used. The word is used both colloquially and politely.

examples[].german: I went horseback riding this morning.
On my days off I enjoy horseback riding.
I tried horseback riding for the first time at a ranch in Hokkaido.
en.notes: 乗馬 means horseback riding as a sport or hobby: 乗馬をする / 乗馬する, 乗馬クラブ, 乗馬体験. The horse itself does not take を; to say "to get on a horse, to ride a horse", use 馬に乗る. 乗馬 therefore sounds somewhat matter-of-fact and suits leisure offerings, hobbies and courses. More rarely it also refers to the riding horse itself.

examples[].german: This is an onomatopoeia that expresses an impression of softness.
Japanese has a lot of onomatopoeia.
When you read manga, you come across many onomatopoeic expressions.
en.notes: オノマトペ comes from French onomatopée and in Japanese covers two groups: 擬音語, which imitate actual sounds (ワンワン, ドンドン), and 擬態語, which describe states or feelings (キラキラ, ふわふわ, イライラ). Japanese has a great many of them; they are everywhere in manga, advertising and everyday speech. They mostly appear with と or する as an adverb or verb (ふわふわする).

en.meaning: at most; up to and including; the following
examples[].german: Free for children ten years old and under.
I'm looking for products costing 500 yen or less.
Please answer the following questions.
en.notes: 以下 after a number includes the limit: 十歳以下 also covers ten-year-olds; 五百円以下 means "500 yen at most". It is a nominal suffix-like word placed after the noun. The dictionary meaning "the following" is a different usage. In these examples, "under ten / under 500" as an exclusive limit would be wrong. 以下の質問, on the other hand, refers to the questions that follow.

examples[].german: We're going to play poker, so go buy some playing cards!
Let's play cards.
On the night of the school trip, we all played cards together.
en.notes: トランプ in Japanese refers to Western playing cards or the card deck as a whole, not a particular game. "To play cards" is トランプをする or トランプで遊ぶ; a single card is called カード. Well-known games are ババ抜き and 七並べ. Do not confuse it with かるた, the traditional Japanese cards.

en.meaning: to go down; to descend; to be granted
examples[].german: I'm scared of going down the ladder.
Let's go down the mountain.
My visa has finally been granted.
en.notes: 下りる is intransitive; the path or place one goes down takes を (階段を下りる, 山を下りる). For getting off vehicles, 降りる is usually written (電車を降りる); 下りる suits stairs, mountains and ladders, as well as 幕が下りる "the curtain falls" and 許可・ビザが下りる "is granted". The transitive partner is 下ろす (荷物を下ろす). Do not confuse with 下がる (to fall, drop) and 下る (くだる, e.g. to go down a river).

en.meaning: to ask; to question; to hold accountable
examples[].german: It is a theme that questions the way society and people should be.
I was held responsible.
Anyone can take part, regardless of age.
en.notes: 問う is elevated and literary; in everyday speech one asks with 聞く or 尋ねる. Typical are set patterns: 責任を問う "to hold accountable" (passive 責任を問われる), ～を問わず "regardless of, no matter whether" (年齢を問わず) and ～を問う "to call into question, to raise as an issue" in media and criticism. Note: the te-form is 問うて, not 問って.

examples[].german: He has the generosity of spirit to accept everything.
We have to accept reality.
This university takes in many international students every year.
en.notes: 受け入れる is transitive (X を受け入れる) and has two main meanings: "to accept" (a proposal, request, criticism, reality) and "to take in" people (refugees, exchange students, patients). Distinguish it from 受け取る (to receive an object), 受ける (to take an exam, to receive a call) and 認める (to recognize, to admit). The noun is 受け入れ; in official documents also written 受入れ.

examples[].german: Could you buy me a bottle of green tea at the convenience store?
I drink green tea every morning.
Which would you like, green tea or black tea?
en.notes: 緑茶 is the general term for green tea. In daily life, Japanese people usually just say お茶, since that already means green tea; 緑茶 is used to distinguish it from 紅茶 (black tea) or ウーロン茶, and on labels and menus. Well-known varieties are 煎茶, ほうじ茶 and 抹茶.

en.meaning: to lick; to suck; to underestimate
examples[].german: Babies lick everything.
I licked an ice cream.
I was taking that team lightly, and we lost.
en.notes: 舐める is transitive (X を舐める) and first means "to lick": アイスを舐める, 犬が手を舐める; with candy also "to suck" (飴を舐める). Very common is the figurative meaning "to underestimate, not take seriously": 相手をなめる, なめるな! "Don't underestimate me!". In this meaning the word is almost always written in kana; the kanji variant 嘗める is rare, and in general なめる is more common than 舐める.

examples[].german: This is the doctor in charge of the outpatient department.
There are many outpatients.
"Pan" (bread) is a loanword.
en.notes: 外来 has two areas: in a hospital it means "outpatient, outpatient department" (外来の患者, 外来受付, 外来で診てもらう) as opposed to 入院 "inpatient". As a prefix it means "introduced from outside or from abroad": 外来語 "loanword" (usually in katakana), 外来種 "invasive species". It is not a true adjective, but is used with の or as part of a compound.

examples[].german: The owner of this hotel is unknown.
The cause is unknown.
If there is anything unclear, please ask at any time.
en.notes: 不明 means "unknown, unclear" and sounds objective to formal; you read it in news and forms: 原因不明 "cause unknown", 行方不明 "missing", 身元不明 "unidentified". As a predicate it is 不明だ/です, before a noun 不明な (不明な点があれば…). Colloquially, 意味不明 means "makes no sense". In conversation people otherwise prefer 分からない.

examples[].german: I'm in the dentist's waiting room right now.
I'm waiting in the hospital waiting room.
The train was delayed by snow, so I rested in the station waiting room.
en.notes: 待合室 is the waiting room at a doctor's office, hospital, train station or airport. You are 待合室にいる or wait 待合室で. Note the spelling without ち: 待合室, although the verbal noun 待ち合わせ "appointment, meeting place" is written with it. For hotels people say ロビー, for performers or speakers 控え室.

examples[].german: I work except on Sundays.
I can also speak languages other than Japanese.
en.notes: 以外 follows the excluded item: 日曜日以外 means "except on Sundays". With の it connects to a noun: 日本語以外の言語, "languages other than Japanese". Depending on the statement, it can mean "except / apart from" or "in addition to". It is a nominal postposed word and not a sentence particle.

examples[].german: Wow, you scared me! Why are you wearing a mask?
I danced wearing a mask.
He was wearing a mask of kindness.
en.notes: 仮面 is a mask that covers the face, for example in a performance. 仮面をつける or かぶる means to put it on or wear it. The word can also figuratively mean a pretended attitude: 親切の仮面 is a mask of kindness. An ordinary medical face mask, on the other hand, is called マスク.

examples[].german: The high school I attended was a very conservative school.
He has a conservative way of thinking.
My father is conservative and hardly ever uses new things.
en.notes: 保守的 is a な-adjective: 保守的な人, 保守的な考え方, 彼は保守的だ. It describes people, institutions or attitudes that stick to what is proven and are cautious about the new. Opposites are 革新的 and 進歩的. The base word 保守 appears in politics (保守派, 保守政党) and in technology also means "maintenance" (システムの保守).

examples[].german: That's quite a classic gag.
It's a classic method, but it is still widely used today.
This movie is a classic love story.
en.notes: 古典的 is a な-adjective and means "classical, traditional, time-tested": 古典的な方法, 古典的なラブストーリー. It often also sounds ironic, like "old-fashioned, hackneyed", for example with 古典的なギャグ or 古典的な手口 "an ancient trick". Classical music is called クラシック(音楽), not 古典的な音楽. The base word 古典 denotes the classics of literature (古典文学).

examples[].german: This word appears in Buddhist scriptures.
I'm studying Buddhist scriptures.
Old Buddhist scriptures are carefully preserved in this temple.
en.notes: 仏典 is the collective term for Buddhist scriptures and sounds technical or literary. The individual sutras that are recited are called お経 in everyday speech. The kanji 典 means "scripture, work" and is also in 辞典, 字典, 事典 and 古典; 仏 stands for Buddha or Buddhism. Typical combinations are 仏典を読む and 仏典に出てくる.

examples[].german: This kanji dictionary contains over 50,000 kanji.
I looked up the kanji in a kanji dictionary.
The calligraphy teacher was checking the shape of the character in an old kanji dictionary.
en.notes: 字典 is a character dictionary that explains individual kanji with their readings, meanings and forms. There are three homophonous じてん: 辞典 (dictionary of words), 字典 (of written characters) and 事典 (encyclopedia of things). To tell them apart, people say, half-jokingly and practically, もじてん, ことばてん and ことてん. In everyday speech one usually just says 辞書 or 漢字辞典; 字典 is more of a technical or title word.

examples[].german: What kind of encyclopedia is that?
I looked it up in the encyclopedia.
This animal encyclopedia has a lot of photos.
en.notes: 事典 is a subject dictionary or encyclopedia that explains things and matters, not words. It mostly appears in compounds: 百科事典 "encyclopedia", 動物事典, 歴史事典. To be distinguished from it are 辞典 or 辞書 (dictionary) and 字典 (character dictionary); since all are read じてん, ことてん is also said for clarity.

examples[].german: We should save our strength for the adventure starting tomorrow.
I like adventure stories.
Quitting my current job and opening a shop seems like quite a gamble to me.
en.notes: 冒険 is an adventure: 冒険に出る "to set out on an adventure", 冒険する, 冒険物語, 冒険家 "adventurer". Figuratively it also refers to a risky undertaking: それはちょっと冒険だ "that's quite a gamble". Unlike 危険 ("danger"), 冒険 emphasizes knowingly taking a risk. For games and films, アドベンチャー is also common.

examples[].german: These jeans are brand new.
I bought a brand-new smartphone.
This bicycle is secondhand, but as good as new.
en.notes: 新品 means a new, unused article, i.e. new goods as opposed to 中古 (secondhand). It is used as a noun (これは新品です) or with の before a noun (新品の靴). For things that are simply "new" in the sense of "newly released" or "different from before", 新しい is used. 新品同様 "like new, as good as new" is common for secondhand goods.

examples[].german: There was only one survivor.
A survivor has been found.
To survive in the desert, water is the most important thing.
en.notes: 生存 is an objective, rather formal word for "survival, being alive" and appears mainly in news, science and reports. Very common are compounds such as 生存者 "survivors", 生存率 "survival rate" and 生存確認 "confirmation of being alive". As a する-verb it is intransitive: 生存する. In everyday speech people more often say 生きる, 生き残る or 助かる.

examples[].german: I went to Koichi's house, but he wasn't in.
I won't be home today.
Could you take care of the cat while I'm away?
en.notes: 留守 means that someone is not at home (or not at the office). Typical patterns: 留守だ "is not in", 家を留守にする "to leave the house empty, to be away", 留守の間 / 留守中 "during one's absence". Related are 留守番 "house-sitting", 留守番電話 or 留守電 "answering machine" and 居留守を使う "to pretend not to be home". For absence from school or work, 欠席 or 休み is used instead.

examples[].german: Is this seat free?
A window seat, please.
en.notes: 席 means a seat, for example on a train, in a restaurant or in a class. 席が空いている means "a seat is free". For a window seat you say 窓側の席. It refers to the usable place, not necessarily the chair as an object; for that, 椅子 fits.

examples[].german: There is always only one truth.
I want to know the truth.
What he said was not the truth.
en.notes: 真実 is "the truth", that is, how something really is, and sounds weightier than the everyday 本当 (本当のこと). It is often used with を: 真実を知る, 真実を話す, 真実を明らかにする. 事実, on the other hand, is an objectively verifiable fact, while 真実 means the truth behind things. Register: rather literary, common in crime stories and news.

examples[].german: That's outside my field of expertise.
His specialty is physics.
What are you majoring in at university?
en.notes: 専門 is a person's field of specialization: 私の専門は経済です, ～を専門にする, 専門外 "not my field". There are many compounds: 専門家 "expert", 専門学校 "vocational school", 専門用語 "technical term". As a suffix, ～専門 means "exclusively for" (女性専門のジム). Specifically for a university major there is also 専攻.

examples[].german: At that time, I learned only that the government would not help its citizens.
The government announced a new policy.
The government says it will raise taxes from next year.
en.notes: 政府 is the government as the state apparatus: 日本政府, 政府の発表, 政府が決める. To be distinguished from it are 政治 "politics", 内閣 "cabinet" and 首相 "prime minister". For local governments, one does not say 政府 but 自治体 or 市役所. Typical combinations: 政府が発表する, 政府に求める, 政府の方針.

examples[].german: The Tokyo dialect is almost the same as the standard language.
A friend from Kansai told me that the Tokyo dialect sounds cold.
In rakugo, old Tokyo speech is often used.
en.notes: 東京弁 is the Tokyo speech. Because today's 標準語 or 共通語 is based on the language of Tokyo, many Tokyoites do not perceive their speech as a dialect at all; people from other regions, especially Kansai, are the ones who often say 東京弁. In a narrower sense, it also means the old Tokyo Japanese of the old town (下町), as heard in rakugo. Formed with the suffix ～弁, like 大阪弁 or 関西弁.

en.meaning: dialect (～弁); speech, eloquence (弁が立つ: to be eloquent)
examples[].german: What dialect is that?
My grandmother still speaks in the Hiroshima dialect.
My older brother is so eloquent that I always lose when we argue.
en.notes: ～弁 attaches as a suffix to place or region names and denotes their dialect: 関西弁, 大阪弁, 東北弁, 博多弁. With 何弁？ one asks which dialect something is; in a factual or scholarly register, 方言 is used. As a word in its own right, 弁 means "speech, eloquence", above all in the phrase 弁が立つ "to be eloquent, to speak well". The kanji 弁 also appears in quite different words such as 弁当 or 弁護士.

examples[].german: Sorry, I'm in a bit of a hurry, so I'm going ahead!
We have no time, so let's hurry.
Eating in a hurry isn't good for your body.
en.notes: 急ぐ means "to hurry, to be in a hurry" and is mostly intransitive: 駅へ急ぐ, and with a route also 道を急ぐ. Transitively it can mean "to speed something up" (仕事を急ぐ). Very common are 急いで＋verb "to do something quickly, in a rush" and 急いでいる "to be in a hurry". Unlike 慌てる (to get flustered, lose one's head), 急ぐ is neutral. Proverb: 急がば回れ "more haste, less speed".

examples[].german: I was a high school student when my father died suddenly.
I was shocked by the news of the sudden death.
A famous singer died suddenly at the age of forty.
en.notes: 急死 is a sudden, unexpected death, for example from heart failure or illness, and as a する-verb it is intransitive: 急死する. The word is matter-of-fact and typical of news and reports. For accidents one rather speaks of 事故死. When talking about one's own relatives in conversation, 急に亡くなりました sounds more considerate.

en.meaning: express train; to rush to (a place)
examples[].german: The express to Kyoto seems to leave from platform three.
I got on an express train.
Hearing the report of the accident, the police rushed to the scene.
en.notes: 急行 is above all the express train: it stops only at the more important stations. The usual ranking is 普通 or 各駅停車 < 快速 < 急行 < 特急; on private railways the 急行 usually costs no extra fare. As a する-verb, 急行する means "to rush (to a place)" and is typical of news reports: 現場に急行する. Common phrases are 急行に乗る and ～行きの急行.

examples[].german: It seems it will take about six months to heal completely.
It's an injury that takes three months to heal.
I'll sit out soccer until the injury has fully healed.
en.notes: 全治 means "complete recovery" and appears mainly in medical statements and news: 全治三か月のけが "an injury expected to take three months to heal". The time span after 全治 thus gives the expected time until recovery. As a する-verb it is intransitive: けがが全治する. In everyday speech one rather says 治る or 完治する.

examples[].german: That disease is still considered incurable at present.
He was diagnosed with an incurable disease.
As medicine advances, incurable diseases are gradually decreasing.
en.notes: 不治 means "incurability" and occurs practically only in the set phrase 不治の病 "incurable disease". The word is elevated or literary; in conversation one rather says 治らない病気. Besides ふじ, the reading ふち is also possible, but rarer. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 富士 (Mt. Fuji).

examples[].german: I plant flowers in the garden.
There is a bird in the tree in the garden.
en.notes: 庭 is a garden or yard at a house. 庭で names it as the place of an activity, 庭に as the place where something exists. With の you connect the word to an object in the garden: 庭の木. The two vowels in にわ are short.

examples[].german: My great-grandmother was born in the Meiji era.
Japan changed greatly in the Meiji period.
This building was built in the 40th year of Meiji.
en.notes: 明治 is the Meiji era (1868-1912), in which Japan modernized greatly. Japanese eras (元号) are also used to count years: 明治四十年, 明治生まれ, 明治時代. The order of the modern eras is 明治 → 大正 → 昭和 → 平成 → 令和. An important term is 明治維新 "Meiji Restoration"; 明治 is also a well-known company name (chocolate, dairy products).

en.meaning: to take a shower; to be showered with; to be exposed to
examples[].german: Our dog likes being showered.
I take a shower in the morning.
The singer was showered with applause from the audience.
en.notes: With 浴びる, the thing that hits the body takes を: シャワーを浴びる (to take a shower), 日光を浴びる (to get sunlight). Figurative uses are also common: 拍手を浴びる (to be showered with applause) and 批判を浴びる (to draw criticism). It is a transitive ichidan verb: 浴びます・浴びて・浴びない. For a bath in a bathtub, you usually say お風呂に入る.

examples[].german: I want to climb onto Totoro's big belly and sunbathe.
I sunbathed in the park.
The cat is sunbathing by the window.
en.notes: 日光浴 means "sunbath, to sunbathe" and is used with をする or as a する-verb: 日光浴(を)する. It also fits animals (猫が日光浴をしている). To be distinguished from 日焼け "suntan, sunburn". 浴 means "to bathe", as in 森林浴 "forest bathing" and 海水浴 "sea bathing".

examples[].german: We decided on a whim to take the limited express.
I'm going to Osaka by limited express.
To take the limited express, you need a limited express ticket.
en.notes: 特急 is the short form of 特別急行 and refers to the fastest train below the Shinkansen. On JR you need a 特急券 (limited express ticket) in addition to your fare; on some private railways the 特急 costs no extra. Ranking: 普通 < 快速 < 急行 < 特急. Figuratively, 特急で also means "at top speed" (特急で仕上げる).

examples[].german: Koichi likes black garlic.
I got deeply tanned from the sun.
I toasted the bread too long and it turned completely black.
en.notes: 真っ黒 means "deep black, pitch black" and is used with な or の before nouns and with になる: 真っ黒な髪, 真っ黒になる. It also means "heavily sun-tanned" (日焼けで真っ黒) and "dirty, charred"; colloquially it even means "clearly guilty", opposite 真っ白 "innocent". The pattern 真っ＋color also exists in 真っ白, 真っ赤 and 真っ青 (also "deathly pale").

examples[].german: In the language of flowers, the cornflower stands for 「幸福」.
I want to lead a happy life.
I put my family's happiness first.
en.notes: 幸福 means "happiness" in the sense of a lasting state of well-being and sounds rather literary or elevated; in everyday speech one mostly says 幸せ. As a な-adjective: 幸福な人生, 幸福な家庭. Luck in the sense of chance or good fortune, on the other hand, is 運 or 幸運 (運がいい). Typical combinations: 幸福を祈る, 人々の幸福.

examples[].german: I really love your smile!
She always has a smile on her face.
The shop assistant said 「いらっしゃいませ」 with a smile.
en.notes: 笑顔 is a smiling face, i.e. "smile" as a facial expression. Typical combinations: 笑顔で～ "with a smile", 笑顔になる "to start smiling", 笑顔を見せる, 笑顔がすてき. To be distinguished from 笑い "laughter" and the more literary ほほえみ "gentle smile". In service and advertising, 笑顔 is a very common word.

examples[].german: What, you're quitting the company?
I made up my mind to leave the company.
I quit the school club and started a part-time job.
en.notes: 辞める is transitive (X を辞める) and means to give up a job, school, club or office: 会社を辞める, 学校を辞める, 部活を辞める. 止める/やめる "to stop an action or habit" (たばこをやめる) is read the same way; it is usually written in kana. The more formal word for leaving one's occupation is 退職する.

examples[].german: Koichi is bad at giving compliments he doesn't mean.
Please don't flatter me.
I'm happy even if it's just flattery.
en.notes: お世辞 is a compliment that is not entirely sincere, that is, flattery: お世辞を言う, お世辞がうまい. In reply to praise, one answers modestly with お世辞でもうれしいです, and お世辞抜きで means "honestly, without flattering". A sincere compliment, on the other hand, is 褒め言葉 or the verb 褒める. The お is a fixed part of the word.

examples[].german: Let's start with the introductory course first.
I joined a beginning Japanese class.
He entered a sumo stable at the age of fifteen.
en.notes: 入門 now mostly means "introduction": 入門書 "introductory book", 入門コース, 入門編, 日本語入門. The original meaning is "to enter as a pupil under a master", for example in sumo, martial arts or rakugo: 相撲部屋に入門する. In contrast to 初級 "beginner level", 入門 emphasizes the very first step into a field.

examples[].german: Please put it in the corner of the room.
There is a bookshelf in the corner of the room.
A small explanation is written in one corner of the map.
en.notes: 隅（すみ）means a corner or edge area within a surface or room. ～の隅に names the place, as in 部屋の隅に. The spelling 角 is also recorded for すみ; for the corner of a room, the ordinary spelling 隅 is suitable. The same kanji 角 can be read かど, つの or かく in other words. The meaning "horn" belongs to つの and is not the meaning of すみ practiced here. In the third example, a small explanation lies in one corner of the map.

examples[].german: Please tell me your opinion on this issue.
I read a book about Japanese culture.
Do you have any questions regarding this matter?
en.notes: 関する occurs practically only in two forms: ～に関する + noun "regarding, about" (環境に関する本) and adverbial ～に関して (この件に関して). It is more formal and literary than ～について, which is more common in conversation. Typical in news, reports and business emails.

examples[].german: I'm planning to go by Hanshin train.
I'm a fan of the Hanshin Tigers.
The area around Osaka and Kobe is called "Hanshin".
en.notes: 阪神 combines 阪 (大阪) and 神 (神戸) and refers to the region between Osaka and Kobe. It is best known as a company name: 阪神電車, 阪神百貨店 and the baseball team 阪神タイガース. Following the same pattern there are 京阪 (Kyoto-Osaka) and 京浜 (Tokyo-Yokohama). As a proper name, it is used without an article or any addition.

examples[].german: The design on the front of this T-shirt is really good.
The front of the building is being repaired.
This poster puts the low price of the products front and center.
en.notes: 前面 is the front side or front of a building, vehicle or garment and sounds somewhat matter-of-fact. To be distinguished from it are 正面 (the side facing you; "straight ahead") and 表 (the front side of a sheet). Figuratively, ～を前面に出す means "to put in the foreground". Do not confuse with the identically read 全面 "entire surface, completely".

examples[].german: Lots of leaves had fallen on the ground.
The ground is wet from the rain.
I caught the ball before it fell to the ground.
en.notes: 地面 is the ground outdoors, whether soil or asphalt: 地面に座る, 地面に落ちる, 地面が濡れる. The floor inside buildings is 床 (ゆか), and 土 denotes soil as a material. Colloquially people also say 地べた (地べたに座る). The particle に for movement onto the ground is typical.

examples[].german: The outside looks nice, but the inside is old.
The outer surface of this ball is made of leather.
Inner beauty is more important than outward beauty.
en.notes: 外面（がいめん） refers to the outer surface or outward appearance of a thing: 建物の外面, ボールの外面. It sounds rather matter-of-fact and written; in everyday speech one usually says 外側 "outside" or 見た目 "appearance". Note: with the reading そとづら the same word means "the face one shows to outsiders" (外面がいい "friendly toward outsiders"). The derivation 外面的 "outward, superficial" is also common.

examples[].german: A famous chef works at this restaurant.
I want to become a cook in the future.
My father is a cook, so he makes delicious food at home too.
en.notes: 料理人 is the general term for someone who cooks professionally, from restaurant cooks to top chefs; the reading is りょうりにん, not りょうりじん. In everyday life the loanwords コック "cook" and シェフ "head chef" are often heard, which suggest Western cuisine more; a cook of Japanese cuisine is traditionally called 板前. Someone who cooks well at home is not a 料理人 but 料理が上手な人.

examples[].german: He is a famous artist.
Many young artists live in this town.
Making a living as an artist is not easy.
en.notes: 芸術家 is the general term for creators of art of any kind; more specific are 画家 "painter", 彫刻家 "sculptor" or 音楽家 "musician". The suffix 家 here denotes someone who practices an art or a field (cf. 作家 "writer"). The loanword アーティスト is also used in everyday speech for pop singers and bands, whereas 芸術家 tends to mean serious, "high" art and sounds somewhat more elevated.

examples[].german: The doors of this train do not open automatically.
When it gets dark outside, the light comes on automatically.
This computer is updated automatically at night.
en.notes: 自動的 is a な-adjective and appears almost always adverbially as 自動的に "automatically, by itself": ドアが自動的に閉まる. Before a noun it is 自動的な. The base word 自動 forms compounds such as 自動ドア or 自動販売機; the opposite is 手動 "manual". Figuratively, 自動的に also describes consequences that occur without any action of one's own, e.g. 会員になると自動的に割引になります.

examples[].german: Basically, I don't believe in spiritual things.
Let's start with the basics.
Basically I have Saturdays off, but when it's busy, I work.
en.notes: 基本的 is a な-adjective: 基本的な + noun means "basic, elementary" (基本的なルール); adverbially, 基本的に means "basically, in principle". 基本的に often hints that there are exceptions - similar to "as a rule". The base noun 基本 "basis" also stands alone (基本が大切). For "from the ground up, radical" one uses 根本的 instead.

examples[].german: He never dog-ears his books.
I made a fold in the paper.
These trousers have a neat pressed crease.
en.notes: 折り目 is the line that forms when paper or cloth is folded: a fold, crease, or the pressed crease of trousers. Typical are 折り目をつける "to make a crease" and 折り目がつく "to get a crease". Unlike しわ "wrinkle, crinkle", 折り目 is a straight, usually deliberate fold line. In the set phrase 折り目正しい it means "correct, well-mannered" in behavior.

examples[].german: Please go in my place.
I drink tea instead of coffee.
In return for your help, I'll treat you to lunch.
en.notes: 代わりに means "instead of" or "in return for". After a noun, の is used: 私の代わりに. It can refer to a substituting person or thing. After a clause such as 手伝ってくれた代わりに, it expresses compensation for the help given. The whole expression is taught here.

examples[].german: Tomorrow is my graduation ceremony.
I cried at the graduation ceremony.
My parents also came to my graduation ceremony.
en.notes: 卒業式 is the graduation ceremony of a school or university; in Japan it usually takes place in March, and its April counterpart is 入学式. One says 卒業式に出る／出席する "to attend the ceremony" and 卒業式で泣く "to cry at the ceremony". 卒業 applies to any school graduation, including elementary and junior high school, not only university.

examples[].german: All human beings are imperfect.
This report is still incomplete.
Making decisions based on incomplete information is dangerous.
en.notes: 不完全 is the opposite of 完全 "complete, perfect" and works as a な-adjective and noun: 不完全な情報, まだ不完全です. It covers both "incomplete" and "imperfect, flawed". For a piece of work that is simply not finished yet, one often says 未完成; for "insufficient", 不十分 fits better. The tone is matter-of-fact and slightly literary.

examples[].german: I hope you can get into the university you want!
I'm hoping to change jobs.
For the airplane seat, I would like a window seat.
en.notes: 希望する means "to wish, to hope for something" and is transitive: 〜を希望する. It sounds more formal than 〜たい and typically appears in applications, forms and when stating preferences (窓側の席を希望します). The derivatives ご希望 "your wish" and 希望者 "applicant, interested person" are very common. The noun 希望 alone also means "hope" (希望を持つ). For personal wishes in daily life, 〜たい or 欲しい is more usual.

en.meaning: to leave behind; to leave over
examples[].german: It's not good to leave food uneaten.
My mother left a note on the table and went out.
I'll set aside a little money for next month.
en.notes: 残す is transitive and means "to leave over, to leave behind": 食べ物を残す, メモを残す. The intransitive partner is 残る "to remain" (ご飯が残っている). With 〜ておく it means "to keep, to put aside" (お金を残しておく); figuratively also "to leave behind" (記録を残す, 名前を残す). Leaving something behind by accident, on the other hand, is 忘れる.

examples[].german: I set the jelly in the refrigerator.
I packed the snow firmly and made a snowman.
I firmed up my resolve.
en.notes: 固める is transitive and means "to make firm, harden, solidify": 雪を固める, ゼリーを冷蔵庫で固める. The intransitive partner is 固まる "to become firm, to set". Figuratively it stands for firming up plans and decisions: 決意を固める, 考えを固める. The expression 身を固める means "to settle down, get married". The underlying adjective is 固い "hard, firm".

examples[].german: What day of the week is it today?
The closing time of this shop differs depending on the day of the week.
I got the day for putting out the garbage wrong.
en.notes: 曜日 means "day of the week" and is in all the day names: 月曜日, 火曜日 etc. The question is asked with 何曜日（なんようび）; do not confuse it with 何日 "which date". In conversation the days are often shortened to 月曜, 火曜. On its own, 曜日 appears mainly in phrases such as 曜日によって "depending on the day of the week" or 曜日を間違える "to get the day of the week wrong".

examples[].german: I was born in Osaka.
Osaka is famous for takoyaki.
From Tokyo to Osaka it takes about two and a half hours by Shinkansen.
en.notes: 大阪 is Japan's second-largest metropolitan area and is both a city (大阪市) and a prefecture (大阪府). It is regarded as the center of 関西 and is known for foods such as たこ焼き and お好み焼き as well as for the 大阪弁 dialect. In Latin script the long vowel is usually omitted ("Osaka"). A person from Osaka is called 大阪の人 or 大阪出身の人.

examples[].german: That guy has no interest in other people, you know.
I am interested in environmental issues.
Young people's interest in politics is declining.
en.notes: 関心 means "interest, concern" and takes に: 〜に関心がある／ない, 〜に関心を持つ. It sounds more matter-of-fact than 興味, which rather expresses personal curiosity and enjoyment (映画に興味がある). 関心 suits social topics in particular and is rated with 高い／低い (政治への関心が低い). Do not confuse it with the identically read 感心 "to admire, to be impressed".

examples[].german: The ball hit me in the face.
I fell and hit my face hard.
This helmet also protects the face.
en.notes: 顔面 is a technical word for the face as a body part, as it appears in medicine, sports and accident reports: 顔面にボールが当たる, 顔面を打つ. In everyday speech people simply say 顔. 顔面 is not used for facial expression or for "face" in the sense of reputation (顔が広い). A well-known phrase is 顔面蒼白 "deathly pale".

examples[].german: On our anniversary, I plan to go out for dinner with him.
We go to a restaurant on our wedding anniversary.
Today is the school's founding anniversary.
en.notes: 記念日 is an anniversary or day of remembrance that commemorates a particular event. 結婚記念日 is a wedding anniversary, 創立記念日 the founding day of an institution. 記念日に indicates what one does on that day. The word does not automatically mean a public holiday with the day off.

examples[].german: Please tell me the exact time.
This clock is accurate.
Please answer the question accurately.
en.notes: 正確 is a na-adjective meaning accurate, correct or precise. 正確な時間 gives an exact time; 正確です judges the accuracy of a clock or of information. With に you describe the manner of an action, e.g. 正確に答える. It is about correctness or precision, not merely about doing something neatly.

examples[].german: I boil water.
I heat the bath water.
en.notes: 沸かす is a transitive godan verb ending in す: you heat a liquid, often until it boils. The thing heated takes を. お風呂を沸かす means to heat the bath water, not merely to run water into the tub. 沸く, by contrast, describes the water becoming hot or boiling.

examples[].german: This is very convenient - you can use it in all kinds of situations!
I like the last scene of this movie.
In important moments, I always get nervous.
en.notes: 場面 refers on the one hand to a scene in a film, play or book (最後の場面), and on the other hand to a concrete situation or occasion in life: いろいろな場面で使える, 大事な場面. In a film context the loanword シーン is also common. 場合 sounds similar, but means a supposed case ("in case"): 雨の場合は中止です. For a general state of affairs one rather uses 状況.

examples[].german: It's a charm that brings good luck.
I wish you good luck.
Luckily, I made it in time for the train.
en.notes: 幸運 means "luck" in the sense of fortunate chance, not in the sense of contentment - for that one says 幸せ or 幸福. It is a noun and a な-adjective: 幸運な人, adverbially 幸運にも "luckily". Set phrases are 幸運を祈ります "I wish you good luck" and 幸運を呼ぶ "to bring good luck". In everyday speech one mostly says 運がいい or, colloquially, ラッキー.

en.meaning: to break; to snap; to fold
examples[].german: When you say things like that, I lose heart.
A branch broke in the strong wind.
I broke a bone in my leg in a soccer match.
en.notes: 折れる is intransitive: something long or thin breaks or snaps (枝が折れる, 骨が折れる). The transitive partner is 折る "to break, to fold". Glass or plates, by contrast, are 割れる, devices 壊れる, threads 切れる. Figuratively, 心が折れる means "to lose heart" and 骨が折れる also means "to be laborious". In directions, 右に折れる means "to turn right" (more common in everyday speech: 曲がる).

examples[].german: On weekends I go to Costco to buy groceries.
The grocery section of this department store is in the basement.
Grocery prices have been rising recently.
en.notes: 食料品 means food as merchandise, i.e. what you buy at the supermarket; typical are 食料品を買う, 食料品売り場 and 食料品店. For food in general, 食べ物 is used in daily life. 食品 is similar but sounds more technical (食品の表示), and 食料 means food as nourishment rather than as stock or supply (食料が足りない).

examples[].german: I'm looking for a luggage tag to put on my travel bag.
I attached a tag to the luggage.
Please write your name and address on the tag.
en.notes: 荷札 is a tag or label attached to luggage or parcels, usually with a name and address: 荷物に荷札をつける. For suitcases, ネームタグ is also often said today. Related words with 札 "sign, slip" are 名札 "name tag" on clothing and 値札 "price tag".

en.meaning: to send back; to let go home
examples[].german: I put the small fish I catch back into the sea.
I sent the child home early.
I'm worried about letting you go home alone at such a late hour.
en.notes: 帰す is transitive and means "to send someone home, to let someone return"; the intransitive partner is 帰る. It refers to people or animals going back to their place: 子供を家に帰す, 魚を海に帰す. Objects, on the other hand, are given back with the identically read 返す (本を返す). Typical is 早く帰す "to send home early", for example when someone is ill.

examples[].german: Stress can make an illness worse.
The weather is getting worse.
The relationship between those two has been getting worse lately.
en.notes: 悪化 is a Sino-Japanese noun used as an intransitive する-verb: 〜が悪化する "to worsen, to get worse". It sounds objective and is typical for news, medical and weather reports (病気が悪化する, 天気が悪化する, 関係が悪化する). In conversation people usually just say 悪くなる. The opposite is 改善する "to improve".

examples[].german: I'll ask the manufacturer.
I inquired about detailed information.
I called the station and inquired about a lost item.
en.notes: 問い合わせる means "to inquire, make an inquiry" - usually to a company or office: 〜に〜を問い合わせる or 〜について問い合わせる. It is more official than 聞く and typical for calls to customer service or authorities. Very common is the noun 問い合わせ, for example お問い合わせ "inquiry, contact" on websites or 問い合わせ先 "contact point".

examples[].german: Medicine is needed to cure this illness.
A doctor cures illnesses.
I want to get over my cold quickly and go to school.
en.notes: 治す is transitive and means "to cure, heal" - for illnesses and injuries: 病気を治す, けがを治す, 風邪を治す. The subject can be the doctor or the patient himself. The intransitive partner is 治る "to get well" (風邪が治った). Note: the identically read 直す means "to repair, correct" (時計を直す, 間違いを直す).

examples[].german: Since about what year BC have people lived in this region?
These ruins date from 3000 BC.
en.notes: 紀元前 refers, in the Christian calendar, to years before Christ, also called before the common era. It stands directly before the year number: 紀元前三千年. 年ごろ makes the dating approximate. This form is suitable for historical dating; for the very distant history of the Earth, expressions such as 何万年前 are usually used.

examples[].german: My body got cold.
My body gets cold at night.
The juice got cold in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 冷える describes something becoming cold or cooling down. It is an intransitive ichidan verb; the thing that cools takes が. It can refer to the body, a drink or a room. 冷やす, by contrast, means to actively cool something and requires an object with を.

examples[].german: My younger brother is a crybaby and cries right away over little things.
I was a crybaby when I was a child.
Crying just because you fell down, what a crybaby you are.
en.notes: 泣き虫 is a teasing expression for someone who cries easily, especially for children. It usually sounds affectionately mocking, but it can also hurt. 虫 is used here as a suffix for people with a typical trait, cf. 弱虫 "weakling, coward" and 本の虫 "bookworm". As a predicate it takes だ／です: 子供の頃は泣き虫でした.

examples[].german: I can hear a baby crying.
I heard crying from the next room and became worried.
My mother explained the circumstances in a tearful voice.
en.notes: 泣き声 is the audible sound of crying or a crying voice. 泣き声が聞こえる describes hearing the crying; 泣き声で話す means someone speaks in a tearful or tear-choked voice. The word names the sound and is not the verb 泣く.

examples[].german: She made a wish on the first star.
I wrote a wish on Tanabata.
I hope your wish comes true.
en.notes: 願い事 is a concrete wish addressed to gods, stars or fate. Typical are 願い事をする "to make a wish" and 願い事がかなう "a wish comes true"; at 七夕 it is written on colorful strips of paper. The more general 願い also includes requests to people (お願い), while 希望 expresses a more matter-of-fact hope or preference.

examples[].german: That comedy duo is from Kansai.
I want to travel to Kansai.
The Kansai dialect has quite a different accent from Tokyo speech.
en.notes: 関西 refers to the region around Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe in the west of the main island; its counterpart is 関東 around Tokyo. You say 関西に住む, 関西出身, 関西の人. The dialect is called 関西弁, and many comedians come from this area. Geographically and officially people also speak of 近畿地方; 関西 is the culturally everyday term.

examples[].german: The steering wheel of Japanese cars is usually on the right side.
Please walk on the right side.
The one on the right side of the photo is my older brother.
en.notes: 右側 means the right side of something: 〜の右側に／を. For the direction of walking or turning, however, only 右 is used: 右に曲がる, not 右側に曲がる. Typical combinations are 右側通行 "right-hand traffic" and 写真の右側 "on the right in the photo". The counterpart is 左側; 側 also forms 内側, 外側 and 両側.

examples[].german: Everyone is standing on the left side of this escalator, aren't they?
There is a school on the left side.
In Japan, cars drive on the left side of the road.
en.notes: 左側 is the left side of something: 〜の左側に／を. In Japan cars drive on the left (道の左側を走る); on escalators people stand on the left in Tokyo, but on the right in Osaka. For the bare direction, 左 suffices (左に曲がる). The counterpart is 右側, and the traffic rule is called 左側通行 "left-hand traffic".

examples[].german: To keep the zombies from getting in, I lowered the shutter and locked it from the inside.
The key is on the inside of the door.
Please stand back inside the yellow line.
en.notes: 内側 is the inner side or inner area of something with a clear boundary: ドアの内側, 線の内側. For "inside" in the sense of "in a room", 中 is usually said (部屋の中). Well known is the platform announcement 黄色い線の内側までお下がりください "Please step back behind the yellow line". The opposite is 外側; 内側から鍵をかける means "to lock from the inside".

examples[].german: I thought it would open outward, but it was a door that opens inward.
I wrote my name on the outside of the box.
The outside of this window is dirty, so I can't see well.
en.notes: 外側 is the outer side or outer area of something: 箱の外側, 外側に開く. General "outdoors, outside" is 外, on the other hand: 外で遊ぶ, not 外側で遊ぶ. The opposite is 内側; the two are often used together, for example with doors, clothing or traffic lanes (外側の車線 "outer lane").

examples[].german: Trees are planted on both sides of the road.
There are small lamps on both sides of the bed.
This bus has doors on both sides.
en.notes: 両側 means "both sides" of something, in a spatial sense: 道の両側, ベッドの両側. For "both" in the general sense, 両方 is used (両方とも好き). With body parts, 両 + noun such as 両手 or 両耳 is preferred. Typical is the structure 〜の両側に〜がある／並んでいる; similar is 左右 "left and right".

examples[].german: You can see Mount Fuji on the east side.
You can see the morning sun from the east-side window.
A new hotel has opened on the east side of the station.
en.notes: 東側 is the east side of something: 駅の東側, 東側の窓. For the pure compass direction, 東 suffices (東へ行く). Correspondingly there are 西側, 南側 and 北側. Historically, 東側 also meant the Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, as opposed to 西側 "the West".

examples[].german: I'm heating up the soup.
I heat the soup in the microwave.
I warmed my hands.
en.notes: 温める means to warm something up or make it warmer. The object takes を. It is a transitive Ichidan verb; 温めて is the て-form. The reading あたためる is chosen here. Heating a liquid to boiling is described more precisely by 沸かす.

examples[].german: There are hardly any troops left in that country anymore.
The troops were assembled.
The troops were transported to the island by ship.
en.notes: 兵員 refers to soldiers as personnel or troop strength, i.e. as a number or group rather than an individual. It is a literary word from news and military reports (兵員を送る, 兵員が不足する). A single soldier is called 兵士; colloquial and somewhat old-fashioned is 兵隊.

examples[].german: This is my ultimate weapon!
Nuclear weapons are dangerous.
That country is developing new weapons.
en.notes: 兵器 denotes military weapons and weapon systems, especially in compounds such as 核兵器 "nuclear weapons" or 化学兵器 "chemical weapons". 武器 is more general and includes any weapon from a knife to a rifle; figuratively people say 笑顔が武器だ, not 兵器. Jokingly, 最終兵器 "ultimate weapon" is heard for a last trump card.

examples[].german: He is a former soldier.
The soldiers are training.
Many soldiers died in the war.
en.notes: 兵士 is the neutral word for an individual soldier, often in the plural 兵士たち. 兵隊 is colloquial and somewhat old-fashioned; 軍人 emphasizes the profession as a member of the military, including officers. Members of the Japan Self-Defense Forces are officially called 自衛官, not 兵士.

examples[].german: There are US soldiers at the base.
An incident involving a US soldier made the news.
That US soldier is very good at Japanese.
en.notes: 米兵 means "US soldier"; 米 stands for the USA in compounds (米国, 日米). The short word is typical of news, especially in connection with the bases on Okinawa. In conversation people more often say アメリカ兵 or アメリカ軍の兵士. 英 for Great Britain (英国) is formed similarly.

examples[].german: Movies based on manga often lose the appeal of the original.
I read the original work of the movie.
The original of this anime is a novel.
en.notes: 原作 is the original work on which an adaptation is based - typically a novel or manga that is made into a film or anime. Typical phrases are 〜が原作の映画 "a film based on ...", 原作を読む and 原作者 "author of the original". 原作通り means "true to the original".

examples[].german: What do you think is the main cause of inflation?
The main cause of the accident has been determined.
According to the doctor, lack of sleep is the main cause of my headaches.
en.notes: 主因 means "main cause" and is a literary word from reports, news and analyses: 事故の主因, 〜が主因となる. In conversation one mostly says 一番の原因 or 主な原因. It almost always follows の after the event whose cause is named.

examples[].german: Want to eat lunch at the cafeteria?
I eat lunch in the school cafeteria.
en.notes: 食堂 is a dining hall or cafeteria. With で you name it as the place of eating. 食べない？ in an invitation is a familiar question in the negative present, used to suggest eating together. 学校の食堂 assigns the cafeteria to a school. しょくどう has a long o at the end.

examples[].german: Seawater is salt water, so you can't drink it as it is.
I boil the pasta in salt water.
If you soak cut apples in salt water, they won't change color.
en.notes: 塩水（しおみず） is the everyday word for salt water, for example in the kitchen: 塩水でゆでる, 塩水につける. In technical texts the same word is also read えんすい. Seawater is more precisely 海水, fresh water 真水. A well-known kitchen trick: cut apples are briefly put in 塩水 so that they do not turn brown.

examples[].german: I feel it's lacking a little saltiness.
These potato chips are salt-flavored.
For ramen, which would you like, salt or soy sauce?
en.notes: 塩味（しおあじ） means "salty taste" and is often used as a flavor variety: 塩味のポテトチップス, 塩味のラーメン. Similar formations are しょうゆ味 and みそ味. To say that something is too salty, the adjectives しょっぱい or 塩辛い are used. In technical texts the word is also read えんみ.

examples[].german: Never lay a hand on government funds!
The management of government funds is strict.
That official used government funds for himself.
en.notes: 官金 means "government funds, public money" and is an outdated, literary word; 官 stands for government and authorities (官庁, 官僚). Today one mostly says 公金 or speaks concretely of 税金. The phrase 官金に手を出す means "to misappropriate government funds".

examples[].german: Please don't step on my foot.
Please don't walk on the grass.
en.notes: 踏む here means "to step on something". The thing stepped on takes を: 足を踏む, 草を踏む. It is a transitive godan verb ending in む; the て-form is 踏んで. With ないでください you ask someone not to step on or walk on something.

examples[].german: He is a former diplomat.
She works as a diplomat.
To become a diplomat, I am studying three foreign languages.
en.notes: 外交官 is composed of 外交 "diplomacy" and 官 "official" and refers to diplomats in the foreign service. An ambassador is more precisely 大使. 官 forms many civil-service occupations, such as 警察官 "police officer" or 裁判官 "judge". Typical are 外交官になる and 外交官として働く.

examples[].german: Before sensing other people's feelings, you should value your own feelings.
I sensed her feelings.
That must have been hard. You have my sympathy.
en.notes: 察する means "to sense, to intuit" - above all the feelings or intentions of others without their being spoken: 気持ちを察する. It is transitive and sounds more refined than 気づく or わかる. The polite phrase お察しします expresses sympathy ("I can imagine how you feel"). The noun 察し appears in 察しがいい "to catch on quickly, to be perceptive".

examples[].german: She has a high ability to sense danger.
I sensed danger.
Dogs are said to be able to sense earthquakes in advance.
en.notes: 察知 means to sense in time something hidden or imminent, especially danger, intentions or changes: 危険を察知する. It is a transitive する-verb with a matter-of-fact, written sound. 察する refers more to the feelings of others, and 気づく is the everyday "to notice". The combination 危険察知能力 "sense for danger" is common.

examples[].german: There are no vacant seats on this flight.
Do you have any seats available?
The manager's seat is still vacant.
en.notes: 空席 refers to a free, unoccupied seat, above all with reservations on trains, planes, cinemas or restaurants: 空席がある, 空席はありますか. On displays you read 空席あり; the opposite is 満席 "fully booked". In daily life people also simply say 空いている席. 空席 can also refer to a vacant post.

examples[].german: He is always smiling.
Please always pay attention to safety while driving.
en.notes: 常に means always or constantly and emphasizes the constancy of a state or behavior. It stands before the predicate it describes and is especially common in explanations or general instructions. 運転中は常に states a requirement for the whole drive; 常に笑顔 describes a permanently friendly appearance.

examples[].german: I want to be able to have everyday conversations in Japanese.
I use Japanese in my daily life.
The trip is over, and I'm back to my daily routine.
en.notes: 日常 means "everyday life, the ordinary" and mostly appears in compounds or with の: 日常生活, 日常会話, 日常の仕事. Adverbially and adjectivally, 日常的 is often used (日常的に使う "to use regularly, in daily life"). 毎日, by contrast, specifically means "every day", and 普段 "usually, normally". 日常に戻る means "to return to everyday life".

examples[].german: They say the pond of this shrine always had water, no matter how dry the weather got.
The dry spell continues and there is a water shortage.
That news was truly a welcome rain after a long drought.
en.notes: 干天 refers to a period of dry weather without rain and is a literary, written word; it is also written 旱天. In everyday speech one says 日照り or 雨が降らない日が続く, and for drought in the news 干ばつ. Today 干天 is known mainly from the saying 干天の慈雨 "longed-for rain after a drought", used figuratively for welcome help in need.

examples[].german: Isn't that just a hallucination?
I had hallucinations from the fever.
Taking this medicine can sometimes cause hallucinations.
en.notes: 幻覚 is a hallucination, i.e. a perception without a real stimulus. Typical are 幻覚を見る and 幻覚が見える; the cause takes で (熱で幻覚を見る). Auditory hallucinations are more precisely 幻聴. 錯覚, by contrast, is a misperception of something real, and 幻 more poetically means "illusion, phantom".

examples[].german: You have chewing gum stuck to the sole of your shoe.
There might be treasure at the bottom of the sea.
I am grateful from the bottom of my heart.
en.notes: 底 is the bottom or lowest surface of a container or body of water (鍋の底, 海の底) and also the sole of a shoe (靴の底). 下, by contrast, means "under": 箱の下 is under the box, 箱の底 is its bottom. The floor of a room is called 床. Figuratively: 心の底から "from the bottom of one's heart", 底をつく "to run out".

en.meaning: from the bottom of one's heart; deeply
examples[].german: I was truly happy.
Hearing that I passed the exam, I felt deeply relieved.
I truly hate people like that.
en.notes: 心底 is an adverb that intensifies feelings: 心底うれしい "happy from the heart", 心底ほっとする "to be deeply relieved", 心底驚く. It sounds more emotional and emphatic than the neutral 心から (心から感謝します) and is often used with negative feelings too: 心底嫌いだ, 心底うんざりする. As a noun it means "the deepest part of the heart, one's true intention" (心底から); in this meaning there is also the literary reading しんてい.

examples[].german: My wallet was stolen.
Somebody stole a bicycle.
en.notes: 盗む is the transitive godan verb for "to steal". The stolen object takes を. 財布を盗まれました is a typical adversative passive: the speaker suffered the loss. The て-form is 盗んで; 盗まれる means "to have something stolen / to be stolen".

examples[].german: Many water plants were growing on the riverbed.
The water is so clear that you can even see the stones on the riverbed clearly.
The key I dropped sank to the bottom of the river.
en.notes: 川底 is the bottom of a river, i.e. what lies beneath the water (底 "bottom", read here with voicing as ぞこ). Typical are 川底に沈む "to sink to the bottom of the river", 川底が見える and 川底の石. The bank, on the other hand, is 川岸 or 川辺; the sea floor is 海底 (かいてい) with the Sino-Japanese reading. In technical texts (geography, hydraulic engineering), 河床 is also used for "riverbed".

examples[].german: He is a very patriotic person.
Watching the Olympics makes me feel patriotic.
Opinions are divided on whether patriotism should be taught at school.
en.notes: 愛国心 is love for one's own country, "patriotism" as a feeling or attitude. Typical combinations are 愛国心が強い, 愛国心を持つ and 愛国心がわく; the person is called 愛国者. In Japan the word is politically sensitive because of the history of the war, for example in the debate about patriotism education at schools. For exaggerated nationalism, ナショナリズム or 国家主義 is more usual.

en.meaning: taking care of oneself; looking after one's health
examples[].german: It has gotten cold, so please take good care of yourself.
I imagine you will continue to have busy days, but please take care of yourself.
At the end of my email to my teacher, I wrote 「ご自愛ください」.
en.notes: 自愛 is found almost only in the polite closing formula ご自愛ください "please take care of your health" in letters, emails and greeting cards to superiors, customers or older people, often reinforced with どうぞ or くれぐれも. Since 自愛 already means "to take care of oneself", お体をご自愛ください is considered redundant, but it is widespread. One does not say it about oneself; among friends one rather says 体に気をつけてね, and to someone already ill one says お大事に. The meaning "self-love" is rare.

examples[].german: There are many themes of sexual love in literature.
The ancient Greeks thought of friendship and sexual love as separate.
This movie has many love scenes, so it is not suitable for children.
en.notes: 性愛 is sexual, physical love, "eros", and belongs to written and technical language (literature, philosophy, psychology). Everyday romantic love is 恋愛, affection in general 愛情. 性愛 is also known as a component of 異性愛 "heterosexuality" and 同性愛 "homosexuality". Typical are 性愛を描く, 性愛のテーマ and 性愛の描写.

examples[].german: Have you ever been to Aichi Prefecture?
Aichi Prefecture is famous for its automobile industry.
Nagoya is in Aichi Prefecture.
en.notes: 愛知県 is a prefecture in the Chūbu region with the capital 名古屋. It is the center of the Japanese car industry; Toyota has its headquarters here. In conversation people often say just 愛知 (愛知の出身です); in addresses the full form comes before the place name: 愛知県名古屋市…. The local dialect is called 名古屋弁.

examples[].german: We were defeated in the final.
Japan lost to Brazil 2-1.
After losing the election, he quit politics.
en.notes: 敗れる "to be defeated, to lose" is intransitive; the opponent takes に (ブラジルに敗れる), the contest takes で or に (決勝で敗れる, 選挙に敗れる). It is more formal than the everyday 負ける and typical of sports reports and news. The transitive counterpart is 破る "to defeat" (相手を破る). Do not confuse it with the identically read 破れる "to tear" (紙が破れる).

examples[].german: You can't know the outcome until the end.
The final goal decided the outcome.
In children's soccer, having fun is more important than winning or losing.
en.notes: 勝敗 denotes the outcome of a contest, literally "victory and defeat". Typical are 勝敗が決まる/つく "to be decided", 勝敗を決める and 勝敗を分ける "to be decisive". Colloquially people say 勝ち負け with the same meaning. Do not confuse it with 勝負, the contest or duel itself (勝負する "to compete against each other").

examples[].german: I don't want to be a loser.
Let's give applause to the losers too.
After the match, the winner and the loser shook hands.
en.notes: 敗者 "loser" is a rather formal word from sports, politics and news; the counterpart is 勝者 "winner". In daily life people mostly say 負けた人 or 負けたほう. Well known is 敗者復活戦 "repechage round" in tournaments. Note, homophones: 歯医者 "dentist" and 廃車 "scrapped car" are also read はいしゃ.

examples[].german: Parents are powerless. Once the kids grow up, there's hardly anything you can do for them.
Faced with a big earthquake, I felt that humans are powerless.
I was frustrated at being powerless, unable to help my friend.
en.notes: 無力 "powerless, helpless" is a noun and な-adjective: 無力な自分, 〜の前では無力だ. It describes a lack of power or ability to change something, not physical weakness (for that, 弱い). The feeling of helplessness is called 無力感, often in 無力感を覚える. The opposite 有力 means rather "influential, promising" (有力な候補).

en.meaning: to make noise; to make a fuss
examples[].german: Please don't make noise.
Please don't make noise at night.
I partied wildly with everyone at the party.
en.notes: 騒ぐ can mean "to make noise" or "to celebrate boisterously". It is an intransitive godan verb ending in ぐ: 騒いで, 騒ぎます. A request like 騒がないでください asks for quiet. In the party sentence, on the other hand, cheerful, loud celebrating is meant.

en.meaning: open every day; no days off
examples[].german: Koichi works without a day off.
This store is open every day of the year.
We will be open on New Year's too.
en.notes: 無休 means "without a closing day" and appears above all on shop signs and in business information: 年中無休 "open all year round", 土日無休 "open on weekends too", 無休で営業する. The opposite is 定休日 "regular closing day". For people, 無休で働く "to work without a day off" is said. Careful when listening: the identically read 無給 means "unpaid".

examples[].german: I bought a painting by an unknown painter.
An unknown newcomer won the tournament.
He too was unknown once, but now he is an actor everyone knows.
en.notes: 無名 "unknown, not famous" mostly stands attributively with の (無名の歌手, 無名の新人) or predicatively as 無名だ; the opposite is 有名. The original meaning "nameless" lives on in set expressions such as 無名戦士の墓 "Tomb of the Unknown Soldier". For an anonymous letter or sender, 匿名 is used instead, and a stranger is not called 無名 but 知らない人.

examples[].german: I'm really glad everyone is safe.
Please come back safely.
Did the package arrive safely?
en.notes: 無事 means "safe and sound, without incident". As a state it appears as 無事だ or 無事で (家族が無事でよかった), as an adverb 無事に "safely, happily, smoothly" with verbs such as 着く, 帰る, 終わる, 届く. Unlike 安全 ("safe" as a property, 安全な場所), 無事 emphasizes the outcome: nothing happened. Set phrases are ご無事で "Arrive safely" and 無事を祈る.

examples[].german: I'm ignorant about economics, so I often don't understand the news.
Ignorance is nothing to be ashamed of.
You must not make fun of ignorant people.
en.notes: 無知 "ignorance, ignorant" is a noun and a な-adjective: 無知な人, 〜について無知だ, 自分の無知を恥じる. The word is judgmental and can come across as insulting; to say politely that you are not familiar with something, 〜に詳しくない or よく知らない is preferable. Do not confuse it with the identically read むち "whip" (鞭).

examples[].german: Don't say unreasonable things.
Running when you have a fever is reckless.
When I was young I did reckless things and was often scolded by my parents.
en.notes: 無茶 describes something unreasonable, reckless or excessive: 無茶を言う "to demand the impossible", 無茶をする "to act recklessly", 無茶な計画. It is colloquial and often sounds reproachful or worried (無茶しないでね). In contrast to 無理 ("impossible; to overexert oneself", 無理をする), 無茶 emphasizes recklessness. Intensified, it becomes 無茶苦茶 or めちゃくちゃ "completely chaotic, extreme"; the kanji are chosen only for their sound.

examples[].german: I want to get into the pharmacy faculty of this university.
I am studying pharmacy at university.
My older sister does pharmaceutical research at her company.
en.notes: 薬学 is pharmacy as a science and field of study: 薬学を学ぶ/専攻する, 薬学部 "faculty of pharmacy", 薬学の研究. The profession is called 薬剤師 "pharmacist", the pharmacy itself 薬局. Alongside 医学 "medicine", it is a subject of its own. The word is a noun; "pharmaceutical" is expressed with 薬学の or 薬学的.

examples[].german: Stop the drugs right now!
The use of drugs is prohibited.
If you have a drug allergy, please tell the doctor.
en.notes: 薬物 is the formal, technical word for a substance with a medicinal effect. In the news it usually means illegal drugs: 薬物乱用, 薬物依存, 薬物事件, 薬物をやめる. In medicine it is neutral for pharmaceutical substances: 薬物アレルギー, 薬物療法. In daily life people simply say 薬 for medicine; colloquially ドラッグ for drugs, and 麻薬 for narcotics in the narrower sense.

examples[].german: It was on sale, so I tried buying a medicated lotion.
I bought a medicated hand cream.
This soap is medicated, so it's said to work on acne.
en.notes: 薬用 "for medicinal purposes" usually stands directly before product names: 薬用石けん, 薬用リップクリーム, 薬用ハンドクリーム, more rarely with の. In Japan it marks care products with an active ingredient (legally 医薬部外品, "quasi-drugs"). Other combinations are 薬用植物 "medicinal plant" and 薬用酒 "medicinal liquor". "Medical" in the sense of "doctor's, relating to medicine" is 医学的 or 医療の instead.

examples[].german: It was so cold that I lost all feeling in my fingers.
She has a very good sense of color.
After living in Japan for a long time, my sense of time has changed.
en.notes: 感覚 is sensory perception and, figuratively, a feel for something: 指の感覚がない "to have no feeling in one's fingers", 色の感覚がいい "to have a good sense of color", 時間の感覚 "sense of time", 金銭感覚 "attitude toward money". Popular is 〜感覚で "as if it were ..." (ゲーム感覚で). For a vague impression one rather says 感じ, for emotions 気持ち or 感情. Despite the dictionary entry, 感覚する is practically never used.

examples[].german: I borrowed a book called 『図説 日本の城』 from the library.
This book explains the structure of the body in an easy-to-understand way with illustrations.
In history class, we use an illustrated reference book.
en.notes: 図説 is an explanation with illustrations, plates and diagrams. It is found mainly in titles of richly illustrated nonfiction books and reference volumes (『図説 日本の歴史』). As a する-verb (〜を図説する) it is literary. More common in everyday speech is 図解 (図解付き "with explanatory graphics"); a single picture or drawing is called イラスト or 挿絵.

examples[].german: I turned down the invitation.
I declined politely.
I didn't have time, so I turned down the job request.
en.notes: 断る here means to decline an invitation or request. The thing declined takes を: 誘いを断る. 丁寧に断る emphasizes a polite refusal. It is a transitive Godan verb ending in る; 断って is the て-form. The other meaning, "to give notice in advance / ask permission", is not used here.

examples[].german: This emergency brake might be broken.
It's an extremely important meeting.
The emergency exit is over there.
en.notes: 非常 has two faces. As a noun it means "emergency" and appears mainly in compounds: 非常口 "emergency exit", 非常ベル, 非常ブレーキ, 非常食, 非常時. As a な-adjective it means "extraordinary, enormous" and appears most often as the adverb 非常に "extremely, very", which sounds more formal than とても. For an acute emergency, everyday speech rather uses 緊急 (緊急の場合).

examples[].german: Picking your nose with your fingers is not okay. Use a tissue to get it out.
Don't pick your nose.
I wiped my child's booger away with a tissue.
en.notes: 鼻くそ is a colloquial, rather crude word for a booger or nasal mucus. 鼻くそをほじる describes picking one's nose. In the first example, the reproach is followed by a casual request with 取りなよ; the expression is suited to familiar conversation, not to a formal description.

examples[].german: You have mustard on the tip of your nose.
The tip of my nose is cold.
When I got to the shop, the door was shut in my face.
en.notes: 鼻先 is the tip of the nose (in everyday speech also 鼻の先 or 鼻の頭). Figuratively it means "right under one's nose": 鼻先でドアを閉められる "to have the door shut in one's face". The phrase 鼻先で笑う means "to laugh contemptuously, to laugh at someone scornfully". For "before one's eyes" in general, 目の前 is more common.

examples[].german: I hum while cooking.
My father hums when he's in a good mood.
I hummed in the train without thinking, and it was embarrassing.
en.notes: 鼻歌 is quietly singing or humming to oneself, usually out of good mood and while doing something else. One says 鼻歌を歌う; 鼻歌まじりに means "cheerfully humming, completely relaxed". Unlike ハミング, pure humming with the mouth closed, 鼻歌 can also be half-aloud with lyrics. The verb 口ずさむ "to hum or sing a tune to oneself" is similar.

examples[].german: I often get nosebleeds.
I suddenly got a nosebleed.
When a nosebleed won't stop, please lean forward and pinch your nose.
en.notes: 鼻血 is written with a voiced ぢ (はなぢ), because 血 on its own is read ち. Typical are 鼻血が出る "to have a nosebleed", 鼻血が止まる/止まらない and 鼻血を出す. In manga and anime, a nosebleed often stands jokingly for sexual arousal. Bleeding in general is 出血.

examples[].german: We cannot issue a certificate.
Please show your ID.
I need a graduation certificate to submit to my new company.
en.notes: 証明書 is a document that officially certifies something. Common compounds are 身分証明書 "ID card", 卒業証明書 "graduation certificate", 在学証明書 "certificate of enrollment" and 印鑑証明書 "seal registration certificate". Typical verbs: 証明書を発行する "to issue", もらう/取る "to get one issued", 提出する "to submit". The base word 証明 means "proof, evidence" (証明する); a driver's license and a membership card are, by contrast, 免許証 and 会員証.

examples[].german: Where can you buy a sailor's uniform?
The sailors are working on the ship.
When he was young, my grandfather was a sailor in the navy.
en.notes: 水兵 is a sailor of the navy (海軍), i.e. an ordinary soldier on a warship. For seafarers on civilian ships one says 船員 or 船乗り. The Japanese school uniform セーラー服 derives from the sailor uniform; 水兵さん sounds childlike and affectionate, as in children's songs. Do not confuse it with the identically read 水平 "horizontal".

examples[].german: His age is unknown.
This is an old song by an unknown author.
"Unknown" was written in the address field of the document.
en.notes: 不詳 means "not known in detail, not determined" and belongs to official written language: on forms, in news and in source citations. Typical are 作者不詳, 年齢不詳, 身元不詳 and 生年不詳. Colloquially, someone whose age is hard to guess is jokingly called 年齢不詳. The broader 不明, by contrast, is used for anything unclear: 原因不明, 行方不明.

examples[].german: I went to see Yoshimoto Shinkigeki in Osaka.
Chaplin's comedies are still funny to watch today.
I like comedies better than tragedies.
en.notes: 喜劇 is comedy as a genre in theater and film; the opposite is 悲劇. Related are 喜劇映画, 喜劇役者 and 喜劇的 "comic". Well known is the Osaka comedy theater 吉本新喜劇. In everyday speech, for comedy shows and comedians people prefer お笑い, and for Western films and series often コメディー. The word is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: That was the beginning of the tragedy.
This is a tragic incident.
In class we read a tragedy by Shakespeare.
en.notes: 悲劇 means, first, a tragedy as a stage play, and second, a tragic event in real life: 悲劇が起きる, 悲劇を繰り返す. The corresponding adjective is 悲劇的 "tragic" (悲劇的な事件). The opposite is 喜劇. Colloquially it is also used in an exaggerated way for small mishaps: それは悲劇だね.

examples[].german: I invited my friend to the movies.
I was invited to go hiking at the weekend, so I decided to go along.
Lured by the sweet smell, I went into the bakery.
en.notes: 誘う is a transitive godan verb ending in う: 誘います・誘って・誘わない. When inviting, the person takes を and the activity takes に: 友達を映画に誘う. It can also mean that something attracts someone; 誘われる is the passive form, "to be invited or lured".

examples[].german: Today I will teach you all a way to dramatically lower your electricity bill.
The match had a dramatic ending.
Reading that book changed my life dramatically.
en.notes: 劇的 is a な-adjective: 劇的な + noun means "dramatic, thrilling, moving" (劇的な勝利, 劇的な再会); the adverb 劇的に means "drastically, suddenly" with verbs of change such as 変わる, 増える, 減る, 良くなる. Unlike ドラマチック, which sounds rather romantic and emotional, 劇的に often describes a strong change soberly. With figures in formal texts, 大幅に is also used.

examples[].german: Have you ever seen an opera?
Let's go see an opera.
The Takarazuka Revue is an all-female theater company.
