en.notes: 歌劇 is the older, formal word for "opera"; in daily life today people almost always say オペラ. 歌劇 lives on in names and titles: 宝塚歌劇団 (the famous all-female revue theater), 歌劇場 "opera house", 歌劇「カルメン」. Typical verbs are 歌劇を見る and 歌劇を上演する "to perform". The word is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: I think this approach is unwise.
This dish tastes bad.
en.notes: 不味い is an i-adjective. For food it means "bad-tasting", for a course of action "unwise" or "problematic". It is often written in hiragana as まずい. 不味くない is the negative form. 不味いと思います marks a personal judgment. Directly judging taste with this word can sound blunt.

examples[].german: These grapes are seedless, so they're easy to eat.
I was absent without a reason.
A coffee without sugar, please.
en.notes: 無し "without, not existing" is almost always written in kana and attaches to nouns as 〜なし: 砂糖なしのコーヒー, 予約なしで入れる, 理由なしに. The counterpart is 〜あり (有り), as in 駐車場あり. With verbs one uses 〜ないで instead (朝ご飯を食べないで). Colloquially, ナシ means "out of the question", as the opposite of アリ "acceptable" (それはナシでしょ).

examples[].german: This manga hasn't been completed yet.
This drama will conclude in ten episodes.
The final installment of this series will be released next year.
en.notes: 完結 is intransitive: a story, a serialized manga or a series 完結する "comes to its conclusion". Typical are 連載が完結する, 全十巻で完結, 完結編 "final part" as well as 完結済み and 未完結. To actively bring something to a conclusion, one says 完結させる. In contrast to 終わる ("to end" in general), 完結 emphasizes completion in terms of content; a finished product or building is 完成 instead.

examples[].german: I get silent phone calls every night.
He stood there without saying a word.
After the quarrel, the two walked silently to the station.
en.notes: 無言 means "without saying a word": 無言で "silently", 無言のまま, 無言の圧力 "silent pressure". 無言電話 is a call in which the caller says nothing, usually as harassment. 沈黙 is silence as a state and rather literary (沈黙が続く); "to fall silent, be quiet" as a verb is 黙る. For a quiet environment, 静か is used, not 無言.

examples[].german: I'm happy to be able to be with the person I love.
I love my family.
He loved music with all his heart.
en.notes: 愛する "to love" is transitive (〜を愛する) and belongs to a special する-class: 愛して, negative 愛さない, potential 愛せる. In everyday speech, feelings are usually expressed with 好き or 大好き; 愛してる sounds very heavy and appears more in songs, films and letters. Very common is the attributive form 愛する + noun: 愛する人, 愛する家族, 愛する故郷. The object can also be music, nature or one's own country.

examples[].german: A weekly magazine wrote that the politician has a lover.
In the drama, the company president went on a trip with his mistress.
The Chinese word "愛人" means "wife" or "husband", but in Japanese it is different.
en.notes: 愛人 in present-day Japanese means the secret lover outside a marriage, i.e. an affair, and sounds negative. For a boyfriend or girlfriend in a normal relationship, 恋人 or 彼氏/彼女 is said. Typical are 愛人がいる and 愛人を作る. Caution for those who know Chinese: in the People's Republic of China, the same written word means "spouse".

en.meaning: to end; to die; (after verb stem) completely
examples[].german: I walked all day and was completely exhausted.
When I returned after a long time, my hometown had changed beyond recognition.
I got lost and was at my wits' end, but a kind person helped me.
en.notes: 果てる on its own is rather literary for "to come to an end" or "to die" (命が果てる). In everyday speech it is encountered mainly after a verb stem meaning "completely, to the extreme": 疲れ果てる "to be completely exhausted", 困り果てる "to be at a total loss", 変わり果てる "to change beyond recognition", あきれ果てる "to be utterly dumbfounded". It is intransitive; related are the noun 果て "end, farthest edge" (世界の果て) and 果てしない "endless".

examples[].german: I've had a fever since the day before yesterday.
The day before yesterday I watched a movie.
en.notes: 一昨日 is read おととい here and means the day before yesterday. おととい is the usual hiragana spelling of the same time expression. The word can stand without a particle; 一昨日から stresses a start on that day that continues up to the time of speaking. The attested reading いっさくじつ is more written and formal and is not practiced here. おととい has four short morae and is not おととし, "the year before last".

examples[].german: I will attend the meeting.
I will attend tomorrow's meeting.
I attended my cousin's wedding.
en.notes: 出席する means to be present at a scheduled event. The event takes に: 会議に出席する. 出席 alone is the noun "attendance". 欠席する is the opposite. The expression suits meetings, classes or a ceremony.

examples[].german: This is a photo of memories from my youth.
This movie depicts the youth of high school students.
I'm already forty, but I still feel young at heart.
en.notes: 青春 is youth as a phase of life, usually emotionally or nostalgically colored: school days, club activities, first love, dreams. Typical are 青春時代, 青春の思い出, 青春を楽しむ and 青春ドラマ/青春映画; literally it means "blue spring". For the quality of "youthfulness" people say 若さ, for young people 若者; childhood is 子どものころ. The word is a noun, not an adverb.

examples[].german: He is fluent in English.
She blabbed her friend's secret.
This paper is flimsy and tears easily.
en.notes: ペラペラ is onomatopoeic and colloquial. Best known is "to speak fluently": 英語がペラペラだ, ペラペラ話す, ペラペラになる. But it can also have the negative sense "to chatter away, to blab" (秘密をペラペラしゃべる), as well as "thin, flimsy" for paper or cloth (ペラペラの紙) and "to flip through quickly" (本をペラペラめくる). It is often written in hiragana too; formally, "fluent" is 流暢.

examples[].german: It seems he injured his head playing soccer.
I wear a helmet to protect my head.
I had an X-ray of my head taken at the hospital.
en.notes: 頭部 is the formal, technical word for the head as a body region and appears in medicine, news and police reports: 頭部を打つ, 頭部のけが, 頭部のレントゲン. In daily life people simply say 頭. By the same pattern there are 胸部 "chest area" and 腹部 "abdominal area". For the "head" of an organization, one does not use 頭部 but トップ or 〜長.

examples[].german: I hear that having something yellow on the west side of your house increases your financial luck.
There is a window on the west side.
en.notes: 西側 refers to the western side of a house, room or area. As a noun it takes に for the place and の before another noun: 西側の窓. 金運がアップするそうです in the first example reports a belief that was heard about luck and is not an established fact. The reading にしがわ here refers to the spatial west side.

examples[].german: Please teach me the Osaka dialect.
The Osaka dialect is interesting.
In the Osaka dialect, "arigatou" is sometimes said as "ookini".
en.notes: 大阪弁 is the dialect of Osaka, the best-known variety of the Kansai dialect (関西弁). Typical are ほんま "really", あかん "no good", おおきに "thanks" and negation in 〜へん (分からへん). One says 大阪弁で話す or 大阪弁をしゃべる. The suffix 〜弁 forms dialect names (博多弁, 東北弁); "dialect" in general is 方言.

examples[].german: I can speak the Kansai dialect.
My friend speaks in the Kansai dialect.
"Akan" in the Kansai dialect means "dame" (no good).
en.notes: 関西弁 is the umbrella term for the dialects of the Kansai region around 大阪, 京都 and 神戸, with sub-varieties such as 大阪弁 and 京都弁. Thanks to comedians on television, it is known all over Japan; typical are あかん, ほんま, なんでやねん and a pitch accent of its own. The counterpart is 標準語 or 共通語 "standard language". One says 関西弁を話す/しゃべる or 関西弁で話す.

examples[].german: This week I have to work on Saturday too.
I go shopping on Saturday.
en.notes: 土曜日 is Saturday. 土曜日に names a point in time for an action; 土曜日も adds this day as well. 今週は土曜日も仕事です says that you work on Saturdays this week too. In どようび, よう is a long o, hence doyōbi.

examples[].german: Next Sunday I have plans.
On Sunday I relax at home.
en.notes: 日曜日 is Sunday. 来週の日曜日 means the Sunday of next week. 日曜日は makes the day the topic. 予定があります says that you have plans; ゆっくりします can describe taking your time and relaxing. にちようび is written nichiyōbi with a long o.

examples[].german: Want to go for a drink after work this coming Monday?
Work starts on Monday.
en.notes: 月曜日 is Monday. 今度の月曜日 names the coming Monday. 仕事の後 places an action in time after work. 飲みに行かない？ is a familiar invitation to go for a drink. 月曜日から names Monday as the start; げつようび has a long o.

examples[].german: On Thursday I have piano from six o'clock.
There is a test on Thursday.
en.notes: 木曜日 is Thursday. 木曜日は names it as the topic, 木曜日に as the date of an event. 六時から means "from six o'clock". ピアノなんです can stand in conversation for a piano-lesson appointment; んです explains your own schedule. もくようび is written mokuyōbi.

examples[].german: I was absent because of illness.
I was absent from school because of illness.
I will be absent from next week's meeting.
en.notes: 欠席する means to be absent from an expected appointment. School, class or a meeting can take を: 学校を欠席する. A cause often follows with で, such as 病気で. The verb describes the absence; by itself it does not say whether the absence is excused.

examples[].german: What we should do on Wednesday can be roughly divided into three things.
I go home early on Wednesday.
en.notes: 水曜日 is Wednesday. 水曜日にするべきこと means things one should do on that day. 大きく分けて sorts them roughly into groups; 三つ names three tasks here. 水曜日は can make the day the topic of a personal plan. すいようび has the vowel sequence ui followed by a long o.

examples[].german: She is an international student from Canada.
There are many international students at the university.
en.notes: 留学生 is someone who studies abroad, such as an exchange student. The word does not necessarily imply an exchange program. カナダからの留学生 gives the origin with からの. 大学に留学生がいる names foreign students at a university. りゅう is a long u after the jointly pronounced sequence りゅ.

examples[].german: I like Japanese comedy.
I watched a comedy show and laughed.
My younger brother says he wants to become a comedian in the future.
en.notes: お笑い is Japanese comedy and entertainment humor, i.e. 漫才, sketches (コント) and 落語 on television and on stage. Typical are お笑い番組 "comedy show", お笑い芸人 "comedian" and お笑いコンビ "comedy duo". 喜劇, by contrast, is comedy as a theater or film genre, and コメディー refers rather to Western comedies. Laughter itself is 笑い, not お笑い.

examples[].german: When I said that in Japan people eat KFC for Christmas dinner, for some reason laughter broke out.
Laughter is good for your health.
en.notes: 笑い is the noun for laughter. 笑いが起きる means that laughter arises; 笑い声を聞く means to hear a laughing voice. The verb is 笑う. In the first example, a remark becomes an occasion for laughter; the sentence does not say that every person in Japan chooses this Christmas meal.

examples[].german: If you write me a proper IOU, I'm happy to lend you the money.
「パン」 is a loanword from Portuguese.
To use the city hall, you need to submit an application.
en.notes: 借用 is the formal word for "to borrow" and appears in contracts, applications and technical texts: 〜を借用する, 借用書 "IOU", 借用語 "loanword". In everyday speech one almost always says 借りる; "to borrow a book from the library" is 本を借りる, not 借用する. The counterpart "to lend" is formally 貸与, in everyday speech 貸す.

examples[].german: Cost-wise, a rented house is more advantageous.
I live in a rented house.
For the ten years since we got married, we have always lived in rented housing.
en.notes: 借家 is a rented house, usually a detached house (一戸建て), as opposed to an owned home, 持ち家. Typical are 借家に住む and 借家暮らし "to live in rented housing". For rental apartments in general one says 賃貸 (賃貸マンション) or アパート. In legal terms such as 借地借家法, 借家 is also read しゃっか.

examples[].german: The Nalanda monastery was the Mecca of Buddhism.
There is an old monastery in the mountains.
In that monastery, the monks get up at five o'clock every morning.
en.notes: 僧院 is a monastery where monks (僧, お坊さん) live and practice religion. It sounds literary and is used mainly for monasteries abroad, for example in Tibet, India or Europe. For Japanese Buddhist temples one says 寺 or お寺 in everyday speech, for Christian monasteries mostly 修道院. Typical are 僧院で暮らす and 古い僧院.

examples[].german: This book was written by a former Buddhist monk.
A Buddhist monk is doing religious training.
en.notes: 仏僧 refers to a Buddhist monk or cleric. 元仏僧 means a former Buddhist monk; 仏僧が修行をする describes religious practice. 方 and 書かれた in the first example express respect toward the author. Do not confuse ぶっそう with the identically read 物騒, "dangerous".

examples[].german: Shh! You can't say that!
Talking about age in front of her is taboo.
In wedding speeches, words like 「別れる」 or 「切れる」 are taboo.
en.notes: 禁句 is a word or topic that one should not bring up in a particular situation or in front of a particular person: 〜は禁句だ, 〜の前では禁句. A well-known example is wedding speeches, in which words like 別れる "to part" or 切れる "to be cut" are considered unlucky (忌み言葉). Broader is タブー "taboo" for actions and topics in general; words that are not broadcast on radio and TV are called 放送禁止用語.

examples[].german: This land is treated as divisible property.
Legally, divisible obligations and indivisible obligations are distinguished.
Things like money, whose value does not change when divided, are called divisible things in the Civil Code.
en.notes: 可分 means "divisible" and is a technical term, mainly in civil law: 可分債務 (divisible obligation), 可分物 (divisible thing), 可分給付. It usually appears as a prefix in compounds or with の (可分の財産). In everyday life one far more often meets the opposite 不可分, for example in 不可分の関係 ("inseparable relationship"). For "can be divided" in ordinary usage one says 分けられる or 分割できる.

examples[].german: It's dangerous here.
It's dangerous to walk alone at night.
en.notes: 危険 as a na-adjective describes something dangerous: 危険な場所. At the end of a sentence it is 危険です. An activity can become the topic with の, as in 夜一人で歩くのは危険です. As a noun, 危険 also means danger; the opposite is 安全. The examples are evaluations of a place and of an activity.

en.meaning: to be late; to arrive late
examples[].german: I was late for school.
The train was delayed and I was late.
en.notes: 遅刻する means to arrive later than the agreed or prescribed time. The destination takes に: 学校に遅刻する. It concerns a person's being late; the delay of a train is described by 電車が遅れる instead. 遅刻 alone is the noun "being late".

examples[].german: I don't have the courage to confess.
I confessed my feelings to the person I like.
He confessed to his mother a lie he had told long ago.
en.notes: 告白 in everyday life today mainly means "declaration of love": 好きな人に告白する, 告白される; afterwards one is often only officially a couple in Japan (付き合う). In youth slang it is shortened to 告る. It also means "to confess, reveal" with を: 秘密を告白する, 罪を告白する. A confession of a crime to the police, on the other hand, is usually 自白.

examples[].german: Did you see the preview for the next episode of that drama?
The company closed the factory without notice.
The teacher announced in advance that there would be a test next week.
en.notes: 予告 is an announcement in advance: 〜を予告する or 〜と予告する, 予告なしに or 予告なく "without warning". In film and television it means "preview": 次回予告 "preview of the next episode", 予告編 "trailer". Do not confuse with 予報 "forecast" (天気予報) and 予約 "reservation"; a general notice is お知らせ.

examples[].german: Smoking is bad for your health.
Smoking is prohibited here.
Excuse me, where is the smoking area?
en.notes: 喫煙 is the formal word for "smoking" and is encountered above all on signs and in official texts: 喫煙所 "smoking area", 喫煙席 "smoking seat", 喫煙者 "smoker". In conversation people almost always say たばこを吸う; 喫煙する sounds official. The counterpart is 禁煙 "no smoking; quitting smoking" - on signs it is usually simply 禁煙 rather than 喫煙禁止.

examples[].german: I like eating the morning set at a coffee shop.
Let's take a break at the coffee shop near the station.
en.notes: 喫茶店 refers to a café or tea room. 喫茶店で names the place of a break or meal. モーニング here means a breakfast offer at the café. 駅の近くの喫茶店 describes a café near the station. The small っ in きっさてん doubles the s: kissaten.

examples[].german: The newspaper reports that a new hospital will be built near the station.
The accident was also reported on the TV news.
You shouldn't believe everything the media report.
en.notes: 報じる "to report, announce" is a literary verb of news language: 新聞が〜と報じる "the newspaper reports that ...", 事故を報じる. Very common is the passive 報じられる "it is reported". In everyday speech people more often say 伝える or ニュースで言っていた; the related noun is 報道 or 報道する. The older variant 報ずる has the same meaning; the sense "to repay" is nowadays usually expressed with 報いる.

en.meaning: house-sitting; staying home to watch the house
examples[].german: I took a job house-sitting for 20,000 yen a day.
I stayed home while my parents were out.
Please leave a message on the answering machine.
en.notes: 留守番 means staying at home and looking after the house or apartment while the others are away: 留守番をする / 留守番する, typical with children: 一人で留守番する. To children one says kindly お留守番. 留守 alone is absence from home (留守にする "to be away"). The answering machine is 留守番電話, short 留守電.

examples[].german: I'm in Ginza now.
I enjoyed shopping in Ginza.
In Japan there are many shopping streets with the name "Ginza".
en.notes: 銀座 is the famous shopping and entertainment district in Tokyo with luxury shops and department stores: 銀座に行く, 銀座で買い物をする. Because Ginza is regarded as the epitome of a lively shopping street, many shopping streets throughout Japan are called 〜銀座 (e.g. 戸越銀座). As a place name it is always written in kanji.

examples[].german: I bought a station bento at the kiosk.
I ate a station bento on the Shinkansen.
The department store sells ekiben from all over the country.
en.notes: 駅弁 is a short form of 駅 and 弁当: a lunch box sold at train stations, often with regional specialties. You typically buy one before a longer trip (駅弁を買う) and eat it on the train, especially on the 新幹線. Department stores hold popular 駅弁大会 with bentos from all over Japan. A bento from a supermarket or convenience store is, by contrast, not a 駅弁.

examples[].german: I can't find Koichi's bow anywhere.
I hit the target with a bow.
My violin bow got old, so I bought a new one.
en.notes: 弓 is the bow as a weapon or sports equipment; the arrow is 矢. Typical combinations: 弓を引く "to draw the bow", 弓で矢を射る "to shoot with a bow". Traditional Japanese archery is called 弓道. 弓 also denotes the bow for string instruments: バイオリンの弓.

examples[].german: To write a good article, it is important to make a draft.
I saved the draft of the e-mail.
I sketch in pencil first and then draw with a pen.
en.notes: 下書き is a draft or preliminary sketch - for texts as well as for pictures (first sketch in pencil, then ink). You say 下書きをする / 下書きする or 〜の下書きを書く. In e-mail and apps, 下書き is the drafts folder: 下書きに保存する. The counterpart, the clean final version, is 清書.

en.meaning: to write in; to fill in
examples[].german: Whenever I have a new appointment, I make a point of writing it into my calendar right away.
I wrote my name in the document.
Please fill in the correct answer in the blank.
en.notes: 書き入れる means to write something into a designated place: the place with に, the content with を - カレンダーに予定を書き入れる, 空欄に答えを書き入れる. Considerably more common is the synonymous 書き込む, which is also used for posts on the internet; on forms you read the formal 記入する. There is no intransitive counterpart.

en.meaning: number of sheets; number of pieces
examples[].german: The minimum order quantity for stickers is 100 sheets.
Please check the number of copies.
There is a limit on the number of tickets one person can buy.
en.notes: 枚数 is the number of things counted with the counter 枚: sheets, copies, photos, tickets, shirts, plates. Typical are 枚数を数える / 確認する and 枚数制限 "limit on the number of pieces". When asking directly for the number, you say 何枚; for other things 数 or 個数, 人数 etc. is used.

examples[].german: I had my car washed at the gas station.
I washed my car on the weekend.
It's going to rain tomorrow, so I'll skip washing the car.
en.notes: 洗車 is washing a car; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 週末に洗車する. To name the car as an object, one says 車を洗う. Related are 洗車場 "car wash, washing area" and 洗車機 "automatic car wash"; at the gas station one often has the car washed: 洗車してもらう.

examples[].german: I feel like eating yakiniku today.
I went to eat yakiniku with my friends.
At a yakiniku restaurant, you grill the meat yourself.
en.notes: 焼き肉 is the grilling of bite-sized pieces of meat at the table, very popular in Japan and similar to Korean barbecue; one goes 焼き肉に行く or to a 焼き肉屋 and grills the meat oneself. In restaurant names it is often written 焼肉 without き. In general it can also simply mean "grilled meat". Grilling outdoors is, by contrast, バーベキュー.

examples[].german: I thought I saw black smoke, and it turns out there's a fire in that apartment building over there!
Black smoke is rising from the factory.
An old bus was driving along belching black smoke.
en.notes: 黒煙 is a written-language word for "black smoke", as known from news about fires and accidents: 黒煙が上がる "black smoke rises", 黒煙を出す. In conversation people usually just say 黒い煙. White smoke is correspondingly 白煙.

examples[].german: What was the name of that Zen temple again?
I visited a Zen temple in Kyoto.
I experienced zazen at a Zen temple.
en.notes: 禅寺 is a temple of Zen Buddhism; note the reading でら (voicing of てら). In general, 寺 or politely お寺 is said for a temple. At many 禅寺, visitors can try 座禅 (seated meditation). Well-known examples are many temples in Kyoto and Kamakura.

examples[].german: He is a Zen monk.
The Zen monk is meditating quietly.
That Zen monk gets up at four every morning and cleans the temple.
en.notes: 禅僧 refers to a monk or priest of Zen Buddhism; 僧 alone is a somewhat formal word for Buddhist monks. In everyday speech one says お坊さん. 禅僧 is encountered mainly in books, documentaries and explanations about temples, often together with 座禅 and 修行 "ascetic training".

examples[].german: People of many different races live in this town.
All people are equal regardless of race.
Racial discrimination is not acceptable.
en.notes: 人種 is the (biologically conceived) human race, today mainly in expressions such as 人種差別 "racism, racial discrimination" and 人種に関係なく "regardless of race". For ethnic groups one says 民族, for nationality 国籍. Colloquially, 人種 is used jokingly for a "type of person": あの人たちは別の人種だ.

examples[].german: Isn't that practically the same as not having done it?
The two quantities are equal.
At this school, everyone has an equal chance.
en.notes: 等しい is a rather literary い-adjective for "equal", especially for quantities, lengths and values: 長さが等しい, AはBに等しい. Very common is the figurative phrase 〜に等しい "as good as, tantamount to": ないに等しい "practically nothing". The adverb form 等しく means "equally". In everyday speech, "equal, the same" is usually 同じ.

examples[].german: So 「イコール」 is also called 「等号」! I didn't know that.
We use the equals sign in mathematical formulas.
I forgot to write the equals sign on the test and lost points.
en.notes: 等号 is the technical term for the equals sign "=" from math class; in everyday speech the sign is usually read as イコール. The inequality signs < and > are called 不等号. Typical: 等号で結ぶ "to connect with an equals sign", 等号を書く.

examples[].german: I want to increase my savings.
I want to expand my vocabulary.
en.notes: 増やす is the transitive Godan verb for "to increase". The thing increased takes を: 貯金を増やす, 語彙を増やす. 増える, in contrast, describes an increase with no acting subject named. The て-form is 増やして; 減らす is the opposite.

en.meaning: first class; first prize; first place
examples[].german: How much is the first prize in this lottery?
I booked a first-class room on the ferry.
I came in first in the foot race at the sports day.
en.notes: 一等 means "first rank, first class, first prize": 宝くじの一等 "jackpot of a lottery", 一等賞, 一等になる "to come first". On ferries there are still 一等 and 二等 as classes; on trains the first class is now called グリーン車. 一等地 is a "prime location". For placement in a competition, 一位 or colloquially 一番 is more common.

examples[].german: We had an evacuation drill at school.
We do tough training every day.
Guide dogs are trained over a long period of time.
en.notes: 訓練 is systematic, often physical training or a drill to practice an ability or behavior: 避難訓練 "evacuation drill", 軍事訓練, 犬を訓練する "to train a dog". As a する-verb it is transitive; the passive 訓練される is common. For practicing sports, music or languages one rather says 練習, for fitness トレーニング, for in-house company training 研修.

examples[].german: How do they determine whether it's brain death?
I was pronounced brain dead.
Whether brain death is considered death of a person differs from country to country.
en.notes: 脳死 is the medical and legal term for brain death: 脳死と判定される "to be declared brain dead", 脳死の状態. It plays a role above all in discussions about organ donation, because in Japan it was long disputed whether brain death counts as the death of a person. Cardiac death is 心臓死; "to die" in general is 死ぬ / 亡くなる.

examples[].german: Use your tiny brain and think hard!
After the exam, my brain is so tired I can't think about anything.
I can't stand scenes in zombie movies where brains come out.
en.notes: 脳みそ (also 脳味噌) is a colloquial word for the brain or brain matter and figuratively for "brains": 脳みそを使え "Use your head!" - this often sounds rude or mocking. In neutral or medical contexts, 脳 is used. With 疲れる it jokingly describes mental exhaustion.

examples[].german: That's media brainwashing.
Please be careful not to be brainwashed.
I watched this commercial every day, got brainwashed, and ended up memorizing the song.
en.notes: 洗脳 is "brainwashing"; as a する-verb it is transitive (人を洗脳する), and very often used in the passive 洗脳される. It is spoken of seriously in connection with cults or propaganda, but colloquially also in an exaggerated, joking way, for example when an advertising jingle won't leave your head or you are completely taken in by someone's opinion.

examples[].german: Who scribbled here?
You must not draw graffiti on the wall.
During class, I was doodling cats in my notebook.
en.notes: 落書き covers everything that is scribbled without permission or on the side: graffiti on walls, scribbles in textbooks and harmless doodles in a notebook. The place takes に: 壁に落書きする, ノートに落書きをする. Do not confuse with 下書き "draft". For graffiti as an art form, グラフィティ is also said.

examples[].german: My father is a pizza delivery person. He can deliver pizzas faster than anyone.
I had the package delivered.
The newspaper is delivered around five o'clock every morning.
en.notes: 配達する means to bring goods or mail to the recipient: 新聞を配達する, ピザの配達, 郵便配達; the person is the 配達員. From the customer's point of view one says 配達してもらう, from the goods' point of view 配達される. More general is 届ける "to bring, to deliver"; 送る is "sending" from the sender's side, and 配送 is more the logistical delivery.

examples[].german: Because of a miscommunication, it turned out to be a pink car.
The transmission of information is important.
I passed the manager's instructions on to everyone on the team.
en.notes: 伝達 is the formal passing on of information, instructions or signals, especially in companies and organizations: 情報伝達, 伝達事項 "announcements", 伝達ミス "communication error". As a する-verb: 指示を伝達する. In everyday speech people simply say 伝える. In biology and technology it also denotes the transmission of signals (神経の伝達).

examples[].german: First, I'll upload the still images.
Please hold still in front of the camera.
Please open the door only after the car has come to a complete stop.
en.notes: 静止 is a rather literary, technical word for "standstill, rest"; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 静止する "to stand still, come to a standstill". Well known are 静止画 "still image" (opposite 動画) and 静止衛星 "geostationary satellite". In everyday speech people say 止まる or じっとする; 静止 is heard more in announcements, instructions and technology.

examples[].german: With so many cute cats like this, I'm not confident I can keep my composure.
Please stay calm.
He lied with a perfectly calm expression.
en.notes: 平静 means "calm, composure, self-possession" and is mostly used as a noun: 平静を保つ "to keep calm", 平静を失う "to lose one's composure"; as a な-adjective 平静な態度 / 平静な顔. It sounds somewhat elevated. In everyday speech one rather says 落ち着く; 冷静, by contrast, emphasizes a cool, level head. Do not confuse it with the identically read era name 平成.

examples[].german: Let's reduce our garbage.
I want to cut down my food costs.
en.notes: 減らす means to actively reduce an amount. The thing reduced takes を: ゴミを減らす, 食費を減らす. It is a transitive Godan verb ending in す. 減る, in contrast, means that something becomes less. The て-form is 減らして.

examples[].german: He is the hope of all humankind.
I think about the future of humankind.
Humans first went to the moon in 1969.
en.notes: 人類 is humankind as a whole or as a biological species: 人類の歴史, 人類の未来, 全人類. It sounds matter-of-fact to solemn. 人間, by contrast, means the individual human or people in general, and 人々 "people". The science of humankind is called 人類学.

examples[].german: That's a relative's company.
Relatives gather at New Year.
That person is a distant relative of mine.
en.notes: 親類 means "relatives, kin" and is somewhat more formal than 親戚, which is much more common in everyday speech. Typical: 遠い親類 "distant relatives", 親類が集まる, 親類の家. In fixed expressions such as 親類縁者 "relatives and kin" only 親類 occurs. For one's own immediate family, 家族 is used.

examples[].german: If you follow the instructions, you'll be fine.
Please read the manual before using it.
The medicine's instruction sheet says to take it three times a day.
en.notes: 説明書 is a written instruction or description that comes with a product: 説明書を読む, 説明書どおりに組み立てる. For appliances it is more precisely 取扱説明書, colloquially 取説; for medicines it is the package insert. Work instructions within a company are more often called マニュアル.

examples[].german: In this town, some people still call trains "kisha".
In the past, I traveled by steam train.
A sightseeing steam train runs only on weekends.
en.notes: 汽車 originally meant the steam train and today sounds old-fashioned or nostalgic, for example in children's songs and memories. In regions without electrified lines (such as Hokkaido or Shikoku), older people still call diesel trains 汽車 too. The normal expression otherwise is 電車, or 列車 in general. Do not confuse with the homophone 記者 "journalist".

examples[].german: You can get to Oshima on a Tokai Kisen ship.
A large steamship is docked in the harbor.
In 1853, an American steamship came to Japan.
en.notes: 汽船 is the steamship; today the word belongs mainly to historical contexts (the arrival of American steamships in 1853) and lives on in the names of shipping companies, e.g. 東海汽船. In daily life people simply say 船, or フェリー for car ferries. The counterpart on rails is 汽車.

examples[].german: On Tuesday evenings I attend a cooking class.
I go to the hospital on Tuesday.
en.notes: 火曜日 is Tuesday. 火曜日の夜 connects the day and the evening with の. 通っています describes the regular attendance of a cooking class here. 火曜日に gives a single Tuesday appointment. かようび contains a long o and is written kayōbi.

examples[].german: It's finally Friday.
On Friday evening I watch a movie.
en.notes: 金曜日 is Friday. ようやく金曜日です expresses relief that this day has finally arrived. 金曜日の夜 means Friday evening. The n before y is separated by an apostrophe in romanization: kin'yōbi. よう contains a long o.

examples[].german: Is it possible to make a reservation for three people on Friday evening at seven o'clock?
That is possible.
Card payment is possible at this hotel.
en.notes: 可能 is a な-adjective/noun for "possible, feasible" and sounds more formal than できる: 予約は可能ですか, 〜することが可能です, 可能な限り "as far as possible". The opposite is 不可能. "Possibility, probability" is 可能性 (〜の可能性がある). In conversation one usually simply asks できますか.

examples[].german: This lid won't close properly.
The shop closes at ten o'clock.
en.notes: 閉まる is an intransitive godan verb: 閉まります, 閉まって. A lid or door closes; a shop shuts. With が you name the thing that closes. 閉める, by contrast, describes actively closing an object. 閉まらないんだけど reports a problem in casual speech.

examples[].german: Where on earth did Koichi and the others go?
The children are playing.
en.notes: 〜達 is usually written as たち and mainly marks a group of people or animals. 子供達 means "the children". After a person's name, on the other hand, it means that person together with others: コウイチ達 means "Koichi and the others". It is not a plural marker that is automatically required for every noun. The sign 〜 shows the place of the preceding expression and is not pronounced; 達 is the kanji spelling of this suffix.

examples[].german: The injury has healed.
Has your cold gotten better yet?
en.notes: 治る means recovering from or healing of an illness or injury. It is an intransitive godan verb ending in る; the thing that heals takes が. The て-form is 治って. 直る, with the same reading, often describes a mistake or a broken object being put right again.

examples[].german: Some kind of warning message popped up... what should I do?
The doctor warned him to quit smoking.
In the soccer match, a player received a caution from the referee.
en.notes: 警告 is an explicit warning or caution: 警告する, 〜に〜ように警告する, 警告を受ける / 出す. Common are 警告文 "warning notice" and 警告音 "warning sound"; in sports, 警告 is the caution (yellow card). 注意 is milder ("notice, admonition"). Official severe-weather warnings, on the other hand, are 警報 (大雨警報) or, weaker, 注意報.

en.meaning: to harden; to set; to freeze (computer)
examples[].german: The pudding should be setting about now.
The cement has hardened.
My computer suddenly froze and I can't do anything.
en.notes: 固まる is intransitive: something becomes hard or firm by itself (セメントが固まる, プリンが固まる); the transitive counterpart is 固める "to harden, firm up". Figuratively, plans or opinions "firm up" (予定が固まる), people huddle together (みんなで固まる) or freeze in fright. Colloquially it is also said of computers and apps that hang: パソコンが固まった.

examples[].german: I'm not wearing my glasses now, so I can't see distant things well.
I can see mountains in the distance.
Thank you for coming from far away.
en.notes: 遠く is the noun and adverb form of 遠い and means "the distance, far away": 遠くに見える, 遠くの町, 遠くへ行く, 遠くから来る. The counterpart is 近く. Before a noun, 遠く needs の (遠くの山), whereas 遠い stands directly before it (遠い山). Figuratively, 遠く及ばない means "to be far from matching".

examples[].german: This is a Japanese lullaby.
My mother sang me a lullaby.
The teacher's voice is just like a lullaby and makes me sleepy.
en.notes: 子守歌 is a lullaby; 子守 means "looking after children". One says 子守歌を歌う; the spelling 子守唄 is equally common. Jokingly, a monotonous speech or a boring lesson is called 子守歌, because one falls asleep during it. Well-known traditional examples are 江戸の子守歌 or 五木の子守歌.

examples[].german: The dictionary form of 「食べた」 is 「食べる」.
Let's learn the dictionary forms of verbs.
If you add 「ことができる」 to the dictionary form, it means "can".
en.notes: 辞書形 is a term from teaching Japanese to foreigners: the basic form of a verb as it appears in the dictionary (食べる, 行く). Many patterns attach to it, e.g. 〜ことができる or 〜前に. In Japanese school grammar the same form is called 終止形 or 基本形. Related terms are ます形, て形 and ない形.

examples[].german: Fortunately, an empty taxi came by just then.
Fortunately, there were no injuries.
I would be grateful if you could send a reply.
en.notes: 幸い is used today mainly adverbially: 幸い / 幸いにも / 幸いなことに "fortunately, luckily" - somewhat more formal than 運よく or よかったことに. In business letters, 〜ていただければ幸いです "I would be grateful if ..." is a set polite request. 不幸中の幸い means "a blessing in disguise". For a personal feeling of happiness one says 幸せ.

examples[].german: Entry by anyone other than authorized persons is prohibited.
Taking photographs is prohibited in this place.
Part-time jobs are prohibited at this school.
en.notes: 禁じる "to prohibit" is literary and often appears on signs and in rules: 〜を禁じる, especially in the passive 禁じられている "is prohibited". The older variant 禁ずる has the same meaning. In everyday speech people say 禁止する, 禁止です or simply だめ. Figuratively it also means "to suppress feelings", for example in 涙を禁じ得ない.

examples[].german: The larynx is an important part for producing the voice.
My grandfather had surgery for laryngeal cancer.
The doctor looked at my larynx with a small camera.
en.notes: 喉頭 is the medical technical term for the larynx, e.g. in 喉頭がん "laryngeal cancer" or 喉頭炎 "laryngitis". In everyday speech one simply says のど (のどが痛い). The ear, nose and throat department is called 耳鼻咽喉科 (not 耳鼻喉頭科); the pharynx is 咽頭.

examples[].german: My father is a master of candy sculpture.
I bought a candy sculpture at the festival.
The craftsman used scissors to make a rabbit candy sculpture in no time.
en.notes: 飴細工 is a traditional craft: soft, hot sugar mass is shaped into animals and figures with the hands and scissors at lightning speed; you often see it at stalls at temple festivals. 飴細工 denotes both the technique and the finished figure; the craftsman is 飴細工の職人. Figuratively, something that is impressive only on the outside is also called 飴細工.

en.meaning: to bully; to pick on; to tease
examples[].german: Kyoko is picking on me.
You must not bully the weak.
It seems my younger brother is being bullied at school.
en.notes: 苛める is almost always written in kana: いじめる "to bully, to torment, to harass". It ranges from teasing among children to systematic bullying; the noun いじめ "bullying" is a major social issue. Typical: 〜をいじめる, passive いじめられる. Harmless teasing is rather からかう. Figuratively: 体をいじめる "to demand a lot of one's body".

examples[].german: I wish for happiness.
I wish for world peace.
I ask that you write your name here.
en.notes: 願う can express a wish or denote a sincere request. The thing wished for takes を: 幸せを願う, 平和を願う. It is a transitive Godan verb ending in う; 願って is the て-form. お願いします is a common polite request that is translated idiomatically in many situations.

examples[].german: What was your first love like?
I won't forget the memories of my first love.
At a class reunion, I met my first love for the first time in twenty years.
en.notes: 初恋 is the first love, both the experience and the person: 初恋の人 / 初恋の相手 "my first love". One says 初恋をする or speaks of 初恋の思い出. A well-known saying is 初恋は実らない "First love never comes true". To fall in love in general is 恋をする or 好きになる.

examples[].german: Wow, my heart is pounding like crazy.
My heart was pounding before I confessed.
My heart is pounding after running.
en.notes: ドキドキ imitates the pounding of the heart and describes excitement, nervousness, fear or being in love: ドキドキする, 胸がドキドキする. It is also written in hiragana as どきどき. ワクワク, by contrast, emphasizes joyful anticipation, and ハラハラ anxious watching when something might go wrong. As an adverb: ドキドキしながら待つ.

examples[].german: If you had to lose one of the five senses, which would you choose? Please also tell me why.
I enjoy cooking using all five senses.
As you get older, your five senses gradually weaken.
en.notes: 五感 are the five senses: 視覚 (sight), 聴覚 (hearing), 嗅覚 (smell), 味覚 (taste) and 触覚 (touch). Typical are 五感を使う, 五感で楽しむ "to enjoy with all the senses" - popular in advertising and travel brochures. The "sixth sense", intuition, is called 第六感.

examples[].german: I'm sick and tired of the politicians' double-talk.
You can't trust someone who is double-tongued.
He is a two-faced man who tells his boss and his subordinates different things.
en.notes: 二枚舌 literally means "two tongues" and refers to someone who tells different people contradictory things or does not keep promises. The fixed phrase is 二枚舌を使う ("to speak with a forked tongue"); attributively: 二枚舌の政治家, 二枚舌外交. It is clearly derogatory; similar are 裏表がある ("to have two faces") and 嘘つき ("liar"), though 二枚舌 specifically stresses the contradiction.

en.meaning: melee; free-for-all (in a fight or game)
examples[].german: That game was a rarely seen free-for-all.
The game turned into a wild fight.
The next election has many candidates, so it looks like it will be a wide-open race.
en.notes: 乱戦 is a chaotic fight, a melee in which everyone fights in confusion. In sports reporting it refers to a wild game with many goals or constant changes of lead (試合が乱戦になる); in elections, an open race with many candidates. The word is rather journalistic and literary. A simple fight is 戦い, a close-quarters man-to-man fight rather 接近戦.

examples[].german: A magazine wrote about a celebrity orgy party.
The men who held an orgy party were arrested by the police.
en.notes: 乱交 refers to sexual promiscuity with changing partners, or group sex; it is most often encountered in 乱交パーティー "sex party" in tabloid media and police reports. The word is crude and matter-of-fact and does not belong in everyday conversation. As a する-verb it is intransitive, but it is rarely used that way. The similar-looking 乱戦, by contrast, means "melee".

examples[].german: I'm collecting the special editions of this comic.
I bought a special issue of the magazine.
The answers to the questions are in the separate booklet.
en.notes: 別冊 is a separate volume or supplement: 別冊付録 "enclosed special booklet" of a magazine, 別冊 as a special edition of a magazine (also in titles of manga magazines such as 別冊マーガレット). In textbooks and workbooks, the solutions are often in the 別冊: 答えは別冊にあります.

examples[].german: I've never seen such an irresponsible person.
Please don't do sloppy work.
Come on, that's enough!
en.notes: いい加減 as a na-adjective means "sloppy, careless, irresponsible": いい加減な人, いい加減な仕事, いい加減な返事. Very common is the exclamation いい加減にしなさい / いい加減にして "That's enough now!". As an adverb it means "quite, really getting to the point of": いい加減疲れた. Similarly derogatory, 適当 is used colloquially. The literal meaning "just right" is nowadays heard almost only in 湯加減 "bath water temperature" (いい湯加減).

en.meaning: good and evil; right and wrong
examples[].german: At this age, surely you know right from wrong.
I can tell right from wrong.
Teaching children right and wrong is the parents' job.
en.notes: 善悪 means "good and evil" or "right and wrong" and is a rather literary, abstract word. Typical are 善悪の判断 "moral judgment", 善悪を区別する or 善悪が分かる "to be able to tell good from evil". In casual conversation people often say the simpler いいことと悪いこと. It is used almost only as a noun with の, を or が.

examples[].german: I'm not good at acting in a group.
Elementary school students go to school in groups every morning.
I've already gotten used to communal life in the dormitory.
en.notes: 集団 is a (usually larger) group or mass of people or animals and sounds more matter-of-fact than グループ. Typical are 集団で行動する "to act as a group", 集団生活 "communal life" (school, dormitory, army) and 集団登校 "going to school together in groups". An organized group with a common purpose, for example for trips, is rather 団体 (団体旅行). In everyday speech, for groups of friends one simply says グループ.

examples[].german: My clothes got dirty.
My clothes got dirty from the mud.
The windows got dirty from the rain.
en.notes: 汚れる with the reading よごれる means "to get dirty". It is an intransitive ichidan verb: the clothes take が, and the cause takes, for example, で. 汚す describes someone making something dirty. The also possible reading けがれる belongs to a different usage and is not taught here.

examples[].german: Only people who pass the entrance test can join this team.
I joined a soccer team.
My younger sister joined a local theater troupe last year.
en.notes: 入団する means "to join a group whose name ends in 団": sports teams (especially professional teams, 球団), theater troupes (劇団), orchestras (楽団) or scouts. The destination takes に: チームに入団する. The opposite is 退団 "leaving". For school clubs, 入部 is said, for companies 入社 and for schools 入学; in daily life, simply 入る also works.

examples[].german: His father is a police officer.
A police officer is directing traffic.
en.notes: 警官 is a noun for a police officer. It can name an occupation with です or だ. 警官が names the person as the one acting. 警官の links the word to a noun. けいかん contains the vowel sequence ei; it is written keikan.

examples[].german: That man seems to be suspected of murder.
The suspect was arrested.
I hear the man admits to the charges.
en.notes: 容疑 is "suspicion of a crime" in the police and legal sense and is typical of news language. Set patterns are Xの容疑で逮捕される "to be arrested on suspicion of X", Xに容疑がかかる "to be under suspicion", 容疑を認める／否認する "to admit/deny the charges". 容疑者 is the "suspect". For everyday suspecting or distrust, 疑い or the verb 疑う is used instead.

en.meaning: to put on; to wear (legwear, footwear)
examples[].german: My younger brother is wearing blue pants today.
I put on new shoes.
Please put on slippers here before entering the room.
en.notes: 履く is used for shoes and clothing on the lower body, such as pants; the kana spelling はく is also possible. For pants and skirts you also see 穿く, while 履く is especially used for shoes. This transitive godan verb forms 履きます and 履いて, read hakimasu and haite. 履いている describes the state of wearing. With を you name the garment. For a shirt you use 着る; the identically read 掃く means "to sweep".

examples[].german: Could I have one wakame soup, please?
I put wakame in the miso soup.
Dried wakame is soaked in water before use.
en.notes: わかめ is an edible brown seaweed and a standard ingredient in みそ汁, salads and soups. The word is almost always written in hiragana (on packages also ワカメ); the kanji 若布 is rarely seen. Usually one buys 乾燥わかめ, which is soaked in water before use. Do not confuse it with 海苔 (dried seaweed sheets for sushi) and 昆布 (kombu for broth).

examples[].german: If the students were robots, they'd hand in their homework properly, and it would probably be easier for the teachers.
There are five hundred students at this school.
en.notes: 生徒 is a noun for a pupil or student. 生徒が names them as the subject; 生徒の links them to a noun. 五百人の生徒 gives the number with the person counter 人. だったら can introduce a hypothetical condition. The reading せいと is seito, with no additional な before a noun.

examples[].german: We are Buddhists.
Many Japanese people are Buddhists.
Both Buddhists and Christians live in this town.
en.notes: 仏教徒 is made up of 仏教 "Buddhism" and 徒 "follower" and means "Buddhist". 'キリスト教徒' and 'イスラム教徒' are formed the same way. When talking about one's own family, one often rather says うちは仏教です, because many Japanese do not see themselves as strictly religious, although funerals are mostly Buddhist. More general for "believers" are 信者 and 信徒.

examples[].german: This religion has followers all over the world.
The church has many believers.
The temple's followers gathered and prepared for the festival.
en.notes: 信徒 refers to the believers or lay members of a religious community, often as opposed to priests, and sounds rather formal. More common in daily life is 信者, which is also used figuratively for fervent fans. In compounds for individual religions, 教徒 is usually used (仏教徒, キリスト教徒). Do not confuse with 神道 (しんとう, with a long o) "Shinto".

examples[].german: At university you can gain not only knowledge but also many human relationships.
I was able to obtain good results.
I decided on studying abroad only after getting my parents' permission.
en.notes: 得る is a formal, rather literary verb for "to obtain, to gain, to receive". Typical objects are 知識, 経験, 情報, 結果 and 許可 (許可を得る "to obtain permission"). In everyday speech one usually says もらう or 手に入れる. In written language the dictionary form is also read うる, especially as an auxiliary verb meaning "to be possible": あり得る "to be possible", but the negative is always あり得ない.

examples[].german: She gave a presentation to persuade her boss.
I persuaded my parents.
His talk is persuasive.
en.notes: 説得する means "to talk someone into or out of something, to convince (with words)" so that they do or don't do something: 親を説得する, 〜するように説得する. When one is persuaded oneself, the passive 説得される is used. Do not confuse it with 納得する, which means "to be satisfied oneself, to accept something". 説得力 is "persuasiveness": 説得力がある "convincing".

en.meaning: to make a mistake; to mix up
examples[].german: I got the phone number wrong.
Sorry, I got your name wrong.
I mistook salt for sugar.
en.notes: 間違える means to do something wrongly or to mix up two things. The thing affected takes を, for example 名前を間違える. It is a transitive ichidan verb; 間違えて is the て-form. The construction と間違える names what one mistakes something for.

examples[].german: The project ended in a complete failure.
The presentation was a total flop.
I made a cake for the first time, but it was a total failure.
en.notes: 大失敗 is a "huge flop, fiasco" - 失敗 intensified by 大. Typical are 〜は大失敗に終わる "ended in a fiasco", 〜が大失敗だった and, as a する-verb, 大失敗する "to go totally wrong". In casual conversation one often hears 大失敗しちゃった. For small mistakes, ミス or 間違い is said, not 大失敗.

examples[].german: You can easily imagine something like that, right?
This problem is not easy.
Isn't there an easier method?
en.notes: 容易 is a formal な-adjective for "easy, simple"; in everyday speech one usually says 簡単 or やさしい. Typical are 容易に想像できる "easily imaginable" and 容易ではない "anything but easy". Note: 用意 "preparation" (用意する) is read exactly the same, ようい, but has nothing to do with it.

examples[].german: I am against violence.
Violence is not tolerated.
He has never used violence against anyone.
en.notes: 暴力 is (usually physical) "violence". To use violence is 暴力をふるう, not 暴力をする. Common compounds are 家庭内暴力 "domestic violence" and 暴力団 "gang, yakuza". For rough, inconsiderate behavior or speech, on the other hand, the adjective 乱暴な is used.

examples[].german: Where did you learn such rough language?
Please don't handle the luggage roughly.
He drives recklessly, so I don't want to ride with him.
en.notes: 乱暴 is used mainly as a な-adjective: "rough, rude, inconsiderate" - 乱暴な言葉 "rough language", 乱暴に扱う "to handle roughly", 運転が乱暴だ "to drive recklessly". The verb 乱暴する "to become violent" is rare and can euphemistically also mean sexual violence, so it is better avoided. The noun for "violence" itself is 暴力.

examples[].german: I love onigiri with pickled plum.
I put a pickled plum in my lunch box.
Pickled plums are sour, but they are said to be good for you.
en.notes: 梅干し are ume fruits pickled in salt and dried (more a type of apricot than plums), very salty and sour (すっぱい). They are eaten in おにぎり, in the お弁当 (for example one umeboshi in the middle of the rice) or with rice porridge. The second part comes from 干す "to dry"; it is also written 梅干. Often just 梅 is said for short: 梅のおにぎり.

examples[].german: The symbol for subtraction is 「−」.
I learned subtraction in arithmetic class.
This problem calls for addition, not subtraction.
en.notes: 減法 is the mathematical technical term for "subtraction" and appears in textbooks alongside 加法 "addition", 乗法 "multiplication" and 除法 "division". In everyday speech and in elementary school lessons one almost always says 引き算 (and 足し算, 掛け算, 割り算). The matching verb is 引く "to subtract".

examples[].german: The Girls' Festival is coming soon, so I put out the hina dolls.
On the Boys' Festival in May, people eat chimaki.
Japan has five traditional seasonal festivals.
en.notes: 節句 are the traditional seasonal festivals; the five classical ones (五節句) fall on 1.1./7.1., 3.3., 5.5., 7.7. and 9.9. Still alive today are mainly 桃の節句 on March 3 (ひな祭り, the Girls' Festival with hina dolls) and 端午の節句 on May 5 (Boys' Festival, today こどもの日). The word is almost always used as X の節句.

examples[].german: Employees came streaming out of the office exit one after another.
Customers are arriving one after another.
New stores are opening one after another near the station.
en.notes: 続々(と) means "one after another, in rapid succession" and is used with verbs of movement or events such as 来る, 集まる, 出てくる, 届く or オープンする. It emphasizes that many come one after another in a short time, and sounds somewhat like a news report; more neutral and more common is 次々(と). The identically pronounced ぞくぞく in kana, on the other hand, describes a shiver or tingle from cold or excitement.

examples[].german: Education is important.
The education of children is very important.
en.notes: 教育 can mean school education and teaching, or the upbringing of a child. 子供の教育 can therefore mean "education" or "raising children", depending on the situation. Here the noun is taught; with する it can also form a verb. The reading きょういく is written kyōiku.

examples[].german: I can't remember the lyrics from here.
The lyrics of this song are lovely.
May I sing while looking at the lyrics?
en.notes: 歌詞 are the "lyrics". The counterpart is 曲 "melody, piece of music"; correspondingly, 作詞 means "to write the lyrics" and 作曲 "to compose". Typical are 歌詞を覚える, 歌詞を見ながら歌う and 歌詞カード (the lyrics booklet of a CD). Do not confuse with the homophone お菓子 (かし, "sweets").

examples[].german: How did Mike learn the numerals?
Japanese numerals are complicated.
The 本 in 「三本」 is not a numeral but a counter.
en.notes: 数詞 is the grammatical technical term "numeral" (一, 二, 百, ひとつ ...). To be distinguished from it is 助数詞, the "counter" or counting unit word such as 本, 枚 or 匹, which is attached to the number. In everyday speech people rather speak of 数 "number" or 数字 "digit"; 数詞 is encountered mainly in grammar lessons.

examples[].german: She was humming that song without realizing it.
I did it without being aware of it.
I was lost in thought, and before I knew it I had arrived in front of my house.
en.notes: 無意識 is mostly used adverbially as 無意識に or 無意識のうちに "unconsciously, without noticing" and attributively with の: 無意識の行動, 無意識のくせ. The opposite is 意識的に "consciously, deliberately". For "unconscious" in the medical sense, everyday speech rather says 意識がない or 意識不明. In psychology, 無意識 also means "the unconscious".

examples[].german: The company president helped the company with his private funds.
He used his own fortune to build a school.
Please keep company money and private funds strictly separate.
en.notes: 私財 is a person's "private property, own money", as opposed to company or public funds. The word is formal and often appears in the set phrase 私財を投じる "to invest one's own fortune", usually for a charitable purpose. In everyday speech one simply says 自分のお金 or 財産.

examples[].german: It is not good to take on debt when you don't know whether you can repay it.
The debt must be repaid.
The shop didn't do well, and a large debt was left behind.
en.notes: 借財 is a literary, somewhat old-fashioned word for "debt, loan". In everyday speech one almost always says 借金. Typical are 借財をする "to take on debt", 借財を返す／返済する "to repay debt" and 借財が残る "debt remains". In casual speech, 借財 therefore sounds stiff.

examples[].german: Accidents keep happening one after another on this road.
It rained for three days in a row.
I look forward to the TV series every morning.
en.notes: 連続 means "succession, series". Very common is number + time unit + 連続(で): 三日連続で "three days in a row", 二年連続優勝 "champion two years in a row". As a verb, 連続する is mostly intransitive: 事故が連続している "accidents are piling up". Compounds include 連続ドラマ "TV series". More neutral for "to go on, to continue" is 続く.

en.meaning: to take along; to bring (a person)
examples[].german: Most people at this event were carrying babies.
I take my child to the park.
Is it okay to bring a friend to the house?
en.notes: 連れる means "to take someone along, to be accompanied by" and takes only people or animals as its object. It almost always appears in the て-form: 連れて行く "to take (there)", 連れて来る "to bring (here)", 連れて帰る "to take home". Attributively one says 子どもを連れた人 "people with a child". For objects, 持って行く／持って来る is used instead.

examples[].german: That zaibatsu dominated the Japanese economy before the war.
After the war, the zaibatsu were dissolved on the orders of GHQ.
In South Korea, large chaebol-affiliated companies are at the center of the economy.
en.notes: 財閥 refers to the large conglomerates controlled by a family through a holding company, such as 三井, 三菱 or 住友, which dominated the Japanese economy before 1945; after the war they were broken up in the 財閥解体 ("dissolution of the zaibatsu"). Their successors are today more often called 企業グループ or 系列. The word is still alive for the Korean chaebol (韓国の財閥) and colloquially for "filthy-rich people": 財閥の御曹司 ("son of a rich family").

examples[].german: Is ranking really that important?
The test rankings were announced.
The team's position in the league rose to third place.
en.notes: 順位 is the "placement, rank" in a competition or ranking. Typical are 順位が上がる／下がる, 順位をつける "to make a ranking" and 優先順位 "priority". The concrete place is given with 〜位: 一位, 三位. For a simple order, for example when queuing, 順番 is used instead.

en.meaning: in descending order of size; largest first
examples[].german: Let's load the luggage into the car in order of size, largest first.
Please arrange the numbers from largest to smallest.
I sorted the files by size, largest first.
en.notes: 大きい順 is a productive formation from adjective + 順 "order": "in order of size, from the largest to the smallest" or, for numbers, "descending". It mostly takes に and verbs such as 並べる, 並ぶ or 並べ替える; the criterion comes before it with の: サイズの大きい順. The counterpart is 小さい順; formed in the same way are 高い順, 安い順, 多い順, 新しい順 and 五十音順.

examples[].german: My grades have improved.
My grades this semester were good.
I showed my exam results to the teacher.
en.notes: 成績 denotes evaluated results or performance. In school it usually means grades: 成績が上がる means "one's grades improve". 今学期の成績 names the results of this semester. Outside school it can also denote, for example, a competition result or a professional track record.

en.meaning: in ascending order of size; smallest first
examples[].german: The rule is to write the answer numbers from smallest to largest.
I numbered them from smallest to largest.
We're taking a photo, so please line up from the front, shortest first.
en.notes: 小さい順 means "in ascending order of size, starting from the smallest" or, for numbers, "ascending". As with 大きい順, it takes に and verbs such as 並べる, 並ぶ or 書く; the criterion comes before it with の: 背の小さい順. With children, 小さい can also mean "young": 小さい順 "the smallest (youngest) first". For body height, 背の低い順 is somewhat more correct.

examples[].german: The seating order was set in the order of the Japanese syllabary.
Let's decide the seating arrangement.
Planning the seating arrangement for a wedding is difficult.
en.notes: 席順 is the "seating order" at celebrations, meetings or in a classroom: 席順を決める, 席順表 "seating chart". On formal occasions it often reflects the hierarchy (seat of honor 上座, lower seat 下座). Do not confuse it with 席替え, the regular swapping of seats in Japanese school classes.

examples[].german: In this museum, the artists' works are displayed in chronological order.
I arranged the photos in chronological order.
Please make a list in chronological order.
en.notes: 年代順 is chronological order. 年代順に並べる means to arrange things by the time of their origin; 年代順の展示 is a chronological exhibition. The noun combines here with に to indicate the arrangement. It is about the order in time, not about the age or rank of the people viewing.

examples[].german: The town names are arranged in gojuon order.
I arranged the roster in gojuon order.
The teacher called the names in gojuon order.
en.notes: 五十音順 is the Japanese "alphabetical" order following the kana table あいうえお・かきくけこ ... up to ん. Dictionaries, name lists and indexes are sorted this way; usually with に + 並ぶ／並べる. Colloquially people also say あいうえお順. For Latin letters it is アルファベット順.

examples[].german: I'm the type who doesn't worry much about details.
Please chop the onion finely.
Sorry, I don't have small change.
en.notes: 細かい has several meanings: "small, fine" for many small pieces (細かく切る "to cut small", 細かい雨 "drizzle"), 細かいお金 "small change", "precise, detailed" (細かい説明) and "petty, picky" (お金に細かい). 細かいことは気にしない means "not to worry about trifles". In contrast to 小さい, which describes a single small object, 細かい emphasizes fineness or detail. Opposite: 粗い "coarse".

examples[].german: Is there a police station near here?
I found a wallet, so I turned it in to the police station.
I was questioned at the police station about the accident.
en.notes: 警察署 is the larger police station of a district (e.g. 新宿警察署). For lost property, directions or small matters, people usually go to a 交番, the small police box; in the countryside there is the 駐在所. The suffix 署 also appears in 消防署 "fire station" and 税務署 "tax office". In conversation people often just say 警察: 警察に行く.

examples[].german: From outside the window, I could hear the whistle of a steam train.
The steam whistle sounded.
The ship sounded its horn and left the harbor.
en.notes: 汽笛 is the steam whistle or signal horn of a train (汽車) or ship; today it is used mainly for ships and often has a nostalgic ring. The pair is 汽笛が鳴る (intransitive) and 汽笛を鳴らす (transitive). A trill whistle or flute is called 笛, a car horn クラクション.

examples[].german: Adding a little salt here brings out the flavor.
We added one new member to the team.
Three plus five makes eight.
en.notes: 加える is transitive: XにYを加える "to add Y to X". It is used in cooking (塩を加える, more everyday 入れる), in arithmetic (more everyday 足す), for people (仲間に加える "to take into the group") and formally for 説明を加える "to add an explanation" or 危害を加える "to inflict harm". The intransitive counterpart is 加わる "to join, to be added".

examples[].german: Here is how to participate.
I plan to take part in the tournament.
Won't you come to the party on Sunday?
en.notes: 参加する is intransitive; the event takes に, not を: パーティーに参加する, 大会に参加する. Common derivations are 参加者 "participant", 参加費 "participation fee" and 不参加 "non-participation". 出席する emphasizes attendance at classes or meetings, whereas 参加 means active participation; joining a club, on the other hand, is 入る.

examples[].german: The sweet potato vendor's truck passed in front of our house.
I like eating roasted sweet potatoes in winter.
We gathered fallen leaves and made roasted sweet potatoes.
en.notes: 焼き芋 is a sweet potato (さつまいも) roasted in an oven or on hot stones, a typical snack in autumn and winter. Street vendors drive around with small trucks and call out "石焼き芋". It has nothing to do with an ordinary baked potato made from じゃがいも. It is also written 焼きいも or やきいも.

examples[].german: This town is safe.
Please evacuate to a safe place.
en.notes: 安全 is a na-adjective meaning safe and, as a noun, safety. 安全な場所 names a safe place; 安全です judges a place as safe. The opposite is 危険. The two examples distinguish a general evaluation of a place from a request to go to a safe place.

examples[].german: I made potato soup.
I put potatoes in the curry.
Please peel the potatoes.
en.notes: じゃがいも is the "potato" and is mostly written in kana (じゃがいも or ジャガイモ); じゃが芋 is a mixed spelling, and the technical word is 馬鈴薯. The name goes back to Jakarta (old ジャガタラ). Typical dishes are 肉じゃが, カレー and ポテトサラダ. The sweet potato, on the other hand, is さつまいも, and french fries are フライドポテト.

examples[].german: He started a new theater company.
I joined a theater company and started acting.
On the weekend I went to see a play by a famous theater company.
en.notes: 劇団 is a "theater troupe, theater ensemble", for example 劇団四季. Typical are 劇団に入る／入団する "to join a troupe", 劇団を作る／立ち上げる "to found" and 劇団員 "ensemble member". Do not confuse it with 劇場 "theater (building)" and 劇 "play".

examples[].german: Those guys are always talking nonsense.
You can't trust those guys.
I'm going out drinking with the guys from work tonight.
en.notes: 連中 is colloquial for "people, guys, bunch". With あの or その it often sounds derogatory (あの連中は信用できない), but among friends it can also stand casually and familiarly for one's own group (会社の連中). It is inappropriate for people one respects; politely, one says 皆さん or 方々.

examples[].german: Dogs express joy by wagging their tails.
I shared the joy of passing with my family.
I will never forget the joy when my child was born.
en.notes: 喜び is the noun of 喜ぶ "to be glad" and means "joy", often about an event: 合格の喜び, 優勝の喜び. Typical are 喜びを感じる, 喜びを表す and 喜びの声. 嬉しさ emphasizes the subjective feeling of happiness, 楽しみ anticipation or enjoyment. In congratulations, the formal お喜び申し上げます is used. Opposite: 悲しみ.

examples[].german: The media reported that news day after day.
Hot days continue day after day.
I'm tired from working overtime day after day.
en.notes: 連日 means "day after day, on several consecutive days" and usually emphasizes something extraordinary that repeats (heat, reports, overtime). It is used adverbially without a particle (連日報道する) or attributively with の (連日の雨). It sounds like news language; in conversation people prefer 毎日 or 何日も続けて. 毎日, by contrast, describes a normal daily routine.

examples[].german: It takes time to get over sadness.
I am feeling deep sorrow.
I couldn't eat anything because of the grief of my pet's death.
en.notes: 悲しみ is the noun of 悲しい and means "grief, sorrow, sadness". Typical are 深い悲しみ, 悲しみを乗り越える "to overcome grief" and Xの悲しみ (別れの悲しみ). 悲しさ describes more the degree of being sad, 寂しさ loneliness. Opposite: 喜び.

en.meaning: to change; to correct; to reform
examples[].german: I decided to postpone it to another day.
I will change my lifestyle habits.
Then, I will contact you again.
en.notes: 改める is transitive and means "to change (for the better), correct, revise"; it sounds more formal than 変える. Typical objects are 態度, 考え, 習慣 and 規則; 日を改める means "to postpone to another day". The intransitive counterpart is 改まる (改まった場 "formal occasion"). Very common is the adverb 改めて "once more, again": 改めてご連絡します.

examples[].german: What was the main reason you decided to quit drinking?
Drunk driving is absolutely not okay.
Until you turn twenty, drinking alcohol is prohibited by law.
en.notes: 飲酒 is the official, written word for "alcohol consumption, drinking alcohol". Typical are 飲酒運転 "drunk driving", 未成年の飲酒 and 飲酒量. In daily life people simply say お酒を飲む; 飲酒する is possible but sounds stiff. In Japan, alcohol is allowed only from the age of 20.

examples[].german: I'd like it to go, please.
Will you eat in, or take out?
Can I take this cake to go?
en.notes: お持ち帰り is the polite word for "to take away" and comes from the verb 持ち帰る. Customers say お持ち帰りでお願いします, while staff ask 店内でお召し上がりですか、お持ち帰りですか. Synonymous but more casual is テイクアウト. Colloquially, お持ち帰り can also mean taking someone home with you after a party.

examples[].german: Let's follow the rules.
Please follow the school rules.
We decided on new rules at the meeting.
en.notes: 規則 means a rule or regulation, for example for a school, a company or a procedure. 規則を守る means "to follow the rules", 規則を決める "to set rules". The word sounds more formal than the loanword ルール. A の phrase names the area concerned, for example 学校の規則.

en.meaning: to be understood; to get through
examples[].german: This phrasing gets the meaning across, but it sounds a bit unnatural.
English wasn't understood.
This road leads to the station.
en.notes: 通じる is mostly intransitive with が and at its core means "to go through, to be connected": 道が駅に通じる "the road leads to the station", 電話が通じる "the call gets through", 英語が通じる "English is understood", 気持ちが通じる "feelings get across". Unlike 分かる, here the language or meaning is the subject, not the person. Xに通じている also means "to be well versed in X"; 〜を通じて means "via, through (someone/something)". Literary variant: 通ずる.

en.meaning: as expected; just as one would expect
examples[].german: Wow! You're amazing, as expected.
As expected of a senior.
As expected, an experienced teacher explains things in an easy-to-understand way.
en.notes: 流石 is usually written さすが and here praises an achievement that one expected from the person: typical for you or "as expected". さすがですね expresses appreciation. The identically written personal name and other sentence patterns such as さすがに with "even so" are separate usages; in these examples the praise is at the center.

examples[].german: When I click here, the text overlaps and becomes unreadable. Is it a bug?
My appointments ended up overlapping.
Bad things piled up, and this week was really tough.
en.notes: 重なる is intransitive: things lie on top of each other (本が重なっている), appointments or events coincide (予定が重なる "to overlap", 祝日と日曜日が重なる) or pile up (悪いことが重なる "one misfortune after another"). The transitive counterpart is 重ねる "to stack, to repeat" (皿を重ねる).

examples[].german: I agree with that opinion, too.
"This movie is a bit long." "Yeah, I agree."
On that point, I completely agree as well.
en.notes: 同感 expresses that one is "of the same opinion" or feels the same way: Xに同感です, 全く同感です. In casual conversation a short 同感！ "I think so too!" is enough. 賛成, by contrast, means "to be in favor of a proposal", 共感 "to empathize, understand emotionally". 同感する is possible, but usually you hear 同感だ／同感です.

en.meaning: awareness (of one's own situation); to be aware
examples[].german: You should have a bit more awareness of being a working adult.
Please act with awareness.
He doesn't seem to be aware that he is in the wrong.
en.notes: 自覚 is awareness of one's own situation, role or condition - not "self-confidence" in the sense of self-assurance (that would be 自信). Typical are 〜としての自覚を持つ "to be aware of one's role as ..." and 〜という自覚がない "not to be aware that ...". As a する-verb, what is recognized takes を: 疲れを自覚する "to realize that one is exhausted". A slightly elevated but commonly used expression, for example in admonitions.

examples[].german: I started a part-time job washing dishes at a restaurant.
I wash the dishes every day.
Can you help me with the dishes after dinner?
en.notes: 皿洗い means "dishwashing" (literally "plate washing") and is used with する: 皿洗いをする. It also refers to the job of dishwasher: 皿洗いのバイト. Synonymous and somewhat more general is 食器洗い; the dishwasher is 食器洗い機. In conversation one often simply says お皿を洗う.

en.meaning: to be renewed; to improve; to become formal
examples[].german: The era name changed and a new era began.
His attitude improved.
In formal settings, let's use honorific language.
en.notes: 改まる is intransitive: something "renews itself" or "changes for the better", for example 年が改まる "a new year begins", 態度が改まる "one's behavior improves". The transitive counterpart is 改める "to change, improve" (規則を改める). Very common is the form 改まった "formal, solemn": 改まった場 "an official occasion"; 改まって何？ colloquially asks "Why so formal?". Rather elevated vocabulary.

examples[].german: Water and oil - do they mix, or don't they?
The colors blend and look pretty.
One adult was playing mixed in among the children.
en.notes: 混ざる is intransitive: things "mix together" or something is "mixed in" somewhere - AとBが混ざる or AにBが混ざる. The transitive counterpart is 混ぜる "to mix, to stir". Almost synonymous is 混じる; for things that remain distinguishable (people in a group), 交ざる is also written. Do not confuse it with 混む "to be crowded".

examples[].german: Where is the parking lot?
The parking lot is full.
en.notes: 駐車場 is a place for parking cars: a parking lot, parking area, or parking garage. It does not mean the individual parked car. 満車 describes a completely full parking lot. The long syllables ちゅう and じょう are written with ū and ō in chūshajō.

examples[].german: I have leftover fish that I caught, so would you like some?
I had money left over.
I had time left over on the test, so I checked it again.
en.notes: 余る is intransitive and means "to be left over, to be in excess" - more than is needed: お金が余る, 時間が余る. In contrast to 残る ("to remain, to still be there"), 余る emphasizes the surplus. In arithmetic, 10を3で割ると1余る means "remainder 1"; the related noun is 余り. Fixed expression: 手に余る "to be beyond one's control".

examples[].german: We had one chair too many.
Don't say unnecessary things.
When I'm told to stop, I want to do it all the more.
en.notes: 余計 is a な-adjective for "superfluous, too much, unnecessary": 余計なこと "unnecessary things", 一つ余計だ "one too many". The phrase 余計なお世話 means "Mind your own business!". As an adverb (余計に / 余計) it means "all the more, even more": 言われると余計にやりたくなる. It often sounds slightly reproachful; more neutral are 不要 and いらない.

examples[].german: This is my personal opinion.
Please protect personal information.
You can also sign up for this tour as an individual.
en.notes: 個人 is a noun: "individual, private person" - as opposed to a group, company or state. It is used attributively with の or in compounds: 個人の意見, 個人情報 "personal data", 個人で "as an individual". The adjective "personal" is 個人的(な): 個人的には "personally, in my own opinion". 私個人の意見 emphasizes that one speaks only for oneself.

examples[].german: I reserved a private room at a cafe and enjoyed a leisurely chat with my friend.
I reserved a private room at the restaurant.
I would like a single room during my hospital stay.
en.notes: 個室 is a room of one's own or a separated room. In a restaurant it means a separate dining room or private booth; in a hospital it can be a single room. 個室を予約する means to reserve such a room. The two restaurant examples do not describe reserving the entire restaurant.

en.meaning: to knock down; to tip over; to defeat
examples[].german: Man, this Bowser is too strong. If anyone knows how to defeat him, tell me!
I defeated the boss in the game.
Excuse me, may I recline my seat?
en.notes: 倒す is transitive: to "knock over, topple, tip down" something (コップを倒す, 木を倒す, 座席を倒す) and, figuratively, to "defeat" an opponent (敵を倒す, ボスを倒す). The intransitive counterpart is 倒れる "to fall over, to collapse". On a plane or bus one politely asks 座席を倒してもいいですか before reclining the seat.

examples[].german: That apartment can't find a tenant because of the rumor that it's haunted.
There is no tenant for this property.
A person who borrows money has to pay it back in small installments every month.
en.notes: 借り手 is "someone who borrows or rents something": the tenant of an apartment, but also a borrower of a loan or an item. The opposite is 貸し手 "landlord, lender, creditor". Typical: 借り手がつく / 見つかる "to find a tenant", 借り手がいない. In contracts, 借主 is more common; in everyday speech one also simply says 借りる人.

examples[].german: So wolverines really exist, huh.
The protagonist of this movie is a person who really existed.
This story is fiction and has no relation to real persons.
en.notes: 実在 means "to actually exist", as opposed to invented things, legends or fiction. As an intransitive する-verb: 実在する動物, 実在した人物 "a person who really lived". Attributively one says 実在の: 実在の人物・団体. Well known is the note at the end of films and novels that the story has nothing to do with real persons. Neutral to slightly formal; in daily life one can also say 本当にいる.

examples[].german: I woke up in the middle of the night from a nightmare.
I had a nightmare last night.
That day was like a nightmare.
en.notes: 悪夢 is a nightmare. 悪夢を見る means to have a nightmare; 悪夢で目が覚める, to wake up from one. The noun also appears in 悪夢のような for a figurative comparison with a very unpleasant experience.

examples[].german: That couple look exactly alike.
Mr. and Mrs. Tanaka have moved.
The company president and his wife also attended the wedding.
en.notes: 夫妻 is "married couple" in formal language and typically follows names or titles: 田中夫妻 "Mr. and Mrs. Tanaka", politely 社長ご夫妻. For one's own couple or in everyday speech, 夫婦 is used (私たち夫婦, 夫婦げんか); you never say 夫妻 about yourself. Frequent in news, invitations and celebratory speeches.

examples[].german: There is a ship in the harbor.
A large ship is docked in the harbor.
I loaded cargo onto the ship at the harbor.
en.notes: 港 with the reading みなと means "harbor". It refers to a place where ships dock and take on cargo or passengers. に can name the location of a ship, で the place of an activity. The reading こう is used in compounds and is not the standalone head word here.

examples[].german: Even though you have a wife and children, you shouldn't go out to eat alone with another woman.
He supports his wife and children.
He left his wife and children in his home country and came to Japan alone to work.
en.notes: 妻子 (read さいし, not つまこ) means "wife and children" as a man's family. It sounds somewhat literary; typical are 妻子を養う "to support wife and children", 妻子を残す and 妻子持ち "family man, married man". In daily life people rather say 奥さんと子ども or 家族.

examples[].german: Even if polygamy became acceptable, without money the declining birthrate couldn't be stopped, right?
Polygamy is not recognized in Japan.
In this country, polygamy used to be normal.
en.notes: 一夫多妻 is a four-character word: literally "one husband - many wives", i.e. polygyny or plural marriage. The system is called 一夫多妻制; antonyms are 一夫一婦(制) "monogamy" and the rare 一妻多夫. It is a matter-of-fact, formal expression from society, law and ethnology; used with が/は as subject or attributively with の. It is read いっぷ with a doubled consonant.

examples[].german: How is Mom's mood today?
You're in a good mood today.
My father has been in a bad mood since morning and isn't talking to anyone.
en.notes: 機嫌 is the outwardly visible "mood", mostly as seen by others: 機嫌がいい / 悪い "in a good / bad mood". 機嫌を取る means "to keep someone in a good mood, to flatter", 機嫌を損ねる "to put someone in a bad mood". ご機嫌 is also a な-adjective "in high spirits" (ご機嫌だね). Unlike 気分 (one's own condition, also physical), 機嫌 mainly describes the mood that others sense.

examples[].german: That man was summoned by the police on suspicion of theft.
He is under suspicion.
As a result of the investigation, the suspicion against him was cleared.
en.notes: 嫌疑 is a formal, legal expression for "suspicion" of having committed a crime or wrong. Typical: 〜の嫌疑で "on suspicion of ...", 嫌疑がかかる "to be under suspicion", 嫌疑が晴れる "to be cleared of suspicion". In police reports 容疑 (容疑者 "suspect") is more common; in daily life people say 疑い or 疑われる.

examples[].german: I left a message on the answering machine.
When I can't answer the phone, I set it to voicemail.
en.notes: 留守番電話 is an answering machine or the corresponding function on a telephone. 留守番電話にメッセージを残す describes leaving a message; 留守番電話にする, switching to this function. 留守番 means looking after the house, but the whole compound refers to a telephone device or a service.

examples[].german: Silicone, which is used in all sorts of processed foods lately - is it really harmless? It's in coffee too, you know.
This insect is harmless.
He looks harmless, but he's very scary when he gets angry.
en.notes: 無害 is a な-adjective (also with の) meaning "harmless, innocuous" and is the opposite of 有害 "harmful". Typical: 人体に無害 "harmless to humans", 無害な虫. Figuratively, 無害そう describes a person who seems harmless. The tone is rather matter-of-fact and technical (products, chemicals, animals); in daily life people also say 安全 or 体に悪くない.

examples[].german: I got a wart on my bottom.
I've been sitting for a long time and my bottom hurts.
I fell and hit my bottom.
en.notes: お尻 is the usual, polite everyday word for "bottom, butt" and is also used with children and at the doctor's: お尻が痛い, お尻を打つ. The form without お, 尻, sounds cruder and lives on mainly in idioms (尻に敷く "to have under one's thumb"). On Japanese toilets, おしり marks the bidet function. Often also written in kana.

examples[].german: This amulet will surely protect you from misfortune.
Don't say unnecessary things. The mouth is the source of calamity.
