Being late for the train kept me from having an accident. Turning misfortune into blessing, as they say.
en.notes: 災い is "misfortune, calamity" in an abstract, somewhat literary sense - that which brings harm. Typical: 災いから守る, 災いを招く "to invite misfortune". Well-known proverbs: 口は災いのもと "Talking gets you into trouble" and 災い転じて福となす "a blessing in disguise, bad turns into good". Concrete disasters are 災害, personal bad luck 災難. Often written in kana as わざわい.

examples[].german: I hear a fire broke out in that building at dawn.
In case of fire, please do not use the elevator.
I bought a house, so I took out fire insurance.
en.notes: 火災 is the formal word for "fire" - in news, announcements and compounds: 火災が発生する, 火災報知器 "fire alarm", 火災保険 "fire insurance". In conversation one mostly says 火事 (火事だ！). "Conflagration" would be too dramatic: 火災 can also be a small fire. 火災 refers to a damaging fire, not an intended fire like 火 or たき火.

examples[].german: There was a fire.
In case of fire, please call 119.
en.notes: 火事 means an uncontrolled fire, for example in a building; for fire as a substance or flame, 火 is usually used. 火事がある reports a fire incident, 火事になる its outbreak. The emergency number 119 is read as いち・いち・きゅう in this context.

examples[].german: That was quite a misfortune.
I lost my wallet and the trains stopped too, so today has been one mishap after another.
I suffered the misfortune of having my bag stolen on my trip.
en.notes: 災難 is a personal "misfortune, mishap" that befalls someone through no fault of their own: 災難にあう "to have bad luck, to meet with misfortune". Very common is the sympathetic phrase とんだ災難でしたね "That was really bad luck!"; 災難続き means "a run of bad luck". In contrast to 災害 (natural disaster), 災難 usually affects individuals, and it sounds more everyday than 災い.

examples[].german: The day of the earthquake disaster is still an unforgettable trauma for me.
Ten years have passed since the earthquake disaster.
I keep water and food at home in preparation for an earthquake disaster.
en.notes: 震災 is the "earthquake disaster", i.e. the damage and consequences of a large earthquake - the quake itself is 地震. Major events bear names with 大震災, such as 東日本大震災 (2011) or 阪神・淡路大震災 (1995). Typical: 震災にあう "to experience an earthquake", 震災から〜年, 震災に備える "to prepare for an earthquake". Serious, rather written tone.

examples[].german: I thought it was smoky somehow, and apparently there was a fire in the neighborhood.
When someone smokes in the room, it's smoky and my eyes hurt.
It's smoky near the bonfire, so let's sit a bit farther away.
en.notes: 煙い is an い-adjective and describes that smoke is bothersome to you - it burns the eyes or scratches the throat: 部屋が煙い, たき火が煙い. It does not mean "smoky" in the sense of taste (that would be スモーキー). 煙たい has the same meaning and, figuratively, also describes an unpleasant, awe-inspiring person (煙たい上司). Redundant phrases such as 煙が煙い are avoided.

examples[].german: The accomplice is said to be likely abroad.
The accomplice was arrested.
I'm not the only one who ate the cake. My little sister is an accomplice too.
en.notes: 共犯者 is the "accomplice" in a crime; 共犯 alone means "complicity". The main perpetrator is 主犯, the perpetrator in general 犯人. Typical in news: 共犯者が逮捕される, 〜の共犯者として. In daily life the word is also used jokingly for someone who joined in a small prank.

examples[].german: The male-to-female ratio at our company is 5 to 2.
When cooking rice, the ratio of rice to water is important.
The ratio of rent to salary is too high.
en.notes: 比率 is the "ratio" or "proportion" of two quantities to each other: AとBの比率, 男女比率. Numerical ratios are read with 対 (5:2 → 五対二). Typical: 比率が高い / 低い "a high / low proportion". The more everyday word is 割合, which can also mean "relatively, fairly"; 比率 sounds more objective and statistical.

examples[].german: The supermarket's back area is off limits.
This area is off limits.
The children were playing in a restricted area and got warned.
en.notes: 立入禁止 (also 立ち入り禁止) is the typical sign text "No entry, no trespassing", composed of 立入 "entering" and 禁止 "prohibition". In a sentence it is a noun with です (ここは立入禁止です) or attributive with の (立入禁止の場所). Common variants: 関係者以外立入禁止 "authorized personnel only", 芝生内立入禁止 "keep off the grass". Official, terse tone.

examples[].german: This place is a hidden gem for pufferfish dishes.
If you want to watch fireworks, this park is a hidden gem.
I'm looking for a hidden-gem ski resort that's empty even on weekends.
en.notes: 穴場 (literally "hole place") is a "hidden gem": a good place that few people know - a restaurant, viewpoint, beach. Typical: 〜の穴場, 穴場スポット, 穴場の店; "X is a hidden gem for Y" is XはYの穴場だ. Colloquial and very common in travel and gourmet magazines. Similar is 隠れ家的なお店 "a place like a hideaway".

examples[].german: My nose was bleeding, so I stuffed tissue in my nostril.
My younger brother flared his nostrils and spoke proudly.
The doctor looked inside my nostril with a light.
en.notes: 鼻の穴 is literally "the hole of the nose" and the normal everyday word for "nostril"; the technical word is 鼻孔. Typical expressions: 鼻の穴をふくらませる "to flare one's nostrils" (from excitement, pride or anger) and 鼻の穴にティッシュを詰める for a nosebleed. "To pick one's nose" is 鼻をほじる, "stuffy nose" is 鼻が詰まる - without 穴.

examples[].german: Today for lunch I had conger eel tempura.
I like conger eel sushi.
Conger eel is lighter than freshwater eel.
en.notes: 穴子 is the "conger eel" (sea eel), named for hiding in holes (穴). On menus it is often written アナゴ in katakana. Popular as 穴子の天ぷら and as sushi with sweet sauce. Do not confuse it with うなぎ, the fattier freshwater eel, usually eaten grilled as うな重.

examples[].german: This chocolate stinks like socks.
The garbage smells bad.
What he's saying smells fishy somehow.
en.notes: 臭い (くさい) is an い-adjective for "stinking, foul-smelling": ゴミが臭い, 足が臭い. Colloquially it also means "suspicious, fishy" (あの話は臭い). As a suffix, 〜くさい forms words such as 面倒くさい "troublesome" or 古くさい "old-fashioned". Note: the same kanji read as a noun, におい, means "smell, stench" (臭いがする); pleasant smells are written 匂い.

examples[].german: The thief was caught.
The thief came in through the window.
en.notes: 泥棒 here means a person who steals: a thief or burglar. 捕まる describes the thief being caught. The dictionary can also use the word for the act; in these sentences the person is meant in each case. The ending ぼう is rendered with ō in dorobō.

examples[].german: I wish I had been born into a wealthy family too.
Many wealthy people live in that town.
We weren't well-off in the past, but every day was fun.
en.notes: 裕福 is a な-adjective meaning "wealthy, well-off" and sounds somewhat more refined than お金持ち. Typical: 裕福な家庭 / 家に生まれる, 裕福に暮らす. Negated: 裕福ではない. In contrast to 豊か ("rich in something", also nature or feelings: 自然が豊か), 裕福 refers only to money and standard of living.

examples[].german: On this community forum, DMs are prohibited to prevent trouble between users.
Let's be careful in order to prevent accidents.
en.notes: 防止 is the prevention of an undesirable event. As a noun it appears in トラブル防止のため; with する it becomes the transitive verb "to prevent": 事故を防止する. The standalone form on this card is the noun. It refers to preventing an event, not to solving it afterwards.

examples[].german: I will definitely make this business a success, also to prevent my hometown from turning into a ghost town.
I wear a hat to prevent sunburn.
The best way to prevent colds is to wash your hands.
en.notes: 防ぐ is transitive: one "prevents" or "fends off" what would cause harm - the unwanted thing takes を: 事故を防ぐ, 日焼けを防ぐ, 風邪を防ぐ. Very common is 〜を防ぐため(に) "in order to prevent ...". Unlike 守る (to protect something valuable: 子どもを守る), 防ぐ is directed against the danger itself. The noun "prevention" is 予防.

examples[].german: I get excited when I face difficulties at work.
Let's overcome the difficulties.
Because of the heavy snow, traveling by car is difficult.
en.notes: 困難 is used as a noun "difficulty, hardship" and as a な-adjective "difficult", but sounds more formal than 難しい. Typical: 困難に直面する "to face difficulties", 困難を乗り越える "to overcome difficulties", 〜は困難だ "... is hardly possible". In bureaucratic language, 困難です is often a polite way of saying "it can't be done".

examples[].german: Many voices of criticism were raised about the content of that article.
His actions were condemned.
Before you blame others, think about yourself.
en.notes: 非難 is sharp "criticism, reproach, condemnation" - one reproaches someone morally. As a transitive する-verb: 人を非難する; passive 非難される, often also 非難を浴びる "to be heavily criticized" and 非難の声が上がる. 批判, by contrast, is objective, also constructive criticism. Note: pronounced the same is 避難 "evacuation, fleeing to safety".

examples[].german: My major is cultural anthropology.
I'm studying anthropology at university.
In anthropology class, we learned about the lives of people in the past.
en.notes: 人類学 is made up of 人類 "humankind" and 〜学 "science, study": "anthropology". It is common in names of fields such as 文化人類学 "cultural anthropology"; the researcher is called 人類学者. Typical: 人類学を勉強する / 専攻する. Related fields are 考古学 "archaeology" and 社会学 "sociology".

examples[].german: Katsu curry for breakfast gives me heartburn!
I have heartburn from eating too much.
I had bad heartburn, so I took stomach medicine.
en.notes: 胸焼け (literally "chest burning", also written 胸やけ) is "heartburn". One says 胸焼けがする or, as an intransitive verb, 胸焼けする. Colloquially it is also used to express that very greasy or sweet food makes you feel sick just by looking at it. The remedy is 胃薬 "stomach medicine".

examples[].german: These days, the internet and the real world have become almost inseparable, haven't they?
These two problems are inseparable.
Language and culture are inseparably linked.
en.notes: 不可分 (不 "not" + 可 "possible" + 分 "to divide") means "inseparable, indivisible". It is a literary word, typical in set patterns: AとBは不可分の関係にある "A and B are inseparably linked", 不可分になる. In conversation one rather says 切り離せない or 分けられない.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to tell on readings from kun readings in kanji.
Kanji have on and kun readings.
In this dictionary, you can look up kanji by their readings.
en.notes: 音訓 combines the two types of kanji readings: 音読み (the reading adopted from Chinese) and 訓読み (the Japanese reading). The word is a technical term from dictionaries and teaching, as in 音訓索引 "index by readings" or 音訓の区別. In conversation one usually names 音読み and 訓読み separately.

examples[].german: The people who live in my neighborhood are all people who love parties.
Those people are kind.
I want to help people who are in trouble.
en.notes: 人達 is the plural form of 人, "people", and is mostly written 人たち, because 達 as a plural suffix is usually in kana. It almost always needs a modifier: あの人たち, 若い人たち, 困っている人たち. More polite is 方々 (あの方々), more general and written is 人々.

examples[].german: I contacted the police.
I called the police right away.
The police are directing traffic at the intersection.
en.notes: 警察 means the police as an institution or the responsible police office. 警察に連絡する means to get in touch with the police; this need not be by phone. 警察に電話する explicitly names a phone call. For an individual police officer, 警察官 is more precise.

examples[].german: At a small restaurant on my Kyoto trip, I enjoyed salt-grilled sweetfish while looking down at a quietly flowing stream.
I left the room quietly and slowly.
en.notes: 静々 is usually written しずしず and describes a calm, slow or dignified movement. It often takes と before the verb: 静々と部屋を出る. The expression has a narrative feel; it describes the manner of movement and not merely the absence of noise.

examples[].german: I only gave my opinion, but my boss yelled at me, "Stop complaining!"
Please don't always complain.
en.notes: 文句を言う means to complain or grumble. 文句 here is the noun "complaint" with を; only 言う is conjugated: 文句を言います, 文句を言わない. 文句を言うな is a curt prohibition. This card treats the whole combination, not the other meaning of 文句 as wording or phrasing.

examples[].german: Bringing electronic devices into this room is prohibited.
Please refrain from using electronic devices on the airplane.
Electronic devices are sensitive to water, so please be careful.
en.notes: 電子機器 (電子 "electronics" + 機器 "equipment, apparatus") is the matter-of-fact umbrella term for "electronic devices" such as smartphones, laptops or tablets. Typical in notices: 電子機器の使用 / 持ち込み "use / bringing of electronic devices". Household appliances are more often called 電化製品 or 家電; in daily life people also simply say スマホやパソコン.

examples[].german: Please check the route to your destination on Google Maps in advance!
Please tell me the shortest route.
The route of infection of the virus is still not known.
en.notes: 経路 is an objective word for the "route, path" that something or someone takes, and also for the "course" of a process. Typical: 経路を調べる / 検索する (in navigation apps), 避難経路 "escape route", 感染経路 "route of infection". In conversation people more often say 道, 道順 or ルート.

examples[].german: How do you close the browser on a smartphone?
Please close your eyes.
Close your books and listen to the teacher.
en.notes: 閉じる is an ichidan verb, mostly transitive (Xを閉じる): to "close" eyes, books, umbrellas, apps or windows on a computer. For doors, windows and shutters, on the other hand, 閉める is usually used. Less often it is intransitive (幕が閉じる "the curtain falls") or means "to end" (会を閉じる). The opposite is 開く (ひらく).

examples[].german: He makes a point of writing text that is easy for readers to understand.
This novel has many readers.
Most readers of this magazine are women in their twenties.
en.notes: 読者 is the "reader" of a book, newspaper or magazine, usually as a group or target audience: 読者が多い, 若い読者, 読者の声 "letters from readers, readers' opinions". A loyal reader is 愛読者. 読み手 sounds more abstract (as the counterpart of 書き手 "writer"); someone who is reading right now is simply 読んでいる人.

examples[].german: I became friends with an American residing in Japan.
I renewed my residence card.
Please complete the procedure at the immigration office before your period of stay expires.
en.notes: 在留 is the official term for "residence", especially the legal residence of foreigners: 在留カード "residence card", 在留資格 "status of residence", 在留期間 "period of stay". As an intransitive する-verb: 日本に在留する. Similar is 在住 "resident of" (東京在住); in daily life people simply say 住む.

examples[].german: Vampires can control people's minds at will.
He commands three languages with ease.
This camera can change its angle freely.
en.notes: 自在 means "at will, freely and effortlessly" and almost always appears adverbially as 自在に + verb: 自在に操る "to master skillfully", 自在に変える "to change at will". Much more common than the single word is the four-character 自由自在 "completely at will". In contrast to 自由 ("free, freedom"), 自在 emphasizes the ability to fully control something.

en.meaning: end of the line; very back
examples[].german: The end of the line is here.
Please line up at the end of the line.
The last car of the train is often empty.
en.notes: 最後尾 (最後 "last" + 尾 "tail") is the "rearmost end" of a row, above all a waiting line or a train. At events, staff carry signs saying 最後尾 "end of the line"; you queue up with 最後尾に並ぶ. The opposite is 先頭 "head, front end". In daily life people also say 列の一番後ろ.

examples[].german: Mr. Chairman, what is on today's agenda?
The chairman opened the meeting.
She was elected chairperson at the student council meeting.
en.notes: 議長 is the "chairperson" of a meeting or assembly, the person who leads the discussion: 議長を務める "to preside, to chair", 議長に選ばれる. The title is also used for presidents of parliaments (衆議院議長). Do not confuse it with 会長 (head of a club or corporation), 委員長 (committee chair) and 司会 (host or emcee of an event). 議長 can be used directly as a form of address.

examples[].german: International exchange is important.
I took part in an international conference.
en.notes: 国際 means "international" and is often used as the first part of a compound: 国際交流, "international exchange", 国際会議, "international conference". Here it is a nominal word component; it is not inflected like an い-adjective.

examples[].german: On your résumé, write the school's name correctly, all the way to "高等学校".
I graduated from high school.
In Japan, after graduating from junior high school, most people go on to high school.
en.notes: 高等学校 is the official name of the three-year "high school" after junior high school (中学校), roughly grades 10 to 12. In daily life people almost always use the short form 高校 (高校生 "high school student"); the full form appears in school names, résumés and documents. Typical: 高等学校を卒業する, 高等学校に進む / 入学する.

examples[].german: Do you have a cough drop?
My throat hurts, so I'll suck on a cough drop.
This herbal cough drop has a refreshing taste.
en.notes: 喉飴 (usually written のど飴) is a "throat lozenge, cough drop", from 喉 "throat" and 飴 "candy". Candies are sucked, hence 喉飴をなめる and not 食べる. People take them when 喉が痛い or with a scratchy throat (喉がイガイガする), for example before karaoke.

examples[].german: When is the baby due?
A baby was born.
This puppy was born only last month.
en.notes: 産まれる is the intransitive counterpart of 産む "to give birth" and refers to the physical birth of a person or animal: 赤ちゃんが産まれる. The more general and more common spelling is 生まれる; only it is also used figuratively (新しいアイデアが生まれる "a new idea arises"). Place and time of birth take で and に respectively: 東京で生まれた, 二〇〇〇年に生まれた. The person who has the child takes に: 姉に男の子が産まれた "my sister had a boy".

examples[].german: If it's that town, you can get there either via Osaka or via Kyoto.
I'm going to Osaka via Nagoya.
I booked the tickets through a travel agency.
en.notes: 経由 means "via, by way of" and comes directly after a place name: 名古屋経由で大阪へ行く. As a する-verb it is 〜を経由して: ドバイを経由してパリへ行く. By extension it also names the route through an office or an intermediary: 旅行会社経由で予約する "to book through a travel agency". Unlike 〜を通って "passing through ...", 経由 emphasizes the intermediate stop of a route; it is typical in timetables, flight information and business language.

en.meaning: to run out; to be lost; to disappear
examples[].german: Oh, we're almost out of toilet paper.
My wallet is gone. I may have dropped it somewhere.
After I took the medicine, the headache went away.
en.notes: 無くなる means that something "runs out" (supplies, time), "gets lost" or "disappears" (pain, desire): 時間が無くなる, 財布が無くなった, 痛みが無くなる. It is mostly written in kana: なくなる. The transitive counterpart is 無くす "to lose" (財布を無くす). Do not confuse with 亡くなる "to pass away" and with the ending 〜なくなる "no longer ..." (食べられなくなる), which consists of ない＋なる.

en.meaning: to connect; to link; to tie
examples[].german: Let's walk holding hands.
I connected the computer to the TV and looked at photos.
I will put you through to the person in charge. Please wait a moment.
en.notes: 繋ぐ means "to connect, to tie up" and is mostly written in kana: つなぐ. Typical uses are 手を繋ぐ "to hold hands", AをBに繋ぐ "to connect A to B" (devices, cables, also tying a dog to a post) and, on the phone, 担当者にお繋ぎします "I'll put you through to the person in charge". The intransitive counterpart is 繋がる: 電話が繋がらない "I can't get through", インターネットに繋がる "to be connected to the internet".

examples[].german: It seems my hometown is in serious trouble because of flood damage.
Flood damage occurred because of the typhoon.
This town has had a lot of flood damage since long ago.
en.notes: 水害 is "flood damage" or a "flood disaster", i.e. damage caused by water after heavy rain, a typhoon or rivers overflowing their banks. The flood itself is 洪水. Typical are 水害が起きる／発生する, 水害に遭う "to be hit by a flood" and 水害で被害を受ける. The word is matter-of-fact and is encountered mainly in news; the umbrella term is 災害 "disaster".

examples[].german: Please enter your answer here.
Please respond to the survey.
I'm waiting for a reply from the company.
en.notes: 回答 is the "answer" to a survey, inquiry or official question: アンケートに回答する, 質問に回答する, 回答を待つ. It sounds more matter-of-fact than the everyday 答え. Do not confuse with the identically read 解答 "solution" to an exam problem. For the response to a letter, an invitation or a call, 返事 is said.

examples[].german: My husband is at work right now.
My husband and I share the housework.
My husband's parents live in Hokkaido.
en.notes: 夫 is the neutral term for one's own husband when talking about him with others, and the standard word in forms and news. 主人 sounds more traditional (literally "master of the house"), 旦那 colloquial. Another person's husband is politely called ご主人 or 旦那さん, not 夫. The married couple is 夫婦.

examples[].german: My wife works at a library.
I made travel plans with my wife.
I bought flowers for my wife's birthday.
en.notes: 妻 is the neutral term for one's own wife toward others and the standard word in forms. 家内 sounds older and humble, 嫁 is colloquial and actually means "daughter-in-law". Another person's wife is politely called 奥さん or 奥様, not 妻. In a matter-of-fact way, 夫と妻 stand side by side.

examples[].german: I wish for world peace.
I want to create a peaceful world.
en.notes: 平和 means peace or peaceful coexistence. As a noun it can name the thing wished for with を: 平和を願う. Used adjectivally before a noun, it takes な: 平和な世界, "a peaceful world". The reading へいわ is written heiwa, not hēwa.

examples[].german: I like soccer.
That bag is mine.
Hey there, what's your name?
en.notes: 僕 is an "I" used mainly by boys and men in daily life; it sounds friendlier and softer than the rougher 俺, but less formal than 私. In meetings or job interviews men usually switch to 私. Adults sometimes address small boys as 僕 themselves ("hey there, little guy"). Plural: 僕たち or 僕ら.

examples[].german: What do you think?
I'm glad I got to talk with you.
I like you.
en.notes: 君 is a familiar "you" among friends, toward younger people, or from superiors to subordinates; in song lyrics it is the typical "you". Toward superiors or strangers it sounds impolite; there you use the name with さん. Do not confuse it with the name suffix 〜君, which is read くん.

examples[].german: My daughter will enter elementary school next year.
I made a cake with my daughter.
How old is your daughter?
en.notes: 娘 refers to one's own daughter when talking about her with others: うちの娘. About another person's daughter, one politely says 娘さん or お嬢さん. In addition, 娘 can mean a "young, unmarried woman", for example in 村の娘; this meaning sounds rather old-fashioned today. The counterpart for sons is 息子.

examples[].german: That child reads a lot of books.
I explained it so that even a small child could understand.
A baby panda was born at the zoo.
en.notes: 子 means "child", but rarely stands alone; it comes with a modifier: あの子, この子, 男の子, 女の子, うちの子. Alone and neutral, 子供 is mostly said. 子 also refers to young animals (パンダの子) and colloquially to young women (かわいい子). あの子 sounds familiar and is used only for children or clearly younger people.

examples[].german: May I visit your home tomorrow?
Is your home close to the station?
Your dog is big, isn't it?
en.notes: お宅 is the respectful term for the other person's home or family: お宅に伺う "to visit you at home", お宅の犬 "your dog". For one's own home, うち is used instead. As a form of address "you" (お宅は…), it sounds distant and sometimes cool, for example among neighbors or between companies. The fan meaning オタク developed from this form of address and is written in katakana.

examples[].german: How is your husband?
Is your husband coming along too?
en.notes: ご主人 is a traditional polite term for another person's husband: "your husband" or "her husband". You can use it to ask how he is or to mention his participation. For your own husband you usually use 夫 instead of the honorific ご主人. 御主人 is the variant written more with kanji; ご主人 is also common. The meaning learned here refers to the husband, not to the also possible meaning of master of the house or employer. The examples distinguish a question about his well-being from a question about accompanying you.

examples[].german: The exam venue is near the station.
Please write your name before entering the venue.
The concert venue was packed with people.
en.notes: 会場 is the "venue" - the hall or grounds where something takes place: 試験会場, 結婚式の会場, コンサート会場. Typical are 会場に入る, 会場に着く and, on signs, 会場はこちら "this way to the venue". An ordinary meeting room is 会議室; 場所 is the general "place" without reference to an event.

en.meaning: way back; return trip; coming home
examples[].german: I'll stop by the supermarket on the way home.
The train home was crowded.
My husband has been coming home late lately.
en.notes: 帰り is the noun of 帰る and means the "way back" or "return". 帰りに means "on the way back" (学校の帰りに, 仕事の帰りに), 帰りの電車 is the train back. The counterpart is 行き "way there": 行きはバス、帰りは電車. 帰りが遅い means "to come home late", and with お帰りなさい one greets someone who comes home.

examples[].german: I have been to Japan once.
I have never once been to this store.
Excuse me, please say that once more.
en.notes: 一度 means "once" and sounds a little more refined than 一回. Typical are 一度〜たことがある "to have ... once", 一度も〜ない "not a single time", もう一度 "once more" and 一度に "at once, at the same time". As a friendly invitation, 一度遊びに来てください means "please come visit sometime". With temperatures, however, 一度 means "one degree".

examples[].german: It's not convenient for me.
Tomorrow is not convenient for me.
Please tell me a day that is convenient for you.
en.notes: 都合 means personal circumstances or time availability here. 都合がいい means "it suits me / I have time", 都合が悪い "it doesn't suit me". In polite questions about appointments, ご都合 is often used. In this use the word is not simply a chance that happens to occur, like 機会.

examples[].german: I'll be back within an hour.
I want to buy lunch for 500 yen or less.
I'm looking for an apartment within a ten-minute walk of the station.
en.notes: 以内 follows a specification of time, quantity or distance and means "within, at most" - the limit value is included: 三日以内に "within three days", 千円以内で "for at most 1000 yen", 駅から歩いて十分以内. With deadlines it usually takes に, with budgets で. Similar is 以下 "... or less"; 未満, by contrast, excludes the limit value.

examples[].german: Please write your name on the front of the paper.
I'm waiting outside the shop.
If the coin comes up heads, I win.
en.notes: 表 (おもて) is the "front side" or "outer side", the counterpart is 裏 "back side": 紙の表と裏, コインの表 "heads". It can also mean "outside, in front of the house": 表で待つ, 表に出る. In the meaning "table, chart", the same character is read ひょう (時刻表 "timetable"). Figuratively, 表 stands for the official, visible side, for example in 表と裏がある人 "a person with two faces".

examples[].german: The principal spoke in the gym.
I wrote a letter to the principal.
Where is the principal's office?
en.notes: 校長 is the head of an elementary, junior high or high school. About the person and in addressing them, 校長先生 is mostly said in school life; 校長 alone sounds matter-of-fact (letters, news) or appears in compounds such as 校長室 "principal's office". The head of a university is, by contrast, 学長.

examples[].german: I checked the schedule with the department head.
The department head is in a meeting right now.
My older brother is the captain of the tennis club.
en.notes: 部長 is the "department head" in a company, above 課長 and below 社長 in the usual hierarchy. As a form of address you use the title instead of さん: 部長 or 山田部長. To customers you refer to your own boss without an honorific: 部長の山田. In schools, 部長 is also the leader of a club, such as テニス部の部長.

examples[].german: My older brother works at a newspaper company.
There was a phone call from the newspaper company.
People from the newspaper came to the school to interview us.
en.notes: 新聞社 is the company that publishes a newspaper, i.e. a "newspaper publisher" or its editorial office: 新聞社に勤める, 新聞社の記者 "newspaper reporter". The newspaper itself is called 新聞, a book publisher is 出版社 and a TV station is テレビ局. In company names it appears as 〜新聞社.

examples[].german: I wash the rice before cooking it.
This rice was grown in Japan.
I bought five kilos of rice at the supermarket.
en.notes: 米 is uncooked rice as a grain and foodstuff: 米を炊く "to cook rice", 米を研ぐ "to wash rice". In everyday speech the polite form お米 is usually used. Cooked rice is called ご飯, in a Western restaurant ライス; the rice plant is called 稲. As an abbreviation for "USA" the same character is read べい (米国).

examples[].german: This cat's fur is soft.
Dog hair is stuck to my clothes.
Lately a lot of my hair has been falling out.
en.notes: 毛 refers to hair in general, animal fur, wool and feathers: 猫の毛, 毛のセーター "wool sweater". Hair on the head is called 髪 or 髪の毛. Typical phrases are 毛が抜ける "hair falls out" and 毛が生える "hair grows". For people, 毛 alone sounds rather physical and matter-of-fact; for hairstyle and haircut, use 髪.

examples[].german: Small birds are singing in the garden.
I could see a small bird from the window.
I feed the small birds every morning.
en.notes: 小鳥 means "small birds", especially songbirds such as sparrows or pet birds such as budgerigars. Typical phrases are 小鳥が鳴く "birds chirp", 小鳥を飼う "to keep a bird" and 小鳥にえさをあげる. The general term is 鳥; 小鳥 sounds friendly and a little cute. Chicks, on the other hand, are called ひな.

examples[].german: You need strength to carry this box.
Let's join forces, everyone.
Whenever you're in trouble, I'm always here to help.
en.notes: 力 is "strength" in both the physical and the figurative sense: 力が強い, 力を入れる "to put effort in, to give it your all", 力を合わせる "to join forces". It also means "ability" (日本語の力 "Japanese skills"), and 力になる means "to help someone, to be a support". As the second part of compounds it is usually read りょく: 能力, 体力.

examples[].german: Please wait behind the red line.
I draw a straight line on the paper.
Please change to the Yamanote Line at the next station.
en.notes: 線 is a "line" or a "stroke": 線を引く "to draw a line", 白い線の内側 on a station platform. As a suffix it denotes railway and transport lines: 山手線 "Yamanote Line", 二番線 "Track 2". It also stands for wires and cables (電話の線). For a line of people, use 列 instead.

examples[].german: The two of them get along well.
Those two get along well.
I used to be on bad terms with my older brother.
en.notes: 仲 describes the relationship between people. 仲がいい means "to get along well", 仲が悪い "to be on bad terms". A partner in the relationship can take と: 兄と仲がいい. It is a noun; "good" or "bad" is expressed by the adjective that follows.

examples[].german: I got 90 points on the exam.
Please ask about the points you don't understand.
I scored two goals in the soccer match.
en.notes: 点 has several basic meanings: a "dot" as a mark, the "score" on tests (九十点を取る, 百点満点), "points" or goals in a game, and, figuratively, an "aspect": この点 "in this respect", いい点 "good point, merit". For the score alone, 点数 is also used. As a counter, 点 also counts items and articles, for example in a shop (三点で千円).

examples[].german: Let's meet on another day.
That is a different problem.
Separate checks, please.
en.notes: 別 means "different, separate". Before a noun, 別の is used: 別の日 "another day", 別の人. 別々に means "separately from each other" (別々に払う "to pay separately"). Very common is 別に with a negative: 別に問題ない "no particular problem"; a curt 別に… as an answer can sound dismissive. As a suffix, 〜別 sorts by category: 国別 "by country".

examples[].german: I heard a strange noise outside.
This sentence is a little odd.
This milk tastes a bit strange.
en.notes: 変 is a な-adjective: 変な音, 変な味, この文は変だ. It means "strange, odd" and often has a slightly negative tone; said about people (変な人) it can sound derogatory. As an adverb it is 変に "in a strange way". Do not confuse it with 辺 "vicinity"; 大変 also has a different meaning ("terrible, very").

examples[].german: I used to live in this town long ago.
I heard stories about the old days from my grandfather.
Once upon a time, there lived an old man and an old woman.
en.notes: 昔 refers to a time far in the past, "in the old days" or "long ago": 昔の友達, 昔はよく泳いだ, 昔から "since time immemorial". Fairy tales begin with 昔々 "Once upon a time". For the more recent past ("a moment ago, the other day") 前 or この前 fit better. As a time adverb, 昔 stands at the start of the sentence without a particle.

examples[].german: I'm not home during the day.
It's warm during the day, but cold at night.
It feels nice to drink beer in broad daylight, doesn't it?
en.notes: 昼間 is the bright part of the day from morning to evening, as opposed to 夜: 昼間は暖かい. 昼, by contrast, rather means noon or lunch (昼ご飯). 日中 is somewhat more formal. 昼間から stresses that something already happens during the day, often with mild disapproval or a wink: 昼間からお酒を飲む.

examples[].german: There is a grove behind the house.
I walked through the woods.
In autumn, the trees in the grove turn red and yellow.
en.notes: 林 is a "grove" or "copse", smaller and sparser than 森 "forest", often consisting of one kind of tree: 松林 "pine grove", 竹林 "bamboo grove". Typical phrases are 林の中を歩く and 林がある. The character consists of two trees (木), 森 of three. 林 is also a common family name.

examples[].german: My throat hurts, so I can't talk today.
I'm thirsty. Please give me some water.
I sang too much at karaoke and lost my voice.
en.notes: 喉 is the throat seen from the inside, i.e. "windpipe, pharynx", and is often written in kana as のど. Important phrases are 喉が痛い "to have a sore throat", 喉が渇く "to be thirsty" (literally "the throat dries out") and 喉がかれる "to become hoarse". The neck seen from the outside, or the nape, is called 首 instead.

examples[].german: Do you know this person?
The teacher knows that story.
As you know, the fees will change from next month.
en.notes: ご存じ is the respectful counterpart of 知っている and is used only for the knowledge of others: 〜をご存じですか "Do you know ...?". About oneself, one answers humbly with 存じております or 存じません, never with ご存じです. The phrase ご存じのとおり "as you know" is common. The spelling ご存知 is just as widespread.

en.meaning: to pull out; to withdraw; to draw out
examples[].german: I withdrew money at the bank.
I pulled a box out from under the desk.
The teacher is good at bringing out the students' abilities.
en.notes: 引き出す literally means "to pull out": 箱を引き出す. In everyday life, お金を引き出す "to withdraw money" is very common; colloquially お金を下ろす is also said. Figuratively it means "to bring out, to elicit": 力を引き出す "to bring out one's potential", 答えを引き出す. The noun 引き出し is a "drawer" or a "withdrawal".

en.meaning: to begin to rain or snow
examples[].german: It started to rain on the way home.
Let's leave before it starts to snow.
The sky is getting dark. It looks like it could start raining any moment.
en.notes: 降り出す means "to start raining or snowing"; the subject is 雨 or 雪: 雨が降り出した. The ending 〜出す stresses a sudden, unplanned start, whereas 降り始める sounds more neutral. Typical are 今にも降り出しそうだ "it could start any moment" and 降り出す前に. The verb is intransitive and is also written 降りだす.

examples[].german: I noticed the mistake.
There are many mistakes in this e-mail.
en.notes: 間違い here is a mistake or error. 間違いに気がつく means to notice a mistake; 間違いがある states that something contains errors. The noun can also be combined with する: 間違いをする. The card does not cover older meanings such as misconduct.

examples[].german: I'm on my way to the station now.
The students are sitting facing the blackboard.
A typhoon is heading toward Kyushu.
en.notes: 向かう means "to head for" (destination with に or へ): 駅に向かう, 東京へ向かう途中. It also means "to face, to sit opposite": 机に向かう "to sit down at one's desk". 〜に向かって means "toward, facing". Related are 向く "to turn, to look toward" and the transitive 向ける "to direct at"; 向かい is "opposite".

examples[].german: I thank you from the bottom of my heart.
I will tell you the details tomorrow.
We look forward to your continued support.
en.notes: 申し上げる is the humble form (謙譲語) of 言う, used when addressing a statement directly to a person of higher status: お礼を申し上げる "to express one's thanks". 申す is plainly humble, for example with one's name: 田中と申します. In the form お／ご〜申し上げる it makes other verbs very polite: お願い申し上げます, お詫び申し上げます, typical of speeches and business letters.

examples[].german: Today is my day off. So I'm staying home.
This shop is always crowded. So you should make a reservation.
That's what I told you, isn't it?
en.notes: だから at the start of a sentence links a previously stated reason with its consequence: "therefore, so". It sounds colloquial; ですから is more polite, なので or そのため more neutral. In an annoyed tone, だから means "I'm telling you ...": だから言ったでしょう. Do not confuse it with 雨だから, where だ＋から gives the reason within a sentence.

examples[].german: I opened the window. Then a cat came in.
You press the button. Then the door opens.
So, you mean Mr. Tanaka isn't coming?
en.notes: すると introduces what happened immediately afterward, often something surprising: 窓を開けた。すると… "Thereupon ...". It is rather narrative and written; the following sentence describes an event, not one's own intention or a request. Besides that, すると draws a conclusion from what was said: "so then, that means". In conversation, そうしたら or そしたら is often used for the temporal sequence.

examples[].german: The train stopped. So I was late.
And how did it turn out?
I got lost. So I asked at the police box.
en.notes: それで ties a consequence to a reason: "so, therefore", for example in excuses. Unlike だから, what follows is not a request or command but a fact. As a question それで？ or それで、どうなったの？ you ask someone to go on with their story. Do not confuse it with それでは "well then", used to close or to move on.

examples[].german: This restaurant is cheap. Besides, the food is good.
It's cold today. Besides, the wind is strong.
I can't go today. I have a lot of homework, and besides, I have a bit of a fever.
en.notes: それに adds a further point pointing in the same direction: "besides, moreover". It is often used to list reasons, frequently together with 〜し: 安いし、それにおいしい. Unlike そして "and" or それから "after that", it is not about a sequence but about an addition. その上 is somewhat more formal.

examples[].german: I've never heard such a story.
Please don't say such things.
No, that's not the case.
en.notes: そんな stands before a noun and means "that kind of, such", referring to something the other person said or something just mentioned. The series: こんな, そんな, あんな, どんな. そんなことはありません is the usual modest way to deflect a compliment, and exclaimed on its own, そんな！ expresses dismay ("That can't be!"). Before adjectives and verbs, そんなに is used instead.

examples[].german: I'd like to live in a house like that.
I've never seen such a big dog before.
I never want to talk to a person like that again.
en.notes: あんな means "that kind of (over there)" and refers to something distant or something both speakers know: あんな家. It often sounds judgmental, both positive (あんな人になりたい) and negative (あんな人とは話したくない). Before adjectives and verbs, あんなに "so much" is used. The series: こんな, そんな, あんな, どんな.

examples[].german: You don't have to hurry that much.
I didn't think it would be that expensive.
This movie wasn't all that interesting.
en.notes: そんなに means "so much, that much" and refers to an extent that the other person mentioned or showed: そんなに急がなくてもいい. Very common is そんなに＋negation "not particularly, not that much": そんなにおいしくない. Correspondingly there are こんなに and あんなに. It stands before adjectives and verbs, whereas before nouns you use そんな.

examples[].german: I've come to understand Japanese quite well.
My cold has gotten much better.
It's still quite a way to the station.
en.notes: だいぶ (also written 大分) means "considerably, quite" and mostly describes a clear change or a large gap: だいぶ慣れた, だいぶよくなった, だいぶ寒くなった. かなり is similar; ずいぶん expresses surprise more strongly. With ある or かかる it describes distance or duration: まだだいぶある "there is still quite a way to go".

en.meaning: visiting a sick person; get-well greeting
examples[].german: I'm going to visit someone who is ill.
I'm going to visit my friend who was hospitalized.
I wrote a get-well letter.
en.notes: お見舞い means a visit or an expression of sympathy during illness or after a misfortune. お見舞いに行く means "to pay a sick visit". It can also mean a get-well letter or a corresponding gift. The お gives the expression a polite form; the attack meaning of the dictionary belongs to a different usage.

examples[].german: If it rains, I'll stay home.
If you have time, please help.
What would you like to do if you won the lottery?
en.notes: もし at the beginning of a sentence announces a condition: "if, in case". It does not replace the conditional form but reinforces it; the verb still ends in 〜たら, 〜ば, 〜なら or 〜ても: もし雨が降ったら. Typical for hypothetical questions (もし〜たら、どうしますか). Related is もしかしたら "perhaps".

examples[].german: Please write with a pen or a pencil.
Please come on Monday or Tuesday.
The game is canceled on days of rain or snow.
en.notes: または connects alternatives: "or". It sounds objective and appears mainly in instructions, forms and announcements: ペンまたは鉛筆. In conversation, simply か (AかB) is usually used. When asking about a choice, use それとも: コーヒーにしますか、それとも紅茶にしますか. It is almost always written in kana, rarely 又は.

examples[].german: I cook for my family.
I'm studying in order to pass the exam.
The train is delayed because of an accident.
en.notes: ため (rarely 為) has two main meanings: purpose and benefit (noun＋のために "for", verb＋ために "in order to", with the same subject and a volitional action) and reason in factual texts: 事故のため "because of an accident". ためになる means "to be useful, instructive". For goals that cannot be controlled, ように is used rather than ために (聞こえるように).

examples[].german: Mr./Ms. Tanaka should be home by now.
The shop should be open today.
I'm sure I put the key in my bag, but I can't find it.
en.notes: はず expresses the speaker's well-founded expectation: "should be, ought to be (according to plan or logic)". It follows the plain form (来るはず), noun + のはず and な-adjective + なはず, and is almost always written in hiragana (筈 is rare). はずがない means "cannot possibly be", はずだった or はずなのに expresses a disappointed expectation. Unlike べき (moral duty) or でしょう (mere supposition), はず rests on concrete grounds such as timetables, arrangements or experience.

examples[].german: Please tell me the reason you were late.
Expensive things are not always good.
This explanation is so difficult that I can't make any sense of it.
en.notes: 訳（わけ）refers to the reason or background of a matter; in conversation it sounds more personal than the matter-of-fact 理由. Fixed expressions are 訳が分からない "can't make sense of something, to not make sense" and 言い訳 "excuse". In grammar patterns it is usually written in hiragana: わけではない "not necessarily", わけがない "no way". With the reading やく the same kanji means "translation" (英訳, 翻訳).

examples[].german: Thanks to my teacher, I was able to pass.
Thanks to the medicine, I slept well.
Thank you for asking; my mother has recovered.
en.notes: おかげ stands for a favorable influence one is grateful for: noun + のおかげで or plain verb form + おかげで (毎日練習したおかげで). For negative causes, のせいで is used instead. The polite phrase おかげさまで "thanks for asking" answers questions about one's well-being, even if the other person did not directly help. The kanji spelling お陰 is possible, but hiragana is usual.

examples[].german: The clock is making a strange noise.
His story was so funny that I laughed.
It's odd that he hasn't come yet.
en.notes: おかしい has two sides: "funny, laughable" and, more common in everyday use, "strange, not right, suspicious". Typical are 体の調子がおかしい "something is wrong with my body" or 〜のはおかしい "it is strange that ...". 面白い, by contrast, rather means "interesting, entertaining", and 変 is a close synonym for "odd, peculiar". As an い-adjective: おかしくて, おかしかった; the kanji spelling 可笑しい is rare.

examples[].german: The child is playing with a toy.
Please put the toys away in the box.
I bought my child a toy for their birthday.
en.notes: おもちゃ is the everyday word for toy and is almost always written in hiragana; the kanji word 玩具（がんぐ）appears more in shops and on signs. Typical are おもちゃで遊ぶ, おもちゃを片付ける and おもちゃ屋 "toy store". Figuratively, 人をおもちゃにする means "to toy with someone".

examples[].german: The other day I met my teacher at the station.
I'll send you the photos from the other day.
Thank you for the other day.
en.notes: この間 refers to a specific point in the recent past, "the other day, a few days ago", and so usually takes the past tense. It is often written in hiragana and colloquially shortened to こないだ. With の it forms attributes (この間の写真), and この間はありがとうございました is a set phrase of thanks when meeting again. For an ongoing state, "lately", you use このごろ or 最近 instead.

examples[].german: Thank you for your words of congratulation.
Let's celebrate your birthday.
I sent flowers as a wedding gift.
en.notes: お祝い can mean congratulations, a celebration or a gift for a joyful occasion. お祝いの言葉 are words of congratulation; 誕生日のお祝い is a birthday celebration. With お祝いとして, a gift can be named as a token of congratulation. The polite form with お is common in everyday speech.

examples[].german: The announcer is reading the news.
I want to become an announcer in the future.
That announcer speaks very beautifully.
en.notes: アナウンサー in Japan are usually salaried broadcasters of a television or radio station who read the news, host programs or commentate on sports. The announcement itself is called アナウンス (駅のアナウンス), and the person who hosts a show or event is usually called 司会者. Typical are アナウンサーになる and ニュースを読む. The profession is considered prestigious and demands especially clean pronunciation.

examples[].german: This drink does not contain alcohol.
I'm driving, so I won't drink alcohol.
Please clean your hands with the alcohol at the entrance.
en.notes: アルコール refers both to the chemical substance and to alcoholic drinks in general. For drinks, however, お酒 is usually used in everyday speech; アルコール sounds more matter-of-fact and appears on labels and notices (アルコール度数, ノンアルコールビール). Since the pandemic, アルコール often also means the hand sanitizer at the entrance of shops. Typical are アルコールを飲む and アルコールが入っている.

examples[].german: My older brother commutes to work by motorcycle.
I wear a helmet when I ride a motorcycle.
I want to get a motorcycle license.
en.notes: オートバイ is a word coined in Japan (from "auto" and "bicycle") for a motorcycle. In everyday speech バイク is much more common, which also includes scooters; オートバイ sounds more matter-of-fact and a little older. One says オートバイに乗る, and as a means of transport オートバイで行く. Do not confuse it with 自転車 "bicycle".

examples[].german: I put gas in the car.
The price of gasoline has gone up.
Is there a gas station nearby?
en.notes: ガソリン is gasoline. To fill up is ガソリンを入れる, the gas station is ガソリンスタンド, a Japanese coinage that does not exist in English in this form. Diesel is called 軽油, and fuel costs are ガソリン代. For price changes one says ガソリンの値段が上がる/下がる.

examples[].german: I cut vegetables and make a salad.
Lunch was a salad and bread.
Would you like dressing on your salad?
en.notes: サラダ refers to the prepared dish, not the plant: lettuce is レタス. Typical are サラダを作る, ドレッシングをかける and compounds such as ポテトサラダ or 野菜サラダ. In Japan, a small salad often comes as a side dish with set menus, including breakfast.

examples[].german: I bought a sandwich at the station.
Two egg sandwiches, please.
I put ham and cheese between slices of bread and made sandwiches.
en.notes: サンドイッチ is a sandwich, in Japan usually made with soft white bread with the crusts cut off. The spelling サンドウィッチ also occurs, and in everyday speech it is often shortened to サンド: 卵サンド, カツサンド. Putting the filling between the slices is called 挟む. In convenience stores, sandwiches usually come cut into triangles in a two-pack.

examples[].german: I grilled a steak for dinner.
The steak at this restaurant is tender.
I'd like my steak well done, please.
en.notes: ステーキ without any addition almost always means a beef steak (ビーフステーキ); other kinds of meat are named, for example ポークステーキ. To fry or grill is ステーキを焼く. In a restaurant you state the doneness with レア, ミディアム or ウェルダン, or simply say よく焼いてください "well done, please". Do not confuse it with ハンバーグ, a kind of meat patty, which is sometimes called ハンバーグステーキ on menus.

examples[].german: I'll wear a suit to the interview.
I need to buy a new suit.
My father goes to work in a suit every day.
en.notes: スーツ refers to a suit made up of a jacket and matching pants or skirt, for men and women alike. You say スーツを着る or スーツで会社に行く; the older word for a man's suit is 背広. For job hunting, students wear a plain, usually black リクルートスーツ. Do not confuse it with スーツケース "suitcase".

examples[].german: This factory produces cars.
Rice production is thriving in this region.
en.notes: 生産 is the noun for production or manufacturing, including in agriculture. With する it becomes the transitive verb "to produce": 車を生産する. 米の生産 means rice production. 盛んです here means that a lot is produced or that production is flourishing.

examples[].german: I often wear sandals in summer.
These sandals are easy to walk in.
I'm going to the sea, so I bought flip-flops.
en.notes: サンダル means sandals and other open shoes. As with all footwear, one says サンダルを履く (not 着る) and, to take them off, サンダルを脱ぐ. Flip-flops are called ビーチサンダル, colloquially ビーサン. With 歩きやすい or 歩きにくい you describe how comfortable it is to walk in them.

examples[].german: Please read the textbook before class.
I forgot my textbook at home.
The explanations in this textbook are easy to understand.
en.notes: テキスト in class usually means the textbook or course material; it is somewhat more general than 教科書, which mainly stands for official school textbooks. In computer language it also means "text" in the sense of text data (テキストファイル). Typical are テキストを開く and テキストの十ページ. For the text of an article or book, 文章 or 本文 is more common.

examples[].german: My mother works part-time at a shop nearby.
I'm looking for a part-time job.
In the chorus, I sing the alto part.
en.notes: パート is the short form of パートタイム and means part-time work or the part-time worker themselves: パートで働く, パートをしている, パートの仕事. Unlike アルバイト, which is mainly associated with students and side jobs, パート typically stands for longer-term part-time positions of adults, often housewives. パート also means "part" or "voice" in music (ソプラノのパート).

examples[].german: I live in a two-story house.
There is a two-story shop in front of the station.
I rode a double-decker bus in London.
en.notes: 二階建て describes a building with two floors; with 〜階建て you count the stories (三階建て, 十階建て), where たて becomes だて through sound change. Since the ground floor counts as 一階 in Japanese, a 二階建ての家 has a ground floor and an upper floor. As a modifier it takes の: 二階建てのバス "double-decker bus".

en.meaning: to come; to go; to be (honorific)
examples[].german: The teacher has already arrived.
Will you come here tomorrow as well?
Do you know where the teacher is right now?
en.notes: おいでになる is a respectful form (尊敬語) for いる, 来る and 行く and refers only to actions of people of higher status, never to oneself. It sounds slightly more formal than the more common いらっしゃる; for one's own actions one humbly uses 参る, 伺う or おる. The ます-form is regularly おいでになります, and the request is おいでください "please come". It is almost always written in hiragana.

examples[].german: What is the teacher doing?
What will you do on the weekend?
I hear the company president plays golf.
en.notes: なさる is the respectful form (尊敬語) of する and describes actions of others: 何をなさいますか, ゴルフをなさる. The ます-form is the irregular なさいます, not なさります, and the imperative なさい appears in gentle commands from parents or teachers such as 早く寝なさい. When ordering, the staff ask 何になさいますか "What will you have?". For one's own actions, the humble いたす is used instead.

examples[].german: I was startled by the loud noise.
I was surprised when I saw the price.
I called out to my friend suddenly from behind and startled him.
en.notes: びっくり is an onomatopoeic word and is almost always used as びっくりする "to be startled, to be surprised"; the trigger is marked by に (音にびっくりする) or a て-form (値段を見てびっくりした). To surprise someone is the causative びっくりさせる. The synonymous 驚く is more neutral and also used in writing; びっくり sounds more colloquial and lively. Spontaneously one exclaims びっくりした！ "You scared me!"; びっくり箱 is a jack-in-the-box.

examples[].german: I waited about ten minutes.
It isn't as cold today as yesterday.
The more I study Japanese, the more interesting it becomes.
en.notes: ほど is mostly written in hiragana and has three main functions. After quantities it means "about, approximately" and sounds somewhat more formal than ぐらい (十分ほど). In the comparison A は B ほど〜ない it means "A is not as ... as B" and always takes a negative. The pattern 〜ば〜ほど means "the more ..., the more ...", and after expressions of degree ほど means "so much that" (泣きたいほど).

examples[].german: Please look at the inside of the box.
I'll reply within today.
Which of these three do you like best?
en.notes: 内（うち）means "inside", but as an independent word it is now mostly used in a temporal or selective sense and then often written in hiragana: 今日のうちに "before today is over", 若いうちに "while one is young", 三つのうち "of the three". For the spatial inside, 中 is more usual in everyday speech, or compounds such as 内側 are used. The same reading うち (mostly as 家 or in kana) also stands for "home, family" and "our" (うちの会社).

examples[].german: Little Hana is already asleep.
I played with Yuki in the park.
Grandma, happy birthday!
en.notes: ちゃん is a familiar, endearing name suffix, used above all for children, girls, close friends and pets; it often attaches to short names or nicknames (ゆうちゃん). In the family it appears in おばあちゃん, お母ちゃん or お兄ちゃん. Compared with the neutral さん and くん, which is used more for boys, ちゃん is very familiar and unsuitable toward superiors or strangers. Only small children use it for their own name.

examples[].german: My father shaves every morning.
My older brother is growing a beard.
The cat's whiskers are very long.
en.notes: ひげ covers every kind of facial hair (beard, mustache, sideburns) and also the whiskers of cats or the antennae of insects. It is mostly written in hiragana; strictly speaking the kanji 髭 denotes the mustache and 鬚 the chin beard. Typical verbs are ひげをそる "to shave", ひげを伸ばす "to grow a beard" and ひげが生える "a beard grows".

examples[].german: I had forgotten something important.
If there is anything you don't understand, please ask.
Have you ever been to Japan?
en.notes: こと refers to abstract things, matters and events, whereas 物（もの）stands for tangible objects. It is written predominantly in hiragana, especially in grammar patterns: た-form + ことがある "to have done something once", ことができる "can", ことにする "to decide to". With adjectives and verbs it forms expressions such as 大事なこと "something important" or 分からないこと "something one doesn't understand".

examples[].german: When the rain stops, I'll go out.
The wind died down in the evening.
The noise from the next room finally stopped.
en.notes: 止む is intransitive and describes something stopping by itself, especially weather and noises: 雨が止む, 風が止む, 音が止む. It is mostly written in hiragana (やむ). The transitive counterpart 止める（やめる）means "to stop doing something" as a deliberate action. Do not confuse it with 止まる（とまる）"to stop" for movement and machines, or with 病む "to be ill".

examples[].german: I quit smoking.
Because of the rain, we called off the game.
Please stop fighting.
en.notes: やめる is transitive: you deliberately stop an activity or drop a plan (たばこをやめる, 行くのをやめる). It is mostly written in hiragana because 止める is also read とめる "to stop, to halt" (a car, a machine). For quitting a job or leaving a school, 辞める is usual. The intransitive counterpart is 止む（やむ）"to stop" for rain or noise.

examples[].german: Please open your textbook.
I'm opening a small shop next month.
We're holding a birthday party for a friend on the weekend.
en.notes: 開く（ひらく）means "to open", especially for things that unfold: 本を開く, 傘を開く, to open a file. It also means "to hold" (パーティーを開く, 会議を開く) and "to open for business" (店を開く); intransitively it can mean that something opens (花が開く). The same kanji is also read あく: 開く（あく）"to open (by itself)" forms a pair with 開ける（あける）and is used more for doors, windows and lids.

examples[].german: I have something to do today, so I'll go home first.
Do you need anything from me?
This is a bicycle for children.
en.notes: 用 means "business, errand": 用がある "to have something to do", 何か用？ "What's up?" (colloquial). In conversation the synonymous 用事 is more common; politely it is ご用 (ご用の方は… "Those who have business, ..."). As a suffix, 〜用 means "intended for ...": 子供用, 女性用, 仕事用.

examples[].german: My wallet was stolen by a pickpocket at the station.
Please watch out for pickpockets in crowded places.
The police arrested a pickpocket.
en.notes: すり refers both to the pickpocket and to pickpocketing and is written in hiragana (the kanji 掏摸 are rare). Typical are すりに遭う "to be pickpocketed", すりに財布を取られる and すりに気を付ける. A thief in general is 泥棒, shoplifting is 万引き, and snatching a handbag in passing is ひったくり.

examples[].german: I had my hair cut at the barber near the station.
My father goes to the barber every month.
At the barber's I also had my beard shaved.
en.notes: 床屋 is the colloquial word for a men's barber, where hair is cut and often the face is shaved. The shop is more formally called 理容室 or 理髪店; a salon with coloring and perms, mainly for women, is a 美容院. Typical are 床屋に行く and 床屋で髪を切る, even when you have your hair cut by someone.

examples[].german: Please complete the procedures.
I completed the formalities for my passport.
I asked at the reception desk how the procedure works.
en.notes: 手続き means a procedure or the formal steps required, for example for a passport. 手続きをする means "to complete the formalities". It refers to the prescribed process, not to practical handiwork. 手続きの方法 names the way of going about it, which you can ask about.

examples[].german: I'm lodging near the university.
I'm looking for new lodging.
The landlady makes me breakfast every morning.
en.notes: 下宿 refers to a room rented in someone else's household, traditionally often with meals provided by the landlord's family, especially for students. As a verb, 下宿する is intransitive: 大学の近くで下宿する. The lodging itself is called 下宿 or 下宿先, the rent 下宿代. Today students more often live in their own アパート or in a dormitory (寮).

examples[].german: Water is essential to life.
I learned about the origin of life.
I took out life insurance.
en.notes: 生命 means "life" in a biological or abstract sense and sounds more objective and more literary than the everyday 命. Typical set phrases are 生命保険 "life insurance", 生命の危険 "danger to life" and 生命の起源 "origin of life". For life in the sense of one's life story or daily life, use 人生 or 生活 instead.

examples[].german: You use this tool like this.
This is how I see it.
If you do it like this, you'll finish faster.
en.notes: こう means "this way, like this" and refers to something the speaker is currently showing or about to carry out. It belongs to the こ・そ・あ・ど series: そう "that way (as you say, as mentioned)", ああ "that way (as over there, as is well known)", どう "how?". Typical are こうする, こう言う and こうすれば; before nouns, こういう is used (こういう本 "a book like this").

en.meaning: from now on; from now; in a moment
examples[].german: I'm going shopping now.
I look forward to continuing to work with you.
From now on I will study Japanese every day.
en.notes: これから means "in a moment, from now" or "from now on, in the future". Without a particle it often stands for an action that follows immediately (これから出かけます), with は or も for the further future (これからは気を付けます, これからもよろしく). これからの + noun means "future, coming". 今から stresses the starting point now more strongly, and 今後 is the formal equivalent.

examples[].german: It rains often these days.
Lately I run every morning.
Young people these days hardly read newspapers.
en.notes: このごろ describes a period up to the present, "lately, nowadays", and mostly appears with the present tense or the ている form for habits and trends. In contrast, この間 refers to a single point in time, "the other day", and 最近 can express both trends and individual recent events. The kanji spelling この頃 is possible; hiragana is common.

examples[].german: I'm full.
The train was full of people.
Lots of cherry blossoms are in bloom in the park.
en.notes: いっぱい means "full" (お腹がいっぱい "full (of food)", 〜でいっぱい "full of") and, colloquially, "a lot, plenty"; たくさん is more neutral. In kanji, 一杯 means "a cup, a glass" (コーヒーを一杯) and also "a drink" (一杯飲みに行く). As a suffix it means "until the end of" (今月いっぱい), and 精いっぱい means "with all one's might".

examples[].german: The person in charge is away from his desk at the moment.
I will be here in the afternoon as well.
Thank you always for your kind support.
en.notes: おる is the humble or polite-formal form of いる and is almost always written in hiragana. It is used for oneself or one's own side, mostly as おります and in the pattern 〜ております instead of 〜ています, typically in business language, on the phone and in e-mails (お世話になっております). For people of higher status, use いらっしゃる instead. In western Japanese dialects, however, おる is the ordinary, non-humble form for "to be there".

examples[].german: The doorbell rang.
If you need anything, please press the bell.
I rang my bicycle bell.
en.notes: ベル refers to a bell or buzzer that gives a signal: 玄関のベル, 自転車のベル, formerly also a telephone or school bell. Intransitively it is ベルが鳴る, transitively ベルを鳴らす, or ベルを押す for buttons. For door intercoms and chimes, インターホン and チャイム are often said today; large temple bells are 鐘, small bells 鈴.

examples[].german: My wallet is in my handbag.
I gave my mother a handbag.
I left my handbag on the train.
en.notes: ハンドバッグ is a small (usually women's) handbag. For bags in general, バッグ or かばん is used; other types are ショルダーバッグ and トートバッグ. The spelling ハンドバック with ク is a common mistake. Typical are ハンドバッグに入れる and ハンドバッグを持つ.

examples[].german: I projected photos onto the screen.
I watched a movie on a big screen.
Please send me a screenshot of your phone.
en.notes: スクリーン mainly means a projection surface: the cinema screen or the screen in a classroom (スクリーンに映す). For the display of a computer, TV or phone, 画面 is the usual word; スクリーン appears there mainly in loanwords such as スクリーンショット. 大きなスクリーンで見る stresses the cinema experience.

examples[].german: The reception desk is on the first floor.
Please write your name at the reception desk.
en.notes: 受付 denotes the reception or front desk here, for example in a hotel, office, or clinic. 受付で names the place where you check in or write your name. The usual spelling 受付 is read うけつけ. The meaning "acceptance of an application" belongs to a further dictionary use.

examples[].german: What is your favorite TV program?
This morning I heard a new song on a radio program.
en.notes: 番組 means an individual show or program on television or radio. 好きな番組 asks about a favorite show; 番組で says on which program something was heard or seen. Here it is not a computer program, which is usually called プログラム.

examples[].german: What a wonderful view.
It was a wonderful performance.
en.notes: 素晴らしい is an i-adjective meaning wonderful or great. It can stand directly before a noun: 素晴らしい景色. At the end of a sentence, the polite past form is 素晴らしかったです. The expression is clear praise and suits both an impression and an achievement.

examples[].german: I want to go to the art museum.
I like art class.
I'm interested in Japanese art.
en.notes: 美術 denotes the fine arts, such as painting or sculpture. 美術の授業 is art class. 美術館 is an art museum and contains the word as a component. For art and artistic activities in a broader sense, 芸術 is a more common umbrella term.

examples[].german: This meat is tough.
This bread is hard and difficult to eat.
This stone is hard and does not break easily.
en.notes: 硬い means hard or tough and is often used for the properties of a material. Hard bread or tough meat is difficult to bite; 硬い石 describes the hardness of a stone. The opposite is 軟らかい. 固い can also express hardness or firmness, while 堅い often emphasizes a solid, reliable quality. The usual combinations help with choosing the spelling. As an i-adjective, it forms 硬くて and 硬くない.

examples[].german: This river is deep.
This river is very deep.
This book has a deeper meaning.
en.notes: 深い is an い-adjective for spatial depth, for example of a river. Before a noun it stands directly: 深い川. It can also mean "profound" in a figurative sense, for example 深い意味, "a deeper meaning". 深く is the adverbial form; 浅い is the opposite, "shallow".

examples[].german: It's shallow here, so it's safe.
The children's pool is shallow.
I slept lightly last night.
en.notes: 浅い means "shallow", for example of water, or "superficial". It is an い-adjective: 浅いプール, "a shallow pool". 浅い眠り, on the other hand, is light sleep. The adverbial form is 浅く; 深い means greater depth.

examples[].german: I envy you for being able to go on a trip.
I envy you for being able to go on an overseas trip.
I envy you for having such a long vacation.
en.notes: 羨ましい can express "I'm envious" or "that is enviable". It is an い-adjective. 羨ましいです often reveals the speaker's feeling even when "I" is not mentioned. It does not have to mean resentment; you can also use it in a friendly way to say you would like to have the opportunity yourself.

examples[].german: The teacher is strict.
This winter is harsh.
en.notes: 厳しい means "strict" for people or rules and "harsh / severe" for conditions. 先生は厳しいです describes a strict teacher; 冬が厳しい means a harsh winter. It is an い-adjective. The reading is きびしい; the identically written form いかめしい belongs to a different word usage.

examples[].german: What a lovely view.
Thank you for the lovely present.
en.notes: 素敵 is a な-adjective for something beautiful, charming, or great. Before a noun, な is used: 素敵な景色, 素敵なプレゼント. It is a personal positive evaluation. The kanji are chosen as phonetic spelling (当て字); the reading is すてき.

examples[].german: There is plenty of time.
I've already eaten enough.
I made sufficient preparations.
en.notes: 十分 with the reading じゅうぶん means "enough / sufficient". As an adverb it stands before the verb, for example 十分食べる. Before a noun it takes な: 十分な準備, "sufficient preparation". The identically written time expression "ten minutes" is read じゅっぷん or じっぷん and does not belong to this card.

examples[].german: I was waiting the whole time.
I've been living here all along.
This shop is much cheaper.
en.notes: ずっと can stress an uninterrupted duration or a large difference. ずっと待つ means "to wait the whole time"; ずっと安い means "much cheaper". With ずっと住んでいる a long period is usually meant, not necessarily one's whole life. The lengthened form ずーっと intensifies the statement.

examples[].german: I'm changing the plan.
I changed my hair color.
en.notes: 変える is a transitive ichidan verb: someone changes something, which takes を. 予定を変える means to change a plan; 髪の色を変える means to change one's hair color. The polite forms are 変えます and 変えました. Its intransitive counterpart 変わる describes something changing on its own.

examples[].german: Spring is coming soon.
The train will depart shortly.
I'll be finished with my homework soon.
en.notes: もうすぐ announces that an event is imminent in time: もうすぐ春です, もうすぐ終わります. Unlike すぐ ("immediately"), it is not suitable for requests or commands - "Please come right away" is すぐ来てください, not もうすぐ. It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: My Japanese is getting better and better.
Don't hold back, please eat as much as you like.
New buildings are going up one after another near the station.
en.notes: どんどん describes a swift, vigorous development, often with ～くなる/～になる: どんどん上手になる. In requests it encourages someone to keep going without restraint: どんどん食べてください, "Please help yourself freely". Do not confuse it with だんだん ("gradually"); as an onomatopoeic word, どんどん also stands for loud knocking or drumming (ドアをどんどんたたく).

examples[].german: I forgot it by mistake.
I carelessly missed my stop.
I wasn't paying attention and mixed up the sugar and the salt.
en.notes: うっかり describes a mishap caused by inattention, not by intention - the opposite of わざと. It often appears together with ～てしまう: うっかり忘れてしまう. As the verb うっかりする it means "to be inattentive, not to pay attention"; a careless mistake is called うっかりミス.

examples[].german: Did you do it on purpose?
My father deliberately lost the game against his child.
It wasn't on purpose. I'm sorry.
en.notes: わざと means "on purpose, intentionally" and usually concerns something undesirable or feigned: わざと負ける "to lose on purpose". To apologize, you say わざとじゃありません "It wasn't on purpose". Do not confuse it with わざわざ ("go out of one's way, take the trouble specially"); it is written in kana.

examples[].german: Is it really true?
I never thought he would come.
It surely won't snow.
en.notes: まさか expresses that one considers something impossible or can hardly believe it. As an adverb it is usually combined with a negative or a supposition: まさか～ないでしょう "surely not", まさか～とは思わなかった "I never thought that ...". On its own as an exclamation, まさか！ means "No way!/You can't be serious!".

examples[].german: Just what you'd expect of a teacher.
After walking for three hours, I was tired after all.
en.notes: さすが + person or noun praises someone for living up to expectations: さすが先生ですね "Typical of a teacher - just what I'd expect". On its own as an exclamation, さすが！ means roughly "Impressive!". さすがに, on the other hand, means "as one would expect, even so", often with a qualification: さすがに疲れました "I was tired after all".

examples[].german: I'm quite tired.
It's quite hot today.
It's quite a distance to the station.
en.notes: かなり means "quite, considerably" and lies in strength between 少し and とても. Before nouns it takes の: かなりの距離, かなりの人. It sounds more matter-of-fact than とても and can intensify both positive and negative things; 割と, by contrast, is weaker and expresses more "surprisingly, actually quite".

examples[].german: It was relatively easy.
This restaurant is relatively cheap.
en.notes: 割と (also 割に) means "relatively, quite" and often implies that something is better or different than expected: 割と簡単でした. It is more colloquial and weaker than かなり. It is often written in kana: わりと.

en.meaning: thanks to you; thanks to your help
examples[].german: I'm well, thank you.
Thanks to your support, I passed the exam.
en.notes: お陰様で is a polite expression for gratefully attributing a good condition or success to someone's support. As a reply to a question about one's well-being, it can also be a friendly routine phrase without naming any concrete help. おかげさまで is often written in hiragana; a following sentence explains what went well.

examples[].german: Please eat, don't hold back.
I have something to do today, so I'll pass on the party.
Please refrain from smoking here.
en.notes: 遠慮する means to hold back out of consideration or to politely decline. 遠慮しないでください or ご遠慮なく encourages a guest to help themselves. With ～は遠慮します you politely decline, and on signs ～はご遠慮ください is a polite prohibition ("please refrain").

examples[].german: I'll look it up on the internet.
I look up words in the dictionary.
I investigated the cause of the accident.
en.notes: With 調べる you check or investigate something in a targeted way; a word is looked up in a dictionary, and a cause is investigated. The object takes を, and the means takes で. It is a transitive ichidan verb.

en.meaning: to endure; to put up with
examples[].german: Even if it hurts, please bear it.
I'm on a diet, so I'm holding off on sweets.
I can't stand this heat any longer.
en.notes: 我慢する means to endure something unpleasant or to deny oneself something. What one endures or goes without takes を: 痛みを我慢する, 甘い物を我慢する. 我慢できない means "cannot bear (any longer)"; 我慢強い describes a patient, resilient person.

examples[].german: Stop complaining all the time.
The food at this restaurant is flawlessly delicious.
A customer complained to me.
en.notes: 文句 is a personal complaint or grumbling; the typical combination is 文句を言う, "to complain". 文句ばかり言う means "to grumble constantly", and 文句なし/文句がない means "flawless, nothing to complain about". A formal complaint to a company is rather 苦情.

examples[].german: Is the rumor about that person true?
The rumor is that a new supermarket is going to open in front of the station.
Speak of the devil - here comes Mr. Tanaka.
en.notes: 噂 is a rumor or gossip about someone; it is often written in kana: うわさ. Typical are 噂を聞く, ～の噂をする "to talk about someone" and ～という噂です "the rumor is that ...". The fixed phrase 噂をすれば（影）corresponds to "Speak of the devil".

examples[].german: Please keep it secret.
This is a secret just between the two of us.
What is the secret of this delicious bread?
en.notes: 秘密 is a secret. Important combinations: 秘密にする "to keep secret", 秘密を守る "to keep a secret" and 秘密を話す "to reveal". It can also refer to the "secret" of a success: おいしさの秘密. Colloquially, among friends, 内緒 is often used.

examples[].german: He has a kind personality.
My older brother and I have completely different personalities.
He and I don't get along in terms of personality.
en.notes: 性格 is a person's character or personality. You describe it with an adjective before it (明るい性格, 優しい性格) or with が: 性格がいい/悪い. 性格が合う means "to get along personality-wise", 性格が合わない "not to be compatible". For things, 性格 also means "nature, character" (問題の性格).

examples[].german: Please change your attitude.
The shop assistant's attitude was very bad.
The company has not yet taken a position on this issue.
en.notes: 態度 is visible behavior or manner toward others: 態度がいい/悪い, 店員の態度. 態度が大きい means "to act arrogantly", 態度を改める "to improve one's behavior". 態度 also denotes the stance on an issue: 態度を決める "to take a stand".

examples[].german: Please don't be so selfish.
My younger brother was a willful child.
Please grant me just one favor.
en.notes: わがまま is almost always written in kana; the kanji 我儘 are rare. As a na-adjective it describes a selfish, spoiled person: わがままな子供. As a noun it appears in わがままを言う "to make selfish demands, to whine"; politely, you ask for a personal favor with わがままを聞いてください.

en.meaning: selfish; arbitrary; of its own accord
examples[].german: Please do not use it without permission.
He really is a selfish person.
The door opened by itself.
en.notes: 勝手 expresses that someone acts only as they please. The most common form is 勝手に "on one's own authority, without asking": 勝手に使わないで. With things, 勝手に means "by itself": ドアが勝手に開く. As a na-adjective, 勝手な人 (or 自分勝手) describes a selfish person; 勝手にしなさい！ means "Do whatever you like!".

examples[].german: Let's exchange phone numbers.
Please change the battery.
Can I exchange this shirt for a bigger size?
en.notes: 交換する means "to exchange, to swap" and also "to replace, to swap out" (電池を交換する). The patterns are AをBと交換する "to exchange A for B" and 友達と～を交換する "to exchange ... with a friend". For exchanging money you say 両替する; the Japanese synonym for "to swap out" is 取り替える.

examples[].german: I wash my hands to prevent illness.
I got a flu shot.
en.notes: 予防する is a formal Sino-Japanese word for preventing illnesses, accidents or disasters: 病気を予防する. Compounds such as 予防注射 "preventive vaccination" are common. In everyday speech, the simpler 防ぐ is often used for "to prevent, to ward off".

examples[].german: I grew up in Tokyo.
This plant grows in sunlight.
en.notes: 育つ describes a child growing up or a plant growing. The living thing takes が, the place of growing up often takes で. For raising a child or growing plants, the transitive 育てる is used. 育つ is a Godan verb ending in つ.

examples[].german: I order a dish.
I ordered a book online.
en.notes: 注文する means "to order", in a restaurant as well as online or from a dealer: 料理を注文する. Waiters politely ask ご注文はお決まりですか, "Have you decided yet?". In casual conversation people often simply say 頼む. As a noun, 注文 can also mean "wish, demand": 注文が多い "to have many special requests".

examples[].german: I'm confirming the reservation.
Before leaving the house, I check whether I turned off the gas.
Let me confirm tomorrow's time once more.
en.notes: 確認する means "to make sure, to check, to verify": 予約を確認する. With an embedded question, ～かどうか確認する means "to check whether ...". In professional life, 確認します and ご確認ください are heard constantly. Approval in the sense of "to authorize", by contrast, is 承認.

examples[].german: I show the guest around.
I take the guest to the conference room.
While looking at the map, I explained the way to the station.
en.notes: 案内する here means to guide someone or to show the way. The person takes を and the destination takes に: お客様を会議室に案内する. Giving directions can also be expressed with 道を案内する. お客様 is a polite term for a guest or customer. The forms of する change, for example in 案内します and 案内しました; 案内 alone is the noun. This card practices the meaning "to guide", not the further meanings "to notify" or "to invite".

en.meaning: to break down; to malfunction (machine, device)
examples[].german: The elevator is out of order.
My car broke down, so I was late for work.
This vending machine is out of order.
en.notes: 故障する is said of machines and devices that no longer work: 車が故障する, エレベーターが故障している. For things that break or are physically damaged (glass, toys), 壊れる is used. The sign 故障中 means "out of order".

examples[].german: I record the lessons.
I record my pronunciation and listen to it.
I recorded bird calls with my phone.
en.notes: 録音する means "to record sound": 授業を録音する. For video recordings, 録画する is used. The device takes で (スマホで録音する); to ask for permission, use 録音してもいいですか.

en.meaning: to broadcast; to announce over a loudspeaker
examples[].german: The news is broadcast every day.
During the earthquake, there was an announcement at school.
en.notes: 放送する means "to broadcast" (TV, radio) and also "to announce over a loudspeaker". Since the broadcaster is usually the one acting, it is often used in the passive: 毎日放送される. A program is 番組, a live broadcast 生放送; 校内放送 is the announcement at school.

examples[].german: I had various experiences.
I was able to have a good experience.
While studying abroad, I experienced living alone for the first time.
en.notes: 経験する means to experience something oneself or to gain experience with it. What is experienced takes を: 一人暮らしを経験する. There is also the combination 経験をする with the noun 経験. いい経験ができました here means that one had the opportunity for a good experience. 留学中に names the time during studying abroad; 初めて marks a first experience. The verb forms are, for example, 経験します and 経験しました.

examples[].german: I imagine my future life.
Summer in Japan was hotter than I had imagined.
I can't imagine life without electricity.
en.notes: 想像する means "to imagine, to picture"; the thing imagined takes を: 将来を想像する. When comparing with reality, you say 想像していたより or 想像以上 ("more than expected"). 想像できない or 想像もつかない means "unimaginable".

en.meaning: to be moved; to be deeply impressed
examples[].german: I was very moved by this movie.
I was moved to see the runners who kept going to the end of the marathon.
en.notes: 感動する means to be deeply moved or touched inside, always in a positive sense. What one is moved by takes に (映画に感動する) or appears as the reason in the て-form (～を見て感動しました). The related adjective is 感動的な, "moving, touching".

examples[].german: I'm relieved that everyone is safe.
You can drink this water without worry.
The medicine will make you better soon, so please don't worry.
