en.notes: 安心する means "to feel reassured, relieved" when a worry disappears; the reason usually appears in the て-form or with で: 無事で安心しました. 安心して～ means "without worry, with peace of mind ...", and 安心してください reassures someone ("Don't worry"). The opposite is 心配する; as a na-adjective: 安心な町.

examples[].german: I don't have enough money.
There isn't enough time.
For three people, this amount is enough.
en.notes: 足りる says that money, time, or an amount is sufficient for a purpose. What is needed takes が; 足りない means "not enough". It is an intransitive ichidan verb. The more formal phrase ～に足りる in the sense of "to be worthy of" belongs to a different use.

en.meaning: to be reluctant; to dislike; to refuse
examples[].german: The child does not like vegetables.
My younger brother is reluctant to go to the hospital.
You must not do things that other people dislike.
en.notes: 嫌がる describes another person visibly disliking something or resisting it; for your own feelings, use 嫌だ or 嫌い. The thing disliked takes を, and an action takes ～のを: 病院に行くのを嫌がる. 人が嫌がることをしない means "do not do things that make others uncomfortable".

examples[].german: My grandmother feels nostalgic about her hometown.
When my father heard songs from his student days, he felt very nostalgic.
en.notes: 懐かしがる describes someone else visibly looking back wistfully on the past; for your own feeling you say 懐かしい. What is missed takes を: 故郷を懐かしがる. It usually appears in the ～ている form or in the past tense.

en.meaning: to be shy; to be embarrassed
examples[].german: The child is shy.
My younger sister is embarrassed about having her picture taken.
Don't be shy, please speak in a loud voice.
en.notes: 恥ずかしがる describes visible shyness or embarrassment in others; for yourself you say 恥ずかしい. The cause takes を or ～のを: 写真を撮られるのを恥ずかしがる. The negative request 恥ずかしがらないで encourages someone; a shy person is called 恥ずかしがり屋.

examples[].german: This pillar is old.
I bumped into a pillar and my head hurts.
This temple has many thick pillars.
en.notes: 柱 is a supporting pillar or post, for example in houses and temples; it is counted with 本. Related words are 電柱 "utility pole" and 大黒柱 "mainstay (of the family)". You bump into a pillar with に: 柱にぶつかる.

examples[].german: I put the futon in the closet.
When I tidied up the closet, an old photo album turned up.
en.notes: 押し入れ is the built-in closet with sliding doors in a Japanese tatami room, in which mainly futons are stored during the day. A Western-style wardrobe is called クローゼット. You put something in with に: 布団を押し入れに入れる; the spelling 押入れ also occurs.

examples[].german: Do you need a blanket?
It's cold, so please give me one more blanket.
I covered the sleeping child with a blanket.
en.notes: 毛布 is a (wool) blanket for covering oneself, for example on an airplane or as an extra cover in winter; it is counted with 枚. To cover someone is 毛布をかける. The thick comforter of a futon, in contrast, is called 掛け布団.

examples[].german: Please turn off the gas.
In winter the gas bill goes up.
I smell gas. Please open the window.
en.notes: ガス in everyday speech usually means the heating and cooking gas in a household. You turn it off with 止める; the gas bill is ガス代, the gas stove ガスコンロ. Gasoline, by contrast, is ガソリン.

en.meaning: detergent; laundry detergent; dish soap; cleaning agent
examples[].german: Please buy some detergent.
We've run out of dish soap.
Please don't put in too much detergent.
en.notes: 洗剤 is the general term for cleaning agents - laundry detergent for clothes as well as dish soap for dishes (食器用洗剤). You put it in with 入れる and use it with で: 洗剤で洗う. Soap, in contrast, is 石けん.

examples[].german: Please brush your teeth before going to bed.
After lunch, I brush my teeth at the office.
I bought a travel toothbrush set.
en.notes: 歯磨き is tooth brushing; you say 歯磨きをする or use the verb 歯を磨く. Toothpaste is usually called 歯磨き粉 and the toothbrush 歯ブラシ. In Japan, many people also brush their teeth after lunch at work or school.

examples[].german: Please take your temperature.
Body temperature rises when you exercise.
en.notes: 体温 is the temperature of the body, as opposed to the air temperature 気温. 体温を測る means to measure it; 体温が上がる describes a rise. The expression denotes the measured value, not automatically a fever or a diagnosis.

examples[].german: Japan's economy is strong.
I'm studying economics.
en.notes: 経済 denotes the economy or the science of economics here. 国の経済 names the economy of a country; 経済を勉強する means to study economics. The first example contains an evaluation with 強い, the second an activity. Other uses for one's personal finances or thriftiness are not part of these examples.

examples[].german: This dictionary is useful.
This experience will be useful in the future.
en.notes: 役に立つ is the fixed phrase for "to be useful" or "to help". The useful thing is the subject; with ～に you can name the purpose or the person. Only 立つ is conjugated: 役に立ちます, 役に立った. The phrase suits tools as well as experiences.

examples[].german: I'm afraid of injections.
I got a shot at the hospital.
Please don't take a bath after the injection.
en.notes: 注射 is a shot or injection. The doctor gives it with 注射をする or 注射を打つ; as a patient you say 注射をしてもらう or 注射を受ける; 予防注射 is a preventive vaccination. Caution: the similar-sounding 駐車 (ちゅうしゃ) means "parking".

examples[].german: I'm having surgery next week.
The surgery went off without a hitch.
My grandfather had eye surgery.
en.notes: 手術 is a surgical operation. 手術をする can be used from the doctor's point of view ("to operate") as well as the patient's ("to be operated on"); to say it unambiguously as the patient, use 手術を受ける. The affected body part precedes it with の: 目の手術, 心臓の手術.

examples[].german: My mother was in the hospital for two weeks.
I'm going to visit a friend who is in the hospital.
en.notes: 入院する means "to be admitted to a hospital as an inpatient"; the hospital takes に: 病院に入院する. The duration stands without a particle (二週間入院する), 入院中 means "being in the hospital". You visit the sick for an お見舞い; the opposite is 退院する, outpatient treatment is 通院.

en.meaning: to be discharged from the hospital
examples[].german: I hear he can be discharged next week.
When I get out of the hospital, I want to go to an onsen.
en.notes: 退院する means "to be discharged from the hospital"; the hospital being left can take を: 病院を退院する. 退院できる and plans with 退院したら "as soon as I am discharged" are common. Congratulations: 退院おめでとうございます. Opposite: 入院する.

examples[].german: Please be kind to the patients.
This hospital has many patients.
en.notes: 患者 is a patient in the medical sense; in a hospital one politely says 患者さん. A sick person in general is 病人. Quantities: 多くの患者, 患者が増える.

en.meaning: to exchange money; to change money
examples[].german: I exchanged dollars for yen at the bank.
Could you change a 1,000-yen bill into 100-yen coins for me?
en.notes: 両替する means "to exchange money", both into another currency and into small change. The pattern is AをBに両替する: ドルを円に両替する. Buses often have a 両替機 for changing bills into coins. For exchanging goods, 交換する is used.

en.meaning: to keep; to take into custody
examples[].german: I'll take care of your luggage.
The neighbor looked after my child for me.
en.notes: 預かる means to take something or someone into temporary custody: 荷物を預かる, 子供を預かる. The counterpart is 預ける ("to leave in someone's care"): 荷物をフロントに預ける. In hotels and at the cash register you hear the polite form お預かりします, e.g. 一万円お預かりします "I have received 10,000 yen from you".

examples[].german: I hand out the worksheets.
I handed out flyers in front of the station.
en.notes: 配る means to distribute something to several people; the recipients take に: 学生にプリントを配る. Typical objects are handouts, flyers, cards or gifts. The expression 気を配る means "to be attentive, to look out for others".

examples[].german: The road is slippery.
I slipped on the ice.
During winter vacation I skied all day at the ski resort.
en.notes: 滑る means both "to slip" and "to glide" (on ice, on skis). 滑りやすい means "slippery", 手が滑る "to slip out of one's hand". Colloquially, 滑る also means "to fail an exam" or that a joke falls flat.

examples[].german: I fell on the stairs.
The child fell down and hurt his knee.
On snowy days, please be careful not to fall.
en.notes: 転ぶ means "to fall down, to tumble" when a person loses their balance; the place takes で: 階段で転ぶ. 倒れる, by contrast, means "to fall over, to collapse" (also for objects), 落ちる "to fall down from a height". Often used with ～てしまう or ～ないように気をつける.

examples[].german: I'll keep studying.
I keep exercising every day.
Let's continue the conversation after the break.
en.notes: 続ける means that someone continues an activity; the activity takes を. By contrast, 続く describes something continuing on its own. 続ける is a transitive ichidan verb. After a verb stem, ～続ける can also express "to keep on ...ing".

examples[].german: The sun sets into the sea.
The ship sank in the storm.
I feel down on rainy days.
en.notes: 沈む means "to sink, to go down" - for ships as well as for the sun (日が沈む; opposite: 昇る). Figuratively, 気分が沈む means "to feel down". The transitive counterpart is 沈める ("to sink something"), the opposite is 浮かぶ.

en.meaning: to float; to drift; to come to mind; to surface
examples[].german: Clouds are floating in the sky.
A good idea came to me.
Tears welled up in her eyes.
en.notes: 浮かぶ means "to float, to drift" (雲が空に浮かぶ, 船が海に浮かぶ) and, figuratively, "to come to mind, to surface": いい考えが浮かぶ. The place takes に. The transitive counterpart is 浮かべる (涙を浮かべる "to have tears in one's eyes"); "to swim" in the sense of swimming as a sport is 泳ぐ.

examples[].german: The sky is cloudy.
It will probably become cloudy from the afternoon.
en.notes: 曇る describes the sky becoming cloudy. It is an intransitive godan verb: 曇ります, 曇って. 空が曇っている states the cloudy condition. 曇るでしょう conveys a weather forecast. The subject takes が; you cannot cloud an object with を.

en.meaning: to clear up; to become sunny
examples[].german: The rain stopped and the sky cleared.
I hope it'll be sunny tomorrow.
en.notes: With the weather, 晴れる means "to clear up" or "to become sunny". The intransitive ichidan verb forms 晴れます and 晴れて. 空が晴れる names the sky as the subject. 晴れるといいですね expresses a wish, not a certain weather forecast. After rain, 晴れました can report that the clearing has already happened.

en.meaning: ceremonial occasions; coming-of-age, wedding, funeral and ancestral rites
examples[].german: There are rules of etiquette for ceremonial occasions.
Weddings, funerals and other family ceremonies cost a lot of money.
en.notes: 冠婚葬祭 is a four-character expression (四字熟語) for the important family ceremonies: 冠 coming of age, 婚 wedding, 葬 funeral, 祭 ancestral rites. It mostly stands as a collective term, for example in 冠婚葬祭のマナー or 冠婚葬祭の費用. The word is rather formal and written.

examples[].german: Next month I'm attending a friend's wedding.
The two of them will hold their wedding next spring.
I was asked to give a speech at the wedding.
en.notes: 結婚式 is the wedding ceremony. As a guest you attend with に: 結婚式に出る/出席する; the couple holds it: 結婚式を挙げる. The reception with food that follows is called 披露宴, the money gift from the guests ご祝儀.

examples[].german: I attended a funeral.
You wear black clothes to a funeral.
We held my grandfather's funeral with family only.
en.notes: 葬式 is the everyday word for a funeral or memorial service; the more polite form is usually お葬式. A person attending uses 葬式に出る or 葬式に行く, while the family uses 葬式をする or, more formally, 葬式を行う. In notices and official texts, 葬儀（そうぎ）is more common.

examples[].german: I write New Year's cards every year.
Many New Year's cards arrived on New Year's Day.
Please mail the New Year's cards by December 25th.
en.notes: 年賀状 are New Year's cards that you mail at the end of December and that the post office delivers together on January 1st. Typical verbs: 年賀状を書く, 年賀状を出す; to arrive: 年賀状が届く. They are counted with 枚: 年賀状を五十枚書きました. Those in a year of mourning send a mourning notice (喪中はがき) as early as November instead.

examples[].german: During Obon I go back to my family home.
At Obon we visit the family grave.
During the Obon period, the Shinkansen are very crowded.
en.notes: お盆 is the Buddhist festival in mid-August (regionally mid-July) at which people welcome the souls of their ancestors. Many companies are then closed (お盆休み), people travel to their hometowns and visit the family graves, and trains and highways are overcrowded. As a time expression, お盆に is used. Note: in everyday speech お盆 also means "tray"; the context decides.

examples[].german: Let's go cherry blossom viewing in the park.
In cherry blossom season, every park is full of people.
The weekend hanami was canceled because of rain.
en.notes: 花見 almost always means viewing the cherry blossoms (桜) in spring, usually as a picnic with food and drinks under the trees. You say 花見をする or 花見に行く; the polite form お花見 is very common. Popular spots fill up quickly, so people often reserve a place early. For autumn leaves, by contrast, you say 紅葉狩り.

examples[].german: The rain continues.
This road goes on further.
en.notes: 続く describes, without a direct object, that something continues or extends further: 雨が続く, 道が続く. It is an intransitive godan verb ending in く. When a person deliberately continues something, it is ～を続ける instead.

examples[].german: I want to go to a hot spring.
Hakone is famous for its hot springs.
On the weekend I went to a hot spring town with my family.
en.notes: Bathing in a hot spring is 温泉に入る (not 泳ぐ). 温泉 denotes both the spring itself and the spa resort with inns: 温泉に行く usually means "to go to an onsen town". An open-air bath is 露天風呂. Before bathing you wash thoroughly, and you do not wear swimwear.

examples[].german: I'm staying at a ryokan.
I ate Japanese food at the ryokan.
The room at the ryokan had tatami and was very quiet.
en.notes: A 旅館 is a traditional Japanese inn with tatami rooms and futons; dinner and breakfast are usually included in the price. To stay overnight is 旅館に泊まる (with に). Unlike at a ホテル, you often wear a yukata in the building. Smaller, family-run guesthouses are called 民宿.

examples[].german: I went to see the temples in Kyoto.
My grandfather's grave is on the grounds of a temple.
Every morning you can hear the temple bell.
en.notes: お寺 is a Buddhist temple; a Shinto shrine, by contrast, is 神社 - do not confuse the two. In everyday speech people almost always say お寺 with the polite お. In proper names, 寺 is usually read じ: 金閣寺（きんかくじ）. To visit: お寺を見学する, お寺を見に行く.

examples[].german: I'd like to try wearing a kimono.
I wear a kimono at New Year.
You can rent kimonos at this shop.
en.notes: You wear or put on a kimono with 着る: 着物を着る; "in a kimono" is 着物で. Today it is mainly worn on special occasions such as New Year, weddings, or Coming of Age Day. In older language 着物 can also mean "clothing" in general. The opposite term is 洋服 (Western clothing); 和服 is a more formal word for Japanese clothing.

examples[].german: I go to the fireworks festival wearing a yukata.
When you stay at a ryokan, there is a yukata in the room.
en.notes: 浴衣 is a light cotton kimono worn in summer to festivals and fireworks; in ryokan and onsen towns it serves as loungewear and a bathrobe. The reading ゆかた is irregular and has to be learned as a whole. To put on: 浴衣を着る, "in a yukata": 浴衣で. The left side goes over the right - the reverse is only done for the deceased.

examples[].german: I'm going to the fireworks festival.
I like watching fireworks in summer.
I set off fireworks in the garden with the children.
en.notes: In Japan fireworks are a summer topic, not a New Year's Eve one: large fireworks festivals are called 花火大会. Watching is 花火を見る, setting off small hand-held fireworks yourself is 花火をする, launching rockets is 花火を上げる. The word is made up of 花 ("flower") and 火 ("fire").

examples[].german: I'm looking forward to the summer festival.
This region's festival is famous.
This Saturday there is a festival at the shrine.
en.notes: In everyday speech 祭り is often said お祭り. That a festival takes place is expressed with がある, and the place takes で: 神社で祭りがあります. In compounds it becomes ～まつり (夏祭り, 雪祭り); in fixed names the り is often dropped (祇園祭). Caution: school and university festivals such as 文化祭 are read ～さい.

examples[].german: Japanese anime is popular all over the world.
As a child, I watched anime every Saturday morning.
en.notes: アニメ is the short form of アニメーション and in Japanese denotes any animated film or cartoon, not only Japanese productions. You say アニメを見る; a feature film is an アニメ映画. Printed comics, by contrast, are called 漫画（まんが）.

examples[].german: I have been learning karate since I was a child.
Karate originated in Okinawa.
en.notes: 空手 literally means "empty hand", that is, fighting without weapons. Taking lessons is 空手を習う, doing the sport is 空手をする or colloquially 空手をやる. Training takes place in a 道場; the black belt is 黒帯. The meaning "with empty hands" is rare; for that, 手ぶら is rather used.

examples[].german: Judo is a Japanese martial art.
I watched a judo match.
My younger brother does judo in his school club.
en.notes: You do judo with 柔道をする or 柔道をやる; taking lessons is 柔道を習う. The judo uniform is the 柔道着, a match is a 試合. Like 剣道, 茶道 or 書道, the word ends in 道（どう）, "way"; the umbrella term for the martial arts is 武道.

examples[].german: The population is increasing.
Recently my workload has increased.
en.notes: 増える describes an increase in people, things, or work; the thing that increases takes が. It is an intransitive ichidan verb. Someone who actively increases an amount uses 増やす with を. The spelling 殖える is used especially for multiplication or growth of capital.

examples[].german: I went to watch sumo.
Sumo wrestlers are very big.
The children are wrestling sumo-style in the park.
en.notes: The reading すもう is irregular. To wrestle sumo is 相撲を取る (not する); to watch is 相撲を見る. The wrestlers are called 力士, colloquially and affectionately お相撲さん. A tournament is called 場所, for example 九州場所.

examples[].german: I am practicing calligraphy.
In calligraphy class, I write kanji.
You use a brush and ink for calligraphy.
en.notes: 書道 is the art of writing characters on paper with a brush (筆) and ink (墨). You say 書道を習う or 書道を練習する; classes are called 書道教室. In elementary school, the subject is usually called 習字（しゅうじ）, which is more like "penmanship".

examples[].german: I would like to try the tea ceremony.
In the tea ceremony, you turn the tea bowl before drinking.
en.notes: 茶道 is read さどう or ちゃどう; both readings are correct. In everyday speech people often simply say お茶: お茶を習っています means "I am learning the tea ceremony". To try it out: 茶道を体験する. What is drunk is powdered green tea, 抹茶.

examples[].german: My mother is learning flower arranging.
I displayed an ikebana arrangement in the entryway.
en.notes: 生け花 denotes both the art of flower arranging and the finished arrangement. Spellings: 生け花, 生花, or いけばな; as an art form it is also called 華道（かどう）. To learn: 生け花を習う; to display an arrangement: 生け花を飾る. The related verb is 花を生ける.

examples[].german: I made a crane out of origami paper.
Could I have a sheet of origami paper?
en.notes: 折り紙 is both the art of paper folding and the square folding paper itself; sheets are counted with 枚. Folding is 折る: 鶴を折る. The material takes で: 折り紙で鶴を作る. The expression 折り紙付き ("guaranteed, proven") comes from the second meaning, "certificate of authenticity".

examples[].german: My grandfather grows vegetables in his field.
There is a small vegetable garden behind the house.
en.notes: 畑 is a dry field for vegetables, grain or fruit, as opposed to the irrigated rice field 田んぼ. To grow vegetables is 畑で野菜を作る. In compounds it becomes ～ばたけ: 麦畑, 茶畑. The kanji is a character created in Japan (国字).

examples[].german: The rice paddies stretch out far and wide.
In spring, water is let into the rice paddy.
At night, frogs croak in the rice paddy.
en.notes: 田んぼ is the usual word for a (flooded) rice paddy; the single kanji 田（た）appears mainly in compounds and names such as 田中. A dry field for vegetables, by contrast, is called 畑. Planting rice seedlings in spring is called 田植え.

examples[].german: This slope is steep.
If you go up the slope, you can see the station.
The school is at the top of the slope.
en.notes: Up a slope is 坂を上る（のぼる）, down is 坂を下りる or 坂を下る（くだる）; the path takes を. An incline is an 上り坂, a descent a 下り坂, the latter also figuratively for "things are going downhill". "Steep" is 急: 急な坂. In place names it often becomes ～ざか.

examples[].german: Go straight along this street.
There are many shops on this street.
At night there are hardly any people on the street.
en.notes: 通り is a busy street with houses and shops, whereas 道 generally means "road, way". Going along a street: この通りをまっすぐ行く (with を). In street names it becomes ～どおり: 中央通り. Do not confuse it with ～とおり "as, just as" (言ったとおり) and the counter for kinds (二通り).

examples[].german: Life in the city is busy.
The city is more convenient than the countryside.
en.notes: 都会 means a larger city or the urban environment, often in contrast to 田舎, the countryside. With の it can modify another noun: 都会の生活. The card uses the word for life in a big city, not for the rare identically written abbreviation of the Tokyo metropolitan assembly.

examples[].german: My money has run low.
The number of tourists falls in winter.
en.notes: 減る describes a quantity or number becoming smaller. The thing that decreases takes が: お金が減る. It is an intransitive Godan verb ending in る: 減ります・減らない・減って; when someone reduces something, the transitive counterpart is 減らす.

examples[].german: The countryside is quiet.
In the future I want to live in the countryside.
I go back to my hometown for New Year.
en.notes: 田舎 is the countryside as opposed to the big city (都会). It also means one's own hometown: 田舎に帰る means "to go back to one's hometown". Depending on context, the word sounds slightly derogatory, as in 田舎者 ("country bumpkin"). The reading いなか is irregular.

examples[].german: I miss my hometown.
I want to eat food from my hometown.
My hometown is a small town in Hokkaido.
en.notes: 故郷 is read ふるさと in everyday use and often also written in kana; the reading こきょう sounds more literary. The word is emotional and fits homesickness: 故郷が懐かしい. To ask neutrally about someone's place of origin, use 出身: ご出身はどちらですか.

examples[].german: The humidity is unpleasantly high in summer.
Because of the humidity, the laundry hardly dries.
en.notes: 湿気 is the perceptible moisture in the air or in rooms. High or low levels are expressed with 湿気が多い and 湿気が少ない. For the measurable relative humidity in percent, 湿度（しつど）is used instead: 湿度は八十パーセントです. Muggy, hot weather is described as 蒸し暑い.

examples[].german: I am going to Kyoto to see the autumn leaves.
The autumn colors are late this year.
en.notes: 紅葉 refers to the red and yellow autumn coloring of leaves; as a する-verb, 紅葉する means "to turn autumn colors". The same kanji are also read もみじ, which sounds more poetic and also means "maple". An outing to view autumn leaves is called 紅葉狩り（もみじがり）, the counterpart to spring 花見.

examples[].german: The cherry blossoms are in full bloom.
I planted a cherry tree in the garden.
en.notes: 桜 can denote both the cherry tree and its blossoms. 桜が満開 means that the trees are in full bloom; 桜を植える speaks of planting a tree. This card practices this plant word, not the other meaning of サクラ for paid or fake audience members.

examples[].german: I set the alarm clock for six o'clock.
The alarm didn't ring this morning, so I was late.
en.notes: 目覚まし is the short form of 目覚まし時計. You set the alarm with 目覚ましをセットする or 目覚ましをかける, and the time takes に: 六時に. The alarm ringing is 目覚ましが鳴る, and turning it off is 目覚ましを止める. In 目覚ましにコーヒーを飲む, the basic meaning "to wake oneself up" is at work.

examples[].german: I renewed my commuter pass.
I forgot my commuter pass.
My commuter pass expires next week.
en.notes: 定期 here is the short form of 定期券, a commuter pass for a fixed route between two stations, often for one, three or six months. Today it is usually stored on an IC card such as Suica. Typical: 定期を買う, 定期を更新する, 定期が切れる ("to expire"). In other words 定期 means "regular": 定期的に, 定期検診.

examples[].german: I was late because of a traffic jam.
I got caught in a traffic jam on the expressway.
On the first day of a long weekend the roads are very congested.
en.notes: 渋滞 is a traffic jam; as an intransitive する-verb: 道路が渋滞している. The cause takes で: 渋滞で遅れる. To get caught in a traffic jam is 渋滞に巻き込まれる or, colloquially, 渋滞にはまる. For crowds of people at stations or in shops, you say not 渋滞 but 混雑 or 混む.

examples[].german: Do you like driving?
Please don't use your phone while driving.
Train service was suspended because of heavy snow.
en.notes: Driving a vehicle is 車を運転する (vehicle with を); the driver is the 運転手, the driver's license 運転免許. For bicycles, by contrast, you say 自転車に乗る. 運転 also refers to the operation of trains and machines: 電車の運転が止まる. With 中 you get 運転中 ("while driving").

examples[].german: I got my license.
I go to driving school in order to get my license.
This job requires a special license.
en.notes: 免許 means an official permit or license. In everyday speech the driver's license is often meant: 免許を取る means to obtain it. The full expression 運転免許 makes this meaning clear; without context, 免許 can also mean another professional or technical qualification.

examples[].german: The train is crowded.
It's crowded everywhere on days off.
If you go early in the morning, the road is not yet congested.
en.notes: Here 込む is the independent intransitive verb for "to be full or crowded". For crowds and traffic, 混む is often written. It is a godan verb ending in む. The attached ～込む in compound verbs such as 申し込む has its own functions and should be distinguished from this use.

examples[].german: I write my appointments in my planner.
I've already bought next year's planner.
I lost my pocket planner.
en.notes: 手帳 is a small notebook or pocket planner in which you mainly enter appointments: 手帳に予定を書く (destination with に). A school notebook, by contrast, is ノート, and a notepad is メモ帳. 手帳 also stands for official booklets such as 母子手帳 (maternal and child health handbook).

examples[].german: We signed a contract.
I changed my mobile phone contract.
Please sign this contract.
en.notes: To conclude a contract is formally 契約を結ぶ or simply 契約する; the contracting partner takes と: 会社と契約する. The contract document is the 契約書. When a contract expires, you say 契約が切れる; 契約社員 are fixed-term employees.

examples[].german: The deadline for the report is Friday.
I didn't make the deadline.
en.notes: 締め切り is the submission or registration deadline. Being on time is 締め切りに間に合う, extending a deadline is 締め切りを延ばす. The spellings 締切 and 〆切 are also seen. The related verb 締め切る means "to close off, to stop accepting".

examples[].german: My father retires next year.
I left the company because of illness.
en.notes: 退職 is leaving a job, whether through retirement (定年退職) or one's own resignation. The company takes を: 会社を退職する. In conversation, people often just say 会社を辞める. Dismissal by the employer, by contrast, is 解雇 or, colloquially, クビ; severance pay is 退職金.

en.meaning: finding a job; starting a job; entering the workforce
examples[].german: I'm starting a job next year.
I started job hunting.
After graduating from university, I got a job at a bank.
en.notes: 就職 means getting a permanent position, especially after university. The company takes に: 銀行に就職する. The job search itself is 就職活動, abbreviated 就活. The counterpart is 退職; changing jobs is 転職.

examples[].german: I'm preparing for the interview.
I was asked various questions in the interview.
This university's entrance exam also includes an interview.
en.notes: 面接 is a personal selection interview, for example for a job application, university admission or a visa application. As an applicant you take part with 面接を受ける; the person conducting it says 面接をする; the interviewer is the 面接官. An interview with journalists, by contrast, is an インタビュー.

examples[].german: I wrote my resume and sent it in.
Please attach a photo to your resume.
en.notes: A Japanese 履歴書 is a standardized form with a passport photo, education and career history; in the past it was often written by hand. Submitting it: 履歴書を出す or formally 履歴書を提出する. Detailed work experience is described additionally in the 職務経歴書.

examples[].german: My older brother works as a technician at a hospital.
A technician came to repair the machine.
en.notes: 技師 is a rather formal job title for technical specialists. In everyday speech 技術者 or エンジニア is more common. Today 技師 is encountered mainly in fixed titles such as 放射線技師 (radiology technologist). "To work as a technician" is 技師として働く.

examples[].german: I consulted a lawyer.
My older sister works as a lawyer at a law office in Tokyo.
en.notes: 弁護士 denotes a person who works professionally as a lawyer. 弁護士に相談する means "to get legal advice"; 弁護士として働く describes the professional activity. The word distinguishes this person from a judge, 裁判官, and a prosecutor, 検察官.

examples[].german: I'm appearing in court.
The trial starts next month.
It took a long time, but we won the case.
en.notes: 裁判 is the legal proceeding itself; the court as a building or institution is 裁判所, the judge 裁判官. To file a lawsuit is 裁判を起こす, to win or lose a case 裁判に勝つ or 裁判に負ける. As a party or witness you appear with 裁判に出る.

en.meaning: to become less crowded; to get hungry
examples[].german: I'm hungry.
After the morning rush, the train gets less crowded.
en.notes: 空く is read すく here. For a train or a shop it means becoming less crowded; 空いている（すいている）describes few crowds. お腹が空く means to get or be hungry. This intransitive godan verb forms すきます and すいて. For a free seat, 空いている with the other reading あいている is usually said; that reading belongs to 空く（あく）. すく is the kana spelling of exactly this reading and these meanings; it denotes neither the reading あく nor the homophone for combing, 梳く.

examples[].german: We must obey the law.
My older sister is studying law at university.
A new law has been enacted.
en.notes: To obey the law is 法律を守る, to violate it 法律に違反する. "Prohibited by law" is expressed with 法律で禁止されている. As a field of study, 法律 means about "law (jurisprudence)": 法律を勉強する. For an individual law with a name, ～法 often stands: 労働基準法.

examples[].german: I'm going to vote.
Next month there is a mayoral election.
In Japan you can vote in elections from the age of 18.
en.notes: "To go and vote" is 選挙に行く; casting your vote is 投票する. That an election takes place is said with 選挙がある or formally 選挙が行われる. To run as a candidate is 選挙に出る. The simple everyday "to choose", by contrast, is 選ぶ.

examples[].german: I work at a trading company.
Japan trades with many countries.
en.notes: 貿易 is trade with foreign countries, that is, import (輸入) and export (輸出). The partner takes と: 多くの国と貿易をする. A trading company is a 貿易会社（ぼうえきがいしゃ）. For trade and business within the country, 商売 or 取引 is rather used.

examples[].german: I pay taxes.
Is tax included in this price?
I hear taxes will go up from next year.
en.notes: 税金 is the general term for taxes; individual kinds of tax end in ～税, for example 消費税 (consumption tax). To pay taxes is 税金を払う, formally 税金を納める. On price tags you read 税込み ("tax included") and 税抜き ("excluding tax").

examples[].german: I'm saving money for the future.
I spent all my savings and bought a car.
en.notes: 貯金 means both saving and the savings themselves. As a する-verb: 貯金する ("to put money aside"); existing savings are expressed with 貯金がある. A piggy bank is a 貯金箱. The more formal 預金 refers specifically to bank deposits.

examples[].german: I want to pay off my debt quickly.
I took out a loan from the bank to buy a house.
en.notes: 借金 is a debt of money. To borrow money or go into debt is 借金をする; from whom is marked with から or に: 銀行から借金をする. To repay is 借金を返す, to be in debt is 借金がある. For borrowing objects, simply use 借りる.

examples[].german: Do you have insurance?
When I go to the doctor, I take my insurance card with me.
I paid for the accident repairs through insurance.
en.notes: Taking out insurance is 保険に入る (with に). Important types are 健康保険 (health insurance) and 生命保険 (life insurance); the insurance card is the 保険証. Do not confuse it with the similar-sounding 保健 ("health care", e.g. 保健室).

examples[].german: I receive a pension.
It's hard to live on the pension alone.
I pay into the pension every month.
en.notes: 年金 is the regular pension and also the pension system. To receive a pension is 年金をもらう or more formally 年金を受け取る; paying contributions is colloquially 年金を払う. Someone who lives on their pension leads a 年金生活. Leaving work itself, by contrast, is 退職 or 定年.

examples[].german: I calculated the expenses for the business trip.
The company has to cut expenses.
en.notes: 経費 are costs in a business context, such as operating or travel costs. Private spending is more often called 費用 or 出費. Charging something to expenses is colloquially 経費で落とす; cutting costs is 経費を減らす or, formally, 経費を削減する.

examples[].german: My income has increased.
I live on my income from a part-time job.
en.notes: 収入 covers all earnings, not just salary (給料). You say 収入が多い or 収入が少ない, and changes with 収入が増える and 収入が減る. The counterpart is expenses, 支出. The source takes で: アルバイトの収入で生活する.

examples[].german: I'm selling my car.
This shop sells bread.
en.notes: 売る is a transitive godan verb: 売ります, 売って. With を you name the goods sold. 店がパンを売っている can describe a shop's regular offering. 売ります can also announce one's own plan to sell; it does not have to describe a sale currently in progress.

examples[].german: I keep track of my monthly expenses.
This month my expenses were higher than my income.
The company cut its advertising expenditure this year.
en.notes: 支出 is the formal word for expenses in a household account book, a company balance sheet or a national budget; the counterpart is 収入 ("income"). Typical combinations: 支出が増える, 支出を減らす, 毎月の支出. In casual everyday speech 出費 or simply 使ったお金 is more usual; as a する-verb (支出する) it sounds official.

examples[].german: The company's profit has gone up.
You must not think only of your own interest.
en.notes: 利益 is the profit of a business: 利益が出る ("a profit arises"), 利益を上げる ("to make a profit"). It also means "benefit, interest": 自分の利益 ("one's own benefit"). The opposite is 損 or 損失; for small personal advantages in daily life, 得 is used more often (得をする).

examples[].german: The typhoon caused great damage.
Because of wrong information, I caused the company great damage.
en.notes: 損害 is material or financial damage, for example from storms, accidents or business mistakes. Typical: 損害が出る ("damage occurs"), 損害を受ける ("to suffer damage"), ～に損害を与える ("to cause damage to someone"). The related 被害 emphasizes the victim's side and is also used when people are injured; 損害 targets the loss of value or money.

examples[].german: Competition is fierce in this industry.
I raced my younger brother to the station.
en.notes: 競争 means competition and rivalry, but also quite concretely a race. Typical: 競争が激しい ("fierce competition"), 競争に勝つ／負ける; the one you compete with takes と: 友達と競争する. A competitor is a 競争相手. For a sports game or tournament, by contrast, you say 試合.

examples[].german: We're advertising the new product.
I tried the sweets that are being advertised on TV.
en.notes: 宣伝 is the activity of advertising, i.e. making something known - through ads, TV commercials or word of mouth; in a political context also "propaganda". As a する-verb the advertised thing takes を: 新商品を宣伝する; as a noun you say ～の宣伝をする. A single ad or advertising poster, in contrast, is a 広告.

examples[].german: I saw the advertisement.
Internet advertising is increasing.
We placed an ad for our shop in the newspaper.
en.notes: 広告 is the concrete advertisement or advertising space: 新聞広告, ネット広告, 駅の広告. To place an ad is 広告を出す. In contrast to 宣伝 (advertising activity as a whole), 広告 means more the medium or the individual ad; TV commercials are colloquially called CM (シーエム).

examples[].german: Please print ten copies of the materials.
I printed the New Year's cards on my home printer.
en.notes: What is printed takes を: 書類を印刷する; the device or method takes で: プリンターで, カラーで印刷する. Copies are counted with 部: 資料を十部. In office life you also hear プリントする; 印刷 sounds more formal and is also used for print shops and books.

examples[].german: Please copy this document.
Before the meeting I made ten copies of the materials.
I copied the photo files to another folder.
en.notes: コピーする means to make a copy of something. The thing copied takes を; for paper, you can count copies with 部. The action can also be copying a file. As a suru-verb it forms コピーして・コピーしない; an advertising slogan as the noun コピー is a different meaning.

examples[].german: I searched for the restaurant's location.
I look up words I don't know in the dictionary on my smartphone.
en.notes: The thing searched for takes を, the medium takes で: ネットで店の場所を検索する. 検索 is targeted searching in databases, dictionaries or on the internet; lost things or people, by contrast, are searched for with 探す (さがす). Colloquially, a Google search is also called ググる.

examples[].german: This book is selling well.
That singer's CDs sell well.
The old bicycle sold for a thousand yen.
en.notes: 売れる means that goods sell or are sold; the goods take が or は as topic. It is an intransitive Ichidan verb. 売る, in contrast, means actively selling something with を. よく売れる means "to sell well", not automatically "to be famous".

examples[].german: I'm repairing the car.
I had the broken watch repaired.
The repair of the air conditioner takes a week.
en.notes: What is repaired takes を: 車を修理する. To have something repaired, you say 修理してもらう or 修理に出す ("to hand in for repair"). In everyday speech 直す (なおす) is the more common word; 修理 sounds more formal and suits devices, cars and buildings in particular - not illnesses (for those, 治す).

en.meaning: to organize; to sort out; to tidy up
examples[].german: I'm tidying up the top of my desk.
Before moving, I sorted through my old clothes.
Let's sort out our thoughts before we speak.
en.notes: 整理する means to put in order systematically, often sorting out what is unnecessary: 書類を整理する, 古い服を整理する. It also works abstractly: 考えを整理する ("to organize one's thoughts"). 片付ける is the everyday "to tidy up, put away"; the fixed phrase 整理整頓 means "order and tidiness".

examples[].german: Let's save water.
To save time, I went by taxi.
I make a bento every day and save on food costs.
en.notes: 節約する means to use something sparingly, i.e. not to waste it: 水・電気・時間・お金を節約する. Putting money aside, in contrast, is 貯金する or お金をためる. The opposite is 無駄遣い ("waste").

examples[].german: The sports day was postponed because of the typhoon.
Let's postpone the meeting until next week.
en.notes: What is postponed takes を, the new date takes に: 会議を来週に延期する. In news reports and announcements the passive is common: 試合が延期されました. Unlike 中止 ("cancellation"), the event still takes place later; in conversation you also say 延ばす or ずらす.

en.meaning: to cancel; to call off; to discontinue
examples[].german: The construction work was halted.
The event was canceled because of rain.
en.notes: 中止する means to cancel something planned entirely or to stop something in progress: イベントを中止する, 工事が中止される. On posters you often see 雨天中止 ("canceled in case of rain"). Unlike 延期 ("postponement"), the event does not take place; giving up a habit, by contrast, is expressed with やめる.

examples[].german: The building has been completed.
I want to finish this painting by next month.
en.notes: 完成する is mostly used intransitively: 建物が完成する ("the building is completed"). Someone who completes something themselves usually says 完成させる: 作品を完成させる. In everyday speech people often just say できる or できあがる; 完成 sounds like a larger, finished work.

examples[].german: A security camera was installed.
A new elevator was installed at the station.
en.notes: 設置する means to set up or install equipment or facilities permanently; the place takes に and the equipment takes を: 入口にカメラを設置する. In notices and news, the passive is common: ～が設置されています. For smaller things, everyday speech prefers つける or 置く; officially, 設置 also means establishing offices or committees.

en.meaning: to deal with; to treat; to border on; to come into contact with
examples[].german: Please treat customers politely.
This park borders the sea.
While studying abroad, I came into contact with many cultures.
en.notes: 接する always takes に. With people, it means "to deal with or treat someone": 子どもに優しく接する. With places, it means "to border on": 海に接する町; it also means "to come into contact with something": 外国の文化に接する. It sounds rather formal; for dealing with customers, everyday speech also uses 対応する.

examples[].german: Walking alone at night is scary.
When I was a child, I was afraid of dogs.
When my father gets angry, he is really scary.
en.notes: こわい is today usually written 怖い; 恐い is a rarer spelling variant with the same meaning. What one is afraid of takes が: 犬が恐い - this is how you talk about your own feelings; for other people you say 怖がる ("to be afraid"). Said of people, it also means "strict, intimidating": 恐い先生.

examples[].german: He is knowledgeable about computers.
Please give a detailed explanation.
For details, please see the website.
en.notes: 詳しい has two usages: before a noun it means "detailed, thorough" (詳しい説明), and with に it means "to be well versed": 彼は車に詳しい. Adverbially it is 詳しく: 詳しく説明する. The phrase 詳しくは～ ("for details ...") often appears in announcements and notices.

examples[].german: Please follow the rules.
I protect the children from danger.
en.notes: 守る can mean to protect people from something or to keep rules and promises. The thing protected or kept takes を; a danger can follow with から. It is a transitive Godan verb ending in る, not an Ichidan verb. The rare reading もる is not taught here.

examples[].german: It's raining heavily.
Competition is fierce in this industry.
en.notes: 激しい describes a strong or violent intensity, for example of rain, movement or competition. It is an i-adjective: 激しい雨 modifies a noun, 競争が激しい evaluates the competition. The adverbial form is 激しく; here the word does not merely mean that something is big.

examples[].german: Agriculture is thriving in this region.
Soccer is very popular in this area.
In class, the students asked questions eagerly.
en.notes: 盛ん is a な-adjective and describes an activity flourishing or being widespread in a place: ～では～が盛んです. Typical subjects are industries, sports or exchange: 農業・スポーツ・交流が盛ん. Adverbially, 盛んに means "eagerly, vigorously, frequently". For individual people, 元気 or 活発 is rather used.

examples[].german: I bought fresh fish at the market.
When you live abroad, every day feels fresh.
en.notes: 新鮮 is a な-adjective: 新鮮な魚, 新鮮な空気. It refers above all to the freshness of food, but figuratively also to impressions that feel new and stimulating: 毎日が新鮮だ. It does not fit freshly washed laundry or a refreshing feeling; there you say きれい or さわやか.

examples[].german: Please always keep the kitchen clean.
This hotel is old, but it's very clean.
en.notes: 清潔 means hygienic cleanliness and is a な-adjective: 清潔なタオル. With にする or に保つ you say "to keep clean". The everyday きれい also means "beautiful", whereas 清潔 clearly means "hygienic"; the opposite is 不潔. 清潔感がある praises a well-groomed appearance.

examples[].german: I had a strange dream.
I wondered why he hadn't come.
en.notes: 不思議 here means strange, puzzling or mysterious. As a na-adjective it stands before a noun with な: 不思議な夢. 不思議に思う describes finding something astonishing or wondering about it. The form 不思議と is another adverbial use and is not practiced here as a separate sentence pattern.

examples[].german: It was a boring class.
I can't go outside because of the rain, so I'm bored.
en.notes: 退屈 is a な-adjective ("boring": 退屈な授業) and at the same time a する-verb: 退屈する ("to be bored"), mostly as 退屈している. Colloquially people often say つまらない about boring things; 暇 only means "having free time" and is not necessarily negative.

examples[].german: The paperwork is a hassle.
My older sister looked after the children for me.
Sorry for the trouble.
en.notes: As a な-adjective, 面倒 means "troublesome, bothersome": 面倒な手続き; colloquially people say 面倒くさい or めんどくさい. The fixed phrase ～の面倒を見る means "to take care of someone". Politely, you apologize with ご面倒をおかけしました ("Sorry for the trouble").

examples[].german: I'm happy when I'm with my family.
Congratulations on your marriage! I wish you all the happiness.
My grandmother lived a happy life.
en.notes: 幸せ is a noun and a な-adjective: 幸せな家庭, 幸せを感じる. It means deeper, lasting happiness in life, whereas 嬉しい expresses joy over a specific occasion. At a wedding one says お幸せに; the more formal synonym is 幸福 (こうふく).

examples[].german: There was an unfortunate accident.
Last week there was a death in the family of a relative.
It was a blessing in disguise that the injury was minor.
en.notes: 不幸 is a noun and a な-adjective: 不幸な事故 ("tragic accident"). The phrase ～に不幸があった is a polite euphemism for a death in the family. 不幸中の幸い means "a blessing in disguise" ("luck within misfortune"). For "I am unhappy", people in everyday speech rather say 幸せじゃない or 悲しい.

examples[].german: I'm good at cooking.
What is your best subject?
My little brother got 100 points on the test and looks proud.
en.notes: What one is good at takes が: 料理が得意です; before nouns: 得意な科目. Unlike 上手, 得意 can be said about oneself without boasting, since it means more "my strong point". The opposite is 苦手. 得意そう or 得意げ means "proud, triumphant", and お得意様 are regular customers.

examples[].german: I'm interested in Japanese culture.
I learned about cultural differences.
en.notes: 文化 refers to the culture of a society or community. 国の文化 means the culture of a country; 文化の違い means cultural differences. 興味がある describes an interest, and 学ぶ describes learning about the topic. The identically written name of the historical Bunka period belongs to a different meaning.

examples[].german: I carry the luggage.
I carried the table to the second floor.
en.notes: 運ぶ here means "to carry" or "to transport". The thing takes を, and the destination takes に. It is a transitive godan verb ending in ぶ; the て-form is 運んで. For floors, Japan counts the ground floor as 一階: 二階 is therefore the floor above the ground floor (the second floor in American usage, the first floor in British usage).

examples[].german: I'm bad at math.
I'm not very fond of spicy food.
I'm not good at speaking in front of people.
en.notes: What one finds difficult or doesn't suit one takes が: 数学が苦手です; activities are embedded with の: 人前で話すのが苦手. 苦手 is also a soft, polite way of saying you don't like something or someone - gentler than 嫌い. 下手, in contrast, describes objectively poor performance, including that of others; the opposite of 苦手 is 得意.

examples[].german: I like plain clothes.
He is rather unassuming, but he works conscientiously.
en.notes: 地味 is the opposite of 派手 and describes colors, clothing or people as plain and restrained: 地味な色, 地味な人. Depending on the context it sounds neutral ("understated") or slightly negative ("drab, dull"). 地味な仕事 is unspectacular but often important work.

examples[].german: Her clothes are always flashy.
We didn't have a lavish wedding; it was just family.
en.notes: 派手 is a な-adjective for anything loud, eye-catching or elaborate: 派手な色, 派手な服, 派手なパーティー. Adverbially, 派手に means "on a large scale, lavishly": 派手にお金を使う. The opposite is 地味. It can be meant admiringly or critically ("gaudy").

examples[].german: We had a luxurious meal.
Payday has come, so let's treat ourselves for once.
I'm lucky just to have a job. I can't be picky.
en.notes: 贅沢 is a noun, a な-adjective and a する-verb: 贅沢な食事, 贅沢する ("to treat oneself, to live in luxury"). Depending on the context it sounds positive ("luxury") or reproachful ("waste"). 贅沢を言う means "to make too high demands, to be picky". Because of the difficult kanji it is often written ぜいたく.

examples[].german: It's just like a dream.
He speaks Japanese as if he were Japanese.
en.notes: まるで strengthens a comparison: "just like" or "as if". It is often followed by ようだ, ように or みたいだ: まるで夢のようです. Something seems like the thing compared, without necessarily being the same. In negative sentences まるで can also mean "not at all"; the examples on this card practice the comparison.

examples[].german: I watch movies once in a while.
You should take a rest once in a while, too.
en.notes: たまに means "occasionally, now and then" and occurs less often than 時々. With は (たまには) it sounds like "for once, for a change" and often appears in suggestions: たまには休もう. Before nouns, you say たまの: たまの休み ("the rare day off"). It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: I rarely eat out.
He rarely gets angry.
You rarely get a chance like this.
en.notes: めったに always appears with a negative: めったに～ない ("hardly ever, rarely"). It is stronger than あまり～ない. めったにない means "rare, extraordinary": めったにないチャンス. The kanji spelling 滅多に exists, but kana is more usual.

en.meaning: going out of one's way; especially
examples[].german: I went all that way, but it was closed.
Since we've come all the way to Kyoto, let's go see some temples.
It was a rare day off, and yet it rained the whole time.
en.notes: せっかく expresses that something took effort or is a valuable opportunity. With ～のに, disappointment follows (せっかく来たのに閉まっていた); with ～から or ～だから, it expresses the wish to make the most of the opportunity. Before nouns, せっかくの is used: せっかくの休み. You can politely decline with せっかくですが…; it is usually written in kana (rarely 折角).

examples[].german: Even if it rains, I'll go.
Even if it's difficult, I'll do my best.
Even if I have no money, I'm happy as long as I have my family.
en.notes: たとえ reinforces a concessive clause and always appears together with ～ても or ～でも: たとえ雨でも, たとえ難しくても. On its own it makes no sense; if you leave it out, the sentence stays grammatical, only less emphatic. Do not confuse it with 例えば ("for example") or the noun 例え ("comparison, analogy").

en.meaning: for now; just in case; more or less
examples[].german: I will check just to be sure.
It might rain, so I'll take an umbrella just in case.
I have written the report, more or less, but I'm still not confident.
en.notes: 一応 has two main meanings: "just in case, to be on the safe side" (一応確認しておきます) and "more or less, so far" - you have done something but are not entirely satisfied. It is often combined with ～ておく. It sounds restrained and modest, and is very common both in daily life and at the office.

examples[].german: I'm moving next month.
I moved from Osaka to Tokyo.
en.notes: 引っ越す is used for changing residence, not for merely moving an object. The previous place takes から, and the new home or city takes に. It is an intransitive godan verb ending in す: 引っ越して, 引っ越した.

en.meaning: first of all; to begin with
examples[].german: First, I'll introduce myself.
First, let's wash our hands.
First press this button, then enter the number.
en.notes: まず introduces the first step and is often continued with 次に or それから: まず～、次に～. 最初に is similar but emphasizes the chronological order more. まず also means "most likely", usually with a supposition or negation: まず大丈夫でしょう. It is almost always written in kana (rarely 先ず).

en.meaning: a little while ago; just now
examples[].german: There was a phone call a little while ago.
Please tell me a bit more about what we were just talking about.
en.notes: さっき refers, from the moment of speaking, to the short time before. It is common in conversation and means "a little while ago" or "just now", without naming a fixed number of minutes. With の it can modify a noun: さっきの話 is the conversation or topic from just now.

examples[].german: You're as energetic as ever.
This shop is crowded as always.
en.notes: 相変わらず says that a quality or state is unchanged from before. This can be friendly, as in 相変わらず元気, or denote a lasting burden, such as a shop that is still crowded. The expression does not automatically mean "always" on every occasion, but compares the present state with a known earlier one.

en.meaning: after all; in any case; simply
examples[].german: After all, it's my first time.
The festival yesterday was exhausting - there were simply a huge number of people.
en.notes: 何しろ stresses a reason that explains everything that follows - similar to "after all, simply, the fact is". It is often followed by ～から, ～ので or a て-form: 何しろ忙しくて…. It is similar to とにかく, but typically introduces a justification. It is also often written in kana: なにしろ.

examples[].german: So, you mean it's impossible?
My mother's older sister, that is, my aunt, lives in Kyoto.
en.notes: つまり sums something up or rephrases it more clearly: "that is" or "in other words". You can also use it to check whether you have understood a conclusion correctly. In 母の姉、つまり私の伯母 the second part names the same person from a different perspective; the card does not cover the noun for a blockage.

examples[].german: The train finally came.
After listening to the teacher's explanation, I finally understood.
It has finally started to get warm.
en.notes: ようやく expresses that something finally happens after a long wait or effort: ようやく電車が来た. It is nearly synonymous with やっと, but sounds a little more matter-of-fact; やっと stresses the relief more. With ～てきた, it describes a gradual change. It is usually written in kana (rarely 漸く).

examples[].german: I live all by myself.
I finished my homework in just five minutes.
I just got home.
en.notes: たった stands before numbers and amounts and stresses how little it is: たった五分, たった千円. It is often reinforced with だけ or しか～ない: たった千円しかない. たった今 means "just now, a moment ago". It is more colloquial and more emotional than ただ or わずか.

examples[].german: I somehow made it in time.
We don't have much money, but we'll manage somehow.
A person named Yamada something called.
en.notes: なんとか means "somehow (with effort)": you cope with something despite difficulties. なんとか間に合う means "to just manage to make it in time", なんとかなる "it will work out somehow", なんとかする "to do something about it, to find a solution". なんとか also serves as a placeholder for something you can't think of at the moment: なんとかさん "Mr./Ms. So-and-so", 山田なんとかという人 "a certain Yamada So-and-so". Mostly written in kana; 何とか is the kanji spelling.

examples[].german: Please explain in even more detail.
As evening came, the rain got even stronger.
This shop is cheap. Moreover, it's close to the station.
en.notes: さらに intensifies an increase: "even (more), still further", often before adjectives or verbs of change: さらに強くなる, さらに詳しく. At the start of a sentence it works as a conjunction, "moreover, in addition", and sounds somewhat more formal than それに. It is mostly written in kana (rarely 更に).

examples[].german: I signed up for the course.
I signed up for the marathon.
I tried to sign up, but the deadline had already passed.
en.notes: 申し込む means to submit a registration or an application. A course or event usually takes に; 参加する, in contrast, means actually taking part. It is a Godan verb ending in む: 申し込んで, 申し込んだ. A rejected or late application can also be described with it.

examples[].german: I decided on my goal for this year.
We're almost at our team's target.
en.notes: 目標 is a concrete, often measurable goal: 目標を立てる／決める, 目標を達成する ("to achieve"). 目的, in contrast, denotes the purpose or intention behind an action (旅行の目的). A travel destination is called 目的地, the goal or finish line in sports ゴール.

examples[].german: If you make an effort, you will succeed.
Thanks to his efforts, we won the match.
en.notes: 努力 is a noun and a する-verb: 努力する ("to make an effort, to strive"). Typical phrases are 努力が足りない, 努力が実る ("the effort bears fruit") and ～の努力のおかげで. A hard-working person is called 努力家. In conversation people often say 頑張る; 努力 sounds more formal and suits applications and speeches.

examples[].german: Let's keep hope.
Please tell us your preferred date.
I passed the entrance exam at my first-choice university.
en.notes: 希望 means both "hope" (希望を持つ) and "wish" in formal contexts: ご希望の日時, 第一希望 ("first choice"). As a する-verb, the thing wished for takes を: 進学を希望する. For personal wishes in everyday life, ～たい or 願い is rather used.

examples[].german: Do you have a good idea?
My proposal was adopted at the meeting.
en.notes: 案 is an idea, plan or proposal that can still be considered or worked out. 案がある means that someone has a proposal; 案を採用する means to adopt it. In compounds such as 改善案, 案 at the end stands for a proposal for improvement. The examples deal with a proposal, not the older meaning "desk".

examples[].german: I checked the content of the email.
The content of this book is a bit difficult.
en.notes: 内容 is the substance of texts, conversations, courses or contracts: メールの内容, 仕事の内容. The physical contents of a container, in contrast, are called 中身 (なかみ): 箱の中身. Common combinations are 内容を確認する and 内容がわかる.

examples[].german: Please line up in order.
Next is your turn.
en.notes: 順番 denotes a fixed order or one's own place in it. 順番に means "in order"; あなたの順番です says that it is now your turn. It can be used when queuing, for tasks or in a game. With の, the person acting is assigned their respective turn.

examples[].german: The proportion of women is increasing.
Mix water and sugar in a ratio of three to one.
Today's test was relatively easy.
en.notes: 割合 is a proportion or ratio: 女性の割合, 三対一の割合で混ぜる. As an adverb, 割合（に） means "relatively, comparatively", similar to わりと or 比較的. Percentages are given with パーセント: 割合は三十パーセントです.

examples[].german: I can understand to a certain extent.
It takes about an hour.
How serious is the injury?
en.notes: 程度 expresses extent or degree: けがの程度, どの程度 ("how much, how far"). ある程度 means "to a certain degree". After numbers it means "about, approximately" and sounds more formal than ぐらい: 一時間程度.

examples[].german: The portion of this dish is big.
There is little rainfall this year.
Quality is more important than quantity.
en.notes: 量 means a quantity that is measured rather than counted: 雨の量, 料理の量 (portion). For countable things you say 数 (かず). Typical are 量が多い／少ない and the saying 量より質 ("quality over quantity"). As a suffix it appears in words such as 雨量 or 運動量.

examples[].german: How tall is this building?
The height of this desk can be adjusted.
en.notes: 高さ is the noun for 高い and means the height of buildings, mountains or furniture, but also pitch: 声の高さ. By the same pattern you form 長さ, 重さ, 大きさ. A person's body height, by contrast, is 身長 (しんちょう). You ask with 高さは何メートルですか or どのくらいですか.

examples[].german: I'm taking part in the party.
Please attend the meeting.
en.notes: 参加する describes actually taking part in an event or activity; the event takes に. For the prior registration, 申し込む is used. It is an intransitive する-verb. The noun 参加 means "participation"; the example sentences use the full verb form.

examples[].german: The number of students has increased.
Please count how many apples are in the box.
en.notes: 数 (かず) is the number of countable things: 学生の数, りんごの数. To count is 数を数える (かぞえる). For uncountable amounts such as water, 量 is used. As a prefix it is read すう: 数人 ("several people"); the number of people is usually 人数 (にんずう).

examples[].german: It has doubled compared to last year.
Rent in Tokyo is about three times that of my town.
Because the exam is coming up, I doubled my study time.
en.notes: On its own, 倍 means "double": 倍になる ("to double"), 倍にする ("to double something"). With a number before it, it is a counter for "-fold": 二倍, 三倍, 十倍. Comparisons are formed with AはBの三倍です ("A is three times B"); 倍 and 二倍 both mean "double".

examples[].german: Please give me half.
I'll give you half of the cake.
en.notes: 半分 is half of a whole. ケーキの半分 uses の to link the half and the whole it refers to. 半分ください asks for half; 半分をあげます announces giving it to someone. In hanbun the n is kept before b.

examples[].german: Please show me the overall plan.
The whole class went on a trip to Kyoto.
It snowed, and the whole town turned white.
en.notes: 全体 regards something as a connected whole, whereas 全部 enumerates all the individual parts ("everything"). Placed after a noun, it forms "the whole ...": クラス全体, 町全体. Attributively it takes の (全体の計画), and adverbially it often appears as 全体的に ("overall").

examples[].german: I don't understand this part.
The last part of the movie was very good.
I repaired the broken part of the chair.
en.notes: 部分 denotes a particular section or spot within a whole, such as a text, a film or an object: この部分, 最後の部分. For "a part of it, some", 一部 is used more often: 一部の人. The adverb 部分的に means "partially".

examples[].german: I'll do the rest of the work tomorrow.
I put the rest of the cake in the refrigerator.
There are only three days left of summer vacation.
en.notes: 残り is the noun of 残る ("to be left over") and denotes the rest. Attributively it takes の: 残りの仕事, 残りのお金. With a quantity it means "... left": 残り三日 ("three days left"). Leftover food is also called 残り物.

examples[].german: It can't be helped.
How people greet each other differs from country to country.
The picnic was canceled because of the rain. Oh well, it can't be helped.
en.notes: N + の仕方 means "the way one does N", especially with する-nouns: 勉強の仕方, 挨拶の仕方. With ordinary verbs, you use the verb stem + 方 instead: 使い方, 書き方. 仕方 is most often met in the fixed phrase 仕方がない / 仕方がありません ("there's nothing to be done"), colloquially shortened to 仕方ない or しょうがない.

examples[].german: Please show me how to do it.
I can't agree with his way of doing things.
When I changed my approach, I finished the work faster.
en.notes: やり方 comes from やる, the casual variant of する, and is very common in everyday speech: やり方を教えてください. It can also refer to a person's personal style or approach, often with a critical undertone: あの人のやり方. Somewhat more formal is 方法 ("method").

examples[].german: I don't understand how to use this app.
Please be careful about how you spend your money.
Is this word used correctly?
en.notes: 使い方 ("how to use something") applies to devices and apps, but also to money, time and words: お金の使い方, 時間の使い方, 言葉の使い方. The object comes before it with の: このアプリの使い方. An instruction manual is a 説明書.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to read this kanji.
The reading of this place name is very difficult.
Even with the same text, the way it is read aloud changes the impression.
en.notes: 読み方 is the way one reads something. With a kanji or place name, the word asks for the reading or pronunciation. With a whole text it can also denote the manner of reading aloud. It is formed from 読み, the verb stem of 読む, and 方, here かた "way, manner".

examples[].german: I will graduate from university next year.
I will work after graduating from high school.
en.notes: 卒業する means to complete a school or course of study. Despite the intransitive する-verb, the school takes を, because you leave it: 大学を卒業する. The mere start of an education is 入学する. Figurative uses, such as giving up a habit, belong to a further sense.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to make miso soup.
The instructions are written on the back of the box.
I taught the children how to make a paper airplane.
en.notes: 作り方 is the way of making something; in cooking it corresponds to "preparation" or "recipe": カレーの作り方. On packaging, 作り方 often appears as a heading above the preparation instructions. It applies just as well to crafting and building: 紙飛行機の作り方.

examples[].german: Please tell me how to get to the station.
I looked up on the internet how to get to the airport.
en.notes: 行き方 here asks by which route one gets to a destination. The destination often precedes the noun with への or までの: 駅への行き方. 行き is the verb stem of 行く, and 方 in this compound is read かた, "way, manner". The card reads the word いきかた and deals with the concrete route, not the general procedure.

examples[].german: The way of thinking differs from person to person.
My father's way of thinking is a bit old-fashioned.
When I changed my way of thinking, the problem seemed smaller.
en.notes: 考え方 means a person's way of thinking or attitude, but also the approach to a problem. Typical are 考え方が違う, 考え方が古い and 考え方を変える. 考え without 方, by contrast, is a single thought or idea: いい考えがあります.

examples[].german: I choose my own way of life.
I respect my grandfather's way of life.
I quit my job and started a new way of life in the countryside.
en.notes: 生き方 means how one leads one's life: values, decisions, life plan. For daily living (housing, work, livelihood), 生活 or 暮らし fits better. Note: the similar-sounding 行き方 (いきかた) means "way to get there": 駅への行き方.

examples[].german: Do you believe in fortune-telling?
I had my palm read by a fortune teller in front of the station.
According to the fortune-telling on TV, today is supposed to be a good day.
en.notes: 占い means fortune-telling or interpreting the future. It is not limited to horoscopes; palm reading is included too. 占いを信じる means to believe in such readings. A person who offers them can be called by the full occupational word 占い師.

examples[].german: A line has formed at the popular ramen shop.
I stood in line and waited for an hour.
The festival procession passed through the town.
en.notes: 行列 is a line of people: 行列ができる ("a line forms"), 行列に並ぶ ("to stand in line"). 行列のできる店 is a shop so popular that you have to queue. 行列 also means "parade, procession", for example at festivals; for a simple row, 列 alone is often used.

examples[].german: Let's avoid the crowds.
The morning trains are crowded.
en.notes: 混雑 is the more formal word for crowding; in conversation people mostly say 混む: 電車が混んでいます. 混雑 is often heard in announcements and read on notices: 大変混雑しております. As a する-verb it is intransitive; the crowded place takes が or は.

examples[].german: I was late because the train was delayed.
I was absent for a week, so I want to catch up on my studies.
The construction work is running behind schedule.
en.notes: 遅れ is the noun of 遅れる and denotes a delay or being behind. For transport, it is 遅れが出る ("delays occur"); the cause takes で: 電車の遅れで. Falling behind in study or work is made up with 遅れを取り戻す.

examples[].german: There was a big change.
I feel the change of the seasons.
This town has changed a great deal in ten years.
en.notes: 変化 is a rather formal word for change; in conversation the verb 変わる is often used. Typical: 変化がある, 気温の変化, 変化する (intransitive). A deliberately made change, for example to a plan, is called 変更.

examples[].german: I entered university.
He starts elementary school in April.
en.notes: 入学する means to begin an education as a pupil or student at a school or university. The institution takes に. It does not denote a single movement into a building; 入る is enough for that. It is an intransitive する-verb, with 入学 as the noun for the start of school or study.

examples[].german: I was delayed because of the weather.
The weather affects my mood.
I started playing guitar because of my older brother's influence.
en.notes: 影響 can be exerted and received: AがBに影響する / 影響を与える ("to influence"), Bの影響を受ける ("to be influenced"). With で it names a cause: 台風の影響で電車が止まりました. This form is very common in news reports and announcements.

examples[].german: This medicine is effective.
The effect of practicing every day is starting to show.
en.notes: 効果 is the effect or result of a measure. 効果がある says that something is effective; 効果が出る shows that the effect is becoming visible. The word can be used for a remedy as well as for practice or work. The card practices this success of an action, not specifically sound or film effects.

examples[].german: I got a good impression.
First impressions are important.
What is your impression of Japan?
en.notes: Typical phrases: いい印象を受ける ("to get a good impression"), 印象を与える ("to make an impression"), 第一印象 ("first impression"), 印象に残る ("to stay in one's memory"). Visitors to Japan very often hear the question 日本の印象はどうですか. The adjective 印象的な means "impressive".

examples[].german: I have hardly any memories of my childhood.
When I hear this song, memories of my student days come back.
My grandfather is ninety, but he has a very good memory.
en.notes: 記憶 is memory, or a stored recollection, and sounds rather formal: 記憶がない, 記憶にない ("not to remember"), 記憶力 ("memory capacity"). For happy personal memories people rather say 思い出: 楽しい思い出. "To remember" is usually 覚えている in everyday speech.

examples[].german: Let's draw on grandmother's wisdom.
Removing stains with lemon is a household tip.
At three years old, my son is becoming quite clever.
en.notes: 知恵 is practical cleverness and life wisdom, not learned knowledge (that would be 知識). Fixed phrases: 知恵を借りる ("to ask someone for advice"), 知恵を出し合う ("to look for a solution together"), 生活の知恵 ("household tip, folk remedy"). For children, 知恵がつく ("to become smarter") is used.

examples[].german: He is very capable.
I'm taking the JLPT in December.
This job requires English ability.
en.notes: 能力 is the general ability to do something, innate or acquired: 能力がある, 能力が高い, ～する能力. Very well known is 日本語能力試験, the JLPT. Distinction: 才能 is talent, 実力 is the ability actually demonstrated.

examples[].german: She has a talent for music.
I think effort is more important than talent.
The teacher noticed his talent for drawing.
en.notes: 才能 is a mostly innate gift, especially in art, music or sports. Typical: Nの才能がある, 才能のある人, 才能を伸ばす ("to develop a talent"). The person who has the talent often takes には: 彼女には才能があります. General abilities, including learned ones, are rather called 能力.

examples[].german: Let's show our real strength.
The exam showed me clearly where I really stand.
He became company president on his own merit.
en.notes: 実力 is the actual ability demonstrated in practice, as opposed to 才能 (talent) or mere potential. Typical: 実力がある, 実力を出す ("to show one's ability"), 実力で ("on one's own merit"). Very common in sports and exams, e.g. 実力テスト.

examples[].german: That's common knowledge.
Keeping appointment times is common sense for working adults.
en.notes: 常識 denotes generally known knowledge, common sense or usual social expectations. 常識です can present something as self-evident; 社会人の常識 speaks of expectations of adults in working life. What counts as 常識 depends on the surroundings. 常識がある describes a person with sensible judgment.

examples[].german: We preserve Japanese traditions.
This shop has a hundred-year tradition.
The kimono is a traditional Japanese garment.
en.notes: 伝統 is a tradition handed down through generations. Typical: 伝統を守る ("to preserve"), 伝統がある, 百年の伝統. As an adjective, 伝統的な ("traditional") is used: 伝統的な料理. For individual customs, for example on festival days, 習慣 or 風習 fit better.

examples[].german: I'm setting off tomorrow morning.
The bus departs at nine o'clock.
en.notes: 出発する means "to set off" or "to depart" and is intransitive. In the first example, a person announces their own departure for tomorrow morning; in the second, it is about the departure time of a bus. An exact time takes に: 九時に. The starting point is given with から, and a destination with へ or に. 出発します and 出発しました are forms of する; 出発 alone is the noun "departure" or "setting off".

examples[].german: I want to learn about local customs.
That custom continues even today.
In Japan, there is a custom of giving children money at New Year.
en.notes: 風習 refers to customs handed down in a region or society, often with a regional or old-fashioned tone. Typical: ～する風習がある, 地方の風習, 古い風習. 習慣 is broader and can also mean personal habits; 伝統 stresses long transmission.

examples[].german: Are you interested in religion?
There are several religions in Japan.
For religious reasons, I don't eat pork.
en.notes: 宗教 means "religion" in general; individual religions are formed with 教: 仏教, キリスト教, イスラム教. Many Japanese people say of themselves 特に宗教はありません, even though they celebrate Shinto and Buddhist festivals. For dietary rules, you often hear 宗教上の理由で ("for religious reasons").

examples[].german: This book introduces interesting ideas.
Freedom of thought is protected in this country.
en.notes: 思想 is a weighty word for an entire system of thought: philosophy, worldview or political ideology, e.g. 東洋の思想 or 思想の自由. For a single thought or idea in everyday life, 考え is used. The word is encountered mainly in school, books and the news, hardly in small talk.

examples[].german: There is an ethics class.
Giving up your seat to elderly people is a basic principle of morality.
Lying is morally wrong.
en.notes: 道徳 is social morality, i.e. generally accepted rules of right conduct. In Japanese schools, 道徳 is also a subject of its own (moral education). The adjective is 道徳的な ("moral"); philosophical or professional ethics is rather called 倫理.

examples[].german: He is a polite person.
When entering someone's house, it is proper to take off your shoes.
Let's observe proper manners toward our superiors.
en.notes: 礼儀 means good manners and decorum. The adjective 礼儀正しい ("polite, well-mannered") is very common. Other phrases: 礼儀を守る, 礼儀を知らない, ～のが礼儀です ("it is proper to ..."). A well-known proverb: 親しき仲にも礼儀あり ("Even among friends, politeness is called for").

examples[].german: Using honorific language is difficult.
Please speak to customers in honorific language.
I learned honorific language at my part-time job.
en.notes: 敬語 is the general term for Japanese honorific language. It is divided into 尊敬語 (respectful language, which elevates the other person), 謙譲語 (humble language, which lowers oneself) and 丁寧語 (the です/ます form). Typical: 敬語を使う, 敬語で話す.

examples[].german: The Kansai dialect is interesting.
My grandmother speaks in dialect, so I sometimes can't understand her.
When I'm nervous, my dialect slips out before I know it.
en.notes: 方言 is a regional dialect; its counterpart is 標準語 ("standard language"). Individual dialects are colloquially named with ～弁: 関西弁, 大阪弁. Typical: 方言で話す, 方言が出る ("the dialect comes out").

examples[].german: Is Japanese pronunciation difficult?
How do you pronounce this word?
My teacher corrected my pronunciation.
en.notes: 発音 is both the noun "pronunciation" and the transitive verb 発音する ("to pronounce", object with を). Typical: 発音がいい / きれい, 発音を直す ("to correct the pronunciation"). Important for learners: long vowels and the small っ can change the meaning.

examples[].german: I learned an interesting expression.
It is hard to put feelings into words.
Please don't use this expression with superiors.
en.notes: 表現 is on the one hand a linguistic phrase (面白い表現, 丁寧な表現), on the other hand the act of expressing itself: 気持ちを表現する (transitive, with を). 表現力 means "expressive ability". In contrast to 言葉 ("word"), 表現 usually means a whole formulation.

examples[].german: The plane has arrived.
The train arrives in five minutes.
The package arrived earlier than planned.
en.notes: 到着する describes people, vehicles or shipments arriving at a destination. The destination takes に, the arriving thing が. It is an intransitive する-verb and sounds more formal than the short 着く. The noun 到着 means "arrival".

examples[].german: I work as a translator.
This novel has been translated into twenty languages.
en.notes: 翻訳 means translating a text or its translated version. 翻訳の仕事 is translation work; with する it becomes the verb 翻訳する. The target language then takes に: 日本語に翻訳する. For oral interpreting, 通訳 is often used.

examples[].german: I asked for an interpreter.
I interpreted at the conference.
My older sister works as an interpreter at a hospital.
en.notes: 通訳 is oral interpreting and at the same time the person who interprets (also 通訳者). Written translation, in contrast, is 翻訳. Typical: 通訳をする / 通訳する, 通訳を頼む, 同時通訳 ("simultaneous interpreting").

examples[].german: I like writing texts.
This text is short and easy to understand.
en.notes: 文章 denotes a written text or composition. With を you name it as the object of writing. 書くのが好き describes a liking for writing; 分かりやすい judges how easily a text can be understood. ぶんしょう is written bunshō with a long o.

examples[].german: Please write an essay.
I wrote an essay in Japanese.
en.notes: 作文 is an essay or the writing of an essay. 作文を書く is a common combination. 作文を names the written text, 日本語で the language in which it is written. 書いてください asks for the writing; 書きました reports the finished essay.

examples[].german: I want to practice Japanese conversation.
On the train I could hear the conversation of the people next to me.
Recently I talk less with my family.
en.notes: 会話 is a conversation between people, especially in language classes: 会話の練習, 英会話 ("English conversation"). The verb 会話する is possible, but in everyday speech people usually say 話す. The person you talk with takes と: 家族との会話.

examples[].german: The president gave a speech.
Elections are coming up, so someone is giving a speech in front of the station.
en.notes: 演説 is a public, often political speech before an audience: 演説をする, 演説を聞く. At weddings, school ceremonies or in class, people rather say スピーチ; a specialist lecture is called 講演. Before elections in Japan you often hear 街頭演説 ("street speech").

examples[].german: I will take part in the debate.
We debated environmental problems.
Last night, I watched a debate between politicians on TV.
en.notes: 討論 is an orderly debate in which different positions argue against each other, for example on TV or in class (討論会). The topic takes について: ～について討論する. 議論 is more general; an informal discussion is 話し合い.

examples[].german: The discussion became heated.
Let's discuss this problem.
After a long discussion, it was decided to change the plan.
en.notes: 議論 is a factual discussion or a dispute of opinions, but not a personal quarrel (that would be けんか or 口論). Typical: ～について議論する, 議論になる, 議論が白熱する ("the discussion gets heated"). 議論 is more general than 討論, which means an organized debate.

examples[].german: I'll state my own view.
I think his claim is correct.
He insisted strongly that he had done nothing wrong.
en.notes: 主張 is an assertion or position that one emphatically upholds, i.e. stronger than 意見 ("opinion"). As the verb 主張する it takes を (権利を主張する) or a quotation with と (～と主張する). 自己主張 means "asserting oneself, assertiveness".

examples[].german: We have finally reached a conclusion.
To start with the conclusion, this plan is impossible.
Please write a conclusion at the end of the report.
en.notes: Fixed combinations: 結論を出す ("to reach a conclusion"), 結論が出る ("a result is settled"), 結論から言うと ("to get straight to the point"). In essays and reports, 結論 also denotes the final section, i.e. the conclusion.

examples[].german: Japan exports cars.
This factory exports electronic devices.
I prepared the documents for exporting abroad.
en.notes: 輸出する means to send goods out of a country to a foreign country. The goods take を, and the destination country takes に or へ. It is a transitive する-verb; the usual reading is ゆしゅつする. The opposite term 輸入する denotes import. Biological uses of the noun are not part of the material here.

examples[].german: I compared the two products.
Compared with last year, it rains a lot this year.
I hate always being compared to my older brother.
en.notes: 比較 is the more formal word for "comparison"; in everyday speech people mostly say 比べる. As a verb: AとBを比較する. The adverb 比較的 ("relatively") is very common: 今日は比較的暖かいです.

examples[].german: We conducted a questionnaire survey.
The police are investigating the cause of the accident.
en.notes: 調査 is a systematic, often official investigation or survey: アンケート調査 ("questionnaire survey"), 世論調査 ("opinion poll"). As a verb: 調査する or formally 調査を行う. In everyday speech, "to look up, to find out" is simply 調べる.

examples[].german: Let's take a look at the statistics.
According to the statistics, Japan's population is declining.
At the shop, we compile sales statistics every month.
