en.notes: 統計 means "statistics" in the sense of collected figures and their analysis. Important expressions: 統計によると ("according to statistics"), 統計を取る ("to compile statistics"). The academic subject is 統計学, and "statistical" is 統計的な.

examples[].german: I'll write a report.
I have to report to my boss.
I told my friends that I got married.
en.notes: 報告 is a notification or report: to whom with に, about what with を or について (上司に結果を報告する). A written report is called 報告書. One also "reports" private news, e.g. 結婚の報告. In Japanese companies the rule ほうれんそう applies: 報告・連絡・相談.

examples[].german: Let's exchange contact information.
Please write your emergency contact here.
I moved, so my contact information has changed.
en.notes: 連絡先 is composed of 連絡 ("contact") and 先 ("destination"): the address, phone number or e-mail at which someone can be reached. Typical: 連絡先を教える, 連絡先を交換する. On forms, 緊急連絡先 ("emergency contact") often appears.

examples[].german: I'll send it by mail.
Has the mail come yet today?
Please write the postal code before the address.
en.notes: 郵便 is the mail as a service and as items sent: 郵便で送る ("to send by mail"), 郵便が来る ("the mail arrives"). Important compounds: 郵便局 ("post office"), 郵便番号 ("postal code"), 郵便受け ("mailbox at the door"). The symbol 〒 stands for the post.

examples[].german: Please send it by express mail.
With express mail, it will arrive by tomorrow.
How much is express delivery?
en.notes: 速達 is express postal delivery for an additional fee: 速達で送る ("to send by express mail"). Such items carry a red stripe or the stamp 速達. Do not confuse it with 書留 ("registered mail"), which is about secure, traceable delivery.

examples[].german: Please open your textbook.
I forgot my textbook.
This story is in the history textbook.
en.notes: 教科書 is the official textbook for a class; additional study and practice books are called 参考書. Books are counted with 冊: 教科書を二冊. Figuratively, 教科書通り means "by the book, exactly according to the rules".

examples[].german: I bought a study guide.
For the exam, I study with a study guide every evening.
My teacher recommended a good study guide to me.
en.notes: 参考書 is a supplementary study or practice book that you use alongside the 教科書, typically for exam preparation. A reference work in the narrower sense, such as a dictionary, is called 辞書 or 辞典. It is counted with 冊: 参考書を三冊.

examples[].german: Let's check next week's schedule.
The itinerary for the trip has been decided.
May we change the date of the meeting?
en.notes: 日程 is a schedule covering one or more days, for example for a trip, conference or event: 旅行の日程. Typical: 日程を決める, 日程を確認する, 日程を調整する ("to coordinate dates"). Personal plans are more often 予定; スケジュール is the casual loanword.

examples[].german: We import food products.
We import wine from France.
Before importing, I checked the quality of the goods.
en.notes: 輸入する means to bring goods from abroad into one's own country. The goods take を, and the country of origin takes から. It is a transitive する-verb; the reading learned is ゆにゅうする. 輸出する denotes the opposite direction. "Import" is used here in the economic sense.

examples[].german: The exam period is two weeks.
This product is available for a limited time only.
The shop gets very crowded during the sale period.
en.notes: 期間 is a span of time with a beginning and an end, i.e. a duration: 試験期間 ("exam period"), 期間中 ("during the period"). 期間限定 ("for a limited time only") is very common for offers and products. Do not confuse it with 期限: 期限 is the end point, i.e. the deadline.

examples[].german: Please submit it by the deadline.
Please check the expiration date of this medicine.
My passport has expired.
en.notes: 期限 is the deadline or expiration date, i.e. the point in time until which something is valid or must be done: 期限までに ("by the deadline"). When the deadline has passed, you say 期限が切れる. Fixed compounds are 賞味期限 ("best-before date"), 有効期限 ("validity period") and 提出期限 ("submission deadline").

examples[].german: This temple was built in the eighth century.
The 21st century is the age of technology.
This shop has been here for half a century.
en.notes: 世紀 is attached directly to the number: 二十一世紀 ("the 21st century"), 八世紀に ("in the eighth century"). The pronunciation of the number often changes: 一世紀 いっせいき, 八世紀 はっせいき. Other phrases are 半世紀 ("half a century") and 世紀の〜 ("... of the century"), e.g. 世紀の発見.

examples[].german: I'm interested in the culture of the Edo period.
I traveled a lot during my student days.
Times have changed.
en.notes: 時代 means an era or period: historical, as in 江戸時代 ("Edo period"), but also personal, as in 学生時代 ("student days") or 子供時代 ("childhood"). 時代が変わる means "times change", 時代遅れ means "outdated, old-fashioned". For a century as a unit of time, by contrast, 世紀 is used.

examples[].german: Young people today use smartphones a lot.
I went to an exhibition of contemporary art.
Nowadays, many people work from home.
en.notes: 現代 means the present time or the modern era and mostly appears attributively with の: 現代の社会, 現代の若者. It is common in compounds such as 現代美術 ("contemporary art") or 現代日本語 ("modern Japanese"). For an everyday "today, nowadays", people rather say 今 or 最近; 現代では sounds more formal.

examples[].german: I studied the history of ancient Egypt.
I saw tools from ancient times at the museum.
The people of ancient Rome also loved baths.
en.notes: 古代 refers to antiquity or the early period of a culture, and is usually placed before country names or used with の: 古代エジプト, 古代ローマ, 古代の文明. Its counterpart is 現代. For an everyday "in the past, long ago", you don't use 古代 but 昔.

examples[].german: I bought stocks.
I made a profit on stocks.
Share prices fell today.
en.notes: 株 is the everyday word for "stock, share": 株を買う／売る, 株で儲ける. The share price is 株価, a joint-stock company 株式会社 - often abbreviated (株) in company names. 株 also serves as a counter for plants with roots (一株 "one clump").

examples[].german: I looked for a room at a real estate agency.
Real estate prices are rising.
My father works at a real estate company.
en.notes: 不動産 is the general term for land and buildings. In daily life, you meet the word mostly in 不動産屋 or 不動産会社 ("real estate agent, real estate company"), where you look for a rental apartment in Japan. A single listed unit, by contrast, is called 物件, not 不動産.

examples[].german: Rent in Tokyo is high.
I pay the rent on the 25th of every month.
How much is the rent for this room?
en.notes: 家賃 is the rent for an apartment or house. Typical are 家賃を払う ("to pay rent"), 家賃が高い／安い, and statements such as 家賃は月八万円. In Japan, 敷金 ("deposit") and 礼金 ("key money") often come on top when moving in.

examples[].german: Utility costs go up in winter.
Are utilities included in the rent?
To save on utility costs, I turn off electricity I'm not using.
en.notes: 光熱費 are a household's energy costs, mainly electricity and gas. Water is strictly counted separately as 水道代; together they are called 水道光熱費. Typical expressions are 光熱費を払う, 光熱費が上がる and 光熱費を節約する ("to save on energy costs").

examples[].german: I'm studying Japanese history.
This building has a long history.
en.notes: 歴史 means history: either as knowledge about the past or as the past of a place, building, or company. 歴史を勉強する means to study history; 長い歴史がある means to look back on a long history. In the second example the building is the topic whose past is described.

examples[].german: Cars are produced at the factory.
This region produces rice.
en.notes: 生産する means to manufacture goods or agricultural products. The product takes を, and the place of production can follow with で. It is a transitive する-verb; 生産 alone is the noun "production". The expression suits a factory as well as growing rice.

examples[].german: What is your nationality?
He acquired Japanese nationality.
Please write your name and nationality on the form.
en.notes: 国籍 is nationality, e.g. on forms and at immigration. Politely you ask 国籍はどちらですか; the answer is the country: 国籍はドイツです. Acquiring and holding it are expressed with 国籍を取る／取得する and 国籍を持つ; 二重国籍 means "dual nationality".

examples[].german: I'm applying for a visa.
You need a visa to go to Japan.
I'll renew my visa before it expires.
en.notes: ビザ is the visa: ビザを申請する ("to apply for"), ビザを取る ("to obtain"), ビザを更新する ("to renew"). When it expires, you say ビザが切れる. The official term for visa is 査証; in everyday speech ビザ often also denotes residence status, such as 学生ビザ or 就労ビザ ("work visa").

examples[].german: I go through immigration control.
Please write your name on the arrival card.
You can't enter the country without a visa.
en.notes: 入国 is entry into a country; as the verb 入国する, the destination country takes に: 日本に入国する. Important compounds at the airport are 入国審査 ("immigration control") and 入国カード ("arrival card"). The opposite is 出国 ("leaving a country").

examples[].german: I'm completing the departure formalities.
Tomorrow morning I leave Japan.
Before leaving the country, I called my parents from the airport.
en.notes: 出国 is leaving a country; as the verb 出国する, the country being left takes を: 日本を出国する. At the airport you encounter 出国手続き ("departure formalities") and 出国審査 ("departure control"). The opposite is 入国 ("entering a country").

examples[].german: My luggage was inspected at customs.
It took thirty minutes to get through customs.
Since I bought a lot of alcohol, I declared it at customs.
en.notes: 税関 is customs, or the customs office at an airport or port. Going through customs is 税関を通る; declaring goods is 申告する. The typical question there is 申告するものはありますか ("Do you have anything to declare?").

examples[].german: I came for sightseeing.
I did some sightseeing in Kyoto.
There are many tourists in this town.
en.notes: 観光 is tourism or sightseeing. As the verb 観光する, the place visited takes を: 京都を観光する; the purpose of travel is expressed with に: 観光に来る. When asked about the purpose of your trip at immigration, you simply answer 観光です. Common compounds are 観光客 ("tourist") and 観光地 ("tourist destination").

examples[].german: I visited famous sights.
This town has many famous sights.
This place is famous for its cherry blossoms.
en.notes: 名所 is a famous place worth seeing. 〜の名所 for "known for ..." is very typical: 桜の名所, 紅葉の名所. Going around the sights is 名所を回る or 名所を巡る. 観光地, by contrast, refers more to a whole tourist area, while 名所 is the individual spot.

examples[].german: Which direction is it?
Please head north.
I lost my sense of direction.
en.notes: 方角 means a compass direction or a direction in the terrain, usually in terms of 東西南北: 北の方角, 駅の方角. Compared with 方向 ("direction" in general, also figurative), 方角 is more geographical. If you have lost your bearings, you say 方角が分からない.

examples[].german: The convenience store is the landmark.
I put a mark on my umbrella.
I will wear a red hat so you can recognize me.
en.notes: 目印 is a feature by which you quickly recognize something: as a waypoint in directions (〜が目印です "the landmark is ...") or as a mark on your own belongings (目印をつける "to mark"). When arranging to meet, people also name a 目印 so they can find each other. An official traffic sign, by contrast, is 標識.

examples[].german: Please follow the signs.
Please pay attention to the traffic signs.
This sign means "stop".
en.notes: 標識 are official signs and markers, especially 道路標識 or 交通標識 ("road signs"). Following a sign is 標識に従う. Shop signs and billboards, by contrast, are 看板, and information boards are 案内板.

examples[].german: I present the research.
The new plan was announced.
en.notes: 発表する means to present results or to announce information publicly. The content takes を, and the setting of a presentation often takes で. It is a transitive する-verb. It describes making something known; publishing a printed work, by contrast, is 出版する.

examples[].german: Where is the exit?
I'm waiting at the station exit.
en.notes: 出口 is the exit of a building or area. 出口はどこですか asks for its location. 駅の出口 assigns it to the station; 出口で待つ names it as a meeting point. 口 is read ぐち in this word, with a voiced g.

examples[].german: The entrance is over there.
Please show your ticket at the entrance.
en.notes: 入口 is the entrance. The spelling 入り口 is also common for the same reading いりぐち. あちら politely points to a place over there. 入口で切符を見せる describes an action at the entrance: で names the place, を the ticket shown.

examples[].german: Please check where the emergency exit is.
In case of fire, please escape through the emergency exit.
Please don't put anything in front of the emergency exit.
en.notes: 非常口 is the emergency exit, in Japan usually marked with the green sign showing a running figure. Typical are 非常口を確認する and 非常口から逃げる ("to escape through the emergency exit"). Related are 非常時 ("emergency") and 非常ベル ("alarm bell"); the normal exit is 出口.

examples[].german: Where is the restroom?
We should wash our hands before eating.
en.notes: 手洗い means washing one's hands and can also mean the washroom or toilet. For polite questions about the toilet, お手洗い is more usual than the plain form 手洗い. 手洗いをする means "to wash one's hands". Context distinguishes this action from a room and from washing laundry by hand.

examples[].german: I can't find the remote control.
Please turn off the TV with the remote control.
I lowered the temperature with the air conditioner's remote control.
en.notes: リモコン is the short form of リモートコントロール and means the remote control. To distinguish, people say テレビのリモコン or エアコンのリモコン. The device used to operate something takes で: リモコンでテレビをつける／消す.

examples[].german: Please lend me a screwdriver.
I need a screwdriver to tighten the screw.
I asked the taxi driver for directions.
en.notes: ドライバー has two everyday meanings: "screwdriver" (ネジを締める／外す) and "driver". For professional drivers, 運転手 is more common, while ドライバー sounds more modern (タクシードライバー). It also refers to the golf club "driver" and the device driver on a computer.

examples[].german: The battery in the remote control has run out.
I replaced the battery with a new one.
I bought four AA batteries.
en.notes: 電池 is a battery. When it is dead, you say 電池が切れる; to replace it is 電池を替える／交換する. Batteries are counted with 本: 単三電池を二本 ("two AA batteries"). For the rechargeable battery of a smartphone or laptop, バッテリー is usually used.

examples[].german: I shop at the convenience store.
I paid the electricity bill at the convenience store.
There is a convenience store in front of the station.
en.notes: コンビニ is the short form of コンビニエンスストア and means the small store, usually open around the clock, found on almost every corner in Japan. The place of an action takes で: コンビニで買う. There you can also pay bills, send packages, or withdraw money.

examples[].german: I bought a present at the department store.
That department store is open until 8 p.m.
en.notes: 百貨店 is a department store with many merchandise sections, such as clothing, household goods and food. It is also called デパート. 百貨店で買う names the department store as the place of shopping; 開いている describes that it is open. The word does not mean a single small specialty shop.

examples[].german: I'm going to the hair salon.
I got my hair cut at the hair salon.
I booked the hair salon by phone.
en.notes: 美容院 (also 美容室) is a hair salon offering cuts, coloring, and styling; the classic men's barber is called 床屋 or 理容室. You go 美容院に行く and have your hair cut there: 美容院で髪を切る. Do not confuse it with 病院 (びょういん, "hospital"): 美容院 is pronounced び・よう・いん.

examples[].german: The experiment succeeded.
I want to succeed in business.
en.notes: 成功する describes an undertaking succeeding or a person being successful. The undertaking can follow with に: 実験に成功する. It is an intransitive する-verb. "To pass a school exam" is usually 試験に合格する; a successful technical trial is a different situation.

examples[].german: I have a toothache, so I'm going to the dentist.
The dentist told me not to eat too many sweets.
My dentist appointment is at three o'clock.
en.notes: 歯医者 denotes the dentist and also the dental practice: 歯医者に行く ("to go to the dentist"). One speaks of the dentist personally in a friendly, polite way as 歯医者さん. On signs and in formal texts, 歯科 or 歯科医 appear instead.

examples[].german: I leave my child at daycare.
I go to pick up my child from daycare at five.
The daycare nearby has no vacancies.
en.notes: 保育園 is a daycare center or nursery for children from 0 to about 5 years old, mainly for working parents, with full-day care. Leaving a child there is 保育園に預ける, picking up is 保育園に迎えに行く. It should be distinguished from 幼稚園, the more education-oriented kindergarten from age 3 with shorter care hours.

examples[].german: I go to cram school three times a week.
Cram school doesn't end until nine in the evening.
The teacher at the cram school explains very well.
en.notes: 塾 is a private tutoring or cram school that many Japanese students attend after regular classes. Regular attendance is 塾に通う, a single trip 塾に行く. Specifically for university entrance exams there is also the 予備校.

examples[].german: I go to a prep school for the university entrance exam.
Classes at the prep school go on into the evening.
After failing the exam, I studied at a prep school for a year.
en.notes: 予備校 is a preparatory school that prepares students specifically for entrance exams, above all those for university (大学受験). In particular, 浪人 - school leavers who did not pass on the first attempt - often study there for a year. Unlike a 塾, a 予備校 is aimed mainly at high school students and school graduates.

examples[].german: I received a scholarship and studied abroad.
I applied for a scholarship.
Since graduating from university, I have been repaying my student loan.
en.notes: 奨学金 is financial support for studies: 奨学金をもらう ("to receive"), 奨学金に申し込む ("to apply"). Note: in Japan many 奨学金 are loans that must be repaid after the studies (奨学金を返す). A scholarship without repayment is more precisely called 給付型奨学金.

examples[].german: I'm taking part in volunteer work.
I do volunteer work on weekends.
I worked as a volunteer at the tournament.
en.notes: ボランティア means both the voluntary activity (ボランティアをする, ボランティアに参加する) and the volunteer person (ボランティアとして働く, ボランティアの人). Common compounds are ボランティア活動 ("voluntary activity") and ボランティア団体 ("aid organization"). It is always understood that the work is unpaid.

examples[].german: I'm going camping in the summer.
We camped in the mountains.
We cooked curry at the campsite.
en.notes: キャンプ is camping: キャンプに行く ("to go camping") or キャンプをする. The campground is キャンプ場, a campfire キャンプファイヤー. In sports, キャンプ also denotes a training camp, such as 春季キャンプ in professional baseball.

examples[].german: I went fishing with my father.
My hobby is fishing.
Fishing is prohibited at this river.
en.notes: 釣り is fishing as an activity and hobby; with the purpose-に you say 釣りに行く ("to go fishing"). The related verb is 釣る: 魚を釣る ("to catch a fish"). Note: as おつり (usually in kana) the same word means "change (money)".

examples[].german: The cooking failed.
No matter how many times I fail, I won't give up.
en.notes: 失敗する means that something fails or that someone makes a mistake. An activity can follow with に, as in 料理に失敗する. The noun 失敗 means "mistake" or "failure". In the second sentence, ～ても shows that the person keeps going despite repeated failures.

examples[].german: I'm going to climb Mt. Fuji.
I plan to go mountain climbing on the weekend.
Please check the weather carefully before a climb.
en.notes: 登山 covers mountaineering as well as hiking in the mountains. The verb 登山する sounds somewhat more elevated; in everyday speech people often simply say 山に登る. The mountain can be given with に: 富士山に登山する. 登山道 ("mountain trail") and 登山靴 ("hiking boots") go with it.

examples[].german: I'm good at swimming.
Swimming is good exercise for the body.
I go to a swimming class every week.
en.notes: 水泳 is swimming as a sport or school subject: 水泳が得意, 水泳教室 ("swimming class"), 水泳部 ("swimming club"). For the concrete activity "to swim", the verb 泳ぐ is usually used: プールで泳ぐ. Competitions are 水泳大会.

examples[].german: I'm in the track and field club.
I ran the 100 meters at a track and field meet.
en.notes: 陸上 literally means "on land". In sports it is the short form of 陸上競技, that is, track and field; this card practices the sports usage. 陸上部 is a corresponding club or school group, 陸上の大会 a competition. The reading is りくじょう, with a long じょう.

examples[].german: I'm taking part in the national tournament.
Next month there is a soccer tournament.
In summer we went to see a fireworks festival.
en.notes: 大会 is a tournament or competition, but also a large event: サッカーの大会, 全国大会 ("national tournament"), 花火大会 ("fireworks festival"). To take part is 大会に出る or more formally 大会に出場する. The school sports festival, by contrast, is the 運動会.

examples[].german: Congratulations on the victory.
The team won the championship.
We won the first round, but we couldn't win the title.
en.notes: 優勝 is the overall victory or title win in a tournament or league, not the win in a single game (for that, 勝つ). As a verb you say 大会で優勝する ("to win the tournament"). Congratulations are expressed with 優勝おめでとうございます; the winning team is the 優勝チーム.

examples[].german: I won the match.
I beat my older brother at tennis.
Whether we won or lost, it was fun.
en.notes: 勝つ is intransitive: whom or what you defeat takes に, never を: 試合に勝つ, 相手に勝つ. The discipline is given with で: テニスで勝つ. The て-form is 勝って; the opposite is 負ける, and winning a tournament title is called 優勝する.

examples[].german: I'm frustrated about losing the match.
Don't let the heat get you down, keep going!
Could you give me a little discount?
en.notes: 負ける is intransitive: what or whom you lose to takes に: 試合に負ける, 相手に負ける. Figuratively it means "to give in, to succumb": 暑さに負けない ("not to let the heat get one down"). When shopping, 負ける also means "to give a discount": 少し負けてください.

examples[].german: The game ended in a draw.
In case of a draw, each team gets one point.
en.notes: 引き分け is the result of a contest in which neither side wins. 試合は引き分けでした reports a drawn game; 引き分けに終わる means that it ends in a draw. It is a noun; the verb 引き分ける has its own form and is not used here as a card reading.

examples[].german: I'm cheering for the team.
Good luck on the exam! I'm rooting for you.
My parents supported my study abroad.
en.notes: 応援する means "to cheer on" in sports, but also quite generally "to support, to keep one's fingers crossed". Whom or what one supports takes を: チームを応援する, 夢を応援する. Among friends you encourage with 応援してるよ ("I'm rooting for you"). An organized cheering section is called 応援団.

examples[].german: A new record was set.
I record my weight every day.
Please take minutes of the meeting.
en.notes: 記録 has two main meanings: "record, minutes" (記録する "to record, to note down") and "record" in sports. For records you say 記録を出す ("to set"), 記録を破る／更新する ("to break, to improve") and 新記録 ("new record"). 記録的な means "record-breaking", e.g. 記録的な大雨 ("record rainfall").

examples[].german: The size fits.
These shoes don't fit me.
The two of them agree in their opinions.
en.notes: 合う here means "to fit" or "to match". What fits takes が; a person can follow with に. Opinions can also agree: 意見が合う. It is an intransitive godan verb ending in う. "To meet someone" is usually written 会う.

examples[].german: Japan scored in the second half.
He is the player with the most points on the team.
en.notes: 得点 is a point scored or the score achieved, such as a goal in soccer or a run in baseball. As a verb, 得点する means "to score, to score a goal"; its counterpart, a goal conceded, is 失点. For test results and school grades, everyday speech prefers 点数 or simply 点.

examples[].german: I follow the referee's decision.
My older brother referees soccer matches.
The referee blew the whistle, and the game started.
en.notes: 審判 is the referee in sports and also the act of refereeing itself: 審判をする ("to be a referee, to officiate"). His decision is called 審判の判定. In a figurative sense 審判 means "judgment", e.g. 最後の審判 ("the Last Judgment").

examples[].german: I met a famous athlete.
That player is very fast.
I want to become a soccer player in the future.
en.notes: 選手 is an athlete or player in competitive sports: サッカー選手, 野球選手, 代表選手 ("national team player"); in general people say スポーツ選手. In the media, 選手 is added respectfully after names: 大谷選手. It is not used for musicians or actors.

examples[].german: I follow the coach's instructions.
I met the film director.
The teacher is proctoring the exam.
en.notes: 監督 is the person in charge: in film the director (映画監督), in sports the head coach or team manager; assistant coaches, by contrast, are called コーチ. As a suru-verb, 監督する means "to supervise, oversee": 試験を監督する ("to proctor the exam").

examples[].german: She is a fan of a famous singer.
Many soccer fans gathered.
en.notes: ファン is a fan or supporter: 〜のファンです ("I am a fan of ..."), 〜のファンになる ("to become a fan of ..."). Organized fans meet in a ファンクラブ. Written the same way is another word for a fan or ventilator (パソコンのファン); this card means the fan (supporter).

examples[].german: This shop is popular.
She is popular in her class.
This game has become popular among children.
en.notes: 人気 means "popularity": 人気がある ("to be popular"), 人気の店 ("popular shop"); among whom is given with に: 若い人に人気がある. To become popular is 人気が出る, a popular person is a 人気者. Note: read as ひとけ, 人気 means "presence of people", for example 人気のない道 ("deserted road").

examples[].german: What is the trend this year?
My older sister always wears fashionable clothes.
The flu is going around at school right now.
en.notes: 流行 refers to what is currently "in fashion" or "trending": 流行の服, 流行に乗る "to follow the trend", 流行遅れ "out of fashion". As an intransitive する-verb, 流行する means "to be in fashion", but also "to be rampant" for diseases (インフルエンザが流行する). In everyday speech the verb is often heard as the identically written 流行る (はやる), which sounds more colloquial. ブーム is a short-lived hype, while ファッション refers only to clothing.

examples[].german: Let's change the subject.
That is an interesting topic.
A café that everyone is talking about has opened in front of the station.
en.notes: 話題 is the topic being talked about: 話題を変える "to change the subject", 話題になる "to get people talking, make headlines". With の before a noun it means "much discussed, trendy": 話題の映画, 話題の店. For the theme of an essay or lecture one says テーマ rather, for a title 題 or タイトル; 話 alone means "talk, story".

examples[].german: Please tell me what you really think.
In Japan, people sometimes show their real opinion or the position they present outwardly, depending on the situation.
en.notes: 本音 is what someone actually thinks or intends. 本音を言う asks for an honest personal statement. The opposite 建前 refers to the position or reason presented outwardly; the two can diverge depending on the situation. This is not a claim that all people in Japan behave the same way.

examples[].german: The façade and the real opinion are different.
In Japan, the official façade is important.
Don't give me the official version; tell me what you really think.
en.notes: 建前 is the outwardly presented, socially expected position - as opposed to 本音, the real opinion. The pair 建前と本音 is a key concept in Japanese communication; 建前を言う means "to say what one is supposed to say", and 建前上 means "officially, in form". The word is not necessarily negative, but describes polite consideration. The second meaning, "topping-out ceremony when building a house", is rare today.

examples[].german: Please don't give up.
I don't want to give up my dream.
Because of the rain, I gave up climbing the mountain.
en.notes: 諦める means to give up a wish or plan or to resign oneself to a situation. The thing given up takes を; a planned activity can follow with ～のを. It is a transitive ichidan verb. 諦めないで is a request not to give up.

examples[].german: I use honorific language with my superiors.
It is better not to sit down before your seniors.
en.notes: 目上 refers to people who rank higher in a given relationship through age or position. It is usually followed by の人: 目上の人. With such people one uses respectful language depending on the situation. The example sentences deal with linguistic and social manners; the expression alone does not set a fixed rule for every encounter.

examples[].german: I am polite even to those junior to me.
You speak differently to those above you and those below you.
The department head also listens to the opinions of his subordinates.
en.notes: 目下 (めした) are people who are below the speaker in rank, age or position; the opposite is 目上. It usually appears with の人 or の者: 目下の人. The distinction determines which language you choose - for example, you say ご苦労さま only to a 目下, not to superiors. For subordinates in a company, 部下 is more concrete. Note: the same 目下 read as もっか means "at present" in written language.

examples[].german: Let's shake hands.
We shook hands when we met.
I was delighted to be able to shake hands with a famous singer.
en.notes: 握手 is the handshake; as a verb 握手する or 握手をする, with the partner marked by と: 先生と握手する. In Japan people usually greet each other with a bow (お辞儀); handshakes occur mostly in business with foreigners, in politics, in sports, and at fan events (握手会). Figuratively, 握手 can also mean "reconciliation, cooperation", for example between countries or companies.

en.meaning: thank you for the meal (after eating)
examples[].german: Thank you for the meal. It was delicious.
Thank you for the meal, senior colleague.
Thanks for the meal, Mom!
en.notes: ごちそうさま is said after the meal, as the counterpart of いただきます before. The polite and most common form is ごちそうさまでした; among family and friends ごちそうさま is enough. You also use it to thank someone who invited you or paid, and to the staff when leaving small restaurants. The kanji spelling ご馳走様 is rare. It is also said jokingly when a couple is being lovey-dovey in front of you.

en.meaning: I'm off (said when leaving home); I'll be back
examples[].german: I'm off. (said when leaving)
I'm off. I'll be back in the evening.
I'm just going to the post office.
en.notes: 行ってきます is said when leaving home or the office when you will come back; literally "I go and come back" (行って + 来る). The reply from those staying behind is 行ってらっしゃい, and on returning ただいま and おかえりなさい follow. To superiors, 行ってまいります is more polite. Someone who leaves for good does not say 行ってきます but さようなら or 失礼します.

examples[].german: Please be careful on your way.
Take care on the way home.
The stairs are slippery, so please be careful.
en.notes: 気をつけて is the て-form of 気をつける "to be careful" and serves as a parting phrase ("take care, get home safely") and as a warning ("Watch out!"). More polite: 気をつけてください or お気をつけて, familiar: 気をつけてね. What one watches out for takes に: 車に気をつけて. The spelling 気を付けて is equally common. 注意する sounds more formal and appears more on signs.

en.meaning: excuse me for leaving before you (said when leaving work)
examples[].german: Excuse me for leaving ahead of you. See you tomorrow.
Sorry, I have to be up early tomorrow, so I'll be leaving before you.
The meeting is still going on, but I'm afraid I have to leave first.
en.notes: お先に失礼します is said when you leave while others are still staying - typically when leaving the office at the end of the day. The usual reply is お疲れさまでした. Among colleagues of equal rank it is shortened to お先に or お先です. Someone who leaves a party or meeting early also uses the phrase. If everyone leaves together, you simply say 失礼します or お疲れさまでした.

examples[].german: I assemble furniture.
I assembled the shelf myself.
Constructing sentences in Japanese is difficult.
en.notes: 組み立てる means "to assemble from individual parts": 家具を組み立てる, 棚を組み立てる. Figuratively, you can also "build up" sentences, plans or arguments: 文を組み立てる. The verb is transitive (を); there is no common intransitive counterpart, and the passive 組み立てられる is used instead. The noun 組み立て means "assembly, structure", and in compounds it is often written without okurigana: 組立工場. 作る is more general, and 建てる is used for buildings.

examples[].german: My friend is sad.
He is grieving over the death of his pet.
en.notes: 悲しむ is the verb for grieving or feeling sadness. A cause can take を, as in ペットの死を悲しむ. It is a transitive Godan verb ending in む; 悲しい, in contrast, is the adjective "sad". Even without an explicitly named cause, someone can simply be 悲しんでいる.

examples[].german: I'm replacing the light bulb.
I'm replacing the old parts with new ones.
I swapped seats with my friend.
en.notes: 取り替える means to exchange something for something else or to replace it with something else. The previous object takes を, the replacement takes に: 古い部品を新しいものに取り替える. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 取り替えます・取り替えて・取り替えない. A mutual exchange can be expressed with と.

examples[].german: Please pull the rope hard.
The child pulled his mother by the hand to the toy section.
The captain is leading the whole team.
en.notes: 引っ張る emphasizes pulling strongly or persistently toward oneself: ロープを引っ張る, 袖を引っ張る. 引く is the more neutral base word; that is why doors are labeled 引く (or 引), not 引っ張る. Figuratively, チームを引っ張る means "to lead the team, carry it along", and 話を引っ張る "to drag something out". The verb is transitive (を); there is no intransitive counterpart, and the passive 引っ張られる is used instead.

en.meaning: to chase; to run after; to pursue
examples[].german: The dog is chasing the cat.
I ran after the person who had dropped their wallet and gave it back.
I came to Tokyo to chase my dream.
en.notes: 追いかける means "to run after, to pursue"; the target takes を: 猫を追いかける. Figuratively, you pursue dreams or trends: 夢を追いかける, 流行を追いかける. 追う is shorter and more literary; 追いつく means "to catch up with" and 追い越す "to overtake". The spelling 追い掛ける exists, but 追いかける is usual. The person being chased is in the passive: 犬に追いかけられる.

en.meaning: to look back; to turn around
examples[].german: I turned around.
Someone called me and I turned around.
Let's look back on this past year.
en.notes: 振り返る literally means "to turn around and look back": 後ろを振り返る. Figuratively, it means "to look back on something, to reflect": 一年を振り返る, 過去を振り返る. 振り向く is purely physical (turning one's head in a direction, e.g. when called), and 戻る means "to go back". The noun 振り返り is a "review, retrospective" in working life.

en.meaning: to jump out; to rush out
examples[].german: A child ran out onto the road.
I had a fight with my mother and stormed out of the house.
In an earthquake, it is dangerous to rush outside right away.
en.notes: 飛び出す means "to suddenly jump out, dash out"; the destination takes に (道路に飛び出す), the place left takes を (家を飛び出す). A typical traffic warning is 飛び出し注意 "Caution, children may run into the road". Figuratively, 家を飛び出す also means "to run away from home", and things can "stick out". 出る is neutral, while 飛び出す stresses suddenness and momentum. The verb is intransitive.

en.meaning: to be connected; to be linked
examples[].german: I can't connect to the internet.
This road leads all the way to the station.
en.notes: 繋がる describes a connection that exists or is being formed. It is an intransitive godan verb: 繋がります・繋がって・繋がらない. The side that is connected to often takes に; for a road, まで can name the place reached. When someone connects things themselves, the transitive counterpart 繋ぐ is used.

examples[].german: I have a lot of stress built up.
The laundry is piling up.
After the rain, water has collected on the road.
en.notes: 溜まる (usually written in kana as たまる) describes something gradually accumulating; often in the ている-form as a state. Typical subjects are ストレス, 疲れ, 仕事, 宿題, ごみ, 洗濯物 and water. For money, one writes 貯まる (お金が貯まる "money builds up"). The transitive counterpart is 溜める or 貯める: ストレスを溜める, お金を貯める.

en.meaning: to be tidied up; to be finished
examples[].german: The room has been tidied up.
The work is finally done.
This problem has not been settled yet.
en.notes: 片付く is the intransitive counterpart of 片付ける "to tidy up, to finish": 部屋を片付ける → 部屋が片付く "the room is tidy". It is also used for work or problems that are "finished" or "solved": 仕事が片付く, 問題が片付く. The ている-form for the state is common: 片付いている部屋. The spelling 片づく is also common. The old meaning "to be married off (a daughter)" is rare today.

examples[].german: I got my clothes dirty.
Don't get your new clothes dirty.
Wastewater from the factory is polluting the river.
en.notes: 汚す is transitive: "to make something dirty, to pollute" (服を汚す, 川を汚す). The intransitive counterpart is 汚れる "to get dirty" (服が汚れる), the adjective is 汚い "dirty". For a mishap, てしまう is often used: 汚してしまった. Note: the same kanji read けがす means, in elevated language, "to dishonor, to stain" (名誉を汚す).

en.meaning: to cool down; to get cold
examples[].german: The coffee has gone cold.
Please eat before it gets cold.
My feelings for him have cooled.
en.notes: 冷める describes something warm cooling to normal temperature: スープが冷める, お茶が冷める. The transitive counterpart is 冷ます (お湯を冷ます). 冷える, by contrast, means "to get cold, to be chilled" (ビールが冷える, 体が冷える). Set phrase: 冷めないうちにどうぞ "please, while it's still warm". Figuratively, feelings or enthusiasm cool off: 気持ちが冷める. Not to be confused with 覚める "to wake up".

en.meaning: to be baked/grilled; to burn down; to get tanned
examples[].german: The bread baked nicely.
After a day at the sea, my face got bright red from the sun.
An old temple burned down in a fire.
en.notes: 焼ける is the intransitive counterpart of 焼く: パンを焼く → パンが焼ける "the bread is done baking". It also describes something burning down (火事で家が焼ける) or getting tanned or sunburned by the sun (日に焼ける, noun 日焼け). 燃える means "to burn, to be in flames", whereas 焼ける emphasizes the result. For meat: よく焼けている "well done".

examples[].german: I deep-fry tempura.
I deep-fried chicken in oil and made karaage.
The children are flying kites in the park.
en.notes: 揚げる means "to deep-fry in oil" in cooking: 天ぷらを揚げる, 油で揚げる. From it come 揚げ物 "fried food" and 揚げたて "freshly fried". The intransitive counterpart is 揚がる (天ぷらが揚がる). 揚げる is also used for flying kites or hoisting flags (たこを揚げる). Not to be confused with the homophones 上げる "to raise" and あげる "to give"; 焼く is "to grill, to bake", 炒める "to stir-fry".

examples[].german: I steam vegetables and eat them.
You steam glutinous rice to make mochi.
It sure is muggy today, isn't it?
en.notes: 蒸す means "to steam" when transitive: 野菜を蒸す, 蒸し器 "steamer", 茶碗蒸し "steamed egg custard". Intransitively it means "to be muggy": 今日は蒸しますね; the adjective 蒸し暑い is more usual for this. 煮る is "to simmer in liquid", ゆでる "to boil in water". Related is 蒸れる "to become hot and damp" (e.g., feet in shoes).

examples[].german: My muscles hurt.
I want to build muscle by exercising.
When you get older, you lose muscle.
en.notes: 筋肉 is a muscle or the musculature. Muscles are "put on": 筋肉をつける (transitive) or 筋肉がつく (intransitive); losing them is 筋肉が落ちる. Sore muscles are 筋肉痛, and strength training is colloquially 筋トレ. 筋 (すじ) alone means "tendon, fiber" or the "plot" of a story.

examples[].german: I fell and broke a bone.
This fish has many bones, so please eat carefully.
This job is quite a lot of work.
en.notes: 骨 is a bone; in fish also a fish bone (魚の骨). Breaking one is 足の骨を折る or, medically, 骨折する. Idiomatically, 骨が折れる means "to be hard work" and 骨を折る "to go to great pains"; context decides. Frames also have 骨, e.g., 傘の骨 "umbrella ribs".

examples[].german: My stomach hurts.
I ate too much, and my stomach feels bad.
I checked where the stomach is located in the diagram.
en.notes: 胃 is the stomach as an internal organ; 腹 or お腹, by contrast, refers more generally to the abdominal area. 胃が痛い names stomach pain, 胃の調子が悪い an upset stomach. The reading consists of a single mora い. The card does not cover an astronomical meaning.

examples[].german: I had a chest X-ray taken.
Cigarettes are bad for the lungs.
en.notes: 肺 is the lung as a breathing organ. 肺のレントゲン refers to an X-ray of this organ. In 肺に悪い, に marks what is harmed by something. The identically sounding はい as the answer "yes" is a different word.

examples[].german: My heart is beating fast.
My grandfather had heart surgery.
en.notes: 心臓 refers here to the heart as a bodily organ. 心臓が動く describes its activity, 心臓の手術 an operation on this organ. For inner feelings or the mind, 心 is used. This card does not practice the figurative meanings "nerve, cheek" or "center".

examples[].german: I had a blood test.
What is your blood type?
Exercise improves blood circulation.
en.notes: 血液 is the technical, medical word for "blood" and appears mainly in compounds: 血液検査 "blood test", 血液型 "blood type". In daily life one says 血 (ち): 血が出る "to bleed", not 血液が出る. People in Japan like to ask about blood type because it is associated with personality. Donating blood is 献血.

examples[].german: I wish you success.
I pray for my family's health.
en.notes: 祈る means "to pray", but it can also express a sincere wish in a situation that is not explicitly religious. What is wished for takes を: 成功を祈る, 健康を祈る. It is a transitive godan verb ending in る; the te-form is 祈って.

examples[].german: I have a cavity, so I'm going to the dentist.
If you eat too many sweets, you'll get cavities.
The dentist pulled one bad tooth for me.
en.notes: 虫歯 means both tooth decay and the decayed tooth itself; it is counted with 本: 虫歯が一本ある. Typical are 虫歯になる "to get a cavity", 虫歯がある and 虫歯が痛い. It is treated at the 歯医者. Literally the word means "insect tooth", from the old belief that worms gnaw at the tooth.

examples[].german: My blood pressure is high.
I measure my blood pressure every morning.
My blood pressure is low, so getting up in the morning is hard.
en.notes: 血圧 is blood pressure. It is 高い or 低い (not 大きい/小さい) and can 上がる "rise" or 下がる "fall". Measuring is 血圧を測る. Medical terms include 高血圧 "high blood pressure" and 低血圧 "low blood pressure". At the doctor's you often hear: 血圧を測りましょう.

examples[].german: Please tell me your symptoms.
What symptoms do you have?
After I took the medicine, my symptoms got milder.
en.notes: 症状 is the medical word for "symptoms, complaints": 風邪の症状, 症状がある, 症状が出る, 症状が重い/軽い. At the doctor's you are asked: どんな症状ですか. For general well-being one says 具合 or 調子 (具合が悪い). 症状 does not fit non-medical "signs"; for those one uses e.g. サイン.

examples[].german: I won the kendo tournament.
I did kendo for three years in junior high school.
I go to the kendo dojo twice a week.
en.notes: 剣道 is the Japanese art of fencing with a bamboo sword (竹刀) and protective armor (防具). You say 剣道をする, 剣道をやる or 剣道を習う; schools have a 剣道部. Training takes place in the 道場, ranks are called 段. The suffix 道 "way" is also found in 柔道 and 茶道.

examples[].german: I do exercises every morning.
During summer vacation, we did radio calisthenics in the park.
A gymnast won a gold medal at the Olympics.
en.notes: 体操 means gymnastics or calisthenics exercises; usually you say 体操をする. Very well known is ラジオ体操, the morning exercises done to radio music, and before swimming you do 準備体操 "warm-up exercises". As a sport, 体操 means artistic gymnastics, and 新体操 is rhythmic gymnastics. 運動 is general "movement, exercise".

examples[].german: This fish is slimy.
The stones in the river were slimy, and I almost slipped.
Okra is so slimy, I don't like it.
en.notes: ぬるぬる describes a slippery, slimy surface: fish, eel, okra, mossy stones, soapy hands. It usually appears as ぬるぬるする / ぬるぬるしている, also ぬるぬるになる. ねばねば is "sticky, stringy" (natto), べたべた "sticky" (sweets, sweat), つるつる "smooth" (ice, skin). ぬるぬる sounds rather unpleasant.

examples[].german: My hands are sticky from touching candy.
That couple clings to each other even in public.
Posters are plastered all over the wall.
en.notes: べたべた describes stickiness: hands after sweets, skin in sweat and humidity (汗でべたべた). Mostly べたべたする or べたべたになる. It also means "all over" (ポスターをべたべた貼る) and, for couples, "to cling together, be constantly lovey-dovey". べとべと is even wetter and more unpleasant, ねばねば is stringy, and ぬるぬる is slimy.

examples[].german: My heart was pounding before the presentation.
When I talk to the person I like, my heart pounds.
I just ran, so my heart is still pounding.
en.notes: どきどき is the pounding of the heart - from excitement, nervousness, being in love, fear or after exertion. It is usually used as どきどきする, often with 胸が or 心臓が. It is also often written in katakana: ドキドキ. わくわく is only positive anticipation, and はらはら is worry while watching; どきどき can be positive or negative.

examples[].german: I'm excited about the trip.
Before opening a present, I'm always excited.
I read the book with excitement, wondering what would happen next.
en.notes: わくわく describes joyful excitement and anticipation of something nice: trips, presents, an exciting story. It usually appears as わくわくする, also ワクワク in katakana. Unlike どきどき, it is never used for fear or nervousness - before an exam you are 緊張する or どきどきする, not わくわく.

examples[].german: I oppose that plan.
My parents opposed my studying abroad.
en.notes: 反対する means to be against a proposal or plan. What the objection is directed at takes に. It is an intransitive する-verb. The noun 反対 can also denote an opposite direction; this directional sense is not taught here as a verb.

examples[].german: I was irritated by the traffic jam.
On days when I haven't slept much, I get irritable quickly.
My little brother annoyed me so much that I ended up raising my voice.
en.notes: いらいら describes inner irritation and impatience: いらいらする. The cause takes で (渋滞でいらいらする), a person who annoys one takes に (弟にいらいらする); "to annoy someone" is いらいらさせる. Often written イライラ too. 怒る shows anger outwardly, while むかつく is colloquial and stronger.

en.meaning: to wander about; to loiter; to pace
examples[].german: I got lost and wandered around.
A suspicious person is loitering in front of the station.
I was worried about the exam results and was pacing around the room.
en.notes: うろうろ describes aimless or restless walking around: when you have lost your way, pace back and forth nervously, or loiter. It is usually うろうろする; the place takes を (部屋の中をうろうろする) or で. It often carries a sense of perplexity or suspicion. ぶらぶら, by contrast, is leisurely strolling, and 迷う means "to get lost".

examples[].german: I slept soundly last night.
The baby is sleeping soundly, so please be quiet.
en.notes: ぐっすり is an adverb for deep, sound sleep. It goes with 寝る or 眠る and can also be combined with と. ぐっすり眠れた says that good sleep was possible; ぐっすり寝ている describes a person who is sleeping right now. It is not used for intense work or other activities.

examples[].german: The documents got scattered.
Opinions are divided.
Since graduating, everyone in our class has scattered in all directions.
en.notes: ばらばら means "scattered, apart, in pieces": ばらばらになる "to fall apart, to scatter", ばらばらにする "to take apart". For opinions, sizes or times it means "inconsistent": 意見がばらばらだ. ばらばらに帰る means "to go home separately". The opposite is そろう "to be uniform, complete"; ぱらぱら describes a light sprinkling or flipping through pages.

examples[].german: You look just like your mother.
This cake looks just like a real flower!
A thief stole all of my money.
en.notes: そっくり has two uses. As a な-adjective it means "strikingly similar, spitting image": Xにそっくりだ, そっくりな. This is stronger than 似ている "to be similar". As an adverb it means "completely, entirely": お金をそっくり盗まれる, そっくりそのまま "exactly as is". そっくりさん is a "look-alike, doppelgänger".

examples[].german: I'm frustrated that I lost the match.
I was so close to winning, how frustrating.
I was furious when my friend made fun of me.
en.notes: 悔しい expresses the bitter frustration over one's own defeat, failure or humiliation, often combined with the wish to do better. 残念 is more neutral, "too bad, regrettable", and also fits things one could not influence; 悲しい is "sad". For other people's feelings one uses 悔しがる or 悔しそう. The noun is 悔しさ.

examples[].german: I watched a heartrending movie.
The farewell song is wistful.
It hurts that I can't see my girlfriend because she lives far away.
en.notes: 切ない describes a bittersweet, tugging pain in the chest - longing, unrequited love, parting, wistfulness. It is typical of songs, movies and manga, but is also common in everyday speech. 悲しい is simply "sad", 寂しい "lonely", 苦しい "agonizing". The noun is 切なさ.

examples[].german: I think I'm pathetic.
We couldn't score a single point in the match; it was a miserable result.
Giving up right away is pathetic!
en.notes: 情けない means "pathetic, miserable, shameful". It is often directed at oneself (自分が情けない) when one is disappointed by one's own weakness; it expresses shame and frustration at the same time. Toward others it is a clear reproach. みっともない emphasizes how something looks to others, 恥ずかしい is one's own embarrassment, 悔しい the annoyance over a defeat.

examples[].german: He is dressed sloppily.
He is careless about time, so he always arrives late.
I don't lend money to people who are careless with it.
en.notes: だらしない describes people who are sloppy and undisciplined - in clothing, lifestyle or behavior: だらしない格好, だらしない生活. With に you indicate the area: 時間にだらしない "unpunctual", お金にだらしない "sloppy with money". For a messy room, 散らかっている is preferred. いいかげん stresses irresponsibility. Colloquially also だらしがない.

examples[].german: He's a quiet child.
That dog is well-behaved.
I prefer clothes in subdued colors to flashy ones.
en.notes: おとなしい means "quiet, well-behaved, gentle" and describes children, animals and reserved people. おとなしくする means "to behave, to keep still". For colors and patterns it means "subdued, plain". The kanji spelling 大人しい ("like an adult") is rare. 静か refers more to sounds and surroundings, 優しい to kindness.

examples[].german: I agree with that opinion.
Everyone agreed.
en.notes: 賛成する means to agree with an opinion or proposal. The content takes に, and the agreeing person takes が. It is an intransitive する-verb; the opposite is 反対する. 賛成 alone can be used as a brief expression of agreement, "I'm for it!".

examples[].german: Please don't ask so persistently.
The constant sales calls are bothering me.
The flavor of this ramen is too heavy.
en.notes: しつこい describes annoying persistence: people, questions, sales calls, but also a cold that won't go away (しつこい風邪). As an adverb: しつこく聞く. With food, it means "too heavy, too greasy" (味がしつこい); the opposite is あっさり. Positive perseverance, by contrast, is described with 熱心 or 粘り強い.

examples[].german: You must not do unfair things.
What, you're the only one who ate two pieces of cake? That's not fair!
He is cunning and always makes others do the hard work.
en.notes: ずるい means "unfair, cunning, sly". As an exclamation, ずるい！ protests an injustice or shows envy ("that's not fair!") - typical among children and friends. ずるをする means "to cheat". 卑怯 is stronger and morally condemning, and 不公平 is the objective "unfairly distributed". The kanji spelling 狡い is rare.

examples[].german: I feel sluggish because of a cold.
On Monday mornings I feel so sluggish that I don't want to get up.
Homework, ugh - can't be bothered.
en.notes: だるい describes a physical feeling of heaviness and listlessness, for example with a cold, fever, heat or exhaustion: 体がだるい, 足がだるい. Colloquially, especially among young people, it also means "annoying, dull, can't be bothered". 疲れた is "tired after exertion", and 眠い "sleepy". In technical language, 倦怠感 is used.

examples[].german: Don't make silly jokes.
Let's stop this silly talk.
The movie I saw yesterday was rubbish.
en.notes: くだらない means "worthless, silly, nonsense" and sounds disparaging: くだらない話, くだらない冗談, くだらない番組. つまらない, by contrast, means "boring, uninteresting" - くだらない goes further and denies the thing any value. The kanji spelling 下らない is rare; colloquially also くだらん.

examples[].german: Stop that disgraceful behavior.
It is embarrassing to do something like that.
Your shirt is hanging out; it looks untidy.
en.notes: みっともない describes what looks embarrassing or improper in the eyes of others - clothing, appearance, behavior in public. Parents often scold: みっともないからやめなさい. 恥ずかしい is one's own feeling of shame, and 情けない is disappointment over weakness. The kanji spelling 見っともない is rare.

examples[].german: Throwing away food is wasteful.
It's a waste to stay home when the weather is so nice.
Those are kinder words than I deserve.
en.notes: もったいない expresses that something valuable is being wasted: food, money, time, talent or an opportunity; as an exclamation もったいない！ "What a waste!". Typical: Xのはもったいない. In humble speech it means "too good for me, undeserved": 私にはもったいない. 残念, by contrast, is "regrettable" without the idea of waste.

examples[].german: Please walk on the sidewalk.
The sidewalk on this road is narrow, so it is dangerous.
en.notes: 歩道 is the path or sidewalk for pedestrians alongside a road. 歩道を歩く uses を for the path traveled. 歩道が狭い describes its small width. A marked crossing over the road, in contrast, is called 横断歩道.

examples[].german: I cross at the crosswalk.
Cross the second crosswalk and then turn right.
Cars must stop in front of the crosswalk.
en.notes: 横断歩道 is any marked pedestrian crossing, both the classic zebra crossing and the crossing at a traffic light. Typical is 横断歩道を渡る, where を marks the stretch crossed. The traffic light for it is 信号, a pedestrian bridge is 歩道橋, and the sidewalk itself is 歩道. 横断 alone means "crossing": 道路を横断する "to cross the road".

examples[].german: Let's take the shortcut.
I know a shortcut.
Is there a quick way to get good at Japanese?
en.notes: 近道 is the shorter route itself and, as a する-verb, taking a shortcut: 近道をする or 近道を通る "to take a shortcut"; when a route becomes shorter, you say ～が近道になる. Figuratively it stands for the fastest way to a goal: 上手になる近道. The opposite is 遠回り "detour". Note: a linguistic "abbreviation" (of a word) is called not 近道 but 略語.

en.meaning: to use; to make use of
examples[].german: I use the library.
I often use the library.
I use my free time to read a book.
en.notes: 利用する means to use a facility, service, or opportunity. What is used takes を. It is a transitive する-verb and suits, for example, libraries or available time. The more general 使う is also used for simple tools and objects.

examples[].german: I paid a fine for speeding.
If you park a car here, you'll be fined.
en.notes: 罰金 is a monetary penalty for a violation. 罰金を払う names the payment; 罰金を取られる describes, from the point of view of the person affected, that they have to pay a penalty. The specific violation can be given with で. The amount and legal basis depend on the situation; the card practices the word's usage.

examples[].german: I change trains at Shinjuku.
There is one transfer on the way to the airport.
We only have five minutes to change trains, so let's hurry.
en.notes: 乗り換え is the noun for the ichidan verb 乗り換える "to transfer". The transfer point takes で (新宿で乗り換える), and the new line takes に (山手線に乗り換える). As a noun you hear 乗り換えがある, 乗り換えなしで行ける or 乗り換えの時間; station signs often use the short form 乗換. Figuratively, it also means switching to another provider or system.

examples[].german: I bought a one-way ticket.
A one-way ticket, please.
It takes an hour each way from home to the office.
en.notes: 片道 is one direction of a trip: 片道切符 "one-way ticket", 片道料金, and with time expressions "each way": 片道一時間. At the ticket counter, 片道でお願いします is often enough. Its counterpart is 往復 "round trip". Note: a one-way street is not 片道 but 一方通行.

en.meaning: round trip; going back and forth
examples[].german: How much is a round-trip ticket?
I bought a round-trip ticket.
Every day I just go back and forth between home and the office.
en.notes: 往復 means "there and back": as a noun in 往復切符 or 往復の切符, and with prices using で: 往復で三万円. As a する-verb, the route takes を: 家と会社を往復する "to commute between home and the company". Its counterpart is 片道. In elevated language, 往復 also means an exchange of letters, e.g. 往復はがき "postcard with a reply card".

en.meaning: first train; first bus; starting station
examples[].german: I take the first train.
I had missed the last train, so I waited for the first train.
This train starts its run at Tokyo Station.
en.notes: 始発 is the first train or bus of the day; you travel 始発で ("on the first train") or wait for the 始発. Its counterpart is 終電 or 終バス. Second meaning: a train that begins its run at a station is 始発 there - 東京駅始発の電車; at such a 始発駅 you can usually get a seat easily.

examples[].german: I made it to the last train.
What time is the last train?
The last train had gone, so I took a taxi home.
en.notes: 終電 is the short form of 最終電車, the last train of the day. Typical phrases: 終電に間に合う "to catch the last train", 終電に乗り遅れる or 終電を逃す "to miss it", and 終電がなくなる "no more trains run". The counterpart is 始発. For buses, people speak of the 終バス or 最終バス.

examples[].german: I renew my commuter pass.
I forgot my commuter pass at home.
My company pays for my commuter pass.
en.notes: 定期券 is a pass for a fixed route, usually for one, three or six months; commuters have a 通勤定期, and school and university students a 通学定期. In everyday speech people often just say 定期. Today the pass is usually stored on an IC card. Typical: 定期券を買う/更新する; many companies pay their employees' 定期券代.

examples[].german: I reserved a seat.
Please put your luggage under the seat.
en.notes: 座席 is a seat, especially on a train, bus, or in a cinema or hall. 座席を予約する secures a specific seat; 座席の下 refers to the space under the seat. The word can mean the assigned place and the physical seat. For a freely movable seat one often says 椅子.

examples[].german: I go through the ticket gate.
I am waiting in front of the ticket gate.
Exit through the north exit ticket gate and go right.
en.notes: 改札 today mainly means the ticket barrier in a station, also 改札口; originally, it meant the inspection of tickets. Typical: 改札を通る, 改札を出る/に入る and 改札で待ち合わせる. Large stations have several gates such as 中央改札 or 北口の改札; automatic gates are 自動改札. A railroad crossing barrier, by contrast, is 踏切.

examples[].german: I'm sorry for being late.
Being late is not tolerated.
I overslept and was late for school.
en.notes: 遅刻 means arriving late for a fixed appointment; the destination takes に: 学校に遅刻する, 会議に遅刻する. It is used only for people; late trains or buses 遅れる, not 遅刻する. To apologize one says 遅刻してすみません or 遅れてすみません. The counterpart for leaving early is 早退.

examples[].german: Life in Japan is enjoyable.
I've gotten used to life living alone.
en.notes: 生活 denotes everyday life and the way someone lives. It is a noun: 日本の生活, 一人暮らしの生活. With する it can mean "to live". It is about daily life here, not biological life or lifespan, which are expressed with 生命 or 寿命, for example.

examples[].german: I'm not feeling well, so I'll leave early.
I have something to take care of today; may I leave at three o'clock?
My son came home early from school because of a fever.
en.notes: 早退 means leaving work or school before the regular end; the place takes を: 会社を早退する, 学校を早退する. To ask permission one uses 早退してもいいですか or 早退させてください. The counterpart is 遅刻; being absent altogether is 休む, or at school 欠席する.

examples[].german: Congratulations on your promotion.
My older sister will be promoted to section chief next month.
en.notes: 昇進 is advancement to a higher professional position or rank. With する it becomes an intransitive verb: 課長に昇進する means "to be promoted to section chief". The new position takes に. A pay raise is 昇給 and is not automatically the same thing.

examples[].german: I'm thinking about changing jobs.
I plan to change jobs next month.
I switched from a bank to a travel company.
en.notes: 転職 is a change of workplace or profession; the new job takes に: 旅行会社に転職する. To be distinguished are 就職 "finding one's first employment" and 退職 "leaving one's job". The job search when changing is called 転職活動. A move because of a transfer within the same company, by contrast, is 転勤.

examples[].german: I visit a business partner.
I have a meeting with a business partner.
We introduced a new product to our client.
en.notes: 取引先 are companies or people with whom you regularly do business - customers as well as suppliers. It belongs to business language; when speaking politely about the people there, you say 取引先の方. For customers in a shop, by contrast, you say お客様. Typical: 取引先を訪問する, 取引先との打ち合わせ, 取引先に連絡する.

examples[].german: I have a meeting in the afternoon.
Before the meeting, I will prepare the materials.
At the planning meeting, we decided the roles for the day.
en.notes: 打ち合わせ is a meeting for preparation or coordination. 打ち合わせがある announces an appointment; 打ち合わせで決める names the meeting as the place of a joint decision. With する, it can also refer to the act of coordinating. This card does not deal with the identically written overlapping of a garment.

examples[].german: I'm going on a business trip next week.
Next week I'm on a business trip to Osaka.
The department head is on a business trip right now.
en.notes: 出張 is a work-related trip; the destination takes に or へ: 大阪に出張する, or you say 出張に行く or 出張で大阪へ行く. On the phone you often hear 出張中です "is on a business trip". A private trip is 旅行, by contrast. In compounds such as 出張修理, 出張 also means "on-site service at the customer's place".

examples[].german: Sales are growing.
This month's sales were good.
On rainy days, the shop's sales drop.
en.notes: 売上 is sales revenue, i.e. the total of goods or services sold - not the profit, which is 利益. Typical: 売上が伸びる/上がる "to rise", 売上が下がる/落ちる "to fall", 売上を伸ばす "to increase". It is also written 売り上げ; in bookkeeping, 売上高 is used.

examples[].german: The deposit is two months' rent.
Will I get the deposit back when I move out?
This apartment requires neither a deposit nor key money.
en.notes: 敷金 is the rental deposit paid on moving in; when moving out, cleaning and repairs are deducted and the rest is refunded. The amount is given in months of rent: 敷金二か月分. Not to be confused with 礼金 "key money", a gift to the landlord that is never returned. In western Japan the deposit is sometimes called 保証金.

examples[].german: There is no key money.
This property requires key money.
I paid key money when I signed the lease.
en.notes: 礼金 here means key money in connection with renting an apartment. It is a payment to the landlord and differs from the deposit 敷金. In apartment listings, 礼金なし says that this payment is waived; 礼金を払う describes paying it. This card practices this rental meaning and not a general monetary gift as thanks.

examples[].german: Please show me the floor plan.
I'll decide after I see the floor plan.
This apartment has a good layout, doesn't it?
en.notes: 間取り is the room layout of an apartment, i.e. its floor plan. In listings it is given with codes like 1K or 2LDK (L = living room, D = dining area, K = kitchen, the number = additional rooms). The drawing for it is called 間取り図. Typical: 間取りがいい, 使いやすい間取り, 間取りを見る.

examples[].german: I have a habit of getting up early.
I want to get into the habit of getting up early.
In this house, it is customary to take off your shoes at the entrance.
en.notes: 習慣 is a personal habit or a customary practice within a group. 習慣がある means to have a habit; 習慣をつける means to acquire one. The identically read 週間, which denotes a number of weeks, is written differently.

examples[].german: I'll contact the landlord.
The landlord lives on the first floor.
I pay the rent to the landlord every month.
en.notes: 大家 (おおや) is the landlord or landlady and is almost always used with さん: 大家さん. 家主 is somewhat more formal. The same kanji read たいか mean something quite different, namely "master, authority" (書道の大家). For larger buildings, contact often goes through a management company (管理会社) rather than directly through the 大家さん.

examples[].german: I'm moving next month.
I'm busy with preparations for the move.
Thank you for helping me move.
en.notes: 引っ越し is the noun for the godan verb 引っ越す "to move" (東京に引っ越す, 新しい家へ引っ越す). As a noun you say 引っ越しをする, 引っ越しの準備, 引っ越しを手伝う. After moving in, it is customary to introduce yourself to the neighbors with a small gift (引っ越しの挨拶). On company signs you often see the shorter spelling 引越し.

examples[].german: When is the bulky waste collection day?
I'm putting the old sofa out as bulky waste.
To dispose of bulky waste, you have to buy a sticker.
en.notes: 粗大ごみ is bulky waste such as furniture, bicycles, or large appliances. In Japan you usually have to register it with the municipality beforehand and buy a paid ticket (粗大ごみ処理券, often simply シール); then you put it out on the agreed day: 粗大ごみに出す. It is also written 粗大ゴミ. Jokingly, the term is also used for a retired husband who is just in the way at home.

examples[].german: Please separate your garbage.
In this town, garbage is separated into eight types.
Please dispose of PET bottles and cans separately.
en.notes: 分別 (ぶんべつ) is separating and sorting, in everyday life mainly of garbage: ごみの分別, ごみを分別する. In Japan garbage is strictly separated into burnable waste, plastic, cans, bottles and so on. Note: the same kanji read ふんべつ mean "discretion, good judgment" (分別のある大人). For simple sorting, 分ける is also used.

examples[].german: There is a neighborhood association meeting.
I took part in the neighborhood association meeting.
At the neighborhood association, I helped clean the park.
en.notes: 町内会 is an association of the residents of a neighborhood. It may organize, for example, meetings, local festivals or communal cleaning. 町内会の集まり means a meeting of this association; 町内会に入る means to join it. Which activities exist depends on the particular neighborhood.

examples[].german: Please pass on the circular.
An announcement about the festival came through the circular.
The circular explains how to put out the trash.
en.notes: 回覧板 is a folder or clipboard with notices from the neighborhood association (町内会) that is passed from household to household. You read it, sign off on it, and pass it on: 回覧板を回す; when it arrives at your place, one says 回覧板が回ってくる. It contains e.g. festivals, garbage rules, or disaster drills. 回覧 alone refers to the circulation of documents, for instance in a company.

examples[].german: I passed a friend at the station.
I passed a car on the narrow road.
I went to the station to pick up my mother, but we missed each other.
en.notes: すれ違う means to pass each other going in opposite directions on foot or by vehicle; the other party takes と: 友達とすれ違う, 車とすれ違う. It also means "to miss each other" when you had meant to meet, and figuratively "to talk past each other, not be in agreement": 気持ちがすれ違う. The noun is すれ違い. Usually only 違う is written with kanji.

examples[].german: I tripped over a stone.
In the dark room, I tripped over the children's toy.
I am struggling with my kanji studies.
en.notes: つまずく means "to trip"; the obstacle takes に: 石につまずく. If a fall follows, you say つまずいて転ぶ - 転ぶ is the falling itself. Figuratively, it means "to run into difficulties, to fail", and the area takes で: 仕事でつまずく. The kanji 躓く is difficult and rare; it is almost always written in kana.

en.meaning: to jump; to hop; to splash
examples[].german: The children are jumping around.
Be careful, the oil splatters.
A fish jumped in the pond.
en.notes: 跳ねる means "to hop, to jump up" - of children, animals, fish or balls; lively jumping around is often 飛び跳ねる. Liquids can also splash: 油が跳ねる, 泥が跳ねる. For comparison: 跳ぶ is a deliberate jump (over something, a long way), and 飛ぶ means "to fly". Do not confuse it with the transitive はねる "to hit with a car" (車にはねられる), which is written 撥ねる.

en.meaning: to dive; to go underwater; to crawl under
examples[].german: I dove into the sea and saw fish.
Because it was cold, I crawled under the futon and slept.
The cat is hiding under the bed.
en.notes: 潜る (もぐる) means "to dive", and the destination takes に: 海に潜る, 水に潜る. Equally often it means "to crawl under something, to hide": 布団に潜る, 机の下に潜る. Figuratively, 地下に潜る means "to go underground". Note: the same kanji read くぐる means "to pass through something" (門をくぐる).

examples[].german: Japan's population is decreasing.
This town's population is small.
en.notes: 人口 refers to the number of people in an area. With ～の人口 you name the area; 多い and 少ない describe a large or small number of inhabitants. 増える and 減る describe how it changes. The identically read 人工 means "artificial" and is a different word.

examples[].german: I grip the steering wheel firmly.
I made onigiri.
I held the child's hand and crossed the street.
en.notes: 握る means "to grip firmly with the hand": ハンドルを握る, 手を握る, つり革を握る. In the kitchen it means shaping rice or sushi by hand, hence the name おにぎり. Figuratively, one has something "in hand": 権力を握る, 秘密を握る. Neutral "to hold, carry" is 持つ, while sudden grabbing is more つかむ.

examples[].german: I stroke the cat's head.
The mother gently stroked her crying child's head.
May I pet the dog?
en.notes: 撫でる means "to stroke, to gently pass a hand over something": 頭を撫でる, 犬を撫でる, 髪を撫でる. If you rub something that hurts, you say さする; mere touching is 触る. Since 撫 is not a Jōyō kanji, it is often written なでる in kana. The idiom 胸をなで下ろす means "to breathe a sigh of relief".

en.meaning: to put between; to insert; to pinch
examples[].german: I put a bookmark in the book.
I got my finger caught in the door.
The bank is across the street from the post office.
en.notes: 挟む means "to put or clamp something between two things": AをBに挟む, e.g. しおりを本に挟む, ハムをパンに挟む. This also applies unintentionally: 指をドアに挟む "to get one's finger caught". With a place: 道を挟んで "across the street". 口を挟む means "to interrupt, to cut in". The intransitive partner is 挟まる (指がドアに挟まる).

en.meaning: to peel off; to tear off
examples[].german: I peel off the sticker.
I took the poster off the wall.
It hurt a little when I peeled off the bandage.
en.notes: 剥がす means "to peel or remove something that is stuck or firmly attached": シール/ポスター/ばんそうこうを剥がす. The intransitive partner is 剥がれる (ペンキが剥がれる "the paint peels off"). Peeling fruit or vegetables, by contrast, is 剥く (むく). The word is often written in kana: はがす.

en.meaning: to wring out; to squeeze; to narrow down
examples[].german: I wring out the towel.
I squeeze a lemon and pour the juice over the fish.
I narrowed down the travel destinations to two.
en.notes: 絞る means "to press liquid out by twisting or squeezing": タオルを絞る "to wring out", レモンを絞る "to squeeze". Figuratively, it means "to narrow down, to reduce": 候補を二つに絞る, 音を絞る "to turn the volume down", 知恵を絞る "to rack one's brains". When extracting milk or juice, 搾る is also written (牛乳を搾る).

en.meaning: to make a mess; to scatter
examples[].german: Don't make a mess of the room.
The child went out leaving the toys scattered everywhere.
en.notes: 散らかす means to scatter things in disorder or to make a room messy. It is transitive: 部屋を散らかす or おもちゃを散らかす name the room or objects with を. As a godan verb ending in す, it forms 散らかします・散らかして・散らかさない. The state of something being messy can be described with the intransitive 散らかる.

examples[].german: I sew on the button.
My mother sewed a yukata for me.
I got injured and had three stitches at the hospital.
en.notes: 縫う means "to sew", by hand or with a sewing machine: 服を縫う, ミシンで縫う. Sewing something on is 縫い付ける (ボタンを縫い付ける). Doctors also stitch wounds: 三針縫う "to stitch with three stitches". Figuratively, 人ごみを縫って歩く means "to weave through the crowd". Knitting, by contrast, is 編む.

en.meaning: to knit; to crochet; to braid
examples[].german: I'm knitting a scarf.
My grandmother is good at knitting sweaters.
I braided my little sister's hair.
en.notes: 編む means to interlace threads or hair: knitting (棒針で編む), crocheting (かぎ針で編む) and braiding (髪を編む; a braid is 三つ編み). The result is called 編み物, hand-knitted items 手編み. In elevated language, 編む also means "to compile, to edit" (an anthology). Sewing, by contrast, is 縫う, weaving 織る.

examples[].german: I dyed my hair brown.
I dyed a white T-shirt blue.
The setting sun was coloring the sky red.
en.notes: 染める means "to dye", especially hair and fabric: 髪を染める, 布を染める. The color takes に (茶色に染める) or appears as an adverb in く (赤く染める). The intransitive partner is 染まる (空が赤く染まる). Unlike 塗る ("to paint"), with 染める the color penetrates the material. Figuratively: 顔を赤く染める "to blush".

en.meaning: to pickle; to soak; to marinate
examples[].german: I pickled cucumbers.
I leave the dirty shirt soaking in water.
I marinate the meat in soy sauce for an hour and then grill it.
en.notes: 漬ける means "to put into a liquid": AをBに漬ける - for soaking (シャツを水に漬ける) or marinating (肉をしょうゆに漬ける), and above all "to pickle, to preserve" as with pickles (きゅうりを漬ける). The result is called 漬物. The intransitive partner is 漬かる (よく漬かっている "well pickled"). Do not confuse with the similar-sounding 付ける "to attach" and つける "to turn on".

examples[].german: I stir-fry the vegetables.
First, sauté the onions until they are brown.
I fried the leftover rice together with egg.
en.notes: 炒める means "to fry in a little oil while stirring", typically in a pan or wok: 野菜を炒める, 油で炒める; a dish made this way is e.g. 野菜炒め. To be distinguished are 焼く (to pan-fry, grill, bake without stirring), 揚げる (to deep-fry) and 煮る (to simmer in liquid). Not to be confused with the identically sounding 痛める "to hurt, injure".

examples[].german: I let the curry simmer slowly.
I stewed beef and vegetables for two hours.
The soup at this restaurant is said to be simmered for ten hours.
en.notes: 煮込む means "to simmer long and slowly, to stew"; compared with the general 煮る ("to cook in liquid"), 込む stresses duration and thoroughness. Typical: じっくり/ゆっくり煮込む, and for the result 煮込み料理 or 煮込みハンバーグ. Cooking various ingredients together is also 煮込む. Cooking only in water is ゆでる.

examples[].german: Please serve the rice into the bowl.
I piled up soil in the garden and planted flowers.
His stories are always a bit exaggerated.
en.notes: 盛る mainly means "to serve food, to fill a bowl": ご飯を茶碗に盛る, サラダを皿に盛る; hence 大盛り ("large portion") and 盛り付け ("plating"). For rice and soup, everyday speech also uses よそう. In addition, 盛る means "to heap up": 土を盛る. Colloquially, 話を盛る means "to exaggerate, to embellish".

examples[].german: I spilled the coffee.
Eat so that you don't drop rice everywhere.
My father often complains about his work.
en.notes: こぼす means "to spill, to drop bits": liquids as well as crumbs or rice: 水/コーヒーをこぼす; often with てしまう because it is an accident. The intransitive partner is こぼれる (水がこぼれる). Set phrases: 涙をこぼす "to shed tears", ぐちをこぼす "to grumble, complain". It is almost always written in kana.

examples[].german: I peeked out of the window.
On the way home I'll drop in at the bookstore.
Please don't peek into other people's rooms.
en.notes: 覗く means "to look in through an opening or secretly": 窓から覗く, 鍵穴から覗く; the thing looked at takes を, the opening takes から. Also "to drop in briefly at a shop": 本屋を覗く. Intransitively it means "to peek out": 雲の間から青空が覗く. Not to be confused with 除く (のぞく) "to remove, to exclude".

en.meaning: to swell; to expand; to grow
examples[].german: The bread has risen.
In spring, the cherry blossom buds swell.
When I heard about studying abroad, my dreams grew.
en.notes: 膨らむ means "to puff up, to swell", for example of dough, balloons or buds: パンが膨らむ. Figuratively, dreams, plans or costs grow: 夢が膨らむ, 費用が膨らむ. The transitive partners are 膨らます/膨らませる (風船を膨らます). The similar 膨れる often sounds negative (お腹が膨れる "to be full") and also means "to sulk".

examples[].german: I untie my shoelaces.
I unpacked my luggage and put away the clothes.
I unraveled an old sweater and knitted a scarf.
en.notes: ほどく means "to loosen something knotted or tied": 靴ひも/結び目/リボンをほどく. Knitted items can also be unraveled (セーターをほどく) and tied-up luggage unpacked (荷物をほどく). The opposite is 結ぶ "to tie"; the intransitive partner is ほどける (靴ひもがほどける "come undone"). The kanji 解く is usually read とく, which is why ほどく is written in kana.

examples[].german: I wrap a scarf around my neck.
I wrap sushi in nori seaweed.
I hurt my leg, so I put on a bandage.
en.notes: 巻く means "to wind around something, to roll up": マフラーを首に巻く, 包帯を巻く, 紙を巻く. The wrapping material takes で: 海苔で巻く, hence 巻き寿司. Other expressions: ねじを巻く "to wind up", 舌を巻く "to be amazed". Wrapping something up completely is 包む. As a counter, 巻 refers to volumes (第一巻).

examples[].german: I turn the page.
Please flip over one card.
When I pulled back the futon, a cat was sleeping there.
en.notes: めくる means "to turn pages or fold back something that covers": ページ/カレンダーをめくる, カードをめくる "to flip a card", 布団をめくる "to pull back the blanket". The intransitive partner is めくれる (スカートがめくれる). The kanji 捲る is rare; it is written in kana. Opening a book is 開く.

examples[].german: I stir the soup.
I stir natto well before eating it.
Please stir the bathwater before you get in.
en.notes: かき混ぜる means "to stir thoroughly, to mix", e.g. with a spoon or chopsticks: スープ/卵/納豆をかき混ぜる. The prefix かき intensifies the simple 混ぜる ("to mix"). Typical is よくかき混ぜる. Intransitively, something blends with 混ざる. In older Japanese baths, one stirs the water before getting in because the hottest water is on top.

examples[].german: There was a traffic accident.
Please be careful to avoid traffic accidents.
Because of an accident at the factory, the machine stopped.
en.notes: 事故 here refers to an accident or an unwanted disruption. 交通事故 is a traffic accident; 事故がある or 起こる describes the event. The noun is read じこ. The older reading ことゆえ and the broader sense "circumstances" do not belong to this card.

examples[].german: I play the guitar.
My older sister is good at playing the piano.
en.notes: 弾く denotes playing a stringed or keyboard instrument, such as guitar or piano. With を you name the instrument. The godan verb forms 弾きます and 弾いて, read hikimasu and hiite. 弾くのが上手 means being good at playing the instrument named.

examples[].german: I paint a landscape.
I drew my dream for the future.
This film portrays the love within a family.
en.notes: 描く (えがく) means "to draw, to paint" and beyond that "to depict" (in film, novels) and "to imagine" (心に描く). The same kanji is also read かく; for everyday drawing one usually says 絵をかく, while えがく sounds somewhat more elevated and is the usual reading for "to depict, to picture". Shapes and paths are also "described": 円を描く.

examples[].german: They are filming a movie.
The filming of the movie has begun.
Photography is prohibited here.
en.notes: 撮影する means "to photograph or film" and sounds more formal than the everyday 写真を撮る. It is often found on signs: 撮影禁止 "no photography". As a noun: 映画の撮影, 撮影中 "filming in progress". The object takes を: 風景を撮影する. For movies, people also simply say 映画を撮る.

examples[].german: I think about the balance of nutrients.
When you are sick, please eat something nutritious.
I've been so busy lately that I'm not getting enough nutrition.
en.notes: 栄養 is nutritional value or nutrient supply: 栄養がある "to be nutritious", 栄養をとる "to take in nutrients", 栄養が足りない, 栄養バランス. For "nutrition" in the sense of eating habits one rather says 食事 or 食生活. A nutritionist is a 栄養士.

examples[].german: I am cutting back on calories.
This cake is high in calories.
This drink has zero calories.
en.notes: カロリー is the energy value of food; packages show kcal (キロカロリー). You say カロリーが高い/低い, less often 多い/少ない. Eating less is カロリーを控える or 抑える. Advertising likes カロリーゼロ, カロリーオフ or 低カロリー; the opposite is 高カロリー.

examples[].german: It is rich in dietary fiber.
Dietary fiber is good for your health.
To get dietary fiber, I eat vegetables every morning.
en.notes: 食物繊維 is dietary fiber, i.e. indigestible plant components found in vegetables, beans, mushrooms or seaweed. Typical: 食物繊維が豊富/多い, 食物繊維をとる. 食物 is read しょくもつ here, not たべもの. 繊維 on its own means "fiber", also in textiles.

examples[].german: I place flowers on the household altar.
Every morning I light incense at the altar.
There is an old Buddhist altar in my grandmother's house.
en.notes: 仏壇 is the Buddhist household altar, a cabinet with doors in which memorial tablets (位牌) and photos of deceased family members stand.
