Typical actions are お花を供える "to offer flowers", お線香をあげる "to light incense" and 仏壇に手を合わせる "to put one's hands together before the altar". Do not confuse it with 神棚, the small Shinto household shrine, which usually hangs high up on the wall.

examples[].german: I took part in the Bon dance.
The Bon dance is a summer pleasure.
I put on a yukata and went to the Bon dance at a nearby park.
en.notes: 盆踊り is the folk dance for お盆, the summer festival commemorating the dead (mid-July or mid-August depending on the region). People dance in a circle around a wooden tower (やぐら) with drums, often in a 浴衣, in parks, at temples or shrines. The word refers both to the dance (盆踊りを踊る) and to the whole event (盆踊りに行く, 盆踊りに参加する).

examples[].german: We celebrated Shichigosan.
We took Shichigosan photos.
Our daughter has her Shichigosan this year, so we're going to the shrine in kimono.
en.notes: 七五三 is the festival around November 15 for children aged three, five and seven (traditionally boys at three and five, girls at three and seven). The family visits a shrine in kimono, prays for health and growth, and has commemorative photos taken; the children receive long lucky candy (千歳飴). Typical are 七五三のお祝い and 七五三で神社にお参りする.

en.meaning: Setsubun (festival marking the start of spring)
examples[].german: On Setsubun we throw beans.
On the evening of Setsubun, my father put on a demon mask.
Setsubun is around February 3 every year.
en.notes: 節分 is the day before the traditional start of spring (立春), usually February 3. People throw roasted soybeans (豆まき) and call out 鬼は外、福は内 "Demons out, good luck in"; often a family member in a mask plays the demon. Afterwards you eat as many beans as your age in years. You say 節分に豆をまく or 節分の日.

examples[].german: I'm investigating the cause of the accident.
The cause of the illness has been found.
en.notes: 原因 is the cause from which an event or problem arises. ～の原因 names the event that was caused; 原因を調べる means to investigate the cause. For a stated motive, 理由 is often used. In gen'in, the apostrophe separates ん from the following vowel.

examples[].german: For Girls' Day, we display dolls.
On Girls' Day, we eat chirashi sushi.
March 3 is Girls' Day, and we celebrate our daughter.
en.notes: ひな祭り (also 雛祭り or 桃の節句) is the festival for girls on March 3. Families display ひな人形, a tiered stand of dolls representing the imperial court, and eat things such as ちらし寿司. The dolls are set up a few weeks beforehand and put away right after. The counterpart for boys is こどもの日 on May 5.

examples[].german: On Children's Day, people hang up carp streamers.
Children's Day is on May 5 and is a national holiday.
en.notes: こどもの日 is Japan's Children's Day on May 5 and a national holiday. The name is read こども・の・ひ; の is part of the name. The examples show a typical custom and the day's place in the calendar. 子供の日 is also a dictionary spelling; the existing card uses the official spelling こどもの日.

examples[].german: It is hot, so I fan myself with a folding fan.
I bought a folding fan as a souvenir from Kyoto.
In summer it is handy to keep a folding fan in your bag.
en.notes: 扇子 is a collapsible folding fan that you open (扇子を広げる) to fan yourself and close again (扇子を閉じる). To fan yourself is 扇子であおぐ (あおぐ is usually written in kana). The flat, round fan often given away at summer festivals, by contrast, is called うちわ; an electric fan is 扇風機.

examples[].german: The sound of the wind chime feels cool.
In summer, I hang a wind chime by the window.
en.notes: 風鈴 is a wind chime, a small wind bell that rings when moved by the wind. It is often hung at a window in summer. 風鈴の音 refers to its sound; 涼しげ describes that this gives an impression of coolness. This does not mean that the wind chime actually cools the air.

examples[].german: I walk in geta.
You wear geta with a yukata.
I went to the summer festival in geta, and my feet hurt afterward.
en.notes: 下駄 are traditional wooden sandals with two crosspieces under the sole; they clatter when you walk. Like all footwear, they are worn with 履く "to put on", nowadays mainly with a 浴衣 at summer festivals. With a kimono, flat 草履 are usually worn instead. The word also appears in 下駄箱, the shoe cabinet at the entrance, even though ordinary shoes are kept in it.

examples[].german: There is a beckoning cat in the shop.
A beckoning cat with its right paw raised is said to beckon money.
I bought a small beckoning cat as a souvenir from Japan.
en.notes: 招き猫 comes from 招く "to beckon, to invite": the cat is not waving goodbye but beckoning luck with a raised paw (the Japanese beckoning gesture with the palm facing down). A raised right paw is said to attract money, a left paw customers. You find them at the entrance or register of shops and restaurants; typical is 招き猫が置いてある.

en.meaning: go out of one's way; take the trouble
examples[].german: Thank you for coming all this way.
You can send it by email, so you don't need to come specially.
en.notes: わざわざ stresses that someone takes special trouble or an extra trip for an action. When thanking, it acknowledges this effort: わざわざ来てくれてありがとう. With a negative, it can say that the effort is not necessary. Depending on tone, the word can also critically highlight needless effort.

examples[].german: I see, so that's how it is.
I see, this method would be faster.
en.notes: なるほど is a reaction to an explanation: "I see" or "indeed". It shows that something has become understandable, and it can introduce a conclusion that follows. In conversation, depending on tone, it can also come across as an assessment of the explanation; for very formal agreement, for example 承知しました or そうですか fit better.

examples[].german: I don't understand at all.
I felt refreshed after taking a shower.
In summer I want to eat something light.
en.notes: さっぱり has two quite different uses. With a negative it means "not at all": さっぱりわからない (colloquially stronger than 全然). With する it describes a fresh, clean, relieved feeling (お風呂に入ってさっぱりする), light, non-greasy food (さっぱりした料理, opposite こってり) or an open, uncomplicated character (さっぱりした性格). Compared with すっきり, さっぱり emphasizes freshness and cleanliness more.

examples[].german: I was disappointed with the result.
I was disappointed that the trip I had been looking forward to was canceled.
Don't be so disappointed. There's always next year.
en.notes: がっかり is almost always used as がっかりする "to be disappointed, to feel let down". The cause is marked with に (結果にがっかりする) or with a て-form (話を聞いてがっかりした). To disappoint someone is がっかりさせる. 残念 expresses more factual regret and is more polite, while がっかり describes the palpable emotional slump.

examples[].german: How was the test result?
When will we find out the exam results?
I summarized the results of the survey in a table.
en.notes: 結果 is the noun "result" or "consequence" here. A test or survey precedes it with の. 結果がわかる means to learn the result; 結果をまとめる, to summarize it. The construction ～した結果 in the sense of "as a result of ..." is another use.

examples[].german: I felt refreshed after taking a shower.
I felt refreshed after cleaning the room.
After I said what I wanted to say, I felt relieved.
en.notes: すっきり describes the feeling that something bothersome is gone: stress, tiredness, clutter, a stuffy nose. Typical are 気分がすっきりする, 頭がすっきりする "to have a clear head" and すっきりした部屋 "a tidy, simple room". Negated (すっきりしない天気, 気持ちがすっきりしない), it means "gloomy, unsatisfying". Similar to さっぱり, but it stresses relief and clarity more than freshness.

examples[].german: Please tidy up properly.
Please take your medicine properly every day.
Let's go to the interview in proper clothes.
en.notes: きちんと means "the way it should be": neatly, cleanly, correctly, punctually, regularly. It stands before verbs (きちんと片付ける, きちんと説明する) or, as きちんとした, before nouns (きちんとした服, きちんとした人). ちゃんと is almost synonymous, but more casual and colloquial; きちんと puts more emphasis on order and precision.

examples[].german: I was sick of being made to listen to the same story again and again.
I'm sick of doing the same work every day.
I'm fed up with the rain of the rainy season.
en.notes: うんざり expresses that you are thoroughly sick of something because it repeats too often or lasts too long. Typical: Xにうんざりする, Xにはもううんざりだ, うんざりした顔. Compared with 飽きる "to get tired of something, to lose interest", うんざり is stronger and contains annoyance or aversion.

examples[].german: I was spacing out.
I'm gazing absent-mindedly out the window.
Without glasses, I see the letters only blurrily.
en.notes: ぼんやり has two main meanings. First, "indistinct, blurry": ぼんやり見える, ぼんやり覚えている "to remember vaguely"; the opposite is はっきり. Second, "absent-minded, lost in thought": ぼんやりする, ぼんやり眺める. A single careless slip from inattention is rather うっかり.

examples[].german: I lead a hectic life.
The end of the year is hectic.
I had no time in the morning and left the house in a rush.
en.notes: 慌ただしい describes a time or situation as hectic and rushed: 慌ただしい毎日, 年末は慌ただしい, adverbially 慌ただしく出かける. It is related to 慌てる "to get flustered". 忙しい mainly says that you have a lot to do; 慌ただしい stresses the restless, rushed atmosphere and sounds somewhat more literary. Often also written in kana: あわただしい.

en.meaning: to act self-important; to be mysterious about something
examples[].german: Stop being so mysterious and tell me.
He always speaks in a pompous way.
The teacher made a show of it and didn't tell us the answer for a long time.
en.notes: 勿体ぶる (usually in kana もったいぶる) means "to put on airs" or "to make it needlessly suspenseful", e.g. when someone deliberately withholds information. Very common is the request 勿体ぶらないで教えて "don't keep me in suspense". As an attribute, 勿体ぶった話し方 describes a pompous, self-important manner. It is intransitive; ぶる means "to act as if one were" (cf. 偉ぶる). Despite the same root, it has nothing to do with もったいない "a pity, wasteful".

examples[].german: Let's stop wasting money.
Please don't waste time.
No matter how often you say it, it's useless.
en.notes: 無駄 is a noun and a な-adjective: "waste, futility". Important patterns are Xを無駄にする "to waste X", 無駄な時間 "wasted time", 〜ても無駄だ "it is useless to ..." and 無駄遣い "wasteful spending". 無駄がない praises something as efficient. もったいない, by contrast, is the exclamation that something valuable is a pity because it is being wasted.

examples[].german: That goes without saying.
I promised, so of course I'll come.
If you do something bad, it's natural that you get scolded.
en.notes: 当然 means "self-evident, natural, as expected". As a noun or な-adjective it appears in 当然のこと and 〜のは当然だ "it is only natural that ...", as an adverb directly before the verb (当然行きます). もちろん is more everyday and also serves as an answer, "but of course!"; 当然 sounds more matter-of-fact, but as a brief answer (当然でしょう) it is slightly blunt. A colloquial synonym is 当たり前.

en.meaning: just in case; if by any chance
examples[].german: I'm preparing for the worst case.
I took out insurance in case something happens.
If, against expectations, you are late, please call.
en.notes: 万が一 stresses that something is highly unlikely ("one in ten thousand"). As an adverb it goes with conditions: 万が一〜たら / 〜場合は "in the unlikely event that ...". As a noun it refers to an emergency: 万が一に備える, 万が一のとき, 万が一のために. The short form 万一 is more literary. Unlike もし, the case is explicitly unlikely; 念のため, by contrast, means "to be on the safe side".

examples[].german: I just arrived.
It just arrived.
The department head has just stepped out.
en.notes: たったいま (usually written たった今) is the emphasized form of 今: "just now, only this very moment". It is used with the past tense (たったいま着きました) and very often with 〜たところ. さっき means "a little while ago" and can already be several minutes or hours back; たったいま is truly immediate.

examples[].german: Please tell me the reason.
Please tell me the reason for your lateness.
Please don't get angry for no reason.
en.notes: 理由 refers to the reason or motive for a behavior. ～の理由 names what an explanation is being sought for; 理由を教える means to tell the reason. For the cause of an accident that is being investigated, 原因 often fits better. The reading learned here is りゆう, not the also recorded reading わけ.

examples[].german: It might rain tomorrow.
I may have left my wallet on the train.
I may not be able to go to the party.
en.notes: もしかしたら "maybe, possibly" almost always goes with かもしれない or のではないか at the end of the sentence. It expresses a rather low probability, weaker than たぶん. もしかすると means the same and is a little more formal; もしかして is used mainly in questions: もしかして田中さんですか "Are you Mr. Tanaka, by any chance?".

examples[].german: It can't be helped.
It can't be helped, so I'll do it myself.
I want the new game so badly.
en.notes: 仕方がない literally means "there is no way (to do it)" and expresses acceptance of a situation: "nothing can be done about it". More casual are 仕方ない and しょうがない; the polite form is 仕方がありません. 〜ても仕方がない means "there is no point in ...", and after the て-form of adjectives it means "unbearably, extremely": 眠くて仕方がない "I'm dead tired". It is conjugated like an い-adjective.

examples[].german: Please don't worry about it.
She cares a lot about what other people think of her.
Don't worry about the price; order whatever you like.
en.notes: Xを気にする means "to worry about X, to pay attention to X", often with the nuance that one worries too much (人の目を気にする "to worry about what others think"). 気にしないで(ください) is the usual reassurance "never mind, don't worry about it". The intransitive counterpart is Xが気になる: something occupies your mind on its own or catches your attention, whereas 気にする is conscious attention.

examples[].german: Do you need help?
I helped with the move.
When I was a child, I often helped around the house.
en.notes: 手伝い is the noun of 手伝う and refers to helping with a task that someone else is doing: 引っ越しの手伝い, 家の手伝い "helping around the house". One says 手伝いをする, humbly お手伝いします / お手伝いしましょうか. 助け, by contrast, is help or rescue in an emergency. お手伝いさん also refers to a housekeeper.

examples[].german: I'll start over from the beginning.
Let's start over from the beginning.
There was a mistake in the calculation, so I redid only the last part.
en.notes: やり直す means to start an activity again or to carry it out once more, often to correct a result. 最初からやり直す stresses a fresh start from the beginning; one can also redo only a certain part. It is a transitive godan verb ending in す: やり直します・やり直して・やり直さない.

en.meaning: to review; to reconsider; to think better of (someone)
examples[].german: We need to review the plan.
Please look over your answers once more before handing them in.
Because he helped me when I was in trouble, I now see him in a new light.
en.notes: 見直す (見る + 直す "once more, anew") has three common meanings: to look something over again (答えを見直す), to reconsider and revise plans or rules (計画を見直す, noun 見直し), and to see someone in a better light (彼を見直した). The last meaning is always positive; a change of opinion for the worse is not expressed by 見直す. Transitive with を.

examples[].german: I remembered the old days.
I remember my student days.
I just can't recall that person's name.
en.notes: Xを思い出す means "to remember X" in the sense of "calling something (back) to mind", so it is a process. That you still know something is expressed by 覚えている instead. When something won't come to mind, the potential form 思い出せない is used. To remind someone of something is 思い出させる; the noun 思い出 means "memory".

examples[].german: Don't repeat the same mistake.
Please repeat after me.
They say history repeats itself.
en.notes: 繰り返す means "to repeat", often several times: 同じ間違いを繰り返す, 何度も繰り返して練習する. Mostly transitive with を, but it can also be used intransitively: 歴史は繰り返す "history repeats itself". The noun or adverb 繰り返し means "repetition, over and over". For a simple "say it once more", もう一度言う is enough in everyday speech.

en.meaning: to calm down; to settle down; to settle in
examples[].german: Take a deep breath and calm down.
I have finally settled into life in the new town.
This café is quiet, and I can really relax here.
en.notes: 落ち着く is intransitive and means "to come to rest": to calm down (落ち着いてください), to subside (熱が落ち着く), to settle in (新しい生活に落ち着く), and to feel comfortable and relaxed in a place (この部屋は落ち着く). 落ち着いた色 or 落ち着いた人 means "subdued" or "composed" respectively. The transitive counterpart is 落ち着ける (気持ちを落ち着ける), and the opposite is 慌てる.

examples[].german: It has to do with my work.
The two of them have a very good relationship.
en.notes: 関係 here means relationship or connection. Aと関係がある means to have to do with A; 二人の関係 is the relationship between two people. The noun can therefore refer to a factual connection or to people. With する, 関係する becomes the verb "to be connected"; the card form is the noun.

examples[].german: What is the purpose of your trip?
It is important to study with a goal in mind.
en.notes: 目的 is the purpose or intended goal of an action. With 旅行の目的 you ask what a trip is for; 目的を持って means to act with a particular goal. Unlike a destination, 目的 here describes the intention behind an activity.

en.meaning: to go out with; to associate with; to accompany
examples[].german: I have been going out with her for three years.
Will you come shopping with me?
After work, I went out drinking to keep my boss company.
en.notes: 付き合う has two main meanings. With と: "to be together with someone, to be in a relationship" or generally "to associate with" (彼女と付き合う, 付き合ってください as a love confession). With に: "to accompany someone, to join in on something" (買い物に付き合う). The noun 付き合い means "association, social obligation", e.g. 付き合いで飲みに行く. Often also written つきあう; intransitive.

en.meaning: to wave; to swing; to reject
examples[].german: I wave to greet someone.
I sprinkle salt on the meat.
I confessed to the person I like, but I got turned down.
en.notes: 振る is a 五段動詞 (振って, 振らない) with the basic meaning "to swing, to shake": 手を振る "to wave", 首を横に振る "to shake one's head", バットを振る. It also means "to sprinkle" (塩を振る) and, in the passive 振られる, "to get turned down, to be dumped". Not to be confused with the identically sounding 降る "to fall (rain, snow)". The intransitive counterpart is 振れる "to swing, to deflect".

examples[].german: May I shift the appointment?
Please move the desk a little to the right.
Since the trains are crowded, I shifted my commuting time by an hour.
en.notes: ずらす means "to shift something a little", spatially (机を右にずらす) or in time (予定をずらす, 時間をずらす), without canceling it; it can be forward or backward. The intransitive counterpart is ずれる "to slip, to shift" (予定がずれる). 延期する, by contrast, explicitly means "to postpone to later" and is more formal; 動かす is a general "to move".

examples[].german: On days off I lie around at home.
Thunder is rumbling in the distance.
I got dirt in my eye and it feels gritty.
en.notes: ごろごろ is an onomatopoeic word with several meanings. Most common is ごろごろする "to lie around lazily, to laze about" (家でごろごろする). It also describes a dull rumbling (雷がごろごろ鳴る, also a growling stomach or a purring cat), the rolling of heavy things, and a scratchy foreign-body feeling in the eye (目がごろごろする). Small children also call thunder ごろごろ.

examples[].german: I'm restless because I'm worried about my exam results.
I have a date today, so I've been jittery since the morning.
Don't fidget; sit down and wait.
en.notes: そわそわ describes visible restlessness: you can't sit still because you are nervous or impatiently waiting for something, e.g. a result or a date. Mostly as そわそわする. どきどき, by contrast, refers to the inner pounding of the heart, and いらいら to irritable impatience. The opposite is 落ち着いている.

examples[].german: I just barely made the train.
I handed in the report right at the deadline.
I passed the exam with a score right at the borderline.
en.notes: ぎりぎり means "just barely, at the last minute, at the very limit". Typical patterns are ぎりぎり間に合う, noun + ぎりぎり (締め切りぎりぎり, 時間ぎりぎり) and ぎりぎりの + noun (ぎりぎりの点数). Colloquially people shout ぎりぎりセーフ "made it just in time". Another word of the same form is the onomatopoeia for grinding teeth (歯をぎりぎりさせる).

examples[].german: It suddenly started to rain.
A stranger suddenly spoke to me, and I was startled.
You shouldn't start with difficult problems right away.
en.notes: いきなり means "suddenly, without warning" and often also "right away, without a preliminary step" (いきなり難しい問題から始める). It stresses that something happens unexpectedly and abruptly, often through an action that one finds startling. 急に is more neutral and describes mainly sudden changes (急に寒くなる); 突然 is somewhat more formal. Almost always in kana.

examples[].german: The room was in a complete mess because of the typhoon.
This cake is super delicious!
What he is saying makes no sense at all.
en.notes: めちゃくちゃ is colloquial. As a な-adjective it means "completely messed up, wrecked" (部屋がめちゃくちゃだ, 〜をめちゃくちゃにする) or "nonsensical, absurd" (めちゃくちゃな話). As an adverb it intensifies like "totally, super": めちゃくちゃおいしい; short forms are めちゃ and めっちゃ. In neutral or polite situations people say とても instead.

examples[].german: He is grumbling and complaining.
Grandpa is watching TV and muttering something.
I got spots on my face.
en.notes: ぶつぶつ describes quiet, discontented muttering to oneself: ぶつぶつ言う, ぶつぶつ文句を言う "to grumble". With ひそひそ, by contrast, you whisper secretly with someone else. As a noun, ぶつぶつ also means "pimples, rash": 顔にぶつぶつができる.

examples[].german: She works briskly and efficiently.
He answered the questions promptly and clearly.
The clerk was quick and capable, which was pleasant.
en.notes: てきぱき praises prompt, efficient and businesslike action: てきぱき(と)働く, てきぱき答える, てきぱきした人 "a capable, brisk person". It is about efficiency and decisiveness, not just speed. Opposites are のろのろ "sluggish" and ぐずぐず "dawdling, hesitant".

examples[].german: Please tell me your opinion.
In the meeting I clearly stated my own opinion.
en.notes: 意見 means an opinion or a point of view here. 意見を言う means to express one's view; 意見を聞く or 聞かせてください asks for another person's view. This card practices this noun, not the other dictionary meaning of 意見する, to admonish someone.

examples[].german: Please stop driving so slowly.
Please don't walk so slowly.
I was so sleepy in the morning that I got ready at a snail's pace.
en.notes: のろのろ describes a sluggish, slow movement and usually sounds annoyed: のろのろ歩く, のろのろ運転 "crawling along, stop-and-go traffic". Related is the adjective のろい "slow, sluggish". ゆっくり, by contrast, is neutral or positive (ゆっくり休む). Opposites: てきぱき, さっさと.

examples[].german: I went out secretly.
I secretly ate sweets.
I'll tell you about a good shop in secret.
en.notes: こっそり means "secretly, unnoticed" and describes actions that others should not notice: こっそり出かける, こっそり食べる, こっそり教える "to tell on the quiet". It stands before the verb, often with と. ひそかに is more literary and can also refer to inner feelings (ひそかに思う); 内緒で stresses that you tell no one.

examples[].german: I like a light flavor.
He readily admitted defeat.
en.notes: あっさり describes two kinds of lightness here. In あっさりした味, the flavor is mild, not heavy or rich. Before an action, it can mean that it happens quickly and without resistance, such as あっさり負けを認める. Both uses are possible; "plain" alone does not always fit the flavor well.

examples[].german: I like rich ramen.
In summer I prefer light food to heavy dishes.
I was late and got a thorough scolding from the teacher.
en.notes: こってり mainly describes heavy, oily, rich food: こってりしたラーメン, こってりした味. Opposites are あっさり and さっぱり "light, not greasy". It can also describe thickly applied makeup. A second meaning is "thoroughly, good and proper" with scolding: こってり叱られる "to get a good talking-to".

examples[].german: I agreed reluctantly.
I accepted it reluctantly.
My mother told me to, so I reluctantly tidied up my room.
en.notes: しぶしぶ (also 渋々, from 渋い "astringent") means "reluctantly, out of necessity": you do something because you must or were asked to, although you don't feel like it (しぶしぶ賛成する, しぶしぶ引き受ける). いやいや shows the aversion even more clearly, while 仕方なく stresses that there was no other choice.

examples[].german: The two of them are whispering to each other.
We were in the library, so we spoke in whispers.
Someone in the seat behind me is whispering about me.
en.notes: ひそひそ describes quiet whispering so that others cannot hear, often with an undertone of muttering or secrecy: ひそひそ話をする, ひそひそ声で話す. ぶつぶつ, by contrast, is discontented muttering to oneself. The verb ささやく "to whisper, to murmur" is more neutral and can also be tender.

examples[].german: He is always smiling.
The grandmother is smiling warmly.
The shop assistant welcomed us with a smile.
en.notes: にこにこ describes a friendly, warm smile without laughing: にこにこする, にこにこ(と)笑う, にこにこ顔. Distinguish it from にやにや "to grin" (smugly or suggestively), くすくす "to giggle" and げらげら "to laugh loudly". A single brief smile is にっこり.

examples[].german: Don't cry like that.
Since her heartbreak, my older sister has been weepy every day.
en.notes: めそめそ describes quiet, tearful sobbing or continuous whining with tears. It goes with 泣く or with する: めそめそしている. The expression can sound disparaging; めそめそ泣かないで is a direct, not very empathetic request and not a neutral description of sadness.

examples[].german: I'm starving.
He is always bowing and scraping to his boss.
en.notes: ぺこぺこ has two meanings practiced here. お腹がぺこぺこです means that you are very hungry; this describes a state. 人にぺこぺこする refers to repeated, often servile bowing toward someone and can sound critical. The listed base forms have different accents depending on the role: the hungry state 0, the adverbial bowing 1.

examples[].german: Don't dawdle; get ready quickly.
If you dawdle, you'll miss the train.
Stop agonizing over it forever and decide already.
en.notes: ぐずぐず describes dawdling, hesitating and indecision: ぐずぐずする, ぐずぐずしないで "don't dawdle, come on". With のろのろ it is about slow movement, with ぐずぐず rather about not getting going. There is also ぐずぐず言う "to grumble". Related is ぐずる "to fuss" (of children). Colloquial and almost always in kana.

examples[].german: I'll make travel plans.
Let's make plans for the summer vacation.
Because the weather is bad, I changed the plan.
en.notes: 計画 is a worked-out plan or project. 計画を立てる means to draw up a plan; 計画を変える means to change it. The activity can precede it with の. With する, the noun can become the verb "to plan"; the card teaches the noun form.

examples[].german: My shoes are worn out.
With overtime every day, my body is completely wrecked.
Watching the movie, tears streamed down my face.
en.notes: ぼろぼろ comes from ぼろ "rags" and as a な-/の-adjective means "worn out, tattered, broken" (ぼろぼろの靴, 本がぼろぼろだ), figuratively also "completely exhausted, at the end of one's rope" (体がぼろぼろ). As an adverb it describes crumbs or drops falling in large quantities: 涙がぼろぼろ出る, パンがぼろぼろこぼれる. Smaller, lighter drops are described by ぽろぽろ.

examples[].german: The stars are twinkling.
The child's eyes were sparkling.
en.notes: きらきら describes many small or changing reflections of light, that is, twinkling or sparkling. It is used with 光る and 輝く, for example; きらきらと is also possible. With stars, actual light is meant; with a child's eyes, the expression can convey enthusiasm at the same time.

examples[].german: It is damp during the rainy season.
This room is so damp that the laundry doesn't dry.
Let's stop the gloomy talk and talk about something fun.
en.notes: じめじめ describes unpleasant, clammy dampness, as in the rainy season or in poorly ventilated rooms: じめじめした天気, 部屋がじめじめする. むしむし, by contrast, stresses muggy heat. Figuratively, じめじめ can also mean "gloomy, dreary" (じめじめした話, じめじめした性格). The opposite is からっと "dry, crisp".

examples[].german: The sun is blazing down.
It's a scorching hot day.
I forgot our appointment, so she is absolutely furious.
en.notes: かんかん has two common meanings. With the sun: "merciless, blazing" (日がかんかん照る, the noun かんかん照り "scorching sun", here read かんかんでり). With people: "livid, hopping mad", mostly about others (かんかんに怒る, 父はかんかんだ). As a sound ("clang, ding") for example of a railroad crossing, it is usually written in katakana カンカン.

examples[].german: It is drizzling softly.
The rainy season has many days of quiet drizzle.
I read while listening to the sound of the soft rain.
en.notes: しとしと describes quiet, even, gentle rain that lasts a long time, and feels rather calm and atmospheric: 雨がしとしと降る, しとしと降る雨. It is used almost only for rain. In contrast to it, ざあざあ stands for pouring downpours and ぱらぱら for scattered drops.

examples[].german: It's pouring.
I can't go out in this pouring rain.
Please don't leave the tap water running nonstop.
en.notes: ざあざあ imitates the roar of heavy rain or a lot of flowing water: 雨がざあざあ降る, ざあざあ降り "downpour" (like 土砂降り). Also for running water: 水をざあざあ流す. Often also in katakana ザーザー. Contrasts with gentle しとしと.

examples[].german: It's pleasantly warm weather today.
It's nice and warm in the sun.
After the bath, my body is nice and warm.
en.notes: ぽかぽか describes soothing, pleasant warmth. It is used for the weather, a sunny spot, or a body that has warmed up; with する it forms a description of a state. It does not mean scorching hot. The other dictionary meaning, for repeated hitting, is not meant here.

examples[].german: It is chilly in the morning.
The cool breeze feels good.
When I touch the cold glass, my hands feel cool.
en.notes: ひんやり describes a noticeable coolness, for example in the air or when touching an object. It can be used with する or modify a noun with した: ひんやりした風. The coolness can be pleasant; it does not automatically mean severe cold. The ん before や is separated with an apostrophe in Hepburn: hin'yari.

examples[].german: It is muggy today.
During the rainy season it's muggy every day, and the laundry won't dry.
It's stuffy in the room, so let's open the window.
en.notes: むしむし describes humid, oppressive hot air, typical of the rainy season and the Japanese midsummer. It is mostly used as a する-verb: 今日はむしむしする "it's muggy today"; also for stuffy rooms: 部屋がむしむしする. The adjective 蒸し暑い has the same meaning but is more neutral. As an onomatopoeic word it is written in kana, in advertising and comics often as ムシムシ.

en.meaning: to fiddle with; to tinker with; to play with
examples[].german: I am fiddling with my smartphone.
Please don't change the computer settings without asking.
When I'm nervous, I have a habit of playing with my hair.
en.notes: いじる means "to fiddle with, to play with something" and takes を: スマホをいじる, 髪をいじる. It also means "to tinker with, to alter something", often without permission or expertise: 設定をいじる. Colloquially, it also means "to tease someone". Unlike 触る "to touch", いじる stresses repeated, often unnecessary handling. The kanji 弄 is rare; in daily life it is mostly written いじる.

examples[].german: Please tell me a good method.
Let's think of other methods.
en.notes: 方法 refers to a method or procedure by which one achieves something. With ～の方法, the activity can precede it. 方法を教える means to explain a procedure; 他の方法を考える means to look for an alternative. The word does not mean a spatial path here.

examples[].german: I peel the apple.
I peeled a mandarin and gave it to the child.
Can you help me peel the potatoes?
en.notes: むく (kanji 剥く, mostly in kana) means "to peel" and takes を: 皮をむく, or the fruit directly as the object, りんごをむく, みかんをむく. Do not confuse it with the identically sounding 向く "to turn toward, to face". The intransitive counterpart is むける "to peel": 日焼けで皮がむけた "after the sunburn, my skin peeled". Peeling with a knife is 包丁でむく.

en.meaning: to pinch; to pick up with fingers; to nibble
examples[].german: Let's chat while nibbling on snacks.
It stank, so I pinched my nose.
It is hard to pick up beans with chopsticks.
en.notes: つまむ means "to pick up with the fingertips or chopsticks": 鼻をつまむ "to hold one's nose", 箸で豆をつまむ. From this comes "to nibble, to snack on the side" - the word おつまみ for small snacks with alcohol derives from it. Unlike つかむ "to grab with the whole hand", you pick up with just two fingers. The kanji 摘む is also read つむ "to pick (flowers)", which is why it is mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: I slurp ramen.
I slurped the miso soup.
I had a cold and was sniffling all day.
en.notes: すする means "to slurp" and refers mainly to noodles and soups: そばをすする, みそ汁をすする. Loud slurping of noodles is not considered impolite in Japan. With 鼻 it means "to sniffle, to snuffle": 鼻をすする. For normal drinking, one says 飲む. The kanji 啜 is difficult; すする is mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: I scoop it up with a spoon.
I scoop the soup with a spoon.
I scooped up river water with both hands.
en.notes: すくう here means to pick up a liquid or small objects with a spoon, a ladle, the hand or a similar tool. The tool takes で, and the thing picked up takes を. It is a transitive godan verb ending in う: すくいます・すくって・すくわない. 救う "to rescue" and 巣くう "to nest" are other words with the same reading.

en.meaning: to tear off; to tear into pieces
examples[].german: I tear the bread into pieces and eat it.
I tore the paper I no longer needed into small pieces and threw it away.
en.notes: ちぎる means to tear something into pieces with the hands or to tear off a piece. The thing torn takes を; 小さく says that small pieces result. It is a transitive godan verb ending in る: ちぎります・ちぎって・ちぎらない. The identically read 契る for a vow or promise does not belong to this card.

examples[].german: The flower wilted because I didn't water it.
This lettuce is a bit wilted, isn't it?
After the teacher scolded him, my little brother was completely downcast.
en.notes: しおれる describes plants that go limp from lack of water or heat and let their heads hang: 花がしおれる, 野菜がしおれる. Unlike 枯れる "to wither, to die", a しおれた plant can recover with water. Figuratively it is also said of people who are dejected after a reprimand or disappointment. Intransitive, with no transitive counterpart; mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: The children are romping in the pool.
On the first trip in a long time, even my mother was as playful as a child.
Stop horsing around on the train!
en.notes: はしゃぐ means "to be boisterous with joy, to romp around" and is intransitive: 子供がはしゃぐ. It describes cheerful, loud excitement, for example on vacation or at a party; in adults it sounds slightly childish, especially はしゃぎすぎ "to be overexcited". Unlike 騒ぐ "to make noise, to raise a racket", the emphasis is on joy, not on the disturbance. Written in kana.

examples[].german: My little brother is sulking because he didn't get any sweets.
She sulked because her birthday was forgotten.
Don't sulk like that; come on, let's play together.
en.notes: すねる means "to sulk, to be in a huff": you show your hurt by stubbornly staying silent or not joining in, often to get attention. Typical for children or in relationships: 無視されてすねる. Unlike 怒る "to get angry", すねる is passive and rather childish. Intransitive; the kanji 拗 is rare, and すねる is mostly written in kana.

en.meaning: to fit in; to get stuck; to get hooked on
examples[].german: Lately I have been hooked on games.
The car's tire is stuck in a hole, and it can't move.
This puzzle piece should fit here.
en.notes: はまる is intransitive and has several meanings: "to fit exactly" (指輪がはまらない), "to fall into, to get stuck" (穴にはまる, 渋滞にはまる) and, colloquially and very commonly, "to be gripped by something, to be addicted to": ゲームにはまっている. The target takes に. The transitive counterpart is はめる "to put in, to put on" (指輪をはめる). Mostly written in kana.

examples[].german: What do you do in this case?
In case of rain, it will be canceled.
en.notes: 場合 names a case or particular circumstances. After a noun, の precedes it, as in 雨の場合. Verbs stand directly before it in their plain form: 雨が降る場合. The expression is especially suited to explaining how to proceed in a possible situation.

en.meaning: to collide; to bump into; to run into
examples[].german: I bumped into the wall.
I ran into someone at the corner.
At work, you sometimes run into difficult problems.
en.notes: ぶつかる means "to collide, to bump against something" and is intransitive: 壁にぶつかる; for a mutual collision と is used: 車と車がぶつかる. The transitive counterpart is ぶつける "to bump something": 頭をぶつける. Figuratively it means "to run into a problem" (問題にぶつかる), "to clash" (意見がぶつかる) and "to coincide in time" (予定がぶつかる).

en.meaning: to slip out of place; to deviate
examples[].german: My glasses slipped.
Because of the typhoon, our trip schedule shifted by one day.
This is going off topic, so let's talk about it another time.
en.notes: ずれる means "to slip, to shift, to deviate from the right position" and is intransitive: メガネがずれる, 予定が一日ずれる. Figuratively: 話がずれる "to get off the topic", 感覚がずれている "to have an odd sense, to be off the mark". The transitive counterpart is ずらす "to shift" (日程をずらす). Written in kana.

examples[].german: My shirt is sticking to my body.
Chewing gum stuck to my shoe.
The child keeps clinging to his mother and won't leave her side.
en.notes: くっつく means "to stick, to adhere" and is intransitive; what something sticks to takes に: ガムが靴にくっつく. It is also used for people who cling closely to each other (子供が母親にくっつく), and colloquially for couples who get together. The transitive counterpart is くっつける "to stick on, to join together". Compared with the neutral 付く, くっつく sounds more colloquial and stresses firm adhesion.

en.meaning: to tease; to make fun of
examples[].german: I tease my younger brother.
Stop teasing your friend.
I was sad because I was teased about being short.
en.notes: からかう means "to tease, to make fun of, to pull someone's leg" and takes the person with を: 弟をからかう. Someone who is teased says からかわれる. It is usually meant playfully, but can hurt; unlike いじめる "to bully, to torment", it lacks the malicious intent. You can also からかう animals. Written in kana.

en.meaning: to meet; to greet (on arrival); to receive
examples[].german: I met my friend at the airport.
The whole family welcomed the guest at the front door.
When we arrived at the hotel, the staff welcomed us with a smile.
en.notes: 出迎える means "to meet or receive someone on their arrival" - at the station, airport or door: 空港で友達を出迎える. In everyday speech people often say the simpler 迎えに行く "to go and pick up"; 出迎える stresses going out to meet and greet someone and sounds somewhat more formal. The noun is 出迎え, politely お出迎え. The opposite is 見送る "to see off".

examples[].german: You spoil your child too much.
Once in a while I pamper myself and eat cake.
If you spoil the dog, it will stop listening to you.
en.notes: 甘やかす means "to spoil, to be too indulgent" and takes を: 子供を甘やかす, 孫を甘やかす. It usually has a reproachful tone. With 自分, it jokingly means "to treat oneself". Do not confuse it with the intransitive 甘える "to let oneself be pampered, to be dependent": parents 甘やかす the child, and the child 甘える toward the parents.

examples[].german: That is his pet phrase.
His pet phrase is "so-so".
I want to break my habit of saying "I'm busy".
en.notes: 口癖 is an expression that someone says over and over out of habit. It need not be a consciously chosen favorite saying. 人の口癖 attributes this verbal habit to a person; 口癖を直す describes trying to break it. The card does not mean just any phrase someone uses only once.

examples[].german: A friend listened to my complaints about work.
When my father drinks, he always complains.
Instead of just complaining, why don't you do something?
en.notes: 愚痴 is complaining about things you can't change anyway - work, the boss, the weather. Typical: 愚痴を言う or 愚痴をこぼす "to complain", 愚痴を聞く "to listen to someone's complaints". Unlike 文句 "complaint, objection", which is directed at someone, 愚痴 serves more to let off steam. Colloquially there is also the verb 愚痴る.

examples[].german: I chatted with a neighbor.
I'm bad at making small talk with the hairdresser at the salon.
After some small talk, the president began to discuss business.
en.notes: 世間話 is casual chatting about everyday matters such as the weather, the neighborhood, or news, i.e. small talk: 近所の人と世間話をする. The conversation partner takes と. Similar is 雑談 "informal conversation", which is also common among colleagues; 世間話 sounds a bit older and neighborly. For gossip about specific people one rather says うわさ話.

examples[].german: I make jokes to make people laugh.
What, you're quitting the company? You're joking, right?
That was just a joke. Don't be angry.
en.notes: 冗談 is a joke or jest in conversation: 冗談を言う "to joke". Very common are 冗談でしょう "You're joking, right?" and 冗談だよ "Just kidding". 冗談じゃない, by contrast, means "This is no joke / No way!". For a told joke with a punchline one rather says ジョーク or 笑い話; 冗談 is mainly the spontaneous jest.

examples[].german: Let's protect the environment.
It is important to protect the environment.
I want to study in a quiet environment.
en.notes: 環境 refers to the environment or the circumstances in which someone lives or works. 環境を守る usually means environmental protection; 静かな環境 describes a quiet surrounding. It is a noun and can therefore stand before another noun with の.

examples[].german: Please don't make excuses.
I ran to the station while thinking up an excuse for being late.
Being busy is not an excuse for not doing your homework.
en.notes: 言い訳 is an excuse or justification that explains a failing - usually with a negative undertone: 言い訳をする, 言い訳ばかりする. ～は言い訳にならない means "... is no excuse". Note: a request for forgiveness is not 言い訳 but 謝る or すみません. Neutral in the sense of "explanation" is 説明.

examples[].german: He is talking to himself.
I have a habit of talking to myself.
Don't mind me. I'm just talking to myself.
en.notes: 独り言 means "talking to oneself, muttering to oneself"; the verb for it is 言う: 独り言を言う. It is often associated with ぶつぶつ "to mutter". The phrase ただの独り言です "I'm just talking to myself" signals that no answer is expected. Besides 独り言, the spelling ひとり言 is also seen.

examples[].german: I overslept and was late.
I have an important exam tomorrow, so I'm setting two alarm clocks so I don't oversleep.
My son is a late riser, and waking him up every morning is hard work.
en.notes: 寝坊 is oversleeping; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 寝坊して遅刻した. 朝寝坊 has the same meaning but is more explicit. The word also refers to a person who likes to sleep late (お寝坊さん "sleepyhead"). Not to be confused with 寝過ごす, which stresses sleeping through a particular moment, such as your train stop.

examples[].german: He sometimes talks in his sleep.
Last night you called my name in your sleep.
Dream on!
en.notes: 寝言 is talking in one's sleep; the verb for it is 言う: 寝言を言う. With で it means "(say) in one's sleep": 寝言で名前を呼ぶ. Figuratively it means "nonsense, babbling"; the cheeky expression 寝言は寝て言え means roughly "Dream on!". Not to be confused with いびき "snoring".

examples[].german: My father's snoring is loud.
My husband snores loudly every night.
I'm told I snore when I'm tired.
en.notes: いびき is snoring. The verb for it is not する but かく: いびきをかく "to snore". Common: いびきがうるさい "the snoring is loud", 大きないびき. The kanji 鼾 is rare; it is almost always written in kana. Quiet breathing in sleep, by contrast, is 寝息.

examples[].german: I dozed off during class.
I dozed off on the train and went past my stop.
Drowsy driving is very dangerous.
en.notes: 居眠り is unintentionally nodding off while sitting, for example in class, on a train, or in a meeting: 授業中に居眠りする. Unlike 昼寝 "nap", which one takes deliberately, 居眠り happens unintentionally. Important compound: 居眠り運転 "falling asleep at the wheel". As a する-verb it is intransitive, also 居眠りをする.

examples[].german: I got sunburned and turned red.
I got a tan at the beach.
I put on sunscreen so I won't get sunburned.
en.notes: 日焼け covers both suntan and sunburn; as a する-verb it is intransitive: 海で日焼けした. Whether brown or red is meant comes from the context (日焼けで赤くなった). Sunscreen is 日焼け止め. Paper, books or tatami that fade in sunlight also 日焼けする. In Japan, great importance is placed on sun protection.

examples[].german: I can't stop yawning.
I'm sleepy and keep yawning.
I yawned during the meeting, and my department head saw me.
en.notes: あくび is a yawn. Typical are あくびが出る "to have to yawn" and あくびをする "to yawn". A suppressed yawn is あくびをかみ殺す. The kanji 欠伸 is rare; it is almost always written in kana. Yawning in front of others, for example in meetings, is considered impolite, as it is for us; you put your hand in front of your mouth.

examples[].german: I have to sneeze.
I can't stop sneezing because of hay fever.
When you sneeze, cover your mouth with a handkerchief.
en.notes: くしゃみ is a sneeze. You say くしゃみが出る "to have to sneeze" or くしゃみをする "to sneeze". Common causes are 風邪 and 花粉症. According to Japanese folk belief, you sneeze when someone is talking about you. The word is written in kana; the kanji spelling 嚔 is not in use.

examples[].german: There was an earthquake yesterday.
There was a big earthquake yesterday.
The window glass broke because of the earthquake.
en.notes: 地震 is the noun for an earthquake. 地震がある or 地震が起こる describes the event; 地震で can introduce its consequence. The identically read 自信 means "self-confidence" and is a different word.

examples[].german: I can't stop hiccupping.
When I drank water, the hiccups stopped.
I laughed so much that I got the hiccups.
en.notes: しゃっくり is the hiccups. Typical: しゃっくりが出る "to get the hiccups", しゃっくりが止まらない "the hiccups won't stop", しゃっくりを止める "to get rid of the hiccups". As a する-verb, it is less common. Home remedies such as drinking water or holding your breath are known in Japan just the same. Always written in kana.

examples[].german: I suffer from lower back pain.
I can't stand up because of lower back pain.
en.notes: 腰痛 means pain in the lower back, that is, in the lumbar region. It is narrower than general back pain. 腰痛に悩む describes a persistent burden; 腰痛で names the pain as the reason for a limitation. The card names the symptom and gives no diagnosis.

examples[].german: I got sore muscles after exercising.
I climbed a mountain for the first time in a long while, so my legs are sore.
They say that as you get older, muscle soreness only comes two days later.
en.notes: 筋肉痛 is, in everyday use, the muscle soreness after sports or unaccustomed exertion. One says 筋肉痛になる, or with a body part 足が筋肉痛だ "my legs are sore". Medically it can also mean muscle pain in general. It is composed of 筋肉 "muscle" and 痛 "pain", like 頭痛 or 腹痛.

examples[].german: I sprained my ankle.
I'll skip soccer practice until the sprain heals.
en.notes: 捻挫 is a sprain. With する it can mean that one has sprained a body part; in the example this is marked with を: 足首を捻挫する. As a noun it can stand for the injury in 捻挫が治る. The card distinguishes a sprain linguistically from a bone fracture, 骨折.

examples[].german: I have a bruise on my arm.
I fell on the stairs and got a bruise.
For a bruise, it helps to put on a cooling patch.
en.notes: 打ち身 is a bruise from a blow or fall, without an open wound: 打ち身ができる. The word is composed of 打つ "to hit" and 身 "body". The medical technical term is 打撲, and the visible bruise mark itself is called あざ. For treatment one cools it and often sticks on a 湿布.

examples[].german: I got a rash from lacquer.
I got a rash from the new cosmetics.
The rash was so bad that I went to a dermatologist.
en.notes: かぶれ is a skin rash as a reaction to something that touched the skin: plants, cosmetics, metal or plasters. More common than the noun is the intransitive verb かぶれる; the cause is marked with に or で: 化粧品でかぶれる. A general rash or eczema is 湿疹. As a suffix, 〜かぶれ means, pejoratively, "enthusiastically influenced by something", e.g. 西洋かぶれ.

examples[].german: I get heat rash in summer.
The baby got heat rash.
The heat rash itches so much that I can't sleep at night.
en.notes: あせも is heat rash, that is, itchy red bumps caused by heavy sweating, especially in babies in summer. Typical: あせもができる, あせもがかゆい. The word is related to 汗 "sweat"; the kanji spelling 汗疹 is rare. Unlike かぶれ, あせも is not caused by contact with a substance but by sweat.

examples[].german: I put a cooling patch on my lower back.
Please peel off the patch before you take a bath.
My shoulders are so stiff that I bought some pain-relief patches at the pharmacy.
en.notes: 湿布 in Japan is above all the medicated pain-relief patch from the pharmacy, cooling (冷湿布) or warming (温湿布). You stick it on with 貼る and peel it off with はがす. Typical uses are 肩こり, back pain, and bruises. For small wounds, 絆創膏 is used instead.

examples[].german: Please put a bandage on it.
I cut my finger and put on a bandage.
Do you have a bandage with you?
en.notes: 絆創膏 is the adhesive bandage for small cuts and wounds. You stick it on with 貼る and peel it off with はがす. Colloquially it is often called by brand names such as バンドエイド or, regionally, カットバン. For pain-relief patches against stiffness, 湿布 is used instead. The difficult kanji mainly need to be recognized when reading.

examples[].german: I do research at a university.
I want to do research at this university.
I explained the research results at the meeting.
en.notes: 研究 refers to the systematic investigation of a topic. As a noun it appears, for example, in 研究の結果; with する it becomes the verb "to research". The research institution can follow with で. For general studying for school or exams, 勉強 is more usual.

examples[].german: I have a mole on my arm.
The mole on my back got bigger, so I had it looked at in the hospital.
The mole next to her mouth is her charm point.
en.notes: ほくろ is a small dark spot on the skin, i.e. a mole or beauty mark: 顔にほくろがある. A ほくろ under the eye is called 泣きぼくろ and is considered attractive. The kanji 黒子 is also read くろこ, so ほくろ is mostly written in kana. Flat pigment spots from age or sun, by contrast, are called しみ, and freckles そばかす.

examples[].german: The freckles are cute.
I get freckles in summer.
I've had freckles around my nose since I was a child.
en.notes: そばかす are freckles, small light-brown spots mainly on the face. One says そばかすがある or, from the sun, そばかすができる / そばかすが出る. Distinction: しみ are larger pigment spots, ほくろ individual dark moles. The word is written in kana; originally it referred to buckwheat chaff, which the spots resemble.

examples[].german: I get dimples when I laugh.
That baby's dimples are very cute.
en.notes: えくぼ is a small dimple, especially on the cheek, that can become visible when smiling. えくぼができる describes its appearance; 人のえくぼ names a person's dimple. The word is often written in hiragana. It refers to a small indentation and not a wrinkle.

examples[].german: My palms are sweating.
Please hold your hand out in front with the palm up.
The snow melted instantly on my palm.
en.notes: 手のひら is the palm of the hand; the back is called 手の甲 "back of the hand". The spellings 手のひら, 手の平 and 掌 exist. Typical: 手のひらに汗をかく "to get sweaty palms", 手のひらを上にする "to turn the palm up". The idiom 手のひらを返す means "to suddenly change one's attitude".

examples[].german: I stand on tiptoe.
These shoes hurt my toes.
It was so cold that my toes got cold.
en.notes: つま先 means the tips of the toes, or the front part of the foot, also of a shoe or sock: 靴のつま先. Typical: つま先で立つ "to stand on tiptoe", つま先立ち. The individual toes are called 足の指, the heel かかと. The spelling 爪先 is also correct.

examples[].german: I'm training my upper arms.
When I wear short sleeves, I'm self-conscious about my upper arms.
A mosquito bit me on the upper arm.
en.notes: 二の腕 is the upper arm between shoulder and elbow. In everyday life the word often comes up in fitness and beauty topics, especially with regard to the soft back side: 二の腕を鍛える, 二の腕が気になる. For "arm" in general one says 腕; medically the upper arm is called 上腕.

examples[].german: My calves are tight.
My calves hurt after running.
In the middle of the night I got a cramp in my calf and woke up.
en.notes: ふくらはぎ is the calf. Common expressions: ふくらはぎが張る "the calves are hard, tense", ふくらはぎがつる "to get a calf cramp". The shin at the front, by contrast, is called すね. The kanji 脹脛 are rare; the word is written in kana.

examples[].german: I sweated under my arms.
With a book tucked under my arm, I went to the library.
I parked my bicycle at the side of the road.
en.notes: 脇 means, first, "armpit", usually as 脇の下 "underarm": 脇の下に汗をかく. Second, it means "side, edge, next to": 道の脇 "roadside", 本を脇に抱える "to tuck a book under one's arm", 脇に置く "to set aside". For "next to", 横 or そば is more common in everyday speech. It is also written わき.

examples[].german: My jaw hurts.
When he thinks, he always puts his hand to his chin.
en.notes: 顎 can refer to the jaw and, on the face, especially the chin. The reading on this card is あご. 顎に手を当てる speaks of putting a hand to the chin; in the case of pain, 顎 can also mean the jaw area depending on the situation. The meaning for a barb on a fishhook is not practiced here.

examples[].german: My cheeks turned red.
The baby's cheeks are plump.
Tears ran down her cheeks.
en.notes: 頬 is the cheek. It has two readings: ほお (standard) and ほほ (also widespread). Colloquially and in child language one says ほっぺ or ほっぺた. Typical: 頬が赤くなる, 涙が頬を流れる, 頬杖をつく "to rest one's chin on one's hand".

examples[].german: I work at a factory.
New products are being made at the factory.
en.notes: 工場 is a factory or production site. It is read こうじょう here; the same spelling also has the reading こうば, which is not automatically equated with this entry. The place of work or production takes で: 工場で働く, 工場で作る.

examples[].german: I'm sleepy and my eyelids are heavy.
I cried a lot, so my eyelids were swollen when I got up in the morning.
I apply eye shadow to my eyelids.
en.notes: 瞼 is the eyelid and is mostly written in kana, まぶた. Common: まぶたが重い "to have heavy lids, to be sleepy", まぶたが腫れる "to have swollen lids". A lid with a crease is 二重まぶた, one without is 一重まぶた - a frequent topic in beauty matters.

examples[].german: I furrow my brow.
When you are tired, pressing the spot between your eyebrows with a finger helps you feel better.
The wrinkle between my eyebrows bothers me.
en.notes: 眉間 is the spot between the eyebrows above the bridge of the nose. An almost fixed phrase: 眉間にしわを寄せる "to knit one's brow, to frown", as a sign of anger, worry or thought. Also 眉間のしわ "frown line". The forehead as a whole is 額 or おでこ, the eyebrow is 眉.

examples[].german: The nape of my neck got sunburned.
When you put your hair up, you can see the nape of your neck.
en.notes: うなじ refers to the nape, especially the back of the neck below the hairline. One can describe that it becomes visible when the hair is put up, or that its skin got sunburned. The word is often written in hiragana. The identically sounding older term for a sea route is a different word.

examples[].german: The shoe rubs against my ankle and it hurts.
I bumped my ankle.
I'm wearing short socks that only reach the ankle.
en.notes: くるぶし is the ankle bone, i.e. the protruding bone on the inside and outside of the ankle joint. The joint itself is called 足首: that is why "to twist one's ankle" is 足首をひねる, not くるぶしをひねる. For socks and trousers, くるぶし serves as a length specification (くるぶし丈). The word is not used for finger knuckles.

examples[].german: I have two hair whorls.
My child's hair whorl is on the right side of the head.
en.notes: つむじ refers to the hair whorl, i.e. the spot where the hair grows in a circular pattern. Such whorls are counted with 一つ・二つ and their position is described with phrases such as 頭の右側など. It refers to the direction of hair growth, not a hairstyle and not a whirlwind.

examples[].german: I have been getting more gray hairs lately.
I can't decide whether to dye my gray hair.
I found a gray hair on my father's head.
en.notes: 白髪 means gray or white hair. In everyday life it is read しらが; the reading はくはつ is literary (白髪の老人). Typical: 白髪が増える, 白髪が生える, 白髪を抜く, 白髪を染める. Hair dye for covering gray hair is called 白髪染め.

examples[].german: I got my bangs cut.
My bangs have grown out and get in my eyes.
If you push your bangs up, the impression changes, doesn't it?
en.notes: 前髪 is the hair at the front that falls onto the forehead, the bangs (fringe). Typical: 前髪を切る, 前髪を伸ばす, 前髪を上げる "to sweep back or put up one's bangs". The counterpart is 後ろ髪 "hair at the back", known from 後ろ髪を引かれる "to find it hard to part". For men, it is more natural to translate it as "the hair at the front".

examples[].german: My split ends bother me.
I went to the hair salon to get my split ends cut.
en.notes: 枝毛 is split ends at the tips of the hair. 枝毛が気になる describes being bothered by split ends; 枝毛を切る means to cut off the split tips. The noun refers to the hair damage, while 美容院 names the hair salon.

examples[].german: My curly hair is a problem for me.
Because of my curls, my hair won't stay in place.
My older sister has curly hair, but mine is straight.
en.notes: くせ毛 (also 癖毛) refers to naturally wavy, curly or unruly hair; 癖 means "peculiarity, habit". It usually means hair that is hard to manage, hence often with 困る or まとまらない. Colloquially one also says 天然パーマ, or 天パ for short. Pretty, intended curls are rather 巻き毛, an artificial perm is パーマ; the opposite is straight hair (ストレート, 直毛).

examples[].german: I had a wisdom tooth pulled.
My wisdom tooth is coming in and it hurts a little.
en.notes: 親知らず means wisdom tooth on this card. 親知らずを抜く describes having such a tooth pulled; 生えてくる its coming through. The expression is often used in conversations about dentist visits. The other dictionary meaning, for unknown biological parents, does not belong to these examples.

examples[].german: We make good products.
The quality of this product is very good.
en.notes: 製品 is a finished manufactured product, especially a good from production. 製品を作る denotes manufacturing; 製品の品質 the quality of the product. The expression fits less well with unprocessed raw materials, for which 原料, for example, is used.

examples[].german: There is a table in the middle of the room.
Please don't stand in the middle of the road.
The one in the middle of the photo is my father.
en.notes: 真ん中 is the exact middle of a space or a row: Xの真ん中に "right in the middle of X", 三人の真ん中. It is more everyday and concrete than 中心 ("center", also abstract: 話の中心) and 中央 (formal, e.g. on signs or in 中央線). Not to be confused with 中 ("in, inside"): 箱の中 is "in the box", 箱の真ん中 "exactly in the middle of the box".

examples[].german: Sales have gradually declined.
Sales increased compared with last month.
The store manager calculates the day's sales every evening.
en.notes: 売り上げ is sales revenue, i.e. the total amount from sales, not the profit (利益). Typical verbs: 売り上げが伸びる/上がる ("to rise"), 売り上げが落ちる/下がる ("to fall"), 売り上げを伸ばす ("to increase"). In business documents, the shortened 売上 or 売上高 is often written; 売り上げ is the usual spelling in running text.

examples[].german: Today's ramen is all sold out.
The tickets are sold out.
"Sold out" is showing on the button of the vending machine.
en.notes: 売り切れ is the noun for the intransitive verb 売り切れる ("to be sold out"): Xは売り切れです, 売り切れになる, attributively 売り切れの商品. On vending machines and signs, 売切 or 売り切れ is often written. The more formal 完売 is used more as a positive success report (チケットは完売しました). Grammatically, 売り切れ is a noun, not an adjective - "to be sold out" is formed with です.

examples[].german: The seller of the camera I bought online was a very kind person.
The seller and the buyer are negotiating.
It's a seller's market right now, so it's easy to find a job.
en.notes: 売り手 is the selling party in a transaction, the counterpart to 買い手 ("buyer"). It is not an occupational title: a shop assistant in a store is called 店員 or 販売員. It is common in 売り手市場 ("seller's market"; in the job market: many jobs, few applicants) and 買い手市場, as well as in online purchases and negotiations.

examples[].german: I was doing volunteer work in Tohoku.
Winters in Tohoku are cold.
en.notes: 東北 here means the Tōhoku region in the north of Japan's main island, Honshū. 東北で marks the place of an activity, 東北の冬 the winter of that region. The same written form can also express the direction northeast; this card and its pronunciation evidence refer to the region name.

en.meaning: resolution; to make up one's mind
examples[].german: I decided to go to Japan.
He made up his mind to quit the company.
I resolved to quit smoking this year for real, but after three days my resolve wavered.
en.notes: 決心 is a firm decision after inner struggle. Typical patterns: 〜と決心する, 〜ことを決心する and 〜決心がつく ("to be able to make up one's mind"), negated 決心がつかない. Other collocations: 決心が固い, 決心が揺らぐ. 決める is neutral for any decision, while 決意 sounds more solemn and stronger and often appears in speeches or written language. For everyday trifles such as choosing a dish, 決心 does not fit.

en.meaning: admission (to a facility); entering; starting a prison term
examples[].german: My grandfather will be admitted to that facility next month.
For applicants, admission is decided after the interview.
He was sent to prison for fraud.
en.notes: 入所 means "to enter or be admitted to an institution (所)": a nursing home (施設に入所する), a daycare (保育所), a research institute (研究所) or an office such as a law firm or talent agency (事務所). It is intransitive: 〜に入所する. For a prison it means "beginning a prison term", and the opposite is then 出所 ("release from prison"); otherwise the opposite is 退所. Other institutions have their own words: 入学 (school), 入社 (company), 入院 (hospital).

en.meaning: first of all; to begin with
examples[].german: First of all, I would like to give a presentation.
First, let's introduce ourselves.
First, please cut the onions.
en.notes: はじめに introduces the first step of a sequence - in speeches, presentations, instructions and recipes: "first of all, to begin with". For this temporal meaning, the spelling 初めに or はじめに is more usual than 始めに; as a heading ("introduction, preface"), it is almost always はじめに. 最初に and まず are more everyday. Note: はじめは means "at first (but later different)": はじめは難しかったが….

examples[].german: Is this lettuce real, by any chance?
This is a real diamond.
Seeing the real Mt. Fuji moved me deeply.
en.notes: 本物 means "the real thing, the original" and is grammatically a noun: attributive 本物の (本物の金), predicative 本物です. The opposite is 偽物 ("fake, imitation"). For true statements one uses 本当 (本当の話), not 本物. Figuratively, 本物 praises real ability: 彼の実力は本物だ ("His ability is the real deal").

examples[].german: I'm preparing for the trip.
The preparations for the party are done.
en.notes: 準備 is preparation. 旅行の準備をする means to make travel preparations; 準備ができる means that everything is ready. With する it can also become a transitive verb: 必要なものを準備する. On this card the noun is the focus. The examples distinguish the act of preparing from the state reached.

examples[].german: Let's go to the festival.
I'm looking forward to the summer festival.
The festival was canceled because of the rain.
en.notes: お祭り refers to a festival, often a local matsuri. The お is part of the polite word form; the plain form is 祭り. Going to the festival is お祭りに行く. The expression can refer to the event visited as well as to an anticipated or canceled festival.

examples[].german: There are many rich people's houses in this area.
That person is famous for being rich.
If I get rich, I want to travel all over the world.
en.notes: 金持ち is a noun ("rich person"); "X is rich" is therefore Xは金持ちです. In conversation the more polite form お金持ち is usually heard; bare 金持ち can sound blunt or even disparaging. The opposite is 貧乏 ("poor"). More formal and written is 裕福 ("wealthy"). Phrases: 金持ちになる ("to get rich"), お金持ちの家.

examples[].german: Please don't fight over me!
Two teams are competing for the championship.
Three people are running against each other in the upcoming election.
en.notes: 争う is intransitive: to quarrel or compete with someone is 〜と争う, the occasion takes で (お金のことで争う), but the prize fought for takes を (優勝を争う, 一位を争う). It sounds more serious and more literary than けんかする, which is used for everyday squabbles among children or friends. Related: 競う ("to vie", fair, sporting), 戦う ("to fight"); noun: 争い.

examples[].german: I have nothing at all in common with Koichi, so I don't know what to talk about.
The two of them have a lot in common.
Japanese and Korean have many things in common.
en.notes: 共通点 is a commonality between people or things: XとYの共通点, (XとYには)共通点がある/ない/多い, 共通点を見つける. The opposite is 違い or, formally, 相違点 ("difference"). 共通 alone means "common" and often stands attributively: 共通の趣味 ("shared hobby"), 共通の友達.

examples[].german: Working together with teammates is fun.
We are carrying out the research jointly.
This apartment building has a shared toilet.
en.notes: 共同 means "joint, communal" and mostly stands as a first element or adverbially: 共同作業 ("collaboration"), 共同研究, 共同で ("jointly"). It also refers to shared use: トイレが共同です ("shared toilet"). The verb 共同する ("to cooperate") is rare; in everyday speech one says 協力する or 一緒にする. Not to be confused with the identically read 協同 (e.g. 協同組合, "cooperative").

examples[].german: I want to become an adult soon.
The dream became reality.
This class consists of twenty students.
en.notes: なる ("to become") is almost always written in kana in everyday use. Connection: nouns and な-adjectives take に (医者になる, 元気になる), い-adjectives take く (寒くなる). The counterpart is する: 〜にする ("to make into, to decide on") versus 〜になる ("to become"). The kanji spelling 成る is seen mainly in 〜から成る ("to consist of", literary).

examples[].german: I wonder what place I'll get this year.
I placed third.
I came in fifth in the marathon.
en.notes: 〜位 is a counter suffix for ranks and placings: 一位, 二位, 三位 (さんい), 何位 (なんい). Typical: 〜位になる, 〜位に入る ("to finish among the top ..."), 〜位を取る. Not to be confused with くらい／ぐらい ("approximately", usually written in kana) and the noun 位 (くらい, "rank, dignity"). In competitions, 〜番 is also said colloquially.

examples[].german: If you take first place, I'll make curry for you every day for a week.
I got first place on the test.
I went to the ramen shop that is number one in the popularity ranking.
en.notes: 一位 is first place in a ranking or competition: 一位になる, 一位を取る, ランキング一位. Colloquially one often says 一番; 首位 is more formal (news, league standings), 優勝 is the overall victory in a tournament. Grammatically 一位 is a noun. With a different meaning, いちい is also the Japanese yew (mostly in kana).

examples[].german: I took first place in the academic achievement test.
The team is in first place.
This book has been at the top of the sales ranking for three weeks.
en.notes: 首位 means "top position, first place" and sounds more formal than 一位 or トップ, typical of sports and business news. Fixed combinations: 首位に立つ ("to move into first place"), 首位を守る ("to defend the lead"), 首位争い ("battle for the top of the table"). In conversation, people usually say 一位 or トップ.

examples[].german: I spend New Year with my family.
My family gets together at New Year.
This shop is also closed at New Year.
en.notes: お正月 denotes New Year, and especially the first days of the new year. The お belongs to the polite word form; 正月 is the plain base. This is about the New Year season, not the further dictionary meaning "January". The expression fits family visits as well as company holidays.

examples[].german: I like men with a deep voice.
The temperature is low today.
en.notes: 低い is an i-adjective: 低くない, 低かった. With 気温 it denotes a low temperature, with 声 a low pitch. A deep voice does not have to be quiet. Before a noun it stands directly: 低い声. 好き names a personal preference here.

examples[].german: That drama was the worst!
The lowest temperature tomorrow is supposed to be three degrees.
I want to sleep at least seven hours a day.
en.notes: 最低 is the opposite of 最高 and has two faces: factual "lowest, minimum" (最低気温, 最低料金) and, as a judgment, "the worst, lousy, unacceptable", very harsh about people: あの人は最低だ. Adverbially, 最低(でも) means "at least". As a な-adjective: 最低な人; the noun 最低限 means "the absolute minimum".

examples[].german: In the first class, we introduce ourselves.
The first time is free.
I couldn't watch the first episode of the drama.
en.notes: 初回 is the first occasion in a series of appointments, episodes or deliveries, typical of service and advertising language: 初回無料, 初回限定 ("first edition only"), 初回の授業, ドラマの初回 ("first episode"). For "to do (something) for the first time", the adverb 初めて is used instead: 初めて来ました, not 初回来ました. The counterpart is 最終回 ("final episode").

examples[].german: Shall we try a different approach?
Excuse me, do you have this in a different color?
I'm busy today, so shall we make it another day?
en.notes: 別の stands before a noun and means "another, a separate": 別の日, 別の方法, 別の人. Unlike ほかの ("other, remaining", more additive: ほかの人も来ます), 別の stresses that it is something different and separate. 違う can also mean "different", but also "wrong" (違う人 = "the wrong person"). Related: 別に (adverb) and 別々.

examples[].german: Could you put the broccoli and the stew in separate containers?
It doesn't particularly bother me.
"What's wrong?" "Nothing really."
en.notes: 別に has two uses. With a negative it means "not particularly, not really": 別に困っていない. Alone as an answer, 「別に。」 means "nothing much, whatever" and can come across as indifferent or curt. Without a negative it means "separately, apart": 別にする, 別に払う. For "each separately" with several parties, 別々に is more usual.

examples[].german: Koichi has become a completely different person since he quit drinking.
With my hair cut, he looks like a different person.
The person in the photo was not my older brother but someone else.
en.notes: 別人 (reading べつじん) is "a different person, someone else". Often figurative for a major change: 別人になる, まるで別人のようだ ("like a different person"). Literally it stands for a person other than the one assumed: 犯人は別人だった. Not to be confused with 他人 ("stranger, unrelated person"); mistaking one person for another is 人違い.

examples[].german: My schedule doesn't match my friend's, so we are going to Hawaii separately.
Separate checks, please.
I wash white and black clothes separately.
en.notes: 別々 means "separately, each on its own" and presupposes several people or things involved. Mostly adverbial: 別々に行く, 別々に払う; attributively 別々の部屋. In a restaurant: お会計は別々で(お願いします) - "separate checks". The opposite is 一緒に. Unlike 別に, 別々に stresses that each part is treated individually.

examples[].german: The brakes on my bicycle don't work.
You have a good nose.
I had a fight with my little brother and haven't spoken a word to him for three days.
en.notes: 利く means "to function, to work (well)" in the sense of an ability: ブレーキが利く, 鼻が利く ("to have a keen nose"), 気が利く ("to be attentive"), 口を利く ("to talk with someone"). To be distinguished from this is 効く for the effect of remedies: 薬が効く, エアコンが効く. Both sound the same and are often simply written in kana as きく; not to be confused with 聞く ("to hear").

examples[].german: The working hours at this job are very long.
Working conditions need to be improved.
Working twelve hours a day is not good for the body.
en.notes: 労働 is "work" as an economic and legal concept (gainful work, labor) and is common mainly in compounds: 労働時間, 労働条件, 労働者, 肉体労働 ("manual labor"). For everyday "to work" one says 働く, for "work, job" 仕事; 労働する sounds stiff and official.

examples[].german: Mr. Koichi, as a company president, what do you think about the labor shortage in Japan?
We protect workers' rights.
Two hundred workers work in this factory.
en.notes: 労働者 is "worker, employee" as an economic and legal concept: 労働者の権利, 外国人労働者, 労働者不足 (ろうどうしゃぶそく, "labor shortage"). In everyday life people rather introduce themselves as 会社員 ("company employee") or say 働く人; 労働者 sounds like newspapers, politics or a trade union. Sense 2 refers specifically to people doing physical work (factory, construction site).

examples[].german: I especially like Japanese food.
There are no particular problems with this plan.
en.notes: 特に highlights something as special: 特に和食が好きです stresses a preference within a larger selection. Before a negated statement it can mean that there is nothing in particular, as in 特に問題はありません. As an adverb it modifies the statement that follows and does not take な.

examples[].german: It was fate that I met you here on that day.
Do you believe in fate?
That accident changed his destiny.
en.notes: 運命 is fate, felt to be predetermined: 運命を信じる, 運命を変える, 運命の人 ("the one, the right person"), 運命的な出会い ("a fateful encounter"). It should be distinguished from 運 ("luck, chance"): 運がいい means "to be lucky", not "to have a good fate". 宿命 sounds even more inescapable and is literary.

en.meaning: to open up; to leave open; to make accessible
examples[].german: In the evening, we open our office as a bar.
Let's open the windows and let in some air.
During summer vacation, the school pool is open to the children.
en.notes: 開放する is transitive: Xを開放する - to leave something open or make it accessible to others (校庭を市民に開放する, 窓を開放する). For the everyday opening of a door or window, 開ける is enough; 開放 stresses keeping something open or releasing it for use. Beware of the identically read 解放する ("to free", e.g. hostages or stress). Also: 開放的 ("open, open-minded").

examples[].german: I ordered ramen.
At this shop you can order with a smartphone.
That customer always has lots of special requests.
en.notes: 注文する is transitive: Xを注文する ("to order X") at a restaurant, in a shop or online (ネットで注文する). Waiters ask ご注文は？ or ご注文はお決まりですか. When eating, one colloquially also says 頼む; a reservation, by contrast, is 予約. Sense 2: 注文 as "request, demand", e.g. 注文が多い ("to be demanding, picky").

examples[].german: If everyone concentrates, this work should be finished by five o'clock.
I can't concentrate on studying.
The population is concentrated in Tokyo.
en.notes: 集中する means "to concentrate" and is mostly intransitive with に: 勉強に集中する. Adverbially: 集中して勉強する ("to study with concentration"). Transitive use is possible when bringing something together: 気持ちを集中する. It also means "to be concentrated, to gather": 人口が都市に集中する. Related: 集中力 ("ability to concentrate").

examples[].german: The customer specified the place for the meeting.
Please specify the date and time.
I reserved a reserved seat on the Shinkansen.
en.notes: 指定する means "to specify, to state, to designate" - usually the place, time or kind of something: 日時を指定する, 指定された場所. It sounds matter-of-fact and is often encountered in forms, online orders (配達日時指定) and instructions. Known from 指定席 ("reserved seat") as opposed to 自由席. General "to decide" is 決める.

examples[].german: It's important to check the size before buying clothes.
I bought new clothes.
en.notes: 洋服 denotes Western-style clothing, as opposed to 和服 such as a kimono. With を you name the clothing bought. 買う前に means "before buying"; the dictionary form 買う precedes it. サイズをチェックする checks the size with a single を. ようふく has a long o.

examples[].german: This house has three small Western-style rooms.
This hotel has Western-style and Japanese-style rooms.
My room is Western-style, with a bed and a desk.
en.notes: 洋室 is a Western-style room with wooden or carpeted floor, a bed, and doors, in contrast to the 和室 with tatami, futon, and sliding doors. The word is ubiquitous in apartment listings (洋室6畳) and hotel bookings. 洋 stands for "Western" as in 洋服 and 洋食.

examples[].german: I sent Koichi a LINE message and got a reply in seconds, lol.
Please wait another thirty seconds.
en.notes: 秒 is the unit of time "second" and follows a number directly in quantities: 三十秒, thirty seconds. It is a noun with a counting function. 秒で is also used in casual messages as an exaggeration for "instantly". The final w in the first example is a written laughter mark; it is not part of the spoken pronunciation of the sentence.

examples[].german: Next week I move up from the beginner to the intermediate level.
I joined a beginner class.
This book is intended for beginner-level learners.
en.notes: 初級 is the beginner level in the series 初級・中級・上級 - in language courses, textbooks, exams or sports. It is used as a noun with の or as the first element: 初級クラス, 初級の文法. A person at that level is a 初級者; 初心者 is more general, "newcomer" (also in driving or hobbies). Grammatically, 初級 is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: What kind of level is intermediate?
I moved up to the intermediate level.
The intermediate ski course was a little difficult.
en.notes: 中級 is the middle level between 初級 and 上級, in language courses, exams, ski slopes or cooking classes. It is used as a noun with の or as the first element of a compound: 中級クラス, 中級者 ("intermediate-level learner"). Grammatically it is a noun. Not to be confused with 中学 ("middle school").

examples[].german: Please be sure to come.
Be sure to do your homework.
This bus always stops in front of the station.
en.notes: 必ず is an adverb meaning "without exception" or "in any case". In a request it strengthens the obligation: 必ず来てください. In a statement it describes something that reliably always happens. It is used directly with the verb and takes no に.

examples[].german: I just can't keep up with the advanced class.
I am taking the advanced exam.
My older sister is an advanced tennis player.
en.notes: 上級 is the highest level in 初級・中級・上級: 上級クラス, 上級の試験, 上級者 ("advanced learner, expert"). Outside courses, it also means "higher-ranking": 上級生 ("student in a higher grade") as opposed to 下級生. For people who are very good at something, 上手な人 or ベテラン is also used.

examples[].german: The police are chasing the culprit.
I will keep pursuing my dream.
I am hounded by work every day.
en.notes: 追う is transitive: Xを追う, to go after someone or pursue something (犯人を追う), also figuratively: 夢を追う, 流行を追う. For physically running after, 追いかける is more everyday. In the passive, 〜に追われる means "to be driven by something": 仕事に追われる. Related: 追いつく ("to catch up"), 追い越す ("to overtake").

examples[].german: Dad always loses his battles with Mom.
The long battle is over.
The fight against the illness lasted a year.
en.notes: 戦い is the noun of 戦う: battle and war, but also competition and figurative struggle (時間との戦い). Typical: 〜との戦い, 戦いに勝つ/負ける. For the fight against illness or poverty it is also written 闘い. A war as a whole is 戦争, an everyday quarrel けんか.

examples[].german: I made a plan for tomorrow's game.
Our surprise plan for Mom's birthday was a great success.
I started a diet plan for losing weight by summer.
en.notes: 作戦 is a tactic or a concrete plan for reaching a goal: 作戦を立てる ("to work out a tactic"), 作戦を変える, 作戦が成功する. Originally military ("operation"), in everyday life it is often used jokingly: ダイエット作戦, サプライズ作戦. A long-term overall strategy is more often 戦略, and a general plan is 計画.

examples[].german: Why is a tank driving around in a place like this?
I saw a tank at the museum.
My younger brother likes building tank models.
en.notes: 戦車 is a tank (tracked military vehicle); historically also the war chariot. It is counted with 台 or 両. One says 戦車に乗る, 戦車が走る. The word is composed of 戦 ("battle") and 車 ("vehicle"); the English "tank" as タンク, by contrast, usually means a container in Japanese.

examples[].german: Sorry. I'm on the battlefield right now, so I can't answer the phone.
A battlefield is a dangerous place.
At lunchtime, this restaurant's kitchen is a real battlefield.
en.notes: 戦場 is the battlefield. In everyday speech it is often used figuratively for a hectic place: 昼の台所はまるで戦場だ ("the kitchen at noon is a real battlefield"). Typical combinations: 戦場に行く, 戦場で戦う. Not to be confused with 会場 ("venue") or 工場 ("factory"), which can also end in 〜じょう.

examples[].german: I have no intention of competing with you at chess.
I compete against athletes from all over the world.
The two are competing for the best grades in the class.
