en.notes: 競う is intransitive and means "to compete, to vie": 〜と競う (with someone), 〜で競う (in a discipline), 〜を競う (for something: 速さを競う). It sounds rather literary and has a sporting, fair-play connotation. In conversation 競争する is more common; 争う, by contrast, stresses quarrel or fierce rivalry.

examples[].german: Oh no. I came to school wearing toilet slippers!
My grandfather still calls the toilet 「便所」.
In old houses, the toilet was outside.
en.notes: 便所 is an old-fashioned, crude word for toilet - today mostly heard from older men or in fixed expressions such as 便所サンダル ("plastic slippers"). The neutral word is トイレ, the polite one is お手洗い, and the very formal one is 化粧室. In polite speech (あちらです), 便所 therefore does not fit.

en.meaning: bargain sale; discount sale; to sell cheap
examples[].german: That supermarket over there is having a tomato sale this week.
The supermarket is having a sale.
Please don't sell yourself short.
en.notes: 安売り is selling at low prices: 安売りをする, 安売りの店, 大安売り ("big clearance sale"). As a する-verb it is transitive: 野菜を安売りする. Similar are 特売 (supermarket special offer) and セール. Figuratively, 自分を安売りする means "to sell oneself short", and 〜を安売りしない means "not to treat something lightly".

en.meaning: revenge; retaliation; getting back at someone
examples[].german: It's annoying; I want to get back at them somehow.
Revenge is not good.
In retaliation for having his toy taken, the younger brother ate his older brother's sweets.
en.notes: 仕返し is retaliation or revenge for wrongs suffered; as a する-verb, the person takes に: 相手に仕返しする. Common are 〜の仕返しに ("as revenge for ...") and 仕返しを恐れる. 仕返し sounds everyday and can also be childishly harmless, whereas 復讐 is serious, often bloody revenge and more literary; colloquially there is also やり返す. The rare meaning "to do something over again" hardly occurs in modern Japanese.

examples[].german: I will never forget.
Please don't be late under any circumstances.
en.notes: 絶対に strengthens a statement: "for sure" or "under no circumstances". With a negative such as 忘れません, it means "by no means". Before a request it can sound very emphatic; the two examples involve a firm promise and a strict prohibition.

en.meaning: to return; to turn over, fold back
examples[].german: I will stay at the office until an email comes back.
It has returned to its original state.
While I was walking, the hem of my trousers folded back.
en.notes: 返る／かえる describes here a return or the return to a former state. For turning over or folding back, the spelling 反る with this reading is also attested, for instance for a folded-back hem. This is an intransitive process: 裾が反る. The reading そる of 反る, by contrast, refers to bending or curving and is learned separately. かえる is a godan verb: かえります, かえって, かえった. The transitive 返す means to give something back or to turn it over.

examples[].german: Where is the gondola station?
Where is the taxi stand?
The bus to the airport leaves from stop number 3.
en.notes: 乗り場 is the place where you board a means of transport: バス乗り場, タクシー乗り場, 〜番乗り場 ("stop/platform no. ..."), also for ferries and cable cars. A bus stop along the route is more often バス停 or 停留所; the platform in a train station is ホーム. The counterpart is 降り場 ("drop-off point").

examples[].german: I don't think you are a loser.
I don't want to be a loser.
Complaining after the game is just the howling of a loser.
en.notes: 負け犬 ("beaten dog") is a derogatory word for a loser or failure. Well known is the saying 負け犬の遠吠え, the "howling of a beaten dog", i.e. complaining after a defeat. In the 2000s it was also used as slang for older unmarried women without children (now felt to be insulting). Neutral is 負けた人, formal 敗者.

examples[].german: Today's game was won by the Japanese team.
I win at rock-paper-scissors!
Whoever arrives first wins.
en.notes: 勝ち is the noun of 勝つ and appears mainly in the form Xの勝ち ("X has won"): 日本チームの勝ち, 私の勝ち！ The opposite is 負け; 勝ち負け means "victory or defeat". 勝利 is more formal (news, speeches). Expressions like 早い者勝ち ("first come, first served") show the pattern "... wins".

examples[].german: Viet, your hairstyle looks a bit delinquent today.
The product had a defect.
I stayed home from work because I wasn't feeling well.
en.notes: 不良 has two meanings. First, "defective, faulty, bad" - almost only in compounds: 不良品 ("defective goods"), 体調不良 ("feeling unwell"), 消化不良. Second, "hoodlum, delinquent": 不良少年, 不良っぽい ("delinquent-looking"). For general "bad", you say 悪い; 不良 does not fit weather or food.

examples[].german: This blanket feels nice.
The massage feels good.
The breeze is pleasant today, isn't it?
en.notes: 気持ちいい describes a pleasant physical feeling or a refreshing mood: 風が気持ちいい, お風呂が気持ちいい. It conjugates like いい: 気持ちよかった, 気持ちよくない. Before nouns people often say 気持ちのいい朝. The opposite 気持ち悪い means "disgusting" or "I feel sick". For enjoyment of activities, 楽しい is used instead.

examples[].german: Try this supplement.
I'll try a new recipe.
I wanted to test my abilities, so I took the exam.
en.notes: 試す is transitive: Xを試す, to try something out or put it to the test (新しい方法を試す, 自分の力を試す). For "to try doing something" one mostly uses the form 〜てみる; the two are often combined: 試してみる. Trying on clothes is 試着する. Also: 試しに ("on a trial basis").

examples[].german: There are only two months left until the entrance exam.
I'm studying for the entrance exam.
My older brother passed the university entrance exam.
en.notes: 入学試験 is the entrance exam of a school or university, often abbreviated 入試 (大学入試). Typical verbs: 入学試験を受ける ("to take"), 入学試験に合格する ("to pass"), 入学試験に落ちる ("to fail"). For companies it is 入社試験; a final exam is 卒業試験.

examples[].german: That's correct!
The correct answer is number three.
It was the right call to bring an umbrella.
en.notes: 正解 is a noun: "the correct answer, the right solution". Typical are 正解は〜です, the quiz exclamation 正解！ and the opposite 不正解 "wrong". As a する-verb, 問題に正解する means "to answer a question correctly". Colloquially, 〜て正解だった means "it was the right decision to ...". Do not confuse it with the adjective 正しい "right, correct", which stands before nouns (正しい答え).

examples[].german: This spoon comes with a case.
I booked a hotel with breakfast.
en.notes: 〜付き here means "equipped with ..." or "including ...". The component in question stands directly before it: ケース付き, 朝食付き. When the whole combination describes another noun, の follows, as in 朝食付きのホテル. The sign 〜 is an unspoken placeholder. This card practices this attached component, not the identically written verb form of 付く or ツキ in the sense of "luck".

examples[].german: Japanese is difficult after all.
Japanese is difficult after all, isn't it?
As forecast, it did rain after all.
en.notes: やはり means "as expected" or "after all / in the end". It often connects the statement with an earlier assumption or a reconfirmed judgment. やっぱり is the common colloquial form. やはり is an adverb here, not a form of the verb やはる.

examples[].german: Is the year-end Jumbo lottery still on sale?
A new game is on sale.
This book is on sale at bookstores nationwide.
en.notes: 発売中 is composed of 発売 "market launch, start of sales" and the suffix 〜中 "in progress", and means "(newly) on the market, available now". It appears mainly on posters, in advertising and in announcements, often as the set phrase 好評発売中 "now available - in great demand". Before a noun it is 発売中の: 発売中の雑誌. Caution: 発売中 does not mean "on special offer, discounted"; for that one says セール中 or 安売り.

examples[].german: Yasuda-san, please bring some food.
Japanese food is delicious.
en.notes: 食べ物 denotes food or something edible. 食べ物を持って来る means to bring food; 持って来てください asks for it. 日本の食べ物 uses の to link the food and its origin. Unlike 食事, 食べ物 denotes the edible thing, not the act or occasion of a meal.

examples[].german: It is neither too big nor too small; it's really just the right size.
The bath water is just right.
Perfect timing. I was just thinking of calling you now.
en.notes: ちょうどいい means "just right, fitting" for size, temperature, amount or timing. It is mostly written in kana; the kanji spelling 丁度いい is less common. It conjugates like いい via よい: ちょうどよかった, ちょうどよくない. ちょうどよかった is also a common reaction, "Perfect timing!", when someone shows up at just the right moment. Similar is ぴったり "a perfect fit", which stresses the exact fit.

en.meaning: to maintain; to retain; to hold
examples[].german: I'm worried whether I can maintain a high level of Japanese if I go to America.
I exercise in order to maintain my health.
That athlete still holds the Japanese record in the 100-meter dash.
en.notes: 保持する means "to keep something, to preserve (in a certain state)" and is a transitive, rather literary する-verb: 記録を保持する, 能力を保持する, 健康を保持する. In conversation 保つ is more natural; for maintaining a level or state one also says 維持する (日本語力を維持する). Common compounds: 記録保持者 ("record holder"), 秘密保持 ("confidentiality").

examples[].german: What, you commute from Tokyo to Kyushu every day?
I commute to work by train every day.
When I was a child, I went to piano lessons regularly.
en.notes: 通う is intransitive and means "to go somewhere regularly", to school, to work, to the hospital, to the gym. The destination is marked with に: 学校に通う, ジムに通う; the means of transport with で. Unlike 行く, 通う stresses repeated, habitual back-and-forth travel, which is why it is mostly used in the ている form. Related nouns are 通勤 "commuting to work" and 通学 "commuting to school".

examples[].german: In middle school, I was in the volleyball club.
I work in the sales department.
Please make three copies of these materials.
en.notes: 〜部 is a suffix after nouns. In companies, it denotes a department (営業部 "sales", 人事部 "personnel department"); 部 is bigger than 課. In schools and universities, it is the club: 野球部, テニス部, and the activity is called 部活. After numbers, 部 counts copies of documents or newspapers: 一部, 三部. As a noun on its own, 部 also means "part" (第一部 "Part 1").

examples[].german: We're having a barbecue on the rooftop today.
The view from the rooftop of the building is beautiful.
There was a small amusement park on the roof of the department store.
en.notes: 屋上 is the walkable flat roof of a building, for example at schools, department stores or office buildings. One says 屋上で (place of action), 屋上に上がる "to go up on the roof" and 屋上から "from the roof". The sloped tile roof or house roof, by contrast, is 屋根; you normally don't stand on a 屋根.

examples[].german: Yoga is indispensable in my daily life.
I never skip breakfast.
My grandfather has never missed his morning walk even for a single day.
en.notes: 欠かす (transitive) means "to omit, to neglect" and occurs almost only in the negative. 欠かさず means "without exception, regularly" (毎日欠かさず運動する), and the potential form 欠かせない means "indispensable" (X に欠かせない). The intransitive counterpart is 欠ける "to be lacking, to chip"; 欠く is the more literary form with a similar meaning.

examples[].german: I'm looking forward to seeing the old town.
Let's go and watch the festival.
We watched the fireworks with the family.
en.notes: 見物 (見物する) means "to look at something as a spectator": sights, festivals, fireworks or sporting events: X を見物する, X を見物に行く. The spectators are 見物人. To be distinguished are 観光 "tourism, traveling to see sights" and 見学 "a visit for learning" (factory, school). With the reading みもの, the same kanji word means "something worth seeing".

examples[].german: Can you read hiragana?
Let's learn hiragana first.
Please write your name in hiragana.
en.notes: 平仮名 is the rounded Japanese syllabary used for particles, verb endings and many native words. The word itself is almost always written in kana: ひらがな. The angular script for loanwords is カタカナ; both together are 仮名 (かな). Typical: ひらがなで書く "to write in hiragana"; the small reading aids above kanji are called ふりがな.

en.meaning: quite; (with negative) not easily; not readily
examples[].german: You're quite good, aren't you?
The bus just won't come.
en.notes: なかなか has two important patterns. With a positive evaluation it means "quite" or "surprisingly good": なかなか上手. With a negation it shows that something does not happen easily or soon despite expectations: なかなか来ません means that the bus just won't come.

examples[].german: This child is literally a "genius".
It is not meant literally.
Because of the heavy snow, the town literally turned white.
en.notes: 文字通り means "literally, word for word". As an adverb it stands directly before the predicate (文字通り真っ白); before nouns it is 文字通りの (文字通りの意味 "the literal meaning"). It is often used to stress that a strong expression is actually true; the word is then often put in 「」. It sounds somewhat more literary than the everyday 本当に.

examples[].german: I made a video teaching the basics of how to use a computer.
I will start learning from the basics.
That's a beginner's mistake, isn't it.
en.notes: 初歩 is a noun for the "first steps, the rudiments" of a subject: 初歩から学ぶ "to learn from the basics", 初歩の日本語. Very common is the na-adjective 初歩的 "elementary, beginner-like", e.g. 初歩的なミス "beginner's mistake". Similar are 基本 "basics (which always remain important)" and 基礎 "foundation"; 初歩, by contrast, stresses the beginner level.

examples[].german: If you level up, you can reach a new stage.
I'm starting a new challenge.
A new supermarket has opened in front of the station.
en.notes: 新た is a na-adjective with a literary tone: 新たな + noun "new, fresh" and adverbially 新たに "newly, anew". It is used mainly with abstract things like challenge, problem or beginning (新たな問題, 新たな一歩) and is common in the news. For concrete everyday objects (new shoes, a new phone) one says 新しい. Set phrase: 気持ちを新たにする "to start afresh, to renew one's motivation".

examples[].german: I have never been to a Western country.
I studied Western culture.
At this restaurant you can also eat Western food.
en.notes: 西洋 means "the West, the Occident" (Europe and North America) and is the counterpart of 東洋 "the Orient, East Asia". It is mostly used with の or in compounds: 西洋の文化, 西洋人, 西洋料理, 西洋風. In everyday speech today, people often say 欧米 "Europe and America" or simply 海外. The short character 洋 appears in 洋食 and 洋服.

examples[].german: A positive mindset is important in everything, isn't it?
I have a happy feeling.
en.notes: 心持ち refers to an inner feeling, a mood, or the attitude with which one approaches something. ポジティブな心持ち concerns the attitude toward a task, 嬉しい心持ち the joyful feeling. The adverbial use meaning "a little", which is also possible, is not meant here.

examples[].german: That's a magnificent tree.
It was a superb performance.
The weather forecast was completely wrong.
en.notes: 見事 is a na-adjective: 見事な "splendid, magnificent, masterly" (見事な桜, 見事な演技). Adverbially, 見事に means "perfectly, skillfully" - often also ironically for a complete failure: 見事に失敗した "failed thoroughly". As praise one calls out お見事！ "Bravo!". Compared with すばらしい, 見事 emphasizes craftsmanship or an impressive sight.

examples[].german: I borrowed a biology book from the library.
I am majoring in biology at university.
My older brother does research in biology.
en.notes: 生物学 is the science "biology"; 〜学 forms names of academic fields (数学, 経済学). At school the subject is usually just called 生物; 生物学 sounds like university and research. A biologist is a 生物学者. Typical combinations: 生物学を勉強する, 大学で生物学を専攻する.

examples[].german: Have you read that pitcher's biography?
I read a biography of a famous scientist.
I would like to write a biography of my grandfather.
en.notes: 伝記 is a "biography, life story", usually as a book about a famous person: 〜の伝記を読む/書く. An autobiography is 自伝, and a biographical film is 伝記映画. Beware when listening: 伝記 sounds exactly like 電気 "electricity, light" - context decides.

examples[].german: I rolled a stone.
We play by rolling the ball around.
Please roll the dice.
en.notes: 転がす is transitive: "to roll something, make it roll" - a ball, a stone, dice (サイコロを転がす) or a rolling suitcase. The intransitive counterpart is 転がる "to roll" (ボールが転がる). Do not confuse it with 転ぶ "to fall down, tumble", which is used only for people and animals.

examples[].german: It's about time to go.
It's about time to head home.
The train should be coming soon.
en.notes: そろそろ can announce that something will happen soon, or say that it is gradually time for an action. そろそろ帰りましょう therefore means "We should be heading home soon". In these sentences it describes the right moment; the dictionary meaning "carefully / slowly forward" is a different use.

examples[].german: Please go ahead and continue with the interview.
Let's move the plan forward.
I set the clock ahead by five minutes.
en.notes: 進める is transitive: "to move forward, to carry on" - 計画を進める, 仕事を進める, 話を進める. Literally also "to move forward", e.g. 時計を進める "to set a clock ahead". The intransitive counterpart is 進む "to advance, to progress" (仕事が進む). Read the same but with a different meaning: 勧める "to recommend, to advise".

en.meaning: to lack; to be wanting in; to chip
examples[].german: I think a diet of only bananas lacks balance.
Behavior lacking in courtesy is not good.
I dropped the plate and chipped its rim.
en.notes: 欠く is transitive and rather literary. It means "to lack, to not have" (バランスを欠く, 常識を欠く) and concretely "to chip off a corner" (皿を欠く). In everyday speech one more often hears the intransitive 欠ける "to be missing, to chip" (お皿が欠けた) or the phrase 欠かせない "indispensable" from 欠かす. Caution: read the same as 書く "to write".

examples[].german: That Italian restaurant closed after only one generation.
My grandfather built this company up to a large one within his own lifetime.
en.notes: 一代 means "one generation, one human life" in the sense of one's own lifetime or period of activity. Typical is 一代で "within a single generation, by one's own efforts", for example when someone builds up a company on their own. The founding generation is 初代, the following ones 二代目, 三代目. For a generation as an age group (the young generation), 世代 is used instead.

examples[].german: Please go straight to the entrance.
I'm going straight to the airport.
I flew from Narita to Paris on a direct flight.
en.notes: 直行 (直行する) means "to go directly, without a stopover"; the destination is marked with に: 空港に直行する. Very common is 直行便 "direct flight, direct service". In office language there is also 直行 "going directly to a client instead of to the office" and 直帰 "going directly home". More colloquially, one says まっすぐ行く.

examples[].german: I think those two are only pretending to be good friends and actually don't get along.
Those two are good friends.
en.notes: 仲良し refers to a good friend or a friendly relationship. 二人は仲良しです means that two people are good friends. Before another noun, の is used here: 仲良しのふり, pretending to be friends. This card covers the friendship meaning, not the euphemistic use of 仲良しする.

examples[].german: I hope that someday I can build a warm family.
We speak Japanese at home.
en.notes: 家庭 is a noun for the family or the home as a domestic sphere of life. 家庭の connects it to a noun; 家庭で names the domestic setting of an activity. 温かい家庭 figuratively means a warm, loving family. 作れたら expresses here the hoped-for possibility of building such a family.

examples[].german: My son is doing well.
My son is getting married next month.
How old is your son?
en.notes: 息子 is one's own son when talking about one's own family. For someone else's son one politely says 息子さん, very formally ご子息. The counterpart is 娘 "daughter" or 娘さん. Small children are often simply called 子ども or by name in daily life.

examples[].german: My father and I share the same basic way of thinking.
Let's rethink it from the ground up.
We have to solve this problem fundamentally.
en.notes: 根本 means "root, foundation, the fundamental part" of something. Common are 根本から "from the ground up", 根本の考え方, and above all the na-adjective 根本的 "fundamental", or adverbially 根本的に. 基本 "basis, basics" is similar but refers more to basic rules. With the reading ねもと, 根本 (also written 根元) denotes the lower part of a tree or object.

examples[].german: I will really do my best.
Eat properly!
Please hold the handrail firmly.
en.notes: しっかり refers to something firm or to a thorough, sufficient action. 手すりをしっかり握る means "to grip the handrail firmly"; しっかり食べる means "to eat properly / enough". It stands before the verb as an adverb and can also emphatically urge careful action.

en.meaning: to let flow; to flush; to play (music)
examples[].german: Please flush the toilet after use.
I shed tears watching the sad movie.
Quiet music is always playing in the shop.
en.notes: 流す is transitive: "to let flow". In everyday life, トイレの水を流す means "to flush the toilet"; also 涙を流す "to shed tears", 汗を流す "to sweat; to work hard" and 音楽を流す "to play music". The intransitive counterpart is 流れる "to flow, to be playing" (水が流れる, 音楽が流れる). As a suffix, 〜流す means "to do in passing, without attention": 聞き流す "to let go in one ear and out the other".

examples[].german: As expected, a first-rate pianist is something else.
I ate at a first-class restaurant.
My older brother works at a top company.
en.notes: 一流 means "first-class, top-" and usually appears as 一流の before nouns: 一流のホテル, 一流企業, 一流大学. The lower grades 二流 and 三流 mean "second-rate" and "third-rate" and sound derogatory; at the very top is 超一流 "absolute world class". An advanced use is 彼一流の… "typical of him".

examples[].german: Apparently the water in the main stream of the Amazon is brown.
The main stream of the river is deep.
This small river joins the main stream farther ahead.
en.notes: 本流 is the "main stream" of a river as opposed to its tributaries (支流). Figuratively it also means the "main direction, mainstream" of a school of thought or party; but this sounds literary. For "mainstream" in everyday speech, one rather says 主流. The word has nothing to do with 本 "book"; here 本 means "main".

examples[].german: I want to increase sales to five times last year's by the end of the year.
The price doubled.
This room is about three times as large as my room.
en.notes: 〜倍 is a counter for multiples: 二倍 "double", 三倍 "triple", 十倍 "tenfold". Typical patterns are X の三倍 "three times as much as X", 〜倍になる "to become x times as much" and 〜倍にする "to multiply by x". Used alone, 倍 already means "double" (値段が倍になった). Note: "twice" in the sense of frequency is 二回 or 二度, not 二倍.

examples[].german: I drank coffee from a cup twice the size of my usual one.
It sold twice as much as last year.
This juice has double the amount, but the price is the same.
en.notes: 二倍 means "double, twice as much". The comparison is made with の: いつもの二倍 "twice as much as usual"; before nouns it is 二倍の (二倍の量). With なる/する it expresses doubling: 二倍になる, 二倍にする. In conversation people often say simply 倍. Not to be confused with 二回 "twice (frequency)".

examples[].german: All of the band members are men.
Has everyone gathered?
We went on a trip with the whole family.
en.notes: 全員 means "all (members of a group)" and applies only to people. Typical are 全員が, 全員で "all together" and combinations like 家族全員, クラス全員. It can also stand adverbially without a particle (全員集まりました). In casual conversation one often says みんな; for things one uses 全部.

examples[].german: A new employee joined the company the other day.
I'm not an employee of this company. I'm a part-timer.
The company cafeteria is cheap and good.
en.notes: 社員 is an "employee, staff member" of a particular company: この会社の社員, 新入社員 "new employee", 正社員 "full-time employee" as opposed to アルバイト or パート. When stating your occupation in general, 会社員です is used instead. Set compounds are 社員食堂 "cafeteria" and 社員旅行 "company trip".

examples[].german: Hiroshima is famous for oysters.
I went to the Peace Memorial Park in Hiroshima.
Have you ever eaten Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki?
en.notes: 広島 is a major city and prefecture in the west of Honshū (広島市, 広島県). It is known for the Peace Memorial Park, the Atomic Bomb Dome (原爆ドーム), oysters (カキ) and Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki (広島風お好み焼き). In reference to the atomic bombing, the name is sometimes written in katakana, ヒロシマ.

examples[].german: Please put your own safety first.
Safety first.
I can't go on the trip. For one thing, I have no money.
en.notes: 第一 is first of all a noun: "the first thing, the most important thing". After a noun, 〜第一 expresses top priority (安全第一 "safety first", 健康第一). 第一に means "in the first place, first of all". At the beginning of a sentence, 第一、… works as an adverb "for one thing, to begin with" when adding another, decisive argument.

en.meaning: as much as possible; as ... as possible
examples[].german: Please come as soon as possible.
I try to eat as many vegetables as possible.
en.notes: できるだけ pushes an action to the limit of what is possible: "as ... as possible". A manner or quantity can follow, for example できるだけ早く for the greatest possible speed. In できるだけ野菜を食べる the target amount is meant; the phrase does not guarantee that the goal is fully achieved.

examples[].german: This work took first place in the essay contest.
Our shop took first place in sales this month.
This song is number one in the popularity ranking.
en.notes: 第一位 is "first place" in a ranking or competition: 第一位になる "to become number one", 〜で第一位 "first place in ...". In conversation people usually say the shorter 一位, likewise 二位, 三位. The prefix 第 turns the number into an ordinal and sounds somewhat more official.

examples[].german: My address is in Shinjuku Ward, Tokyo.
I live in Tokyo.
The Tokyo Metropolis has a population of about 14 million.
en.notes: 東京都 is the administrative unit "Tokyo Metropolis". 都 is a type of prefecture of its own next to 道 (北海道), 府 (大阪府, 京都府) and 県, and there is only one 都. 東京都 is used in addresses, forms and official language (都知事, 都庁); in everyday speech people simply say 東京.

examples[].german: Kyoto used to be the capital of Japan.
There are beautiful gardens in Kyoto.
It takes about two hours from Tokyo to Kyoto by Shinkansen.
en.notes: 京都 is both a city and a prefecture (京都市, 京都府) and was Japan's capital from 794 until the beginning of the Meiji period (1868/69). It is known for temples, shrines, gardens and traditional districts. The kanji 都 means "capital"; 東京 literally means "eastern capital". Typical: 京都に行く, 京都駅, 京都の人.

en.meaning: to move; to work; to run
examples[].german: Something moved over there.
The clock isn't running.
I'm going to take a photo, so please don't move.
en.notes: 動く is intransitive: "to move", and for machines "to run, to work" (時計が動かない "the clock isn't running", 電車が動いていない "the trains aren't running"). Figuratively it also means "to act, to become active". The transitive counterpart is 動かす "to move, to set in motion" (机を動かす). For "to move house", one does not say 動く but 引っ越す.

examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka had great success in business.
Business is going well.
My older brother started a new business in Tokyo.
en.notes: 商売 is "trade, business" in the sense of buying and selling, often for small shops and self-employed people: 商売をする, 商売を始める, 商売がうまくいく. 商売繁盛 is the wish for "a thriving business". Colloquially 商売 can also mean "occupation, job" (商売道具 "tools of the trade"). For companies and industries, ビジネス or 事業 sound more modern.

examples[].german: This used to be a merchant's house.
Merchants of the past traveled by ship.
Osaka merchants are said to be good talkers.
en.notes: 商人 is a "merchant, trader" and often sounds historical, for instance for merchants of the Edo period or the proverbial 大阪商人. For today's businesspeople one rather says 商売人, ビジネスマン or 店の人. Easily confused when listening: 証人 "witness" is read the same way, and 職人 is a "craftsman".

examples[].german: He's a villain, but also a gardening pro who loves flowers.
The villain in the movie was scary.
He is not a bad person. He just has a bit of a sharp tongue.
en.notes: 悪人 is a "bad person, villain" and sounds somewhat literary or like stories and films. In everyday speech people mostly say 悪い人. The opposite is 善人 "good person". The villain role in film or theater is 悪役.

examples[].german: That wicked woman has good ears, at least.
The wicked woman in this drama is interesting.
The protagonist of that novel is a femme fatale who deceives men.
en.notes: 悪女 refers to a "wicked, scheming woman", often in the sense of a femme fatale in novels, dramas and gossip. Used of real people, it is a strong insult. The gender-neutral word is 悪人. The old secondary meaning "ugly woman" is hardly used today.

examples[].german: Today was the worst day.
I lost my wallet. Ugh, the worst!
In the worst case, we can just walk home.
en.notes: 最悪 means "the worst" and is the opposite of 最高. Before nouns it is 最悪の or, colloquially, 最悪な (最悪の場合 "in the worst case"). As an exclamation, 最悪！ means "Damn! Terrible!" and is very colloquial. At the start of a sentence, 最悪 can work adverbially as "at worst".

en.meaning: late at night; dead of night
examples[].german: What's the matter, at this hour of the night?
I worked until late at night.
I'm going to Osaka by night bus.
en.notes: 深夜 is the "late night", roughly from midnight until early morning. Typical are 深夜に, 深夜まで, 深夜バス "night bus", 深夜番組 "late-night show" and 深夜料金 "late-night surcharge" for taxis. 夜中 has the same meaning but is more colloquial; 夜遅く only means "late in the evening".

examples[].german: Watch out for cars.
Before the test, I read the instructions.
en.notes: 注意 refers to attention, caution, or a notice. 人や物に注意する means to pay attention to a person or thing. 注意事項 are points that should be observed. The examples show attention in traffic and reading notices before a test. The combination 注意する is an intransitive suru-verb here; the card form 注意 is a noun.

examples[].german: Let's help each other.
The two looked at each other.
en.notes: お互いに means that an action takes place reciprocally between people. It can stand before the verb: お互いに顔を見合わせる means to look at each other. The お belongs to the more polite form of 互いに; in お互いに助け合う, the adverb and the verb both emphasize mutual help.

examples[].german: The water is a hundred feet deep here.
The water depth of this pool is two meters.
Please check the water depth before jumping in.
en.notes: 水深 is the depth of the water at a certain spot. A measurement is stated with 水深は二メートルです or checked with 水深を確認する. The word is a noun; 深い, by contrast, is the adjective "deep". The measurements in the first two examples refer to specific, mutually unrelated places.

examples[].german: The water depth is as much as 300 meters at the deepest point.
The deepest part of the sea is very dark.
The map shows the deepest spot.
en.notes: 最深 here refers to the greatest depth or the deepest spot. The noun appears in 最深で, at the deepest point, and combines with の: 最深の場所. In 最深部, 部 is the area or part. In a dictionary the word can also have an adjectival role; the examples and the accent evidence of this card deal with the nominal use. Do not confuse it with 最新, which means newest.

examples[].german: When the term ends, summer vacation begins.
The new term begins.
My grades in the second term improved.
en.notes: 学期 is a division of the school year. Japanese schools usually have three 学期 (一学期 from April, 二学期 from September, 三学期 from January), which corresponds more to trimesters. At universities one speaks of 前期/後期 or likewise of 学期 "semester". Common are 新学期 "new school year/term" and 学期末 "end of the term". Read the same: 楽器 "musical instrument".

examples[].german: The snowboarding and skiing season has finally come around again this year.
I like the cherry blossom season best.
We haven't decided yet when we will move.
en.notes: 時期 is a "period, point in time, the time for something": この時期 "at this time of year, at this stage", 桜の時期, 時期が早い "it's still too early". Unlike 季節 (the four seasons), 時期 refers to a particular phase for an event or activity. 時代, by contrast, refers to an era, and ころ to an approximate point in time.

examples[].german: The tea ceremony is an important part of Japanese culture.
My grandmother has been learning the tea ceremony since she was young.
The utensils for the tea ceremony are all old and expensive.
en.notes: 茶の湯 is a traditional term for the Japanese tea ceremony, literally "hot water for tea". Today 茶道 (さどう) is more common; in everyday speech also simply お茶を習う "to learn the tea ceremony". Typical are 茶の湯の道具 "tea utensils" and 茶の湯を習う. The word sounds cultivated and somewhat old-fashioned.

examples[].german: Steam is coming out of the kettle.
The mirror fogged up from the steam of the bath.
Steaming ramen looks delicious.
en.notes: 湯気 is the visible steam rising from hot water, food or the bath. Typical are 湯気が出る and 湯気が立つ "it steams". Technical steam (steam engine) is 蒸気, smoke is 煙 and fog is 霧. Figuratively, 頭から湯気を出す means "to boil with rage".

examples[].german: Where did you buy that dagger?
An old dagger is on display at the museum.
The samurai wore a sword and a short sword at his waist.
en.notes: 短刀 is a short knife or short sword with a blade of at most about 30 cm, especially the traditional Japanese short sword of the samurai era. The word is encountered mainly in museums, history, and samurai films; in everyday speech one says ナイフ for a knife and 包丁 for a kitchen knife. The long samurai sword is called 刀. Wearing it at the waist is expressed with 差す: 刀を差す.

examples[].german: The short-term experiment is finished.
I'm looking for a short-term part-time job.
During summer vacation I did a three-week short study stay abroad.
en.notes: 短期 means "short duration, short-term" and is a noun, not an い-adjective: it takes の before a noun (短期のアルバイト) or forms compounds such as 短期留学 "short stay abroad for study" or 短期間 "short period of time". The opposite is 長期 "long-term". For everyday "short" (a short time, a short way), 短い is used. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced 短気 "short-tempered, impatient".

examples[].german: Hey Mom, has it been decided what's for dinner tonight?
The date for the meeting has been decided.
In this dormitory, it is the rule that you must be back by ten at night.
en.notes: 決まる is the intransitive counterpart of 決める "to decide, to fix": 日程を決める → 日程が決まる "the date is set". The result is marked with に: 行き先が北海道に決まる. ～ことに決まる or ～ことに決まっている means "it is fixed / it is the rule that ...". In the ている form, 決まっている expresses a fixed state or something taken for granted. Colloquially, 決まってる also means "looks perfect, looks great" (clothes, hairstyle).

examples[].german: Each one is different.
Let's hear each person's opinion.
en.notes: それぞれ means "each individually" or "respectively". It can itself stand for a group of people or things, as in それぞれ違います. Before a noun it takes の: それぞれの意見, "the respective opinion / each person's opinion". The dictionary lists this nominal use alongside the adverbial one.

examples[].german: My father is a drinker too.
This pub is popular with people who like to drink.
He drinks a lot, but he is conscientious at work.
en.notes: 酒飲み refers to someone who likes to drink a lot of alcohol regularly; 酒 here stands for alcohol in general, not just sake. The word is colloquial and often sounds self-deprecating or mildly reproachful, but does not necessarily mean alcohol addiction (that would be アルコール依存症). Intensified, it is 大酒飲み "heavy drinker". 酒好き, by contrast, stresses only the liking for alcohol.

examples[].german: Have you ever heard the sound a giraffe makes?
I can hear birds singing.
I woke up in the middle of the night to a cat meowing.
en.notes: 鳴き声 is the sound of an animal: the chirping of birds, meowing, barking, also the chirping of insects (虫の鳴き声). It comes from the verb 鳴く, which is used for animal sounds. The identically read 泣き声 with 泣く, by contrast, means the "crying" of a person, such as a baby. A human voice is simply 声. Typical: 鳴き声が聞こえる, 鳴き声を聞く.

examples[].german: When you have worries, it is best to talk to friends or parents.
Do you have any worries?
I have so many worries that I can't sleep well at night.
en.notes: 心配事 is a concrete thing that worries you, a single "worry" or problem. 心配 alone, by contrast, is the feeling or the act of worrying (心配する, 心配だ). Typical are 心配事がある and 何か心配事がありますか. Through compounding, 事 becomes ごと; it is also written 心配ごと. Similar is 悩み, which means more of an inner problem you wrestle with.

examples[].german: Let's gather fallen leaves and make a fire.
In autumn there are more falling leaves.
The path in the park is full of fallen leaves.
en.notes: 落ち葉 are leaves that have fallen from the tree - a compound of 落ちる and 葉, which becomes ば here. Typical combinations: 落ち葉を集める, 落ち葉を掃く "to sweep leaves", 落ち葉を踏む. Colored leaves still on the tree are 紅葉 (こうよう/もみじ); dried-up leaves are called 枯れ葉. The word is a noun, not an adjective.

examples[].german: Our father always gives us advice.
People often tell me I look like my father.
As a father, I want to cherish the time I spend with my children.
en.notes: 父親 is the matter-of-fact, neutral word for "father" as the male parent, often in contrast to 母親. It is used descriptively, e.g. 父親として "as a father" or 父親に似ている. To outsiders one politely refers to one's own father as 父, and to other people's fathers as お父さん; a father is addressed as お父さん, never as 父親. When speaking of oneself as a "father" in a role, one also uses 父親.

examples[].german: My mother is always full of energy.
I miss my mother's home cooking.
The child was gripping her mother's hand tightly.
en.notes: 母親 is the matter-of-fact, neutral word for "mother" as the female parent, the counterpart of 父親. It is used descriptively, e.g. 母親の手料理 or 母親として. Politely about one's own mother one says 母, about other people's mothers お母さん; she is addressed as お母さん. うちの母親 sounds casual and colloquial and is common among friends.

examples[].german: I probably like this song third best among the Beatles songs.
Please get off at the third station.
I am the third of three brothers.
en.notes: With the suffix 番目, numbers become ordinal numbers: 一番目, 二番目, 三番目 "the third". Before a noun, の is used: 三番目の駅; the counting direction is given with から: 右から三番目. 三番 alone, on the other hand, denotes a number or rank ("number three", 三番線 "platform 3"). For things you also hear 三つ目, and in formal written language 第三.

examples[].german: His way of talking really gets on my nerves.
His way of speaking is easy to understand.
I practiced how I speak before the interview.
en.notes: 話し方 is the way someone speaks: tempo, tone, word choice and politeness. It follows the pattern verb stem + 方 "way of doing", like 書き方 or 読み方. Typical: 話し方が丁寧だ, 話し方が速い, 話し方を練習する. 言い方 refers more narrowly to the phrasing of a specific utterance (その言い方はひどい), whereas 話し方 refers more to a person's general speaking style.

examples[].german: That's all.
The ending of the movie was moving.
I'm moving at the end of this month.
en.notes: 終わり is the noun for 終わる and means "end, finish". With の it gives the point in time: 今月の終わりに "at the end of this month", 映画の終わり. これで終わりです or 今日はこれで終わりにしましょう end a class or a meeting. The opposite is 始まり or 初め. Casually you also say おしまい; as the closing word of a film, often just 終 appears.

en.meaning: to open; to become vacant or free (空く)
examples[].german: What time does this shop open?
The door won't open.
Is this seat free?
I have time in the afternoon.
en.notes: 開く is read あく here: a door opens or a shop opens. For an empty or free seat as well as available time, the spelling 空く with the same reading is used. 空いています describes the state of being free or available. The intransitive godan verb forms あきます and あいて; what opens or becomes free takes が. 空く with the reading すく, by contrast, often describes less crowding or hunger.

examples[].german: It's finally over.
The work is finally finished.
I ran and just barely made the train.
en.notes: やっと means either "finally" after effort or waiting, or "just barely / with difficulty". やっと終わりました emphasizes the completion achieved. With やっと間に合いました, the narrow time margin can come to the foreground. The situation shows which meaning fits.

examples[].german: I never thought something like this would happen.
What happened?
If an earthquake occurs, please get under a desk.
en.notes: 起こる is intransitive: an event "happens, occurs" - 事故が起こる, 地震が起こる, 問題が起こる. The transitive counterpart is 起こす "to cause" (事故を起こす). In spoken Japanese, 起きる is just as common in this meaning (事故が起きる). Caution: the identically read 怒る means "to get angry, to scold".

en.meaning: to be conveyed; to spread; to be handed down
examples[].german: My mother's feelings came across through this letter.
The news spread quickly throughout the town.
This is a story that has been handed down in this village since long ago.
en.notes: 伝わる is the intransitive counterpart of 伝える "to communicate, to convey": 気持ちを伝える → 気持ちが伝わる "the feelings get across". It also means that news or rumors spread (ニュースが伝わる), that customs are handed down (昔から伝わる話) and that something reaches a country (仏教が日本に伝わった). Often in the negative: 言いたいことが伝わらない "they don't understand what I mean".

examples[].german: Could you project the slides onto the screen?
Before going out, I check my appearance in the mirror.
The quiet lake reflected the blue sky.
en.notes: 映す is transitive and means "to cast an image onto something": X を スクリーン/テレビ に映す "to project, to display" or X を鏡に映す "to look at in the mirror"; a water surface also "reflects" something. The intransitive counterpart is 映る "to be reflected, to appear" (鏡に顔が映る). Not to be confused with 写す "to copy, to photograph" and 移す "to move, to transfer", which are read the same way.

examples[].german: Yogurt helps with the digestion of food.
Digesting food takes time.
Even if you learn a lot at once, you can't absorb it.
en.notes: 消化 is "digestion"; as a transitive する-verb: 食べ物を消化する. Common are 消化がいい/悪い "easy/hard to digest". Figuratively it means to "absorb" knowledge (習ったことを消化する), or to "use up, work through" something (休みを消化する, 予定を消化する). Do not confuse it with the identically read 消火 "extinguishing a fire" (消火器 "fire extinguisher").

en.meaning: to come off; to come out (stain, pain)
examples[].german: The button came off.
This stain won't come out even after washing.
I was finally able to take my summer vacation.
en.notes: 取れる is the intransitive counterpart of 取る. It means "to come off, to come loose" (ボタンが取れる), "to disappear" for stains, pain or fatigue (しみが取れる, 痛みが取れる) and "to be harvested/caught" (then often written 採れる/獲れる). At the same time it is the potential form of 取る: 休みが取れる "to be able to take time off", 予約が取れる "to get a reservation".

examples[].german: They are all Canadians.
They came together.
I got to know them at university.
en.notes: 彼ら is the plural of 彼 and means "they" for a group of men or a mixed group; for all-female groups one says 彼女たち. In spoken Japanese, third-person pronouns tend to be avoided; people use names or say あの人たち. 彼ら therefore sounds somewhat distant and literary; it is not used for superiors or customers. The ending ら is less polite than たち.

examples[].german: "Oh, there's someone over there." "Huh, there's no one there, is there?"
Can someone help me?
en.notes: 誰か is an indefinite pronoun for "someone". 誰かいる states that someone is there; 誰か助けてください calls for help from any person. 誰もいない, by contrast, means "no one is there", with the negative form いない. The か here belongs to the expression and is not a sentence-final question particle.

examples[].german: "Which floor?" "The fourth, please." "This elevator doesn't stop at the fourth floor."
Please go up to the second floor.
The toilets are on the third floor.
en.notes: 階 is the counter for floors of a building. Japanese counts the ground floor as 一階, so 二階 is the "first floor" in the British sense (second floor in the American sense); basement floors are 地下一階 etc. Sound changes: いっかい, にかい, さんがい, よんかい, ろっかい, はっかい, じゅっかい; 何階 is read なんがい or なんかい. Do not confuse it with the counter 回 "-times", which is also read かい.

examples[].german: Why not become a library member first?
Do you have a membership card?
Only members can use this gym.
en.notes: 会員 is a "member" of a society, club, gym or a service with registration. Typical are 会員になる "to become a member", 会員カード, 会員登録 "registration" (e.g. on websites) and 会員制 "members only". For members of a band or team, メンバー is more common, for school clubs 部員, for company employees 社員.

examples[].german: I used to be a sailor on this ship.
I traveled around the world as a sailor.
Sailors cannot see their families for a long time.
en.notes: 船員 is the general term for a crew member of a ship, that is, a "sailor". The captain is 船長; the entire crew (also on aircraft) is 乗組員. Colloquial and a bit more romantic is 船乗り "seafarer". Navy soldiers, by contrast, are 水兵. The word is a noun: 船員として働く, 船員になる.

examples[].german: It went well.
I can't explain it well.
en.notes: うまく is the adverbial form of うまい. Here it describes successful or skillful action: うまくいく, "to go well", and うまく説明する, "to explain well". The statement concerns the execution or the result; the use of うまい for tasty food is not taught in these examples.

examples[].german: I like stories with a punchline.
The punchline of this story is funny.
Even if we leave now, all we'll end up doing is being late.
en.notes: 落ち here means the "punchline" of a joke or story and is usually written in katakana as オチ. It comes from the storytelling art 落語; オチのない話 "a story without a punchline" is a typical criticism. It also means "outcome, the end of the story": ～のが落ちだ "all that comes of it is ..." (mostly negative). Not to be confused with the verb 落ちる "to fall".

examples[].german: Today there is a gathering of people from the lab.
I took part in a gathering of friends.
Because of the rain, few customers are coming today.
en.notes: 集まり is the noun of 集まる and refers to a rather informal "gathering, get-together": 友達の集まり, 家族の集まり, 研究室の集まり. A formal meeting is a 会議, a larger assembly a 集会. 集まりがいい/悪い describes the "turnout", i.e. whether many or few people come. Typical: 集まりがある, 集まりに参加する/出る.

examples[].german: I passed a yakuza boss in the underpass.
I follow the boss's orders.
When he was a child, my older brother was the leader of the neighborhood kids.
en.notes: 親分 is the "boss, leader" of a group, above all a yakuza gang or traditional craftsmen; the followers are 子分. Casually, the leader of a gang of kids can also be called this. For the boss in a company, one does not say 親分 but 上司 or 社長. 親分肌 describes someone with a natural, caring leadership style. Similar is 親方 (master in a craft or sumo).

examples[].german: Please express your current feelings with kaomoji.
I use kaomoji in messages.
You should avoid using kaomoji in business emails.
en.notes: 顔文字 are faces built from characters such as (^_^) or (T_T); unlike Western emoticons, they are upright and are not read sideways. Literally the word means "face characters" (顔 + 文字). To be distinguished from them are 絵文字 "emoji" (pictograms) and スタンプ "stickers" in chat apps. They are used in casual messages, rather not in business emails.

examples[].german: There are lots of CDs in the media club's clubroom.
We practice in the clubroom after school.
en.notes: 部室 is the room of a school or university club. 部室に describes what is located there; 部室で what one does there. The word means the clubroom and not the club itself, which is expressed by 部 or クラブ, for example.

examples[].german: This library is popular with graduate students.
I do research as a graduate student.
After graduating from university, I became a graduate student.
en.notes: 大学院生 is someone studying at a 大学院 ("graduate school") - this includes master's (修士) and doctoral (博士) students. In short, 院生 is often used. Undergraduate students are called 大学生 or 学部生. Typical: 大学院生として研究する, 大学院生になる; moving on after the bachelor's degree is 大学院に進む.

examples[].german: My girlfriend is active as a cosplayer on weekends.
I take part in volunteer activities.
This volcano is still active.
en.notes: 活動 is an "activity" (usually organized or regular); as a する-verb it is intransitive: 活動する "to be active". Typical compounds are ボランティア活動, クラブ活動 or 部活動 (short: 部活) and 就職活動 (short: 就活, "job hunting"). It also applies to organizations, animals and volcanoes. 行動, by contrast, means the actions or behavior of an individual, and 運動 physical exercise or sport.

examples[].german: Today is a holiday, so my usual cafe was closed.
Banks are closed on public holidays.
en.notes: 祭日 denotes a festival day or public holiday. As a noun it can be used with です or だ; 祭日の休み links it to another noun via の. In the examples, the holiday explains why shops or banks are closed. The official Japanese national holidays are called 国民の祝日.

examples[].german: That office worker always got his work done steadily.
The plan is progressing steadily.
I'm preparing step by step for next month's match.
en.notes: 着々 almost always appears as 着々と and describes something moving toward a goal step by step and according to plan - typically with 進む: 準備が着々と進む, 工事が着々と進む. It sounds rather objective and is common in news and reports. だんだん, by contrast, means a gradual change, and どんどん rapid, vigorous progress. The mark 々 repeats the preceding kanji.

examples[].german: Don't torment me any more!
The illness is making him suffer.
Please stop tormenting the animals.
en.notes: 苦しめる is transitive: X を苦しめる "to torment someone, make someone suffer". The subject is often a cause such as illness, heat or a problem: 病気が彼を苦しめる. The intransitive counterpart is 苦しむ "to suffer" (病気に苦しむ), which is related to the adjective 苦しい. For deliberately bullying people, for example at school, いじめる is used instead. The word sounds serious and emotional.

examples[].german: Well then, let's look at the answers.
I checked the answers of the test.
Please answer the following questions in Japanese.
en.notes: 解答 is the "solution, answer" to an exam or exercise question: 解答用紙 "answer sheet", 解答欄 "answer box", 問題に解答する. Note: the identically read 回答 is the "reply" to a survey, inquiry or complaint. In everyday speech people simply say 答え or 答える; 解答 is more academic and literary.

examples[].german: Why do you stick out your little finger when you drink from a glass?
I bumped my little finger and it hurts.
I made a pinky promise with the child.
en.notes: 小指 is the little finger; on the foot, more precisely 足の小指 "little toe". The other fingers are 親指, 人差し指, 中指 and 薬指. In the childhood promise 指切り, the little fingers are hooked together. 小指を立てる (sticking out the little finger) used to be a gesture for "girlfriend, lover".

examples[].german: I added butter and gave the udon a Western twist.
I like Western-style buildings.
Which would you prefer for breakfast, Japanese or Western?
en.notes: 洋風 means "in the Western style" and is the counterpart of 和風 "in the Japanese style". It usually takes の before a noun (洋風の建物, 洋風の朝ごはん); 洋風な is also possible; 洋風にする/アレンジする means "to give a Western twist". Related are 洋食 "Western food" and 洋室 "Western-style room" (as opposed to 和室).

examples[].german: Do you think you'll get along with Satomi?
Let's all get along.
Don't fight; play nicely together.
en.notes: 仲良く is the adverbial form of 仲がいい / 仲良い and means "on good terms, harmoniously". Very common are 仲良くする "to get along well" and 仲良くなる "to become friends", each with と: 友達と仲良くする. It also stands directly before verbs: 仲良く遊ぶ, 仲良く暮らす. The noun 仲良し means "good friends, best friend".

examples[].german: I just arrived at Narita Airport.
What time will we arrive in Tokyo?
en.notes: 着く means "to arrive" and is an intransitive godan verb: 着きます, 着いて. With に you name the destination of arrival. 着きました reports that you have already arrived; 何時に着きますか asks for the arrival time. It differs from 着る, "to put on (clothes)", with a different reading and conjugation.

examples[].german: My boyfriend likes to drink.
He is known for liking alcohol.
I gave sake to my father, who likes to drink.
en.notes: 酒好き describes someone who likes to drink alcohol; in compounds 好き becomes ずき (本好き, 犬好き). It is used as a noun or な-adjective: 酒好きの人, 彼は酒好きだ, intensified 大の酒好き. Compared with 酒飲み ("a drinker who drinks a lot"), it emphasizes the fondness more and sounds friendlier. How much someone can handle is expressed with 酒に強い/弱い.

examples[].german: What, does this painting really cost a hundred million yen?
I won a hundred million yen in the lottery.
What would you do if you had a hundred million yen?
en.notes: 一億円 is 100,000,000 yen. Japanese counts large numbers in steps of four digits: 万 (10,000) and 億 (100,000,000); so "one million" is 百万 and "one billion" is 十億. As with 万, 一 must stand before 億: いちおく, never just おく. 一億円 is proverbial as a huge sum, for example for a lottery win (宝くじで一億円当たる). With も one stresses the size: 一億円もする.

examples[].german: It is doubtful whether Koichi really can't eat meat.
I have doubts about this result.
If you have any questions, please ask at any time.
en.notes: 疑問 is a doubt or an open question that one asks oneself: 疑問を持つ, 疑問に思う "to wonder, to doubt", ～かは疑問だ "it is questionable whether ...". 何か疑問があれば means "if there are any questions". 質問, by contrast, is a question that one asks someone (質問する), and 問題 is a task or a problem. Grammar: 疑問文 "interrogative sentence", 疑問詞 "question word".

examples[].german: This bowl is my mother's.
I served the food in a beautiful vessel.
He doesn't have what it takes to be company president.
en.notes: 器 is a vessel, especially tableware such as bowls and plates, often with an aesthetic undertone (器にこだわる "to care about beautiful tableware"). In general, "tableware" is 食器, a container for packaging is 容器. Figuratively, 器 means a person's "caliber": 器が大きい "big-hearted", 社長の器 "having what it takes to be a boss".

examples[].german: Thank you for your hard work. / Good work today.
Thank you for your hard work. You did a good job today, too.
I'm heading home first. Thanks for your hard work, everyone.
en.notes: お疲れ様 acknowledges the effort of others. The common forms are お疲れ様です and お疲れ様でした. Among colleagues, the phrase can mean "Have a good evening" when parting; it is not a literal statement that someone looks tired. For unfamiliar customers or superiors, the appropriate address depends on the relationship and the situation.

examples[].german: Could you set this tableware out on the table?
Please wash the dishes.
When I moved, I wrapped the dishes in newspaper.
en.notes: 食器 is the collective term for dishes and cutlery: plates, bowls, cups, often also chopsticks. Typical are 食器を洗う "to wash the dishes", 食器を並べる "to set the table", 食器棚 "dish cabinet" and 食器洗い機 "dishwasher". Individual pieces are called specifically 皿, 茶わん or コップ; 器 sounds more refined and emphasizes the beauty of a single vessel.

examples[].german: My boyfriend is a sumo wrestler.
A sumo wrestler's body is very big.
Sumo wrestlers often eat chanko stew.
en.notes: 力士 is the official term for a professional sumo wrestler. In everyday speech people affectionately say お相撲さん; the sport itself is 相撲, the highest rank 横綱. Wrestlers in the upper divisions are called 関取. For wrestlers in other combat sports (pro wrestling), レスラー is used.

examples[].german: The shower in this hotel in Shinjuku only gives cold or lukewarm water.
I went shopping in Shinjuku.
Shinjuku Station is so big that I often get lost.
en.notes: 新宿 is a ward (新宿区) and a business and entertainment district in Tokyo. 新宿駅 is considered the busiest station in the world; also located there are the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (東京都庁), the nightlife district 歌舞伎町 and the park 新宿御苑. Watch the reading: しんじゅく with voiced じゅ, not しゅく. As a place name it takes で/に/へ: 新宿で買い物する, 新宿に行く.

examples[].german: I really like this flashback scene in the movie.
I looked back on the past.
My grandmother recalled her life during the war and wrote a book about it.
en.notes: 回想 is the deliberate "looking back, recalling" of the past and sounds rather literary; as a する-verb it is transitive: 昔のことを回想する. Common are 回想シーン "flashback" in film and manga and 回想録 "memoirs". In everyday speech people more often say 思い出す "to remember" or 振り返る "to look back".

examples[].german: The drinking parties at my company are a lot of fun!
We have a drinking party on Friday.
I was invited to a drinking party, but I declined.
en.notes: 飲み会 is a social drinking party among colleagues, fellow students or friends, mostly in a pub (居酒屋). It is an important social ritual and not a binge; people who don't drink alcohol take part anyway. Special forms are 歓迎会 "welcome party", 送別会 "farewell party" and 忘年会 "year-end party"; the second round is 二次会. Typical: 飲み会がある, 飲み会に誘う/参加する.

examples[].german: When I glanced back, he was still looking at me.
I looked back while walking.
When someone called my name from behind and I turned around, my teacher was standing there.
en.notes: 見返る means "to turn around and look back" - literally, over one's shoulder. It sounds somewhat literary; in everyday speech one mostly says 振り返る, which also figuratively means "to look back on the past". Well known is the woodblock-print motif 見返り美人. Not to be confused with 見返す "to look at again; to show someone up" and the noun 見返り "return, reward".

examples[].german: I met Hana at the beginning of April.
First, let's decide on the goal.
First, let me introduce myself.
en.notes: 初めに means "first, at the beginning" and opens a sequence, often followed by 次に and 最後に. With の before it, it means "at the beginning of": 四月の初めに "at the beginning of April". Not to be confused with 初めて "for the first time". For the start of an action, the spelling 始めに is also found. As a heading (mostly in kana: はじめに) it stands for "introduction, preface".

examples[].german: The "wind god" created the divine wind.
I learned about the kamikaze in history class.
When the Mongol army came, a huge typhoon blew. People called it the "divine wind".
en.notes: 神風 literally means "divine wind". Originally it refers to the typhoons that destroyed the Mongol invasion fleets in the 13th century and thus supposedly saved Japan. In the West the word is known mainly through the suicide pilots of World War II; in Japan these are usually called 特攻 or 特攻隊. The word is a noun and rare in everyday life, mainly found in history and literature.

examples[].german: I am left-handed.
These scissors are hard to use for left-handed people.
As a child, I was trained out of being left-handed into being right-handed.
en.notes: 左利き refers both to left-handedness and to a left-handed person; 利き comes from 利く "to work well". It is a noun: 私は左利きです, 左利きの人, 左利き用のはさみ. The opposite is 右利き, ambidextrous is 両利き, the dominant hand is 利き手. An older, humorous meaning is "someone who likes to drink".

examples[].german: We have P.E. tomorrow.
We ran in P.E. class.
On rainy days we play basketball in the gym.
en.notes: 体育 is the school subject "sports, physical education": 体育の授業, 体育の先生, 明日は体育がある. The gym is called 体育館. The holiday 体育の日 was renamed スポーツの日 in 2020. For sports as a leisure activity one says スポーツ, for physical exercise 運動.

examples[].german: I help people in trouble.
I want to help people in need.
I rescued a child who had fallen into the river.
en.notes: 助ける is a transitive ichidan verb for helping or rescuing. The person takes を: 人を助ける. It can denote everyday support as well as rescue from danger. The te-form is 助けて; 助かる, by contrast, describes someone receiving help or being saved.

examples[].german: My son is not right-handed.
Most Japanese people are right-handed.
That shop only had guitars for right-handed players.
en.notes: 右利き means right-handedness or a right-handed person and is a noun: 右利きです, 右利きの人, 右利き用 "for right-handers". The opposite is 左利き, ambidextrous is 両利き, the preferred hand 利き手. 利き comes from 利く "to work well"; it is always written with kanji.

examples[].german: I think I'll catch up with you in about five minutes.
I ran and caught up with my friend.
I want to study hard and catch up with everyone in my class.
en.notes: 追い付く is intransitive; the person caught up with takes に: 友達に追い付く. It is also used figuratively, for example for level of study or performance (クラスのみんなに追い付く), and in the negative for "can't keep up" (生産が追い付かない). 追い越す, by contrast, means "to overtake" (with を), and 追いかける "to chase, to run after". It is often also written 追いつく.

examples[].german: Do you intend to fight alone?
Let's fight to the end.
My grandfather has been fighting his illness for a long time.
en.notes: 戦う is intransitive: the opponent is marked with と (敵と戦う, 強いチームと戦う), not with を. Besides war and combat, it also means "to compete against someone" in sports and "to struggle against" difficulties (病気と戦う). For the struggle with illness or poverty, the spelling 闘う is often seen; the noun is 戦い "fight". For a personal quarrel among friends, one says けんかする instead.

en.meaning: to like very much; to love
examples[].german: I love you.
I love chocolate.
en.notes: 大好き expresses strong affection or a great liking. The object is named with が: あなたが大好き, チョコレートが大好き. It behaves like a na-adjective: 大好きな食べ物. With people it can mean "to be very fond of"; with things, "to like very much". It is not a transitive verb with を.

en.meaning: to break free; to get loose
examples[].german: The balloon slipped out of the girl's hand.
The bird got out of the cage.
During the walk, the dog broke loose from its leash.
en.notes: 放れる is a rare spelling of はなれる and emphasizes "tearing oneself loose, getting free" from a grip or a restraint: 手から放れる, ひもから放れる. In everyday writing, 離れる ("to move away, to be separated") is used almost always, and for animals that escape, 逃げる is the usual word. The transitive counterpart is 放す "to let go, to release" (鳥を放す), which is encountered far more often.

examples[].german: How much is the admission fee?
Admission to the art museum is 1,000 yen for adults.
On the first Sunday of every month, admission is free.
en.notes: 入館料 is the admission fee for a building such as a museum, library, aquarium or art gallery; 館 means "building, hall". For events, stadiums or parks, 入場料 is used, for zoos and gardens 入園料. Typical are 入館料を払う, 入館料がかかる and 入館料は無料です; on signs it often appears with price tiers such as 大人・子ども.

examples[].german: Are gas prices high in Japan?
I paid the parking fee.
Taxi fares go up at night.
en.notes: 料金 is the charge for a service or use: 電気料金, 電話料金, タクシーの料金, 駐車料金. For the price of goods, one says 値段 instead; colloquially, 料金 is often replaced by the suffix 〜代 (電気代, ガス代). Typical combinations are 料金を払う, 料金が高い/安い and 料金が上がる; 運賃 is specifically the fare, 料金所 the toll booth.

examples[].german: Oh, a new movie theater has been built.
I saw a new movie at the movie theater.
en.notes: 映画館 is the movie theater as a building or place, 映画 the film. 映画館で names the place where a film is seen. できてる is the spoken short form of できている and here describes a newly built movie theater. It is about the finished state, not a personal ability.

examples[].german: That yakuza boss ended up being assassinated.
The president was assassinated.
Lincoln was assassinated in 1865.
en.notes: 暗殺 is the targeted, usually politically motivated murder of a well-known person, that is, an "assassination". As a verb it appears almost always in the passive: 大統領が暗殺される. For killing in general, 殺す is used; for murder as a crime, 殺人; the assassin is 暗殺者, the case 暗殺事件. The word belongs mainly in news and history books.

examples[].german: I'm not good at memorizing.
Memorizing kanji is hard work.
I memorized all the vocabulary before the test.
en.notes: 暗記 is deliberate memorization, word for word: 単語を暗記する, 九九を暗記する. The general 覚える means "to remember, to learn" and is less technical; 暗記 emphasizes mechanical memorization, often before exams. Related are 丸暗記 "rote memorization", 暗記カード "flashcards" and 暗記が得意/苦手.

examples[].german: If you make a mistake, you should apologize.
I apologized for being late.
en.notes: 謝る means "to apologize". The reason can be expressed with ことを: 遅れたことを謝る. The person one apologizes to takes に. Despite the ending る, it is a godan verb: 謝ります, 謝って. The similar-sounding spelling 誤る means "to make a mistake".

examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka, you have a phone call.
I wrote "Hanako Yamada" with 様 on the envelope.
Sir/Madam, please come this way to your seat.
en.notes: 〜様 is the more polite form of 〜さん and is attached to names when addressing customers, guests or business partners, as well as on envelopes and in e-mails (山田様). Service staff constantly say お客様. You never use it for yourself or your own company. It is also found in fixed words such as 神様, 王様, 皆様, お疲れ様 and ご馳走様.

examples[].german: How do you plan to kill that fly?
Please don't kill insects.
I held my breath and hid behind the door.
en.notes: 殺す is transitive ("to kill", 虫を殺す); the passive 殺される means "to be killed", and the intransitive counterpart is 死ぬ "to die". Figuratively it means "to suppress": 息を殺す "to hold one's breath", 声を殺す "to muffle one's voice", 才能を殺す "to let a talent wither". Colloquially, 殺される is also used jokingly and exaggeratedly (母に殺される "Mom's going to kill me").

examples[].german: I also can't stand murder scenes in dramas.
A murder case occurred.
Murder is a serious crime.
en.notes: 殺人 is murder or killing as an act and a crime; it mostly appears in compounds such as 殺人事件 "murder case", 殺人犯 "murderer" or 殺人を犯す "to commit murder". For the action itself in a sentence, the verb 殺す is used more often. Colloquially, 殺人的 means "murderous": 殺人的な暑さ, 殺人的な混雑.

examples[].german: You must not commit suicide.
We are working on suicide prevention.
Climbing a mountain in this snow is suicidal, you know.
en.notes: 自殺 is an intransitive する-verb: 自殺する "to take one's own life", with no を-object. An attempt is 自殺を図る, prevention is 自殺防止 or 自殺予防. News reports often use more cautious wording, such as 自ら命を絶つ. Figuratively, 自殺行為 means "sheer suicide", i.e. an extremely reckless act.

examples[].german: Huh, that's not true at all.
I don't understand at all.
"Did you wait long?" "No, it's totally fine."
en.notes: 全然 normally goes with a negation: 全然わからない "not to understand at all", 全然おいしくない. It also fits words with a negative meaning such as 全然だめ. In colloquial speech today you often hear it with positive statements as an intensifier (全然大丈夫 "totally okay"), which is avoided in formal texts. あまり〜ない means only "not very", and 全く is the more formal counterpart of 全然.

examples[].german: I like hot tea.
This tea is hot, so be careful.
en.notes: 熱い is an i-adjective for a hot object or hot liquid: 熱くない, 熱かった. Hot tea is 熱いお茶. For hot weather, the other spelling 暑い is used. 熱いので can give the heat as the reason for the warning 気をつけて.

examples[].german: Please decide that among yourselves.
Good morning, everyone.
en.notes: 皆さん politely addresses a group as "all of you" or "everyone". It can be used as a form of address: 皆さん、おはようございます. With が it marks the group that does or decides something. The casual みんな is a different form; 皆さん suits, for example, a greeting to a group.

examples[].german: This cat has green eyes.
In spring the trees turn green.
en.notes: 緑 is a noun for the color green. Before a noun it usually appears as 緑の, as in 緑の目. 緑になる describes a change to this color. 緑なんだ explains or stresses a fact in conversation. The word is read みどり and is not an i-adjective.

examples[].german: Why is this egg green?!
I'm wearing a green sweater.
In Japan, a green traffic light is also called "blue".
en.notes: 緑色 is a noun and is placed before nouns with の (緑色のセーター) or used as a predicate with だ/です; there is no い-form as with 赤い or 青い. Often 緑 alone is enough, which additionally means "greenery, plants". Note: traffic lights and some vegetables are traditionally called 青 ("blue") even though they are green. 黄緑 is light green.

examples[].german: When I was a child, I wanted to become a poet.
I read the works of a famous poet.
This poet's poems are even included in textbooks.
en.notes: 詩人 is "poet" - someone who writes 詩 (poems): 詩を書く, 詩人になる. For novelists one says 作家 or 小説家; someone who writes traditional tanka is a 歌人, and someone who writes haiku is a 俳人. Jokingly, someone who expresses themselves in a very emotional way is also called 詩人, as in 詩人だね.

examples[].german: I was praised by my teacher.
I was happy to be praised by my teacher.
I praised the child's efforts.
en.notes: 褒める is the transitive ichidan verb for "to praise". A person or their achievement takes を. The passive form 褒められる means "to be praised"; the person who praises then takes に. In the active example, the child's effort is explicitly what is praised.

examples[].german: Last month I became a section chief.
I reported to the section chief.
Section Chief Tanaka, the materials for the meeting are ready.
en.notes: 課長 is the head of a 課 ("section, department"), ranking below 部長 and above 係長 in the company hierarchy. The title is used directly as a form of address instead of さん: 課長、ちょっといいですか / 田中課長. When talking to outsiders about your own boss, you drop the honorific address and say 課長の田中.

examples[].german: Did you know that there is actually a bounty on Koichi's head?
The prize money for the tournament is one million yen.
I won a quiz show and received prize money.
en.notes: 賞金 is money you receive as a prize or reward: 賞金をもらう, 賞金を獲得する. A prize in kind, by contrast, is 賞品, the prize as an honor 賞. 賞金をかける means "to put up prize money / a bounty"; for criminals one also speaks of 懸賞金.

examples[].german: The wheel of my motorcycle came off.
The wheel of my bicycle got bent.
This suitcase has four wheels.
en.notes: 車輪 is the whole wheel of a vehicle (rim with tire), on cars, bicycles, trains or suitcases. In everyday speech people often say タイヤ for cars or bicycles; so it is the タイヤ that goes flat (タイヤがパンクする), not the 車輪. The expression 車の両輪 denotes two things that work only together.

examples[].german: Mercury accumulates in some fish.
Mercury is harmful to the body.
en.notes: 水銀 is the chemical element mercury. It is a substance name and a noun: 水銀がたまる describes an accumulation, 水銀を使う its use. The character 銀 alone means silver; the whole word refers to a different element. The examples talk about accumulation in some fish and about harmfulness to the body.

examples[].german: I think silver would be a good eye color for this character.
I like silver cars.
This spoon is silver-colored, but it is not real silver.
en.notes: 銀色 is a noun ("silver color") and stands before nouns with の (銀色の車) or with に (銀色に光る); there is no い-form. It describes only the color; the metal itself is 銀. For cars and electrical appliances people also often say シルバー; the counterpart is 金色 "gold-colored".

en.meaning: all you can; as much as you like
examples[].german: Whenever I go to an all-you-can-eat place, I always eat too much.
I enjoyed all-you-can-sing karaoke.
When their parents aren't around, my younger brother does whatever he wants.
en.notes: 〜放題 is attached to the verb stem and means "as much as you like": 食べ放題 "all-you-can-eat", 飲み放題, 使い放題 (flat rate). With the たい form it sounds negative: 言いたい放題 / やりたい放題 "to say or do whatever one wants, without consideration". Also negative is 荒れ放題 "completely overgrown", when something is left to itself.

examples[].german: I heard that the stationmaster's child is apparently adopted.
We took in an adopted child.
When he was a child, he was adopted by his uncle.
en.notes: 養子 is an adopted child, traditionally mostly a son; for a daughter there is 養女. Common are 養子にする "to adopt", 養子になる "to be adopted" and 養子をもらう/迎える "to take in a child". A Japanese peculiarity is the 婿養子: a son-in-law who is adopted into the wife's family and takes her name.

en.meaning: in front of the station; station area
examples[].german: I live in an apartment in front of the station.
There is a cafe in front of the station.
I met a friend in front of the station.
en.notes: 駅前 is the area directly in front of the station with shops, bus stops and taxi stands, not only the square itself, which is called 駅前広場. One says 駅前に住む, 駅前で待ち合わせる; 駅前通り is the street in front of the station. For the exact position "right in front of the station building", people more often say 駅の前.

examples[].german: Let's ask the station attendant over there.
I asked a station attendant for directions.
My father worked as a station attendant for thirty years.
en.notes: 駅員 are the employees of a station, for example at the ticket gate or platform; politely one says 駅員さん. The conductor on the train is 車掌, the train driver 運転士, the head of the station 駅長. When you have questions, you turn to the 駅員: 駅員に聞く.

examples[].german: Today my favorite idol is honorary stationmaster for a day at this station.
The stationmaster gave a welcoming speech.
At a station in Wakayama there was a cat as stationmaster.
en.notes: 駅長 is the stationmaster, i.e. the head of a station; his office is the 駅長室. The regular staff are 駅員. In promotional events a celebrity is often appointed 一日駅長 "honorary stationmaster for a day"; the cat Tama also became famous as the 駅長 of a small station.

examples[].german: I'm tidying up the desk.
I sorted the travel photos and put them in an album.
Let me sort out my thoughts for a moment, then I'll tell you.
en.notes: 整理 means "to put in order, to sort", often involving getting rid of what is unnecessary: 書類を整理する, 写真を整理する; also abstractly, 考えを整理する. In 整理整頓 it stands next to 整頓 "to put neatly in place"; 片付ける is more general, "to tidy up, to put away". Other meanings are "to regulate" (交通整理) and "to cut down" (人員整理 "staff reduction"); 整理券 is a numbered ticket.

examples[].german: Hey, isn't that Kaoru's boyfriend?
I went to see a movie with my boyfriend.
My relatives asked me whether I have a boyfriend.
en.notes: 彼氏 is a steady boyfriend in a romantic relationship: 彼氏がいる, 彼氏ができる, 彼氏と別れる. A man who is merely a friend is 男友達 or simply 友達. The counterpart is 彼女 "girlfriend"; the ex is colloquially 元彼. The word is casual-neutral; more formally one says 交際相手 or 恋人.

examples[].german: I'll have a draft beer.
I'll do it.
Have you seen my umbrella?
en.notes: 俺 is a markedly masculine, casual "I" used among friends, in the family or toward younger people. At work, toward superiors or strangers it sounds rough; there people say 私 or 僕. 僕 sounds more boyish and softer. In manga it is often written in katakana as オレ; the plural is 俺たち or 俺ら.

examples[].german: We are first-years.
We won't lose.
Our town has a new station now, too.
en.notes: 俺たち is the plural of 俺 and means "we" in casual, masculine speech among friends or in a team. Even more casual is 俺ら; more neutral are 僕たち and 私たち, formal 私ども. The ending is usually written in hiragana たち, less often 達.

examples[].german: This is not juice. It's canned beer.
I put the canned beer in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 缶ビール is beer in a can. 缶 names the packaging; ビール the drink. With 缶ビールです you identify the contents, with 缶ビールを冷蔵庫に入れる you describe chilling it. The card refers to the product, not a counting unit; individual cans are usually counted with 本.

examples[].german: Please put empty cans in here.
Please put empty cans out for recycling.
There was an empty can lying in the park, so I picked it up.
en.notes: 空き缶 is an empty beverage can; 空き (from 空く "to become empty") also appears in 空き瓶 "empty bottle", 空き箱 and 空き家. In Japanese waste separation, 空き缶 usually belong to the recyclables category "缶・びん". Cans thoughtlessly thrown away are called 空き缶のポイ捨て.

examples[].german: My dog is old, so he gets tired quickly.
I got tired after a long day.
en.notes: 疲れる is an intransitive ichidan verb: 疲れます, 疲れて. It describes someone becoming tired. 疲れました can report present tiredness after exertion. すぐ疲れる explains that someone tires quickly. んです adds an explanatory tone in conversation.

examples[].german: Cats help you relieve your tiredness.
Let's get rid of our tiredness in the hot spring.
I'm still worn out from the trip.
en.notes: 疲れ is the noun form of 疲れる and means tiredness or exhaustion. Typical expressions are 疲れが取れる "to recover", 疲れを取る "to get rid of fatigue", 疲れがたまる "exhaustion builds up" and 疲れが出る "the exhaustion starts to show". 疲労 is the formal word; the greeting お疲れ様 comes from the same root.

examples[].german: Hokkaido is in the north of Japan.
I saw the lavender fields in Hokkaido.
I'm going skiing in Hokkaido during the winter vacation.
en.notes: 北海道 is the northernmost of the four main islands and also an administrative unit of its own: the only 道 among the 都道府県, so one never says 北海道県. Its capital is 札幌. One goes 北海道へ/に, and residents are called 道民. It is known for snow, skiing, dairy products and lavender fields.

examples[].german: I'm interested in Japan.
Are you interested in this movie?
While reading, I lost interest in this book.
en.notes: 興味 is interest or curiosity in something. The topic takes に: 日本に興味がある. 興味を持つ means to show or develop interest; 興味を失う means to lose interest. The card shows a noun that is often used with these fixed verb combinations.

examples[].german: I'm going to the airport to pick someone up.
I pick up my friend at the airport.
We welcomed the new year with our family.
en.notes: 迎える is a transitive ichidan verb. It means, for example, to receive or pick up an arriving person; the person takes を. 迎えに行く stresses that you go in order to pick someone up. With time periods such as 新年, it can also mean to experience or welcome the beginning.

examples[].german: How are you planning to share that data?
Let's share the information.
I share the kitchen with my roommate.
en.notes: 共有する means "to own or use jointly, to share": 情報を共有する, ファイルを共有する, 部屋を友達と共有する. It stresses that several people have the same thing at their disposal; "to divide" in the sense of distributing is 分ける instead. In apps and social media, シェアする is also often heard. Compounds are 共有スペース and 情報共有.

examples[].german: The population of Tashirojima is no more than a hundred people.
Tashirojima is famous as a cat island.
en.notes: 田代島 is the name of Tashirojima, an island in Miyagi Prefecture that belongs to the city of Ishinomaki. 地名 (place name) + の人口 talks about the population; 猫の島として有名です talks about its fame as a cat island. 以下 includes the stated limit: 百人以下 means at most a hundred people. The limit given in the example is supported by the city's population figures from 2026.

examples[].german: I really like the expression on the girl's face in this illustration.
Her expression changed.
I'm going to take a photo, so please look a bit more cheerful.
en.notes: 表情 is the facial expression: 表情が明るい/暗い, 表情が豊か "expressive", 表情が硬い "to look tense", 表情を変える. 無表情 means "expressionless". In an extended sense it also describes the mood or atmosphere of a place (町の表情), whereas 顔 is the face itself.

examples[].german: A cat licked my middle finger.
I'm wearing a ring on my middle finger.
I got my middle finger caught in the door.
en.notes: 中指 is the middle finger, also the middle toe (足の中指). The fingers are, in order, 親指, 人差し指, 中指, 薬指, 小指. The insulting gesture 中指を立てる was adopted from the West and is less common in Japan.

examples[].german: She is my goddess!
I studied the goddesses of Greek mythology.
I went to New York to see the Statue of Liberty.
en.notes: 女神 is a goddess, that is, a female 神; with 様 (女神様) it sounds reverent or besotted, for example when admiring a woman. Well-known phrases are 自由の女神 "Statue of Liberty" and 勝利の女神 "goddess of victory" (勝利の女神がほほえむ "luck is on someone's side"). For gods in general, 神 or 神様 is used.

examples[].german: The king loves cooking.
Once upon a time, there was a king.
This country still has a king today.
en.notes: 王様 is the everyday, child-friendly word for "king", typical in fairy tales (昔々、王様が…). In news and official texts one says 国王 or simply 王. Related words are 女王 "queen", 王子 "prince" and お姫様 "princess". Figuratively, someone who behaves in a domineering way is also called 王様.

examples[].german: Let go of my thumb!
I gave the OK sign with my thumb up.
