I bumped my big toe and it hurts a lot.
en.notes: 親指 is the thumb; on the foot it is the big toe (足の親指). The "thumbs up" gesture is 親指を立てる. The other fingers are 人差し指, 中指, 薬指 and 小指. On a smartphone you usually tap with the 親指.

examples[].german: He is called the god of soccer.
I made a request to God.
In Japan, it is said that there is a god even in the toilet.
en.notes: 神様 is the respectful form of 神 and the usual word for gods in everyday speech; in Shintō there are countless gods, for example in mountains or houses; the Christian God is also called this. One prays to a god with 神様にお願いする / 祈る. Figuratively, someone is the "god" of their field: サッカーの神様. Also well known is the saying お客様は神様です.

examples[].german: My mother is very good with her hands and can make anything.
In winter my fingertips get cold.
Please touch the screen lightly with your fingertip.
en.notes: 指先 is the fingertip: 指先が冷たい, 指先で触る. 指先が器用 means "nimble-fingered, skillful". It can also mean the tips of the toes, but つま先 is the usual word for that. 先 here means "tip, end", as in 鼻先.

examples[].german: The boss's painting won the special selection prize at the competition!
We use specially selected ingredients.
This restaurant's premium wagyu is very expensive.
en.notes: 特選 has two uses: on products it stands for "selected, premium quality" (特選品, 特選和牛, 特選しょうゆ), and at art exhibitions and competitions it is a high distinction (特選に選ばれる, 特選に入賞する). It is not a "special offer" in the sense of a reduced price; that is 特売 or セール. The word is rather literary.

en.meaning: to see off; to put off for now
examples[].german: I see my friend off.
I saw my family off at the station.
Because of the rain, we put off our departure for now.
en.notes: 見送る means to say goodbye to someone as they set off, often by accompanying them part of the way. The person takes を. For a plan or a departure, 見送る can also mean "to put off for now". It is a transitive godan verb ending in る; 見送って is the て-form.

en.meaning: to pass (an exam); to be accepted
examples[].german: Yes! I got into a university in Seattle!
I finally passed the driving license test on the third try.
I passed the interview for the part-time job, so I'll start working next week.
en.notes: 受かる is intransitive and means "to pass (an exam), be accepted"; the target takes に: 試験に受かる, 大学に受かる. The opposite is 落ちる "to fail". The transitive 受ける means "to take (an exam)", the more formal synonym is 合格する. 受かる is colloquial-neutral and very common in conversation.

examples[].german: This is an image of Uranus.
Uranus is a planet of the solar system.
In science class we looked up information about Uranus.
en.notes: 天王星 is the planet Uranus, the seventh planet from the sun. The planet names end in 星: 水星, 金星, 地球, 火星, 木星, 土星, 天王星, 海王星. When reading, てん and おう merge into てんのう; do not confuse it with 天皇 "emperor", which is also read てんのう.

examples[].german: That dress is so cute!
I bought a new dress.
In summer it's easy because you can go out in just a dress.
en.notes: ワンピース is a wasei-eigo word from "one-piece" and means a (summer) dress made in one piece, that is, top and skirt together. A formal evening dress is more likely called ドレス. You say ワンピースを着る; for swimwear it denotes the one-piece swimsuit. In capitals, "ONE PIECE" is also the famous manga.

examples[].german: It's not good to keep people waiting.
I'm sorry to have kept you waiting.
I overslept and kept my girlfriend waiting for a whole hour.
en.notes: 待たせる is the causative of 待つ: "to make someone wait" (人を待たせる). Very common are the fixed polite formulas お待たせしました (staff or someone arriving), humble お待たせしてすみません, and casual お待たせ！. The opposite perspective is 待たされる "to be kept waiting" (causative-passive).

examples[].german: The underwear section is over there.
I'm going to buy new underwear.
I'm taking three days' worth of underwear on the trip.
en.notes: 下着 is underwear of all kinds, including undershirts; its counterpart is 上着 "jacket". Note: パンツ in Japanese usually means "underpants", and 肌着 is the undershirt worn directly against the skin. In department stores the section is called 下着売り場; for women's underwear you also hear ランジェリー.

examples[].german: Did you bring your swimsuit?
I'm taking a swimsuit because I'm going to the pool.
After arriving at the sea, I changed into my swimsuit.
en.notes: 水着 is any kind of swimwear: swimsuit, swim trunks or bikini (ビキニ). You say 水着を着る and 水着に着替える "to change into". Colloquially, men's swim trunks are also called 海パン. The word is composed of 水 "water" and 着 "clothing", like 下着 and 上着.

examples[].german: That person gives a bad impression, don't you think?
That looks good.
It feels like spring has already come.
en.notes: 感じ is the noun form of 感じる and means "feeling, impression". Typical are 〜感じがする "to feel like, to have the impression that", 感じがいい/悪い "likeable/unlikeable", and colloquially いい感じ "going well" or こんな感じ "something like this". Do not confuse it with the identically read 漢字; 気持ち is more the inner feeling.

examples[].german: I am here now thanks to all of you.
I thank you all for your cooperation.
An announcement for all passengers.
en.notes: 皆様 is the most polite form of "everyone": みんな is casual, 皆さん polite, 皆様 especially respectful. It is heard in speeches, announcements, business letters and customer service. Typical are 皆様のおかげで "thanks to all of you" and 皆様、こんにちは.

examples[].german: Um, how do I get to the main building again?
The main building is under renovation.
The main building and the new building are connected on the second floor.
en.notes: 本館 is the main building as opposed to 別館 "annex" or 新館 "new building" - typical for department stores, hotels, ryokan, schools and hospitals. On signs, 本館 also means "this building, our building", for example 本館は全館禁煙です.

examples[].german: I was invited to a party.
I invited my friends to the party.
en.notes: 招待する means to invite someone explicitly. The invited person takes を, and the occasion takes に: 友達をパーティーに招待する. 招待される is the passive "to be invited". 招待 alone is the noun "invitation"; the verb form combines it with する.

examples[].german: I'm sorry, I didn't mean any harm.
I know he means no harm, but I felt a little sad.
A child said it, so there's no ill intent.
en.notes: 悪気 (read わるぎ) means "ill intent" and is almost always used in the negative: 悪気はない/なかった "it wasn't meant maliciously". It is used to apologize or to defend someone. The more formal word for "malice", also a legal term, is 悪意.

examples[].german: Do you go mountain climbing, Mr. Yamada?
I go hiking in the mountains on weekends.
When you go hiking, bring plenty of water.
en.notes: 山登り is the everyday word for "climbing a mountain" and usually means hiking in the mountains, not technical climbing. One says 山登りをする or 山登りに行く; with a place name: 富士山に登る. The Sino-Japanese 登山 is more matter-of-fact and sounds more like sport or alpinism, ハイキング like an easier hike without a summit.

examples[].german: Huh, isn't the word 「流行歌」 a bit old-fashioned? It sounds like something grandparents would say.
My grandmother often sings the hit songs of her youth.
A nostalgic old hit came on the radio.
en.notes: 流行歌 refers to a popular song that was sung everywhere in a certain period, especially the hits of the Showa era. The word sounds old-fashioned today; for current hits one says ヒット曲 or simply 流行っている歌. Typical combinations are 昭和の流行歌 or 昔の流行歌.

examples[].german: The dishes at this restaurant are all delicious without exception.
Every rule has exceptions.
Just this once, as an exception, you may hand it in tomorrow.
en.notes: 例外 is a noun: 例外がある, 例外を認める. Very common are the set phrase 例外なく "without exception" and 例外として "as an exception". As an adjective, 例外的な means "exceptional, as an exception". The opposite would be the rule: ルール or 原則.

examples[].german: This is just one example.
To give one example, in Japan you take off your shoes when entering a house.
As an example, let me tell you about my own case.
en.notes: 一例 means "one example, a single case" and sounds somewhat more formal than 例. Typical are ほんの一例 "just one example (of many)", 一例を挙げる "to give an example" and 一例として "as an example". In everyday speech one usually just says 例えば or 例を出す.

examples[].german: Isn't this example sentence a bit strange?
I read the example sentences in the textbook.
Let's try making an example sentence using this word.
en.notes: 例文 is an "example sentence" as found in textbooks and dictionaries. Typical combinations are 例文を読む, 例文を作る and 辞書の例文. Not to be confused with 例 "example" in general or 文 "sentence"; 作文 is a composition one writes oneself.

examples[].german: That runner went from tenth to first place in the last lap.
Let's go once around the park.
Someday I want to cycle all the way around Japan.
en.notes: 一周 is "one lap, one circuit". As a する-verb, the place circled takes を: 公園を一周する, 世界一周する "to make a trip around the world". As a noun it denotes a lap in sports: 最後の一周. For further laps you count 二周, 三周. Do not confuse it with 一週 (one week, 一週間), which is pronounced the same.

examples[].german: There are always yakuza-looking men around that woman.
The surrounding environment is very quiet.
The circumference of this lake is about ten kilometers.
en.notes: 周囲 means "surroundings", often also "the people around" (周囲の人), and also the "circumference" of an object: 池の周囲は二キロ. It is more formal and literary than the everyday 周り, which is usually preferred in conversation. Typical: 周囲を見回す, 周囲に気をつける.

examples[].german: I'm busy preparing for the anniversary event.
We celebrated the company's tenth anniversary.
Next year is our fifth wedding anniversary.
en.notes: 周年 almost always follows a number and refers to a round anniversary: 創立十周年 "tenth anniversary of the founding", 結婚五周年. Watch the pronunciation: 十周年 is read じゅっしゅうねん or じっしゅうねん. The yearly recurring day itself is called 記念日 (結婚記念日); 周年 counts the years and is often combined with 記念.

examples[].german: This café has a nice atmosphere, doesn't it?
One remark from him made the mood in the meeting turn bad.
The new teacher has a gentle air about her.
en.notes: 雰囲気 is the "atmosphere, mood" of a place or situation, but also the "aura" of a person: 優しい雰囲気の人. Typical: 雰囲気がいい／悪い, 雰囲気のある店, 雰囲気を壊す. The correct reading is ふんいき; the often heard ふいんき is considered a mistake.

examples[].german: I respect my teacher.
The person I respect most is my grandmother.
I disagree with his opinion, but I respect his sincerity.
en.notes: 尊敬する means to hold someone in high regard because of their abilities, attitude or achievements. The person respected takes を; 尊敬しています describes an existing attitude. As a suru-verb it forms 尊敬して・尊敬しない. Respect does not rule out a differing opinion.

examples[].german: Japan has four seasons.
Japan's four seasons are beautiful.
In this park you can enjoy the flowers of each season throughout the year.
en.notes: 四季 means the four seasons as a whole and sounds somewhat more elevated than 季節, which refers to a single season (好きな季節は秋です). A popular cliche is 日本には四季がある or 四季がはっきりしている. Set combinations: 四季の花, 四季折々 "in every season".

examples[].german: You totally beat me.
I understood it completely.
There's no such thing as a perfect person.
en.notes: 完全 is a な-adjective: 完全な答え "a complete answer". Very common is the adverb 完全に "completely, totally", also used colloquially as an intensifier: 完全に忘れてた. Unlike 完璧 "flawless, perfect", 完全 emphasizes that nothing is missing. Opposite: 不完全.

examples[].german: Can you wake me up before it's finished?
The work is finally finished.
The new station building is scheduled to be completed next year.
en.notes: 完成 is the "completion" of a work, building or plan. It is mostly intransitive: 作品が完成する "the work gets completed"; transitively one more often says 作品を完成させる. In everyday speech, for small things one rather says できた; 完成 sounds like a bigger project. Nouns: 完成品, 完成まであと一週間.

examples[].german: I'm thinking about human nature.
This novel depicts the weakness of human nature.
Anger and sadness are also part of human nature.
en.notes: 人性 "human nature" is a rare, literary word from philosophy and literature. In normal Japanese one says 人間性 or 人間の本性 instead. Do not confuse it with the identically pronounced and very common 人生 "life, course of life".

examples[].german: I caught a sexually transmitted disease.
I got tested for sexually transmitted diseases.
Use condoms to prevent sexually transmitted diseases.
en.notes: 性病 is the general term for "venereal diseases". One says 性病にかかる "to catch" and 性病の検査を受ける "to get tested". In medicine and educational texts, the more neutral technical term 性感染症 is used today.

en.meaning: especially; going to the trouble; precious
examples[].german: Are you going to waste the advice I took the trouble to give you?
I went to the trouble of making it, but nobody ate it.
Since we've come all the way to Kyoto, let's go see a temple.
en.notes: せっかく is almost always written in kana. Three patterns: せっかく〜のに "went to the trouble of ..., but in vain" (regret), せっかく〜から "since we're here ..., (let's make use of the opportunity)" and せっかくの＋noun "precious, long-awaited", often with disappointment: せっかくの休みが雨だ. The polite formula せっかくですが introduces a refusal.

examples[].german: I'm disappointed in you.
I was disappointed by his attitude.
After losing the match, the fans' disappointment was enormous.
en.notes: 失望 is "disappointment" and sounds stronger and more formal than the everyday がっかりする. The person or thing one is disappointed in is marked with に: 彼の態度に失望する. To disappoint someone is 失望させる; as a noun: 失望が大きい.

examples[].german: What are your wishes?
There is still hope.
My long-held wish has finally come true.
en.notes: 望み is the noun of 望む and means "wish" as well as "hope, prospect". Typical: 望みがかなう "the wish comes true", 望みを捨てない "not to give up hope", まだ望みがある. By comparison, 願い sounds more personal and emotional, 希望 more matter-of-fact (e.g. on forms).

en.meaning: to wish for; to hope for; to look out over
examples[].german: My parents wish for me to become a doctor.
I wish for peace.
From the rooms of this hotel you can see Mt. Fuji.
en.notes: 望む "to wish, to hope for" is more formal than 〜たい or 欲しい and often appears in speeches or texts: 平和を望む. One can also expect something from others: 親は子供が医者になることを望んでいる. In written language it also means "to look out at something": 富士山を望む部屋. Colloquially: 望むところだ "Bring it on, that suits me just fine!".

examples[].german: I plan to go to the home improvement store tomorrow to buy lumber.
I'm building a house out of wood.
Japan imports a lot of lumber from abroad.
en.notes: 木材 is "wood" as a material and commodity, for example in home improvement stores, industry or statistics. In everyday speech, for objects people prefer 木でできた "made of wood"; 木 alone also means "tree". The closely related 材木 refers specifically to cut construction timber such as beams and boards.

examples[].german: I feel happiness.
I feel the warmth of spring.
en.notes: 感じる means to perceive or feel, for instance warmth, happiness or a mood. The thing perceived takes を. It is an Ichidan verb; 感じます and 感じて are regular forms. The examples distinguish an inner feeling from a physically perceptible warmth.

examples[].german: I made a table out of old lumber.
I'm transporting lumber.
My grandfather ran a small lumber yard in town.
en.notes: 材木 is cut "construction timber" such as beams and boards, as you buy at a 材木屋 "lumber yard". It sounds more traditional and concrete than 木材, which generally denotes "wood as a raw material". Typical: 材木を運ぶ, 材木を切る.

examples[].german: Oh, so the leaves of a pine are called 「松葉」. I didn't know that.
Pine needles are lying on the ground.
Even in winter, pine needles stay green.
en.notes: 松葉 is the "pine needle", composed of 松 "pine" and 葉 "leaf", which here becomes voiced to ば. In conversation one also says 松の葉. Well-known compounds are 松葉杖 "crutch" (after its forked shape) and 松葉ガニ, a regional name for the snow crab.

examples[].german: Saying such a thing makes me doubt his character.
He is a person of noble character.
Some people become a completely different person when they drink.
en.notes: 人格 is "character" in the moral sense, the personality as a whole, and sounds serious. Typical: 人格を疑う "to doubt someone's decency", 人格者 "person of noble character", 二重人格. For everyday temperament people say 性格 (明るい性格), for a person's likable manner 人柄.

en.meaning: to pass (an exam); to be accepted
examples[].german: I'm definitely going to pass!
I'm glad I was able to pass the exam.
My older brother got into a university in Tokyo.
en.notes: 合格する means "to pass an exam" or "to be admitted"; the exam or school is marked with に: 試験に合格する, 大学に合格する. Colloquially one also says 受かる; the opposite is 落ちる or 不合格になる. Related: 合格点 "passing mark", 合格発表 "announcement of results".

examples[].german: That's a great outfit.
You're wearing stylish clothes.
Aren't you cold in that getup?
en.notes: 格好 here means appearance, getup or clothing. 素敵な格好 praises the outfit; その格好 refers to a person's actual clothes. 格好いい is a fixed combination for good-looking or stylish, which is pronounced kakkoii in the example. The standalone base form of the card, by contrast, is the noun kakkō. かっこう is the kana spelling of this noun for appearance or getup; it is not the short form かっこ or the noun かっこう "cuckoo".

examples[].german: I like men with a sturdy build.
He has a sturdy bone structure.
At last the framework of the new plan is in place.
en.notes: 骨格 is the "skeleton" or the "bone structure, physique": 骨格がしっかりしている "to be solidly built". Figuratively it means the "framework" of a plan or text: 計画の骨格. For the general build of the body, 体格 is also used in daily life; 骨格 stresses the bone structure.

examples[].german: I'll stay here.
There is still work left.
That trip has stayed in my heart to this day.
en.notes: 残る is intransitive: "to remain, to be left over, to stay behind"; the transitive counterpart is 残す "to leave over". The place is marked with に: ここに残る, 会社に残る. Something left over takes が: 仕事が残っている, ご飯が残る. Figuratively: 心に残る, 記憶に残る "to stay in one's memory". For "to stay" in general, いる is often enough.

examples[].german: That's a very Japanese way of thinking, isn't it?
This garden is very typically Japanese.
Deciding everything together is a characteristic of Japanese companies.
en.notes: 日本的 "typically Japanese" describes above all ways of thinking, values and culture: 日本的な考え方, 日本的な会社. For the look and style of rooms, food or design, 和風 or 日本風 is used more often. 日本らしい, by contrast, usually sounds appreciative: "just the way you would expect from Japan".

examples[].german: I want to get into show business.
She made her debut in show business at fifteen.
I'm not very interested in entertainment news.
en.notes: 芸能界 is the "show business, entertainment industry" with actors, singers and TV stars. Typical are 芸能界に入る, 芸能界デビュー and 芸能界を引退する. A person from this world is called 芸能人; gossip about it is 芸能ニュース.

examples[].german: Please think carefully.
I'm thinking about the future.
en.notes: 考える means "to think / to consider" and can also express planning an action. The topic can take のことを: 将来のことを考える. よく考えてください is a request to think thoroughly. It is a transitive ichidan verb; the te-form is 考えて.

examples[].german: That comedian is really funny, isn't he?
My dream is to become a comedian in the future.
A street performer was juggling at the festival.
en.notes: 芸人 today mainly refers to comedians on television, in full お笑い芸人. Originally it means "performer, entertainer" in general, such as 大道芸人 "street performer". Not to be confused with 芸能人 (celebrity, star in general) or 芸者 (geisha).

examples[].german: A geisha performed a dance for us at the banquet.
I saw a geisha in Kyoto.
Geisha's work is to entertain guests with song and dance.
en.notes: 芸者 is a traditional female entertainer who entertains at banquets with dance, song and conversation; respectfully one says 芸者さん. In Kyoto she is called 芸妓, the apprentice 舞妓. The image of the geisha as a prostitute that is widespread in the West is false.

examples[].german: I think this will take some time to digest.
Greasy food is hard to digest.
I have to use up my remaining paid leave this month.
en.notes: 消化する means "to digest" (食べ物を消化する) and, figuratively, "to absorb material": 授業の内容を消化する. In working life it also means "to use up, work through": 有給を消化する "to take remaining leave". Common: 消化にいい／悪い "easy／hard to digest". Do not confuse it with the identically read 消火 "extinguishing a fire".

examples[].german: This will come off with an eraser.
The light went out.
en.notes: 消える is an intransitive ichidan verb: 消えます, 消えて. A light can go out, and writing can disappear. With が you name the thing affected. 消しゴムで names the eraser as the means. The transitive 消す, by contrast, describes someone erasing or switching something off.

examples[].german: This picture is really creepy.
I feel sick from motion sickness.
My socks got wet in the rain, and it feels yucky.
en.notes: 気持ち悪い covers two areas: physically "I feel sick" (乗り物酔いで気持ち悪い) and emotionally "disgusting, creepy, repulsive" (虫が気持ち悪い). It also expresses an unpleasant feeling on the skin: 汗で気持ち悪い. In youth slang it is shortened to キモい, which is very hurtful when said about people. Opposite: 気持ちいい.

en.meaning: to move; to set in motion
examples[].german: It's impossible for me to move this piano by myself.
Please move this box.
That movie moved many people.
en.notes: 動かす is transitive: "to move something, to shift, to set in motion"; the intransitive counterpart is 動く "to move". Typical are 机を動かす, 体を動かす "to move around, to exercise" and 機械を動かす "to operate a machine". Figuratively, 心を動かす means "to move, to touch someone".

examples[].german: Do you wear earrings like these?
Let's put on a necktie.
Please wear a mask on the train.
en.notes: 着ける is "to put on, to wear" for accessories and things fastened to the body: マスク, ネックレス, 指輪, イヤリング. It is mostly just written つける. For clothing on the upper body 着る applies, for trousers and shoes はく, for hats かぶる, for ties and belts more often しめる. Fixed phrase: 身に着ける "to wear on the body; to acquire (a skill)".

examples[].german: You have to study properly every day.
I study three hours every day.
Before the exam, I studied at the library with a friend.
en.notes: 勉強する means "to study" or "to work on a subject of learning" here. The subject or language can take を: 日本語を勉強する. The duration comes without に, as in 三時間勉強する. The phrase 〜するんだよ can be an emphatic instruction in this context, not just a description. In the third example, と names the study partner and で the place of study. For repeatedly practicing a skill, 練習する often fits. This card practices the meaning "to study", not a price discount.

examples[].german: When are you planning to travel?
I'm traveling around Europe in the summer.
I like traveling alone.
en.notes: 旅行する means "to travel, to take a trip". The area traveled takes を (ヨーロッパを旅行する "to travel around Europe"), and the destination can take に or へ. In everyday speech 旅行に行く is even more common. 旅 sounds more poetic, and 出張 is a business trip.

examples[].german: Whatever you do, don't wake him up.
Please wake me up at seven in the morning.
That driver caused an accident last year, too.
en.notes: 起こす is the transitive counterpart of 起きる and means "to wake someone" or "to set upright": 子供を起こす, 倒れた自転車を起こす. Also very common is "to cause, to trigger": 事故を起こす, 問題を起こす. To ask to be woken: 七時に起こしてください.

en.meaning: to notice; to come to (regain consciousness)
examples[].german: I noticed the mistake.
I noticed that I had forgotten my wallet.
When I came to after a while, I was in a hospital bed.
en.notes: 気がつく is a fixed phrase for "to notice / to become aware of something". What is noticed takes に, also after a sentence with こと: 忘れたことに気がつく. In a different situation the phrase can mean "to regain consciousness". The verb component is a godan verb ending in く: 気がつきます, 気がついて.

examples[].german: Most of the visitors to this ski resort are foreign tourists.
Many travelers visit Kyoto.
The information center for travelers is inside the station.
en.notes: 旅行者 is a "traveler" in general, rather matter-of-fact, as in news or on signs: 外国人旅行者. Someone traveling to see the sights is a 観光客 "tourist", the more common word in conversation. 旅人 sounds literary and romantic.

examples[].german: I don't like that person because he's always badmouthing others.
Please don't speak ill of others.
I was sad to learn that people had been badmouthing me behind my back.
en.notes: 悪口 means "gossip, disparaging remarks" about someone; almost always in the phrase 悪口を言う, often 人の悪口. Behind someone's back: 陰で悪口を言う. The reading is わるぐち; the Sino-Japanese reading あっこう is literary. A complaint about something, by contrast, is 文句.

examples[].german: What do you think is necessary to have good communication?
My state of health is good.
Relations between the two countries are still good.
en.notes: 良好 is a formal な-adjective for "good, satisfactory" and typically appears in reports, news and medical findings: 経過は良好です, 良好な関係. In everyday conversation people simply say いい or よい. It is often used predicatively with です.

examples[].german: What, this is fully automatic?
This door opens automatically.
There is a vending machine in front of the station.
en.notes: 自動 means "automatic" and is not a な-adjective: one says 自動で開く or 自動の機械; as an adverb also 自動的に. It appears in many compounds: 自動ドア, 自動販売機, 自動車, 全自動. The opposite is 手動 "manual". In grammar, 自動 is the short form of 自動詞 "intransitive verb".

examples[].german: I feel sick from indigestion.
I ate too much and got indigestion.
There were so many explanations that class ended before I had absorbed everything.
en.notes: 消化不良 is "indigestion": 消化不良になる, 消化不良を起こす. Figuratively it means that one has not properly absorbed material or information: 授業が消化不良のまま終わった. In everyday speech, for stomach trouble people also say お腹の調子が悪い or 胃がもたれる.

examples[].german: A new conveyor-belt sushi restaurant has opened.
We went to a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant as a family.
At this conveyor-belt sushi place, every plate costs one hundred yen.
en.notes: 回転ずし is sushi from a conveyor belt, literally "rotating sushi"; 寿司 becomes voiced ずし here. It is also written 回転寿司. One says 回転ずしに行く and usually pays by plate (一皿百円). Colloquially also 回るお寿司.

en.meaning: closing time; (store) closing; going out of business
examples[].german: This store closes at nine o'clock.
I bought bread before closing time.
I hear the bookstore in front of the station will close for good next month.
en.notes: 閉店 means two things: the daily closing of a shop (閉店時間, 閉店は九時) and the permanent closure of a business (来月閉店する, 閉店セール). As a する-verb it is mostly intransitive, with the shop as the topic: この店は九時に閉店する. The opposite is 開店 "opening, grand opening". In conversation, for the daily closing one often simply says 店が閉まる; 閉店 sounds more businesslike and typically appears on signs and in announcements.

examples[].german: This door opens and closes automatically.
The attendant opened and closed the window many times a day.
Please be careful of the train doors opening and closing.
en.notes: 開閉 combines "to open and close" in one word and is a する-verb of written and technical language, for example in instructions and announcements: ドアの開閉にご注意ください. It can be used both transitively (窓を開閉する) and intransitively (ドアが自動で開閉する). Common in compounds: 開閉式の屋根 ("retractable roof"), 開閉ボタン. In everyday speech people prefer 開け閉め (あけしめ): 窓の開け閉め.

examples[].german: If you feel like it, how about going to karaoke with us now?
Let's sort it out ourselves somehow.
Our school is pretty far from the station.
en.notes: 俺ら is the casual masculine form for "we, us", formed from 俺 and the casual plural suffix ら. It sounds rougher than 俺たち and much more informal than 僕ら or 私たち; it is used only among friends. Rarely, it also simply means "I" (dialectal).

examples[].german: There's a well over there.
In the old days we drew water from this well.
The water from the well is cold even in summer.
en.notes: 井戸 is a "well" for drawing water, not an ornamental fountain (that would be 噴水). Typical: 井戸を掘る, 井戸の水 (井戸水), 井戸から水をくむ. The expression 井戸端会議 "chat at the well" denotes gossip among neighbors.

examples[].german: The morning light is beautiful.
The morning light comes in through the window.
I read the map by the light of a flashlight.
en.notes: 光 here means "light" or "ray of light". The reading is ひかり; the reading こう belongs to other uses, for example in compounds. With で, light can denote the means of an action: 光で地図を読む. The examples involve natural morning light and an artificial light source.

en.meaning: to adjust; to match; to combine
examples[].german: He's good at adapting to the other person's pace, isn't he?
I set the clock to the correct time.
Let's all join forces and do our best.
en.notes: 合わせる is the transitive counterpart of 合う "to fit": "to adjust, to coordinate, to put together". With に you state what one adjusts to: 相手に合わせる, 時計を時間に合わせる. Set phrases: 力を合わせる "to work together", 手を合わせる "to put one's hands together", 間に合わせる "to make it in time".

examples[].german: Watch your opponent's movements closely!
The cat's movements are fast.
Every morning I check price trends in the news.
en.notes: 動き is the noun of 動く: the "movement" of a body or object (猫の動き) and, figuratively, "development, trend" (物価の動き, 新しい動き). Typical: 動きが速い／遅い, 動きを見る, 動きがない "nothing is happening". For athletic movement or physical exercise, 運動 is used instead.

examples[].german: I collect coins with serrated edges.
Let's look around before crossing the street.
Let's be careful not to bother the people around us.
en.notes: 周り is a noun: "surroundings" (家の周り), "circumference, edge" (池の周り) and often "the people around one" (周りの人). Place expressions are formed with 〜の周りに／で. It is the everyday word; 周囲 is more formal. It is also written 回り; 身の回り means "personal belongings, one's immediate surroundings".

examples[].german: Please tell me the depth of this pool.
The depth of this lake is fifty meters.
Only after I became an adult did I understand the depth of my teacher's words.
en.notes: 深さ is the noun for 深い and refers to the measurable "depth": 深さは五メートル, 深さを測る. Figuratively it also means the "depth" of feelings or thoughts: 愛の深さ. The variant 深み stresses more a quality (taste, character) and is not measurable.

examples[].german: My menstrual cycle is always about 28 days.
Fashions are said to go in cycles.
The Earth orbits the Sun in a cycle of one year.
en.notes: 周期 is the "cycle, period" of a regularly recurring process: 生理周期, 公転周期, 〜年の周期で. It sounds technical or scientific. For intervals between buses or appointments, 間隔 is used instead; for a single lap, 一周.

examples[].german: I'll wait in the waiting room!
I waited for my friend in the station waiting room.
The hospital waiting room was very crowded.
en.notes: 待合 on its own is a short form; almost always 待合室 "waiting room, waiting hall" is used, in doctors' offices, hospitals and stations. One waits 待合室で. The spelling 待ち合い室 also occurs. Do not confuse it with 待ち合わせ "appointment, meeting point".

examples[].german: The voice was a child's, but the way of speaking was completely adult.
His manner of speaking is polite.
When he gets angry, his way of speaking suddenly turns rough.
en.notes: 言葉つき (also written 言葉付き) describes how someone speaks, the tone and manner that come through in speech: 丁寧な言葉つき "polite manner of speaking", 乱暴な言葉つき "rough manner of speaking", 言葉つきが変わる. It is rather literary; in daily life people more often say 口調 "tone of voice" or 言葉遣い "choice of words, language use". 言葉遣い stresses the chosen words (keigo or not), 言葉つき more the impression the way of speaking makes.

examples[].german: My mother isn't feeling very well.
I don't feel well today.
Please fold the paper like this.
en.notes: 具合 refers to the condition of something, but above all to one's state of health: 具合が悪い "to feel unwell, to be sick", politely お具合はいかがですか. Devices also have a 具合: パソコンの具合がおかしい "something is wrong with the PC". In こんな具合に / そういう具合に it means "in this way". 調子 is similar, but stresses form and performance (調子がいい); 気分が悪い means more nausea or a bad mood.

examples[].german: Isn't that an image of propaganda that was created deliberately?
I ignored it on purpose.
en.notes: 意図的 describes something that happens on purpose. Before a noun it takes な, as in 意図的な行動; as an adverbial it takes に: 意図的に無視する. It stresses the contrast with an oversight. The question in the first example expresses a conjecture about how the image came about, not an established fact.

examples[].german: This is really modern, isn't it?
This building has a modern design.
The small village of old has turned into a modern town.
en.notes: 近代的 is a な-adjective: 近代的な建物, 近代的に発展する. It means "modern" in the sense of "modernized, up to date", often in contrast to traditional or old-fashioned - typical for cities, buildings, facilities and ways of thinking. 近代 is the modern era (in Japan from the Meiji period on); 現代的 emphasizes "contemporary, of today", and モダン is often used for stylish, modern design.

examples[].german: There are various kinds.
This store has many kinds of cake.
en.notes: 種類 refers to a kind, type, or category. Before another noun, の is used: いろいろな種類のケーキ, "various kinds of cake". たくさんの種類 emphasizes variety, not the number of individual pieces. The independent noun is taught here; an attached counting use is a separate grammatical use.

examples[].german: When I give the signal, please jump high.
The teacher gave the signal.
Let's wait for the signal to depart.
When I give the signal, please start the squats.
Please send the signal.
en.notes: 合図 is an agreed-upon sign or signal. 合図をする and 合図を出す mean to give a signal; 合図を待つ means to wait for it. The bare form is a noun that is also used with する. In the first example the action begins only after the signal. 相図 is a rare spelling of the same word.

examples[].german: I instinctively felt that it was bad news.
Animals act on instinct.
Protecting one's children is a mother's instinct.
en.notes: 本能 is a noun: "instinct, innate drive". Typical are 本能で行動する "to act instinctively" and the adverb 本能的に "instinctively"; also compounds such as 母性本能 "maternal instinct" or 生存本能 "survival instinct". 直感, on the other hand, is "intuition, gut feeling" in a specific situation, while 本能 means the innate behavior of humans and animals.

examples[].german: Tomorrow is sports day.
There is a sports day in autumn.
At sports day, my son ran in the relay.
en.notes: 運動会 is the sports day at Japanese kindergartens and schools, usually in autumn (sometimes in spring), with relay races, tug-of-war and 玉入れ; families come to watch and bring bento. One says 運動会がある, 運動会に出る, 運動会で走る. At middle and high schools the event is often called 体育祭; companies and communities also hold 運動会.

en.meaning: to warm up; to get warm
examples[].german: I'll wait here until the shower water gets warm.
I got into the bath and warmed up.
Hearing that story warmed my heart.
en.notes: 温まる is intransitive: something or someone gets warm (体が温まる, スープが温まる); the transitive counterpart is 温める "to warm up" (スープを温める). For rooms, air and weather one usually writes 暖まる (部屋が暖まる), for liquids, food and the body 温まる. Figuratively: 心が温まる "it warms one's heart", 心温まる話 "heartwarming story".

examples[].german: There is a bad wolf in "Little Red Riding Hood".
There was a wolf in the forest.
He is the lone wolf of the class.
en.notes: 狼 is the wolf; in Japan the native wolf (ニホンオオカミ) is extinct, and in zoo and nonfiction texts オオカミ is often written in katakana. Wolves howl: 狼が遠吠えする. Fixed expressions: 一匹狼 "lone wolf, loner" and, colloquially, 狼 or 送り狼 for a man who is after women. They are counted with 匹 or 頭.

examples[].german: A werewolf has apparently shown up again.
I watched a werewolf movie.
It is said that werewolves transform on full-moon nights.
en.notes: 狼男 is the werewolf of Western legends and horror films, who turns into a wolf on full-moon nights (満月の夜に狼に変身する). The word is mostly encountered in movies, games and Halloween costumes. For a man who pursues women, one does not say 狼男 but simply 狼.

examples[].german: That man is a famous bestselling author.
I want to become a writer in the future.
A new book by my favorite author has come out.
en.notes: 作家 is a writer or author as a profession (人気作家, 作家になる); in the arts also an artist (陶芸作家 "ceramic artist"). 小説家 is specifically "novelist". The author of a particular work is 作者 (この本の作者), the author of the present text, formally, 筆者. Manga artists, by contrast, are 漫画家.

examples[].german: He is a person who prefers classical music.
I prefer quiet places.
This dish is popular with young people.
en.notes: 好む is transitive (X を好む) and much more literary than 好き; in conversation one says 静かな所が好きです instead of 静かな所を好みます. Common are the passive 好まれる "to be popular" (若い人に好まれる), the negative 好まない, and 好んで～する "to do something gladly, of one's own will". Related are the noun 好み "taste, preference" and お好み焼き.

examples[].german: Since there are all kinds of people, it is only natural that different opinions come up.
You can eat dishes from various countries.
Favorite foods differ from person to person.
en.notes: 様々 is a な-adjective: 様々な国, 様々な意見; as a predicate 人によって様々だ "it differs from person to person". It means the same as いろいろ or, colloquially, 色んな, but sounds a little more formal and is typical of writing, news and talks. 々 is the repetition mark; さまざま is also often written in hiragana.

examples[].german: This band's vocalist is from Fukushima.
The fruit from Fukushima is delicious.
In summer vacation I'm going to my grandmother's house in Fukushima Prefecture.
en.notes: 福島 is a proper name: the prefecture 福島県 in the Tōhoku region and its capital 福島市; also a common family name. To distinguish, one says 福島県 or 福島市. Fukushima is known for peaches and other fruit, sake and onsen; internationally also for the nuclear accident of 2011 (福島第一原発).

examples[].german: Buddhism began in ancient India.
I learned about the teachings of Buddhism.
In Japan, many families hold funerals in the Buddhist way.
en.notes: 仏教 is Buddhism; a Buddhist is 仏教徒, Buddhist temples are called お寺 (as opposed to the Shintō shrines 神社). Buddhism came to Japan via Korea in the 6th century. Many Japanese combine both religions: weddings and New Year are often Shintō, funerals mostly Buddhist (仏式).

examples[].german: That great Buddha statue is about 15 meters tall.
Let's go see the Great Buddha in Kamakura.
The Great Buddha of Nara is at Tōdai-ji Temple.
en.notes: 大仏 is a large Buddha statue, usually with a place name: 奈良の大仏 at the temple 東大寺 and 鎌倉の大仏 are the best known. A Buddha statue in general is 仏像; 大仏 are only the especially large ones. One says 大仏を見る, 大仏にお参りする.

examples[].german: My mother is a very devout person.
There is a proverb, "Even a sardine head becomes sacred through faith".
Young people are not as devout as they used to be.
en.notes: 信心 is religious faith, piety toward gods or Buddha. It is most often encountered in 信心深い（しんじんぶかい）"pious, devout" and in the proverb 鰯の頭も信心から. More general and formal is 信仰 "faith, religion" (信仰する); trust in people, by contrast, is 信用 or 信頼.

examples[].german: Honestly, I felt a little distrust toward that shop assistant's words.
Distrust of politicians is growing.
After being lied to so many times, I came to distrust people.
en.notes: 不信 is a noun: "distrust, disbelief". It rarely stands alone, but mostly in compounds: 不信感 "feeling of distrust" (不信感を持つ／抱く), 政治不信 "disillusionment with politics", 人間不信 "distrust of people". Beware of the identically pronounced 不審 "suspicious" (不審な人 "suspicious person"). In daily life, people often simply say 信じられない or 信用できない.

examples[].german: No, I haven't replied yet.
Please reply to the email.
Sorry for the late reply.
en.notes: 返信 is the written reply to an email, letter or message: メールに返信する, 返信が来る, 返信を待つ. 返事 is more general and also applies to spoken replies ("Yes!" in response to a call); 答え is the answer to a question, 回答 to a survey or inquiry. Not to be confused with the homophone 変身 "transformation".

examples[].german: This district is family-oriented and comfortable to live in.
This district is quiet.
The baseball club won the district tournament.
en.notes: 地区 is a noun for a delimited area, neighborhood or district, often with a function: 住宅地区 "residential area", 商業地区 "business district", 地区大会 "district tournament". It sounds somewhat official. 地域 is broader and means "area, region, community", 地方 "region, province"; 区 is the administrative ward of a large city (新宿区).

examples[].german: WaniKani is good for studying Japanese vocabulary.
I learn new words every day.
I don't understand the meaning of this word.
en.notes: 単語 is the individual word as a unit of learning: 単語を覚える "to learn vocabulary", 英単語 "English vocabulary word", 単語帳 "vocabulary notebook". 言葉 is much broader ("word, language, utterance"), and 語彙 ("vocabulary") means the whole stock of words. When asking about the meaning of a word, you say この単語の意味 or simply この言葉の意味.

examples[].german: There seem to be a lot of oddballs in this town.
He is a bit of an oddball.
Geniuses are often said to be eccentrics.
en.notes: 変人 refers to an oddball or eccentric, slightly derogatory, but among friends also jokingly affectionate. More neutral are 変わった人 or 変わり者; 変な人 is the plain description "strange person" and can also mean "suspicious person". Typical: 変人扱いされる "to be treated as a weirdo".

examples[].german: The body of a man was found in the mountains under unexplained circumstances.
The cause of the unnatural death is being investigated.
The singer died under mysterious circumstances while traveling.
en.notes: 変死 is a term from police and news reports for an unnatural or unexplained death (accident, suicide, crime or unknown cause). Common are 変死体 "body found under unexplained circumstances" and, in writing, 変死を遂げる; 変死する is intransitive. In everyday speech one rather says 不自然な死に方 or names the cause directly (事故で亡くなる).

examples[].german: In what year did the Shanghai Incident occur?
In history class, we learned about the Manchurian Incident.
At that time, the Japanese government called the war an "incident".
en.notes: 事変 is a historical term for an armed conflict or incident without a formal declaration of war, above all in names such as 満州事変 (Mukden Incident, 1931) or 上海事変. The Japanese government of the time euphemistically called wars 事変. In everyday speech, 事件 "incident, crime", 事故 "accident" or 出来事 "event" are used instead.

examples[].german: Ah, I left my umbrella on the train.
Oh, there's a kitten in the garden!
en.notes: あ is a short exclamation used when you suddenly notice or remember something: "ah!" or "oh!". It can stand before a whole sentence. In writing, a comma often follows. あっ is a related form, abruptly cut off; this card practices the short あ. The long ああ has its own meanings and cards. The examples show remembering a forgotten item and the surprising discovery of an animal.

examples[].german: I want to become like that in the future, too.
When someone says it like that, I can't refuse.
en.notes: ああ means "in that way" or "like that" and points to something that speaker and listener regard as distant or known. ああなりたい names a role model; ああ言われると reacts to the way something was said. This card covers the adverb of the series こう・そう・ああ・どう, not the identically sounding exclamation "Ah!".

examples[].german: Asked "Have you made the reservation yet?", I answered, "Yeah, yesterday."
My friend said, "That movie was good, wasn't it?" so I nodded and said, "Yeah, it really was."
en.notes: ああ here is a short affirmative reply: "yes", "right" or "exactly". You use it to confirm a question or agree with a statement. This reply belongs in casual conversation and, depending on tone, can sound calm or a bit curt; for a polite answer you would rather use はい or ええ. It is pronounced with a long a. The emotional exclamation "ah!" and the adverb ああ "in that way" have their own cards. The examples distinguish confirming a completed action from agreeing with a shared assessment.

examples[].german: I saw wild lions in Africa.
There are more than fifty countries in Africa.
en.notes: アフリカ is the continent of Africa and is written in katakana. アフリカで names the place of an activity; アフリカには describes what exists on the continent. The origin is expressed with アフリカの, for example for goods. 五十以上 includes fifty and means at least fifty.

en.meaning: to greet; to give a speech
examples[].german: When I arrive at the office in the morning, I greet everyone.
I haven't greeted my new neighbor yet.
At the wedding, the company president gave a speech first.
en.notes: 挨拶する means "to greet"; the person greeted takes に (先生に挨拶する), and the form 挨拶をする is equivalent. At celebrations it also means "to give a short speech". The noun 挨拶 "greeting, words of welcome" has its own card. The kanji are difficult, so in daily life it is often written in kana as あいさつする.

examples[].german: Japan is an Asian country.
I like all Asian cuisines.
en.notes: アジア is the continent Asia. アジアの国 refers to a country in Asia; アジアの料理 dishes from Asian cuisines. 東南 in 東南アジア means southeast. To express origin or relation to the continent, the noun is often linked with の.

examples[].german: I created a new account.
This account is for work.
en.notes: アカウント here means a user account with a digital service. アカウントを作る means to create it; 仕事用です means it is intended for work purposes. A bank account is usually 口座. The noun アカウント refers to the access or the account, not to the associated password.

examples[].german: I hear it will rain tomorrow.
Please submit these documents by tomorrow.
en.notes: 明日 is read あす on this card and means "tomorrow". There is also the everyday reading あした. A time expression like 明日 stands without に in these sentences. 明日は names the topic of the weather report; 〜そうです here reports information that was heard. 明日までに sets a deadline: the documents are to be handed in tomorrow at the latest.

en.meaning: only, nothing but; about, approximately; just (〜たばかり)
examples[].german: My little brother does nothing but play games.
I just ate lunch a little while ago.
I waited about ten minutes at the station.
en.notes: ばかり follows nouns or verb forms: 肉ばかり食べる "to eat only meat", 遊んでばかりいる "to do nothing but play", 食べたばかり "just ate". After quantities it means "about" (一時間ばかり), similar to ぐらい. Unlike だけ, ばかり often sounds reproachful ("always only"). Colloquially often ばっかり; written almost always in kana, the kanji form 許り is rare.

examples[].german: The second person from the right is my older brother.
What is the second highest mountain in Japan?
Which position from the top is your name in the roster?
en.notes: Suffix attached after a number for the position in a sequence: 二番目, 三番目, 何番目; with に for rankings such as 二番目に高い "the second highest". Unlike 一番 ("most; number one"), 〜番目 counts neutrally; the prefixed 第〜 is more literary, 〜回目 counts repetitions. 一番目 and 三番目 have their own cards.

examples[].german: There is a Vietnamese student in my class.
Vietnamese coffee is sweet.
en.notes: ベトナム is the country name Vietnam. ベトナムの学生 describes the origin of a student; ベトナムのコーヒー the origin or national style of the coffee. For a person from Vietnam you say ベトナム人. The noun is written in katakana.

examples[].german: In Brazil they speak Portuguese.
I bought Brazilian coffee.
en.notes: ブラジル is the country name Brazil. ブラジルでは introduces a statement about the country; ブラジルのコーヒー names the origin of a product. The official language is called ポルトガル語. The word is written in katakana and is a noun.

examples[].german: I saw pigs and cows on the farm.
Pigs are animals with a very good sense of smell.
en.notes: 豚 here means the animal pig. 豚を飼う means to keep pigs; 豚の鼻 means the snout or the nose of the animal. Pork is unambiguously called 豚肉. As a term for a person, 豚 can be strongly insulting; the examples speak exclusively about animals.

examples[].german: I chat with my friends in the evening.
We also accept questions by chat.
en.notes: チャット here means a digital chat. With する it becomes a verb, "to chat"; 友達と names the conversation partner. チャットで describes the communication channel, for example for questions to a service. The identically sounding word for the currency kyat is a different meaning.

examples[].german: I check the weather forecast before going out.
He always wears checked shirts.
Please sign this check.
en.notes: チェック here means checking or a check pattern. チェックする describes checking, for example a weather forecast. チェックのシャツ denotes a checked shirt; in this meaning the noun connects with の. To check in is チェックイン and is not taught on this card. In financial language, チェック can also mean a cheque, for example in Japanese information about American banks. 小切手 is the unambiguous Japanese term for this means of payment. In このチェックに署名する it is about signing a cheque, not about checking.

en.meaning: not at all; not a bit (with negative)
examples[].german: This movie wasn't interesting at all.
No matter how many times I explain, he doesn't understand at all.
en.notes: "Not at all, not a bit", only with a negative. More colloquial than 少しも or 全然.

examples[].german: The electricity bill was high this month.
The company pays the taxi fare.
en.notes: 〜代 here is an attached word element for costs or a fee: 電気代 is the electricity cost, タクシー代 the taxi fare. The wavy line shows that another word comes before it. This suffix is not an independent sentence particle. Other uses of 代, such as decades of age or generations, do not belong to this card.

examples[].german: I downloaded this app for free.
The download is taking a long time.
en.notes: ダウンロード is the downloading of digital data. ダウンロードする is a transitive verb: the app or file takes を. As a noun it can take に to name the activity that requires time. Transferring in the opposite direction is アップロード.

examples[].german: My grandfather received a telegram saying "Come home at once".
Since I couldn't attend the wedding, I sent my friend a congratulatory telegram.
en.notes: 電報 is a telegram: a message delivered as a written document. 電報を送る means to send a telegram, 電報を受け取る to receive one; 電報を打つ is also a fixed expression for sending. The word appears in older stories for urgent messages and, in Japan, also for formal congratulations or condolences. The examples contrast receiving an urgent summons with a wedding congratulation.

examples[].german: I bought cold medicine at the drugstore.
The drugstore in front of the station is open until ten at night.
en.notes: ドラッグストア is a store for over-the-counter medicines and other everyday goods. ドラッグストアで買う names the place of purchase; 駅前のドラッグストア refers to a specific branch at the station. 薬局 is also used for a pharmacy; the name alone does not say whether a branch processes prescriptions.

examples[].german: I dry my hair with a hair dryer.
Is there a hair dryer in the hotel room?
en.notes: ドライヤー here means a hair dryer. ドライヤーで髪を乾かす describes drying the hair with the device; ドライヤーはありますか asks whether there is one. The long final syllable is written doraiyā. The card shows the name of the device, not a verb.

examples[].german: On Saturday night I'm going out for drinks with friends.
We are open only in the morning on Saturdays too.
Are you free next Saturday?
en.notes: 土曜 is the short form of 土曜日 (its own card) and is very common in conversation, timetables and opening hours: 土曜の夜, 土曜休み; 土日 means "weekend". The meaning is the same; the short form just sounds a little more casual, while 土曜日 is preferred in letters and announcements. Do not confuse it with the homophone 土用 "dog days".

examples[].german: Please send the application form by fax.
This hospital still uses fax.
en.notes: ファックス refers to a fax and also to the fax machine. ファックスで送る means to send something by fax; ファックスを使う can refer to the machine or to the transmission. With する it becomes a verb for faxing. The stand-alone form on this card is a noun; the spelling FAX is also common.

en.meaning: Hello, is anybody home?; may I come in?
examples[].german: Hello. Is anyone there?
I called out 「ごめんください」 at the entrance of the shop.
No matter how many times I called 「ごめんください」, there was no answer.
en.notes: ごめんください is here the polite call at the entrance of a house or shop: you draw attention to yourself and, in effect, ask for admission. With どなたかいらっしゃいますか you ask whether anyone is there. It is not a general greeting for every encounter. The spelling ご免ください is attested; the usual kana form is what is learned.

en.meaning: there is; to exist (very polite for ある)
examples[].german: The restroom is on the second floor.
Do you have any questions?
en.notes: Very polite form of ある ("there is, to have") and, in でございます, of です. Typical in service situations: こちらにございます. The kanji 御座います is rare.

en.meaning: drinking cup, sake cup (in set phrases)
examples[].german: At the banquet, everyone raised their cups and prayed for the couple's happiness.
Even after the banquet ended, the two kept refilling their cups.
en.notes: 杯／はい can denote a cup for alcoholic drinks, especially in fixed or elevated phrases. 杯を挙げる means to raise the cup to drink or toast; 杯を重ねる means to drink repeatedly. The spelling 盃 is also attested. The common reading さかずき is learned separately. As a counter in 一杯／いっぱい, 杯 has a different function; this card shows the drinking cup in the phrases mentioned.

examples[].german: Today's dinner is hamburger steak.
Kids love hamburger steak.
I'm cooking hamburger steaks in a frying pan.
en.notes: ハンバーグ is a hamburger steak, i.e. the meat dish without a burger bun. The hamburger in a bun is called ハンバーガー. ハンバーグです can name the dish on the menu; ハンバーグを焼く describes its preparation. The long syllable バー is rendered with ā in hanbāgu.

examples[].german: I went to the airfield to pick up my father.
There is a small airfield on this island.
en.notes: 飛行場 refers to an airfield or landing field where aircraft take off and land. 空港 is the term for an airport; both words can refer to the same facility. 飛行場まで names the way there, 飛行場がある the presence of such a facility. The reading has two long vowels: hikōjō.

examples[].german: The child's cheeks are red from the cold.
While watching the movie, tears ran down my cheeks.
My grandmother held my cheeks in both hands and said, "You've grown big."
en.notes: The second, equally valid reading of 頬 "cheek" besides ほお (its own card). ほお is regarded as the standard and dictionary form and appears in the fixed words 頬杖（ほおづえ）and 頬張る（ほおばる）; ほほ is very common in spoken Japanese and is found in ほほえむ "to smile" (微笑む). In free use (頬が赤い) both readings are correct; ほほ sounds somewhat softer and more colloquial.

examples[].german: I checked the opening hours on the shop's website.
There are photos on the school's website.
en.notes: ホームページ can mean the start page, a web page or the whole website. In the examples it means the web presence of a shop or a school. ホームページで調べる describes looking something up there; ホームページに出ている says that something can be seen there. Both long vowels appear in hōmupēji.

examples[].german: I bought this plate at a 100-yen shop.
The 100-yen shop also has stationery.
en.notes: 百円ショップ is the name of a type of store associated with the base price of 100 yen. It does not follow that every single product there has the same price. 百円ショップで買う describes a purchase there; 百円ショップには…もある names a further part of the assortment. Colloquially such a store is also called 百均（ひゃっきん）.

en.meaning: not good, wrong; must not (…てはいけません); hopeless
examples[].german: You must not take photographs inside the museum.
I have to submit the report by tomorrow.
What, you have a fever? That's not good.
en.notes: Polite form of いけない; central in …てはいけません "you must not" (prohibition) and …なければいけません "you must" (obligation). On its own, それはいけませんね expresses sympathy: "That's terrible." Almost always written in kana, because 行けません is at the same time the potential form of 行く, "cannot go". Casually one says …ちゃだめ or …てはだめ.

en.meaning: must not (...てはいけない); bad; wrong; useless; too bad
examples[].german: You must not talk loudly in the library.
I have to hand in the report by tomorrow.
Oh no, I left my umbrella on the train!
en.notes: The plain (non-polite) form of いけません (its own card); it is the core of the patterns …てはいけない "must not" and …なければいけない "must". On its own, いけない means "bad, wrong" (いけない子) or serves as an exclamation "Damn!, Oh no!" when one notices a mistake. Almost always in kana; when written 行けない it is more likely read as "cannot go" (potential of 行く).

en.meaning: as much as one likes; any amount
examples[].german: You can have as many refills of rice as you like.
As for time, I have plenty.
en.notes: いくらでも expresses a freely chosen or very large amount. For refills of rice it means "as much as you like"; 時間ならいくらでもある stresses that there is plenty of time. The expression is used here as an adverb and does not denote a number. The meaning follows from the thing mentioned and the situation of the conversation.

examples[].german: My older brother is a bank employee and leaves the house early every morning.
I didn't know the way, so I asked a station employee.
If you become a member of this gym, you can also use the pool.
en.notes: Suffix for persons who belong to an organization or work there: 会社員 "company employee", 店員 "shop clerk", 駅員 "station employee", 会員 "member", 公務員 "civil servant". 員 practically never stands alone; as a standalone word people say メンバー or 一員（いちいん）. Unlike 〜者（しゃ） "person who does ...", 〜員 emphasizes belonging to a group or staff. Do not confuse it with the homophone 韻（いん） "rhyme".

examples[].german: Indian curry is spicy.
A lot of people live in India.
en.notes: インド is the country name India. インドの… assigns something to the country; インドに住む describes living there. A person from India is called インド人. インドネシア, by contrast, means Indonesia, a different country. What is learned is the usual katakana spelling, not the kanji spelling 印度.

examples[].german: I booked the hotel on the Internet.
The Internet can't be used in this room.
en.notes: インターネット refers to the Internet and is also shortened to ネット. インターネットで names the means of an action, such as an online booking. インターネットが使える or 使えない describes whether you can use an Internet connection. The long syllable ター is rendered with ā in intānetto.

examples[].german: On the trip I made friends with people from various countries.
This shop has all kinds of bread.
en.notes: 色んな stands directly before a noun and means "various" or "all sorts of". It is a colloquial prenominal word（連体詞）; neither な nor だ is attached to it. In familiar conversation it is often written いろんな. 色々な has a different form. The examples show different countries of origin and various kinds of bread.

examples[].german: I saw a dolphin show at the aquarium.
Dolphins are very intelligent animals.
en.notes: イルカ means a dolphin. The katakana spelling is usual here; 海豚 is a rare kanji spelling with the reading いるか. イルカのショー names a performance with dolphins, イルカは… a statement about the animals. 頭がいい in the second example means that they are intelligent.

examples[].german: Threading a needle is difficult.
I sewed my name with red thread.
A string on the shamisen broke.
en.notes: 糸 means thread, yarn or a thin string. 針に糸を通す means to pull a thread through the eye of a needle; 糸で縫う describes sewing with thread. With the 三味線, 糸 can mean the string. The identically read 意図, by contrast, means "intention" and is a different word.

examples[].german: I want to climb Mt. Fuji someday.
Let's meet again somewhere sometime.
I tried going to the ramen shop I talked about the other day.
en.notes: Refers to an indefinite point in time, mostly in the future ("someday"), more rarely in the past ("the other day, once"). Almost always in kana; 何時か is a rare spelling. Do not confuse it with 五日/いつか "the 5th of the month; five days" (own card), which sounds the same. Also to be distinguished from いつでも "any time" and いつも "always".

en.meaning: I'll be going (and coming back) - humble-polite
examples[].german: Well then, I'll go to the bank.
Saying 「行ってまいります」, he bowed to the department head.
en.notes: 行ってまいります is said by the person leaving when departing temporarily. まいります is the humble polite form; the greeting corresponds functionally to 行ってきます and implies a return is expected. In the office it can be used to announce going to an appointment. The person staying can reply with 行ってらっしゃい.

en.meaning: See you later! (said to someone leaving home)
examples[].german: "I'm off." "See you later. Be careful."
The hotel staff said 「行ってらっしゃいませ」 to me.
en.notes: The reply to 行ってきます: the person who stays says this to bid farewell to someone who is leaving and will come back. More polite: 行ってらっしゃいませ (for example in a hotel). On the return, ただいま and おかえりなさい follow.

examples[].german: How do you read this character?
She has very beautiful handwriting.
en.notes: Written character, letter; also handwriting: 字がきれい (beautiful writing). Kanji in general: 漢字; written characters in general: 文字.

en.meaning: throughout; all over; all; until the end (suffix)
examples[].german: It rained all day yesterday.
I will finish this work within today.
This song is known all over the world.
Congratulatory letters arrived from all my relatives.
en.notes: じゅう covers an entire period, place or group of people: 一日中 "all day", 世界中 "all over the world", 親戚中 "all the relatives". With に, a time limit can be meant: 今日中に means "within today, before today is over". Which reading 中 takes depends on the combination and meaning; 工事中, by contrast, is read こうじちゅう.

examples[].german: It's about ten minutes on foot to the station.
The meeting starts in ten minutes.
There is a ten-minute break between classes.
en.notes: As a time expression, 十分 is read じっぷん or, in conversation nowadays more often, じゅっぷん "ten minutes". The same spelling read じゅうぶん means "enough, sufficient" (its own card); for this reason minutes are mostly written with numerals as 10分. With 〜間, 十分間 emphasizes the duration.

en.meaning: person with a profession, interest or inclination (suffix)
examples[].german: A photographer is taking pictures of the sea.
My younger brother is a hard worker who practices every day.
en.notes: 家（か）forms a word for a person after a noun. 写真家 is a photographer; 努力家 names someone who makes great efforts. The suffix can thus express an occupation or a pronounced trait. It is attached directly to the preceding element. 家（いえ）for "house" and 家（け）after a family name are other readings.

en.meaning: opening; leaving open; opening to the public
examples[].german: Every Saturday is a day when the schoolyard is open to the public.
The government is pushing ahead with opening up the agricultural products market.
This room has a high ceiling and a feeling of spaciousness.
en.notes: The noun of the verb 開放する (to open, make accessible); typical in 校庭開放 "opening of the schoolyard", 市場の開放 "opening of the market" and 開放感 "feeling of spaciousness". Do not confuse it with the homophones 解放 (liberation from coercion or captivity) and 介抱 (nursing a sick person): 開放 opens doors, spaces and markets, 解放 frees people.

examples[].german: It might rain from this afternoon.
The road is crowded, so I might be a little late.
What he is saying may be true.
en.notes: Expresses a possibility and stands at the end of a sentence after the plain form of verbs and i-adjectives, or directly after nouns and na-adjectives (本当かもしれない, 静かかもしれない). Polite: かもしれません; colloquially shortened: かも. It is less certain than でしょう/だろう "probably". Usually in kana; かも知れない is rarer.

examples[].german: I studied English in Canada.
The mountains in Canada were very beautiful.
en.notes: カナダ is the country name Canada. カナダで names the place of an activity, such as a language course. カナダの… assigns something to the country, such as its mountains. The usual katakana spelling is the one to learn; the kanji spelling 加奈陀 is rare.

en.meaning: (my) wife; family, household; inside the home
examples[].german: My wife is out at the moment.
My wife and I went to a hot spring, just the two of us.
My whole family is deeply grateful.
I did cottage-industry work at home.
en.notes: 家内 has three related meanings here with the same reading かない. As a humble term it means one's own wife when speaking to others; 妻 is another term for this, while 奥さん is used for another person's wife. In 家内一同, 家内 refers to the whole family. The spatial meaning "inside the house" also appears as a component of 家内工業, home industry. For an everyday statement of location, 家の中 is used. The respective combination shows which meaning is intended.

examples[].german: In the Showa era, my grandmother worked as a nurse in a hospital.
In that story, a night-shift nurse encourages an anxious patient.
en.notes: 看護婦 means a nurse and is an older job title referring to women. It appears in earlier stories and occasionally still colloquially. The common job title today is 看護師, regardless of gender. 看護婦として働く describes the work; a 看護婦 can also appear as a character in an older story. The examples contrast a former profession with the care of a patient in a story.

examples[].german: A new confectionery shop opened in front of the station.
I bought a sweet bun at the convenience store for breakfast.
Tea and sweets had been prepared in the guest room.
en.notes: The base word without the polite prefix お. When speaking on its own, people almost always say お菓子（おかし）in everyday life; 菓子 alone sounds written or technical and appears mainly in compounds: 菓子パン "sweet bun", 菓子店 "confectionery shop", 和菓子（わがし）"Japanese sweets", 洋菓子（ようがし）"Western sweets" (with voiced が there). Do not confuse it with the homophones 歌詞 "song lyrics" and 貸し "lending".

examples[].german: This castle is easy to defend and hard to attack.
It is not hard to imagine that he was disappointed.
en.notes: 難い（かたい） is a standalone i-adjective meaning "difficult". It sounds literary and appears, for example, in 想像するに難くない "not hard to imagine". The form 難く（かたく） stands before ない. The attached suffix ～難い（がたい） in 信じ難い and ～難い（にくい） in 読み難い have their own readings and are not equated here. The old proverbial form 難し（かたし） is not a modern base form. 固い, 硬い and 堅い denote other kinds of hardness or firmness.

examples[].german: The price is high, but you can use it for a long time.
I practiced, but I couldn't win the match.
en.notes: けど joins two clauses with a contrast in spoken language: "but" or "although". It is a short form of けれども and stands directly after the first clause, for example 高いけど "it's expensive, but ..." or 練習したけど "although I practiced ...". After a noun or な-adjective, だけど is usually used. In formal writing, けれども and が are more common. The independent けど at the start of a new sentence has its own card.

examples[].german: I'm busy today. But I can talk for a little while.
He took the wrong road. But he still made it by the agreed time.
en.notes: As an independent conjunction, けど can stand at the start of a new sentence: "but" or "however". It picks up a previously stated fact and contrasts it with a qualification or an unexpected result. This short form of けれども is colloquial; in more formal writing, けれども or しかし fit. The particle けど, which directly joins two clauses, is practiced on its own card.

examples[].german: I fell down the stairs and hurt my leg.
I hear three people were injured in the accident.
When you use a kitchen knife, be careful not to hurt yourself.
en.notes: Verb form of the noun card 怪我（けが）"injury". In everyday use, 怪我をする is just as common as 怪我する; the injured body part takes を (足を怪我する). It means "to injure oneself (unintentionally)"; to injure someone else is 怪我をさせる. Often written in kana (けがする); compare 傷（きず）"wound" and 痛める "to hurt, to strain something".

examples[].german: We are planning a family trip for the summer vacation.
I secretly planned a friend's birthday party.
The company is planning to build a new factory next year.
en.notes: 計画する is transitive: the thing planned takes を (旅行を計画する), whole undertakings take 〜ことを計画する. With the noun 計画 (own card) one also says 計画を立てる "to draw up a plan". 予定, by contrast, is a fixed appointment or an item in the calendar, whereas 計画 stresses preparation and organization.

en.meaning: counter for houses, buildings and shops
examples[].german: There is one bookstore near the station.
There are as many as three convenience stores on this street.
Yesterday I went around many izakaya with my friends.
en.notes: Counts houses, shops, restaurants and other buildings: 一軒 (いっけん), 二軒, 三軒 (さんげん), 六軒 (ろっけん), 八軒 (はっけん), 十軒 (じゅっけん), question word 何軒 (なんげん). 一軒家 means "detached house". The card 軒/のき, on the other hand, teaches the noun "eaves"; do not confuse it with 〜件 (cases, matters) and 〜県 (prefecture).

examples[].german: This restaurant is expensive, but very delicious.
It had been raining. Nevertheless, the match was held.
en.notes: "But, however", at the beginning of a sentence or after a sentence. More polite and more written than けど, more casual than しかし. Also as a soft introduction: すみませんけれども… (Excuse me, but ...).

examples[].german: This keyboard is easy to type on.
I spilled coffee on the keyboard.
My older sister plays keyboard in a band.
en.notes: キーボード means "keyboard" on a computer and, in a band, usually the "keyboard" as an electronic keyed instrument. For typing, 打つ or 入力する fits; for playing, 弾く. The two long vowels are written with ī and ō in kībōdo. Which object is meant follows from the situation.

examples[].german: Giraffes have very long necks.
The giraffe is eating the leaves of a tall tree.
en.notes: Mostly in katakana; the kanji 麒麟 also denote the Chinese mythical creature qilin (logo of the Kirin brewery).

examples[].german: I calculated this data on a computer.
My father writes computer programs at his company.
en.notes: General term for a computer; for your own machine you usually say パソコン in daily life. The spelling without the long-vowel mark（コンピュータ）is widespread in technology and administration.

examples[].german: When I was a child, I often swam in the river.
Tomorrow I will arrive at the station around ten o'clock.
en.notes: After times of day and dates it is read ごろ and often written in hiragana: 十時ごろ "around ten o'clock". After nouns with の or after clauses it is ころ: 子どもの頃 "when I was a child". Related: この頃（このごろ）"these days, lately".

examples[].german: The entrance ceremony is held in the auditorium.
All the students gathered in the auditorium.
en.notes: Auditorium, assembly hall of a school or university. Same sound: 行動 (action).

examples[].german: I live in Setagaya Ward in Tokyo.
Many foreigners live in this ward.
en.notes: Ward (of a large city), e.g. the 23 wards of Tokyo (渋谷区). Ward office: 区役所.

examples[].german: White clouds are floating in the sky.
Dark clouds have appeared, so it looks like rain.
en.notes: Cloud. Cloudy: 曇り（くもり）. Same sound: 蜘蛛 (spider), in standard Japanese even with the same pitch pattern.

examples[].german: I was in the photography club in high school.
I practice at a tennis club on weekends.
I borrowed a golf club.
I drew the ace of clubs.
en.notes: Association, club (テニスクラブ; at schools also クラブ活動 = 部活), nightclub, golf club. The card suit of clubs is also called クラブ.

examples[].german: Please click the button at the top right.
You can order with a single click.
en.notes: As a verb with する: ボタンをクリックする. Double-click: ダブルクリック. On a smartphone, タップ is used more.

examples[].german: Something urgent came up, so I can't go.
This slope is very steep, so be careful.
en.notes: な-adjective: sudden (急な雨), urgent (急な用事) or steep (急な坂). Adverb: 急に (suddenly). Same sound: 九.

en.meaning: as it is, unchanged; while (a state remains); as one likes
examples[].german: Please don't enter the room with your shoes on.
I fell asleep with the window open and caught a cold.
Many old houses remain in this town just as they were in the past.
en.notes: A formal noun that expresses an unchanged state: verb in た-form + まま (窓を開けたまま寝る "to sleep with the window open"), noun + のまま (昔のまま), also 言われるままに "as one is told". Unlike 〜ながら, まま does not describe a second action but a state that remains, often unexpectedly. そのまま has its own card; do not confuse it with ママ "mama" and 間々 "occasionally". Almost always in kana.

examples[].german: The mouse stopped working.
Please select the file with the mouse.
en.notes: The computer mouse. The animal is called ネズミ in everyday speech; マウス otherwise refers to laboratory mice.

examples[].german: I'll send the details later by email.
Last night I messaged a friend.
en.notes: Mostly email or mobile messages; as a verb, メールする means "to send a message". Postal mail is called 郵便 or 手紙.

examples[].german: Please tell me your email address.
I'm contacting you because I changed my email address.
en.notes: Often shortened to メアド or アドレス. The @ sign is called アットマーク.

examples[].german: She laughed innocently like a child.
It's getting dark outside. It looks like it will rain.
Winning the lottery would be like a dream.
en.notes: みたい is the colloquial equivalent of ようだ: noun + みたい "like, similar to" (子供みたい), sentence + みたい "apparently" (雨みたいだ). It inflects like a na-adjective: みたいな + noun, みたいに + verb. Compared with らしい, みたい expresses more one's own impression. Do not confuse it with 〜てみたい "want to try" (from みる).

en.meaning: -th year student (suffix, e.g. 三年生, 大学二年生)
examples[].german: My younger brother is a third-year elementary school student.
"What year are you in?" "I'm a second-year university student."
The sixth-graders go on a school trip next month.
en.notes: Suffix after a number for the grade level or year of study: 小学三年生, 高校二年生, 大学四年生; you ask with 何年生ですか. The separate card 一年生 additionally covers "beginner, newcomer". Do not confuse it with 〜年 (years, year number) and the identically pronounced 粘性 "viscosity".

examples[].german: I bought this book online.
The ball hit the net.
en.notes: Short form of インターネット (ネットで買う = to buy online). Also a real net, e.g. in tennis.

examples[].german: On Sunday mornings I sleep in.
My father's hobby is DIY carpentry.
That shop's regular closing day is Sunday.
en.notes: 日曜 is the short form of 日曜日 (its own card) with the same meaning, typical of conversation, timetables and opening hours (日曜休み, 日曜の朝). It is fixed in compounds such as 日曜大工 "DIY" and 日曜版 "Sunday edition". In formal texts and announcements, the full form 日曜日 is preferred.

examples[].german: According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
According to the news, there was an accident near the station.
According to what Mr./Ms. Tanaka says, that shop will close next month.
en.notes: 〜によると names the source of information and usually stands at the beginning of the sentence: 天気予報によると "according to the weather forecast". The sentence then typically ends with a hearsay form such as 〜そうです or 〜ということです. Equivalent and somewhat more written is 〜によれば. Do not confuse it with ことによると "possibly" and with the verb 拠る "to be based on"; the kanji spelling に依ると is rare.

en.meaning: Welcome back! (short for お帰りなさい); homecoming, way back (polite)
examples[].german: "I'm home!" "Welcome back. You're early today."
Please use the exit over there on your way out.
About what time will the company president be back?
en.notes: As a greeting, the casual short form of お帰りなさい (own card): family and friends answer ただいま with it, whereas お帰りなさい sounds somewhat more polite and complete. As a polite noun, お帰り means the "homecoming, way home" of a respected person, for example 社長のお帰り, or on signs お帰りはこちら "Exit". In the greeting it is often written in kana (おかえり).

examples[].german: Please, have a seat here.
I will call you in order, so please have a seat on the chairs over there.
Interviewer: "Please have a seat." Student: "Excuse me." (thank you)
en.notes: A polite request to sit down, formed from お + stem of 掛ける (here "to sit down") + ください; usually written in kana. You hear it at reception, at a doctor's office or in a job interview. Simpler is 座ってください, even more polite おかけになってください. The card 掛ける teaches only "to hang"; this sense "to sit down" lives mainly in this phrase.

examples[].german: In the future I want to become rich and live in a big house.
That person is rich, yet always wears cheap clothes.
She was born into a wealthy family.
en.notes: The polite, softer form of 金持ち（かねもち）"rich person", with the prefix お. In conversation お金持ち sounds more natural and friendly; 金持ち is neutral to somewhat blunt (金持ちのくせに) and appears in compounds like 大金持ち. Common in お金持ちになる "to become rich" and お金持ちの家 "wealthy family".

examples[].german: How old is your child?
I hear Mr./Ms. Tanaka's child is a university student.
en.notes: Polite for other people's children; about one's own children, 子ども or うちの子 is said.

examples[].german: Japan's population is about 120 million.
This painting sold for 300 million yen.
en.notes: The Japanese number system groups in steps of four digits: 万 = 10,000, 億 = 100,000,000, 兆 = 1,000,000,000,000. 一億 is "one hundred million", 十億 "one billion".

en.meaning: Sorry to keep you waiting; thank you for waiting
examples[].german: Sorry to keep you waiting. Here is your coffee.
Excuse me, sorry to keep you waiting.
en.notes: "Sorry to keep you waiting" - very common in restaurants and shops; among friends, simply お待たせ！ Even more polite: 大変お待たせいたしました.

examples[].german: Congratulations on your marriage.
Happy New Year. I look forward to your continued support this year as well.
en.notes: Polite form of おめでとう. The occasion comes first, often with ご／お: 誕生日おめでとうございます, ご結婚おめでとうございます, at New Year 明けましておめでとうございます.

examples[].german: The main industry of this town is tourism.
The main cause of the accident was excessive speed.
First, I will explain the main purpose of the meeting.
en.notes: 主な stands only directly before a noun and is not conjugated: 主な原因 "main cause", 主な目的 "main purpose", 主な産業 "most important industry". As a predicate (～は主だ) it is uncommon; for that, 中心だ or 一番大事だ is rather said. The related adverb is 主に "mainly"; 主なる is the stiff, literary variant of the same word. Do not confuse it with 主（しゅ）"lord" or 主（ぬし）"owner".

examples[].german: There are kangaroos in Australia.
December is summer in Australia.
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Note: オーストリア is Austria, a difference of just one ラ. In news also 豪州（ごうしゅう）.

examples[].german: My swimming teacher taught me how to do the crawl.
When I switched to a less tiring way of swimming, I could swim longer than before.
en.notes: 泳ぎ方 is the way one swims, or a swimming technique. The noun combines the stem form 泳ぎ with 方 "manner, way". 泳ぎ方を教える means to teach someone swimming or a technique; 泳ぎ方を変える means to change one's way of swimming. It denotes the method and can refer to a particular stroke such as クロール. The examples contrast learning a technique with adapting it to tire less quickly.

examples[].german: I saw a baby panda at the zoo.
Pandas eat bamboo all day long.
en.notes: A zoo animal in katakana; very popular in Japan. A police patrol car is jokingly called パンダ because of its black-and-white paint job.

examples[].german: Dad, look, look!
Our dad is good at cooking.
en.notes: Child-language "Dad"; adults also use it within the family. Formal: 父, 父親; as a form of address: お父さん.

examples[].german: I forgot my password.
Please make your password at least eight characters long.
en.notes: "To enter a password": パスワードを入力する. The PIN of a bank card, on the other hand, is called 暗証番号.

examples[].german: Penguins are birds, but they can't fly.
The children laughed when they saw the penguins walk.
