en.notes: A zoo animal, written in katakana. Penguins live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere; in Japan you see them in zoos and aquariums (水族館).

examples[].german: The printer is out of paper.
I printed the documents on the printer at the convenience store.
en.notes: Also written プリンタ. "To print out": 印刷する or, colloquially, プリントする.

examples[].german: The lion was sleeping at the zoo.
The lion is called the "king of beasts".
en.notes: A zoo animal, written in katakana. The lion as a zodiac sign: しし座.

examples[].german: I'll send the link to the meeting by email.
Please click this link.
en.notes: As a verb with する (to link). "To send a link": リンクを送る. Same sound: リンク (skating rink).

examples[].german: This library is used a lot by students.
On a day of heavy snow, I refrained from using the car.
en.notes: 利用 is the noun for the use or utilization of something. One speaks, for example, of 学生の利用 "use by students" or 車の利用 "use of a car". 利用が多い describes frequent use; 利用を控える means to limit or forgo use. With する it becomes the verb 利用する "to use", which has its own card. Here the examples show the frequent use of a facility and the deliberate renunciation of a means of transport.

examples[].german: You log in with your email address and password.
I haven't been able to log in since this morning and I'm at a loss.
en.notes: As a verb with する: サイトにログインする. Opposite: ログアウト.

examples[].german: Russia is the largest country in the world.
I hear the winters in Russia are very cold.
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Language: ロシア語. In compounds it is abbreviated as 露（ろ）, e.g. 日露.

examples[].german: I can't read Russian script.
She speaks Russian and Japanese.
en.notes: Country + 語（ご）= language. The Cyrillic script is called キリル文字.

en.meaning: -ness (nominalizing suffix for adjectives, e.g. 高さ, 寒さ, 便利さ) (suffix)
examples[].german: The height of this mountain is about three thousand meters.
I'm still not used to the cold of winter in Hokkaido.
Once you know how convenient a smartphone is, you can't give it up.
en.notes: Attaches to the stem of i- and na-adjectives and turns it into a noun for degree or extent: 高い → 高さ ("height"), 寒い → 寒さ ("cold"), 便利 → 便利さ ("convenience"). Very productive and neutrally measurable, whereas 〜み (e.g. 甘み, 痛み) rather expresses a felt quality and works only with a few adjectives. Do not confuse it with the sentence-final particle さ or with 差/さ ("difference").

examples[].german: You can find cheap hotels on this website.
Please see the company's website for details.
en.notes: Short for ウェブサイト. Also "site, grounds" (e.g. キャンプサイト).

examples[].german: My older brother called late last night.
It has been raining continuously since last night.
en.notes: 昨夜 with the reading さくや means "yesterday evening" or "last night". It seems more written or formal than ゆうべ, which can also be written 昨夜. 昨夜遅く means late yesterday evening or late last night; 昨夜から describes the beginning of a state during last night. As a time expression, 昨夜 often stands without a particle before the verb.

examples[].german: This watch is made in Switzerland.
Plastic cups are hard to break.
en.notes: Suffix meaning "made in / made of": 日本製 (made in Japan), ドイツ製, プラスチック製 (made of plastic).

en.meaning: to live; to spend one's daily life
examples[].german: I've been living on my own since I entered university.
Living on 100,000 yen a month is hard.
I lived for a week on an island without electricity.
en.notes: Suru-verb for the noun 生活 "life, daily life"; the place takes で (東京で生活する), and so do the means (年金で生活する). It stresses the way of life and livelihood, whereas 暮らす sounds somewhat warmer and more everyday, and 住む means only "to reside". For "to be alive", 生きる is used instead.

en.meaning: to take care of; to look after
examples[].german: My younger brother looks after the dog every day.
My mother takes care of my grandmother, who is in the hospital, every day.
Could you look after the cat while I'm on my trip?
en.notes: Most common is the form 〜の世話をする (犬の世話をする "to take care of the dog"); X を世話する is also possible but sounds a little more written. The person who receives help, on the other hand, says 世話になる or politely お世話になる (own cards). In the meaning "to arrange, to find for someone", one also says 仕事を世話する "to arrange a job".

examples[].german: The city library is open on Sundays too.
This city has three large parks.
en.notes: City as an administrative unit: 横浜市, 市役所 (city hall), 市長 (mayor). The reading いち means "market" (朝市).

examples[].german: We, the whole family, mourned grandfather's death.
The protagonist of this novel does not fear death.
en.notes: 死（し）is the noun for death, as in 死を悼む "to mourn a death" or 死を恐れる "to fear death". The verb is 死ぬ（しぬ）. The reading し applies here to the independent noun; it is not derived from the polite title 氏. The special use in baseball is not part of this card.

examples[].german: It's raining and it's already late, so let's go home today.
I'd like to go to that shop, but I have no money this month either.
en.notes: し here attaches to a completed statement and names one of several possible reasons. You can link reasons with …し、…し; not all of them need to be spoken. After nouns and na-adjectives, the plain form だし is used, for example 雨だし; after polite statements ですし is also possible. At the end of a sentence, し often leaves the conclusion unspoken and sounds conversational. The identically sounding number names and nouns belong to their own cards.

en.meaning: to put away; to store; to close (a shop)
examples[].german: Please put the scissors you used back in the drawer.
The rain got heavy, so we closed the shop early today.
en.notes: As a full verb, しまう means "to put away in its place" (usually written in hiragana, kanji 仕舞う). After the て-form (〜てしまう, colloquially 〜ちゃう) it expresses completion or regret; that grammar is covered in the grammar section.

examples[].german: Get ready quickly! You'll be late for school.
I'll be ready in five minutes, so please wait a moment.
I have already prepared everything needed for the trip.
en.notes: 支度する means practical preparation in daily life: getting ready to go out, preparing food, packing luggage. The form with the noun is also common: 出かける支度をする, 夕飯の支度をする (the noun 支度 has its own card). 準備する is more general and more formal (also for plans, events), 用意する stresses laying things out ready. The spelling 仕度する has the same meaning.

examples[].german: Shall we have a meal together before the movie?
I had a meal with my family at a restaurant.
en.notes: 食事する means to have a meal. 食事 alone is the noun "meal"; 食事をする is also possible. The full verb 食事する is intransitive. For a particular food as an object, one uses something like パンを食べる. With 〜しませんか you can politely invite someone to eat together. 一緒に means "together", と names the companion and で the place. The forms of する change, for example in 食事します, 食事しました and 食事して.

en.meaning: to agree, consent; to know, understand (polite)
examples[].german: Yes, understood. Please wait a moment.
I am fully aware of the danger.
My father wouldn't agree to my studying abroad for a long time.
en.notes: 承知する is a formal "to take note of, to consent". Very common at work is the humble-polite reply 承知しました "Understood, will do"; even more humble is かしこまりました, more casual 分かりました or 了解. ご承知のとおり means "as you know". With an object: X を承知する or X は承知している "to be aware of something". The noun 承知 has its own card.

examples[].german: An invitation to a wedding arrived from a friend.
Thank you for the invitation.
I was busy, so I declined the invitation to the party.
en.notes: 招待 is the formal invitation as a noun: 招待を受ける "to accept an invitation", 招待を断る "to decline", politely ご招待. The invitation card is called 招待状. The verb "to invite" is 招待する (own card); 正体 "true identity" is read the same but is a different word.

examples[].german: I bought a new video game.
She speaks in a soft voice.
en.notes: Several meanings: soft, gentle (ソフトな声); software (ゲームソフト); soft-serve ice cream (ソフトクリーム).

examples[].german: It's not that cold today.
If you insist that much, let's try it once.
en.notes: "So much, to that extent." Mostly with a negative: それほど難しくない = "not that difficult". Similar: そんなに.

examples[].german: Wednesday is the regular closing day, so the shop is closed.
I go to a yoga class every Wednesday night.
The meeting was postponed to next Wednesday.
en.notes: Short form of 水曜日 (its own card), especially in schedules, notices and casual conversation (水曜の夜, 毎週水曜, 水曜休み). In calendars often just 水. In formal texts and announcements, 水曜日 is more usual; all weekdays have such short forms (月曜, 金曜).

examples[].german: I taught my grandmother how to use a smartphone.
If you have a smartphone, please show the screen.
en.notes: Full form of スマホ; common in manuals and news, but in conversation almost always スマホ.

examples[].german: Many people look at their smartphones on the train.
I looked at the map on my smartphone.
en.notes: Colloquial short form of スマートフォン; much more common in everyday speech than the long form. Older mobile phones are called 携帯（けいたい）.

examples[].german: This recording is in stereo, so you hear different sounds from the left and right.
After repairing the old stereo, I was able to listen to records again.
en.notes: ステレオ denotes stereo sound with separate left and right channels and also a stereo system. ステレオで録音する means to record in stereo; ステレオを修理する to repair a stereo system. The opposite in sound format is モノラル "mono". This card practices the independent noun for sound and device. The word element ステレオ in terms for spatial vision has a different use.

en.meaning: straight, directly; quickly, suddenly; quietly, smoothly; (〜する) to feel relieved
examples[].german: When his name was called, he stood up smoothly.
After I took the medicine, the headache vanished all at once.
After I said everything I wanted to say, I felt relieved.
en.notes: Onomatopoeic adverb for a smooth, effortless and often sudden movement: すっと立ち上がる, 痛みがすっと消える, 手をすっと出す. With する, 気持ちがすっとする / 胸がすっとする means "to feel relieved, liberated". Do not confuse it with ずっと "all the time; much more" and そっと "quietly, gently"; すっと stresses the smooth and quick. In speech it is often drawn out as すーっと.

examples[].german: On the way home I buy milk at the supermarket.
This supermarket is open until 10 p.m.
en.notes: Short form of スーパーマーケット. As a prefix, スーパー also means "super-"; in daily life "supermarket" is the most common meaning.

examples[].german: The child is playing games on a tablet.
I take a tablet to meetings.
en.notes: Tablet computer. In a medical context it also means "tablet" (pill), but for that 錠剤（じょうざい）is mostly said.

examples[].german: It's hot all year round in Thailand.
I had dinner at a Thai restaurant.
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Similar-sounding are タイ (necktie) and 鯛（たい）(sea bream); context decides.

examples[].german: Even if it rains, the match will be held.
Even though it's expensive, I want this bag.
I envy people who don't gain weight no matter how much they eat.
en.notes: Concessive particle attached to the te-form of verbs and i-adjectives: 雨が降っても "even if it rains", 高くても "even if it's expensive". After nouns and na-adjectives, and with the voiced te-form, でも is used (学生でも, 読んでも). With いくら, どんなに or 何度 it means "no matter how (much/often)". Not to be confused with the conjunction でも "but" (vocab-n5:1195).

examples[].german: I bought a dictionary at the bookstore in front of the station.
This coffee shop is open from seven in the morning.
en.notes: 店（てん） stands at the end of names for shops or restaurants, such as 書店（しょてん）, bookstore, and 喫茶店（きっさてん）, cafe. The first part of the word says what kind of shop it is. As a standalone word for a shop, 店 is usually read みせ: 店に入る. Practice the compound names each with their full reading.

examples[].german: I borrowed a book from the Metropolitan library.
The trains in Tokyo are very convenient.
en.notes: The capital prefecture Tokyo (東京都) as an administrative unit; mostly in compounds: 都内 (within Tokyo), 都庁 (prefectural government), 都知事 (governor).

en.meaning: at last; finally; in the end
examples[].german: After three years, the house was finally completed.
I waited, but he didn't come in the end.
en.notes: "At last, finally", after a long wait or as a final result, positive or negative. The kanji 到頭 is rare. Similar: ついに, やっと (positive only, after effort).

examples[].german: I exercise in the park for thirty minutes every morning.
It rained yesterday, so I exercised at home.
en.notes: 運動する means here to move physically or to do sports. The place takes で; a duration like 三十分 comes without に. 毎朝 describes a habit, while 〜ので in the second example gives the reason for the choice of place. The verb is intransitive; place and duration describe the activity. The forms are, for example, 運動します, 運動した and 運動して. 運動 alone is a noun; the meanings "campaign" and "motion of a body" are not practiced here.

en.meaning: gossip; slander; abuse (reading わるくち)
examples[].german: It's not good to speak ill of people.
She is always badmouthing her boss behind his back.
I was very sad when I was badmouthed in class.
en.notes: 悪口 has two equally standard readings, わるくち and わるぐち (its own card); meaning and usage are identical, and わるくち is somewhat more common and often listed first in dictionaries. Typical is 〜の悪口を言う "to badmouth someone", passive 悪口を言われる. The Sino-Japanese reading あっこう occurs only in written language and set phrases such as 悪口雑言.

examples[].german: On the desk there are books, notebooks and so on.
On days off, I do things like cooking and cleaning.
en.notes: や connects nouns in a list that allows for further, unnamed items. 本やノート names, for example, books and notebooks among other objects. と, by contrast, presents the listed items as a complete list in the given context. The whole group of words can stand before が or を: 本やノートが, 料理や掃除を. This use is to be distinguished from 〜屋 for shops or occupations and from the regional copula や.

examples[].german: Explaining is easy, but actually doing it is hard.
If it's a repair of this scale, it's an easy job even for me.
en.notes: 易い means easy or simple here. Standing alone it is found, for example, in 易い仕事 or in contrast with 難しい. For easily understood tasks and texts, やさしい is also common. 易い（やすい）must be distinguished from 安い（やすい）"cheap": the same pronunciation means a different meaning and kanji spelling here. After a verb stem such as 読み in 読みやすい, やすい acts as a suffix; the examples on this card practice the standalone adjective. Its negation is 易くない, the past tense 易かった.

examples[].german: I traveled around Europe during the summer vacation.
There are many old towns in Europe.
en.notes: Continent in katakana (from Portuguese "Europa"). In compounds: 欧（おう）, e.g. 欧米 "Europe and America, the West".

en.meaning: manner, way; appearance; like (〜ような, 〜ように, 〜ようだ)
examples[].german: Mr./Ms. Tanaka seems very tired today.
I practice every day so that I can speak Japanese well.
The joy I felt then is beyond words.
en.notes: A formal noun that is almost always written in kana and never occurs alone: ようだ "seems", ような "like a ...", ように "so that / as"; after a verb stem it denotes the manner (言いようがない "there are no words for it"). Do not confuse it with 〜様 (さま, polite name suffix), 様子 (ようす, state, appearance) or 用 (よう, business).

examples[].german: Who is that person?
There are a lot of people in this shop.
en.notes: Refers to a human being without specifying gender; あの人 points to a particular person. To count people, use 一人、二人、三人 with their own special readings, rather than simply putting a number before ひと. 人が多い describes a large crowd.

examples[].german: My mother is good at cooking.
I call my mother.
Mom, I'm off. See you later!
en.notes: お母さん is used to address your own mother or respectfully for another person's mother. In familiar conversation it can also refer to your own mother. In a formal introduction to outsiders, you normally say 母（はは）.

examples[].german: There is a black cat.
I'm wearing black clothes.
en.notes: 黒い is an i-adjective: 黒い猫 "black cat". The color name as a noun is 黒（くろ）, as in 黒の服. Here the color is being described; in other contexts, 黒い can also be used figuratively. The negative is 黒くない.

en.meaning: famous or outstanding piece of music; masterpiece (music)
examples[].german: This is a jazz classic.
Please listen to this masterpiece.
en.notes: 名曲 is a famous or especially successful piece of music. The word can honor a song as well as an instrumental piece; it is not a general word for masterpieces of painting or literature. ジャズの名曲 assigns the piece to a music genre. この名曲を聴いてください explicitly recommends a particular piece for listening.

examples[].german: The bodies of the two people were found in the mountains.
There was a corpse on the road.
The police are examining the body.
en.notes: 死体 is a noun for a dead body, that is, a corpse. In reports you can say 死体が見つかった; 見つかる means that something is found. Because the body is no longer alive, 死体がある is the fitting phrase here. 死亡, by contrast, refers to dying or death as an event. For two people, the counter 二人 is read ふたり here.

examples[].german: Nobody died on this flight.
One person died in the accident.
I write the date of death on the document.
en.notes: 死亡 means death and sounds factual, for example in news or documents. With する it becomes the intransitive 死亡する: 事故で一人が死亡した reports that someone died in an accident. The person takes が, and 事故で names the circumstance. In everyday personal speech you often hear 死ぬ; 死亡した日 fits, for example, giving a date on a form.

examples[].german: I received a wool blanket as a Christmas present.
This sweater is made of wool.
I wash the wool and then spin it into thread.
en.notes: 羊毛 is wool from sheep. As a material it can modify a product with の: 羊毛のブランケット. 羊毛でできている explains what an object is made of. The word names the fiber itself; 毛糸, by contrast, means yarn, as used for knitting. When processed, 羊毛 can become 糸.

examples[].german: China's population is larger than Japan's.
China is a big country.
I got a letter from a friend in China.
en.notes: 中国 means the country China in this entry. 中国の人口 gives the population, 中国の友達 links the country to a person. The same word with the same reading can also refer to Japan's Chūgoku region; for travel plans, the context must therefore be clear. Here the examples refer to the country.

examples[].german: I have never been to Shikoku.
I bought a map of Shikoku.
en.notes: 四国 is the name of one of Japan's four main islands. The whole word is read しこく. 四国に行く names the island as a travel destination; 四国の地図 links the name to a map. With 行ったことがありません, one says that one has not yet had this trip experience.

examples[].german: I have never been abroad.
I collect foreign stamps.
en.notes: 外国 is another country, or abroad, from the speaker's point of view. It is a noun: 外国に行く names a travel destination, 外国の切手 describes stamps from other countries. 外国に行ったことがない reports a lack of experience abroad; がいこく has no long vowel.

examples[].german: In June, a friend from abroad is coming to Japan.
There are many foreigners in this town.
en.notes: 外国人 is a person from another country; which country counts as "foreign" depends on the context. 人 is read じん here. 外国人の友人 links the origin to a friend. The word does not describe a particular language or region of origin.

examples[].german: I like red cars.
A red apple, please.
The light is red, so please stop.
en.notes: 赤い means "red" and is an i-adjective: 赤いりんご. 赤（あか）, by contrast, is the noun for the color. For traffic lights, red is also described with 赤; "to turn red" is 赤くなる. The negative is 赤くない.

examples[].german: My husband is in the United States.
I read the brochure of a university in the United States.
en.notes: 米国 is a term for the United States and is a noun. It is read べいこく; 米 has the reading べい here. 米国にいる names a person's location, 米国の大学 a university there. The expression is often found in written texts and news.

examples[].german: Those two look like sisters, don't they?
Do you have sisters?
en.notes: 姉妹 refers to sisters collectively, without naming each one as an older or younger sister. The reading is しまい. 姉妹みたい describes an impression or comparison, not necessarily a family relationship. 姉妹がいますか, by contrast, asks about sisters that actually exist.

examples[].german: Please come to the hotel later.
I'll call you later.
en.notes: 後で means "later" or "afterwards". Without further detail, it leaves the time open: 後で電話します. 食事の後で would explicitly be "after the meal". In 後でホテルに来てください, で belongs to the time expression; ホテルに names the destination of the coming.

examples[].german: I'd like to go abroad.
I read news from overseas.
en.notes: 海外 refers to foreign countries, that is, regions beyond one's own country. It is a noun: 海外に行く names the travel destination, and 海外のニュース means news from abroad. Although 海 means "sea", present-day usage does not presuppose any particular trip by ship.

examples[].german: My bag is brown.
I bought brown shoes.
en.notes: 茶色 is the color brown. As a color noun, it takes の before a thing: 茶色の靴. In 私のカバンは茶色です, the color is stated with です. The reading is ちゃいろ; ちゃ forms a single syllable. The related i-adjective 茶色い has an additional い at the end.

examples[].german: Last month, I got fired from the company.
I do my work carefully so that I don't get fired.
en.notes: 首になる is colloquial for being dismissed or "fired". In 会社を首になる, を marks the company one has to leave; it is not the object of an action on the neck. The なる part conjugates as a Godan verb: 首になりました, 首にならない. In formal conversations, "fired" as a translation may sound correspondingly harsh.

examples[].german: My mother passed away last year.
I looked at a photo of my late grandfather.
en.notes: 亡くなる is a gentle term for "to die", especially when talking about people. This Godan verb is intransitive: the deceased person takes が. 亡くなった祖父 describes the late grandfather. The same reading なくなる, when written 無くなる, can instead mean the disappearance of a thing.

examples[].german: Please enter the whole email address in lowercase.
This character is a lowercase a.
en.notes: 小文字 here means lowercase letters such as a, as opposed to capital letters such as A. It is about the letter form, not merely the font size. 小文字で入力する states the form when typing; 小文字のエー describes a small a. The full reading is こもじ.

examples[].german: Winter vacation starts next week.
I'm going skiing during winter vacation.
en.notes: 冬休み is the winter vacation, or a wintry holiday period. 冬休みは来週からです gives its start; 冬休みにスキーに行く names it as the period of a planned activity. The word itself does not fix particular months or vacation dates.

en.meaning: can; to be able to; to be done; to be completed
examples[].german: I can read this kanji.
The meal is ready.
en.notes: 出来る is an intransitive Ichidan verb: 出来ます, 出来て. With verb + ことが出来る, one talks about ability or possibility. In 料理が出来ました, by contrast, it means the meal is finished. These two meanings depend on the sentence. The word is often written in hiragana: できる.

examples[].german: The sky is blue.
The blue sea is beautiful.
This blue shirt, please.
en.notes: 青い is an i-adjective and usually means "blue", as in 青い空. In set contexts, 青 can also denote green, especially for traffic lights or unripe fruit. For the color green in general, 緑（みどり）is usual. The negative of 青い is 青くない.

examples[].german: My older brother talks very fast.
Please do not speak so fast.
en.notes: 早口 means fast speech or a fast way of speaking. It is a noun: 兄は早口です describes the brother's way of speaking. 早口で話す states the manner of speaking; 早口で話さないでください asks for a slower pace. The word does not by itself mean the person as a "fast talker".

examples[].german: I'm ten yen short.
There isn't enough time, so I'll read the rest tomorrow.
en.notes: 足りない means "to be not enough, to be lacking". The thing that is insufficient takes が: お金が足りない. An amount such as 十円 says how much is missing. The expression is the negative form of 足りる; politely it is 足りません. ので can give the missing supply or time as a reason.

examples[].german: My former partner is older than me.
I asked an older friend for advice.
en.notes: 年上 describes a higher age relative to another person. 私より年上 means "older than me". As a noun, it modifies a person with の: 年上の友達. It refers to age, not automatically to professional experience or a higher position.

examples[].german: This year I want to go on a diet.
This year the summer was hot.
en.notes: 今年 is the calendar year in which one is speaking. 今年は sets this year as the topic of an intention or a retrospective. The reading ことし must be learned as a whole. A statement about a past summer can still contain 今年 if that summer belongs to the current year.

examples[].german: There are many children younger than me in this class.
My younger brother is three years younger than me.
en.notes: 年下 describes a lower age compared with another person. 年下の子 links the age relationship to a child. In 三歳年下, 三歳 gives the difference: three years younger. Who is meant as the point of comparison is stated with より or is clear from the situation.

examples[].german: Is there a convenience store at the east exit?
Please go out through the east exit.
en.notes: 東口 is the entrance or exit on the east side, for example of a train station. 東 is read ひがし and 口 is read ぐち here. 東口にある names something at this place; 東口から出る describes where one exits. Whether one goes in or out is determined by the sentence.

examples[].german: Please turn this way.
This window faces south.
en.notes: 向く can describe a person turning or the orientation of an object. This godan verb forms 向きます, 向いて. こっちを向く means to turn this way; 南を向く means to face south. In these sentences, を marks the direction of the gaze or orientation.

examples[].german: The stress in my private life is great.
I want to value my private life.
en.notes: 私生活 is private life, such as personal relationships and everyday life outside work. In this compound, 私 is read し. 私生活のストレス links an area of strain to private life. 私生活を大切にする means giving importance and attention to this part of life.

examples[].german: I want to enter a private university.
This is a private school.
en.notes: 私立 refers to an institution under private management, especially schools and universities. As a noun it connects with の: 私立の学校. The reading しりつ sounds like 市立 "municipal"; to tell them apart, 私立 is sometimes also called わたくしりつ.

examples[].german: The blue sea stretches out before my eyes.
The rumor spread.
en.notes: 広がる is an intransitive godan verb: 広がります, 広がって. It describes spatial expansion or spreading, including of rumors. With が you name what expands or spreads. The transitive 広げる, by contrast, describes someone extending or spreading something.

examples[].german: I don't eat pork.
Let's make cutlets from pork.
en.notes: 豚肉 is pork and a noun. When eating, it takes を as an object: 豚肉を食べる. In 豚肉でカツを作る, on the other hand, で names the meat as an ingredient or material. The reading ぶたにく combines ぶた "pig" with にく "meat".

examples[].german: I bought a lottery ticket.
I won the lottery.
en.notes: 宝くじ can refer to the lottery or to a single lottery ticket. With 宝くじを買う you buy a ticket; 宝くじに当たる means to win the lottery. The reading is たからくじ. Having bought a ticket says nothing yet about winning.

examples[].german: The goal is just one step away.
Let's move forward step by step.
en.notes: 一歩 is one step. The reading いっぽ contains a small っ and a p, not an h. あと一歩 names the one remaining step; 一歩ずつ means "step by step". 前に進む states the direction in which one keeps going.

examples[].german: This car is big, isn't it?
The door of the car closed.
en.notes: 車両 means a vehicle or a car of a train. The reading しゃりょう ends with a long o. この車両は大きいです describes a particular car; 車両のドア links the word with its door. When counting railway cars, 両 is usually used, as in 十両.

examples[].german: On weekdays I go to the office early.
Please come quickly.
en.notes: 早く can mean "early" or "quickly". 早く会社に行く can refer to an early time; with 早く来てください one usually asks someone to come quickly. It is the ku-form of 早い. For speed, the spelling 速く is also seen. The situation shows which meaning is intended.

examples[].german: I knocked on the door of the president's office.
Where is the meeting room?
en.notes: 〜室 is a word element at the end of a room name: 会議室 "meeting room", 社長室 "president's office". 〜 marks the spot for the preceding part of the word. 室 is read しつ. The particle follows the whole room word, as in 会議室は or 社長室のドア. The spelling without the placeholder is 室; 〜 stands here for the preceding part of the word.

examples[].german: There was a big tree in the meadow.
Let's sit on the grass.
en.notes: 草地 is an area covered with grass, such as a meadow. 草地に names it as a place; 草地の木 is a tree on that area. The reading is くさち. 座りましょう suggests sitting down together, without saying that one is already seated.

examples[].german: I looked at a photo of the king.
In this story, the king comes to the castle.
en.notes: 国王 refers to the head of a monarchy, usually translated as "king". It is a noun: 国王の写真 is a photo of the king, and 国王が来る names him as the one acting. こくおう is read with a long o at the end. By itself, the word does not name a particular country.

examples[].german: The moon is smaller than Mercury.
I drew a picture of Mercury.
en.notes: 水星 is the name of the planet Mercury. It is read すいせい; here it does not mean the "comet" 彗星, which is also read すいせい. 水星より names Mercury as the basis of comparison. 水星の絵 connects the planet's name with a drawing.

examples[].german: That thing you can see over there is Venus.
I looked at a photo of Venus.
en.notes: 金星 is the planet Venus and is read きんせい. The same spelling can mean a special victory when read きんぼし; this card practices the planet name. あそこに見えるのが金星です identifies a visible celestial body. 金星の写真, on the other hand, names a picture of it.

examples[].german: This curry is spicy.
This kimchi is spicy.
I don't like spicy food.
en.notes: 辛い（からい）here refers to spicy food. 辛いもの means spicy dishes. The same spelling also has the reading つらい, "painful, hard to bear"; that reading is not part of the taste meaning practiced here. The negative of からい is 辛くない（からくない）.

en.meaning: to grow; to sprout; to come in (teeth)
examples[].german: Mushrooms grow on this tree.
The baby got a tooth.
en.notes: 生える describes something growing out of a surface or emerging. It is an intransitive ichidan verb: 生えます, 生えて. With が you name what grows, and with に the place: 木にキノコが生える. For the first emergence of teeth, too, you say 歯が生える.

examples[].german: I looked up Saturn in a reference book.
Saturn has rings.
en.notes: 土星 is the planet Saturn. 土 is read ど here, and 星 せい. 土星を調べる makes the planet the object of the research; 土星には輪がある describes its rings. The spelling is a planet name and not a free description of earth or stars.

examples[].german: This town is very lively.
On the day of the festival, life returned to the shop.
en.notes: 活気 means liveliness or vigorous activity, for example in a town or a shop. With 活気がある you say that a place is lively. 活気が戻る describes the liveliness returning. The small っ in かっき lengthens the k sound.

examples[].german: There are many insects in the ground.
I buried a cable in the ground.
en.notes: 地中 is the area inside the soil. As a place noun, it combines with に: 地中に虫がいる. 地中に埋める names the ground as the destination of burying. It is read ちちゅう with a long u; the word describes the position below the surface of the earth.

en.meaning: going to work; going to the office
examples[].german: Are you going to the office alone today?
I go to work at eight every morning.
Working from home is over, and from next month I have to go to the office every day.
en.notes: 出社 means "to come to the office/company" and is used almost only in a work context. As an intransitive する-verb, the time takes に: 九時に出社する. Nearly synonymous is 出勤 ("to report for duty"), which also fits work outside an office, whereas 出社 refers to the company; 会社に出社する is therefore redundant. Since the pandemic it is often set against 在宅勤務 or リモートワーク. The opposite is 退社 - but note that 退社 can also mean "to leave the company".

examples[].german: I got a text from my ex-partner.
I returned my ex-partner's book.
en.notes: 元パートナー is a former partner. 元 is read もと here and comes before パートナー. It can mean a former personal or business partnership; the context clarifies which. から names the sender of a message. の links the person to a thing, as in 元パートナーの本 "the former partner's book".

examples[].german: An orange stone fell into the river.
The child picked up a pebble.
en.notes: 石ころ is a small stone or pebble. In 石ころが落ちる the stone is the subject of falling; in 石ころを拾う someone picks it up. The reading is いしころ. The word does not refer to a particular type or color of stone.

examples[].german: That's fine, I'll have someone else do it!
I took someone else's bag home by mistake.
en.notes: 他の人 means another person or other people. の links 他 with 人; in this phrase it is read ほかのひと. The other people need not be unknown strangers. 他の人にしてもらう means to have someone else do something; 他の人のカバン names the owner of a bag.

examples[].german: I wish I had ten million dollars.
Ten million people live in this country.
en.notes: 一千万 is ten million: 千 "thousand" is combined here with 万 "ten thousand". The reading is いっせんまん with a small っ. The unit follows the number, as in 一千万ドル or 一千万人. With 一千万円, an audible n comes before えん.

examples[].german: Who is this person?
This movie is interesting.
en.notes: この comes directly before a noun and points to something near the speaker: この人, この映画. It is not connected with な and, unlike これ, does not stand alone here. この人、だれ？ is a shortened, colloquial question. この映画は makes the movie the topic of an evaluation. 此の is a rare kanji spelling with the same reading この. This pointer to a person, thing or idea is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: The moon is round.
There is a round ball.
We eat at a round table.
en.notes: 丸い describes a round, circular or spherical shape. 丸い is especially common for spherical things; the alternative spelling 円い tends to emphasize a circular shape. As an i-adjective, 丸い stands directly before the noun and forms 丸くない. 円い is also listed as a spelling; the note on circular shape also applies when searching via this form.

examples[].german: Isn't that Emily over there?
What is that over there?
Did that thing from yesterday go well?
en.notes: あれ stands alone and refers to something over there, away from both speaker and listener. In familiar conversation it can also mean a person; for polite naming, あの人 or あの方 fit better. Before a noun, use あの: あの本. あれは何ですか asks about a distant thing. In familiar conversation, あれ can also mean a thing that both people already know, without naming it. 彼 is a rare kanji spelling for it; it is usually written あれ. The same kanji meaning "he" is read differently: かれ.

examples[].german: This bread is supposedly five dollars.
How many yen is a hundred dollars?
en.notes: ドル is the currency unit dollar and follows a number: 五ドル, 百ドル. It is not a sentence particle. Which dollar is meant depends on the country or context. だって can colloquially report a price one has heard; 何円 asks for an amount in yen.

examples[].german: Which child is Maria?
Which book do you want?
en.notes: どの asks directly before a noun which one from a selection is meant: どの子, どの本. It connects to the noun without な. If the noun is missing, ask with どれ. どの本が欲しいですか asks about the book the person wants. 何の is a rare kanji spelling for どの; in everyday use the hiragana spelling is usual. The same characters can be read なんの in other phrases, but this card explicitly practices どの.

en.meaning: there is not; to not have
examples[].german: I have no money at all.
I don't have any time today.
en.notes: ない negates the existence of a thing here: お金がない, 時間がない. What is lacking takes が. It behaves like an i-adjective: ないです is more polite, and なかった describes the lack in the past. ありません is also possible. 無い is the kanji spelling for this lack of existence; hiragana is very common. The ない attached directly to a verb, as in 行かない, is an auxiliary form and is usually written without kanji.

examples[].german: Oh, my bag isn't here!
I left my bag behind.
en.notes: カバン means a bag, often for carrying books or personal belongings. It can also be written 鞄. カバンがない states that the bag is missing; カバンを忘れてきた says that one left it behind when leaving. が marks the missing thing, を the forgotten object.

examples[].german: I want to go to Western Europe.
I bought a map of Western Europe.
en.notes: 西ヨーロッパ is Western Europe. 西 is read にし here; ヨーロッパ contains a long o and a small っ before p. に names the region as a travel destination. 西ヨーロッパの地図 links the region name to a map; the exact division of Europe may depend on the context.

examples[].german: We share the pasta between the two of us.
Let's divide the cake into three pieces.
en.notes: 分ける is a transitive ichidan verb: 分けます, 分けて. The thing that is divided or shared takes を. 二人で names the two people involved; 三つに names the three resulting parts. 二人で分ける speaks of sharing together, not of two parts alone.

en.meaning: to take someone's place; to be replaced
examples[].german: I answered the phone in place of my mother.
The teacher has changed.
en.notes: 代わる is an intransitive godan verb: 代わります, 代わって. 先生が代わる says that another person takes over as teacher. 母に代わって names the mother as the person whose place one temporarily takes. The spelling 代わる often emphasizes substitution; the meaning comes from the whole sentence. 代る is another recorded spelling for this meaning of substitution and replacement.

examples[].german: I have no intention of enrolling in a university.
I have a good idea.
en.notes: 考え is a noun: a thought, an idea or an intention. In いい考えがある it is about an idea. Verb + 考えがある can express an intention, such as 入学する考え. It is not the full verb form 考える "to think". かんがえ is read with a short e at the end.

examples[].german: I read Mr. Tanaka's book.
Mr. Yamada gave a speech.
en.notes: 〜氏 is a formal suffix after a name, especially in written reports: 田中氏. It can refer to men or women. 〜 marks the spot for the name here. In normal direct address, さん is used more often. After the whole name including 氏, particles such as が or の follow. The spelling without the placeholder is 氏; 〜 stands here for the preceding name. The independent meaning "clan" belongs to a different use of 氏.

examples[].german: How are you?
The children are playing energetically.
en.notes: 元気 is a na-adjective: 元気な子供 "lively child", 元気に遊ぶ "to play energetically". お元気ですか politely asks how someone is doing. The word can refer to health and energy; it is not conjugated like an i-adjective. The negative is 元気ではありません.

examples[].german: Please enter your full name.
I do not know that person's full name.
en.notes: 氏名 is the full name, usually family name and given name. It often appears on forms. 氏名を入力する means to enter one's name; 氏名が分かる says that one knows it. The reading is しめい, not うじめい.

examples[].german: I have two 1,000-yen bills in my wallet.
Please break this 10,000-yen bill.
en.notes: 〜札 after an amount of money denotes a bill: 千円札 "1,000-yen bill", 一万円札 "10,000-yen bill". This word element is read さつ. The finished bills are counted with 枚: 二枚. 〜 is a placeholder for the stated value, not a spoken syllable.

examples[].german: I'm short of 1,000-yen bills.
I paid with a 1,000-yen bill.
en.notes: 千円札 is a single bill worth a thousand yen. In せんえんさつ there is an audible n between せん and えん. To count the bills, use 枚. 千円札で払う names the bill as the means of payment; 千円札が足りない means there are too few such bills.

examples[].german: There are few people in this area.
Is there a convenience store around here?
en.notes: この辺 is the area nearby. With は you make it the topic of a description; with に you ask about something at this place. The card uses the reading このへん. この辺 is a place noun, not a freely conjugating i- or na-adjective.

en.meaning: to attach; to add; to put on
examples[].german: Do you want ketchup on your hot dog?
Please put on your name tag.
en.notes: 付ける is a transitive Ichidan verb: 付けます, 付けて. You name with を what you attach or add, and with に the place. With ケチャップを付ける, it is about adding a sauce; 名札を付ける can mean putting on a name tag. In casual conversation, を can be omitted.

examples[].german: A hotel that costs 10,000 yen or more is fine too.
Only people aged eighteen or older may enter.
en.notes: After a number, 〜以上 means "at least" or "or more". The stated number is included: 十八歳以上 also covers eighteen-year-olds. The reading is いじょう with a long o. 一万円以上のホテル links the minimum amount to the hotel. 以上 on its own can have other meanings in other contexts.

examples[].german: He lost his friend's trust.
I do not want to lose anything important.
en.notes: 失う is a transitive godan verb: 失います, 失って. What is lost takes を. It is used for important things or trust. 失いたくない expresses not wanting to lose something. The passive form 失われる can say that something is lost.

examples[].german: What a rude man.
Excuse me, what is your name?
en.notes: 失礼 as a na-adjective means "rude": 失礼な人. With 失礼ですが, on the other hand, you politely introduce a possibly personal question, similar to "Excuse me, but ...". The form does not say that the person addressed is rude. The reading しつれい ends in えい.

examples[].german: Mom is working desperately at dieting.
I asked for help with a desperate look on my face.
en.notes: 必死 describes very intense, often desperate effort. It is a na-adjective: 必死な顔. With に it describes the manner of an action: 必死に勉強する. 必死 does not have to mean that someone has lost all hope; strenuous effort can also be meant. The small っ in ひっし is part of the reading.

examples[].german: I do not know about the future.
I am thinking about the children's future.
en.notes: 未来 is the future, especially the time still ahead of us. It is a noun: 未来のこと refers to future matters, and 未来を考える makes the future the object of thought. みらい is read with short vowels. The word itself does not give a specific date.

examples[].german: At the end of the year, my family eats soba.
I'm busy at the end of the year.
en.notes: 年末 is the end of the year. 年末に names it as the time of an action; 年末は can make it the topic of a description. It denotes a period around the end of the year and need not mean only the last day. The reading is ねんまつ.

examples[].german: I will move out of this apartment by the end of the month.
I get my salary at the end of the month.
en.notes: 月末 is the end of a month. 月末までに names a deadline: by the end of the month at the latest. 月末に, by contrast, names a point in time around the end of the month. The reading is げつまつ. 末 means "end" in this word, not "weekend".

examples[].german: It takes ten minutes by car to get to high school.
I met a friend from high school.
en.notes: 高校 is the short form of 高等学校, an upper secondary school. 高校まで names it as the destination or endpoint of a route. 高校の友達 can mean friends from one's high school days. こうこう has two long o sounds. In the route sentence, 十分 is read じゅっぷん "ten minutes" here.

examples[].german: Summer vacation starts next week.
I want to go to the sea during summer vacation.
en.notes: 夏休み is the summer vacation or a summery holiday period. 夏休みは来週からです gives the start; 夏休みに海に行く names the vacation as the period of a trip. The word itself does not fix particular vacation months. It is read なつやすみ.

examples[].german: Math is my weak point.
I found the weak point of this plan.
en.notes: 弱点 is a weakness or weak point, for example in a person, a device or a plan. 私の弱点 names one's own weakness. 弱点を直す describes working on a weak spot. The reading is じゃくてん; じゃ forms a single mora.

examples[].german: It's already half past two now.
Let's meet at half past two.
en.notes: 二時半 is half past two, that is, 2:30. 半 adds half an hour; here it does not mean "half past one". 二時半です states the time, 二時半に会う the time of a meeting. Whether morning or afternoon is meant must be clarified by the context or by a word like 午後.

examples[].german: The two lights became bright at the same time.
It is difficult to speak and write at the same time.
en.notes: 同時 is the same point in time. With に it becomes "at the same time": 同時に明るくなる. Before another noun, 同時の is possible, as in 同時の到着. Two events on the same day are not necessarily 同時. The reading どうじ has a long o.

examples[].german: This hair dryer is quite powerful.
I use a powerful light on dark roads.
en.notes: 強力 means "strong" or "powerful", for example for a device or an effect. It is a na-adjective: 強力なライト. With です or だ you describe the strength of something. The reading きょうりょく has a long o in the first part.

examples[].german: I went to university to study geography.
I like geography class.
en.notes: 地理 is geography, as a field of knowledge or a school subject. 地理を学ぶ names it as the subject of study; 地理の授業 is a class in this subject. ために can name the purpose of attending a university. ちり has two short syllables; it is not the country name チリ (Chile).

examples[].german: I can see many balloons in the sky.
The child is holding a balloon.
en.notes: 風船 is a balloon, for example as a toy or decoration. 風 is read ふう here, with a long u. 風船が見える describes that balloons can be seen; 風船を持つ names them as objects being held. For a hot-air balloon, the word usually encountered is 気球.

examples[].german: I dislike insects.
I dislike exercise.
I don't like vegetables, but I eat them every day.
en.notes: Despite its い ending, 嫌い is a na-adjective: 嫌いな食べ物. The disliked thing usually takes が. 嫌いです can express a clear dislike; 好きではありません "I don't like it" often sounds more reserved. 嫌いではありません means "I don't mind it".

examples[].german: Last week my company was closed.
I looked at the photos from last week.
en.notes: 先週 is the week before the current week. It is read せんしゅう with a long u. 先週は frames a retrospective description; 先週の写真 means photos from that week. An action with 先週 refers to the previous week and is often in a past form.

examples[].german: There is a big test this week.
Are you free this Friday?
en.notes: 今週 is the current week. 今週は makes it the topic of a plan or announcement. 今週の金曜日 means the Friday of this week; の links the week with the day here. It is read こんしゅう with a long u. 今週 alone does not yet name a single date.

examples[].german: On the weekend, I stay on my bed or sofa.
What are you doing on the weekend?
en.notes: 週末 is the weekend. As a topic, 週末は describes a habit or a plan, while 週末に names the time of an action. For a single upcoming weekend, 今週末 helps; for the past weekend, 先週末. The second question leaves open which activity is planned; it does not require naming a particular day of the week.

examples[].german: Is this a goldfish? Or a carp?
I played goldfish scooping at the festival.
en.notes: 金魚 is a goldfish. It is an animal name; for a living animal you use いる. The first question distinguishes 金魚 from コイ, a carp. 金魚すくい names a game at festivals in which you scoop goldfish out of the water with a small scoop. Here 金魚 is part of a compound game name.

examples[].german: Swan feathers are white and beautiful.
There are swans on the lake.
en.notes: 白鳥 means "swan" here. Although the characters mean "white" and "bird", 白鳥 usually names this group of birds and not every white bird. 白鳥の羽 describes the feathers, 湖に白鳥がいる the location of living animals. The reading はくちょう ends with a long vowel: hakuchō.

examples[].german: My raincoat is yellow.
The yellow flowers are beautiful.
The yellow sign at the entrance is the landmark.
en.notes: 黄色 is the color name yellow and can stand as a noun with です: 黄色です. Before a noun, 黄色の is possible; the usual i-adjective form is 黄色い, as in 黄色い花. The form 黄色い thus belongs to the related adjective form, while the entry names the color 黄色. In directions, you can use the color as a landmark.

examples[].german: There is a large Black community in Toronto.
There is a Black student in the class.
en.notes: 黒人 is a noun for a Black person. Before another noun, の is used, as in 黒人の学生 or 黒人のコミュニティ. The word does not describe any particular nationality; a person can at the same time be, for example, カナダ人. The examples name a community and an individual student, without deriving further characteristics from the term.

examples[].german: This is my little sister's doll.
I bought my daughter a doll.
en.notes: 人形 is a doll or a figure that represents a human being. 人形です identifies the object; 娘に人形を買ってあげた names a gift for the daughter. あげる emphasizes that you did something for someone else. For living people 人 is used; for a doll, ある is the usual existence verb.

examples[].german: This table was handmade by Hayashi.
These are handmade sweets.
en.notes: 手作り as a noun means "made by hand" or "homemade". Before a product, の is used: 手作りのお菓子. 林さんの手作りです names the person who made the item himself or herself. It can describe both crafted items and self-prepared food; the examples make no statement about whether they are sold.

examples[].german: As soon as you leave through the south exit, there is a tea shop.
Let's meet at the south exit.
en.notes: 南口 denotes the entrance or exit on the south side, often at a train station. 南口から出る names the starting point of a movement, 南口で会う the meeting point. The reading みなみぐち contains the voiced form ぐち of 口. Naming the exact exit is helpful for meetings when a station has several entrances.

examples[].german: She is good at cooking.
He is good at tennis.
My mother grills fish skillfully.
en.notes: 上手（じょうず）is a na-adjective for skill or ability. The activity often takes が: 料理が上手です. 上手に describes how an action is performed. The word is often suited to praising others; for your own strong point, 得意（とくい）is often more natural.

examples[].german: The teacher corrected how I say 「すみません」.
Please phrase it more politely.
en.notes: 言い方 is the way of saying something: the wording, the tone or the chosen manner of expression. 言う supplies the stem 言い, and 方 means the manner or way here. 丁寧な言い方 asks for a more polite wording, without necessarily changing the content. A teacher can also correct the way in which one says a particular expression.

en.meaning: to get ahead of; to forestall; to anticipate
examples[].german: The patrol car got ahead of the fleeing car and blocked its path.
I got there ahead of time and was waiting.
My mother prepared everything I needed before I even said anything.
en.notes: 先回り means to beat someone to a place by taking a different or faster route and arrive at the destination before them; 先回りして待つ often follows. Figuratively, it means to anticipate something, e.g. 相手の考えを先回りする or 話を先回りする ("to jump ahead"). It is an intransitive する-verb, and the destination takes に. Unlike 先に行く ("to go on ahead"), 先回り carries the nuance of intercepting someone or getting there before them.

examples[].german: Let's meet soon.
I plan to move soon.
en.notes: 近々 means "soon" or "in the near future" here. It does not fix an exact day and fits plans or invitations: 近々会いましょう. It is used directly before the action, without adding する or な. The reading is ちかぢか, chikajika in Hepburn. A concrete deadline such as 明日 is more precise than this open-ended time expression.

examples[].german: The blue sky stretches out overhead today.
The blue sky stretches out overhead today.
I ate my bento under the blue sky.
en.notes: 青空 is a blue, clear-looking sky. 青空が広がる describes the visible sky above a place; 青空の下で names the surroundings of an outdoor activity. The word is a noun, so の comes before 下. What is emphasized is not the size but the blue of the sky; 大空 emphasizes its vastness more.

examples[].german: Both of those brothers are still elementary school students.
My younger brother is an elementary school student.
When I was in elementary school, I walked to school every day.
en.notes: 小学生 refers to a child who attends elementary school. The noun is gender-neutral; in one example, 弟 makes clear that the younger brother is meant. 二人とも says that both people attend this school level, and まだ stresses "still". 小学生の時 can place an activity in one's own elementary school years.

examples[].german: My child is a junior high school student now.
My older sister played tennis when she was in junior high school.
en.notes: 中学生 is a student at a Japanese junior high school, that is, the school level between elementary school and high school. 中学生です states the current status. 中学生の時, by contrast, looks back on the junior high school years. In the first example, 今 is read いま; it means "now" and is not part of the word 中学生.

examples[].german: Were there any anime that were unpopular this year?
This singer has become unpopular.
en.notes: 不人気 means "unpopular" or "not very popular". As a na-adjective it can stand before a noun, as in 不人気な番組. 不人気だった describes a past state; 不人気になる describes a change toward less popularity. The word first of all says something about the reception by the public, not about whether a work is good or bad on its merits.

examples[].german: This is how you cut out a heart shape.
I cut out the newspaper article.
en.notes: 切り取る means to detach a part by cutting or separating it. The cut-out piece takes を: ハートの形を切り取る, 記事を切り取る. Unlike plain 切る, the word emphasizes removing or detaching. It is a godan verb with 切り取ります and 切り取って. The two examples show crafting and keeping a newspaper clipping.

examples[].german: I saw a man take a smartphone out of Michael's bag.
I took a book out of the box.
en.notes: 取り出す means to take something out of a container or an enclosed area. The object takes を and the place it comes from takes から: 箱から本を取り出す. This godan verb forms 取り出します and 取り出して. のを見た can present an observed action as a whole clause: you saw someone taking something out.

examples[].german: My older brother is a university student.
My older brother is tall.
Big brother, help me with this problem.
en.notes: お兄さん respectfully refers to another person's older brother and serves as a form of address for your own older brother. The first examples should be understood as familiar family conversation. To outsiders, you normally call your own older brother 兄（あに）. It does not mean "younger brother".

examples[].german: I'm bad at singing.
I'm bad at drawing.
I'm not good at singing, so I practice every day.
en.notes: 下手（へた）is a na-adjective and means "not skilled at something". The activity often takes が: 歌が下手です. 下手な is the form before a noun, 下手に the adverbial form. The term can be hurtful when used to judge others; the opposite is 上手.

examples[].german: Why do elephants have long trunks?
I saw an elephant at the zoo.
en.notes: 象 means "elephant". For a living animal, use いる; when observing, 象 becomes the object of 見る. 鼻 can mean the trunk of an elephant, whereas for humans it means the nose. The first question asks about the long trunk, the second tells of one's own observation at the zoo.

examples[].german: The convenience store in 1-chome has just opened.
I turn right at the intersection in 3-chome.
en.notes: 〜丁目 is an address element after a number and denotes a numbered section of a city district. 一丁目 is read いっちょうめ here, 三丁目 さんちょうめ. It is neither a standalone place designation without a number nor a grammatical conversation particle. In place names, 一丁目の店 names a shop in the first block, and 三丁目の交差点 an intersection in the third block. The spelling without the placeholder is 丁目; 〜 stands here for the preceding number.

examples[].german: Let's meet here at 3 p.m. on the 3rd.
What time is it now?
en.notes: 〜時 follows a number and gives a clock time: 三時 is さんじ, 午後三時 is 3 p.m. 何時 is read なんじ and asks "what time is it?". For a duration, use 時間, not just 時. In the first example, 三日 is a calendar day and is read みっか; the time follows as 午後三時. The spelling without the placeholder is 時; 〜 stands here for the preceding number.

en.meaning: big; largely; with a large motion
examples[].german: When you see a taxi, please raise your right hand high.
Please write the characters large.
en.notes: 大きく describes how an action is carried out. It is the ku-form of 大きい: 字を大きく書く means "to write large". With 大きく手を上げる, the movement is made clearly and broadly. The form attaches directly to the verb; before a noun, the adjective form 大きい is used instead, as in 大きい字.

examples[].german: The hull was big.
The hull is big, isn't it?
At the harbor, I checked whether the hull was damaged.
en.notes: 船体 is the body or hull of a ship. The word is more technical than 船, which means the whole ship. 船体が大きい describes the hull, 船体を調べる an inspection of this part. As a noun, it is worked into the sentence with が or を; it is not a size specification on its own.

examples[].german: This is room 302.
Where is room 305?
en.notes: 〜号室 follows a room or apartment number. 三〇五号室 is read さんまるごごうしつ here; the zero can be read まる when digits are read one by one. こちらが302号室です identifies a room, どこですか asks for its location. The 〜 in the entry is a placeholder for the number and is not part of the spoken reading.

examples[].german: On a day like this, let's look up at the sky.
It feels good to look at the wide sky.
An airplane is flying through the big sky.
en.notes: 大空 is the wide, open sky. It sounds more vivid than plain 空 and emphasizes vastness. 大空を見上げる describes looking up, 大空を飛ぶ a movement through the sky. 青空, by contrast, emphasizes the blue color. The beginning おお is pronounced long: ōzora.

en.meaning: to be found; to turn up
examples[].german: I found a cheap hotel near the station.
The key is nowhere to be found.
en.notes: 見当たる means to be found or spotted while searching or looking around. It is intransitive: 鍵が見当たらない means "the key can't be found". どこにも with a negative reinforces "nowhere". The positive form can report that one has found a suitable thing. This godan verb forms 見当たります and 見当たらない.

examples[].german: This is how to make a triangular rice ball.
This sign is triangular.
en.notes: 三角形 is a triangle and is read さんかくけい here. As a noun it can modify another thing with の: 三角形のおにぎり is a triangular rice ball. 三角形です describes the shape of an object. The also common pronunciation さんかっけい is a shortened variant; this entry's romanizations follow the given reading さんかくけい.

examples[].german: I do not know the conjugated forms of 「立つ」.
Please learn the conjugated forms of verbs.
「書か」 is a conjugated form of 「書く」 and is used in 「書かない」.
en.notes: 活用形 names a form of an inflecting word. In Japanese school grammar it refers to forms such as 未然形 and 連用形. For verbs, what matters is which form comes before an ending: 書か is used, for example, in 書かない. The reading ends in けい, not がた. 分かりません reports a comprehension problem here, and 覚えてください is a request to learn.

examples[].german: This person is famous.
This temple is famous.
It's a famous shop, so there are always a lot of people.
en.notes: 有名 is a na-adjective: 有名な人 "famous person". For "to be known for something", ～で有名 is usual, such as 桜で有名 "famous for cherry blossoms". 有名 says something about renown; whether the person or thing is good only becomes clear from context.

examples[].german: "Thank you," I said in a low voice.
Please speak quietly.
en.notes: 小声 is a quiet voice. With で, the noun describes how someone speaks: 小声で言う or 小声で話す. The first phrase can render a softly spoken word of thanks, the second can ask someone to lower their volume. Unlike 耳打ち, 小声 does not require closeness to another person's ear. Before a noun, の is used, as in 小声の会話.

examples[].german: Neptune is blue in color.
Neptune is far from the sun.
en.notes: 海王星 is the planet Neptune. 太陽から遠い states its great distance from the sun; 海王星の色 refers to its color. The name is read かいおうせい, with a long おう. It names a planet, not a general type of star. In the examples, visible color and spatial distance are distinguished.

examples[].german: Do you have a used TV for 5,000 yen or less?
Children aged ten and under are free.
en.notes: 〜以下 sets an upper limit and includes the stated value. 五千円以下 means at most 5,000 yen, and 十歳以下 means up to and including ten years. For a limit that excludes the stated value, with numbers you would use something like 未満. After 以下, の can connect a noun: 五千円以下のテレビ. The examples show a price limit and an age condition.

examples[].german: Every year the townspeople all go cherry blossom viewing together.
The townspeople take part in the festival.
Only town residents can use this facility.
en.notes: 町民 are the residents of a town or small municipality. 町民が names them as an acting group, 町民だけ stresses a rule that applies only to this group. 町民 is not a nationality. For residents of a city called 市, 市民 is used; in the entry, the municipality is designated with 町.

examples[].german: The next class is next week.
Please tell me the plans for next week.
en.notes: 来週 is the week after the current week. The word can give the time directly or specify a plan with の: 来週の予定. 来週です answers the question of when something takes place. For an appointment exactly one week later, 一週間後 is more precise; that is not always the same date as "next week".

examples[].german: From now on, please send emails to this address.
I will be careful from now on.
I have not seen my teacher since I graduated.
en.notes: 以後 refers to the time from a reference point onward. Without an earlier point in time, it often means "from now on", for example with a changed email address or a resolution. After a te-form it can mean "since then": 卒業して以後 looks back at the time after graduation. The word sounds more formal than これから and can stand directly before the action as a time expression.

examples[].german: A loaf of bread is often sold sliced into six or eight slices.
One loaf of sandwich bread, please.
en.notes: 一斤 is a quantity word for one loaf of bread. The number of slices is stated separately: 6枚切り means this amount of bread is cut into six slices, 8枚切り accordingly into eight. When ordering, the quantity can stand directly after the object: 食パンを一斤ください. What is practiced here is the loaf of bread, not the older weight unit 斤.

examples[].german: This bread is 500 yen for two loaves.
I ordered two loaves of bread.
I baked two loaves of bread and gave one to my neighbor.
en.notes: 二斤 gives a bread quantity of two loaves and is read にきん. 斤 is a counter for bread here, not a statement of the number of slices. 二斤で五百円 gives the price for the whole quantity of two loaves. When ordering or baking, the quantity can stand after the object without any further particle: パンを二斤注文する.

examples[].german: Is there water on Mars?
Mars is a red planet.
en.notes: 火星 is the planet Mars. With 火星には you ask about something on this planet, such as water. 星 can also mean a planet in general usage; astronomically more precise is 惑星. The name is a noun. The の in 火星の写真 would denote a picture of this planet.

examples[].german: This town is quiet.
The library is quiet.
Please speak quietly in the library.
en.notes: 静か is a na-adjective for quiet or little noise: 静かな町. 静かに describes a quiet action, such as 静かに話す "to speak quietly". For a negative assessment of a deserted environment, 静か alone is not always enough; the word can mean pleasantly quiet.

examples[].german: Have you ever seen Jupiter?
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
en.notes: 木星 is Jupiter, a planet of our solar system. 木星を見たことがありますか asks about a past observation. With "the largest planet", the frame of reference must be clear: 太陽系で一番大きい惑星 limits the statement to the solar system. 木星 is a name; the general term for a group of planets is 惑星.

examples[].german: After coming down the mountain, I finally reached a populated area.
It is a place far from human settlements.
en.notes: 人里 refers to a place inhabited by people, especially in contrast to mountains, forests or wilderness. 人里に着く describes reaching a settlement. 人里離れた場所 is a place away from human settlement; 離れた connects directly to 場所 here. The word sounds more descriptive than a specific municipality term such as 町.

examples[].german: It takes about two minutes.
I will arrive in ten minutes.
en.notes: 〜分 expresses minutes. The pronunciation changes after numbers: 二分 is にふん, and 十分 is read じゅっぷん here. For a duration, you ask how many minutes an action takes; あと十分で, by contrast, gives the time remaining until arrival. 十分 can also be read じゅうぶん and mean "sufficient"; in the example, the time expression shows the minutes reading. The spelling without the placeholder is 分; 〜 stands here for the preceding number.

examples[].german: The jacket of this suit has no inside pocket.
I keep my wallet in the inside pocket.
en.notes: 内ポケット is a pocket on the inside of a garment. The word combines 内 with the loanword ポケット and is pronounced うちポケット. 内ポケットがない describes a property of a jacket; 内ポケットに財布を入れる names the place something is put into. It means the pocket inside a garment, not a separate handbag.

examples[].german: Today, let's learn about Napoleon III.
Napoleon III was a famous emperor.
en.notes: ナポレオン三世 is the personal name Napoleon III. The ending 三世 is read さんせい and distinguishes him from other bearers of the same name. について names the topic of a lesson, は introduces the person as the topic of a description. The entry practices this name; 三世 is not translated here as "three worlds".

examples[].german: That person is a celebrity.
Please show me that book.
I heard that story yesterday as well.
en.notes: その comes directly before a noun. It often refers to something near the listener or something already mentioned: その本, その話. It cannot replace a thing on its own; それ exists for that. The demonstrative use should be distinguished from the hesitating filler その…. In conversation, the context helps recognize what is being pointed at or referred to. 其の is the rare kanji spelling of the demonstrative その. In normal usage, kana is used here; this spelling does not denote a family name.

examples[].german: I feel like I've seen that person over there somewhere before.
That mountain is Mt. Fuji.
en.notes: あの comes before a noun and refers to something distant from both conversation partners, such as あの山. It can also mean a person known to both whom one points out. To stand alone as a substitute for a thing, use あれ. The filler あの… at the start of a conversation is a different use; in the examples, あの belongs to 人 or 山 respectively. The rare kanji spelling 彼の belongs here to the reading あの; this demonstrative is usually written in kana. In another context, 彼の can be read かれの "his"; that is a different use.

examples[].german: The clownfish is a saltwater fish.
I saw saltwater fish at the aquarium.
en.notes: 海水魚 are fish that live in the sea, that is, in salt water. The opposite is 淡水魚 for freshwater fish. 海水魚です assigns a species of fish to this group; 水族館で海水魚を見る tells of an observation in an aquarium. The ending 魚 is read ぎょ here and belongs to the compound word for the animal group.

examples[].german: What is life like in the northern region?
Winters in the north are cold.
en.notes: 北国 can denote a northern country or region. In a Japanese context it often means an area in the north; it is not a fixed country name. 北国のくらし asks about life there, and 北国の冬 describes a season in that area. The reading きたぐに contains ぐに as the voiced form of 国.

en.meaning: evening sun; afternoon sun from the west
examples[].german: The evening sun is so bright that I cannot see the TV.
The evening sun is dazzling.
I closed the curtains to keep out the western sun.
en.notes: 西日 is sunlight coming in from the west, especially in the afternoon or toward evening. 西日がまぶしい describes this light being dazzling. It can interfere with watching TV or be a reason to close curtains. The word is read にしび; it does not refer only to a sunset on the horizon.

examples[].german: This street is bustling.
The festival is lively.
en.notes: 賑やか describes a bustling environment or a lively, often cheerful atmosphere: 賑やかな通り, 賑やかな祭り. It is a na-adjective; the adverbial form is 賑やかに. The word is often positive or neutral, whereas うるさい criticizes disturbing noise.

examples[].german: There are many mountains in East Asia.
I'm interested in the culture of East Asia.
en.notes: 東アジア denotes the geographic region of East Asia. The reading here is ひがしアジア: 東 is read ひがし, and アジア is a loanword. 東アジアには names something within the region; 東アジアの文化 relates something to this region. It is a region name and not the nationality of an individual person.

examples[].german: Ramadan will be over soon.
Night has given way to dawn.
en.notes: 明ける is an intransitive Ichidan verb in these examples. 夜が明ける means that the night ends and it gets light. With a longer period like ラマダーンが明ける, it means "to come to an end". The subject takes が. The spelling 明ける emphasizes this change of time; 開ける often describes opening an object.

examples[].german: I gave a round frisbee to the puppy as a present.
This stone has a round shape.
I folded the round piece of paper in half.
en.notes: 円い means "round" here, especially with a circular, flat shape. The spelling 丸い, read the same, is often used for ball-shaped things. As an i-adjective, 円い stands directly before the noun: 円い紙. Before an action, 円く can describe the manner; the past is 円かった. The examples look at shapes and at handling a round piece of paper.

examples[].german: I tell the brothers apart by their eye color.
It is difficult to tell twins apart.
This machine distinguishes red balls from blue balls.
en.notes: 見分ける means to tell things or people apart by recognizable features. The thing distinguished takes を, the feature often で: 目の色で見分ける. 見分けるのは makes the action the topic. This transitive Ichidan verb forms 見分けます and 見分けない; the spelling should not be equated with 分ける in the sense of dividing.

examples[].german: When is the next time?
Let's do our best next time too.
en.notes: 次回 denotes the next issue, session or occasion of a repeated thing. It sounds more formal than 今度 and does not fix a particular day. 次回は、いつですか asks for the date; 次回も connects the next occasion to the previous one. With の it can modify a noun, as in 次回の授業.

examples[].german: I just saw news about the Middle East on TV.
Have you ever been to the Middle East?
en.notes: 中東 is the region name "Middle East". With の it combines with topics like 中東のニュース; with 行く, に names the travel destination. The word is a noun, not an adjective that can be used independently. The boundaries of the region so named can be drawn differently depending on the context; the entry therefore gives no fixed list of countries.

examples[].german: The sun came up, and it is gradually getting lighter all around.
It's quiet around here, isn't it?
en.notes: 辺り here refers to the immediate surroundings without drawing an exact boundary. この辺り is "around here"; 辺りが明るくなる describes a change in the surroundings. The word can also appear in approximate statements, but the examples practice its spatial meaning. For a precisely defined address, you name the place more concretely.

examples[].german: Lots of cars pass by.
I go to school by this road.
en.notes: 通る here means passing by, driving past, or using a route. Although the verb is intransitive, を in この道を通る marks the route traveled. The destination follows with に: 学校に行く. This godan verb ending in る forms 通ります, 通って and 通らない; it therefore does not belong to the ichidan group like 見る.

examples[].german: Many people live in this apartment building.
I am a resident of this apartment building.
en.notes: 住人 is a person who lives in a place. このマンションの住人 assigns someone to a residential building, while 住人がいます names the people who live there. The word concerns the place of residence, not nationality. アパート refers to the residential building in the examples; for a single apartment, 部屋 would be more precise.

examples[].german: This flower is pretty.
This room is clean.
en.notes: きれい means "beautiful" or "clean, tidy", depending on context. Despite the い ending, it is a na-adjective: きれいな花, きれいな部屋. The negative is きれいではありません, not きれくない. The kanji spellings 綺麗 and 奇麗 are also in use.

examples[].german: Getting into a medical university costs money.
I want to get into a medical university.
en.notes: 医大 is the short form for a medical college or university. 医大に入る here means to be admitted there and start studying; it is not merely about entering a building. 入るには names the requirement or cost of this admission. With 入りたい, one expresses one's own wish to study at such a university.

examples[].german: I study medicine at university.
I'm studying medicine.
This book describes the history of medicine.
en.notes: 医学 is medicine as a science or field of study. 医学を学ぶ and 医学を勉強する describe studying this subject; の connects it with, for example, 発展, the development of the field. Neither a single medication nor medical treatment is meant here. For a medication 薬 is used, and for treatment something like 治療.

examples[].german: I hear this country used to be a monarchy.
The United Kingdom is a monarchy.
en.notes: 君主国 is a state with a monarch as head of state. The word refers to the state, not to the individual ruler. By itself it does not say how much political power that person holds. かつて and だったそうです report a former form of government, while 君主国です gives a present classification.

en.meaning: -kun (name suffix, often for boys or young men)
examples[].german: Michael has no siblings.
Good morning, Yamada!
en.notes: 〜君 is read くん and attached to a name, for example 山田君. It is often used to address boys or younger men who are familiar to the speaker and of equal or lower status. The form is not a general respectful address for just anyone; when in doubt, さん is often the better choice. It can occur both in direct address and when speaking about someone. The symbol 〜 is only a placeholder for the name. The spelling without the placeholder is 君; 〜 stands here for the preceding name.

en.meaning: to be against; to be toward; regarding
examples[].german: What is the exchange rate of the yen against the dollar right now?
I have an opinion on this problem.
en.notes: In these examples, 対する connects a topic or a standard of comparison with a statement. 名詞に対する stands before a noun: ドルに対する円のレート. 名詞に対して stands before the predicate, for example when expressing an opinion about a problem. The te-form is 対して, the polite form 対します. "Against" here means a relationship or comparison, not necessarily a spatial position.

examples[].german: Please return from the Tokyo branch office to the headquarters in Portland.
I work at a branch office of a newspaper company.
en.notes: 支局 is a branch office, especially of an agency, news agency or newspaper editorial office. 本社, by contrast, denotes the headquarters of a company. 支局から names the starting point of a return; 支局で names the workplace. For an ordinary bank or store branch, 支店 is the more common word.

examples[].german: Becoming a teacher at this school is a big responsibility.
I was entrusted with an important task.
en.notes: 大役 is a particularly important or responsible task. This entry's reading is たいやく. 大役を任される means that someone entrusts you with this responsibility; 大役です assesses an activity as a great responsibility. The word means more than merely long-lasting work. The examples use the general meaning of a task, not a special role in the theater.

examples[].german: Let's do yoga every day for mind and body.
I am healthy in both mind and body.
en.notes: 心身 combines mind and body. 心身のために names both as the purpose of an action; 心身ともに emphasizes that a statement applies to both. The word itself is a noun and connects to another noun with の. しんしん is pronounced without long vowels; the components 心 and 身 are not separate words in this compound.

examples[].german: Please spray your whole body once a day.
My whole body has sore muscles.
en.notes: 全身 means the whole body. With に it can name the target of an application, with が the body as the bearer of a sensation: 全身が筋肉痛です. Before a noun, の is often used, such as 全身の写真 for a photo showing the whole person. 全身 is itself a noun, not an i- or na-adjective.

examples[].german: This dictionary is handy.
It's convenient to live near the station.
en.notes: 便利 is a na-adjective for practical usefulness or a favorable location: 便利な辞書, 便利な場所. It does not necessarily mean physically comfortable; a comfortable seat might be 座り心地がいい, for example. 便利ではありません is the polite negative; 不便（ふべん）means "inconvenient".

examples[].german: The two sides' views are not the same.
I listened to the opinions of both sides.
en.notes: 両者 sums up two people, groups or sides that are already known. It sounds more formal than 二人 and can also refer to two parties. 両者の考え compares their views; 両者の意見を聞く describes letting both have their say. For more than two parties, 両者 is not the right collective term.

examples[].german: I want to meet the author of this book.
The author of this book is famous.
The creator of this picture is a friend of mine.
en.notes: 作者 is the person who created a work. For a book it means "author"; for a picture it can denote its creator or artist. 作品の作者 assigns the person to the work. 作者に会う names them as the target of a meeting, and 作者が書く or 描く names them as the acting person. Not every artist is automatically the 作者 of the work currently being looked at.

examples[].german: That man is a famous engineer.
The engineer built a new machine.
en.notes: 工学者 is someone who works professionally in engineering. The word is built from 工学 and 者 but is used as a whole noun. 有名な工学者 describes a well-known specialist; 工学者が names them as the actor in developing a machine. The examples use "engineer" without specifying a particular academic degree or job title.

examples[].german: This is the place where an old plate was found in the soil.
Where is the meeting place?
en.notes: 場所 names a place or a specific spot. この場所です can point to a spot where something happened. 待ち合わせの場所 identifies it as the meeting point; the question どこですか asks for the location. This entry practices the spatial meaning, not the special use for a sumo tournament.

examples[].german: Please buy a ticket before you enter.
The admission fee is 500 yen.
en.notes: 入場 refers to entering an event hall or venue. With する it becomes the intransitive 入場する, "to enter"; no direct object with を is needed. 入場料, by contrast, is the compound noun for the admission fee. In the first example, buying the ticket counts as a step before entering; in the second, the price is stated.

en.meaning: elsewhere; other places; other people or groups
examples[].german: Let's go to some other store instead of this one.
Please do not worry about other people's affairs.
en.notes: 他所 is read よそ here and is often written only in kana. 他所の店 is a store other than the current one; 他所のこと here means the affairs of other people or groups. The word contrasts something outside one's own place or circle. The reading よそ must not be replaced by the other possible character readings as different words. 余所 is another kanji spelling of よそ; the kana form is common here as well.

examples[].german: My daily breakfast is bacon and bread.
I eat breakfast every morning.
I had no time this morning, so I did not eat breakfast.
en.notes: 朝ごはん is breakfast as a meal. In everyday use, ごはん here is not limited to rice: breakfast can also consist of bread. 朝ごはんは describes the content of the meal, 朝ごはんを食べる the eating. In the additional example, 時間がなくて gives the reason the meal was skipped.

examples[].german: I do yoga in the bright morning sun.
The morning sun is beautiful, isn't it?
Morning sunlight comes into this room through the east window.
