en.notes: 朝日 is the sun, or its light, in the morning. 朝日の中 names the light as the surroundings of an activity; 朝日がきれい describes the sight. 朝日が入る can express that morning sunlight falls in through a window. The nature word is meant here, not a family, place or company name with the same characters.

examples[].german: On my days off, I go to a tea ceremony class.
I watched a judo match.
en.notes: 〜道 serves as a word element for a way or a practiced art, as in 茶道 "tea ceremony" and 柔道 "judo". Here it is read どう with a long o. 〜 shows the place of the preceding word part. The standalone 道 "road, way" with the reading みち is a different use.

examples[].german: One day until the exam. I don't have enough time.
I had a nice time with a friend.
en.notes: 時間 is time that one has or needs for something. 時間が足りない means that it is not enough. With a number, 時間 also gives a duration in hours: 三時間 "three hours". 楽しい時間 is a pleasantly spent time. For a clock time, 時 without 間 is used, as in 三時.

examples[].german: It was very cold yesterday.
Moving is hard work.
en.notes: As an adverb, 大変 intensifies a following adjective or verb in the sense of "very"; as a な-adjective in 大変だ／です it describes a difficult or strenuous situation.

examples[].german: I studied for three hours at the library.
I traveled for two weeks.
en.notes: 〜間 after a time expression denotes a duration: 三時間 "three hours", 二週間 "two weeks". Here it is read かん. Three o'clock is 三時, a duration of three hours is 三時間. 〜 is a placeholder for the preceding word part; the whole duration can stand with the verb without any further particle. The spelling without the placeholder is 間; 〜 stands here for the preceding time expression.

examples[].german: Humans convey their thoughts with words.
In this story, humans and animals live together.
en.notes: 人間 is a human being or humankind as a whole. 人 is read にん here, 間 げん. 人間が names humans as the subject; 人間と動物 connects humans with animals. In a general statement about 人間, a single person is not necessarily meant.

examples[].german: My home is a space where I can feel at ease.
I made some space between the two desks.
en.notes: 空間 is a space or free room, not necessarily an enclosed room. It can also denote an area perceived as pleasant. 安心できる空間 describes a place where one can feel secure. 空間を作る means to make room. くうかん has a long u.

examples[].german: I am bad at entering numbers.
This digit is a six.
en.notes: 数字 are numerals or numbers, for example when reading or entering them. この数字は六です identifies a digit. 数字を入力する makes them the content being entered. The expression 下手です judges a person's ability, not the number itself. すうじ begins with a long u.

examples[].german: The number of staff at this company is twenty.
Please tell me the number of participants.
en.notes: 人数 is the number of people. A number of people is stated with 人: 二十人 "twenty people". 人数 stands for the count itself, for example when asking for the number of participants. The reading is にんずう with a long u; 人数 is not translated as a single person.

examples[].german: This time my score was 100 points.
My score has gone up compared to before.
en.notes: 点数 is a score, for example on a test or in a game. 百点 gives one hundred points; 点数 says what kind of figure is involved. 点数が上がる describes improved performance. The reading てんすう ends with a long u. The number of points can be stated explicitly in the sentence or left open.

examples[].german: Tokyo is a big city.
I live in Tokyo.
en.notes: 東京 is Tokyo. It is read とうきょう with two long o sounds; きょ forms a single mora. 東京に住む names the city as the place of residence. With 東京は大きい町です, a property of the city is described. The name itself is a noun and is not inflected like an adjective.

examples[].german: What can you see on the other side of the mountains?
There is a hospital over there.
en.notes: 向こう can mean the other side or a place over there. 山の向こう is the other side of the mountains. With 向こうに, one asks or reports about something at a distant place. It is a place noun here; the reading むこう has a long o.

examples[].german: This movie is popular across the U.S.
I checked the weather across the U.S.
en.notes: 全米 here means the whole United States. 全米で names the U.S. as the area of an action or a widespread property. 全米の天気 refers to the weather in the whole country. 米 is read べい; the reading of the whole word is ぜんべい.

en.meaning: to approach; to get close to
examples[].german: Do not go any closer to the river!
Spring is approaching.
As the two kept meeting through work, they gradually grew closer.
en.notes: 近づく is an intransitive godan verb: 近づきます, 近づいて. With に you name the target of the approach. Seasons can also figuratively come closer: 春が近づく. Verb + な is a harsh prohibition and sounds much stronger than a polite request. The reading ちかづく is written with z in Hepburn (chikazuku). 近付く is another spelling with the same reading ちかづく. With people, the verb can also mean getting closer to each other or getting to know someone better; the social context makes this meaning clear.

examples[].german: Are you all right?
I have no fever, so I'm fine.
Tomorrow is a day off, so it's fine even if it gets late.
en.notes: 大丈夫 here means "all right, no problem". 大丈夫ですか asks how someone is or whether something is possible. In conversation, 大丈夫です can also decline an offer, so pay attention to situation and tone. It is a na-adjective, not an i-adjective.

examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka is off today, so a substitute teacher is coming.
What shall we do instead?
en.notes: 代わり is a replacement or substitute, and a noun. 代わりの先生 refers to a substitute teacher. その代わりに can mean "instead" and suggest a different action. The reading is かわり; the related verb 代わる, by contrast, ends in る.

examples[].german: I have exactly the same opinion as you.
There is no problem at all.
en.notes: 全く intensifies a statement: "completely", "entirely" or "at all". 全く同じ考え emphasizes complete agreement; 全く問題ありません emphasizes that there is no problem. It is not limited to negative sentences. まったく exclaimed on its own can also express annoyance; here the examples practice the intensifying meaning.

examples[].german: The other day, there was a caterpillar on the tree.
Last Sunday I watched a movie.
en.notes: この前 is a time expression here for "the other day" or an earlier point in time. The distance from the present remains open. この前の日曜日 means the most recent Sunday. 前 is read まえ on this card. The phrase can place the sentence in time directly or, with の, specify a time expression.

examples[].german: A notice was in the mailbox.
I have an important announcement.
en.notes: お知らせ is a notice or announcement. The お belongs to the polite word form. お知らせの紙 means a sheet of paper with a notice; お知らせがあります announces that there is something to report. The meaning does not specify whether the notice is printed, spoken or electronic.

en.meaning: to be completed; to be finished
examples[].german: It took three days for the craft project to be finished.
The meal is ready.
en.notes: 出来上がる is an intransitive godan verb: 出来上がります, 出来上がって. With が you name what is finished, such as a craft project or a meal. In 出来上がるのに三日かかる, のに names the time required here, not a contrast. Three days is read みっか.

examples[].german: Black hairs are mixed in among the white ones.
The child is playing, mingling with the adults.
en.notes: 交じる is an intransitive godan verb even though it ends in いる: 交じります, 交じって. It can mean being mixed in or mingling among people. With が you name who or what is among them; に names the group or area. For material mixtures, the spelling 混じる is often seen.

examples[].german: Our dog runs around when it sees snow.
The children are running around in the park.
en.notes: 走り回る means to run around in various places. The whole verb is intransitive and takes godan endings: 走り回ります, 走り回って. With が you name the person or animal running, with で the place. 雪を見ると can describe an event that regularly triggers something.

examples[].german: My father is good at guessing the price of tea.
Please guess the answer.
en.notes: 当てる here means to guess something correctly. The sought answer or detail takes を. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 当てます, 当てて. お茶の値段を当てる means to guess the price of the tea; 答えを当ててください is a request to give the right answer.

examples[].german: I transformed into a different person with makeup.
In this story, a fox turns into a person.
en.notes: 化ける describes a transformation, for example in stories, or figuratively a greatly changed appearance. It is an intransitive ichidan verb: 化けます, 化けて. With に you name the assumed form: 人に化ける, 別人に化ける. メイクで names the means of the change.

examples[].german: After the knock, I heard the sound of a doorknob turning.
Please turn the steering wheel to the right.
en.notes: 回す is a transitive godan verb: 回します, 回して. With を you name what is turned, such as a doorknob or steering wheel. ドアノブを回す音 contains a whole action as a description of the sound. 右に gives the direction of the turn. The intransitive 回る means that something turns by itself.

examples[].german: Water, please.
Cold water, please.
I water the flowers.
en.notes: 水 means water, in everyday speech especially cold or unheated water. Hot water is normally お湯（おゆ）. 水を飲む means "to drink water", and 水をあげる means, for example, "to water a plant". For a polite order, お水をください is also common.

examples[].german: I myself drink both coffee and tea.
I will do it myself.
en.notes: 私自身 emphasizes "I myself" or "I personally". 私自身は can highlight one's own habit; 私自身が emphasizes that I am the one taking on the action. 私自身の考え highlights one's own opinion. The reading on this card is わたしじしん.

examples[].german: I want to enroll in a private university.
The tuition at this private university is high.
en.notes: 私立大学 is a privately run university. The word is read しりつだいがく. 私立大学に入学する means to enroll or be admitted there. 私立大学の学費 refers to its tuition; the term alone does not fix any particular fee level.

examples[].german: I learned that conjugation form in the last class.
Last time, I ate lunch here.
en.notes: 前回 is the last time, that is, the previous episode or session in a series. 前回のクラス names the previous class. 前回は can set an earlier occasion as the topic. The reading is ぜんかい; it means the previous repetition, not automatically yesterday.

examples[].german: It's a building with five floors above ground and two below.
From the plane, you can see the town on the ground.
en.notes: 地上 denotes the area above the ground or the surface of the earth. With の it describes a noun: 地上のフロア "an above-ground floor". 地上に names a place above the ground. In building specifications, 地上 comes before the number of above-ground floors. ちじょう ends with a long o.

en.meaning: to point; to direct; to turn (something) toward
examples[].german: Can you point it a little further back?
Please do not point the camera at me.
en.notes: 向ける is a transitive ichidan verb: 向けます, 向けて. You aim an object or body part in a direction. The object takes を, the target takes に. 向けないでください asks that something not be pointed. The intransitive 向く describes the orientation of the person or thing itself.

examples[].german: What on earth are you doing here?
What do you think?
en.notes: お前 is a very informal "you", often in male-coded speech. Depending on the relationship, it sounds familiar, rough or condescending. You also hear it in arguments. As a form of address it is unsuitable for polite conversation with unfamiliar people. It is a pronoun here; before は or が it behaves like a noun. おまえ is the kana spelling of the same pronoun. Another dictionary meaning refers to the presence of a person of high rank or a deity; it should be distinguished from the familiar pronoun on this card.

examples[].german: A beautiful beach stretches along the Mediterranean.
During summer vacation, I took a cruise on the Mediterranean.
en.notes: 地中海 is the proper name of the Mediterranean Sea. It is read ちちゅうかい with a long u; ちゅ is pronounced together. 地中海で names it as the place of an activity, 地中海の as a link to a noun. 地中海でクルーズをする means to take a cruise on the Mediterranean.

examples[].german: No water is coming out of the tap.
I put tap water in a bottle.
en.notes: 水道 is the water supply or water pipe system. 水道の水 is tap water, and 水道から水が出る describes water coming out of it. 水道から names the source of the water. すいどう ends in a long o; the beginning すい stays sui.

en.meaning: to turn on; to switch on
examples[].german: At night I turn on the car's headlights.
Please turn on the TV.
en.notes: 点ける is a transitive ichidan verb: 点けます, 点けて. It is used to switch on a light or a device; the device takes を. The verb is also often written つける. 点けてください is a request to turn something on. The spelling 点ける makes the meaning "turn on/light" clear here.

examples[].german: Cooking dinner every day is Dad's job.
I was entrusted with an important role.
en.notes: 役目 is a task, role or function that someone takes on. お父さんの役目 names the person to whom the task is assigned. 役目を任される means to be given a task. A regular responsibility can be a 役目 just as much as a newly assumed task.

examples[].german: Would you like some tea?
I drink tea after meals.
en.notes: お茶 is the usual polite word for tea; the お often stays even in your own everyday speech. Without further detail, Japanese green tea is often meant, or other tea depending on the situation. For black tea, 紅茶（こうちゃ）is usual. A cup of tea can be counted with お茶を一杯.

examples[].german: This shirt is made of cotton fabric.
This fabric is soft.
en.notes: 生地 here is fabric, that is, textile material. コットン生地 is cotton fabric. In 生地で出来ている, で names the material. この生地 can point to a fabric one is looking at or feeling. The reading on this card is きじ.

examples[].german: At my school, we study nine subjects.
What is your favorite subject?
en.notes: 科目 is a teaching or study subject. 好きな科目 asks about a favorite subject. With a number, you state the number of subjects: 九科目 "nine subjects". 科目を学ぶ names the subject as what is learned. The number of subjects depends on the particular curriculum.

examples[].german: Several years have passed since I came to Japan.
Let's meet again in a few years.
en.notes: 数年 is an imprecise expression for a few years. 数年前 means "a few years ago", 数年後 "in a few years". 来てから数年がたつ describes the time that has passed since an arrival. The reading is すうねん with a long u; the exact number of years remains open.

examples[].german: Let's type a message with some emoji mixed in.
What does this emoji mean?
en.notes: 絵文字 are emoji, small pictographic characters in messages. 絵文字を入れる or 使う describes inserting or using such characters. You can ask the meaning of a single emoji with この絵文字はどういう意味ですか. It is read えもじ; the j in the romanization represents じ.

examples[].german: My father is a professional pitcher.
That pitcher throws fast balls.
Who is today's starting pitcher?
en.notes: 投手 is the technical term for the pitcher in baseball; in conversation and sports broadcasts you hear the loanword ピッチャー just as often. Typical compounds are 先発投手 "starting pitcher", 救援投手 "reliever" and エース投手. The opponent is the batter 打者 (バッター), and the catcher is 捕手 (キャッチャー). The related verb is 投げる: 投手が球を投げる.

examples[].german: But I can't do it.
It's expensive. But it's delicious.
en.notes: でも links two statements here with "but" and stands at the beginning of the second statement. It can introduce an objection or a contrasting evaluation. でも、できないよ is a personal objection; 高いです。でも、おいしいです contrasts price and taste. This use is common in conversation.

examples[].german: Let's eat here!
Please sit here.
en.notes: ここ points to a place near the speaker: "here". ここで names the place of an action, ここに a destination or position. ここで食べよう suggests eating at this place. ここに座ってください asks someone to sit at the indicated spot. 此処 is a rare kanji spelling of ここ. For the ordinary location "here", kana is mostly used.

examples[].german: Today I had a muffin as a snack.
I am going to buy a three o'clock snack.
I ate a small snack during my lunch break.
en.notes: おやつ is a between-meal snack, often in the afternoon, but also at lunchtime. It does not have to be exactly at three o'clock. おやつに names something eaten as a snack; 三時のおやつ specifies a planned snack by time. The お belongs to the usual word form and is read together with やつ. お八つ is a rare kanji spelling; お八 without つ is also attested as a historical or rare spelling for this snack meaning. Today おやつ in kana is the usual form. 八つ historically belongs to a time designation; the meaning learned here is a between-meal snack, not a quantity of eight snacks and not an old term for a time of day.

examples[].german: Hello, this is Yamakawa.
Hello, can you hear me?
en.notes: もしもし is used on the phone to make contact or to check whether the other person is still listening. Afterwards, one can state one's own name: もしもし、山川です. もしもし、聞こえますか asks whether one can be heard. The phrase is read as a fixed greeting.

examples[].german: The two rivals are finally going to face off.
Ahead of the showdown, the two teams are practicing.
en.notes: 対決 is a confrontation or direct encounter; with する it becomes an intransitive verb. 対決します and 対決して are regular する forms. The participants can be named together with が, an opponent also with と. 対決することになった describes that the encounter is now scheduled.

examples[].german: My older sister lives in Tokyo.
My older sister became a teacher.
Big sister, look at this.
en.notes: お姉さん is a respectful term for an older sister and a possible form of address for your own older sister. In the first examples, someone is talking about their own sister in a familiar setting. To outsiders, 姉（あね）is normally used. For a younger sister, say 妹.

examples[].german: I buy milk.
I drink milk every morning.
en.notes: 牛乳 means cow's milk. It is a noun and takes を as a drink or purchase: 牛乳を飲む, 牛乳を買う. Plant-based drinks are normally named more precisely, such as 豆乳（とうにゅう）"soy milk". For quantity, 一杯 or a packaging word such as 一本 is possible.

examples[].german: My friend lives in South Africa.
I'd like to go to South Africa sometime.
en.notes: 南アフリカ here denotes the state of South Africa. 南 is read みなみ, アフリカ afurika. 南アフリカに住む names the country as a place of residence, 南アフリカに行く as a travel destination. The proper name stays unchanged even before に or の.

examples[].german: A cold north wind is blowing.
The north wind is strong, so I closed the window.
en.notes: 北風 is wind from a northern direction. 北 is read きた here, 風 かぜ. 北風が吹く names the wind as what blows. With 北風が強いので you can give the wind strength as a reason for an action. 北風 names the direction, not automatically a particular temperature.

examples[].german: The sky at dawn today was pink.
I woke up at daybreak.
en.notes: 夜明け is dawn or daybreak. 夜明けの空 describes the sky at that time, and 夜明けに names the time of an event. It is read よあけ without a long vowel. Time expressions can specify which dawn is meant more precisely, such as 今日の夜明け.

examples[].german: I bought a heart-shaped balloon.
Please cut this paper into a heart shape.
en.notes: ハート形 is a heart shape. It is read はーとがた with a long a and がた. ハート形の describes an object as heart-shaped; ハート形に names the desired shape in a transformation, for example when cutting out. The word can describe balloons, pieces of paper or other shapes.

examples[].german: First, please look at the table of contents of the book.
I looked in the table of contents for the chapter I wanted to read.
en.notes: 目次 is the table of contents of a book or document. 本の目次 names the book it belongs to. 目次を見る means to look into it; 目次で章を探す describes searching for a chapter using the table. It is read もくじ, not もくつぎ.

examples[].german: Is salmon a saltwater fish? Or a freshwater fish?
There are many sea fish at this market.
en.notes: 海魚 are sea fish, that is, saltwater fish. The reading on this card is うみざかな; 魚 is read ざかな there. The word is often contrasted with 川魚 "river fish". A question with それとも offers two possible classifications and does not answer it yet.

examples[].german: I like Japanese-style sweets.
I stayed in a Japanese-style room.
en.notes: 和風 is a Japanese style. It can stand directly before a noun, as in 和風スイーツ, or with の: 和風の部屋. For food it concerns its design or manner of preparation; for a room, its furnishings. わふう ends with a long u.

examples[].german: I'm thinking of buying an antique sofa for this Japanese-style room.
This inn has a Japanese-style room.
en.notes: 和室 is a room in the traditional Japanese style. 和室があります states that such a room exists. 和室に can indicate it as the destination of furnishing or of a stay. The reading わしつ has no long vowels.

examples[].german: Traditional Japanese clothing such as the kimono is part of Japanese culture.
I wore traditional Japanese clothing at the wedding.
en.notes: 和服 is traditional Japanese clothing, such as a kimono. 和服を着る means to put on or wear such clothing. キモノなどの和服 names the kimono as an example. The word denotes a clothing style and says nothing by itself about when or by whom it is worn.

examples[].german: What are the regional specialties of Kyushu?
I bought a specialty of this town as a souvenir.
en.notes: 名物 is a well-known specialty or typical product of a place. It can be something edible, but does not have to be. 九州の名物 or この町の名物 names the regional connection with の. 名物を買う describes buying such a product. めいぶつ is romanized as meibutsu.

examples[].german: I eat meat.
I buy meat at the supermarket.
en.notes: In a food context, 肉 means "meat". The type of animal can be given with a compound: 牛肉（ぎゅうにく）, 豚肉（ぶたにく）, 鶏肉（とりにく）. "To eat meat" is 肉を食べる; as a substance, meat is often ordered by weight, such as 百グラム.

examples[].german: I feel uncomfortable because I ate too much.
I went through a hard time because I had no friends.
en.notes: 苦しい is an i-adjective for physical discomfort or a burdensome situation. The forms are 苦しかった and 苦しくない. 食べすぎて苦しい describes discomfort after eating too much. 苦しい時期 can mean a difficult period of life. Which burden is meant depends on the context.

examples[].german: The guest room was spacious and had two beds.
A staff member showed me to the guest room.
en.notes: 客室 is a guest room here, for example in a hotel. 客室は広い describes its size; 客室に案内する means to guide someone to the room. きゃ forms a single mora. In other contexts the word can also mean a passenger cabin; in these examples it is a room.

examples[].german: When I was little, I thought I wanted to become a cake shop owner when I grew up.
That flower shop is pretty.
en.notes: 〜屋 is attached to a word and denotes a shop or a person with the corresponding trade: 花屋 "flower shop", 肉屋 "butcher shop/butcher". さん can make the term more polite. With ケーキ屋さんになりたい it is about a career wish, with 花屋 about the shop. 〜 is a placeholder and is not pronounced. The spelling without the placeholder is 屋.

examples[].german: I bought 400 grams of beef at the butcher.
There is a butcher shop near the station.
en.notes: 肉屋 denotes a butcher shop or a butcher. 肉屋で買う names the shop as the place of purchase. With さん one can make the term more polite: 肉屋さん. 牛肉 is beef; 四百グラム names a concrete purchased amount and is read よんひゃくグラム.

examples[].german: This town has an old teahouse.
I drank tea at a teahouse in Kyōto.
en.notes: 茶屋 here means a teahouse where one can take a break and drink tea. 茶屋があります states that a teahouse exists. 茶屋でお茶を飲む describes it as the place of drinking. The reading is ちゃや; ちゃ forms a single mora.

examples[].german: I bought raw salmon at the fish shop.
I am waiting for a friend in front of the fish shop.
en.notes: 魚屋 is a fish shop or fishmonger. 魚 is read さかな here; with 屋 it becomes さかなや. 魚屋で names the place of shopping, 魚屋の前 the area in front of the shop. 魚屋さん is a more polite term for the shop or the seller.

examples[].german: My friend works as a designer in Nagoya.
Have you ever been to Nagoya?
en.notes: 名古屋 is the name of the city of Nagoya. It is read なごや without long vowels. 名古屋で names the city as the place of an activity, 名古屋に as a travel destination. 行ったことがありますか asks about a past visit, not about a current travel plan.

examples[].german: I get the same error every time.
Thank you for your continued patronage.
en.notes: 毎度 means "every time" and refers to repeated occasions. 毎度、同じエラーが出る describes a regularly recurring problem. In 毎度ありがとうございます, it becomes the usual thanks to repeat customers or for continued support. It does not name a specific number.

examples[].german: Today it is thirty degrees.
This angle is ninety degrees.
I have seen this movie twice.
en.notes: 〜度 follows a number. For temperatures and angles it means "degree": 三十度 "thirty degrees", 九十度 "ninety degrees". As a counter for occurrences it means "time(s)": 二度 "twice". In the third example, 二度 counts how often the movie was seen. The temperature scale must be clear from the context. The reading on this card is ど; 〜 marks the place for the number and is not pronounced. The spelling without the placeholder is 度.

examples[].german: The new book goes on sale tomorrow.
The limited edition sold out on the release day.
en.notes: 発売 is the start of sales of a product; 発売する means to put it on the market. 発売される is the passive form "to be released/to go on sale". 発売日 names the release or sales start day. The verb with する is transitive; the product can be named with を.

examples[].german: I like fish.
I grill fish.
There are fish in the river.
en.notes: 魚（さかな）refers both to live fish and to fish as food. For a live fish, use いる, not ある, for "there is". The reading うお also occurs, especially in compounds; here the common everyday reading さかな is practiced.

examples[].german: Which prefecture are you from?
I went to Osaka Prefecture, Kyoto Prefecture and Hyogo Prefecture.
What is the highest mountain in this prefecture?
en.notes: 〜県 is attached to place names and forms the names of prefectures: 千葉県, 兵庫県. Japan has 47 administrative units (都道府県), of which 43 are 県; exceptions are 東京都, 北海道 and 大阪府 and 京都府. You ask about someone's origin with 何県 or どこの県; 県 also stands alone as a noun (この県, 県の代表). Common compounds are 県庁 ("prefectural government") and 県民 ("prefectural resident").

examples[].german: That woman is a very elegant beauty, isn't she?
I painted a picture of a beautiful woman.
en.notes: 美人 denotes a beautiful woman as a person. It is a noun: 美人です can describe a person, and 美人の絵 a picture of a beautiful woman. The meaning is an assessment of appearance. びじん has no long vowels; じん is written jin.

examples[].german: The match ended in a draw.
I played a game against my friend.
en.notes: 勝負 here means a contest or game in which people compete against each other. 勝負する is an intransitive する verb; 勝負します and 勝負して are regular forms. 勝負は引き分けだった describes the result. With と you can name the opponent, as in 友達と勝負する.

examples[].german: The winner of this race gets money.
I'll give the winner a trophy.
en.notes: 勝者 is the person or group that has won a contest. このレースの勝者 names the competition in question with の. 勝者に names the recipient when an award is handed over. しょうしゃ contains two syllables pronounced together, しょう and しゃ, the first with a long o.

examples[].german: Hoping for certain victory, I bought a good-luck charm.
I wrote 「必勝」 ("certain victory") on the flag.
en.notes: 必勝 is a certain victory. The word is encountered as a motto or wish before a contest. 必勝を願う means to wish for a certain victory. The word expresses confidence or a goal; a written motto does not by itself say how the contest will end. ひっしょう contains a small っ and a long o.

examples[].german: This test was a piece of cake, wasn't it?
Our team won easily.
en.notes: 楽勝 is an easy victory and is also used figuratively for something very easy. 楽勝だった can therefore say of a test that it was a piece of cake. In 楽勝する, the する verb describes an effortless victory. らくしょう ends with a long o.

examples[].german: How many kilograms does Anna weigh?
I have gained weight recently.
en.notes: 体重 is body weight. With 何キロ you ask about weight in kilograms. 体重が増える means that weight increases. The word alone does not judge a number as good or bad. たいじゅう ends with a long u; じゅ is pronounced as one unit.

examples[].german: Please draw a double line under the characters you do not understand.
It has a double meaning.
en.notes: 二重 is a doubling or a double version. With の it modifies a noun: 二重のライン "a double line". 二重に can name a double arrangement or action. The reading on this card is にじゅう with a long u. 二重の意味 can mean a double meaning.

examples[].german: Have you already learned all the kana?
Please write your name in kana.
en.notes: 仮名 refers to kana, that is, the Japanese scripts hiragana and katakana. 仮名で書く names the script used with で. 仮名を学ぶ names it as what is learned. The reading here is かな. In a specific writing task, the context can determine which of the two kana scripts is meant.

examples[].german: Peru is one of the countries in South America.
I want to travel around South America.
en.notes: 南米 is South America; it is a short form of 南アメリカ. 南米の国 names a country of this continent. In 南米を旅行する, を marks the area traveled. なんべい is written Nanbei; the n before b is kept in this romanization.

examples[].german: Let's eat vegetables.
The child doesn't like vegetables.
en.notes: 野菜 is the collective term for vegetables and has no plural ending in Japanese. 野菜を食べる means "to eat vegetables"; individual kinds or quantities are named more precisely when needed. 果物（くだもの）is the everyday counterpart for fruit.

en.meaning: to cross; to intersect; to associate with
examples[].german: I am bad at mingling with all kinds of people at parties.
Two roads intersect.
en.notes: 交わる is an intransitive godan verb: 交わります, 交わって. Paths can cross; people can associate with each other or mingle among others. With が you name the crossing paths, with と the people someone has contact with. The meaning depends on the context.

examples[].german: I am an elementary school teacher.
I live near an elementary school.
en.notes: 小学校 is an elementary school. 小学校の先生 means a teacher at this type of school. 小学校の近くに describes a place near the school. しょうがっこう has two long o and a small っ; the romanization is shōgakkō.

examples[].german: Please be careful with the fire of the heater.
Please be careful on your way home.
en.notes: 気を付けて is a fixed request to be careful. It contains the て-form of 付ける; with ください the request becomes more polite. 火に気を付けて names the danger with に, 気を付けて帰って names careful behavior on the way home. 気をつけて without the character 付 is also common.

examples[].german: My younger brother is a high school student.
When I was a high school student, I often studied in the library.
en.notes: 高校生 is a student at an upper secondary school. 高校生です states the current student status. 高校生の時 can look back on one's own earlier school days. こうこうせい is written kōkōsei: two long o sounds, followed by the vowel sequence ei.

examples[].german: Junior high school students often come to this convenience store.
My younger brother attends junior high school.
en.notes: 中学校 refers to a junior high school, that is, a lower secondary school. 中学校の生徒 refers to its students. 中学校に通う means to attend this school regularly. ちゅうがっこう has a long u, a long o and a small っ.

en.meaning: to stick; to be attached; to come on (light)
examples[].german: This letter doesn't have a stamp on it yet.
The light is on, isn't it?
en.notes: 付く is intransitive here: 切手が付く describes a stamp that is attached, and 電気が付く a light that comes on. The te-form with いる describes the existing state. The place of attachment can be named with に, as in 手紙に. For actively attaching something, the transitive 付ける is used. For lights, 点く is also written; the entry keeps the spelling given here.

examples[].german: Can you find my mother?
I finally found a job.
en.notes: 見付ける means to find someone or something. The object found or sought takes を. The also common spelling 見つける has the same reading; here 見付ける is kept. This ichidan verb forms 見付けます and 見付けない. In the second example, やっと stresses that the search took longer or was harder than hoped.

examples[].german: They say my younger brother is a wimp.
That child is a wimp, isn't it?
Please don't call me a wimp.
en.notes: 弱虫 is a derogatory term for a "coward" or a fearful person. 虫 in this compound does not mean an actual insect. 弱虫だ calls the person that; 弱虫だと言われる reports being called that by others. The word can be used as a noun; the additional sentence shows how to object to this hurtful label.

examples[].german: My husband ran with all his strength despite his frail body.
I can see a faint light.
en.notes: 弱々しい describes something that looks weak or powerless: a body, a voice or even a light. This i-adjective stands before a noun without な: 弱々しい光. In the first example, 体ながら means "despite the body being in this state". It is about the impression of lacking strength; the word does not specify any particular medical cause.

en.meaning: to be chipped; to be lacking; to be missing
examples[].german: The rim of the mug got chipped.
The edge of the plate got chipped.
This plan lacks a concrete explanation.
en.notes: 欠ける is an intransitive ichidan verb here. The damaged edge takes が: 端が欠ける. It can also express that something essential is missing; the thing it concerns then often follows with に. The form 欠けてしまった emphasizes the undesired result. The examples show material damage and a missing explanation, without claiming that anyone caused the damage on purpose.

examples[].german: I like fruit.
I eat fruit every day.
Apples are fruit, but carrots are vegetables.
en.notes: 果物 is the collective term for fruit and refers to edible fruits such as apples or oranges. It takes no plural ending. For individual pieces, suitable counters are used depending on the fruit, often 個. 野菜（やさい）means vegetables.

examples[].german: The old TV at my grandmother's house was black and white.
It is a black-and-white photo.
Please print these materials in black and white.
en.notes: 白黒 means black and white here, that is, an image without colors. The noun connects to another noun with の: 白黒の写真. 白黒で印刷する names the printing mode, 白黒でした an earlier state. The examples use the image and color meaning; in other contexts, the word can also refer to a decision about right and wrong.

examples[].german: That is really nice footage, isn't it?
I saw the footage on TV.
en.notes: 映像 here refers to film or video footage. It can comprise several moving images and is not limited to a single movie. 映像を見る describes watching it, and いい映像 evaluates the footage. The word is a noun; in 映像の編集, の connects it with "editing", for example. The examples do not use a reflection or a mere mental image.

examples[].german: That's an interesting image.
I downloaded the image.
en.notes: 画像 is an image, here especially a digital image file or its visible content. 画像をダウンロードする means downloading this file. おもしろい画像, by contrast, evaluates what can be seen in the image. With の one can add a property, for example 画像の大きさ for the image size; the word is a noun.

examples[].german: A sales manager from a life insurance company came to our house earlier.
Do you have life insurance?
en.notes: 生保 is an abbreviation here for 生命保険, life insurance. 生保に入っている asks about an existing insurance contract, not about entering an office. In the first example, 生保の refers to the field of the sales manager. The same characters can form a different abbreviation in other contexts; here, sales and insurance make clear that life insurance is meant.

examples[].german: To keep up my physical strength, I walk every morning.
Please keep it in a clean condition.
en.notes: 保つ here means to keep something in its state or at its previous level. What is preserved takes を: 体力を保つ or 状態を保つ. This transitive godan verb forms 保ちます, 保って and 保たない. In the first example, daily walking is a personal habit; the second sentence asks to maintain a clean condition.

examples[].german: I tried to persuade my friend, but it did not work out.
I attempted to make bread with a new recipe.
en.notes: 試みる means to make an attempt. It sounds more written or formal than the everyday やってみる. The undertaking takes を, as in 説得を試みる. This ichidan verb forms 試みます and 試みた. The examples contrast trying out a new cooking idea with trying to persuade someone; an attempt does not guarantee success.

examples[].german: First, try it without saying anything.
I tried a sample at the department store.
en.notes: 試食 is tasting food, often before a purchase or as a sample of a new dish. With する it becomes the transitive 試食する; the dish tried can take を. 試食してみて is a familiar request to try it once. The word concerns food and not testing devices or an exam.

examples[].german: This book contrasts the city and the countryside.
Bright scenes and dark scenes are strongly contrasted.
The contrast between the white snow and the red camellias is very beautiful.
en.notes: 対比 means placing two things side by side to make their differences clear - more "juxtaposition, contrast" than a mere "comparison". Typical: AとBを対比する, Aと対比して, 〜の対比が鮮やかだ (for colors, light and shadow, novel characters). 比較 is the general word for "to compare", often with an evaluation of which is better; 対照, like 対比, stresses the contrast. Rather literary, often found in texts on art, literature and statistics.

examples[].german: Now I will announce it. The winner of the speech contest is Ms. Tanaka!
I presented a new product.
en.notes: 発表 is announcing or publicly presenting something. 発表する takes the content with を, for example 新商品を発表する. With an announcement, the content can instead follow in the next sentence. The word also means a presentation; it does not require that the content was secret. 発表 itself is the noun, and 発表します is the polite verb form.

examples[].german: Two eggs, please.
I make an omelet with eggs.
en.notes: 卵 means an egg, in everyday speech often a chicken egg. In cooking, the spelling 玉子 is also seen. Eggs can be counted with 個; the general counting form 二つ is also possible. In 医者の卵 "doctor in the making", on the other hand, it has a figurative meaning.

examples[].german: This graph represents the population of the town.
What does this picture express?
en.notes: 表す can mean to represent what something stands for, or to express a meaning. What is represented follows with を: 人口を表す. With この絵は何を表していますか you ask about the content or message of a picture. This transitive godan verb ending in す forms 表します and 表して. The examples use the representing and expressing meanings that go with this spelling.

examples[].german: There are five minutes until departure.
The train departs at nine o'clock.
en.notes: 出発 means departing or setting off. With する it becomes an intransitive verb: 電車が出発する. 出発まで names the time that remains until departure; 九時に, by contrast, names the point in time itself. The word can also refer to a journey on foot and is not limited to trains.

examples[].german: Oden really calls for mustard, doesn't it?
Do you eat it with mustard?
en.notes: 辛子 is mustard, in Japanese everyday life often the hot yellow mustard served with dishes like oden. The word is often written からし; this entry keeps its kanji spelling. 辛子をつける means to put some of it on the food. In the first sentence, the familiar でしょ asks for agreement on a preference, while the second asks about eating habits.

examples[].german: The other day, I went to the bookstore with a friend.
I bought a new novel at the bookstore.
en.notes: 本屋 is a bookstore here. With 行く, に marks the destination of a visit; with 買う, で marks the place of purchase. The reading ほんや contains ん before や, not a combined syllable にゃ; in romanization it is therefore written hon'ya. The examples concern the shop, not a publisher or a main building, which the word can denote in other contexts.

examples[].german: The puppy was like an angel.
The angel in that painting is beautiful, isn't it?
en.notes: 天使 is an angel as a religious or pictorially represented figure. 天使みたい can affectionately describe an especially lovable being as a comparison; the puppy does not literally become an angel. あの絵の天使, by contrast, names the depicted figure in a picture. The word is used as a noun.

examples[].german: We will hold a big sale in the new year.
Happy New Year!
en.notes: 新年 is the new year, or the time of its beginning. 新年に names it as the time of an event. 新年おめでとうございます is a polite New Year's greeting. The final とう in おめでとう is pronounced as a long tō. The ん of しん and the following ね of ねん remain recognizable in shinnen instead of merging into a single syllable.

examples[].german: I went to hear a conversation between an engineer and a psychologist.
I watched a conversation on TV.
en.notes: 対談 is a conversation or dialogue between two people, often before an audience or for publication. 対談を聞く and 対談を見る treat the conversation as an event or media content. With する it can also express that someone holds such a dialogue with another person. It means more than a brief greeting in passing.

examples[].german: My mother has difficulty walking, so she often uses a car.
There are also people with difficulty walking.
I am hard of hearing, so please write it on paper to tell me.
en.notes: 不自由 can express that a bodily function is limited. 足が不自由 describes an impairment of the legs or of walking. As a na-adjective it connects to a person with な: 足が不自由な方. なので gives the reason for choosing the car in the first example. Here a specific limitation is described, not a trait of the whole person.

examples[].german: "Live with all your strength every day" is a teaching from my father.
I treasure my teacher's teachings.
en.notes: 教え is a teaching, instruction or a principle that has been passed on. 父からの教え names the person it comes from; 先生の教え names the source. 教えを大切にする means to value and preserve this teaching. Here 教え is the noun, not the identically written verb form of 教える.

examples[].german: Is there a convenience store in this area?
There is a hotel near the station.
Near the station, you can hear car noise even at night.
en.notes: 付近 is the immediate surroundings of a place. この付近 names the area around the current reference point; 駅の付近 names the station as the starting point of orientation. The term does not presuppose a fixed distance in meters. In the examples, に marks the place of existing shops or buildings; 付近 itself is a noun.

examples[].german: I eat bread in the morning.
I like freshly baked bread.
en.notes: パン means bread and in everyday Japanese also covers various rolls and sweet baked goods such as 菓子パン. It is a noun, not a verb. 焼きたてのパン means bread that has just been freshly baked.

examples[].german: Michael is a better swimmer than a fish!
He is good at swimming.
Today I will practice swimming at the pool.
en.notes: 泳ぎ is swimming or the way someone swims. In 泳ぎが上手, the swimming ability becomes the object of an evaluation with が. 泳ぎを練習する treats swimming as a practiced activity. The word is a noun here; the identically written connective form of 泳ぐ is a separate grammatical use.

en.meaning: to let through; to show in
examples[].german: Glass lets light through.
Please show the guest into the room.
en.notes: 通す is transitive here. 光を通す means to let light through; お客様を部屋に通す means to show a guest into the room. を marks what is let through or shown in, に the destination. This godan verb ending in す forms 通します and 通して. Unlike 通る, here it describes someone or something making the passage possible.

examples[].german: Excuse me, I do not know how to use this coupon.
This machine is in use.
en.notes: 使用 is the use of an object or means and sounds more formal than 使う. 使用する forms the transitive verb; 使用の仕方 asks as a noun about the way of using something. 使用中 means that something is currently being used, not merely that it is usable. The よう in しよう is pronounced long; it is not the shortened sound sequence しょう.

examples[].german: I'm from Malaysia.
Where are you from?
He is a graduate of this university.
en.notes: 出身 names a person's origin, for example a place, a country or a school. マレーシア出身です means that one comes from Malaysia; it does not automatically determine nationality. 出身はどこですか asks about origin, not about the current place of residence. A place name often stands before 出身 without an additional particle.

examples[].german: The pitcher is being replaced.
The person in charge changed partway through.
en.notes: 交代 is replacing, changing or taking turns in a role. With する, the person who takes over or hands over the place can take が. In sports it concerns, for example, the pitcher; in a work situation, the person in charge. 途中で here means a change during the process; it need not mean a journey "on the way". 交替 is another spelling for this change or replacement; with する it also forms a verb.

examples[].german: I met my teacher there.
Please sit over there.
en.notes: そこ denotes a place near the listener or a place just mentioned. そこで names the place of an action; そこに with 座る the spot where one sits down. For a place far from both conversation partners, あそこ is often used. 其処 is a rare kanji spelling; in everyday writing, そこ is usually used. It is the place demonstrative that is meant, not 底, "bottom".

examples[].german: My house is over there.
There's a shop over there.
en.notes: あそこ is "over there", that is, a place that is distant from the speaker and the listener. The demonstrative needs no additional noun after it: あそこだ indicates the place directly. With に, it names the place where a building exists. あの, by contrast, comes before a noun, such as あの店; the two forms are therefore built into the sentence differently. 彼処 is a rare kanji spelling of this place demonstrative. Normally, あそこ is written in kana.

examples[].german: I lost five kilos in one month.
I ran five kilometers.
en.notes: キロ is the short form of キログラム or キロメートル. The topic decides whether weight or distance is meant: やせる refers to body weight, 走る to the distance covered. A number before キロ gives the amount. If the context allows both, the full term is clearer. In other compounds, キロ can also be the prefix for thousand; the two examples practice the units as nouns.

examples[].german: All that's left is to go back down the same way we came.
I went down the slope.
We slowly went down the mountain road by bus.
en.notes: 下る here means going or driving down along a route. 坂を下る uses を for the path covered; the verb is nonetheless intransitive. This godan verb ending in る forms 下ります and 下って. In the romanizations, this entry's reading くだる is kept; the related 下りる, おりる, is a different verb.

examples[].german: Let's eat.
I like rice and miso soup.
en.notes: ご飯 means cooked rice and, depending on context, a meal as a whole. ご飯を食べる can therefore simply mean "to eat". Uncooked rice grains are called 米. In ご飯とみそ汁, on the other hand, the rice is meant as an individual component.

examples[].german: Is there a way to receive a pension from abroad?
I received the package.
en.notes: 受け取る means to receive or accept something. What is received takes を, and the source can be named with から. A payment can be 受け取る just like a package. This transitive godan verb forms 受け取ります and 受け取って. The examples deal with actually receiving, not interpreting a statement, which is also possible with this word.

examples[].german: Let's rest here for ten minutes.
Let's take a ten-minute break.
I was able to solve this problem in ten minutes.
en.notes: 十分間 means a duration of ten minutes and is read じゅっぷんかん here. The also common reading じっぷんかん is not used in the entry. 間 makes the duration explicit; 十分間で names a span of time within which something is accomplished. The characters 十分 are the number with the counter for minutes here and are not read じゅうぶん, "sufficient".

examples[].german: Last year, I spent the winter in a warm southern country.
This flower is a plant from a southern region.
en.notes: 南国 denotes a southern country or region, often with the idea of a warm climate. It is a noun and connects to another noun with の. It fixes no particular national border and no exact climate type. The examples name a personal travel memory and the origin of a plant from a southern area.

examples[].german: A warm south wind is blowing.
A south wind is blowing today.
The flag is fluttering in the south wind.
en.notes: 南風 is wind coming from the south. This entry's reading is みなみかぜ; the wind direction names where the wind comes from, not where it goes. 南風が吹く describes the blowing. 南風で, by contrast, can give the cause of a movement, such as a fluttering flag. Whether the wind is warm depends on the place and the weather.

examples[].german: The car went toward the southeast.
This room faces southeast.
en.notes: 南東 is the compass direction southeast. With の it connects to 方, the direction, while 向き gives the orientation of a room. The word is a noun, not a na-adjective. 方 is read ほう here; 南東の方に行く means moving in this direction without naming a particular destination.

en.meaning: to give a ride; to take on board; to put on
examples[].german: In Japan, can you take a dog in a taxi?
I put the child in the car.
en.notes: 乗せる here means to let someone board a vehicle or take them along in it. The person or animal takes を, the vehicle takes に. It is the transitive counterpart of 乗る: the child gets in, while someone else puts or takes it in the car. This ichidan verb forms 乗せます and 乗せて; the examples state no general rule about taking animals in taxis.

examples[].german: My internet speed is so slow that it irritates me.
Please reduce your speed.
en.notes: 速度 is the speed or pace of a process. 速度が遅い describes a low speed; 速度を落とす means to reduce it. The word can refer to traffic and to technical processes such as an internet connection. The examples state no particular unit of measurement, so speed is judged qualitatively.

examples[].german: This train runs to the last stop.
The last stop of this bus is Tokyo Station.
At the terminal, all the passengers got off.
en.notes: 終点 is the last station or the end of a transport route. 終点まで names the end point to which a train runs. 終点は東京駅です identifies the specific terminal of a bus route under discussion. 終点で names the place of getting off. It concerns the route of this service, not the general end of every journey.

examples[].german: The meeting has ended.
The game has ended.
Please save first and then finish your work.
en.notes: 終了 is the end or conclusion of a process. 終了する can express that something comes to an end, or that someone ends something; the sentence structure decides. 試合が終了する names the game as ended, 作業を終了する the activity someone finishes. 終了しました reports an end that has occurred, while the additional sentence asks for a deliberate conclusion.

examples[].german: I like Japanese food.
My mother's cooking is delicious.
I like cooking.
en.notes: 料理 can refer to the activity of cooking, a prepared dish or a cuisine as a style. 日本料理 means "Japanese cuisine", 母の料理 the food prepared by one's mother. For the activity, 料理する or 料理をする is used.

examples[].german: When does the last bus leave?
This is the last bus.
Please send it once the final check is finished.
en.notes: 最終 denotes the last position or phase in a series. Before a noun, の often follows, as in 最終のバス or 最終の確認; compounds such as 最終確認 are also common. The bus examples refer to the last scheduled service, the additional example to a final checking step. The word itself is a noun, not a na-adjective.

examples[].german: I heard the sound of a ball rolling.
The ball is rolling.
Empty cans are lying around on the floor.
en.notes: 転がる is intransitive: the ball is described as rolling, without naming the cause of this movement. The verb forms 転がります and 転がって. 転がっている can also mean "lying around" in a suitable context, such as empty cans on the floor. The examples therefore show both a movement and objects lying scattered.

examples[].german: My father drives a car or motorcycle between the office and home every day.
My father is driving the car.
Please drive the car slowly on rainy days.
en.notes: 運転する here means to operate a vehicle. 車を運転する names the vehicle being driven with を; a route driven can also be given with を. 間 is read あいだ in the route between the company and the house. The suru-form gives 運転します and 運転して. Merely riding along without steering oneself is not meant.

examples[].german: When a car drives, its tires rotate.
This chair swivels.
Please turn this handle one full turn.
en.notes: 回転 is a rotation around an axis or a turning movement. 回転する is intransitive here: the tires or the chair turn. 一回転 denotes one complete revolution. 回転させる makes something turn; the handle being moved then follows with を. The examples use the physical rotating movement, not the turnover rate of goods and not mental agility.

examples[].german: Please move forward a little more.
Please go straight ahead.
I made good progress on my work today.
en.notes: 進む is intransitive and can describe spatial movement forward or progress in a piece of work. 前に names the direction for movement; 仕事が names the process that is progressing. This godan verb forms 進みます and 進んで. For a direct object that someone deliberately moves forward, 進める would be used rather than 進む in this contrast.

examples[].german: The road construction is progressing.
The construction work is progressing smoothly.
Let's first confirm how the meeting will proceed.
en.notes: 進行 here denotes the progress of a piece of work or an event. In the examples, 進行する is used for a process that moves forward. 順調に additionally says that this happens smoothly; 進行 alone does not yet judge the course positively. 会議の進行 names, as a noun, the course of a meeting. The entry practices this meaning for work and events.

examples[].german: Last summer, we went to a mountain with beautiful fresh green leaves.
The fresh green leaves of early summer are beautiful.
When I opened the window, I smelled the scent of fresh green leaves.
en.notes: 青葉 are fresh green leaves, or young foliage. In this nature word, 青 is used for green; the leaves are not blue. 青葉が美しい describes their sight, 青葉の香り their smell. The plant word is meant here and not a personal or place name with the same characters.

examples[].german: Winning the lottery, you're lucky.
You're lucky today, aren't you?
Luckily, I was able to buy the last ticket.
en.notes: 運がいい means to have luck: a favorable coincidence benefits someone. 運 takes が and いい evaluates this coincidence; it is not simply about the feeling of being happy. 運がいいことに introduces a fortunate circumstance and can be translated as "luckily". The examples show an unexpected win and the luck of still getting a ticket.

en.meaning: release; making public; opening to the public
examples[].german: That movie will be released next week.
The minutes of the meeting are scheduled to be made public later.
The garden of this temple is open to the public only in spring and autumn.
en.notes: 公開 means making something accessible to the public: films (映画が公開される = "is released in theaters"), information, data, gardens or buildings. As a transitive する-verb the object takes を: 情報を公開する; the passive 公開される is very common. 公表 stresses the official announcement of facts, 発表 announcing or presenting, while 公開 puts making accessible in the foreground. Opposite: 非公開 ("not open to the public"). Common: 一般公開, 公開日, 情報公開.

examples[].german: Did you have breakfast?
For breakfast I eat bread.
My father is preparing breakfast for the family.
en.notes: 朝ご飯 refers to the whole breakfast meal, even if you eat bread instead of rice. 朝ご飯を食べる means "to have breakfast"; 朝ご飯にパンを食べる names what you eat for breakfast. 朝食 is the more formal term, for example on a hotel schedule. 朝御飯 is an attested, less common spelling with the same reading.

examples[].german: Today is the day for collecting money.
Someone comes to collect the money every month.
I put the collected money in an envelope.
en.notes: 集金 is the collecting or gathering of money, such as payments that are due. 集金の日 names a day set aside for it, and 集金に来る the purpose of a visit. With する it forms a verb; 集金したお金 is money that has already been collected. It concerns collecting a payment, not automatically a voluntary donation, for which 寄付, for example, is used.

examples[].german: At school, we learned about the lives of farmers in the past.
That farmer grows rice.
en.notes: 農民 refers to people who engage in agriculture and also appears in historical descriptions. As a noun it can be described with の: むかしの農民 are farmers of earlier times. 農民のくらし means their way of life, 農民が米を作る their activity. The word names a group of people and is not an adjective; it does not claim that all these people grow the same crops.

examples[].german: Our company president is an ironman who comes to work even after a triathlon.
That person is as strong as an iron man.
en.notes: 鉄人 is here, figuratively, a person with extraordinary strength or endurance. The fact that the company president still works after a triathlon is the basis for this comparison; he is not made of iron. 鉄人のように means "like an iron man" and compares a trait. The noun can also denote a robot in fictional contexts; this meaning is not used in the examples.

examples[].german: When I grow up, I want to join an electric railway company.
This railway line is convenient.
en.notes: 電鉄 is an electric railway and often appears as part of the name of a railway company. 電鉄会社 names the company where someone wants to work; この電鉄 refers, in the second example, to the railway line under discussion. 会社に入社する means to join a company. The characters 電 and 鉄 help in recognizing the word, but do not replace its full reading でんてつ.

examples[].german: The arithmetic teacher is Mr. Tanaka.
Let's do our arithmetic homework.
en.notes: 算数 is arithmetic, or elementary mathematics as a school subject. 算数の先生 names the teacher for this subject, 算数の宿題 the corresponding homework. The word is a noun and connects here to the following noun with の. The more general term for mathematics is 数学; the two words are not used in the same way in every educational context.

examples[].german: I attend a Japanese class once a week.
I'm studying Japanese.
Please write your name in Japanese.
en.notes: 日本語 is the Japanese language and is used as a noun. 日本語を勉強する names it as the object of study; 日本語で書く names with で the language in which something is written. 日本語の教室 denotes a Japanese course. 一回 is read いっかい, so 週に一回 means "once a week". A subject of study and the linguistic means of an action fulfill different roles in the sentence.

examples[].german: I went to university to study French.
I can speak a little French.
en.notes: フランス語 denotes the French language; 語 is read ご in this language name. フランス語を学ぶ names the subject of study, フランス語が話せる the language one can speak. ために explains the purpose of going to university in the first example. In the usual writing, the syllables of the country name are in katakana; the entry's continuous hiragana reading gives the same pronunciation.

examples[].german: I taught Spanish to a friend.
I want to study Spanish.
en.notes: スペイン語 is Spanish as a language. 人にスペイン語を教える names the learner with に and the subject taught with を. 教えてあげる presents the teaching as a favor to this person; the form suits a familiar relationship better than a neutral statement about teaching. 勉強したい, by contrast, expresses one's own wish to study. The 語 of the language name is read ご.

examples[].german: How are you doing today?
How are you feeling physically?
This computer hasn't been working well lately.
en.notes: 調子 here means the condition of a person or the functioning of a device. 体の調子 asks explicitly about physical well-being; without this addition, the context can clarify the reference. 調子がいい and 調子が悪い evaluate how well something is going or working. For a computer, 調子が悪い describes a malfunction, not an illness. Other meanings such as a musical tone are not practiced here.

examples[].german: The teacher emphasized the important points.
Please emphasize this word.
I highlighted the places to watch out for with red lines.
en.notes: 強調 is the special emphasizing or highlighting of a statement. With する it is transitive: the emphasized word or important point takes を. 強調 can happen in speech or through visible markings; in the additional example, a red line is the means of directing attention. Here it does not mean greater loudness as such, but the special weighting of a content.

examples[].german: My younger brother is ten years old.
I play soccer with my younger brother.
en.notes: 弟 means a younger brother, whether he is a child or an adult. For your own brother you normally say 弟; for another person's younger brother, 弟さん is polite. The age is relative to the person in question, not to the speaker in every situation.

examples[].german: What's for lunch?
Let's have lunch together.
en.notes: 昼ご飯 refers to the midday meal. 昼御飯 and 昼ごはん are also found as spellings. With 何ですか you ask what food there is; 一緒に食べましょう invites someone to have lunch together.

examples[].german: I have only told close friends so far.
He and I are close friends.
en.notes: 親しい here describes a close, familiar relationship with people. 親しい友人 are close friends; 人と親しい names with と the person one is close to. It is an i-adjective and stands before 友人 or 友達 without な. しか with a negative form limits the circle of those in the know to close friends in the first example. Physical closeness would be expressed with 近い instead.

examples[].german: Your expression has become calmer than last time.
You have a frightening look on your face, don't you?
The actor changed his expression and played a different person.
en.notes: 顔付き denotes the facial expression or the outward appearance of the face. 顔付きが穏やかになる describes a change to a calmer expression; 怖い顔付きをしている describes the visible impression. With 顔付きを変える, someone can deliberately change their expression, for example when acting. The first sentence compares with an earlier meeting, not with another person's face.

examples[].german: Because of Alzheimer's disease, there are times when I cannot remember various things.
My grandfather is in the hospital with heart disease.
My father has diabetes, so he cuts back on sweets.
en.notes: 〜病 is a suffix for names of diseases: 心臓病 ("heart disease"), 糖尿病 ("diabetes"), アルツハイマー病. On its own, 病 is not read びょう; the everyday word for illness is 病気, and literary there is 病（やまい）. For syndromes and complaints, 〜症 is often used instead, such as 花粉症 ("hay fever") or 熱中症 ("heatstroke").

examples[].german: Is anyone sick or injured?
I took the sick person to the hospital.
en.notes: 病人 is a sick person, not necessarily someone already being treated in a hospital. 病人がいる states the presence of such a person with いる, which is used for living beings. 病人を病院に連れて行く names the accompanied person with を and the destination with に. ケガ人 is read けがにん and, in contrast, denotes injured people in the first example.

examples[].german: Shaved ice is best eaten in summer.
The weather is wonderful today.
Today's highest temperature was thirty degrees.
en.notes: 最高 can express an enthusiastic evaluation such as "wonderful" or name the highest value of a quantity. 天気は最高です praises the weather; 最高気温 is the highest temperature. Before a noun, compounds such as 最高気温 and connections with の are common. The examples therefore distinguish a personal judgment from a measurable maximum. かき氷 is shaved ice.

examples[].german: The panda ate bamboo one piece after another.
Problems came up one after another.
en.notes: 次々 describes a series of events in which the next one keeps being added. It can be used adverbially with に or と: 次々に竹を食べる and 問題が次々と出てくる. It emphasizes the sequence and not simply a large total quantity. In the second example, problems arise one after another; 出てくる means "to crop up" here, not people coming out of a room.

examples[].german: Shall we replace this part with gold?
I replaced the old part with a new one.
In today's game, we substituted one player.
en.notes: 代える is a transitive ichidan verb: what or who is replaced can take を, the replacement に. For things, this word family is often written 替える, and for another person as a stand-in or replacement, often 代える. When replacing things, the spelling 代える also appears next to 替える. The player substitution shows the typical use with a person. The forms are 代えます and 代えて, not a godan form ending in って.

examples[].german: Many of the town's residents go to the eye doctor.
I have to go to the eye doctor.
en.notes: 目医者 is an understandable term for an eye doctor. 目医者に通う describes repeated visits; 目医者に行く can mean a single trip to this practice. に names the destination. The first sentence describes the behavior of many local residents, the second a personal necessity. The reading めいしゃ is romanized as meisha; the vowel sequence remains recognizable.

examples[].german: Please turn right and enter the first room.
My name was called first.
en.notes: 一番目 is the first position in a sequence. 一番目の部屋 identifies the first room with の; 一番目に names the rank of an event, such as in the calling of names. 目 makes it an ordinal number explicitly. Being first in the order is not a claim that this room or person is qualitatively the best. The reading is いちばんめ without a small っ.

examples[].german: I'm looking forward to the date tomorrow.
I'm looking forward to the trip.
Looking at the flowers in the garden every morning is my pleasure.
en.notes: 楽しみ can be anticipation of an event or a regular joy in everyday life. デートが楽しみです means that you are looking forward to the date; the noun is combined with です here. 毎朝花を見るのが楽しみです, by contrast, names a recurring pleasant activity. 楽しみにしている is also a common form for anticipation. The entry is the noun 楽しみ, not the identically written continuative form of the verb 楽しむ.

examples[].german: I make dinner.
I eat dinner at seven o'clock.
en.notes: 晩ご飯 means the evening meal. 晩御飯 and 晩ごはん are other common spellings; 夕食 is another term for dinner. A mealtime is attached with に, such as 七時に食べる.

examples[].german: This curry uses spices intended for Japanese people.
This book is intended for children.
This car is made for the overseas market.
en.notes: 〜向け attaches to a noun and denotes the target group or the intended market. 子供向けです means "intended for children"; 子供向けの本 uses の before the following noun. 海外向けに作る names, with に, the market for which something is made. It is a word suffix, not an independent sentence particle. The sign 〜 only shows the attachment point and is not pronounced. The spelling without the placeholder is 向け.

en.meaning: to be saved; to be helped
examples[].german: You will surely be saved. Don't worry.
Everyone was saved.
It would help me if you carried the luggage.
en.notes: 助かる is intransitive: it describes the person who is rescued or the one who benefits from help. It can mean being rescued from danger, but also "that would be a help to me". 荷物を持ってくれると助かります asks for support indirectly and says that carrying would be a relief. The active "to save or support someone" is 助ける. As a godan verb, 助かる forms 助かります and 助かって.

examples[].german: Summer is the season for eating shaved ice and enjoying fireworks.
Let's enjoy the trip.
en.notes: 楽しむ means to take pleasure in an activity or experience. The thing enjoyed takes を: 花火を楽しむ or 旅行を楽しむ. This transitive godan verb ending in む forms 楽しみます and 楽しんで; the invitation 楽しみましょう suggests enjoying something together. Unlike 楽しみです, which often expresses anticipation, the verb here describes experiencing something pleasant. 楽む is an additional dictionary and search spelling with the same reading たのしむ. 楽しむ remains the usual form; the variant is not a different verb.

en.meaning: to hurl at; to throw at
examples[].german: Throwing pebbles at people is rude!
Please do not throw the ball at anyone.
I ended up hurling hurtful words at the other person.
en.notes: 投げ付ける is a forceful throw or one aimed at someone. The thrown object takes を, and the target can be named with に. With 言葉 or insults as the object, it is figurative: one hurls hurtful words at someone. This ichidan verb forms 投げ付けます and 投げ付けて. The negative 投げ付けないでください asks to refrain from this action; an unnamed target is not added in translation.

examples[].german: In this folktale, a tanuki bewitches people.
I feel as if I had been bewitched by a fox.
en.notes: 化かす is a transitive godan verb: 化かします, 化かして. In stories it can mean "to bewitch" or "to deceive by magic". With を you name the person deceived. 狐に化かされたような気分 means figuratively to feel as if bewitched or completely confused; 化かされた is the passive form.

examples[].german: As soon as Koichi's baby's name is decided, I will let you know right away.
We decided on the plan at the meeting.
en.notes: 決定する means "to decide" or "to determine" and forms する forms: 決定します, 決定して. With を you name what someone decides. With が you can say that something is settled: 名前が決定する. 決定したら names the settling as the condition for the next action. けってい contains a small っ and the vowel sequence ei.

en.meaning: to meet by chance; to come across; to meet up (flow together)
examples[].german: I ran into a friend on my trip.
I came across a wonderful book at the library.
Two rivers flow together in this valley.
en.notes: 出会う is an intransitive godan verb: 出会います, 出会って. It means a chance encounter or discovering something. With に you name the person or thing you come across. With すてきな本に出会う, it is figuratively about discovering an appealing book. 出合う is another spelling with the same reading であう. For rivers flowing together or paths meeting, 出合う is especially typical. An older "rendezvous" is a secret meeting in dictionary examples; for a normal appointment, one uses, for example, 待ち合わせる instead.

examples[].german: In April, I joined a private railway company.
I commute by private railway.
en.notes: 私鉄 is a private railway. 私鉄の会社 names a corresponding railway company, 私鉄で the means of transport. 入社する describes joining a company. 私鉄で通勤する means to commute to work by this railway. してつ is read without a long vowel.

examples[].german: Our dog makes a lot of demands.
The workers made a demand.
en.notes: 要求 is a demand or an insistent request. 要求する is a transitive する verb: 要求します, 要求して. With を you name what is demanded. 要求が多い describes many wishes or demands; 要求を出す means to make a demand. The reading ようきゅう has a long o and a long u.

examples[].german: I'd like to enroll at a private university.
My older sister attends a private university.
en.notes: 私大 is an abbreviation of 私立大学, i.e. a private university. 私大に入学する means entering such a university, 私大に通う means attending it regularly. The reading is しだい with no long vowel. The word by itself says nothing about tuition or quality.

examples[].german: I go to school.
School starts at nine.
en.notes: 学校 refers to a school as an institution and, in everyday speech, also to school life. 学校に行く names the school as a destination; 学校で勉強する names the school as a place of learning. The small っ in がっこう is written as a double consonant kk, the long o as ō.

examples[].german: What time does the event start?
The class has started.
en.notes: 開始 is the start of an action or event. 開始する forms a する-verb and can be transitive or intransitive: 作業を開始する "to start the work", 授業が開始する "the class starts". 開始時間 asks for the start time. 開始します and 開始して are regular する-forms.

examples[].german: This dress shows off the curves of the body beautifully.
I drew a curved line on the paper.
en.notes: 曲線 is a curved line or curve. 曲線を描く describes drawing one, 体の曲線 the contours of a body. 見せてくれる describes the impression something gives. きょ forms a single mora; きょくせん has no long vowels.

examples[].german: I went abroad to learn various languages.
This book is written in three languages.
en.notes: 言語 is a language as a system. 言語を学ぶ names it as the subject being learned; 色々な言語 means various languages. 学ぶために explains the purpose of an action. The reading on this card is げんご. Here the word refers to languages in general, not to a single spoken sentence.

examples[].german: The Tokyo Disney Resort is in Chiba Prefecture.
I have a friend who lives in Chiba.
en.notes: 千葉 can mean the city or the prefecture of Chiba. 千葉県 explicitly names the prefecture, and 千葉市 explicitly names the city. 千葉に住む gives Chiba as a place of residence; without an addition, the context determines the exact reference. ちば has no long vowels.

examples[].german: I blurted out what I really think.
I couldn't help laughing.
en.notes: 思わず describes a reaction that happens involuntarily or without prior intention. It stands before the action as an adverb. 思わず本音を口にする means letting one's true thoughts slip out. 思わず笑ってしまう describes laughter that escapes you. してしまいました can emphasize that the action was completed unintentionally.

examples[].german: This standing bar has cheap draft beer and tasty snacks.
You can drink standing up here.
en.notes: 立ち飲み is drinking while standing. 立ち飲み屋 or 立ち飲みの店 refers to a shop or bar where people drink standing. 立ち飲みができます is about the possibility of drinking in this way. The reading is たちのみ, with no long vowels.

examples[].german: I'm going to do the cleaning work now.
The work is finished.
en.notes: 作業 is a concrete piece of work or task. 作業する forms an intransitive する-verb; 作業をする is also common. 作業が終わる describes completion. 作業をします can announce an upcoming task. さぎょう contains a long o and the jointly pronounced sequence ぎょ.

en.meaning: to fall ill; to suffer mentally
examples[].german: I was ill for a long time.
In this story, the protagonist is mentally troubled.
en.notes: 病む is a Godan verb: 病みます, 病んで. It can refer to illness or suffering. 病んでいる describes a continuing state. In 心を病む, 心 is named with を as the affected area. This expression denotes mental suffering; the exact condition must be inferred from the context.

examples[].german: I went to the town hall this morning.
I submitted a notification to the town hall.
en.notes: 役場 is a town hall, i.e. the local government office. 役場に行く names it as the destination of a visit. 役場に届を出す describes submitting a notification there. 行ってきました expresses that one went there and came back. The reading is やくば.

en.meaning: tone of voice; manner of speaking
examples[].german: My father's tone toward my older sister was harsh.
Please speak in a gentle tone.
en.notes: 口調 is the way someone speaks, i.e. their tone of voice. 人に対する口調 states who the tone is directed at. 優しい口調で describes a gentle tone as the manner of speaking. The reading is くちょう with a long o; here 口 is read only as く.

examples[].german: I study Japanese at university.
The university is far from home.
en.notes: 大学 means a university or college. The place of an activity takes で: 大学で勉強する. In 大学は家から遠い, 家から names the reference point of the distance. This card does not cover historical administrative schools or the classic book title 大学.

examples[].german: I ate raw corn at a farm in Aomori.
I work on a large farm.
en.notes: 農場 is an agricultural operation or farm. 農場で names it as the place of an activity. 青森の農場 places it in a region; 大きな農場 describes its size. のうじょう has two long o sounds and is written nōjō.

examples[].german: It was only this morning that I remembered, "Oh! The test is today!"
It was cold this morning, wasn't it?
en.notes: 今朝 means "this morning" and is read けさ. It can stand as a time expression without any particle, or become the topic with は. 今朝になってから stresses that one only noticed something this very morning. The expression refers to the morning of the day on which it is spoken.

examples[].german: My older brother is good and fast at addition.
Let's learn addition first.
en.notes: 足し算 is addition, i.e. adding numbers together. 足し算が上手 describes good arithmetic skill. 足し算を習う names addition as what is being learned. In this word 算 is read ざん; たしざん has no long vowels.

examples[].german: Of course I can do subtraction!
Next, let's practice subtraction.
en.notes: 引き算 is subtraction, i.e. taking numbers away. 引き算ができる describes the ability to do it; 引き算を練習する names what is practiced. 算 is read ざん here. With 次は you can announce subtraction as the next learning step. 引算 is a spelling variant of 引き算 with the same reading ひきざん and the same meaning. The usual spelling on this card is 引き算.

examples[].german: When someone comes, the security light comes on.
Because the light came on, I started reading a book.
en.notes: 点く is an intransitive godan verb: 点きます, 点いて. It describes a light or device coming on; it takes が. With the transitive 点ける, someone switches something on. 点いたので can name the coming on as the reason for a following action. The spelling つく is also often seen.

examples[].german: Walking on a mountain path takes physical stamina.
I rested partway along the mountain path.
en.notes: 山道 is a path or road in the mountains. The reading on this card is やまみち. In 山道を歩く, を marks the path that is traversed. 山道の途中 names a point along the way on this path. The word alone does not say how difficult or steep the path is.

examples[].german: Oh, I smell tobacco.
Please don't smoke cigarettes here.
en.notes: タバコ means tobacco or a cigarette. タバコのにおい describes the smell that is perceived. タバコを吸う means "to smoke"; 吸わないでください asks someone not to. The word is often written in kana. All vowels in タバコ are short. 煙草（たばこ） is a kanji spelling of the same word; タバコ or たばこ is commonly used. The characters are read as a whole word, たばこ.

examples[].german: The service at that restaurant is so-so, don't you think?
I am grateful for the staff member's service.
en.notes: サービス here means service, i.e. attendance or care. レストランのサービス refers to what the restaurant provides. サービスに感謝する describes thanks for this care. ビミョーじゃない？ is a colloquial, skeptical assessment. サービス is written sābisu, with a long a.

examples[].german: However, that was a lie.
Japanese is difficult. However, it is interesting.
en.notes: しかし is a conjunction meaning "however/but". It introduces a statement that contrasts with the preceding one. しかし、それはウソだった corrects an earlier account; 難しいです。しかし面白いです sets two evaluations against each other. It is often used in explanatory or written texts. 然し is a rare kanji spelling of しかし. The usual spelling of the conjunction is in kana.

examples[].german: My company is in that office building over there.
That building is tall, isn't it?
en.notes: ビル is a short form of ビルディング and refers to a multi-story building. オフィスビル is an office building. 会社がビルに入っている describes the company as being housed there. 入ってる is the colloquial short form of 入っている. ビル has two short vowels; ビール, by contrast, means beer.

examples[].german: I go to the hospital.
I got medicine at the hospital.
en.notes: 病院 means a hospital or clinic. 病院に行く can also mean a visit to the doctor in everyday speech, without anyone being admitted. For the destination use に, for an action there で. Do not confuse it with 美容院（びよういん, hair salon）.

en.meaning: to be taught; to learn from someone
examples[].german: You should learn the apple pie recipe from Grandma.
I learned Japanese from my teacher.
en.notes: 教わる is a transitive Godan verb: 教わります, 教わって. に names the person you learn from, and を the thing learned. The focus is on the learner. 教える, in contrast, describes teaching from the teacher's point of view. 教わるといいよ is friendly advice to have someone teach you something.

en.meaning: to leave; to go away; to pass
examples[].german: The fad will be over soon anyway.
My friend left this town last year.
en.notes: 去る is an intransitive Godan verb here: 去ります, 去って. In 町を去る, を marks the place that is left. ブームが去る means a trend is over. どうせ can express a resigned or dismissive expectation: "anyway". The reading さる has short vowels.

examples[].german: Could you tell me the plans for the day after tomorrow?
