I'm going on a trip starting the day after tomorrow.
en.notes: 明後日（あさって）is the day after tomorrow, counted from today. As a time expression it often stands without に; with の it can modify a noun: 明後日の予定. The more formal reading みょうごにち belongs to a separate reading entry. The fixed phrase あさっての方向, on the other hand, means a completely wrong direction.

examples[].german: I made a mistake in only one place on the test.
Please gather in one place.
en.notes: 一ヶ所 means "one place" or "one spot". The reading is いっかしょ with a small っ; the small ヶ is read か here. 一ヶ所だけ limits something to exactly one place. 一ヶ所に集まる means that everyone comes together in one place. 一箇所 and 一カ所 are also common spellings.

examples[].german: Please draw a straight line on the paper.
On the map, this road is shown as a straight line.
en.notes: 直線 is a straight line. 直線を引く means to draw such a line; に names the surface and で a tool used. 直線になる describes a line as straight. The sequence ちょ forms a single mora. 曲線, by contrast, means a curved line.

examples[].german: The car was driving straight ahead slowly.
Please go straight along this road.
At intersections, cars going straight have priority over cars turning right.
en.notes: 直進 means "to go straight ahead" and is typical of traffic language, navigation announcements and physics (光は直進する). It is intransitive; the route you travel along takes を, as with other verbs of movement: この道を直進する. In everyday speech people often simply say まっすぐ行く; 直進 sounds more matter-of-fact. At intersections, 直進 is contrasted with 右折/左折, e.g. 直進車 ("vehicle going straight ahead").

examples[].german: My father lives in Tokyo.
Yesterday I talked with my father on the phone.
en.notes: 父 is the humble term for one's own father when speaking about him to others. The reading is ちち. 父と話す names him as the conversation partner, 父は introduces him as the topic. For another person's father, polite everyday speech usually uses お父さん.

examples[].german: My mother works at a school.
I gave flowers to my mother.
en.notes: 母 is the humble term for one's own mother when talking with others. The reading はは has two short a's. In 母に花をあげる, she is marked with に as the recipient and the flowers with を as the gift. For another person's mother, one usually says お母さん politely.

examples[].german: My older brother is a university student.
On Sunday I watched a movie with my older brother.
en.notes: 兄 means one's own older brother when speaking about him. Age is part of the meaning; 弟 is the younger brother. 兄と映画を見る names the brother as a companion. The reading is あに. For another person's older brother, お兄さん is often used politely.

examples[].german: My older sister teaches Japanese.
I received a letter from my older sister.
en.notes: 姉 is the term for one's own older sister when telling others about her. 姉から names her as the source of a letter or gift. 姉は日本語を教えています describes her occupation. The reading あね contains no long vowels. A younger sister is 妹.

examples[].german: The bank is near the station.
I withdraw money at the bank.
en.notes: 銀行 means a financial institution, not a bench. The location can be described with ～の近く. For "to withdraw money", the combination お金をおろす is used; the bank as the place of action takes で.

examples[].german: My uncle lives in Osaka.
I asked a man I didn't know the way to the station.
en.notes: おじさん can mean an uncle or, informally, a middle-aged man. Among relatives, 伯父さん is also written for an older brother and 叔父さん for a younger brother of a parent. For a stranger, the other meaning is clear from the context. おじさん has a short i; おじいさん has a long i.

examples[].german: I drank tea with my aunt.
I asked a woman I didn't know the way.
en.notes: In the family, おばさん means "aunt". 伯母さん refers to an older sister and 叔母さん to a younger sister of a parent. In informal speech, おばさん can also mean a middle-aged woman. The context shows whether a relative is meant. ば has a short a; おばあさん has a long a.

examples[].german: My grandfather takes a walk every morning.
That old man is very energetic.
en.notes: おじいさん can mean a grandfather or an elderly man. 私のおじいさん makes it clear that one's own grandfather is meant. The i-sequence in じい is pronounced long; the shorter おじさん means uncle or middle-aged man. With あのおじいさん, the context decides whether a relative is meant.

examples[].german: Please use the red pen.
The traffic light is red.
en.notes: 赤 is the noun for red. Before another noun it is connected with の: 赤のペン. 赤い, on the other hand, is an adjective and stands directly before the noun. 信号は赤です states the state of a traffic light. This card uses the reading あか and the color meaning.

examples[].german: This paper is white.
I bought a white shirt.
en.notes: 白 is a noun for the color white. 白です can state the color as a predicate; 白のシャツ connects the noun with a piece of clothing. The adjective 白い needs no の before シャツ. The reading しろ has short vowels. The color meaning is intended here.

examples[].german: My favorite color is black.
The black bag is mine.
en.notes: 黒 is the noun for black. 好きな色は黒です states a color preference. 黒のかばん uses の between the color noun and the bag. 私のです omits the noun that was already mentioned and here means "it's mine". 黒い is the adjective form.

examples[].german: Yellow flowers are blooming.
My younger sister has a yellow bag.
en.notes: 黄色い is an i-adjective. It stands directly before the noun it describes: 黄色い花, 黄色いかばん. As a predicate you can use 黄色いです; the negative form is 黄色くないです. The color noun is 黄色. The sequence きい contains a long i.

examples[].german: There is a small pond in the park.
I ate my packed lunch by the pond.
en.notes: 池 is a pond. 池があります states its existence; に marks the place. 池のそば refers to the area right by the pond. The reading is いけ. Bodies of water take あります, while fish in the water are expressed with います.

examples[].german: Where is the post office?
I mail a letter at the post office.
en.notes: 郵便局 means a post office or postal branch, that is, the place for postal services. 郵便 on its own is mail as items sent or as a service. With 郵便局で手紙を出す you describe mailing a letter at the post office.

examples[].german: Hokkaido is in the north of Japan.
Please walk north from the station.
en.notes: 北 here is the noun for north and is read きた. 日本の北に gives the location in the north of Japan. 北へ names a direction of movement; the particle へ is pronounced e. 北という方角 can be used without a specific place name. In compounds, 北 is often read ほく.

examples[].german: Okinawa is in the south of Japan.
The window of the room faces south.
en.notes: 南 is the noun for south. The reading on this card is みなみ. 日本の南に describes the location in the south of Japan. 南を向いている describes something as facing south. With 南へ you can name a direction of movement; the verb that follows determines the sentence structure.

examples[].german: The sun rises in the east.
The school is east of the station.
en.notes: 東 is the noun for east and is read ひがし here. 東から出る names the east as the starting direction. 駅の東に describes a location east of the station. In compounds, 東 can also be read とう, as in 東京; the reading on this card remains ひがし.

examples[].german: The sun sets in the west.
It's a ten-minute walk west from the station.
en.notes: 西 is the noun for west. 西に沈む describes the sun setting in the west. 西へ names the direction of movement; へ is pronounced e. 十分 as a length of time is read じゅっぷん here, i.e. ten minutes. The reading にし contains short vowels.

examples[].german: I take medicine after the meal.
I'll call you later.
Please follow me.
en.notes: On this card, 後 is read あと. For the time meaning, a noun is connected with の後: ご飯の後 "after the meal". 後で can mean "later" without an explicitly stated reference point. Spatially, 後 can mean the area behind someone: 私の後について来る means to follow me, walking behind me. あと contains two short vowels.

en.meaning: before; ahead; beforehand; the point further ahead
examples[].german: May I go home before the others?
There is a shop further down this road.
en.notes: 先 is read さき here. 先に means "first" or "before the others" in terms of time. この道の先に describes, spatially, a point further ahead on this road. 帰ってもいいですか asks for permission. The rest of the sentence shows whether 先 is meant in terms of time or space.

examples[].german: What time is the next train?
I'll read next.
en.notes: 次 is a noun for the next one in a sequence. Before another noun it is connected with の: 次の電車. 次は makes the next step or the next person the topic. 次に can mean "next". The reading is つぎ, with short vowels.

examples[].german: I'm eating at home this evening.
May I call you this evening?
en.notes: 今晩 means "this evening" or "tonight". It refers to the evening of the day on which it is spoken. As a time expression it can stand without a particle; 今晩は makes the evening the topic, with は read wa. 今晩、電話してもいいですか asks permission for a call this evening.

examples[].german: In the early evening I go for a walk with my dog.
I'll be back by early evening.
en.notes: 夕方 refers to late afternoon through early evening, roughly the time around dusk. It does not name a fixed time of day. 夕方までに means "by early evening" and sets a latest point in time. The reading ゆうがた has a long u; 方 is read がた here.

examples[].german: Dinner is at seven.
Shall we cook dinner together?
en.notes: 夕飯 is the evening meal. The reading on this card is ゆうはん, with a long u. 夕飯は七時です gives the planned mealtime. 夕飯を作る names dinner as something that is prepared. 作りませんか is a polite invitation to cook together.

examples[].german: I borrow books from the library.
I study at the library.
en.notes: 図書館 is a library with books to read or borrow, not a bookstore（本屋）. For activities there, the place takes で. 本を借りる means to borrow a book; 本を返す means to return it.

examples[].german: It rained from morning till night.
That evening I went to bed early.
en.notes: 晩 refers to the evening or the night. 朝から晩まで covers the span from morning to evening. その晩 refers to an evening that has already been mentioned. With a time expression and は, that evening can become the topic. The reading ばん contains the moraic n.

examples[].german: When I was a child, I lived in Tokyo.
When I have free time, I read books.
en.notes: 時 is read とき here and names a point in time or an occasion. After a noun, の comes before 時: 子供の時. A na-adjective takes な before it: 暇な時. With a verb, the plain form is used, e.g. 出かける時. The whole expression states when something happens.

examples[].german: Please listen to what the teacher says.
That story is interesting.
en.notes: 話 is a noun for a conversation, a speech or a story. 話を聞く means to listen to what is said; 先生の話 names the teacher as the source. The reading is はなし. The verb 話す "to speak/to tell", on the other hand, has a す; the spelling on this noun card ends with the kanji.

examples[].german: I'm free on Sunday.
Please come when you have time.
en.notes: 暇 can mean "free time" as a noun and "not busy" as a na-adjective. 暇です describes that someone has time. Before a noun, な is used: 暇な時. With 暇がある, free time is named as time that is available. The reading ひま has two short vowels.

examples[].german: Please don't carry heavy things.
There are old things in this box.
en.notes: 物 is a general noun for things or objects. An adjective can stand directly before it: 重い物, 古い物. With を you name objects at which an action is directed; with が you can describe their presence. The reading on this card is もの. In this usage, 物 is not used for people.

examples[].german: I want to study in a quiet place.
What kind of place is this?
en.notes: 所 here is a place or spot and is read ところ. 静かな所 connects a na-adjective with the place; 所で gives the place of an action. どんな所 asks what kind of place something is. The spelling ところ in kana is also common, especially in grammatical expressions.

examples[].german: Is there a bank around here?
Let's take a short break around here.
en.notes: In these examples, 辺 means "area/vicinity". この辺 refers to the area here; あの辺 to an area over there. With に you ask about something that exists there. With で you name the place of an activity. The reading is へん; the word can mean an approximate area rather than an exact point.

examples[].german: There is a bookstore next to the bank.
Please lay the paper sideways.
Please write your name on the side of the box.
en.notes: 横 can refer to the side, the place next to something, or a horizontal direction. 銀行の横に means "next to the bank". 紙を横に置く describes laying the paper sideways. 箱の横の面 names the side surface of a box. With の you connect 横 with its reference point. The reading よこ has short vowels.

examples[].german: My grandmother lives in a small village.
This village has no train station.
en.notes: 村 is a village. The reading on this card is むら. 村に住む names the village as the place of residence; この村には makes it the place and topic of a further statement. 駅がありません means that there is no station there. With 小さな you describe a small village.

examples[].german: I'm waiting in front of the school gate.
We close the gate at night.
en.notes: 門 is a gate, e.g. the entrance of a school ground. 門の前 names the area in front of the gate; 門を閉める names it as the thing that is closed. 閉めます is a transitive verb, because someone closes the gate. もん ends in a moraic n.

examples[].german: I go to the office.
The company is big.
en.notes: 会社 means a company and in everyday speech can also refer to one's own workplace. That is why 会社に行く often means "to go to work". An activity at the workplace is linked with で, such as 会社で働く. 大きい会社 can mean a large organization, not just a large building.

examples[].german: There are books in the box.
Please open this box.
en.notes: 箱 is a box. 箱の中に describes the interior as a place. 箱を開ける names the box as the object of opening; 開けてください is a polite request. The exact size depends on the context. はこ has short vowels.

examples[].german: It's cold, so I'll put on a jacket.
I hung my jacket over the chair.
en.notes: 上着 is a jacket or a garment for the upper body. To put it on, 着る is used: 上着を着ます. 上着を椅子に掛ける marks the jacket with を and the chair with に. The reading is うわぎ; in this compound 着 is read ぎ.

examples[].german: There is a calendar on the wall.
I write the days off on the calendar.
en.notes: カレンダー is a calendar. カレンダーがあります names it as an existing object; カレンダーに書く uses に for the surface or place of the entry. 休みの日 refers to days off. The stroke ー lengthens the last a: karendā.

examples[].german: I take a shower in the morning.
This room has a shower.
en.notes: シャワー means a shower. シャワーを浴びる is the expression for "to take a shower"; 浴びる is an ichidan verb: 浴びます, 浴びて. シャワーがあります names an existing shower. シャ is pronounced as a single sequence, and ー lengthens the final a.

examples[].german: I put plates on the table.
There is a cat under the table.
en.notes: テーブル is a table. テーブルに置く names it as the destination of placing; テーブルの下 refers to the space beneath it. テーブルの上に explicitly names the tabletop as the place. The first syllable has a long e because of ー: tēburu.

examples[].german: Please write your name with a ballpoint pen.
I bought a blue ballpoint pen.
en.notes: ボールペン is a ballpoint pen. ボールペンで書く names the writing tool with で. ボールペンを買う names it as the object bought. 青い describes the color of the item. ー lengthens the o; at the end is a moraic n: bōrupen.

examples[].german: I pour coffee into the cup.
This cup is small.
en.notes: カップ here means a cup or mug. カップに入れる names the vessel with に and the contents with を. カップは小さいです describes the size of the vessel. The small ッ is written as a double p: kappu. コーヒー, by contrast, has long vowels.

examples[].german: I ate curry for lunch.
This curry is not very spicy.
en.notes: カレー refers to curry or a curry dish and can also be short for カレーライス. 昼ご飯にカレーを食べる names curry as the lunch. あまり辛くない describes the dish as not particularly spicy. あまり is used here with a negative form. ー lengthens the e in karē.

examples[].german: I'm wearing a new shirt.
Please wash this shirt.
en.notes: シャツ here means a shirt as an upper garment. To wear it, you say シャツを着る. 着ています describes the state of having it on. シャツを洗う names the garment as the object being washed. シャ is pronounced together as sha.

examples[].german: I bought a blue skirt.
This skirt is a little long.
en.notes: スカート is a skirt. 青いスカート connects the color adjective directly with the garment. スカートは長いです judges its length. With the degree word 少し the statement becomes "a little long". The stroke ー lengthens the a: sukāto.

examples[].german: That shop is cheap.
The cake at this shop is delicious.
en.notes: 店（みせ）means a shop and can also refer to a food and drink business. この店のケーキ are the cakes that this shop sells. In compounds, 店 is often read テン, as in 喫茶店; this card uses みせ.

examples[].german: I'm wearing black trousers.
These trousers are too big.
en.notes: ズボン means trousers and is usually written in katakana. For putting on or wearing them, 履く is used: 履きます, 履いて. 大きすぎます means "too big"; before すぎる, the final い of the i-adjective 大きい drops. ズボン has short vowels and a moraic n at the end.

examples[].german: I put on slippers in the entrance area.
Please put the toilet slippers here.
en.notes: スリッパ are light house shoes, i.e. slippers. Footwear is put on with 履く; スリッパを履く names them as the object with を. トイレのスリッパ refers to the slippers intended for the toilet. The second sentence asks to put this pair in a particular place. The small ッ briefly stops the airflow before p: surippa, not suripa.

examples[].german: It's cold, so I turned on the heater.
Please turn off the heater before going to bed.
en.notes: ストーブ here is a heater, i.e. a room heating device. For an appliance, つける means "to turn on" and 消す accordingly "to turn off". 寒いので gives the reason for turning it on; 寝る前に fixes the time for turning it off as before going to sleep. In these examples the word means the room heater. A kitchen stove would be called something like コンロ in another context.

examples[].german: The key is in my pocket.
I took money out of my pocket.
en.notes: ポケット is a pocket in or on a garment. ポケットにある names the location of an object, whereas ポケットから出す names taking it out of the pocket. に and から therefore express different spatial relations. For a carried handbag or shopping bag, かばん or バッグ fits better. The small ッ before t belongs to the pronunciation poketto.

examples[].german: I put the letter in the mailbox.
There is a red postbox in front of the station.
en.notes: ポスト here is a mailbox for posting mail. 手紙をポストに入れる names the letter with を and the destination with に. 駅の前にポストがある, by contrast, describes where a mailbox stands. The noun has other meanings, such as a professional position; the reference to a letter and to the red box makes the mail meaning clear here.

examples[].german: You can keep pets in this house.
My pet is a small dog.
en.notes: ペット is an animal kept as a pet. ペットを飼う uses を for the animal and 飼う for keeping animals; 飼えます is the potential form. In connection with a house, it can express that keeping pets is allowed there. 私のペットは犬です, by contrast, identifies one's own animal. The word meant here is the animal word borrowed from English, not the identically sounding abbreviation PET for plastic.

examples[].german: I buy vegetables at the greengrocer.
There is a greengrocer near the station.
en.notes: 八百屋 is a vegetable and fruit shop or the person who runs it. The reading やおや is learned as a whole; in this word, 八百 is not pronounced as the number はっぴゃく. 八百屋で names the place of shopping, 八百屋がある the existence of a shop. The examples deal with the actual shop and not with a figurative term for someone who does many different things.

examples[].german: There's a big dog.
Please read in a loud voice.
en.notes: 大きな stands directly before a noun. With 犬 it describes physical size, with 声 loudness: 大きな声で means "in a loud voice". It is a fixed prenominal form and does not form a predicate such as 大きなです. For a stand-alone statement, 大きいです is used. The な belongs to the whole form 大きな here; no further な is added.

examples[].german: I bought bread at a small shop.
Small flowers are blooming in the garden.
I'll fix even small mistakes right away.
en.notes: 小さな is a fixed prenominal form that stands directly before a noun: 小さな店 or 小さな花. A stand-alone statement is formed with 小さいです instead. The word can also express little importance or a small extent, as in 小さな間違い. In the extra example, でも means "even" and shows that even a small mistake gets corrected. No additional な is inserted after 小さな.

examples[].german: I don't like rainy days.
Let's forget the unpleasant things.
en.notes: 嫌 can express one's own dislike or an unpleasant quality. 雨の日は嫌です means that one doesn't like rainy days; 嫌なこと are unpleasant things. Before a noun, as a na-adjective, it takes な; at the end of a sentence, です can follow. 嫌です said on its own can sound quite clearly like a refusal. The examples thus contrast a personal dislike with the description of unpleasant experiences.

examples[].german: My younger sister is a high school student.
My younger sister sings well.
Tomorrow I'm going to a movie with my younger sister.
en.notes: 妹 means "younger sister" and does not fix an absolute age. 妹 is used for your own sister, and 妹さん is polite for another person's younger sister. The sister can therefore also be an adult. 妹と＋verb describes a joint action.

examples[].german: I eat at a restaurant.
I made a reservation at a restaurant.
en.notes: レストラン means a restaurant; the word is used especially often for restaurants with Western-style cuisine, without being strictly limited to them. The place of eating takes で. 予約する describes a reservation, for example for a restaurant visit.

examples[].german: This tea is lukewarm.
The bath water has become lukewarm.
en.notes: ぬるい describes a lukewarm temperature, for example of tea or bath water. It can imply that more warmth was expected. As an i-adjective, it forms ぬるく before なる: ぬるくなった means "has become lukewarm". The first example describes an existing temperature, the second a change. Laxity or an overly lenient attitude is a different usage and is not practiced here.

examples[].german: Please say it once more.
I want to see that movie once more.
en.notes: もう一度 asks for or describes another performance of the same action. With 言ってください it is a request for repetition, with 見たいです the wish to watch a movie one has already seen again. もう is pronounced long here and together with 一度 means "once more". It does not refer to an additional time of day, and on its own it says nothing about how often the action is repeated in total.

examples[].german: Please, have a seat.
Please have some of these sweets.
"May I use this pen?" "Go ahead."
en.notes: どうぞ can accompany an invitation, a permission, or the friendly handing over of something. Before 座ってください it turns the request into an invitation to take a seat. このお菓子をどうぞ offers sweets, even without an explicit verb. In the extra example, it agrees to a request to use a pen. It therefore means "please", "here you are" or "go ahead", depending on the situation.

examples[].german: Thank you very much.
Thanks, as always.
Somehow this explanation is hard to understand.
en.notes: どうも can strengthen thanks or be used on its own as a brief thank-you. どうもありがとうございます is fuller and more polite than the brief いつもどうも. In another context, どうも means "somehow" and expresses an impression that is hard to explain exactly. So the translation "thanks" does not fit everywhere. The examples distinguish explicit thanks from the subjective impression of a hard-to-understand explanation.

examples[].german: Yes, that's right.
Yes, I have tomorrow off.
"Is this seat free?" "Yes, go ahead."
en.notes: ええ is an affirmative "yes" in conversation. It can confirm a statement or introduce the answer to a question. In casual conversation it often sounds softer than a curt はい; in formal procedures, はい is the natural answer. The reading has a long e sound. What is meant here is agreement, not a hesitant えー or the regionally used adjective ええ meaning "good".

examples[].german: Well then, let's begin.
Hmm, I don't really know.
en.notes: さあ can prompt action or introduce an uncertain answer. さあ、始めましょう invites everyone to begin together; さあ、よく分かりません can be rendered as "Hmm, I don't really know". The speaking situation and intonation distinguish these functions. As an introductory exclamation, the word is not inflected like an ordinary adjective or verb.

examples[].german: I'm looking for a book like this.
So there's a shop in a place like this.
en.notes: こんな stands before a noun and refers to this kind of thing. A speaker can use it to refer to a book being shown or to a place just experienced. こんな本 is therefore "a book like this", not necessarily exactly this one book. こんな所に can additionally express surprise at the place. The word already stands as a complete form before the noun; no further な is inserted.

examples[].german: What kind of music do you like?
What kind of work do you do?
Whatever the job, I do my best until the end.
en.notes: どんな asks before a noun about its kind or characteristics: どんな音楽 or どんな仕事. It does not simply pick a particular item from a series, as どの can. With でも a different function arises: どんな仕事でも means "for any job, no matter what kind". The extra example makes this all-encompassing statement clear and is not a question.

examples[].german: I don't eat much meat.
It's not very cold today.
en.notes: あまり is used here with a negative form and weakens a quantity or a degree. あまり食べません means "don't eat much", あまり寒くない "not particularly cold". In these sentences it does not mean that nothing at all is eaten or that there is no cold at all. The negation can stand with the verb or be formed with くない for an i-adjective.

examples[].german: The weather is nice today.
May I sit here?
en.notes: いい describes something good or pleasant and is also used for permission. いい天気 praises the weather; ～てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted. The usual inflected forms come from よい: よくない and よかった. They are not formed simply by adding くない or かった to いい. The second example is about permission to sit, not about the quality of sitting.

examples[].german: I stay at a hotel.
The hotel room is spacious.
en.notes: ホテル means a hotel. For staying overnight in accommodation, ～に泊まる is used: ホテルに泊まる. ホテルの部屋 is a hotel room; の links the accommodation and the room belonging to it.

examples[].german: Well then, see you tomorrow.
In that case, I'll take this one, please.
en.notes: じゃあ is the spoken form of では and introduces a next step in the conversation. じゃあ、また明日 prepares for a farewell; じゃあ、これをください shows the decision after a choice. It therefore means "well then", "in that case" or "okay then", depending on the context. In more formal speech, では is often more suitable. The long a sound belongs to the form じゃあ used here.

examples[].german: Well then, let's begin.
Well then, see you next week.
en.notes: では here introduces a new step in the conversation or a farewell. では、始めます announces the start; では、また来週 prepares for the end of the meeting. In such transitions it usually sounds a little more formal than じゃあ. The written は is pronounced wa in this combination. What is meant here is the conversational transition, not the identically written combination of a place expression with で and the topic marker は.

en.meaning: and then; after that; and also
examples[].german: I eat breakfast. After that I go to school.
Bread, and also milk, please.
en.notes: それから connects a temporal sequence or supplements a list. After the breakfast sentence it means "after that" and places the trip to school in time. In an order, it can add a further desired item, i.e. "and also". It picks up the previous content of the conversation. It should therefore be translated according to the context and not rendered in every sentence with a bare "from there".

examples[].german: This room is spacious. And it's bright.
I read a book and then went to sleep.
en.notes: そして connects additional statements or successive actions. Two qualities of the same room are joined as "and"; for reading and then sleeping, "and then" fits. The word stands as a link between the statements and is not inflected like a verb. In the second example, the temporal order follows from the completed actions and their context.

examples[].german: Well then, I'll take my leave.
Then let's meet at the station.
"The shop is closed today." "In that case, let's go tomorrow."
en.notes: それでは picks up what has been discussed so far and leads to the next step in the conversation. It can introduce a polite farewell or formulate an agreement that follows from it. After a stated situation, it can also be translated as "in that case": if the shop is closed today, a visit tomorrow is proposed. 失礼します is a polite farewell in the first example. The は is pronounced wa here; the shorter spoken form is それじゃあ.

examples[].german: Why were you absent from school?
Why are you studying Japanese?
Please explain why you were late.
en.notes: どうして here asks for a reason or motivation. The question about the absence calls for an explanation of a past event; the question about studying Japanese can ask about the personal goal. In a sentence with どうして～のか, the why-question is embedded, for example as the subject of an explanation. The word can also ask about a method; the examples specifically practice its "why" usage.

examples[].german: Who is that person?
Who did you come with?
en.notes: どなた is the polite question about a person and corresponds to 誰. It stands as a question word itself: どなたですか asks about identity, どなたと names the companion with と. 方 and the respectful verb form いらっしゃる fit the polite tone of the examples. The word does not ask about an object; 何 would be used for that. The politeness concerns the person addressed or talked about.

examples[].german: Which would you prefer, tea or coffee?
Where are you from?
May I ask who this person is?
en.notes: どちら asks about a direction or place, about a choice, and also politely about a person. お茶とコーヒーはどちらがいいですか contrasts two possibilities. お国はどちらですか politely asks about the country of origin. どちら様ですか asks about a person's identity; 様 makes the question additionally respectful. For more than two items, どれ is often used for the choice.

examples[].german: Please come this way.
This is Mr./Ms. Yamada.
en.notes: こちら politely refers to the speaker's side or area and can also introduce a nearby person. こちらへ来てください names the direction toward the speaker with へ. こちらは山田さんです, by contrast, introduces Yamada as a person. The reference depends on the situation; こちら is not just a place word in every sentence. In casual conversation, the form こっち is used.

en.meaning: over there (near you); that way; you (polite)
examples[].german: Please sit over there.
How is the weather where you are?
Is Japanese used at your company?
en.notes: そちら refers to the area of the person addressed. It can mean a direction toward the other person's area, a seat there, or the place where the other person is. In そちらの会社 it can politely refer to the other person's company. そちらに座る names a destination seat with に, whereas そちらの天気 refers to the weather at the other location. The casual form is そっち.

examples[].german: It takes an hour to the airport.
The airport is very big.
en.notes: 空港 means an airport, not an airplane（飛行機）. ～まで names a destination point; 一時間 then describes the time needed to get there. The long vowels u and o in くうこう are written with macrons in Hepburn: kūkō.

examples[].german: The entrance is over there.
I bought it at the shop over there.
en.notes: あちら refers to a place or direction that is distant from both speakers. あちらです points to the entrance over there. あちらの店 specifies with の a shop in that distant area; で names it as the place of shopping. The form sounds more polite than あっち. Here it indicates spatial distance, not temporal order.

examples[].german: Come here.
This road is shorter.
en.notes: こっち is the casual form of こちら and refers to the speaker's side. こっちに来て calls someone over; こっちの道 selects the road on this side. の connects the demonstrative with 道. A request without ください suits close conversation partners. The small っ before ち is written tch in Modified Hepburn: kotchi.

examples[].german: The station is over there.
Wait over there.
en.notes: あっち is the casual form of あちら: "over there" or "in that direction". 駅はあっちです shows the location or direction of the station. あっちで待っていて names with で the place where someone should wait. In the described situation, the place is distant from both speakers. The small っ belongs to the whole reading atchi; it is not left out.

examples[].german: Which do you like better, red or blue?
Which way is the station?
en.notes: どっち is the casual form of どちら. It can ask about a choice between two possibilities or about a direction. 赤と青、どっちが好き？ offers colors to choose from; 駅はどっち？ asks for the direction to the station. Short questions without ですか suit casual conversation here. In Modified Hepburn, the small っ before ち is written tch: dotchi.

examples[].german: This movie is boring.
It's boring alone, so I invited friends.
Please don't fight over trivial things.
en.notes: つまらない describes something boring or uninteresting and can also mean "trivial". For the movie it is about a lack of interest, for つまらないこと about a minor matter. The word is often written in hiragana and is a separate i-adjective here. It does not have to be understood literally as the negation of 詰まる in every context. ので gives the reason in the second example for why friends were called.

examples[].german: Let's take a photo all together.
Has everyone arrived yet?
en.notes: みんな refers to all the people of a group known from the context. みんなで invites a joint action; みんな来ましたか asks whether the whole expected group has come. The situation determines who belongs to it. みんな is less formal and more emphatic than みな. Before さん, the usual form of address みなさん is used, not simply みんなさん.

examples[].german: The students are all in the classroom.
Let's discuss it all together.
en.notes: 皆 is read みな here and refers to all members of a group. It is somewhat more formal than みんな. 学生は皆 names the complete group of students, and 皆で相談する a joint discussion. The following で describes acting together. The form みな is also in the address 皆さん; its full pronunciation is みなさん.

examples[].german: Let's meet again tomorrow.
It has started raining again.
This room is spacious. It is also close to the station.
en.notes: また often indicates a repetition or a renewed meeting. また明日会いましょう looks ahead to another meeting the next day; また雨が降ってきた to rain setting in again. As a link between statements, また can also mean "in addition". In the extra example, it adds the closeness to the station to the room's spaciousness. The context decides between repetition and additional information.

examples[].german: That's right. I'm a student.
I think so too.
en.notes: そう picks up content that has already been expressed or understood. そうです confirms the other person's statement; そう思います agrees with a thought. The word means "so" or "that's right" here. It is not the identically written そう that attaches to a verb stem and forms an impression like "looks like". The long o sound is romanized as sō.

examples[].german: Where is the station?
It's a ten-minute walk to the station.
en.notes: 駅 means a train station or rail stop, including city trains and subways. A bus stop is normally called バス停. 駅まで歩いて十分 describes the walking time to the station; 十分 is read じゅっぷん here.

examples[].german: That person is a teacher.
Which person is Mr./Ms. Yamada?
en.notes: 方 is read かた here and is a respectful term for a person. あの方 politely describes a distant person; どの方 asks about a person from a selection. The construction is noun plus particle, such as 方は or 方が. The same character is often read ほう in expressions of direction and comparison. There is also the attached form ～方 for a method; these roles are to be distinguished from the polite word for a person.

examples[].german: This one is cheaper.
I walk toward the station.
en.notes: 方 is read ほう here and refers to a direction or a side in a comparison. 駅の方へ歩く means to walk in the direction of the station; the station need not be the destination reached. こちらの方が安いです compares the alternative here with another one. の connects the reference with 方, が marks the compared alternative. The polite person reading かた belongs to a different usage.

examples[].german: I live near the station.
Please sit next to me.
en.notes: 側 is read そば here and indicates spatial proximity. 駅の側 is the vicinity of the station, 私の側 the place right next to me. の establishes the reference; に names the place of residence with 住む and the destination seat with 座る. In this meaning the word is often written そば. The identically sounding buckwheat noodles are a different word and not a place expression.

examples[].german: Please show me another book.
Do you have any other questions?
They don't have it in this shop, so I'll look elsewhere.
en.notes: 他（ほか）refers to something else or additional. Before a noun, の is used: 他の本 "another book". 他に often means "in addition, besides", 他で "elsewhere". The kana spelling ほか is also common; the reading ほか is to be distinguished from 他（た）in other compounds.

en.meaning: to put on (the head); to wear on the head
examples[].german: Please put on your hat.
The child is wearing a red hat.
en.notes: 被る is read かぶる here and means to put something on the head or wear it there. The hat is the object, marked with を. 被ってください asks someone to put it on, 被っています describes the resulting state of wearing it. Despite its る ending it is a Godan verb and forms 被って. The other reading こうむる belongs to meanings such as "to suffer" and is not used here.

examples[].german: I'll play after I do my homework.
What are we doing today?
en.notes: やる here means to do a task or activity, and in usage it feels more casual than する. 宿題をやる names the task as the object; やってから places the playing after finishing the homework. The polite ending in やります makes the sentence more polite, while the verb itself remains rather colloquial. This godan verb forms やります and やって.

examples[].german: Please put out the fire.
Please don't go near the fire.
en.notes: 火 is fire or a flame. 火を消す names with を the fire that is to be extinguished or switched off. 火の近く, by contrast, names a place near the fire. The form 行かないでください asks you to refrain from approaching. The word is read ひ like 日, "day", but has different characters and a different meaning.

examples[].german: Today was a good day.
The days have gotten longer.
This room gets a lot of sun in the morning.
en.notes: 日 is read ひ here and can mean a day, the bright part of the day, or sunlight. いい日でした evaluates a day as a good experience; 日が長くなる describes longer daylight. 日が当たる means that the sun shines on a place. The extra room example uses this sunlight meaning. Dates and compounds have their own readings; the single reading ひ is not simply used everywhere.

examples[].german: I came to Japan alone.
There is one student in the classroom.
en.notes: 一人 is read irregularly as ひとり when counting people. 学生が一人います counts a single person; 一人で says that someone acts without company. In the Japan example this means "come to Japan alone", not necessarily being unmarried. In the second sentence the number of people stands after the subject and before います. Another common counting form is 二人, ふたり.

examples[].german: I'm traveling with a friend, just the two of us.
There are two children in the room.
en.notes: 二人 means two people and is read ふたり. 子供が二人います counts the children, 二人で旅行する describes a trip as a pair. 友達と二人で in the first example means the speaker and a friend, i.e. two people in total. The most common reading is ふたり; ににん is also attested. The word alone does not claim a romantic relationship between the two people.

examples[].german: I go by train.
The train has come.
en.notes: 電車 means a train, literally an electrically powered train in particular. As a means of transport it takes で: 電車で行く. When boarding, に is used: 電車に乗る. 電車が来る describes the arrival of a train.

examples[].german: I turn twenty this year.
My older brother is twenty years old.
en.notes: 二十歳 is read はたち when giving this age and means twenty years old. 二十歳になる describes reaching this age; 二十歳です states the current age. 今年 places the birthday in the current year without naming a specific date. The special reading applies to the age; the number 二十 alone is usually read にじゅう.

examples[].german: I was at home all day.
You take this medicine three times a day.
en.notes: As a duration, 一日 is read いちにち. 一日中 covers the whole day, whereas 一日に三回 gives a frequency per day. The first day of a month, by contrast, is read ついたち. So pay attention to 中 or the following frequency expression before choosing the reading.

en.meaning: the first day of the month
examples[].german: Today is May 1st.
The shop is closed on the 1st.
en.notes: ついたち is the fixed calendar reading for the first day of a month. It remains after the month name: 五月一日 is read ごがつついたち. A duration of one day, by contrast, is read いちにち. A stand-alone 一日 can, in connection with an appointment, mean the 1st of the month in question.

examples[].german: We're having a party on Saturday.
I invited friends to the party.
en.notes: パーティー here means a celebration with several guests. パーティーをする describes hosting or celebrating, パーティーに友達を呼ぶ inviting friends to it. に marks the event as the destination of the invitation. The ending ティー is pronounced with a long i; パーティ is also attested.

examples[].german: Please open to page ten.
I read five pages every day.
en.notes: ページ refers to a page of a book and also follows a number. 十ページを開く names the page that is to be opened; 五ページ読む the number of pages read. The verb helps to distinguish a page number from an amount of pages. The kanji spelling 頁 is also read ページ in this usage; you find it in books and indexes, for example. For ten, じっページ and じゅっページ are both in use.

examples[].german: Please press this button.
A button came off the shirt.
en.notes: ボタン can refer to a button on clothing or a button on a device. With ボタンを押す you press a button; ボタンが取れる describes a button that has come off. The rare kanji spelling 釦 is read ボタン in both meanings. In everyday writing, the katakana form is usual. The identically sounding plant name 牡丹 is a different word.

examples[].german: There are twenty people in my class.
The Japanese class is on Monday.
en.notes: クラス can mean a group of learners or a particular course. クラスには二十人います describes how many people belong to the group; 日本語のクラスは月曜日です gives the date of the course. For people, います is used here. The similarly sounding verb 暮らす, by contrast, means to live or to spend one's daily life.

examples[].german: I'll be back right away.
If you don't understand, please ask right away.
en.notes: すぐに places the start of an action close to the present or a previously mentioned point in time. Before 帰ります it announces a soon return; after 分からない時は it urges one to ask without waiting long. に stands before the verb and can be omitted in many such sentences. It is about the point in time here, not the speed of the action.

en.meaning: etc.; and so on; for example
examples[].german: I bought apples, bananas and so on.
On days off I read books and the like.
en.notes: など shows that the things mentioned are examples from a larger selection. In りんごやバナナなど it closes an open-ended list. After just one noun, as in 本など, it can be rendered as "for example". A following case particle remains possible: などを marks the things named as examples as the object.

examples[].german: I take the bus.
What time does the bus come?
en.notes: バス here means the bus as a means of transport. For boarding or riding along, say バスに乗る, and for the way of travelling, バスで行く. Identically written loanwords for bath, bass or fish belong to other meanings.

examples[].german: I only drank water.
Please wait just five minutes.
en.notes: だけ limits a selection or quantity to what is named. 水だけ excludes other drinks, 五分だけ limits the waiting time to five minutes. Unlike しか, だけ does not require a negated verb: 飲みました and 待ってください stay affirmative here. The limitation stands directly after the noun or quantity in question.

examples[].german: It's warmer today than yesterday.
The train is faster than the bus.
I want to live in a place quieter than here.
en.notes: より follows the standard of a comparison. In 今日は昨日より暖かい, 昨日 is the reference point: today is warmer than yesterday. AはBより～ thus describes that the quality is more pronounced in A than in B. The same comparison can stand before a noun, as in ここより静かな所 for a place that is quieter than this one.

examples[].german: I asked a police officer the way.
The police officer is at the police box.
en.notes: お巡りさん is a familiar everyday term for a police officer. The word refers to the person: お巡りさんに道を聞く means to ask them the way. 交番, by contrast, is the small police box where the person may work. お and さん are part of the fixed term here and are kept when using it.

examples[].german: Excuse me. May I come in?
Well then, I'll be going.
en.notes: 失礼します is a polite formula for announcing a small interruption or entering or leaving a room. Before 入ってもいいですか it serves as an introduction to the request to enter. At the end of a conversation it can express farewell. The ending します belongs to the polite form; the formula need not be understood as an actual apology for a mistake.

examples[].german: I'm going to bed now. Good night.
Good night. See you tomorrow.
en.notes: おやすみなさい is the greeting when going to bed and when parting at night. You can use it to announce that you yourself are going to sleep, or to wish the other person a good night. It does not replace the evening greeting こんばんは. The shorter form おやすみ suits close friends; おやすみなさい is the more polite full formula.

examples[].german: I take a bath every evening.
This room doesn't have a bath.
en.notes: 風呂 refers to the bath, the bathtub or bathing. The common phrase 風呂に入る means to take a bath; に is used here with 入る. In everyday life you often encounter the more polite form お風呂. この部屋には風呂がありません, by contrast, is about the fact that a bath is not part of the room's equipment.

examples[].german: Please fold the paper in half lengthwise.
I wrote the name vertically.
en.notes: 縦 refers to the vertical direction or the lengthwise direction of an object; the opposite is 横. With に it becomes a direction expression for the action: 縦に折る means to fold lengthwise, 縦に書く to write vertically. With paper and writing, the intended direction depends on how the surface lies in front of you or is viewed.

examples[].german: This room is three meters wide.
There is a station a hundred meters ahead.
en.notes: This entry practices メートル as a unit of length. The word follows a number: 幅が三メートルあります describes a width, 百メートル先 a distance ahead. The rare kanji spelling 米 is read メートル in this meaning and is to be distinguished from the rice word 米（こめ）. メートル or the symbol m is usual. The secondary meaning as a measuring device is practiced separately; for that, メーター is mostly used today.

examples[].german: I go back by taxi.
Please call a taxi.
en.notes: タクシー means a taxi. With で you name it as a means of transport, with を as the vehicle being called: タクシーを呼ぶ. The long i at the end of the word comes from ー and is romanized takushī.

examples[].german: It's two kilometers to the school.
Today I walked five kilometers.
en.notes: キロメートル refers to longer distances and distances covered. 学校まで二キロメートルあります gives the distance to the school; 五キロメートル歩く the distance one walks. In conversation, キロ can suffice when a distance is meant. The rare kanji spelling 粁 has the same reading; the katakana form and the symbol km are usual.

examples[].german: This luggage weighs ten kilograms.
I bought two kilograms of rice.
en.notes: キログラム follows a number and gives weight. この荷物は十キログラムです describes the weight of a piece of luggage; 米を二キログラム買う the quantity measured out at purchase. The short form キロ is enough when the context is clear. The rare kanji spelling 瓩 is also read キログラム; in everyday life you mostly encounter the katakana form or the symbol kg.

examples[].german: Two hundred grams of meat, please.
I add fifty grams of sugar.
en.notes: グラム gives smaller weights when shopping and cooking. 肉を二百グラムください orders a specific amount; 砂糖を五十グラム入れる states the quantity of an ingredient. The rare kanji spelling 瓦 can also mean グラム. Here it belongs to the unit word and is to be distinguished from the ordinary word 瓦（かわら）, roof tile. In recipes and on packaging, グラム or g is usual.

examples[].german: I wear a dress shirt to work.
I ironed the dress shirt.
en.notes: ワイシャツ refers to a dress shirt, as worn for example to work or with a suit. 着る is used for this; 着て行く additionally describes going somewhere in these clothes. ワイシャツにアイロンを掛ける means to iron the shirt. The spelling Ｙシャツ is also read ワイシャツ. Although the term goes back to the English "white shirt", the shirt can have a different color.

examples[].german: I sealed the box with tape.
This tape sticks well.
I heard my grandfather's voice on an old tape.
en.notes: テープ means tape; the object and the verb show which kind is meant. When sealing a box or with よく付く, it is adhesive tape. With 声を聞く, a recording tape may be meant. テープで names the tape as an aid or medium, while テープは makes the tape itself the topic.

en.meaning: likewise; the pleasure is mine; thank you
examples[].german: "Pleased to meet you." "Likewise."
Thank you, too.
en.notes: こちらこそ answers a friendly remark by turning it back on oneself: "likewise" or "the pleasure/thanks is mine". After よろしくお願いします it returns the wish for good cooperation. After ありがとうございました it stresses that one is grateful too. In this fixed phrase, こそ emphasizes one's own side.

examples[].german: The answer is 1.
I'm still one yen short.
en.notes: 一 as a stand-alone number is read いち. In 一円 this reading is kept: いちえん. With certain counters, however, the form changes, for example 一回（いっかい）or 一人（ひとり）. So learn a number and its counter together. In 答えは一です, the number itself is the answer, with no counted thing.

examples[].german: The answer is 2.
I bought two tickets.
en.notes: 二 is the number two and is read に on this card. When counting flat things, it is combined, for example, with 枚: 二枚 "two pieces". In an answer, the number can stand alone before です. People and days of the month have their own forms such as 二人 and 二日, which are learned as whole words.

examples[].german: The answer is 3.
I took three photos.
en.notes: 三 is the number three and is read さん. The n is a separate sound at the end of the number. With 枚 you count photos, for example: 三枚. The number 三 is different from the honorific ending さん after a name. In larger numbers, it can likewise stand before other number words, such as 三十.

examples[].german: The answer is 4.
Four stamps, please.
en.notes: 四 means four; this card uses よん. The moraic n remains audible in 四枚 as well. In 四月, however, the same kanji is read し: しがつ. The right reading therefore depends on the whole expression. 四枚ください asks for four flat objects that were mentioned beforehand.

examples[].german: I travel by plane.
I bought a plane ticket.
en.notes: 飛行機 means an airplane. As a means of travel it takes で. 飛行機のチケット is a flight ticket; a shorter term for it is 航空券. Do not confuse it with 空港 ("airport"). ひこうき is written hikōki.

examples[].german: The answer is 5.
I found a five-yen coin.
en.notes: 五 is the number five and is read ご here. The vowel is short in the basic form. 五円玉 refers to a five-yen coin; 玉 is read だま in this compound. With other counters, other expressions are formed, such as 五枚 for five flat things. Number and counter are read together.

examples[].german: The answer is 6.
Please show me six photos.
en.notes: 六 is read ろく and means six. With 枚, 六枚 means "six pieces", for example of photos. With some other counters, the pronunciation changes: 六百 is read ろっぴゃく. Such combinations are learned as whole forms. ろく has two short vowels in its basic form.

examples[].german: The answer is 7.
I laid out seven cards side by side.
en.notes: 七 means seven; the reading on this card is なな. 七枚 means, for example, "seven cards/sheets". Another common reading is しち, as in 七月. なな has two short a's and no long a. Which reading is used must be noted for each expression.

examples[].german: The answer is 8.
I bought eight envelopes.
en.notes: 八 is the number eight and is read はち. 八枚 counts, for example, eight envelopes. Before certain counters, shortened forms with a small っ arise, such as 八百 はっぴゃく. In 八枚, the basic reading はち is kept. はち has no long vowels.

examples[].german: The answer is 9.
I chose nine photos.
en.notes: 九 is the number nine. This card reads it きゅう with a long u; きゅ forms a sequence pronounced together. 九枚 means "nine pieces" for flat things. In 九月, however, the reading is く: くがつ. Number combinations are therefore read to match the counter.

examples[].german: The answer is 10.
A ten-yen coin is lying there.
en.notes: 十 is the number ten and is read じゅう with a long u here. 十円玉 is a ten-yen coin. With some counters the form changes, for example 十分 じゅっぷん for ten minutes. とお appears in other number expressions such as 十日; this card uses じゅう.

examples[].german: The answer is 100.
I'm still 100 yen short.
en.notes: 百 is a hundred and is read ひゃく. ひゃ forms a sequence pronounced together. 百円 means one hundred yen. In larger numbers, some combinations change their reading: 三百 さんびゃく, 六百 ろっぴゃく, 八百 はっぴゃく. In the basic form 百, there is normally no 一 before ひゃく.

examples[].german: The answer is 1000.
This book costs 1,000 yen.
en.notes: 千 is a thousand and is read せん. 千円 is the amount of a thousand yen; before 円, an apostrophe in sen'en separates the n from the following e. For exactly one thousand, one usually says 千, without 一 before it. In building larger numbers, forms such as 二千 and 三千 occur, where 三千 is read さんぜん.

examples[].german: The answer is 10,000.
This watch costs 10,000 yen.
en.notes: 万 is the unit for ten thousand. Exactly 10,000 is 一万 いちまん; here, the one is explicitly stated before 万. 二万 means 20,000. 一万円 is an amount of 10,000 yen. When reading larger numbers, grouping by four digits helps, since 万 bundles 10,000 each time.

examples[].german: I'm going to Japan in April.
I counted out loud: "one, two, three, four."
en.notes: On this card, 四 is read し. This reading appears in 四月 しがつ for April and when reciting the number sequence 一、二、三、四. Other expressions need よん, for example 四枚. The card therefore practices the reading し without carrying it over to all combinations with 四.

examples[].german: I go to school by bicycle.
I pump air into the bicycle tire.
en.notes: 自転車 is a bicycle. For the means of transport, use で: 自転車で学校に行く. For getting on or riding a bicycle, 乗る takes に. The reading is じてんしゃ, not じでんしゃ.

examples[].german: I get up at seven.
July is hot.
en.notes: 七 is read しち here. This is the reading in 七時 しちじ and 七月 しちがつ. With other counters, なな may be common, for example 七枚 ななまい. The two short syllables in しち should be read clearly. This card practices the しち combinations with time of day and month.

examples[].german: I go to bed at nine.
School starts in September.
en.notes: 九 has the reading く on this card. It is used in 九時 くじ and 九月 くがつ. In 九枚, by contrast, it is read きゅうまい. く has a short u; the other basic reading きゅう has a long u. The whole word determines the right reading.

examples[].german: Today is May 2nd.
The trip takes 2 days.
en.notes: 二日 is read ふつか. As a date, it is the second day of a month: 五月二日 "May 2nd". In 二日かかる, by contrast, a duration of two days is meant. 二日間 also emphasizes the time span. The reading has neither long vowels nor a small っ.

examples[].german: Today is May 3rd.
The trip takes 3 days.
en.notes: 三日 is read みっか with a small っ. It can name the third day of a month or a duration of three days. With a month before it, such as 五月三日, the date is clear. In 三日かかります, it gives the time needed. The reading is みっか in both cases.

examples[].german: Today is May 4th.
The trip takes 4 days.
en.notes: 四日 is よっか, with a small っ and a short o. It refers to the fourth day of a month or a duration of four days. 五月四日 is thus May 4th. For a duration, 四日間 can also be said. ようか with a long o, by contrast, is 八日, i.e. eight days or the eighth day.

examples[].german: Today is May 5th.
The trip takes 5 days.
en.notes: 五日 is the fifth day of a month or a duration of five days and is read いつか. 五月五日 means May 5th. 五日かかる gives five days of time needed. The identically pronounced いつか can mean "someday"; with this kanji spelling 五日, it is about the number five.

examples[].german: Today is May 6th.
The trip takes 6 days.
en.notes: 六日 is read むいか. The u and the following i are pronounced as two vowels; there is no small っ. 五月六日 is May 6th. When you say something takes 六日, six days are meant. The duration can be explicitly marked as a time span with 六日間.

examples[].german: Today is May 7th.
The trip takes 7 days.
en.notes: 七日 is the seventh day of a month or a duration of seven days. The reading is なのか, i.e. not なな plus か. 五月七日 names May 7th; 七日かかります describes the time needed of seven days. All vowels in なのか are short.

examples[].german: Today is May 8th.
The trip takes 8 days.
en.notes: 八日 is read ようか and has a long o: yōka. It refers to the eighth day of a month or a duration of eight days. 五月八日 is May 8th. Four days, by contrast, is よっか with a small っ. So pay attention to the length of the o and the difference from っ.

examples[].german: Today is May 9th.
The trip takes 9 days.
en.notes: 九日 is the ninth day of a month or nine days' duration. The reading is ここのか with four short syllables: こ・こ・の・か. 五月九日 is May 9th. 九日かかる gives the duration; 九日間 explicitly highlights the time span. The reading stays the same in these usages.

examples[].german: I drive a car.
I like red cars.
en.notes: 車（くるま）usually means a car in everyday speech, but can refer to a vehicle more generally. 車を運転する means to drive or steer a car. For "to go by car" as a means of travel, say 車で行く. The meaning "wheel" is not intended here.

examples[].german: Today is May 10th.
The trip takes 10 days.
en.notes: 十日 is read とおか with a long o: tōka. It is the tenth day of a month or a duration of ten days. 五月十日 means "May 10th". In 十日かかる, it is about a time span of ten days. The spelling とお has the same length here as a long o in other words.

examples[].german: Today is May 20th.
The trip takes 20 days.
en.notes: 二十日 has the special reading はつか. It refers to the twentieth day of a month or a duration of twenty days. 五月二十日 means "May 20th". 二十日かかります gives twenty days of time needed. This form is learned as a whole; the basic numbers 二 and 十 are not read individually here.

examples[].german: Four apples, please.
There are 4 boxes on the table.
en.notes: 四つ counts four things without a more specific counter. The reading is よっつ with a small っ; it is written yottsu. The quantity can follow the object: りんごを四つ. 四つあります states the quantity of existing objects. A construction before the noun is also possible: 四つの箱.

examples[].german: Five apples, please.
There are 5 boxes on the table.
en.notes: 五つ is the general counting form for five things and is read いつつ. The two つ are normal syllables; there is no small っ. You can count after the noun, as in りんごを五つ, or stand before a noun with 五つの. The plain number word 五, by contrast, is read ご.

examples[].german: Six apples, please.
There are 6 boxes on the table.
en.notes: 六つ counts six things in general. The reading むっつ contains a small っ and is written muttsu. This is a different form from the plain number word 六 ろく. In 箱が六つあります, the quantity stands between the object and あります. With 六つの箱, the quantity can also stand before the noun.

examples[].german: Seven apples, please.
There are 7 boxes on the table.
en.notes: 七つ means seven things and is read ななつ. It has three short syllables and no small っ. The つ belongs to the general counting form, so no further counter such as 枚 is needed for this usage. In 七つの箱, の connects the quantity with the following noun.

examples[].german: Eight apples, please.
There are 8 boxes on the table.
en.notes: 八つ is the general counting form for eight things. It is read やっつ with a small っ and written yattsu. The plain number word 八 is はち, whereas this counting form begins with や. 八つあります states the quantity present; 八つください asks for this quantity.

examples[].german: I'd like nine apples, please.
There are nine boxes on the desk.
en.notes: 九つ counts nine things in general and is read ここのつ: こ・こ・の・つ. All vowels are short. ここのつ ends in つ, whereas the day form 九日 ここのか ends in か. When ordering, 九つ follows the noun you want, as in りんごを九つください.

examples[].german: It's zero degrees today.
Please count from zero.
en.notes: 零 is zero and is read れい. 零度 names a temperature of zero degrees; the unit is given with 度. 零から数える takes zero as the starting point of a count. Another common word for the number is ゼロ. The romanization of this reading stays rei.

examples[].german: There is nothing left.
The temperature is zero degrees.
en.notes: ゼロ names the number zero and can also mean that there is none of something or nothing left. 残りはゼロです says that nothing is left. ゼロ度 gives zero degrees. 零 れい is another word for the number. ゼロ has two short vowels.

examples[].german: I eat breakfast.
I want to eat sushi.
en.notes: 食べる is a transitive ichidan verb: 食べます・食べて・食べない. The food usually takes を. 食べたい expresses a wish to eat; depending on context, 食べる can mean "to eat" or "to have a meal".

examples[].german: Please go straight along this road.
This road is dark.
en.notes: 道（みち）means a street, a path or a route. When moving, the stretch traversed can take を: この道を行く. In directions, まっすぐ means "straight ahead". Figurative meanings such as the path of life are not taught here.

examples[].german: I cross the bridge.
A new bridge has been built.
en.notes: 橋（はし）is a noun for a bridge. "To cross a bridge" is 橋を渡る; for a position, use something like 橋の上 "on the bridge". The identically pronounced 箸 means "chopsticks"; the script, context and pitch accent help to tell them apart.

examples[].german: I go home.
I moved into a new house.
en.notes: 家（いえ）means a house or home. 家に帰る means "to return home"; with a place of residence, に is used. For your own home, うち is also very common. The reading いえ is practiced here; 家 also has other readings in compounds.

examples[].german: The room is clean.
I clean the room.
I reserved a room at this hotel.
en.notes: 部屋 means "room". The place of presence usually takes に, an action in the room takes で: 部屋にいる, 部屋で勉強する. "To clean the room" is 部屋を掃除する. The word can also refer to a hotel room.

examples[].german: I cook in the kitchen.
I eat in the kitchen.
en.notes: 台所 means the kitchen as a room or work area in the household. For activities, で is used: 台所で料理する. キッチン is a common alternative. In 台所にいる, on the other hand, に is used because only the location is stated.

examples[].german: I take a bath.
The bath feels very nice.
The water in the bathtub is hot.
en.notes: お風呂 is the usual polite word for a bath or bathtub; the お is often used even for one's own bath. お風呂に入る means "to take a bath". A shower, by contrast, is taken with シャワーを浴びる. The hot bathwater is usually called お湯.

examples[].german: Where is the restroom?
May I use the restroom?
en.notes: トイレ means the toilet or the restroom. トイレはどこですか asks the way there; トイレに行く means "to go to the restroom". お手洗い（おてあらい）is a more polite term often seen on signs or in restaurants.

examples[].german: Please open the window.
You can see the mountain from the window.
en.notes: 窓 is the noun for a window. "To open or close a window" is 窓を開ける・閉める. 窓から describes the view from there, as in 窓から山が見える. For a window seat, 窓側（まどがわ）is common.

examples[].german: Please close the door.
There are shoes in front of the door.
en.notes: ドア means a door, often one on hinges. ドアを開ける・閉める means "to open or close the door". ドアの前 is the area in front of the door. For the entrance area of a house, 玄関（げんかん）is often used.

examples[].german: There is a book on the desk.
I bought a new desk.
en.notes: 机 is a table for working, studying or writing, usually a desk. 机の上 means "on the desk" and 机の下 "under the desk". A dining or living room table is often called テーブル; the usage matters for word choice.

examples[].german: Please sit down.
This chair is comfortable to sit in.
I set up ten chairs before the meeting.
en.notes: 椅子に座る means to sit on a chair; the seat is marked with に. 椅子を運ぶ or 椅子を並べる, on the other hand, describe moving or arranging chairs. When counting, 一脚（いっきゃく）is often used. Figuratively, 椅子 can also mean a post or position, as in 社長の椅子.

examples[].german: I make a phone call.
I am talking on the phone.
The phone is ringing.
en.notes: 電話 can mean the telephone or a phone call. 電話をかける means "to call" and 電話で話す "to talk on the phone". 電話する is also common. In 電話が鳴る "the phone rings", the device itself is in the foreground.

examples[].german: Please look at the clock.
The clock has stopped.
en.notes: 時計 means a clock or watch; the context shows whether a wristwatch, wall clock or other timepiece is meant. 腕時計（うでどけい）is explicitly a wristwatch. 時計を見る means "to look at the clock"; for the time of day, 時間 or an expression with 時 is used.

examples[].german: I forgot my umbrella.
Since it is raining, I will take an umbrella.
en.notes: 傘 means a rain umbrella or parasol; in everyday speech it usually means the rain umbrella. "To put up or use an umbrella" is 傘を差す（さす）. 傘を持つ can mean holding it or carrying it along. Umbrellas are counted with 本, as in 傘を一本.

examples[].german: Do you have the key?
Please lock up.
en.notes: 鍵 is a key; the word can also mean the lock. 鍵をかける means "to lock" as a fixed expression, and 鍵を開ける "to unlock". The door is often the topic or marked with に. Keys are usually counted with 本.

examples[].german: I forgot my wallet.
There is money in the wallet.
en.notes: 財布 is a wallet or purse for cash and cards. 財布にお金を入れる means "to put money into the wallet"; 財布を忘れる "to forget one's wallet". For a small coin purse, 小銭入れ（こぜにいれ）is also used.

examples[].german: What is in the bag?
I put the book in the bag.
en.notes: かばん means a bag, such as a school bag, travel bag or briefcase. The kanji spelling is 鞄. かばんに本を入れる means "to put a book in the bag" and かばんの中 "the inside of the bag". A simple sack or plastic bag is more likely called 袋（ふくろ）.

examples[].german: This book is interesting.
I borrowed a book from the library.
en.notes: As an independent noun, 本 means "book". Books are counted with 冊: 本を一冊 "one book". The character 本 also appears as a counter for long, thin objects; in that case it is not the noun "book". 図書館で本を借りる means "to borrow a book from the library".

examples[].german: I read the newspaper.
I read the newspaper in the morning.
I bought a newspaper at the station.
en.notes: 新聞 is a newspaper, not just any news. 新聞を読む means "to read the newspaper" and 新聞を買う "to buy a newspaper". A magazine is called 雑誌. A single copy of a newspaper can be counted with 部, as in 新聞を一部.

examples[].german: I bought a magazine.
This magazine is interesting.
en.notes: 雑誌 means a magazine, that is, a periodically published publication. 新聞, by contrast, is a newspaper. 雑誌を読む・買う are common combinations. Individual issues can be counted with 冊, as in 雑誌を一冊.

examples[].german: I go to school.
I'm going to Tokyo tomorrow.
Work is going well.
en.notes: 行く describes movement away from the respective reference point; the destination takes に or へ. Depending on the means of transport, it can mean "to go" or "to travel". This godan verb has the special forms 行って・行った, but regular 行きます・行かない. In うまくいく it means "to go well".

examples[].german: Please write in pencil.
This pencil is short.
en.notes: 鉛筆 means a pencil, usually a wooden one. 鉛筆で書く means "to write in pencil"; で marks the writing tool. For a mechanical pencil, シャープペンシル or the short form シャーペン is common. Pencils are counted with 本.

examples[].german: Please lend me a pen.
A red pen, please.
I write my name with a pen.
en.notes: ペン is a writing instrument with ink, or a nib pen; a pencil is called 鉛筆. ボールペン explicitly means a ballpoint pen. ペンで書く means "to write with a pen"; individual pens are counted with 本.

examples[].german: Let's take a photo.
Please show me your trip photos.
en.notes: 写真 is a photo or photograph. "To take a photo" is 写真を撮る, not 写真を作る. 写真を見せる means "to show photos". Photos, as flat objects, are counted with 枚, as in 写真を一枚.

examples[].german: I am going to see a movie.
I like Japanese movies.
en.notes: 映画 means a film as a work, or a film screening. 映画を見る means "to watch a movie"; 映画を見に行く "to go out to see a movie". The cinema as a building is 映画館（えいがかん）. "Japanese films" can be expressed as 日本の映画.

examples[].german: I listen to music.
I like classical music.
Music can be heard from the next room.
en.notes: 音楽 is the general term for music. 音楽を聞く means "to listen to music"; for attentive or enjoyable listening, 聴く is also written. A genre can come before it, as in クラシック音楽. A single piece of music is called 曲（きょく）.

examples[].german: I like traveling.
I am going on a trip next month.
en.notes: 旅行 means a trip and forms the verb "to travel" with する. 旅行に行く is also a common combination. A single everyday trip to school is normally not a 旅行; the word emphasizes a journey or excursion.

examples[].german: I take a walk in the park.
I go for a walk with the dog every morning.
en.notes: 散歩 is a walk, often without a particular destination and for relaxation. 散歩する means "to take a walk". The space walked through can be marked with を, and a companion with と: 公園を散歩する, 犬と散歩する.

examples[].german: How is the weather today?
Tomorrow's weather will be sunny.
en.notes: 天気 means the weather in general. With どうですか you ask about its condition, and with 晴れ, 雨 or 雪 you state the weather situation. "Nice weather" is いい天気. 今日の天気 connects the day with the noun by の.

examples[].german: A friend is coming.
I came from Japan.
Spring has come.
en.notes: 来る describes movement toward the speaker or another reference point. This irregular verb changes its reading: 来ます（きます）・来て（きて）・来ない（こない）. 日本から来ました names the place of origin; with a season, 来る can also express its arrival.

examples[].german: It will rain tomorrow.
I stay home on rainy days.
en.notes: 雨 is a noun: 雨です means "it is raining/there will be rain" in a weather report. For ongoing precipitation, 雨が降っています is used. 雨の日 means a rainy day; の connects the weather with the day.

examples[].german: It is snowing.
There is a lot of snow this year.
en.notes: 雪 means snow and snowfall. 雪が降る means "it snows"; 雪が降っています describes snow that is falling right now. For an amount of snow, 雪が多い is one example. Personal names with the same reading are not meant here.

examples[].german: The wind is strong today.
In autumn the wind is cool.
en.notes: 風（かぜ）means wind here. 強い describes its strength and 涼しい its pleasantly cool effect. A cold is normally written 風邪, also read かぜ. The reading ふう in other uses is not the reading of this card.

examples[].german: The sky is beautiful.
You can see stars in the sky.
en.notes: 空（そら）means the sky or the air space. 空に星が見える describes the position of visible stars with に. The same kanji is also read から or くう in other words; those readings are not used here.

examples[].german: I climb the mountain.
Mt. Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.
en.notes: 山（やま）means a mountain or hill. 山に登る means to climb a mountain. In many mountain names, 山 is read さん, as in 富士山（ふじさん）; so 富士山 is not *ふじやま in the standard name used here.

examples[].german: I swim in the river.
The river water is clean.
en.notes: 川（かわ）means a river or stream. For an activity in the river, the place is marked with で. 川の水 means river water. In river names the reading can change to がわ through sound linking, as in 多摩川（たまがわ）. 河 is also a recorded spelling of かわ for a river; the first example spelling remains 川.

examples[].german: I want to swim in the sea.
I go to the sea in summer.
en.notes: 海 means the sea or ocean. The combination 海に行く can mean a trip to the coast, not necessarily into the water. For an activity in the sea, で is used: 海で泳ぐ. The destination with 行く is marked with に.

examples[].german: The flowers are beautiful.
I planted flowers in the garden.
en.notes: 花（はな）means a flower or blossom. It can mean several flowers, although the noun needs no separate plural form. A planting place is given with に: 庭に花を植える. 鼻 ("nose") has the same reading but is a different word.

examples[].german: There is a big tree.
I rest under the tree.
en.notes: 木（き）means a tree here. 木 can also mean wood, but the examples concern a living tree. 木の下 means under the tree; the place of an activity is then marked with で.

examples[].german: I like dogs.
I go for a walk with my dog.
en.notes: 犬 means dog. To express the presence of a dog, いる is used, since it is a living being. 犬と散歩する means to go for a walk with a dog; と names the companion. Dogs are usually counted with 匹, and large animals, depending on context, with 頭.

examples[].german: I go home.
I'll be home at five o'clock.
The guest has already left.
en.notes: 帰る means returning home or to a familiar place of origin. For guests, it can mean "to leave, to say goodbye". Despite its -える ending, it is a godan verb: 帰ります・帰って・帰らない. 帰る and 変える（to change）are different words.

examples[].german: There is a cat.
This cat likes fish.
en.notes: 猫 means a cat. As a living being, its existence is expressed with いる. 猫は魚が好きです has two roles: 猫は is the topic and 魚が is what is liked. Cats are usually counted with 匹.

examples[].german: A bird is flying.
Birds are singing in the morning.
en.notes: 鳥 means bird. For flying, one says 鳥が飛ぶ; bird calls are normally described with 鳴く. Poultry meat is often written 鶏肉; this card deals with living birds. For animals of this kind, 羽 is a common counter.

examples[].german: What day of the week is it today?
The weather is nice today.
en.notes: 今日（きょう）means today. As a simple time expression it normally needs no に; は highlights today as the topic. Before a noun it is connected with の: 今日の天気. The long reading きょう is written kyō.

examples[].german: I watched a movie yesterday.
I was busy yesterday.
en.notes: 昨日（きのう）means the day before today. Statements about completed actions are often in the past tense, as in 見ました. Adjectives also form a past tense: 忙しかった. The long o is written kinō.

examples[].german: I get up early in the morning.
I wash my face before breakfast.
en.notes: 朝 means the morning as a time of day, not the next day（明日）. It can stand directly as a time expression: 朝早く起きる. 朝ご飯 is breakfast; 朝ご飯の前に means before breakfast. The card uses the reading あさ.

examples[].german: I eat lunch.
It is hot during the day.
en.notes: 昼 can mean the midday period or, more generally, the bright part of the day. 昼ご飯 means lunch. In contrast to 夜, 昼 is often "during the day", not just exactly twelve o'clock. The reading is ひる.

examples[].german: I watch TV in the evening.
It is quiet at night.
en.notes: 夜（よる）can mean the evening after dark or the night. As a time expression it can stand directly before the activity: 夜テレビを見る. 夜は highlights the night time as the topic. For "every night/every evening", 毎晩 is used.

examples[].german: What time is it now?
I am watching TV now.
en.notes: 今 means now, the present moment. It is narrower than 今日 ("today"). 今何時ですか asks for the current time; 今～ています emphasizes an action in progress. Normally no に follows 今 as a time expression.

examples[].german: I study Japanese every day.
I take a walk every day.
en.notes: 毎日 means every day and describes regular repetition. It usually stands before the activity without に. A period within the day can be added, as in 毎日一時間 ("one hour every day"). 今日, by contrast, means only today.

examples[].german: That man is a teacher.
A boy is running.
en.notes: 男 on its own can sound rather blunt when referring to someone you do not know. 男の人 is often the more polite form in everyday speech, and 男性 the neutral, formal one. 男の子 means a boy, so adding の changes the reference.

en.meaning: to see; to watch; to look
examples[].german: I watch TV.
Let's go see the cherry blossoms.
en.notes: 見る is a transitive ichidan verb: 見ます・見て・見ない. What is looked at takes を. 見に行く combines the verb stem 見 with に and 行く: you go somewhere in order to look at something. For deliberate watching, 観る is also used; it is not necessarily interchangeable with 見る in every sense.

examples[].german: I drink coffee every morning.
I get up at six every morning.
en.notes: 毎朝 means every morning. It denotes repetition on each morning and is normally used without に. A specific time can be added with に: 毎朝六時に. The first あ in あさ is kept: まいあさ.

examples[].german: I read a book every evening.
I take a bath every evening.
en.notes: 毎晩 means every evening or every night. It is a regular time expression that does not need に. 毎日, by contrast, covers the whole daily rhythm. 晩 is read ばん in this word; both examples describe recurring evening habits.

examples[].german: I play tennis every week.
I go shopping every Sunday.
en.notes: 毎週 means every week and usually stands before an activity without に. You can add the day of the week: 毎週日曜日に ("every week on Sunday"). 毎日, by contrast, describes daily repetition; 週 is the week.

examples[].german: I always eat here.
I always walk along this street.
en.notes: いつも means always or regularly as usual. It stands before the habit described, for example いつもここで食べる. 時々, by contrast, is only occasionally. The card deals with the frequency usage, not a place name read the same way. The kanji spelling 何時も is read いつも; the kana form is usual.

examples[].german: I sometimes watch movies.
I sometimes eat at a restaurant.
en.notes: 時々 means sometimes or from time to time, that is, not a daily or exceptionless habit. The character 々 repeats 時 in the spelling; the reading is ときどき. As a time adverb it normally stands without に.

examples[].german: I often eat Japanese food.
I understand Japanese well.
en.notes: よく means "often" or "well/thoroughly", depending on the context. よく食べる can describe a frequent activity; よく分かる a good understanding. It is an adverb, not the predicate adjective いい. 欲 ("desire") and 翼 ("wing") are other words with the same reading.

en.meaning: at once; right away; just nearby
examples[].german: I will go right away.
The station is just over there.
en.notes: すぐ can mean "immediately" in time or "close by" in space. すぐ行く is to go at once; すぐそこ is right there, without much distance. The word here is an adverb, not the old verb すぐ ("to pass by").

examples[].german: It is still raining.
My homework is not finished yet.
en.notes: まだ with an affirmative statement means "still": まだ雨が降っています. With a negated statement it means "not yet": まだ終わっていません. It signals that an expected change or completion has not yet occurred.

examples[].german: I have already eaten.
Let's head back now.
I won't eat any more.
en.notes: もう denotes a point in time or a state that has already been reached: もう食べました. With a negation it means "no longer": もう食べません. It thus contrasts with まだ ("still/not yet"). もう帰りましょう means that it is time to go back now.

examples[].german: This flower is very beautiful.
I am very tired, so I will go to bed early.
en.notes: とても intensifies a gradable quality and means "very". It can be used with い- and な-adjectives and suitable expressions of state. It does not state a quantity of objects; たくさん is suitable for that. The stronger everyday form とっても is also common. 迚も is a rare kanji spelling of とても; the kana form is usual.
