en.meaning: to hear; to listen; to ask
examples[].german: I listen to music.
Please ask the teacher.
en.notes: 聞く can mean "to hear, to listen" or "to ask". 音楽を聞く names what is heard with を; 先生に聞く names the person asked with に. This transitive godan verb forms 聞きます・聞いて・聞かない. Context decides between the two meanings.

examples[].german: I understand a little Japanese.
Let's rest for a little while.
en.notes: 少し can mean a small amount, a low degree or a short time. 少し分かる means to understand somewhat; 少し休む to take a short break. To describe a small amount of something as a quality, 少ない is used instead, as in お金が少ない.

examples[].german: I read a lot of books.
I did a lot of shopping.
en.notes: たくさん means a large amount or number. It can directly accompany the action, as in 本をたくさん読む. Before a noun, の is often used: たくさんの本. The spelling 沢山 is possible; here the word is shown in kana.

examples[].german: I ate all of it.
It is 1,000 yen in total.
en.notes: 全部 means all or the whole. It can sum up a whole quantity as the object of an action. 全部で indicates a total sum, such as a price. It should be distinguished from たくさん: "a lot" need not be "all".

examples[].german: Let's go together.
I live together with a friend.
en.notes: 一緒に means together or jointly. Another person involved is added with と: 友達と一緒に. The に is part of the adverbial phrase taught here; it is not attached again in addition.

examples[].german: One apple, please.
Please choose one.
en.notes: 一つ is the general counting form for one thing, often used when no special counter applies. It can follow the object: りんごを一つ. Before a noun it is connected with の: 一つのりんご. The reading is ひとつ, not いちつ.

examples[].german: I buy two eggs.
There are two roads.
en.notes: 二つ counts two things with the general ～つ series. After an object the counter can stand without a particle: 卵を二つ買う. Before a noun, の is needed: 二つの道. The reading is ふたつ, not につ.

examples[].german: There are three boxes.
I ate three mandarins.
en.notes: 三つ counts three things in the general ～つ series. The small っ in みっつ is written as a double consonant in romaji: mittsu. The number can follow the counted thing with が or を: 箱が三つある, みかんを三つ食べる.

examples[].german: I have no money.
I spent too much money.
en.notes: お金 is the usual word for money. The お belongs to the common polite word form; it is also used for one's own money. お金がある describes available money, お金を使う spending it. 円, by contrast, names the currency yen.

examples[].german: I buy a ticket.
I lost my ticket.
en.notes: 切符 means a ticket, especially for transport. Paper tickets are counted with 枚: 切符を二枚. The small っ leads to a double p in romanization: kippu. Do not confuse it with 切手 ("postage stamp").

examples[].german: A stamp, please.
This stamp is pretty, isn't it?
en.notes: 切手 means a postage stamp for mailing. The common combination 切手を貼る means to stick on a stamp. As flat pieces of paper, they are counted with 枚. The reading きって has a small っ; 切符（きっぷ）, by contrast, is a ticket.

examples[].german: I read a book.
I read the newspaper every day.
How do you read this kanji?
en.notes: 読む is a transitive godan verb: 読みます・読んで・読まない. Besides reading texts, it can indicate how a character is pronounced: 何と読みますか asks for the reading. The material being read usually takes を.

examples[].german: I write a letter.
A letter has come from my friend.
en.notes: 手紙 is a letter or written message, normally a personal one. 手紙を書く means to write a letter. When receiving, から names the sender: 友達から手紙が来る. 手紙 does not stand for a postage stamp or ticket.

examples[].german: What is your name?
Do you know the name of this flower?
en.notes: 名前 means a name in general and, depending on the context, also a first name. お名前 is the polite form when asking another person. With の you name whose or what's name is meant: この花の名前.

examples[].german: What does this word mean?
I don't understand the meaning of this kanji.
en.notes: 意味 is the meaning or sense of a word, character or statement. この言葉の意味は何ですか asks for an explanation. When understanding, 意味 takes が with 分かる. It is not the same as 読み方, the pronunciation or reading.

examples[].german: Do you have any questions?
May I ask the teacher a question?
en.notes: 質問 is a question asked of someone. 質問する means to ask a question. The person asked is attached with に: 先生に質問する. 質問がありますか asks whether someone has a question; it is not a school exercise item like 問題.

examples[].german: Please write the answer.
I don't know the answer to this problem.
en.notes: 答え is an answer and, for problems, also the solution. The combination 答えを書く means to write down the answer. This noun has no verb conjugation; the related verb is 答える. 問題の答え means the solution to a problem.

examples[].german: There is no problem.
This question is difficult.
en.notes: 問題 can mean a practical problem or a question or exercise on an exam. 問題はありません means "there is no problem". この問題は難しい can mean a difficult school problem. A question put to someone is usually called 質問.

examples[].german: There is a test tomorrow.
The test is next Monday.
I got a hundred points on the test.
en.notes: テスト means a test or an examination of knowledge and skills here. テストがある announces an exam date; テストを受ける means "to take an exam". The result can be given with 点, such as 百点 "a hundred points".

examples[].german: Did you do your homework?
I forgot my homework.
en.notes: 宿題 means homework or an assigned task; Japanese needs no plural ending for it. 宿題をする means "to do homework". 宿題を忘れる can mean that one did not do it or did not bring the material; the context decides.

examples[].german: Studying Japanese is fun.
I study for two hours every day.
en.notes: 勉強 is the noun for studying or learning; with する it becomes "to study". The subject studied can stand with の, as in 日本語の勉強, or with を before 勉強する. 二時間勉強する gives the duration; for a fixed point in time, に is used instead.

examples[].german: I write a letter.
Please write your name.
en.notes: 書く refers to writing a text or individual characters. What is written takes を: 手紙を書く, 名前を書く. The て-form is 書いて; the polite form is 書きます.

examples[].german: The work is finished.
I will go home after work is finished.
I am looking for a new job now.
en.notes: 仕事 can mean a concrete job, a task, or one's occupation. 仕事をする means "to work" and 仕事が終わる "the work ends". 新しい仕事を探す usually means looking for a new position; for a single task, the context is decisive.

examples[].german: I practice every day.
I am practicing the piano.
I drink water after practice.
en.notes: 練習 is practice or training to improve a skill. 練習する means "to practice"; the practice subject often stands with を or の, as in ピアノを練習する, ピアノの練習. It denotes targeted repetition and application; general studying is often 勉強.

examples[].german: Please turn right.
Please turn right at the next corner.
There is a key in the right pocket.
en.notes: 右 is a location and direction noun: 右に曲がる "to turn right". Before another noun, の is used, as in 右のポケット "the right pocket". "On the right side of ..." is ～の右に. The direction depends on the point of view; the opposite is 左.

examples[].german: Please go left.
Please go straight along the left road.
The post office is to the left of the bank.
en.notes: 左 means the left side or direction. 左に行く means "to go left" and 左の道 "the left road". For position relative to something, ～の左に is used. The opposite is 右; the word is a noun and often needs の for further specification.

examples[].german: It is on the desk.
There is a book on the table.
Please look up.
en.notes: 上（うえ）is a location noun here meaning "above, over, on". "On the desk" is 机の上; with に you describe the place of a thing, with で the place of an action. 上を見る means "to look up". Other readings of 上, such as じょう in compounds, are to be learned separately.

examples[].german: It is under the desk.
There is a cat under the desk.
I am waiting on the floor below.
en.notes: 下（した）here means the area under something or a lower position. 机の下に means "under the desk"; for an action taking place there, で is used. 下の階 is the floor below. The word is a noun, not an i-adjective; other readings such as げ belong to other combinations.

examples[].german: It is in the bag.
What is in the box?
Since it is raining, I will play inside the house.
en.notes: 中（なか）here means the inside of a container or room: かばんの中, 家の中. For the place where one is, に is used, and for an action carried out there, で. The readings ちゅう or じゅう occur in other combinations, such as 勉強中 or 一日中; they are not the reading of the location noun practiced here.

examples[].german: It is cold outside.
The shoes are dirty, so please take them off outside the house.
en.notes: A location noun: 外に出る denotes movement outside, 外で遊ぶ an action outdoors. 建物の外 denotes the area outside a building. The reading ほか belongs to another use and is not treated here as an equivalent reading.

examples[].german: I am in front of the station.
I am waiting in front of the station.
I read a book before going to bed.
en.notes: 前（まえ）can mean "in front of, ahead" spatially and "before" in time. 駅の前 denotes the area in front of the station. For the time before an activity, the plain verb form comes before 前に: 寝る前に "before going to bed". With a noun, の connects, as in 食事の前に.

examples[].german: Please look behind you.
There is a park behind the school.
en.notes: 後ろ（うしろ）is the spatial back or the area behind something. ～の後ろに means "behind ..." and 後ろを見る "to look behind". For "afterwards" or "after an activity", 後（あと）is usually used, as in 食事の後で; that is a different reading and use. The spelling 後 without ろ is also recorded for the same reading; it deviates from the usual okurigana spelling 後ろ. Here the meaning remains spatial "back, behind"; a future point in time is not meant.

examples[].german: I speak Japanese.
I talked with a friend on the phone.
en.notes: With a language as the object, 話す means "to speak a language": 日本語を話す. The person you talk to is attached with と, the means of communication with で: 友達と電話で話す. Do not confuse it with the similar 離す ("to separate").

examples[].german: Who is next door?
Please ask the person next to you.
en.notes: 隣（となり）denotes the person, thing or apartment immediately adjacent. 隣の人 means "the person next to me/next door" and ～の隣に "right next to ...". 隣 alone can stand for the house next door. 近く, by contrast, denotes closeness in general and does not require immediate adjacency.

examples[].german: I live near the station.
Is there a convenience store nearby?
en.notes: 近く is a location noun here for the vicinity or surroundings. 駅の近くに means "near the station" and この近く "near here". Unlike 隣, the place need not be directly adjacent. 近い is the related i-adjective for "near"; the form 近く practiced here is used as a noun.

examples[].german: It is between the house and the station.
I travel between Tokyo and Osaka by Shinkansen.
Please be quiet during class.
en.notes: 間（あいだ）denotes a spatial gap or a span of time. Between two things is ～と～の間; "during class" is 授業の間. 間は usually covers the whole duration, while 間に highlights an event within that time. The reading ま denotes other uses, such as a pause or gap.

examples[].german: It is warm in spring.
When spring comes, the cherry trees bloom.
en.notes: 春 is spring as a season. In general statements 春は can be used; 春になる means "it becomes spring". For an action in this season, 春に is also possible. The related 春休み（はるやすみ）means spring vacation.

examples[].german: It is hot in summer.
It is hot in summer, so I go to the sea.
en.notes: 夏 is summer. 夏は暑いです describes the typical weather; 夏に海へ行く an activity in the season. 夏休み（なつやすみ）is the summer vacation. 暑い is written for hot weather; 熱い, by contrast, is used for hot water or hot objects, for example.

examples[].german: It is cool in autumn.
The autumn leaves are beautiful in autumn.
en.notes: 秋 is autumn. 秋は涼しいです describes the season in general; 秋に旅行する names an activity in autumn. 紅葉（こうよう）here denotes the autumn coloring of leaves, not just foliage without a color change.

examples[].german: It is cold in winter.
I want to go skiing in winter.
en.notes: 冬 is winter. 冬は寒いです describes the typical weather; 冬にスキーに行く names an outing in this season. 冬休み（ふゆやすみ）is the winter vacation. 寒い denotes the cold of the surroundings, while 冷たい denotes, for example, the coldness of a touched object.

examples[].german: The moon is beautiful.
The moon is beautiful, isn't it?
The next month is March.
en.notes: 月（つき）means the moon and, as an independent noun, can also mean a month. Calendar months, by contrast, are named with ～月（がつ）, such as 三月（さんがつ）"March". For a counted duration, ～か月（かげつ）is usual. These forms have different readings from the つき practiced here.

examples[].german: It rained a lot this year.
A new year has begun.
en.notes: 年（とし）is the independent noun for a year and can also denote age, as in 年を取る "to grow older". Calendar years and counted years mostly use ねん, such as 二〇二六年（にせんにじゅうろくねん）. That reading does not belong to the independent form とし practiced here.

examples[].german: There is a test next week.
I exercise three times a week.
en.notes: 週 is the week. Compounds such as 来週（らいしゅう）refer to a specific week; 一週間（いっしゅうかん）is a duration of one week. 一週間に三回 means "three times a week". The doubled consonant in いっしゅうかん is part of the pronunciation of this counting form.

examples[].german: I buy bread.
How much did you pay for that bag?
en.notes: 買う means to buy something with money. The item takes を; the purchase price can be given with で: いくらで買う ("to buy for how much"). For this godan verb, う becomes って in the て-form: 買って.

examples[].german: It starts at nine in the morning.
I go shopping in the morning.
en.notes: 午前 denotes the morning and, in clock times, the period from midnight until before noon, that is, a.m. 午前九時 is 9 a.m.; 午前二時 would be 2 a.m. 午前中 means the morning as a period. The opposite term for clock times is 午後.

examples[].german: Let's meet at three in the afternoon.
I have class from the afternoon.
en.notes: 午後 denotes the afternoon and, in clock times, the period from noon until before midnight, that is, p.m. 午後三時 is 3 p.m. (15:00); 午後八時 is 8 p.m. (20:00) and falls in the evening. 午後から means "from the afternoon". The opposite term for clock times is 午前.

examples[].german: When is your birthday?
I eat cake on my birthday.
en.notes: 誕生日 denotes the yearly recurring birthday. For an event on this day, に is used: 誕生日にケーキを食べる. With いつですか you ask for the date. 日 is read び in this word, not ひ.

examples[].german: I have tomorrow off.
There is a ten-minute break between classes.
en.notes: 休み is a noun for a break, free time or vacation. 休みです means "I have the day off" or "it is closed", depending on the context. A short break is also 休み, for example during class. The related verb is 休む, not *休みる.

examples[].german: What color do you like?
The color of the car is blue.
en.notes: 色 means a color. 何色 asks "what color" and is read なにいろ in this sentence. With の you name the object: 車の色. Blue as a color name is the noun 青; 青い is the related い-adjective.

examples[].german: I bought new clothes.
I wash clothes.
en.notes: 服 means clothes and in daily life often refers to Western-style garments. 服を着る means to get dressed or wear clothes, 服を洗う to wash them. It can mean several items without the Japanese noun getting a special plural form.

examples[].german: Please take off your shoes.
These shoes are a little small.
en.notes: 靴 means shoes or footwear. To put them on, 履く is used, and to take them off, 脱ぐ. Shoes as a pair are counted with 足（そく）, but the word itself needs no separate plural form. この靴は小さい can mean that the shoes do not fit.

examples[].german: I put on a hat.
I am wearing a hat today.
en.notes: 帽子 covers hats and caps. For headwear, かぶる is used, not the general 着る for clothing. 帽子をかぶります denotes putting it on; 帽子をかぶっています the subsequent wearing as a state.

examples[].german: I am wearing glasses.
The person wearing glasses is Mr. Tanaka.
en.notes: メガネ means glasses; the spelling 眼鏡 is also common. The matching verb is かける: メガネをかける. ～かけています describes wearing. A person can be identified by メガネをかけている人 ("the person who is wearing glasses").

examples[].german: Take care of your health.
Exercise is good for the body.
en.notes: 体（からだ）is the body and, in a health context, can mean one's physical condition. 体に気をつける means to take care of one's health, 体にいい "good for the body". The card uses からだ; other kanji readings in compounds are not equated with it. 身体 can also be read からだ; this special whole-word reading is treated as gikun. There is also the reading しんたい; this card continues to use からだ.

examples[].german: I study.
Won't you play tennis with me?
en.notes: する is irregular: します, して, した. It forms verbs with action nouns, such as 勉強する; 勉強をする is also possible. For sports, you say, for example, テニスをする. The form ～しませんか invites someone to do something together. 為る is a rare kanji spelling of this verb; する in hiragana is the norm.

examples[].german: I have a headache.
I bowed my head.
en.notes: 頭（あたま）means the head here. 頭が痛い is the usual way to say you have a headache. 頭を下げる means to lower one's head and, in the right context, can describe a bow. This card deals neither with a leader nor with a down payment.

examples[].german: I wash my face.
I remember her face.
en.notes: 顔 means face. 顔を洗う is to wash one's face. Faces can also be recognized or remembered, as in 顔を覚えている. Meanings such as reputation or influence are figurative uses and are not taught here.

examples[].german: My eyes are big.
Please close your eyes.
en.notes: 目（め）means one eye or both eyes; the number is understood from the context. 目を閉じる means to close one's eyes. The kanji also serves as an ordinal suffix, as in 二つ目, but this card deals with the body part.

examples[].german: My ear hurts.
Please cover your ears.
en.notes: 耳 means ear. For earache, 耳が痛い is used; when covering, the ear is the object with を. 耳 can mean both ears without a plural marker. Meanings such as the crust of bread belong to other uses.

examples[].german: Please open your mouth.
Please eat with your mouth closed.
en.notes: 口（くち）means the mouth here. Opening is 口を開ける, closing 口を閉じる. It appears with を as the body part being moved. Openings of objects or the activity of talking are other uses that the card does not treat as the basic meaning.

examples[].german: Please wash your hands.
Please raise your right hand.
en.notes: 手（て）means a hand; the form can also mean several hands. 右手 and 左手 mean the right and left hand. 手を洗う is to wash one's hands, 手を上げる to raise a hand. Other meanings such as method are not meant here.

examples[].german: My foot hurts.
He has long legs.
en.notes: 足（あし）can mean a foot or the whole leg; the context decides. 足が痛い can therefore describe foot or leg pain, depending on the body area meant. For the leg, 脚 is also common. 足が長い normally refers to long legs.

examples[].german: I'm hungry.
I have a stomachache.
en.notes: お腹（おなか）means stomach or belly. The usual polite form with お is also used for one's own belly. お腹がすく means to get hungry, お腹が痛い to have a stomachache. The reading is the whole-word form おなか, not an arbitrary combination of other 腹 readings.

examples[].german: He/She is tall.
I sit with my back to the wall.
en.notes: 背（せ）can mean back or body height. 背が高い means physically tall; 背が低い short. In 背を向ける, by contrast, the back is meant. For the body's back, the longer word 背中（せなか）is also used.

examples[].german: The voice is loud.
That singer has a nice voice.
en.notes: 声 means voice. 声が大きい means a loud voice, not its physical size. いい声 is a pleasant or beautiful voice. The examples concern people; general noises are often called 音.

examples[].german: There is a book on the desk.
I don't have time today.
en.notes: ある expresses the existence of inanimate things and the availability of, for example, time. A place takes に, and the thing that exists takes が: 机の上に本がある. For people and animals, いる is normally used. The plain negative is ない, the polite one ありません.

examples[].german: Please take your medicine.
I went to the pharmacy to buy medicine.
en.notes: 薬 is medicine or a medication. For tablets and other oral medication one says 薬を飲む; an ointment is applied with 塗る. 薬局 is the pharmacy. The card deals with medicines, not illegal drugs or other chemicals.

examples[].german: I got sick.
When you are sick, please rest.
en.notes: 病気 means illness and, with です, can also express "to be sick". 病気になる means to become ill. Before the noun 時, の is used: 病気の時 ("when one is sick"). The word is not an い-adjective; forms like *病気い are wrong.

examples[].german: Which country do you come from?
Which country do you want to go to?
en.notes: 国（くに）means a country or state here. どの国 asks "which country". With から you name the country of origin, with に a travel destination. The word does not automatically mean a city or a state within any given country.

examples[].german: This town is quiet.
There is no station in this town.
en.notes: 町（まち）can mean a town, a smaller place or a neighborhood. The exact administrative category does not follow from the word alone. The location of a place is given with に; 町には can introduce a statement about existing facilities. 街 is another recorded spelling of まち; this card practices the place and neighborhood sense.

examples[].german: I play in the park.
The park is next to the station.
en.notes: 公園 is a public park. An activity in the park takes で: 公園で遊ぶ. For its location, に with ある is used, as in 駅の隣にある. The place itself is not a living being and therefore takes ある instead of いる.

examples[].german: I swim in the pool.
In summer I go to the pool.
en.notes: プール means a swimming pool or the swimming pool as a facility here. For swimming, で is used; for a visit as a destination, に. Identically written meanings for pool billiards or pooled resources are not meant here; the long u is written pūru.

examples[].german: Please enter the classroom.
There are twenty students in the classroom.
en.notes: 教室 means a classroom or teaching room here. For entering and for the location of people present, に is used. Classes as a course or university departments are further meanings but not the rooms of these examples. きょうしつ has a long o.

examples[].german: Please look at the blackboard.
The teacher writes characters on the blackboard.
en.notes: 黒板 is the board people usually write on with chalk. 黒板に字を書く means "to write characters on the blackboard": に marks the surface on which the writing appears. For a white writing board, ホワイトボード is usual; 黒板 does not refer to just any board.

examples[].german: I look at the map.
Let's look at the map and find the way.
I draw a map from the station to my house.
en.notes: 地図 is a map or plan for spatial orientation; a city map can also be called that. 地図を見る means "to look at the map", 地図で調べる "to check using the map". A drawn route map is also called 地図, not just a map of a whole country.

examples[].german: I watch TV.
I watched the news on TV.
I bought a new TV.
en.notes: テレビ can mean the television set or television as a medium. テレビを買う means "to buy a TV", テレビを見る "to watch TV". テレビのニュース is TV news. テレビをつける and テレビを消す are about switching the set on and off.

examples[].german: I have an older brother.
There is a cat in the room.
en.notes: いる refers to the existence or presence of people and animals; for things, ある is used. Do not confuse it with similarly pronounced verbs like 要る ("to need"). In statements of location, the place takes に and the living being takes が: 部屋に猫がいる.

examples[].german: I use the computer.
I send e-mail from the computer.
I bought a computer for work.
en.notes: パソコン is the common short form of パーソナルコンピューター and means a personal computer, such as a desktop PC or laptop. パソコンでメールを送る uses で for the means. A laptop is also called ノートパソコン; パソコン does not automatically mean a smartphone.

examples[].german: Do you have a camera?
I take a camera on the trip.
en.notes: カメラ is a camera for taking pictures. カメラを持っている can express owning or carrying one; カメラを持って行く means "to take a camera along". The picture itself is called 写真. "To take a photo with a camera" is カメラで写真を撮る, with で for the device used.

examples[].german: Please turn on the air conditioner.
May I turn on the air conditioner?
There is no air conditioner in this room.
en.notes: エアコン is the short form for an air conditioner. エアコンをつける means "to turn the air conditioner on", エアコンを消す "to turn it off". Many units can also heat; the word alone does not specify cooling. 冷房 denotes cooling mode, 暖房 heating mode.

examples[].german: Please turn on the light.
Please turn off the light.
Without electricity, the computer can't be used.
en.notes: 電気 means electricity or, in everyday speech, electric light. With 電気をつける and 電気を消す, the light is usually meant. 電気で動く means "to run on electricity"; で marks the energy source. Whether "electricity" or "light" fits is decided by the action in the sentence.

examples[].german: I bought souvenirs.
I will buy souvenirs and go home.
At my friend's house, I handed over a gift.
en.notes: お土産 is often a gift one buys for others on a trip, for example something typical of the place visited. It can also be a gift a guest brings when visiting. The お is a polite prefix; the full reading is おみやげ. お土産を渡す means "to hand over a souvenir/gift".

examples[].german: There is a lot of luggage.
I have a lot of luggage and it is tiring.
Please put your luggage here.
en.notes: 荷物 means luggage or transported goods and, depending on the context, can also mean a package. The word has no plural ending: 荷物が多い means "to have a lot of luggage". 荷物を預ける means "to check in luggage", 荷物を持つ "to carry luggage". How many individual pieces are meant follows from the sentence.

examples[].german: What do you eat?
What do you want to eat?
What is in the box?
en.notes: 何 is read なに here and asks about a thing or action: 何を食べる "eat what", 何がある "what is there". Before です, the reading なん is usual, as in 何ですか. The reading should therefore be learned together with its combination; the examples here practice なに specifically.

examples[].german: Where is the restroom?
Where are you going?
en.notes: どこ asks about a place. どこですか means "where is it?", どこに行く "where to go", どこで買う "where to buy". に marks the destination of a movement or a location, で the place of an action. The particle therefore provides the more precise meaning of the place question. The spelling 何処 is also read どこ. In normal text, the kana form どこ is usual.

examples[].german: When are you going to Japan?
When did you come to Japan?
Until when will you wait?
en.notes: いつ asks about a point in time or a date. Unlike a fixed clock time, the simple question form normally needs no に: いつ行きますか. いつから asks for the start, いつまで for the endpoint of a time span. The answer may be a clock time, a day or a longer period. The rare kanji spelling 何時 can be read いつ. For this question, the kana form いつ is usual; the same kanji can also be read なんじ "what time".

examples[].german: I understand Japanese.
I don't understand this problem.
en.notes: With 分かる, the thing understood normally takes が: 日本語が分かる. Despite its -る ending, the verb is a godan verb: 分かります, 分かって. 分かりました can also mean "Understood!" as a reply.

examples[].german: Why do you study Japanese?
Why are you studying Japanese?
Why is the train stopped?
en.notes: なぜ asks for a reason or cause. With a person, the question can aim at a motive, with an event at its explanation. なぜ often sounds matter-of-fact or probing; in everyday conversation, どうして and the more casual なんで are also common. A direct why-question can sound demanding depending on tone.

examples[].german: How is Japanese?
How is life in Japan?
How do you use this computer?
en.notes: どう asks about a manner or an assessment. 日本の生活はどうですか asks for an impression of life in Japan; どう使いますか asks about operation. Before a noun, どんな is normally used for "what kind of ...", not どう. In more polite questions, いかが can be used. 如何 is a rare kanji spelling of どう. The kana form どう is usual; the kanji can also be read いかが.

examples[].german: Yes, I understand.
Yes, please.
en.notes: はい is the polite answer "yes" and can also signal "understood" or "I'm listening". はい、分かりました confirms understanding; はい、お願いします accepts an offer. A single はい while listening does not yet mean agreement with a proposal. To decline, the answer itself is explained, for example with いいえ.

en.meaning: no; not at all; don't mention it
examples[].german: No, that's not right.
No, not yet.
"Thank you." "Not at all, you're welcome."
en.notes: いいえ is a negative answer. いいえ、違います corrects an assumption; いいえ、まだです means "no, not yet". As a modest reply to thanks, いいえ can also mean "don't mention it". This use does not deny the thanks itself but plays down one's own help. The kanji spelling 否 is documented as a rare form for this reading in older dictionary entries. For ordinary answers, the kana spelling いいえ is used. The same kanji is also read いな or いや in other expressions; those readings belong to other words.

examples[].german: Good morning, teacher. (Greeting to a teacher.)
I said "Good morning" to the teacher.
On the phone I said: "Good morning. This is Tanaka."
en.notes: おはようございます is the polite morning greeting, for example to teachers or at work. Among familiar people, おはよう is often enough. On the phone, one's own name can follow the greeting. Some workplaces also use the greeting at the start of a shift at other times of day; normally it is a morning greeting. お早うございます is also read おはようございます; the phrase is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: Hello, how are you?
Hello, Mr./Ms. Tanaka.
At noon, I entered the shop and said "Hello".
en.notes: こんにちは is a daytime greeting, especially from late morning to the afternoon. The final は is pronounced わ: konnichiwa. You can then ask how someone is or start a conversation. The form is also common as a greeting when entering a small shop; other greetings are used in the morning and evening.

examples[].german: Good evening, Mr./Ms. Tanaka.
"Good evening, nice weather, isn't it?"
When I talk by video in the evening, I first say "Good evening".
en.notes: こんばんは is the greeting when meeting in the evening. The final は is pronounced わ: konbanwa. The form opens contact, for example in person or in an evening video call. It is not a greeting for going to bed; for that, おやすみなさい is said.

examples[].german: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.
I waved goodbye to my friend.
Before leaving Japan, I said "Goodbye" to my friends.
en.notes: さようなら is a farewell greeting. It is used at school, for example, and can seem more serious for longer separations. Among friends, またね or じゃあ、また are often used for a quick reunion. However, さようなら does not necessarily mean a final farewell; さようなら、また明日 is possible. 左様なら is a rare kanji spelling; さようなら is usual.

examples[].german: Thank you very much. That helped me.
I received a present and said "Thank you".
en.notes: ありがとうございます is the polite expression of thanks, for example for help, information or a gift. Among familiar people, ありがとう can be enough. For help that has already been given, ありがとうございました is also said. The fixed phrase is pronounced arigatō gozaimasu; the long ō belongs to the pronunciation. 有難うございます is a dictionary spelling of the thanks formula; the kana form ありがとうございます is usual.

examples[].german: Excuse me, please tell me the way.
Sorry for being late.
en.notes: すみません is used both to apologize and to politely get attention. すみません、道を教えてください opens a request for directions; 遅れてすみません apologizes for one's own lateness. In such an apology, the cause can stand in the te-form directly before すみません. 済みません is a dictionary spelling of the phrase; normally すみません is written in kana.

examples[].german: That woman is a doctor.
A girl is singing.
en.notes: 女 on its own can sound abrupt when referring to a stranger. 女の人 is often more polite in everyday speech, and 女性 is common in neutral texts. 女の子 means a girl; 女 is not a polite form of address.

examples[].german: Please wait here.
I'm waiting for the bus.
en.notes: What or whom you wait for takes を: バスを待つ. A waiting place is marked with で. The て-form is 待って; ～待ってください is a request, and ～待っています describes ongoing waiting.

examples[].german: A coffee, please.
I said "please" to the shop assistant.
Please take care of this work.
en.notes: お願いします politely asks for something or asks someone to take on a task. The thing requested can come before it with を: コーヒーをお願いします "a coffee, please", この仕事をお願いします "please take care of this work". The phrase can stand alone when it is clear what is meant. It makes a request of others and is not a general reply to thanks.

examples[].german: Itadakimasu! (Phrase said before eating.)
Before the meal, one says "Itadakimasu".
Even when I eat alone, I say "Itadakimasu".
en.notes: いただきます is said by the person who is about to eat, as an expression of thanks before the meal. It is therefore not a wish of "Enjoy your meal" to someone else. The phrase can also be used when eating alone. After the meal, ごちそうさまでした is usually said; the two phrases play different roles in time. 戴きます is listed in dictionaries only as a search spelling of this meal phrase. For your own writing, use いただきます.

examples[].german: Thank you for the meal. It was delicious.
When I left the restaurant, I said to the staff: "Thank you for the meal".
en.notes: ごちそうさまでした is the fixed expression of thanks after a meal. It can be addressed to the person who cooked or invited, but it is also said without direct address. Before eating, いただきます is used. The form with でした looks back on the finished meal. ご馳走様でした is another spelling with the reading ごちそうさまでした. The phrase is usually written in kana.

examples[].german: Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka.
At the beginning of the e-mail I wrote: "Nice to meet you".
en.notes: 初めまして is said when meeting for the first time, often before stating one's own name. The phrase can also open a first message to a previously unknown person. It does not fit again when meeting a second time. The common kana form はじめまして has the same reading. Although the ending looks like a て-form, it is learned as a fixed greeting. 始めまして is also recorded as a spelling of the greeting; はじめまして is commonly written.

examples[].german: I'm back!
When I returned to the office, I said to a colleague: "I'm back."
en.notes: ただいま accompanies a return, usually coming home: "I'm back!" Others often reply with おかえり or おかえりなさい. Among familiar colleagues it can also be said when returning to the office; a formal report would be something like ただいま戻りました. The spelling ただ今 has the same reading here. Temporal meanings such as "right now" belong to a different use from the greeting of this card.

examples[].german: Welcome back. Thank you for your hard work.
When the family comes home, one says "Welcome back".
en.notes: おかえりなさい greets a person who is coming back home. The reply to ただいま is often this phrase or the shorter おかえり. なさい is learned here as part of the greeting: the phrase does not tell the arriving person to leave again or to come home first.

examples[].german: Class begins.
The movie starts at eight o'clock.
en.notes: 始まる is intransitive: an event begins, as in 授業が始まる. To actively begin something, use the transitive 始める with を: 授業を始める. Despite the ending る, 始まる is a Godan verb; the て-form is 始まって.

examples[].german: The movie is over.
Class ends at three o'clock.
en.notes: 終わる here describes an event or activity ending. The ending event takes が or, as the topic, は. 終わりました reports that the end has occurred, while 終わります can state a scheduled end time. The て-form of this Godan verb is 終わって.

en.meaning: to memorize; to learn; to remember
examples[].german: I learn kanji.
I remembered my friend's name.
en.notes: 覚える here means to take something into memory or to commit it to memory. The content learned takes を. 覚えました says that one has learned it; 覚えています means, in the right context, "I remember" or "I have it in memory". It is an Ichidan verb: 覚えて, 覚えない.

examples[].german: Please stand up.
I stand in front of everyone.
en.notes: 立つ means "to stand up" or "to stand". For an existing position, 立っています is often used; the spot takes に. The て-form is 立って. For "to set up someone or something", the transitive 立てる is used.

examples[].german: I forgot the name.
I left my umbrella on the train.
en.notes: 忘れる can mean to forget a memory or to accidentally leave an object behind. Both take を as the object. For an object left behind, に names the place: 電車に忘れる. This is not automatically the same as losing, for which, for example, なくす is used. The て-form is 忘れて.

en.meaning: to become; to be useful (ためになる)
examples[].german: I want to become a doctor.
It has become cold.
This book is useful for studying Japanese.
en.notes: なる here means to become or to take on a state. After nouns and な-adjectives, に is used: 医者になる, 静かになる. An い-adjective takes く: 寒くなる. なる is intransitive and a Godan verb; なって is the て-form. The identically read 鳴る, by contrast, means to sound. The phrase ためになる means to be useful or to benefit someone, as in 日本語の勉強のためになる. The rare kanji spelling 為る is also recorded for this verb; normally it is written なる. 為る can be read する for another verb, while this card specifically practices なる.

examples[].german: Please lend me a book.
I lent a book to my friend.
en.notes: 貸す means to lend something to someone, from the lender's point of view. The object takes を, the recipient に: 友達に本を貸す. 借りる describes the same lending situation from the borrower's point of view. 貸してください therefore asks to be given something to use. The て-form is 貸して.

examples[].german: I borrow a book at the library.
I borrowed an umbrella from a friend.
en.notes: 借りる means to borrow something, from the borrower's point of view. を marks the object, から or に the person one gets it from. 図書館で, by contrast, names the place of borrowing. Despite りる, it is an Ichidan verb: 借りて, 借りない. The counterpart for the lender is 貸す.

examples[].german: Please wash your hands.
After eating, I wash the dishes.
en.notes: 洗う means to wash or clean something with water. The thing being washed takes を: 手を洗う or お皿を洗う. It applies both to personal hygiene and to objects. As a godan verb ending in う, it forms 洗って and 洗わない; *洗うて is not a standard form.

en.meaning: to put on; to wear (upper-body clothing)
examples[].german: I put on a coat.
I am wearing a white shirt.
en.notes: 着る is used for clothing worn from the shoulders down, such as a shirt, coat or dress. 着ます can refer to the act of putting on; 着ています describes wearing as a state. For shoes and trousers one uses 履く, for hats かぶる. 着る is an ichidan verb with the te-form 着て; 切る, which is read the same, is a different verb.

examples[].german: Please take off your shoes.
Because it was hot, I took off my coat.
en.notes: 脱ぐ means to take off clothing or shoes. Unlike putting on, where different verbs are used depending on the item, the same verb works for both coats and shoes here. The item taken off takes を. This godan verb ending in ぐ forms 脱いで and 脱いだ, that is nuide and nuida, not *nugite.

en.meaning: to put on (glasses); to make (a phone call)
examples[].german: I make a phone call.
I am wearing glasses.
en.notes: かける has many meanings; on this card the fixed collocation decides. 電話をかける means to make a phone call, メガネをかける to put on glasses. メガネをかけています means to be wearing glasses. For a phone call, に can name the person called: 友達に電話をかける. Both uses are transitive and ichidan: かけて.

examples[].german: The wind is blowing.
I blew a whistle.
en.notes: With 風が, 吹く describes the wind blowing. With a wind instrument and を, it means to play it or blow into it: 笛を吹く. Depending on the chosen meaning, the verb is intransitive or transitive. The te-form of this godan verb ending in く is 吹いて, not *吹って.

examples[].german: Please sit on the chair.
My father is sitting by the window.
en.notes: 座る means "to sit down"; 座っています describes sitting as a state. The seat or place to sit takes に: 椅子に座る. Despite -る, it is a godan verb, hence 座って and 座ります.

examples[].german: A bird is flying.
I will fly to Tokyo by plane.
en.notes: Here 飛ぶ means to fly. The flying creature takes が, a travel destination takes に. 飛行機で names the means of transport. As a godan verb ending in ぶ, it forms 飛んで and 飛んだ. The other possible meaning, to jump, is not taught here as the same movement.

examples[].german: I climb the mountain.
I climbed the stairs.
en.notes: 登る means to climb up or ascend, especially a mountain. 山に names the goal of the climb; 階段を the route traversed. This を does not make the verb transitive. 登る is godan and forms 登って. 上る is also read のぼる, but 登る particularly emphasizes climbing.

en.meaning: to stop; to come to a halt; to perch (留まる)
examples[].german: The bus stopped.
The clock stopped.
A small bird is perched on a branch of a tree in the garden.
en.notes: 止まる（とまる）describes a movement or operation coming to a standstill; the vehicle or device affected takes が. For a bird that settles on a branch and sits there, 留まる can also be written. The perch takes に. This intransitive godan verb forms とまります and とまって. 留まる with the longer reading とどまる means to remain; 泊まる（とまる）means to stay overnight.

examples[].german: I will stay at a hotel.
I stayed at a friend's house.
en.notes: 泊まる means to stay overnight or to stay temporarily in lodgings. The place of stay takes に: ホテルに泊まる, 友達の家に泊まる. 一泊（いっぱく）counts one overnight stay. 泊まる is godan and forms 泊まって; 止まる, which sounds the same, means to stop.

examples[].german: I pay.
I paid by card.
en.notes: Here 払う means to pay. The amount or bill takes を; the method of payment takes で, as in カードで払う. お金を払う does not yet specify whether one pays in cash or by card. This godan verb ending in う forms 払って and 払わない; other meanings such as brushing off dust do not belong to this card.

en.meaning: to send; to see off, to accompany
examples[].german: I send a letter.
I accompany my friend to the station.
en.notes: 送る means to send when something is dispatched: 手紙を送る. With a person as the object it can also mean to see off or accompany, as in 友達を駅まで送る. を marks the object sent or the person accompanied, and まで marks the end point of the accompanying. For the recipient of a letter, に is used. This godan verb forms 送って.

examples[].german: The package has arrived.
A letter will arrive tomorrow.
en.notes: Intransitive verb: the item that arrives takes ga. Todokimashita describes an arrival that has already happened. The destination can be added with に: 家に届く. By contrast, 届ける is transitive and means actively delivering something, with を. 届く is a Godan verb: 届いて.

examples[].german: I go up to the second floor (the first floor above ground level, counting the Japanese way).
The temperature has risen.
en.notes: 上がる describes someone going up or a value rising: 二階に上がる, 温度が上がる. In these meanings it is intransitive; the thing that rises takes が, and a spatial destination takes に. "To raise something" is 上げる instead. Despite the ending る, 上がる is a godan verb: 上がります, 上がって. The dictionary spelling 上る for あがる is marked as irregular okurigana. Normally write this reading as 上がる; 上る with the reading のぼる can denote a different verb.

en.meaning: to fall, to go down; to step back
examples[].german: The temperature has dropped.
The price has gone down.
Please step back a little.
en.notes: 下がる describes a value falling: 温度が下がる, 値段が下がる. It can also mean "to step back", as in 少し後ろに下がる. The verb is intransitive: the price drops without a direct object being named. "To lower something" is 下げる. The godan forms are 下がります and 下がって. The dictionary spelling 下る for さがる has irregular okurigana; normally write this reading as 下がる. 下る can denote a different verb with other readings.

en.meaning: to put; to place; to leave behind
examples[].german: Please put it on the desk.
Please put it on the table.
I left my luggage at home and went out.
en.notes: 置く means "to put down, to set" or "to leave behind". The object takes を, the place where it is put takes に: 本を机に置く. The word does not specify whether something lies or stands; the object determines that. The te-form is 置いて. The auxiliary-verb construction ～ておく, for preparation, is a different use.

en.meaning: to sleep; to go to bed
examples[].german: I go to bed at eleven o'clock.
The baby is already asleep.
en.notes: 寝る can mean "to sleep" or "to go to bed". A clock time with に often indicates bedtime: 十一時に寝る. 寝ています means "is sleeping" in the right context. The ichidan forms are 寝ます and 寝て.

en.meaning: to take; to pick up; to remove
examples[].german: I take a pen.
Please take the book from the shelf.
I remove the lint from my clothes.
en.notes: 取る is a transitive verb meaning "to take, to pick up"; the object takes を. A source can be marked with から: 棚から本を取る. 服についたごみを取る, on the other hand, means "to remove dirt that is stuck on". The te-form is 取って. For taking photographs one usually writes 写真を撮る, not 写真を取る.

examples[].german: Please choose the one you like.
Please choose the color you like.
I chose a cheap hotel and made a reservation.
en.notes: 選ぶ means "to choose from several possibilities". The thing chosen takes を; the set of options can take から, as in 三つから一つ選ぶ. A decision can be based on preferences or on a criterion such as price. This godan verb forms 選びます and 選んで, not 選ぶて.

en.meaning: to line up; to stand in a row
examples[].german: Please line up here.
Everyone is standing in line, waiting.
Small shops line this street.
en.notes: 並ぶ describes people or things standing in a row. For people it can mean "to queue up"; 店が並んでいる describes a row of shops. The verb is intransitive: 店が並ぶ. When someone actively lines objects up, 並べる with を is used. The te-form of 並ぶ is 並んで.

en.meaning: to be in trouble; to be troubled
examples[].german: I'm in trouble.
I got lost and was in trouble.
It is a problem for me if you park a car here.
en.notes: 困る describes being at a loss, having difficulties, or being affected by something. 道に迷って困る gives the cause with the te-form. ここに車を止めると困ります can be a polite way to point out that parking causes a problem. 困りました can also express a problem that has just arisen and still persists.

examples[].german: That is wrong.
This answer is wrong.
This bag is a different color from my bag.
en.notes: 違う is a verb meaning "to be different, to differ" and "to be incorrect". この答えは違います judges an answer as wrong. For a comparison と is often used: 私のかばんと違う "different from my bag". The polite form is 違います, the negative 違いません or 違わない; the word is not a na-adjective.

examples[].german: A passport is necessary.
Time is needed.
I put the things I need into my bag.
en.notes: 必要 is a na-adjective: 必要な物 means "needed things". In ～が必要です it is said that something is necessary, such as a passport or time. The negative is 必要ではありません or 必要じゃありません. 必要 denotes a requirement; it does not express that someone merely wants something.

examples[].german: I have been to various countries.
There are all kinds of shops.
I thought about this problem in many ways.
en.notes: 色々 expresses variety, not just a large number of identical things. Before a noun, な usually follows: 色々な国 "various countries". As an adverb, 色々考える or 色々と考える can mean "to think about something in many ways". The mark 々 indicates repetition of 色; the kana spelling いろいろ is also common.

examples[].german: It is the same school.
It's the same as my bag, isn't it?
en.notes: 同じ means "the same". Before a noun it normally appears without な: 同じ学校 "the same school". As a predicate it is 同じです; the thing compared can take と, as in 私のかばんと同じ. Whether the very same item or an identical model is meant depends on the context.

examples[].german: Please wait a moment.
It is a little cold today.
"Will you come tomorrow?" "Tomorrow is a bit difficult ..."
en.notes: Before an adjective, ちょっと means "a little"; in a request it can mean "briefly, for a moment". 明日はちょっと…… can be a reserved refusal: the difficulty is left unsaid. The context decides whether a small amount, a short duration, or a politely hinted problem is meant. The rare kanji spelling 一寸 can be read ちょっと. As a unit of length, however, it is read いっすん; normally write the adverb as ちょっと.

en.meaning: to get up; to wake up
examples[].german: I get up at six every morning.
The baby is still awake.
en.notes: 起きる refers to waking up or getting up. 起きています can mean "to be awake", while 立っています describes physically standing. The clock time takes に. This ichidan verb forms 起きます and 起きて.

examples[].german: Please go straight ahead.
Go straight and turn right.
I sit with my back straight.
en.notes: まっすぐ means "straight, straight ahead, upright" in a spatial sense. まっすぐ行く is a direction; まっすぐにする means "to make straight". The word can be used before a verb or with に. The small っ is pronounced as a double s: massugu. Physical straightness should be distinguished from a moral judgment.

examples[].german: Please speak slowly.
I walk slowly.
Today I will rest at home in peace.
en.notes: ゆっくり describes a slow, unhurried pace or resting at ease. It comes before the verb: ゆっくり話す, ゆっくり休む. In these combinations the particle と can be added: ゆっくりと休む. ゆっくりと is thus the same adverbial use with と; the meaning does not become a new word.

examples[].german: It gets gradually warmer.
I have gradually come to understand Japanese.
en.notes: だんだん describes a step-by-step change, for example in the weather or in acquiring a skill. With なる, a state comes about gradually: 暖かくなる, 分かるようになる. The change can also be a decrease, as in だんだん寒くなる. と can often follow; だんだん alone is also complete.

examples[].german: Please eat more.
Please speak louder.
en.notes: もっと means "more" or "even more strongly" than before. In もっと食べる it is about the amount of food; もっと大きい声で話す asks for a higher volume. The point of comparison can be left unspoken when it is clear from the conversation. The word denotes an increase, not a mere repetition of the same action.

examples[].german: I came to Japan for the first time.
I saw Mount Fuji for the first time.
My first trip was fun.
en.notes: 初めて means that one experiences or does something for the first time. Before a noun, の follows: 初めての旅行 "the first trip". Here the word describes not a mere order among several activities but a first experience. The similar-sounding 始めて is a form of 始める "to begin" and is written differently.

examples[].german: I like this the most.
This restaurant is the most delicious.
I came first in the test.
en.notes: 一番 stands before a quality for "most, -est": 一番好き "like best", 一番おいしい "most delicious". It can also denote first place or number one. 一番になる means "to take first place". What is being compared must be clear from the sentence or the conversation.

examples[].german: It will probably rain.
It will probably rain tomorrow.
Mr./Ms. Tanaka is probably at home.
en.notes: 多分 marks a conjecture, not a certain fact. It can introduce a prediction or an assessment of a present situation. でしょう often appears at the end of the sentence, but it is not required. As "probably, perhaps", 多分 describes the certainty of a statement; here it is not a quantity word meaning "much".

examples[].german: It is really delicious.
This movie is really interesting.
Are you really coming tomorrow?
en.notes: 本当に means "really, truly". It can intensify an evaluation, as in 本当においしい, or check whether a statement actually holds: 本当に明日来ますか. The combination is pronounced hontō ni with a long ō. A follow-up question with it can signal surprise or doubt; tone and context decide.

examples[].german: I understood it on the whole.
It's about a thousand yen.
en.notes: 大体 can express an approximate quantity or a general overview; before a number it means "about". 大体分かりました means "I understood it on the whole", not necessarily completely and in every detail. 大体千円 is an approximate price. The informal spelling だいたい is also common.

en.meaning: quite; fine, sufficient; no, thank you
examples[].german: That's fine, thank you.
That's fine, thank you very much.
This amount is enough.
This book is quite interesting.
"Would you like some tea?" "No, thank you."
en.notes: Before an adjective, 結構 means "quite", as in 結構おもしろい. この量で結構です confirms that an amount is sufficient. As a reply to an offer, however, いいえ、結構です can mean "no, thank you". A bare 結構です therefore depends on the context; a clear refusal additionally says いいえ or explains that one needs nothing more.

examples[].german: I work at a bank.
I work eight hours a day.
en.notes: 働く here means to do a job. The workplace is attached with で: 銀行で働く. Regular professional activity is often described with 働いています. A work duration can be given with ～時間.

examples[].german: Of course I'll go.
Of course I'll go!
"May I eat in this room?" "Of course."
en.notes: もちろん marks something as self-evident or gives a firm yes. もちろん行きます is a confident commitment; as an answer to a question about permission, もちろんです can be used. Unlike 多分, the word does not express a mere conjecture. It can answer on its own when the intended statement is clear from the question.

examples[].german: Would you like sugar?
Do you take sugar in your coffee?
I use a hundred grams of sugar for this cake.
en.notes: 砂糖 is sugar as an ingredient or sweetener. "To put sugar in coffee" is コーヒーに砂糖を入れる: を marks the sugar, に the drink. The amount can be given with グラム. The word itself denotes the substance; the quality "sweet" is 甘い.

examples[].german: Please pass the salt.
Please add a little more salt.
en.notes: 塩 is salt as a substance or seasoning. 塩を取ってください is a request at the table to pass the salt; 塩を入れる means "to add salt". もう少し塩を入れる means "to add a little more salt". For "salty" one uses an adjective such as しょっぱい or 塩辛い; 塩 itself is a noun.

examples[].german: I put soy sauce on it.
This soy sauce is a bit sweet.
en.notes: 醤油 is soy sauce. 醤油をかける means to pour soy sauce over something; かける here means neither to make a phone call nor to put on glasses. The food it is poured on can take に. The full reading is しょうゆ with a long o, that is shōyu. 醬油 is a rare kanji spelling of 醤油; the reading remains しょうゆ.

examples[].german: I add a little miso and make miso soup.
The miso is in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 味噌 is miso, the fermented seasoning paste, often made from soybeans. It is an ingredient; 味噌汁, by contrast, is the miso soup made from it. 味噌を入れる describes adding the paste. The card deals with the food, not the colloquial meaning "the key point".

examples[].german: I take a bento with me.
I eat my bento.
en.notes: お弁当 is a meal packed in a box to take along. The usual お is part of the polite full form taught here and can also be used for one's own bento. 持っていく means to take something to another place; 食べる refers to the contents, not the box.

examples[].german: I bought some sweets.
I gave the children some sweets.
en.notes: お菓子 means sweets and sweet baked goods, for example candy or cake. It need not refer to one particular kind or number of pieces. The polite お is often used in everyday speech even for one's own sweets. When giving, the gift takes を and the recipient takes に.

examples[].german: One apple, please.
I eat an apple for breakfast.
en.notes: Here りんご means the apple as a fruit. The word is usually written in kana; 林檎 is the corresponding kanji spelling. For whole apples the general counter つ can be used: 一つ, 三つ. An apple at breakfast is expressed with 朝ご飯に as part of the meal.

examples[].german: I like mandarin oranges.
I peel a mandarin orange and eat it.
en.notes: みかん is a mandarin orange, in everyday Japanese especially the satsuma mandarin. The word is often written in hiragana; the kanji are 蜜柑. 皮をむく means to remove the peel. 未完 and 未刊, which are read the same, mean unfinished and unpublished respectively.

examples[].german: I drink coffee.
The coffee at this cafe is delicious.
en.notes: コーヒー means coffee. The two ー marks here indicate a long o and a long i: kōhī. コーヒーを飲む describes drinking; 店のコーヒー can refer to the coffee served at a particular cafe. The noun needs no special plural form for several servings. 珈琲 is a kanji spelling of コーヒー marked as ateji. The katakana form コーヒー is the usual one; the reading remains kōhī.

examples[].german: I'm tired, so I'll rest for a bit.
I'll be absent from school on Monday.
en.notes: 休む can express a rest break or staying away from work or class. What is missed takes を: 学校を休む. Therefore 学校を休みます means "I don't go to school", not "I rest at school".

examples[].german: Would you like some juice?
An orange juice, please.
en.notes: Here ジュース means juice. A flavor can come directly before it, as in オレンジジュース. In everyday speech the word can also refer to sweet fruit drinks; it does not by itself guarantee any particular fruit content. The small ュ forms one syllable together with ジ, and ー lengthens u: jūsu.

examples[].german: Do you drink alcohol?
I don't drink alcohol.
en.notes: お酒 refers to alcoholic drinks in general and, depending on the context, can mean sake specifically. The お is an ordinary polite prefix and does not oblige you to speak only of another person's drink. お酒は飲みません is a natural way to say that you do not drink alcohol.

examples[].german: One beer, please.
This beer is cold.
en.notes: ビール means beer. 一杯（いっぱい）counts a filled drinking vessel or one serving here and is read ippai. For an order, をください is used; for an evaluation of temperature, は冷たいです. The long i in ビール is written bīru.

examples[].german: I wash the plates.
Two plates, please.
en.notes: お皿 is a plate or dish for food. The polite prefix お is common in everyday speech. Flat plates are counted with 枚: 二枚（にまい）. お皿を洗う means to wash the dishes; the card names the tableware and not automatically the food on it.

examples[].german: I pour water into the glass.
This glass is broken.
en.notes: コップ is a drinking glass or a simple drinking cup. In コップに水を入れる, に is the container and を the contents poured in. コップは割れています, on the other hand, describes a glass that is already broken as a state. The small ッ doubles the p: koppu.

examples[].german: Can you use chopsticks?
Please show me how to use chopsticks.
en.notes: 箸（はし）are chopsticks for eating. 箸を使う means to use chopsticks; 箸の使い方 is the way of using them. A pair is counted with 一膳（いちぜん）. 橋, which is read the same, means bridge and has a different meaning; the kanji spelling prevents confusion here.

examples[].german: A spoon, please.
I eat soup with a spoon.
en.notes: スプーン means spoon. You ask for a spoon with スプーンをください. As an eating tool it takes で: スプーンで食べる. The long u is written supūn; the fishing lure that can also be called a spoon does not belong to the cutlery on this card.

examples[].german: I use a fork.
The fork is in the drawer.
en.notes: Here フォーク means the fork as cutlery. フォークを使う describes using it, フォークで食べる eating with it. The long o is written fōku. The same katakana word for folk music or a baseball pitch is not meant on this card.

examples[].german: I cut it with a knife.
Please wash the knife.
en.notes: ナイフ is a knife, for example for eating or cutting. As a cutting tool it takes で, while the thing cut takes を: ナイフで肉を切る. ナイフを洗う, on the other hand, treats the knife itself as the object. The reading naifu has no long ai.

examples[].german: The refrigerator is in the kitchen.
Please put the milk in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 冷蔵庫 is a refrigerator. For its location, に is used with ある; for something put into it, に is likewise used with 入れる. The food itself can be the topic with は or the object with を. ぞう has a long o, so reizōko; れい remains rei in Modified Hepburn.

en.meaning: to teach; to tell; to explain
examples[].german: I teach English.
Please tell me the way to the station.
en.notes: 教える means not only "to teach" but also "to tell or show someone something". The person addressed takes に, and the content conveyed takes を: 人に英語を教える. 道を教えてください is a request for directions.

examples[].german: The washing machine has broken down.
I wash the clothes in the washing machine.
en.notes: 洗濯機 means a washing machine for clothes. With で it is named as the appliance used: 洗濯機で服を洗う. As an appliance that breaks down, it takes が with こわれる. The card reading is せんたくき; the accent of the whole word is not composed from 洗濯 and 機.

examples[].german: I clean the room.
After cleaning, I open the window.
en.notes: 掃除 is cleaning, for example of a room. With する it becomes the activity: 掃除をする or 掃除する. 部屋の掃除 names the cleaning of the room; 掃除の後 is the time after cleaning. The card remains a noun, even though it can be used as a する expression.

examples[].german: I do the laundry.
When the laundry is done, I hang the clothes up to dry.
en.notes: 洗濯 is the washing of clothes, or laundry as a chore. 洗濯をする means to do laundry; 洗濯が終わる reports the end of this process. Hanging the clothes up afterwards is 服を干す. 選択, which is read the same, means selection and is a different word.

examples[].german: I'm going shopping.
Before shopping, I write down what I need.
en.notes: 買い物 is shopping and can also mean the goods bought. 買い物に行く names shopping as the purpose of going; 買い物をする is the activity itself. A shopping list can be made before the purchase. The word is not a freely conjugating verb ending in もの.

examples[].german: Let's have a meal.
It is mealtime.
en.notes: 食事 denotes a meal or the act of having a meal. 食事をする means to eat, and 食事の時間 means mealtime. The invitation 食事をしましょう is polite and consists of する with the ending ましょう. Diet as a lasting regimen is another meaning and is not meant here.

examples[].german: I like sports.
On weekends I play sports in the park.
en.notes: スポーツ means sports in general. With が好き one expresses interest or preference, without specifying whether one plays or watches. スポーツをする means to play sports; で names the place. The long o is written supōtsu and is not pronounced as an additional syllable.

examples[].german: I play soccer.
I watched a soccer match.
en.notes: サッカー means soccer. サッカーをする means to play soccer oneself; サッカーの試合を見る means to watch a match. The small ッ doubles k and ー lengthens a: sakkā. Names or textile terms with the same spelling do not belong to this sport.

examples[].german: He/She is good at tennis.
Have you ever played tennis?
en.notes: テニス means tennis. テニスが上手です evaluates skill at playing; テニスをする means to play. ～したことがありますか, on the other hand, asks whether someone has ever had the experience, without claiming good performance. 上手 is read じょうず here, that is jōzu.

examples[].german: I watch baseball.
Baseball is popular in Japan.
en.notes: 野球 is baseball as a sport. 野球をする means "to play baseball", 野球を見る "to watch baseball". A single game can be called 野球の試合. The long ū belongs to the reading やきゅう; the spelling consists of 野 and 球.

examples[].german: I'm going to watch a game.
Today's game was interesting.
I will take part in tomorrow's match.
en.notes: 試合 is a sports game or a contest between opponents. 試合を見る means "to watch a game", 試合に出る "to take part in a contest". A game for entertainment can be called ゲーム; 試合 emphasizes competition. The noun can also be combined with する, but is learned here as a noun.

examples[].german: I'm taking piano lessons.
I learned how to write kanji from a teacher.
en.notes: 習う emphasizes learning through lessons or instruction, for example in music or a language. The subject learned takes を, and the teacher takes に or から. For general learning or studying on your own, 勉強する is often used.

examples[].german: Let's play a game.
I played a game with the child.
The rules of this game are simple.
en.notes: ゲーム is a game and is often used with する: ゲームをする. Depending on the context it can mean a board game, a video game or another rule-based game. ゲームのルール are the rules of the game. The long ē in gēmu corresponds to the length mark ー.

examples[].german: I play the piano.
Can you play the piano?
The piano is big, so it won't fit in the room.
en.notes: ピアノ means the piano as an instrument here. It is played with 弾く: ピアノを弾く. The construction ～ことができる asks about an ability. With ピアノが大きい, on the other hand, the size of the instrument can be described. The musical direction "softly" is a different use of the identically written word.

examples[].german: I am playing the guitar.
I like playing the guitar.
I borrowed a guitar from a friend.
en.notes: ギター is a guitar. For playing it, 弾く is used: ギターを弾く, with the te-form 弾いて. ギターを借りる means "to borrow a guitar"; the person you borrow it from takes に. The long ā at the end is written with ー.

examples[].german: I draw a picture.
Who painted this picture?
I hung a picture on the wall.
en.notes: 絵 is a picture, drawing or painting. 絵を描く means "to draw or paint a picture"; the verb is read かく in both cases. A photograph is normally 写真. A physical 絵 can be looked at, hung up or drawn; the word does not distinguish between painting and drawing techniques.

examples[].german: She dances well.
I saw a Japanese dance.
en.notes: 踊り is the noun "dance"; the related verb is 踊る "to dance". 踊りが上手 describes a person's skill at dancing. 日本の踊り can mean a Japanese dance form or a corresponding performance. For one's own action, one says 踊る, not 踊りです.

examples[].german: I brush my teeth.
I brush my teeth every day.
My tooth hurts, so I am going to the dentist.
en.notes: 歯 means one tooth or several teeth; the number is clear from the context. 歯を磨く means "to brush one's teeth". For a toothache, 歯が痛い is used, with が marking the aching part of the body. 歯医者 is a dentist or a dental practice. The meaning practiced here is a person's teeth.

examples[].german: I got my hair cut.
I want to get my hair cut.
My younger sister has long hair.
en.notes: 髪 refers to the hair on the head. 髪を切る means "to cut one's hair" and in everyday speech can also describe a visit to the hairdresser, where one has it cut. 髪が長い describes long hair. For body hair or animal hair, 毛 is often used; the 髪 learned here is hair on the head.

examples[].german: I cut my finger.
I accidentally cut my finger.
I count with my fingers.
en.notes: 指 is a finger or toe. For a clear distinction one says 手の指 "finger" and 足の指 "toe". 指を切る in everyday use often means "to cut one's finger", not necessarily to cut it off. With 指で the finger can be named as a tool, for example when counting.

examples[].german: My younger brother has a small nose.
I breathe through my nose.
en.notes: 鼻 is the nose. 鼻が小さい describes its size; 鼻で息をする means "to breathe through the nose". The reading はな is also used for 花 "flower"; the spelling distinguishes the two words. The examples explicitly describe the body part and its function.

examples[].german: My neck hurts.
Because it is cold, I wrapped a scarf around my neck.
en.notes: 首 denotes the neck area as the connection between head and body. 首が痛い can mean "my neck hurts" or "my throat area hurts", depending on the spot. For pain in the throat, のど is often used instead. 首にマフラーを巻く means "to wrap a scarf around one's neck".

examples[].german: I use a computer.
I spent a lot of money on the trip.
en.notes: 使う refers to using a tool or means. With money, お金を使う means "to spend money", and with time, 時間を使う means "to spend time". What is used or consumed takes を; the て-form is 使って.

examples[].german: My shoulder hurts.
My shoulders are stiff.
I hang my bag over my shoulder.
en.notes: 肩 is a shoulder or the shoulder area. 肩が痛い describes pain, 肩がこる describes stiffness. Both are expressed in Japanese with が on the body part. A bag is carried over the shoulder, for example, with かばんを肩にかける; に then marks the place where it hangs.

examples[].german: My arm hurts.
Are you wearing a wristwatch?
Please raise your arm.
en.notes: 腕 is the arm. 腕が痛い describes arm pain; 腕を上げる means "to raise one's arm". In 腕時計 "wristwatch", 腕 is a component of a compound word of its own. Its pronunciation and accent must be learned separately; the accent given here belongs to the full word 腕.

examples[].german: My knee hurts.
My knee hurts and I can't run.
There is a cat on my lap.
en.notes: 膝 is the knee; when sitting it can also mean the lap. 膝が痛い means "my knee hurts". 猫が膝の上にいる describes a cat on the lap, not necessarily on a single knee joint. The reading is ひざ; how many knees are meant becomes clear from the context.

examples[].german: I caught a cold.
My cold has gone, so I am going to school.
en.notes: 風邪 is a cold. The fixed phrase 風邪をひく means "to catch a cold"; 風邪が治る means "the cold goes away". The spelling distinguishes 風邪 from 風 "wind", although both are read かぜ. The examples use 風邪 in the everyday sense of "cold".

examples[].german: I have a fever.
I have a fever, so I am going to the hospital.
The heat of the stove makes the room warm.
en.notes: 熱 is fever, or warmth and heat. In a conversation about the body, 熱がある usually means "to have a fever". ストーブの熱, on the other hand, means the warmth of a stove. The word is a noun; "hot" as a property of an object is 熱い, which has a different form.

examples[].german: My head hurts.
My stomach hurts.
If it hurts, please raise your hand.
en.notes: 痛い is an i-adjective for pain. The aching part of the body takes が: 頭が痛い, お腹が痛い. Without a named body part, 痛い can also mean "that hurts". The negative is 痛くない, the past tense 痛かった. "To be in pain" is therefore not expressed with 痛いをする.

examples[].german: I am very sleepy.
I couldn't sleep well yesterday, so I am sleepy.
Because I am sleepy, I will go to bed early today.
en.notes: 眠い means "sleepy", that is, wanting to sleep. It is not the same as 疲れた "exhausted, tired", although both can apply at once. This i-adjective forms 眠くない and 眠かった. 眠くなる means "to become sleepy"; 眠いので gives sleepiness as the reason for a further action.

examples[].german: I am happy to have received a present.
I am glad to see you again.
en.notes: 嬉しい describes personal joy about something, such as a present or a reunion. A cause can be given with the te-form: もらって嬉しい, 会えて嬉しい. It is an i-adjective with the forms 嬉しかった and 嬉しくない. 楽しい, on the other hand, often describes an activity or experience being fun.

examples[].german: I was sad after watching the movie.
My friend moved away and I am sad.
This is a sad story.
en.notes: 悲しい can describe one's own feeling of being sad or the sad content of a story. 映画を見て悲しかった means here that the person was sad after the movie; 悲しい話 judges the story itself. This i-adjective forms 悲しかった in the past tense and 悲しくない in the negative.

examples[].german: I feel lonely being alone.
My friend went back to his/her home country, and I have become lonely.
There are few people on this road; it feels deserted.
en.notes: 寂しい describes loneliness or a lack of closeness to other people. For a place it can also mean "deserted, sparsely populated". 寂しくなる means "to become lonely"; the i-ending changes to く before なる. Sadness and loneliness can occur together, but here 寂しい emphasizes the absence of company or of life in a place.

examples[].german: The child is playing in the park.
I have three children.
en.notes: Can refer to one child or several; the number is clear from context. 子供がいる means, depending on context, that children are present or that someone has children. 子ども is a common alternative spelling. Adult offspring can also be called 子供.

examples[].german: I make a cake.
I made a small box out of paper.
This company builds ships.
en.notes: 作る emphasizes that something comes into being or is prepared, such as an object or food. The result takes を, the material takes で: 紙で箱を作る. The general する, by contrast, denotes an activity without necessarily producing something new. 造る is often used for building larger things or for industrial production, as in 船を造る ("to build ships"). The reading stays つくる.

examples[].german: That movie is scary.
That movie was scary.
I am afraid of dogs and can't go near them.
en.notes: 怖い describes something frightening or one's own fear of it. あの映画は怖い judges a movie as scary. 犬が怖い, on the other hand, can mean "I am afraid of dogs"; the frightening trigger takes が. This i-adjective forms 怖かった and 怖くない. It does not mean "bad" in general.

examples[].german: I am embarrassed that I made a mistake.
I am embarrassed to speak in front of everyone.
en.notes: 恥ずかしい describes embarrassment, shame or self-consciousness. After a mistake it can mean "I am embarrassed"; in front of many people it can express shyness about speaking. It is an i-adjective: 恥ずかしかった, 恥ずかしくない. A te-form like 間違えて can name the cause of the feeling.

examples[].german: The room next door is noisy.
How annoying! Be quiet for a bit.
en.notes: うるさい means "noisy, disturbing" and can also describe something annoying. In 隣の部屋がうるさい, it is about disturbing noise. Saying うるさい！ directly to a person can sound harsh and is meant to silence them. The examples distinguish a description from an irritated demand. A polite request would be something like 静かにしてください. 五月蝿い is a special spelling of うるさい marked as ateji. The usual kana form is easier to use; the reading is not built up from the individual kanji.

examples[].german: My hands are dirty.
The room is dirty, so I will clean it.
en.notes: 汚い is an い-adjective meaning dirty. It stands directly before a noun: 汚い手. As a polite statement it is 汚いです, and in the negative 汚くないです. With から, dirtiness can give the reason for cleaning afterwards. This card does not use it as an insulting judgment of a person.

examples[].german: Watch out! A car is coming.
This road is dangerous, so please be careful.
en.notes: 危ない means dangerous or risky. Exclaimed on its own, 危ない！ is also the warning "Watch out!"; this fixed warning function supplements the normal adjectival statement. This い-adjective forms 危なくない for "not dangerous". It refers to a concrete danger and is not a general translation of "difficult".

examples[].german: I want a new computer.
What do you want for your birthday?
en.notes: 欲しい is an い-adjective for the wish to have something. The desired object takes が, not を as with an ordinary purchase verb. In a statement one typically speaks of one's own wish; a question can ask about the other person's wish. For a desired action, the verb form ～たい is used instead.

examples[].german: Which is the correct answer?
Please write your name correctly.
en.notes: 正しい means correct or right. Directly before a noun it stays 正しい, as in 正しい答え. When the correct performance of an action is meant, it becomes 正しく: 正しく書く. The negative is 正しくない. The moral sense "just" is another meaning that is not taught here.

examples[].german: That's a rare flower, isn't it?
It is snowing today. That is unusual here.
en.notes: 珍しい means rare or unusual in the given context. It can describe a thing or evaluate an event that does not often occur in that place. It does not automatically mean "newly bought". As an い-adjective it stands directly before 花 and forms 珍しくない for "not unusual".

examples[].german: I am reading a thick book.
Because it is cold, I will wear a thick coat.
en.notes: 厚い describes the thickness of an object, for example a book or a coat. It is the counterpart of 薄い. For the width of a pen or a trunk, 太い is used instead. 暑い and 熱い, which are read the same, concern heat; they are not spelling variants of this thickness word.

examples[].german: I enter the room.
I joined the school tennis club.
en.notes: 入る means "to go in" and also "to join a group". The place entered or the group takes に: 部屋に入る, クラブに入る. Although the word ends in -いる, it is a godan verb: 入ります, 入って. For "to put something in", 入れる is used.

examples[].german: I use a thick pen.
This singer has a deep, full voice.
en.notes: 太い describes, for example, a thick pen or trunk, that is, a large cross-section. For a voice it can also mean deep and full: 声が太い. This second use is not a statement about the singer's physical thickness. As an い-adjective it forms 太く; for the thickness of a book or material, 厚い is usually used.

examples[].german: I walk along a narrow road.
I sew the button on with a thin thread.
en.notes: 細い means thin or narrow, as in a thread or a narrow path. It describes a small width or a small cross-section. A thin sheet of paper, on the other hand, is usually 薄い紙. As an い-adjective it stands directly before 糸 or 道 and forms 細く.

examples[].german: There are many young people.
The teacher is young and energetic.
en.notes: Here 若い refers to young age. It stands directly before 人 and is joined to another quality with ～くて: 若くて元気. The negative is 若くない. The word does not automatically mean immature; that judgment is a different, context-dependent use.

examples[].german: What time does class start?
What class do you have in the afternoon?
en.notes: 授業 means a class or a lesson. 何時から asks for its start time; 午後の授業 asks about the class in the afternoon. It denotes the event, whereas 教室 is the room. じゅぎょう has a long o at the end and is written jugyō.

examples[].german: I give a present.
I bought a birthday present.
en.notes: プレゼント is a present. When giving, it takes を with あげる; when receiving, for example, を with もらう. 誕生日のプレゼント means a present for a birthday. With する the word can also be used as "to give a present"; the card itself remains a noun.

examples[].german: I keep my promise.
I have an appointment with a friend.
en.notes: 約束 can be a promise or an appointment. 約束を守る means to keep a promise; 約束がある means to have a fixed appointment. と names the other person involved. The word alone does not say whether the appointment is romantic, friendly or business-related.

examples[].german: She has a warm heart.
I made up my mind about something important.
en.notes: 心（こころ）denotes inner feeling, the mind, or the heart in a figurative sense. 心が温かい describes warm-heartedness; 心に決める means to firmly resolve something inwardly. For the physical heart, 心臓 is common. The card uses こころ, not other 心 readings automatically taken from compounds.

examples[].german: It is a good memory.
I tell a friend about my memories of the trip.
en.notes: 思い出 is a memory of a past experience. A single pleasant memory can be いい思い出; one can tell about travel memories with 思い出を話す. The noun denotes the content of the memory. Actively recalling something, by contrast, is expressed with the verb 思い出す.

examples[].german: I want to travel all over the world.
There are various countries in the world.
en.notes: Here 世界 means the world in the geographical sense. 世界中（せかいじゅう）means the whole world or everywhere in the world; 中 is read じゅう there. In 世界には, に names the space in which countries exist. A field of expertise as a particular "world" is another use that these examples do not need.

en.meaning: to go out; to come out; to attend
examples[].german: I leave the house.
I'm attending Japanese class today.
en.notes: When leaving a place, 出る is used with を: 家を出る. It can also mean "to attend/be present"; then an event or class takes に: 授業に出る. This ichidan verb forms 出ます and 出て.

examples[].german: Please write the characters.
I can't read this character.
en.notes: 文字 is a written character, such as a letter or a kanji. It does not by itself mean a whole word. 文字を書く means to write characters, 文字が読めない means to be unable to read them. The reading of this card is もじ; other readings in technical terms are not equated with it.

examples[].german: I memorize kanji.
This kanji is difficult.
en.notes: 漢字 are the characters of Chinese origin used in Japanese. The word can refer to one character or several, with no special plural ending. 漢字を覚える means to memorize them; この漢字は難しい judges a specific character as difficult. A character and its complete word are not automatically the same thing.

examples[].german: Can you write hiragana?
Please write your name in hiragana.
en.notes: ひらがな is the Japanese kana script, used among other things for grammatical endings and particles. で is used for writing in this script: ひらがなで書く. ひらがなを書けますか asks about the ability to write the characters. The word itself is often written in hiragana.

examples[].german: Katakana is used for loanwords.
