I am studying katakana too.
en.notes: カタカナ is the Japanese kana script, used especially for loanwords. It is also used for other purposes such as emphasis; it therefore does not mean exclusively foreign names. カタカナを勉強する means to study the script. The a vowels in カ and ナ are short.

examples[].german: Please give me some paper.
Please write your name on the paper.
en.notes: 紙（かみ）means paper. A request for paper uses をください; the surface written on takes に: 紙に名前を書く. Sheets of paper are counted with 枚. 髪 for hair and 神 for a deity are different words that are read the same, not meanings of this paper card.

examples[].german: Please put it in the envelope.
I put a stamp on the envelope.
en.notes: 封筒 is an envelope. 封筒に入れる means to put something inside; 封筒に切手を貼る means to stick a stamp on its surface. に can therefore mean a target container or a place to stick; the verb decides. Both vowels in ふうとう are long: fūtō.

examples[].german: Please tell me your telephone number.
What is your room number?
en.notes: 番号 is a number or sequence of digits used for identification. 電話番号 means telephone number; 部屋の番号 the room number. 何番（なんばん）asks which number. It is about an identifier, not automatically the quantity of things present. The long o at the end is written bangō.

examples[].german: Please write your address.
I told my friend my new address.
en.notes: 住所 is the postal or physical address of a home or business. 住所を書く means to write it down, 住所を教える to tell it to someone. The person who learns it takes に. An e-mail address is normally called メールアドレス and is not designated by 住所 alone.

examples[].german: I take the subway.
I go to work by subway.
I lost my wallet on the subway.
en.notes: 地下鉄 is the subway. 地下鉄に乗る describes boarding or using a subway; 地下鉄で行く names it as the means of transport. に belongs to 乗る here, and で marks the means of travel. The word refers to the railway and its network, not merely to the underground space 地下.

examples[].german: Please cross the street at the traffic light.
The light is red, so please stop.
en.notes: Here 信号 means a traffic light. 信号が赤 is a red light; 信号のところで道を渡る means "to cross the street at the traffic light". The light serves as a landmark. The more precise 信号機 is also possible; the examples practice the everyday short form 信号.

examples[].german: I'm going out shopping.
I'm going out with friends.
en.notes: 出かける means to set off from home or one's previous location to do something. The purpose can take に: 買い物に出かける; a companion takes と. 出掛ける is another spelling of the same word.

examples[].german: I turn right at the intersection.
Please turn left at the next intersection.
There is a bank near the intersection.
en.notes: 交差点 is a road intersection. In directions, 交差点を右に曲がる can be used: を marks the point where the route changes direction. 交差点の近く, on the other hand, means the area around the intersection. The long ō in kōsaten belongs to the reading こうさてん.

examples[].german: Please turn at the corner.
Please turn at that corner.
I bumped my foot on the corner of the desk.
en.notes: Here 角 is read かど and means a corner or edge. In directions, 角を曲がる means "to turn at the corner". 机の角 is the corner of a desk. Other readings of 角, such as つの "horn" or かく in geometric words, do not belong to the reading かど practiced here.

examples[].german: I can see a large building.
What is that building?
en.notes: 建物 is a building as a structure, such as a house, a school or an office building. 建物が見える describes that a building is visible. あの建物は何ですか asks what a particular building is or what it is used for. The word is more general than a specific building type such as 学校 or 病院.

examples[].german: I'm going to the 3rd floor.
How many stories does this building have?
en.notes: 階 denotes a floor of a building and is used after numbers to count floors. In Japan 一階 is usually the ground floor; 三階 is therefore the floor two levels above it (the 3rd floor in the American sense). 三階 is read さんがい or さんかい, 何階 なんがい or なんかい. The question about a building's height is 何階建てですか. The accent of the single word 階 does not automatically apply to number combinations.

examples[].german: I take the elevator.
I take the elevator to the 5th floor.
The elevator is not working, so I will take the stairs.
en.notes: エレベーター is an elevator. エレベーターで行く names it as the means of reaching another floor; the destination takes に. エレベーターが動かない means "the elevator is not working". The two length marks in エレベーター are rendered as ē and ā.

examples[].german: You take off your shoes at the entrance.
Please take off your shoes in the entryway.
I am waiting for a friend in the entryway.
en.notes: 玄関 is the entrance area of a house or apartment. In many Japanese homes, shoes are taken off there. で is used for an action performed there: 玄関で靴を脱ぐ. For something located there, に is usually used, as in 玄関に靴がある. The word can mean more than just the front door.

examples[].german: I sleep in bed.
I bought a new bed.
en.notes: ベッド is a bed as a piece of furniture. ベッドで寝る means "to sleep in bed"; で marks the place of the sleeping. ベッドを買う means buying the bed itself. The small ッ produces the double d in beddo and is not pronounced as a separate syllable tsu.

examples[].german: I lay out the futon.
In Japan, some people sleep on a futon.
en.notes: 布団 is Japanese bedding, which can include a mattress pad and a quilt. 布団を敷く means "to lay out the futon, that is, the sleeping mat". 布団で寝る describes sleeping with or on it. In Japan, a futon is not necessarily a Western-style folding sofa bed; the examples refer to bedding.

examples[].german: I put the book on the shelf.
I lined up the books on the shelf.
I made a new shelf.
en.notes: 棚 is a shelf or a shelf board. 棚に本を置く means "to put books on the shelf"; 棚に本を並べる emphasizes lining them up neatly. For things on an upper surface, 棚の上 can be used. The word denotes the shelf, not automatically a closed cupboard.

examples[].german: Please look inside the drawer.
There is a pen in the drawer.
The drawer won't open.
en.notes: 引き出し is a drawer. 引き出しの中 means its inside; 引き出しが開かない means that it cannot be opened. The word is a complete noun. The identically written stem form of 引き出す belongs to a different grammatical use and does not provide the accent of the drawer.

examples[].german: I walk in the park.
I walk to the station.
en.notes: 歩く explicitly means "to go on foot", as opposed to running, 走る. A route traversed can take を: 公園を歩く. The destination or end of the route can be given with まで: 駅まで歩く.

examples[].german: Please press the button.
Please press this button.
I pushed the heavy box into the room.
en.notes: 押す means "to press" or "to push". ボタンを押す means "to press a button"; 箱を押す "to push a box". The thing moved or pressed takes を. This godan verb forms 押します and 押して. On a door, 押す can be the instruction "push"; the opposite is 引く "pull".

examples[].german: Please pull the door open.
Please draw a line with the ruler.
en.notes: Here 引く means "to pull", and in 線を引く "to draw a line". With a door, you pull it toward you; with a ruler, you draw a line. The object takes を, a tool such as 定規 takes で. The godan forms are 引きます and 引いて, with a long i in hiite.

examples[].german: I cut paper.
I cut the vegetables small.
I hung up the phone.
en.notes: 切る means "to cut", for example paper or vegetables. 電話を切る also means "to end the call, to hang up". The object takes を. It is a godan verb: 切ります, 切って. 着る "to put on", which is read the same, is by contrast an ichidan verb and has different forms.

examples[].german: I brush my teeth.
I brush my teeth and then go to bed.
Before going out, I polish my shoes.
en.notes: 磨く refers to cleaning or polishing by rubbing or brushing. 歯を磨く means "to brush one's teeth", 靴を磨く "to polish shoes until they shine". The object takes を. This godan verb forms 磨きます and 磨いて; with ～てから, the second action follows only after the brushing.

examples[].german: Please do not touch.
Please do not touch this painting.
The child touched snow for the first time.
en.notes: 触れる means "to touch" here. In the usual construction the thing touched takes に: 絵に触れる, 雪に触れる. The negative is 触れない; 触れないでください asks someone not to touch something. It is an Ichidan verb with 触れます and 触れて, not a Godan verb despite the ending る.

examples[].german: I throw the ball.
Please throw the ball.
Please do not throw trash into the river.
en.notes: 投げる means "to throw" or "to hurl". The thing thrown takes を; a destination can follow with に, as in 川にごみを投げる. It is an ichidan verb: 投げます, 投げて. A request is 投げてください, a prohibition 投げないでください. The examples practice literal throwing.

en.meaning: to catch; to stop (e.g. a taxi)
examples[].german: I caught an insect.
I caught a fish.
I caught a taxi in front of the station.
en.notes: 捕まえる means "to catch" and can also mean "to stop, to nab". 虫を捕まえる means catching an insect; タクシーを捕まえる means stopping or getting a taxi. The object takes を. It is an ichidan verb: 捕まえます, 捕まえて. 捕まる, by contrast, describes someone or something being caught.

examples[].german: I deliver the package.
I am going to deliver the package.
I took the wallet I found on the street to the police box.
en.notes: 届ける means "to deliver, to hand in" and describes bringing something to a recipient or place. The thing delivered takes を, the recipient or destination takes に. 届けに行く uses the verb stem to name the purpose of going. 届く, by contrast, means "to arrive": 荷物が届く.

en.meaning: to give (to others); to do for someone
examples[].german: I give my friend a present.
I gave my friend a present.
I taught my younger brother Japanese.
en.notes: あげる describes giving to another person: 友達にプレゼントをあげる. The recipient takes に, the gift takes を. After a te-form, ～てあげる means doing something for someone, such as 教えてあげる. The focus is on the giving or helping side; the identically read meanings "to raise" and "to deep-fry" are not meant here.

examples[].german: I received a present from my friend.
I was praised by the teacher.
en.notes: もらう describes receiving: 友達にプレゼントをもらう. The giver can take に or から, the thing takes を. After a te-form, ～てもらう means that one receives an action as a help or favor: ほめてもらう. This godan verb forms もらいます and もらって; it is not an ichidan verb.

examples[].german: I run every morning.
I had no time, so I ran to the station.
en.notes: 走る here means "to run/jog", while 歩く refers to walking on foot. Despite -る, 走る is a godan verb: 走ります, 走って. With まで the endpoint of the run can be named, for example 駅まで走る.

en.meaning: to give (to me or my circle)
examples[].german: My friend gave me a book.
My mother made a bento for me.
en.notes: くれる means that someone gives something to me or to a person close to me. The giver takes が, the gift takes を. After a te-form, ～てくれる can express an action done for me: 作ってくれる. The viewpoint lies with the receiving side. The verb is ichidan but has the special imperative くれ. 呉れる is a rare kanji spelling. For giving to me and the ～てくれる construction, the kana form くれる is usual.

examples[].german: I call a taxi.
Please call a taxi.
The teacher called my name.
en.notes: 呼ぶ can mean "to call over, to summon". タクシーを呼ぶ means "to call or order a taxi"; 名前を呼ぶ "to call out a name". The thing called takes を. The godan forms are 呼びます and 呼んで, with んで in the te-form. You can call a taxi without 呼ぶ itself meaning exclusively "to telephone".

examples[].german: Everyone is laughing.
The baby is laughing.
Please smile when the photo is taken.
en.notes: 笑う can mean "to laugh" or "to smile". In みんな笑っている laughing is meant; for a photo, 笑ってください can ask someone to smile. The person usually takes が. This godan verb forms 笑います and 笑って. The examples concern joy or a friendly face, not laughing at a person.

examples[].german: The baby is crying.
I cried while watching the movie.
en.notes: 泣く means to cry or to shed tears. The person crying takes が. 泣いています describes crying that is going on right now; 映画を見て泣く links it with watching a movie. The godan verb ending in く forms 泣いて and 泣いた, not *泣って.

examples[].german: The teacher got angry.
Please listen to me without getting angry.
en.notes: 怒る here means to get angry. 怒っています can describe the state of being angry; 怒らないで asks someone not to get angry. It is an intransitive godan verb with 怒って as its て-form. The other use, to scold someone, is not automatically included in every statement about anger.

examples[].german: The child is happy.
My friend was pleased with the present, which made me happy.
en.notes: 喜ぶ means to be glad or pleased. With が one describes the person who is pleased; with を one can name what pleases them: プレゼントを喜ぶ. 喜んでくれる makes the other person's joy appear as something pleasing to the speaker. The godan verb ending in ぶ forms 喜んで.

en.meaning: to be surprised; to be startled
examples[].german: I was startled by the loud noise.
I was surprised by the unexpected present.
en.notes: 驚く can mean to be surprised or to be startled by something. The triggers often take に: 音に驚く, プレゼントに驚く. The context decides whether the reaction is pleasant or frightened. This intransitive godan verb forms 驚いて; actively surprising another person is 驚かす.

examples[].german: I ordered a coffee at the restaurant.
I asked my friend for help.
en.notes: 頼む means to ask someone for something and can also mean to order. に names the person, を the thing requested: 友達に手伝いを頼む. In a restaurant, コーヒーを頼む orders a coffee. This godan verb ending in む forms 頼んで. For "to ask a favor", お願いする is also common.

examples[].german: Please help me.
I helped my younger brother with his homework.
en.notes: 手伝う means to help out with a task. The activity being assisted can take を: 宿題を手伝う. The person to whom the task belongs can be specified with の. This transitive godan verb ending in う forms 手伝って and 手伝わない. A request for help is 手伝ってください.

examples[].german: The money for the trip has been collected.
Everyone gathered in front of the station.
en.notes: 集まる describes people coming together or things accumulating. The thing gathered takes が, and the meeting place can take に. Someone who actively collects something uses 集める with を instead. 集まる is godan with 集まって; its る ending does not make it ichidan. The usual spelling is 集まる. The dictionary variant 集る has irregular okurigana; use 集まる in your own writing.

examples[].german: I swim in the pool.
Fish are swimming in the river.
en.notes: 泳ぐ describes swimming by people and animals. The place of a swimming activity takes で, and a space swum through can take を. For this godan verb ending in -ぐ, the て-form is 泳いで, not 泳いて.

examples[].german: I said goodbye to my friend at the station.
I broke up with my partner.
en.notes: 別れる means to part from one another. With friends it can simply mean going separate ways after meeting; with 恋人 it can mean ending a relationship. と names the other person. 別れる is intransitive and ichidan: 別れて, 別れない. The context decides between a temporary farewell and a permanent separation.

en.meaning: to be able to; to be possible
examples[].german: Can you speak Japanese?
You can take photos here.
en.notes: できる means to be able to or to be possible. With a noun and が, it names an ability or a field one has mastered, as in 日本語ができる. An action expressed by a verb uses the dictionary form plus ことができる: 写真を撮ることができる. This ichidan verb forms できない; additional meanings such as "to be finished" are not automatically meant in every ability statement.

examples[].german: Two plus three makes five.
Do you add sugar to your coffee?
en.notes: 足す means to add numbers or to add one thing to another. In 二に三を足す, 三 is the added value and 二 is the starting value. In コーヒーに砂糖を足す, the coffee is the target and the sugar is the addition. This transitive godan verb ending in す forms 足して.

examples[].german: The phone is ringing.
The alarm clock rang at six in the morning.
en.notes: 鳴る means that something produces a sound, such as a phone or an alarm clock. The thing that sounds takes が. 鳴っています describes ringing that is audible right now. This godan verb forms 鳴って; actively causing a sound is 鳴らす. The identically read なる meaning "to become" is a different lexeme.

examples[].german: The stars are shining.
This ring is sparkling.
en.notes: 光る means to shine or to glitter. With 星 "shine" usually fits, with a piece of jewelry "glitter". The shining or glittering object takes が, or は as the topic. 光っています describes the visible state. The godan verb ending in る forms 光って, not *光いて.

examples[].german: I was born in Tokyo.
A baby was born, so the family is delighted.
en.notes: 生まれる means to be born, but in Japanese it is already a verb in its own right, an intransitive ichidan verb. It is not formed by adding a passive ending. で names the place of birth: 東京で生まれる. 生まれました reports a birth; 生まれたので can give it as the reason for the joy that follows.

examples[].german: My grandfather died last year.
This fish is already dead.
en.notes: 死ぬ means to die. 死にました reports death as an event; 死んでいます means to be already dead and describes the state. The form ends in ぬ and belongs to godan: 死んで, 死なない. The word is direct; for people who have passed away, the more reserved 亡くなる is also common.

en.meaning: to gain weight; to get fat
examples[].german: I have put on weight lately.
I have gained weight, so these trousers are tight.
en.notes: 太る means to gain body weight or to become fatter. 太りました states the change; 太っている can describe the resulting state. It is an intransitive godan verb with 太って. A statement about weight does not automatically contain a health-related or moral judgment.

en.meaning: to lose weight; to get thin
examples[].german: I have lost a little weight.
My older brother is slim.
en.notes: 痩せる means to lose weight or to become thinner. 痩せました reports a change; 痩せています can describe a slim state and does not automatically mean currently losing weight. It is ichidan: 痩せて, 痩せない. A statement about body shape alone does not specify a cause of the change.

examples[].german: I hang out with friends.
The children are playing in the park.
en.notes: 遊ぶ can mean children's play or spending free time together. 友達と遊ぶ can also mean "to spend time with friends", depending on the situation, without naming a particular game. For a specific sport or instrument, use more fitting verbs, such as テニスをする and ピアノを弾く.

examples[].german: The cherry trees are blooming.
When spring comes, many flowers bloom in the park.
en.notes: 咲く means to bloom or to open as a blossom. The flowers that bloom take が. 咲いています describes that they are in bloom right now; 春になると can introduce a recurring blooming season. This godan verb ending in く forms 咲いて, without an additional small っ.

examples[].german: Where is the food department?
I asked a clerk at the sales floor.
en.notes: 売り場 is the area where goods are sold, such as a sales department or a sales stand. The type of goods can precede it: 食品売り場. For an action in this area, で is used. The word denotes the place of sale, not a favorable time to sell here.

examples[].german: Here is your change.
Please do not forget your change.
en.notes: おつり is the change after a purchase, that is, the amount returned. The spelling お釣り is also common. おつりをどうぞ accompanies the handing over; おつりを忘れないでください reminds someone to take it along. When paying, one can ask with おつりをください for the change that is still missing.

examples[].german: I pay at the register.
Three people are lined up in front of the register.
en.notes: レジ is the cash register, both the machine and the checkout area in a store. It is a short form of レジスター. For paying, レジで is used; レジの前に names the area in front of it. The word alone does not say whether one pays in cash or by card.

examples[].german: May I have a bag?
Please put it in a bag.
en.notes: 袋（ふくろ）is a bag, pouch or sack. When requesting one it takes を; as a container for packed goods it takes に. 袋をもらえますか politely asks whether one can get one. The word itself does not specify whether it is made of paper, cloth or plastic.

examples[].german: A guest came to our house.
This store always has many customers.
en.notes: お客さん can be a visitor or guest and, in a shop, a customer. お and さん form a respectful way to refer to the other person here. The context decides between a private visit and business customers. The full reading is おきゃくさん, in which きゃ forms a single mora.

examples[].german: I greet my neighbor.
I received vegetables from my neighbor.
en.notes: 隣人（りんじん）is a neighbor or a person in the neighborhood. The word sounds more formal than the common everyday 近所の人. When greeting, the neighbor takes に; when receiving something from them, から. The term alone says nothing about gender or kinship.

en.meaning: to stop; to turn off; to fasten or hold (留める)
examples[].german: Please stop the car.
Please turn off the air conditioner before you go out.
I fastened the name tag to my clothes with a safety pin.
The police held the man at the station and questioned him about the circumstances.
en.notes: 止める（とめる）is transitive: one stops something or switches it off, and the object takes を. For fastening, for example with a pin, 留める is used in particular. 留める can also mean to hold someone or keep them in custody. This ichidan verb forms とめます and とめて. 止まる, by contrast, describes stopping without an active object; the readings やめる and とどめる belong to other entries.

examples[].german: I hand over the letter.
Please hand over the documents.
Please hand this key to the person at the reception desk before you leave.
en.notes: Here 渡す means "to hand over, to pass". The thing takes を, the receiving person takes に. A handover can be personal, for example a letter or leaving a key at the reception desk. This godan verb forms 渡します and 渡して. 渡る, on the other hand, means to cross something oneself; it is not the form for "to hand something to someone".

examples[].german: Please do not touch.
Please do not touch the wall.
Please feel this cloth. It is very soft.
en.notes: 触る means "to touch". One can say 絵に触る; when touching deliberately, the thing touched can also take を, as in 布を触る. 触らないでください prohibits touching, and 触ってみてください invites someone to try. Despite the ending る, it is a godan verb: 触ります, 触って.

examples[].german: I sing at karaoke.
Please sing this song.
en.notes: 歌う means "to sing". The song takes を, and the place takes, for example, で: 歌を歌う, カラオケで歌う. This godan verb forms the te-form 歌って and the negative 歌わない.

en.meaning: to drop; to lose; to remove (dirt)
examples[].german: I dropped my wallet.
I accidentally dropped my wallet.
I wash the dirt off my hands with soap.
en.notes: 落とす means "to drop" and, for lost objects, also "to lose". The object affected takes を: 財布を落とす. 汚れを落とす, by contrast, means "to remove dirt". 落としてしまう emphasizes an undesired outcome. This transitive verb differs from 落ちる: an apple falls with が, while someone drops it with を. The dictionary variant 落す is also read おとす; use 落とす in your own writing.

en.meaning: to fall; to drop; to fail (an exam)
examples[].german: The apple fell.
An apple fell from the tree.
I failed the exam, so I will study again.
en.notes: 落ちる describes something falling; the thing that falls takes が, and the starting point can take から. In 試験に落ちる, "to fail an exam", the exam takes に. This ichidan verb forms 落ちます and 落ちて. 落とす, by contrast, describes someone dropping an object. The dictionary spelling 落る is marked as irregular okurigana; use 落ちる in your own writing.

examples[].german: I return the book.
I have to return the book to the library.
I borrowed money, so I will pay it back next week.
en.notes: 返す means "to give back" or "to pay back". The thing returned takes を, the person or institution takes に. With borrowed money, お金を返す is a repayment. It is a godan verb with 返します and 返して. 帰る, on the other hand, means to go back or go home oneself.

en.meaning: to receive; to take (an exam), to undergo
examples[].german: I am taking the exam.
I took the test.
I received an explanation from the teacher.
en.notes: 受ける has several meanings. 試験を受ける means "to take an exam", not "to pass it". 説明を受ける means "to receive an explanation". The exam or the service received takes を; the person explaining can take から. This ichidan verb forms 受けます and 受けて.

en.meaning: to leave in someone's care; to deposit
examples[].german: I check my luggage.
May I leave my luggage with you?
I deposit money at the bank every month.
en.notes: 預ける means to hand something over for safekeeping or care. The item handed over takes を, the responsible person or institution takes に. With luggage it is temporary storage; with a bank it can mean depositing money. The Ichidan verb forms 預けます and 預けて. 預かる describes the point of view of the person who takes something into their care.

examples[].german: I will let you know the result.
Please let me know the result.
If you will be late, please let us know by phone.
en.notes: 知らせる means "to inform, to notify" and makes information known to someone. The information takes を, the person notified takes に. 知らせてください asks for a message; a condition like 遅れるときは explains when one should get in touch. This ichidan verb forms 知らせます and 知らせて.

examples[].german: Please give them my regards.
Please tell the teacher.
I conveyed my feelings through a picture.
en.notes: 伝える means "to convey, to communicate". The person receiving takes に, the content takes を. よろしく伝えてください is the fixed request "Please give my regards to them". Not only words but also a picture can convey feelings. This ichidan verb forms 伝えます and 伝えて.

en.meaning: to be visible, to be seen; to look, to seem
examples[].german: I can see the mountain.
You can see the mountains from here.
This room looks spacious.
en.notes: 見える describes that something is visible without one having to look at it deliberately. The thing visible takes が; ここから names the vantage point. With 広く見える it means "to look big or spacious", without fixing the actual size. This ichidan verb is intransitive: 見ます "I look" and 見えます "it can be seen" are different verbs.

en.meaning: to be audible, to be heard
examples[].german: I can hear music.
Excuse me, I can't hear you well. One more time, please.
en.notes: 聞こえる means that a sound is audible or reaches the ears. The thing audible takes が: 音楽が聞こえる. よく聞こえません explains that one cannot hear well, for example on the phone; the request to repeat fits with this. It is an intransitive ichidan verb with 聞こえます and 聞こえて. 聞く, by contrast, also denotes deliberate listening or asking.

examples[].german: I found the key.
I finally found the key.
On my walk I discovered a small bakery.
en.notes: 見つける means "to find, to discover". The thing found takes を. It can be the result of a search, such as for a key, or an unexpected discovery along the way. やっと emphasizes that it finally succeeded. This transitive ichidan verb forms 見つけます and 見つけて; 見つかる, by contrast, describes something being found.

examples[].german: I take a photo.
I took a photo of Mt. Fuji.
Please don't take photos here.
en.notes: 写真を撮る is the usual combination for "to take a photo"; the person or thing photographed can also take を. 撮る here refers to taking pictures and should be distinguished from 取る ("to take") and 捕る ("to catch"). The te-form is 撮って.

examples[].german: I am looking for a job.
I am looking for my key.
I searched inside the bag, but the key was not there.
en.notes: 探す describes the search, not its success. 仕事を探す means "to look for work", 鍵を探す "to look for a key". In かばんの中を探す, を marks the area searched. This godan verb forms 探します and 探して. 見つける says that something was actually found.

examples[].german: I got lost.
I ended up getting lost.
I can't decide which of the two dishes to eat.
en.notes: 迷う means "to get lost" or "to be unable to decide". 道に迷う is "to lose one's way". In どちらを食べるか迷う one is unsure which of two options to choose. This intransitive Godan verb forms 迷います and 迷って. A decision with か can come before it as the content of the uncertainty.

examples[].german: I lost my wallet.
I lost something important.
To eliminate mistakes, I will check once more.
en.notes: 無くす means "to lose" when something can no longer be found. It can also mean "to eliminate": ミスを無くす means to avoid mistakes or eliminate them entirely. The affected object takes を. This godan verb forms 無くします and 無くして. The kana spelling なくす is also common; 亡くす, for a death, is a different spelling.

examples[].german: Please don't worry.
I am worried about my mother.
My parents are worried about my exam.
en.notes: 心配する means "to worry". The cause stands before the verb, for example as 私の試験のことを; のことを highlights what one is worried about. 心配しないでください is a reassuring request not to worry. There is also the state description 心配です, as in 母のことが心配です. Without する, 心配 is also used as a noun, or with な before a noun. The forms of する change, for example 心配します, 心配した and 心配して.

examples[].german: I'm exhausted today.
I'm exhausted from walking a lot.
My father came home with a tired look on his face.
en.notes: 疲れた means "exhausted, tired from exertion", not simply "sleepy" like 眠い. It is the ta-form of 疲れる and can express exhaustion felt at present. Before a noun it stays unchanged: 疲れた顔. The polite form in the examples is 疲れました; neither な nor another い is attached to 疲れた.

examples[].german: The train is fast.
This train is fast.
I ran to the station fast, so I made it in time for the train.
en.notes: 速い denotes high speed. A train can be 速い; 速く走る describes running fast and uses the ku-form before a verb. For "early" in the temporal sense, 早い is usually written, although the reading is the same. As an i-adjective, 速い forms the negative 速くない and the past 速かった.

examples[].german: It is a square box.
This box is square.
I fold a square sheet of paper in half and make a card.
en.notes: 四角い describes a four-cornered shape and can mean "square" or "rectangular". It does not say that all sides must be equally long. Before a noun it is used directly, as in 四角い紙, without な. The ku-form is 四角く. The word is more precise than a general "angular", which could include other shapes.

examples[].german: This bread is hard.
This bread is hard, isn't it?
The lid of this jar is so tight that I can't open it.
en.notes: 固い means hard or firm and can also mean stuck fast. 固いパン is hard bread; a stiff bottle cap can also be 固い. 硬い often emphasizes the hardness of a material, such as stone, while 堅い is used for a solid, reliable nature. The spellings overlap but have different typical combinations. 固い is correct for bread. This i-adjective forms 固く and 固くない.

examples[].german: It is a soft cushion.
This cloth is soft.
The soft morning light comes in through the window.
en.notes: 柔らかい means "soft" or, for impressions, also "mild, gentle". A cushion or cloth gives way when touched; 柔らかい光 describes gentle light. Before a noun this i-adjective stands without な. The forms are 柔らかく and 柔らかくない. The reading is やわらかい; the shorter form やわらか has a different grammatical use.

examples[].german: This flower is beautiful.
This park is beautiful, isn't it?
I cleaned, and the room became tidy.
en.notes: 綺麗 can mean "beautiful" or "clean, tidy". With flowers, beauty is meant; after cleaning, a room can be 綺麗. Despite the reading きれい, it is not an i-adjective: before a noun it is 綺麗な, and for change 綺麗になる. The kana spelling きれい is also common. The kanji spelling 奇麗 is also read きれい and can mean "beautiful" or "clean".

examples[].german: I watched a movie with a friend.
I wrote a letter to a friend.
en.notes: Common in everyday speech; depending on context it can mean one friend or several. 友達と marks doing something together, while 友達に marks, for example, the recipient of a message. 友人 is more neutral or formal. The word does not by itself denote a romantic relationship.

examples[].german: Please open the window.
May I open the door?
I open the shop at nine in the morning.
en.notes: 開ける is transitive: someone opens something, such as 窓を開ける. The matching intransitive verb is 開く（あく）: 窓が開く "the window opens". 開ける can also refer to opening a business; as an ichidan verb it forms 開けて and 開けない.

examples[].german: It is a splendid building.
It's an impressive building, isn't it?
My younger brother helps with the housework every day. That's admirable, isn't it?
en.notes: 立派 means "impressive, splendid" and can also acknowledge a praiseworthy achievement or attitude. A 立派な建物 looks impressive; a helpful person can be called 立派 for their behavior. It is a na-adjective with 立派な before a noun. The small っ in the reading appears as a double p in rippa.

examples[].german: They are sturdy shoes.
This bag is sturdy.
My grandmother is physically robust and goes for a walk every morning.
en.notes: 丈夫 means "sturdy, durable" for objects and "healthy, resilient" for people. 丈夫な靴 withstands wear; 体が丈夫 describes a strong constitution. This na-adjective takes な before a noun and です as a statement. The reading じょうぶ contains a long ō: jōbu.

examples[].german: Family is important.
This is a precious watch that I got from my grandmother.
en.notes: 大切 means "important" and, for personal belongings, "precious, dear". 家族は大切です expresses the importance of family. A 大切な時計 can have sentimental value without being expensive. Before a noun, な is used; 大切にする means to treat something with care or to cherish it. The context shows whether significance or personal attachment is in the foreground.

examples[].german: Please take good care of it.
Health is the most important thing.
en.notes: 大事 denotes something important or precious. As a な-adjective it takes な before a noun: 大事なもの. 大事にする means to treat something carefully or to value it; 大事にしてください therefore asks for careful handling. 大事です, by contrast, evaluates how important something is.

examples[].german: This problem is easy.
This dish can be made easily.
en.notes: 簡単 describes something that is easy to solve or can be done without much effort. It is a な-adjective: 簡単な問題. With に it describes the manner of an action, as in 簡単に作れる: easy to make. Here "simple" means low difficulty, not automatically low quality.

examples[].german: This map is complicated.
Please explain complicated things in a simple way.
en.notes: 複雑 means complicated or complex, for example when many parts or relationships interlock. Before a noun it takes な: 複雑なこと. 複雑です describes the thing itself; a difficult explanation can nevertheless be put in an understandable way. The opposite for a simple structure is 簡単.

examples[].german: It is inconvenient because there is no train.
If you can't use the phone, it is inconvenient to get in touch.
en.notes: 不便 means impractical or inconvenient because something makes everyday life harder. It is the counterpart of 便利 and a な-adjective: 不便な場所. 電車がなくて names a reason, while ～のに不便です states for which activity something is a hindrance. For an uncomfortable chair, 座りにくい fits better depending on the context.

examples[].german: He/She is a kind person, isn't he/she?
The clerk kindly showed me the way.
en.notes: 親切 describes helpful, considerate kindness. 親切な人 is a kind person; 親切に explains how someone helps or explains something. It is about how one treats others, not merely a friendly face. 親切にしてくれました emphasizes that the kindness benefited oneself.

examples[].german: He/She is a serious student.
Please answer seriously.
en.notes: 真面目 means serious or conscientious. 真面目な学生 describes a person's attitude; 真面目に答える asks for a serious answer. The word does not necessarily mean sad or humorless. な stands before a noun, に before an action; the predicate form is 真面目です.

examples[].german: I will go after all.
Japanese food really is delicious, isn't it?
en.notes: やっぱり is the spoken form of やはり. It can confirm an expectation: "as I thought" or "after all". In a decision such as やっぱり行きます it often means "I'll go after all", after one had hesitated or thought differently. It therefore does not simply express an uncertain guess like たぶん. 矢っ張り is a rare kanji spelling marked as ateji; やっぱり is usual.

examples[].german: Please close the door.
Please close the window.
I close the shop at eight in the evening.
en.notes: 閉める means "to close something" and takes its object with を: ドアを閉める. 閉まる, by contrast, describes something closing or being shut: ドアが閉まる. This ichidan verb forms 閉めて; the identically pronounced 締める means, among other things, "to tighten".

examples[].german: It's probably all right.
It will probably rain tomorrow.
en.notes: たぶん marks a conjecture: probably or perhaps. The speaker considers something plausible but does not guarantee it. That is why it also goes with でしょう, which expresses a conjecture. Compared with きっと, たぶん usually sounds less convinced; it does not fix a specific percentage.

examples[].german: You will surely get good at it.
The key is surely at home.
en.notes: きっと shows strong conviction or confident expectation: "surely". It is usually more decisive than たぶん, but remains the speaker's assessment. When encouraging, it expresses trust; for a presumed location, a firm assumption. No factual guarantee follows from it. 屹度 is a rare kanji spelling marked as ateji. In normal text, きっと is used.

examples[].german: It is exactly three o'clock.
This shirt is just the right size.
en.notes: ちょうど means exactly, just or fitting. With a clock time it concerns a precise point in time; in ちょうどいい, a fitting amount or size. It is an adverb and takes neither な nor its own verb ending. Homophones meaning furniture or consistency do not belong to this card. 恰度 is a rare spelling of ちょうど marked as ateji. The kana form ちょうど is the usual one.

examples[].german: I understood it roughly.
It takes about thirty minutes.
en.notes: だいたい expresses an approximate quantity or the greater part of something. だいたい三十分 is about half an hour, not an exact duration. With 分かりました, it means that one has understood the essentials; individual details may be missing. The usual kanji spelling is 大体.

examples[].german: I don't understand at all.
I am not tired at all.
en.notes: ぜんぜん strengthens negative sentences to "not at all": ぜんぜん分かりません. The negation is contained in the verb or adjective, not in the adverb alone. Colloquially one also hears positive phrases such as 全然いいよ: "That's perfectly fine". For basic polite usage, the negative examples are especially useful.

examples[].german: It's incredibly fun.
My younger brother can run very fast.
en.notes: すごく intensifies an adjective or a description: very, incredibly. It is the ku-form of すごい, but is often used like a degree adverb in its own right. すごく楽しい evaluates an experience; すごく速く走る intensifies the speed of an action. In conversation it often sounds more lively than とても.

en.meaning: after a long time; long time no see
examples[].german: Long time no see!
I rode a bicycle for the first time in a long time.
en.notes: 久しぶり is said when meeting again after a longer time. With ですね the greeting is polite, and with お久しぶりです it is somewhat more respectful. In 久しぶりに～する, on the other hand, it means doing something again after a long pause. It does not fix a specific number of days or years. 久し振り is another spelling with the same reading ひさしぶり.

examples[].german: Happy birthday!
I sent a friend who got married an email saying "Congratulations".
en.notes: おめでとう congratulates someone on a happy occasion, such as a birthday, a wedding or a passed exam. Among friends the short form fits; おめでとうございます is more polite. The occasion can come before it: 誕生日おめでとう. The phrase also suits a written message of congratulations. お目出度う is listed only as a dictionary search spelling. Normally write the congratulation as おめでとう.

examples[].german: Welcome! How many people are in your party?
When you enter a shop, you are greeted with "Welcome".
en.notes: いらっしゃいませ greets customers or guests in a shop or restaurant. It is said by the staff; customers do not normally have to answer the greeting with the same phrase. In a restaurant, a question about the number of people may follow. To welcome a friend to your home, いらっしゃい is more fitting.

en.meaning: to turn on; to switch on
examples[].german: Please turn on the light.
May I turn on the TV?
It's dark, so I'll turn on the light.
en.notes: Here つける means "to turn on a device or light" and is also written 点ける or 付ける. Depending on context, つける can also mean "to attach" or "to wear"; the identically pronounced 浸ける means "to soak".

examples[].german: Excuse me for intruding. Wow, what a spacious room.
Before entering a friend's house, you say "Excuse me for intruding".
en.notes: お邪魔します is said by a visitor when entering someone else's home. It politely acknowledges that one is making use of the other person's private space. "Excuse me for intruding" is a visiting greeting here; there does not have to be any actual disturbance. When leaving after the visit you hear お邪魔しました.

examples[].german: Welcome back. How was the trip?
When I heard "I'm home", I answered, "Welcome back".
en.notes: お帰りなさい greets someone who is coming back home. The returning person often says ただいま, and the person who stayed at home answers with お帰りなさい. The greeting also fits when someone returns home after a trip. The なさい at the end is part of the fixed phrase and is not a command to come back here.

examples[].german: Do your best!
I will do my best for the test.
en.notes: 頑張る means to make an effort, to persevere or to do one's best. 頑張ってください encourages another person; 頑張ります announces one's own effort. This godan verb forms the て-form 頑張って. It promises effort, but not yet a successful outcome.

examples[].german: I made it to the train in time.
If you don't hurry, you won't make it to class on time.
en.notes: 間に合う means to be on time or to still reach something in time. The train, class or appointment takes に: 電車に間に合う. The verb is intransitive and godan with 間に合って. 間に合いません negates being in time; here it does not mean that something is sufficient in quantity.

examples[].german: I intend to go tomorrow.
I intend not to watch TV today.
en.notes: つもり expresses a personal intention. The dictionary form of the planned action stands before it: 行くつもりです. A negative dictionary form like 見ないつもりです means that one intends not to do something. It is a noun, not a verb of its own, and describes the plan rather than an action that has already happened. The dictionary spelling 積もり is read つもり; for this construction of intention the kana form is usual.

examples[].german: What are your plans for tomorrow?
The meeting is scheduled to start at three o'clock.
en.notes: 予定 means plans or a scheduled timetable. 明日の予定 asks about the plans for tomorrow. In ～予定です, an action whose course is planned can also stand before 予定: 始まる予定です. In contrast to the personal intention of つもり, 予定 often emphasizes arranged or planned organization.

examples[].german: May I ask for your advice?
I discussed the travel plans with my family.
en.notes: 相談 is a consultation or discussion; with する it means to consult or ask for advice. 先生に相談する names the person one seeks advice from; 家族と相談する emphasizes discussing together. The topic can take ～について. 相談してもいいですか politely asks whether one may discuss a matter.

examples[].german: Please contact me.
There was a message from the school.
en.notes: 連絡 means making contact or a message. 連絡する means to get in touch or to notify someone; the person contacted often takes に. 連絡がある means that a message arrives, and ～から names its source. The word does not specify whether one phones, writes or sends a message.

examples[].german: I will introduce my friend.
Please introduce yourself.
en.notes: 紹介 is an introduction. With する it becomes "to introduce": the person introduced takes を, the person they are introduced to takes に. 自己紹介 is introducing oneself. One can also introduce a place or a product. The accent of 紹介 alone does not automatically apply to the whole word 自己紹介.

examples[].german: Please reply.
The reply to the email still hasn't come.
en.notes: 返事 is a reply or response to a message, question or call. 返事をする means "to reply", 返事が来る "a reply comes". In メールの返事, の marks the message being replied to. The word can also be a short spoken reaction; it is not limited to written replies.

examples[].german: Please turn off the light.
Please turn off the TV.
I erased the wrongly written character.
en.notes: 消す is used both for switching off lights or devices and for erasing writing: 電気を消す, 字を消す. It is transitive; 消える, by contrast, describes going out or disappearing. This godan verb forms 消して and 消さない.

examples[].german: Did you understand?
I understood the teacher's explanation.
I understood the reason why I was late.
en.notes: 理解 means "understanding"; 理解する means to understand some content. 理解できる says that one can understand it or has understood it. With the potential form the content understood can take が: 説明が理解できる. A connection or a reason can also be understood; 理解する does not automatically mean agreeing with an opinion.

examples[].german: Please explain.
Please explain it once more.
Next to the machine, there is a written explanation of how to use it.
en.notes: 説明 is an explanation or description. 説明する means "to explain"; the thing explained takes を, the listener takes に. A 説明 can also exist in writing, for example next to a device. もう一度説明してください asks for a repetition without saying that the first explanation was wrong.

examples[].german: It is a good experience.
It turned out to be a good experience.
I have no work experience in cooking, but I cook at home every day.
en.notes: 経験 is an experience one has had oneself, or accumulated practical experience. いい経験になった evaluates an experience in retrospect. 経験がある means to already have experience with something; 経験する means "to experience oneself". The word does not yet say whether the experience was positive or negative.

examples[].german: I failed.
I did badly on the test.
From this failure, I decided to prepare earlier next time.
en.notes: 失敗 is a failure or mistake. 失敗する means that something fails or one makes a mistake. For a test, テストに失敗した first says only that it went badly; a formal failure is more precisely 試験に落ちた. The expression 失敗から学ぶ means to learn from a mistake.

examples[].german: It was a success.
The project was a success.
We talked together about the reason for the success.
en.notes: 成功 means "success"; 成功する means "to succeed, to be successful". A successful project can take が, a successful action takes に: 実験に成功する. 成功の理由 asks about the reason for the success. The word describes a successful result and is not the same as the mere attempt to do something.

examples[].german: Everything is ready.
I am preparing for the party.
I prepared tea for the guests.
en.notes: 用意 is preparation or the providing of something. 用意ができた means that everything is prepared. 用意する is also used for concrete things one provides, such as drinks or documents. The thing provided takes を; パーティーの用意 means the preparations for the party, not automatically only the food.

examples[].german: I have something to take care of.
I have something to take care of today.
Let's meet at the station once I'm done with my errand at the bank.
en.notes: 用事 is something one has to take care of, or another obligation. 用事がある can explain why one has no time, without giving private details. 用事で出かける gives an errand as the reason for going out. The word is a noun; for "to run an errand", 用事する is not normally said.

examples[].german: Please guide me.
A station attendant guided me.
I read the information at the entrance and then entered the venue.
en.notes: 案内 is guiding, directions or information. 案内する can mean to lead someone to a place or to show something. A written 案内, by contrast, informs about a place or procedure. With 駅員さんに案内してもらう one receives help from the station staff; it is not about guiding this person oneself.

examples[].german: The view is beautiful.
The mountain scenery is beautiful.
I reserved a room with a nice view.
en.notes: 景色 is the visible landscape or view, also in a city. 景色がきれい describes what one sees. 景色のいい部屋 is a room with a nice view, literally a room whose view is good. の can mark the subject of いい here instead of が. The word denotes the scene being looked at, not the weather or a travel plan.

examples[].german: There is abundant nature.
I like walking in nature.
The smile in this photo looks natural.
en.notes: 自然 as a noun is nature, as in 自然の中 "in nature". As a na-adjective it means "natural": 自然な笑顔 looks unforced and not artificial. 自然です evaluates this impression. The two uses differ grammatically; the meaning "by itself" has other constructions and is not practiced here.

examples[].german: Do you have an umbrella?
I carry heavy luggage.
en.notes: 持つ can mean "to hold in the hand", "to carry" or "to own"; the thing takes を. 持っています often describes an ongoing state, such as having an umbrella. This godan verb forms 持って; "to take along" is often 持っていく.

examples[].german: The air is clean.
The air in the mountains is delicious.
The teacher got angry, so the atmosphere in the classroom became heavy.
en.notes: 空気 refers to the air we breathe. 空気がおいしい is a common positive description of fresh air, not literal eating. In conversation, 空気 can also mean the mood. 教室の空気が重い describes an oppressive atmosphere. The context shows whether air as a substance or the social atmosphere is meant.

examples[].german: The Earth is round.
Let's reduce garbage for the sake of the Earth.
en.notes: 地球 is the Earth as a planet. 地球は丸い describes its shape; 地球のために gives protecting our planet as the purpose. For earth as soil or material, other words are used, such as 土. The long ū belongs to the reading ちきゅう; the small ゅ forms a single syllable kyu with き.

examples[].german: The sun is out.
The sun rises in the east.
en.notes: 太陽 is the sun as a celestial body. 太陽が出ている means that the sun can be seen or is shining. 太陽が昇る describes its rising; 東から names the direction it rises from. The word is a noun, and the long final syllable is rendered with ō.

examples[].german: I can see many stars.
The stars are beautiful tonight, aren't they?
I drew a star shape on a card.
en.notes: 星 is a star in the sky and can also be a star shape used as a symbol. 星が見える says that stars are visible; 星の形を描く means to draw a star shape. In everyday use the points of light visible at night are meant, without distinguishing every astronomical type exactly. The spelling for the family name Hoshi does not provide the accent of this noun.

examples[].german: Japan is an island country.
Japan has many islands.
I will go by boat to meet a friend who lives on this island.
en.notes: 島 is an island. One can name an island as a destination with 船で島に行く; 島に住む describes living there. 島国 is a compound word of its own, "island country". Its accent cannot be read off from 島 alone. Names written with 島 also have their own readings and accents.

examples[].german: I walked along the coast.
I took a walk along the coast.
There is a small hotel near the coast.
en.notes: 海岸 is the coast or the area by the sea and can also denote a beach. Not every 海岸 consists of sand. 海岸を歩く or 散歩する describes the route of a walk; 海岸の近くに, by contrast, names a location on the coast. The word is more general than a specific bathing bay.

examples[].german: It is cool in the forest.
I walked through the forest.
en.notes: 森 is a forest. 森の中は涼しい describes a property of the space in the forest; 森の中を歩く the route through it. For an action at a place, で is often suitable, for the route traversed を. 森 can also occur in names; here the ordinary word for a forest is practiced.

examples[].german: I swam in the lake.
This lake is very big.
en.notes: 湖 is a lake, that is, an inland body of water. 湖で泳ぐ names the lake as the place of swimming; この湖は大きい describes its size. The word is not the sea and is read みずうみ, romanized mizuumi, not みずみ. For a location by the lake, 湖のそば can be used.

examples[].german: Please do not throw stones.
The child is throwing stones.
I put a stone on the paper so that it would not be blown away by the wind.
en.notes: 石 is a stone or pebble. 石を投げる means throwing a stone; 石を置く, by contrast, can use it as a weight. In both cases the object takes を. A request like 投げないでください is a prohibition. The meaning practiced here is the ordinary stone, not automatically a gemstone or a game piece.

examples[].german: I play with sand.
The sand on the beach is white.
Sand got into my shoes, so I took it out.
en.notes: 砂 is sand. 砂で遊ぶ describes playing with sand as a material; 海岸の砂 means the sand on a coast. When there is sand in a shoe, one can say 靴の中に砂が入った. The word can denote an indefinite amount; it does not automatically need a number or a plural.

examples[].german: I live in Tokyo.
I want to live in Osaka.
Nobody lives in this house.
en.notes: With 住む, the place of residence takes に: 東京に住んでいます. For a current residence, 住んでいます is usual; 住みたい expresses the wish to live somewhere. 住む is intransitive and, as a godan verb, forms 住んで.

examples[].german: I am afraid of insects.
Our child likes insects.
In the garden, insects are eating the leaves.
en.notes: 虫 here means an insect or small crawling creature in everyday language. It is not a special word only for a beetle. 虫が怖い means that one is afraid of insects; 虫が好き describes interest or preference. In a garden, 虫 can also appear as animals that eat leaves.

examples[].german: Leaves have fallen on the road.
In autumn, the leaves of this tree turn red.
There was a small insect on the underside of the leaf.
en.notes: 葉 is a leaf of a plant. 木の葉 are the leaves of a tree; 葉の裏 is the underside of a leaf. 葉が落ちている can describe the result of falling: the leaves are already lying on the ground. Not all plants change the color of their leaves in the same way; the autumn sentence therefore refers to a specific tree.

examples[].german: Please do not break the branches.
The branch of the tree broke.
A bird is perched on the branch.
en.notes: 枝 is a branch or twig. 枝を折る means that someone breaks it off; 枝が折れる describes the branch breaking by itself. A branch can also be a perch for a bird: 枝に止まる. The word is more general than just a thick branch and also fits a thin twig.

examples[].german: I sat down on the grass.
On the weekend I weeded the garden.
en.notes: 草 means grass or weeds, depending on where the plants grow. 草の上に座る describes sitting on grass. 庭の草を取る means removing unwanted plants in the garden, that is, weeding. The internet use of 草 for laughter does not belong to this plant usage.

examples[].german: The ice has melted.
Please put ice in the drink.
en.notes: 氷 is frozen water. In a drink it usually means ice cubes or pieces of ice, not ice cream. 氷が溶ける describes melting; 氷を入れる describes putting it in. The reading こおり has a long o sound: kōri.

examples[].german: I can see smoke.
Smoke got into my eyes and tears came out.
en.notes: 煙 means smoke, for example from a fire or from cooking. 煙が見える describes its visibility. 煙が目に入る means that smoke gets into the eyes; 目に is the destination here. Unlike 湯気, 煙 does not simply denote water vapor.

examples[].german: There is a strange noise.
I woke up to the sound of the rain.
en.notes: 音 is a sound or noise. 音がする says that a sound is produced or perceptible; 音が聞こえる emphasizes hearing. 雨の音 names the source of the sound with の. A voice is normally 声, even though both are audible.

examples[].german: It smells good.
The smell of tobacco clings to these clothes.
en.notes: 匂い means smell or scent. いい匂いがする is "to smell good"; 匂いがつく describes a smell that sticks to something. For unpleasant smells the spelling 臭い is also common, but 匂い is not limited to pleasant scents. The reading におい is nioi. The kana form におい can also stand for this smell.

examples[].german: How does it taste?
This dish tastes good, doesn't it?
en.notes: 味 denotes the taste of food or drinks. 味はどうですか asks for an assessment. 味がいい praises the taste; 味が濃い, by contrast, describes a strong taste and is not automatically praise. The figurative meaning of 味 for appeal or charm is not needed here.

examples[].german: It has an interesting shape.
I cut the paper into a round shape.
en.notes: 形 means the visible shape or form of an object. 面白い形 evaluates an unusual shape. In 丸い形に切る, に names the shape that results from cutting. The word says nothing yet about material or size.

examples[].german: Do you know this person?
Do you know that shop?
Yesterday I learned about that news for the first time.
en.notes: "I know it" or "I know ..." is usually 知っています. The usual negative is 知りません. 知る can also denote the moment of finding out, as in ニュースを知る "to learn of a piece of news"; it is a transitive godan verb with the te-form 知って.

examples[].german: How big is it?
The size of this bag is just right.
en.notes: 大きさ is the size of an object. The noun is formed from 大きい with さ and often follows の: かばんの大きさ. 大きさはどのくらいですか asks about the extent; ちょうどいい evaluates the size as fitting. For weight, 重さ is used.

examples[].german: I measure the weight.
How much does this luggage weigh?
en.notes: 重さ means weight and is a noun formed from 重い with さ. 重さを量る means to determine the weight, usually with a scale. ～の重さ asks for the weight of the object named. 大きさ, by contrast, describes its size, not its mass.

examples[].german: How long is it?
The length of this room is six meters.
en.notes: 長さ is length, formed from 長い with さ. ～の長さ names the length of a particular object. An answer like 六メートル describes a linear dimension; it is not the area of the room. In a question, どのくらい leaves the unit of measurement open at first.

examples[].german: The room is ten tatami mats in size.
I was surprised by the size of the park.
en.notes: 広さ describes the area or spatial extent. For a room the measurement can be given in 畳, a unit based on tatami mats. 公園の広さに, on the other hand, names the extent that impresses someone. 長さ measures only a length; 広さ can mean all the available space.

examples[].german: How fast is the car?
The speed of the Shinkansen is amazing, isn't it?
en.notes: 速さ is speed or quickness and a noun from 速い. 車の速さ asks about the speed of the car. For the early time of day or an early point in time, the identically read spelling 早さ is often used. This card uses 速さ for the speed of movement.

examples[].german: I have an exam tomorrow.
I passed the exam.
en.notes: 試験 is an exam or a test. 試験がある announces that an exam is taking place. 試験に合格する means to pass the exam; 試験を受ける only means to take part and says nothing about the result. The part of speech of the card remains a noun.

examples[].german: Please lend me an eraser.
I erased the wrong part with an eraser.
en.notes: 消しゴム is an eraser. 消しゴムを貸してください asks to borrow one. When erasing, で marks the tool: 消しゴムで消す. 消し is fixed in this compound noun; the verb form of the action comes from 消す.

examples[].german: I draw a line with the ruler.
This ruler is thirty centimeters long.
en.notes: 定規 is a ruler for measuring or drawing straight lines. 定規で線を引く uses it as a tool; で corresponds to "with" here. A value in センチ can state the length of the ruler. The reading じょうぎ has a long o: jōgi.

examples[].german: Let's sing a song.
Do you know that song?
en.notes: 歌 means song and can also refer to singing as an activity. 歌を歌う is the normal combination "to sing a song". あの歌 names a particular song; 知っていますか asks whether it is known. A classical Japanese poem is not meant here.

examples[].german: What is your hobby?
My hobby is reading.
en.notes: 趣味 means hobby or leisure pastime. 趣味は何ですか asks about such an activity, 趣味は読書です names it. There can be several hobbies; the word alone does not require the singular. The meaning "taste" or "preference" in other phrases is not needed here.

examples[].german: I think it's good.
I think it will rain tomorrow.
en.notes: Before 思う comes a statement in plain form with と: 雨だと思います "I think it will rain". With nouns and na-adjectives, だ is included; with i-adjectives there is no だ. 思います here marks a personal assessment, not an established fact.

examples[].german: I like exercise.
I exercise every morning.
en.notes: 運動 here means physical movement, training or sports. 運動が好きです expresses a preference; 運動する means actually being physically active. 毎朝運動しています describes a habit. Political movements or physical motion are other uses of this word.

examples[].german: I went to the art museum.
The art museum is closed on Mondays.
en.notes: 美術館 is an art museum or an art gallery. With に one names the destination of a visit, with で the place of an activity in the museum. Opening and closing days can be given with ～は休みです. The じゅ in びじゅつかん forms a single mora.

examples[].german: I saw a panda at the zoo.
How much is a ticket to the zoo?
en.notes: 動物園 is a zoo. 動物園で names the place where one sees animals, 動物園に the destination of an outing. When planning a visit, one can ask about the ticket price. The reading どうぶつえん is dōbutsuen; つ and え remain separate syllables.

examples[].german: Where is the police box?
If you don't know the way, please ask at the police box.
en.notes: 交番 is a small police station in a neighborhood. You can ask there for directions, for example. 交番はどこですか looks for its location; 交番で聞く names it as the place to get information. The reading is kōban, with a long o.

examples[].german: I buy medicine at the pharmacy.
The pharmacy is next to the post office.
en.notes: 薬局 is a pharmacy. 薬局で薬を買う describes a purchase; 薬局は～の隣です gives its location next to another building. 薬 means medicine, 薬局 is the place. In やっきょく the small っ doubles the k sound; きょ is a single mora.

examples[].german: I pray at the Shinto shrine.
This Shinto shrine has a large torii gate.
en.notes: 神社 is a Shinto shrine. The word does not mean a Buddhist temple; that is 寺. 神社にお参りする means a religious visit or praying at the shrine. 鳥居 is the characteristic gate that can be seen at a shrine.

examples[].german: I toured the temple.
This temple is a ten-minute walk from the station.
en.notes: 寺 is a Buddhist temple. With the polite お one often hears お寺. 見学する means a visit for observation; ～から歩いて十分 gives a distance as walking time. The Shinto shrine, by contrast, is 神社. The reading てら is tera, and with お accordingly otera.

examples[].german: There is a supermarket in the neighborhood.
I greet the people in the neighborhood.
en.notes: 近所 is the neighborhood or nearby surroundings. 近所に names a place in this area; 近所の人 means the people living there. The word is not itself "a neighbor" but denotes the area. With の it can stand before another noun.

examples[].german: Please go up the stairs.
The stairs are next to the elevator.
en.notes: 階段 is a staircase. In 階段を上がる, を marks the route traveled and not an object being worked on. With ～の隣です one can explain the location of the stairs. For the floors of a building, however, 階 is used, as in 三階.

examples[].german: There is a cat on the roof.
The roof of the house was damaged by the typhoon.
en.notes: 屋根 is the roof of a building, not the ceiling of a room. 屋根の上に names a place on the roof. 屋根が壊れる describes damage without naming a person who caused it as an object. 家の indicates the building it belongs to.

examples[].german: I meet a friend.
Yesterday I met my teacher.
Let's meet at the station tomorrow.
en.notes: The person you meet often takes に: 友達に会う. と can emphasize an arranged or joint meeting. 会う is intransitive; its te-form is 会って. For meeting someone for the first time, 初めて会う is a natural combination.

examples[].german: I hang a picture on the wall.
This wall is white.
en.notes: 壁 is a wall. 壁に絵を掛ける means to hang a picture on the wall; に marks the place of attachment. 壁は白いです, by contrast, describes the color. The figurative meaning "obstacle" is not used in these examples.

examples[].german: The floor is clean.
Please sit on the floor.
en.notes: 床 means floor. 床がきれいです can describe it as clean or well kept; 床に座る names the floor as a seat. The reading ゆか refers here to the floor of a room. The identically written reading とこ is used for other words and phrases.

examples[].german: The ceiling is high.
I cleaned the ceiling of the room.
en.notes: 天井 is the ceiling of a room. 天井が高い describes its large distance from the floor. 天井を掃除する names it as the surface being cleaned. For a blanket on a bed a different word is used, such as 毛布; the roof of a house is 屋根.

examples[].german: The futon is in the closet.
I cleaned the inside of the closet.
en.notes: 押入れ is a built-in closet, often used for storing futons. The spelling 押し入れ is also common. 押入れにある describes an object lying there; 押入れの中を掃除する the cleaning of the interior. The long i sound in おしいれ arises from two consecutive い.

examples[].german: I like tatami rooms.
Please take off your shoes before entering the tatami room.
en.notes: 畳 is a tatami mat, a traditional Japanese floor covering. 畳の部屋 means a room with this covering. Before entering, one may be asked to take off one's shoes. The card reading is たたみ; as a unit of area after a number, one often hears じょう.

examples[].german: The pillow is soft.
I bought a new pillow.
en.notes: 枕 is a pillow or headrest for sleeping. 枕が柔らかい judges its texture; 新しい枕を買う describes a purchase. For a general seat or sofa cushion you often hear クッション. The narrator's introduction, which can also be called 枕, is not meant here.

examples[].german: I look in the mirror.
There is a large mirror on the wall.
en.notes: 鏡 is a mirror. 鏡を見る means to look in the mirror; the reflection does not need to be named as an object of its own. 壁に鏡がある describes the mirror as a piece of furnishing. The figurative meaning "model" belongs to a different dictionary entry.

examples[].german: I wash my hands with soap.
This soap smells nice.
en.notes: 石鹸 means soap. When washing hands, 石鹸で marks the means used and 手を the body part washed. いい匂いがする can describe the scent of a soap. The small っ in せっけん doubles k: sekken. 石鹼 is listed in the dictionary only as a search form; 石鹸 is suitable for writing.

examples[].german: I buy a toothbrush.
The toothbrush is in the bathroom.
en.notes: 歯ブラシ is a toothbrush. The word combines 歯, tooth, with the katakana word ブラシ. 歯ブラシを買う describes a purchase; 歯ブラシは～にあります gives its storage place. The reading is はぶらし, with no long vowel.

examples[].german: Please lend me a towel.
Please wipe your hands with the towel.
en.notes: タオル is a towel. タオルを貸してください asks for a borrowed towel. When drying off, タオルで names the tool and 手を the hands being dried. 拭く has the て-form 拭いて, read ふいて.

en.meaning: to ride; to board; to get on
examples[].german: I get on the train.
Let's take the bus.
Every day I ride my bicycle to school.
en.notes: With 乗る, the means of transport takes に: 電車に乗る, バスに乗る. The verb can refer both to boarding and to the ride itself. It is an intransitive godan verb and forms 乗って; the opposite, for getting off, is 降りる.

examples[].german: Please take out the trash.
Please do not throw trash on the street.
en.notes: ゴミ means trash or garbage. ゴミを出す means to take it out for collection or disposal. ゴミを捨てる means to throw away; in the negative request, 道に names the unwanted place of disposal. The spellings ごみ and ゴミ are both common. For the reading ごみ, the kanji spelling 塵 is also recorded; in everyday life the usual kana forms ごみ and ゴミ are suitable. 塵芥 is also attested as a difficult kanji spelling with the reading ごみ. The same kanji can also be read じんかい or ちりあくた; this card practices only ごみ. In ordinary notices and conversations, ごみ and ゴミ remain a good choice.

examples[].german: Please throw it in the trash can.
The trash can is over there.
en.notes: ゴミ箱 is a trash can or waste container. ゴミ箱に捨てる names it as the destination for discarded trash. With ゴミ箱はどこですか you can ask for its location. In ごみばこ, 箱 is read ばこ here, unlike the standalone はこ.

examples[].german: I like pickled vegetables.
Have you ever eaten Japanese pickled vegetables?
en.notes: 漬物 is pickled vegetables as a food. 漬物が好きです expresses a preference; 食べたことがありますか asks about past experience. The spelling 漬け物 is also common. The word does not say which kind of vegetable is pickled.

examples[].german: This bowl is big.
I had a donburi rice dish for lunch.
en.notes: 丼（どんぶり）can mean a deep bowl or a rice dish served in such a bowl. With 食べる, the dish is meant, not the tableware. In compound dish names you often hear どん, as in 牛丼: gyūdon. The full reading on this card remains donburi.

examples[].german: I made a bento.
I took a bento and went to the park.
en.notes: 弁当 is a prepared meal in a box, for example to take along. It means the food together with how it is put together; the empty box is called 弁当箱. With the polite お the form is お弁当. 弁当を作る is to prepare a bento, 弁当を持って行く is to take one along.

examples[].german: I bought two rice balls.
At school I ate the rice balls my mother made.
en.notes: おにぎり are shaped portions of rice, often triangular and sometimes filled. "Rice ball" names the food, not necessarily a round ball. 二つ counts two pieces here. A description such as 母が作った names the person who prepared them.

examples[].german: I eat udon noodles.
In winter I want to eat udon.
en.notes: うどん are thick Japanese wheat noodles. うどんを食べる refers to actual eating; うどんが食べたい expresses the wish for it. たい attaches to the verb stem and means "want to", not an action that has already begun. The kana spelling is usual for this food.

examples[].german: I like soba noodles.
I ate cold soba noodles.
en.notes: そば here means soba noodles made from buckwheat. The kanji spelling 蕎麦 makes the food meaning clear. The identically pronounced そば meaning "nearby" is a different word. 冷たいそば means noodles served cold, not a cold place nearby.

examples[].german: The sashimi is fresh.
The three of us shared the sashimi.
en.notes: 刺身 is sashimi, sliced raw fish or other raw seafood. 新鮮です judges the freshness of the food. 刺身を分ける means dividing a portion among several people. The card does not say which kind of fish is used.

en.meaning: teacher; respectful title for teachers, doctors, etc.
examples[].german: The teacher is very kind.
I ask the teacher a question.
Doctor, my throat hurts.
en.notes: Used as an occupational term and as a form of address for teachers, but also for doctors, for example. A name can come directly before it: 田中先生. When stating your own occupation, you normally say 教師です or 教員です rather than calling yourself by the honorific 先生.

examples[].german: I get off at the next station.
Let's get off here.
After getting off the bus, I walk.
en.notes: When getting off, the vehicle often takes を and the place of getting off takes で: バスを降りる, 駅で降りる. 降りる is nonetheless intransitive and belongs to the ichidan group; the te-form is 降りて. The reading おりる must not be confused with 降る（ふる）"to fall, to rain".

examples[].german: Let's go eat sushi.
I made sushi at home.
en.notes: 寿司 is sushi, a dish of seasoned vinegared rice with various toppings. It does not always contain raw fish. 寿司を食べに行く means going out to eat sushi; 寿司を作る describes preparing it. With the polite お you also hear お寿司.

examples[].german: I ate yakitori.
Let's go eat yakitori.
en.notes: 焼き鳥 is yakitori, grilled meat on skewers, usually chicken. 焼き鳥を食べました reports a meal. 食べに行きましょう, on the other hand, invites someone to go out together for this food. The word names no particular shop and no particular seasoning.

examples[].german: I boil water.
Please pour hot water into the cup.
en.notes: お湯 is hot water. お湯を沸かす is the fixed combination for heating or boiling water. カップにお湯を入れる describes pouring it in afterward; に names the vessel. The polite お belongs to the usual word, and the full reading is おゆ.

examples[].german: Ice water, please.
I cooled the drink with ice water.
en.notes: 氷水 is water with ice or very cold ice water. 氷水をください orders it as a drink. With 氷水で冷やす it can also be used to cool other things. The reading of this card is こおりみず, kōrimizu; other dictionary readings are not confused with it.

examples[].german: Let's raise a toast!
At the party I said "Cheers!"
en.notes: 乾杯 is the call "Cheers!" and can also refer to the act of clinking glasses. 乾杯しましょう invites people to toast together. 乾杯と言う quotes the call. The combination with する uses the noun; it is not an independent godan verb.

en.meaning: thank you for the meal (said after eating)
examples[].german: Thank you for the meal. (after eating)
In a note to my mother I wrote "thank you for the meal".
en.notes: ご馳走様 thanks someone for the food after a meal. The kana spelling ごちそうさま is also common. With でした it becomes the polite longer form ご馳走様でした. Besides thanking someone directly, the short formula can also be written in a message to the person who cooked. ご馳走さま is another spelling of the short formula of thanks.

examples[].german: I put on a sweater.
Can this sweater be washed in the washing machine?
en.notes: セーター is a sweater. セーターを着る means to put it on or wear it, depending on the verb form. With 洗濯機で洗えますか you ask whether it is machine washable; で names the appliance. The long katakana vowels are shown with macrons in sētā.

examples[].german: Please put on your coat.
I hung my coat on a hanger.
en.notes: コート here is a coat. The identically sounding word for a sports court is a different word. コートを着る means to put on a coat; ハンガーに掛ける means to hang it on a hanger. The reading kōto contains a long o.

examples[].german: I am wearing gloves.
You need gloves in winter.
en.notes: 手袋 are gloves or mittens. 手袋をする is the usual combination for putting them on or wearing them. 手袋をしています describes the state of wearing them. 手袋が必要です says they are needed, without naming a particular number of pairs.

examples[].german: Please turn right.
I turn left at the next corner.
This road bends near the river.
en.notes: When turning, に indicates the direction: 右に曲がる, 左に曲がる. The corner passed through can take を, even though 曲がる is intransitive. The verb also means "to bend, to be curved"; for actively bending an object, 曲げる is used. The te-form is 曲がって. The shortened dictionary spelling 曲る has the same reading まがる; in your own writing, 曲がる is the usual spelling.

examples[].german: I wrap a scarf around my neck.
I got this scarf from my mother.
en.notes: マフラー here means a scarf. マフラーを巻く describes wrapping it around the neck; 母からもらう names the source of a gift. The similar-sounding word for an exhaust muffler is not meant in these contexts. In mafurā, the last a is long.

examples[].german: I tie my necktie.
I have to wear a necktie.
en.notes: ネクタイ is a necktie. ネクタイを締める means to put it on or tie it; ネクタイをする means to wear it. しなければなりません expresses an obligation. It does not automatically say whether one is already wearing a tie.

examples[].german: Do you have a handkerchief?
I dried my hands with a handkerchief.
en.notes: ハンカチ is a cloth handkerchief. 持っていますか asks whether someone has one with them. With ハンカチで手をふく you can dry your hands. It is not the usual word for a paper tissue; for that you hear ティッシュ.

examples[].german: I received a ring.
What a pretty ring!
en.notes: 指輪 is a finger ring as jewelry. 指輪をもらう means to receive a ring; きれいな指輪 praises its appearance. The word alone does not say whether it is a wedding ring. Before 指輪, the na-adjective きれい takes な.

examples[].german: I wear glasses.
I can't see without my glasses.
en.notes: 眼鏡 is a pair of glasses. 眼鏡をかける means to put them on; 眼鏡をかけています means to be wearing them. 眼鏡をかけないと見えません expresses "I can't see without glasses" as a condition. The figurative meaning of good judgment is not intended here.

examples[].german: What is in the bag?
I want to buy a new bag.
en.notes: 鞄 is a bag, for example for carrying personal items. The kana spelling かばん is also common. 鞄の中に asks about its contents; 鞄を買いたい expresses a wish to get one. The word does not refer to a trouser pocket.

examples[].german: I wash the dishes.
There is cake on the plate.
en.notes: 皿 is a plate or a flat serving dish. 皿を洗う describes washing up, 皿の上に the place of a food on it. As a counter, 皿 can also count a portion; here the examples are ordinary objects. The card reading is さら.

examples[].german: I put rice in the bowl.
I got this bowl from my grandmother.
en.notes: 茶碗 can be a rice bowl or a teacup. In 茶碗にご飯を入れる a rice bowl is meant; に names the container. 茶碗をもらう describes receiving such a piece of tableware. The ちゃ in ちゃわん forms a single mora. 茶わん and the kana form ちゃわん also refer to the same item.

examples[].german: I brew tea in the teapot.
I lost the lid of the teapot.
en.notes: 急須 is a small teapot for brewing and pouring tea. 急須でお茶を入れる names it as the device used for preparation. 急須のふた is its lid; の connects the part with the object. The reading きゅうす is kyūsu, with a long vowel in きゅう.

examples[].german: I turn on the fan.
The breeze from the fan feels nice.
en.notes: 扇風機 is an electric fan. 扇風機を回す means to run it; the verb describes the rotating motion. 扇風機の風 names the air flow of the device. The reading せんぷうき has a long u: senpūki.

examples[].german: I cross the bridge.
Please cross the street.
I crossed the river by boat.
en.notes: With 渡る, the road, river or bridge crossed takes を: 橋を渡る, 川を渡る. This を marks the space traversed; 渡る remains intransitive. For the means of transport, で is usual, such as 船で. This godan verb forms 渡って.

examples[].german: First, I will introduce myself.
At first I didn't understand Japanese, but now I understand a little.
en.notes: 最初 means beginning or first. 最初に names the first step of a sequence. 最初は, by contrast, describes the state at the beginning, often in comparison with later. With 最初の, the word can also modify a noun, for example 最初の日.

examples[].german: I will do my best until the end.
When was the last time we met?
en.notes: 最後 is the end or the last time. 最後まで means until the end and marks the limit of an activity. 最後に can mean "lastly", for example at the last meeting. For the last piece or the last person, 最後の stands before the noun.

examples[].german: I have been busy lately.
I recently bought a new bicycle.
en.notes: 最近 means recently or lately. It can refer to a state that is still continuing or to a single recent event. It does not fix an exact number of days. 最近の before a noun means, for example, "the latest" or "the more recent".

examples[].german: What do you want to be in the future?
In the future I want to live in Japan.
en.notes: 将来 is the future, often with a view to later life plans. 将来何になりたいですか asks about a future occupation or role. 将来、日本に住みたい states a wish for later in life. It does not fix a concrete date such as tomorrow or next year.

examples[].german: I went to Japan last year.
Last summer was very hot.
en.notes: 去年 is the year before the current year. It can stand as a time expression without a particle: 去年行きました. With の it refers to a part of that year, such as 去年の夏. The reading きょねん contains きょ as a single mora and no long vowel.

examples[].german: I'll come again next year.
Next year I will start university.
en.notes: 来年 is the year after the current year. As a time expression it often needs no particle, but it can become the topic with は. また来ます announces another visit; 大学に入ります the start at a university. No particular month is meant.

examples[].german: Let's go together next time.
This time I did it well.
en.notes: 今度 can mean the next time or this time. In an invitation it often looks ahead to an upcoming occasion. In 今度は上手にできました, by contrast, it is about this successful attempt as opposed to earlier ones. The verb tense and the context help you choose.

examples[].german: It is exactly three o'clock.
It's just the right size, isn't it?
en.notes: 丁度 is the kanji spelling of the common ちょうど. With a clock time it means "exactly"; with いい it judges a size or amount as fitting. It modifies the following word as an adverb and takes no な. The reading remains chōdo with a long o.

examples[].german: It suddenly rained.
It suddenly started to rain.
The phone call was suddenly cut off, so I called back.
en.notes: 急に here describes a sudden, unexpected event. It stands before the process described, for example 急に雨が降る. It does not simply say that someone acts quickly on purpose; 急いで may fit for that.
