The whole combination きゅうに is practiced as an adverb. For a noun, 急な is used instead, for example 急な予定変更.

examples[].german: I occasionally watch a movie.
Once in a while I go to see a movie.
Occasionally I finish work early, so on those days I eat dinner with my family.
en.notes: 偶に means "once in a while, occasionally" and describes a low frequency. It fits recurring activities or exceptions to the daily routine. The kana spelling たまに is very common in ordinary text. It means neither "by chance" in the sense of a random event nor "every time".

examples[].german: This house is big.
This dog is big.
This bag is big, so a lot fits in it.
en.notes: 大きい is an i-adjective: 大きい家, 家が大きい. Here it describes physical size; for a person's height, 背が高い is usual. 大きな also stands before nouns, but is not used as a sentence predicate with です. The negative is 大きくない.

examples[].german: I completely forgot.
I had completely forgotten.
The snow has completely melted, so I can walk on the road now.
en.notes: すっかり means "completely, entirely". It emphasizes, for example, total forgetting or a completed change. すっかり忘れていた describes the state of having completely forgotten something. すっかり溶けた says that none of the snow in question is left. It does not merely mean "very" in every adjective sentence.

examples[].german: This outfit fits perfectly.
These shoes fit perfectly.
I arrived at exactly five o'clock.
en.notes: ぴったり means "fitting exactly" and also "exact". Clothes or shoes can be ぴったり when the size is right. 五時ぴったりに着く means "to arrive at exactly five o'clock". The small っ is rendered as a double t in pittari. A fitting garment does not automatically have to be uncomfortably tight.

examples[].german: I spent the time leisurely.
On days off I spend my time leisurely.
I don't have work today, so I will take it easy at home.
en.notes: のんびり describes a relaxed time without haste. Before a verb it names the manner of the activity, for example のんびり過ごす. With する, のんびりする means "to relax, to take it easy". It can describe a pleasant break and does not automatically mean laziness. The reading is written nonbiri, with n before b.

examples[].german: Please say it clearly.
You can see the mountains clearly today.
The plans still aren't settled.
en.notes: はっきり means "clear, distinct". It can concern pronunciation or visibility. はっきりする also means that something is settled or becomes clear; はっきりしない means that it is still unclear. The request はっきり言ってください can ask for clear pronunciation or an unambiguous statement, depending on the conversation.

examples[].german: Please eat properly.
Do your homework properly.
This clock is working properly.
en.notes: ちゃんと means "properly, reliably, sufficiently", depending on the context. With eating it asks for a proper or sufficient meal, with homework for careful work. ちゃんと動く says that something works as it should. It is colloquial; しなさい sounds like a clear instruction, for example from a parent to a child.

examples[].german: Please come as early as possible.
For my health, I take the stairs whenever possible.
en.notes: なるべく means "as much as possible, as far as it goes". It expresses a goal and allows for practical limits. なるべく早く asks for the earliest time possible; なるべく階段を使う means taking the stairs when it is practicable. It does not demand the same action without exception under all circumstances. 成るべく is also recorded; the kana form なるべく is usual.

en.meaning: to tidy up; to finish off
examples[].german: Please tidy up the room.
I will finish today's work first and then go home.
en.notes: 片付ける means "to tidy up, to put away" and, with work, also "to get done". A room takes を as the area being tidied; 今日の仕事を片付ける means finishing off the tasks. This ichidan verb forms 片付けます and 片付けて. The reading contains づ, which in Hepburn is written zu: katazukeru.

examples[].german: I throw away the trash.
Please throw away the old newspapers.
Please do not throw trash here. Take it home with you.
en.notes: 捨てる means "to throw away, to dispose of". The thing thrown away takes を. A place can follow with に: ここにゴミを捨てる. 捨てないでください prohibits throwing things away at this spot. This ichidan verb forms 捨てます and 捨てて; it does not simply describe dropping something by accident.

examples[].german: I picked up a wallet.
I picked up some money on the street.
I picked up the trash in the park and put it in a bag.
en.notes: 拾う means "to pick up, to gather". It can concern an object that has been found or collecting trash while cleaning. The thing takes を, the place where it is found or the work is done takes で. This godan verb forms 拾います and 拾って. Picking up a wallet does not say that it belongs to oneself.

en.meaning: to get used to; to become tame (馴れる)
examples[].german: I have gotten used to life in Japan.
Have you gotten used to life in Japan?
I practiced every day and got used to driving.
The cat that ran away at first has gradually become tame around people.
This bird is not yet used to people, so it flees when you get close.
en.notes: 慣れる means to get used to something or to become familiar with it. What one gets used to stands before に. Practice can lead to familiarity with an activity. For an animal that becomes tame or trusting, the spelling 馴れる is especially encountered; here 人に names the people the animal becomes more familiar with. This intransitive ichidan verb describes the change in the animal itself and forms なれます and なれて.

examples[].german: There is a small cat.
A small child is crying.
en.notes: 小さい is an i-adjective and describes small size: 小さい猫. For children it can also mean "still young, little". 小さな is an alternative form directly before a noun; as a sentence predicate, use 小さいです. The negative is 小さくない.

examples[].german: You look like your mother.
These two people look very much alike, don't they?
The pronunciation of these two words is similar.
en.notes: 似る means "to resemble". The point of comparison takes に: お母さんに似ている. For an existing resemblance, 似ている is usually appropriate. The similarity can concern appearance, characteristics or pronunciation. This ichidan verb forms 似ます and 似て; a similarity does not mean that two things are identical.

examples[].german: The weather has changed.
The name of the station has changed, so I can't tell on the old map.
en.notes: 変わる describes something changing. The thing that changes takes が, without the sentence having to name an agent who causes it. The counterpart 変える means to change something oneself, with を. 変わる is godan: 変わります, 変わって. When a name changes, an old map may therefore no longer fit.

examples[].german: Have you decided?
Let's decide on the day of the trip.
en.notes: 決める means "to decide, to fix". A chosen date or content takes を; a question such as 何にするか can state what is being decided. 決めましょう invites a joint decision. This ichidan verb forms 決めます and 決めて. 決まる, by contrast, describes that something is settled.

examples[].german: I collect stamps.
Collecting stamps is my hobby.
Before the trip, I gathered everyone's opinions.
en.notes: 集める means "to collect, to gather". It fits a collection of objects and also information or opinions. The thing collected takes を. 集めています can describe a regular collecting activity. This ichidan verb forms 集めます and 集めて; 集まる describes coming together without the same active collector.

examples[].german: I broke the window.
Please do not break the toy.
I worked too much and ruined my health.
en.notes: 壊す means "to break, to destroy". The thing affected takes を. It can also mean to damage one's health: 体を壊す means to become unwell. This godan verb forms 壊します and 壊して. 壊れる describes something breaking; 壊す names the damaging action or cause on the acting side.

examples[].german: The computer has broken.
This chair is old, so it looks like it will break soon.
en.notes: 壊れる means "to break" or "to stop working". The thing affected takes が. A computer can lose its function, an old chair can fall apart. 壊れそうです describes an expected danger, not yet an actual break. This intransitive ichidan verb forms 壊れます and 壊れて.

examples[].german: I am repairing the bicycle.
I had the watch repaired.
I corrected the mistake in the essay.
en.notes: 直す means "to repair, to correct". The thing repaired or the mistake corrected takes を. 直してもらう says that someone else took over the repair for one. This godan verb forms 直します and 直して. The whole expression 書き直す, as a compound verb, has its own usage and accent.

en.meaning: to be fixed; to be corrected
examples[].german: The bicycle is fixed, so I can use it again.
The mistake in this sentence has already been corrected.
en.notes: 直る describes something being in order again: a repaired bicycle or a corrected mistake. The thing affected takes が. It is an intransitive godan verb: 直ります, 直って. 直す, by contrast, means repairing or correcting something oneself. For recovering from an illness, the spelling 治る is usual.

examples[].german: The laundry has dried.
The rain stopped and the road dried quickly.
en.notes: 乾く means "to become dry". The thing drying takes が: 洗濯物が乾く. It names the process or its result, without anyone drying as an agent. For deliberate drying, 乾かす is used. 乾く is godan and forms 乾きます and 乾いて; thirst is expressed with the differently written 渇く.

examples[].german: I got wet in the rain.
My clothes got wet in the rain.
Water spilled from the glass and the desk got wet.
en.notes: 濡れる means "to get wet". The thing that got wet takes が, a cause like rain takes で. Spilled water can also cause it. This ichidan verb forms 濡れます and 濡れて. 濡れている describes the wet state, not necessarily the moment of getting wet. The kana spelling ぬれる denotes the same verb.

examples[].german: I bought a new car.
I want to buy new shoes.
The new teacher starts today.
en.notes: 新しい can mean "newly made or bought" as well as "newly added": 新しい車, 新しい先生. It is an i-adjective and stands directly before the noun. The past form is 新しかった; the opposite for things is 古い.

examples[].german: It shook in the earthquake.
The building shook in the earthquake.
The curtain is swaying slowly in the wind.
en.notes: 揺れる means "to move, to sway, to shake". The thing moving takes が; 地震で names an earthquake as the cause, 風で the wind. The movement can be violent or go slowly back and forth. This intransitive ichidan verb forms 揺れます and 揺れて. It does not say that someone deliberately shakes the object.

examples[].german: The flower has withered.
The flower has unfortunately withered.
The grass withered from the summer heat, and the garden turned brown.
en.notes: 枯れる describes plants withering or dying. The plant takes が. 枯れてしまった can express regret that it has withered. It is an intransitive Ichidan verb: 枯れます, 枯れて. The word is not the general "to dry" used for laundry or a road.

en.meaning: to raise, to bring up; to grow (plants)
examples[].german: I am growing vegetables.
Raising children is hard work.
en.notes: 育てる means "to raise" or to promote growth. It fits children and also plants, such as vegetables in the garden. The thing cared for or raised takes を. This transitive ichidan verb forms 育てます and 育てて. 育つ, by contrast, describes something growing; 育てる does not automatically mean genetic breeding.

examples[].german: I planted flowers.
I planted flowers in the garden.
I want to plant a tree in the garden and create a place where I can rest in summer.
en.notes: 植える means "to plant": one sets a plant or seed in a place. The plant takes を, the place takes に. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 植えます, 植えて. 植える denotes the planting itself; 育てる describes the subsequent care and raising.

examples[].german: The snow has melted.
The ice cream has unfortunately melted.
The sugar dissolved in the water.
en.notes: 溶ける describes something melting or dissolving in a liquid. The substance affected takes が; 水に names the water in which it dissolves. It is intransitive: 溶けます, 溶けて. 雪が溶ける concerns warmth, 砂糖が水に溶ける concerns dissolving. 溶けてしまう can express regret about melted ice cream.

examples[].german: The water has frozen.
This lake freezes over in winter.
en.notes: 凍る means "to freeze, to freeze over". Water or a lake takes が as the thing that freezes. It is an intransitive Godan verb even though it ends in る: 凍ります, 凍って. The reading こおる has a long o: kōru. 冬になると describes, in a suitable context, a regularly occurring result, not a claim about every lake.

examples[].german: The water has boiled.
When the water boils, please turn off the heat.
en.notes: 沸く describes water starting to boil or boiling. The water takes が: お湯が沸く. It is intransitive; 沸かす, by contrast, means bringing water to a boil. This godan verb forms 沸きます and 沸いて. 沸いたら names here the point from which the heat should be turned off.

en.meaning: to fry, to grill, to bake
examples[].german: I grill the meat.
Let's grill the meat.
I baked a cake in the oven and took it to a friend's birthday.
en.notes: 焼く denotes frying, grilling, baking or roasting with heat. The food prepared takes を; オーブンで names the appliance. It does not mean boiling something in water. This transitive godan verb forms 焼きます and 焼いて. Whether to translate it as "fry" or "bake" depends on the food and the preparation.

examples[].german: I simmer the vegetables.
I am simmering the vegetables.
If you simmer meat for a long time over low heat, it becomes tender.
en.notes: 煮る means to cook, simmer or braise food in liquid. The food takes を. The Ichidan verb forms 煮ます and 煮て. 野菜を煮ている can describe cooking that is going on right now. 弱い火で is about low heat; 煮る does not always require vigorously boiling water. It is a different word from 似る "to resemble".

examples[].german: Please mix it well.
Please toss the salad.
If you mix red and white paint, you get pink.
en.notes: 混ぜる means "to mix, to blend, to stir". The things mixed take を; と can connect two ingredients. For a liquid "stir" fits, for salad or paint "mix" often fits. The Ichidan verb forms 混ぜます and 混ぜて. よく混ぜてください asks for thorough mixing without naming a particular ingredient itself.

examples[].german: This building is old.
I looked at old photos.
en.notes: 古い describes old things or something from long ago: 古い建物, 古い写真. For a person's old age, you normally use 年を取っている rather than 古い. This i-adjective forms 古くない and 古かった; the opposite for new things is 新しい.

examples[].german: I wrap the present.
I wrapped the present.
I wrapped the glass in newspaper so that it would not break.
en.notes: 包む means "to wrap, to pack". The thing wrapped takes を; the material can follow with で. A present is wrapped for handing over, a glass to protect it from breaking. This godan verb forms 包みます and 包んで. 包む does not automatically mean using a solid box; paper or cloth is enough in a suitable context.

examples[].german: I count from one to ten.
Please count the money.
en.notes: 数える means "to count". One can recite a sequence of numbers or count objects or money. The thing counted takes を; から and まで give the start and end of a sequence. It is an Ichidan verb: 数えます, 数えて. The verb stays the same even though different counters are needed when stating the result.

examples[].german: I compare the two.
I compared the two prices.
Compared with last year, this year is warm.
en.notes: 比べる means "to compare". AとBを比べる names both objects of comparison; Aと比べると sets A as the point of comparison for the following statement. One can compare prices or compare today's state with earlier. This transitive ichidan verb forms 比べます and 比べて. Comparing alone does not yet say that one has decided.

examples[].german: I bow.
At the start of class you stand up and bow to the teacher.
The shop assistant said "Thank you very much" and bowed.
en.notes: お辞儀 means "bow". お辞儀をする or お辞儀する means "to bow"; に names the person one bows to. It occurs in greetings and when thanking. In the school routine 起立、礼、着席 one first stands up, bows and then sits down. The spellings お辞儀 and 御辞儀 refer to the same word here.

examples[].german: Let's greet each other.
In the morning I greeted my neighbor.
At the start of the ceremony, the principal gave a short address.
en.notes: 挨拶 means "greeting" and can also refer to a short speech of welcome at an event. With する it becomes "to greet" or "to give a short address". The person greeted takes に. 朝の挨拶 concerns the everyday greeting; 校長先生の挨拶 a speech by the school principal. The kana reading is あいさつ, without a small っ.

examples[].german: It feels good.
Let's respect other people's feelings.
en.notes: 気持ち denotes a feeling, a sensation or a mood. 気持ちがいい means "it feels pleasant", for example with pleasant air or movement. 相手の気持ち, by contrast, concerns the inner experience of the other person. 気持ちを大切にする means to take their feelings seriously. The noun here is not the similarly written adjective 気持ちいい.

examples[].german: Please don't worry.
I am worried about the exam.
en.notes: 心配 denotes worry or concern. 心配する means "to worry"; 心配しないでください tries to reassure someone. In 試験のことが心配です, the exam stands with が as the object of the worry. With the verb, 試験のことを心配する is also possible. 心配な顔 is a worried face; the form before a noun needs な here.

examples[].german: I am relieved.
I was relieved that the test was over.
At this store I can shop with peace of mind.
en.notes: 安心 denotes reassurance or a feeling of security. 安心する means "to be reassured, to be relieved". After a stressful task, 安心した can express relief. 安心して買い物ができる, by contrast, describes being able to shop with confidence. 安心して names the inner attitude; it is not an objective guarantee that every risk is excluded.

examples[].german: Please be patient.
Please be patient a little longer.
There was something I wanted, but I held back and did not spend the money.
en.notes: 我慢 means "to endure" or "to hold oneself back", with する as the verb. A request like 我慢してください asks someone to put up with an unpleasant situation a little longer. It can also mean doing without something one wants. 我慢 is therefore not just waiting for the next person; the context shows which burden or which desire is meant.

examples[].german: Please don't push yourself too hard.
That is impossible.
en.notes: 無理です can mean "that's impossible, that won't work", for example when time or means are lacking. 無理する, by contrast, means taking on too much or overexerting oneself. 無理しないでください is a request to limit one's own strain. Before a noun, な is often used: 無理な計画, an unworkable plan.

examples[].german: This mountain is high.
These clothes are expensive.
en.notes: 高い means both height and a high price. 山が高い means "the mountain is high", 服が高い "the clothes are expensive"; 背が高い means "tall in stature". Depending on the meaning, the opposites are 低い "low" and 安い "cheap".

examples[].german: It is a special day.
Today is a special day.
Today, as a special exception, we will finish class early.
en.notes: 特別 means "special". Before a noun, 特別な is usual: 特別な日, a special day. 特別に can say that something is done differently as an exception. 特別に授業を早く終わる describes a deviation from the normal routine. "Special" here does not automatically mean "very" before any adjective.

examples[].german: I want to live a normal life.
I like a normal life.
Only local trains stop at this station.
en.notes: 普通 describes what is normal or ordinary. Before a noun, の is very common: 普通の生活, a normal life. In rail contexts, 普通 also means the local train that stops at all the designated stations. 普通しか止まらない means in this context that only such trains stop there. The long final syllable is written futsū in Hepburn.

examples[].german: Please go to the other side.
I am against it.
en.notes: 反対 can mean "opposite" spatially or "against" in a discussion. 反対側 is the opposite or other side. 私は反対です expresses opposition to a proposal. With する, Aに反対する means "to speak out against A". The context separates a statement of place from an opinion; an opposite side is not an objecting person.

examples[].german: Please feel free to use it.
I have free time on the weekend.
en.notes: 自由 means "free, freedom". 自由に使う allows use at one's own discretion; 自由な時間 is time one can dispose of oneself. Before a noun, な is used here, for the manner of an action に. 自由 does not automatically mean "free of charge"; there is 無料 for that. The reading じゆう ends with a long u: jiyū.

examples[].german: Where is the bus stop?
I am waiting at the bus stop.
en.notes: バス停 is a bus stop. どこですか asks about its location; で marks an activity there, such as waiting. The mixed spelling バス停 combines the katakana word バス with 停, read てい. バス停 refers to the stopping point, not the bus itself and not necessarily a large bus terminal.

examples[].german: The ticket office is over there.
A long line has formed in front of the ticket office.
en.notes: 切符売り場 is the place where you buy tickets, whether travel or admission tickets. In these examples the ticket office is meant. 売り場 is the place of sale; 切符 says what is sold. の前に describes the area in front, for example for a queue. The word does not refer to the ticket gate you pass through to reach the platform.

examples[].german: I go through the ticket gate.
I go through the ticket gate to the platform.
I am waiting for a friend outside the ticket gate.
en.notes: 改札口 is the entrance with the ticket check, often with barriers between the entrance area and the platforms. 改札口を通る means to pass this checkpoint; を marks the place passed through here. 改札口の外 is the area outside. It is a handy meeting point, but not a counter for buying tickets.

examples[].german: Please go to platform 3.
The train arrives at platform three.
en.notes: ホーム means "platform" here. 三番ホーム is platform three, which one can go to or where a train can arrive. に names the destination in both examples. The pronunciation has a long o: hōmu. This word comes from "platform" and in a railway context is not the similar-sounding English "home" meaning a residence.

examples[].german: Which vehicle will you go by?
Which vehicle do you like?
en.notes: 乗り物 is a vehicle or means of transport that one travels in. どの乗り物 asks which one among several is meant. With で it names the transport used, with が in 好きです the preferred one. The word says nothing yet about schedule or propulsion; bus, train and bicycle are possible examples.

examples[].german: Please cross the pedestrian bridge.
You can see Mt. Fuji well from this pedestrian bridge.
en.notes: 歩道橋 is a pedestrian bridge, often over a road. 歩道橋を渡る means to cross it; を marks the path that is crossed. 歩道橋から names it as the starting point of the view. The word means a bridge for pedestrians and not just the sidewalk at the edge of the road. The long vowels are written hodōkyō.

examples[].german: This restaurant is cheap.
Do you know a cheap shop?
This bag cost a thousand yen and was cheap.
en.notes: 安い here means "inexpensive, good value" and refers to the price, not automatically to poor quality. 安い店 is a shop with low prices. This i-adjective forms 安かった and 安くない. For "easy to do", on the other hand, the verb suffix ～やすい is used.

examples[].german: I park my bicycle at the bicycle parking area.
Please park your bicycle at the bicycle parking area.
The bicycle parking area at the station was full, so I looked for another place.
en.notes: 駐輪場 is an area for parking bicycles. With に you name the parking place, with で an activity there. The word differs from 駐車場, the parking lot for cars and, in the right context, other vehicles. By itself it gives no information on whether the bicycle parking is free. The reading is chūrinjō.

examples[].german: I wait at the railroad crossing.
If you cross the railroad crossing, the post office is on the right.
en.notes: 踏切 is a railroad crossing where a road or path crosses the tracks at the same level. で names the place of an activity such as waiting, を names a path that is crossed. You do not normally board the train there; for that you go to the station and platform. In these examples only the railroad crossing is meant.

examples[].german: I shop at the shopping street.
I shopped at the shopping street.
The shops in the shopping street are open on Sundays too.
en.notes: 商店街 is a shopping street or a district with many shops. で names it as the place of shopping. の describes something within this shopping area, such as 商店街の店. It does not have to be a single shopping mall; it often includes several small, independent shops. The long first syllable is written shōtengai.

examples[].german: My back hurts.
My back itches, but I can't reach it with my hand.
en.notes: 背中 is the back as a part of the body. With が one names it, for example, as the place of pain or itching. 背中がかゆいのに connects the itch with the unexpected difficulty of reaching the spot. The word here denotes neither the rear part of a building nor in general everything that lies "behind".

examples[].german: My lower back hurts.
My lower back hurts, so I'm going to rest.
I put my hand on my hip for the photo.
en.notes: 腰 refers to the lower back or the area around the waist and hips. 腰が痛い is commonly understood in everyday speech as "I have back pain"; it does not have to mean the hip joint specifically. 腰に names a position on this part of the body. The body-part sense practiced here is not コシ, the firmness of noodles or paper.

examples[].german: I sprained my ankle.
I sprained my ankle.
My socks are short, so my ankles are showing.
en.notes: 足首 is the ankle joint, or the area around the ankle connecting foot and lower leg. 足首をひねる means to twist or roll it. The form with を names the affected spot; 足首が見える says it is visible. It does not mean the whole foot, even though 足 is in the word.

examples[].german: The skin is dry.
In winter my skin starts to itch.
en.notes: 皮膚 is skin as body tissue. It is more technical than the common everyday word 肌, which often stresses the visible condition of the skin. 皮膚が乾燥している describes dry skin; かゆくなる describes a change toward itching. The word alone does not name a cause or a particular skin disease.

examples[].german: I am bleeding.
I cut my finger and it bled.
Blood got on my shirt, so I washed it right away.
en.notes: 血 means "blood". 血が出る is the usual combination for "to bleed"; the blood takes が as what comes out. 血が付く describes blood sticking to something, such as a shirt. The reading of the single word is ち; in compound words the same kanji can be read differently.

examples[].german: This road is long.
This movie is long.
en.notes: 長い describes spatial length and duration in time: 長い道, 長い映画. It is an i-adjective and forms 長くない and 長かった. For the height of a mountain or person, 高い is used; the opposite of 長い is 短い. 永い is another spelling for length of time. For spatial length, such as a long road, 長い is used.

examples[].german: I sweated.
I exercised and worked up a sweat.
I wiped the sweat off my face with a towel.
en.notes: 汗 is sweat. The usual combination 汗をかく means "to sweat"; かく in this combination does not mean "to write". 汗を拭く means to wipe off the sweat. 運動して can name the preceding activity. The examples concern sweat on the body, not condensation on a cold glass.

examples[].german: It's hard for me to breathe.
Please breathe deeply.
en.notes: 息 is breath or breathing. 息をする means "to breathe"; 息が苦しい describes difficulty breathing. 深く息をする asks for deep breathing and does not by itself mean only breathing in. For "to breathe in" 息を吸う is more exact, for "to breathe out" 息を吐く. In these examples physical breathing is meant.

examples[].german: My cough won't stop.
When you have a cough, please wear a mask.
en.notes: 咳 means "cough" as a noun. 咳が出る describes having to cough; 咳が止まらない, that the cough does not stop. 咳をする is also a common combination. ときは names, in the second sentence, the situation in which the request to wear a mask applies. The word itself does not specify any cause of illness.

examples[].german: I got hurt.
I got injured playing soccer.
My injury has healed, so I can walk to school again.
en.notes: 怪我 is an injury. 怪我をする and 怪我する mean "to get injured". で can name the occasion, such as サッカーで. It is not the general word for illness; an injury can come from a fall or an accident. The kanji are read as the word けが, not assembled individually from their usual readings.

examples[].german: My grandfather is well.
My grandfather is eighty years old.
en.notes: 祖父 means "grandfather" and is used especially when talking to others about one's own grandfather. When addressing him directly, おじいさん or おじいちゃん is usual. 祖父は元気です describes his well-being; 八十歳 names his age. When speaking about one's own family, this plain family term usually takes no さん.

examples[].german: I played with my cousin.
My cousin lives in Osaka; I see him during the summer vacation.
en.notes: 従兄弟 means a male cousin in this spelling. The reading いとこ is often written in kana in everyday use and, depending on the context, can also be used without regard to gender. For a female cousin there is the spelling 従姉妹. With と you name the person you play with; に in 夏休みに gives the time of the meeting.

examples[].german: My nephew came.
My nephew is five years old.
en.notes: 甥 is a nephew, that is, the son of one's own brother or sister. It is a male kinship term; 姪 means niece. 甥が来た reports his arrival, 甥は五歳です his age. The reading おい contains two separate vowels and is written oi.

examples[].german: I am a university student.
There are a lot of students.
Can students buy this ticket at a discount?
en.notes: Mainly used for people studying at universities and colleges; depending on context it can be broader. For school pupils, 生徒 is more accurate, and for elementary school children, 児童. Common in 大学生, 学生生活 and 学生証. 学生の＋noun assigns something to the student sphere.

examples[].german: My hair is short.
I'm using a short pencil.
The lunch break is short.
en.notes: 短い means "short" in terms of length or duration: 短い髪, 短い休み. It does not refer to small size in general; 小さい is used for that. This i-adjective forms 短くない and 短かった; its opposite is 長い.

examples[].german: My niece is five years old.
I gave my niece a present.
en.notes: 姪 is a niece, that is, the daughter of one's own brother or sister. 甥 is the male counterpart, "nephew". 姪にプレゼントをあげる names the recipient with に and the present with を. The reading めい is written mei; here it is not a single long e in the Hepburn spelling.

examples[].german: I am still single.
Mr. Tanaka is still single.
Unmarried people can also take part in this meeting.
en.notes: 独身 means "unmarried, single". By itself it does not say whether someone lives alone or is in a relationship at all. Before a noun, use の: 独身の人. まだ独身です stresses "still"; without まだ the statement is more neutral. The word describes current marital status and does not prove that someone was never married.

examples[].german: They are a happily married couple.
That couple gets along very well.
That couple opened a small shop together.
en.notes: 夫婦 means a married couple and refers to both married partners together. 仲の良い夫婦 describes their good relationship; 夫婦で can say that they do something together as a couple. It is not a general word for two friends. The reading ふうふ has a long u: fūfu.

examples[].german: They are twin brothers.
I celebrated the twins' birthday.
en.notes: 双子 refers to twins as a pair or to a single twin child. With の you describe the relationship: 双子の兄弟 are twin brothers. Even for a joint birthday party, 双子 remains an ordinary noun; it needs no separate plural ending.

examples[].german: A baby was born.
The baby is crying.
en.notes: 赤ちゃん is the usual word for a baby. The ちゃん is part of the whole word here; the meaning is not literally "little red". 赤ちゃんが生まれる reports a birth, and 赤ちゃんが泣いている describes a baby that is crying right now. The kana form あかちゃん has the same meaning and reading.

examples[].german: I want to become an adult.
Adults are 1,000 yen.
en.notes: The reading of 大人 is おとな. With 大人になる you talk about growing up. On price lists, 大人 is the category "adults": in 大人は千円です the admission price is meant, even though 料金 is not stated explicitly.

examples[].german: It is popular with young people.
Young people are playing sports in the park.
en.notes: 若者 can refer to one young person or to young people in general. In 若者に人気がある, に names the group among whom something is popular. With 若者が, on the other hand, you describe the young people themselves as the ones acting; the number is clear from the context.

examples[].german: An elderly person is walking slowly.
I work at a nursing home.
en.notes: 老人 means an old or elderly person. In 老人ホーム it comes before the loanword ホーム and forms the term for a nursing home. Note the long vowels in rōjin and hōmu; in a sentence about a person, 老人 can also stand alone.

examples[].german: There are three men.
That man is Mr. Tanaka.
en.notes: 男性 is a neutral, formal term for a man or a male person. To count people, 人 follows the number: 男性が三人. With あの男性 you refer to a man at some distance; あの corresponds to "that" here.

examples[].german: She is a female teacher.
That woman is very kind.
en.notes: 女性 refers to a woman or a female person. 女性の先生 makes it explicit that the teacher is a woman; 先生 alone does not specify gender. In あの女性は… a particular woman at some distance becomes the topic of the sentence.

examples[].german: The weather is good.
This book is good.
en.notes: 良い（よい）is the slightly more literary form of いい. When conjugating, the stem よ is also used for いい: よくない "not good", よかった "was good". Here the word evaluates weather or a book positively; it is an i-adjective.

examples[].german: I served tea to a guest.
There are a lot of customers in that shop.
en.notes: 客 means "guest" or "customer" depending on the situation. When hosting, a guest is meant; in a shop, customers. The polite form is お客さん. In a report the plain 客 can also appear, for example in 客にお茶を出す: to serve tea to a guest.

examples[].german: Please ask a shop assistant.
A shop assistant is arranging the goods.
en.notes: 店員 refers to a person who works in a shop. The word does not specify gender. 店員に聞く means to turn to the shop staff; 店員さん is the polite form. In Hepburn romanization, the apostrophe in ten'in separates ん from the following い.

examples[].german: My father is a taxi driver.
I asked the bus driver.
en.notes: 運転手 is a driver, especially as a job title. The vehicle can precede it with の: タクシーの運転手 or バスの運転手. When speaking politely about the person, 運転手さん is possible; さん does not change the meaning of the occupation.

examples[].german: I want to become a nurse.
The nurse was kind.
en.notes: 看護師 refers to a nurse, regardless of gender. 看護師になる describes entering this profession; になりたい expresses a career wish. 看護師さん is a polite way to refer to the person, for example in a hospital.

examples[].german: A police officer is standing in front of the station.
I asked a police officer for directions.
en.notes: 警察官 is the job title for a police officer. When you ask the person something, に is used: 警察官に道を聞く means "ask the police for directions". 警察 means the police, 警察官 the individual person in this occupation.

examples[].german: A firefighter helped me.
Many children want to become firefighters.
en.notes: 消防士 refers to a person in the fire department. The ending 士 is part of the occupational title. 消防士になりたい is a career wish; 消防士が助けてくれた describes help that benefited oneself. In shōbōshi both o are long.

examples[].german: A farmer is selling vegetables.
My grandfather is a farmer.
en.notes: 農家 can mean a farmer or a farming family. 農家の人 explicitly makes the person from an agricultural household the topic. In 祖父は農家です the grandfather's occupation is meant; 家 is read か in this word.

examples[].german: The carpenter builds a house.
I asked the carpenter to repair the door.
en.notes: 大工 is a craftsman who mainly does woodwork on houses. 大工さん is the polite way to refer to the person. For a repair job the person takes に and the requested work takes を: 大工さんに修理を頼む.

examples[].german: I will do my best together with my comrades.
I went on a trip with my soccer buddies.
en.notes: 仲間 are people with whom you do something together or share an interest. サッカーの仲間, for example, are the people from your own soccer group. 仲間と一緒に emphasizes acting together; the word itself can refer to one person or several.

examples[].german: I had my senpai teach me.
Senpai, I'll be leaving ahead of you.
en.notes: 先輩 is a person who has been at the same school or workplace for longer. What matters is this relationship, not just age. You can learn from a 先輩 or address someone that way; お先に失礼します is the polite phrase for leaving before others.

examples[].german: The weather is bad.
The grades are bad.
en.notes: 悪い is the general opposite of 良い: 天気が悪い "bad weather", 成績が悪い "poor performance". With things and results, it usually denotes an unfavorable state or low quality. This i-adjective forms 悪くない and 悪かった.

examples[].german: I got an email from my kōhai.
I taught the work to a newly joined kōhai.
en.notes: 後輩 is the counterpart of 先輩: a person who joined the same school or workplace later. They do not have to be younger. 後輩から names them as the sender of a message; 後輩に names them as the recipient of an explanation.

examples[].german: I report to my boss.
I attended a meeting with my boss.
en.notes: 上司 is a superior in the workplace. Reporting to a 上司 is 上司に報告する; に names the recipient. In 上司と会議に出る, on the other hand, と indicates the person accompanying you to the meeting. In jōshi and hōkoku the first o is long in each.

examples[].german: I train my subordinates.
I asked my subordinate to take on a task.
en.notes: 部下 refers to a person who is under one's authority at work. 部下を育てる means professional development, not raising children. 部下に仕事を頼む means to ask this person to take on a task; に names the person being addressed.

examples[].german: I eat lunch with my colleagues.
A colleague helped me with my work.
en.notes: 同僚 are colleagues from the same work environment. With 同僚と you name the companion in a shared activity. 同僚に手伝ってもらう emphasizes that you receive help from colleagues. Both o in dōryō are long.

examples[].german: I met the company president.
The company president is very busy.
en.notes: 社長 refers to the head of a company. By itself it does not say who owns the company. In 社長にお会いしました, 会う is expressed politely as お会いする; the person met takes に. 社長は makes the company president the topic of a description.

examples[].german: I got an email from a friend who is a company employee.
My father is a company employee.
en.notes: 会社員 is a person employed at a company. The word names the type of employment, not a concrete task such as sales or accounting. With の you can add this information to a person: 会社員の友達 is a friend who is employed at a company.

examples[].german: I want to become a public servant.
My older brother is a public servant.
en.notes: 公務員 refers to people employed in the public service, for example at a government agency. 公務員になる means to take up this kind of employment. 公務員になりたい expresses a career wish; 公務員です, by contrast, describes a person's current employment.

examples[].german: Payday is on the 25th.
My salary goes up from next month.
en.notes: 給料 is the salary or wages from a job. 給料日 is payday. For a raise you say 給料が上がる: the salary goes up. 来月から names the start of the change; 給料 itself says nothing about the amount or the payment date.

examples[].german: Let's take a break.
The break lasts until two o'clock.
en.notes: 休憩 is a break during work or an activity. With する it becomes "to take a break": 休憩しましょう is an invitation to do so together. As a noun, 休憩 can also refer to the period of time; 休憩は二時までです gives the end of the break.

examples[].german: I'm working overtime today.
After overtime, I had dinner with a friend.
en.notes: 残業 refers to work beyond regular working hours. 今日は残業です is a short statement that you are working overtime today. With 残業の後で you link overtime, as a noun, to a following activity.

examples[].german: It's hot today.
It's hot, so I'll open the window.
en.notes: 暑い describes heat in the surroundings, especially in weather. For a hot object or hot drink, 熱い is written instead; both words are read あつい. The negative is 暑くない, the past 暑かった.

examples[].german: The commute takes an hour.
I commute to work by train.
en.notes: 通勤 is the regular trip to work, not the trip to school. 通勤する means "to commute to work". In 通勤に一時間かかる, に names the activity that takes time; 電車で, on the other hand, names the means of transport.

examples[].german: There is a meeting from three o'clock.
I gave my opinion at the meeting.
en.notes: 会議 is a meeting or conference. 会議がある announces that one is taking place; から names the start. In 会議で意見を言う, で marks the setting in which one voices an opinion. The spelling 会議 belongs here to the noun.

examples[].german: Let's exchange business cards.
Even though it's an important meeting, I forgot my business cards.
en.notes: 名刺 is a business card with a name and contact details. 名刺を交換する means to exchange business cards. 名刺を忘れてしまう describes forgetting them with a tone of regret; なのに contrasts it with the important occasion.

examples[].german: Please sign the document.
I put the papers in my bag.
en.notes: 書類 are documents or papers; the word can also refer to a single document. 書類にサインする means to sign the document. In 書類をかばんに入れる, on the other hand, 書類 is the object that you put in the bag.

examples[].german: I made a reservation at the restaurant.
Is a reservation necessary?
en.notes: 予約 means a reservation, booking or appointment made in advance. As a noun it appears in 予約をする; with する alone it becomes 予約する. 予約は必要ですか asks whether a reservation is required. The context says what is to be booked.

examples[].german: Please submit the notification.
I don't know how to fill out the notification.
en.notes: 届 is a written notification or report submitted to an office. The reading is とどけ; the spelling 届け is also encountered. 届を出す means "to submit a notification", and 届の書き方 refers to how one writes the notification.

examples[].german: Please fill out the application form.
The application forms are at the reception desk.
en.notes: 申込書 is an application or registration form. In 申込書に記入する, に marks the form into which details are entered. You can also ask for the form itself with 申込書はどこにありますか. The ending 書 is read しょ here.

examples[].german: Please give me my change.
The change is 300 yen.
en.notes: お釣り is the change you get back after paying. It does not simply mean coins in a wallet. The お is the polite prefix and belongs to the form on this card. お釣りは三百円です states the amount to be returned.

examples[].german: How much is it?
This price is high, isn't it?
en.notes: 値段 refers to the price of something. 値段はいくらですか asks for the amount. With 値段が高い or 値段が安い you judge the price as high or low; 高い with 値段 does not mean spatial height. The kana spelling ねだん also means this price.

examples[].german: Is there a discount?
Thanks to the discount, I was able to buy it cheaply.
en.notes: 割引 is a discount or price reduction. 割引はありますか asks whether there is a reduction. In 割引で安く買えました, で names the discount as the reason for being able to buy cheaply; 買えました is the potential form of 買う. 割引き is another spelling of the noun "discount".

examples[].german: It's cold in winter.
It's cold, so I'll wear a coat.
en.notes: 寒い describes cold weather, a cold environment or the feeling of being cold. 冷たい, by contrast, is used for something cold to the touch, such as water. As an い-adjective, 寒い forms the negative 寒くない and the past 寒かった.

examples[].german: Please wrap the present.
The wrapping is pretty, isn't it?
en.notes: 包装 refers to wrapping something or to the packaging of a thing. 包装する means "to wrap"; in a shop you can say 包装してください. When you say 包装がきれいです, you are commenting on the packaging. Both o in hōsō are long.

examples[].german: I choose the goods.
How much is this article?
en.notes: 品物 is an object or article, often as goods when shopping. 品物を選ぶ describes choosing; この品物は… makes a particular article the topic of a question. The word can refer to a single item as well as to goods in general.

examples[].german: It is cloudy today.
On cloudy days I take a walk in the park.
en.notes: 曇り is the noun for cloudy weather. That is why a weather statement uses です: 今日は曇りです. Before another noun it is joined with の, as in 曇りの日. The verb form 曇る, by contrast, means "to become cloudy". 曇 is also listed for this reading; the fuller spelling 曇り shows the noun clearly.

examples[].german: It will be sunny tomorrow.
On sunny days I do laundry.
en.notes: 晴れ is the noun for clear, fine weather. 明日は晴れです is a weather statement for tomorrow. With 晴れの日に you name a day with this weather as the time of an activity. In this meaning, 晴れ is joined with の, not with な.

examples[].german: A typhoon is coming.
School was canceled because of the typhoon.
en.notes: 台風 is a typhoon. 台風が来る speaks of its approach. With 台風で you name it as the cause of a consequence, such as a school closure. In taifū the u is long; the word refers to the cyclone, not simply to any strong wind.

examples[].german: It is the rainy season.
During the rainy season, laundry hardly dries.
en.notes: 梅雨 is read つゆ and means the East Asian rainy season, not each individual rainy day. 梅雨の季節 means "the season of the rainy season". 梅雨には sets this period as the frame for a statement, for example that laundry hardly dries.

examples[].german: Which season do you like?
There are four seasons in Japan.
en.notes: 季節 is a season or a period of the year. どの季節 asks which one out of several is meant. For four seasons use 四つの季節; 四つ is read よっつ. With 季節の you can assign other things to the respective season.

examples[].german: I add a little vinegar.
The vinegar is on top of the shelf.
en.notes: 酢 is vinegar as an ingredient. In 酢を少し入れる, 酢 is what is added, and 少し describes the small amount. When talking about where it is kept, a place takes に and あります. The short reading す consists of only one mora.

examples[].german: I make bread with wheat flour.
I bought a bag of wheat flour.
en.notes: 小麦粉 is wheat flour. With 小麦粉で you name it as the material something is made from. When shopping, the amount can be given with 袋: 一袋 is read ひとふくろ and means "one bag". The whole word is read こむぎこ.

examples[].german: Let's eat cake.
I made a cake for his/her birthday.
en.notes: ケーキ is cake; the exact kind depends on the context. The ー makes the e long: kēki. ケーキを食べましょう invites people to eat together; 誕生日にケーキを作る describes making a cake for a birthday.

examples[].german: It's warm today.
Please bring warm clothes.
en.notes: 暖かい is used especially for pleasantly warm air and for clothing that protects against the cold. 温かい often refers to the tangible warmth of food or drinks; both are read あたたかい. Before a noun the い is kept: 暖かい服.

examples[].german: The miso soup is warm.
I drink miso soup every morning.
en.notes: 味噌汁 is soup made with miso, that is, fermented soybean paste. For drinking or eating this soup, 飲む is often used. 味噌汁が温かい comments on its temperature; 毎朝味噌汁を飲む describes the habit of having it in the morning.

examples[].german: I made side dishes to go with the rice.
What is today's side dish?
en.notes: おかず are dishes eaten with rice, such as vegetables, fish or meat. The word can mean one such dish or several side dishes together. 今日のおかずは何ですか asks about the side dish of the day; before です, 何 is read なん here. お菜 is a rare kanji spelling; 御数 is listed in the dictionary only as a search form. For writing, the usual kana form おかず is suitable.

examples[].german: I suck on a candy.
I gave the child a candy.
en.notes: 飴 is a hard candy that you can suck on. 飴をなめる means "to suck on a candy". In 子供に飴をあげる, に marks the person who receives the candy. The same reading あめ also belongs to 雨 "rain"; the script and the context tell the words apart.

examples[].german: I eat rice crackers.
I bought rice crackers as a souvenir.
en.notes: 煎餅 are Japanese rice crackers; the hiragana spelling せんべい is also often seen. 煎餅を食べる describes eating them, 煎餅をお土産に買う describes buying them as a souvenir. The に after お土産 names the purpose of the purchase.

examples[].german: People eat mochi at New Year.
I eat grilled mochi with soy sauce.
en.notes: 餅 is mochi, a small rice cake made from glutinous rice. お正月に names the New Year festival as the occasion for eating it. In 焼いた餅, 焼いた describes how the mochi is prepared; 醤油をつけて食べる means to eat it with soy sauce.

examples[].german: One apple, please.
The apple is red.
en.notes: 林檎 is the apple as a fruit; the word is often written りんご. You can count an apple with 一つ: 林檎を一つください. 赤い describes the color of the fruit under discussion; the reading of the whole word remains りんご.

examples[].german: Mandarin oranges are delicious in winter.
I peeled the mandarin orange.
en.notes: 蜜柑 are mandarin oranges, especially the satsuma mandarins common in Japan. The common spelling みかん reads the same. 蜜柑の皮 refers to the peel; 皮をむく means to peel the fruit. The word 蜜柑 alone does not fix a number of pieces.

examples[].german: I like strawberries.
I want to eat strawberry cake.
en.notes: 苺 means strawberry; いちご is often written instead. In 苺が好き, 苺 is what one likes. In 苺のケーキ, の connects the strawberries with a cake; 食べたい expresses the wish to eat it.

examples[].german: I eat watermelon in summer.
I cut the watermelon in half.
en.notes: 西瓜 is a watermelon; すいか or スイカ is often seen. In 夏は西瓜を食べる, 夏 is the time frame. 西瓜を半分に切る, on the other hand, describes preparation: the watermelon is divided into two halves.

examples[].german: I bought grapes.
Grapes are delicious in autumn.
en.notes: 葡萄 are grapes; the common kana spelling is ぶどう. The last o in budō is long. 葡萄を買う describes shopping, and 葡萄がおいしい is a judgment of taste. Whether it means one bunch or several comes from context.

examples[].german: It's cool in autumn.
I want to study in a cool room.
en.notes: 涼しい usually means pleasant, refreshing coolness in the air or weather. It is therefore more positive than 寒い ("cold/chilly"). The form 涼しく can be used adverbially; before a noun, say 涼しい部屋.

examples[].german: The peach is delicious.
Please peel the peach.
en.notes: 桃 is a peach. 桃がおいしい describes its taste. With 桃の皮 you name the skin of the fruit; 桃の皮をむいてください asks someone to peel the peach. Both syllables in もも are short.

examples[].german: It is nashi pear season.
This nashi pear is very big.
en.notes: 梨 is the nashi pear, an Asian pear; it is often written なし. 梨の季節 means "pear season". With この梨は… you describe a specific fruit, for example its size. The identically pronounced なし meaning "without/not existing" is a different word.

examples[].german: I cut the carrot.
I put carrots in the curry.
en.notes: 人参 means carrot here and is read にんじん; you also often see にんじん or ニンジン. When cutting, the carrot takes を. In カレーに人参を入れる, に names the dish into which the carrot goes as an ingredient.

examples[].german: I sauté the onion.
When you cut onions, tears come to your eyes.
en.notes: 玉葱 is an onion; the reading is たまねぎ. 玉葱を炒める means to sauté onions. In 玉葱を切ると涙が出る, と links the cutting to the reaction that follows: your eyes water.

examples[].german: I make grated daikon.
I bought a daikon radish.
en.notes: 大根 is the large white daikon radish. 大根おろし is grated daikon. When shopping, the long root is often counted with 本: 一本 is read いっぽん. In the plain word 大根, the reading is だいこん.

examples[].german: I grill the eggplant.
I like eggplant tempura.
en.notes: 茄子 is an eggplant; the common kana spelling is なす. 茄子を焼く describes preparing it by pan-frying or grilling. In 茄子の天ぷら, の connects the eggplant with the dish tempura. In Modified Hepburn, tenpura is written with n before p.

examples[].german: I make cucumber salad.
I bought two cucumbers.
en.notes: 胡瓜 means cucumber; きゅうり or キュウリ is often used instead. The u in kyūri is long. 胡瓜のサラダ is cucumber salad. When shopping, cucumbers can be counted with 本 as long objects: 二本 is read にほん.

examples[].german: I buy tofu.
I put tofu in the miso soup.
en.notes: 豆腐 is tofu. In tōfu the first o is pronounced long. 豆腐を買う describes shopping; 味噌汁に豆腐を入れる names tofu as an ingredient of miso soup. Here 豆腐 is the object with を and 味噌汁 is the receiving dish with に.

examples[].german: I wrap the onigiri in nori.
I cut the nori into thin strips.
en.notes: 海苔 means nori, edible seaweed often used as thin sheets. 海苔でおにぎりを包む names nori as the material for wrapping. 海苔を細く切る describes cutting it into thin strips; を then marks nori as the object being worked on.

examples[].german: I make simmered pumpkin.
This pumpkin is heavy.
en.notes: 南瓜 is a pumpkin; the reading かぼちゃ cannot be derived from the individual characters. It is often written かぼちゃ or カボチャ. 南瓜の煮物 is a dish of cooked pumpkin. With この南瓜は... you describe a particular fruit, for example its weight.

examples[].german: This cake is delicious.
It was so delicious that I ate another one.
en.notes: おいしい evaluates the taste of food and drinks positively. The spelling 美味しい is also common. For the past, い is replaced by かった: おいしかった. Figurative uses for attractive offers are not meant here.

examples[].german: I put napa cabbage in the pot.
The napa cabbage is in the refrigerator.
en.notes: 白菜 is napa cabbage and is read はくさい. 白菜を鍋に入れる describes its use in a hot pot dish. When storage is the point, 冷蔵庫に names the place; あります says the napa cabbage is there.

examples[].german: I chop the green onions.
I put green onions on the ramen.
en.notes: 葱 is a green onion or spring onion, often also written ねぎ. 葱を刻む describes fine slicing or chopping. In ラーメンに葱をのせる, the green onion is the garnish placed on the ramen.

examples[].german: I slice the lotus root thinly.
Lotus root tempura is delicious.
en.notes: 蓮根 is lotus root as a vegetable; れんこん is often written. The reading ends in ん. 蓮根を薄く切る describes thin slices, 蓮根の天ぷら is a tempura dish made with lotus root. In Hepburn the n remains visible in renkon and tenpura.

examples[].german: I make a salad with burdock root.
Where can I buy burdock root?
en.notes: 牛蒡 is gobo, burdock root as a vegetable; ごぼう is often written. The final o of gobō is long. 牛蒡をサラダにする describes preparing it as a salad. 牛蒡はどこで買えますか asks where it can be bought.

examples[].german: I grill shiitake mushrooms.
I bought shiitake mushrooms at the supermarket.
en.notes: 椎茸 is the shiitake mushroom; the reading is しいたけ, with a long i at the start. For shopping, 椎茸を買う is used, for preparation 椎茸を焼く. When buying, で names the place, for example スーパーで for "at the supermarket".

examples[].german: I put water in the pot.
I ate a Japanese hot pot with my family.
en.notes: 鍋 can mean the cooking pot or a Japanese stew-style dish prepared in it. In 鍋に水を入れる the vessel is meant. With 鍋を食べる you eat the dish, not the pot. 鍋料理 is the fuller term for such a dish.

examples[].german: I washed the frying pan.
I fry an egg in the frying pan.
en.notes: フライパン is a frying pan. フライパンで names the cooking utensil used for frying. When you clean the pan itself, it takes を: フライパンを洗う. The word is written entirely in katakana.

examples[].german: I bought a cutting board.
I cut vegetables on the cutting board.
en.notes: まな板 is a cutting board; 板 is read いた here. まな板の上で names the work surface on which you cut. With まな板を買う, by contrast, the board itself is the object of the purchase. The reading is まないた, with no additional consonant between な and い.

examples[].german: I cut with the kitchen knife.
I cut the fish with the kitchen knife.
When I'm done cooking, I wash the kitchen knife and put it away.
en.notes: 包丁 is a kitchen knife for cutting and preparing food. で names it as the tool, を the thing cut. 包丁を洗う, on the other hand, describes cleaning the knife itself. The reading ほうちょう contains two long o: hōchō. The knife is meant here, not the older meaning "cooking". 庖丁 is also listed as a spelling for this kitchen knife; the reading stays ほうちょう.

examples[].german: I scoop soup with the ladle.
I serve soup with the ladle.
I washed the ladle I used and put it in the drawer.
en.notes: お玉 is a ladle for portioning soup or other liquid food. With で you name it as the tool: お玉でスープをすくう. お玉を洗う makes the ladle itself the object. The word is often written in kana as おたま. In these examples the kitchen tool is meant, not a personal name or the also attested meaning "egg".

examples[].german: This dish tastes bad.
This coffee tastes so bad that I can't drink it.
en.notes: With food, まずい means "bad-tasting" and comes across as a clearly direct judgment. In polite conversation, あまりおいしくない ("not particularly tasty") is often more reserved. The connecting form is まずくて. This card deals with taste, not the meaning "problematic".

examples[].german: Do you have a bottle opener?
I open the bottle with a bottle opener.
en.notes: 栓抜き is a bottle opener. ありますか asks whether one is available; で names it as the tool for opening a bottle. The reading せんぬき has an n at the end of the first syllable and an n at the start of the next: sennuki. Before this n, Hepburn needs no separating apostrophe, unlike before a vowel.

examples[].german: Please turn off the faucet.
No water comes out of the faucet.
en.notes: 蛇口 is the faucet. 蛇口を閉める means to turn it off; から names the starting point of the water. 蛇口から水が出ない therefore describes that no water comes out of the tap. The word is read as a whole as じゃぐち; the literal meaning of the individual kanji does not reliably explain the present reading.

examples[].german: I change the light bulb.
The light bulb has burned out.
en.notes: 電球 is a light bulb. 電球を替える means to replace the bulb. 電球が切れる is the usual expression for it no longer lighting up, that is, having burned out. を marks the thing being replaced; が marks the bulb in which the failure occurs. The reading ends with a long ū: denkyū.

examples[].german: Please plug it into the outlet.
There are only two outlets in this room.
en.notes: コンセント is the word for an electrical outlet in Japanese. に names the target when plugging in a plug; the thing being plugged in can be omitted in conversation. コンセントが二つしかない means "there are only two outlets". It is not the English "consent" meaning agreement. For the plug itself, プラグ is used, for example.

examples[].german: Please turn it on.
Please press the switch.
This switch is broken; the light doesn't come on even when I press it.
en.notes: スイッチ is a switch for operating a device here. スイッチを入れる means "to turn on", スイッチを切る "to turn off". 押す describes pressing; not every switch is operated by pressing. In these examples the word does not mean a change between topics or a game console.

examples[].german: I vacuum.
I clean the room with the vacuum cleaner.
The vacuum cleaner is so loud that I can't hear the voice on the phone.
en.notes: 掃除機 is the vacuum cleaner. 掃除機をかける is the set expression for "to vacuum". 掃除機で掃除する names the appliance with で as the means. The word contains 掃除 "cleaning" and 機 "machine", but is read as the name of the appliance as a whole. The first syllable is long: sōjiki.

examples[].german: I do the ironing.
I iron the shirt.
After the iron had cooled down, I put it in the box.
en.notes: アイロン here is the iron for clothes. アイロンをかける means "to iron"; the garment can come before it with に, as in シャツにアイロンをかける. The word refers to the appliance and not to the metal iron in general. The combination シャツをかける alone can mean "to hang up a shirt" and is inaccurate for "to iron".

examples[].german: I heat it in the microwave.
Please heat it in the microwave.
I left a plate in the microwave.
en.notes: 電子レンジ is the microwave oven. With で you name it as the appliance or place of heating: 電子レンジで温める. In suitable conversation it is often shortened to レンジ. The examples do not say that you use an oven for baking. 電子レンジの中 means the interior of the appliance.

examples[].german: I cook rice in the rice cooker.
With the new rice cooker, the rice turns out very delicious.
en.notes: 炊飯器 is a rice cooker. 炊飯器でご飯を炊く names the appliance as the means for cooking rice. 炊ける can describe a possible or successful cooking result; ご飯が炊ける makes the rice the subject. 炊飯器 refers to the appliance, not to a pot for just any dish. The reading is suihanki.

examples[].german: I hang the laundry on the rack.
Because it started to rain, I brought the laundry in from the drying rack.
en.notes: 物干し is a device for drying laundry, such as a drying rack. に names the place where the laundry is hung. 物干しの洗濯物 means the laundry hanging there. 物干し is the device; 洗濯物 is what is being dried. The term does not always have to mean a freestanding folding rack.

examples[].german: Traveling is fun.
The party yesterday was a lot of fun.
en.notes: 楽しい describes something that gives pleasure, such as an activity or time spent together. It is an い-adjective: 楽しかった ("was fun") and 楽しく ("in an enjoyable way"). Do not equate it with 楽な ("effortless/comfortable").

examples[].german: I wash my face at the washbasin.
I brush my teeth in front of the washbasin.
en.notes: 洗面台 is the washing area with a basin, often also with a shelf or mirror. 洗面台で顔を洗う names it as the place where the face is washed. 洗面台の前で describes the spot in front of it. It is not the kitchen sink where dishes are usually washed. The whole word is read senmendai.

examples[].german: I fill the bathtub with hot water.
You should wash the bathtub every day.
en.notes: 浴槽 is the bathtub as a container, not the bathroom as a room. 浴槽にお湯を入れる means to run hot water into it. 浴槽を洗う means cleaning the tub. たほうがいい gives advice; the example sentence explicitly mentions daily cleaning, without that being part of the word's meaning.

examples[].german: I clean the toilet bowl.
I cleaned the toilet bowl.
Please close the toilet lid.
en.notes: 便器 refers to the toilet bowl, the sanitary fixture, not the whole toilet room. 便器を掃除する means to clean this fixture. 便器のふた is the toilet lid. トイレ is broader in everyday use and can mean either the toilet or the toilet room; 便器 names the bowl more precisely.

examples[].german: I grow flowers on the balcony.
I hang the laundry out on the balcony.
en.notes: ベランダ here means the balcony of an apartment. With で you name it as the place of an activity: tending flowers or hanging laundry. The word can also be used for a veranda; in the examples a balcony is meant. It describes the place, not automatically a garden. In the flower example, 育てる means tending and letting them grow.

examples[].german: I sit on the carpet.
I bought a new carpet.
en.notes: 絨毯 is a carpet, either covering a large area or as a single runner or rug. の上に names its top side as a place to sit. 絨毯を買う, on the other hand, concerns acquiring one. In everyday writing the kanji can also be replaced by the kana spelling じゅうたん. The long u is rendered as ū: jūtan.

examples[].german: I arrange flowers in the vase.
I put flowers in the vase.
The vase broke, so I bought a new one.
en.notes: 花瓶 is a flower vase. 花瓶に花を活ける means to arrange flowers in it; 入れる is more general, "to put in". The vase takes に as the container, the flowers take を as the object. 花瓶が割れる, by contrast, describes the vase itself breaking. The spelling combines "flower" with "bottle", but the whole word is read kabin.

examples[].german: I set the alarm clock.
The alarm clock rang.
en.notes: 目覚まし時計 is an alarm clock. をセットする means to set it to a wake-up time; が鳴る describes its ringing. In this compound, 時計 is read どけい, with d instead of t. The full reading is めざましどけい. The word refers to the device, not just the time of waking up.

examples[].german: I step on the scale.
I step on the scale every morning.
The numbers on the scale are small, so I can't see them well.
en.notes: 体重計 is a scale for measuring body weight. 体重計に乗る means to stand on the scale; に marks the destination of the movement. 体重計の数字 means the numbers on the display; 見る can refer to reading that display. The word means the measuring device, not the weight itself. The reading is taijūkei.

examples[].german: There are four people in my family.
I go on a trip with my family.
en.notes: 家族は四人です counts the members of a family. 家族で＋verb means the family does something together; で marks the acting group here. For another person's family, ご家族 is a polite form.

examples[].german: This movie is interesting.
His story was funny, and everyone laughed.
en.notes: 面白い can mean "interesting" or "funny". With a movie or book, context decides whether interest or humor is emphasized. The connecting form is 面白くて; the い-adjective can also stand directly before a noun: 面白い話.

examples[].german: I write in my diary every day.
I write in my diary every day.
Reading an old diary, I remembered my student days.
en.notes: 日記 is a diary or a personal daily record. 日記を書く means "to write a diary". 毎日 gives the frequency; 書いています can express an ongoing habit here. 古い日記を読む concerns rereading one's own memories later. The small っ in にっき is written as a double k: nikki.

examples[].german: I like reading manga.
Japanese manga are interesting.
en.notes: 漫画 are drawn stories, comics or manga. 漫画を読むのが好き means that you like reading them; の turns reading into an activity that you can evaluate. 日本の漫画 means manga from Japan. The word describes the medium and says nothing by itself about whether it is meant for children or adults.

examples[].german: I'm reading a novel.
I'm reading this novel.
After work, my friend is writing a short story.
en.notes: 小説 is a literary narrative text, often a novel, but also a shorter story. It is not used only for a very long book. 小説を読む refers to reading; 小説を書く to writing such texts. 書いている can describe work currently in progress. The first syllable is long: shōsetsu.

examples[].german: I send a postcard.
I sent my friend a postcard.
I wrote the address on the postcard and then put on a stamp.
en.notes: 葉書 is the postcard. In everyday writing it is very often spelled はがき. 葉書を送る names the sending; に can give the recipient. 葉書に住所を書く, by contrast, makes the card the place of writing. Here the word does not mean a short note slip, even though that further meaning is in the dictionary.

examples[].german: I want to send a parcel.
A parcel has arrived.
en.notes: 小包 is a package or parcel for sending. Despite 小, it does not necessarily have to be a very small shipment. を marks the parcel being sent; が marks the parcel that arrives. The reading こづつみ is written kozutsumi in Hepburn. The づ becomes zu here, not dzu.

examples[].german: Please change this money.
I exchanged money at the bank.
I changed a thousand-yen bill into hundred-yen coins.
en.notes: 両替 means "money exchange". It can refer to exchange between currencies or into other bills and coins of the same currency. 両替する is the verb for it. 両替をお願いします is a polite request for this service. For paying for a purchase you don't simply use 両替する.

examples[].german: I bought a lucky charm.
I bought a lucky charm at the shrine.
When I travel, I carry this lucky charm with me.
en.notes: お守り is an amulet or lucky charm meant to symbolize protection or luck. You receive or buy such items at a shrine, for example. お守りを持ち歩く means to carry it with you. The word's meaning describes the object and its attributed function, not a proven protective effect.

examples[].german: I sent a picture postcard.
I sent a picture postcard from my travel destination.
When I see the photo on this picture postcard, I remember the trip.
en.notes: 絵葉書 is a picture postcard with an image on it. It is a special kind of 葉書, but an ordinary postcard need not have such a picture. を marks the card being sent; から can name the place you send it from. 絵葉書の写真, by contrast, refers to the picture on the card. The reading is ehagaki.

examples[].german: I buy juice from the vending machine.
I bought a drink from the vending machine.
I forgot to take my change from the vending machine.
en.notes: 自動販売機 is a vending machine. It often sells drinks, but the word is not limited to juice or drinks. で names the machine as the place of purchase. 自動販売機のおつり means the change from the machine. The full reading is じどうはんばいき; the first o is long.

examples[].german: Japanese is difficult.
This problem is so difficult that I don't know the answer.
en.notes: 難しい describes something that is hard to understand or to cope with. For great weight, 重い is used instead. The form 難しくて connects the difficulty with a further statement; the negative is 難しくない.

examples[].german: I put the big blanket up on the loft.
Please raise your hand.
en.notes: 上げる here means to lift something or bring it to a higher place. The thing lifted takes を; に can name the higher destination. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 上げます, 上げて. ロフト here means a raised living level or mezzanine. Distinguish this "lifting" from the also-read あげる "to give" by context.

examples[].german: Push the lever down as hard as you can!
Please lower the temperature a little.
en.notes: 下げる here means "to lower, bring down, reduce". The thing lowered takes を, for example a lever or a temperature. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 下げます, 下げて. 力いっぱい下げて is a direct, forceful command; 少し下げてください is a polite request for a small change. The word does not require physical force in every context.

examples[].german: One miso ramen, please.
Please give me some water.
Please write your name on this paper.
en.notes: 下さい is the polite request "please give me ...". In orders, を can be omitted in conversation: みそラーメン下さい. It is usually written ください in kana. It is the special imperative form of くださる and is practiced here as a ready-made expression. After the て-form of another verb, ください instead means "please do ...".

examples[].german: Where is the entrance?
Where is the entrance?
I am waiting for a friend at the entrance.
en.notes: 入り口 is the entrance. This reading contains g: iriguchi, not irikuchi. 入り口はどこ？ is a short, casual question; どこですか is more polite. 入り口で names the entrance as the place of an activity, such as waiting. The spelling 入口 is also common and is read the same way in the right context.

examples[].german: It's no big deal.
It's nothing special.
To think you made everything by yourself, that's really something.
en.notes: 大した comes before a noun and means "significant, considerable, remarkable". It very often appears with a negative: 大したことじゃない, "it's no big deal". In a positive sentence it can express recognition. It is used here as an attributive expression; you do not simply attach な to it as with an ordinary な-adjective.

examples[].german: Oh, that's Mt. Fuji!
Someday I want to climb Mt. Fuji.
en.notes: ふじ山 is a learner-friendly mixed spelling of 富士山, Mt. Fuji. In this name 山 is read さん; this is not the polite name suffix さん. In normal kanji text 富士山 is usual. あっ expresses a sudden discovery; に names the destination when climbing. The proper name is written Fujisan.

examples[].german: There is an artificial pond in this park.
This is an artificial flower.
en.notes: 人工 means "artificial, man-made". Before a noun it often takes の: 人工の花, an artificial flower. In fixed compounds の can be missing, for example 人工芝 for artificial turf. It refers to human production as opposed to natural origin. The identically read 人口 means "population" and is a different word.

examples[].german: I gave it my all!
I ran with all my strength.
I pushed the heavy door with all my strength, but it didn't open.
en.notes: 力いっぱい means "with all one's strength, as hard as possible". It stands before an action as an expression of manner. It can describe physical effort or stress strong effort in trying. The small っ in いっぱい is written as a doubled p. It does not merely mean repeating a task very often.

examples[].german: My roommate climbs up to the loft.
I go up the stairs.
en.notes: 上る here means to go up or climb. It is intransitive, even though the path covered takes を: 階段を上る. に can name the destination, such as a higher living level. This godan verb forms 上ります and 上って. The spelling 登る is especially common when climbing a mountain; both can express "to climb up" depending on the context.

examples[].german: I saw the moon last night.
Last night I had a meal with a friend.
I couldn't sleep well last night, so I'm sleepy today.
en.notes: 夕べ here means "yesterday evening, last night" and can stand at the start of a sentence as a time expression. It refers to the evening before today. In other contexts the word can also simply mean "evening", for instance in event titles with の; that meaning is not the one in these examples. The long first syllable is written yūbe. 昨夜 can also refer to yesterday evening or last night with the reading ゆうべ.

examples[].german: This problem is easy.
This book is written in simple words.
en.notes: 易しい means "easy/simple" and is often written やさしい. Do not confuse it with 優しい ("kind, gentle"). This い-adjective can evaluate a task or stand before a noun: 易しい言葉 ("simple words").

examples[].german: The girl in the white dress is Rachel.
A girl is singing a song.
en.notes: 女の子 means "girl". It can refer to a female child; whether a daughter is meant depends on the context. 女の子が names a girl as an identified person or as the one acting. の belongs to the fixed compound 女の子. For adult women the term can sound too familiar or diminutive depending on the situation.

examples[].german: The women's restroom is over there.
Where is the women's restroom?
In this class there are ten girls and eight boys.
en.notes: 女子 means girls or women and often appears in categories, such as 女子トイレ or 女子学生. In direct personal conversation it is not always the most fitting term for an adult woman. そっち is a casual direction word, while どこですか politely asks about the place. The counterpart 男子 appears in corresponding categories.

examples[].german: I am five years old.
My grandmother is ninety years old.
You can attend this class from age six.
en.notes: 〜才 is the age counter "... years old". The wavy line marks a place for a number and is not pronounced. 才 is here the simplified spelling of the age character 歳. With numbers the pronunciation sometimes changes: 一才 is いっさい, 十才 is じゅっさい or じっさい; 二十才 has the special reading はたち. The examples practice concrete statements of age.

examples[].german: This curry is quite delicious.
Quite an interesting book, isn't it?
I'm looking for my key, but I just can't find it.
en.notes: 中々 is usually written なかなか. In a positive evaluation it means "quite, fairly, considerably". With a negated verb it often means that something does not come easily despite effort or waiting: なかなか見つからない, "not easy to find". So it is not always a mere intensifier like "very". 中中 is also listed as a spelling; the kana form なかなか is more common.

examples[].german: I returned to New York on May 1st.
May is pleasant.
en.notes: 五月 is the month of May and is read ごがつ. A month can take に; as the topic of a statement it is followed by は. 五月一日 is May 1st: ごがつついたち, not ごがついちにち. 過ごしやすい here evaluates the pleasant weather or conditions; this is a statement in the given context, not a worldwide weather rule.

examples[].german: I went to the United States in June.
In this town it rains a lot in June.
en.notes: 六月 is the month of June, read ろくがつ. に links it as a point in time to an activity; は makes it the topic of a statement. 雨が多い means it rains a lot. With この町では it is clear which place the weather statement refers to. In month names, 月 is read がつ, not つき.

examples[].german: I will turn fifty in October.
On this mountain, October is the season of autumn leaves.
en.notes: 十月 is October, read じゅうがつ. に names the month as a point in time, for example for a birthday. 五十才になる means "to turn fifty"; the common reading is ごじゅっさい. 紅葉の季節 describes the season of changing leaves at the given place. 十月 is a month name, not a statement of "ten months long".

examples[].german: The wedding party was in January.
In this town it is very cold in January.
en.notes: 一月 is January and is read いちがつ as a month name. The same spelling with a different reading can mean "one month": ひとつき. The examples mean the calendar name. A celebration can have taken place in January; the cold in the second sentence describes a specific place. In month names, 月 is read がつ.

examples[].german: Valentine's Day is in February.
February is the shortest month.
en.notes: 二月 is February, read にがつ. Not every number has the same reading before 月 as when counting; this combination is learned as a month name. は can make the month the topic. 一番短い月 means "the shortest month"; here 月 is read as the independent word つき. The examples use the modern calendar.

examples[].german: She is a kind person.
The teacher explained it to me kindly.
en.notes: 優しい describes kindness, gentleness or caring behavior. For "easy", the identically pronounced 易しい is written instead. The form 優しく describes how someone acts: 優しく説明する ("to explain kindly").

examples[].german: The puppy is cute.
What a cute puppy!
I gave the puppy some water and then went for a walk.
en.notes: 子犬 is a puppy, that is, a young dog. 子 here names the young of an animal. かわいい子犬 judges it as cute; 子犬に水をあげる, by contrast, describes caring for it. With に you name the animal as the recipient. The reading is koinu with the vowels o and i kept separate.

examples[].german: "Good morning!" said the prince.
The prince lives in the castle.
The British prince visited Japan.
en.notes: 王子 is a prince as the son of a king; the female counterpart is 王女, in fairy tales usually お姫様. In fairy tales and children's language you almost always hear 王子様, and 白馬の王子様 ("prince on a white horse") stands for the dream man. For the Japanese imperial family one does not use 王子 but separate words such as 皇太子 ("crown prince") or 親王.

examples[].german: That is the queen's necklace.
The queen is very beautiful.
en.notes: 女王 means "queen", here a female monarch. 女王のネックレス means her necklace; 女王は makes her the topic of a description. It is a different term from 王女 "princess". The reading is じょおう: joō, with the syllable jo before a long o. You do not insert an extra syllable じょう.

examples[].german: In this story, the princess is always right.
The princess is a kind person.
The princess visited the town and talked with the children.
en.notes: 王女 is a princess, especially a daughter from a royal house. 女王, on the other hand, is the queen. The words have similar kanji in reverse order but are not interchangeable. In the example sentence この話では a claim is limited to the story being told. The reading おうじょ is written ōjo.

examples[].german: April 1st is April Fools' Day.
The new term starts in April.
en.notes: 四月 is April and is read しがつ, not よんがつ. 四月一日 is しがつついたち, "April 1st". に can name a point in time, から a start. 新学期 is the new school term or new academic period; it is not in every context the whole new school year. The examples mean the modern calendar.

examples[].german: Japanese curry is delicious.
Have you ever been to Japan?
en.notes: 日本 is Japan. The name has the common readings にほん and にっぽん; this entry practices にほん. 日本のカレー names Japanese curry, 日本に行く names Japan as the travel destination. 行ったことがありますか asks about past experience. の shows origin or affiliation here, not ownership of a country.

examples[].german: My task is to correct system errors.
I corrected the mistake.
Before listening to the teacher, I straightened my posture.
en.notes: 正す means "to correct, to put right". A mistake takes を; 姿勢を正す also means to straighten one's posture. This godan verb forms 正します and 正して. For an ordinary repair, 直す is often more fitting. The similarly read 質す "to inquire" is a different dictionary entry and not the meaning of the examples.

examples[].german: What is this ball?
The child is playing with a ball.
en.notes: 玉 here means "ball" or a small round object. なんだ、この玉？ is a casual question about the ball; 玉で遊ぶ names it as something to play with. The reading is たま. With coins you often find the altered ending だま, such as 百円玉; that is not simply the reading of the standalone word in these examples. 球 is also a spelling of たま for a sphere or ball. The other meanings of this word depend on the spelling and the context.
