examples[].german: Please give me that round onion.
Please buy some onions and bring them back.
When I cut onions, tears come to my eyes.
en.notes: 玉ねぎ is the onion. The word part ねぎ does not make it an ordinary long spring onion; 玉ねぎ is its own vegetable name. を names it as the object bought or prepared. 買ってきてください asks someone to buy them and bring them back. In conversation, を can be omitted when ordering.

examples[].german: I live in Japan with a white partner.
That white woman over there is American.
en.notes: 白人 refers to a white person as a population or ancestry category. の can precede another noun, as in 白人のパートナー. By itself it says nothing about nationality; 白人 and アメリカ人 are different pieces of information. 女性 explicitly names a woman in the second example. The modern meaning practiced here is not one of the older dictionary meanings.

examples[].german: I'm very busy today.
I'm so busy that I have no time to eat lunch.
en.notes: 忙しい means that many tasks or appointments take up one's time. It describes being busy, not merely moving around. The connecting form is 忙しくて; for the negative, say 忙しくない. A time period can be emphasized with は.

examples[].german: Salmon eyes are tasty too.
I made a fried egg.
The main attraction of this festival is the fireworks at night.
en.notes: 目玉 literally means the eyeball. Figuratively it can name the main attraction or special highlight of an event. The fixed compound 目玉焼き, by contrast, means "fried egg (sunny-side up)"; no eyeball is meant. The examples show a food with eyes, the fixed dish name and an event highlight. The reading is medama.

examples[].german: The jacket has pockets on the left and right sides.
Please look left and right.
Before I cross the road, I look carefully left and right.
en.notes: 左右 names left and right together. ジャケットの左右 describes both sides of the jacket. 左右を確認する means to look at or check both sides, for example before crossing a road. In 道路を渡る, 道路 is the path being crossed. The reading さゆう has a long u: sayū.

examples[].german: Good morning, Miho-chan!
I said "good morning" to my friend.
In the morning I greeted the teacher with "good morning".
en.notes: おはよう is the casual morning greeting. To people you address more politely you usually say おはようございます. With friends the short form fits. In some occupations it is also used at the start of work later in the day; that is a usage in particular environments, not a general greeting for every time of day. お早う is a kanji spelling of the same short greeting; normally おはよう is written in kana.

examples[].german: Are you American?
There is an American student in the class.
en.notes: アメリカ人 is a person from the USA, that is, a U.S. American. In this nationality term, 人 is read じん. の can precede another noun: アメリカ人の学生. The compound term is learned as a whole and does not by itself say which language a person is currently using.

examples[].german: There are two French people.
I have a French friend.
en.notes: フランス人 is a French man or woman. In this combination 人 is read じん. When two people are counted, 二人 is read ふたり, not ににん. フランス人の友達 describes the nationality of a friend. The expression does not fix the person's gender.

examples[].german: A marble is a small, round ball.
The child is playing with marbles.
en.notes: ビー玉 is a small glass marble for playing. The word refers to a particular round plaything, not any small ball of any material. With で you name the marbles as the thing played with. The long first syllable is written bī; 玉 is read だま in this compound. The general ball, on the other hand, is 玉, tama.

examples[].german: There is an important test this month.
I am busy this month.
I wrote this month's schedule in my planner.
en.notes: 今月 is the current month, the month in which you are speaking. As a time expression it often needs no に; with は the month becomes the topic. 今月の予定 means the appointments of this month. It is not always "the next thirty days": the expression is based on the calendar month.

examples[].german: Michael is a friend of my father's.
I met a friend.
en.notes: 友人 means "friend" and sounds more factual or formal than 友達. It suits reports, for example, or introducing a person to others. 父の友人 names a friend of the father; 友人に会う names the friend as the person one meets. The word alone does not indicate a romantic relationship and does not specify gender.

examples[].german: The station is close.
The summer vacation is near.
en.notes: 近い can express spatial or temporal closeness. 駅が近い means "the station is close", 夏休みが近い "the summer vacation is coming up". As a place noun, 近く is used, for example 駅の近く ("near the station").

examples[].german: The design of this apartment's doorway is cute.
Who is the person standing at the doorway?
en.notes: 戸口 is the door opening, or the entrance right at the door. 戸口のデザイン describes its design; 戸口に立つ means to stand there. It is narrower than any access to a large building or site. 入り口 is often more general for "entrance" in everyday use. The item practiced here is not a family name.

examples[].german: This Benz is secondhand.
I bought a used car.
It's used, but it has no scratches.
en.notes: 中古 means "used, secondhand" and before a noun is usually followed by の: 中古の車. It describes previous use or resale, not automatically a bad condition. 中古です is also possible as a predicate. The use practiced here is not the historical meaning "Middle Ages".

examples[].german: We went on a double date with a foreign couple.
There is a foreigner in this class.
en.notes: 外人 is a colloquial term for a foreign person and can sound exclusionary or derogatory. The usually more neutral form is 外国人. The examples help you understand the shorter form in conversation; it is not a generally polite form of address. By itself the word does not specify a concrete nationality.

examples[].german: You can get into the municipal pool for three dollars.
I am going to the municipal library.
en.notes: 市立 means that a facility is run or established by a city. It appears in compounds like 市立プール or before a noun with の. The reading しりつ sounds exactly like 私立 "private"; to tell them apart, people sometimes say いちりつ in speech. The examples concern municipal facilities, not general visits to the city.

examples[].german: I live in the city of Seattle now.
I looked at a map on the City of Seattle website.
en.notes: シアトル市 is the city of Seattle. 市 is read し as the ending of a city name. シアトル市に住む names the place of residence; シアトル市のウェブサイト, by contrast, refers to the city's website. The name シアトル is written in katakana.

examples[].german: This is a machine used for fitness training.
Please use this tool.
en.notes: 用いる means "to use" and is especially useful in explanations or instructions. It is a transitive Ichidan verb: 用います, 用いて. The means used takes を, the purpose often takes に. Before a noun, 用いる describes what the thing is used for.

examples[].german: Life is wonderful.
I traveled abroad for the first time in my life.
en.notes: 人生 means life as a personal path through life. 人生って... is a casual way of making life the topic of conversation. 人生で初めて means "for the first time in one's life"; で names the frame of experience here, not a place of residence.

examples[].german: Jenny is British.
I talked in English with a British friend.
en.notes: イギリス人 is a British person. The ending 人 is read じん in nationality terms. イギリス人です states nationality; イギリス人の友達 links this information with a person, such as a friend.

examples[].german: Hello, how are you?
I started an email to a friend with "hello".
en.notes: Here 今日は means the greeting: it is read こんにちは, with wa at the end. It is usually written in hiragana. It suits a daytime greeting in conversation and a friendly opening for a message. The same spelling can otherwise mean きょうは "as for today ..."; this card practices the greeting.

examples[].german: That's a quiet dog, isn't it?
Please be quiet in the library.
en.notes: 大人しい describes quiet, gentle or good-natured behavior, including in animals. As an i-adjective it stands directly before the noun: 大人しい犬. With 大人しくする you talk about behaving quietly or well; for this, い becomes く.

examples[].german: The airport is far.
The school is far away, so I go by bus.
en.notes: 遠い here denotes a large spatial distance. A reference point can be named with から: 家から遠い ("far from home"). For a large or spacious room, 広い is used instead. The reading とおい contains a long o and is romanized tōi.

examples[].german: I knocked on the door.
Please close the door.
en.notes: 戸 means a door, especially one in Japanese-style construction, such as a sliding door. In 戸をノックする and 戸を閉める the door is the object with を. The reading と is short; 戸 by itself does not specify which way the door opens.

examples[].german: That woman? That's Mami.
A woman explained the way to me.
en.notes: 女の人 means "woman" and is a term for a person made of 女＋の＋人. In あの女の人, あの points to a woman farther away. When you get something explained by her, に is used: 女の人に教えてもらう. The reading also includes the ん in おんな.

examples[].german: I want to widen my circle of friends.
I spread out the map and looked at it.
en.notes: 広げる is a transitive Ichidan verb: 広げます, 広げて. With it you can unfold something, such as a map, or expand an area. 友達の輪を広げる means to widen one's circle of friends. What is spread out or expanded takes を.

examples[].german: It's an echo! Can you hear it?
Because I wanted to hear an echo, I called out loudly.
en.notes: 山びこ is an echo, especially one in the mountains. 聞こえる describes that one can hear it without actively listening for it. 山びこを聞きたくて, on the other hand, names the wish to hear an echo as the reason for a call.

examples[].german: The book is on the table.
I wiped the tabletop.
en.notes: テーブルの上 means the tabletop or the place on the table. の links テーブル with 上, which is read うえ here. For a location, に follows; when you wipe the surface, it takes を as the area being worked on.

examples[].german: There are lots of manga under the bed.
I cleaned under the bed.
en.notes: ベッドの下 is the area under the bed. の links the bed with the position word 下, read した. With ベッドの下に you name the place of objects; with ベッドの下を掃除する, the area being cleaned. The small ッ doubles the d in beddo.

examples[].german: Then I watched the sunrise from Mt. Fuji.
What time is sunrise?
en.notes: 日の出 is sunrise. The part の belongs to the fixed term; the reading is ひので. With 日の出を見る you report watching it. With 日の出の時間は何時ですか, on the other hand, you ask for the time of sunrise.

examples[].german: One draft beer, please.
Please show me the draft beer menu.
en.notes: 生ビール is nama beer, often ordered as draft beer in restaurants. In this meaning, 生 is read なま, and ビール has a long i. To count glasses of beer use 杯: 一杯 is いっぱい. 生ビールのメニュー names the corresponding drinks menu.

examples[].german: I'm at the north exit!
Let's meet at the north exit.
en.notes: 北口 is the northern entrance or exit, for example at a train station. 口 is read ぐち here. 北口にいる says where a person is; 北口で待ち合わせする names the meeting point. Whether an entrance or an exit is meant depends on the situation.

examples[].german: This is a photo of Mt. Fuji.
What is this?
About the plan we just talked about, what do you think of it?
en.notes: これ is an independent demonstrative pronoun: "this one". It refers to something near the speaker or the thing just pointed out. Unlike この, これ needs no following noun. これが… identifies the thing, これは何ですか asks about it. これ can also pick up the thing or idea just discussed. 此れ is a rare kanji spelling; in everyday writing これ is usual.

examples[].german: This room is spacious.
Children are playing in a big park.
en.notes: 広い refers to a large area or lots of available space: a spacious room or an expansive park. It does not mean "far away"; 遠い is used for that. Before a noun the い is kept: 広い公園.

examples[].german: Two apple juices, please.
I wash the apple and then eat it.
en.notes: リンゴ is the katakana spelling for apple. In リンゴジュース it forms the first part of "apple juice". In an order, 二つ counts two servings. リンゴを洗ってから食べる, by contrast, describes a sequence: wash the apple first, then eat it.

examples[].german: I read a book by lamplight.
I turned on the light in the room.
en.notes: 明かり is light or a light source. ランプの明かり means the light of a lamp; 明かりで本を読む names it as an aid for reading. 部屋の明かりをつける means to switch on the light in the room. Here つける is used as the verb for switching on.

examples[].german: I have no strength in my right hand.
I hold the pen in my right hand.
en.notes: 右手 is the right hand and is a noun. With 右手で you name the hand as the means of an action, such as holding a pen. 右手に力が入らない describes having no strength in the right hand. In this word, 手 is read て.

examples[].german: I held a spoon in my left hand.
I wear a ring on my left hand.
en.notes: 左手 is the left hand and is a noun. 左手で names it as the means of holding or using an object. 左手に指輪をする, by contrast, describes the place where one wears a ring.

examples[].german: I want to live to be a hundred years old.
Fish live in water.
en.notes: 生きる is an intransitive ichidan verb: 生きます, 生きて. It speaks of living, that is, being alive. 生きている describes this state. In 百歳まで生きたい, まで names the desired age as the limit; for the place where one lives, 住む is usually used instead.

examples[].german: This class is suspended for a while.
I temporarily suspended the construction work.
en.notes: 休止 is the suspension or interruption of an activity or operation. It is not simply a rest break like 休憩. このクラスは休止です describes a class that is suspended. With 工事を休止する you say that you are interrupting the construction work; the project affected takes を.

examples[].german: On days off I drink wine.
Tomorrow is a day off.
en.notes: 休日 is a day off or a holiday; the word need not mean a legal public holiday. 休日は… describes what one does on such days. 明日は休日です says that tomorrow is a day off. The u in kyūjitsu is long.

examples[].german: First, I cut the tomatoes.
Please wash your hands first.
en.notes: 先ず means "first" here and is mostly written まず. It places an action before the following steps. The adverb needs no particle: 先ずトマトを切る. A request can also begin with 先ず to highlight the first step.

examples[].german: The month before last, I went to Cuba.
How much was the rent the month before last?
en.notes: 先々月 is the month before last, that is, two months before the current month. You can use it as a time expression without a particle. With 先々月の you connect this period to a noun, such as 先々月の家賃 for the rent of the month before last.

examples[].german: Last month was June.
I went to Japan last month.
en.notes: 先月 is the month immediately before the month in which you are speaking. As a time expression it often stands before the verb without a particle: 先月日本に行きました. With 先月は you make the past month the topic; 先月の写真 would be photos from that month.

examples[].german: This road is narrow.
This room is small.
en.notes: 狭い describes little width or little available space. With a road it means "narrow", with a room "cramped/small". It is the counterpart of 広い. The negative is 狭くない, the past 狭かった.

examples[].german: Thank you very much for the other day.
I read the book I bought the other day.
en.notes: 先日 refers to a certain day not long ago: "the other day" or "a few days ago". Unlike 先月, it does not specify a whole calendar month. 先日はありがとうございました thanks someone for an earlier meeting or help. In 先日買った本, the time expression belongs to the purchase, not to the later reading.

examples[].german: My father is a Frisbee expert.
I had a master of cooking teach me some tricks.
en.notes: 名人 is someone who masters an activity superbly. With activity + の名人 you name the field, such as 料理の名人. The word can also be used admiringly in daily life and does not claim any particular professional qualification. 名人に教えてもらう describes having such a person teach you something.

examples[].german: My surname is "Tanaka".
Please tell me your surname.
en.notes: 名字 is the family name and is a noun. With 名字は田中です you state your surname; 名字を教えてください asks for this information. The whole reading is みょうじ, with a long ō. It does not refer to the given name, which is called 下の名前, for example.

examples[].german: The girl got angry and pressed her lips into a straight line.
Birds were lined up in a straight line on the power line.
en.notes: With the reading いちもんじ, 一文字 means "straight line", like the shape of the character 一. 口を一文字に結ぶ describes lips pressed firmly together into a straight line; 一文字に並ぶ describes a straight-line arrangement. The reading ひともじ for "one character" belongs to a different usage and is not practiced here.

examples[].german: I went to Japan in 2011.
I looked at photos from 2011.
en.notes: ２０１１年 refers to the calendar year 2011 and is read にせんじゅういちねん. After this year number, 年 is read ねん. With ２０１１年に you name the year of an event; with ２０１１年の写真 you assign photos to this year. The full-width digits change neither the number nor the reading.

en.meaning: within the year; by the end of the year
examples[].german: A calf will be born within this year.
I will finish it by the end of the year.
en.notes: 年内 means the part of the year in question that is still left. 年内に means "within this year" or "by the end of the year": the event should happen before the turn of the year, not necessarily exactly on the last day. 終わらせます is "I will bring it to an end"; this differs from the intransitive 終わります "it ends".

examples[].german: First-year students, please raise your hands.
I am a first-year university student.
en.notes: 一年生 refers to a person in the first year of a school or college. For elementary school children "first grader" fits, for 大学の一年生 "first-year student". It is about the year of schooling, not age. 一年生の子 connects the grade level with the children.

examples[].german: Thank you for your prompt email.
The phone rang right after I got home.
en.notes: 早々に means "quickly" or "promptly". In 早々にメールをくれて、ありがとう you thank someone for a quick message. After a noun, 早々 can also mean "right after ...": 帰宅早々 is immediately after getting home. The reading そうそう contains two long ō sounds; here the word is an adverb, not a particle.

en.meaning: in one go; all at once, suddenly
examples[].german: My father ate the chocolate on the table in one go.
The temperature dropped all at once.
en.notes: 一気に describes an action done without interruption, such as eating something up in one go. With a change of state it can mean "all at once" or "suddenly": 気温が一気に下がる. The っ is rendered as a doubled k in ikki. に belongs to the expression practiced here.

examples[].german: My mother is in a good mood today.
I'm not in the mood to watch a movie today.
en.notes: 気分 refers to one's mood or state of feeling. 気分がいい can mean "to be in a good mood" or "to feel well", depending on context. With 映画を見る気分ではありません you say that you are not in the mood for a movie right now; it is not about the ability to watch a movie.

examples[].german: This room is bright.
The morning sky is bright.
My older sister has a cheerful personality and has many friends.
en.notes: As an i-adjective, 明るい stands directly before a noun: 明るい部屋 (a bright room). It also describes a cheerful person or good prospects for the future. The negative is 明るくない. With a field of expertise, ～に明るい means "to be well versed in something". 明い is recognized as a search variant; for your own writing, use 明るい.

examples[].german: When are you finally going to get serious?
Do you mean that seriously?
en.notes: 本気 speaks of seriousness and genuine commitment. 本気で言う means to mean something seriously; 本気を出す means to really exert oneself or to get seriously started. The question いつになったら、本気を出すんですか can sound reproachful. 本気で describes the attitude toward the action that follows.

examples[].german: It's amazing that you can stay so calm.
Don't worry, I'm fine.
en.notes: 平気 describes calmness or a lack of worry. In casual speech 平気です can also assure that everything is fine. Depending on tone, 平気でいる sounds admiring or critical. よく平気でいられますね expresses astonishment; よく here does not mean "often" or "always".

examples[].german: Nick has something of a single-minded streak, doesn't he?
He is a straightforward, single-minded person.
My grandfather had a single-minded character and never went back on anything he had once decided.
en.notes: 一本気 describes a character that is "straightforward" and "unwavering" in devotion to one thing: honest, without ulterior motives, but also not very willing to compromise. Typical patterns are 一本気な人, 一本気な性格 and 一本気なところがある; less often as a noun with の (一本気の男). The tone is usually appreciative, unlike 頑固 ("stubborn"), which is clearly negative; 一途, by contrast, stresses devotion to a person or goal, for example in love. The word sounds somewhat old-fashioned.

examples[].german: Oh! A bamboo shoot is poking out of the ground!
I simmered bamboo shoots.
en.notes: 竹の子 is a bamboo shoot, not literally a "bamboo child". It can mean the growing plant or the food. 出てる is the casual short form of 出ている, "is coming out / has grown out". 土 has the reading つち here; the whole reading of the card word remains たけのこ.

examples[].german: A villager went into the river.
The villagers are preparing the festival.
en.notes: 村人 are people who live in a village. In this word, 人 is read びと: むらびと. 一人の村人 names a single person; here 一人 is read ひとり. Without a number, 村人 can also mean several villagers depending on the context, such as the helpers at a festival.

examples[].german: It's not a kitchen worth showing to other people.
Please show me the photo.
en.notes: 見せる means "to show" and is a transitive ichidan verb: 見せます, 見せて. The thing shown takes を, the person it is shown to takes に. 人に見せるほどの… describes something worth showing to others. 見る, by contrast, means "to see/look at" and distributes the roles differently.

en.meaning: way of looking; how to read
examples[].german: Do you know how to read this chart?
Let's try changing our way of looking at it.
en.notes: 見方 can refer to a viewpoint or to the way of reading or understanding something. このチャートの見方 asks how to read the chart. 見方を変える, on the other hand, means to take a different perspective. In 変えてみましょう, てみる invites trying that once.

examples[].german: There are lots of shellfish in the river.
I picked up shells at the seaside.
en.notes: 貝 can refer to the living shellfish or to its shell. For living shellfish, いる fits as with other animals. 貝を拾う at the beach often means picking up shells; there 拾う is the verb of the action. The reading かい stays the same in both meanings.

examples[].german: Last year this area had a water shortage.
There is a shortage of staff.
en.notes: 不足 means shortage or scarcity. As a する-verb, 不足する means "to be lacking / to be insufficient" and is intransitive: 水が不足する, not 水を. 不足しています describes an existing shortage. The card shows the noun stem 不足; the verb forms belong to 不足する.

examples[].german: There are lots of people inside the car.
Please be quiet inside the vehicle.
en.notes: 車内 is the interior of a vehicle, including a train or bus. It is a noun: 車内に人がいる names the place where someone is, and 車内ではお静かにお願いします asks for quiet behavior there. Vehicle + の車内 can specify which vehicle is meant.

examples[].german: My father is an office worker.
My father reads the newspaper every morning.
Dad, will you help me?
en.notes: お父さん is a respectful term for another person's father and a common way to address your own father. In familiar family conversation it can also mean "my father", as in the first examples. When speaking to outsiders, you normally use 父（ちち）for your own father.

examples[].german: It's dark at night.
The room is dark, so I'll turn on the light.
en.notes: 暗い here describes low brightness in a room or outdoors. The negative 暗くない means "not dark"; the opposite is 明るい. A color can also be dark, but this card focuses on lighting conditions.

examples[].german: I taught Japanese to a friend who is second-generation Japanese-descended.
He is a second-generation Japanese emigrant descendant.
en.notes: 二世 here means the second generation of a family with a migration background, such as 日系二世 for people of Japanese descent. It is not a statement of age. The addition 日系 makes clear which origin is meant. The statement of origin alone says nothing about which language the individual person speaks.

en.meaning: third generation; the Third (after a name)
examples[].german: My friend is third-generation Japanese-descended.
I read a book about Henry III.
en.notes: 三世 can refer to the third generation of a family with a migration background, such as 日系三世. After a name it also means "the Third", as in ヘンリー三世. Here the reading is さんせい. The statement of origin and the number in a ruler's name are different uses of the same word.

examples[].german: On weekends I mainly spend my time at home.
This company mainly makes cars.
en.notes: 主に means "mainly" or "chiefly". It names the main emphasis without excluding other possibilities. 主に家で過ごす says where one mostly spends time; 主に車を作る names the most important product. The adverb comes before the statement it qualifies.

en.meaning: one's husband; master of the house, owner
examples[].german: This person is my husband.
The owner of this shop is good at cooking.
en.notes: 主人 is a noun. In わたしの主人 one's own husband is meant; in この店の主人 the owner of the shop. The context therefore decides the meaning. For another person's husband the polite form ご主人 is often encountered; this card practices the form without ご.

examples[].german: On the left is Mami, in the middle is Jenny, and on the right is Michael.
There is a table in the middle of the room.
en.notes: 中央 is the middle or center and is a noun. 部屋の中央に names a place within the room. In 中央がジェニーです, on the other hand, が identifies the person in the middle position. In ちゅうおう both ū and ō are long; as a noun, 中央 often needs の before another noun.

examples[].german: That mountain is flat, isn't it?
I pitched the tent on a level spot.
en.notes: 平ら describes a level or flat surface. As a na-adjective it takes な before a noun: 平らな場所. In a sentence you say この道は平らです. 平らにする describes making something level; ら is part of the word and not a sign of an i-adjective.

examples[].german: On weekdays, dinner is mainly curry.
I have work on weekdays.
en.notes: 平日 refers to the ordinary days as opposed to days off or holidays. In the usual weekly schedule this typically means Monday to Friday; the actual schedule determines the boundary. 平日のディナー uses の for dinner on such days. 平日は makes these days the topic of a habit or work arrangement.

examples[].german: That was a hit with all your strength, wasn't it?
A single blow decided the match.
en.notes: 一打 is a single blow or hit, for example in sports. The reading is いちだ. 力いっぱいの一打 evaluates a powerful blow; 一打で names a single blow as the means or the decisive cause. Here the word counts the act of striking, not a person.

examples[].german: There were many small plates on the table in the bar.
I put soy sauce in the small dish.
en.notes: 小皿 is a small plate or small dish for serving. The reading こざら has a z: 皿 alone is read さら. 小皿がある describes tableware that is there; 小皿に醤油を入れる names the small dish as the destination and the soy sauce as the contents.

examples[].german: I got a beer as a thank-you.
I want to express my thanks.
en.notes: お礼 is a polite word for thanks. お礼に means "as a thank-you" and names the occasion for a gift or action. お礼を言う means to express one's thanks; お礼を言いたい expresses the wish to do so. The initial お is part of the word form practiced here.

examples[].german: This luggage is heavy.
This box is so heavy that I can't carry it alone.
en.notes: 重い here means "heavy" in terms of weight. For a difficult task, 難しい is used, not automatically 重い. The form 重くて can link the weight with a consequence; 軽い is the opposite.

examples[].german: This is an unfair method.
Fraud is not tolerated.
en.notes: 不正 describes dishonest or unlawful behavior. As a noun it can mean "fraud / wrongdoing" and as a na-adjective it can modify a noun: 不正な方法. 不正は許されません rejects such behavior. The meaning comes from the context, not from one particular kind of crime alone.

examples[].german: This calf is still a very small baby.
There are calves on the farm.
en.notes: 子牛 is a calf. The whole reading is こうし, with a long ō; it is not split into ko ushi. 子 here describes the young animal. For living calves you use いる, as in 牧場に子牛がいます for where they are.

examples[].german: This is a precious gem of my mother's.
The ring is set with a gem.
en.notes: 宝石 is a gem or jewel and is a noun. 母の大切な宝石 can mean a stone that means a great deal to the mother personally; 大切 does not have to claim a high monetary value. 宝石がついている describes a piece of jewelry fitted with a gem. The reading ほうせき has a long ō.

examples[].german: Please give me one whole piece, not just half.
I copied the whole folder.
en.notes: 丸ごと means "whole / in its entirety". It refers to the extent, not to how quickly something happens. 丸ごと一つ orders a complete piece instead of a half. A folder can also be 丸ごとコピーする, that is, copied together with all its contents. The word is used as an adverb.

examples[].german: I looked into air pollution.
The air is clean.
en.notes: 大気 refers to the atmosphere or the air as part of the environment. You encounter the word in connection with weather or environmental topics. 大気の汚れ means "pollution of the air"; 大気がきれい describes its cleanliness. The reading たいき stays short, with no long vowel.

examples[].german: My mother often says "It's okay".
He doesn't mention that story.
en.notes: Here 口にする means to utter or mention something. A topic takes を: その話を口にする. For words quoted literally, use と: 「大丈夫」と口にする. You change the する part, for example to 口にします or 口にしません; 口 stays くち in this expression.

examples[].german: Canada is in North America.
I looked at a map of North America.
en.notes: 北アメリカ is North America as a continent. 北 is read きた here; アメリカ is in katakana. 北アメリカにある names a geographic location; 北アメリカの地図 is a map of the continent. It does not merely mean the north of the USA.

examples[].german: Which tie shall we get as a present?
Which one is your book?
Well then, I'll have the soup while it's warm.
en.notes: どれ asks independently about one thing out of several possibilities: どれがあなたの本ですか. With どれにする you choose something; directly before a noun, however, どの is used. As an interjection, どれ can also mean "well then" or "let's see" and introduce an action. 何れ is a rare kanji spelling for this reading; どれ is usually in hiragana. 何れ can also be read いずれ, a different word.

examples[].german: Yeah, let's do that!
"Have you eaten yet?" "Yeah, I have."
en.notes: うん is a casual affirmative reply: "yes". It suits familiar conversations, for instance among friends or in the family. With うん、そうしよう you agree to a suggestion; in response to a question, うん can confirm a fact. In more polite situations はい is usually the better reply.

en.meaning: to put in; to pour in; to let in
examples[].german: I put water in the bottle every day.
I let the child into the room.
en.notes: 入れる is a transitive ichidan verb: 入れます, 入れて. With を you name what goes in, with に the destination. With water it means "to fill"; 子供を部屋に入れる can mean to let the child into the room. The intransitive 入る, by contrast, describes someone or something going in by itself.

examples[].german: This bag is light.
I take a light bag on trips.
en.notes: 軽い here means "light" in the sense of low weight. For a low level of difficulty, 易しい is used. The opposite of 軽い is 重い. The adjective stands before a noun without な: 軽いかばん.

examples[].german: Today is the day to put out the recycling.
I took my wallet out of my bag.
en.notes: 出す is a transitive godan verb: 出します, 出して. It describes taking something out or putting it outside. The thing takes を, and the place it comes from can follow with から: かばんから財布を出す. 出す日 is the day of the action; 出る, by contrast, describes going out without a direct object.

en.meaning: to give birth to; to produce
examples[].german: This plan created new jobs.
The cat gave birth to kittens.
en.notes: 生む can mean "to give birth to" or "to bring forth". A living being or a thing takes を as what comes into being: 子猫を生む, 仕事を生む. It is a transitive Godan verb: 生みます, 生んで. The intransitive 生まれる, on the other hand, says that something is born or comes into being.

en.meaning: to stand (something) up; to set up
examples[].german: A book stand is for standing books upright.
I set up a tent.
en.notes: 立てる here means to set something upright or to put it up. It is a transitive ichidan verb: 立てます, 立てて. The object that is set up takes を. In 本を立てるためのもの, ための names the purpose of the object; テントを立てる is setting up a tent. 立つ, by contrast, describes standing itself.

examples[].german: Please make this character bold.
I read the headline in bold type.
en.notes: 太字 is bold type or thick lettering and is a noun. 太字にする switches the text to bold; 太字の見出し links the style with a headline. 太字で書く names the lettering as the manner of writing. The reading is ふとじ, with no long vowel.

examples[].german: Please shuffle the cards well.
I let the child join in the adults' game too.
en.notes: 交ぜる is a transitive Ichidan verb: 交ぜます, 交ぜて. It fits shuffling cards together and including a person in a group or a game. In カードをよく交ぜる, よく means "thoroughly". With に you can name the group or game that someone is added to.

examples[].german: The moonlight was very beautiful last night.
I could see the road by moonlight.
en.notes: 月光 is moonlight and is read げっこう: the doubled k for っ and ō for こう. 月光がきれい evaluates the light; 月光で道が見える describes being able to see the road by moonlight. で names the illumination here, が the thing that is visible.

examples[].german: This apartment gets a lot of sunlight.
I avoided the sunlight and sat in the shade.
en.notes: 日光 is sunlight here. In このアパートは日光がよく入る you say that a lot of light comes into the apartment. 日光を避ける means to avoid direct sunlight. っ gives kk and こう a long ō. The identically written city Nikkō is a different meaning.

examples[].german: The DVD and the CD were released on the same day.
I have a problem because two exams fall on the same day.
en.notes: 同日 means "on the same day". The events concerned can still take place at different times; 同日 does not claim simultaneity to the minute. 同日に names the shared day as a time expression. You often meet the word in announcements or when planning several appointments.

examples[].german: The coin spins on the table.
The Earth revolves around the Sun.
en.notes: 回る is an intransitive godan verb: 回ります, 回って. It can describe turning in place or circling around something. In コインが回る the coin is the subject. 太陽の周りを回る names with を the path traveled; を does not make the verb transitive here.

examples[].german: I'll pass this time.
The test this time was difficult.
en.notes: 今回 means the present occasion or "this time". 今回は、やめておきます is a polite decision to forgo something this time. 今回のテスト connects the expression to the test in question. Even when the exam is already over, 今回 can still mean the current round that was discussed most recently.

examples[].german: There are many people.
I have so much homework that I'm not done yet.
en.notes: 多い can describe a large number or a large quantity. The usual sentence form is 人が多い ("there are many people"). Before a noun, 多くの or たくさんの is usually used for "many ...", not simply 多い. おおい is written as ōi with a long o.

examples[].german: The same three people go to that meeting every time.
Please don't be late every time.
en.notes: 毎回 means "every time" and refers to recurring occasions, not necessarily fixed days. In a sentence it often stands without a particle. 毎回この三人 stresses that the same three people always take part. 毎回遅刻しないでください objects to repeated lateness; it does not describe a single exception.

examples[].german: Apparently you can win a TV.
I won the lottery.
The ball hit the window.
en.notes: 当たる means, among other things, "to hit" and "to win". In these meanings it is intransitive: the ball or the prize takes が; the target that is hit can take に. 宝くじが当たる means to win a lottery prize. The Godan verb forms 当たります and 当たって. An object that someone hits deliberately is expressed differently with the related 当てる.

examples[].german: The word "Winner!" caught my eye.
Today is a lucky day, isn't it?
This ticket is a winner, so I get a prize.
en.notes: 当たり here is a hit or a lucky success. On a ticket or package, 当たり can indicate a win; as a short exclamation "Bingo!" fits. 当たりの日 names an especially successful day. Do not confuse it with the identically read place word 辺り "area". In these examples the form is a noun, not the verb form 当たり or the ending "per".

examples[].german: Is this workshop held every month?
I read three books every month.
en.notes: 毎月 means "every month", read まいつき here. It names a regular repetition; 来月, by contrast, refers only to the next month. For an event, 毎月ありますか asks about the monthly occurrence. 毎月本を三冊読む states a monthly quantity; 三冊 counts books. Before 毎月 you usually need no に.

examples[].german: Every April I go cherry blossom viewing.
I go to see the cherry blossoms every year.
Every year we take a family photo on his/her birthday.
en.notes: 毎年 is "every year", here with the reading まいとし. It describes habits or regularly recurring events. 毎年四月に links the yearly repetition with a month; the に belongs to 四月 here. お花見 is viewing cherry blossoms and does not have to be an organized festival. The second common reading まいねん does not change the meaning.

examples[].german: Is beef okay for you?
Beef has gotten more expensive.
en.notes: 牛肉 is beef. The noun names the meat, not the living animal 牛. 牛肉は平気ですか asks in a food context whether someone can eat beef without a problem or finds it acceptable. 高くなる means "to become more expensive" here. The long first syllable is written gyū; 牛 and 肉 together form the fixed food name.

examples[].german: I was the only man there.
I take care of my own things myself.
en.notes: 自分 refers to the person in question, oneself; who is meant is clear from the sentence. In the examples it is the speaker. 自分のこと names one's own affairs, 自分でする means "to do it oneself". It does not automatically stand for "I" in every conversation: in narration it can refer to another person mentioned earlier.

examples[].german: I'd like that light blue bag.
I am wearing a light blue shirt.
en.notes: 水色 is light blue or a pale shade of blue. Before a noun, の is usually used: 水色のバッグ, 水色のシャツ. The word is not an i-adjective; 水色い is not formed. ほしいんですが is a reserved way to introduce a wish, for example in a shop. The color term names only the shade, not the material of the bag or shirt.

examples[].german: This bus goes to Seattle.
I take the train bound for Tokyo.
Please put the items bound for Tokyo in this box.
en.notes: 行き is used after the name of a destination and means "heading to ..." or "destined for ...". This entry practices the reading ゆき, as in 東京行き. You also hear いき; the reading shown here remains ゆき. After the compound, の can come before the vehicle. It is a destination label attached to a noun, not an ordinary sentence particle like に.

examples[].german: The error occurred thousands of times.
Thousands of people came.
en.notes: 何千 means "many thousands" and is often combined with a counter: 何千回 "thousands of times", 何千人 "thousands of people". も emphasizes the large number. Here 何 is not a question about a specific number; the sentence asserts a vaguely large quantity. With 人 you say にん, with 回 かい.

examples[].german: There is little money.
There are few students today, so the classroom is quiet.
en.notes: 少ない evaluates a small number or amount, as in 人が少ない and お金が少ない. As an adjective it describes the quantity of something; 少し, by contrast, is a quantity adverb, for example 少し食べる ("to eat a little"). The connecting form is 少なくて.

examples[].german: What month were you born?
What month did you come to Japan?
en.notes: 何月 asks "which month?" and is read なんがつ. The combination 何月生まれ asks about the birth month, not the birthday as a calendar date. 何月に names the month of an event. In this calendar question, 月 is read がつ; "how many months?" needs a different combination, such as 何か月.

examples[].german: There is a lot to learn in life.
I studied economics at university.
en.notes: 学ぶ means "to learn, to study" and takes the subject of learning with を: 経済学を学ぶ. It can refer both to instruction and to learning from experience. 大学で names the place of study here. The Godan verb ends in ぶ and forms 学びます, 学んで and 学んだ. 勉強する is another common form for focused study.

examples[].german: My brother is one year above me.
Before the new school year begins, I buy new textbooks.
en.notes: 学年 can refer to the school year as a period of time or to a student's grade level. 一つ上の学年 means "one grade higher". For "I am in third grade" one usually says 三年生; 学年, on the other hand, can be compared directly or made the topic. The reading is がくねん, gakunen.

examples[].german: I want to take a robotics class.
I am studying engineering.
I use knowledge of engineering to build a new machine.
en.notes: 工学 is engineering, or the engineering sciences. It names a field of study and takes を as a subject of study. ロボット工学 is robotics; の can attach a course to it. クラスに入りたい means wanting to take part in this course. Identically read words such as 高額 "large sum of money" have different kanji and meanings.

examples[].german: That is not a testicle.
That way of putting it is vulgar, so I say 「睾丸」 rather than 「金玉」.
en.notes: 金玉, read きんたま, is a vulgar colloquial term for the testicles. In a medical or polite description, 睾丸 is the appropriate neutral term. The individual kanji do not literally mean "golden balls" here. The reading きんぎょく belongs to a different dictionary entry; this entry explains the vulgar form so that you can understand such conversations.

examples[].german: Along with sweat, fluid leaves the body.
The fluid in the body is important.
en.notes: 体内 means the inside of the body. As a noun it is combined with particles: 体内から "from inside the body", 体内の水分 "the fluid in the body". It is not an i-adjective. The examples describe a process and a component inside the body; for the surface of the body you need a different expression.

examples[].german: "Psycho" is Hitchcock's masterpiece.
This film is a masterpiece, isn't it?
It took five years to complete this large-scale work.
en.notes: 大作 can refer to a substantial, large-scale work or an important masterpiece. For films it can stress the large scale of production without praising every single scene. の names the creator, as in ヒッチコックの大作. In the second sentence, ね is an invitation to agree with an evaluation. Do not confuse it with 対策 "countermeasure", which is read the same way.

examples[].german: I raised my voice without meaning to.
Please don't speak in a loud voice.
en.notes: 大声 is a loud voice. With で it becomes the manner of speaking: 大声で話す "to speak loudly". 大声が出る describes a loud utterance slipping out. つい and てしまった stress the unintentional occurrence in the first sentence. As a polite notice, the request 大声で話さないでください can be used.

examples[].german: Those two are brothers.
I have two siblings.
We sisters run a small shop together.
Of the two sisters, the elder lives in Tokyo and the younger in Osaka.
en.notes: 兄弟 can mean brothers or siblings in general; sisters are not excluded in the general meaning. The kanji do name an older and a younger brother, but the overall usage is broader. 二人 is read ふたり. With 兄弟は二人います the speaker usually means two siblings besides themselves; for the total number of siblings including oneself you can phrase it differently, for example 三人兄弟です. The spelling 姉妹 can also be read きょうだい as a special meaning reading (gikun) when sisters are explicitly meant. Normally, however, 姉妹 is read しまい. The examples with 姉妹 deliberately use the special reading きょうだい here.

examples[].german: Is the piano competition next month?
I will start a new job next month.
en.notes: 来月 is the next calendar month after the current one. As a time expression it often stands without に. 来月ですか asks about a date, and 来月から marks the start of an activity that lasts for some time. The expression does not mean exactly "in thirty days"; the distance depends on today's date.

examples[].german: I get up early in the morning.
He replies quickly.
en.notes: 早い refers to an early point in time or to quick completion or reaction. 速い is used mainly for high speed of movement or progress. Before a verb, 早い becomes 早く: 早く起きる ("to get up early").

en.meaning: since ancient times; from of old
examples[].german: Customs from olden times remain in this region.
This tradition has continued since ancient times.
en.notes: 古来 means "since ancient times, for a long time" and usually sounds written or elevated. It suits traditional customs and traditions. 古来の習慣 is "a custom that has existed since ancient times". You also find 古来から; the から underlines the starting point in time. For a short personal "for a while now", 昔から is often more everyday.

en.meaning: for ... years; for the past ... years
examples[].german: Michael has been a friend of my father's for thirty years.
He has been a friend for ten years.
A dream I have held for ten years has finally come true.
en.notes: 〜年来 links a number of years with a relationship or thing that has existed over that period: 三十年来の友人 "a friend of thirty years". The sign 〜 shows the place for a number and is not pronounced. の often follows. Even without a number, 年来 means "existing for a long time". Here it names the duration up to now, not a calendar year or a future deadline.

examples[].german: The company has in-house designers.
Please follow the company's internal rules.
en.notes: 社内 means "inside the company, in-house". 社内に names the internal area as a place, 社内のルール the company's internal rules. The word does not by itself say whether the whole operation is in a single building. Contrast 社外 "outside the company"; the identically read 車内, by contrast, means the interior of a vehicle.

en.meaning: joining a company; entering a firm
examples[].german: My older sister joins that company next month.
The new graduates all joined the company at the same time in April.
It has already been five years since I joined the company.
en.notes: 入社 means joining a company as an employee; as an intransitive する-verb, the company takes に: 会社に入社する. It stresses the formal start of employment, often in connection with 新卒 and the 入社式 in April. 就職 is more general, "finding a job", and is not limited to companies. The counterpart is 退社 ("leaving the company", but also "finishing work for the day") or 退職. Common compounds: 入社試験, 入社式, 中途入社.

examples[].german: The cheese was triangular.
This shape is a triangle.
Please fold the paper into a triangle.
en.notes: 三角 is a triangle or a triangular shape. You describe something with 三角です or use 三角の before a noun. With the cheese the shape is meant; the second statement names a geometric figure. 三角に折る means to fold something into a triangle. The word says nothing about equal sides: a triangle does not have to be equilateral.

examples[].german: The keys on my keyboard are square.
This box is square.
I drew a square in my notebook and wrote my name inside it.
en.notes: 四角 refers to a four-cornered shape and, depending on the object, can also mean a square. For exactly "square", 正方形 is clearer. 四角です describes the shape; 四角い is the related i-adjective. In this entry the reading is しかく, not the identically read 資格 "qualification". The examples show objects and the drawing of a figure.

examples[].german: The staff member says, "Thank you very much."
Please say it clearly.
en.notes: 言う means "to say". Direct speech comes before と, as in 「ありがとう」と言う. This Godan verb forms 言います, 言って and 言った; despite its short reading, it is not an Ichidan verb. はっきり言う asks for a clear statement. In conversation the dictionary form often sounds like ゆう, but the dictionary reading practiced here remains いう.

examples[].german: Please reduce your driving speed.
We are driving on the expressway.
en.notes: 走行 refers to driving or the movement of a vehicle. As a noun it appears in 走行スピード, for example; with する it becomes a verb: 走行しています. 高速道路を here names the route being driven; を is not marking an object that is changed. In everyday speech 車で走る often fits as well, while 走行 sounds more technical.

examples[].german: This restaurant will open soon.
We will notify you shortly.
en.notes: 近日 means "soon, within the next few days" and is often used in announcements. It does not yet name an exact date. 近日中に limits an announced action to the near future. オープンする means "to open" for a restaurant. For a binding appointment, a specific day or time is clearer.

examples[].german: In recent years, Japanese whisky has been trending.
In recent years, the number of foreign tourists has increased.
Research in recent years has revealed new things.
en.notes: 近年 means "in recent years". It suits developments over a longer recent period, not just yesterday or today. 近年の before a noun can refer, for example, to recent research. 最近 is more general in everyday speech for "lately". The reading きんねん contains two consecutive n sounds.

examples[].german: It's already late.
He walks slowly.
en.notes: 遅い can describe a late point in time or a slow pace. もう遅いです means "it's already late" in the right context. 歩くのが遅い, by contrast, means "to walk slowly". For arriving late, 遅れる is often used.

examples[].german: A boy was born in 2018.
Two boys are playing.
en.notes: 男の子 is a boy or a male baby. The fixed compound contains の, but in ordinary usage it does not simply mean "a man's child". With 生まれる, the boy is the child who was born; 二人 counts two boys and is read ふたり. For an adult man, 男の人 is the usual other term.

examples[].german: There was a hairy caterpillar in the cabbage.
There are hairy caterpillars in the garden.
A hairy caterpillar is eating a leaf.
en.notes: 毛虫 is a hairy caterpillar. 毛 means hair; there are other words for caterpillars in general, such as イモムシ. がいる names the animal in a place. 毛虫が葉を食べる describes its feeding, not its effect on people. The figurative dictionary meaning for an annoying person is not practiced here.

examples[].german: My father was born in the old downtown district.
I took a walk through the old downtown district.
en.notes: 下町 traditionally refers to the lower-lying part of a city, characterized by shops, crafts and residential houses. It is not simply any city center or the modern business district. In Tokyo the term can especially mean the traditional eastern districts. The examples mention a place of origin and a walking route, without specifying a particular Tokyo district.

examples[].german: Tanaka-sensei is a man.
That man is a teacher.
A man showed me the way at the station.
en.notes: 男の人 means a man and is a common, neutral description of a person. 男の子, by contrast, means "boy". The の belongs to the fixed compound; the whole term is understood as a unit. A sentence can identify the person or ask about what he does. When addressing someone directly, one usually uses a name or an appropriate role title.

examples[].german: Thank you for everything until now.
What have you been doing until now?
en.notes: 今まで means "until now, so far" and sets the present as the endpoint of a period. 今までありがとう can be a farewell thanks for the time spent together so far. 今まで何をしていましたか asks about activities up to this moment. With に one can refer to past experiences; that is a separate construction, not the meaning "from now on".

examples[].german: Please give me some pink yarn.
I knitted a scarf with yarn.
en.notes: 毛糸 is wool yarn for knitting or crocheting. It means a processed thread and not just any raw wool. ピンク色の毛糸 names the color of the yarn; 毛糸で編む names the material used. 編む forms the past tense 編みました. For a scarf, マフラー is the usual word in the example.

examples[].german: I'm going to the supermarket right now and will be back.
Please come right away.
en.notes: 今すぐ means "right now" and stresses that an action should begin without delay. It is often used as a time expression without any further particle. 今すぐ来てください can sound urgent depending on the situation. 行ってきます announces leaving with a later return; the return is implied in this phrase.

examples[].german: In this village, rice has been grown since long ago.
I go back to my hometown for Obon.
During summer vacation, I went back to my hometown for the first time in a long while.
en.notes: 里 can mean a village or one's home, that is, the family's home. It often sounds more traditional than 村 or 故郷. 里に帰る describes returning there. The fixed compound 里帰り means "homecoming, visit to one's hometown". 里 is not normally used on its own for just any animal habitat.

examples[].german: I'm feeling a little homesick.
I got homesick and cried.
When I look at family photos, I get homesick.
en.notes: 里心 is homesickness or longing for one's hometown. The fixed expression 里心がつく means that this feeling arises. ついちゃった is the casual contraction of ついてしまった and describes the feeling that has arisen. With が the homesickness is named as a state that arises; 里心 is not itself a verb.

examples[].german: Is that true?
Please tell me the truth.
en.notes: 本当 means "truth", and 本当です means "it is true". Before a noun, の often follows: 本当のこと means "the truth, what really happened". 本当に strengthens a statement as "really"; by contrast, 本当ですか is a follow-up question about whether something is true. It is not an i-adjective and forms no 本当い here. The kana form ほんとう refers here to the same truth or reality.

examples[].german: He is a strong person.
The wind is strong today.
en.notes: 強い can express physical strength or high intensity, as with a person or a strong wind. The opposite is 弱い. The form 強く is used adverbially; before a noun, say 強い人 without な.

examples[].german: I wonder if that coin parking lot has a free space.
A vacant taxi came.
en.notes: 空車 can indicate an unoccupied taxi or free spaces in a parking lot. For a taxi, the sign means it can take passengers. For a parking facility, the available parking area is meant. The counterpart 満車 means complete occupancy in a parking context. The examples show these two different everyday situations.

examples[].german: My husband is my partner for life.
It became a memory for a lifetime.
I will never forget what happened on this day as long as I live.
en.notes: 一生 is a person's whole life. With の it describes a lifelong relationship or memory: 一生のパートナー, 一生の思い出. It can also limit an action in time without a particle, as in 一生忘れない. The small っ appears in the romanization as an extra s: isshō; 一緒 "together" is a different word.

examples[].german: That child's gestures are just like an adult's.
The cat's mannerisms are cute.
He signaled "Over here" by waving his hand.
en.notes: 仕草 is a visible movement, gesture or typical way of moving. It can describe people or animals. まるで大人の仕草だ compares the behavior to that of an adult. 仕草で shows that a gesture conveys something even without words. The focus here is on observed movements, not a full theatrical performance.

examples[].german: The te-form of 「出る」 is 「出て」.
Please use the "masu form" in your essay.
en.notes: 〜形, read けい, denotes a form in compounds, especially a grammatical verb form: て形, ます形. The mark 〜 shows the place of the preceding element and is not pronounced. The reading here is not the standalone word for shape, かたち. For a round plate, 丸い形 with かたち is therefore correct, not this attached grammatical term. Without the placeholder mark, the element is written 形; in て形 and ます形 the reading is けい.

examples[].german: I am Japanese, but I was born in San Francisco.
Where were you born?
I was born in a small village, but now I live in a big city.
en.notes: 生まれ here is birth, or the birthplace, as a noun. 生まれはサンフランシスコです names the place, while 日本人 names the nationality; the two do not have to be the same country. 生まれはどちらですか asks specifically about the place of birth. In these sentences the form is not simply a truncated verb form of 生まれる.

examples[].german: Please recycle the rest of the trash.
Do you have any other questions?
The shop sells bread. Besides that, you can also buy drinks.
en.notes: その他 means "the rest" or "in addition". This entry practices そのほか; especially in written lists そのた is also usual. Before a noun it takes の: その他のご質問, further questions. As an addition, そのほか can also introduce a further item. The spelling その外 is an attested variant, while そのほか explicitly shows the reading practiced here. What is left over or added comes from the context.

examples[].german: The elevator is at the west exit.
Let's meet at the west exit.
en.notes: 西口 is the west exit or west entrance, often at a train station. The compound names a specific side of the building. 西口にあります gives the location of an elevator; 西口で待ち合わせる gives the meeting point of an appointment. In this compound, 口 is read ぐち. A family name written the same way is not part of the location usage practiced here.

examples[].german: Today there is a crescent moon.
The crescent moon is beautiful, isn't it?
I drew a small crescent moon in the corner of the picture.
en.notes: 三日月 is a slender crescent moon. The name contains 三日, but in ordinary use it names the visible shape of the moon, not a freely counted period of three days. The reading is みかづき, mikazuki in Hepburn. It can refer to the moon in the sky or to a drawn crescent; 月 remains part of the fixed word here.

examples[].german: That looks interesting!
How much is that?
en.notes: それ means "that" for something near the listener or something just mentioned in the conversation. It stands alone; before a noun you need その instead. それはいくらですか asks for the price of that item. 面白そう describes an impression. 其れ is a rare kanji spelling of the same word; それ in hiragana is the usual form. The examples practice the demonstrative, not an exclamation or a verb form.

examples[].german: I'm in the department store restroom right now.
I bought clothes at the department store.
en.notes: デパート is a department store with various departments. This shortened English loanword does not refer to a single department of a company here. デパートのトイレ names a facility in the department store; デパートで服を買う gives the place of shopping. に fits the location of presence in the first sentence, で the action carried out there in the second.

examples[].german: I'm physically weak, so I often rest.
This team is weak.
en.notes: 弱い denotes little strength, little resilience or little competitive strength. 体が弱い describes a weak physical constitution, チームが弱い the low playing strength of a team. The opposite is 強い; the connecting form is 弱くて.

examples[].german: Is this your blog?
What is your name?
en.notes: あなた means "you", but it is not automatically a polite form of address. In direct conversation, people often use the name, the job title, or omit the person altogether. あなたの here marks possession, that is, the person in question. The questions are understandable but can seem distant with unfamiliar people. The special intimate address between spouses is not the meaning of these examples. 貴方 and 貴女 are recorded kanji spellings of あなた. The kana form is the usual one; the kanji do not guarantee a polite tone.

examples[].german: Dad is good at tennis.
Well done!
Since my older sister is good at cooking, she taught me how to make it.
en.notes: 上手い describes an ability here: テニスが上手い means "to be good at tennis". The reading is うまい, not じょうず; unlike 上手, 上手い is an i-adjective and forms 上手かった and 上手く. In casual conversation, 上手いですね can praise a skillful action. For this spelling we practice "skilled"; the other possible meaning "delicious" is often written うまい or 旨い.

examples[].german: That man over there is in his thirties.
He is in his thirties.
After I turned thirty, I started learning piano.
en.notes: 三十代 means the life stage from 30 to 39 years. The suffix 代 forms an age group here; "exactly thirty years old" is 三十歳. 三十代です places a person in this group, 三十代になってから looks back at the start of this life stage. The pronunciation is run together: さんじゅうだい.

examples[].german: I pay for the book by card.
Please pay the amount.
Shipping is included in the price.
en.notes: 代金 is the amount one pays for goods or a service. 本の代金 names the purchase price of the book, 代金を払う the payment of this amount. With カードで the means of payment is stated. 代金に含まれる explains what is included in the amount; the shipping costs are called 送料. General expenses or financial outlay are more often described with 費用.

examples[].german: This thread snaps easily.
The thread snapped.
My visa expires next month.
en.notes: 切れる is an intransitive Ichidan verb here: 糸が切れる means "the thread snaps". The affected thing takes が; someone who cuts something uses 切る with を instead. With 期限が切れる a deadline or validity expires. The forms are 切れます, 切れて and 切れない. 切れてしまった stresses the resulting, often undesired state.

examples[].german: Please write the whole title in capital letters.
Please write your name in capital letters.
I type capital letters while holding down the Shift key.
en.notes: 大文字 is read おおもじ here and means capital letters, such as A instead of a. It is about letter case, not a larger font size. 大文字で書く uses で to indicate how something is written; when typing, the Shift key can help. The opposite term is 小文字. The first example's romanization therefore uses ōmoji.

examples[].german: I whispered "thank you" in his ear.
I whispered a secret in my friend's ear.
en.notes: 耳打ち refers to whispering directly into someone's ear. With する it becomes a verb: 耳打ちしました. The person is marked with に, and the whispered content with を or as a quotation before と. So you can whisper a short "thank you" or tell someone a secret. Any quiet voice without this closeness to the ear is not automatically 耳打ち.

examples[].german: I substituted yogurt for sour cream.
I use margarine as a substitute for butter.
There was no pillow, so I used a towel instead.
en.notes: 代用 means using something else as a substitute. In サワークリームをヨーグルトで代用する, the product being replaced comes before を and the substitute before で: yogurt replaces sour cream. Xの代用にYを使う expresses the same relationship as a noun. The word also fits outside recipes, for example when a towel temporarily replaces a pillow.

en.meaning: to appear (in a photo or video); to be captured
examples[].german: My father does not like appearing in videos.
I came out nicely in the photo.
en.notes: 写る means to appear in a photo or video. It is intransitive: the person shown is the subject, and 写真に or ビデオに names the medium. 写す, by contrast, is the verb for photographing or depicting someone or something. 写る ends in る but is a godan verb: 写ります, 写って, 写らない. The identically read 移る describes a change of place.

examples[].german: I intend to hold the meeting at the hotel.
We will hold an event next month.
I conducted an experiment and wrote the results in my notebook.
en.notes: 行う means "to carry out" or "to conduct" and sounds more formal than plain する. The action performed takes を: ミーティングを行う, 実験を行う. 場所で names the place of the activity. Despite the character 行, it is read おこなう here, not いく. This godan verb forms 行います, 行って and 行わない; the te-form is pronounced おこなって.

examples[].german: The white flowers are pretty.
Snow is white.
When I go to school, I wear a white shirt.
en.notes: 白い is the i-adjective "white" and stands directly before a noun: 白い花. The color name as a noun is 白（しろ）. For a piece of clothing, you can therefore say 白いシャツ or 白のシャツ; the negative of the adjective is 白くない.

examples[].german: The vehicle entered the underground area.
There is a parking lot in the basement.
en.notes: 地下 is a noun for the area beneath the ground or the basement level. 地下に入る names a destination, 地下にある a location. Before another noun, の is used, as in 地下の駐車場. The examples use the spatial meaning; political or secret activities are not described with it here.

examples[].german: They raised both hands and shouted banzai.
Please hold it with both hands.
en.notes: 両手 means the two hands of a person. In 両手を上げる they are the object of the movement; 両手で持つ, on the other hand, names the means by which one holds something. 両 stands for both parts of a pair, not for any number of hands. The word is a noun; before a following noun it needs の.

examples[].german: Please email me the schedule for both days.
The weather was good on both days.
en.notes: 両日 refers to two already known days and means "both days" or "on both days". The word suits schedules and announcements in particular. 両日のスケジュール sums up the planning of both days, 両日とも stresses that a statement applies to both. The days need not be consecutive; 二日間, by contrast, describes a duration of two days.

examples[].german: My father and my mother are both French.
I want to eat both.
en.notes: 両方 refers to both members or sides of a group of two. 父も母も names the two people explicitly; 両方とも confirms that the statement applies to both. With two dishes, 両方食べたい can mean that you want both. Before another noun, の is used, as in 両方の店. For more than two things, 全部 is usually more suitable.

examples[].german: Shall I cut all the onions?
Everything is finished.
en.notes: 全て refers to everything within a given group or to the full extent of an action. 全ての本 means "all the books": の is used before a noun. In 全て終わりました, the whole process in question is complete. 玉ねぎは全て切りますか asks whether all the onions on hand should be cut completely. すべて is often written in hiragana; it is not a na-adjective.

examples[].german: I ran to the office with all my strength.
I ran as hard as I could.
I helped my friend move with all my might.
en.notes: 全力 is all of one's strength or the greatest possible effort. 全力で describes the manner of an action: doing it with everything one has. This can apply to physical running or committed help. The common pattern is 全力で plus a verb. The word is a noun, not a na-adjective.

en.meaning: all Japan; All-Japan (as in national championships)
examples[].german: A notice has arrived from the All Japan Judo Federation.
The All Japan Championships are about to begin.
en.notes: 全日本 can mean "all-Japan, nationwide" before names of competitions or associations. 全日本選手権 is a national championship, 全日本柔道連盟 the All Japan Judo Federation. In both examples, 全日本 is part of a name with nationwide scope. Event titles may have a set pronunciation; here the dictionary reading ぜんにほん is kept.

examples[].german: Today was a peaceful day.
It was a peaceful era.
I wish peace and well-being for my family.
en.notes: 平安 means peace, tranquility or well-being and sounds rather solemn or literary. As a na-adjective it appears in 平安な日; as a noun one can say 家族の平安を願う, that is, to wish one's family peace and well-being. In everyday descriptions, 穏やか or 平和 often fit better. 平安な時代 here means a peaceful era, not the name of the historical 平安時代.

examples[].german: Have you ever been to Kyushu?
I took a trip to Kyushu.
I bought a map of Kyushu.
en.notes: 九州 is the name of one of Japan's four main islands. As a place name it takes に for a travel destination and の as in 九州の地図. 行ったことがありますか asks about past travel experience, while 旅行に行きました reports a specific trip. The long vowels in きゅうしゅう are rendered as Kyūshū.

examples[].german: What is the population of Honshu?
Honshu is the largest island in Japan.
en.notes: 本州 is Honshu, the largest of Japan's four main islands. 本州の人口 asks about the population of this island. In size comparisons, 一番 needs a recognizable frame of reference; 日本で一番大きい島 therefore explicitly means "the largest island in Japan". 本州に行く names Honshu as a travel destination.

examples[].german: Ah, the game I was looking forward to was canceled.
Ah, I'm so glad you came back safely.
en.notes: ああ expresses a feeling as an exclamation, such as disappointment or relief. The tone and the following sentence show what is meant. 嗚呼 is a rare, rather literary spelling; in everyday writing, ああ is usually used. A short pause often follows the exclamation. Distinguish this use from ああ meaning "that way"; it does not replace a polite answer to a question.

examples[].german: My older brother lives in America.
I often watch American movies.
en.notes: Usually the USA is meant (officially アメリカ合衆国, short 米国（べいこく）). In compounds: 米, e.g. 日米 "Japanese-American".

examples[].german: Um, excuse me. Where is the station?
Um, I have a small favor to ask ...
en.notes: Hesitant "Um, excuse me ..." - used to politely address someone or to buy time to think. Shorter: あの.

examples[].german: Please take bus number two.
I don't understand question number three.
en.notes: 番（ばん）follows a number and denotes a number within a series. 二番のバス is the bus with the number two; 問題の三番 names question number three. The number and 番 form a unit. For the order of people there is also 私の番 "it's my turn"; this separate meaning is not practiced here.

examples[].german: I ate a banana for breakfast.
This banana is still green and hard.
en.notes: Loanword in katakana. Long, thin things are counted with 本（ほん／ぼん／ぽん）: バナナ一本.

examples[].german: One medium coffee, please.
My test results were average.
en.notes: 中（ちゅう）denotes medium size or a middle rank here. For sizes, you can contrast 大・中・小（だい・ちゅう・しょう）. As a noun, 中 alone can name the chosen item, as in 中を一つ. This meaning is to be distinguished from the suffix in 工事中 or 授業中.

examples[].german: Chinese pronunciation is difficult.
My father uses Chinese at work.
en.notes: Usually Standard Chinese (Mandarin) is meant. Many kanji are shared, but pronunciation and grammar are completely different.

examples[].german: My roommate is Chinese.
Many Chinese tourists come to this store.
en.notes: Country + 人（じん）= national. More polite when speaking of a person: 中国の方（かた）.

examples[].german: Please put the box on this stand.
This platform is too low, so I can't reach the upper shelf.
en.notes: 台 denotes a base or platform on which something stands or on which you put something. With 台の上に you name a place on this base. In 作業台, for example, it denotes a work surface. The same spelling can also serve as a counter for machines and vehicles; that is a different use.

examples[].german: Well then, let's meet next week.
Thank you for today. See you then.
en.notes: "See you then" - somewhat more formal than じゃあ、また. Often used at the end of emails or conversations with acquaintances.

examples[].german: Thank you very much for carrying my luggage.
Thank you very much for your invitation. I would be glad to come.
en.notes: どうもありがとうございます is a polite, complete expression of thanks. どうも intensifies the thanks compared with ありがとうございます. In letters and messages as well as in conversation, the kana spelling is usual; 有難う is also read ありがとう. With an occasion placed before it, the thanks becomes specific: ご招待どうもありがとうございます. For something already completed, ありがとうございました is also used.

examples[].german: My grandfather's old camera needs film.
I put a screen protector on my phone.
en.notes: Film for cameras, but also a thin protective film (保護フィルム = screen protector for a phone). A movie is called 映画.

examples[].german: I'm traveling to France during the summer vacation.
French bread is delicious, isn't it?
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Language: フランス語, person: フランス人. Abbreviation in compounds: 仏（ふつ）, e.g. 日仏.

examples[].german: Learning foreign languages is fun.
At this school, you learn two foreign languages.
en.notes: 外国 (foreign country) + 語 (language). "To learn a foreign language": 外国語を勉強する／学ぶ.

en.meaning: to show signs of a feeling; to act as if feeling (verb-forming suffix)
examples[].german: My younger brother acted cold and closed the window.
My younger sister is reluctant to take this medicine.
If he is praised even a little, he immediately acts proud.
en.notes: Here がる attaches to the stem of an adjective and describes visible signs of a feeling, often in another person. With 寒い the い drops: 寒がる. With 嫌な the stem 嫌 remains: 嫌がる. The resulting verbs are godan verbs: 寒がります, 嫌がっている. It describes an observed reaction; you are not claiming to know the other person's thoughts for certain. With 得意がる the combination means that someone acts proud. The word part がる does not stand alone in this use.

en.meaning: month of the calendar year (after a number or question word)
examples[].german: I'm going to a new school in April.
What month is your birthday?
en.notes: がつ denotes the month within the calendar year: 四月（しがつ）is April, and 何月（なんがつ）asks "which month?". After a month name, に is often used to give a point in time. For the duration "four months", say 四か月（よんかげつ）. The moon, by contrast, is read 月（つき）.

examples[].german: Please walk on the right side of the road.
The store's side and the customer's side had different opinions.
en.notes: 側 is read がわ here and denotes a side. Combined with other words you get, for example, 右側（みぎがわ）, the right side, and 店の側, the store's side as a party involved. どちら側 asks "which side?". The reading そば of the same kanji, by contrast, means "nearby" or "next to".

examples[].german: Please write your address and name.
Thank you for your message.
en.notes: 御 is read ご in this use and is mostly written in kana. The prefix makes a word more polite or expresses respect: ご住所, ご家族, ご連絡. It often stands before words of Chinese origin, but it cannot be added to just any noun. In ご連絡ありがとうございます, the thanks go to the other person's message. お is a related prefix with other common combinations.

examples[].german: Please write your name in Japanese.
This movie is in French, but it has Japanese subtitles.
en.notes: 語（ご）follows the name of a country or language and forms the name of a language. 日本語 means Japanese, フランス語 French. The suffix describes the language, not the nationality of a person; 日本人 is a different word for that. The use as a free noun meaning "word" is practiced separately.

examples[].german: Please tell me the meaning of this word.
I changed the word so as not to keep using the same one.
en.notes: 語（ご）as a noun denotes a word or a term. この語 names a particular word, for example when asking about its meaning; 別の語 means a different word. This use is common in explanations about language and text. The suffix for languages, as in 日本語, has its own card.

en.meaning: about, approximately (after an amount); as much as; at least (voiced form of くらい)
examples[].german: It takes about ten minutes to walk to the station.
You can at least clean your own room yourself.
I was so happy I could have cried.
en.notes: The voiced variant of the particle くらい (the same word, separate card くらい). After amounts and time expressions it means "about, approximately" (三十分ぐらい); after nouns "at least" (挨拶ぐらいしなさい); after verbs and adjectives "so much that" (泣きたいぐらい). After nouns and numbers ぐらい is somewhat more common, after この/その/あの くらい is more usual; mostly the two are interchangeable. For clock times, however, ごろ is used (三時ごろ).

examples[].german: August is very hot.
I go back to my home country in the middle of August.
en.notes: Read regularly: はち + がつ. The Obon festival（お盆）falls in August, when many people travel back to their hometowns.

examples[].german: I'm moving at the beginning of next month.
At first I didn't understand much, but gradually I got used to it.
en.notes: Beginning, start. 初め is used more for points in time (月の初め = beginning of the month), 始め for the start of an action (仕事始め). 初めに = first of all; do not confuse it with 初めて (for the first time).

examples[].german: There are three cats in the garden.
I bought two fish.
en.notes: 匹 counts smaller animals here, for example cats, dogs, or fish. After a number the initial sound often changes: 一匹（いっぴき）, 二匹（にひき）, 三匹（さんびき）, 六匹（ろっぴき）. The combination states the number; 猫が三匹います means that there are three cats. For people, use 人.

examples[].german: My older brother lived in Kyoto for a month.
Once a month I clean all the windows of the room.
en.notes: 一月 is read ひとつき here and denotes the duration of one month. The same kanji spelling can denote January when read いちがつ; the reading and context decide. The also attested spelling ひと月 makes the duration easier to recognize. 一月に一度 means once a month, while a span of time placed before an activity gives its duration.

examples[].german: My older brother is studying at a British university.
It often rains in Britain.
en.notes: The usual name for the United Kingdom (formally and in newspapers 英国（えいこく）). The language is not called "イギリス語" but 英語.

examples[].german: There is salmon roe on this sushi.
I put the salmon roe into a small container and stored it in the fridge.
en.notes: イクラ refers to the individual, usually salted or seasoned eggs of the salmon as food, for example on sushi or a rice bowl. The word comes from Russian and is usually written in katakana. Do not confuse it with いくら／幾ら ("how much").

en.meaning: the day before yesterday (reading いっさくじつ)
examples[].german: At the meeting the day before yesterday, a new plan was decided.
Since the day before yesterday, the library's opening hours have changed.
en.notes: 一昨日 is read いっさくじつ here and means the day before yesterday. This Sino-Japanese reading suits written notices or reports; in everyday conversation おととい is usual. Both readings refer to the same day. 一昨日の refers to something from that day, 一昨日から to a start on that day. The small っ doubles the s sound: issakujitsu.

en.meaning: two years ago; the year before last (reading いっさくねん)
examples[].german: Sales two years ago were higher than last year.
This company has been selling its products overseas since the year before last.
en.notes: 一昨年 is read いっさくねん here and means the year before last year, i.e. two years ago. The reading suits reports and retrospectives; in everyday conversation おととし is usual. 一昨年の assigns something to that year. 一昨年から names a start two years ago. It refers to the calendar year, not necessarily a distance of exactly 24 months. The small っ doubles the s sound: issakunen.

examples[].german: I love Italian food.
I want to go to Italy next year.
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Language: イタリア語, Italian food: イタリア料理.

examples[].german: I'm taking an Italian class at university.
"Ciao" is an Italian greeting.
en.notes: Country + 語（ご）= language. Music terms such as ピアノ or テンポ come from Italian.

examples[].german: I look up words I don't know in the dictionary.
My grandfather's dictionary is big and heavy.
en.notes: 字引（じびき）, also written 字引き, is an older term for a dictionary. In everyday use today 辞書 is the more common choice. 字引で調べる means "to look something up in a dictionary". The word is still understood; the label does not mean it is unusable or purely historical.

examples[].german: When November comes, the trees in the mountains turn red and yellow.
My birthday is November 3rd.
en.notes: Composed of 十一（eleven）and 月（がつ）. Do not confuse it with 十一日（じゅういちにち, the eleventh）.

examples[].german: I am very busy at work in December.
On December 31st, my family eats soba noodles.
en.notes: The last month of the year; December 31st is called 大晦日（おおみそか）. An old, poetic name is 師走（しわす）.

en.meaning: question particle at the end of a sentence
examples[].german: Is this seat free?
What time are you coming tomorrow?
en.notes: か marks a question at the end of a sentence here: 行きますか. In polite questions it often follows です or ます. It does not change the verb and needs no question mark in a Japanese sentence. In casual speech, rising intonation alone can also indicate a question. A curt か after a plain verb form can sound much more direct than a polite question, depending on the situation.

en.meaning: counter for a number of months
examples[].german: I studied Japanese for three months.
