You can use this ticket for one month from the day of purchase.
en.notes: か月 counts a duration or number of months; it does not name a month of the year. It follows a number and also appears as ヶ月, カ月, or 箇月. Common forms are 一か月（いっかげつ）, 三か月（さんかげつ）, and 六か月（ろっかげつ）. 三月（さんがつ）, by contrast, means March. For a duration, 間 can follow: 三か月間.

examples[].german: I go to the library three times a week.
Please say your name one more time.
en.notes: 回 counts how often an action or event occurs. After a number, 一回 means once and 三回 three times; 一回 is pronounced いっかい. 週に三回 gives the frequency per week. もう一回 asks for a repetition. This counter counts occurrences; the identically read words 階 and 貝 have other meanings.

examples[].german: I learned Korean by watching Korean dramas.
The station signs are also written in English and Korean.
en.notes: The usual term for the language spoken in South Korea; the more neutral, linguistic term is 朝鮮語（ちょうせんご）.

examples[].german: A Korean exchange student lives in the next room.
He is Korean, but he was born in Japan.
en.notes: Country + 人（じん）= national. More polite when speaking of a person: 韓国の方（かた）.

examples[].german: This document examines the production volume of chicken meat.
Please put the chicken and the pork in separate bags.
en.notes: 鶏肉 can be read けいにく as well as とりにく. The reading けいにく consists of the Chinese readings of 鶏 and 肉 and denotes the same chicken meat. In spoken pronunciation, えい usually becomes a long e; the romanization of this reading is keiniku. The spelling 鳥肉 with the more general kanji 鳥 has other readings and also denotes the meat of other birds.

examples[].german: I bought two eggs.
There is only one piece in the box.
en.notes: 個（こ）counts small individual things, such as eggs or items in a box. It follows the number: 二個 is two pieces, and 一個 is read いっこ. The quantity can stand directly before を or follow the item named. For people, other counters are used. Only the counting of things is practiced here.

examples[].german: Please make ten copies of the meeting materials.
The print on this copy is too faint to read.
en.notes: Noun; as a verb コピーする (already N4). A photocopy, but also a copy made on a computer. Advertising copy: キャッチコピー.

examples[].german: I will study abroad in Japan in September.
Even in September, hot days still continue.
en.notes: Read くがつ, not きゅうがつ - one of the irregular month readings, along with 四月（しがつ）and 七月（しちがつ）.

examples[].german: It takes about fifteen minutes to walk to the station.
This bag cost about three thousand yen.
en.notes: Here くらい follows a quantity or time expression and means "about": 十五分くらい, 三千円くらい. The pronunciation ぐらい also occurs. This card practices the reading くらい and the approximate quantity; other uses for a degree or comparison are not covered here. Kana is the usual way to write it. Distinguish it from 暗い "dark" and the noun 位 "rank/place value".

examples[].german: I lit the candle with a match.
While camping we started a fire using matches.
en.notes: Match (the kanji 燐寸 is very rare); nowadays mostly replaced by lighters (ライター). Same-sounding words: マッチ "contest" (タイトルマッチ) and マッチする "to match; go well together".

examples[].german: Please give me three sheets of paper.
I bought two tickets, but one friend can't come after all.
en.notes: 枚 counts thin, flat objects, such as sheets of paper, plates, or tickets. The number comes first: 一枚（いちまい）, 三枚（さんまい）. The initial sound of まい stays unchanged. 紙を二枚ください orders two sheets of paper; 切符が二枚あります describes two tickets being on hand.

examples[].german: I pay rent every month.
This magazine arrives on the tenth of every month.
en.notes: まいげつ is a reading of 毎月 alongside まいつき and means "every month". As a time expression, the word can stand directly before the sentence. If you also name a specific day, に follows that day: 毎月十日に. "For a month", by contrast, is 一か月; 毎月 describes repetition.

examples[].german: I go to the sea every year in summer.
I'm looking forward to our annual trip.
en.notes: まいねん is a reading of 毎年 alongside まいとし. The word denotes something that repeats every year. Before a noun, の is used, as in 毎年の旅行 for "the annual trip". For a duration of one year, use 一年 or 一年間; 毎年 does not denote a duration.

en.meaning: also, too; both ... and (AもBも); even, as many as (三時間も); (negative) not ... either, neither ... nor
examples[].german: Mr. Tanaka is a student. I am a student too.
My younger sister eats neither meat nor fish.
The train stopped, and I waited for as long as three hours.
en.notes: Basic particle that replaces は or が (usually also を; after other particles it is attached: にも, からも) and expresses "also": 私も学生です. Used twice, AもBも means "both A and B", and negated, "neither A nor B". After quantities, も stresses a surprisingly large amount (三時間も "as long as three hours"); after question words with a negative, it yields "nothing / no one" (何も...ない, 誰も...ない). In contrast to は (topic, contrast) and が (subject), も adds something of the same kind.

en.meaning: while; at the same time as another action
examples[].german: I cook while listening to music.
My father eats breakfast while reading the newspaper.
en.notes: In this use it is usually written ながら. It attaches to the stem before ます: 聞きます → 聞きながら. It connects two actions by the same person that take place at the same time. The action at the end of the sentence is usually the main statement: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する means that you listen to music while studying. Other meanings, such as "although", depend on the construction.

examples[].german: What is this?
How many times a week do you exercise?
en.notes: 何ですか is usually read なんですか. Before a counter, なん asks for the number, as in 何回（なんかい）for "how many times". The reading depends on the combination, so you cannot replace なに with なん everywhere. 何を in a question about the object is normally read なにを.

examples[].german: Excuse me, what time is it now?
What time are you getting up tomorrow?
en.notes: Question word with 時（じ, o'clock）: 今何時ですか. The same spelling can be read いつ ("when"), but "when" is nowadays usually written in hiragana, so 何時 is almost always なんじ.

examples[].german: How many people are in your family?
How many people came to the party?
en.notes: Question word with the counter 人（にん）. Do not confuse it with 何人（なにじん）"what nationality", which is written the same way.

examples[].german: Once a year, my family takes a photo together.
I lived in Japan for three years.
I went to Japan in 2025.
en.notes: 年（ねん）follows numbers in years of the calendar and when counting years. 三年 is read さんねん. Without a preceding number, ねん appears, for example, in 年に一度: "once a year". For the year as an independent time noun, 年（とし）is also common. This card does not replace the different reading とし.

examples[].german: In this schedule, "日" stands for Sunday.
The opening hours column says "Sun: closed".
en.notes: 日 is used in calendars and opening hours as a short form of 日曜日, Sunday. This abbreviation appears together with the other days of the week, for example 土・日 for Saturday and Sunday. The reading にち belongs to the weekday name here; the word 日 meaning "day" or "sun" is read ひ in other contexts.

examples[].german: I have a lot of Japanese friends.
Japanese people often bow.
en.notes: Country + 人（じん）. Also read にっぽんじん, but in everyday speech it is usually にほんじん.

examples[].german: There are three students in this classroom.
How many people are you traveling with?
en.notes: 人 is read にん here as the counter for people: 三人 さんにん, 四人 よにん. One person is 一人 ひとり, two people 二人 ふたり. 何人 なんにん asks "how many people?". The number with 人 can follow the noun it belongs to: 学生が三人います. 何人で describes the size of a group doing something together. The standalone noun 人 "person" has the other reading ひと.

en.meaning: polite or honorific prefix, mostly before native Japanese words (prefix, e.g. お茶, お名前)
examples[].german: Would you like another cup of tea?
Excuse me, could you give me your name once more?
Teacher, how are you?
en.notes: A polite prefix before nouns and adjectives, mostly before native Japanese words: お茶, お金, お名前, お元気. Before Sino-Japanese words ご (御/ご, separate card) is usual: ご家族, ご連絡; but exceptions such as お電話 and お時間 are common. It is also part of the humble form お + verb stem + する (お持ちします). Almost always written in kana; the kanji 御 is seen mainly in formal texts.

examples[].german: Long time no see. How are you?
At the beginning of the letter I wrote "How are you?".
en.notes: "How are you?" - only used when you haven't seen each other for a while, not as an everyday greeting. Answer: はい、元気です／おかげさまで.

examples[].german: I ate an orange for breakfast.
The person in the orange sweater is my older sister.
en.notes: Fruit and color; as a color also オレンジ色. Mandarins are called みかん.

en.meaning: party; group (e.g. in mountain climbing); political party
examples[].german: We're having a party at a friend's house.
The three of us formed a party and climbed a mountain.
In this book, political parties are called "パーティ".
en.notes: パーティ is a form without the long final i of パーティー. The word can denote a celebration or a group doing something together, especially in mountain climbing: パーティを組む means to form such a group. The meaning "political party" is also attested; in present-day general usage, 政党 is clearer for that. Context decides which meaning is intended.

examples[].german: I listen to music on my father's old radio cassette player.
I recorded my own singing on the radio cassette player.
en.notes: ラジカセ is the short form of ラジオカセット: a device combining a radio and a cassette recorder. ラジカセで音楽を聞く names the device as the means of listening. ラジカセで録音する describes a recording made with the device; 録音する means to record. An ordinary radio without a cassette function is called ラジオ.

examples[].german: I put a cassette into the radio cassette player and pressed the play button.
Because the radio cassette player was broken, I asked for it to be repaired.
en.notes: ラジオカセット is the full name for a combined radio and cassette recorder; in conversation it is often shortened to ラジカセ. カセットを入れる describes inserting a cassette, ラジオカセットが壊れる a malfunction of the device. The term refers to the whole device, whereas カセット alone denotes the cassette or a module.

examples[].german: My father has a lot of old records.
Recently more people are listening to music on records again.
en.notes: Phonograph record; also a record in sports (but 世界記録 is more common than ワールドレコード).

examples[].german: I undid the wrongly sewn seam with a seam ripper.
Please lend me a seam ripper so I can cut the thread of the button.
en.notes: リッパー here means a seam ripper for cutting sewing thread. It is used, for example, to undo a wrongly sewn seam or to remove a button. リッパーで names the tool used. The small ッ doubles the following p sound, and ー lengthens the last vowel: rippā. Other fields use the same loanword for other devices or software.

examples[].german: I graduate from university in March.
In Japan, the cherry trees begin to bloom around the end of March.
en.notes: Month names = number + 月（がつ）. 三月 is the month of March; "three months", by contrast, is 三か月（さんかげつ）.

en.meaning: counter for books, notebooks and volumes
examples[].german: I borrowed two books from the library.
This novel has three volumes in total.
en.notes: 冊 counts bound books, notebooks, or individual volumes of a work. 二冊 にさつ means "two books/volumes" and 三冊 さんさつ "three books/volumes". One is 一冊 いっさつ; the double s in the romanization stands for a geminate consonant. 本を二冊借りる states the number of books borrowed; 全部で三冊 states the total number of volumes. The similar-sounding 札 さつ belongs to banknotes and is a different word.

examples[].german: Goodbye, teacher. See you tomorrow.
He left the town without even saying goodbye.
en.notes: Casual short form of さようなら. It often sounds final ("farewell"); in everyday life people more often part with じゃあね or またね.

examples[].german: My younger brother is taller than me.
I measure the child's height every month.
en.notes: 背（せい）means body height here. 背が高い means "to be tall", 背を測る "to measure one's height". せい sounds longer than せ, another common reading of 背. The meaning "back" does not belong to the reading せい learned here.

examples[].german: July 7th is Tanabata.
Summer vacation starts in July.
en.notes: Standard reading しちがつ. Because しち is easily confused with いち, you also hear なながつ colloquially; in exams and textbooks しちがつ is the standard.

en.meaning: I apologize; sorry to have disturbed you
examples[].german: I dialed the wrong number. I apologize.
I said "Sorry to have disturbed you" and left the staff room.
en.notes: A polite apology for a small disturbance or a mistake, also when leaving a room (for example, the staff room). The present tense 失礼します is used when entering.

examples[].german: I was in Japan for three weeks.
Please hand in this homework within two weeks.
en.notes: 週間 states a duration in weeks and follows a number: 一週間（いっしゅうかん）, 二週間（にしゅうかん）. It denotes a span of time, whereas 週 can also denote a particular calendar week. 一週間以内 means "within a week". The identically read 習慣 means "habit".

examples[].german: Spain is warmer than Japan.
My friend watched a soccer game in Spain.
en.notes: Country name in katakana. Language: スペイン語 (already N5).

examples[].german: There are ten mandarin oranges in the box.
I counted with the child from one to ten in the native counting series.
en.notes: 十 is read とお here, as the end of the native counting series 一つ、二つ、三つ…九つ、十. With it you can count ten things without naming a particular counter. Unlike 一つ through 九つ, とお is not followed by つ. In the Sino-Japanese number series, ten is じゅう. Both forms have a long vowel; the romanization of とお is tō.

examples[].german: I'm having dinner at home today.
Please come over to my place sometime soon.
My household is a family of four.
en.notes: うち often means one's own home or household and is frequently written in hiragana. 家で means "at home" here, and 私の家に "to my place". The family can also be meant as a unit: 家は四人家族です. The reading いえ often denotes the house as a building; うち often emphasizes the connection to the people living there.

examples[].german: My name is Tanaka.
I wrote that letter.
en.notes: 私 is read わたくし here. This self-reference is more formal than わたし and suits, for example, a professional introduction or a public speech. It is used by people of all genders. As a pronoun, わたくし can be followed by は or が. In the first example someone introduces themselves; in the second, が emphasizes who wrote the letter. The reading わたし remains another common self-reference.

en.meaning: to go; to travel along a path (reading ゆく)
examples[].german: I am going to the town in the north.
The traveler goes along a narrow mountain path.
en.notes: ゆく and いく can both mean "to go". ゆく sounds more literary than いく; this reading is deliberately practiced here. The destination takes へ or に, and a path traveled along takes を. The polite form is ゆきます. For the present-day て-form and simple past, use いって and いった, not ゆいて and ゆいた.

examples[].german: Please take two apples each.
I'm gradually coming to understand Japanese little by little.
en.notes: Follows a quantity: 一人一つずつ (one each), 少しずつ (little by little). Formerly also written づつ.

examples[].german: I treat people in the spirit of ichigo ichie, treasuring each encounter.
I want to cherish the once-in-a-lifetime encounters I have while traveling.
The shop owner welcomes customers every day in the spirit that each encounter happens only once.
en.notes: 一期一会 is composed of 一期 (いちご) "a whole lifetime" and 一会 (いちえ) "one encounter": every encounter occurs in one's life only once in just this way. The expression comes from the tea ceremony and urges one to honor every meeting with full attention and hospitality. Typical are 一期一会の出会い, 一期一会を大切にする and 一期一会の精神. It sounds elevated, but as a life motto it is also popular in everyday life (travel, farewells, the restaurant trade).

en.meaning: karma; what goes around comes around; as you sow, so shall you reap
examples[].german: He had always deceived others, and now he himself was deceived. It is truly karma.
They say what goes around comes around, so be kind to people.
That the student who bullied others was later isolated himself can probably be called karma.
en.notes: 因果応報 is composed of 因果 ("cause and effect") and 応報 ("retribution") and comes from Buddhist teaching: good deeds bring good results, bad deeds bring bad ones. Today it is mostly used in a negative sense, when the consequences of one's own wrongdoing catch up with someone: まさに因果応報だ, 因果応報というものだ. Closer to "having only oneself to blame" is 自業自得. The tone is rather literary to elevated-colloquial.

en.meaning: independent and self-reliant; going one's own way
examples[].german: She has a spirit of independence and self-reliance.
Without help from his parents, he started a company entirely on his own.
The company does not join any large corporate group and continues to run its business independently.
en.notes: 独立独歩 combines 独立 ("independence") with 独歩 ("walking alone"): one does not rely on others but goes one's own way by one's own strength. Typical are 独立独歩の精神/人生 and 独立独歩で〜する; also used of companies that belong to no conglomerate. The expression is praising and rather literary.

en.meaning: getting rich quick; making a fortune in one stroke
examples[].german: He bought a lottery ticket, dreaming of getting rich quick.
Putting all your assets into stocks in hopes of striking it rich is dangerous.
In the Gold Rush era, many people headed west chasing the dream of instant riches.
en.notes: 一攫千金 means "a thousand pieces of gold (千金) in one grab (一攫)": to get rich in one stroke and without much effort. Typical are 一攫千金を狙う, 一攫千金を夢見る and 一攫千金の夢. It is often about lotteries, gambling, speculation or gold rushes and often has a slightly skeptical undertone. The kanji 攫 is rare; in the media 一獲千金 is sometimes written.

en.meaning: fair and square; open and honest
examples[].german: Let's fight fair and square.
She stated her opinion openly and honestly.
The athletes' representative took the oath: "We swear to compete fairly."
en.notes: 正々堂々 doubles 正 "right, correct" and 堂 "dignified, stately" and means "fair, open and upright", without tricks or secrecy. Typically adverbial with と: 正々堂々と戦う, 正々堂々と勝負する; adnominal 正々堂々たる態度 or 正々堂々の勝負. Classic is the athletes' oath: 正々堂々と戦うことを誓います. The tone is elevated to solemn; the spelling 正正堂堂 is rare.

en.meaning: a mixture of good and bad; gems and stones jumbled together
examples[].german: Information on the Internet is a mixed bag.
The submitted works were of very mixed quality, so the judging took a long time.
The books at the used book fair are a mixed lot, but occasionally there is a hidden gem.
en.notes: 玉 is a gemstone, 石 an ordinary stone, 混交 "mixed": valuable and worthless things lie jumbled together. 玉石混交 describes collections whose quality varies greatly, such as information, applications, products or books. Mostly predicative: 〜は玉石混交だ. The original spelling is 玉石混淆; 混交 is the simplified form common today. The expression implies that one has to do the selecting oneself.

examples[].german: Her talent is one of a kind.
He is my one and only irreplaceable best friend.
The taste of the ramen at this shop is unique - nobody else can imitate it.
en.notes: 唯一無二 combines 唯一 "sole" and 無二 "without a second": there is only one of it, and it is irreplaceable. It mostly stands with の before a noun (唯一無二の存在, 唯一無二の親友) or predicatively with のものだ. It is more emphatic than 唯一 alone and stresses special value. It sounds rather elevated and is readily used in advertising, speeches and song lyrics.

examples[].german: Without a just cause, people will not follow.
The country started the war under the banner of self-defense.
I bought an expensive massage chair under the pretext of "it's for my health."
en.notes: Originally the subject's duty toward the ruler (大義) and the correct order of ranks (名分). Today 大義名分 mainly means a plausible, morally defensible justification for an action, often with the undertone of "pretext". Typical: 大義名分がある／ない, 大義名分を掲げる, 〜という大義名分のもとに. Unlike 理由, it stresses the public justification before others.

en.meaning: diverse; of many kinds; wide variety
examples[].german: A wide variety of goods are lined up in this shop.
A wide range of opinions was expressed at the meeting.
A great variety of creatures live in this forest.
en.notes: 多種多様 means "many kinds and many forms": very diverse, of great range. It stands as a な- or の-adjective before nouns (多種多様な商品, 多種多様な意見, 多種多様な生き物) and stresses the large number of different kinds. It is somewhat more formal and stronger than さまざまな or いろいろな and appears often in reports, advertising and non-fiction. The related noun is 多様性 "diversity".

examples[].german: He remained unruffled even in a critical situation.
Even when a big earthquake struck, my grandmother was calmly drinking tea.
The prime minister answered the reporters' tough questions with composure.
en.notes: 泰然 means "calm, serene", 自若 "to remain oneself, unchanged". 泰然自若 describes someone who stays perfectly composed even in danger or under pressure. It is a たる-adjective: adverbially 泰然自若として（いる）, attributively 泰然自若たる態度; a な-use is uncommon. Related are 冷静 and 落ち着いている; 泰然自若 is more elevated and stresses inner imperturbability.

en.meaning: half-hearted; neither one thing nor the other
examples[].german: If you're going to do it half-heartedly, you're better off not doing it.
My work is still half-done.
I woke up at an awkward time and now I can't sleep.
en.notes: 中途 "halfway" and 半端 "incomplete, odd" together give "half-finished, half-hearted". As a na-adjective: 中途半端な気持ち, 中途半端にやる, 中途半端なままにする. It also describes things that are neither one thing nor the other, such as 中途半端な時間 "an awkward time of day" or 中途半端な長さ. Neutral, but often critical in conversation.

en.meaning: natural and flawless; as if made by heavenly hands
examples[].german: Her performance was natural and flawless, and it captivated the audience.
This poem is perfectly natural; one senses not the slightest trace of artifice.
His unaffected, artless character made him beloved by everyone.
en.notes: Literally "heavenly robe without a seam": the garments of celestial beings have no seams. 天衣無縫 therefore praises works such as poems, texts or performances that seem perfectly natural, without a trace of artificiality. Applied to people, it means an unaffected, unselfconscious nature, similar to 天真爛漫. Common: 天衣無縫な／の, 天衣無縫で.

examples[].german: He is so honest to a fault that he can't tell a lie.
In an interview, you don't need to be naively honest and badmouth your previous company.
He honestly turned in the lost wallet with every last yen in it.
en.notes: 馬鹿正直 combines 馬鹿 "stupid" (here as an intensifier) with 正直 "honest": so honest that it is unwise, for example because one also says things one had better keep quiet. It is a な-adjective and often adverbial: 馬鹿正直に答える, 馬鹿正直に話す. The tone is half critical, half affectionate - one blames the clumsiness but acknowledges the sincerity. It is rather colloquial and, strictly speaking, not a classic four-character idiom but a compound.

examples[].german: You should have your own opinion and not just follow the crowd.
If everyone just goes along with other people's opinions, there is no point in a discussion.
One must be careful about the herd-like criticism online.
en.notes: 付和雷同 consists of 付和 ("to join in") and 雷同 ("to echo like thunder"): one simply agrees with the majority or a loud voice without any conviction of one's own. It is an intransitive する-verb (〜に付和雷同する) and clearly pejorative; it often appears negated as an admonition: 付和雷同せず. The tone is literary; in colloquial speech people more often say 周りに流される.

en.meaning: swift as the wind, silent as the forest, fierce as fire, immovable as a mountain
examples[].german: Takeda Shingen's battle standard was Fūrinkazan.
The coach made "Fūrinkazan" his team's slogan.
The expression Fūrinkazan originally derives from Sunzi's "The Art of War".
en.notes: Abbreviation of a passage from Sunzi's "The Art of War": 疾きこと風の如く、徐かなること林の如く、侵掠すること火の如く、動かざること山の如し. 風林火山 became famous as the banner of the warlord 武田信玄. Today it serves as a motto for a flexible, resolute strategy, in sports, business or as a title; in everyday life it usually appears as a quotation, not as a freely usable adjective.

en.meaning: peaceful and uneventful; calm and safe
examples[].german: I want to spend peaceful, quiet days.
I'm relieved that this year, too, ended without incident.
The festival, about which there had been worries, ended peacefully without any accidents.
en.notes: 平穏無事 combines 平穏 "calm, peaceful" and 無事 "without incident, safe and sound": a state in which nothing bad happens. Typical are 平穏無事な毎日, 平穏無事に暮らす and 平穏無事に終わる. The expression sounds warm and somewhat formal and is readily used in New Year's greetings or retrospectives. It stresses the absence of problems, not luck or excitement; similar but broader is 無病息災 "free from illness and misfortune".

en.meaning: ruthlessly inconsiderate; acting as if no one else were there
examples[].german: Those around him were appalled at his inconsiderate attitude.
There were young people making a racket on the train without regard for others.
Even the staff are struggling with that customer's utter disregard for others.
en.notes: Literally "beside one, as if there were no one" (傍らに人無きが若し): 傍若無人 describes ruthless, brazen behavior as if there were no other people. Typical: 傍若無人な態度／振る舞い, 傍若無人に振る舞う, 傍若無人ぶり. It is strongly reproachful and sharper than 失礼 or わがまま; similar is 厚かましい, which stresses brazenness in making demands.

en.meaning: unanimous; with the approval of everyone present
examples[].german: The proposal was passed unanimously.
Mr. Tanaka was unanimously elected as the new chairman.
By the unanimous decision of the judges, her work was awarded the grand prize.
en.notes: 満場一致 means "the whole hall (満場) is of one opinion (一致)": everyone present agrees. It almost always appears with で: 満場一致で可決される, 満場一致で選ばれる, 満場一致で決まる. It belongs to the language of assemblies, parliaments, juries and clubs and is rather formal. 全会一致 is a close synonym, especially in committees; in everyday speech people also simply say 全員賛成.

en.meaning: utterly chaotic; all mixed up; nonsensical; (colloq.) extremely, totally
examples[].german: The room is a complete mess.
Please don't talk nonsense.
The test yesterday was incredibly hard.
en.notes: The kanji are ateji; it is usually written むちゃくちゃ in kana. 無茶 alone means "unreasonable, absurd" (無茶をする). As a na-adjective: 無茶苦茶な話 "absurd story", 無茶苦茶になる "to get completely messed up". Colloquially also an intensifier, "extremely": むちゃくちゃおいしい. The variant めちゃくちゃ (short: めっちゃ) means the same and is even more casual.

en.meaning: no discussion needed; nothing to discuss
examples[].german: He was thrown out without further discussion.
In this tournament, a rule violation means disqualification, no ifs or buts.
"No arguments! Clean up your room right now."
en.notes: 問答 is "question and answer, discussion", 無用 "unnecessary": 問答無用 declares any further discussion superfluous. Adverbial 問答無用で means "without ifs and buts, summarily" (問答無用で退場／追い出す); as an exclamation, 問答無用！ cuts off any objection. The tone is authoritarian and curt; a politer alternative would be 議論の余地はない.

en.meaning: living at leisure in comfort; a carefree life
examples[].german: After retirement, he lives a leisurely and contented life.
My dream is to live carefree in the countryside someday.
He sold his company and, in his thirties, was able to live entirely as he pleased.
en.notes: 悠々自適 combines 悠々 "calm, unhurried" and 自適 "to arrange things as one pleases": to live as one wishes, free from obligations and worries. Most often it describes retirement: 悠々自適の生活, 悠々自適に暮らす, 定年後は悠々自適. It usually presupposes that one is financially secure. The tone is positive and somewhat elevated; in everyday speech one also says のんびり暮らす.

examples[].german: Because our interests coincided, we decided to cooperate.
People with a stake in that company cannot take part in the review.
Once interests are involved, discussion becomes difficult even among friends.
en.notes: 利害関係 means "the relationship of benefit (利) and harm (害)": a relationship in which one's own economic or other interests are at stake. Typical are 利害関係がある／ない, 利害関係が一致する／対立する and 利害関係者 "stakeholder, parties concerned". It is a factual expression from business, law and politics, often in connection with conflicts of interest. Strictly speaking, it is not a four-character idiom but an ordinary compound of 利害 and 関係.

en.meaning: blend of Japanese and Western styles
examples[].german: This building has a design combining Japanese and Western styles.
Our breakfast is a Japanese-Western mix of rice and scrambled eggs.
We had a wedding in a mixed style: a Shinto ceremony followed by a reception at a hotel.
en.notes: 和 stands for "Japanese", 洋 for "Western", 折衷 for "combining the best of both, finding a middle way". 和洋折衷 describes architecture, interiors, cuisine, fashion or ceremonies that mix Japanese and Western elements. Mostly attributive: 和洋折衷の建物／料理／結婚式. It is a neutral, very common expression; analogously there is 和洋中 for "Japanese, Western and Chinese".

en.meaning: changing repeatedly; going back and forth
examples[].german: The plan keeps changing, and there is confusion.
The suspect's testimony keeps changing.
The game swung back and forth, and I couldn't take my eyes off it until the end.
en.notes: 二転三転 literally means "to turn over two times, three times": something changes again and again, so that one does not know where one stands. It is used as a する-verb (計画が二転三転する) and typically describes plans, statements, decisions, scores or negotiations. The tone is often critical, for example with witness statements or political decisions (証言が二転三転する). Similar is コロコロ変わる, which is more colloquial.

en.meaning: drawing water to one's own paddy; acting out of self-interest
examples[].german: His argument is self-serving.
Interpreting data in a way that suits oneself is self-serving.
Each party kept repeating arguments in its own interest, and the reform made no progress.
en.notes: 我田引水 literally means "to channel water into one's own (我) rice field (田) (引水)". It means interpreting arguments, data or rules so that they serve only one's own advantage. Typical are 我田引水の議論/解釈 and 〜は我田引水だ. The expression is critical and rather literary, for example in commentary on politics and business.

en.meaning: asking oneself and answering oneself; self-reflection
examples[].german: I searched for the answer, repeatedly asking myself questions.
Every day I ask myself whether this job is really right for me.
After losing the game, he asked himself, "What was I missing?"
en.notes: 自問自答 means "to ask oneself and answer oneself": to brood inwardly over something and wrestle with oneself. It is used as a する-verb or noun, often with a quoted thought: 「これでいいのか」と自問自答する, 自問自答を繰り返す. It describes serious reflection on decisions, mistakes or one's own path. More neutral is 考え込む; 反省, by contrast, stresses remorse.

en.meaning: looking right and left indecisively; hesitating
examples[].german: Don't hesitate; stick to your convictions.
You can't expect anything from a government that dithers over every opinion poll.
The department head only watches the executives' expressions and dithers.
en.notes: 右顧 means "to look to the right", 左眄 "to glance to the left": 右顧左眄 describes someone who, out of consideration for others' opinions, constantly hesitates and cannot decide. As an intransitive する-verb: 右顧左眄する, negated 右顧左眄せず（に）. The expression is literary and critical, often about politicians or superiors. Similar is 優柔不断; however, that stresses weakness of character, whereas 右顧左眄 stresses glancing at others.

en.meaning: fighting valiantly alone; doing one's best without support
examples[].german: He fought on alone and completed the project.
In the understaffed shop, the manager is struggling single-handedly.
The game was lost, but the ace's one-man effort stood out.
en.notes: 孤軍 is an isolated army without reinforcements, 奮闘 "to fight doggedly". 孤軍奮闘 describes someone who battles great difficulties alone and without help, at work, in sports or in a task that actually needs a team. Used as a する-verb (孤軍奮闘する) or as a noun (〜の孤軍奮闘). It expresses recognition of the effort, often with the undertone that others did not help.

en.meaning: screams and cries of agony; hellish chaos
examples[].german: The accident site presented a scene of utter pandemonium.
Right after the earthquake, the town turned into a hellish scene.
On the first day of the sale, the sales floor was sheer pandemonium.
en.notes: 阿鼻 and 叫喚 are two of the Buddhist hells, where the damned scream in torment. 阿鼻叫喚 therefore describes a scene in which people scream in panic and pain, for example after disasters or accidents. Fixed frames: 阿鼻叫喚の地獄絵図, 阿鼻叫喚の様相を呈する, 阿鼻叫喚の巷と化す. In everyday life it is also used jokingly as an exaggeration for chaotic situations.

en.meaning: groping in the dark; searching for a solution without clues
examples[].german: Since the cause was unknown, we continued to grope in the dark.
The new business is still at the stage of groping for a way.
The development team felt its way forward and created a new drug.
en.notes: 暗中模索 means "to grope (模索) in the dark (暗中)": to search for a solution or a way without any clues. It is used as a noun (暗中模索の状態, 暗中模索が続く) or as a する-verb (暗中模索する), often for new projects, research or investigations. Synonymous but more everyday is 手探り（で）. The expression is not necessarily negative, but often describes the difficult initial phase.

en.meaning: different bodies, one heart; united in deep solidarity
examples[].german: The two overcame the difficulties as one in heart.
My grandfather often said that husband and wife should be two bodies with one heart.
Let us all, the entire staff, unite as one and take on the new goal.
en.notes: Literally "different bodies, same heart": 異体同心 describes people who are separate individuals but hold firmly together and pursue the same goal, such as married couples, teams or communities. Typical frames: 異体同心で〜する, 異体同心となって. It is elevated and known mainly from Buddhist (Nichiren) texts and speeches; in everyday speech people say 心を一つにする. The opposite is 同体異心.

en.meaning: sharing the same fate; sink or swim together
examples[].german: We are in this together. Let's do our best until the end.
If you knew about the fraud and kept silent, you are in it just as deep.
If the parent company collapses, the subcontractors will go under with it.
en.notes: Originally Buddhist: after death, to be reborn together (托生) on the same lotus blossom (一蓮) in paradise. Today 一蓮托生 means that one shares the same fate for better or worse, often with the undertone that it concerns failure, guilt or shared responsibility. Typical: 〜とは一蓮托生だ, 一蓮托生の関係. Comparison: 呉越同舟 stresses rivals who happen to come together; 一蓮托生 stresses the shared fate.

en.meaning: consistency between words and deeds; practicing what one preaches
examples[].german: People whose words and deeds match are trusted.
Above all, politicians are expected to practice what they preach.
If the teacher who says "Don't be late!" is late himself, you can't say he practices what he preaches.
en.notes: 言行一致 means "words (言) and deeds (行) agree": one does what one says. It is used as a noun (言行一致が求められる, 言行一致の人) or as a する-verb (言行が一致している) and is a typical requirement for politicians, teachers and executives. The opposite is 言行不一致. The tone is rather formal and moral; colloquially one says 言うこととやることが同じ／違う.

en.meaning: dry and dull; boring and colorless
examples[].german: The dry and dull explanation made the listeners sleepy.
I don't feel like reading a dry report full of nothing but numbers.
I want to escape from a dull life consisting only of work.
en.notes: 無味乾燥 means "without taste (無味) and dried out (乾燥)": boring, dry, without any appeal. It is a な-adjective and describes texts, explanations, speeches, work or a whole life (無味乾燥な説明, 無味乾燥な毎日). It never means literally dry food, but a lack of liveliness or emotion. More everyday are つまらない or 退屈.

en.meaning: peerless in the world; the best under heaven
examples[].german: His swordsmanship was praised as unrivaled in the land.
The legendary sumo wrestler is said to have possessed unrivaled brute strength.
My older brother proudly declared, "When it comes to making gyoza, I'm unbeatable."
en.notes: Literally: 天下 "under heaven, the whole world" + 無双 "without a second, peerless", that is, "unsurpassed in the whole world". It is used for outstanding strength or martial skill, mostly with a historical or heroic ring: 天下無双の剣豪, 天下無双の怪力, 天下無双と称される. Close in meaning are 天下一 and 古今無双. In today's everyday speech it sounds exaggerated and is therefore gladly used jokingly for one's own talents; attributively it takes の.

en.meaning: someone who gives up quickly; flash in the pan; unable to stick with anything
examples[].german: I started a diet, but it ended after three days.
I'll try hard not to give up after three days.
Even if I start keeping a diary, I always quit after a few days.
en.notes: Literally "three-day monk": someone who becomes a monk and gives up after three days. It refers to a person or behavior lacking perseverance, a "flash in the pan". Typical frames are 三日坊主で終わる "to stop after a short time" and 三日坊主になる; often used self-ironically about diets, diaries or exercise. Colloquial and slightly humorous.

examples[].german: He apologized sincerely to the victim's family.
We will respond to our customers' requests with all sincerity.
I devoted myself to her wholeheartedly, but her feelings did not change.
en.notes: 誠心誠意 doubles 誠 "sincerity" in 誠心 "sincere heart" and 誠意 "sincere intention": with complete honesty and devotion. It is mostly used directly as an adverb before a verb: 誠心誠意謝る, 誠心誠意対応する, 誠心誠意尽くす. It is polite-formal and typical of apologies, customer service and company statements. 誠心誠意を込めて is redundant (it says the same thing twice); correct is 誠意を込めて or simply 誠心誠意.

en.meaning: self-sufficiency; being able to provide for oneself
examples[].german: He lives a self-sufficient life in the countryside.
Japan cannot be self-sufficient in food.
At our house, we produce almost all our vegetables ourselves.
en.notes: 自給 "supplying oneself" and 自足 "being content with oneself" together make "self-sufficiency". One speaks of a 自給自足の生活 in the countryside, but also of states that are 自給自足する in food or energy. As a する-verb, the supplied good takes を: 野菜を自給自足する. Related is 自給率 "self-sufficiency rate". Neutral.

en.meaning: on the verge of explosion; touch-and-go situation
examples[].german: Relations between the two countries are on a knife's edge.
The meeting room had a volatile atmosphere, and no one opened their mouth.
The two were so tense that a fight could have broken out at any moment.
en.notes: 一触即発 means "one touch (一触) and immediately (即) explosion (発)": a situation is so tense that even a small trigger sets off a conflict. Typical are 一触即発の状態／事態／雰囲気 and 一触即発の危機. It is used for international crises, but also for quarrels between people or tense meetings. The expression is rather formal and appears a lot in the news; more everyday is ピリピリしている.

examples[].german: We should aim for coexistence and mutual prosperity between nature and humans.
They are exploring a way for local shops and large supermarkets to coexist and thrive together.
We would like to build a mutually beneficial relationship with our business partners.
en.notes: 共存共栄 means "to exist together (共存) and to prosper together (共栄)": two or more sides live side by side and both profit from it. Typical are AとBの共存共栄, 共存共栄を目指す／図る and 共存共栄の関係. The expression comes from business, politics and environmental discussions and is formal. 共存 alone means only "coexistence"; 共存共栄 additionally stresses mutual benefit. The reading きょうそん for 共存 is also common.

examples[].german: She prepared for the trip meticulously.
Always well prepared, he had brought two umbrellas in case of rain.
According to the police, the crime had been carefully planned.
en.notes: 用意周到 combines 用意 "preparation" and 周到 "thorough, careful": everything is prepared down to the detail, and every eventuality has been thought of. It is a な-adjective: 用意周到な人, 用意周到に準備する／計画する. It is mostly praise, but in crime and news texts it is also neutral for carefully planned crimes (用意周到な犯行). Similar but more everyday is 準備がいい; 念入り stresses more the thoroughness of an action.

en.meaning: to make a fresh start; to change one's whole attitude
examples[].german: He made a fresh start and began a new job.
Taking the move as an opportunity, he made a completely fresh start.
In the new year I'm making a fresh start and plan to jog every morning.
en.notes: 心機 means "state of mind" and 一転 means "to turn completely": you change your inner attitude and start anew. Typically used as an introductory phrase (心機一転、〜を始める), as a する-verb (心機一転する), and with a triggering occasion: 〜を機に心機一転. Note: writing it as 新規一転 is a common mistake. Neutral; often found in New Year's and farewell greetings.

en.meaning: crisis management; handling of dangerous situations
examples[].german: Because crisis management was lax, great damage resulted.
The company created a crisis management manual in preparation for earthquakes.
A leader needs the ability to manage crises.
en.notes: 危機 "crisis, danger" and 管理 "administration, management": crisis management, that is, prevention and response in disasters, accidents or scandals. Not a figurative idiom but a technical term from business, politics and administration. Typical: 危機管理が甘い "crisis management is lax", 危機管理能力, 危機管理マニュアル. Formal and common in the news.

examples[].german: In a fiercely competitive industry, natural selection takes place.
Through natural selection, species suited to their environment survive.
Old services that do not fit the times will eventually be weeded out naturally.
en.notes: 自然淘汰 is the technical term for "natural selection" in biology: 淘汰 originally means "to sift out, to sort out". Figuratively it describes how, in business or society, what does not fit drops out by itself; then it often appears in the passive: 淘汰される, 自然淘汰されていく. Typical are 自然淘汰が起こる／働く and 自然淘汰によって. The expression is factual-formal; for competition among companies one also hears 生き残り競争.

en.meaning: overwhelmed with deep emotion; immeasurably moved
examples[].german: I was filled with deep emotion at the graduation ceremony.
Returning to my hometown for the first time in thirty years, I am filled with deep emotion.
Seeing his daughter in her wedding dress, the father had a look of deep emotion.
en.notes: 感慨 is the deep feeling when looking back on something, and 無量 means "immeasurable": 感慨無量 describes the overwhelming emotion at graduations, reunions or anniversaries. Typical: 感慨無量だ／です, 感慨無量の思い／面持ち. The short form 感無量 is also common. It is more solemn than 感動する; while 感動 reacts to something beautiful, 感慨無量 carries a sense of looking back on a long road.

examples[].german: This may sound like bragging, but this cake turned out delicious.
The president praised the quality of the new product to the skies.
If you keep praising yourself, others will stop trusting you.
en.notes: 自画自賛 literally means to write a eulogy (賛) on one's own painting (自画), that is, self-praise. It is a する-verb (〜を自画自賛する) and is often placed in front self-deprecatingly: 自画自賛になりますが / 自画自賛ですが, similar to "not to toot my own horn". Said of others, it sounds critical. Similar is 手前味噌.

en.meaning: it is too early; the time is premature
examples[].german: It is too early to draw a conclusion.
I think it is still premature to open a new shop.
The plan was shelved as premature.
en.notes: 時期 "time, timing" and 尚早 "still too early": something is premature, the time is not yet ripe. Almost always predicative: 〜するのは時期尚早だ, or in 時期尚早として見送る "to shelve as premature". Formal and typical of politics, business and discussions; in daily life one rather says まだ早い.

en.meaning: indecisive; hesitant; unable to make up one's mind
examples[].german: He is so indecisive that he can hardly make a decision.
I want to change my indecisive personality.
Even when the shop assistant asked which one I'd take, I was so indecisive that I couldn't choose.
en.notes: 優柔 means "soft, yielding" and 不断 means "lacking resolve", together giving "indecisive, wavering". It describes a character trait of being unable to decide: 優柔不断な性格／人／態度, 優柔不断で決められない. Slightly critical; its opposite is 決断力がある "decisive". Neutral, common in everyday speech, also used self-critically.

en.meaning: standing united; coming together as one
examples[].german: The team stood united and won the victory.
The whole class worked together as one to prepare for the school festival.
Now is the time for the people of the town to stand together.
en.notes: 一致 "agreement" and 団結 "solidarity": a group stands together and works toward a common goal. Mostly as 一致団結して〜する or 一致団結する. Typical for teams, classes, companies or whole communities; often in appeals and speeches. Neutral to slightly solemn, with a positive connotation.

en.meaning: to carry out one's original resolve to the end
examples[].german: Sticking to his original resolve, he realized his dream over ten years.
She often wanted to quit, but she stayed true to her goal and became a doctor.
My motto is to see through the resolve I made at the start.
en.notes: 初志 means "original resolve" and 貫徹 means "to carry through, to realize to the end": you stay true to your first decision even when it gets hard. Patterns: 初志貫徹する, 初志貫徹で〜, often as a life motto (「初志貫徹」が座右の銘). Rather literary and solemn, popular in interviews with athletes or in graduation speeches.

en.meaning: with all one's might; to do one's best
examples[].german: I am studying Japanese with all my might.
I ran as hard as I could, but I did not make it in time.
I bought a car with money I earned by working hard.
en.notes: Literally: 一生 "one's whole life" and 懸命 "to risk one's life"; originally it was 一所懸命, that is, defending one's own fief at the risk of one's life. Today it simply means, in an everyday way, "with all one's might, to the best of one's ability". It is used as an adverb before verbs (一生懸命(に)働く), as a な-adjective before nouns (一生懸命な人) or predicatively (一生懸命だ), and goes well with 頑張る. The register is neutral and it is very common.

en.meaning: full of energy; bursting with vitality
examples[].german: The children are playing full of energy.
I've recovered from the illness, and now I'm full of energy.
en.notes: 元気一杯 means full of energy or vitality. With に it describes an activity: 元気一杯に遊ぶ. With な it stands before a noun: 元気一杯な子ども. The also attested spelling 元気いっぱい is kept as an alias. This card is about the whole compound, not about 一杯 as a single word for a glass or a full amount.

en.meaning: open all year round; open every day without a day off
examples[].german: This convenience store is open all year round without a day off.
My mother works for her family without a single day off.
At the entrance of the shop it says "Open every day".
en.notes: Literally: 年中 "throughout the year" and 無休 "without a day off". It means "open every day of the year"; this often appears on signs and in advertising. Typical frames are 年中無休で営業する, 年中無休の店 and, jokingly for people, 年中無休で働く. Related are 24時間営業 "open around the clock" and the opposite 定休日 "regular day off".

en.meaning: through the changing of the four seasons; in every season
examples[].german: Japan has its own beauty in every season.
In this garden you can enjoy different flowers in every season.
This ryokan serves dishes of the respective season.
en.notes: Literally: 四季 "the four seasons" and 折々 "each at its own time". It refers to what each season brings that is its own. It almost always stands with の before a noun: 四季折々の花, 四季折々の景色, 四季折々の料理; adverbial 四季折々に is rarer. The expression sounds elevated and is typical of travel brochures, garden descriptions and menus.

en.meaning: day after day; every single day
examples[].german: Day after day, the same work - I'm exhausted.
I practiced day after day, and now I can finally play this piece.
en.notes: 毎日毎日 intensifies 毎日 and means day after day, every single day. The repetition can emphasize weariness, as with the same work every day, or the persistence of an activity. As an adverb, the compound stands before the content of the sentence without an additional particle; with の it can also modify a noun.

examples[].german: Her explanation was logical and well-organized.
Although he was nervous, he laid out his thoughts clearly and logically.
Logically structured writing is easy to read.
en.notes: 理路整然 combines 理路 ("line of reasoning, logic") with 整然 ("orderly"). It almost always appears with と: 理路整然と話す/説明する or attributively 理路整然とした説明/文章. The opposite is 支離滅裂 ("incoherent, disjointed"). The expression is praising and rather elevated.

en.meaning: trip around the world; once around the world
examples[].german: Someday I want to take a trip around the world.
After he stopped working, my grandfather went around the world by ship.
About how much does a round-the-world ticket cost?
en.notes: Literally: 世界 "world" and 一周 "one round, once around". It means a journey once around the world. Typical frames are 世界一周の旅, 世界一周旅行 and, as a する-verb, 世界一周する; with a means of transport: 船で世界一周する. The register is neutral; 一周 alone is also used for laps on a track or around a lake.

en.meaning: today or tomorrow; in the very near future
examples[].german: I will reply to you today or tomorrow.
This problem won't be solved as soon as today or tomorrow.
en.notes: 今日明日 here means today or tomorrow, or in the very near future. 今日明日中に sets a very near deadline. On this card the compound is read きょうあす, with あす as the reading of 明日. With 今日明日には…ない one denies that something can be expected within this short time. The meaning "today and tomorrow together" is a different usage.

en.meaning: spring, summer, autumn and winter; the four seasons
examples[].german: In Japan the four seasons - spring, summer, autumn and winter - are distinct.
I took photos of the scenery in spring, summer, autumn and winter.
en.notes: 春夏秋冬 names the four seasons in order: spring, summer, autumn and winter. The whole compound is read しゅんかしゅうとう. With の it can express a seasonal reference before a noun. The card shows the Sino-Japanese reading of the compound; the individual seasons are also read 春／はる, 夏／なつ, 秋／あき and 冬／ふゆ.

examples[].german: It is important to believe in yourself.
This is my own problem, so I'll decide myself.
Traveling taught me a lot about myself.
en.notes: Literally: 自分 "oneself" and 自身 "oneself, one's own person" - the doubling is emphatic: "oneself and nobody else". It works like a pronoun with particles: 自分自身を信じる, 自分自身で決める, 自分自身のために. Compared with plain 自分 it stresses that it really is about one's own person, often in advice and reflections. The register is neutral.

examples[].german: At a construction site, safety comes first.
On snowy days, safety comes first, so please drive slowly.
Safety comes first in mountain climbing, so let's call it off on days with bad weather.
en.notes: Literally: 安全 "safety" and 第一 "number one, first" - "safety first". The expression is a well-known slogan on construction sites and in factories (often with a green cross), but is also used in everyday life. Typical frames are 〜は安全第一だ, 安全第一で〜する and 何よりも安全第一. The register is neutral; on a sign it is terse and formulaic.

en.meaning: to do what one says; to keep one's word and act
examples[].german: He always keeps his word, so you can trust him.
I announced that I would lose ten kilos this year - and now I'm going to follow through.
The company president kept his word and built a new factory as promised.
en.notes: Literally: 有言 "to have words, to announce something" and 実行 "to carry out" - you say beforehand what you will do, and then you actually do it. The expression is a play on the older 不言実行 "act without making many words". Typical frames are 有言実行の人, 有言実行する and 〜は有言実行だ; it sounds appreciative and motivating. The register is neutral to slightly formal.

en.meaning: one heart and soul; inseparably united
examples[].german: That married couple is one heart and soul.
Players and fans are one inseparable unit.
The employees pulled together as one and put the company back on its feet.
en.notes: Literally "one heart, same body": two or more people are so closely united that they think and act like one person. Typical for married couples, partners, or teams and fans: 〜は一心同体だ, 一心同体となって〜する. Not to be confused with 以心伝心 "understanding each other without words". Neutral, warm and positive.

en.meaning: words and deeds do not match; hypocrisy
examples[].german: His words and deeds don't match, so he can't be trusted.
Saying "health comes first" and then drinking every night - your words and deeds don't match.
The prime minister's gap between words and deeds was sharply criticized in the newspapers.
en.notes: 言行不一致 is composed of 言行 "words and deeds" and 不一致 "lack of agreement": someone says one thing and does another. The opposite is 言行一致, which is regarded as a virtue. Typical patterns are 言行不一致な人, 〜は言行不一致だ and 言行不一致を指摘される; the reproach hits politicians and superiors especially often. The expression is rather matter-of-fact and formal, and sounds clearly like criticism.

en.meaning: free and uninhibited; living as one pleases
examples[].german: She lives freely and uninhibitedly.
My younger brother is a free spirit and often surprises the family.
The children were drawing freely and uninhibitedly on a big sheet of paper.
en.notes: 自由 means "free" and 奔放 means "unrestrained, exuberant": someone lives or acts freely, without caring about rules and conventions. Patterns: 自由奔放な性格／生き方, 自由奔放に生きる／描く. Depending on context admiring ("unconventional, creative") or slightly critical ("unruly"). Neutral to literary.

en.meaning: This Way Up! Do not turn upside down (on packages)
examples[].german: "Tenchi muyō" is written on this box.
Since I am sending a cake, I put a "this way up" sticker on the box.
"Tenchi muyō" does not mean "it doesn't matter which way is up or down."
en.notes: 天地 "top and bottom" and 無用 "prohibited, not allowed" (as in 他言無用 "do not tell anyone"): the notice on packages means "do not drop, do not turn upside down". Many Japanese people misunderstand it as "top and bottom don't matter", which is why an arrow or 上 is often added as well. A fixed print or sticker (天地無用のシール); formal, almost only in writing.

en.meaning: to pitch with all one's strength; to give it everything
examples[].german: I'm tackling this project with everything I've got.
Right now I'm devoting myself to raising my children more than to my job.
The pitcher threw with all his strength until the very last pitch.
en.notes: Literally "to pitch with full strength" (全力 + 投球), originally from baseball. Figuratively it means to devote oneself to something with all one's strength: 〜に全力投球する, 全力投球で取り組む. Common in interviews and resolutions about work, training or family. Neutral, sporty and motivating.

en.meaning: natural stance; being relaxed and authentic
examples[].german: In a job interview, it is important to be natural and relaxed.
I get nervous before the match, but I want to take it on in a relaxed way.
Her natural smile is loved by many fans.
en.notes: 自然体 comes from martial arts such as judo, where it refers to the relaxed, upright basic stance. In everyday life it means a natural, unforced manner - without pretending or putting yourself under pressure. Typical are 自然体でいる, 自然体で臨む and 自然体の〜 (自然体の笑顔); the word has positive connotations and often appears in interviews with athletes or actors. Its opposites would be, for example, 無理をする or かっこつける.

examples[].german: His explanation made no sense.
This email makes no sense to me.
My little brother was saying incomprehensible things in his sleep in the middle of the night.
en.notes: 意味 "meaning" and 不明 "unclear": something is unintelligible or makes no sense. As a na-adjective or predicate: 意味不明な言葉／行動, 〜は意味不明だ. In youth slang it is very common as an exclamation ("What's that supposed to mean?"), even shortened to イミフ. Neutral in writing, in conversation often annoyed and colloquial.

examples[].german: This manga is extremely popular with young people.
The new bakery in front of the station is so popular that there is always a line.
This hugely popular game sold out immediately on the release date.
en.notes: 大人気（だいにんき） intensifies 人気 "popularity" with 大 to "hugely popular". Typical are 〜に大人気だ (子どもに大人気), 大人気の店 and 大人気商品 - a favorite word in advertising and the news; 超人気 sounds even more casual. Note: the same kanji read おとなげ appear in 大人気ない "childish, immature (for an adult)"; this has nothing to do with popularity and is therefore often written 大人げない.

examples[].german: This law is provoking divided opinions.
The ending of that movie received very mixed reactions.
Opinions are divided on the new school uniform, even within the school.
en.notes: 賛否 means "approval and disapproval" and 両論 means "both opinions": on a topic there are both supporters and opponents. Typical patterns: 賛否両論がある, 賛否両論を呼ぶ "to provoke controversial reactions" and 〜は賛否両論だ. Related: 賛否が分かれる "opinions are divided". Neutral, common in the news and in reviews.

en.meaning: action over words; deeds, not words
examples[].german: He is a man of action rather than words.
She did not talk about her goal and quietly earned the qualification.
Deeds over words is all well and good, but in a team reporting matters too.
en.notes: 不言実行 literally means "not speaking (不言) but carrying out (実行)": one does not announce things loudly but simply gets them done. Typical are 不言実行の人 and 不言実行で〜する; it is praise. The counterpart 有言実行 ("announce and then also carry out") was coined later and is now just as common.

en.meaning: every single word; not a single word
examples[].german: I didn't miss a single word of the teacher's talk.
He didn't say a single word about that matter.
The author's manuscript was made into a book without changing a single word.
en.notes: 一言 (read いちごん here, not ひとこと) means "one word" and 半句 means "half a phrase": the smallest conceivable amount of words. Almost always with も and a negative: 一言半句も聞き漏らさない "not to miss a single word", 一言半句も話さない. Literary and elevated; in everyday speech one rather says 一言も.

en.meaning: to show weakness; to complain; to want to give up
examples[].german: Don't complain; let's hang in there until the end.
My mother never once complained, even while she was ill.
Work was so hard that I ended up venting my weakness to a friend.
en.notes: 弱音を吐く is composed of 弱音 "faint-hearted talk, complaints" and 吐く "to spit out, to utter": you whine, complain about difficulties or say you can't go on. It is mostly used in the negative or as an admonition: 弱音を吐くな, 弱音を吐かずに頑張る, 一度も弱音を吐かなかった. If you do pour your heart out to a confidant for once, you say つい弱音を吐いてしまった. The expression is neutral and common in everyday speech.

en.meaning: sense of responsibility; sense of duty
examples[].german: She is a person with a strong sense of responsibility.
I can't entrust this job to someone with no sense of responsibility.
In the interview, I answered that my strength is my strong sense of responsibility.
en.notes: 責任感 is the feeling of being responsible for something, that is, a sense of responsibility or duty. It almost always appears with 強い / ある / ない: 責任感が強い "very conscientious", 責任感がない "irresponsible". In job interviews and references, 責任感が強い is a typical compliment. Not to be confused with 責任 itself, responsibility as duty or liability (責任を取る).

examples[].german: This project is being carried out as joint work.
Cutting the cake is the couple's first joint task.
When working in a group, it is important to assign roles.
en.notes: 共同 means "joint" and 作業 means "work, task": work that several people do together. Not a figurative idiom but an ordinary compound: 共同作業をする, 共同作業で進める. Well known is the wedding phrase 二人の初めての共同作業 at the cake cutting. Neutral; 協力 stresses helping more, 共同作業 the doing together.

en.meaning: personal responsibility; at one's own risk
examples[].german: Please invest at your own risk.
Entering a prohibited area is at your own risk.
It is not good to dismiss everything by saying it's your own responsibility.
en.notes: 自己 means "oneself" and 責任 means "responsibility": you bear the consequences of your actions yourself. Typical in warning notices and terms and conditions: 自己責任で〜してください "at your own responsibility". In debates 自己責任論 refers to the attitude of blaming victims themselves, and then sounds critical. Neutral to formal.

examples[].german: I am deeply grateful and moved by everyone's support.
To receive such a lovely present - I'm so grateful and touched!
Thank you for helping me move - I can't thank you enough!
en.notes: 感謝 "thanks" and 感激 "deep emotion": one is overjoyed, thankful and moved. Typical as the exclamation 感謝感激です！ or with the occasion marked by に: 応援に感謝感激です. Jokingly lengthened, one says 感謝感激雨あられ ("thanks and emotion like rain and hail"). Casual and emphatic; in formal letters one prefers 心より感謝申し上げます.

en.meaning: serious contest; everything is at stake
examples[].german: Tomorrow's match is a serious contest, with everything at stake.
The samurai of old fought with real swords, staking their lives.
I treated the job interview as the real thing and prepared thoroughly.
en.notes: 真剣 here means "real sword" (as opposed to a wooden sword) and 勝負 means "fight, contest": originally a fight with sharp blades to the death. Figuratively it means a confrontation in which everything is seriously at stake, with no playing around: 真剣勝負だ, 真剣勝負をする, 真剣勝負の場. Neutral; common in sports, exams or negotiations.

en.meaning: with body and soul; with all one's strength and heart
examples[].german: I played with body and soul.
The new company president said, "I will work for the company with all my strength."
My mother raised us with all her devotion.
en.notes: 全身 means "the whole body" and 全霊 means "the whole soul": with body and soul, with everything one has. Fixed patterns are 全身全霊を込める／かける／傾ける and 全身全霊で〜する. Solemn and emphatic, typical for pledges, politicians' inaugural speeches and interviews with athletes or artists.

examples[].german: I was ecstatic at the news that I had passed.
My younger brother got his first girlfriend and is on cloud nine.
I was on cloud nine after being praised, then failed miserably on the next test.
en.notes: 有頂天 denotes the highest heaven in Buddhism; in everyday use it means to be beside oneself with joy. Typical are 有頂天になる and 〜に有頂天になる; often it carries the implication that someone becomes careless or arrogant out of sheer joy: 有頂天になって失敗する. More neutral expressions for great joy are 大喜び or, colloquially, 舞い上がる.

examples[].german: It may sound like boasting, but our products are of high quality.
I don't mean to praise myself, but I think this plan turned out well.
The department head's talk is always just self-praise, and listening to it is tiring.
en.notes: 手前 "I myself, one's own" and 味噌 "miso": one praises one's own homemade miso, that is, one's own things or achievements. Mostly used as a modest preface before praising something of one's own: 手前味噌ですが…／手前味噌になりますが… "it may sound like self-praise, but...". As criticism of others: 手前味噌ばかり. Polite-colloquial, common in working life.

examples[].german: After repeated trial and error, I finally succeeded.
Programming is a series of trial and error.
My mother worked out a new way to make curry through trial and error.
en.notes: 試行 "trial" and 錯誤 "error" together make "trial and error": one tries things, makes mistakes and thus approaches the solution. Typical are 試行錯誤を重ねる "to make many attempts", 試行錯誤の末に "after much trial and error" and, as a する-verb, 試行錯誤する or 試行錯誤しながら. Neutral to slightly formal; frequent in reports on development, research and cooking.

examples[].german: I searched in all directions, but couldn't find it.
The pigeons were startled and flew off in all directions.
At the press conference, the company president was bombarded with questions from all sides.
en.notes: 四方 means "the four directions" and 八方 means "the eight directions"; they reinforce each other to mean "in all directions, from all sides". Typical with に or から: 四方八方に散らばる／探す, 四方八方から集まる. Neutral and vivid; similar to but stronger than あちこち. Related is 八方ふさがり "blocked in every direction, with no way out".

examples[].german: The two are a couple who love each other.
The two married out of mutual love and still get along very well.
The player and the team really wanted each other, so the contract was quickly settled.
en.notes: 相思 means "to be fond of each other" and 相愛 means "to love each other": two people love one another. Patterns: 相思相愛の二人／カップル, 〜と相思相愛だ. Figuratively it is often used for mutual interest, for example between a company and an applicant or a club and a player. Neutral, slightly humorous in the figurative sense.

examples[].german: This street is one-way.
His love was one-sided.
Let's set aside time for questions so that communication doesn't become a one-way street.
en.notes: 一方通行 is composed of 一方 "one side, one direction" and 通行 "traffic, passage". Literally it is one-way traffic; road signs say 一方通行, and one says 一方通行の道 or 一方通行を逆走する "to drive the wrong way down a one-way street". Figuratively it describes something that runs in only one direction: 一方通行の恋 "unrequited love", 一方通行のコミュニケーション "communication without feedback". To be distinguished from this is the adjective 一方的 "one-sided, unilateral", which tends to judge a person's inconsiderate behavior.

examples[].german: Next year I want to take a trip abroad.
I got a passport for my first trip abroad.
I lost my wallet during my trip abroad, and it was a real mess.
en.notes: 海外旅行 combines 海外 "overseas, abroad" (literally "beyond the sea") with 旅行 "trip". Since Japan is an island nation, every foreign country is "beyond the sea"; 海外旅行 is therefore the usual expression, while 外国旅行 sounds noticeably rarer. Typical combinations are 海外旅行に行く, 海外旅行をする and 海外旅行中に "during the trip abroad"; the counterpart is 国内旅行 "domestic trip". For a study stay abroad, on the other hand, one says 留学.

examples[].german: An experienced guide will show us the way.
When you're in trouble, it's good to ask an experienced senior colleague for advice.
This company is looking for experienced engineers.
en.notes: 経験豊富 consists of 経験 "experience" and 豊富 "abundant, rich in" and means "experienced, with a lot of experience". It is used like a な-adjective, mostly attributively before people: 経験豊富な先生, 経験豊富なスタッフ; predicatively it is 彼は経験豊富だ. In an ordinary sentence the split form 経験が豊富だ is also very common. The opposite is 経験不足 or 経験が浅い. The expression is neutral to slightly formal and typical for job ads, introductions and advertising.

en.meaning: to make a firm resolution; to resolve to change something
examples[].german: I made a firm resolution and started a diet.
At forty, my father made up his mind and started studying at university.
My room was so messy that I finally pulled myself together and did a thorough cleaning.
en.notes: 一念発起 comes from Buddhism: 一念 means "a single (firm) thought" and 発起 means "to bring forth, to make a resolution" - originally the resolution to take the path to enlightenment. Today it means making a firm resolution, after long hesitation, to start something new or change one's life. It almost always appears as a する-verb in the form 一念発起して〜を始める/〜する, e.g. for a diet, studies, or quitting smoking. It sounds somewhat elevated, but is widespread in everyday conversation and personal accounts; a simpler word would be 決心する.

en.meaning: simple and clear; easy to understand
examples[].german: His explanations are always simple and clear.
The rules of this game are so simple and clear that even children understand them right away.
The answer is simple and clear: you just have to practice every day.
en.notes: 単純明快 combines 単純 "simple, plain" with 明快 "clear, unambiguous" and means "simple and clear, easy to understand". Unlike 単純 alone, which can also mean "simplistic, naive", 単純明快 is almost always positive: 単純明快な説明, 単純明快なルール, 答えは単純明快だ. It is used like a な-adjective; when followed by another clause it takes the form 単純明快で. Neutral to slightly literary; in casual conversation one also simply says 分かりやすい.

en.meaning: unrivaled; the best in the world
examples[].german: My grandmother's cooking is unrivaled.
His skill at magic tricks is second to none.
The hot spring of this inn is said to be one of a kind.
en.notes: 天下一品 consists of 天下 "all under heaven, the whole world" and 一品 "a unique piece, a masterpiece" and means "unsurpassed, uniquely good". It is strong praise, often somewhat jokingly exaggerated, especially for food and skill: 〜の味は天下一品だ, 天下一品の腕前. It is mostly used predicatively with だ or attributively with の. In normal conversation it sounds somewhat old-fashioned and flowery; more neutral would be 最高 or 抜群. The expression is also known as the name of a ramen chain.

examples[].german: The pitcher achieved a perfect game.
It was a perfect game through the ninth inning, but the last batter got a hit.
A perfect game is a record you only get to see once every few decades.
en.notes: 完全試合, from 完全 "complete, perfect" and 試合 "game, match", is a technical term from baseball: the perfect game, in which the pitcher lets no opposing player reach base over the whole game. Typical combinations are 完全試合を達成する and 完全試合を逃す "to narrowly miss a perfect game". It should be distinguished from ノーヒットノーラン, in which no hit, but for example a walk, is allowed. Outside sports 完全試合 is hardly used figuratively; for a "flawless performance" one rather says 完璧.

examples[].german: Studying abroad is a good opportunity for cross-cultural exchange.
A cross-cultural exchange event with foreign residents was held at city hall.
Food easily becomes an occasion for cross-cultural exchange.
en.notes: 異文化交流 is composed of 異文化 "foreign culture" (異 "different" + 文化) and 交流 "exchange": "intercultural exchange". It is not a classic four-character idiom but a modern compound that is common in schools, communities and universities: 異文化交流イベント, 異文化交流会, 異文化交流を深める. Similar is 国際交流, which stresses exchange between countries more.

en.meaning: getting straight to the point; without beating around the bush
examples[].german: I'll ask you directly: do you agree?
To put it bluntly, I am against this plan.
Her straightforward way of speaking is sometimes misunderstood.
en.notes: 単刀直入 literally means "to charge straight in with a single sword (単刀) (直入)", that is, to get straight to the point without preamble. Most common is 単刀直入に言う/聞く, often as an introduction: 単刀直入に言うと / 単刀直入に伺いますが. Attributively: 単刀直入な質問/物言い. It can be used neutrally to politely; it announces that something direct is about to follow.

en.meaning: every moment is precious; time is worth its weight in gold
examples[].german: The line of poetry "A moment of a spring evening is worth a thousand gold pieces" is the origin of this phrase.
For examinees just before the exam, every day is precious.
It would be a waste to spend a precious day off sleeping.
en.notes: 一刻千金 means "one moment (一刻) is worth a thousand pieces of gold (千金)": precious time that should not be wasted. It comes from the poem of Su Shi 「春宵一刻値千金」, which praises a beautiful spring evening. Today it mostly stands predicatively (今は一刻千金だ) or with の before time words (一刻千金の時間). It is elevated and literary; in everyday speech one more often says 時は金なり or 時間がもったいない.

en.meaning: reading between the lines; unspoken meaning
examples[].german: You need to pick up on what he is implying.
The reply "I'll think about it" carries the unspoken meaning that it's a refusal.
I didn't notice the implied meaning in my boss's email and repeated the same mistake.
en.notes: 言外之意 means "the meaning (意) outside the words (言外)": what someone means but does not say explicitly. 之 here is the classical Chinese equivalent of の; in modern Japanese one almost always writes 言外の意味 or 言外の意, and the four-character form is found rather in idiom collections. Typical are verbs such as 汲み取る "to read into", 読み取る or 察する. In content it is close to 行間を読む "to read between the lines", which plays a large role in Japanese communication.

en.meaning: isolated and helpless; completely alone without support
examples[].german: He kept fighting while isolated and without help.
After exposing the wrongdoing, he found himself utterly isolated and unsupported in the company.
When I fell ill in a foreign country where I knew no one, I felt the anxiety of being alone and without help.
en.notes: 孤立無援 combines 孤立 "isolated, cut off" and 無援 "without support": to stand completely alone with no one helping. Typical are 孤立無援の状態／戦い and 孤立無援になる. Originally it describes besieged troops, today also people who have no backing at work, in politics or in everyday life. The expression is formal and more dramatic than 一人ぼっち "all alone, lonely".

en.meaning: to come into one's talent; to blossom
examples[].german: She finally came into her talent and gained worldwide recognition.
A newspaper headline read: "Eighteen years old, talent in bloom."
After meeting a good mentor, he brought his musical talent to full bloom.
en.notes: 才能開花 is a shortened, headline-style form of 才能が開花する "one's talent blossoms, develops"; 開花 literally means "flowers coming into bloom". In ordinary sentences you therefore say 才能が開花する or 才能を開花させる (transitive: "to bring one's talent to full bloom"). The four-character form is seen mainly in headlines, advertising and sports reports. It is not a classical four-character idiom but a modern compound.

examples[].german: In the martial arts, the unity of body and mind is important.
According to the idea of the unity of body and mind, mental fatigue also shows up in the body.
As I keep up my zazen, I feel I am getting closer to a state of unity of body and mind.
en.notes: 心身一如 means "body (身) and mind (心) are one (一如)"; 一如 is a Buddhist term for "unity, non-duality". The expression comes from Zen Buddhism and is used today in martial arts, yoga, medicine and health writing: mental and physical condition influence each other. Typical are 心身一如の境地 and 心身一如の考え方. It is elevated and technical; in everyday speech one says 心と体はつながっている.

en.meaning: from beginning to end; thoroughly; uncompromisingly
examples[].german: From beginning to end, he held fast to his convictions.
I am thoroughly opposed to that plan.
This novel is written entirely from the culprit's point of view.
en.notes: 徹頭徹尾 means "to go through the head (頭) and go through the tail (尾)": from beginning to end, completely, without deviation. It is mainly an adverb and stands before verbs or judgments: 徹頭徹尾反対する, 徹頭徹尾貫く. It often stresses an uncompromising attitude or that something is consistent throughout. It is elevated; more everyday are 最初から最後まで and 一貫して.

en.meaning: to travel constantly; to be always on the move
examples[].german: He leads a life of constant travel.
As a young salesman, I spent my days traveling all over the country.
The professor receives so many lecture requests that he travels restlessly around the whole country.
en.notes: 南船北馬 literally means "by ship in the south, on horseback in the north": in ancient China people traveled by boat in the water-rich south and on horseback in the north. From this came the meaning "to be constantly on the road, to travel restlessly about". It is usually used with の (南船北馬の日々／生活) and describes travel required by work, for example by sales representatives, politicians or lecturers. The expression is literary and rare; in everyday speech one says 全国を飛び回る or 出張続き.

examples[].german: We must not be taken in by ignorant prejudice.
It is wrong to write off people of the past as ignorant and unenlightened.
Listening to the expert, I felt ashamed of my own ignorance.
en.notes: 無知蒙昧 combines 無知 "ignorance" and 蒙昧 "intellectual darkness, lack of enlightenment": utterly ignorant and unenlightened. It is a な-adjective or noun (無知蒙昧な人々, 自分の無知蒙昧を恥じる). The expression is very derogatory and condescending, so it is rude when applied to others; applied modestly to oneself it is more acceptable. It is a written-language word; normally one simply says 無知 or 物を知らない.

en.meaning: to live up to one's reputation; to show one's true worth
examples[].german: He gave a performance that lived up to his reputation.
It was the veteran who scored the winning goal, truly living up to his name.
All the guests were moved by the hospitality of the long-established ryokan, which did full honor to its reputation.
en.notes: 面目躍如 literally means "the face (面目, honor) leaps to life (躍如)": someone impressively shows what he is made of and fully lives up to his reputation. Typical forms are 面目躍如たるものがある, 面目躍如の活躍 and 〜の面目躍如だ, often used of veterans, experts or long-established companies. It is positive and elevated, frequent in sports and culture reports. Do not confuse it with 面目丸つぶれ "to lose face completely"; the reading めんぼくやくじょ is also correct.

en.meaning: mutual affection; falling blossoms and flowing water
examples[].german: The two of them are truly drawn to each other, like blossom and water.
The novel depicts the love of two people bound by mutual affection.
Seeing cherry petals drifting on the river, I remembered the expression 落花流水 ("falling blossoms, flowing water").
en.notes: 落花流水 means "falling blossoms and flowing water": the blossom wants to drift with the water, and the water wants to carry the blossom, an image of mutual affection between a man and a woman. Originally it also describes the scenery of late spring and, in the sense of 落花流水の如し, can stand for decline or dispersal. It is found with の: 落花流水の情, 落花流水の仲. The expression is literary and rare in everyday speech.

en.meaning: learn the new from the old
examples[].german: He carries out his research in the spirit of learning the new from the old.
Reading the classics is learning the new from the old.
Urban development that makes use of the old townscape is exactly this idea of learning the new from the old.
en.notes: 温故知新 goes back to the Analects of Confucius: 故きを温ねて新しきを知る ("to study the old and learn the new from it"). It means gaining insights for the present from history and tradition. Typical are 温故知新の精神/姿勢 and まさに温故知新だ. It is elevated in tone and often appears in speeches, school mottos or advertising copy.

en.meaning: to respond flexibly; to adapt to the situation
examples[].german: People who can respond flexibly as the situation demands are in demand.
When things don't go as planned, let's think flexibly.
Not only the manual but also flexible judgment is necessary.
en.notes: Literally: 臨機 "to meet the moment" and 応変 "to adapt to change". It means acting flexibly and appropriately according to the situation instead of rigidly following a plan or rules. Typical are 臨機応変に対応する／考える and 臨機応変な判断. Common in job ads, in working life and in advice; neutral to slightly formal.

en.meaning: to endure hardship to achieve a goal; to nurse a desire for revenge
examples[].german: With a spirit of enduring hardship, he takes on the rematch.
Since losing last year's final, I have spent a year of hardship to make it this time.
Passing the entrance exam on my third attempt was the result of working hard through hardship.
en.notes: 臥薪嘗胆 literally means "to sleep on brushwood (臥薪) and taste gall (嘗胆)": according to a Chinese legend, two kings toughened themselves this way so as not to forget the shame of a defeat and to take revenge.
