Today it means to take on great hardship to reach a goal or to make up for a defeat. Typical are 臥薪嘗胆の日々／思い and 臥薪嘗胆して. It is elevated and sounds heroic, often used in sports and success stories.

en.meaning: a warrior worth a thousand; outstandingly strong
examples[].german: She is an outstanding programmer, worth a thousand others.
This team consists only of players who are each worth a thousand.
In the Warring States period, he was known as a commander who could take on thousands single-handedly.
en.notes: 一騎当千 means "one rider (一騎) is a match for a thousand (千)": a fighter who alone is as strong as a thousand opponents. Originally applied to warriors, it is now used figuratively for exceptionally capable people in sports, work or games. It almost always stands before a noun with の: 一騎当千の武将, 一騎当千の強者（つわもの）. The expression is elevated and appreciative, and is also used jokingly as an exaggeration.

examples[].german: Everyone around him was surprised at his bold and fearless behavior.
Attacking a bank openly in broad daylight, what an audacious criminal.
Newcomer that he is, he audaciously argued against the president's opinion in the meeting.
en.notes: 大胆不敵 combines 大胆 "bold, daring" and 不敵 "fearless, without respect for the opponent": so bold that one shrinks from nothing. It is a な-adjective (大胆不敵な行動, 大胆不敵な笑み) and also appears as 大胆不敵にも "brazenly". The tone ranges between admiration and criticism; in the news it often describes brazen crimes (大胆不敵な犯行). It is stronger than 大胆 alone; 無謀, by contrast, stresses recklessness.

examples[].german: With an indomitable spirit, he overcame the difficulties.
He is an indomitable person who never gives up, no matter how many times he fails.
In his promotion greeting, he said, "I will strive with an indomitable spirit."
en.notes: 不撓不屈 means "not to bend (不撓) and not to yield (不屈)": unbending, not to be broken by any difficulty. It almost always appears in the fixed combination 不撓不屈の精神 or as 不撓不屈の人／努力. In Japan it also became well known through sumo wrestlers who used it in their speech on promotion to yokozuna. It is very elevated and solemn; in everyday speech one says 何度でもあきらめない or 粘り強い.

en.meaning: to make a career; to get ahead in the world; social advancement
examples[].german: He moved to Tokyo dreaming of getting ahead in the world.
The son of a poor farming family rose in the world and even became a minister.
I value time with my family more than career success.
en.notes: 立身出世 combines 立身 "to establish oneself in life" and 出世 "to rise, make a career": to move up socially and professionally and gain standing. Typical are 立身出世を夢見る／目指す and 立身出世する. The expression sounds somewhat old-fashioned and recalls the Meiji era, when advancement through education was an ideal. In everyday speech today one usually just says 出世する or キャリアアップ.

en.meaning: two sides of the same coin; inseparably linked
examples[].german: Freedom and responsibility are two sides of the same coin.
The effect and the side effects of a medicine are inseparably linked.
His stubbornness is a strength, but it is also the flip side of his weakness.
en.notes: 表裏一体 means "front and back (表裏) form one body (一体)": two seemingly opposite things are inseparably linked, like two sides of a coin. Typical are AとBは表裏一体だ and 表裏一体の関係にある. It often concerns abstract pairs such as freedom and responsibility, success and failure, effect and side effect. The expression is matter-of-fact and elevated, and frequent in commentaries and essays.

en.meaning: excelling in both academics and sports; mastery of both learning and martial arts
examples[].german: He is a student who excels in both academics and sports.
This high school has put excellence in both study and sports forward as its educational policy.
Samurai of the Edo period were expected to excel in both literary and martial arts.
en.notes: 文武両道 means "both paths, that of the pen (文) and that of the military profession (武)": originally the samurai was required to master both education and martial arts. Today it mostly means that someone is equally good in school or studies and in sports. Typical are 文武両道の生徒 and 文武両道を目指す／掲げる, for instance as a school motto. The expression is positive and slightly formal.

en.meaning: warm-hearted and sincere; good-natured and reliable
examples[].german: He is trusted by those around him for his warm-hearted and sincere character.
The letter of recommendation said, "He is a kind and conscientious person."
I have never once seen my gentle, upright grandfather angry.
en.notes: 温厚篤実 combines 温厚 "gentle, friendly" and 篤実 "sincere and conscientious": a calm, warm and dependable character. Typical is 温厚篤実な人柄／人物. The expression is very formal and appears mainly in letters of recommendation, obituaries, wedding speeches and personal descriptions. In conversation one is more likely to say 優しくて真面目な人.

en.meaning: quick-witted; to respond on the spot with apt wit
examples[].german: Everyone laughed at her quick-witted answer.
The host's quick-witted patter instantly livened up the hall.
Few people can answer on the spot even when asked unexpected questions in an interview.
en.notes: 当意即妙 means "suited (当) to the occasion (意), and apt (妙) on the spot (即)": quick-witted, responding with spontaneous wit in just the right way. It is a な-adjective: 当意即妙な答え／受け答え, 当意即妙に切り返す. It is used to praise hosts, speakers or conversation partners who answer surprising questions wittily. In everyday speech one says 頭の回転が速い or 機転が利く.

en.meaning: the right person in the right place
examples[].german: Placing the right people in the right positions is important.
The new department head assigned each employee to the position that suited them best.
For the school festival, we decided roles according to aptitude, for example leaving the posters to someone good at drawing.
en.notes: 適材適所 literally means "the suitable timber (適材) in the suitable place (適所)", originally from carpentry. It means deploying people according to their abilities. Typical are 適材適所の人事/配置 and 適材適所に配置する; used mainly in companies, administration and teamwork.

en.meaning: to punish one to warn a hundred; to make an example of someone
examples[].german: He was severely punished as an example to others.
To make an example, the manager did not let the player who arrived late play in the match.
Some say that drunk driving calls for harsh penalties as a deterrent.
en.notes: 一罰百戒 means "one punishment (一罰), a hundred warnings (百戒)": to punish one person severely so that everyone else is deterred, making an example of him. Typical are 一罰百戒の意味で／として and 一罰百戒の処分. It appears in news about disciplinary punishment, sports and company rules, and is formal. It is often used to justify a harsh penalty, and sometimes it is also critically questioned.

en.meaning: soft outside, strong inside; gentle in manner but strong-willed
examples[].german: She is gentle on the outside but strong-willed within.
The new department head is soft outside and firm inside: calm, but he never gives up his opinion.
A leader is expected to have an attitude that is gentle yet firm.
en.notes: 外柔内剛 means "soft outside (外柔), hard inside (内剛)": someone appears gentle and friendly but has a firm will. It is mostly used of people, with の or な: 外柔内剛の人, 外柔内剛なタイプ. It is a compliment that combines kindness with inner strength. The opposite is 内柔外剛 "hard outside, weak inside"; the expression is elevated and rather literary.

en.meaning: the finishing touch; the final stroke that brings something to life
examples[].german: The report is good in content, but the conclusion is weak, so it lacks the finishing touch.
The yuzu peel placed on top at the end is the finishing touch of this dish.
Even if the preparation is perfect, it will lack the finishing touch if the closing greeting goes wrong.
en.notes: 画竜点睛 literally means "to put the pupils into a painted dragon": according to legend, a painted dragon came to life as soon as the painter painted in its eyes. It means the decisive final touch that makes a work come alive. By far the most common use is in the fixed phrase 画竜点睛を欠く "the decisive final touch is missing". It is an elevated, written-language expression; note that 睛 (pupil) is often wrongly written as 晴.

examples[].german: There is a Q&A session after the presentation.
Now, I would like to move on to the Q&A session.
In the Q&A of the press conference, the minister was asked tough questions.
en.notes: 質疑応答 is made up of 質疑 "asking questions, inquiry" and 応答 "answer, reply" and refers to the question round after a lecture, a presentation or at a press conference. Typical combinations are 質疑応答の時間, 質疑応答に移る "to move on to the Q&A" and 質疑応答を行う. The word is neutral to formal; in everyday speech one also casually says Ｑ＆Ａ or 質問コーナー.

en.meaning: painstaking effort, grain by grain; diligent toil
examples[].german: This work is the fruit of painstaking labor.
He opened his own shop with money he had painstakingly saved.
When I think of the farmers' hard work, I cannot leave any rice uneaten.
en.notes: 粒粒辛苦 (usually written 粒々辛苦) literally means "every grain is hardship" and goes back to a Chinese poem according to which every grain of rice contains the hard work of the farmers. Figuratively it means patient, laborious effort over a long time. Typical are 粒粒辛苦の末 "after years of effort", 粒粒辛苦の結晶 "the fruit of painstaking work" and 粒粒辛苦して "with great effort". It is a written-language expression and rather rare; in conversation one says more simply 苦労して.

en.meaning: peace under heaven; everything is peaceful and calm
examples[].german: I hope the peaceful world continues.
In the Edo period, an age of peace lasted about 260 years.
It's the day before the exam and my little brother does nothing but sleep. He's carefree, isn't he?
en.notes: 天下泰平 (also 天下太平) literally means "great peace under heaven" and describes a time when calm and order prevail throughout the country, for example 天下泰平の世 or 天下泰平の時代. As a な-adjective it is also used slightly ironically for people who are carefree and unconcerned although there would be reason to worry: "He's got a sunny disposition." In the historical sense it is rather elevated, in the ironic sense colloquial.

en.meaning: to fizzle out; to fade away naturally
examples[].german: As we did not keep in contact, the friendship fizzled out.
The project got no budget and fizzled out before long.
Once we were in a long-distance relationship, we could no longer meet, and things between him and me just faded away.
en.notes: 自然消滅 means "to disappear by itself" and is used as an intransitive する-verb: plans, clubs, rules or relationships 自然消滅する when nobody takes care of them any more and they fade away without a formal end. It is particularly common for romantic relationships: 彼女とは自然消滅した "We just stopped getting in touch, and it fizzled out". Unlike 解散 or 中止, there is thus no deliberate decision. A neutral expression, common in daily life and in the news.

en.meaning: out of the frying pan into the fire; no sooner is one difficulty over than another comes
examples[].german: Just when I thought the car repair was finally done, I lost my wallet. One misfortune after another.
Just when the earthquake cleanup was finally over, a typhoon came. It really is one thing after another.
I fixed one bug and another one showed up. One problem after another.
en.notes: 一難去ってまた一難 literally means "When one misfortune (一難) has gone (去って), another (また) misfortune comes". It means: as soon as one problem is solved, the next one appears, roughly "out of the frying pan into the fire". Unlike 泣きっ面に蜂 ("it never rains but it pours", misfortunes pile up), it stresses the sequence: first relief, then new worry. It usually stands as a comment at the end of a sentence: …。一難去ってまた一難だ.

examples[].german: His arrogant and insolent attitude drew the resentment of those around him.
Though he's a newcomer, he speaks to his seniors in an insolent tone.
Once he took power, he started behaving arrogantly.
en.notes: 傲岸 means "haughty, unyielding", 不遜 "disrespectful, presumptuous": 傲岸不遜 condemns an arrogant attitude in which someone treats others condescendingly. Typical: 傲岸不遜な態度／物言い, 傲岸不遜に振る舞う. It is strongly judgmental and literary; in everyday speech people say 偉そう or 生意気. 傲慢 is the ordinary word for "arrogant"; 傲岸不遜 sounds even sharper.

en.meaning: vague and unclear; hazy and indistinct
examples[].german: That plan is vague and lacks concreteness.
The minister's reply was so nebulous that the main point could not be grasped.
My memories of early childhood are hazy.
en.notes: 曖昧 means "unclear, ambiguous", 模糊 "blurred, misty": 曖昧模糊 intensifies the meaning of 曖昧 and describes plans, statements, memories or boundaries that cannot be clearly grasped. Most often with と: 曖昧模糊とした説明, 曖昧模糊としている. It is literary; in everyday speech 曖昧 or はっきりしない is enough. The opposite would be 明確 or 明瞭.

en.meaning: the beauties of nature; flowers, birds, wind and moon
examples[].german: Japanese culture values the beauties of nature.
The poets of old composed waka about the beauties of nature.
After retirement, I want to live a peaceful life enjoying the beauties of nature.
en.notes: 花鳥風月 lists flowers, birds, wind and moon and stands for the beauties of nature as classic motifs of Japanese aesthetics. Typical are 花鳥風月を愛でる/楽しむ/詠む. In a second sense, it also denotes the artful engagement with these themes in poetry, painting or the tea ceremony. The expression is elevated and literary.

en.meaning: uncontrollable desires; the mind like a wild horse and a monkey
examples[].german: Even though the exam is coming up, I can't suppress my urge to play, and my mind is restless.
To curb my restless desires, I sit in Zen meditation every morning.
It is said that even monks in training are sometimes plagued by unruly desires.
en.notes: From Buddhism: the will (意) gallops like a horse (馬), the heart (心) leaps about like a monkey (猿). 意馬心猿 describes worldly desires and passions that cannot be reined in, leaving one inwardly restless. Typical: 意馬心猿を抑える, 意馬心猿の状態. It is very literary and concerns desire and temptation, not mere nervousness; for general restlessness people say 落ち着かない or そわそわする.

en.meaning: recasting something old in a new form; taking the essence and reworking it
examples[].german: The classic work was reworked and arranged in a modern style.
This film is a free reworking of one of Shakespeare's tragedies.
Rather than simply imitating, he transformed the source and finished it as an original work.
en.notes: Literally "to change the bones and take over the womb": originally a term from Chinese poetry for taking the idea of an older work and recasting it into something of one's own. 換骨奪胎 is a transitive する-verb: 〜を換骨奪胎する. Used correctly it is positive (creative reinvention); however, it is often used disparagingly for mere rewriting or copying. Not to be confused with 盗作 ("plagiarism").

examples[].german: He's all talk and no action.
Having so boldly declared, "We will definitely win the championship," I can't afford to lose.
Voters are no longer fooled by the grand talk before an election.
en.notes: 大言 is "big words", 壮語 "grandiose talk": 大言壮語 means to boast, to announce things one cannot deliver. It can stand as a noun (大言壮語ばかり) or as an intransitive する-verb (〜と大言壮語する). The tone is pejorative and literary; colloquially people say 大口を叩く or ビッグマウス. Unlike 自慢 ("showing off about something one has"), it is mostly about boastful promises.

examples[].german: This region has picturesque scenery and attracts many tourists.
In retirement, I want to live in a scenic seaside town.
A small hotel stands on the shore of a scenic lake.
en.notes: 風光 is the scenery, 明媚 "clear and lovely": 風光明媚 is the most common expression for a picturesque area and frequent in travel brochures and descriptions of places. As a na-adjective: 風光明媚な土地／湖畔, predicatively 風光明媚だ／で. Compared with 山紫水明, which is more literary and refers specifically to mountains and clear water, 風光明媚 is more general and also suits coasts or islands.

en.meaning: staking everything on one throw; a desperate gamble
examples[].german: He made an all-or-nothing bet.
Staking the company's fate on it, they unveiled a make-or-break new product.
Just before the end of the game, a desperate long shot went in.
en.notes: 乾坤 means "heaven and earth", 一擲 "a single throw" (of the dice): one stakes everything, even heaven and earth, on one throw. 乾坤一擲 describes a decisive, risky commitment. Fixed frames: 乾坤一擲の勝負／大勝負に出る, 乾坤一擲の一手. It is pathetic in tone and literary; in everyday speech people say 一か八か or 大きな賭けに出る.

en.meaning: undisputed authority; a leading figure in a field
examples[].german: He is the undisputed authority in this field.
The late Professor Yamada was revered as the foremost authority in Japanese physics.
I asked a calligrapher said to be the undisputed master to take me on as a disciple.
en.notes: 泰山 is Mount Tai, the sacred mountain in China, 北斗 the Big Dipper: both are points of orientation to which everyone looks up. 泰山北斗 denotes an outstanding, universally revered authority in a field. Typical: 〜界の泰山北斗, 泰山北斗と仰がれる. More common is the short form 泰斗 (医学の泰斗). It is very formal and said about others; more neutral would be 第一人者 or 権威.

en.meaning: with an open and unprejudiced mind; frankly
examples[].german: One should listen to opinions with an open mind.
The leaders of the two countries talked frankly and without reservations.
Even if I am criticized, I want to accept it without bias and improve.
en.notes: 虚心 means "without prejudice, with an empty heart", 坦懐 "open and calm in temperament": 虚心坦懐 describes an attitude with which one listens or speaks without bias and ulterior motives. Mostly adverbial: 虚心坦懐に話し合う／耳を傾ける. Popular in politics and negotiations. Related is 素直 ("sincere, obedient"), which describes more of a character trait; 虚心坦懐 means a deliberately adopted attitude.

en.meaning: impregnable fortress; secure stronghold; unassailable position
examples[].german: That company has built an unassailable position in its industry.
This electoral district was for many years a stronghold of the conservatives.
A start-up is breaking into a market that had been the stronghold of the big corporations.
en.notes: 金城 is a castle with metal walls, 湯池 a moat of boiling water: a fortress that cannot be taken. Today 金城湯池 mainly denotes a secure stronghold or firmly held territory, for example of a politician or party in an electoral district or of a company in a market. Typical: 〜の金城湯池だ, 金城湯池を守る／崩す. Similar are 牙城 and 地盤.

en.meaning: a hundred flowers in full bloom; a profusion of talents or styles
examples[].german: A dazzling profusion of art styles is spreading.
The garden in spring was truly a sea of blossoms.
This year's candidates for the newcomer award are a lineup of diverse talents.
en.notes: Literally "a hundred flowers bloom in wild profusion". 百花繚乱 first describes a lush display of flowers, and figuratively the simultaneous appearance of many talents, beautiful people or different styles and works. Typical: 百花繚乱の時代／顔ぶれ, predicatively 百花繚乱だ. Also written 百花撩乱. Positive and colorful in tone, often used in culture and sports reports.

en.meaning: natural disaster; upheavals of heaven and earth
examples[].german: I prepared disaster-preparedness supplies in case of natural disasters.
People in the past considered natural disasters to be the wrath of the gods.
Unless some cataclysm happens, the game will be held as scheduled.
en.notes: 天変地異 combines 天変 ("unusual celestial phenomena" such as storms or eclipses) with 地異 ("upheavals of the earth" such as earthquakes or floods). It denotes great, extraordinary natural events and sounds weightier than 自然災害. The exaggeration 天変地異でも起きない限り ("unless the world ends") is also common. The tone is literary.

en.meaning: moving three times like Mencius's mother; choosing the environment for raising a child
examples[].german: Moving for the sake of the child's education is exactly the example of Mencius's mother.
Following the lesson of Mencius's mother, we bought a house near the library.
As the story of Mencius's mother shows, children are greatly influenced by their environment.
en.notes: According to tradition, the mother of Mencius (孟母) moved three times (三遷): away from the cemetery, away from the market, until she lived next to a school, where her son imitated the learning. 孟母三遷 stresses how important a good environment is for upbringing. Mostly quoted as a lesson: 孟母三遷の教え, 孟母三遷というように. A related expression about the same mother is 孟母断機.

en.meaning: to laugh loudly and heartily; roaring laughter
examples[].german: Everyone burst into roaring laughter at his joke.
When the president heard about his subordinate's mistake, he laughed heartily and forgave him.
The old monk did not answer his disciple's question but simply laughed heartily.
en.notes: 呵呵 is onomatopoeic for loud laughter (like "haha"), 大笑 "to laugh big, heartily". 呵呵大笑 describes a booming, carefree laugh, often from someone with a generous, composed manner. Mostly as a する-verb: 呵呵大笑する. It is very literary; in everyday speech people say 大笑いする or 爆笑する. The expression sounds more like a serene old master than like giggling.

en.meaning: to extinguish all thoughts; to attain absolute inner calm
examples[].german: If you clear your mind completely, even fire feels cool.
In the intense heat, I cleared my mind and kept practicing.
I dispel stray thoughts and concentrate on Zen meditation with an empty mind.
en.notes: 心頭 is "the inside, the mind", 滅却 "to extinguish": 心頭滅却 means to switch off all disturbing thoughts and sensations. Famous is the saying 心頭滅却すれば火もまた涼し, which the Zen monk 快川紹喜 is said to have uttered as his temple was burned: with a purified mind, even fire is cool. Today it is mostly quoted for enduring heat, pain or stress through willpower; also as a する-verb: 心頭滅却して.

en.meaning: deep and far-sighted planning; shrewd foresight
examples[].german: Thanks to his far-sighted planning, the company avoided a crisis.
The seemingly reckless decision was actually the result of deep foresight.
Ieyasu laid far-sighted plans to unify the country.
en.notes: 深謀 is "profound planning", 遠慮 here "thinking far ahead", not the everyday meaning "restraint". 深謀遠慮 denotes careful, far-sighted strategies that take future developments into account. Typical: 深謀遠慮をめぐらす, 〜の深謀遠慮, 深謀遠慮に富む. It is appreciative; for cunning schemes in a pejorative sense there is 権謀術数.

en.meaning: onlookers see more than the players; outsiders have a better overview
examples[].german: As they say, a third party can judge more calmly than those involved.
If I may say so as an outsider, I think your plan is a bit unrealistic.
A friend who was watching the go game from the side noticed the winning line, as onlookers do.
en.notes: Literally: 傍目 "watching from the side" + 八目 "eight moves": someone who merely watches go sees eight moves further than the players. It means that outsiders often judge a situation more clearly than those involved. Common frames: 傍目八目というように, 傍目八目で言わせてもらうと ("speaking as an outsider"). It is also written 岡目八目; the reading remains おかめはちもく. Slightly elevated, but also common in conversation.

en.meaning: the mutability of all things; the impermanence of life
examples[].german: To live in a world of constant change, one needs flexibility.
Change may be the way of the world, but I never thought that large company would go bankrupt.
My grandfather lived through the turbulent era of war and reconstruction.
en.notes: A Buddhist expression: 有為 ("the conditioned", everything that arises through causes) + 転変 ("unceasing change"): nothing in the world remains as it is. Well known is the phrase 有為転変は世の習い ("change is the way of the world"); attributively: 有為転変の世, 有為転変の人生. Note: here 有為 is read うい, not ゆうい ("capable, promising"). Related are 諸行無常 and 栄枯盛衰; literary, typical of speeches, essays and obituaries.

en.meaning: but to return to the subject; ending a digression
examples[].german: Anyway, let's get back to the main topic.
But enough digressing; today's main topic is a review of the new camera.
My reminiscing has gone on too long, but to get back to the point, I will now talk about plans for the next fiscal year.
en.notes: 閑話休題 is composed of 閑話 "idle talk, digression" and 休題 "to let the topic rest" and means "enough of the digression, back to the topic". It stands as a conjunction at the beginning of a sentence, mostly in essays, columns, blogs or speeches, often reinforced by 本題に戻ろう. Many native speakers wrongly understand it as introducing a digression ("by the way"); the correct meaning is the opposite. In everyday speech, people say more simply それはさておき or 話を戻すと.

en.meaning: adding flowers to brocade; making the good even better
examples[].german: On top of winning the championship, he also took the MVP, the icing on the cake.
A new fountain was added to the beautiful garden, which really put the finishing touch on it.
Their former teacher also rushed to the couple's wedding, making it a day crowned with joy.
en.notes: 錦上添花 literally means "to add (添) flowers (花) onto brocade (錦)" and comes from Chinese: something already beautiful or pleasing is crowned by yet another good thing. In Japanese the expression is rather rare and elevated; it appears in speeches and texts, for example 錦上添花だ or 錦上添花となる. More common is the resolved form 錦上花を添える or simply 花を添える. Opposite: 泣きっ面に蜂 (misfortune upon misfortune); do not confuse it with 蛇足 (superfluous addition).

en.meaning: narrow escape from death; barely escaping death
examples[].german: He narrowly escaped death and returned alive.
The climber rescued from the mountain disaster told of his brush with death.
He was buried under a building in the big earthquake but survived by a hair's breadth.
en.notes: 九死一生 literally means "nine parts death, one part life": the situation was almost hopeless, and yet one survived. By far the most common form is the phrase 九死に一生を得る "to narrowly escape death"; as a compound it appears attributively, for example 九死一生の体験 or 九死一生の思い. Typical in reports about accidents, disasters or serious illness; the tone is serious and rather literary.

en.meaning: telepathy; unspoken understanding from heart to heart
examples[].german: With old friends, you can understand each other without words.
We understand each other without saying anything - real telepathy.
At work, you should not rely on unspoken understanding but state things clearly in words.
en.notes: 以心伝心 literally means "to transmit (伝心) from heart to heart (以心)" and comes from Zen Buddhism, where the teaching was passed from master to disciple without words. Today it means "tacit understanding, comprehension without words" between close friends, couples or well-coordinated colleagues. Typical patterns: 以心伝心で通じる, 以心伝心の仲. Critically, it is often said that in companies one should not rely on 以心伝心.

en.meaning: full of troubles and difficulties; eventful
examples[].german: It was a year full of troubles, but I got through it.
In his New Year's address, the president looked back on last year as an eventful, difficult year.
I listened to the stories of my grandfather, who lived through a time of turmoil and hardship.
en.notes: 多事多難 combines 多事 "many incidents" and 多難 "many difficulties" and describes a time full of problems and unsettling events. It is very typical in year-end reviews, New Year's addresses and editorials: 多事多難な一年, 多事多難の年, 多事多難な時代. It is used as a na-adjective or with の. Do not confuse it with 多事多端 ("a lot to do, very busy") and 前途多難 (difficulties that still lie ahead).

en.meaning: cheap and shoddy mass production; poor-quality goods
examples[].german: Shoddily made products cannot win consumers' trust.
Riding the boom, similar-looking programs are being churned out.
At that time there were also many shoddily built ready-made houses.
en.notes: 粗製乱造 consists of 粗製 "crude, careless manufacture" and 乱造 "indiscriminate mass production": cheap goods are turned out in large numbers with no regard for quality. The original spelling is 粗製濫造; 乱 is the simplified substitute. It is also a transitive する-verb (〜を粗製乱造する, passive 粗製乱造される) and is often applied figuratively to TV programs, books, laws or qualifications. The expression is always critical and rather literary.

examples[].german: I played the piano in a state of complete absorption.
When the fire broke out, I frantically picked up my child and fled outside.
I was running in a daze, and before I knew it I had arrived at the station.
en.notes: Literally: 無我 "without self, selfless" and 夢中 "as in a dream, completely absorbed". It means being so wrapped up in something, or acting under pressure in such a way, that one forgets oneself and one's surroundings. Almost always adverbial as 無我夢中で + verb (走る, 逃げる, 練習する), also 無我夢中になる. Neutral; fits both enthusiasm and emergencies.

examples[].german: I listened to the story half believing, half doubting.
Even after receiving the news that I had passed, I still could not quite believe it.
The medicine I tried skeptically worked surprisingly well.
en.notes: 半信半疑 means "half believing, half doubting". Typical are 半信半疑で聞く/試す, 半信半疑の顔 and 半信半疑だった. It describes skepticism toward surprising news or a promise, often with the undertone that it turns out to be true after all. The expression is neutral and common in everyday speech.

en.meaning: swinging between joy and worry; emotional roller coaster
examples[].german: I swing between joy and worry over the exam results.
You shouldn't get worked up over the ups and downs of stock prices.
Watching the election projections, the campaign team swung between elation and anxiety.
en.notes: 一喜一憂 literally means "now joy, now worry": one reacts to every small change alternately with joy and worry. It is an intransitive する-verb used with に: 結果に一喜一憂する. It often appears negated as advice to stay calm: 〜に一喜一憂しない(ほうがいい). Neutral and common in everyday speech and in the media.

en.meaning: writhing in pain; in great agony
examples[].german: I writhed in agony from a stomachache.
I suffered agonizing toothache pain all night long.
Before the deadline, I was agonizing because I couldn't get the manuscript written.
en.notes: 七転八倒 literally means "to roll over seven times, to fall eight times" and describes writhing in violent pain: 七転八倒する, 七転八倒の苦しみ. Figuratively also for desperately struggling with a task. Do not confuse it with 七転び八起き ("to fall down and get up again and again"), which praises perseverance. The reading しってんばっとう is also widespread.

en.meaning: in one ear and out the other; ignoring advice
examples[].german: No matter how often you warn him, it goes in one ear and out the other.
He let the criticism go in one ear and out the other and stuck to his own way.
Even the doctor's advice falls on deaf ears; my father still hasn't quit smoking.
en.notes: 馬耳東風 literally means "east wind in a horse's ear" (after a poem by Li Bai): just as a horse does not notice the mild spring wind, someone completely ignores advice or criticism. Typical are 〜も馬耳東風だ and 馬耳東風と聞き流す. Synonymous but more colloquial is 馬の耳に念仏. The tone is mildly reproachful.

en.meaning: self-inflicted; you reap what you sow
examples[].german: Failing the exam is his own fault, since he didn't study.
You caught a cold from staying up too late all the time; you brought it on yourself.
It's his own doing, but I feel a little sorry for him having to leave the company.
en.notes: 自業自得 comes from Buddhism: 自業 "one's own deeds (karma)" and 自得 "to receive oneself" - one experiences the consequences of one's own actions. It is used almost only for bad consequences, often coolly or reproachfully: それは自業自得だ "You brought that on yourself". Typical frames are 〜のは自業自得だ and 自業自得だけど (with some sympathy). Said directly to the person concerned, it comes across as harsh.

examples[].german: Everyone agreed unanimously.
The participants answered with one voice, "It was fun."
Experts are unanimously pointing out that early countermeasures are needed.
en.notes: 異口同音 means "different mouths (異口), the same sound (同音)": many people say the same thing independently of one another. Almost always adverbial with に: 異口同音に言う/答える/賛成する. Watch the reading: いくどうおん, not いこうどうおん. Neutral to literary, common in reports.

en.meaning: much the same; only minor differences
examples[].german: All the proposals are much the same.
Smartphones from different companies have become more or less identical in terms of functions.
The two of them held nearly the same opinion, so they quickly reached an agreement.
en.notes: 大同小異 means "the same in the large (大同), different in the small (小異)". It states that several things hardly differ, often with a slightly disappointed undertone: どれも大同小異だ. It is used predicatively with だ, as 大同小異の〜 or 大同小異になる. Similar but more colloquial is 似たり寄ったり.

en.meaning: in name only; without actual substance
examples[].german: That committee exists in name only.
Since there are no penalties, the rule has become a dead letter.
The title is department head, but in reality it is a post without any authority.
en.notes: 有名無実 means "the name (名) exists, the substance (実) is missing"; 有名 has nothing to do with "famous" here. It describes rules, bodies or titles that exist only on paper: 有名無実の規則/ポスト, 〜は有名無実だ. Very common is 有名無実化する ("to become an empty shell"). Critical and literary.

en.meaning: saving oneself from a hopeless situation; a turnaround
examples[].german: He turned the game around with a game-saving home run.
Hoping to rescue itself from the crisis, the company launched a new product.
The final last-ditch strategy also ended in failure.
en.notes: Literally: 起死 "to wake the dying" and 回生 "to bring back to life". It means a rescue or turnaround from a seemingly hopeless situation. Typically attributive: 起死回生の一打, 起死回生のホームラン, 起死回生の策; also 起死回生を狙う／図る. Common in sports and business reports; rather elevated to journalistic.

en.meaning: a hundred shots, a hundred hits; always hitting the mark
examples[].german: His weather forecasts are always right.
After lots of practice, every one of her shots goes in.
It's impossible for fortune-telling to be right every time.
en.notes: Literally: "a hundred shots, a hundred hits". Originally from archery, today used for someone or something that always hits or never errs - predictions, throws, tips. Typical as the predicate 百発百中だ or 百発百中になる, also adverbially 百発百中で当たる. Neutral, often appreciative or, in negated form, skeptical.

en.meaning: fair wind and full sails; smooth sailing
examples[].german: His career is going smoothly.
It is not the case that things have gone smoothly since the founding.
The couple's newlywed life seemed to be going smoothly.
en.notes: 順風満帆 means "tailwind (順風) with full sails (満帆)": everything goes smoothly and successfully. Typical for life, career, marriage or companies: 順風満帆な人生, 順風満帆だ. Very often negated to hint at difficulties: 順風満帆ではなかった. Reading まんぱん, not まんぽ.

en.meaning: once-in-a-lifetime chance; an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years
examples[].german: This is a once-in-a-lifetime chance.
Getting to work with the director I admire is a golden opportunity.
He deeply regretted missing the chance of a lifetime.
en.notes: 千載一遇 literally means "to meet once (一遇) in a thousand years (千載)". It appears almost exclusively before nouns such as チャンス, 好機 or 機会: 千載一遇のチャンス. Typical verbs are 掴む ("to seize") and 逃す ("to miss"). A common writing mistake: 一隅 instead of 一遇.

en.meaning: overnight; in a very short time (usually negated: not overnight)
examples[].german: A foreign language cannot be mastered overnight.
A relationship of trust cannot be built overnight.
The town's traditions were not created overnight but nurtured over hundreds of years.
en.notes: 一朝一夕 means "one morning, one evening", that is, a very short time. It appears almost always in negated sentences: 一朝一夕には身につかない, 一朝一夕にできるものではない ("not overnight"). Typical topics are languages, skills, trust and traditions. The expression is slightly elevated.

examples[].german: I studied with total concentration.
The children were building a sand castle, completely absorbed.
He devoted himself wholeheartedly to practicing the piano.
en.notes: 一心不乱 means "one heart (一心), not distracted (不乱)": completely absorbed in an activity without letting oneself be disturbed. It almost always appears adverbially: 一心不乱に勉強する/祈る/働く. Similar are 無我夢中 (more like being lost in one's zeal) and 脇目も振らず. Neutral, praising.

en.meaning: surrounded on all sides; completely isolated
examples[].german: I am completely isolated within the company.
After the scandal came to light, the minister found himself isolated on all sides.
Because I was the only one in the class who opposed it, I found myself totally isolated.
en.notes: 四面楚歌 goes back to a Chinese story: the besieged general Xiang Yu heard songs of his homeland Chu (楚歌) from all sides (四面) and thought his own people had gone over to the enemy. Today it means to be attacked from all sides and to have no allies. Typical are 四面楚歌の状態, 四面楚歌に陥る and 四面楚歌になる.

en.meaning: survival of the fittest; the strong eat the weak
examples[].german: The business world is dog-eat-dog.
In nature the law of the jungle applies; weak animals are quickly eaten.
Many young people have doubts about a competitive society ruled by survival of the fittest.
en.notes: 弱肉強食 literally means "the flesh of the weak is the food of the strong" (弱/肉/強/食). It describes a world in which the stronger displaces the weaker, originally in nature, and by extension in business, sports or society. Typical are 弱肉強食の世界/社会 and 〜は弱肉強食だ; it often carries a note of criticism or resignation.

examples[].german: I was driven into a desperate predicament.
I had lost my way and my phone battery was dead - I thought it was all over.
The team came back to win from a seemingly hopeless situation.
en.notes: Literally: 絶体 and 絶命 - "the body at its end, life at its end" (from astrology). It means a seemingly hopeless situation. Very common is 絶体絶命のピンチ, also 絶体絶命の状況／危機 and 絶体絶命だ. Note: it is written 絶体, not 絶対 - a classic writing mistake. Neutral, often dramatizing in sports, thrillers and everyday storytelling.

examples[].german: An unprecedented incident occurred.
For a minister to be three hours late to a meeting is unheard of.
Because of a snowfall unlike any before, all the trains stopped.
en.notes: Literally: 前代 "earlier ages" and 未聞 "never heard of". It means something completely unprecedented, mostly in a negative or indignant sense (scandals, mistakes, accidents), more rarely appreciative. Typical are 前代未聞の事件／出来事 and 〜なんて前代未聞だ. Somewhat elevated; similar is 空前絶後, which stresses even more strongly "unique for all time".

examples[].german: I sold my old books for next to nothing.
Even if I tried to sell my grandfather's land, it would fetch only a pittance.
Even the game console that was once expensive would now be haggled down to a pittance.
en.notes: 二束三文 literally means "two bundles for three mon" (an old copper coin), that is, a bargain-basement price. It is mostly used with selling: 二束三文で売る, 二束三文で買いたたかれる, 二束三文にしかならない, or attributively 二束三文の値段/土地. The tone is colloquial and idiomatic and often regretful.

examples[].german: I was surprised by his wildly original idea.
The film became a talking point for its outlandish story.
Children's ideas are sometimes so unconventional that they amaze adults.
en.notes: 奇想天外 combines 奇想 ("strange idea") with 天外 ("beyond the heavens"): an idea nobody else would come up with. It is a na-adjective: 奇想天外なアイデア/発想/ストーリー. Mostly positive and astonished about surprising creativity, but it can also suggest "far-fetched". Neutral, common in reviews and advertising.

en.meaning: groping in the dark; being utterly at a loss
examples[].german: There are no clues to the culprit, and we are groping in the dark.
The new job is full of things I don't understand, and I'm still completely at sea.
Negotiations remained in the dark for three months.
en.notes: 五里霧中 means "in the middle of a fog five ri (an old unit of length) wide": you have no orientation at all and don't know how things will continue. Typical are 五里霧中だ, 五里霧中の状態, 五里霧中のまま. A common writing mistake: 夢中 instead of 霧中. Neutral to literary, e.g. for investigations, negotiations or a new job.

en.meaning: struggling hard; going through great trouble
examples[].german: I'm struggling with the preparations for moving.
I struggle to pay the rent every month.
I struggled quite a bit with the unfamiliar honorific language.
en.notes: Literally: "four sufferings, eight sufferings" - a Buddhist term for the basic sufferings of life (birth, old age, illness, death and four more). Today it means to struggle hard with something, often with money or a difficult task. Typical is 〜に四苦八苦する or 〜のに四苦八苦する. Colloquial to neutral, with a slightly humorous tone.

en.meaning: making a mountain out of a molehill; gross exaggeration
examples[].german: He always exaggerates when he talks.
The weekly magazine blew a minor slip of the tongue out of all proportion.
I only fell down a little, but my mother made a huge fuss of it all over the neighborhood.
en.notes: Literally "needle small, stick big": something as small as a needle is presented as big as a stick. 針小棒大 criticizes the excessive exaggeration of trifles, almost always in the form 針小棒大に言う／話す／報じる／書き立てる. A neutral everyday expression for it is 大げさに言う or 話を盛る; 針小棒大 is more literary and sounds reproachful.

en.meaning: by a hair's breadth; at the last moment
examples[].german: I caught the train by a hair's breadth.
I was rescued at the last moment.
The brakes worked in time, and an accident was narrowly avoided.
en.notes: Literally: 危機 "crisis, danger" and 一髪 "one (single) hair" - the danger hangs by a hair. It means an extremely narrow rescue or a success that comes just in time. Typical are 危機一髪で助かる／間に合う and 危機一髪のところで. Note: 危機一発 is a common writing mistake. Neutral, often in storytelling.

examples[].german: Such conduct is outrageous.
Drunk driving is out of the question.
Selling customers' personal information is an outrageous scandal.
en.notes: Originally a Buddhist term: the deepest truth lies beyond language (言語 "words", 道断 "the way is cut off"). Today 言語道断 means "so outrageous that words fail". Note the reading: 言語 is read ごんご here, not げんご. Typical frames are 〜とは言語道断だ, 〜なんて言語道断だ and 言語道断な／の行為; the expression is a sharp moral condemnation, stronger than とんでもない or ひどい.

en.meaning: a strong start and a weak finish; starting with a bang and ending with a whimper
examples[].german: This project ended in an anticlimax.
The first half was interesting, but the final episode was a letdown.
Please don't let your guard down until the end so that the reform does not fizzle out.
en.notes: Literally "dragon head, snake tail": something begins big and magnificent and ends miserably. Typical are 竜頭蛇尾に終わる and 竜頭蛇尾だ／になる, referring to projects, reforms, novels or series. Also written 龍頭蛇尾 and occasionally read りょうとうだび. The opposite, a consistently strong effort to the very end, is described with expressions such as 初志貫徹 or 有終の美を飾る.

examples[].german: Carelessness is your worst enemy, so don't let your guard down.
Even with a three-point lead, we can't get complacent. Let's stay focused until the end.
A cold that is almost over is exactly when you must not be careless.
en.notes: 油断大敵 combines 油断 ("carelessness, negligence") with 大敵 ("great enemy"): anyone who feels too safe makes mistakes. It is usually used as a stand-alone warning, often with a reason before it or an exhortation after it: 最後まで油断大敵だ, 油断大敵だから気を抜くな. It is a common saying in sports, at school and in health contexts.

en.meaning: has both strengths and weaknesses; pros and cons
examples[].german: Every method has its pros and cons.
This product has strengths and weaknesses and is not perfect.
I think life in the city and life in the country each have their pros and cons.
en.notes: Literally "one long, one short", that is, one strength and one weakness. It means that something has both advantages and disadvantages and no option is clearly superior. Typical are 一長一短がある and 〜は一長一短だ, often when comparing methods, products or ways of living. It is neutral; it is not used for people in the sense of "strengths of character", but for things and options.

en.meaning: running around in confusion; being thrown into a panic
examples[].german: After the earthquake, the residents were running around in confusion.
Employees flustered by the sudden change.
I didn't know where the venue was and wandered around the station in confusion.
en.notes: Literally: 右へ往き、左へ往く - "to go to the right, to go to the left". It means headless, confused running back and forth, mostly out of panic or helplessness. As a する-verb: 右往左往する; often with the trigger marked by に (突然の変更に右往左往する). Neutral, slightly critical or vividly descriptive.

en.meaning: desperate struggle; struggling against difficult conditions
examples[].german: I struggled with how to use the new software.
He is wrestling hard with a difficult problem.
To meet the deadline, the whole team struggled desperately.
en.notes: Literally: 悪戦 "bad (difficult) fight" and 苦闘 "agonizing struggle". It means to struggle doggedly with something under adverse circumstances. Typical is 〜に悪戦苦闘する, for example with new technology, difficult tasks or tight deadlines. Neutral; unlike 四苦八苦, it stresses the stubborn fight more than the distress.

en.meaning: hitting it off immediately; taking to each other at once
examples[].german: The two hit it off at their first meeting.
We had a shared hobby and hit it off.
At the izakaya, I hit it off with the customer at the next seat, and we exchanged contact information.
en.notes: Literally: 意気 "spirit, disposition" and 投合 "to agree, to match". It means that people understand each other at once and are on the same wavelength. Typical: 〜と意気投合する or 二人は意気投合した, often with an occasion such as 初対面で or 共通の趣味で. Neutral and positive, common when telling how one got to know someone.

en.meaning: triumphantly; full of pride and enthusiasm
examples[].german: He came back triumphantly after passing the exam.
The winning team paraded proudly.
Having been chosen as leader, he strode into the meeting room in high spirits.
en.notes: Literally: 意気 "spirit, courage" and 揚々 "raised high, proud". It means a triumphant, confident bearing after a success or full of confidence. Almost always adverbial as 意気揚々と + a verb of motion (帰る, 引き上げる, 入ってくる). Slightly elevated; can also be used ironically for exaggerated confidence of victory.

en.meaning: catching everyone in one sweep; netting the lot in a single cast
examples[].german: The police rounded up the criminal group in one sweep.
A method for exterminating pests all at once.
In the game, I used a special attack and wiped out all the enemies at once.
en.notes: Literally "to catch everything with a single cast of the net" (一網 "one net", 打尽 "to capture completely"). Figuratively it means catching a whole group in one go, typically criminals in a raid. Fixed frames are 〜を一網打尽にする and 〜が一網打尽になる. Rather literary and known from the news; jokingly also used for games or pests.

en.meaning: obvious at a glance; plain as day
examples[].german: If you look at the graph, the result is obvious at a glance.
His talent is obvious.
Which one is genuine is obvious if you put them side by side.
en.notes: Literally: 一目 "one glance" and 瞭然 "clear, distinct". It means that something is obvious at first sight, often in comparisons or from graphs. Typical are 〜は一目瞭然だ and 〜ば一目瞭然だ (見れば, 比べれば). Neutral to slightly elevated, common in presentations, advertising and explanations.

en.meaning: killing two birds with one stone; double gain
examples[].german: Listening to music while exercising kills two birds with one stone.
With this method you can save both time and money - two benefits at once.
en.notes: Literally: 一挙 "a single action" and 両得 "double gain". It means achieving two advantages at the same time with one measure - "killing two birds with one stone". Mostly as the predicate 〜は一挙両得だ. Synonymous and much more common in everyday speech is 一石二鳥; 一挙両得 sounds somewhat more elevated.

en.meaning: cutting in two with one stroke of the sword; deciding decisively and clearly
examples[].german: The company president resolved the problem decisively.
She turned down the proposal flatly.
The samurai cut the bamboo in two with a single stroke.
en.notes: Literally "in two pieces with one sword stroke" (一刀 "one sword (stroke)", 両断 "to cut in two"). Figuratively it means dealing with a problem or opinion decisively and without hesitation, e.g. 一刀両断に解決する or 一刀両断に切り捨てる. Often also in 〜を一刀両断する about critics who tear an argument apart in a single sentence. Rather literary and vivid.

examples[].german: That politician is a shrewd old hand.
Watch out for that cunning negotiator.
The dealer in second-hand goods is an old fox, so he won't give you a discount easily.
en.notes: According to legend, a snake that has lived a thousand years in the sea and a thousand years in the mountains becomes a dragon. 海千山千 therefore denotes a person who has become seasoned and cunning through a great deal of life experience. Mostly attributive: 海千山千の商人／政治家／したたか者. Unlike 経験豊富 ("experienced", positive), there is always an undertone of distrust; it should not be used as a compliment for someone.

en.meaning: getting priorities backward; putting the cart before the horse
examples[].german: Stressing yourself out for the sake of your health is putting the cart before the horse.
If you work too hard for money and ruin your health, you've got it backward.
Caring only about scores without understanding the content is putting the cart before the horse.
en.notes: Literally: 本 "root, the main thing" and 末 "tip, the side issue" are 転倒 "reversed, turned upside down". It means that one confuses means and ends, or the important and the unimportant. Typical is the frame 〜のは本末転倒だ or 〜たら本末転倒だ, often as a critical comment on absurd behavior. Neutral to slightly elevated, equally usual in conversation and in writing.

en.meaning: many twists and turns; a long and complicated path
examples[].german: After many twists and turns, he finally realized his dream.
This plan had many twists and turns, but succeeded in the end.
The labor-management negotiations finally reached agreement after many twists and turns.
en.notes: 紆余 means "to wind, meander" and 曲折 "to bend": 紆余曲折 describes a path full of turns, complications and setbacks before one reaches the goal. Fixed frames are 紆余曲折を経て, 紆余曲折の末（に） and 紆余曲折がある. The expression usually looks back at a difficult but ultimately completed process; for mere ups and downs of fortune, 浮き沈み fits better.

en.meaning: rise and fall; the ebb and flow of prosperity
examples[].german: History is a repetition of rise and fall.
The rise and fall of companies is the way of the world.
Walking through the deserted mining town, one cannot help feeling the transience of glory.
en.notes: 栄枯 is "flourishing and withering", 盛衰 "prosperity and decline"; together 栄枯盛衰 describes the inevitable alternation of rise and fall in empires, families, companies or cities. The classic phrase is 栄枯盛衰は世の習い／世の常. Other patterns: 栄枯盛衰を見る／感じる, 〜の栄枯盛衰. The tone is reflective and slightly melancholy, comparable to the Buddhist 諸行無常.

en.meaning: fair and just; open and honest
examples[].german: I demand a fair and just trial.
His fair and upright attitude earned trust.
Elections must be conducted fairly and openly.
en.notes: 公明 means "open and clear", 正大 "upright and great": 公明正大 describes conduct without ulterior motives that anyone can verify. Typically a na-adjective: 公明正大な態度／裁判／選挙, adverbially 公明正大に行う. Unlike 公平 ("impartial"), it additionally stresses transparency and honesty; 正々堂々, on the other hand, is said more of fighting fairly and openly in competition.

en.meaning: in all ages and all places; throughout history and across the world
examples[].german: In all ages and all places, love is a universal theme of humankind.
A library that has collected masterpieces from all times and countries.
en.notes: Literally: 古今 "past and present" and 東西 "east and west". It means "at all times and in all places", that is, universally. Typical adverbially at the start of a sentence (古今東西、〜は変わらない) or attributively as 古今東西の〜 (名作, 料理, 物語). Slightly elevated, often in essays, advertising and TV titles.

en.meaning: talent and beauty combined; both gifted and attractive
examples[].german: She is known as a woman who has both talent and beauty.
People with both talent and beauty are hard to find.
She is an actress of both brains and beauty who even holds a medical license.
en.notes: 才 is "talent, intelligence", 色 "appearance, beauty", 兼備 "to possess both at once". 才色兼備 is traditionally said almost only of women (才色兼備の女性／女優); for men it sounds unusual, and people rather say 文武両道 or 眉目秀麗. Usual forms are 才色兼備の and 才色兼備な. It is praise, but today, depending on the context, it may be felt to be old-fashioned or fixated on appearance.

en.meaning: self-abandonment; despair; giving up on oneself
examples[].german: After repeated failures, he fell into despair.
Don't give up on yourself; look ahead.
After losing his job, he lived a reckless, self-destructive life.
en.notes: Literally: 自暴 "to do violence to oneself" and 自棄 "to throw oneself away". It means giving up all hope out of despair and letting oneself go. Typical are 自暴自棄になる and 自暴自棄な／の生活; in advice it is often negated: 自暴自棄にならないで. Colloquially, やけになる corresponds to it.

examples[].german: It is important to sift and select information carefully.
When moving, you choose which belongings to keep and which to discard.
en.notes: Literally: 取捨 "to take and to throw away" and 選択 "selection". It means deliberate sorting out: keeping what is useful and discarding what is unnecessary. Typical are 情報の取捨選択 and 〜を取捨選択する, also 取捨選択が必要だ. Slightly elevated, common in texts about media literacy, work and organizing.

en.meaning: consistent from beginning to end; coherent throughout
examples[].german: His argument is consistent from beginning to end.
One should stick to a consistent policy.
His story is inconsistent, so he can't be trusted.
en.notes: Literally: 首尾 "head and tail, beginning and end" and 一貫 "running through on one line". It means that statements, attitude or actions remain free of contradiction from beginning to end. Typical are 首尾一貫している, 首尾一貫した態度／方針 and, negated, 首尾一貫していない "contradictory". Rather elevated, used in discussions, criticism and evaluations.

en.meaning: to spur each other on and improve; to grow together
examples[].german: I grew by spurring each other on with my friends.
It is important to improve through mutual competition with rivals.
I want to create a workplace where young employees can spur each other on.
en.notes: 切磋琢磨 comes from the image of working bone and ivory (切・磋) and jade and stone (琢・磨): by cutting and polishing, something becomes ever finer. Today it mainly means "to spur each other on and get better together", i.e. friendly rivalry. Typical is the form with と or 互いに: 仲間と切磋琢磨する, 互いに切磋琢磨し合う. It sounds positive and rather elevated and is readily used in speeches, school and company texts; in everyday speech one says more simply 競い合う or 刺激し合う.

en.meaning: constantly changing one's mind; issuing orders in the morning and revising them in the evening
examples[].german: The public is confused by the government's constant flip-flopping.
The president's instructions keep changing, and the staff on site are being jerked around.
If the rules keep being changed, nobody will follow them anymore.
en.notes: 朝令暮改 literally means "to give an order in the morning (朝令), to change it in the evening (暮改)". It criticizes governments, authorities or superiors whose instructions and rules change constantly and without a clear line: 朝令暮改の政策, 方針が朝令暮改だ, also as a する-verb 朝令暮改する. In business language it is occasionally used positively for flexible course corrections, but the basic tone remains reproachful and literary.

en.meaning: unprecedented; never before reached by anyone
examples[].german: He set a record that no one had ever achieved before.
They take on a challenge in uncharted territory.
The expedition finally stood on a summit no one had ever reached.
en.notes: 前人未到 literally means "earlier people have not yet arrived": a place, area or record that no one has reached before. It almost always stands attributively with の before a noun: 前人未到の記録, 前人未到の領域, 前人未到の地. It is especially common in sports reports about records and in texts about research or expeditions. The expression is elevated and literary; similar is 史上初 "first time in history", whereas 空前絶後 additionally stresses that it will never happen again.

en.meaning: charging blindly ahead; rushing headlong like a wild boar
examples[].german: He charges ahead recklessly and has no sense of planning.
A leader who charges ahead blindly is dangerous.
Instead of rushing in headlong, let's make a plan first.
en.notes: Literally "to rush (突) like a wild boar (猪) and press wildly forward (猛進)". It means heading blindly toward a goal without thinking. Mostly critical (計画性がない), but sometimes also appreciative of drive. Frames: 猪突猛進する, 猪突猛進型の人, 猪突猛進で〜. Often used in New Year's greetings in the Year of the Boar (亥年).

en.meaning: deceiving through superficial changes; the same thing in different packaging
examples[].german: That is nothing more than a trick of superficial changes.
If the monthly payment decreases but the total stays the same, it's a shell game.
Keeping the price the same and reducing the quantity is a sleight-of-hand tactic.
en.notes: From the Zhuangzi: a monkey keeper wants to give his monkeys three chestnuts in the morning and four in the evening; the monkeys protest, but with "four in the morning, three in the evening" they are satisfied, although the total is the same. 朝三暮四 therefore means being dazzled by superficial differences, or deceiving others with such tricks. Typical: 朝三暮四だ, 朝三暮四の策／やり方. Do not confuse it with 朝令暮改 ("constantly changing orders").

examples[].german: He solved the problem with lightning-fast skill.
She reacted like lightning.
Right after the start of the match, they took the lead with a lightning goal.
en.notes: 電光石火 combines 電光 "lightning" and 石火 "the spark that arises when stone is struck": something happens in a tiny instant, lightning-fast. Typical combinations are 電光石火の早業 "lightning-fast feat", 電光石火の速さ and 電光石火のごとく (elevated). It describes quick actions and reactions, especially in sports, fight scenes or surprisingly quick decisions. In everyday speech one usually simply says あっという間に or 素早く; 電光石火 sounds vivid and somewhat dramatic.

en.meaning: running about busily; rushing hither and thither
examples[].german: I ran around in all directions to raise funds.
Every day is spent rushing about preparing for the event.
The president is dashing about in search of new business partners.
en.notes: Literally "to rush east, to run west": 東奔西走 describes someone hurrying about everywhere for a cause, for example raising money, making preparations or looking for supporters. It is used as an intransitive する-verb: 〜のために東奔西走する. Unlike a simple 忙しい, it stresses constantly being on the move and working toward a goal; colloquially people say 走り回る or 駆けずり回る.

en.meaning: progress by the day and month; steady advancement
examples[].german: Technology is advancing steadily.
The field of medicine advances constantly.
Smartphones advance so fast that they become outdated in two or three years.
en.notes: Literally "forward by the day, a step by the month" (日進 + 月歩). It means constant, rapid progress, almost always for technology, medicine or science, hardly for personal skills. Typical frames are 〜は日進月歩だ, 日進月歩の技術 and 日進月歩で進歩する. Neutral to literary, common in news and advertising copy.

en.meaning: people-pleaser; someone who is nice to everyone
examples[].german: If you try to be everyone's friend, you can't make real friends.
He tries to please everybody, so he can't be trusted.
So that people don't call you a people-pleaser, state your own opinion clearly too.
en.notes: Literally "a beauty from all eight directions", originally a flawless beauty. Today it is used almost only pejoratively: someone who is friendly to everyone and wants to please everybody, but shows no stance of his own - a "people-pleaser". Frames: 八方美人だ, 八方美人な人, 八方美人と言われる. Not a compliment, so use with care.

examples[].german: Leonardo da Vinci was a learned and versatile man.
I want to be taught by a teacher who is both learned and versatile.
My grandfather was both learned and talented, and he could answer whatever I asked.
en.notes: 博学 is "widely learned", 多才 "versatilely talented": 博学多才 praises someone who has both broad knowledge and many skills. Common are 博学多才な人物 and 博学多才で…. 博学 or 博識 alone stresses knowledge only, 多才 or 多芸 only the talents. The expression is elevated and is usually said about others, not about oneself.

en.meaning: good health and no illness; being in the best of health
examples[].german: I go to the first shrine visit of the year, wishing for my family's good health.
Good health is the greatest happiness.
I bought my grandmother an amulet for good health.
en.notes: 無病 "without illness" and 息災 "safe and sound, free from misfortune" (a Buddhist expression) together make "healthy and well". It is used above all in wishes and prayers: 家族の無病息災を願う, 無病息災を祈る, often at the first shrine visit of the year or on good-luck charms. It often stands next to 家内安全. Elevated and somewhat traditional; in daily life one simply says 元気 or 健康.

examples[].german: He is a student of impeccable conduct.
A politician who had been considered upright was arrested for corruption.
Unlike his exemplary older brother, the younger one was always playing pranks.
en.notes: 品行方正 combines 品行 ("conduct, way of life") with 方正 ("upright, correct") and describes a blameless, morally impeccable person. It is used as a na-adjective or with の: 品行方正な生徒, 品行方正で知られる. The expression is elevated and sounds somewhat stiff; it is also used ironically for model students or for people whose spotless reputation turns out to be false.

en.meaning: clear mirror and still water; a calm and serene mind
examples[].german: I approach the match with a calm and serene state of mind.
Through meditation he reached a state of perfect calm.
I want to set my anger aside and make my judgment with a clear, calm mind.
en.notes: 明鏡 is a brightly polished mirror, 止水 still, unmoving water: both reflect things without distortion. 明鏡止水 describes a clear, calm mind without agitation, greed or ulterior motives. Fixed frames: 明鏡止水の心境／境地, 明鏡止水の心で. It is more elevated than 落ち着いている or 冷静 and is gladly used before competitions, exams or important decisions.

en.meaning: old and young, men and women; everyone
examples[].german: This event can be enjoyed by people of all ages and genders.
It is popular regardless of age or gender.
On the festival day, young and old gathered at the shrine in great numbers.
en.notes: Literally "old and young, men and women"; it means "all people, regardless of age or gender". Note the special readings 老若 (ろうにゃく) and 男女 (なんにょ) instead of the usual ろうじゃく and だんじょ. Typical frames: 老若男女を問わず "regardless of age and gender" and 老若男女が楽しめる. Neutral, common in advertising and event announcements.

examples[].german: I fondly remember my younger days when I worked with all-out determination.
I kept running doggedly and reached the finish line.
In the month before the exam, I studied like mad.
en.notes: The kanji 我武者羅 are a purely phonetic spelling (ateji); the word is mostly written in kana: がむしゃら. It describes someone who goes at something regardless of the cost, doggedly and with all their strength. Almost always adverbial as がむしゃらに働く／勉強する／走る. Colloquial and rather positive about dedication, but can also hint at recklessness.

en.meaning: with all one's might; wholeheartedly; giving one's all
examples[].german: Thanks to studying with all my might, I passed.
The way he works with total dedication is admirable.
You did your best, so you don't have to worry about the result.
en.notes: 一所懸命 is the original form: samurai staked their lives (懸命) on their single fief (一所). Today the variant 一生懸命 "staking one's whole life" is much more common; both mean "with all one's might, to the best of one's ability". Typically adverbial (一所懸命（に）勉強する) or as a na-adjective (一所懸命な姿). Neutral; in newspapers 一所懸命 is sometimes preferred.

en.meaning: unprecedented and never to be repeated; once in history
examples[].german: A film that became a hit like none before or since.
He achieved a record unmatched before or since.
That earthquake caused damage unlike anything before, and probably unlike anything to come.
en.notes: 空前絶後 is composed of 空前 "never before" and 絶後 "never after": so extraordinary that it has never happened and probably never will again. It mostly stands with の before a noun (空前絶後の大ヒット, 空前絶後の記録) and can describe both positive things and catastrophes. It is stronger than 前人未到 or 前代未聞, which stress only the "never before". The expression is elevated, but is readily used with exaggeration in advertising and the media.

en.meaning: all things in the universe; all of creation
examples[].german: Philosophy is a discipline that takes all things in the universe as its subject.
I feel gratitude toward all of creation.
In Shinto, it is believed that gods dwell in all things in nature.
en.notes: 森羅 means "densely lined up like trees in a forest", 万象 "all phenomena": 森羅万象 encompasses everything there is in the universe. It usually stands as an object or theme: 森羅万象を対象とする, 森羅万象に宿る. The expression is solemn and appears in philosophy, religion and descriptions of nature; in everyday speech one simply says あらゆるもの or 世の中のすべて.

en.meaning: innocent and unaffected; naive and unselfconscious
examples[].german: Her innocent, natural smile is soothing.
The natural openness of children is wonderful.
The new colleague has such an open, unaffected nature that she quickly became friends with everyone.
en.notes: 天真爛漫 combines 天真 "naturally unadulterated" and 爛漫 "in full bloom, radiant": someone shows their nature openly, without ulterior motives or pretense. It is a な-adjective: 天真爛漫な子ども, 天真爛漫な笑顔, and as a noun 天真爛漫さ. It is almost always positive ("unselfconscious, warm, childlike-open") and is used especially for children and young women. A derogatory "naive" is expressed more with 世間知らず or 単純.

en.meaning: joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure; the full range of emotions
examples[].german: He is a person who expresses his emotions honestly.
He has a temperamental personality with strong emotions.
My father hardly shows his emotions on his face.
en.notes: 喜 "joy", 怒 "anger", 哀 "sorrow", 楽 "pleasure": the four basic emotions together stand for the whole range of human emotions. Typical frames: 喜怒哀楽を表す／顔に出す "to show emotions", 喜怒哀楽が激しい "very emotional, moody" and 喜怒哀楽がない. Neutral, often in descriptions of character or acting.

en.meaning: simple and sturdy; down-to-earth and strong
examples[].german: It is a school known for its simple and sturdy school spirit.
He is trusted for his plain and sturdy character.
This manufacturer's furniture is unadorned and solid and lasts for decades.
en.notes: 質実 means "plain and honest, without ostentation", 剛健 "strong and steadfast". 質実剛健 praises a down-to-earth, unpretentious and at the same time robust nature, in people, schools (often as a school motto, 校訓), companies or products. As a na-adjective: 質実剛健な人柄／校風. In contrast to 地味 ("unobtrusive", rather negative), it is clearly positive; the opposite would be 華美 or 軟弱.

en.meaning: three-legged race; working closely together; hand in hand
examples[].german: The couple runs the shop hand in hand.
They overcame the difficulties through close cooperation.
At the sports day, I entered the three-legged race with my father.
en.notes: Literally "two people, three legs": the three-legged race at the sports day, in which two runners tie one leg together. Figuratively it means that two partners work closely and in step, such as married couples, coaches and athletes or two companies. Typical: 二人三脚で〜する and 〜と二人三脚で歩む. Neutral and positively connoted.

en.meaning: freely; at will; having full command
examples[].german: He commands English freely.
He pilots the drone freely.
The height of this desk can be changed freely.
en.notes: Two expressions for freedom (自由 "free", 自在 "at will") reinforce each other: to do or master something completely freely and effortlessly at one's own will. Almost always adverbial with verbs such as 操る, 使いこなす, 動かす or 変える: 自由自在に操る "to wield masterfully". Also possible as a na-adjective (自由自在な動き). Neutral.

en.meaning: scenic beauty; beautiful scenery of mountains and waters
examples[].german: He built a villa in a place of scenic beauty.
Kyoto is a beautiful city of scenic mountains and clear waters.
Outside the inn's window spread a landscape of picturesque mountains and rivers.
en.notes: Literally "mountains purple, waters clear": in the evening light the mountains shimmer violet and rivers run clear. 山紫水明 praises a picturesque, seemingly unspoiled landscape; the expression became known through the scholar 頼山陽 and his view over Kyōto. Almost always attributive: 山紫水明の地／景色. For a simple view people say 景色がいい or 風光明媚; 山紫水明 is more literary.

en.meaning: onlookers see more than the players; one sees more clearly from the outside
examples[].german: As they say, onlookers see more, so let's hear a third party's opinion as well.
The saying about onlookers is well put; my friend's advice was spot on.
Watching shogi from the side, you can see the good moves right away as an onlooker.
en.notes: From the game of go: someone who merely watches (岡目, "view from the side") sees eight moves (八目) further than the players themselves. 岡目八目 means that uninvolved people can often judge a situation more clearly than those affected. Mostly quoted as a proverb: 岡目八目というように／とはよく言ったもので. Also written 傍目八目. It is often used to justify why one should seek the opinion of third parties.

en.meaning: excessive suspicion; a suspicious mind sees ghosts everywhere
examples[].german: Consumed by suspicion, he even doubted his friends.
Let's be careful not to fall into excessive suspicion.
Because the boss explains nothing, suspicion is spreading among the employees.
en.notes: 疑心暗鬼 is the short form of 疑心暗鬼を生ず: a "suspicious heart" (疑心) produces "demons in the dark" (暗鬼) - once someone is suspicious, they see threats everywhere. Typical are 疑心暗鬼になる, 疑心暗鬼に陥る and 疑心暗鬼が広がる; it is often about groups in which, after an incident, everyone suspects everyone. The expression is somewhat elevated, but well known from the news and everyday conversation.

en.meaning: to give one's all; to work with total dedication
examples[].german: He rebuilt the company through tireless effort.
I am grateful to the employees who worked with total devotion.
Even in my new post, I intend to devote myself with all my strength to the company.
en.notes: Literally "to grind the bones to powder, to shatter the body": 粉骨砕身 means to give one's all, to the point of self-sacrifice. Typical in inaugural speeches and pledges: 粉骨砕身努力いたします, 粉骨砕身（して）働く／尽くす; also 粉骨砕身の努力. It is very formal and solemn; in everyday speech people say 一生懸命 or 全力で.

en.meaning: perfect and flawless; completely without defects
examples[].german: There is no such thing as a perfectly flawless person.
I thought I had made a flawless plan.
Even a hero who seems flawless has an unexpected weakness.
en.notes: 完全無欠 means "complete and without any deficiency" (無欠 = "without a flaw"), that is, absolutely perfect. It is used as a な- or の-adjective: 完全無欠な人, 完全無欠の計画. It often appears in negated or ironic sentences such as 完全無欠な人間なんていない, because absolute perfection is rare. It is stronger and more formal than 完璧; in everyday speech one usually simply says 完璧.

en.meaning: one step forward, one step back; stalemate; ups and downs
examples[].german: The patient's condition keeps fluctuating between better and worse.
The negotiations are in a back-and-forth stalemate.
The match swung back and forth, and the outcome was unclear until the end.
en.notes: Literally "once forward, once back" (一進 + 一退). It means a state that fluctuates back and forth without a clear direction emerging - with illnesses, negotiations, games or share prices. Typical frames: 一進一退を繰り返す, 一進一退の状態／攻防 and 〜は一進一退だ. Neutral to literary, common in news.

examples[].german: His explanation was totally incoherent.
Nothing gets decided in a muddled discussion.
The drunken department head began saying incoherent things.
en.notes: 支離滅裂 combines 支離 "fragmented, fallen apart" and 滅裂 "torn, destroyed": speech, thoughts or actions lack a common thread and make no sense. It is a な-adjective and is often used predicatively: 話が支離滅裂だ, 支離滅裂なことを言う. Typical subjects are 説明, 話, 言い訳, 主張 or 文章. It is clearly critical; more neutral are 筋が通らない "not logical" or まとまりがない "unstructured".

examples[].german: He gave a speech with a majestic, dignified bearing.
The team marches in with an imposing air.
An old castle towers majestically on the hill.
en.notes: 威風堂々 combines 威風 "dignity, awe-inspiring presence" with 堂々 "stately, confident": imposing, majestic. It mostly stands adverbially with と or as とした before nouns: 威風堂々と行進する, 威風堂々とした態度. It is used to describe people, appearances, buildings or landscapes. 堂々 alone is more everyday ("confident, unabashed"); 威風堂々 sounds solemn; in Japan it is also the title of Elgar's marches "Pomp and Circumstance".

examples[].german: That shameless attitude is appalling.
Shamelessly, he went home without apologizing.
Acting unfazed even after the lie was exposed - that is the height of shamelessness.
en.notes: 厚顔無恥 literally means "thick face, no shame": impudent and shameless; someone acts brazenly without feeling ashamed. It is a な-adjective (厚顔無恥な態度, 厚顔無恥な人) and also appears in the phrase 厚顔無恥にも "shamelessly" and 厚顔無恥にもほどがある "this is the height of shamelessness". It is a strong, condemnatory expression, often directed at politicians or companies. Milder and more everyday are 図々しい and 厚かましい.
